Ford's TSB 23-2218 for 2021–2023 F-150 with the DCACA inverter shows radio-frequency interference from the inverter upsetting the tyre pressure system, so the BCM stores B124D and lights the TPMS lamp; the procedure confirms the inverter as source and suppresses the interference. Toyota Industries' patent US10050558B2 describes a 12 V-fed inverter that only runs between about 11 and 16 V and shuts down on overvoltage or when its power devices overheat. Which unit module B is remains unpublished; no maker documents B012D. Supply, ground and data lines come before a new module.
c: Supply voltage outside the permitted window, weak 12 V battery or poor ground
Module B overheating, blocked air path or cooling fan failed
Module B internally defective or emitting interference
s: Outlets switch off or are unavailable
Side effects on radio-based systems such as tyre pressure monitoring
Module handles 120/240 V AC from a high-voltage source; work only with the system de-energised

B012E.t: DC/AC Converter A High Voltage Power Outlet Control Module "C"
B012E.d: B012E concerns outlet control module C. GM's name for the part is accessory AC and DC power control module: in program N222385490, 2023 Silverado and Sierra 1500 built from September 2022 without a working inverter, because of the chip shortage, received this module, a fuse and BCM reprogramming, with separate inverters for 110 V (RPO KI4) and 230 V (KI5). Ford's patent US11043801B2 describes the control side: relays switching each socket, run timers and power limits, all managed by the DCACA controller. Whether module C is a third unit or another function is not published, and no manufacturer documents B012E. Typical causes are supply, ground, network faults or missing configuration after replacement.
c: Module C or BCM not configured or programmed after installation or replacement
Fuse, supply or ground of module C faulty
s: Power outlets in cab and bed inoperative
Outlet functions missing from the display menu
Module handles 120/240 V AC from a high-voltage source; work only with the system de-energised

B012F.t: A/V Sensor Washer Fluid A Control Circuit
B012F.d: B012F reports a fault in the control circuit for A/V sensor washer fluid A, the first of six such circuits, with B0130 to B0134 following. A/V most likely stands for autonomous vehicle; the circuit drives the pump or valve that delivers fluid to one sensor. Uber's patent family (US20180015907A1, US10220817B2) shows the layout: one reservoir, a set of pumps the vehicle computer starts individually for each camera or lidar cleaner, plus compressed air through solenoid valves. Ford's US10569746B2 has the computer run a wash pump when it judges a sensor window dirty. Which sensor A serves is not published; no maker documents B012F. If the circuit fails, sensor A goes uncleaned and automated driving functions may restrict themselves.
c: Pump motor or valve coil for fluid circuit A open or shorted
Damaged wiring or corroded connector in the control circuit
Driver stage in the controlling module defective
s: Sensor A is no longer washed, camera or lidar view stays dirty
Assistance or automated driving functions report sensor blocked or become unavailable

B0130.t: A/V Sensor Washer Fluid B Control Circuit
B0130.d: B0130 reports a fault where the module switches A/V sensor washer fluid B, the second of six channels running from B012F (A) to B0134 (F). A/V almost certainly stands for autonomous vehicle. Uber's cleaning layout (US20180015907A1) shows what such a channel switches: a compressor charges an air accumulator, one reservoir with a level sensor holds the fluid, and several pumps feed the cleaning heads, each started separately by the vehicle computer. Kautex sells its Allegro system for cameras and lidar on vehicles from level 1 to level 5, mixing water and air jets. Which sensor channel B serves is not published, and no carmaker documents B0130. With the circuit open or shorted, the sensor on channel B is no longer washed.
c: Pump motor or valve coil on fluid channel B open or shorted
Corroded or loose connector at the pump, exposed to washer spray and road salt
Output stage for channel B in the controlling module failed
s: The camera or lidar on channel B stays dirty while the others are cleaned
Driver assistance or automated driving reports a blocked sensor or is withdrawn

B0131.t: A/V Sensor Washer Fluid C Control Circuit
B0131.d: B0131 points to the circuit that switches A/V sensor washer fluid C, the third channel of the B012F to B0134 series for autonomous vehicle sensors. Ford's patent US10569746B2 describes a rotating sensor cover: the computer first tries a contactless cleaner with fluid or air and only brings in a wiper when the window's measured opacity stays above a limit. A Korean lab study of lidar windows ran its washer at 0.5 bar and its air jet at 2 bar and found the type of dirt, its concentration and whether it had dried to matter most. No carmaker documents B0131 with this meaning. General Motors lists B0131 among the keywords of bulletin PIP5094 from 2013, which belongs to an older, unrelated numbering. Fault effect: sensor C goes unwashed.
c: Pump or solenoid valve of channel C with open or shorted winding
Harness to the sensor cleaning unit chafed or pinched at a bracket
Controlling module output for channel C defective
s: Washing of sensor C stops; dirt, salt or insects stay on its window
A wiper or air jet, if fitted, has to do the cleaning alone

B0132.t: A/V Sensor Washer Fluid D Control Circuit
B0132.d: B0132 concerns washer fluid channel D of a self-driving vehicle's sensor cleaning, the fourth in the series that starts at B012F. In Uber's patent US10173646B1 the vehicle computer judges how dirty each sensor is and then works out a cleaning order, so the cleaning units fire one after another instead of all at once; a dead channel removes one sensor from that rotation. Rain, snow, road salt, pollen, insect remains and bird droppings are the deposits named there. A KTH thesis written for Scania compared cleaning methods for heavy autonomous trucks and tuned fluid use by varying pump output. Nobody publishes which sensor sits on channel D, and no carmaker documents B0132. Typical faults are an open pump circuit or a short in its supply.
c: Open circuit in the channel D pump or valve, often a burnt-out winding
Supply or control lead of channel D shorted to ground or battery voltage
Pump blocked by frozen or contaminated fluid, drawing excess current
s: Sensor D is skipped in the cleaning sequence and stays dirty
Automated driving may limit itself or ask the driver to take over

B0133.t: A/V Sensor Washer Fluid E Control Circuit
B0133.d: B0133 covers the control circuit of A/V sensor washer fluid E, the fifth channel after B012F to B0132. Autonomous vehicles carry many cameras and lidar units, so cleaning is split into several separately switched fluid paths. Uber's patent US10220817B2 shows a sensor platform whose grooves and raised rim carry fluid and air to the sensor heads. Kautex says its Allegro control software assigns priority among the sensors when coordinating the actuators. In a lab study on lidar windows, results depended above all on the kind of deposit, its density and whether it had dried. Which sensor is on channel E is not disclosed, and no carmaker documents B0133. If the channel stays switched off, deposits on that sensor are no longer removed.
c: Pump or valve of channel E defective, coil open or shorted
Water ingress or corrosion in the connector of channel E
Output for channel E in the cleaning control module damaged
s: The sensor on channel E keeps a film of dirt or dried spray
Message that a sensor is blocked or an assistance function is unavailable

B0134.t: A/V Sensor Washer Fluid F Control Circuit
B0134.d: B0134 is the last of the six A/V sensor washer fluid circuits (B012F for A up to B0134 for F) and covers channel F. The module drives a pump or valve on this channel and reports the code when it finds an open or shorted output. Ford's US10569746B2 lets the computer decide from the measured opacity of a sensor window whether spraying is enough or a wiper must follow. Uber's US10173646B1 runs the cleaning units in an order derived from sensor condition. The KTH thesis for Scania found that changing pump output moved the wave front of fluid across a sensor fascia. Which sensor channel F supplies is not published, and no carmaker documents B0134. Until it is repaired, sensor F loses its washer supply.
c: Winding of the channel F pump or valve open or shorted
Wiring of channel F damaged, for example after bodywork near the sensor mount
Driver stage for channel F in the module failed
s: Sensor F no longer gets washer fluid; only air or a wiper, if present, still works
Assistance functions that rely on sensor F report reduced availability

B0140.d: Neither the J2012 code lists available here nor any carmaker's public material contains B0140; its wording repeats B0061, the J2012 code for the front passenger belt tension sensor, and resembles B0182. The part itself is well described. In Delphi's design (US6554318B2) the webbing runs through a slider that moves against springs, while a Hall element between two magnets reads the travel. A second Delphi patent (US6605877B1) sends the tension value over a two-wire line to the module that classifies the occupant, which uses it to tell a tightly strapped child seat from an adult. FMVSS 208 allows automatic passenger airbag suppression for small occupants. A fault in this circuit usually lights the airbag lamp.
c: Loose or corroded plug at the passenger belt tension sensor
Sensor signal out of range, for example from a jammed slider
Sensor lead trapped under the seat or at the sill panel
s: Airbag warning lamp on
Passenger airbag status indicator may show an unexpected state
Safety note: the sensor sits near pretensioner and side airbag plugs; unplug only with the battery disconnected and the wait time observed

B0150.d: No publicly available J2012 code list includes B0150, and no carmaker publishes it with this meaning. The mode door decides whether air leaves at the face vents, the footwell or the windscreen. A range/performance fault means the door does not reach the commanded position or its feedback does not fit the command. Many actuators carry a potentiometer geared to the motor that returns roughly 0 to 5 V, as a Motor magazine article explains; Calsonic's patent EP0771679A2 pairs each door motor with such a position detector. GM's Global A climate control, as documented for the 2011 Saab 9-5, uses stepper motors and logs mode actuator circuit faults under B0233 instead. Expect air from the wrong outlets or a door that hunts.
c: Mode door or its linkage binding, broken lever or stripped gear
Mode door actuator worn, feedback track of the potentiometer dirty
End positions not relearned after actuator replacement
s: Air comes out of the wrong vents or the selected mode is not reached
Clicking or knocking behind the dashboard while the door moves
Windscreen demisting weaker because too little air reaches the defrost outlets

B0152.d: B0152 appears in no J2012 code list and in no public carmaker document. In J2012 the driver's buckle sensor is B0050, so the title duplicates that code. The switch tells the vehicle whether the tongue is latched. TRW's patent US5898366A places a Hall device, a magnet and an armature in the buckle, and the latch movement changes the flux and thus the output; US5966784A uses a flux reversal for the same purpose and adds that the signal can steer airbag deployment. FMVSS 208 S7.3 requires a driver belt warning: a lamp and a 4 to 8 second chime, or a lamp lasting at least 60 seconds. A circuit fault can leave the reminder on with the belt fastened, or silent without it.
c: Buckle plug under the driver seat loose or corroded
Buckle lead pinched or broken by seat movement
Hall sensor or contact in the buckle defective, buckle must be replaced
s: Belt reminder for the driver stays on or does not come on
Airbag warning lamp on in vehicles that read the buckle in the airbag module
Safety note: the buckle plug sits under the seat near airbag and pretensioner plugs; unplug only with the battery off and the wait time observed

B0154.d: B0154 has no entry in the publicly available J2012 lists, and carmakers do not describe it in public material; J2012 assigns the front passenger buckle sensor to B0052, which this title duplicates. On the passenger side the buckle signal does more than drive a reminder: together with seat occupancy it helps the restraint module choose how the passenger airbag and pretensioner act. TRW's US5966784A reads latch state from the direction of a magnetic field through a Hall device; US5898366A guides the flux through a spring-loaded armature that touches the latch. For passenger cars built from 1 September 2028, FMVSS 208 applies its new belt warning rules (S7.5) to the front outboard seats as well. Typical result: wrong or missing passenger reminder, often with the airbag lamp.
c: Buckle connector under the passenger seat loose, corroded or kicked off
Buckle wire chafed by the seat rail or a seat adjustment
Switch inside the buckle worn or soiled by spilled drinks
s: Passenger belt reminder wrong, permanently on or missing
Airbag warning lamp on
Safety note: seat plugs share space with airbag and pretensioner wiring; disconnect the battery and wait before unplugging anything

B0156.d: The publicly available J2012 lists skip B0156, and public carmaker documents do not mention it; the same meaning is covered by code B0305. A sun load sensor on top of the dashboard tells automatic climate control how strongly sunlight heats the cabin, so the system can add cooling early. HELLA's solar sensor sits centrally on the dash, measures radiation across different zones and reports over LIN. Patent US6888120B2 uses two light-collecting lenses, each aimed at its own photodiode, to separate driver and passenger sides. GM files this sensor under B0183 instead: in the 2011 Saab 9-5 the HVAC module sets it when the 5 V identifying pulse fails to arrive and then works with zero sun intensity.
c: Sensor plug under the dash top cover loose or damaged after windscreen work
Photodiode or electronics in the sun load sensor failed
Signal or supply wire shorted or open behind the dashboard
s: Cabin gets too warm in strong sun because the system does not add cooling
Automatic blower and temperature react only to air temperature

B0158.d: Although B0158 is absent from the publicly available J2012 lists, General Motors and Saab use it with exactly this meaning. In the 2011 Saab 9-4X the instrument cluster reads the outside air sensor and stores B0158 02 when the signal implies more than 88 °C, B0158 05 below −40 °C; the display then shows dashes. Saab 9-3 manuals place it in the body module: under 0.25 V means short to ground, above 5 V means open or short to supply, and the last known value is kept. GM bulletin PIC5656F (LaCrosse 2010–13, Verano 2012–16, Malibu 2013–16, Cascada 2017) links B0158 to a missing outside temperature and an HVAC display stuck in Celsius, and starts with the sensor plug and circuits 61 and 636.
c: Sensor at the front bumper unplugged or connector damaged after front-end work
Thermistor in the outside air sensor open or shorted, often after stone impact
Signal or low reference wire to the cluster damaged
s: Outside temperature display missing or showing dashes
Automatic climate control works with a stored or default temperature
On some GM models the HVAC display switches to Celsius

B0159.d: No public J2012 source lists B0159. General Motors uses it: bulletin PIP5094 from 2013 lists B0159 among its service information keywords, though without a description, so no public GM text states the exact fault logic. Its neighbour B0158 is GM's outside air sensor circuit code. The sensor is an NTC thermistor behind the front bumper; per the 2011 Saab 9-5 manual the cluster supplies 5 V, sees high resistance and voltage when it is cold and low values when it is hot. A range/performance fault, unlike B0158, concerns a signal that stays inside the electrical limits but is implausible, for example frozen at one value or far from what other temperatures suggest. Result: wrong outside reading.
c: Outside air sensor drifted or slow to react, giving plausible but wrong values
Sensor mounted where engine or road heat reaches it, e.g. after a bumper repair
Corroded contact adding resistance and shifting the reading
s: Displayed outside temperature clearly too high or too low
Climate control or A/C compressor behaves oddly because of the wrong outside value

B0160.d: B0160 is not among the publicly available J2012 entries, and no maker publishes it with this meaning; a similar title belongs to B0250. The in-car sensor tells automatic climate control the actual cabin temperature. To read real cabin air it is usually aspirated: Denso's patent US20040016537A1 draws cabin air across the sensor with an aspirator fed by the HVAC case, so air keeps flowing in every mode. Manufacturers use other numbers for this circuit. In GM's Global A system, as in the 2011 Saab 9-5, B0163 covers the passenger compartment sensor with limits of 0.1 and 4.9 V. Older Saab 9-3 models use B0165 when the input drops below 0.2 V (grounded) and B0166 for an open.
c: Thermistor in the in-car sensor open or shorted
Sensor plug behind the dash or headliner loose or corroded
Signal or reference wire damaged during interior work
s: Automatic climate control overheats or overcools the cabin
Blower speed does not settle as the cabin reaches the set temperature

B0162.d: No public carmaker source and no publicly available J2012 list covers B0162. The title implies a second sun load channel, as used for dual-zone climate control: Eaton's patent US5957375A describes a sensor that sees how much sun reaches separate areas of the cabin so each side can be cooled on its own. US6888120B2 achieves this with two lenses and two photodiodes split by an opaque section, one for the driver and one for the passenger side. GM, by contrast, covers its whole multi-zone sensor with one code, B0183, in the 2011 Saab 9-4X; if no value is available the module assumes 0 W/m², 45° elevation and −75° azimuth. Losing the second channel leaves one side poorly compensated.
c: Second photodiode or channel of a dual-zone sun sensor failed
Connector of the sensor in the dash top cover loose or damaged
Signal wire of the second channel open or shorted
s: One side of the cabin gets too warm in sun while the other is fine
Dual-zone automatic reacts to sunshine only on one side

B0164.t: Air Bag In-Vehicle Temperature Sensor Circuit
B0164.d: B0164 is not listed in any publicly available J2012 table. General Motors does use the number: bulletin PIP5094 from 2013 lists it as a service information keyword, but no public GM text gives its wording. The airbag meaning in the title is not documented by any carmaker. GM's neighbouring code B0163 is the passenger compartment sensor of the HVAC system, which makes a climate control meaning more likely than an airbag one. Temperature sensing for airbags does exist: Delphi's US7000946B2 adjusts restraint output to the measured inflator temperature, using the control chip's own die temperature as a guide, and Bosch's US5697639A puts a temperature sensor inside the airbag module. Treat any B0164 by the make's own definition.
c: Temperature sensor or its wiring open or shorted
GM: fault in the climate control sensor group around B0163 rather than the airbag
Internal temperature measurement of the control module faulty
s: Airbag or climate warning, depending on which module stored the code
Climate control may run on a substitute cabin temperature
Safety note: if the airbag module is involved, work only with the battery disconnected and the wait time observed

B0166.d: The public J2012 lists do not contain B0166, and no make describes it as a discharge air sensor. Saab does use it, for the cabin rather than the outlet: in 9-3 climate control manuals from 2003 to 2012, B0166 05 marks the indoor or compartment temperature sensor as open or shorted to supply once the module input rises above 4.8 V, checked continuously with the ignition on; B0165 02 is the matching short to ground. Discharge or duct air sensors are NTC thermistors in the outlet ducts that let the module check what it actually delivers. GM's Global A system, per the 2011 Saab 9-5 manual, numbers them B0173, B0178, B0509 and B0514. A B0166 therefore needs the make's own definition.
c: Sensor open or signal shorted to supply (Saab 9-3 cabin sensor)
Sensor connector loose or left unplugged after dashboard work
On other makes, the outlet duct sensor itself failed
s: Automatic climate control misjudges cabin or outlet temperature and over- or undercorrects
Set temperature is not held steadily

B0168.d: B0168 shows up neither in the publicly available J2012 lists nor, with this meaning, in public carmaker documents; air mix door circuits have the codes B0258 and B0263. The air mix or blend door divides the airflow, sending part across the heater core and part past it, and so sets outlet temperature. A performance fault means it does not reach or hold its target. An older Japanese patent (CA1266779A) shows how sensitive this is: in the door range where a small movement changes air temperature a lot, the motor gets lower voltage to stop the door hunting. In US5529112A the temperature door motor runs into its end stop and stays stalled there. GM's Global A climate control drives this door with a stepper motor and logs it under B0408.
c: Blend door shaft or lever broken or slipping on the actuator
Air mix actuator gear worn or motor weak
Foreign object or debris in the HVAC case blocking the door
s: Outlet air stays hot or cold regardless of the temperature setting
Temperature swings or clicking behind the dash

B0170.d: Searching the available J2012 lists and public manufacturer material turned up no entry for B0170 with this title. Unlike B0150, which concerns how the mode door moves, this code points at the sensor that reports its position. In most electronic climate actuators that sensor is a potentiometer on the gear train; a Motor magazine article puts its signal at about 0 to 5 V and notes that simple recirculation actuators often have none. Hyundai's patent US9960727B2 drives intake, temperature, mode and defog door motors until the feedback voltage matches the target and watches the motor current for stalls. A lost or noisy position signal leaves the module unsure where the door is, so it may stop driving it.
c: Worn or dirty potentiometer track inside the mode actuator
Feedback signal, 5 V supply or reference wire open or shorted
Bent or pushed-back pin in the actuator connector
s: Air distribution stays fixed in one position
Actuator runs repeatedly or ticks after switching on

B0173.t: Upper Left Duct Air Temperature Sensor Circuit
B0173.d: B0173 lacks an entry in the public J2012 lists, but General Motors documents it clearly in its Global A climate control. In the 2011 Saab 9-5 and 9-4X manuals it covers the upper left duct air temperature sensor: B0173 02 when the signal is grounded, 05 for high voltage or an open; the module flags a signal under 0.1 V or over 4.9 V and continues with a default value. B0178 is the lower left sensor, B0509 and B0514 the right side. GM bulletin 17-NA-049 (2017 Bolt EV, Opel Ampera-e) traces B0173 and B0178 to a duct sensor harness pinched between HVAC case and tie bar, and PIT5383 lists B0173 for 2015 models needing new K33 HVAC software. GM files the air inlet door under B022A.
c: Duct sensor harness pinched between HVAC case and cross-car beam (GM 17-NA-049)
Upper left duct sensor thermistor open or shorted
HVAC module calibration needing an update (GM PIT5383, 2015 models)
s: Left vents too warm or too cold, or heating or cooling seems not to work
Climate control runs on a default duct temperature

B0175.d: The J2012 tables at hand leave out B0175, and no maker ties it to the recirculation door; a recirculation door circuit has the code B0273. Saab assigns the number to a temperature sensor instead. Its 9-3 climate control manuals read B0175 02 as a grounded left vent air mix temperature sensor, with the 2003 manual naming an input below 0.2 V, and the module then borrows the value of the left floor sensor; B0176 is its open circuit. GM's Global A system logs recirculation door actuator faults under B0223 and B022A instead. The recirculation door switches between fresh and cabin air, and HELLA notes that an air quality sensor can move it automatically. Check the make's definition first.
c: Recirculation door sticking or its actuator gear stripped
Saab 9-3: left vent air mix sensor or its lead shorted to ground
Actuator wiring or connector fault behind the glovebox
s: Recirculation cannot be switched or windows fog because the door stays on recirculate
Saab 9-3: left outlet temperature regulated less precisely

B0181.d: B0181 is missing from every publicly available J2012 code list, and no carmaker publishes it as a front blower code. Saab does use the number, for something else: its 9-3 climate control stores B0181 05 when the left floor air mix temperature sensor input rises above 4.8 V, i.e. open or shorted to B+. In GM's later Global A climate control the front blower speed circuit is B0193; a general blower circuit has the code B0283. Read as titled, a circuit low fault means the blower feed or speed line sits too low. In the 2011 Saab 9-5 the climate module sends a PWM command that the blower module turns into 2 to 13 V at the motor; with that line grounded or open the fan stops. Older systems step the speed through resistor paths instead.
c: Speed command line between climate module and blower module open or chafed to ground
Blower control module or series resistor burnt out, often after a sluggish motor drew too much current
Blown fuse or melted connector in the blower power feed
s: Front blower does not run at all or only at the highest stage
Windscreen demists slowly because almost no air reaches it

B0182.t: Right Front/Passenger Side Buckle Tension Sensor Circuit
B0182.d: B0182 appears in no J2012 list and in no public document of any carmaker, so the code cannot be verified. Its meaning overlaps B0061, the passenger belt tension sensor, and B0140. Such a sensor sits at the lower belt anchor and tells the occupant detection system how hard the belt is pulled. Delphi's patent US6605877B1 feeds the sensor and reads its data over the same two wires; a tension above a calibrated value points to a child seat strapped down tightly, and the seat weight reading is corrected by the belt load. FMVSS 208 lets carmakers switch the passenger airbag off automatically for small children, which is where this signal matters. A circuit fault leaves the module unsure whether to permit the airbag, so it lights the airbag lamp.
c: Plug at the belt anchor sensor loose, corroded or pulled off when the seat was moved
Two-wire lead to the occupant detection module pinched or chafed under the seat
Sensor electronics faulty, for instance after a crash load on the belt
s: Airbag warning lamp lit
Passenger airbag off indicator behaves unexpectedly with a child seat or adult in the seat
Safety note: airbag and pretensioner plugs are close by; disconnect the battery and wait before unplugging anything

B0184.d: No publicly available J2012 list includes B0184, and no maker documents it as a rear blower code. In Saab's 9-3 climate control the number belongs to the solar sensor: B0184 06 means that circuit is open or shorted to ground, and the system then regulates as on an overcast day. GM's Global A models report a rear blower speed circuit fault as B0208; GM bulletin PIT5383A lists B0208 among the HVAC codes of several 2015 GM models. Rear blowers serve the second and third rows of vans and large SUVs. In the 2011 Saab 9-5 an auxiliary blower module converts a PWM command into a motor voltage between 2 and 13 V, and a grounded, open or shorted command line stops the rear fan. A Hyundai patent notes that a stalled HVAC motor can draw several hundred mA. A related code is B0330.
c: Long harness run to the rear blower open or shorted, often at body joints or under trim
Auxiliary blower control module or rear resistor failed
Rear blower motor worn or blocked by debris drawn in through the rear intake
s: No airflow from the rear roof or floor vents
Rear seats stay warm in summer or cold in winter while the front is comfortable

B0186.d: B0186 is not in the publicly available J2012 lists, and no manufacturer uses it for front blower speed. Saab assigns it to the solar sensor of the 9-3: B0186 01 is a short to B+ in that circuit, after which the climate control assumes cloudy weather. A speed performance fault, as the title puts it, differs from the circuit faults B0181 and B0283: the wiring is intact, but the fan does not turn at the commanded speed. Denso's patent US10300764B2 shows how a blower control module checks this with a Hall sensor. If the rotor has not moved after about 2.7 s it reports a locked rotor to the climate module, power is cut and a in one example a restart follows after 20 s, five times at most until the next start. US5554913A names the classic cause: foreign objects sucked into the intake jam the wheel.
c: Leaves or other debris drawn in through the air intake, braking or jamming the fan wheel
Worn blower motor bearings or brushes, motor runs slowly or stalls
Heavily clogged cabin filter loading the motor
s: Blower speed does not match the selected stage or fluctuates
Fan stops and restarts after a pause, sometimes with a grinding noise

B0188.d: B0188 cannot be traced: it appears in no publicly available J2012 list and in no public carmaker material. The rear wiper meaning repeats B0910, titled Wiper Motor Rear Circuit. Bosch describes the part: unlike the front system, the rear wiper has a single arm driven straight off the motor, with sweep angles from 88 to 177 degrees and wiped radii of 250 to 500 mm. Because motor and harness sit in the tailgate, the circuit must cope with hinge flexing and moisture. Audi traced dead or intermittent rear wipers on the 2010–2015 Q5 to corrosion at splice B538 in the motor control circuit; the voltage drop pushed the control signal out of range, and the splice was repaired. With the circuit open or shorted, the rear window stays unwiped.
c: Wires broken in the rubber boot between body and tailgate after years of opening
Corroded splice or connector in the rear wiper control circuit causing a voltage drop
Rear wiper motor seized, for example from a corroded spindle, or internally shorted
s: Rear wiper does not move or works only now and then
Rear wiper stops away from its rest position

B0190.d: No known public source lists B0190, neither a J2012 table nor a carmaker document. The part named in the title is common: a cam on the wiper gear opens or closes contacts, so the control knows when the blades are at rest and can keep the motor running until they get there. Controllers also use this signal for protection. In US5694011A a timer set longer than one wipe cycle cuts the motor if the park signal stops changing, which catches blades frozen to the glass; US4320329A treats a missing park position after a cycle as a blocked motor and lengthens the pause. A patent by FCA, US8598828B2, filters the contact signal so noise is not taken for a state change. With a faulty circuit the blades may stop anywhere, keep sweeping after switch-off, or intermittent mode misbehaves.
c: Park contacts in the wiper motor gear housing worn, dirty or corroded by water
Park signal wire or connector at the wiper motor open or shorted
Fuse or relay in the park supply circuit failed
s: Wipers stop in the field of view instead of at the bottom of the screen
Wipers keep running after being switched off or intermittent mode fails

B0192.d: B0192 is publicly unverifiable: it appears neither in a J2012 list nor in any carmaker's documents. A performance fault, unlike the circuit fault B0220, means the wiring may be fine while the wipers sweep too slowly or irregularly. Speed is usually judged from the park contact, which closes once per revolution. US5216340A uses exactly this on cars with two wiper motors: from the timing and the back-EMF voltage seen at each park contact it detects that one motor runs faster and briefly holds it back until both are in step again. US5694011A shows the extreme case, a motor so loaded by frozen or stuck blades that the park signal stops. Bosch now also offers brushless and reversing drives whose electronics set speed and end positions themselves. Typical result: smeared, slow or out-of-step wiping.
c: Wiper linkage pivots dry, corroded or binding, slowing the motor
Worn motor brushes or commutator, reduced torque and speed
Blades frozen to the glass or heavily loaded by snow
s: Wipers sweep noticeably slower than usual, especially on high speed
Wiper arms judder, hesitate or run out of step with each other

B0200.t: Air Bag System Voltage Out of Range
B0200.d: B0200 is not documented in public: no publicly available J2012 list and no carmaker uses it with this meaning. What the title describes is real. An airbag control unit runs from the vehicle battery and needs a stable supply to fire reliably; Bosch rates its commercial vehicle unit for 8.5 to 32 V. An energy reserve capacitor, 2 x 4.2 mF in that unit, keeps it working for a defined autonomy time if the battery is torn off in a crash (Bosch EP1526986B1). Airbag system chips such as Bosch CG903 monitor their supply voltages and test the reserve capacitor all the time. A patent for an airbag ECU (US20140142812A1) logs how long the supply stayed in a set range, for instance during cranking dips. Outside the range the module turns on the airbag lamp, the readiness indicator FMVSS 208 demands.
c: Weak battery or charging fault letting system voltage sag, often while cranking
Poor ground or loose supply pin at the airbag control unit connector, or a corroded fuse contact
Airbag control unit faulty, for example its internal supply or reserve capacitor
s: Airbag warning lamp on, sometimes only after a cold start or jump start
Other modules may also log low-voltage faults
Safety note: airbags may not deploy while the fault is present; work on the system only with the battery disconnected and the wait time observed

B0205.d: B0205 is absent from the published J2012 lists, and no carmaker documents it for the defroster door; a defrost door circuit has the code B0278. Saab files its 9-3 defrost door motor under B0240 06 and B0241 01, where an open, grounded or B+ shorted motor circuit leads to wrong air distribution. The defroster door sends air to the windscreen. MOTOR magazine notes that most electronic climate actuators report door position through a potentiometer driven by their gear train, as a signal of roughly 0 to 5 V. Older layouts get by without one: in Hitachi's CA1266779A a two-position actuator just flips the vent door between face vents and defroster, and US4819715A drives a shutter that opens either the upper vents or the defroster nozzle. A position fault means the door is not where it was commanded.
c: Defroster door actuator with stripped gears or worn feedback potentiometer
Door or linkage binding, broken or blocked by foreign objects
Position feedback or reference wire open or shorted
s: Little or no air reaches the windscreen in defrost mode
Air comes from the wrong outlets or a clicking noise is heard behind the dashboard

B0210.d: No publicly available J2012 table mentions B0210, and no carmaker documents it; lost or invalid communication with a rain sensing module is covered by U0231 and U0532. The sensor is mounted behind the windscreen, inside the car and within the wiped area. According to HELLA, light-emitting diodes shine infrared light through a prism into the glass; on a dry screen it is totally reflected to a photodiode, while drops let part of it escape. A gel pad couples the sensor optically to the glass, and a poorly fitted pad can cause malfunctions. From the received light the electronics estimate the rain and set the wiper interval, switching to the highest stage in heavy spray. HELLA's fourth generation also reports streaks and dirt. If the sensor fails, the wiper module falls back to normal interval wiping.
c: Gel pad aged or with air bubbles, often after a windscreen replacement
Rain sensor electronics failed or moisture inside the housing
Supply or data wire to the sensor at the headliner damaged
s: Automatic wiping does not react to rain or wipes on a dry screen
Wipers only work in fixed interval or manual stages
Automatic headlamps may also stop working on combined rain/light sensors

B0220.d: B0220 is absent from the openly accessible J2012 lists and from carmaker documents, so it cannot be proven publicly; the front wiper motor circuit itself has the code B0900. The speed circuit is the part that selects slow or fast wiping. Classic wiper motors have three brushes, one for low speed, one for high and a shared one. In the prior art described in Denso's US6917173B2, a relay feeds the high brush while a MOSFET switches the low brush, both commanded by a wiper control unit; that patent replaces the arrangement with a two-brush motor whose speed is set by PWM duty, 100 % meaning fast. US5216340A also shows the low and high brush layout. Bosch's brushless EC drive does without brushes. An open speed line leaves one stage dead; a short can lock the wipers at one speed.
c: High/low speed relay or its contacts failed in the fuse box or control module
Wire or plug to the low or high speed brush of the motor open or shorted
One speed brush worn out or burnt inside the wiper motor
s: Wipers work at only one speed, slow or fast
Wipers run at one speed and cannot be switched to the other

B0223.d: B0223 does not appear in the publicly available J2012 lists, but General Motors uses it for the recirculation door actuator. On GM Global A cars such as the Saab 9-5 and 9-4X of model year 2011 that actuator is a stepper motor with four control lines; B0223 01 means command circuit 1 is shorted to battery, B0223 06 that it is open or low. The module only checks the outputs when the motor starts to move, not while it runs or once the target is reached; it then switches the output off and deactivates that motor. B022A is the second recirculation command circuit. GM bulletin PIT5383A for 2015 Buick, Cadillac, Chevrolet and GMC models lists B0223 among HVAC codes and inoperative recirculation, fixed by reprogramming the HVAC module. The airbag lamp meaning once given here belongs to B00D2 in J2012.
c: Recirculation door stepper motor faulty or its gears stripped
Control line 1 to the actuator open, grounded or shorted to battery voltage
HVAC control module software, as in GM bulletin PIT5383A, or module output stage
s: Recirculation cannot be switched on or off
Windows mist up or outside smells get in because the door is stuck

B0226.d: The publicly available J2012 lists have no B0226, and no maker documents it for headlamp levelling. Saab uses the number in its 9-3 climate control: B0226 01 is a short to B+ in the recirculation motor circuit, possibly causing stale air or misted windows. Automatic levelling, as HELLA explains, keeps the beam cut-off steady as the load changes. A control unit compares front and rear axle sensors with stored values and drives small motors in the headlamps; dynamic systems, found on almost all xenon cars, also correct for braking and acceleration. Compact cars often omit the front sensor. Each axle sensor is an angle sensor whose lever is clipped to a suspension arm; older ones use a potentiometer, newer ones inductive measurement. With the front sensor failed, the beam stays where it was.
c: Lever or coupling rod of the front axle sensor bent, broken or detached
Connector or wire at the sensor corroded or damaged by road splash
Sensor worn out internally or not calibrated after replacement or suspension work
s: Headlamp levelling warning shown and beam height no longer adjusts
Oncoming drivers flash because the beam is set too high under load

B0228.d: B0228 appears in none of the publicly available J2012 lists, and no carmaker publishes it as a fog lamp code. General Motors does use the number, but inside climate control: bulletin PIT5383 lists B0228 among the HVAC codes of 2015 Cadillac, Chevrolet and GMC models whose K33 climate module needed new software; GM does not publish its exact wording. Read as titled, the code concerns the drive of the front fog lamps. In patent US8125101B1 the fog switch grounds dedicated signal lines that act straight on the fog lamp relays; in US7230350B2 a fog switch shifts the voltage on the headlamp switch resistor chain, and the controller then adds the fog function. A circuit fault leaves the lamps dark or hides the request from the module.
c: Fog lamp relay or fuse failed, so the lamps get no supply although the switch is on
Low-mounted harness in the front bumper torn or corroded, often after a parking knock or water ingress
Bulb burnt out or lamp housing flooded through a cracked lens
Fog position of the light switch worn or its signal line open
s: Front fog lamps stay dark although the switch is on
Fog lamp indicator lights up but only one lamp or none works

B0231.d: B0231 is found neither in any publicly available J2012 list nor in public service documents of a carmaker, so the code cannot be verified. The title points to the front marker or position lamps. FMVSS 108 places side marker lamps close to the leading and trailing ends of the body so that, seen from the side, they reveal how long the vehicle is. HELLA lists front marker lights as white, or amber where the headlamps are amber, and mandatory on vehicles wider than 1600 mm. They normally light in the park position of the light switch. A module that switches them electronically can spot a missing load: Ford's patent US4667187A briefly toggles each lamp for about 300 µs and flags a fault when no current change follows. Expect a dark marker lamp and, where fitted, a bulb warning.
c: Bulb or LED module of the marker lamp failed
Corroded bulb holder or plug in the headlamp area, where spray water reaches it
Feed or ground wire to the front lamp open or shorted
s: One front marker or position lamp stays dark with parking lights on
Bulb failure warning in the instrument cluster, where the car has one

B0233.d: Public J2012 listings leave B0233 out, yet GM assigns it in its Global A climate control for the air distribution (mode) actuator. On 2011 Saab 9-5 and 9-4X cars that actuator is a stepper motor: the HVAC module feeds it a 12 V reference and switches its four coils to ground in pulses. B0233 01 means one of its control lines is shorted to voltage, B0233 06 that a line is open or low. The module tests the outputs only as the motor starts a move, not during travel or at the target. GM bulletin PIT5383 names B0233 among HVAC codes of 2015 models cured by reprogramming the K33 module. The rear distribution actuator reports B3531 instead. With the front actuator out, air keeps coming from the outlets last selected.
c: Mode stepper actuator failed internally, e.g. a burnt coil or worn gear
One of the four control lines or the 12 V reference chafed, open or shorted behind the dash
HVAC module software fault on affected GM models, fixed by reprogramming
s: Air comes from the wrong outlets and the selected distribution is ignored
Windscreen cannot be demisted because air will not switch to defrost

B0235.d: No publicly available J2012 list contains B0235, nor does any carmaker describe it, which leaves it unverified; side-specific brake lamp codes are B0850 and B0851. Stop lamps send a steady red signal rearward while the driver brakes, and FMVSS 108 also demands a third stop lamp mounted high. The brake light switch at the pedal triggers them, directly or via a body module. HELLA describes a Golf V in which one 21 W bulb works as tail lamp on a PWM signal of about 5.7 V and as stop lamp at a full 13.5 V, so one wiring fault can hit both jobs. On a Mitsubishi Grandis, moisture inside the brake light switch even lit the traction and stability warning lamps. A dark brake lamp raises the risk of being hit from behind.
c: Stop lamp bulb or LED unit failed
Brake light switch misadjusted, worn or wet inside
Blown fuse or broken wire, often in the tailgate or boot lid harness
Corroded lamp holder or plug in the rear light cluster
s: One or more brake lamps stay dark when the pedal is pressed
Bulb warning shown, sometimes together with traction or stability warning lamps
Safety note: following traffic gets no braking signal; repair before further driving

B0237.d: Neither the publicly available J2012 lists nor any public service literature mention B0237, so it remains unconfirmed. In the words of FMVSS 108, backup lamps light the road behind the car and warn pedestrians and drivers that it is reversing or about to. HELLA notes that the circuit may only be live with the ignition on and reverse engaged. Manual gearboxes close a plunger switch in reverse; on automatics the range sensor or the transmission controller supplies the signal. In patent US5065135A, held by Automotive Products, logic that decodes the selector position energises a relay feeding the lamp for as long as reverse is reported. A fault leaves the lamps dark in reverse, or lit outside reverse when the line is shorted to supply.
c: Reverse light switch on the gearbox worn or its plug corroded by road spray
Reversing lamp bulb burnt out or LED unit failed
Missing reverse signal from the range sensor or transmission module on automatics
Broken wire in the tailgate harness feeding the lamp
s: Reversing lamps stay dark with reverse gear engaged
Reversing lamps lit while driving forward

B0239.d: B0239 cannot be traced in any J2012 source or factory document, so its use stays unproven; the same title belongs to B0860. The licence plate lamp lights the rear registration plate and is usually wired with the tail lamps. FMVSS 108 asks that it illuminate the plate without obstruction by body parts. HELLA quotes the European rule that the plate must be readable from 25 m, with no part of it below 2.5 cd/m². Body modules today monitor lighting outputs, and HELLA's Golf 6 example shows the other side of that: after fitting LED rear lamps the module must be recoded, or it reports lamp faults. A circuit fault here leaves the plate dark, which can lead to a police stop.
c: Plate lamp bulb or LED unit failed, often from water inside the housing
Wire broken in the flexible tube between body and tailgate or boot lid
Retrofitted LED lamp not matched by the body module coding
s: Rear number plate is not lit with the lights on
Bulb warning in the cluster, where the car monitors this lamp

B0240.d: Searching J2012 sources turned up no B0240, and no maker applies it to the headlamp switch; the identical title belongs to B0800. Saab gives the number another job: in the 9-3 climate system B0240 06 means the defrost door motor circuit is open or grounded, with wrong air distribution as a result, and B0241 01 that this motor is shorted to B+. Going by its title, the code concerns the light switch input. Modern switches rarely carry lamp current. In US7230350B2 a series resistor chain gives each position (Auto, Off, Park, Headlamp) its own voltage band, read by an 8-bit converter, and the bands stay clear of 0 and 255 so a grounded line or one shorted to battery lands outside all of them. US8125101B1 then falls back to the mode closest to the driver's choice.
c: Worn or dirty contacts or resistor track inside the light switch
Switch plug loose or corroded behind the dashboard trim
Signal line to the body module shorted to ground or supply
s: Lights do not follow the switch position or fall back to a fixed setting
Automatic lights or parking lights cannot be selected

B0245.d: B0245 is unknown to every publicly available J2012 source and undocumented by carmakers, so nothing public backs it; driver window faults have the code B0500. The driver's door usually holds the master switch block, which commands its own window and, by signal lines or a bus, the other doors. Honda's patent US7145299B2 replaces two heavy wires per door with a single line that the master ties to battery for up, to ground for down and leaves floating for stop, so contact wear and relay surges no longer stress the switch. A circuit code here means the module sees a switch state that cannot be right, such as a contact held closed by corrosion or a broken line. Windows that can close on their own must reverse before pressing 100 N under FMVSS 118.
c: Master switch contacts corroded or sticking, often after drinks or rain got into the door panel
Wires broken in the rubber boot between body and driver's door
Plug of the switch block loose or with pushed-back pins
s: Driver's window or other windows do not respond to the master switch
A window moves on its own or the one-touch function misbehaves

B0247.d: B0247 is listed in none of the publicly available J2012 sources and no carmaker publishes it; passenger window circuit faults have the code B0501. The passenger switch is the simpler partner of the driver's master block: it moves only its own window, and the master can override it or lock it out. In Honda's US7145299B2 the passenger door unit keeps its own up and down buttons wired across its drive transistors, so they still work while the master line is idle; should the master command up while the local down button is pressed, a relay lifts one motor terminal off ground. A circuit code therefore points to the passenger switch, its plug in the door or the line to the master. FMVSS 118 restricts when such a window may move without the ignition key.
c: Passenger window switch worn or contaminated
Signal line between passenger door and master switch broken at the door hinge
Window lock button on the master stuck or its circuit faulty
s: Passenger window works from the driver's switch but not from its own
Passenger switch moves the window only in one direction

B0250.t: HVAC Air Temperature Internal Sensor Circuit
B0250.d: None of the publicly available J2012 lists contain B0250. On the Saab 9-3 the number marks an actuator fault instead: B0250 06 means the floor door motor circuit is open or grounded, which upsets air distribution, while B0251 01 is the B+ short. Taken by its title, the code is about the cabin temperature sensor, which also has the code B0160. These sensors are NTC elements whose resistance falls as they warm, as HELLA documents for its own air temperature sensor. To measure real cabin air rather than still air behind the dash, TGK's patent US6622924B2 pulls air past the thermistor with a small brushless fan whose rotation is reported on its own pin. If the circuit fails, automatic climate control works with a substitute value and the cabin ends up too warm or too cold.
c: Sensor plug or wiring behind the dashboard open or shorted to ground
NTC element in the sensor damaged
Aspirator fan seized or its intake grille blocked, so the reading lags behind cabin temperature
s: Automatic climate control holds the wrong cabin temperature
Blower speed and outlet temperature no longer adapt as the cabin warms up

B0252.d: For B0252 there is neither a J2012 entry nor any factory description, so the code is unverified. The title names one direction of the driver's window motor. A reversible DC motor moves the glass; the down path is the half of the drive that puts supply on one motor terminal and ground on the other. In patent US6906487B2 (International Rectifier, now Infineon) two smart high-side switches and two low-side MOSFETs form that H-bridge, read the motor current and shut down on shorts or overheating. If only the down path fails, the window still closes but will not open, which points to one driver stage, a relay contact or one motor lead. Pinch protection under FMVSS 118 reverses the glass downwards, so a dead down path disables it as well.
c: Down relay contact or driver transistor in the door module burnt
One motor lead broken in the door or at the motor plug
Worn motor brushes or commutator with a dead spot in one direction
s: Driver's window closes but will not go down
Pinch protection or one-touch down no longer works

B0255.t: HVAC Air Temperature External Sensor Circuit
B0255.d: B0255 shows up in no publicly available J2012 source. Saab's 9-3 uses it for a door motor: B0255 06 reports the right vent door motor circuit open or grounded, B0256 01 the B+ short on that motor. By its title, though, the code means the outside air sensor; that component also has the codes B0158 and B0159. HELLA's ambient sensor is an NTC resistor read through a voltage divider, rated −40 to +65 °C with a time constant under 35 s, and the module turns its resistance into a temperature using the sensor curve. Mounted behind the grille or under a mirror, it suffers from stone chips, salt and pinched wiring. Climate control uses the value to choose mode and fan speed, so a fault means poor regulation and a blank or wrong outside temperature.
c: Outside sensor broken by stone impact or corroded by road salt
Sensor wiring behind the bumper pinched or torn, often after front-end repairs
Moisture in the sensor plug changing the measured resistance
s: Outside temperature display shows dashes or an implausible value
Automatic climate control regulates poorly, especially in cold or hot weather

B0258.d: The public J2012 sources do not list B0258, and no carmaker documents it publicly; it cannot be verified. GM's Global A system logs its left, or main, temperature actuator under B0408 instead, as the 2011 Saab 9-5 manual shows. Air mix door 1 is normally the main or driver-side blend door and divides the air between heater core and bypass. In dual-zone units each side has its own doors: Valeo's US6484755B1 places both zone actuators on one side of the case so that one access route serves both. Most actuators are reversible DC motors with a position potentiometer on the gear train, giving a signal between about 0 and 5 V according to MOTOR magazine. A circuit fault leaves the door where it stopped, so the outlet temperature no longer follows the setting.
c: Blend door actuator motor or its feedback potentiometer failed
Actuator plug or wires under the dashboard loose, chafed or shorted
Door jammed by debris or a broken shaft, overloading the motor drive
s: Air from the vents stays hot or cold whatever temperature is set
Clicking or knocking behind the dashboard when the temperature is changed

B0260.d: No publicly available J2012 list contains B0260 with this meaning, and the same title belongs to B0970. Saab uses the number in the climate control of the 2003 9-3: B0260 06 stands for the left vent door motor circuit open or grounded, B0261 01 for a short to B+. By its title, the code means the courtesy lamp supply. Door ajar switches ground an input when a door opens; in Ford's patent US6133827A a module then lights the dome and footwell lamps, keeps them on for 25 s after the last door shuts and cuts them through a battery saver relay after 40 minutes. Ram's owner's manual describes a 10-minute cut-off for a door left ajar. A circuit fault means lamps that stay dark, never switch off, or drain the battery overnight.
c: Door contact switch or lock contact sticking, so the module sees a door open
Lamp feed shorted in the roof liner or a lamp unit with water damage
Battery saver relay or output stage in the body module faulty
s: Interior lamps do not come on when a door opens
Interior lamps stay lit or the battery is flat after the car stood overnight

B0263.d: B0263 shares the fate of its sibling B0258: no publicly available J2012 source lists it and no maker describes it. The second blend door usually serves the passenger side or the rear zone. Saab's 9-5 and 9-4X service data, which follow GM's Global A scheme, file the right temperature actuator under B0418 and the rear one under B0428, each a stepper motor checked for shorts to voltage and for opens. Some designs save the second motor: Denso's US7793706B2 drives the front door and a pair of rear doors from one servo through cams and a rocker, so a single failure would affect both zones. When the second door's circuit fails, the passenger or rear side stays at a fixed temperature while the driver side keeps regulating.
c: Passenger-side or rear blend actuator failed
Wiring to the second actuator open or shorted, often near the centre console
Shared linkage or door shaft broken, overloading the drive
s: Passenger side or rear outlets stay at one temperature whatever is set
Noticeable temperature difference between left and right outlets

B0265.d: Nothing in the publicly available J2012 sources or carmaker literature mentions B0265, so it is unverifiable; related codes are B0270 and B0272. The lock/unlock button in the driver's door tells the body or door module to run all lock motors, as HELLA's overview of central locking describes. In the Sumitomo patent US6365986B1 the switch pulls one of two inputs, each held high by a pull-up, to ground, and the module acts on the high-to-low edge rather than the level; after a reset it assumes the switch is pressed so that no second, false lock cycle follows. A circuit fault therefore means a line stuck low, which can block other lock commands or cycle the locks, or an open line that makes the button dead.
c: Lock/unlock button sticking or shorted by moisture in the door panel
Switch wires broken in the boot between body and driver's door
Input stage in the body or door module damaged
s: Doors cannot be locked or unlocked with the interior button
Locks cycle on their own or ignore the remote key

B0268.d: B0268 is not in the published J2012 lists, but General Motors uses the number: bulletin PIP5094, written for 2014 and older GM cars and light trucks, includes it in its keyword list of body codes, without a descriptor. The mode door routes air to face vents, footwell or windscreen. GM's later Global A system files the mode actuator under B0233; B0150 and B0170 also exist for this door. Such actuators are often a DC motor with a geared potentiometer returning about 0 to 5 V, per MOTOR magazine; newer ones count commutator pulses instead. In Nissan Shatai's patent US4819715A one actuator sets a shutter to open the upper vents, the defroster or neither. A circuit fault leaves the door in its last position.
c: Mode door actuator motor or position feedback failed
Actuator over-travelling or binding at the door, overloading its drive
Actuator plug or wiring behind the dash open or shorted
s: Air stays on one outlet, for example defrost, whatever mode is chosen
Pressing the mode button no longer changes where the air comes out

B0270.d: Public evidence for B0270 is lacking: it is absent from every publicly available J2012 list, and no manufacturer describes it. The title points to the lock/unlock rocker in the front passenger door. Saab, for instance, files that switch in the 9-3 (2003–2012) under its own number B3270: when the passenger door module reads a grounded switch line, the button is ignored and central locking only responds to the remaining controls. In the active-low input of US5619075A a pressed switch pulls the module input to ground. A circuit fault therefore means the module sees a button held permanently, never pressed or giving an implausible level. Remote key and driver switch normally keep working; the driver-side switch has its own code, B0265.
c: Lock rocker in the passenger door worn, sticking or contaminated
Switch signal wire chafed to ground or broken in the door hinge passage
Water ingress or corrosion at the door trim switch connector
Door or body control module input stage faulty
s: Passenger door lock button has no effect on central locking
Doors lock or unlock by themselves when the switch line is shorted
Remote key and driver switch still lock the car normally

B0272.d: Neither the reachable J2012 lists nor any carmaker's documents mention B0272, which leaves the code unproven. Its title covers the interior central-locking button in general, without naming a door. Saab logs a held button in the 9-3 driver door module as B3270 61: if the input stays low, the module waits until the key is released and pressed again before acting. In US6365986B1 such a manual switch inside the door is one of two inputs, next to the key-cylinder contact, from which the control unit drives the lock motors. US6157090A codes each switch position with its own resistor, so the body module reads the position as a current level. The door-specific switch codes are B0265 and B0270; actuator faults are B0530 ff.
c: Central-locking button mechanically stuck or contacts worn
Switch wire shorted to ground or open between switch and module
Spilled liquid or condensation in the switch panel
Door or body control module misreads the switch input
s: Interior lock button does not lock or unlock the doors
Locks cycle unexpectedly or only react to the remote key

B0273.d: B0273 could not be traced in the code lists at hand, nor in any manufacturer publication. The title concerns the electrical circuit of the actuator that swings the intake door between outside air and cabin air. Saab uses its own numbers here: in the 9-3 climate module B0225 06 stands for an open or grounded recirculation motor circuit and B0226 01 for a line shorted to battery voltage; the 2011 Saab 9-5 (GM) reports the stepper command lines as B0223/B022A. Patents such as US5181553A and US8641490B2 show the intake door driven by its own motor on command of the climate controller. With the circuit dead the door stays where it last stopped, which can mean stale air, fogging windows or weak cooling. B0175 covers door performance rather than the circuit.
c: Recirculation door actuator motor burnt out or internally open
Actuator wiring behind the glovebox chafed, shorted or unplugged
Door jammed by leaves or debris so the motor stalls at high current
Driver stage in the climate control module defective
s: Recirculation button changes nothing at the air intake
Windows fog up or outside odours enter the cabin
Reduced cooling on hot days

B0274.d: Nothing public confirms B0274 – the publicly available J2012 tables skip it and no maker explains it. The title refers to the switch the driver or a passer-by uses to release the boot lid electrically. Saab treats the button separately in the 9-3: the driver door module sets B2730 61 when the boot button stays active for more than 20 s, after which the lid will not open. Downstream, Saab and GM log the release output itself (9-3 B3265, 9-5 2011 B3265 02 for a grounded relay control line). Remote-release patents such as US4979384A and US3917330A show the basic layout: a switch energises a solenoid or motor in the latch. A switch-circuit fault leaves the lid shut or, if shorted, can pop it open unexpectedly.
c: Exterior release button corroded or full of water and dirt
Wires broken in the flexible boot lid hinge loom
Interior release button held or jammed by trim
Door or body module input reading the switch defective
s: Boot lid cannot be opened with the button, only by key or remote
Lid unlatches without anyone pressing the button

B0278.d: B0278 appears neither in J2012 tables nor in factory service material, so its existence is open. By its title it covers the electrical side of the defrost door actuator, the flap that routes air to the windscreen. Saab's 9-3 climate module stores the matching fault as B0240 06 (actuator circuit open or grounded) and B0241 01 (short to battery or excessive current); both lead to wrong air distribution. Hitachi's US5181553A drives the defroster door with a dedicated actuator motor, and MOTOR magazine describes how such actuators are tested electrically. A dead circuit leaves the door parked, so demisting may be weak or air may blow at the screen constantly. Door position problems without an electrical fault fit B0205.
c: Defrost door actuator motor open or shorted internally
Actuator wiring under the dashboard damaged or connector loose
Door or linkage seized so the motor draws excessive current
Actuator driver in the climate control module failed
s: Windscreen clears slowly because little air reaches it
Air keeps blowing at the windscreen whatever mode is selected

B0283.d: B0283 is not in any publicly available J2012 list; it is documented by Saab/GM, where it means the heated rear window relay, not a blower. In the Saab 9-3 (2003–2012) the rear electrical centre sets B0283 01 when the relay output exceeds 6 V with heating on, and B0283 06 when it stays below 6 V (open or grounded line). The GM-built Saab 9-5 and 9-4X of 2011 run the test in the climate module at 9–16 V: 02 means a grounded relay control line and the grid heats nonstop, 05 means open or short to voltage and the grid stays cold; a history code clears after 50 ignition cycles. As US4673797A shows, such relays are usually timed and drop out after a set period. Front blower faults belong to B0181/B0186; the heating grid itself is B0950.
c: Rear window heater relay with open coil or welded contacts
Relay control wire open, grounded or shorted to battery voltage
Poor ground or corroded socket at the relay
Output stage of the climate or electrical centre module faulty
s: Heated rear window does not work when switched on
Rear window heats continuously and cannot be switched off
Battery drained if the grid keeps heating

B0288.d: A search found B0288 in no J2012 list and in no carmaker's service data; it stays unconfirmed. The refrigerant pressure sensor it names sits on the high-pressure line; its signal decides whether the compressor may run and how fast the cooling fan turns. On most cars the engine controller reads it and stores P0530–P0533. Saab's 9-3 with Trionic 8, for example, sets P0532 below 0.25 V and P0533 above 4.2 V, each for over 1 s with the engine running above −7 °C, and then cuts the A/C relay. Patent US9259992B2 routes the sensor to the engine module in the same way, and US5623835A uses it to drive the fan. A body code would only be used where the climate module reads the sensor itself.
c: Refrigerant pressure sensor failed or signal drifting
Sensor connector near the condenser corroded by road spray
5 V reference, ground or signal wire open or shorted
Very low refrigerant charge giving an implausible reading
s: Air conditioning blows warm because the compressor is disabled
Radiator fan runs constantly or at the wrong speed

B0290.d: B0290 has no public source: the publicly available J2012 tables omit it, and service literature is silent. The title names the push button that requests the heated rear window. On the 2011 Saab 9-5 (GM) that button sits in the climate control faceplate, which passes the request to the climate module; only the relay output has its own code there (B0283). Saab's 9-3 monitors the button lamp separately as B0969 02. Patents US4555743A and US4673797A describe the usual logic: a momentary switch starts a timer of about ten minutes and can cancel it again. A switch fault means requests are lost or seen all the time, so the rear window either never heats or restarts by itself.
c: Rear defrost button contacts worn or button stuck in the panel
Climate control faceplate or its circuit board defective
Signal or data line between panel and module interrupted
s: Pressing the rear defrost button has no effect
Rear window heating switches on by itself or cannot be cancelled
Indicator lamp in the button stays dark or lit

B0292.d: Whether B0292 is used anywhere is unknown; no consulted J2012 list carries it and no maker documents it. Its title points to the electromagnetic clutch that couples a belt-driven compressor to its pulley, and the relay feeding the clutch coil. Usually the engine controller owns this circuit and logs P0645–P0647; on the Saab 9-3 with Trionic 8, for instance, P0646 sets when the relay output stays below 2 V for over 1 s, and the compressor may then run without stop. Patent US20040211197A1 explains that the climate unit cannot see a failed clutch unless an extra feedback path exists, and US4481784A shows the classic battery–relay–coil chain. Electric compressors without a clutch do not use such a code.
c: Clutch coil open or shorted, often after overheating
A/C clutch relay failed or contacts welded
Excessive clutch air gap so the plate does not pull in
Clutch feed or ground wire at the compressor damaged by heat
s: No cooling, compressor hub does not turn with A/C on
Compressor runs permanently even with A/C switched off

B0300.d: Public code lists do not show B0300, and factory documentation for it is missing too. The evaporator temperature sensor is a thermistor on or just behind the evaporator core; the climate controller cycles or throttles the compressor with it so that the core does not ice up (US6427465B1, US4326386A). Saab's 9-3 uses its own numbers: B0521 02 below 0.2 V and B0522 05 above 4.8 V at the module input, after which the outside temperature serves as a substitute value. HELLA reports that a badly sealed or drifting sensor can freeze the evaporator and choke the airflow. A circuit fault therefore tends to cost cooling comfort rather than leave the car without air.
c: Evaporator thermistor open, shorted or out of tolerance
Sensor pushed out of the core or poorly sealed after service
Connector at the HVAC housing loose or corroded by condensate
Sensor input in the climate control module faulty
s: Cooling weak or fluctuating, especially in hot weather
Airflow drops after a long drive because the evaporator ices up

B0305.d: B0305 is unconfirmed by any public J2012 list or manufacturer, and its subject matches B0156. The sun load sensor is a photodiode on top of the dashboard that tells automatic climate control how much solar heat enters the cabin (US6888120B2, US5957375A). Real codes for it carry other numbers: Saab's 9-3 uses B0183 08 for an implausible signal and B0184 06 for an open or grounded circuit, and then regulates as if the sky were overcast; the GM-built 2011 Saab 9-5 reports B0183 02/05. A circuit fault rarely stops the system, but in strong sun the cabin tends to run warm and the blower reacts late.
c: Sun load sensor photodiode aged or damaged
Sensor unclipped from the dashboard grille, connector pulled off
Signal or ground wire to the sensor open or shorted
s: Cabin too warm in bright sunshine with auto climate
Blower speed does not rise when the sun comes out

B0310.d: For B0310 there is neither a J2012 list entry nor a known manufacturer description. The title refers to the position feedback of the power driver seat. GM's 2011 Saab 9-5 uses Hall sensors built into each seat motor; the memory module feeds them 12 V and counts their pulses (0–65,535) to know where the seat is; its codes are B1825, B2355, B2365 and B2375. Saab's 9-3 files the fore-aft sensor as B2375: 04 above 0.5 V for an open line, 29 when no pulses arrive. Then memory recall stops and end-stop learning is lost. US5751129A names potentiometers, Hall sensors and commutator pulses as the usual principles. Manual seat movement normally still works.
c: Hall sensor inside a seat motor failed
Wiring under the seat pinched by the rails or pulled off
Sensor supply or ground circuit open or shorted
s: Memory buttons do not recall stored seat positions
Seat moves jerkily or stops short of its end position
Easy-entry function does not move the seat back

B0312.d: B0312 is undocumented in public: no accessible code list includes it and no automaker defines it. The title means the switch that moves the driver seat fore and aft. GM's 2011 Saab 9-5 tracks it as B1755 (forward) and B1760 (rearward): a switch line shorted to ground, or one direction active while the opposite is pressed, disables that motor both ways and blocks memory recall. Saab's 9-3 seat module reports B1755 01/B1760 01 when a switch line is shorted to battery voltage; the seat then only moves away from the faulty direction. In US4467252A a bank of reversible manual switches, one per adjustment direction, drives the seat motor alongside the memory logic. Motor and wiring faults on the same axis are B0560.
c: Seat switch contacts worn or the knob stuck in one direction
Drink spilled into the side-mounted switch
Switch wiring chafed under the seat cover
Seat module misreading the switch inputs
s: Driver seat moves only forward or only backward
Seat fore-aft movement dead while other axes work
Memory recall ignored

B0320.d: None of the J2012 lists on hand names B0320, and no vehicle maker publishes a definition. The title concerns position feedback on a powered front passenger seat, which exists mainly where that seat has memory or an easy-entry function. Saab's 9-3 passenger seat module uses B2375 for its fore-aft sensor: 01 when the input exceeds 7 ± 0.2 V, 04 for an open line; either way memory functions stop and calibrated end stops are lost. US6320341B1 avoids a separate sensor by counting the current ripple of the DC motor, while US5751129A builds the sensors into the memory module. The driver-side counterpart is B0310; fore-aft motor faults on this seat are B0570.
c: Position sensor in the passenger seat motor failed
Seat loom damaged by objects or feet under the seat
Sensor signal shorted to supply voltage
s: Passenger seat memory or easy-entry does not work
Seat jerks when starting or stopping

B0322.d: B0322 lacks any public definition, either in J2012 lists or from a manufacturer. The title describes the sensor reporting the cushion tilt of the power driver seat, normally made by raising or lowering the front edge. Saab's 9-3 driver seat module calls it the tilt position sensor and stores B3923: 01 above 7 ± 0.2 V, 02 when shorted to ground, 04 for an open line and 29 when no pulses arrive while the engine runs. Memory recall then stops and the end-stop calibration of the tilt motor is lost. US4682088A measures front and rear cushion height with potentiometers, while US6320341B1 restores the front cushion portion by pulse counting. Fore-aft feedback is B0310.
c: Sensor in the cushion tilt motor failed
Tilt motor wiring pinched in the seat frame
Shared sensor supply shorted or open
s: Cushion tilt not restored by memory recall
Tilt adjustment jerks or stops before the end

B0325.d: Searches turned up B0325 in no J2012 list and in no factory documentation. The title names the SET or M button used to store the current seat position under one of the memory buttons. Saab's 9-3 driver seat module knows it as the memorize button: B2765 01 when its line is shorted to battery voltage, B2765 61 when it is held or stuck for more than 60 s; the module then treats it as released until it is pressed afresh. US4682088A and US4463426A describe the classic sequence – press SET, then memory 1 or 2 within a short window – and US4264849A uses the same buttons both to recall and, with a store key, to save. A faulty set switch blocks saving but not manual adjustment.
c: Memory set button stuck in the door or seat panel
Button wire shorted to supply voltage or broken
s: New seat positions cannot be stored
Memory buttons recall old settings only

B0327.d: No known public list or manufacturer document defines B0327. The title is vague: it suggests a fault in storing or restoring positions of a power passenger seat. For that a module needs working position feedback; in Saab's 9-3 passenger seat module a lost slide sensor signal (B2375) switches off all memory functions and erases the end-stop calibration. US4264849A shows stored positions recalled by push buttons for any vehicle seat, and US6320341B1 restores several cushion and backrest positions from pulse counts. Without a manufacturer definition the exact trigger is unknown; it likely corresponds to lost stored data or failed recall.
c: Missing position feedback from a passenger seat motor
Stored positions lost after battery disconnection or low voltage
End stops not relearned after seat or motor replacement
s: Passenger seat does not return to its stored position
Stored settings forgotten after the ignition is switched off

B0330.d: B0330 cannot be found in accessible J2012 lists or carmaker sources, and it overlaps B0184 in content. The rear blower moves conditioned air to the back rows, often as a second fan in a rear duct (US6915650B2) or a separate rear unit with its own speed control (US4949779A). GM's 2011 Saab 9-5 and 9-4X log the circuit as B0208: the climate module sends a PWM speed command to an auxiliary blower control module that converts it into 2–13 V at the motor; 01 means that line is always high, 06 always low or floating, and the rear blower stops. Typical faults are a seized motor, a burnt speed controller or a broken command wire.
c: Rear blower speed controller or resistor burnt out
Rear blower motor seized or brushes worn
Speed command wire open or shorted between modules
Rear blower fuse or supply relay failed
s: No air from the rear vents
Rear blower runs only at one speed or cannot be switched off

B0335.d: B0335 is unsupported by J2012 lists and by service information; its topic duplicates B0341. The circuit is the heating mat in the driver cushion and backrest plus its supply. Real codes elsewhere: Saab's 9-3 climate module stores B2428 01 when the left heater is shorted to battery voltage and B2429 06 for an open left heater; GM's 2011 Saab 9-5 measures current and voltage every 10 s and sets B2425 0B/0D/0E for high current, high or low resistance. Chrysler bulletin 08-049-14 (Wrangler 2011–12) replaced elements whose resistance fell out of range below −12 °C (B1092). Patent US5229579A cuts power on a detected short or open to prevent overheating.
c: Heating wire in the driver cushion broken by repeated flexing
Seat heater connector under the seat loose or burnt
Element or feed wire shorted to the seat frame
Output stage of the seat heating or climate module defective
s: Driver seat stays cold although heating is switched on
Seat heating indicator flashes or goes out after a few seconds
Only the backrest or only the cushion warms up

B0337.d: There is no public trace of B0337 in J2012 lists or factory data; its subject repeats B0342. It covers the passenger seat heating mat and its feed. Because that seat is often empty, a fault may go unnoticed for a long time. Saab's 9-3 climate module reports B2433 01 when the right heater is shorted to battery voltage and B2434 06 for an open or grounded circuit; GM's 2011 Saab 9-5 uses B2430 0B/0D/0E. Chrysler's bulletin 08-049-14 covered both front seats (B1096 on the right). US6252208B1 shows how a control circuit combines heating current and an NTC seat sensor; a broken element or feed simply leaves the passenger seat cold.
c: Heating wire in the passenger cushion or backrest broken
Connector under the passenger seat kicked loose or corroded
Damage during work on the occupant detection mat in the same cushion
Heater output in the controlling module defective
s: Passenger seat heating does not warm up
Heating switches off shortly after activation

B0339.d: B0339 shows up neither in the public code lists nor in published service material. Rear seat heating is an option on larger cars; the GM-built 2011 Saab 9-4X with heated rear seats has a dedicated control module behind the rear backrest. It feeds both mats through a common supply, regulates by switching their ground with PWM and checks current and voltage every 10 s: B2425/B2430 0D mean element resistance too high, 0B/0E too much current or too little resistance.
