Each rear seat also carries an NTC sensor (B1925/B2170), and B2345 13 reports the shared disable line. US5229579A shows why such controllers shut off on a short or an open circuit.
c: Heating mat in a rear seat cushion broken
Connector damaged when the rear seat was folded or removed
Rear seat heating control module or its supply faulty
Seat temperature sensor implausible so heating is disabled
s: One or both rear seat heaters stay cold
Rear seat heating indicator flashes or goes out

B0341.d: B0341 is not backed by any known J2012 list or carmaker text, and it covers the same ground as B0335. The HVAC prefix fits cars whose climate control module also runs the seat heaters. Saab's 9-3 is one: its climate module drives the left seat heater and reads a seat temperature sensor; B1927 02 (input below 0.2 V) switches the left heater off, and B2429 06 reports an open element. US6252208B1 shows such a set-up, where an NTC sensor in the seat forms a voltage divider whose tap the controller reads to regulate heating current. The mats are the same as with a separate seat heating module; what differs is the module that owns the output and sets the code.
c: Seat temperature sensor shorted or open so heating is blocked
Long harness from climate module to seat damaged at the seat rail
Seat heater output in the climate control module failed
s: Driver seat heating dead while climate control works
Heating starts but stops after a short time

B0342.d: No accessible J2012 list or manufacturer source mentions B0342; it matches B0337 in substance. As with the driver side, the HVAC prefix implies a climate module that also drives the passenger seat heater. In Saab's 9-3 that module reads a right seat temperature sensor too: B2172 02 below 0.2 V or B2173 05 above 4.8 V (tested only while the cabin is warmer than −10 °C) shuts the right heater down, while B2434 06 flags an open or grounded heater output. US5229579A puts a thermistor next to the heating element so the controller can regulate and spot faults. A failed sensor can therefore disable a heating mat that is itself intact.
c: Right seat temperature sensor open or shorted
Connector under the passenger seat loose
Climate module seat heater driver or sensor input faulty
s: Passenger seat heating switches off immediately
Passenger seat stays cold

B0420.d: No public J2012 list carries B0420 with this meaning, and no carmaker describes an audio-system fault under it. The one documented use is unrelated: Saab files B0420 06 in the 9-3 (2003–2012) climate control as an open or grounded circuit to the right air-mix flap motor, which upsets temperature control. Read literally, the title points to a fault inside the head unit, the part that feeds every speaker channel. Saab's 2011 9-5 shows how such units judge their outputs: the radio stores B1025–B1055 for a shorted or open speaker line and mutes only that channel. Klippel describes how the DSP, amplifier and microphones already fitted in a car could run a self-test of the whole system. Lost bus contact with the radio belongs under U0184.
c: Internal electronics or software of the head unit faulty
Low or unstable supply voltage or poor ground at the head unit
Unit overheated because of blocked ventilation behind the dash
s: No sound from any speaker, or the radio restarts by itself
Head unit freezes or ignores its buttons
Code stored together with other infotainment faults

B0425.d: Every accessible J2012 list lacks B0425, and no maker's literature mentions it, leaving the code itself unverified. The title concerns a fault inside the separate audio amplifier rather than in its wiring. Amplifier chips such as TI's TAS6424E-Q1 check each channel for open load, shorted load and shorts to battery or ground, and raise a warning on clipping or overtemperature. In GM's Global A electronics, as fitted to 2011 Saab 9-5 and 9-4X cars, the amplifier stores no codes of its own; the radio watches the PWM mute line and logs B1287 if that line is open or shorted 0.4 s after it switches the amplifier on. Typical signs are silence or crackling on all amplified channels. Communication loss with the amplifier is U0186, a fault of the head unit B0420.
c: Output stage or internal electronics of the amplifier failed
Amplifier overheated, e.g. under a seat or in the boot without airflow
Moisture or water in the amplifier housing or plug
Shorted speaker or wiring that has overloaded the output stage
s: No sound or only very low volume from the amplified speakers
Crackling, hum or distortion, often worse when warm
Subwoofer or premium sound channels drop out

B0440.d: No public J2012 source lists B0440, and no carmaker explains it, so the code cannot be verified. The title concerns the Bluetooth unit that pairs a phone for hands-free calls and music streaming. Automotive chips such as NXP's AW300, qualified to AEC-Q100, handle the HFP and A2DP profiles; TI's WiLink 8Q family combines Bluetooth with Wi-Fi and GNSS for infotainment units. Often the radio part sits inside the telematics or head unit: the Saab 9-5 (2011) places it in the OnStar module and switches Bluetooth off when B2485 reports its antenna open or grounded. A module fault shows as failed pairing, dropped calls or no streaming. The antenna circuit has its own title, B0460, the microphone B0450; bus loss to the telematics unit is U0198.
c: Software fault or hung state of the Bluetooth/telematics unit
Bluetooth chip or its module failed internally
Poor supply or ground connection at the module
s: Phone cannot be paired or is not found
Hands-free calls drop or music streaming stops
Bluetooth menu greyed out or missing

B0445.d: B0445 does not appear in any reachable J2012 list and is not described by a manufacturer, so its existence is unproven. A USB hub in the car splits one host port of the head unit across several sockets for media and charging. Because a loose cable can touch battery voltage, TI's TPD3S714-Q1 shields the bus supply and both data lines against shorts up to 18 V in hubs and head units, and the TPS254900A-Q1 turns its switch off quickly on such a short so that the upstream converter and the hub data lines survive. TI's charging-port overview bundles power conversion, USB-PD and this protection for media hubs. A hub fault leaves sockets without data or charge, or lets a phone connect only now and then. Bus faults of the head unit itself are separate U codes.
c: Socket damaged or contaminated, short between pins
Cable between hub and head unit loose or chafed
Hub electronics or protection switch failed
Connected device or cable draws too much current
s: USB stick or phone not recognised
Socket charges but transfers no data, or vice versa
Phone projection drops out repeatedly

B0450.d: The code B0450 is absent from the publicly accessible J2012 lists, and no carmaker publishes it, so it remains unverified. Its title covers the hands-free microphone line. The module puts a bias voltage on the signal wire and reads speech back on the same wire. On the 2011 Saab 9-5 and its 9-4X sibling the OnStar module logs B2455 once the signal wire has been broken, grounded or tied to supply, or the low-reference return has lost contact, for 10 s; the status LED turns red and the other party cannot hear the caller. Audio converters like TI's PCM6240-Q1 supply a 5–9 V bias and flag open or shorted inputs and shorts to ground, bias or battery. Calls and voice control still start, but the far end hears nothing. Pairing problems belong to B0440.
c: Microphone in the headliner or mirror failed
Microphone wire pinched or broken in the headliner or A-pillar
Plug at microphone or module loose or corroded
s: Caller cannot hear the driver during hands-free calls
Voice control does not react to spoken commands
Emergency call or telematics status lamp shows a fault

B0455.d: No J2012 list available to the public includes B0455, and factory literature is silent on it, so the code is unverified. It names an internal fault of a display module, such as the centre screen or a cluster panel, not its wiring or data link. Saab's 2011 9-5 sets B1020 when the radio gets an improper status reply from its display assembly, pointing to an electronics fault or a jammed button; on the 9-4X the same number covers the radio/HVAC control panel. Denso's US11348495B2 lets each display test its own circuit, report to the image ECU and, if it fails, hand speed and warnings to another screen. Hyundai Mobis (US11961434B2) spots a frozen picture through hidden test pixels. Bus loss to a display is U0162 or U0255; a dark screen with live content suggests B0490.
c: Display controller or panel electronics failed
Software fault, often curable by an update
Button on the display unit jammed and reported as a fault
s: Screen stays black, flickers or freezes on one picture
Touch input or buttons on the display do not respond
Information moves to another display or a warning appears

B0460.d: B0460 appears in none of the accessible J2012 lists and in no manufacturer document, so it remains unproven. Its title concerns the Bluetooth antenna circuit. GM's Global A system in the Saab 9-5 and 9-4X (2011) covers the same part under its own number B2485: the small antenna sits directly on the OnStar module without a cable, is tested once a second, and an open or grounded antenna disables Bluetooth and turns the status LED red. Visteon's US20040116084A1 sends DC down an antenna feed and judges open or short from the current drawn, while Delphi's US6999858B2 detects a removed antenna by a floating DC node or by a mismatch at the transmitter output. Poor range or lost pairing points here; a dead Bluetooth chip belongs to B0440.
c: Antenna contact or plug at the module loose or corroded
Antenna or its lead damaged, e.g. after work behind the dash
Antenna detection or radio stage inside the module faulty
s: Phone pairs only at very short distance or not at all
Bluetooth switched off by the module, status lamp red
Calls and streaming break up repeatedly

B0490.d: B0490 is not listed in any accessible J2012 source, nor does a carmaker's literature cover it, so public proof is lacking. The title covers the backlight of a display, today usually LED strings fed by a boost driver. TI's LP8866-Q1 and LP8872-Q1 flag open strings, shorted LEDs and LED shorts to ground and report them to the host; TI adds that quick short-to-ground detection avoids glare that could blind the driver at night. GM's 2011 9-4X logs B1289 when the radio finds the PWM brightness line to the rear-seat screens open or shorted 400 ms after enabling it, and the screens then fall back to a fixed brightness. A dark screen whose picture is still faintly visible in sunlight points here rather than to B0455.
c: LED string or single LED of the backlight failed
Backlight driver or its boost stage defective
Brightness control line open or shorted
s: Screen dark although content is faintly visible in bright light
Brightness cannot be adjusted or follows no day/night change
Uneven, flickering or partly dark backlight

B0500.d: No public J2012 list includes B0500, and no carmaker documents it, so the code is not verified. The title concerns the driver's power window circuit. Saab handles this under its own numbers: in the 9-3 (2003–2012) the driver door module logs B3205/B3210 for an open, shorted or overloaded down or up path and retries on every new drive cycle; on the 2011 9-5 the BCM sets B3205 for an incompatible, internally failed or unlearned motor, the latter without one-touch travel. In US6906487B2 an H-bridge reads motor current for pinch detection. FMVSS 118 requires a window that closes by itself to reverse before 100 N, so a fault may block automatic closing. Switch faults belong to B0245, the down path alone to B0252.
c: Window motor worn, sluggish or with a dead spot
Wires broken in the rubber boot between body and door
Regulator or glass runs bind, motor overloads
End positions lost after battery disconnection, relearn needed
s: Driver window does not move or only in one direction
One-touch up/down and pinch protection out of action
Window stops or reverses partway without reason

B0501.d: For B0501 neither the reachable J2012 lists nor any manufacturer offer a definition, so the code is unverified. The title points to the front passenger window circuit. Saab's 9-3 passenger door module uses B3205/B3210 for its own motor paths and B3932 when it measures current while the motor should be idle; one-touch travel then stops. GM's 2011 9-4X sets B3210 for the passenger motor if its compatibility code does not match the BCM. Honda's US7145299B2 shows the classic layout in which the driver's master switch commands the passenger door over a single line, so the fault may sit in the master switch, the line or the local switch. Without working reversal, FMVSS 118's 100 N limit rules out automatic closing. The passenger switch circuit is B0247.
c: Passenger window motor worn or internally faulty
Passenger button in the driver's master switch faulty
Wiring broken in the passenger door hinge passage
Replacement motor not coded or not matched to the body module
s: Passenger window dead from both the local and the master switch
Window works only while the button is held
Window moves slowly or stops partway

B0502.t: Left Rear Power Window Circuit Malfunction
B0502.d: B0502 has no entry in any accessible J2012 list, and no carmaker describes it, so the code stays unproven. Its title concerns the left rear window circuit. In the Saab 9-3 the left rear door module logs B3210 04 when the motor's up path is open and the glass will not close, and B3543 if the two Hall signals arrive in reverse order for 150 ms, which disables one-touch travel. GM's 2011 9-5 assigns the left rear motor B3215. Microchip's AVR480 note shows why the Hall pulses matter: speed, current and glass position feed the pinch check. FMVSS 118 demands reversal before 100 N for any window that closes on its own. Many rear doors carry a child lockout; a locked-out rear switch is intended and not a fault.
c: Hall sensor in the motor or its supply faulty
Left rear window motor worn or with an open winding
Wires broken in the rear door hinge passage
s: Left rear window will not close or will not open
One-touch function and pinch protection not available
Window reverses on its own without an obstacle

B0503.t: Right Rear Power Window Circuit Malfunction
B0503.d: Public J2012 lists do not contain B0503, and no carmaker publishes a description, so the code is unverified. The title names the right rear window circuit. In the 9-3, Saab's right rear door module sets B3205 04 for an open down path and b3992 11 when the glass travels further than expected between its end stops; one-touch up and pinch protection then stop working. GM's 2011 9-4X gives this motor B3220, for example after an internal motor fault. FMVSS 118 lets a window close by itself only if it reverses before 100 N, which a module that has lost track of the glass cannot ensure. International Rectifier's US6906487B2 drives such a motor through an H-bridge with short-circuit and overtemperature cut-off.
c: Regulator cable or guide slipped, glass travel no longer matches
Right rear window motor worn or internally faulty
Motor or door plug corroded by water in the door
s: Right rear window does not open or moves only jerkily
One-touch closing and pinch protection disabled
Window stops short of the top seal or runs past it with noise

B0510.d: B0510 is missing from the publicly available J2012 lists, and no manufacturer defines it in accessible documents. GM does list B0510 among the circuit DTC keywords of bulletin PIP5094 (2014 and earlier cars and light trucks), but without a descriptor. The title points to the switch that tells the body electronics the driver door is being opened. In GM's 2011 Saab 9-5 the comparable input is the driver exterior handle switch, coded B3849 02: if the keyless entry module sees that line grounded or closed for over 180 s, it ignores the handle. Toyota's EP2372055A1 shows why such inputs matter: a door courtesy switch that fails to report an opening can let auto-lock trap the key inside. The passenger door counterpart is B0520.
c: Driver door switch worn, dirty or stuck in one position
Wire broken or chafed in the driver door hinge passage
Moisture or corrosion at the switch connector
Input stage of the body or keyless entry module faulty
s: Interior light stays off when the driver door is opened
Keyless opening at the driver handle does not respond
Door-open message or chime missing or shown permanently

B0520.d: No accessible J2012 list contains B0520, and its meaning is not published by any carmaker. The code exists at GM: PIP5094, a circuit-testing bulletin for 2014 and earlier GM vehicles, lists it as a keyword but leaves it undefined. The title describes the switch reporting that the front passenger door is opening. GM's 2011 Saab 9-5 monitors the matching right front exterior handle switch as B1474 02 and disables that handle once the line is grounded or stays closed beyond 60 s. Toyota's EP2372055A1 adds a plausibility check for intermittent switch faults: if a smart-key unlock is followed by the key being found inside the cabin without any door-open signal, the switch is judged faulty. Driver side: B0510.
c: Passenger door switch contacts worn, greased up or frozen
Wire break in the passenger door hinge passage
Exterior handle switch shorted by water ingress
Body or keyless entry module input faulty
s: Passenger door opening not detected by interior light or alarm
Passenger exterior handle ignored by the keyless system
Auto-lock may relock the car with the key inside

B0530.d: B0530 does not appear in the publicly available J2012 lists. GM names it among the circuit keywords of PIP5094 without a descriptor, and the GM-era Saab 9-3 (2003–2012) uses B0530 for something else entirely: the left turn indicator. There the front electrical centre logs B0530 04 when the lamp draws under 50 mA, and the rear centre logs B0530 02 for a grounded output, after which the indicators flash at double rate. For the driver door lock motor named in the title, the same 9-3 uses its own numbers in the driver door module, B3135 02 (motor line grounded) and B3130 02 (common line), both leaving central locking dead. HELLA lists supply, ground, broken wires and stiff lock mechanics as typical actuator faults.
c: Lock motor in the driver door latch worn or seized
Wire break in the door hinge passage
Stiff or contaminated latch mechanism overloading the motor
Output stage of the door or body control module faulty
s: Driver door does not lock or unlock with remote or switch
Other doors keep locking normally
On a Saab 9-3 the code instead comes with a left turn signal fault

B0531.d: B0531 is neither in the accessible J2012 lists nor in any public manufacturer document, so the code itself cannot be verified. Its title covers the lock motor in the front passenger door. The Saab 9-3 checks that motor in the passenger door module and stores B3135 02 when the line is grounded during a lock or unlock request. In GM's 2011 Saab 9-5, by contrast, the body control module drives grouped lock and unlock lines (B3125, B3130, B3135 02) at 9–18 V; a grounded line disables the power locks; once repaired, the stored entry ages out after 50 starts. Mitsuba's US7218120B2 describes how a driver stage can be checked with a small test current for shorts to supply or ground before the motor is powered. Driver door: B0530.
c: Passenger door lock motor burnt out or seized
Lock motor wire chafed to ground in the door
Water ingress at the latch connector
Door or body control module output faulty
s: Passenger door stays locked or unlocked while others follow
Whole central locking inoperative if a shared line is grounded
Audible click without latch movement

B0532.t: Left Rear Door Lock Actuator Circuit
B0532.d: Public J2012 lists do not include B0532. At GM it exists only as an undefined keyword in PIP5094, the general circuit-testing bulletin for GM cars and light trucks up to model year 2014. Its title refers to the lock motor in the left rear door. Rear doors carry an extra duty here: FMVSS 206 requires each rear side door to have a lock that, when engaged, also blocks the inside handle. The Saab 9-3 places this motor under the left rear door module and logs B3135 02 when the module input reads a short to ground during locking; after the fault clears the motor tries again. A failed rear actuator usually leaves that one door out of step with the rest of the car. Right rear: B0533.
c: Left rear lock motor worn or jammed
Broken wire in the left rear door boot
Latch linkage stiff from dirt or corrosion
Rear door or body module output faulty
s: Left rear door does not follow central locking
Vehicle cannot be fully secured from outside
Inside handle locking at that door may not work

B0533.t: Right Rear Door Lock Actuator Circuit
B0533.d: B0533 is absent from the J2012 lists that can be consulted publicly; GM's PIP5094 merely names it as a circuit keyword for 2014-and-earlier models without saying what it covers. The title assigns it to the lock motor of the right rear door. In the Saab 9-3 the right rear door module watches this motor and reports B3135 02 if its line is shorted to ground while the car is being locked or unlocked. Rear doors often add a second actuator: the 2011 Saab 9-5 drives a child security relay feeding both rear latches and stores B3930 02 when that circuit is grounded, which also takes the power locks out of service. Separating such a child-lock fault from the main lock motor is the first diagnostic step. Left rear: B0532.
c: Right rear lock motor worn or jammed
Electric child lock motor or its wiring shorted
Broken wire in the right rear door boot
Rear door or body module output faulty
s: Right rear door stays locked or unlocked
Electric child lock at the rear may not engage
Power locks inoperative if a shared rear circuit is grounded

B0540.d: Neither the public J2012 lists nor any accessible maker document define B0540, so the code is unverified. The title concerns the circuit of the switch that signals the driver door is not fully shut. The GM-era Saab 9-3 tracks this input in the body control module as B2976: subtype 02 when the line sits below 2.9 V (short to ground), 05 above 10.2 V (open or short to battery), checked with ignition on or while the alarm is armed, and the driver gets a display message. In Ford's US6133827A each ajar switch is open with the door closed and grounds the input when it opens; a failed switch can keep the courtesy lamp burning. The door-open switch itself is B0510.
c: Ajar switch in the latch or door frame stuck or corroded
Switch wire chafed to ground in the door hinge passage
Open wire or loose pin at the latch connector
s: Door-open warning shown although the driver door is shut
Interior light stays on and may drain the battery
Alarm or auto-lock behaves erratically

B0541.d: B0541 cannot be traced in public J2012 lists or published manufacturer data. By its title it covers the ajar switch circuit of the front passenger door. Saab's 9-3 monitors that switch as B2991 in the body control module using the driver-side thresholds: 02 for a grounded line under 2.9 V, 05 for an open line or battery short over 10.2 V. Many modern doors have no separate jamb plunger; ArvinMeritor's US20030182863A1 puts the ajar switch on the latch claw, where it changes state roughly halfway between the fully latched and the safety position, so a door that only reached the safety catch still reads as ajar. A latch replacement can therefore be the fix. Driver side: B0540.
c: Ajar switch inside the passenger door latch worn
Door only reaching the safety catch due to misaligned striker
Switch wire open or grounded in the hinge passage
s: Passenger door reported open while driving
Courtesy light does not react to the passenger door
Alarm cannot be armed or triggers falsely

B0560.d: B0560 is not part of the publicly available J2012 lists. GM does use the code: preliminary information PIT5404 for the 2015 Tahoe, Suburban, Yukon and Escalade tells technicians to check B0560 together with B1277, B127C and B127D while chasing active-noise-cancellation drone, but it gives no descriptor, so a seat meaning is not supported there. For the fore/aft seat motor of the title, Saab's 9-3 driver seat module uses B1770: subtype 04 when an output stays below 6 V (or below battery minus 0.7 V in the other direction), 0B above 40 A; memory recall is then disabled. Aisin's US8781691B2 counts Hall pulses from this motor to know the seat's fore-aft position.
c: Seat track blocked by objects or debris, overloading the motor
Fore/aft motor or its gear drive worn
Wiring under the seat pinched or connector loose
Relay or driver stage in the seat module faulty
s: Driver seat does not move forward or backward
Stored seat positions cannot be recalled
Seat stops after a short distance or moves in one direction only

B0561.d: B0561 has no entry in the accessible J2012 lists and no public manufacturer definition. The title refers to the motor that raises and lowers the driver seat; Chrysler's US4682088A splits this into front and rear cushion motors with about 1.5 in of travel. In the Saab 9-3 the height motor circuit is B1765 in the driver seat module: 04 for an open output, 0B for more than 40 A; the output is shut off and retried once per ignition cycle. GM's 2011 Saab 9-5 instead tests a shared 2.5 V bias point before any seat motor runs and sets B3920 if it stays above 2.78 V or under 1.47 V for a tenth of a second, blocking every motor on that power rail. A failed height axis therefore often stops other axes too.
c: Height motor or spindle gear seized
Motor wires pinched by the seat frame when lowering
Short on a motor line shared with other seat axes
s: Driver seat height cannot be adjusted
Other seat axes may stop working as well
Memory recall incomplete or blocked

B0562.d: B0562 is missing from public J2012 lists, and no manufacturer documents it. The title names the circuit of the backrest recline motor in the driver seat, which in Chrysler's US4682088A tilts the seatback through roughly 38 degrees. Saab's 9-3 reports this motor as B1785 in the driver seat module: 04 when an output voltage stays too low (open circuit), 0B when draw exceeds 40 A, for example with a jammed recliner gear; memory positions are then unavailable. GM's 2011 Saab 9-5 adds a Hall sensor inside the recline motor, fed with 12 V; its signal faults are logged separately as B1825 01/06. For the driver this usually means the backrest stays at its last angle.
c: Recliner gear jammed or worn, motor draws excess current
Recline motor open winding or brushes worn
Wiring between seat base and backrest broken
s: Driver backrest angle cannot be changed
Memory positions are not reached
Motor hums or clicks without backrest movement

B0570.d: B0570 is not found in any J2012 list open to the public, nor in published manufacturer material. Its title covers the fore/aft motor of the front passenger seat. The Saab 9-3 passenger seat module shows how such a circuit is policed: B1770 04 for an open output, 0B above 40 A, and 61 when a relay is stuck to ground, detected right after a soft start because the output exceeds 6 V. In the last case the seat no longer moves in the selected direction but still travels the other way; in all cases memory functions stop. As TI's note on memory seats explains, position is commonly tracked by Hall sensors on the motor whose revolutions are converted into seat travel. Driver side: B0560.
c: Objects under the passenger seat blocking the track
Seat module relay stuck, seat moves one way only
Fore/aft motor open circuit or worn brushes
Connector under the seat loose or corroded
s: Passenger seat does not slide forward or back
Seat moves only in one direction
Passenger seat memory or easy-entry function unavailable

B0580.d: B0580 is absent from publicly available J2012 lists and lacks a public manufacturer definition. The title describes an internal fault of the driver seat memory module. GM's 2011 Saab 9-5 shows what such a module checks in itself: B3920 42 when its calibration was never programmed, B3920 00 when the current leaving a motor rail differs from the returning current, plus voltage faults on the rail; the module then refuses those motors, and a stored code disappears once 40 ignition cycles pass without the fault. In the Saab 9-3, B3920 01 (output above 12 V while inactive) cancels all memory functions, while a stuck memory button (B2755 01) is merely ignored. Chrysler's US4682088A keeps stored positions in non-volatile memory.
c: Replacement module installed without calibration or setup
Internal electronic fault of the memory module
Liquid under the seat reaching the module
Low battery voltage or poor module ground
s: Memory buttons do not recall seat or mirror positions
Power seat partly or completely inoperative
Stored positions lost after power interruption

B0600.d: B0600 is not listed in the J2012 tables that are publicly accessible, and no manufacturer explains it. The title refers to the adjustment circuit of the driver's exterior mirror, which FMVSS 111 requires the driver to be able to tilt horizontally and vertically while seated. Saab's 9-3 monitors the two mirror motors in the driver door module: B1723 01 for the left/right output shorted to battery, B1724 02 for the up/down output shorted to ground, both evaluated only while the common motor line (B1600) is fault-free. The module then retries that axis four times per driving cycle. Memory mirrors also read the glass position; Britax's US6254242B1 uses a potentiometer linked directly to the glass for that.
c: Mirror adjustment motor seized by corrosion or ice
Mirror wires broken in the door hinge passage
Water in the mirror housing shorting the motor or sensor
s: Driver mirror does not move in one or both axes
Mirror memory position not restored
Rear view to the driver's side limited until adjusted by hand

B0601.d: B0601 is not covered by the public J2012 lists or by any accessible manufacturer documentation. By title it concerns the adjustment circuit of the passenger exterior mirror; FMVSS 111 only demands that it can be tilted, not remote control from the driving position, yet most are motorised. TI's application brief describes the usual layout: two small brushed motors below 1 A, driven by three half-bridges sharing one common leg. Saab's 9-3 passenger door module logs B1723 02 or B1724 01 for a shorted motor output. GM's 2011 Saab 9-5 drives this mirror from the passenger window switch; an internal fault there sets B154B 39 and suspends mirror movement while it persists, and the stored code clears after 40 cycles.
c: Passenger mirror motor seized or worn
Shared motor line shorted, affecting both axes
Wire break in the passenger door hinge passage
Passenger door module or window switch electronics faulty
s: Passenger mirror cannot be adjusted electrically
Reverse tilt-down or memory position of the mirror missing
Driver mirror usually keeps working

B0610.d: Public J2012 lists, OEM manuals and NHTSA bulletins all lack B0610; its use cannot be verified. The title describes the heating element behind the outside mirror glass. In the 2003–2012 Saab 9-3 each door module watches this load on its own: if the heater draws too much current when switched on, it stores B1640 02 and tries again only in the next drive cycle. Magna's US9481304B2 gives a typical pad of roughly 23 W (1.8 A at 13 V), often a PTC element, whose power is cut back while the car stands still. According to TI, a mirror module has to supervise both the folding motor and the heater load for faults. A dead heater only affects demisting; adjustment faults have their own codes (B0600, B0601).
c: Heating pad behind the mirror glass broken or shorted
Corroded plug at the mirror glass or in the mirror base
Wire chafed in the door hinge passage
Heater output of the door or body control module faulty
s: Outside mirror stays fogged or iced while the rear window clears
Mirror glass does not warm up when the heating is switched on
Code returns after every restart

B0700.d: No accessible J2012 list, public manufacturer manual or NHTSA bulletin contains B0700, so the code cannot be verified. Its title points to the circuit that drives a power sunroof open and shut. GM-era Saab cars report such faults under their own numbers: the 9-3 sunroof module stores B3661 0E when motor current is too high and B3664 04 for an open switch line, after which button presses are ignored; B3664 0A follows if the same switch position is seen for over 30 s. In the 2011 Saab 9-5 the module reads the switch as a resistor ladder and reports B3664 to the BCM via LIN. FMVSS 118 demands that a closing roof panel reverses before it squeezes with 100 N, which is why motor current is supervised at all. Position feedback: B0710.
c: Dirty or dry guide rails raising motor current
Sunroof switch or its wiring faulty
s: Sunroof does not move when the button is pressed
Roof stops or reverses on its own while closing
Motor hums without the panel moving

B0710.d: Nothing public confirms B0710: it is missing from J2012 extracts, workshop manuals and recall bulletins alike. The title refers to the position feedback of a power sunroof. Typical designs count pulses from a Hall sensor at the motor shaft: Nedap's NL1001829C2 derives panel position and speed from the pole changes, and Bosch's DE19815960A1 resets such a counter at a mechanical stop and uses it to separate sliding from tilting travel. Without valid pulses neither the anti-trap function required by FMVSS 118 nor one-touch travel can work. In the 2011 Saab 9-5 the motor unit reports an unlearned calibration as B3697 4B; the 9-3 disables express operation with B3696 0B when the motor is misfitted or the mechanism blocked. Drive circuit: B0700.
c: End positions not relearned after battery disconnection or motor replacement
Hall sensor or motor electronics faulty
Signal wire or connector at the motor damaged
s: One-touch opening or closing no longer works
Roof stops short of its end position or reverses unexpectedly
Roof can only be moved step by step until reinitialised

B0800.d: B0800 lacks any public evidence; no J2012 extract or service document mentions it. The title concerns the light switch that tells the body control module which lamps to energise. In the GM-developed Saab 9-3 the BCM checks switch positions 1 and 2 and logs B2585 05 or B2575 05 when the respective line rises above 10.2 V; dipped beam then stays on whatever the switch says. GM's 2011 Saab 9-5 compares its headlamp-on and headlamp-off inputs, stores B257A on an implausible combination and falls back to automatic headlamp control. FMVSS 108 requires every car to have a dipper switch and a high-beam telltale. Both fallbacks keep the lights usable, so the fault mostly shows as lost manual control rather than darkness.
c: Worn or corroded contacts in the light switch
Switch signal wire shorted to battery voltage
Loose or damaged plug behind the switch
Switch input of the body control module faulty
s: Dipped beam stays on regardless of switch position
Lights only work in automatic mode
Parking lights cannot be selected separately

B0810.d: Whether any carmaker sets B0810 is unknown – the number shows up in no J2012 excerpt and no service literature. The title covers the left dipped-beam output. The GM-era Saab 9-3 checks it in the front electrical centre under the number B2575: with the switch at dipped beam (position 2), a draw below 0.8 A sets B2575 04 (open) and one of 7.9–30 A sets B2575 0B, which may also mean a bulb of the wrong rating. With xenon lamps the ignition has to be on for 30 s before the test can run. HELLA explains why: the xenon ballast first fires the lamp with up to 30 kV and only then regulates it to a steady 35 W. A dark left dipped beam is a road-safety defect and should be repaired before driving at night. Right side: B0811.
c: Bulb of the wrong wattage fitted
Corroded headlamp plug or poor ground
Lamp output of the lighting or body module faulty
s: Left dipped beam dark, lamp failure message in the display
Reduced view of the left road edge at night; repair before driving in the dark
Light flickers or fails only after the lamp has warmed up

B0811.d: No J2012 excerpt or published service text uses B0811, which leaves the code undocumented. The title names the right dipped-beam circuit. In GM's 2011 Saab 9-5 the body control module powers low beam or daytime running lamps, while a separate headlamp control module stores B2699 (02 grounded, 04 open, 00 malfunction) when it sees a commanded lamp stay dark. The older 9-3 uses the same number B2699 for its right dipped beam and sets 04 below 0.8 A or 0B at 7.9–30 A, for instance after a bulb of the wrong rating has been fitted. FMVSS 108 sets the lower-beam requirements every car has to meet. A failed right dipped beam leaves the kerb side poorly lit at night and should be fixed quickly. Left side: B0810.
c: Right low-beam bulb or LED unit failed
Incorrect bulb rating after a replacement
Open or grounded supply wire to the headlamp
Headlamp or body control module output faulty
s: Right dipped beam or daytime running lamp stays dark
Lamp warning shown in the instrument cluster
Kerb side poorly lit at night; have it repaired promptly

B0820.d: B0820 is undocumented: neither open J2012 material nor factory or NHTSA papers list it. The title refers to the left main-beam output. In the second-generation Saab 9-3 the front electrical centre flags B2580 04 when the left main beam draws under 0.8 A while switched on and B2580 0B for 7.9 to 30 A. GM's 2011 Saab 9-5 works differently: both main beams are fed through one relay whose coil the body control module grounds, and if that control line is shorted to battery plus, B2580 01 is stored with both high beams off. HELLA points out that bi-xenon units form low and high beam in one module by moving a shutter, so a fault can also sit in that mechanism. FMVSS 108 requires an upper-beam indicator for the driver. Right side: B0821.
c: High-beam relay or its control line faulty
Shutter actuator in a bi-xenon module stuck
s: Left main beam stays dark when high beam is selected
Both main beams fail if the shared relay circuit is affected
Lamp failure message in the display

B0821.d: For B0821 there is no public trace in J2012 extracts, factory manuals or NHTSA files. The title describes the right main-beam circuit. Saab's 9-3 (type 9440) watches it under its own number B3866: open (04) when the lamp draws under 0.8 A with main beam on, overcurrent (0B) in the 7.9–30 A band; apart from the warning the module takes no action. Because high beam is only used on empty roads, a one-sided failure is often noticed late, mostly as a darker right verge. In GM's 2011 Saab 9-5, by contrast, a fault on the shared relay line (B2580 01) switches off both sides together. FMVSS 108 lists the beam switching device and the upper-beam indicator as required equipment. Left side: B0820.
c: Supply wire to the right headlamp open or shorted
Main-beam output of the lighting module faulty
s: Right main beam stays dark, left one works
Lamp warning in the display when high beam is switched on

B0830.d: Open J2012 sources do not include B0830, and no workshop or NHTSA text quotes it, so it remains unconfirmed. The title covers the left front indicator. The GM-developed Saab 9-3 monitors this lamp as B0530 in its front electrical centre: a draw above 6 A for longer than 6 ms counts as a short to ground and the output is switched off, while less than 50 mA counts as an open circuit. FMVSS 108 (S9.3.6) requires that a failed turn lamp becomes visible to the driver through the pilot indicator, as steady light, no light or a clearly changed flash rate. HELLA advises checking the bulb, corrosion in the holder, the fuse and the plug before suspecting electronics. A dead front indicator hides turning intentions from oncoming traffic. Other corners: B0831, B0840, B0841.
c: Corroded bulb holder or plug in the headlamp housing
Supply wire shorted to ground, output shut off
Indicator output of the electrical centre faulty
s: Left front indicator dark, warning in the display
Pilot light stays steady or flashes noticeably faster
Turning intention not visible to oncoming traffic; repair promptly

B0831.d: B0831 has no published definition; J2012 extracts, factory literature and NHTSA records are silent on it. Its title names the right front indicator circuit. In the GM-era Saab 9-3 this lamp is checked as B0525 by the front electrical centre, with the same limits as on the left: under 50 mA means open (04), while over 6 A lasting beyond 6 ms is read as a short to ground (02) and cuts the output. The same number B0525 is reused by the rear centre for the right rear lamp, so the module reporting the code matters. FMVSS 108 makes every car carry a flasher, a pilot indicator and a hazard warning system. HELLA lists defective bulbs, corroded contacts and damaged plugs as the common culprits. Left front: B0830; right rear: B0841.
c: Water in the lamp housing corroding the contacts
Wire damaged after front-end repair or impact
s: Right front indicator dark when signalling right
Changed flash rate or steady pilot light in the cluster
Hazard lights incomplete on the right front corner

B0840.d: Neither J2012 extracts nor any OEM or NHTSA publication name B0840; its use is unproven. The title concerns the left rear indicator. In the 2003–2012 Saab 9-3 the rear electrical centre supervises this lamp under the number B0530: an open lamp (04) or a short to ground (02) shows up as a warning message and the remaining indicators flashing at double speed, which is exactly the pilot-indicator behaviour FMVSS 108 permits for a failed turn lamp. HELLA notes that modern rear lamps are driven by body or lighting control units and may consist of LED segments, so diagnosis should include fault codes, connectors and the supply to the lamp unit. A failed rear indicator hides lane changes from following traffic. Right rear: B0841.
c: Rear indicator bulb or LED segment failed
Corroded plug or bulb carrier in the rear lamp
Wire break in the boot lid or tailgate harness
s: Indicators flash at double speed when signalling left
Left rear indicator dark, warning message shown
Lane changes not visible to following traffic; repair promptly

B0841.d: No public record of B0841 exists in J2012 lists, OEM manuals or bulletins. The title refers to the right rear indicator circuit. The second-generation Saab 9-3 logs this lamp in its rear electrical centre as B0525: under 50 mA is treated as open (04), more than 6 A for over 6 ms as a short to ground (02), after which the output is switched off. In both cases the driver sees a message and a doubled flash rate. FMVSS 108 accepts such a change in flash rate as the required failure indication. HELLA recommends checking lamp, holder and plug for corrosion and, on PWM-driven lamps, checking the PWM signal on a scope or scan tool. A dark right rear indicator means turns and lane changes go unannounced to following traffic. Left rear: B0840.
c: Right rear indicator bulb burnt out
Corroded contacts in the bulb holder
Pinched wire shorting to body ground
Lamp driver in the rear module faulty
s: Indicators flash at double speed when signalling right
Right rear indicator does not light, message in the display

B0850.d: B0850 cannot be confirmed from any open source – J2012 tables, OEM documentation and NHTSA bulletins omit it. The title covers the left stop lamp. In Saab's 9-3 (type 9440) the rear electrical centre checks it while braking under its own number B3445: below 50 mA it records an open circuit (04), and once current tops 6 A for over 6 ms a short to ground (02), shutting the output down. The third, high-level brake light is logged separately there (B3884). FMVSS 108 makes stop lamps mandatory and defines the high-mounted lamp as a steady stop warning visible through other vehicles. HELLA lists bulbs, holders, fuses and plug connections as the first checks. A missing brake light weakens the warning to following drivers and should be repaired at once. Right side: B0851.
c: Left stop-lamp bulb or filament failed
Corroded bulb holder in the tail lamp
Open or grounded wire to the left tail lamp
Stop-lamp output of the rear module faulty
s: Left brake light stays dark when braking, warning shown
Weaker warning to following traffic; repair before further driving
Tail light on the same side may also be affected with combined bulbs

B0851.d: Published J2012 tables skip B0851, and service literature and NHTSA filings never cite it either. The title names the right stop-lamp circuit. The GM-developed Saab 9-3 tests this lamp whenever the brake light is on and stores B3878 04 once the right lamp draws less than 50 mA; the high-mounted lamp is judged separately under B3884 with a lower limit of 20 mA. If both sides and the third lamp go dark together, the cause usually lies upstream, at the brake light switch or a shared fuse, not in one lamp circuit. For today's networked rear lamps HELLA names failed LED segments and faulty plugs as typical findings. FMVSS 108 requires working stop lamps on every car. Repair without delay; left side: B0850.
c: Right stop-lamp bulb or LED segment failed
Loose or corroded plug at the right tail lamp
Wire to the right tail lamp broken
Lamp driver in the rear module faulty
s: Right brake light dark while the left one and the third lamp work
Brake light warning in the display
Reduced braking signal to following drivers; repair at once

B0860.d: B0860 is not traceable in public J2012 extracts, and no manufacturer or regulator text refers to it. The title describes the lamp lighting the rear number plate. GM's 2011 Saab 9-5 switches it through the body control module whenever parking or dipped lights are selected, logging B3883 02 for a grounded and B3883 04 for an open feed. The older Saab 9-3 uses the same number in its rear electrical centre with stated limits: an open circuit below 20 mA, a short once over 3.5 A flows for longer than 10 ms, which also cuts the output. FMVSS 108 defines the licence plate lamp and requires it on every car. A dark plate light is not a driving hazard, but it is a roadworthiness defect that police checks can pick up.
c: Water in the lamp housing corroding contacts
Wire break in the boot lid hinge area
Lamp output of the body or rear module faulty
s: Number plate not illuminated with lights on
Lamp warning in the display
Plate lamp stays on permanently in some short-circuit cases

B0900.d: Open J2012 material, factory manuals and NHTSA bulletins contain no entry for B0900, so it is unconfirmed. The title concerns the windscreen wiper motor circuit. GM-era Saab models diagnose it at the relays: the 9-3 sets B3874 06 or B3875 06 when the low- or high-speed relay output stays below 6 V, so the wipers stop, run constantly or only at high speed. GM's 2011 Saab 9-5 logs B3715 and B3875 for the relay control lines and B371A when the park-switch signal does not match the switch position. FMVSS 104 asks for two or more speeds: a fast one with 45 or more wipes a minute and a slower one with 20 or more, separated by 15 or more. Bosch supplies brushless and reversing wiper drives; TI names position control with stall detection as a design requirement. Rear: B0910.
c: Wiper relay sticking or with burnt contacts
Wiper motor worn or park switch faulty
Damaged wiring in the scuttle area
s: Wipers do not run, run continuously or only at one speed
Wipers stop outside the park position
Poor visibility in rain; do not drive in wet weather until repaired

B0910.d: A public definition of B0910 is lacking in J2012 extracts as well as in OEM and NHTSA documents. The title refers to the rear window wiper motor circuit. On the second-generation Saab 9-3 the rear electrical centre drives it through a relay and stores B3720: 01 if more than 6 V sits on the output during activation, so the wiper does not work, and 06 if over 6 V is present with the wiper off, where a short to ground makes the wiper run constantly and an open line stops it. In Bosch's rear wiper a single arm is driven directly by a compact drive unit. TI names stall detection and low losses as key requirements for any wiper drive. Unlike the front wiper (B0900) no safety standard prescribes it, so failure is a comfort and visibility issue.
c: Wire break in the tailgate hinge harness
Rear wiper motor or spindle seized by corrosion
s: Rear wiper does not run when switched on
Rear wiper keeps running after switching off

B0920.d: B0920 has no verifiable source: it is absent from J2012 excerpts and from all published service information. The title covers the washer fluid pump circuit. GM's 2011 Saab 9-5 lets the body control module start the pump together with low-speed wiping as soon as washing is requested; with a supply of 9 to 16 V it watches the relay control line, stores B3873 02 on a short to ground and suspends washing. Headlamp washing there is a separate circuit (B3810) and only runs with low or high beam on, then pauses for 4 wash cycles or 48 hours. The 9-3 sets B3873 06 below 6 V on its relay output. FMVSS 104 requires a windscreen washing system on passenger cars, and HELLA describes centrifugal pumps in the reservoir for such systems. Wipers: B0900, B0910.
c: Washer pump motor seized, often after running dry or freezing
Corroded plug at the pump in the wheel arch
Washer relay or its control line faulty
Relay driver in the body control module faulty
s: No washer fluid sprays when the wash switch is used
Washer pump runs continuously
Headlamp washers inoperative as well on shared circuits

B0950.d: None of the accessible J2012 lists, OEM manuals or NHTSA bulletins mention B0950; it is therefore unverified. The title refers to the electrically heated rear window. GM-era Saab cars monitor this heater under other numbers: in the 2011 Saab 9-5 the climate control module energises the relay coil that switches battery voltage to the grid, and faults on that control line are stored as B0283. The 9-3 checks the relay output in the rear electrical centre (B0283 06 below 6 V) and the indicator lamp in the button separately (B0969 02 above 1 A). A broken grid line or a loose tab on the glass usually disables only part of the heated area, while relay or supply faults stop it entirely. The main consequence is poor rear visibility in cold or damp weather.
c: Broken heater line or detached terminal tab on the glass
Wire break in the tailgate or boot lid harness
Climate or body control module output faulty
s: Rear window does not clear when the heater is switched on
Only some heater lines warm up
Indicator in the button does not light

B0960.t: Parking Assist Rear Sensor Right Middle Circuit
B0960.d: B0960 does not appear in the accessible J2012 lists; it is documented by GM and the GM-era Saab models as the right middle rear parking sensor. The 2011 Saab 9-5 and 9-4X list B0960 01 (short to battery), 06 (low voltage or open), 08 (invalid signal), 21 (incorrect period) and 3A (wrong part fitted); B0958, B0959 and B0961 cover the other rear sensors. The older 9-3 uses B0960 for its right centre distance sensor and checks it with reverse gear engaged and more than 9 V; on a fault the system stops measuring and mutes the warning tones. Bosch explains that such sensors emit short ultrasonic pulses and pass the echoes to a central unit, measuring up to 5.5 m. The horn relay, by contrast, is monitored by the same makers as B2750.
c: Sensor face dirty, iced or covered
Ultrasonic sensor defective or wrong part fitted
Bumper harness damaged after a parking knock or repair
s: Parking assist switches off with a message when reversing
No warning tones although an obstacle is close
Obstacles behind the car must be checked visually until repaired

B0970.d: B0970 is not documented anywhere public, whether in J2012 extracts, workshop literature or NHTSA bulletins. The title covers the interior lighting circuit. The 2003–2012 Saab 9-3 supervises it through its BCM: B2556 02 when more than 10 A flows on the lamp feed, B2555 0F when the lamps are powered although they should be off, and B2610 02 when the dimmed PWM line drops below 2.0 V. GM's 2011 Saab 9-5 reports a grounded courtesy lamp feed as B2615 02, stops driving the lamps and clears the history entry after 100 fault-free ignition cycles. HELLA warns that fitting bulbs of higher wattage overheats lamps and surrounding trim. A constantly lit interior lamp can drain the battery overnight.
c: Door contact switch stuck, keeping the lamps on
Short in a roof or footwell lamp, often after bulb changes
Chafed wire in the headliner or A-pillar
Lamp output of the body control module faulty
s: Interior lights stay off when a door is opened
Interior lights stay on permanently
Battery flat after the car has stood overnight

B0980.d: Public sources give no meaning for B0980: J2012 extracts and OEM or NHTSA documents leave it out. The title concerns the signal by which the ignition switch reports its run and start positions. GM-era Saab vehicles use other numbers for this: the 9-3 column module sets B1440 0F when the +15 supply from the ignition switch module is open and B1368 00 when that input is shorted to battery; in both cases it blocks cranking and deactivates the steering lock. GM's 2011 Saab 9-5 energises an ignition 1 relay in run and start and stores B144A 02 for a grounded control line, giving a no-start or an engine that keeps running after the key is removed. FMVSS 114 defines the key-operated starting system and its anti-theft requirements.
c: Worn contacts in the ignition switch
Open or shorted ignition feed wire
Ignition relay or its control line faulty
Low battery voltage causing implausible signals
s: Engine does not crank although the key is turned
Ignition cannot be switched off or key cannot be removed
Steering lock or electrical consumers behave erratically

B0990.d: For B0990 no public evidence exists, be it in J2012 lists or in carmaker or NHTSA papers. The title describes a self-detected failure inside the body control module. GM-era Saab models report this as B1000 or B101D: on the 2011 Saab 9-5 the module runs its internal test at every power-up, refuses further inputs on a fault and clears a history entry after 50 fault-free ignition cycles; a module should only be replaced if the code is current. The 9-3 BCM stores B1000 37 for an internal timeout, and its column module logs B3985 when the immobiliser code cannot be written into the BCM. TI lists open-load and short detection and fail-safe behaviour among the core BCM functions. Rule out supply and ground faults before replacing it.
c: Poor supply voltage or ground at the module
Moisture or corrosion inside the module
Internal electronic failure of the module
s: Several body functions fail at once, such as lights, locks or wipers
Car will not start if the immobiliser data cannot be read
Code stored only as history without any noticeable effect

C0001.d: C0001 concerns the first traction control valve of hydraulic channel A, usually one of the two brake circuits in the ABS/ESC modulator. To brake a spinning drive wheel without driver input, a TCS-capable modulator carries an extra isolation valve and priming valve per circuit: the normally open isolation valve closes off the master cylinder, while the normally closed priming valve opens so the pump can draw fluid and build pressure. Which of the two a maker numbers as valve 1 is not published. The module watches the coil circuit and whether pressure follows the command; a fault switches off traction and usually stability control and lights the warning lamp, while ordinary braking remains. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
c: Corroded or chafed wiring to the modulator
s: ABS warning lamp on
Traction and stability control disabled
Normal braking retained without ABS

C0002.d: C0002 points to the second traction control valve of channel A. Together with valve 1 it forms the valve pair a TCS modulator adds to each brake circuit: an isolation valve that cuts the circuit off from the master cylinder and a priming valve that opens the path from the master cylinder to the return pump, so pressure can rise at a driven wheel while the pedal is released. The public record does not say which of the pair J2012 calls valve 2. The module flags an open or shorted coil, an implausible current or a pressure response that does not match the command. Traction and stability control are switched off and the ABS or ESC lamp comes on; foundation braking still works. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
c: Corroded or chafed wiring to the modulator
s: ABS warning lamp on
Traction and stability control disabled
Normal braking retained without ABS

C0003.d: C0003 is the counterpart of C0001 in channel B, the second brake circuit of the modulator. A pump patent for such units shows the layout plainly: two normally open isolation valves and two normally closed priming valves, one of each per circuit, operated by the control unit alongside the apply and release valves when traction control intervenes. Valve 1 of channel B therefore matches the first valve of the other circuit; the published sources do not fix which function carries the number. A coil open or short, a current outside the expected window or a pressure that fails to follow the command sets the code. Traction and stability control are disabled and the warning lamp lights, while ordinary braking is unaffected. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
c: Corroded or chafed wiring to the modulator
s: ABS warning lamp on
Traction and stability control disabled
Normal braking retained without ABS

C0004.d: C0004 completes the set with the second traction control valve of channel B. During an intervention the module closes the isolation valve and opens the priming valve of the circuit concerned so the pump can supply pressure to a wheel that is spinning; afterwards both return to rest so the driver's pedal again acts through the master cylinder. A valve that sticks or a coil that fails can therefore leave the pump without supply or keep the circuit isolated from the pedal, which is why the module reacts at once. It sets the code for an electrical fault or an implausible pressure response, switches off traction and stability control and lights the warning lamp. Base braking stays available. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
c: Corroded or chafed wiring to the modulator
s: ABS warning lamp on
Traction and stability control disabled
Normal braking retained without ABS

C0010.d: Covers the left front inlet (apply) solenoid valve of the ABS hydraulic modulator. During ABS, traction or stability control the module closes this valve to isolate the left front brake circuit from the master cylinder and hold wheel pressure, then opens it to let pressure back in. The module checks the coil for opens, shorts and out-of-range resistance and monitors valve response. GM documents code C0010 (sub-type .5A) setting in the electronic brake control module of 2018-2019 Equinox, Terrain, Envision and Canyon, where it could store falsely and was under engineering review. A fault disables ABS and related functions; the red brake or amber ABS lamp illuminates and conventional braking remains.
c: Inlet valve coil open or shorted
Brake control module fault or false setting
s: ABS warning lamp on
ABS and stability control disabled
Normal braking retained

C0011.d: Covers the left front outlet (release) solenoid valve of the ABS hydraulic modulator. This valve opens to dump brake fluid from the left front caliper into the low-pressure accumulator so the module can reduce wheel pressure during an ABS or stability event, then closes to allow reapply. The control module monitors the coil for opens, shorts to power or ground and resistance outside the normal range. It is the release counterpart to the left front inlet valve C0010. A confirmed fault disables ABS, traction and stability control and lights the ABS indicator while leaving base braking functional. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; NHTSA's brake safety study names the release valve the module opens to lower wheel pressure, and a pump patent shows it as a normally closed valve beside each apply valve.
c: Outlet valve coil open or shorted
s: ABS warning lamp on
ABS and stability control disabled
Normal braking retained

C0012.t: Left Front Hydraulic Release Too Long
C0012.d: Set when the ABS modulator cannot release pressure at the left front wheel within the expected time during a control cycle. Rather than a pure electrical fault it is a performance or plausibility code: after the module commands the left front outlet valve to dump pressure, it expects wheel speed to recover and pressure to fall; if the release takes longer than the calibrated limit the module concludes the hydraulic path is restricted, the valve is sticking or the pump/accumulator cannot accept fluid. ABS and stability control are disabled and the ABS lamp is set. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. NHTSA describes ABS control as a hold, release and reapply cycle, and a patent explains that a well-filled low-pressure accumulator can keep the outlet valves from lowering pressure as demanded.
c: Restricted hydraulic path or contaminated fluid
Pump or accumulator cannot accept fluid
s: ABS warning lamp on
ABS and stability control disabled
Extended or firm pedal during hard braking

C0014.d: Covers the right front inlet (apply) solenoid valve of the ABS hydraulic modulator, the mirror of C0010 on the right front corner. The module closes this valve to isolate the right front brake circuit and hold wheel pressure during ABS, traction or stability control, then opens it to reapply pressure from the master cylinder or pump. It monitors the coil for opens, shorts to supply or ground and resistance outside the calibrated window. A confirmed electrical fault disables ABS and the stability functions and turns on the ABS warning lamp, with conventional foundation braking unaffected. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; NHTSA's safety study of hydraulic ABS/ESC brakes describes the hold valve used per wheel, and a pump patent shows it as a normally open apply valve.
c: Inlet valve coil open or shorted
s: ABS warning lamp on
ABS and stability control disabled
Normal braking retained

C0015.d: Covers the right front outlet (release) solenoid valve of the ABS hydraulic modulator, the release counterpart to inlet valve C0014. It opens to dump brake fluid from the right front caliper into the low-pressure accumulator so wheel pressure can fall during an ABS or stability cycle, then closes for reapply. The module monitors the coil circuit for opens, shorts and out-of-range resistance and checks valve response. A confirmed fault disables ABS, traction and stability control and sets the ABS warning lamp while base hydraulic braking stays available. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the inlet/outlet pair per wheel is described in NHTSA's brake safety study and in a pump patent for ABS/ESC units.
c: Outlet valve coil open or shorted
s: ABS warning lamp on
ABS and stability control disabled
Normal braking retained

C0016.t: Right Front Hydraulic Release Too Long
C0016.d: Set when the ABS modulator cannot release pressure at the right front wheel within the expected time during a control cycle, the right front equivalent of C0012. After commanding the right front outlet valve to dump pressure the module expects wheel speed to recover and line pressure to fall; if the release exceeds the calibrated time limit it infers a sticking valve, a restricted hydraulic path or an accumulator/pump that cannot take fluid. The module disables ABS and stability control and sets the ABS warning lamp. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. A patent on ABS low-pressure accumulators shows why release can stall: once the accumulator pressure is high, fluid no longer leaves the wheel through the outlet valve as requested.
c: Restricted hydraulic path or contaminated fluid
Pump or accumulator cannot accept fluid
s: ABS warning lamp on
ABS and stability control disabled
Extended or firm pedal during hard braking

C0018.d: Covers the left rear inlet (apply) solenoid valve of the ABS hydraulic modulator, the rear-axle counterpart of C0010. The module closes this valve to isolate the left rear brake circuit and hold wheel pressure during ABS, traction or stability control, then opens it to reapply pressure. On many vehicles the rear channel also carries electronic brake-force distribution. The module monitors the coil for opens, shorts to supply or ground and resistance outside the calibrated range. A confirmed electrical fault disables ABS and the stability functions and lights the ABS warning lamp while leaving base braking intact. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; NHTSA's brake safety study and a pump patent describe the per-wheel apply valve.
c: Inlet valve coil open or shorted
s: ABS warning lamp on
ABS and stability control disabled
Normal braking retained

C0019.d: Covers the left rear outlet (release) solenoid valve of the ABS hydraulic modulator, the release counterpart to inlet valve C0018. It opens to dump brake fluid from the left rear caliper or wheel cylinder into the low-pressure accumulator so pressure can fall during an ABS or stability cycle, then closes for reapply. The module monitors the coil circuit for opens, shorts and out-of-range resistance and verifies valve response. A confirmed fault disables ABS, traction and stability control and sets the ABS warning lamp while base hydraulic braking remains. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the release valve per wheel appears in NHTSA's brake safety study and, normally closed, in a pump patent.
c: Outlet valve coil open or shorted
s: ABS warning lamp on
ABS and stability control disabled
Normal braking retained

C001A.t: Left Rear Hydraulic Release Too Long
C001A.d: Set when the ABS modulator cannot release pressure at the left rear wheel within the expected time during a control cycle, the left rear equivalent of C0012 and C0016. After the module commands the left rear outlet valve to dump pressure it expects wheel speed to recover and line pressure to fall; a release that exceeds the calibrated time limit indicates a sticking valve, a restricted hydraulic path or an accumulator or pump unable to accept fluid. ABS and stability control are disabled and the ABS warning lamp is set. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; NHTSA's study covers the release step of the ABS cycle, and a patent shows how a full low-pressure accumulator slows it.
c: Restricted hydraulic path or contaminated fluid
Pump or accumulator cannot accept fluid
s: ABS warning lamp on
ABS and stability control disabled
Extended or firm pedal during hard braking

C001C.d: Covers the right rear inlet (apply) solenoid valve of the ABS hydraulic modulator, the right rear counterpart of C0010 and C0018. The module closes this valve to isolate the right rear brake circuit and hold wheel pressure during ABS, traction or stability control, then opens it to reapply pressure; on the rear axle the same channel often supports electronic brake-force distribution. It monitors the coil for opens, shorts to supply or ground and resistance outside the calibrated range. A confirmed electrical fault disables ABS and stability control and lights the ABS warning lamp while base braking remains. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the apply valve per wheel is described by NHTSA and in a pump patent.
c: Inlet valve coil open or shorted
s: ABS warning lamp on
ABS and stability control disabled
Normal braking retained

C001D.d: Covers the right rear outlet (release) solenoid valve of the ABS hydraulic modulator, the release counterpart to inlet valve C001C. It opens to dump brake fluid from the right rear caliper or wheel cylinder into the low-pressure accumulator so pressure can fall during an ABS or stability cycle, then closes for reapply. The module monitors the coil circuit for opens, shorts and out-of-range resistance and checks valve response. A confirmed fault disables ABS, traction and stability control and sets the ABS warning lamp while base hydraulic braking remains available. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; NHTSA's brake study and a pump patent describe the release valve that sits beside each apply valve.
c: Outlet valve coil open or shorted
s: ABS warning lamp on
ABS and stability control disabled
Normal braking retained

C001E.t: Right Rear Hydraulic Release Too Long
C001E.d: Set when the ABS modulator cannot release pressure at the right rear wheel within the expected time during a control cycle, completing the per-wheel set with C0012, C0016 and C001A. After commanding the right rear outlet valve to dump pressure the module expects wheel speed to recover and line pressure to fall; a release longer than the calibrated limit points to a sticking valve, a restricted hydraulic path or an accumulator or pump that cannot accept fluid. ABS and stability control are disabled and the ABS warning lamp is set. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the release phase is covered by NHTSA's brake study, the accumulator limit by a patent on low-pressure accumulators.
c: Restricted hydraulic path or contaminated fluid
Pump or accumulator cannot accept fluid
s: ABS warning lamp on
ABS and stability control disabled
Extended or firm pedal during hard braking

C0020.d: Covers the electric pump (return) motor of the ABS hydraulic unit and its control circuit. The motor drives the piston pump that returns brake fluid from the low-pressure accumulators and builds pressure for ABS, traction and stability interventions. The control module commands the motor and monitors the drive circuit and motor-run feedback; it sets the code for an open or shorted motor circuit, a seized motor or a run signal that does not match the command. RAM assigns code C0020-01 to a general electrical failure of the ABS pump-motor control on its 2500 and 3500 trucks. A fault disables ABS and the stability functions; the ABS lamp illuminates and base braking remains.
c: Pump motor seized or windings failed
Open or shorted motor supply or ground
s: ABS warning lamp on
ABS, traction and stability control disabled
No pump noise during self-test

C0021.d: A performance code for the power brake booster, set when the booster does not deliver the expected level of assist or does not respond to the control module as commanded. On vehicles with an electronic or vacuum booster the module compares driver pedal demand, measured boost and the resulting brake pressure, and stores the code when assist is weak, slow or inconsistent. GM documents C0021 setting on 2019-2020 Silverado and Sierra together with reduced engine power and service brake messages, in some cases after a module programming event with low battery voltage. The driver may feel a hard pedal and longer stopping distance; a warning message and the brake or ABS lamp appear.
c: Booster worn or not holding vacuum/pressure
Low battery voltage during module programming
Faulty boost or pressure sensor input
s: Hard brake pedal and reduced assist
Service brake or reduced power message
ABS or brake warning lamp on

C0022.d: C0022 covers the solenoid valve of an electronically controllable brake booster. Patent literature shows a vacuum booster that works in two ways: by the driver's pedal in normal braking, and through a solenoid valve that changes the pressure in an auxiliary chamber so the booster applies the brakes without the pedal. NHTSA's brake study describes the conventional vacuum booster, which this valve extends, sitting ahead of the master cylinder. The module checks the coil circuit for opens, shorts and resistance out of range and whether assist follows the command. A fault removes automatic braking and can change pedal effort; the brake or ABS lamp lights. No manufacturer documents this code publicly with a retrievable bulletin.
s: Changed brake pedal effort or feel
Noise from the brake system
ABS or brake warning lamp on

C0023.d: Covers the stop lamp (brake light) control circuit as driven or monitored by the brake or stability control module. Modern ABS/ESC systems can command the stop lamps during autonomous braking events such as traction control, stability control and automatic emergency braking, independent of the driver pressing the pedal, and they monitor the circuit for opens, shorts and lamp-output disagreement. The code is stored when the commanded stop lamp state does not match the measured output or the circuit is faulty. Effects range from stop lamps that stay on or off to disabled driver-assist functions that rely on brake-light actuation. Mazda stores C0023:14 as a brake light circuit malfunction and names a retrofitted brake light flasher as one trigger (service alert SA-041-26). NHTSA's brake study lists brake lights on/off as a CHB output.
c: Open or shorted stop lamp wiring
s: Stop lamps stay on or do not light
Stability or driver-assist functions disabled
ABS or stability warning lamp on

C0024.t: Brake Pedal Feedback Pressure Solenoid Circuit
C0024.d: Covers the solenoid that generates brake pedal feedback pressure in an electronic or brake-by-wire braking system. Because the driver is hydraulically decoupled during controlled braking, a pedal-feel simulator uses this solenoid to build a controlled counter-pressure so the pedal feels natural. The module monitors the coil circuit for opens, shorts and out-of-range resistance and checks that feedback pressure tracks the command. GM documents C0024 on 2019-2020 Cadillac XT6, Chevrolet Blazer and GMC Acadia with reduced brake assist, warning messages in the driver display and an altered pedal feel. A fault alters pedal feel and may reduce controlled assist; the brake or ABS warning lamp is set.
s: Changed or abnormal pedal feel
Loss of brake assist, driver messages
ABS or brake warning lamp on

C0025.t: Brake Pedal Feedback Pressure Sensor Circuit
C0025.d: C0025 covers the pressure sensor on the pedal feedback side of a decoupled or brake-by-wire system, the measuring partner of the feedback valve C0024. In such systems the pedal pushes fluid into a pedal feel simulator via a simulator valve the module can open or close, while separate sensors read pressure in the simulator circuit and in the wheel circuit. A patent for this layout reads the driver's request from a pressure sensor on the master cylinder side and describes a standstill self-test that opens the simulator valve and watches the pressure rise. The module sets C0025 for a signal out of range, an open or short, or a value that does not fit pedal travel. Pedal feel changes, assist may drop to a mechanical fallback, and the brake or ABS lamp lights. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
c: Feedback pressure sensor out of range
s: Changed or abnormal pedal feel
Loss of brake assist, driver messages
ABS or brake warning lamp on

C0030.d: Covers the left front tone wheel (reluctor or encoder ring) that the wheel speed sensor reads to measure rotation. This is a signal-plausibility code rather than a sensor circuit fault: the module sees an erratic, noisy or intermittent speed signal consistent with a damaged, contaminated or loose tone ring rather than a sensor electrical failure. Volvo documents BCM-C0030 on the S80 together with a grinding noise at the wheel hub when the hub has shifted within the steering knuckle. A fault disables ABS, traction and stability control and lights the ABS warning lamp while base braking remains.
s: ABS warning lamp on
ABS and stability control disabled
Grinding noise from wheel hub

C0031.d: Covers the left front wheel speed sensor and its circuit. The sensor, usually an active Hall-effect type, reports wheel rotation to the ABS/ESC module for anti-lock, traction and stability control and for speed-dependent functions. The module monitors the circuit for opens, shorts to power or ground, a signal outside the valid range and a missing signal while the vehicle is moving. Jaguar documents C0031 on the F-Pace and XE with several fault sub-types (C0031-2F, -29, -31, -62) while the ABS warning lamp is lit. A fault disables ABS, traction and stability control and lights the ABS warning lamp while base braking remains.
c: Open, shorted or chafed sensor wiring
s: ABS warning lamp on
ABS and stability control disabled
Speedometer may read erratically

C0032.t: Left Front Wheel Speed Sensor Supply
C0032.d: Covers the supply circuit that powers the left front active wheel speed sensor. Active sensors need a regulated voltage from the ABS/ESC module; this code is set when that supply is open, shorted to ground or to another voltage, or is outside the regulated range so the sensor cannot report a valid signal. It is distinct from the sensor-signal code C0031 in that the fault is on the feed rather than in the sensor element or its output. A fault disables ABS, traction and stability control for that corner and lights the ABS warning lamp while base braking remains. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; NHTSA reproduces the J2012 wheel speed sensor codes, with C0032 as left front supply, in its EPS safety report.
c: Open or shorted sensor supply wire
Corroded connector on the supply side
s: ABS warning lamp on
ABS and stability control disabled
No wheel speed signal from this corner

C0033.d: Covers the right front tone wheel (reluctor or encoder ring) read by the right front wheel speed sensor, the mirror of C0030. It is a signal-plausibility code: the module sees an erratic, noisy or intermittent speed signal consistent with a damaged, contaminated or loose tone ring rather than a sensor electrical failure. Volvo documents BCM-C0033 on the S80 together with a grinding noise at the wheel hub caused by a hub that has shifted within the steering knuckle. A fault disables ABS, traction and stability control and lights the ABS warning lamp while base braking remains available.
s: ABS warning lamp on
ABS and stability control disabled
Grinding noise from wheel hub

C0034.d: Covers the right front wheel speed sensor and its circuit, the mirror of C0031. The active sensor reports wheel rotation to the ABS/ESC module for anti-lock, traction and stability control and speed-dependent functions. The module monitors the circuit for opens, shorts to power or ground, a signal outside the valid range and a missing signal while the vehicle is moving. Jaguar documents C0034 on the F-Pace and XE with several fault sub-types (C0034-2F, -29, -41) alongside C0031 while the ABS warning lamp is lit. A fault disables ABS, traction and stability control and lights the ABS warning lamp while base braking remains.
c: Open, shorted or chafed sensor wiring
s: ABS warning lamp on
ABS and stability control disabled
Speedometer may read erratically

C0035.t: Right Front Wheel Speed Sensor Supply
C0035.d: C0035 reports a fault in the feed that powers the right front active wheel speed sensor, the right-hand partner of C0032. The ABS/ESC module supplies the sensor with a regulated voltage; an open feed, a short to ground or to another voltage, or a supply outside its window leaves the sensor unable to send a speed signal. NHTSA's EPS safety report lists C0035 with this meaning in its table of J2012 wheel speed codes. Caution with older GM vehicles: GM numbers its four wheel speed sensor circuits C0035 to C0050 in its own scheme (bulletin 16-NA-248, PIE0456), so a GM C0035 is a sensor circuit fault rather than a supply fault. ABS, traction and stability control switch off and the ABS lamp lights; normal braking remains.
