AAM's EcoTrac, introduced on the 2014 Jeep Cherokee, separates the driveline at both the PTU and the rear module under command of its own control unit. In an AAM patent a power-operated actuator, for example a solenoid, moves the PTU mode collar only after the rear clutch has brought the propshaft up to speed; a Linamar patent energises a PTU coil with brief pulses of about 3 to 4 A and tracks the sleeve with a Hall or linear sensor. C00A2 means the output stage feeding that actuator reports a fault, such as overcurrent, short, open load or overtemperature, the classes that automotive driver ICs like TI's DRV8873-Q1 flag. No manufacturer publishes a C00A2 case.
c: Short to ground or battery on the PTU actuator circuit
PTU actuator coil or motor open or internally shorted
Damaged output stage inside the driveline module
s: AWD unavailable, vehicle stays in front-wheel drive
AWD warning lamp or message

C00A3.t: Driveline Control Module Rear Differential Unit A Control Circuit Driver
C00A3.d: C00A3 points to the driver stage inside the driveline module that powers actuator A of the rear differential unit, not to the actuator itself. The module's own transistor monitoring reports something wrong at that output. A Mitsubishi Electric patent illustrates the principle on an electromagnetic clutch: a PWM high-side and a low-side transistor feed the coil, the filtered terminal voltages are checked with the selector in P or N, and if they deviate from normal both transistors are switched off so the clutch opens. Modern H-bridge drivers such as TI's DRV8873-Q1 separately flag overcurrent, short to battery or ground, open load and overtemperature. On hydraulically actuated twin-clutch units, a dedicated ECU drives solenoid valves instead. No manufacturer publishes a C00A3 case; actuator A's own codes are C0095 and C0096.
c: Short to ground or battery in the actuator A supply lines
Actuator A motor or coil drawing excessive current (binding, winding short)
Output stage in the module overheated or defective
s: Rear clutch released, AWD inactive
AWD warning in the instrument cluster

C00A4.t: Driveline Control Module Rear Differential Unit B Control Circuit Driver
C00A4.d: Where a rear unit carries a second actuator, for example the second clutch of a twin-clutch module that can drive each rear wheel on its own, the driveline module needs a second output stage, and C00A4 reports a fault in that one. If actuator B is a brushless motor, the stage is a three-phase bridge: automotive gate drivers such as TI's DRV8343-Q1 detect short to battery, short to ground, MOSFET overcurrent and gate driver faults, and offer an offline open-load and short check before the motor is switched on. BorgWarner's latest AWD coupling uses exactly such a brushless motor with integrated electronics. A driver fault on side B leaves actuator A usable, so some systems can keep partial AWD. No manufacturer publishes a C00A4 case; the actuator's own codes are C0097 and C0098.
c: Phase or supply line of actuator B shorted to ground or battery
Winding fault or blocked rotor in actuator B causing overcurrent
Failed output stage B in the module
s: AWD or torque vectoring warning
One rear clutch or locking function inactive

C00A5.t: Driveline Control Module Transfer Case Unit Control Circuit Driver
C00A5.d: C00A5 concerns the output stage in the driveline module that powers the transfer case actuator, typically a DC gearmotor that shifts range and mode or presses a multi-plate clutch. Bosch describes such a transfer case clutch driven by a DC motor with worm gear through an H-bridge, with motor speed, worm wheel position and motor current measured; Magna's shift patent regulates the gearmotor speed by PWM and switches to closed-loop position control near the end of travel. The code is set when the module sees a fault at its own driver, such as overcurrent, a short to ground or battery, an open load or thermal shutdown, the categories listed for H-bridge ICs like TI's DRV8873-Q1. The actuator itself is covered by C00A6. No manufacturer publishes a C00A5 case. The transfer case then usually holds its last state or drops to 2WD.
c: Shorted transfer case motor wiring or connector
Binding or worn transfer case motor causing overcurrent
Defective H-bridge in the driveline module
s: 4WD/AWD cannot be engaged or range shift refused
4WD service warning in the cluster

C00A6.d: C00A6 is the general code for the transfer case actuator, the motor unit that presses the transfer case clutch or moves its shift mechanism. Ford uses it with many failure-type suffixes. SSM 49669 covers 2020–2021 Explorer and Aviator AWD with C00A6:07, :18, :19, :4B, :66, :71, :74 or :99 and an AWD lamp, noting that the clutch actuator is not always at fault and that revised pinpoint tests should be followed. SSM 52152 links C00A6:71/:74/:99 with C00A7 and C00A8 codes on 2020–2023 Explorer/Aviator to a harness rubbing on a heat shield where it runs to the actuator motor. TSB 25-2373 ties C00A6 together with C0631 on 2020–2021 models built up to 30 August 2021 to the unit that decouples the front axle, which is swapped together with an updated intermediate shaft. Bosch describes this kind of transfer case clutch actuator in detail.
c: Harness to the actuator motor chafed on the underbody heat shield
Front axle disconnect actuator/intermediate shaft fault (Ford Explorer/Aviator)
Transfer case clutch actuator motor worn or seized
s: Wrench (powertrain malfunction) indicator or AWD lamp (Ford)
4WD Fault Service Required message
AWD function lost

C00A7.t: 4WD/AWD Transfer Case Unit Actuator Position Sensor A
C00A7.d: Position sensor A reports where the transfer case actuator, and thus the range or mode mechanism, currently stands. Magna patents a linear Hall sensor bolted from outside into the case, reading a stepped sector plate (four positions over about 60 degrees) or a plate on the range fork, with a duty-cycle output. Stellantis uses C00A7-13, circuit open: TSB 08-237-23 (2023 Ram 1500) and 08-239-23 (2023 Wagoneer models from a nine-day June 2023 build window, later superseded by 08-122-24) list it with C00A8-13 and other transfer case codes, an illuminated MIL and a 4WD Service light; the cause is a transfer case shift motor connector not fully seated, fixed by a push-pull-push check. Ford's SSM 52152 lists C00A7:11 and :13 on Explorer/Aviator, traced to a chafed harness at the actuator motor.
c: Transfer case shift motor connector not fully seated (Stellantis 2023)
Harness chafed where it routes to the actuator motor (Ford)
Position sensor A in the actuator failed
s: MIL on (Stellantis) or wrench indicator (Ford)
4WD Service light or 4WD Fault Service Required message
4WD modes cannot be selected

C00A8.t: 4WD/AWD Transfer Case Unit Actuator Position Sensor B
C00A8.d: C00A8 is the second position signal of the transfer case actuator. Whether B is a redundant copy of A or tracks a different part, the motor or the cam, is not published by any maker; BorgWarner, for example, puts a contact probe on the shift drum cam instead of the motor because a torsion spring sits in between, and reads five plateaus from 2WD high to 4WD low. Stellantis lists C00A8-13, circuit open, in TSB 08-237-23 and in 08-122-24, which replaced 08-239-23 for 2023 Wagoneer and Grand Wagoneer built 16 to 24 June 2023: the MIL must be on, and a loose shift motor connector is the cause, verified by pushing, pulling and pushing the plug again. Ford SSM 52152 names C00A8:11 and :13 on 2020–2023 Explorer/Aviator. Magna's Hall sensor patent shows a sensor that can be exchanged from outside.
c: Harness damage at the heat shield near the transfer case (Ford)
s: MIL illuminated (Stellantis), wrench indicator (Ford)
4WD Service light, four-wheel drive not available

C0110.d: C0110 does not appear in the accessible J2012 code tables; it is documented by General Motors, whose brake modules use it for the electric motor of the ABS return pump. In the Saab 9-5 (2010–2011) and 9-4X service data the motor sits in the brake pressure modulator valve while its relay is inside the EBCM; the module leaves the motor off during ordinary braking and runs it only for ABS, traction or stability intervention. The 9-5 logs symptom 06 after an open or grounded feed lasting 0.01 s, the 9-4X uses a 1.8 s window, and symptom 61 marks a seized or worn motor. ABS, TCS and ESC are then disabled for the ignition cycle with ABS and brake lamps lit. A GM bulletin for the 2014 Cadillac ELR also lists C0110.
c: Open or high-resistance pump motor supply or ground (fuse, connector, ground point)
Seized or worn pump motor in the modulator valve assembly
Faulty pump motor relay inside the brake control module
s: ABS and red brake warning lamps on
Traction and stability control indicator on, systems disabled
No ABS intervention on slippery surfaces

C0111.d: No accessible J2012 table, manufacturer index or NHTSA bulletin lists C0111, so the code cannot be traced to any published application. The title describes a plausibility monitor rather than a wiring fault: the controller notices that an anti-lock intervention, or one of its pressure-release phases, lasts longer than makes physical sense. Bosch patented such a guard in 1988. If a wheel shows slip above a threshold for about 20 s while the driver is not braking, the controller first becomes less sensitive and then switches ABS off and lights a lamp; a spare wheel or uneven tyre pressures were the named triggers. A Toyota/Denso patent ends a pressure reduction after about 3 s and checks for abnormal prolongation. Mismatched tyres or a weak speed signal are the likely roots.
c: Spare wheel, mixed tyre sizes or very uneven tyre pressures
Weak or disturbed wheel speed signal (air gap, dirty sensor ring)
Sluggish valve in the hydraulic unit prolonging a control phase
s: ABS warning lamp on, anti-lock function switched off
Pedal pulsing or long release phases during gentle braking

C0112.d: C0112 is not found in any accessible J2012 table or in the NHTSA bulletin index, and no manufacturer documents it publicly. Read literally, the title flags anti-lock control that starts again and again although the wheel situation does not justify it, as opposed to one overlong event (C0111). Nissan and Unisia patented a counter that sums pressure-release time across successive control cycles; when it keeps growing past roughly 0.5 s because one wheel speed sensor reads too high, that sensor is judged faulty and left out of the reference speed. The Bosch patent of 1988 switches ABS off when slip persists without braking. Plausible causes are a tyre of the wrong size, a cracked or loose sensor ring and electrical noise on a speed signal.
c: Tyre or wheel of the wrong rolling circumference
Cracked, loose or contaminated sensor ring
Interference or intermittent contact on a wheel speed sensor circuit
s: ABS kicks in at low speed or on dry road without reason
ABS warning lamp on after repeated interventions

C0121.d: C0121 is absent from the accessible J2012 lists. GM includes it in the chassis code keyword list of bulletin PIP5094 (2013), and AA1Car's ABS code table, which follows GM numbering, names it Valve Relay Circuit Malfunction. This relay passes battery voltage to all solenoid valves of the hydraulic unit, while the controller grounds each valve on its own. A Hella/Lucas patent describes the monitoring: the module checks the relay coil current and the voltage behind the contact, and if either is wrong it drops the relay so the valves fall back to their rest position; a Toyota/Denso patent uses a cut-off relay in the same way. Ordinary braking remains, but ABS and the functions built on it are lost and the warning lamp lights. A sticking contact, a blown valve feed fuse or a poor module ground are typical causes.
c: Blown fuse or poor battery feed to the valve relay
Corroded or loose ground of the brake control module
Valve relay contact sticking or burnt (relay often inside the module)
s: ABS warning lamp on, often together with traction or stability lamp
No anti-lock action, wheels can lock under hard braking

C0128.d: C0128 is not part of the accessible J2012 tables. GM lists it among its chassis codes in bulletin PIP5094, and the GM-based ABS table published by AA1Car words it Low Brake Fluid Circuit Low. The input comes from the level switch in the master cylinder reservoir: a float carrying a magnet closes a reed contact once the fluid drops, as patents from ITT and from Nabco/Nissan show. FMVSS 135 requires the red brake warning to light when the level falls below the maker's safe mark or a quarter of a compartment, whichever is higher. A genuinely low level usually means worn pads or a leak and calls for a brake check before driving on; a full reservoir with the code points to a stuck float, a shorted switch or chafed wiring.
c: Fluid level genuinely low from pad wear or a leak
Stuck float or shorted reed switch in the reservoir
Chafed switch wiring shorted to ground
s: Red brake warning lamp or low fluid message
Possibly longer pedal travel if fluid is really missing

C0131.d: C0131 is not in the accessible J2012 lists; GM and Saab use it for the brake pressure sensor that measures master cylinder pressure inside the modulator. In the Saab 9-5 up to 2010 a signal above 4.75 V or under 0.25 V lasting 0.1 s, or a supply outside 4.4–5.6 V, sets it and ABS, TCS and ESP go out of service. The later 9-5 and the 9-4X call it Traction Control System Pressure Circuit, check the sensor against the pedal message from the body module and against vehicle deceleration, and switch off traction and stability control. GM bulletins PIC5704C to H (Sonic, Spark, Trax, Encore 2012–2022) report C0131 after a modulator swap when shipping material was left on the sensor, which then reads 5 V all the time.
c: Brake pressure sensor in the modulator faulty or out of calibration
Shipping material left on the sensor after modulator replacement (GM)
Fault on the 5 V reference or signal circuit of the sensor
Incorrect brake pedal signal used for the plausibility check
s: Traction/stability control warning on, systems switched off
On some models ABS lamp on as well

C0136.d: No public J2012 list, NHTSA bulletin or manufacturer table carries C0136, so it cannot be matched to a vehicle. Its title is word for word that of C0205, and at GM the brake switch input of ABS/TCS modules is C0161; which number a given car uses can only come from its own service data. The function itself is well described. Bosch patented a monitor for ABS and traction control units that stores a suspected short or stuck switch when the signal is already present at ignition-on, and an open line when no signal appears during a later drive; with automatic gearboxes it waits for three repeats. A second Bosch patent rechecks a switch reported stuck high by demanding a clean low-high-low pattern at standstill. Stop lamps and cruise control share this signal.
c: Brake light switch misadjusted, worn or sticking
Open or short in the switch circuit or connector
s: Stop lamps stay on or do not work
Cruise control will not engage or cancels
ABS or stability warning lamp may come on

C0141.t: Left Front ABS Inlet Solenoid Circuit
C0141.d: C0141 is not listed in the accessible J2012 tables. Saab documents it for the Bosch 5.3 TC/ABS of the 9-3 and 9-5 from 1998 and for the later 9-5 ESP as the left pressure-increase valve, kept apart from the wheel valve group code C2450; GM's chassis keyword list (PIP5094) includes it, and AA1Car's GM-based table calls it Left TCS Solenoid #1. Describing it as the left front inlet valve is therefore one reading of a valve that builds pressure in the left front brake circuit, above all during traction control. Saab tests the coil without pause for breaks and shorts, with the rolling check running above 6 km/h; a fault shuts down ABS, TCS and ESP and lights several warning lamps at once. Coil, wiring and the valve block are the usual suspects.
c: Open or shorted coil of the left pressure-increase valve
Poor contact between control unit and valve block
Failed valve driver in the control module
s: ABS, brake and central warning lamps on
TCS/ESP off indicator lit, no ABS, TCS or ESP function

C0146.t: Left Front ABS Outlet Solenoid Circuit
C0146.d: Like its neighbours, C0146 is missing from the accessible J2012 tables and is documented only in Saab and GM material. Saab's 9-3/9-5 data for the Bosch 5.3 TC/ABS name it the left pressure-reduction valve, the ESP version of the 9-5 calls it the left pressure relief valve; the GM keyword list PIP5094 includes the number and AA1Car's GM-based table labels it Left TCS Solenoid #2. Its job is the opposite of C0141: it lets pressure out of the left circuit again. Its title reads it as the left front outlet valve, which matches that role. With the Saab diagnostic tool the valve can be clicked at 1 Hz for about 30 seconds to confirm whether it responds. A failure takes ABS, traction control and ESP out of service.
c: Open or shorted coil of the left pressure-reduction valve
Control module fault (Saab replaces the control module after checks)
Weak supply or ground to the brake control unit
s: Several brake-related warning lamps on together
ABS, traction and stability control unavailable

C0148.t: Right Front ABS Outlet Solenoid B Circuit Malfunction
C0148.d: C0148 is listed neither in the publicly available J2012 tables nor in maker indexes or NHTSA bulletins, so what the letter B stands for cannot be verified. The title suggests a second release solenoid for the right front wheel, as some hydraulic units pair two valves per channel. In any ABS unit the outlet side lets fluid escape from the caliper so the wheel can spin up again. Controllers check each coil electrically; a MOTOR article on the ATE system shows the module sending short test pulses to every inlet and outlet coil and setting a code within about 65 ms of key-on if one pulse is missing or too strong. A Toyota/Denso patent pairs such open/short checks with a relay that cuts all valves. With the code stored, the anti-lock function is usually off.
c: Solenoid coil open, shorted or out of resistance range
Corroded contact between coil and control module
Failed output stage in the ABS module
s: ABS warning lamp on immediately after key-on
Anti-lock and related functions switched off

C0151.t: Right Front ABS Inlet Solenoid Circuit
C0151.d: C0151 mirrors C0141 on the right side and, like it, is not in the accessible J2012 tables. Saab's 9-3 and 9-5 workshop pages for the Bosch 5.3 TC/ABS and for the 9-5 ESP define it as the right pressure-increase valve, separate from the right front wheel valve code C2455; GM's PIP5094 keyword list carries it, and AA1Car's GM-based table reads Right TCS Solenoid #1. In the diagonal brake layout of those cars the valve feeds pressure into the right front circuit when traction control brakes a spinning wheel. Saab watches the circuit for breaks and shorts continuously and runs the valve test above 6 km/h. Once the code sets, ABS, TCS and ESP stay off, and the brake, ABS and central warning lamps come on.
c: Defective coil of the right pressure-increase valve
Contact fault at the module-to-valve-block interface
Valve driver fault in the brake control module
s: Brake, ABS and central warning lamps on
No traction control when a front wheel spins

C0153.t: Right Front ABS Inlet Solenoid B Circuit Malfunction
C0153.d: C0153 cannot be found in any accessible J2012 list, NHTSA bulletin or manufacturer table; neither the code nor its B suffix is publicly documented. By title it concerns a second inlet solenoid for the right front wheel. Inlet valves are open at rest and close to hold caliper pressure while the module decides whether to release or rebuild it. Bosch combines the per-wheel valves, the return pump and the control electronics in one hydraulic unit. The MOTOR study of the ATE system shows that coil faults are found by timed current pulses, and that the module records exactly which valve misbehaved before shutting down anti-lock. In practice, the coil, the plug between coil and module, or the module itself are suspects.
c: Poor plug contact between coil and module
Internal fault in the ABS control module
s: ABS lamp on, anti-lock unavailable
Stability control may also be switched off

C0156.t: Right Front ABS Outlet Solenoid Circuit
C0156.d: C0156 completes the Saab/GM group of four and is likewise absent from the accessible J2012 tables. Saab lists it as the right pressure-reduction valve for the 9-3/9-5 with Bosch 5.3 traction control and as the right pressure relief valve in the 9-5 ESP; GM's PIP5094 keyword list names the code, and AA1Car's GM-based table gives Right TCS Solenoid #2. Reading it as the right front outlet valve fits its task of releasing pressure from that circuit after a traction or ABS intervention. Saab's fault page ends, after the wiring and actuator checks, with replacing the control module, since the coils are tied to the electronic unit. Until then the car brakes normally but without ABS, TCS or ESP support.
c: Open or shorted coil of the right pressure-reduction valve
Fault inside the control unit carrying the valve coils
Moisture or corrosion at the control unit connector
s: ABS, brake and TCS/ESP OFF lamps on
Wheels may lock under emergency braking

C0158.t: Left Rear ABS Inlet Solenoid Circuit Malfunction
C0158.d: C0158 is publicly undocumented: it appears in no accessible J2012 table, NHTSA bulletin or manufacturer index. Saab, for example, reports the rear left valve group under C2415 instead. The title points to the electrical circuit of the inlet solenoid for the left rear brake. That valve stays open during normal braking and closes when the rear wheel starts to lock, trapping pressure in the caliper. Toyota and Denso patented a routine check that tests every actuator solenoid for breaks and shorts, raises a fault flag, lights the warning lamp and trips a cut-off relay so the brakes revert to plain pedal operation. MOTOR's measurements on the ATE system add that a coil with wrong resistance reaches its current limit too fast or too slowly.
c: Rear left inlet coil open, shorted or with wrong resistance
Corrosion at the hydraulic unit connector
Failed output stage in the control module
s: ABS warning lamp on, anti-lock switched off
Rear wheels can lock under hard braking

C0161.d: C0161 is outside the accessible J2012 tables but well documented at GM. Service data for the later Saab 9-5 and the 9-4X define it as an implausible ABS brake switch signal: the EBCM receives the pedal-applied message from the body module and compares it with brake pressure and vehicle motion. The 9-4X sets it after four starts to over 40 km/h without any switch change, or when the pedal reads applied for 360 s above 20 km/h with less than 15 bar; the 9-5 uses 122 s and 6.2 bar plus a check for more than 15 bar for 2 s with the pedal released. GM bulletin PIT5181A for 2012–2014 full-size trucks and SUVs links C0161 and C0277 to a loose terminal in connector X205. Hill start assist may be disabled; braking while accelerating can also set it.
c: Brake pedal position sensor or switch out of adjustment
Loose or backed-out terminal in the pedal sensor wiring (GM X205)
Brake pressure sensor reading that contradicts the pedal signal
s: Service stability or traction message
Cruise control or brake lights may misbehave
Hill start assist unavailable

C0163.t: Left Rear ABS Outlet Solenoid Circuit Malfunction
C0163.d: None of the reachable J2012 lists, maker indexes or NHTSA bulletins mention C0163, so its use cannot be shown for any vehicle. The title names the outlet solenoid of the left rear brake, the valve that opens during anti-lock control to dump caliper pressure toward the return pump and lets the wheel recover. If it cannot open, the rear wheel may lock; if it sticks open, the rear brake loses pressure during regulation. Electrically, controllers verify the coil with short current pulses: MOTOR describes the ATE module checking every outlet and inlet coil in a fixed sequence and flagging the missing one, and the Toyota/Denso patent cuts all valve power through a relay after such a finding. Bosch places these valves together with the pump in the hydraulic unit.
c: Rear left outlet coil open or shorted
Poor contact at the hydraulic unit connector
Outlet valve mechanically stuck by contaminated fluid
s: ABS warning lamp on
Unstable rear axle under hard braking without ABS

C0168.t: Right Rear ABS Inlet Solenoid Circuit Malfunction
C0168.d: C0168 has no public trace: it is missing from the accessible J2012 tables, from the NHTSA bulletin index and from the manufacturer pages checked, where Saab for instance uses C2485 for the rear right valves. Taken at face value it covers the inlet solenoid of the right rear brake, which isolates that caliper from master cylinder pressure while the module regulates the wheel. Typical findings are a coil with an open winding, a short between coil and housing, or a corroded plug at the valve block. Toyota and Denso patented the self-test that checks each solenoid for these faults and then trips a cut-off relay, while MOTOR documents how the ATE module times test pulses per valve and shuts anti-lock down when one is wrong.
c: Open winding in the rear right inlet coil
Corroded plug at the valve block
s: ABS lamp on, often directly at key-on
No anti-lock control on any wheel

C0173.t: Right Rear ABS Outlet Solenoid Circuit Malfunction
C0173.d: No accessible J2012 list, maker index or NHTSA bulletin contains C0173, so the code cannot be tied to any vehicle; Saab, for instance, reports a fault in either valve of the right rear wheel as C2485. By its title it covers the release valve of the right rear brake. In the Saab hydraulic unit this valve is closed at rest and opens, together with the return pump, only when that wheel nears lock-up, letting fluid out of the caliper into a small accumulator. Saab energises every valve for 20 ms in a self-test at each key-on and switches ABS, traction and stability control off when one fails. An outlet coil that cannot open leaves the rear wheel prone to locking during ABS braking; a leaking one lets the caliper lose pressure.
c: Open or shorted coil of the right rear outlet valve
Corroded or loose contact between valve block and control module
Faulty valve driver stage inside the control module
s: ABS and brake warning lamps on, ABS/TCS/ESC switched off
Right rear wheel may lock under hard braking

C0185.d: C0185 is missing from the accessible J2012 lists and from the NHTSA bulletin index, and no maker documents it, so it is not publicly verifiable; its title is shared with C0499. It describes a lateral acceleration signal that is electrically intact but does not fit the motion of the car. GM-based service data for the Saab 9-4X file exactly this case under C0186 with symptom 5A: an offset outside its window, or a value that disagrees with yaw rate, steering angle and speed. Honda patented a check that flags the sensor when its reading exceeds the smaller of V²/R and 1 g in both left and right turns, so a slope offset alone does not trip it. A Bosch patent covers clearing such a fault only after offset and model comparisons pass while driving straight and cornering.
c: Sensor offset drifted or calibration not learned after replacement
Sensor or module loose or mounted at the wrong angle
Implausible comparison signal (steering angle, wheel speeds)
s: Stability control warning lamp on, ESC switched off
Unwanted stability interventions when cornering

C0186.d: C0186 lies outside the publicly available J2012 tables but is firmly established at GM and Saab for the lateral accelerometer. On Saab 9-5 models through 2010 the ESP module sets it when the 0–5 V signal leaves the 0.25–4.75 V band for over 0.1 s or makes no sense; at standstill the reading should be close to 0 m/s². Later GM designs such as the 9-4X read the sensor as part of a multi-axis module over CAN, with symptom 71 for invalid data and 5A for an implausible value. GM bulletins link C0186 together with C0196 and C0287 to a failed multi-axis sensor (PIT5187A, SRX/Equinox/Terrain 2011–2012), to corrosion in connector X411 of Equinox/Terrain 2010–2017 (PIT5427B) and to airbag module software (PI1525). Stability control then stays off.
c: Corroded connector or terminals in the sensor or bus wiring
Outdated software in the module that hosts the sensor (e.g. airbag module)
s: Service StabiliTrak / ESP OFF message or lamp
Traction and stability control unavailable
Further chassis codes (C0196, C0287, U-codes) stored

C0196.d: C0196 is absent from the accessible J2012 lists, yet it is the yaw rate code of GM and Saab and is also used by Karma. The Saab 9-5 sets it when the sensor output leaves 0.25–4.75 V for longer than 0.1 s or its 2.1–2.9 V reference strays for 0.2 s; GM's multi-axis sensor reports 00 for a faulty signal and 5A when offset or plausibility against lateral acceleration, steering angle and speed fail. GM bulletin 15-05-25-001 traces C0196-5A on 2014–2016 full-size trucks and SUVs to stone hits that make the sensor in the airbag module resonate at 12–14 kHz. GM (Volt, ELR) and Karma (Revero 2017–2018) report it after transport on a carrier, when the car senses motion without wheel speed; a relearn, rest and a drive above 20 mph clear it.
c: Code set during transport or flat towing while modules were awake
Faulty or unlearned yaw rate / multi-axis sensor
Signal spikes from body vibration, stone impacts or loose mounting
Corroded connector or CAN wiring fault
s: Service StabiliTrak message, traction/ABS or ESP OFF lamp
Stability control and hill start assist disabled
Red brake lamp on in some vehicles

C0200.t: ABS Solenoid Valve Front Left Circuit
C0200.d: Neither the reachable J2012 tables nor NHTSA's bulletin index nor the manufacturer indexes checked contain C0200, so no published vehicle is known to use it. Its title, a circuit fault of the front left ABS solenoid valves, matches what Saab records as C2450 on 9-5 cars equipped with Bosch 5.3 TC/ABS. Each wheel channel of such a unit has an inlet valve that is open at rest and an outlet valve that is closed at rest, so the controller can hold, lower or rebuild pressure at this wheel alone; in Saab's ESP version both valves also act during stability braking. A shorted or open coil shows up in the brief valve test after key-on, which MOTOR captured as one short current pulse per coil, after which ABS and the functions built on it stay off and the lamps light.
c: Open or shorted coil of a front left valve
Poor contact between valve coils and control module (solder joint, contact strip)
Faulty valve driver in the control module
s: ABS warning lamp on from key-on, ABS inactive
Traction and stability control also switched off

C0201.d: Searches of J2012 tables, NHTSA bulletins and maker indexes found no trace of C0201, so no vehicle use can be shown; GM files its low-fluid input under C0128. The title concerns the wiring of the float switch fitted to the master cylinder reservoir. On the Saab 9-5 that switch sits in the filler cap: a float with two contacts closes once the level has dropped to about two thirds and grounds the warning lamp, which the cluster also lights for 3 s at key-on as a bulb check. A Nabco/Nissan patent places a reed switch under the reservoir floor, worked by a magnet in the float, with a push-down test. Under FMVSS 135 the driver must be warned once any chamber drops under the maker's safe mark or one quarter of its capacity. A circuit code points to a broken lead, a corroded plug or an internally shorted switch.
c: Corroded or loose connector at the reservoir cap or switch
Level switch shorted or open internally, float stuck
Chafed wiring between switch and module
Actually low fluid from worn pads or a leak
s: Red brake warning lamp on or flickering
Low-fluid message although the reservoir is full

C0202.d: No accessible J2012 list, NHTSA bulletin or maker index mentions C0202; the code is publicly unverifiable, and C0230 carries an almost identical title. A brake pedal position sensor reports how far the pedal moves instead of a mere on/off state. GM patented a resistive design with two outputs: one goes to the engine module for diagnosis, the other to the brake module, which uses it to release the shift interlock. Besides out-of-range checks, GM looks for faults inside the valid range by weighting how much the reading changes while the interlock is released. Bosch's PWG travel sensor works without contact through a Hall element and sends two PWM signals so the control unit can compare them. Such sensors are needed above all where braking is blended with energy recovery.
c: Worn, misadjusted or not relearned pedal position sensor
Loose or corroded connector at the pedal
Pedal bracket or return spring binding
s: Brake or stability warning lamp on
Shift lever cannot be moved out of park, cruise control inactive

C0203.t: ABS Solenoid Valve Front Right Circuit
C0203.d: C0203 has no public trace: neither the accessible J2012 lists nor the NHTSA bulletins or maker indexes include it. Read literally it is the front right counterpart of C0200; Saab's 9-5 fitted with the Bosch 5.3 traction/ABS unit reports this case as C2455. GM's wording for the TRW EBC450 unit of the 2011 Saab 9-5 calls the two valves per wheel isolation and dump valves: the first closes to freeze pressure, the second opens to bleed it into the low-pressure accumulator, from which the pump returns the fluid, and the control module powers both coils itself. A Toyota/Denso patent describes the classic reaction to a broken or shorted coil: a fault flag is set, the warning lamp is latched and a cut-off relay is dropped so the car brakes like one without ABS.
c: Open or shorted coil of a front right valve
Poor contact between control module and valve block
Faulty valve driver in the control module
s: ABS lamp on, anti-lock function off
Front right wheel can lock under hard braking

C0205.d: C0205 cannot be found in the accessible J2012 lists, in NHTSA bulletins or in maker indexes; its title is identical to that of C0136, and GM-designed brake modules such as that of the Saab 9-4X use C0161 for the brake switch input. The switch itself is a closing contact that passes battery voltage to the brake module and the stop lamps when the pedal is pressed, as Saab's 9-3 ESP data show. Saab's 9-5 ESP module supervises the line by feeding a small current into it that returns to ground through the stop lamp bulbs; an interruption there is stored as C2470. Bosch and Nissan Diesel patented a scheme with two pedal switches that must agree, counting repeated mismatches before declaring both failed. Dark or permanently lit stop lamps are the first hint.
c: Stop lamp switch misadjusted, worn or broken
Blown stop lamp bulbs or fuse interrupting the monitoring path
Broken wire or corroded connector at the pedal
s: Stop lamps stay off or stay on
Cruise control will not engage or does not switch off when braking
ABS/ESC warning lamp on

C0206.t: ABS Solenoid Valve Rear Left Circuit
C0206.d: C0206 is not documented publicly; the publicly available J2012 lists, the NHTSA bulletin index and maker indexes do not contain it. The title describes an electrical fault of the left rear ABS valves, which Saab's 9-5 TC/ABS data file as C2415 and watch for opens and shorts at all times, with the active valve check above 6 km/h. On the rear axle these valves matter even without wheel lock: Saab's 9-3 ESP description explains that electronic brake-force distribution operates each wheel's inlet and outlet valve, without the pump, to keep rear pressure from locking the rear wheels first. A failed rear valve therefore costs EBD as well as ABS, which is why the brake lamp lights next to the ABS lamp. MOTOR's current-probe recordings show such a coil fault as a missing test pulse.
c: Open or shorted coil of a rear left valve
Cracked solder joint or contact strip, often worse when cold
Faulty valve driver in the control module
s: ABS and red brake warning lamps on
No ABS or electronic brake-force distribution, rear may lock early

C0209.t: ABS Solenoid Valve Rear Right Circuit
C0209.d: C0209 appears in none of the accessible J2012 tables, NHTSA bulletins or manufacturer indexes and is therefore not publicly verifiable. Its title, a circuit fault of the rear right ABS solenoid valves, corresponds to Saab's C2485 on the 9-5 with Bosch TC/ABS. In the Saab ESP unit twelve valves share one block: an inlet and an outlet valve for each wheel plus two pairs used only for traction control. At every key-on the module pulses all valves for 20 ms alongside the pump test, and any failure turns off ESP, TCS and ABS together. Bosch describes the same layout of per-wheel valves, return pump and electronics in one hydraulic unit. MOTOR notes that a single bad solenoid often means replacing the whole valve block, so exact coil and wiring tests come first.
c: Open or shorted coil of a rear right valve
Poor contact between control module and valve block
Internal failure of the hydraulic unit
s: ABS, brake and ESP OFF lamps on
No anti-lock, traction or stability intervention

C0220.d: C0220 has not turned up in any accessible J2012 table, NHTSA bulletin or maker index; there is no public evidence of its use. The title refers to the voltage that feeds the solenoid valves of the hydraulic unit. In GM-designed systems such as the TRW EBC450 of the 2011 Saab 9-5, the brake control module itself feeds both the valve coils and the pump motor. A Hella/Lucas patent routes battery voltage to all valves through the contact of a fail-safe relay and checks the switched voltage behind it; a wrong value drops the relay and lights the lamp. Saab's older ESP shows a typical limit for a supply fault, below 9 V for 0.5 s above 6 km/h, stored there as C1532. A weak battery, a blown fuse, poor grounds or charging faults are frequent causes.
c: Low system voltage from a weak battery or charging fault
Blown fuse or high resistance in the module supply line
Poor ground connection of the brake control module
Faulty valve supply relay or driver inside the module
s: ABS, brake and stability lamps on, often intermittently
ABS and traction control unavailable

C0225.d: C0225 is missing from the accessible J2012 lists. GM does use the number: its terminal-test bulletin PIP5094 for 2014 and older cars and light trucks lists it among the chassis codes, and AA1Car's table of GM ABS codes gives it as Left Front Wheel Speed Sensor Circuit Open, not as a valve relay fault. No maker on record documents a valve relay meaning. For the relay named in the title, a Hella/Lucas patent explains the job: one relay contact supplies all ABS valves, and the module checks both coil current and switched voltage, opening the relay on a fault so the valves return to rest. On a GM vehicle with C0225, the left front sensor circuit deserves the first look; HELLA notes that only passive sensors can be checked by resistance.
c: On GM vehicles open left front wheel speed sensor or its wiring
Burnt or sticking valve relay contact
Blown fuse or poor ground in the relay circuit
s: ABS warning lamp on, ABS disabled
Traction control or speedometer function affected on some vehicles

C0230.d: C0230 is in none of the accessible J2012 tables and in no NHTSA bulletin or manufacturer index, so it cannot be traced to a vehicle. The title points to the electrical side of a brake pedal position sensor: a supply, signal or ground line that is open or shorted, so the reading falls outside the band the module accepts. GM's patent for a two-output resistive sensor names these out-of-range low and high conditions as the standard on-board check before it adds a test for faults within the range. Bosch's Hall-type PWG sensor delivers two independent PWM outputs; if one disappears or both disagree, the controller can tell a wiring fault from a real pedal movement. Expected effects are stop lamp or cruise control trouble, a lit warning lamp and, on hybrids, limited brake blending.
c: Open or shorted supply, signal or ground wire of the sensor
Corroded or loose connector at the pedal sensor
Internal sensor fault (worn track, failed Hall element)
s: Brake or stability warning lamp on
Stop lamps or cruise control behave incorrectly

C0234.d: C0234 is publicly unverifiable: the publicly available J2012 tables, NHTSA's bulletins and maker indexes all lack it; in AA1Car's list of GM ABS codes the same wording belongs to C0245. The title describes a speed signal whose frequency is implausible. The control module derives wheel speed from frequency alone: the inductive sensors of the Saab 9-5 with a 29-tooth ring give roughly 70 Hz at 20 km/h, and the Hall sensors of the 9-3 run on a 48-pole ring up to about 2000 Hz. A frequency far off those of the remaining wheels points to a wrong tone ring, a mismatched tyre size or missing teeth. Nisshinbo patented a test that compares every pulse period with a reference at steady speed; a gap of three or five periods marks one or two broken teeth.
c: Damaged, cracked or wrong tone ring (missing teeth, wrong tooth count)
Tyre or wheel size differs from the other wheels
Excessive air gap or metal debris on the sensor
s: ABS and traction lamps on, sometimes only above a certain speed
Unwanted ABS or traction intervention

C0235.d: C0235 does not show up in the publicly available J2012 lists. GM's bulletin PIP5094 names the number among chassis codes for cars and light trucks up to 2014, and AA1Car's GM-based ABS table renders it as Rear Wheel Speed Signal Circuit Open; an erratic-signal meaning is not documented by any maker. Taken by its title, the code concerns a speed signal that jumps or briefly drops out while the wheel turns steadily. HELLA's workshop guide names broken wires, internal shorts, heavy dirt and a growing air gap as the usual reasons, with pseudo control interventions or locking wheels as symptoms, and recommends comparing the wheel signals in live data and on a scope. Bosch's Hall sensors turn the encoder field into square current pulses, so a loose plug shows as missing pulses.
c: Intermittent wire break or loose connector, often at moving harness sections
Dirt, rust or metal debris on the sensor, enlarged air gap
Wheel bearing play letting the encoder wobble
s: ABS lamp comes and goes
Pulsing pedal or ABS intervention at low speed without reason

C0237.t: Loss of Speed Sensor Signal Front Left
C0237.d: The publicly available J2012 tables skip C0237. GM lists the number in PIP5094, and AA1Car's GM-based code table reads it as Rear Wheel Speed Signal Erratic, so GM's use concerns the rear axle, not the front left wheel of the title. Other makers code a lost front left signal differently: the Saab 9-5 records an open or shorted front left sensor as C1372 and a mechanical or functional fault as C1371, switching ABS, TCS and ESP off. A total loss means no pulses reach the module although the other wheels turn; typical reasons are a cable torn at the steering knuckle, a sensor pushed away from its 29-tooth ring or a damaged connector. HELLA advises checking supply and signal with a meter and oscilloscope before a new sensor is fitted.
c: Broken sensor cable or damaged connector at the front left wheel
Sensor failed or pushed out of position after suspension work
Tone ring damaged or missing after drive shaft or hub replacement
s: ABS, traction and stability lamps on
No ABS; speedometer may misread if it uses this wheel

C0238.d: C0238 does not appear in the publicly available J2012 code lists. GM uses it: the terminal-check bulletin PIP5094 for 2014 and older GM cars and light trucks names it as a chassis keyword, and AA1Car's table of GM ABS codes calls it Wheel Speed Mismatch, which fits the title. GM does not publish its setting rule for this number. A related GM test on the 2011 Saab 9-5 shows the principle: above 14 km/h, brake off and driving straight, a wheel reading more than 20 percent off the others is treated as a fault. Typical reasons are one tyre of a different size or pressure, a spare wheel, a damaged tone ring or a sensor with too much air gap. ABS and traction control are normally switched off until the next ignition cycle.
c: One tyre with different size, wear or pressure, or a space-saver spare fitted
Cracked, corroded or wrong tone ring on one wheel
Wheel speed sensor loose or with excessive air gap, or worn wheel bearing
s: ABS and traction control warning lamps on
ABS and traction control disabled for the rest of the trip

C0240.d: C0240 cannot be verified publicly: it is missing from the accessible J2012 lists, from the NHTSA bulletin index, from GM's PIP5094 keyword list and from the Saab and Mitsubishi indexes. Only the part in the title can be described. In a modern brake control unit a pressure sensor reports how hard the driver presses; on the TRW EBC450 of the 2011 Saab 9-5 it is built into the valve block. The module feeds it 5 V and expects about 0 V with the pedal released and more than 1 V when braking. A broken supply or signal line, or a reading that does not fit the deceleration or brake switch, disables ABS, traction and stability control; GM files that fault under C0131. Brake assist and stability control use this signal to judge braking demand.
c: Open or shorted 5 V supply or signal wire to the pressure sensor
Faulty pressure sensor inside the hydraulic unit
Sensor offset not calibrated after module or valve block replacement
s: ABS, traction and stability warning lamps on
Brake assist and stability control unavailable

C0241.d: None of the reachable J2012 tables contain C0241, and a warning lamp meaning is documented nowhere. GM's PIP5094 keyword list includes the number; AA1Car's table of GM ABS codes names it EBCM Control Valve Circuit. Saab used it in the TC/ABS 5.3 system of the first 9-5 model year, 1998, for a bad engine torque limitation signal: if the Trionic engine module has a torque control fault, a break in that line or the brake module carries the wrong engine variant, the engine side sends a fixed 96 percent pulse ratio and traction control shuts down with the TCS OFF lamp lit. The lamp in the title is required by FMVSS 135, which demands a brake warning indicator for any electrical failure of the antilock system. Check which system and maker stored the code before testing anything.
c: On Saab 9-5 (1998) open or shorted torque limitation line or throttle fault in the Trionic engine module
On GM vehicles fault in a control valve circuit driven by the brake module
Brake module programmed for the wrong engine variant
s: TCS OFF or ABS warning lamp on
Traction control not working
Check engine lamp on at the same time when the engine module is the source (Saab)

C0242.d: C0242 is a GM brake module code that the accessible J2012 lists do not contain. The Saab 9-5 and 9-4X of 2011 describe it as Powertrain Control Module Indicated Traction Control Malfunction, and the GM bulletin PIC4740C for the 2007 Cadillac STS calls it ECM Indicated TCS Malfunction. During traction control the brake module asks the engine module over the data bus for less torque. When the engine module holds certain faults of its own, it replies that it cannot cut torque, and the brake module stores C0242. Traction and stability control then stay off for the ignition cycle and their lamp comes on. The real fault sits in the engine or transmission module, so its codes are read first; in PIC4740C a loose transmission connector X1 was the cause.
c: Stored fault in the engine control module that blocks torque reduction
Loose or poorly seated terminals at the transmission connector (GM PIC4740C)
Faulty engine control module, rarely the brake module
s: Traction or stability control lamp on, systems disabled
Check engine lamp or reduced engine power from the engine side fault

C0244.d: No public J2012 table carries C0244, and no maker documents a meaning matching the title. The only public use is Saab's, and it concerns the engine torque signal. On the 1998 9-5 with TC/ABS 5.3 the Trionic engine module reports actual torque to the brake module as a pulse-width signal; C0244 is stored when that line is open or shorted. On the 2004 9-5 with ESP the torque value arrives over the data bus, and C0244 means the engine module flagged its own value as invalid. Either way the TCS or ESP OFF lamp comes on and the function is lost, while ABS keeps working. The pulse-width idea in the title fits this signal, not a brake pressure valve. Diagnosis starts in the engine module; the current torque can be read with a scan tool.
c: Open or shorted torque signal line between engine and brake module (Saab 9-5 1998)
Fault in the engine control module that invalidates the torque value
Data bus problem between engine and brake module
s: TCS OFF or ESP OFF lamp on
No traction or stability control, ABS still active

C0245.d: C0245 is missing from the reachable J2012 lists but is a documented GM code: PIP5094 lists it, AA1Car's GM table names it Wheel Speed Sensor Frequency Error, and the 2010 and 2011 Saab 9-5 manuals call it Wheel Speed Sensor Frequency Malfunction. The active sensors there get 12 V from the brake module and return a square wave whose frequency gives the wheel speed. The check runs above 9 mph with no open-circuit sensor code, brake released and no cornering; if one wheel differs from the rest by more than 20 percent, ABS, hill start assist, traction and stability control shut down for that ignition cycle and three warning lamps light. GM first checks tyre size and pressure, then the tone ring and sensor seating.
c: Tyre with wrong size or pressure on one wheel
Damaged or contaminated tone ring or magnetic encoder
Sensor not seated correctly or excessive wheel bearing play
s: ABS, traction/stability and brake warning lamps on together
ABS, stability control and hill start assist disabled

C0246.d: The accessible J2012 tables lack C0246, and an internal brake module fault is not what any maker uses it for. Two makers use it differently. In the 2011 Saab 9-5 (GM) it is set by other modules on the fast CAN network when the periodic wheel speed message from the brake module stops arriving: Invalid Data Received From Electronic Brake Control Module. Toyota stores it in the skid control ECU of the 2014 to 2020 4Runner together with C0226, C0236 and C0256; Tech Tip T-TT-0597-20 traces the ABS lamp to a ground that fluctuates when aftermarket LED or HID headlight bulbs are fitted. The meaning therefore depends on make and on which module holds the code. On GM, start with the wheel speed sensors.
c: On GM vehicles wheel speed message from the brake module missing on the CAN bus
On Toyota 4Runner unstable ECU ground caused by aftermarket LED or HID headlight bulbs
Damaged brake module connector or ground wires
s: ABS warning lamp on
Functions that use wheel speed run degraded in other modules (GM)

C0250.d: C0250 is publicly unverifiable: neither the reachable J2012 lists, nor NHTSA's bulletin index, nor GM's PIP5094 keywords, nor the Saab manuals contain it. What can be described is the part named in the title. On hydraulic power steering a pressure switch or sensor at the pump outlet tells the engine control when steering adds load. Chrysler's patent US6152106 uses a voltage-output sensor so the idle air control can open earlier and avoid idle dips while parking. Mazda's patent US6012541 shows a plausibility test: a switch that stays closed for 60 s at over 60 km/h with warm fluid is judged stuck, because nobody steers that long at speed. For the electrical faults of such a sensor, the powertrain codes P0550 to P0554 exist.
c: Faulty or stuck power steering pressure sensor or switch
Damaged wiring or connector at the pressure sensor
Low fluid level or worn pump giving abnormal pressure
s: Idle speed dips or stalls when steering at standstill
Warning lamp or stored code without noticeable steering change

C0252.d: C0252 has no entry in the publicly available J2012 tables, nor does any maker tie it to a pump motor ground. Saab and GM use it for stability control plausibility. The 2002 to 2010 Saab 9-5 with Bosch ESP sets it after a rare event while ABS or ESP is regulating, such as the car sliding sideways with locked wheels, or after a brief voltage drop at the steering angle or yaw rate sensor. The 2011 9-5 (GM) calls it Vehicle Stability Control Module Sensors Correlation Malfunction: steering angle, yaw rate and lateral acceleration disagree, or straight driving is not recognised within 2.5 km. GM bulletin PIC3171E links C0252 on the 2005 to 2006 Cadillac STS to a loose lower steering column bearing that corrupts the steering position signal.
c: Steering angle sensor not calibrated, misaligned or disturbed by column play
Loose or wrongly mounted yaw rate / multi-axis acceleration sensor
Incorrect wheel alignment after suspension work
Rare driving situation during regulation (sliding with stationary wheels)
s: ESP OFF or stability control lamp on
Unwanted stability control intervention when turning
Stability control and hill start assist disabled

C0258.d: No public record of C0258 exists: the publicly available J2012 lists, the NHTSA bulletin index and the GM and Saab indexes all lack it. Only the sensor named in the title can be described. A booster vacuum sensor tells the control unit whether enough vacuum is stored for power-assisted braking; GM needs it on cylinder-deactivation engines, which return to all cylinders when vacuum gets low. GM patent US7076347 checks the sensor with the throttle almost closed: over one second the gap to manifold vacuum must shrink to near zero. GM patent US7467544 also catches a reading biased high or low. Electrical faults of such a sensor are normally stored as powertrain codes P0556 to P0559 rather than as a chassis code.
c: Open or shorted sensor supply, ground or signal wire
Leaking vacuum hose, check valve or booster diaphragm
s: Warning lamp or message about brake assistance
Cylinder deactivation or engine stop-start inhibited on affected vehicles

C0265.d: C0265 does not appear in the published J2012 lists; it belongs to GM's numbering. PIP5094, GM's terminal-check bulletin for 2014 and older vehicles, includes it, and in AA1Car's listing of GM ABS faults it is EBCM Relay Circuit, matching the title. GM does not publish the setting rule for this number. The task of such a relay is described in a Hella/Lucas patent: one contact switches battery voltage to all ABS valves, and the module watches both coil current and the voltage behind the contact. If either is wrong, the relay is dropped, the valves lose power, and the car brakes conventionally without ABS while the warning lamp is lit. Check fuses, relay contacts and the module ground before replacing the brake module.
c: Blown fuse or poor battery feed to the relay
Burnt or sticking relay contacts (internal relay in later modules)
Poor ground at the brake control module
s: ABS warning lamp on, ABS disabled
Traction control unavailable on equipped vehicles

C0266.d: Active brake booster faults are filed under C0266 by no maker, and the reachable J2012 lists omit the code. The number is a GM one: it shows up among PIP5094's keywords, and AA1Car words it exactly like C0265, EBCM Relay Circuit, so on GM vehicles it points to the relay that powers the ABS valves and pump rather than to a booster. The part in the title is a booster that builds pressure without the driver, either a vacuum unit with a solenoid or an electromechanical design such as Bosch's iBooster, whose motor works independently of engine vacuum and can brake on its own for assistance functions. On a vehicle with such a booster, its own maker-specific codes cover faults; with C0266, first find out which module stored it.
c: On GM vehicles fault in the brake module relay supply (fuse, contact, ground)
Faulty actuator or motor of an active booster
Damaged wiring or connector to the booster or relay
s: ABS or brake warning lamp on
Assistance functions such as automatic braking unavailable

C0267.d: C0267 is missing from the accessible J2012 lists; GM has used it with two meanings. AA1Car's table of older GM ABS codes names it Pump Motor Circuit Open/Shorted, matching the title, and PIP5094 confirms the number. In the later GM Global A systems, as in the 2011 Saab 9-4X, it reads Low Brake Fluid Indicated: the brake module sees the level switch circuit grounded, or the level below MIN, for 60 seconds, disables traction and stability control and asks the cluster for the brake lamp. Bulletin PIC6156 for the 2014 to 2016 Malibu traces false low-fluid messages with C0267 to a missing ground ring at stud G203; PIT5499 for the 2015 to 2016 Colorado and Canyon to water in the brake module connector.
c: On newer GM vehicles brake fluid below MIN (check pad wear and leaks)
Loose ground (GM G203) or corroded brake module connector
On older GM ABS open or shorted pump motor circuit or worn pump motor
s: Red brake warning lamp or low brake fluid message
Traction and stability control disabled, ABS lamp on with older systems

C0268.d: C0268 appears in no public J2012 table. It is a GM number named in PIP5094, and AA1Car repeats for it the wording of C0267, Pump Motor Circuit Open/Shorted. A run-time limit as in the title is documented by no maker for this code. Why pump run time matters is shown by a Kelsey-Hayes patent for GM-type ABS: one DC motor drives the return pumps that empty the low-pressure accumulators after the dump valves open; if the motor runs too slowly the accumulators fill and pressure at the wheel can no longer be lowered. The patent starts the motor at full voltage for about 0.3 s, then regulates speed by PWM and back EMF. A motor running too long or too slow points to wear, low voltage or a poor ground.
c: Worn or sluggish ABS pump motor
Low supply voltage or poor ground at the pump motor circuit
Open or shorted pump motor wiring or connector (GM wording)
s: ABS warning lamp on, ABS and traction control disabled
Pump runs audibly long during self-test or ABS events

C0269.d: C0269 lacks a J2012 entry in the sources available, and a vacuum sensor meaning appears nowhere. On GM vehicles, where PIP5094 names the code, AA1Car translates it as Excessive Dump/Isolation Time: the brake module has held wheel pressure isolated or released for longer than its software allows. In GM-type ABS the isolation valve closes to stop pressure rise and the dump valve opens to let fluid into a low-pressure accumulator. A Lucas patent explains why dump time is limited: at very low speed a recovering wheel still looks locked, so dumping is cut off once it exceeds a weighted average of earlier cycles. Typical causes are a faulty wheel speed signal, a sticking valve or a weak return pump.
c: Erratic or weak wheel speed signal making a wheel appear locked
Sticking isolation or dump valve in the hydraulic unit
Weak return pump or full low-pressure accumulator
s: ABS warning lamp on, ABS disabled
Long or soft brake pedal feel during an ABS stop

C0273.t: Brake Booster Pressure Sensor Circuit Malfunction
C0273.d: Neither the reachable J2012 lists nor any maker describe C0273 as a booster pressure sensor code. GM's PIP5094 does include the number, and AA1Car translates it, like C0271 and C0272, as EBCM Malfunction, meaning an internal fault of the brake module. In that case the module is normally replaced after supply, ground and connector have been checked. The sensor in the title measures the vacuum or pressure stored in the brake booster. GM's patent US7467544 compares it with manifold vacuum at closed throttle and flags a reading drifted high or low, and can even correct a moderate drift. Electrical faults of that sensor are usually stored under the powertrain codes P0556 to P0559.
c: On GM vehicles internal fault of the brake control module
Low supply voltage, poor ground or corroded module connector
Faulty booster pressure sensor or its wiring
s: ABS and traction warning lamps on
ABS and stability functions disabled

C0277.d: The publicly available J2012 tables omit C0277; GM assigns it to the brake pedal position sensor, not for a booster vacuum sensor. In the 2011 Saab 9-4X the body module watches the sensor with 9 to 16 V supply and the brake applied: failure type 06 means the signal or 5 V reference line is grounded or interrupted, 07 that a line touches battery voltage or the low reference is open, 09 a signal changing too fast, 4B a sensor whose rest position was never learned. GM bulletin 19-NA-202 for the 2016 to 2019 Malibu lists the same subcodes and fixes false C0277 with brake module software; PIT5181A for 2012 to 2014 full-size trucks points to connector X205. Effects include dead stop lamps, cruise control faults and a Service Stabilitrak message.
c: Loose, backed-out or bent terminals in the sensor connector or GM connector X205
Short or open in signal, 5 V reference or low reference wire
Brake module software (GM 19-NA-202) or rest position not learned
s: Rear stop lamps inoperative
Service Stabilitrak message, traction control lamp on
Cruise control cannot be set or drops out

C0279.t: Brake Booster Boost Sensor Circuit Malfunction
C0279.d: C0279 is absent from every publicly available J2012 list, and no maker describes it as a booster sensor code. GM does use the number: its bulletin PIP5094 names it among the chassis keywords for 2014 and older cars and light trucks, and the GM brake code chart published by AA1Car renders it as Powertrain Configuration Not Valid, meaning the brake module received engine or driveline data it was not set up for. The part in the title reports how much vacuum or boost pressure the brake booster holds. On the 2011 Saab 9-4X the brake module feeds such a sensor with 5 V and switches an electric vacuum pump on when the reading drops; Bosch uses the same signal for start/stop and brake assist. With the circuit faulty, the module loses that reading.
c: Open or shorted 5 V supply, signal or ground wire of the booster sensor
Booster pressure sensor failed or its grommet leaking
Brake module not configured for the fitted engine or driveline (GM meaning of the number)
s: Brake or ABS warning lamp on
Electric vacuum pump runs constantly or not at all
Start/stop or brake assist unavailable

C0287.d: The publicly available J2012 lists do not contain C0287, and no maker uses it for an ESP Performance fault. In later GM brake systems the number belongs to the longitudinal acceleration sensor: the Saab 9-5 of 2010 and 2011 and the 2011 Saab 9-4X file it under the multi-axis sensor that also delivers lateral acceleration and yaw rate over CAN. It sets when that signal is missing, disagrees with the speed change of the car or has an offset outside its window; subcode 4B marks a calibration never learned, 71 invalid data. Only hill start assist is switched off. GM bulletins PI1525 (2014–15 Regal, Malibu, Sonic) and PIT5427 (2010–15 Equinox and Terrain, corroded connector X411) list it with C0186 and C0196. Older GM tables used the number otherwise.
c: Multi-axis sensor replaced or disturbed without setup and yaw sensor learn
Corroded or loose connector in the sensor supply or CAN lines
Faulty multi-axis sensor or outdated software in the module hosting it
s: Hill start assist not available
Stability control or airbag warning lamp on when stored together with C0186 or C0196

C0288.d: No reachable J2012 list carries C0288, and no known maker files a yaw rate range fault under it. GM's PIP5094 contains the number, and AA1Car's GM brake table gives it a quite different meaning: Brake Warning Lamp Circuit Shorted to B+. The title describes a yaw rate signal that leaves its permitted span. Where GM documents that case, it uses C019B instead: on the 2011 Saab 9-5 the brake module flags a yaw signal out of its specified range and then turns ESP and the hill start aid off until the next ignition cycle. The older Saab 9-5 sensor covers about ±138 degrees per second, reads zero at rest and is checked every 20 ms. Bosch explains the micromechanical Coriolis measurement used in such sensors.
c: Sensor bracket loose, bent or sensor mounted crooked after body repair
Unstable supply or ground at the sensor
s: Stability and traction control warning lamp on
Stability control disabled for the rest of the trip

C0290.t: Brake Pedal Stroke Sensor Circuit Malfunction
C0290.d: C0290 does not show up in the publicly available J2012 lists, and no maker ties it to a pedal stroke sensor. GM lists the number in PIP5094; AA1Car's GM brake table translates it as Lost Communications With PCM, a data bus fault between brake and engine module. A pedal stroke sensor measures how far the driver pushes the pedal or brake rod. Bosch builds such sensors on the Hall principle for up to 45 mm of travel or 55 degrees of rotation, and its iBooster reads the pedal through a differential travel sensor before its motor adds force. Electric boosters and blended regenerative brakes depend on this signal; when its circuit fails, the system falls back to an unassisted or less refined mode and the brake warning appears.
c: Damaged wiring or connector at the pedal travel sensor
Pedal travel sensor failed or its magnet displaced
Data bus fault between brake and engine module (GM meaning of the number)
s: Brake warning lamp on
Higher pedal effort or changed pedal feel
Regenerative braking reduced on hybrid or electric cars

C0291.t: Brake Pedal Apply Sensor Circuit Malfunction
C0291.d: C0291 is in no publicly available J2012 table, and no maker uses it for a brake apply sensor. GM names the number in its PIP5094 keyword list, and AA1Car's table of GM brake codes reads it as Lost Communications With BCM, a lost data link to the body module. An apply sensor tells the control units whether, and how firmly, the pedal is pressed. GM handles that job with a pedal position sensor: on the 2011 Saab 9-4X it is read by the body module, which needs 9 to 16 V supply and stores separate subcodes for grounded or open lines, battery shorts, implausible jumps and a missing rest position learn. A failure there affects stop lamps, shift lock and the electric park brake release.
c: Chafed wire or loose connector at the pedal sensor
Pedal sensor replaced or pedal adjusted without relearning the rest position
Data link to the body module interrupted (GM meaning of the number)
s: Stop lamps stay on or do not light
Cruise control or shift lock release not working
ABS or stability control warning lamp on

C0295.d: Public evidence for C0295 is lacking. The code appears neither in the publicly available J2012 tables nor in GM's PIP5094 keywords, the AA1Car chart, the Saab manuals or the NHTSA bulletin index. What remains is the fault the title names, a steering angle sensor whose zero point no longer matches straight-ahead driving. GM stores this case as C0710 5A on the 2011 Saab 9-5, comparing steering angle with yaw rate; ESP and the hill start aid then stay off for the ignition cycle. The earlier Saab 9-5 disables the system once the stored correction reaches 15 degrees. GM bulletin 16-NA-151 cures a 2016 Malibu C0460 after a voltage dip by turning the wheel lock to lock. Bosch measures the angle with two magnet gears.
c: Wheel alignment or steering parts changed without recentring the sensor
Calibration lost after battery disconnection or a voltage dip
Steering angle sensor or clock spring assembly faulty
s: Stability control warning lamp on
Steering wheel off centre when driving straight
Unexpected stability control interventions

C0300.d: C0300 appears in none of the published J2012 lists, and no maker documents it as an ABS valve code. GM uses the number: it is among the chassis keywords of PIP5094, and AA1Car's GM table calls it Rear Speed Sensor Malfunction, listed in the same block as the transfer case motor codes C0306 to C0315. The title describes the front left inlet valve of the ABS valve block. That valve is open at rest and closes during a regulation cycle to hold pressure at the wheel; TRW, in the 2011 Saab 9-5, calls it the isolation valve. Saab's older 9-5 pulses every valve for 20 ms at each ignition-on and, on a fault, switches off ABS, traction and stability control with their warning lamps. A sluggish front left inlet valve leaves that wheel under- or overbraked during ABS.
c: Inlet valve sticking from contaminated or aged brake fluid
Valve coil or driver in the brake module faulty
On GM 4WD trucks, rear speed sensor fault in the transfer case system (GM meaning of the number)
s: ABS and stability control warning lamps on
Car pulls during hard braking

C0301.d: No reachable J2012 table, no GM keyword list such as PIP5094, no AA1Car chart and no NHTSA bulletin carries C0301. Makers that document this fault use their own numbers. Mercedes-Benz stores open-circuit compressor actuation on AIRMATIC cars as C1562 and, after moisture froze in the compressor and the start current blew the 40 A fuse, replaces compressor, fuse and relay together. Lexus reports C1752 on the 2013–17 LS460 when water corrodes the height control compressor, and Volvo tells dealers to swap fuse and compressor on 2017–18 models. The relay switches the compressor's heavy current on command of the suspension module. A worn compressor overloads its contacts; a relay that sticks closed keeps it running and can overheat it.
c: Relay contacts burnt or welded by excessive compressor current
Worn, seized or water-damaged compressor drawing too much current
Blown compressor fuse or corroded relay socket and wiring
s: Air suspension warning message, compressor silent
Vehicle sinks or leans after standing
Compressor runs continuously when the relay sticks

C0302.d: C0302 has no public footprint: the publicly available J2012 tables, GM's PIP5094, the AA1Car chart and the NHTSA bulletin index all lack it. This text therefore covers only the front left outlet valve named in the title. Unlike the inlet valve it stays closed at rest and opens only when the brake module wants to drop pressure at a locking wheel; the released fluid goes into an accumulator from which the return pump feeds it back. TRW calls this part the dump valve. If it opens too slowly, the front left wheel can lock; if it leaks, pressure escapes and the pedal sinks or the car pulls right. Bosch places these valves, the return pump and the control unit together in one hydraulic unit, so a valve fault usually means repairing that unit.
c: Outlet valve seat leaking because of dirt or wear
Valve coil or its driver in the brake module faulty
Old or wrong brake fluid slowing the valve
s: ABS warning lamp on, ABS switched off
Front left wheel locks or pedal sinks slowly

C0303.d: C0303 has no public evidence at all: the accessible J2012 lists, GM's PIP5094 keyword list, AA1Car's GM table and the NHTSA index all lack it. The title points to the front right inlet valve. A performance fault here means the brake module saw the valve respond wrongly, for example a coil current out of range during the self-test or a wheel that does not hold pressure as commanded. In the Saab 9-5 ESP valve block twelve solenoid valves sit together, including an inlet/outlet pair for every wheel, and any valve fault switches ABS, traction and stability control off and lights their lamps. A front right inlet valve that stays shut leaves that wheel underbraked, so the car may pull to the left; one that will not close lets the wheel lock in ABS braking.
c: Inlet valve stuck from debris after brake work
Open or shorted valve coil inside the hydraulic unit
Low supply voltage to the valve circuit during self-test
s: ABS, traction and stability control lamps on
Car pulls to the left when braking

C0304.d: No public source confirms C0304; searches of the J2012 tables at hand, of GM's keyword bulletin PIP5094, of AA1Car and of the NHTSA bulletin index came up empty. The title concerns the front right outlet valve, the part that bleeds pressure off that caliper when the wheel starts to lock. In the TRW brake system of Saab's 2011 9-5, the EBC450, the module first holds pressure by closing the inlet valve and only then opens this dump valve, sending fluid into the accumulator, from where the pump returns it. A valve that will not open lets the front right wheel lock; a valve that does not reseal drains pressure, gives a long pedal and can make the car pull left. Saab's ESP version uses the same valves for stability braking, so the fault disables ABS and ESP alike.
c: Outlet valve not resealing because of dirt in the seat
Valve coil or brake module output stage defective
Accumulator or return pump unable to take the released fluid
s: ABS and stability control warning lamps on
Long brake pedal or front right wheel locking

C0305.d: C0305 is missing from the published J2012 lists and is not described by any maker as an ABS valve code. GM does use it: PIP5094 lists the number, and AA1Car's GM table calls it Front Speed Sensor Malfunction, the partner of C0300 in the block before the transfer case motor codes. The title refers to the rear left inlet valve. Besides ABS work, the rear inlet valves carry the electronic brake force split: on the 2011 Saab 9-5 the TRW module lowers rear pressure by cycling the rear valves instead of using a mechanical proportioning valve, and it also uses the valves to hold pressure for hill start assist. A sluggish rear left inlet valve can let that wheel lock early or brake too little, and the module then disables ABS and stability control.
c: Rear left inlet valve sticking from contaminated fluid
Valve coil or brake module driver defective
On GM 4WD trucks, front speed sensor fault in the transfer case system (GM meaning of the number)
s: ABS and brake warning lamps on
Rear wheel locking early or hill start assist unavailable

C0306.t: Transfer Case Motor A or B Circuit
C0306.d: C0306 is not in the publicly available J2012 lists, and nobody uses it for a ride height sensor. GM uses it in its transfer case module (TCCM) for the two circuits that drive the shift motor: AA1Car's GM table names it Motor A or B Circuit, and bulletins PIP5080 and PIP5080B for 2012–13 Silverado, Sierra, Tahoe, Suburban, Avalanche and Yukon point to terminals at X109 and to connector X3 of the module, which carries motor circuits 1552 and 1553. Gears Magazine describes the 2013–14 Canyon and Colorado: the module powers one motor line, reads the voltage drop on the other and sets the code after four seconds of wrong values; subcodes 01, 02, 04 and F1 mean short to battery, short to ground, open and performance.
c: Loose, corroded or poorly crimped terminals at the motor or module connector
Transfer case shift motor with internal short or open winding
Faulty motor driver in the transfer case control module
s: Service 4WD message in the driver information centre
Transfer case does not shift between 2WD, 4WD and low range

C0307.d: C0307 has no public trace: not in the accessible J2012 lists, not in GM's PIP5094 or AA1Car's GM table, and not in the NHTSA bulletin index. Described here is the rear right inlet valve of the title. In an ESP valve block it does more than ABS work: Saab explains for the 9-5 that both valves of each rear wheel are also driven during stability interventions, so that pressure can be shaped at all four corners while the pump runs. A rear right inlet valve that answers slowly therefore spoils both ABS stops and stability corrections that brake the right rear wheel. The self-test at ignition-on catches coil faults; hydraulic slowness shows up during regulation. Either way ABS and ESP are switched off with their lamps.
c: Rear right inlet valve slowed by dirt or aged fluid
Coil of the valve or brake module output defective
Poor contact between brake module and valve block
s: ABS and stability control lamps on
Stability control unavailable

C0308.t: Transfer Case Motor A/B Circuit Low
C0308.d: None of the publicly available J2012 lists contains C0308, and no source links it to a ride height sensor. GM uses it for the transfer case shift motor: PIP5094 lists the number, AA1Car's GM chart labels it Motor A/B Circuit Low, and Dorman's guide for its replacement motor covers 1998–2005 S10 Blazer, Sonoma, Tahoe, Suburban, Yukon, Silverado, Sierra, Escalade, Avalanche and related trucks. The transfer case module sets it when it finds motor control line A or B shorted to ground, or when the feedback voltage on those lines is far too low. Once stored, the module stops every 4WD shift and lights Service 4WD. The sibling codes C0309 and C0310 cover a high voltage and an open circuit on the same lines.
c: Motor control wire A or B chafed against the frame and grounded
Transfer case control module output stage faulty
s: Service 4WD lamp on
No shifting into or out of four-wheel drive

C0309.d: C0309 is no part of any public J2012 table, and no manufacturer documents it as a valve code. GM does use it: it is among the keywords of PIP5094, and the GM code chart on AA1Car calls it Motor A/B Circuit High, a transfer case shift motor fault next to C0308 and C0310; that meaning rests on this single source. The title instead names the rear right outlet valve. It opens to let fluid out of the right rear caliper into the accumulator when that wheel tends to lock and stays shut otherwise. Saab's 9-5 checks each valve with a 20 ms pulse at every ignition-on, and a fault turns ABS, traction and stability control off. A valve stuck open would keep the right rear wheel from building pressure.
c: Rear right outlet valve not closing fully
Valve coil or brake module driver faulty
On GM 4WD trucks, transfer case motor circuit shorted to voltage (GM meaning of the number)
s: ABS and stability control warning lamps on
Weak braking at the right rear wheel

C0310.t: Transfer Case Motor A/B Circuit Open
C0310.d: C0310 is not listed in any publicly available J2012 table; no maker uses it for a rear left ride height sensor. GM assigns the number to the transfer case shift motor: it is in PIP5094, AA1Car gives the GM wording Motor A/B Circuit Open, and Dorman describes it for GM trucks and SUVs of 1998 to 2005. The transfer case module drives the motor through two lines, one switched to supply and the other to ground depending on direction. When it commands a low level on a line and reads a high voltage back instead, it concludes that line A, line B or the motor winding is open and stores C0310. Shifting is then blocked and Service 4WD lights up. A broken motor pigtail or connector is the usual cause.
c: Broken motor control wire or pigtail exposed under the vehicle
Corroded or unseated connector at the shift motor
Open winding or worn brushes in the shift motor
s: Service 4WD lamp on, 4WD switch lights flash
Transfer case stays in its last range

C0312.d: Searches for C0312 in reachable J2012 lists, in GM sources and in the NHTSA bulletin index returned nothing, so only the component is described here. A ride height sensor at the right rear converts the swing of a lever arm linked to the suspension into an electrical signal, usually by inductive or Hall measurement, and feeds air suspension, damping or headlamp levelling. HELLA lists bent lever arms, broken wires, corroded plugs and water ingress as the usual failures. Makers use their own numbers here: RAM stores a stuck right rear height sensor on the 2022–23 1500 as C152A-2A and fixed it with module software, and BMW had to inspect rear sensor control rods on 2019 X5 and X7 models.
c: Bent, detached or wrongly clipped sensor lever or link rod
Corroded connector or broken wire at the rear right sensor
Sensor failed internally after water ingress
s: Air suspension or levelling warning message
Rear right corner sits too high or too low
Headlamp levelling incorrect
