C0317.d: C0317 is publicly undocumented: it is missing from every publicly available J2012 list, from GM's keyword bulletin PIP5094 and from the whole NHTSA bulletin index. What follows describes only the part named in the title. On air or self-levelling suspension a relay carries the heavy compressor current and is energised by the suspension module. Land Rover ships the compressor relay together with the replacement compressor for the 2010 Range Rover, whose compressor could fail by running too long. Audi has technicians open relay J403 of the self-levelling compressor on A6 and Q7 models and judge its contacts: burnt contacts mean compressor and relay are both renewed. Volvo checks fuse and relay before it blames the compressor. A circuit fault here leaves the vehicle unable to raise or hold its ride height.
c: Relay contacts burnt or welded by a compressor drawing too much current
Open or shorted control line between suspension module and relay coil
Worn or seized compressor overloading the relay
Blown compressor fuse or corroded relay socket
s: Suspension warning or air suspension fault message
Vehicle sits low and does not rise
Compressor runs constantly or never starts

C0327.d: C0327 has no entry in the published J2012 tables, but GM documents it: the transfer case control module (TCCM) of 4WD trucks and SUVs uses it for the encoder that tells the module where the motor has turned the shift shaft. Dorman's instruction sheets for GM pickups and SUVs from 1998 to 2009, the Saab 9-7X included, describe it as a voltage outside the expected window on the encoder circuit; play in a worn shift shaft can also make the encoder report a false position. GM bulletin PIP5098 for the 2004–12 Colorado and Canyon links it to a Service 4WD message after cold or damp standing and points to ground circuit 550 of the encoder motor channels, terminal F7 of connector 2 in the underhood fuse block. PIP5094 lists the number among GM chassis codes.
c: Loose or corroded ground terminal for the encoder channels (GM circuit 550)
Damaged encoder harness or water in the motor connector
Encoder in the shift motor assembly defective
Worn shift shaft lets the encoder read a false position
s: Service 4WD message or flashing 4WD switch lamps
Transfer case does not shift or shifts only intermittently
Fault appears mainly on the first drive after cold or damp standing

C0374.d: No publicly available J2012 list carries C0374; GM uses it in the transfer case control module of its 4WD trucks and SUVs, and PIP5094 names it among GM chassis codes. Dorman's sheets for the S10, Blazer, Astro and Safari, the Trailblazer, Envoy and Isuzu Ascender call it General 4WD Failure: in Auto 4WD the module notices rear wheel slip, commands torque to the front axle and still sees the front and rear propshafts turning at different speeds. After ten attempts that fail to couple the front drive it stores the code. Auto 4WD is then unavailable and Service 4WD stays lit until the next engine start. The fault thus points to the coupling path as a whole, encoder motor, clutch and speed sensors, rather than one circuit.
c: Encoder motor too weak or sticking, so the clutch is not applied
Front or rear propshaft speed sensor or its wiring giving false values
Worn transfer case clutch pack or wrong fluid
Tires of unequal size or pressure faking a speed difference
s: Service 4WD message until the next engine start
Auto 4WD does not engage, rear wheels spin on slippery ground

C0376.d: C0376 is not in the published J2012 lists. The number exists at GM, whose bulletin PIP5094 lists it next to transfer case codes such as C0374 and C0387, but no reachable GM document states what it means. The title part decouples the front axle so the front driveline stands still in two-wheel drive. GM handles the front axle actuator of 2007–13 Silverado, Sierra, Tahoe and Yukon under C0379 and blames moisture at the actuator plug. FCA stores such faults as C1463 or C147B: on the 2018 Wrangler the drivetrain module sets C147B-14 when the lock signal of the disconnect stays under 1.19 V for over 500 ms and then leaves the actuator where it is; for Ram 3500/4500 it advises checking the harness 6–8 inches from the plug. If the disconnect fails, 4WD may not engage or release.
c: Water or corrosion in the axle actuator connector
Chafed actuator harness near the axle
Disconnect actuator or its position switch defective
s: Service 4WD message or flashing 4WD indicator
Front wheels not driven although 4WD is selected
Grinding or clicking from the front axle when shifting

C0387.t: Transfer Case Unable to Complete Shift
C0387.d: C0387 is absent from the publicly available J2012 lists. GM uses it in its transfer case control module as Unable to Complete Shift; there is no evidence of a position sensor code. PIP5003C for 2010–13 Silverado, Sierra, Tahoe, Yukon, Avalanche, Escalade and hybrids explains that once a range change or a slip correction has been commanded, the module watches the shift shaft and sets the code when the motor has not begun to move it within 50 ms; heat, cold and supply voltage influence this. If it is history only and cannot be reproduced, a slow encoder motor is the likely culprit, not the module. PIP5080 has technicians check terminal fit in plugs X109 and X3. Per PIP5089A, if the fault is still present at the next start the failed relearn sets C0569 instead. Dorman adds that the module may default to 4HI or 4LO.
c: Encoder motor too slow to start moving the shift shaft
Poor terminal fit at the module connectors (GM X109, X3)
Low supply voltage or extreme temperatures during the shift
Mechanical binding inside the transfer case shift mechanism
s: Service 4WD message, often intermittent
Requested range or mode is not reached
Transfer case stays in a default 4HI or 4LO

C0388.t: Transfer Case High Range Switch Circuit Malfunction
C0388.d: No public source can be found for C0388; neither the reachable J2012 tables nor GM's PIP5094 or NHTSA's index of bulletins contain it. The text therefore covers only the title part. A transfer case reports its engaged range to the control module through a switch or position sensor; the high range is the normal road gear. Makers that document this file it under their own numbers. GM checks circuits 7477 to 7479 between gear position sensor B2227 and the module when C0398 repeats on 2014–15 trucks. Since a 2014 calibration the GM module also compares the stored shift shaft position at shutdown with the value at start and, beyond 5 degrees of drift, holds 4HI. Nissan replaced the transfer case range sensor on 2023 Frontier and Titan in campaign PC984.
c: Open, shorted or corroded wire or terminal of the range switch
Range switch or position sensor on the transfer case defective
Transfer case module calibration needing an update
s: Service 4WD or 4x4 warning displayed
Range indicator does not match the selected gear
Shifts out of high range refused

C0389.t: Transfer Case Low Range Switch Circuit Malfunction
C0389.d: There is no evidence that any maker uses C0389. Neither the publicly available J2012 tables nor GM's chassis keyword bulletin PIP5094 nor NHTSA's index name it, so only the switch named in the title is described. The low range signal matters beyond the transfer case: under FMVSS 126 the stability control must return to its default mode at each new ignition cycle, yet it may stay in a reduced mode if the driver chose low-range 4WD on the previous cycle. A wrong low range signal can therefore affect ESC as well as shifting. GM reads range from a gear position sensor and flags a mismatch as C0398 (PIP5220B); Nissan renewed the range sensor on 2023 Frontier and Titan models. Typical results are a 4WD warning and 4LO that will not engage or release.
c: Damaged or corroded wiring of the low range switch
Low range switch or range sensor defective
Transfer case stuck between ranges so no switch position is reached
s: 4LO cannot be selected or left
4WD warning and low range indicator flashing
Stability control behaves unexpectedly after restart

C0399.d: C0399 cannot be traced publicly. Publicly available J2012 tables do not list it, PIP5094 from GM omits it, and the only matches in NHTSA's index are Mack recall numbers. Only the switch itself is therefore described. With the 4WD mode switch on the dash the driver chooses 2WD, Auto, 4HI or 4LO, and the transfer case module turns that choice into shift commands. GM does not file switch faults under C-codes: on the 2015 Colorado and Canyon its module stores B2725 when a switch with an Auto position is fitted to a truck without Auto 4WD and sends an invalid voltage, and B0770 for the Auto LED circuit; PIP5256 and PIP5256A order the correct switch. With a faulty switch signal the module usually ignores mode requests and keeps the current range.
c: Switch variant not matching the transfer case (e.g. Auto position without Auto 4WD)
Worn switch contacts or resistor ladder giving invalid voltages
Open or shorted lead between switch and transfer case module
s: Service 4WD message
Mode changes ignored or 4WD indicators flash

C0400.d: C0400 is publicly undocumented: none of the published J2012 lists contains it, neither does GM's PIP5094, and a search of NHTSA's bulletin index finds nothing. Only the part from the title is described here. For traction control the brake unit must build pressure without the driver pressing the pedal. In the TC/ABS unit of the 2004 Saab 9-5 one pressure build valve and one pressure release valve per front wheel are used only in TCS mode, while the return pump supplies fluid; Bosch likewise places all control valves and the pump in one hydraulic unit. Each time the ignition comes on, the Saab module tests each valve with a 20 ms pulse; if one fails it switches off ESP, TCS and ABS and lights ABS, brake and ESP OFF lamps.
c: Open or shorted coil of a traction control valve
Valve driver inside the brake control module failed
Poor supply or ground of the brake control module
s: ABS, traction control and stability warning lamps on
Wheels spin freely when pulling away on slippery ground

C0401.d: There is no public evidence that any maker uses C0401. The code is missing from the publicly available J2012 lists and from GM's PIP5094; the only NHTSA index hit is a BMW program number. The description is limited to the switch itself. On the 2004 Saab 9-5 a spring-loaded dash button beside the steering wheel turns ESP and TCS off together; it grounds a supply from the brake module, works for switching off only below 60 km/h, and after more than ten seconds pressed forces the system on until the next ignition cycle without storing a code. FMVSS 126 allows such an off control but demands that stability control come back in its default mode at every new ignition cycle. A shorted or open button circuit leaves the driver unable to change the mode.
c: Button stuck pressed or contacts dirty
Open or grounded lead between button and brake module
Liquid spilled into the switch panel
s: Traction or stability control cannot be switched off or on
TCS OFF or ESP OFF lamp lit permanently

C0402.d: Publicly available J2012 tables skip C0402, yet GM assigns it in its rear differential clutch control module: the 2010–11 Saab 9-5 and the 2011 9-4X call it Transfer Case Solenoid Valve and describe the rear drive clutch solenoid, which the module drives by PWM to set the clutch pressure and so the torque sent rearward; the 2008–12 Saab 9-3 XWD calls it Differential Clutch Solenoid Valve. No maker documents it as a traction control lamp circuit. Subcode 02 is a short with coil resistance below 2 Ω, 04 an open with current off target by over 200 mA for 100 ms, 42/43/4B missing or bad calibration, 61 a valve that does not engage. AWD is switched off and Service Rear Axle appears; valve and module are replaced as a matched pair.
c: Open or shorted solenoid valve circuit at the rear drive unit
Valve calibration not stored after module replacement
Solenoid valve sticking because of contaminated or aged clutch fluid
Corroded connector on the rear axle module
s: Service Rear Axle or AWD warning displayed
Car drives on the front wheels only

C0405.d: C0405 could not be found in any public source, including the public J2012 tables, GM's PIP5094 and NHTSA's bulletin index, and no maker publishes a time limit for a traction control intervention. So only the monitored function is outlined. Traction control brakes a spinning drive wheel and asks the engine for less torque; Bosch counts it among the functions of ESP. In the 2004 Saab 9-5 the return pump runs throughout every TCS or ESP braking event while the control valves raise, hold and lower pressure, and the function lamp lights only when braking and torque reduction act together. An intervention lasting far longer than expected suggests a false wheel speed or a stuck valve; how and when a system then reacts is maker specific.
c: Erratic wheel speed signal faking continuous wheel spin
Spare wheel or tires of different size on one axle
Hydraulic control valve sticking in the brake unit
s: Traction control lamp flashes for a long time or stays on
Engine power reduced and a wheel braked without reason
Hot or smelling brake on one wheel

C0410.t: Adaptive Cruise Control Sensor Circuit Malfunction
C0410.d: C0410 has no public trace; searches of the publicly available J2012 tables, of GM's keyword bulletin PIP5094 and of NHTSA's bulletin index came up empty. The text is therefore restricted to the sensor named in the title. Adaptive cruise control relies mostly on a radar sensor behind the front fascia that watches the lane ahead; Bosch describes how ACC holds the set speed while the road is clear and keeps a chosen gap once a slower vehicle appears, with a stop-and-go version that brakes to a halt below 30 km/h. Makers that document sensor faults use their own codes: Nissan stores C2581-78 or C2581-92 for the distance sensor on the 2022 Pathfinder and prescribes a check of mounting and alignment before parts are replaced. A sensor circuit fault switches ACC off.
c: Loose or corroded connector of the front radar sensor
Sensor or bracket bent after a minor impact, alignment lost
s: Adaptive cruise control unavailable with a warning message
Forward collision warning or emergency braking disabled

C0420.t: Adaptive Cruise Control Module Internal Performance
C0420.d: No public document shows a maker using C0420. It does not appear in the openly accessible J2012 lists, in GM's PIP5094 or in the NHTSA bulletin index, so only the module from the title is covered. The ACC module evaluates the radar data and requests engine torque and braking to keep speed and gap, as Bosch outlines. Faults of the module itself are mostly cured by software: Jeep reprograms the ACC module of the 2024 Compass when C0063-9A, a yaw rate operating-condition code, is set with the check engine lamp, naming ACC software as the cause; Land Rover corrected a wrong ACC module calibration on 2019 Range Rover Sport mild hybrids in service action N343NAS1. An internal performance fault normally disables adaptive cruise and related assists until the module passes its self-test.
c: ACC module software or calibration out of date
Low or unstable supply voltage during self-test
Internal hardware fault of the ACC module
s: Adaptive cruise control and related assists unavailable
Driver assist warning in the instrument cluster

C0440.d: C0440 cannot be verified publicly; searches of the available J2012 tables, GM bulletin PIP5094 and the full NHTSA index found no hit. Its title is word for word that of C0455, which GM does use for the steering wheel position sensor read by the brake module; the description here sticks to the sensor. It sits on the steering column and gives stability control the driver's intended direction. Bosch builds it with two measuring gears of different tooth counts, so the absolute angle is known over several turns, and sends angle and rate over CAN with internal plausibility checks. Saab's 9-5 sensor uses gears with 28 and 26 teeth and needs a zero calibration after front end work. GM bulletin PI0639D traces C0455 on 2007–17 trucks and vans to fretting corrosion at the connector.
c: Fretting corrosion or loose fit at the sensor connector
Zero position not calibrated after alignment or column work
s: Stability control and traction control warning lamps on
Service StabiliTrak or ESP message

C0445.d: No accessible J2012 list contains C0445, and no manufacturer bulletin or service page using it could be found, so its exact meaning cannot be proven publicly. The title points to a steering wheel position sensor whose zero point was never learned or has been lost. Saab explains for the 9-5 that the sensor only knows straight ahead after a calibration, which is due after front-end work or a sensor swap. Mitsubishi resets both the sensor neutral point and the value stored in the stability unit after an alignment, and HELLA warns that a wrong zero upsets stability control. On the 2011 Saab 9-5, GM files this condition under C0710 symptom 42 instead. Expect the stability warning lamp and ESC out of action until the sensor is calibrated.
c: Zero-point calibration skipped after alignment, steering work or sensor replacement
Stored calibration lost after battery disconnection or low voltage
Stability control module replaced or reprogrammed without relearning the angle
s: ESC or traction control warning lamp on
Stability control unavailable
Steering wheel reading not zero when driving straight (scan tool)

C0450.t: Rear Wheel Steering Position Sensor Circuit
C0450.d: C0450 does not occur in the accessible J2012 lists. Its only public manufacturer use is GM: bulletin PIC5321A for the 2010–2011 Cadillac DTS links C0450 with Service Power Steering and Service Brake System messages, a lit check-engine lamp and cycling door locks, caused by an engine harness chafed through on the transmission. The DTS has no rear-wheel steering, so GM evidently uses the number for a front steering function; the bulletin does not name it. For the rear-steer meaning of the title: systems such as ZF's AKC set rear toe electrically, a patent for an electric rear-steer actuator reads ball-screw travel with Hall elements, and a ONE80 patent drives the wheels back to straight ahead and locks out rear steer once the position signal is lost or wrong.
c: Wiring harness chafed or pinched (GM DTS case at the transmission)
Faulty position sensor in the rear steering actuator
Corroded or loose connector on the actuator
s: Steering or brake system warning message in the cluster
Rear steering locked straight ahead, larger turning circle
Check-engine lamp on some GM models

C0455.d: C0455 is absent from the accessible J2012 lists but well documented at GM, where the electronic brake control module (EBCM) stores it for the steering wheel position sensor circuit. Bulletin PI0639C, covering 2007–2016 full-size pickups, SUVs, vans and the Colorado/Canyon, blames rising resistance between sensor and EBCM caused by fretting corrosion and a connector with too much play; it says not to replace the sensor but to fit shim stock and apply dielectric grease. PIT4225F adds a steering wheel fitted off its master spline, and PIT5207 an EBCM programmed for the wrong sensor design on 2010 hybrids. The driver sees Service StabiliTrak, often together with C0710.
c: Fretting corrosion and play at the sensor connector (GM PI0639C)
Steering wheel not aligned with the shaft master spline
EBCM programmed for the wrong sensor design
s: Service StabiliTrak message and stability lamp on
ABS lamp may come on first
Stability control unavailable

C0460.d: C0460 is not in the accessible J2012 lists; GM and Saab use it for the steering angle signal. On the 2016 Malibu the EBCM sets it after a brief low-voltage event, and turning lock to lock with ignition on resets the sensor (16-NA-151). On 2017–2018 XT5 and Acadia, C0460 symptom 5A in the power steering module came from a sensor trim error and is fixed by reprogramming (17-NA-284); PIE0481A pairs it with C0545 on 2009–2012 Malibu, G6 and Aura. The Saab 9-3 sets it if the angle rate passes 3000°/s, the computed offset passes 18°, the angle exceeds ±720° or freezes. Lotus uses C0460 for something else: the pressure sensor in Bosch ESP8 units, often tripped by a misadjusted brake light switch.
c: Brief low voltage leaving the sensor uninitialised
Sensor trim error or control module software (GM 17-NA-284)
Angle offset after alignment or steering work
Steering angle sensor or column module defective
s: Traction or stability control lamp on
Reduced Steering Assist message, sometimes without actual loss of assist
Stability control switched off

C0496.d: C0496 appears in no accessible J2012 list, and neither the NHTSA bulletin index nor the manufacturer portals checked contain it, so the code is not publicly verifiable; the established code with this title is C0196. What the title covers: a micromechanical gyro, usually combined with the lateral accelerometer and mounted near the centre of gravity. The Saab 9-5 unit gets a 50 Hz reference from the ESP module, reports yaw over ±138°/s and has its own self-test every 20 ms; the ESP module flags open circuits and shorts to ground or supply. Later designs such as the Saab 9-3 sensor or Bosch's SMI810 deliver digital data over a bus. Without the signal, stability control cannot work; whether a lamp lights depends on the maker.
c: Open circuit or short in the sensor wiring
s: Stability and traction control unavailable
ESC warning lamp on, depending on the make

C0497.d: Neither the accessible J2012 lists nor any manufacturer bulletin or service text mention C0497, so its use cannot be confirmed publicly. The title describes a yaw rate signal that is electrically present but does not match how the car moves. Stability units test this against estimates: a Siemens patent builds a reference yaw rate from steering angle, wheel speeds and accelerations, expects a value near zero at standstill and marks the sensor faulty when the gap passes a threshold. A Ford patent turns yaw rate and lateral acceleration into two road-bank estimates and counts a yaw fault when one exceeds a limit taken from the other, then disables brake control. A Linköping thesis for ZF tried such residual checks with injected faults. Saab gives a ±138°/s test range.
c: Yaw rate sensor offset or drift
Sensor loose, twisted or mounted in the wrong orientation
Wrong comparison input (steering angle not calibrated, wheel speed fault)
s: ESC lamp on, stability control switched off
Unwanted brake interventions when cornering

C0498.d: C0498 is in none of the accessible J2012 lists. GM does use the number: bulletin PIP5094, a terminal-test reminder for GM cars and light trucks of 2014 and earlier, names C0498 and C0499 among many chassis codes, but without any wording, so GM's meaning stays undocumented and a lateral accelerometer fault is not confirmed; the established code with this title is C0186. The part itself is a capacitive sensor whose middle plate swings between two fixed plates under sideways force. On the Saab 9-5 it puts out 0–5 V, about 2.6 V straight ahead, and the ESP module recognises a broken wire or one shorted to ground or battery. A GM EBCM shows the same signal as 0–5 V. Losing it takes away a key ESC input.
c: Open circuit or short in the signal, reference or ground wire
Loose or corroded connector at the sensor cluster
s: Stability control unavailable, ESC lamp depending on the make
Lateral acceleration reads a fixed value on the scan tool

C0499.d: C0499 is missing from the accessible J2012 lists. GM bulletin PIP5094 names C0499 next to C0498 without saying what it stands for, so no manufacturer confirms a lateral acceleration meaning; the established code with this title is C0185. The title describes a lateral acceleration reading that is wired correctly but implausible. Saab explains that its ESP unit compares measured lateral acceleration with what the steering angle implies. A Ford patent derives a road-bank angle from lateral acceleration and steering angle, accepts an accelerometer fault only while the car is stable, then disables brake control until the next key-on and warns the driver. The ZF thesis from Linköping detected offset and drift faults of this sensor with model residuals.
c: Offset or drift of the lateral acceleration sensor
Sensor cluster loose or not mounted level
s: ESC lamp on, stability control switched off until restart
Unexpected ESC interventions on banked roads

C0500.t: Left Front Wheel Speed Sensor A Circuit/Open
C0500.d: C0500 flags lost continuity in the left front wheel speed sensor circuit. An active sensor draws a steady current even with the car parked; Allegro gives 7 and 14 mA as the usual levels of a two-wire interface, so a reading near zero means a broken path. GM's 2016 hybrid OBD tables set C0500 once the signal-line current stays under 3.8 mA for 0.12 s, rated Type A (MIL on the first trip), and suppress it while C05A4 reports a low sensor supply. Mitsubishi maps C1061-13 to C0500 with a delay of at most 1 s and the check-engine lamp after one trip. Unrelated: a Stellantis brake bulletin for the 2022–2023 Wagoneer uses C0500-00 for a hydraulic leak. With this code ABS, stability and traction control shut down.
c: Sensor plug corroded or loose, or a wire broken along the wheel arch
ABS module supply, fuse or fusible link faulty (Mitsubishi lists these)
s: ABS, ESC and traction control warning lamps on, check-engine lamp on some makes
ABS, stability control and hill start assist unavailable
Scan tool shows no left front wheel speed while driving

C0501.t: Left Front Wheel Speed Sensor A Range/Performance
C0501.d: C0501 means the left front speed signal is present but does not fit the situation. GM shows how differently this is judged: its 2016 hybrid tables flag the code when that wheel reads 0 mph while the other three exceed 7.45 mph at a vehicle speed above 11.8 mph (Type A), whereas the 2023 tables test the air gap and set it when magnetic flux stays below 2.2 mT for at least five wheel turns, as Type B with two trips. Mitsubishi derives C1061-92, its C0501, from a speed gap to the other wheels between 10 and 60 km/h and names wrong tire sizes and the sensor rotor. Stellantis reprogrammed engine controllers of the 2017 Cherokee 3.2 because C0501 was being stored falsely there, adding that on that model it does not light the MIL.
c: Sensor not fully seated or air gap to the tone ring too large
Tire on the left front differs in size from the specified one
Tone ring or magnetic encoder damaged or dirty
Control module software sets the code falsely (Stellantis reflash)
s: ABS and stability warning lamps on after driving, not at key-on
Unexpected ABS or traction control intervention at low speed
Code stored in the engine controller without MIL (Stellantis)

C0502.t: Left Front Wheel Speed Sensor A Circuit Low
C0502.d: C0502 reports the left front sensor circuit below its valid level, mostly a grounded wire or a supply that has sagged. In GM's 2019 tables (19OBDG03D) the brake module's Polaris ASIC sets C0502 for three conditions: the low side shorted to ground, tested only at power-up or after clearing codes (100 ms); sensor undervoltage (20 ms); and, unusually, an open sensor drawing under 3.5 mA, which other GM tables file as C0500. All are Type A. Audi bulletin 2061331/1 for 2017–2021 A4, A5, S and RS models stores C050200 as short to ground: a wire was poorly crimped in the front sensor connector, and the remedy is a new speed sensor and pad-wear harness. Mitsubishi's C1061-11 covers short and open circuits and even lights the parking brake warning.
c: Sensor wire chafed through to ground or poorly crimped in the connector
Sensor supply voltage too low (battery, fuse or module output)
Internal short in the left front sensor
s: ABS and ESC lamps on right after starting
Parking brake warning or electric parking brake functions restricted on some models

C0503.t: Left Front Wheel Speed Sensor A Circuit High
C0503.d: With C0503 the left front circuit reads above its permitted level, which in practice means the signal wire is in contact with battery voltage. GM's 2016 hybrid tables set it when the signal line exceeds 12 V for 0.12 s; the 2023 tables look at current instead and react above 50 mA, many times what a healthy active sensor draws. Both rate it Type A, with a MIL on the first trip. GM also names C05A4, a low common sensor supply, among the codes that block C0503, so a supply fault should be dealt with first. Mitsubishi assigns C1061-12, a short in the front left sensor circuit, to C0503, detected within 1 s, check-engine lamp after one trip. Look for a harness pressed against a live feed or a sensor with an internal short.
c: Signal wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Internal short in the left front sensor
Sensor input stage in the ABS module defective
s: ABS and ESC warnings directly after switching on
Check-engine lamp on some makes (GM Type A, Mitsubishi)
Brake assist and hill descent control switched off

C0504.t: Left Front Wheel Speed Sensor A Intermittent/Erratic
C0504.d: C0504 points to a left front speed signal that jumps or produces far too many edges, not one that is missing. GM's 2016 hybrid brake module stores a time stamp for every sensor edge in a buffer and sets C0504 within 0.03 s when that buffer overflows; the 2023 tables apply the same idea to a DMA transfer unit receiving time stamps too often. For 2020 Chevrolet Silverado and GMC Sierra 2500/3500HD, GM preliminary information PIT5707 ties C0504 and its right-hand twin C050A to manufacturing debris on the reluctor ring: clean it without using a magnet, which may mean removing the hub bearing. Mitsubishi (C1061-38) checks the signal between 10 and 60 km/h, needs two trips for the MIL and lists the sensor rotor among the causes.
c: Metal debris or dirt on the reluctor ring (GM PIT5707)
Loose contact in the sensor plug or a wire breaking under movement
s: ABS lamp and service stability message on the driver display
Fault comes and goes with road surface or steering angle

C0505.t: Left Front Wheel Speed Sensor A Correlation
C0505.d: C0505 says the left front wheel speed is out of step with the other wheels although the circuit tests pass. GM's 2019 tables (19OBDG03D) group several comparisons under this code: a missing sensor, meaning this wheel shows under 1.5 km/h while another exceeds 6 km/h (3 to 120 s depending on speed); a dropout check paused after sudden accelerations; a start-up check that runs until 15 km/h; and the reverse case, where only this wheel turns. Named causes are a badly seated sensor, an air gap out of tolerance and a demagnetized tone ring. Mitsubishi files speed gaps caused by non-specified tires as C1061-64 = C0505, evaluated between 10 and 60 km/h. For comparison, Toyota decides wheel sensor plausibility from about 6 mph, as FenderBender explains.
c: Tire of a different size or heavily worn tire on the left front
Sensor not seated correctly, air gap out of tolerance
Demagnetized or damaged magnetic encoder ring
s: ABS/ESC lamps after a drive, often following a tire change
Traction control intervenes although wheels are not slipping

C0506.t: Right Front Wheel Speed Sensor A Circuit/Open
C0506.d: C0506 reports an open or grounded circuit at the right front wheel speed sensor. GM's 2023 tables describe it as a grounded or interrupted line, recognized from the signal-line current: below 3.8 mA for 0.12 s, Type A, and only evaluated after the start-up sensor test has finished without a supply undervoltage. On GM's 2019 platform an open drawing under 3.5 mA is filed as C0508 instead, so the same broken wire can carry different numbers. Mitsubishi assigns C1063-13 to C0506 and warns not to replace the ABS unit for a code that is stored but not active; it may simply mean the car was not driven after the last repair. HELLA advises checking supply voltage and wiring with a multimeter, as the internal resistance of active sensors cannot be measured.
c: Broken wire or open contact between ABS module and right front sensor
Old stored code after repair, vehicle not yet driven
s: ABS, ESC and traction control lamps on from start-up
Right front wheel speed reads zero in live data

C0507.t: Right Front Wheel Speed Sensor A Range/Performance
C0507.d: C0507 flags an implausible right front speed signal. In GM's 2019 tables the brake module's ASIC watches the sensor current itself: a level hanging in the grey zones between 7 and 14 mA or 14 and 28 mA for 750 ms points to a high-resistance harness or leakage to battery voltage. Those bands sit between the base, data and speed-pulse levels Allegro lists for AK-protocol sensors. Further C0507 checks there look at standstill pulse width and timing. Mitsubishi assigns C1063-92, evaluated from 10 to 60 km/h. Stellantis bulletins show engine controllers storing the code too, for example on the 2016 Jeep Renegade 2.4 (18-061-16) and the 2026 Dodge Charger Sixpack (18-022-26); for the Charger, the bulletin blames a monitor lacking robustness and prescribes reprogramming.
c: Corroded contacts or damaged insulation causing resistance or leakage current
Damaged tone ring or wrong tire size on the right front
Engine controller software storing the code falsely (Stellantis)
s: ABS/ESC lamps after driving off
Code present only in the engine controller during a full vehicle scan

C0508.t: Right Front Wheel Speed Sensor A Circuit Low
C0508.d: C0508 reports the right front sensor circuit below range. A 2024 Jeep Wrangler case from the Stellantis STAR center shows a typical picture: after an earlier repair the ABS lamp came on with C0508-00, ABS disabled and implausible-speed network codes; the sensor harness had been pinched and only needed rerouting. Audi's bulletin 2061331/1 for 2017–2021 A4 and A5 family cars stores C050800 as short to ground when a wire is poorly crimped in the front sensor connector. GM's 2023 tables use C0508 for signal patterns that the current, supply and voltage monitors cannot classify as either a fault or a valid signal (0.12 s, Type A). Mitsubishi's C1063-11 covers short and open circuits on the right front and also lights the parking brake warning.
c: Sensor harness pinched or misrouted after suspension or brake work
Poorly crimped terminal in the sensor connector (Audi)
s: ABS lamp on, often right after a repair
Additional network codes about implausible wheel or vehicle speed
Parking brake warning on some models

C0509.t: Right Front Wheel Speed Sensor A Circuit High
C0509.d: C0509 means the right front sensor line carries more current or voltage than allowed. GM's 2019 tables (19OBDG03D) set it within 100 ms when the high-side current passes 40 mA, or when the Polaris ASIC reports either sensor line shorted to battery or an overcurrent on the low side; it is Type A. That limit sits well above anything a working sensor consumes, so a stuck reading there is a wiring or sensor fault, not a speed signal. Bosch describes its active sensors as working with a two-wire interface that follows an international standard and signals by current; there the brake module feeds the sensor and reads its pulses over the same pair, so one chafed spot affects both supply and signal. Mitsubishi assigns C1063-12, a short in the front right circuit, detected within 1 s and with MIL after one trip.
c: Sensor line chafed against a battery-voltage wire
Right front sensor drawing excess current due to an internal short
Sensor supply driver in the ABS module defective
s: ABS and ESC lamps on immediately, check-engine lamp on some makes
ABS, EBD and hill start assist suspended

C050A.t: Right Front Wheel Speed Sensor A Intermittent/Erratic
C050A.d: C050A is the erratic-signal code for the right front sensor. GM's 2019 tables show how this is judged: an unfiltered wheel acceleration above 491 m/s² feeds a counter that latches the fault at 40 s and decays again on clean readings, so only persistently unrealistic jumps set it; a separate check trips when the edge count exceeds 55 (25 ms). Listed causes are a loosely mounted sensor, missing tone-ring teeth and electromagnetic interference. GM preliminary information PIT5707 for 2020 Silverado and Sierra HD trucks found metal debris on the front reluctor ring; its labor time for removing the hub and cleaning is 1.1 h. HELLA adds heavy dirt and increased bearing play as typical sensor faults. Mitsubishi assigns C1063-38 to C050A with a two-trip MIL.
c: Metal debris or heavy dirt on the right front reluctor ring
Missing tone-ring teeth or excessive wheel bearing play
Electromagnetic interference or intermittent contact in the harness
s: ABS lamp and stability system message that appear and disappear
Pulsing brake pedal or ABS action at low speed without wheel lock

C050B.t: Right Front Wheel Speed Sensor A Correlation
C050B.d: C050B is the correlation code for the right front wheel. GM's 2025 tables (25OBDG04A) rate it Type B, so the MIL waits for a second trip, and add a check not found under C0505 in the 2019 tables: the brake module compares the switching state it requests from the sensor supply driver with the state reported back, an internal module fault rather than a sensor problem. The plausibility checks stay: from start-up to 15 km/h a wheel below 1.2 km/h counts as missing, and if only this wheel exceeds 6 km/h while another stays under 1.5 km/h, a 40 s wait precedes storing the fault. Mitsubishi lists C1063-64 as C050B, naming tire size and sensor rotor. Bosch's active sensors resolve speed down to about 0.1 km/h, so a dead channel shows up early.
c: Right front tire of a different size or circumference
Sensor-to-ring gap out of tolerance or demagnetized encoder
Internal fault in the ABS module's sensor supply switch (GM)
s: ABS/ESC lamps after the second drive with the fault
Stability and traction control unavailable, normal braking retained

C050C.t: Left Rear Wheel Speed Sensor A Circuit/Open
C050C.d: C050C is stored when the brake controller loses the current path to the left rear speed sensor. GM's 2023 OBD tables (23OBDG07) read 0.12 s at under 3.8 mA in the signal wire as a ground short or a break and rate the code Type A, so the MIL can come on in the first trip. Mitsubishi lists C1065-13 of the Outlander PHEV as C050C, detected within one second, with ABS, ASC and engine lamps lit. Its fail-safe list shows what a dead rear sensor costs: besides ABS, EBD and stability control, the electric parking brake function is suspended. The rear harness runs past the trailing arm or axle and flexes with every bump, which makes chafed or pulled leads typical; a sensor with an internal open is the other usual finding.
c: Sensor lead chafed or torn where it follows the rear suspension
Left rear sensor connector corroded or not latched
s: ABS and stability warning lamps on right after key-on, check-engine lamp on some makes
ABS, stability control and on some models electric parking brake functions restricted
Live data shows no left rear wheel speed

C050D.t: Left Rear Wheel Speed Sensor A Range/Performance
C050D.d: C050D says the left rear signal exists but is not trustworthy. In GM's 23OBDG07 tables several checks share this code: a weak magnetic flux under 2.2 mT across at least five wheel turns (detected after 8 s at 3.1 mph or 22 s at 1.24 mph), missing standstill pulses for 3.6 s, and an undervoltage on the sensor supply; all are Type B with two trips, and the tables list Bosch, Continental and DF11i sensor variants. GM's 2019 tables add a grey-zone current between 7 and 28 mA for 750 ms. Stellantis lists C050D as a left rear plausibility error in PCM reflash bulletins such as 18-075-20 for the 2018 Jeep Compass. Mitsubishi files C1065-92 as C050D and points to tire size and the sensor rotor.
c: Air gap to the rear encoder too large (sensor not seated, worn or loose hub bearing)
Contact resistance or leakage in the rear sensor wiring
Left rear tire differs in rolling circumference
Control module software sets the code falsely (Stellantis reflash)
s: ABS and stability lamps come on only after some driving
Stability or traction control intervenes without reason at low speed
Code may be stored without a lit MIL on some Stellantis models

C050E.t: Left Rear Wheel Speed Sensor A Circuit Low
C050E.d: C050E reports the left rear sensor circuit pulled below its expected level. GM's 2019 EBCM tables (19OBDG03D) let the Polaris ASIC set it for three separate findings: an open sensor bit, a grounded low side, looked for only at start-up or once codes have been cleared, and sensor undervoltage, which needs only 20 ms; all are Type A with the MIL. The 2025 tables quantify the open-sensor bit as high-side current under 3.5 mA. Mitsubishi's C1065-11, its C050E, covers both short and open circuits and is one of the few wheel sensor faults there that also turns on the electric parking brake warning next to the ASC, ABS and engine lamps. A wire grounded against the rear subframe or a water-logged connector is the usual cause.
c: Sensor wire grounded against the subframe or body
Moisture or corrosion in the left rear connector
Low supply voltage at the brake module (fuse, battery)
s: ABS, stability and electric parking brake warnings on (Mitsubishi)
ABS and stability control disabled for the rest of the trip

C050F.t: Left Rear Wheel Speed Sensor A Circuit High
C050F.d: C050F covers the opposite electrical case: the left rear circuit sits too high, as when the signal wire touches a battery-fed conductor. For GM's 2016 hybrids, 12 V surpassed on the signal wire for 0.12 s, with more than 6.9 V system voltage, is the trigger; the 2023 tables instead look at current and flag a signal wire carrying over 50 mA, again within 0.12 s and as Type A. Mitsubishi lists C1065-12 as C050F, a short circuit found within one second that lights the MIL after one trip. Rear harnesses often share a loom with parking brake motor, trailer socket or tail lamp feeds, so insulation damage near those conductors is worth checking before a sensor is replaced.
c: Signal wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit in the rear loom
Left rear sensor draws excessive current internally
s: ABS and stability lamps on immediately, MIL on some makes
No ABS regulation, rear brake force distribution in fallback mode

C0510.t: Left Rear Wheel Speed Sensor A Intermittent/Erratic
C0510.d: C0510 flags a left rear speed signal that jumps instead of changing smoothly. GM's 19OBDG03D EBCM logic counts every moment in which the unfiltered wheel acceleration exceeds 491 m/s² at vehicle speeds beyond 3.58 m/s and sets the code once that tally reaches 40 s; a second path latches it within 25 ms when more than 55 edges arrive too quickly. GM names loose mounting, missing teeth on the tone ring and electromagnetic interference as causes. Mitsubishi's C1065-38 runs between 10 and 60 km/h and counts as C0510 after two trips. On the rear axle, load matters: a Stellantis STAR case for the Ram 3500 describes erratic rear sensor codes only with payload or a trailer on rough pavement, without a part fault.
c: Sensor loose in its bore or play in the rear wheel bearing
Missing or damaged teeth, rust flakes on the tone ring
Wire breaking up intermittently as the rear suspension moves
Heavy payload or trailer on rough roads (Ram 3500 case)
s: ABS or stability lamp on after bumps, railway crossings or rumble strips
Brief, unexpected ABS pulsing at the rear
Fault often gone after the next ignition cycle

C0511.t: Left Rear Wheel Speed Sensor A Correlation
C0511.d: C0511 means the left rear speed does not match what the other three wheels report. In GM's 19OBDG03D tables four monitors feed it: missing sensor (this wheel below 1.5 km/h while the rest exceed 6 km/h, 3 to 120 s), dropout (no edges for 150 ms after a valid reading above 30 km/h, with thresholds that depend on axle and brake pedal), fast missing (counted from key-on until 15 km/h is first reached) and too fast (this wheel faster than 6 km/h with the others standing, 40 ms). All are Type A. Mitsubishi calls C1065-64 its C0511 and blames a wrong tire size, checked between 10 and 60 km/h. GM bulletin PIT5950 for the 2019–2023 Silverado 1500 lists C0511 among codes that keep returning after a front sensor of the wrong side was fitted.
c: Left rear tire of a different size or heavily worn compared with the others
Demagnetized encoder or damaged tone ring at the left rear
Wrong sensor fitted after a repair (GM PIT5950)
s: ABS and stability lamps on after setting off or at moderate speed
Speedometer and driver aids act up after a tire change

C0512.t: Right Rear Wheel Speed Sensor A Circuit/Open
C0512.d: C0512 is the open-circuit code for the right rear wheel. GM's 2016 hybrid tables run the check only after the sensor self-test has finished and system voltage is above 6.9 V; then 0.12 s with less than 3.8 mA flowing in the signal wire is enough for a Type A entry. The XT4 section of GM's 2019 tables words the same test as a ground short or interruption and monitors the supply line separately. Mitsubishi assigns C1067-13 to C0512 with a delay of at most one second and lists harness, sensor and the brake unit's power feed as suspects. Because an active sensor modulates a two-wire current, as Bosch describes it, a reading near zero cannot be a slow wheel; it points to a broken lead, an unplugged connector or a dead sensor.
c: Broken lead or unplugged connector at the right rear
Fuse or power feed of the brake module (Mitsubishi lists it)
s: ABS and stability lamps on at key-on, sometimes the MIL
Right rear wheel speed reads zero in live data
ABS and traction control unavailable

C0513.t: Right Rear Wheel Speed Sensor A Range/Performance
C0513.d: C0513 marks a right rear signal that is present but implausible. GM's 2016 hybrid tables catch two patterns: the wheel shows 0 mph while the other three turn and the car exceeds 11.8 mph, and a start-up check in which the right rear stays at zero while the others pass 7.45 mph; both mature at once as Type A, but not during ABS or traction control action. GM bulletin 24-NA-125 for the 2024 Silverado EV traces C0513 to C0516 to the ABS harness rubbing against the upper rim of the rear motor housing over the right-hand axle shaft and fixes it by repair and rerouting. Stellantis reflashed the 2017 Cherokee because C0513 was set falsely and notes it does not light the MIL there. Mitsubishi's C1067-92 relates the code to tire size.
c: Excessive air gap or damaged encoder at the right rear
ABS harness rubbing on the rear drive unit (2024 Silverado EV)
Right rear tire of a different size
False setting by control module software (Stellantis)
s: ABS lamp with a service stability message
Lamps come on after driving off, not at key-on
Code stored without MIL on some Stellantis models

C0514.t: Right Rear Wheel Speed Sensor A Circuit Low
C0514.d: C0514 reports the right rear sensor circuit below its valid range. GM's 2025 EBCM tables (25OBDG04A) show how broadly that is read: the Polaris ASIC raises an open-sensor bit when the high-side current drops under 3.5 mA, and a separate bit for a low side shorted to ground, both after 100 ms as Type A; the listed suspects run from sensor and harness to the printed circuit board and the ASIC. GM's 2023 tables also file signal patterns under C0514 that fit neither a known electrical fault nor a valid signal. On the 2024 Silverado EV, bulletin 24-NA-125 ties the code to a harness worn through on the rear drive unit. Mitsubishi's C1067-11 adds the parking brake warning lamp.
c: Harness worn through and grounded near the rear axle or drive unit
Brake module circuit board or ASIC faulty (GM lists it)
s: ABS lamp and service stability message
Electric parking brake warning on some models (Mitsubishi)
ABS and stability control switched off

C0515.t: Right Rear Wheel Speed Sensor A Circuit High
C0515.d: C0515 says the right rear sensor circuit draws or sees too much. GM's 2025 tables bundle four ASIC flags under this code: high-side current above 40 mA, high side shorted to battery, low-side overcurrent and, perhaps unexpectedly, a low side shorted to ground; each sets it after 100 ms as Type A. The 2023 tables keep it simpler: 50 mA exceeded for 0.12 s in the signal wire. Mitsubishi's C1067-12 equals C0515 and is described as a short circuit found within one second. GM's Silverado EV bulletin 24-NA-125 lists C0515 among the codes caused by the ABS harness touching the rear drive unit. A sensor shorted inside its housing is the other common source of overcurrent.
c: Insulation damage in the right rear harness causing a short
Sensor supply stage in the brake module defective
s: ABS and stability lamps on as soon as the self-test ends
Stability and traction control unavailable

C0516.t: Right Rear Wheel Speed Sensor A Intermittent/Erratic
C0516.d: C0516 stands for a right rear signal that stutters or spikes. GM's 2025 tables use the 491 m/s² wheel acceleration limit at speeds beyond 3.58 m/s but let the fault mature in about 200 ms of near-continuous violation, sampled every 5 ms, and decay the counter when the signal calms; the 2016 hybrid tables instead set it after a 0.03 s overflow of the timer buffer that stores sensor edges. Mitsubishi files C1067-38 as C0516, checked between 10 and 60 km/h, MIL after two trips. GM's program 18316 shows a rear-specific trigger: on 2018 Express and Savana vans with four-wheel discs, axle vibration over rumble strips made the right rear signal erratic, fixed by a brake module calibration. Bulletin 24-NA-125 lists C0516 too.
c: Damaged tone ring teeth or loosely mounted right rear sensor
Rear axle vibration disturbing the signal (GM program 18316)
Brake module calibration too sensitive, update available
s: ABS, stability and traction lamps after rough road sections
Functions return only after the next ignition cycle

C0517.t: Right Rear Wheel Speed Sensor A Correlation
C0517.d: C0517 reports that the right rear speed disagrees with the rest of the vehicle. GM's 2025 tables (25OBDG04A) run missing, dropout, fast-missing and too-fast checks for this wheel; the missing-sensor test, a wheel under 1.5 km/h while others exceed 6 km/h, is rated Type B there, i.e. MIL after two trips. The same tables park an internal fault under C0517: when the sensor supply driver's requested and reported states, exchanged with the ASIC over SPI, disagree for 100 ms, the code is set without any wiring fault outside. Mitsubishi lists C1067-64 as C0517 and checks the right rear against the others between 10 and 60 km/h, citing tire size. GM bulletin PIT5950 includes C0517 among repeat codes after a wrong sensor was fitted.
c: Right rear tire not matching the others in size or wear
Weak encoder or excessive air gap at the right rear
Wrong sensor installed during an earlier repair
Sensor supply driver inside the brake module faulty (GM)
s: ABS and stability lamps after driving off or at moderate speed
Code returns after sensor replacement if the true cause is elsewhere

C0518.t: Left Front Wheel Speed Sensor - Mechanical
C0518.d: C0518 points to a mechanical rather than electrical problem at the left front speed sensor: wrong part, wrong position, a damaged or soiled encoder, or play in the hub. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's tables and Mitsubishi's index file such faults under range or correlation codes instead. The mechanics are well described elsewhere. GM bulletin PIT5950 for Silverado and Sierra 1500 warns that left and right front sensors look alike, that a swapped part keeps setting codes, and that the flat side of the tip must face the magnetic encoder ring on the wheel bearing. An Infiniti bulletin asks technicians to check the sensor head and the encoder for dirt, cracks, missing teeth, corrosion and looseness, since contamination alone can cause intermittent faults.
c: Magnetic encoder or tone ring dirty, cracked or missing teeth
Sensor for the other side fitted or tip turned away from the encoder
Worn or loose left front hub bearing changing the air gap
s: ABS and stability lamps on, often recurring after a repair
Uneven or missing left front speed reading at low speed

C0519.t: Right Front Wheel Speed Sensor - Mechanical
C0519.d: C0519 is the mechanical-fault code for the right front sensor. It appears in code lists, but no manufacturer publishes a setting rule for it; the known diagnostics put such faults under range, erratic or correlation codes. What goes wrong mechanically at a front wheel is documented in GM bulletin PIT5707: on 2020 Silverado and Sierra HD trucks, manufacturing debris on the reluctor ring set C0504 or C050A, and the cure was cleaning the ring without a magnet, sometimes with the front hub removed. Allegro explains why geometry matters at all: the magnetic field reaching a Hall sensor weakens steeply as the air gap grows, so a sensor that is not fully seated, a bent bracket or bearing play can leave the signal too weak to read.
c: Metal debris or rust buildup on the right front reluctor ring
Sensor not fully seated or bracket bent, air gap too large
s: ABS lamp and stability service message
ABS may regulate unexpectedly at walking pace

C051A.t: Left Rear Wheel Speed Sensor - Mechanical
C051A.d: C051A names a mechanical fault at the left rear sensor. Like its siblings it is listed but not documented by any manufacturer, so the actual setting rule is unknown. At the rear axle the encoder sits in different places: inside the hub bearing seal on many cars, as HELLA describes for multipole rings, or on the axle shaft or hub of rigid axles. Ford special service messages show the rear-specific risks: on Ford's F-53 motorhome chassis of 2020, rear axle tone rings bent during hub and rotor installation, and on 2021–2022 F-150 trucks with a three-quarter floating axle, metal particles on axle tone rings and sensors set rear sensor codes until the axle tubes were cleaned. Those Ford cases were stored as C0037 and C0036, not as C051A.
c: Metal particles or rust on the rear encoder or sensor tip
Rear tone ring bent or cracked, often after hub or brake work
Left rear hub bearing worn, encoder seal damaged
s: ABS lamp, sometimes only under load or on rough roads
Rear wheel speed drops out or jitters in live data

C051B.t: Right Rear Wheel Speed Sensor - Mechanical
C051B.d: C051B covers a mechanical defect at the right rear wheel. No public manufacturer document defines when it is set; the cases known from bulletins carry other codes. They still show what to inspect at a right rear wheel. GM's 2018 program 18316 for Express and Savana vans found that axle vibration over rumble strips shook the right rear sensor signal into erratic values, and changed the brake module calibration rather than any part. Ford's message on the F-53 chassis covers tone rings deformed while hub and rotor were refitted. Infiniti's sensor bulletin adds loose or corroded tone wheels and bearings to the list. A mechanical code therefore calls for a look at encoder, bearing and sensor fit before electrical testing.
c: Right rear tone ring deformed or corroded
Right rear hub bearing loose or worn
Axle vibration disturbing the signal on rough surfaces
s: ABS, stability and traction lamps after rough stretches
Driver aids unavailable until the next ignition cycle

C051C.t: Multi-axis Acceleration Sensor Module A Range/Performance
C051C.d: Module A delivers yaw rate and accelerations along several axes, but at least one channel sits outside what the vehicle's motion allows, for example a turn rate while parked or a lateral g that does not fit speed and steering. No manufacturer documents C051C publicly, so exact limits are unknown. Patents show why such checks matter: in a Kelsey-Hayes (now ZF) filing a sensor tilted by 5 degrees reports about 8.7 deg/s of yaw during a hard pitch, while stability control typically reacts at 3 to 7 deg/s; an Autoliv patent tracks slowly creeping offsets with a moving average. Unlike the calibration and correlation codes, here the reading itself is implausible. Stability control usually switches off with its warning lamp lit.
c: Module A loose, tilted or mounted on a deformed bracket
Internal offset of the inertial sensor drifted beyond tolerance
Defective sensing element inside module A
Wrong module variant fitted or installed in the wrong orientation
s: ESC or traction control warning lamp on
Stability control unavailable or intervening without reason
Yaw rate or acceleration not zero at standstill (scan tool)

C051D.t: Multi-axis Acceleration Sensor Module A Missing Calibration
C051D.d: The module holds no valid zero point or mounting orientation, typically after it or the brake controller was replaced and the setup step was skipped. Corrections like these live in non-volatile memory: Kelsey-Hayes measures the offset of the whole assembly on a turning stand and adds the in-car tilt. GM's Saab 9-4x shows the workshop side: a new multi-axis module (called IMU in the programming tool) must first be configured, then the yaw sensor learned on level ground. On its Super Cruise controller GM files missing offset or orientation learning and a detected swap of the high-performance IMU under C0520 instead. No public source uses C051D itself. Stability control stays off until the learn is done.
c: Module A or brake control module replaced without configuration and yaw sensor learn
Learn procedure aborted, e.g. vehicle not level or voltage dropped
Stored calibration lost after software update or module fault
s: ESC warning lamp on right after a repair
Stability and traction control unavailable
Driver assistance such as adaptive cruise may be disabled

C051E.t: Multi-axis Acceleration Sensor Module A Intermittent/Erratic
C051E.d: Module A's data arrive, but values jump, freeze briefly or vanish for short moments instead of changing smoothly. Modern units digitise yaw rate and accelerations inside the module and pass them on over a serial link: Bosch's SMI810 uses SafeSPI with 16-bit data, and a Hyundai/Kia design checks each value against the sensor's measuring range before sending it over CAN to the stability controller. Loose plugs, vibration or supply dips can therefore show up as erratic samples. No manufacturer publishes C051E, so limits are unknown. The intermittent label separates it from a steady implausible value (C051C) and from a disagreement with other signals (C051F). The ESC lamp may come and go between drives.
c: Loose or corroded connector at module A
Brief supply or ground dropouts, weak battery
Module not firmly fastened, picks up vibration
Sporadic internal fault of the sensor electronics
s: ESC warning lamp comes and goes
Stability control occasionally unavailable
Jumping yaw or acceleration values in live data

C051F.t: Multi-axis Acceleration Sensor Module A Correlation
C051F.d: The brake controller finds that module A's signals do not agree with a second source of the same motion. Audi uses this code on the e-tron: the ABS unit (address 0003) stores C051F00, and Audi's 2019 bulletin names the suspension control module as sensor module A. Waking the bus while the car falls asleep could set it, along with implausible lateral acceleration and yaw codes and a lost airbag-unit message; often an ignition cycle clears it, otherwise a drive above about 30 mph with the wheel turned 60 degrees each way. Bulletin 2061908 (2019 to 2024 e-tron and Q8 e-tron) logs it sporadically and fixes it with new ABS and suspension software. Bosch patents cross-check redundant inertial sensors the same way.
c: ABS or suspension control software fault (Audi e-tron update)
Bus woken while modules enter sleep mode (door, charger)
Module A misaligned so its axes no longer match the reference
Fault in the comparison source (second inertial sensor, steering angle, wheel speeds)
s: ESC warning lamp and several cluster messages
Yellow drive fault message (Audi e-tron)
Fault often gone after the next ignition cycle

C0520.d: General fault of module A without a narrower fault type. GM gives the most detail: in the 2023 and 2025 OBD tables of its Super Cruise controller (EOCM3), C0520 watches the high-performance IMU and sets when initialisation does not finish in time, the unit resets, its temperature status is invalid, offset or orientation learning is missing, or a swapped IMU is detected via its serial number. GM rates it Special Type C, emissions neutral, so no check-engine lamp; adaptive cruise and Super Cruise are switched off. Audi lists C052000 on the 2019 e-tron next to C051F00 for module A in the suspension control module. Compared with C051C to C051F, the code says only that the module as a whole failed.
c: IMU fails to initialise in time or resets during operation
Module swapped, offset or orientation calibration not learned
Software fault in the module or the receiving controller
Internal electronic failure of module A
s: ESC warning lamp or service message for stability control
Adaptive cruise or hands-free driving assistance unavailable (GM)
No check-engine lamp

C0521.t: Multi-axis Acceleration Sensor Module B Range/Performance
C0521.d: Same fault type as C051C, but for a second inertial module B: its rates or accelerations lie outside what driving physics permits. No manufacturer explains C0521 publicly, and which unit is B on a given car is not documented either. A second unit is common on vehicles with automated driving, where Bosch offers IMUs up to two-fold ASIL-D and stresses redundancy. A GM patent explains what corrupts such readings: six bias terms and three mounting angles, which plant calibration only partly removes and which change over time; GM estimates them from satellite navigation data. Assistance features that rely on module B, and possibly stability control, are suspended while the code is present.
c: Module B loose, tilted or bracket bent after a repair or impact
Bias of the accelerometers or gyros drifted out of tolerance
Defective sensing element inside module B
s: Driver assistance or ESC warning message
Adaptive cruise or lane functions unavailable
Module B reading not zero at standstill (scan tool)

C0522.t: Multi-axis Acceleration Sensor Module B Missing Calibration
C0522.d: Module B lacks its stored zero point or installation data, so its readings cannot be trusted. No manufacturer publishes C0522, and which unit carries the letter B is not documented. A Hyundai/Kia design that moves the inertial sensor into the airbag control unit applies offset correction inside the sensor according to the vehicle set-up and keeps data in one-time-programmable memory; Kelsey-Hayes stores assembly and in-car offsets in the controller's non-volatile memory. GM's Saab 9-4x procedure shows the practical rule: a replacement multi-axis module is configured with the programming tool and the yaw sensor learned afterwards. Without that step, functions using module B stay unavailable.
c: Module B or its host control unit replaced without configuration
Vehicle variant or mounting position coded incorrectly
Calibration data lost after software update
s: Warning message appears directly after a repair
Assistance or stability functions unavailable

C0523.t: Multi-axis Acceleration Sensor Module B Intermittent/Erratic
C0523.d: Module B sends values that jump or drop out now and then. No manufacturer publishes C0523, so limits and the identity of module B stay open. GM bulletins show that a separate multi-axis module is a networked unit of its own: on 2013 to 2014 Malibu, LaCrosse and Regal it logs U0121 in history at key-up because the brake module answers late, which GM calls normal, and on 2018 to 2020 Equinox and Terrain U0125 for a lost module is cured by brake controller software. Such communication codes are separate from C0523, which concerns erratic content. Bosch's SMI810 sends 16-bit SafeSPI frames, so contact faults appear as sporadic bad samples. Warnings may come and go.
c: Loose or corroded connector or ground at module B
Supply dips from a weak battery or poor connections
Sporadic internal fault in module B
s: Assistance or ESC warning comes and goes
Code stored in history without current fault
Jumping values from module B in live data

C0524.t: Multi-axis Acceleration Sensor Module B Correlation
C0524.d: Module B's readings disagree with another source for the same motion, most likely module A or values computed from steering angle and wheel speeds. No manufacturer publishes C0524; Audi documents only the A counterpart. A Bosch patent places two sensor devices on opposite sides of the car and treats yaw rate as measured twice, directly and via the centrifugal accelerations at each spot, so a control unit can spot a device giving falsified data. A Hyundai/Kia design moves the yaw and g sensors into the airbag unit and sends them over CAN to the stability controller, a layout where the airbag and brake systems can each hold a set. Which side is wrong is left to further testing.
c: Module A or B rotated on its mount after repair or impact
Drifting sensor in one of the two modules
Software or timing fault in the comparing controller
s: ESC or assistance warning message
Stability or assistance functions limited

C0525.d: General fault of module B, without stating whether range, calibration, signal stability or correlation is at fault. No manufacturer publishes C0525, and the location of module B is not documented. According to Bosch, one inertial unit can feed stability control as well as the airbag electronics, and an integrated version exists; the 2013 Buick Regal, for example, carries its multi-axis sensor in a module of its own at GM. FCA files a comparable internal failure as C006A-49 on Ram pickups and says that replacing the ABS or occupant restraint module is unnecessary if the code clears after a software update. Whether module B means a second IMU or a sensor in another controller therefore depends on the make.
c: Software fault, fixed by an update of the host module
Internal electronic failure of module B
Supply or ground fault at module B
s: ESC, airbag-related or assistance warning depending on host module
Stability or assistance functions unavailable

C0526.d: C0526 is the base code for the steering angle sensor module, used when a fault is reported without a more specific failure type. MINI documents it for the 2017 Countryman F60 plug-in hybrid: an on-board diagnosis error in the electric power steering software stored C0526, readable only with a generic OBD tool, and lit the check-engine lamp. It occurred after the car had been in transport mode and the terminals were switched twice without steering; turning lock to lock, a driving-readiness routine and later software clear it. Sensors such as Bosch's derive the absolute angle from two gear-driven magnets read by GMR elements and send angle and rate over CAN. Typical consequences are an ESC lamp and, on EPS cars, reduced assist.
c: Power steering software error (MINI F60 PHEV 2017)
Supply loss or battery disconnection without relearning
Internal fault in the steering angle sensor module
s: Check-engine lamp on (MINI F60 PHEV)
ESC warning lamp on, stability control limited

C0527.d: C0527 marks a mechanical rather than electrical fault of the steering angle sensor module. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Many sensors are gear-driven: Bosch and Saab describe a hub gear on the steering shaft turning two measuring gears with different tooth counts (28 and 26 on the Saab 9-5), whose magnet positions encode the absolute angle. Broken teeth, a cracked housing, a worn drive dog or a sensor clipped in out of position make the reported angle stop following the wheel although supply and bus are fine. Bourns' contactless type checks its own angular speed and reports an error beyond 1016°/s, which a jumping gear would cause. Stability control is usually switched off; the cure is a new sensor and re-centring.
c: Worn or broken measuring gears inside the sensor
Sensor drive dog or mounting loose on the steering shaft
Sensor installed out of position after column or clock spring work
s: ESC warning lamp on
Angle on the scan tool jumps or stops changing while steering
Possible noise from the steering column

C0528.d: C0528 means the module delivers an angle that is out of range or behaves implausibly while it still communicates. Audi documents it on the 2015–2018 A3 e-tron as C052800, steering angle sender with implausible signal, sometimes stored together with P060700 after ESC had been switched off (TSB 2060682/1); the ESC lamp lights. A Kelsey-Hayes patent shows how such checks work: an offset that moves more than 15° after re-zeroing counts as a shift fault, more than 10 s of cumulative dropouts or 1000 events as intermittent, and yaw control stays off until the signal is trusted again. Bosch builds plausibility tests between the measuring channels into its GMR sensor. Unlike C052A, the error lies in the sensor value itself.
c: Steering angle sensor module delivering implausible values
ABS/ESC module software issue (Audi A3 e-tron)
Offset after alignment or steering work without re-zeroing
s: ESC warning lamp on
Stability control unavailable or intervening at odd moments

C0529.t: Steering Angle Sensor Module Missing Calibration
C0529.d: C0529 is set when the steering angle sensor module has no valid zero point. Stellantis documents it as C0529-00 on the 2023 Dodge Hornet and the 2023–2024 Alfa Romeo Tonale: if the wheel was turned without assist between key-off and key-on, the calibration was lost and the MIL came on, going out again after a lock-to-lock turn; an EPS software update fixes it (TSB 08-148-23, 08-163-23). For the 2022–2023 Ram ProMaster, an internal note asks for sensor initialisation by turning lock to lock with the engine running, or via wiTECH, after battery disconnection and before any steering gear replacement. Saab and Mitsubishi likewise require a straight-ahead calibration after alignment or sensor replacement.
c: Calibration lost after battery disconnection or steering while switched off
Initialisation skipped after steering gear, sensor or alignment work
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on (Stellantis)
ESC warning lamp on, stability control limited until calibrated
Lamp goes out after turning the wheel from lock to lock

C052A.d: The steering angle sensor module reports wheel angle and turn rate to the stability control unit, which cross-checks that value against an independent estimate. Correlation means the reading and the estimate disagree for longer than the calibrated window; the signal itself is present. A Bosch patent derives a model yaw rate from the angle and the left/right wheel-speed difference, and a Ford patent lets the ESC unit judge an angle supplied by electric power steering from yaw rate, wheel speeds and lateral acceleration, switching ESC off with a warning lamp if the check fails. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. Typical triggers are an offset after an alignment or steering repair and an internal module fault. Unlike C0528 or C0529, the sensor may look sane on its own.
c: Angle offset after wheel alignment or steering work without zero-point adjustment
Internal fault in the steering angle sensor module
Faulty comparison signal (yaw rate, wheel speed or steering angle from power steering)
s: ESC or traction control warning lamp on
Stability control switched off or intervening at the wrong moment
Steering wheel off-centre when driving straight

C052B.d: Range/performance fault of the ABS pump motor: the drive is commanded, but the motor or its relay does not behave as expected. On the 2023 Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV the brake unit maps C1051-04 (and C1051-49, added by bulletin TSB-23-35-002) to C052B; it is checked with normal supply voltage, set within 12 s; after a single trip the ASC, ABS and brake warnings plus the check-engine lamp come on. ESC, traction control, ABS, EBD, brake assist and regenerative braking are suspended. An AlliedSignal patent, now held by Bosch, shows one test: a healthy motor coasts after switch-off and its voltage decays slowly, so a decay faster than about 134 V/s marks a motor that did not turn. Usually motor or pump in the hydraulic unit are worn or seized; basic braking stays.
c: Pump motor worn (brushes) or pump seized in the hydraulic unit
Motor relay or switching stage in the ABS unit faulty
Marginal supply or ground connection under motor load
s: ABS, ESC and brake warning lamps on
ABS and stability control unavailable, normal braking remains
No pump noise during the self-test after starting off

C052C.d: Open circuit in the ABS pump motor drive: the control unit finds no current path through motor or relay where one should exist. Mitsubishi lists C1051-13 as C052C on the 2023 Outlander PHEV within the same frame as C052B (normal supply, up to 12 s, ABS, ASC, brake and engine lamps after one trip, stability and regenerative braking functions off). Its confirmation drive runs at roughly 50 km/h for about two minutes, so a cleared code may only return on the road. A Bosch patent spots an interruption while the motor is not driven: two resistors bias both terminals to a middle level, and a broken loop drags one terminal down and the other up. Likely causes are a loose connector, burnt brushes or an open winding inside the hydraulic unit.
c: Loose or corroded connector at the ABS unit
Worn brushes or open winding in the pump motor
s: ABS and ESC warning lamps on
ABS, traction and stability control switched off
Code returns only after a short drive

C052D.t: ABS Pump Motor Control Circuit High
C052D.d: The pump motor control circuit reads higher than the commanded state allows, which normally means the control line or motor terminal is shorted toward battery voltage or the switching stage is stuck on. No manufacturer publishes this code; Mitsubishi, for example, reports its pump motor faults under C052B and C052C. The Bosch fault-monitoring patent US5329238 shows the principle: terminal voltages are compared with supply-referenced limits, a level above the upper one is taken as a short to plus, and the drive is then cut. With a stuck-on stage the pump may hum continuously and drain the 12 V battery. The US brake standard FMVSS 135 requires a warning for any electrical ABS failure; normal braking without ABS remains.
c: Motor relay or semiconductor switch in the ABS unit stuck closed
Motor lead or control line shorted to battery voltage
Moisture bridging pins in the ABS connector
s: ABS warning lamp on
Pump motor runs continuously or hums with ignition on
Battery discharged after standing

C052E.t: ABS Pump Motor Control Circuit Low
C052E.d: Low counterpart of C052D: the pump motor control signal stays near ground when it should rise, pointing to a short to ground on the control side, a failed driver stage or a weak ground path of the hydraulic unit. No maker documents C052E publicly. In the Bosch patent US5329238 a terminal below the lower threshold is treated as a short to minus, and the drive is limited or switched off. Ford traced its older pump code C0020 on 2020 Explorer, Aviator and Police Interceptor Utility (bulletin 20-2364) to bad ground contact at G108, partly due to unsuitable bolt plating, and replaced the fasteners instead of the module, a reminder to check grounds first. While the code is active the pump cannot run on demand, so ABS and stability control are disabled.
c: Poor ground connection of the ABS unit or hydraulic block
Control line or motor lead shorted to ground
Driver stage in the ABS control unit failed
s: ABS and ESC warning lamps on
ABS and stability control unavailable

C052F.t: ABS Pump Motor Supply Voltage Circuit/Open
C052F.d: The pump motor has its own battery feed, separate from the logic supply, and this code reports that feed as missing or open. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV manual shows the layout: motor and motor relay draw from a 60 A fusible link and must see 10–16 V at the unit connector, the valves from a separate 50 A link, the electronics from a 5 A fuse. Mitsubishi itself reports such a loss through its pump motor code and lists fuse, fusible link and 12 V battery as causes, not via C052F. An AlliedSignal patent (now Bosch) logs a separate fault when the motor voltage at switch-off is below about 7 V. Because the electronics stay powered, the module still communicates and lights the ABS lamp while the pump is dead.
c: Pump motor fuse or fusible link blown
Corroded or loose battery feed terminal at the ABS connector
Open or high-resistance ground of the ABS unit
s: ABS and ESC warning lamps on
Pump motor never runs, ABS and stability control off

C0530.d: Plausibility fault of motor control A: the circuit is electrically intact, but the motor does not answer its command as the module expects – it stalls, runs too slowly or keeps turning. SAE J2012 lists the code in the chassis block beside the ABS pump motor and valve codes without naming the motor, and no manufacturer was found that publicly assigns it, so which drive counts as A stays open. A typical check comes from an Advics patent for brake pump motors: after the relay opens, the back-EMF is watched; if it falls below a lower threshold too early for several 1 ms cycles in a row, the motor is judged seized rather than merely loaded. The affected chassis function is switched off and its warning lamp lit.
c: Motor or driven mechanism stiff or seized
Worn motor (brushes, bearings) delivering too little speed
Fault in the control unit's motor stage or feedback evaluation
s: Chassis or brake warning lamp on
The function driven by motor A is unavailable

C0531.d: Motor control A sees an open circuit: with the stage switched off, the module cannot detect the expected current path through the motor. J2012 names no specific motor and no public manufacturer assignment was found, so the actuator behind A depends on the vehicle. Detection usually runs while the motor rests: in the Bosch patent US5329238 resistors bias both motor terminals, and an interruption pushes them apart toward opposite rails; automotive H-bridge drivers such as TI's DRV8873-Q1 offer an open-load test for the same purpose, before the motor is commutated and while it runs. Typical causes are an unplugged connector, a broken wire or a burnt-out winding or brush. The motor stays still until the circuit is closed, and the related function is disabled.
c: Connector to motor A unplugged or corroded
Broken motor lead in the harness
Open winding or worn brush in motor A
s: Warning lamp of the affected system on
Motor A does not run at all

C0532.d: Motor control A reads high: a motor output sits near supply voltage although the driver commands it low or off. That points to a short to battery voltage in the motor leads or a high-side switch that no longer opens. J2012 leaves the motor unnamed and no manufacturer publication assigning C0532 was found. Bosch's US5329238 compares each terminal with limits scaled to the measured supply and treats an exceeded upper limit as a short to plus, after which drive is cut in one or both directions; TI's DRV8873-Q1 guards against shorts to battery with overcurrent protection that disables the affected half-bridge. If the motor stays energised it may run on or overheat; otherwise the function simply drops out with its warning lamp.
c: Motor lead chafed against a live wire
High-side switch in the control unit stuck on
Moisture bridging pins in the connector
s: Warning lamp of the affected system on
Motor A runs on or gets hot

C0533.d: Motor control A reads low: an output that should be driven up stays close to ground. Typical reasons are chafed motor wiring touching the body, water in a connector or a failed low-side stage; a stalled motor drawing excess current can look similar to the driver.
