The J2012 title gives no motor, and no maker was found that documents C0533, so the A assignment remains vehicle-specific. In the Bosch patent US5329238 a terminal under the lower threshold during active drive indicates a short to minus; TI's DRV8873-Q1 handles shorts to ground through its overcurrent protection and can latch the affected half-bridge off. Because a ground short can draw high current, the module disables the motor and the associated function and sets its warning.
c: Motor lead chafed through to body ground
Water ingress in the motor connector
Low-side stage in the control unit failed
s: Warning lamp of the affected system on
Motor A does not start; a fuse may blow

C0534.t: Motor Control A Supply Voltage Circuit/Open
C0534.d: The power feed of motor control A is missing or open, so the driver stage has nothing to switch even though the logic side of the module is alive. Chassis motors often get a dedicated battery feed: in the brake unit of the 2023 Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV, for example, the pump motor hangs on its own 60 A fusible link and needs 10–16 V at the connector. Driver ICs watch this rail as well; TI's DRV8873-Q1 locks out its outputs on supply undervoltage. J2012 does not say which motor is A, and no public manufacturer assignment of C0534 was found. Check the fuse or fusible link, the feed wire and the ground before suspecting the module; the function remains off until the supply is restored.
c: Fuse or fusible link of the motor feed blown
Open feed wire or loose supply terminal
Missing ground of the control unit's power stage
s: Warning lamp of the affected system on
Motor A never runs while other functions of the module work

C0535.d: Second motor channel B fails its plausibility check: wiring and supply test fine, yet the motor's reaction to commands is wrong, for example too little speed, a delayed start or no stop. Where a controller drives two motors or two channels, A and B separate them; J2012 does not say which motor B is, and no manufacturer publicly assigns C0535, so the meaning must come from the vehicle's own service data. How such a check can work is shown by an AlliedSignal patent now held by Bosch: after shut-off a spinning DC motor acts as a generator, and a voltage collapse faster than roughly 134 V/s means it never really turned. Causes lie mostly in the motor or the driven mechanism; the channel A counterpart is C0530.
c: Driven mechanism of motor B binding or blocked
Motor B worn and too slow
Faulty speed or position feedback in the control unit
s: Warning lamp of the affected system on
Function of motor B slow, incomplete or unavailable

C0536.d: Motor control B finds its load missing. The module expects a closed path through the windings of channel B and sees an open circuit instead – a pulled connector, a cut lead, corroded pins or an internal break in the motor. Brake controllers have run dedicated open-circuit routines for pump motors for decades, as in a Kelsey-Hayes patent (now ZF) that checks the motor circuit while the pump is not requested; current bridge driver chips like the DRV8873-Q1 from TI provide open-load detection both in standby and during operation. J2012 does not identify the motor behind B and no public manufacturer documentation of C0536 was found. Until repaired the motor stays dead and the function it serves is unavailable; compare C0531 for channel A.
c: Connector to motor B pulled off or pins corroded
Motor lead cut or broken in the harness
Internal break in motor B (winding, brush)
s: Warning lamp of the affected system on
Motor B shows no reaction

C0537.d: Channel B of the motor control reads high, meaning a motor terminal is pulled toward battery voltage against the command. A pinched lead touching a live wire, moisture bridging pins in a shared connector, or a high-side switch stuck in the conducting state are the usual suspects. For the shut-down logic, the Bosch patent US5329238 distinguishes this case from a short to minus and can block drive in just one direction; TI's DRV8873-Q1 covers shorts to battery with its overcurrent monitoring, which can latch, retry or only report. C0537 appears in no public manufacturer document found, and J2012 leaves the motor unnamed. Expect the function to be off, possibly with a motor that briefly runs on; the A-side equivalent is C0532.
c: Pinched motor B lead contacting a live wire
Moisture between pins of a shared connector
High-side switch for channel B not opening
s: Warning lamp of the affected system on
Motor B runs on briefly or the function is switched off

C0538.d: Motor control B reads low: a channel-B output is held near ground. Besides a direct short of a motor lead to the body, the Bosch patent US5329238 also covers the case where both terminals deviate at once while driven, which it reads as a short across the motor itself or between its two lines. Driver chips such as TI's DRV8873-Q1 react to a short to ground through their overcurrent protection and switch the half-bridge off. J2012 does not tie the code to a specific motor and no public manufacturer assignment of C0538 appears in the sources reviewed. Inspect harness routing near moving parts and connectors for water before replacing the motor or module; channel A uses C0533 for the same fault.
c: Motor B lead shorted to body near moving parts
Short across motor B or between its two lines
Water in the connector of motor B
s: Warning lamp of the affected system on
Motor B does not start

C0539.t: Motor Control B Supply Voltage Circuit/Open
C0539.d: Motor control B has lost its power supply, or the supply circuit is open. In many brake and chassis controllers the motor stage is fed by its own fused battery line while the logic runs from ignition, so the module can still communicate and store this code. A Hitachi patent for electric brake actuators monitors the vehicle supply line and, once it drops to a set level, switches to backup power and limits motor current; driver ICs like TI's DRV8873-Q1 enforce an undervoltage lockout on their motor supply. J2012 does not specify the motor behind B and no manufacturer was found that documents C0539 publicly. Check the fuse or fusible link, the supply wire, connector and ground; for channel A see C0534.
c: Fuse or fusible link of the channel B feed open
Weak 12 V battery pulling the motor supply below the limit
s: Warning lamp of the affected system on
Motor B never runs although the module communicates

C053A.d: The brake control unit holds no valid calibration for its ABS valves. Analog-controlled inlet valves open at a current that depends on the pressure difference, manufacturing scatter and wear, so the controller needs a stored opening-current curve to meter pressure finely. Continental patents describe how it is learned: the pump builds pressure (about 130–150 bar, or points at 150 and 50 bar) against a valve held shut by roughly 1800 mA, then the current is lowered until the valve opens. One of them notes the data are lost when the electronics are replaced. Hence the code typically follows a module or hydraulic unit swap, or an aborted learning run. No manufacturer documents C053A publicly; running the calibration with a scan tool usually clears it.
c: ABS control unit or hydraulic unit replaced without valve calibration
Calibration run aborted (low voltage, air in the system, conditions not met)
Software update or memory fault erased the calibration data
s: ABS and ESC warning lamps on
ABS and stability control limited or switched off

C053B.d: Supply fault on the ABS solenoid valves: the feed that powers the inlet and outlet valves, usually switched through a valve relay inside the brake unit, is missing or open. On the 2023 Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV the code is C1048-11 (valve relay), shown as C053B; it is checked with normal supply, set within 2 s, and lights ASC, ABS, brake and check-engine lamps after one trip. A confirmation run needs only ignition on and a 10 s wait. The valve side is fed from a 50 A fusible link and should read 10–16 V at the connector. The fail-safe suspends ABS, EBD, ESC and traction control together with brake assist and the electric parking brake. Without valve power the module cannot modulate pressure, while the foundation brakes keep working.
c: Valve relay inside the ABS unit faulty
Fusible link of the valve supply blown
Damaged or loose terminal in the ABS connector
s: ABS, ESC and brake warning lamps on
ABS, stability control and electric parking brake functions unavailable

C053C.d: A wheel speed signal is implausible, but the fault is reported generically rather than for one named wheel. Mitsubishi uses C106A-64 as C053C on the 2023 Outlander PHEV and runs four detection paths, one per sensor, each with a delay of at most 1 s; listed causes include the sensor, its rotor and a wrong tire size, and the code needs two trips before ASC, ABS, brake, parking brake and check-engine lamps light. Active Hall sensors, as Bosch describes them, read a rotating encoder and send pulses whose frequency follows wheel speed down to about 0.1 km/h, so mismatched tires or a damaged encoder ring distort the comparison. Wheel-specific circuit faults use C0500 ff., wrong parts C0555–C0558.
c: Mismatched tire sizes or a space-saver spare fitted
Damaged or dirty encoder ring (sensor rotor)
Wheel speed sensor faulty or not seated correctly
s: ABS, ESC and brake warning lamps on after two trips
ABS, traction control and stability control switched off
Speed-dependent assistance functions unavailable

C053D.d: The brake pressure sensor A signal is electrically present, but its value does not fit the braking situation. GM stores C053D in the brake system control module, calling it a circuit performance fault: on 2019 Silverado/Sierra 1500 drivers got a hard pedal plus the Service Brake Assist warning (PIT5638), and bulletin 20-NA-073 lists it among faults that drop the brake-by-wire system into its mechanical Push-Thru mode; the fix is BSCM software. Stellantis logs it as Brake Pressure Sensor 1 Performance in the PCM of the 2023 Grand Cherokee, where the PCM compares the sensor with the pedal position sensor inside the BSCM; remedy is a PCM flash or an ABS initialization. Mitsubishi maps C106C-02 to it (Outlander PHEV 2023, ASC lamp plus MIL after two trips).
c: Brake or engine control software with an over-sensitive plausibility check (several bulletins)
Pressure and pedal sensors not initialized after module or hydraulic unit replacement
Air in the brake lines distorting the pressure build-up
Stop-light switch or pedal sensor delivering a mismatching reference
Drifting pressure sensor in the hydraulic unit
s: Brake assist or stability control warning shown
Brake pedal hard or travelling further than usual
Check-engine lamp on some models

C053E.t: Brake Pressure Sensor A Circuit Low
C053E.d: The voltage on the signal line of brake pressure sensor A has dropped under the lower limit the brake module accepts. Such ratiometric 5-V sensors normally stay within a window: an older Saab 9-5 brake unit faults its pressure sensor below 0.25 V held for 0.1 s. Usual triggers are a signal wire shorted to ground, a lost 5-V feed or a sensor failing internally. GM shows a second pattern: on 2024 Silverado/Sierra 2500HD/3500HD, C053E with a MIL message at start-up came from the sensor still initializing and warming up; bulletin 24-NA-016 prescribes new EBCM software and warns against replacing the modulator valve. Mitsubishi lists C106C-16 as this code (Outlander PHEV 2023). Unlike C053F the reading is too low; unlike C053D it is electrically out of range.
c: Signal wire chafed through and touching ground
Missing or weak 5-V reference to the sensor
Module software flagging the sensor during start-up warm-up (GM HD trucks 2024)
s: ABS or stability control warning lamp lit
Message in the driver display right after start-up
Stability, traction control or brake assist switched off

C053F.t: Brake Pressure Sensor A Circuit High
C053F.d: Brake pressure sensor A reports a voltage above the upper limit of its valid band. Since the sensor is fed with 5 V, a short of the signal line to the reference or to battery voltage, a broken ground wire or an internal fault can push the reading up; a Saab 9-5 brake unit draws the line at 4.75 V lasting 0.1 s. GM-built Saab 9-5 models from 2011 check both the 5-V reference and the signal wire of the pressure sensor, which sits in the brake modulator valve block, and then disable ABS, traction and stability control for the ignition cycle. The only public code mapping comes from Mitsubishi: C106C-17 equals C053F on the 2023 Outlander PHEV, with ASC lamp and MIL after two trips and a detection delay of a second at most. C053E is the opposite fault.
c: Signal wire shorted to the 5-V reference or battery voltage
Pressure sensor in the hydraulic unit defective
s: ABS and stability control warning lamps on
Traction control, stability control and hill-start assist unavailable
Check-engine lamp on some hybrids

C0540.d: General electrical fault in the circuit of brake pressure sensor A, typically an interrupted signal, reference or ground wire, or a connection with excessive resistance. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; Mitsubishi, for example, maps its sensor-A faults to C0044 and C053D to C053F instead. The function is well described elsewhere: a Bosch patent has the master-cylinder pressure sensor report to the ESC controller, which lights ABS and ESC lamps and changes to a reduced or off state on a fault, and Saab 9-5 (2011) service data checks the 5-V feed and the signal wire for opens within 0.1 s and then shuts off ABS, traction and stability control until the next ignition cycle. Ordinary braking remains. Low and high voltages have their own codes, C053E and C053F.
c: Loose, corroded or pushed-out pin at the sensor or brake module connector
Broken signal, reference or ground wire
Internal open circuit in the pressure sensor
s: ABS and ESC warning lamps on
Stability and traction control out of service
Brake assist or hill-start assist missing

C0541.d: Brake pressure sensor B delivers a valid voltage, yet the value is implausible. Which sensor carries the letter B varies by maker. Bentley documents the code for the Continental GT/GTC (2018–2022) and Flying Spur (2020–2022): C054100 in the ESC unit J104 is labelled as a fault of the rear-left pressure sensor, adaptive cruise control becomes unavailable, and the repair is a new J104 because the sensor is built into it. Typical tests behind such a fault are described by Saab, whose 9-5 brake module rejects a pressure reading that does not match deceleration or the brake switch, and by a Honda patent that declares the sensor failed when pedal stroke grows but pressure does not. A Bosch patent adds an offset that has drifted too far. C0542 to C0544 are the electrical faults.
c: Pressure sensor inside the ESC hydraulic unit drifting or sluggish
Zero-point calibration not done after module or valve block replacement
Brake light switch or pedal sensor giving a contradictory reference
s: Adaptive cruise control unavailable
ESC or ABS warning in the cluster
Assistance functions such as brake assist reduced

C0542.t: Brake Pressure Sensor B Circuit Low
C0542.d: Brake pressure sensor B pulls its signal below the lowest voltage the receiving module treats as valid. Two makers name the code in public bulletins. Bentley lists C054200 in the ESC unit J104 of the Continental GT/GTC and Flying Spur alongside C054100, with adaptive cruise switched off and the J104 replaced. Stellantis lists C0542 as Brake Pressure Sensor 2 Circuit Low among powertrain-module faults of the 2019 Jeep Cherokee with 3.2-litre V6 and engine stop-start; there a PCM software update was the remedy, with a check-engine lamp as the complaint. As a reference for the electrical limit, a Saab 9-5 brake unit treats anything under 0.25 V lasting 0.1 s as a sensor fault. Signal shorts to ground, a missing 5-V feed or a failed sensor are the usual causes.
c: Sensor or the ESC unit with integrated sensor defective
Engine control software misjudging the signal (Jeep Cherokee 2019)
s: Check-engine or ESC warning lamp on
Adaptive cruise control or stop-start unavailable

C0543.t: Brake Pressure Sensor B Circuit High
C0543.d: Here the signal of brake pressure sensor B sits above the top of its permitted range, which points to a signal wire touching the 5-V reference or battery voltage, an open sensor ground, or a sensor that has failed high. Stellantis is the one maker naming the code publicly: bulletins covering the stop-start Cherokee of model year 2019 with the 3.2-litre V6 list Brake Pressure Sensor 2 Circuit High next to the matching low fault, logged in the engine control module and cleared up by new PCM software (18-023-19, 18-077-22). For the electrical threshold, a Saab 9-5 brake module flags readings above 4.75 V held for 0.1 s. Unlike C0541 this is a pure voltage fault; C0542 is the low counterpart and C0544 the open circuit.
c: Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage
Sensor ground open or high resistance
Engine control software fault (Jeep Cherokee 2019 bulletins)
Sensor failed with permanently high output
s: Check-engine lamp on
Stop-start or brake-related assistance not working

C0544.d: The brake module sees a general electrical fault in the circuit of pressure sensor B, usually an interruption in signal, feed or ground. No maker publishes this exact meaning; note that GM bulletins use C0544 for a different, steering-related fault in its power steering module, so a GM scan result must be read with GM definitions. For the component itself, Saab 9-5 (2011) data shows how such circuits are watched: the brake module watches both the sensor feed and its output line, sets a fault after 0.1 s of open or high resistance and disables ABS, traction and stability control for that ignition cycle. Bentley shows that sensor B can sit inside the ESC unit, which then has to be replaced as a whole. C0541 covers implausible values, C0542 and C0543 low and high voltage.
c: Connector at sensor or brake module loose or corroded
Interrupted signal, feed or ground wire
Open inside the sensor or the ESC unit carrying it
s: ABS, traction and stability warning lamps on
Driver assistance relying on brake pressure unavailable

C0545.t: VIN Not Programmed or Incompatible - BSCM
C0545.d: The brake system control module (BSCM) holds no vehicle identification number, or one that does not belong to the car it is fitted to. Modules store the VIN in non-volatile memory; GM patents describe a replacement module comparing its own stored VIN with the one held by another control unit and running a configuration routine when they differ, and point out that a swapped or tampered module shows up as a VIN discrepancy. The code therefore appears mainly after a used or new brake module has been installed without the programming and setup the maker requires; Saab 9-5 (2010) service data, for instance, demands programming plus configuration and setup after an EBCM replacement. No maker documents C0545 publicly with this meaning; GM uses the number for a power steering fault.
c: New brake module installed without VIN programming
Used module from another vehicle still carrying its old VIN
Programming session interrupted, for example by low battery voltage
s: ABS or ESC warning lamp on after a module replacement
Brake-related functions limited or disabled

C0546.d: Generic variant without a named module: a chassis control unit reports that its stored vehicle identification number is blank or does not match the car. Which unit sets it is left to the maker, so the scan tool entry shows the module concerned. The principle is documented in GM patents: each unit keeps the VIN in memory, possibly in write-once storage set at the factory; a replaced or manipulated module reveals itself because its number differs from the others, and a fresh module can adopt the vehicle VIN and its configuration on start-up. In practice the code follows a module swap without the required programming. No maker documents C0546 publicly. C0545 is the same fault tied to the brake system module; P0630 and P0631 cover engine and transmission control.
c: Replacement chassis module not programmed with the vehicle VIN
Second-hand module carrying a foreign VIN
Software level not matching the vehicle configuration
s: Warning lamp of the affected chassis system on
Function of the replaced module missing or limited

C0547.d: Fault in the feed circuit powering the vacuum sensor on the brake booster, usually an open or a short on the regulated supply. Such sensors need a stable 5 V: HELLA specifies 4.5 to 5.5 V for its three-pin vacuum sensor (output, ground, supply), whose analogue signal tells the brake control unit when to run the electric vacuum pump. Bosch describes the same sensor as the basis for pump control, stop-start and ESP assistance. A Saab 9-5 brake module shows how a supply is policed on a brake sensor: outside 4.4 to 5.6 V lasting 0.06 s is a fault. No maker documents C0547 publicly. Without valid supply the vacuum value is lost, so assist functions and an electric pump may run on fallback. C0548 is the narrower case of a supply that is merely too low.
c: Supply wire or connector pin interrupted
Supply line shorted to ground or another circuit
Vacuum sensor shorting the supply internally
s: Brake system or ESC warning shown
Stop-start inactive or electric vacuum pump running constantly

C0548.d: The supply reaching the vacuum sensor is present but sags below its lower limit. With a ratiometric sensor every output voltage scales with the feed, so an under-supplied sensor reports a wrong vacuum even if it is healthy. HELLA rates its brake booster vacuum sensor for 4.5 to 5.5 V and maps 0 to −1000 hPa onto 0.5 to 4.5 V; a feed near the bottom of that window already shifts the reading. On a Saab 9-5 the brake module reacts to a sensor supply under 4.4 V within 0.06 s. Typical causes are a weak module output, an extra load on a shared 5-V rail or high resistance in the feed wire. No maker documents C0548 publicly. C0547 covers an open or shorted supply, C054B and C054F low sensor signals.
c: Another sensor on the same 5-V rail drawing it down
Corroded contact or damaged feed wire adding resistance
Weak sensor supply output in the control module
s: Brake or ESC warning lamp on
Vacuum reading implausible in live data
Further codes for sensors on the same supply

C0549.d: General circuit fault of vacuum sensor A, usually a broken or disconnected signal, ground or feed line. The sensor measures the vacuum in the brake booster; Bosch notes that its value lets the system run the electric vacuum pump, permits engine stop-start and supports ESP functions. Mitsubishi shows how a brake unit watches it on the 2023 Outlander PHEV: with power on and normal supply, an open or a short in the brake vacuum sensor circuit, or signal noise, is detected within a second and stored as C1073, after which brake assist is suspended; Mitsubishi does not map that fault to an SAE code. Which physical sensor is called A is manufacturer-specific, and no maker documents C0549 publicly. C054A to C054C cover plausibility, low and high signal.
c: Sensor plug loose or not latched after work in the engine bay
Broken signal, ground or supply wire
Internal open in the vacuum sensor
s: Brake assist warning or ABS lamp on
Stop-start no longer switching off the engine

C054A.d: Vacuum sensor A delivers an in-range voltage that does not agree with what the booster should hold. Patents show the logic: GM compares booster vacuum with engine vacuum from the MAP sensor while the throttle is closed, because the two should track each other without braking, and flags a sensor biased high or low when the difference persists too long; Ford relies on the check valve and treats a booster pressure clearly above manifold pressure as sensor degradation. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV brake unit has a related check that faults a booster vacuum of about 0 kPa while the engine runs (C106D-01), though that may also mean a real leak. No maker documents C054A publicly; A-B assignment varies. Electrical faults are C0549, C054B and C054C.
c: Vacuum sensor drifted or contaminated (oil, moisture)
Real leak in hose, check valve or booster making the reading look wrong
Faulty comparison value, such as manifold pressure
s: Brake assist warning or reduced assist feel
Electric vacuum pump running more often than normal
Stop-start or cylinder deactivation inhibited

C054B.d: The signal of vacuum sensor A has fallen below the lowest voltage a working sensor can produce. In HELLA's design the output runs from 0.5 V at no vacuum to 4.5 V at −1000 hPa and is clamped to a 0.4–4.8 V band, so anything under that floor must be electrical: a grounded signal line, an absent 5-V feed or an internally failed sensor. Because low voltage in such a characteristic means little or no vacuum, the brake control unit cannot trust the value and may run the electric pump as a precaution or block functions that depend on it, which Bosch names as pump control, stop-start and ESP assistance. Mitsubishi detects short circuits on its brake vacuum sensor within a second. No maker documents C054B publicly. C054C is the high counterpart.
c: Sensor failed with output stuck low
s: Brake assist or brake system warning lit
Electric vacuum pump running continuously

C054C.d: Vacuum sensor A reports a voltage above its upper clamp. HELLA's booster sensor never exceeds 4.8 V when intact, even at full vacuum, so a higher reading indicates a signal shorted to the 5-V supply or to battery voltage, an open ground, or an internal defect. On a characteristic where more volts mean more vacuum, such a fault pretends a deep vacuum that may not exist; that is the riskier direction, because the electric pump could stay off. Brake units therefore check the circuit continuously; the 2023 Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV reports a shorted vacuum sensor circuit in at most one second and suspends brake assist. Bosch describes the sensor as the input for pump control and stop-start. No maker documents C054C publicly. C054B is the low counterpart, C0550 the same fault on sensor B.
c: Signal line shorted to supply or battery voltage
Sensor failed with output stuck high
s: Brake assist warning on
Harder brake pedal if the booster really runs short of vacuum

C054D.d: Circuit fault on a second vacuum sensor, labelled B, typically an open in its signal, ground or feed. Some systems carry more than one vacuum measurement, for example a booster sensor next to one on the pump or supply line, but which sensor is B is not published by any maker, and no manufacturer documents C054D. The monitoring follows the same pattern as for sensor A: Mitsubishi's brake unit in the 2023 Outlander PHEV recognises an open, a short or a noisy vacuum sensor signal within a second (its own code C1073) and drops brake assist. HELLA's sensor wiring is simple – one pin each for output, ground and supply – so inspection starts at the connector. C0549 is the same fault on sensor A; C054E to C0550 are plausibility, low and high faults of B.
c: Connector of sensor B unplugged, loose or corroded
Interrupted wire in the sensor harness
s: Brake system or brake assist warning
Vacuum pump control in fallback, pump running longer

C054E.d: Sensor B reports a plausible-looking voltage, but the vacuum it represents contradicts the expected value. With two vacuum sensors a module can also compare them with each other; publicly, the comparison methods come from patents on booster sensors: Ford treats booster pressure lying clearly above manifold pressure as sensor degradation, since a working check valve prevents that state, and checks whether booster pressure moves after brake applications; GM tracks booster vacuum against MAP-based engine vacuum with the throttle closed. A real leak or a weak pump can look identical, so the vacuum system is tested before replacing the sensor. No maker documents C054E publicly, and the meaning of B is maker-specific. C054A is the counterpart on sensor A.
c: Leak, faulty check valve or weak vacuum pump
Wrong sensor type fitted after repair
s: Brake assist or brake system warning
Pedal feels firmer after several brake applications

C054F.d: The voltage from vacuum sensor B is lower than any value its characteristic allows. Taking HELLA's booster sensor as the reference, the output should never drop below 0.4 V, while 0.5 V corresponds to no vacuum at all; a reading underneath that is electrical rather than physical. A signal line grounded through chafing, a lost 5-V supply or a sensor with a dead output stage are the usual sources, and a low supply (C0548) can contribute. Mitsubishi's brake unit shows that short circuits on the brake vacuum sensor are caught within one second. Bosch lists pump control and stop-start among the functions fed by this measurement, so they fall back when it is lost. No maker documents C054F publicly. C0550 is the high fault, C054B the low fault of sensor A.
c: Signal wire of sensor B grounded
Output stage of sensor B failed
s: Brake assist warning shown
Stop-start unavailable

C0550.d: Vacuum sensor B puts out more voltage than its design permits. HELLA caps the output of its booster sensor at 4.8 V, with 4.5 V already standing for −1000 hPa, so anything above is a wiring or sensor fault: signal touching the supply or battery voltage, a broken ground return or a failed sensor. Because a high voltage simulates strong vacuum, the control unit must not rely on it for switching the electric vacuum pump; Bosch describes that pump control as the core job of the measurement. Mitsubishi's brake unit catches vacuum sensor shorts within a second and suspends brake assist. No maker documents C0550 with this meaning; one GM bulletin cites C0550 at a rear differential clutch module, a GM-specific use. C054F is the low counterpart, C054C the same fault on A.
c: Signal of sensor B shorted to supply or battery voltage
Ground return of sensor B broken
Sensor B stuck at high output
s: Brake assist or brake system warning on
Firm pedal possible if the pump is not switched on when needed

C0551.d: C0551 reports an electrical break in the longitudinal acceleration sensor circuit: the brake or stability module no longer gets a usable fore-aft signal, usually because the signal or supply wire is open or a plug has lost contact. Earlier layouts mounted a separate g-sensor close to the centre of gravity and cabled it to the ABS unit; a Kelsey-Hayes patent (now ZF) describes a capacitive element whose analog voltage rises with acceleration and moves it onto the ABS circuit board to drop wiring and connectors. No manufacturer explains C0551 in a public document. Without the input, four-wheel-drive ABS loses its wheel-independent speed reference and stability functions are normally switched off with ABS/ESC lamps lit, while base braking remains. C0553 and C0554 cover a low or high voltage, C0552 an implausible value.
c: Broken signal or supply wire between sensor and brake module
Corroded, loose or pushed-back terminal at the sensor plug
Internal open in the sensor or, on integrated designs, in the ABS/ESC unit
s: ABS and/or ESC warning lamp on
Stability, traction or hill-start assistance unavailable
ABS on four-wheel-drive vehicles regulates less precisely

C0552.d: Here the fore-aft acceleration signal arrives but does not match how the car is actually moving. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV brake controller reports its built-in decel G sensor fault C1071-64 as C0552; the check needs a healthy supply and takes up to 2 s, and a second faulty drive turns on the ASC and ABS warnings as well as the check-engine lamp. ASC, traction control, brake LSD, brake assist, brake force distribution and hill start assist are suspended. Mitsubishi lists altered vehicle attitude (different tyre sizes front and rear, overload) and a wrongly angled ABS unit among the causes. Patents describe the test: Sumitomo (now Advics) relates the sensor value to the derivative of the fastest wheel speed and, after repeated misfits, has ABS use wheel data only; Bosch adds offset and range checks on straight roads.
c: Changed vehicle attitude, e.g. different tyre sizes front and rear or overload
ABS/ESC unit or sensor mounted at the wrong angle or loose
Sensor offset drifted or internal sensor defect
Faulty wheel speed data used as comparison value
s: ESC/ASC and ABS warning lamps on, MIL possible on some models
Stability control, traction control and hill start assist switched off
Fault returns after load or tyre changes

C0553.d: C0553 is stored when the longitudinal acceleration signal sits below the lowest voltage the module accepts. Analog acceleration sensors idle at mid-scale; a Hyundai/Kia patent gives 2.5 V as the zero point of a G-sensor on a 5 V reference, so a level dragged toward 0 V cannot come from real braking but points to the wiring: signal shorted to ground, missing sensor supply, or a sensor whose output stage has failed. The same patent has the controller check the sensor at ignition-on and switch to a fallback mode with a warning on failure. No manufacturer publishes C0553 itself. As with the open circuit, stability and related assist functions drop out and the ESC/ABS lamp lights, base brakes keep working. C0554 is the opposite case, C0551 an open line.
c: Signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Sensor reference supply missing or collapsed
Sensor output stage failed at the lower end
s: ESC and ABS warning lamps on from start-up
Stability control and hill-hold unavailable

C0554.d: C0554 is the upper counterpart of C0553: the fore-aft acceleration voltage stays above the highest value that a real sensor reading may take. With a mid-scale zero point, as in a Hyundai/Kia G-sensor patent (2.5 V on a 5 V supply), a value pinned near the reference voltage would mean an absurd, constant acceleration, so the module treats it as a circuit fault. Typical reasons are a signal wire touching a supply line, moisture bridging pins in the plug, or an internal sensor defect; Bosch also names supply fluctuations among the disturbances its check has to catch. No public manufacturer text covers C0554. The module drops the signal, suspends stability and related assist functions and lights the ESC/ABS lamp, while normal braking stays available. C0551 is an open line, C0552 a plausible-looking but wrong value.
c: Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the sensor connector
Sensor output stage failed at the upper end
s: ESC and ABS warning lamps on
Traction and stability assistance switched off

C0555.t: Left Front Wheel Speed Sensor A Incorrect Component Installed
C0555.d: The left front wheel speed signal is present, but the ABS module concludes that the part behind it is not the one it expects. Mitsubishi maps its code C1061-4A on the 2023 Outlander PHEV to C0555 and defines it as the front left sensor fitted in the wrong position; the module needs no more than 3 s to flag it, provided the sensor supply is intact, and the second affected drive brings on the MIL together with the ASC and ABS warnings. ABS, EBD, ASC, traction control, hill descent control and the electric parking brake function are suspended. One way a module can spot this: sensor ICs such as Allegro's A19302 report rotation direction, with forward defined by mounting orientation, so a sensor of the wrong variant or side reads the wheel as turning backwards. After replacing a sensor, check the part number before anything else.
c: Wrong sensor variant fitted (other side, other axle or passive instead of active)
Sensors or their connectors swapped between wheel positions
ABS control unit misjudges a correct sensor
s: ABS and ESC/ASC warning lamps on after a sensor or hub repair
Check-engine lamp on some models
Electric parking brake and hill descent control unavailable

C0556.t: Right Front Wheel Speed Sensor A Incorrect Component Installed
C0556.d: Mirror of C0555 for the right front wheel: the sensor delivers pulses, yet the ABS module rejects it as the wrong component. Mitsubishi lists its code C1063-4A on the 2023 Outlander PHEV as C0556, with the same rule (fitted at the wrong position, at most 3 s, two trips to MIL plus ASC and ABS lamps). Worth noting from that procedure: a code that is only stored, not active, may simply mean the car was not driven after the last repair, and the ABS unit should not be replaced for it; the check needs about 2 minutes at 50 km/h or more. HELLA notes that powered (active) and self-generating (passive) sensors are often hard to tell apart by eye and that carmakers have mostly fitted active ones since 1998, which makes a mixed-up spare part a realistic cause. Circuit faults on this wheel show up as C0506 or C0034 instead.
c: Replacement sensor of the wrong type (passive instead of active, other side)
Stored code left over because no test drive followed the repair
s: ABS and stability warning lamps on, MIL on some models
No ABS or ESC intervention on slippery roads

C0557.t: Left Rear Wheel Speed Sensor A Incorrect Component Installed
C0557.d: C0557 concerns the speed sensor at the left rear wheel: its signal exists, but the ABS module judges the fitted part as not matching. Mitsubishi lists C1065-4A on the 2023 Outlander PHEV as C0557 (sensor in the wrong position, up to 3 s, MIL after two trips). Ford reports the same fault type with its base code plus failure byte, C0037:4A. On 2025 Bronco and Ranger, special service messages 53875 and 53988 (plus their Ranger counterparts) show it together with C003A:4A at start-up as an ABS software issue; replacing sensors or the module does not help, the fix is reprogramming the ABS module. So before buying a sensor, compare part numbers and look for software bulletins. Unlike C050C (circuit open) or C0510 (erratic), the wiring is usually fine here.
c: Wrong or other-side sensor fitted at the left rear
ABS module software misjudges the sensor (fixed by reprogramming)
Rear sensor connectors swapped left and right
s: Several brake system warnings at start-up
ABS and stability control unavailable
Check-engine lamp on some models

C0558.t: Right Rear Wheel Speed Sensor A Incorrect Component Installed
C0558.d: For the right rear wheel, C0558 says the ABS module does not accept the installed speed sensor as the correct part. Mitsubishi maps C1067-4A on the 2023 Outlander PHEV to C0558 (wrong installation position, detection within 3 s, MIL after two trips). Ford uses C003A:4A for the same failure type: on the 2025 Mustang GTD, bulletin 26-2102 traces it, together with circuit codes such as :01 and :07, to heat generated by the rear brake discs damaging the heat shield over the sensor harness, and replaces the damaged rear sensors with an updated part. So a physically harmed sensor can trigger this code too, not only a wrong spare part. Beware of older GM data: on the 2013 Chevrolet Malibu, preliminary information PIC5751A lists C0558 for an electric parking brake fault fixed at ground G401, a meaning unrelated to wheel speed.
c: Wrong sensor variant fitted at the right rear
Sensor or harness damaged by brake heat
s: Yellow or red ABS warning indicator on
Stability and traction control switched off
Check-engine lamp on some models

C0559.t: Power Steering Control Module Range/Performance – Rear
C0559.d: C0559 covers the rear steering controller, the electronics of active rear-wheel steering, when it fails its own performance or plausibility checks. Systems such as ZF's AKC turn the rear wheels by up to 12° opposite to the front ones at low speed and in the same direction from about 60 km/h. No maker documents C0559 publicly, but the faults are known under other codes: Bentley logs P060700 (control module performance) in the rear axle steering unit J1019 and checks damage, ground point 710, replaces the rack and realigns; Audi updates J1019 software for C12A329 and asks for an alignment; on the 2017 Q7 a sensor signal discrepancy lit the steering lamp. A Mazda patent compares three position detectors, uses the agreeing pair and returns the wheels to centre. The car then drives like one without rear steering.
c: Rear steering control module software fault (update available)
Disagreeing position or angle signals inside the rear steering actuator
Poor ground or supply of the rear steering unit
Damaged, contaminated or worn rear steering actuator
s: Steering or rear steering warning in the instrument cluster
Larger turning circle, rear wheels held straight
Driver assistance functions limited on some models

C055A.t: ABS Pump Motor Supply Voltage Circuit A High
C055A.d: Supply voltage A of the ABS pump motor is above its upper limit. The motor draws heavy current, so overvoltage stresses motor, relay or semiconductor switch; typical causes are a faulty alternator regulator, a jump-start or charger at too high a voltage, or a measuring fault in the module. No maker documents C055A publicly. Mitsubishi shows comparable limits on the 2023 Outlander PHEV: the motor feed is specified at 10–16 V, and the brake unit stores C1056-17 (generic C0565, ABS module system voltage high) once its ignition supply reaches at least 16 V, with a detection delay of at most 1 s, suspending ABS, ASC and related functions. Circuit B has its own codes (C05A5 ff.). Measure the charging voltage first.
c: Alternator regulator or DC/DC converter delivering too high a voltage
Jump-start or battery charger with excessive voltage
Voltage measurement fault in the ABS control unit
s: ABS and ESC warning lamps on
Other overvoltage warnings or flickering lights at the same time

C055B.t: ABS Pump Motor Supply Voltage Circuit A Low
C055B.d: Supply voltage A of the pump motor is below its lower limit. Under load the motor pulls the feed down, so a weak 12 V battery, a corroded terminal, a high-resistance fusible link or a poor ground can all set it, and the relay may chatter. No maker publishes C055B. On the 2023 Outlander PHEV Mitsubishi specifies 10–16 V at the motor feed and flags an ignition supply of 10 V or less at its brake unit within 1 s under C1056-16, a code without generic equivalent. A patent originally filed by AlliedSignal and now owned by Bosch flags its own fault if the motor sits under roughly 7 V at shut-off, and a Hitachi patent for electric brake actuators limits motor current once the vehicle supply falls under a set level. Charge and test the battery before replacing parts.
c: Corroded terminal or high-resistance fusible link in the motor feed
Poor ground connection of the ABS unit
s: ABS and ESC warning lamps on, often after cold starts
Pump runs sluggishly or ABS functions drop out

C055C.t: ABS Pump Motor Supply Voltage Circuit A Range/Performance
C055C.d: The return pump motor of the ABS/ESC hydraulic unit has its own power feed, usually a fused line from the battery switched through a relay or a transistor stage in the module. C055C means this feed is present but its voltage does not behave as expected while the motor is off or running – sagging under load, slow to rise or drifting – as opposed to the hard open or short codes C052F, C055A and C055B. No maker publishes a C055C threshold. Ford checks the same motor supply under C052B: below 6 V with the pump off or 7.3 V with it on for 1.8 s. Mitsubishi files a motor or motor-relay fault (C1051-1C, up to 12 s) without an SAE code. GM used C055C in older power steering modules for an unrelated fault. With the pump unusable, ABS and stability control switch off.
c: Corroded or loose pump motor fuse, feed terminal or ground at the hydraulic unit
Weak battery or charging fault letting the supply collapse under motor load
Worn or sticking pump motor drawing excessive current
Faulty motor relay or driver stage inside the ABS module
s: ABS and stability control warning lamps on
No pump buzz during the start-up self-test
Normal braking remains, but without ABS regulation

C055D.d: Passenger-car brakes are split into two hydraulic circuits so that one can still stop the car if the other fails. Brake-by-wire units with a motor-driven plunger can estimate fluid loss directly: they compare the plunger travel with the measured pressure. In GM's 2025 EBCM tables C055D is the leak check of one circuit (listed as circuit 1): if the calculated leakage passes 500 mm³/s (a second stage 2000 mm³/s) for 0.1–0.5 s while braking with the circuits separated, a Type A fault with MIL is set after one trip. C055E covers the other circuit. FMVSS 135 requires a red brake warning when a split system suffers a major drop in fluid level or pressure. The car then brakes with reduced effect and longer pedal travel; it must be checked before further driving.
c: Leaking brake line, hose, fitting or caliper in this circuit
Worn seal in the master cylinder or the brake-by-wire unit
Air left in the circuit after service, read as compliance or leakage
Overly sensitive leak calculation in the brake module software
s: Red brake warning and amber ABS or stability lamp
Soft or sinking brake pedal, longer stopping distance
Falling fluid level or wet spots at a wheel

C055E.d: C055E reports a leak in hydraulic circuit A, the counterpart of C055D. Land Rover documents it on the Defender L663 from 2020 as C055E-7A, meaning lost fluid or a failed seal, with amber ABS and DSC lamps. By design the code survives a simple clear: after the repair the ignition is cycled until the car sleeps, switched on again, left 15 s without touching the pedal, then the pedal is held firmly for up to 120 s while the valves click through a self-check (SSM 74988). If lamps stay lit, the leak is still there. GM's 2025 EBCM tables list C055E for the second circuit with the same leakage limits as C055D and Type A MIL. Driving on is risky, because only one circuit may be braking.
c: Fluid escaping from a line, hose, union or caliper of circuit A
Internal seal failure in master cylinder or hydraulic unit
Repair done but the required self-check was not completed, so the code stays
Air trapped after bleeding or component replacement
s: Amber ABS and DSC/ESC lamps, possibly red brake warning
Longer pedal travel or spongy feel
Warning returns after clearing until the self-check passes

C055F.d: The brake system control module (BSCM) or electronic brake boost controller (EBBC) has found that its hydraulic unit – master cylinder, pedal simulator, separation valves or boost plunger – does not perform as calculated. GM's 2019 tables test it during shutdown: a simulator leak sets C055F if secondary pressure drops under 15 bar; in 2025 a master cylinder leakage above 200 mm³/s also counts, Type A with MIL. On 2026 Silverado/Sierra 1500 GM replaces the master cylinder (PIT6450A); on 2022–26 trucks and SUVs the code appeared below −23 °C from low battery voltage (PIT6476). Jeep logs it as ABS Hydraulic Unit Performance on the 2021 Wrangler 4xe with MIL and fixes stored cases by ABS software (08-032-22). Expect a hard or changed pedal.
c: Internal leak or failure of the master cylinder or pedal simulator
Low battery voltage, especially in severe cold, during the self-test
Brake module software flagging the unit too readily (update available)
Poor power or ground terminals at the brake module
s: Service Brake System message, ABS and stability lamps
Hard pedal or changed brake pedal effort
Check-engine lamp on some models

C0560.t: Brake Pressure Sensor A Missing Calibration
C0560.d: The brake module expects stored calibration data for pressure sensor A, normally the master cylinder pressure sensor: zero offset, sensor identity and a flag that the end-of-line or service calibration succeeded. C0560 means this data is absent or does not match the fitted sensor. GM's 2019 and 2025 tables check only the stored status, 500 ms after wake-up, Type A with MIL; GM's 2016 hybrid tables also call it when a test pulse reads above 110 % or below 90 %. Ford hybrids set it when checksum or sensor ID stored in sensor and module disagree (150 or 70 ms). Mitsubishi has a similar uncalibrated sensor code without SAE number (C105E-92). It typically follows a module or hydraulic unit swap; the scan tool calibration usually clears it.
c: Pressure sensor calibration skipped after replacing the brake module or hydraulic unit
Calibration interrupted, e.g. pedal touched or voltage dropped during the routine
Used or wrong hydraulic unit whose sensor data do not match the module
Non-volatile memory error in the brake module
s: ABS, traction or stability lamp on after brake repair
Brake assist or stability functions unavailable
Check-engine lamp on some GM models

C0561.d: Where two vacuum signals describe the brake booster supply, the module expects them to track each other; C0561 means sensor A and sensor B disagree beyond the allowed band. No maker documents this code number publicly. The principle is patented: Ford compares the booster vacuum sensor with a second reservoir sensor after the vacuum pump stops and flags a sensor mismatch; GM checks the booster sensor against manifold vacuum at closed throttle and marks it biased high or low after set times. Sensors such as HELLA's run on 5 V and output 0.5–4.5 V. GM uses C0561 differently: in its brake modules it means stability control was disabled because another module reported a fault. Brake assist and stop/start may be limited.
c: One vacuum sensor drifting or reading offset
Leaking or kinked vacuum hose or check valve between the two measuring points
Corroded connector or damaged wiring on one sensor
Unstable 5 V reference or ground shared by the sensors
s: Brake or stability warning lamp
Electric vacuum pump runs too often or not at all
Stop/start or brake assist unavailable on some cars

C0562.t: Brake Pedal Position Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit/Open
C0562.d: Hybrids, EVs and brake-by-wire cars measure how hard the driver wants to brake with a contactless pedal angle or travel sensor. Bosch builds these with a magnetic field sensor on a 5 V supply and two redundant outputs, often pulse-width modulated, so the module can cross-check them. C0562 reports that this 5 V feed is interrupted – the module sees no usable supply at all, unlike C056D (too low) and C056E (too high). No maker publishes a C0562 threshold; Ford's hybrids watch the same supply for a window of 4.87–5.13 V over 50 ms. Without the sensor the module cannot split braking between regeneration and friction, so regenerative braking and some assist functions are lost.
c: Broken 5 V supply wire or pin pushed out at the pedal sensor
Sensor connector loose or left unplugged after pedal-area work
Internal open circuit in the pedal sensor
Brake module no longer providing the 5 V reference
s: Brake system or ABS warning lamp
Regenerative braking reduced or off, pedal feel changes
Brake lights or cruise control affected on some cars

C0563.d: C0563 is a summary code: the ABS control module reports that it cannot carry out its own function correctly, without pinning the fault on one sensor or valve. Ford shows how it is used. In its 2015–2019 hybrids the ABS module stores internal faults as U3000 (control module) or U2200 (corrupt data), and the hybrid powertrain module mirrors both as C0563 so that regenerative braking faults appear in the OBD system. On 2025–26 F-150, Ranger, Bronco, Expedition and Navigator C0563 sits in the ABS module alongside the message Check Brake System, traced to air left in the system after bleeding or to brake service mode still active; the workshop manual test was revised (SSM 54733). Clear underlying faults first, then check software.
c: Air in the hydraulic system or brake service mode left active after work
Internal ABS module fault or corrupted memory
Outdated or incomplete module software or configuration
Unstable supply or ground at the ABS module
s: Check Brake System message and ABS lamp
ABS and stability control unavailable
Regenerative braking limited on hybrids

C0564.t: ABS Control Module System Voltage Low
C0564.d: The ABS module needs a stable 12 V supply to switch its valves and pump. C0564 means its measured system voltage has dropped below the permitted minimum. Ford's hybrids accept 9.0 to 16.9 V and log anything outside as C0564 (low) or C0565 (high), suspending pump motor checks meanwhile. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV detects 10 V or less within 1 s under C1056-16 – without SAE number or MIL – and suspends ABS, EBD, ASC, traction control, brake assist and the electric parking brake. Typical triggers are a tired battery, cranking dips or a poor feed or ground to the module. Unlike C055B, which concerns only the pump motor feed, C0564 affects the whole module.
c: Weak or deeply discharged 12 V battery
High resistance in the module fuse, feed wire or ground
Alternator or DC/DC converter not supplying enough voltage
Parasitic drain or aftermarket equipment pulling the battery down
s: ABS, stability and brake warnings, often together with other modules' warnings
Electric parking brake or hill hold unavailable
Warnings disappear after recharging the battery

C0565.t: ABS Control Module System Voltage High
C0565.d: C0565 is set when the ABS module measures a supply voltage above its permitted maximum; excess voltage can damage the valve and pump drivers, so the module stops regulating. Mitsubishi maps its C1056-17 to C0565 on the 2023 Outlander PHEV: 16 V or more on the ignition feed within 1 s, ASC, ABS, brake and parking brake lamps plus the MIL after two trips; ABS, EBD, ASC, brake assist and the electric parking brake are suspended. Ford's hybrids flag voltage above 16.9 V. Causes lie in the charging side – a faulty regulator or DC/DC converter, or jump-starting or charging with too high a voltage. The low-voltage counterpart is C0564.
c: Faulty alternator regulator or DC/DC converter overcharging the 12 V system
Jump-start or battery charger set to an excessive voltage
Poor ground making the module read voltage too high
s: ABS, stability, brake and parking brake warnings
Check-engine lamp on some models
Bulbs burning out or other modules reporting overvoltage

C0566.d: Some vacuum brake boosters carry an electrically operated valve that lets air into the working chamber without pedal input – for emergency brake assist or, on hybrids, to blend friction and regenerative braking. An Aisin patent shows the idea: when energised, the solenoid admits atmospheric pressure to an auxiliary chamber and raises boost. C0566 reports an open circuit in this solenoid's wiring or coil. Ford's 2015–2019 hybrids store the ABS fault C0022 (brake booster solenoid) and mirror it as C0566 in the hybrid powertrain module; while it is active, Ford's pump motor and valve tests are suspended. Normal pedal boost usually remains, but automatic brake assist and smooth blending are lost.
c: Solenoid connector loose, unlatched or corroded at the booster
Broken wire between ABS module and booster solenoid
Open solenoid coil inside the booster
s: Brake system or stability warning
Brake assist or regenerative blending unavailable
Pedal feel changes on hybrids

C0567.d: C0567 flags the brake booster solenoid circuit as too low – typically a short to ground on the line between the module's high-side driver and the coil. Ford describes the check in its 2015–2019 hybrid summaries: with both high-side and low-side drivers switched off, the module measures the voltage on the solenoid supply; below 3.0 V for 380 ms the fault is stored, and Ford's hybrid powertrain module shows it as C0567 (ABS module code C0022). Because a grounded line can overload the driver, the module stops using the solenoid. Brake assist from the booster then fails and hybrids lose part of the blended braking. Look for chafed harness near the booster or water in the connector before replacing the booster.
c: Chafed solenoid wire shorting to body ground
Moisture or corrosion bridging the connector pins
Shorted solenoid winding inside the booster
s: Brake system warning lamp
No automatic brake assist
Less regenerative braking on hybrids

C0568.d: C0568 is the high-side counterpart of C0567: the solenoid circuit carries voltage when it should be dead. In Ford's 2015–2019 hybrid logic both drivers are commanded off and the solenoid supply line must stay near zero; more than 3.0 V for 80 ms points to a short to battery voltage or a driver that will not switch off, and the hybrid powertrain module reports C0568 (ABS code C0022). The risk is a solenoid energised without command, which would add boost the driver did not ask for, so the module blocks the function. An Aisin patent explains why that matters: energising the valve alone raises the booster output. Check for a short to a neighbouring powered wire before suspecting the module.
c: Solenoid wire chafed against a powered circuit
High-side driver in the ABS module not switching off
Contamination bridging pins in the solenoid connector
s: Brake system warning lamp
Brake assist switched off
Unusual pedal feel on hybrids

C0569.d: C0569 covers booster solenoid faults that are neither a clear open nor a clean short: the circuit reacts, but not as the module expects. Ford's hybrids (2015–2019) run three checks during operation, each over 80 ms: more than 2 V over the low-side driver while the high side is off, less than 160 mA in the test pulse with the high side on, or under 3.0 V supply with the high side on. Pump motor faults C052B–C052E block this test. A partly corroded connector or a coil with drifting resistance is the usual cause. GM used C0569 for something else entirely – a system configuration error in the transfer case module (PIP5089A) – so check the brand before diagnosing.
c: Corroded or loose terminals adding resistance in the solenoid circuit
Degraded driver stage in the ABS module
s: Intermittent brake system warning
Brake assist occasionally unavailable
Code returns after clearing

C056A.t: Brake Booster Pressure Sensor Power Supply Circuit
C056A.d: Pressure sensors in the brake system are ratiometric parts fed with 5 V from the control module; HELLA's booster vacuum sensor, for example, is specified for 4.5–5.5 V and answers with 0.5–4.5 V. If that supply is missing or out of range, every reading is wrong, so C056A is checked before the sensor signals are judged. Ford's 2015–2019 hybrids use C056A exactly this way: the missing-calibration and erratic checks of the brake pressure sensors (C0560, C056B) only run when no C056A supply fault is present. No maker publishes a C056A threshold. Bosch notes the booster vacuum signal also governs the electric vacuum pump and start/stop. Expect brake assist and stability functions to be limited.
c: Open or shorted 5 V supply wire to the sensor
Another sensor on the same reference pulling the supply down
Faulty 5 V regulator in the control module
s: Brake or stability warning, often with further sensor codes
Brake assist or electric vacuum pump control affected
Stop/start inactive on some cars

C056B.d: C056B means the signal from brake pressure sensor A drops out or jumps for short moments instead of being steadily wrong. Ford's hybrid summaries (2015–2019) name two triggers: a checksum error in the digital data coming from the sensor for 70 ms, or a commanded control signal that does not show up at the sensor within 70 ms; the check runs only with a healthy sensor supply (no C056A). Ford's ABS module stores the same event as C0044. Saab's 2011 9-5 shows the consequence of an erratic pressure signal under its own code C0131: ABS, hill start assist, stability and traction control are disabled for the rest of the ignition cycle. Shaking the harness while watching live data helps find the loose contact.
c: Loose or corroded contact in the pressure sensor connector or harness
Disturbed digital sensor line, e.g. damaged shielding or poor ground
Sensor electronics failing intermittently, often in the hydraulic unit
Brief dips in the 5 V sensor supply
s: ABS and stability lamps that come and go
Stability control or hill start assist off until next start
Regenerative braking reduced on hybrids

C056C.d: C056C is the intermittent fault of the second brake pressure sensor, B. Which pressure B measures depends on the system – in Ford's hybrid ABS modules the two sensors read different points of the hydraulic unit, and other makers fit sensor B in a separate circuit or in the boost chamber. No maker documents C056C publicly. By analogy with sensor A (Ford C056B: corrupted sensor data or a missing control response for 70 ms), the code points to brief signal loss rather than lasting drift, which belongs under C0541. Honda's patent shows how a pressure sensor is judged: if pedal stroke rises but pressure does not follow, the sensor is deemed faulty. Typically stability functions shut down until the next start.
c: Intermittent contact at the sensor B connector or harness
Sensor B electronics dropping out under heat or vibration
Poor ground or unstable reference voltage
s: Sporadic ABS or stability warning
Traction and stability control briefly unavailable
No noticeable change in normal braking

C056D.t: Brake Pedal Position Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit Low
C056D.d: The brake pedal angle sensor of a hybrid or brake-by-wire car is fed from a regulated 5 V line. C056D means this supply is present but sagging. Ford's 2015–2019 hybrid summaries set a joint window for C056D and C056E: if the supply leaves 4.87–5.13 V for 50 ms, the code for the low or high side is stored; in Ford's ABS module both appear as C100F and the hybrid powertrain module shows C056D for the low case. A drooping reference usually means a short to ground inside the sensor, a damaged supply wire or another load on the same rail. GM uses C056D in its own way, for example with parking brake faults on 2017–2019 Acadia, Traverse, Enclave and XT5 (PIT5662A).
c: Pedal sensor loading the supply through an internal fault
Supply wire chafed to ground near the pedal box
Another sensor on the same 5 V rail pulling it down
Weak 5 V regulator in the brake module
s: Brake system warning and possibly stability lamp
Regenerative braking reduced, firmer friction braking
On GM models parking brake messages instead

C056E.t: Brake Pedal Position Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit High
C056E.d: C056E is stored when the 5 V feed of the brake pedal position sensor rises above its limit. In Ford's 2015–2019 hybrid logic that means more than 5.13 V for 50 ms; the ABS module records C100F and the hybrid powertrain module C056E. An elevated reference usually comes from a short between the supply and a battery-voltage wire, from a missing sensor ground that lets the line float up, or from a failing regulator. Since Bosch-type pedal sensors deliver two redundant outputs referenced to the same supply, a high supply skews both and the plausibility check can no longer help. GM uses C056E in its own way, for instance in the 2017–2019 parking brake case on Acadia, Traverse, Enclave and XT5 (PIT5662A).
c: Supply wire shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
Open sensor ground letting the reference float high
Faulty 5 V regulator in the brake module
s: Brake system warning lamp
Regenerative braking limited
Pedal sensor plausibility codes may follow

C056F.t: Brake Booster Travel Sensor Circuit Low
C056F.d: The travel sensor tells the booster control how far its input side has moved. On older vacuum boosters it followed the movable wall; on Bosch's iBooster a differential travel sensor measures the offset between the pedal-driven input rod and the motor-driven booster body, and the controller works to bring that offset back to zero. C056F means the signal sits below its valid band – typically a short to ground, a lost sensor supply or an open reference. No maker publishes a C056F threshold; GM, for instance, files its pedal travel sensors as master cylinder piston position sensors (C05CC, C05CF). Without this input the module cuts or limits electric assist, so the pedal gets hard while the base brakes keep working.
c: Travel sensor signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Missing 5 V supply to the sensor, e.g. corroded connector pin at the booster
Internal fault of the travel sensor, usually built into the booster assembly
Defective sensor input stage in the booster control unit
s: Hard brake pedal with clearly higher pedal force
Brake system or stability warning lamp and a message to service the brakes
Brake assist, automatic emergency braking or regenerative braking unavailable

C0570.t: Brake Booster Travel Sensor Circuit High
C0570.d: C0570 is the high-side counterpart of C056F: the booster travel signal reads above its plausible maximum. Typical triggers are a signal wire touching the 5 V reference line or battery positive, or a broken sensor ground that lets the input float upward. Travel sensing in boosters dates back to vacuum units in which an electrical sensor in the housing reported the position of the movable wall and had to be set against housing tolerances; electromechanical units like the iBooster measure pedal travel with a sensor inside the unit instead. No manufacturer documents C0570 publicly. A value stuck at the top can look like a fully pressed pedal, so the module normally disables electric assist and brake assist; stopping then needs much more pedal effort.
c: Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage
Open sensor ground letting the signal float to the upper limit
Travel sensor damaged internally, e.g. after water ingress at the booster
Wrong or not properly installed booster or sensor after a repair
s: Electric brake assist switched off, pedal much harder
Brake warning and stability control lamp on
Driver assistance braking functions disabled

C0571.t: Brake Pressure Sensor C Circuit Low
C0571.d: Brake pressure sensor C is an additional hydraulic pressure sensor whose job depends on the brake system; each maker assigns the letter itself. GM uses C0571 in three variants. In the 2016–2019 hybrid brake control modules it is master cylinder pressure sensor 1, set when the signal line shows no voltage difference to ground for 0.1 s. In a 2019 EBCM with integrated booster it is the secondary circuit pressure sensor, set below 4.61 % of its supply within 100 ms. In the 2023 and 2025 tables a SENT master cylinder sensor pinned at its minimum of −1480 kPa for 0.96 s sets it. GM rates every variant Type A, MIL after one trip. ABS, stability control and regenerative blending are then restricted.
c: Sensor signal line shorted to ground in the harness or connector
Sensor supply missing, so the output stays at its lowest value
Defective pressure sensor, often integrated in the hydraulic or brake module
s: Check engine light together with ABS or stability warning (GM)
Regenerative braking or brake assist reduced, pedal feel changed
Brake pressure reading on the scan tool stuck at its minimum

C0572.t: Brake Pressure Sensor C Circuit High
C0572.d: C0572 marks the upper end of the same sensor C channel: the pressure signal is at or above its top limit. GM's 2016–2019 hybrid brake modules check the signal voltage against the supply voltage and set the code when the two are practically equal for 0.1 s. The 2019 EBCM uses more than 95.24 % of supply voltage and explicitly includes an open signal line, so GM has no separate open-circuit code for this sensor. In the 2023 and 2025 tables the SENT master cylinder sensor reporting its maximum of 30,000 kPa for 0.96 s triggers it. All variants are Type A with MIL. A short to the reference voltage is the usual wiring cause; since the module would otherwise see heavy braking that is not happening, it stops trusting the sensor and limits brake functions.
c: Signal line shorted to the 5 V reference or another supply
Open signal line pulled high by the module input (GM counts this here)
Pressure sensor reporting full scale because of an internal fault
s: Check engine light plus ABS or stability lamp (GM)
Scan tool shows high brake pressure with the pedal released
Brake assist and regenerative braking restricted

C0573.d: C0573 is reserved for an interrupted circuit of brake pressure sensor C – a broken signal, supply or ground wire, or a connector that has lost contact. No manufacturer documents it publicly; GM, which uses C0571 and C0572 for this sensor, books an open signal line under C0572. How an open shows up depends on the input circuit: with a pull-down resistor at the module, a lost supply or signal wire drops the reading to 0 V, while a lost ground can push it above 4.7 V, as a Denso patent on vehicle pressure sensors explains. Ratiometric transducers such as Honeywell's also drive power or ground loss to a defined rail. Sensor C usually sits in the brake module or hydraulic unit, and ABS, stability control or brake assist may be switched off.
c: Loose, corroded or pushed-back pin at the sensor or module connector
Broken signal, supply or ground wire in the harness
Internal open circuit in the pressure sensor
s: ABS, stability or brake warning lamp on
Pressure value missing or fixed at a rail on the scan tool
Fault may come and go when the connector is moved

C0574.t: Brake Pressure Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
C0574.d: Here the sensor C signal is electrically within limits but does not make sense. GM's 2016–2019 hybrid brake modules learn the zero point while the pedal is released and set C0574 if the offset exceeds ±1,500 kPa; to confirm a repair the car is driven at about 37 mph for 5 s without braking. A 2019 EBCM compares its two secondary circuit pressure signals with each other and with pedal travel (difference above 5 bar), checks each learned offset (above 10 bar) and catches erratic readings within 80 ms. The 2023 and 2025 tables allow an offset of 12 bar. All are Type A with MIL. A Lucas/ZF patent shows why several sensors are needed: only a comparison of three or more at a shared pressure tells which one has drifted.
c: Pressure sensor zero point drifted with age or temperature
Residual pressure while learning, e.g. dragging pedal or sticking valve
Poor sensor ground shifting the signal level
Sensor values not relearned after replacing the brake module
s: Check engine light and ABS or stability lamp (GM)
Uneven or changed braking feel when regeneration blends in
Code returns after clearing once the car has been driven

C0575.t: Brake Pressure Sensor D Circuit Low
C0575.d: Brake pressure sensor D is a further hydraulic pressure sensor whose position is set by the manufacturer. In GM's hybrid brake control modules of 2016–2019 it measures brake pressure at the left rear wheel, and C0575 is stored when its signal stays under 0.3 V for 0.1 s while the ignition is on, rated Type A with MIL after one trip. Without that value the module lacks the rear wheel pressure it uses to blend regenerative and friction braking. Older GM vehicles used the same number for something unrelated: the left front damper actuator circuit of the electronic suspension (Saab 9-5, and GM full-size trucks whose engine harness chafed on the vacuum pump pulley, PIT5307G). Typical causes are a short to ground, lost sensor supply or a failed sensor.
c: Signal line of sensor D shorted to ground
Sensor supply interrupted, output drops to near 0 V
s: Check engine light with brake or stability warning (GM hybrids)
Regenerative braking reduced, more friction braking
Rear pressure reading near zero even when braking

C0576.t: Brake Pressure Sensor D Circuit High
C0576.d: C0576 is set when the signal of brake pressure sensor D sits too high. GM's 2016–2019 hybrid brake tables, where D is the left rear wheel pressure sensor, compare the signal line against the supply: a level over 3.3 V lasting 0.1 s at ignition on stores the code, Type A with MIL after one trip. A short to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage and a broken sensor ground are the usual reasons; an internally damaged sensor can also report full scale. A Bosch trainer describes such a sensor as 5 V supplied, giving under 1 V with the brakes released and rising with pressure, which makes a high reading at rest easy to spot on live data. The module then no longer trusts the value, and regenerative blending and ABS/ESC are restricted.
c: Signal line shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage
Open sensor ground, signal floats high
Sensor internally damaged, reports maximum pressure
s: Check engine light and brake warnings (GM hybrids)
High rear pressure shown with the pedal released
Less regenerative braking, ABS/ESC restricted

C0577.d: C0577 stands for an open circuit of brake pressure sensor D. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM, which assigns sensor D to the left rear wheel pressure sensor in its hybrid brake modules, uses only C0575, C0576 and C0578 there; C0577 also appears in GM's code list for 2014 and older vehicles (PIP5094), where it belongs to GM's earlier numbering. An open wire is recognised because the reading moves into a band reserved for faults: if the module input has a pull-up resistor it goes high, with a pull-down it goes low, as Honeywell specifies for its ratiometric transducers. Brake-by-wire units monitor each extra pressure sensor separately; Bosch's EBS, for example, flags caliper and axle sensor faults one by one.
c: Connector of sensor D unplugged, corroded or with a spread terminal
Wire broken near the sensor, e.g. at a flex point toward the rear axle
Internal open circuit in sensor D
s: Brake, ABS or stability warning lamp
No valid value for sensor D on the scan tool
Regenerative braking or brake assist limited

C0578.t: Brake Pressure Sensor D Circuit Range/Performance
C0578.d: For sensor D the range/performance check targets a signal that is electrically fine but implausible. In GM's 2016–2019 hybrid brake modules, where D measures left rear brake pressure, the zero offset is learned while the car is being driven above about 4.5 mph with the brake released and the hydraulic pump idle; an offset beyond ±1,500 kPa sets C0578 at once, Type A with MIL. To prove the repair GM asks for driving at roughly 37 mph for at least 5 s. Wheel pressure sensors can also be checked against each other when valves connect them to one common pressure, a method described in a Lucas/ZF patent that singles out the drifting sensor and its error. Likely causes are sensor drift, trapped pressure in the rear circuit or a ground offset.
c: Zero point of sensor D drifted
Pressure trapped in the rear circuit, e.g. sticking caliper or valve
Ground offset between sensor and brake module
s: Check engine light and brake warnings (GM hybrids)
Rear brake pressure shown although no brake is applied
Code sets again after a short drive

C0579.t: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
C0579.d: Electromechanical brake boosters watch the heat in their motor and power electronics so they can scale back assist before damage; a Hitachi Astemo patent, for example, describes one sensor on the motor and one in the drive circuit, with assist limited above set temperatures. GM reads two temperature channels from its booster: A under P25C6/P25C7, B under C0579/C057A. C0579 means channel B reads too low, which GM treats as a short to ground: under 0.03 V on five consecutive checks within 0.6 s in the 2023 and 2025 tables, Type B with MIL after two trips. GM's 2019 Cadillac XT4 tables use the same voltage with two detections between about 7 and 124 mph, but as Type C without MIL. The booster then runs a protective strategy.
c: Temperature signal B shorted to ground inside the booster or its harness
Fault in the booster control electronics reading the channel
s: Check engine light after two trips (GM 2023/2025), brake warning
Brake assist may be reduced as a precaution
Booster temperature B shows an implausible value on the scan tool

C057A.t: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
C057A.d: C057A is the high counterpart: temperature channel B of the booster reads at its upper end, which GM interprets as the signal shorted to supply. GM's 2023 and 2025 EBCM tables set it above 3.14 V when five checks in a row fail within 0.6 s and rate it Type B, with MIL after two trips; the 2019 Cadillac XT4 version uses 3.34 V and is Type C without MIL. Channel A trips at 3.27 V under P25C7, so the two channels have slightly different limits. Whether a high voltage means hot or cold depends on where the thermistor sits in its divider, which is why the module treats a value at the rail as a wiring fault rather than a temperature. Without a usable reading the booster cannot protect its motor and may reduce assist.
c: Temperature signal B shorted to the sensor supply or another voltage
Thermistor or its return line open, pulling the input to the rail
Moisture or corrosion inside the booster electronics
s: Check engine light after two trips (GM 2023/2025) and brake warning
Temperature B reading stuck at a limit
Reduced brake assist during long downhill braking

C057B.t: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor B Circuit/Open
C057B.d: C057B is defined for an interrupted circuit of booster temperature sensor B. No manufacturer publishes it; GM maps the faults of this channel to C0579 and C057A only. Temperature sensors of this kind are normally NTC thermistors placed near the motor or on the power stage and read through a voltage divider. If the thermistor or one of its wires opens, the divider node is pulled toward the excitation voltage, and a thermistor design guide advises placing diagnostic thresholds beyond the usable temperature range to catch that. Microchip points out that an NTC on a power module follows case and heatsink temperature rather than the chip junction. Because the sensor is usually inside the booster, an open circuit often means replacing the unit.
c: Open wire or loose pin between thermistor and booster electronics
Cracked thermistor body or broken lead after thermal or mechanical stress
Failed solder joint on the booster circuit board
s: Brake system warning and service message
Temperature B missing or at an extreme value on the scan tool
Assist possibly limited to protect the motor

C057C.t: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
C057C.d: C057C covers a temperature B value that is electrically valid but behaves implausibly – it stays frozen, climbs too slowly after hard use, or departs from what the module's thermal estimate predicts. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. In Hitachi Astemo's electric booster patent the measured motor and drive circuit temperatures decide when current and thus assist are limited and when they are restored, with an intermediate step if the pedal is still pressed; a wrong but believable value would therefore throttle assist too early or let the motor run too hot. Thermistor makers name moisture, cracking, solder stress and resistance drift as typical long-term failures. The module may restrict assist as a precaution.
c: Thermistor resistance drifted through age, moisture or heat cycling
Sensor lost thermal contact with motor or power stage
Plausibility model in the booster software too strict
s: Brake warning, often after long or repeated braking
Temperature B frozen or lagging behind temperature A
Assist reduced earlier than usual

C057D.t: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor Circuit B Intermittent/Erratic
C057D.d: C057D is meant for a temperature B signal that drops out or jumps for brief moments instead of failing for good – a loose connector pin, a cracked solder joint or a wire breaking under vibration are the classic reasons. No manufacturer publishes a threshold for it. GM's monitors for this channel require several consecutive out-of-range samples (two or five) before storing C0579 or C057A, which filters single spikes; a separate code for unsteady behaviour is not listed in GM's public tables.
