Thermistor suppliers name mechanical stress, moisture and solder damage as frequent sources of unstable readings. The fault tends to come and go with temperature or road shocks and may return after clearing; while the signal is unreliable the booster can limit assist.
c: Loose or fretting pin in the booster connector
Cracked solder joint of the thermistor on the circuit board
Moisture ingress causing leakage currents at the sensor
s: Brake warning that appears and disappears
Temperature B jumping on the scan tool
Code returns some time after clearing

C057E.t: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor A/B Correlation
C057E.d: With two temperature sensors in the booster the module can cross-check them: after a long rest both should be close to ambient, and under load they should move in a consistent pattern. C057E is set when sensors A and B disagree beyond a plausible margin. GM fits two such channels in its booster (A: P25C6/P25C7, B: C0579/C057A), but its public tables do not list C057E, and no other maker documents it either. The idea is known from related systems: Safran compares redundant temperature sensors in electric brake actuators and discards inconsistent ones, and Hitachi Astemo's electric booster carries separate motor and drive circuit sensors. As the module cannot tell which reading is wrong, it usually protects the motor by reducing assist.
c: One of the two thermistors drifted or lost thermal contact
Added resistance in one sensor circuit, e.g. corroded contact
Real local overheating of motor or power stage, e.g. after jammed mechanics
s: Brake system warning with service message
Temperatures A and B clearly apart on the scan tool after a cold start
Reduced brake assist

C057F.t: Brake Booster Motor A Phase U-V-W Circuit/Open
C057F.d: C057F covers an interrupted drive path in the three-phase motor of an electric brake booster: a winding, a phase lead or a power transistor that no longer carries current. GM documents it in several brake modules, always as Type A with MIL after one trip. Its 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables switch single bridge transistors while the motor is not being driven and set the code within 5 ms if the phase W voltage does not respond. The 2023 and 2025 EBCM tables measure coil resistance and trip above 0.20358 Ω (or below 0.01258 Ω) for 0.12 s, or when the voltage vector is off by more than 1.5 V. In GM's 2019 IBC unit C057F also covers phases that fail to rise above 3.46 V or sit near battery level before start-up. The brakes keep working, only without electric assist.
c: Bridge transistor in the brake module no longer switching (drive stage defect)
Broken winding or failed internal phase connection in booster motor A
Corroded or loose phase contact between control unit and motor, raising coil resistance
s: Hard brake pedal, noticeably more pedal force needed
Brake system, ABS/traction and check engine lamps on
Message about reduced brake assist

C0580.t: Brake Booster Motor A Phase U-V-W Circuit Low
C0580.d: C0580 flags a phase of booster motor A that is pulled too low, or a driver stage that cannot lift it properly. GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables use it when the gate-drive supply of the bridge driver falls too far below the motor supply (7 V limit, 5 ms). In the 2019 IBC unit it covers a phase that does not drop under 0.99 V while its lower transistor conducts, a phase already near 0 V before the bridge is enabled, and an undercharged bootstrap capacitor – all Type A with MIL. Automotive gate drivers such as TI's DRV8305-Q1 report this charge-pump undervoltage themselves. Note the older meaning: on the 2011 Saab 9-5 and related GM cars, C0580 was the right front damper actuator of the adaptive suspension. In the booster meaning the module normally switches assist off.
c: Gate-driver or charge-pump supply in the brake module too low (internal defect or weak supply)
Phase lead of motor A chafed through and shorted to ground
Lower bridge transistor shorted or permanently driven
s: Electric brake assist off, pedal feels hard
Brake and stability warning lamps, on GM also the check engine lamp
Fault may appear right after switching the ignition on

C0581.t: Brake Booster Motor A Phase U-V-W Circuit High
C0581.d: C0581 is reserved for a phase of booster motor A whose voltage sits too high – typically a phase lead touching battery positive or an upper power transistor that stays conductive. No manufacturer publishes C0581: GM's brake tables list only C057F, C0580 and C0582 for the phase circuits of this motor, and its 2019 IBC unit books stuck-high phases under C057F. How such a fault is detected is laid out in gate-driver data sheets: TI's DRV8343-Q1 runs an offline short-to-supply test while the bridge is off, and the DRV3245Q-Q1, intended for electric brake and brake assist, watches drain-source voltages and phase comparators. Because a stuck upper transistor can lock the motor, the module turns assist off; the hydraulic base brake stays available.
c: Upper bridge transistor in the brake module shorted or stuck on
Phase lead of motor A shorted to battery voltage
Moisture in the booster connector creating a leakage path to supply
s: Brake assist switched off, high pedal effort
Brake system warning lamp and service message

C0582.t: Brake Booster Motor A Phase U-V-W Circuit Range/Performance
C0582.d: C0582 is the plausibility check of the drive stage for booster motor A and the best documented code of this group. GM's 2016/2019 hybrid tables switch an upper and a lower transistor of different phases in all six pairings and trip above 150 A; the 2023/2025 EBCM tables expect an idle phase at 1.65 V during start-up and also file a temperature-sensor plausibility test here. Type A, MIL. GM bulletin 22-NA-100 (2022 Cadillac XT5/XT6, Chevrolet Blazer, GMC Acadia with eBoost) reports check engine, traction and ABS lamps and possible loss of assist in a panic stop: reprogram if stored, new BSCM if active. Stellantis tells Jeep Wagoneer dealers to renew eBooster and BSCM together; GM's PIC6614 says Lyriq codes may show only in OnStar data.
c: Software fault in the brake system control module (GM 22-NA-100, fixed by reprogramming)
Defective bridge driver or shorted transistor pair in the drive stage
Internal fault of the eBooster unit, requiring booster and module replacement
s: Check engine, traction control and ABS lamps on together
Brake assist failure message, abnormal pedal feel
Reduced assist especially during hard or panic braking

C0583.t: Brake Booster Motor B Phase U-V-W Circuit/Open
C0583.d: C0583 refers to the second motor or second winding system, B, of an electric brake booster and reports an interrupted phase path there. Not every booster has a B side: GM's public tables diagnose motor A only, and no manufacturer documents C0583 in this meaning. GM's keyword list for 2014 and older vehicles (PIP5094) contains C0583 from an earlier numbering. A B channel makes sense in redundant layouts such as the dual-winding gear motor in a Hyundai Mobis patent, where two power modules each feed one three-phase winding and either one can carry the full current. An open B phase is found the same way as on side A, for example using the driver chip's open-load check. The module drops the faulty channel; depending on design, assist continues on A or is reduced.
c: Open winding or internal phase connection of motor/winding system B
Power module B with a transistor that no longer conducts
Loose or corroded phase contact on the B side
s: Brake warning lamp with a service message
Weaker or slower brake assist if only side A remains

C0584.t: Brake Booster Motor B Phase U-V-W Circuit Low
C0584.d: C0584 means a phase of booster motor B is held too low – shorted to ground, a lower transistor that will not switch off, or a driver whose gate supply has collapsed. No manufacturer publishes the code in its booster meaning; it shows up only in GM's older keyword list (PIP5094), where the number belonged to another system. Gate drivers such as TI's DRV8343-Q1 test every phase for a short to ground while the bridge is disabled, and the DRV8305-Q1 reports when its charge pump falls too far below the motor supply. With two independent winding systems, as in the Hyundai Mobis patent, a fault in one system must not pull down the other, so the module isolates side B and, where the design allows, keeps braking assist going on side A.
c: Phase lead of side B shorted to ground or housing
Lower transistor of power module B shorted
Gate-driver supply of channel B too low
s: Brake system warning and possibly reduced assist
Driver assistance braking functions may be limited

C0585.t: Brake Booster Motor B Phase U-V-W Circuit High
C0585.d: C0585 stands for a phase of booster motor B reading too high, for instance a lead shorted to battery positive or an upper transistor stuck on. The number had another use on older GM-platform cars: on the 2011 Saab 9-5 it identified the left rear damper actuator of the adaptive suspension. In its booster meaning no manufacturer publishes it. The checks required mirror those for C0581 on side A – offline short-to-supply tests and drain-source voltage monitoring as in TI's DRV3245Q-Q1. Redundant drives then isolate the faulty side: Kollmorgen's early patent on redundant windings already shared the torque among the healthy winding sets, and in the Hyundai Mobis design the remaining power module takes over the whole current command.
c: Phase lead of side B shorted to battery voltage
Upper transistor of power module B shorted or stuck on
Code read on an older GM-platform vehicle where C0585 belongs to a damper actuator
s: Brake system warning lamp
Reduced or switched-off electric assist

C0586.t: Brake Booster Motor B Phase U-V-W Circuit Range/Performance
C0586.d: C0586 is set when the B drive stage of the booster motor is electrically connected but behaves implausibly: phase currents that do not match the command, a transistor pair conducting at once, or a bridge driver that fails its start-up self-test. Nobody publishes limits for side B. GM's tests for motor A under C0582 – more than 150 A in a cross-switching test, an idle phase not at 1.65 V – show what such a check looks like. TI's DRV3245Q-Q1, designed for electric brake and brake assist, adds shoot-through prevention and gate-source monitoring for the same purpose. In a dual-winding motor like the Hyundai Mobis one, diagnostics classify each power module as healthy or failed; the failed one is switched off, so the driver may notice a weaker or slower pedal response.
c: Bridge driver of channel B failing its self-test
Current measurement of channel B drifting, currents no longer match the command
Control unit software issue, resolved by update where available
s: Brake warning or service message
Pedal response weaker or slower than usual

C0587.t: Brake Booster Motor A Position Sensor Circuit/Open
C0587.d: C0587 concerns the rotor position sensor of booster motor A – a resolver, a sine/cosine magnetic sensor or a set of Hall elements that tells the controller where the rotor stands so it can commutate the windings. The code reports an open sensor circuit. No manufacturer documents it publicly: GM books position faults of this motor under C0588, C0589 and C058A, and C0587 appears in GM's older keyword list only from a different numbering. Hitachi's resolver patent shows how a break is caught: a bias placed on one winding terminal must reappear at the other, otherwise a pull-up drives the reading high. Bosch describes a fallback for a booster whose rotor sensor goes silent – the motor is run open-loop with capped speed and speed changes, so assist becomes weaker.
c: Broken signal or supply wire of the position sensor
Pushed-back or corroded pin at the sensor or module connector
Sensor element inside the booster failed, booster unit usually replaced
s: Electric brake assist reduced or off, hard pedal
Brake warning lamp and message

C0588.t: Brake Booster Motor A Position Sensor Circuit Low
C0588.d: C0588 is set when the position signal of booster motor A sits below its valid band. GM documents it in its EBCM tables: the 2019 Cadillac XT4 unit trips when a raw sine or cosine value drops under 1,300 counts, or their sum under 3,876, for 10 ms; the 2023 and 2025 tables use a cosine value under 10 counts for 0.15 s, a sine line under 1.047 V or a vector length below 0.25. GM rates every variant Type A, lighting the MIL on the first trip. A low value points to a grounded signal line or missing sensor supply; Hitachi's resolver patent notes that a ground short pulls the output to 0 V. Infineon's TLE5009, a sine/cosine angle sensor intended for motor commutation, specifies a valid vector band for the same reason. Assist is cut or limited, and often the booster unit must be replaced.
c: Sine or cosine line of the sensor shorted to ground
Missing sensor supply, signals collapse toward zero
Sensor element or target magnet damaged, amplitude too small
s: Check engine lamp together with brake/ABS warning (GM)
Electric assist switched off, high pedal effort

C0589.t: Brake Booster Motor A Position Sensor Circuit High
C0589.d: C0589 is the high counterpart: a sine or cosine line of motor A's position sensor reads above its permitted maximum. In GM's 2019 XT4 brake module a raw value above 2,795 counts, or a sum above 4,327, for 10 ms sets it; the 2023 and 2025 EBCM tables trip on a cosine reading above 4,075 counts lasting 0.15 s, a sine input above 2.252 V, or a calculated vector length above 1.14. GM classifies it as Type A, MIL on the first trip. Typical causes are a sensor line touching supply voltage or a broken sensor ground. Hitachi describes how a short to battery drives the evaluated signal to its upper limit, after which motor current is cut. Without a trustworthy rotor angle the booster cannot commutate its motor, so electric assist is withdrawn.
c: Sensor signal line shorted to the sensor supply or battery voltage
Open sensor ground lifting the signals to the upper limit
Internal sensor fault in the booster unit
s: Brake assist warning with check engine lamp (GM)
Hard pedal, assist withdrawn

C058A.t: Brake Booster Motor A Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
C058A.d: C058A covers a position signal of booster motor A that is electrically valid but not believable. GM uses it widely: its 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables flag a rotor angle changing faster than 73° per ms, the 2019 IBC unit an invalid Hall pattern (all three high or all low) and a frozen signal, the XT4 module a vector length outside 0.6889–1.2996, and the 2023/2025 tables angle jumps beyond 711.2 rad/s – each Type A with MIL. NXP likewise treats Hall patterns 000 and 111 as an interface fault. GM's PIC6614 lists C058A for the Cadillac Lyriq with a brake assist failure message; Stellantis names it alongside C0582 for the Jeep Wagoneer and asks for BSCM and eBooster to be replaced together.
c: Position sensor delivering implausible angles (Hall element or sine/cosine sensor degraded)
Intermittent contact or interference on the sensor lines causing angle jumps
Booster unit internal fault or position data no longer matching the stored calibration
s: Brake assist failure message, abnormal pedal feel
Check engine and brake warning lamps (GM)
Fault may be hard to read out with a normal scan tool

C058B.t: Brake Booster Motor B Position Sensor Circuit/Open
C058B.d: C058B reports an open circuit at the position sensor of booster motor B. Such a second sensor exists where the booster has a second motor or winding system with its own commutation, or where the rotor angle is measured twice for safety. Stellantis shows that the eBooster of the Jeep Wagoneer has a motor B position channel, since its parts bulletin names C058E (range/performance) for it; C058B itself is not published by any maker. Kollmorgen's early patent on redundant windings gives every winding set its own group of Hall sensors, so losing one group only affects that set. An open line is detected as in Hitachi's resolver circuit: the bias signal no longer arrives and the input floats to its pull-up level. The module then drops channel B and runs on A or with reduced assist.
c: Broken signal or supply wire of position sensor B
Loose or corroded contact in the sensor B connector
Failed sensor element B inside the booster
s: Brake system warning with service message
Possibly reduced assist or limited assistance functions

C058C.t: Brake Booster Motor B Position Sensor Circuit Low
C058C.d: C058C applies when the motor B position signal sits below its lower limit – usually a sensor line shorted to ground, a missing sensor supply or a damaged sensor element. No manufacturer publishes this code; GM limits its documented position checks to motor A, where C0588 trips in the XT4 module below 1,300 counts. The physics are the same on either side: Hitachi's resolver patent attributes a reading near 0 V to a ground short, and a vector-length check like the one Infineon specifies for its TLE5009 sine/cosine sensor exposes an amplitude that has collapsed. In a dual-winding booster as described by Hyundai Mobis, the inverter for winding B depends on this angle, so the module shuts that inverter down and relies on the remaining channel.
c: Signal line of sensor B shorted to ground
Supply of sensor B missing or too low
Sensor element B or its magnet degraded, signal amplitude too small
s: Brake warning lamp
Assist may continue on one channel with reduced dynamics

C058D.t: Brake Booster Motor B Position Sensor Circuit High
C058D.d: C058D is set when a signal of motor B's position sensor exceeds its upper limit, for example because a sensor line touches supply voltage or the sensor ground has opened. No manufacturer documents C058D publicly; the range/performance case of the same sensor is C058E, which Stellantis lists for the Jeep Wagoneer eBooster. A short to battery in a resolver path pushes the evaluated signal to its ceiling, as Hitachi's patent explains. Bosch's booster patent outlines what a controller can still do when rotor position feedback is lost: drive the motor open-loop with capped speed and limited speed changes. Depending on the design, the module therefore continues with motor A, runs a degraded mode or switches assist off entirely.
c: Signal line of sensor B shorted to supply or battery voltage
Open ground of sensor B lifting the signal
Internal fault of sensor B in the booster
s: Brake system warning and message
Assist weaker or switched off depending on design

C058E.t: Brake Booster Motor B Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
C058E.d: C058E concerns a second rotor angle channel of the electric booster motor whose readings are electrically valid but not believable. In GM's 2019 integrated brake control unit this is MPS2, a SENT sensor checked against the faster SPI sensor MPS1 of the same motor: a gap above 2° plus a 3° speed allowance, opposite directions or a changed rest offset for 100 ms set it, Type A with MIL. GM's PIT5638 series for the 2019 Silverado and Sierra 1500 covers cases where the cluster showed Service Brake Assist and the pedal turned hard; the fix was new BSCM calibration, and the ECM adds P25A2. Stellantis names C058E for the eBooster of the 2022–25 Wagoneer and Grand Wagoneer; if it returns after the revised test, BSCM and booster are replaced as a pair.
c: Brake control module calibration causing false correlation faults (GM PIT5638)
Second rotor position sensor in the booster drifting or failing
Fault inside the brake control module or eBooster unit (replaced together)
Poor contact in the booster sensor connector
s: Service Brake Assist message in the instrument cluster
Hard brake pedal needing more effort, longer stopping distance
Check engine lamp via the brake module request (P25A2)

C058F.d: C058F covers the case where regenerative braking does not deliver the torque the brake system has planned with. In a blended brake the brake module asks the electric drive for generator torque, usually the smaller of the available capacity and the driver's demand, estimates what actually arrives and adds friction braking for the rest, as a GM/BMW/Daimler/Chrysler patent explains. Ford Otosan describes inferring the regenerative share from vehicle deceleration and switching to friction braking at once when regeneration is unavailable, for example with a full or hot battery. Ford notes that its ABS module may cap regenerative torque and that on plug-in hybrids lost regeneration shortens electric range. No manufacturer documents C058F publicly; expect reduced recuperation.
c: Electric drive or inverter delivering less generator torque than requested
Traction battery unable to absorb charge (full, hot or cold)
Torque arbitration or estimation software in the brake or hybrid module
Missing or delayed torque messages between brake and drive modules
s: Regenerative braking reduced or disabled, friction brakes do more work
Uneven deceleration or changed pedal feel during light braking
Shorter electric range on plug-in hybrids and EVs
Brake or hybrid system warning message

C0590.t: Brake Booster Motor A Phase U-V-W Current High
C0590.d: C0590 means the current measured in the drive of booster motor A is too high, mostly checked while the bridge is idle and almost nothing should flow. GM uses it in several units, always Type A with MIL: its 2016/2019 hybrid booster trips on leakage current above 20 A for 5 ms, the XT4 module on an idle offset above 36.1 A or a phase current above 200 A, and the 2023/2025 EBCM tables on a shunt offset above 38 A for 0.2 s. In GM's 2019 IBC unit it also flags a bridge driver whose overcurrent detection fails its power-up self-test. Mitsubishi maps C18E1-19 of the Outlander PHEV brake unit to C0590 with MIL after one trip; booster assist, regeneration and automatic braking stop. On the 2011 Saab 9-5 the number was a damper actuator code.
c: Leaking or partly conducting MOSFET in the booster motor bridge
Shunt or measuring amplifier offset drifted upward
Winding short in booster motor A drawing excess current
Bridge driver chip failing its overcurrent self-test
s: Brake assist warning, much higher pedal effort
Check engine, ABS or brake warning lamps on
Regenerative braking and automatic brake functions unavailable

C0591.t: Brake Booster Motor A Phase U-V-W Current Low
C0591.d: C0591 is the low counterpart: the current value of booster motor A lies below what is plausible, in practice a negative reading when the motor is at rest. In GM's 2016/2019 hybrid booster a leakage reading under −20 A counts while a half bridge is idle; the 2023/2025 EBCM tables set it when the offset taken from the internal shunt falls below −38 A for 0.2 s. The XT4 module is stricter: any idle offset under 0 A with the motor not actuated, under −36.1 A in general, or a phase current under −200 A for 0.3 s. All are Type A with MIL. A negative value at standstill points less to the motor than to the measuring chain: amplifier offset, shunt solder joints or the module's analog input. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV reports it as C18E1-18 with MIL and switches off assist.
c: Current sense amplifier or ADC offset drifted below zero
Cracked solder joint or damaged shunt in the power stage
Unexpected reverse current through a faulty bridge transistor
s: Loss of electric brake assist, hard pedal
Check engine and brake warning lamps after one drive
Regenerative braking switched off

C0592.t: Brake Booster Motor B Phase U-V-W Current High
C0592.d: C0592 reports excessive current in the second motor or second winding system, B, of an electric brake booster. No manufacturer publishes it in this sense; the number appears only in GM's keyword list PIP5094 for 2014 and older vehicles, from an earlier numbering. Side B exists in redundant layouts such as the Hyundai Mobis dual-winding booster motor, where two power modules with six MOSFETs each drive one winding and the healthy module takes over the full current command once the other is diagnosed as failed. Overcurrent on such a stage is caught by MOSFET drain-source monitoring and shunt amplifiers, as offered by TI's DRV8343-Q1. GM's side A limits (above 20 A leakage, 38 A offset) show the order of magnitude. Expect assist on side A only or reduced.
c: Shorted or leaking transistor in power module B
Insulation fault in winding system B
Measuring offset of the side B current sensing
s: Brake assist warning, possibly weaker or slower assist
Brake or ABS warning lamp on

C0593.t: Brake Booster Motor B Phase U-V-W Current Low
C0593.d: C0593 is meant for a current value on booster side B that is too low or negative where the controller expects about zero or a commanded positive current. It is not documented by any manufacturer; like C0592 it shows up only in GM's old keyword list PIP5094 with a different meaning. Unlike the high fault, a low value rarely reflects real current: more often the measuring chain has an offset. TI's DRV8343-Q1 has a calibration input that shorts the amplifier inputs internally so the controller can store the zero point and subtract it, and a drifted zero leads exactly to such readings. GM's matching test for side A trips below −20 A or −38 A. In a dual-winding motor like the Hyundai Mobis design, module B is then shut down and module A carries the load alone.
c: Zero point of the side B current measurement drifted
Defective power module B or its driver chip
High resistance in a side B phase connection
s: Brake assist warning message
Assist weaker under hard braking if only side A remains

C0594.d: C0594 judges whether booster motor A moves as commanded, not its wiring. GM's 2016/2019 hybrid booster flags a motor turning against the commanded direction (under 15 rad/s while more than 25 rad/s is requested), more than seven direction reversals, oscillation with the brake applied, or unintended backward rotation above 40 rad/s. In the XT4 unit and the 2023/2025 EBCM tables the plunger must reach its end position at start-up; the code also sets if the motor test finds a hardware fault, if pressure sensor 2 stays at or below 10 bar while the motor moves, or if modelled and measured pressure differ by over 40 bar for 0.2 s. All Type A with MIL. Mitsubishi files C18E1-49 (motor not operating normally) of the Outlander PHEV as C0594 with MIL.
c: Binding gear, spindle or plunger inside the booster
Worn or damaged booster motor A
Air or leakage in the hydraulic circuit so pressure does not follow motor travel
Faulty rotor position feedback causing wrong direction or oscillation
s: Loss of brake assist with a heavy pedal
Check engine and brake warning lamps on
Booster noise or pedal vibration before the fault sets

C0595.t: Brake Booster Internal Power Driver Range/Performance
C0595.d: C0595 covers the power path inside the booster electronics: master switch, safety relay and the six-transistor bridge driver. GM's 2016/2019 hybrid booster switches its master switch on, off and on again at start-up and expects the voltage ratio behind it above 0.88. In GM's IBC unit the feedback behind the motor safety relay must stay above or below 80 % of supply for 50 ms, besides configuration and SPI checks of the bridge driver; XT4 and the 2023/2025 tables test the bridge driver chip at start-up. All Type A with MIL. GM bulletin 20-NA-073 (2019–20 CT6, XT5, XT6, Blazer, Acadia, Silverado, Sierra) lists C0595 with lost assist and push-through braking, fixed by BSCM software; 19-NA-202 does the same for the 2016–19 Malibu. Mitsubishi maps C18ED-04 here.
c: Defective bridge driver chip or its SPI communication
Motor safety relay or master switch not switching correctly
Supply voltage dips or poor module ground
s: Loss of brake assist, longer and softer pedal with more force needed
Service StabiliTrak or brake messages, traction lamp on
Check engine lamp (requested by the brake module)

C0596.t: Brake Booster Motor A Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
C0596.d: C0596 questions the current measurement of booster motor A itself rather than the motor. GM's 2016/2019 hybrid booster tests its overcurrent comparator at start-up by forcing minimum and maximum PWM and reading the comparator output back over a feedback line, while the voltage behind the master switch must sit near zero or near battery voltage; a hardware overcurrent flag on that line during operation also sets it (30 ms). GM's 2019 IBC unit injects zero, positive, negative and common-mode offsets into the current sense path at power-up, with the motor almost still and 7.1–18 V supply, and compares the results with their allowed bands. All Type A with MIL. Driver chips such as TI's DRV8343-Q1 short the amplifier inputs on command for this zero calibration.
c: Faulty current sense amplifier or motor driver chip
Overcurrent comparator or its feedback line not responding
Supply voltage outside the test window during start-up
s: Brake assist warning right after switching on
Heavy brake pedal, check engine lamp on

C0597.t: Brake System Control Module A Performance
C0597.d: C0597 is a summary code for the first brake system control module: it cannot carry out its function properly, and the failure type byte narrows the cause. Toyota uses C059746 (calibration or parameter memory) on 2020–22 Corolla, Corolla Cross and RAV4 with a parking brake warning, cured by reprogramming the skid control unit (T-SB-0078-21), and C059704 (internal failure) on the 2022–23 Tundra, covered by a software campaign. Stellantis asks for current software before an ABS module and booster are replaced for C0597-00 on the 2021–22 Grand Cherokee and 4xe. On 2026 GM full-size SUVs C0597 replaced C055F: a Service Brake System message led to a new master cylinder (PIT6450A), and cold-weather cases trace to weak battery voltage (PIT6476).
c: Outdated or corrupted brake module software or calibration data
Low battery voltage or poor power and ground connections, especially in cold
Internal fault of the brake control unit or integrated master cylinder
s: Service Brake System or parking brake malfunction message
ABS, stability control and possibly check engine lamps on
Changed brake pedal effort

C0598.t: Brake System Control Module B Performance
C0598.d: C0598 is the same summary check for a second brake control module, B. Such a module is found where braking is split between two units: Bosch gives its integrated power brake a separate backup unit for automated driving, so the vehicle still stops if the main unit fails. A BWI patent describes such a backup unit with its own control unit, motor and pumps for the front axle, linked to the main unit over a private CAN line and taking over pedal boost in the fallback mode. C0598 reports that unit B fails its internal checks. No manufacturer documents C0598 publicly; Toyota's use of C0597 for control module A shows the lettering. Redundancy or assist is reduced while it is stored.
c: Software or calibration fault in brake module B
Power supply or ground problem of module B
Internal hardware fault of module B
Fault on the link between the two brake modules
s: Brake system warning message
Driver assistance or automated driving functions unavailable
Reduced brake assist if the module handles boosting

C0599.t: Brake Booster Control Module Missing Calibration
C0599.d: C0599 means the control unit of an electric brake booster finds no valid calibration data. Stand-alone electromechanical boosters such as Bosch's iBooster carry their own controller, which converts the reading of a built-in differential travel sensor into motor commands; how the pedal feels is set by software parameters. A Bosch patent describes keeping the characteristic between booster travel and driver input in exactly this unit. If that data set or its learned values are absent, typically after a booster or module swap or an aborted flash, the code is stored. No maker documents C0599 publicly. As a yardstick, GM's check for a pressure sensor calibration (C0560) only reads the stored end-of-line status 500 ms after wake-up. Expect weak or missing assist and a hard pedal until the setup routine has run.
c: Booster or its control module replaced without running the setup/calibration routine
Software update or programming of the booster module aborted or incomplete
Internal memory fault in the booster control module losing stored data
s: Brake warning or service brake assist message in the cluster
Hard brake pedal with reduced power assist
Driver assistance functions using the booster (e.g. emergency braking) unavailable

C059A.t: Power Steering Control Module - Rear Missing Calibration
C059A.d: C059A concerns active rear-axle steering: its control module lacks the calibration it needs to position the rear wheels. Systems like ZF's AKC turn the rear wheels by a few degrees with an electrically driven spindle, either through one central actuator or one per wheel. A Magna patent shows what has to be calibrated: a coarse absolute travel sensor and a fine rotor sensor are referenced to the geometric centre between both mechanical end stops, and these values are stored so the actuator can return to straight-ahead. Without them the module cannot hold the rear wheels centred and disables rear steering. No maker documents C059A publicly. GM names the part K92 Rear Power Steering Control Module; on the 2024 Hummer EV it stopped working after vehicle-wide programming until authentication was repeated (PIT6350), logged as U3000/U1961/U1962.
c: Rear steering module or actuator replaced without centre calibration
Programming or setup after a software update not completed
Suspension or alignment work requiring a new rear steering zero point
Low 12 V supply interrupting the calibration routine
s: Rear steering warning in the cluster and rear wheel steering inactive
Larger turning circle and changed handling at speed
Steering wheel slightly off centre on straight roads

C059B.t: Brake Pressure Sensor B Missing Calibration
C059B.d: The brake module cannot confirm that pressure sensor B has been calibrated and that its sensitivity is right. GM uses C059B in the brake controller of its 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables for the rear-left wheel pressure sensor: during a test pulse the sensor response must stay between 90 % and 110 %, checked only after at least one completed offset learn, with low master cylinder pressure and no ABS, traction or stability intervention. Type A, MIL after one trip; to confirm a fix, drive above about 6 mph for a minute without braking. In those same tables the rear-left sensor's circuit faults use C0575–C0578. A Bosch patent likewise treats a failed test pulse as a sensitivity fault with ABS and ESC lamps on. Ford checks sensor data by checksum and ID, but only for sensor A (C0560).
c: Calibration or offset learn not completed after module or hydraulic unit replacement
Pressure sensor responding outside the allowed test-pulse window
Brake control module storing or evaluating calibration data incorrectly
s: ABS and stability control warning lamps on, MIL possible
Regenerative braking blending or ESC functions restricted

C059C.t: Brake Pressure Sensor C Missing Calibration
C059C.d: For pressure sensor C the module finds no confirmed calibration record. Such a record usually holds the zero offset and a status flag written on the assembly line or by the scan tool. No maker documents C059C publicly. Related checks are published: GM's 2019 EBCM reads only that status flag for its master cylinder sensor (C0560) 500 ms after wake-up, Type A with MIL, and Ford hybrids compare checksum and sensor ID between sensor and module (150 or 70 ms). GM's 2016 hybrid controller uses C0571–C0574 for a master cylinder sensor but files its calibration fault under C0560, so letters in calibration codes need not match circuit codes. Saab names module and modulator replacement as reasons to recalibrate with the brake released and the car secured.
c: Sensor calibration not performed after replacing the brake module or modulator
Calibration aborted because the pedal was pressed or the vehicle moved
Stored data does not match the fitted sensor (checksum or ID)
s: ABS/ESC warning lamp on
Stability control or brake assist functions switched off

C059D.t: Brake Pressure Sensor D Missing Calibration
C059D.d: C059D flags missing calibration data for a fourth hydraulic pressure sensor. No manufacturer publishes this code. Where the letter D appears elsewhere, GM's 2016 hybrid brake controller uses it for the rear-left wheel pressure sensor (C0575–C0578), yet reports that sensor's calibration fault as C059B; the letters of the calibration codes therefore follow each maker's own list. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV has a comparable fault without SAE number, C105E-92 for an uncalibrated pressure sensor, detected within 1 s, and tells technicians to clear a merely stored code instead of replacing the unit. A Bosch patent describes resetting an offset fault only after a successful check while driving. Practically, the module limits ABS/ESC functions until the scan tool calibration has passed.
c: Calibration of the sensor not done after hydraulic unit or module replacement
Code stored from an earlier event, sensor already calibrated
Brake module losing calibration data in its memory
s: ABS and ESC warning lamps on
Brake pressure based functions such as hill hold or brake blending limited

C059E.t: Brake Pressure Sensor E Missing Calibration
C059E.d: C059E reports that sensor E, one more pressure sensor in a multi-sensor brake unit, has never been calibrated successfully or that its record is lost. No maker documents C059E publicly; for sensor E only the circuit codes C059F–C05A2 exist. GM's published logic for related sensors shows what can go wrong: for its pedal travel sensor (C05D4) the stored status reports a failed zeroing if the sensor had an electrical fault, the car moved or the brake was applied during calibration, or the offset was too big, too small or unsteady. For pressure sensor A GM's 2025 tables check only the status flag, 500 ms after wake-up, Type A. Saab lists module or modulator replacement as reasons to recalibrate. Rerun the calibration with the car stationary and the pedal untouched.
c: Calibration run while the vehicle moved or the brake pedal was pressed
Calibration skipped after replacing the brake module or hydraulic unit
Sensor offset too large or unstable so the calibration is rejected
s: ABS/ESC or brake system warning lamp on
Brake assist or stability functions disabled

C059F.t: Brake Pressure Sensor E Circuit Low
C059F.d: The signal of brake pressure sensor E sits below its valid window. Analogue brake pressure sensors run on 5 V and report roughly 0.5–4.5 V; a Bosch trainer notes such a sensor shows under 1 V with the brake released. A Denso patent on vehicle pressure sensors reserves 0–0.3 V as an error band and explains that, with a pull-down resistor at the module, a broken supply or signal wire also drags the reading to 0 V, so an open circuit can appear as low here. Other causes are a short of the signal to ground or a failed sensor. No maker documents C059F publicly. GM's hybrid brake controller uses the same kind of check on its wheel pressure sensors: below 0.3 V lasting 100 ms, rated Type A. Sensor E is usually built into the hydraulic unit, so a sensor fault often means replacing that unit.
c: Signal wire of the sensor shorted to ground
Open 5 V supply or signal wire pulled low by the module input
Pressure sensor failed internally (often part of the hydraulic unit)
s: ABS/ESC warning lamp on
Stability control and pressure-based brake functions switched off

C05A0.t: Brake Pressure Sensor E Circuit High
C05A0.d: C05A0 is set when sensor E reports a voltage above its usable range. In the Denso patent on vehicle pressure sensors the band from 4.7 to 5 V is reserved for faults, and a lost ground wire pushes the output into it through the divider formed by the sensor's internal resistance and the module's pull-down resistor. Honeywell's ratiometric transducers deliberately drive their output to 97.5 % of supply on an internal fault or overpressure, so a high code can also come from the sensor itself. A short to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage is the other common case. No maker publishes C05A0; GM's 2019 EBCM uses more than 95.24 % of supply for 100 ms on comparable sensors, Type A. The module would otherwise see braking that is not happening, so it ignores the sensor and limits ESC.
c: Signal shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage
Open sensor ground lifting the output to the upper rail
Sensor signalling an internal fault at full scale
s: ABS/ESC warning lamp on
Stability control unavailable, brake lights may be requested falsely on some systems

C05A1.d: This code points to an interrupted circuit of sensor E: a broken signal, 5 V supply or ground wire, or a connector that has lost contact. No maker documents C05A1 publicly. Whether an open is recognised as such or as low or high depends on the input circuit, which is why many systems book it under C059F or C05A0 instead. Honeywell specifies that with an external pull-up resistor a power or ground loss drives the output high, with a pull-down low. A Denso patent adds a check for creeping contact resistance, which produces in-between voltages that such resistor schemes miss: the supply is briefly raised so the sensor outputs a fixed test voltage. Bosch's EBS monitors each of its pressure sensors separately. Check connector and wiring before condemning the sensor.
c: Corroded or loose connector at the sensor or hydraulic unit
Broken signal, supply or ground wire
Internal open circuit in the sensor
s: ABS/ESC warning lamp on, possibly coming and going
Stability control and brake assist switched off

C05A2.d: Here sensor E delivers a voltage that is electrically valid but does not fit the braking situation: a drifting zero point, wrong gain or a value that disagrees with other pressure signals. No maker documents C05A2 publicly. The usual tests are known from related sensors. GM's hybrid brake controller learns each wheel sensor's zero while the pedal is released and flags an offset beyond ±1,500 kPa at once. A Bosch patent sets an offset fault when the compensation passes a limit, lights the ABS and ESC lamps and clears it only after a good check while driving. A Lucas/ZF patent opens the valves at standstill so all sensors see one pressure; with at least three of them the drifting one and its error can be identified. Trapped pressure, sensor drift or a ground offset are typical causes.
c: Sensor zero point or gain drifted with age or temperature
Residual pressure trapped in the circuit during the zero learn
Ground offset between sensor and module distorting the reading
s: ABS and ESC warning lamps on
Stability or regenerative brake functions reduced

C05A3.t: Wheel Speed Sensors Supply Circuit High
C05A3.d: Active wheel speed sensors are fed by the ABS module and send their pulses back as a current on the same pair of wires, as HELLA explains. C05A3 reports that this common supply is too high or cannot be switched off. GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid brake controllers look for reverse current on the supply line, the sign of a short to the battery feed, for over 3.5 s. A 2019 GM EBCM with a system ASIC uses C05A3 for two cases: the sensor supply exceeds its overvoltage limit, after which the ASIC turns off all four high-side switches, and a periodic test in which a supposedly switched-off high side is still live. Both are Type A with MIL. Allegro rates its wheel speed sensor IC for 24 V and clamps at 28 V. With no wheel speeds, ABS, ESC and traction control stop working.
c: Wheel speed sensor wire chafed and shorted to battery voltage
Supply switch or ASIC in the brake module stuck on
Water in a wheel speed sensor connector bridging to a powered circuit
s: ABS, traction and stability control warning lamps on at the same time
Several or all wheel speed signals lost, speedometer may drop out
MIL on (GM)

C05A4.t: Wheel Speed Sensors Supply Circuit Low
C05A4.d: The shared feed for the active wheel speed sensors is too low for them to work. In GM's hybrid tables of 2016 and 2019 the brake controller measures, via an internal comparator, the voltage between the sensor supply line and the signal line and sets C05A4 below 6.7 V for 0.06 s while system voltage is above 6.9 V, Type A with MIL; it also blocks the single-wheel codes such as C0500–C0504. A 2019 GM EBCM reads the supply through its ASIC, on units without a regulated sensor feed also against the 12 V input, and sets the code within 15 ms. Allegro's sensor IC needs at least 4 V, or 5.2 V for one variant. On the 2021 Jeep Wrangler 4xe a weak 12 V battery set C05A4 together with other low-voltage codes and a MIL; the fix was to charge, test and replace the battery (08-106-21). Check battery and charging before parts.
c: Wheel speed sensor wiring shorted to ground, pulling the shared supply down
Sensor supply stage inside the brake module failing
s: ABS, traction and stability control lamps on, MIL possible
Several wheel speed codes at once, often with low-voltage codes
Hard starting or no start when the 12 V battery is the cause

C05A5.t: ABS Pump Motor Supply Voltage B Circuit/Open
C05A5.d: Supply B is a second power feed for the pump motor of the brake unit; C05A5 reports it as missing or open. A second feed is found where the motor or its drive is built redundantly. Hyundai Mobis patents a brake motor with two windings, each with its own power module and own supply input from the battery; if one side fails it is shut off and the other carries the full current. Ipgate describes a brake-by-wire drive with two three-phase strands and electronics on two redundant voltage supplies. No maker documents C05A5 publicly. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV shows the usual single-feed layout: 60 A fusible link to the motor, 10–16 V at the connector. Feed A has its own code C052F. Depending on design, the pump runs on with reduced power or brake functions are cut back.
c: Blown fuse or fusible link in the B supply
Open wire or loose terminal in the B feed to the brake unit
Internal fault in the second power stage of the brake module
s: ABS/ESC or brake system warning on
Reduced pressure build-up or loss of redundancy message

C05A6.t: ABS Pump Motor Supply Voltage B Circuit High
C05A6.d: C05A6 says the second pump motor feed, supply B, carries more voltage than allowed. Overvoltage strains the motor and above all the transistors that switch it; gate driver ICs for brake motors such as TI's DRV8305-Q1 therefore watch their supply and raise an overvoltage warning in the mid-30 V range. Typical causes are a faulty alternator or DC/DC converter regulator, jump-starting or charging at too high a voltage, or a measuring fault in the module. No maker documents C05A6 publicly. As an orientation, Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV specifies 10–16 V for the motor feed and stores C1056-17 once the brake unit's supply reaches 16 V within 1 s. Where the motor has two power modules on separate inputs, as in a Hyundai Mobis patent, the faulty side can be disabled while the other keeps working.
c: Alternator or DC/DC converter regulating too high
Jump start or battery charger with excessive voltage
Voltage measurement fault in the brake module
s: ABS/ESC warning lamp on, possibly with other overvoltage codes
Very bright lights or battery warning if charging is the cause

C05A7.t: ABS Pump Motor Supply Voltage B Circuit Low
C05A7.d: Supply B of the pump motor reads below its lower limit. The pump motor draws high current, so a weak 12 V battery, corroded terminals, a fuse holder with high resistance or a poor ground show up first under load. No maker documents C05A7 publicly. Published low-voltage checks for the single feed give a sense of scale: Ford hybrids flag the pump circuit if it is under 7.3 V for 1.8 s while running (C052B), Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV stores C1056-16 at 10 V or less, and an AlliedSignal patent, now Bosch, sets a separate fault if the motor sees less than about 7 V at switch-off. For a motor with two power modules on their own inputs, as patented by Hyundai Mobis, one weak side can be dropped. Circuit A has its own code C055B.
c: Corroded terminal, fuse holder or ground in the B feed
Charging system not keeping up (alternator or DC/DC converter)
s: ABS/ESC lamp on, often after cold starts or long standstill
Pump motor running audibly slower during self-test

C05A8.t: ABS Pump Motor Supply Voltage B Circuit Range/Performance
C05A8.d: C05A8 means supply B is present but behaves implausibly: it sags too far once the pump starts, recovers too slowly, or does not match the state the module has commanded. That is different from a hard open (C05A5) or a steady high or low reading (C05A6, C05A7). No maker publishes a threshold for C05A8. Ford's hybrid brake module shows the logic on its single pump feed under C052B: below 6 V with the pump off or below 7.3 V with it on, each for 1.8 s. Mitsubishi lists 10–16 V for the motor feed on the 2023 Outlander PHEV, measured once with the motor switch off and once on. Systems with a second feed, such as the redundant brake-by-wire drive in an Ipgate patent, need this check to know whether the backup path is really usable. Load-test battery and feed.
c: Excessive voltage drop in the B feed when the pump starts
Relay or semiconductor switch in the B path responding slowly or partly
Aged 12 V battery with high internal resistance
s: Intermittent ABS/ESC warning, mostly during pump activity
Message about reduced braking redundancy on brake-by-wire vehicles

C05A9.t: ABS Pump Motor Supply Voltage Circuit A/B Correlation
C05A9.d: With two feeds for the pump motor, the module can compare them: both come from the same vehicle supply and should read almost alike. C05A9 is set when the two drift apart beyond the allowed margin, even though each may still lie in its own window. A Hitachi patent for electric brakes uses this idea: the control unit compares the voltages of several branch supply lines and, if the largest difference exceeds a limit, concludes that a main line is broken and switches in a backup path. Hyundai Mobis gives each winding of a dual brake motor its own power module and supply input, and Ipgate runs its brake-by-wire electronics on two redundant supplies. No maker documents C05A9 publicly. Likely causes are a high-resistance connection in one feed or a measuring error in the module.
c: Corroded terminal, fuse or connector in only one of the two feeds
Voltage measurement channel in the brake module drifting
Poor ground affecting only one supply path
s: ABS/ESC or brake system warning lamp on
Pump operation or brake redundancy restricted

C05AA.t: ABS Pump Motor Temperature Too High
C05AA.d: C05AA signals that the ABS return or high-pressure pump motor, or its switching stage, has become too hot. Few units have a sensor on the motor, so the temperature is usually modelled. A Kelsey-Hayes (now ZF) patent estimates the heat of the transistor that drives the pump from separate heating and cooling curves, starting from the module's ambient sensor; above a limit of about 90–150 °C (60–110 °C in deep cold) the pump is disabled until the estimate falls below a lower threshold, optionally with a warning lamp. Bosch describes a staged response in an electrohydraulic brake: as limits are passed, heat-producing functions are cut back down to the mechanical fallback. Long ABS or stability events, hot climates and a stiff pump favour it. No manufacturer publishes C05AA.
c: Long ABS, traction or stability interventions, e.g. on rough or slippery roads
Stiff pump or worn motor brushes raising current and heat
Module ambient sensor or temperature model giving false values
s: ABS or stability control temporarily unavailable
ABS or brake warning lamp on, often clearing after cooling down

C05AB.d: C05AB concerns the separation valve that decouples the driver's master cylinder from the wheel circuits while the brakes work by wire, so that pedal pressure does not cut into regenerative braking. It is usually open without current, so the pedal acts on the wheels if power fails, as in Continental's brake-by-wire layout. A performance fault means it does not seal or switch as expected. Mando's patent shows how a leak is found: if pedal simulator pressure follows circuit pressure too closely, fluid is getting through; the valve is re-energised to free a stuck seat, and after repeated failures the system warns and returns to direct pedal braking, as leaking pressure can kick back into the pedal. Toyota patents isolate a valve by response delays. No manufacturer publishes C05AB.
c: Dirt or debris on the valve seat causing leakage
Valve coil or its driver in the module not switching properly
Old or wrong brake fluid making the valve sluggish
Pressure sensor errors making the valve look faulty
s: Pedal kickback or vibration during braking
Regenerative braking reduced, brake warning message
Brakes switch to direct pedal operation with higher effort

C05AC.t: Brake Blending Separation Valve Stuck Closed
C05AC.d: C05AC names one specific failure: the separation valve of the blended brake stays closed when it should open. Toyota's patent for a hybrid brake defines this closure failure and shows how it is pinned down: the control pressure sensor lags its target by more than a set amount for too long, the sensor passes its self-test and the upstream linear valve demonstrably delivers fluid, so the blockage must be the separation valve. The brake then drops into a no-current backup mode with master cylinder pressure on the front axle. Designs differ in how much a closed separation valve costs: Lucas showed a layout in which both front brakes still respond to the pedal although the isolating valve stays shut. No manufacturer publishes C05AC; assist and regeneration are typically suspended.
c: Valve armature stuck by contamination or corrosion
Open coil or wiring so a normally closed valve cannot open
Valve driver stage in the brake module defective
s: Brake warning, assist and regeneration off
Higher pedal effort, longer stopping distance in backup mode
Uneven braking between axles possible

C05AD.d: C05AD is the overall check of a blended brake: does the hydraulic pressure built by wire match what the controller asked for? GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables (brake module BSC1) compare actual and target boost-piston pressure, for the by-wire side as well as the master cylinder side: more than 4,000 kPa too high points to a false high sensor value, more than 1,500 kPa too low to a low sensor value, an empty accumulator, a weak pump, air or a leak. It sets within 0.5–1 s, Type A with MIL. GM proves the repair by driving to about 25 mph and braking gently at around 3,000 kPa rear pressure twice. Bosch notes that blending generator and hydraulic braking is a core job of brake-by-wire, and Ford Otosan's patent compensates regeneration gaps with friction braking.
c: Brake pressure sensor reading too high or too low
Low accumulator pressure or weak hydraulic pump
Air in the hydraulic circuit after service
External or internal leak in the brake hydraulics
s: Brake warning and check engine lamps
Soft or inconsistent pedal, braking stronger or weaker than expected
Regenerative braking reduced

C05AE.t: ABS Pump Motor Calibration Not Learned
C05AE.d: C05AE means the brake module lacks a valid zero calibration for the measuring channels of its pump motor. In GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid brake module (BSC1) the motor voltages are read through a sigma-delta modulator that needs a 0 V calibration; with the ignition on, more than 6.9 V system voltage and the pump off, the code sets if the raw generator voltage reading falls outside 14–23.8 or the drop across the pump relay outside 13–18, for 3 s. A second test flags supply undervoltage: shunt voltage under 7.5 V or relay drain voltage outside 1.5–3 V for 2 s. Type A with MIL; the check passes after 20 s of driving above 18.6 mph. Such offset calibration is standard for delta-sigma converters, as TI's ADS131M04 data sheet shows.
c: Stored zero calibration missing or invalid after module replacement or programming
Low or unstable supply voltage during the calibration
Pump motor relay or shunt in the module out of tolerance
s: ABS and brake warning lamps plus check engine lamp
ABS or stability functions limited until the calibration succeeds

C05AF.t: Brake Booster Motor B Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
C05AF.d: C05AF is the plausibility check of the current measurement on booster side B, the second motor or winding system. No manufacturer publishes it. A separate sensing chain for B is needed wherever each power module controls its own winding, as in the Hyundai Mobis dual-winding booster motor, since every module must know its phase currents to regulate torque and to judge its own health. Typical checks run at start-up, before current flows: the controller shorts the amplifier inputs (TI's DRV8343-Q1 offers a pin for this), records the zero point and rejects values outside a band. GM's counterpart for side A, C0596, additionally injects test offsets. A failed B measurement normally leads to side B being switched off and assist relying on side A, possibly with lower power.
c: Faulty current sense amplifier of side B
Zero offset of side B outside its allowed band
Damaged shunt or solder joint in power module B
s: Brake assist or brake system warning
Possibly weaker assist under hard braking

C05B0.d: C05B0 reports lost fluid or volume in a hydraulic circuit the maker designates C; at GM its meaning has changed over time. GM's 2016–2019 hybrid brake controllers used it for the front axle circuit: wheel behaviour not matching vehicle deceleration during ABS or EBD for 1 s, or master cylinder pressure above rear axle pressure at constant pedal. A 2019 EBCM with integrated booster flags dynamic leaks when a pressure error integral passes 20 bar. In GM's 2023 and 2025 tables C05B0 means air in the plunger circuit: a volume deviation over 2 cm³ during replenishment, or over 1.5 cm³ in the other tests. All Type A with MIL. GM bulletin 22-NA-247 warns of false C05B0 on eBoost models after pad work; pump the pedal firm before clearing. On 2019 Silverado/Sierra it came with Service Brake Assist.
c: Caliper pistons pushed back during pad work and not reseated before driving (GM 22-NA-247)
Air in the plunger or brake circuit after service or bleeding
Real fluid leak at a line, hose, caliper or valve
Brake module software calibration causing false detection (GM PIT5638)
s: Service brake assist or brake system message, brake warning lamp
Longer or softer pedal travel
MIL on (GM)

C05B1.d: C05B1 is the leak code for hydraulic circuit D. The only public maker use is GM's hybrid brake controller of 2016–2019, where it covers the rear axle circuit. Two checks feed it: during pressure hold phases with the pump off and the car at rest, a calculated rear leakage above 0.3 ml/s, judged over more than 300 s of cumulative braking; and, with more than 5,000 kPa at the front axle and a steady pedal for 3 s, a master cylinder pressure lower than the rear axle pressure. Type A, MIL after one trip. Its partner C05B0 covered the front axle there. A Continental patent shows another approach: build pressure with a motor-driven plunger and judge tightness from the slope of the pressure decay. FMVSS 135 demands a red warning on major fluid loss. Inspect lines, rear calipers and the hydraulic unit.
c: Fluid leak at a rear brake line, hose or caliper
Internal leakage of an inlet or outlet valve in the hydraulic unit
Air in the rear circuit after service
s: Brake and ABS warning lamps on, MIL possible
Longer pedal travel and weaker rear braking

C05B2.t: Steering Wheel Angle Sensor Signal - Yaw Rate Sensor Signal Correlation
C05B2.d: C05B2 flags a mismatch between how far the driver has turned the wheel and how quickly the car actually rotates about its vertical axis. The stability controller turns steering wheel angle and road speed into an expected yaw rate through a single-track vehicle model; a Siemens patent applies that model only up to about 4 m/s² of lateral acceleration. Bosch gives a permitted gap of roughly 1 to 4.5 deg/s between the yaw sensor and the steering-based value and keeps stability control switched off while the fault stands, with traction control still working. No manufacturer publishes C05B2 itself. Frequent triggers are a steering angle sensor left uncalibrated after alignment or steering repairs, a loose or shifted yaw sensor, or a drifting offset. ESC is unavailable and its warning lamp remains lit.
c: Steering angle sensor not recalibrated after wheel alignment, steering or column work
Yaw rate sensor or sensor cluster loose, rotated or wrongly installed
Offset drift or internal fault in the yaw rate or steering angle sensor
Mismatched tyres or bent steering parts making the vehicle model invalid
s: ESC and often traction control warning lamp on
Stability control interventions unavailable
Steering wheel off-centre when driving straight, if alignment is the cause

C05B3.t: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor C Circuit Low
C05B3.d: C05B3 means the third temperature channel of an electromechanical brake booster has dropped below its usable band. Mitsubishi documents the code for the Outlander PHEV: the DTC index pairs it with the brake unit's own code C18FC-18, EBA temperature sensor 1, and lights the brake system warning lamp plus the MIL after two trips. The value comes from the control electronics inside the electric intelligent brake unit. With the motor switch on, Mitsubishi stores the fault within one second if that reading is at or below −43 °C or at or above 169 °C. The fail-safe column says normal condition, so assist keeps working. Mitsubishi files its second sensor under C0579/C057A. Listed causes are harness, connector and the brake unit itself.
c: Fault in the temperature detection inside the electric brake unit's control module
Corroded or loose brake unit connector or damaged harness
Supply disturbance during start-up distorting the reading
s: Brake system warning lamp on
Check engine lamp on after two trips (Mitsubishi)
Braking assist usually unchanged

C05B4.t: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor C Circuit High
C05B4.d: C05B4 is the upper-limit counterpart: temperature channel C of the electric booster reports a value above its permitted maximum. In Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV index it stands next to C18FC-19, again EBA temperature sensor 1, with the same lamp logic – brake system warning lamp and MIL after the second trip. Mitsubishi's description page for this subcode repeats the criteria of C05B3 word for word (−43 °C or colder, 169 °C or hotter, detected within one second), so the split into low and high lies in the electrical evaluation, not in the published temperatures. Whether a high signal stands for heat or cold depends on how the thermistor is wired in its divider. Because the sensor sits on the control board, a persistent fault usually means replacing the brake unit.
c: Temperature circuit on the brake unit's control board defective
Poor contact at the brake unit connector or chafed wiring
Genuinely excessive electronics temperature after heavy booster use
s: Brake system warning lamp on
MIL on after the second trip (Mitsubishi)
Code returns immediately after clearing if the unit is defective

C05B5.t: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor C Circuit/Open
C05B5.d: C05B5 is reserved for an interrupted circuit of booster temperature sensor C. No manufacturer documents it publicly; Mitsubishi, the one maker naming sensor C codes, reports problems with this channel only as C05B3 or C05B4. Boosters typically carry several NTC thermistors: Hitachi Astemo places one on the motor and one in the controller near the motor drive stage and caps motor current when either runs hot. If a thermistor or its lead breaks, the divider sits at one rail; a supplier overview cautions that such a rail reading alone cannot separate every wiring, reference or converter fault. Microchip adds that a board or module NTC follows case temperature, not the transistor junction. As the sensor is mostly internal, repair normally means a new booster unit.
c: Cracked thermistor body or broken lead inside the booster
Fractured solder joint on the control board from vibration or heat cycles
Open wire or pin where the sensor is wired externally
s: Brake or brake system warning lamp on
Booster may restrict assist as a precaution, depending on design

C05B6.t: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
C05B6.d: C05B6 targets a sensor C reading that is electrically inside its band yet does not behave like a real temperature: it stays flat during long assist phases, lags far behind the other channels, or contradicts the thermal estimate of the module. No manufacturer publishes this code. The risk is clear from Hitachi Astemo's booster patent, where measured motor and controller temperatures decide when motor current is cut back and when full assist returns; a believable but wrong value either throttles assist early or lets the drive overheat. Microchip notes that an NTC mounted in a power module tracks the case and heatsink, so a junction estimate has to be derived from it. Long-term drift through moisture or cracking is a known NTC weakness. A plausibility fault normally needs a drive with booster activity to set.
c: Thermistor resistance drifted through ageing, moisture or micro-cracks
Sensor lost thermal contact with the part it should measure
Thermal model or calibration in the booster control unit not matching the hardware
s: Brake system warning lamp on
Assist reduced earlier than usual during long descents or repeated braking

C05B7.t: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
C05B7.d: C05B7 is meant for a temperature C signal that jumps or briefly drops out rather than failing permanently. No manufacturer documents it publicly. In Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV the sensor C channel is judged against fixed limits with a detection time of up to one second, so short spikes there end up as C05B3 or C05B4 instead of a separate erratic code. Thermistor specialists attribute unstable readings mainly to mechanical stress: bent leads, board flex or shocks can produce intermittent contact before the part opens completely, and damaged coatings let moisture in. Because the sensor often sits on the booster's own board, a cracked solder joint is the usual suspect. The lamp may come and go with temperature or rough roads, and the fault tends to reappear after clearing.
c: Cracked solder joint or lead at the thermistor
Loose pin or fretting corrosion at the booster connector
Moisture reaching the sensing element through a damaged coating
s: Brake system warning lamp flickers or appears only at times
Code returns after clearing, often after rough roads or temperature changes

C05B8.t: Brake Booster Motor A Position Sensor Supply Circuit/Open
C05B8.d: The rotor position sensor of booster motor A – Hall, magnetoresistive or a digital SENT angle sensor – is fed from a regulated 5 V output of the brake control unit. C05B8 reports that this feed is interrupted. No manufacturer documents the code publicly; GM's 2019 integrated brake control lists supply faults of its two motor position sensors under C05D1 and C05BB only. Denso's sensor patent shows why an open feed is hard to tell from a dead sensor: with a pull-down input the signal simply falls to 0 V. Hitachi Astemo's steering patent therefore monitors each sensor supply separately so the failed one can be identified. Without a rotor angle the booster cannot commutate its motor, so assist is cut back or lost and the brake warning appears.
c: Broken supply wire or pin between control unit and motor position sensor
Sensor supply output in the brake control unit failed
Internal open in the position sensor's supply path
s: Brake warning lamp and message such as service brake assist
Noticeably harder brake pedal
Regenerative or electronic brake functions unavailable

C05B9.t: Brake Booster Motor A Position Sensor Supply Circuit Low
C05B9.d: C05B9 is set when the feed voltage for motor A's position sensor sags below its lower limit. No manufacturer publishes C05B9; as a reference point, GM's 2019 brake module calls its 5 V sensor supplies low below 4.85 V lasting 100 ms, but books that under C05D1 or C05BB. A low supply usually means the line is shorted to ground or a sensor is drawing too much current. Supplies of this kind are often tracking regulators such as TI's TPS7B4253-Q1, built for sensors on long cables: the output is short-proof to ground and current-limited at typically 450 mA, so instead of failing it lets the voltage collapse. Since the same rail can also feed pedal sensors, related codes may appear together. Motor commutation becomes unreliable and assist is reduced or removed.
c: Supply line chafed through and shorted to ground
Defective position sensor or another sensor on the same rail loading the supply
Weak sensor supply regulator in the control unit
s: Brake warning lamp, often with several sensor codes at once
Brake pedal feels hard, assist reduced

C05BA.t: Brake Booster Motor A Position Sensor Supply Circuit High
C05BA.d: C05BA covers the opposite case: the 5 V feed of motor A's position sensor rises above its upper limit. The usual culprit is a supply line touching a battery-voltage wire, less often a regulator that has lost control. No manufacturer publishes C05BA; GM's 2019 brake module treats its sensor supplies as high above 5.15 V for 100 ms, filing them under C05D1 or C05BB. TI's TPS7B4253-Q1 tracker shows how such outputs are protected: it survives a short to battery and opens its internal switch within about 1 ms. Hitachi Astemo deliberately places its supply monitor voltage at 3.75 V, below 5 V, so overvoltage stays measurable. An overvoltage can also damage the sensor, so assist is withdrawn and the booster runs without motor support.
c: Supply line shorted to a battery-voltage circuit in the harness
Sensor supply regulator in the control unit no longer regulating
Poor control unit ground shifting the measured supply voltage
s: Brake warning lamp and assist warning message
Hard brake pedal, longer stopping effort

C05BB.t: Brake Booster Motor A Position Sensor Supply Circuit Range/Performance
C05BB.d: GM uses C05BB in the integrated brake control of 2019 models. There the processor generates two 5 V sensor supplies; each feeds one pedal travel channel plus one motor position channel. C05BB belongs to the second supply (PTS2 and MPS2), C05D1 to the first. GM sets it below 4.85 V or above 5.15 V for 100 ms, and also for an unsteady supply: every out-of-band sample adds 50 points and the fault matures at 800, so after 80 ms at the earliest; every good one subtracts 1, and the fault stays latched until ignition off. All three variants are Type A, MIL on the first trip. GM names a faulty motor position sensor, pedal travel sensor or circuit board as causes. GM thus books its MPS2 under a motor A code, though its MPS2 plausibility fault is C058E.
c: Defective motor position sensor loading the shared supply
Defective pedal travel sensor on the same supply
Fault on the brake control unit's circuit board
Intermittent contact in the sensor supply wiring
s: Check engine lamp and brake warning on the first trip (GM)
Service brake assist message, hard pedal
Fault remains until the ignition is switched off

C05BC.t: Brake Booster Motor B Position Sensor Supply Circuit/Open
C05BC.d: C05BC reports an interrupted supply for the position sensor of booster motor B. A B channel exists where the actuator carries a second motor or winding set, or measures its rotor angle twice for redundancy. No manufacturer documents C05BC publicly. Hyundai Mobis describes a brake actuator with a dual-winding motor whose two power modules are fed separately; when one is diagnosed faulty it is shut down and the full current command passes to the other. Hitachi Astemo pairs each sensor supply with its own angle and torque sensor and keeps the motor running on the healthy set. As in Denso's analysis, a broken feed drags the signal to 0 V. The usual result is a brake warning with reduced assist, while full failure of boosting is avoided.
c: Broken wire or pushed-back pin in the motor B sensor supply
Second sensor supply output in the control unit failed
Open inside the motor B position sensor
s: Brake warning lamp, assist may remain partly available
Reduced maximum assist or slower pressure build-up

C05BD.t: Brake Booster Motor B Position Sensor Supply Circuit Low
C05BD.d: C05BD means the supply of motor B's position sensor reads below its permitted minimum – a ground short, a sensor pulling excess current or a weak regulator. No manufacturer publishes this code. Hitachi Astemo explains why two supplies need cross-checking: both share one ground, so without comparison the controller could not say which supply sagged. Each microcontroller there reads a 2.5 V reference from its own supply and a 3.75 V monitor of the other, and a low supply leaves a distinct pattern across those four values. A tracking regulator like the TPS7B4253-Q1 from TI holds its output current at a limit during a short, so the voltage drops instead of the part burning out. With channel B lost, the actuator relies on motor A or its first sensor and may lower assist gradually.
c: Motor B sensor supply line shorted to ground
Damaged motor B position sensor drawing too much current
Second sensor regulator in the control unit weak
s: Brake warning lamp on
Assist fades gradually or is limited at high demand

C05BE.t: Brake Booster Motor B Position Sensor Supply Circuit High
C05BE.d: C05BE is stored when the 5 V feed of motor B's position sensor exceeds its upper limit. No manufacturer documents it publicly. Two mechanisms are typical: the supply line has contacted a wire carrying battery voltage, or the reference ground of the sensor side has lifted, which makes every voltage measured against it look too high. Denso's patent illustrates the ground effect for a sensor read through a pull-down: a broken ground drives the signal above 4.7 V. In Hitachi Astemo's cross-check a rising ground pulls both references down while the monitor values stay put, which separates a ground fault from a true overvoltage. TI's tracker cuts its output path when shorted to battery. The booster then drops channel B and runs with motor A or reduced assist.
c: Motor B sensor supply shorted to a battery-voltage wire
Open or high-resistance sensor ground raising the measured voltage
Second sensor supply regulator out of regulation
s: Brake warning lamp and assist warning
Possibly further sensor codes if a shared ground is affected

C05BF.t: Brake Booster Motor B Position Sensor Supply Circuit Range/Performance
C05BF.d: C05BF concerns a motor B sensor supply that stays inside its hard limits but behaves implausibly – it fluctuates, disagrees with the independent monitor, or does not match the first supply. No manufacturer documents C05BF publicly. GM's comparable check for its own two supplies, filed under C05BB and C05D1, shows the principle: brief excursions outside 4.85–5.15 V are weighted and accumulated, while good samples slowly reverse the count, so only a persistent disturbance latches. Hitachi Astemo chooses non-overlapping A/D windows of 475–575 and 699–849 counts for reference and monitor signals so that even a stuck comparator input is caught. A supply that drifts or ripples can corrupt the rotor angle without tripping simple low or high checks, so the module treats channel B as unreliable.
c: Intermittent contact or corrosion in the motor B sensor supply wiring
Unstable sensor supply regulator or failing filter capacitor in the control unit
Fault in the supply monitoring circuit itself
s: Brake warning lamp appearing at times
Assist occasionally reduced, code returns after clearing

C05C0.t: Brake Pedal Position Sensor A Not Learned
C05C0.d: The control unit has no valid learned rest position for channel A of the brake pedal position sensor, so it cannot turn the raw signal into a reliable pedal travel. No manufacturer documents C05C0 publicly. The closest GM analogue is C0277 with failure type 4B: the body module reports that the home position of the pedal sensor was never learned and asks for a recalibration. Stellantis likewise requires a brake pedal learn in the ABS module after a PCM swap or update (C0042-54). Hitachi describes learning the stroke sensor zero only while no brake request is present. Typical triggers are a new sensor, a replaced module or an interrupted learn. C05C1 covers channel B, C0619 an offset outside the learn limit.
c: Learn procedure not run after sensor or module replacement
Learn routine aborted because the pedal was touched or the vehicle moved
Sensor channel A faulty or mounted out of position
Learned values lost in the control module memory
s: Brake or ABS warning lamp and message in the cluster
Brake lights or cruise control cancel react late or not at all
Regenerative braking or brake assist functions restricted

C05C1.t: Brake Pedal Position Sensor B Not Learned
C05C1.d: Set when the second, redundant channel B of the brake pedal position sensor lacks a stored zero point. Many electric and hybrid brake pedals read travel twice so that one channel can cross-check the other; Bosch builds such pedal travel sensors with a magnetic field sensor and two redundant outputs. Without a learned rest value for B, that cross-check is lost even when channel A is fine. No manufacturer publishes C05C1. GM handles the comparable fault as C0277-4B and simply recalibrates, and Hitachi only accepts a new zero if the complete learn run finished without pedal input. After fitting a new pedal sensor or control unit, run the learn with the pedal fully released. C05C0 is the twin for channel A, C061A the offset-limit fault.
c: Channel B not learned after a repair or software update
Learn conditions not met (pedal pressed, vehicle rolling)
Channel B of the pedal sensor faulty or out of tolerance
s: Brake warning lamp or service message
Reduced redundancy, some assist or regeneration functions disabled

C05C2.t: Brake Booster Motor A Over Temperature
C05C2.d: The electric booster or integrated brake unit has found its drive motor A, or the power stage feeding it, too hot. GM uses the code in several EBCM tables, all Type A with MIL: one design trips above 154 °C estimated motor temperature or on a bridge driver over-temperature shutdown, the Cadillac XT4 unit above 120 °C and 142 °C rotor/ECU temperature, 23OBDG07 and 25OBDG03B also when torque limiting stops the plunger refill, and 25OBDG04B above 140/160 °C magnet or 210/240 °C winding temperature. Mitsubishi lists C05C2 for Outlander PHEV code C18E1-4B with MIL after two trips, although that page describes a missing supply to the stroke sensor. Expect reduced boost after long or repeated hard braking. C0594 covers motor performance.
c: Long downhill braking or repeated hard stops overheating the motor
Hydraulic fault making the motor run longer than normal
Power stage or bridge driver reporting false or real over-temperature
Low supply voltage forcing current limitation
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and brake warning on GM models
Reduced brake assist, pedal feels harder
Regenerative braking temporarily disabled

C05C3.t: Brake Booster Motor A Supply Circuit
C05C3.d: Points to the power feed of booster motor A: fuse, supply cable, ground or the module input that carries battery current to the motor stage, rather than the motor windings themselves. No manufacturer documents C05C3 publicly. Bosch specifies its iBooster for supply voltages above 9.8 V with up to 450 W of motor power, so a weak feed shows up quickly under load.
