Hitachi describes cutting the booster motor current when the supply drops below or rises above set limits, and motor gate drivers such as the TI DRV8343-Q1 lock out on supply undervoltage. Check voltage drop on feed and ground while braking. Phase current faults are C0590/C0591, internal driver faults C0595, and the position sensor supply has its own codes.
c: Blown fuse or corroded high-current feed to the booster
Loose or corroded ground of the brake unit
Weak 12 V battery or charging fault causing voltage dips
Internal supply path of the brake module damaged
s: Brake warning lamp, loss or reduction of brake assist
Hard brake pedal, especially at low battery voltage
Further faults for regeneration or driver assistance braking

C05C4.t: Brake Pressure Sensor F Missing Calibration
C05C4.d: The brake controller finds no stored calibration (offset or zero point) for pressure sensor F, the sixth hydraulic pressure sensor in its numbering. Which physical sensor carries the letter F is up to the maker, and none publishes C05C4. Comparable codes exist for sensors A and B: GM checks sensor B in its hybrid brake controller via test pulses after offset compensation, and Saab/GM calls for a scan-tool pressure sensor calibration after replacing the EBCM or the modulator. Hitachi learns pressure sensor zeros only while the master cylinder is pressureless and the pedal is released. A new module or hydraulic unit without the follow-up calibration is the usual cause. C05C5 to C05C8 cover the sensor's signal faults.
c: Calibration skipped after module or hydraulic unit replacement
Calibration interrupted by brake application or low voltage
Calibration data lost in the module memory
s: ABS, ESC or brake warning lamp on
Stability control or brake assist functions disabled

C05C5.t: Brake Pressure Sensor F Circuit Range/Performance
C05C5.d: Pressure sensor F delivers a voltage inside the electrical window, yet the value does not fit the braking situation: wrong offset at rest, a reading that disagrees with deceleration or the brake switch, or a pressure that does not match pedal travel. No manufacturer documents C05C5 for sensor F. GM shows the method on other channels: the XT4 brake module flags pressure sensor A when its offset exceeds 12 bar with the pedal released, and Saab/GM treats a pressure signal that conflicts with vehicle deceleration as not plausible. Bosch compares measured pressure against a stored curve over input rod stroke. Unlike C05C6 and C05C7, the wiring is usually intact; suspect the sensor, its calibration or the hydraulics.
c: Pressure sensor F drifting or with offset out of tolerance
Calibration not matching after component replacement
Air in the system or hydraulic fault falsifying pressure
Increased contact resistance at the sensor connector
s: ABS/ESC warning lamp, stability control off
Unusual pedal feel or uneven braking assistance

C05C6.t: Brake Pressure Sensor F Circuit Low
C05C6.d: The signal of pressure sensor F sits below its valid band. Ratiometric 5 V pressure sensors normally output roughly 0.5 to 4.5 V; Denso describes treating 0 to 0.3 V as a fault zone, and with a pull-down resistor at the input a broken supply or signal wire also drags the reading toward zero. Saab/GM sets its brake pressure circuit code when signal or 5 V reference has a ground short or an open lasting 0.1 s and then disables ABS and traction control. No manufacturer publishes C05C6 for sensor F, so the letter-to-sensor mapping is not public. Measure supply, ground and signal at the connector before replacing the sensor. C05C7 is the high side, C05C8 the open circuit, C05C9 the shared supply.
c: 5 V reference interrupted or shorted to ground
Internal fault of pressure sensor F
s: ABS, ESC and traction control warning lamps on
Stability and traction control unavailable

C05C7.t: Brake Pressure Sensor F Circuit High
C05C7.d: Here the voltage of pressure sensor F rises above the top of its measuring range. With the common pull-down input, Denso explains that a lost sensor ground lifts the output past 4.7 V, which lies in the upper fault band; a short of the signal to a voltage source has the same effect. Industrial sensors such as the Honeywell MIP series deliberately park their output near 97.5 % of supply to signal an internal fault or overpressure. Saab/GM detects a short to voltage on the brake pressure signal or reference within 0.1 s. No carmaker documents C05C7 for sensor F. Check the ground wire first, then insulation of the signal line. C05C6 is the low counterpart, C05C5 the in-range plausibility fault.
c: Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
Sensor F reporting an internal fault at the upper rail
s: ABS/ESC lamp on, stability functions switched off
Live data shows implausibly high brake pressure with pedal released

C05C8.d: General circuit fault of pressure sensor F, most often a break in one of its three wires (supply, signal, ground) or a connector that has lost contact. Where the reading ends up depends on the input circuit: Honeywell notes that after a power or ground loss the output goes high with a pull-up and low with a pull-down resistor, so an open line can look like C05C6 or C05C7 unless the module tells them apart. Saab/GM flags an open or high resistance on the brake pressure signal or 5 V reference after 0.1 s. Bosch advises checking the live value of a modulator-mounted pressure sensor before buying an expensive part. No manufacturer publishes C05C8 for sensor F. Repair wiring or connector, then clear and retest.
c: Connector unplugged, corroded or with pushed-back pins
Broken wire in the sensor harness
Internal open circuit in sensor F
s: ABS and ESC warning lamps on
Stability control and brake assist functions not available

C05C9.d: Refers to the reference voltage the brake module provides to its hydraulic pressure sensors, not to one sensor's signal. If this feed collapses or rises, every sensor on it reads wrong at once, which is why the module checks the supply separately. Saab/GM monitors the 5 V reference of the brake pressure sensor and reacts within 0.1 s when that line touches ground or a voltage source. GM's integrated brake controller shows the usual window for such feeds: 4.85 to 5.15 V, held for 100 ms, on the pedal and motor sensor supplies (C05D1, C05BB). Tracking regulators like the TI TPS7B4253-Q1 are built for exactly this off-board sensor duty. No maker documents C05C9 itself. Unplug sensors one by one to find a shorted load.
c: Reference line shorted to ground or to battery voltage
One pressure sensor internally shorted, pulling down the shared feed
Sensor supply regulator inside the brake module defective
s: Several brake pressure codes at the same time
ABS, ESC and brake assist warnings, functions off

C05CA.t: Brake Master Cylinder Piston Position Sensor A Circuit Voltage High
C05CA.d: Channel A of the travel sensor at the master cylinder input rod reports a signal beyond its upper limit. In GM's booster-type brake modules this channel is a linear position sensor (LiPS) that talks to the EBCM digitally over SENT, so the high error is a message from the sensor itself: the Cadillac XT4 table in 19OBDG03D reacts within 0.033 s on the fast channel, 23OBDG07 and 25OBDG03B after 0.96 s on the slow channel, Type A with MIL. Line shorts and lost messages are filed under separate network codes there. Continental describes pedal modules that read travel with two sensors so one bad channel can be identified. Check the sensor connector and supply before replacing the booster assembly. C05CB is the low counterpart.
c: Position sensor A reporting out-of-range high internally
Supply voltage of the sensor out of tolerance
Sensor magnet or input rod out of position
s: Malfunction indicator lamp plus brake warning on GM models
Reduced brake assist or changed pedal feel

C05CB.t: Brake Master Cylinder Piston Position Sensor A Circuit Voltage Low
C05CB.d: Mirror image of C05CA: channel A of the master cylinder piston travel sensor reports that its value fell below the permitted range. GM documents it for its booster-type EBCMs, where the linear position sensor encodes travel digitally and flags its own low limit violation: the XT4 module acts after 0.033 s on the SENT fast channel, while the 2023 and 2025 tables wait 0.96 s for the slow-channel status, Type A, one trip, MIL. A low report often follows a sensor that loses its magnet reference or sees a sagging supply. Bosch builds such travel sensors around a Hall element that tracks a magnetic field over up to 45 mm of rod stroke. If the code returns after wiring checks, the sensor is usually part of the booster unit and replaced with it.
c: Position sensor A reporting out-of-range low
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and brake system message
Brake assist reduced, regeneration possibly off

C05CC.t: Brake Master Cylinder Piston Position Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
C05CC.d: Channel A (GM calls it PTS1) delivers a travel value that is electrically valid but physically wrong. GM's integrated controller with pedal simulator, the vacuum-free design ZF supplies, checks three things: travel above 38 mm (normal input piston travel is about 25 mm, about 36 mm without boost), a change faster than 700 mm/s, and a learned offset beyond 2.5 mm, each 100 ms, Type A. In the XT4 booster module the zero offset with pedal released may not exceed 0.9 mm while driving and accelerating; 23OBDG07 and 25OBDG03B allow +1.1/-1.5 mm. Causes range from a failed sensor to a bent sensor rod or wrong mounting. C05CF is the same check on channel B, C05D0 compares both channels.
c: Sensor A offset drifted beyond the learn limit
Damaged travel sensor rod or mounting
Pedal not fully returning (floor mat, return spring)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and brake warning
Changed pedal feel or reduced assist
Brake lights may react inconsistently

C05CD.t: Brake Master Cylinder Piston Position Sensor B Circuit Voltage High
C05CD.d: Channel B of the master cylinder piston travel sensor is stuck at a permanent high level. In GM's booster-type EBCMs the second channel is not sent over SENT like channel A but as a PWM signal around 1 kHz, which is why high and low here mean a line that no longer toggles: the module sets C05CD when it sees a steady high state for 0.2 s, read as a short of the PWM line to supply (19OBDG03D XT4 section, 23OBDG07, 25OBDG03B; Type A, one trip, MIL). Duty cycle or frequency outside 8.5-92 % or 900-1120 Hz falls under a separate communication code. Look for chafed wiring touching a supply wire or a sensor output stage that has failed high. C05CE is the stuck-low partner.
c: PWM signal line shorted to supply voltage
Output stage of sensor channel B failed high
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the connector
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and brake warning on GM models
Booster runs on channel A only or reduces assist

C05CE.t: Brake Master Cylinder Piston Position Sensor B Circuit Voltage Low
C05CE.d: Here the second, PWM-coded output (channel B) of the piston travel sensor stays permanently low. GM's XT4 brake module and the later 23OBDG07 and 25OBDG03B tables interpret a constant low level for 0.2 s as the signal line shorted to ground, Type A, one trip, MIL. Because a PWM line at 0 V also results when the sensor loses its supply or ground, a dead channel B together with a working channel A suggests a wiring fault close to the second output, while both channels failing hints at the shared supply (C05D1). The module can usually still brake with channel A, but with less redundancy. Inspect the harness at the booster for crush or water damage before condemning the unit. C05CD is the stuck-high case.
c: PWM signal line shorted to ground
Sensor channel B without supply or ground
Output stage of channel B failed low
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, brake system warning
Possibly reduced assist or regeneration off

C05CF.t: Brake Master Cylinder Piston Position Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
C05CF.d: Plausibility fault on channel B (GM: PTS2) while its signal is electrically in range. GM's integrated controller with pedal simulator runs the same checks on B as on A: more than 38 mm of travel, a step faster than 700 mm/s that disagrees with channel A and the simulator pressure model, or an offset beyond 2.5 mm, all with 100 ms and Type A. In the booster-type units the B offset with released pedal is limited to 0.9 mm (XT4) or +1.1/-1.5 mm (2023/2025 tables). Wards reported that this vacuum-free ZF system for GM full-size trucks reads the driver's braking wish from a pedal sensor, so a bad channel directly affects brake request. C05CC handles channel A, C05D0 the A/B comparison.
c: Offset of sensor B outside the allowed range
Loose contact causing implausible jumps on channel B
Sensor rod or mounting worn or bent
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and brake warning
Pedal feels different, assist may be reduced

C05D0.t: Brake Master Cylinder Piston Position Sensor A/B Correlation
C05D0.d: Both travel channels are individually plausible, but they disagree with each other. GM's integrated controller votes two out of three: PTS1, PTS2 and a third travel estimate (BAS); if PTS1 and PTS2 differ by more than 2 mm and one of them also deviates from the third value by over 2 mm, that channel is declared failed after 100 ms. The XT4 booster module allows 2.71 mm, the 23OBDG07 and 25OBDG03B tables 1.5 mm, each for 0.12 s with both channels initialised and otherwise fault-free; all Type A with MIL. Continental describes pedal modules with two travel sensors precisely so a single bad one can be identified. Loose sensor mounting, contamination and connector faults on one channel are typical causes. C05CC/C05CF cover each channel alone.
c: One sensor channel drifting away from the other
Mechanical play at the sensor or input rod
Contact resistance on one channel only
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and brake warning
Brake system switches to reduced mode, regeneration may be off

C05D1.t: Brake Master Cylinder Piston Position Sensor Supply Circuit
C05D1.d: Fault on the reference supply of the master cylinder piston (pedal travel) sensor. GM's integrated brake controller provides two 5 V supplies, each feeding one pedal travel channel and one motor position channel; C05D1 covers the first (PTS1/MPS1), C05BB the second. The supply fails below 4.85 V or above 5.15 V for 100 ms; for erratic dips a counter adds 50 per sample towards 800 (fastest 80 ms) and latches until key-off. All are Type A with MIL in 19OBDG03D and 25OBDG04B. Because the motor position channel shares the feed, motor sensor codes can appear at the same time. Tracking regulators such as the TI TPS7B4253-Q1 show how such off-board sensor supplies are built and protected.
c: Supply line shorted to ground or to another voltage
Pedal travel or motor position sensor loading the supply
Supply circuit on the control module board defective
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, brake warning and loss of assist
Further codes for pedal travel and motor position sensors

C05D2.t: Master Cylinder Piston Position Higher Than Expected
C05D2.d: The piston has travelled further than the measured pressure justifies, a sign that fluid escapes or a sensor misreads. GM's integrated controller models the simulator pressure from pedal travel and sets C05D2 when the model exceeds the measured value by more than 20 bar (250 ms in 19OBDG03D, 500 ms in 25OBDG04B), naming master cylinder or simulator seal leakage and an in-range pressure sensor fault. The XT4 module reacts after 0.2 s when pressure lags behind the measured travel. GM bulletin 20-NA-073 (2019-2020 pickups and SUVs) lists C05D2 as excessive piston travel with loss of brake assist and fixes it by reprogramming the BSCM. Bosch and Continental patents describe the same travel-versus-pressure leak check. C05D3 is the opposite case.
c: Internal leakage at master cylinder or simulator seals
Simulator pressure sensor reading too low within range
Air in the hydraulic system after service
s: Longer, softer brake pedal with higher pedal force
Loss of brake assist and messages in the driver information centre
Malfunction indicator lamp on GM models

C05D3.t: Driver Applied Pressure Higher Than Expected
C05D3.d: The pressure the driver generates is higher than the measured pedal travel would predict, a hard pedal pattern. GM's integrated controller sets C05D3 when the measured simulator pressure is more than 20 bar above its travel-based model, outside fast applications, naming a closed or blocked simulator valve, a seized simulator and an in-range sensor fault. The booster-type EBCMs (XT4, 23OBDG07, 25OBDG03B) call the check hard pedal and react after 0.2 s without ABS or ESC activity; Type A with MIL. GM PIT6012/PIT6012A for 2023-2024 Colorado and Canyon pair C05D3 with P25A2, a lit check engine lamp and a soft pedal, and point first to a weak battery. Bosch maps the same hard-pedal zone over input rod stroke.
c: Weak or discharged 12 V battery (GM PIT6012)
Pedal simulator valve closed or blocked
Pressure or travel sensor misreading within range
s: Check engine lamp on together with brake system message
Brake pedal feels spongy, hard or unusual

C05D4.t: Brake Master Cylinder Piston Position Sensor Calibration Not Learned
C05D4.d: No valid zero calibration exists for the master cylinder piston travel sensors. GM's integrated controller stores the end-of-line zeroing of its pedal travel sensors in non-volatile memory and reloads it each drive; C05D4 sets within 10 ms after start if the stored status shows the learn failed. GM lists sensor electrical faults, a moving vehicle or applied brake during calibration, and an offset too large, too small or unsteady, plus memory errors (19OBDG03D and 25OBDG04B, Type A with MIL). Hitachi learns stroke sensor zeros only with no brake request and discards a run that is interrupted. After replacing the brake unit, perform the calibration with a scan tool on a stationary vehicle. C05CC/C05CF cover offsets learned but out of limit.
c: Zeroing not done after replacement of the brake unit
Calibration disturbed by vehicle movement or pedal input
Sensor offset too large, too small or unsteady
Memory error in the brake control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and brake warning after start
Brake system in reduced mode until calibrated

C05D5.t: Brake Master Cylinder Cut Off Valve
C05D5.d: Electrical fault of the solenoid valve that separates the master cylinder from the wheel circuits in by-wire operation, so pressure comes from the motor and the pedal works against a simulator. In GM's booster-type EBCMs (XT4, 23OBDG07, 25OBDG03B) the valve driver reports over-current of about 4 to 6.5 A, an output stage above 195-220 °C, a lost power ground or lost freewheeling within 0.03 s. GM's integrated controller maps open and shorted driver tests of its simulator-side valve to C05D5 (Type A, MIL) but a coil above 265 °C as Type C without MIL; 25OBDG04A uses it for the traction control isolation valves. Bosch describes these isolation valves closing during by-wire braking. Expect reduced assist or a mechanical push-through fallback.
c: Valve coil shorted or open inside the hydraulic unit
Valve driver stage or ASIC in the module defective
Poor power ground of the brake module
Valve overheated by excessive activation time
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and brake warning
Loss of brake assist, pedal works on the master cylinder directly
ESC and traction control limited

C05D6.t: Power Steering Control Module Processor Performance
C05D6.d: The electric power steering controller has found that its own processor, or the cross-check between its processors, is not working as expected. Toyota documents the code as C05D604 in the ECU of the EPS steering gear: 2019–2020 RAV4 and RAV4 Hybrid light the EPS warning in red or yellow at start-up or while driving (T-SB-0061-20), and the 2022 Tundra and Lexus LX 600 log it at start-up, often together with C15D704. In each case the fix is reprogramming the gear ECU with revised logic. Many EPS units pair a main and a monitoring microcontroller that must both enable the motor relay; Mando describes such a start-up check. If the self-test fails, assist is reduced or switched off, so steering becomes heavy.
c: EPS controller software flags a false processor fault, update available
Supply voltage dip during engine start disturbs the self-test
Internal hardware fault in the steering control module
s: Red or yellow power steering warning lamp
Steering suddenly heavier or assist reduced
Fault appears mainly right after starting the vehicle

C05D7.t: Brake Transmission Shift Interlock (BTSI) Control Circuit
C05D7.d: Covers the output that drives the brake transmission shift interlock, the solenoid that keeps the selector in park until the brake pedal is pressed. In the US, FMVSS 114 has required this lock since 1 September 2010 on vehicles up to 4,536 kg fitted with an automatic gearbox and a park position. A patent by Pontiac Coil shows the usual layout: a spring holds a blocking pin in the locked position, and a transistor energizes the coil only with ignition on and brake switch closed, so the system fails locked. The code points to the driver stage, wiring or coil. No manufacturer publishes C05D7; Ram logs P0928-00 for an internal BTSI fault in its rotary shifter. P081F is the signal correlation counterpart.
c: Interlock solenoid coil open or shorted
Damaged wiring or corroded connector at the shifter
Driver stage in the shifter or body module faulty
Brake light switch signal missing, so the lock is never released
s: Selector cannot be moved out of park despite pressing the brake
Selector leaves park without the brake applied
No clicking of the interlock when the brake is pressed

C05D8.d: The AWD controller sees no plausible current path in the output that drives the actuator of clutch A, typically an open coil, motor winding or wire. Depending on the design, the actuator is an electromagnetic coil (JTEKT ITCC: coil current sets the transmitted torque) or an electric motor that turns a ball ramp through a worm gear, as in a Magna disconnect coupling. Ford names C05D8:19 for the Bronco Sport with the 2.0L engine, model years 2021–2022, in SSM 51117, together with C05D9:71 and the clutch B codes C05E7/C05E8; the cause there is a misaligned magnet ring in the rear drive unit motor, fixed by replacing the motor alone. With the circuit open the clutch cannot close, AWD is switched off and a warning appears.
c: Actuator coil or motor winding open
Rear drive unit motor with misaligned magnet ring (Ford Bronco Sport 2.0L)
Broken wire or loose connector at the rear axle
Output stage in the AWD control module faulty
s: AWD warning lamp or message, vehicle drives on one axle only
Wheel spin on slippery surfaces when pulling away

C05D9.t: 4WD/AWD Clutch A Actuator Control Circuit Performance
C05D9.d: The actuator circuit of clutch A is electrically intact, but the actuator does not respond as commanded, for example the measured current, motor speed or achieved torque differs from the target. Ford uses this code widely in its AWD module. Bronco 2021–2022: C05D9:19 or :99 with the wrench lamp and AWD off, caused by a discharged battery; check the battery and reprogram the module (TSB 22-2136, 22-2447). Bronco Sport 2.0L: C05D9:71 from a misaligned rear drive unit motor magnet ring (SSM 51117). E-Transit 2023 and Nautilus 2024: C05D9:74 with C0095:18 and loss of AWD until the next key cycle (SSM 52112); for Escape/Corsair 2023–2024 SSM 52788 blames AWD module software.
c: Low battery state of charge or weak supply voltage
Actuator motor worn or misassembled (magnet ring)
Ball ramp or gear train of the actuator binding
s: AWD fault message, AWD inoperative for the rest of the trip
Powertrain malfunction (wrench) lamp on
Function returns after restarting the vehicle

C05DA.t: 4WD/AWD Clutch A Actuator Control Circuit Low
C05DA.d: The voltage measured on the clutch A actuator line stays below the expected level, which usually means a short to ground somewhere between the control module and the coil or motor. Mitsubishi Electric describes a method for an electromagnetic driveline clutch: a high-side PWM transistor and a low-side switch feed the coil, the terminal voltages are compared with their normal values, and on a ground fault both transistors switch off so the clutch opens. JTEKT's ITCC likewise sets its clutch force through coil current, and BorgWarner also offers electromagnetically actuated couplings. No manufacturer publishes a case for C05DA. C05DB covers the opposite fault, a short to supply; C05D8 an open circuit.
c: Actuator wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Water or corrosion in the connector at the axle
Coil or motor winding shorted to the housing
s: AWD switched off with warning lamp
Fault returns immediately after clearing

C05DB.t: 4WD/AWD Clutch A Actuator Control Circuit High
C05DB.d: Set when the clutch A actuator line reads too high, typically because it touches battery voltage or because the low-side switch cannot pull it down. For an electromagnetic clutch, Mitsubishi Electric checks for this short with the selector in P or N by comparing the terminal voltages against normal values, then releases the clutch by turning off both drivers. A line stuck at supply can keep a coil partly energized, so on an ITCC-type coupling (current controls torque) the clutch may drag even when open is commanded. Newer BorgWarner couplings instead use a brushless motor with electronics integrated into the actuator unit. No public manufacturer case exists for C05DB; C05DA is the short to ground.
c: Actuator wire shorted to a supply line in the harness
Output transistor in the AWD module stuck on
Corrosion bridging pins in the actuator connector
s: AWD warning, all-wheel drive disabled
Possible binding or tyre scrub in tight turns if the clutch drags

C05DC.d: The calculated or measured temperature of clutch A has passed the protection limit, usually after long slipping in sand, snow or while towing. Audi stores C05DC00 in the AWD control unit of quattro ultra models: in TSB 2075681/1 the technician drives circles at full lock below 10 km/h for up to 15 minutes until the yellow four-wheel drive overheating lamp comes on, then erases the entry. Suppliers protect the clutch in steps. A BorgWarner patent cuts engine torque from 130 °C and stops at 110 °C; JTEKT estimates the oil temperature from transmitted torque and speed and lowers the target torque above a threshold; GKN's actuator controller also tracks clutch temperature. After cooling, AWD normally returns.
c: Long periods of wheel slip in deep snow, sand or mud
Towing or steep climbs with heavy load
Different tyre sizes or wear front to rear force constant slip
s: Yellow AWD overheating warning
Less drive to the secondary axle until the clutch has cooled
Engine power briefly reduced during wheel spin

C05DD.d: The AWD controller has commanded clutch A to close, but the speed difference across it or the actuator feedback shows that it is not transmitting the expected torque or has stayed open. Typical reasons are worn plates, a sticking actuator or a ball ramp that cannot travel far enough. Disconnect systems make the check routine: Audi quattro ultra opens a plate clutch behind the gearbox plus a separate disconnect clutch inside the rear differential and reconnects both within about 200 ms, and GKN's actuator controller monitors connection feedback and compensates for clutch wear. In a Magna coupling the ECU first indexes the ball ramp to a ready point with light plate contact. No manufacturer publishes a case for C05DD. C05DE is the reverse fault, a clutch that will not open.
c: Clutch plates worn, slipping under load
Actuator or ball ramp sticking short of full travel
Wrong, aged or low clutch fluid
Damaged shift fork or dog teeth in the decoupling unit
s: AWD malfunction message, vehicle behaves like two-wheel drive
Wheel spin and traction control interventions on slippery roads

C05DE.d: Clutch A keeps transmitting torque or stays connected although the controller has ordered it to open. Front and rear axles are then forced to turn together, which shows up as binding, tyre scrub or droning in tight, slow turns. Audi documents the twin code C05ED00 (clutch B stuck engaged) in its quattro ultra AWD module J492; TSB 2051558 traces it to a worn shift fork in the rear differential. For closed clutch 1 in tight corners Audi bulletin 2059057 describes humming and binding and prescribes fresh ATF for that clutch. In Magna's coupling a return spring pushes the plates apart; a seized ball ramp or welded plates defeat it. No public case names C05DE itself.
c: Clutch plates welded or swollen after overheating
Actuator or ball ramp seized in the applied position
Aged clutch fluid causing drag and stick-slip
Worn shift fork keeps a dog clutch engaged
s: Binding, hopping or tyre scrub when parking or in tight turns
Droning or vibration from the rear axle
AWD malfunction message

C05DF.d: The engagement sequence of clutch A did not finish correctly: the actuator ran, but synchronisation, connection feedback or the timing check failed. This matters most for disconnecting systems that must reconnect a stationary driveline on the move. Audi states that quattro ultra synchronises the disconnected parts and closes the rear decoupling clutch in about 200 ms; BorgWarner lists rapid synchronisation for AWD availability on its disconnect couplings; GKN's disconnect controller operates the dog clutch and checks a connection feedback signal plus self-diagnosis. A missed sequence is distinct from C05DD, where the clutch slips or stays open, and from C05E6, a position control error. No manufacturer publishes a C05DF case.
c: Speeds not matched in time before the clutch closes
Actuator too slow because of low voltage or wear
Engagement feedback sensor reports wrong state
s: AWD unavailable message, sometimes only for one trip
Clunk from the driveline when AWD tries to engage

C05E0.d: General electrical fault in the sensor that reports where the clutch A actuator stands, without the controller narrowing it down to low, high or intermittent. Electromechanical AWD clutches need this signal because the motor angle maps to plate travel and clamping force. Bosch describes a transfer-case clutch driven by a DC motor, worm gear and lifting disc, with its own position sensor on the worm wheel plus speed and current sensing; Dana reads the motor shaft position with Hall sensors or encoders. Without a valid position the controller cannot meter torque and opens the clutch. No manufacturer publishes C05E0; C05E1 to C05E4 are the more specific variants.
c: Position sensor in the actuator faulty
Sensor supply or ground from the AWD module missing
s: AWD warning, all-wheel drive switched off
Traction loss when pulling away on low grip

C05E1.t: 4WD/AWD Clutch A Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
C05E1.d: The clutch A position signal is electrically within limits but does not fit what the actuator should be doing, for instance it barely changes while the motor runs or jumps further than the gearing allows. Bosch's transfer-case clutch provides the data for such a cross-check: worm wheel position, motor speed and motor current are all measured, so a position that drifts away from the counted motor rotation stands out. Dana relates motor shaft position to the rise of motor current when the ball ramp starts to clamp. Causes are a loose sensor magnet, a slipping gear or a sensor drifting with temperature. No manufacturer documents C05E1; the plain circuit fault is C05E0.
c: Sensor magnet or target loose or misaligned
s: AWD warning, torque transfer to the secondary axle stopped
Fault often sets only after some driving

C05E2.t: 4WD/AWD Clutch A Position Sensor Circuit Low
C05E2.d: The position signal from the clutch A actuator has dropped below its valid band. On a sensor powered by a reference supply this normally means the signal line is shorted to ground, the supply is missing, or the sensor output is dead. Position sensing on such actuators is described by Bosch (sensor on the worm wheel of a transfer-case clutch drive) and by Dana (Hall sensors or encoders on the motor shaft of a ball ramp actuator). Since a reading stuck at the bottom could be mistaken for an open clutch, the controller stops using it and disables the AWD clutch. No manufacturer publishes C05E2; C05E3 is the high-side counterpart.
s: AWD warning lamp on
Vehicle drives with one axle only

C05E3.t: 4WD/AWD Clutch A Position Sensor Circuit High
C05E3.d: Here the clutch A position signal sits above the highest value a working sensor can deliver. Usual explanations are a signal line touching the supply or battery voltage, a lost sensor ground that lets the output float up, or an internal sensor fault. Bosch and Dana both describe actuator position sensing for motor-driven AWD clutches, on the worm wheel or on the motor shaft, so the controller can relate angle to clamping force. A value pinned at the top would suggest a fully closed clutch, which the controller cannot trust; it therefore releases the clutch and reports the fault. No manufacturer documents C05E3; the low-side variant is C05E2.
c: Signal wire shorted to supply or battery voltage
s: AWD warning lamp on
All-wheel drive disabled until the fault is repaired

C05E4.t: 4WD/AWD Clutch A Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent
C05E4.d: The clutch A position signal drops out or jumps for short moments and then recovers, so the controller sees implausible steps between consecutive samples. The pattern points to a loose pin, a chafed wire that touches only on bumps, or moisture in the connector near the axle, rather than a dead sensor. Bosch's actuator design measures worm wheel position together with motor speed, and Dana reads motor shaft position continuously while the clutch is applied, which makes short glitches visible. AWD may drop out briefly and come back after the next start. No manufacturer publishes C05E4. Permanent faults use C05E2 or C05E3.
c: Loose or corroded pin in the sensor connector
Harness chafing at the axle or subframe
s: AWD warning that comes and goes
Short losses of drive to the secondary axle

C05E5.d: The controller has no valid stored reference for clutch A, typically the touch or kiss point where the plates begin to carry torque. Bosch finds this point on a transfer-case clutch by running the motor at constant speed and intersecting two regression lines from the free-travel and loaded ranges; the run is repeated at engine start or at standstill because wear shifts the curve. Dana notes that each motor and control unit pairing gives its own kiss point. Magna moves the plates to a stand-by position just before contact. A new actuator, controller or clutch, an interrupted learn or lost memory leaves the value missing; a learn routine with a scan tool usually clears it. No manufacturer publishes C05E5.
c: Learn not run after replacing actuator, clutch or module
Learn routine aborted, for example by low voltage or vehicle movement
Stored values lost after battery disconnection or module fault
s: AWD warning directly after a repair
All-wheel drive disabled or harsh engagement

C05E6.d: The closed-loop control that drives clutch A to a target position cannot hold or reach it: the deviation between commanded and measured position stays too large for too long. Magna describes an ECU that controls the angular position of the ball ramp actuator ring; Bosch drives its transfer-case clutch motor with a cascaded current and speed controller through an H-bridge; GKN's actuator controller handles fast clutch actuation and compensates for wear. A mechanical load, a weak motor, low voltage or a wrongly learned reference can each prevent the actuator from settling. Unlike C05E1, the sensor itself is plausible here. No manufacturer publishes C05E6; C05EF is the clutch B equivalent.
c: Actuator gear train or ball ramp binding
Weak actuator motor or low supply voltage
s: AWD malfunction message, AWD disabled
Uneven or delayed torque transfer before the fault sets

C05E7.d: The AWD module finds no usable current path in its driver output for the clutch B actuator, most often an open coil, motor winding, connector or wire. A second clutch exists either in a twin-clutch rear drive unit with one clutch per rear wheel, or as a disconnect stage in the rear axle. Ford is the only maker with a public case: SSM 51117 lists C05E7:19 for 2021–2022 Bronco Sport 2.0L, the engine sold with the twin-clutch Badlands rear drive unit, while the single-clutch models in the same bulletin only log C0095. Ford traces it to a magnet ring that sits out of position inside the rear drive unit motor; the motor is now replaced on its own. Ford does not state which rear wheel belongs to B. Driver chips such as TI's DRV8873-Q1 test for an open load before switching on.
c: Open coil or motor winding in the clutch B actuator
Misaligned magnet ring in the rear drive unit motor (Ford Bronco Sport 2.0L)
Broken wire or corroded connector between AWD module and rear drive unit
Faulty driver stage in the AWD module
s: AWD warning lamp or message, rear axle no longer driven
Rear locking or torque vectoring function unavailable on twin-clutch units
Fault is present again immediately after clearing

C05E8.t: 4WD/AWD Clutch B Actuator Control Circuit Performance
C05E8.d: The clutch B actuator circuit is electrically intact, yet its response does not match the command: current, motor movement or the torque built up stays outside the expected band. Ford stores C05E8:71 in the AWD module of 2021–2022 Bronco Sport 2.0L vehicles (SSM 51117), together with C05D9:71 for clutch A; both lead back to the misaligned magnet ring of the rear drive unit motor, and the repair is a new motor instead of a complete unit. On twin-clutch modules such as GKN's Twinster each wheel clutch is set separately; GKN's actuator controller compensates for wear and runs its own self-diagnosis, so a clutch that lags behind its partner stands out. Once one side no longer follows, left-right torque control is lost and AWD is usually switched off for the trip.
c: Misaligned magnet ring in the rear drive unit motor (Ford Bronco Sport 2.0L)
Worn or sluggish actuator motor or hydraulic control for clutch B
Low battery voltage limiting actuator current
Binding in the actuator mechanism or clutch pack
s: AWD fault message, all-wheel drive off for the rest of the trip
Reduced traction off-road because one rear wheel is no longer controlled

C05E9.t: 4WD/AWD Clutch B Actuator Control Circuit Low
C05E9.d: The voltage on the clutch B actuator line reads below the expected value, which points to a short to ground between AWD module and coil or motor, or to a driver stage that pulls the line down. A Mitsubishi Electric clutch patent shows how such a fault is caught: high-side and low-side transistors feed the coil, with the selector in P or N the module checks both terminal voltages against what they should read, and a deviation turns off both drivers, leaving the clutch released. Modern motor driver ICs such as TI's DRV8873-Q1 report a short to ground as a separate fault class. In a twin-clutch rear unit, B may serve only one rear wheel, so drive on that side is lost first. No manufacturer publishes a C05E9 case; C05EA is the opposite fault.
c: Chafed actuator wire shorting to ground near the rear axle
Water or corrosion in the rear drive unit connector
Internal short in the clutch B coil or motor
s: AWD warning, all-wheel drive disabled
Fault returns at once after clearing, often after driving through water

C05EA.t: 4WD/AWD Clutch B Actuator Control Circuit High
C05EA.d: The clutch B actuator line reads too high, usually from contact with a battery feed or because the low-side switch no longer pulls it down. With coil-type clutches the danger is current flowing although the module wants the clutch open: in JTEKT's ITCC the coil current sets the transmitted torque, so a partly energised coil lets the clutch drag. Mitsubishi Electric's patent checks for shorts via the terminal voltages in P or N and then turns both drivers off; TI treats a short to battery as its own diagnostic in the DRV8873-Q1 motor driver. A dragging clutch B can show up as tyre scrub or binding in tight, slow turns. No public manufacturer case exists for C05EA; C05E9 covers the short to ground and C05E7 the open circuit.
c: Actuator wire shorted to a supply line
Low-side switch in the AWD module defective
Corrosion bridging pins in the actuator connector
s: AWD warning, all-wheel drive disabled
Possible binding or tyre scrub when manoeuvring

C05EB.d: The AWD module has calculated or measured that clutch B has passed its permitted temperature, usually after long slipping in deep snow, sand or mud, or when towing. In a twin-clutch rear module the two wheel clutches heat up separately, so one side can reach its limit while the other is still cool, for instance when only one rear wheel spins. GKN's actuator controller tracks clutch temperature, and suppliers patent staged protection: BorgWarner reduces engine torque from about 130 °C until the clutch drops below 110 °C, JTEKT estimates oil temperature from torque and wheel speed and then lowers the target torque. Audi documents the twin code C05DC00 for clutch A only. Once cooled, the system normally returns to full function. No manufacturer publishes a C05EB case.
c: Long wheel spin on one rear wheel in snow, sand or mud
Towing or climbing with high, continuous torque transfer
Different tyre sizes or wear front to rear causing permanent slip
Aged or wrong fluid in the rear drive unit
s: AWD overheating or temporarily disabled message
Less drive to the rear until the clutch has cooled
Engine power briefly reduced during wheel spin

C05EC.d: Clutch B was commanded to connect, but speed signals or actuator feedback show that it carries no torque or has stayed open. In disconnecting systems the second clutch is often a positive shift element rather than a friction pack: Audi's quattro ultra releases both a gearbox-side multi-plate clutch and a decoupler in the rear differential, which autozine describes as an electromechanically operated dog clutch on the right half shaft. For this unit Audi's guided fault finding can end in replacing actuator 2 (V623) or the driveshaft speed sensor G970, as its bulletins note. BorgWarner's dog-clutch patent uses a single Hall sensor to confirm sleeve speed and position before full torque is allowed. No manufacturer publishes a C05EC case; C05ED is the reverse, a clutch that will not open.
c: Clutch B actuator sticking or too weak to shift the sleeve
Worn shift fork or damaged dog teeth in the rear differential
Worn friction plates on twin-clutch units
Low or wrong fluid in the rear drive unit
s: AWD malfunction message, vehicle drives on the front axle only
Wheel spin and traction control interventions on slippery roads

C05ED.d: Clutch B is still connected although the AWD module has ordered it to open. It is the one code of the clutch B group that a manufacturer documents in detail. Audi stores C05ED00 with symptom code 29725 in the AWD control unit J492 of quattro ultra models (A4, A5, A6, A7, Q5 and their S versions, mainly 2018–2020), and the instrument cluster sporadically reports a four-wheel drive malfunction. The first issue of TSB 2051558 (2018) had the rear differential replaced if the code came back after the test plan; since revision 3 in mid-2020 Audi names wear on the rear differential's shift fork as the cause, removes actuator 2 (V623) and fits a new fork from a repair kit instead of a new differential. Production received an improved fork material.
c: Worn shift fork in the rear differential (Audi quattro ultra)
Clutch B actuator seized in the engaged position
Welded or swollen plates on friction-type clutch B
s: Sporadic four-wheel drive malfunction message
Rear driveline keeps turning when it should be decoupled, possible noise

C05EE.d: The connection sequence of clutch B did not complete: the actuator moved, but speed matching, position feedback or the time window failed. This concerns above all positive dog clutches, which may only close once both halves turn at almost the same speed. BorgWarner's dog-clutch patent starts engagement within roughly 100–200 rpm speed difference and allows full torque only after a Hall sensor confirms about two thirds engagement; Ford's synchronisation patent first spins up the stationary driveline with the rear clutch and then closes a synchroniser in the PTU. Audi states that quattro ultra completes the whole reconnection in around 200 ms. C05EC means the clutch stays open or slips, C05EF a position control deviation. No manufacturer publishes a C05EE case.
c: Speed of the disconnected driveline not matched in time
Slow actuator, often from low voltage or cold, thick fluid
Faulty position or shaft speed feedback
Worn or chipped dog teeth blocking engagement
s: AWD unavailable message, sometimes only for one trip
Clunk or rattle from the rear when AWD tries to connect

C05EF.d: The position loop that moves clutch B to a target cannot reach or hold it: commanded and measured actuator position stay apart for too long. Such loops depend on a learned reference. Dana's patent finds the kiss point from motor current plotted against Hall or encoder shaft position; Bosch derives it from two regression lines while the motor pushes against the rising clutch load; in Magna's design the ECU sets how far the ball-ramp ring is rotated. For a dog clutch, BorgWarner reads the axial sleeve position with a Hall sensor. Typical reasons are binding mechanics, a weak motor or low supply voltage, and a reference that no longer matches worn plates. Unlike C05EE, the sequence itself is not the issue. No manufacturer publishes C05EF; C05E6 is the clutch A counterpart.
c: Binding ball ramp, gear or shift mechanism
Weak actuator motor or low supply voltage
Learned reference no longer valid after wear or part replacement
s: AWD malfunction message, AWD disabled
Delayed or uneven torque transfer before the fault sets

C05F0.t: Rear Drive Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit Low
C05F0.d: The signal of the rear drive shaft speed sensor stays below its valid range, typically due to an open circuit, a short to ground or a missing sensor supply. The AWD module needs this speed to match a disconnected rear driveline to the wheels before a clutch closes; American Axle's patent feeds a pinion shaft speed sensor into exactly that synchronisation check. Audi lists the driveshaft speed sensor G970 among the parts tested in quattro ultra fault finding for C05ED00. Many such sensors are two-wire Hall ICs that toggle between two supply currents; Allegro's A19420 uses about 7 and 14 mA, so a current below the lower band, or none at all, cannot be a valid pulse. No manufacturer publishes C05F0 itself; C05F1 is the high counterpart.
c: Open sensor wire or loose connector
Signal or supply line shorted to ground
s: AWD warning, all-wheel drive not connected
Vehicle drives in front-wheel drive only

C05F1.t: Rear Drive Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit High
C05F1.d: Here the rear drive shaft speed signal reads above its valid range, as caused by a short to supply voltage, a damaged sensor IC or a fault at the module input. With a two-wire Hall sensor the module watches the current between a low and a high level (Allegro A19420: about 7 and 14 mA); a current clearly above the upper band cannot be a speed pulse. Without a plausible prop shaft speed, a disconnecting AWD system cannot judge when the rear driveline has caught up with the wheels, which the American Axle and BorgWarner patents require before engagement. Audi's quattro ultra uses such a sensor as G970. No manufacturer publishes C05F1; C05F0 is the low case, C05F4 the plausibility check.
c: Sensor signal line shorted to supply voltage
Damaged sensor IC drawing excessive current
Faulty sensor input in the AWD module
s: AWD warning, all-wheel drive not connected
Fault sets immediately at ignition on

C05F2.t: Rear Drive Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit Intermittent
C05F2.d: The speed signal from the rear drive shaft drops out or jumps for short moments and then recovers, so the AWD controller sees pulse gaps or sudden speed steps that no real shaft could make. Such sensors are often two-wire Hall ICs whose supply current toggles between two levels; Allegro specifies about 7 and 14 mA for its A19420 and stresses stable output despite sudden air gap changes, so short dropouts usually point to wiring, connector or mounting rather than the IC. American Axle uses a speed sensor on the rear drive module pinion shaft to judge synchronisation before a disconnect clutch engages; Audi lists the drive shaft speed sensor G970 for quattro ultra. No maker documents C05F2 itself; permanent faults are C05F0, C05F1 or C05F3.
c: Loose, corroded or water-affected connector at the sensor
Harness chafed or broken where it flexes near the axle or drive shaft
Sensor not seated firmly, air gap varies with vibration
Damaged or dirty target ring on the shaft
s: AWD or 4WD warning appears now and then and disappears again
All-wheel drive briefly unavailable, often on rough roads
Code stored as history without a current fault

C05F3.t: Rear Drive Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit
C05F3.d: Catch-all electrical fault for the rear drive shaft speed sensor circuit, stored when the controller detects a problem but does not narrow it to low, high or intermittent. Typical are an open supply or signal wire, a failed sensor IC or a fault in the module input. Two-wire Hall sensors such as the Allegro A19420 report speed as alternating current levels and can also signal an internal error; a current outside both bands cannot be read as speed. The value matters for disconnecting AWD systems: BorgWarner reads sleeve speed and position with one Hall sensor and engages a dog clutch only within about 100 to 200 rpm, and Audi names sensor G970 in its quattro ultra diagnosis. No maker documents C05F3 itself; C05F0 and C05F1 are the more specific variants.
c: Open signal or supply wire between sensor and module
Connector not latched or pins pushed back
Faulty input stage in the AWD control module
s: AWD or 4WD service message, all-wheel drive switched off
Vehicle drives on the primary axle only
No drive shaft speed shown in live data

C05F4.t: Rear Drive Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
C05F4.d: The rear drive shaft speed is electrically valid but does not fit the rest of the driveline. The controller can compare it with wheel speeds, the axle ratio and the clutch state: with AWD engaged the shaft must follow the rear wheels, and a reading that stays near zero, lags or runs too fast is implausible. American Axle relies on a pinion shaft speed sensor to confirm that the disconnected rear driveline has reached primary speed before a dog clutch shifts, and BorgWarner times engagement by a speed difference of about 100 to 200 rpm. A wrong reading would break exactly that check. Likely causes are an enlarged air gap, a damaged target ring, a wrong part or a slipping clutch. No maker documents C05F4; electrical faults are C05F0 to C05F3.
c: Air gap too large, sensor not fully seated or wrong spacer
Target ring damaged, loose or covered with metal debris
Wrong sensor, target ring or axle ratio after repair
Slipping AWD clutch makes shaft speed deviate
s: AWD warning and all-wheel drive disabled
Rear axle no longer connects in a disconnecting AWD system
Live data shows shaft speed that does not match wheel speeds

C05F5.d: The range actuator is the electric gear motor that moves the transfer case between high range, neutral and low range. With this code the controller finds no usable current path in the motor drive circuit, usually an open winding, wire or connector. Automotive H-bridge drivers such as the TI DRV8873-Q1 run a dedicated open-load test besides short and overcurrent checks. Stellantis uses its own code C140A-13 for an open shift motor drive in bulletin 08-237-23 for 2023 Ram 1500 trucks, caused by an unseated shift motor connector; Ford asks in SSM 48300 for Super Duty trucks to check loose pins, contamination and broken wires before replacing a shift motor. No maker documents C05F5 itself. With the circuit open, range shifts are impossible.
c: Shift motor connector not fully seated or corroded
Broken wire between control module and motor
Open motor winding or worn brushes in the range actuator
Failed output stage in the control module
s: 4WD service message, low range cannot be selected
Range indicator flashes or does not change
Transfer case stays in its last position

C05F6.d: The drive circuit of the range actuator is electrically present, but the response does not match the command: motor current, run time or achieved travel fall outside the window the controller expects. Magna describes a range shift motor driven by pulse width modulation in phases, fast to neutral, slower through synchronisation at about 55 to 80 percent of travel, and under PID position control from about 90 percent. A circuit with high resistance or a weak supply cannot follow such a profile. GM bulletin PIP5098 for Colorado and Canyon traces intermittent 4WD faults to a poor ground terminal for the encoder motor, easiest to reproduce under high electrical load while cranking and shifting. No maker documents C05F6 itself; mechanical binding is C05FA.
c: High resistance in ground or supply of the motor circuit
Weak battery or low system voltage during the shift
Worn shift motor drawing abnormal current
Degraded driver stage in the control module
s: Range shifts slow or incomplete
Intermittent 4WD service message, often when cold or at start-up
Shift attempt aborted, transfer case returns to previous range

C05F7.d: A range actuator drive line sits below its expected voltage, typically because a motor lead is shorted to ground or the driver pulls it down when it should not. In a reversing gear motor each terminal is alternately the high and the low side, so a ground short on either lead shows up depending on shift direction. The TI DRV8873-Q1 is an example of a driver that reports a short to ground separately from overcurrent and open load and shuts the affected half-bridge off. Ford advises in SSM 48300 to inspect Super Duty transfer case connectors for damaged wires before condemning the motor; Magna's patent shows the motor turning a screw and sector shaft to move the range fork, so without drive the fork stays put. No maker documents C05F7; C05F8 is the high-side fault.
c: Motor lead chafed through and shorted to the body or transfer case
Water or corrosion in the shift motor connector
Internal short in the shift motor
Faulty low-side driver in the control module
s: 4WD service message, range change refused
Fault may appear only when shifting in one direction
Blown fuse for the transfer case motor possible

C05F8.d: A range actuator drive line carries more voltage than the controller expects, for example from a short to battery voltage or because a low-side switch no longer pulls the line down. The risk is a motor that runs or is braked when it should be idle, or a driver that cannot complete a commanded direction. The TI DRV8873-Q1 lists short to battery as its own protection case and disables the output that sees it. Magna drives the range shift motor with pulse width modulation and controls speed, direction and revolutions per shift, which presumes both motor leads can be switched cleanly. Stellantis bulletin 08-237-23 shows how many transfer case codes an unseated shift motor connector can trigger at once. No maker documents C05F8 itself; C05F7 covers the ground side.
c: Motor lead shorted to a battery-fed wire
Low-side switch in the control module failed open
Corrosion bridging pins in the shift motor connector
s: 4WD service message, range shift disabled
Shift motor may hum or run unexpectedly
Transfer case remains in the last selected range

C05F9.d: The controller has measured or estimated that the range actuator motor is too hot and blocks further shifts until it cools. Most designs model temperature from motor activity; a Denso patent for a similar shift actuator adds a fixed increment per motor start, lets the estimate decay over time and limits the motor above a protection value of 137 degrees C in its example. Ford TSB 22-2136 for 2021–2022 Bronco names C05F9:19 together with C05D9:99 in the AWD module, with the wrench lamp on and 4WD off, linked to low battery charge: test the battery, clear codes and shift through 2H, 4H, 4A and 4L. Its headline and the follow-up 22-2447 only list C05D9, so the C05F9 entry may be a typo. Stellantis reports motor overheating as its own C1444-98.
c: Many range shifts in a short time, motor protection active
Low battery charge prolongs motor run time and current
Stiff shift mechanism or blocked shift loads the motor
Worn shift motor drawing excess current
s: Message that 4WD is overheated or temporarily unavailable
Range shifts refused until the system cools
Wrench or 4WD service lamp on

C05FA.d: The range actuator received a valid command and its circuit looks fine, yet the transfer case did not reach the requested range in time or stays in one position. Range shifts use toothed sleeves that can meet tooth on tooth; BorgWarner places a torsion spring between motor and barrel cam so the motor can keep turning and the stored energy finishes the shift once the teeth align. If the block persists, or the fork, cam or motor gear binds, the controller sees no progress. GM describes this case in PIP5089A for 2007–2015 full-size trucks as C0387, a shift that could not be finished: if the encoder motor still cannot move as required at the next start-up relearn, the module sets C0569 instead. No maker documents C05FA itself; overheating from repeated attempts is C05F9.
c: Shift blocked tooth on tooth, often when not rolling or not in neutral
Binding range fork, cam or shift rail inside the transfer case
Worn or seized shift motor gear train
Low or wrong transfer case fluid
s: Low range does not engage or does not release
Range indicator keeps flashing
Grinding or clicking from the transfer case during the shift

C05FB.d: General electrical fault in the circuit of the sensor that reports where the range actuator stands, without narrowing it to low, high or implausible. Designs vary: Magna mounts a programmable linear Hall IC on the transfer case housing that reads a stepped sector plate or the range fork and outputs a duty cycle; BorgWarner uses a single sensor whose probe rides five plateaus on the cam; GM full-size trucks combine rotary and incremental position sensors in the encoder motor. Stellantis files comparable faults under the separate SAE codes C00A7-13 and C00A8-13 (actuator position sensor A or B circuit open), triggered in bulletin 08-237-23 by an unseated connector. No maker documents C05FB itself; C05FD and C05FE are the narrower variants.
c: Sensor or actuator connector not fully latched
Open supply, ground or signal wire of the position sensor
Failed position sensor, often integrated in the shift motor
s: 4WD service message, range shifts disabled
Range indicator blank or flashing
Further transfer case codes stored at the same time

C05FC.t: 4WD/AWD Range Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
C05FC.d: The range actuator position signal is electrically valid but does not agree with what the actuator is doing: it does not change while the motor runs, lands between defined positions or contradicts a second position input. Magna's sensor resolves its four sector positions to about plus or minus 1.5 degrees, and BorgWarner's target has five plateaus, so a reading between steps is suspicious. Toyota shows the comparison principle on 2024–2025 Tacoma models with P178462 and P17AC62, where the limit switch of the shift motor disagrees with the H4-L4 switch; bulletin T-SB-0093-25 replaces the transfer shift actuator and fits a new breather hose. GM notes that position faults can block the startup relearn. No maker documents C05FC itself; pure circuit faults are C05FB, C05FD and C05FE.
c: Sensor target or magnet shifted, loose or worn
Moisture in the actuator, for example via a faulty breather
Sensor drifting with temperature or age
Actuator or module replaced without matching calibration
s: Flashing 4WD indicator, range display does not match actual range
Range shifts refused or repeated
4WD service message

C05FD.t: 4WD/AWD Range Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Low
C05FD.d: The range actuator position signal sits below the lowest value an intact sensor can deliver. With a sensor powered from a reference supply this usually means the signal line is shorted to ground, the supply is missing or the sensor output has failed low. Fixed diagnostic bands are common for such position inputs; a Honda and Denso patent for a comparable shift range actuator treats any sensor voltage at or below 0.5 V as abnormal. Sensors with PWM output, as in Magna's transfer case design, show the same fault as a duty cycle stuck at the lower limit. GM bulletin PIP5098 points to a corroded ground terminal for the encoder motor channels on Colorado and Canyon. No maker documents C05FD itself; C05FE is the opposite case.
s: 4WD service message, range shifts disabled
Range indicator shows no valid position

C05FE.t: 4WD/AWD Range Actuator Position Sensor Circuit High
C05FE.d: The range actuator position signal lies above the highest value a working sensor produces. Usual explanations are a signal line touching supply voltage, a lost sensor ground that lets the output float up, or an internal sensor fault. In a patent shared by Honda and Denso on a park-by-wire shifter, anything from 4.5 V up counts as faulty and then relies on learned values or end-stop learning to keep limited operation. Magna's transfer case sensor reports position as a duty cycle, where the same fault appears as a ratio pinned near the top. Stellantis bulletin 08-237-23 shows that a loose shift motor connector can upset several position inputs at once. No maker documents C05FE itself; C05FD covers readings that are too low.
c: Signal wire shorted to supply or battery voltage
s: 4WD service message, range shifts disabled
Range display flashes or shows a wrong range

C05FF.d: The controller lacks valid reference positions for the range actuator, so it cannot translate sensor readings into high, neutral and low. GM full-size trucks run such a relearn at every start-up: per PIP5089A the transfer case module drives the encoder motor to locate its position, and if a sensor, motor or circuit problem prevents this it sets C0569 and runs no further checks. Lear's actuator patent shows why the limits matter, as about 270 degrees of worm gear travel are used inside a 330 degree mechanical range and a full turn could lock the transfer case. A Honda and Denso patent for a similar shift actuator falls back to driving against both end stops when sensor data are unusable. New actuators, modules or lost memory are typical triggers. No maker documents C05FF itself.
c: Actuator or control module replaced without running the learn routine
Learn routine aborted by a sensor, motor or wiring fault
Stored values lost after battery disconnection or low voltage
s: 4WD service message right after a repair
Range shifts unavailable until the learn has run
Range indicator flashes at start-up

C0600.d: The position loop that drives the range actuator to a target does not reach or hold it: commanded and measured position stay apart for too long, although sensor and drive circuit pass their own checks. Magna describes such a loop for a transfer case range shift, with speed profiles per shift phase and PID control over the last tenth of travel down to a stop at the target. Lear's actuator patent notes that the feedback should stop the worm gear at about 270 degrees but can overrun towards the 330 degree stop. Typical causes are binding, a weak motor, low voltage or poor learned limits. GM used C0600 earlier for a suspension accelerometer (PI0954, 2010 LaCrosse); that is a different, older assignment. No maker documents C0600 in this meaning.
c: Stiff range fork, cam or shift rail slows the actuator
Weak shift motor or low supply voltage
Learned end positions no longer match the hardware
Play between sensor target and shift mechanism
s: Range shift incomplete, indicator flashes
4WD service message and range shifts blocked
Noise from the transfer case while the motor hunts for position

C0601.d: An active air dam is a panel below the front bumper that an electric drive lowers at speed to reduce drag and raises for slow driving, towing or rough ground. Ford's patent for this design moves the panel with two motor-driven screw jacks under command of the PCM or body module over LIN or CAN; a GM patent closes the loop with position, motor current and back-EMF feedback. C0601 means the drive path to the actuator is open: the controller switches its output on, yet no load current flows. Integrated motor drivers such as TI's DRV8873-Q1 report exactly this as an open load. No maker documents C0601 publicly; Ford and Stellantis only publish the performance code C0604. The panel usually stays where it last stopped.
c: Actuator connector loose, unplugged or corroded after water entry
Wire broken in the exposed harness behind the bumper, often after impact or road debris
Open motor winding or internal fault in the air dam actuator
s: Active Air Dam System Fault message in the cluster
Air dam no longer moves and stays raised or lowered
Slightly higher fuel use on the highway when stuck raised

C0602.t: Active Air Dam Control Circuit Low
C0602.d: C0602 says the control line to the air dam actuator is held below its expected voltage, most often because a motor lead touches ground or because water has bridged pins in the connector. Smart H-bridge drivers such as the DRV8873-Q1 see a grounded output as overcurrent, trip within a few microseconds and turn that half-bridge off, so the motor never gets drive. For a 2025 Ram 1500 with air dam codes, Stellantis has technicians look for corrosion, cut or chafed wires and excess resistance before replacing the dam. Ford fits separate left and right actuators on the F-150, so one side can be at fault alone. No maker documents C0602 itself. The panel stops moving and a warning text may show; high and open faults are C0603 and C0601.
c: Actuator wire chafed through and touching the body or frame
Water and corrosion in the actuator connector after a damaged seal
Shorted motor or electronics inside the actuator
s: Air dam warning message in the instrument cluster
Air dam stays in one position
Fault returns as soon as the system commands movement

C0603.t: Active Air Dam Control Circuit High
C0603.d: With C0603 the air dam control circuit reads above its permitted level, which points to a lead shorted to battery voltage or to another powered wire in the front-end harness. Motor driver ICs like the DRV8873-Q1 list a short to battery as a separate protected fault and disable the affected output. GM's patent on air dam self-diagnosis compares commanded position with measured position and motor current, which lets the controller tell a wiring problem from a blocked or broken panel. No maker documents C0603 publicly. Ram's X96 warranty extension for 2019 Ram 1500 trucks shows that air dam faults can light the MIL there, but that case is the lost-communication code U0645. Expect a stationary panel and a system message.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-fed wire in the front harness
Fault in the actuator electronics holding the line high
Wrong pin assignment or splice after a previous bumper or harness repair
s: Air dam system fault message
Air dam does not deploy at highway speed
Possible blown fuse for the air dam circuit

C0604.t: Active Air Dam Control Circuit Performance
C0604.d: C0604 is the air dam code that makers really publish: the panel does not reach or hold its commanded position even though the circuit itself looks sound. Ford stores C0604:00 in the PCM of 2021–2023 F-150s, often with a cluster warning that the air dam system has failed; its fixes are new left and right actuators for an actuator firmware issue (SSM 51718), a PCM reflash (TSB 24-2404, later 25-2155 and 25-2236) and, on 2021–2025 trucks, new bolts where the actuator-to-dam bolts broke (SSM 54705). Stellantis ties C0604 to water in the connector and to fascia contact causing a clunk at 15–35 mph, and on a 2025 Ram 1500 to impact damage, with the MIL lit. GM's patent splits such faults into sensor, actuator and panel cases.
c: Actuator firmware or PCM software level with known false or real faults (Ford F-150)
Broken bolts between actuator and air dam, panel hangs
Air dam bent, cracked or jammed after ground contact or debris
Water or corrosion in the actuator connector
Air dam lip rubbing on the front fascia
s: Active Air Dam System Fault See Manual message
Air dam hangs down or does not retract
Clunk from the front end when driving at moderate speed or decelerating
Check engine lamp on some Ram trucks

C0605.d: The steering wheel angle sensor tells the stability system how far and how quickly the driver turns. C0605 means its circuit is open or no usable signal arrives at all: a broken supply, ground or signal wire, an unplugged connector or a dead sensor. In a Bosch patent for a PWM-output sensor, the control unit treats the signal as missing when no high level appears within one PWM period; a Kelsey-Hayes patent declares an open or short once the phase lines stay out of range for about 5 ms and blocks yaw control. Bosch's GMR sensor today sends angle and rate over CAN. No maker publishes C0605 with this meaning; GM's PI0954 used C0605 on the 2010 Buick LaCrosse for a suspension accelerometer, an unrelated older assignment.
c: Connector at the steering column loose or not latched after airbag or column work
Broken supply, ground or signal wire in the column harness
s: ESC/stability control warning lamp on, system off
Traction control and lane or parking assistants may be unavailable
Steering angle reads zero or not available in scan data

C0606.t: Steering Wheel Angle Sensor Circuit Low
C0606.d: C0606 flags a steering angle signal or sensor supply that reads too low, as caused by a short to ground, a sagging supply or an output stuck at the bottom of its range. In the Kelsey-Hayes design the two phase lines swing between roughly 0.6 V and 4.4 V on a 5 V feed, and anything below the lower band is a fault; Bosch's PWM sensor maps −720° to +720° onto 10–90 % duty cycle, so a line pinned to ground leaves that window, and the patent lists a short to ground as detectable. Sensors that talk over CAN, such as the Bourns type 6002 running on 8–18 V, report their errors on the bus instead. No maker documents C0606 publicly. Stability control shuts down; after repair the centre position may need relearning.
c: Signal wire chafed against the steering column and shorted to ground
Low sensor supply from a weak battery or a damaged feed circuit
s: ESC warning lamp on and stability control unavailable
Steering angle in scan data pinned at one end value
Driver assistance messages about limited function

C0607.t: Steering Wheel Angle Sensor Circuit High
C0607.d: C0607 is the mirror image of C0606: the steering angle signal sits above its allowed ceiling. Usual reasons are a signal wire shorted to the sensor supply or to battery voltage, an open ground at the sensor, after which the line drifts up, or an internal fault driving the output to its top end. In the Kelsey-Hayes quadrature sensor a valid high state is near 4.4 V and readings beyond the upper limit are faults; in the Bosch PWM concept a line stuck at battery level yields no valid duty cycle, and the patent names a short to battery as detectable. HELLA points out that a redundant double angle sensor lets such single-channel failures be caught. No maker publishes C0607. The ESC lamp lights and stability control stays off until the fault is gone.
c: Signal wire shorted to the sensor supply or battery voltage
Open sensor ground, signal floats high
s: ESC and traction control warning lamps on
Steering angle shown at an implausible maximum value
Lane keeping or park assist switched off

C0608.t: Steering Wheel Angle Sensor Circuit Performance
C0608.d: C0608 covers a steering angle signal that is electrically in range but cannot be trusted: it jumps, drifts, freezes or disagrees with what yaw rate, lateral acceleration and wheel speeds imply. The Kelsey-Hayes patent rejects a centre offset that moves by more than about 15° after a dropout, and Bosch builds plausibility checks of the individual measuring channels into its GMR sensor. HELLA reminds workshops to zero the sensor after alignment or steering work, since a wrong zero point disturbs stability control. FMVSS 126 defines ESC as a system that monitors driver steering inputs, so the module switches ESC off once that input is doubtful. No maker publishes C0608; related checks are C0528, C052A and C05B2.
c: Sensor not zeroed after wheel alignment, steering or column repair
Steering wheel fitted off centre or toe out of adjustment
Worn or faulty sensor giving jumping or frozen values
Brief signal dropouts from a loose connector
s: ESC lamp on, sometimes only after a few turns or straight driving
Unexpected ESC braking interventions
Steering angle not zero with the wheels pointing straight

C0609.d: The park brake switch is the driver's apply and release button for an electric parking brake; on some cars it also reports lever or button state to other modules. C0609 covers an electrical fault in its circuit, such as an open contact, a short to ground or supply, or an unplugged connector. Continental's patent for a redundant EPB button gives each switch level its own supply and ground and measures resistor potentials to find these faults, then still reads the driver's request from the intact channel. Audi logs C060900, under the same switch title, in J623, the engine control unit of 2022–2024 Q4 e-tron models, with a drive system warning and sometimes no gear engagement; TSB 2074088 calls for a 15-minute terminal 30 reset and earth strap work.
c: Connector at the switch or in the dash not fully engaged
Poor ground or control unit software (Audi Q4 e-tron case)
Worn, contaminated or corroded switch contacts, e.g. after spilled drinks
s: Park brake or drive system warning in the cluster
Parking brake does not respond to the button
Gear selection refused in some electric models

C060A.d: C060A means the park brake switch reports a state that does not change when it should, or that contradicts itself: a jammed or welded contact, a button held down mechanically, or paired contacts that disagree. EPB buttons carry duplicated contacts for safety; a TRW patent notes that the controller flags an error when the paired signals do not arrive within about 30 ms, and that a blocked actuator can close just one of them. Advics counts apply and release signals seen together as a switch failure, lights a warning lamp and stores a code. Continental's design falls back to a majority vote and, while moving, chooses release over apply. No maker publishes C060A itself. The button may stop working in one or both directions.
c: Button jammed by dirt, sticky residue or a broken housing
One contact of the redundant pair welded or worn
Object in the console pressing the button
s: Park brake warning lamp or message
Brake does not apply or release from the button
Code returns right after clearing while the button is untouched

C060B.t: Left Park Brake Actuator Control Circuit/Open
C060B.d: On motor-on-caliper parking brakes, a small DC motor drives a gear stage and a spindle that pushes the rear piston; ZF quotes up to 19 kN clamping force with its early swash plate gearbox and up to 25 kN with a two-stage planetary set for heavy vehicles. C060B means the control unit (ESC module or separate EPB module) finds the drive circuit of the left motor open: broken lead, unplugged caliper connector or burnt winding. Hyundai uses its own code C2416 for an open or shorted left motor and fixed 2019–2022 Ioniq hybrids with new connector extension harnesses; GM's PIT5662A, filed under C056D/C056E, asks for no more than 6 Ω per rear circuit measured at the EBCM. No maker publishes C060B itself. The left caliper cannot clamp.
c: Corroded or loose connector or extension harness at the left caliper
Wire broken where the harness flexes with the suspension
Open winding in the left actuator motor
s: Red park brake lamp flashing or Service Parking Brake message
Left rear brake does not apply when the switch is pulled
Auto-hold or hill-start assist unavailable

C060C.t: Left Park Brake Actuator Control Circuit Low
C060C.d: C060C indicates that a drive line of the left parking brake motor is pulled toward ground. Typical reasons are a motor lead chafed against the body or axle, water standing in the caliper connector, or a shorted motor. The motor is reversed through an H-bridge, and protected bridge drivers such as TI's DRV8873-Q1 treat a grounded output as overcurrent and cut that half-bridge within microseconds. Both public cases on this hardware point at the wiring: Hyundai's 2023 bulletin for left-side motor short/open (its own code C2416) replaces the Ioniq connector extension, and GM's PIT5662A traces park brake messages to resistance in the rear circuits. No maker publishes C060C. The left motor is not driven, so secure the car in Park or in gear.
c: Motor lead chafed and shorted to the body or axle
Water and corrosion in the left caliper connector
s: Park brake warning lamp and service message
Left rear brake does not apply or release
Fuse for the park brake motor may blow

C060D.t: Left Park Brake Actuator Control Circuit High
C060D.d: Here one of the two left motor leads reads high: it is shorted to battery voltage, or touches another live wire, so the low side of the bridge cannot pull it down. A bridge driver such as the DRV8873-Q1 detects an output shorted to the battery and disables the stage to protect itself. The motor sits in the rear caliper, where ZF's design drives a spindle through a gearbox, so its leads run along the moving suspension and through a weather-exposed plug. Hyundai's left-side motor short/open bulletin (code C2416) and GM's rear-circuit resistance check in PIT5662A show the same weak spots. No maker publishes C060D. The left side stays as it was, and the driver gets a park brake warning.
c: Motor lead shorted to a battery-fed wire
Moisture bridging pins in the caliper connector
Failed driver stage in the brake control module
s: Park brake warning lamp on
Left rear brake does not respond to the switch
Electronic pad change mode cannot be entered

C060E.t: Left Park Brake Actuator Performance/Stuck Off
C060E.d: C060E is set when the left actuator is driven but does not build or keep the clamping force it should, so the brake effectively stays off. Bosch's EPB patents derive clamping force from motor current: during apply it rises as pads meet the disc and then levels off at the target force. A current that never climbs points to a slipping belt, a stripped gear or a spindle that turns without pushing the piston. FMVSS 135 tests parking brakes by holding a vehicle loaded to GVWR on a 20 % grade, so a weak left side can let the car creep. GM's PIT5662A shows that excess resistance in a rear circuit can also starve the motor. No maker publishes C060E. Expect a park brake warning and limited auto-hold.
c: Worn gearbox, belt or spindle inside the left actuator
Pads or piston not set up correctly after brake service without maintenance mode
High resistance in the left motor circuit limits motor torque
s: Vehicle may creep on a slope with the parking brake applied
