Park brake warning lamp or message
Motor noise without the usual clamping sound at the left rear

C060F.t: Left Park Brake Actuator Stuck On
C060F.d: C060F is the reverse of C060E: the left actuator does not release, or the module cannot confirm that it has. An Advics patent recognises release by watching motor current while the motor runs backwards: once the current stops changing after a minimum time of around 200 ms, the clamping force is taken as zero and the motor runs on briefly to set pad clearance. A release that never shows this pattern, or a motor that stalls, fits a stuck-on fault. Seized pistons, a corroded spindle nut, pads frozen to the disc or a broken gear stage are typical. ZF's workshop guide requires the scan tool maintenance mode before the actuator unit is replaced. Driving with the brake applied overheats the rear brake.
c: Seized caliper piston or corroded spindle nut
Pads frozen or rusted to the disc after standing
Broken gear stage in the actuator
s: Left rear brake drags, smells hot or the car pulls away sluggishly
Park brake lamp stays on after release
Release message or refusal to drive off

C0610.t: Right Park Brake Actuator Control Circuit/Open
C0610.d: C0610 reports that the drive circuit of the right rear parking brake motor is open, so the controller switches its bridge but no motor current flows. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV shows how such a check works under its own code C10B0-01: during apply or release the ABS unit looks for an open motor circuit on the right side and reacts within about one second, then suspends the electric parking brake and hill start assist. Hyundai calls the same fault C2417 on the Ioniq hybrids and replaces a connector extension harness, and GM's PIT5662A wants no more than 6 ohms per rear circuit at the EBCM. None of these makers emits C0610 itself. The right caliper cannot clamp; the left side is C060B.
c: Right caliper motor connector unplugged, corroded or with pushed-back pins
Broken wire in the harness that flexes with the right rear suspension
Open winding or worn brushes in the right actuator motor
Blown fuse or fusible link feeding the parking brake output stage
s: Parking brake warning lamp and service message
Right rear caliper neither applies nor releases electrically
Hill start assist or auto hold unavailable

C0611.t: Right Park Brake Actuator Control Circuit Low
C0611.d: C0611 means one of the two leads to the right parking brake motor is dragged toward ground. The harness to the right rear caliper rides on the suspension and passes close to the brake disc, so chafing against the knuckle or water in the plug are the usual suspects, followed by a shorted motor. H-bridge drivers such as TI's DRV8874-Q1 sense an output tied to ground as overcurrent and switch the bridge off, which leaves the motor without drive. Hyundai's bulletin for the Ioniq hybrids names C2417, short or open on the right motor, and fits an improved extension harness on that side. No maker publishes C0611. GM once listed C0611 in its connector test bulletin PIP5094 under an older, unrelated meaning.
c: Motor lead chafed through at the right rear knuckle or bracket
Water and corrosion bridging pins in the right caliper connector
Internal short in the right actuator motor
s: Parking brake warning lamp on
Right side does not apply; vehicle may roll on a slope if not in Park or in gear
Fuse for the parking brake circuit may blow

C0612.t: Right Park Brake Actuator Control Circuit High
C0612.d: With C0612 a lead of the right parking brake motor stays at or near battery voltage while the bridge tries to pull it low. Likely causes are a short to a live wire in the rear harness, a wrong splice after body or axle repair, or a defect in the output stage. Driver ICs such as the DRV8873-Q1 treat a short to the supply as its own protected fault and disable the output. GM's PIT5662A, written for park brake messages on the Acadia, XT5, Enclave and Traverse, has technicians measure both rear circuits at the brake module with the actuators plugged in; a reading above 6 ohms means wiring or actuator repair. No maker publishes C0612. The right brake keeps its last position, and a parking brake warning lights up.
c: Motor lead shorted to a battery-fed wire in the rear harness
Failed low-side switch in the control unit holding the lead high
Wrong pin or splice after an earlier harness or body repair
s: Service parking brake message and warning lamp
Right parking brake does not respond to the switch
Code may return as soon as an apply is commanded

C0613.t: Right Park Brake Actuator Performance/Stuck Off
C0613.d: C0613 covers a right actuator that is powered but fails to clamp. The wiring is intact, yet the module never sees the motor turn or the current rise that marks pads pressed against the disc. Mitsubishi gives a concrete case with C10B0-09 on the 2023 Outlander PHEV: during apply the right motor does not rotate, and after ten seconds or more the ABS unit flags it and disables both the parking brake and hill start assist. Bosch patents read clamping force from motor current, so a flat current curve points to a slipping belt, stripped gear or idle spindle; ZF's actuator drives the spindle through a belt and a gearbox. FMVSS 135 requires the parking brake to hold a loaded car on a 20 % grade. No maker publishes C0613; the left twin is C060E.
c: Stripped gear, slipping belt or broken spindle inside the right actuator
Motor seized by corrosion after water entry
High resistance in the right circuit starving the motor of current
Pads or disc worn far beyond limit, or caliper not calibrated after a brake job
s: Parking brake warning lamp and message
Parked vehicle may creep on a slope
No motor noise from the right rear when the brake is applied

C0614.t: Right Park Brake Actuator Stuck On
C0614.d: C0614 is set when the right parking brake will not let go, or when the module cannot confirm that it has. To release, the motor runs in reverse; Advics treats the force as released when, after a minimum run of roughly 200 ms, the current has settled, and then lets the motor run on briefly to restore pad clearance. If that pattern never appears, or the motor stalls, the right side counts as stuck on. Bosch also uses current monitoring to spot abnormal behaviour and may command a release on its own. Causes are mostly mechanical: a seized piston or spindle nut, pads rusted to the disc after standing, or a jammed gearbox. ZF notes that the actuator must be wound back with a scan tool before service. Driving off overheats the right rear brake.
c: Seized caliper piston or corroded spindle nut on the right side
Pads rusted to the disc after the car stood for a long time
Jammed gearbox or damaged motor in the right actuator
s: Right rear brake drags; car pulls or feels held back when driving off
Hot right rear wheel and burning smell
Parking brake warning and release request not completed

C0615.t: Park Brake Control Module Control Circuit/Open
C0615.d: C0615 points at the circuit that feeds or enables the parking brake control electronics, not at a single caliper: it reads as open. Today the parking brake logic often runs as a software block inside the ESC unit (VDA recommendation 305-100), while the host supplies the motor power stage; a few cars keep a separate module. GM's EBCM tables for 2025 trucks show what such a check looks for, filed under C0616: if the motor supply line stays below 2 V for 500 ms during an apply or release, the clamp 30 feed counts as open. Mitsubishi sets C10B7-16 when the feed falls to 10 V or less. No maker publishes C0615 with this meaning; on 2014–2019 GM trucks C0615 is listed beside ride control codes in PIT5307G, which reflects an older GM assignment.
c: Blown fuse or fusible link in the parking brake power feed
Loose or corroded terminal on the power or enable line at the module
Broken wire between fuse box and module
Internal fault in the module's supply stage
s: Electric parking brake inoperative on both sides
Parking brake warning lamp and service message
Auto hold and hill start assist unavailable

C0616.t: Park Brake Control Module Control Circuit Performance
C0616.d: C0616 is the one code in this range that GM really uses. Its 2025 EBCM tables file over twenty parking brake self-tests under it, all Type C without MIL: the left and right H-bridge supplies may not differ by more than 12 % at 8–20 V, the current measuring path must read 10.5–17 A in its self-test, the motor voltage must stay between 7 and 18 V for 700 ms, plus watchdog, ASIC and rollaway checks. The 2019 tables for the L3B engine list C0616 for an ADC reference fault in the EBCM as Type A with MIL. Bulletin 24-NA-122 traces a parking brake warning on 2024 Silverado and Sierra HD trucks to EBCM software; the fix is reprogramming, not a new module. Mitsubishi reports similar faults as C10B3.
c: Software anomaly in the brake module (GM 2024 HD trucks, fixed by reprogramming)
Weak battery, poor ground or charging fault pushing motor voltage outside its window
Internal hardware fault in the parking brake ASIC, bridge or measuring path
Parking brake assembly check not completed after module replacement
s: Service Parking Brake message in the driver information center
Parking brake warning lamp; parking brake may be inhibited
Check engine lamp on some GM models

C0617.t: Park Brake Control Module Control Circuit Low
C0617.d: C0617 says the supply or control line feeding the parking brake electronics reads too low. Because both caliper motors draw several amps when they clamp, a weak battery, a poor ground or a corroded feed shows up here first. Mitsubishi's ABS unit on the 2023 Outlander PHEV sets C10B7-16 when the ignition feed drops to 10 V or less for about a second and then suspends the parking brake and hill start assist. GM's 2025 EBCM tables stop the motor and block actuation when its voltage stays under 7 V for 700 ms, but they store that as C0616. In the integrated layout described for VDA 305-100 the power stage belongs to the ESC host, so the feed is shared. No maker publishes C0617; charge the battery before chasing it.
c: High resistance in the module ground or power feed
Control or enable line shorted to ground
s: Parking brake warning lamp, often together with other low-voltage messages
Parking brake applies slowly or not at all
Hill start assist unavailable

C0618.t: Park Brake Control Module Control Circuit High
C0618.d: C0618 is the overvoltage counterpart of C0617: the feed or control line of the parking brake electronics reads above its window. A regulator fault in the alternator or DC/DC converter, jump starting with a booster set to 24 V, or a short between the enable line and a live wire are the usual reasons. Mitsubishi's ABS unit sets C10B7-17 once the ignition feed reaches 16 V or more, with a detection delay of up to one second, and the parking brake is then locked out. In GM's 2025 EBCM tables a motor voltage above 18 V for 700 ms halts the motor and blocks further actuation, logged as C0616. No maker publishes C0618. Check charging voltage with the engine running before blaming the brake module.
c: Faulty voltage regulator in the alternator or DC/DC converter
Overvoltage from a jump starter or charger on a 24 V setting
Enable or control line shorted to a battery-fed wire
s: Parking brake warning lamp, possibly with a battery or charging warning
Parking brake does not respond to the switch
Other modules may log overvoltage codes at the same time

C0619.t: Brake Pedal Position Sensor A Offset Exceeded Learning Limit
C0619.d: Pedal position sensors are taught their rest value, and C0619 says the offset found for channel A lies outside the band the controller will accept. A Hitachi patent on electric boosters learns the stroke sensor zero only with the pedal released and no brake request, and treats a zero beyond a prescribed range as a sensor fault. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV maps C18EE-96 (abnormal stroke sensor value) to C0619, with MIL and brake warnings after two trips; boost, regenerative braking and automatic braking stop. GM's PIT5206D shows the field side: a wiring dropout made the ECM learn 0.61 V instead of about 1 V, so it saw the brake applied. GM relearns after any sensor or module service (16-NA-155).
c: Intermittent connection in the sensor circuit that skewed the learned value
Pedal not returning fully (floor mat, stiff pivot, wrong adjustment)
Sensor drifted or fitted out of position after replacement
Learn procedure skipped or disturbed after sensor or module service
s: Brake or brake system warning lamp; check engine lamp on some vehicles
Brake lights, cruise control or shifting behave as if the pedal were pressed
Reduced brake assist or regenerative braking on electrified models

C061A.t: Brake Pedal Position Sensor B Offset Exceeded Learning Limit
C061A.d: C061A is the same learn-limit check for the second channel, B. Many pedal sensors hold two independent elements; on GM trucks since 2012 one potentiometer feeds the ECM and the other the BCM, each with its own 5 V reference, ground and signal. Each controller keeps its own released-position value and updates it whenever it sees a lower voltage, so a short dropout on one channel can leave B with a skewed zero while A stays correct. The Hitachi patent rejects a learned zero outside its prescribed range as a sensor fault. Snap-on and GM's 16-NA-155 stress relearning in both modules without touching the pedal. Which physical channel a maker calls B is not public, and no maker documents C061A; channel A is C0619.
c: Dropout or fretting corrosion on the channel B reference, ground or signal pin
Learn done in only one module, or the pedal moved during the learn
Pedal rest position changed by a mat, bracket damage or adjustment
Drifting second element inside the pedal sensor
s: Brake system warning or message
Mismatch between modules about pedal state, e.g. brake lights versus cruise control
Shift interlock or start function may act up

C061B.t: ECM Request - Forced Traction Control Disable
C061B.d: C061B is not a brake fault at all. It records that the engine control module told the brake module to switch traction control off, usually because the engine can no longer cut torque on demand. A Hyundai patent spells out the logic: the TCS asks for a torque cut over CAN, the engine reports the torque it delivers, and if the gap stays outside ±10 % too often, TCS is turned off and a warning lamp lit. GM handled this with its own codes: PIC4740C lists C0242 ECM Indicated TCS Malfunction next to C0561, and PIT4169F tells technicians that the PCM usually holds a code too, possibly without a check engine lamp, and not to replace the EBCM. Fix the engine fault first. No maker documents C061B publicly.
c: Engine misfire or other engine fault that blocks torque reduction
Electronic throttle or torque model fault stored in the ECM
Corrupt or missing torque messages between engine and brake module
ECM software issue setting the disable request without a real fault
s: Traction control off lamp or Service Traction Control message
Stability control may also be unavailable
Engine codes stored, sometimes with the check engine lamp

C061C.t: Variable Effort Steering Actuator Control Circuit/Open
C061C.d: Variable effort steering changes how hard a hydraulic system steers with road speed. In GM's Magnasteer a coil and permanent magnets on the rotary valve add or subtract from the torsion bar's stiffness; the GM and Steering Solutions patent EP2028081B1 describes this actuator, and ±3 A coil current is cited in a later patent. Ford's older variable-assist systems used a stepper-driven or solenoid orifice instead. C061C means the actuator circuit is open: the controller drives it but no current flows. Coil resistance should be about 2 ohms; an open reading means a new rack, as the coil is not serviceable. GM used its own C1241 for this. No maker publishes C061C. Expect light steering at speed or heavy steering when parking.
c: Connector at the steering gear loose, corroded or soaked with fluid
Open actuator coil inside the steering gear
Broken wire between control module and steering gear
s: Steering effort no longer changes with speed
Heavier steering when parking or lighter, nervous steering on the highway
Steering or stability warning on some vehicles

C061D.t: Variable Effort Steering Actuator Control Circuit Low
C061D.d: C061D flags an actuator line held too low, most often a coil lead shorted to the steering gear housing or to the vehicle body. The Magnasteer coil sits in the cast valve housing, which forms part of its magnetic circuit, so insulation damage there grounds the winding; checking each coil terminal against the housing is a standard test. Because the current must flow in both directions, the controller uses a full bridge, and drivers such as the DRV8874-Q1 shut down on overcurrent when an output is grounded. With the actuator dead, assist depends solely on torsion bar stiffness and the pump's delivery. No maker publishes C061D; open and high are C061C and C061E.
c: Actuator coil insulation broken down to the steering gear housing
Actuator wire chafed against subframe or exhaust heat shield
Failed output stage in the controlling module
s: Speed-dependent steering feel lost
Steering feels the same at all speeds
Fuse for the steering actuator may blow

C061E.t: Variable Effort Steering Actuator Control Circuit High
C061E.d: C061E means an actuator line reads above what the controller expects, typically a lead shorted to battery voltage or a driver stage stuck on. Delphi describes Magnasteer as electronically modulating the magnetic torsional rate, with coil polarity deciding whether effort rises or falls; a line stuck high can therefore hold the actuator in one direction or stop the bridge from regulating. Ford's older variable-assist valve shows the other pattern: no current means a wide open valve and full assist, while 550 mA at 80 mph closes it. A bridge IC like the DRV8873-Q1 recognises a short to the supply and turns off. No maker documents C061E. The driver feels steering effort that no longer tracks speed.
c: Actuator lead shorted to a battery-fed wire
Output transistor in the module stuck on
Wrong pinning after a steering gear swap
s: Unusually heavy or unusually light steering that does not change with speed
Steering warning message on some vehicles

C061F.t: Variable Effort Steering Actuator Control Circuit Performance
C061F.d: C061F covers an actuator circuit that is electrically intact but does not behave as commanded: the current does not follow the request, or the expected change in effort fails to show up. In Magnasteer the coil runs from about −3 A to +3 A, and the current reverses around mid speed, so tracking errors appear as wrong feel in town or on the highway. The Steering Solutions patent stresses that the magnetic null must line up with the valve's centre for the gear to work properly; a later variant without permanent magnets only raises effort with speed. Coil heating, a sticky valve or a damaged magnet ring fit this code. GM's scan tool can run a function test that sweeps the current. No maker publishes C061F.
c: Magnetic null shifted from valve centre, damaged magnet ring
Sticking rotary valve from contaminated fluid
High resistance in connector or wiring limiting coil current
Wrong or missing vehicle speed input to the controlling module
s: Steering effort wrong for the speed or changing unexpectedly
Pull to one side with no alignment fault
Steering warning on some vehicles

C0620.t: Variable Effort Steering Lock/Safety Actuator Control Circuit/Open
C0620.d: Some steering systems that vary effort or ratio carry a second actuator whose only job is safety: a solenoid lock that blocks the motor or gear so the wheel turns the wheels directly. Delphi's patent combining Magnasteer with an active steering actuator uses a solenoid that is energised to unlock and drops into lock without power; JTEKT and Continental lock their superimposed steering the same fail-safe way. C0620 means this lock's circuit is open, so the unit cannot release and the variable function stays off. No maker publishes C0620 in this sense. On 2014–2019 GM trucks C0620 appears among suspension codes in PIT5307G, an older, unrelated assignment.
c: Connector to the lock solenoid unplugged or corroded
Open lock solenoid coil, for example after overheating
Broken wire between the steering module and the lock
s: Variable steering function disabled; steering works with a fixed characteristic
Steering system warning
Possible click or no click from the steering when switching on

C0621.t: Variable Effort Steering Lock/Safety Actuator Control Circuit Low
C0621.d: C0621 reports the lock or safety actuator line held too low. In JTEKT's variable-ratio design a PNP transistor switches the lock coil, and the ECU holds the line low on purpose when it wants to lock, for instance after a motor or sensor fault or a broken cable. An unintended short to ground therefore looks like a permanent lock request: the solenoid cannot lift the arm, and the steering stays mechanically coupled. GM's active front steering patent locks the motor electrically first and falls back to the mechanical lock if that has not happened within about 42 ms. No maker publishes C0621. The car steers normally but without the variable feature, and a warning appears.
c: Lock solenoid wire shorted to ground in the column or gear harness
Shorted turns in the lock solenoid
Failed drive transistor in the steering module
s: Variable ratio or effort function off
Steering warning lamp or message

C0622.t: Variable Effort Steering Lock/Safety Actuator Control Circuit High
C0622.d: C0622 is the critical direction for a fail-safe lock: the actuator line reads high even when the controller wants it off. Since the lock in these designs releases when powered, a line shorted to battery voltage would keep it open when it should engage, so the safety path no longer works. Continental's superimposed steering unit, for example, stays open while powered and only blocks the planet carrier once power is gone, after which the normal steering gear still steers the car. JTEKT varies the holding duty with battery voltage to keep the coil cool. Controllers that detect a stuck-high line therefore shut the variable function down. No maker documents C0622 publicly.
c: Lock solenoid wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit
Drive transistor in the module stuck on
s: Steering system warning; variable function switched off
No noticeable change in normal steering

C0623.t: Variable Effort Steering Lock/Safety Actuator Control Circuit Performance
C0623.d: C0623 covers a lock or safety actuator whose circuit is sound but whose action does not match the command: it does not release when energised, does not engage in time, or its current is implausible. JTEKT's lock coil first gets full duty for about one second to pull the arm free, then 60 % below 13 V or 40 % above 14 V to hold it, which keeps the coil at or below 100 °C instead of near 200 °C. GM's active steering patent switches to the mechanical lock if electrical locking has not taken effect within about 42 ms. A worn lock pin, a sticky arm, a weak spring or a hot coil can each upset such timing. No maker publishes C0623; the variable steering function is switched off until the code clears.
c: Sticking lock arm or pin, worn lock teeth
Solenoid weakened by heat, pull-in force too low
Weak or broken return spring, lock engages late
s: Steering warning and variable function off
Clicking or knocking from the steering column at start or stop
Steering wheel slightly off-centre after the system locks

C0624.d: Variable effort steering tunes hydraulic assist to the situation, and besides road speed some systems also read a steering wheel sensor. Ford's variable-assist steering, first used on the 1988 Lincoln Continental, fed its module from an optical sensor tracking how the wheel turns; a Ford patent describes that encoder with 20 slots and two detectors, good for 4.5° steps, and drops the actuator current during quick evasive turns so full assist comes back. A GM patent adds a handwheel angle input to Magnasteer control. C0624 is the general electrical fault in this sensor circuit: broken signal wire, lost feed or ground. No maker publishes C0624. Effort then follows road speed alone, or the system falls back to one fixed level.
c: Loose or corroded connector at the steering column sensor
Wire broken where the harness flexes in the steering column
Failed sensor, for example a dead optical detector
s: Steering effort no longer reacts to quick wheel movements
Effort stays at one level or follows only road speed
Steering warning on some vehicles

C0625.t: Variable Effort Steering Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
C0625.d: Here the sensor signal is electrically present but its content does not add up. With an incremental steering wheel sensor the module derives rate or angle from pulse counts; a Ford patent computes steering rate from the counts in a fixed sampling window, so lost pulses give a wrong rate. A Kelsey-Hayes patent on a two-channel sensor checks after each dropout whether the newly learned zero has moved by more than about 15° and then reports a shift fault; levels that sit between the valid low and high bands are rejected too. No maker publishes C0625 for steering. On GM vehicles the number turns up in PIP5094 (2014 and older) and among suspension-related codes in PIT5307G for 2014–2019 trucks, an older and unrelated use.
c: Dirt or damage on the encoder disc causing lost pulses
Intermittent contact at the connector producing short dropouts
Sensor loose or misaligned after column or steering work
Implausible road speed input used for the cross-check
s: Steering effort changes unexpectedly while turning
Variable assist switched off with a fixed steering feel
Steering or stability warning on some vehicles

C0626.t: Variable Effort Steering Sensor Circuit Low
C0626.d: C0626 means the signal of the variable effort steering sensor reads below the lowest level the module accepts. A Kelsey-Hayes patent shows the typical window for such a steering wheel sensor: with a 5 V supply each channel switches between roughly 0.6 V and 4.4 V, and anything under the lower band counts as low. After about 5 ms out of range the module stops trusting the signal, and after roughly 100 ms it latches an open or short fault. A Ford patent lists steering wheel rate and position among the inputs of a speed-dependent effort controller. Typical causes are a signal wire shorted to ground, a lost 5 V feed or a failed output stage. No maker publishes C0626. Unlike C0627, the fault lies on the ground side.
c: Signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
5 V sensor feed missing or pulled down by another fault
Sensor output stage failed and stuck low
s: Variable assist disabled, steering effort fixed
Steering warning lamp or message

C0627.t: Variable Effort Steering Sensor Circuit High
C0627.d: The high counterpart: the sensor signal sits above the top of the band the module treats as valid. In the Kelsey-Hayes design a healthy channel peaks near 4.4 V on a 5 V supply, so a reading close to the supply rail or beyond it points to a short to the reference or to battery voltage, or to a broken sensor ground that lets the input float high. That patent handles high, low and in-between levels as separate faults so service can tell them apart. Ford's variable-assist systems used such a steering wheel rotation sensor together with road speed, and Ford's effort patent names steering rate and angle as inputs. No maker publishes C0627. As with C0626, the module ignores the sensor and steers on a fixed or speed-only curve.
c: Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage
Open sensor ground letting the signal float high
Sensor output stage failed and stuck high
s: Variable assist disabled, steering effort fixed
Steering warning lamp or message

C0628.d: C0628 says the unit that runs variable effort steering fails its own function checks. On GM's Magnasteer that unit was a separate module in 1996–97 and became part of the brake control module from 1998. A GM patent describes the logic: a microcomputer reads coil current from speed and lateral acceleration tables, limits the total and its rate of change and drives the coil by PWM; a Steering Solutions patent gives ±3 A full scale. Performance faults cover a driver stage that cannot reach the commanded current, a failed internal self-test or corrupt calibration. GM's Tech 2 can run a function test sweeping the coil current. No maker publishes C0628 in this sense; GM's PIP5094 list (2014 and older) carries the number with an older meaning.
c: Internal fault in the controlling module or its coil driver stage
Low or unstable supply voltage so the commanded current cannot be reached
Corrupt calibration or software after a module replacement or flash
s: Steering effort no longer changes with speed
Heavy steering when parking or light steering at highway speed
Steering, ABS or stability warning where the brake module hosts the function

C0629.t: Variable Effort Steering Control Module Incorrect Component Installed
C0629.d: C0629 flags a mismatch between what the variable effort steering module expects and what is fitted. Variable-effort gears exist in versions that cannot be swapped blindly: replacement racks come with or without the EVO solenoid, and GM's second Magnasteer generation dropped the permanent magnet and only raises effort with speed, whereas the first one reverses coil current around 45 mph. A Steering Solutions patent shows why this matters: the current's direction decides whether effort goes up or down. A module that detects the wrong part, wrong position or wrong variant blocks its function, much like Mitsubishi's brake unit flags a wheel sensor fitted in the wrong place within 3 s. No maker publishes C0629. It usually follows a gear or module swap.
c: Replacement steering gear of the wrong variant, for example without actuator
Module from another vehicle or not configured for this equipment
Actuator connected with reversed polarity after a repair
s: Variable assist inactive after a steering or module repair
Steering effort behaves the wrong way round, heavy when slow
Steering warning on some vehicles

C062A.t: Variable Effort Steering Module Temperature Too High
C062A.d: The variable effort steering module, or its coil driver, reports a temperature above its permitted limit. Heat matters twice here: a GM patent on magnetic variable effort steering notes that fluid viscosity, magnet properties and coil current all drift with temperature and either fits a sensor in the fluid sump or infers temperature from the current error. A JTEKT patent warns that a continuously energised steering coil can reach about 200 °C and holds it at or below 100 °C by pulsing it. Driver chips set their own limits; TI's DRV8873-Q1 warns at a die temperature of roughly 140–160 °C and shuts down at 165–185 °C. No maker publishes C062A. The function is typically reduced or suspended until things cool down.
c: Very high underhood or fluid temperature, for example after long parking manoeuvres in heat
Partly shorted coil drawing excess current and heating the driver
Faulty internal temperature measurement reporting heat that is not there
s: Variable effort reduced or switched off temporarily
Steering feel changes after hard use and returns after cooling

C062B.t: Variable Effort Steering Module Temperature Too Low
C062B.d: C062B is set when the module or its coil driver reads a temperature below the range it is designed for. Automotive driver chips such as TI's DRV8873-Q1 are specified down to an ambient of −40 °C, so a lower reading means either an extreme cold soak or a measurement that has failed. Cold also changes the steering itself: the GM patent on temperature compensation for magnetic variable effort steering points to thicker fluid and changed electrical and magnetic behaviour, and corrects the coil current with tables tested at different temperatures, either from a fluid temperature sensor or from the current deviation. Outside its table the module cannot compensate and suspends variable effort. No maker publishes C062B. Unlike C062A, warming up usually clears it.
c: Vehicle parked for a long time in severe frost
Open or failed temperature measurement inside the module or at the fluid sensor
Moisture or corrosion at the connector distorting the reading
s: Variable effort inactive after a cold start
Heavy or uneven steering until the system warms up

C062C.d: C062C judges whether the second drive, B, of an electric brake booster moves as commanded; the circuit may be intact. Boosters like Bosch's iBooster turn motor torque through a three-stage gear into force on the master cylinder, and in redundant layouts such as a Hyundai Mobis design a dual-winding motor is fed by two power modules, each able to carry the whole current command alone if the other is declared failed. No maker documents C062C publicly. The yardstick is its twin C0594 for motor A: GM's 2016 hybrid tables flag a motor below 15 rad/s while more than 25 rad/s is requested, more than seven direction changes, or reverse rotation above 40 rad/s, within 0.15 s, Type A. With side B out, assist may still come from side A only.
c: Worn or damaged motor B, for example bearing or winding damage
Fault in the power module or driver stage feeding side B
Binding in gear stage or booster mechanism
Booster control software needing an update
s: Brake system or brake assist warning
Harder pedal or reduced assist in some situations
Driver assistance functions with automatic braking restricted

C062D.d: C062D means the ABS valve group does not work as expected, although no single valve or plain supply fault explains it. Mitsubishi is the one maker that maps it publicly: in the 2023 Outlander PHEV brake unit, valve relay code C1048-92 shows as C062D, set within 2 s with normal supply and the system switched on, with ASC, ABS, brake lamp and MIL after one trip; bulletin 23-35-002 adds C1048-01 to the same number. Stability, traction, ABS, EBD, brake assist, hill start and electric parking brake functions are then suspended. Brake units check valves and relay with test pulses: a Tokico patent tells relay, switch and coil faults apart with a tiny test current, and MOTOR describes key-on pulse tests lasting about 65 ms.
c: Internal fault in the ABS control unit or its valve relay
Weak supply through fuse, fusible link, wiring or 12 V battery
Corroded or loose connector at the hydraulic unit
s: ABS, stability control and brake warning lamps on
Check engine lamp on (Mitsubishi)
ABS, traction control and electric parking brake unavailable

C062E.t: Active Air Dam Supply Voltage Circuit Low
C062E.d: The active air dam actuators run from the vehicle battery while the PCM or body module commands them over LIN or CAN, as Ford's patent lays out. C062E reports that the supply reaching the actuator or its module is too low to move the panel safely. Small LIN motor drivers made for flaps and grille shutters watch this themselves: Melexis' MLX81350 has an undervoltage threshold selectable between about 4 and 9 V. Stellantis shows a related field case on the Ram 1500: lost contact with the air dam plus system-voltage-low codes in several modules, traced to loose grounds G921/G933/G904 and fluid wicking into inline connector XY110A. No maker publishes C062E. The panel stops where it is until supply recovers.
c: Loose or corroded ground point in the front harness
Water or washer fluid wicking into an inline connector
Weak battery or low charging voltage
High resistance in fuse or feed wire to the actuator
s: Air dam no longer moves and stays in its last position
Air dam fault message in the cluster
Low-voltage codes in other modules at the same time

C062F.t: Active Air Dam Supply Voltage Circuit High
C062F.d: C062F is the overvoltage side: the supply at the air dam actuator or its module lies above the permitted window. Ford's patent powers the screw-jack actuators from the vehicle battery, so a regulator fault in the charging system, jump-starting with a higher voltage or a load dump spike can push the feed too high. Driver electronics guard against this: Melexis' MLX81350 LIN motor driver, offered for flaps and grille shutters, trips at about 22, 24 or 40 V depending on setting, and TI's DRV8873-Q1 is rated for at most 38 V. A GM air dam patent checks position, current and back-EMF but takes the supply as given, so the supply code stands apart. No maker publishes C062F. The actuator usually stops until the voltage drops.
c: Charging system overvoltage from a faulty regulator
Jump start or battery charger with excessive voltage
Faulty voltage measurement inside the actuator electronics
s: Air dam stops moving, often together with other overvoltage codes
Air dam fault message in the cluster
Flickering lights or charging warning if the regulator is at fault

C0630.d: C0630 says the air dam panel itself does not move although the actuator is driven and reports sensible values. GM's patent defines exactly this case: if measured position and motor current agree with each other but both differ from the commanded position, or back-EMF shows unusual load, the panel is at fault rather than sensor or drive. Ford's patent lowers the panel above 45 mph for 15 s or above 55 mph and raises it for 4WD, towing or high temperatures, so a stuck panel stays in the wrong place. Field causes are documented around C0604: broken actuator-to-dam bolts on 2021–2025 F-150s (SSM 54705) and impact damage on Ram trucks. No maker publishes C0630; GM's PIP5094 and PIT5307G list the number with an older meaning.
c: Panel bent or jammed after ground contact, debris or a kerb
Broken bolts between actuator and panel
Ice, snow or packed mud blocking the guides
Worn or seized screw jack in the actuator
s: Air dam hangs down or does not deploy
Air dam fault message in the cluster
Scraping on ramps or slightly higher fuel use on the highway

C0631.d: A front axle disconnect separates the front shaft from the driveline when only the rear or primary wheels need to drive, cutting drag; a BorgWarner patent shows a shift fork sliding a splined sleeve, with a cone synchroniser matching speeds first. Ford uses C0631 in the AWD module of 2020–2021 Explorer and Aviator built up to 30 Aug 2021: the powertrain malfunction (wrench) lamp comes on, often with C00A6, and the cause is the disconnect actuator and intermediate shaft. TSB 23-2114, later 23-2174, 25-2373 and 25-2568, swaps them for a redesigned intermediate shaft without disconnect, seals off the four-wire pigtail, fits a new halfshaft and updates the AWD module, at 2.0–7.8 h depending on engine.
c: Failed disconnect actuator or intermediate shaft (Ford Explorer/Aviator 2020–2021)
Loose, corroded or damaged actuator connector
Shift sleeve or synchroniser binding, often from wear or fluid problems
s: Wrench or 4WD/AWD warning lamp on
All-wheel drive not available or front axle does not engage
Possible noise from the front axle area

C0632.d: C0632 concerns the electrical path that drives the front axle disconnect, not the shift itself. The actuator may be electromagnetic or electromechanical; BorgWarner's patent even reads its position from the coil's inductance, which changes between engaged and released. Ford's Explorer and Aviator actuator has a four-wire connector. No maker publishes C0632; Stellantis uses its own codes, and its STAR cases show where such faults sit: on 2019–2021 Ram heavy-duty trucks damaged wires within 6–8 inches of the FAD connector, on Ram 1500 a check of harness and connector before the actuator is replaced, and on the Jeep Wrangler a signal below 1.19 V for 500 ms from moisture in a 34-way connector; the actuator then keeps its position.
c: Chafed or cut wires close to the actuator connector
Water or corrosion in the actuator or inline connector
Spread or pushed-out terminals in the connector
s: 4WD/AWD service message or warning lamp
Front axle does not engage or disengage

C0633.d: On all-wheel-drive systems that can uncouple the front axle, a speed sensor on a front shaft tells the controller how fast the uncoupled part turns, so it can match speeds before re-engaging. A BorgWarner patent uses a Hall sensor on the shift sleeve to read both speed and position and engages once the gap to wheel speed is within about ±100–200 rpm; an American Axle patent uses a pinion speed sensor the same way before moving its shift collar. Ford documents C0633 in the AWD module of 2020 Explorer, Aviator and Police Interceptor Utility 4WD built up to 20 Mar 2020: warning messages with C0633, C00A6:07 or both came from an oil-soaked front halfshaft speed sensor; TSB 21-2270 replaces it (0.8 h).
c: Sensor contaminated with axle oil (Ford Explorer/Aviator 2020)
Failed sensor or damaged wiring and connector
Wrong air gap or damaged sensor target on the shaft
s: AWD or 4WD warning messages in the cluster
All-wheel drive limited or not engaging
Possible oil seepage near the sensor

C0634.d: Two brake pressure sensors that see the same hydraulic pressure should report nearly the same value; C0634 means sensors A and B disagree beyond the allowed margin, even if each signal is valid on its own. Which sensor bears which letter depends on the maker. GM's 2019 brake module tables show the method but file it under C0574: two secondary circuit sensors are compared, with pedal travel as third reference, and a gap above 5 bar for 100 ms sets the fault, Type A with MIL. A Kelsey-Hayes patent places two elements on one diaphragm and disables hydraulic brake assist with a warning lamp when they differ, and a Lucas patent notes that two sensors only show that one is wrong, not which. No maker publishes C0634.
c: One sensor drifting in offset or gain
Fault in the brake control unit with integrated sensors, often replaced as a unit
Air or a blocked passage making the sensors see different pressures
Brake module software or calibration needing an update
s: ABS, stability or brake system warning lamp on
Brake assist or driver assistance functions with automatic braking off

C0635.d: C0635 flags a broken circuit at brake pressure sensor G: a supply, signal or ground wire without continuity, or a plug that has lost contact. No manufacturer publishes C0635 in this meaning, so it is unknown which part carries the letter G. A seventh sensor only exists in large units, for example the Lucas/ZF electro-hydraulic layout with four wheel sensors, one supply sensor and two front push-through sensors. What the module reads after an open depends on its input: per Honeywell, losing feed or ground sends the signal to the top rail if the input is pulled up, to the bottom if it is pulled down. Saab/GM books such an interruption after 0.1 s and switches off ABS and stability control. GM's PIP5094 lists C0635 from an older, unrelated GM numbering.
c: Plug at the sensor or hydraulic unit loose, corroded or with pushed-back terminals
Broken supply, signal or ground wire in the sensor harness
s: ABS and ESC warning lamps on
Stability control and pressure-based brake functions switched off

C0636.t: Brake Pressure Sensor G Circuit High
C0636.d: The voltage of sensor G sits above anything a valid pressure can produce. A Toyota patent shows how a brake gets seven pressure sensors: one for the accumulator, two for the master cylinder chambers and four for the wheel cylinders, all read by the brake ECU. If one of them stops delivering sensible values, that ECU de-energises every valve and motor, and the front wheels are then braked with boosted pedal pressure. Whether Toyota or anyone else calls one of them G is not published. Denso reserves 4.7–5 V as an upper fault band and describes how a missing sensor ground raises the line into that band. GM's 2019 EBCM sets its high codes for brake pressure sensors above 95.24 % of supply for 100 ms. Typical causes: short to 5 V or battery, open ground.
c: Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Open or high-resistance sensor ground lifting the output
Sensor G failed internally and driving its output to the top
s: ABS/ESC warning lamp on
Live data shows high pressure with the pedal released
Brake assist and stability functions unavailable

C0637.t: Brake Pressure Sensor G Circuit Low
C0637.d: C0637 reports that sensor G delivers less voltage than its lowest valid reading. Brake pressure sensors keep a live zero at rest, so a signal near 0 V means a fault rather than zero pressure: Saab's 9-5 ESP flags a pressure signal under 0.25 V lasting 0.1 s, and GM's 2016 hybrid brake module treats under 0.3 V for 0.1 s on its left rear wheel pressure sensor (sensor D there) as a short to ground, Type A. Common causes are a signal wire chafed through to the body, a 5 V reference pulled down, or a failed sensor. Which component G is stays open; in a seven-sensor unit like the Lucas/ZF design it would be one of the wheel, supply or push-through sensors. G usually sits in the hydraulic block, so a sensor defect often means replacing that block.
c: Signal wire chafed and shorted to ground
5 V sensor reference shorted to ground or interrupted
Sensor G defective, often only replaceable with the hydraulic unit
s: ABS and ESC warning lamps on
Live data shows no pressure even when the pedal is pressed

C0638.d: Here sensor G produces a voltage inside its window, but the pressure it reports disagrees with what the system expects. Lucas/ZF describe the classic test for multi-sensor EHB units: after the driver brakes to a stop, the isolation valve stays closed and all wheel valves open, so three or more sensors share one pressure; the odd one out is the faulty sensor, with size and direction of its error. Two sensors alone would only reveal that something is wrong. A Bosch patent learns offsets while driving, flags a fault once the correction grows beyond a threshold and keeps ABS lamp and ESC telltale lit until a later good check. No manufacturer documents C0638; GM's PIP5094 contains the number from an earlier GM scheme. Causes: drift, trapped pressure, a sticking valve.
c: Zero point or gain of sensor G drifted
Pressure trapped in the circuit during the comparison or zero learn
Valve sticking so the sensor does not see the shared test pressure
s: ABS lamp and ESC telltale on
Stability control reduced or off, regenerative braking possibly limited

C0639.d: Brake pressure sensor H has lost its electrical connection: an interrupted 5 V feed, signal or ground line, or a loose plug at the hydraulic unit. No published service data ties C0639 to a real part. Layouts with eight sensors do exist: a Toyota patent places pressure sensors at the pump and accumulator output, ahead of the pressure-increasing valve, in the master cylinder and booster chambers and at all four wheel cylinders. With a pull-down input, Denso shows that a cut supply or signal line ends at 0 V while a cut ground climbs above 4.7 V, so an open may surface as C063B or C063A instead. Kelsey-Hayes plugs its sensor straight into the module board to avoid a harness and watches for an open or shorted bridge; on a failure ABS is disabled and a lamp lit.
c: Sensor plug loose or terminals corroded
Supply, signal or ground conductor broken
Open measuring bridge or failed electronics inside the sensor
s: ABS and ESC lamps on, possibly flickering with vibration
ABS or stability control disabled

C063A.t: Brake Pressure Sensor H Circuit High
C063A.d: The output of pressure sensor H is too high to be real. C063A is not documented by any carmaker. Another Toyota patent shows seven pressure points in one brake: accumulator, two master cylinder passages and four control pressures standing for the wheel cylinders. Which of them a system might label H is not public. An excessive signal usually means the line touches a voltage source or the sensor ground is lost; some sensors also park their output at the top on purpose, as Honeywell's MIP transducers do at 97.5 % of supply after an internal fault or overpressure. Saab's 9-5 ESP sets its pressure sensor code above 4.75 V within 0.1 s and also checks that the sensor supply stays between 4.4 and 5.6 V. Measure ground and feed at the plug before replacing parts.
c: Signal line touching a 5 V or battery feed
Sensor ground open or high resistance
Sensor reports an internal fault or overpressure at its upper rail
s: ABS/ESC warning lamp on, ESC unavailable
Implausibly high brake pressure in live data at rest

C063B.t: Brake Pressure Sensor H Circuit Low
C063B.d: C063B says sensor H reads below its valid floor. Unlike C063C the problem is electrical, not a believable but wrong pressure. A Bosch workshop article on a Teves MK60 unit describes the integrated sensor: fed with 5 V, it stays below 1 V with the brakes off and climbs as pedal pressure builds, so the fault limit has to sit well under that rest level. GM's 2019 EBCM flags its circuit pressure sensor as shorted low when the main channel falls under 4.61 % of supply, or the reference channel under 4.85 %, for 100 ms. Where H sits is not published; in Toyota's eight-sensor design the candidates would be a wheel cylinder, the booster chamber or the pump output. Likely: signal shorted to ground, collapsed 5 V reference or a dead sensor.
c: 5 V reference collapsed by a short in another sensor on the same feed
Sensor H without output due to an internal defect
s: ABS and ESC lamps on
Brake assist and stability control not available

C063C.d: Sensor H gives an electrically valid yet implausible pressure. In Toyota's eight-sensor patent the check connects a pressure source to a brake cylinder: both readings should then nearly match, and a gap beyond a threshold means one of the two sensors, the passage or the cylinder is at fault; the switch-over is preferably made at standstill. Ford's hybrid brake, which has only two pressure sensors, shows typical limits: a P1 offset outside ±16 bar, or both sensors more than 50 bar apart for 100 ms. That Ford needs no letters beyond A and B also shows that H exists only in larger systems. No maker documents C063C. FMVSS 126 requires a telltale for ESC malfunctions, so the driver gets a warning lamp that goes out only after the fault has gone.
c: Offset or gain of sensor H drifted out of tolerance
Restricted passage or faulty brake cylinder so pressures really differ
Air in the brake fluid distorting the pressure build-up
s: ESC malfunction telltale and ABS lamp on
Changed pedal feel or reduced brake assistance

C063D.d: A wire or contact of brake pressure sensor J is interrupted. No manufacturer ties C063D to a specific sensor. Continental's one-box brake patent names sensors for the master cylinder and for the pressure supply unit and mentions optional further ones for brake circuits or wheel brake circuits, so a J sensor could be among those. Bosch Motorsport's EBS illustrates per-channel fault flags: internal axle pressure, internal master cylinder pressure and the external caliper and master cylinder sensors each have their own bit. GM's 2019 EBCM does not separate an open from a short to voltage at all; both end up as open or shorted high above 95.24 % of supply. So check plug, terminals and harness first, even if the stored code says high instead of open.
c: Spread or corroded terminal in the sensor connector
Conductor interrupted between sensor and control unit
s: Brake system or ESC warning lamp on
Pressure-controlled brake functions switched off

C063E.t: Brake Pressure Sensor J Circuit High
C063E.d: C063E: sensor J sends more voltage than its range allows. GM's 2016 hybrid brake controller shows the method on a wheel pressure sensor: if the signal line exceeds 3.3 V and so no longer differs from the supply, a short to supply is stored after 0.1 s with the ignition on, rated Type A. Denso's patent explains the second route: with a pull-down at the input, an open sensor ground forms a divider that pushes the line beyond 4.7 V. No public source says which part is sensor J; brake-by-wire units such as Bosch Motorsport's EBS already measure axle, driver, caliper and master cylinder pressure separately. A falsely high value would look like braking that is not happening, so the module discards the signal and limits its functions.
c: Signal line shorted to the sensor supply
Sensor ground interrupted, output lifted through the input divider
Sensor J electronics failed with output stuck high
s: Brake or ESC warning lamp on
Live data shows brake pressure although no one is braking

C063F.t: Brake Pressure Sensor J Circuit Low
C063F.d: The signal of brake pressure sensor J is stuck below its lower limit. Ipgate's double-stroke-piston patent fits one pressure sensor to each brake circuit and checks the delivered fluid volume against the pressure-volume curve of that circuit; such a circuit sensor is one possible J position, though no manufacturer confirms the letter. Denso defines 0–0.3 V as the low fault band and notes that a broken feed or signal line also lands there when the input has a pull-down. Saab/GM detects a ground short or open on the signal or 5 V reference after 0.1 s and then turns off ABS, traction and stability control for the rest of the ignition cycle. Usual suspects: a chafed signal wire, a shorted reference, a failed sensor element.
c: Broken feed or signal wire pulled to 0 V by the module input
Failed sensing element in sensor J
s: ABS, traction and stability warning lamps on
ABS and ESC inoperative until the next ignition cycle

C0640.d: C0640 marks sensor J as valid in voltage but wrong in content. In plunger-based brakes the pressure can be cross-checked against what the actuator did: Ipgate compares delivered piston volume with the pressure-volume curve and closes the inlet valves one by one to find a leaking circuit, while Continental's one-box layout carries separate sensors for master cylinder and pressure supply that can be set against each other. GM's 2016 hybrid module re-zeroes its wheel pressure sensor only while the pedal is released and reports a correction larger than ±1,500 kPa. A circuit leak, air or a seized valve can therefore set C0640 as well as a drifting sensor. No maker documents this code publicly; PIP5094 lists C0640 under GM's old numbering.
c: Sensor J drifting so its zero correction exceeds the limit
Leak or air in the brake circuit so pressure and delivered volume disagree
s: Brake warning and ESC lamps on
Longer pedal travel or reduced brake boost in fallback mode

C0641.d: Brake pressure sensor K has an open circuit. Because the letter I is skipped in this series, K stands for a tenth pressure sensor, which is rare in cars; no carmaker publishes C0641 and the assignment is unknown. Heavy vehicles show how many pressure inputs one brake ECU can have: Bendix's EC-80 ESP reads a brake demand sensor in each of the two air circuits plus a load sensor and keeps a separate open-or-shorted code for each; ESP is then switched off while ABS and traction control stay active. In passenger cars the sensor often plugs straight into the module, as in a Kelsey-Hayes design, which removes harness opens but not contact faults. Honeywell notes that the resulting level after an open depends on whether the input has a pull-up or a pull-down resistor.
c: Poor contact between sensor and module or harness connector
Open conductor where an external harness is used
s: ESC or ABS warning lamp on
Stability control off, basic ABS may remain available

C0642.t: Brake Pressure Sensor K Circuit High
C0642.d: C0642 means the output of sensor K exceeds its upper limit. Electro-hydraulic brakes like Mercedes' Sensotronic Brake Control work with a high-pressure accumulator and a pedal value sensor with two Hall elements; during a pre-drive check the unit pressurises the calipers to test, among other things, its pressure sensors. A high fault on any such sensor would make the module believe the brakes are applied. Saab's 9-5 sets its sensor code above 4.75 V for 0.1 s; GM's 2019 EBCM uses 95.24 % of supply on the main channel and 94.50 % on the reference channel. No maker says which sensor would be K, so the letter cannot be linked to a location. Typical: short to 5 V or battery, lost sensor ground, internal fault.
c: Signal shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Internal fault of sensor K signalled at the upper rail
s: Brake system and ESC warning lamps on
Brake lights or hold functions may be requested wrongly on some systems

C0643.t: Brake Pressure Sensor K Circuit Low
C0643.d: Sensor K reports less voltage than any valid pressure would give. Bendix's truck ESP treats brake demand and load sensors individually and, if one of them fails, disables only ESP while ABS and traction control carry on; this graded reaction shows why the code may leave basic ABS working. GM's 2016 hybrid module compares the wheel pressure signal with ground and sets its low code under 0.3 V within 0.1 s. Denso points out that a broken supply wire reads exactly like this when the module pulls its input down, so a low code does not rule out an open. Which sensor K would be is not published by any carmaker. GM's PIP5094 keyword list contains C0643 from its old numbering, unrelated to this sensor.
c: Broken sensor supply read as 0 V through the input pull-down
s: ESC lamp on, ESC switched off
ABS and traction control may keep working

C0644.d: The voltage from sensor K is in range, yet the pressure is not believable. Bendix's EC-80 stores a plausibility error when the primary and secondary brake demand sensors disagree and asks for a static calibration after an ECU swap. Mercedes' SBC repeats self-tests about every 16 brake applications, pressurising the calipers to check sensors, valves and leaks; if the system fails, two valves stay open so pedal force acts on the brakes directly. A Bosch patent keeps an offset fault stored, with ABS and ESC lamps lit, until a later good check on a roughly straight drive passes. No manufacturer documents C0644 or says which sensor K is. Look for drift, air, a leak or a valve that does not close.
c: Sensor K offset or gain drifted
Sensor values not re-learned after module replacement
Leak, air or a valve that does not seal distorting the pressure
s: ABS and ESC lamps on until a later successful check
Stability control reduced, pedal may feel different in fallback mode

C0645.d: C0645 reports lost continuity in the circuit of brake pressure sensor L, the eleventh letter of the series because I is not used. That is far beyond a normal car: a Bosch patent names one, three or five sensors as the usual ESP layouts and calls five the current maximum. No carmaker publishes which sensor would carry the L. Where it does exist, the sensor is often clinched straight into the valve block, and Continental and Bosch both describe its four contacts (supply, ground, two signal pads) touching spring contacts on the module board instead of a harness. An open is then frequently a bent spring, a corroded pad or a crack inside the unit, not a broken wire. Expect the ESC and ABS lamps; ordinary braking is kept.
c: Spring contact between sensor and module board bent, dirty or corroded
Plug or harness of an externally mounted sensor without continuity
s: ESC and ABS warning lamps on
Pressure-based functions such as brake assist or hill hold unavailable

C0646.t: Brake Pressure Sensor L Circuit High
C0646.d: C0646 means the signal of brake pressure sensor L lies above the band a real pressure can produce. A Kelsey-Hayes patent spells out the logic for a bridge-type brake sensor: a healthy output stays between zero and the supply voltage, so a reading equal to supply points to an open circuit, not to maximum pressure. A high code can therefore hide a lost ground or a broken signal line as well as a short to 5 V. Truck trailer brakes show where extra analog pressure sensors appear: WABCO's Trailer EBS D feeds an optional external brake pressure sensor from the modulator and reads it on a 0–5 V analog input. No carmaker documents C0646 or names its sensor L. Because a phantom pressure would suggest an application that is not taking place, the module stops trusting the channel.
c: Sensor ground open, so the signal floats up to supply level
Signal line shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Sensor electronics driving the output to its upper limit
s: ABS/ESC warning lamp on
Stability control or electronic brake pressure control switched off

C0647.t: Brake Pressure Sensor L Circuit Low
C0647.d: Sensor L reads below its lowest valid value. In the Kelsey-Hayes scheme a near-zero bridge output is read as a probable short, because the sensor never reaches 0 V with a working circuit. Where the fault lies depends on the architecture: in a Continental Teves design the sensor in the hydraulic unit is only a bare Wheatstone bridge, and amplifier, offset correction and digitising sit in an IC on the control module, so a low reading can start on the board just as well as in the sensor. That patent also loads the factory calibration of each sensor, tied to its serial number, into the module. Typical causes: signal shorted to ground, collapsed sensor supply, damaged bridge. Which part a system calls L is not public; C0647 has no documented carmaker.
c: Sensor supply missing or pulled down
Amplifier or input stage in the brake control module defective
s: ABS/ESC warning lamp on
Brake assist and stability control unavailable

C0648.d: Sensor L delivers an electrically valid signal whose pressure does not fit the situation. Commercial vehicle EBS shows how such a check works with many sensors: WABCO's tractor EBS has pressure sensors in the front axle relay valve, in each channel of the rear axle modulator and in the trailer control valve. During normal braking the left and right rear pressures must almost match, and a deviation beyond the permitted value is stored as a fault. Each sensor carries individual calibration data; in Continental's process they are matched to its serial number and stored in the module, so a mismatch after a repair could also appear as an offset. No carmaker documents C0648 or the letter L. Look for drift, trapped pressure, a sticking valve or a leak.
c: Sticking valve, leak or trapped pressure in the measured circuit
Calibration data not matching the fitted sensor after a repair
s: ABS/ESC warning lamp on, sometimes only after several brake applications
Uneven or reduced electronic brake force distribution

C0649.d: The circuit of brake pressure sensor M, the twelfth in the series, has no continuity. Where so many pressure inputs exist, they are often not reachable from outside: WABCO notes that the two rear axle pressure sensors of its truck EBS are wired inside the axle modulator, so the cabling cannot be tested from outside and a fault means work on the modulator. Passenger-car units behave similarly; Actronics points out that the ATE MK60 carries its brake pressure sensor inside the unit, while some VW models use separate sensors near the master cylinder. External sensors, as on WABCO's trailer brake, take their supply from the modulator through a plug. No carmaker assigns C0649 or the letter M. Check plug and terminals first, then the unit.
c: Loose or corroded plug at an external sensor or at the modulator
Open in the internal wiring of the modulator or hydraulic unit
Broken wire in the sensor harness
s: Brake or ABS warning lamp on
Electronic pressure control replaced by a fallback mode

C064A.t: Brake Pressure Sensor M Circuit High
C064A.d: C064A: the voltage from sensor M exceeds what any valid pressure would give. On WABCO's Trailer EBS D the brake pressure sensor of an extra EBS relay valve, for example on a drawbar trailer's front axle, draws its supply from the trailer modulator and returns its actual value as an analog signal; all active sensors share supply outputs that are protected against short circuits. A short from that supply to the signal pin therefore drives the reading to the top. Kelsey-Hayes adds the opposite path: an open circuit lets a bridge output rise to supply level, so a high code does not exclude a broken wire. No passenger-car maker documents C064A. With the channel discarded, the system falls back to reduced functions.
c: Signal pin shorted to the sensor supply or battery voltage
Open sensor ground or signal line letting the input float high
Sensor output stuck at its upper limit
s: Brake or ABS warning lamp on
Load-dependent or electronic pressure control disabled

C064B.t: Brake Pressure Sensor M Circuit Low
C064B.d: Sensor M sits below its lower signal limit. Because modules often supply several pressure sensors together, a single low code can be the visible part of a wider fault: WABCO's trailer modulator powers all active sensors jointly, so a short on one sensor supply can pull others down too, and codes for neighbouring letters may then appear at the same time. In an ESP block, Bosch describes each sensor with four contacts, two for supply and two for the analog pressure signal, which makes a shorted or contaminated spring contact a plausible cause. GM's 2019 brake module flags its secondary circuit pressure sensor low under 4.61 % of supply for 100 ms; no maker publishes C064B itself. Check the shared supply before replacing sensor M.
c: Shared sensor supply shorted, pulling several sensors low
Signal line or contact of sensor M shorted to ground
s: Warning lamp on, possibly with further pressure sensor codes
Electronic brake functions reduced to a fallback mode

C064C.d: Sensor M stays inside its electrical window, but the pressure it reports is not believable. Trailer EBS shows an active test: when the control pressure exceeds 0.3 bar, WABCO's modulator switches its redundancy valve to reservoir pressure and starts EBS braking; during the stop it briefly switches back and uses its internal actual-pressure sensors to confirm that pneumatic pressure is present, otherwise it changes to purely pneumatic braking. Kelsey-Hayes lists in-range checks for hydraulic sensors: high pressure lasting unusually long, or high pressure while the brakes are not applied. No carmaker documents C064C or says which sensor is M. Possible causes: drift, a sticking valve, a leak, contamination in the sensor port.
c: Sensor reading drifted from the true pressure
Valve in the measured circuit not switching as commanded
Contamination or air at the sensor port
s: Warning lamp on after a brake application
Braking switched to a backup mode with less precise pressure control

C064D.d: C064D concerns an interrupted circuit at brake pressure sensor N, the thirteenth of the series. Larger sensor counts push makers towards digital links. A Bosch patent proposes PSI5 or DSI current interfaces on which up to four pressure sensors share two wires for power and data; an open in such a pair would silence every sensor on it at once. SENT sensors, which Pico Technology shows with two pressure channels in one housing, can likewise lose two readings through one broken line. Continental's integrated module groups several sensors under one combined plug with the pump motor. Hence: if several pressure codes appear together, look for the common line or plug. No carmaker publishes C064D or assigns the letter N.
c: Open in a line or plug shared by several sensors
Poor contact at the sensor plug or spring contact
s: ABS/ESC warning lamp on, often with other pressure sensor codes
Stability control and brake assist unavailable

C064E.t: Brake Pressure Sensor N Circuit High
C064E.d: The signal of sensor N is above its permitted maximum. What the brake does next is described well for truck EBS: WABCO checks every analog pressure sensor signal against its authorised values; if one is lost, the module may keep producing electrical brake pressure by auxiliary means with limited accuracy, and if electronic control is impossible the axle falls back on purely pneumatic backup braking. For digital sensors the equivalent of a high reading is often a value pinned at full scale or a fault flag; Pico Technology notes that SENT frames carry a status nibble with diagnostic information and a CRC the receiver checks. C064E has no documented user, and nobody publishes which sensor N would be. Likely: short to supply, lost ground, failed sensor.
c: Signal shorted to sensor supply or battery voltage
Sensor electronics reporting full scale or an internal fault
s: Brake or ESC warning lamp on
Less precise brake pressure control or pure backup braking

C064F.t: Brake Pressure Sensor N Circuit Low
C064F.d: C064F: sensor N reports less than its smallest valid signal. In integrated units the sensor element and its evaluation are split: Continental Teves fits a bare measuring bridge into the hydraulic block and leaves amplification and offset to an IC in the module, while Actronics, which repairs such units, names the ATE MK60 with its internal pressure sensor as the system with the most pressure sensor problems and recommends repair or replacement of the unit rather than of a single sensor. A low reading can thus come from the sensor, the contacts or the module input. GM's 2016 hybrid brake module, for comparison, sets the low code of its left rear wheel pressure sensor below 0.3 V within 0.1 s. Nobody documents C064F or the letter N.
c: Internal pressure sensor of the hydraulic unit failed
Signal contact or line shorted to ground
Evaluation IC in the control module defective
s: ABS/ESC warning lamp on
Stability control unavailable

C0650.d: Sensor N reports a pressure that is electrically valid but disagrees with the commanded or expected value. WABCO's truck EBS runs a matching test: with a defined magnetic flux in the proportional valve a minimum brake pressure must build up at the front axle brakes, or at the valve that controls the trailer, and when the vehicle brakes via pneumatic backup the rear axle must reach a set minimum once the front exceeds a threshold. A Kelsey-Hayes patent avoids a second complete sensor by putting two sensing elements on one diaphragm and flagging a fault when their readings differ beyond a threshold. Neither source uses the code; C0650 and the letter N are not assigned publicly. Causes: drift, valve faults, leaks, air.
c: Valve or modulator not building the commanded pressure
Leak or air in the measured circuit
s: Warning lamp on after braking
Pressure control falls back to an emergency mode

C0651.t: Left Front Wheel Speed Sensor B Circuit/Open
C0651.d: C0651 reports an open circuit at the second speed sensor of the left front wheel. Sensor B exists only where a wheel carries two independent speed signals, mainly in redundant brake systems for automated driving. Continental describes two layouts: two separate sensors per wheel, each wired to its own brake control unit, or one housing with two sensing elements, each with its own two-wire cable that can run to a different controller. On such two-wire sensors the signal rides on the supply current, and Allegro notes that the module can spot opens and shorts simply from the current drawn. No carmaker publishes C0651. Sensor A (C0500) usually keeps ABS working, but the redundancy is lost.
c: Broken wire in the sensor B cable near the wheel
Plug of the second channel loose or corroded
Second sensing element inside the sensor failed open
s: Warning for brake or driver assistance system
Automated driving or redundant brake functions unavailable

C0652.t: Left Front Wheel Speed Sensor B Range/Performance
C0652.d: The second left front wheel speed signal is present but implausible. With two channels per wheel the module has a direct partner to compare: Volvo Truck's patent for a dual-element sensor merges both signals with an integrity index, averages them while they agree within a band, takes the higher value when both run but differ, and drops a channel that reads zero. Bosch's patent for shared wheel sensors lists the usual checks, among them air gap, pulse width and speed plausibility. For single sensors, Toyota, as described by FenderBender, judges plausibility from about 10 km/h forward and flags an 8 km/h gap to vehicle speed; how B is judged is not published. Causes: worn encoder, excessive air gap, wrong part.
c: Air gap too large from bearing play or a sensor not seated fully
Sensor variant not matching the vehicle
s: Driver assistance or redundant braking warning
Automated functions withdrawn while ABS on sensor A continues

C0653.t: Left Front Wheel Speed Sensor B Circuit Low
C0653.d: C0653 means the circuit of left front sensor B sits below its valid level. Active wheel speed sensors usually signal through current steps; Allegro gives 7 and 14 mA as typical levels and a safe state below about 3.9 mA that a sensor uses to report its own fault. A reading under the lower band can therefore come from a shorted or chafed line, a supply that has dropped, or the sensor itself flagging an error. In Bosch's shared-sensor design each ECU feeds its sensors and checks supply voltage and the lines for shorts and opens. Bosch also offers a redundant-signal version of its wheel speed sensor, so the second channel is always ready for the backup actuator. No carmaker documents C0653.
c: Sensor B line chafed through and shorted to ground
Supply from the secondary control unit too low
Sensor in its fault (safe) state after an internal error
s: Warning for brake or driver assistance system
Redundant braking or automated driving not available

C0654.t: Left Front Wheel Speed Sensor B Circuit High
C0654.d: Here the circuit of the second left front sensor reads above its permitted level, typically a short to the battery feed or to the supply of another channel. That risk follows from the packaging: Continental's dual-element sensor gives each element its own two-wire cable but allows both to share one outer sheath, so a crushed or heat-damaged cable can affect both channels. Volvo Truck lets both brake ECUs supply the sensor through a power multiplexer that switches over when one ECU fails. Aumovio, Continental's former automotive arm, markets the dual sensor with two electrically isolated signals under ISO 26262, so the second channel must stay separate. No carmaker publishes C0654; repair the cable or replace the sensor.
c: Sensor B line shorted to battery voltage
Short between the two channels in a shared cable sheath
Internal fault in the second sensing channel
s: Warning for brake or driver assistance system
Possibly both speed signals of the wheel affected

C0655.t: Left Front Wheel Speed Sensor B Intermittent/Erratic
C0655.d: C0655 points to a second left front speed signal that drops out or jumps. Active sensors read the wheel through closely spaced sensing elements whose phase-shifted signals also give the rotation direction, as FenderBender explains, so small mechanical faults show up as irregular pulses. HELLA lists the usual reasons a wheel sensor fails: broken wiring, internal shorts, heavy dirt, extra wheel bearing play and a damaged encoder. Volvo Truck's dual-element design discards a channel that reads zero and carries on with the other. Bosch stresses that the redundant signal must be permanently available to avoid delays when the backup actuator takes over. GM's PIP5094 lists C0655 only as an unrelated old GM number.
c: Loose contact or partly broken wire that moves with the steering and suspension
Dirt or damage on the magnetic encoder
Excessive wheel bearing play changing the air gap
s: Warning that comes and goes, often on rough roads or while steering
Automated or redundant brake functions intermittently withdrawn

C0656.t: Left Front Wheel Speed Sensor B Correlation
C0656.d: C0656 flags a mismatch between the B signal at the left front hub and the values it is checked against, typically sensor A on the same hub, while the circuit itself tests good. No carmaker publishes this code or its limits. Two patent designs show what such a comparison can catch. Continental Teves placed two magnetoresistive paths of different sensitivity in one housing; a comparator inside the sensor checks whether both deliver the same frequency, because a disturbed path can flip and even double the reading. Audi proposed pairing an active Hall sensor with a passive inductive one on the same pulse wheel, so that a supply failure cannot silence both. Likely causes: a damaged encoder, a sensor sitting too far from its encoder, mixed-up parts.
c: Sensor not seated correctly, air gap out of tolerance
Damaged, dirty or partly demagnetized encoder ring
Sensor of a different type or side fitted
s: Warning for brake or driver assistance system
Automated or redundant brake functions withdrawn, ABS usually still active

C0657.t: Left Front Wheel Speed Sensor B Incorrect Component Installed
C0657.d: Here the module receives something on the second left front speed channel but decides that the fitted sensor is not the type it expects. No carmaker documents C0657, so the exact detection rule is unknown. A mix-up is easy: Continental designed its dual-element sensor to fit the same mounting position as a conventional single-element sensor, so an ordinary part bolts in without complaint and the second channel is missing or delivers the wrong signal. Allegro's A19350 shows how interchangeable modern chips are: thanks to flexible orientation it can stand in for xMR or Hall sensors, and it uses a pulse-width protocol carrying speed, direction and safety data that the controller must be set up for. GM's old keyword list PIP5094 contains C0657 only as an unrelated earlier number.
c: Conventional single-channel sensor fitted instead of the dual-channel part
Sensor variant with other protocol or for the other side
Brake module not configured or coded for the fitted sensor
s: Warning appears soon after a sensor or hub replacement
Redundant braking or automated driving functions not available

C0658.t: Right Front Wheel Speed Sensor B Circuit/Open
C0658.d: C0658 reports an open in the wiring of right front sensor B, so the module sees no supply current on that channel. Sensor B is the redundant partner found mainly in brake systems built for automated driving; ABS normally keeps running on sensor A, where an open would show as C0506. Audi's patent for such a pair gives each sensor its own data line to the controller, so that one broken line cannot remove both signals, and suggests a passive inductive sensor as the second one because it works without any supply. For the anti-lock function itself, UN Regulation 13-H demands that every electrical fault, external wiring included, lights the yellow warning. Check plug, cable and sensor. No carmaker publishes C0658; GM's old PIP5094 list uses the number for something else.
c: Broken or torn sensor cable, often near the steering knuckle
Connector not latched, corroded or with spread terminals
s: Warning for brake or driver assistance system
Redundant braking or automated driving not available

C0659.t: Right Front Wheel Speed Sensor B Range/Performance
C0659.d: The second right front speed signal arrives, but its quality or value does not fit. For sensors using the VDA AK protocol, Infineon's TLE5046SiC shows what a module can read besides speed: a 3-bit air gap gauge and, in one variant, a reserve bit that is set once the magnetic signal drops below twice the value at the limit air gap. A weakening signal thus becomes visible before pulses are lost. UN Regulation 13-H requires ABS sensor anomalies that cannot be seen at standstill to be detected by 10 km/h, or by 15 km/h where a wheel that is not turning could cause a false alarm; how quickly a B channel gets rated remains unpublished, and no carmaker documents C0659. Likely causes: too large an air gap from bearing play or a loose holder, a dirty or damaged encoder, a wrong sensor.
c: Air gap too large from wheel bearing play or a loose sensor holder
