Encoder ring dirty, cracked or weakened
s: Warning for brake or driver assistance system, often only while driving
Automated functions withdrawn while ABS on sensor A continues

C065A.t: Right Front Wheel Speed Sensor B Circuit Low
C065A.d: C065A means the current in the circuit of right front sensor B stays below its lowest valid level. TI's TPIC7218-Q1, an interface chip that powers and reads four wheel speed sensors, rates a current under about 4.5 mA as undercurrent and labels it a possible short to ground. A low reading can also come from the sensor itself: Infineon's TLE5046SiC drops to a constant error current of at most 3.8 mA when it detects an internal fault, and falls back to that level too when its supply sinks below 3.5 V. So the supply voltage at the plug is the first thing to measure. Normal levels for such sensors are 7 and 14 mA, plus 28 mA for the speed pulse in the AK protocol. No carmaker publishes C065A; the left front counterpart is C0653.
c: Signal line chafed through and touching ground
Supply at the sensor too low, e.g. from contact resistance
Sensor reports an internal fault with its error current
s: Warning for brake or driver assistance system right after switching on
Redundant braking or automated driving not available

C065B.t: Right Front Wheel Speed Sensor B Circuit High
C065B.d: In C065B the line of sensor B at the right front shows a level above its allowed window, which mostly means a short to the supply. TI's TPIC7218-Q1 sets this limit by sensor type: for active two-level sensors any current over 20 mA counts as overcurrent, for three-level VDA sensors only above 40 mA, in both cases marked as a possible short to battery. A separate flag reports a short to battery while the channel is switched off, and the supply switch caps current at 50 to 150 mA when the line is shorted to ground. Infineon's TLE5046SiC explains the wide band: its speed pulse alone may draw up to about 32 mA. Inspect the harness near hot or moving parts and for contact with another channel, then test the sensor. No carmaker documents C065B.
c: Signal line shorted to battery voltage
Contact with the supply of another sensor channel in a shared cable
Sensor draws excessive current due to internal damage
s: Warning for brake or driver assistance system
Channel switched off by the module, redundant functions unavailable

C065C.t: Right Front Wheel Speed Sensor B Intermittent/Erratic
C065C.d: C065C describes a second right front speed signal that vanishes now and then or carries irregular pulses. With AK protocol sensors, Pico's oscilloscope guide shows that the sensor keeps sending a data packet roughly every 147 ms even while the wheel stands still, so a break in that rhythm exposes a loose contact without the car moving. Pico also notes that some data bits are assigned by the sensor or vehicle maker, and that filtering helps to separate noise from real pulses when measuring. Inside Infineon's TLE5046SiC one safety check fires when more than two consecutive pulses appear on the speed path without a matching event on the direction path, or the reverse, and an EMC feature rides through short supply interruptions. No carmaker documents C065C.
c: Loose contact in plug or cable, often where the cable flexes with steering
Encoder ring with dirt, metal chips or cracks
Interference from nearby high-current lines or damaged shielding
s: Warning that comes and goes, e.g. on rough roads or while steering
Automated or redundant brake functions intermittently withdrawn

C065D.t: Right Front Wheel Speed Sensor B Correlation
C065D.d: C065D says the second right front speed value disagrees with its comparison partners although no circuit fault is found. What it is compared with depends on the architecture. A Knorr-Bremse patent for commercial vehicles lets a separate redundancy system read part of the wheel speeds, for instance one wheel per axle, and exchanges all values over CAN, which makes a second sensor at every wheel unnecessary; there a mismatch can also stem from the data link between two control units. Continental's sensor with two elements can either switch to the healthy element or average both, which first requires deciding whether they agree. For automated driving, Bosch Engineering adds a redundant brake unit to its integrated power brake. No carmaker publishes C065D or its tolerance.
c: Sensor B badly seated or air gap differing from sensor A
Encoder track damaged where only one element reads it
Disturbed data exchange between the brake control units
s: Warning for brake or driver assistance system after a drive
Automated driving functions refused, ABS usually unaffected

C065E.t: Right Front Wheel Speed Sensor B Incorrect Component Installed
C065E.d: C065E means the module rejects the part fitted as the second speed sensor on the right front hub. Wheel speed sensors differ in their output scheme, and the receiving electronics are set up for one of them: TI's TPIC7218-Q1 is configured per sensor type, using two current thresholds for active sensors and four for VDA sensors that add 9 data bits. Allegro's A81415, a power management chip for electromechanical brakes, decodes two-level, PWM and three-level AK sensors, high-resolution versions included. Even within one family, Infineon sells the TLE5046SiC as an LR and an ERR variant in which bit 0 means air gap reserve in one case and an error flag in the other. Compare part numbers before suspecting the wiring; no carmaker documents C065E.
c: Replacement sensor with a different output protocol or variant
Single-channel sensor fitted where a dual-channel part belongs
Brake module not configured or coded for the fitted sensor
s: Warning appears soon after a sensor or hub replacement
Redundant braking or automated driving functions not available

C065F.t: Left Rear Wheel Speed Sensor B Circuit/Open
C065F.d: C065F reports that the second speed channel at the left rear wheel has no closed circuit. No carmaker publishes this code and no service bulletin mentions it, so the exact test is unknown. With active sensors an open is easy to recognise: NXP's KMI25 draws a constant base current of about 7 mA through the same two wires that carry its speed pulses, so a broken lead or a loose plug leaves the module with no current at all. A Motor magazine test on Honda sensors found 10 to 11 V supplied by the ABS unit and stressed that the sensor goes silent once that feed is lost, which is why the supply is checked before the sensor is condemned. As long as sensor A still works, ABS normally carries on; functions that need the second signal are withdrawn.
c: Broken lead or loose, corroded plug between sensor and module
Supply output for channel B in the brake module not switched on
s: Warning for brake or driver assistance system right after switching on
Functions relying on the second rear left signal not available

C0660.t: Left Rear Wheel Speed Sensor B Range/Performance
C0660.d: C0660 means the wiring of sensor B at the left rear tests good, yet its output fails to act like a wheel speed: it may vanish at speed, jump or show an odd pulse pattern. No published service data defines the check. Mounting is a common reason. NXP's application note for magnetoresistive speed sensors explains that a sensor placed off-centre to its target delivers a weaker signal with extra offset, which shows up as a duty cycle well away from 50 %, while a tilt below about 4° hardly matters. The KMI25 even reports the problem itself: one bit of its AK protocol is set when the magnetic field becomes too weak for normal operation. GM's keyword list PIP5094 contains C0660 only as an older GM number with a different meaning.
c: Sensor seated off-centre or too far from its encoder
Encoder ring worn, dirty or weakly magnetised
s: Warning only appears while driving, often above a certain speed
Assistance functions withdrawn while ABS on sensor A continues

C0661.t: Left Rear Wheel Speed Sensor B Circuit Low
C0661.d: With C0661 the second left rear speed signal sits below the lowest level an intact sensor ever outputs, typically because the signal lead touches ground or the sensor feed has collapsed. No carmaker documents this code. What normal looks like is shown by a Motor magazine measurement on Honda sensors: a healthy unit switches cleanly between about 0.70 V and 1.40 V with a 50 % duty cycle, and a pickup magnet held against the sensor tip makes it switch. A level that stays below the lower band therefore points to wiring rather than to the encoder. Rear wheel speeds matter beyond ABS: in an HL Mando design the electric parking brake on the rear wheels uses them to calculate slip and backs off before a wheel locks during an emergency stop.
c: Signal lead chafed through and touching ground
Sensor supply pulled down, e.g. by water in the plug
s: Warning for brake or stability system shortly after start
Emergency braking support of the electric parking brake may be restricted

C0662.t: Left Rear Wheel Speed Sensor B Circuit High
C0662.d: C0662 is stored when the second left rear speed channel reads above anything the sensor itself can deliver. NXP's KMI25 uses three current steps: about 7 mA at rest, 14 mA for a logic one of its data protocol and 28 mA for each speed pulse. A higher value can only come from outside the sensor, such as contact with battery voltage, a chafed wire touching another feed or moisture bridging the plug. Motor magazine measured 10 to 11 V on the supply wire of Honda sensors; a signal lead that has worn through against that wire will climb towards the same voltage. No carmaker documents C0662 publicly. It also appears in GM's keyword list PIP5094, but only as a former GM code with an unrelated meaning.
c: Signal lead shorted to battery voltage or to the sensor feed
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the connector
Sensor B drawing excessive current internally
s: Warning lamp for ABS or stability control
Module switches channel B off, redundant functions unavailable

C0663.t: Left Rear Wheel Speed Sensor B Intermittent/Erratic
C0663.d: Here the second left rear speed signal drops out for moments or jumps, without a lasting circuit fault. No public service data describes the code, so diagnosis has to follow the sensor principle. NXP's application note on magnetoresistive speed sensors warns that outside magnetic fields add to the measuring field: motors, relays and even wires carrying large currents close by can shift the signal far enough to lose pulses, and very strong fields can permanently change the magnet built into the sensor. On many cars the encoder is a magnetised ring in the wheel bearing seal; NTN-SNR points out that a magnetic screwdriver can erase its poles, which leaves gaps in the pulse train. C0663 also appears in GM's PIP5094 list, but only as an old, unrelated GM number.
c: Loose contact in plug or harness that opens on bumps
Encoder ring partly demagnetised or damaged
Interference from nearby motors or high-current cables
s: Warning comes and goes, often on rough roads
Brief, unexpected stability or ABS interventions

C0664.t: Left Rear Wheel Speed Sensor B Correlation
C0664.d: C0664 flags that the second left rear speed value disagrees with its reference speeds, although its circuit is sound. No carmaker publishes the comparison. Two patents show how a rear wheel can be cross-checked. Bosch uses the left rear wheel as its example of a failed or omitted sensor: the module estimates that wheel from the other three, for instance as the front average or as front left plus front right minus rear right, and checks the result against the gearbox output speed. A fault counts only when the deviation stays above a threshold for a set time. Ford relies on the differential: the mean of both rear wheels follows from the output shaft speed and the final drive ratio. A sensor that disagrees with such references gets flagged even though it still sends pulses.
c: Damaged or wrong encoder ring giving a false pulse count
Tyre of different size or heavily worn on the left rear
Sensor B losing pulses at high speed
s: Warning set after a longer drive, not at start
Automated or redundant brake functions refused

C0665.t: Left Rear Wheel Speed Sensor B Incorrect Component Installed
C0665.d: C0665 says the part on the second left rear speed channel is not the one the module expects. No carmaker documents the code or how it identifies the part. Typical mix-ups arise at the wheel bearing. Motor magazine describes bearings whose magnetic encoder ring sits on the inboard face: pressed in the wrong way round, nothing passes the sensor and speed codes appear right after the repair, while the reversed bearing is usually ruined. On the sensor side, NXP sells the KMI25 in two variants, one for magnetised multipole rings and one for steel gear wheels, so a sensor matched to the other encoder type will not work properly. GM's PIP5094 lists C0665 merely as an earlier GM number with another meaning.
c: Wheel bearing fitted with the encoder facing away from the sensor
Sensor made for a different encoder type or vehicle
Replacement hub without encoder ring fitted
s: Warning appears right after a bearing, hub or sensor replacement
Redundant brake functions not available

C0666.t: Right Rear Wheel Speed Sensor B Circuit/Open
C0666.d: The second speed channel at the right rear wheel is open: a wire, terminal or the sensor itself no longer conducts. C0666 is not documented by any carmaker. Where the repair ends depends on the hub design. Schaeffler's wheel bearing brochure notes that some third-generation bearings carry all speed sensors inside the bearing unit, so an internal open there can mean replacing the whole hub assembly. The loss also affects the parking brake. A ZF patent on electric parking brakes handles a missing or implausible speed signal by closing the brake only while the switch is held and with a steady rise in force, so the car stays stable; full clamping follows only once maximum force is reached. Normal ABS often stays available through sensor A.
c: Harness or connector open at the right rear wheel
Sensor inside the hub bearing unit failed open
Input stage for channel B in the brake module defective
s: Warning for brake or stability system on every start
Electric parking brake may only apply gradually while the switch is held

C0667.t: Right Rear Wheel Speed Sensor B Range/Performance
C0667.d: C0667 reports that the second right rear speed signal arrives but is not plausible, while the circuit itself is fine. No maker documents the code. At the rear axle the air gap can change while driving. A Ford patent observes that on semi-floating axles the shaft can deflect by more than 0.5 mm, enough to push a Hall sensor out of range of its tone ring so the signal turns wrong or vanishes, especially on the more heavily loaded side in a turn. On non-driven rear axles with two tapered roller bearings, Schaeffler requires the bearing clearance to be set by the maker's specification; too much play spreads the load unevenly and makes the hub less rigid, which can likewise disturb the gap. Faults that come with load or cornering point in this direction.
c: Worn or wrongly adjusted wheel bearing letting the gap vary
Axle shaft deflection under load or a bent shaft
Sensor not fully seated in its bore
s: Warning mainly with load, towing or in fast bends
Stability control functions temporarily withdrawn

C0668.t: Right Rear Wheel Speed Sensor B Circuit Low
C0668.d: C0668 points to a channel reading that is too low for the second right rear sensor. No carmaker documents the code, so the limit is not public. With a current-output sensor the floor is easy to define: in NXP's KMI25 a constant source of about 7 mA runs the whole chip and is always present, even when no pulse is sent. A reading under that level means current is leaking past the sensor to ground or the sensor is not getting enough voltage. NXP's application note for the older KMI15 explains why this interface is chosen: the module turns the sensor current into a voltage across a load resistor, which keeps the signal robust over longer leads. A partly crushed lead along the rear suspension can produce exactly such a low reading.
c: Crushed or chafed lead leaking current to ground
High contact resistance lowering the sensor voltage
Sensor B internal current source defective
s: Warning lamp for ABS or stability control
Redundant speed information at the right rear missing

C0669.t: Right Rear Wheel Speed Sensor B Circuit High
C0669.d: With C0669 the second right rear speed channel shows a level above the valid range, which usually means it is connected to a voltage source it should not see. No carmaker publishes this code. Sensor chips are built to survive such faults for a while: NXP builds the input die of the KMI25 with a process rated for high voltage, precisely to shield the measuring parts from the harsh conditions on the supply line. For the older KMI15 NXP recommends extra parts against voltage spikes and reverse polarity and notes that many vehicle networks already cap load-dump surges at about 40 V. The brake module, however, will not accept the reading and shuts the channel off until the short to battery, the damaged lead or the faulty sensor has been dealt with.
c: Signal lead shorted to battery voltage
Repaired or replacement harness wired to the wrong pins
s: Warning lamp right after switching on
Channel B switched off, assistance functions reduced

C066A.t: Right Rear Wheel Speed Sensor B Intermittent/Erratic
C066A.d: C066A describes a second right rear speed signal that keeps dropping out or jumping. No carmaker documents it. Apart from loose contacts, the encoder deserves a close look. Schaeffler explains that many wheel bearings carry a multipole encoder just inside the seal: a ring magnetised in alternating poles that the sensor reads. NSK adds that this surface must not be pressed on during fitting and must be kept away from magnets and dirt. A ring with a cracked section, a spot of attracted metal swarf or a weakened pole produces a pulse train with gaps, which reads as an erratic speed rather than a dead channel. Such a ring cannot be repaired on its own when it is part of the bearing, so the bearing or hub has to be replaced.
c: Encoder ring with metal swarf, cracks or weakened poles
Intermittent contact in plug or harness
Worn wheel bearing letting the encoder wobble
s: Warning appears and clears again during a drive
Speed of the right rear wheel jumps in live data

C066B.t: Right Rear Wheel Speed Sensor B Correlation
C066B.d: The second right rear speed value is electrically fine but disagrees with its references. No carmaker documents C066B or its limits. A Ford patent shows a check that suits a driven rear axle: the right rear speed is calculated as twice the output shaft speed divided by the axle ratio, minus the measured left rear speed. If measured and calculated values differ beyond a tolerance on consecutive passes or for more than 0.2 s, the fault is registered, and the calculated value stands in meanwhile. The tolerance can be tightened with lateral acceleration, and the side under more load gets the closer look. Bosch describes a similar estimate from the three other wheels, validated against the gearbox output. Wrong tyre sizes or a damaged encoder can trigger such a mismatch.
c: Mismatched tyre size or tread depth at the right rear
Encoder with missing or extra pulses
Axle ratio or tyre data in the module not matching the vehicle
s: Warning after a fast or long drive
Traction or stability functions temporarily reduced

C066C.t: Right Rear Wheel Speed Sensor B Incorrect Component Installed
C066C.d: C066C indicates that the part on the second right rear speed channel differs from the one the module is set up for. No carmaker documents the code or its detection logic. Parts for the rear hub come in several versions: Schaeffler lists wheel bearings both with a multipole encoder and without one, plus third-generation units with the sensors built in, so a hub from the wrong range may lack the encoder or the second sensor altogether. Orientation matters too. NSK advises identifying the encoder side with a magnetic test card and fitting the bearing so that this face ends up next to the sensor; NTN-SNR suggests a paper clip for the same check. Since the code points to the part rather than to wiring, the fitted hub and sensor numbers are compared with the vehicle's specification first.
c: Hub or bearing from a variant without encoder or second sensor
Bearing fitted with the encoder side facing away from the sensor
Sensor of another type or vehicle fitted
s: Warning appears right after work on the right rear hub
Redundant or automated brake functions not available

C066D.d: C066D covers a fault in the transducer reporting the air pressure inside the service/spring brake chambers of an air-braked vehicle. No maker documents the code, but the diagnosis of real systems is published. Bendix's Intellipark electronic parking brake measures the delivery pressure of every channel with its own transducer and logs J1939 faults for signals shorted high or to ground; if a sensor fails, park status for that unit cannot be shown, rollaway mitigation is lost and the driver is told to chock the wheels. A WABCO (now ZF) patent uses such a sensor to decide whether the spring brakes are applied or released. Knorr-Bremse, which also builds the parking brake into its electronic air control unit, places sensors at the control inlet and the outlet of the relay valve so each reading can serve as a cross-check on the other.
c: Sensor signal or 5 V supply shorted to ground or voltage
Pressure transducer in the valve module defective
Sensor outputs shorted together or connectors swapped
s: Parking brake indicator flashes, park status unknown
Automatic park functions such as rollaway protection unavailable

C066E.t: Service/Park Brake Chamber Pressure Too High
C066E.d: C066E means the measured chamber pressure is higher than the module allows in the present state. No maker documents the code, so its limit is not public. Too much pressure in the service section raises the push on the brake directly: Bendix calculates about 1,800 lbf on the pushrod when 60 psi reaches a type 30 chamber, and its chamber tests are not to exceed 120 psig. A specific risk is compounding. A ZF patent from the WABCO family explains that adding service brake force on top of applied spring brakes can permanently damage downsized brakes, and uses the axle's service pressure to release the springs before that happens. Haldex's trailer EBS warns separately when reservoir pressure rises above 9.8 bar, pointing to a governor or valve fault upstream.
c: Governor or pressure regulator letting system pressure rise too far
Anti-compound function not working, both forces add up
s: Brake warning or fault message on the dash or trailer lamp
Harsh braking or overheated wheel ends after parking manoeuvres

C066F.t: Service/Park Brake Chamber Pressure Too Low
C066F.d: C066F reports chamber pressure below what the brake system needs. No maker documents this code. For the spring section the consequences are clear: inside Bendix's piggyback unit the main spring starts to apply the brake once its chamber pressure falls under 78 psi, so a leak or weak supply makes the brakes drag. UN Regulation 13 requires that the springs of a motor vehicle do not start acting above 80 % of the lowest normal pressure, and that the driver is warned when the feed to the spring chamber sinks far enough for the brake components to start moving. FMVSS 121 asks for a warning once the service reservoir falls below 60 psi. Haldex lets its trailer EBS monitor spring brake pressure through an extra 5 V sensor and light a lamp under a set limit.
c: Leaking diaphragm, chamber seal or supply line
Insufficient reservoir pressure from compressor or dryer
Park valve or relay valve not delivering full pressure
s: Red brake or low-air warning, parking brake indicator flashing
Brakes dragging or spring brakes applying on their own

C0670.t: Left Front Acceleration or Position Sensor Circuit
C0670.d: C0670 is absent from the publicly available J2012 lists, but GM assigns it in its electronic damping control. In Saab's 2011 workshop data for the 9-5 and 9-4X it covers the vertical acceleration sensor at the left front wheel, which the suspension module supplies with 5 V and which answers with 0.5 to 4.5 V. Subcode 02 sets when the signal remains below 0.5 V longer than 1.5 s, 05 when it remains above 4.5 V as long, and 0A when it changes too rarely for 2.5 s above 30 km/h. Variable damping is then switched off until the next ignition cycle and a suspension warning appears. GM bulletin PI0954 names C0670 among five accelerometer codes on the 2010 LaCrosse with real-time damping when a service sensor meets an early controller. Nothing public ties the code to the park brake; C0675 is the right-hand twin.
c: Wheel acceleration sensor, its 5 V supply or signal wire faulty
Replacement sensor not compatible with early suspension module (GM PI0954)
Corroded or loose connector at the wheel housing
s: Service suspension message in the instrument cluster
Adaptive damping inactive, firmer or less controlled ride

C0671.t: Electric Park Brake Actuator Right Circuit
C0671.d: C0671 cannot be traced publicly: no publicly available J2012 list, no NHTSA bulletin, no GM keyword list and no Saab index contains it. GM even uses the neighbouring C0670 for a damping sensor and logs the electric park brake motor of the 2011 Saab 9-5 under C028A, with subcodes for shorts to plus or to ground, an open circuit and wrong frequency. The title points to the right rear caliper actuator. In the TRW design a motor turns a gearbox via a toothed belt, which drives a spindle and nut against the piston; swash-plate units reach about 19 kN, planetary ones about 25 kN. To release, the module reverses the motor polarity. Corrosion at the plug or a dead motor leaves that wheel unclamped or stuck, and ZF warns against freeing it with an external power source.
c: Moisture or corrosion at the actuator plug in the wheel housing
Chafed or broken wire between module and actuator
s: Park brake warning light or message
Right rear brake does not apply or does not release

C0680.t: Electric Park Brake Module Internal Fault
C0680.d: Public evidence for C0680 is lacking: it is in none of the public J2012 tables, bulletins or maker indexes. The title describes a park brake controller that fails its own checks. How GM handles that is documented for the 2011 Saab 9-5, just under other numbers: C056E flags software that is missing, an absent calibration or implausible software, and C0558 a calibration or mechanical fault; depending on the case the brake is disabled outright or allowed one more release. In many current cars the park brake logic lives inside the ABS/ESC module, which drives both motors directly. After pad or caliper work the system must be put into maintenance mode and calibrated again, so a skipped calibration or interrupted programming is a likely trigger alongside a genuinely failed board.
c: Calibration after brake service skipped or programming interrupted
Electronics inside the park brake or ABS/ESC module failed
Low battery voltage during self-test or programming
s: Park brake warning, function disabled or degraded
Brake cannot be applied, or only one more release is allowed

C0700.d: No public record shows a carmaker using C0700; public J2012 lists, NHTSA bulletins and maker indexes are silent. The title concerns superimposed steering such as the system from the Bosch-ZF venture that BMW introduced on the 2004 5 Series. A compound planetary set in the steering shaft adds an angle from an electric motor that turns the carrier, and an electromagnetic lock holds that carrier still whenever the function is off. A separate controller needs the angles at the wheel and at the pinion plus vehicle and wheel speeds over the network to compute the extra angle. If that exchange breaks down, the logical reaction is to lock the gear set, leaving a fixed ratio with full hydraulic assist; the car steers normally but feels slower at parking speeds. Lost communication is more often filed under U codes.
c: Damaged bus wiring or connector to the active steering controller
Steering angle or wheel speed message missing from another module
Active steering controller without power or defective
s: Steering warning in the instrument cluster
Steering ratio stays fixed, more wheel turns when parking

C0710.d: C0710 does not appear in the publicly available J2012 lists, yet GM uses it widely in the brake control module for the steering angle it feeds to stability control. Saab 9-5 2011 wording matches the title for subcode 00 and adds 42 (centering not stored) and 5A (signal missing, offset out of range or at odds with yaw rate); the 9-4X adds 71 for invalid data. The sensor should sweep from -550 to +550 degrees. When the code sets, StabiliTrak is switched off for that ignition cycle. GM bulletins give typical causes: a wheel mounted one spline off (PIT4225F, 2007-13 trucks), lift kits, other wheelbases or tyre sizes (PIT4322G), a worn lower column bearing on the 2005-06 STS (PIC3171E), and the wrong sensor calibration after programming 2010 hybrid trucks (PIT5207).
c: Steering angle sensor not centred after alignment or repair
Steering wheel mis-splined, or suspension, wheelbase or tyres changed
Faulty steering angle sensor, connector or worn column bearing
Brake module programmed for the wrong sensor design
s: Service StabiliTrak or stability message, ESC indicator on
Unwanted stability intervention while cornering

C0712.d: No carmaker is known to document C0712; it is not in the J2012 tables, bulletins or maker indexes searched. The title points to a position input of the power steering whose value is outside the expected band or does not track the other signals. An electric power steering relies on three position measurements: driver torque, the angle of the assist motor and the absolute steering wheel angle; Infineon offers separate angle sensors for the last two. How much an implausible angle hurts is shown by GM bulletin PI0800D for 2013 Equinox, Terrain, Malibu, LaCrosse and Regal: after a botched steering angle alignment the EPS logs a code that will not clear, assist drops to manual after only part of a turn and the car tries to steer to one side at speed. A new calibration or reflash usually follows.
c: Steering angle or position learn skipped or done wrongly
Position sensor in the steering gear or column defective
Intermittent connection in the sensor wiring
s: Power steering warning, assist reduced or lost
Steering wheel off centre or vehicle drifts to one side

C0715.d: C0715 is not traceable in public material; the publicly available J2012 tables, the NHTSA bulletin index and maker code lists all lack it. The function it names is well known from engine diagnostics, where the same check runs as P0551. On hydraulic steering the pump pressure rises with steering effort and a switch or sensor tells the engine controller to raise idle. Mitsubishi flags the circuit when the switch stays on after a stop that follows at least 4 s above 50 km/h; Saab sets P0551 on the 9-3 when the switch state changes for 600 s above 50 km/h and keeps the higher idle meanwhile. Toyota replaced the sensor on the 2007-08 Tundra to cure circuit low and high codes. Typical results are stalling or dipping idle at full lock, or a raised idle when driving straight.
c: Pressure sensor or switch stuck or drifting
Fluid seeping into the sensor connector
Pump pressure abnormal due to low fluid or worn pump
s: Idle dips or engine stalls at full steering lock
Idle stays raised while driving straight

C0720.t: Electric Power Steering Torque Sensor Circuit
C0720.d: No publicly available J2012 list contains C0720, and the only maker that uses it means something else: GM files C0720 71 on the 2011 Saab 9-5 and 9-4X as invalid engine torque data received by the suspension module over CAN; the damping control stays off for that ignition cycle and a history entry clears after 41 fault-free cycles. For the torque sensor in the title, GM uses C0545 instead (bulletin PIT5213B for 2014-15 full-size trucks) and Stellantis C1593. The sensor measures the twist of a torsion bar between steering wheel and gear, often with linear Hall chips such as Infineon's TLE499x family. GM's special coverage 15356 for the 2007-12 Malibu, G6 and Aura shows the effect of a failed sensor: sudden loss of assist with a warning chime, fixed by a new sensor or motor/controller.
c: Loose or corroded connector between sensor and EPS module
Sensor zero point not learned after replacement
s: Sudden loss of steering assist with warning message and chime
Heavy steering at low speed

C0725.d: C0725 has no public documentation; the publicly available J2012 tables, NHTSA bulletins and maker indexes leave it out. Carmakers file assist motor faults elsewhere: GM uses C0475, including symptom 64 for a detected slip in the motor circuit (bulletin PIT5213B), and Stellantis C1592, which the 2019 Jeep Cherokee could log as a general electrical failure and which a software flash addressed under bulletin 08-034-20, sometimes together with a MIL. The motor is usually a brushless machine fed by a power stage; NXP describes control units that measure rotor position and the current in each phase and set PWM duty cycles through field-oriented control. A circuit fault here means a phase, the power stage or the wiring does not behave as commanded, so the module cuts or reduces assist and steering becomes heavy.
c: Motor winding or power stage in the EPS unit defective
Module software misdiagnoses the motor circuit (update available)
Poor connection between module and motor
s: Steering warning, assist reduced or lost
Steering feels notchy or jerks while turning

C0727.d: C0727 has no public trace in the public J2012 tables, NHTSA bulletins or maker indexes, and trailer faults usually sit in B or U codes. The circuits behind the title are documented. GM trucks with the trailering app have a trailer lighting module that powers the socket with pulse-width signals; in 2019 the park, stop and turn circuits had to draw at least 55 mA before a trailer was recognised, and the module watches for bulb outage and overcurrent. Trailers with their own lighting module can confuse it. Ford traced false trailer connected messages on the 2019-20 Ranger to moisture in the 4-pin and 7-way connectors, and Stellantis advises packing the Ram 2500 bumper socket with dielectric grease against corrosion. Lamps on the trailer then fail or flicker.
c: Moisture or corrosion in the vehicle trailer socket
Short, LED load too low or own lighting module on the trailer
Damaged vehicle harness or trailer lighting module
s: Trailer lamps inoperative or flickering
Trailer connected/disconnected message without reason

C0730.t: Electric Power Steering Motor Position Sensor Circuit
C0730.d: Neither the publicly available J2012 lists nor NHTSA bulletins or maker indexes show C0730, so its use is not publicly verifiable. The sensor it names reports the rotor angle of the brushless assist motor, without which the module cannot commutate the phases or run field-oriented current control. Infineon places a rotary magnetic angle sensor on the motor and offers dual-die parts such as TLE5012BD and TLE5x09D so that two independent readings can be compared; NXP lists encoder or resolver processing and rotor position among the core jobs of the steering controller. A circuit fault means the angle signal is missing, shorted or electrically implausible. Without a trustworthy rotor angle the motor cannot be driven safely, so assist is withdrawn, often abruptly, and the steering turns heavy.
c: Rotor position sensor in the EPS motor defective
Poor connection between sensor and control board
Sensor magnet loose or misaligned after repair
s: Steering assist drops out suddenly, warning lamp on
Steering jerky or uneven while turning

C0735.t: Electric Power Steering Module Internal Fault
C0735.d: No known public source uses C0735; it is absent from the published J2012 lists, from NHTSA bulletins and from maker indexes. Carmakers report an internal EPS controller fault under other codes. GM uses C056D as a general hardware fault and asks technicians to reprogram the module first when symptom 39 is set (PIT5213B, 2014-15 trucks and SUVs). Stellantis uses C2217-00; on the 2023 Wagoneer and Grand Wagoneer it came with loss of assist and a steering lamp and was improved by new software (08-147-23), while on the 2019 Cherokee bulletin 08-034-20 excludes cases where C2217 is active and assist is gone with the engine running. Nexteer stresses redundant hardware and parallel software paths so that a single internal fault does not remove all assist at once.
c: Module software fault, cleared by reprogramming
Internal hardware failure of the EPS controller
Wrong steering gear or module installed, setup not completed
s: Service power steering message, steering lamp on
Assist reduced or absent from start-up

C0740.d: C0740 is not publicly documented by any carmaker; publicly available J2012 lists, NHTSA bulletins and maker indexes do not contain it. The title concerns the heavy supply feed of an electric steering, which draws high currents when the wheel is turned at standstill. GM bulletin PIT5405C for 2014-17 Silverado, Sierra, Tahoe, Suburban, Yukon and Escalade shows what a weak feed does: reduced assist, kickback in the wheel, even stalling and blank displays, traced to a poor body ground, a battery cable shorting on the starter shield, high-resistance battery connections, a weak battery or a loose main power and ground connector at the rack. GM logs device power faults there as C0800. NXP describes EPS control units with integrated undervoltage monitoring that limit or stop assist when supply sags.
c: Loose or corroded main power or ground connection at the rack
Discharged or failing battery, high-resistance battery cables
Battery cable shorting elsewhere or poor body ground
s: Assist weakens or cuts out at low speed and full lock
Steering wheel jerks, other displays flicker

C0745.d: Public documentation of C0745 is missing; it is not in the publicly available J2012 tables, in NHTSA bulletins or in maker indexes. GM reports an overheated EPS controller as C0176 (PIT5213B). The protection itself is well described in a Delphi patent: instead of relying on thermistors, the controller squares the motor current and runs it through several low-pass filters, each standing for one thermal time constant, the slowest close to 2,000 s. When a filter exceeds its limit, motor current is reduced step by step, more strictly when the motor is stalled against a lock. The example motor handles 15 A continuously or 75 A for about 5 s. Long parking manoeuvres or holding full lock therefore make the steering heavier until the unit cools down.
c: Long parking manoeuvres or holding the wheel at full lock
Stiff steering gear, joints or tyres raising motor load
Temperature estimate or sensor in the module faulty
s: Steering gradually heavier after repeated manoeuvring
Power steering warning message

C0750.d: None of the public code lists carries C0750. GM, however, uses it in its tire pressure monitoring for the left front wheel transmitter, and the Saab 9-5 (2010-2011) and 9-4X service pages define the subcodes: 03 for a weak sensor battery, 29 for a sensor that sends too few telegrams, 39 for an internal sensor defect. The check runs above 40 km/h, when the roll switch in each wheel unit should wake the transmitter; if it stays silent or its data are invalid, the body control module sets the code and the TPMS lamp blinks for a minute, then stays lit. GM bulletin PIC5650M lists C0750 among the effects of radio interference from add-on devices. C0755, C0760 and C0765 cover the other wheels. No evidence ties the code to a cruise control brake switch.
c: Built-in battery of the wheel sensor exhausted (subcode 03)
Sensor damaged during tire service, after a flat or replaced by a valve without sensor
Radio interference from aftermarket devices or metallised window tint (GM PIC5650M)
Remote receiver or its antenna unplugged or faulty
s: TPMS lamp flashes about one minute after start, then stays on
Dashes instead of a pressure value for the left front tire
Service tire monitor message in the driver display

C0784.t: Trailer Brake Force Sensor Circuit Malfunction
C0784.d: Searches for C0784 came up empty: the public code lists, the NHTSA bulletin index, GM's keyword table and the Saab and Mitsubishi indexes all miss it. The title points to the signal an integrated trailer brake controller uses to gauge how hard the driver is braking. Patents show the usual choices: a pressure transducer on the master cylinder, a pedal travel sensor or an accelerometer, whose proportional output sets the current to the trailer's electric brakes. Continental adds a gain optimiser that compares master cylinder pressure with measured deceleration, for example 0.5 g expected at 80 bar, and raises the trailer gain when the rig stops too weakly. Without a valid signal the controller can no longer scale trailer braking to the driver's demand.
c: Open, shorted or corroded wiring or connector of the brake force or pressure signal
Brake pressure transducer or deceleration sensor defective
Trailer brake controller module faulty or wrongly configured
s: Trailer brakes weak, delayed or not applied when the vehicle brakes
Trailer brake warning message in the instrument cluster

C0800.d: Generic code lists omit C0800, but GM uses it widely for the supply voltage that a chassis module sees, often the brake control module. Saab workshop pages for the 2011 models list the subcodes are 03 below threshold, 07 above, 0D high resistance and 11 high input; the module flags a supply under roughly 9 V or over 18 V lasting about 5 s and may switch itself off. Saab's 2009 9-3 ESP unit sets 03 under 8 V for 0.5 s, or under 9.5 V above 15 km/h, and drops ABS and ESP. GM bulletins tie it to a loose negative cable on the 2011-15 Cruze (PI1398A), to faults reproducible under heavy electrical load (PIC6037) and to poor connections on 2014-17 trucks (PIT5405C); on the 2013 LaCrosse and Malibu wheel speed faults come first (PIC5837). It is not a drive system low voltage code.
c: Loose or corroded battery cable or ground connection (GM PI1398A)
Weak battery or charging system fault, also after jump start or charger use
High resistance in the module's supply or ground circuit
s: ABS, traction and stability warnings light up, sometimes only briefly
Radio or displays switch off and on, lights flicker
Heavier steering at low speed on vehicles with electric power steering

C0805.d: Public evidence for C0805 is lacking: it appears neither in code lists nor in the NHTSA index, GM's keyword table or the Saab and Mitsubishi indexes. The title describes a steering angle sensor whose zero point has not been learned. GM files exactly that fault elsewhere: in both 2011 Saab models, 9-5 and 9-4X, the brake module stores C0710 subcode 42 when the sensor reports no calibration, then switches off ESC and the hill holder until the next ignition cycle. Stellantis uses the J2012 code C0529 for the same condition on the ProMaster and advises an initialisation first, by turning lock to lock with the engine running or by scan tool, before any steering gear is replaced. The bulletin names a battery disconnect or a new steering gear as typical triggers for a fresh learn.
c: Zero point not learned after battery disconnect or steering gear replacement
Steering wheel or sensor mounted off centre, so the learned offset is out of range
Steering angle sensor defective and unable to store the calibration
s: Stability or traction control lamp stays on
ESC and hill start assist unavailable

C0810.d: C0810 cannot be located anywhere public, whether in code lists, the NHTSA index or the GM, Saab and Mitsubishi material. The title concerns the electrical drive of the air suspension compressor, an electric motor that Continental describes with carbon brushes stressed by inrush current. Lexus uses its own code C1752 for the motor circuit on the 2013-17 LS460 and traces it to corrosion inside the compressor after water enters through the intake tubes; the fix is a new compressor and motor assembly. Mercedes-Benz likewise reports moisture and corrosion in the compressor that cut its output and leave deposits on the valve block seats, and counters it with software. A dead circuit means the springs can no longer be filled, so the body sinks or stays at one level.
c: Water ingress and corrosion seizing or loading the compressor motor
Open, shorted or corroded wiring or connector at the compressor
s: Air suspension warning message in the cluster
Vehicle sits low or does not change ride height

C0815.d: C0815 has no public owner: code lists and maker indexes skip it, and the NHTSA index only matches it inside unrelated BMW bulletin IDs. The title names thermal protection of the air suspension compressor. Most systems have no temperature sensor and estimate the heat from running time instead. Continental patents describe two strategies: switching the pump off above a calculated limit and back on only when it has cooled enough for one full level change on a loaded vehicle, or pulsing it near the limit so that a lift of 20 to 30 s can still finish. Long lifts at standstill, frequent level corrections, fast off-road driving and heavy sound insulation heat it most; a leak that keeps it running has the same effect.
c: Leak in an air spring, line or valve block keeps the compressor running
Repeated manual level changes at standstill or heavy load changes
Worn or moisture-damaged compressor delivering too little air
s: Ride height change stops or is refused for several minutes
Air suspension warning, vehicle sits low after long standing

C0820.t: Air Suspension Height Sensor Front Left
C0820.d: Nobody documents C0820 in the open; apart from Honda bulletin IDs that happen to contain the string, searches of lists and indexes found nothing. The title concerns the ride height sensor at the left front corner, a lever on the control arm turning an angle sensor that reports body height to the air suspension module. Stellantis uses its own numbers here: C151E for a stuck left front sensor on the 2022-23 Ram 1500, fixed by new module software (08-127-23, 08-150-24), and C1567 for an implausible left front level on the 2021 Grand Cherokee, where pinched front air lines were the cause. Without a valid front left height, the module stops levelling that corner or the whole car and shows a service message.
c: Bent, detached or seized sensor lever or link at the front left control arm
Water, corrosion or chafing at the sensor plug or harness in the wheel arch
Air suspension module software reporting a false stuck sensor (Stellantis 08-150-24)
s: Service air suspension message
Front left corner sits too high or too low, height changes refused

C0821.t: Air Suspension Height Sensor Front Right
C0821.d: C0821 leaves no public trace in public lists, bulletins or maker indexes; going by its name it means the front right level sensor. HELLA builds such sensors as a housing on the body with a lever and ball joint to the axle, using potentiometer, Hall or contactless inductive elements, fed with 4 to 11 V and sending analogue, PWM, SENT or PSI5 signals. Stellantis logs the front right sensor as C1522: subcode 11, a grounded signal wire, on the 2022 Grand Wagoneer, where its STAR case notes the code can also appear after the car was jacked up or lifted, and subcode 2A for a stuck signal on the 2022-23 Ram 1500. A ground fault often hides in a wet or damaged connector at the wheel arch.
c: Signal wire shorted to ground by chafing, water or corrosion
Code stored after the car was jacked or lifted, sensor at end of travel
Front right height sensor or its lever defective
s: Service air suspension message
Vehicle leans to the front right or levelling is switched off

C0822.t: Air Suspension Height Sensor Rear Left
C0822.d: For C0822 the search of code lists, NHTSA and the GM, Saab and Mitsubishi sources returned nothing. Per its title it covers the rear left level sensor of an air suspension. At the rear axle the harness runs close to the subframe and fuel tank, which is where Stellantis found the cause of its own code C1526 subcode 11, short to ground, on a 2019 Grand Cherokee: the wiring rubbed on bracket edges and had to be repaired, isolated and tied away (STAR S2108000161). On the 2022-23 Ram 1500 the same sensor sets C1526-2A when the module considers it stuck. HELLA notes that many such sensors work with two redundant channels, so the module can spot a split between them before the reading is used.
c: Harness rubbing on subframe or bracket edges near the fuel tank
Rear left height sensor or its link rod damaged
Module software misjudging the sensor as stuck
s: Service air suspension message
Rear left sags or rear ride height not adjusted

C0823.t: Air Suspension Height Sensor Rear Right
C0823.d: C0823 is unknown to every public source, from code lists to the NHTSA index and maker documentation. The title refers to the rear right level sensor. Its reading matters most when loading, since the module uses the rear heights to keep ground clearance and headlamp aim constant. Stellantis gives the rear right corner its own code, C152A, and on the 2022-23 Ram 1500 with four-corner air suspension a stuck rear sensor reading was resolved by reprogramming the module, with the battery held between 13.2 and 13.5 V during the flash (08-127-23). HELLA's level sensor brief lists a 12-bit resolution and an operating range from -40 to 125 °C. A suspect sensor is checked against its lever position before replacement.
c: Rear right height sensor, lever or ball joint worn or broken
Corroded or loose sensor connector, damaged harness
Air suspension module software needing an update (Stellantis 08-127-23)
s: Service air suspension message
Rear right sits low or high, load levelling inactive

C0825.d: No public code list, bulletin or service manual assigns C0825, so its use by any carmaker cannot be shown. The title points at the torque sensor of electric power steering: a torsion bar in the column or pinion twists under the driver's hand force, and Hall elements read that twist as a torque value. A range or performance fault means the reading stays inside its electrical limits but does not make sense, for example when the main and backup channels disagree. A Mitsubishi Electric patent checks both channels against a torque estimated from the motor current and stops assistance when none of them agree. Makers that publish torque sensor faults use their own numbers, e.g. Honda C1423-14 for the sensor supply on the 2022 CR-V. Expect an EPS warning and heavier steering.
c: Torque sensor channel drifting or reading implausibly against the second channel
Unstable sensor supply or internal short in the sensor (as in Honda bulletin 22-011)
Poor contact at the sensor or steering module connector
s: Power steering warning lamp or message
Steering assist reduced or switched off, wheel feels heavy
Uneven assistance between left and right turns

C0827.d: C0827 appears in no accessible code list, bulletin or manufacturer table, so no carmaker can be named for it. The title describes a steering torque signal that freezes: the value no longer follows the driver, either because a short pins the output at a supply rail or because the sensor delivers a constant value while the wheel is clearly being turned. An NSK patent shows how such a case is handled: outputs close to 0 V or 5 V (about 0.3 V and 4.7 V) count as faulty, the controller then works with the smallest of the last few good samples and fades assistance to zero over a set time rather than cutting it at once. Unlike the plausibility fault C0825, here the signal stops changing. The driver sees an EPS warning and the steering turns heavy within seconds.
c: Sensor output shorted to supply or ground, holding the signal at a rail
Hall element or sensor electronics frozen, usually requiring a new steering gear or column
Chafed or pinched harness between sensor and steering module
s: Power steering warning lamp on
Assistance fades out and steering becomes heavy

C0830.t: Steering Wheel Angle Sensor Center Position Not Learned
C0830.d: No public list or bulletin uses C0830; its content overlaps with C0529 (missing calibration) and C0805. The stability control needs to know which sensor reading means wheels straight ahead; until that zero point is stored, it cannot compare steering input with yaw. GM files this as C0710-42 (calibration not programmed): Saab 9-5 and 9-4X of 2011 then disable both the stability system and the hill holder and light the indicator. Ram ProMaster 2022-23 sets C0529-00 after battery disconnect or gear replacement; turning lock to lock or a scan tool relearn fixes it (9100119). Kia asks for a centred wheel within 5 degrees when calibrating the Sorento column (PS547), and recalibrated 2025 Seltos sensors set wrong at the plant (SA641).
c: Zero point not relearned after battery disconnect, alignment, sensor or steering gear replacement
Steering wheel not centred or alignment off during calibration
Incorrect calibration from the factory (Kia service action SA641)
s: Stability and traction control lamp on, ESC switched off
Hill start assist or lane functions unavailable
Steering wheel slightly off centre when driving straight

C0840.d: C0840 is not documented anywhere in public; no list, bulletin or manual of any carmaker uses it. The title concerns the electrical side of the valves that route air in a self-levelling suspension. Some systems carry one switching valve per air spring in a central block next to the compressor, as in a Continental patent that also places fast lowering valves there; older Ford and Lincoln designs put a two-position vent solenoid on top of each spring, opened by the vehicle dynamics module to fill or vent. A circuit fault means the module sees an open, a short or wrong current on a coil. Bentley logs such a case as C11C613, an open circuit at the rapid filling valve of the Bentayga, and checks the connector first. The affected corner can no longer be raised or lowered.
c: Water or corrosion in the valve connector (Bentley 2064579/1 checks the plug first)
Open or shorted valve coil, often after moisture got into the system
Chafed harness at the valve block or air spring
s: Air suspension warning or service message
One corner sags or ride height cannot be changed

C0850.d: No manufacturer publishes C0850, and no code list carries it, so its use cannot be shown. The title refers to the electrically adjusted shock absorber at the left front. Its control unit sends a pulse width modulated current through a valve coil in the damper and measures the current that really flows; when the two differ, it stores a fault. GM does exactly this under its own number C0575 (Left Front Damper Actuator Circuit) on the 2011 Saab 9-5 and 9-4X, a meaning that differs from the J2012 use of C0575. The module then turns electronic damping off for that ignition cycle and shows SERVICE SUSPENSION SYSTEM. Stellantis uses C15C2 and C15C3 for the two left front valves (compression, rebound) on Ram 1500 and Charger from 2024.
c: Damaged or loose cable and plug at the front left strut
Valve coil inside the damper open or shorted, damper must be replaced
Faulty driver stage in the suspension control module
s: Service suspension message
Damping no longer adapts, ride feels harsher or floatier

C0851.d: C0851 has no public owner: neither code lists nor bulletins name it. Its subject is the adjustable damper at the right front corner. GM's electronic suspension on the 2011 Saab 9-5 files this corner as C0580 with three failure types: 02 when the high side is shorted to ground or to voltage, 04 for an open control line, 0F for an erratic coil current. The system works only between 9 and 16 V; a stored history entry clears after 41 fault-free ignition cycles. ZF's CDC design shows why wiring matters at this point: the proportional valve sits either inside, fed through the piston rod, or outside on the tube with its own sealed plug, and it is reset within milliseconds. Stellantis uses C15C4 and C15C5 for this corner. Damping falls back to a fixed setting.
c: Corroded or loose plug at the right front damper
Proportional valve in the damper failed
Supply outside 9-16 V causing erratic current readings
s: Suspension warning in the instrument cluster
Body movements less controlled over bumps

C0852.d: Nothing public ties C0852 to a manufacturer; it is absent from every public list and index. The title covers the adjustable rear left damper. Some modern units use two valves per damper, one for compression and one for rebound. Stellantis does so on the 2024-26 Ram 1500 and Dodge Charger and logs the rear left pair as C15C6 and C15C7; its bulletin S2623000031 warns that these faults can only be diagnosed while active, so a module should not be replaced for stored entries, and tap tests on harness and pin fit come first. GM's older single-valve layout on the 2011 Saab 9-4X calls the same corner C0585. Rear dampers sit low and close to road spray, so plugs and cables there suffer most. Electronic damping is switched off until the fault clears.
c: Loose pin fit or intermittent contact in the rear left damper connector
Harness damaged by road spray, stones or corrosion near the rear axle
Compression or rebound valve in the damper failed
s: Service suspension warning
Rear feels bouncy or harsh, drive modes no longer change damping

C0853.d: C0853 is undocumented in public sources; no carmaker's list, bulletin or manual mentions it. The title is about the adjustable damper at the right rear. Such dampers only work as well as the inputs behind them: the control unit takes in body and wheel motion from accelerometers and sets each valve accordingly. BMW reprogrammed the variable damper control of X6 (F16) cars built in late 2014 because tolerance spread in the wheel accelerometers made it shut electronic damping off and leave the car on a conventional setting. For the actuator itself, GM's 2011 Saab models (9-5, 9-4X) use C0590 for this corner, and Stellantis uses C15C8 and C15C9 on the Ram 1500 from 2024. A failed rear right channel makes the car ride on fixed damping and shows a suspension warning.
c: Open or shorted circuit to the right rear damper valve
Implausible wheel acceleration sensor input causing shutdown (BMW SI B37 01 14)
Damper control unit software needing an update
s: Suspension fault message
Car stays on a fixed damper setting regardless of mode

C0860.d: No carmaker documents C0860 openly, and it does not appear in any accessible list. The title names trailer sway control, an extra function of the stability control that uses the existing ESC sensors to spot a swinging trailer and then brakes single wheels and trims engine torque until the combination calms down. A Bosch patent detects sway as the gap between target and measured yaw rate, filtered to roughly 0.5 to 1.5 Hz so that normal steering is ignored, and can counter it by shifting drive torque between rear wheels instead of braking. A performance fault means the function cannot work as intended. Acura shows how makers label this: on the 2007-11 MDX the warning for trailer stability assist lit up together with codes 59-1, 66-1, 67-1 or 69-1, and a faulty brake pedal position switch was to blame.
c: Fault in an ESC input such as brake pedal switch, yaw or wheel speed signal
Trailer not recognised because of trailer socket or wiring faults
Stability control software or configuration needing an update
s: Trailer stability or ESC warning lamp on
No automatic braking when the trailer sways

C0870.t: Control Module Voltage Reference Output Circuit
C0870.d: C0870 is missing from the accessible J2012 code lists; it is documented at GM, where it covers the 5 V reference that a module feeds to its sensors. Saab workshop pages for the 2011 9-5 and 9-4X use it in the suspension control module, which feeds five acceleration sensors on the body and at the wheels: subcode 03 means that line is shorted to ground and 07 that it touches battery voltage, each for 1.5 s, checked between 9 and 16 V. Electronic damping then shuts off for the ignition cycle. The fix is to unplug the sensors one by one and watch the reference return to 4.8-5.2 V. Under the older name Device Voltage Reference Output 1 Circuit, GM hybrid pickups of 2005 and 2007 used it for the pedal sensor supply of the steering pump (above 4.65 V or below 3.95 V, type C, no MIL).
c: One acceleration sensor shorting the shared 5 V reference
Reference line chafed to ground or to battery voltage
Module reference supply faulty, module replacement after wiring checks (Saab WIS)
s: SERVICE SUSPENSION SYSTEM message
Adaptive damping inactive for the rest of the trip
Several acceleration sensor codes stored at once

C0900.d: C0900 does not appear in the publicly available J2012 code lists, and no carmaker publishes it for tire pressure monitoring. The one official mention points elsewhere: GM upfitter bulletin 80C for the 2008-2014 Silverado and Sierra HD chassis cab lists C0900 subcode 07 as Device Voltage High, a supply fault logged by the PTO module. The title instead means the battery inside the first wheel transmitter. A Schrader patent describes a single lithium cell and spare function bits in every radio word that can carry a low battery message. Mitsubishi books exactly this case for tire 1 as C1910 and names the cell built into the transmitter as the likely cause. Expect the TPMS lamp; the unit is replaced and its ID registered again.
c: Built-in lithium cell of the wheel transmitter at end of life
Aged cell whose voltage sags in cold weather
On GM vehicles the code may instead stem from excessive module supply voltage (Device Voltage High)
s: TPMS warning lamp flashes after start, then stays lit
Pressure reading for one wheel drops out intermittently, more often in cold weather

C0901.d: Nothing public ties C0901 to a carmaker: no public code list, NHTSA bulletin or service index contains it. Its title concerns the automatic assignment of wheel transmitter 1 to a corner of the car. Without that link the system knows a pressure value but not which tire it belongs to. Saab's 9-5 of 2011 learns the side from the sensor's turning direction and the axle from signal strength, which takes 3 to 9 minutes of driving. A Schrader patent instead compares the phase angle each sensor reports with ABS tooth counts and picks the best matching wheel. Land Rover's TPM module sets C1D18-55 while locations are still unknown and clears it after 10 minutes above 20 km/h. A performance fault means the learning did not finish or gave a doubtful result.
c: Learning drive too short or too slow after wheel change or sensor replacement
Wheel speed data from the ABS module missing or implausible, so phase comparison fails
Transmitters of a spare wheel or a nearby vehicle disturbing the assignment
s: TPMS warning lamp lit or flashing although tire pressures are correct
Pressures shown at the wrong wheel position or no position display at all

C0902.d: C0902 cannot be traced in public sources; the NHTSA index only matches it inside an unrelated vehicle number. The title covers the cell feeding wheel transmitter 2. Which corner counts as number 2 is up to each maker; Mitsubishi numbers tires 1 to 4 and uses C1920 for a weak transmitter battery on tire 2. A CM Automotive patent shows how such a sensor watches itself: a resistor divider feeds the cell voltage to the microcontroller, every message carries a byte with that level, and the monitor lights a separate lamp once readings could become inaccurate. Honda splits the same fault by wheel, with codes 31, 33, 35 and 37. Because the cell is sealed into the transmitter, the fix is a new sensor plus ID learning.
c: Transmitter cell discharged after years of service
Sensor electronics drawing excess current, draining the cell early
After rotating wheels the battery warning is attributed to the wrong position
s: TPMS lamp or a service tire monitor message
Readings from one wheel update less often or vanish

C0903.d: Searches found C0903 neither in code lists nor in maker documents; a single NHTSA hit is a truck maker's campaign number. The title addresses locating transmitter 2 on the vehicle. Two methods are documented. A Ford patent puts a low frequency initiator into each wheel well: the controller fires it above about 20 mph, waits 3 seconds for the sensor to answer with its ID and a special status flag, raises the transmit power step by step and declares an error once the limit is reached without reply. A 2022 Mitsubishi system without initiators derives the position from the timing between the wheel speed sensors and each tire sensor. If either check ends without a clear match, the corner of sensor 2 stays unknown.
c: Location learning interrupted, e.g. short trips at low speed after tire service
Sensor does not answer the wheel well initiator (weak LF field, misaligned initiator)
Acceleration or rotation detection inside the sensor faulty
s: TPMS lamp on with all tires correctly inflated
Display shows pressures without assigning them to wheel positions

C0905.d: No manufacturer is known to use C0905; none of the code lists, service indexes or NHTSA bulletins searched contains it. The title names a weak battery in the third wheel transmitter. GM and Saab file this condition by wheel rather than by number, as subcode 03 Low Voltage under C0750 to C0765; on the 2011 Saab 9-5 the check needs more than 40 km/h, when a centrifugal roll switch puts each sensor into rolling mode and the door lock receiver forwards its data to the body module. Mitsubishi's counterpart for tire 3 is C1930, raised when the reception warning stems from low transmitter voltage. A low battery alone leaves pressures readable at first, so this is an early warning; the sensor will soon need replacing.
c: Sensor cell near end of life (typically after many years)
Sensor stuck in a fast transmit mode, drawing the cell down early
s: TPMS lamp flashes about a minute after start, then stays on
Pressure values still shown, warning returns after every restart

C0907.d: C0907 has no public owner: code lists, the NHTSA index and the GM, Saab and Mitsubishi service indexes all lack it. Per its title it flags a fading battery in transmitter 4. How that state is noticed: the sensor measures its cell through a voltage divider and sends a battery byte with each pressure message, as a CM Automotive patent shows. Mitsubishi stores C1940 for tire 4 in this case; once the cell sags further, the receiver stops hearing the sensor and the same family sets C1941 after roughly 20 minutes of driving without its ID. The 2011 Saab 9-4X handles it per corner, subcode 03 under C0750 to C0765. The code thus heralds a coming loss of signal; replacing the sensor before that avoids a dark pressure display.
c: Cold weather pushing an ageing cell below the warning level
Fault in the sensor's voltage measurement
s: TPMS warning lamp with a sensor fault message
Later, dashes instead of a value for the affected wheel

C0910.d: There is no public evidence that any carmaker assigns C0910. It describes a fault in the circuit of the radio receiver that collects the wheel sensor telegrams. Designs differ: GM and Saab route the sensors through the remote door lock receiver, which passes the decoded telegrams on to the BCM; Nissan-built cars lacking keyless entry use a stand-alone TPMS receiver that reports to the BCM as well. Honda keeps a separate code 41 for abnormal signal reception. GM bulletin PIC5650M lists sensor codes C0750 to C0765 and C0775 among the effects of radio interference from toll passes, other key fobs, LED lamps or phone chargers. A circuit fault of the receiver itself, such as lost supply, ground or data line, silences all four wheels at once rather than a single sensor.
c: Lost supply voltage or ground at the receiver, e.g. corroded connector
Open or shorted data line between receiver and body control module
Radio interference from aftermarket devices (GM PIC5650M)
Receiver module or its antenna defective
s: TPMS malfunction indication with no pressure shown for any wheel
Poor remote key range where the receiver is shared with the door locks

C0912.d: C0912 could not be found in any code list, bulletin or service index, so its use remains unproven. The title refers to the front initiator: a coil near the wheel that wakes the tire sensor with a low frequency field so the system can tell which corner answered. A TRW patent mounts one such induction coil per wheel well and sends at about 125 kHz, relying on the field fading quickly with distance so only the adjacent sensor reacts. A Ford patent wires each initiator straight to the controller and raises the drive current step by step until the sensor replies. Honda reports a shorted initiator line as code 45. An open or shorted front circuit leaves the front sensors unlocated, so pressure values may lack their position.
c: Initiator wiring in the wheel arch chafed, corroded or unplugged
Initiator coil open or shorted internally
Initiator knocked out of its mount by wheel arch liner damage
Output stage in the TPMS module defective
s: TPMS malfunction lamp on
Front tire pressures shown without wheel position or not at all after a tire change

C0915.t: Active Roll Stabilisation Front Actuator Circuit
C0915.d: No list, bulletin or manual shows C0915 in use; the NHTSA index only matches unrelated BMW document numbers. The title names the front actuator of active roll control, which splits the anti-roll bar and twists its halves against each other to hold the body level in bends and to decouple them on rough roads. Schaeffler's 48 V design for the Audi SQ7 front axle drives this with a brushless motor and a three-stage planetary gearbox, up to about 30 degrees of twist and 850-1200 Nm; ZF quotes up to 1400 Nm. A circuit fault concerns motor or sensor wiring between actuator and control unit. Audi's Q7/Q8 family logs control unit faults as C129700 at addresses 00D4/00D5, while Land Rover's older hydraulic system used C1119 and needed bleeding.
c: Damaged plug or harness at the front stabiliser actuator
Actuator motor or internal sensor failed
Fault in the 48 V supply feeding the actuator
s: Suspension or roll stabilisation warning
Noticeably more body lean in corners

C0916.t: Active Roll Stabilisation Rear Actuator Circuit
C0916.d: C0916 has no documented user; it is absent from every accessible list, bulletin and index. It names the rear axle actuator of active roll control. Systems with actuators on both axles split the stabilising torque between front and rear, which also lets them tune self-steering; ZF describes this for its electromechanical roll control. Faults at the rear unit therefore change balance as well as body lean. Bulletins show how carmakers handle such cases under their own codes: Mercedes updated the front and rear roll stabilisation units of 2021 GLE and GLS models whose software could display a warning not to exceed 50 mph, and Land Rover quarantined 2022-23 Range Rover and Range Rover Sport cars whose front and rear roll control modules sometimes failed to initialise, lighting an amber suspension lamp.
c: Damaged harness or plug at the rear stabiliser actuator, exposed to road spray
Roll control software needing an update (Mercedes 2021060016, Land Rover N733)
Rear actuator motor or gearbox failed
s: Amber suspension warning lamp
Speed limit advice in the cluster, more body roll and changed handling balance

C0920.d: C0920 is not found in any accessible list or bulletin. The title describes a suspension control unit that fails its own checks. GM names such a fault C0550 Electronic Control Unit, as the 2011 Saab 9-5 pages show: the self-test runs at power-up and needs only supply and ground, the module ignores further inputs, and it should only be replaced if the code is present as current and history entry; a history entry clears after 50 clean ignition cycles. Not every module swap is an internal fault: GM's PI0954 had 2010 LaCrosse suspension modules replaced because they did not accept service accelerometers, and Stellantis warns against replacing the damping module for stored codes. Audi logs C129700 for a limiting fault inside its roll stabiliser units.
c: Internal hardware or memory fault confirmed as current and history code
Poor supply or ground at the module triggering self-test failures
Software or parts incompatibility (GM PI0954, Audi 2067804/3)
s: Suspension service message, adaptive damping or levelling off
Other suspension codes may be stored alongside

C0950.t: Tire Pressure Monitoring Sensor Front Left
C0950.d: No public source links C0950 to a carmaker. The same content, the left front tire sensor, is documented under other numbers: GM and Saab use C0750, whose 2011 Saab 9-5 subcodes split a weak cell (03), too few telegrams (29) and an internal defect (39); Mitsubishi's 2022 index carries C1731 for the front left sensor and C1741 when its data stay away. GM bulletin PIC5650M lists C0750 among the codes that radio interference from aftermarket devices can cause, so the environment belongs in the diagnosis. As a catch-all for the front left unit the code covers a sensor that falls silent, reports nonsense or is not learned. Air pressure itself is not the issue; the indicator shows a system fault and that wheel loses its value.
c: Cell of the left front sensor exhausted
Sensor broken during tire fitting or wheel swapped for one without sensor
New sensor ID not registered for the front left position
Radio interference from aftermarket devices (GM PIC5650M)
s: TPMS lamp flashes, then stays on
No pressure value for the left front tire

C0951.t: Tire Pressure Monitoring Sensor Front Right
C0951.d: C0951 is not documented by any known maker. For the front right sensor GM and Saab rely on C0755 instead, on the 2011 9-4X with the subcodes 03, 29 and 39. Mitsubishi's 2022 data spell out the no-data case in detail as C1742-21: the BCM watches for the right front signal once the car has covered 10 minutes in total at 40 km/h or more, and it stores the code if nothing arrives. Its listed causes reach beyond the sensor: driving through radio interference, an incomplete ID registration, wiring or the BCM itself. A front right sensor code therefore calls for checking the learned ID and the surroundings before buying a sensor. The driver loses the front right reading and sees the TPMS warning.
c: ID registration of the front right sensor incomplete
Radio interference along the route or from devices in the car
s: Dashes instead of a value for the right front tire
TPMS lamp lit after about ten minutes of driving

C0952.t: Tire Pressure Monitoring Sensor Rear Left
C0952.d: A manufacturer using C0952 is not on record; the number is absent from all lists and bulletins searched. What it names, the left rear tire sensor, carries other codes elsewhere: C0760 at GM and Saab, C1734 and C1744 in Mitsubishi's 2022 index, and on a 2008 Honda Accord the codes 37 for a low sensor battery and 38 for a sensor that stopped transmitting at the left rear. Relearning follows a fixed sequence of corners; Honda starts with the front left wheel, moves on to the rear left one, then the rear right, and finishes at the front right, and Saab's autolearn tells the axles apart by signal strength. A left rear fault therefore often follows a wheel rotation or a missed relearn step. The left rear pressure is no longer monitored.
c: Wheels rotated without relearning sensor positions
Cell of the left rear sensor exhausted
Sensor damaged or missing after tire work
s: No reading for the left rear tire
TPMS warning after a tire rotation

C0953.t: Tire Pressure Monitoring Sensor Rear Right
C0953.d: C0953 stays without a documented user; neither J2012 lists nor bulletins name it. The right rear sensor appears at GM and Saab as C0765, where subcode 39 marks an internal malfunction. Mitsubishi's 2022 page for C1733-68 shows how implausible data from that corner are caught: above 40 km/h the BCM checks pressure, temperature and G sensor values in each telegram from the right rear unit and flags a fault within one second; the only cause listed is the sensor. Unlike a silent sensor, this one still transmits, but its content is unusable. Replacing the right rear sensor and registering its ID is the usual cure. Until then the TPMS lamp stays on and no valid right rear pressure is shown.
c: Pressure, temperature or acceleration element inside the right rear sensor defective
Sensor damaged by tire fitting, sealant or impact
s: TPMS lamp on with no valid value for the right rear tire
Implausible or jumping pressure reading at the right rear

C0960.t: Tire Pressure Monitoring Module Internal Fault
C0960.d: Public material does not show C0960 in use by any maker; it is missing from the public lists, indexes and bulletins. The title points to a self-test failure in the control unit that evaluates the tire sensors. Makers with their own codes for this: Honda's TPMS unit reports code 81 when its RAM, ROM, A/D converter, EEPROM or arithmetic unit fails the check, and Mitsubishi's 2022 BCM-based system lists C1700 control unit faults with several subcodes. Land Rover keeps the function in a separate TPM module. FMVSS 138 requires a malfunction telltale within 20 minutes of any fault that stops the system working, so the warning lamp is the visible sign. Wheel sensors are usually fine; the module is reprogrammed or replaced.
c: Memory or processor fault inside the TPMS control unit
Corrupted or incomplete software after programming
Low supply voltage or poor ground disturbing the self-test
s: TPMS malfunction lamp lit permanently
No tire pressures shown at all

P0001.t: Fuel Volume Regulator A Control Circuit/Open
P0001.d: The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure. P0001 is set when the control module detects that the control circuit of this valve is open, i.e. no plausible current flows when the valve is driven. Rail pressure can then no longer be controlled as intended. Whether the valve is open or closed without current depends on the design, so the same fault can cause excess pressure in one system and no pressure in another.
c: Connector at the regulator loose, corroded or unplugged
Solenoid coil of the regulator open
Broken wire in the harness, e.g. chafing or rodent damage
Output driver in the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Engine cranks but does not start, or stalls (normally closed valve)
Loss of power or limp mode (normally open valve)
Additional rail pressure codes possible

P0002.t: Fuel Volume Regulator A Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0002.d: The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure. With P0002 the circuit is electrically intact, but command and effect do not match: the measured current does not fit the duty cycle, or rail pressure does not follow the regulator position plausibly.
