The cause is often mechanical, for example a sticking valve, rather than the wiring.
c: Regulator sticking or worn due to dirt, debris or water in the fuel
High resistance at connector or wiring causing wrong current
Low-pressure supply problem: clogged filter or air in the fuel
Rail pressure sensor reading wrong values
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power or limp mode
Jerking or unstable idle
Hard starting or stalling

P0003.t: Fuel Volume Regulator A Control Circuit Low
P0003.d: The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure. P0003 means the control module measures a voltage or current below the expected range on the control circuit, typically because of a short to ground. On some output stages an open circuit is also reported as low. A short on the switched ground side can keep the valve permanently energised.
c: Harness chafed through, short to ground
Shorted turns in the regulator coil (resistance too low)
Water or corrosion in the connector
Output driver in the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Hard starting or stalling
Loss of power or limp mode
Low rail pressure code possible

P0004.t: Fuel Volume Regulator A Control Circuit High
P0004.d: The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure. P0004 means the voltage on the control circuit stays too high for the commanded duty cycle, typically because of a short to battery voltage, or, with a switched ground side, an open circuit. The valve can then not be energised; a normally open design delivers maximum fuel and rail pressure rises.
c: Short to battery voltage in the harness
Open coil or wire, reported as high with ground-side switching
Output driver in the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power or limp mode
Rough running or diesel knock possible
Excess rail pressure codes possible

P0005.t: Fuel Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit/Open
P0005.d: The fuel shutoff valve is a solenoid valve that opens or blocks the fuel supply. On diesel engines it is usually closed without current, so that the engine stops reliably when switched off. The engine control module energises it to let fuel flow and monitors its control circuit continuously. P0005 is set when this control circuit is open. A normally closed valve then cannot open, so the engine does not start or cuts out while driving. Which vehicles use this valve and code varies by manufacturer.
c: Wire or connector interrupted or corroded
Fuse or relay in the valve supply faulty
Output driver in the engine control module faulty
s: Engine cranks but does not start
Engine cuts out suddenly
Check engine light on

P0006.t: Fuel Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit Low
P0006.d: The fuel shutoff valve is a solenoid valve that opens or blocks the fuel supply. On diesel engines it is usually closed without current, so that the engine stops reliably when switched off. The engine control module energises it to let fuel flow and monitors its control circuit continuously. P0006 means voltage or current in the control circuit is below the expected range, typically because of a short to ground; depending on the output stage an open circuit can also show up this way. The valve is then not energised correctly, which can prevent starting or make the engine stall.
c: Short to ground in the harness
Shorted turns in the valve coil
Output driver in the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Hard starting or no start
Engine stalls

P0007.t: Fuel Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit High
P0007.d: The fuel shutoff valve is a solenoid valve that opens or blocks the fuel supply. On diesel engines it is usually closed without current, so that the engine stops reliably when switched off. The engine control module energises it to let fuel flow and monitors its control circuit continuously. P0007 means the voltage in the control circuit stays too high, because the control module expects the line to be pulled to ground. Typical causes are a short to battery voltage or, with ground-side switching, an open circuit. The valve cannot be switched, which leads to starting problems or stalling.
c: Control wire open or shorted to battery voltage
Output driver in the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Hard starting or no start
Engine stalls

P0008.d: The engine control module learns how far each camshaft of bank 1 is offset from the crankshaft and compares this with a reference. P0008 is set when both camshafts of this bank are shifted in the same direction beyond a threshold. That points to the drive shared by the bank: a stretched primary timing chain, a worn tensioner, an idler gear or a crankshaft reluctor wheel that has slipped. A single faulty camshaft phaser does not set this code, because it affects only one camshaft.
c: Timing drive fitted incorrectly after an engine repair
s: Check engine light on
Timing chain rattle, especially at cold start
Loss of power or rough running
Often stored together with P0016 to P0019

P0009.d: The engine control module learns how far each camshaft of bank 2 is offset from the crankshaft and compares this with a reference. P0009 is set when both camshafts of this bank are shifted in the same direction beyond a threshold. That points to the drive shared by the bank: a stretched primary timing chain, a worn tensioner, an idler gear or a crankshaft reluctor wheel that has slipped. A single faulty camshaft phaser does not set this code, because it affects only one camshaft. Bank 2 exists only on V and boxer engines.
c: Timing drive fitted incorrectly after an engine repair
s: Check engine light on
Timing chain rattle, especially at cold start
Loss of power or rough running
Often stored together with P0016 to P0019

P000A.t: A Camshaft Position Slow Response Bank 1
P000A.d: This monitor does not judge the end position of the intake camshaft on bank 1 but how fast it follows a change of the commanded angle. The code is set when the actual angle lags behind the target for too long during several adjustments. The adjustment speed depends directly on oil flow, so worn or wrong oil and a partly clogged screen are the usual causes. Drivability is often hardly affected; the fault is an early warning before the camshaft misses its target position altogether. Bank 1 is the cylinder bank that contains cylinder 1.
c: Oil too thick or too thin, sludged, or oil level low
Screen at the oil control valve partly clogged
Cam phaser leaking internally or worn
Generally weak oil pressure, e.g. worn oil pump or bearings
s: Check engine light on
Slight hesitation when accelerating
Often no noticeable symptoms

P000B.t: B Camshaft Position Slow Response Bank 1
P000B.d: This monitor does not judge the end position of the exhaust camshaft on bank 1 but how fast it follows a change of the commanded angle. The code is set when the actual angle lags behind the target for too long during several adjustments. The adjustment speed depends directly on oil flow, so worn or wrong oil and a partly clogged screen are the usual causes. Drivability is often hardly affected; the fault is an early warning before the camshaft misses its target position altogether. Bank 1 is the cylinder bank that contains cylinder 1.
c: Oil too thick or too thin, sludged, or oil level low
Screen at the oil control valve partly clogged
Cam phaser leaking internally or worn
Generally weak oil pressure, e.g. worn oil pump or bearings
s: Check engine light on
Slight hesitation when accelerating
Often no noticeable symptoms

P000C.t: A Camshaft Position Slow Response Bank 2
P000C.d: This monitor does not judge the end position of the intake camshaft on bank 2 but how fast it follows a change of the commanded angle. The code is set when the actual angle lags behind the target for too long during several adjustments. The adjustment speed depends directly on oil flow, so worn or wrong oil and a partly clogged screen are the usual causes. Drivability is often hardly affected; the fault is an early warning before the camshaft misses its target position altogether. Bank 2 exists only on V and boxer engines; it is the cylinder bank without cylinder 1.
c: Oil too thick or too thin, sludged, or oil level low
Screen at the oil control valve partly clogged
Cam phaser leaking internally or worn
Generally weak oil pressure, e.g. worn oil pump or bearings
s: Check engine light on
Slight hesitation when accelerating
Often no noticeable symptoms

P000D.t: B Camshaft Position Slow Response Bank 2
P000D.d: This monitor does not judge the end position of the exhaust camshaft on bank 2 but how fast it follows a change of the commanded angle. The code is set when the actual angle lags behind the target for too long during several adjustments. The adjustment speed depends directly on oil flow, so worn or wrong oil and a partly clogged screen are the usual causes. Drivability is often hardly affected; the fault is an early warning before the camshaft misses its target position altogether. Bank 2 exists only on V and boxer engines; it is the cylinder bank without cylinder 1.
c: Oil too thick or too thin, sludged, or oil level low
Screen at the oil control valve partly clogged
Cam phaser leaking internally or worn
Generally weak oil pressure, e.g. worn oil pump or bearings
s: Check engine light on
Slight hesitation when accelerating
Often no noticeable symptoms

P000E.t: Fuel Volume Regulator Control Exceeded Learning Limit
P000E.d: The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure. To compensate for tolerances and wear, the control module learns a long-term correction of the regulator control. P000E is set when this correction leaves its calibrated range. The regulator is electrically fine, but the system needs an unusually large correction all the time, which points to wear or contamination of regulator or pump, a weak low-pressure supply, or a missing calibration after a pump replacement.
c: Fuel volume regulator worn or contaminated
Low-pressure side: clogged filter, weak lift pump or air in the fuel
Not calibrated after pump or regulator replacement
s: Check engine light on
Often hardly noticeable at first, later loss of power
Hard starting if rail pressure is wrong
Additional rail pressure codes possible

P000F.t: Fuel System Over Pressure Relief Valve Activated
P000F.d: On common-rail diesel and some gasoline direct-injection systems a spring-loaded pressure relief valve protects the rail and injectors: if pressure rises too far, it opens and returns fuel to the tank, often holding a reduced pressure for limp-home operation. The control module recognises the opening from the rail pressure signal and stores P000F. The code reports an event, not a defect of the relief valve itself; the actual cause usually lies in pressure control, for example a regulator that delivers too much fuel.
c: Fuel volume regulator stuck open or without current, pump over-delivers
Rail pressure sensor reading wrong, control runs into overpressure
Pressure control valve faulty, where fitted
Fuel return line blocked or kinked
Relief valve itself leaking or fatigued
s: Check engine light on
Sudden loss of power or limp mode
Engine may stall
Excess rail pressure code possible

P0010.d: The engine control module drives the oil control valve (a pulse-width modulated solenoid) of the variable valve timing on the intake camshaft on bank 1. It checks the electrical state of this output and sets the code when the circuit is open, or when the measured state does not match the command, for example because of a short. Camshaft adjustment is then disabled and the phaser stays in its locked rest position: the engine keeps running, but with less torque and higher consumption. Bank 1 is the cylinder bank that contains cylinder 1.
c: Solenoid coil of the oil control valve open or shorted
Connector corroded, loose or soaked with engine oil wicking through the valve
Wiring harness chafed through or broken
Supply voltage missing, e.g. blown fuse
Output driver in the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Less pulling power at low and medium engine speed
Rough idle in some engines
Slightly higher fuel consumption

P0011.t: "A" Camshaft Position - Timing Over-Advanced or System Performance (Bank 1)
P0011.d: The engine control module compares the commanded position of the intake camshaft on bank 1 with the actual position it calculates from the camshaft and crankshaft sensors. This code is set when the camshaft sits further advanced than commanded for longer than a calibrated time, or, depending on the manufacturer, when the target is missed in either direction ("system performance"). Typical cause is a phaser that does not return to its rest position, for example because the oil control valve sticks open or its screen is clogged. Bank 1 is the cylinder bank that contains cylinder 1.
c: Oil level too low, oil sludged or wrong viscosity
Screen at the oil control valve clogged with debris
Cam phaser worn or its locking pin sticking
Timing chain worn or fitted incorrectly after a repair
s: Check engine light on
Rough or unstable idle, as valve overlap is too large
Engine may stall at idle
Rattling from the timing drive at cold start
Higher fuel consumption

P0012.d: The engine control module compares the commanded position of the intake camshaft on bank 1 with the actual position from the camshaft and crankshaft sensors. This code is set when the camshaft stays further retarded than commanded for longer than a calibrated time. Usually the phaser does not move far enough out of its rest position, because oil pressure is too low to release the locking pin, the oil control valve does not open, or the oil screen is blocked. A stretched timing chain also shifts the camshaft towards retarded. Bank 1 is the cylinder bank that contains cylinder 1.
c: Oil pressure or oil level too low, oil worn out
Oil control valve sticking closed or its screen blocked
Cam phaser defective or seized in its rest position
Timing chain stretched or jumped a tooth
Wear debris in the oil circuit, e.g. from a thrust bearing
s: Check engine light on
Noticeably less torque and pulling power
Higher fuel consumption
Harder starting in some cases
Rattle from the timing drive if the chain is stretched

P0026.t: Intake Valve Control Solenoid Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1)
P0026.d: A solenoid valve routes engine oil to a valve control element on the intake side of bank 1. Depending on the manufacturer this is a valve lift changeover or a camshaft phaser. P0026 is a plausibility fault: the electrical control is in order, but the expected effect does not occur or comes too late. The control module recognises this from feedback such as an oil pressure switch or the camshaft sensor. Pure circuit faults of the same solenoid have their own codes. The engine usually remains drivable, but with less power and higher consumption.

Feedback oil pressure switch faulty or leaking (systems with switch)
Screen in front of the solenoid clogged, or solenoid sticking
Mechanical fault in the valve train, e.g. locking pin or phaser sticking
Contact resistance in wiring or connector
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power, no extra pull at higher engine speed
Higher fuel consumption
Rough idle possible if a phaser is affected

P0030.d: The upstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 (sensor 1, before the catalytic converter) only delivers a usable signal once its ceramic element is hot. A heating element inside the sensor gets it there quickly after a cold start. Typically the heater receives battery voltage via a fuse or relay, and the engine control module switches the ground side with a pulsed signal while comparing the commanded state with the measured voltage or current. P0030 is the general circuit fault: the measured state does not fit the command, most often because the circuit is interrupted. Which physical fault sets P0030, P0031 or P0032 is defined by each manufacturer. Without heating, closed-loop mixture control starts late and cold-start emissions rise.
c: Heater circuit interrupted, e.g. broken or chafed wire near the exhaust
Heating element inside the sensor burnt out
Connector corroded or terminal pushed back
Heater supply fuse or relay faulty
Output driver in the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable drivability problem
Closed-loop control starts late after a cold start
Emissions test or readiness check failed

P0031.t: HO2S Heater Control Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P0031.d: The upstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 (sensor 1, before the catalytic converter) only delivers a usable signal once its ceramic element is hot. A heating element inside the sensor gets it there quickly after a cold start. Typically the heater receives battery voltage via a fuse or relay, and the engine control module switches the ground side with a pulsed signal while comparing the commanded state with the measured voltage or current. P0032.d: The upstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 (sensor 1, before the catalytic converter) only delivers a usable signal once its ceramic element is hot. Typically the heater receives battery voltage via a fuse or relay, and the engine control module switches the ground side with a pulsed signal while comparing the commanded state with the measured voltage or current. P0033.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Control Circuit
P0033.d: The turbocharger bypass valve A is the compressor recirculation (diverter) valve: it connects the pressure side of the compressor with the intake side upstream of the turbocharger. It opens when the throttle closes quickly at high boost, so the compressor does not surge and the compressor wheel keeps its speed for the next acceleration. Output driver in the engine control module faulty

P003A.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Position Exceeded Learning Limit
P003A.d: The electric boost actuator A positions the variable turbine vanes or the wastegate and reports its position through a sensor. In a learning run, for example with the engine warm at idle or after switching off, the control module drives the actuator to its mechanical end stops and stores the sensor values as reference. P003A is set when a learned end position or the total travel lies outside the permitted limits. Typical reasons are worn or sticking vanes or linkage, a faulty actuator, a broken actuator lever, or a replacement actuator that has not been learned in. A usually denotes the first turbocharger in the exhaust flow.

Position sensor or its wiring faulty
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power mode
Underboost or overboost codes possible
Sometimes no noticeable symptoms

P003C.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Performance/Stuck Off Bank 1
P003C.d: The camshaft profile actuator A switches the intake camshaft (camshaft A) on bank 1 between fixed cam profiles, usually a low-lift base profile and a high-lift profile. In most designs the unactuated state ("off") is the base profile; which profile counts as "on" is defined by the manufacturer. The control module does not need a position sensor to check the switchover: it detects the actual profile indirectly, for example from oil pressure in the switching gallery, intake pressure per cylinder or crankshaft speed fluctuations. This code is set when the switchover is commanded but the camshaft stays on the base profile, or switches too slowly or incompletely. The engine then lacks power at higher engine speed.
c: Oil level too low, wrong viscosity or sludged oil, so switching pressure is missing
Profile switching solenoid sticking or its screen clogged
Oil supply to the switching elements leaking or restricted, e.g. worn seals
Locking pin in tappet or rocker arm, or sliding cam piece, sticking
Consequence of a circuit fault of the same actuator
s: Check engine light on
Lack of power at higher engine speed
Reduced power mode on some vehicles

This code is set when the base profile is commanded but the camshaft stays on the switched profile. Large lift and long opening at low engine speed cause rough idle and poor low-speed running.

Sliding cam piece stuck in the high-lift position

Poor running when cold
Misfire codes possible

P0040.t: O2 Sensor Signals Swapped Bank 1 Sensor 1/Bank 2 Sensor 1
P0040.d: On engines with two exhaust banks, the control module checks whether the upstream oxygen sensors are assigned to the right bank. It changes the mixture on one bank only, actively or as part of normal bank-wise control, and watches which sensor responds. If the sensor that should sit on the other bank reacts, the signals are swapped. This logic is documented for the manufacturer-specific predecessor codes; the usual cause is connectors plugged in crosswise after a repair. If the swap remains, each bank is controlled by the other bank's signal, so fuel trims drift towards their limits.

Harness routed wrongly or pins swapped in a connector
Wrong harness, control module or calibration after a replacement
s: Check engine light on

Unstable idle or higher consumption possible

P005A.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Performance/Stuck Off Bank 1
P005A.d: The camshaft profile actuator A switches the exhaust camshaft (camshaft B) on bank 1 between fixed cam profiles, usually a low-lift base profile and a high-lift profile. In most designs the unactuated state ("off") is the base profile; which profile counts as "on" is defined by the manufacturer. The control module does not need a position sensor to check the switchover: it detects the actual profile indirectly, for example from oil pressure in the switching gallery, intake pressure per cylinder or crankshaft speed fluctuations. This code is set when the switchover is commanded but the camshaft stays on the base profile, or switches too slowly or incompletely. The engine then lacks power at higher engine speed.
c: Oil level too low, wrong viscosity or sludged oil, so switching pressure is missing
Profile switching solenoid sticking or its screen clogged
Oil supply to the switching elements leaking or restricted, e.g. worn seals
Locking pin in tappet or rocker arm, or sliding cam piece, sticking
Consequence of a circuit fault of the same actuator
s: Check engine light on
Lack of power at higher engine speed
Reduced power mode on some vehicles

P005B.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator A Control Stuck On Bank 1

The control module does not need a position sensor to check the switchover: it detects the actual profile indirectly, for example from oil pressure in the switching gallery, intake pressure per cylinder or crankshaft speed fluctuations. This code is set when the base profile is commanded but the camshaft stays on the switched profile. Large lift and long opening at low engine speed cause rough idle and poor low-speed running.
c: Profile switching solenoid stuck open, oil pressure is not released
Locking pin does not return (weak spring, burr or dirt)
Oil pressure too high or drain from the switching gallery blocked
Sliding cam piece stuck in the high-lift position
s: Check engine light on
Rough idle and jerking at low engine speed
Poor running when cold
Misfire codes possible

P005E.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control B Supply Voltage Circuit Low
P005E.d: "Boost control B" is the electrically driven actuator the engine control module uses to set boost pressure: depending on the engine a pulse-width modulated solenoid or vacuum converter at the wastegate, the control valve of variable turbine vanes, or an electric actuator with position feedback. B is the second actuator, for example on the high-pressure turbocharger of a two-stage system or on the second turbocharger; it does not denote cylinder bank 2. This code concerns the supply voltage that the control module switches to the actuator (high side): it is too low, for example because of a short to ground or an open circuit. Without control the actuator usually falls back to its rest position, which on most engines means low boost; depending on the design too much boost is also possible.
c: Supply wire shorted to ground or interrupted
Fuse or relay of the supply faulty
High-side driver in the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power or reduced power mode
Weak acceleration, noticeable turbo lag
Overboost possible in rare cases

P0065.d: Air-assisted injectors have an air sleeve around the nozzle tip: air flowing past at high speed breaks the fuel spray into finer droplets, which improves combustion and cold starts and lowers hydrocarbon emissions. On port-injected engines this air is taken upstream of the throttle and dosed by a pulse-width modulated bypass solenoid; because it bypasses the throttle, it is part of the idle air. The system is rare and mainly found on older engines. P0065 means the control is electrically in order, but the effect is implausible. One documented method compares the idle speed controller correction with the air assistance switched on and off during stable idle; if the difference is too large, the code is set.
c: Air hoses to the injectors leaking, disconnected or blocked
Air passages at the injectors coked
s: Check engine light on
Rough or unstable idle
Poorer cold starting

P0068.d: The engine control module compares the air quantity measured by the manifold pressure and/or mass air flow sensor with the quantity the throttle position leads it to expect. P0068 is set when they do not match, typically because more air arrives than the nearly closed throttle allows, i.e. an air leak behind the throttle, or because the throttle body is dirty or a sensor reads wrong. On engines with electronic throttle this check protects throttle control, so the engine often goes into reduced power. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own.
c: Air leak behind the throttle: intake manifold, vacuum or MAP hoses
Mass air flow or manifold pressure sensor faulty
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power mode
Rough or unstable idle
Jerking

P0069.t: Manifold Absolute Pressure - Barometric Pressure Correlation
P0069.d: With the ignition on and the engine stopped, the intake manifold is at ambient pressure, so the manifold pressure sensor and the barometric pressure sensor (often inside the control module) must read almost the same. P0069 is set when they differ by more than a threshold. Some systems also compare the barometric reading with a value estimated from manifold pressure at wide-open throttle while driving. Altitude and weather shift both values equally and do not cause the code. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own.
c: MAP sensor hose blocked, kinked or leaking
Barometric pressure sensor (often inside the control module) faulty
s: Check engine light on
Often no further symptoms
Mixture or power deviations possible

P006A.t: MAP - Mass or Volume Air Flow Correlation Bank 1
P006A.d: The engine control module compares the air quantity measured by the mass air flow sensor with the quantity it calculates from manifold pressure, engine speed and temperature. P006A is set when the two deviate too far. A typical cause is an exhaust gas recirculation valve that does not close: recirculated exhaust raises manifold pressure without passing the air flow sensor. Air leaks, a leaking crankcase ventilation hose or a dirty sensor have the same effect. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own.
c: EGR valve dirty or sticking open
Air leak or crankcase ventilation hose leaking
Mass air flow sensor dirty or manifold pressure sensor faulty
s: Check engine light on
Rough running
Slight hesitation when accelerating

P006B.d: On engines with an exhaust pressure sensor, mostly turbocharged diesels, the control module checks whether manifold pressure and exhaust back pressure fit each other, for example with the engine stopped, when both should be at ambient pressure. P006B is set when they do not. No manufacturer description of this code was found; the explanation follows the general rule for plausibility checks of input sensors. Suspects are the exhaust pressure sensor or its sooted hose, and the manifold pressure sensor. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own.
c: Exhaust pressure sensor faulty or its hose sooted or blocked
EGR or turbocharger fault distorting pressures
s: Check engine light on
Often no further symptoms

P006C.d: On turbocharged or supercharged engines the control module compares manifold pressure with the pressure measured upstream of the throttle, for example at idle or with the throttle wide open, where the two must lie close together. P006C is set when the difference exceeds a threshold. Manufacturers interpret "inlet pressure" differently: some mean boost pressure upstream of the throttle, others the pressure at the compressor inlet. Typical causes are a leak in the charge-air path or a faulty pressure sensor. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own.
c: Leak or disconnected hose in the charge-air path
Boost or inlet pressure sensor faulty
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power possible
Hissing from a charge-air leak

P006D.t: Barometric Pressure - Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Correlation Bank 1
P006D.d: Without boost, for example with the engine stopped or at low load, the pressure sensor ahead of the turbocharger or supercharger must read about the same as the barometric pressure sensor. P006D is set when the difference is too large; some manufacturers compare against an estimated barometric value instead and run the check once per ignition cycle. Typical causes are a faulty inlet pressure sensor, a faulty barometric sensor (often inside the control module) or a wiring or reference-voltage fault. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own.
c: Barometric pressure sensor or control module faulty
Wiring, connector or 5 V reference faulty
Clogged air filter lowering pressure ahead of the compressor
s: Check engine light on
Often no further symptoms
Reduced boost possible

P006E.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Supply Voltage Circuit Low
P006E.d: "Boost control A" is the electrically driven actuator the engine control module uses to set boost pressure, for example a wastegate solenoid, the control valve of variable turbine vanes or an electric actuator. Some engines supply it through two driver stages in the control module: a high side that switches the supply voltage and a low side that switches ground. The low side is covered by P0045 to P0048; this code concerns the high side. P006E is set when the switched supply voltage is too low, typically because the supply wire is shorted to ground or interrupted. Without supply the actuator stays in its rest position, which on most engines means low boost and reduced power.
c: Supply wire shorted to ground or interrupted
Connector at the actuator corroded or loose
High-side driver in the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power or reduced power mode
Weak acceleration, noticeable turbo lag

P006F.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Supply Voltage Circuit High
P006F.d: "Boost control A" is the electrically driven actuator the engine control module uses to set boost pressure, for example a wastegate solenoid, the control valve of variable turbine vanes or an electric actuator. Some engines supply it through two driver stages in the control module: a high side that switches the supply voltage and a low side that switches ground. The low side is covered by P0045 to P0048; this code concerns the high side. P006F is set when the voltage on the supply circuit is too high, typically because the supply wire is shorted to battery voltage, so the control module can no longer switch the actuator off. Without supply the actuator stays in its rest position, which on most engines means low boost and reduced power.
c: Supply wire shorted to battery voltage
Water or corrosion in the connector
High-side driver in the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power or reduced power mode
Weak acceleration, noticeable turbo lag

P0070.t: Ambient Air Temperature Sensor Circuit A
P0070.d: The ambient air temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as temperature rises. Its value is used by the climate control, the outside temperature display and the engine control module, which needs it to enable other diagnostics and to correct its maps. Depending on the vehicle the engine control module reads the sensor directly, or the instrument cluster or another module sends the value over the data bus; some vehicles have no sensor and estimate ambient temperature from intake air temperature. P0070 is the general circuit fault or an invalid signal, for example when the instrument cluster reports the value as invalid or the reading is implausibly low.
c: Sensor faulty (exposed to spray and stone chips at the front)
Connector corroded or wire damaged, e.g. after front-end damage
Instrument cluster or data transmission faulty (vehicles with bus-supplied value)
s: Wrong or missing outside temperature display
Climate control regulates incorrectly
Check engine light on (manufacturer-dependent)
Other monitors may not complete

P0071.t: Ambient Air Temperature Sensor Circuit A Range/Performance
P0071.d: The ambient air temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as temperature rises. Its value is used by the climate control, the outside temperature display and the engine control module, which needs it to enable other diagnostics and to correct its maps. Depending on the vehicle the engine control module reads the sensor directly, or the instrument cluster or another module sends the value over the data bus; some vehicles have no sensor and estimate ambient temperature from intake air temperature. P0071 is a plausibility check: after a long standstill (several hours) ambient, intake air and coolant temperatures should be close together. If the ambient reading deviates by more than a threshold at the next start, the code is set; an engine block heater or strong sunshine are excluded where the system can detect them.
c: Sensor mounted in a heat-affected spot, e.g. after a repair
Actually the comparison sensor (intake air or coolant) is faulty
s: Wrong or missing outside temperature display

Depending on the vehicle the engine control module reads the sensor directly, or the instrument cluster or another module sends the value over the data bus; some vehicles have no sensor and estimate ambient temperature from intake air temperature. c: Instrument cluster or data transmission faulty (vehicles with bus-supplied value)
s: Outside temperature display shows implausibly low values
Climate control regulates incorrectly
Check engine light on (manufacturer-dependent)
Other monitors may not complete

Valve control is then switched off or stays in its base position.

Oil at the connector, e.g. from a leaking valve O-ring
Output driver or supply in the engine control module faulty

Less power, especially at high engine speed with lift changeover

P0087.d: On common-rail diesel and gasoline direct-injection engines, a high-pressure pump feeds the fuel rail, a sensor measures rail pressure, and the engine control module regulates it towards a target from its maps. P0087 is set when the actual pressure stays below the target by more than a threshold for some time. It is a system code: it does not say which component is at fault. Typical causes are a weak low-pressure supply, a worn high-pressure pump, a sticking control valve, a leak or a drifting pressure sensor; the engine usually goes into reduced power.
c: Low-pressure supply too weak: lift pump, clogged filter, low tank level or waxing
Pressure control or metering valve sticking
High-pressure leak or excessive injector return flow
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power or reduced power mode
Hard starting or stalling
Jerking under load

P0088.d: On common-rail diesel and gasoline direct-injection engines, a high-pressure pump feeds the fuel rail, a sensor measures rail pressure, and the engine control module regulates it towards a target from its maps. P0088 is set when the actual pressure stays above the target by more than a threshold for some time. On many gasoline systems the pump can only raise pressure, which is then reduced only by injecting. Typical causes are a sticking pressure control or metering valve, a drifting pressure sensor or, on diesels with a pressure control valve, a blocked return. Real overpressure can cause harsh combustion noise and smoke.
c: Pressure control or metering valve sticking
Fuel return blocked (diesel with pressure control valve)
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power or reduced power mode
Harsh combustion noise
Smoke from the exhaust

P0089.d: On common-rail diesel and gasoline direct-injection engines, a high-pressure pump feeds the fuel rail, a sensor measures rail pressure, and the engine control module regulates it towards a target from its maps. The fuel pressure regulator A is the actuator the manufacturer designates for this: depending on the system a pressure control valve that releases fuel from the rail, or the control valve on the high-pressure pump. Some manufacturers report the pump valve under the "fuel volume regulator" codes instead. P0089 is a function check: pressure may still be plausible, but the regulator works at its limit, needs too much correction, or pressure does not follow its control signal. Typical causes are a sticking or worn regulator, a weak pump or a faulty pressure sensor.
c: Pressure regulator or pump control valve sticking or worn
s: Check engine light on
Jerking or hesitation
Loss of power, reduced power mode possible

P008A.t: Low Pressure Fuel System Pressure - Too Low
P008A.d: Some engines, mainly gasoline direct injection with a demand-controlled in-tank pump, have their own pressure sensor in the low-pressure line between the tank pump and the high-pressure pump. The engine control module compares this supply pressure with its target. P008A is set when the supply pressure stays too low. Besides a weak tank pump or its control unit, a clogged filter or a faulty sensor, simply running the tank empty can set this code.
c: Tank run empty or very low fuel level
In-tank pump or its control unit faulty
s: Check engine light on
Hard starting
Jerking under load
High-pressure codes may follow

P008B.t: Low Pressure Fuel System Pressure - Too High
P008B.d: Some engines, mainly gasoline direct injection with a demand-controlled in-tank pump, have their own pressure sensor in the low-pressure line between the tank pump and the high-pressure pump. The engine control module compares this supply pressure with its target. P008B is set when the supply pressure stays too high. Manufacturer bulletins name a faulty low-pressure sensor as the most common cause, for example from fuel entering the sensor and falsifying its signal; a mechanical gauge test clarifies whether the pressure is really too high.
s: Check engine light on
Often no drivability symptoms

P008C.d: On some common-rail diesels, fuel returning from the injection system is cooled in a heat exchanger connected to a low-temperature coolant circuit. An electric coolant pump, switched by the engine control module depending on fuel temperature, drives this circuit. P008C reports an open control circuit of this pump or its relay. If the pump fails for long, the fuel runs hotter; some systems then limit power to protect components.
c: Output driver in the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Often no further symptoms
Reduced power when fuel gets hot possible

P008F.d: After the engine has been switched off long enough, coolant and fuel should have approached the same temperature. The engine control module compares the coolant temperature sensor with the fuel temperature sensor at the next cold start and sets P008F if they differ too much. From this alone it cannot tell which sensor is wrong, so both have to be checked. Regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors; the exact conditions are manufacturer-specific.
c: Values distorted, e.g. by an auxiliary heater
s: Check engine light on
Usually no drivability symptoms
Cold-start behaviour may be affected

P0093.t: Fuel System Leak Detected - Large Leak
P0093.d: A leak in the high-pressure fuel system is not measured directly but inferred from a pressure and volume balance. P0093 means the pump is already delivering at its limit and rail pressure still stays well below target. The leak can be external (line, rail) or internal (injector return, relief valve). An external leak is a fire hazard: stop the engine and inspect it.
c: High-pressure line or rail fitting leaking
Pressure relief or control valve leaking
Weak pump or low-pressure supply mistaken for a leak
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power or reduced power mode
Long cranking
Fuel smell or visible leak

P0094.t: Fuel System Leak Detected - Small Leak
P0094.d: A leak in the high-pressure fuel system is not measured directly but inferred from a pressure and volume balance. P0094 is typically detected when rail pressure drops too fast during overrun with injection cut off, or when more pump delivery than expected is needed at idle. Possible leaks are injectors with too much leak-off, fittings or relief valves; internal leakage can dilute the engine oil with fuel, so a rising oil level is a warning sign.
s: Check engine light on
Long cranking
Rising engine oil level from fuel dilution
Slight loss of power

P0095.t: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 2 Circuit Bank 1
P0095.d: Intake air temperature sensor 2 is the second air temperature sensor in the intake path. On many turbocharged engines it sits in the intake manifold behind the compressor and charge air cooler, often combined with the manifold pressure sensor, and is used to calculate cylinder filling and ignition timing. The numbering is not standardised, so its position can differ between manufacturers. P0095 is the general circuit fault; low and high signals have their own codes. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found.
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable symptoms
Slightly changed power or retarded ignition possible

P009A.t: Intake Air Temperature/Ambient Air Temperature Correlation
P009A.d: After a long standstill with the engine cold, intake air temperature and ambient air temperature should be about the same. P009A is set when the two sensors disagree by more than a threshold at the next start. A detected engine block heater usually suspends the test. Several manufacturers perform this comparison under other codes; no manufacturer description naming P009A itself was found. Suspects are both sensors, an ambient sensor in a heat-affected position and contact resistance at a connector.

P009B.d: The fuel pressure relief control is an electrically controlled valve on the fuel rail that the engine control module opens to reduce rail pressure deliberately, for example on overrun, on load drops or when the engine is switched off. It differs from the purely mechanical pressure relief valve, which opens passively at overpressure, and from the pressure regulator, which controls pressure continuously. Manufacturer documents show this code mainly on heavy-duty diesel engines. P009B reports an open control circuit of this valve. Rail pressure can then not be reduced as intended, and the engine may be derated.
c: Output driver in the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power (derate) possible

P00AF.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Module Performance
P00AF.d: Boost control A here is an electronic actuator with its own electronics (a "smart" actuator), usually on the variable turbine geometry, with its own position sensor and controlled over a data bus or a pulsed signal. It checks itself and reports internal faults to the engine control module; documented examples are pattern errors, overcurrent and checksum errors. The control module cannot narrow down a fault inside the actuator further. P00AF is set when actuator A reports such an internal fault. Manufacturer bulletins recommend checking the vane mechanism for free movement and, if it moves freely, replacing only the actuator rather than the whole turbocharger.
c: Electronics or motor inside the actuator faulty
Sector gear or vane mechanism sticking (soot, coking), causing overcurrent
Weak supply or ground, corroded connector
Software of actuator or control module
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power or limp mode with reduced boost
Often stored with actuator position or boost codes

P00B0.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control B Module Performance
P00B0.d: Boost control B here is an electronic actuator with its own electronics (a "smart" actuator), usually on the variable turbine geometry, with its own position sensor and controlled over a data bus or a pulsed signal. It checks itself and reports internal faults to the engine control module; documented examples are pattern errors, overcurrent and checksum errors. The control module cannot narrow down a fault inside the actuator further. B denotes the second, separate actuator. P00B0 is set when actuator B reports an internal fault. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found; the explanation follows its documented counterpart.
c: Electronics or motor inside the actuator faulty
Sector gear or vane mechanism sticking (soot, coking), causing overcurrent
Weak supply or ground, corroded connector
Software of actuator or control module
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power or limp mode with reduced boost

P00B1.d: The radiator coolant temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor that measures coolant temperature on the radiator side, typically at the radiator outlet; the exact position depends on the manufacturer. Together with the engine coolant temperature sensor it gives a second measuring point, which the control module uses to diagnose the thermostat and coolant flow, for example on engines with an electrically heated map-controlled thermostat. P00B1 is the general circuit fault; low and high signals have their own codes. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found.
c: Connector or wiring at the radiator corroded or damaged (exposed front position)
s: Check engine light on
Thermostat and coolant flow diagnostics are suspended
Often no noticeable symptoms

P00B6.t: Radiator Coolant Temperature/Engine Coolant Temperature Correlation
P00B6.d: The radiator coolant temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor that measures coolant temperature on the radiator side, typically at the radiator outlet; the exact position depends on the manufacturer. Together with the engine coolant temperature sensor it gives a second measuring point, which the control module uses to diagnose the thermostat and coolant flow, for example on engines with an electrically heated map-controlled thermostat. After a long standstill (eight hours in a documented case) engine and radiator should be at the same temperature. P00B6 is set at the next start when the engine and radiator coolant temperature sensors differ by more than a threshold that may depend on intake air temperature. A detected engine block heater cancels the test. From this alone the control module cannot tell which sensor is wrong.
c: Retrofitted engine preheater or auxiliary heater not detected by the system
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable symptoms

P00B7.d: When the engine is hot, the thermostat should be open and coolant should flow through the radiator. P00B7 is set when the engine coolant temperature is very high (above about 117 to 119 °C in documented cases) while the radiator side stays much colder, so too little coolant flows through the radiator. The usual cause is a thermostat stuck closed; low coolant, air in the system, a pump that delivers too little or a blocked radiator have the same effect. If the temperature keeps rising, stop driving to avoid engine damage.
c: Low coolant level or air in the cooling system
Coolant pump delivering too little (impeller, drive; known cases on some engines)
One of the temperature sensors reading wrong
s: Check engine light on
Coolant warning light
High engine temperature up to overheating
Weak or fluctuating cabin heating

P00B8.t: MAP - Mass or Volume Air Flow Correlation Bank 2
P00B8.d: On engines with two intake paths, the control module compares the manifold pressure of bank 2 with the measured or calculated air quantity of that bank. P00B8 is set when the two do not fit together; the code does not say which value is wrong. As with its bank 1 counterpart, typical causes are an air leak, an exhaust gas recirculation valve that does not close, or a dirty or drifting sensor. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found; the explanation follows its documented counterpart.
c: Air leak in the intake of bank 2
EGR valve dirty or sticking open
Manifold pressure sensor or air flow meter dirty or drifting
s: Check engine light on
Rough running
Mixture codes possible

P00B9.t: Low Pressure Fuel System Pressure - Too Low. Low Ambient Temperature
P00B9.d: This code reports too low a pressure in the low-pressure fuel supply between the lift pump and the high-pressure pump under the additional condition of low ambient temperature. It separates cold-related supply problems from the general case. A typical mechanism, documented for diesel engines, is wax separating from insufficiently winterised fuel at sub-zero temperatures and clogging the filter or tank strainer. No manufacturer description naming this exact code, its thresholds or the vehicles using it was found.
c: Wax separation from summer or insufficiently winterised diesel in frost
Fuel filter clogged or water in the filter frozen
s: Check engine light on
Hard or no cold start
Jerking or loss of power after starting

P00BA.t: Low Fuel Pressure - Forced Limited Power
P00BA.d: "Forced limited power" is a term for a protective strategy in which the engine control module deliberately limits engine power. Regulations require the check engine light to come on within seconds when such an emissions-relevant limp-home mode is active. These codes report the reason for the limitation; usually further codes point to the actual cause. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found. P00BA: power has been limited because fuel pressure is too low, which protects the engine and the pump against running lean or losing rail pressure.
c: Fuel filter clogged, suction-side leak or air in the system
Lift pump or high-pressure pump weak
Pressure regulator or relief valve leaking
s: Check engine light on
Marked loss of power, limp mode
Hard starting or jerking

P00BB.t: Fuel Injector Insufficient Flow - Forced Limited Power
P00BB.d: "Forced limited power" is a term for a protective strategy in which the engine control module deliberately limits engine power. These codes report the reason for the limitation; usually further codes point to the actual cause. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found. P00BB: power has been limited because the injectors do not deliver enough fuel, for example due to coking or wear; low rail pressure or missing injector coding after a replacement have a similar effect.
s: Check engine light on
Marked loss of power, limp mode

P00BC.t: Mass or Volume Air Flow A Circuit Range/Performance - Air Flow Too Low
P00BC.d: The control module compares the air mass measured by the air flow meter with the air mass it expects from a model, for example from manifold pressure, boost pressure and throttle position. These codes report the deviation with its direction: "too low" means the meter measures less air than expected, "too high" more. Regulations allow manufacturers to use one code for both directions or separate codes, as here. P00BC concerns air flow meter A. Typical causes are air entering behind the meter, a charge-air leak, a dirty meter or a restricted intake. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found; the explanation follows its documented counterpart.
c: Air leak behind the meter or charge-air leak
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power
Lean mixture codes possible

P00BD.d: The control module compares the air mass measured by the air flow meter with the air mass it expects from a model, for example from manifold pressure, boost pressure and throttle position. Typical causes are a drifting or oil-coated meter or a wrong model value, for example from a faulty manifold pressure sensor or an open exhaust gas recirculation valve. P00C0.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Control Circuit
P00C0.d: Bypass valve B is the compressor recirculation (diverter) valve of turbocharger B, not the wastegate: it lets charge air flow back to the compressor inlet when the throttle closes quickly, so the compressor does not surge. Turbocharger B is the second turbocharger in exhaust flow on series systems and the turbocharger of bank 2 on parallel twin-turbo engines. P00C0 is the general circuit fault, usually an open circuit in the control circuit of this valve; the circuit is monitored continuously.
c: Wiring or connector damaged by turbocharger heat
Output driver in the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Fluttering or surging noise when lifting off the throttle
Boost fluctuations, loss of power

P00C2 reports too high a voltage, typically a short to battery voltage in the control circuit of this valve; the circuit is monitored continuously.
c: Wiring or connector damaged by turbocharger heat
Output driver in the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Fluttering or surging noise when lifting off the throttle
Boost fluctuations, loss of power

No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found; the explanation follows its documented counterpart.

Fluttering or surging noise when lifting off the throttle
Boost fluctuations, loss of power

A documented method detects this on overrun from the pulsation of the measured air mass that compressor surge causes when the valve should open.

s: Check engine light on

P00C5.d: The control module has detected that turbocharger B runs above its permitted maximum speed. Speed is measured by a dedicated sensor per turbocharger where fitted, or estimated from a model of pressure ratio and air mass. Turbocharger B is the second turbocharger in series systems or the one on bank 2 in parallel systems. Typical causes are sticking boost control of this turbocharger or a charge-air leak; find the cause before driving on, as overspeed can destroy the turbocharger. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found; the explanation follows its documented counterpart.
c: Boost control of turbocharger B sticking (wastegate or vanes)
Leak on the pressure side making the turbocharger work harder
Speed sensor or its wiring delivering wrong values
Operation at high altitude or software
s: Check engine light on
Limp mode with reduced power
Whistling from the turbocharger

P00C6.t: Fuel Rail Pressure Too Low - Engine Cranking
P00C6.d: Direct-injection engines release injection only once the rail has reached a minimum pressure. P00C6 is set when this pressure is not reached quickly enough while cranking, or, in another documented variant, when it drops below the minimum again right after the high-pressure start. Cranking then takes longer or the engine does not start. The check runs once per start; some manufacturers only enable it above a minimum tank level.
c: High-pressure pump weak, or its drive cam or follower worn
Lift pump or low-pressure supply too weak
Control valve on the pump faulty
Leak or check valve fault letting pressure bleed off after shutdown
s: Check engine light on
Long cranking
No start
Jerking after starting

P00C7.t: Intake Air Pressure Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 1
P00C7.d: With the engine stopped, all pressure sensors in the intake system (manifold pressure, boost pressure, barometric pressure) should read ambient pressure; some diesels also compare them at idle. The control module compares them: if one sensor stands out, it sets that sensor's own code. P00C7 is set when the readings disagree but no single sensor can be identified as faulty, which points to a fault affecting several sensors, such as a shared reference voltage or ground.
c: Shared 5 V reference or ground of the pressure sensors disturbed
Two sensors drifting at the same time (contamination, oil mist, ageing)
Pressure hose to a sensor leaking or blocked
s: Check engine light on
Often no further symptoms
Substitute values with loss of power possible

P00C8.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator A Solenoid Supply Voltage Control Circuit/Open
P00C8.d: Some engine control modules switch the solenoid of fuel pressure regulator A on both sides: the ground side is monitored by P0090 to P0092, the supply side (high-side driver) by P00C8 to P00CA. On gasoline direct injection the regulator is typically the control valve on the high-pressure pump. P00C8 reports an open circuit on the supply side. Rail pressure can then not be controlled, causing starting problems, stalling or reduced power.
c: Supply wire or connector to the pump solenoid damaged by heat or chafing
High-side driver in the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Hard starting or stalling
Loss of power or limp mode

P00CB.t: Fuel Volume Regulator Solenoid Supply Voltage Control Circuit/Open
P00CB.d: The fuel volume regulator is the solenoid valve that meters how much fuel the high-pressure pump delivers (metering unit on diesels, pump control valve on some gasoline direct-injection engines). None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors.

P00CE.t: Intake Air Temperature Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 1
P00CE.d: After a long standstill (six hours in a documented case) all intake air temperature sensors, for example intake air, charge air cooler and manifold temperature, should read about the same. The control module compares them in pairs: if one sensor stands out, it sets that sensor's own plausibility code. This code is set when no pair agrees, so no single sensor can be identified as faulty. A detected engine preheater suspends the test. Since it runs only after a long standstill, the code may take a night to return after being cleared. Some vehicles also disable start-stop while this code is stored.
c: One temperature sensor drifting without setting its own code
Uneven cooling, undetected preheater or strong sunshine
Shared ground or reference line disturbed, falsifying several sensors
s: Check engine light on
Start-stop disabled on some vehicles
Usually no drivability symptoms

P00CF.t: Barometric Pressure - Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor A Correlation
P00CF.d: With the engine stopped or without boost, the boost pressure sensor A (between compressor and throttle) must read practically ambient pressure. This code is set when it deviates from the barometric pressure sensor by more than a threshold; the code does not say which of the two is wrong. Manufacturers that publish their diagnostics run the same comparison under other codes. None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors.
c: Boost pressure sensor dirty, oil-coated or drifting
Barometric sensor drifting, also when inside the control module
Contact resistance at connector, ground or 5 V reference
Sensor port or hose leaking or blocked
s: Check engine light on
Reduced boost or limp mode possible
Often no further symptoms

P00D1.t: HO2S Heater Control Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1 Sensor 1
P00D1.d: This code concerns the heated oxygen sensor upstream of the catalytic converter (sensor 1) on bank 1. Unlike the heater circuit codes, which report an open or short circuit, this code means the heater is driven but does not bring the oxygen sensor to the expected temperature. One documented method, used where no current-measuring shunt is fitted, measures the internal impedance of the sensor element: a hot element has a low impedance. If the impedance stays above a limit that depends on the calculated element temperature and the voltage at the sensor connector, the heating is judged insufficient. The test runs once per trip. Typical causes are an aged heating element or added resistance from corrosion in the heater circuit. For this sensor position no manufacturer description of the test was found; the code appears in a manufacturer's code list, and the explanation follows the documented counterpart for sensor 2.
c: Corrosion or contact resistance at connector or harness of the heater circuit
Too low supply voltage at the sensor connector, e.g. poor ground
Diagnostic software (manufacturer updates exist for some vehicles)
Replacement sensor with a different heater
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable drivability problem
Oxygen sensor heater readiness stays incomplete

P00D5.t: HO2S Sensor Correlation Bank 1 Sensor 1/Bank 1 Sensor 2
P00D5.d: During fuel cut-off on overrun the exhaust gas is pure air, so the oxygen sensors before and behind the catalytic converter must both report the same lean value. A documented method averages and normalises the signals of both sensors during fuel cut-off and sets the code when they differ by more than a limit; it runs once per drive cycle and needs several overrun phases. The code points to one of the sensors having drifted, not to the catalytic converter. The manufacturer documenting it uses wide-band sensors in both positions.
c: Air or exhaust leak between the sensors falsifying the lean signal
Retrofitted sensor with wrong characteristic, or software
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable drivability problem
Catalyst readiness may stay incomplete

P00D7.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Temperature Too High
P00D7.d: Bypass valve A is the electric compressor recirculation valve, mounted close to the hot compressor and turbine housing. This code reports that its temperature is too high. How the temperature is detected is not described in published manufacturer documents; a documented principle for comparable turbocharger solenoids estimates the coil temperature from current, supply voltage and duty cycle and protects the coil by limiting or switching it off. With the valve switched off, the compressor may surge when lifting off the throttle. None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors.
c: Valve energised for unusually long periods, e.g. due to boost control problems
Coil with shorted turns or aged
Heat shield missing or exhaust leak near the turbocharger
Contact resistance or supply fault distorting the estimate
s: Check engine light on (manufacturer-dependent)
Whistling or fluttering when lifting off the throttle
Slight loss of power

P00D9.t: Ambient Air Temperature Sensor Circuit B
P00D9.d: Ambient air temperature sensor B is a second, separate ambient temperature circuit in addition to sensor A. What the second measuring point is used for in a given vehicle could not be documented; the value may be wired directly to the control module or come over the data bus. Regulations require monitoring of such inputs because ambient temperature is often an enabling condition for other diagnostics. None of the manufacturer documents searched uses these codes; the explanation follows sensor A. P00D9: This is the general circuit fault or an invalid signal.

Connector corroded or wiring damaged, often after front-end work
Module supplying the value over the data bus faulty
s: Wrong or missing outside temperature display
Climate control regulates incorrectly

P00DE.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P00DE.d: With indirect charge air cooling, a water-to-air charge air cooler cools the charge air; it sits in a separate low-temperature coolant circuit with an electric pump and its own radiator. The charge air cooler coolant temperature sensor A measures the coolant temperature of this circuit. The control module uses it to control the pump and to monitor cooling performance. Documented users are diesel engines from Ford and GM. P00DE: This is the general circuit fault; low and high signals have their own codes. P00E3.t: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Stuck Open
P00E3.d: Some engines, mainly hybrids and fuel-saving designs, have an exhaust heat exchanger behind the catalytic converter that transfers exhaust heat into the coolant for faster warm-up of engine and cabin. A bypass valve sends the exhaust either through the heat exchanger or around it. Documented diagnostics compare the coolant temperature rise at the heat exchanger with the commanded mode: if it behaves like bypass while recovery is commanded, or the other way round, the valve is considered stuck. P00E3 reports the valve stuck open. How "open" and "closed" map to bypass and recovery is not publicly documented, so both possible effects should be considered: slow warm-up and weak heating, or excessive coolant heat. None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors.
c: Valve flap coked or corroded and sticking
Heat exchanger temperature sensor faulty, simulating a stuck valve
s: Check engine light on
Slow warm-up and weak heating in winter
Or high coolant temperature and long fan run-on

Shared 5 V reference or ground faulty
Sensor port blocked or hose leaking
s: Check engine light on
Boost limitation or uneven power possible

P00E7.t: Intake Air Temperature Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 2
P00E7.d: After a long standstill (six hours in a documented case) all intake air temperature sensors, for example intake air, charge air cooler and manifold temperature, should read about the same. The control module compares them in pairs: if one sensor stands out, it sets that sensor's own plausibility code. This code is set when no pair agrees, so no single sensor can be identified as faulty. A detected engine preheater suspends the test. Since it runs only after a long standstill, the code may take a night to return after being cleared. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found; bank 2 codes are intended for engines with two separate intake paths.
c: One temperature sensor drifting without setting its own code
Uneven cooling, undetected preheater or strong sunshine
Shared ground or reference line disturbed, falsifying several sensors
s: Check engine light on
Usually no drivability symptoms

P00F2.d: The humidity sensor measures the relative humidity of the intake air; on documented vehicles it is built into the mass air flow sensor or a combined sensor. The engine control module uses the value, for example, to correct torque and in emission models. One documented design is capacitive and reports humidity as a pulsed signal with a duty cycle that the control module converts back. P00F2 reports an open or general circuit fault of the humidity sensor. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found.

s: Check engine light on

P00F7.t: Barometric Pressure - Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Correlation Bank 2
P00F7.d: This is the bank 2 counterpart of the comparison between barometric pressure and the pressure ahead of the turbocharger or supercharger. At low air flow the inlet pressure sensor reads close to ambient pressure, minus the small loss across the air filter, so it must match the barometric reading. The code is set when the difference is too large; a clogged air filter or a leaking intake hose on bank 2 can cause it as well as a drifting sensor. None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors.
c: Inlet pressure sensor of bank 2 drifting or dirty
Air filter or intake of bank 2 clogged
Intake hose between air flow meter and turbocharger leaking or slipped off
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power or boost limitation possible
Whistling from an intake leak

P00F8.t: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit
P00F8.d: The turbocharger outlet pressure sensor A measures the pressure directly at the compressor outlet. It is a separate code family from the boost pressure sensor, which usually measures the pressure just ahead of the throttle; engines use it where the pressure behind the compressor is needed in addition, for example to judge the pressure loss across the charge air cooler or to protect against compressor surge. One manufacturer documents it as a combined temperature and pressure sensor. P00F8 is the general circuit fault of this sensor. None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors.
c: Connector loose or not fully engaged, or sensor not seated properly
Wire interrupted, short to ground or 5 V reference missing
Leak at the sensor flange or seal
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power or limp mode with boost limitation
Jerking under load possible

P00F9.d: The turbocharger outlet pressure sensor A measures the pressure directly at the compressor outlet. P00FB.t: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit High
P00FB.d: The turbocharger outlet pressure sensor A measures the pressure directly after the compressor, usually ahead of the charge air cooler; FCA fits it as a combined temperature and pressure sensor. Boost control and compressor protection use the value. P00FB means the signal voltage is above its valid range: typically a signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage, an open ground, or a failed sensor. It does not mean the boost really is too high – that would be P0234. The circuit is monitored continuously from key-on; comparable GM pressure sensors fail above 86–97 % of the reference for about 4 s. The engine then works with a substitute value and may limit boost. GM and Ford do not use this code family in their published summaries – they rely on the boost sensor ahead of the throttle (P0235–P0238) – so no manufacturer document naming exactly this code was found.
c: Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Ground (low reference) wire open or connector corroded
Sensor faulty internally (oil mist, heat at compressor outlet)
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power or limp mode with boost limit
Further pressure plausibility codes possible

P00FC.t: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A Intermittent/Erratic
P00FC.d: The turbocharger outlet pressure sensor A measures the pressure directly after the compressor, usually ahead of the charge air cooler; FCA fits it as a combined temperature and pressure sensor. Boost control and compressor protection use the value. P00FC covers short dropouts or jumps in the signal that are each too brief for the low or high code, or changes faster than real pressure can move. Comparable intermittent monitors count range violations per drive cycle – Ford's MAP check, for example, sets after 25 events. The FCA case for the sibling code P00F9 was a sensor not fully seated with an unlatched connector, exactly the kind of fault that produces erratic signals; heat and vibration near the turbocharger add to it. GM and Ford do not use this code family in their published summaries – they rely on the boost sensor ahead of the throttle (P0235–P0238) – so no manufacturer document naming exactly this code was found.
c: Connector loose, not latched, or terminals corroded or spread
Harness chafed or broken near the turbocharger (heat, vibration)
s: Check engine light on, possibly only after several drives
Occasional hesitation or brief loss of power under load
Fault comes and goes

P00FD.t: Battery B State of Charge Performance
P00FD.d: 'Battery B' here is not a hybrid high-voltage battery (those have codes from P0B27) but, in the only documented use by FCA/Stellantis, the 12 V auxiliary battery of the start-stop system. When the engine restarts automatically, a relay separates main and auxiliary battery so that the auxiliary one keeps the control units stable while the main battery cranks. The engine module sets P00FD if the auxiliary battery is disconnected on the first start, drops below about 8 V during an auto-start, or repeatedly falls below 10.3 V (counter reaches ten). Start-stop is then disabled; often it follows a jump start or many short trips. Whether the MIL comes on is not stated in the sources.
c: Loose or corroded positive or ground connections at either battery
150 A fuse or fuse array in the power distribution centre open or poorly contacting
s: Start-stop out of service, 'Service Start/Stop' message
Engine does not crank once
'Service Shifter' message with electronic gear selector

P00FE.t: EVAP System Tank Vapor Line Restricted/Blocked
P00FE.d: The evaporative emission system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister and later purges it into the engine. P00FE means the vapour path between tank and canister is restricted or blocked. That matters because a blocked line can hide the tank side from the leak test and disturb tank venting and refuelling. Ford, where P00FE replaces its own code P144A, checks this once per drive cycle during the cruise leak test, while purging with the vent valve closed, and confirms suspicious pressure responses with an intrusive test. VW used the same code on the 2013–2019 Golf, where the diagnosis covers the purge valve and the leak detection module. Typical causes are kinked or pinched lines and charcoal grains from a broken canister.
c: Kinked, pinched or misrouted vapour line between tank and canister
Charcoal canister broken down, grains blocking lines or valves
Rollover or fill-limit valve at the tank stuck closed (e.g. after overfilling)
Purge valve or leak detection module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Fuel nozzle clicks off early when refuelling
Hiss or vacuum when opening the fuel cap
Usually no change in driving

P00FF.t: Body Control Module Requested MIL Illumination
P00FF.d: P00FF is an information code in the engine control module: the body control module has detected an emissions-relevant fault of its own and asks over the data bus for the check engine light. The engine module stores P00FF so that a generic OBD scanner can see why the MIL is on; the actual fault is stored in the body control module as B or U codes and must be read there. GM documents two cases – a 2020 Cadillac CT5 with climate flap actuator codes and 2025 full-size SUVs with U1962 – both cured by reprogramming the body control module, not by replacing parts. The mechanism matches other 'module requested MIL' codes such as P069E. P00FF itself causes no limp mode.
c: Emissions-relevant fault in the body control module or its sensors/actuators (own B/U codes)
Software or calibration fault in the body control module
Communication fault on the data bus
s: Check engine light on without an engine fault
Other messages depending on the body module fault
Driving behaviour unchanged

P0100.t: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit
P0100.d: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0100 means the control module gets no usable signal at all. Ford uses it for a broken sensing element on digital sensors (period longer than 1.3 ms, i.e. below about 0.78 kHz, for half a second); on GM's 3.0 V6 in the Saab 9-4X it is set at 0 Hz. Many systems with voltage sensors skip P0100 and report low or high directly. The engine then runs on air mass calculated from manifold pressure, throttle angle and speed; Ford also disables start-stop.
c: Connector unplugged or corroded, signal or supply wire open
Sensor faulty internally (broken element, failed electronics)
s: Check engine light on
Rough idle, hesitation, lack of power (substitute value)
Hard starting or stalling
Higher fuel consumption

P0101.t: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0101.d: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0101 is a plausibility fault: the signal is electrically fine but does not match the engine's state. GM petrol engines model the expected air flow from manifold pressure, throttle, speed and boost and blame the MAF if it is off by more than 20 g/s; GM diesels check the measured-to-estimated ratio (0.8–1.2) with EGR closed; Bosch ME9 compares it with the throttle angle. Common causes are air leaks after the sensor, a soiled element (oiled sport filters) or a disconnected crankcase vent; GM also documents a bad crimp in the fuse box. Ford uses P0068 instead. Two trips are needed.
c: Air leak between sensor and engine (cracked or loose intake duct, boost leak)
Contaminated sensing element (oil from oiled sport filter, dust)
Clogged or wrongly fitted air filter, modified intake
Aged sensor or poor contact in the wiring
s: Check engine light on, often without driveability problems
Hesitation, flat spot, poor throttle response
Rough idle or stalling
Higher consumption, often with lean codes P0171/P0174

P0102.t: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Low
P0102.d: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0102 means the signal is below its electrical lower limit – a frequency that is too low or a voltage that is too low. Documented limits: GM petrol 450 Hz or less, GM diesel below 276 Hz, Ford digital below 1.5 kHz for 5 s, Ford analogue below 0.244 V. 'Low' describes the signal: typically an open or grounded signal wire, missing supply voltage or failed electronics. Saab notes that a large leak between sensor and throttle can also cause it. GM and Saab need two trips; the engine runs on a calculated substitute value.
