s: Check engine light on (not on GM 2016 diesels)
Brief stumbling or misfire-like dropouts
Occasional limp mode, fault often not reproducible

P0195.t: Engine Oil Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0195.d: The engine oil temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor fed with 5 V through a resistor: the hotter the oil, the lower the signal voltage. The engine module uses the oil temperature for variable cam timing (Ford disables it with cold oil or a sensor fault), engine protection and the oil life monitor; many engines have no such sensor and use a calculated oil temperature instead. P0195 is the general circuit fault without telling low from high. With analogue sensors most manufacturers use P0197/P0198 instead. The documented use is Ford's 2023 diesels with a digital SENT oil temperature sensor: P0195 is set when the sensor reports a status or data fault for 5 s, while a complete loss of communication is U0667. The module then uses a substitute value (Saab: 100 °C), and functions relying on oil temperature are restricted.
c: Connector or harness damaged, corroded or oil-soaked
Sensor faulty internally (electronics fault on SENT sensors)
5 V reference or ground problem in the sensor circuit
s: Check engine light on (depending on manufacturer)
Oil temperature display missing or fixed
Restricted cam timing, slightly reduced power
Oil life calculation less accurate

P0196.t: Engine Oil Temperature Sensor A Range/Performance
P0196.d: The engine oil temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor fed with 5 V through a resistor: the hotter the oil, the lower the signal voltage. The engine module uses the oil temperature for variable cam timing (Ford disables it with cold oil or a sensor fault), engine protection and the oil life monitor; many engines have no such sensor and use a calculated oil temperature instead. P0196 means the signal is electrically valid but implausible – stuck, offset or rising wrongly. GM's LT4 runs three tests: after a cold soak oil, coolant and intake air must agree within 16 °C; during warm-up the oil must reach 90 °C after enough air mass; and continuously it is compared with a model (fault above 30 °C); two trips. Saab expects at least 50 °C once coolant has held 80 °C for 3 min. Caution: on Ford's 2023 diesels P0196 actually checks the coolant sensor against oil temperature (35 °C after 6 h), and Nissan traced it on the Rogue to a faulty coolant control valve.

Comparison sensor (coolant, intake air) or its wiring wrong
Thermal management or coolant control valve, or thermostat faulty (oil genuinely too hot or cold)
s: Check engine light on (usually after two drives)
Implausible oil temperature reading
Possibly a cam timing code alongside
Often no noticeable symptoms

P0197.t: Engine Oil Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low

P0198.t: Engine Oil Temperature Sensor A Circuit High

P019A.t: O2 Sensor Delayed Response - Rich to Lean Bank 1 Sensor 3
P019A.d: Sensor 3 on bank 1 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick; it exists on Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (on both banks) and on Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. 'Delayed response' means the sensor starts reacting too late after a mixture change – unlike 'slow response' (P0145/P0165), where the transition itself is too flat. This code covers the rich-to-lean direction, tested during forced fuel cut-off. For sensor 2, GM checks whether the signal falls below 450 mV before a calibrated air mass has passed; behind two converters their oxygen storage buffers the change, so limits are wide. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found – the Jaguar Land Rover bulletins list only P0142ff/P0162ff for sensor 3 – so the description rests on CARB's response requirement and the sensor 2 logic. There is no limp mode; the converter monitor cannot complete.
c: Converter with strongly differing oxygen storage (aftermarket or new)
s: Check engine light on
No noticeable change in driving
Catalyst readiness not set (emissions test)

P019E.t: Alternative Fuel Tank A Pressure Sensor Circuit
P019E.d: These codes only apply to vehicles that run on a gaseous alternative fuel – compressed natural gas (CNG) or LPG – either as bi-fuel models alongside petrol (for example GM's 2015–2016 Impala Bi-Fuel or 2013–2016 Silverado/Sierra 2500HD) or as dedicated gas engines. CNG is stored at up to about 250 bar (3600 psi); a regulator reduces it to a few bar for the gas rail and injectors. The tank pressure sensor A sits at or in the regulator; together with the tank temperature it gives the gas level, and it decides whether gas operation is possible. P019E is the general circuit fault of this sensor without telling low from high. Ford's earlier bi-fuel CNG system showed the gauge as empty on a tank pressure sensor fault. Typical reaction: gas operation is blocked and a bi-fuel vehicle switches to petrol. No manufacturer document naming exactly this code was found; GM's bulletins only state that faults are reported like on petrol models. The description rests on CARB, which treats such vehicles like petrol engines for model years 2004–2018, and on the documented system design.
c: Connector or harness at the tank pressure sensor (at the regulator) corroded, loose or chafed
Engine or alternative fuel control module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Gas level gauge wrong, jumping or showing empty
Gas operation blocked or automatic switch to petrol
Dedicated gas engines: limp mode or starting problems possible

P01AA.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Temperature Sensor Circuit
P01AA.d: These codes only apply to vehicles with a gaseous alternative fuel – compressed natural gas (CNG) or LPG – as bi-fuel models alongside petrol or as dedicated gas engines; on bi-fuel vehicles a fault usually blocks gas operation and the vehicle runs on petrol. The tank temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor: with CNG there is no float, so the gas level is calculated from tank pressure and tank temperature (GM: full at about 3600 psi at 21 °C, empty at about 400–500 psi). On GM's 2015 Impala Bi-Fuel the sensor is built into the tank and cannot be replaced separately. P01AA is the general circuit fault of this sensor without telling low from high. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the description rests on CARB, which treats such vehicles like petrol engines for model years 2004–2018, and on the documented system design.
c: Connector or wiring of the tank temperature sensor open, corroded or chafed
Gas module, CAN link or engine module
s: Stored fault code (warning light depending on system)
Gas level display wrong
Gas operation blocked, switch to petrol

P01AF.t: Alternative Fuel Tank A Level Sensor Circuit
P01AF.d: These codes only apply to vehicles with a gaseous alternative fuel – compressed natural gas (CNG) or LPG – as bi-fuel models alongside petrol or as dedicated gas engines; on bi-fuel vehicles a fault usually blocks gas operation and the vehicle runs on petrol. Tank level sensor A only exists where there is a real sender – typically LPG tanks with a float whose position is transmitted magnetically through the tank wall (Roush propane systems: 0.1–4.9 V). With CNG the 'level' is a calculated value. The documented systems report level faults under the petrol fuel level codes (Roush propane P0460–P0463, GM CNG van P0463), so no manufacturer document using exactly this code was found. P01AF is the general circuit fault of this sender.
c: Connector or wiring of the level sensor open, corroded or chafed
Gas module, CAN link or engine module
s: Check engine light on
Gas level display wrong, jumping or empty
Range or refuelling information unreliable

P01B4.t: Alternative Fuel Rail Temperature Sensor Circuit
P01B4.d: These codes only apply to vehicles with a gaseous alternative fuel – compressed natural gas (CNG) or LPG – as bi-fuel models alongside petrol or as dedicated gas engines; on bi-fuel vehicles a fault usually blocks gas operation and the vehicle runs on petrol. The gas rail temperature sensor, often combined with the rail pressure sensor, measures the gas temperature at the injectors: gas cools strongly when it expands in the regulator, and the injected mass depends on density, i.e. on rail pressure and temperature, so the module corrects injection time with it. A Ford patent describes plausibility checks against engine bay temperature at idle and an expected cold rail at full load with a full tank. Roush propane systems report rail temperature faults as P0181–P0183; no manufacturer document using exactly this code was found. P01B4 is the general circuit fault of this sensor.
c: Connector or wiring of the rail temperature sensor open, corroded or chafed
Gas module, CAN link or engine module
s: Check engine light on
Gas operation blocked or switch to petrol
Mixture errors or stumbling in gas mode

P01B9.t: Engine Oil Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P01B9.d: The engine oil temperature sensor B is an NTC thermistor fed with 5 V through a resistor: the hotter the oil, the lower the signal voltage. The engine module uses the oil temperature for variable cam timing (Ford disables it with cold oil or a sensor fault), engine protection and the oil life monitor; many engines have no such sensor and use a calculated oil temperature instead. Sensor B is a second oil temperature sensor whose position is defined by the manufacturer. P01B9 is the general circuit fault of sensor B, the counterpart of P0195. No manufacturer document using the B-sensor codes was found, so it is unclear who fits a sensor B; the description follows sensor A and CARB's circuit monitoring requirement.
c: Wiring or connector of sensor B
s: Check engine light on (depending on manufacturer)
Oil temperature reading possibly wrong
Usually no driving symptoms

P01BE.t: Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor Circuit Bank 2
P01BE.d: The bank 2 rail pressure sensor measures the pressure in a second, separate high-pressure rail on V engines that have one rail with its own sensor per bank. Many V engines connect both rails and use only one sensor (P0190–P0194); the only documented user of the bank 2 codes is GM's 5.5 litre LT6 (Corvette Z06 2023–2024) with a digital sensor per rail. P01BE is the general circuit fault of the bank 2 sensor, the counterpart of P0190. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the logic follows the bank 1 sensor and CARB's circuit monitoring requirement. On a fault the module uses a substitute value and usually limits power.
c: Connector or harness of the bank 2 sensor corroded or wet
s: Check engine light on
Limp mode or 'Reduced Engine Power'
Rough running

P01BF.t: Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance Bank 2
P01BF.d: The bank 2 rail pressure sensor measures the pressure in a second, separate high-pressure rail on V engines that have one rail with its own sensor per bank. Many V engines connect both rails and use only one sensor (P0190–P0194); the only documented user of the bank 2 codes is GM's 5.5 litre LT6 (Corvette Z06 2023–2024) with a digital sensor per rail. P01BF is the plausibility fault of the bank 2 sensor, the counterpart of P0191. GM documents it on the LT6 as an 'internal component fault' of the sensor, appearing together with codes for low rail pressure at start (P00C6), pressure regulation at its limit and injector faults: a wrong 12-pin intermediate connector to the bank 2 rail let water in. The fix was a new engine/injector harness and rail pressure sensor. Thresholds are not published; GM's dual-channel comparison on bank 1 (1.0 MPa) suggests similar logic. On a fault the module uses a substitute value and usually limits power.
c: Water or corrosion at the bank 2 intermediate connector (GM LT6: wrong 12-pin connector)
Bank 2 rail pressure sensor faulty internally
Genuine pressure fault on bank 2 (pump, control valve)
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power
Starting problems (with P00C6)
Misfires with injector codes at the same time

P01C0.t: Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor Circuit Low Bank 2

P01C2.t: Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic Bank 2

P01C3.d: Fuel pressure sensor A is a fuel pressure sensor without 'rail' in its name and without a bank – unlike the rail pressure sensors P0190–P0194 and P01BE–P01C2; which sensor it is depends on the manufacturer. The only documented case is FCA, where sensor A is the low-pressure sensor in the supply line, read together with the fuel pump control module. GM calls its low-pressure sensor 'sensor B' (P018A–P018E). P01C3 is its general circuit fault without telling low from high. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the description rests on CARB's circuit monitoring requirement, the FCA sibling code P01C6 and GM's equivalent low-pressure sensor checks.
c: Connector corroded or wet, wire open or shorted
Fuel pump control module or engine module
s: Check engine light on
Hard starting or stalling possible
Hesitation or lack of power under load

Occasional starting problems

P01C8.t: Fuel Rail/System Pressure - Too Low Bank 2
P01C8.d: Some V engines have a separate high-pressure fuel circuit per bank, each with its own pump or rail – for example Audi's 4.0 TFSI V8 with a second high-pressure pump for bank 2. These codes are the bank 2 counterparts of the system pressure codes for bank 1. P01C8 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0087: the actual pressure stays below target over time. Typical causes are a weak high-pressure pump on bank 2, a faulty volume control valve, low supply pressure or a leak. No manufacturer using exactly this code was found; the logic follows P0087 and CARB's requirement for pressure control. Not every two-rail engine uses them: GM's LT6 reports bank 2 pressure problems under other codes.
c: High-pressure pump of bank 2 weak or worn
Volume control valve faulty or its control disturbed
Supply pressure too low (lift pump, filter)
Leak in the bank 2 high-pressure circuit
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power or limp mode
Hard starting, misfires on bank 2

P01C9.t: Fuel Rail/System Pressure - Too High Bank 2
P01C9.d: Some V engines have a separate high-pressure fuel circuit per bank, each with its own pump or rail – for example Audi's 4.0 TFSI V8 with a second high-pressure pump for bank 2. These codes are the bank 2 counterparts of the system pressure codes for bank 1. P01C9 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0088: the actual pressure is above target. Audi documents it on 2013–2014 A8/S8 and S6/S7 4.0 TFSI models together with P0088: at low supply voltage the duty cycle of the volume control valve was no longer sufficient, the valve stayed shut and the pump delivered full flow – audible as noise from pump 2, sometimes with slightly reduced power. The fix was a software update. Not every two-rail engine uses them: GM's LT6 reports bank 2 pressure problems under other codes.
c: Volume control valve not controlled properly (e.g. at low supply voltage), software
Bank 2 rail pressure sensor reading too high
s: Check engine light on (possibly intermittent)
Noise from the bank 2 high-pressure pump
Slightly reduced power possible

P01CA.t: Fuel Rail Pressure Too Low - Engine Cranking Bank 2
P01CA.d: Some V engines have a separate high-pressure fuel circuit per bank, each with its own pump or rail – for example Audi's 4.0 TFSI V8 with a second high-pressure pump for bank 2. These codes are the bank 2 counterparts of the system pressure codes for bank 1. P01CA is the bank 2 counterpart of P00C6: during cranking the rail pressure on bank 2 does not rise quickly enough to the minimum needed to release injection. For bank 1 GM checks once per start that pressure exceeds about 3 MPa and does not fall below 2 MPa, with two trips. No manufacturer using exactly this code was found; GM's two-rail LT6 reports the same situation with the bank-neutral P00C6.
c: High-pressure pump of bank 2 or its drive weak
Low supply pressure at start (lift pump, check valve)
Leak or leaking injector on bank 2
Bank 2 rail pressure sensor or connector
s: Check engine light on
Long cranking or no start
Rough running right after start

P01CB.t: Cylinder 1 Injection Timing Performance - Over Retarded
P01CB.d: Diesel engines must detect when fuel can no longer be injected at the correct crank angle – CARB requires this for every injector individually, hence one code per cylinder. The start of injection is not measured directly: during overrun with fuel cut-off the control module fires a tiny test injection into one cylinder (GM: about 1.5 mm³) and evaluates the resulting speed change at the crankshaft sensor. From this it learns how much extra energizing time the injector needs (Bosch calls this zero fuel calibration). This code means injector 1 needs clearly more energizing time than intended, i.e. it opens too late – GM sets it above 80 µs of extra time, after two trips. Documented users are GM's 6.6 litre Duramax (LML, L5P) and FCA's 3.0 litre EcoDiesel; Ford reports the same function under P2B11ff. Bulletins often point away from the injector: GM fixed false settings on 2020–2021 L5P trucks with new software and warns that vibration, for example from off-road tyres, disturbs the evaluation; FCA lists wrong injector correction codes, boost leaks and loose injector clamps.
c: Injector worn, coked or sticking (opens late, delivers too little)
False setting from software or vehicle vibration (e.g. off-road tyres)
Wrong injector correction code stored after an injector replacement
Boost leak or loose injector clamp
s: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
Louder combustion noise or knocking
Rough idle
Possibly smoke

From this it learns how much extra energizing time the injector needs (Bosch calls this zero fuel calibration). This code means injector 10 needs clearly less energizing time than intended, i.e. it opens too early or delivers too much – GM sets it below −90 µs, after two trips. No manufacturer document using the codes for cylinders 9–12 was found; the description follows CARB's requirement and the documented measuring principle (Bosch patent, GM tables for cylinders 1–8). Such codes can only appear on engines with at least that many cylinders.
c: Injector worn or leaking (delivers too much in small quantities)
False setting from software or vehicle vibration (e.g. off-road tyres)
Wrong injector correction code stored after an injector replacement
Boost leak or loose injector clamp
s: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
Louder combustion noise or knocking
Rough idle
Possibly smoke

P01E3.d: Coolant temperature sensor 3 is a third NTC coolant sensor on engines with thermal management or split cooling circuits; its position is defined by the manufacturer – on Jaguar Land Rover's 2018–2019 Ingenium petrol engines it sits in the engine block water jacket, on Audi's 3.0 TFSI V6 it is part of the thermal management. As with every NTC sensor, a low signal voltage means hot and a high one cold. CARB requires such additional sensors to be monitored from model year 2019 onwards. P01E3 is the general circuit fault of this sensor without telling low from high. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; it is described by analogy with its documented sibling codes and the NTC principle.
c: Open circuit or loose contact at connector or wiring of sensor 3
Short to ground or voltage in the harness
s: Check engine light on
Coolant temperature or cooling fan behaviour possibly affected
Often no change in driving

P01E4.t: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 3 Circuit Range/Performance
P01E4.d: Coolant temperature sensor 3 is a third NTC coolant sensor on engines with thermal management or split cooling circuits; its position is defined by the manufacturer – on Jaguar Land Rover's 2018–2019 Ingenium petrol engines it sits in the engine block water jacket, on Audi's 3.0 TFSI V6 it is part of the thermal management. As with every NTC sensor, a low signal voltage means hot and a high one cold. CARB requires such additional sensors to be monitored from model year 2019 onwards. P01E4 means the signal is electrically valid but implausible. Audi documents it on 2017–2021 3.0 TFSI V6 models together with cooling system, cylinder head temperature and 'engine temperature too low' codes: the cause was a thermostat that did not close fully, and Audi states that replacing the sensor does not fix it.
c: Low coolant or air at the sensor
s: Check engine light on
Engine warms up slowly, heater output weak
Often together with cooling system codes

P01E5.t: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 3 Circuit Low
P01E5.d: Coolant temperature sensor 3 is a third NTC coolant sensor on engines with thermal management or split cooling circuits; its position is defined by the manufacturer – on Jaguar Land Rover's 2018–2019 Ingenium petrol engines it sits in the engine block water jacket, on Audi's 3.0 TFSI V6 it is part of the thermal management. As with every NTC sensor, a low signal voltage means hot and a high one cold. CARB requires such additional sensors to be monitored from model year 2019 onwards. P01E5 means the signal voltage is too low, so the module would read an implausibly hot coolant – typically a signal wire shorted to ground, coolant or moisture in the connector, or an internally shorted sensor. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; it is described by analogy with its documented sibling codes and the NTC principle.
c: Signal wire of sensor 3 shorted to ground (chafing, water in connector)
Coolant in the connector, corrosion with leakage current
s: Check engine light on
Coolant temperature or cooling fan behaviour possibly affected
Often no change in driving

P01E6.t: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 3 Circuit High
P01E6.d: Coolant temperature sensor 3 is a third NTC coolant sensor on engines with thermal management or split cooling circuits; its position is defined by the manufacturer – on Jaguar Land Rover's 2018–2019 Ingenium petrol engines it sits in the engine block water jacket, on Audi's 3.0 TFSI V6 it is part of the thermal management. P01E6 means the signal voltage sits near the reference, so the module would read very cold coolant (around −40 °C) – typically an open signal or ground wire, a loose connector with poor terminal tension, an open sensor or a short to voltage. Jaguar Land Rover documents the code on its 2018–2019 Ingenium petrol engines and has the wiring checked first, then the sensor replaced.
c: Signal or ground wire open, connector loose, poor terminal tension
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or 12 V
s: Check engine light on

Often no change in driving

P01E7.t: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 3 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P01E7.d: Coolant temperature sensor 3 is a third NTC coolant sensor on engines with thermal management or split cooling circuits; its position is defined by the manufacturer – on Jaguar Land Rover's 2018–2019 Ingenium petrol engines it sits in the engine block water jacket, on Audi's 3.0 TFSI V6 it is part of the thermal management. c: Loose contact at connector or pins
Wire break in the harness (movement, vibration)
Sensor opening internally with temperature changes
Corrosion or moisture in the connector
s: Check engine light on
Jumping coolant readings
Usually no change in driving

P01E8.t: Engine Coolant Heater A Control Circuit/Open
P01E8.d: Engine coolant heater A is an electric coolant heater switched by the engine module, directly or via a relay or power stage, to shorten warm-up – less cold-start emissions and faster cabin heat; A and B denote two separately switched heaters or stages. It is not the same as a mains-powered block heater (which the vehicle does not control) or the electrically heated thermostat (P0597–P0599). CARB requires output components to be checked for correct response or at least for circuit faults. This code reports an open control circuit – the module detects missing continuity, typically with the driver switched off. No manufacturer using these codes was found in the GM, Ford or NHTSA documents checked; the typical driver diagnosis (open circuit detected with the driver switched off, as GM does for other outputs) is an analogy, and thresholds are unknown.
c: Control wire or connector to the heater or relay open
Heater element burnt out or relay coil open
Fuse in the load circuit blown
s: Check engine light on
Longer warm-up, cabin heat slower in winter
Usually no change in driving

P01E9.t: Engine Coolant Heater A Control Circuit Low
P01E9.d: Engine coolant heater A is an electric coolant heater switched by the engine module, directly or via a relay or power stage, to shorten warm-up – less cold-start emissions and faster cabin heat; A and B denote two separately switched heaters or stages. This code reports a control circuit voltage that is too low – typically a short to ground in the control line or the heater/relay. No manufacturer using these codes was found in the GM, Ford or NHTSA documents checked; the typical driver diagnosis (open circuit detected with the driver switched off, as GM does for other outputs) is an analogy, and thresholds are unknown.

Moisture or corrosion in the connector
s: Check engine light on

P01F0.t: Coolant Temperature Relapsed Below Diagnostic Monitoring Temperature
P01F0.d: Since model years 2019–2021 CARB requires petrol engines to detect a thermostat fault not only during warm-up but also when the coolant, after reaching operating temperature, drops back below the temperature needed for other diagnostics. P01F0 is this check. GM sets it when coolant falls below 64 °C with a conventional thermostat or 70.5 °C with an electrically heated one (2019 Corvette: 65/78.5 °C) after having been above it, with at least 0.8 km driven, ambient above −7 °C, enough heat input and no long overrun downhill; two trips. GM also uses it on the 6.6 litre Duramax diesel as a 'stuck open thermostat' check. Ford does not use the code in the documents checked. Usual cause is a thermostat stuck open.
c: Thermostat stuck open or not sealing
Heated map thermostat, thermal management valve or switchable water pump faulty
Low coolant or air in the system
s: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
Temperature gauge drops while driving
Weak cabin heating, higher consumption

P01F1.d: Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, behind a third converter or converter brick. The OBD standard provides for up to four sensors per bank, and the code standard defines sensor 4 for bank 1 only. No manufacturer or vehicle using these codes could be identified; the description rests on CARB's requirements for downstream oxygen sensors and the logic of sensors 2 and 3. A switching sensor delivers about 0.1–0.9 V. P01F1 is the general circuit code of this sensor, the counterpart of P0136/P0142 for sensors 2 and 3. Typical causes are an aged sensor, open or high-resistance wiring and a failed heater.
c: Wiring or connector open, high-resistance or corroded
s: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Catalyst monitor readiness possibly not set
Usually no change in driving

P01F2.t: O2 Sensor Circuit Low Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 4
P01F2.d: Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, behind a third converter or converter brick. The OBD standard provides for up to four sensors per bank, and the code standard defines sensor 4 for bank 1 only. No manufacturer or vehicle using these codes could be identified; the description rests on CARB's requirements for downstream oxygen sensors and the logic of sensors 2 and 3. A switching sensor delivers about 0.1–0.9 V. P01F2 means the signal stays near 0 V – typically a signal wire shorted to ground, a faulty sensor or an exhaust leak ahead of it; GM checks its other downstream sensors for a signal below about 40–60 mV.
c: Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor
s: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Catalyst monitor readiness possibly not set
Usually no change in driving

P01F3.t: O2 Sensor Circuit High Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 4
P01F3.d: Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, behind a third converter or converter brick. The OBD standard provides for up to four sensors per bank, and the code standard defines sensor 4 for bank 1 only. No manufacturer or vehicle using these codes could be identified; the description rests on CARB's requirements for downstream oxygen sensors and the logic of sensors 2 and 3. A switching sensor delivers about 0.1–0.9 V. P01F3 means the signal is above about 1.05–1.1 V, which a switching sensor cannot produce – typically the heater supply or another voltage on the signal wire, or a heater-to-signal short inside the sensor.
c: Signal wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
s: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Catalyst monitor readiness possibly not set
Usually no change in driving

P01F4.t: O2 Sensor Circuit Slow Response Bank 1 Sensor 4
P01F4.d: Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, behind a third converter or converter brick. The OBD standard provides for up to four sensors per bank, and the code standard defines sensor 4 for bank 1 only. No manufacturer or vehicle using these codes could be identified; the description rests on CARB's requirements for downstream oxygen sensors and the logic of sensors 2 and 3. A switching sensor delivers about 0.1–0.9 V. P01F4 means the sensor reacts too slowly to mixture changes; CARB requires at least a rich-to-lean response test of downstream sensors during fuel cut-off. Behind several converters the oxygen storage buffers the change, so limits are wide.
c: Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor
s: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Catalyst monitor readiness possibly not set
Usually no change in driving

P01F5.t: O2 Sensor Circuit No Activity Detected Bank 1 Sensor 4
P01F5.d: Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, downstream of a further converter. No manufacturer or vehicle using sensor 4 codes could be identified (GM and Ford documents stop at sensor 3); the description follows CARB's requirements for downstream sensors and GM's checks on sensor 2. P01F5 means that with a warm engine and heated sensor the signal does not switch between rich and lean but stays in the middle or at the bias voltage the module applies. For sensor 2, GM detects this when the signal stays above 1.7 V of a 1.9 V bias, a two-trip fault. Usual causes are an open signal or ground wire or a dead sensor.
c: Signal or ground wire open, connector corroded
Sensor aged or poisoned, produces no voltage
Sensor heater faulty, sensor does not reach operating temperature
Exhaust leak upstream of the sensor
s: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Catalyst monitor readiness possibly not set
Usually no change in driving

P01F6.t: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean Bank 1 Sensor 4
P01F6.d: Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, downstream of a further converter. No manufacturer or vehicle using sensor 4 codes could be identified (GM and Ford documents stop at sensor 3); the description follows CARB's requirements for downstream sensors and GM's checks on sensor 2. P01F6 means the sensor stays lean: the module deliberately enriches the mixture, and if the sensor does not reach the expected rich voltage before a set amount of air has passed, it counts as stuck lean. GM runs this test on sensor 2 once per trip as a two-trip fault. Usual causes are an aged sensor, an exhaust leak ahead of it or a signal wire shorted to ground.
c: Exhaust leak or false air upstream of the sensor
Signal wire shorted to ground or contact resistance
s: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Catalyst monitor readiness possibly not set
Usually no change in driving

P01F7.t: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Rich Bank 1 Sensor 4
P01F7.d: Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, downstream of a further converter. No manufacturer or vehicle using sensor 4 codes could be identified (GM and Ford documents stop at sensor 3); the description follows CARB's requirements for downstream sensors and GM's checks on sensor 2. P01F7 means the sensor stays rich: when the module leans the mixture or cuts fuel on overrun, the signal does not drop into the lean range. CARB names exactly this rich-to-lean transition during fuel cut-off as the minimum check for downstream sensors; GM tests sensor 2 this way as a two-trip fault. Usual causes are a sooted or oil-fouled sensor or a signal wire shorted to the heater supply.
c: Signal wire shorted to voltage (e.g. heater supply)
Mixture genuinely rich (leaking injector, coolant or oil burning)
s: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Catalyst monitor readiness possibly not set
Usually no change in driving

P01F8.t: Engine Coolant Heater A Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P01F8.d: The engine module switches an electric coolant heater A through a power stage (driver). This code means the driver itself has reported excessive current or overheating and has shut down to protect itself – it concerns the control circuit, not the coolant temperature. Such heaters warm the coolant around a cold start, shortening warm-up and providing cabin heat sooner; a GM patent describes how the module recognises a pre-heated engine so other temperature diagnostics do not misfire. No manufacturer using this code family was found in GM, Ford or FCA documents; the description rests on CARB's requirements for output components. Siblings for heater A are P01E8–P01EB.
c: Short or partial short in heater element A
Wiring or connector chafed to ground, moisture in connector
Driver stage in the module or relay faulty or overheated
Heater running without coolant (low level, air pocket)
s: Check engine light or warning message (manufacturer-dependent)
Slow warm-up, little heat in cold weather
Further heater codes possible (P01E9)

P01F9.t: Engine Coolant Heater B Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P01F9.d: The engine module switches an electric coolant heater B – a second heater or heating stage – through a power stage (driver). This code means the driver itself has reported excessive current or overheating and has shut down to protect itself – it concerns the control circuit, not the coolant temperature. Such heaters warm the coolant around a cold start, shortening warm-up and providing cabin heat sooner; a GM patent describes how the module recognises a pre-heated engine so other temperature diagnostics do not misfire. No manufacturer using this code family was found in GM, Ford or FCA documents; the description rests on CARB's requirements for output components. Siblings for heater B are P01EC–P01EF.
c: Short or partial short in heater element B
Wiring or connector chafed to ground, moisture in connector
Driver stage in the module or relay faulty or overheated
s: Check engine light or warning message (manufacturer-dependent)
Slow warm-up, little heat in cold weather

P01FA.t: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor B Circuit
P01FA.d: Turbocharger outlet pressure sensor B is a second pressure sensor at a compressor outlet – for example one per turbo on twin-turbo engines or a second measuring point; sensor A has the codes P00F8–P00FC. It is a separate family from the boost pressure sensor: GM and Ford report the pressure ahead of the throttle under the boost sensor codes P0236–P0238. No manufacturer using the sensor B codes was found; FCA documents sensor A and a second outlet sensor. P01FA is the general electrical fault that the module does not classify as low or high. Without a plausible actual pressure, boost control usually limits boost.
c: Connector or pins at sensor B loose or corroded
Harness damaged (5 V reference, signal, ground)
Engine module or 5 V supply disturbed
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power, boost limited
Limp mode possible

P01FB.t: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor B Range/Performance
P01FB.d: Turbocharger outlet pressure sensor B is a second pressure sensor at a compressor outlet – for example one per turbo on twin-turbo engines or a second measuring point; sensor A has the codes P00F8–P00FC. It is a separate family from the boost pressure sensor: GM and Ford report the pressure ahead of the throttle under the boost sensor codes P0236–P0238. No manufacturer using the sensor B codes was found; FCA documents sensor A and a second outlet sensor. P01FB is the plausibility fault: the signal is electrically valid but does not fit. After a long stop all pressures should equal barometric pressure; while running the value is compared with a pressure modelled from airflow, speed and throttle – GM flags its boost sensor at deviations of roughly 25–30 kPa.
c: Leaking charge air hose or blocked pressure port
Fault in other model inputs (MAF, MAP)
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power, boost limited
Limp mode possible

P01FC.t: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor B Circuit Low
P01FC.d: Turbocharger outlet pressure sensor B is a second pressure sensor at a compressor outlet – for example one per turbo on twin-turbo engines or a second measuring point; sensor A has the codes P00F8–P00FC. It is a separate family from the boost pressure sensor: GM and Ford report the pressure ahead of the throttle under the boost sensor codes P0236–P0238. No manufacturer using the sensor B codes was found; FCA documents sensor A and a second outlet sensor. P01FC means the signal voltage stays below its lower limit – usually a signal wire shorted to ground or a missing 5 V reference. For comparison, GM sets its boost sensor low code below 14.4 % of 5 V, Ford below 0.19 V for 5 s.
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power, boost limited
Limp mode possible

P01FF.t: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A/B Correlation
P01FF.d: Turbocharger outlet pressure sensor B is a second pressure sensor at a compressor outlet – for example one per turbo on twin-turbo engines or a second measuring point; sensor A has the codes P00F8–P00FC. P01FF compares sensors A and B: with the engine off both should read barometric pressure, and in comparable operation they must agree within a tolerance. On twin-turbo engines a genuinely weaker turbo on one bank can also cause it.

P0200.d: P0200 is the injector circuit fault without a cylinder assignment. The large US manufacturers do not use it – GM and Ford report injector faults per cylinder (P0201 ff) or as faults of the shared injector supply (P062D/P062E, P2146 ff). Saab documents it on the 3.0 V6 diesel of the 9-5, whose injectors are driven by a separate power stage behind the glovebox: there P0200 means an electrical fault in that power stage or its wiring, and the engine is shut down. Generally the cause lies in something all injectors share – supply, fuse, relay, ground or driver stage – so several cylinders are affected at once. CARB does not require separate codes for each kind of circuit fault.
c: Shared injector supply open (fuse, relay, harness connector)
Separate injector power stage or its wiring faulty (diesel)
Driver stage in the engine module faulty
Ground fault of the module or power stage
s: Check engine light on
Engine does not start or shuts down
Severe misfire on several cylinders
Limp mode, loss of power

P0201.d: P0201 reports an electrical fault, mainly an open circuit, in the injector circuit of cylinder 1. The engine module watches each injector output: GM flags an open circuit at an impedance of 200 kΩ or more – on direct injection and diesel engines in 10 of 20 or 5 of 10 samples and with the warning light in the first trip, on some port-injected engines only after two trips. Ford's port injection reads a fault bit from the driver chip that covers open, short to ground and short to voltage alike; Ford diesels report only the open circuit here and shorts as P0261/P0262. On direct injection the affected injector is switched off; the cylinder misfires.

Injector supply missing (fuse, relay) – then usually several cylinders at once

s: Check engine light on

Loss of power, rough idle

P020A.d: P020A reports a fault in the injection timing of cylinder 1 on a diesel engine. Unlike P01CB/P01CC ('over retarded/advanced', the result of the injector learning routine in overrun), this code has no direction, and what it checks is up to the manufacturer. GM uses it as an electrical check on a four-cylinder diesel and on the 6.6 litre L5P Duramax V8: at every injection the engine module measures how long the injector current takes to reach its pull-in level of 13 A. If on the V8 that time is outside 60–150 µs in 10 of 20 samples, the code sets and the warning light comes on in the first trip. FCA lists it for the 3.0 litre EcoDiesel V6 together with the learning codes: check injector coding, charge air leaks and the injector clamp, reset the zero fuel calibration and repeat the learning drive; if the code returns, the injector is replaced.
c: Injector of cylinder 1 faulty (coil, armature, wear, deposits)
Injector wiring or connector: contact resistance, corrosion, chafing
Engine software sets the code falsely (update available for some models)
Injector driver stage or boost voltage in the engine module
Wrong injector code, contaminated fuel or loose injector clamp
s: Check engine light on
Rough running or misfire, rough idle
Loss of power, smoke or knocking possible

P0213.d: A cold start injector is an additional injector in the intake manifold that sprays extra fuel for a few seconds while a cold engine is cranked. In classic Bosch systems a thermo-time switch on the block powers it directly, without the engine module – such systems cannot set a code at all. A code is only possible where the engine module drives the valve and monitors its circuit, as CARB requires for output components. From the 1990s the main injectors took over cold-start enrichment, so the code only fits early OBD II engines. P0213 concerns cold start injector 1. No manufacturer using it was found in GM, Ford or Saab documents.
c: Connector or wire corroded or open
Valve coil open or valve stuck
Thermo-time switch or control relay faulty
Driver stage in the engine module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Poor cold start, long cranking in cold weather
Leaking valve: hot-start problems, flooding, black smoke

P0215.d: The engine shutoff solenoid is the electric stop valve on older diesel injection pumps, mainly distributor pumps. It is energised with the ignition on and lets fuel into the pump; with no current a spring closes it, the pump runs dry and the engine stops – also as a safety backup if the governor fails. P0215 reports a fault in this solenoid or its supply, typically a broken coil, a sticking plunger, a blown fuse or relay, or a wiring fault. The result is either an engine that will not start or dies, or one that keeps running after switch-off. Newer diesels stop through the injectors or a fuel shutoff valve with its own codes P0005–P0007. No manufacturer document describing P0215 was found; the description rests on CARB's requirements for output components and a Bosch patent on the valve.
c: Shutoff solenoid faulty (open coil, sticking plunger)
Relay or fuse in the supply circuit faulty
Broken wire, corrosion or ground fault at the pump connector
s: Engine does not start or stalls while driving
Engine keeps running after ignition off (solenoid stuck open)
Check engine light on
Stumbling with a loose contact

P0216.d: P0216 is a diesel code for the control of injection timing. On 1990s distributor pumps with an electronic timing advance it meant that actual injection timing missed its target; today manufacturers use it for the electronic injector control, with different meanings. GM's Duramax diesels compare, inside the engine module, the summed injection pulse widths from the hardware driver with those calculated by the software; a mismatch in 30 of 124 or 60 consecutive checks sets the code with the warning light in the first trip. On GM's 3.0 litre LM2 it appeared together with P0202 from a broken pin in the injector 2 connector. Saab's 3.0 V6 diesel uses it for a fault in the separate injector power stage. The result can be loss of power, rough running, smoke and limp mode.
c: Injector harness or connector (broken pin) – common rail
Engine module or injector power stage faulty internally
Distributor pump electronics or timing advance faulty
Low supply pressure on distributor pumps (lift pump, filter)
Pump installed incorrectly, drive gear misaligned
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power, limp mode
Rough running, jerking
Hard starting or stalling (distributor pump), smoke

P0217.d: P0217 is a condition code: the engine module reports that coolant temperature has passed a protection threshold. The limit and the reaction depend on the manufacturer – Saab's 2.2 diesel sets it at 120 °C for over 10 s, limits fuel quantity and suspends EGR and boost diagnostics until the temperature drops; heavy-duty diesels cut power sharply and may shut down; Ford petrol engines use their own code P1299 and cut fuel to individual cylinders. Whether the warning light comes on varies, because CARB exempts overheat protection that only engages once the gauge reads red. Usual causes are low coolant, a thermostat stuck closed, a failed fan or water pump – but Ford traced some cases to a faulty coolant sensor or harness.
c: Radiator fan, fan clutch or water pump faulty, radiator clogged
Coolant temperature sensor or harness faulty (false reading)
Extreme load (towing, gradient, heat) with an intact cooling system
s: Temperature gauge in the red, overheat warning
Loss of power, limp mode, cylinders possibly shut off
Air conditioning switches off
Steam or coolant smell, coolant loss

P0218.t: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Over Temperature Condition
P0218.d: P0218 is a condition code: the transmission or engine module reports that transmission fluid temperature sensor A reads above an overheat limit. Saab's Aisin automatic sets it above 170 °C for more than 10 s, or above 140 °C for two minutes at high speed, shows a 'transmission overheating' warning and shifts less smoothly; afterwards a fluid change is advised because the additives are spent. Ford uses its own code on diesels and lists P0218 without the warning light on other models. Reactions include earlier torque converter lock-up, a modified shift pattern and sometimes reduced power. Causes are real overheating – towing, hills, low or old fluid, a clogged cooler – or a sensor reading wrongly.
c: High load (towing, hills, sustained full throttle, stop-and-go in heat)
Fluid cooler, thermostat or lines clogged, weak cooling system
Torque converter clutch slipping or internal damage
Temperature sensor or wiring reading wrongly
s: Transmission overheating warning
Changed or harsh shifting
Limp mode or reduced power possible
Burnt fluid smell

P0219.d: P0219 is a condition code: engine speed has exceeded the overspeed limit even though the rev limiter already cuts fuel – so the engine was driven from outside, usually by downshifting at too high a road speed or descending in too low a gear, or the speed signal was wrong. Limits: Ford 6.7 litre diesel above 4,200 rpm, 3.0 litre above 4,800 rpm, after 0.1 s; GM/Saab 2.8 V6 petrol with manual gearbox above 7,000 rpm for 1 s; Saab 2.2 diesel above 6,200 rpm, although fuel is cut from 5,000 rpm. Many manufacturers store it without the warning light. Saab advises: together with a camshaft sensor code it was real overspeed, alone check the speed signal; after real overspeed inspect the engine for valve train damage.
c: Downshift at too high a road speed (manual gearbox)
Descending in too low a gear
Fault in the speed signal (crankshaft sensor, wiring)
Diesel runaway (oil drawn into the intake) or sticking injection
s: Usually no lasting symptoms, only a stored code
Briefly very high revs, limiter intervening
Check engine light possible (manufacturer-dependent)
After real overspeed: rattling, loss of power

P021A.d: P021A reports a fault in the injection timing of cylinder 7 on a diesel engine. Unlike P01D7/P01D8 ('over retarded/advanced', the result of the injector learning routine in overrun), this code has no direction, and what it checks is up to the manufacturer. GM uses it as an electrical check on the 6.6 litre L5P Duramax V8: at every injection the engine module measures how long the injector current takes to reach its pull-in level of 13 A. If on the V8 that time is outside 60–150 µs in 10 of 20 samples, the code sets and the warning light comes on in the first trip. For 2020–2021 Silverado/Sierra HD, GM issued a software update against false setting. FCA's V6 and Ford do not use it.
c: Injector of cylinder 7 faulty (coil, armature, wear, deposits)
Injector wiring or connector: contact resistance, corrosion, chafing
Engine software sets the code falsely (update available for some models)
Injector driver stage or boost voltage in the engine module
Wrong injector code, contaminated fuel or loose injector clamp
s: Check engine light on
Rough running or misfire, rough idle
Loss of power, smoke or knocking possible

P021C.d: P021C reports a fault in the injection timing of cylinder 9 on a diesel engine. Unlike P01DB/P01DC ('over retarded/advanced', the result of the injector learning routine in overrun), this code has no direction, and what it checks is up to the manufacturer. A cylinder 9 code only applies to engines with 9 or more cylinders. No manufacturer or vehicle using it was found – GM's documents stop at cylinder 8 (P021B), FCA's at cylinder 6, and Ford uses other codes. The description therefore follows the documented siblings: GM checks the injector's current rise electrically, FCA ties the code to injector learning. CARB requires diesel engines to detect injection that is too early or too late.

P0220.d: With electronic throttle control the throttle body carries two position sensors, A and B, usually with opposite or offset signals, and the engine module compares them (correlation code P2135). GM and Ford give the pedal sensors their own codes (P2120 ff), so B is in practice the second throttle sensor. P0220 is the general circuit fault of sensor B without telling low from high. GM uses it in a special sense on 2015–2016 V8 engines: the signal lies outside 0.25–4.59 V only in the monitoring processor while the main processor sees it as valid; this sets immediately with the warning light. Newer GM and Ford engines report sensor B faults as P0222/P0223. The module carries on with sensor A, limits throttle opening and power and switches off cruise control.
c: Throttle body or sensor B faulty (worn track)
Wiring or connector at the throttle body (corrosion, break)
5 V reference disturbed (short in another sensor on the same reference)
Engine module input or monitoring processor faulty
s: Check engine light and throttle warning light
Reduced power, limp mode
Poor throttle response, jerking
Cruise control disabled

P0221.t: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch B Circuit Range/Performance
P0221.d: With electronic throttle control the throttle body carries two position sensors, A and B, usually with opposite or offset signals, and the engine module compares them (correlation code P2135). GM and Ford give the pedal sensors their own codes (P2120 ff), so B is in practice the second throttle sensor. P0221 is the plausibility fault: the signal of sensor B is electrically valid but does not match sensor A or the throttle position expected from airflow. Bosch ME9 engines (Saab) set it at a deviation of more than 9 %, older Ford systems at more than 7 degrees between the sensors without the warning light; many newer engines report this only as P2135. The module carries on with sensor A, limits throttle opening and power and switches off cruise control.
c: Worn track of sensor B (signal jumps)
Contact resistance at connector or wiring
Mass airflow sensor fault or false air
s: Check engine light on
Limp mode, reduced power
Rough idle, jerking
Cruise control disabled

P0222.t: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch B Circuit Low
P0222.d: With electronic throttle control the throttle body carries two position sensors, A and B, usually with opposite or offset signals, and the engine module compares them (correlation code P2135). GM and Ford give the pedal sensors their own codes (P2120 ff), so B is in practice the second throttle sensor. P0222 means the signal of sensor B is below its lower limit – GM about 0.25 V, Ford below 0.25 V – typically a short to ground, an open signal wire or a missing 5 V reference. Both detect it within about a second and switch the warning light on in the first trip. If the shared reference fails, several sensors report low at once. The module carries on with sensor A, limits throttle opening and power and switches off cruise control.
c: Signal or 5 V wire open or shorted to ground
Throttle body or sensor B faulty internally
5 V reference pulled down by another sensor
s: Check engine light and throttle warning light
Reduced power, limp mode
Poor throttle response, jerking
Cruise control disabled

P0223.t: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch B Circuit High
P0223.d: With electronic throttle control the throttle body carries two position sensors, A and B, usually with opposite or offset signals, and the engine module compares them (correlation code P2135). GM and Ford give the pedal sensors their own codes (P2120 ff), so B is in practice the second throttle sensor. P0223 means the signal of sensor B is above its upper limit – GM above 4.59 V, Ford above 4.75 V – typically an open sensor ground, a signal shorted to 5 V or battery voltage, or an open signal wire on a pulled-up input. Both detect it within about a second and switch the warning light on in the first trip. The module carries on with sensor A, limits throttle opening and power and switches off cruise control.
c: Sensor B or throttle body faulty
Signal shorted to 5 V or 12 V in the harness
s: Check engine light and throttle warning light
Reduced power, limp mode
Poor throttle response, jerking
Cruise control disabled

P0224.t: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch B Circuit Intermittent
P0224.d: With electronic throttle control the throttle body carries two position sensors, A and B, usually with opposite or offset signals, and the engine module compares them (correlation code P2135). GM and Ford give the pedal sensors their own codes (P2120 ff), so B is in practice the second throttle sensor. P0224 reports brief dropouts or jumps of sensor B that do not last long enough for the steady fault codes. No manufacturer using exactly this code was found: GM counts intermittent faults within P0222/P0223, and Ford's digital sensors report intermittent faults as P0124 for sensor A and P0229 for sensor C – after more than 0.4 s, while a steady fault needs over 4 s. Depending on frequency the result is jerking or brief limp mode.
c: Loose contact or corroded connector at the throttle body
Worn spot on the sensor track
Wire breaking from engine movement or vibration
s: Occasional jerking or power dips
Brief limp mode
Check engine light (sometimes only intermittently)

P0225.d: Sensor C is a third throttle or pedal position sensor whose role depends on the manufacturer. Ford uses it for the sensor of the second throttle body on engines with two throttles and digital (SENT) sensors; with other makes it can be a further pedal or throttle channel. P0225 is the general circuit fault of sensor C without telling low from high (those are P0227/P0228). Ford sets it when the digital sensor of the second throttle body has been faulty for more than 4 s and switches on the warning light and the powertrain fault lamp; communication faults of the sensor line have their own codes. The result is reduced power.
c: Sensor C or second throttle body faulty
s: Check engine light and powertrain fault lamp
Reduced power
Rough idle, jerking

P0226.t: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch C Circuit Range/Performance
P0226.d: Sensor C is a third throttle or pedal position sensor whose role depends on the manufacturer. Ford uses it for the sensor of the second throttle body on engines with two throttles and digital (SENT) sensors; with other makes it can be a further pedal or throttle channel. P0226 is the plausibility fault: the signal of sensor C is electrically valid but does not match its partner sensor or the airflow model. No manufacturer using exactly this code was found – Ford does not report sensor C plausibility separately. The logic follows the sibling checks on sensors A and B (Bosch: more than 9 % deviation, Ford: more than 7 degrees). The result is limp mode with reduced power.
c: Wear or dirt on sensor C or the second throttle body
Contact resistance at connector or wiring
s: Check engine light on
Limp mode, reduced power
Jerking, poor throttle response

P0227.t: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch C Circuit Low
P0227.d: Sensor C is a third throttle or pedal position signal; its role depends on the manufacturer. Ford uses it for the sensor of the second throttle body on engines with two throttles and digital (SENT) sensors, GM does not use it. P0227 means the signal of sensor C is below its lower limit – on an analogue sensor a signal wire shorted to ground or an open signal or 5 V reference wire. The module discards sensor C and runs in limp mode with limited power. Ford reports low and high faults of its digital sensor C as U2111/U2112 instead, so no manufacturer using exactly this code was found; the description follows CARB's input monitoring requirement and the sensor A/B siblings.
c: Signal wire of sensor C shorted to ground or open (chafing, connector)
5 V reference to the sensor open or loaded
Sensor C or second throttle body faulty
Corrosion or water in the throttle body connector
s: Check engine light (Ford also the wrench light)
Limp mode with limited power
Delayed or missing throttle response
Rough or raised idle

P0228.t: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch C Circuit High
P0228.d: Sensor C is a third throttle or pedal position signal; its role depends on the manufacturer. Ford uses it for the sensor of the second throttle body on engines with two throttles and digital (SENT) sensors, GM does not use it. P0228 means the signal of sensor C is above its upper limit – typically an open sensor ground, which pulls the signal up to the reference, or a signal wire shorted to voltage. The module discards sensor C and runs in limp mode with limited power. Ford reports low and high faults of its digital sensor C as U2111/U2112 instead, so no manufacturer using exactly this code was found; the description follows CARB's input monitoring requirement and the sensor A/B siblings.
c: Signal wire shorted to 5 V or system voltage
Sensor C or throttle body faulty
s: Check engine light (Ford also the wrench light)
Limp mode with limited power
Delayed or missing throttle response
Rough or raised idle

P0229.t: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch C Circuit Intermittent
P0229.d: Sensor C is a third throttle or pedal position signal; its role depends on the manufacturer. Ford uses it for the sensor of the second throttle body on engines with two throttles and digital (SENT) sensors, GM does not use it. P0229 reports a fault of sensor C that comes and goes. Ford documents it exactly: if its digital sensor on the second throttle body reports a fault for more than 0.4 s, P0229 sets; if the fault persists beyond 4 s it becomes P0225. Both switch on the warning light and the wrench light. Typical causes are a loose contact at the second throttle body's connector or chafed wiring.
c: Loose contact at the second throttle body connector (spread pins, corrosion)
Harness chafing with intermittent short or open
Sensor or second throttle body with an internal intermittent fault
Voltage dips in the supply or ground
s: Check engine light and wrench light (Ford)
Brief jerking or loss of power
Occasional limp mode

P022A.t: Charge Air Cooler Bypass Control A Circuit/Open
P022A.d: The charge air cooler bypass is a flap or valve that routes compressed air around the charge air cooler, so the engine and exhaust warm up faster after a cold start; when warm it closes or opens partly to control intake air temperature. It is driven by an electric motor with a built-in position sensor or by a solenoid and vacuum can. P022A is the general circuit fault of the actuator drive, mainly an open circuit: the driver sees no current or an output voltage outside its window. The module then switches bypass control off and the flap stays in its rest position. No manufacturer document using this code was found – GM and Ford do not use the bypass codes; the description rests on CARB's component monitoring requirement and a Bosch patent on the bypass valve.
c: Wire or connector at the bypass actuator open
Actuator or solenoid of the bypass flap faulty (coil, motor)
Fuse or relay of the actuator supply
Driver stage in the engine module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Depending on the rest position: longer warm-up or higher charge air temperature with slight loss of power
Often nothing noticeable while driving
