P037A.t: Glow Plug/Heater Indicator Control Circuit Low
P037A.d: Diesel engines show the driver a wait-to-start lamp while the glow plugs preheat; the engine module switches it with a high-side driver. P037A means the lamp control circuit is too low – in practice a short to ground on the line to the instrument cluster. GM's diesels detect it in the driver itself: about 0.5 Ω to ground with the lamp commanded, only with a lamp configured, ignition on, more than 11 V and not while cranking. The 2015 engines need 3 s of fault, the 2016/2018 engines 10 of 15 samples; the check engine light follows after two trips. The glow plugs keep working; only the indication is missing, so the driver may start too early. CARB requires monitoring of the wait-to-start lamp circuit. Ford reports lamp faults under P0381 and does not use P037A.
c: Lamp control wire chafed through to ground between engine module and cluster
Lamp or LED driver in the instrument cluster shorted internally
Moisture or corrosion in the module or cluster connector
Driver in the engine module faulty
s: Glow plug light does not come on or stays dim
Check engine light on (GM after two trips)
Driver starts too early, possibly poor cold start

P037B.t: Glow Plug/Heater Indicator Control Circuit High
P037B.d: P037B is the counterpart of P037A: the control circuit of the wait-to-start lamp is too high, i.e. the line carries voltage although the engine module's driver is off, or the driver sees a short to battery voltage. GM's 2015 diesels check in the off state and set the fault after 1 s with more than 11 V; the 2016/2018 engines evaluate a short of about 0.5 Ω to a voltage source in the driver, 10 of 20 samples at 100 ms. In both cases the check engine light comes on after two trips. The lamp then stays on permanently or cannot be switched off, so the driver no longer gets a usable preheat signal; the driver may protect itself when commanded. There is no limp mode. Ford and Saab do not use P037B; CARB requires monitoring of the lamp circuit and of output components for shorts.
c: Lamp control wire chafed against battery or ignition positive
Fault in the instrument cluster feeding voltage back
Water damage in a connector bridging to a neighbouring pin
Driver in the engine module faulty
s: Glow plug light stays on or flickers
Check engine light on (after two trips)
No recognisable preheat indication

P037C.t: Cold Start Camshaft Profile System Performance
P037C.d: To heat the catalyst quickly after a cold start, some engines select a particular camshaft profile; CARB counts altered valve timing among these cold-start measures and requires components of the cold-start strategy to have their own diagnostics. P037C checks whether the requested profile is actually engaged during this phase. It is documented by code only at GM, on the 2.7-litre turbo four-cylinder (L3B) with a three-step sliding camshaft: while catalyst heating is active, the measured lift state is compared with the cold-start target, and if it is wrong in 100 of 120 cylinder events the code is set in the first trip. Two GM bulletins (19-NA-145 for 2019 Silverado/Sierra 1500 with stalling on remote start below −6 °C, 20-NA-174 for the 2020 Cadillac CT4) trace P037C to a software fault and reprogram the engine module.
c: Profile actuator (sliding cam pin) sticking or not switching
Wrong oil viscosity or low oil level, mechanism stiff when cold
s: Check engine light on
Rough running or stalling when cold (for example on remote start)
Often no noticeable symptoms

P037D.d: To check the glow plugs, the engine module reads back the voltage or current of the glow plug supply through a sense circuit – CARB requires glow plug circuits to be monitored for correct current and voltage drop, and from model year 2010 the failure of a single plug to be detected. In the J2012 scheme P037D is the general code for this sense circuit, P037E and P037F its low and high counterparts. None of the manufacturer documents available to us uses P037D: GM's 2016/2018 diesels use only P037E/P037F, Ford 2023 its own glow plug codes (P0671 ff, P064C) and Saab reports the feedback of its glow plug control module as P0380/P0382. The description therefore follows CARB and the GM sister codes. Typically glow plug monitoring is inactive; glowing itself can work normally.
c: Sense wire open or high resistance, connector corroded
Glow relay or glow plug control module giving an implausible feedback
Fuse or fusible link of the glow plug supply blown
s: Check engine light or glow plug light on
Possibly poor cold start if the cause also affects the glow plug supply
Further glow plug codes stored

P037E.d: P037E means the voltage read back from the glow plug supply is too low. GM's 2016/2018 diesels, whose glow plug output stages sit in the engine module, compare the feedback with the battery voltage while glowing: if it is lower by more than a calibrated, current-dependent threshold – excessive voltage drop or a short to ground of the sense line – a sample counts as faulty, and 60 of 120 samples in a 50 ms grid set the code, roughly 3 of 6 s. The check only runs with the engine running (afterglow), not while cranking, and is suspended if a single plug or the supply already has an electrical fault. GM classes the cause as internal to the module (measuring circuit) and turns on the check engine light after two trips. There is no limp mode; glow plug monitoring is restricted.
c: High contact resistance in the glow plug supply (connector, ground, fusible link)
Measuring circuit or output stage in the engine module
Sense or supply wire shorted to ground
Weak battery or vehicle voltage at the edge of the enable range
s: Check engine light on
Possibly hard starting or knocking when cold
Further glow plug codes

P037F.d: P037F means the voltage read back from the glow plug supply is too high. GM's 2016/2018 diesels set it when the feedback lies above a threshold derived from the run/crank relay voltage, with a feedback above 5.0 V – for example voltage is reported although the plugs are not energised, or the sense line is shorted to positive. The code needs 40 of 80 samples at 50 ms, about 2 of 4 s, only with the engine running, and turns on the check engine light after two trips; GM classes the cause as internal to the module. If there is a real short to positive or a stuck relay or output stage, the plugs can stay energised permanently, overheating them and draining the battery – then also check the single plug codes P0671 ff and P066x. CARB requires glow plug circuits to be monitored for correct current and voltage drop.
c: Sense wire chafed against positive or bridged in the connector
Glow relay sticking or output stage shorted (supply stays on)
Measuring circuit in the engine module
s: Check engine light on
Glow plugs possibly energised permanently (flat battery, plug damage)
Glow plug light implausible

P0380.d: P0380 concerns glow plug circuit A – depending on the manufacturer the first group of plugs, glow relay 1 or feedback line A of the glow plug control module. Saab's 3.0 TiD (9-5, 2002) has two feedback lines from the control module; if line A at the engine module stays above 4.0 V for more than 3 s while glowing, the module is reporting a plug or circuit fault, checked once per drive cycle with the warning lamp on. In Saab's 1.9 TiD (EDC16) the glow plug control module drives two pairs of plugs, monitors them itself and reports faults over a diagnostic line that should switch inversely to the activation line. The 2010/11 Saab 9-5 2.0 TiD sets P0380 for implausible feedback or a missing supply of the module, there without check engine light. Newer GM and Ford diesels report single plugs under P0671 ff instead.
c: Glow plug(s) in circuit A burnt out
Glow plug control module or glow relay faulty
Wiring or connector fault (feedback line, plug connector, supply)
Missing battery or ignition supply of the control module (fuse)
s: Hard starting when cold, long cranking
White or blue smoke and rough running after a cold start
Glow plug light or check engine light on or flashing

P0381.d: P0381 monitors the circuit of the wait-to-start lamp for an open circuit or, more generally, for faults that keep the lamp dark when commanded – CARB names a burnt-out bulb as the example, with exemptions for LCD clusters and for engines that only release the starter after preheating. GM's 2015–2018 diesels detect an open circuit in the driver by a high load impedance (about 200 kΩ in 2015), in 0.2 s or 10 of 15 samples, with the check engine light after two trips; on the 2014 Duramax LML P0381 still covered all lamp circuit faults including a short to ground. Ford's 2023 diesels check via the instrument cluster: if it reports the lamp off although on is commanded, P0381 is set within about 1 s at key-on. There is no limp mode; the risk is starting too early in the cold.
c: Control wire open or connector fault between engine module and cluster
Lamp or LED in the instrument cluster burnt out
Instrument cluster faulty or communication problem (Ford)
s: Glow plug light does not come on at key-on
Check engine light on (GM after two trips)
Driver starts too early in the cold

P0382.d: P0382 is the counterpart of P0380 for glow plug circuit B – depending on the manufacturer the second group of plugs, glow relay 2 or feedback line B of the glow plug control module. A code-specific manufacturer description exists from Saab: the 3.0 TiD V6 diesel in the 9-5 (2002) reads two feedback lines from its glow plug control module, and if line B stays above 4.0 V for more than 3 s while glowing, the module is reporting a fault in the second group of plugs; the check runs once per drive cycle, the warning lamp comes on and there is no further system reaction. Newer GM and Ford diesels report single plugs under P0671 ff and do not use P0382. CARB requires glow plug circuits to be monitored for correct current and voltage drop. The typical consequence is a poor cold start with smoke.
c: Glow plug(s) in circuit B burnt out
Glow plug control module or glow relay 2 faulty
Feedback line B, plug connector or busbar faulty
s: Hard starting when cold, long cranking
White or blue smoke and rough running after a cold start
Glow plug light or check engine light on or flashing

P0383.t: Glow Plug Control Module 1 Control Circuit Low
P0383.d: Many diesels have a separate glow plug control module that the engine module commands over a control line. P0383 means this line is too low. In GM's logic for the 2010/11 Saab 9-5 2.0 TiD the engine module drives the module with a PWM signal and holds about 10 V on the line at rest (9.5–10.5 V at the signal terminal); if it reads too little voltage for more than 0.5 s – short to ground, or an open circuit or high resistance – it sets P0383, with ignition on, 9–16 V, once per ignition cycle. In that European version the code does not turn on the check engine light. Without a valid command the module does not glow, so the engine starts poorly when cold. Ford uses P0384 differently and not P0383; GM's 2016/2018 diesels have their output stages in the engine module and no such line. For US vehicles there is no code-specific source.
c: Control line between engine module and glow plug module shorted to ground or open
Corroded connector at the glow plug module in the engine bay
Glow plug control module faulty (input pulls the line down)
s: No preheating, poor cold start
Smoke after a cold start
Warning lamp depending on the manufacturer

P0384.t: Glow Plug Control Module 1 Control Circuit High
P0384.d: P0384 is the counterpart of P0383: the control line from the engine module to the glow plug control module is too high, i.e. shorted to positive. In GM's logic for the 2010/11 Saab 9-5 2.0 TiD the signal terminal should show 9.5–10.5 V; a higher voltage for more than 0.5 s, with ignition on and 9–16 V, sets the code, there without check engine light. Ford's 2023 diesels (6.7 and 3.0 litre) use P0384 differently from the J2012 name, for the supply voltage of the glow plug module: below 6.5 V, above 16.5 V or open, detected in about 1 s – today J2012 has P052F for that. So with Ford, check battery, alternator and the module's supply first. The consequence is missing or irregular preheating or a protective shutdown of the module, with a poor cold start.
c: Control line chafed against positive or bridged in the connector
Glow plug control module faulty internally (feeding back)
Ford: supply of the module outside 6.5–16.5 V or open (battery, alternator, fuse)
s: No or irregular preheating, hard starting when cold
Smoke after a cold start
Warning lamp depending on the manufacturer

P0385.d: Some engines have a second crankshaft sensor or a second track on the tone wheel, which the engine module checks against sensor A or the camshaft. P0385 means its signal is missing or does not match. GM's 2004 Northstar 4.6 V8 counts the crank pulses per cam pulse (target 48 ± 1, fault in 8 of 10 tests) and also flags 2 s while cranking or 0.4 s running without a match, after two trips; an active P0385 suspends the cam sensor check. GM's 3.8-litre V6 (2006) sets it when its low resolution track stays silent while the medium resolution track delivers 36 pulses, 40 of 50 samples. The Honda 3.5-litre in the 2004 Saturn Vue Redline sets it when the second crank signal is missing while the first runs, judged after 17 revolutions, in the first trip. The engine usually keeps running on sensor A.
c: Connector or wiring open or corroded
Tone wheel or second track damaged
s: Check engine light on
Longer cranking
Tachometer flickers, rough running
Rarely stalling

P0386.t: Crankshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0386.d: P0386 means the signal of the second crankshaft sensor or second tone wheel track is present but implausible. GM's 2004 Northstar 4.6 V8 sets it after 5 resynchronisations within 10 s, after two trips. GM's 3.8-litre V6 (2006) expects exactly 0 or 6 low resolution pulses per 36 medium resolution pulses and one cam pulse; any other count in 40 of 50 samples sets the code, also after two trips. The Honda 3.5-litre in the 2004 Saturn Vue Redline counts implausible signals of its second crank sensor (target 44 crank pulses per 3 cam pulses, checked every half revolution, the counter dropping by one every 10 s) and sets the code at 30, about 2.2 s at idle, in the first trip. Typical causes are interference pulses, a dirty sensor or a wrong air gap; the result is jerking, misfire or longer cranking.
c: Interference pulses (wiring near the ignition, shielding)
Sensor dirty or air gap wrong
s: Check engine light on
Jerking, misfire
Longer cranking

P0387.t: Crankshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Low
P0387.d: By its J2012 name P0387 means the signal of the second crankshaft sensor stays at a low level – typically a short to ground of the signal wire, a missing or shorted sensor supply, or with an inductive sensor an amplitude that is too small. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0387: the engines with a sensor B that we found (GM Northstar 4.6 and 3.8-litre V6, the Honda 3.5-litre in the Saturn Vue Redline) report its electrical faults under P0385 and implausible signals under P0386. The description therefore follows the J2012 name, the function of sensor B and CARB's monitoring requirement for crank angle sensors. As long as sensor A works, the engine usually keeps running; together with a sensor A fault it may not start.
c: Sensor supply too low or shorted
s: Check engine light on
Longer cranking
Rough running, no start if sensor A also fails

P0388.t: Crankshaft Position Sensor B Circuit High
P0388.d: Some engines have a second crankshaft sensor or a second track on the tone wheel – GM's 3.4/3.5/3.8-litre V6 use the low resolution track of a dual Hall sensor, the Honda 3.5-litre in the Saturn Vue Redline a second sensor – which the engine module checks against sensor A or the camshaft. By its J2012 name P0388 means the signal of sensor B stays above its upper limit – with a Hall sensor typically an open signal wire held high by the module's pull-up, or a short to positive. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0388: the engines with a sensor B report its electrical faults under P0385 and implausible signals under P0386. The description therefore follows the J2012 name, these component sources and CARB's monitoring requirement for crank angle sensors. The engine usually keeps running on sensor A; longer cranking is possible.
c: Signal wire of sensor B open or connector corroded or loose
Signal wire shorted to positive or reference voltage
s: Check engine light on
Longer cranking or starting problems
Possibly rough running or misfire
Often no noticeable symptoms while sensor A takes over

P0389.t: Crankshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Intermittent
P0389.d: Some engines have a second crankshaft sensor or a second track on the tone wheel – GM's 3.4/3.5/3.8-litre V6 use the low resolution track of a dual Hall sensor, the Honda 3.5-litre in the Saturn Vue Redline a second sensor – which the engine module checks against sensor A or the camshaft. By its J2012 name P0389 means the signal of sensor B drops out for moments or becomes erratic – missing or extra edges – without staying permanently low or high. Such faults are typically found by counting pulses against sensor A or the camshaft, as GM's 3.8-litre V6 and the Honda engine do; both, however, report the result under P0385/P0386, and no manufacturer document available to us uses P0389. The description therefore follows the J2012 name, these component sources and CARB. Typical causes are a loose contact, a broken wire and interference.
c: Loose contact or corrosion at the sensor B connector
Wire break or chafing that appears with engine movement
Electrical interference (add-on devices, routing near ignition or relays)
Tone wheel damaged or dirty, air gap too large
s: Check engine light on, possibly only after several trips
Occasional stalling or jerking
Sporadic starting problems

P038A.d: Ignition I is one of the control signal lines from the engine module to an ignition module, ignition output stage or group of coils; which cylinders it serves is defined by the manufacturer, not by the code standard. The code concerns the logic-level control signal, not the coil's primary current (that has its own codes, P0351 ff and P2300 ff). P038A means the control line is open – the module sees a voltage with its driver off that indicates high resistance. No manufacturer using these codes was found – neither GM nor Ford use the Ignition A to J codes; GM reports coil control faults as P0351 ff – so the description follows CARB and that analogy. The affected coils fire wrongly or not at all, causing misfire; many modules then shut off injection to those cylinders to protect the catalyst.
c: Control line or connector pin open (corrosion, pushed-back pin)
Ignition module or coil with integrated driver of this group faulty
Supply or ground of the ignition module faulty
Driver stage in the engine module
s: Check engine light on
Misfire, jerking, rough idle
Loss of power, possibly cylinders shut off
Additional misfire codes P0300 ff

P038B.t: Ignition I Control Signal Circuit Low
P038B.d: Ignition I is one of the control signal lines from the engine module to an ignition module, ignition output stage or group of coils; which cylinders it serves is defined by the manufacturer, not by the code standard. The code concerns the logic-level control signal, not the coil's primary current (that has its own codes, P0351 ff and P2300 ff). P038B means the control line reads low – typically shorted to ground. No manufacturer using these codes was found – neither GM nor Ford use the Ignition A to J codes; GM reports coil control faults as P0351 ff – so the description follows CARB and that analogy. The affected coils fire wrongly or not at all, causing misfire; many modules then shut off injection to those cylinders to protect the catalyst.
c: Input of the ignition module or coil shorted
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Driver stage in the engine module
s: Check engine light on
Misfire, jerking, rough idle
Loss of power, possibly cylinders shut off
Additional misfire codes P0300 ff

P038C.t: Ignition I Control Signal Circuit High
P038C.d: Ignition I is one of the control signal lines from the engine module to an ignition module, ignition output stage or group of coils; which cylinders it serves is defined by the manufacturer, not by the code standard. The code concerns the logic-level control signal, not the coil's primary current (that has its own codes, P0351 ff and P2300 ff). P038C means the control line reads high – typically shorted to voltage. No manufacturer using these codes was found – neither GM nor Ford use the Ignition A to J codes; GM reports coil control faults as P0351 ff – so the description follows CARB and that analogy. The affected coils fire wrongly or not at all, causing misfire; many modules then shut off injection to those cylinders to protect the catalyst.
c: Control line shorted to a supply wire
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Driver stage in the engine module

P038F.t: Ignition J Control Signal Circuit High
P038F.d: Ignition J is one of the control signal lines from the engine module to an ignition module, ignition output stage or group of coils; which cylinders it serves is defined by the manufacturer, not by the code standard. The code concerns the logic-level control signal, not the coil's primary current (that has its own codes, P0351 ff and P2300 ff). P038F means the control line reads high – typically shorted to voltage. No manufacturer using these codes was found – neither GM nor Ford use the Ignition A to J codes; GM reports coil control faults as P0351 ff – so the description follows CARB and that analogy. The affected coils fire wrongly or not at all, causing misfire; many modules then shut off injection to those cylinders to protect the catalyst.
c: Control line shorted to a supply wire
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Driver stage in the engine module
s: Check engine light on
Misfire, jerking, rough idle
Loss of power, possibly cylinders shut off

P0390.t: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Bank 2
P0390.d: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor; bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1, so the code only occurs on V and boxer engines with one exhaust cam sensor per bank. P0390 means no or too few exhaust cam pulses arrive from bank 2 while the crankshaft turns. GM's 3.0 twin-turbo V6 (LGW) sets it after 5.5 s without a cam pulse, 4 s of cranking or fewer than 4 pulses in 3 s, after two trips; for GM it collects all circuit faults. GM's 3.6-litre V6 in the Saab 9-4X also counts 800 of 1,000 engine cycles without a pulse. Ford checks the crank-to-cam ratio from 200 rpm within 5 s, and the 2004 Northstar counts missing signal changes up to 16. The bank 2 exhaust phaser then locks in its base position; the engine keeps running on the crank and intake cam sensors. FCA advises saving the synchronisation data before replacing the sensor.
c: Connector or wiring of the bank 2 exhaust sensor open or corroded (signal, 5 V, ground)
Oil contamination or leak at the sensor, sensor loose
Tone wheel on the phaser damaged or wrongly fitted after timing chain work
Engine module, or 5 V reference shorted by another sensor
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power (bank 2 exhaust cam timing in its base position)
Longer cranking
Rough idle
Higher fuel consumption

P0391.t: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance Bank 2
P0391.d: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor; bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1, so the code only occurs on V and boxer engines with one exhaust cam sensor per bank. P0391 means the bank 2 exhaust cam signal is present, but the number or position of its pulses does not fit the crankshaft. GM's 3.0 twin-turbo V6 (LGW) expects 4 to 6 pulses in the first 12 reference events and 398 to 402 per 100 engine cycles on the four-tooth wheel, after two trips; the Saab 9-4X 2.8 turbo V6 (LAU) checks pulses per crank revolution below 2,520 rpm. The 2004 Northstar requires each edge within a window of crank teeth, and GM's 2004 3.6-litre V6 (LY7) counts implausible signals over two drive cycles. The phaser then goes to its base position and the engine cranks longer. Mechanical causes – damaged tone wheel, jumped chain – matter more here than with P0390.
c: Tone wheel on the bank 2 exhaust phaser damaged, loose or wrongly fitted
Interference or loose contact producing extra edges
Sensor loose, wrong O-ring or gap, chips on the magnet
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power (bank 2 exhaust cam timing in its base position)
Longer cranking
Rough idle
Occasional stalling

P0392.t: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Low Bank 2
P0392.d: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor; bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1, so the code only occurs on V and boxer engines with one exhaust cam sensor per bank. P0392 means the bank 2 exhaust cam signal stays low without edges – typically a short to ground of the signal wire, a sensor output stuck low or a missing 5 V reference. Only manufacturers with separate low and high codes use it: on the Saab 9-4X 2.8 turbo V6 (GM LAU) the signal must stay low without pulses for more than 1 s, or 10 s cumulatively, after more than 10 crank revolutions and below 2,520 rpm, after two trips; GM's 2004/2005 3.6-litre V6 (LY7, LP1) counts the fault over two drive cycles. Newer GM petrol engines (2015–2020) and Ford report the same fault as P0390. The consequence is as for P0390: cam timing on bank 2 in its base position, loss of power, longer cranking.
c: 5 V reference missing (shorted by another sensor on the same circuit)
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power (bank 2 exhaust cam timing in its base position)
Longer cranking
Rough idle

P0393.t: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit High Bank 2
P0393.d: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor; bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1, so the code only occurs on V and boxer engines with one exhaust cam sensor per bank. P0393 means the bank 2 exhaust cam signal stays high without edges. Because the engine module pulls the Hall sensor's signal line up, an open wire leads to 'high' just like a short to positive – GM's 2004 3.6-litre V6 (LY7) therefore calls the fault 'circuit continuity or high' and counts it over two drive cycles. On the Saab 9-4X 2.8 turbo V6 (GM LAU) the signal must stay high without pulses for more than 1 s, or 10 s cumulatively, after two trips. Only manufacturers with separate low and high codes use it; newer GM petrol engines and Ford report the fault as P0390. The consequence is as for P0390: cam timing on bank 2 in its base position, loss of power, longer cranking.
c: Signal wire open or connector off
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power (bank 2 exhaust cam timing in its base position)
Longer cranking
Rough idle

P0394.t: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Intermittent Bank 2
P0394.d: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor; bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1, so the code only occurs on V and boxer engines with one exhaust cam sensor per bank. P0394 means the bank 2 exhaust cam signal now and then appears at a position where it is not expected relative to the crank reference – sporadic extra or missing edges. Ford checks this in its camshaft ignition system test from 200 rpm and decides within 5 s. FCA also uses the code and asks dealers to save the cam/crank synchronisation event data before replacing parts, a hint that the sensor itself is often not the culprit. GM does not use P0394 and reports such faults under P0391. Typical causes are a loose contact, interference or a damaged tone wheel.
c: Loose contact or corrosion at the sensor connector or harness
Interference (ignition wiring, add-on devices, ground problems)
Tone wheel or phaser damaged, or sensor loose
s: Check engine light on
Sporadic jerking or stalling
Occasionally longer cranking

P0395.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P0395 is the general circuit code for this pressure sensor, meant for modules that do not separate open circuits and shorts into low and high. The only manufacturer we found using this code family – GM's European 2.0 CDTI diesel, documented in Saab 9-5 workshop information – splits the faults into low and high (P0397, P0398) and does not use P0395; VW's US 2.0 TDI engines with pressure-sensing glow plugs report such faults with their own codes (P13CE ff). The description therefore follows CARB's requirement to monitor input sensors for circuit faults. The sensor has three wires (5 V reference, ground, signal); without it the module drops combustion control for that cylinder.
c: Connector at the pressure-sensing glow plug loose or corroded
Reference, signal or ground wire open or shorted
Sensor electronics in the glow plug faulty
s: Check engine light on (often after two trips)
Usually barely noticeable – combustion control for the cylinder is switched off
Possibly rougher running, more noise or slightly higher consumption

P0396.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P0396 means the sensor signal is electrically fine but does not fit the expected value. No manufacturer document available to us describes the code; a GM patent shows how such a check works: in overrun the measured peak pressure is compared with a compression pressure calculated from manifold pressure and compression ratio, and the pressure values are also compared with limits and with crankshaft speed fluctuation. GM's European diesel in the Saab 9-5 uses the peak pressure in overrun anyway to find top dead centre. Typical causes are sensor drift from combustion deposits or a glow plug that leaks or is wrongly torqued. CARB requires a two-sided plausibility check of input sensors where feasible.
c: Sensor in the glow plug drifting (deposits, ageing)
Glow plug leaking or wrongly torqued (pressure transmitted wrongly)
Contact resistance in connector or ground
s: Check engine light on
Combustion control for the cylinder off – slightly rough running, more noise
Possibly more smoke or consumption

P0397.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P0397 means the sensor signal stays below its lower limit. GM's European 2.0 CDTI diesel (Saab 9-5, 2010) sets it when the signal is below the threshold for more than 2 s with the engine running, checked once per drive cycle, with the check engine light after two trips; the displayed maximum combustion pressure then reads 0 kPa instead of the normal 0–9,000 kPa. Saab names an open or grounded 5 V reference and a signal wire shorted to ground as causes; the glow plug should measure 3–12 Ω between reference and ground. Without the signal, combustion control for this cylinder is switched off, which is usually barely noticeable.
c: 5 V reference wire open or shorted to ground
Sensor electronics of the glow plug faulty
s: Check engine light on (often after two trips)
Usually barely noticeable – combustion control for the cylinder is switched off
Possibly rougher running, more noise or slightly higher consumption

P0398.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P0398 means the sensor signal stays above its upper limit. GM's European 2.0 CDTI diesel (Saab 9-5, 2010) sets it when the signal is above the threshold for more than 2 s with the engine running, checked once per drive cycle, with the check engine light after two trips; the displayed maximum combustion pressure then reads 10,000 kPa instead of the normal 0–9,000 kPa. Saab names a 5 V reference shorted to positive, an open signal wire or one shorted to positive, and an open ground wire as causes – an unplugged connector is the most common. Without the signal, combustion control for this cylinder is switched off, which is usually barely noticeable.
c: Connector off or loose, signal wire open
Sensor in the glow plug faulty
Signal or reference wire shorted to positive
s: Check engine light on (often after two trips)
Usually barely noticeable – combustion control for the cylinder is switched off
Possibly rougher running, more noise or slightly higher consumption

P0399.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P0399 means the sensor signal is erratic or drops out for moments. GM's European 2.0 CDTI diesel (Saab 9-5, 2010) calls it 'circuit erratic' and sets it when the signal is outside its range for more than 0.2 s with the engine running; its fault table groups the erratic and pressure variation codes together as signal performance faults. The test plan checks a reference of 4.8–5.2 V and a ground below 5 Ω before the glow plug is replaced. Typical causes are a loose contact at the glow plug connector, a chafed engine harness or sensor electronics that become unstable with temperature. The code often comes and goes; combustion control for the cylinder is suspended while it is active.
c: Loose contact at the glow plug connector
Chafing or broken wire in the engine harness
Sensor electronics of the glow plug unstable with temperature
s: Check engine light on
Occasionally rough running
Often no symptoms, the code comes and goes

P039A.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P039A means the pressure measured in the cylinder is lower than expected while the sensor itself is electrically fine. No manufacturer document available to us describes the code; GM patents show how such an evaluation works: peak and minimum pressure are compared with limits and with a motoring pressure calculated from manifold pressure and compression ratio, and the ratio of measured to motoring pressure is compared between cylinders. A low value can mean weak combustion or compression – leaking valve, worn rings, leaking glow plug seat, an injector delivering too little – or a sensor drifting downwards. The usual consequence is rough running and more smoke.
c: Compression loss (valve, piston rings, leaking glow plug seat)
Injector delivering too little or coked
s: Check engine light on
Lack of power, rough running, possibly misfire on this cylinder
More smoke

P039B.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. P039B means the pressure measured or calculated for the cylinder is higher than expected. It is documented by code at Audi, surprisingly on a petrol engine: on the 2015 S3 (2.0 TFSI, engine CYFB) the four 'pressure too high' codes came on with the EPC lamp, usually together with misfire codes P0300–P0304 and the manufacturer code for hiding a cylinder; the cause was a software fault that mis-detected misfire, and a software update fixed it. How Audi determines the pressure, the bulletin does not say. On diesels with pressure-sensing glow plugs GM patents describe a peak pressure above its limit – too much or too early injection, or a sensor drifting upwards. If the cylinder is shut off, power drops noticeably.
c: Engine module software (Audi S3 2015, engine CYFB)
Injector delivering too much or dripping
Sensor drifting upwards (diesel pressure-sensing glow plug)
Knock or pre-ignition on a petrol engine
s: EPC or check engine light on
Misfire codes, possibly a cylinder shut off with noticeable loss of power
Rough running

P039C.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. GM's European 2.0 CDTI diesel (Saab 9-5, 2010) uses P039C as 'pressure variation too low', with three sub-checks, and sets it when the signal is outside its range for more than 0.2 s with the engine running; its fault table counts it among the signal performance faults together with the erratic code. What exactly is measured, Saab does not explain; presumably it is the swing of the pressure signal within an engine cycle – too small a swing means the signal barely responds, for example because the glow rod is stuck by carbon and no longer transmits the pressure, or because pressure build-up is missing. Usually there are no noticeable symptoms.
c: Pressure-sensing glow plug faulty or coked (glow rod stuck)
Contact resistance in connector or ground
Actual compression loss or misfire in the cylinder
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable symptoms
Possibly rough running or combustion noise because control is off

P039D.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 1. GM's European 2.0 CDTI diesel (Saab 9-5, 2010) uses P039D as 'pressure variation too high' and sets it when the signal is outside its range for more than 0.2 s with the engine running; its fault table counts it among the signal performance faults together with the erratic code. What exactly is measured, Saab does not explain; presumably it is the swing of the pressure signal within an engine cycle – too large a swing points to a noisy or overshooting signal or implausible pressure peaks, for example from faulty sensor electronics, interference on the signal wire or, less often, a combustion anomaly such as a dripping injector. Usually there are no noticeable symptoms.
c: Sensor in the glow plug faulty (signal noise)
Loose contact or interference on the signal wire
s: Check engine light on

Typical causes are sensor drift from combustion deposits or a glow plug that leaks or is wrongly torqued. CARB requires a two-sided plausibility check of input sensors where feasible.
c: Sensor in the glow plug drifting (deposits, ageing)
Glow plug leaking or wrongly torqued (pressure transmitted wrongly)
Contact resistance in connector or ground
s: Check engine light on
Combustion control for the cylinder off – slightly rough running, more noise
Possibly more smoke or consumption

P03DD.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 8. P03DD means the sensor signal stays below its lower limit – typically an open or grounded 5 V reference or a signal wire shorted to ground. The only manufacturer we found using this code family, GM's European 2.0 CDTI four-cylinder diesel (Saab 9-5, 2010), uses it for cylinders 1 to 4: signal below the threshold for more than 2 s with the engine running, check engine light after two trips, displayed pressure 0 kPa. For cylinder 8, which only engines with at least 8 cylinders have, no manufacturer document available to us uses the code; the description follows that logic and CARB. Without the signal, combustion control for this cylinder is switched off.
c: 5 V reference wire open or shorted to ground
Sensor electronics of the glow plug faulty
s: Check engine light on (often after two trips)
Usually barely noticeable – combustion control for the cylinder is switched off
Possibly rougher running, more noise or slightly higher consumption

P03DE.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 8. P03DE means the sensor signal stays above its upper limit – typically an unplugged connector, an open signal or ground wire, or a short to positive. The only manufacturer we found using this code family, GM's European 2.0 CDTI four-cylinder diesel (Saab 9-5, 2010), uses it for cylinders 1 to 4: signal above the threshold for more than 2 s with the engine running, check engine light after two trips, displayed pressure 10,000 kPa. For cylinder 8, which only engines with at least 8 cylinders have, no manufacturer document available to us uses the code; the description follows that logic and CARB. Without the signal, combustion control for this cylinder is switched off.
c: Connector off or loose, signal wire open
Sensor in the glow plug faulty
Signal or reference wire shorted to positive
s: Check engine light on (often after two trips)
Usually barely noticeable – combustion control for the cylinder is switched off
Possibly rougher running, more noise or slightly higher consumption

P03DF.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 8. P03DF means the sensor signal is erratic or drops out for moments – typically a loose contact at the glow plug connector, a chafed harness or sensor electronics unstable with temperature. The only manufacturer we found using this code family, GM's European 2.0 CDTI four-cylinder diesel (Saab 9-5, 2010), uses it for cylinders 1 to 4 as 'circuit erratic': signal outside its range for more than 0.2 s with the engine running. For cylinder 8, which only engines with at least 8 cylinders have, no manufacturer document available to us uses the code; the description follows that logic and CARB. The code often comes and goes.
c: Loose contact at the glow plug connector
Chafing or broken wire in the engine harness
Sensor electronics of the glow plug unstable with temperature
s: Check engine light on
Occasionally rough running
Often no symptoms, the code comes and goes

P03E0.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 8. P03E0 means the pressure measured in the cylinder is lower than expected while the sensor itself is electrically fine. No manufacturer document available to us describes the code; GM patents show how such an evaluation works: peak and minimum pressure are compared with limits and with a motoring pressure calculated from manifold pressure and compression ratio, and the ratio of measured to motoring pressure is compared between cylinders. A low value can mean weak combustion or compression – leaking valve, worn rings, leaking glow plug seat, an injector delivering too little – or a sensor drifting downwards. The usual consequence is rough running and more smoke.
c: Compression loss (valve, piston rings, leaking glow plug seat)
Injector delivering too little or coked
s: Check engine light on
Lack of power, rough running, possibly misfire on this cylinder
More smoke

P03E1.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 8. P03E1 means the pressure measured or calculated for the cylinder is higher than expected. The 'pressure too high' codes are documented only at Audi, for cylinders 1 to 4 of the 2015 S3 petrol engine, where a software fault mis-detected misfire. On diesels with pressure-sensing glow plugs GM patents describe a peak pressure above its limit – too much or too early injection, or a sensor drifting upwards. For cylinder 8, which only engines with at least 8 cylinders have, no manufacturer document available to us uses the code; the description follows that logic and CARB. If the cylinder is shut off, power drops noticeably.
c: Injector delivering too much or dripping
Sensor drifting upwards (diesel pressure-sensing glow plug)
Knock or pre-ignition on a petrol engine
s: EPC or check engine light on
Misfire codes, possibly a cylinder shut off with noticeable loss of power
Rough running

P03E2.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 8. P03E2 means the swing of the pressure signal is too small. The only manufacturer we found using this code family, GM's European 2.0 CDTI four-cylinder diesel (Saab 9-5, 2010), uses 'pressure variation too low' for cylinders 1 to 4: signal outside its range for more than 0.2 s with the engine running; what exactly is measured, Saab does not explain – presumably the signal barely responds, for example because a coked glow rod no longer transmits the pressure. For cylinder 8, which only engines with at least 8 cylinders have, no manufacturer document available to us uses the code; the description follows that logic and CARB. Usually there are no noticeable symptoms.
c: Pressure-sensing glow plug faulty or coked (glow rod stuck)
Contact resistance in connector or ground
Actual compression loss or misfire in the cylinder
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable symptoms
Possibly rough running or combustion noise because control is off

P03E3.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 8. P03E3 means the swing of the pressure signal is too large. Usually there are no noticeable symptoms.
c: Sensor in the glow plug faulty (signal noise)
Loose contact or interference on the signal wire
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable symptoms
Possibly rough running or combustion noise because control is off

P03E4.d: Some diesels have a combustion pressure sensor in the glow plug; the engine module uses it to control injection for each cylinder. This code concerns cylinder 8. P03E4 means the combustion quality in the cylinder, evaluated from the combustion pressure, is abnormal. No manufacturer document available to us describes the code; a GM patent shows the method: the ratio of measured to motoring pressure is turned into a measure of combustion energy, an inequality index against the neighbouring cylinders in firing order is formed, and a two-sided threshold detects partial combustion, misfire, injector and compression faults. CARB requires engines with a combustion or combustion quality sensor to detect misfire more sharply (5 % in 1,000 revolutions). Typical causes are a coked or leaking injector, compression loss or poor fuel; the engine runs roughly and smokes more.
c: Injector coked, leaking or delivering the wrong quantity
Partial combustion or misfire (fuel quality, EGR distribution)
s: Check engine light on
Rough running, vibration
Loss of power, more smoke and consumption

P03E5.t: A Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor C Circuit Bank 1
P03E5.d: On some engines the intake cam phaser (camshaft position actuator A) has its own position sensors, which tell the engine module where the phaser actually is; sensor C is the third of them, bank 1 the side with cylinder 1. P03E5 is the general circuit code for this sensor: the module sees an open circuit or a signal outside its valid window on the supply, signal or ground line. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. GM's 2.7-litre engine monitors comparable position sensors on its sliding camshaft under other codes (P2C05 ff), with an open circuit above 200 kΩ and a short below 0.5 Ω in 4 of 5 samples – only as a comparison. The phaser is then usually held in its base position. CARB requires electronic parts of variable valve timing systems to be monitored as comprehensive components.
c: Connector or harness to position sensor C open or corroded
5 V reference or ground disturbed (also by another sensor on the same circuit)
s: Check engine light on
Cam phasing held in its base position, loss of power
Possibly rough idle or higher consumption

P03E6.t: A Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor C Range/Performance Bank 1

P03E6 means the sensor signal is electrically valid but implausible – for example the number or position of its edges per engine cycle does not match the crankshaft sensor, it jumps, or it lies outside the phaser's adjustment range. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. GM's 2.7-litre engine monitors comparable position sensors on its sliding camshaft under other codes (P2C05 ff), with an open circuit above 200 kΩ and a short below 0.5 Ω in 4 of 5 samples – only as a comparison. Typical causes are a dirty sensor or wrong air gap, a damaged or wrongly fitted phaser, or interference.
c: Sensor dirty (metal debris on the magnet) or air gap wrong
Phaser or sensor target damaged or wrongly fitted (timing)
s: Check engine light on
Cam phasing held in its base position, loss of power
Possibly rough idle or higher consumption

c: Sensor ground open or connector corroded

s: Check engine light on

P03E9.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor A Exceeded Learning Limit
P03E9.d: Engines with cam profile switching move the intake camshaft between lift profiles with actuators – for example pins that shift a sliding cam – and position sensors report which profile is engaged. The engine module learns reference values of position sensor A, such as its end-position levels or the expected pulse position relative to the crankshaft and camshaft sensors; a Ford patent describes correcting this position for the cam phase. P03E9 means the learned value lies outside the permitted adaptation limit, so profile detection is no longer reliable and the module usually stays in a safe profile. No manufacturer document available to us describes the code or its limits; GM's 2.7-litre sliding cam has no learning-limit code. CARB lists a pin that does not reach its position among the faults to be detected.
c: Position sensor A or actuator with integrated sensor worn or faulty (signal drift)
Actuator pin or sliding piece stiff, guide worn, dirty oil
Actuator not relearned or wrongly fitted after replacement
Connector or wiring with contact resistance
s: Check engine light on
Profile switching disabled: less power at high revs or higher consumption
Possibly further profile actuator or sensor codes

P03EC.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator C Control Circuit/Open Bank 1
P03EC.d: With a sliding camshaft, the intake camshaft (camshaft A) carries movable cam pieces with several lift profiles; solenoid actuators shoot a pin into a groove in the piece and shift it axially. Actuator C is the third of these actuators – not a profile position. The only known user is GM's 2.7-litre turbo four (L3B, three-step sliding cam, from model year 2019). P03EC means the actuator's control circuit is open: GM checks the circuit with the driver on and sets the code at an impedance of 200 kΩ or more (4 of 5 samples, above 11 V, MIL on the first trip). The actuator can then not shift its cam piece, and lift switching and cylinder deactivation are blocked.
c: Actuator connector loose, corroded or pin pushed back (often after valve cover work)
Wire broken in the engine harness
s: Check engine light on
Lift switching and cylinder deactivation blocked, higher consumption
Possibly rough running if a cam piece stays in the wrong position

P03ED.d: With a sliding camshaft, the intake camshaft (camshaft A) carries movable cam pieces with several lift profiles; solenoid actuators shoot a pin into a groove in the piece and shift it axially. Oil or moisture in the connector

P03EF.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator C Control Performance/Stuck Off Bank 1
P03EF.d: With a sliding camshaft, the intake camshaft (camshaft A) carries movable cam pieces with several lift profiles; solenoid actuators shoot a pin into a groove in the piece and shift it axially. GM uses this code for a pin that extends without being commanded (4 of 5 cylinder events, MIL on the first trip); a pin that does not extend on command shows up there through the cam piece position sensors (GM-specific codes P30BE ff). GM bulletins name swapped actuator connectors and actuators fitted to the wrong camshaft after repairs.
c: Actuator faulty inside: pin extends uncommanded (weak return spring)
Actuator connectors swapped, or intake and exhaust actuators fitted to the wrong camshaft
Interference in the Hall feedback signal (ground, connector)
Cam piece sticking or shift groove worn
s: Check engine light on
Ticking or rattling at the camshaft carrier
Misfire, rough idle or less power in the wrong lift profile
Lift switching and cylinder deactivation out of service

P03F0.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator C Control Stuck On Bank 1
P03F0.d: With a sliding camshaft, the intake camshaft (camshaft A) carries movable cam pieces with several lift profiles; solenoid actuators shoot a pin into a groove in the piece and shift it axially. GM checks whether the pin returns past its retraction threshold by the end of the engine cycle; a single failure in 5 samples sets the code (MIL on the first trip), because a pin left extended can drag in the groove and shift the piece wrongly.

Solenoid stays energized (control wire shorted to ground)
s: Check engine light on

P03F6.d: On some engines the exhaust cam phaser (camshaft position actuator B) has its own position sensors, which tell the engine module where the phaser actually is; sensor C is the third of them, bank 1 the side with cylinder 1. P03FA.d: Ignition K is one of up to twelve control signal lines (A to L) from the engine module to an ignition coil with integrated output stage or to an ignition module – plausibly the 11th channel, but the code standard leaves the assignment to the manufacturer. The code concerns this logic-level signal, not the coil's primary circuit (coil K has its own codes, P0361 and P2330 ff). P03FA means the control line is open or high-resistance: with its driver switched off the module sees a voltage that indicates a missing load (GM uses more than 30 kΩ for comparable coil drivers). The coil fires wrongly or not at all; the misfire usually also sets P0300 ff, and many modules shut off injection to that cylinder to protect the catalyst. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – it would only concern twelve-cylinder engines, whose makers publish no OBD summaries; GM and Ford tables stop at eight and ten cylinders.
c: Control line or connector pin open (corrosion, pushed-back pin)
Coil with integrated output stage or ignition module faulty
Supply or ground of the coil or module missing
s: Check engine light on, may flash with severe misfire
Misfire on the cylinder of this channel, rough running
Loss of power, cylinder possibly shut off

P0400.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P0400 is the general flow fault of EGR system A, used where the module does not classify the error as too little (P0401) or too much (P0402). Ford petrol engines with a stepper-motor valve open and close the valve at steady part load and compare intake manifold pressure with and without EGR; too small a normalised difference (below 1.0) sets P0400, MIL after two trips. GM diesels use the code differently, for air-mass checks with excessive EGR rate. EGR is then usually switched off.
c: EGR passages or valve carboned up
Leak in the intake or EGR pipe
s: Check engine light on
Pinging under load or rough idle, depending on direction
Higher NOx, emission test failed

P0401.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P0401 means too little exhaust is recirculated. Petrol engines open the valve briefly and expect a rise in manifold pressure (GM 2004 V6, MIL on the first trip); older Ford systems measure the pressure drop across an orifice (DPFE sensor). Diesels balance the air mass: if the meter sees more fresh air than the target EGR rate allows, too little exhaust flows (GM, Ford, Saab, usually MIL after two trips). Diesel causes are mostly a coked valve or cooler, petrol causes blocked passages.
c: EGR passages, valve or cooler carboned up
EGR valve faulty or stuck closed
Ford: DPFE sensor or its hoses blocked, cracked or swapped
Diesel: air mass meter drifting or air leak after the turbo
Vacuum control of the valve faulty
s: Check engine light on
Pinging or knocking under load (petrol)
Higher NOx, emission test failed
Often no noticeable symptoms

P0402.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P0402 means too much exhaust is recirculated, or exhaust flows although the valve should be closed – CARB explicitly requires a leaking valve to be detected. Ford's DPFE check at idle with EGR off expects no pressure difference above the engine-off value; Ford diesels compare the measured EGR rate with the expected one, GM diesels the fresh-air deviation in the opposite direction. Petrol engines idle roughly or stall, diesels smoke and may lose power.
c: EGR valve stuck open, dirt under the seat
Ford: DPFE sensor drifting or hose wrong
Diesel: air leak between air mass meter and turbo, MAF drift
s: Check engine light on
Rough idle or stalling (petrol)
Jerking at part load
Diesel: black smoke, loss of power

P0403.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P0403 concerns the electrical drive of the EGR valve – solenoid, stepper motor, DC motor or vacuum regulator. The module checks the output and sets the code for an open circuit (GM: above 200 kΩ, MIL after two trips; Ford after 4 s, MIL after two trips). Newer systems report shorts separately as P0489 (low) and P0490 (high); Ford and older GM systems include them in P0403. EGR is then switched off for the rest of the trip.
c: Connector at the EGR valve corroded or loose
Coil or motor in the EGR valve burnt out
s: Check engine light on
EGR switched off: pinging (petrol) or higher NOx
Usually no loss of power

P0404.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P0404 is the function check of the valve drive: on valves with a position sensor the module compares commanded and actual position, and a persistent deviation means the valve sticks, is coked or its drive is too weak (GM diesel 2018 above 10 %, GM petrol 2004 above 15 %, both MIL after two trips). Ford calls it control stuck. Saab's V6 diesel deviates and uses P0404 for a short to positive. EGR control is then switched off and the valve de-energised.
c: Position sensor in the valve inaccurate
Supply voltage too low or ground fault
s: Check engine light on
EGR deactivated
Rough idle or jerking if the valve hangs open
Diesel: possibly reduced power

P0405.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. EGR sensor A is usually the valve position sensor with a 5 V supply; on Ford until about 2011 it was the DPFE differential pressure sensor. P0405 means its signal is below the lower limit – GM 2018 below 11 % of 5 V (MIL after two trips), Ford below 5 % of full scale for 4 s, Saab below 0.26 V. The cause is a short to ground or an open signal or 5 V wire. EGR position control is then switched off.
c: Wire or connector to the EGR valve open or shorted to ground
Position sensor in the EGR valve faulty (usually one unit with the valve)
s: Check engine light on
EGR switched off
Diesel: possibly reduced power
Otherwise hardly noticeable

P0406.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. EGR sensor A is usually the valve position sensor; on Ford until about 2011 the DPFE differential pressure sensor. P0406 means its signal is above the upper limit – GM 2018 above 97.7 % of 5 V, GM 2005 above 94.7 % (both MIL after two trips), Ford petrol above 95 % for 4 s, Ford diesel above 4.70 V, Saab above 4.75 V. Typical is a signal wire shorted to positive or an open sensor ground, which GM names explicitly. EGR is then switched off.
c: Sensor ground or return wire open
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or positive
Sensor in the EGR valve faulty
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
s: Check engine light on
EGR switched off
Diesel: possibly reduced power
Otherwise hardly noticeable

P0407.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. What EGR sensor B is depends on the manufacturer – on systems with a second valve or pressure sensor it is that second sensor. GM's diesels of 2017/18 use P0407 for the coolant temperature sensor at the inlet of the high-pressure EGR cooler: low means a resistance below 55 Ω, i.e. very hot or shorted to ground, MIL after two trips. No manufacturer document available to us uses the code for a second position sensor. A substitute value is used.
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving
EGR or EGR cooler protection possibly restricted

P0408.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. What EGR sensor B is depends on the manufacturer – on systems with a second valve or pressure sensor it is that second sensor. GM's diesels of 2017/18 use P0408 for the coolant temperature sensor at the inlet of the high-pressure EGR cooler: high means a resistance above 134 kΩ, i.e. an open circuit or extreme cold (20 of 24 samples, MIL after two trips). A substitute value is used.
c: Signal or ground wire open, connector off
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving
EGR or EGR cooler protection possibly restricted

P0409.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. EGR sensor A is usually the valve position sensor (on older Fords the DPFE pressure sensor). P0409 is its general circuit code, for a missing or implausible signal that the module does not classify as low or high. No manufacturer document available to us uses it – GM, Ford and Saab report sensor A as P0405/P0406, Ford intermittent faults as P046D – so the description follows CARB, which requires input circuits to be checked for continuity and range. EGR is usually switched off.
c: Connector or wire of the position sensor open or loose
EGR valve with integrated sensor faulty
s: Check engine light on
EGR switched off
Otherwise usually unremarkable

P040A.d: EGR temperature sensor A measures the gas temperature in the EGR path – for cooler monitoring, component protection and the EGR model. Whether it sits before or after the cooler depends on the maker: GM diesels have sensor A after and B before the cooler, Ford diesels sensor B after it. Like a coolant sensor it is an NTC, so a low voltage means hot. P040A is its general circuit code. No manufacturer document available to us uses it – GM and Ford report this sensor as P040B to P040E – so the description follows CARB's requirement to check input circuits for continuity and range. A substitute value is used and the EGR cooler check is suspended.
c: Connector or wire at the sensor (heat, corrosion)
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving
Substitute value used, EGR cooler check suspended

P040B.t: EGR Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P040B.d: EGR temperature sensor A measures the gas temperature in the EGR path – for cooler monitoring, component protection and the EGR model. Whether it sits before or after the cooler depends on the maker: GM diesels have sensor A after and B before the cooler, Ford diesels sensor B after it. Like a coolant sensor it is an NTC, so a low voltage means hot. P040B is its plausibility check: after a cold start the sensor must warm up once hot exhaust flows. Ford diesels set the code if it rises by less than 10 °C after load; GM diesels if it barely changes after at least 8 hours off and a defined EGR flow (MIL after two trips). A sooted sensor tip or a lack of EGR flow are typical causes.
c: No EGR flow (valve or cooler blocked), sensor sees no heat
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving
Substitute value used, EGR cooler check suspended

P040C.t: EGR Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P040C.d: EGR temperature sensor A measures the gas temperature in the EGR path – for cooler monitoring, component protection and the EGR model. Whether it sits before or after the cooler depends on the maker: GM diesels have sensor A after and B before the cooler, Ford diesels sensor B after it. Like a coolant sensor it is an NTC, so a low voltage means hot. P040C means the signal is below its lower limit – very hot or a signal wire shorted to ground. Thresholds: GM's Duramax LML below 0.46 V for 5 s, GM 2014 below 0.14 V, GM 2018 a resistance below 404 Ω, Ford diesel below 0.69 V for 5 s; MIL after two trips. A substitute value is used and the EGR cooler check is suspended.
c: Signal wire shorted to ground (chafed on the exhaust)
Actual extreme gas temperature (EGR cooler faulty)
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving
Substitute value used, EGR cooler check suspended

P040D.t: EGR Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P040D.d: EGR temperature sensor A measures the gas temperature in the EGR path – for cooler monitoring, component protection and the EGR model. Whether it sits before or after the cooler depends on the maker: GM diesels have sensor A after and B before the cooler, Ford diesels sensor B after it. Like a coolant sensor it is an NTC, so a low voltage means hot. P040D means the signal is above its upper limit – very cold or, far more often, an open circuit (connector off, broken wire). Thresholds: GM's Duramax LML above 4.84 V for 5 s, GM 2014 above 4.98 V, GM 2018 a resistance above 1268 Ω (40 of 50 samples, MIL after two trips); Ford diesel lists the code without figures. A substitute value is used.
c: Connector off, broken wire or open circuit
Ground wire open or short to positive
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving
Substitute value used, EGR cooler check suspended

P040E.t: EGR Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P040E.d: EGR temperature sensor A measures the gas temperature in the EGR path – for cooler monitoring, component protection and the EGR model. Whether it sits before or after the cooler depends on the maker: GM diesels have sensor A after and B before the cooler, Ford diesels sensor B after it. Like a coolant sensor it is an NTC, so a low voltage means hot. P040E means the signal jumps. GM diesels of 2016–18 set it when the measured resistance changes by more than 25 Ω between two samples 100 ms apart – faster than any real temperature change, so a loose contact or a cracked sensor is the cause (40 of 50 samples, MIL after two trips). Ford and GM's earlier Duramax LML do not use the code.
c: Loose contact in the connector or chafed wire
Sensor with an internal hairline crack
s: Check engine light on, may come and go
No change in driving

P040F.d: The two EGR temperature sensors measure the gas temperature in the EGR path, before and after the cooler – which is A and which is B depends on the maker. P040F compares sensors A and B: after a long stop (GM: at least 8 hours) both must read about ambient temperature. If they differ by more than the calibrated limit at start-up (GM Duramax LML table, at least 20 °C, with exclusions for block heaters), the code is set, MIL after two trips. It does not say which sensor is wrong – compare both with intake air and coolant temperature. Ford diesels cover the same goal with P041B.
c: Contact resistance at one sensor's connector
s: Check engine light on, may come and go
No change in driving

P0410.d: After a cold start the secondary air (AIR) pump blows fresh air behind the exhaust valves so that unburnt fuel burns off and the catalyst heats up faster; a shut-off valve opens the path and stops exhaust from flowing back. P0410 is the general function code for secondary air system A. Many Bosch-managed engines check it passively: with the pump running, the front oxygen sensor must read lean or the fuel control must react; Pierburg lists P0410 as no lean signal, i.e. no air detected. Saab's Motronic 900, by contrast, uses it for too much air. GM's systems with a pressure sensor use P0411 and P2440 ff instead. The check runs once per trip after a cold start; driving is unaffected.
c: Secondary air pump failed (water ingress, seized)
Combination or shut-off valve carboned up or stuck
Vacuum hose or electric changeover valve leaking or faulty
Air ducts in the head carboned up or hose off
s: Check engine light on
Secondary air readiness not set (emission test)
Pump silent after a cold start, or unusually loud
Driving normal, higher cold-start emissions

P0411.t: AIR System A Incorrect Flow Detected
P0411.d: After a cold start the secondary air (AIR) pump blows fresh air behind the exhaust valves so that unburnt fuel burns off and the catalyst heats up faster; a shut-off valve opens the path and stops exhaust from flowing back. P0411 means the measured air flow does not match the expected value. Passive systems judge it from the oxygen sensor or fuel control (Saab 900: less than 12 points of correction within 12 s). GM measures actively with a pressure sensor between pump and valve and compares it with a model while pump and valve are on – from 2018 a deviation above 5.0 kPa or below −4.9 kPa sets the code, MIL after two trips. The test needs a cold engine after a long stop, so short warm trips do not complete it.
c: Pump weak or failed (water, filter debris)
Combination valve partly stuck or check valve faulty
Hoses blocked, leaking or off; ducts in the head carboned up
Pressure sensor port blocked or sensor drifting (pressure-sensor systems)
Pump relay or supply with contact resistance
s: Check engine light on
Secondary air readiness not set (emission test)
Pump silent after a cold start, or unusually loud
Driving normal, higher cold-start emissions

P0412.t: AIR System Switching Valve A Circuit
P0412.d: The switching valve is the electrically driven valve of this path – a solenoid valve, or on Pierburg/VW systems an electric changeover valve that applies vacuum to the pneumatic combination valve; valve A serves the first path or bank 1, valve B the second. P0412 is the general electrical fault in the control circuit of valve A, detected by comparing the driver's feedback with its commanded state. GM has used it since about 2015 specifically for an open circuit (200 kΩ or more, 20 of 25 samples, MIL after two trips) and reports shorts as P041F and P044F; older GM systems and Toyota use it for any driver fault. The valve then stays shut, so secondary air is missing and P0411 or P2441 may follow.
c: Switching valve A faulty (coil open or shorted, water ingress)
Connector corroded or wire open or chafed
s: Check engine light on
Secondary air inactive
Secondary air readiness not set (emission test)
Driving normal

P0413.t: AIR System Switching Valve A Circuit Open
P0413.d: The switching valve is the electrically driven valve of this path – a solenoid valve, or on Pierburg/VW systems an electric changeover valve that applies vacuum to the pneumatic combination valve; valve A serves the first path or bank 1, valve B the second. P0413 means the control circuit of valve A is open: with the driver switched off the module does not see the expected supply or pull-up level. The check runs continuously. Subaru's two-valve system assigns valve A to bank 1, and its bulletin advises checking the valve of the other bank as well. The valve stays shut and the bank gets no secondary air; flow codes such as P0411 may follow.
c: Wire to the valve open or connector loose or corroded
Fuse of the valve supply blown
s: Check engine light on
Secondary air inactive
Secondary air readiness not set (emission test)
Driving normal

P0414.t: AIR System Switching Valve A Circuit Shorted
P0414.d: The switching valve is the electrically driven valve of this path – a solenoid valve, or on Pierburg/VW systems an electric changeover valve that applies vacuum to the pneumatic combination valve; valve A serves the first path or bank 1, valve B the second. P0414 means the control circuit of valve A is shorted. A short to ground keeps the valve energized and open; a short to supply or a shorted coil overloads the driver, which many modules then switch off for the rest of the trip. An open valve with the pump running can also set P2440, and exhaust can reach the pump if the check valve leaks. Subaru names P0414 in its bulletin for the two-valve system.
c: Valve coil with shorted turns (water ingress)
Wire chafed against ground or supply
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
s: Check engine light on
Secondary air inactive
Secondary air readiness not set (emission test)
Driving normal

P0415.t: AIR System Switching Valve B Circuit
P0415.d: The switching valve is the electrically driven valve of this path – a solenoid valve, or on Pierburg/VW systems an electric changeover valve that applies vacuum to the pneumatic combination valve; valve A serves the first path or bank 1, valve B the second. P0415 is the general electrical fault in the control circuit of valve B, the second valve on two-valve or two-bank systems such as V engines or Subaru's turbo boxer. It is detected like P0412 for valve A, by comparing the driver's feedback with its commanded state. No manufacturer document available to us describes P0415 specifically; Pierburg's fault table lists it with the same remedies as valve A.
c: Wire or connector to valve B faulty
s: Check engine light on
Secondary air inactive on the second bank
Secondary air readiness not set (emission test)
Driving normal

P0416.t: AIR System Switching Valve B Circuit Open
P0416.d: The switching valve is the electrically driven valve of this path – a solenoid valve, or on Pierburg/VW systems an electric changeover valve that applies vacuum to the pneumatic combination valve; valve A serves the first path or bank 1, valve B the second. P0416 means the control circuit of valve B is open – the module does not see the expected level with its driver switched off. On Subaru's two-valve system valve B serves bank 2; the bulletin advises checking the valve of the other bank too, because a shared supply can be the cause. The valve stays shut and that bank gets no secondary air.
c: Wire or connector to valve B open
Coil of valve B burnt out
Shared supply of both valves faulty
s: Check engine light on
Secondary air inactive on bank 2
Secondary air readiness not set (emission test)
Driving normal

P0417.t: AIR System Switching Valve B Circuit Shorted
P0417.d: The switching valve is the electrically driven valve of this path – a solenoid valve, or on Pierburg/VW systems an electric changeover valve that applies vacuum to the pneumatic combination valve; valve A serves the first path or bank 1, valve B the second. P0417 means the control circuit of valve B is shorted. As with valve A (P0414), a short to ground keeps the valve open, while a short to supply or a shorted coil overloads the driver, which is then often switched off for the rest of the trip. Subaru names P0417 for its two-valve system, with valve B on bank 2.
c: Coil of valve B with shorted turns (water ingress)
Wire chafed against ground or supply
s: Check engine light on
Secondary air inactive on bank 2
Secondary air readiness not set (emission test)
Driving normal

P0418.d: After a cold start the secondary air (AIR) pump blows fresh air behind the exhaust valves so that unburnt fuel burns off and the catalyst heats up faster; a shut-off valve opens the path and stops exhaust from flowing back. Control A is the drive circuit of pump A – in practice the coil of the pump relay, which the module switches to ground; the old wording was Relay A. GM uses P0418 for an open circuit (200 kΩ or more, 20 of 25 samples, MIL after two trips) and P2257/P2258 for shorts; Saab and Toyota describe the same circuit. If the pump does not run, P0411 may follow. A relay with welded contacts keeps the pump running – Subaru recalled cars because the pump could overheat.
c: Pump relay faulty (coil open, contacts burnt or welded)
Control wire or connector to the relay open or corroded
Fuse blown, often due to a seized pump
Pump stiff or blocked by water or debris
s: Check engine light on
Pump does not run after a cold start – or runs constantly if the relay is welded
Secondary air readiness not set (emission test)
Hot pump or burning smell if it runs constantly

P0419.d: After a cold start the secondary air (AIR) pump blows fresh air behind the exhaust valves so that unburnt fuel burns off and the catalyst heats up faster; a shut-off valve opens the path and stops exhaust from flowing back. Control B is the drive circuit of a second pump or pump relay, found only on systems with two pumps or relays, for example large V engines with one pump per bank. It is checked like P0418 by comparing the driver's feedback with its commanded state. No manufacturer document available to us describes P0419 specifically; Pierburg's fault table lists it as relay B with the same remedies as relay A.
c: Wire or connector to relay B faulty
s: Check engine light on
Second pump does not run
Secondary air readiness not set (emission test)
Driving normal

Like a coolant sensor it is an NTC, so a low voltage means hot. P041A is its general circuit code. No manufacturer document available to us uses it – GM and Ford report sensor B as P041B to P041D – so the description follows CARB's requirement to check input circuits for continuity and range. A substitute value is used and the EGR cooler check is suspended.
c: Connector or wire at the sensor
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving
Substitute value used, EGR cooler check suspended

P041B.t: EGR Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P041B.d: EGR temperature sensor B measures the gas temperature in the EGR path – for cooler monitoring, component protection and the EGR model. Whether it sits before or after the cooler depends on the maker: GM diesels have sensor A after and B before the cooler, Ford diesels sensor B after it. Like a coolant sensor it is an NTC, so a low voltage means hot. P041B is its plausibility check. Ford diesels compare it at a cold start, after at least 6 hours off, with two other air temperatures (limit 25 °C, 30 °C with a block heater); GM diesels set the code if it barely changes after 8 hours off and EGR operation. Ford petrol engines list P041B with the electrical checks (5 s). MIL after two trips.

s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving
