P04D8.t: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop EGR Control
P04D8.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Where EGR is closed-loop controlled – on flow, valve position or pressure difference – CARB requires the control to start within a time set by the maker after starting; otherwise a fault is due, and P04D8 is that code. Typical prerequisites are coolant or cooler temperature, valid sensors and an operating range; Ford diesels, for example, run their EGR monitors only with EGR in closed loop. No manufacturer document available to us uses P04D8 – many monitor the inputs individually instead, as CARB permits.
c: Engine reaches release temperature too late (thermostat stuck open, very short trips, cold weather)
Faulty input sensor blocks the release (EGR temperature, air mass, position)
EGR valve or actuator not ready (stuck, learned value missing)
s: Check engine light on
Usually no driveability problems
Often together with coolant or sensor codes

P04D9.t: Closed Loop EGR Control At Limit - Flow Too Low
P04D9.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P04D9 means the EGR control has used up its authority and still gets too little flow – CARB requires this to be detected. Ford's 6.7-litre diesel sets it when the desired minus the measured EGR rate stays above 50 points for 20 s. Volvo cars from 2022 also set it after long low-load driving and fix it with a software update and an activation drive; a Mack/Volvo truck bulletin traces it to wrong EGR temperature readings from worn connector contacts.
c: EGR cooler, valve or pipes sooted or narrowed
EGR valve sticking or not opening fully
EGR rate mismeasured (temperature sensor contacts, air mass meter, pressure sensor)
Software or driving profile with long low-load operation
s: Check engine light on
Often no noticeable symptoms
Higher NOx, petrol engines may knock

P04DA.t: Closed Loop EGR Control At Limit - Flow Too High
P04DA.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P04DA is the counterpart of P04D9: the control cannot lower the flow far enough even at the end of its range. CARB requires this for petrol engines from model years 2019–21 and for diesels. Ford's 6.7-litre diesel sets it when the desired minus the measured EGR rate stays below −60 points for 20 s with EGR in closed loop. Too much exhaust in the cylinder causes soot, rough running and, on petrol engines, misfire up to stalling at idle.
c: EGR valve not closing (soot at the seat, stuck open)
Air mass meter reading too little fresh air (EGR rate calculated too high)
Position or EGR temperature sensor giving a wrong value
Intake or exhaust throttle wrong (pressure difference too large)
s: Check engine light on
Rough idle, jerking
Smoke or soot (diesel), possibly stalling at idle (petrol)

P04DB.d: The crankcase ventilation (PCV) system routes blow-by gas from the crankcase into the intake; CARB requires a disconnection between crankcase and intake to be detected. GM's 2.0-litre LSY has a pressure sensor in the PCV hose: with the hose connected it must see a pressure drop that grows with air flow, plus pressure pulses from the pistons. Ford reports the same sensor type as crankcase pressure sensor A (P051A ff). P04DB means a disconnection: without the pressure drop the clean-air side is off, without the pulses the crankcase side. GM's LSY uses the product of normalised offset and noise (below 0.63 kPa², MIL after two trips); Ford's EcoBoost checks the dirty side at cranking and the clean side above 5 lb/min of air. Engines without such a sensor may report a disconnection through mixture or load codes, as CARB allows. FCA bulletins cover it on the Alfa Romeo 2.0 turbo and the Ram 3.0 EcoDiesel.
c: Ventilation hose off or quick connector not latched (often after intake work)
Hose cracked or porous, or nipple broken
PCV valve stuck closed or oil separator blocked or frozen (simulates a disconnection)
Pressure sensor in the hose giving a wrong signal
s: Check engine light on
Hissing, false air, rough idle or lean running
Oil mist or smell in the engine bay

P04DC.t: Fuel Fill Door Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Range/Performance
P04DC.d: Plug-in and some full hybrids keep the fuel tank sealed while driving, separated from the charcoal canister by a valve. When the driver presses the fuel button, the system opens the valve, lets the pressure escape into the canister and only then unlocks the filler door. A switch reports whether the door is open or closed, so that the tank can be sealed again afterwards. P04DC means the door switch signal is electrically valid but implausible. A GM patent detects refuelling from a rising fuel level at standstill with low tank pressure; if the switch reported open for less than about 20 s, or closed for too long, it is faulty. A Ford patent sets a fault if the fuel level rose and the car drove off without the switch ever reporting open – the valve then stays open and the driver is warned. If the door state is unknown, the system leaves the tank open to the canister as a precaution and suspends the leak tests. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB's input component rules and patents for the door switch.
c: Switch mechanically jammed or misadjusted (reports one state permanently)
Door or actuator damaged or missing
Signal or connector fault with a valid but wrong level
s: Check engine light on
Fuel door open message although the door is closed, or missing when it is open
Door may not open or only after a delay
EVAP readiness not set

P04DD.t: Cold Start EGR A Flow Insufficient Detected
P04DD.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P04DD monitors EGR A while a cold-start emission reduction strategy is active and commands EGR: if the flow does not react as intended, too little exhaust is recirculated in the warm-up phase. CARB requires separate codes for such cold-start faults, which is why P04DD exists alongside P0401. The only manufacturer reference is a FCA bulletin for a six-cylinder diesel with high- and low-pressure EGR, naming it as a consequence of a failed position sensor (P0407/P0408) – repair that first.
c: EGR valve position sensor faulty (follow-on code)
EGR valve sticking or not opening when cold (soot, icing, condensate)
Pressure, temperature or air mass sensor misreading
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable symptoms
Higher NOx after a cold start

P04DE.t: Cold Start EGR A Flow Excessive Detected
P04DE.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P04DE is the counterpart of P04DD: during an active cold-start strategy the flow of EGR A is too high – the strategy calls for little or limited EGR, but the valve lets more through. CARB requires separate codes for cold-start faults. No manufacturer document available to us uses P04DE; FCA uses the neighbouring code P04DD, so its use there is plausible but not documented. Too much exhaust in a cold engine causes rough running, smoke and in extreme cases stalling.
c: EGR valve not closing fully (soot, condensate, stuck open)
Position sensor reports a wrong position
Air mass or pressure difference misreading
s: Check engine light on
Rough idle after a cold start
Smoke or soot after a cold start (diesel), stalling possible

P04DF.t: EVAP System Purge Control Valve A Performance/Stuck Open
P04DF.d: Purge valve A is the main EVAP purge valve between charcoal canister and intake manifold (on turbo engines the low-load path); its electrical circuit faults are P0443, P0458 and P0459. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows GM's comparable check P0496, Subaru's valve B counterpart P04AE and CARB's purge flow requirement. P04DF means valve A does not react as commanded or lets vapour through when closed: with the system sealed and the valve not driven, vacuum must not reach the tank. Intake vacuum then draws vapour all the time – rich mixture and hard starting after refuelling are typical.
c: Purge valve A leaking or stuck open (charcoal dust or dirt on the seat)
Canister broken down, charcoal dust in the valve
Tank pressure sensor giving a wrong signal
s: Check engine light on
Hard starting or stumbling idle right after refuelling
Rough idle, rich fuel trim

P04E0.t: EVAP System Purge Control Valve A Stuck Closed
P04E0.d: Purge valve A is the main EVAP purge valve between charcoal canister and intake manifold (on turbo engines the low-load path); its electrical circuit faults are P0443, P0458 and P0459. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows GM's comparable check P0496, Subaru's valve B counterpart P04AE and CARB's purge flow requirement. P04E0 means valve A does not open although it is driven: no vacuum builds up in the tank and the mixture does not react while purging – CARB requires missing purge flow to be detected. The canister is then not purged and saturates, causing fuel smell and early nozzle shut-off.
c: Purge valve A stuck closed (gummed, charcoal dust, spring or armature)
s: Check engine light on
Fuel smell
Nozzle clicks off early when refuelling

P04E1.t: Crankcase Ventilation Hose Connection Sensor Circuit
P04E1.d: The crankcase ventilation (PCV) system routes blow-by gas from the crankcase into the intake; CARB requires a disconnection between crankcase and intake to be detected. GM's 2.0-litre LSY has a pressure sensor in the PCV hose: with the hose connected it must see a pressure drop that grows with air flow, plus pressure pulses from the pistons. Ford reports the same sensor type as crankcase pressure sensor A (P051A ff). P04E1 is the sensor's general circuit fault, typical of digital sensors with invalid signal patterns or where low and high are not separated. Its circuit diagnosis is a precondition for the disconnection check P04DB. No manufacturer document available to us uses P04E1 itself; GM uses P04E2/P04E3, Ford P051A ff.
c: Sensor connector not latched or corroded
Signal, 5 V reference or ground wire open
s: Check engine light on
Disconnection check P04DB does not run
Usually no change in driving

P04E2.t: Crankcase Ventilation Hose Connection Sensor Circuit Low
P04E2.d: The crankcase ventilation (PCV) system routes blow-by gas from the crankcase into the intake; CARB requires a disconnection between crankcase and intake to be detected. GM's 2.0-litre LSY has a pressure sensor in the PCV hose: with the hose connected it must see a pressure drop that grows with air flow, plus pressure pulses from the pistons. Ford reports the same sensor type as crankcase pressure sensor A (P051A ff). P04E2 means the sensor signal is too low: GM's LSY sets it at 4.3 % of 5 V or less (about 0.22 V) in 1280 of 1600 samples, MIL after two trips. With this ratiometric sensor an open signal line also reads low, as does a missing 5 V reference. The disconnection check P04DB is then suspended.
c: Signal line open or shorted to ground
5 V reference open or shorted (often shared with other sensors)
s: Check engine light on
Disconnection check P04DB does not run
Usually no change in driving

P04E3.t: Crankcase Ventilation Hose Connection Sensor Circuit High
P04E3.d: The crankcase ventilation (PCV) system routes blow-by gas from the crankcase into the intake; CARB requires a disconnection between crankcase and intake to be detected. GM's 2.0-litre LSY has a pressure sensor in the PCV hose: with the hose connected it must see a pressure drop that grows with air flow, plus pressure pulses from the pistons. Ford reports the same sensor type as crankcase pressure sensor A (P051A ff). P04E3 means the sensor signal is too high: GM's LSY sets it at 95.5 % of 5 V or more (about 4.78 V) in 1280 of 1600 samples, MIL after two trips. Typical is a signal line shorted to 5 V or battery voltage; an open sensor ground can also pull the signal up. The disconnection check P04DB is then suspended.
c: Signal line shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
s: Check engine light on
Disconnection check P04DB does not run
Usually no change in driving

P04E4.t: Crankcase Ventilation Hose Connection Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P04E4.d: The crankcase ventilation (PCV) system routes blow-by gas from the crankcase into the intake; CARB requires a disconnection between crankcase and intake to be detected. GM's 2.0-litre LSY has a pressure sensor in the PCV hose: with the hose connected it must see a pressure drop that grows with air flow, plus pressure pulses from the pistons. Ford reports the same sensor type as crankcase pressure sensor A (P051A ff). P04E4 means the sensor signal jumps or drops out briefly – usually a loose contact, a chafed wire or a measuring port blocked by oil sludge or ice. The disconnection check P04DB is then suspended or may report falsely. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows the GM sibling codes P04E2/P04E3 and CARB.
c: Loose contact at the sensor connector
Sensor faulty or measuring port blocked (oil sludge, ice)
s: Check engine light on
Disconnection check P04DB does not run
Usually no change in driving

P04E5.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. The code standard allows up to four EGR temperature sensors, A to D – for example before and after the cooler, or in the high- and low-pressure circuits; which is which depends on the maker. Sensor D is the fourth of them, usually an NTC whose low voltage means hot. P04E5 is its general circuit fault, conceivable on systems with high- and low-pressure EGR and two sensors per circuit. No manufacturer document available to us uses sensor D – GM, Ford and FCA use at most A to C – so the description follows CARB's requirement to check input circuits for continuity and range. EGR then uses a substitute value or is switched off.
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving (EGR on a substitute value or off)
Possibly EGR flow or cooler codes (P0401, P2457)

P04E6.t: EGR Temperature Sensor D Circuit Range/Performance
P04E6.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Sensor D is the fourth of up to four EGR temperature sensors, conceivable on engines with high- and low-pressure EGR and a sensor before and after each cooler; it is usually an NTC whose low voltage means hot. No manufacturer document available to us uses sensor D; the description follows CARB and Ford's checks on sensor B as a comparison. P04E6 means the signal is electrically valid but implausible – for example it differs from other temperatures after a long stop, does not react when EGR opens, or freezes. Ford compares sensor B with intake and charge air after at least 6 hours off and flags more than 25 °C.
c: Sensor drifting (soot or oil crust, ageing)
Contact resistance in connector or harness (heat, corrosion)
Real temperature deviation: EGR cooler or bypass faulty, valve sticking
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving
EGR possibly reduced, higher NOx

P04E7.t: EGR Temperature Sensor D Circuit Low
P04E7.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Sensor D is the fourth of up to four EGR temperature sensors, conceivable on engines with high- and low-pressure EGR and a sensor before and after each cooler; it is usually an NTC whose low voltage means hot. No manufacturer document available to us uses sensor D; the description follows CARB and Ford's checks on sensor B as a comparison. P04E7 means the signal is below its lower limit – a signal line shorted to ground or, theoretically, an extremely high temperature. For sensor B Ford uses below 0.19 V. A substitute value is used and EGR may be reduced.
c: Signal line chafed against ground or the engine
Water or corrosion in the connector
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving
EGR possibly reduced, higher NOx

P04E8.t: EGR Temperature Sensor D Circuit High
P04E8.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Sensor D is the fourth of up to four EGR temperature sensors, conceivable on engines with high- and low-pressure EGR and a sensor before and after each cooler; it is usually an NTC whose low voltage means hot. No manufacturer document available to us uses sensor D; the description follows CARB and Ford's checks on sensor B as a comparison. P04E8 means the signal is above its upper limit – an open circuit in sensor, connector, line or ground, or a short to positive; the reading looks very cold. For sensor B Ford uses above 4.95 V. A substitute value is used.
c: Connector off or loose, or pin corroded
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving
EGR possibly reduced, higher NOx

P04E9.t: EGR Temperature Sensor D Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P04E9.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Sensor D is the fourth of up to four EGR temperature sensors, conceivable on engines with high- and low-pressure EGR and a sensor before and after each cooler; it is usually an NTC whose low voltage means hot. No manufacturer document available to us uses sensor D; the description follows CARB and Ford's checks on sensor B as a comparison. P04E9 means the signal briefly leaves its valid range or changes impossibly fast – typically a loose contact. Ford detects such sporadic faults on other sensors with short limit violations of about 0.4 s.
c: Loose contact in connector or harness (vibration, heat)
Sensor with an internal hairline crack
s: Check engine light on, may come and go
Usually no change in driving

P04EA.t: EVAP System Small Leak Detected - Fuel Tank Side
P04EA.d: Hybrids with a sealed fuel tank have a valve separating the tank from the charcoal canister and its vent side. CARB allows such sections to be leak-checked separately with their own codes; a Ford patent checks the tank side via tank pressure with the valve closed and the canister side with a leak check module. Conventional systems report the same leak as P0442, P0455 or P0456. P04EA reports a small leak (0.040 in) in the tank section – tank, filler neck, cap and lines up to the tank valve. No manufacturer document available to us names this code; the description follows CARB and the Ford patent.
c: Fuel cap or seal leaking or not closed properly (tether trapped)
Filler neck or tank vent line leaking
Sender or pump flange seal leaking
Tank valve or tank pressure sensor faulty
s: Check engine light on
Possibly check fuel cap message or slight fuel smell
No change in driving

P04EB.t: EVAP System Small Leak Detected - Fresh Air Side
P04EB.d: Hybrids with a sealed fuel tank have a valve separating the tank from the charcoal canister and its vent side. CARB allows such sections to be leak-checked separately with their own codes; a Ford patent checks the tank side via tank pressure with the valve closed and the canister side with a leak check module. Conventional systems report the same leak as P0442, P0455 or P0456. P04EB reports a small leak (0.040 in) in the canister and vent section – canister, vent valve or leak check module, dust filter and lines up to the purge valve – typically checked with the leak check pump with the engine off. No manufacturer document available to us names this code; the description follows CARB and the Ford patent.
c: Crack or leaking connection at the canister or vent lines
Vent valve or leak check module not sealing
Rodent bite or chafing on lines under the car
s: Check engine light on
Possibly check fuel cap message or slight fuel smell
No change in driving

P04EC.t: EVAP System Large Leak Detected - Fuel Tank Side
P04EC.d: Hybrids with a sealed fuel tank have a valve separating the tank from the charcoal canister and its vent side. CARB allows such sections to be leak-checked separately with their own codes; a Ford patent checks the tank side via tank pressure with the valve closed and the canister side with a leak check module. Conventional systems report the same leak as P0442, P0455 or P0456. P04EC reports a large leak in the tank section: it cannot be brought to test pressure or loses it at once – cap missing or open, line off. Stellantis documents it on the Jeep Wrangler 4xe plug-in hybrid only, whose conventional models report P0455; several bulletins name a cap not closed properly or a trapped tether, with a forced leak test via the scan tool.
c: Fuel cap not closed properly or tether trapped
Cap or filler neck sealing surface poor
Recirculation or vent line loose at the quick connector
Tank pressure sensor or valve faulty
s: Check engine light on
Check fuel cap message, often right after refuelling
Possibly fuel smell

P04ED.t: EVAP System Large Leak Detected - Fresh Air Side
P04ED.d: Hybrids with a sealed fuel tank have a valve separating the tank from the charcoal canister and its vent side. CARB allows such sections to be leak-checked separately with their own codes; a Ford patent checks the tank side via tank pressure with the valve closed and the canister side with a leak check module. Conventional systems report the same leak as P0442, P0455 or P0456. P04ED reports a large leak in the canister and vent section: the leak check module builds up no meaningful vacuum – line off, canister broken, vent valve open. Purging may be suspended. No manufacturer document available to us names this code; the description follows CARB and the Ford patent.
c: Line at the canister or leak check module off or broken
Vent valve or leak check module not closing
s: Check engine light on
Possibly check fuel cap message or slight fuel smell
No change in driving

P04EE.t: EVAP System Very Small Leak Detected - Fuel Tank Side
P04EE.d: Hybrids with a sealed fuel tank have a valve separating the tank from the charcoal canister and its vent side. CARB allows such sections to be leak-checked separately with their own codes; a Ford patent checks the tank side via tank pressure with the valve closed and the canister side with a leak check module. Conventional systems report the same leak as P0442, P0455 or P0456. P04EE reports a very small leak (0.020 in) in the tank section, usually checked with the engine off. Stellantis documents it on the Jeep Wrangler 4xe – cap, tether or filler tube, with a scan-tool leak test before replacing parts – and Ford on the C-Max, Fusion and MKZ hybrids and Energi of 2013–17, together with P0456 and P0457, fixed by a tighter purge valve and software.
c: Fuel cap seal deformed or dirty, tether trapped
Purge valve not sealing (Ford hybrids) – plus software
Leaking quick connector or vent line at the tank
Hairline crack in tank lines or flange seal
s: Check engine light on
Check fuel cap message
No change in driving

P04EF.t: EVAP System Very Small Leak Detected - Fresh Air Side
P04EF.d: Hybrids with a sealed fuel tank have a valve separating the tank from the charcoal canister and its vent side. CARB allows such sections to be leak-checked separately with their own codes; a Ford patent checks the tank side via tank pressure with the valve closed and the canister side with a leak check module. Conventional systems report the same leak as P0442, P0455 or P0456. P04EF reports a very small leak (0.020 in) in the canister and vent section; the leak check module compares the vacuum against a 0.020 in reference and the section does not reach it. On Ford's C-Max, Fusion and MKZ hybrids and Energi a leaking purge valve is the typical trigger, fixed per bulletin with the valve and software.
c: Vent valve or leak check module leaking
Hairline crack or leaking connections at the canister
s: Check engine light on
EVAP readiness not set
No change in driving

P04F0.t: EVAP System High Load Purge Line A Performance
P04F0.d: Turbocharged engines also purge the charcoal canister under boost, through a high-load line to the compressor inlet via a venturi; check valves keep boost out of the EVAP system, and CARB requires this path to be monitored. P04F0 checks it: Ford (2020–23, replacing P144C) runs the test once per trip under boost with the vent closed and purge open, and sets the code if tank pressure rises faster than 0.5 or 1 inH2O/s or the vacuum rate is out of range, within 5–10 s. VW, Audi and Bentley monitor the line with their own pressure sensor.
c: Check valve in the purge line leaking, stuck open, fitted wrongly or missing
High-load purge line to the turbo or venturi off, cracked or blocked
Purge line pressure sensor wrongly connected or faulty (VW group)
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving
Possibly fuel smell, EVAP readiness not set

P04F1.d: P04F1 is the function check of a purge line that is not the high-load path A – by the wording of another code list the low-pressure path to the intake manifold, counterpart of P04F0. The purge valve opens and the tank pressure or mixture reaction is missing or wrong: the line is blocked or off, or a check valve sticks. CARB requires every purge path to be checked; a FCA patent describes such a stepwise test. No manufacturer document available to us names this code.
c: Purge line to the intake manifold off, kinked or blocked
Check valve in the low-load path sticking
s: Check engine light on
Possibly fuel smell
No change in driving

P04F2.d: An electrically heated catalyst has a heating disc ahead of the catalyst so that it works soon after a cold start; Emitec's EMICAT runs on 12, 24 or 48 V and draws up to about 300 A. It is in series production on 48-volt mild-hybrid diesel vans since 2022. P04F2 concerns the heated catalyst of bank 1. The code monitors the supply voltage of the heater: if it lies outside its window when heating is requested, the heater cannot deliver its power and is limited or switched off, so the catalyst lights off later. A Subaru patent detects faults in the supply path when the heater is commanded. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – Ford, for example, states that heated catalyst monitoring is not supported – so thresholds and warning-lamp logic are not documented; the description follows CARB and patents for the same part.
c: 48 V or high-voltage supply weak (battery, charge, cold, DC-DC converter)
Fuse, relay or power switch faulty
Contact resistance or corrosion at high-current connector or ground
s: Check engine light on (depending on the maker)
Higher emissions after a cold start
Otherwise usually unremarkable

P04F3.d: An electrically heated catalyst has a heating disc ahead of the catalyst so that it works soon after a cold start; Emitec's EMICAT runs on 12, 24 or 48 V and draws up to about 300 A. It is in series production on 48-volt mild-hybrid diesel vans since 2022. P04F3 concerns the heated catalyst of bank 2 – no production vehicle with two heated catalysts is known. The code monitors the supply voltage of the heater: if it lies outside its window when heating is requested, the heater cannot deliver its power and is limited or switched off, so the catalyst lights off later. A Subaru patent detects faults in the supply path when the heater is commanded. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – Ford, for example, states that heated catalyst monitoring is not supported – so thresholds and warning-lamp logic are not documented; the description follows CARB and patents for the same part.
c: 48 V or high-voltage supply weak (battery, charge, cold, DC-DC converter)
Fuse, relay or power switch faulty
Contact resistance or corrosion at high-current connector or ground
s: Check engine light on (depending on the maker)
Higher emissions after a cold start
Otherwise usually unremarkable

P04F4.d: An electrically heated catalyst has a heating disc ahead of the catalyst so that it works soon after a cold start; Emitec's EMICAT runs on 12, 24 or 48 V and draws up to about 300 A. It is in series production on 48-volt mild-hybrid diesel vans since 2022. P04F4 concerns the heated catalyst of bank 1. The code means the measured voltage or current in the heater circuit is too low for the commanded state – typically the feed or the heating element is shorted to ground; depending on the driver also an open circuit. The heater is switched off. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – Ford, for example, states that heated catalyst monitoring is not supported – so thresholds and warning-lamp logic are not documented; the description follows CARB and patents for the same part.
c: Feed shorted to ground (chafed at the exhaust, heat)
Heating disc shorted to its housing (insulation damage)
s: Check engine light on (depending on the maker)
Higher emissions after a cold start
Otherwise usually unremarkable

s: Check engine light on (depending on the maker)

P04FA.t: EGR A Control Temperature Too High
P04FA.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. P04FA is a protective check of the electrically driven EGR valve A (DC motor on an H-bridge with position sensor): the module detects overtemperature or thermal overload of the actuator, modelled from current, actuating work and position behaviour, and limits or switches off EGR. Ford petrol engines from 2020 run it continuously with 4 s to fault above 8.25 V and 400 rpm. Pierburg documents heat damage to VW's 12 V electric EGR valves. EGR then closes, NOx rises.
c: EGR valve stiff from coking (motor working against resistance)
High thermal load (full load, poor valve cooling, low coolant)
Valve motor or H-bridge driver faulty (overcurrent)
s: Check engine light on
Rough idle or jerking if the valve hangs
Loss of power, possibly limp mode

P04FB.t: Crankcase Ventilation Hose Connection Sensor Range/Performance
P04FB.d: The crankcase ventilation hose connection sensor is a pressure sensor in the PCV line that measures pressure relative to atmosphere; it is the basis for detecting a disconnected hose (P04DB). P04FB is its plausibility check: GM's 2.0-litre LSY checks the zero point with the engine stopped (at least 10 s, coolant 70 °C or more) – a reading outside ±0.63 kPa or a frozen value sets the code in 128 of 160 samples, MIL after two trips. The disconnection check P04DB is then not possible.
c: Sensor port or line blocked by oil or ice (value frozen)
Contact resistance in supply, ground or signal
Residual crankcase pressure after switch-off (blocked ventilation)
s: Check engine light on
No change in driving

P04FC.d: The crankcase ventilation routes blow-by gas into the intake, and CARB requires it to be monitored. P04FC is a general function check: pressure or flow in the system deviates from the model. FCA uses it on the 2.0-litre turbo in the Wrangler and Cherokee (2018–19) and the 3.6 Pentastar in the Challenger (2020), with known false triggers fixed by engine module software; the strategy is not published, a FCA patent evaluates a pressure sensor in the fresh-air line.
c: PCV valve or oil separator blocked or sticking
Ventilation or fresh-air hose leaking or loose, oil filler cap leaking
s: Check engine light on
Possibly oil consumption or oil in the intake
Whistling from false air

P04FD.t: EGR Actuator A Control Processor Performance
P04FD.d: Exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) routes part of the exhaust back into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx. Some EGR actuators have their own electronics (smart actuators), with position control inside the actuator and communication with the engine module by bus or PWM. P04FD means the actuator reports an internal processor or electronics fault, or its self-test failed. CARB does not require such internal faults to be reported, so the code is a voluntary detail. Volvo and Mack trucks with turbocompound document it with false triggers fixed by engine software. The actuator then goes to its default position and EGR is off.
c: Electronics in the EGR actuator faulty (heat, moisture)
Valve stiff, causing a control fault in the actuator
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power possible
Higher NOx

P04FE.d: An electrically heated catalyst has a heating disc ahead of the catalyst so that it works soon after a cold start; Emitec's EMICAT runs on 12, 24 or 48 V and draws up to about 300 A. It is in series production on 48-volt mild-hybrid diesel vans since 2022. P04FE concerns the heated catalyst of bank 1. The code is the function check: the circuit is electrically sound but the effect does not fit – for example the energy delivered in a time window after switch-on stays below target, which a Toyota patent evaluates as a ratio, or the catalyst temperature does not rise as modelled. Ageing of the disc raises its resistance. The pure temperature result code is P0424/P0434. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – Ford, for example, states that heated catalyst monitoring is not supported – so thresholds and warning-lamp logic are not documented; the description follows CARB and patents for the same part.
c: Heating disc aged (resistance increased, cracks, electrode damage)
Supply drops under load (cold or weak 48 V battery, contact resistance)
Catalyst or exhaust temperature sensor implausible
s: Check engine light on (depending on the maker)
Higher emissions after a cold start
Otherwise usually unremarkable

P04FF.d: An electrically heated catalyst has a heating disc ahead of the catalyst so that it works soon after a cold start; Emitec's EMICAT runs on 12, 24 or 48 V and draws up to about 300 A. It is in series production on 48-volt mild-hybrid diesel vans since 2022. P04FF concerns the heated catalyst of bank 2 – no production vehicle with two heated catalysts is known. The code is the function check: the circuit is electrically sound but the effect does not fit – for example the energy delivered in a time window after switch-on stays below target, which a Toyota patent evaluates as a ratio, or the catalyst temperature does not rise as modelled. Ageing of the disc raises its resistance. The pure temperature result code is P0424/P0434. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code – Ford, for example, states that heated catalyst monitoring is not supported – so thresholds and warning-lamp logic are not documented; the description follows CARB and patents for the same part.
c: Heating disc aged (resistance increased, cracks, electrode damage)
Supply drops under load (cold or weak 48 V battery, contact resistance)
Catalyst or exhaust temperature sensor implausible
s: Check engine light on (depending on the maker)
Higher emissions after a cold start
Otherwise usually unremarkable

P0500.d: The vehicle speed signal A comes, depending on the maker, from a sensor on the gearbox, the transmission output speed, the wheel speeds via ABS/ESP or a CAN message; CARB explicitly names it as an input to be monitored. P0500 is the general code for this signal. Ford checks plausibility: the car must be moving (high load, positive torque), yet the signal stays below 1–5 mph for 5 s; Ford diesels flag a missing CAN message after 0.5 s. GM's Saturn ION of 2004 used high load with below 3 mph for 6.2 s (MIL after two trips); GM's 2018 tables use P0502/P0503 instead. Cruise control is then disabled and substitute values are used.
c: ABS/ESP module or wheel speed sensor faulty (signal source)
Output speed sensor or vehicle speed sensor faulty or dirty (metal debris on the magnet)
Wire or connector open or shorted, corrosion
Wrong tyre or axle data programmed
s: Check engine light on
Speedometer dead or jumping
Cruise control not working
Automatic shifts harshly or wrongly

P0501.t: Vehicle Speed Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0501.d: The vehicle speed signal A comes, depending on the maker, from a sensor on the gearbox, the transmission output speed, the wheel speeds via ABS/ESP or a CAN message; CARB explicitly names it as an input to be monitored. P0501 means the signal is present but does not fit the driving state or lies outside the physically possible range. Saab's Trionic T5 sets it above 270 km/h; other makers typically compare it with engine speed times gear ratio, wheel speeds or the transmission output speed. GM's 2018 tables and Ford do not use P0501 (GM: P0503, Ford: P0500). Cruise control is then disabled.
c: Wheel speed sensor or tone ring damaged or dirty (ABS source)
Wrong tyre size, axle ratio or coding
Sensor with weak signal or damaged tone wheel
Interference from damaged shielding or ground
s: Check engine light on
Speedometer dead or jumping
Cruise control not working
Automatic shifts harshly or wrongly

P0502.t: Vehicle Speed Sensor A Circuit Low
P0502.d: The vehicle speed signal A comes, depending on the maker, from a sensor on the gearbox, the transmission output speed, the wheel speeds via ABS/ESP or a CAN message; CARB explicitly names it as an input to be monitored. Despite its wording, all makers found check plausibility: the car is clearly moving (load, torque, overrun), yet the signal stays at zero. GM's 2018 tables use the transmission output speed: below 12 rpm (petrol) or 60 rpm (diesel) for 4.5 s, MIL on the first trip. Subaru (also in the Saab 9-2X) sets it below 1 km/h on overrun for over 4 s with the MIL at once; Saab's T5 after 4 s without signal above 1800 rpm. Electrical faults give the same picture.
c: Speed or output speed sensor faulty
Wire open or shorted to ground, connector corroded
ABS module sends no speed signal
Tone wheel damaged or sensor dirty
s: Check engine light on
Speedometer dead or jumping
Cruise control not working
Automatic shifts harshly or wrongly

P0503.t: Vehicle Speed Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic/High
P0503.d: The vehicle speed signal A comes, depending on the maker, from a sensor on the gearbox, the transmission output speed, the wheel speeds via ABS/ESP or a CAN message; CARB explicitly names it as an input to be monitored. P0503 combines three fault patterns: sporadic signal loss, jumping values and a value that is too high. GM detects a sudden signal drop quickly (0.3 s, 5 counts, MIL on the first trip); Subaru sets it at 240 km/h or more for a cumulative 4 s, Saab's diesel above 220 km/h. In limp mode Subaru sets the speed to zero, disables fuel cut-off on overrun and raises the fan.
c: Loose contact, chafed wire, corroded connector
Interference from damaged shielding or the ignition
Sensor with weakened magnet or damaged tone wheel
s: Check engine light on
Speedometer needle jumps
Cruise control drops out, jerky shifting

P0504.d: The brake pedal switch has two contacts – A usually for the brake lights, B for cruise control and brake information – working in opposite sense, so the module expects opposite states on every brake application. P0504 means they disagree. The signal is used for cruise control cut-off, brake override with electronic throttle, the shift interlock and start-stop. Ford sets it only after more than 25 (petrol) or 40 (diesel) disagreeing brake applications, with the wrench lamp instead of the warning lamp; a NHTSA investigation covers Hyundai brake light switches.
c: Brake light switch faulty (burnt or corroded contact)
Switch misadjusted or retaining clip or stop pad worn
Wire, connector or brake light fuse faulty
Moisture in fuse or junction boxes
s: Cruise control cannot be switched on
Brake lights stay on or do not come on
Selector lever cannot be moved out of P
Wrench or ESC lamp on

P0505.d: CARB requires the idle speed control to be monitored: petrol engines must flag a fault if the target idle speed is not reached within +200/−100 rpm, diesels within ±30 %. Older engines use a separate idle air control valve that bypasses the closed throttle; with electronic throttle the throttle itself controls idle and no separate valve exists. P0505 is the general fault of the idle control, used where the maker does not separate too low from too high or the control is at its limit. With an idle valve it is typically sticking or gummed (Saab T5: idle outside 700–1200 rpm); on electronic throttles a Ford investigation shows P0505 from deposits in the throttle body. Ford's 2020–23 engines disable start-stop with P0505–P0507. Warning lamp behaviour depends on the maker.
c: Throttle body or idle valve dirty or gummed
False air (hoses, intake gasket, crankcase ventilation)
Idle valve faulty mechanically or electrically
Learned values not reset after cleaning
s: Idle speed fluctuates, too high or too low
Engine stalls at idle or when coasting
Start-stop not working

P0506.t: Idle Control System RPM - Lower Than Expected
P0506.d: CARB requires the idle speed control to be monitored: petrol engines must flag a fault if the target idle speed is not reached within +200/−100 rpm, diesels within ±30 %. Older engines use a separate idle air control valve that bypasses the closed throttle; with electronic throttle the throttle itself controls idle and no separate valve exists. P0506 means the idle speed of the warm engine at standstill stays too low despite fully used control. GM uses more than 91 rpm filtered for 10 s (MIL after two trips), Ford petrol −100 rpm plus a correction above 1 lb/min, Ford diesel −100 rpm for 5 s, Subaru −100 rpm with the correction at its limit for 10 s three times. Typical are deposits, extra load or a restricted intake or exhaust.
c: Deposits at the throttle or bypass channel, or gummed idle valve
Extra load: stiff accessory drive, gearbox or converter
Intake or exhaust restricted (air filter, catalyst)
Idle valve or throttle actuator faulty, wrong learned value
s: Idle too low, engine shakes
Engine stalls when stopping or with A/C on
Check engine light after two trips

P0507.t: Idle Control System RPM - Higher Than Expected
P0507.d: CARB requires the idle speed control to be monitored: petrol engines must flag a fault if the target idle speed is not reached within +200/−100 rpm, diesels within ±30 %. Older engines use a separate idle air control valve that bypasses the closed throttle; with electronic throttle the throttle itself controls idle and no separate valve exists. P0507 means the idle speed stays above target although the control is at its minimum – air bypasses the control or the throttle does not close. GM uses more than 182 rpm filtered (MIL after two trips), Ford petrol +200 rpm, Ford diesel +160 rpm, Subaru +200 rpm for 10 s three times; on the Saab 9-4X three overspeed fuel cut-offs at standstill also set it. False air is the classic cause.
c: False air (vacuum hose, intake gasket, brake booster)
Crankcase ventilation leaking or wrongly routed
Throttle not closing fully (deposits, ice, stop misadjusted)
Wrong throttle learned value after cleaning or replacement
s: Idle speed too high
Automatic car creeps at standstill
Hissing from false air

P0508.t: Idle Air Control System Circuit Low
P0508.d: CARB requires the idle speed control to be monitored: petrol engines must flag a fault if the target idle speed is not reached within +200/−100 rpm, diesels within ±30 %. Older engines use a separate idle air control valve that bypasses the closed throttle; with electronic throttle the throttle itself controls idle and no separate valve exists. P0508 is an electrical fault in the drive circuit of a separate idle valve. Subaru (also in the Saab 9-2X) feeds the valve from the main relay and pulses it to ground; the module counts signal edges and sets P0508 at 8 or fewer in 64 ms instead of about 160 – the output hangs at one level – with the warning lamp at once and limp mode without idle control. Many makers, Ford among them, report all circuit faults under P0511 instead.
c: Control wire shorted to ground or open
Connector contact at valve or module
s: Idle fluctuates or is wrong
Engine stalls at idle
Check engine light on at once

P0509.t: Idle Air Control System Circuit High
P0509.d: CARB requires the idle speed control to be monitored: petrol engines must flag a fault if the target idle speed is not reached within +200/−100 rpm, diesels within ±30 %. Older engines use a separate idle air control valve that bypasses the closed throttle; with electronic throttle the throttle itself controls idle and no separate valve exists. P0509 is the counterpart of P0508: the drive circuit of the idle valve is shorted to positive or shows implausibly many signal edges – Subaru sets it at 225 or more in 64 ms, with the warning lamp at once and limp mode without idle feedback. It only exists on engines with a separate idle valve.
s: Idle too high or fluctuating
Stalling at idle
Check engine light on at once

P050A.t: Cold Start Idle Control System Performance
P050A.d: After a cold start the engine module raises idle speed and air mass and retards the ignition so that much heat goes into the exhaust and the catalyst lights off quickly. CARB requires this cold-start strategy to be monitored with its own codes, separate from ordinary idle and ignition faults. Ford collects data during the first 15 s after a cold start (coolant and catalyst 20–100 °F) and judges after 300 s, once per trip. P050A checks whether the raised idle speed or air mass commanded at a cold start is actually reached: Ford sets it when the average deviation between target and actual speed exceeds 200 rpm, with the warning lamp. GM does not use P050A as its own monitor and reports cold-start system faults under its manufacturer code P1400.
c: Throttle or idle valve dirty or coked, not enough air when cold
Fault in the throttle or idle valve circuit
Extra load at cold start (alternator, A/C), stiff engine
s: Check engine light on
Idle after a cold start too low, too high or hunting
Occasional stalling shortly after a cold start

P050B.d: After a cold start the engine module raises idle speed and air mass and retards the ignition so that much heat goes into the exhaust and the catalyst lights off quickly. CARB requires this cold-start strategy to be monitored with its own codes, separate from ordinary idle and ignition faults. Ford collects data during the first 15 s after a cold start (coolant and catalyst 20–100 °F) and judges after 300 s, once per trip. P050B checks the ignition part of the strategy – the retard for catalyst heating; CARB allows checking only the commanded value. Ford sets it when desired and commanded cold-start timing differ by more than 10°, for example because knock, torque or idle control take back the retard. FCA fixed P050B on the 2.0-litre turbo Wrangler of 2018–19 with software. GM has no separate monitor.
c: Idle control takes back the retard because speed would drop (false air, dirty throttle)
Knock control or knock sensor intervenes
Extra load or alternator at cold start
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable symptoms
Catalyst warms up more slowly after a cold start

P050C.t: Cold Start Engine Coolant Temperature Performance
P050C.d: P050C is documented only on Bosch ME9 in the Saab 9-3 V6 2.8 turbo: a cold-start plausibility check of the coolant temperature sensor. After a long stop coolant and intake air must read about the same; the code sets if coolant is more than 10 °C below or 15 °C above intake air, once per trip with the warning lamp. A wrong coolant reading distorts cold-start enrichment and can run the fan on a cold engine. The common reading 'coolant warms up too slowly' does not fit – that is P0125/P0128. GM, Ford and FCA do not use P050C.
c: Coolant temperature sensor drifting, wrong characteristic
Contact resistance or corrosion at the coolant or intake air sensor connector
Intake air temperature sensor reading wrong
Auxiliary heater or block heater not recognised, very short stop
s: Check engine light on
Rough running after a cold start
Radiator fan runs with a cold engine

P050D.d: GM's direct-injection petrol engines (from about 2016) split the injection into two pulses and retard the ignition after a cold start to heat the catalyst. P050D counts engine cycles with incomplete combustion via the crankshaft misfire detection during this strategy; if the rate reaches the catalyst-damaging misfire threshold, the code sets – once per trip, while the strategy is active (under 45 s running, coolant up to 66 °C). Mostly MIL after two trips, some calibrations without MIL. Ford and FCA do not use P050D.
c: Injector with poor spray pattern or deposits, or injector circuit fault
Spark plug or ignition coil weak
Poor fuel or low fuel pressure
s: Check engine light on (depending on calibration)
Rough idle or jerking in the first seconds after a cold start
Usually unremarkable when warm

P050E.t: Cold Start Engine Exhaust Temperature Too Low
P050E.d: After a cold start the engine module raises idle speed and air mass and retards the ignition so that much heat goes into the exhaust and the catalyst lights off quickly. CARB requires this cold-start strategy to be monitored with its own codes, separate from ordinary idle and ignition faults. Ford collects data during the first 15 s after a cold start (coolant and catalyst 20–100 °F) and judges after 300 s, once per trip. P050E is the system check of the strategy: does enough heat reach the exhaust and catalyst? Ford uses no exhaust temperature sensor but a catalyst temperature model – actual against target – and sets the code when the temperature deficit divided by the target rise exceeds 0.4, with the warning lamp. FCA uses P050E on the 3.0-litre EcoDiesel (Ram 1500, Grand Cherokee 2014), where it concerns heating the oxidation catalyst, fixed by software. GM uses its manufacturer code P1400 instead.
c: Idle or air control does not reach the cold-start target (dirty throttle, false air)
Ignition not retarded enough (knock or torque intervention)
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving
Higher cold-start emissions

P050F.d: GM (from about model year 2017/18) monitors the brake booster with a vacuum sensor: with the pedal at rest and high intake vacuum the booster must hold its vacuum; a loss over time is filtered as a drift ratio, and above a threshold P050F sets, MIL after two trips. It runs with the engine on, during start-stop auto-stops and after switch-off. Without enough brake vacuum the module must throttle, restart the engine from auto-stop or request a pump – which affects idle and start-stop – and brake assistance can drop. Ford and FCA do not use P050F.
c: Leaking vacuum hose or check valve
Leaking diaphragm in the brake booster
Vacuum sensor or its seal faulty
Electric or mechanical vacuum pump weak (where fitted)
s: Check engine light on
Hard brake pedal, especially after auto-stop
Hissing at the pedal, start-stop stops less often

P0510.d: Older engines with a mechanical throttle have a separate idle contact on the throttle or the combined throttle position sensor (Bosch Motronic throttle switch, Nissan and Toyota sensors with idle switch). The module uses it to recognise idle – for idle control, fuel cut-off on overrun and idle ignition timing – and as a substitute if the position sensor fails. P0510 flags an implausible switch: closed with the throttle open, or open at idle. Manufacturer thresholds were not found in accessible documents; with electronic throttle the switch no longer exists.
c: Idle switch or throttle sensor misadjusted
Switch contacts worn, dirty or corroded
Wire or connector open or shorted
Throttle not closing (deposits, sticking cable, stop misadjusted)
s: Idle too high or fluctuating
Engine stalls when coasting
No fuel cut-off on overrun (higher consumption)

P0511.d: CARB requires the idle speed control to be monitored: petrol engines must flag a fault if the target idle speed is not reached within +200/−100 rpm, diesels within ±30 %. Older engines use a separate idle air control valve that bypasses the closed throttle; with electronic throttle the throttle itself controls idle and no separate valve exists. P0511 is the general circuit fault of the idle valve – open, short to ground or to positive – without separating low and high, which CARB permits. Ford (up to about 2012, engines with an idle valve) has the output stage report it via a diagnostic status bit, continuously. Valve types are PWM solenoid or rotary valves (two wires) or stepper motors (four wires, typical of GM). Without a working valve the engine runs on a fixed bypass or the mechanical stop and may stall.
c: Idle valve faulty (coil open or shorted)
s: Idle too high, too low or fluctuating
Engine stalls at idle
Check engine light on

P0512.d: The engine module reads a start request – from the ignition switch, a start button via the body module, or start-stop – and drives the starter relay with it. P0512 flags a fault in this signal. Subaru (also in the Saab 9-2X) checks plausibility: if the engine runs above 500 rpm and the start signal stays active for more than 3 minutes, a short or sticking switch is assumed, MIL after two trips. On a Jeep Cherokee diesel a chafed harness caused P0512 with a no-start. The starter then does not crank – or with a short to positive keeps running.
c: Ignition or start switch, or start button, faulty or sticking
Harness chafed, short to ground or positive
Selector or clutch switch in the start path
s: Engine does not start, starter does not crank
Starter keeps running after the start (noise)
Check engine light (Subaru after two trips)

P0513.d: The engine module receives a secret code from the immobiliser or body module (Chrysler SKIM/SKREEM/RF hub, Saab CIM); if it does not match the stored code, P0513 sets and starting is prevented – Saab cuts fuel and blocks the starter. The most common trigger is a replaced or reflashed engine module that was not taught to the immobiliser (FCA, Saab), less often handshake timing on FCA hybrids or a key not programmed. FCA lists it as invalid SKIM key. It is not emission-related; CARB does not require immobiliser monitoring, and no source documents a warning lamp.
c: Engine module replaced or reflashed and not taught to the immobiliser
Key or transponder not programmed or faulty
Immobiliser, body or RF hub module replaced or faulty
s: Engine does not start or stops after 1–2 s
Immobiliser or security lamp flashes
Starter does not crank (Saab)

P0514.d: The battery temperature sensor – usually an NTC in the battery tray or inside an intelligent battery sensor on the negative terminal – lets the module adjust the charging voltage (higher when cold, lower when warm) and supports battery management and start-stop. P0514 is the plausibility check of the temperature signal. On FCA/Alfa Romeo the temperature comes from the intelligent battery sensor on the negative terminal; P0514 means its value is implausible, and several cases on the Alfa Giulia 2.0 were fixed by engine module software. A fixed substitute temperature is then used; CARB requires plausibility faults to have their own code.
c: Corrosion at sensor or connector near the battery acid
Sensor fitted wrongly after a battery change
s: Possibly check engine light
Charging voltage too high or too low
Start-stop not working

P0515.d: The battery temperature sensor – usually an NTC in the battery tray or inside an intelligent battery sensor on the negative terminal – lets the module adjust the charging voltage (higher when cold, lower when warm) and supports battery management and start-stop. P0515 is its general circuit fault – open or short – without separating low and high; the charging voltage is then fixed or conservative. No manufacturer document available to us names this code; the description follows CARB's input component rules. A fixed substitute temperature is then used.
c: Sensor not plugged in after a battery change
s: Possibly check engine light
Charging voltage not temperature-compensated
Start-stop or battery management limited

P0516.d: The battery temperature sensor – usually an NTC in the battery tray or inside an intelligent battery sensor on the negative terminal – lets the module adjust the charging voltage (higher when cold, lower when warm) and supports battery management and start-stop. P0516 means the signal voltage stays below its limit for a minimum time; with an NTC in a voltage divider a low voltage means very hot, or more often a signal line shorted to ground or an internal short. The module then assumes a hot battery and may charge too little. No manufacturer document available to us names this code; the description follows CARB's input component rules. A fixed substitute temperature is then used.
c: Signal line shorted to ground (chafed at the battery tray)
Moisture or acid in the connector
s: Possibly check engine light
Charging voltage too low
Battery weak, starting problems in the cold

P0517.d: The battery temperature sensor – usually an NTC in the battery tray or inside an intelligent battery sensor on the negative terminal – lets the module adjust the charging voltage (higher when cold, lower when warm) and supports battery management and start-stop. P0517 means the signal voltage is above its limit, close to the reference; with an NTC that means very cold, or more often an open circuit – sensor unplugged, wire broken – or a short to positive. The module then assumes a cold battery and may charge too high. No manufacturer document available to us names this code; the description follows CARB's input component rules. A fixed substitute temperature is then used.
c: Sensor unplugged or forgotten after a battery change
Wire or connector open or corroded
s: Possibly check engine light
Charging voltage too high
Battery gassing or overcharged

P0518.d: Older engines without electronic throttle have a separate idle air control valve bypassing the closed throttle; CARB requires its output to be checked but not the fault types to be coded separately. P0518 means its circuit fails sporadically – the signal or current briefly leaves its valid range and returns. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0518; GM and Ford report idle valve faults as P0505–P0507 and P0511. Engines with electronic throttle do not set it.
c: Loose contact or corrosion at the idle valve connector
Broken or chafed wire in the harness
s: Fluctuating idle
Engine stalls when coasting or stopping
Check engine light (depending on the maker)

P0519.d: P0519 means the idle control fails functionally with an electrically sound circuit – the actual idle speed deviates strongly despite fully used control. It is documented only on Subaru (also in the Saab 9-2X, electronic throttle, around 2005): idle at least 1000 rpm above target with the control already at zero for 2 or 5 s sets the code with the warning lamp at once, and a fail-safe cuts fuel to cylinders to stop the engine racing. GM and Ford use P0506/P0507 instead; CARB's mandatory limit is +200/−100 rpm.
c: False air behind the throttle (intake, gasket, vacuum hose)
Throttle or idle valve stuck open (foreign body, coking)
Follow-on fault of other codes (sensors, pedal)
s: Idle far above target, engine races
Jerking from cylinder cut-off in limp mode
Check engine light on

P051A.d: The crankcase pressure sensor measures pressure in the crankcase ventilation (PCV) against atmosphere; Ford's EcoBoost engines use it for the disconnection check P04DB, which needs a sound sensor. P051A is the sensor's general circuit fault. Ford uses it only for the digital SENT sensor, when the module receives invalid messages or signal patterns (together with U060E for lost communication); analogue sensors report P051B–P051D instead. It is checked continuously with 5 s to fault.
c: Connector or supply, ground or SENT signal wire open or corroded
Oil or moisture in the connector
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving
Disconnection check P04DB suspended

P051B.t: Crankcase Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P051B.d: The crankcase pressure sensor measures pressure in the crankcase ventilation (PCV) against atmosphere; Ford's EcoBoost engines use it for the disconnection check P04DB, which needs a sound sensor. P051B is its plausibility check. Ford flags a zero-point deviation above 0.15 inHg (about 0.5 kPa) from ambient with the engine stopped, and in operation at low air flow a pressure above 5 inHg (about 17 kPa) or below −0.6 inHg – so Ford also reports a real excess crankcase pressure under P051B. Maserati and Alfa Romeo bulletins name blow-by valves or software.
c: PCV or blow-by valve sticking, ventilation blocked or frozen (real overpressure)
s: Check engine light on
Possibly oil leaks or oil mist (real overpressure)
Often no change in driving

P051C.t: Crankcase Pressure Sensor A Circuit Low
P051C.d: The crankcase pressure sensor measures pressure in the crankcase ventilation (PCV) against atmosphere; Ford's EcoBoost engines use it for the disconnection check P04DB, which needs a sound sensor. P051C means the signal of the analogue ratiometric sensor is too low – Ford sets it below 0.44 V for 5 s. Typical is a signal shorted to ground, an open or shorted 5 V reference, or an open signal line pulled down.
c: 5 V reference or signal line open or shorted to ground
5 V reference pulled down by another sensor
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving
Disconnection check P04DB suspended

P051D.t: Crankcase Pressure Sensor A Circuit High
P051D.d: The crankcase pressure sensor measures pressure in the crankcase ventilation (PCV) against atmosphere; Ford's EcoBoost engines use it for the disconnection check P04DB, which needs a sound sensor. P051D means the signal is too high – Ford sets it above 4.56 V for 5 s. Typical is a signal shorted to 5 V or battery voltage, an open sensor ground, or an open signal pulled up. A real excess pressure in the crankcase does not set P051D.
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving
Disconnection check P04DB suspended

P051E.t: Crankcase Pressure Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P051E.d: The crankcase pressure sensor measures pressure in the crankcase ventilation (PCV) against atmosphere; Ford's EcoBoost engines use it for the disconnection check P04DB, which needs a sound sensor. P051E means the signal jumps or briefly drops below or above its limits – physically impossible changes, usually from a loose contact. No manufacturer document available to us uses P051E; Ford, Maserati and FCA use only P051A–P051D. The description follows CARB's input component rules.
c: Loose contact at the sensor connector
Oil or water in the connector
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in driving
Disconnection check P04DB suspended

P051F.d: The crankcase ventilation has an oil mist separator or filter element that can clog; the crankcase pressure sensor then sees rising pressure at a given flow. P051F reports this restriction. No manufacturer document available to us uses it – Ford reports high pressure under P051B. BMW and GM bulletins describe the consequences of a blocked separator: oil pushed past seals, oil mist in the intake and charge air cooler, higher oil consumption. CARB requires the PCV system to be monitored.
c: Separator or filter clogged with oil, soot or sludge
Icing in the separator or hose on short winter trips
s: Check engine light on
Oil leaks at seals or dipstick
Oil mist in the intake, higher oil consumption

P0520.t: Engine Oil Pressure Sensor/Switch A Circuit
P0520.d: The oil pressure sensor matters for emissions control because modern engines use it as an input – for two-stage or regulated oil pumps, hydraulic cam phasers and GM's cylinder deactivation, whose lifters switch by oil pressure. P0520 is the general circuit fault, used differently: Ford petrol and diesel engines set it for the digital SENT sensor when it reports an internal fault, does not initialise or sends values out of range (lost communication is U0600), after 5 s. GM's 1.4 L turbo with an oil pressure switch sets it when the switch reports pressure although the engine has been off long enough to be pressureless – type C, without warning lamp.
c: Connector corroded or oily (oil creeping through a leaking sensor)
Signal line open or shorted to ground
5 V reference or supply faulty (usually with other sensor codes)
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Oil pressure gauge or warning wrong
Cam phasing or cylinder deactivation possibly disabled

P0521.t: Engine Oil Pressure Sensor/Switch A Range/Performance
P0521.d: The oil pressure sensor matters for emissions control because modern engines use it as an input – for two-stage or regulated oil pumps, hydraulic cam phasers and GM's cylinder deactivation, whose lifters switch by oil pressure. P0521 is the plausibility check. With the engine off the sensor must read about zero (GM: above 40 kPa after 10 s is a fault, Ford diesel above 70 kPa); with it running the value is compared with a model of speed and oil temperature (GM single-stage pump ±50 kPa). GM checks two-stage pumps against limits per stage and calibrates P0521 with the pump valve – so a real pressure fault can also set it. GM type B, two trips.
c: Oil pump control valve or two-stage pump stuck in the wrong stage
Wrong viscosity, low oil level or foaming oil
s: Check engine light on
Oil pressure reading implausible or fluctuating
Cylinder deactivation or cam phasing possibly disabled

P0522.t: Engine Oil Pressure Sensor/Switch A Low
P0522.d: The oil pressure sensor matters for emissions control because modern engines use it as an input – for two-stage or regulated oil pumps, hydraulic cam phasers and GM's cylinder deactivation, whose lifters switch by oil pressure. P0522 means the signal voltage is below its limit: GM 2018 below 5 % of the 5 V reference, Ford petrol below 0.25 V, Ford diesel below 0.018 V, about 5 s. As the sensor gives about 0.5 V at zero pressure, this is an electrical fault – real low pressure is P0524. GM's 2006 V8s used the warning lamp only with cylinder deactivation; GM's 4.6 L Northstar then allows cam phasing only above 1500 rpm.
c: Signal line shorted to ground or open
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Oil pressure gauge at zero or warning despite normal pressure
Cam phasing or cylinder deactivation possibly disabled

P0523.t: Engine Oil Pressure Sensor/Switch A High
P0523.d: The oil pressure sensor matters for emissions control because modern engines use it as an input – for two-stage or regulated oil pumps, hydraulic cam phasers and GM's cylinder deactivation, whose lifters switch by oil pressure. P0523 means the signal voltage is above its limit: GM 2018 above 95 % of the 5 V reference, GM 2006 above 4.89 V, Ford petrol above 4.75 V, Ford diesel above 4.992 V, about 5 s. Typical are an open sensor ground or a signal shorted to 5 V or battery voltage. Real excess pressure is not reported here – Ford uses P055F for that. GM's 2006 V8s used the warning lamp only with cylinder deactivation.
c: Signal shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Oil or moisture in the connector
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Oil pressure gauge at maximum
Cam phasing or cylinder deactivation possibly restricted

P0524.d: P0524 is not a sensor fault but a condition: the measured oil pressure is below a minimum depending on speed, load and temperature (Ford diesel 30–90 kPa) for about 5 s, with the sensor itself plausible. Its purpose is engine protection; Ford petrol engines with mid-lock cam phasers drive them into the locked position. GM's tables do not use it; FCA updated the Ram EcoDiesel software against false setting in the cold. Stop the engine, check the oil level and confirm with a mechanical gauge.
c: Oil level too low, oil loss or consumption
Too thin oil, fuel dilution or clogged pick-up screen
Oil pump or pressure control valve faulty or stuck
False setting by software in the cold (Ram EcoDiesel)
s: Oil pressure warning and/or check engine light
Engine noise (lifters, timing chain)
Possible power reduction

P0525.t: Cruise Control Servo Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0525.d: P0525 concerns vehicles with a separate cruise control servo – a vacuum or electric actuator on the throttle cable driven by the engine module: the control circuit is electrically sound, but the response does not match the command. With electronic throttle the engine module controls the throttle itself, so the code hardly applies there. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0525. CARB names cruise control as the example of an emission-neutral diagnosis: switching it off as the default reaction suffices, so usually no warning lamp.
c: Servo worn or sticking, cable misadjusted
Vacuum leak at hose or diaphragm (vacuum servo)
Wiring, connector or fuse to the servo
Brake or clutch switch interrupting the servo release
s: Cruise control inoperative or switches off
Speed not held or fluctuating
Usually no check engine light

P0526.d: Engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch (GM petrol SUVs and pick-ups 2004–2006, GM Duramax, Ford 6.7 L Power Stroke) have a Hall sensor reporting fan speed; the fan checks P0483, P0494 and P0495 need it. P0526 means no usable signal although the clutch is driven: GM Duramax below 500 rpm with fan duty at least 36 % for 2 s; the 6.6 L LML distinguishes a level stuck low or high; GM petrol V8s set it when no pulses arrive with the engine running. Type B, two trips. GM also reports a missing signal under P0526. A GM bulletin for 2011–2013 Duramax vans and pick-ups names loud fan noise and weak air conditioning at low speed.
c: Hall sensor at the fan clutch faulty
Wiring or connector (chafing at the shroud, corrosion)
s: Check engine light on
Fan permanently on or off, loud fan noise
Weak air conditioning at low speed, overheating under load

P0527.d: Engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch (GM petrol SUVs and pick-ups 2004–2006, GM Duramax, Ford 6.7 L Power Stroke) have a Hall sensor reporting fan speed; the fan checks P0483, P0494 and P0495 need it. P0527 means a signal is present but implausible – spikes, jumps or a speed that does not fit the clutch command and engine speed. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0527; GM covers implausibility through P0483 (target versus actual) and P0493. CARB requires input components used by other diagnoses to be checked for plausibility.
c: Sensor or trigger element damaged, wrong air gap
Interference or ground fault on the sensor line
Viscous clutch slipping or sticking (real speed off)
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Unsteady fan control
Fan permanently on

P0528.t: Fan Speed Sensor Circuit No Signal
P0528.d: Engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch (GM petrol SUVs and pick-ups 2004–2006, GM Duramax, Ford 6.7 L Power Stroke) have a Hall sensor reporting fan speed; the fan checks P0483, P0494 and P0495 need it. P0528 means no pulses arrive from the sensor although the fan should be turning. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0528 – GM detects exactly this state (fan below 4 rpm with the engine running) but reports it as P0526. CARB requires input components to be checked for open and short circuits.
c: Fan or clutch really not turning
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Fan permanently on or not at all
Tendency to overheat

P0529.d: Engine-driven fans with an electronically controlled viscous clutch (GM petrol SUVs and pick-ups 2004–2006, GM Duramax, Ford 6.7 L Power Stroke) have a Hall sensor reporting fan speed; the fan checks P0483, P0494 and P0495 need it. P0529 means the speed signal drops out or jumps at times. It is documented only for Ford's 6.7 L Power Stroke in the 2016–2019 Super Duty and F-650/750: a Ford service message lists it with P0480, P0494, P0495 and P0691–P0694 for fans running permanently or not at all, and warns against replacing the clutch too early – check wiring, connector and sensor first. Ford's summaries give no thresholds.
c: Loose contact at connector or wiring at the fan (vibration, chafing)
Sensor in the fan clutch intermittently faulty
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Fan running permanently or not at all
Loud fan noise

P052A.t: Cold Start A Camshaft Position Timing Over-Advanced Bank 1
P052A.d: Some engines shift the intake (A) camshaft right after a cold start so that more exhaust heat reaches the catalyst; CARB requires each commanded element of this cold-start strategy to be monitored under its own codes. Documented only by Ford (from 2008): during the first 60 s it checks the cam position for 5 s and sets a code above 11° deviation, plus a stuck-pin test (10° commanded, under 2° movement) and an averaged deviation index. Warning lamp after two trips; afterwards the normal cam codes take over. P052A means bank 1 was too far advanced. Outside cold start, P0011 applies.
c: Cam phaser sticking or lock pin not releasing
Low oil level, wrong viscosity or sludged oil
Oil control valve sticking or screen clogged
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable driving symptoms
Possibly rattle or rough idle on cold start
Higher cold-start emissions

P052B.t: Cold Start A Camshaft Position Timing Over-Retarded Bank 1
P052B.d: Some engines shift the intake (A) camshaft right after a cold start so that more exhaust heat reaches the catalyst; CARB requires each commanded element of this cold-start strategy to be monitored under its own codes. Documented only by Ford (from 2008): during the first 60 s it checks the cam position for 5 s and sets a code above 11° deviation, plus a stuck-pin test (10° commanded, under 2° movement) and an averaged deviation index. Warning lamp after two trips; afterwards the normal cam codes take over. P052B means bank 1 was too far retarded – typical for a phaser stuck in its locked base position.
c: Cam phaser sticking or lock pin not releasing (stuck in base position)
Low oil level, wrong viscosity or sludged oil
Oil control valve sticking or screen clogged
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable driving symptoms
Possibly rattle or rough idle on cold start
Higher cold-start emissions

P052C.t: Cold Start A Camshaft Position Timing Over-Advanced Bank 2
P052C.d: Some engines shift the intake (A) camshaft right after a cold start so that more exhaust heat reaches the catalyst; CARB requires each commanded element of this cold-start strategy to be monitored under its own codes. Documented only by Ford (from 2008): during the first 60 s it checks the cam position for 5 s and sets a code above 11° deviation, plus a stuck-pin test (10° commanded, under 2° movement) and an averaged deviation index. Warning lamp after two trips; afterwards the normal cam codes take over. P052C means bank 2 of a V engine was too far advanced. Outside cold start, P0021 applies.
c: Cam phaser sticking or lock pin not releasing (bank 2)
Low oil level, wrong viscosity or sludged oil
Oil control valve sticking or screen clogged
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable driving symptoms
Possibly rattle or rough idle on cold start
Higher cold-start emissions

P052D.t: Cold Start A Camshaft Position Timing Over-Retarded Bank 2
P052D.d: Some engines shift the intake (A) camshaft right after a cold start so that more exhaust heat reaches the catalyst; CARB requires each commanded element of this cold-start strategy to be monitored under its own codes. Documented only by Ford (from 2008): during the first 60 s it checks the cam position for 5 s and sets a code above 11° deviation, plus a stuck-pin test (10° commanded, under 2° movement) and an averaged deviation index. Warning lamp after two trips; afterwards the normal cam codes take over. P052D means bank 2 of a V engine was too far retarded. Outside cold start, P0022 applies.
c: Cam phaser sticking or lock pin not releasing (bank 2)
Low oil level, wrong viscosity or sludged oil
Oil control valve sticking or screen clogged
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable driving symptoms
Possibly rattle or rough idle on cold start
Higher cold-start emissions

P052E.d: P052E is a function fault of the crankcase ventilation pressure regulating valve. Audi's 3.0 TFSI has a diaphragm valve whose torn diaphragm or elbow causes false air and whistling; Mercedes' M270/M274 have a switched part-load ventilation valve that blocks with oil carbon and lets oil into the intake – blue smoke, rough running, lack of power; Mercedes extended the emission warranty on the intake module. GM Europe's 2.0 diesel in the Saab 9-5 uses P052E differently, for PCV heater performance – which J2012 lists as P053D.
c: Diaphragm of the regulating valve torn or fatigued
Part-load ventilation valve blocked (oil carbon, sludge)
Elbow or hose at the valve cracked, clamp leaking
s: Check engine light on
Whistling or hissing in the engine bay
Rough idle, blue smoke or oil consumption, lack of power

P052F.t: Glow Plug Control Module 1 System Voltage
P052F.d: Diesel glow plugs are switched by a separate glow plug control module fed from the battery, with its own ground, a command from the engine module and a diagnostic line back. P052F means its supply voltage is out of range. Ford's 6.7 L and 3.0 L Power Stroke set it below 6.5 V, above 16.5 V or with an open supply, after about 1 s, continuously. An FCA bulletin shows P052F together with all six glow plug open codes P0671–P0676, because without supply no current flows – check main feed, connector and grounds first. GM does not use it.
c: Main feed to the module open or high-resistance (fuse, connector, corroded ring terminal)
Poor ground of the glow plug module
System voltage too low or too high (weak battery, regulator fault)
s: Check engine light on
Hard cold start, long cranking, white smoke
Several glow plug codes at once

P0530.t: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor A Circuit
P0530.d: The engine module reads the high-side refrigerant pressure sensor (5 V reference, signal rising with pressure) to switch or regulate the compressor, raise the radiator fans at high pressure and pre-control the compressor load at idle. CARB therefore requires A/C components to be monitored where they alter fuel or ignition control or feed other diagnoses (from 2006–2008). P0530 is the general circuit fault; GM and the Saab 9-4X use the more precise P0532/P0533 instead. Saab's 2006 9-5 diesel (Bosch EDC16) assigns P0530 differently, to a short to ground below 0.1 V for 0.6 s, switching off the A/C relay. Warning lamp depends on the maker.
c: Connector or contacts corroded or loose
5 V reference shorted by another sensor
s: Air conditioning not cooling (compressor off)
Radiator fan running permanently
Check engine light (depending on the maker)

P0531.t: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0531.d: The engine module reads the high-side refrigerant pressure sensor (5 V reference, signal rising with pressure) to switch or regulate the compressor, raise the radiator fans at high pressure and pre-control the compressor load at idle. CARB therefore requires A/C components to be monitored where they alter fuel or ignition control or feed other diagnoses (from 2006–2008). P0531 means the signal is electrically valid but does not fit the expected pressure. GM compares the pressure rise after compressor engagement with a model of ambient and coolant temperature, road speed and fan speed, 100 samples of 100 ms, type X without warning lamp. Saab's 2006 9-5 diesel assigns P0531 differently, to a short to positive above 4.9 V with 101 kPa substitute value.
c: Refrigerant charge wrong (too little or too much)
Compressor or control valve delivering poorly
s: Weak or no cooling
Compressor cycling unusually
Usually no check engine light

P0532.t: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor A Circuit Low
