c: Debris or ice blocking the louvres
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Higher coolant temperature under load or slower warm-up
Slightly higher fuel consumption
Often no noticeable symptoms

P05FF.t: Brake Pressure Sensor/Brake Pedal Position Sensor Correlation
P05FF.d: Stop-start decides when to stop and restart the engine from the brake: Ford stops it when the pedal switch is on and master cylinder pressure is high enough, and restarts when pressure falls below a filtered reference. P05FF means brake pressure (from the sensor in the ABS unit, sent over the network) and brake pedal position do not agree – for example pedal pressed without pressure build-up, or pressure without pedal. Ford's 2020–23 petrol vehicles check this continuously in the section 'Brake Diagnostics for Stop-Start Dependability' and set the code within 1 s, without the check engine light; stop-start is blocked so the engine is not stopped or started unexpectedly. Ford gives no threshold for the deviation. GM monitors the pedal travel sensor under P057x instead. Brake switch disagreement is P0504.
c: Brake pedal position sensor or switch misadjusted or faulty
Master cylinder pressure sensor in the ABS unit faulty
Network communication or software between ABS module and engine module
Air in the brake system or hydraulic fault (long pedal travel without pressure)
s: Stop-start disabled
No check engine light at Ford, possibly wrench or service warning
Possible related codes P0504 or brake pressure codes

P0600.d: P0600 means a serial data link that the module relies on has failed. At Ford it is the internal link between the main processor and the monitoring processor ('quizzer') of the electronic throttle safety concept: if data cannot be exchanged or check bytes are invalid, the code sets within about a second (diesel: 5 s), usually with the check engine and wrench lamps and a throttle failure mode such as an RPM limit. Subaru (also sold as Saab 9-2X) uses it for the dedicated serial line between engine and transmission module. GM does not use P0600. Lost CAN messages from a named module are reported separately as U0100 and following. Before replacing anything: check battery, grounds and supply, look for a software bulletin, reprogram with a stable power supply, and replace the module only if the code returns.
c: Internal module fault in the processor-to-processor link
Open or short in a dedicated serial line between engine and transmission module (e.g. Subaru)
Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module
Fault in the transmission module at the other end of the line
s: Check engine light, at Ford also the wrench lamp
Reduced power or RPM limit (throttle failure mode)
Harsh shifts or transmission limp mode where the line links engine and gearbox
Other monitors such as the catalyst monitor do not run

P0601.t: Internal Control Module Memory Checksum Error
P0601.d: The module continuously calculates a checksum over its program and calibration memory (flash) and compares it with the stored value; on newer units the flash error correction also reports bit errors it cannot repair. A mismatch means the stored software is corrupted. GM sets P0601 in the engine module after one failed pass (or five once the first pass is complete) and turns on the lamp in the first trip; in body modules after two trips. Ford reports the same check as P0605, while GM, VW and Mazda use P0601. Typical causes are an interrupted reflash and manufacturer software errors – VW (2.0 TFSI) and Mazda (MX-5 2013) fixed it by reprogramming. The code alone does not say which module set it – the scan tool shows whether it is the engine, transmission, brake or body module.
c: Defective flash memory in the module
Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module
s: Check engine light on
Often no change in driving
Possibly no start or limp mode if the software is badly damaged
Transmission limp mode if the transmission module is affected

P0602.d: P0602 reports that the module is not, or not completely, programmed for this vehicle. GM checks at power-up and then every second whether a service replacement module still carries no calibration, and sets the code in the first trip; in brake modules a missing calibration set or a sensor ID that does not match also counts. Ford uses P0602 when the checksum of the vehicle identification block (tyre size, axle ratio, VIN) is wrong. Typical triggers are a new module that was never programmed, a reflash interrupted by a voltage dip or lost connection, or wrong software. Depending on the maker the engine may not start, run with reduced power or only show the lamp; GM Europe engines show a service lamp instead of the check engine light. The fix is almost always reprogramming with a stable power supply; replace the module only if the code returns.
c: Programming interrupted by a voltage dip or lost connection
Wrong or incompatible software, calibration or configuration block
Internal memory defect in the module
s: Check engine light or service lamp
Engine may not start or runs in limp mode
Reduced engine power
Appears right after a module replacement or software update

P0603.t: Internal Control Module Keep Alive Memory (KAM) Error
P0603.d: Keep alive memory holds learned values – fuel trim, idle and shift adaptation, readiness status – while the engine is off, as long as the module has constant battery power; CARB defines it as memory that is lost when the battery or fuse is disconnected. The module stores a checksum of this memory at shutdown and compares it at the next start (Ford, GM Europe); GM calls the check 'long term memory reset', and the Ford diesel watches the supply of its engine-off timer chip (below 0.25 V). By far the most common trigger is outside the module: a disconnected, flat or replaced battery or an interrupted constant feed – Nissan bulletins name exactly this and ask for at least 11 V before clearing. Learned values then start from default and the readiness monitors are reset. Whether the lamp comes on depends on the maker.
c: Battery disconnected, deeply discharged or replaced
Interrupted constant power feed to the module (fuse, wire, corrosion)
Main relay drops out too early, memory not saved completely at shutdown
s: Check engine light on (depending on the maker)
Rough idle or changed shifting until values are relearned
Readiness monitors reset
Often right after battery work

P0604.t: Internal Control Module Random Access Memory (RAM) Error
P0604.d: P0604 means the module's working memory (RAM) failed its self-test: a value written to a cell does not read back correctly, a built-in hardware test fails, error correction reports faults, or protected memory is written without permission. GM's engine module scans the whole RAM within 30 s of start-up and then keeps checking in the background, setting the code after repeated failures with the lamp in the first trip; Ford tests RAM during initialisation, the GM gateway with error correction at start (two trips). Unlike most memory codes, P0604 is used the same way by GM, Ford, Chrysler and Saab. Consequences depend on the module: a transmission module goes into limp mode with maximum line pressure and a fixed gear, an engine module may reduce power. The code alone does not say which module set it – the scan tool shows whether it is the engine, transmission, brake or body module.
c: Internal hardware defect of the module (RAM)
Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module
Moisture or corrosion in the module or at its connector
s: Check engine light on
Limp mode or transmission limp mode
Intermittent stalling or starting problems
Several module codes at the same time

P0605.t: Internal Control Module Read Only Memory (ROM) Error
P0605.d: P0605 reports an error in the module's program memory (ROM, today flash), found by a checksum or error-correction check at start-up or in the background. Ford is the main user: its engine and transmission modules compare a ROM checksum and set P0605 with the check engine light; the diesel transmission module tests once per trip at start. GM's engine module does not use P0605 and reports the same fault as P0601; the GM gateway (2025) uses it for uncorrectable ROM bit errors with two-trip logic, and GM Europe's 1.6 L engine even assigns it to processor faults of the throttle control. Which of P0601 and P0605 appears is therefore the manufacturer's choice. The usual repair is reprogramming, which restores the memory contents; replace the module only if the code returns.
c: Program memory corrupted by an interrupted reflash
Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module
s: Check engine light on
Possibly starting problems
Transmission limp mode if the transmission module is affected
Reduced power (GM Europe assignment)

P0606.d: P0606 means the module doubts the integrity of its own processor. Checks include a question-and-answer game between main and monitoring processor (GM: new seed via SPI within 450 ms; Ford: 'quizzer' level 3), arithmetic unit and register tests, stack overflow, the order in which safety-critical software runs, and the internal voltage supply (Ford diesel: 5 V rail outside 4.7–5.3 V). Because it belongs to the electronic throttle safety concept, the module usually reacts with a failure mode – reduced power, RPM limit or throttle default position – and the lamp in the first trip. Many cases are software issues fixed by reprogramming (Chrysler 3.6 L 2014, VW Routan, GM brake module 2024), so check bulletins before replacing hardware. The code alone does not say which module set it – the scan tool shows whether it is the engine, transmission, brake or body module.
c: Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module
Internal hardware defect (processor, voltage regulator, output stage chip)
Short on a 5 V sensor reference loading the internal supply
s: Check engine light, at Ford also the wrench lamp
Limp mode with reduced power or RPM limit
Poor throttle response
Rarely stalling or no start
Often together with voltage codes P0562/P0563

P0607.d: P0607 is the general 'module not working correctly' code, used when no specific memory or processor part is named. Ford sets it for wrong instruction execution or too many processor resets in engine and transmission modules; the Ford diesel after five communication errors with its monitoring chip within 20 s (a complete loss of that link is P0600). GM introduced it in the engine module only recently: the 2025 tables evaluate the results of built-in self-tests and error-correction counters, with the lamp in the first trip. Resets can cause brief stumbling or stalling, and some systems switch to limp mode. Software updates fixed it on the Alfa Romeo Giulia 2.9 V6 and Ram 6.7 Cummins, so check bulletins first. The code alone does not say which module set it – the scan tool shows whether it is the engine, transmission, brake or body module.
c: Internal module defect (processor, clock, monitoring chip)
Low voltage, voltage dips or a poor ground or supply at the module
Electrical interference, e.g. from a faulty alternator or ignition
s: Check engine light on
Limp mode or reduced power
Brief stumbling or stalling (module reset)
Several implausible codes at once

P0608.d: Many engine or powertrain modules turn the raw wheel or output-shaft speed into a cleaned-up vehicle speed signal and pass it on through their own driver – a square-wave signal whose frequency rises with speed – to the instrument cluster, cruise control, radio or steering. P0608 concerns output A: the module compares the commanded driver state with the actual line state and reports a short to ground or voltage, an open circuit or an internal driver fault, as CARB requires for output components. Output A is the first such output, usually the speedometer feed. If the speed sensor itself fails, P0500–P0503 set instead. No manufacturer table available to us gives thresholds; GM lists the code in older vehicles. On modern cars speed is shared over CAN, so the code mainly affects older vehicles with a hard-wired speedometer signal.
c: Short or open in the output line A to the receiving module
Corroded or spread connector pins at the module or receiver
Faulty receiving module pulling the line to ground
Internal driver fault in the module
s: Speedometer dead or jumping
Cruise control not working
Odometer stops counting
Speed-dependent functions (steering, radio volume) disturbed

P0609.d: Many engine or powertrain modules turn the raw wheel or output-shaft speed into a cleaned-up vehicle speed signal and pass it on through their own driver – a square-wave signal whose frequency rises with speed – to the instrument cluster, cruise control, radio or steering. P0609 concerns output B: the module compares the commanded driver state with the actual line state and reports a short to ground or voltage, an open circuit or an internal driver fault, as CARB requires for output components. Output B is a second output; which device hangs on it (cruise module, radio, body builder interface) depends on the wiring diagram. If the speed sensor itself fails, P0500–P0503 set instead. No manufacturer table available to us gives thresholds; GM lists the code in older vehicles. On modern cars speed is shared over CAN, so the code mainly affects older vehicles with a hard-wired speedometer signal.
c: Short or open in the output line B to the receiving module
Corroded or spread connector pins at the module or receiver
Faulty receiving module pulling the line to ground
Internal driver fault in the module
s: Speed-dependent function of the receiver on output B disturbed
Cruise control or add-on device without speed signal
Often no noticeable driving symptom

P060A.t: Internal Control Module Monitoring Processor Performance
P060A.d: Electronic throttle systems use three levels: level 1 runs the engine, level 2 recalculates key values independently on the same processor, and level 3 is a separate monitoring processor that quizzes the main one and can shut down the throttle outputs. P060A means this monitoring processor (level 3) or its cooperation with the main processor is faulty: the question-and-answer game fails, an operating system call ends with an unrecoverable error, or the self-test of the monitoring module fails (Ford diesel: 5 s). Ford sets it with the check engine and wrench lamps since generation 3 throttle systems (older generation 2 without the check engine light); GM Europe's 1.6 L turbo rates it type C with a service lamp and reduced power. GM North America does not use P060A. Nissan (Rogue 2021) and Ford (Explorer 2.3 2025) fixed it by reprogramming – often there are no driving symptoms at all.
c: Unstable supply voltage or poor ground at the module (weak battery, voltage spikes)
Moisture or corrosion in the module or connector
s: Check engine light, at Ford also the wrench lamp
Reduced power or limp mode
Often no driving symptoms
Rarely stalling or starting problems

P060B.t: Internal Control Module A/D Processing Performance
P060B.d: The analog-to-digital converter turns every analog sensor voltage into a number, so a faulty converter can falsify many values at once. The module checks it by timing its start-up calibration (GM 6.6 L diesel: 0.30 s or longer is a fault), by converting fixed internal reference voltages (about 4.73–4.83 V must be read), by grounding a test channel that must then read near 0 V (Ford diesel: over 249 mV is a fault) and by comparing with a second converter. GM sets it in the first trip, Ford with the check engine and wrench lamps as a level 3 check; the module usually enters limp mode. Ford fixed an F-150 2.7 L case (with misfire codes) by reprogramming. GM also uses P060B in the brake module – then ABS warnings appear and the engine module is not the culprit. The old wording 'A and D' simply spelled out 'A/D'.
c: Unstable supply voltage or poor ground at the module (weak battery, voltage spikes)
Internal defect of the converter or its chip
Shorted sensor input pulling the converter reference
s: Check engine light, at Ford also the wrench lamp
Reduced power or limp mode
Several sensor or misfire codes at the same time
ABS/ESC warning if the brake module set the code

P060C.t: Internal Control Module Main Processor Performance
P060C.d: P060C reports a fault in the main processor that actually runs the engine, found either by the monitoring processor (Ford 'quizzer', level 3) or by duplicate storage and recalculation (GM). Typical findings are corrupted RAM or ROM data, arithmetic unit errors, memory address violations, a wrong program sequence or internal supply or temperature out of range (Ford diesel: internal voltage outside 1.3–3.3 V, 5 s). GM's 2025 petrol table flags a torque compensation outside ±52.9 Nm for 475 ms and sets the code in the first trip. Reactions range from reduced power to engine shutdown. Software is the most common cause: GM (2022 full-size trucks and SUVs), VW (Tiguan 2021, with cruise control faults), Nissan and Mercedes (transmission module, E-Class hybrid) fixed it by reprogramming.
c: Unstable supply voltage or poor ground at the module (weak battery, voltage spikes)
Overheating or moisture in the module
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power or limp mode
Driver assistance such as adaptive cruise unavailable
Rarely stalling or no start
Transmission limp mode if the transmission module is affected

P060D.t: Internal Control Module Accelerator Pedal Position Performance
P060D.d: The accelerator pedal has two sensor tracks. With P060D the module's own cross-check of the pedal value fails: two processors (GM: main and 'motor' processor) calculate pedal position independently and must agree, and an active test briefly pulls one track to ground – the other must not follow, otherwise the tracks are shorted together. Thresholds: GM 2005 difference over 0.142 V or track 2 over 2.05 V during the test; GM 2006 over 5 %; Ford diesel compares track 1 against twice track 2 (half slope), fault above 547 or 1055 mV for 5 s. GM sets it in the first trip, Ford since 2020 with the check engine and wrench lamps (2012 only the wrench lamp). Unlike P2138, where the two pedal tracks disagree outside the module, P060D is the internal plausibility check.
c: Short between the two pedal sensor signal lines or moisture in the pedal connector
s: Reduced power, engine barely responds to the pedal
Check engine light or wrench lamp
Cruise control disabled
Raised idle or limp mode

P060E.t: Internal Control Module Throttle Position Performance
P060E.d: P060E is the throttle counterpart of P060D. The throttle body also has two position sensor tracks, and the module checks whether it can still detect a short between them: during an active test one track is influenced briefly, and the second processor (GM 'motor processor') confirms that the test actually ran. GM 2005 sets the code when track 2 exceeds 1.75 V during the test or no test activity is seen for 500 ms, GM 2006 at 2.05 V or 498 ms, each after two counts of about 155 ms, with the lamp in the first trip; GM Europe rates it type C with reduced power. Ford does not use P060E. The throttle opening is limited or set to its default position. External disagreement between the two tracks is P2135; circuit faults of single tracks are P0120–P0123 and P0220–P0223.
c: Short between the throttle sensor signal lines or moisture in the throttle connector
Internal module fault (test circuit, second processor)
s: Reduced power
Check engine light (GM) or service lamp (GM Europe)
Hesitant or jerky throttle response
Cruise control not working

P060F.t: Internal Control Module Coolant Temperature Performance
P060F.d: Coolant temperature feeds the torque model of the engine (friction, cold start), which the level 2 monitoring of the electronic throttle concept recalculates. P060F means the module's internal cross-check of this value failed: the temperature used by the main software and the value captured or recalculated by the monitoring level or a second converter path do not agree. No manufacturer table available to us (GM 2004–2025, Ford 2012/2020–23/diesel 2023, Saab) describes P060F with thresholds, so this explanation follows the pattern of P060D/P060E and CARB's rationality requirement for the coolant temperature sensor. Expect a substitute temperature, a permanently running fan and possibly reduced power. Sensor faults themselves are P0115–P0119; if those are present, start there.
c: Internal module fault in a converter or processor path
Loose contact at the coolant temperature sensor that jumps between samples
Unstable supply voltage or poor ground at the module (weak battery, voltage spikes)
s: Check engine light or service lamp
Possibly reduced power
Radiator fan runs constantly (substitute value)
Implausible temperature gauge

P0610.d: The module checks its vehicle-specific configuration for completeness and validity: at Ford the vehicle identification block or as-built data with tyre circumference, axle ratio, transmission and options; at GM the programmed vehicle options. Ford 2012 sets P0610 when one or more fields of that block are configured wrongly, the Ford diesel checks continuously within 0.5 s; GM and Saab V6 engines set it in the first trip, also for incomplete programming. Typical triggers are a new or used module without correct configuration, an interrupted reprogramming, or changed tyres or axle without updating the data. Symptoms include wrong speedometer readings or shift points and missing functions such as cruise control. The fix is rewriting the configuration or VIN-specific programming with the manufacturer's tool; replace the module only if the code returns.
c: Module not or wrongly configured after replacement (used part, missing as-built data)
Changed tyre size or axle ratio without updating the data
Internal memory fault of the module
s: Check engine light (depending on maker and variant)
Wrong speedometer reading or shift points
Optional functions such as cruise control missing

P0611.d: P0611 concerns systems with a separate injector control module or injector driver stage. On GM's 6.6 L Duramax LB7/LLY the injector driver unit reports a microcontroller, monitoring or converter fault or a timeout to the engine module over CAN; the code sets after 30 of 50 checks at 125 ms with battery voltage of 10–18 V, and the lamp follows after two trips. On Ford's 6.0 L Power Stroke the injector module steps battery voltage up to about 48 V; Ford's bulletin requires it to stay above 45 V during the last 10 s of the injector prime, with the battery at 11.5 V or more – weak batteries strain and damage the converter. Newer Ford diesels check an internal reference measurement (0–3300 mV, 5 s). Results are hard or no starting, rough running and low power.
c: Faulty voltage converter or driver stage in the injector module (Ford 6.0 L)
Low battery voltage, weak batteries or poor ground
CAN or supply line between engine and injector module disturbed
s: Hard or no start, especially when cold
Rough running, misfires
Lack of power
Check engine light (GM after two trips)

P0612.t: Fuel Injector Control Module Relay Control
P0612.d: Some diesels have a separate injector driver module that is powered through a relay switched by the engine module – GM's 6.6 L Duramax LB7/LLY with its injector driver unit, Ford's 6.0 L Power Stroke with its injector control module. P0612 means the commanded relay state and the voltage measured back at the output do not match. GM checks this with ignition on and the CAN link initialised, outside the shutdown phase, and sets the code after 30 of 50 checks at 125 ms; the lamp follows after two trips. If the relay fails, the injector module gets no power – the engine does not start or stalls; if it does not drop out, the module stays powered and drains the battery. Newer diesels have the injector drivers inside the engine module and use P062D/P062E instead. A fault reported by the injector module itself is P0611.
c: Injector module relay faulty (coil open, contacts welded)
Relay control or feedback wire open or corroded, fuse
Low battery voltage or ground problems
Driver in the engine module faulty
s: Engine does not start or stalls while driving
Check engine light (GM after two trips)
Battery drain if the relay does not drop out
Often together with P0611 or injector codes

P0613.d: P0613 reports an internal processor or calculation fault in the transmission control module. It is usually set by the transmission module itself – the scan tool shows which module stored it; on some architectures the engine module reports it on the transmission module's behalf. The only manufacturer document found is Subaru's bulletin for the 2022 BRZ 2.4 L automatic: an internal plausibility check (a calculated gear ratio) set P0613 falsely in rare cases, and the fix was reprogramming the transmission module with improved self-diagnosis. Depending on the maker the transmission may go into limp mode with a fixed gear and harsh shifts. Check supply, ground and battery first, then look for a software update. The engine module's processor fault is P0606; an ECM/TCM mismatch is P0614.
c: Voltage dip, poor ground or supply at the transmission module
s: Check engine light or transmission warning
Transmission limp mode (fixed gear, harsh shifts)
Implausible shifting
Often no noticeable symptoms (sporadic false report)

P0614.d: P0614 means the software or calibration variant of the engine module does not match the fitted transmission module or transmission type, or the transmission module is not registered. CARB allows modules with several calibration variants (for example manual and automatic) to share one calibration ID only if a wrong variant turns on the lamp – exactly this check. GM's V6 engines (Saab 9-5 2010) run it continuously with ignition on and light the lamp in the first trip, also for incomplete programming; Saab's Bosch ME9 sets it when a wrong variant is programmed, without any other system reaction. Typical cases are a used module from a car with a different gearbox or a software update applied to only one of the two modules.
c: Engine or transmission module replaced and not matched or registered
Used module with the wrong variant (different gearbox or engine)
Software update on only one of the two modules
s: Check engine light on
Possibly transmission limp mode or limited shifting
Sometimes no other symptoms

P0615.d: The engine module switches the starter relay coil through its own driver – GM petrol engines with 12 V stop-start use a low-side driver, the Saab 9-4X switches 12 V to the coil. CARB requires output components to be checked for open and short circuits. GM sets the codes after two trips on stop-start engines, while GM diesels (2016) and the Saab 9-4X store them without the check engine light. At Ford an active starter code blocks stop-start. P0615 is the open or general circuit fault: GM measures the driver output with the driver off and sets the code at 200 kΩ or more after 40 of 50 samples at 50 ms. Chrysler traced no-start cases with P0615 to a harness chafed or pinched at the engine mount near the starter. Short to ground and to voltage are P0616 and P0617; the start request input is P0512.
c: Control wire open, harness chafed or pinched, connector corroded
Relay ground, fuse or supply faulty
Driver in the engine module faulty
s: Engine does not crank
Stop-start not working
Intermittent starting problems
Check engine light only with some makers

P0616.d: The engine module switches the starter relay coil through its own driver – GM petrol engines with 12 V stop-start use a low-side driver, the Saab 9-4X switches 12 V to the coil. CARB requires output components to be checked for open and short circuits. GM sets the codes after two trips on stop-start engines, while GM diesels (2016) and the Saab 9-4X store them without the check engine light. At Ford an active starter code blocks stop-start. P0616 means the control wire is shorted to ground: GM detects 0.5 Ω or less to ground with the driver off (8 of 10 samples in 2018 and 2025, 40 of 50 in 2019). With a low-side driver the short can energise the relay permanently; with a high-side driver (Saab) the relay no longer pulls in. Saab's check: a test lamp across the coil terminals must flash during cranking.
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion in the relay or fuse box
Driver in the engine module faulty
s: Engine does not crank
Stop-start disabled
Possibly blown fuse in the relay circuit
Check engine light only with some makers

P0617.d: The engine module switches the starter relay coil through its own driver – GM petrol engines with 12 V stop-start use a low-side driver, the Saab 9-4X switches 12 V to the coil. CARB requires output components to be checked for open and short circuits. GM sets the codes after two trips on stop-start engines, while GM diesels (2016) and the Saab 9-4X store them without the check engine light. At Ford an active starter code blocks stop-start. P0617 means the control wire is shorted to battery voltage: GM detects it with the driver on, when the voltage stays high although the driver pulls to ground (40 of 50 samples in 2018 and 2025, 8 of 10 in 2019). With a high-side circuit such as the Saab's, the short can close the relay permanently and keep the starter turning – a risk for starter and ring gear; with a low-side circuit the relay loses its control.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery feed (harness damage)
Relay faulty internally (contact to coil, welded)
Voltage fed in by retrofitted electrics (remote start, alarm)
Driver in the engine module faulty
s: Engine does not crank, or the starter keeps running
Stop-start not working
Battery drained
Check engine light only with some makers

P0618.t: Alternative Fuel Control Module KAM Error
P0618.d: CARB treats gas-fuelled vehicles (CNG, LPG, also the gas mode of bi-fuel cars) like petrol cars up to model year 2018 and under an approved manufacturer plan afterwards. P0618 is meant for vehicles with a separate control module for the alternative fuel: it reports an error in that module's keep alive memory, which holds learned values while the ignition is off and loses them when power is cut – the gas counterpart of P0603. No manufacturer was found that uses P0618 this way; Roush's Ford propane conversions, for example, report a failed gas module as U0108. One Chrysler bulletin lists 'P0618' with the title of P061B – apparently a typo, not a second meaning. Expect lost adaptations; bi-fuel cars may switch to petrol. Check supply, fuse and ground of the gas module first.
c: Power interruption at the gas module (battery disconnected, fuse, loose contact)
Poor supply, ground or corrosion at the module (underbody mounting)
Software or programming fault of the gas module
s: Check engine or gas system warning light
Switch to petrol, gas mode blocked (bi-fuel)
Rough idle until values are relearned
Often no symptoms

P0619.t: Alternative Fuel Control Module RAM/ROM Error
P0619.d: CARB treats gas-fuelled vehicles (CNG, LPG, also the gas mode of bi-fuel cars) like petrol cars up to model year 2018 and under an approved manufacturer plan afterwards. P0619 means the separate alternative fuel module reports an error in its working memory (RAM, read/write test) or program memory (ROM/flash, checksum) – one code for both, while the engine module uses P0604 and P0605. No manufacturer was found that uses the code; Roush's Ford propane systems report gas module failures as U0108 and the engine module's own memory errors as P0604/P0605. A module whose memory cannot be trusted will typically shut down gas operation: bi-fuel cars run on petrol, dedicated gas engines may not start. The usual remedies are reprogramming the gas module with a stable supply, then replacement.
c: Interrupted or faulty programming of the gas module
Voltage dips, supply, ground or corrosion
s: Check engine or gas system warning light
No gas operation, switch to petrol
Starting problems on dedicated gas engines
Possibly communication code U0108

P061A.d: Electronic throttle systems run a second, independent calculation on the same processor (level 2, at Ford 'IPC – independent plausibility check') that recomputes driver demand, permitted and actual torque and their inputs, and compares them with the main software. P061A is the result of the torque comparison: the commanded or estimated torque exceeds the permitted torque for the current operating point (Ford diesel 2023: within 0.1 s). The module reacts at once by limiting torque – RPM guard, pedal-follower mode, in severe cases engine shutdown. Ford petrol engines report it without the check engine light (CARB allows that for emission-neutral reactions), GM Europe as type C; GM North America does not use the code. Ram 6.7 L Cummins (2019) fixed it by reprogramming. Fix input sensor codes first, then check supply and ground, then look for a software update.
c: Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Contradictory inputs (pedal, throttle, air mass, cruise request) produce an implausible torque demand
Voltage dips, poor ground or supply at the module
Internal defect of the engine module
Unapproved power upgrade (torque model no longer fits)
s: Reduced power or limp mode, poor throttle response
Wrench, service or check engine lamp depending on the maker
Cruise control disabled
Rarely the engine shuts off

P061B.t: Internal Control Module Torque Calculation Performance
P061B.d: Electronic throttle systems run a second, independent calculation on the same processor (level 2, at Ford 'IPC – independent plausibility check') that recomputes driver demand, permitted and actual torque and their inputs, and compares them with the main software. P061B means the torque calculation itself is inconsistent: main software and monitoring compute the torque differently. On Ford petrol engines it sets within 1 s with the check engine and wrench lamps and blocks the catalyst monitor. On Ford's 2023 diesel torque equals injected fuel, so P061B checks the injection control instead – energising times outside 10–850 ms, more than 127.2 µs between programmed and actual, or more than 5 mg difference in quantity correction (5 s). Software updates fixed it on Chrysler's 3.0 L EcoDiesel and the Ram 6.7 L Cummins; on the Ford Five Hundred it came with idle codes and a dirty throttle body.
c: Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Dirty throttle or air path, idle adaptation at its limit (petrol)
Voltage dips, poor ground or supply at the module
Injector quantity deviation pushing the zero-fuel calibration out of range (diesel)
Internal defect of the engine module
s: Check engine light and wrench lamp
Reduced power or limp mode
Fluctuating idle (Ford petrol with dirty throttle)
Sometimes only the lamp

P061C.t: Internal Control Module Engine RPM Performance
P061C.d: Electronic throttle systems run a second, independent calculation on the same processor (level 2, at Ford 'IPC – independent plausibility check') that recomputes driver demand, permitted and actual torque and their inputs, and compares them with the main software. P061C means the two internal engine speed calculations from the crankshaft signal disagree. GM's 6.6 L Duramax sets it at 400 rpm or more difference once the redundant speed is at least 600 rpm and the engine is synchronised, after 0.32 s, with the lamp after two trips; Ford's diesel also uses 400 rpm (5 s), Ford petrol engines react within 1 s with the check engine light. Because speed is a base value of torque monitoring, limp mode follows. A disturbed crankshaft signal can make both paths react differently, so fix P0335–P0339 first.
c: Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Disturbed crankshaft signal (sensor, reluctor, shielding, connector, interference)
Voltage dips, poor ground or supply at the module
Internal defect of the engine module
s: Check engine, wrench or service lamp
Reduced power or RPM limit
Stumbling or brief misfires with a disturbed signal
Rarely stalling

P061D.t: Internal Control Module Engine Air Mass Performance
P061D.d: Electronic throttle systems run a second, independent calculation on the same processor (level 2, at Ford 'IPC – independent plausibility check') that recomputes driver demand, permitted and actual torque and their inputs, and compares them with the main software. P061D means the independent recalculation of air mass or engine load disagrees with the main software's value. On petrol engines air mass is the main input for actual torque, so torque monitoring needs it to be plausible. Ford sets P061D within 1 s with the check engine and wrench lamps and blocks the catalyst monitor; GM Europe's 1.6 L turbo runs the check only without mass air flow circuit codes (P0100/P0102/P0103) and rates it type C. Ford's diesel does not use the code. No maker publishes a threshold. Fix air flow and mixture codes first; vacuum leaks after the sensor and a dirty MAF are typical triggers.
c: Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Implausible air mass or load signal (dirty MAF, vacuum leak after the sensor)
Voltage dips, poor ground or supply at the module
Dirty throttle, adaptation at its limit
Internal defect of the engine module
s: Check engine and wrench lamp (Ford) or service lamp
Reduced power, poor throttle response
Often air flow or mixture codes as well

P061E.t: Internal Control Module Brake Signal Performance
P061E.d: Electronic throttle systems run a second, independent calculation on the same processor (level 2, at Ford 'IPC – independent plausibility check') that recomputes driver demand, permitted and actual torque and their inputs, and compares them with the main software. Torque monitoring needs a reliable brake signal: brake applied means zero driver demand, cruise is cancelled, and in pedal limp mode the engine returns to idle. Ford introduced a brake switch with two outputs for this. P061E means the brake information is implausible inside the module – main software and monitoring do not see the same state, or the redundant brake data from the ABS module is invalid. Ford petrol engines set it within 1 s with the wrench lamp but no check engine light; from model year 2018 Ford replaced it with U1012. Ram 6.7 L Cummins (2019) fixed it by reprogramming. Brake switch circuit faults are P0571–P0573 and P0504.
c: Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Brake light switch misadjusted or faulty (both outputs do not switch together)
Faulty brake data from the ABS module or CAN disturbance
Connector or wiring fault at the brake switch
Internal defect of the engine module
s: Wrench lamp (Ford), no check engine light
Cruise control not working
Possibly reduced power
Stop-start possibly blocked

P061F.t: Internal Control Module Throttle Actuator Controller Performance
P061F.d: P061F monitors the throttle position controller inside the engine module and its communication with the main processor. At Ford the main processor sends the target throttle angle to this controller (generation 2: a 312.5 Hz duty cycle signal, 10–92 % for 0–82°), which drives the throttle motor via an H-bridge; the monitoring checks that the target is implemented and reported back correctly. Ford 2012 sets it within 1 s – with the check engine light on generation 2 (2003–2007, separate controller chip), without it on generations 3/4 where the controller is integrated. A fault puts the throttle into its default position with an RPM limit. Ford 2020–23 no longer uses P061F (throttle controller faults run under P2107 ff). No other manufacturer document available to us uses it. Throttle motor circuit and function codes are P2100–P2112.
c: Internal fault in the throttle controller of the engine module
Throttle stiff, sooted or iced, controller at its limit
Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Throttle motor connector or wiring resistance
Voltage dips, poor ground or supply at the module
s: Wrench lamp (Ford), check engine light on generation 2
Throttle in default position, raised idle, barely any response
RPM limit

P0620.d: The alternator regulator is linked to the engine module by an L (turn-on) line, an F (field) line reporting field load as a duty cycle, or on newer cars a LIN bus. P0620 is the general control circuit code. On LIN alternators it stands for disturbed control or communication: a manufacturer table published via NHTSA (gateway module with LIN alternator) lists it with the battery lamp on and stop-start disabled, alongside P065B for range/performance. Saab's 9-3 diesel uses it for the L line – open between module and alternator for more than 6 s, or a charging signal in an implausible state. Ford's 6.8 L V10 reports it with or without the check engine light depending on the variant. GM does not use P0620 and reports L and F line faults as P0621/P0622.
c: Connector or wire between module and alternator (corrosion, break, chafing)
Alternator or regulator faulty, including its LIN interface
Battery flat or faulty, jump start or charger connected
s: Battery warning lamp on
Battery not or incorrectly charged, starting problems
Stop-start not working
Sometimes no noticeable symptoms

P0621.d: The alternator regulator is linked to the engine module by an L (turn-on) line, an F (field) line reporting field load as a duty cycle, or on newer cars a LIN bus. P0621 concerns the L line: the engine module applies voltage through a high-side driver and so switches the regulator's field control on and off. GM's 2023 and 2025 engine modules check the output impedance – open at 200 kΩ or more, short to ground or 5 V at 0.5 Ω or less – with ignition on or engine running and at least 11 V, after 5 s (short to ground 15 s), without the check engine light as an 'emission neutral' diagnostic. The Saab 9-4X switches on the battery lamp 15 s after setting the code; Saab's T8 flags an open D+ line after 0.5 s and raises the idle speed. Low and high on this line are P2500 and P2501.
c: L line or alternator connector open or shorted
Ground problems between engine and body
s: Battery warning lamp on
Battery not or incorrectly charged, starting problems
Raised or fluctuating idle
Starting problems after a longer drive

P0622.d: The alternator regulator is linked to the engine module by an L (turn-on) line, an F (field) line reporting field load as a duty cycle, or on newer cars a LIN bus. P0622 checks the F feedback: its duty cycle equals the field on-time, from which the module calculates alternator torque and raises idle under load. Two plausibility tests: with ignition on and engine off the duty cycle must be near 0 % – a fault at 65 % or more; with the engine running (below 3000 rpm) it must be 5–99 % – a fault at 5 % or less. GM's 2023 and 2025 modules use 5 s each and, unusually, set the check engine light in the first trip; the Saab 9-4X uses 5 s and 15 s without it and only when P0621 is not set. Other systems split the same check into P0625 (low) and P0626 (high).
c: F line or alternator connector open or shorted
Alternator not charging (belt, brushes), duty cycle implausible
s: Battery warning lamp on
Check engine light possible on GM from model year 2023
Idle fluctuates or drops when large loads switch on
Flat battery with a real charging fault

P0623.d: P0623 concerns the control of the battery warning lamp by a module's output driver, not the alternator itself. Traditionally the regulator switches the lamp through terminal L; where a module switches it instead – GM's Saab 9-4X turns the lamp on 15 s after a charging code – it can monitor its lamp output for open or short circuits. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0623, so the description follows the principle of other lamp outputs. Under CARB a pure indicator lamp needs the check engine light only if other diagnostics depend on it, which is rarely the case. The lamp then never lights (not even at the bulb check) or stays on, and real charging faults may go unnoticed. The L line itself is P0621; the fuel cap lamp P0624 belongs to a different system.
c: Wire or connector to the lamp or instrument cluster
s: Battery lamp never lights (not even at bulb check) or stays on
Real charging faults may not be displayed
Otherwise usually no driving symptoms

P0624.d: Despite its neighbours, P0624 has nothing to do with the alternator: it is the control circuit of the 'check fuel cap' warning lamp of the evaporative system. Ford's evaporative monitor lights such a lamp when, after refuelling, the tank cannot be pulled into vacuum – a gross leak or missing cap (P0457) – and turns it off once the cap is secured; not every vehicle has this lamp. The module driving the lamp (engine or body module, depending on the vehicle) can monitor its output for open or short circuits. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0624 itself. The lamp is only a hint; the leak is reported with the check engine light as P0455/P0457, so P0624 itself is practically emission neutral under CARB. The lamp then never lights or stays on, and a loose cap is no longer indicated.
c: Wire or connector to the warning lamp or instrument cluster
Output driver in the engine or body module
s: Fuel cap lamp never lights or stays on
A loose cap is no longer indicated
No driving symptoms

P0625.d: The alternator regulator is linked to the engine module by an L (turn-on) line, an F (field) line reporting field load as a duty cycle, or on newer cars a LIN bus. P0625 means the F feedback is too low: with the engine running the regulator reports (almost) no field duty cycle – typically an open or grounded F line, or the alternator is not charging. The Saab 9-4X sets it below 3000 rpm when the duty cycle stays under 5 % for 15 s; Saab's T8 when it stays under 0.5 % for over 30 s with the L line active, and raises the idle speed. Ford's 6.8 L V10 reports it with or without the check engine light depending on the variant. GM's newer engines combine low and high in P0622.
c: F line open or shorted to ground, connector corroded
Regulator or alternator faulty or not charging (brushes, field winding)
Alternator B+ feed missing or high resistance
s: Battery warning lamp on
Battery not or incorrectly charged, starting problems
Raised or fluctuating idle
Check engine light on some Ford variants

P0626.d: The alternator regulator is linked to the engine module by an L (turn-on) line, an F (field) line reporting field load as a duty cycle, or on newer cars a LIN bus. P0626 means the F feedback is too high – a duty cycle near 100 % when little or no field current is expected, typically a short to battery voltage. The Saab 9-4X sets it with ignition on and engine off above 65 % for 15 s, Saab's ME9 above 65 % for 3 s with the engine running, and raises the idle speed. Chrysler fixed P0626 on the 2019 Ram 3500–5500 chassis cab 6.7 L Cummins by reprogramming, as part of a check engine light bulletin; Ford's 6.8 L V10 reports it with or without the lamp. The former obdex title 'Performance' was wrong – all lists and manufacturers use 'High'.
c: F line shorted to battery voltage (chafing), connector
Regulator faulty (field permanently on, possibly overcharging)
s: Battery or check engine lamp (Chrysler/Ford partly with MIL)
Raised idle
Possibly overvoltage or overcharging with a regulator fault
Often no driving symptoms

P0627.d: What 'fuel pump A control circuit' means differs by maker: at GM petrol engines it is the control line from the engine module to the fuel pump relay (high-side driver), at GM's LML diesel the lift pump, at Ford petrol engines with a pump driver module the secondary circuit from that module to the pump (reported as a duty cycle on a monitor line), and at Ford's 6.7 L diesel (F-650/750) the high or low side of the pump relay. P0627 is the open or general circuit fault. GM measures with the relay driver on and sets the code at 200 kΩ or more after 8 of 10 samples at 250 ms – after two trips in 2018, in the first trip in 2025; some modules also set P0629. Ford's petrol pump module reports an open, short or overheating in its secondary circuit (2012: 80 % duty cycle, 2–5 s), Ford's 6.7 L diesel an open relay side within 0.2 s. Without the pump the engine does not start or stalls.
c: Fuel pump relay or pump driver module faulty
Wire or connector to relay or pump open or corroded (tank, underbody)
Driver in the engine module faulty
s: Engine does not start or stalls
Lack of power or stumbling under load
Pump not audible with ignition on
Check engine light on

P0628.t: Fuel Pump A Control Circuit Low
P0628.d: What 'fuel pump A control circuit' means differs by maker: at GM petrol engines it is the control line from the engine module to the fuel pump relay (high-side driver), at GM's LML diesel the lift pump, at Ford petrol engines with a pump driver module the secondary circuit from that module to the pump (reported as a duty cycle on a monitor line), and at Ford's 6.7 L diesel (F-650/750) the high or low side of the pump relay. P0628 means a short to ground: GM detects 0.5 Ω or less to ground with the driver on (8 of 10 samples at 250 ms; two trips in 2018, first trip in 2025); the driver then shuts off, the relay does not pull in and the pump stops. Ford's 6.7 L diesel reports a short to ground on the high side of the pump relay within 0.2 s. Ford petrol engines do not use P0628. A blown fuse is a frequent companion.
c: Control wire to relay or pump shorted to ground (chafing)
Pump or pump module shorted internally (Ford high side)
Driver in the engine module faulty
s: No start or stalling
Pump does not run
Blown fuse
Check engine light on

P0629.t: Fuel Pump A Control Circuit High
P0629.d: What 'fuel pump A control circuit' means differs by maker: at GM petrol engines it is the control line from the engine module to the fuel pump relay (high-side driver), at GM's LML diesel the lift pump, at Ford petrol engines with a pump driver module the secondary circuit from that module to the pump (reported as a duty cycle on a monitor line), and at Ford's 6.7 L diesel (F-650/750) the high or low side of the pump relay. P0629 means a short to battery voltage: GM detects voltage at the output while the driver is off (8 of 10 samples at 250 ms, two trips in 2018); because the driver hardware cannot always separate open circuit and short to voltage, P0627 may set as well. Ford's 6.7 L diesel reports a short to voltage on the high side of the pump relay within 0.2 s. If the pump can no longer be switched off it may keep running after switch-off and drain the battery.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery feed
Relay contacts welded or relay faulty internally
Moisture in the relay or fuse box
Driver in the engine module shorted
s: Pump runs constantly or after switch-off
Battery drained
Possibly no start
Check engine light on

P062A.t: Fuel Pump A Control Circuit Range/Performance
P062A.d: P062A is a plausibility check of the fuel pump control circuit, not a plain short or open. On Ford's 2023 diesels (F-250 to F-550 and 3.0 L) the lift pump module reports its status as a duty cycle; outside 78–82 % – the expected 'good' signal – the code sets after 0.5 s. On the Alfa Romeo Giulia 2.0 turbo (2017) P062A was a false trigger fixed by reprogramming the engine module, without parts. GM and Ford petrol engines do not use P062A; Ford reports duty cycle deviations there under P025B and P064A. Depending on the cause the pump runs on a substitute value or pressure drops, with lack of power or long cranking. Circuit faults are P0627–P0629, fuel pressure itself P0087 and P0190 ff.
c: Pump driver module faulty or reporting an error status
Contact problems or resistance in signal or supply wires
s: Check engine light on
Lack of power or stumbling
Delayed start
Often no noticeable symptoms (software case)

P062B.t: Internal Control Module Fuel Injector Control Performance
P062B.d: P062B monitors the injector driver stage inside the engine module. On direct injection engines a separate driver chip generates the boost voltage for opening the injectors and is configured by the main processor via SPI; GM checks initialisation, boost voltage (petrol: 90 V or more or 40 V or less), self-test, data download and communication, and sets the code in the first trip – while it is active, single injector circuit codes are suppressed. Saab's 2.0 L turbo also counts a short to ground in an injector circuit (10 s, two trips). Ford's diesel uses it as a plausibility check of the injection command (post injection, energising over 200 µs during overrun), Ford petrol engines only with cylinder deactivation. Chrysler's 3.0 L EcoDiesel was fixed by software. Misfires, loss of power or stalling follow.
c: Short to ground on an injector high-voltage or control wire, or a faulty injector
Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Undervoltage or supply problem (battery, main relay)
Faulty driver chip in the engine module
s: Check engine light (GM in the first trip)
Stumbling, misfires, loss of power
Starting problems or stalling
Other injector codes are not reported while P062B is active (GM)

P062C.t: Internal Control Module Vehicle Speed Performance
P062C.d: Electronic throttle systems run a second, independent calculation on the same processor (level 2, at Ford 'IPC – independent plausibility check') that recomputes driver demand, permitted and actual torque and their inputs, and compares them with the main software. Vehicle speed feeds torque monitoring through cruise control, speed limiter and gear-dependent limits. P062C means the module's internal cross-check of vehicle speed fails – main software and monitoring determine it separately, for example from transmission output or wheel speeds, and the values disagree. Ford sets it within 1 s with the wrench lamp; the check engine light came on only on generation 2 (2003–2007), since 2020 not at all. Cruise control and speed limiter are disabled, power may be limited. Ram 6.7 L Cummins (2019) fixed it by reprogramming. No threshold is published. Fix speed sensor codes P0500–P0503 first; a wrong tyre size or axle ratio in the module can also contribute.
c: Engine module software or calibration fault (update available)
Disturbed vehicle or output speed signal (sensor, reluctor, ABS CAN data)
Wrong tyre size or axle ratio configured in the module
Internal defect of the engine module
s: Wrench lamp (Ford), check engine light only on older Ford
Cruise control not working
Possibly reduced power

P062D.t: Fuel Injector Driver Circuit Performance Bank 1
P062D.d: Direct-injection injectors (petrol and common-rail diesel) need a high boost voltage generated in the module to open fast; the module then holds them with pulsed battery voltage. P062D monitors this boost voltage or the shared injector supply of bank 1. GM's 2018 Duramax sets it when the internal boost voltage is above 75 V or below about 52 V, the supply line to the injectors is open or the module has an internal fault, in 14 of 20 samples at 6.25 ms, with the lamp in the first trip (2025: above 60 V or below 40 V). Ford's petrol direct injection flags it when the opening current is not reached in time (10 s, no cylinder named), Ford's diesel when the driver chip reports a loss of high voltage (0.5 s). Injectors then open late or not at all: misfires, rough running, loss of power or no start. GM uses only P062D, also on V8s. Single injector circuits are P0201 ff.
c: Short in an injector high-side wire or injector collapsing the boost voltage
s: Check engine light (GM in the first trip)
Misfires, rough running, stumbling
Loss of power or limp mode
Hard start or no start

P062E.t: Fuel Injector Driver Circuit Performance Bank 2
P062E.d: Direct-injection injectors (petrol and common-rail diesel) need a high boost voltage generated in the module to open fast; the module then holds them with pulsed battery voltage. P062E is the bank 2 counterpart of P062D for V engines with separate driver circuits per bank. The only user found is Ford's 2023 diesel (6.7 L Power Stroke V8): the driver chip's internal logic reports a loss of the high-voltage supply and the code sets within 0.5 s; group supply faults of the injectors are P2150/P2151 and P2153/P2154. GM monitors the same boost voltage only under P062D. The injectors of bank 2 then open incorrectly – misfires on one side of the engine, rough idle, loss of power and possibly limp mode. Check wiring and connectors under the bank 2 valve cover and each injector for shorts before suspecting the engine module.
c: Short in an injector wire or injector of bank 2
Engine module or driver chip faulty internally
Connector or harness under the bank 2 valve cover
s: Check engine light on
Misfires on one side of the engine
Loss of power or limp mode
Rough idle, starting problems

P062F.d: Learned values, adaptations, counters and configuration are saved to non-volatile memory (EEPROM or flash-emulated NVM) when the module shuts down. P062F means this memory failed a check: GM and GM Europe test at start-up whether the last write at shutdown completed, GM's 6.6 L diesel checks a checksum per data block and whether sectors can be erased, Ford's diesel reports read, write or erase errors (5 s). Lamp behaviour varies: GM petrol engine modules after two trips, the Duramax 2014 and Saab 2.0 L turbo in the first trip, GM transmission modules and GM Europe's 1.6 L turbo without it. Most often the shutdown was interrupted – battery disconnected, voltage dip, main relay dropping out too early. Learned values are lost and relearned. The code also appears in transmission and other modules.
c: Shutdown interrupted (battery disconnected, voltage dip, main relay drops out too early)
Weak battery, poor ground or supply at the module
Memory defect in the module (write cycles, ageing)
s: Check engine or service lamp (depending on the maker, sometimes after two trips)
Learned values lost: rough idle or harsh shifts until relearned
Often no driveability symptoms

P0630.t: VIN Not Programmed or Incompatible ECM/PCM
P0630.d: Since model year 2005 CARB requires exactly one module to report the VIN to a scan tool, and reprogramming the VIN must erase all emission-related diagnostic data. P0630 means the engine module holds no valid VIN or one that does not fit. GM checks continuously whether every VIN position is a valid ASCII character (older tables: bytes 00 or FF count as empty), 250 ms, with the lamp in the first trip. At Ford the body module sends VIN, tyre circumference and axle ratio at every start, and P0630 sets while only default values are stored – so it covers more than the VIN; the 2023 diesel checks within 0.5 s. Hyundai requires writing the VIN after replacement; once written it cannot be changed. The engine runs normally; inspection stations may reject a missing VIN.
c: New replacement module without written VIN
Used module from another vehicle (VIN does not match)
Interrupted programming or missing configuration data from the body module (Ford)
s: Check engine light (some Ford trucks without)
Scan tool shows no or a wrong VIN
Ford: wrong tyre or axle data, speedometer errors
Driving usually normal

P0631.t: VIN Not Programmed or Incompatible TCM
P0631.d: P0631 is the transmission module counterpart of P0630: the transmission control module holds no VIN, an invalid one, or one that does not match the vehicle – usually compared with the VIN of the engine or body module. Typical is a replaced transmission module or mechatronic unit (on dual-clutch and automatic gearboxes with integrated control) that was not VIN-programmed, or a used part. Depending on the architecture the transmission module itself or the engine module sets the code. No manufacturer table or bulletin available to us names P0631; the description follows CARB's VIN rules and the documented P0630 procedure (Hyundai, Ford), where the VIN is distributed to all modules that need it and stored once. Shifting is usually normal, but adaptations or configuration may be blocked.
c: Transmission module or mechatronic unit replaced, VIN not written
Used transmission module from another vehicle
CAN communication fault during the VIN comparison
s: Check engine light or transmission warning
Scan tool shows no or a wrong VIN in the transmission module
Transmission adaptation possibly impossible
Driving often normal

P0632.d: Engine modules increasingly keep their own copy of the odometer reading or take it over from the instrument cluster or body module; for model years 2019–2021 onward CARB requires mileage in the module's operating data records and explicitly mentions the case 'odometer is lost'. P0632 means the engine module holds no valid odometer value. It typically appears after the engine module was replaced and the mileage was neither transferred with the tool nor taken over from the cluster. GM notes for the 2019–20 Cadillac CT6-V that mileage is stored redundantly in engine module, body module and cluster, and that programming several of them at once can corrupt it – program one after the other. No manufacturer table available to us names P0632 itself. Driving is normal; service and operating counters may be implausible.
c: Engine module replaced, mileage not transferred
Several modules (engine, body, cluster) replaced or programmed at the same time
No communication to the cluster or body module during takeover
s: Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Scan tool shows no or a different mileage in the engine module
Implausible service or oil change displays

P0633.d: The immobiliser couples the engine module to the immobiliser control module (GM body module, Chrysler SKIM/WCM) through a secret key and a challenge-response exchange – 'key' here means these security data, not the ignition key. P0633 means the engine module has not learned this secret key yet. At GM and Saab the code is set automatically whenever the engine module enters learn mode, for example as a new part, and clears after a successful learn and engine start; it is only a real fault if learn mode does not end, often because the engine fails to start for another reason. Chrysler calls it 'SKIM secret key not stored in PCM' and fixed false settings on the 2012–13 Grand Voyager 2.8 diesel by software. The engine does not start or dies after one or two seconds; the security lamp, not the check engine light, comes on.
c: Engine module replaced, immobiliser not learned
Learn procedure aborted or learn mode not exited (no start for another reason)
Communication fault to the immobiliser module
s: Engine does not start or dies immediately
Security or immobiliser lamp on or flashing
Code present after engine module replacement until learned
Sometimes immobiliser communication codes

P0634.t: Control Module Internal Temperature A Too High
P0634.d: The module measures its own circuit board temperature with an internal sensor and sets P0634 when it overheats. In practice this concerns mainly transmission modules mounted in or on the gearbox, such as GM's 6T70/6T75 and 6L units with the module in the valve body, surrounded by transmission fluid. GM sets it at 142 °C or more for 5 s (Saab 9-4X: 146 °C), or at 50 °C or more with system voltage of 18 V or higher for 2 s, because overvoltage heats the output stages. The Saab 9-4X then goes into limp mode with only reverse and 5th gear, manual shifting disabled and maximum line pressure; GM's table rates it without the check engine light. Check transmission overtemperature (P0218) first, then fluid level and cooler, engine cooling and charging voltage. Faults of the internal temperature sensor circuit are P0666–P0669.
c: Transmission fluid too hot: cooler clogged, lines kinked, air flow blocked, wrong level
Charging system overvoltage (18 V or more)
Faulty internal temperature sensor or valve body module
High sustained load (towing, mountain driving, heat)
s: Transmission limp mode (fixed gear), harsh shifts
Manual shifting disabled
Transmission warning, check engine light depending on the maker
Often together with transmission overtemperature (P0218)

P0635.d: P0635–P0637 concern the control or signal circuit between engine module and power steering – depending on the maker the drive of an electro-hydraulic pump or the steering load signal the engine module uses to raise idle. CARB requires power steering components to be monitored only if another diagnostic uses them, so these codes are rare and maker-specific. Mercedes-Benz stores P0635 in the electric steering module itself (no assist after start, software update); no engine module table available to us uses P0635–P0637. P0635 is the general or open-circuit code; output components must be checked for circuit faults, but separate low/high codes (P0636/P0637) are not mandatory. Steering assist may fail or be reduced; without the load signal idle can sag at full lock. The power steering pressure switch family is P0550–P0554.
c: Wire or connector between engine module and steering module or pump open or corroded
Software or calibration fault in the steering module (Mercedes)
Steering module or electro-hydraulic pump faulty
Undervoltage from weak battery, alternator or poor ground
s: Power steering warning, heavy steering
Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Idle drops when steering
Fault possibly only after engine start

P0636.d: P0635–P0637 concern the control or signal circuit between engine module and power steering – depending on the maker the drive of an electro-hydraulic pump or the steering load signal the engine module uses to raise idle. CARB requires power steering components to be monitored only if another diagnostic uses them, so these codes are rare and maker-specific. Mercedes-Benz stores P0635 in the electric steering module itself (no assist after start, software update); no engine module table available to us uses P0635–P0637. P0636 means the voltage in this circuit is too low – the wire is shorted to ground, supply voltage is low, or the driver sees a low state although it commanded 'on'. No manufacturer threshold is published.
c: Signal or control wire shorted to ground (chafing)
Undervoltage from battery, alternator or ground
Steering module or pump module faulty internally
s: Power steering warning, heavy steering
Check engine light (depending on the maker)
Idle drops when steering

P0637.d: P0635–P0637 concern the control or signal circuit between engine module and power steering – depending on the maker the drive of an electro-hydraulic pump or the steering load signal the engine module uses to raise idle. CARB requires power steering components to be monitored only if another diagnostic uses them, so these codes are rare and maker-specific. Mercedes-Benz stores P0635 in the electric steering module itself (no assist after start, software update); no engine module table available to us uses P0635–P0637. P0637 means the voltage in this circuit is too high – a short to battery voltage, or the driver or steering module reports a high state although 'off' was commanded; an electro-hydraulic pump may then keep running. No manufacturer threshold is published.
c: Control or signal wire shorted to battery voltage
Steering module or pump module faulty internally
s: Power steering warning
Heavy steering or pump running constantly
Check engine light possible

P0638.d: The electronic throttle motor positions the throttle plate; P0638 means the actuator does not follow its command on bank 1 (or the only throttle): target and actual angle from the two position sensors differ, or the motor needs too much duty cycle to hold the position. Subaru (also sold as Saab 9-2X) sets it at more than 3.5° deviation for 250 ms or over 95 % duty cycle for 2 s, lights the lamp at once and lets the spring set the plate to about 6° – raised idle, almost no power. GM's Saab 9-4X V6 uses more than 80 % duty cycle for over 1 s, lamp in the first trip. Mazda's CX-9 set it after frosty nights when condensation froze the throttle and fixed it with software that moves the plate after switch-off. Ford reports the same function as P2111/P2112.
c: Resistance in the motor control wires
s: Check engine or electronic throttle light
Limp mode: much reduced power, raised idle
Delayed or jerky throttle response
Often after a cold start in frost

P0639.d: P0639 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0638 and only applies to engines with two separate electronic throttles, one per cylinder bank (some V8, V10 and V12 engines with separate intake paths). The module compares target and actual angle and the duty cycle the motor needs; if the plate does not follow, it is de-energised and springs to its rest position, and power is limited. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0639 – this follows P0638 (Subaru: more than 3.5° deviation for 250 ms) and CARB's function check of output components. Ford calls a second throttle 'throttle actuator B' and reports it as P211A ff, its sensors as sensor C (P0225/P0229). Uneven filling of the two banks can also cause a rough idle.
c: Bank 2 actuator motor or gears faulty
s: Check engine light
Limp mode, loss of power
Rough idle from uneven bank filling

P063A.d: Some charging systems measure the actual battery or alternator voltage through a separate sense line (regulator terminal S or an input of the module) to compensate voltage drops in the charging cable; without it the system reports a charging fault. No manufacturer document available to us uses P063A–P063D, so these descriptions follow the circuit principle and CARB, under which a charging-system input needs the check engine light only if it affects emissions or other diagnostics. P063A is the general or open-circuit code of sense circuit A; range, low and high are P063B–P063D. It differs from the F feedback (P0622/P0625/P0626) and the L line (P0621); the module's own supply voltage is monitored as P0560–P0563.
c: Sense wire, fuse or connector between battery and alternator or module open or corroded
Contact resistance at battery terminals or grounds
s: Battery warning lamp on
Charging voltage too high or too low (flat or overcharged battery)
Flickering lights
Further voltage codes (P0562/P0563)

P063B.t: Generator Voltage Sense Circuit A Range/Performance
P063B.d: Some charging systems measure the actual battery or alternator voltage through a separate sense line (regulator terminal S or an input of the module) to compensate voltage drops in the charging cable; without it the system reports a charging fault. No manufacturer document available to us uses P063A–P063D, so these descriptions follow the circuit principle and CARB, under which a charging-system input needs the check engine light only if it affects emissions or other diagnostics. P063B is the plausibility check: the measured sense voltage does not fit battery or system voltage or the target value – often because of a voltage drop from contact resistance. Open circuit, low and high are P063A, P063C and P063D.
c: Sense wire, fuse or connector between battery and alternator or module open or corroded
Contact resistance at battery terminals or grounds
s: Battery warning lamp on
Charging voltage too high or too low (flat or overcharged battery)
Flickering lights
Further voltage codes (P0562/P0563)

P063C.t: Generator Voltage Sense Circuit A Low
P063C.d: Some charging systems measure the actual battery or alternator voltage through a separate sense line (regulator terminal S or an input of the module) to compensate voltage drops in the charging cable; without it the system reports a charging fault. No manufacturer document available to us uses P063A–P063D, so these descriptions follow the circuit principle and CARB, under which a charging-system input needs the check engine light only if it affects emissions or other diagnostics. P063C means the sense voltage is below its limit or below battery voltage – open circuit, short to ground or high resistance; the regulator may then overcharge or fall back to a fixed target.
c: Sense wire, fuse or connector between battery and alternator or module open or corroded
Contact resistance at battery terminals or grounds
s: Battery warning lamp on
Charging voltage too high or too low (flat or overcharged battery)
Flickering lights
Further voltage codes (P0562/P0563)

P063D.t: Generator Voltage Sense Circuit A High
P063D.d: Some charging systems measure the actual battery or alternator voltage through a separate sense line (regulator terminal S or an input of the module) to compensate voltage drops in the charging cable; without it the system reports a charging fault. No manufacturer document available to us uses P063A–P063D, so these descriptions follow the circuit principle and CARB, under which a charging-system input needs the check engine light only if it affects emissions or other diagnostics. P063D means the sense voltage is above its limit – a short to a higher voltage, overvoltage or a regulator fault.
c: Sense wire, fuse or connector between battery and alternator or module open or corroded
Contact resistance at battery terminals or grounds
s: Battery warning lamp on
Charging voltage too high or too low (flat or overcharged battery)
Flickering lights
Further voltage codes (P0562/P0563)

P063E.t: Auto Configuration Throttle Input Not Present Bank 1
P063E.d: Some modules configure themselves at start-up by detecting which inputs are present. P063E means the module expects a throttle position input for bank 1 but does not detect it. Unlike circuit codes such as P0122/P0123 or P2135, which judge a present but faulty signal, this says the input was not found for the configuration. No manufacturer document or patent available to us describes this check; the explanation is derived from the J2012 wording. CARB requires input components to be checked for circuit continuity and plausibility, and modules with several variants to detect a wrong one. Possible causes are an unplugged throttle body or open wiring, or software meant for a different vehicle. Without a throttle signal an electronic throttle runs in limp mode.
c: Throttle sensor or unit not connected, connector or wire open
Wrong module software or variant for the vehicle (module from another model)
s: Check engine light
Limp mode, reduced power
Rough idle, poor throttle response
Additional throttle circuit codes

P063F.t: Auto Configuration Engine Coolant Temperature Input Not Present
P063F.d: Some modules configure themselves at start-up by detecting which inputs are present. P063F means the module expects a coolant temperature input but does not detect it during this self-configuration. It differs from the circuit codes P0117/P0118 (signal low/high) and the plausibility codes P0116, P0125 and P0128, which judge a present signal. No manufacturer document or patent available to us describes this check; the explanation is derived from the J2012 wording. CARB requires the coolant temperature sensor to be monitored for circuit, range and warm-up. Possible causes are an unplugged NTC sensor, an open wire or software for a different vehicle. Expect a substitute temperature, a constantly running fan, a dead temperature gauge and poorer cold starts.
c: Coolant temperature sensor not connected, connector or wire open
s: Check engine light
Radiator fan runs constantly
Temperature gauge not working
Poor cold start, higher consumption

P0640.d: Some diesels (for example GM's 6.6 L Duramax LML and the Cummins in Ram trucks) warm the intake air with a heater grid switched by a relay or semiconductor switch. P0640 reports a fault in its control circuit. GM's LML glow plug module expects a digital feedback from the heater while it is commanded on; if it is missing for 2 s (75 % of 4 s), the code sets and the lamp follows after two trips. Current, voltage and temperature faults run under GM's own codes P154A–P154D. CARB requires intake air heaters to be checked for response, current and voltage drop. The result is poor cold starts, white smoke and rough running after a cold start; a relay stuck on drains the battery – Ram recalled 2021 trucks because a shorted heater relay could overheat. Ford's 2023 diesel does not use P0640.
c: Heater relay or switching module faulty
Control wire or connector open or corroded
Heater grid burnt out or shorted to ground
Heater main cable or fuse loose or faulty
Glow plug or engine module faulty
s: Check engine light
Poor cold start in low temperatures
White smoke, rough running after cold start
Flat battery if the relay sticks

P0641.d: The engine module feeds several sensors (pedal, throttle, pressure and position sensors) from shared, regulated 5 V reference circuits; 'A' is circuit 1. A short on one sensor or its wire pulls down every sensor on that circuit and triggers many follow-up codes – so look for the one faulty sensor or chafed wire, for example by unplugging the sensors one at a time. P0641 is the general code for circuit A. GM puts everything into this one code: reference outside 4.875–5.125 V or jumping (filtered against unfiltered value), 19 of 39 counts or 0.19 s in a row, lamp in the first trip; circuits 2–4 are P0651, P0697 and P06A3, and GM does not use P0642/P0643. GM Europe's 2.0 L diesel flags it outside 4.5–5.5 V for 0.5 s with reduced engine power (two trips), the 2.0 L petrol after 1 s or 10 s cumulative (first trip). Because throttle and pedal sensors may be affected, limp mode is common.
c: Short to ground or voltage at one of the supplied sensors or its wire
A sensor signal wire shorted to voltage
Harness damage (chafing, rodent bite, water in connector)
s: Check engine light
Limp mode with reduced power
Many codes from several sensors at once
Possibly starting or boost problems

P0642.t: Sensor Reference Voltage A Circuit Low
P0642.d: The engine module feeds several sensors (pedal, throttle, pressure and position sensors) from shared, regulated 5 V reference circuits; 'A' is circuit 1. A short on one sensor or its wire pulls down every sensor on that circuit and triggers many follow-up codes – so look for the one faulty sensor or chafed wire, for example by unplugging the sensors one at a time. P0642 means the voltage of reference circuit A is too low – typically the 5 V wire or a connected sensor is shorted to ground. Ford checks continuously from ignition on and sets it below 4.75 V after 5 s; GM Europe's 2.0 L petrol after 1 s or 10 s cumulative, lamp in the first trip. GM North America reports it as P0641. All sensors on the circuit then read near 0 V, with matching 'low' codes. High is P0643, range/performance P06A6.
c: 5 V wire or sensor shorted to ground
Internal short in a supplied sensor (e.g. pressure sensor)
s: Check engine light
Limp mode with reduced power
Many codes from several sensors at once
Possibly starting or boost problems

P0643.t: Sensor Reference Voltage A Circuit High
P0643.d: The engine module feeds several sensors (pedal, throttle, pressure and position sensors) from shared, regulated 5 V reference circuits; 'A' is circuit 1. A short on one sensor or its wire pulls down every sensor on that circuit and triggers many follow-up codes – so look for the one faulty sensor or chafed wire, for example by unplugging the sensors one at a time. P0643 means the voltage of reference circuit A is too high – the 5 V wire is shorted to battery voltage or to a higher potential, for example a sensor signal wire shorted to voltage. Ford sets it above 5.25 V after 5 s; GM Europe's 2.0 L petrol after 1 s or 10 s cumulative, lamp in the first trip; GM North America reports it as P0641. Sensors then read too high, and battery voltage on the reference can damage them. Low is P0642.
c: 5 V wire shorted to battery voltage
Signal wire of a supplied sensor shorted to voltage
s: Check engine light
Limp mode with reduced power
Several 'high' sensor codes
Implausible readings (pressure, pedal)
