P06E9.d: On cars with stop-start or keyless start the engine module operates the starter relay itself and watches the start: if cranking is commanded but the engine does not turn, turns too slowly or the start is aborted, it sets P06E9. CARB counts an engine start from 150 rpm below warm idle. Thresholds for speed and time are not published. Bulletins show both sides: VW traces P06E9 on the Tiguan to dirt inside the starter that opens its contacts intermittently, and on the Atlas has relays, battery and voltage drop checked; Audi's SQ5 and FCA's Jeep Compass need module software instead. Ford lists P06E9 among the starter faults that disable stop-start.
c: Starter worn or solenoid contacts intermittently open
Weak battery, voltage drop on main cables or ground
s: Intermittent no-start or only clicking
Stop-start not working
Check engine light depending on manufacturer (FCA: yes)
Long cranking

P06EA.t: NOx Sensor Processor Performance Bank 1 Sensor 1
P06EA.d: A modern NOx sensor is a smart sensor: a ceramic sensing element with pump cells and heater plus its own control unit with a microcontroller, which regulates the pump currents, calculates NOx and oxygen and sends them to the engine module over CAN. P06EA means this control unit of sensor 1 (before the SCR catalyst) reports an internal fault – its self-tests of RAM and ROM or EEPROM checksums fail – so the electronics, not the sensing element, are at fault. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code: Ford's 2023 diesels run exactly these checks continuously, with a fault after 5 s, but report them as P2200; GM uses the P2200 family and U029D/U029E. The NOx value is then invalid, so SCR dosing runs on a model or stops, a warning appears and, depending on market, a countdown to a start lock.
c: Faulty electronics in the NOx sensor control unit
Moisture or corrosion in control unit or connector (underbody location)
Under- or overvoltage or dips in the sensor supply
s: Check engine light or emissions warning
Message to check AdBlue/emission system, possibly countdown to start lock
Follow-up codes for SCR efficiency or NOx plausibility
Driveability usually unchanged

P06EB.t: NOx Sensor Processor Performance Bank 1 Sensor 2
P06EB.d: A modern NOx sensor is a smart sensor: a ceramic sensing element with pump cells and heater plus its own control unit with a microcontroller, which regulates the pump currents, calculates NOx and oxygen and sends them to the engine module over CAN. P06EB means this control unit of sensor 2 (after the SCR catalyst) reports an internal fault – its self-tests of RAM and ROM or EEPROM checksums fail – so the electronics, not the sensing element, are at fault. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code: Ford's 2023 diesels run exactly these checks continuously, with a fault after 5 s, but report them as P229E; GM uses the P2200 family and U029D/U029E. The NOx value is then invalid, so SCR dosing runs on a model or stops, a warning appears and, depending on market, a countdown to a start lock.
c: Faulty electronics in the NOx sensor control unit
Moisture or corrosion in control unit or connector (underbody location)
Under- or overvoltage or dips in the sensor supply
s: Check engine light or emissions warning
Message to check AdBlue/emission system, possibly countdown to start lock
Follow-up codes for SCR efficiency or NOx plausibility
Driveability usually unchanged

P06EC.t: Fuel Injector Control Module Requested MIL Illumination
P06EC.d: P06EC is a notice code like P0700: a separate fuel injector control module has stored an emission-related fault of its own and asks the engine module over CAN to switch on the check engine light. The actual fault is stored in that module and must be read there; simple OBD readers show only P06EC. GM uses it on the 2019 Corvette ZR1, whose LT5 engine adds port injection driven by its own module with its own crank and cam inputs; the code runs continuously from key on and is listed as type A without its own MIL – the lamp comes from the module's fault. Older separate injector modules (Ford 6.0 L Power Stroke, GM bi-fuel CNG trucks) report through P0611 or U codes instead. Any limp mode follows the module's fault.
c: Emission-related fault in the injector control module or its injectors/sensors (code stored there)
Supply, ground or relay problem of the module
Software level of engine or injector module
s: Check engine light on
Generic scanner shows only P06EC – details in the injector module
Depending on the fault, power loss, misfire or limp mode

P06ED.d: The engine module turns the crankshaft signal into a cleaned-up square wave for the tachometer, transmission or body-builder modules – Saab's 1999 9-3, for example, sends two pulses per revolution, about 30 Hz at idle. P06ED means this output is too low, typically shorted to ground, so it can no longer switch high. It is the counterpart of P0654 (open circuit) and P06EE (high). CARB requires output circuits to be checked; the signal is emission-relevant only if a receiving module uses it for emission functions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB, the component and P0654. The tachometer then reads zero or jumps, and modules using the signal lose it, while the engine runs normally.
c: Speed output wire chafing against ground
Aftermarket tachometer or accessory wired wrongly
s: Tachometer at zero or jumping
Other modules without speed signal
Engine runs normally

P06EE.d: The engine module turns the crankshaft signal into a cleaned-up square wave for the tachometer, transmission or body-builder modules – Saab's 1999 9-3, for example, sends two pulses per revolution, about 30 Hz at idle. P06EE means this output is too high, typically shorted to supply voltage, so it can no longer switch to ground; the driver may shut down for protection. It is the counterpart of P0654 (open circuit) and P06ED (low). CARB requires output circuits to be checked. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB, the component and P0654. The tachometer then reads nothing or full scale, and modules using the signal lose it, while the engine runs normally.
s: Tachometer shows nothing or full scale
Other modules without speed signal
Engine runs normally

P06EF.d: P06EF concerns the automatic restart after the system itself has stopped the engine – stop-start or hybrid. The restart, by starter, reinforced stop-start starter or belt starter-generator, takes too long or fails. CARB does not count such a commanded shutdown as a stall. No manufacturer publishes the time limit. VW's Tiguan bulletins list P06EF together with P06E9 and trace both to dirt inside the starter; FCA fixes it on the 2019 Jeep Wrangler with engine-module software and lights the check engine light. Stop-start is then disabled. Besides the starter, a weak stop-start battery or fuel and ignition problems at restart can be the cause.
c: Starter or starter-generator worn, contacts intermittently open
Weak stop-start battery (AGM/EFB) or battery sensor
Fuel pressure or ignition at restart
s: Engine does not restart or restarts late after stop-start
Stop-start disabled
Check engine light (FCA)

P06F0.t: Reductant Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit
P06F0.d: Some SCR diesels have a separate reductant control module that drives the DEF pump, heaters and dosing valve – Ford calls it the pump motor controller (fault above 130 °C under P20FF), GM's L5P an SCR power module. It measures its own board temperature with an internal sensor to protect itself from heat. P06F0 is the general circuit fault of this internal sensor: the signal is missing, open or cannot be evaluated. Range, low and high are P06F1–P06F3; the DEF tank temperature sensor is a different part. No manufacturer document available to us uses P06F0–P06F3; Ford and GM report related faults under P20FF or own codes. Without a valid temperature the module limits or stops heaters and pump, so dosing is restricted and an SCR warning, up to a start lock countdown, may follow.
c: Reductant control module or pump unit faulty (sensor is on the board)
Water ingress or corrosion in the module (DEF crystals, underbody location)
Supply or ground problems at the module
s: Check engine light or SCR warning
Message to check AdBlue system, possibly countdown to start lock
DEF heating or pump inactive (no thawing in frost)
Driveability usually unchanged

P06F1.t: Reductant Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Range/Performance
P06F1.d: Some SCR diesels have a separate reductant control module that drives the DEF pump, heaters and dosing valve – Ford calls it the pump motor controller (fault above 130 °C under P20FF), GM's L5P an SCR power module. It measures its own board temperature with an internal sensor to protect itself from heat. P06F1 means the signal is electrically valid but implausible – it jumps, freezes or differs from comparison temperatures such as ambient or tank temperature after a long stop. Circuit faults are P06F0, P06F2 and P06F3. No manufacturer document available to us uses P06F0–P06F3; Ford and GM report related faults under P20FF or own codes. Without a valid temperature the module limits or stops heaters and pump, so dosing is restricted and an SCR warning, up to a start lock countdown, may follow.
c: Reductant control module or pump unit faulty (sensor is on the board)
Water ingress or corrosion in the module (DEF crystals, underbody location)
Supply or ground problems at the module
s: Check engine light or SCR warning
Message to check AdBlue system, possibly countdown to start lock
DEF heating or pump inactive (no thawing in frost)
Driveability usually unchanged

P06F2.t: Reductant Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
P06F2.d: Some SCR diesels have a separate reductant control module that drives the DEF pump, heaters and dosing valve – Ford calls it the pump motor controller (fault above 130 °C under P20FF), GM's L5P an SCR power module. It measures its own board temperature with an internal sensor to protect itself from heat. P06F2 means the signal is below its minimum; with the usual NTC voltage divider that is a short to ground, and the reading appears implausibly hot. The opposite fault is P06F3, an implausible reading P06F1. No manufacturer document available to us uses P06F0–P06F3; Ford and GM report related faults under P20FF or own codes. Without a valid temperature the module limits or stops heaters and pump, so dosing is restricted and an SCR warning, up to a start lock countdown, may follow.
c: Reductant control module or pump unit faulty (sensor is on the board)
Water ingress or corrosion in the module (DEF crystals, underbody location)
Supply or ground problems at the module
s: Check engine light or SCR warning
Message to check AdBlue system, possibly countdown to start lock
DEF heating or pump inactive (no thawing in frost)
Driveability usually unchanged

P06F3.t: Reductant Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit High
P06F3.d: Some SCR diesels have a separate reductant control module that drives the DEF pump, heaters and dosing valve – Ford calls it the pump motor controller (fault above 130 °C under P20FF), GM's L5P an SCR power module. It measures its own board temperature with an internal sensor to protect itself from heat. P06F3 means the signal is above its maximum; with the usual NTC voltage divider that is an open circuit or short to positive, and the reading appears implausibly cold. The opposite fault is P06F2, an implausible reading P06F1. No manufacturer document available to us uses P06F0–P06F3; Ford and GM report related faults under P20FF or own codes. Without a valid temperature the module limits or stops heaters and pump, so dosing is restricted and an SCR warning, up to a start lock countdown, may follow.
c: Reductant control module or pump unit faulty (sensor is on the board)
Water ingress or corrosion in the module (DEF crystals, underbody location)
Supply or ground problems at the module
s: Check engine light or SCR warning
Message to check AdBlue system, possibly countdown to start lock
DEF heating or pump inactive (no thawing in frost)
Driveability usually unchanged

P06F4.d: When the engine module switches a lamp through its own wire, it checks the output driver electrically like other lamp outputs: with the lamp off the line must carry supply voltage, with it on nearly 0 V – GM's MIL driver, for example, flags an open circuit at 200 kΩ or more. It cannot see whether the bulb lights, and on cars that send the lamp command over CAN such faults appear as U codes. P06F4 concerns the indicator showing that stop-start is active or disabled; the code reports a fault in its control circuit. No manufacturer document available to us uses it; the description follows CARB's output check and other lamp circuits. Only the display is affected – the stop-start function itself has its own codes (P06E9, P06EF).
c: Wire or connector to the indicator open or shorted
s: Stop-start indicator not working or permanently lit
Usually no check engine light

P06F5.d: SAE J2012 provides a complete code family for a second glow plug control module, mirroring module 1 code for code. P06F5 is the general or internal fault of module 2, the counterpart of P064C. For module 1, GM's L5P groups driver faults (under 3.2 A with 0 V at the plug for 3.5 s) and a ROM checksum error under P064C, after two trips; Ford's 2023 Power Stroke lists P064C among the module checks with detection in about 1 s. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P064C). The plugs fed by module 2 then heat poorly or not at all.
c: Glow plug control module 2 faulty internally
Poor supply or ground of module 2
s: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp
Hard cold start, long cranking in frost
Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only
Usually no symptoms when warm

P06F6.t: Glow Plug Control Module 2 Control Circuit/Open
P06F6.d: P06F6 means the command line from the engine module to glow plug control module 2 is open or has a general circuit fault – the counterpart of P0670 for module 1. The engine module's output driver detects an open load while the driver is off. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P0670). Shorts on the same line are P06F7 (to ground) and P06F8 (to positive); the feedback line back to the engine module is P06FC/P06FD. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank.
c: Line from engine module to glow module 2 open, connector loose or corroded
Input of glow module 2 faulty or module not connected
s: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp
Hard cold start, long cranking in frost
Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only
Usually no symptoms when warm

P06F7.t: Glow Plug Control Module 2 Control Circuit Low
P06F7.d: P06F7 means the command line from the engine module to glow plug control module 2 is too low, typically shorted to ground – the counterpart of P0383 for module 1. The engine module's output driver detects the short by its current when switched on or by the line voltage when switched off. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P0383). An open line is P06F6, a short to positive P06F8. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank.
c: Command line to glow module 2 chafed through to ground
Moisture or corrosion in the connector bridging to ground
Input of glow module 2 or engine module driver faulty
s: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp
Hard cold start, long cranking in frost
Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only
Usually no symptoms when warm

P06F8.t: Glow Plug Control Module 2 Control Circuit High
P06F8.d: P06F8 means the command line from the engine module to glow plug control module 2 is too high, typically shorted to positive – the counterpart of P0384 for module 1. Note that Ford's 2023 diesels use P0384 differently, for the supply voltage of the glow module (below 6.5 V or above 16.5 V); in J2012 that is P052F, and for module 2 P06F9. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P0384). An open line is P06F6, a short to ground P06F7. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank.
c: Command line shorted to positive or supply
Corrosion in the connector bridging to a B+ pin
s: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp
Hard cold start, long cranking in frost
Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only
Usually no symptoms when warm

P06F9.t: Glow Plug Control Module 2 System Voltage
P06F9.d: P06F9 means the supply voltage of glow plug control module 2 is out of range – the counterpart of P052F for module 1. For module 1, Ford's 2023 Power Stroke flags below 6.5 V, above 16.5 V or an open supply after about 1 s; GM's L5P checks the same under P163C (below 6.0 V with ignition above 9 V, or implausible against ignition voltage, 4 s). An FCA bulletin shows P052F together with the glow plug open codes, because without supply no current flows. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P052F). Check main feed, fuses and ground first.
c: Main feed to glow module 2 open or high-resistance (fuse, fusible link, B+ wire)
Weak battery or discharged auxiliary battery
s: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp
Hard cold start, long cranking in frost
Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only
Usually no symptoms when warm

P06FA.d: P06FA means glow plug control module 2 does not respond correctly to the glow command – the counterpart of P06E5 for module 1. For module 1, Ford's 2023 Power Stroke flags internal drivers that fail to switch or overheat for more than 1 s; GM's L5P files the same check under P064C (under 3.2 A with 0 V at the plug for 3.5 s, two trips). No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P06E5). Internal checksum errors are P06FB, overheating P263F. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank.
c: Glow module 2 faulty internally (drivers do not switch)
Poor supply or ground of module 2
s: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp
Hard cold start, long cranking in frost
Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only
Usually no symptoms when warm

P06FB.t: Glow Plug Control Module 2 Memory Checksum Error
P06FB.d: P06FB means glow plug control module 2 has found a memory checksum error – the counterpart of P06DF for module 1. The module forms a checksum over its memory at power-up and compares it with the stored value. For module 1, Ford's 2023 Power Stroke checks the RAM checksum at power-up (about 1 s); GM's L5P checks the ROM checksum (4.5 s, two trips) and reports it as P064C. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P06DF). The usual remedy is reprogramming or replacing the module. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank.
s: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp
Hard cold start, long cranking in frost
Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only
Usually no symptoms when warm

P06FC.t: Glow Plug Control Module 2 to PCM Communication Circuit
P06FC.d: P06FC means the feedback or communication from glow plug control module 2 to the engine module is missing, or the line is open or shorted – the counterpart of P0683 for module 1. Depending on design the module reports over a single feedback wire (Bosch-type systems expect it inverse to the command line) or over the bus; GM and Ford report a lost bus link as U0106 rather than P0683. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P0683). The engine module then loses the plug status reports; implausible messages are P06FD. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank.
c: Feedback or bus line open or shorted, connector corroded
Glow module 2 without supply (does not transmit)
Glow module 2 or engine module interface faulty
s: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp
Hard cold start, long cranking in frost
Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only
Usually no symptoms when warm

P06FD.t: Glow Plug Control Module 2 to PCM Communication Circuit Range/Performance
P06FD.d: P06FD means signals or messages from glow plug control module 2 arrive at the engine module but are implausible – wrong duty cycle or pattern, feedback not matching the command, or single messages timing out. It is the counterpart of P0684 for module 1; Saab's Bosch-based diesels, for example, expect the feedback signal to be inverse to the command line. No manufacturer document available to us uses a second glow module – Ford's and GM's V8 diesels drive all eight plugs from one; the code suits systems with one module per cylinder bank. The description follows module 1 (P0684). A missing signal or open line is P06FC, a lost bus link usually U0106. The plugs of module 2 then heat poorly or not at all, typically on one bank.
c: Loose contact or contact resistance in the feedback or bus line
Ground offset between module and engine module from glow currents
Software mismatch between modules or module faulty
s: Check engine light, possibly glow plug/wait-to-start lamp
Hard cold start, long cranking in frost
Rough cold idle and white smoke, often one cylinder bank only
Usually no symptoms when warm

P06FE.t: Cold Start Diesel Intake Air Flow Control Performance
P06FE.d: 'Diesel intake air flow control' is the diesel's electric intake throttle with position sensor (P02E0 ff). During cold start many diesels close it partly: the extra load raises exhaust temperature so the catalysts light off sooner. CARB requires such cold start elements to be monitored, with their own codes separate from normal operation. P06FE means the throttle does not reach its target position while the cold start strategy is active – it is not the intake air heater. No manufacturer document available to us uses P06FE: GM's 2025 diesels run this check under P2957 (deviation above 16 % or 10 %, two trips), Ford's 2023 diesels under P02E4 in cold start mode. Cold start emissions rise; driveability usually stays normal.
c: Intake throttle coked with soot and oil (EGR, crankcase ventilation)
Throttle motor or gear stiff, position sensor faulty
Ice or condensate in the intake in frost
Contact resistance in connector or wiring, low voltage
s: Check engine light, usually after two trips
Hardly any change in driveability
Possibly more smoke or smell while warming up
Further throttle codes (P02E1/P02E4/P02E5) possible

P06FF.d: When the engine module switches a lamp through its own wire, it checks the output driver electrically like other lamp outputs: with the lamp off the line must carry supply voltage, with it on nearly 0 V – GM's MIL driver, for example, flags an open circuit at 200 kΩ or more. It cannot see whether the bulb lights, and on cars that send the lamp command over CAN such faults appear as U codes. P06FF concerns an economy indicator such as an ECO lamp that the engine module switches directly; the code reports a fault in its control circuit. It should not be confused with a body electrics 'economy mode' that saves battery energy. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code; the description follows CARB's output check and other lamp circuits. Driving is not affected.
c: Wire or connector to the lamp open or shorted
s: ECO indicator not working or permanently lit
No effect on driving

P0700.d: P0700 is a notice code: the separate transmission control module has stored an emission-related fault of its own and asks the engine module to switch on the check engine light. The actual fault – a sensor, solenoid, ratio or speed sensor code – is stored in the transmission module and must be read with a tool that can address it; simple OBD readers often show only P0700. GM's engine module reads the request message from 3 s after start; Subaru-based systems (Saab 9-2X) light the MIL at once and clear it after three fault-free cycles. Ford's engine modules with integrated transmission control do not use P0700. Any limp mode comes from the transmission fault, not from P0700.
c: Actual fault stored in the transmission module (sensor, solenoid, ratio, speed sensor)
Wrong transmission fluid level or condition causing slip or ratio codes
Harness or connector at the transmission corroded or damaged
Low system voltage or weak battery
s: Check engine light, possibly transmission warning
Depending on the transmission fault: limp mode, harsh or delayed shifts
Often no symptoms if the fault was intermittent
Simple OBD reader shows only P0700

P0701.d: P0701 means the transmission control system works outside its expected range or its function is implausible – without a circuit fault. What exactly is checked is up to the manufacturer; no GM, Ford, Saab or bulletin document available to us describes the strategy. The only manufacturer evidence is Ford's engine module list for 6.8 L E- and F-Series trucks, where P0701 is stored without the check engine light. Typically the control cannot plausibly achieve the requested gear, pressure or torque, and the transmission goes into limp mode. Individual components have their own codes (P0705 ff range sensor, P0715 ff speed sensors, P0750 ff solenoids).
c: Transmission control faulty internally or software
Implausible input signals (speed or range sensor) without own circuit fault
Wrong fluid level or quality – hydraulics do not respond
Harness or connector with contact resistance
s: Transmission warning (at Ford no check engine light)
Limp mode with fixed gear or missing gears
Harsh or irregular shifts

P0702.d: P0702 reports an electrical fault in the transmission control system as a whole – typically the supply of the transmission actuators (solenoid supply, transmission relay, supply switch in the module) or a circuit fault not assigned to a single component. No manufacturer document available to us describes it in detail; Ford's engine module list for 6.8 L E- and F-Series trucks stores it without the check engine light. If the solenoid supply is lost, transmissions usually fall back to a hydraulic limp gear. Individual solenoids have their own codes (P0750 ff); actuator supply is P0657 ff.
c: Transmission actuator supply interrupted (fuse, relay, ground)
Harness or connector at transmission or module damaged, corroded or oil-soaked
Transmission module output stage or supply switch faulty
s: Transmission limp mode with fixed gear
Transmission warning; check engine light depending on the maker
No or harsh shifts, further solenoid codes

P0703.d: Brake switch A is usually the brake light switch, B a second, redundant contact or signal used to cancel cruise control, release the converter clutch, check 'brake before throttle' and for stop-start. Since about 2014 GM receives it as a CAN message from the body module and checks its integrity (rolling counter, protection value: 3 of 10 faulty in 2014, 9 of 17 in 2025) without the check engine light; cruise control is disabled. Subaru-based systems (Saab 9-2X) check the circuit electrically during stops and starts and light the MIL after two trips. An NHTSA investigation of Hyundai and Kia brake light switches lists P0703 with a brake light that stays on. Brake switch A codes are P0571–P0573, disagreement between A and B is P0504.
c: Brake light or double switch worn, corroded or misadjusted
Wiring or connector at the pedal damaged, fuse blown
CAN message from the body module disturbed (GM: software, bus fault)
Aftermarket LED lamps or trailer module distorting the circuit
s: Cruise control cannot be engaged or drops out
Brake light stays on or does not work
Selector cannot be moved out of P (shift lock)
Check engine light depending on the maker

P0704.d: Only on cars with a clutch pedal: the clutch switch tells the engine module that the clutch is depressed, used to cancel cruise control, smooth load changes when shifting and for stop-start. The check is a plausibility test over driving events rather than a voltage check: Saab's Trionic T8 expects a change of state every time the car pulls away from 3 to 50 km/h (four misses in a row), the EDC16 diesel at gear changes (25 in a row, above 35 km/h and 1500 rpm), and Ford compares its two clutch switches continuously. None of them lights the check engine light; cruise control is disabled. Separate clutch pedal switch codes are P0830–P0835.
c: Clutch switch faulty or misadjusted (does not switch or too late)
Connector or wiring at the pedal box damaged or corroded
Floor mat or pedal stop shifted, switch bracket broken
Driving style (pulling away or shifting without fully depressing the clutch)
s: Cruise control not working or not cancelling when declutching
Jerks or rev hang when shifting
Stop-start inactive
Usually no check engine light

P0705.t: Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit (PRNDL Input)
P0705.d: The transmission range sensor (selector or multifunction switch, PRNDL) reports the selected range; it may be a multi-contact switch with a bit pattern per position, an analog sensor with two opposing voltages adding up to 5 V, or a contactless PWM sensor. Its second channel has its own codes (P2801–P2805). P0705 is the circuit or pattern fault: the module receives a combination that matches no valid position. Ford flags an invalid pattern after 5 s (digital sensor) or 200 ms (4-bit sensor), checking continuously with the check engine light; Saab's 9-5 (9600) detects an impossible combination of its four contacts and goes into limp mode with the gearbox warning. The transmission no longer knows the range reliably – limp mode, start interlock or reversing light may be affected. Check the harness for shorts to ground before replacing the sensor.
c: Range sensor worn, dirty or with oil or water ingress
Sensor misadjusted or selector cable out of adjustment
Harness or connector at the transmission damaged, short to ground
Transmission or engine module input faulty
s: Check engine and/or transmission warning lamp
Transmission limp mode, fixed gear, harsh shifts
Starting problems in P/N or start interlock
Wrong gear indication, reversing light not working

P0706.t: Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0706.d: The transmission range sensor (selector or multifunction switch, PRNDL) reports the selected range; it may be a multi-contact switch with a bit pattern per position, an analog sensor with two opposing voltages adding up to 5 V, or a contactless PWM sensor. Its second channel has its own codes (P2801–P2805). P0706 means the signal is present but implausible. Ford uses it per transmission: for its PWM sensor when the frequency leaves 100–175 Hz (nominal 125 Hz), for the 6F digital sensor when it stays in the transition zone between two positions. Saab's 9-5 (9650), whose sensor sits in the transmission module, flags a sum of the two opposing channels more than 0.29 V away from 5 V, with the lamp in the first trip; adaptations are frozen, the gearbox holds 2nd gear in D and the engine may not restart after switch-off.
c: Range sensor or transmission module with integrated sensor faulty
Selector cable or sensor misadjusted (position between two ranges)
Contact resistance in sensor supply or ground
Moisture or oil in harness or connector
s: Check engine and/or transmission warning lamp
Transmission limp mode, fixed gear, harsh shifts
Starting problems in P/N or start interlock
Wrong gear indication, reversing light not working

P0707.t: Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit Low
P0707.d: The transmission range sensor (selector or multifunction switch, PRNDL) reports the selected range; it may be a multi-contact switch with a bit pattern per position, an analog sensor with two opposing voltages adding up to 5 V, or a contactless PWM sensor. Its second channel has its own codes (P2801–P2805). P0707 means the sensor A signal is too low – usually a short to ground or lost supply. GM's T87A transmission module flags a PWM duty cycle below 8.8 % for 0.5 s within 1.5 s, with the lamp in the first trip; Ford flags a duty cycle below 10 %, an analog sensor below 0.2 V for 5 s or a dual-analog channel below 0.127 V for 200 ms; Saab's 9-5 (9650) below 0.127 V for 100 ms twice. 'Low' refers to the signal, not to a gear.
c: Signal wire shorted to ground (chafing at the transmission case)
Sensor supply missing (5 V reference, fuse)
Connector corroded or oil in the connector
s: Check engine and/or transmission warning lamp
Transmission limp mode, fixed gear, harsh shifts
Starting problems in P/N or start interlock
Wrong gear indication, reversing light not working

P0708.t: Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit High
P0708.d: The transmission range sensor (selector or multifunction switch, PRNDL) reports the selected range; it may be a multi-contact switch with a bit pattern per position, an analog sensor with two opposing voltages adding up to 5 V, or a contactless PWM sensor. Its second channel has its own codes (P2801–P2805). P0708 means the sensor A signal is too high – a short to voltage or, depending on the circuit, an open line pulled up. GM's T87A transmission module flags a PWM duty cycle above 91.2 % for 1.8 s within 2.25 s, lamp in the first trip; Ford flags a duty cycle above 90 %, an analog sensor above 4.8 V for 5 s, a dual-analog channel above 4.84 V for 200 ms, and explicitly an open circuit on its digital sensor (all switches open, e.g. unplugged); Saab's 9-5 (9650) above 4.87 V for 100 ms twice, with 2nd gear held and a restart interlock.
c: Sensor connector off or signal/ground wire open
s: Check engine and/or transmission warning lamp
Transmission limp mode, fixed gear, harsh shifts
Starting problems in P/N or start interlock
Wrong gear indication, reversing light not working

P0709.t: Transmission Range Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
P0709.d: The transmission range sensor (selector or multifunction switch, PRNDL) reports the selected range; it may be a multi-contact switch with a bit pattern per position, an analog sensor with two opposing voltages adding up to 5 V, or a contactless PWM sensor. Its second channel has its own codes (P2801–P2805). P0709 means the sensor A signal jumps briefly to invalid values or drops out without being permanently low or high. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0709 – Ford catches short invalid states under P0705 and P0706 instead – so the description follows the sibling codes. Sliding contacts in older selector switches are a typical source; the transmission may briefly lose the range and go into limp mode.
c: Loose contact or corrosion in the range sensor connector
Worn sliding contacts in the selector switch
Harness chafing on transmission or bracket, breaking when moved
Misadjusted sensor or selector cable (position at the limit)
s: Intermittent transmission warning or check engine light
Gear indication flickers, brief shift jolts
Occasional starting problems in P/N
Occasional limp mode

P070A.d: Fluid level sensors in the transmission sump (capacitive or voltage-based) report the oil level to the transmission module; measurements are only valid under defined conditions – an Allison patent names fluid temperature, vehicle at rest, low input speed and a tilt correction. Such sensors are mainly found in heavy automatic transmissions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. P070A is the general circuit fault of this sensor (open or fault in the signal circuit). Because the oil level does not usually affect emissions directly, a rating without the check engine light is likely; expect a transmission warning or a missing level display. An actually low oil level is not a P070A fault. Range, low, high and intermittent are P070B–P070E; fluid temperature has its own codes (P0710 ff).
c: Wire or connector to the sensor (often through the sump or transmission connector) open or oil-soaked
s: Transmission warning or 'check fluid level' message
Fluid level display missing
Usually no driveability problems

P070B.t: Transmission Fluid Level Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P070B.d: Fluid level sensors in the transmission sump (capacitive or voltage-based) report the oil level to the transmission module; measurements are only valid under defined conditions – an Allison patent names fluid temperature, vehicle at rest, low input speed and a tilt correction. Such sensors are mainly found in heavy automatic transmissions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. P070B means the signal is present but implausible – it does not change, does not fit temperature or operating state, or lies outside the physically possible range. Such checks only make sense within the valid measuring window. A truly wrong oil level (overfilled, underfilled) or the wrong fluid can also appear as an implausible signal. The circuit fault is P070A.
c: Fluid level sensor drifting or dirty (wear debris, sludge)
Fluid level actually wrong (over- or underfilled) or wrong fluid
Contact resistance in connector or wire
Faulty tilt or temperature compensation (fluid temperature sensor fault)
s: Warning or message about transmission fluid level
Fluid level display implausible or unavailable
Usually no driveability problems

P070C.t: Transmission Fluid Level Sensor Circuit Low
P070C.d: Fluid level sensors in the transmission sump report the oil level to the transmission module as a voltage; an Allison patent converts it to millimetres and only accepts readings with the vehicle at rest, warm fluid, low input speed and a tilt correction. Such sensors are mainly found in heavy automatic transmissions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. P070C means the sensor signal is below its lower limit – typically the signal wire shorted to ground or a sensor shorted internally. Because the oil level does not usually affect emissions directly, a rating without the check engine light is likely; expect a transmission warning or a missing level display. An actually low oil level is P070F.
c: Signal wire to the level sensor shorted to ground (chafing, transmission connector)
Transmission connector soaked in oil or corroded
s: Fluid level display missing or warning to check transmission fluid
Usually no driveability problems
Transmission warning lamp depending on manufacturer

P070D.t: Transmission Fluid Level Sensor Circuit High
P070D.d: Fluid level sensors in the transmission sump report the oil level to the transmission module as a voltage; an Allison patent converts it to millimetres and only accepts readings with the vehicle at rest, warm fluid, low input speed and a tilt correction. Such sensors are mainly found in heavy automatic transmissions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. P070D means the sensor signal is above its upper limit – typically an open signal or ground wire, pulled up inside the module, or a short to positive. Because the oil level does not usually affect emissions directly, a rating without the check engine light is likely; expect a transmission warning or a missing level display. The opposite fault is P070C.
c: Wire or connector to the level sensor open
s: Fluid level display missing or warning to check transmission fluid
Usually no driveability problems
Transmission warning lamp depending on manufacturer

P070E.t: Transmission Fluid Level Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P070E.d: Fluid level sensors in the transmission sump report the oil level to the transmission module as a voltage; an Allison patent converts it to millimetres and only accepts readings with the vehicle at rest, warm fluid, low input speed and a tilt correction. Such sensors are mainly found in heavy automatic transmissions. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. P070E means the level signal drops out briefly or jumps unrealistically – usually a loose contact or a wire breaking under movement. Sloshing and tilt also make readings vary, which is why valid measurements need the vehicle at rest. Because the oil level does not usually affect emissions directly, a rating without the check engine light is likely; expect a transmission warning or a missing level display.
c: Loose contact in transmission connector or harness
Contaminated or foaming fluid at the sensor
s: Fluid level display jumps or drops out at times
Intermittent warning message

P070F.d: P070F is not a circuit fault but a condition: a working fluid level sensor reports a level below the target band. In the Allison patent the module compares the measured height in millimetres with a tilt-dependent band and reports at least a quart too little or too much – only with the vehicle at rest, fluid above about 30–40 °C and low input speed. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code. Take it seriously: real fluid loss leads to slipping, overheating (P0218) and ratio errors. Leaks at the pan gasket, seals or cooler lines and wrong filling after service are the usual causes.
c: Leak (pan gasket, shaft seals, cooler lines)
Underfilled after fluid change or repair
s: Warning: transmission fluid level low
Slipping gears, delayed engagement
Transmission overheating
Oil spots under the vehicle

P0710.t: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0710.d: The transmission fluid temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as the fluid warms; the module feeds it with 5 V through a resistor. A low signal therefore means very hot or a short to ground, a high signal very cold or an open circuit. P0710 is the general circuit code used when a manufacturer does not separate low and high. Subaru-based systems (Saab 9-2X) flag 0.1 V or less or 4.7 V or more, light the MIL after two consecutive trips and use 80 °C as substitute. Ford's 2023 diesels use P0710 alongside P0712/P0713 for open and short circuits, without MIL, after 5–12 s, substituting coolant temperature. GM uses only the split codes. With the substitute value the shift quality suffers: harsh shifts and a late converter clutch.
c: Fluid temperature sensor faulty (often part of the internal harness or valve body)
Transmission connector leaking or corroded, oil in the connector
s: Harsh or late shifts
Torque converter clutch applies late or not at all
Check engine or transmission lamp depending on manufacturer
Implausible fluid temperature in the scan tool

P0711.t: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0711.d: P0711 means the fluid temperature signal is electrically valid but implausible. Manufacturers check three things: the fluid does not warm up as expected (GM 2025 still below 15 °C after the calibrated warm-up time, Saab's AF40 below 20 °C after 10 minutes of driving), the value is stuck (Ford: within ±2 °F for about 2.5 minutes below 70 or above 225 °F), or it jumps unrealistically. GM's 6T70 compares it with the module's internal temperature. The MIL rating varies: GM's newer modules after two trips, Saab AF40 none, Ford none; a 2013 Ram 6.7 bulletin moved P0711–P0714 from one to two trips. A substitute value then limits adaption and converter clutch control.
c: Fluid temperature sensor drifting or stuck
High contact resistance in connector or harness (oil, corrosion)
Very cold weather or short trips (fluid does not reach warm-up threshold)
s: Harsh or late shifts
Torque converter clutch applies late or not at all
Check engine or transmission lamp depending on manufacturer
Implausible fluid temperature in the scan tool

P0712.t: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0712.d: The transmission fluid temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as the fluid warms; the module feeds it with 5 V through a resistor. A low signal therefore means very hot or a short to ground, a high signal very cold or an open circuit. P0712 means the signal is too low – the sensor reads extremely hot, or the signal wire is shorted to ground. GM's 2025 transmission modules flag below 13.5 Ω for 5 of 6 s after two trips; the 2018 LT4 engine module below 17.88 Ω (over 150 °C) without MIL; the 2007 Allison 1000 150 °C or more for 2.5 s; Saab's AF40 over 200 °C; Ford below 0.05 V for 5–12 s without MIL. The module substitutes a value (coolant temperature, 80 °C or a hot mode) and may shift with hot-fluid strategy. Real overheating with a good sensor is P0218.
c: Signal wire shorted to ground (internal harness, chafing)
s: Transmission in hot mode (early converter clutch, changed shift points)
Harsh shifts
Extremely high fluid temperature shown
Check engine or transmission lamp depending on manufacturer

P0713.t: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0713.d: The transmission fluid temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as the fluid warms; the module feeds it with 5 V through a resistor. A low signal therefore means very hot or a short to ground, a high signal very cold or an open circuit. P0713 means the signal is too high – the sensor reads extremely cold, or the circuit is open or shorted to positive. GM's 2025 modules flag above 284 kΩ for 5 of 6 s after two trips; the 2007 Allison 1000 −45 °C or below for 2.5 s; Saab's AF40 below −43 °C; Ford above 4.6 V for 5–12 s without MIL. Many require prior running time or a warm engine so a genuine −40 °C cold start does not count (Allison: coolant above 20 °C; Saab: over 10 minutes of driving). The transmission then stays in its cold strategy: open converter clutch, late upshifts.
c: Transmission connector loose or corroded, wire open
s: Fluid temperature shown around −40 °C
Converter clutch stays open, late upshifts
Higher fuel consumption
Check engine or transmission lamp depending on manufacturer

P0714.t: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
P0714.d: The transmission fluid temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as the fluid warms; the module feeds it with 5 V through a resistor. A low signal therefore means very hot or a short to ground, a high signal very cold or an open circuit. P0714 means the signal drops out or jumps briefly – not long enough for P0712 or P0713. Ford's 2012 6R80 transmission names P0714 among its fluid temperature checks for open, short and in-range faults. Ram 6.7 bulletins of 2013 changed P0711–P0714 from a one-trip to a two-trip MIL to avoid needless warnings. GM files such jumps under P0711 instead. No source publishes thresholds for P0714 itself. A loose contact in the transmission connector or a chafing internal harness is the usual cause.
c: Loose contact in transmission connector (oil, corrosion, spread pins)
Internal harness chafing from movement or vibration
s: Harsh shifts at times
Jumping fluid temperature display
Check engine or transmission lamp depending on manufacturer

P0715.t: Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit
P0715.d: The input or turbine shaft speed sensor – a Hall sensor with square-wave output or an inductive sensor with sine output – reports the speed behind the torque converter. With output and engine speed it gives the actual gear ratio, converter slip and shift timing. P0715 is the general circuit code. Ford uses it for 'no signal' too: the vehicle is moving under power (engine above converter stall speed, output speed plausible) but the sensor reports under 200 rpm for 5–30 s; Ford's DPS6 dual-clutch sets it for a hardware-detected fault of input shaft sensor 1. Subaru-based systems flag an open or shorted circuit, Saab's Aisin box no input signal while the output sensor works, substituting output speed. GM does not use P0715. Limp mode, harsh shifts and a disabled converter clutch follow.
c: Speed sensor faulty (Hall IC or coil open or shorted)
Connector or harness corroded, chafed or loose pins (with internal sensors also the pass-through connector)
Metal debris on the sensor magnet or damaged reluctor wheel
Transmission module or its sensor supply faulty
s: Check engine and/or transmission warning lamp
Limp mode with fixed gear, harsh shifts
Torque converter clutch does not apply
Input speed shows 0 or implausible in the scan tool

P0716.t: Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0716.d: The input or turbine shaft speed sensor – a Hall sensor with square-wave output or an inductive sensor with sine output – reports the speed behind the torque converter. With output and engine speed it gives the actual gear ratio, converter slip and shift timing. P0716 means a signal is present but implausible: too high, or dropping suddenly without recovering. GM's 2025 modules count drops of more than 650 rpm between 25 ms samples and fail after more than three; the 6T70 in the Saab 9-4X flags a 1350 rpm drop for 1 s; the 2007 Allison 1000 also detects noise and swapped sensor wires; all after one trip. Ford's 6R80 flags turbine speed above 7700 rpm. The 6T70 then runs only reverse and fifth gear, with maximum line pressure and no converter clutch.
c: Loose contact or chafing in the sensor circuit
Sensor faulty, wrong air gap or metal debris
Reluctor wheel or clutch drum damaged
Sensor wires swapped after repair or interference
s: Check engine and/or transmission warning lamp
Limp mode with fixed gear (6T70: reverse and fifth only)
Harsh or delayed shifts
Torque converter clutch locked out

P0717.t: Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit No Signal
P0717.d: The input or turbine shaft speed sensor – a Hall sensor with square-wave output or an inductive sensor with sine output – reports the speed behind the torque converter. With output and engine speed it gives the actual gear ratio, converter slip and shift timing. P0717 means there is practically no input speed signal although the vehicle is driving under power. GM's 2025 modules flag under 200 rpm for more than 4 s with torque applied, the 6T70 under 50 rpm for 5 s, the Allison 1000 under 61 rpm with output above 500 rpm; Ford under 200 rpm for 5–30 s; all after one trip. GM calls it 'circuit low voltage', but means missing frequency. On GM's 10-speed both input and output sensors share a supply – P0717 together with P0722 points to that supply rather than two sensors.
c: Speed sensor faulty (Hall IC or coil open or shorted)
Connector or harness corroded, chafed or loose pins (with internal sensors also the pass-through connector)
Metal debris on the sensor magnet or damaged reluctor wheel
Transmission module or its sensor supply faulty
s: Check engine and/or transmission warning lamp
Limp mode with fixed gear, harsh shifts
Torque converter clutch does not apply
Input speed shows 0 or implausible in the scan tool

P0718.t: Input/Turbine Shaft Speed Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
P0718.d: The input or turbine shaft speed sensor – a Hall sensor with square-wave output or an inductive sensor with sine output – reports the speed behind the torque converter. With output and engine speed it gives the actual gear ratio, converter slip and shift timing. P0718 means the signal is present but jumps or drops out briefly. Ford's petrol modules from 2012 to 2023 count 200 turbine speed spikes above 400 rpm with at most 1.5 s between them in a forward gear. GM's Honda-built five-speed of 2006 flags jumps of more than 3 mph per 10 ms three times in 500 ms, after two trips; GM's own transmissions file such jumps under P0716 instead. Loose contacts and electrical interference are the usual causes; shifts become erratic and limp mode may follow at times.
c: Loose contact, corroded connector or chafing
Metal debris on the sensor or loose mounting
s: Occasional harsh or unexpected shifts
Warning lamp
Converter clutch applies and releases unevenly
Limp mode at times

P0719.d: Brake switch B is the brake signal to the transmission module or a second brake switch channel, used to release the converter clutch, adapt shift strategy on grades and cancel cruise control. Low and high describe the signal voltage, and what that means depends on polarity: GM's converter clutch brake switch is closed at rest (12 V), while Saab's Trionic 8 sees 12 V when braking. Detection is always a plausibility check against driving: the brake reads applied during accelerations or never applied during decelerations. P0719 means the signal stays low. For GM that reads as brake applied: 2006 transmission modules flag it after eight accelerations without the brake releasing, without MIL. Saab's Trionic 8 flags the brake light signal not changing during four decelerations from 40 to 3 km/h and disables cruise control. The opposite is P0724.
c: Brake light switch faulty or misadjusted
Wire to the module open (GM) or shorted to ground (Saab T8)
Connector at the pedal box corroded
s: Cruise control cannot be activated or switches off
Unusual shifting, converter clutch behaviour changed
No downshift on uphill grades (Subaru)
Brake lights stay off or on

P071A.d: A transmission mode switch selects an alternative shift schedule such as sport, winter or tow/haul; J2012 does not define which button is A or B. No manufacturer document available to us uses P071A–P071F: GM monitors its analog drive mode switch under its own codes (low below 21–29 % of 5 V, high from 94 %, 200 of 250 samples, two trips), which shows how such buttons are read as coded voltages. P071A is the general circuit fault of mode switch A: its state is invalid or implausible. The transmission then usually stays on its normal schedule. Low and high are P071B/P071C, switch B has P071D–P071F; the range sensor (PRNDL) is P0705 ff.
c: Mode switch A faulty (selector lever or console)
Wiring or connector in the console damaged (spilled drinks, chafing)
s: Mode A cannot be selected or stays active
Mode indicator missing or flashing
Transmission stays on the normal shift schedule

P071B.t: Transmission Mode Switch A Circuit Low
P071B.d: A transmission mode switch selects an alternative shift schedule such as sport, winter or tow/haul; J2012 does not define which button is A or B. No manufacturer document available to us uses P071A–P071F: GM monitors its analog drive mode switch under its own codes (low below 21–29 % of 5 V, high from 94 %, 200 of 250 samples, two trips), which shows how such buttons are read as coded voltages. P071B means the signal of mode switch A is below its lower limit: with analog, resistor-coded buttons a short to ground, with digital buttons switching to ground a button stuck pressed. The opposite is P071C.
c: Moisture or dirt in the button
s: Mode A cannot be selected or stays active
Mode indicator missing or flashing
Transmission stays on the normal shift schedule

P071C.t: Transmission Mode Switch A Circuit High
P071C.d: A transmission mode switch selects an alternative shift schedule such as sport, winter or tow/haul; J2012 does not define which button is A or B. No manufacturer document available to us uses P071A–P071F: GM monitors its analog drive mode switch under its own codes (low below 21–29 % of 5 V, high from 94 %, 200 of 250 samples, two trips), which shows how such buttons are read as coded voltages. P071C means the signal of mode switch A is above its upper limit – typically an open circuit pulled up inside the module, or a short to positive. The mode then cannot be selected. The opposite is P071B.
c: Wire or connector to the button open
s: Mode A cannot be selected or stays active
Mode indicator missing or flashing
Transmission stays on the normal shift schedule

P071D.d: A transmission mode switch selects an alternative shift schedule such as sport, winter or tow/haul; J2012 does not define which button is A or B. No manufacturer document available to us uses P071A–P071F: GM monitors its analog drive mode switch under its own codes (low below 21–29 % of 5 V, high from 94 %, 200 of 250 samples, two trips), which shows how such buttons are read as coded voltages. P071D is the general circuit fault of a second mode switch B, for example a separate winter and sport or tow/haul button. The second mode is then unavailable. Low and high are P071E/P071F; switch A has P071A–P071C.
c: Mode switch B faulty (selector lever or console)
Wiring or connector in the console damaged (spilled drinks, chafing)
s: Mode B cannot be selected or stays active
Mode indicator missing or flashing
Transmission stays on the normal shift schedule

P071E.t: Transmission Mode Switch B Circuit Low
P071E.d: A transmission mode switch selects an alternative shift schedule such as sport, winter or tow/haul; J2012 does not define which button is A or B. No manufacturer document available to us uses P071A–P071F: GM monitors its analog drive mode switch under its own codes (low below 21–29 % of 5 V, high from 94 %, 200 of 250 samples, two trips), which shows how such buttons are read as coded voltages. P071E means the signal of mode switch B is below its lower limit – a short to ground or a button stuck against ground. Mode B may then be unavailable or permanently active. The opposite is P071F.
c: Moisture or dirt in the button
s: Mode B cannot be selected or stays active
Mode indicator missing or flashing
Transmission stays on the normal shift schedule

P071F.t: Transmission Mode Switch B Circuit High
P071F.d: A transmission mode switch selects an alternative shift schedule such as sport, winter or tow/haul; J2012 does not define which button is A or B. No manufacturer document available to us uses P071A–P071F: GM monitors its analog drive mode switch under its own codes (low below 21–29 % of 5 V, high from 94 %, 200 of 250 samples, two trips), which shows how such buttons are read as coded voltages. P071F means the signal of mode switch B is above its upper limit – an open circuit or short to positive. Mode B then cannot be selected. The opposite is P071E.
c: Wire or connector to the button open
s: Mode B cannot be selected or stays active
Mode indicator missing or flashing
Transmission stays on the normal shift schedule

P0720.d: The output shaft speed sensor (Hall or inductive) reports the speed of the transmission output; it gives the gear ratio together with input speed and on many vehicles also the road speed for speedometer and cruise control. P0720 is the general circuit code. Ford also uses it for 'no signal': while engine and turbine speed show the vehicle moving, the sensor reports under 100–200 rpm for 5–30 s; ZF's 6HP26 in Ford vehicles flags an open or short after 0.6 s. Subaru-based systems (Saab 9-2X) flag an impossible 255 km/h or 0 km/h while driving and light the MIL after two trips, substituting the other sensor. GM does not use P0720 but P0722. Speedometer and cruise control may fail, often with a vehicle speed code as well.
c: Speed sensor faulty (Hall IC or coil open or shorted)
Connector or harness corroded, chafed or loose pins (with internal sensors also the pass-through connector)
Metal debris on the sensor magnet or damaged reluctor wheel
Transmission module or its sensor supply faulty
s: Speedometer drops out or jumps
Warning lamp, limp mode or fixed gear
Harsh shifts, cruise control not working

P0721.t: Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0721.d: The output shaft speed sensor (Hall or inductive) reports the speed of the transmission output; it gives the gear ratio together with input speed and on many vehicles also the road speed for speedometer and cruise control. P0721 means the output speed is present but implausible: too high (Ford 6R80 above 7450 rpm), not matching wheel or input speed in the engaged gear (ZF 6HP26 more than 200 or 250 rpm apart, Ford's F21 more than 15 % for 10 s), or jumping (Allison 1000: 500 rpm within 0.15 s). On GM's 10-speed with a direction-sensing sensor, P0721 means the reported direction of rotation does not fit – since 2025 after two trips, earlier after one. Wrong tyre sizes or a faulty wheel speed sensor can also falsify the comparison.
c: Output speed sensor faulty or dirty (metal debris)
Contact problems or interference in the sensor circuit
Wrong tyre size or axle ratio, faulty wheel speed sensor
Reluctor wheel damaged or sensor mounted wrongly
s: Speedometer jumps
Warning lamp
Wrong shifts, limp mode
ABS/ESP warning possible if wheel speed is affected

P0722.t: Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit No Signal
P0722.d: The output shaft speed sensor (Hall or inductive) reports the speed of the transmission output; it gives the gear ratio together with input speed and on many vehicles also the road speed for speedometer and cruise control. P0722 means the output speed signal is missing while the vehicle is driving. GM's 2025 modules flag under 60 rpm for 3.5–5 s with more than 50 Nm torque and check wheel speeds as well; a 2006 GM table flags no output pulse during 6000 input pulses; Ford under 100–200 rpm for 5–30 s; Saab's Aisin box from 4 km/h. GM rates it after one trip. The transmission goes into limp mode, and speedometer and cruise control may stop working. On GM's 10-speed, P0717 and P0722 together point to the shared sensor supply.
c: Speed sensor faulty (Hall IC or coil open or shorted)
Connector or harness corroded, chafed or loose pins (with internal sensors also the pass-through connector)
Metal debris on the sensor magnet or damaged reluctor wheel
Transmission module or its sensor supply faulty
s: Speedometer reads 0
Limp mode or fixed gear
Warning lamp (MIL, transmission)
Cruise control not working

P0723.t: Output Shaft Speed Sensor Circuit Intermittent
P0723.d: The output shaft speed sensor (Hall or inductive) reports the speed of the transmission output; it gives the gear ratio together with input speed and on many vehicles also the road speed for speedometer and cruise control. P0723 means the output speed drops or jumps briefly. GM's 2006 tables flag road speed falling below 61 rpm while driving; the 2019–2025 modules count sudden drops (for example 700 rpm) and fail after more than five, after one trip. In Ford vehicles the ZF 6HP26 flags a drop of more than 1000 rpm with the converter clutch locked, the CFT30 more than 6000 rpm per second. The speedometer needle twitches, shifts become erratic and limp mode may follow at times. Loose contacts are the usual cause.
c: Loose contact, corroded connector or chafing
Metal debris on the sensor or loose mounting
s: Speedometer needle twitches or drops briefly
Occasional wrong shifts or downshift jolts
Warning lamp
Limp mode at times

P0724.d: Brake switch B is the brake signal to the transmission module or a second brake switch channel, used to release the converter clutch, adapt shift strategy on grades and cancel cruise control. Low and high describe the signal voltage, and what that means depends on polarity: GM's converter clutch brake switch is closed at rest (12 V), while Saab's Trionic 8 sees 12 V when braking. Detection is always a plausibility check against driving: the brake reads applied during accelerations or never applied during decelerations. P0724 means the signal stays high. For GM that reads as brake never applied: 2006 transmission modules flag it after eight decelerations without a brake signal of at least 2 s, without MIL. Saab's Trionic 8 flags a brake light signal that reads on while accelerating from 3 to 40 km/h, four times, and disables cruise control. The opposite is P0719.
c: Brake light switch sticking or misadjusted
Signal wire shorted to positive (Saab T8) or switch permanently closed (GM)
Retrofitted trailer or LED lights feeding back
s: Cruise control cannot be activated or switches off
Unusual shifting, converter clutch behaviour changed
No downshift on uphill grades (Subaru)
Brake lights stay off or on

P0725.d: The transmission module needs engine speed for converter slip, shift quality and to check the turbine speed. Today it almost always arrives over CAN from the engine module with a validity flag; only GM's 2007 Allison 1000 tables show a separate engine speed sensor read by the transmission module. P0725 is the general fault of this input; with CAN it means the engine module marks its speed value as invalid. Saab's Aisin transmissions and a 2006 GM table set it after about 4 s, the GM table with immediate MIL. A Saab bulletin notes that behind P0725 there is always a crankshaft or camshaft sensor code in the engine module (P0016, P0335–P0339) – so read the engine module first. Limp mode follows; a completely missing CAN message is U0100.
c: Crankshaft or camshaft sensor fault in the engine module (speed invalid there)
CAN fault between engine and transmission module (wiring, termination, connector)
s: Transmission warning lamp, possibly check engine light
Torque converter clutch locked out
Harsh shifts or limp mode
Often an engine code (crankshaft sensor) as well

P0726.d: The transmission module needs engine speed for converter slip, shift quality and to check the turbine speed. Today it almost always arrives over CAN from the engine module with a validity flag; only GM's 2007 Allison 1000 tables show a separate engine speed sensor read by the transmission module. P0726 means the engine speed value is present but implausible. The Allison 1000, which reads its own sensor, flags a jump of 600 rpm within 0.15 s or noise of ±650 rpm, with the engine above 600 rpm and a gear engaged, after two trips. Saab's 9-3 of 2000, which receives the value over the bus, flags more than 7200 rpm for at least 10 s. The converter clutch is then locked out and shifts may be harsh. No signal at all is P0727.
c: Engine speed sensor at the transmission (Allison) dirty or faulty, loose contact
Wrong bus value from the engine module (crankshaft sensor problem)
s: Transmission warning lamp, possibly check engine light
Torque converter clutch locked out
Harsh shifts or limp mode
Often an engine code (crankshaft sensor) as well

P0727.t: Engine Speed Input Circuit No Signal
P0727.d: The transmission module needs engine speed for converter slip, shift quality and to check the turbine speed. Today it almost always arrives over CAN from the engine module with a validity flag; only GM's 2007 Allison 1000 tables show a separate engine speed sensor read by the transmission module. P0727 means the engine speed signal is missing although the transmission is turning. The Allison 1000 flags under 61 rpm for 4 s with turbine speed of 400 rpm or more, after two trips; Saab's 9-3 of 2000 input speed above 2000 rpm for more than 5 s without engine speed; a 2006 GM table the CAN engine speed failing to answer. The module then works without converter slip information, usually locks out the converter clutch and may enter limp mode.

CAN communication between engine and transmission module disturbed
Crankshaft sensor fault in the engine module
s: Transmission warning lamp, possibly check engine light
Torque converter clutch locked out
Harsh shifts or limp mode
Often an engine code (crankshaft sensor) as well

P0728.d: The transmission module needs engine speed for converter slip, shift quality and to check the turbine speed. Today it almost always arrives over CAN from the engine module with a validity flag; only GM's 2007 Allison 1000 tables show a separate engine speed sensor read by the transmission module. P0728 means the engine speed signal at the transmission module drops out briefly. No manufacturer document available to us uses this code: GM's Allison 1000 detects jumps and noise of this input under P0726/P0727, and Saab's bus-based systems use those codes, too. By analogy with P0718/P0723 dropouts are counted. A loose contact in the signal or CAN circuit or an intermittent crankshaft sensor fault in the engine module is the likely cause; shifts may be harsh at times.

Intermittent crankshaft sensor fault in the engine module
s: Occasional transmission warning lamp

P0729.d: The transmission module divides input (turbine) speed by output speed and compares the result with the ratio of the commanded gear; a deviation means slip – a clutch or brake not holding, too little pressure – or a wrong gear. Thresholds: Ford more than 30 rpm off for 1.8 s three times (diesel 2023: over 20 % for 12 s), GM's 2006 tables and the Allison 1000 converter slip of 200–230 rpm for 2.25 s after one trip, Saab's Aisin boxes over 20 % twelve times without MIL. P0729 concerns sixth gear. Saab's Aisin six-speed also checks whether the actual ratio matches fourth or fifth – the sixth gear clutch is not holding and the box drops into another gear. Ford stores it only if the fault does not fit a particular solenoid (otherwise P0751 ff). On GM manual transmissions (LT4) it checks the gear position sensor instead.

P0730.d: P0730 reports a wrong transmission ratio without assigning it to a gear. Two uses are documented. Older Aisin-type automatics (a 2006 GM table, Saab's 9-5 of 2002) set it when fourth or fifth gear shows the ratio of third – a shift solenoid (Saab: S3) is not switching; GM lights the MIL at once, Saab enters limp mode. GM's continuously variable transmissions of 2023 and 2025 use it when the pulleys do not reach the commanded variator ratio – the belt or chain slips or clamping pressure is too low – after one trip. Ford and newer GM step automatics use gear-specific or clutch valve codes instead. Check fluid level and condition first.

P0737.d: Some transmission modules pass an engine speed signal on to other devices such as a tachometer over a wire of their own. CARB requires output circuits to be checked. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0737–P0739 – engine speed is shared over CAN today; the description follows CARB and the engine module's own speed output (P0654), which sends, for example, two pulses per revolution. P0737 is the general circuit fault of this output; low and high are P0738/P0739. Not to be confused with the engine speed input at the transmission module (P0725 ff). A tachometer or dependent display then reads wrong or nothing, while driving is usually unaffected.

P0738.t: TCM Engine Speed Output Circuit Low
P0738.d: Some transmission modules pass an engine speed signal on to other devices such as a tachometer over a wire of their own. CARB requires output circuits to be checked. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0737–P0739 – engine speed is shared over CAN today; the description follows CARB and the engine module's own speed output (P0654), which sends, for example, two pulses per revolution. P0738 means this output is too low, typically shorted to ground, so it can no longer switch high. The opposite is P0739, the general fault P0737. A tachometer or dependent display then reads zero or jumps, while driving is usually unaffected.

P073D.d: P073D means neutral is commanded but not reached or not held. GM uses it on vehicles with electronic gear selection (shift-by-wire, e.g. Cadillac XT4): the selector or engine module compares commanded and actual range from the range sensor and flags it after 1.8–2 s in the selector module or 10 s in the engine module, after two trips. For Ford's 6F35 the supplier Sonnax describes a mechanical cause: a forward or direct clutch dragging in neutral, visible as turbine speed staying only 200–400 rpm below engine speed. The car may creep in N; range changes may be locked. The opposite, stuck in neutral, is P072A.

Shift-by-wire: range actuator or park module, range sensor or its calibration
Valve body (manual valve, missing check ball, sticking solenoid)
s: Vehicle creeps in N or engine is loaded when shifting to N
N selection not accepted, warning message
Harsh engagement N to D/R (6F35)
Check engine light after two trips (GM)

P073E.d: P073E means reverse is commanded but not reached. Two uses are documented. With electronic gear selection (shift-by-wire) GM compares the commanded range with the actual range reported by the transmission and flags it if reverse is not reached within 1.8–3 s in the selector or diesel engine module, or 10 s in petrol engine modules, after two trips; GM bulletins name a range actuator centred wrongly (LaCrosse, XT5) and software after an over-the-air update (2025 Equinox/Terrain). On dual-clutch transmissions (2020–23 Corvette, Maserati MC20) it means the reverse gear cannot be engaged. Stuck in reverse is P072B, slip in reverse P0736.

Range sensor reports the wrong actual range

P073F.d: 'Unable to engage' means the transmission does not reach the commanded gear – the opposite of 'stuck in gear', where a gear cannot be disengaged. Documented users are dual-clutch transmissions, whose shift forks are moved hydraulically and watched by travel sensors: GM's 8-speed in the 2020–23 Corvette, Maserati's MC20 and – for the odd gears only – Acura's RLX Sport Hybrid, whose 'odd gear monitor' is part of an emission recall with permanent codes. No manufacturer publishes thresholds. P073F means the first gear, on the odd sub-gearbox, cannot be engaged; a gear that will not disengage is P072C, slip in an engaged gear P0731. GM's bulletin first runs a learn procedure and cleans valves only if system pressure codes are present; Maserati checks system pressure (20–30 bar). If neither helps, the mechanics are at fault.

System pressure unstable or too low (pressure valve, pump, fluid level)

Transmission warning or check engine light, possibly limp mode with one sub-gearbox locked out

P0740.d: The torque converter clutch (lock-up) connects pump and turbine mechanically; a solenoid – on/off, pulse-width modulated or proportional – moves a control valve in the valve body. Slip is engine speed minus turbine speed. Manufacturers do not use P0740–P0744 uniformly: Ford uses P0740 for open, P0742 for short to ground and P0744 for short to power, and reports stuck on as P2758. P0740 concerns the control circuit of the converter clutch solenoid. Ford flags an open circuit when the driver feedback line disagrees with the command for 0.5–5 s, with MIL; a 2006 GM table checks 0/12 V with more than 43 of 50 failed counts after two trips – newer GM units use P2761/P2763/P2764. FCA's Ram 6.7 reads P0740 as converter slip out of range and moved it to two trips by software in 2013. The clutch is then switched off: higher engine speed when cruising, more fuel, hotter fluid.
c: Open or corroded harness or transmission pass-through connector
Internal transmission harness or mechatronic unit
Driver stage in the module faulty
FCA: actual converter slip (clutch wear, fluid) or software
s: Check engine light or transmission warning
No lock-up: engine speed about 100–300 rpm higher when cruising
Higher fuel consumption, hotter transmission fluid

P0741.t: Torque Converter Clutch Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
P0741.d: P0741 means the converter clutch does not lock although commanded – slip stays too high while the circuit is electrically fine. Thresholds: GM's T43 at least 130 rpm for 5 s twice, the 6T70 50 rpm for 5 s three times, Saab's Aisin AF40 over 100 rpm for 2 s, all after two trips; Ford over 100–200 rpm or a speed ratio below 0.93 over five lock-up events; Subaru engine speed more than 9/8 of target for 10.2 s. The module then locks out the clutch, sometimes the top gear, and uses a hot-mode shift pattern. Low or burnt fluid, a worn control valve in the valve body and a glazed converter clutch are the usual causes; Hyundai's 8-speed bulletin calls for a new converter.
c: Fluid level too low, old or burnt fluid
Converter clutch control valve worn or sticking, bore worn
Lock-up clutch in the converter worn or glazed
Leaking turbine shaft seals or pump
s: Check engine light or transmission warning
Higher engine speed when cruising, 'rubber band' feel
Higher consumption, rising fluid temperature
Possibly shudder when the clutch applies

P0742.t: Torque Converter Clutch Circuit Stuck On
P0742.d: P0742 means the converter clutch stays applied although commanded off – there is almost no slip. GM's T43 flags −50 to +13 rpm for 1.5 s six times and the 6T70 −20 to +30 rpm for 2.5 s, both after one trip; Allison and Saab's Aisin AF40 after two trips, the AF40 also when the engine stalls without slip. Typical is the engine stalling when stopping or when selecting D or R, plus jerking at low speed. Note the different uses: Ford's P0742 is a short to ground in the clutch solenoid circuit (stuck on is P2758 there), and Saab's 9-3 of 2003 uses it for a mechanical lock-up fault.

Solenoid stuck open (or short to ground with low-side control)
Lock-up clutch seized in the converter
Wrong fluid level or contaminated fluid
Engine or turbine speed signal implausible
s: Engine stalls when stopping or selecting D/R
Jerking or bucking at low speed
Check engine light or transmission warning

P0743.d: The torque converter clutch (lock-up) connects pump and turbine mechanically; a solenoid – on/off, pulse-width modulated or proportional – moves a control valve in the valve body. Slip is engine speed minus turbine speed. Manufacturers do not use P0740–P0744 uniformly: Ford uses P0740 for open, P0742 for short to ground and P0744 for short to power, and reports stuck on as P2758. P0743 is the collective electrical code for the converter clutch solenoid circuit – open, short to ground or to positive – detected by terminal voltage, driver feedback or current. Subaru flags it after 0.14 s and lights the MIL after two trips, Saab's 9-3 of 2003 above 1356 mA for 500 ms, Allison after 1.5 s; older Ford transmissions also use it. The clutch is switched off; Saab's Aisin boxes go into limp mode, Subaru does not.
c: Transmission harness or pass-through connector (corrosion, chafing, oil in connector)
Driver stage in the transmission or engine module
s: Check engine light or transmission warning

P0744.d: The torque converter clutch (lock-up) connects pump and turbine mechanically; a solenoid – on/off, pulse-width modulated or proportional – moves a control valve in the valve body. Slip is engine speed minus turbine speed. Manufacturers do not use P0740–P0744 uniformly: Ford uses P0740 for open, P0742 for short to ground and P0744 for short to power, and reports stuck on as P2758. In J2012 P0744 is an intermittent fault in the converter clutch circuit, but no manufacturer document available to us uses it that way: Ford flags a short to power via the driver feedback line after 0.5–5 s with MIL, and Nissan's CVT bulletins treat it as a functional converter fault checked at the valve body and belt. GM does not use it. Short interruptions make the clutch drop out and reapply, and lock-up may be disabled for the trip.

Ford: control wire shorted to positive
Nissan CVT: converter or valve body mechanical
