A shorted turn or a damaged phase lead to ground gives the same picture on other vehicles. A Hyundai patent describes two measured phases with the third calculated. P0A61 is the low side, P0A60 the general V code, P0A5F and P0A65 phases U and W.
c: Coolant inside the traction motor with loss of insulation (Hyundai Ioniq Hybrid)
Phase V lead or winding shorted to ground or to another phase
Inverter power stage fault in phase V
s: Check Engine and hybrid warning lights
Weak acceleration, air conditioning inoperative

P0A63.t: Drive Motor A Phase W Current
P0A63.d: P0A63 concerns the current in phase W of drive motor A. In the Toyota field reports filed with NHTSA it always appears beside P0A60: on a 2006 Highlander Hybrid with sub code 502, after P0A60 sub code 501, together with P0A78 and P0AEF, master warning on and no drive; the inverter assembly was replaced. These Toyota reports name only V and W, for the motor and for the generator (P0A72, P0A75), which fits a design where two phase currents are measured and U follows from the rule that all three add up to zero, as a Hyundai patent describes. Audi stores P0A6300 in module J841 of the 2021-23 Q5 e quattro when the welded high-voltage phase lead fails. P0A64/P0A65 are low and high, P0A5D and P0A60 phases U and V.
c: Internal fault in the inverter assembly (Toyota Highlander Hybrid)
High-voltage phase W cable or weld joint faulty (Audi Q5 e quattro)
s: Master warning or drive system fault message, MIL
Vehicle will not move or start

P0A64.t: Drive Motor A Phase W Current Low
P0A64.d: P0A64 means phase W of drive motor A shows too little current at the moment it should peak, typically an open W lead or a W sensor stuck at zero. GM completes its three-phase sequence with this code on the 2016 Chevrolet Volt motor control processor and in the 2018 hybrid tables: when the rotor sits within 30 degrees of the W phase axis, the inverter runs normal PWM above 50 V and the squared current command exceeds 900 A2 (2016) or 4,900 A2 (2018), a W peak below 9 A for 0.4 s of a 0.6 s window sets P0A64 as Type A, MIL on the first trip. Because the rotor passes each axis in turn, only the open phase is flagged. A Caterpillar patent uses a near-zero phase reading the same way. P0A65 is the high side, P0A5E and P0A61 cover U and V.
c: Open circuit in the phase W cable, connector or terminal
Phase W current sensor reads zero
Phase W switch of the inverter not conducting
Open winding of phase W in drive motor A
s: MIL and propulsion system warning
Uneven or reduced electric drive torque

P0A65.t: Drive Motor A Phase W Current High
P0A65.d: P0A65 reports overcurrent in phase W of drive motor A. It is the third phase code in Hyundai bulletin 17-01-057-1 for the 2017 Ioniq Hybrid, campaign T2J: with an internal coolant leak in the traction motor, P0A65, P0A5F or P0A62 set with Check Engine and hybrid lights, often joined by the isolation fault P0AA6. Reduced power when accelerating and a non-working air conditioner followed. The fix path is the scan tool isolation test, a coolant inspection of the motor and, if confirmed, a new traction motor. In general, a W-phase winding short or a pinched cable has the same effect. Hyundai inverters measure two phases and calculate the third, per a Hyundai patent. P0A64 is the low side, P0A63 the general W code, P0A5F and P0A62 phases U and V.
c: Internal coolant leak in the traction motor (Hyundai Ioniq Hybrid)
Phase W lead or winding shorted to ground or to another phase
Inverter power stage fault in phase W
s: Check Engine and hybrid warning lights
Reduced power when accelerating
Air conditioning inoperative (Hyundai Ioniq Hybrid)

P0A66.t: Drive Motor B Phase U Current
P0A66.d: P0A66 is the general fault code for the current in phase U of drive motor B, the second electric machine of a two-motor hybrid or an electric rear-axle motor. No manufacturer documents P0A66 publicly; GM, for instance, only uses the open-phase code P0A67 for this phase. The checks behind such a code are described in patents: a Caterpillar patent declares a phase sensor failed when the three phase currents no longer add up to roughly zero, and a Hyundai patent shows inverters that measure two phases and calculate the third. CARB requires circuit and rationality monitoring of electric drive components. P0A67 and P0A68 are the low and high variants, P0A69 and P0A6C cover phases V and W, P0A5D is the same code on motor A. Motor B is normally shut off.
c: Phase U current sensor of motor B failed (inside the inverter)
Phase U high-voltage cable or terminal between inverter and motor B faulty
Internal fault in the motor B power stage
Winding fault in phase U of drive motor B
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Motor B switched off, less power or no electric all-wheel drive

P0A67.t: Drive Motor B Phase U Current Low
P0A67.d: P0A67 reports that phase U of drive motor B carries too little current at the moment it should peak, which GM interprets as an open circuit in that phase. In the 2016 Chevrolet Volt tables for motor control processor B the test runs while the rotor is within 30 degrees of the U axis, the inverter is above 50 V in normal PWM and the squared current command exceeds 900 A²; a peak below 9 A for 0.4 s within a 0.6 s window sets a Type A fault with MIL on the first trip. GM's 2018 tables shared by the Volt and the CT6 plug-in keep the test but raise the command threshold to 4,900 A². P0A68 is the high side, P0A6A and P0A6D are phases V and W, P0A5E the motor A counterpart. Motor B is disabled.
c: Open circuit in the phase U cable, connector or terminal of motor B
Phase U switch of the motor B inverter not conducting
Phase U current sensor stuck at zero
Open winding of phase U in drive motor B
s: MIL on the first trip and propulsion system warning
Jerky or weak electric drive, reduced power

P0A68.t: Drive Motor B Phase U Current High
P0A68.d: P0A68 means the current measured in phase U of drive motor B rises above its plausible maximum, either because a real overcurrent flows, for example through damaged insulation, a winding short or a shorted power switch, or because the phase sensor reads too high. No manufacturer documents P0A68 publicly. For the motor A counterpart P0A5F, Hyundai links phase-high codes on the 2017 Ioniq Hybrid to coolant leaking inside the traction motor, together with an insulation fault. A Toyota patent explains why the inverter must react quickly: overcurrent loads the power switches and can destroy them, so the drive is cut. CARB requires monitoring of electric drive components. P0A67 is the low side, P0A6B and P0A6E cover V and W. Motor B is shut down.
c: Winding short or insulation breakdown in phase U of motor B (e.g. coolant ingress)
Shorted power switch in the phase U leg of the inverter
Phase U current sensor reading too high (gain or offset fault)
s: Hybrid warning and MIL, often with an insulation fault code
Sudden loss of drive from motor B

P0A69.t: Drive Motor B Phase V Current
P0A69.d: P0A69 flags a general fault in the current of phase V of drive motor B. No manufacturer documents P0A69 publicly. Phase V matters doubly on many inverters: a Hyundai patent describes designs that measure only two of the three phase currents and calculate the remaining one, so a faulty V reading also distorts the computed phase. A Caterpillar patent detects a failed sensor through the zero-sum rule of the three phase currents and can then estimate the missing value. CARB requires monitoring of electric drive components for circuit faults and plausibility. P0A6A and P0A6B are the low and high variants, P0A66 and P0A6C phases U and W, P0A60 the motor A equivalent. The driver sees a hybrid warning and motor B is taken out of service.
c: Phase V current sensor of motor B failed
Fault on the motor B inverter board or power stage
Phase V high-voltage cable or terminal loose or damaged
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Reduced power, motor B no longer contributes

P0A6A.t: Drive Motor B Phase V Current Low
P0A6A.d: P0A6A is GM's open-circuit test for phase V of drive motor B. The controller checks each phase on its own as the rotor turns; for phase V it looks at the window of 30 degrees either side of the V axis, where the current should be largest. With the inverter above 50 V in normal PWM and a squared current command above 900 A² (2016 Volt) or 4,900 A² (2018 and 2019 tables), a peak below 9 A for 0.4 s out of 0.6 s is a Type A failure with MIL after one trip. The 2016 Volt table describes this motor B code with the words drive motor A, an evident copy slip. A missing V current points to a broken lead, a dead switch or a sensor stuck at zero. P0A6B is the high side, P0A67 and P0A6D phases U and W, P0A61 the motor A code.
c: Phase V lead, connector or bolted terminal of motor B open
Phase V switch of the motor B inverter not switching
Phase V current sensor output stuck at zero
Open phase V winding in motor B
s: MIL and propulsion system warning after the first trip
Vibration or uneven torque from motor B before shutdown

P0A6B.t: Drive Motor B Phase V Current High
P0A6B.d: P0A6B is stored when phase V of drive motor B reports more current than the operating state allows. No manufacturer documents P0A6B publicly. Two causes must be told apart: a real overcurrent from a shorted switch, a winding fault or an insulation breakdown, and a sensor that reads high because its gain or zero offset has drifted. Patents show how inverters separate them: Toyota compares a control sensor against a monitoring sensor and the commanded current, Caterpillar checks that the three phase currents still sum to about zero. CARB requires plausibility monitoring of electric drive components. P0A6A is the low side, P0A68 and P0A6E the U and W phases, P0A62 the motor A counterpart. The inverter shuts motor B down to protect itself.
c: Phase V current sensor gain or offset drifted high
Shorted power switch in the phase V leg
Winding or insulation fault in phase V of motor B
s: Hybrid warning and MIL
Motor B cut out, reduced acceleration

P0A6C.t: Drive Motor B Phase W Current
P0A6C.d: P0A6C covers a general fault in the phase W current of drive motor B. No manufacturer documents P0A6C publicly. Where motor B sits on a separate axle, its three high-voltage phase leads are long and exposed, so cable and terminal faults are a realistic cause; for the motor A phase codes P0A5D, P0A60 and P0A63, Audi blames welding variances in the high-voltage wiring of the 2021-23 Q5 e quattro. On the sensing side, a Caterpillar patent recognises a dead phase sensor by its near-zero reading combined with a violated zero-sum of the three currents. CARB requires circuit and plausibility checks of drive components. P0A6D and P0A6E are the low and high cases, P0A66 and P0A69 phases U and V, P0A63 motor A. Motor B is switched off.
c: Phase W high-voltage lead or terminal to motor B damaged or loose
Internal fault of the motor B inverter
s: Hybrid warning lamp and MIL
Loss of electric drive on the axle driven by motor B

P0A6D.t: Drive Motor B Phase W Current Low
P0A6D.d: P0A6D completes GM's set of open-phase tests for drive motor B with phase W. Because each phase is only judged while the rotor sits within 30 degrees of its own axis, the code points to W alone rather than to the motor as a whole. GM's tables for the 2016 Volt require a running drive, more than 50 V on the inverter in normal PWM and a squared current command above 900 A²; the 2018 tables for Volt and CT6 use 4,900 A². If the W peak stays under 9 A for 0.4 s within 0.6 s, the Type A fault turns on the MIL after one trip. Typical findings are an interrupted W lead or terminal, a non-conducting switch or a sensor reading zero. P0A6E is the high side, P0A67 and P0A6A phases U and V, P0A64 the motor A test.
c: Phase W lead or terminal of motor B interrupted
Phase W switch of the inverter not conducting
Phase W current sensor stuck at zero
Open phase W winding in motor B
s: MIL on the first trip with propulsion warning
Rough or reduced electric drive

P0A6E.t: Drive Motor B Phase W Current High
P0A6E.d: P0A6E indicates excessive current, measured or real, in phase W of drive motor B. No manufacturer documents P0A6E publicly. On the motor A side, Hyundai's 2017 Ioniq Hybrid campaign shows the typical real-world pattern: coolant leaking inside the traction motor set phase-high codes for U, V and W alongside a high-voltage isolation fault, with motor replacement once the leak is confirmed. A Toyota patent describes the protective logic: if current runs far above the command, the inverter is at risk, so the system stops switching and opens the relays. CARB requires monitoring of electric drive components. P0A6D is the low side, P0A68 and P0A6B the U and V phases, P0A65 motor A. Drive from motor B is lost until repair.
c: Insulation breakdown or winding short in phase W (moisture, coolant)
Shorted switch in the phase W leg of the inverter
Phase W current sensor reading too high
s: MIL and hybrid warning, possibly with an isolation fault
Motor B no longer drives; possible air conditioning shutdown

P0A6F.d: P0A6F is the general fault code for the phase U current of the hybrid generator, the motor-generator that is mainly driven by the engine, starts it and charges the battery, such as Toyota's MG1 or Hyundai's hybrid starter-generator. No manufacturer documents P0A6F publicly; Toyota's published field reports show generator codes for phases V and W only. A Hyundai patent describes an inverter that senses two or three generator phase currents through its own sensors, separate from those of the drive motor. CARB requires monitoring of electric drive components. P0A70 and P0A71 are the low and high variants, P0A72 and P0A75 phases V and W, P0A59 the generator current sensor circuit. Without the generator, engine start and charging may fail.
c: Generator phase U current sensor failed
Fault in the generator section of the inverter assembly
Generator phase U cable or terminal faulty
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Engine cannot be started electrically or battery is no longer charged

P0A70.d: P0A70 means phase U of the hybrid generator carries or reports too little current while the generator is loaded, typical of an open phase or a sensor stuck near zero. No manufacturer documents P0A70 publicly. The closest published test is GM's open-phase check for the drive motors (P0A67 and siblings), which compares the peak current near each phase axis against a 9 A threshold; GM publishes no such test for the generator. A Caterpillar patent identifies a failed phase sensor by a reading close to zero while the currents no longer sum to zero. CARB requires circuit monitoring of electric drive components. P0A71 is the high side, P0A73 and P0A76 phases V and W, P0A6F the general code. Engine start and charging can be affected.
c: Open circuit in the generator phase U lead or terminal
Generator phase U current sensor stuck near zero
Phase U switch in the generator inverter not conducting
s: Hybrid warning and MIL
Engine runs rough at start or battery charge level keeps dropping

P0A71.d: P0A71 is set when the current in phase U of the hybrid generator exceeds its permitted level. No manufacturer documents P0A71 publicly. The Toyota patent on current sensor monitoring applies directly, since its machine also runs as an engine-driven generator and starts the engine: a sensor stuck too low makes the controller push the real current far above command, and an overcurrent through the inverter can damage its switches, so the relays are opened. A real overcurrent can also come from a winding or insulation short in the generator or a shorted switch. CARB requires monitoring of electric drive components. P0A70 is the low side, P0A74 and P0A77 phases V and W, P0A6F the general code. The hybrid system usually shuts down.
c: Shorted power switch in the generator phase U leg
Winding or insulation short in generator phase U
Faulty phase U current sensor or its evaluation in the inverter
s: Master warning or hybrid warning with MIL
Hybrid system shuts down; vehicle may not move or restart

P0A72.d: P0A72 reports a fault in the phase V current of the hybrid generator. Toyota uses it: a field report filed with NHTSA covers a 2006 Highlander Hybrid with the MIL on and P0A72 stored together with P0A75 for generator phase W, P0A60 and P0A63 for drive motor A, and inverter performance codes including P0A78; after checking connector fit and the resistance of the three-phase cables, the inverter/converter assembly was replaced. The pairing of V and W codes fits inverters that measure two phases and calculate the third, as a Hyundai patent describes for its starter-generator. P0A73 and P0A74 are the low and high cases, P0A6F and P0A75 phases U and W. Expect a hybrid warning and possibly no drive.
c: Internal fault in the inverter/converter assembly (Toyota Highlander Hybrid)
Generator phase V current sensor failed
Poor pin fit or damaged three-phase cable to the generator
s: MIL and master warning, several hybrid codes at once
Vehicle may not move or enter ready mode

P0A73.d: P0A73 indicates that phase V of the hybrid generator delivers or reports too little current under load. No manufacturer documents P0A73 publicly. On inverters that measure only phases V and W, a low V reading has a knock-on effect: the calculated U current is wrong as well, so the generator torque control loses accuracy. A Caterpillar patent shows the logic for three-sensor systems, where a near-zero reading plus a violated zero-sum identifies the failed sensor; a Toyota patent compares a control sensor with a monitoring sensor and the current command. CARB requires circuit monitoring of electric drive components. P0A74 is the high side, P0A70 and P0A76 phases U and W, P0A72 the general code. Charging and engine start can suffer.
c: Generator phase V current sensor reading near zero
Generator phase V lead or terminal open
Phase V switch in the generator inverter not conducting
s: Hybrid warning and MIL
Engine runs more often, battery charge does not recover

P0A74.d: P0A74 appears when phase V of the hybrid generator shows more current than its limit allows. No manufacturer documents P0A74 publicly. A drifting sensor zero point is one candidate: a Hyundai patent covering both the traction motor and the starter-generator corrects phase sensor offsets and flags a fault when the correction fails. Real overcurrent is the other, for example from a winding or insulation short or a power switch that no longer turns off; a Toyota patent explains why the inverter then shuts down quickly. CARB requires monitoring of electric drive components. P0A73 is the low side, P0A71 and P0A77 phases U and W, P0A72 the general code. The hybrid system typically stops, and in power-split hybrids the car may lose drive entirely.
c: Phase V sensor offset drifted or offset correction failed
Power switch in the generator phase V leg not turning off
Winding or insulation short in generator phase V
s: Master warning or hybrid warning with MIL
Hybrid system shutdown, possibly no propulsion

P0A75.d: P0A75 stands for a fault in the phase W current of the hybrid generator. Toyota documents it in practice: in a field report from an NHTSA investigation of 2006 Highlander Hybrid inverters, P0A75 appeared next to P0A72, the drive motor phase codes P0A60 and P0A63 and inverter performance codes, and the root cause was inside the inverter/converter, which was replaced. A sudden cluster like this points more to the shared inverter than to the generator winding. A Toyota patent shows how a control and a monitoring current sensor are cross-checked so that a defective sensor is caught before it causes overcurrent. P0A76 and P0A77 are the low and high variants, P0A6F and P0A72 phases U and V. Ready mode or drive may be lost.
c: Internal fault in the inverter/converter assembly (Toyota Highlander Hybrid)
Generator phase W current sensor failed
Generator phase W cable or connector faulty
s: MIL and master warning, usually with other hybrid codes
Vehicle will not become ready or will not move

P0A76.d: P0A76 signals that phase W of the hybrid generator conducts or reports too little current while the generator should be producing or absorbing torque. No manufacturer documents P0A76 publicly. Physically, the generator phase leads run from the inverter into the transaxle or engine bay, so a loose bolted terminal, a cracked lead or a corroded connector can open the W path; electrically, a sensor fixed near zero gives the same reading. A Caterpillar patent separates both: a sensor fault is assumed when one phase reads about zero while the sum of the three no longer balances. A Hyundai patent shows separate generator phase sensors in the inverter. CARB requires circuit monitoring. P0A77 is the high side, P0A70 and P0A73 phases U and V.
c: Loose terminal, cracked lead or corroded connector in generator phase W
Generator phase W current sensor stuck near zero
Open phase W winding in the generator
s: Hybrid warning and MIL
Engine start harsh or delayed, charging reduced

P0A77.d: P0A77 is the excess-current code for phase W of the hybrid generator. No manufacturer documents P0A77 publicly. When the engine drives the generator hard, for instance while charging or during engine start, a short between turns, a breakdown to the housing or a switch that fails closed can let the W current climb beyond its limit; a sensor with too much gain produces a similar picture without real overcurrent. A Toyota patent, whose machine also works as generator, describes stopping the inverter and opening the relays when current runs away; a Caterpillar patent checks the zero-sum of the phase currents to unmask a bad sensor. CARB requires monitoring of electric drive components. P0A76 is the low side, P0A71 and P0A74 phases U and V.
c: Turn-to-turn short or insulation breakdown in generator phase W
Power switch in the generator phase W leg failed closed
Generator phase W current sensor with excessive gain
s: Master warning or hybrid warning with MIL
Hybrid system shuts down during charging or engine start

P0A78.d: P0A78 means the inverter stage feeding drive motor A has reported a power-switch fault. GM explains the check in its hybrid OBD tables: the IGBT module watches each phase for desaturation, a sign of a short between the upper and lower switch; if that status persists for about 2 ms the code sets as Type A, MIL on the first trip. Stellantis replaced the power inverter module on 2021 Jeep Wrangler 4xe with P0A78 and P0A79, which ran on engine power only, and refreshed hybrid control software on the 2017 Pacifica Hybrid. Land Rover logs P0A78 in the inverter converter of 2024-25 Range Rover models and asks not to clear it before diagnosis. P0A79 is motor B, P0A7A the generator inverter, P0A3C overheating of inverter A. Expect a warning and loss of electric drive.
c: IGBT desaturation or short in the inverter power stage
Power inverter module defective (replaced on Jeep Wrangler 4xe)
Shorted winding or phase cable of drive motor A
s: MIL and hybrid or high-voltage warning
No electric drive, engine-only operation
Stop safely warning on some models

P0A79.d: P0A79 is the drive motor B counterpart of P0A78: the inverter stage for motor B has detected a power-switch fault. In GM hybrid OBD tables the IGBT module reports a desaturation status on a high or low side switch of any phase; persisting for about 2 ms it sets P0A79 as Type A with MIL on the first trip. Stellantis documents P0A79 several times: on the 2021 Jeep Wrangler 4xe together with P0A78 and an engine-only limp mode, fixed by a new power inverter module; on the 2017 Pacifica Hybrid with improved hybrid control software, and with a loose high-voltage cable at the inverter terminal that also caused loss of propulsion. P0A78 is motor A, P0A7A the generator inverter, P0A3D overheating of inverter B. The driver loses electric drive.
c: IGBT desaturation or short in the motor B power stage
Loose high-voltage cable at the inverter terminal (Pacifica Hybrid)
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
No electric drive, engine-only operation
Loss of propulsion in severe cases

P0A7A.d: P0A7A reports that the inverter stage driving the generator has signalled a fault, for example overcurrent or a failed power switch. Toyota uses the code across its hybrids and splits it with information codes. Bulletin T-SB-0142-16 covers 2012-2016 Avalon, Camry and RAV4 Hybrid with MIL on and P0A7A plus information code 122, a generator inverter fail signal caused by overcurrent; the repair replaces inverter and transaxle. A Toyota field report filed with NHTSA describes a 2006 Highlander Hybrid with P0A7A sub code 325, master warning, MIL and Check Hybrid System, traced to a fault inside the inverter assembly. P0A78 and P0A79 are the drive motor inverters, P0A3E generator inverter overheating, P0A92 generator performance.
c: Internal generator inverter fault with overcurrent (Toyota information code 122)
Fault in the generator inside the transaxle
Insufficient inverter cooling stressing the power stage
s: MIL, master warning and Check Hybrid System message
Reduced power or vehicle will not enter ready mode

P0A7B.t: Battery Energy Control Module Requested MIL Illumination
P0A7B.d: P0A7B is a request code: the battery energy control module, which has found an emissions-relevant fault of its own, asks the engine control module to switch on the MIL, and the engine controller stores P0A7B. The actual cause sits in a separate code in the battery module. GM documents this on the 2024-25 Corvette E-Ray: P0A7B in the K20 engine controller appears together with P0E3C in the battery module, caused by air trapped around the battery coolant pump after a repair; purging the air is the fix. Subaru reports P0A7B in the engine controller of the 2014 XV Crosstrek Hybrid alongside battery and drive motor codes after a frozen power relay. Diagnose the battery module codes first. P0AC4 is the matching request from the hybrid control module.
c: Emissions-relevant fault stored in the battery energy control module
Air trapped at the battery coolant pump (Corvette E-Ray, with P0E3C)
Frozen power supply relay of the drive motor control module (Subaru Crosstrek Hybrid)
s: MIL on
Additional codes stored in the battery control module

P0A7C.d: P0A7C reports that the electronics controlling the hybrid motors, mainly the inverter, have run hotter than allowed. Ford uses the code on its hybrids and stores it in the PCM. A Ford bulletin for 2010-11 Fusion and Milan Hybrid and 2011 MKZ Hybrid built up to 9 September 2010 describes a wrench light with no drivability concern and P0A7C, cured by a PCM software update. Ford warranty statistics supplied to NHTSA list P0A7C as a recurring code on 2010-12 Escape, Tribute and Mariner Hybrid. Common physical causes are a failed coolant pump of the motor electronics cooling loop, low coolant, air in the loop or a blocked radiator. CARB requires monitoring of inverter thermal management. P0A3C and P0A3D cover the individual inverters. Power is reduced to protect the electronics.
c: Coolant pump of the motor electronics cooling loop failed
Low coolant or air in the electronics cooling loop
PCM calibration triggering the code without real overheating (Ford Fusion Hybrid)
Blocked electronics radiator or faulty cooling fan
s: Wrench or hybrid warning light
Reduced power, especially under high load or heat

P0A7D.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack State of Charge Low
P0A7D.d: The battery controller watches whether the traction or mild-hybrid pack stays inside its usable state-of-charge (SOC) window. GM sets P0A7D (Type B, two trips) when SOC stays below a program threshold (30 % or 10.5 %) for more than half of a drive cycle longer than 50 km, after allowing generator time to recover. Ford reports it on 2020 Escape/Explorer Hybrid after a deep discharge from long standing or crank/no-start, and Audi on 48 V systems whose protection relays open at low SOC. Unlike P0A7F/P0A80 the pack itself is not judged worn; it is simply too empty. Expect no EV mode, weak assist or, in severe cases, a no-start until the pack is recharged.
c: Pack discharged by long standing time or repeated crank/no-start attempts
Generator, DC/DC or charging path not replenishing the pack
48 V battery in low-voltage protection state (relays open)
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning
No electric driving or reduced motor assist
Engine runs longer to recharge the pack
Vehicle may not start or reach ready mode

P0A7E.d: The pack controller compares the hottest module temperature with a protection limit. GM sets P0A7E, mostly as Type A (MIL after one trip), when the maximum module temperature exceeds a program limit between about 61 and 73.5 °C, unless a temperature sensor fault is active. Subaru documents it on the 2014–16 Crosstrek Hybrid, where too strict logic for heat after shutdown cut assist and auto start-stop; GM links it on eAssist cars to a cooling fan that stops at low system voltage; Porsche saw it with implausible sensor signals on the 911 GTS T-Hybrid. Sensor circuit faults have their own codes (P0A9B–P0A9E). The car limits charge and discharge power to protect the cells.
c: Battery cooling fan inoperative or intake/filter clogged
Battery controller software logic (update released by Subaru, Porsche)
Low 12 V system voltage stopping the cooling fan
Aged cells with high internal resistance heating up
s: Hybrid system warning and check engine light
Reduced electric assist and regeneration
Auto start-stop no longer works
In rare cases warning with no-start

P0A7F.d: This is the state-of-health monitor that CARB requires for hybrid storage systems. GM compares the calculated pack power capability with an end-of-life table at mid state of charge and sets P0A7F as Type B (two trips) when it falls short. Honda reports it as battery module deterioration on the 2009 Civic Hybrid and as serious capacity deterioration on the 2014 Accord Plug-In; Mercedes uses it when the 48 V module reaches its health limit, partly fixed by software. Toyota bulletins for Prius, Prius v and Camry Hybrid name a clogged battery cooling fan as a trigger. P0A80 is the harder replace-pack verdict. Drivers notice weaker assist, more engine running and higher fuel use.
c: Pack capacity or power capability lost through ageing
Dust or debris in the battery cooling fan or filter overheating cells
Battery controller software misjudging health (Honda, Mercedes)
Individual weak modules pulling the pack down
s: Check engine or hybrid/IMA warning light
Weak acceleration assist, especially from a stop
Engine runs more often, higher fuel consumption
Shorter electric range on plug-in models

P0A80.d: The battery controller has concluded that the pack is at end of life. In GM tables this is a resistance test: the maximum cell or pack resistance, measured from current and voltage swings, exceeds a temperature-dependent end-of-life threshold, and the code sets as Type A after one trip. Toyota bulletins for Prius (2004–09, 2013–15), Prius v and Camry Hybrid report P0A80, often together with P0A7F, caused by dust in the battery cooling fan; cleaning the fan comes first. Honda recalled the 2018 Accord Hybrid because software wrongly set this code as a permanent fault after pack replacement. Compared with P0A7F it is the final verdict; assist and economy drop and the MIL stays on.
c: Cell or module resistance above end-of-life limit
Clogged battery cooling fan or intake filter (Toyota)
Controller software misreading a replaced pack (Honda Accord Hybrid 2018)
s: Check engine and hybrid system warning on
Noticeably weaker electric assist
Higher fuel consumption, engine runs more

P0A81.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Control Circuit/Open
P0A81.d: The controller watches the output that drives battery cooling fan 1 for an open circuit. In the 2016 GM table the fan is commanded at low duty (under 10 %) and the circuit voltage sits between about 1.6 and 5.85 V instead of being pulled low; 16 failures in 20 samples set it as Type B. An older GM program used it as a general fan unit fault judged by a monitor voltage. Ford found P0A81, often with P0A96 for fan 2, in the battery control module of 2005–12 Escape and Mariner Hybrids and replaced both fans; drivers usually noticed nothing. Low and high faults have their own codes (P0A84, P0A85). Without airflow the pack heats up and power may be limited.
c: Fan motor or its internal electronics open
Loose or corroded fan connector, broken control wire
Faulty output stage in the battery control module
s: Check engine or hybrid warning, often no other complaint
Battery cooling fan does not run when commanded
Reduced hybrid power in hot conditions

P0A82.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Performance/Stuck Off
P0A82.d: This code covers a fan 1 that is electrically intact but does not deliver the requested cooling, up to standing still. No manufacturer publishes code-exact criteria; CARB requires a functional check of battery cooling where feasible. Typical methods: GM compares commanded and fed-back fan speed (filed under its own sense code P0BC8), Toyota flags a fan whose feedback-corrected duty deviates too far from the expected value, and Honda compares expected and measured battery temperature rise. Causes are mostly mechanical: dust on the blades, a clogged intake filter, worn bearings. Circuit faults use P0A81/P0A84/P0A85; the stuck-on case is P0A83. The pack runs hotter and power may be limited.
c: Dust or debris on fan blades or in the duct
Clogged or covered battery air intake or filter
Worn or seized fan motor bearings
s: Hybrid warning or check engine light
Fan audibly weak or silent under load
Reduced electric assist in warm weather

P0A83.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Stuck On
P0A83.d: P0A83 means battery cooling fan 1 keeps turning although the controller has switched it off. No manufacturer publicly documents this exact code. CARB asks for fan outputs to be checked for proper response to commands. GM shows the method under its sense code P0BC8: with the fan off for more than 20 s, a reported speed above 120 rpm counts as a fault. Likely causes are a control wire shorted to supply, a welded fan relay (GM files that as P0BC1) or a fan controller that ignores the command. The pack stays cool, but the fan drains the 12 V battery when parked and stays loud. Do not confuse it with P0A82 (fan too weak or off) or the circuit codes P0A81/P0A84/P0A85.
c: Fan control wire shorted to supply voltage
Welded fan relay keeps power applied
Fan's internal speed controller ignores off command
Battery control module output stuck active
s: Battery fan heard running with the vehicle off or idle
Discharged 12 V battery after parking
Hybrid or check engine warning

P0A84.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Control Circuit Low
P0A84.d: The controller detects a short to ground on the control output of battery cooling fan 1. GM tests it while the fan is commanded at low duty: a circuit voltage below about 0.26 V counts as a failure, and 16 fails in 20 samples at 250 ms set a Type B code (MIL after two trips). Another GM hybrid program detects it through the output stage status flag (20 of 25 samples). Mitsubishi lists P0A84 in the BMU and PHEV ECU of the 2018–20 Outlander PHEV among codes caused by a frozen battery heater relay, so meaning can differ by maker. Open and high faults are P0A81 and P0A85. With the output pulled low the fan may not respond, the pack warms up and power can be reduced.
c: Fan control wire chafed and shorted to ground
Internal short in the fan's control input
Moisture or corrosion in the fan connector
Defective output stage in the controller
s: Check engine or hybrid warning after two trips
Battery cooling fan does not follow commands
Reduced hybrid power when the pack gets warm

P0A85.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Control Circuit High
P0A85.d: The controller detects a short to voltage on the control output of battery cooling fan 1. GM runs the test while the fan is commanded between 11 % and 100 % duty: a circuit voltage above 9 V counts as a failure, and 16 fails in 20 samples set a Type B code with MIL after two trips. GM tables from 2013, 2016, 2018 and 2019 hybrid programs carry it, partly via the output stage status flag. Depending on the circuit, the fan may run constantly at full speed or not respond. The low and open counterparts are P0A84 and P0A81; a fan that keeps running without a circuit fault is P0A83.
c: Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Fan control input internally open or shorted to its supply
Corroded connector creating leakage to supply
s: Check engine or hybrid warning after two trips
Battery fan runs constantly or not at all
Possible 12 V battery drain when parked

P0A86.t: 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor A Circuit
P0A86.d: The 14 volt power module is the DC/DC converter that feeds the 12 V network of a hybrid or electric vehicle from the high-voltage battery; GM calls it the Accessory Power Module (APM). Current sensor A measures the current flowing through this converter. P0A86 is the general circuit code for that sensor, used when the controller recognises a fault in the sensor circuit without classifying it as low, high, implausible or intermittent (P0A87 to P0A8A). No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's published tables for the same APM input sensor use only the low/high codes P0A88 and P0A89. With an untrustworthy current reading the hybrid controller may limit or switch off the converter, so the 12 V battery can run down over time.
c: Current sensor inside the 14 V power module faulty (usually not replaceable separately)
Damaged wiring or corroded connector between module and hybrid controller
Software fault in the module or hybrid controller
s: Hybrid or charging system warning lamp on
12 V battery discharges, low-voltage warnings
Possibly no other noticeable change in driving

P0A87.t: 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0A87.d: This code means the current sensor of the 14 V power module (DC/DC converter, GM: APM) delivers values that are electrically valid but implausible. GM's 2016 eAssist tables (hybrid control processor HPC1) describe a stuck-in-range test: once per key cycle, while the high-voltage contactors are open and then move to precharge, the converter should be off, so the averaged input current must be near zero. If the average is 0.50 A or more, P0A87 sets as a Type B code, so the MIL comes on after two failed trips. The test is skipped while P0A88 or P0A89 is active. Unlike those circuit low/high codes, the wiring is usually intact here; a sensor with offset drift is the typical finding.
c: Current sensor zero-point drift inside the power module
Converter actually conducting current when it should be off (internal module fault)
Ground or reference fault distorting the sensor signal
s: MIL on after two drive cycles
Usually no driveability change
Possible reduced 12 V charging if the converter is limited

P0A88.t: 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor A Circuit Low
P0A88.d: P0A88 reports that the current sensor of the 14 V power module (DC/DC converter feeding the 12 V system) reads too low while the converter should be delivering power. GM documents it for the Accessory Power Module: in the 2013 eAssist tables the input current must stay below 0.5 A for 1.5 s within a 2 s window while calculated output power is 0.25 to 1.5 kW; the 2016 tables use 0.50 A or less in 640 of 800 samples, enabled only when the APM is on, the hood is closed and the 12 V target is reached. Both rate it Type B, two trips to MIL. A short to ground, an open signal line or a dead sensor are typical; P0A89 is the opposite high fault, P0A87 the plausibility check.
c: Sensor signal shorted to ground or open
Current sensor in the power module failed
s: MIL and hybrid/charging warning
12 V battery not charged properly
Start/stop function may be disabled

P0A89.t: 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor A Circuit High
P0A89.d: P0A89 is set when the current sensor of the 14 V power module reports more current than the converter can physically carry. GM's eAssist tables show how: in 2013 the APM input current reading had to exceed 22.5 A for 1.5 s while calculated output power was 1.5 kW or less; in 2016 the limit is 45.25 A or more in 200 of 250 samples (about 5 s) with the APM commanded on and 9 to 32 V supply. Both versions classify it Type B, so the MIL lights after the second failing trip. Typical causes are a signal short to voltage or an internal sensor fault. P0A88 is the low counterpart, P0A87 the in-range plausibility test, and the APM output sensor has its own codes (P0C9E/P0C9F).
c: Sensor signal shorted to supply voltage
Current sensor in the power module failed
Open sensor ground pulling the signal high
s: MIL and hybrid/charging warning
Converter output limited, 12 V voltage drops
Start/stop function may be disabled

P0A8A.t: 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
P0A8A.d: P0A8A covers short dropouts or jumps in the signal of the current sensor in the 14 V power module, the DC/DC converter that charges the 12 V battery in hybrids and EVs. The signal is valid most of the time but briefly leaves its range or changes faster than physically possible. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's APM tables only show the hard limits for the same sensor (P0A88 below 0.5 A, P0A89 above 22.5 A or 45.25 A), which indicates what the intermittent check guards against. Loose terminals, chafed wiring near the module and vibration are the usual suspects. Compared with P0A88/P0A89 the fault often clears and returns, which makes freeze-frame data valuable.
c: Loose or fretted terminals at the module connector
Chafed wiring with intermittent short or open
Intermittent internal fault of the current sensor
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Occasional 12 V voltage fluctuations

P0A8B.d: The 14 V power module (DC/DC converter) regulates the voltage of the 12 V network in hybrid and electric vehicles. P0A8B is the general code for a fault in the voltage this module produces or senses, without the more specific labels unstable, low, high or performance (P0A8C to P0A8F). No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's 2013 eAssist tables show how the sibling codes are used for the same function: the APM low-voltage sensor is checked against fixed limits and against the separately measured run/crank voltage. A fault here means the 12 V system may no longer be supplied reliably, so the 12 V battery and consumers should be checked before the module is condemned.
c: Internal fault of the DC/DC converter
Loose or corroded 12 V output cable or ground connection
Weak 12 V battery distorting the system voltage
s: Charging or hybrid system warning
Electrical consumers behave erratically
12 V battery discharged

P0A8C.t: 14 Volt Power Module System Voltage Unstable
P0A8C.d: P0A8C indicates that the output voltage of the 14 V power module, the DC/DC converter supplying the 12 V network of a hybrid or EV, fluctuates beyond what the control strategy accepts instead of settling at its target. Possible reasons include a poor 12 V connection, an aged 12 V battery that no longer buffers the network, or a regulation problem inside the converter. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's APM tables only cover low, high and performance faults of the same voltage (P0A8D, P0A8E, P0A8F). For the driver, flickering lights, resets of electronic units or start/stop being disabled are typical. Unlike P0A8D/P0A8E the average voltage may still be normal.
c: Loose or corroded 12 V battery terminal or ground strap
Aged 12 V battery no longer buffering the network
Unstable regulation inside the DC/DC converter
s: Flickering lights or display resets
Charging or hybrid system warning
Start/stop disabled

P0A8D.t: 14 Volt Power Module System Voltage Low
P0A8D.d: P0A8D reports too low a voltage at the 14 V power module (DC/DC converter feeding the 12 V network). GM uses it in its 2013 eAssist tables as the circuit-low check of the APM low-voltage sensor: if that sensor reads below 1 V for 1.5 s within a 2 s window while ignition voltage is 9 to 32 V, the code sets; it passes again above 1.5 V. It is Type B, two trips to MIL. Because a real 12 V network cannot be at 1 V with the ignition on, GM's version really points to an open or shorted voltage sense line or a failed sensor, not a flat battery. Other makers may apply the code to genuine undervoltage. P0A8E is the high counterpart, P0A8F the correlation check.
c: Voltage sense line open or shorted to ground
Voltage sensor inside the power module failed
Converter not delivering output (fuse, output cable)
s: MIL and charging/hybrid warning
12 V battery discharges
Start/stop disabled

P0A8E.t: 14 Volt Power Module System Voltage High
P0A8E.d: P0A8E signals too high a voltage at the 14 V power module, the DC/DC converter supplying the 12 V side. In GM's 2013 eAssist tables it is the circuit-high check of the APM low-voltage sensor: a reading above 20 V for 1.5 s within a 2 s window, with ignition voltage 9 to 32 V, sets the code, and it passes below 19.5 V. GM rates it Type B, so the MIL comes on after two failing trips. Since the network should sit around 14 V, a reading over 20 V usually means a sense line shorted to a higher potential or a faulty sensor; a genuinely over-regulating converter would also threaten bulbs and modules. P0A8D is the low counterpart, P0A8F compares the sensor with the ignition voltage.
c: Voltage sense line shorted to a higher potential
Voltage sensor inside the power module failed
Converter regulating its output too high
s: MIL and charging/hybrid warning
Very bright lights or failing bulbs if overvoltage is real
Converter may be shut down

P0A8F.d: P0A8F means the 14 V power module (DC/DC converter for the 12 V network) does not perform as expected even though its signals are electrically in range. GM's 2013 eAssist tables use it as a correlation test: with the APM commanded on and ignition voltage 9 to 32 V, the APM's own low-voltage reading and the run/crank voltage measured by the controller must agree within 4.5 V. A larger difference over 3.75 s in a 5 s window sets the code as Type B, two trips to MIL. A high resistance in the 12 V output path or ground, a drifting sensor or a converter that cannot hold its target can all cause this. P0A8D and P0A8E cover sensor circuit low/high faults.
c: High resistance in 12 V output cable, fuse link or ground
Drifting voltage sensor in the module
Converter unable to hold its target voltage
s: MIL and charging/hybrid warning
Low or fluctuating 12 V voltage

P0A90.d: P0A90 reports that electric drive motor A does not behave as commanded. In GM's eAssist mild hybrid the motor/generator is belt-driven from the crankshaft, so GM uses P0A90 to detect a slipping or broken belt: the motor speed is compared with the engine speed. In 2013 a difference above 1000 rpm for 1.5 s, or repeated smaller slips above 500 rpm on two key cycles, set it; the 2016 tables use more than 1500 rpm for about 5.6 s or repeated 1000 rpm slip events. GM rates it Type A, MIL on the first trip. In full hybrids the generic definition applies to speed or torque deviations of the traction motor. P0A91 is the equivalent for motor B, P0A92 for the generator.
c: Slipping, worn or broken drive belt on belt-driven motor/generators
Faulty belt tensioner or contamination on the belt
Motor, position sensor or inverter fault in full hybrids
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Belt squeal or auto-stop/start not working
Reduced electric assist or limp mode

P0A91.d: P0A91 is set when the second electric drive motor (motor B) of a hybrid or electric vehicle does not deliver the expected speed or torque, although no electrical circuit fault is detected. Motor B exists only on systems with two traction motors, such as power-split or dual-motor layouts. CARB requires hybrid OBD systems to monitor electric motor performance. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's tables describe the motor A equivalent P0A90 as a comparison between motor speed and a reference speed, which illustrates the approach. Causes range from inverter or resolver faults to mechanical damage. The vehicle usually limits power or enters a reduced mode. P0A79 covers inverter B performance.
c: Inverter B fault limiting motor current
Mechanical damage to motor B or its gearing
s: Hybrid/EV system warning and MIL
Reduced power or limp mode

P0A92.d: P0A92 indicates that the generator of a hybrid system, the electric machine mainly used to convert engine power into electrical energy, does not reach the expected output, speed or torque. CARB requires manufacturers to describe how they monitor the generator so that faults preventing it from working are detected. FCA documents the code for the 2020 Jeep Compass and Renegade plug-in hybrids (bulletin 08-057-21): it appears together with drive motor phase current sensor codes, and the fix is a software update of the hybrid control processor and power inverter module. A turtle (limp home) lamp may accompany it. P0A90/P0A91 cover the drive motors; P0A3F and similar codes cover generator position sensing.
c: Hybrid controller or inverter software needing update (documented by FCA)
Internal generator fault (winding, bearing, position sensor)
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Limp home (turtle) lamp, reduced power
Reduced charging of the high-voltage battery

P0A93.d: The power inverter of a hybrid has its own coolant circuit with an electric pump, radiator and fan, separate from engine cooling. P0A93 is set when this circuit does not cool as intended. CARB lists inverter thermal management among the components that hybrid OBD must monitor. Hyundai documents the code for the 2011 Sonata Hybrid (bulletin 14-HC-001), assigning it, like P0C73, to the electric water pump; symptoms include a hybrid warning, no EV mode and poor acceleration. Toyota recalled 2004–2009 Prius models (12V-536) because the inverter water pump could fail and cause a stall; that notice does not name a code. A leaking or air-locked circuit should also be checked.
c: Electric inverter coolant pump failed or seized
Low coolant or air in the inverter circuit
Pump wiring, fuse or relay fault
Radiator fan not running or radiator blocked
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
No EV mode, reduced power
Vehicle may not start or may stall

P0A94.d: P0A94 reports that a DC/DC converter in the high-voltage system does not perform as commanded. In Toyota hybrids this is the boost converter inside the inverter assembly, which raises the battery voltage before it reaches the motor inverters. Toyota documents P0A94 for 2010–2015 Prius and 2012–2017 Prius v together with P0A1A, P324E and P3004 (bulletin T-SB-0003-21): the cause is damage in the inverter with converter, and the repair depends on the detail code. Recalls 14V-053 and 18V-684 address transistors in the intelligent power module that could overheat; the car then enters a fail-safe mode with reduced power. Not to be confused with the 14 V power module codes P0A86 to P0A8F.
c: Damaged power transistors in the boost converter / inverter assembly
Thermal stress from insufficient inverter cooling
Outstanding recall or software update not performed
s: MIL, hybrid system and other warning lamps
Fail-safe mode with greatly reduced power
Vehicle may stop and not restart

P0A95.d: P0A95 means the battery management detects that a fuse in the high-voltage circuit has opened, usually by comparing the voltage before and after the fuse. Several makers document it: Jaguar for the I-PACE battery energy control module, where a shorted high-voltage auxiliary component blows fuses in the junction box and battery module; Porsche for the Taycan as the main high-voltage fuse with a vehicle that will not become ready to drive; Volvo, whose procedure compares the voltage after the fuses with pack voltage; and Audi, which found an intermittent false entry in hard cornering fixed by software. P0E2F and P0E30 cover fuses B and C. Mostly the car cannot be driven until the cause is found.
c: Short circuit in a high-voltage auxiliary component (e.g. compressor, heater)
Fuse opened after overload or ageing
Faulty voltage measurement or software misdetection in the battery control module
s: Vehicle not ready to drive, propulsion warning
MIL or yellow warning lamp
Climate compressor or heater inoperative

P0A96.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 2 Control Circuit/Open
P0A96.d: Some packs use two cooling fans; P0A96 reports an open or general fault in the control circuit of the second one. Ford documents it code-exact: on 2005–12 Escape Hybrid and 2006–11 Mariner Hybrid the traction battery control module may store P0A96, often together with P0A81 for fan 1, and the repair is to replace both high-voltage battery fans with a kit (about 3 hours, pack removal included). Ford notes the code alone usually causes no noticeable symptom. CARB requires the electronic outputs used for battery thermal management to be monitored. Short-circuit faults on fan 2 are P0A99 and P0A9A. If one fan fails, cooling capacity drops and power may be limited in heat.
c: Fan 2 motor or electronics failed (Ford replaces both fans)
Loose connector or broken wire to fan 2
s: Code found during other diagnosis, often no complaint
Check engine or hybrid warning
Reduced hybrid power in hot conditions

P0A97.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 2 Performance/Stuck Off
P0A97.d: P0A97 is the fan 2 counterpart of P0A82: the second battery cooling fan is electrically reachable but does not reach its requested speed or does not turn at all. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. CARB requires a functional check of battery cooling where feasible, and the methods are published for fan 1: GM compares commanded and measured speed (its sense code P0BC8), Toyota judges the deviation of the feedback-corrected duty, Honda compares expected and actual battery temperature rise. Blocked air paths and worn motors are the usual causes. Circuit faults on fan 2 are P0A96, P0A99 and P0A9A; the stuck-on case is P0A98. With one fan weak the pack runs warmer.
c: Dust or debris on fan 2 or in its duct
Blocked air intake to the battery
s: Hybrid warning or check engine light
Weak airflow from the battery vents
Reduced electric assist in warm weather

P0A98.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 2 Stuck On
P0A98.d: P0A98 reports that battery cooling fan 2 keeps running after the controller has commanded it off; it mirrors P0A83 for fan 1. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. CARB calls for fan outputs to be checked for correct response to commands. GM's published method for fan 1 (sense code P0BC8) flags a fan that still reports more than about 250 rpm after being off for over 20 s; the same logic applies to a second fan. Typical causes are a welded relay, a control wire shorted to supply or fan electronics that ignore the stop command. Cooling is not at risk, but the fan can drain the 12 V battery and is audible after shutdown. Fan 2 circuit codes are P0A96, P0A99 and P0A9A.
c: Fan 2 control wire shorted to supply
Fan 2 internal controller ignores off command
s: Battery fan audible after the vehicle is switched off
12 V battery discharged after parking
Hybrid or check engine warning

P0A99.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 2 Control Circuit Low
P0A99.d: P0A99 reports a short to ground on the control circuit of the second battery cooling fan. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; Ford's two-fan Escape/Mariner Hybrid packs show that a second fan exists (there with P0A96). CARB requires the outputs used for battery thermal management to be monitored for circuit faults. The fan 1 counterpart P0A84 shows the usual GM logic: with the fan commanded at low duty, an output voltage below about 0.26 V in 16 of 20 samples sets a Type B code. The same approach is to be expected for fan 2. With the output held low the fan may not respond, cooling capacity falls and power may be limited. Open and high faults are P0A96 and P0A9A.
c: Fan 2 control wire shorted to ground
Internal short in fan 2 control input
Moisture or corrosion in the fan 2 connector
s: Check engine or hybrid warning
Fan 2 does not run when commanded
Reduced hybrid power in hot conditions

P0A9A.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 2 Control Circuit High
P0A9A.d: P0A9A reports a short to voltage on the control circuit of the second battery cooling fan. No manufacturer publishes this exact code; CARB requires the electronic outputs of battery thermal management to be checked for circuit faults. The fan 1 counterpart P0A85 shows the usual method: GM samples the output while the fan is commanded between 11 % and 100 % duty and counts a voltage above 9 V as a failure, setting a Type B code after 16 of 20 samples. A fan 2 diagnosis would work the same way. Depending on the circuit design the fan runs constantly or stops responding; a constantly running fan can drain the 12 V battery. Open and low faults are P0A96 and P0A99; a mechanically stuck-on fan is P0A98.
c: Fan 2 control wire shorted to supply voltage
Fan 2 control input internally open or shorted to supply
Corroded connector with leakage to supply
s: Check engine or hybrid warning
Fan 2 runs constantly or not at all
Possible 12 V battery drain when parked

P0A9B.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0A9B.d: Temperature sensor A is one of the thermistors the battery controller uses to track cell or module temperature for cooling, charge limits and power limits. P0A9B is the general circuit code for this sensor: the controller finds an electrical fault it does not classify further as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM, for example, reports the sibling codes P0A9C to P0A9F instead. In those tables a failed sensor input is excluded from protection logic, and GM's Volt bulletin notes several sensors per pack. Expect a hybrid warning and reduced charge and assist power while the controller works with fewer valid temperatures. Check the sensor harness at the module sensing board before condemning the pack.
c: Open, corroded or loose sensor wiring or connector inside the pack
Failed thermistor on the module or cell sensing board
Battery controller input or software fault
s: Hybrid or EV system warning and check engine light
Reduced electric assist, regeneration or charging power
Battery cooling fan or pump runs more than usual

P0A9C.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0A9C.d: This is a plausibility check: the reading of temperature sensor A is compared with the other sensors in the same pack, which should agree within a few degrees. GM sets P0A9C (Type B, two trips) when sensor A deviates from the average of the others by more than 25 °C for 50 of 67 samples (19OBDG02); Two-Mode hybrids use more than 15 °C against each other sensor for 90 of 100 samples, other programs more than 20 °C. The check is suspended while circuit low/high codes are active, so P0A9C points to a sensor that reads wrongly but stays in range. GM's Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists it as sensor 1 performance and cures false sets with new module software. The pack then limits power to protect the cells.
c: Thermistor drifted or poorly seated on its cell or module
High-resistance connection in the sensor circuit shifting the reading
Battery controller calibration causing false sets (GM Volt update)
Genuine local temperature difference from a cooling or cell problem
s: Check engine light after two drive cycles
Reduced hybrid assist or charging power
Message such as battery too cold, plug in to warm (GM Volt)

P0A9D.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0A9D.d: Sensor A is an NTC thermistor fed through a pull-up resistor, so the voltage falls as the temperature rises; a short to ground looks like an absurdly hot cell. GM sets P0A9D (Type B, two trips) when the converted value exceeds 160 °C in 8 of 10 samples (19OBDG02); Two-Mode hybrids use above 95 °C while the other sensors read below 70 °C, other programs above 87.5 °C for 1.4 s. GM's Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 names it sensor 1 circuit low voltage. The low-voltage case is the counterpart of P0A9E (open circuit, reads very cold) and differs from P0A7E, which reports a real overtemperature. Because the controller must assume heat, it cuts charge and discharge power and may run cooling at full speed.
c: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground or chafed inside the pack
Internally shorted thermistor on the sensing board
Moisture or coolant in the sensor connector
Battery controller software causing false sets (GM Volt)
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Strongly reduced electric power or no EV mode
Battery cooling running at high speed without reason

P0A9E.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0A9E.d: With the NTC thermistor of sensor A on a pull-up circuit, an open sensor or wire drives the input voltage toward the reference, which the controller reads as an extremely cold cell. GM sets P0A9E (Type B, two trips) when the value falls below -69 °C in 8 of 10 samples (19OBDG02); Two-Mode hybrids flag readings below -45 °C, other programs below -40 °C for 1.4 s. GM's Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists it as sensor 1 circuit high voltage and pairs it with a battery too cold message at mild ambient temperatures. Unlike P0A9D the fault suggests an open circuit rather than a short. Because cold cells accept little current, the car restricts charging, regeneration and electric drive.
c: Open sensor wire or unplugged connector inside the pack
Open (failed) thermistor on the sensing board
Signal shorted to the reference voltage
Battery controller software causing false sets (GM Volt)
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Battery too cold message although it is not cold
Little or no electric drive and weak regeneration

P0A9F.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0A9F.d: Cell temperature changes slowly, so a reading that jumps back and forth points to the circuit, not the battery. GM monitors this by summing the absolute sample-to-sample change of sensor A over a 10-sample window every 100 ms; if the sum exceeds 10, that window fails, and four failed windows out of five set P0A9F as Type B (two trips) in the 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables (16OBDG02, 19OBDG02). GM names a loose or intermittent connection as the typical trigger. The signal may still sit inside its valid range, which separates P0A9F from the hard low/high codes P0A9D/P0A9E and from the plausibility code P0A9C. The car protects the pack by limiting power and may show the fault only now and then.
c: Loose, fretted or corroded pin in the sensor connector
Partly broken sensor wire that opens with vibration or heat
Electrical interference on the sensor line from high-voltage components
s: Warning light that comes and goes
Temporarily reduced hybrid or EV power
Battery temperature value jumps in the scan tool data

P0AA0.d: The positive main contactor is a high-voltage relay that connects the positive pole of the traction battery to the propulsion bus. P0AA0 is the general fault code for this contactor circuit, used when the controller sees a problem it does not split into stuck closed (P0AA1), stuck open (P0AA2) or the control-circuit codes P0AD9 to P0ADC. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM, Audi, Jeep and Mitsubishi report the specific siblings instead. NHTSA's Mach-E recall query shows the underlying failure modes: overheated contacts that stay open or weld shut. With the positive side unusable the car may refuse ready mode or drop propulsion; work on it requires high-voltage qualification.
c: Positive contactor or battery junction box worn or damaged
Fault in the contactor coil feed or its connector
Weak 12 V supply so the contactor does not pull in reliably
s: Vehicle does not enter ready or propulsion-active mode
Hybrid or EV system warning with check engine light
Possible loss of propulsion while driving

P0AA1.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Positive Contactor Circuit Stuck Closed
P0AA1.d: P0AA1 means the positive main contactor conducts although it should be open, typically because its contacts have welded. GM checks this with all contactors commanded open for over 120 s (or the bus already below 9 % of pack voltage): more than 30 V on the positive bus in 4 of 6 samples sets Type B (two trips, 19OBDG02). Older GM programs test during precharge instead and set Type A after one trip if bus voltage exceeds 80 % (2011) or 60 % (2016) of pack voltage. GM bulletins cover the 2017 Bolt EV and welded contactors on the 2019 Volt; Jeep fixes false sets on the 2023 Grand Cherokee 4xe with software, Mitsubishi lists it as main contactor (+) seizure on the i-MiEV. The car may refuse to start.
c: Positive contactor contacts welded, e.g. after high current or arcing
Battery or hybrid controller software (GM Volt 2019, Jeep 4xe updates)
Faulty battery disconnect unit (GM Bolt EV bulletin)
Bus voltage sensing error making an open contactor look closed
s: Vehicle will not switch into ready or propulsion-active mode
Check engine light and service high voltage system message
Often stored together with P0AA4 or a slow discharge code such as P0C76

P0AA2.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Positive Contactor Circuit Stuck Open
P0AA2.d: P0AA2 means the positive main contactor does not close, or does not conduct, when the controller commands it closed, so the high-voltage bus cannot be energised from the pack. Audi documents it for the 2020-2022 Q5 e quattro and 2021-2022 A7 e quattro plug-in hybrids: the car does not start and the battery management module stores P0AA2 (often with P0AA5). Audi traces rare cases to oxidised contact surfaces in the battery junction box after long standing or high humidity, and first prescribes repeated ignition cycles and an EV road test before replacing the junction box. GM lists the code among high-voltage faults for which Ultium EV pack data must be collected. Unlike P0AA1, the contacts are open, not welded.
c: Oxidised contact surfaces after long standing or high humidity (Audi)
Failed battery junction box or burnt contactor
Contactor coil not energised due to wiring or 12 V supply fault
s: Vehicle does not start or reach ready mode
Service high voltage battery or hybrid warning message
Possible sudden loss of propulsion if the contactor opens while driving

P0AA3.d: The negative main contactor switches the negative pole of the traction battery onto the propulsion bus; together with the positive contactor it isolates the pack completely when the car is off. P0AA3 is the general code for this contactor circuit when the fault is not reported more precisely as stuck closed (P0AA4), stuck open (P0AA5) or a control-circuit fault (P0ADD to P0AE0). No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM, Audi, Jeep and Mitsubishi publish the specific siblings. Contact damage from heat and arcing, as described in NHTSA's Mach-E recall query, is the usual background. Expect a hybrid or EV warning and possibly no ready mode; diagnosis belongs to a high-voltage trained workshop.
c: Negative contactor or battery junction box worn or damaged
Fault in the contactor coil wiring or connector
Battery controller driver or software fault
s: Vehicle does not enter ready mode
Hybrid or EV system warning with check engine light
Charging may be refused

P0AA4.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Negative Contactor Circuit Stuck Closed
P0AA4.d: P0AA4 reports that the negative main contactor still conducts while it should be open, usually through welded contacts, so the pack is no longer fully isolated on the negative side. GM tests it once all contactors have been commanded open for more than 120 s, or the bus has already decayed below 9 % of pack voltage: over 30 V on the negative bus in 4 of 6 samples at 12.5 ms sets Type B (two trips, 19OBDG02). GM's 2017 Bolt EV bulletin prescribes contactor cycling and then a new battery disconnect unit; the 2019 Volt update links welded contactors to P0AA1, P0AA4 and P0C76. Jeep cures false sets on the 2023 Grand Cherokee 4xe by software, and Mitsubishi calls it main contactor (-) seizure on the i-MiEV.
c: Negative contactor contacts welded after high current or arcing
Battery or hybrid controller software (GM Volt 2019, Jeep 4xe updates)
Faulty battery disconnect unit (GM Bolt EV bulletin)
s: Vehicle will not start or switch into ready mode
Check engine light and high voltage system message
Often stored together with P0AA1 or the slow discharge code P0C76

P0AA5.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Negative Contactor Circuit Stuck Open
P0AA5.d: P0AA5 is set when the negative main contactor stays open or fails to conduct after the controller has commanded it closed, so the negative side of the high-voltage bus never connects. Audi reports it, alone or with P0AA2, on the 2020-2022 Q5 e quattro and 2021-2022 A7 e quattro plug-in hybrids with a no-start complaint; the stated cause is oxidation of the contact surfaces in the battery junction box after very long standing or extreme humidity. Audi's procedure: several ignition cycles and an EV road test with many consumers on, and a new junction box only if the fault returns. GM includes P0AA5 among the Ultium EV high-voltage codes that require pack data retrieval. It is the counterpart of P0AA4 (welded contacts).
c: Oxidised contact surfaces after long standing or high humidity (Audi)
Failed battery junction box or burnt negative contactor
Contactor coil not energised due to wiring or 12 V supply fault
s: Vehicle does not start or reach ready mode
Hybrid or high voltage battery warning
Charging not possible

P0AA6.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage System Isolation Fault
P0AA6.d: The high-voltage system floats free of the chassis, and an isolation monitor measures the resistance from each HV rail to body ground. P0AA6 sets when that resistance falls below a calibrated limit. GM tables measure with the contactors open and fail below 75,000 ohms (2016) or 213,000 ohms (2019), Type A, one trip; Volt bulletins expect over 275 kOhm after repair, while FMVSS 305 sets 100 ohms per volt DC as the post-crash floor. Documented causes: Volt battery coolant leaks, a chafed HV harness on Ford Aviator/Explorer hybrids, a traction motor coolant leak on the 2017 Ioniq Hybrid; Toyota adds INF codes naming the area. P0AA7 to P0AAB flag the measuring circuit itself. Expect warnings, no charging or a stop-safely message.
c: Coolant or moisture inside the battery pack, inverter or drive motor
Chafed or crushed orange HV cable shorting to the body
Insulation breakdown in the electric A/C compressor or a motor winding
Electrolyte leakage or contamination inside the battery sections
s: Check engine and hybrid or EV system warning lights
Vehicle will not charge or will not enter ready mode after restart
Stop safely now message or reduced power

P0AA7.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Isolation Sensor Circuit
P0AA7.d: To measure isolation, the battery controller reads the voltage of each HV rail against chassis ground through an isolation sensor circuit and can switch in a known bias resistor. P0AA7 means this measuring circuit itself does not work, so the controller can no longer judge isolation. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables use it for a bias switch self-test: with all contactors open for 8 seconds after shutdown, switching the bias resistor must change both sensor readings; a combined change below 5 V squared sets the code, Type B, two trips. Mitsubishi lists P0AA7 to P0AA9 as leak detection circuit faults; on 2018 Outlander PHEVs noise caused false setting and a 60 km/h limit until restart, fixed by a sub-BMU update. P0AA6 is the actual insulation fault.
c: Failed isolation bias switch or measuring circuit inside the battery controller
Controller software misreading electrical noise (update available on some models)
Open or loose isolation sense lead or connector at the battery
s: Check engine and EV system service warnings
Power reduced or speed limited until the system is switched off and on
Regenerative braking warning on some models

P0AA8.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Isolation Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0AA8.d: The two isolation sensor readings, positive rail to ground and negative rail to ground, should together equal the total pack voltage. P0AA8 is the plausibility check of that relation. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables fail it when the sum of both readings differs from the measured battery voltage by more than 5 V in 40 of 50 samples, with the bias switch open, Type B, two trips. GM's 2013 table compares mid-pack sensors with the motor controller's voltage reading and allows 15 V. Mitsubishi groups P0AA8 with P0AA7 and P0AA9 as leak detection circuit faults, which on 2018 Outlander PHEVs were set falsely by noise. Unlike P0AA9 or P0AAA, the signal stays in range but is implausible; P0AA6 is a real insulation loss.
c: Isolation measuring amplifier or reference in the battery controller out of tolerance
Pack voltage sense lead fault making the comparison value wrong
Controller software misreading electrical noise (update available on some models)
s: Check engine and hybrid or EV system warnings
Reduced power or speed limit until restart
Isolation monitoring unavailable, so related faults may go unreported

P0AA9.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Isolation Sensor Circuit Low
P0AA9.d: P0AA9 reports that the isolation sensor signal sits below its valid window, typically because the sense line or the measuring input is pulled toward ground or has lost its supply. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables flag it when the sensor reads under 5 V with the bias switch open in 320 of 400 samples (about 5 s), Type B, two trips; the 2013 GM table uses a negative mid-pack reading under 5 V with contactors closed. Mitsubishi includes P0AA9 in its 2018 Outlander PHEV sub-BMU campaign together with P0AA7 and P0AA8, where noise caused false setting. The high counterpart is P0AAA. A low reading is a measuring fault, not proof of an insulation leak; that is P0AA6. Expect warnings and possibly reduced power.
c: Isolation sense line shorted to ground or open input
Failed isolation measuring circuit in the battery controller
Controller software misreading electrical noise (update available on some models)
s: Check engine and EV system warning lights
Reduced power or speed limit on some models

P0AAA.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Isolation Sensor Circuit High
P0AAA.d: P0AAA is the high-side counterpart of P0AA9: the isolation sensor reports a rail-to-ground voltage above anything the pack can produce. GM's tables tie the limit to the pack: over 333 V in the 2016 table and over 416 V in the 2019 table, each in 320 of 400 samples with the bias switch open, Type B, two trips. The 2013 GM table instead flags a mid-pack reading that differs from the motor controller's voltage by more than 15 V. Likely sources are an open reference or ground in the measuring circuit or a failed input stage in the battery controller. No public bulletin from another maker names this code. The car usually stays drivable with warnings, but isolation monitoring is lost, and P0AA6 cannot be trusted until it is fixed.
c: Open ground or reference in the isolation measuring circuit
Failed isolation input stage in the battery controller
Sense lead shorted to another HV potential inside the pack
s: Check engine and hybrid or EV warning lights
Isolation monitoring disabled while the code is active

P0AAB.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Isolation Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0AAB.d: P0AAB covers an isolation sensor signal that jumps or drops out briefly instead of staying wrong. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's hybrid tables use only P0AA7 to P0AAA for the measuring circuit. CARB requires hybrid input components to be monitored for circuit and rationality faults, which is the basis for this code. The best public analogue is Mitsubishi's 2018 Outlander PHEV campaign, where noise from the shift selector, brakes or A/C made the sub-BMU misjudge its leak detection circuit, setting P0AA7 to P0AA9. Check for software updates, then for loose connectors at the battery controller. Erratic readings can mask a true insulation fault (P0AA6). Expect warnings that come and go.
c: Electrical noise misinterpreted by controller software
Loose or corroded sense connector at the battery controller
Failing isolation measuring circuit inside the controller
s: Hybrid or EV warning lights that come and go
Occasional power limitation that clears after restart

P0AAC.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0AAC.d: Air-cooled hybrid batteries carry a thermistor in the cooling air path; GM calls sensor A the inlet air sensor. The battery controller uses it to run the fan and to judge cooling. P0AAC is the general circuit code, set for an electrical fault that is not classified as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM reports the siblings P0AAD to P0AAF instead, with Type B, two-trip logic. CARB requires hybrid component temperature sensors to be monitored like other input components. If the controller has no valid air temperature, it typically falls back to fixed fan control and may restrict battery power. Check connector and wiring at the air inlet duct first, then the sensor.
c: Loose, corroded or damaged sensor connector or wiring at the air duct
Battery controller input or reference voltage fault
s: Check engine or hybrid system warning light
Battery cooling fan runs constantly or at fixed speed
Reduced electric assist in hot conditions

P0AAD.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0AAD.d: P0AAD is the plausibility check for battery air temperature sensor A: the signal is electrically valid but does not fit other temperatures. GM documents two methods. In the 2011 and 2013 full-size two-mode hybrid tables, at power-up the inlet air reading may not exceed the outlet air reading by more than 20 °C, checked once per start. In GM's 2013 table (13OBDG05C), after more than 8 hours off the inlet sensor may not differ from the average battery core temperature by more than 10 °C, 50 of 62 samples. Both are Type B, two trips. A sensor stuck at a plausible value, a sensor out of the air stream or a faulty core sensor can cause it. The car keeps running, but fan control and power limits may be wrong.
c: Thermistor drifted or stuck at a plausible value
Sensor displaced from the air stream or duct blocked
Fault in the comparison sensor (outlet air or cell temperature)
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Battery cooling fan behaves unusually

P0AAE.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0AAE.d: The battery air temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor, so a low signal voltage reads as very hot air. P0AAE sets when the signal stays below the lower limit, usually a short to ground. GM's 2013 table (13OBDG05C) uses under 0.3 V, about 90 °C, in 7 of 10 samples; the two-mode hybrid tables of 2011 and 2013 flag an inlet reading above 95 °C in 30 of 40 samples. Both are Type B, two trips. Since the controller then assumes overheated cooling air, it may run the fan hard and cut battery power although nothing is hot. Look for chafed sensor wires touching ground or a sensor shorted internally. The opposite case, an open circuit reading as very cold, is P0AAF.
c: Sensor signal wire chafed and shorted to ground
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Battery cooling fan runs at high speed without reason
Reduced electric assist and regeneration

P0AAF.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0AAF.d: Air temperature sensor A is the thermistor GM places at the cooling air inlet of air-cooled hybrid packs.
