Being an NTC type, a high signal voltage means the controller sees implausibly cold air, typically from an open wire or a lost ground. GM's 2013 table 13OBDG05C sets P0AAF above 4.63 V, equal to about -45 °C, in 7 of 10 samples; the two-mode hybrid tables of 2011 and 2013 use a reading below -45 °C in 30 of 40 samples. All are Type B, two trips. The controller then ignores the inlet value, so fan control and the inlet-to-outlet comparison lose their reference. Check the connector at the inlet duct for a pushed-out pin first. The shorted counterpart reading as very hot is P0AAE.
c: Open signal or ground wire between sensor and battery controller
Connector at the air inlet duct loose or with pushed-back pin
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Scan tool shows inlet air near -40 °C regardless of weather
Battery fan runs on a fixed default speed

P0AB0.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0AB0.d: P0AB0 flags a battery air temperature sensor A signal that jumps faster than real air temperature can change, usually a sign of a loose contact rather than a dead sensor. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's two-mode and 2013 tables for sensor A only list the low, high and plausibility codes. GM does describe the method for the analogous cell sensor code P0A9F: the controller adds up the absolute signal changes over a 10-sample window and fails it when the sum exceeds a limit, 4 of 5 windows, Type B. CARB requires hybrid temperature inputs to be checked for such faults. Wiggle-test harness and connector at the inlet duct while watching live data before replacing the sensor.
c: Loose or corroded contact at the inlet air sensor connector
Wire chafed through at the duct, intermittently touching ground
Electrical interference on the sensor line
s: Hybrid warning light that comes and goes
Inlet air reading jumps in live data
Battery fan speed changes without obvious reason

P0AB1.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P0AB1.d: Air temperature sensor B is a second thermistor in the battery cooling air path; in GM's two-mode hybrid tables it is the outlet air sensor behind the modules. P0AB1 is the general circuit code for it, used when the controller sees an electrical fault without sorting it into low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM reports the siblings P0AB2 to P0AB4 instead. CARB requires temperature inputs of hybrid components to be monitored for circuit faults. Without a valid outlet value the controller cannot judge how much heat the air carries away, so it usually falls back to a default fan strategy and may limit battery power. Inspect the outlet-side connector and wiring first.
c: Damaged wiring or poor contact at the outlet air sensor
s: Hybrid or check engine warning light
Battery fan runs on a default setting
Possibly reduced electric assist

P0AB2.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0AB2.d: P0AB2 checks whether air temperature sensor B reads sensibly. GM uses it on the full-size two-mode hybrids, where sensor B measures outlet air: in the 2011 and 2013 tables, with the battery fan commanded on, the outlet air may not be more than 10 °C warmer than the hottest battery module, 90 of 100 samples, Type B, two trips. The logic is simple physics: air leaving the pack cannot be much hotter than the modules that heated it. The test is skipped while module sensor or fan faults are present. A drifting thermistor, a sensor that has slipped out of the air stream or a faulty module sensor can trigger it. Unlike P0AB3 and P0AB4, the circuit itself is electrically in range.
c: Outlet air thermistor drifted from its characteristic
Sensor displaced from its position in the air duct
Battery module temperature sensor used for comparison reads wrong
s: Hybrid or check engine warning light
Outlet air reads clearly above module temperatures in live data
Usually no change in driving behavior

P0AB3.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P0AB3.d: P0AB3 means the signal of air temperature sensor B sits below its valid range. Because the sensor is an NTC thermistor, a low voltage translates into very hot air, so a short to ground is the usual cause. GM documents the code for the outlet air sensor of its full-size two-mode hybrids: in the 2011 and 2013 tables it fails when the outlet reading exceeds 95 °C in 30 of 40 samples while at least one module sensor still reads below 70 °C, Type B, two trips. That extra condition separates a real overheat from a wiring fault. The controller may then run the fan at full speed and cut battery power without need. The open-circuit counterpart is P0AB4.
c: Sensor B signal wire shorted to ground
Moisture or debris bridging the connector pins
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Battery fan runs loud even when the pack is cool
Reduced electric assist and regeneration

P0AB4.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
P0AB4.d: P0AB4 reports a signal from air temperature sensor B above the valid range. For an NTC thermistor that reads as extremely cold air, which points to an open circuit, a broken ground or a disconnected plug. GM uses the code for the outlet air sensor of its full-size two-mode hybrids; the 2011 and 2013 tables set it when the outlet reading falls below -45 °C in 30 of 40 samples, Type B, two trips. With the outlet value rejected, the controller also suspends the outlet plausibility test P0AB2 and runs the fan on a substitute strategy. Look for a connector left off after battery work or a broken wire at the duct. The shorted counterpart is P0AB3, the inlet-side equivalent P0AAF.
c: Open signal or ground wire of sensor B
Connector not refitted after battery or duct work
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Outlet air shows about -40 °C in live data
Battery fan on default operation

P0AB5.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0AB5.d: P0AB5 is set when the signal of battery air temperature sensor B fluctuates in a way real air temperature cannot, typically from an intermittent contact. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's two-mode tables, which use sensor B as the outlet air sensor, list only P0AB2 to P0AB4. As an analogy, GM's 2019 table judges the battery cell sensor code P0A9F by summing signal changes within 10-sample windows, failing after 4 of 5 bad windows, Type B. CARB requires hybrid temperature inputs to be checked for erratic behaviour. The fault often comes and goes with vibration or temperature. Move the outlet-side harness while watching live data to locate the weak point.
c: Loose or corroded terminal at sensor B
Partly broken wire near the outlet duct
Interference coupled into the sensor line
s: Hybrid warning light that appears intermittently
Outlet air value jumps in live data
No noticeable driving change in most cases

P0AB6.d: Some engines sit on switchable or actively driven hydraulic mounts whose solenoid or actuator is energised by the engine controller. P0AB6 reports that the driver output for the second mount (B) sees an open or otherwise faulty circuit. Ford lists the code in its 2020-23 gasoline OBD summary under active mounts, assigns mount B to bank 2, monitors continuously and lets the low-level driver fault mature for about 5 seconds before storing it. On the 2008 Honda Pilot the same code covers the rear mount actuator. Mount A has the matching codes P0A14 to P0A16. Drivers mostly notice more vibration at idle or in cylinder-deactivation mode; the engine itself keeps running normally.
c: Broken or chafed control wire to the mount actuator
Corroded or loose connector at the mount (splash zone)
Mount solenoid or actuator coil open internally
Output driver in the engine controller defective
s: Check engine light on
Noticeable vibration at idle or with cylinder deactivation active
Cylinder deactivation may be suspended on some models

P0AB7.t: Engine Mount B Control Circuit Low
P0AB7.d: P0AB7 means the engine controller sees the control line of active engine mount B pulled too low, the usual signature of a short to ground or an actuator coil with too little resistance. Ford's 2020-23 gasoline OBD summary lists it among the active-mount checks for bank 2: the output driver flags the fault continuously and the PCM matures it within roughly 5 seconds. Honda describes the code on the 2008 Pilot as a low-current fault in the rear mount actuator circuit. P0AB6 covers the open circuit, P0AB8 the high side, and P0A15 the same fault on mount A. The driver usually feels more engine shake at idle; drivability is otherwise unaffected.
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Water ingress in the mount connector
s: Check engine light on
Increased vibration felt through seat and steering wheel at idle

P0AB8.t: Engine Mount B Control Circuit High
P0AB8.d: With P0AB8 the controller finds the control circuit of active engine mount B at too high a level, for example because the line has a short to battery voltage or the driver cannot pull it down. Ford names the code in its 2020-23 gasoline OBD summary as the bank 2 high fault of the active-mount circuit check, which runs continuously and needs about 5 seconds of driver-reported fault before a code is stored. Honda's 2008 Pilot uses the B codes for the rear mount actuator. The open circuit is P0AB6, the low side P0AB7, and the mirror code for mount A is P0A16. Consequences are comfort-related: the mount stays in its default state and vibration rises at idle.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
Output driver in the engine controller defective
s: Check engine light on
Rougher feel at idle and when pulling away

P0AB9.d: Despite the broad title, GM uses P0AB9 for one concrete check: a failed engine auto-start or auto-stop in its hybrids, including an engine stall during that process. In the 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables the hybrid controller sets the code when the engine still reports no torque about 15 seconds into an auto-start although more than 20 Nm is commanded, provided fuel level is sufficient and no cam or crank fault is present. The 2011 and 2013 tables describe the same idea with a stall during start/stop. GM rates it Type A, so the MIL comes on after one trip. Other faults that prevent starting, such as P0A0F, point at more specific causes; P0AB9 itself is the symptom.
c: Fuel delivery problem (weak pump, nearly empty tank, clogged filter)
Ignition or injector fault that prevents the engine from firing
Starter-generator or motor unable to spin the engine to start speed
s: Check engine light on
Engine hesitates, fails or stalls when restarting at a stop
Auto-stop disabled for the rest of the trip

P0ABA.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense A Circuit
P0ABA.d: The battery management system measures the total voltage of the high-voltage pack through a dedicated sense circuit and uses it for state of charge, power limits and contactor checks. P0ABA is the general circuit fault for sense circuit A, set when the reading is unusable without being clearly low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM, for instance, monitors the same circuit with the more specific P0ABB to P0ABD. CARB requires hybrid battery inputs that feed emission-relevant control to be checked for circuit faults. Expect a warning light and reduced hybrid assistance, because the controller then works with conservative limits.
c: Damaged or loose voltage sense lead inside the battery pack
Measurement input of the battery controller defective
Blown sense fuse or failed divider resistor
s: Check engine or hybrid system warning light
Reduced electric assist or EV range
Vehicle may not enter ready mode

P0ABB.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense A Circuit Range/Performance
P0ABB.d: P0ABB is a plausibility check: the measured pack voltage is within electrical limits but does not agree with what the individual cells add up to. GM documents it in several hybrid tables. From 2016 the battery controller flags it when pack voltage and the sum of cell voltages differ by more than 10 V in 32 of 40 samples; the 2013 table compares the pack reading with 32 times the average cell voltage and uses a 5.49 V limit. Both are Type B, so the MIL needs two trips. The check is suppressed while cell voltage circuit faults are active. P0ABC and P0ABD cover hard low or high readings, P0AF8 compares the pack sensor with the inverter bus voltage.
c: Pack voltage measurement drifted (divider or input aging)
Faulty cell voltage tap distorting the cell sum
s: Check engine or hybrid system warning light
Erratic state-of-charge display
Reduced electric power

P0ABC.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense A Circuit Low
P0ABC.d: P0ABC is stored when the pack voltage sensor reports a value below anything the battery could really have, pointing to a short to ground or a lost sense signal rather than a discharged pack. GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables set it below 4.8 V with system voltage above 10.2 V, after 8 failed samples out of 10 taken every 25 ms, and rate it Type A with MIL on the first trip. The 2013 table for an earlier hybrid uses a limit of 30 V, 7 of 10 samples and Type B. A real deep discharge is handled by other codes such as P0AFA. Because the controller no longer trusts pack voltage, hybrid operation is restricted or the vehicle will not go ready.
c: Sense line shorted to ground or disconnected
Sense fuse or link open so no voltage reaches the input
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning on
Vehicle may refuse to enter ready mode
Engine runs continuously, no electric drive

P0ABD.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense A Circuit High
P0ABD.d: The counterpart to P0ABC: the pack voltage reading is above the highest value the battery could physically reach, which suggests an open reference, a failed divider or a damaged input rather than real overcharging. GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables set P0ABD above 392 V, again with 8 failed samples out of 10 at 25 ms intervals and Type A, so the MIL comes on immediately. For the smaller pack in its 2013 table the limit is 190.1 V, with 7 of 10 samples and Type B. Range and plausibility problems are reported by P0ABB, the low limit by P0ABC. The vehicle typically limits or blocks electric operation until the fault is cleared.
c: Open ground or reference side of the sense circuit
Voltage divider component failed in the battery controller
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning on
Electric drive limited or unavailable

P0ABE.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0ABE.d: P0ABE flags a pack voltage signal that jumps or drops out briefly instead of changing smoothly, as a battery voltage physically would. A loose sense connection or a cracked solder joint inside the pack are the classic triggers. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM covers the same sensor with P0ABB, P0ABC and P0ABD, and its battery controller cross-checks the pack reading against the cell sum and the inverter bus voltage (P0AF8). CARB demands circuit and rationality monitoring for such battery inputs. Because the faults come and go, the code may be stored without lasting symptoms, but power limits and warning lights can appear during the dropouts.
c: Loose or fretted voltage sense connection
Cracked solder or crimp joint on the sense board
Electrical noise from damaged shielding or ground
s: Warning light that comes and goes
Sudden short drops in electric power

P0ABF.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor A Circuit
P0ABF.d: The pack current sensor, usually a Hall-effect unit around the main cable, tells the battery controller how much current flows in and out. P0ABF is the general fault of sensor A. GM uses it in its 2019 hybrid controller tables as a stuck-in-range check: before the high-voltage bus is precharged the controller stores a zero-current baseline, then expects a measurable change once precharge starts or the main contactor closes and loads such as the inverter and auxiliary power module draw current. If the reading moves by less than 1 A, P0ABF fails. Out-of-range readings are P0AC1 and P0AC2, offset errors P0AC0. Without a valid current value state of charge cannot be tracked, so power is limited.
c: Sensor supply, ground or signal wire faulty
Sensor not seated around the conductor after repair
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning on
Reduced electric power and erratic charge display
Vehicle may not go ready

P0AC0.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0AC0.d: P0AC0 belongs to the battery current sensor family, not to battery cooling. It reports a sensor whose reading is electrically valid but implausible. GM's 2011 to 2013 hybrid tables describe the check: with the contactors open, when no current can flow, the reading in each of the sensor's high, mid and low ranges must stay within 5 A of zero, and the controller also checks that the measured current fits the change in pack voltage. A failure sets the code as one-trip Type A in the 2013 table. The check waits while circuit codes P0AC1 or P0AC2 are active. Effects are a drifting charge estimate, reduced hybrid power and, in severe cases, a vehicle that will not go ready.
c: Unstable sensor supply or reference voltage
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning on
State of charge display drifts or jumps
Reduced electric assist

P0AC1.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor A Circuit Low
P0AC1.d: P0AC1 is set when the output of the pack current sensor falls below the valid window, so that the converted current would be an impossible discharge or charge value. GM documents it in several hybrid tables. In the 2016 and 2019 versions the Hall-effect sensor fails when the result is below -365.1 A for 8 of 10 samples at 25 ms with system voltage above 10.2 V; the code is Type A with MIL on the first trip. An earlier GM pack in the 2013 table uses an output below 0.2 V, equal to about -230 A, with 7 of 10 samples and Type B. Typical causes are a lost supply or a signal shorted to ground. P0AC2 is the high side and P0AC0 the plausibility check.
c: Sensor 5 V supply open or shorted
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning on
Electric drive limited or vehicle will not go ready

P0AC2.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor A Circuit High
P0AC2.d: With P0AC2 the current sensor output sits above its valid window, which after conversion would mean an implausibly large current in the opposite direction to P0AC1. GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables set it when the Hall-effect sensor reads above 274.6 A in 8 of 10 samples taken every 25 ms, again as Type A with immediate MIL. The 2013 table for an earlier pack uses an output above 4.65 V, roughly 215 A, with 7 of 10 samples and Type B. A signal shorted to the 5 V supply or an open sensor ground are common reasons. Because the controller can no longer count charge, it caps battery power; the low limit is P0AC1 and implausible offsets are P0AC0.
c: Signal wire shorted to the 5 V supply or another voltage
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning on
Battery power limited, engine runs more often

P0AC3.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0AC3.d: P0AC3 describes a battery current signal that jumps, spikes or drops out in a way real current flow could not explain, typically through a loose connector, a chafed signal wire or interference on the sensor ground. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM monitors the same Hall-effect sensor with the stuck check P0ABF, the offset check P0AC0 and the range limits P0AC1 and P0AC2, and CARB requires circuit and rationality monitoring for battery inputs that influence emissions. As the fault is not permanent, the code may be the only trace; during the dropouts the controller may still cut battery power or turn on a warning light.
c: Loose or corroded current sensor connector
Chafed signal or supply wire with intermittent contact
Interference on sensor ground or shield
s: Warning light that comes and goes
Short drops in electric power while driving

P0AC4.t: Hybrid/EV Powertrain Control Module Requested MIL Illumination
P0AC4.d: In many hybrids the hybrid powertrain controller has its own emission-related diagnostics but does not drive the malfunction indicator lamp itself. When it detects such a fault it sends a MIL request to the engine controller, which then stores P0AC4 as a pointer. GM documents this in its 2011, 2013, 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables: the engine controller watches the request message continuously once 3 seconds have passed after power-up and logs P0AC4 after one trip, listed as Type A but marked No MIL because the lamp is owed to the original fault. The real cause is therefore stored in the hybrid controller and must be read there. P0A7B is the equivalent request from the battery energy control module.
c: Emission-related fault stored in the hybrid controller
Request still present because codes were cleared only in the engine controller
s: Check engine light on (caused by the underlying hybrid fault)
Further codes present only in the hybrid controller

P0AC5.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P0AC5.d: Battery temperature sensor B is one of several thermistors that measure cell or module temperature inside the high-voltage pack; GM's Volt bulletin calls it sensor 2 of nine. P0AC5 is the general circuit code for it, used for an electrical fault the controller does not classify as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM, for instance, reports P0AC6 to P0AC9 instead. CARB requires hybrid battery temperature inputs to be monitored for circuit faults. With one sensor missing the controller has a gap in its temperature picture and tends to limit charge and discharge power. The sensor usually sits on a module or sensing board inside the pack, so checks need high-voltage safety procedures.
c: Poor contact or damaged wire between sensor B and sensing board
Fault in the battery controller input stage
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning
Reduced electric power and regeneration
Charging may be slower on plug-in models

P0AC6.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0AC6.d: P0AC6 is the plausibility test for battery temperature sensor B: its reading is compared with the other pack sensors. GM documents several calibrations. The 2016 and 2019 tables fail it when the sensor differs from the average of the other sensors by more than 25 °C, 50 of 67 samples; the two-mode hybrid tables of 2011 and 2013 use more than 15 °C, 90 of 100 samples; GM's 2013 table 13OBDG05C allows 8.55 °C after more than 6 hours off. All are Type B, two trips. Bulletin 18-NA-342 for the Chevrolet Volt lists P0AC6 among false sensor codes in cold weather and fixes them by reprogramming. Otherwise a drifting sensor or a real local hot spot in a module is likely.
c: Sensor B drifted from its characteristic
Controller software flags the sensor falsely (GM Volt bulletin 18-NA-342)
Corroded contact adding resistance in the sensor circuit
Real temperature difference from a weak cell or blocked cooling
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
One sensor reading far off the others in live data
Battery too cold message on the Volt in mild weather

P0AC7.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P0AC7.d: P0AC7 means the voltage of battery temperature sensor B is below its valid range. GM's sensors are NTC thermistors, so a low voltage equals an extremely hot reading, usually from a short to ground. The thresholds differ by program: the 2016 and 2019 tables fail it above 160 °C in 8 of 10 samples; the two-mode tables of 2011 and 2013 above 95 °C in 30 of 40 samples; GM's 2013 table 13OBDG05C below 0.3 V, about 90 °C, in 7 of 10. All are Type B, two trips. GM's Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 names P0AC7 among sensor codes that can set falsely and calls for a software update. A genuine hot pack would trip far lower thresholds first, so treat P0AC7 as an electrical fault.
c: Sensor B signal shorted to ground inside the pack harness
Controller software setting the code falsely (Volt bulletin 18-NA-342)
Moisture or coolant at the sensing board connector
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Sensor B shows an implausibly high temperature
Charging and drive power reduced

P0AC8.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
P0AC8.d: P0AC8 reports that battery temperature sensor B delivers a voltage above its valid range, which for an NTC thermistor reads as extreme cold. An open wire, a disconnected sensing board plug or a broken sensor are typical. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables set it below -69 °C in 8 of 10 samples, the two-mode hybrid tables of 2011 and 2013 below -45 °C in 30 of 40, and GM's 2013 table 13OBDG05C above 4.63 V, about -45 °C, in 7 of 10; all Type B, two trips. In the Chevrolet Volt, bulletin 18-NA-342 links such codes to a Battery Too Cold message above -25 °C ambient and prescribes reprogramming. A pack believed to be frozen gets strict charge and power limits.
c: Open signal or return wire of sensor B
Controller software issue on the Volt (bulletin 18-NA-342)
Signal shorted to the reference voltage
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Battery too cold message although it is not cold
Strongly reduced charging and electric power

P0AC9.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0AC9.d: P0AC9 catches a battery temperature sensor B signal that changes erratically. Pack temperatures move slowly because of the large thermal mass, so rapid swings point to a bad connection. GM documents the method in its 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables: the controller integrates the absolute change of the sensor value over a 10-sample window at 100 ms per sample; a window fails when the sum exceeds 10, and the code sets after 4 of 5 failed windows, Type B, two trips. The older two-mode and 2013 tables have no erratic code for this sensor. The fault is often intermittent and may clear by itself, so check connector locking and terminal tension at the sensing board.
c: Loose terminal or unlatched connector at the sensing board
Partly broken sensor wire inside the pack
Interference from high-voltage switching on the sensor line
s: Hybrid warning light that comes and goes
Sensor B value jumps in live data
Occasional power limitation

P0ACA.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor C Circuit
P0ACA.d: Battery temperature sensor C is a further thermistor inside the high-voltage pack, corresponding to sensor 3 in GM's Volt bulletin. P0ACA covers a general electrical fault in its circuit that the controller does not narrow down to low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM reports the more specific siblings P0ACB to P0ACE instead. CARB requires temperature sensors of hybrid batteries to be monitored like other input components. Losing one temperature input makes the controller more cautious: expect reduced charge and assist power and a hybrid warning. Since sensors C and B often share the same sensing board, check whether neighbouring sensor codes are stored as well.
c: Poor contact or damaged wire between sensor C and sensing board
Fault in the battery controller input stage
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning
Reduced electric power and regeneration
Further battery sensor codes may be stored

P0ACB.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P0ACB.d: With P0ACB the controller judges battery temperature sensor C implausible: its value deviates too far from what the other pack sensors report. GM applies the same limits as for sensors A and B. In the 2016 and 2019 tables the threshold is more than 25 °C away from the average of the other sensors in 50 of 67 samples; the 2011 and 2013 two-mode tables use more than 15 °C in 90 of 100; the 2013 table 13OBDG05C uses 8.55 °C after a soak of more than 6 hours. All are Type B, two trips. The Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 includes P0ACB among codes corrected by software. Without a bulletin, compare all sensors after an overnight soak to see whether only sensor C stands out.
c: Sensor C drifted from its characteristic
Controller software flags the sensor falsely (GM Volt bulletin 18-NA-342)
Real temperature difference in the module monitored by sensor C
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Sensor C reads clearly off the others after a long soak
Possibly reduced charge and drive power

P0ACC.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor C Circuit Low
P0ACC.d: P0ACC sets when the signal of battery temperature sensor C drops below the valid voltage window. For the NTC sensors GM uses, that equals an impossibly hot reading, most often caused by a short to ground in the pack wiring. GM's thresholds for sensor C mirror those for B: above 160 °C in 8 of 10 samples in the 2016 and 2019 tables, above 95 °C in 30 of 40 in the two-mode tables of 2011 and 2013, and below 0.3 V, about 90 °C, in 7 of 10 in the 2013 table 13OBDG05C; always Type B, two trips. Bulletin 18-NA-342 lists P0ACC for the Chevrolet Volt and prescribes a software update first. After that, inspect the sensor C wiring and the sensing board for chafing or moisture.
c: Sensor C signal shorted to ground
Controller software setting the code falsely (Volt bulletin 18-NA-342)
Moisture at the sensing board connector
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Sensor C shows an implausibly high temperature
Reduced charging and electric drive power

P0ACD.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor C Circuit High
P0ACD.d: P0ACD indicates that battery temperature sensor C reports a voltage above its plausible range, which an NTC sensor translates into extreme cold. Common reasons are an open circuit, a pin backed out of the sensing board connector or a cracked thermistor. GM sets the code below -69 °C in 8 of 10 samples in its 2016 and 2019 tables, below -45 °C in 30 of 40 on the 2011 and 2013 two-mode hybrids, and above 4.63 V, about -45 °C, in 7 of 10 in the 2013 table 13OBDG05C; Type B, two trips. On the Chevrolet Volt, bulletin 18-NA-342 ties it to a false Battery Too Cold message and a reprogramming fix. A seemingly frozen pack is heavily limited in charge and discharge.
c: Open signal or return wire of sensor C
Controller software issue on the Volt (bulletin 18-NA-342)
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Battery too cold message in mild weather
Strongly reduced charging and electric power

P0ACE.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0ACE.d: P0ACE flags erratic behaviour of battery temperature sensor C, meaning the reading jumps faster than the heavy battery mass could ever warm or cool. In GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables the controller sums the absolute changes of the sensor value across a 10-sample window taken every 100 ms; a sum above 10 fails the window, and 4 failed windows out of 5 store the code as Type B, two trips. This is the same logic GM uses for sensors A and B. The older two-mode and 2013 programs do not list an erratic code for sensor C. Typical culprits are a loose terminal, a partly broken wire or a connector not fully latched after pack service. Several jumping sensors at once point to the sensing board.
c: Loose terminal or unlatched connector at sensor C
Partly broken sensor wire inside the pack
Fault on the battery sensing board affecting several inputs
s: Hybrid warning light that appears intermittently
Sensor C value jumps in live data
Occasional power limitation

P0ACF.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 3 Control Circuit/Open
P0ACF.d: Air-cooled traction batteries can use several blowers; P0ACF belongs to the third one and means the battery controller sees an open or otherwise invalid control line while it drives fan 3. CARB 1968.2 (e)(15.2.3)(B) requires the electrical inputs and outputs of the battery thermal management to be monitored like other comprehensive components. No manufacturer publicly documents this code; GM shows the method on fan 1 (P0A81): it checks the control voltage on the driver output and needs 16 failures before a Type B code is stored. Fan 1 and fan 2 have their own sets P0A81 and P0A96. Without the third blower the pack heats up faster, and power is limited.
c: Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at fan 3
Broken control wire between battery controller and fan 3
Fan motor or its built-in driver open internally
Fan output stage in the battery controller defective
s: Hybrid or EV system warning light, often with check engine light
Electric drive power reduced when the battery gets warm
No fan noise from the battery area when cooling is expected

P0AD0.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 3 Performance/Stuck Off
P0AD0.d: P0AD0 is a functional fault: the control line of battery fan 3 may be electrically fine, but the blower does not deliver what was commanded, or stays still. Depending on design, the controller compares fan speed feedback with the request, or, as a Honda patent describes, compares the expected battery temperature change for the known cooling capacity with the measured one. CARB asks for such a functional check of the battery cooling where feasible. No manufacturer publicly documents P0AD0 itself; circuit faults of the same fan are P0ACF, P0AD2 and P0AD3, the opposite case is P0AD1. The driver usually sees a hybrid warning and reduced power on hot days.
c: Fan intake or duct blocked by dirt, pet hair or objects (often under or beside a seat)
Worn bearings or debris slowing the fan wheel
Speed feedback signal from fan 3 missing or implausible
Weak 12 V supply or poor ground at the fan
s: Hybrid or EV system warning light
Power or regeneration limited after longer drives or in heat
Battery temperature rises faster than usual

P0AD1.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 3 Stuck On
P0AD1.d: P0AD1 is the counterpart to P0AD0: fan 3 of the traction battery keeps turning although the controller has switched it off or commanded a lower level. A speed feedback or the current in the fan circuit shows that the blower still runs. CARB 1968.2 requires the battery thermal management outputs to be checked for proper response to commands. No manufacturer publicly documents P0AD1; for fan 1 GM treats an unwanted speed above about 250 rpm with the fan off under its own code P0BC8. Typical causes are a driver stage stuck on or a short to supply voltage. Effects are an audible fan after shutdown and possible 12 V battery drain rather than a drivability problem.
c: Fan output stage in battery controller or fan module stuck on
Control wire chafed against a supply voltage
s: Battery fan audible after the vehicle is switched off
12 V battery discharged after standing
Hybrid or EV warning light

P0AD2.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 3 Control Circuit Low
P0AD2.d: P0AD2 reports that the control signal for battery fan 3 is pulled too low, typically a short to ground on the line between battery controller and blower. Such fans are mostly speed-controlled by a PWM duty cycle, as a Toyota patent on battery fan control explains. No manufacturer publicly documents P0AD2; GM sets the analogous fan 1 code P0A84 when the control voltage stays below 0.257 V with system voltage above 9.1 V, Type B with two trips. The open circuit is P0ACF, a short to voltage P0AD3. CARB requires these electrical checks for battery thermal components. Fan 3 then cannot be driven, and the battery may run warm with limited power.
c: Control wire chafed through to body ground
Internal short in fan 3 motor or its electronics
Moisture or spilled liquid in the fan connector
Output stage in the battery controller defective
s: Hybrid or EV system warning light, often with check engine light
Electric drive power reduced when the battery gets warm
No fan noise from the battery area when cooling is expected

P0AD3.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 3 Control Circuit High
P0AD3.d: With P0AD3 the battery controller finds the control line of cooling fan 3 at a voltage that is too high for the commanded state, pointing to a short to a supply voltage or a fan input that no longer pulls the line down. No manufacturer publicly documents this code; GM's analogous fan 1 code P0A85 trips when the control voltage exceeds 9 V while the fan is driven, Type B. Siblings: P0AD2 for the low side, P0ACF for an open line, P0AD1 if the fan keeps running. CARB 1968.2 calls for this circuit monitoring on battery thermal management parts. Depending on the fault the fan runs permanently or not at all, and the pack may be derated.
c: Control wire shorted to 12 V or another supply
Fan electronics no longer loading the control line
Bent or bridged pins in the fan connector
s: Hybrid or EV system warning light
Fan 3 runs constantly or not at all
Reduced electric power when the battery is warm

P0AD4.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Flow System Insufficient Air Flow
P0AD4.d: P0AD4 is a system-level check of air-cooled traction batteries: the controller concludes that too little air passes the cells, for example because the cell temperatures rise faster than the commanded fan level allows, as a Honda fan diagnosis patent describes. CARB 1968.2 asks for a functional check of the battery cooling performance where feasible. Stellantis lists P0AD4 for the 48 V eTorque battery of the Ram 1500 (TSBs 08-033/034/035-24, 2022-24) and cures some cases with a battery pack control module software update. Unlike the fan circuit codes, P0AD4 is often caused by a blocked intake or duct. Expect a warning lamp and limited assist or electric power.
c: Cabin air intake grille or duct of the battery blocked (bags, clothing, dust, pet hair)
Battery air filter clogged, where fitted
Battery controller software sets the code falsely (Ram eTorque, fixed by update)
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Reduced electric assist or start-stop not available
Battery fan runs loud for long periods

P0AD5.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Flow Valve A Control Circuit/Open
P0AD5.d: Some air-cooled battery packs route their cooling air through a motorized flap that switches between cabin air, recirculation or an outlet. P0AD5 means the battery controller finds the drive circuit of this valve A open or otherwise faulty. No manufacturer publicly documents P0AD5; the same component appears in Audi's Q5 hybrid (2012-15) bulletin, where the battery management module J841 works with the learned end stops of the air supply valve in the cooling module. CARB 1968.2 requires electrical monitoring of all battery thermal management outputs. Sibling codes are P0AD6 (range/performance), P0AD7 (low) and P0AD8 (high). The flap stays where it is, and the controller may cut electric operation.
c: Loose or corroded connector at the flap actuator
Broken wire in the actuator harness
Output stage in battery controller defective
s: Hybrid warning, electric drive may be switched off
Check engine light on
Battery temperature not controlled as usual

P0AD6.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Flow Valve A Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0AD6.d: P0AD6 flags that the air flow valve A of the battery cooling does not behave as expected: the circuit is intact, but position, travel or the learned end stops do not fit the command. Audi documents exactly this code as P0AD600 on the 2012-15 Q5 hybrid (TSB 2038152): a software error made the battery management module J841 lose the learned end stops of the air supply valve, electric and hybrid drive were disabled, and a software update to version 0543 fixed it. CARB 1968.2 calls for functional monitoring of battery thermal management. Pure circuit faults are P0AD5, P0AD7 and P0AD8. Besides software, a sticking flap or a slipping actuator can cause it.
c: Battery controller software loses learned end stops (Audi Q5 hybrid, fixed by update)
Flap binding from dirt or a deformed duct
Actuator gears or position feedback worn
End stops not relearned after battery or actuator work
s: Hybrid drive system error message in the cluster
Electric and hybrid operation no longer available
Check engine light on

P0AD7.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Flow Valve A Control Circuit Low
P0AD7.d: P0AD7 sets when the control circuit of the battery air flow valve A reads too low a voltage, usually a short to ground in the line or actuator. The valve is a motorized flap in the battery cooling duct, as in the Audi Q5 hybrid cooling module, whose bulletin covers the range/performance sibling P0AD6. No manufacturer publicly documents P0AD7 itself, so thresholds and debounce times are unknown. CARB 1968.2 requires battery thermal management outputs to be checked for circuit faults. Neighbours are P0AD5 (open) and P0AD8 (high). With the flap no longer movable, cooling may be impaired and the hybrid system may restrict electric operation.
c: Actuator control wire shorted to ground
Internal short in the flap actuator
s: Hybrid warning, electric drive may be switched off
Check engine light on
Battery temperature not controlled as usual

P0AD8.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Air Flow Valve A Control Circuit High
P0AD8.d: With P0AD8 the battery controller sees too high a voltage in the drive circuit of air flow valve A, typically a short to a supply voltage or an actuator that no longer draws current. The component is the motorized flap that directs cooling air through an air-cooled traction battery, documented for example in Audi's Q5 hybrid bulletin on the related code P0AD6. No manufacturer publicly documents P0AD8; exact limits are not published. CARB 1968.2 requires circuit monitoring of battery thermal management outputs. Compare P0AD7 for the low side and P0AD5 for an open circuit. The flap may stay in one position, so cooling and electric drive can be restricted.
c: Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Actuator no longer loading the circuit
Bridged or bent pins in the connector
s: Hybrid warning, electric drive may be switched off
Check engine light on
Battery temperature not controlled as usual

P0AD9.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Positive Contactor Control Circuit/Open
P0AD9.d: The positive main contactor connects the traction battery to the high-voltage bus; its coil is driven by the battery or hybrid controller. P0AD9 covers an open in this coil circuit. GM documents it in detail: in hybrid tables from model year 2011 the HPC2 sets it on open load during the commanded state, Type B. 2016-19 tables use a control voltage between 1.15 and 2.81 V with the contactor commanded off, 40 of 50 samples at 12.5 ms; 2019 versions also check coil current below 194 mA when on. CARB requires circuit monitoring of hybrid outputs. Low and high faults are P0ADB and P0ADC; a contactor stuck open is P0AA2. The car usually cannot go ready.
c: Open in the contactor coil or its pigtail inside the battery disconnect unit
Loose or corroded low-voltage connector at the battery disconnect unit
Broken control wire in the battery harness
High-side driver in the battery controller defective
s: Vehicle will not enter ready mode or start
Hybrid or EV warning light and check engine light
Charging not possible

P0ADA.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Positive Contactor Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0ADA.d: P0ADA describes a positive contactor coil circuit that is electrically present but does not behave plausibly: coil current, voltage or response time outside the expected window, for instance due to high resistance or an unstable PWM hold signal. No manufacturer publicly documents this code; GM, which details the positive contactor driver codes P0AD9, P0ADB and P0ADC with Type B logic and sample counters, does not list P0ADA. CARB 1968.2 requires functional and rationality checks of hybrid output components. It must be separated from the contact-side codes P0AA1 (stuck closed) and P0AA2 (stuck open). Drivers may see intermittent no-start or loss of ready mode.
c: High resistance in coil wiring or connector (corrosion, fretting)
Contactor coil degraded or partially shorted
Low 12 V supply during contactor closing
s: Vehicle will not enter ready mode or start
Hybrid or EV warning light and check engine light
Charging not possible

P0ADB.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Positive Contactor Control Circuit Low
P0ADB.d: P0ADB means the drive circuit of the positive main contactor reads too low, mostly a short to ground. GM uses it widely: 2016-19 tables set it when the control voltage stays under 5.35 V with the contactor commanded on, 13 of 16 samples, Type B. The 2013 eAssist battery controller checks the low-side driver in the off state for a short to ground or an open circuit, 3 of 5 samples, two trips. Audi lists P0ADB00 in battery management 2 (J1120) of 2019-22 A6 to Q8 models with a software fix (TSB 2066205), and Dodge names it for the 2024 Charger EV (TSB 08-071-25). The battery then cannot be connected, so the vehicle will not become ready.
c: Coil control wire shorted to ground
Battery controller software sets the code (Audi, Dodge bulletins)
Driver stage in the battery controller defective
s: Vehicle does not start; multiple warnings in the cluster
Hybrid or EV warning light
Charging not possible

P0ADC.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Positive Contactor Control Circuit High
P0ADC.d: P0ADC indicates that the positive contactor drive circuit carries too much voltage for the commanded state, usually a short to battery voltage. In GM's 2016-19 hybrid tables the driver output, with the contactor commanded off, reads between 5.27 and 19.7 V for 40 of 50 samples at 12.5 ms, Type B with two trips. The 2013 eAssist controller sets it for a short to power on the low-side driver in the on state, 3 of 5 samples. CARB requires such circuit monitoring for hybrid components. Siblings are P0AD9 (open) and P0ADB (low). A short to power can energize the coil unintentionally, so the contactor may not open when it should.
c: Coil control wire shorted to 12 V
Damaged harness or connector at the battery disconnect unit
Driver stage in the battery controller shorted
s: Hybrid or EV warning light
High-voltage system disabled, vehicle not ready
Possible related stuck-closed codes

P0ADD.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Negative Contactor Control Circuit/Open
P0ADD.d: The negative main contactor closes the return path of the traction battery; P0ADD reports an open in its coil drive circuit. GM documents the code in parallel to the positive side: tables since model year 2011 detect open load in the HPC2 and store it after two trips; 2016-19 tables evaluate a control voltage between 1.15 and 2.81 V while off, 40 of 50 samples, Type B, and 2019 tables add a coil current check below 194 mA when on. CARB 1968.2 covers this circuit monitoring of hybrid components. Related codes are P0ADF and P0AE0 for low and high, P0AA5 for a contactor stuck open, P0AD9 for the positive side. Without this contactor the HV system stays off.
c: Open in negative contactor coil or its pigtail
Loose or corroded connector at the battery disconnect unit
Broken control wire in the battery harness
Driver in the battery controller defective
s: Vehicle will not enter ready mode or start
Hybrid or EV warning light and check engine light
Charging not possible

P0ADE.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Negative Contactor Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0ADE.d: P0ADE is set when the coil circuit of the negative main contactor works electrically but its values are implausible, such as coil current or hold voltage out of range or a slow response after the command. No manufacturer publicly documents this code; GM, whose tables cover the negative contactor driver codes P0ADD, P0ADF and P0AE0 in detail, does not use P0ADE. CARB 1968.2 requires rationality and functional checks on hybrid output components. The contact-side faults P0AA4 (stuck closed) and P0AA5 (stuck open) are separate diagnoses. Possible effects are an intermittent failure to reach ready mode or charge.
c: High resistance in coil wiring or connector
s: Vehicle will not enter ready mode or start
Hybrid or EV warning light and check engine light
Charging not possible

P0ADF.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Negative Contactor Control Circuit Low
P0ADF.d: P0ADF reports that the drive circuit of the negative main contactor is pulled too low, typically a short to ground in the coil line. GM documents the code in its 2016-19 hybrid tables: control voltage below 5.35 V while the contactor is commanded on, 13 of 16 samples at 12.5 ms (20 of 25 in one 2016 group), Type B with two trips, enabled above about 9 to 10 V on the 12 V system. CARB 1968.2 requires this kind of circuit monitoring for hybrid outputs. Counterparts are P0ADD (open), P0AE0 (high) and, on the positive side, P0ADB. As the contactor cannot close properly, the high-voltage system does not come up and the vehicle will not drive or charge.
c: Coil control wire shorted to ground
Moisture in the battery disconnect unit connector
Driver in the battery controller defective
s: Vehicle will not enter ready mode or start
Hybrid or EV warning light and check engine light
Charging not possible

P0AE0.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Negative Contactor Control Circuit High
P0AE0.d: P0AE0 is stored when the negative contactor drive circuit shows too high a voltage for its state, which mostly means a short to battery voltage. GM's 2016-19 hybrid tables set it with the contactor commanded off and the driver output between 5.27 and 19.7 V for 40 of 50 samples at 12.5 ms, Type B, two trips. CARB 1968.2 requires hybrid output components to be monitored for such circuit faults. Siblings are P0ADD (open) and P0ADF (low); the positive side equivalent is P0ADC. A coil energized by a short could keep the contactor closed, so a stuck-closed code P0AA4 may follow. The controller usually disables the high-voltage system.
c: Coil control wire shorted to 12 V
Damaged harness or connector at the battery disconnect unit
Driver stage in the battery controller shorted
s: Hybrid or EV warning light
High-voltage system disabled, vehicle not ready
Possible additional stuck-closed code

P0AE1.d: Before the main contactors close, a precharge contactor routes battery current through a resistor so the inverter capacitors fill slowly instead of drawing a damaging inrush. P0AE1 is the general fault of this precharge path when it is not split into stuck closed (P0AE2), stuck open (P0AE3) or a driver fault (P0AE4 to P0AE7). Honda lists P0AE1 as a bypass contactor malfunction in bulletins 20-030 (2012-15 Civic Hybrid) and 20-021 (2013 ILX Hybrid); there a cracked solder joint in the motor power inverter is the cause and the whole inverter is replaced. Mercedes-Benz names P0AE173 on the G 580 with EQ technology after unplugging the AC charger too early. Expect no ready mode or no charging.
c: Defective solder joint in the motor power inverter (Honda IMA)
Precharge contactor or precharge resistor failed
Fault logged by battery controller software after an interrupted charging sequence
Wiring or connector fault in the contactor circuit
s: Hybrid or EV system warning in the cluster
Vehicle does not become ready to drive
Charging not possible

P0AE2.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor Circuit Stuck Closed
P0AE2.d: P0AE2 means the precharge path conducts although it should be open, for example welded contacts or a precharge switch that no longer turns off. GM's 2011 Volt table checks it once per precharge event: if the bus voltage already exceeds 80 % of pack voltage before precharge begins, the precharge FET is judged stuck closed, 4 of 4 samples, Type A with MIL after one trip. Mitsubishi lists P0AE2 as charging contactor seizure on the 2012 i-MiEV (TSB-12-54-014). Audi names it for the 2022 e-tron GT with a software fix, and Dodge and Jeep list P0AE2-00 for the 2025 Charger EV and 2024 Wagoneer S, where a battery pack replacement may be required. The car may refuse to start.
c: Precharge contactor contacts welded or precharge switch shorted
Battery controller software sets the code falsely (Audi, Stellantis bulletins)
Contactor driver held on by a short to power
Bus voltage not discharged before the next precharge
s: Vehicle does not become ready to drive
MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
Wrench symbol or service message in the cluster

P0AE3.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor Circuit Stuck Open
P0AE3.d: P0AE3 is set when the precharge path does not conduct after it has been commanded closed, so the bus voltage fails to rise and the main contactors are not allowed to close. GM documents several cases: preliminary information PIC6165A for the 2016-17 Chevrolet Volt describes a rare P0AE3 in cool weather right after a completed charge, without driveability effects; parts should not be replaced, a new calibration followed, and the MIL goes out after three clean drive cycles. GM bulletin 23-NA-151 lists P0AE3 among high-priority codes on Ultium EVs that call for battery stability checks. Audi includes P0AE300 for the 2022 e-tron GT. Unlike P0AE2, the contacts stay open; a slow precharge is P0C78.
c: Battery controller calibration sets the code under certain conditions (GM Volt, Audi)
Precharge contactor contacts burnt or coil not pulling in
Precharge resistor or its fuse open
Internal fault in the battery disconnect unit
s: Vehicle does not become ready to drive
MIL or service engine soon light on
No battery charge level shown after switching on

P0AE4.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor A Control Circuit/Open
P0AE4.d: P0AE4 concerns the circuit that drives the coil of precharge contactor A, not its contacts. GM uses it in many hybrid and EV tables, with changing logic: the 2016 and 2019 OBDG02 tables look for an open high-side driver circuit, a control voltage between 1.15 and 2.81 V while commanded off, 40 of 50 samples at 12.5 ms, Type B, two trips. The 2019 OBDG01 version also catches a short to power while off and a coil current below 194 mA while on. The 2011 Volt table instead flags a short to battery voltage in the off state, Type A, one trip. With the coil not driven, precharge cannot start and the high-voltage system stays off. Low and high variants are P0AE6 and P0AE7.
c: Open control wire or loose connector at the contactor coil
Control wire shorted to 12 V (GM 2011 and 2019 logic)
Driver stage in the battery or hybrid controller defective
s: Vehicle does not become ready to drive
MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
Charging not possible

P0AE5.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor A Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0AE5.d: P0AE5 reports that the precharge function works electrically but does not deliver the expected result, so the controller judges the circuit implausible. Ford documents it in special service message SSM 47129: 2013-18 C-MAX and Fusion Hybrid and Energi models and the MKZ Hybrid may not start, with P0AE5 stored in the battery energy control module. When pinpoint tests show that the DC/DC converter, the cabin coolant heater or the A/C compressor has a low internal resistance on its high-voltage side, Ford replaces only that component, not the battery junction box. A load that drags the bus down keeps the precharge from reaching its target. Open, low and high driver faults are P0AE4, P0AE6 and P0AE7.
c: High-voltage consumer with low internal resistance (DC/DC converter, coolant heater, A/C compressor)
Precharge resistor degraded or wrong value
Precharge contactor responding slowly or with high contact resistance
s: Vehicle does not start or become ready
Red warning triangle or hybrid warning in the cluster
Possible additional codes from the faulty high-voltage consumer

P0AE6.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor A Control Circuit Low
P0AE6.d: P0AE6 means the control line of precharge contactor A is pulled too low, usually a short to ground. GM documents it in several programs. The 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables test the high-side driver while the contactor is commanded on and fail it below 5.35 V, 13 of 16 samples at 12.5 ms, Type B with two trips, enabled above 10.2 V system voltage. GM's 2013 eAssist battery controller uses a low-side driver and flags low voltage in the off state, which there points to a short to ground or an open circuit, 3 of 5 samples at 50 ms, Type B. CARB requires such circuit checks on hybrid outputs. Because the coil cannot pull in, precharge never starts; the positive main contactor equivalent is P0ADB.
c: Control wire chafed and shorted to ground
Open circuit on low-side driven designs (GM eAssist)
Driver stage in the battery controller defective
s: Vehicle does not become ready to drive
MIL and hybrid warning on
Engine start or electric drive unavailable

P0AE7.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor A Control Circuit High
P0AE7.d: P0AE7 is stored when the control line of precharge contactor A carries too much voltage for its commanded state, typically a short to the 12 V supply. In GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables the high-side driver output reads between 5.27 and 19.7 V while the contactor is commanded off, 40 of 50 samples at 12.5 ms, Type B, two trips. GM's 2013 eAssist controller looks for a short to power on its low-side driver in the on state, 3 of 5 samples at 50 ms, Type B. A coil energized by a short may keep the precharge path closed when it should be open, so P0AE2 can follow. CARB requires circuit monitoring of such hybrid outputs. The negative and positive main contactor counterparts are P0AE0 and P0ADC.
c: Control wire shorted to 12 V supply
Driver stage stuck on in the battery controller
s: Vehicle may not start or become ready
MIL and hybrid warning on
Possible additional stuck-closed code P0AE2

P0AE8.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit
P0AE8.d: Battery temperature sensor D is a further thermistor inside the high-voltage pack; GM's Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists the matching codes as temperature sensor 4 of nine. P0AE8 is the general circuit code for it, used when the controller finds an electrical fault without classifying it as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's hybrid tables report the more specific siblings P0AE9 to P0AEC instead. CARB requires temperature inputs of hybrid batteries to be monitored for circuit faults. With one value missing, the controller has a gap in its temperature picture and usually limits charge and discharge power. The sensor sits on a module or sensing board inside the pack, so checks require high-voltage safety procedures.
c: Poor contact or damaged wire between sensor D and sensing board
Fault in the battery controller input stage
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning
Reduced electric power and regeneration
Further battery sensor codes may be stored

P0AE9.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit Range/Performance
P0AE9.d: P0AE9 is the plausibility check for battery temperature sensor D, GM's sensor 4: its reading is compared with the other pack sensors. In GM's 2016 and 2019 tables it fails when the value is more than 25 °C away from the average of the others in 50 of 67 samples; the two-mode hybrid tables of 2011 and 2013 use more than 15 °C in 90 of 100; the eAssist table 13OBDG05C allows 8.55 °C after a long module off time; GM's 2018 table uses 20 °C for 5 s within 6.7 s. All are Type B, two trips. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 counts P0AE9 among sensor codes that set falsely in cold weather and fixes them by reprogramming. Otherwise a drifting sensor or a real hot spot in one module is the likely cause.
c: Temperature sensor D drifting out of tolerance
Genuine local temperature difference in one battery module
Increased contact resistance in the sensor circuit
s: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips
Battery Too Cold message despite mild weather (Volt)
Reduced charge and electric drive power

P0AEA.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit Low
P0AEA.d: P0AEA means the voltage of battery temperature sensor D is below its valid range. GM uses NTC thermistors with a pull-up on the sensing board, so a low voltage reads as an extremely hot cell, usually from a short to ground. Thresholds vary: above 160 °C in 8 of 10 samples in the 2016 and 2019 tables; above 95 °C in 30 of 40 on the 2011 and 2013 two-mode hybrids; below 0.3 V, about 90 °C, in 7 of 10 in the eAssist table 13OBDG05C; above 87.5 °C for 1.4 s within 2 s in a 2018 controller. All are Type B, two trips. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists P0AEA among codes that can set falsely and calls for a software update first. A genuinely hot pack would trip lower limits earlier, so treat it as electrical.
c: Sensor D signal wire shorted to ground
Moisture or damage on the battery sensing board
s: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips
Charge and drive power strongly limited
Battery cooling running more than usual

P0AEB.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit High
P0AEB.d: P0AEB reports that battery temperature sensor D delivers a voltage above its valid range. For GM's NTC sensors this reads as extreme cold, pointing to an open wire, a backed-out pin at the sensing board or a cracked thermistor. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables set it below -69 °C in 8 of 10 samples, the 2011 and 2013 two-mode hybrids below -45 °C in 30 of 40, the eAssist table 13OBDG05C above 4.63 V, about -45 °C, in 7 of 10, and a 2018 controller below -40 °C for 1.4 s within 2 s; all Type B, two trips. On the Chevrolet Volt, bulletin 18-NA-342 links such codes to a Battery Too Cold message above -25 °C ambient and prescribes reprogramming. A pack the controller believes frozen gets strict charge and power limits.
c: Open circuit or unplugged connector at sensor D
s: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips
Battery Too Cold message (Volt)
Charging and electric drive restricted

P0AEC.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0AEC.d: P0AEC flags erratic behaviour of battery temperature sensor D: the reading jumps faster than the heavy battery mass could ever warm or cool. GM documents the method in its 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables. The controller sums the absolute changes of the sensor value across a 10-sample window taken every 100 ms; a sum above 10 fails the window, and 4 failed windows out of 5 store the code as Type B, two trips. GM applies the same logic to sensors A to C. The older two-mode and eAssist tables list no erratic code for sensor D. Typical culprits are a loose terminal, a partly broken wire or a connector not fully latched after pack service. If several sensors jump at once, suspect the sensing board rather than the individual thermistor.
c: Loose terminal or connector not fully latched at sensor D
Partly broken or chafed sensor wire
Fault on the battery sensing board
s: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips, may go out again
Jumping battery temperature in live data
Occasional power limitation

P0AED.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0AED.d: The inverter of an electric drive motor carries thermistors near its power switches so the controller can derate before the IGBTs overheat. In GM's hybrid tables, inverter temperature sensor A is the phase U sensor of the inverter for motor A. P0AED is the general circuit code for it, used for an electrical fault that is not classified as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM reports the specific siblings P0AEE, P0AEF and P0AF0 instead. CARB requires monitoring of hybrid components and their sensors for circuit faults. Without a valid inverter temperature the controller has to assume the worst and usually limits motor torque. The sensor is built into the power inverter module, so repair often means replacing that unit.
c: Internal fault of the sensor inside the power inverter module
Corroded or loose connector at the inverter module
Software fault in the motor control processor
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine lamp
Reduced electric drive power
Possible loss of electric drive

P0AEE.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0AEE.d: P0AEE checks whether inverter temperature sensor A reads sensibly. GM's 2016 to 2019 tables compare it after a cold soak with an average temperature of the vehicle; more than 20 °C apart sets Type B, two trips. The 2011 Volt compares it with the other power electronics sensors (20 °C, Type A), the 2013 two-mode trucks after 360 minutes off (15 °C), eAssist with module and MGU temperatures (20 °C). GM bulletin PIC6303A notes that on Volt, Malibu and LaCrosse with 5ET50 the code alone triggers no remedy; the inverter is only replaced with P0AC4. Audi fixes P0AEE00 on Q5 and A7 e quattro by software, and Honda lists it among inverter faults of the 2012-15 Civic Hybrid with extended warranty.
c: Controller software error (Audi Q5/A7 e quattro bulletin)
Inverter temperature sensor A drifting out of tolerance
Failing power inverter module (e.g. Honda MPI solder joints)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, often without drivability change
Drive system fault warning (Audi)
Vehicle may not start in hybrid mode

P0AEF.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0AEF.d: P0AEF means the signal of inverter temperature sensor A is below its valid range. GM describes it as an NTC thermistor with a pull-up on the sensing board, so a low voltage reads as an impossibly hot inverter, usually a short to ground or an internal sensor fault. GM's thresholds: above 170 °C for 2.5 of 3.5 s, Type B, in the 2016 to 2019 hybrid tables; above 159 °C, Type A, one trip, in another 2019 table; above 150 °C on eAssist; above 130 °C, Type A, on the 2011 Volt; above 125 °C, Type B, on the 2011 and 2013 two-mode trucks. Stellantis lists P0AEF-11 for the 2026 Jeep Compass PHEV outside the US among codes behind an Electric Traction System Fault and a no-start, repaired by replacing the inverter.
c: Shorted sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module
Sensor signal shorted to ground in external wiring, where present
Moisture or coolant inside the inverter housing
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning
Electric drive power cut back strongly
Vehicle may not start (Jeep Compass PHEV)

P0AF0.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0AF0.d: P0AF0 reports a signal from inverter temperature sensor A above its valid range, which for an NTC sensor reads as an extremely cold inverter: open wire, lost ground or a broken sensor. GM's 2016 to 2019 hybrid tables set it below -50 °C for 2.6 of 3.65 s, but only after at least 90 s of inverter warm-up at 20 Nm or more, so a really cold car does not trigger it; Type B, two trips. The 2011 Volt uses below -58 °C (Type A), eAssist below -70 °C and the two-mode trucks below -40 °C (Type B). Kia's 2025 Sorento Hybrid bulletin lists P0AF0 with P0A3C and P1B77 after intermittent motor operation during engine clutch learning and fixes it with a motor control unit update.
c: Open sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module
Motor control unit software (Kia Sorento Hybrid 2025)
Loose or corroded connector at the inverter
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning
Reduced electric drive power
Traction motor noise or inoperative A/C (Kia)

P0AF1.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0AF1.d: P0AF1 is meant for an inverter temperature sensor A signal that jumps or drops out briefly instead of failing permanently. Inverter heat sinks are liquid-cooled and change temperature smoothly, so sudden steps point to a contact problem or an internal fault in the sensing circuit. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's hybrid tables cover sensor A only with the plausibility, low and high codes P0AEE, P0AEF and P0AF0. GM's method for erratic battery sensors, such as P0AEC, sums signal changes over 10-sample windows and fails after 4 of 5 bad windows, which shows how such a check usually works. CARB requires hybrid sensor inputs to be monitored for this kind of fault. Freeze-frame data help, since the fault often comes and goes.
c: Loose or corroded connector at the inverter module
Intermittent fault inside the power inverter module
Electrical interference on the sensor signal
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Brief power reductions while driving
Jumping inverter temperature in live data

P0AF2.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P0AF2.d: Inverter temperature sensor B is, in GM's hybrid tables, the phase U thermistor of the second inverter, the one that drives motor B in two-motor systems. P0AF2 is its general circuit code for an electrical fault that the controller does not narrow down to low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's tables report the specific siblings P0AF3, P0AF4 and P0AF5 instead. CARB requires monitoring of hybrid components and their sensor circuits. Without a valid temperature the controller cannot protect the power switches of inverter B and usually limits that motor's torque. Whether a vehicle uses sensor B at all depends on its layout, so read the full code list and check the inverter connectors.
c: Internal fault of the sensor inside the power inverter module
Corroded or loose connector at the inverter module
Software fault in the motor control processor
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine lamp
Reduced electric drive or generator power
Higher fuel consumption in hybrid operation

P0AF3.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0AF3.d: P0AF3 is the plausibility test for inverter temperature sensor B, the phase U sensor of GM's motor B inverter. In the 2016 to 2019 tables the sensor is compared after a cold soak with a calculated average vehicle temperature; a difference above 20 °C sets the code, Type B, two trips. The 2011 Volt compares it with the other power electronics sensors at 20 °C, Type A, and the 2011 and 2013 two-mode trucks after 360 minutes off at 15 °C, Type B. GM bulletin PIC6303A lists P0AF3 with P0AEE and the other inverter thermistor codes on 2016-18 Volt, Malibu, LaCrosse and Regal with the 5ET50 drive: alone they cause no noticeable effect, and the inverter is replaced only if P0AC4 set at the same time.
c: Inverter temperature sensor B drifting out of tolerance
Uneven inverter coolant flow after soak
s: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips
Often no noticeable drivability change
Further inverter temperature codes may be stored

P0AF4.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P0AF4.d: P0AF4 reports a signal of inverter temperature sensor B below the valid range. GM uses an NTC thermistor with a pull-up, so a low voltage reads as an inverter far hotter than possible, usually from a short to ground or an internal sensor fault in the motor B inverter. GM's thresholds: above 170 °C for 2.5 of 3.5 s, Type B, two trips, in the 2016 to 2019 hybrid tables; above 159 °C, Type A, one trip, in another 2019 table; above 130 °C, Type A, on the 2011 Volt; above 125 °C, Type B, on the 2011 and 2013 two-mode trucks. A genuine overheat is reported separately as an over-temperature code such as P0A3D or P0C14. Because the sensor sits inside the inverter, the fix is usually the inverter assembly.
c: Shorted sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module
Sensor signal shorted to ground in external wiring, where present
Moisture or coolant inside the inverter housing
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning
Motor B power strongly limited
Reduced hybrid assist and regeneration

P0AF5.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
P0AF5.d: P0AF5 means inverter temperature sensor B delivers a voltage above its valid range. For GM's NTC sensor that equals an implausibly cold inverter, so an open circuit, a lost ground or a cracked thermistor is likely. In GM's 2016 to 2019 tables the code sets below -50 °C for 2.6 of 3.65 s, but only once the inverter has run at least 90 s at 20 Nm or more, which rules out a genuinely cold start; Type B, two trips. The 2011 Volt uses below -58 °C with Type A, one trip; the 2011 and 2013 two-mode trucks use below -40 °C, Type B. Until the value is valid, the controller protects inverter B with substitute values and may reduce motor B power. Check connectors at the inverter before condemning the unit.
c: Open sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module
Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the inverter
s: Malfunction indicator lamp after two trips
Reduced motor B power
Implausibly cold inverter temperature in live data

P0AF6.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0AF6.d: P0AF6 targets an inverter temperature sensor B signal that jumps or drops out briefly. Since the heat sink of the motor B inverter is liquid-cooled and warms or cools gradually, abrupt changes in the reading indicate a contact problem or an intermittent fault in the sensing circuit rather than real temperature. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's hybrid tables only list P0AF3, P0AF4 and P0AF5 for sensor B. For erratic battery temperature sensors such as P0AEC, GM sums the signal changes over 10-sample windows and fails after 4 of 5 bad windows, a likely model for this check. CARB requires sensor inputs of hybrid systems to be checked for erratic behaviour. Watch live data while gently moving the inverter harness.
c: Loose or corroded connector at the inverter module
Intermittent fault inside the power inverter module
Electrical interference on the sensor signal
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Brief reductions of motor B power
Jumping inverter temperature in live data

P0AF7.t: 14 Volt Power Module Internal Temperature Too High
P0AF7.d: The 14 V power module is the DC/DC converter that feeds the 12 V network from the high-voltage battery in hybrids and EVs. P0AF7 reports that its internal temperature has exceeded the protection limit, a real overheat rather than a sensor circuit fault. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM's 2013 eAssist table shows how the same module is watched: its Accessory Power Module has two temperature sensors with their own circuit codes, and the separate code P0C32 compares sensor 1 with a thermal model and fails if they differ by more than 15 °C. CARB requires monitoring of hybrid components. Common causes are a blocked cooling path, a weak coolant pump or fan, or a constantly high 12 V load. The module then derates its output, so the 12 V battery may run down.
c: Restricted cooling, weak coolant pump or failed cooling fan
Sustained high 12 V load or weak 12 V battery
Internal fault of the DC/DC converter
s: Warning lamp or 12 V charging warning
Low 12 V voltage, flickering lights
Comfort consumers switched off

P0AF8.d: P0AF8 compares the battery pack voltage reported by the battery controller with an independent measurement on the high-voltage bus. GM calls it system voltage correlation: with the contactors closed, the 2019 tables fail it when the pack reading differs from the inverter bus voltage by more than 13.95 V, or from the charger bus voltage by more than 14.95 V, 400 of 500 samples at 25 ms, Type A. The 2011 Volt table uses 12 V and Type A, the 2013 eAssist table 5.77 V against the motor controller, Type B. GM's Saturn Vue Hybrid PIP4005A links P0AF8 with P0AFB to a loose negative battery cable, and Volt PIC6089B mentions it with low 12 V system faults. P0AFA and P0AFB judge the voltage level itself.
c: Loose or arcing high-voltage battery cable connection
Pack or bus voltage sensing circuit inaccurate
Low 12 V supply or loose 12 V power fuse affecting the measuring modules
High resistance in a pack fuse or main contactor
s: MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
Battery saver or low battery message
Intermittent no crank or reduced hybrid power

P0AF9.d: P0AF9 is meant for a traction battery voltage that fluctuates more than load changes can explain, for example through a loose terminal, an intermittent contactor or a cell group that collapses under load. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM, for instance, covers system voltage with P0AF8 (correlation), P0AFA and P0AFB (low and high), and reports uneven cell groups as P0BBE pack voltage variation, which bulletin 19-NA-117 ties to degraded cells in the Volt and ELR. CARB requires hybrid battery inputs to be monitored for circuit and rationality faults. Typical effects are intermittent power limits and warnings; check high-voltage connections and cell voltages under load.
c: Loose high-voltage terminal or busbar connection
Degraded cell group collapsing under load
s: Intermittent hybrid or EV warning
Sudden power reductions while driving
Code may come and go without lasting symptoms

P0AFA.d: P0AFA protects the traction battery from deep discharge: the pack voltage, or in some versions any cell voltage, has fallen below a temperature-dependent limit. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables set it after 320 of 400 samples (about 10 s) for the pack or 112 of 140 for a cell, Type A, and latch it so that only a technician command can clear it. GM bulletins name causes: degraded cell groups in 2011-15 Volt and ELR (19-NA-117), a blown fuse in the Bolt EV manual disconnect lever (18-NA-225), cell contamination in the 2015 Spark EV (17-NA-131) and repeated cranking that empties the Malibu Hybrid pack (PIC6229). A Ram eTorque parts notice names it for the 48 V power pack. Expect a no-start.
c: Pack drained by repeated failed engine starts or long standing
Open high-voltage fuse or manual disconnect
Loose or high-resistance ground on 48 V systems
s: Vehicle does not start; restart blocked while the code is latched
Reduced or lost propulsion before the no-start
Plug-in charging not possible

P0AFB.d: P0AFB guards against overcharging: the pack voltage, or a single cell, exceeds a temperature-dependent upper limit. GM's 2016 and 2019 tables use 320 of 400 samples (about 10 s) for the pack and 112 of 140 for a cell, Type A, and latch the code until a technician clears it by command; the 2011 Volt table also uses Type A. On the 2007-09 Saturn Vue Hybrid, GM's PIP4005A finds P0AFB together with P0AF8 caused by a loose negative battery cable. Mercedes-Benz uses P0AFB00 on 48 V starter-alternator systems for an on-board voltage that is too high, with software fixes for M256 engines, S-Class and GLE/GLS. Toyota's Prius Prime tech tip uses P0AFB11 with a current sensor text.
c: Loose or arcing battery cable causing voltage spikes
Control unit software allows overvoltage (Mercedes 48 V bulletins)
Cell imbalance so that one cell overcharges
Faulty voltage sensing reporting too high a value
s: Hybrid system or MIL warning
Start-stop or regenerative braking disabled
Possible no crank on mild hybrids

P0AFC.d: Some hybrid packs carry a separate sensor module that measures block voltages and passes them to the battery controller; Toyota calls it the battery voltage sensor or battery smart unit. P0AFC reports a fault of this module itself, such as a failed self-check or disturbed data transfer. Toyota documents it for the 2012-2015 Camry Hybrid in tech tip T-TT-0359-15 (repair manual entry P0AFC-123): an aftermarket antenna in the trunk, for example for CB radio, can set the code, and relocating it is the first step before following the regular diagnosis. CARB requires hybrid battery inputs to be monitored. Without valid block voltages the hybrid system usually shuts down or limits power.
c: Radio interference from an aftermarket antenna near the battery (Toyota Camry Hybrid)
Battery voltage sensor module internally defective
Supply or communication wiring of the sensor module faulty
s: MIL and check hybrid system warning on
Hybrid drive disabled or reduced
Code may return when the radio transmitter is used

P0AFD.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Temperature Too Low
P0AFD.d: P0AFD indicates that the traction battery is colder than its permitted operating range. At very low temperatures cell resistance rises and charging risks lithium plating, so the controller restricts or blocks charging and discharging. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
