Cell or NiMH block on channel S actually discharged
s: MIL and hybrid or EV warning message
Restricted power, engine may run more often on hybrids

P0B98.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense S Circuit High
P0B98.d: P0B98 marks a sense S value that is too high to be a cell voltage. The thresholds vary with the battery chemistry and controller: GM's 2016 Volt and 2019 battery controllers flag 4.8 V or more after 1.4 s in 2 s (Type A), the 16OBDG02 programme 4.90 V in 14 of 18 samples (Type A), and the eAssist mild hybrid more than 4.65 V in 7 of 10 samples with the 12 V supply above 8.8 V (Type B). On the 2012 two-mode trucks S is NiMH block 19 and its limit is 23 V, 15 of 20 samples, Type B. Like the low test, the high test waits until open sense line faults are ruled out. The fix is usually wiring or the monitoring board; a truly overcharged cell is rare but must be excluded.
c: Sense lead S shorted to a higher cell or busbar
Measuring chip reading channel S incorrectly
Real overvoltage of the cell or block on channel S
s: MIL and service hybrid system message
Charging and regeneration limited

P0B99.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense S Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0B99.d: P0B99 is the erratic variant within the sense S group. A public manufacturer description does not exist. GM's tables cover channel S from the 2011 Volt via the 2012 two-mode trucks and eAssist to the 2019 controllers, yet only with circuit, range, low and high codes (P0B95 to P0B98). CARB 1968.2 obliges manufacturers to monitor battery voltage sensors of a hybrid storage system for circuit and rationality faults and to separate the fault codes by replaceable unit, which is why J2012 reserves this slot. Should a vehicle set it, the technician would look for a sense S connection that works most of the time but breaks briefly, typically a fretting terminal or a cracked solder joint on the board.
c: Fretting corrosion on the terminal of sense lead S
Cracked solder joint for channel S on the monitoring board
Harness chafing that only shorts under movement
s: Sporadic hybrid warning without a pattern
Code often stored as history, hard to reproduce

P0B9A.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit
P0B9A.d: P0B9A is the open-circuit code for sense T, the twentieth cell channel. GM uses it only on lithium-ion packs. The 2011 Volt compares adjacent cells for a difference above 1 V and checks the busbar cap voltage against 0.7 V; the 2016 Volt and ELR raise the adjacent-cell limit to 1.3 V, add a balancing-gate test below 36 mV and decide within 0.6 s, and the 2019 controller keeps those values but stretches the window to 0.8 s of 1.6 s, Type A in both cases. The 2012 two-mode trucks also have a channel T, their last nickel-metal hydride block 20, yet their tables carry range, low and high codes for it and no circuit code. A genuinely open lead usually means opening the high-voltage pack.
c: Open sense lead T at the cell tab or connector
Poor busbar or splice joint in the channel T path
Monitoring board input for channel T failed
s: MIL, hybrid or EV system warning
Ready mode or charging blocked

P0B9B.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit Range/Performance
P0B9B.d: On the 2012 two-mode trucks sense T is block 20, the last of their twenty nickel-metal hydride blocks, and P0B9B shows how GM handles the missing neighbour: block 20 alone is multiplied by twenty and compared with the pack voltage, and a gap above 70 V in 160 of 170 samples sets the code as Type B. All other channels there use a pair of blocks. On lithium-ion packs the code means that cell T does not follow the pack average: the 2019 hybrid processor demands 0.005 V of movement when the average shifts by more than 0.022 V (35 of 40 samples, Type A), the 2016 Volt the same with a 7 s in 8 s window, and eAssist half the average movement in 20 of 40 samples, Type B.
c: Channel T measurement stuck or sluggish
Block 20 voltage diverging from pack voltage on two-mode NiMH packs
Faulty pack voltage reference used for the comparison
s: MIL, drivability usually unchanged
Hybrid assist or EV range slightly reduced

P0B9C.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit Low
P0B9C.d: P0B9C signals that sense T reads too low. On the 2012 two-mode trucks this is block 20, and because no block 21 exists the low test there looks at block 20 alone: below 2 V in 15 of 20 samples, Type B, while channels R and S each need their upper neighbour to read low as well. GM's lithium-ion controllers from the 2016 Volt to 2019 work with 0.2 V or less for 1.4 s within 2 s, Type A, the 16OBDG02 programme with under 0.20 V in 14 of 18 samples, and the eAssist mild hybrid with 1.4 V in 7 of 10 samples, Type B. Open sense line faults are evaluated first. For the driver the result is a warning and reduced power until the cause is repaired.
c: Sense lead T shorted to ground or a lower potential
Weak or discharged NiMH block 20 on two-mode packs
Failed measuring input for channel T
s: MIL and hybrid warning
Reduced power, engine may not shut off on hybrids

P0B9D.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit High
P0B9D.d: If sense T reports more voltage than its cell can hold, the battery controller stores P0B9D. GM documents it on several systems. The 2019 battery energy control module and the 2016 Volt set it at 4.8 V or above for 1.4 s within 2 s, Type A, and only when no open sense line fault is pending. The 16OBDG02 programme with a dedicated battery sensor module uses 4.90 V in 14 of 18 samples. The eAssist mild hybrid sets it above 4.65 V in 7 of 10 samples, Type B. In the 2012 two-mode trucks the channel is block 20, the final NiMH block, with a limit of 23 V and 15 of 20 samples, Type B. Most such readings come from wiring touching a higher potential or a faulty measuring input.
c: Sense lead T shorted to a higher cell or busbar
Measuring input for channel T drifting high
Cell or block T genuinely overcharged
s: MIL and service hybrid or EV system message
Charging power reduced

P0B9E.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0B9E.d: P0B9E would describe a sense T signal that flickers. It lacks any public manufacturer documentation. Even the 2012 two-mode trucks, whose last NiMH block is channel T, monitor it only for range, low and high, and GM's lithium-ion controllers add a circuit test but no intermittent one. The requirement behind the whole code family comes from CARB 1968.2: battery voltage sensors of a hybrid energy storage system are monitored components, and manufacturers must store separate codes that lead to the smallest part replaceable in service. A technician facing this code would wiggle-test the channel T wiring while watching the cell voltage live and look for a reading that dips or spikes for a fraction of a second.
c: Loose or spread terminal in the channel T connector
Connection that opens with temperature changes
Electrical interference coupling into sense lead T
s: Intermittent warning lamp
Occasional brief loss of electric drive

P0B9F.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense U Circuit
P0B9F.d: P0B9F covers an open or high-resistance sense U lead, channel twenty-one. From U onward the 2012 two-mode trucks drop out, as their pack has only twenty blocks, so this code is a lithium-ion matter at GM. In the eAssist mild hybrid the test is the familiar one, lines N and N-1 both under 1.4 V with a change above 0.5 V within 200 ms in 7 of 10 samples, Type B, but it is now blocked by P1B38 instead of P1B37. The 16OBDG02 programme measures the sense line resistance and sets above 30.00 in 7 of 9 samples, Type A. The 2016 Volt and ELR decide in 0.6 s, the 2019 controller in 0.8 s of 1.6 s, both on adjacent-cell differences of 1.3 V and splice checks.
c: Sense lead U interrupted or detached from its cell
Corroded terminal raising the resistance of lead U
Fault in the balancing circuit used for the channel U test
s: MIL and hybrid or EV system warning
No start or ready mode on some vehicles
Charging not possible

P0BA0.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense U Circuit Range/Performance
P0BA0.d: P0BA0 tells the technician that channel U gives a number, but the number does not move with the pack. GM checks this rationality only on lithium-ion systems, since the two-mode NiMH trucks end at block 20. The Cadillac ELR of 2016 reacts to the smallest movement: when the average cell voltage changes by more than 0.006 V, cell U must follow, and 20 failures in 40 samples at 200 ms set a Type A fault. The Volt of the same year looks at 0.022 V of average movement and a 7 s in 8 s window, the 2019 hybrid processor at 0.005 V with 35 of 40 samples, and eAssist at half the average movement, Type B. Circuit, low and high faults are excluded before the test runs, so wiring is less likely than the controller.
c: Measuring channel U holding a fixed value
Software or calibration issue in the battery controller
Cell U behaving differently from its neighbours due to ageing
s: MIL, often without driver-noticeable change
Electric range may be reduced

P0BA1.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense U Circuit Low
P0BA1.d: P0BA1 is stored when sense U reads close to zero. GM's lithium-ion controllers of the 2016 Volt and ELR and of 2019 treat 0.2 V or less over 1.4 s in a 2 s window as a Type A fault, provided no open sense line, lost slave communication or balancing fault is already active. The 16OBDG02 programme with its own battery sensor module uses under 0.20 V in 14 of 18 samples. GM's eAssist mild hybrid applies a much higher limit of 1.4 V in 7 of 10 samples, Type B. The two-mode NiMH trucks have no channel U. A short in the sense lead or a failed measuring input is the most likely finding.
c: Sense lead U shorted towards ground or a lower cell
Dead measuring input for channel U
Cell U internally shorted or deeply discharged
s: MIL and EV or hybrid system warning
Propulsion power limited

P0BA2.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense U Circuit High
P0BA2.d: P0BA2 flags an excessive voltage on channel U. GM's eAssist mild hybrid uses the lowest threshold of the documented systems: above 4.65 V in 7 of 10 samples with the 12 V supply above 8.8 V, Type B. The 2016 Volt and the 2019 battery controller set it at 4.8 V or more held for 1.4 s within 2 s, Type A; the 16OBDG02 programme at above 4.90 V in 14 of 18 samples, Type A. As with the low code, the high test is held back while an open sense line or module communication fault is active. Channel U does not exist on the twenty-block two-mode trucks. Before replacing parts, the actual cell voltage should be measured, because a lead touching a higher potential is far more common than a real overcharge.
c: Sense lead U in contact with a higher potential
s: MIL and hybrid or EV warning
Charging stopped early

P0BA3.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense U Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BA3.d: Within the sense U group, P0BA3 is the slot for a signal that is present but unsteady. No manufacturer documents it publicly; GM, the only maker whose tables cover channel U in detail, uses P0B9F to P0BA2 and nothing more. CARB 1968.2 demands monitoring of the hybrid storage system's voltage sensors and separate codes per repairable unit, and SAE reserves the intermittent code so that a manufacturer could report unstable sensing separately from a hard open or short. Physically this points to a connection that breaks for milliseconds, such as a fatigued crimp, a loose screw at a busbar tap or vibration damage to a flexible printed circuit. Repair follows the same path as for the circuit code.
c: Fatigued crimp on sense lead U
Loose fastener at the busbar tap of channel U
Vibration damage to the flexible printed circuit
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Brief reduced-power events

P0BA4.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense V Circuit
P0BA4.d: P0BA4 reports an open or poorly connected sense V lead, the twenty-second channel and the last before W begins at P0BA9. GM's 2019 battery energy control module recognises it through seven cases, including 1.3 V between neighbouring cells, less than 36 mV with the balancing gate on and splice voltages above 0.1 or 0.5 V, with 0.8 s of failure in 1.6 s, Type A. The 2011 Volt already listed P0BA4 among its open sense line codes. In GM's 16OBDG02 programme a measured line resistance above 30.00 in 7 of 9 samples triggers it, in the eAssist mild hybrid low readings on lines N and N-1 together with a 0.5 V jump, Type B, gated by P1B38. Without a good sense lead the pack cannot balance or protect that cell.
c: Broken or unplugged sense lead V
High-resistance splice or busbar joint on channel V
Cell monitoring board fault on channel V
s: MIL and hybrid or EV system warning
Vehicle may not become ready to drive
Charging blocked

P0BA5.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense V Circuit Range/Performance
P0BA5.d: P0BA5 describes a sense V value that stays within limits but fails a rationality check against the other cells. GM's 16OBDG02 programme demands a trend of at least 0.002 V in the same direction as the average whenever that average moves more than 0.022 V, with 35 failures in 40 evaluations giving Type A. The 2019 hybrid processor works the same way with 0.005 V. For the 2016 model year GM lists two variants: the Volt with a 7 s in 8 s window and the ELR with 0.006 V of average movement and 20 of 40 samples at 200 ms. GM's eAssist expects half the average movement, Type B. Since the test is skipped while circuit, low or high faults are active, P0BA5 alone points to the measurement rather than an open lead.
c: Channel V reading stuck while other cells move
Aged cell V responding differently to load
s: MIL, little change in driving
Reduced regeneration or assist possible

P0BA6.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense V Circuit Low
P0BA6.d: A sense V reading that collapses towards zero produces P0BA6. The threshold depends on the system: GM's eAssist mild hybrid uses under 1.4 V in 7 of 10 samples with at least 8.8 V on the 12 V side, Type B, while GM's lithium-ion battery controllers of 2016 and 2019 go down to 0.2 V or less for 1.4 s within 2 s, Type A. The 16OBDG02 programme sets it below 0.20 V in 14 of 18 samples. Because these tests are blocked by an active open sense line fault, P0BA4 would be reported first if the lead were simply broken; P0BA6 alone tends to mean a short to a lower potential or a failed input. The driver sees a hybrid or EV warning and reduced power.
c: Sense lead V shorted to ground or a lower cell
Monitoring board input for channel V failed
s: MIL and service hybrid or EV system message
Power limited, restart may be refused

P0BA7.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense V Circuit High
P0BA7.d: P0BA7 is the high-voltage plausibility code for channel V. The battery controller compares the measured value against a ceiling no healthy cell should reach: 4.8 V for 1.4 s within 2 s in GM's 2016 Volt and ELR and in the 2019 battery energy control module (Type A), 4.90 V in 14 of 18 samples of 100 ms in the 16OBDG02 programme (Type A), and 4.65 V in 7 of 10 samples in the eAssist mild hybrid (Type B). Each of these checks waits for the open sense line monitor to pass. A high reading usually comes from a sense lead V pressed against a higher cell tab or busbar, or from a measuring chip that has lost its reference, and only rarely from a cell actually overcharged.
c: Sense lead V touching a higher cell tab or busbar
Measuring chip with faulty reference reading channel V high
s: MIL and hybrid or EV warning
Charging and regeneration reduced

P0BA8.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense V Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BA8.d: P0BA8 completes the five codes of channel V and is meant for an unstable rather than a failed sense V signal. There is no public manufacturer documentation for it. GM covers channel V in its 2011 Volt, eAssist, 2016 and 2019 tables but never with an intermittent monitor, only with P0BA4 to P0BA7. The code exists because CARB 1968.2 requires battery voltage sensors of hybrid storage systems to be monitored and fault codes to isolate the smallest replaceable unit, and J2012 provides an intermittent slot for every sense channel. A fault of this kind would typically be traced to a connection that loses contact under vibration or thermal cycling. Channel W follows from P0BA9.
c: Contact of lead V lost intermittently under vibration
Joint on channel V opening with thermal cycling
Corroded connector pin for channel V
s: Occasional hybrid or EV warning
Fault not reproducible during short workshop test

P0BA9.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense W Circuit
P0BA9.d: P0BA9 opens the W group, the twenty-third cell voltage channel, and flags a sense lead that is open or badly connected. GM's 2019 battery energy control module checks seven cases, ranging from a reading under 36 mV while the balancing gate of that cell is switched on to at least 1.3 V between neighbouring cells and splice voltages above 0.1 V or 0.5 V at busbar joints; 0.8 s of failure within 1.6 s sets it as Type A. The 2016 Volt module uses a 0.6 s window instead. GM's eAssist mild hybrid needs readings under 1.4 V on lines N and N-1 plus a change of more than 0.5 V within 200 ms in seven of ten samples, Type B. With the lead lost, the cell behind it can neither be balanced nor protected.
c: Broken, chafed or unplugged sense lead W
High-resistance busbar or splice joint at channel W
Failed input on the cell monitoring board for W
s: MIL with hybrid or EV system warning
Reduced propulsion power or no ready mode
Charging interrupted or refused

P0BAA.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense W Circuit Range/Performance
P0BAA.d: Here the W reading is not missing but implausible: it fails to follow the rest of the pack. GM's 2019 hybrid powertrain control processor 2 watches for the average cell voltage to move more than 0.022 V between samples and then expects channel W to trend at least 0.005 V in the same direction; 35 failures in 40 samples at 100 ms give a Type A fault. The 16OBDG02 programme applies the same logic with 0.002 V. The eAssist system is more tolerant and only asks the cell to move half as far as the others once the average shifts more than 0.045 V, 20 of 40 samples, Type B. In the 2011 Volt tables W appears as sensor 23 of the rationality check. Drivers often notice nothing beyond the warning lamp.
c: Measuring input for W frozen at a fixed value
Battery controller software needing an update
Cell W reacting differently to load because of ageing
s: Warning lamp with little change in driving
Possibly limited regeneration or electric assist

P0BAB.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense W Circuit Low
P0BAB.d: A W channel reading at or near zero sets P0BAB. How low is too low depends on the battery: GM's lithium-ion modules of 2016 and 2019 react to 0.2 V or less held for 1.4 s within a 2 s window, Type A, and the 16OBDG02 programme to under 0.20 V in 14 of 18 samples at 100 ms. The eAssist mild hybrid already fails below 1.4 V, seven of ten samples, as long as the 12 V supply exceeds 8.8 V and P1B38 is not active; that fault is Type B. All of these tests stand down while an open sense line fault is present, so a simply broken lead shows up as P0BA9. P0BAB on its own suggests a short towards a lower potential, a dead measuring input or a deeply discharged cell. Power and charging are usually restricted.
c: Sense lead W shorted to a lower cell potential
Measuring input for W on the monitoring board failed
Cell W deeply discharged or internally shorted
s: Hybrid or EV warning and MIL
Reduced power output
Charging limited or blocked

P0BAC.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense W Circuit High
P0BAC.d: P0BAC is the upper counterpart to P0BAB: channel W reports more voltage than a single cell can plausibly hold. GM sets the limit at 4.8 V or more for 1.4 s within 2 s in the 2011 and 2016 Volt battery modules, which makes it a one-trip fault. The 16OBDG02 programme fails at above 4.90 V in 14 of 18 samples, Type A, while the eAssist battery is stricter with more than 4.65 V in seven of ten samples, Type B. A high reading usually comes from a lead touching the potential of the next cell up or from a faulty input, less often from a genuinely overcharged cell. Because overcharging is a safety risk, the controller typically cuts charging and regeneration until the cause is found.
c: Sense lead W in contact with a higher cell potential
Monitoring board input for W reading too high
Cell W actually overcharged after a balancing fault
s: MIL and battery system warning
Charging and regeneration stopped
Possible reduced power mode

P0BAD.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense W Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BAD.d: P0BAD is reserved for a W signal that drops out or jumps for short moments instead of failing outright. No manufacturer documents the code publicly. GM monitors channel W in several programmes, from the 2011 Volt to the eAssist and the 2019 tables, but only through P0BA9 to P0BAC; none of them contains an intermittent test. The slot exists because J2012 gives every sense channel five codes and CARB 1968.2 requires the battery voltage sensors of a hybrid energy storage system to be monitored with fault codes that point to the smallest replaceable part. If a vehicle did store it, the usual suspects would be a crimp or connector that loses contact under vibration or with temperature changes.
c: Loose or fretting connector pin on lead W
Crimp on lead W opening with temperature changes
Cracked solder joint on the monitoring board input W
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Occasional short power reduction

P0BAE.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense X Circuit
P0BAE.d: Channel X, number twenty-four, starts with P0BAE, the open-lead code. The first-generation Volt of 2011 already detected it through several cases: two neighbouring readings more than 1 V apart, a busbar sense voltage above 0.7 V combined with an implausible cell voltage, or adjacent cells differing by more than 0.5 V on a shared supply line. GM's later 16OBDG02 programme measures the sense line resistance directly and fails it above 30.00 in seven of nine samples, Type A; the unit is not printed. In the 2019 battery energy control module the familiar 1.3 V and 36 mV criteria apply with 0.8 s in 1.6 s. Whichever method is used, the controller loses sight of one cell and normally restricts the battery.
c: Sense lead X broken or disconnected
Loose busbar fastener at the X sensing point
Sense harness X damaged during earlier battery work
s: MIL and service message for the high-voltage system
Vehicle may stay out of ready mode
Charging stops early

P0BAF.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense X Circuit Range/Performance
P0BAF.d: P0BAF covers a sense X signal that is electrically present yet does not behave like a real cell. For model year 2016 GM documents two versions in the same booklet. The Volt controller fails it when X moves in a different direction from the pack average, or by less than 0.005 V while that average moves more than 0.022 V, for 7 s within 8 s, Type A. The ELR variant samples every 200 ms, needs average movement above 0.006 V and fails after 20 of 40 samples, one trip. The eAssist hybrid asks for at least half of the average change, Type B over two trips, and GM's 2019 processor uses a 0.005 V trend test. Since the check pauses during circuit, low or high faults, P0BAF points to a stuck measurement rather than a broken wire.
c: Sense X value stuck while the pack voltage changes
Calibration of the battery controller requiring reprogramming
Cell X with deviating internal resistance
s: MIL without obvious driving change
Reduced electric range in some cases

P0BB0.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense X Circuit Low
P0BB0.d: When channel X reads too low, P0BB0 is stored. In GM's eAssist mild hybrid the battery interface module sets it below 1.4 V in seven of ten samples at 200 ms, provided the 12 V system is above 8.8 V and the group fault P1B38 is not active, as a two-trip Type B fault. The 2011 Volt and the 16OBDG02 programme work with a far lower limit of about 0.2 V, the latter in 14 of 18 samples at 100 ms, Type A. That difference reflects the cell chemistry and how much voltage a healthy cell can lose. Because an open lead is caught first by P0BAE, a stand-alone P0BB0 is more often a short in the sense harness, a failed input or a cell that has collapsed. Expect reduced power and blocked charging.
c: Short between sense lead X and a lower potential
Defective measuring channel X in the monitoring electronics
Cell X collapsed or internally shorted
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Electric assist or propulsion reduced
Charging not possible

P0BB1.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense X Circuit High
P0BB1.d: P0BB1 means the battery controller sees too much voltage on sense X. In GM's 2019 battery energy control module the threshold is 4.8 V or more, held for 1.4 s within a 2 s window, and the code is Type A, so the MIL comes on in the first trip. The 16OBDG02 programme allows up to 4.90 V and needs 14 failing samples out of 18, while the eAssist battery treats anything above 4.65 V in seven of ten samples as a Type B fault. These tests are suppressed while an open sense line or a lost communication with the cell monitoring slave is active. A real cell at that voltage would be dangerously overcharged, so a wiring fault towards the neighbour cell or a defective input is the more frequent finding.
c: Sense lead X shorted to the next higher cell
s: MIL in the first trip
Charging and regenerative braking disabled

P0BB2.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense X Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BB2.d: Of the five X codes, P0BB2 is the only one without any public manufacturer description. It is intended for a sense X signal that flickers, drops out briefly or jumps between values. GM's Volt tables of 2011 and 2016 list channel X with circuit, range, low and high monitors, P0BAE to P0BB1, and no intermittent check. The code therefore rests on the J2012 structure and on CARB 1968.2, which requires hybrid battery voltage sensors to be monitored and the fault to be isolated to the smallest replaceable unit. In practice a technician would look for a contact that opens under vibration, moisture in a connector or a harness rubbing against the module housing.
c: Contact on lead X opening under vibration
Moisture or corrosion in the X sense connector
Harness X chafing against the module housing
s: Intermittent warning lamp
Sporadic hybrid system message

P0BB3.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Y Circuit
P0BB3.d: P0BB3 reports that the sense lead of channel Y, the twenty-fifth cell group, is no longer properly connected. GM's 16OBDG02 programme does not wait for odd voltages but calculates the resistance of the sense line and fails it above 30.00 in seven of nine samples, which is a one-trip Type A fault; the unit is missing in the table. The 2019 battery energy control module instead looks at the cell voltages themselves, for example 1.3 V between neighbours or a reading below 36 mV while that cell is being balanced, with 0.8 s of failure in 1.6 s. The eAssist mild hybrid sets it as a Type B fault when lines N and N-1 both read under 1.4 V and jump by more than 0.5 V. Low and high monitors for Y are blocked while P0BB3 is active.
c: Open circuit in sense lead Y
Corroded or loose terminal raising line resistance at Y
Cell monitoring slave board fault on input Y
s: MIL and high-voltage system warning
Vehicle may not start in electric mode
Charging aborted

P0BB4.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Y Circuit Range/Performance
P0BB4.d: P0BB4 is a plausibility code: the controller compares how the Y reading changes over time with the behaviour of all other cells. In the 16OBDG02 programme a sample counts as failed when the pack average moves by more than 0.022 V but Y has not trended at least 0.002 V the same way; 35 such results in 40 evaluations set a one-trip Type A fault. The 2019 hybrid powertrain control processor 2 uses the same frame with a 0.005 V trend. For the 2016 Volt the window is 7 s in 8 s. A frozen analogue input or a software problem in the battery controller are the typical findings, while a real cell defect is rarer. Unlike P0BB3, the signal is present, so the car usually keeps driving.
c: Analogue input Y frozen at one value
Weak cell Y with sluggish voltage response
s: MIL, vehicle still drivable
Battery power occasionally limited

P0BB5.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Y Circuit Low
P0BB5.d: P0BB5 stands for a sense Y voltage below the plausible minimum. GM's 2016 Volt module and the 2019 battery energy control module both use 0.2 V or less for 1.4 s inside a 2 s window and flag it as Type A. Before testing, the 2019 module makes sure that no open sense line, no lost communication with the cell monitoring slave and no balancing or internal slave fault is active, and that the second protection self test is not running. The eAssist mild hybrid sets the code below 1.4 V in seven of ten samples, Type B. The likely culprits are a pinched sense wire touching a lower potential, a failed measuring channel or a cell that has really lost its charge. The driver sees a warning and reduced performance.
c: Pinched sense wire Y shorting to a lower potential
s: Hybrid or EV warning with MIL
Noticeably reduced power

P0BB6.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Y Circuit High
P0BB6.d: The battery controller logs P0BB6 when the Y channel climbs above a level no healthy cell reaches. GM's first Volt of 2011 put that limit at 4.8 V or more, 1.4 s within 2 s, with the MIL after one trip. The 16OBDG02 programme samples every 100 ms and fails above 4.90 V in 14 of 18 samples, Type A; the eAssist battery fails above 4.65 V in seven of ten samples at 200 ms, Type B. A wiring fault that connects the Y input to the potential of the next cell is the most common explanation, followed by a failed input. Overcharging of a single cell is possible after a balancing problem and must be ruled out before the pack is charged again.
c: Sense input Y bridged to the next cell potential
Defective input Y on the monitoring board
Overcharged cell Y after a balancing problem
s: MIL and charging stopped
Regeneration disabled

P0BB7.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Y Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BB7.d: P0BB7 would describe an unstable sense Y signal, one that is mostly correct but drops out or jumps from time to time. No manufacturer publishes a monitor for it. Where GM covers channel Y, in the 16OBDG02 programme and the 2019 battery and hybrid processor tables, it does so with P0BB3 to P0BB6: line resistance, trend comparison, low and high limits. A brief interruption would there show up as a counted failure inside one of those tests rather than under its own code. P0BB7 thus exists as a J2012 placeholder that satisfies the CARB 1968.2 demand for monitored battery voltage sensors. Diagnosis would focus on connectors, crimps and solder joints that react to movement or heat.
c: Intermittent contact in the Y sense connector
Crimp or weld on lead Y opening when hot
Hairline crack in a solder joint of input Y
s: Warning lamp appears now and then
Short-lived power limitation

P0BB8.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Z Circuit
P0BB8.d: P0BB8 is the open-circuit code of channel Z, the twenty-sixth and last cell channel with a generic P0 code. GM packs with more channels continue with manufacturer codes, for example P1B28 for the circuit of AA in the 2019 tables. The 2019 battery energy control module sets P0BB8 through the same seven cases as its neighbours, with 1.3 V between adjacent cells, under 36 mV on an active balancing gate or excessive splice voltage, 0.8 s in 1.6 s, Type A. GM's eAssist uses the voltage of lines N and N-1 below 1.4 V together with a change above 0.5 V in 200 ms, seven of ten samples, Type B and gated by P1B38. The 2011 Volt already listed P0BB8 among its open sense line faults.
c: Excessive resistance at the splice or busbar of Z
s: MIL and stop or service warning for the drive system
Ready mode may be refused
No charging

P0BB9.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Z Circuit Range/Performance
P0BB9.d: With P0BB9 the controller says that sense Z does not track the pack: the value is within limits, but it stays still or moves the wrong way while the other cells change. GM's 2019 hybrid powertrain control processor 2 enables the comparison once the system voltage is above 10.20 V and the average cell voltage shifts by more than 0.022 V, then demands a trend of at least 0.005 V on Z; 35 failures in 40 samples are Type A. The 2016 Volt variant fails after 7 s within 8 s. In the eAssist mild hybrid, Z has to follow at least half of an average movement above 0.045 V, 20 of 40 samples, Type B. A recalibrated controller or a replaced monitoring board is a more common fix than a new cell.
c: Z reading static despite changing pack voltage
Monitoring board or controller calibration fault
Cell Z with abnormal charge and discharge behaviour
s: MIL, driving largely unaffected
Possibly lower assist or regeneration

P0BBA.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Z Circuit Low
P0BBA.d: P0BBA is stored when the voltage measured on channel Z falls below the lower limit. In the 16OBDG02 programme the hybrid processor checks Z every 100 ms and fails it below 0.20 V in 14 of 18 samples, a Type A fault, but only with a system voltage above 10.20 V and no open-circuit fault on the cell. GM's 2019 battery energy control module and the 2011 Volt use 0.2 V or less over 1.4 s within 2 s. This rules out a simple open lead, which would have set P0BB8 first. What remains is a short in the Z wiring or connector, a failed channel on the monitoring board or a cell whose voltage has actually collapsed. The battery is normally limited to protect the other cells.
c: Short in the Z sense wiring or connector
Failed channel Z on the monitoring board
s: MIL and hybrid or EV warning
Limited power and charging

P0BBB.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Z Circuit High
P0BBB.d: If the Z channel shows a cell voltage above the upper limit, the controller sets P0BBB. The 2016 Volt battery module uses 4.8 V or more for 1.4 s in a 2 s window, Type A, and checks first that the cell monitoring slave is communicating and no open sense line is reported. The 16OBDG02 programme fails above 4.90 V in 14 of 18 samples, and the eAssist mild hybrid fails above 4.65 V in seven of ten samples with a healthy 12 V supply, Type B over two trips. Lithium-ion cells are not meant to exceed these values, so the reading normally points to a short towards the higher neighbour, a faulty input or a corrupted measurement, and only rarely to a truly overcharged cell. Charging is stopped as a precaution.
c: Sense lead Z shorted towards the higher neighbour cell
s: MIL and charging stopped
Reduced regeneration

P0BBC.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Z Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BBC.d: P0BBC closes the generic block of 26 cell voltage channels from A to Z; after it J2012 moves on to pack-level codes such as P0BBD and P0BBE. The code is meant for a Z signal that is unstable rather than absent. There is no manufacturer documentation for it: GM monitors channel Z from the 2011 Volt to the 2019 battery energy control module, but always with P0BB8 to P0BBB only, and no table contains an intermittent monitor. Its basis is CARB 1968.2, which requires battery voltage sensors of hybrid storage systems to be checked and faults to be narrowed down to the smallest replaceable unit. Should it appear, contacts that fail under vibration or heat cycling are the logical starting point.
c: Intermittent contact on sense lead Z
Joint at channel Z opening with heat cycling
Corrosion in the Z sense connector
s: Warning lamp appearing irregularly
Occasional brief loss of electric drive power

P0BBD.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Variation Exceeded Limit
P0BBD.d: P0BBD means the spread between cells or blocks of the pack has grown beyond what the controller accepts. GM used it on the two-mode hybrids, where a difference of more than 1.5 V between adjacent block voltages in three of three samples at 1 s, with battery current above 0.2 A, set a Type B fault labelled as end-of-life deviation. On the Chevrolet Bolt EV, bulletin 22-NA-151 links it to reduced propulsion and charging capped at 30 % and names cases induced by driving style that need reprogramming, otherwise a pack replacement. Volkswagen reports it on the ID.4 from cells with increased self-discharge, Audi on the Q4 e-tron with a drive system that cannot be activated, and Stellantis on the Wrangler 4xe.
c: Cells or modules with increased self-discharge or capacity loss
Controller software or cell capacity adaptation needing an update
Aged battery pack at end of life
Cell balancing unable to equalise the pack
s: MIL or electrical system warning
Reduced propulsion power and capped state of charge
Reduced electric range
Drive system cannot be activated in severe cases

P0BBE.d: P0BBE watches the gap between the highest and the lowest cell voltage in the pack. GM's first-generation Volt sets it when that difference exceeds 0.3 V in 50 of 245 samples taken every 100 ms, provided the cell voltage rationality fault is not active; it is a one-trip Type A fault. Stellantis lists the code on the Jeep Grand Cherokee 4xe and Wrangler 4xe together with P0B24, P0DAB and a state-of-health code, where updated battery pack control module software is the remedy and an unresolved case can end in a no-start. Chrysler's warranty extension for the 2017 to 2021 Pacifica Hybrid replaces the whole high-voltage pack for this code. Its companion P0BBD reports a spread that has exceeded a set limit.
c: Cells drifted apart beyond what balancing can correct
Battery pack control module software needing an update
Defective or aged high-voltage battery pack
Faulty cell voltage measurement simulating a spread
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Reduced electric range or propulsion
Vehicle may not start

P0BBF.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan Supply Voltage Circuit/Open
P0BBF.d: Air-cooled hybrid packs draw cooling air through a 12 V blower that is fed through a fuse and often a relay; the controller watches the voltage reaching the fan, and Toyota even uses that measured supply voltage to correct the fan duty. P0BBF means this feed is open or missing while the fan should be powered. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's Two-Mode hybrid monitors the same feed but reports only the high case, a welded relay, as P0BC1. CARB requires the electrical inputs and outputs of battery thermal management to be monitored. Low and high faults are P0BC0 and P0BC1, faults in the fan's own control line P0A81 to P0A85. Without power the fan stops, the pack warms up and the controller limits power.
c: Blown fuse in the battery fan feed
Fan relay contacts not closing or relay coil open
Open supply wire or loose terminal at the fan connector
s: Hybrid system warning or MIL on
Battery fan silent when it should run
Reduced electric assist in hot weather or under load

P0BC0.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan Supply Voltage Circuit Low
P0BC0.d: P0BC0 reports that the voltage feeding the battery cooling fan is lower than expected while the fan is switched on. A short to ground downstream of the fuse, a corroded connector or a relay with burnt contacts drops the voltage, so the fan turns slowly or not at all. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. Toyota's hybrid controller measures the fan supply on the auxiliary battery side and raises the duty when it is low, which shows why a sagging feed matters for cooling. CARB asks for circuit monitoring of all battery thermal management parts. The open case is P0BBF, the high case P0BC1 (GM: welded relay). A weak 12 V battery can cause a sag too, so check it first. Expect reduced power when the pack heats up.
c: Fan supply wire chafed and shorted to ground
Burnt fan relay contacts or corroded terminals causing voltage drop
Weak 12 V auxiliary battery or poor ground
Seizing fan motor pulling excessive current
s: Hybrid system warning or MIL on
Battery fan runs slowly or noticeably weaker
Reduced electric assist when the pack is warm

P0BC1.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan Supply Voltage Circuit High
P0BC1.d: P0BC1 flags voltage on the battery fan feed when there should be none, or more than expected. GM documents it for the battery pack control module of its Two-Mode hybrid SUVs and pickups (Tahoe, Yukon, Escalade, Silverado, Sierra; 2012 and 2013 tables) as a welded fan relay: with the fan commanded off, a fan monitor voltage of at least 0.9 V in 10 of 20 samples at 100 ms sets it, provided the 12 V system is between 9 and 18 V and no fan circuit code (P0A81) is active. It is Type B, MIL after two trips. A stuck relay keeps the fan running with the vehicle off and drains the 12 V battery. The open and low cases are P0BBF and P0BC0; a fan that keeps turning without this fault is P0A83.
c: Fan feed shorted to a constant battery voltage wire
Relay control output in the module stuck on
s: MIL on after two trips
Battery fan keeps running after the vehicle is switched off
Discharged 12 V battery after standing

P0BC2.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor E Circuit
P0BC2.d: Battery temperature sensor E is the fifth thermistor in the high-voltage pack; GM's Chevrolet Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists the E codes as temperature sensor 5 of nine. P0BC2 is the general circuit code, used when the controller detects an electrical fault without classing it as low, high or erratic. GM's hybrid tables report only the specific siblings P0BC3 to P0BC6. NHTSA's summary of an Audi pending service solution for 2027 Q6 and A6 e-tron models names P0BC2 with a failure type byte among implausible temperature sensor errors. CARB requires battery temperature sensors to be monitored for circuit faults. With one value missing the controller limits charge and discharge power. The sensor sits inside the pack, so checks call for high-voltage safety procedures.
c: Loose or corroded connector of sensor E at the sensing board
Faulty input on the battery sensing board or module
s: Hybrid or EV system warning and MIL
Reduced power or charging rate
Battery cooling running more than usual

P0BC3.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor E Circuit Range/Performance
P0BC3.d: P0BC3 is the plausibility check for battery temperature sensor E, GM's sensor 5: its reading is compared with the other pack sensors, which should agree closely. GM's 2016 hybrid table fails it when E is more than 25 °C away from the average of the others in 50 of 67 samples; the 2018 CT6 plug-in table more than 20 °C for 5 s within 6.7 s; the eAssist mild hybrid (13OBDG05C) allows only 8.55 °C, and only after the module has been off for more than six hours. All are Type B, two trips. The check is suspended while circuit codes are active, so it points to a sensor that reads wrongly but in range, or to a real hot spot. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 counts it among codes that set falsely in cold weather and fixes them by reprogramming.
c: Sensor E drifting or poorly seated on its cell group
Module software setting the code falsely in the cold (GM Volt)
Real local hot spot from a weak cell group or blocked airflow
s: MIL on after two trips
Battery too cold or reduced power message
Limited charge and discharge power

P0BC4.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor E Circuit Low
P0BC4.d: Sensor E is an NTC thermistor with a pull-up resistor, so its voltage falls as it gets hotter; a short to ground therefore looks like an extremely hot cell group. GM's 2016 table sets P0BC4 when the converted value exceeds 160 °C in 8 of 10 samples; the 2011 Volt table and GM's 2019 battery module table use above 87.5 °C for 1.4 s within 2 s; the eAssist mild hybrid flags a sense voltage under 0.3 V, about 90 °C, in 7 of 10 samples. All are Type B, two trips. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 names it sensor 5 circuit low voltage. Its counterpart is P0BC5 (open circuit, reads very cold); a genuinely overheated pack is reported as P0A7E. Because the controller must assume heat, it cuts charge and discharge power and may run cooling at full speed.
c: Sensor E signal wire shorted to ground inside the pack
Moisture or contamination on the sensing board
s: MIL on after two trips
Implausibly high temperature for sensor E on the scan tool
Reduced power and battery fan or cooling at full speed

P0BC5.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor E Circuit High
P0BC5.d: P0BC5 reports that battery temperature sensor E delivers a voltage above its valid range. With GM's NTC sensors that reads as extreme cold, pointing to an open wire, a backed-out pin at the sensing board or a cracked thermistor. GM's 2016 table sets it below -69 °C in 8 of 10 samples, the 2011 Volt table and GM's 2019 battery module table below -40 °C for 1.4 s within 2 s, and the eAssist mild hybrid above 4.63 V, about -45 °C, in 7 of 10 samples; all Type B, two trips. On the Chevrolet Volt, bulletin 18-NA-342 links these codes to a Battery Too Cold message at ambient temperatures above -25 °C and prescribes reprogramming. Its counterpart is P0BC4. A pack the controller believes frozen gets strict charge and power limits.
c: Open sensor E wire or backed-out pin at the sensing board
Module software misreading in the cold (GM Volt, reprogramming)
s: MIL on after two trips
Battery too cold, plug in to warm message
Very limited power or charging

P0BC6.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor E Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BC6.d: P0BC6 flags erratic behaviour of battery temperature sensor E: the reading jumps far faster than the heavy battery mass could warm or cool. GM documents the method in its 2016 and 2018 hybrid tables (16OBDG02, 18OBDG02). Sampling every 100 ms, the controller adds up the absolute changes of the sensor value over a 10-sample window; a sum above 10 fails the window, and 4 failed windows out of 5 store the code as Type B, two trips, provided system voltage is above 10.2 V. The same logic covers the other pack sensors. The older Volt, Two-Mode and eAssist tables list no erratic code for sensor E. Typical culprits are a loose terminal, a cracked wire or a connector not fully latched after pack work; if several sensors jump at once, suspect the sensing board.
c: Loose terminal or unlatched connector of sensor E
Cracked or chafed sensor wire breaking contact intermittently
Sensing board fault affecting several temperature inputs
s: MIL on after two trips
Sensor E value jumping on the scan tool
Occasional power reduction

P0BC7.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Sense Circuit/Open
P0BC7.d: Many battery cooling fans report their actual speed back to the controller as a pulse signal; Toyota patents describe a rotation sensor on the fan motor whose measured speed is compared with the target. P0BC7 means this feedback line for fan 1 is open or carries no usable signal. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's 2016 and 2018 hybrid tables cover the same feedback only through P0BC8, P0BC9 and P0BCA. CARB requires the electrical inputs of battery thermal management to be monitored. The fan may still turn, but the controller can no longer confirm it and usually limits power to protect the pack. Faults in the drive circuit are P0A81 to P0A85; fan 2 feedback has its own codes P0D5F to P0D63.
c: Open feedback wire or loose pin at the fan connector
Failed speed sensor or electronics inside the fan unit
Faulty feedback input in the controlling module
s: Hybrid system warning or MIL on
Reduced electric assist or charging power
Fan audible even though the code reports no feedback

P0BC8.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Sense Range/Performance
P0BC8.d: P0BC8 compares the speed fed back by battery cooling fan 1 with what the controller commanded. GM's 2016 and 2018 hybrid tables run two checks. With the fan enabled at 11 to 89 % duty for more than 11 s, the filtered difference between commanded and reported speed must stay inside calibrated limits; large errors fail within seconds, small ones after up to 43 s. With the fan off for more than 20 s, a reported speed above 120 rpm fails in 24 of 32 samples at 250 ms. It is Type B, two trips, and waits while drive or sense circuit codes are active. A dusty or worn fan that cannot reach its speed is the usual cause; a fan turning while commanded off points to a stuck drive. The circuit cases are P0BC7, P0BC9 and P0BCA.
c: Dust-clogged impeller, blocked intake or worn fan bearing
Fan keeps running while commanded off (stuck drive or relay)
Fan electronics reporting a wrong speed
s: MIL on after two trips
Weak airflow or unusual fan noise from the battery intake
Reduced electric assist when the pack warms up

P0BC9.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Sense Circuit Low
P0BC9.d: P0BC9 means the speed feedback of battery cooling fan 1 is implausibly low while the fan is running. GM evaluates the feedback as a frequency: in its 2016 and 2018 hybrid tables the code counts a failure when the frequency stays below 8 Hz with the fan enabled at 11 to 89 % duty for more than 8 s and system voltage above 10.2 V; 16 failures in 20 samples at 250 ms set it as Type B, two trips. A frequency near zero comes either from a fan that is not turning or from a feedback line shorted to ground or interrupted. The high case is P0BCA, a speed that is merely too far from the target is P0BC8, and drive circuit faults are P0A81 to P0A85. Expect power limits when the pack warms up.
c: Fan seized, blocked or without power
Feedback wire shorted to ground or interrupted
Failed speed sensor inside the fan unit
s: MIL on after two trips
No airflow from the battery cooling fan
Reduced power when the battery gets warm

P0BCA.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Sense Circuit High
P0BCA.d: P0BCA means the speed feedback of battery cooling fan 1 is implausibly high. GM's 2016 and 2018 hybrid tables count a failure when the feedback frequency exceeds 290 Hz with the fan enabled at 11 to 89 % duty for more than 8 s and system voltage above 10.2 V; 16 failures in 20 samples at 250 ms set it as Type B, two trips. No real fan reaches that frequency, so the cause is electrical: noise coupled into the feedback line, a line shorted to another signal or to voltage, or fan electronics sending garbage. Check wire routing and grounds before replacing the fan. The low case is P0BC9, speed errors within range P0BC8, an open line P0BC7. While the feedback is untrusted the controller may limit power.
c: Electrical noise on the feedback line from poor routing or a bad ground
Feedback wire shorted to voltage or another signal
Fan electronics sending an invalid speed signal
s: MIL on after two trips
Implausible fan speed reading on the scan tool
Possible power reduction

P0BCB.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 1 Sense Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BCB.d: P0BCB flags a speed feedback from battery cooling fan 1 that drops out or jumps in a way no rotating fan can, typically a loose contact in the feedback line. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's 2016 and 2018 hybrid tables, which watch the same pulse feedback, list only performance, low and high (P0BC8, P0BC9, P0BCA). Toyota's battery cooling patents show the principle: the speed measured by a rotation sensor on the fan motor is compared with the target under steady command, so a jumping signal makes that comparison worthless. CARB requires the inputs of battery thermal management to be monitored. Wiggle-test the fan connector and harness. An open line is P0BC7; fan 2 has P0D63.
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the feedback circuit
Chafed harness near the fan or battery case
Intermittent fault in the fan's speed sensor
s: Hybrid system warning or MIL, sometimes coming and going
Fan speed reading jumping on the scan tool
Occasional power reduction

P0BCC.t: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0BCC.d: In a two-machine hybrid one inverter feeds the traction motor and a second one the generator, the machine that is mainly driven by the engine to charge the battery or start it. Its power switches carry thermistors so the controller can cut current before they overheat. P0BCC is the general circuit code for sensor A of that generator inverter, used for an electrical fault the controller does not classify as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; CARB requires hybrid components and their sensor inputs to be monitored for circuit faults. Without a valid reading the controller limits generator power, which can reduce charging and hybrid performance. The sensor normally sits inside the inverter assembly.
c: Fault of the sensor or its circuit inside the inverter assembly
Loose or corroded connector at the inverter
Software fault in the inverter or hybrid control module
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine lamp
Reduced generator output and battery charging
Engine runs more often or hybrid mode limited

P0BCD.t: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0BCD.d: P0BCD flags a generator inverter temperature sensor A whose signal is electrically valid but does not fit the operating state, for example a value stuck at one temperature or far from the other temperatures after a long soak. Ford documents this exact code: on 2020 Lincoln Aviator 3.0L hybrids built up to 18 July 2020, P0BCD stored in the inverter system controller (SOBDMC) lights the MIL and is caused by software; the fix is reprogramming that module. Patents by Hino and Mitsubishi Electric describe how such checks work, comparing heat generated in the inverter with the measured temperature change or detecting a stuck sensor. Circuit faults go to P0BCE or P0BCF instead.
c: Inverter controller software (Ford SSM 49120, Lincoln Aviator 2020)
Sensor drifting or stuck at one value
Uneven inverter coolant flow distorting the comparison
s: Malfunction indicator lamp
Often no noticeable change in driving
Hybrid system warning message possible

P0BCE.t: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0BCE.d: P0BCE means the signal of generator inverter temperature sensor A is below its valid range. Inverter thermistors are usually NTC types with a pull-up resistor, as GM's tables describe for the drive motor inverter sensors: a short to ground or a shorted element pulls the voltage down, which the controller reads as an impossibly hot inverter. GM sets the comparable drive motor codes at roughly 125 to 170 °C, depending on generation. No manufacturer documents P0BCE itself publicly; CARB requires this circuit monitoring for hybrid sensor inputs. The controller then protects the generator inverter with a substitute value and limits generator power. A real overheat is reported separately as P0A3E.
c: Shorted sensor or circuit inside the inverter assembly
Signal shorted to ground in external wiring, where present
Moisture or coolant inside the inverter housing
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning
Generator power strongly limited
Battery charge drops, engine runs more

P0BCF.t: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0BCF.d: P0BCF reports a signal from generator inverter temperature sensor A above its valid range. With the usual NTC thermistor and pull-up, an open circuit, a lost sensor ground or a cracked element drives the voltage up, which reads as an extremely cold inverter. GM's comparable drive motor checks set below -40 to -58 °C and wait until the inverter has worked for about 90 s at 20 Nm or more, so a genuinely cold start does not trigger them. No manufacturer documents P0BCF itself publicly; CARB requires circuit monitoring of hybrid sensor inputs. Until the value is valid the controller uses conservative substitutes and may limit generator power. Check the inverter connectors before replacing the unit.
c: Open sensor or circuit inside the inverter assembly
Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the inverter
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning
Reduced generator output
Implausibly low inverter temperature in live data

P0BD0.t: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BD0.d: P0BD0 is reserved for a generator inverter temperature sensor A signal that jumps or briefly drops out instead of failing for good. A liquid-cooled inverter changes temperature slowly, so sudden steps point to a contact problem or to interference: a Hitachi patent on inverter systems explains that the small sensor signal can pick up noise from the high-voltage main circuit and has to be filtered statistically. No manufacturer documents P0BD0 itself publicly; CARB requires hybrid sensor inputs to be checked for such faults as well. Permanent faults are reported as P0BCE or P0BCF. Freeze-frame data and a wiggle test at the inverter connector help find the cause.
c: Loose or corroded contact at the inverter connector
Intermittent fault inside the inverter assembly
Interference from the high-voltage circuit on the sensor signal
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Brief drops in generator or hybrid power
Jumping inverter temperature in live data

P0BD1.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit
P0BD1.d: Which thermistor is called sensor C depends on the maker. In GM's hybrid tables it is the second sensor of the motor A inverter: the phase V sensor in the 2016 to 2019 tables, labelled temperature sensor 2 in the Volt and ELR. P0BD1 is its general circuit code for an electrical fault that is not classified as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM reports only the specific siblings P0BD2, P0BD3 and P0BD4. CARB requires hybrid sensor circuits to be monitored. Without a valid value the controller cannot protect that phase and normally limits motor torque. The sensor sits inside the inverter, so repairs often mean replacing the assembly.
c: Internal fault of the sensor inside the power inverter module
Corroded or loose connector at the inverter module
Software fault in the motor control processor
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine lamp
Reduced electric drive power
Possible loss of electric drive

P0BD2.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P0BD2.d: P0BD2 checks whether inverter temperature sensor C, GM's second sensor in the motor A inverter, agrees with the other temperatures after a cold soak. More than 20 °C apart sets it: Type B, two trips, on the 2016 Volt; Type A in a 2019 table; Type A on the 2011 Volt and 2016 ELR, compared with coolant and transmission temperature after 6 h off. GM's 2012 and 2013 tables use 15 °C after 360 min. GM bulletin PIC6303A says that on 2016-18 Volt, Malibu, LaCrosse and Regal the code alone needs no repair; the inverter is replaced only with P0AC4. GM fixes it by software on the 2017 Bolt EV and Ampera-e. Porsche replaces a coolant hose with a sticking thermostat on the Cayenne S E-Hybrid.
c: Inverter module software (GM bulletin 18-NA-064, Bolt EV/Ampera-e)
Sticking thermostat in the power electronics coolant hose (Porsche Cayenne S E-Hybrid)
Inverter temperature sensor C drifting out of tolerance
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, often without drivability change
Propulsion power reduced message (Bolt EV)
Red hybrid warning in the cluster (Porsche)

P0BD3.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Low
P0BD3.d: P0BD3 means the signal of inverter temperature sensor C, the phase V sensor of GM's motor A inverter, is below its valid range. GM uses an NTC thermistor with a pull-up on the sensing board, so a short to ground reads as an impossibly hot inverter. GM's thresholds: above 170 °C for 2.5 of 3.5 s, Type B, two trips, on the 2016 Volt and in a 2018 table; above 159 °C for 6.25 of 8.75 s, Type A, in a 2019 table; above 130 °C, Type A, on the 2011 Volt and 2016 ELR; above 125 °C, two trips, in the 2012 and 2013 tables. A genuine overheat of that phase is reported as P0C12. Since the sensor is part of the inverter, the usual fix is the inverter assembly.
c: Shorted sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module
Sensor signal shorted to ground in external wiring, where present
Moisture or coolant inside the inverter housing
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning
Drive motor power strongly limited
Reduced regeneration

P0BD4.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit High
P0BD4.d: P0BD4 reports a voltage from inverter temperature sensor C above its valid range. For GM's NTC sensor this is an implausibly cold inverter, typically caused by an open circuit, a lost ground or a cracked element. To avoid false alarms on a cold day GM waits until the inverter has run at least 90 s at 20 Nm or more. The 2016 Volt and a 2018 table then set it below -50 °C for 2.6 of 3.65 s, Type B, two trips; a 2019 table uses -50 °C with Type A. The 2011 Volt and 2016 ELR use below -58 °C, Type A; the 2012 and 2013 tables below -40 °C, two trips. Until the reading is valid the controller protects the inverter with substitute values and may cut motor power.
c: Open sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module
Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the inverter
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, depending on model after two trips
Reduced electric drive power
Implausibly low inverter temperature in live data

P0BD5.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BD5.d: P0BD5 is meant for an inverter temperature sensor C signal that jumps or drops out for short moments. Because the heat sink of a liquid-cooled inverter changes temperature smoothly, sudden steps point to a contact fault or to interference; a Hitachi patent explains that the small thermistor signal can pick up noise from the high-voltage main circuit. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM covers its sensor C, the phase V sensor of the motor A inverter, only with P0BD2, P0BD3 and P0BD4. CARB requires hybrid sensor inputs to be monitored for erratic faults too. Freeze-frame data and a careful check of the inverter connector are the best starting points.
c: Loose or corroded contact at the inverter module
Intermittent fault inside the power inverter module
Interference from the high-voltage circuit on the sensor signal
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Brief power reductions while driving
Jumping inverter temperature in live data

P0BD6.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor D Circuit
P0BD6.d: Sensor D is, in GM's hybrid tables, the second thermistor of the motor B inverter, the counterpart of sensor C in the motor A inverter: phase V in the 2016 to 2019 tables, temperature sensor 2 of inverter B on the Volt. Other makers assign the letter differently. P0BD6 is its general circuit code for an electrical fault that the controller does not narrow down to low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM reports P0BD7, P0BD8 and P0BD9 instead. CARB requires monitoring of hybrid sensor circuits. Without a valid value the controller cannot protect that inverter and usually limits the motor it drives. Read all stored codes, since several inverter codes often appear together.
c: Internal fault of the sensor inside the power inverter module
Corroded or loose connector at the inverter module
Software fault in the motor control processor
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine lamp
Reduced electric drive or generator power
Higher fuel consumption in hybrid operation

P0BD7.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor D Circuit Range/Performance
P0BD7.d: P0BD7 is the plausibility check for inverter temperature sensor D, GM's second sensor in the motor B inverter. After a cold soak its reading is compared with an average vehicle temperature; more than 20 °C apart sets the code, Type B, two trips, on the 2016 Volt and Type A in a 2019 table. The 2011 Volt compares with power electronics coolant and transmission temperature after 6 h off (20 °C, Type A); GM's 2012 and 2013 tables use 15 °C after 360 min, two trips. GM bulletin PIC6303A lists P0BD7 with the other inverter thermistor codes on 2016-18 Volt, Malibu, LaCrosse and Regal: alone it causes no noticeable effect, and the inverter is replaced only if P0AC4 set at the same time.
c: Inverter temperature sensor D drifting out of tolerance
Uneven inverter coolant flow after soak
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, often after two trips
Often no noticeable drivability change
Further inverter temperature codes may be stored

P0BD8.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor D Circuit Low
P0BD8.d: P0BD8 means the signal of inverter temperature sensor D is below its valid range; with an NTC thermistor and pull-up that reads as an extremely hot inverter, usually from a short to ground or an internal sensor fault. GM sets it above 170 °C for 2.5 of 3.5 s, Type B, two trips, on the 2016 Volt, above 159 °C, Type A, in a 2019 table, above 130 °C, Type A, on the 2011 Volt and above 125 °C, two trips, in the 2012 table. Stellantis lists P0BD8-11 for the 2026 Jeep Compass 1.6 PHEV outside the US among the codes behind a no-start with the message Electric Traction System Fault; the repair is the traction inverter of the hybrid dual-clutch transmission.
c: Shorted sensor or circuit inside the inverter (Jeep Compass PHEV bulletin)
Sensor signal shorted to ground in external wiring, where present
Moisture or coolant inside the inverter housing
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning
Vehicle does not start, Electric Traction System Fault (Jeep)
Electric drive power strongly limited

P0BD9.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor D Circuit High
P0BD9.d: P0BD9 means inverter temperature sensor D delivers a voltage above its valid range. For GM's NTC sensor in the motor B inverter that equals an implausibly cold inverter, so an open circuit, a lost ground or a cracked thermistor is likely. GM checks only after the inverter has run at least 90 s at 20 Nm or more, so a real cold start is excluded. The 2016 Volt then sets it below -50 °C for 2.6 of 3.65 s, Type B, two trips; a 2019 table uses -50 °C with Type A; the 2011 Volt below -58 °C, Type A; the 2012 table below -40 °C, two trips. Until the value is valid the controller uses substitute values and may limit motor B. Check the inverter connectors before replacing the unit.
c: Open sensor or circuit inside the power inverter module
Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the inverter
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, depending on model after two trips
Reduced motor B power and regeneration
Implausibly low inverter temperature in live data

P0BDA.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor D Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BDA.d: P0BDA covers an inverter temperature sensor D signal that changes in steps or drops out briefly. Real temperatures of a liquid-cooled inverter move smoothly, so such jumps suggest a contact problem or interference from the high-voltage switching, which a Hitachi patent on inverter systems names as a typical disturbance of the small sensor signal. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's tables cover sensor D, the second sensor of the motor B inverter, only with P0BD7, P0BD8 and P0BD9. CARB requires hybrid sensor inputs to be monitored for erratic behaviour as well. Because the fault comes and goes, freeze-frame data and live data during a wiggle test are the most useful clues.
c: Loose or corroded contact at the inverter module
Intermittent fault inside the power inverter module
Interference from the high-voltage circuit on the sensor signal
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Brief power reductions while driving
Jumping inverter temperature in live data

P0BDB.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor E Circuit
P0BDB.d: Which thermistor counts as inverter temperature sensor E is set by the manufacturer. In GM's hybrid tables it is the third sensor of the motor A inverter (PIM sensor #3), assigned to phase W in the 2016 to 2019 tables. P0BDB is the general circuit code for an electrical fault that is not classed as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM uses only the siblings P0BDC, P0BDD and P0BDE. CARB requires hybrid sensor circuits to be monitored for circuit faults. Without a valid reading the controller cannot protect the phase W power switches and usually limits motor torque. The sensor is built into the inverter, so the repair is often the inverter assembly.
c: Internal fault of the thermistor or its circuit inside the power inverter module
Corroded or loose connector at the inverter module
Software fault in the motor control processor
s: Malfunction indicator lamp or hybrid system warning
Reduced electric drive power
Further inverter temperature codes stored at the same time

P0BDC.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor E Circuit Range/Performance
P0BDC.d: P0BDC checks whether inverter temperature sensor E, GM's phase W sensor in the motor A inverter, agrees with the vehicle after a long stand. The 2016 and 2018 tables compare it after a cold soak with a calculated average temperature; more than 20 °C apart for 0.525 of 0.625 s sets Type B, two trips. A 2019 table uses the same 20 °C as Type A. The 2011 Volt compares it with power electronics coolant temperature (20 °C, Type A); the 2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks use 15 °C after at least 360 minutes off (Type B). GM bulletin PIC6303A says that on 2016-18 Volt, Malibu, LaCrosse and Regal the code has no remedial action; the inverter is replaced only together with P0AC4.
c: Phase W thermistor drifting out of tolerance
Uneven inverter cooling or residual heat after the soak period
Failing power inverter module (replace only with P0AC4 per GM PIC6303A)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp after two drives, often without any drivability change
Code found during inspection without customer complaint

P0BDD.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor E Circuit Low
P0BDD.d: P0BDD reports that the signal of inverter temperature sensor E, the phase W thermistor of GM's motor A inverter, sits below its valid range. GM uses an NTC thermistor with a pull-up on the sensing board, so a short to ground appears as an impossibly hot inverter. Thresholds: above 170 °C for 2.5 of 3.5 s, Type B, two trips, in the 2016 and 2018 tables; above 159 °C for 6.25 of 8.75 s, Type A, in a 2019 table; above 130 °C, Type A, on the 2011 Volt; above 125 °C, Type B, on the 2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks. A real overheat of that phase is reported separately as P0C13. With the sensor inside the inverter, the usual fix is the inverter assembly.
c: Shorted thermistor or signal line inside the power inverter module
Signal shorted to ground in external wiring, where the design has any
Moisture or coolant inside the inverter housing
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning
Drive motor A power strongly limited
Reduced regenerative braking

P0BDE.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor E Circuit High
P0BDE.d: P0BDE means the signal of inverter temperature sensor E is above its valid range. For GM's NTC thermistor with pull-up that reads as an extremely cold phase W in the motor A inverter, typically an open circuit, lost reference ground or a failed sensor. GM sets it below -50 °C, but only after at least 90 s of inverter warm-up at 20 Nm or more, so a genuinely cold car does not trip it: 2.625 of 3.65 s, Type B, two trips, in the 2016 and 2018 tables, 6.25 of 8.75 s, Type A, in a 2019 table. The 2011 Volt uses below -58 °C (Type A), the 2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks below -40 °C (Type B). The controller usually limits power to protect the unmonitored phase.
c: Open thermistor or broken connection inside the power inverter module
Loose or corroded connector at the inverter
Lost sensor reference ground on the sensing board
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning
Reduced electric drive power once the inverter has warmed up

P0BDF.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor E Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BDF.d: P0BDF flags an unstable signal from inverter temperature sensor E: the reading jumps or drops out briefly instead of staying out of range, typically from a loose connector, a cracked solder joint or an ageing thermistor. In GM's hybrid tables sensor E is the phase W sensor of the motor A inverter, but GM does not list this erratic code; no manufacturer documents P0BDF publicly. CARB requires hybrid sensor circuits to be checked for circuit faults, which includes intermittent signals. Unlike P0BDD and P0BDE, the value returns to plausible levels between faults, so the code may come and go. Because the controller cannot trust the sensor, it usually reduces motor power while the fault is present.
c: Loose, corroded or vibrating connector at the inverter
Cracked solder joint on the inverter sensing board
s: Malfunction indicator lamp that comes and goes
Occasional loss of electric drive power

P0BE0.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor F Circuit
P0BE0.d: Sensor F is, in GM's hybrid tables, the third thermistor of the motor B inverter (inverter B sensor #3), the counterpart of sensor E in the motor A inverter; the 2016 to 2019 tables assign it to phase W. Other makers may use the letter differently. P0BE0 is its general circuit code for an electrical fault the controller does not narrow down to low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM reports P0BE1, P0BE2 and P0BE3 instead. CARB requires hybrid sensor circuits to be monitored. Without a valid reading the controller cannot protect that inverter phase and usually limits the motor it drives. Read all stored codes, since inverter faults rarely come alone.
c: Internal fault of the thermistor or its circuit inside the power inverter module
Corroded or loose connector at the inverter module
Software fault in the motor control processor
s: Malfunction indicator lamp or hybrid system warning
Reduced power from drive motor B
Higher fuel consumption in hybrid operation

P0BE1.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor F Circuit Range/Performance
P0BE1.d: P0BE1 is the plausibility check of inverter temperature sensor F, GM's phase W thermistor in the motor B inverter. After the car has stood long enough, its reading must match a reference: in the 2016 and 2018 tables a calculated average after cold soak, with more than 20 °C difference for 0.525 of 0.625 s setting Type B over two trips, Type A in a 2019 table. The 2011 Volt compares against power electronics coolant temperature (20 °C, Type A), the 2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks after 360 minutes off with a 15 °C limit (Type B). GM bulletin PIC6303A lists P0BE1 for 2016-18 Volt, Malibu, LaCrosse, Velite and Regal: no customer-noticeable reaction, inverter replacement only with P0AC4.
c: Phase W thermistor of inverter B drifting out of tolerance
Uneven inverter cooling or residual heat after the soak period
Failing power inverter module (replace only with P0AC4 per GM PIC6303A)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp after two drives, usually without drivability change
Code found during inspection without customer complaint

P0BE2.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor F Circuit Low
P0BE2.d: P0BE2 is set when the voltage from inverter temperature sensor F, the phase W thermistor in GM's motor B inverter, drops below the valid window. Because GM pairs an NTC element with a pull-up resistor, a short to ground is converted into a temperature far above anything the inverter can survive. Limits found in GM's tables: more than 170 °C for 2.5 of 3.5 s, Type B, two trips (2016 and 2018); more than 159 °C for 6.25 of 8.75 s, Type A (2019); more than 130 °C, Type A (2011 Volt); more than 125 °C, Type B (2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks). Genuine overheating of this phase has its own code, P0C16. The thermistor is part of the inverter, so it is rarely replaced on its own.
c: Shorted thermistor or signal line inside the power inverter module
Signal shorted to ground in external wiring, where the design has any
Moisture or coolant inside the inverter housing
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning
Power of drive motor B strongly limited
Engine runs more often in hybrid operation

P0BE3.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor F Circuit High
P0BE3.d: P0BE3 is the high-signal fault of inverter temperature sensor F, GM's phase W thermistor in the motor B inverter. With an NTC element and pull-up, an open circuit or a sensor that has lost ground drives the voltage up, which the controller reads as an implausibly cold inverter. GM only judges this after the inverter has worked for at least 90 s at 20 Nm or more: below -50 °C for 2.625 of 3.65 s sets Type B, two trips (2016 and 2018 tables), or Type A for 6.25 of 8.75 s (2019). The 2011 Volt uses below -58 °C (Type A), the 2012 and 2013 two-mode trucks below -40 °C (Type B). Expect limited output from motor B until the circuit is repaired.
c: Open thermistor or broken connection inside the power inverter module
Loose or corroded connector at the inverter
Lost sensor reference ground on the sensing board
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning
Reduced power from drive motor B once warmed up

P0BE4.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor F Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0BE4.d: P0BE4 stands for brief dropouts or jumps in the signal of inverter temperature sensor F, which GM's hybrid tables place at phase W of the motor B inverter. The reading returns to normal between events, which separates it from the steady low and high faults P0BE2 and P0BE3. GM does not list this code, and no other manufacturer documents P0BE4 publicly. CARB's monitoring requirement for hybrid sensor circuits covers such intermittent faults as well. Typical sources are a connector with poor contact, a cracked solder joint or a thermistor whose resistance has become unstable. While the signal is distrusted, the controller tends to cut motor B power, and the fault can disappear before the workshop sees it.
c: Loose, corroded or vibrating connector at the inverter
Cracked solder joint on the inverter sensing board
s: Malfunction indicator lamp that comes and goes
Occasional power reduction of drive motor B

P0BE5.t: Drive Motor A Phase U Current Sensor Circuit
P0BE5.d: The inverter of drive motor A measures the current in each motor phase with a current sensor; the controller needs these values for torque control and overcurrent protection. P0BE5 is the general circuit code for the phase U sensor, used for an electrical fault that is not classed as offset, low or high. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM's hybrid tables (2011 Volt through 2019) only use the siblings P0BE6, P0BE7 and P0BE8, and CARB requires hybrid sensor circuits to be monitored. Without a reliable phase U reading the inverter typically switches to a reduced or alternate control mode, so motor A loses power. The sensor sits inside the inverter, which usually means inverter replacement.
c: Failed phase U current sensor inside the inverter
Supply or signal fault on the inverter's sensor board
Software fault in the motor control processor
s: Hybrid system warning and malfunction indicator lamp
Reduced power from drive motor A
Possible loss of electric drive

P0BE6.t: Drive Motor A Phase U Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0BE6.d: GM uses P0BE6 as the offset check of the phase U current sensor in the motor A inverter. At every start, while no current flows, the controller learns the sensor's zero offset; if it exceeds 30 A (2011 Volt and 2016 tables, Type A; 2012 two-mode trucks, Type B) or 35 A (2019 table, Type A), the code sets. In GM's BAS Plus (eAssist) table a fault of this sensor makes current control switch to an alternate mode that does not use the current sensors. Jeep lists P0BE6 with the other phase current codes on the 2020 Renegade and Compass 1.3 PHEV for Europe, with the turtle and Service 4WD lights, and fixes it by reprogramming the hybrid control processors.
c: Zero offset of the phase U current sensor drifted beyond the limit
Faulty sensing electronics in the power inverter module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp
