Weak or failed electric coolant pump of the circuit
Clogged radiator or inoperative cooling fan
s: Hybrid or EV system warning and MIL
Reduced drive power, especially under load or in heat
Coolant level low in the electronics reservoir

P0C32.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cooling System A Performance
P0C32.d: P0C32 is the functional check of the battery thermal system that CARB asks for. GM tunes it per vehicle: the 2012 Volt (12OBDG01A) fails it when the average pack temperature stays above 40 °C in active cooling or below −17 °C in active heating, after 4200 s or 9000 s, Type A, one trip. The Two-Mode trucks (12OBDG06) compare the hottest module with a limit that rises with inlet temperature, from 45 °C to about 65 °C, Type B. The air-cooled eAssist (13OBDG05C) models the power pack temperature after six hours off and fails above 15 °C deviation, Type B. GM bulletin PIP4992C links P0C32 on 2012–2016 eAssist cars to a pack fan that stops at low 12 V voltage and calls for reprogramming and fan replacement. B and C circuits use P2D3F and P2D40.
c: Battery cooling fan stopping at low 12 V system voltage (GM eAssist)
Low coolant, air or a weak pump in a liquid-cooled pack circuit
Blocked cooling air intake or ducts of an air-cooled pack
Failed pack heater or chiller valve
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Reduced electric range or assist
Charging system or battery warning message (eAssist)

P0C33.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit
P0C33.d: Battery temperature sensor F is the sixth thermistor in the high-voltage pack; GM's Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists the F codes under temperature sensor 6 of nine. P0C33 is the general circuit code for an electrical fault the controller does not classify as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly: GM's hybrid tables use only the more specific siblings P0C34 to P0C37. CARB requires battery temperature sensors to be monitored for circuit faults and, where possible, separate codes that point to the smallest replaceable part. With one temperature missing the controller has to assume the worst and limits charge and discharge power. The sensor sits inside the pack, so checks need high-voltage safety procedures.
c: Loose or corroded connector of sensor F at the sensing board
Faulty input on the battery sensing board or module
s: Hybrid or EV system warning and MIL
Reduced power or charging rate
Battery cooling running more than usual

P0C34.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit Range/Performance
P0C34.d: P0C34 checks whether sensor F, GM's sensor 6, agrees with the rest of the pack. The controller compares its reading with the average of the other battery temperature sensors. GM's 2016 hybrid table fails it above 25 °C difference in 50 of 67 samples; the Volt and plug-in tables of 2016 to 2019 use 20 °C, in 2018 for 5 s within 6.7 s; the air-cooled eAssist (13OBDG05C) allows only 8.55 °C and tests only after more than six hours with the module off. All are Type B, two trips. Active circuit codes suspend the test, so P0C34 means a sensor that reads wrongly but within range, or a real local hot or cold spot. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 names it sensor 6 performance among codes that set in cold weather without a hardware fault.
c: Sensor F drifting or poorly seated on its cell group
Module software setting the code falsely in the cold (GM Volt)
Real local temperature difference from a weak cell group or uneven cooling
s: MIL on after two trips
Battery too cold or reduced power message
Limited charge and discharge power

P0C35.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit Low
P0C35.d: Sensor F is an NTC thermistor with a pull-up on the sensing board, so its voltage drops as temperature rises; a short to ground looks like an extremely hot cell group. Low refers to the signal, not to the temperature. GM's 2016 table sets P0C35 when the converted value exceeds 160 °C in 8 of 10 samples; the Volt battery tables of 2016 to 2019 use above 87.5 °C for 1.4 s within 2 s; the eAssist mild hybrid flags a sense voltage under 0.3 V, about 90 °C, in 7 of 10 samples. All are Type B, two trips. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 calls it sensor 6 circuit low voltage. The opposite fault is P0C36; a pack that is really too hot is reported as P0A7E. Because the controller must assume heat, it cuts power and may run the cooling hard.
c: Sensor F signal wire chafed and shorted to ground
Faulty input on the battery sensing board
s: MIL after two trips
Battery cooling running at high speed
Strongly reduced charge and drive power

P0C36.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit High
P0C36.d: P0C36 means the voltage from battery temperature sensor F sits above its valid range. With GM's NTC thermistor and pull-up, an open circuit, a broken wire or an unplugged connector pulls the input up and reads as an impossibly cold cell group. GM's 2016 table fails it below −69 °C in 8 of 10 samples, the Volt battery tables of 2016 to 2019 below −40 °C for 1.4 s within 2 s, and the eAssist table above 4.63 V, about −45 °C, in 7 of 10 samples, each as Type B, two trips. Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists it as sensor 6 circuit high voltage and links the F group to a Battery Too Cold message. The counterpart for a short to ground is P0C35. Expect limited power and possibly pack heating that is not needed.
c: Open circuit or unlatched connector of sensor F
Module software setting the code falsely in the cold (GM Volt)
s: MIL after two trips
Battery too cold, plug in to warm message
Reduced electric power

P0C37.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0C37.d: P0C37 targets a sensor F signal that jumps instead of following the slow temperature change of a heavy battery. GM documents the logic in its 2016 to 2018 hybrid tables (16OBDG02, 17OBDG02, 18OBDG02): every 100 ms the controller adds up the absolute changes of the sensor value over a window of 10 samples; a sum above 10 fails the window, and 4 failed windows out of 5 set the code as Type B, two trips, with system voltage above 10.2 V and no communication fault active. The Volt, Two-Mode and eAssist tables have no erratic code for this sensor. Unlike P0C35 and P0C36, the signal stays inside its valid range, so the cause is usually a loose terminal or a cracked wire. If several sensors jump at once, the sensing board is the likelier suspect.
c: Loose terminal or connector of sensor F not fully latched after pack work
Cracked sensor wire with intermittent contact
Faulty battery sensing board, often with several sensors affected
s: MIL after two trips
Intermittent hybrid warning, often on rough roads
Temporarily reduced power

P0C38.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0C38.d: The DC/DC converter steps the high-voltage battery down to the 12 V system and replaces the alternator in hybrids and EVs. Its power stage carries temperature sensors so the controller can derate before the semiconductors overheat. P0C38 is the general circuit code for sensor A. Hyundai documents it on the 2027 Palisade Hybrid as P0C381C (failure type 1C, voltage out of range): the hybrid warning light comes on after the car has been parked for a long time, and bulletin 26-01-071H and campaign 9D8 cure it with an HPCU software update that improves the detection logic, so the sensor itself is usually fine. CARB requires the converter's inputs to be monitored as comprehensive components. Low, high and erratic signals have their own codes P0C3A to P0C3C.
c: Control unit software misjudging the sensor after long parking (Hyundai Palisade Hybrid)
Fault in the circuit of sensor A inside the converter or power control unit
Internal fault of the DC/DC converter requiring replacement
s: Hybrid system warning light
12 V charging reduced or switched off
Code appearing after the car has stood for a long time

P0C39.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A Range/Performance
P0C39.d: P0C39 is the plausibility check of DC/DC converter temperature sensor A: its reading lies within the electrical range but does not fit the converter's operating state or a second sensor. FCA uses it on the 2021 Ram 1500 with the 3.6 litre eTorque mild hybrid, where the code is called temperature sensor 1 performance. Bulletin 08-037-21 updates the HCP software and changes this code from a two-trip to a one-trip DTC, so the MIL can come on after a single fault. Sensor B, sensor 2 at Ram, has the matching code P0C3E. CARB requires rationality checks for such inputs. A drifting sensor or poor thermal contact is typical; outright circuit faults are reported as P0C38, P0C3A or P0C3B instead.
c: Outdated hybrid control software (Ram 1500 eTorque, bulletin 08-037-21)
Sensor A drifting or with poor thermal contact to the power stage
Uneven cooling of the converter making the readings disagree
s: MIL, after one trip with updated Ram software
Mild hybrid assist or 12 V supply reduced

P0C3A.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A Low
P0C3A.d: P0C3A means the signal of DC/DC converter temperature sensor A is below its valid range. Low refers to the signal voltage: with an NTC thermistor and pull-up, as GM uses for its hybrid temperature sensors, a short to ground or a failed element reads as extreme heat. No manufacturer documents P0C3A publicly. Mercedes-Benz shows the opposite case for the same sensor, P0C3B as a short to positive, on the EQB and the G-Class, and Ram the plausibility code P0C39. CARB requires the converter's inputs to be checked for out-of-range values. Because the controller must assume an overheated power stage, it limits or stops the converter output; the 12 V battery then supplies the car alone and a low-voltage warning may follow. The sensor is usually built into the converter.
c: Sensor A signal shorted to ground inside the converter or its harness
Shorted temperature element A, usually requiring converter replacement
Converter really overheated due to a cooling fault
s: Hybrid or EV system warning
12 V battery warning, system voltage dropping
Reduced power or restricted functions

P0C3B.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A High
P0C3B.d: P0C3B reports a signal from DC/DC converter temperature sensor A above its valid range, typically a short to positive or an open circuit pulled up by the input. Mercedes-Benz documents it on series 243 (EQB) and 465 (G-Class, including the electric G 580): information LI54.10-P-079533 describes P0C3B00 as a short circuit to positive of temperature sensor A, stored together with P0E9700, P0E5400 and P0C4000 after faulty wake-up behaviour of the converter. Drivers see a red 12 V battery message and white or yellow HV warnings. The remedy is a converter check in XENTRY, clearing the fault memory and a converter reset; parts are not replaced first. The low-signal sibling is P0C3A, sensor B's high code is P0C40.
c: Faulty wake-up behaviour of the converter putting it into an error state (Mercedes 243/465)
Open circuit or short to positive in the sensor A circuit
Internal defect of the DC/DC converter
s: Red 12 V battery warning in the cluster
White or yellow high-voltage system warning
12 V battery no longer charged while driving

P0C3C.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A Intermittent/Erratic
P0C3C.d: P0C3C covers a signal from DC/DC converter temperature sensor A that drops out or jumps for short moments while staying mostly within range. The heat sink of a converter warms and cools slowly, so fast jumps point to the signal path rather than to real temperature changes. No manufacturer documents P0C3C publicly. The method is known from GM's hybrid tables for comparable thermistors, such as P0C37 for battery sensor F: the controller adds up signal changes in short windows and fails the test when several windows exceed a limit. CARB requires such inputs to be monitored for faults. Typical causes are a loose terminal, vibration damage or moisture at the converter connector. Unlike P0C3A and P0C3B, the fault may vanish between tests, so a wiggle test helps.
c: Loose terminal or moisture at the converter connector
Harness damaged by vibration with intermittent contact
s: Intermittent hybrid or EV warning
Occasional 12 V charging interruptions

P0C3D.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P0C3D.d: P0C3D is the general circuit code for the second temperature sensor of the DC/DC converter, which turns high-voltage battery power into 12 V supply. Converters with two sensors watch separate parts of the power stage or cross-check one sensor against the other. No manufacturer documents P0C3D publicly. Sensor B itself appears in bulletins: Mercedes-Benz lists P0C4000, a short to positive of sensor B, on the EQB and the G-Class, and Ram the plausibility code P0C3E as temperature sensor 2 on the 2021 1500 eTorque. Sensor A uses P0C38 for the same fault class. CARB requires such converter inputs to be monitored. A circuit fault makes the controller limit or stop the converter, so the 12 V battery may run down and warnings follow.
c: Connector or wiring fault in the sensor B circuit
Failed temperature element B inside the converter
Converter or hybrid control software misjudging the sensor
s: Hybrid or EV system warning
12 V battery warning

P0C3E.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor B Range/Performance
P0C3E.d: P0C3E flags DC/DC converter temperature sensor B as electrically valid but implausible, for instance when it disagrees with sensor A or with what the converter load should produce. FCA uses it on the 2021 Ram 1500 with the 3.6 litre eTorque mild hybrid under the name temperature sensor 2 performance. Bulletin 08-037-21 reflashes the hybrid control processor and changes P0C3E, together with P0C39 for sensor 1, from a two-trip to a one-trip code, so one failed test can light the MIL. CARB requires rationality checks for converter inputs. Typical causes are a drifting element, poor thermal contact or outdated software. Circuit faults of sensor B are reported as P0C3D, P0C3F or P0C40; a converter that is really too hot sets P0D32 instead.
c: Outdated hybrid control software (Ram 1500 eTorque, bulletin 08-037-21)
Sensor B drifting or with poor thermal contact
Uneven converter cooling making sensors A and B disagree
s: MIL, after one trip with updated Ram software
Mild hybrid assist or 12 V supply reduced

P0C3F.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor B Low
P0C3F.d: P0C3F is stored when the voltage from the second temperature sensor of the DC/DC converter falls below the lowest plausible value. These sensors are normally NTC thermistors fed through a pull-up resistor, so a low voltage corresponds to an extremely hot reading; a short to ground or a shorted element produces exactly that. No manufacturer documents P0C3F publicly. GM uses the same logic for comparable hybrid thermistors, flagging a low circuit once the computed temperature reaches about 88 °C. Mercedes-Benz lists the opposite fault of the same sensor, P0C40, on the EQB and G-Class. CARB requires hybrid component inputs to be checked for out-of-range signals. The converter usually derates to protect itself, so 12 V charging suffers. Sensor A's low code is P0C3A.
c: Sensor B signal line shorted to ground in the converter or harness
Shorted thermistor B, usually only fixable by replacing the converter
Converter actually overheating because its cooling fails
s: Hybrid or EV system warning in the cluster
12 V battery warning or falling on-board voltage
Reduced power or switched-off comfort consumers

P0C40.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor B High
P0C40.d: P0C40 means the second temperature sensor of the DC/DC converter delivers a voltage above its valid window, which on a thermistor circuit points to a short to positive or an open line pulled up to the reference. Mercedes-Benz documents it for the EQB (series 243) and the G-Class including the electric G 580 (series 465). Information LI54.10-P-079533 describes P0C4000 as a short to positive of temperature sensor B and lists it among up to four converter codes, with P0C3B00, P0E9700 and P0E5400, that appear after the converter wakes up incorrectly. The car shows a red 12 V battery message plus HV warnings. Workshops check the converter with XENTRY, erase the memory and reset the unit before replacing anything. P0C3F is the low counterpart; sensor A uses P0C3B.
c: Converter entering a fault state after incorrect wake-up (Mercedes 243/465)
Open circuit or short to positive in the sensor B wiring
Internal defect of the DC/DC converter
s: Red 12 V battery message in the instrument cluster
White or yellow high-voltage warning
12 V battery no longer charged while driving

P0C41.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor B Intermittent/Erratic
P0C41.d: P0C41 concerns a reading from DC/DC converter temperature sensor B that jumps or briefly drops out while it mostly remains inside the valid range. A converter heat sink changes temperature slowly, so abrupt steps indicate a signal problem rather than real heating. No manufacturer documents P0C41 publicly. GM's 2019 hybrid tables show the usual method on the battery coolant thermistor: the controller adds the absolute differences of ten consecutive 100 ms samples and counts a failure when the sum exceeds 64 °C, setting the code after 4 s within a 5 s window. CARB requires hybrid component inputs to be monitored for such faults. Typical culprits are a loose terminal, moisture or vibration damage. Unlike P0C3F and P0C40, the fault can disappear between checks.
c: Loose terminal or moisture at the converter connector
Harness chafed or cracked by vibration
s: Hybrid or EV warning that comes and goes
Short interruptions of 12 V charging

P0C42.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0C42.d: P0C42 is the general circuit code for the first coolant temperature sensor in the liquid loop of a hybrid or EV battery, typically placed at the pack inlet. The battery controller uses it to decide when to pump, heat or chill the coolant. Volvo documents P0C4200 in the battery energy control module of the XC90 T8 plug-in hybrid from model year 2016, as either an intermittent or a permanent entry with a possible check engine lamp; according to technical journal TJ 33546, once the current software is verified the entry is simply erased and no parts are needed. GM reports faults of the same sensor more precisely as P0C44 and P0C45. CARB requires the inputs of the battery thermal management to be monitored. P0C43 covers implausible readings, P0CD5 sensor B.
c: Battery controller software flagging the circuit wrongly (Volvo XC90 T8)
Corroded or loose connector or damaged wire at the coolant sensor
s: Check engine lamp, often without other complaints
Battery cooling or heating running on substitute values
Reduced charging or drive power in hot or cold weather

P0C43.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0C43.d: P0C43 flags battery coolant temperature sensor A as electrically valid but not believable. GM's 2019 hybrid tables describe a cold-soak comparison: once all high-voltage contactors and the battery heater have been off for at least 14,400 s, the hybrid controller compares inlet coolant temperature with the average cell temperature and with outside air, failing when the gaps reach about 23 °C and 22 °C; 8 s out of 10 s set a Type B code, so the MIL follows on the second trip. Audi uses P0C4300 in the thermal management module of the 2020 Q5 TFSI e. Bulletin 2059530 and update 80C9 explain that the stored limits were set too tightly for everyday conditions, so the code and P0CE100 appeared without a defect; new software fixes it. CARB demands rationality checks for battery thermal inputs.
c: Too tight plausibility limits in the control software (Audi Q5 TFSI e, update 80C9)
Coolant sensor A drifting away from its characteristic
Added resistance in the sensor circuit shifting the reading
s: MIL after a cold start, often with no other complaint
Battery thermal management working on substitute values

P0C44.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0C44.d: P0C44 reports that the voltage of battery coolant temperature sensor A is too low. The sensor is an NTC thermistor, so a low voltage translates into a very hot reading, and a short to ground or a shorted element is the classic cause. GM documents the code in the battery energy control module: the 2011 Chevrolet Volt sets it when the inlet coolant value reaches 87.9 °C (ADC count 130 or less), the 2019 hybrid tables use the same temperature at an ADC count of 133 or less. The fault must be present for 1.75 s within a 2.5 s window; as a Type B code it turns on the MIL after the second trip. Because the controller can no longer trust the coolant value, it may limit battery power. P0C45 is the high counterpart, P0C42 the generic circuit code.
c: Sensor signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Coolant or water in the connector bridging the pins
s: MIL and hybrid or EV system message
Coolant temperature shown implausibly high in live data
Limited charging or drive power

P0C45.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0C45.d: P0C45 indicates that the signal of battery coolant temperature sensor A sits near the reference voltage. On an NTC circuit with pull-up this looks like extreme cold and usually comes from an open circuit, an unplugged connector or a short to voltage. GM uses the code in the battery energy control module: the 2011 Chevrolet Volt fails the test below -40 °C at an ADC count above 3823, the 2019 hybrid tables at a count above 3890. In both cases 1.75 s within 2.5 s are needed, and the Type B rating lights the MIL after two trips. With the inlet reading lost, the controller runs the battery cooling and heating on substitute values and may cut power in hot or cold weather. The low counterpart is P0C44; sensor B reports the same fault as P0CD8.
c: Open signal or ground wire, or connector not latched
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
s: MIL after two trips
Coolant temperature shown at about -40 °C in live data
Reduced charging power in extreme temperatures

P0C46.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0C46.d: P0C46 points to a battery coolant temperature signal that jumps faster than liquid in the loop can physically change temperature. GM's 2019 hybrid tables explain the check: every 100 ms the hybrid controller takes the difference to the previous inlet coolant value, adds up ten of these absolute steps and counts a failure when the sum exceeds 64 °C. Four seconds of failures within a five second window set the code, rated Type B with the MIL on the second trip. The test is suppressed while the hard circuit faults P0C44 or P0C45 are active, so P0C46 usually means a signal that is present but noisy. Loose terminals, contact corrosion or a harness that moves with the battery are the usual causes; wiggling the wiring with live data running helps locate it. Sensor B uses P0CD9.
c: Loose or spread terminal at the coolant sensor connector
Corrosion at connector or ground point
Harness rubbing or cracked near the battery coolant lines
s: MIL that may go out again for a while
Jumping coolant temperature in live data

P0C47.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump A Control Circuit/Open
P0C47.d: P0C47 means the controller sees an electrical fault on the line that commands battery coolant pump A. GM's 2019 tables catch open, short to ground and short to power by current: with the pump on, less than 200 mA or more than 3 A on the control line count as failures, with the pump off less than 120 µA; 4 s within 5 s set a Type B code. Porsche reports P0C4700 on the 2015–2017 Cayenne plug-in hybrid (92A), often with the MIL as the only symptom, and blames corroded ground pin 6B, a corroded pump connector or poor wiring. Audi links it on the 2024 Q4 e-tron to corrosion at splice J1 with reduced power. Bentley warns that on 2025–2026 Continental GT and Flying Spur hybrids it can keep the car from switching to ready mode. P0C48 and P0C49 are the low and high variants.
c: Corroded or painted ground point or corroded pump connector (Porsche Cayenne 92A)
Corroded splice or chafed harness in the pump circuit (Audi Q4 e-tron, Bentley)
Failed electric coolant pump or its relay
s: MIL, frequently the only sign
Electrical or drive system warning with reduced power
Vehicle refuses to become ready to drive

P0C48.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump A Control Circuit Low
P0C48.d: P0C48 narrows a fault on the control line of battery coolant pump A down to a signal that stays too low, as caused by a short to ground or a driver output that cannot pull the line up. Ford lists the code for the 2020 Explorer, Police Interceptor Utility and Lincoln Aviator with the hybrid powertrain. Bulletins 20-2293 and 20-2345 group it with P0C49, P0C4A, P0C4B, P0CFF, P2B29 and other pump and battery codes that light the MIL and are stored in the PCM; the cause is the software of the battery energy control module, which is reprogrammed. Other makers, GM for instance, cover the same failure inside the broader code P0C47. CARB requires output components of battery thermal management to be checked for circuit faults. If the pump really stops, battery power is limited.
c: Battery control module software (Ford/Lincoln 2020 hybrids, TSB 20-2345)
Pump control wire shorted to ground
Internal fault in the pump electronics pulling the line low
s: MIL on
Hybrid system message, battery power possibly limited

P0C49.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump A Control Circuit High
P0C49.d: P0C49 is set when the control signal to battery coolant pump A remains too high, for example because the line is shorted to battery voltage or, on a pulled-up input, interrupted. Ford uses it on the 2020 Explorer, Police Interceptor Utility and Lincoln Aviator hybrids. Bulletins 20-2293 and 20-2345 list it right after P0C48 among a group of MIL codes for the battery and electronics coolant pumps; Ford traces them to the battery energy control module software and fixes them by reprogramming. GM, by contrast, folds short to power into P0C47. CARB requires the outputs of battery thermal management to be monitored for circuit faults. If the pump actually loses its command, the battery heats up faster under load and the system reduces power. P0C48 is the low counterpart, P0C4D concerns the supply voltage instead.
c: Battery control module software (Ford/Lincoln 2020 hybrids, TSB 20-2293/20-2345)
Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Control line interrupted at the pump connector
s: MIL on
Battery power reduced during long climbs or fast charging

P0C4A.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump A Control Performance
P0C4A.d: P0C4A says pump A runs electrically but does not achieve its cooling effect. The 2011 Chevrolet Volt fails the test when the pump has been on for over 60 s and the pack inlet coolant temperature has moved by less than 5 °C, rated Type B. GM's bulletin PI0798A (Volt 2011–2015, Ampera 2012, ELR 2014–2016) traces the code after draining and refilling to trapped air, cured by a vacuum purge. Porsche explains for the 2018 Panamera 4 E-Hybrid that the pump reports dry running when its speed rises while current drops, a condition that can need a long stretch of driving before it is logged. Audi (Q4 e-tron 2022) and Bentley (Bentayga and Flying Spur Hybrid, EV speed capped near 48 km/h) also bleed first, Ford reflashes the battery module. FCA's Pacifica Hybrid uses P0C4A for inverter overtemperature instead.
c: Air trapped in the battery coolant loop, often after a coolant service
Low coolant level or a leak in the low-temperature loop
s: MIL shortly after cooling system work
Electric drive warning, reduced power or capped EV speed
Gurgling noise from the coolant loop

P0C4B.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump A Supply Voltage Circuit/Open
P0C4B.d: P0C4B refers to the power feed of battery coolant pump A rather than its command line: the controller sees no or only an implausible supply voltage at the pump, typically because a fuse, relay, connector or wire in the feed is open. Ford documents the code on its 2020 hybrids. On the Escape HEV built up to 10 June 2020, bulletin 20-2221 lists P0C4B with other battery codes in the battery energy control module and cures the MIL by reprogramming PCM and BECM; bulletins 20-2293 and 20-2345 name it for the Explorer and Aviator hybrids. Without a software cause, the fuse and relay in the pump feed come first. CARB requires the electrical components of battery thermal management to be monitored. P0C4C and P0C4D are the low and high variants of the same supply.
c: Battery control module software (Ford Escape HEV, Explorer and Aviator 2020)
Blown fuse or failed relay in the pump supply
Open feed wire or pushed-out pin at the pump connector
s: MIL on
Battery coolant pump not running, power limited when warm

P0C4C.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump A Supply Voltage Circuit Low
P0C4C.d: P0C4C reports that the supply voltage reaching battery coolant pump A is below the expected level while the circuit is not fully open. Typical reasons are high resistance in the feed, a corroded fuse contact, a weak relay, a poor ground or a short to ground that drags the line down. No manufacturer documents P0C4C publicly. Ford uses the sibling P0C4B for the open supply circuit on its 2020 Escape, Explorer and Aviator hybrids, and Bentley's bulletin on P0C4700 for 2025–2026 Continental GT and Flying Spur hybrids shows what such a feed contains: a 10 A fuse, a relay and a harness route that can chafe at the rear suspension. CARB requires the electrical parts of battery thermal management to be monitored. A pump that receives too little voltage runs slowly or not at all.
c: High resistance from corroded fuse, relay contacts or connector
Supply wire chafed and shorted to ground
s: MIL or hybrid or EV warning
Coolant pump running slowly or intermittently
Battery power reduced when the pack warms up

P0C4D.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump A Supply Voltage Circuit High
P0C4D.d: P0C4D is the counterpart to P0C4C: the voltage measured on the supply of battery coolant pump A is higher than the controller allows. That can come from a feed wire shorted to another, more highly loaded circuit, from a relay that stays closed when the pump should be off, or from an overall excessive on-board voltage, for example a faulty DC/DC converter. No manufacturer documents P0C4D publicly. Ford's bulletins for the 2020 Escape, Explorer and Aviator hybrids name the sibling P0C4B for the open supply, and Bentley describes the feed of the same pump with fuse and relay for 2025–2026 hybrids. CARB requires the electrical components of battery thermal management to be monitored. If several modules log overvoltage at once, the 12 V supply is the more likely culprit than the pump circuit.
c: Supply wire shorted to another voltage-carrying circuit
Excessive 12 V system voltage from a faulty DC/DC converter
s: MIL or hybrid or EV warning
Coolant pump running although the system is switched off

P0C4E.t: Drive Motor A Position Exceeded Learning Limit
P0C4E.d: P0C4E says the resolver offset of drive motor A was learned, yet the learned value is unacceptable. That offset lines up the zero point of the resolver with the rotor magnets. GM rejects a correction angle beyond 30 degrees, or a new value that differs from the stored one by more than 10 degrees; the learn happens at key-off with the motor under 20 rpm and over 192 V on the DC link. Volt and ELR tables rate it Type A, and from 2016 the deviation has to show up on five key-off cycles. Kia links P0C4E00 on 2022-24 Sorento PHEV AWD to a jerky change between electric and hybrid drive and cures it with a new transaxle plus updated hybrid control software (TSB TRA112). P0C17 is the case with no valid learn at all.
c: Resolver or rotor position shifted after replacing the motor, resolver stator or transaxle
Internal transaxle fault on affected Kia Sorento PHEV models (TSB TRA112)
Hybrid or motor control software that needs an update
Damaged resolver that delivers a shifted angle
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, often first noticed after a repair
Jerk or rough feel when switching between electric and hybrid drive
Reduced electric drive power

P0C4F.t: Drive Motor B Position Exceeded Learning Limit
P0C4F.d: P0C4F covers the second traction motor: its resolver offset learn finished, but the angle it produced lies outside what the controller will accept. GM applies the same two tests as for motor A, an absolute correction above 30 degrees or a change of over 10 degrees against the value kept from earlier learns, both checked at key-off with the rotor nearly still and more than 192 V available. The 2011 Volt sets it on one trip as Type A; the 2016 and 2019 Volt tables also say Type A but wait for five key-off cycles with the angle out of range. No bulletin for this code has been published. A large offset jump usually means something mechanical changed, so the check after a motor or sensor job matters most. P0C18 means motor B was never learned.
c: Motor B resolver stator fitted in a different position after a repair
Learn disturbed by a moving rotor or unstable high voltage at key-off
Damaged motor B resolver giving a shifted angle
s: Malfunction indicator lamp after shutdown cycles
Reduced propulsion or motor B unavailable
Unusual noise or shudder under electric drive

P0C50.t: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit A
P0C50.d: A resolver has two pickup windings set 90 degrees apart, one giving a sine and one a cosine signal. The codes P0C50 onward judge each of those circuits on its own, while P0A3F to P0A43 judge the combined angle signal. GM names the S1/S3 winding Circuit A and the S2/S4 winding Circuit B. P0C50 is the general entry for Circuit A of motor A, used when the controller sees a fault in that line without classing it as a low or high reading. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM covers the same winding only through P0C52 and P0C53. CARB requires circuit faults of such inputs to be detected and stored separately from out-of-range faults. Expect a warning lamp and possibly lost electric drive.
c: Open wire or loose terminal in the Circuit A (first pickup winding) lines
Corroded or damaged connector between resolver and motor control module
Defective pickup winding inside the resolver stator
Fault in the resolver input stage of the motor control module
s: Hybrid or drive system warning together with the check engine lamp
Electric drive switched off or reduced power
Vehicle may not reach ready mode

P0C51.t: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit A Range/Performance
P0C51.d: P0C51 means the first resolver winding of motor A (Circuit A) delivers a signal that is electrically present but not believable, for example unsteady or out of step with the second winding. Bentley uses it on 2025 Continental GT, GTC and Flying Spur hybrids, logged by the e-drive control unit at address 0051 next to P0A4000 and later P0C5B00, with a drive system message in the cluster. Bulletin 2080242 asks for logged measured values, a check of the sensor and power electronics plugs for bent pins, weak terminal grip, moisture or corrosion, then basic settings; revision 3 adds a new 90-degree connector. No set threshold is published. P0C52 to P0C54 cover low, high and sporadic faults of the same line.
c: Weak terminal grip or bent pins at the sensor or power electronics connector
Moisture, oil or corrosion in the resolver connectors
Faulty 90-degree connector on the affected Bentley models (TPI 2080242/3)
s: Drive system fault message in the instrument cluster
No electric or hybrid driving mode available
Fault may come and go with temperature or vibration

P0C52.t: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit A Low
P0C52.d: P0C52 reports that the DC reference level on Circuit A of the motor A resolver, the S1/S3 winding in GM terms, has dropped too low, which points to a short to ground or a line pulled down. GM fails it below 0.5 V on the 2011 Volt, 2012 two-mode trucks, 2013 eAssist and 2016 ELR, and below 0.10 V on the 2019 Volt. Timing ranges from 50 of 80 samples taken every 10.4 ms (one trip, Type A) to 0.525 s within 0.8375 s on the 2016 Volt or 0.25 s within 0.375 s on the 2019 Volt (both Type B). Bentley finds P0C5200, often with P0C5C00, on 2020-22 Bentayga Hybrids with a chafed 12 V transmission harness. Unlike P0A41, which rates the whole signal, this code names one winding.
c: Chafed or pinched transmission harness shorting a Circuit A line to ground (Bentley TPI 2066714)
Water or corrosion in the resolver connector
Shorted S1/S3 winding inside the resolver stator
Faulty resolver input in the motor control module
s: Check engine lamp, often with P0C5C stored at the same time
Electric drive shut off or power reduced
On some hybrids the engine runs constantly or the car will not start

P0C53.t: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit A High
P0C53.d: P0C53 is the high counterpart of P0C52: the reference level on the S1/S3 winding circuit of the motor A resolver rises above its window, typical of a short to a voltage source or an open line that floats up. GM uses an upper limit of 4.5 V on the 2011 Volt, 2013 eAssist and 2016 Volt and ELR, 4.9 V on the 2019 Volt and only 3.0 V on the 2012 two-mode Tahoe, Yukon, Escalade, Sierra and Silverado hybrids. It reacts faster than on the low side: 20 of 30 samples (about 208 ms) on the 2011 Volt, 0.2125 s within 0.3125 s on the 2016 Volt. MIL logic is Type A on the 2011 Volt and the 2012 trucks, Type B on eAssist and the later Volt. No bulletin names this code for motor A.
c: Open S1 or S3 line or a terminal that has backed out, letting the input drift high
Circuit A line shorted to a voltage-carrying wire in the harness
Broken S1/S3 winding in the resolver stator
Faulty resolver input in the motor control module
s: Check engine lamp with hybrid system message
Reduced propulsion or electric drive unavailable
Rough engine running on vehicles that use motor A for starting

P0C54.t: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit A Intermittent/Erratic
P0C54.d: P0C54 stands for short dropouts or jumps on Circuit A of the motor A resolver that never last long enough to count as a steady low or high fault. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM handles the same situation differently: on its 2013 eAssist cars the resolver circuit checks run a retry scheme that lets the drive recover from brief faults, and only light the MIL through P0C52 or P0C53 once the trouble repeats, either about 5 s of failure within roughly 10 s or 10 s of accumulated failure over 30 minutes. Typical triggers are loose terminals, a cable that moves with the drivetrain or moisture in the plug. The fault often vanishes after a restart and returns under vibration or heat.
c: Loose or poorly crimped terminal in a Circuit A line
Harness rubbing or flexing at a point that moves with the powertrain
Moisture or contamination in the resolver plug
s: Warning lamp that appears and disappears between trips
Brief loss of electric drive or a short jerk
Fault often gone after a restart

P0C55.t: Drive Motor B Position Sensor Circuit A
P0C55.d: P0C55 is the general circuit code for the first pickup winding (Circuit A) of the resolver on the second traction motor. It applies when the motor B controller recognises a fault on that winding but cannot assign it to a low or high level. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM, which runs two motors in the Volt, ELR and the two-mode trucks, files motor B winding faults under P0C57 and P0C58 instead. Compared with P0A45, which reports the motor B angle signal as a whole, P0C55 narrows the search to one winding and its two wires. CARB requires such circuit faults to be detected separately from out-of-range faults. The result is usually a warning lamp and the loss of motor B for drive or charging.
c: Open wire or loose terminal in the motor B Circuit A lines
Damaged or corroded motor B resolver connector
Defective first pickup winding in the motor B resolver
s: Check engine lamp with hybrid system warning
Motor B unavailable, reduced propulsion
Engine may run more often because the second motor is offline

P0C56.t: Drive Motor B Position Sensor Circuit A Range/Performance
P0C56.d: P0C56 flags a plausibility problem on Circuit A of the motor B resolver: the winding is connected and its level sits inside the electrical window, yet the signal it carries does not fit, for instance because it wanders or no longer matches the second winding. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The closest published case is the motor A version P0C51, which Bentley traces to connector pin fit and contamination on its 2025 Continental hybrids. Possible reasons on motor B are the same kind of contact issue, a resolver with weakened output or interference on poorly shielded lines. P0C57 to P0C59 cover hard low, high and sporadic faults, and P0A46 judges the overall motor B angle signal.
c: Poor pin fit or contamination at the motor B resolver connector
Damaged shield or twisted pair letting interference onto Circuit A
Motor B resolver winding with weakened output
s: Hybrid warning and check engine lamp
Motor B torque limited or switched off
Occasional shudder when motor B takes load

P0C57.t: Drive Motor B Position Sensor Circuit A Low
P0C57.d: P0C57 means the reference level on Circuit A of the motor B resolver, the S1/S3 winding in GM wiring, has sunk below its limit. GM checks it exactly like the motor A line: under 0.5 V on the 2011 and 2016 Volt and the 2012 two-mode trucks, under 0.10 V on the 2019 Volt, with Type A on the early cars and Type B from 2016. In the field it rarely stands alone. GM preliminary information PIC5856A to F for 2011-13 Volt and 2014-16 ELR groups P0C57 with P0C58 and P0C62: if wiring checks and normal diagnosis find nothing, the motor B position sensor is replaced and the drive motor generator control module is brought to its latest calibration. A genuine harness fault to ground still has to be excluded before any parts are ordered.
c: Faulty motor B position sensor (resolver stator) on Volt and ELR (GM PIC5856)
Circuit A line of motor B shorted to ground in the harness
Drive motor generator control module not on the latest calibration
s: Service engine soon lamp, current or in history
Often stored together with P0C58 and P0C62
Reduced propulsion

P0C58.t: Drive Motor B Position Sensor Circuit A High
P0C58.d: P0C58 sets when the S1/S3 winding circuit of the motor B resolver shows a reference level above its window, as from an open lead drifting up or a short to voltage. GM limits are 4.5 V on the 2011 and 2016 Volt, 4.9 V on the 2019 Volt and 3.0 V on the 2012 two-mode trucks, with the fast high-side timing of 20 out of 30 samples on early cars. This is one of the most frequent resolver codes on the first-generation Volt. GM's first note PIC5856 from 2013 already paired P0C58 with P0C62, the S2/S4 high code, on 2011-13 Volts: if wiring is fine, a new motor B position sensor goes in, a part ordered through GM's technical assistance center, and update the module calibration.
c: Faulty motor B position sensor on 2011-13 Volt and 2014-16 ELR (GM PIC5856)
Open S1 or S3 line or spread terminal at the resolver connector
Motor control module running an older calibration
s: Check engine lamp, frequently together with P0C62
Reduced propulsion power
Fault may only be in history memory

P0C59.t: Drive Motor B Position Sensor Circuit A Intermittent/Erratic
P0C59.d: P0C59 reports that Circuit A of the motor B resolver drops out or jumps for moments only, without a fault that persists as low, high or implausible. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Where a dual-motor system uses it, the cause is nearly always mechanical: a terminal that loses grip under vibration, a cable section that flexes with the transmission, or water creeping into a plug. The GM truck note PIP4607A shows how a single poorly crimped terminal at the transmission pass-through connector can upset resolver signals of motor B. Since short glitches on a position signal disturb torque control, the controller may still cut motor B briefly. P0C57 and P0C58 are the steady faults on the same winding.
c: Poorly crimped or loose terminal in the motor B Circuit A path
Wire breaking inside its insulation where the harness flexes
Water ingress at the resolver or pass-through connector
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Short loss of motor B assistance or a jerk
Intermittent start problems on some hybrids

P0C5A.t: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit B
P0C5A.d: P0C5A is the base circuit code for Circuit B, the second pickup winding of the motor A resolver; GM calls it the S2/S4 winding, set 90 degrees from the S1/S3 winding of Circuit A. The code is meant for a fault on that winding which the controller cannot class as a low or high level. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM checks the S2/S4 line only through P0C5C and P0C5D. If P0C5A appears on its own, the problem is limited to the second winding and its two wires; if P0C50 is stored too, a shared part such as the connector or the excitation side is more likely. P0A3F, by contrast, covers a lost angle signal without naming a winding. Expect a warning and possibly no electric drive.
c: Open wire or loose terminal in the S2/S4 (Circuit B) lines
Defective second pickup winding in the resolver stator
s: Check engine lamp with drive system warning
Electric drive limited or unavailable
Vehicle may refuse to enter ready mode

P0C5B.t: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit B Range/Performance
P0C5B.d: P0C5B is set when the second resolver winding of motor A (Circuit B) stays within its electrical limits yet carries a signal that does not make sense next to the first winding. Bentley added it in revision 3 of bulletin 2080242 for the Continental GT, GTC and Flying Spur hybrids: P0C5B00 now appears alongside P0C5100 and P0A4000, which shows that both windings lose plausibility at once when the shared connection is poor. The repair path is the same, measured value logs, inspection of the 8-pin and 32-pin plugs for pin drag and corrosion, replacement of a 90-degree connector after approval, then basic settings. No threshold is published. P0C5C to P0C5E are the low, high and sporadic Circuit B faults.
c: Insufficient terminal grip at the sensor or power electronics connector
Faulty 90-degree connector on affected Bentley hybrids (TPI 2080242/3)
Corrosion, oil or moisture in the resolver plugs
s: Drive system fault shown in the cluster
Electric drive mode not available
Usually stored together with P0C51 and P0A40

P0C5C.t: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit B Low
P0C5C.d: P0C5C tells that the reference level on the S2/S4 winding of the motor A resolver, Circuit B, has fallen below its floor. GM uses 0.5 V on the 2011 Volt, 2012 two-mode trucks, 2013 eAssist and the 2016 Volt and ELR, 0.10 V on the 2019 Volt; the low side needs a longer confirmation than the high side, for example 0.525 s within 0.8375 s on the 2016 Volt. On the single-motor eAssist it is a two-trip Type B code. Bentley lists P0C5C00 first in its Bentayga Hybrid note 2066714: damaged 12 V transmission wiring, often with P0C5200 and a temperature sensor code P0A2D00, so a harness worn through on one spot can pull down both windings and other motor sensors at once.
c: Transmission harness chafed or pinched, grounding an S2/S4 line (Bentley TPI 2066714)
Moisture or corrosion in the resolver connector
Shorted S2/S4 winding in the resolver stator
s: Engine warning light, often with P0C52 and a motor temperature code
Electric drive limited or switched off
On mild hybrids loss of start-stop and assist

P0C5D.t: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit B High
P0C5D.d: P0C5D means the S2/S4 winding circuit of the motor A resolver, Circuit B, reads a reference level above its ceiling. This hints at an open wire whose input floats toward the supply, or contact with a voltage-carrying conductor. GM applies 4.5 V on most of its hybrids, 4.9 V on the 2019 Volt and a much lower 3.0 V on the 2012 two-mode Tahoe, Yukon, Escalade, Sierra and Silverado. On the 2013 eAssist cars, 20 failed samples out of 30 at 10.4 ms set a two-trip Type B fault; the 2011 Volt uses the same count as a one-trip Type A. When P0C5D appears with P0C53, the shared plug or the resolver itself is more likely than a single wire. No bulletin names this code.
c: Open S2 or S4 wire or backed-out terminal
S2/S4 line touching a voltage-carrying conductor
Broken S2/S4 winding in the resolver stator
Faulty resolver input stage in the motor control module
s: Check engine lamp after one or two trips depending on the vehicle
Electric assist or drive unavailable
Auto stop disabled on mild hybrids

P0C5E.t: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit B Intermittent/Erratic
P0C5E.d: P0C5E captures brief interruptions or spikes on Circuit B, the second winding of the motor A resolver, that clear again before a firm low, high or plausibility fault can be confirmed. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM leaves such events to the debounce of P0C5C and P0C5D, which on its eAssist cars tolerates short outages and only reports a repeating pattern. Where P0C5E is used, the search starts at the mechanical joints of the S2/S4 path: crimp quality, terminal grip, a cable clip that lets the harness rub on the transmission. Checking resistance while flexing the harness tends to reveal it. P0C54 is the same fault on Circuit A; both together point to the common connector.
c: Loose or weak terminal in the S2/S4 path
Harness rubbing on the transmission because of a missing or broken clip
s: Warning light appearing only now and then
Momentary drop of electric torque
No fault found on a stationary check

P0C5F.t: Drive Motor B Position Sensor Circuit B
P0C5F.d: P0C5F is the umbrella circuit code for Circuit B of the motor B resolver, which GM wires as the S2/S4 winding of the second traction motor. It fits a fault on that winding that the controller notices but cannot assign to a low or high reading. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; on GM's dual-motor hybrids the same winding is covered by P0C61 and P0C62 only. Together, P0C55 and P0C5F let a technician see whether one or both windings of motor B are affected: one alone points to that winding's wires, both together to the shared plug, the excitation or the motor control module. P0A45 reports the overall motor B angle signal. Expect a warning lamp and the loss of motor B.
c: Open wire or loose terminal in the motor B S2/S4 lines
Damaged motor B resolver or pass-through connector
Defective second pickup winding in the motor B resolver
s: Hybrid warning and check engine lamp
Motor B shut off, lower propulsion
Possible no-start on hybrids that crank with motor B

P0C60.t: Drive Motor B Position Sensor Circuit B Range/Performance
P0C60.d: P0C60 indicates that the second winding of the motor B resolver (Circuit B) is electrically intact but delivers values the controller rejects as unrealistic, for example an amplitude that no longer agrees with the first winding or an angle that jumps against the measured speed. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The idea behind it is the separate rationality test that CARB demands for input sensors, apart from circuit and range checks. Practical suspects are contact resistance at the plug, a resolver stator that has moved or been damaged, and stray coupling from the high-voltage phase cables onto a poorly shielded line. P0C61 to P0C63 cover low, high and sporadic Circuit B faults, P0A46 the combined signal.
c: Raised contact resistance at the motor B resolver connector
Motor B resolver stator shifted or damaged
Interference from the high-voltage phase cables through a damaged shield
s: Hybrid system warning with check engine lamp
Motor B output limited
Vibration or noise when motor B is under load

P0C61.t: Drive Motor B Position Sensor Circuit B Low
P0C61.d: P0C61 reports a reference level below the lower limit on the S2/S4 winding circuit of the motor B resolver. GM uses 0.5 V on the 2011 and 2016 Volt and the 2012 two-mode trucks, 0.10 V on the 2019 Volt, and needs the low reading for 50 of 80 samples on early cars, 0.25 s within 0.375 s on the 2019 model. A documented field case comes from the 2008 Tahoe and Yukon Hybrid: GM's PIP4607A describes no-crank or intermittent start complaints with P0A45, P0C61, P0A46 and P1B04, traced to a badly crimped pin 20 in the 24-way transmission pass-through connector X176; vehicles built before VIN 8R217000 receive a new internal transmission harness. P0C62 is the high side.
c: Poor crimp at the transmission pass-through connector (GM PIP4607A, 2008 Tahoe/Yukon Hybrid)
S2/S4 line of motor B shorted to ground
Shorted S2/S4 winding in the motor B resolver
s: Engine does not crank or cranks only intermittently
Check engine lamp with several resolver codes of motor B
Reduced propulsion

P0C62.t: Drive Motor B Position Sensor Circuit B High
P0C62.d: P0C62 means the reference level on the S2/S4 winding circuit of the motor B resolver climbs above its upper limit. GM triggers it at 4.5 V on the 2011 and 2016 Volt and ELR, 4.9 V on the 2019 Volt and 3.0 V on the 2012 two-mode trucks; on the 2016 Volt the level must stay high for 0.2125 s within 0.3125 s, rated Type B over two trips. P0C62 shows up in every GM note of the PIC5856 series, from the 2013 original to version F of 2019, for 2011-13 Volt and 2014-16 ELR, usually paired with P0C58 and sometimes P0C57. Because both windings of the same resolver report high at once, GM's remedy after clean wiring checks is a new motor B position sensor plus the latest module calibration.
c: Faulty motor B position sensor on 2011-13 Volt and 2014-16 ELR (GM PIC5856)
Open S2 or S4 wire or terminal backed out of the connector
Drive motor generator control module without the latest calibration
s: Service engine soon lamp, often with P0C58
Reduced propulsion power
Code may return after clearing until the sensor is replaced

P0C63.t: Drive Motor B Position Sensor Circuit B Intermittent/Erratic
P0C63.d: P0C63 is reserved for short-lived dropouts or erratic jumps on Circuit B, the second winding of the motor B resolver, that do not settle into a steady fault. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The best public illustration comes from GM's 2008 Tahoe and Yukon Hybrid: a weak crimp at the transmission pass-through connector produced intermittent starting with motor B resolver codes, though GM files them under P0C61 and the general P0A45 and P0A46 rather than an intermittent code. That case shows where to look first, crimp joints, pass-through connectors and harness sections near moving parts. Wiggle tests under live data help catch it. P0C59 is the same fault type on Circuit A of motor B.
c: Weak crimp or loose terminal in the motor B S2/S4 path, including pass-through connectors
Intermittent wire break near moving powertrain parts
Moisture or corrosion causing unstable contact
s: Intermittent warning lamp
Occasional start problems or short loss of motor B
Fault not present during a workshop check

P0C64.d: P0C64 is the catch-all entry for the first pickup circuit of the generator resolver, the sensor that reports rotor angle so the inverter can energise the generator phases at the right moment. It is used when the controller judges that circuit faulty without sorting the fault into low, high, implausible or sporadic. No manufacturer documents P0C64 publicly. Mitsubishi shows how such faults get split on the 2023 Outlander PHEV: the sine winding, which it treats as circuit A, has its own low and high codes (P0C66, P0C67), and a failed internal status goes to P0A4B. CARB asks for an approved generator monitoring plan and for circuit and range checks on hybrid inputs. Expect a hybrid system warning and, depending on the design, reduced power or no charging by the engine.
c: Open, chafed or shorted lead in the first resolver pickup winding circuit
Corroded or loose resolver connector between generator and inverter
Damaged pickup winding inside the generator resolver stator
Fault in the generator control electronics of the inverter or power drive unit
s: Hybrid system or malfunction indicator lamp on
Engine runs but the high-voltage battery is no longer charged by the generator
Reduced power or hybrid functions disabled

P0C65.t: Generator Position Sensor Circuit A Range/Performance
P0C65.d: P0C65 flags circuit A of the generator resolver as electrically present but not believable. The trace stays between the hard low and high limits, yet its amplitude, centre voltage or relation to the second winding no longer fits the rotor angle the controller expects, for example after the sensor stator has shifted or when the phase cables couple noise into it. No manufacturer documents P0C65 publicly. Mitsubishi runs an analogous window test on the 2023 Outlander PHEV: a sine or cosine level outside 2.1 to 2.9 V for 0.28 s counts as a plausibility fault, but it is filed under P0A4C for the whole sensor. P0C66 and P0C67 cover hard low and high readings on the same circuit. Typical consequences are a hybrid warning and limited use of the generator.
c: Resolver stator loose or shifted, for instance after work on the generator or transaxle
Interference from the phase cables because of a misrouted or damaged resolver harness
Partially damaged winding that weakens the circuit A signal
Generator control software that misjudges a sound signal
s: Hybrid system warning light
Generator use restricted, less charging while driving
Occasional roughness when the engine starts or stops in hybrid mode

P0C66.t: Generator Position Sensor Circuit A Low
P0C66.d: P0C66 means the signal of circuit A of the generator resolver has dropped below its lower limit. Mitsubishi uses it on the 2023 Outlander PHEV for the sine winding: the generator control unit, supplied with at least 8 V, watches the line continuously and sets the code when the sine voltage stays at or below 2.000 V for 0.21 s. A short to ground on a sine lead or a damaged winding are the classic causes; a Bosch patent shows that the averaged potential of the coil lines reveals whether a lead touches ground or supply. Mitsubishi first checks for radiator fan codes and tests the resolver circuit, and replaces the power drive unit, or later the generator, only if the code comes back. P0C67 is the high counterpart, P0C6B the same test on the cosine side.
c: Sine lead of the resolver shorted to ground or to the housing
Shorted or damaged sine winding in the generator resolver
Faulty input stage in the power drive unit (generator control unit)
Damaged or contaminated resolver connector pins
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning shortly after switching on
Generator out of service, no charging by the engine
Reduced driving power

P0C67.t: Generator Position Sensor Circuit A High
P0C67.d: With P0C67 the controller sees circuit A of the generator resolver stuck above its upper limit. On the 2023 Outlander PHEV Mitsubishi assigns it to the sine winding and trips it once that voltage stays at or above 4.900 V for 0.21 s; the check runs continuously while the generator control unit has 8 V or more. Note the uneven window, since the lower limit is 2.0 V. A lead shorted to a supply potential is the textbook cause, and depending on the input stage an open line can also float high. The Bosch patent on resolver short detection separates both short types by the averaged line potential. Mitsubishi's repair path matches P0C66 and ends with a new power drive unit or generator. P0C6C is the matching cosine code.
c: Sine lead of the resolver shorted to a supply or excitation potential
Open sine lead that floats high at the input stage
Faulty resolver input in the power drive unit
Insulation fault between windings inside the resolver
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning
Engine-driven charging stops, battery charge falls faster
Power limitation or hybrid functions switched off

P0C68.t: Generator Position Sensor Circuit A Intermittent/Erratic
P0C68.d: P0C68 is stored when circuit A of the generator resolver drops out or jumps for short moments and then looks normal again, so neither the low nor the high limit is held long enough to set P0C66 or P0C67. Vibration at a connector, a chafed lead or contacts that loosen with heat are the usual suspects. No manufacturer documents P0C68 publicly. GM gives a practical example for this kind of weakness: on the 2011-12 Volt it replaced the original 2x4 resolver plug of motor A, a part GM lists as the generator position sensor stator, with a sealed 1x6 plug because the signal suffered under vibration, and warns that a misplaced harness lets the phase cables disturb the signal (PIC6136A). Such faults often appear only on rough roads or when hot.
c: Resolver connector with poor contact that opens under vibration
Harness rubbing through intermittently in the transaxle or generator area
Bursts of interference from nearby phase cables due to harness routing
Contact or winding joint that fails only at high temperature
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Brief jolts or interruptions in generator operation
Fault appears mainly on bad roads or after long drives

P0C69.d: P0C69 is the general fault entry for the second pickup winding of the generator resolver. A resolver needs both windings, set 90 degrees apart, to give an unambiguous rotor angle; with only one, the inverter can no longer place the current in the generator phases correctly. The code applies when circuit B is judged faulty but not classified further. No manufacturer documents P0C69 publicly. At Mitsubishi on the 2023 Outlander PHEV circuit B corresponds to the cosine winding, and that design reports it only through the low and high codes P0C6B and P0C6C. CARB's hybrid rules require the generator to be monitored under an approved plan and circuit faults of input components to be detected. P0C64 is the same entry for circuit A.
c: Open or damaged lead in the second resolver pickup winding circuit
Bent, corroded or pushed-back pins at the resolver connector
Faulty second pickup winding in the resolver stator
Internal fault in the generator control electronics
s: Hybrid warning or malfunction indicator lamp
Generator switched off, battery is no longer recharged by the engine
Limited driving power

P0C6A.t: Generator Position Sensor Circuit B Range/Performance
P0C6A.d: P0C6A concerns circuit B of the generator resolver, the cosine side at Mitsubishi: its signal stays inside the electrical limits but does not agree with what the controller expects. Because sine and cosine together describe one angle, a cosine trace with the wrong amplitude or a drifting centre shows up as a mismatch against circuit A, even though no line is shorted. Possible reasons are a loose or twisted sensor stator, a winding with partial damage, or noise picked up from nearby phase leads. No manufacturer documents P0C6A publicly; Mitsubishi's comparable window check on the 2023 Outlander PHEV (2.1 to 2.9 V, 0.28 s) is stored as P0A4C. Hard low or high readings on this circuit belong to P0C6B and P0C6C; the circuit A version is P0C65.
c: Loose or twisted resolver stator changing the cosine amplitude
Partially shorted cosine winding with weakened output
Noise from phase leads due to damaged shielding or poor routing
High contact resistance in the circuit B connector
s: Hybrid warning lamp
Generator used only partly or not at all
Unusual noise or vibration from the transaxle under load

P0C6B.t: Generator Position Sensor Circuit B Low
P0C6B.d: P0C6B tells you that circuit B of the generator resolver, the cosine winding, reads too low. In the 2023 Outlander PHEV, Mitsubishi stores it if the cosine signal is no higher than 2.000 V throughout 0.21 s; the test never pauses while the generator control unit receives 8 V or more. To confirm a repair, the matching drive cycle only asks for the power supply mode to be switched ON and a wait of five seconds or more. Likely causes are a cosine lead with a short to ground, a pinched harness near the transaxle or a failing winding. If the resolver circuit tests fine and the code returns, Mitsubishi fits a new power drive unit and, once the EV oil cooling has been checked, a new generator. P0C66 is the sine-side twin, P0C6C the high reading on the same line.
c: Cosine lead of the resolver shorted to ground
Pinched or crushed resolver harness near the transaxle
Shorted cosine winding in the generator resolver
Faulty cosine input in the power drive unit
s: Malfunction indicator lamp right after switching on
No charging of the drive battery by the engine
Reduced performance in hybrid mode

P0C6C.t: Generator Position Sensor Circuit B High
P0C6C.d: P0C6C is the high-side fault of circuit B in the generator resolver. On the 2023 Outlander PHEV, where circuit B is the cosine winding, Mitsubishi triggers it when the cosine voltage sits at 4.900 V or above for 0.21 s; the monitor stays active as long as the generator control unit is supplied with 8 V. First rule out a cosine lead that touches a voltage source, followed by connector damage and an internal fault in the power drive unit, which houses the generator control unit. Mitsubishi also has the radiator fan codes dealt with first and, before fitting a new generator, the EV oil cooling inspected. Unlike P0C6D, the voltage here is held out of range rather than leaving it briefly. P0C67 is the same fault on the sine side.
c: Cosine lead shorted to a supply or excitation line
Damaged resolver connector with bridged pins
Internal fault in the power drive unit holding the generator control unit
Open cosine lead that drifts high at the input
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and hybrid warning
Generator inactive, state of charge drops while driving
Engine may run more often or the car limits power

P0C6D.t: Generator Position Sensor Circuit B Intermittent/Erratic
P0C6D.d: P0C6D records short, irregular disturbances on circuit B of the generator resolver: the signal flickers, loses samples or jumps, but each event is too brief to count as a hard low or high reading (P0C6B, P0C6C). Because the angle is computed from both windings, even short glitches on the second winding can make the inverter lose track of the rotor for a moment, which may be felt as a jolt or a brief break in charging. No manufacturer documents P0C6D publicly. Typical sources are a terminal with reduced contact pressure, a seal that lets moisture in, or a harness that moves against a bracket. GM's 2011-12 Volt shows how much vibration matters for resolver plugs (PIC6136A). Wiggle tests with live data help to localise such faults; P0C68 is the circuit A equivalent.
c: Terminal with reduced contact pressure in the circuit B connector
Moisture entering through a damaged connector seal
Harness moving against a bracket or edge and breaking contact
Interference spikes from phase cables near the resolver lines
s: Intermittent warning lamp
Short jerks or charging interruptions in hybrid mode
Fault hard to reproduce in the workshop

P0C6E.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor A/B Correlation
P0C6E.d: P0C6E compares two battery temperature sensors, A and B, with each other rather than judging either one alone. After a long rest the pack should be close to one temperature, so a lasting gap between the two points to a sensor that reads wrongly while staying electrically valid. No manufacturer documents P0C6E publicly; GM and Mitsubishi run the same idea against the pack average and store per-sensor codes instead. GM's eAssist table 13OBDG05C flags sensor 1 (P0A9C) or sensor 2 (P0AC6) beyond 8.55 °C after more than six hours off, Type B; Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander PHEV allows 13 °C after one hour of soak. A Subaru patent compares a sensor pair after parking once both cool at a similar rate. P0C6F covers the B/C pair.
c: Thermistor A or B drifted while staying inside its electrical range
Sensor no longer seated against its cell or module
Genuine temperature difference from uneven cooling or a weak cell group
Battery management software with an over-sensitive comparison
s: Hybrid or EV system warning lamp
Reduced charge and discharge power
Battery fan or cooling running more than usual

P0C6F.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor B/C Correlation
P0C6F.d: P0C6F sets when battery temperature sensors B and C disagree by more than the calibrated margin. Sensor B also takes part in the A/B check (P0C6E), so the pattern of stored codes helps: if P0C6E and P0C6F appear together, B is the shared suspect, while P0C6F alone points more towards C. No manufacturer documents P0C6F publicly. A Toyota patent describes a second way to catch such faults while the pack is working: if the spread between sensors is large during charging or discharging and one output barely moves, that sensor is treated as frozen. GM files the physical fault per sensor; on the eAssist, sensor 3 is P0ACB with 8.55 °C after six hours off. A real local hot spot inside a module can also open the gap.
c: Sensor C reading off, especially when P0C6F is stored alone
Sensor B reading off, likely when P0C6E is stored as well
Sensor output stuck at one value while the pack temperature changes
Real local heating in a module, for example from a cell with high resistance
s: Hybrid or EV system warning
Power or charging rate limited
Displayed battery temperatures differ noticeably in live data

P0C70.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor C/D Correlation
P0C70.d: P0C70 is the correlation check between battery temperature sensors C and D. The controller expects both to settle at nearly the same value once the pack has rested, and it stores the code when their difference stays too large. No manufacturer documents P0C70 publicly. Where GM and Mitsubishi publish this monitor, they compare each sensor with the pack average and name the single sensor; GM's sensor 4 code P0AE9 is the D counterpart. Before replacing parts it is worth knowing that GM cured false sets of these Volt sensor codes, shown with a battery-too-cold message, by reprogramming the module (18-NA-342). Genuine faults are a drifting thermistor, a sensor that lost contact with its cells, or uneven cooling. The battery controller usually limits power. P0C71 continues with D/E.
c: Thermistor C or D drifted out of agreement with the other
Battery control software that sets the code falsely, for example in cold weather
Sensor C or D detached from its cell group
Uneven cooling across the pack, such as a blocked air duct or coolant channel
s: Malfunction indicator lamp or EV system warning
Message asking to plug in or warm the battery
Reduced electric power and slower charging

P0C71.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor D/E Correlation
P0C71.d: P0C71 checks whether battery temperature sensors D and E agree with each other. Both sit in the same pack, so after a long soak they should report almost the same value; a lasting gap means one of them reads wrong although its circuit looks healthy. No manufacturer documents P0C71 publicly. GM and Mitsubishi run this plausibility test against the pack average instead and log the single sensor: on the eAssist cars (13OBDG05C) GM flags sensor 4 (P0AE9) or sensor 5 (P0BC3) beyond 8.55 °C after more than 21,600 s off, Type B, while the 2022 Outlander PHEV tolerates 13 °C after one hour. P0C70 covers the C/D pair and P0C72 the E/F pair; open or shorted sensors set their own circuit codes.
c: Thermistor D or E drifted while staying inside its electrical range
Sensor no longer pressed against its cell or module
Genuine temperature difference from uneven cooling or a weak cell group
Battery management software with an overly tight comparison
s: Hybrid or EV system warning lamp
Reduced battery charge and discharge power
Battery cooling running more often than usual

P0C72.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor E/F Correlation
P0C72.d: P0C72 is the agreement test between battery temperature sensors E and F. The controller stores it when the two readings stay apart by more than a calibrated margin after the pack has had time to even out. No manufacturer documents P0C72 publicly; GM names the matching single-sensor plausibility codes P0BC3 (sensor 5) and P0C34 (sensor 6) and compares each with the pack average, Type B. On the Chevrolet Volt GM traced false sensor codes, together with a battery-too-cold message above -25 °C, to module software and cured them by reprogramming (18-NA-342), so a software check comes before any pack work. If the fault is real, a drifting thermistor, a sensor that lost contact with its module or uneven coolant flow are typical. Battery power is then limited. The D/E pair is P0C71.
c: Thermistor E or F drifted without an electrical fault
Battery module software that reports sensor faults falsely, fixed by reprogramming
Sensor detached from its cell group
Uneven coolant or air flow through the pack
s: Hybrid or EV system warning lamp
Battery-too-cold or similar message although it is not very cold
Reduced electric power and range

P0C73.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump A Control Performance
P0C73.d: P0C73 reports that coolant pump A of the motor electronics, the loop that cools the inverter and often the drive motor, does not run the way the controller commands. Kia's bulletins for Niro and Carnival hybrids use exactly this name. The 2018 Outlander PHEV sets it when, with at least 30 % pump command for over 2 s, pump speed stays between 100 and 1,000 rpm or exceeds 5,300 rpm for 0.5 s; Mitsubishi lists air in the loop, wrong coolant level or mix and frozen coolant first. Toyota tied P0C73 on the 2014-2016 Highlander Hybrid to water corroding the inverter pump connector, Kia to water entering the pump can, Mercedes (M264) to trapped air. Battery pack pump faults use P0C47-P0C4D. Power is reduced to protect the inverter.
c: Air trapped in the inverter cooling loop, often after coolant service
Water ingress and corrosion at the pump connector or inside the pump housing
Low coolant level, wrong mixture or frozen coolant
Control-unit software with faulty judgement logic
s: Malfunction indicator lamp or hybrid warning lamp
Coolant warning in the instrument cluster
Reduced electric drive power at high load

P0C74.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump B Control Performance
P0C74.d: P0C74 is the performance check for coolant pump B of the motor electronics, found on vehicles with a second electric pump in the power electronics cooling. The controller compares how the pump should run with how it actually runs and stores the code when the two disagree for longer than calibrated. Stellantis is the only maker found documenting it by code: for 2023-2024 Jeep Renegade and Compass 4xe with the 1.3 L plug-in hybrid, bulletins 08-165-24, 08-193-24 and 08-064-25 cure a lit MIL with P0C74 by flashing new software into the hybrid controller and the power inverter module, with no parts replaced. Where software is current, air in the loop, a worn or blocked pump and wiring faults remain. Pump A uses P0C73, pump C P2BD7.
c: Hybrid control or inverter module software, fixed by an update
Air pocket in the power electronics coolant loop
Pump B worn, blocked or seized
Damaged wiring or corroded connector at pump B
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Reduced electric drive power when the electronics run hot

P0C75.t: Hybrid/EV Battery System Discharge Time Too Short
P0C75.d: P0C75 is logged when the high-voltage bus loses its voltage faster than expected after the contactors open. At shutdown the inverter's DC-link capacitor is drained through a discharge resistor or an active discharge circuit, and from capacitance and resistance the controller knows roughly how long that should take. A much quicker drop points to lost capacitance, a lower resistance than designed, a leakage path or a wrong voltage reading. A capacitor diagnostic patent (EP2682769B1) uses the same comparison to detect capacitor ageing. No manufacturer documents P0C75 publicly; GM publishes only the opposite check, P0C76. The driver usually sees a hybrid warning lamp, and depending on the make the next start may be blocked.
c: DC-link capacitor lost capacitance through ageing or damage
Additional load or leakage path on the high-voltage bus
Bus voltage measured incorrectly by the inverter or battery module
Discharge resistor or circuit with too low a resistance
s: Hybrid or EV system warning lamp
Vehicle may not become ready to drive

P0C76.t: Hybrid/EV Battery System Discharge Time Too Long
P0C76.d: P0C76 means the high-voltage bus is still too high a set time after the contactors opened, so the inverter capacitor was not drained as intended. GM publishes thresholds: the 2011 Volt flags more than 200 V after 3.5 s (Special Type C, no MIL), the 2013 eAssist cars more than 65 V after 6.5 s and the 2019 tables more than 200 V after 3.5 s, both Type A after two failed runs. Bulletins name welded contactors on the 2019 Volt (software update, N192226060), a high-voltage cable that had worked loose on the inverter terminal of the 2017 Pacifica Hybrid (08-107-17) and, on GM two-mode trucks, jump-starting with the key on (PIT4585E). A failed discharge circuit is the classic part fault. Treat the bus as live until measured.
c: Active discharge circuit or discharge resistor in the inverter failed
Main contactor welded closed so the battery keeps feeding the bus
Loose high-voltage cable or terminal at the inverter
Low 12 V supply during shutdown or module software
s: Hybrid warning lamp or service high voltage message
Vehicle may not start or become ready
Loss of propulsion

P0C77.t: Hybrid/EV Battery System Precharge Time Too Short
P0C77.d: P0C77 is stored when the inverter side reaches battery voltage too quickly during precharge. Before the main contactor closes, the controller charges the inverter capacitor through a precharge resistor and watches the ratio of bus to battery voltage. GM's 2011 Volt sets the code if that ratio passes 95 % within 50 ms of precharge start, Type A; the 2013 eAssist uses 75 ms, Type B, and both require the bus to be below 40 V beforehand. A rise that fast suggests a bypassed or shorted resistor, a main contactor that is welded or closes early, or far less capacitance on the bus than expected. Chrysler lists P0C77 for the 2017 Pacifica Hybrid together with a high-voltage cable that had worked loose on the inverter terminal (08-107-17). Propulsion may be unavailable.
c: Main contactor welded or closing before precharge ends
Loose high-voltage cable leaving the inverter capacitor partly disconnected
Faulty bus or battery voltage measurement
s: Malfunction indicator or hybrid warning lamp
Vehicle does not become ready or loses propulsion

P0C78.t: Hybrid/EV Battery System Precharge Time Too Long
P0C78.d: P0C78 means precharge took too long: the inverter side did not come up to battery voltage within the allowed time. GM's 2011 Volt allows 700 ms to reach 95 % (Type A), the 2013 eAssist 1,000 ms or more than 5 A for over 100 ms (Type B), and the 2019 tables demand 95-105 % at 0.700 s, Type A. The 2018 Outlander PHEV flags a gap of 12 V or more between battery and inverter after 1 s. Typical causes are an open precharge resistor or fuse, a high-voltage load pulling the bus down, and software. Bulletins cover a blown fuse in the service disconnect (Bolt EV, 18-NA-225), a failed coolant heater (Spark EV, 16-NA-072) and battery-module software at Chrysler and Volvo. The vehicle then normally will not become ready.
c: Precharge resistor, precharge contactor or high-voltage fuse open
Faulty high-voltage consumer such as a coolant heater loading the bus
Battery module software, fixed by an update
Loose high-voltage cable or bus bar
s: Vehicle does not become ready to drive
Malfunction indicator lamp and drive system message
Loss of propulsion

P0C79.t: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Too High
