Compared with the open-circuit code P0CC1 and the short-to-voltage code P0CC4, the repair focuses on finding the point of ground contact.
c: Faulty output stage in the control module
s: Check-engine lamp after two trips
Pump running constantly or not at all
Reduced electric assist

P0CC4.t: Drive Motor A Coolant Pump Control Circuit High
P0CC4.d: P0CC4 stands for a control line of the drive motor A coolant pump that is held at supply voltage or overloaded. In GM's 2013 eAssist table 13OBDG05C the output driver reports a high-circuit status, and unlike the open and low checks this one runs while the pump is commanded on; 20 failures in 25 samples at 250 ms in run/crank set a Type B code, two trips. Sampling with the output switched on lets the driver recognise excess current or a voltage that should not be there. Causes include a control wire chafed against a battery-positive feed, a pump drawing too much current because of a jammed rotor, or water in the connector. The output stage normally switches off to protect itself, so the pump stops and the motor generator loses active cooling; P0CC3 and P0CC1 are the other circuit codes of this pump.
c: Control wire shorted to a voltage-carrying line
Water ingress in the pump connector
s: Check-engine lamp after two trips
Pump silent when it should run

P0CC5.t: 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor A/B Correlation
P0CC5.d: P0CC5 compares the two current sensors of the 14 V power module, the DC/DC converter that feeds the 12 V network from the high-voltage battery. In GM's 2013 eAssist table 13OBDG05C, where the unit is the accessory power module (APM), sensor A measures the input and sensor B the output side. The module computes an input power, multiplies it by an efficiency factor taken from a table (0.99 down to 0.90) and compares the result with the power derived from the output side; a gap above 0.4 kW for 3.75 s within a 5 s window, at 9 to 32 V and with the input power inside the enabling window the table ties to 1.25 kW, is a Type B fault. The check is suspended while the single-sensor codes P0A88/P0A89 or P0C9E/P0C9F are active. One drifting sensor is the usual reason, and a 12 V battery that stays poorly charged is a typical sign.
c: Offset or gain drift of one current sensor
Internal fault of the power module, e.g. real efficiency loss
Calibration or software fault in the module
s: Check-engine lamp after the second faulty trip
12 V battery not fully charged or low-voltage warning

P0CC6.t: Charge Port Door A Open Request Switch Wake-Up Circuit
P0CC6.d: On plug-in vehicles the button that asks for the charge flap to open must also be able to rouse a sleeping control module, so it drives a separate wake-up line besides its normal signal. P0CC6 records that these two signals disagree. GM documents the code for the 2011 Chevrolet Volt, where the hybrid control module 2 (VICM) checks two cases: wake-up active although the switch reads released, and switch pressed with no wake-up seen. Both are filtered over 50 ms samples and stored as Type B after two trips with the warning lamp. The test is skipped while P0CC7, P0CC9 or P0CCA is active, so P0CC6 points to the wake-up wire or the switch contact itself. The driver mostly notices that pressing the button sometimes does not open the flap.
c: Open, chafed or shorted wake-up wire between switch and control module
Worn or contaminated contact in the open request switch
Corroded or loose pins at the switch or module connector
Faulty wake-up input inside the control module
s: Charge flap opens only after several presses or not at all
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)
Possible extra drain on the 12 V battery if the module is kept awake

P0CC7.t: Charge Port Door A Open Request Switch Circuit
P0CC7.d: P0CC7 is the general circuit fault of the button that requests opening of charge flap A. GM reads this switch as a percentage of its reference and expects defined states; on the 2011 to 2013 Chevrolet Volt the code sets when the reading sits in a forbidden band between 65.9 and 81.6 percent, which indicates a wrong resistance, for instance a damaged switch or a partly broken wire. Six bad readings out of eight (50 ms steps in 2011/2012, 500 ms in the 2013 table) trigger it, and it is a Type B code with the lamp after two trips. Hard shorts are split off into P0CC9 (to ground) and P0CCA (to battery voltage); unstable signals belong to P0CCB. In daily use the flap may ignore the button, while opening via the key or screen can still work.
c: Open request switch with wrong internal resistance
Partly broken wire or corroded connector raising circuit resistance
Faulty switch input in the control module
s: Charge flap does not open with the button
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)
Opening via key, app or screen still possible on some models

P0CC8.t: Charge Port Door A Open Request Switch Circuit Performance
P0CC8.d: P0CC8 covers a plausibility fault of the charge flap A open request switch: the signal is electrically within limits, yet its behaviour makes no sense, for example a button that reports pressed for far too long or never changes state over many wake-ups. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's Volt tables of 2011 to 2013 monitor the same switch only for invalid range, low and high (P0CC7, P0CC9, P0CCA), so the performance check is not used there. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15) requires rationality checks only for inputs that affect emissions or serve another diagnostic, which explains why such comfort inputs are often left out. A GM patent shows the typical layout, in which the release button makes the controller energize the flap actuator. Expect a flap that reacts erratically to the button.
c: Mechanically sticking or jammed open request switch
Worn switch contact giving an implausible signal
Wiring fault that keeps the signal in an unexpected state
s: Charge flap opens unexpectedly or ignores the button
Message about the charge flap in the instrument cluster

P0CC9.t: Charge Port Door A Open Request Switch Circuit Low
P0CC9.d: P0CC9 means the open request switch of charge flap A reads lower than any valid state, which typically results from the signal wire touching ground or from a switch that has failed short. In the Chevrolet Volt tables of 2011 to 2013, GM sets it once the reading drops under 22.9 percent of the reference in six of eight samples; the code is Type B, so the warning lamp follows after two consecutive trips. The monitor belongs to the hybrid control module 2 (VICM). The opposite fault, a reading above 94.5 percent, is P0CCA, and a value stuck between valid states is P0CC7. Because a grounded signal may look like a permanently pressed button, the flap can fail to respond or the module may stay awake longer than intended.
c: Signal wire chafed through to body ground
Water in the switch connector creating a leakage path to ground
s: Charge flap does not react to the button
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)

P0CCA.t: Charge Port Door A Open Request Switch Circuit High
P0CCA.d: With P0CCA the control module sees the charge flap A open request switch signal above its highest valid level. Depending on the circuit, a wire shorted to battery voltage or an interrupted ground or switch path pushes the reading up. GM's Volt monitor from 2011 onward flags it when more than 94.5 percent of the reference is measured in six of eight samples, then stores it as a Type B code with the lamp after two trips; the 2013 table stretches the sample spacing to 500 ms. Low readings below 22.9 percent go to P0CC9 instead, and an invalid middle value to P0CC7. Since a high reading usually looks like a button that is never pressed, the typical complaint is a charge flap that cannot be opened from the switch.
c: Signal wire shorted to a 12 V supply
Interrupted ground or switch return path
Pin pushed back in the connector
s: Charge flap cannot be opened with the button
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)

P0CCB.t: Charge Port Door A Open Request Switch Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0CCB.d: P0CCB flags a charge flap A open request switch whose signal jumps between states without a matching press, or drops out briefly. Such signals usually come from loose terminals, a cracked solder joint in the switch or a harness that flexes with a door or body panel. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's Volt tables of 2011 and 2012 cover the same switch only with P0CC7, P0CC9 and P0CCA, which use six of eight samples as a filter and would hide short dropouts. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15) makes intermittent checks mandatory only for emission-related inputs, so a comfort switch like this one rarely carries one. The GM charge port patent shows how the button press leads the controller to fire the flap actuator. The driver sees the flap answer only now and then.
c: Loose or spread terminal at the switch or module connector
Cracked solder joint or worn contact inside the switch
Harness damaged where it flexes with a door or panel
s: Charge flap opens only occasionally when the button is pressed
Fault comes and goes, often with temperature or road vibration

P0CCC.t: Charge Port Door A Position Sensor Circuit
P0CCC.d: The position sensor of charge flap A tells the vehicle whether the flap is open or shut; GM has patented a version in which a magnet on the flap acts on a magnetic sensor in the housing. P0CCC is the general circuit code for this sensor. On the 2011 to 2013 Chevrolet Volt it sets when the reading lands in the invalid window of 65.9 to 81.6 percent of reference in six of eight samples, as a Type B code with the lamp after two trips. GM uses the flap state as an enable condition for the control pilot check P0CF4, which is why the sensor is part of the OBD system there; GM's 2016 hybrid table no longer lists these flap codes. Short circuits have their own codes, P0CCE (low) and P0CCF (high). The driver may see a false flap-open message or a charging refusal.
c: Faulty flap position sensor or switch
Sensor or its harness pigtail not fully seated in the housing
Damaged wire or corroded connector in the sensor circuit
s: Flap-open message although the flap is closed
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)
Charging or charge pilot checks may be blocked

P0CCD.t: Charge Port Door A Position Sensor Circuit Performance
P0CCD.d: P0CCD is set when the charge flap A position signal is electrically valid but does not fit what the flap should be doing, for example a state that disagrees with the last commanded movement. GM bulletin 25-NA-049 (March 2025) names the code for the Ultium models Cadillac Lyriq 2023 to 2025, Chevrolet Blazer EV and Equinox EV 2024 to 2025, and Cadillac Optiq and Escalade IQ 2025: drivers see a Service High Voltage message, the cause is attributed to software, and dealers are told to reflash the BECM (battery energy control module) through vehicle wide programming without replacing parts. Porsche describes a related hardware case for the Taycan, where a wrong end-position signal locked the opposite flap and new harnesses fixed it. Circuit faults proper are P0CCC, P0CCE and P0CCF.
c: Software anomaly in the battery control module (GM Ultium, bulletin 25-NA-049)
Position sensor giving a wrong end-position signal
Faulty harness between flap module and control unit
Flap not reaching its end position because of mechanical binding
s: Service High Voltage message (GM Ultium models)
Flap status shown wrongly; another flap may be locked

P0CCE.t: Charge Port Door A Position Sensor Circuit Low
P0CCE.d: P0CCE reports that the charge flap A position sensor signal has fallen below its lowest valid level, the classic sign of a signal wire shorted to ground or a sensor that has failed short. GM documents it for the 2011 to 2013 Chevrolet Volt: the hybrid control module 2 sets it when the reading is under 22.9 percent of reference in six of eight samples, and as a Type B code the lamp comes on after two trips. While it is active, GM suspends dependent tests such as the control pilot check P0CF4 and the flap opening check P0CD2. The high-side counterpart is P0CCF, the invalid middle window P0CCC. For the driver this mostly means a wrong flap status in the display and, depending on software, blocked charging.
c: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Water in the flap area or sensor connector
s: Wrong flap status in the display
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)
Charging may be refused

P0CCF.t: Charge Port Door A Position Sensor Circuit High
P0CCF.d: P0CCF stands for a charge flap A position sensor signal above its highest valid level. A signal wire touching a 12 V feed, or an interrupted sensor ground that lets the input float upwards, are the usual explanations. In GM's Chevrolet Volt tables from 2011 to 2013 the threshold is 94.5 percent of reference, confirmed in six of eight samples; the 2013 table samples at 500 ms. The code is Type B, so the lamp lights after the second trip with the fault. As with P0CCE, an active P0CCF stops GM's dependent tests P0CF4 and P0CD2 from running. Low readings are P0CCE, plausibility problems P0CCD. A driver typically gets a flap status that never changes or a message that the flap is open.
c: Sensor signal wire shorted to a 12 V feed
Interrupted sensor ground or open sensor
s: Flap status stuck or shown as open
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)

P0CD0.t: Charge Port Door A Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0CD0.d: P0CD0 completes the position sensor group of charge flap A: the module sees the flap signal flicker or drop out for moments, without a lasting open, short or implausible state. Loose connector terminals, a sensor that is not held firmly in its seat, or a harness strained by the flap mechanism are the usual triggers. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Two official sources describe faults of the same part: Porsche replaced the flap harnesses on the 2020 Taycan because a faulty sensor signal misjudged the end position, and GM patented a magnet and sensor pair that reports whether the flap is shut. The steady faults have their own codes, P0CCC, P0CCE and P0CCF, and P0CCD covers plausibility. A driver may see the flap status switch back and forth or get sporadic charging warnings.
c: Loose terminal in the position sensor connector
Harness to the flap module chafed or under strain
Sensor or magnet not held firmly in its mounting
s: Flap status in the display changes without reason
Sporadic charging or flap warnings

P0CD1.t: Charge Port Door A Unlock Control Circuit
P0CD1.d: P0CD1 is the circuit fault of the output that releases charge flap A, normally a relay or driver that briefly powers the latch actuator. A GM patent shows such an actuator retracting a post so the spring-loaded flap can pop open. On the 2011 to 2013 Chevrolet Volt the hybrid control module 2 relies on the fault status its driver reports and covers two cases: short to ground, judged while the unlock is commanded, and a short to 12 V or an open line, judged while it is not, using sample counts such as 64 of 80 at 50 ms. It is a Type B code with the lamp after two trips, and an active P0CD1 blocks the opening check P0CD2. Split low and high codes (P0CD3, P0CD4) are not used there. Result for the driver: the flap stays shut.
c: Unlock actuator coil open or shorted
Faulty charge flap relay or its control wire
Chafed or corroded wiring to the actuator
Output driver in the control module damaged
s: Charge flap does not unlock
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)
Emergency release needed to reach the charge socket

P0CD2.t: Charge Port Door A Unlock Control Circuit Performance
P0CD2.d: P0CD2 is a functional test: after commanding charge flap A to unlock, the module waits for the position sensor to report the flap open. GM documents it for the Chevrolet Volt. The 2011 table allows 5 seconds, the 2012 and 2013 tables 13 seconds, and the 2013 version only runs above minus 12 °C. The test is skipped while P0CCC, P0CCE, P0CCF or P0CD1 is active, so P0CD2 means the electrics look fine but the flap did not move. It is a Type B code with the lamp after two trips. Frozen or binding flaps are a typical cause: GM bulletin PI0936 covers 2013 Volts whose flap would not open in the cold because of a misaligned hinge pin, and Porsche replaced jamming flap switching elements on the 918 Spyder.
c: Flap frozen, stuck to the seal or binding at the hinge
Weak or mechanically blocked unlock actuator
Misaligned charge port housing or hinge pin (GM PI0936)
Position sensor not registering the open flap
s: Flap does not open, especially in frost
Warning lamp after two trips (GM Volt)

P0CD3.t: Charge Port Door A Unlock Control Circuit Low
P0CD3.d: P0CD3 narrows the unlock output fault of charge flap A down to a low level: the monitored voltage on the actuator or relay control line stays near ground when it should be higher, which typically means a short to ground on the control wire or a failed actuator coil pulling the line down. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's Volt tables of 2011 and 2012 fold the short to ground into the combined circuit code P0CD1 instead of using P0CD3. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15) asks for circuit checks on outputs only where emissions or other diagnostics depend on them. The GM charge port patent illustrates the actuator that this output powers. The high-side case is P0CD4, the functional test P0CD2. A driver usually finds that the flap no longer releases, and a blown fuse is possible.
c: Actuator control wire shorted to ground
Shorted winding in the unlock actuator
s: Charge flap does not unlock
Possibly blown fuse in the actuator supply

P0CD4.t: Charge Port Door A Unlock Control Circuit High
P0CD4.d: P0CD4 is the high-level variant of the charge flap A unlock output fault. The control line reads high when the driver should be pulling it low or holding it off, as happens with a short to a 12 V wire, and on many low-side drivers also with an open actuator or broken wire. A flap actuator that is powered all the time may overheat, while an open one simply never releases. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's Volt tables cover short to battery and open circuit within P0CD1. A Tesla patent describes the same principle, in which a controller closes a switch to supply the flap release actuator. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15) explains why comfort outputs like this rarely receive split low and high codes. Siblings: P0CD3 for low, P0CD2 for the movement check.
c: Actuator control wire shorted to a 12 V feed
Open actuator winding or broken wire
Output driver in the control module damaged
s: Charge flap does not unlock or unlocks unexpectedly
Actuator may become hot from continuous current

P0CD5.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P0CD5.d: P0CD5 is the general circuit fault for the second coolant temperature sensor in the liquid loop of a hybrid or EV battery. In GM's tables for the Chevrolet Volt and Cadillac ELR, sensor B is the one at the pack outlet, an NTC thermistor read by the battery energy control module, while sensor A sits at the inlet. GM splits electrical faults of sensor B into P0CD7 and P0CD8 and does not list P0CD5 itself. No manufacturer publicly documents this general code; it suits controllers that only recognise an unusable signal without telling low from high. CARB requires battery thermal management inputs to be checked for circuit faults. Without the outlet value the controller no longer knows how much the coolant warms across the pack and may limit charging or drive power. Implausible readings fall under P0CD6.
c: Loose, corroded or unplugged connector or damaged wire at the outlet sensor
Input circuit or reference in the battery control module faulty
s: Check engine or hybrid system warning lamp
Reduced charging or drive power, especially in heat or cold
Battery heating or cooling runs on substitute values

P0CD6.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0CD6.d: P0CD6 means that coolant temperature sensor B at the battery outlet is electrically fine, yet its value does not fit the rest of the thermal system. GM runs the check in the hybrid controller of the Volt with the coolant pump above 20 % and no circuit faults present: if the outlet reading is more than 10 °C away from both the inlet reading and the mean cell temperature (2011 Volt, 80 of 100 samples at 100 ms), or at least 20 °C in the 2016 ELR (32 of 40 samples at 250 ms, pump running for over a minute), the result is a Type B code with the MIL following on the second trip. Volvo lists ECM-P0CD623 on the 2016-17 XC90 T8 as an incorrect entry cured by a total software upgrade (TJ 32193). Otherwise a drifting sensor, contact resistance or trapped air are likely.
c: Outlet coolant temperature sensor reading off (drift)
Contact resistance at connector or terminals
Air or low coolant in the battery loop after service
Control module software sets the code incorrectly (e.g. Volvo XC90 T8)
s: MIL on, often without noticeable driving symptoms
Battery cooling or heating behaves unexpectedly

P0CD7.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P0CD7.d: P0CD7 reports that the signal of battery coolant temperature sensor B at the pack outlet has dropped toward ground. On an NTC thermistor with pull-up resistor a low voltage reads as very hot coolant, so a short to ground or a damaged sensor is the usual explanation rather than real overheating. GM's battery energy control module in the 2011 Chevrolet Volt and 2016 Cadillac ELR stores the code once the outlet value reaches 87.9 °C, an ADC count of 130 or less, for 1.75 s within a 2.5 s window; it is rated Type B, so the MIL lights after the second trip. While it is active, GM suspends the outlet plausibility test P0CD6 and the coolant pump checks that rely on this value. Expect reduced charging or power until the signal is back. The open-circuit counterpart is P0CD8, sensor A low is P0C44.
c: Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground
Sensor B internally shorted or water-damaged
Input stage of the battery control module faulty
s: MIL on after two trips (GM)
Displayed outlet coolant temperature implausibly high
Charging or drive power reduced

P0CD8.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
P0CD8.d: P0CD8 is the high-voltage fault of battery coolant temperature sensor B at the pack outlet. On the usual NTC circuit the signal rises to the reference when the loop is broken, so the controller sees an impossible temperature below -40 °C. The battery energy control modules of the 2011 Chevrolet Volt and 2016 Cadillac ELR use exactly this limit, an ADC count above 3823, held for 1.75 s within 2.5 s; the code is Type B with the MIL on the second trip. Connectors left unplugged after work on the battery, corroded pins, a broken wire or a short to a supply line are the common findings, an open sensor element is rarer. Until it is fixed the battery may not be heated or cooled as intended and cold-weather power can be limited. The low counterpart is P0CD7, sensor A high is P0C45.
c: Connector of sensor B unplugged or not latched after service
Broken signal or ground wire, corroded terminals
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
s: MIL on after two trips (GM)
Outlet coolant temperature shows about -40 °C
Limited power or charging in cold weather

P0CD9.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0CD9.d: P0CD9 covers a signal from battery coolant temperature sensor B that drops out or jumps for short moments while staying inside the electrical limits most of the time. It is meant for loose terminals, chafed wires or a sensor that misbehaves only with vibration or temperature. Volvo documents ECM-P0CD900 as a permanent entry on several 2021-2022 plug-in hybrids: according to TJ 36929, charging in outside air warmer than 20 °C can light the engine lamp although nothing is broken, and software release 2024 week 34 (version 3.2.4) improves the detection; in any other situation VIDA fault tracing applies. GM does not list P0CD9 and handles the comparable erratic case for sensor A as P0C46 with a step-sum test. Hard short or open faults are P0CD7 and P0CD8.
c: False detection after charging in warm weather (Volvo, software update)
Loose or corroded terminal at the sensor or module connector
Chafed harness that moves with the battery or body
Sensor B with an intermittent internal fault
s: Check engine light, often after charging
Jumping outlet temperature value in live data

P0CDA.t: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit C
P0CDA.d: P0CDA belongs to the rotor position sensor of drive motor A, normally a resolver: an excited stator winding induces signals in pick-up windings so the motor controller can work out rotor angle and speed. SAE counts the circuits of this sensor as A, B and C; GM, for instance, assigns circuit A to the S1/S3 winding and circuit B to S2/S4. What circuit C carries is not described in any public manufacturer document; the excitation winding or an additional signal path would be plausible, but neither is confirmed. No manufacturer publicly documents P0CDA, so CARB's demand to monitor electric drive inputs for circuit faults is the basis. Without a trustworthy angle the inverter cannot control torque, and the system limits or stops electric drive. Plausibility faults are P0CDB, low and high P0CDC and P0CDD.
c: Loose, corroded or damaged resolver connector between motor and inverter
Resolver winding of circuit C defective
Evaluation circuit in the motor control module faulty
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Electric drive limited or unavailable, engine runs more
Reduced regenerative braking

P0CDB.t: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit C Range/Performance
P0CDB.d: P0CDB flags circuit C of the drive motor A position sensor as present but implausible: its amplitude or phase, or the angle calculated from it, no longer agrees with the other circuits or with the observed motor speed. GM runs comparable tests on the main resolver signals, for example an amplitude check of the sine and cosine windings under P0A3F rated Type A, and limits for circuits A and B. No manufacturer publicly documents P0CDB itself, and none explains what circuit C carries; CARB requires rationality monitoring of electric drive inputs. Plausible causes are a resolver that has shifted on its mount, rotor bearing play, a winding or terminal whose values change with heat, or a controller calibration issue. Drivers usually see a hybrid warning and reduced electric power. Hard circuit faults are P0CDC and P0CDD.
c: Winding or terminal of the resolver changing its values when hot
Resolver shifted on its mount or rotor bearing play
Motor control module software or calibration
s: Hybrid system warning, MIL
Reduced electric power, engine starts in EV mode
Fault appears more often when the drivetrain is warm

P0CDC.t: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit C Low
P0CDC.d: P0CDC reports that circuit C of the rotor position sensor on drive motor A reads below its permitted window. Typical reasons are a short to ground, a short between windings or a low-resistance path through moisture in the connector. For circuits A and B GM shows how such a test works: the motor control processor compares the sensed resolver voltage with a threshold and sets a Type B code when it stays out of range for 0.25 s within a 0.375 s window (P0C52, P0C5C). No manufacturer publicly documents the circuit C version, and what that circuit carries is not published. As soon as the angle signal becomes unreliable, the inverter reduces or stops electric drive torque, and regeneration may be cut as well. Check plug and harness to the inverter before replacing parts. The high fault is P0CDD.
c: Circuit C wire shorted to ground or to another resolver wire
Moisture or corrosion in the resolver connector
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Electric drive limited, engine runs instead
Reduced or no regenerative braking

P0CDD.t: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit C High
P0CDD.d: P0CDD indicates that circuit C of the drive motor A position sensor reads above its limit, which in general points to an open winding, a disconnected plug or a short to a voltage source. Subaru uses the code in the drive motor control module of the 2014 XV Crosstrek Hybrid. Bulletin 07-82-14R explains that P0CDD together with P0A3F could be stored whenever the 12 V auxiliary battery sagged below specified limits; the module then requests the MIL via P0CA1 in the engine controller, and C1424 appears in the stability control unit. The remedy is reprogramming the module with revised logic, which production adopted in January 2014. On such cars check the 12 V battery and software first. Electric drive is usually limited while the fault is active. The low counterpart is P0CDC.
c: 12 V auxiliary battery voltage dips with outdated module logic (Subaru)
Open winding, broken wire or disconnected resolver plug
Circuit C wire shorted to a voltage source
s: MIL on (requested via P0CA1 on Subaru)
Hybrid system warning, electric assist missing

P0CDE.t: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit C Intermittent/Erratic
P0CDE.d: P0CDE describes a circuit C signal from the drive motor A position sensor that drops out or jumps briefly instead of failing for good. That pattern suits loose terminals at the resolver plug, a harness strained by drivetrain movement, or a winding or contact that opens only when hot. Short glitches matter because the inverter needs the rotor angle continuously; GM therefore evaluates its resolver circuits A and B within fractions of a second (0.25 s in a 0.375 s window). No manufacturer publicly documents P0CDE or the meaning of circuit C, so CARB's requirement to monitor electric drive inputs is the general basis. A dropout can cause a jolt, a hybrid warning or a switch to engine operation, and after a restart the car often drives normally again. A wiggle test with the motor warm helps.
c: Loose or spread terminal in the resolver connector
Harness strained or chafed by drivetrain movement
Resolver winding or joint that opens when hot
s: Occasional jolt or hybrid system warning
Temporary switch to engine operation
Fault disappears after restart

P0CDF.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve A Control Circuit/Open
P0CDF.d: P0CDF signals an electrical fault in the drive circuit of coolant control valve A, the valve that routes or shuts off coolant to the hybrid or EV battery. Mercedes-Benz uses it in the battery management unit N82/2 of the S-, E- and C-Class hybrids, where it marks the actuation of the battery module coolant shutoff valve as electrically faulty or interrupted (service information LI83.30-P-061224, together with the stuck codes P0CE0 and P0CE1). An open coil, a broken wire, a corroded plug or a failed driver stage in the control unit are typical. CARB requires output drivers of the battery thermal management to be checked for circuit faults. If the valve cannot be operated, the battery may run too warm or too cold and charging or power can be limited. Shorts to ground or voltage appear as P0CE2 and P0CE3.
c: Valve coil or actuator motor open
Broken wire or corroded connector at the valve
Driver stage in the battery or thermal control unit failed
s: MIL or hybrid system warning
Battery cooling or heating not working as intended
Reduced charging or drive power

P0CE0.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve A Performance/Stuck Off
P0CE0.d: P0CE0 means coolant control valve A of the battery loop is electrically sound but does not reach or hold its commanded position. GM's 2011 Chevrolet Volt checks the four-port valve in stages: an end-stop learn, reaching the target within 1.5 s, drift above 3 % and a noisy feedback; 1280 of 1600 samples at 6.25 ms set a Type B code. GM's 2016 ELR tables use P1F56 for this. Audi stores P0CE000 in the thermal management unit of the 2020-2022 Q5 TFSI e and fixes it with new software (TSB 2067066). Mercedes reads it as a battery coolant shutoff valve that does not close. Toyota reports its RAV4 Prime fault P0CDF72, a stuck-open battery cooling valve, as SAE P0CE0 and revised the air conditioner amplifier logic (T-SB-0057-21). The opposite case is P0CE1.
c: Control software or limits too strict (Audi, Toyota updates)
Valve sticking or actuator too weak
s: MIL on, often without other symptoms
Battery temperature regulation less effective

P0CE1.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve A Stuck On
P0CE1.d: P0CE1 reports that coolant control valve A of the battery circuit remains in its active position although the controller commanded a change. Manufacturers phrase it differently: Mercedes hybrid battery management speaks of a shutoff valve that does not open, Volvo of a valve stuck on in the BECM of the XC90 T8 from model year 2016. Volvo's TJ 32903 first advised erasing the intermittent entry and test driving, a later revision a software upgrade. For the 2020 Audi Q5 TFSI e, bulletins 2059530 and 80C9 state that the temperature difference limits used to judge the valve were too tight; new software followed (also TSB 2067066). Bentley's TPI 2058049 for the Bentayga Hybrid starts with the coolant level of the battery circuit and an actuator test of changeover valve N632. P0CE0 is the opposite fault.
c: Monitoring limits or software too strict (Audi, Volvo updates)
Low coolant level or air in the battery coolant circuit
s: MIL on, usually without driving symptoms
Battery cooled or heated longer than needed

P0CE2.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve A Control Circuit Low
P0CE2.d: P0CE2 points to a ground short on the drive circuit of coolant control valve A. In the 2011 Chevrolet Volt and 2016 Cadillac ELR, GM's four-port battery valve is moved by a small motor with two driver lines. The hybrid controller sets P0CE2 when driver line 1 reads low while the valve should be travelling in reverse, with system voltage above 9 V (2011) or 10.2 V (2016); 90 failed samples out of 100 at 6.25 ms create a Type B code, so the MIL comes on after two trips. As long as it is active, the valve performance test is blocked. Typical findings are a wire chafed against the body, water in the connector or an internal short in the valve motor. With the valve stuck in its last position, battery cooling or heating may be restricted. Short to voltage is P0CE3, open circuit P0CDF.
c: Driver wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Water or corrosion in the valve connector
s: MIL after two trips (GM)
Valve does not move, battery thermal conditioning limited

P0CE3.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve A Control Circuit High
P0CE3.d: P0CE3 is the short-to-voltage fault of the coolant control valve A drive circuit. GM tests it on the motor-driven four-port battery valve of the 2011 Chevrolet Volt and 2016 Cadillac ELR: driver line 1 reads high while the valve should be stopped or moving forward. System voltage must exceed 9 V or 10.2 V, and 90 of 100 samples at 6.25 ms set a Type B code with the MIL on the second trip. Unlike P0CE2, the check is made in the other direction of travel, which helps tell which condition was detected. Pinched wires touching a supply line, harness damage near the battery or a faulty driver stage in the module are typical causes. Battery temperature control then works only in a fallback mode. Short to ground is P0CE2, mechanical sticking P0CE0 and P0CE1.
c: Driver wire pinched against a supply line
Harness damage near the battery or valve
Driver stage in the control module faulty
s: MIL after two trips (GM)
Battery heating or cooling in fallback mode

P0CE4.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve Position Sensor Circuit
P0CE4.d: P0CE4 is the general circuit fault of the position feedback from the battery coolant control valve. On motor-driven valves the actuator reports its actual position as a share of the sensor supply voltage, letting the controller confirm that coolant really flows toward the battery, chiller or heater. GM's Volt and ELR monitor this feedback but report its electrical faults as P0CE6 and P0CE7; no manufacturer publicly documents P0CE4 itself. CARB requires battery thermal management inputs to be checked for circuit faults. Likely causes are an open signal, reference or ground wire, a damaged connector at the valve or a failed sensor inside the actuator, which is normally replaced together with the valve. Without feedback the controller may park the valve and limit charging or power. Implausible positions are P0CE5.
c: Open signal, reference or ground wire of the position sensor
Damaged or corroded connector at the valve
Position sensor inside the valve actuator failed
s: MIL or hybrid system warning
Valve held in a default position, thermal conditioning limited

P0CE5.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0CE5.d: P0CE5 means the position feedback of the battery coolant control valve is electrically valid, but the valve has not arrived where the controller sent it. In GM's 2016 Cadillac ELR tables the hybrid controller allows up to 22 s; if the feedback still shows a different position once the end-stop learn routine P1F56 has finished, 1280 of 1600 samples at 6.25 ms set a Type B code with the MIL on the second trip. In the 2011 Volt the same situation still fell under P0CE0. Causes include a valve that runs stiff because of deposits or cold, a weak actuator motor, a sensor that has moved away from its learned end stops, and air or low coolant in the loop. Battery cooling or heating then works less effectively. Circuit faults are P0CE6 and P0CE7, valve faults P0CE0 and P0CE1.
c: Valve stiff from deposits or low temperature
Actuator motor weak or gearing worn
Position sensor drifted from learned end stops
Air or low coolant in the battery circuit
s: MIL after two trips (GM)
Battery reaches its target temperature more slowly

P0CE6.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve Position Sensor Circuit Low
P0CE6.d: P0CE6 reports that the position feedback of the battery coolant control valve has fallen below its permitted window. GM expresses the signal relative to the reference voltage: the 2011 Chevrolet Volt fails it below 5 % in 40 of 50 samples at 100 ms, the 2016 Cadillac ELR below 28 % in 640 of 800 samples at 6.25 ms, a value under the lowest end stop the ELR accepts during learning (just over 30 %). Both are Type B, so the MIL comes on after two trips, and while the code is active the valve performance test is suspended. A short of the signal wire to ground, a missing reference voltage or a defective sensor track in the actuator are the likely causes. The controller can then no longer position the valve reliably. The high fault is P0CE7, plausibility P0CE5.
c: Feedback signal wire shorted to ground
Sensor reference voltage missing or open
Worn or defective sensor track in the actuator
s: MIL after two trips (GM)
Valve position shown as near 0 % in live data

P0CE7.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve Position Sensor Circuit High
P0CE7.d: P0CE7 is the high-side fault of the battery coolant control valve position feedback. GM sets it when the signal exceeds 95 % of the reference voltage in the 2011 Chevrolet Volt (40 of 50 samples at 100 ms) or 72 % in the 2016 Cadillac ELR (640 of 800 samples at 6.25 ms), in both cases with system voltage above 9 V or 10.2 V and rated Type B, so the MIL lights on the second trip. The ELR value sits just above the highest end stop it accepts while learning (about 69.5 %). An interrupted sensor ground, a signal line shorted to the reference or to battery voltage, or a worn sensor track are typical. The coolant path can then no longer be confirmed, and thermal conditioning may be restricted. The low counterpart is P0CE6.
c: Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage
Worn sensor track in the actuator
s: MIL after two trips (GM)
Valve position shown near 100 % in live data

P0CE8.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0CE8.d: P0CE8 stands for a valve position feedback that drops out or jumps briefly while the hard low and high limits are not violated long enough to set P0CE6 or P0CE7. Such patterns come from loose pins at the valve plug, a cracked solder joint or a worn sensor track that loses contact at certain angles. GM's 2011 Volt catches a related symptom inside P0CE0: when the summed noise of the feedback exceeds 12 %, the valve performance test fails (8 of 10 samples at 1 s). No manufacturer publicly documents P0CE8 itself; CARB's requirement to monitor battery thermal management inputs applies. Effects range from a brief warning to temporarily limited charging, often with no lasting complaint. Watching the feedback in live data while moving the connector usually reveals the fault.
c: Loose or corroded pin in the valve connector
Worn sensor track losing contact at certain positions
Cracked solder joint inside the actuator
s: Occasional warning lamp that may go out again
Jumping valve position in live data

P0CE9.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump A Control Circuit/Open
P0CE9.d: The hybrid controller checks the control line of the electric pump that moves coolant through the power electronics loop, which in GM's Volt and ELR serves the inverter module and the high-voltage charger. GM tables from 2011 to 2016 fail it when the output driver reports an open line or a short to ground or voltage in 16 of 20 samples at 250 ms. The 2019 HPC2 table measures line current instead: below 200 mA or above 3 A while the pump is commanded on, below 120 µA while it is off, for 4 s within a 5 s window. All variants are Type B, two trips. Audi logs P0CE900 on the e-tron and Q8 e-tron in thermal management unit 00C5. P0CEB and P0CEC split the fault into low and high, P0CEA covers pump function. With the pump idle, inverter and charger heat up and power is reduced.
c: Open or chafed control wire, or corroded connector at the electronics coolant pump
Failed electronics in the pump itself, drawing no current or far too much
Coolant loss from a damaged hose letting the pump run dry (Audi e-tron/Q8 e-tron bulletin)
Faulty output driver in the hybrid or thermal management control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp or hybrid/drive system warning on
Reduced drive power because inverter and charger temperatures rise
Charging power reduced or charging interrupted
Pump not audible after switch-on when commanded via scan tool

P0CEA.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump A Performance
P0CEA.d: Here the pump circuit is electrically intact, yet the coolant it should move does not seem to arrive. GM documents it in the VICM tables of 2014 and 2016, the latter explicitly for the Cadillac ELR: with the pump enabled above 30 % speed for more than 300 s, the controller compares the power electronics coolant temperature with the temperature of the high-voltage charger. A gap larger than a calibrated value, separate for charging and for driving, or a charger hotter than 60 °C for over 600 s while charging counts as a failure; 32 of 40 samples at 250 ms set the code, Type B, two trips. Circuit faults (P0CE9, enable line) block the test. Weak flow from air in the loop, low coolant or a worn pump is the usual background; charging and drive power are cut back to protect the electronics.
c: Air trapped in the power electronics coolant loop after service or a leak
Low coolant level in the electronics loop reservoir
Worn or partly blocked pump delivering too little flow
Skewed coolant or charger temperature signal distorting the comparison
s: Malfunction indicator lamp or hybrid system message
Charging slows down or stops, especially in hot weather
Reduced propulsion power during long or demanding drives

P0CEB.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump A Control Circuit Low
P0CEB.d: The control line of the electronics coolant pump sits at too low a level, typically because it is shorted to ground or the driver cannot pull it up. No manufacturer publishes setting criteria for this code. GM's 2019 HPC2 table names P0CEB only as a blocking code alongside P0CE9, P0CEC and P0CED: while any of them is active, the plausibility test of the electronics coolant temperature sensor (P0CEF) does not run. GM folds a grounded line into P0CE9 in other years, so how P0CEB is used depends on the controller. CARB requires inverter cooling components to be checked for circuit faults. The counterpart for a line stuck high is P0CEC. A shorted line can keep the pump from running, which lets the inverter and charger loop overheat and leads to power limits.
c: Control wire chafed through and touching body ground
Water or corrosion in the pump connector bridging pins to ground
Faulty output stage in the controlling module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp or hybrid warning
Electronics coolant pump does not run
Power or charging limited as electronics temperatures rise

P0CEC.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump A Control Circuit High
P0CEC.d: P0CEC flags a pump control line that is held too high, normally a short to battery voltage on the output. GM's HPC2 tables of 2016 and 2019 (16OBDG02, 19OBDG02) look for it while the pump enable is on and the commanded duty cycle is between 0 and 10 %: a line reading high when it should be nearly off counts as a failure, and 16 of 20 samples at 250 ms set the code, Type B, two trips, with system voltage above 10.2 V. A pump with a line pinned high may run constantly or ignore speed requests, depending on its electronics. Open circuits belong to P0CE9, a line pulled low to P0CEB, the separate enable wire to P0CED. The fix is usually in the harness: a pinched wire touching a feed or moisture in a connector.
c: Control wire shorted to a 12 V feed in the harness
Moisture or corrosion in the pump connector linking supply and control pins
Pump electronics feeding voltage back onto the control line
Output stage in the control module stuck high
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Pump runs permanently or does not respond to speed changes
Possible power limitation of the hybrid system

P0CED.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump A Enable Circuit
P0CED.d: Some electronics coolant pumps receive two signals: a speed command and a separate enable wire that switches the pump on. P0CED concerns that enable wire. In GM's 2011 Volt (11OBDG01) any open or short on it sets the code after 16 of 20 samples at 250 ms with more than 9 V supply, Type B, two trips. Later GM controllers split the short cases into their own codes and keep P0CED for an open: the HPC2 tables 16OBDG02 and 19OBDG02 fail it when, with enable commanded on, the line rests between 1.14 V and 2.81 V, a level that points to a floating wire. The speed command line itself is P0CE9 to P0CEC. Without enable the pump stays off even though its command looks normal, so electronics temperatures climb and power may be reduced.
c: Broken enable wire or terminal pushed out of the connector
Enable wire shorted to ground or voltage (codes it on older GM controllers)
Defective enable input inside the pump
Faulty enable driver in the control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Electronics coolant pump remains off
Reduced power or charging rate when electronics get warm

P0CEE.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0CEE.d: Sensor A reports the coolant temperature in the loop that cools the hybrid power electronics. P0CEE is the general circuit code for it, used where a controller does not tell low from high. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM, for example, reports the same sensor only through P0CF0 (below 2 or 4 % of the reference voltage), P0CF1 (above 98 %) and the plausibility and noise checks P0CEF and P0CF2. CARB requires temperature inputs of inverter cooling systems to be checked for open circuits and for readings outside their valid band, so a controller may file an open or shorted sensor here instead. Because the system can no longer judge the coolant, it usually runs the pump harder and caps inverter and charging power as a precaution.
c: Loose, corroded or water-soaked sensor connector
Damaged signal or ground wire of the sensor
s: Malfunction indicator lamp or hybrid system warning
Electronics coolant pump runs continuously
Reduced drive or charging power as a precaution

P0CEF.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0CEF.d: The sensor stays electrically within range but reports a temperature that does not fit its surroundings. GM uses two kinds of comparison. In the 2011 Volt and the ELR it is checked against the high-voltage charger temperature with the pump running at 30 % or more for over 60 or 300 s; the limit is 38 to 40 °C (2011) or 35 °C (ELR). From the 2016 Volt on the test runs once after a long rest (propulsion off over 18,000 or 21,600 s, pump and A/C off for 3,600 s) and compares with outside air, transmission fluid and A/C high-side temperature; limits are 27/27/28 °C, 21/35 °C in 16OBDG02. GM uses 32 of 40 samples or 8 s in 10 s, Type B, two trips. Hard circuit faults are P0CF0/P0CF1, noise P0CF2. A wrong reading misleads the cooling and power limits.
c: Sensor element drifted and reads offset from the real coolant temperature
Added resistance from corroded terminals shifting the signal
Genuine temperature gap from poor flow or air in the electronics loop
Comparison sensor (charger, outside air or transmission fluid) reading wrong without its own code
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on, often without noticeable drivability change
Electronics coolant pump runs at odd times or longer than usual
Occasional power or charging limitation

P0CF0.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0CF0.d: The signal voltage of the electronics coolant temperature sensor drops close to zero, which almost always means the signal wire touches ground or the sensor is shorted internally. Low refers to the voltage, not to the temperature. GM sets the code below 2 % of the 5 V reference (0.1 V) in the 2011 Volt, the ELR and the 2016 HPC2 table, and below 4 % (0.2 V) in the 2016 Volt and the 2019 HPC2 table. Counting is 16 of 20 samples at 250 ms or 4 s in a 5 s window, with more than 9 or 10.2 V supply, Type B, two trips. The open or high case is P0CF1, a plausible but wrong value is P0CEF. With no usable reading, the controller assumes the worst, runs the pump and can limit inverter and charging power.
c: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Water in the connector bridging signal and ground
s: Malfunction indicator lamp or hybrid warning
Scan tool shows an implausibly high coolant temperature
Pump running constantly, power or charging reduced

P0CF1.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0CF1.d: The sensor signal rises nearly to the 5 V reference, the typical picture of an open circuit, an unplugged connector or a signal wire shorted to voltage. GM sets it above 98 % of the reference (4.9 V) in all published tables from the 2011 Volt to the 2019 HPC2 controller, 16 of 20 samples at 250 ms or 4 s within 5 s, Type B, two trips. Chrysler's Pacifica Hybrid shows it in practice: STAR case S2008000119 (2020, revised 2021) links P0CF1 together with P1B71-00 and B12B0-00 and the message Service Hybrid Electrical System to water entering the grey 16-pin inline connector XY291A under the battery skid plate. Cleaning and dielectric grease cure light moisture; corroded pins mean new dash and underbody harnesses. P0CF0 is the grounded counterpart.
c: Water or corrosion in an underbody inline connector (Chrysler Pacifica Hybrid XY291A)
Open signal or ground wire, or unplugged sensor
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
s: Service Hybrid Electrical System or similar warning
Scan tool shows an implausibly low coolant temperature
Charging or drive power limited

P0CF2.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0CF2.d: This code catches a coolant temperature signal that jumps around faster than a liquid can actually change temperature, without necessarily leaving the valid voltage window. GM computes a string length: the controller adds up the absolute steps between four consecutive readings taken 250 ms apart. If that total exceeds 90 °C (2016 Volt, 19OBDG01) or 95 °C (16OBDG02), the window counts as failed; 4 of 5 windows, 5 of 7 windows or 1 s in a 1.25 s window then set the code, Type B, two trips. Loose terminals, a cracked solder joint in the sensor or a chafed wire that touches intermittently produce such spikes. Steady faults are P0CF0/P0CF1, a stable but wrong value P0CEF. The erratic reading can make the pump and power limits react without reason.
c: Loose or spread terminal in the sensor connector
Chafed wire making intermittent contact with ground or another circuit
Cracked internal connection in the sensor
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, sometimes coming and going
Coolant temperature value jumps in live data
Pump speed or power limits change without reason

P0CF3.d: The control pilot is the signal line between charging station and vehicle: the station drives a 1 kHz square wave of about ±12 V, the vehicle loads it through a diode and resistors and thereby moves the level between the charging states. P0CF3 means the charge control module sees this line as interrupted, so no usable pilot reaches it although a connector is expected. FCA lists P0CF3-00 for the Chrysler Pacifica Plug-in Hybrid 2018 and 2019 (hybrid control processor, North America) and for the Jeep Renegade and Compass 4xe 2020-2021 (integrated dual charging module, Europe); each bulletin cures false entries with new module software. Implausible levels fall under P0CF4, shorts under P0CF5 and P0CF6, dropouts under P0CF7. Usually the car refuses to start charging or stops shortly after plugging in.
c: Charging or hybrid control module software misjudging the pilot (FCA reflash bulletins)
Bent, pushed-back or corroded pilot pin in the charge inlet, or a broken pilot wire
Defective charging cable or station that delivers no pilot signal
s: Charging does not start although the cable is plugged in
Charging aborts shortly after connection
Malfunction indicator lamp on and code not clearing (FCA)

P0CF4.d: P0CF4 flags a pilot signal that is electrically present but does not fit what the vehicle expects. GM spells out the test for the Chevrolet Volt (2011-2019, VICM/HPC2): with no cord connected and the car moving at 8 km/h or more, pilot voltage divided by battery voltage must stay below 0.03 and both processor logic states must agree; in a self-test with the internal diagnostic switch closed and the charging and ventilation switches open, the ratio must sit between 0.30 and 0.55. 30 of 50 samples at 100 ms set it as Type A, MIL after one trip; older tables also require the charge door to be closed. FCA names P0CF4-00 together with P0CF3 on the Pacifica Plug-in Hybrid and the Renegade/Compass 4xe and fixes it by reflash. Opens and shorts have their own codes. Charging may fail or be refused.
c: Faulty pilot measuring or self-test circuit inside the charging/hybrid control module
Module software needing an update (FCA Pacifica and 4xe bulletins)
Moisture or dirt in the charge inlet creating a leakage path on the pilot line
Charge door position fault blocking or distorting the test (GM Volt enable condition)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after one trip (GM)
Charging refused or interrupted
Charge status indicator shows a fault

P0CF5.d: Circuit Low means the pilot level sits under the lowest value any regular charging state can produce, as happens when the pilot wire is shorted to ground or to the protective earth contact. GM checks it in the Chevrolet Volt VICM/HPC2 tables from 2012 to 2019: with the cord unplugged, the controller feeds its own test signal through the internal diagnostic switch, and the ratio of pilot voltage to 12 V battery voltage must not fall below 0.03. 30 failures within 50 samples at 100 ms set the code as Type A, so the MIL lights after a single trip. A missing signal is P0CF3, an excessive level P0CF6, an implausible one P0CF4. While the line is pulled down, the vehicle cannot show the station that it is connected and ready, so charging does not begin.
c: Pilot wire chafed through and touching ground or the protective earth conductor
Water or corrosion bridging pilot and earth pins in the charge inlet
Failed pilot input or test circuit in the charging control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on (GM Type A)
Station does not detect the vehicle, charging never starts
Charge status indicator shows a fault after plugging in

P0CF6.d: A pilot level above the valid range usually means the line touches a supply voltage, or the measuring path in the module reads wrongly. GM evaluates it on the Chevrolet Volt (VICM/HPC2, 2012-2019) only while no cord is connected and the car is travelling at 8 km/h or faster, a moment when the pilot should be practically dead: a normalized pilot voltage (pilot voltage over battery voltage) above 0.55, or 0.58 in the 2012 table, in 30 of 50 samples at 100 ms sets the code. It is Type A, so the MIL comes on after one trip. The low-side counterpart is P0CF5, plausibility errors belong to P0CF4, an open line to P0CF3. With the pilot held high, the vehicle cannot pull the level down to request energy, and the station does not switch power on.
c: Pilot wire shorted to a 12 V feed in the harness or inlet
Pilot measuring circuit in the charging control module reading too high
Moisture in a connector coupling a neighbouring voltage onto the pilot
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after a drive (GM Type A)
Charging does not begin at the station
Charging fault message in the cluster

P0CF7.d: This code stands for a pilot signal that comes and goes or jumps between levels, typically from a loose contact in the charge inlet, a plug that is not fully latched or interference on the line. Ford documents P0CF7 on the 2021-2022 Mustang Mach-E and the 2022 e-Transit, logged by the SOBDM (secondary OBD module A), and on the 2022 F-150 Lightning by the same unit, there called BCCM, the charger control module. The bulletins link it to a charge status indicator flashing red, often alongside P0A7F from the battery controller; for the Mach-E an EVSE plug that is not properly secured is named as the trigger, and for both models the fix is new SOBDM/BCCM software. Steady opens, shorts and plausibility faults use P0CF3 to P0CF6. Charging stops now and then or is aborted.
c: Charger module software reacting too sensitively (Ford SOBDM/BCCM reprogramming)
Charging plug not fully seated or latched in the inlet
Worn or loose pilot contact in the inlet or on the charging cable
Charging station producing an unstable pilot signal
s: Charge status indicator flashing red (Ford)
Charging stops intermittently
Additional warning lamp with related codes such as P0A7F

P0CF8.t: Control Pilot Charging Switch A Circuit/Open
P0CF8.d: On the vehicle side the pilot is loaded permanently by about 2.7 kΩ, which drops the station's +12 V to roughly 9 V once a cable is connected. To ask for energy the vehicle closes charging switch A, often called S2, which adds a 1.3 kΩ branch and brings the level to about 6 V, the state in which the station closes its contactors. P0CF8 reports that the control circuit of this switch is open, so the module cannot operate it. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM tests the same switch on the Chevrolet Volt only for plausibility (P0CF9, normalized pilot voltage 0.14-0.28 in a self-test), and CARB requires plug-in vehicles to monitor charging system function. Shorts are P0CFA/P0CFB, a switch that will not close is P0CFD. Expect a car the station recognises that still never starts charging.
c: Open control wire or loose connector between module and charging switch
Charging switch or its 1.3 kΩ branch open inside the module or inlet electronics
Failed driver stage in the charging control module
s: Station detects the vehicle but charging never begins
Charging fault message after plugging in

P0CF9.t: Control Pilot Charging Switch A Range/Performance
P0CF9.d: Charging switch A is the vehicle-side switch that adds a resistor across the pilot to tell the charging station that the car is ready to take current. P0CF9 says the effect of that switch is implausible. GM documents the check for the Chevrolet Volt 2011-2019 (VICM/HPC2): with the cord unplugged, the controller closes its diagnostic switch together with the charging switch and expects the ratio of pilot voltage to battery voltage between 0.14 and 0.28; outside that band in 30 of 50 samples at 100 ms the code sets, Type A, MIL after one trip. The test only runs once the pilot circuit check has passed in the same key cycle, and it comes before the ventilation switch test P0D01. Opens and shorts of the switch are P0CF8, P0CFA and P0CFB. A car with this fault may be recognised but not charge.
c: Charging switch resistor branch out of tolerance or switch with high contact resistance
Internal fault in the VICM/charging module measuring or switching circuit
Leakage on the pilot line from moisture in the charge inlet
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on (GM Type A)
Charging does not start or is refused

P0CFA.t: Control Pilot Charging Switch A Circuit Low
P0CFA.d: Charging switch A shifts the control pilot from the connected state at about 9 V to the charge-request state at about 6 V by switching in an extra 1.3 kΩ path. P0CFA indicates that the control or feedback line of this switch reads too low, typically a harness wire touching ground or a driver stage in the charging module that has failed shorted. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; CARB requires hybrids and plug-ins to monitor the charging system, and GM's Chevrolet Volt checks the same switch only indirectly through P0CF9 by measuring the pilot voltage it causes in a self-test. Depending on the design, a grounded control line can hold the switch permanently closed or permanently open. The high-side fault is P0CFB, the open circuit P0CF8. Charging may then start unexpectedly or not at all.
c: Switch control or feedback wire shorted to ground
Shorted driver stage in the charging control module
Corrosion in the inlet or module connector bridging to ground
s: Charging does not start, or starts as soon as the plug is inserted
Charging fault message in the cluster

P0CFB.t: Control Pilot Charging Switch A Circuit High
P0CFB.d: P0CFB is the high-side counterpart: the control or feedback line of charging switch A, which loads the pilot with an extra 1.3 kΩ to request charging, shows a voltage above its valid band. Typical are a short to a supply voltage in the harness or connector, or an output stage in the charging module that no longer pulls the line down. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the closest documented test is GM's P0CF9 on the Chevrolet Volt, which judges the switch by the pilot voltage it produces in a self-test (ratio 0.14-0.28), while CARB requires plug-in vehicles to monitor the charging system. Low readings are P0CFA, an open line P0CF8, dropouts P0CFC. For the driver the station typically stays in the plugged-in state without supplying power, or a session cannot be ended cleanly.
c: Switch control or feedback wire shorted to a supply voltage
Output stage in the charging module no longer switching to ground
Lost ground at the switch letting the line float high
s: Vehicle detected at the station but no energy flows
Charging cannot be stopped normally

P0CFC.t: Control Pilot Charging Switch A Intermittent/Erratic
P0CFC.d: With P0CFC the module sees the circuit of charging switch A, which places the charge request on the pilot line, change state erratically: the signal toggles briefly or vanishes for moments, whereas lasting faults would set P0CF8, P0CFA or P0CFB. Likely triggers are a loose pin, corrosion in the charge inlet or module connector, or a chafed wire that loses contact only under vibration or temperature change. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; it follows the pattern of the pilot codes, and Ford's P0CF7 bulletins show how an insufficiently secured plug can produce such dropouts on the pilot itself. CARB requires plug-in vehicles to monitor the charging system. Because each lost charge request makes the station switch off, sessions are interrupted repeatedly and may restart on their own.
c: Loose or spread terminal in the switch circuit connector
Corrosion or moisture in the charge inlet
Chafed wire losing contact under vibration or temperature change
s: Charging interrupted repeatedly, sometimes restarting by itself
Code returns after clearing

P0CFD.t: Control Pilot Charging Switch A Stuck Off
P0CFD.d: Stuck Off means the module commands charging switch A closed, but the pilot does not show the expected effect: the level stays at the connected value of about 9 V instead of dropping to around 6 V, so the station never receives a charge request. Possible are a switch or relay that no longer closes, an open resistor in the 1.3 kΩ branch, or a fault in the pilot measuring path. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's plausibility test P0CF9 on the Chevrolet Volt evaluates the same switch from the pilot voltage during a self-test, and CARB requires the charging system to be monitored on plug-in vehicles. Its opposite is P0CFE, a switch that will not open; circuit faults are P0CF8 to P0CFB. The car is detected at the station and may report that it is plugged in, but charging never starts.
c: Charging switch or relay in the module no longer closing
Open resistor or solder joint in the 1.3 kΩ branch
Charging module software not issuing the close command correctly
s: Vehicle shows plugged in, but charging never begins
Charging station remains in standby or connected state

P0CFE.t: Control Pilot Charging Switch A Stuck On
P0CFE.d: Stuck On describes a charging switch A that stays closed while the module wants it open, so the pilot keeps signalling a charge request. Mercedes-Benz documents P0CFE00 in the AC charger N83, whose fault text states that the charger’s internal charge-start switch does not open. A 2023 bulletin for models 206, 223 and 243 reports it after charging has finished or at the start of a timed-charging pause, only with pre-entry climate control active, together with a charging error message in the cluster; NHTSA's index lists the same bulletin for many Mercedes plug-in and electric models up to 2026. The cause there is software, cured by SCN coding, and the bulletin advises against replacing parts. Its counterpart is P0CFD, circuit faults are P0CF8 to P0CFB. Charging may not end properly or is aborted.
c: On-board charger software, cured by SCN coding (Mercedes-Benz N83)
Charging switch or relay contacts sticking closed
Control line fault holding the switch permanently on
s: Charging error message in the instrument cluster after charging
Charging aborts at home socket, wallbox or public station
Fault appears mainly with pre-entry climate control active (Mercedes-Benz)

P0CFF.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump A Stuck/Stalled
P0CFF.d: Unlike the electronics codes above, P0CFF belongs to the pump that circulates coolant through the high-voltage battery. It means the pump is commanded but does not turn, or stops. Volkswagen and Audi log P0CFF00 in the battery management unit J840 (address 008C): VW bulletin 93-21-02 for the 2021 ID.4 blames trapped air when pump V590 did not run during the fill-and-bleed routine, and Audi's 2068363 series for the Q4 e-tron prescribes two bleed runs at a battery temperature of 3 to 26 °C, replacing V590 only if the code returns. Ford lists P0CFF with MIL for the 2020 Escape HEV (20-2221, stored in the BECM) and the Explorer/Aviator hybrids (20-2345) and fixes it with BECM software. Related: P2B28 performance, P2B29 dry run, P2CF3 underspeed, P0C4A control. A stalled pump soon limits charging and drive power.
c: Air trapped in the battery coolant loop, pump running dry and stalling (VW ID.4, Audi Q4 e-tron)
Battery control module software misjudging pump state (Ford 2020 hybrids)
Seized or mechanically blocked battery coolant pump
Low coolant level in the battery loop
s: Warning such as Electric drive fault or Electrical system not working correctly
Malfunction indicator lamp on (Ford)
Reduced charging speed, especially DC fast charging
Reduced drive power when the battery warms up

P0D00.t: Control Pilot Charging Ventilation Switch Circuit/Open
P0D00.d: Some battery types can give off gases while charging; for that case the conductive charging standards provide a state in which the vehicle asks the station for ventilation. The vehicle signals it by switching a much smaller resistor of about 270 Ω onto the pilot, which drags the level to around 3 V; the station then only delivers power where ventilation is assured. P0D00 reports that the control circuit of this ventilation switch is open. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's Chevrolet Volt monitors the switch for plausibility only (P0D01, normalized pilot voltage 0.04-0.10 in a self-test), and CARB requires plug-in vehicles to monitor the charging system. During normal charging the switch stays open, so an open circuit often goes unnoticed except for the stored code. Shorts are P0D02/P0D03.
c: Open control wire or loose connector of the ventilation switch circuit
Ventilation switch or its resistor branch open inside the module
Failed driver stage in the charging control module
s: Stored code, charging usually still works
Charging system warning in the cluster

P0D01.t: Control Pilot Charging Ventilation Switch Range/Performance
P0D01.d: The ventilation switch lets the vehicle request charging state D, in which a small resistor pulls the pilot down to about 3 V and the station may only deliver power with ventilation. P0D01 means this switch does not produce a plausible pilot level. GM documents the check for the Chevrolet Volt (VICM/HPC2): in a self-test with the cord unplugged and the diagnostic and ventilation switches closed, the ratio of pilot voltage to battery voltage must lie between 0.05 and 0.10 in the 2011 table, or between 0.04 and 0.10 in the 2016 and 2019 tables. 30 failed samples out of 50 at 100 ms set it as Type A, MIL after one trip; the pilot circuit and charging switch tests must have finished first. Circuit faults are P0D00, P0D02 and P0D03. If the switch really sticks closed, stations without ventilation will not supply power.
c: Internal fault in the VICM/charging module switching or measuring circuit
Ventilation resistor branch out of tolerance or high contact resistance
Leakage on the pilot line, for example moisture in the charge inlet
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on (GM Type A)
Charging possibly refused at stations without ventilation

P0D02.t: Control Pilot Charging Ventilation Switch Circuit Low
P0D02.d: P0D02 marks the control or feedback line of the ventilation switch as too low, usually a harness wire grounded somewhere along its route or a charging module driver that has failed shorted. That switch places a resistor of about 270 Ω across the pilot so that the level falls to roughly 3 V, the state in which a vehicle demands charging with ventilation. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's Chevrolet Volt evaluates the same switch by the pilot level it causes (P0D01, ratio 0.04-0.10 in a self-test), and CARB requires plug-in vehicles to monitor the charging system. If the short holds the switch closed, a station without ventilation will refuse to deliver power; if it holds it open, the fault mostly shows only as a stored code. The high-side fault is P0D03, the open line P0D00.
c: Ventilation switch control or feedback wire shorted to ground
Shorted driver stage in the charging control module
Corrosion in a connector bridging the line to ground
s: Charging refused at stations without ventilation
Stored code without noticeable effect

P0D03.t: Control Pilot Charging Ventilation Switch Circuit High
P0D03.d: Here the line that drives or reports the ventilation switch reads above its valid range, which points to a short to a supply voltage or a driver stage that no longer switches. The ventilation switch is the vehicle-side element that requests charging with ventilation by loading the control pilot with roughly 270 Ω and lowering it to around 3 V. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the closest documented test is P0D01 on the Chevrolet Volt, where GM judges the switch from the pilot voltage it produces in a self-test with the cord unplugged, and CARB requires plug-in vehicles to monitor the charging system. Low readings are P0D02, an open circuit P0D00, intermittent faults P0D04. Effects range from a stored code only to a refused charging session, depending on which switch state the fault forces.
c: Ventilation switch control or feedback wire shorted to a supply voltage
Output stage in the charging module no longer switching
Lost ground at the switch letting the line float high
s: Stored code, sometimes with a charging system warning
Charging refused if the switch is forced closed

P0D04.t: Control Pilot Charging Ventilation Switch Intermittent/Erratic
P0D04.d: P0D04 covers short, irregular disturbances in the ventilation switch circuit: the signal drops out or flickers, while lasting faults would be stored as P0D00, P0D02 or P0D03. Worn or corroded contacts in the charge inlet or module connector, and wires that lose contact under vibration, are the obvious suspects. Whenever the ventilation switch closes even briefly, it pulls the pilot toward about 3 V, so a station without ventilation suddenly sees a demand it cannot meet and may switch off. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's Chevrolet Volt shows how the switch is checked via P0D01, and CARB requires plug-in vehicles to monitor the charging system. In practice the driver notices charging sessions that stop for no obvious reason and a code that comes back after clearing.
c: Loose or spread terminal in the ventilation switch circuit
Corrosion or moisture in the charge inlet or module connector
Chafed wire with contact loss under vibration
s: Charging sessions stop without obvious reason
Code returns after clearing

P0D05.t: Control Pilot Charging Ventilation Switch Stuck Off
P0D05.d: Stuck Off for the ventilation switch means the module commands the switch closed, yet the pilot does not drop to the level around 3 V that marks a request for charging with ventilation. Possible causes are a switch that no longer closes, an open resistor in the roughly 270 Ω branch, or a measuring fault in the module. Because ordinary charging takes place without a ventilation request, this fault rarely restricts charging; it mainly shows up during the self-test the module runs on the circuit. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's Chevrolet Volt performs that kind of self-test as P0D01, with a normalized pilot voltage window of 0.04-0.10, and CARB requires plug-in vehicles to monitor the charging system. The opposite case is P0D06, circuit faults are P0D00 to P0D03. Expect a stored code and charging that still works.
c: Ventilation switch in the module no longer closing
Open resistor or solder joint in the ventilation branch
Pilot measuring fault in the charging module
s: Stored code, charging normally still possible
Charging system warning in the cluster on some vehicles

P0D06.t: Control Pilot Charging Ventilation Switch Stuck On
P0D06.d: Stuck On means the ventilation switch remains closed when it should be open, so the pilot is held near 3 V and the station reads a permanent demand for charging with ventilation. Stations that cannot provide ventilation do not supply power in that state, which in practice stops charging altogether. Likely causes are a welded or sticking switch, a short across the 270 Ω branch, or a module output that no longer releases. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's Chevrolet Volt checks the same switch through P0D01 by the pilot level it causes in a self-test, and Mercedes-Benz documents the matching failure of charging switch A as P0CFE00 (switch not opening, cured by software). The counterpart is P0D05, circuit faults are P0D00 to P0D03. The car is detected at the station but does not charge.
c: Ventilation switch contacts welded or sticking closed
Short across the ventilation resistor branch
Module output or software holding the switch on
s: Charging station does not supply power
Charging error message after plugging in

P0D07.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor A Circuit
P0D07.d: P0D07 is the general circuit code for positive contactor A of the charging system, the switch that joins the plus side of a charging path to the traction battery. Depending on the design this path comes from the DC fast-charge inlet or from the on-board charger; the Chevrolet Volt, for instance, places charging contactors between charger and pack. The code stands for an electrical fault in that contactor branch which fits no more specific case. No manufacturer documents P0D07 publicly; a GM patent describes judging such contactors by their coil current, and CARB requires plug-in vehicles to monitor charging components. Welded or non-closing contacts are P0D08/P0D09, driver faults P0D0A–P0D0D, the main pack contactors P0AA0 ff. Usually charging is blocked while driving still works.
c: Damaged wiring or corroded connector in the contactor branch
Fault in the module that drives and monitors the contactor
s: Charging not possible or aborted
Charging system warning in the instrument cluster

P0D08.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor A Stuck Closed
P0D08.d: P0D08 means positive charging contactor A has stayed closed although the control module commanded it open, typically because the contacts have welded. The module notices this when voltage remains on the charging side, for instance at the charge port once a session has ended, as a Toyota patent on charge-relay sticking explains. GM stores P0D08 in the BECM of the 2023 Cadillac Lyriq; bulletin 23-NA-096 traces a joint setting with P0D0F to a software fault after an interrupted level 2 AC session and confirms it with a one-minute test charge. Stellantis lists P0D08-00 for the 2024–2025 Ram ProMaster EV with MIL and a vehicle that may not enable, remedied by BPCM reflash. The negative side is P0D0F, the opposite fault P0D09. A live inlet is a safety risk, so charging or driving gets locked out.
c: Contactor contacts welded, for example after switching under load
Battery module software misjudging the contactor state (GM Lyriq, Ram ProMaster EV bulletins)
Driver stage or coil supply that does not switch off
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and high-voltage service message
Charging refused
Vehicle may not switch to ready mode

P0D09.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor A Stuck Open
P0D09.d: P0D09 is set when positive charging contactor A fails to close: after the command the expected voltage never shows up on the charger side. GM documents the check for the Chevrolet Volt (VICM 2016, HPC2 2019): during charger precharge, with charging and precharge contactors on and the negative main contactor still off, a charger voltage under 10 V ends the test; 2016 needs 8 failing samples out of 9, 2019 waits for at least 0.7 s of precharge. Both are Type A, MIL after one trip. Kia lists P0D0972 for the 2023 Niro EV (bulletin 298, ICCU replacement), Stellantis P0D09 for Wagoneer S and Charger Daytona (BPCM update), GM preliminary PIT6083 for the 2024 Lyriq after very long charging. Charging then stops or never starts; the welded case is P0D08.
c: Contactor mechanically failing to close or burnt contacts
Fault in the on-board charger or integrated charging unit (Kia ICCU bulletin)
Control software needing an update (Stellantis, GM Lyriq)
Missing coil supply because of a wiring or fuse fault
