GM and Mitsubishi publish only fixed limits (P0D53 and P0D54) and, at Mitsubishi, a zero-point test (P0D52) for this sensor; a sudden step that returns to normal would not necessarily trip those. CARB's charger requirement for plug-in hybrids is the regulatory basis for monitoring the signal at all. Typical triggers are intermittent internal contacts, solder fatigue from heat cycles during charging, or electrical noise from the charger's switching stage. The likely result is charging that stops and restarts or finishes much later than expected.
c: Intermittent contact in the current measuring path of the charger
Solder joints fatigued by charging heat cycles
Switching noise coupling into the sensor signal
s: Charging pauses and resumes repeatedly
Charging takes much longer than usual
Occasional charging system warning

P0D56.d: P0D56 is the general circuit fault of proximity detection circuit A, the line through which the vehicle notices that a charging plug sits in its inlet. Under SAE J1772 this proximity pin runs to protective earth through resistors in the plug and a switch tied to the latch button, so the car can block driving away and end charging before the plug is pulled; under IEC 62196 a resistor on the same pin also codes the cable's current rating. This is a different line from the control pilot, which carries the PWM dialogue with the charging station and has its own codes P0CF3-P0CF6. No manufacturer documents P0D56 publicly. A fault can mean no charging, or a car that thinks it is still plugged in.
c: Damaged or corroded proximity contact in the charge inlet
Open or chafed wire between charge inlet and evaluating module
Evaluation input in the charger or control module failed
s: Charging does not start although the cable is plugged in
Vehicle refuses to drive or shows the cable as connected without a plug
Charging system warning

P0D57.d: P0D57 means the plug-present signal of proximity circuit A is electrically within limits but its value or behaviour does not fit the situation, for instance a level between the defined states for plugged, unplugged and latch pressed. FCA uses the code on the Chrysler Pacifica plug-in hybrid: bulletins 08-044-20 (2017) and 08-042-20 (2018) list P0D57 with control pilot codes P0CF3 and P0CF4 behind an illuminated MIL and cure it by reflashing the hybrid control processors HCP and AHCP. FCA publishes no thresholds. The J1772 proximity circuit relies on defined resistor steps, so worn inlet contacts or an off-standard charging cable can shift the reading. Hard short circuits are P0D58 and P0D59.
c: Hybrid control software needs update (FCA HCP/AHCP)
Worn or contaminated proximity contact shifts the resistance
Charging cable or adapter with off-standard proximity resistor
s: MIL on (FCA)
Charging starts unreliably or not at all
Plug status shown incorrectly

P0D58.d: P0D58 reports a voltage on proximity circuit A that is too low while no plug can possibly be inserted. GM's Volt checks this in its hybrid control processor: in 2011 with the charge door closed or above 12.4 mph in a range other than Park, from 2016 above 20 km/h outside Park, the signal must sit in a window, and less than 4.2 V for 30 of 50 samples (later 240 of 400) sets the code as a Type A fault with immediate MIL. In the third-generation smart electric drive with 22 kW charger, Mercedes defines P0D5800 as a short to ground of this contact sensing; bulletin LI54.10-P-067823 links it to loose low-voltage plugs at the charger, a car that will not start and a cable-plugged-in message. The high counterpart is P0D59.
c: Proximity signal wire shorted to ground or chafed against body
Loose low-voltage connector at the on-board charger (smart)
Moisture or contamination bridging the inlet contacts
Evaluation input of the control module failed
s: MIL on (GM)
Vehicle will not start or shift because a plug appears connected
High-voltage battery cannot be charged

P0D59.d: P0D59 is logged when proximity circuit A shows a voltage above its expected resting level at a moment when the charge port must be empty. GM's Volt uses the same plausibility window as for P0D58 but trips above 4.8 V: in 2011 with the door shut or above 12.4 mph in a range other than Park, from 2016 at more than 20 km/h outside Park, over 30 of 50 or 240 of 400 samples; the fault is Type A and turns on the MIL. Mercedes defines P0D5900 for the 22 kW charger of the third-generation smart electric drive as a short to positive in the plug contact sensing, and the same bulletin blames loose charger connectors for charging and start-up problems. Electrically, a short to a supply line or a broken reference path can raise the level.
c: Proximity signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Interrupted ground or reference path of the detection circuit
Loose connector at the charger or charge inlet
s: MIL on (GM)
Inserted charging plug not recognised, no charging
Start-up problems after charging (smart)

P0D5A.d: P0D5A points to a proximity signal on circuit A that flips between states or jumps erratically, so the vehicle sees the plug come and go although nobody touched it. No manufacturer documents P0D5A publicly. The function itself is laid down in SAE J1772: the plug-present contact tells the car when a connector is seated and when its latch button is pressed, which lets it stop drawing current before disconnection. An unstable signal can therefore cause charging to abort without reason or a drive lock that appears and vanishes. Mercedes' smart bulletin for the 22 kW charger shows the typical background: loose low-voltage contacts that act up only when parts are warm or cold. Hard faults are P0D58 and P0D59.
c: Loose contact in the inlet or at the charger connector
Worn latch switch or contacts in the charging plug
s: Charging aborts sporadically
Plug status message appears and disappears
Occasional refusal to drive off

P0D5B.t: Battery Charger 14 Volt Output Power Performance
P0D5B.d: P0D5B checks whether the power leaving the charger's built-in 14 V output is physically possible. GM's charger module for the Volt and ELR multiplies the measured 14 V output voltage and current and compares the product with the AC input power times a factor of about 2 plus an offset: 2.5 W in the 2011 table, 125 W in the 2014 Volt/ELR and 2016 ELR tables. Exceeding that for 1.6 s within a 2 s window sets a Type A fault with MIL. The test only runs when the sensor codes P0D44, P0D45, P0D49 and P0D4A are clear, and the same low-voltage power also enters GM's total output check P1ECE. Because the 12 V side only takes part while charging, failures mostly show up as charging faults.
c: Voltage or current measurement of the 14 V stage reads too high
AC input power measured too low
Low-voltage stage of the on-board charger faulty
s: MIL on (GM)
Charging interrupted
12 V battery not supported while plugged in

P0D5C.t: Battery Charger Hybrid/EV Battery Output Power Performance
P0D5C.d: P0D5C judges the power the charger feeds into the traction battery against what it draws from the grid. GM's first-generation Volt and ELR charger module calculates high-voltage output power and flags it when it exceeds AC input power times about 2 plus 30 W (2011) or 120 W (2014 and 2016 ELR), for 1.6 of 2 s, Type A. The 2016 Volt checks the opposite direction: efficiency below 67 % of the nominal value for the coolant temperature and input power, with at least 600 W commanded on Level 1 or 2 charging, sets a Type B fault. Ford stores P0D5C in the secondary OBD module of the 2020 Lincoln Aviator plug-in hybrid; SSM 49289 cures a MIL after charging by reprogramming that module.
c: Power stage of the charger degraded, efficiency too low
Module software miscalculates power (Ford SOBDM update)
Output voltage/current or AC input measurement inaccurate
Insufficient cooling of the power electronics during charging
s: MIL on after a charging session
Charging slower than expected
Charging interrupted

P0D5D.t: Battery Charger Hybrid/EV System Discharge Time Too Short
P0D5D.d: P0D5D concerns the active discharge of the charger's high-voltage side after charging ends: the stored voltage collapses faster than the circuit design allows. No manufacturer documents P0D5D publicly; GM's Volt only publishes the opposite case P0D5E. Patent literature explains why a fast drop is suspicious too: a German application on high-voltage diagnostics describes detecting a discharge path that is permanently switched on, and a quick decay can equally point to lost capacitance or a faulty voltage reading. Safety is not at risk, since the voltage does fall below the touch-safe level, but the electronics may be degraded. CARB requires detection of charger faults that disable or limit charging. Charging may be refused until the fault is repaired.
c: Discharge switch inside the charger stuck closed
Charger voltage measurement reads falsely low
s: Charging system warning after the end of charging
Next charging session may not start
No noticeable effect while driving

P0D5E.t: Battery Charger Hybrid/EV System Discharge Time Too Long
P0D5E.d: P0D5E means the high-voltage side of the charger did not drop to a safe level in time after it was disconnected. GM's 2011 Volt charger module fails the test if 60 V or more remain 1.5 s after the discharge command, or 6.75 s after a confirmed communication loss with the hybrid controller; a backup routine then checks for battery current that would reveal a stuck contactor. The 2016 Volt allows 4 s after the contactors open, the 2019 Volt also 4 s against 58 V and adds a case for a failed voltage sensor combined with a stuck negative contactor. All are Type A with immediate MIL. A patent for on-board charger discharge circuits cites roughly 60 V as the safety limit. The opposite fault is P0D5D.
c: Active discharge circuit of the charger not working
High-voltage contactor stuck closed keeps the bus energised
Lost communication between charger and hybrid controller
Charger voltage sensor reads falsely high
s: MIL on (GM)
Charging blocked after the fault
Further high-voltage codes such as contactor faults may be stored

P0D5F.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 2 Sense Circuit/Open
P0D5F.d: Where a traction battery is cooled by two fans, each one can report its actual speed back to the controller on a separate sense line. P0D5F is the general circuit code for that return path of fan 2: the line is open or delivers nothing the controller can evaluate. No manufacturer documents P0D5F publicly. Volkswagen's 2014 Touareg Hybrid reads the same fan 2 feedback as a voltage but only defines P0D60 to P0D62, and Toyota patents show why the signal matters: measured fan speed is compared with the speed the duty command should give. CARB requires electrical inputs of battery thermal management to be monitored. Fan 2 may keep turning, yet its operation can no longer be confirmed, so the pack may be protected by reduced power. Drive-side faults of fan 2 are P0A96 and its siblings; fan 1 feedback uses P0BC7 to P0BCB.
c: Broken feedback wire or terminal pushed out at the fan 2 connector
Corroded or loose connector between fan 2 and the battery controller
Speed signal output inside the fan 2 motor electronics failed
Feedback input of the battery control module defective
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Reduced electric assist or charging power when the battery warms up
Often no noticeable change while fan 2 still runs

P0D60.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 2 Sense Range/Performance
P0D60.d: P0D60 means the feedback of battery cooling fan 2 is electrically present but does not fit what the fan was told to do. Volkswagen documents it for the 2014 Touareg Hybrid: the battery controller reads the fan 2 feedback as a voltage and flags this code when it crosses a limit that moves with the commanded duty, somewhere between 1.37 and 3.43 V; fan 1 is judged the same way under P0BC8. Behind such a mismatch usually sits a fan that turns too slowly or too fast for its command, for example from a worn bearing, debris in the impeller or a blocked intake duct, less often a drifting feedback stage. The reading stays inside its valid window, which separates P0D60 from the hard faults P0D61 (low) and P0D62 (high). Battery temperatures may climb and the system can cut power to protect the pack.
c: Fan 2 runs off its commanded speed due to worn bearing or debris on the impeller
Clogged intake grille, filter or duct of the battery cooling air
Drifting speed feedback stage in the fan electronics
High resistance in the feedback or supply connection of fan 2
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Fan noise that is louder, rougher or weaker than usual
Battery temperature rises faster and electric power is limited

P0D61.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 2 Sense Circuit Low
P0D61.d: P0D61 reports that the feedback signal of battery cooling fan 2 sits at or near zero. In Volkswagen's 2014 Touareg Hybrid the battery controller sets it once the fan 2 feedback voltage drops below 0.1 V; the matching fan 1 code is P0BC9. Such a flat reading comes from a feedback wire shorted to ground, a feedback stage inside the fan that has failed low, or a fan that has no supply and therefore produces no signal at all. Unlike P0D60, where a valid signal merely disagrees with the command, here the value is simply out of range at the bottom; the opposite end is P0D62. Because the controller cannot tell whether fan 2 still moves air, it may treat the cooling as lost and limit battery power under load or in warm weather.
c: Fan 2 feedback wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Fan 2 without supply (fuse, relay or supply wire), so no signal is generated
Feedback output of the fan 2 electronics failed low or motor seized
Feedback input of the battery control module defective
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Fan 2 audibly silent although battery cooling is requested
Reduced electric power, especially in warm conditions

P0D62.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 2 Sense Circuit High
P0D62.d: P0D62 is set when the feedback of battery cooling fan 2 rises above its plausible maximum. Volkswagen gives the threshold for the 2014 Touareg Hybrid as a fan 2 feedback voltage above 3.45 V, mirroring P0BCA for fan 1. A real fan cannot drive the signal that high, so the cause is electrical: the feedback wire touching a supply or another signal, a missing ground at the fan so the line floats up, or fan electronics stuck at their upper output. Check the ground and the harness routing before condemning the fan. The bottom end of the range is P0D61, while P0D60 covers a valid signal that disagrees with the command. With the speed information unusable, the controller cannot verify cooling and may restrict battery power.
c: Fan 2 feedback wire shorted to a supply or neighbouring signal
Open ground at fan 2 letting the feedback line float high
Fan 2 electronics stuck at their upper feedback level
Feedback input of the battery control module defective
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Electric power limited when the battery gets warm
Fan 2 may still run normally

P0D63.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 2 Sense Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0D63.d: P0D63 flags a feedback signal from battery cooling fan 2 that drops out or jumps in steps no spinning fan could produce. The typical culprit is a loose pin or cracked wire that opens and closes with vibration, or interference coupled into the feedback line. No manufacturer documents P0D63 publicly; Volkswagen's 2014 Touareg Hybrid watches the fan 2 feedback only for performance, low and high (P0D60 to P0D62). Toyota's battery cooling patents explain why an unsteady signal is a problem: the controller compares measured speed with the speed expected for the duty command, and a jumping value defeats that comparison. CARB requires the inputs of battery thermal management to be monitored. A wiggle test at the fan 2 connector while watching live data is the quickest check. The fan 1 counterpart is P0BCB.
c: Loose or spread terminal in the fan 2 feedback connector
Cracked feedback wire that opens under vibration
Electrical interference from nearby high-current or high-voltage wiring
Unstable feedback stage in the fan 2 electronics
s: Warning light that comes and goes
Occasional short phases of reduced electric power
Often no noticeable change in fan operation

P0D64.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan Enable Circuit/Open
P0D64.d: Besides its speed command, a battery cooling fan can have a separate enable line that switches the fan electronics on. P0D64 means the controller has found this enable output open. GM documents it in its hybrid OBD tables 16OBDG02 to 19OBDG02 under the battery system module, there named fan 1 enable: with the enable commanded off and system voltage above 10.2 V, an output voltage stuck between 1.14 and 2.81 V counts as an open circuit, and 16 failures in 20 samples at 250 ms set it as Type B, MIL after two trips. The fan speed diagnostic P0BC8 is suspended while P0D64 to P0D66 are active. Typical causes are a broken wire or an unplugged fan connector. Without enable the fan stays off, so the battery heats faster and power may be reduced. Short to ground is P0D65, short to voltage P0D66.
c: Broken enable wire between battery controller and fan
Fan connector unplugged or not latched, often after battery or trim work
Open enable input inside the fan electronics
Enable driver in the battery system module defective
s: Check engine light or hybrid warning after two trips
Battery cooling fan does not run
Reduced electric assist when the battery gets hot

P0D65.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan Enable Circuit Low
P0D65.d: P0D65 reports a short to ground on the enable output of the battery cooling fan: the line stays low even though the controller is trying to switch the fan on. GM's 2013 eAssist mild hybrid table 13OBDG05C detects it from the output driver's fault flag for the power pack fan, 20 failures in 25 samples at 250 ms, Type B. The later hybrid tables 16OBDG02 to 19OBDG02 test it with the enable commanded on: a voltage under 5.35 V at system voltage above 10.2 V counts, and 16 failures in 20 samples set the code, again Type B with MIL after two trips. A chafed wire touching the body or a shorted input inside the fan are the usual finds. The fan cannot start, so expect higher battery temperatures and possibly reduced electric support. Open circuit is P0D64, short to voltage P0D66.
c: Enable wire chafed and shorted to body ground
Shorted enable input inside the fan electronics
Moisture or corrosion bridging the enable pin to ground
Enable driver in the battery controller defective
s: Check engine light or hybrid warning after two trips
Battery cooling fan never switches on
Engine runs more and electric assist drops in hot weather

P0D66.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan Enable Circuit High
P0D66.d: P0D66 stands for a short to voltage on the enable output of the battery cooling fan. Because the line is pulled high from outside, the fan may run although the controller wants it off, or the controller simply loses authority over it. GM's 2013 eAssist table 13OBDG05C flags it through the output driver's fault status, 20 failures in 25 samples at 250 ms, Type B. In the hybrid tables 16OBDG02 to 19OBDG02 the check runs with the enable commanded off: 5.27 to 19.7 V on the output at system voltage above 10.2 V counts as a failure, 16 in 20 samples set the code, Type B, MIL after two trips. Look for the enable wire rubbing against a supply wire or water in the connector. A fan that never stops drains the 12 V battery. Open circuit is P0D64, short to ground P0D65.
c: Enable wire rubbed through and touching a 12 V supply wire
Moisture in the fan connector bridging enable and supply pins
Internal fault in the fan electronics feeding voltage back onto the enable line
Enable driver in the battery controller defective
s: Check engine light or hybrid warning after two trips
Battery cooling fan runs continuously, even with the vehicle off
Discharged 12 V battery after standing

P0D67.t: Battery Charger Control Module A Performance
P0D67.d: P0D67 says that the control electronics of the on-board charger are not working properly. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV manuals (2019 and 2022) spell out what that means there: with the charger supplied at 10 to 16 V, the code sets when one of its internal supply rails leaves its window for 1 s, 3.0 to 3.6 V for the 3.3 V rail, 5.3 to 6.8 V for the 6 V rail or 9.4 to 14.9 V for the 12 V rail. Charging is then stopped, and the only listed remedy is a new charger/DC-DC converter unit. Kia's bulletin 298 for the 2023 Niro EV names P0D67 among codes that lead to replacing the integrated charging control unit (ICCU) and mentions a possible MIL. Driving usually still works, but plug-in charging does not. Processor faults of the same module are P0E5E.
c: Internal low-voltage supply of the on-board charger out of tolerance
On-board charger or integrated charging unit failed
Weak 12 V supply or poor ground at the charger
Charger software fault, fixed by an update where available
s: Plug-in charging stops or does not start
Electric vehicle system warning in the cluster, possibly MIL
Vehicle can still be driven on stored energy or fuel

P0D68.t: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor A Circuit
P0D68.d: An electric A/C compressor in a hybrid or EV runs its motor from the high-voltage battery through an inverter in the compressor housing, and a sensor there measures the incoming high voltage. P0D68 is the general circuit code for that sensor: its signal is missing or unusable as a whole, without a specific low or high reading. No manufacturer documents P0D68 publicly. GM (Volt) and Mitsubishi (Outlander PHEV) monitor the same sensor but use P0D69 for plausibility against the battery voltage and P0D6A/P0D6B for out-of-range values. CARB requires electronic A/C components to be monitored where they affect engine control or other diagnostics. In practice the compressor controller stops the compressor when it cannot trust its input voltage, so cabin cooling and any refrigerant-based battery cooling are lost.
c: Voltage measurement inside the electric compressor's inverter failed
Compressor reports its sensor value over a faulty data link
Poor high-voltage connection at the compressor
s: Air conditioning does not cool
Warning message or warning light, depending on the vehicle
Battery cooling via refrigerant may be limited

P0D69.t: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor A Performance
P0D69.d: P0D69 is a plausibility check: the high voltage that the electric A/C compressor measures at its input should match the traction battery voltage, since both see the same supply. GM's Volt sets it when the two differ by more than 15 V in the 2011 table (35 of 40 samples at 250 ms) and by more than 30 V in the 2016 and 2019 tables (8 of 10 s in 2019), each Type B with MIL after two trips and only with contactors closed and no battery voltage codes active. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV uses 20 V for 2 s, with the compressor reading 205 to 415 V, a battery above 15 °C and intake air above 0 °C; the 2023 model lights only the MIL for it. Usual causes are the compressor's internal measurement, the data link carrying its value, or the hybrid controller. Range faults are P0D6A and P0D6B.
c: Drifting high-voltage measurement inside the electric compressor
Fault on the data bus that carries the compressor voltage value
Hybrid or vehicle controller misjudging the comparison
Error in the battery voltage measurement used as reference
s: Check engine light
Air conditioning weak or switched off
Often no other noticeable change

P0D6A.t: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor A Circuit High
P0D6A.d: P0D6A means the electric A/C compressor reports an input voltage higher than the high-voltage system can actually deliver. GM's 2011 Volt table sets it at 450 V or more (30 of 60 samples at 50 ms); the 2016 and 2019 Volt tables use more than 527.25 V, judged by the compressor itself and sent over the data bus (2019: 4 of 5 s). Both are Type B, MIL after two trips. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV flags it when the compressor reads above 415 V for 2 s while the battery shows 220 to 400 V; its 2019 and 2022 manuals label the code inconsistently as low and high, but the threshold is a high one. The 2023 model lights the MIL. A real overvoltage is unlikely, so the compressor's measurement or the hybrid controller is the main suspect. The low end is P0D6B, plausibility P0D69.
c: Voltage measurement in the compressor inverter reading too high
Hybrid controller or data link fault
s: Check engine light
Air conditioning stops cooling
Driving otherwise normal

P0D6B.t: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor A Circuit Low
P0D6B.d: P0D6B reports that the high-voltage input reading of the electric A/C compressor sits below the plausible range. GM's first-generation Volt (2011–2015) and the 2016 ELR set it at 190 V or less in 30 of 60 samples at 50 ms, checked only with the contactors closed for over a second and fault-free. The 2016–2019 Volt uses below 27.75 V, judged by the compressor and passed on over GMLAN (2019: 4 of 5 s); all are Type B, MIL after two trips. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV flags under 205 V for 2 s while the battery shows 220 to 400 V; the 2019/2022 page header mislabels it as high, but the threshold is a low one, and the 2023 list calls it Circuit Low with MIL only. Suspects: compressor inverter, CAN link, hybrid ECU. A real supply loss is P0D6D.
c: Voltage measurement in the compressor inverter reads too low
Faulty data link between compressor and hybrid controller (named by Mitsubishi)
Hybrid or vehicle controller evaluates the value incorrectly
s: Check engine light after two trips (GM) or immediately (Mitsubishi 2023)
Air conditioning stops cooling
Battery cooling via refrigerant may be restricted

P0D6C.t: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0D6C.d: P0D6C covers a voltage-sensor signal from the electric A/C compressor that jumps or drops out briefly instead of staying wrong: single readings outside the expected window or abrupt steps that do not last long enough for the low or high code. No manufacturer documents P0D6C publicly. GM (Volt, ELR) and Mitsubishi (Outlander PHEV) monitor the same input but only publish P0D69 (comparison with battery voltage), P0D6A and P0D6B, each with fixed fail counts such as 30 of 60 samples or 2 s. CARB requires the sensor inputs of hybrid thermal-management parts, which include a compressor that also cools the battery, to be checked for circuit and rationality faults. Loose low-voltage plugs, a marginal HV contact or a failing inverter board are typical; cooling may cut in and out.
c: Loose or corroded low-voltage connector at the compressor
Intermittent fault on the compressor's inverter board
Marginal high-voltage contact at the compressor connector
s: Air conditioning cools intermittently
Code returns sporadically after clearing
Often no warning light

P0D6D.t: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage A Low
P0D6D.d: P0D6D concerns the high voltage actually reaching the electric A/C compressor motor rather than the sensor circuit: the supply is too low to run it. Mazda documents it for the CX-90 PHEV (2024–2026) and CX-70 PHEV (2025–2026) in bulletin 07-002/26: an overcurrent can short the compressor internally and blow the A/C high-voltage fuse, after which the PCM stores P0D6D, often with U0605. The fix is an updated compressor, followed by a continuity check of the HV circuit including the fuse. Bentley's 2022 Flying Spur Hybrid logs P0D6D00 in thermal management together with an open HV wiring circuit when the HV cable between battery and on-board charger breaks internally; the battery then stops charging as well. The sensor-range code is P0D6B, the high side P0D6E.
c: Internal short in the compressor that has blown the A/C high-voltage fuse (Mazda)
Broken high-voltage cable in the supply path (Bentley, battery to on-board charger)
Open A/C fuse or poor high-voltage connection without a compressor defect
s: Air conditioning does not cool at all
Further codes such as lost communication with the compressor
High-voltage battery may not charge (cable fault)

P0D6E.t: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage A High
P0D6E.d: P0D6E means the high voltage supplied to the electric A/C compressor motor is above what the compressor is built to accept, as opposed to a sensor circuit reading too high (P0D6A). No manufacturer documents P0D6E publicly. GM handles the situation its own way: the 2011–2015 Volt and 2016 ELR compressor sets P0D6A at 450 V or more and a separate maker code, P1ECA, for a single peak of 480 V; Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV treats over 415 V for 2 s as P0D6A. Real overvoltage is rare because the traction battery clamps the bus; possible triggers are spikes during charging or regeneration, a faulty charger or converter, or a misreading inverter. The compressor usually shuts down to protect its power stage. CARB covers such inputs under hybrid thermal-management monitoring.
c: Voltage measurement in the compressor inverter reads too high
Voltage spikes on the high-voltage bus during charging or regeneration
Charger or DC/DC converter regulating the bus voltage incorrectly
s: Air conditioning switches off
Possibly further high-voltage codes
Warning message depending on the vehicle

P0D6F.d: P0D6F flags excessive current drawn by the electric A/C compressor on its high-voltage DC link while the motor is running. GM's first-generation Volt (2011–2015) and the 2016 Cadillac ELR set it when the DC link current exceeds 27 A in 30 of 60 samples taken every 50 ms with a compressor speed request above zero; it is Type B, MIL after two trips. A separate maker code, P1EC9, catches momentary peaks above 60 A. The second-generation Volt tables no longer list P0D6F. High current points to a mechanically binding or liquid-slugging compressor, a shorted motor winding or a failing power stage; overcharged refrigerant or very high head pressure can also raise the load. Phase-specific current faults are P0D7A to P0D7F.
c: Shorted winding in the compressor motor
Refrigerant overcharge or excessive high-side pressure
Failing power stage in the compressor inverter
s: Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning cuts out under load
Unusual noise from the compressor

P0D70.t: A/C Compressor Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0D70.d: The control electronics inside an electric A/C compressor carry a temperature sensor on the processor board, called internal sensor A; the compressor uses it to protect itself and reports the value to the vehicle. P0D70 is the general circuit code for it: the value is missing or invalid without a defined low or high reading. No manufacturer documents P0D70 publicly. GM's Volt and ELR tables only use P0D71 (comparison with other temperatures), P0D72 (below −40 °C) and P0D73 (above 150 or 274 °C) for this sensor. A Hyundai patent on temperature sensors of power electronics lists open connectors, shorts, noise and board faults as the usual origins. As the sensor sits on the module's circuit board, a confirmed fault usually means a new compressor assembly; cooling may be reduced or stop.
c: Temperature sensor or its circuit on the compressor board failed
Value not transmitted correctly over the data link
Unstable 12 V supply or ground of the compressor electronics
s: Air conditioning weak or off
Battery cooling via refrigerant may be limited
Warning depending on the vehicle

P0D71.t: A/C Compressor Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Performance
P0D71.d: P0D71 is a plausibility test for the compressor control module's internal (CPU) temperature sensor: after a long rest, every temperature in the compressor should be close to its surroundings. GM's 2011 Volt compares it with intake air and with the output-stage sensor and fails above 6 °C in 35 of 40 samples at 250 ms. The 2016 Volt uses more than 22 °C against outside air and the IGBT sensor once the compressor has been off for over 7,200 s, the 2016 ELR 10 °C, and the 2019 Volt 22 °C in 8 of 10 s; outside air has to be above −7 °C. All are Type B with MIL after two trips. A drifting sensor, a faulty reference sensor or a compressor still warm from use can trigger it; range faults are P0D72 and P0D73.
c: Drifting internal temperature sensor in the compressor electronics
Outside air, intake air or IGBT sensor used for comparison is wrong
Compressor not fully cooled down when the test ran
s: Check engine light after two trips
Usually no noticeable change in A/C operation

P0D72.t: A/C Compressor Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0D72.d: P0D72 is the high-signal circuit code for the compressor module's internal temperature sensor. With the usual NTC thermistor a high signal means the reading looks extremely cold, and that is how GM defines it: every Volt and ELR table from 2011 to 2019 sets it when the reported CPU temperature is below −40 °C. Timing is 30 of 60 samples at 50 ms in the first-generation Volt, 40 of 50 at 100 ms in 2016 and 4 of 5 s in 2019, each Type B with MIL after two trips; the older tables only check with outside air above −7 °C. In the J2012 list this High code comes before the Low code P0D73. Typical cause is an open sensor path or a cracked solder joint on the compressor board, so the assembly is usually replaced.
c: Open circuit in the internal temperature sensor path
Cracked solder joint on the compressor electronics board
Faulty value transmission to the host controller
s: Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning limited or switched off

P0D73.t: A/C Compressor Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0D73.d: P0D73 is the low-signal circuit code for the internal (CPU) temperature sensor of the compressor control module. For an NTC sensor a low signal corresponds to an implausibly hot reading. GM sets it above 274 °C in the 2011–2015 Volt and 2016 ELR, and above 150 °C in the 2016–2019 Volt, where the compressor itself detects the condition and reports it over GMLAN; counting is 30 of 60 samples at 50 ms, 40 of 50 at 100 ms or 4 of 5 s depending on the year, Type B. Values like these suggest a shorted sensor rather than real heat, although genuine overheating of the electronics should be ruled out by checking. The compressor may limit or stop operation. The cold-side code is P0D72, plausibility P0D71.
c: Short circuit in the internal temperature sensor path
Real overheating of the compressor electronics
Faulty value transmission to the host controller
s: Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning reduced or switched off

P0D74.t: A/C Compressor Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0D74.d: P0D74 reports an unsteady signal from the internal temperature sensor of the A/C compressor control module: the reading jumps or drops out in short bursts rather than sitting at one wrong value. No manufacturer publishes a threshold for P0D74. GM's 2019 Volt table names it, together with P0D71 to P0D73, as a fault that blocks other compressor diagnostics, which ties it to the same sensor, but it gives no set criteria. A Hyundai patent on temperature sensors of power switches describes how loose connectors, noise, board defects or cold solder joints produce exactly such erratic values. Because the sensor is part of the compressor electronics, a confirmed fault usually ends with a new assembly; check the 12 V supply, ground and data connections first.
c: Cold or cracked solder joint on the compressor board
Loose low-voltage connector or ground at the compressor
Electrical interference on the sensor signal
s: Air conditioning cuts out now and then
Code appears sporadically

P0D75.t: A/C Compressor Control Module Output Driver Temperature Sensor Circuit
P0D75.d: The output driver temperature sensor watches the power transistors (IGBTs) that switch the three motor phases of an electric A/C compressor; they heat up under load, and the compressor reduces speed or stops before they overheat. P0D75 is the general circuit code for this sensor without a defined low or high value. No manufacturer documents P0D75 publicly; GM's Volt and ELR use P0D76 to P0D78 for the same sensor and mention P0D79 in enable conditions. A Denso patent on hybrid compressor control describes throttling the compressor when the IGBT module runs hot, which is why losing this signal normally halts it. CARB requires such thermal-management inputs to be monitored. The sensor is built into the inverter, so repair usually means a new compressor.
c: Temperature sensor at the IGBT module or its circuit failed
Sensor value not transmitted correctly to the vehicle
Unstable 12 V supply or ground of the compressor electronics
s: Air conditioning switched off
Battery cooling via refrigerant may be limited

P0D76.t: A/C Compressor Control Module Output Driver Temperature Sensor Performance
P0D76.d: P0D76 checks whether the compressor's output driver (IGBT) temperature sensor agrees with other temperatures after a cold soak. GM's 2011 Volt fails it when the IGBT reading differs from outside air by more than 11 °C and from the CPU sensor by more than 7 °C after the compressor has been off for over 21,600 s, with coolant and outside air within 15 °C of each other; 35 of 40 samples at 250 ms. The 2016 Volt uses 22 °C for both comparisons after 7,200 s off, the 2016 ELR 15 °C, and the 2019 Volt 22 °C in 8 of 10 s, where every comparison must fail together. Each is Type B, MIL after two trips. Causes: drifting sensor, wrong reference value, residual heat. Range codes are P0D77 and P0D78.
c: Drifting IGBT temperature sensor in the compressor inverter
Outside air or CPU temperature used for comparison is wrong
Power stage still warm when the test ran
s: Check engine light after two trips
Usually no noticeable change in A/C operation

P0D77.t: A/C Compressor Control Module Output Driver Temperature Sensor Circuit High
P0D77.d: P0D77 is the high-signal circuit code of the output driver (IGBT) temperature sensor in the electric A/C compressor. As with an NTC sensor, the high signal shows up as an impossibly cold temperature: GM sets it when the IGBT reading is at or below −40 °C, in all Volt and ELR tables from 2011 to 2019. The first-generation Volt needs 30 of 60 samples at 50 ms and evaluates only with outside air above −7 °C; the 2016 Volt counts 40 of 50 samples at 100 ms, the 2019 Volt 4 of 5 s, with the compressor reporting the fault over GMLAN. Type B, MIL after two trips. Without a valid power-stage temperature the compressor cannot protect itself and is normally switched off. Likely an open sensor path on the inverter board; hot-side code P0D78.
c: Open circuit in the IGBT temperature sensor path
Cracked solder joint on the inverter board
Faulty value transmission to the host controller
s: Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning switched off

P0D78.t: A/C Compressor Control Module Output Driver Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
P0D78.d: P0D78 is set when the output driver (IGBT) temperature sensor of the electric A/C compressor signals low, which for an NTC sensor means an implausibly hot value. GM uses 274 °C or more in the 2011–2015 Volt and the 2016 ELR, and above 150 °C in the 2016–2019 Volt; detection takes 30 of 60 samples at 50 ms, 40 of 50 at 100 ms or 4 of 5 s, Type B with MIL after two trips. Temperatures like these are beyond what the power stage survives, so a shorted sensor is more likely than real heat, although a seized compressor or a failed condenser fan can drive the IGBTs hot. Expect the A/C to switch off. The cold-side counterpart is P0D77, plausibility P0D76.
c: Short circuit in the IGBT temperature sensor path
Real overheating of the power stage from high load or poor condenser cooling
Faulty value transmission to the host controller
s: Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning switched off

P0D79.t: A/C Compressor Control Module Output Driver Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0D79.d: P0D79 marks an erratic signal from the output driver temperature sensor, the sensor that guards the compressor's power transistors: values flicker or drop out briefly instead of staying wrong. No manufacturer publishes set criteria. GM's 2019 Volt table lists P0D79 next to P0D77 and P0D78 as an IGBT-sensor circuit fault that suspends the plausibility checks, which shows the code is in use, but without thresholds. A Hyundai patent on temperature sensors for power switches names loose connectors, electrical noise, board defects and cold solder joints as typical origins of such unstable readings. Because the compressor can no longer trust its overheat protection, it may cut out repeatedly. CARB requires thermal-management inputs to be checked for circuit faults.
c: Cold or cracked solder joint at the IGBT sensor
Loose low-voltage connector or ground at the compressor
Switching noise from the inverter coupling into the sensor signal
s: Air conditioning cuts out repeatedly
Code appears sporadically

P0D7A.t: A/C Compressor Motor Phase U Current Low
P0D7A.d: Electric A/C compressors run a three-phase motor whose phase currents U, V and W are measured inside the inverter. P0D7A belongs to phase U. GM's 2011–2015 Volt and 2016 ELR test the sensors while the motor is stopped and the speed request is zero, when no current should flow: a phase U reading of +68 A or more in 30 of 60 samples at 50 ms sets P0D7A, Type B with MIL after two trips, and a 12 V reset is needed before it can pass again. In other words, GM uses the code for a current-sensor offset at standstill rather than for weak current during operation. The cause lies in the inverter's current sensing; the compressor normally stops. The negative counterpart is P0D7B, other phases P0D7C and P0D7E.
c: Offset or failure of the phase U current sensor in the inverter
Fault in the inverter's current measuring circuit
s: Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning does not start

P0D7B.t: A/C Compressor Motor Phase U Current High
P0D7B.d: P0D7B is the second phase U current code of the electric A/C compressor. In GM's first-generation Volt (2011–2015) and the 2016 Cadillac ELR it sets when the phase U current sensor reads −68 A or less although the motor is stopped and no speed is requested, counted as 30 failures in 60 samples at 50 ms; Type B, MIL after two trips, with a 12 V reset required before a pass. A real current of that size at standstill is impossible, so the fault lies in the sensor or its evaluation on the inverter board, which normally means replacing the compressor. The A/C stays off while the code is active. GM's positive-direction code for the same phase is P0D7A; phases V and W use P0D7D and P0D7F.
c: Phase U current sensor reading negative at standstill
Fault in the inverter's current evaluation
s: Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning stays off

P0D7C.t: A/C Compressor Motor Phase V Current Low
P0D7C.d: P0D7C relates to phase V of the three-phase motor in an electric A/C compressor. GM documents it in the 2011–2015 Volt and 2016 ELR tables as a standstill check: with the compressor speed request at 0 rpm the measured phase V current should be near zero, and a value of +68 A or above in 30 of 60 samples (50 ms each) sets the code. It is Type B, so the MIL comes on after two trips, and the result only returns to pass after a 12 V reset. The later Volt tables from 2016 do not list it. As the motor cannot carry that current while stopped, an offset in the inverter's phase V current sensor is the likely cause, and the compressor is normally replaced. Related: P0D7D for the negative side, P0D7A and P0D7E for the other phases.
c: Offset or failure of the phase V current sensor in the inverter
Fault in the inverter's current measuring circuit
s: Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning inoperative

P0D7D.t: A/C Compressor Motor Phase V Current High
P0D7D.d: P0D7D marks a phase V current reading of the electric A/C compressor that is far negative while the motor should be idle. GM's first-generation Volt and the 2016 ELR set it at −68 A or less, judged in 30 of 60 samples every 50 ms whenever the speed request is zero, as Type B with MIL after two trips. A 12 V reset is needed before the diagnostic can report a pass again. Because the check runs only with the motor stopped, it catches a drifting or failed current sensor rather than an operating overload; running overcurrent is P0D6F. Expect the climate control to lose cooling, with battery cooling affected on vehicles that share the refrigerant circuit. The counterpart on the same phase is P0D7C.
c: Phase V current sensor reading negative at standstill
Fault in the inverter's current evaluation
s: Check engine light after two trips
No cooling from the air conditioning
Battery cooling via refrigerant may be limited

P0D7E.t: A/C Compressor Motor Phase W Current Low
P0D7E.d: P0D7E applies to phase W, the third winding of the electric A/C compressor motor. GM's 2011–2015 Volt and 2016 Cadillac ELR check the W-phase current sensor while the motor is at rest: a reading of +68 A or more in 30 out of 60 samples at 50 ms sets the code, Type B with the MIL after two trips, and only a 12 V reset re-enables a pass. With all three phase sensors tested the same way, a fault on just one phase points to that sensor channel on the inverter board, while faults on several phases at once suggest a common supply or reference problem in the inverter. The compressor stays off. P0D7F is the negative direction on phase W; P0D7A and P0D7C cover the other two phases.
c: Offset or failure of the phase W current sensor channel
Common supply or reference fault in the inverter (several phases affected)
s: Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning does not run

P0D7F.t: A/C Compressor Motor Phase W Current High
P0D7F.d: P0D7F is the negative-direction current code for phase W of the electric A/C compressor motor. In GM's first-generation Volt and the 2016 ELR the inverter reports a W-phase current of −68 A or lower while the motor is stopped and no speed is requested; 30 such readings in 60 samples at 50 ms set the code, Type B with MIL after two trips, and a 12 V reset is required before it can pass. Since no current can flow in a stopped motor, a sensor offset or a fault in the measuring circuit is the cause, not the refrigerant system. Repair is normally a compressor assembly. GM's second-generation Volt no longer lists these phase codes. Related: P0D7E on the same phase, P0D7B and P0D7D on the others.
c: Phase W current sensor reading negative at standstill
Fault in the inverter's current measuring circuit
s: Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning inoperative

P0D80.d: P0D80 means the on-board charger sees no usable AC supply at its input even though the charging handshake says power should be there. Ford documents the check for its plug-in hybrids in the OBD summaries for model years 2014 to 2018: with the cable connected, the EVSE active and the S2 switch closed, an input below 85 VAC lasting 30 seconds sets the code, and Ford's code dictionary marks it as a MIL code. The fault can therefore lie outside the car, for example a dead EVSE or a tripped breaker, as well as in the charge inlet, the AC harness or the charger itself. P0D81 to P0D84 cover implausible or electrically wrong input signals, P0D27 a supply that is present but too low. The driver notices that the car does not charge.
c: Charging station or outlet delivers no AC after the handshake (fault, tripped breaker)
Open AC contact or wire between charge inlet and charger
Fault in the charger's input stage or voltage measurement
s: Vehicle does not charge although the cable is plugged in
Charging fault message or flashing fault pattern at the charge port
Check engine light

P0D81.d: P0D81 is the plausibility code for the charger's AC input: a signal is present and electrically valid, yet contradicts the stage the charging sequence has reached. No manufacturer documents this code publicly with thresholds. A Ford patent on charger-to-EVSE detection outlines the kind of check meant here: the charger watches for line voltage while its S2 switch is still commanded open, debounces the condition and may only report it after it recurs over several charge cycles. Such a mismatch typically comes from a station that energises its contacts too early. CARB does not require faults caused by the off-board supply to be told apart, so the code often points at the EVSE rather than the car. P0D80 covers missing input, P0D82 and P0D83 electrical out-of-range values, P0D90 a wrong frequency.
c: Charging station switches AC on before the vehicle has closed S2 (faulty or welded EVSE relay)
Charger's input voltage measurement reports an implausible value
Improvised supply that feeds the inlet directly without a proper EVSE
s: Charging does not start or stops shortly after plugging in
Charging fault message

P0D82.d: P0D82 reports that the charger's input circuit signal has dropped below the lowest value the module accepts as electrically valid. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; Ford, for instance, folds missing input into P0D80 with its 85 VAC/30 s limit. By analogy with other circuit-low codes, the cause is usually in the measuring path: a sense line shorted to ground, moisture or corrosion at the inlet terminals, or a failed input stage inside the charger. That separates P0D82 from P0D27, which judges a real but weak mains supply, and from P0D3F, which is reserved for the input voltage sensor circuit itself. CARB asks for such circuit faults on charger inputs to be detected. To the driver the result is a charge that will not begin or ends early.
c: Input sense line or harness shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion at the charge inlet terminals
Failed input stage inside the on-board charger
s: Charging does not start
Charging ends earlier than expected
Charging fault message

P0D83.d: P0D83 is set when the charger reads its input circuit above the highest electrically valid level, i.e. a reading the measuring stage could not produce from a healthy mains connection. No manufacturer publishes a threshold for it. Likely culprits are a sense line shorted to a voltage source, a damaged inlet whose pins bridge to one another, or a measuring channel in the charger that has drifted or failed. P0D28 should be kept apart: it rates a real mains voltage above what the charger accepts, whereas P0D83 doubts the signal itself; P0D40 is the matching fault of the separate input voltage sensor. Because the charger cannot trust the reading, it normally refuses to convert power, so the battery stays uncharged while driving is unaffected.
c: Input sense line shorted to a voltage source
Damaged charge inlet with bridged or burnt contacts
Drifted or failed measuring channel in the charger
s: Charger refuses to charge
Charging fault message

P0D84.d: P0D84 stands for an input signal that keeps jumping or dropping out during a charge rather than sitting steadily at a wrong value. There is no public manufacturer description of the code. In practice such patterns come from contacts that make and break: a worn or loose charging plug, a heat-damaged inlet socket, a cable damaged by being driven over, or a loose connector between inlet and charger. A supply that sags under load, such as a long extension lead, can look the same. The Ford P0D80 check with its 30-second debounce shows how short dropouts are filtered before an open circuit is declared; P0D84 catches what remains unstable. Charging may stop and restart repeatedly, take longer than usual or abort without a clear pattern.
c: Worn, loose or heat-damaged charging plug or inlet contacts
Supply sagging under load, e.g. long extension lead
Loose connector between inlet and charger
s: Charging stops and restarts repeatedly
Charging takes noticeably longer

P0D85.t: Battery Charging Output Voltage Too High
P0D85.d: P0D85 means the charger is putting more voltage onto the traction battery side than it should. In Ford's 2019 plug-in hybrid OBD summary the battery controller compares the charger's output voltage with its own request and flags a surplus of 20.82 V lasting 20 seconds. Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander PHEV judges a change of output voltage of more than 450 V while the PHEV-ECU allows charging, stops the charge and points to the charger/DC-DC unit after checking the high-voltage fuse and the P/N lines; the 2023 list lights the hybrid warning and the MIL. Porsche reuses P0D8500 on 911 (992) petrol models for a battery voltage judged too high at cold start, fixed by DME software (TI 203/23). Related: P0D20, P0D21 and the sensor code P0D4F.
c: Voltage control fault inside the on-board charger/DC-DC unit
Open high-voltage fuse or P/N line between charger and battery (output unloaded)
Control unit software error (e.g. Porsche DME, reprogramming)
s: Charging stops
Hybrid system warning and check engine light

P0D86.t: Battery Charger Coupler Status Indicator Control Circuit A/Open
P0D86.d: Many plug-in vehicles light up the charge inlet to show whether the plug is recognised, charging is running or a fault exists; a Ford summary describes a four-segment ring, a supplier patent multi-coloured LEDs at the port. P0D86 says the control module driving channel A of this indicator finds no continuity in that circuit. Which colour or segment A stands for is up to the manufacturer, and none documents this code publicly. GM's Volt watched its single charge-status LED under P0D2C instead and caught an open line while the LED was commanded off, Type B. Typical reasons are an unplugged lamp connector, a broken wire near the flap or a burnt-out LED. Charging itself keeps working; only the status display at the port is missing. P0D87 and P0D88 are the low and high faults of the same channel.
c: Indicator connector at the charge inlet unplugged or not latched
Broken wire in the harness near the charge port flap
Failed LED or lamp element of channel A
s: Part of the charge port lighting stays dark
Charging status not visible at the inlet, charging itself works

P0D87.t: Battery Charger Coupler Status Indicator Control Circuit A Low
P0D87.d: P0D87 flags channel A of the charge port status indicator as pulled low, which in practice means a short to ground somewhere between driver and lamp. Such a fault only shows when the channel is switched on: the driver tries to raise the line and current flows straight to ground. GM's Volt checked its comparable charge-status LED (P0D2C) exactly that way, with 40 failed samples out of 50 taken every 100 ms while the LED was commanded on. No maker publishes thresholds for P0D87 itself. Chafed insulation on a body edge, water that has entered the inlet lighting or a shorted LED module are the usual suspects. Most drivers protect themselves by switching off, so the light stays dark; charging is not affected. An open circuit on the same channel is P0D86, a short to voltage P0D88.
c: Chafed wire of channel A touching body ground
Water ingress into the charge inlet lighting
s: Indicator channel A stays dark when it should light
Charging status hard to read at the port

P0D88.t: Battery Charger Coupler Status Indicator Control Circuit A High
P0D88.d: P0D88 is stored when channel A of the charge port status indicator sits at a high level although the driver is holding it off, typically because the line touches a voltage-carrying wire or the driver stage leaks. The fault is therefore seen in the switched-off state; GM's Volt evaluated its own charge-status LED (P0D2C) for short to battery only while the LED was meant to be dark. No manufacturer documents P0D88 publicly. The visible result is often the reverse of P0D87: channel A glows constantly or faintly, so the port may suggest a charging state that does not exist. A pinched harness at the flap hinge, a bridged connector or a defective output in the control module are the causes to check. Charging works normally; P0D86 and P0D87 cover open and grounded faults of the same channel.
c: Channel A wire shorted to a voltage-carrying wire (pinched harness)
Bridged or corroded connector at the indicator
Leaking or failed output stage in the control module
s: Indicator channel A lights constantly or glows faintly
Port shows a misleading charging status

P0D89.t: Battery Charger Coupler Status Indicator Control Circuit B/Open
P0D89.d: P0D89 reports lost continuity in the second output channel, B, of the charge port status indicator. Where an indicator has several channels, they usually stand for different colours or segments, as in the multi-colour port lighting of a supplier patent; which one is B depends on the vehicle, and no manufacturer documents this code publicly. For diagnosis the pattern across channels helps: if only B is open while A and C work, the break lies in the B branch or its LED; if P0D86 and P0D8C are stored at the same time, a shared connector, supply or ground at the inlet is more likely. CARB lets makers combine open and shorted output faults in one code, so not every vehicle separates them. The visible effect is a missing colour or segment at the port; charging continues.
c: Break in the channel B wire or its connector pin
Failed LED or segment of channel B
Shared connector or ground at the inlet (when A and C are also affected)
s: One colour or segment of the port lighting missing
Charging works normally

P0D8A.t: Battery Charger Coupler Status Indicator Control Circuit B Low
P0D8A.d: P0D8A means channel B of the charge port status indicator is held at ground level when it ought to rise, i.e. a short to ground on the B line or inside its lamp. The inlet is one of the most exposed electrical points of the car: rain, car-wash water and road salt reach it every time the flap opens, so corroded or wet contacts that bridge to ground are a frequent finding. No manufacturer documents P0D8A publicly; the closest published logic is GM's P0D2C test on the Volt, which checks for a grounded LED line while the lamp is commanded on and sets a Type B fault. The channel normally switches off to protect its driver, so the related colour or segment remains dark. Charging is not restricted. P0D89 covers an open B circuit, P0D8B a short to voltage.
c: Wet or corroded contacts at the inlet lighting bridging to ground
Channel B wire chafed through to body ground
Shorted LED or segment of channel B
s: Colour or segment B stays dark
Charging status only partly shown

P0D8B.t: Battery Charger Coupler Status Indicator Control Circuit B High
P0D8B.d: P0D8B is set when the B line of the charge port status indicator carries voltage while its driver has it switched off. The detection logic mirrors what GM published for the Volt's charge-status LED (P0D2C): a short to battery is looked for during the off phase. No manufacturer documents P0D8B itself. In everyday use the consequence can be more confusing than a dark lamp: segment or colour B stays lit, so the port may display a charge level or state that does not match reality, which matters when owners rely on the light to check progress. Insulation damage where the harness bends at the flap, a connector bridged by moisture or a stuck driver output are the main candidates. Charging is unaffected. P0D89 and P0D8A are the open and low faults of channel B.
c: Insulation damage where the harness bends at the flap, contact with a supply wire
Driver output in the control module stuck on
s: Colour or segment B stays lit
Displayed charge level does not match the actual state

P0D8C.t: Battery Charger Coupler Status Indicator Control Circuit C/Open
P0D8C.d: P0D8C points to an open third channel, C, of the charge port status indicator. Only systems with at least three separately driven lighting outputs use it, for instance one per colour in an RGB-type port lamp of the kind a supplier patent describes, or individual ring segments. No manufacturer documents the code publicly. A common trigger is work at the inlet: after body repair, a flap or inlet replacement or paint work, the lamp connector may be left unplugged or a pin pushed back in its housing. On integrated inlets, where the LEDs sit inside the socket assembly, a failed LED can mean replacing the whole inlet. If A and B report open at the same time, look at the common connector first. The port loses one colour or segment; charging continues unaffected.
c: Lamp connector left unplugged or pin pushed back after work at the inlet
Failed LED of channel C (on integrated inlets the whole inlet assembly)
s: One colour or segment of the port lighting missing
Fault appears after body or inlet repair

P0D8D.t: Battery Charger Coupler Status Indicator Control Circuit C Low
P0D8D.d: P0D8D marks channel C of the charge port status indicator as shorted toward ground: when the module switches C on, the line does not reach the expected level and the driver registers overcurrent or a low voltage. As with A and B, the code is defined in the standard but no manufacturer publishes its own conditions for it; GM's Volt logic for P0D2C, which tests a grounded LED line only while the LED is commanded on, shows the usual principle. Because the third channel is often the last LED or segment in a chain, damage tends to sit at the far end of the harness inside the inlet housing. A grounded driver output inside the module is the rarer case. Expect the channel to go dark and possibly the whole indicator to be disabled for protection; charging stays possible. P0D8C and P0D8E complete the C trio.
c: Short to ground at the far end of the harness inside the inlet housing
Shorted LED or segment of channel C
Grounded driver output inside the control module
s: Colour or segment C stays dark
Whole port indicator may switch off

P0D8E.t: Battery Charger Coupler Status Indicator Control Circuit C High
P0D8E.d: P0D8E is recorded when channel C of the charge port status indicator shows a high level that the driver did not command, a short to a supply voltage or a driver that no longer turns off. Following the pattern GM published for the Volt's charge-status LED, this is checked while the output is meant to be inactive. No manufacturer documents P0D8E publicly. What the owner sees depends on what C signals on that vehicle: in multi-colour designs, where each LED colour carries a meaning such as fault, charging or complete, a constantly lit C channel can display a fault or a finished charge that is not real. Look for chafing where the harness passes the flap mechanism, a connector bridged by water or a stuck output stage. Charging is unaffected. P0D8C and P0D8D are the open and low faults of channel C.
c: Chafed channel C wire touching a supply wire at the flap mechanism
Output stage in the control module stuck on
s: Colour or segment C lit permanently
Port shows a fault or complete status that is not real

P0D8F.t: Battery Charger A Cooling System Performance
P0D8F.d: P0D8F means the cooling of on-board charger A is not keeping the unit within its temperature limits, so the charger has to restrict its function. Mercedes documents the code with failure type 97 for the AMG GLE 53 Hybrid (bulletin LI47.70-P-079963, 2025): AC charging stops after about 15 minutes, the cluster reports AC charging inoperative and severely limited hybrid performance, and alongside P0D8F the charger stores an implausibility between its two coolant temperature sensors. The cause was the low-temperature circuits of power electronics and charger with swapped coolant lines; the remedy is to exchange them, not the charger. Air-cooled chargers, such as in Ford's older plug-in hybrids, report overheating under P0D24 instead. Charger B uses P2DB6.
c: Low coolant level or air in the charger's cooling circuit
Coolant lines connected to the wrong circuit (Mercedes AMG GLE 53 Hybrid)
Failed coolant pump of the low-temperature circuit
Blocked low-temperature radiator or inactive cooling fan
s: AC charging stops after a short time or runs at reduced power
Warning that AC charging is inoperative
Hybrid drive performance limited

P0D90.d: P0D90 is stored when the AC supplied to the on-board charger does not have a believable mains frequency. No official manufacturer document available to the public names the code with a threshold. A Ford patent on charger-to-EVSE detection describes the obvious method: after the pilot signal is present and S2 is closed, the charger measures the interval between successive zero passes of the incoming AC, increments an error counter whenever the result is under 40 Hz or over 70 Hz and stores a code after a set number of errors. The patent notes that the frequency fault need not stop charging, and that a frequency error together with a lost pilot is treated as the higher-ranking loss of AC power. Unstable sources such as small generators or faulty portable EVSEs are the usual trigger; often the driver notices nothing at all.
c: Charging from a source with unstable frequency (small generator, inverter)
Faulty portable charging unit or wall box
Fault in the charger's frequency measurement
s: Often no noticeable effect apart from the stored code
Charging interrupted at certain supply points

P0D91.t: Battery Charger Coupler Lock Control Circuit/Open
P0D91.d: P0D91 means the module that drives the charge-plug latch sees its lock output as electrically open: when it commands the latch closed, no current flows through the wiring and actuator winding. Without a confirmed lock, the car normally refuses to start a charging session, because the plug could be withdrawn under load. Mercedes-Benz documents P0D9100 in the drivetrain control unit (PTCU, N127) of its recent P3 plug-in hybrids such as the S 580 e and the AMG GT 63 S E and C 63 S E: bulletin LI47.70-P-078127 describes a car that will not charge on AC with the check engine light on and names hardware or software as possible causes still under investigation. Shorts on this output are P0D92/P0D93, a driven but ineffective lock is P0D94, and the release side has P0D95–P0D98.
c: Connector at the lock actuator loose, corroded or backed out
Broken wire in the harness between control unit and inlet
Motor winding inside the lock actuator burnt through
Driver stage or software of the controlling module (Mercedes names both)
s: Vehicle does not charge on AC
Check engine light on (Mercedes)
Charging system warning in the instrument cluster

P0D92.t: Battery Charger Coupler Lock Control Circuit Low
P0D92.d: P0D92 says the voltage on the lock control output stays too low, typically because the drive line is shorted to ground or the actuator draws far too much current, so the module cannot energise the latch properly and shuts its driver off. No manufacturer publishes this exact code. The hardware it supervises is described in patents: a small geared DC motor pushes a pin or cam across the plug latch (GM, US9279276B2), and a position sensor reports whether the pin really reached the locked end, otherwise fast charging is withheld (GM, US8936482B2). Which module drives the lock differs by maker (on-board charger at the VW group, drivetrain unit at Mercedes, SOBDM at Ford). The open-circuit case is P0D91, a short to supply P0D93; for the driver, the charging session simply never starts.
c: Lock drive wire chafed and shorted to body ground
Actuator jammed or binding, drawing excessive current
Water in the actuator connector at the inlet
Driver output of the controlling module defective
s: Charging session does not start after plugging in
Charge plug is not held in the inlet
Charging fault message in the cluster or app

P0D93.t: Battery Charger Coupler Lock Control Circuit High
P0D93.d: P0D93 reports a lock control circuit that reads higher than the module expects, classically a drive line shorted to a supply voltage. Ford shows that mechanical damage leads there as well: TSBs 22-2355 and 23-2014 list P0D93:00, alongside P0D94, P0D98, P0D9E and P0DA0, as stored by the SOBDM (secondary on-board diagnostic module) of Mach-E, e-Transit and F-150 Lightning built 2021–2023. If the DC fast-charge plug is pulled without the release button held fully down, the locking pin of the actuator can break or go missing; the cluster then shows Charger Service Required and the next level 3 session fails. Ford replaces only the actuator, quoting 1.2 to 1.7 hours of labour. A short to ground on this output would be P0D92, an open circuit P0D91.
c: Locking pin broken or missing after the plug was pulled while latched (Ford)
Lock drive wire shorted to a supply voltage
Internal electrical fault in the lock actuator
Driver stage of the controlling module defective
s: DC fast charging (level 3) inoperative
Charger Service Required indicator in the cluster (Ford)
Locking pin visibly broken or absent at the inlet

P0D94.t: Battery Charger Coupler Lock Control Circuit Performance
P0D94.d: P0D94 is the functional check of the locking step: the wiring tests fine, yet after a lock command the feedback from the actuator does not confirm that the pin arrived in its locked position. Two makers publish it. Ford's TSBs 22-2355 and 23-2014 tie it to a broken or missing pin in the DC charge-port lock actuator of 2021–2023 Mach-E, e-Transit and Lightning models, cured with a new actuator. Audi logs P0D9400 in charger J1050 (address 00C6) of 2024–2026 Q4 e-tron models: the plug at times neither locks nor releases, the charge LED switches to red and the cluster reports restricted AC charging. Audi blames charger software, warns that a new control unit does not help and fixes it with the combined update ID.S 5.6.3 (TSB 2083187). Electrical faults are P0D91–P0D93.
c: Software fault in the on-board charger, fixed by update (Audi)
Actuator mechanism binding from dirt, ice or wear
Charge plug not fully seated, so the pin cannot engage
s: Charging aborts or does not start; DC fast charging unavailable
Charge cable cannot be removed except with the manual release
Charge LED changes from green to red, AC charging restricted message (Audi)

P0D95.t: Battery Charger Coupler Unlock Control Circuit/Open
P0D95.d: P0D95 concerns the release direction: the output that withdraws the locking pin shows an open circuit when the module commands unlock. Because J2012 assigns lock and unlock separate control circuits, the module watches each drive direction on its own, and a break can disable only the release. That is the more awkward failure, since the cable may stay latched in the inlet after charging; inlets therefore carry a mechanical emergency release, which Audi's Q4 e-tron bulletins mention as the fallback when the plug will not come out. No manufacturer documents P0D95 publicly; it rests on CARB's rule that output components be checked for circuit faults and proper response to commands, and on lock actuator patents such as GM's geared-motor design (US9279276B2). The shorted variants are P0D96/P0D97, the locking side P0D91–P0D94.
c: Open unlock drive wire or loose pin in the actuator connector
Motor winding or internal contact of the actuator open
Corrosion in the connector at the inlet from road splash
Unlock driver stage of the controlling module defective
s: Charge cable stays locked in the inlet after charging
Plug can only be freed with the emergency release
Charging system fault message

P0D96.t: Battery Charger Coupler Unlock Control Circuit Low
P0D96.d: P0D96 indicates that the voltage on the unlock control output is too low, which usually means the release line is shorted to ground or the actuator pulls an overcurrent as soon as it is energised in the release direction. To protect its driver, the module stops commanding, so the pin stays where it is. If it was latched, the plug remains captive until the emergency release is used; if it was already open, the car may refuse the next session because it can no longer trust the lock. No manufacturer publishes this code, so the explanation draws on CARB's monitoring logic for output components and on actuator patents in which a position sensor confirms each end stop (GM, US8936482B2). Compared with P0D95 the circuit is not broken but shorted; the opposite fault, a short to supply, is P0D97.
c: Unlock drive wire shorted to ground at a chafe point
Actuator seized, for example by ice or dirt, causing overcurrent
Unlock driver stage of the module defective
s: Charge plug cannot be unplugged after charging
Emergency release needed to free the cable
Next charging session refused

P0D97.t: Battery Charger Coupler Unlock Control Circuit High
P0D97.d: P0D97 reports that the unlock control output sits higher than it should while the module is not driving it, or does not follow the command, which points to a release line touching a supply voltage. Such a fault is critical for safety logic: a release path that may be energised unintentionally could free the plug during current flow, so control units typically end the charging session or refuse to begin it while the code is active. No manufacturer documents P0D97 openly. CARB's comprehensive-component rules require output circuits to be checked for shorts and correct response, and the TE Connectivity actuator patent EP3252879B1 stresses that the lock position must be reliably detected to prevent unsecured charging. P0D96 is the short to ground, P0D93 the matching fault on the locking side.
c: Unlock drive wire shorted to a supply wire in the harness
Internal short inside the lock actuator
Unlock driver stage of the module stuck on
s: Charging session stops or does not start
Plug is not held firmly in the inlet
Charging system fault message

P0D98.t: Battery Charger Coupler Unlock Control Circuit Performance
P0D98.d: P0D98 is set when the release command is carried out electrically but the feedback does not confirm that the pin has retracted, or the actuator never reaches its open end stop. Ford is the only maker that names it publicly: TSBs 22-2355 and 23-2014 list P0D98:00 in the SOBDM of Ford's electric Mach-E, e-Transit and Lightning pickup (2021–2023), together with P0D93, P0D94 and the lock position codes P0D9E/P0DA0. Root cause there is a damaged DC charge-port lock actuator after the plug was yanked out without fully pressing the release button; the result is no level 3 charging and a Charger Service Required warning. Ford reminds owners that the latch can also be released from the centre screen or the button on the fast charger. Wiring faults on this side are P0D95–P0D97.
c: Actuator pin damaged by pulling the plug while latched (Ford)
Release movement blocked by ice, dirt or a worn gear train
s: DC fast charging (level 3) inoperative
Charger Service Required indicator (Ford)
Plug hard to remove or held in the inlet

P0D99.t: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0D99.d: P0D99 flags a general electrical fault in temperature sensor A of the charging inlet, the element that tells the car how hot the power contacts are. At high current, contact resistance heats the pins; the reading lets the car throttle or stop charging (TE Connectivity, US10960781B2). Inlet suppliers fit resistive sensors: Phoenix Contact strings PTC elements along the AC pins and puts a Pt 1000 on each DC pin, with shutdown above +90 °C at the contact. For the third-generation smart electric drive with 22 kW charger, Mercedes defines P0D9900 as an electrical fault of the inlet contact temperature sensor; bulletin LI54.10-P-067823 traces it, like neighbouring sensor codes, to loose low-voltage plugs at the charger. Without a usable reading, charging is refused or limited. Implausible, low and high readings are P0D9A–P0D9C.
c: Loose low-voltage connector at the on-board charger (smart)
Damaged sensor wiring between inlet and charger
Temperature element in the inlet failed (usually replaced with the inlet harness)
Evaluation input in the charger module defective
s: High-voltage battery cannot be charged
Charging only at reduced power
Charging system fault message

P0D9A.t: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0D9A.d: P0D9A covers a coupler temperature signal that is electrically valid but does not make sense, for example a rise that the charging current cannot explain or a value that disagrees with the rest of the system. GM's preliminary information PIT5904 lists it, with P298C and P0E5F, for the 2022 GMC Hummer EV and BrightDrop EV600: the MIL comes on and charging fails or aborts, often at heavily used public or dealer stations. GM suspects software or oversized and damaged terminals in the cable plug, advises clearing codes and trying another station, and notes that the test only re-runs after about 10 minutes of driving above 2 mph. Mercedes stores it as P0D9A97 (sensor malfunction) in the smart's 22 kW charger. Unlike P0D99, a worn station plug can trigger it on a healthy car; true overheating is P0E5F.
c: Oversized or damaged terminals in the charging station plug (GM)
Charging software calibration, update pending or available (GM)
Raised contact resistance at the vehicle inlet pins
Temperature element drifting out of its characteristic
s: MIL on (GM)
Charging fails or stops, often at busy public stations
Code returns only after a drive of about 10 minutes (GM)

P0D9B.t: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0D9B.d: P0D9B means the voltage of coupler temperature sensor A has dropped below its valid window. Low refers to the signal, and what that implies about temperature depends on the element: with an NTC a low voltage stands for an extremely hot reading, whereas the PTC chain and Pt 1000 sensors Phoenix Contact builds into its inlets lose resistance as they cool, so in the usual pull-up wiring a low signal looks implausibly cold. A short to ground drives the signal low with either type. Bentley publishes the code for the 2024 Bentayga Hybrid: TPI 2075291/1 reports that the on-board charger (address 00C6) displays the texts of P0D9B and P0D9C swapped, and confirms that P0D9B is the low fault, so technicians should diagnose by code, not by the displayed wording. No thresholds are public. The high fault is P0D9C.
c: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion bridging the sensor contacts in the inlet
Diagnosis misled by swapped fault texts in the charger (Bentley)
s: Charging refused or limited
Charging system fault message
Fault stored as intermittent or static in the charger

P0D9C.t: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0D9C.d: P0D9C is stored when the signal of coupler temperature sensor A climbs above its valid window, the typical result of an open sensor loop, an unplugged connector or a short to a supply voltage. Read as temperature, a high signal means cold for an NTC but hot for the resistive PTC and Pt 1000 elements found in CCS inlets from Phoenix Contact, which is why an interrupted Pt 1000 wire can look like a contact far above the +90 °C shutdown limit and stop charging at once. Bentley's TPI 2075291/1 for the 2024 Bentayga Hybrid confirms that P0D9C is the high fault, although the on-board charger (address 00C6) shows the text of the low fault; the diagnostic path must follow the code number. Bentley gives no thresholds. Unlike true overtemperature (P0E5F), nothing is actually hot here; the circuit is at fault. Its low counterpart is P0D9B.
c: Open sensor wire or connector at the inlet or charger
Sensor signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Temperature element open inside the inlet
Diagnosis misled by swapped fault texts in the charger (Bentley)
s: Charging stops immediately or does not start
Charging system fault message
Fault stored as intermittent or static in the charger

P0D9D.t: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0D9D.d: P0D9D is logged when the signal of temperature sensor A in the charging inlet jumps or drops out for short moments instead of failing for good.
