The sensor sits beside the power pins so the car can cut back or end charging once contact resistance heats them; TE Connectivity patents US10960781B2 and US11117478B2 name thermistors and resistance thermometers for this job. No manufacturer documents P0D9D publicly. A related smart case shows the pattern: with the 22 kW charger, Mercedes blamed inlet sensor codes on loose low-voltage plugs at the charger and warned that the fault may only show up with warm or cold parts. Typical is a session that stops for no clear reason and works again later. Steady circuit, plausibility, low and high faults are P0D99 to P0D9C.
c: Sensor wiring between inlet and charger with a loose or chafed contact
Low-voltage connector at the on-board charger not fully seated (seen on smart for sibling codes)
Moisture or corrosion in the inlet harness connector
Temperature element in the inlet with an internal intermittent break
s: Charging stops now and then and resumes on a later attempt
Charging power reduced for a while without an obvious reason
Charging fault message that comes and goes

P0D9E.t: Battery Charger A Coupler Lock Position Sensor Circuit
P0D9E.d: The lock position sensor tells the vehicle whether the pin that holds the charging plug in the inlet is extended or retracted. Without that feedback the car cannot confirm a latched plug and refuses fast charging. A GM patent, US8936482B2, measures how far the actuator has moved the pin, with a Hall element, a potentiometer or an end-stop switch as options. P0D9E is the general circuit fault of this feedback. Ford lists P0D9E:00 in TSBs 22-2355 and 23-2014 for the F-150 Lightning, Mach-E and e-Transit built 2021 to 2023, stored by the SOBDM together with P0D93, P0D94, P0D98 and P0DA0. The cause there is mechanical: pulling the DC plug without holding the release button down breaks or loses the actuator pin, and Ford swaps only the lock actuator. Range, low, high and intermittent faults are P0D9F to P0DA2.
c: Actuator pin broken or missing after the plug was pulled while latched (Ford)
Open or shorted feedback wire between lock actuator and control module
Corroded or loose connector at the lock actuator
Evaluation input of the controlling module defective
s: DC fast charging inoperative
Charger Service Required message in the cluster (Ford)
Locking pin visibly damaged or absent at the inlet

P0D9F.t: Battery Charger A Coupler Lock Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0D9F.d: P0D9F covers a lock position signal that is electrically in range but does not fit the situation: the pin is reported in a position the actuator was not told to reach, or it gets there too late. The sensing principle in GM patent US8936482B2 works on pin travel, so a jammed or worn mechanism shows up here as well as a drifting sensor. Mercedes names the code for the third-generation smart electric drive with 22 kW charger built before 25 March 2013. Bulletin LI54.10-P-067823 lists P0D9F00 (position sensor of the cable lock faulty) among sporadic interlock faults: the car will not start and shows a plugged-in cable, or the battery will not charge. The cause was loose low-voltage contacts on the charger; technicians gently move each plug and wait up to 5 s for charging to begin. Hard circuit faults are P0D9E, P0DA0 and P0DA1.
c: Loose low-voltage contacts at the 22 kW on-board charger (smart)
Lock mechanism sluggish from ice, dirt or a worn gear train
Position sensor in the actuator drifting or misaligned
s: Vehicle will not start and reports a connected charging cable (smart)
High-voltage battery does not charge
Fault may appear only at the start or end of charging, with cold or warm parts

P0DA0.t: Battery Charger A Coupler Lock Position Sensor Circuit Low
P0DA0.d: P0DA0 means the lock position feedback sits at the bottom of its range, typically from a signal wire shorted to ground. Mitsubishi documents it for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: with the IGCT supply on, the PHEV-ECU detects a low input from the lock position reading. The sensor sits in the charge connector lock actuator, part of the inlet harness; the signal line should carry battery voltage at the unplugged connector, and the sensor should measure 16.8 kΩ, give or take 0.84 kΩ. Depending on the result, technicians repair the line, replace the inlet harness or replace the PHEV-ECU. Ford names P0DA0:00 in TSBs 22-2355 and 23-2014 for its 2021 to 2023 electric models, alongside P0D9E, after a broken lock pin; there only the actuator is replaced. The opposite fault is P0DA1.
c: Lock position signal line shorted to ground (Mitsubishi)
Actuator pin broken after the plug was pulled while latched (Ford)
Position sensor in the inlet harness outside its resistance specification
s: DC fast charging not possible
Charger Service Required message (Ford)
Plug is not latched or charging ends right after start

P0DA1.t: Battery Charger A Coupler Lock Position Sensor Circuit High
P0DA1.d: P0DA1 is the high-side fault of the lock position feedback: the signal stays near its upper limit, which points to an open circuit somewhere in the sensor loop rather than a grounded wire. In the 2023 Outlander PHEV, Mitsubishi sets it in the PHEV-ECU when the supply is on and a high input from the lock position reading is seen. The test steps reveal the likely weak spots: terminal 1 of the lock actuator connector must have a ground path of no more than 2 Ω, terminal 2 must show battery voltage, the signal line to the PHEV-ECU must be intact, and the sensor in the inlet harness must read 16.8 kΩ within 5 percent. A failed ground, a broken wire or an open sensor therefore all end here. Mitsubishi's warning lamp table does not list it. The low counterpart is P0DA0.
c: Ground connection of the lock actuator connector interrupted
Open signal line between inlet harness and PHEV-ECU
Position sensor in the inlet harness open or far above 16.8 kOhm
s: Charging plug lock not confirmed, DC charging refused
Charging system message, no MIL documented

P0DA2.t: Battery Charger A Coupler Lock Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0DA2.d: P0DA2 is stored when the lock position feedback flickers or drops out briefly, while it never sits at one limit long enough for the low or high verdict. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The sibling procedures from Mitsubishi for the 2023 Outlander PHEV show where to look: the sensor lives in the lock actuator of the inlet harness, gets its supply and ground through a connector at the inlet, and Mitsubishi explicitly allows for intermittent faults when a code does not return after clearing. GM patent US8936482B2 explains why the reading matters: the module judges the lock state from how far the pin has travelled, so a jumping signal can make a latched plug look unlocked. CARB demands circuit checks on such inputs. Expect fast charging that aborts at random. Steady faults are P0D9E to P0DA1.
c: Loose or corroded contact at the lock actuator connector
Inlet harness chafed where it moves with the charge port flap or body
Worn lock mechanism letting the pin rattle near a switching point
s: DC fast charging aborts at random
Lock status message that appears and clears again

P0DA3.t: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor A Circuit
P0DA3.d: The inverter of drive motor B, usually the rear electric motor in all-wheel-drive hybrids, measures its own DC link voltage; sensor A delivers that value to the motor controller. P0DA3 is the general circuit fault for this channel, with no finer verdict such as low or high. No manufacturer documents P0DA3 publicly. Mitsubishi watches the same sensor in the rear motor unit of the Outlander PHEV but reports it with the specific codes P0DA5 and P0DA6, whose diagnosis starts with the high-voltage fuse, cabling and battery terminals before the motor control unit is replaced. Denso describes in patent US9819293B2 how the input voltage reading of an inverter is judged against a battery reading or an estimate from the control loop. Without a valid voltage the rear drive is usually limited or switched off. Specific faults are P0DA4 to P0DA7.
c: Voltage sensing circuit inside the rear motor control unit defective
Loose high-voltage cable or terminal at the rear inverter
Low-voltage connector or harness to the inverter controller faulty
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Rear electric drive reduced or unavailable
Reduced power or no READY state

P0DA4.t: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0DA4.d: P0DA4 flags a rear inverter voltage that is electrically valid but disagrees with the other voltage readings on the same high-voltage bus. Mitsubishi spells out the check for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: once the power drive unit has at least 8 V, voltage control is off, CAN is healthy and the rear value is available, all three comparisons must fail together, namely capacitor 2 main, capacitor 2 sub and capacitor 1 each differing from the rear inverter reading by at least 100 V, held 0.2 s or longer. Because a single deviating reading is not enough, the rear sensor itself is the prime suspect. The manual first clears higher-priority codes and the rear unit's P0C7A, P0DA5, P0DA6 and P30D1, then replaces the power drive unit. The warning light and MIL come on. The battery-side correlation code is P0DA9.
c: Rear inverter voltage sensing drifts against the other bus readings
Power drive unit faulty (Mitsubishi final repair step)
Underlying fault in the rear motor control unit (P0C7A, P0DA5, P0DA6, P30D1)
s: Plug-in hybrid system warning and MIL on
Rear motor power limited
Code returns only after the OBD-II drive cycle

P0DA5.t: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor A Circuit Low
P0DA5.d: P0DA5 reports that the rear inverter voltage signal sits at the bottom of its range, the classic result of an open circuit, a short to ground or no high voltage arriving at all. Mitsubishi sets it in the rear motor control unit of the 2018 Outlander PHEV when, with the propulsion system active, the sensor output stays below 0.5 V, roughly 10 V on the bus, for 0.3 s. If the front unit and the generator unit report undervoltage too (P1A1B, P104D), the manual inspects the high-voltage fuse, cabling, battery section voltages and bus bars; otherwise it checks the torque of the rear battery cable at both ends before replacing the rear unit. A loose cable can therefore mimic a sensor fault. The 2023 model lists the code as a minimum range check with MIL. The high side is P0DA6.
c: Rear high-voltage battery cable (P and N lines) loose or damaged
High-voltage fuse not seated or loose bus bar in the battery
Sensing circuit in the rear motor control unit failed
Fault inside the traction battery pack
s: MIL and plug-in hybrid warning on
Rear motor drive switched off
Possible no-READY condition if other units also lose voltage

P0DA6.t: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor A Circuit High
P0DA6.d: P0DA6 is the upper-limit fault of the rear inverter voltage signal: the reading sticks near the top, as with a short to the sensor supply, or the bus really is overvolted. Mitsubishi checks it in the rear motor control unit of the 2018 Outlander PHEV whenever that unit is powered with 8 to 16 V; a sensor output above 4.7 V, standing for about 440 V, held for 0.3 s sets the code. The manual then looks at the other units: only if the front unit also stores P0D30 and the generator unit P1078 does it go on to the high-voltage fuse and cabling, because a shared high reading points to the battery or HV circuit. If the rear unit is alone, it is replaced straight away. The 2023 model lists the code as a maximum range check with MIL. True overvoltage at the rear inverter has its own code, P0C7A.
c: Rear motor control unit sensing faulty when no other unit reports high voltage (Mitsubishi)
Fault in the high-voltage circuit or battery when front and generator units also report high
Signal shorted to the sensor supply inside the inverter
s: MIL and plug-in hybrid warning on
Rear motor drive switched off, reduced power

P0DA7.t: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0DA7.d: P0DA7 is meant for a rear inverter voltage reading that jitters or drops out briefly without staying out of range long enough for P0DA5 or P0DA6. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The neighbouring Mitsubishi checks give the time scale: the rear motor unit of the Outlander PHEV needs 0.3 s outside its window for the low or high fault, and the 2023 plausibility test waits 0.2 s, so faster glitches call for a separate detector. Denso's patent US9819293B2 compares the measured inverter input voltage with a value estimated from the motor control loop, an approach that also exposes an unsteady sensor. Likely triggers are a loose low-voltage plug at the inverter, a high-voltage terminal with poor contact, or sensing electronics that fail with heat. The hybrid warning may come and go.
c: Low-voltage connector at the rear inverter with intermittent contact
High-voltage terminal at the rear inverter not tightened properly
Voltage sensing electronics failing with temperature or vibration
s: Hybrid warning that appears and clears
Brief loss of rear drive power

P0DA8.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage/Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Correlation
P0DA8.d: P0DA8 compares the traction battery voltage with the voltage measured at the inverter of drive motor A; both should match closely once the contactors are closed. Denso cites earlier diagnostics that blame a voltage sensor when the two differ by more than a set amount (US9819293B2). Honda describes it as a voltage fault of its MPI inverter module: recall 15-057 for the 2014–15 Accord Hybrid ties it to the battery cell voltage sensor misreading inverter noise, with an electric-only emergency mode capped near 40 mph, and was a vehicle emissions recall in California. Warranty extensions 20-030 and 20-021 for Civic Hybrid 2012–15 and ILX Hybrid 2013 list it among codes from a cracked solder joint in the inverter, which is replaced. Ford logs P0DA8 on 2021–22 Mach-E with a flat 12 V battery and replaces the HV junction box.
c: Cracked solder joint in the motor power inverter (Honda Civic/ILX Hybrid)
Battery cell voltage sensor software misreading inverter noise (Honda Accord Hybrid recall)
High-voltage battery junction box faulty (Ford Mach-E)
Battery-side or inverter-side voltage sensor drifting
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Fail-safe electric mode with strongly limited speed (Honda)
Discharged 12 V battery (Ford Mach-E)

P0DA9.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage/Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Correlation
P0DA9.d: P0DA9 is the motor B counterpart of P0DA8: the controller compares traction battery voltage with the voltage seen at the inverter of drive motor B, typically the rear motor, and logs the code when the two drift apart with the contactors closed. No manufacturer documents P0DA9 publicly. Denso describes the underlying test, a battery sensor and an inverter sensor checked against a permitted difference, in the background of patent US9819293B2. Mitsubishi runs a closely related check on the 2023 Outlander PHEV but compares the rear inverter with the capacitor voltages of its power electronics and reports it as P0DA4 at 100 V for 0.2 s. A mismatch may come from either sensor, from a contactor or cable with high resistance, or from the inverter itself. CARB requires hybrid systems to monitor electric motor performance.
c: Voltage sensing in the motor B inverter drifting
Battery pack voltage measurement in the battery management faulty
High resistance in a contactor, fuse or cable between battery and rear inverter
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Rear electric drive limited or disabled

P0DAA.d: P0DAA reports that the resistance between the charging-side HV bus and chassis ground has fallen too low, so the charging path or the battery is no longer safely insulated. GM documents the logic for the 2014 Chevrolet Volt and Cadillac ELR in the HPC2 (VICM): in charge-only mode the active isolation resistance is measured, at most once per wake-up; below 325 kOhm, or 400 kOhm while the code is active, for 10 s, and with five of the last ten results low, the code sets as Type A with MIL after one trip. GM preliminary information PIC5920 links it to vehicles that will not charge and points to coolant leaking into the battery pack or insulation loss in the cells; technicians check the pack drain plug and reprogram HPCM2 and BECM, and call support if isolation stays under 275 kOhm. GM used P0AA6 for this on 2011–13 Volts.
c: Coolant leaking into the battery pack (GM)
Insulation loss within battery cells or sections (GM)
Damaged insulation in the on-board charger or charging cables
s: Vehicle will not charge
MIL on (GM Type A)
Low coolant level in the battery coolant reservoir

P0DAB.d: P0DAB is the overall verdict on cell balancing: the battery controller sees that bleeding charge off the fuller cells no longer brings the pack back into line, so the spread between cells stays too wide. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15.2.3) requires hybrids to check exactly this. Mazda sets it on the 48 V M Hybrid Boost of the CX-90 and CX-70 (MHB module: P0DAB:17; SGC2/DMCM: P0DAB:00) with the check engine light; if it returns at once after clearing, the 48 V battery is replaced, otherwise program MSP66 reflashes. Jeep lists P0DAB-00 with MIL for Wrangler 4xe and Grand Cherokee 4xe and cures it with BPCM software. Faults of a single balancing circuit carry their own codes from P0DAC on.
c: Battery controller software that judges balancing too strictly (FCA BPCM and Mazda MSP66 reflash)
Cells aged unevenly so the spread grows faster than balancing can correct it
Internal fault in the battery assembly (Mazda 48 V battery replaced when the code returns at once)
One or more balancing switches or resistors no longer working
s: Check engine light and hybrid system warning in the cluster
Mild hybrid assist, start-stop and regeneration switched off (engine-only operation on Mazda)
Reduced electric range or usable battery capacity

P0DAC.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit A
P0DAC.d: P0DAC reports an electrical fault in balancing circuit A, meaning the wiring, switch or monitoring chip behind it, not a balancing result. Audi uses it on the e-tron GT (2022-2026) in battery management address 008C and spells it out as an electrical fault of cell controller 1. Bulletin 2074056 explains that a short power interruption while the 12 V battery is reconnected can log this entry; the guided fault finding then proposes new HV modules, which Audi calls unnecessary and resets remotely. A later reporting case (2078729) pairs P0DAC00 with the red onboard supply lamp and a car that will not start. Audi already listed P0DAC00 for the 2016 A3 e-tron (bulletin 2046556), where new software cured it. Stuck states and implausible results are P0DAD to P0DAF.
c: Brief 12 V supply interruption, e.g. while reconnecting the 12 V battery (Audi e-tron GT)
Defective cell monitoring controller or balancing switch of circuit A
Loose or corroded sense/balancing lead connector at the module
s: Battery management warning or red onboard supply lamp
Vehicle may refuse to start or enter drive readiness
Diagnostic tester proposes replacing HV battery modules

P0DAD.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit A Stuck On
P0DAD.d: P0DAD means balancing circuit A keeps draining its cells although the controller has not asked for it: the bleed switch is stuck closed and the resistor keeps pulling those cells down. Ford uses the code in the BECM of its hybrids; the 2019 OBD summary gives each of 14 circuits six cells and, at key-on with the contactors still open, rates a circuit faulty when one of its cells departs from the mean for 0.1 s by over 75 mV. Toshiba's patent US20130026994A1 detects such a shorted balancing switch with a comparator. Left alone, the affected cells sink below the rest, particularly while the car is parked, and the usable pack window shrinks. Which cells form group A is up to the maker.
c: Balancing transistor of circuit A shorted (fails closed)
Monitoring chip or its drive output keeps the switch enabled
Controller software leaving a balancing request active
s: Hybrid or EV battery warning with the MIL
Cells of one group noticeably lower after the car has been parked
Range or electric assistance decreasing over days

P0DAE.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit A Stuck Off
P0DAE.d: With P0DAE the controller has commanded balancing on circuit A, yet nothing happens: the switch stays open or the bleed resistor is broken, so the targeted cells keep their charge. Ford documents the code for its hybrid BECM; in the 2014 OBD summary the verdict rests on a 100 ms check at power-up with open contactors, in which one cell of the six-cell group lying beyond 75 mV from the average on two successive starts is enough. For a related code, GM checks on eAssist with the ignition off that the cell moves by more than 0.1 V once the resistor is switched in. The penalty is slow: the high cells limit charging, the pack loses usable capacity and the overall verdict P0DAB may follow.
c: Bleed resistor of circuit A open or its solder joint cracked
Broken balancing/sense lead or terminal between module and cells
s: MIL and battery system warning
Charging ends early because individual cells reach full first
Growing cell voltage spread in the live data

P0DAF.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit A Range/Performance
P0DAF.d: P0DAF is a plausibility code: circuit A switches and is electrically intact, but the effect on the cell voltages does not match what the controller expects. FCA is the visible user. Ram 1500 pickups with the 48 V eTorque system (2019-2024, bulletin 08-030-24 and its yearly versions) list P0DAF among the MIL codes fixed by new BPCM software. The 2026 Jeep Cherokee 1.6 hybrid (bulletin 08-186-26) logs P0DAF-00 together with low cell voltage P0DE6; the car may not start or switch off, and the update improves the robustness of the P0DAF check. So a software update is the first step before touching hardware. Pure circuit faults are P0DAC, stuck states P0DAD and P0DAE.
c: Battery pack control module software with an oversensitive check (FCA bulletins 08-030-24, 08-186-26)
Weak or deeply discharged cells that respond differently to balancing, e.g. after cold cranking
Bleed resistor or switch of circuit A with changed resistance
s: MIL on, often together with other battery codes
Vehicle may not start or cannot be switched off (Jeep Cherokee hybrid)
Reduced mild hybrid assistance

P0DB0.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit B
P0DB0.d: P0DB0 flags an electrical defect in the second balancing circuit, B. The battery controller finds an open, short or implausible voltage on the switch, resistor or lead serving that cell group, independent of whether balancing would be needed right now. One way to test this hardware is shown in LG Chem's patent US20110285539A1: a floating capacitor is charged to the cell voltage and then drained via the bleed path, and a high leftover voltage marks the circuit as faulty. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requires functional monitoring of these parts on hybrids. Audi lists P0DB000 in bulletin 2046556, written for the 2016 A3 e-tron, next to the other circuit codes; there it came with intermittent charging refusal and was fixed by software for J840 and JX1.
c: Damaged balancing/sense lead or connector of cell group B
Cell monitoring chip or controller of group B defective
Short 12 V supply dropout during service work
s: Battery system warning and MIL
Electric drive or assistance possibly limited

P0DB1.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit B Stuck On
P0DB1.d: P0DB1: in circuit B the bleed path stays closed even after the controller withdrew the command. The cells of group B are drained without pause, so their voltage falls behind the others, worst during long standstill. Detection usually compares commanded and reported switch state; GM's eAssist logic for a related code needs 7 failed of 10 samples before a Type B entry. Toshiba describes a comparator check that spots a shorted balancing switch while it should be off. Ford names P0DB1 for its hybrid BECM; the 2015 OBD summary flags it when, at start-up with open contactors, one of the six cells served by circuit B differs from the pack mean by more than 75 mV. The electrical fault of the same circuit is P0DB0, the opposite stuck state P0DB2.
c: Shorted balancing transistor in circuit B
Drive output of the monitoring chip stuck active
Moisture or contamination on the module board creating a leakage path
s: MIL with battery warning
Group B cells clearly low after parking
Usable charge and range shrinking

P0DB2.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit B Stuck Off
P0DB2.d: Stuck off on circuit B (P0DB2) is the passive failure: the command arrives, but the bleed resistor of that group carries no current, so its high cells are never trimmed. LG Chem's patent EP2730933A1 tests for this by switching the balancing circuit on and off and watching how the voltage across a diagnosis resistor reacts; no change means a dead circuit. The result builds up over many charges: cells of group B reach the upper limit first and end charging early, while the rest stay below. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 counts this as a balancing malfunction. Ford lists P0DB2 in its 2016 hybrid OBD summary: the BECM bleeds only the highest cells down to the others and judges each six-cell circuit once per power-up against a 75 mV limit. Compare P0DB1 for the opposite fault.
c: Bleed resistor of group B burnt open
Balancing transistor of circuit B no longer switching
Open terminal or cell tap connection in group B
s: MIL and battery warning
Charging stops before the expected state of charge
High cell voltages in group B in live data

P0DB3.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit B Range/Performance
P0DB3.d: P0DB3 concerns how well circuit B works rather than whether it switches. The controller balances group B for a set time and then checks the outcome; if the cells moved too little, too much or in an unexpected direction, the result is called implausible. The LaunchPoint patent US8598840B2 describes this kind of check: voltages are read during a planned balancing period, and a side that fails to produce the expected effect is declared faulty and disabled. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 sets the rule that balancing must keep the intended cell voltages. Volvo uses P0DB3: on the SPA Twin Engine plug-ins (XC90, XC60, S90, V90, 2016-2019) the BECM logs P0DB300 as intermittent, and Technical Journal 33931 blames BECM software that also distorted the electric range display; updating it is the fix.
c: Controller software with too narrow expectations (cf. FCA updates for P0DAF)
Aged or high-resistance cell in group B reacting atypically
Bleed resistor value drifted so balancing current is wrong
s: MIL, sometimes without any noticeable drivability change
Cell spread in group B not shrinking after charging

P0DB4.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit C
P0DB4.d: P0DB4 belongs to the third balancing channel, C, and points to its hardware: an interrupted or shorted lead, a failed switch or a monitoring chip reporting nonsense for that cell group. A common test method sits in LG Chem's EP2730933A1, where a diagnosis resistor between cell and balancing circuit lets the controller see a defined voltage step each time the circuit is toggled; a missing or wrong step betrays the fault. Since sense and balancing leads often share pins, a sense-lead problem can show up here as well. For hybrids, CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 makes watching these parts mandatory. Audi records P0DB400 on the 2016 A3 e-tron; bulletin 93 17 04 links it to software that began CAN traffic late, so a reflash comes before any hardware work.
c: Fault in a lead shared by voltage sensing and balancing in group C
Cell monitoring chip of group C defective
Corroded module connector after water ingress
s: MIL with battery or hybrid warning
Further cell voltage codes stored alongside
Electric operation possibly reduced

P0DB5.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit C Stuck On
P0DB5.d: Circuit C stuck on (P0DB5) means the cells of group C bleed energy permanently, also with the car switched off. Designers guard against exactly this: the LaunchPoint patent US8598840B2 lets every balance enable expire on a timer unless the central controller renews it, so a lost command cannot leave a switch on. When the hardware itself fails closed, that guard does not help and the controller can only spot the falling voltage or the mismatch between command and switch state. Over a few days the group C cells can drop far enough to trigger low cell voltage codes. Ford's 2017 hybrid OBD summary tests circuit C in a 100 ms window each time the car wakes, contactors still open, and sets P0DB5 if one of its six cells is more than 75 mV off the average.
c: Balancing transistor in circuit C failed closed
Enable or watchdog logic of the module not releasing the switch
Leakage path on the module board
s: MIL with battery warning, often after standing
Low cell voltage codes in group C as a follow-up
Electric range dropping

P0DB6.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit C Stuck Off
P0DB6.d: P0DB6 says that the bleed function of group C does not respond: commanded on, circuit C stays dead. In LG Chem's US20110285539A1 such a case shows up because a test capacitor charged to cell voltage is not emptied through the balancing path and keeps a high residual voltage. Typical culprits are an open resistor, a transistor that no longer conducts or a broken cell tap. While driving there is little to feel; the effect is that group C cannot be trimmed, so the strongest cell there caps every full charge. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 demands detection of this. Ford documents P0DB6 in the 2018 OBD summary for its hybrids, one of fourteen balancing circuits there; a 75 mV spread inside the six-cell group, seen on two consecutive power cycles before the contactors close, triggers it.
c: Bleed resistor of circuit C open
Balancing transistor of circuit C not conducting
Broken cell tap or weld in group C
s: MIL with battery warning
Shorter charging sessions and lower usable capacity

P0DB7.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit C Range/Performance
P0DB7.d: P0DB7 covers a circuit C that works electrically but whose outcome does not add up. A typical trigger is a cell in group C that needs trimming far more often or far less often than its neighbours. Southwest Electronic Energy's patent US9097774B2 counts balancing events per cell and flags one whose count runs away, because that hints at an internal short. So this code can point at the cells as well as at the circuit. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requires the system to keep the cell voltages it aims for. Volvo lists P0DB700 as an intermittent BECM fault on its 2016-2019 SPA plug-in hybrids; Technical Journal 33931.6.0 ties it, combined with charging voltage or communication codes, to a BECM software product.
c: Cell in group C with rising self-discharge or an internal short
Controller software with unsuitable plausibility limits
Bleed resistor of circuit C out of tolerance
s: MIL, often with no other immediate effect
One cell in group C repeatedly lower than the rest

P0DB8.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit D
P0DB8.d: P0DB8 is the circuit code for balancing channel D. Here the controller sees a hardware problem: the switch, resistor or cell tap of group D reports a state that cannot be valid, typically an open lead or a short to a neighbouring line. Toshiba's patent US20130026994A1 shows how a monitoring chip can tell which balancing terminal is open and pass that to the main controller, which then decides whether the module or the cell unit must be repaired. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 calls for this monitoring on hybrids. Audi's bulletin 2046556 names P0DB800 for the 2016 A3 e-tron, where the car could also wrongly report a plugged-in charger; new software cured it.
c: Open balancing terminal or lead in group D
Monitoring chip of group D defective
s: MIL and battery system message
Possible limitation of electric power

P0DB9.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit D Stuck On
P0DB9.d: A stuck-on circuit D (P0DB9) drains group D continuously. The usual check is simple: does the switch state reported back equal the state the controller asked for? GM applies this on the eAssist battery for a related code, sampling every 200 ms and logging a Type B fault after 7 mismatches in 10. Here the reported state stays on while the command says off. Besides the voltage loss, the bleed resistor keeps warming its part of the module, which can upset temperature readings nearby. On Ford hybrids the code is real: the 2019 OBD summary checks circuit D for 0.1 s at each start, before the high voltage contactors close, against a 75 mV deviation of any of its six cells from the average. The broken-circuit case is P0DB8, the inactive case P0DBA.
c: Balancing transistor of circuit D shorted
Status feedback of the module wrong, switch actually fine
Drive output of the monitoring chip stuck on
s: MIL with battery warning
Group D cells and their local temperature deviating
Loss of charge while parked

P0DBA.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit D Stuck Off
P0DBA.d: P0DBA: circuit D refuses to bleed. Toshiba's patent US20130026994A1 lists an open balancing terminal as one of the faults a monitoring chip should report, and this is the typical root of a stuck-off result. Because no charge is taken away from the high cells in group D, the pack's top end is governed by them; the charger and the controller stop earlier and the displayed range creeps down. The fault rarely causes a sudden breakdown. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requires balancing to stay functional. Ford uses P0DBA in its hybrid BECM (OBD summary 2015); the stuck-off decision comes from comparing the six cells of circuit D with the pack average at power-up, 75 mV being the limit. The always-on opposite is P0DB9, the overall verdict P0DAB.
c: Open balancing terminal or cell tap in group D
Bleed resistor of circuit D open
Balancing transistor of circuit D failed open
s: MIL and battery warning
Range slowly decreasing, charging finishing early

P0DBB.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit D Range/Performance
P0DBB.d: For P0DBB the controller judges the effect of balancing in circuit D as implausible. A clear reference is GM's eAssist key-off test for a related code: engaging the bleed load has to pull the cell at least 0.1 V away from its rest value. A result outside the expected window, even with intact wiring, is what a performance code captures. Passive balancing turns excess charge into heat, as the Wikipedia article on battery balancing outlines, so a weak resistor or a cell with changed internal resistance shifts the outcome. Volvo documents P0DBB00 for the BECM of its SPA Twin Engine models; Technical Journal 33931.3.0 traces it to software from week 18w17 and prescribes improved BECM software.
c: Cell in group D with changed internal resistance or capacity
Plausibility limits in the controller software too tight
Bleed resistor of circuit D drifted
s: MIL without obvious driving symptoms
Cell spread in group D persisting after long charging

P0DBC.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit E
P0DBC.d: P0DBC is set for an electrical fault in the fifth balancing channel, E: the controller cannot trust the path through which group E would be bled, because a lead, switch or resistor reads open, shorted or out of range. The floating-capacitor method in LG Chem's US20110285539A1 is one way to test that path without loading the cells: charge, discharge through the balancing circuit, then compare the residual voltage with a limit. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requires the balancing parts of a hybrid to be monitored. In bulletin 93 17 04 from Audi, covering the A3 e-tron of model year 2016, P0DBC00 appears with the circuit codes of A to H; late CAN start-up was the cause, removed by software for the battery controller at address 008C.
c: Open or shorted balancing lead in group E
Monitoring chip responsible for group E faulty
Module connector of group E loose or corroded
s: MIL and battery warning
Electric drive possibly restricted

P0DBD.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit E Stuck On
P0DBD.d: With P0DBD the controller finds circuit E active when it should be idle. LG Chem's EP2730933A1 offers a way to see it: with the balancing circuit commanded off, the voltage across the diagnosis resistor should match the idle pattern; if it looks like the active pattern, current is still flowing. Group E then loses charge around the clock and drifts below the others, which in time can block charging or limit power because the lowest cell sets the lower limit. A shorted transistor is the classic cause. Ford's hybrid BECM sets P0DBD as well; the 2017 OBD summary describes a 100 ms start-up test with open contactors in which any cell of circuit E deviating more than 75 mV from the mean marks the circuit. The circuit fault is P0DBC, the inactive case P0DBE.
c: Balancing transistor of circuit E shorted
Drive line of the switch held active by the monitoring chip
Leakage on the module board after moisture
s: MIL with battery warning
Power reduced as group E cells drop
Charge loss after a few days parked

P0DBE.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit E Stuck Off
P0DBE.d: P0DBE means circuit E does nothing when told to bleed. The LaunchPoint patent US8598840B2 describes reading the cells while a planned bleed phase is running and treating a balancing side that shows no effect as faulted; this is the logic behind a stuck-off verdict. That patent also keeps a second balancing path in reserve, a reminder that some designs can carry on with reduced function. For the driver the code is mostly a long-term matter: group E stays high, charging ends sooner and capacity seems to fade. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 asks for detection of such faults. Ford has carried P0DBE since its 2014 hybrid OBD summary, where a deviation above 75 mV within the six-cell circuit E must recur on two consecutive power-ups.
c: Bleed resistor of circuit E open
Balancing transistor of circuit E does not turn on
Enable signal for group E not reaching the module
s: MIL and battery warning
Apparent loss of capacity over weeks

P0DBF.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit E Range/Performance
P0DBF.d: P0DBF tells that balancing in circuit E produces results the controller cannot explain, though the circuit switches. One reason can be a cell that keeps needing correction: the Southwest Electronic Energy patent US9097774B2 tracks how often each cell gets balanced and treats an outlier as a warning of internal shorting, well before overheating. A drifting bleed resistor or too tight software limits can also trigger it; FCA's P0DAF updates for circuit A show the software route. Under CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 the target cell voltages must be maintained. Volvo's XC90, XC60, S90 and V90 Twin Engine (2016-2019) store P0DBF00 as intermittent, and the TJ 33931 series cures it with new BECM software, sometimes followed by a 12 V reset. Measure cell voltages and self-discharge before replacing modules.
c: Cell in group E with increased self-discharge
Software limits for the balancing check too narrow
Bleed resistor of circuit E out of tolerance
s: MIL, usually without immediate drivability change
Recurring deviation of a single cell in group E

P0DC0.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit F
P0DC0.d: P0DC0 marks an electrical fault in balancing circuit F, the sixth cell group whose bleed path the battery controller can switch. Audi lists P0DC000 for the 2016 A3 e-tron in bulletin 93 17 04 (2046556/1), together with the circuit codes for groups A to H and B200000. Owners noticed that charging failed now and then or that the car claimed a charger was plugged in when none was. Audi traced this to software that started CAN communication too late; reflashing the high voltage battery controller J840 (address 008C) and the power electronics JX1 (00C6) cured it. On this car the entry therefore describes a timing problem rather than burnt parts. California's OBD rule (13 CCR 1968.2) obliges hybrids to supervise balancing. Stuck states and implausible results of group F use P0DC1 to P0DC3.
c: Battery controller software that starts CAN communication too late (Audi A3 e-tron, J840/JX1 update)
Open or chafed balancing/sense lead of cell group F
Defective cell monitoring chip serving group F
s: Charging fails intermittently
Cluster shows a connected charger although no cable is plugged in
Several balancing circuit codes stored at the same time

P0DC1.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit F Stuck On
P0DC1.d: P0DC1 says that the bleed path of cell group F appears to stay engaged. Ford lists it for the BECM of its full and plug-in hybrids in the OBD system summaries of model years 2014 to 2019. The battery there is split into fourteen balancing circuits, A to N, each looking after six cells. The check runs for 100 ms at every power-up while the main contactors are still open, so no load current blurs the readings: if any of the six cells in a circuit strays more than 75 mV from the mean of all cell voltages (in the 2019 summary for 0.1 s), the circuit is judged stuck. A group drained by a closed switch during standstill shows up exactly this way. Paragraph (e)(15.2.3) of the CARB regulation explicitly allows such switch-response monitoring. Opposite case: P0DC2.
c: Bleed transistor of group F shorted, so the resistor stays connected
Monitoring chip output keeps the switch of circuit F enabled
A cell of group F with high self-discharge mimicking a drained group
s: Check engine light with hybrid battery warning after a cold start
Cells of group F clearly below the pack average after standstill
Reduced electric range or assistance

P0DC2.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit F Stuck Off
P0DC2.d: With P0DC2 the controller concludes that circuit F does not bleed when asked to, so the fullest cells of group F are never trimmed. Ford's 2014 hybrid OBD summary applies the same 75 mV deviation test over the six cells of each circuit as for the stuck-on code, but the 2014 to 2018 versions want the deviation seen at two power-ups in a row, before the contactors close. The practical cost lies in charging: the group that cannot shed charge reaches its upper limit first and stops the charge for the whole pack. An Intersil (now Renesas) application note estimates that lithium cells 150 mV apart at full charge can lose up to a quarter of usable pack capacity. CARB's section 1968.2 counts the missing response as a malfunction. The always-on opposite is P0DC1.
c: Bleed resistor of group F burnt open
Bleed transistor of circuit F no longer conducting
Loose cell tap or connector pin on the balancing lead
s: Charging ends earlier than usual, displayed full charge gives less range
Cells of group F remain highest after charging
Check engine light, usually without noticeable driving change

P0DC3.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit F Range/Performance
P0DC3.d: P0DC3 is the plausibility code for balancing circuit F, and Volvo is a documented user. On the SPA Twin Engine plug-in hybrids (XC90, XC60, S90, V90, model years 2016-2019) the BECM stores P0DC300 as an intermittent fault, listed alongside the range/performance codes of circuits A to E. Technical Journal 33931.3.0 of 2018 links them to BECM software released in week 18w17, which could make the displayed electric range fluctuate or drop unreasonably; improved software was the remedy. The later version 33931.6.0 adds a software product and sometimes a 12 V reset, about 20 minutes disconnected. Before suspecting cells, check the software level. Pure circuit faults of group F are P0DC0, stuck states P0DC1 and P0DC2.
c: BECM software version with faulty balancing evaluation (Volvo TJ 33931)
Cells of group F with changed capacity respond differently to bleeding
Bleed resistor value drifted so the balancing current is off target
s: Displayed electric range fluctuates or is unreasonably low
Combustion engine runs more often than expected in hybrid mode
Check engine light, fault often stored as intermittent

P0DC4.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit G
P0DC4.d: P0DC4 points to the hardware path of balancing circuit G: lead, switch, resistor or the chip that drives them. On the 2016 Audi A3 e-tron it appears as P0DC400 in bulletin 93 17 04, never alone but in a row with the circuit codes of groups A to H. When so many channels fail at once, a shared cause is far more likely than eight broken circuits; Audi blamed late CAN start-up and fixed it with software for J840 and JX1. A genuine defect looks different: Texas Instruments describes for its BQ79616-Q1 monitor a test that turns the bleed FET on and expects the voltage across it to fall below half the cell voltage; a channel that fails this is singled out. Supervision of these parts is mandated in CARB's OBD regulation, 13 CCR 1968.2. Siblings: P0DC5 to P0DC7.
c: Common software or communication cause when circuit codes A to H appear together (Audi A3 e-tron)
Bleed FET of channel G failing the on-state check
Corroded or loose connector on the cell harness of group G
s: Hybrid battery warning with check engine light
External charging refused now and then
Scan tool lists several circuit codes plus a control module fault

P0DC5.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit G Stuck On
P0DC5.d: P0DC5 reports that the bleed switch of group G seems to stay closed. Ford lists the code for the BECM of its 2018 hybrids and plug-ins; there, a sticking circuit is inferred at start-up, with contactors open, from any of its six cells straying more than 75 mV from the pack average. A more direct test can sit in the monitoring chip. Renesas patent US9735567B2 gives each balancing terminal a comparator plus a pull-up: with the switch commanded off, the measured cell voltage should come through, and a reading near zero reveals a switch stuck in conduction. Untreated, group G keeps losing charge while parked and can end up triggering low-cell warnings. CARB lets makers watch the switches instead of every cell voltage. Circuit fault: P0DC4, inactive: P0DC6.
c: Balancing switch of group G stuck in conduction
Enable signal from the controller or chip never withdrawn
Moisture or contamination forming a leakage path on the module board
s: Check engine light and hybrid battery warning
Low cell voltage codes may follow after longer parking
Electric range decreasing from day to day

P0DC6.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit G Stuck Off
P0DC6.d: P0DC6 is set when circuit G stays idle although balancing is requested, so group G cannot give up charge. Ford names the code in its 2015 hybrid OBD summary and decides it from the start-up voltage comparison of the six cells per circuit. Ford's own patent application US20130030617A1 shows why this matters during charging: a resistor placed across a nearly full cell routes some of the charging current past it, or the higher cells are bled down at the end and the pack is topped up again. With circuit G dead, neither route works, and the cells of G define when charging must stop. The driver sees a slowly shrinking electric range, not a breakdown. Detecting it is a CARB requirement for hybrids. Opposite: P0DC5.
c: Shunt resistor of group G open, no current can bypass the cells
Balancing switch of group G does not close on command
Pin backed out of the cell harness connector
s: Electric range shrinks gradually over weeks
Charging stops before the indicated target
Check engine light without immediate drivability change

P0DC7.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit G Range/Performance
P0DC7.d: P0DC7 means circuit G switches but its effect on the cells does not fit the controller's model. The code is not tied to passive bleeding. Ford's patent application US20120293129A1 describes active balancing, where charge taken from the highest cell is moved to weaker ones, for example by a switched capacitor or a flyback transformer, and the transfer time depends on the gap between highest and lowest cell. In such a design a weak converter or worn capacitor shows up as a correction that falls short, not as an open circuit. Public documentation of P0DC7 by a maker could not be found; Volvo's bulletins for the neighbouring P0DC3 point to software first. CARB wants the balancing system to keep the desired cell voltages. Electrical fault: P0DC4.
c: Controller software with too tight plausibility limits
Weak transfer stage in active balancing (capacitor or transformer aged)
Cells of group G aged so that they react differently to correction
s: Check engine light with hybrid system message
Cell spread in group G does not shrink after balancing
Usable battery capacity slightly reduced

P0DC8.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit H
P0DC8.d: P0DC8 covers an electrical fault of balancing circuit H. Audi's bulletin 93 17 04 for the 2016 A3 e-tron lists P0DC800 as the last of its circuit codes; no letter beyond H appears there, which suggests eight circuits in that pack. Since the fix was software that let CAN communication begin on time, the entry can also stem from the controller not hearing its cell electronics early enough. GM's eAssist table 13OBDG05C shows the same idea under its own codes: losing LIN contact with a balance processor (P1B34, P1B35) counts as a fault after 7 of 10 checks every 200 ms and is rated Type B. California makes this supervision mandatory for hybrid OBD. Stuck and plausibility faults of H use P0DC9 to P0DCB.
c: Cell electronics not answering in time after wake-up (Audi software fix)
Damaged internal bus or supply wiring to the monitoring board of group H
Open bleed path or lead in circuit H
s: Charging not possible at times
Hybrid battery warning and check engine light
Fault returns after clearing until software is updated

P0DC9.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit H Stuck On
P0DC9.d: P0DC9: the bleed path of group H keeps conducting. Ford lists the code for its 2016 hybrid and plug-in BECM, judged at start-up from the cell spread within the six-cell circuit. Besides draining charge, a switch that cannot open turns energy into heat around the clock. Monitoring chips are built to limit that heat: TI's BQ79616-Q1 pauses all balancing when sensors next to its internal bleed FETs exceed about 105 °C, or when a thermistor near the external resistors passes a set limit. A shorted FET ignores such a pause, so the hot spot persists. Expect group H to sit low after standstill. The CARB rule permits judging balancing by switch response. Circuit fault: P0DC8, inactive case: P0DCA.
c: Bleed FET of group H shorted and unaffected by thermal pause
Heat damage on the monitoring board around the bleed resistors of H
Chip logic keeping the balancing enable of channel H active
s: Check engine light and hybrid battery warning
Group H noticeably lower than the rest after parking
Locally raised temperature reading in the battery module

P0DCA.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit H Stuck Off
P0DCA.d: P0DCA flags circuit H as inactive: balancing was ordered, but group H keeps its charge. Ford includes the code in its 2017 hybrid OBD summary, again decided by the start-up comparison of six cells per circuit with the pack average. Not every pause is a fault, which makes this code tricky. TI's BQ79616-Q1 stops a channel when its timer runs out, when the cell drops below a programmable floor between 2.45 and 4 V, on an unmasked fault, or for a thermal pause. A controller has to separate such intended stops from a bleed path that never conducts, for instance an open resistor or broken tap. Over many charges the unbalanced group H caps the charge. Under 13 CCR 1968.2 this must be detected. Opposite: P0DC9.
c: Bleed resistor of group H open
Broken cell tap or weld on the balancing lead of H
Intended stop (timer, thermal pause) wrongly judged as no response by the software
s: Full charge reached earlier, with less range than before
Cells of group H stay at the top of the cell list
Check engine light

P0DCB.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit H Range/Performance
P0DCB.d: P0DCB is raised when circuit H works electrically but the result of a balancing run does not match the plan. Ford's patent US9145064B2 shows how such a plan can be made: from each cell's capacity surplus and the pack charge current the controller computes how long that cell's resistor must stay active during charging so that all cells reach the target together. If group H still stands apart when that time has passed, the outcome is implausible, whether because of a resistor that drifted, a cell whose capacity changed or wrong estimates. A public maker document for P0DCB was not found; Volvo cures the F counterpart P0DC3 with BECM software. The CARB requirement is that intended cell voltages be maintained. Circuit fault: P0DC8.
c: Wrong capacity or state-of-charge estimate for the cells of group H
Battery controller software (update first, as Volvo does for P0DC3)
Bleed resistor of H drifted from its nominal value
s: Check engine light, often only after charging sessions
Group H remains out of line after a full charge
Fluctuating range estimate

P0DCC.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit I
P0DCC.d: P0DCC concerns the hardware of balancing circuit I, the ninth group, so only packs split into at least nine balancing channels can raise it. No maker publishes this exact code: Ford's hybrid summaries assign letter I only to the stuck codes P0DCD and P0DCE, and Audi's A3 e-tron bulletin stops at H. How an electrical fault of such a channel can be caught is shown in Renesas patent US9735567B2: a pull-up resistor lifts the balancing terminal to cell potential when the switch fails to close, so commanding it on and still seeing the full cell voltage exposes an open path. Broken leads, corroded connectors or a faulty monitoring chip are the usual suspects. California's regulation demands monitoring of such parts on hybrids. Related: P0DCD to P0DCF.
c: Broken balancing or sense lead of group I
Corroded connector between cell group I and its monitoring board
Defective monitoring chip for channel I
s: Hybrid battery warning with check engine light
Electric drive or charging limited by the battery controller

P0DCD.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit I Stuck On
P0DCD.d: P0DCD tells that circuit I is drained although no balancing is wanted. In Ford's 2014 hybrid OBD summary the code belongs to the start-up check with open contactors; that early version only sets it after the 75 mV spread within the six-cell group has shown up on two consecutive power-ups. A diagnosis must also know when a switch is on deliberately. Samsung SDI's patent US11327122B2 turns balancing switches on in groups to warm the voltage monitoring chip when it is cold, and switches them off again as the chip warms up. Such intended activity must not count as stuck on; a switch that keeps conducting after every command to open does. Expect group I to lag after parking. CARB section (e)(15.2.3) accepts checks on the switches themselves. Inactive case: P0DCE.
c: Balancing switch of group I permanently conducting
Driver stage of the monitoring chip stuck active on channel I
Software leaving a deliberate switch activation (e.g. chip warming) active
s: Check engine light with hybrid battery warning at start-up
Group I lower than the rest after longer standstill
Shorter electric range

P0DCE.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit I Stuck Off
P0DCE.d: P0DCE means the bleed path of group I does not respond to a balancing request. Ford lists it in the 2019 OBD summary for its full and plug-in hybrids, where the BECM discharges only the highest cells to match the rest and runs this check for 100 ms at power-up before the contactors close. Because the code concerns a switch that never conducts, nothing happens suddenly while driving. The penalty grows from charge to charge: the Intersil application note AN141 explains that in a series string the unbalanced cells hit full charge before the others and the weakest cell then limits what the pack can deliver. For a plug-in that means less electric range. The fault has to be found under CARB's hybrid rules. The stuck-on opposite is P0DCD.
c: Open bleed resistor in circuit I
Balancing switch of group I that no longer closes
Cell tap of group I loose at the busbar
s: Electric range decreases over many charging cycles
Cells of group I highest at the end of charging
Check engine light without noticeable effect while driving

P0DCF.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit I Range/Performance
P0DCF.d: P0DCF closes the series for the ninth balancing group: circuit I is electrically intact, yet balancing does not bring its cells to where the controller intended. No maker publishes this code. Ford's hybrid OBD summaries cover letter I only with the stuck codes P0DCD and P0DCE. A Ford patent, US20130030617A1, describes a target-based approach: while the pack is being charged for a set period, selected cells feed a load so that every cell ends up at or above a planned energy level. If group I misses that level when the period ends, the verdict is implausible operation rather than a dead switch. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requires hybrids to detect when desired cell voltages can no longer be held. Range or capacity may shrink gradually.
c: Cells of group I aged differently, so the planned balancing time no longer fits
Battery controller calibration with an unsuitable target or time window
Bleed resistor of circuit I off its nominal value, giving too little current
s: Check engine light, typically noticed after charging
Group I stays apart from the other cells after a full charge
Slowly shrinking electric range

P0DD0.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit J
P0DD0.d: P0DD0 reports an electrical fault in balancing circuit J, the tenth group. Only packs split into ten or more balancing channels can set it; Audi's A3 e-tron bulletin ends its circuit codes at H and Volvo's SPA Twin Engine journal at F, so those packs never reach J. No manufacturer documents P0DD0 publicly, and Ford uses J only for stuck faults. Toshiba patent US20130026994A1 describes one way to spot a broken link: a small current source parallel to the balancing switch lets the chip compare the sense pin with the balancing pin and flag an open terminal. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 asks for separate fault codes that point to the smallest replaceable part. Stuck and plausibility faults of J use P0DD1 to P0DD3.
c: Open balancing or sense terminal of group J (lead, crimp or weld)
Loose or corroded connector between group J and its monitoring board
Faulty monitoring chip channel serving circuit J
s: Hybrid battery warning with check engine light
Charging or electric drive limited by the battery controller

P0DD1.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit J Stuck On
P0DD1.d: P0DD1: group J's bleed path keeps drawing current after balancing should have ended. Ford's 2014 OBD summary for its hybrids and plug-ins assigns the code to the BECM, which checks at power-up, before the contactors close, for 100 ms: if one of the six cells in the circuit sits more than 75 mV away from the mean of all cells, and this repeats on two consecutive power cycles, the fault is stored. Ford's 2014 code list marks it as a MIL code. Designers guard against this failure: LaunchPoint patent US8598840B2 lets current flow through a bleed resistor only with an encoded, redundant enable that a timer cancels if it is not withdrawn. Group J will sag during standstill. Opposite case: P0DD2.
c: Balancing transistor of group J shorted and conducting permanently
Balancing enable for channel J not withdrawn by the monitoring electronics
Cell in group J with high self-discharge producing the same voltage pattern
s: Check engine light and hybrid battery warning after switching on
Group J clearly lower than the rest after parking
Shorter electric range

P0DD2.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit J Stuck Off
P0DD2.d: P0DD2 marks circuit J as unable to bleed: balancing is commanded, but the six cells of group J keep their charge. Ford lists the code in its 2015 hybrid OBD summary with the same power-up test as for the stuck-on case, run for 100 ms with the contactors still open, two consecutive power cycles and the 75 mV limit against the average cell voltage. GM's 2013 eAssist table documents a more direct test under its own code P1EAA: with the key off and the contactors open, a cell's balancing resistor is switched on and the cell voltage has to move by at least 0.1 V; two failed samples across key cycles give a Type A fault. Over many charges group J ends up high and caps the full charge. Opposite: P0DD1.
c: Bleed resistor of circuit J open or burnt
Balancing switch of group J no longer closing
Interrupted balancing lead between cell tap and board
s: Check engine light without noticeable change in driving
Cells of group J at the top of the cell list at the end of charging
Usable battery capacity declining over time

P0DD3.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit J Range/Performance
P0DD3.d: P0DD3 is a plausibility verdict on circuit J: the switch reacts, but the effect of balancing on group J does not match what the controller expected. No maker documents this code publicly, so the reasoning rests on CARB and on how balancing is planned. Ford patent US20120293129A1 describes active balancing in which the highest cell is discharged for a time that depends on its charge gap to the lowest cell, and the removed charge is moved back into the pack. A gap that stays after such a run, or a run that ends too soon, points to wrong estimates or a weak path rather than an open circuit. 13 CCR 1968.2 requires detection once balancing can no longer hold desired cell voltages. Electrical faults of J: P0DD0.
c: Wrong charge estimate for the cells of group J
Battery controller software or calibration (check for updates first)
Balancing path of J with raised resistance, so less charge moves than planned
s: Check engine light, often only after several charges
Group J remains out of line despite balancing
Unsteady range prediction

P0DD4.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit K
P0DD4.d: P0DD4 is the electrical fault code for balancing circuit K, the eleventh group, so it only exists on packs with at least eleven balancing channels. Public maker documents for this exact code were not found; Ford's summaries give K only to the stuck faults P0DD5 and P0DD6. How a monitoring chip catches broken wiring is shown in Infineon's TLE9012DQU data sheet: during its round-robin cycle the chip sinks a test current of about 15 mA into each balancing pin, odd channels in one cycle and even ones in the next, and flags a broken wire or missing load when the resulting change in cell voltage falls outside a set window. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requires such components to be monitored on hybrids. Related: P0DD5 to P0DD7.
c: Open wire or loose cell tap in group K
Corrosion or moisture at the connector of the monitoring board for K
Defective monitoring chip or external balancing part of channel K
s: Check engine light and hybrid system warning
Missing or implausible cell voltages for group K in the scan tool
Reduced charging or drive power

P0DD5.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit K Stuck On
P0DD5.d: P0DD5 tells that circuit K is discharging its cells without a balancing request. Ford's 2016 hybrid OBD summary links the code to the BECM start-up check: before the contactors close it looks at the six cells of the circuit for 100 ms and fails it when one of them is more than 75 mV away from the average, confirmed on a second power cycle. A switch that conducts by itself can also be caught directly: in Toshiba patent US20130026994A1 the balancing switch is held off while a comparator watches the nodes on both sides of it; if one side sinks below the other, the switch is judged short-circuited. Apart from charge loss, the shorted path heats its resistor all the time. Inactive case: P0DD6.
c: Shorted balancing switch of group K
Heat damage or contamination bridging the balancing path of K on the board
Driver stage of the monitoring chip holding channel K on
s: Check engine light at start-up
Group K drops faster than the other cells while parked
Locally higher battery module temperature

P0DD6.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit K Stuck Off
P0DD6.d: P0DD6: group K's bleed path stays dead when balancing is called for. Ford includes it in its 2017 hybrid OBD summary; the BECM decides at power-up with open contactors, within 100 ms and over two power cycles, using the 75 mV deviation of one of the six cells from the average. LG's patent US20110285539A1 offers a direct check of the path: a sampling capacitor first takes on the cell's voltage and is then emptied through the balancing circuit; whatever voltage is left over must be close to zero, otherwise the circuit is faulty. Because nothing is drained, the car drives normally, but group K keeps reaching full charge first and the pack loses usable capacity. The stuck-on counterpart is P0DD5.
c: Open bleed resistor in circuit K
Balancing switch of group K failing to turn on
Cracked solder joint in the balancing path of K
s: Check engine light while the car drives normally
Group K highest at the end of charging
Electric range decreasing over many charges

P0DD7.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit K Range/Performance
P0DD7.d: P0DD7 points to balancing of group K that works, but not within the expected limits. No maker publishes this code. A monitoring chip can deliver exactly this kind of finding: Infineon's TLE9012DQU checks every channel during active balancing for overcurrent and undercurrent through a sense resistor and switches balancing off when either threshold is crossed. Its per-cell timer runs up to roughly 3.9 hours in steps of about 7.5 minutes. A current that is too low over such a period moves far less charge than planned, so group K stays apart without any open or shorted part. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 accepts checking the commanded switches as long as the system notices that desired cell voltages are no longer held. Electrical fault: P0DD4.
c: Balancing current of K below the expected value (aged resistor, raised contact resistance)
Controller calibration with too short balancing time for group K
A cell in group K drifting faster than balancing can compensate
s: Check engine light, often after charging
Spread of group K returns soon after a balancing session
Fluctuating range estimate

P0DD8.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit L
P0DD8.d: P0DD8 concerns the hardware of balancing circuit L, the twelfth group. No manufacturer documents it publicly; Ford, whose hybrid BECM runs through letter N, uses L only in the stuck codes P0DD9 and P0DDA. LG Chem's patent EP2730933A1 shows a way to test one balancing circuit through its neighbour: diagnosis resistors sit between each balancing circuit and its cell terminals, and when the circuit under test is switched on or off, the voltage measured across the adjacent circuit has to change in a known pattern. A missing or wrong pattern exposes a broken resistor, switch or connection. The CARB regulation requires separate codes that lead the technician to the replaceable unit. Stuck and plausibility faults of L: P0DD9 to P0DDB.
c: Open resistor, switch or solder joint in circuit L
Poor connection of the cell taps of group L
Faulty voltage measuring channel next to circuit L
s: Hybrid battery warning and check engine light
Power or charging limited

P0DD9.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit L Stuck On
P0DD9.d: P0DD9: the balancing path of group L will not switch off. The 2018 edition of Ford's hybrid OBD summary contains the code; the BECM catches it at power-up with the contactors still open, in a 100 ms check that compares each of the six cells of circuit L with the average and fails above 75 mV, again over two power cycles. GM shows a different route in its 2013 eAssist table: code P1B33 compares the reported balancing switch status with the commanded one and fails after 7 of 10 samples, as a two-trip fault. A switch that reads on while it should be off is exactly what P0DD9 describes. While parked the group drains, and the warm resistor stresses the module. Inactive opposite: P0DDA.
c: Balancing switch of group L shorted
Balancing command for L not cleared by the monitoring electronics
Switch status feedback of channel L reporting on although the switch is open
s: Check engine light after switching on
Group L lower than the others after standing
Less electric range

P0DDA.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit L Stuck Off
P0DDA.d: P0DDA says circuit L does not discharge when it is told to. In Ford's 2019 hybrid OBD summary the start-up test has been simplified: it still runs for 100 ms before the contactors close, but the requirement of two consecutive power cycles is gone, and the 75 mV deviation of a cell from the average must instead persist for 0.1 s. Ford's 2014 code list flags the code for the MIL. Renesas patent US9735567B2 explains why a switch that never closes can be seen electrically: a pull-up lifts the balancing pin to cell potential, so a switch that is told to close while the pin still shows the full cell voltage means the path is open. Group L then lags behind in every balancing run and limits the charge. Opposite case: P0DD9.
c: Balancing switch of group L stays open when commanded on
Bleed resistor of circuit L open
Missing gate drive for the balancing switch of L
s: Check engine light with no change in drivability
Group L reaches full charge before the rest
Gradual loss of usable capacity

P0DDB.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit L Range/Performance
P0DDB.d: P0DDB stands for balancing of group L whose result is out of range although the circuit answers. No maker documents P0DDB publicly. A patent by Southwest Electronic Energy, US9097774B2, adds an important angle: it counts how often each cell has to be balanced and flags a cell that needs it far more or less often than the others, since an internal short can be the reason. Applied here, a plausibility fault of L may not be a balancing defect at all but a cell that keeps losing charge. That makes a careful look at self-discharge and cell voltages worthwhile before parts are replaced. CARB requires hybrids to flag a balancing system that fails to keep cells at their target voltage. Electrical fault of L: P0DD8.
c: Cell in group L with an internal soft short, needing balancing again and again
Controller calibration of expected balancing effect for L
Drifted bleed resistor of circuit L
s: Check engine light, sometimes only after long parking
Group L drifting low between charges
Range estimate varying from day to day

P0DDC.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit M
P0DDC.d: P0DDC reports an electrical fault of balancing circuit M, the thirteenth group, which only large packs with at least thirteen channels possess. No maker publishes this exact code; in Ford's BECM documents M appears only as stuck on (P0DDD) and stuck off (P0DDE). LaunchPoint's patent US8598840B2 describes how such faults can be found while the system runs: built-in tests feed every cell measurement its own distinct test signal and are run from a circuit domain kept separate from the balancing and measuring electronics they check, so one failure cannot hide itself. Wiring breaks, damaged connectors and chip faults are typical findings. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requires these parts to be watched on hybrids. Related: P0DDD to P0DDF.
c: Broken sense or balancing wire of group M
Damaged or poorly seated connector at the board for M
Fault in the monitoring electronics of channel M
s: Check engine light and hybrid warning
Battery controller restricting power or charging

P0DDD.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit M Stuck On
P0DDD.d: P0DDD reports a balancing path of group M that keeps conducting. Ford's 2015 hybrid OBD summary places it in the BECM monitor, judged at power-up before the contactors close: 100 ms, six cells per circuit, more than 75 mV from the average, two consecutive power cycles. A properly working chip should never leave a channel on indefinitely. Infineon's TLE9012DQU, for example, gives each cell its own balancing timer of up to about 3.9 hours and ends balancing on its own once that runs out, or when its over- or undercurrent check trips. If group M still loses charge after such limits, the switch itself is most likely shorted. Expect a low group M after a night of parking. Inactive counterpart: P0DDE.
c: Shorted balancing switch of group M that no timer can stop
Damaged external balancing transistor on the board for M
High self-discharge cell in group M imitating a stuck switch
s: Check engine light at start-up
Group M noticeably low after overnight parking
Raised module temperature near group M

P0DDE.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit M Stuck Off
P0DDE.d: P0DDE means group M is not bled when it should be. Ford carries the code in its 2016 hybrid OBD summary with the usual BECM start-up rule: 100 ms with open contactors, six cells per circuit, a 75 mV gap to the average, confirmed over two power cycles. A balancing channel can also be stopped on purpose, which a diagnosis must keep apart from a real failure. TI's BQ79616-Q1 data sheet lists such ends: the per-channel timer expires, the cell falls below a set voltage, an unmasked fault appears or the host stops balancing. Only a path that never conducts after a valid start counts here. Left alone, the fuller cells of M reach their limit first at every charge, and the pack gives away capacity. Stuck-on case: P0DDD.
c: Bleed resistor of circuit M open
Balancing switch of group M that no longer turns on
Intended balancing stop for M misjudged as no response by the software
s: Check engine light while driving feels normal
Group M highest at the end of each charge
Less usable battery energy over time

P0DDF.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit M Range/Performance
P0DDF.d: P0DDF covers group M when balancing responds but its outcome is not credible. No manufacturer publishes this code. Ford patent US9145064B2 shows what the expected outcome can be built on: the controller derives a bleed time per cell from that cell's surplus capacity and the charging current, so that all cells arrive at the target together at the end of charging. If group M is still out of line once its time is used up, the plan or the hardware behind it is off. Typical reasons are a capacity estimate that no longer matches an aged cell or a resistor that has drifted. The CARB hybrid rule in 13 CCR 1968.2 calls for exactly this functional check. Electrical fault of M: P0DDC.
c: Stored capacity value for cells of group M out of date
s: Check engine light following charging sessions
Group M not aligned with the rest after full charge
Inconsistent range display

P0DE0.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit N
P0DE0.d: P0DE0 flags a wiring or driver fault in balancing circuit N, the fourteenth and last letter of the series; the next code, P0DE4, belongs to a different system. Packs with more balancing groups than fourteen must therefore map several groups to one letter or use their own codes. Ford's hybrid BECM is one of the few documented users that fills all fourteen letters, but only with stuck codes, so P0DE0 itself has no public maker source. How a broken balancing terminal is found is shown in Toshiba patent US20130026994A1, where comparing the sense pin with the balancing pin reveals an open connection. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requires codes that point to the smallest replaceable unit. Stuck and plausibility faults of N: P0DE1 to P0DE3.
c: Open balancing terminal or lead of group N
Corroded or loose connector at the last module board
Monitoring chip channel for N defective
s: Hybrid battery warning with check engine light
Electric operation or charging restricted

P0DE1.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit N Stuck On
P0DE1.d: P0DE1 is the last stuck-on code of the series: group N keeps bleeding when it should rest. Ford lists it in every hybrid OBD summary from 2014 to 2019; in the 2017 edition the BECM spends 100 ms after key-on, while the contactors are still open, checking whether any of the six cells of circuit N sits more than 75 mV from the average, with two consecutive power cycles needed. A balancing switch that cannot open drains the group constantly, even with the car parked, and turns that energy into heat on the board. A cell with an internal short can produce the same falling voltage, so a check of the switch on the bench is worthwhile before the cells are condemned. Ford's 2014 code list ties the code to the MIL. Inactive case: P0DE2.
c: Balancing switch of group N permanently conducting
Monitoring electronics keeping the balancing command for N active
Cell of group N with an internal short causing the same voltage drop
s: Check engine light after switching on
Group N drops while the car is parked
Shorter electric range

P0DE2.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit N Stuck Off
P0DE2.d: P0DE2 closes Ford's list of balancing codes: circuit N does not discharge when commanded. Ford's 2018 hybrid summary has the BECM judge this during a 100 ms window at key-on, contactors still open, comparing each of the six cells with the average against 75 mV over two power cycles. A switch that stays open has no immediate effect on driving, but the imbalance adds up. Intersil's application note AN141 puts numbers on this: cells count as matched when their capacities lie within 3 percent, and a gap of only 150 mV at full charge can cost a series pack a quarter of its capacity or more. Group N will therefore be full first and limit what the whole pack can store. Stuck-on counterpart: P0DE1.
c: Open bleed resistor in circuit N
Balancing switch of group N not turning on
Cell tap of group N detached from the busbar
s: Check engine light without driving complaint
Charging ends early because group N is full first
Electric range shrinking over months

P0DE3.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit N Range/Performance
P0DE3.d: P0DE3 is the final code of the balancing series and judges whether balancing of group N achieves a believable result. No maker documents it publicly. The Wikipedia article on battery balancing explains why such a check matters: unless the upper and lower cut-offs line up with the weakest cell, the energy the pack can take in and give back stays limited, so a mismatched group throttles the whole battery. Passive systems burn the surplus in resistors, active ones move it over to the emptier cells. If group N stays apart although its circuit reacts, the cause lies in estimates, cell ageing or a weak bleed path. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 obliges hybrid monitors to catch cells drifting away from their balancing target. Electrical fault: P0DE0.
c: Cells of group N aged unevenly
Controller estimates or calibration for group N off
Bleed path of N with too little current
s: Check engine light, mostly after charging
Group N never quite levels with the other groups
Reduced and unsteady range

P0DE4.t: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Over Temperature
P0DE4.d: P0DE4 reports that the electric motor of auxiliary transmission fluid pump A has run too hot. Such a pump keeps the transmission pressurised while the engine is stopped, either by start-stop or during electric driving in a hybrid. No manufacturer documents P0DE4 publicly. Ford's 2019 hybrid OBD summary shows how its plug-in hybrids treat pump heat under other codes: once the pump circuit board exceeds 130 °C for 3 s the TCM logs P175A and disables the pump, and above 135 °C the event feeds the stall code P0C2A. Heat builds when the motor labours against low, aged or very cold fluid, against a binding rotor, or in a hot transmission.
