The car then usually keeps the engine running instead of stopping or driving electrically. P0C1B is the controller electronics, P277D the motor of pump B.
c: Low, aged or wrong transmission fluid making the pump work harder
Binding rotor or worn bearing in the pump motor
Transmission running hot (towing, heat, restricted fluid cooler)
Faulty temperature evaluation in the pump controller or outdated software
s: Start-stop no longer shuts the engine off
Electric driving limited, engine keeps running
Harsh engagement when pulling away after a stop
Malfunction indicator lamp on

P0DE5.t: Charge Status Indicator B Control Circuit/Open
P0DE5.d: P0DE5 flags an interrupted drive circuit for charge status indicator B, a second lamp or LED that tells the owner whether the vehicle is charging, for instance one at the charge port next to the one on the dashboard. Which light gets the letter B is up to the maker. No manufacturer documents P0DE5 publicly. GM's tables for the Chevrolet Volt and Cadillac ELR only cover indicator A (P0D2C): the hybrid controller samples the LED driver every 100 ms, needs 40 bad results out of 50 and checks for a short to battery or an open line while the LED is commanded off. In the current code set, shorts on B have their own codes, P0E41 and P0E42, so P0DE5 narrows the fault to a break: a cut wire, a loose connector or a dead LED. Charging itself still works.
c: Broken wire or unplugged connector to indicator B
Burnt-out LED or failed indicator unit
Corroded contacts in the weather-exposed charge port area
Failed output driver in the controlling module
s: Charge status indicator B stays dark while charging
Charging works normally
Warning lamp possible depending on the manufacturer

P0DE6.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cell Voltage Low
P0DE6.d: P0DE6 means the battery controller has measured at least one cell of the high-voltage pack below its lower voltage limit. It concerns a real reading, not the sensing lines (P0B3D and similar), and it looks at the weakest cell rather than the charge of the whole pack (P0A7D). Ford pairs it with P0A7D on 2020 Escape and Explorer hybrids drained by long standing or failed starts; a rescue charge needs the lowest cell above 1.45 V and a cell spread under 2.5 V (SSM 49163, later 51460, 52230 and 52773 for 2023-24 models). Stellantis fixes P0DE6 with BPCM software on the 2024-25 Dodge Charger EV and Jeep Wagoneer S, and on the 2026 Cherokee hybrid lengthened its maturing time for cold cranks. A no-start or reduced power is typical.
c: Pack deeply discharged after long standing or repeated failed starts
Battery controller software judging too strictly (e.g. cold cranking)
Single weak cell with high self-discharge or lost capacity
Cell balancing circuit draining one cell
s: Vehicle will not start or switch to ready
Reduced power, no electric driving
Malfunction indicator lamp on

P0DE7.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cell Voltage High
P0DE7.d: P0DE7 is stored when a single cell of the high-voltage pack climbs above the upper voltage limit the battery controller permits. Overcharged lithium-ion cells age quickly and can become unsafe, so the controller usually restricts charging and regenerative braking until the cell is back in range. The only public manufacturer use found is Ram: bulletin 08-030-24 and its sister bulletins for the 2019-2024 Ram 1500 with eTorque mild hybrid (3.6 L V6 and 5.7 L V8) list P0DE7 together with cell supervisory, voltage sense and balancing codes and prescribe new BPCM software, pointing to a calibration cause. Other plausible causes are failed balancing, a cell with raised internal resistance during regen, or a drifting measurement chip. Low cell voltage is P0DE6, pack overvoltage P0AFB.
c: Battery controller software or calibration (documented by Ram)
Cell balancing no longer bleeding off the highest cell
Aged cell with raised internal resistance overshooting during regen
Drifting cell monitoring chip reporting too high a value
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Weaker regenerative braking, charging limited
Mild-hybrid assist or start-stop unavailable

P0DE8.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve C Control Circuit/Open
P0DE8.d: P0DE8 reports an open or otherwise faulty drive circuit for coolant control valve C, a third switchable valve in the coolant loop of the hybrid or EV battery. What it switches depends on the layout, for example whether coolant passes through the radiator, the air-conditioning chiller or a heater, and the maker decides which valve is called C. No manufacturer documents P0DE8 publicly. The closest documented case is valve A: the battery management of Mercedes S-, E- and C-Class hybrids flags its actuation as electrically faulty or open with P0CDF00 (LI83.30-P-061224). CARB demands circuit checks on every output used to heat or cool the energy store. Expect a broken wire, a loose plug or an open coil. Shorts are P0DEB and P0DEC, an overloaded driver P0E22.
c: Broken wire or loose connector at valve C
Open coil or motor winding inside valve C
Corroded pins from coolant or water ingress
Failed driver stage in the controlling module
s: Battery temperature control works only in a fallback mode
Charging or drive power reduced when the pack is too hot or cold
Malfunction indicator lamp on

P0DE9.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve C Performance/Stuck Off
P0DE9.d: P0DE9 says coolant control valve C is electrically fine but does not do its job: it fails to reach the commanded position or remains in its off state. No manufacturer documents P0DE9 publicly. GM's 2011 Chevrolet Volt tables show what such a test can look like for valve A, which has a position feedback: on start-up the valve must find its end stop within 800 ms, later it must reach each target within 1.5 s, and an erratic feedback with more than 12 % noise counts as well; enough failed samples set a Type B code with the MIL on the second trip. Where no feedback exists, makers judge the valve from coolant or pack temperatures, which CARB requests as a functional check of cooling. Dirt, a seized valve body or a weak actuator are typical. Stuck on is P0DEA.
c: Valve body seized or sluggish from deposits
Worn actuator motor or gearing in valve C
Low coolant or air in the battery loop distorting the temperature check
s: Battery heats up faster under load or while fast charging
Charging power or drive power limited
Malfunction indicator lamp on

P0DEA.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve C Stuck On
P0DEA.d: P0DEA means coolant control valve C stays in its active position even though the controller has asked it to return. A wiring check cannot see this, because the circuit is intact; the controller needs a position feedback, as on GM's Volt valve with its own sensor codes, or it infers the state from coolant and pack temperatures that keep moving the wrong way. No manufacturer documents P0DEA publicly. Mercedes battery management shows for valve A that the same mechanical fault can be named in both directions, with separate codes for a shutoff valve that will not close and one that will not open (P0CE000, P0CE100). Depending on what C controls, coolant keeps flowing through the chiller or heater path, so the pack may be overcooled in winter or kept warm in summer. Stuck off is P0DE9.
c: Valve jammed in the active position by debris or wear
Driver stage that does not switch off
s: Pack too cold in winter or too warm in summer
Reduced range or charging speed
Malfunction indicator lamp on

P0DEB.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve C Control Circuit Low
P0DEB.d: P0DEB is set when the drive line of coolant control valve C reads too low, which almost always means a short to ground somewhere between controller and valve. No manufacturer documents P0DEB publicly. GM's 2011 Volt tables for valve A show the logic: with system voltage above 9 V, a low reading on driver line 1 during reverse travel counts as a failure, and 90 failures out of 100 samples at 6.25 ms set a Type B code. A short to ground lets current bypass the load, so many drivers protect themselves by shutting off; an overheated or overloaded driver has its own code, P0E22. Chafed insulation near brackets, coolant in the connector and an internal short in the valve motor are the usual finds. The valve then stays wherever it was. Open circuit is P0DE8, short to voltage P0DEC.
c: Chafed wire shorting to body ground
Coolant or water in the valve connector
Internal short in the valve motor
s: Valve C no longer moves, temperature control in fallback mode
Charging or drive power reduced at temperature extremes
Malfunction indicator lamp on

P0DEC.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve C Control Circuit High
P0DEC.d: P0DEC is the short-to-voltage case for coolant control valve C: its drive line reads high at a moment when the controller expects it low. No manufacturer documents P0DEC publicly. For valve A, GM's 2011 Volt checks driver line 1 for a high level while the valve should be stopped or moving forward, again needing 90 failures in 100 checks for a Type B code. Unlike a ground short, a line held at supply voltage can keep the valve energised, so the valve may creep to an end stop instead of freezing. Keep the drive circuit apart from the feedback: on valves with a position sensor, a signal above the valid range is a sensor code such as P0CE7, not P0DEC. A wire pinched against a live feed or a driver that will not switch off is typical. Short to ground is P0DEB, open circuit P0DE8.
c: Wire pinched against a supply line
Driver stage in the module not switching off
Moisture bridging pins in the connector
s: Valve C runs to an end position and stays there
Pack temperature drifts, power or charging limited
Malfunction indicator lamp on

P0DED.d: P0DED points to an open or faulty hard-wired circuit between the powertrain side and the pedestrian alert control module, the unit that makes a quiet hybrid or EV audible at low speed. It is not a network fault, which is U013F, nor a speaker fault, which uses B0122 and B0123. No manufacturer documents P0DED publicly. The module exists because of law: US standard FMVSS 141 requires a sound whenever propulsion is active and the car is not in Park, in reverse and up to about 30 km/h, and the EU has demanded such a system for new types since July 2019. Ford calls the unit PACM; on the 2020-21 Escape Hybrid it sits in the right rear quarter (TSB 21-2271). An open line typically means a silent car, so pedestrians lose their warning and the driver usually sees a message.
c: Broken wire or loose connector at the alert module
Blown fuse or interrupted supply to the module
Internal fault of the pedestrian alert module
s: No artificial driving sound at low speed or in reverse
Pedestrian alert warning message in the instrument cluster

P0DEE.t: Pedestrian Alert Control Module Circuit Low
P0DEE.d: P0DEE is set when the hard-wired circuit to the pedestrian alert control module sits below its expected voltage, typically from a short to ground. No manufacturer documents P0DEE publicly, so the exact signal behind it, whether supply, wake-up or a command line, is not known in detail. A ground short often blows a fuse or makes the driving module disconnect the line, and the alert then falls silent, even though FMVSS 141 expects a sound from standstill with propulsion on, in reverse and up to around 30 km/h; EU vehicles must carry such a system as well. Look along the whole harness run, which can be long: on Ford's 2020-21 Escape Hybrid the module sits in the right rear quarter. Open circuit is P0DED, short to voltage P0DEF.
c: Chafed or crushed wire shorting to ground
Water ingress in a connector near bumper or wheel arch
Internal short in the alert module
s: Pedestrian warning sound missing
Warning message in the instrument cluster
Fuse for the alert module may be blown

P0DEF.t: Pedestrian Alert Control Module Circuit High
P0DEF.d: P0DEF reports a voltage above the permitted window on the wired link to the pedestrian alert control module, most often because a wire touches a supply line or the line has lost its ground reference. No manufacturer documents P0DEF publicly. The consequence differs from the low case: a line stuck high may leave the module permanently woken or commanded, so instead of silence the alert can behave oddly, for example sounding when it should not or draining the 12 V battery while parked. Whether that happens depends on the design. The legal background is the same as for the siblings: FMVSS 141 and the EU require a warning sound for quiet vehicles at low speed. Ford names the unit PACM. P0DED is an open circuit, P0DEE a short to ground, U013F lost communication.
c: Wire pinched against a 12 V supply line
Loose or corroded ground connection of the module
Internal fault of the alert module or its driver
s: Pedestrian sound missing or sounding at the wrong time
Warning message in the instrument cluster
Possible 12 V battery drain while parked

P0DF0.t: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P0DF0.d: P0DF0 is the catch-all circuit code for temperature sensor B in the generator inverter, the power stage that drives the generator of a two-machine hybrid. The controller sets it when the sensor line is electrically faulty but the fault is not sorted into low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents P0DF0 publicly. Mitsubishi fits one thermistor per IGBT in the generator unit of the Outlander PHEV and reports the second high-side sensor (V phase) only through P0DF4 to P0DF6, never through this general code; Ford likewise names only open and short checks for its generator inverter sensor. CARB requires every input that feeds inverter thermal management to be checked for circuit faults. Without a valid value the controller has to assume the worst and usually limits generator output.
c: Loose, corroded or damaged connector at the inverter or power unit
Thermistor or its signal path inside the inverter module faulty
Faulty evaluation input in the generator control unit
s: Hybrid or engine warning light on
Reduced generator output, weaker charging while driving
Hybrid system may switch to a restricted mode

P0DF1.t: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0DF1.d: P0DF1 means the signal of generator inverter temperature sensor B drops out or jumps for short moments and then looks normal again. Typical triggers are temperature steps faster than the power module could physically heat or cool, or brief readings that resemble an open line. No manufacturer documents P0DF1 publicly: Ford's monitors for its generator inverter sensor cover only opens and shorts (P0BCE, P0BCF), and Mitsubishi has no intermittent code for the corresponding V-phase sensor at all. CARB still expects inverter thermal inputs to be monitored. Because the fault comes and goes, freeze frame data and a wiggle test of the inverter harness tell more than swapping parts. A steady fault on this sensor would be logged as P0DF0, P0DF5 or P0DF6 instead.
c: Loose or fretted terminal in the inverter connector
Harness chafing or vibration damage near the power unit
Intermittent contact inside the inverter module
s: Warning light that comes and goes
Occasional short loss of generator power
Fault often not reproducible at the workshop

P0DF2.t: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit
P0DF2.d: P0DF2 covers an electrical fault on temperature sensor C of the generator inverter that the controller cannot assign to a more specific low, high or intermittent code. Which power switch carries sensor C is up to the manufacturer; in Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV the third high-side IGBT sensor sits on the W phase, and its faults are logged only as P0DF7 to P0DF9. No manufacturer documents P0DF2 itself. CARB demands circuit monitoring for inputs of inverter thermal management. As these thermistors are usually built into the IGBT module, a confirmed sensor fault often means replacing the inverter or the complete power unit, so the harness and connector deserve a careful check first. The general circuit code for sensor B is P0DF0.
c: Thermistor inside the IGBT module defective
Connector or signal line fault between module and controller
Faulty input stage in the generator control unit
s: Hybrid or engine warning light on
Generator power reduced as a precaution
Higher engine use or weaker battery recharge

P0DF3.t: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0DF3.d: P0DF3 is logged when sensor C in the generator inverter delivers an unsteady signal: short spikes, gaps or values that change faster than the module temperature ever could. Such faults often start at connectors that loosen under engine vibration and repeated heating cycles, or at pins attacked by moisture. No manufacturer documents P0DF3 publicly, and Mitsubishi, which does monitor a W-phase sensor in its generator unit, defines no intermittent code for it. CARB requires these thermal inputs to be monitored nonetheless. The warning may vanish after a restart and return days later, so it pays to note when and under which load it appeared. Constant faults of the same sensor are P0DF2, P0DF8 and P0DF9; the matching fault on sensor B is P0DF1.
c: Terminal losing contact under vibration or heat cycles
Moisture or corrosion in the inverter connector
Intermittent connection inside the inverter module
s: Warning light that appears only now and then
Brief drops in generator power
Code stored as history fault without current symptoms

P0DF4.t: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0DF4.d: P0DF4 reports that temperature sensor B of the generator inverter delivers an electrically valid signal whose value does not fit the other sensors. Mitsubishi documents the check for the Outlander PHEV: a single time in each drive cycle, following at least 600 s of standstill and with the IGBTs switched off, the V-phase high-side sensor may not differ by more than 47 °C from the other two phase sensors for 0.1 s; otherwise P0DF4-00 is stored and the power drive unit is replaced. Volvo lists ECM P0DF400 for 2022-on T8 plug-in hybrids and warns it can be misdetected, showing Propulsion System Service Required; for builds from week 202147 to 202446 ECM software 3.4.4 cures it. Out-of-range signals are P0DF5 and P0DF6.
c: Control software misdetection (Volvo T8, ECM update available)
Sensor in the power module drifted or stuck at one value
Internal fault in the power drive unit (Mitsubishi replaces the unit)
s: Message such as Propulsion System Service Required
Engine warning light on
Turtle symbol and reduced power in some cases

P0DF5.t: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P0DF5.d: P0DF5 sets when the signal voltage of generator inverter temperature sensor B stays below its valid window. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV checks this continuously: if the V-phase high-side IGBT sensor reads at most 1.25 V during 0.08 s while the generator control unit has at least 8 V supply, P0DF5-00 is stored. Mitsubishi does not say which temperature this means, but with a thermistor whose resistance falls as it warms, a low voltage looks like an extremely hot switch, the usual picture of a short to ground or a shorted element. The guided repair ends with a new power drive unit because the sensor is internal. Expect reduced generator power while the fault is present. The high case is P0DF6, an implausible in-range value P0DF4.
c: Shorted thermistor inside the IGBT module
Internal fault of the power drive unit
s: Engine or hybrid warning light on
Generator output limited, engine runs more often
Displayed inverter temperature implausibly high

P0DF6.t: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
P0DF6.d: P0DF6 is the high-signal case for sensor B in the generator inverter. In the Outlander PHEV Mitsubishi stores P0DF6-00 when the V-phase high-side IGBT sensor voltage reaches at least 3.75 V during 0.08 s, again only with a GCU supply of at least 8 V. A voltage at the upper limit mostly points to an interrupted sensor line, a lost reference ground or a cracked element; with the common NTC layout it reads as an implausibly cold module. Since the inverter can then no longer protect its switches against overheating, the controller works with a safe substitute and may cut generator output. Mitsubishi's procedure ends with a new power drive unit. Too low a signal on this sensor is P0DF5; the same open-type fault on sensor C would be P0DF9.
c: Open signal line or backed-out terminal
Cracked sensor element or internal fault of the power drive unit
s: Engine or hybrid warning light on
Inverter temperature shown far too low
Generator power reduced

P0DF7.t: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P0DF7.d: P0DF7 is the plausibility code for temperature sensor C of the generator inverter. The idea behind it: after a long rest every power switch should be at roughly the same temperature, so a sensor that stands out is suspect. In Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV the W-phase high-side sensor is compared once per trip, after 600 s or more of soak and with the IGBTs off, against the U- and V-phase sensors; a gap above 47 °C lasting 0.1 s stores P0DF7-00. The circuit itself is electrically fine in this case, so wiring checks rarely help, and Mitsubishi's procedure replaces the power drive unit. A genuine overheat of the inverter is reported separately as P0A3E. The same comparison on sensor B is P0DF4.
c: Sensor C drifted or stuck inside the IGBT module
Internal fault of the power drive unit
s: Engine warning light on after a cold start
Usually no noticeable change in driving
Possibly reduced generator power

P0DF8.t: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Low
P0DF8.d: P0DF8 tells that temperature sensor C in the generator inverter delivers a voltage below its valid range. Mitsubishi uses the code in the Outlander PHEV for the W-phase high-side IGBT sensor: a reading at or under 1.25 V for 0.08 s, with at least 8 V GCU supply, stores P0DF8-00, and the check runs all the time. Physical causes are a short between signal and ground or a breakdown inside the module, for instance after coolant has reached the electronics. The value suggests a far too hot switch, so the controller derates the generator to stay on the safe side. The sensor cannot be replaced on its own, which is why Mitsubishi lists the power drive unit. The same fault on sensor B is P0DF5, the high case on this sensor P0DF9.
c: Signal line of sensor C shorted to ground
Shorted sensor or internal fault of the power drive unit
Coolant or moisture inside the inverter electronics
s: Hybrid or engine warning light on
Generator power limited
Implausibly high inverter temperature in live data

P0DF9.t: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit High
P0DF9.d: P0DF9 is stored when the C temperature sensor of the generator inverter reports a voltage at or beyond the upper end of its window. For the Outlander PHEV Mitsubishi defines the limit as 3.75 V for 0.08 s on the W-phase high-side IGBT sensor, monitored continuously whenever the GCU has at least 8 V. An open line, a backed-out terminal in the inverter connector or a broken sensor element are the usual explanations. Unlike a real cold start, the reading does not climb as the generator works, which separates the fault from a true low temperature. Generator power may be held back until the value is valid again, and Mitsubishi fixes it by replacing the complete power drive unit. Too low a voltage on the same sensor is P0DF8; the B-sensor counterpart is P0DF6.
c: Open signal line of sensor C
Terminal pushed back in the inverter connector
Broken sensor element inside the power drive unit
s: Engine or hybrid warning light on
Inverter temperature stuck at a very low value
Generator output held back

P0DFA.t: Generator Phase U-V-W Current Sensor Correlation
P0DFA.d: In a three-phase machine the currents of phases U, V and W add up to nearly zero at every instant, so a sum far from zero shows that at least one current sensor is wrong. P0DFA is the code for this cross-check on the generator side. Mitsubishi documents it for the Outlander PHEV: with the IGBTs switching, the summation check must not report a failure, and with them off the sum must stay below 140 A; either condition held for 0.35 s sets P0DFA-00. Ford counts P0DFA among the generator inverter faults of its power-split hybrids, and SSM 50151 notes that on 2020 to 2021 hybrid models it can be caused by a 12 V dip at key-on, so check for low voltage first. Single-phase sensor faults are P0E00 to P0E0B.
c: 12 V voltage drop at key-on (Ford SSM 50151)
One phase current sensor with offset or gain error
Internal fault of the inverter or power drive unit
s: Stop Safely Now or hybrid system warning
Vehicle may not start or ready mode is refused
Generator shut down, restricted driving

P0DFB.d: The position sensor of a hybrid generator, normally a resolver, is never mounted exactly in line with the magnetic poles of the rotor. The remaining angle error is determined once and saved in the controller; Hyundai describes doing this after assembly and again whenever the machine or its control unit is replaced, and Ford describes an in-vehicle routine started by a scan tool that sweeps the current angle and reads the offset where the q-axis current crosses zero. P0DFB means such a learned offset lies outside the window the software accepts, so it cannot be used for field-oriented control. No manufacturer documents P0DFB publicly. Possible reasons are a resolver that moved on its shaft, an aborted learning run or a faulty controller. A missing value is P0DFC instead.
c: Offset learning interrupted or run under wrong conditions
Resolver rotor or stator shifted after repair or damage
Fault or wrong software in the generator control unit
s: Hybrid system warning and engine warning light
Generator not used, reduced charging or engine start problems
Code returns after clearing until relearned

P0DFC.d: P0DFC is stored when the controller has no valid learned position offset for the generator resolver. Ford explains it in the OBD summary of its power-split hybrids: the code appears when the resolver was not configured at the assembly plant or after the inverter system controller has been replaced, and the check fails if the value held in EEPROM is outside its accepted range. It runs continuously from 700 ms after power-up with 6 to 19 V on the 12 V system, and Ford's 2014 code list marks P0DFC as a MIL code. Volvo reported intermittent IGM-P0DFC00 entries without symptoms on 2016 to 2017 XC90 T8 models and later released new IGM software. After a module or generator replacement, run the learn procedure. The drive motor counterpart is P0C17.
c: Inverter or hybrid controller replaced without resolver learning
Software fault in the inverter generator module (Volvo, update available)
Stored offset lost or corrupted in EEPROM
s: Engine warning light on
Generator or hybrid functions restricted
Sometimes only stored as history code without symptoms

P0DFD.t: Battery Charger Coolant Control Valve Control Circuit/Open
P0DFD.d: P0DFD flags an open or otherwise faulty drive circuit of the valve that controls coolant flow through the on-board charger. Such a valve lets the thermal system send coolant to the charger during AC charging and bypass it while driving. No manufacturer documents P0DFD publicly. The nearest documented case is the coolant shutoff valve of the battery module in Mercedes S-, E- and C-Class hybrids, whose actuation fault or open circuit the battery management logs as P0CDF00 (LI83.30-P-061224). CARB names thermal management of the battery and of the inverter explicitly, not the charger, so whether the MIL lights is up to the maker. A charger that runs too hot will cut its power, so charging may become slower. Shorts are P0DFE and P0DFF.
c: Broken wire or unplugged connector at the valve
Open coil or motor winding in the valve
Faulty output stage in the controlling module
s: Charging slower than usual or interrupted
Charging or service message
Driving usually unaffected

P0DFE.t: Battery Charger Coolant Control Valve Control Circuit Low
P0DFE.d: P0DFE means the control line of the charger coolant valve reads low, usually because it is shorted to ground somewhere between driver and valve. No manufacturer documents P0DFE publicly. GM's 2011 Volt tables show how such a check works on battery coolant valve A (P0CE2): with system voltage above 9 V and the valve commanded in reverse, a low sense level on drive 1 counts as a failure, and the code needs a fault in 90 of 100 checks spaced 6.25 ms apart before it is set as a two-trip Type B code. For the charger valve a similar logic is likely but not published. A ground short typically freezes the valve where it is, so the charger may be left without coolant and lower its power. Look for chafed wires and wet connectors. Open circuit is P0DFD.
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Coolant or water in the valve connector
Internal short in the valve actuator
s: Reduced charging power, longer charging time
Charger warning or charging stops
Driving normally unaffected

P0DFF.t: Battery Charger Coolant Control Valve Control Circuit High
P0DFF.d: P0DFF is the short-to-voltage case for the valve that cools the on-board charger. The controller sees the drive line high while commanding it low. No manufacturer documents P0DFF publicly. The closest published logic is GM's 2011 Volt monitor for battery coolant valve A (P0CE3). It watches for a high sense level on drive 1 while the valve is stopped or moving forward, above 9 V system voltage, and stores a two-trip Type B code only after 90 bad results in 100 samples taken at 6.25 ms intervals. If the wire is stuck at battery potential the actuator stays powered, and the valve can travel to its end position rather than stopping where it was. If that leaves the charger uncooled, charging power drops. Usual causes are chafed insulation touching a powered conductor or an output stage that fails to turn off. Ground short is P0DFE.
c: Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Output stage in the controlling module will not switch off
Internal fault in the valve actuator
s: Charging slower or charger warning
Valve audibly running to its end stop
Driving normally unaffected

P0E00.t: Generator Phase U Current Sensor Circuit
P0E00.d: P0E00 is the general circuit code for the current sensor in phase U of the generator. Each phase sensor, usually a Hall-type device inside the inverter, outputs a voltage around a mid-point when no current flows. No manufacturer documents P0E00 publicly. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV shows how its generator unit judges the U-phase sensor: at standstill below 20 rpm with the IGBTs off the signal must stay between 2.3 and 2.7 V (P0E01-00 after 0.32 s), and readings of 0.5 V and lower, or 4.5 V and higher, held for 0.2 s set P0E02-00 or P0E03-00. P0E00 is meant for circuit faults outside these categories. Without the signal the inverter cannot regulate generator torque properly. Phases V and W are P0E04 and P0E08.
c: Supply or reference fault of the current sensor
Defective phase U current sensor inside the inverter
Faulty internal connection between sensor and control board
s: Hybrid system warning and engine warning light
Generator switched off, reduced performance
Vehicle may not reach ready mode

P0E01.t: Generator Phase U Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0E01.d: P0E01 flags an implausible zero point of the U-phase current sensor inside the generator inverter. Sensors of this kind put out a voltage near the middle of their span while no current flows, so the test is only run when the machine cannot carry current. Mitsubishi documents the code for the Outlander PHEV: on the 2023 model the generator control unit evaluates the U-phase signal with the IGBTs switched off, the generator turning below 20 rpm and at least 8 V supply, and stores P0E01-00 if the value leaves the 2.3 to 2.7 V band for 0.32 s; MIL and hybrid warning light come on. The 2018 code chart calls the same code an offset fault of current sensor 1. A shifted zero distorts generator torque control. Hard signal faults of this sensor appear as P0E02 or P0E03.
c: Zero point of the phase U current sensor drifted (sensor inside the power drive unit)
Unstable sensor supply or reference voltage inside the inverter
Evaluation circuit of the generator control unit faulty
s: MIL and hybrid system warning light on
Generator output reduced, less charging while driving
Code often returns after clearing at the next standstill check

P0E02.t: Generator Phase U Current Sensor Circuit Low
P0E02.d: P0E02 is stored when the output of the generator inverter's phase U current sensor falls to the bottom of its range, a level no real current would produce. Mitsubishi uses it on the Outlander PHEV: from model year 2023 the generator control unit, supplied with at least 8 V, sets P0E02-00 once the U-phase signal drops to 0.5 V or lower and stays there for 0.2 s; unlike the zero-point test, no standstill is needed. The 2018 code chart describes the same code as a ground short or a broken line at current sensor 1. Because the sensor is built into the power drive unit, Mitsubishi's procedure ends with replacing that unit after a confirming drive cycle. The offset check is P0E01, the opposite fault P0E03. Without a valid U-phase value the generator usually runs only in a limited way.
c: Sensor signal shorted to ground or sensor output failed low
Open signal or supply connection of the sensor inside the power drive unit
Input stage of the generator control unit faulty
s: MIL and hybrid system warning light on
Generator power limited or generator not used
Battery charge falls faster in hybrid operation

P0E03.t: Generator Phase U Current Sensor Circuit High
P0E03.d: P0E03 is the upper-limit fault of the current sensor that measures phase U of the generator inverter: its signal is pinned near the supply rail. In the 2023 Outlander PHEV, Mitsubishi lets the generator control unit set P0E03-00 when the U-phase voltage climbs to at least 4.5 V and remains there for 0.2 s with the unit supplied by at least 8 V; for the 2018 model the code list blames a short to the supply or a shorted current sensor 1. A reading this high would mean a phase current far beyond anything the generator delivers, so the controller treats it as an electrical defect and not as overcurrent; genuine overcurrent has codes of its own, at Ford for instance P0A71. On the 2023 model the MIL is switched on as well. Low signal: P0E02, zero-point fault: P0E01.
c: Sensor signal shorted to its supply voltage
Current sensor in the power drive unit failed with high output
Lost sensor ground or reference inside the inverter
s: MIL and hybrid system warning light on
Generator switched off or strongly limited
Engine runs more often without charging the battery

P0E04.t: Generator Phase V Current Sensor Circuit
P0E04.d: P0E04 is the general circuit code for the generator inverter's V-phase current sensor, meant for an electrical fault that is not narrowed down to offset, low or high. No manufacturer documents P0E04 publicly. Phase V is a special case: the 2018 Outlander PHEV measures generator current with only two sensors, on phases U and W (P0E01 to P0E03, P0E09 to P0E0B), since the third current follows arithmetically from the other two. Only the 2023 model adds its own V-phase sensor, and there its faults are reported solely through P0E05 to P0E07. CARB requires electrical monitoring of hybrid components that affect emissions. If the code does appear, check the inverter connectors and look for further phase sensor codes. Matching codes for phases U and W: P0E00 and P0E08.
c: Electrical fault in the V-phase sensor circuit inside the inverter
Poor contact at the inverter or generator control unit connector
s: Hybrid or engine warning light on
Reduced generator output

P0E05.t: Generator Phase V Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0E05.d: P0E05 reports an implausible zero point of the current sensor in phase V of the generator inverter. Mitsubishi describes it only for the 2023 Outlander PHEV, the first of its generator units with a sensor in phase V; the earlier model measured just U and W. The test mirrors that of the other phases and runs at rest: IGBTs off, generator below 20 rpm, control unit fed with at least 8 V. If the V-phase signal then sits outside 2.3 to 2.7 V for 0.32 s, P0E05-00 is logged and the MIL turns on. As no current can flow in this state, any deviation points to the sensor itself. A zero error left in place would also disturb the three-phase sum check P0DFA, so both codes may appear together. Open or shorted signals of this sensor are P0E06 and P0E07.
c: Zero point of the phase V current sensor drifted
Disturbed sensor supply or reference in the power drive unit
s: MIL and hybrid system warning light on
Possibly also the phase sum code P0DFA stored
Less generator support during hybrid driving

P0E06.t: Generator Phase V Current Sensor Circuit Low
P0E06.d: P0E06 means the phase V current sensor of the generator inverter delivers a signal at the floor of its range. The 2023 Outlander PHEV is the only documented user: Mitsubishi's generator control unit, running on 8 V or more, stores P0E06-00 when the V-phase voltage remains at 0.5 V or below for 0.2 s, and the MIL comes on. Electrically this fits an interrupted signal or supply line or a signal shorted to ground, which is how Mitsubishi's older chart explains the matching U-phase fault. On this model the sensor is integrated in the power module, so the official remedy after a confirming test drive is a new unit. The older Outlander PHEV has no V-phase sensor and therefore never sets P0E06. Related: P0E05 (offset) and P0E07 (signal high).
c: V-phase sensor signal shorted to ground or sensor failed low
Open sensor signal or supply inside the power drive unit
Input of the generator control unit faulty
s: MIL and hybrid system warning light on
Generator power limited

P0E07.t: Generator Phase V Current Sensor Circuit High
P0E07.d: P0E07 is set when the phase V current sensor in the generator inverter reports a signal stuck high. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV has its generator control unit flag P0E07-00 as soon as the V-phase voltage is at 4.5 V or above for 0.2 s while its own supply is at least 8 V; MIL and hybrid warning both illuminate. Real current cannot cause such a value, so the fault lies in the sensor, a short to its supply or in the evaluation circuit. The earlier Outlander PHEV, which measured only phases U and W, has no counterpart. When several phase sensors report high at the same moment, a shared supply problem inside the unit is a more likely explanation than three separate defects. Siblings for phase V: P0E05 (offset) and P0E06 (low).
c: V-phase sensor signal shorted to its supply
Common sensor supply in the power drive unit too high or faulty
Current sensor failed with high output
s: MIL and hybrid system warning light on
Generator switched off or limited
Other phase current sensor codes stored at the same time

P0E08.t: Generator Phase W Current Sensor Circuit
P0E08.d: P0E08 covers an electrical fault of the generator inverter's W-phase current sensor that falls outside the offset, low and high categories. No manufacturer documents P0E08 publicly. Unlike phase V, the W-phase sensor exists on both Outlander PHEV generations Mitsubishi describes: the 2018 model uses it as current sensor 2, the 2023 model as one of three, yet both log its faults only as P0E09, P0E0A and P0E0B. CARB demands circuit monitoring of hybrid components relevant to emissions. A sensor that delivers no usable value at all keeps the inverter from controlling generator torque, so the system will typically cut generator power and rely more on the engine or the battery. Phase U counterpart: P0E00, phase V: P0E04.
c: Electrical fault in the W-phase sensor circuit inside the inverter
Loose or corroded connector at the power drive unit
s: Hybrid or engine warning light on
Reduced generator output, battery charged less while driving

P0E09.t: Generator Phase W Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0E09.d: P0E09 is the zero-point check of the phase W current sensor in the generator inverter. Mitsubishi uses it on two Outlander PHEV generations. The 2018 code chart lists it as an offset fault of current sensor 2, the second of only two generator current sensors. For 2023 the generator control unit runs the same standstill test as for U and V: IGBTs off, generator under 20 rpm, at least 8 V supply, and the W-phase voltage has to stay inside 2.3 to 2.7 V; 0.32 s outside that band sets P0E09-00 and the MIL. On a two-sensor layout an offset in W also corrupts the V current derived from it, so control quality suffers on two phases at once. Hard signal faults of the same sensor are P0E0A and P0E0B.
c: Zero point of the phase W current sensor drifted
Sensor supply or reference in the power drive unit unstable
Evaluation in the generator control unit faulty
s: MIL and hybrid system warning light on
Rough or reduced generator operation
Fault reappears at the next standstill check after clearing

P0E0A.t: Generator Phase W Current Sensor Circuit Low
P0E0A.d: With P0E0A the phase W current sensor of the generator inverter reports a signal at or near zero volts. Mitsubishi covers this code in its Outlander PHEV service information: the 2018 chart attributes it to a short to ground or an open circuit of current sensor 2, and in the 2023 model the generator control unit sets P0E0A-00 after the W-phase voltage has stayed at 0.5 V or lower for 0.2 s with at least 8 V supply, lighting the MIL. On the 2018 two-sensor layout, losing phase W leaves a single measured phase, too little for current control, so generator operation is heavily restricted. Mitsubishi's procedure first deals with codes of higher priority, confirms the fault with a drive cycle and then replaces the power drive unit. Related: P0E09 and P0E0B.
c: W-phase sensor signal shorted to ground or sensor failed low
Open sensor signal or supply inside the power drive unit
Input stage of the generator control unit faulty
s: MIL and hybrid system warning light on
Generator largely out of operation
Battery is charged noticeably less while driving

P0E0B.t: Generator Phase W Current Sensor Circuit High
P0E0B.d: P0E0B marks a phase W current sensor signal in the generator inverter that sits at the top of its range. In the 2023 Outlander PHEV, Mitsubishi's generator control unit records P0E0B-00 when the W-phase voltage stays at no less than 4.5 V over a period of 0.2 s with a supply of at least 8 V, and turns on the MIL; the 2018 code chart names a short to the supply or a short circuit of current sensor 2. A value like this would match a current well above the generator's capability, so it is judged as a sensor fault, not as overcurrent, which Mitsubishi handles separately with P30A3. The code concerns the W-phase sensor alone; an open phase winding or cable shows up as P0E0C instead. Lower-limit and offset faults of this sensor: P0E0A and P0E09.
c: W-phase sensor signal shorted to its supply voltage
Current sensor in the power drive unit failed with high output
Lost sensor ground or reference inside the inverter
s: MIL and hybrid system warning light on
Generator switched off or limited

P0E0C.d: P0E0C concerns the three power phases between generator inverter and generator, not the current sensors. The J2012 title fits the use Mitsubishi documents for the 2023 Outlander PHEV under its own label of generator current deviation: with at least 50 A commanded, the generator between 500 and 4,500 rpm and 8 V supply, a U, V or W current stuck within about 17 A either side of zero for 0.4 s, or a failed comparison with the target current, sets P0E0C-00 and the MIL. A phase that carries no current despite a demand is just what an open line looks like; GM checks drive motor phases in a similar way under P0C05. Likely causes are loose high-voltage terminals, a damaged phase cable or winding, or the inverter. Phase sensor faults are P0E00 to P0E0B.
c: Loose or burnt high-voltage phase terminal between inverter and generator
Phase cable or generator winding interrupted
Power drive unit does not drive one phase (switch or driver fault)
s: MIL and hybrid system warning light on
Generator no longer charges, engine runs without series hybrid support
Possible noise or vibration from the generator under load

P0E0D.d: P0E0D is the low member of the generator phase circuit group: a U, V or W line between inverter and generator is pulled toward the negative high-voltage rail or to ground, for instance through damaged insulation or a lower power switch that conducts when it should not. No manufacturer documents P0E0D publicly. From this trio, Mitsubishi's generator unit in the Outlander PHEV only uses the open-circuit code P0E0C and catches dangerous currents with its own code P30A3; for the comparable drive motor trio GM's hybrid tables use only P0C05. CARB requires circuit monitoring of hybrid components. A low phase usually goes together with overcurrent or insulation warnings, so an insulation test of cable and winding belongs in the diagnosis. High counterpart: P0E0E.
c: Phase cable or winding insulation damaged, leakage to ground
Lower IGBT of one phase leaking or shorted
Phase voltage evaluation in the inverter faulty
s: Hybrid system warning light, possibly with insulation fault message
Generator shut down

P0E0E.d: P0E0E reports a generator phase line that reads high: one of the U, V or W connections is held near the positive high-voltage potential, typically by an upper power switch that stays on or by a short to the positive rail. No manufacturer documents P0E0E publicly; the generator units Mitsubishi describes for the Outlander PHEV only use P0E0C here, and in GM's tables only the open-phase check P0C05 is used for the corresponding drive motor group. CARB still requires circuit faults of hybrid components to be detected. Because a phase stuck high lets current flow without control, inverters normally shut the gate drive off at once; the generator then stops supplying charge and the vehicle runs with restricted hybrid function. Low and open counterparts: P0E0D, P0E0C.
c: Upper IGBT of one phase shorted or not switching off
Phase line shorted to the positive high-voltage rail
Phase monitoring in the inverter faulty
s: Hybrid system warning light and MIL on
Generator shut down, no charging while driving

P0E0F.t: Generator Inverter Power Supply A Circuit/Open
P0E0F.d: P0E0F is set when the generator inverter loses one of its internal supplies, supply A, or the line to it is interrupted. Which supply carries the letter A is up to the manufacturer; usually it is the low-voltage feed of the gate drivers that switch the power transistors. No manufacturer documents P0E0F publicly. The drive motor counterpart P0C0B shows how such a check works at GM: the IGBT module itself reports a bias fault once its gate drive supply drops below a threshold, which the 2011 Volt treats as Type A after a single 2.08 ms event and a 2019 table after 0.168 s within a 0.2 s window. CARB requires circuit monitoring of hybrid components. Without gate drive supply the generator cannot be controlled at all. Low and high variants: P0E10, P0E11; supply B: P2CC5.
c: Gate driver supply inside the inverter failed
12 V feed, fuse or connector of the inverter interrupted
s: Hybrid system warning light and MIL on
Generator out of operation, vehicle may not reach ready state

P0E10.t: Generator Inverter Power Supply A Circuit Low
P0E10.d: P0E10 means supply A of the generator inverter is present but too low. Ford lists the code in the HEV OBD system summary for its power-split hybrids (OBDSM1901): in the paragraph on the gate signal lines of motor and generator, P0E10 appears with P0BCE and P0BCF among the generator-side open-circuit faults, while the motor side is covered by P0C0C. For Ford, P0E10 is therefore tied to the gate drive path of the generator inverter rather than to a separate supply part, and no voltage limit is published. CARB requires circuit monitoring for such hybrid components. A weak gate drive supply can leave the power switches only partly turned on so they overheat, which is why the inverter limits or stops the generator. Siblings: P0E0F and P0E11.
c: Gate drive supply or gate signal path in the inverter faulty (Ford)
Low 12 V supply to the inverter, e.g. weak battery or poor ground
s: Hybrid system warning light and MIL on
Generator limited or switched off, reduced hybrid performance

P0E11.t: Generator Inverter Power Supply A Circuit High
P0E11.d: P0E11 is stored when supply A of the generator inverter is above its permitted range. Overvoltage on the gate driver feed can overstress the control inputs of the power transistors, so controllers usually react by blocking the inverter. No manufacturer documents P0E11 publicly. Ford's hybrid summary shows that such supplies are watched: a gate drive power supply above 15.08 V counts as a fault there, though Ford files it under a rotor position circuit voltage check and not under P0E11. CARB asks for circuit fault detection on hybrid parts. A short between two supply rails or a faulty regulator inside the inverter are the likely causes; a charging system fault on the 12 V side can also contribute. Siblings: P0E0F and P0E10; supply B high: P2CC7.
c: Voltage regulator of the gate driver supply in the inverter faulty
Short between two internal supply rails
Overvoltage in the 12 V system (DC/DC converter or charging fault)
s: Hybrid system warning light and MIL on
Generator blocked, no charging while driving

P0E12.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Heater A Control Circuit/Open
P0E12.d: P0E12 concerns the command circuit of battery coolant heater A, the electric element that warms the coolant sent to the hybrid or EV battery when the pack is too cold for charging or full power. The controller flags it when this circuit is open or otherwise electrically faulty. No manufacturer documents P0E12 publicly. GM's 2016 Volt shows the same check under its own code P1EC3: above 10.2 V system voltage, 20 failed readings within 40 samples taken every 100 ms set a Type B code. CARB requires every electronic output used to heat the energy store to be checked for circuit faults. Typical finds are a cracked conductor, an unseated connector or a dead output stage. In frost the car may then limit charging or rely on the engine. Shorts to ground or voltage are P0E13 and P0E14.
c: Broken or chafed wire in the heater A command circuit
Loose, corroded or unlocked connector at the heater or controller
Open circuit inside the heater A assembly
Failed output driver in the controlling module
s: Check engine light on
Slow or reduced charging in cold weather
Engine runs more often than usual on cold days
Reduced electric power until the pack warms up

P0E13.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Heater A Control Circuit Low
P0E13.d: P0E13 is the low-signal case on the command line of battery coolant heater A: the controller reads the line near ground at a moment when it expects a higher level, which points to a short to ground or a driver that cannot pull the circuit up. No manufacturer documents P0E13 publicly. GM's 2016 Volt folds open circuit, ground short and voltage short of its battery heater transistor into the single code P1EC3, rated Type B. Keep this low-voltage command fault apart from an isolation fault of the high-voltage heater element: GM bulletin PIC5920B lists the battery heater of the 2011–2014 Volt and 2014 ELR as one possible cause of isolation codes. CARB requires circuit checks on battery heating outputs. With the heater stuck off, winter charging slows down. P0E12 is the open circuit, P0E14 the high case.
c: Command wire shorted to ground, e.g. chafed against the body
Moisture or coolant in the heater connector
Internal short in the heater's control input
Output driver in the controller stuck low
s: Check engine light on
Battery heater does not work at low temperatures
Longer charging times in winter

P0E14.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Heater A Control Circuit High
P0E14.d: P0E14 is logged when heater A's control wire sits too high, typically because it touches a supply voltage or because a pulled-up input has lost its connection. No manufacturer documents P0E14 publicly; GM's 2016 Volt reports open, ground and voltage faults of its heater transistor together as P1EC3 (Type B). The high case deserves care because, depending on the design, a line held at supply voltage can keep the heater energised against the controller's will. Heater makers guard against that: a patent now held by PTI EV Hybrid describes a battery coolant heater with a thermistor in its housing that cuts power when the coolant warms faster than a set rate. CARB requires circuit monitoring of battery heating outputs. P0E13 is the low counterpart, P0E12 the open circuit.
c: Command wire shorted to a supply or neighbouring live wire
Open connection on a pulled-up heater input reading as high
Output driver in the controller that will not switch off
s: Check engine light on
Heater shut down by its own overheat protection
Battery heating unavailable or erratic in cold weather

P0E15.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Heater A Control Performance
P0E15.d: P0E15 means heater A can be addressed electrically but does not deliver the heat it was asked for. Stellantis uses the code on Chrysler Pacifica plug-in hybrids from 2017 onward and the 2021–2023 Jeep Wrangler 4xe for the high-voltage electric coolant heater (ECH), a LIN-controlled unit that on these models heats the cabin loop. The ECH locks itself after low or high voltage, lost communication or overheating; repeated overheating locks it until service or, on the Wrangler after the third event, for good, and P0E15 must be present for the reset routine. Causes named are coolant leaks, air, frozen or wrong coolant, a faulty auxiliary pump, supply problems or the heater itself. Several bulletins (08-052-22, 08-080-26) cure false or permanent P0E15 entries with HCP/AHCP software. The MIL comes on and EV mode may be lost.
c: Low coolant, leaks or trapped air in the heater loop
Hybrid control software that needs an update (Stellantis HCP/AHCP)
Heater unit permanently locked or internally failed
Faulty auxiliary coolant pump or restricted hoses
High- or low-voltage supply fault or LIN bus problem at the heater
s: Check engine light on
Message that electric mode is unavailable, engine keeps running
Little or no heat from the electric heater
Permanent code may block an emissions inspection

P0E16.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Heater B Control Circuit/Open
P0E16.d: P0E16 is the open-circuit code for a second battery coolant heater, B. Why a car has two: some thermal systems pair the pack heater with another heater, for example one for the cabin loop, and can route its heat to the battery. A patent from Magna E-Car describes exactly that fallback when the battery pack heater fails, so the letter depends on how the maker splits the heaters. No manufacturer documents P0E16 publicly, and none of the GM, Ford or Stellantis papers checked used it. The logic matches heater A, which GM's 2016 Volt checks as P1EC3 with 20 failures in 40 samples (Type B). CARB requires circuit monitoring of each output used to heat the energy store. Look for a broken wire, a loose connector or an open element. P0E17 and P0E18 are the shorts.
c: Broken wire in the heater B command circuit
Loose or corroded connector at heater B
Open element or electronics inside heater B
s: Check engine light on
Battery warms up slowly in cold weather
Reduced charging power at low temperatures

P0E17.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Heater B Control Circuit Low
P0E17.d: P0E17 reports that the command signal to battery coolant heater B stays too low, most often from a short to ground between controller and heater. No manufacturer documents P0E17 publicly. Some designs give the second heater a different job, such as warming the cabin loop, and only borrow it for the pack when needed, as a Magna E-Car patent outlines; the wiring of heater B may then run through other areas than that of heater A. GM covers ground shorts of its battery heater command inside the broader code P1EC3 on the 2016 Volt (Type B), so an exact low-only threshold is not public. CARB requires circuit checks on heating outputs of the energy store. Chafing near brackets and water in the plug are the classic finds. Open circuit is P0E16, short to voltage P0E18.
c: Heater B command wire shorted to ground
Water or coolant in the heater B connector
Internal short at the control input of heater B
s: Check engine light on
Second heater does not support battery warm-up
Slower charging in winter

P0E18.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Heater B Control Circuit High
P0E18.d: P0E18 says the command line of battery coolant heater B reads high when the controller expects it low, for example from contact with a supply wire or an interrupted pulled-up input. No manufacturer documents P0E18 publicly. The risk here is a heater that cannot be switched off. Many coolant heaters therefore carry their own guard; one patent design with a thermistor in the heater housing stops current when the coolant temperature climbs faster than a limit. GM's 2016 Volt groups voltage shorts of its battery heater command into P1EC3 (Type B). CARB requires circuit monitoring of energy-store heating outputs and, where possible, a functional check of heating. A pinched wire against a live feed or a driver that sticks on is typical. Short to ground is P0E17, open circuit P0E16.
c: Heater B command wire shorted to a voltage source
Interrupted pulled-up input at heater B
s: Check engine light on
Heater B switched off by its overheat protection
Battery heating unavailable in cold weather

P0E19.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Heater B Control Performance
P0E19.d: P0E19 means heater B is commanded and electrically intact but the expected warming does not follow. No manufacturer documents P0E19 publicly. How such a test works is visible in GM's 2016 Volt, where the battery heater performance code P1EC6 runs once per drive or charge: during an active heat request the pack inlet coolant must gain more than 3 °C within 154.1 s, otherwise a Type B fault is stored; it is skipped while coolant level or inlet temperature sensor codes are active. CARB asks for such a functional check of heating where feasible. Air in the loop, a weak pump, a blocked hose or a failing element are the usual causes, and a wrongly routed valve can send the heat elsewhere. Unlike P0E15 for heater A, this concerns the second heater. P0E16 to P0E18 are its circuit codes.
c: Air pocket or low coolant level in the battery loop
Heater B element producing too little heat
Weak pump, restricted hose or coolant valve in the wrong position
Inlet coolant temperature sensor reading wrongly
s: Check engine light on
Battery stays cold for a long time after a cold start
Reduced charging and drive power in winter

P0E1A.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump B Control Circuit/Open
P0E1A.d: P0E1A reports an open or otherwise faulty command circuit for battery coolant pump B, a second electric pump found where the battery loop is split or a separate circuit feeds a chiller or heater. No manufacturer documents P0E1A publicly. For pump A, GM's 2019 tables show how the controller judges such a line by current: while running, below 200 mA or above 3 A is a fault, while off, below 120 µA; failing for 4 s within a 5 s window gives a Type B code. A second pump would usually be monitored the same way. CARB requires every electronic output of battery thermal management to be checked for circuit faults. Usually a wire has parted, a connector has backed out or the pump itself is dead. The low and high cases are P0E1B and P0E1C; supply and speed faults of pump B have their own codes, P2CF4 to P2CF7.
c: Broken wire in the pump B command circuit
Loose or corroded connector at pump B
Failed pump output in the controlling module
s: Check engine light on
Battery or electronics temperatures rise faster under load
Reduced power or charging rate

P0E1B.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump B Control Circuit Low
P0E1B.d: P0E1B narrows a pump B command fault down to a level below the expected window, normally because the control or PWM wire has a ground fault, or because a driver that cannot raise it. No manufacturer documents P0E1B publicly. The nearest documented relative is P0C48 for pump A, which Ford listed for the 2020 Explorer, Police Interceptor Utility and Lincoln Aviator hybrids and traced to battery energy control module software that is reprogrammed. A software cause of that kind is worth ruling out first before cutting into the harness. Physically, a low reading often comes from insulation rubbed through on a bracket or from coolant wicking into the connector. CARB wants each thermal management output checked for such faults. If pump B stops as a result, the loop it serves loses flow. Open circuit is P0E1A, short to voltage P0E1C.
c: Pump B control or PWM wire shorted to ground
Coolant or water in the pump connector
Control module software fault, as seen by Ford on the pump A sibling
Internal short at the pump B control input
s: Check engine light on
Pump B does not run
Power limited when the components it cools get hot

P0E1C.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump B Control Circuit High
P0E1C.d: P0E1C is set when the command signal to battery coolant pump B stays above what the controller allows, for instance because the line is shorted to battery voltage or, on a pulled-up PWM input, interrupted. No manufacturer documents P0E1C publicly. Its pump A counterpart P0C49 appears in Ford bulletin 20-2293 for the 2020 Lincoln Aviator hybrid among MIL codes for the coolant pumps, with BECM reprogramming as the fix. In contrast to a ground short, a line held high can either keep a simple on/off pump running continuously or, with PWM pumps that read a steady high as an invalid command, make the pump fall back to a default speed or stop. CARB requires circuit monitoring of thermal management outputs. Look for a wire touching a live feed. P0E1B is the low case, P0E1A the open circuit.
c: Pump B control wire shorted to battery voltage
Interrupted pulled-up PWM input at the pump
Control module software fault, as Ford found for pump A
s: Check engine light on
Pump B runs constantly or not at all
Reduced power under heavy load

P0E1D.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump B Control Performance
P0E1D.d: P0E1D says pump B accepts its command electrically but the effect the controller looks for does not appear, such as the expected flow, speed or temperature change in its loop. No manufacturer documents P0E1D publicly. The model is pump A on the 2011 Chevrolet Volt: once the pump has run for over 60 s, the pack inlet coolant temperature must have shifted by at least 5 °C, otherwise a Type B code is set. GM bulletin PI0798A traces that pump A code after a drain and refill to trapped air, cleared with a vacuum purge, which is also the first check for pump B after service work. CARB calls for a functional check of battery cooling where feasible. Worn bearings, a clogged inlet or a sensor reading wrongly are further causes. Pump B speed faults may also show as P2CF6 or P2CF7.
c: Air trapped in the loop after a coolant service
Worn pump B or debris blocking its impeller or inlet
Low coolant level or leak in the battery loop
Coolant temperature sensor giving an implausible value
s: Check engine light on
Battery or electronics temperatures higher than normal
Gurgling noise from the coolant loop
Power or charging rate limited

P0E1E.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump B Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P0E1E.d: P0E1E does not describe the wire or the pump directly but the switching stage that drives pump B: that driver has reported excess current or overheating and has protected itself. Such smart switches measure their own state; a TI automotive high-side switch, for example, turns off at about 150 °C junction temperature or on reaching its current limit and signals the fault on a diagnostic pin. No manufacturer documents P0E1E publicly. GM's 2019 tables show a comparable monitor for a different load, the fuel pump driver code P1255: a board temperature of 160 °C or more, 3 failures in 15 samples, Type B. A pump that drags or seizes, a partial short in the motor or a hot mounting spot of the module are typical. Pump A has the same code as P0E1F.
c: Pump B binding or seized, drawing too much current
Partial short in the pump motor or its wiring
Driver in the module overheating due to location or poor cooling
Degraded output driver in the control module
s: Check engine light on
Pump B switches off intermittently
Battery or electronics temperature rises, power is limited

P0E1F.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump A Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P0E1F.d: P0E1F reports that the output stage switching battery coolant pump A has hit its current or temperature limit. Ford uses the code on its 2020 hybrids. On the Escape HEV built up to 10 June 2020, bulletin 20-2221 lists P0E1F in the battery energy control module beside pump and battery codes and blames strategies in the BECM software, fixed by reprogramming PCM and BECM. Bulletins 20-2293 and 20-2345 name it for the Explorer, Police Interceptor Utility and Aviator hybrids, with the MIL on and a BECM update as the cure. If software is ruled out, the hardware logic applies: smart switches such as TI's automotive high-side parts shut off at their current limit or around 150 °C and report the event. A stiff pump, a short in the motor or a heat-soaked module remain. Pump B has the same code as P0E1E.
c: Battery energy control module software (Ford 2020 hybrids)
Pump A binding or seized and drawing excess current
Partial short in the pump motor or harness
Output driver overheating in the module
s: Check engine light on
Battery coolant pump stops intermittently
Hybrid power limited when the battery gets warm

P0E20.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve A Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P0E20.d: P0E20 points at the driver that powers coolant control valve A: its output has exceeded a current limit or run too hot and switched itself off. No manufacturer documents P0E20 publicly. Valve A is often a small motor actuator; on the 2011 Chevrolet Volt it is driven in both directions through two drive lines, each with its own ground and voltage short checks (90 failures in 100 samples at 6.25 ms, Type B). Driving a motor into a jammed end stop is exactly what heats such a stage, so a sticking valve is a prime suspect. Mercedes reports the electrical fault of its battery shutoff valve as P0CDF00 instead. TI's automotive smart switches illustrate the protection itself: shut-off at the current limit or near 150 °C, with a fault flag. P0E21 and P0E22 cover valves B and C.
c: Valve A sticking or jammed so the actuator stalls
Partial short in the valve actuator motor or its wiring
Degraded valve driver in the control module
s: Check engine light on
Valve A stays in its last position
Battery runs too warm or too cold, power or charging limited

P0E21.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve B Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P0E21.d: P0E21 is the overload or overheat report of the driver for coolant control valve B. No manufacturer documents P0E21 publicly. What B means differs between makers: on the 2011 Chevrolet Volt, GM's own codes for valve B (P1EC7, P1EC8) actually watch the second drive line of the same valve motor that serves as valve A, whereas other layouts have a physically separate second valve for a chiller or radiator branch. For diagnosis it is therefore worth checking first which actuator the maker calls B. The protection itself works like that of TI's integrated high-side switches for cars, which cut off at their current limit or near 150 °C and report it. CARB obliges makers to monitor these outputs electrically. Electrical circuit faults of valve B are P0D1A, P0D1D and P0D1E.
c: Valve B binding so its actuator stalls against the stop
Short or low resistance in the valve B actuator or harness
Degraded driver stage in the control module
s: Check engine light on
Coolant routing does not change as commanded
Battery temperature drifts, power or charging limited

P0E22.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve C Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P0E22.d: P0E22 tells that the driver for a third coolant control valve, C, has protected itself against excessive current or heat. No manufacturer documents P0E22 publicly, and none of the reviewed GM, Ford, Stellantis or Mercedes documents uses a valve C at all. Three valves suggest a loop with several branches, for example radiator, air-conditioning chiller and heater, with C switching one of them. Unlike a plain ground short (P0DEB), the overload code catches a load that still conducts but draws too much, so a stiff valve or a shorted turn in its motor is the likely trigger rather than a broken wire. CARB requires that every electronic output of battery thermal management be checked for circuit faults; TI's automotive smart switches show the mechanism: they disconnect once current reaches the limit or the junction nears 150 °C.
c: Valve C stiff or jammed by deposits
Shorted turn in the valve C actuator motor
Degraded driver stage in the control module
s: Check engine light on
One branch of the coolant loop no longer switches
Battery overcooled in winter or kept too warm in summer

P0E23.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor G Circuit
P0E23.d: P0E23 is the catch-all circuit code of drive motor inverter temperature sensor G, a thermistor that watches the power switches of the motor inverter. It stands for an electrical fault the controller cannot pin down as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents P0E23 publicly. The only published user of the G series is Mitsubishi: in the 2023 Outlander PHEV the seventh IGBT sensor of the front motor unit (U-phase H2) reports its faults as P0E24, P0E25 and P0E26, but not as P0E23. CARB requires hybrid input components to be tested for open circuits and out-of-range signals. Without a valid temperature the inverter is usually run with reduced torque; the sensor sits inside the inverter, so repair often means that assembly.
c: Temperature sensor or sensing board inside the inverter failed
Poor contact at an internal or external inverter connector
Faulty evaluation input in the motor control unit
s: Hybrid system warning light and MIL on
Reduced electric drive power

P0E24.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor G Circuit Range/Performance
P0E24.d: P0E24 is the plausibility test of inverter temperature sensor G: the signal is electrically fine, but the temperature it reports does not fit. Mitsubishi uses the code on the 2023 Outlander PHEV for IGBT sensor number 7 in the front motor control unit, labelled U-phase H2. The check runs only after a soak of at least 600 s, with the IGBTs shut down and the unit fed with 8 V or more, within 1.5 s of these conditions being met. Should it then deviate from either of two other IGBT temperatures by more than 47 °C for 0.1 s, P0E24-00 is logged; MIL and plug-in hybrid warning light both light up. After a long stand all switches should be equally warm, so the code points to a drifting sensor. Mitsubishi's flow ends with a new power drive unit.
c: Sensor G reads offset against the other IGBT sensors
Fault on the sensing circuit of the power drive unit
Uneven inverter cooling, e.g. air in the coolant circuit
s: MIL and plug-in hybrid warning light on
Often no noticeable change in driving

P0E25.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor G Circuit Low
P0E25.d: P0E25 means the voltage of inverter temperature sensor G has fallen below its valid window. In the 2023 Outlander PHEV, Mitsubishi assigns it to the U-phase H2 sensor of the front motor control unit and sets P0E25-00 once that signal does not rise above 1.25 V during 0.08 s with a unit supply of 8 V upward; the MIL is switched on together with the hybrid warning lamp. Mitsubishi states only the voltage. For an NTC element fed through a pull-up resistor, as GM describes for its inverter sensors, a low voltage equals a very hot sensor, so a ground short or a damaged sensing line looks like an overheated switch. Real overheating is reported by separate temperature codes. The opposite limit is P0E26; the sensor is not sold separately.
c: Sensor signal shorted to ground inside the inverter
Damaged sensing board, e.g. after coolant ingress
s: MIL and hybrid warning light on
Motor power limited as if the inverter were overheating

P0E26.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor G Circuit High
P0E26.d: P0E26 is logged when the signal of inverter temperature sensor G climbs above its permitted range. In the 2023 Outlander PHEV it belongs to the front motor unit's U-phase H2 sensor: at least 3.75 V lasting 0.08 s, with at least 8 V supply to the unit, sets P0E26-00 together with MIL and hybrid warning light. With an NTC element and pull-up resistor, the layout GM documents for its inverter thermistors, such a voltage would mean an extremely cold power switch, which a working inverter never shows; the usual reasons are an open sensing line, a lost reference ground or a broken thermistor. The low-side fault is P0E25. Because the sensor is built into the unit, Mitsubishi replaces the power drive unit.
c: Open sensing line or broken thermistor
Signal shorted to the sensor supply
s: MIL and hybrid warning light on
Reduced electric drive power as a precaution

P0E27.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor G Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E27.d: P0E27 marks short dropouts or jumps in the signal of inverter temperature sensor G. Between the events the reading is normal again, which is what separates it from the steady faults P0E25 and P0E26. No manufacturer documents P0E27 publicly; Mitsubishi, the one documented user of sensor G on the 2023 Outlander PHEV, checks that sensor for plausibility and for both voltage limits only. CARB expects hybrid sensor circuits to be monitored for circuit faults, which covers unstable signals as well. Likely sources are a connector with poor contact, a cracked solder joint on the sensing board or a thermistor with unstable resistance. The code can vanish before the workshop sees it, and the drive may be limited while it is active.
c: Intermittent contact at an inverter connector
Cracked solder joint on the sensing board
s: Warning light that comes and goes
Brief drops in electric drive power

P0E28.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor H Circuit
P0E28.d: Sensor H is the eighth temperature sensor of a drive motor inverter, and P0E28 is its general circuit code for an electrical fault without a more precise low, high or erratic finding. No manufacturer documents P0E28 publicly. Mitsubishi, whose 2023 Outlander PHEV is the documented user of the H series, calls the part FMCU IGBT temperature sensor 8 (V-phase H2) and files its faults under P0E29, P0E2A and P0E2B; the general circuit code is not listed. Which component carries letter H is up to each maker. CARB requires hybrid input components to be checked for interruptions and for readings outside their range. When the value is missing, the controller has to protect that phase by limiting torque; the sensor is part of the inverter assembly.
c: Sensor H or its sensing board in the inverter failed
Connector or internal wiring fault in the inverter
Evaluation input of the motor control unit faulty
s: Hybrid warning light and MIL on
Limited motor torque

P0E29.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor H Circuit Range/Performance
P0E29.d: With P0E29 the controller doubts the reading of inverter temperature sensor H although its voltage is valid. On the 2023 Outlander PHEV Mitsubishi uses it for IGBT sensor 8 of the front motor unit, the V-phase H2 position. The cold-start comparison is the same one used for sensors 1 to 7: soak of 600 s or more, IGBTs off, supply at least 8 V, test window of 1.5 s; a difference above 47 °C to either of two reference IGBT temperatures, held for 0.1 s, stores P0E29-00 and lights the MIL and the hybrid warning light. A sensor that is wrong by that much after a cold soak is offset, not overheated. The sibling for the U-phase sensor is P0E24. Mitsubishi verifies it on a test drive before installing a new power drive unit.
c: Sensor H offset against the other IGBT sensors
Measuring circuit in the power drive unit faulty
s: MIL and hybrid warning light on
Driving usually unaffected

P0E2A.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor H Circuit Low
P0E2A.d: P0E2A reports that inverter temperature sensor H delivers a voltage below its lower limit. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV assigns the code to IGBT sensor 8 (V-phase H2) of the front motor control unit, triggered by a voltage at or under 1.25 V lasting 0.08 s while the supply is 8 V or higher; the MIL comes on. Sensor 8 is the last one with a generic code there: for sensors 9 to 12 Mitsubishi falls back on its own P301x codes, since the generic list stops at H. If the circuit is an NTC divider of the type GM documents, low voltage reads as excessive heat, so a ground short makes the inverter look overheated and power is cut back. Genuine phase overheating is a separate code; the high-side fault is P0E2B.
c: Signal of sensor H shorted to ground
Moisture or coolant damage on the sensing board
s: MIL and hybrid warning light on
Power reduction similar to an overheating inverter

P0E2B.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor H Circuit High
P0E2B.d: P0E2B is the upper-limit fault of inverter temperature sensor H. Mitsubishi documents it for the 2023 Outlander PHEV, where sensor H is IGBT sensor 8 at the V-phase H2 position of the front motor unit: a signal reaching 3.75 V for 0.08 s while the unit receives 8 V or more sets P0E2B-00, and the function list shows MIL and hybrid warning light for it. In an NTC circuit with pull-up, as GM uses in its inverters, the controller would read this as an implausibly cold phase, so the cause is almost always electrical: an interrupted signal path, a missing sensor ground or an element that has gone open. Its low-side partner is P0E2A, the U-phase counterpart P0E26. The repair at Mitsubishi is a new power drive unit.
c: Interrupted signal path of sensor H
s: MIL and hybrid warning light on
Drive power may be limited

P0E2C.t: Drive Motor Inverter Temperature Sensor H Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E2C.d: P0E2C covers an unsteady signal from inverter temperature sensor H: it flickers, jumps or drops out for moments and then recovers. That pattern differs from P0E2A and P0E2B, where the voltage stays beyond a limit. No manufacturer documents P0E2C publicly. Mitsubishi watches its sensor 8 on the 2023 Outlander PHEV only for plausibility and the two voltage limits and gives no erratic code for it. CARB's monitoring rules for hybrid input components include such intermittent faults. In practice the trigger tends to be mechanical, such as vibration at a connector, a fine crack in the sensing board or a terminal with corrosion. Freeze frame data and wiggle tests help, since the fault may be gone when the car arrives.
c: Corroded terminal in the sensor circuit
Hairline crack in the sensing board
s: Intermittent warning light
Occasional short power reductions

P0E2D.t: Internal Control Module Hybrid/EV Battery Monitor Performance
