P0E2D.d: P0E2D is an internal self-test result of the module that supervises the high-voltage pack: the part that measures cell voltages, usually a dedicated monitor chip with its own converter and reference, does not behave as expected. It casts doubt on the measurement itself, not on a cell. Battery monitor patents such as Renesas US9735567B2 show the kind of checks involved, for example self-diagnosis of the A/D converter, detection of a broken sense line between cell and chip, or a second, simpler fault monitor. No manufacturer document on an official server explains P0E2D. CARB requires computers and hybrid components feeding the drive to be monitored. Without trusted cell voltages the pack cannot be shielded from over- or undercharge, so power is limited or the car will not get ready.
c: Cell monitoring circuit in the battery control module faulty
Software error in the battery control module
s: Hybrid or EV system warning and MIL on
Reduced power or vehicle not ready to drive

P0E2E.d: P0E2E concerns the high-voltage fuse that protects the branch from the battery to on-board charger A. Battery managements usually judge such a fuse by comparing the voltage ahead of and behind it, as Volvo describes for its HV fuses. Audi documents P0E2E00 for the 2022 Q5 plug-in hybrid: the hybrid battery regulation module J840 stores it intermittently with symptom code 28733, often next to P0A95, and the driver sees an electrical system fault message or the car does not start. According to Audi, a diagnostic irregularity during very dynamic cornering creates the entry without a real defect; replacing the switching unit, as guided fault finding suggests, does not help, a software update does. A truly open charger fuse stops AC charging. P0A95, P0E2F and P0E30 cover other HV fuses.
c: False entry from the battery management software (Audi Q5 PHEV)
Fuse opened after a short in the on-board charger or its cable
Faulty voltage measurement at the fuse
s: Electrical system fault message
No AC charging or vehicle does not start

P0E2F.d: P0E2F says the battery management has found a second high-voltage fuse open, or believes it has. Several makers use it. Mercedes calls it electrical fuse B, the battery-internal fuse protecting auxiliary HV consumers in its plug-in hybrids: a shorted belt starter-alternator or another short in that line blows it, the engine no longer starts and only electric driving remains; once the short is fixed, the 2024 bulletin for series 206, 223, 254 and 290 has the HV battery replaced. On EQB models a DC/DC wake-up fault can set it without a blown fuse. Porsche lists it as fuse 2 on the 2020-22 Taycan, which is then not ready to drive. Volvo and Polestar compare the voltages after the front and rear fuse outputs with pack voltage. Main fuse: P0A95.
c: Short circuit in an HV consumer on the protected branch
False detection by the battery management or DC/DC wake-up fault
Faulty voltage measurement behind the fuse
s: Engine does not start, electric driving only (plug-in hybrids)
Vehicle not ready to drive or propulsion warning
MIL or HV drive system warning on

P0E30.d: P0E30 is the code for a third fuse in the high-voltage system, after A (P0A95) and B (P0E2F). No manufacturer documents P0E30 publicly. How such a fuse is checked can be seen from the siblings: Volvo and Polestar have the battery control module compare the voltage measured after each fuse output with the pack voltage, and Porsche numbers its Taycan fuses as fuse and fuse 2 under P0A95 and P0E2F. A pack with only two fused branches never sets P0E30. What the third fuse protects, for example a heater, compressor or charger branch, is decided by the maker. If it opens, the consumers on that branch lose power; a blown fuse normally follows a short circuit that has to be found before the fuse or the battery unit is replaced.
c: Short circuit in a consumer on the third fused branch
Faulty voltage measurement behind the fuse
Software error in the battery control module
s: HV system warning message
Consumers on the affected branch without function

P0E31.t: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor A Circuit
P0E31.d: P0E31 is the general circuit code of voltage sensor A in a DC/DC converter, the measurement the converter or its controller uses to regulate output voltage. It is used for electrical faults that do not fit the low, high or erratic categories. P0E31 itself is not documented publicly by any manufacturer. GM's 2025 engine tables use the neighbouring codes for the same sensor in a converter that steadies the 12 V supply during engine auto-starts: P0E33 below 1 V, P0E34 above 28 V, P0E32 for implausible values. FCA names sensor A as voltage sensor 1 on the 2021 Ram 1500 eTorque. CARB wants open circuits and out-of-range signals of such inputs reported separately where feasible. With a lost voltage signal the converter tends to stop or run in a fallback mode.
c: Voltage measurement inside the DC/DC converter failed
Wiring or connector fault on the converter
Poor ground connection of the converter
s: Warning light and possibly 12 V battery warning
Engine auto-stop disabled or reduced 12 V supply

P0E32.t: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor A Range/Performance
P0E32.d: P0E32 flags a voltage reading of DC/DC converter sensor A that is electrically valid but does not match a reference. GM's 2025 engine tables (25OBDG03A, ECM) apply it to a converter that holds the 12 V supply steady during auto-starts: in bypass mode the raw output voltage may differ from the ECM run/crank voltage by no more than 2 V, and Type B (two trips) follows once 320 of 400 samples, taken every 12.5 ms, fail. During an auto-crank 8 of 16 samples with at least 6.6 V battery voltage count, as do more than 2 failed auto-cranks out of 3. FCA's flash 08-037-21 for the 2021 Ram 1500 eTorque turns P0E32-00 into a one-trip code. Mercedes ties P0E32FA in the HV converter of S-Class hybrids to sporadic red 12 V messages.
c: Voltage measurement in the converter drifting
Voltage drop on supply, ground or reference wiring
Control software needing an update (FCA, Mercedes)
Weak 12 V battery distorting the comparison during cranking
s: MIL on after two trips (GM)
Red 12 V warning message (Mercedes)
Auto stop/start unavailable

P0E33.t: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor A Low
P0E33.d: P0E33 means the controller reads an implausibly low value from voltage sensor A of a DC/DC converter, typically because the signal wire is shorted to ground. GM documents it in its 2025 engine control tables (25OBDG03A) for a converter that keeps the 12 V network stable while the engine restarts automatically: the raw voltage value 1 must drop below 1 V, and 320 failing samples out of 400 taken every 12.5 ms, about four seconds, are needed. The test runs with at least 6.6 V battery voltage in run/crank or accessory mode. GM rates it Type B, so the MIL comes on after two trips. P0E34 is the opposite case on the same sensor, P0E38 the matching fault on sensor B. Start-stop and the 12 V support can be limited.
c: Sensor signal wire chafed through to ground
Voltage measurement inside the converter failed
Moisture in the converter connector bridging to ground
s: MIL on after two trips (GM)
Auto stop/start no longer available
Possible 12 V voltage dips during engine restarts

P0E34.t: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor A High
P0E34.d: With P0E34 the controller sees a voltage on sensor A of the DC/DC converter that is too high to be real, which points to the signal being shorted to a battery feed or another live wire. In GM's 2025 tables (25OBDG03A) the ECM flags it when raw voltage value 1 exceeds 28 V, far above anything a 12 V converter output should reach. Sampling and confirmation mirror the low case: 320 of 400 readings must fail, battery voltage must be 6.6 V or more, and as a Type B fault it needs two trips before the MIL lights. A real overvoltage of the converter would not normally reach that value, so the wiring and the sensing path come first. Low readings on the same sensor use P0E33; sensor B has P0E39 for the same fault.
c: Signal wire shorted to a battery feed or other live circuit
Lost reference ground of the measurement, signal floats high
Faulty measuring circuit in the converter
s: MIL on after two trips (GM)
Engine auto-stop disabled

P0E35.t: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor A Intermittent/Erratic
P0E35.d: P0E35 is reserved for a voltage sensor A signal that jumps or drops out briefly instead of staying wrong: the reading is erratic, but not low or high long enough for P0E33 or P0E34 to mature. No manufacturer documents P0E35 publicly. The neighbouring GM codes for the same sensor (25OBDG03A, a converter backing up the 12 V network during engine auto-starts) show the frame: valid readings lie between 1 V and 28 V and are sampled every 12.5 ms. CARB expects input faults to be split into circuit, out-of-range and, where feasible, rationality checks; an erratic code captures the unstable signal in between. Loose terminals, a cracked solder joint or a ground that only fails under vibration are the usual suspects, so the fault may come and go.
c: Loose or spread terminal in the converter connector
Ground connection that fails under vibration
Cracked solder joint in the converter's measuring circuit
s: Warning light that appears and disappears
Start-stop works only now and then

P0E36.t: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor B Circuit
P0E36.d: P0E36 is the catch-all circuit code for the second voltage measurement of a DC/DC converter, sensor B. Where a converter reads both its input and its output, or monitors one rail twice, the second path gets the letter B; FCA names it voltage sensor 2 on the 2021 Ram 1500 eTorque. No manufacturer documents P0E36 itself in public sources. GM's 2025 engine tables treat sensor B through its sibling codes only: below 1 V is P0E38, above 28 V is P0E39, and a gap of more than 2 V to the ECM run/crank voltage is P0E37. P0E36 is left for electrical faults that fit none of those, such as an open line the controller recognises as such. CARB asks for circuit faults of inputs to be detected separately where feasible. Converter output may be reduced.
c: Open sense wire or unplugged connector
Second measuring path inside the converter failed
s: Warning light, possibly 12 V battery warning
Start-stop disabled or converter output reduced

P0E37.t: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor B Range/Performance
P0E37.d: P0E37 says that voltage sensor B delivers a believable number which nevertheless disagrees with what the vehicle measures elsewhere. GM's 2025 engine tables (25OBDG03A) check raw voltage value 2 of the converter against the ECM run/crank voltage: in bypass mode a gap above 2 V counts, and 320 failed samples out of 400 at 12.5 ms set a Type B code. During an automatic engine restart the converter stabilises the 12 V supply, and then 8 of 16 samples are enough. FCA, which calls this channel voltage sensor 2, changed the code from a two-trip to a one-trip code with flash 08-037-21 for the 2021 Ram 1500 eTorque. Drift in the measurement, voltage drop on wiring or outdated software are typical; hard shorts are P0E38 and P0E39.
c: Second voltage measurement in the converter drifting
Voltage drop on supply or ground wiring distorting the comparison
Controller software needing an update (FCA eTorque)
s: MIL on, after one or two trips depending on maker and software
Start-stop unavailable

P0E38.t: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor B Low
P0E38.d: P0E38 is stored when the second voltage reading of the DC/DC converter, sensor B, sits at the bottom of its scale. GM uses it in the 2025 engine tables (25OBDG03A) with the same limits as on sensor A, only applied to raw voltage value 2: under 1 V, confirmed by 320 of 400 samples taken at 12.5 ms intervals and only checked at 6.6 V battery voltage or more. GM's description calls it a test for short to ground, and the result is Type B with the MIL on the second trip. Because GM uses two independent paths, a fault on just one of them points to that path's wiring or circuit rather than the converter output itself. Sensor A's low code is P0E33; P0E39 covers sensor B reading too high.
c: Sensor B signal wire shorted to ground
Failed second measuring circuit in the converter
Bent or corroded pin in the converter connector
s: MIL on after two trips (GM)
Auto stop/start inhibited

P0E39.t: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor B High
P0E39.d: P0E39 reports that sensor B of the DC/DC converter reads far too high, a pattern GM attributes to a short to battery. The 2025 engine tables (25OBDG03A) set the bar at more than 28 V for raw voltage value 2, again needing 320 failing samples within 400 at 12.5 ms and a battery voltage of at least 6.6 V, with Type B confirmation over two trips. If only sensor B shows the excess while sensor A and the ECM's own run/crank reading stay normal, a wiring fault on the B path is far more likely than a converter that really puts out such a voltage. A lost reference ground can also let the signal float upward. Sensor A's high code is P0E34; a low reading on sensor B is P0E38, an implausible but valid one P0E37.
c: Sensor B signal shorted to a voltage-carrying wire
Open reference ground letting the signal float high
Failed measuring circuit for sensor B
s: MIL on after two trips (GM)
Start-stop switched off

P0E3A.t: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor B Intermittent/Erratic
P0E3A.d: P0E3A covers an unsteady signal from voltage sensor B of a DC/DC converter: short spikes, dropouts or noise that never last long enough for the hard low or high codes. Publicly, no manufacturer documents P0E3A. For orientation, GM's 2025 engine tables (25OBDG03A) accept 1 to 28 V on raw voltage value 2 and only set P0E38 or P0E39 after roughly four seconds out of five of continuous failure, so brief disturbances slip past those tests. FCA calls this channel voltage sensor 2 on the Ram 1500 eTorque. CARB wants inputs checked for circuit, range and rationality faults; an erratic code is the gap filler. A fault confined to sensor B while sensor A is steady narrows the search to the B wiring and its terminals, often in a spot that moves with the engine.
c: Harness rubbing intermittently where it moves with the engine
Poor terminal tension in the sensor B circuit
Electrical interference on an unshielded sense line
s: Sporadic warning light, sometimes cleared on its own
Start-stop unavailable from time to time

P0E3B.d: P0E3B indicates that the electric pump circulating coolant through the high-voltage battery turns faster than commanded. A pump that suddenly spins too freely has usually lost its load, because it is moving air instead of coolant after a leak, a low reservoir or a poorly bled system. No manufacturer documents P0E3B publicly. GM's 2019 hybrid tables (19OBDG01) show how such a check works under a maker-specific code (P19FF): the controller filters the difference between commanded and reported pump speed and flags a deviation in either direction; if the pump is meant to be off but still reports over 250 rpm, that counts as well, all as Type B. The sibling P0E3C covers a pump that is too slow. Battery cooling may be reduced and charge or power limited.
c: Low coolant level or leak, pump running partly dry
Air left in the battery loop after a repair
Faulty pump electronics or speed feedback signal
s: Hybrid or EV system warning
Reduced charging or drive power when the battery warms up

P0E3C.d: P0E3C is set when the battery coolant pump stays below the speed it has been asked for. GM documents it specifically for the 2024–25 Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray: the battery energy control module (K16) stores P0E3C, and the ECM may add P0A7B to switch on the MIL. Bulletin 24-NA-160 traces it to air collecting in the hoses next to the pump after an earlier repair; the pump halts to protect itself, which the module reads as underspeed. The fix is to lower the pump below the other plumbing and have a scan tool spin it for a quarter of an hour at 4,000 rpm, topping up the 1.9 litre loop, and to repeat if needed. Only if the code returns after two or more purges is the pump itself diagnosed. Overspeed of the same pump is P0E3B.
c: Air trapped around the pump after earlier service (GM 24-NA-160)
Worn pump bearing or debris slowing the impeller
Low supply voltage or poor ground at the pump
s: MIL on, with P0A7B stored in the ECM (Corvette E-Ray)
Electric front-axle drive limited when the battery gets hot

P0E3D.t: Control Pilot Indicator Control Circuit Low
P0E3D.d: P0E3D concerns the lamp or LED that shows the state of the pilot connection to the charging station, not the pilot signal itself. Low means the driver circuit reads too little voltage, typically because the line to the LED is shorted to ground. No manufacturer documents P0E3D publicly. GM's Volt tables for 2011 and 2012 (11OBDG01, 12OBDG01A) fold this case into the older open-circuit code P0D2B: a ground short is detected while the LED is commanded on, with 12 failed samples out of 15 at one sample every 100 ms, Type B. The current code set gives the ground short its own code, while P0E3E takes the short to voltage. The indicator stays dark or wrong, charging normally continues. Pilot line faults are P0CF3 and P0CF4.
c: Wire to the indicator LED shorted to ground at the charge port
Faulty output driver in the controlling module
s: Pilot indicator stays dark when it should light
Charging itself usually unaffected

P0E3E.t: Control Pilot Indicator Control Circuit High
P0E3E.d: P0E3E is the high-side counterpart for the control pilot indicator circuit: the module senses voltage on the LED line when there should be little or none, the classic sign of a short to a supply wire. Publicly, no manufacturer documents P0E3E. On the Chevrolet Volt, GM's 2011 and 2012 tables still handle this under P0D2B, as a second case checked while the LED is commanded off, where 40 of 50 readings, one per 100 ms, have to fail. Shorts to voltage tend to come from chafed wiring at the charge port, where several feeds run side by side, or from a failed driver stage. The LED may glow permanently or flicker regardless of the real pilot state. P0E3D is the low case, P0D2B the open circuit; charging is normally not blocked.
c: Indicator wire chafed against a supply wire near the charge port
Output stage in the module stuck on
Water in the charge port connector bridging pins
s: Pilot indicator lit or flickering without reason
Misleading charge port light while charging works

P0E3F.t: Charge Status Indicator A Control Circuit Low
P0E3F.d: P0E3F reports that the output feeding charge status indicator A sits too low in voltage. That light confirms to the owner that the vehicle is charging, and the expected cause is an LED line touching ground. No manufacturer documents P0E3F publicly. GM's Chevrolet Volt tables for 2012 (12OBDG01A) still count this situation under P0D2C: the ground short is looked for while the LED is commanded on, and 40 failing samples out of 50, one every 100 ms, confirm it as Type B. Newer code sets split it off as P0E3F, with P0E40 for the short to voltage and P0D2C left for the open circuit. The charge status light stays dark, so the owner cannot tell at a glance whether charging has started, though the charger itself keeps working.
c: LED supply wire pinched or chafed to ground
Failed driver in the controlling module
s: Charge status light stays off during charging
Charging continues normally

P0E40.t: Charge Status Indicator A Control Circuit High
P0E40.d: P0E40 is logged when the drive circuit of charge status indicator A carries voltage although the light is commanded off, typically because the line touches a live wire. P0E40 has no public documentation from any manufacturer. In GM's 2012 Volt tables (12OBDG01A) this is the second case inside P0D2C: with the LED switched off, the hybrid controller looks for a short to battery and needs 40 bad samples out of 50 at 100 ms. A light that glows while nothing is charging, or keeps glowing after charging has ended, is the visible result and can mislead the owner about the charge state. Suspects are wiring near the dash or charge port, water in a connector or a driver stage that no longer switches off. P0E3F is the low case on the same light.
c: Indicator wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit
Output driver no longer switching off
Moisture bridging pins in the indicator connector
s: Charge status light on although nothing is charging
Owner misled about the actual charge state

P0E41.t: Charge Status Indicator B Control Circuit Low
P0E41.d: P0E41 refers to a second charge status light, indicator B, whose driver circuit is pulled too low, usually by a short to ground. Which light carries the letter B is the maker's choice; a lamp at the charge port alongside the dashboard light would be a typical pair. No manufacturer documents P0E41 publicly, and the GM Volt and ELR tables only cover indicator A. By analogy with GM's P0D2C test on light A (12OBDG01A), a ground short would be checked while the LED is commanded on, with 40 of 50 samples at 100 ms. Because indicator B usually sits in the exposed charge port area, a pinched harness or water ingress there deserve the first look. Indicator A keeps working if only B is affected. The open-circuit code for B is P0DE5, the high case P0E42.
c: Indicator B wire pinched to ground near the charge port flap
Water ingress into the charge port light assembly
s: Second charge light (e.g. at the port) stays dark
Main charge indicator and charging unaffected

P0E42.t: Charge Status Indicator B Control Circuit High
P0E42.d: P0E42 means the driver circuit of charge status indicator B shows voltage at a moment when the light should be switched off, pointing to a short to a supply wire or a driver that stays on. P0E42 appears in no public manufacturer document. Indicator A gives the reference: on the 2012 Chevrolet Volt, GM's table 12OBDG01A includes in P0D2C a check for a short to battery while the LED is off, requiring 40 out of 50 failed readings at 100 ms intervals. The same logic would apply to light B. In practice indicator B often belongs to the charge port, so wet or corroded contacts and harness damage at the flap are common starting points. Expect a second light that glows or flickers out of turn. Low is P0E41, open is P0DE5.
c: Indicator B wire touching a live wire at the charge port
Wet or corroded contacts bridging to a supply pin
Output driver for indicator B stuck on
s: Second charge light glowing or flickering when not charging
Charging itself works

P0E43.d: P0E43 is the module-B counterpart of P0A1D: it reports that a second hybrid/EV powertrain controller has detected an internal failure or can no longer be trusted. Vehicles with two such processors, for example GM's Bolt EV with a second powertrain module labelled K114B (HPCM2), are where the letter B makes sense. No manufacturer documents P0E43 publicly. The A code shows what is meant: GM's 2013 hybrid tables store P0A1D when a status message from motor control processor A reports a controller failure in 3 of 4 counts, Type B, and Ford's 2019 hybrid summary uses P0A1D when the serial link between its processors fails, checked continuously. CARB requires the MIL for computer faults that impair OBD. Reprogramming or module replacement is likely; power may be limited.
c: Internal processor or memory fault in module B
Supply, ground or internal bus fault at the module
s: MIL and hybrid or EV system warning
Reduced propulsion power or no ready mode

P0E44.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense E Circuit
P0E44.d: P0E44 is the basic circuit code for the fifth pack voltage measurement, channel E, which follows channels A to D (P0ABA, P0B14, P0B19, P0B1E) in the code list. The battery controller stores it when this input is electrically unusable, for example open, without a plausible raw value or failing a self-test of its measuring stage, and none of the more specific low, high or erratic codes fits. No manufacturer documents P0E44 publicly, and which tap a maker labels E is its own decision. CARB requires every voltage sensor of the hybrid energy storage system to be monitored as an input component, with codes narrowing the fault down to a replaceable part. Without this value the controller restricts or blocks high-voltage operation.
c: Open or unplugged voltage sense lead or connector inside the pack
Faulty measuring stage or input of the battery controller
Blown fuse or open resistor in the sense path
s: Hybrid or high-voltage system warning lit
Reduced electric assist or limited battery power
Vehicle may not switch to ready mode

P0E45.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense E Circuit Range/Performance
P0E45.d: P0E45 says pack voltage measurement E delivers a value that is electrically valid but does not fit the rest of the battery data. Such a rationality test usually compares the channel with the summed block or cell voltages, or with a second pack measurement. No manufacturer documents P0E45 publicly. GM's 2013 two-mode hybrid trucks (Tahoe, Yukon, Escalade, Silverado, Sierra) show the method on channel A: their battery pack control module fails P0ABB once the gap between pack voltage and the added-up block voltages exceeds 50 V in 70 of 80 checks taken every 100 ms, Type A, one trip. CARB requires plausibility monitoring for battery voltage sensors. Circuit, low, high and erratic faults of channel E are P0E44, P0E46, P0E47 and P0E48. Battery power is usually limited.
c: Corroded or loose sense connection adding resistance and skewing the reading
Drifting measuring stage or outdated software in the battery controller
Fault in the reference value, e.g. a block or cell voltage channel
s: Warning light with reduced hybrid or electric power
Displayed state of charge or range jumps unexpectedly

P0E46.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense E Circuit Low
P0E46.d: P0E46 is stored when pack voltage measurement E reads below the lowest value the connected battery could physically present. That points to the measuring path, such as a sense lead shorted to ground, a blown sense fuse or a failed input stage, not to an empty battery. No manufacturer documents P0E46 publicly. On GM's 2013 two-mode hybrid trucks the comparable channel A code P0ABC sets below 40 V, but only after the contactors have been closed for more than 200 ms, and needs 300 failures in 400 samples at 10 ms, Type A, one trip. CARB requires out-of-range checks for battery voltage sensors. The high counterpart is P0E47; a pack that is really deeply discharged sets its own codes such as P0AFA. Hybrid operation may be blocked.
c: Sense lead of channel E shorted to ground or chassis
Blown fuse or open resistor in the sense path pulling the reading down
Defective input stage of the battery controller
s: Vehicle does not become ready to drive or drops out of ready mode
Hybrid system warning and MIL lit
Electric drive or engine assist unavailable

P0E47.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense E Circuit High
P0E47.d: P0E47 means pack voltage measurement E reports more voltage than the pack can reach even when fully charged. A sense lead touching a higher potential, a broken divider resistor or a damaged input of the measuring chip are the usual explanations; real overcharging is unlikely when only one channel shows it. P0E47 is not documented by any manufacturer in public. The 2013 GM two-mode hybrid pickups and SUVs test the analogous channel A against 430 V (P0ABD), using the same 300-of-400 counter at 10 ms and running the test only while the 12 V network sits between 9 and 18 V. CARB requires battery voltage sensors to be tested against plausible limits. Low and plausibility faults of channel E are P0E46 and P0E45. Expect a warning and restricted electric drive.
c: Sense lead of channel E chafed through and touching a higher potential
Broken divider resistor or lost reference in the measuring circuit
Damaged measuring input or software fault in the battery controller
s: MIL and hybrid warning on
Charging or regenerative braking restricted
Electric drive limited or blocked

P0E48.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense E Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E48.d: P0E48 marks pack voltage measurement E as unsteady: the signal jumps, drops out for fractions of a second or changes faster than a battery voltage can, and then returns to normal. Because the fault comes and goes, it is often found only as a stored code after a brief warning. No manufacturer documents P0E48 publicly, and GM's published hybrid tables, for example those of the 2013 two-mode trucks, test pack voltage only for low, high and rationality faults on channel A. CARB requires circuit monitoring of battery voltage sensors in the energy storage system. Steady faults of the same channel are P0E44 to P0E47; channel F uses P0E4D for this fault type. Loose or corroded sense terminals and chafed leads that react to vibration or heat are the usual suspects.
c: Loose, pushed-back or corroded terminal on the channel E sense lead
Chafed sense lead that shorts briefly under vibration
Intermittent fault in the battery controller input
s: Warning light that comes and goes
Brief losses of electric power, often on rough roads
Stored code without a current fault

P0E49.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense F Circuit
P0E49.d: Channel F is the sixth and last pack voltage measurement in this series and comes after channel E (P0E44 to P0E48). P0E49 is its general circuit fault: the battery controller cannot use the input, for instance because the sense line is open, the measuring chip reports an internal error or the raw value is missing, while no clear low, high or erratic pattern applies. No manufacturer documents P0E49 publicly. Systems that compare several high-voltage measurements, as GM's 2019 hybrids do between the pack sensor and the inverter and charger bus voltages, depend on every channel being valid. CARB requires all battery voltage sensors of the storage system to be monitored. The vehicle typically limits or refuses high-voltage operation.
c: Open sense lead or disconnected connector of channel F
Internal fault of the voltage measuring chip or battery controller
Moisture or corrosion in the pack-side connector
s: High-voltage warning and reduced power
Vehicle may refuse to become ready

P0E4A.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense F Circuit Range/Performance
P0E4A.d: P0E4A reports that pack voltage measurement F lies within its electrical range but disagrees with a reference value. No manufacturer documents P0E4A publicly. GM's 2019 hybrid tables show two plausibility checks such a channel could face: P0ABB fails when pack voltage and the summed cell voltages differ by more than 12 V in 20 of 25 samples at 25 ms, and P0AF8 compares the pack sensor with the inverter bus voltage, failing at more than 13.95 V difference in 400 of 500 samples, or at more than 14.95 V against the charger bus. Both are Type A, so the MIL comes on in the first trip. CARB requires rationality monitoring of battery voltage sensors. The electrical faults of channel F are P0E49, P0E4B and P0E4C; channel E uses P0E45.
c: Contact resistance at a sense terminal distorting the channel F value
Fault in the comparison value, such as the inverter bus or cell voltage measurement
Measuring drift or software issue in the battery controller
s: MIL on in the first trip with reduced battery power
Implausible state of charge display

P0E4B.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense F Circuit Low
P0E4B.d: P0E4B sets when pack voltage measurement F falls below its plausible minimum, which normally points to a sense path shorted to ground, an open sense fuse or a defective input of the battery controller. No manufacturer documents P0E4B publicly. As a reference, the battery energy control module in GM's 2019 hybrid tables sets the channel A code P0ABC when pack-side voltage stays under 24 V for 1.6 s within a 2 s window, Type A, one trip, as long as system voltage is at least 9 V. CARB requires out-of-range checks of battery voltage sensors. P0E4C is the high counterpart, P0E4A the plausibility fault, and the matching low code of channel E is P0E46. Because precharge and contactor checks rely on the reading, the vehicle may not reach ready mode.
c: Channel F sense lead shorted to ground or pack housing
Open fuse or resistor in the channel F sense path
Failed analog input of the battery controller
s: No ready mode or contactors do not close
MIL and high-voltage warning on

P0E4C.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense F Circuit High
P0E4C.d: P0E4C means pack voltage measurement F reports a value above anything the battery can produce. Common reasons are a sense line in contact with a higher potential, a lost ground reference in the measuring circuit or a faulty analog input, so the channel rather than the cells is suspect. No manufacturer documents P0E4C publicly. In GM's 2019 hybrid tables the channel A code P0ABD sets above 479 V, again 1.6 s within 2 s and Type A. CARB requires battery voltage sensors to be checked against upper and lower limits. Real overvoltage of single cells is reported by cell voltage codes such as P0DE7, while the low fault of channel F is P0E4B and the same high fault on channel E is P0E47. The controller usually blocks or limits electric operation.
c: Channel F sense line touching a higher potential
Lost ground reference or broken divider in the measuring circuit
Faulty analog input or software of the battery controller
s: Warning lamp and limited electric drive
Charging interrupted or not started

P0E4D.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense F Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E4D.d: P0E4D flags pack voltage measurement F as intermittent: short dropouts, spikes or steps that a real high-voltage battery cannot make, followed by normal readings again. Where a vehicle cross-checks several voltage sensors, as GM does in its 2019 hybrids between the pack sensor and the inverter or charger bus (P0AF8), such glitches can also surface as correlation faults. No manufacturer documents P0E4D publicly. Under CARB rules the storage system's voltage sensors must be watched for circuit faults. Permanent faults of channel F are P0E49 to P0E4C, the same fault type on channel E is P0E48. Typical triggers are loose sense terminals, corrosion inside connectors and leads that move with vibration, so the symptoms appear and vanish.
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the channel F sense circuit
Sense lead that loses contact when the harness moves
Interference or intermittent fault in the measuring electronics
s: Intermittent warning light
Sporadic power limitation
Additional correlation codes stored

P0E4E.d: P0E4E reports that the hybrid system commanded an engine start but the crankshaft did not turn, or did not reach the cranking speed it expected. It differs from P0A0F, where the engine is turned over but does not fire and keep running. In most hybrids a motor-generator fed by the high-voltage battery cranks the engine, so causes range from a seized engine or transaxle to missing battery energy or a drive fault. No manufacturer documents P0E4E publicly. GM's bulletin PIC6229C for the 2016-2019 Malibu hybrid shows why charge matters: below a pack voltage of 154 to 210 V, depending on temperature, the system stops trying to crank until a recovery charge is done. CARB requires the energy storage monitor to catch faults that prevent engine starts.
c: High-voltage battery too low to crank, often after repeated failed starts
Mechanically seized engine or blocked transaxle
Fault in the cranking motor-generator, its inverter or a conventional starter
Crankshaft speed not detected because of a sensor or signal fault
s: Engine does not turn over when the hybrid system calls for it
Vehicle runs electrically only or shows a stop-safely warning
No start at all once the battery is depleted

P0E4F.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump A Control Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E4F.d: P0E4F covers coolant pump A of the motor electronics loop, which cools the inverter and drive motor, and sets when the signal exchanged with the pump becomes unstable rather than permanently open or shorted. Ford uses exactly this code in the OBD summaries for its hybrid and plug-in hybrid models of 2015 to 2019: the pump reports back to the module, and P0E4F is stored when that feedback is outside the expected frequency or duty cycle for more than 1 s. The check runs continuously from 500 ms after power-up with 6 to 19 V on the 12 V network, next to P0A05 (no response for over 9.25 s), P0A06 and P0A07 (driver faults) and P0C73 (pump reports an internal fault). Loose pins or moisture in the pump connector are typical; overheat protection may cut power.
c: Loose, corroded or wet pins in the pump A connector
Chafed command or feedback wire that loses contact intermittently
Failing electronics inside the pump sending an unstable feedback signal
Unstable 12 V supply or poor ground at the pump
s: MIL or hybrid system warning
Power reduction when inverter or motor temperature rises
Fault may clear itself and return later

P0E50.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump B Control Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E50.d: P0E50 is the intermittent or erratic fault of the control circuit for coolant pump B, the second electric pump some hybrids use in the inverter and motor electronics cooling. No manufacturer documents P0E50 publicly. The closest published example is Ford's pump A version, P0E4F, stored when the pump's feedback leaves its expected frequency or duty cycle for over 1 s. Second pumps of this kind are in service: on the 2024 Jeep Compass 4xe, Stellantis bulletin 08-200-24 cures the pump B performance code P0C74 by reprogramming the hybrid control processors. CARB requires inverter cooling outputs to be monitored for circuit faults. Steady open, low and high faults of pump B are P0B38 to P0B3A. Short dropouts briefly reduce coolant flow and may trigger a power limit.
c: Intermittent contact at the pump B connector or a harness splice
Pump B electronics producing an unstable signal
Control module software evaluating the pump signal too strictly
s: Warning light that appears now and then
Temporary power reduction under high load or heat

P0E51.t: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor A Circuit
P0E51.d: P0E51 is the general circuit fault of current sensor A in a DC/DC converter, the element that tells the converter's controller how many amps flow through its power stage. The code covers a signal path that is broken in a way the controller cannot sort into low, high or implausible. No manufacturer documents P0E51 publicly. The same sensor appears in Mercedes-Benz information LI54.10-P-079533 for the EQB and G-Class, where a short to positive is stored as P0E5400. Ford's hybrid summaries show what such a check looks at: at power-up the inductor current sensor of the boost converter must show less than 15 A offset and a raw signal between 4.5 and 6.0 V, though Ford files these faults under P0A11. CARB requires circuit checks on hybrid input components. Converter output is usually limited.
c: Current sensor inside the converter defective (usually not replaceable separately)
Loose, corroded or damaged sensor connection or harness
Fault on the converter control board or its sensor supply
Converter or hybrid control software needs an update
s: Hybrid or 12 V battery warning in the instrument cluster
12 V battery is charged poorly or not at all
Reduced electric power or limited hybrid functions

P0E52.t: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0E52.d: P0E52 is the plausibility test of current sensor A: the signal is electrically valid, yet the measured current does not fit what the converter is doing. Two makers name it. FCA lists it for the 2021 Ram 1500 with the 3.6 litre eTorque mild hybrid; bulletin 08-037-21 brings new HCP software and turns P0E52 from a two-trip into a one-trip code, so the MIL may light after a single faulty drive. Ford reports it from the inverter system controller of the 2024–2026 Lincoln Nautilus and the 2025–2026 Maverick hybrid, together with several motor and inverter codes; the car loses power and shows Stop Safely Now or Service Vehicle Soon, and the special service message tells dealers to replace that controller. Pure circuit faults are P0E51, P0E53 and P0E54.
c: Control software with unsuitable limits (FCA eTorque HCP update)
Internal fault of the inverter system controller (Ford hybrid)
Current sensor drifting or offset out of tolerance
High resistance at sensor connector or ground
s: MIL on, often after only one drive
Limited power with Stop Safely Now or Service Vehicle Soon message
Reduced eTorque assist or start/stop function

P0E53.t: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor A Circuit Low
P0E53.d: P0E53 means the signal of DC/DC converter current sensor A sits below its valid window. On a Hall-type sensor with a mid-scale zero point, that usually points to a short to ground, a missing sensor supply or an open signal wire pulled low, not to a real drop in current. No manufacturer documents P0E53 publicly. Ford's hybrid summaries show the kind of window involved: the boost stage's inductor current signal counts as valid only from 4.5 to 6.0 V, so a lower raw value is a fault, although Ford stores it under the collective code P0A11. Mercedes-Benz reports the opposite fault of the same sensor on the EQB and G-Class as P0E5400. CARB demands out-of-range checks on such inputs. With no usable current reading the converter is normally throttled or shut down.
c: Sensor supply missing or too low
Current sensor or converter electronics defective
s: Hybrid or charging-system warning lamp
12 V battery discharges because the converter does not supply it
Reduced power or electric drive not available

P0E54.t: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor A Circuit High
P0E54.d: P0E54 reports a current sensor A signal above the range the DC/DC converter accepts. Mercedes-Benz uses it explicitly: its bulletin LI54.10-P-079533, covering the EQB (series 243) and the G-Class including the electric G 580 (series 465), defines P0E5400 as a short to positive of the converter's current sensor A. It is one of up to four converter codes, with P0C3B00, P0E9700 and P0C4000, that appear after the converter wakes up incorrectly; drivers see a red 12 V battery message and HV warnings. Mercedes treats it as a state error rather than a broken part: the technician runs the buck mode in XENTRY for about 30 s, checks that output current settles from a high initial value, then clears the memory or resets the converter. The low-signal sibling is P0E53.
c: Converter stuck in a fault state after incorrect wake-up (Mercedes 243/465)
Signal line shorted to a supply voltage
Current sensor or converter electronics defective
s: Red 12 V battery message
White or yellow high-voltage system warnings
Reduced drive power

P0E55.t: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E55.d: P0E55 deals with a current sensor A reading that flickers or vanishes for moments instead of failing for good. FCA documents it repeatedly for the Ram 1500 with eTorque mild hybrid, where the DC/DC converter sits in the 48 V battery pack and is run by the battery pack control module (BPCM). Bulletin 08-030-24 for the 2019 model lists P0E55 among ten BPCM codes; 08-333-25 and its revision 08-283-26 for the 2025 truck with the 3.6 litre V6 name it alone and describe the result: the 12 V battery is not kept charged, runs flat soon after driving and may leave the truck needing a tow, later also with limp-home mode and disabled start/stop. In all cases the fix is new BPCM software, not a part. Steady circuit faults are P0E51, P0E53 and P0E54.
c: Battery pack control module software (FCA eTorque, reflash)
Loose or corroded contact in the sensor path
Current sensor or converter electronics failing intermittently
s: MIL on
12 V battery not charging, flat soon after driving
Limp-home mode and start/stop disabled

P0E56.t: DC/DC Converter Input Voltage Too Low
P0E56.d: P0E56 says the voltage arriving at the input of the DC/DC converter, normally the high-voltage bus of the traction battery, is lower than the converter needs to work. Unlike the sensor codes, the reading itself is believed; the supply is the problem. No manufacturer documents P0E56 on an official public server. Converter makers build in the matching guard: Poclain's 48 V unit runs from 36 V upward and switches off by undervoltage lockout near 28 V, restarting only around 30 V. Ford's hybrid summaries apply a similar floor to the inverter input under a different code, P1A07, below 150 V for 100 ms. CARB requires hybrid components to be monitored. Causes range from a deeply discharged or disconnected battery to open contactors or a fault in the HV cabling; the 12 V system then loses its charge source.
c: Traction battery deeply discharged or limited by its management system
Main contactor not closing or high-voltage cable/connector fault
Input voltage measurement inside the converter faulty
s: 12 V battery warning, battery discharges while driving
Hybrid system warning, vehicle may not reach ready mode
Reduced power

P0E57.t: DC/DC Converter Input Voltage Too High
P0E57.d: P0E57 is set when the DC/DC converter sees more voltage on its input than it is rated for. Excess input voltage stresses the switching transistors and input capacitors, so a converter typically stops working to protect itself. No manufacturer documents P0E57 on an official public server. Supplier data show the limits involved: Poclain specifies 96 V as the highest continuous input for its 48 V converter. Ford's hybrid summaries treat a comparable overvoltage on the inverter side as P0C79, triggered when the DC bus measurement exceeds 516 V for 10 ms. CARB requires such hybrid components to be monitored. Typical triggers are a boost stage regulating too high, a charging or regenerative event without proper voltage control, or a faulty voltage measurement. The 12 V supply may stop while the code is active.
c: High-voltage bus driven too high by boost stage, regeneration or charging
Input voltage measurement in the converter reads too high
Hybrid or battery control software needs an update
s: Hybrid system or 12 V battery warning
Converter switches off temporarily, 12 V voltage drops
Reduced power or limited regeneration

P0E58.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor C Circuit
P0E58.d: P0E58 stands for a general circuit fault of the third temperature sensor in a DC/DC converter, after sensors A (P0C38 ff.) and B (P0C3D ff.). Which part of the converter sensor C watches is up to the maker. At Ford it is the inductor of the variable voltage converter, the boost stage of its full hybrids, but Ford uses only the plausibility code P0E59 for it. No manufacturer documents P0E58 publicly. The code is meant for a fault the controller can detect without being able to classify it as too low, too high or implausible, for example an unstable reference or supply. CARB requires circuit monitoring of hybrid input components. Without this reading the controller protects the converter by limiting its power, which can cut electric assist.
c: Sensor connection or wiring damaged or corroded
Temperature sensor in the converter defective
Sensor reference or evaluation circuit in the converter faulty
s: Hybrid system warning
Reduced electric assist or power

P0E59.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P0E59.d: P0E59 is the best-documented member of this group. Ford's hybrid OBD summaries from 2015 to 2019 assign it to the inductor temperature sensor of the variable voltage converter and monitor it without pause once 500 ms have passed since power-up, provided the 12 V supply lies between 6 and 19 V. It fails on any of three conditions: a sensor voltage under 0.067 V or over 4.86 V, an inductor reading above 165 °C for 1 s, or a value more than 30 °C away from engine coolant temperature after a soak of 180 minutes. Ford thus folds the electrical range checks into this code instead of using P0E5A/P0E5B. FCA also uses P0E59 on the 2021 Ram 1500 eTorque; bulletin 08-037-21 makes it a one-trip code with new HCP software. Sensors A and B have P0C39 and P0C3E as their plausibility codes.
c: Inductor temperature sensor drifting, reading off after cold soak
Inductor really overheating, e.g. due to weak electronics cooling
Short or open in the sensor circuit (Ford range limits)
s: MIL on, at FCA after one faulty drive
Reduced hybrid assist or electric driving
Hybrid system warning

P0E5A.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Low
P0E5A.d: P0E5A means the voltage from DC/DC converter temperature sensor C has fallen below its valid window. With the NTC thermistors common in power electronics, a low voltage translates into an implausibly hot reading, so a grounded signal wire or a failed sensor is far more likely than genuine overheating. No manufacturer documents P0E5A publicly. Ford gives an idea of the window for its sensor C, the inductor sensor of the boost converter: anything under 0.067 V counts as a fault, but Ford stores it as P0E59, not as P0E5A. CARB requires out-of-range monitoring of hybrid input components. Because the controller must assume overtemperature, it usually derates the converter at once, which can reduce electric power. The high-signal counterpart is P0E5B.
c: Evaluation circuit in the converter faulty
s: Hybrid system warning
Converter derated, reduced electric power

P0E5B.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor C Circuit High
P0E5B.d: P0E5B is stored when the signal of DC/DC converter temperature sensor C rises above its valid window. On an NTC circuit with pull-up resistor, that is the typical picture of an unplugged connector, a broken wire or a short to a supply voltage, and it reads as a converter far colder than possible. No manufacturer documents P0E5B publicly. Ford's limit for its sensor C, the boost converter inductor sensor, lies at 4.86 V; above that a fault is logged, yet Ford reports it as P0E59. Range checks of this kind are mandatory under CARB for hybrid inputs. Since a cold reading would hide real overheating, the controller treats the converter temperature as unknown and usually limits power. A connector check is the obvious first step. P0E5A is the low-signal counterpart.
c: Connector unplugged or sensor wire broken
Signal shorted to a supply voltage
s: Hybrid system warning
Power limited as a precaution

P0E5C.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E5C.d: P0E5C flags a sensor C signal that changes faster than the part it watches could heat or cool. A converter inductor or heat sink has thermal mass, so a jump of many degrees within a few milliseconds points to a contact problem in the circuit, not to the converter itself. No manufacturer documents P0E5C publicly. The sensor is known from Ford, where sensor C watches the boost converter inductor and is checked only through P0E59 with fixed voltage and temperature limits; an erratic check is not described there. CARB requires hybrid input components to be monitored for circuit faults. Typical causes are a loose terminal, vibration damage or moisture at the converter connector. The fault may come and go between drives, so a wiggle test with live data helps more than a static measurement.
c: Loose or widened terminal at the sensor or converter connector
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
s: Hybrid warning that comes and goes
Short episodes of reduced electric power

P0E5D.d: P0E5D adds the intermittent case to the DC/DC converter enable codes P0A11 (open), P0A12 (low) and P0A13 (high). Through the enable line a hybrid or body controller switches the converter on and off; if that line flickers, the converter keeps stopping and restarting. Converter data sheets show how simple the input often is: on Poclain's 48 V unit the converter runs while the enable pin is tied to input positive or left floating and shuts off when it is pulled to input negative, so a poor ground or chafed wire can cycle it. No manufacturer documents P0E5D publicly. Ford's hybrid summaries use only P0A11 and attach several internal boost converter faults to it. CARB requires output components to be checked for circuit faults. The driver may see the 12 V voltage dip or a battery warning that comes and goes.
c: Loose or corroded terminal on the enable line
Poor ground reference between controller and converter
Chafed enable wire touching ground intermittently
Output stage in the commanding controller faulty
s: 12 V battery warning that comes and goes
Fluctuating system voltage, flickering lights
Hybrid warning, possibly reduced power

P0E5E.t: Battery Charger Control Module A Processor Performance
P0E5E.d: P0E5E reports that the processor of the on-board charger's control unit fails its self-tests. Mitsubishi spells this out for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: P0E5E-00 means a ROM checksum (CRC) error or a RAM read/write error in the charger control; the code lights both the PHEV warning and the MIL. In the Volkswagen group the code is stored by the battery management module (address 8C). Bentley's information 2066497/1 for the 2021 Bentayga Hybrid lists it with charger faults when the car will not charge or stops charging, and the remedy there is a new on-board charger (AX4). Audi's on-car analysis list of June 2026 names P0E5E00 for Q5 PHEV 2024–2025 with a check engine light after charging and asks dealers to contact technical support. Non-processor faults of the module are P0D67.
c: Control electronics of the on-board charger defective (unit replacement)
Unstable 12 V supply or ground of the charger during start-up
s: Plug-in charging impossible or interrupted
MIL and hybrid/PHEV warning, sometimes right after charging

P0E5F.t: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature A Too High
P0E5F.d: P0E5F is not a sensor fault: the coupler temperature sensor A works, but the charging inlet really got too hot. Three makers document it. Ford links it on the 2021–2023 Mustang Mach-E (stored in the SOBDM) to a red flashing charge indicator and no charging from a 48 A level 2 station, while 32 A or less may still work; SSM 51866 calls for a new charge port. GM's PIT5904 for the 2022 Hummer EV and BrightDrop EV600 says the pin temperatures are watched all the time and that, once the code has tripped, charging resumes only after the plug is pulled and reinserted, even when the pins have cooled; worn station plugs are a suspect. Mercedes stores P0E5F97 in the AC charger of several 2024 plug-in hybrids in strong sun and calls it no fault, with power cut back until the temperature drops.
c: Excessive contact resistance in the vehicle charge port (Ford replaces the port)
Worn or damaged plug of the charging cable or station
High ambient temperature or direct sun while charging (Mercedes)
s: Charging stops or runs at reduced power
Charge indicator red or flashing red, warning in app or cluster
Charging restarts only after unplugging and replugging

P0E60.t: Battery Charge Mode Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0E60.d: P0E60 concerns a wired control line that tells the on-board charger which mode to run in, set by the module that coordinates charging. Range/Performance means the line shows a valid level, but its state or response disagrees with the command. No manufacturer documents P0E60 or the modes it selects publicly. The closest documented analogue is GM's charger control circuit P0E65 in the 2016 Volt and the 2019 hybrid tables, a separate command line checked by a hardware fault flag (30 failures in 40 samples, Type B), and Ford's P0E64, which flags a missing ready answer after the charge wake-up line goes high. Under CARB, a plug-in hybrid must notice charger faults that block charging or cut its rate. Expect charging to fail, run in the wrong mode or stop, depending on how the maker has defined the modes.
c: High resistance or damage on the mode control line
Input stage of the on-board charger faulty
Output stage or software of the commanding module faulty
s: Plug-in charging does not start or stops
Charging runs at an unexpected rate

P0E61.d: P0E61 means the 12 V enable line that wakes or permits the on-board charger has a circuit fault, most often an open. GM documents it codegenau. In the 2016 Volt the VICM watches this charger enable circuit; in the 2019 hybrid tables the HPC2 module does so. The test reads a fault flag reported by the driver hardware and runs when system voltage is at least 10.2 V; 30 failed samples out of 40, taken every 25 ms, set the code as Type B, so the MIL lights after two trips with the fault. GM also uses P0E61 as a blocking condition: while it is active, the high-voltage battery heater test is not run. CARB's charger rule for plug-in hybrids covers exactly such failures. With no enable signal the charger stays off and plug-in charging fails.
c: Enable wire open or connector at charger/module not seated
Output driver in the controlling module (VICM/HPC2) faulty
Enable input of the on-board charger defective
s: Plug-in charging does not start
MIL on after two trips
Battery heating in cold weather may be unavailable

P0E62.t: Battery Charger A Enable Circuit Low
P0E62.d: P0E62 reports that the enable line of on-board charger A is held at a lower level than its commanded state allows, typically by a short to ground. If the module drives the line high to permit charging, the charger never sees the request. Should the line instead carry a low-active signal, a grounded wire could leave the charger permitted at all times, which is why manufacturers separate low from high. No manufacturer documents P0E62 publicly. GM's 2016 Volt and 2019 hybrid tables cover only the generic enable fault P0E61, using a hardware fault flag at 10.2 V or more, 30 failures in 40 samples and Type B. CARB requires plug-in hybrids to catch charger faults that prevent charging. A shorted enable wire can also overload the driver stage in the commanding module.
c: Enable wire chafed and shorted to ground
Enable input of the charger shorted internally
Driver stage in the commanding module faulty
s: Charging does not start when plugged in
Charging system warning

P0E63.t: Battery Charger A Enable Circuit High
P0E63.d: P0E63 is the high-level counterpart: the enable signal to charger A sits above the level its commanded state allows, for instance because it touches a 12 V feed. In practice the charger may then be woken although no charging is requested, which can drain the 12 V battery while parked, or it may ignore a switch-off command. No manufacturer documents P0E63 publicly. GM documents only the generic enable fault P0E61 for the 2016 Volt (VICM) and in the 2019 hybrid tables (HPC2), evaluated via a hardware fault flag with 30 failures in 40 samples as Type B; separate low and high codes are not listed there. CARB counts any charger fault that disturbs charging as one a plug-in hybrid must detect. A wire chafed against a powered harness or an internal short in the charger are the usual suspects.
c: Enable wire shorted to a 12 V supply
Enable input of the charger faulty
Driver stage in the commanding module stuck on
s: 12 V battery drained while parked
Charger active or charging not ending as expected
Charging system warning

P0E64.t: Battery Charger A Enable Circuit Range/Performance
P0E64.d: P0E64 covers an enable line that is electrically intact while the charger still does not respond as it should. Ford documents it in its 2019 hybrid OBD summary, there titled Battery Charger Enable Circuit Range/Performance: the check runs once the charger is in its ready state and the charge wake-up signal Chrg_Wkup has gone high, and it fails when the battery energy control module still reports not ready after 30 seconds. The same monitor group checks the charger's output power against the expected value under P0D20. A BECM that does not wake, a slow start-up of either module or software disagreement between charger and BECM can therefore set P0E64 without any wiring fault. For plug-in hybrids, CARB demands detection of such charging failures. Open, low and high circuit faults are P0E61 to P0E63.
c: Charger and BECM do not complete start-up within 30 s (software or wake-up timing)
Battery energy control module not waking or not reporting ready
High resistance on the wake-up line producing a marginal level
s: Charging does not start although the cable is connected
Charging system warning or charge port light shows a fault

P0E65.d: P0E65 flags a fault on the wired command line through which the hybrid control unit operates the on-board charger, most often an interrupted line. GM uses it codegenau: in the 2016 Volt the VICM runs the test, in the 2019 hybrid tables (19OBDG01) the HPC2 module. The check relies on a fault flag raised by the output driver hardware itself and only runs while system voltage is 10.2 V or higher and the charger enable mask is active. Samples are taken every 25 ms; 30 bad ones among 40 store the code. GM classes it Type B, so the MIL comes on once the fault returns on a second trip. Low, high and plausibility faults on the same line have their own codes, P0E66 to P0E68. Plug-in charging is usually refused until the line is repaired.
c: Broken or disconnected charger control wire
Corroded or pushed-out terminal at charger or control unit
Defective output driver in the commanding control unit
s: Vehicle does not charge when plugged in
MIL after the second trip with the fault (GM)
Charging fault message in the instrument cluster

P0E66.d: With P0E66 the controller finds the charger command line pulled lower than the state it is driving, which typically means the wire touches ground somewhere between the control unit and the on-board charger. If the command is active-high, the charger simply never receives it; a grounded line can also overload the output stage that drives it. No manufacturer documents P0E66 publicly. GM's Volt and 2019 hybrid tables check this line only through the general code P0E65, based on a hardware fault flag sampled every 25 ms at 10.2 V or more. California's OBD rule requires plug-in hybrids to recognise charger faults that stop or limit charging. P0E67 is the opposite case, a line stuck high; P0E68 covers a line that is electrically sound but answers wrongly.
c: Control wire chafed through to body ground
Moisture in a connector bridging the signal to ground
Internal short in the charger's command input
s: Charging does not start after plugging in
Charge indicator shows a fault or goes out

P0E67.d: P0E67 is set when the charger command line reads higher than commanded, for instance close to battery voltage while the control unit is holding it off. A short to a live wire is the classic cause; with some driver designs an open line also floats high and lands here. The risk is the reverse of P0E66: depending on how the signal is defined, the charger may see a permanent request and try to start, or the module may stop charging as a precaution. No manufacturer documents P0E67 publicly. GM covers the line in the 2016 Volt (VICM) only with the general code P0E65, Type B, 30 of 40 samples at 25 ms. CARB expects a plug-in hybrid to detect charger malfunctions that disable or restrict charging, which applies here as well.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery feed or other supply
Open line read as high by the driver circuit
Output stage of the control unit stuck switched on
s: Charging aborted or not offered at all
Charger wakes up or runs without a charging request

P0E68.d: P0E68 is the plausibility code of the charger command line: no short or open is present, yet the charger does not react to the command in the expected way or in the expected time. Typical triggers are a charger that wakes too slowly, a voltage drop on the line that leaves the level ambiguous, or software in the two modules that disagrees. No manufacturer documents P0E68 publicly. A close analogue is Ford's P0E64 on its 2019 hybrids: once the charge wake-up line is high, the battery energy control module must report ready within 30 seconds. GM's general circuit code for the same line is P0E65. CARB requires detection of charger faults that block charging or reduce its rate. Pure wiring faults are P0E65 to P0E67; a software update is often the first step.
c: Charger and control unit software not matching
Charger responding late or not at all to the command
Excess resistance in the line distorting the signal level
s: Charging starts late, stops or fails intermittently
Charge timer or scheduled charging not working

P0E69.t: Control Pilot Indicator Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0E69.d: P0E69 belongs to the output that drives the small lamp or LED showing the state of the pilot connection to the charging station. Range/Performance means the driver circuit reports a state that does not fit what the module commanded, without a clear short or open. No manufacturer documents P0E69 publicly. GM's Volt tables for 2011 and 2012 show how such a driver is watched, under the older code P0D2B: one sample every 100 ms, a ground short counted while the LED is commanded on with the cord plugged in (12 of 15 samples), a short to battery or an open while it is off and unplugged (40 of 50), Type B. Today the hard faults are split into P0D2B, P0E3D and P0E3E. The pilot signal itself is not affected; charging usually works, only the indication is wrong.
c: Indicator LED aged or partially failed, drawing the wrong current
Loose contact at the charge port lamp connector
Faulty feedback of the LED driver in the control unit
s: Charge port indicator flickers, stays dark or shows the wrong state
Charging itself usually unaffected

P0E6A.t: Battery Charging System Precharge Contactor Circuit
P0E6A.d: P0E6A is the general code for the precharge contactor of the battery charging system. Before the main charging contactors close, this small contactor feeds the charger side through a resistor so the voltage can rise gently towards pack voltage; without it the main contacts would arc. The code collects faults of this branch that fit none of the more specific siblings. No manufacturer documents P0E6A publicly. GM's 2019 hybrid tables watch the same function under their own codes: the charger bus must reach 95 to 105 percent of pack voltage within 0.7 seconds (P0D26), and battery current above 3 A for about 87 ms during precharge sets P3061, both Type A. CARB requires charger malfunctions that block charging to be detected. Stuck faults are P0E6B and P0E6C, coil circuit faults P0E6D to P0E70.
c: Precharge resistor burnt open or overheated
Worn or sluggish precharge contactor in the charging path
s: Charging session aborts right at the start
Charging not possible, driving usually still possible

P0E6B.t: Battery Charging System Precharge Contactor Circuit Stuck Closed
P0E6B.d: P0E6B means the precharge contactor of the charging system appears to stay closed although it has been told to open, usually because its contacts have welded. The battery management notices this when the charger side carries voltage before any precharge was requested, or when it does not drop after switch-off. That is a safety matter: the charging path may remain live. No manufacturer documents P0E6B publicly. Mitsubishi's i-MiEV manual, published as a 2019 bulletin, handles the comparable weld of its charging contactor under P0AE2 and checks it as the high-voltage system is activated; besides wiring and the contactor itself it lists the combined charger and DC-DC unit and other high-voltage loads as possible causes. CARB requires faults that disable charging to be detected. The opposite fault is P0E6C.
c: Coil kept energised by a control line fault
Residual voltage from another high-voltage unit misread as a closed contactor
s: Charging blocked and high-voltage warning displayed
Vehicle may refuse to switch to ready mode

P0E6C.t: Battery Charging System Precharge Contactor Circuit Stuck Open
P0E6C.d: P0E6C reports that the precharge contactor of the charging system does not close, or that no current flows through the precharge branch, even though the command was given. The charger side then cannot be brought up to pack voltage, the main charging contactors stay open and the session ends before any energy flows. No manufacturer documents P0E6C publicly. GM's 2019 hybrid tables show the measurable symptom under other codes: if the charger bus is still outside 95 to 105 percent of pack voltage after 0.7 seconds, P0D26 is set, and if charger voltage stays under 10 V once a precharge attempt has failed, GM blames the positive charging contactor with P0D09, both Type A. CARB counts such charging failures among the faults a plug-in hybrid must detect. A welded contactor is P0E6B instead.
c: Open precharge resistor interrupting the branch
Burnt or contaminated contactor contacts not conducting
Contactor coil not pulling in due to low supply
s: Charging stops a few seconds after plugging in
Repeated clicking from the battery area at charge start

P0E6D.t: Battery Charging System Precharge Contactor Control Circuit/Open
P0E6D.d: P0E6D concerns the low-voltage side of the charging precharge contactor: the coil circuit through which the control unit switches it, typically interrupted. Unlike P0E6C, which judges what happens on the high-voltage side, this code comes from the driver output itself. No manufacturer documents P0E6D publicly. GM uses the same method on the positive charging contactor of its 2019 hybrids (P0D0A): an open is recognised when the switched-off output still shows more than 4 V, or when less than 194 mA flows with the output on; 40 failed samples out of 50 at 12.5 ms set a Type B code. Mitsubishi's i-MiEV compares a coil monitor with the command and stores P0AE6 for the charging contactor. Range, low and high faults of the coil circuit are P0E6E to P0E70.
c: Broken coil control wire or unplugged connector
Open winding in the contactor coil
Failed driver stage in the battery management unit
s: Charging cannot be started
High-voltage system fault message

P0E6E.t: Battery Charging System Precharge Contactor Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0E6E.d: P0E6E is stored when the coil circuit of the charging precharge contactor neither shows a clean short nor an open, but its electrical behaviour does not match the command: coil current outside the expected window, a slow pull-in, or feedback that lags behind the switching command. Rising contact resistance in the connector, a coil with changed resistance or a weak supply to the driver are typical. No manufacturer documents P0E6E publicly. Related GM monitoring in the 2019 hybrid tables shows the measured quantity, a current sense feedback of the contactor driver with a 194 mA minimum while on, used there for the positive charging contactor (P0D0A). CARB requires output components to be checked for proper function, not only for circuit faults. Hard faults on the same circuit are P0E6D, P0E6F and P0E70.
c: Increased contact resistance in the coil connector
Contactor coil resistance out of specification
Low supply voltage at the contactor driver
s: Charging starts only on some attempts
Fault appears mostly in cold weather or with a weak 12 V battery

P0E6F.t: Battery Charging System Precharge Contactor Control Circuit Low
P0E6F.d: P0E6F points to the coil control line of the charging precharge contactor sitting too low, most likely shorted to ground. With a high-side driver the coil then cannot be energised, so precharge never starts; the driver itself may shut down to protect itself. No manufacturer documents P0E6F publicly. GM notes for the comparable high-side monitor of its positive charging contactor (P0D0A, 2019 hybrid tables) that it cannot detect a short to ground at all, which is why a separate low code makes sense. Mitsubishi's i-MiEV stores P0AE6 when the coil feedback of its charging contactor stays off while the module commands it on; it names wiring, the contactor and the EV-ECU as causes. P0E70 is the high counterpart, P0E6D an open coil circuit.
c: Coil control wire shorted to ground inside or near the battery
Shorted turns in the contactor coil
Driver stage switched off by its overcurrent protection
s: Charging does not start, contactor click missing
High-voltage fault message when plugging in

P0E70.t: Battery Charging System Precharge Contactor Control Circuit High
P0E70.d: P0E70 is the high-side counterpart of P0E6F: the coil line of the charging precharge contactor carries voltage although the driver is off. A short to a 12 V feed can energise the coil without a command, which would let the precharge branch conduct unasked; the battery management therefore usually locks out charging. No manufacturer documents P0E70 publicly. For its positive charging contactor GM tests exactly this case in the 2019 hybrid tables (P0D0A): with the driver off, an output voltage above the 12 V battery voltage minus 0.4 V counts as a short to power, confirmed by 40 of 50 samples at 12.5 ms, Type B. Mitsubishi's i-MiEV sets P0AE7 when the coil monitor stays on after an off command. An open coil circuit is P0E6D.
c: Coil control wire shorted to a 12 V supply
Driver stage in the battery management unit stuck on
Open ground return of the coil leaving the line at supply level
s: Charging locked out with a high-voltage fault message
Contactor clicks without a charging request

P0E71.d: P0E71 compares the torque that the hybrid generator or motor-generator actually provides with the value requested by the hybrid control. If the two drift apart beyond a calibrated margin, the code is set. Ford uses it codegenau in its 2024 to 2025 gasoline OBD summary: in the three-byte format P0E71-48 replaces the older P061B for a motor torque plausibility error on vehicles with the modular hybrid transmission (MHT), rated MIL plus wrench lamp. The monitor runs continuously and needs less than one second to register a fault. Under CARB, powertrain components whose failure can raise emissions fall under the comprehensive component checks. Causes range from inverter faults and position sensor errors to winding damage. Expect reduced power, limited hybrid operation or a disabled hybrid system.
c: Fault in the inverter stage feeding the generator
Rotor position sensor (resolver) delivering a wrong angle
Damaged generator winding or internal contamination
s: MIL and service wrench lamp on (Ford)
Reduced power or emergency running mode
Engine runs more often, hybrid assistance missing

P0E72.d: P0E72 refers to the pulse train that an AC charging station places onto the pilot wire. Under SAE J1772, matched by IEC 61851-1, this is a rectangular ±12 V signal at 1 kHz, and its duty cycle tells the car how much current it may draw. The vehicle measures the period of this signal; if it is clearly slower than 1 kHz, the reading is distrusted and P0E72 is stored, because a wrong frequency also makes the current limit unreliable. No manufacturer documents P0E72 publicly. A US Department of Energy test report on pilot-line communication (PNNL) treats the 1000 Hz frequency and pulse width as values that added equipment must not disturb. Causes are a faulty station or adapter, interference on the line, or the car's measuring circuit. P0E73 is the high case; voltage faults are P0CF4 to P0CF6.
c: Charging station or portable charger generating an off-spec pilot
Faulty charging adapter or extension in the cable path
Pilot measuring circuit in the vehicle charger misreading
s: AC charging does not start or stops at one station
Charging works normally at other stations

P0E73.d: P0E73 is set when the control pilot pulses from the charging station arrive faster than the nominal 1 kHz. Above the permitted band the vehicle can no longer be sure that it decodes the duty cycle, and with it the allowed charging current, correctly; in practice it refuses or ends the session. Short spikes or ringing on the pilot line can mimic extra edges and be counted as a higher frequency, so cable condition and nearby interference matter as much as the station itself. No manufacturer documents P0E73 publicly. Simulation notes from Typhoon HIL describe the station side of this interface, a PWM signal of ±12 V at 1 kHz evaluated by a resistor network in the car. If the fault follows the vehicle across several stations, check the charge port and the charger's input. P0E72 is the low case.
c: Electrical interference or ringing on the pilot line
Charging station with a faulty pilot oscillator
Damaged charging cable or corroded charge port pin
Faulty pilot input in the on-board charger
s: AC charging refused or stopped shortly after start
Fault tied to a specific station or cable

P0E74.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Internal Isolation Fault
P0E74.d: P0E74 reports that the insulation between the cells or internal high-voltage parts of the traction battery and its housing has become too weak, as measured inside the pack. P0AA6, by contrast, covers isolation of the whole high-voltage system. Audi uses P0E74 codegenau: a 2018 bulletin for the A3 e-tron (model years 2017 and 2018) names it together with P0AA6 in the battery regulation control module J840, with the battery warning lamp on; workshops were asked to quarantine the car and contact technical support before replacing parts. As a reference for typical limits, GM's 2019 hybrid tables flag P0AA6 below 325,000 ohm. CARB treats high-voltage isolation detection as a safety-only system. Coolant or water inside the pack, damaged cell wiring and a faulty isolation monitor are typical.
c: Coolant leak or water ingress inside the battery pack
Chafed or damaged insulation of internal high-voltage wiring
Faulty isolation measurement in the battery management
s: Battery or high-voltage warning lamp on
Vehicle may not enter ready mode or blocks charging
Electric driving disabled

P0E75.t: Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Circuit/Open
P0E75.d: P0E75 is the basic electrical code for coolant bypass valve A: the control unit finds that the output switching the valve, or the wire leading to it, does not form a closed circuit, in most cases because of an open. Valves of this kind usually divert coolant between loops, for example between the engine and a heater loop that keeps the cabin warm while a hybrid drives electrically. No manufacturer documents P0E75 publicly. Ford's 2019 hybrid and plug-in summary watches a comparable valve under the older codes P2682 and P2683 and relies on the fault status of its smart driver, which must persist beyond 5 s. CARB counts such actuators among the comprehensive components that need circuit checks. Low, high and plausibility faults of this circuit are P0E76 to P0E78; drivers mostly notice weaker heating.
c: Broken wire or loose connector on the valve A control circuit
Burnt or internally open coil/motor in valve A
Coolant or water ingress corroding the valve connector pins
Faulty output driver in the engine or hybrid control module
s: Check engine light
Little or no cabin heat, especially in electric mode
Engine warms up more slowly or runs more often than usual

P0E76.t: Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Circuit Low
P0E76.d: With P0E76 the voltage on the control line of coolant bypass valve A stays lower than the driver expects for its current state, which points to a short to ground somewhere in the harness or inside the actuator. What happens next depends on the driver layout: a low-side output may leave the valve energised all the time, a high-side output can no longer move it at all, and the driver may switch off to protect itself. No manufacturer documents P0E76 publicly. In Ford's 2019 hybrid summary the matching job falls to P2682, flagged once the driver has signalled a fault continuously for over 5 s; only after that does Ford run its stuck-valve check P26AB. CARB requires circuit monitoring of output devices like this one. P0E77 is the high case, P0E75 an open; P0E79 and P0E7A cover a valve that is mechanically stuck.
c: Chafed control wire touching body or engine ground
