Internal short in the valve A actuator
Moisture bridging pins in the valve connector
s: Check engine light
Valve stays in one position, heating behaves oddly
Possible blown fuse if the short is hard

P0E77.t: Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Circuit High
P0E77.d: P0E77 is logged when valve A's drive line carries more voltage than the driver should allow, typically because the wire has rubbed through against a 12 V feed. A low-side driver then sees battery voltage while it is trying to pull the line down and usually reports overcurrent; with some designs an open line can float high and end up here too. In either case the valve no longer follows commands reliably. No manufacturer documents P0E77 publicly. Ford's 2019 hybrid summary handles the same situation on its bypass valve as P2683, again set after more than 5 seconds of driver fault status. CARB expects such outputs to be checked for circuit faults. A grounded line is P0E76 and an interrupted one P0E75; replacing the valve without checking the harness first rarely helps.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Open circuit that the driver interprets as high
s: Check engine light
Cabin heat unstable or missing

P0E78.t: Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0E78.d: P0E78 is the plausibility code for the actuator circuit of bypass valve A. Neither an open nor a short is present, yet current, feedback or response time of the actuator do not fit what the module has commanded: a coil whose resistance has drifted, a motor that labours against a sticky shaft, or a supply that sags under load. For motor-driven valves with position feedback the module may also see the valve arrive late or stop short. No manufacturer documents P0E78 publicly. Ford's hybrid summary for 2019 shows the general idea of checking the actual valve position once an electrical problem is known, under P26AB. CARB asks for functional checks of output components in addition to circuit tests. Hard electrical faults are P0E75 to P0E77; a valve that stays put is P0E79 or P0E7A.
c: Deposits or wear making the valve A mechanism sluggish
High resistance at connector or ground of the valve circuit
Low supply voltage to the actuator under load
s: Check engine light
Heating output varies from trip to trip

P0E79.t: Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Stuck/Open
P0E79.d: P0E79 reports that bypass valve A apparently remains open although the module has asked it to close. The control unit cannot see the valve directly; it infers the position from temperatures, typically by comparing two coolant sensors that should drift apart when the loops are separated. No manufacturer documents P0E79 publicly. Ford's 2019 hybrid summary describes exactly this logic for its older code P26AB, a valve stuck in the combined loop: if the heater-loop sensor reads more than 5 °F above the engine sensor within 60 seconds after a circuit fault, the valve is taken as stuck. An open valve lets heat escape into the larger loop, so cabin heat in electric mode suffers and the engine may warm up differently. CARB requires functional monitoring of such outputs. The opposite case is P0E7A.
c: Valve A jammed open by debris or a broken internal part
Actuator no longer moves the valve
Hoses swapped at the valve after a repair
Skewed coolant temperature sensor misleading the check
s: Weak cabin heat in electric mode
Engine starts more often to supply heat
Check engine light

P0E7A.t: Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Stuck Closed
P0E7A.d: P0E7A is the reverse of P0E79: valve A should open and let coolant pass, but the temperature picture says it has stayed shut. Depending on what the valve connects, the result is a loop that gets no flow from the engine side, so heater output or heat transfer drops, or a branch that heats up because it is cut off from circulation. No manufacturer documents P0E7A publicly. The closest published case is the sibling on valve B: Stellantis sets P0E80 once the engine coolant reading and the electric heater inlet are over 40 °F apart, and blames misrouted hoses or a clogged three-way valve on Wrangler and Pacifica plug-in hybrids. Under CARB, actuators of this kind need a functional check as well. Electrical faults on valve A are P0E75 to P0E78.
c: Debris or deposits blocking valve A
Actuator or gear stuck in the closed position
Air pocket after a coolant service blocking flow
s: Little or no cabin heat
Rising coolant temperature in the affected loop
Check engine light

P0E7B.t: Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Circuit/Open
P0E7B.d: P0E7B covers an interrupted control circuit of the second coolant bypass valve, B. The module sees no proper load on its output, so the valve cannot be positioned and stays wherever it last was or springs back to its rest position. Stellantis does use the valve B family: its 2025 and 2026 bulletins for the RAM 1500 and the Wagoneer with the 3.0 litre Hurricane engine list P0E7C to P0E7F together with U063C, a lost link to the valve B actuator, and its plug-in hybrids use P0E7F and P0E80. P0E7B itself appears in none of these published documents. Ford's 2019 hybrid summary shows the usual circuit test on a comparable valve, a driver fault lasting over 5 seconds. CARB requires circuit checks on such outputs. Short and plausibility faults are P0E7C to P0E7E.
c: Broken wire or unplugged connector at valve B
Internal open in the valve B actuator
Missing supply or ground at a networked valve actuator
s: Check engine light
Heating or engine warm-up behaves differently

P0E7C.t: Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Circuit Low
P0E7C.d: P0E7C says that the wiring which operates bypass valve B reads too low, typically because a wire or the actuator itself has a ground fault. Stellantis documents the code: bulletin 18-071-26 (revisions A and B, October 2026) for 2025 RAM 1500 pickups fitted with the Hurricane straight-six, SO or HO twin-turbo and bulletin 18-082-26 for the 2025 Wagoneer and Grand Wagoneer name it among the faults cured by new engine control software, with the check engine light on. That points to calibration as a frequent trigger on these engines, besides real wiring damage. A low reading on the line keeps the valve from being driven as intended, so the coolant split between loops is no longer under control. CARB lists such outputs among the components that need circuit monitoring. High and open faults are P0E7D and P0E7B.
c: Engine control software needing the update from the manufacturer bulletin (Stellantis 3.0 Hurricane)
Valve B control wire shorted to ground
Internal short in the valve B actuator
s: Check engine light
Often no noticeable driving symptom

P0E7D.t: Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Circuit High
P0E7D.d: P0E7D is stored when the line driving valve B sits above its expected level, for instance with the wire chafed against a powered line or a driver that cannot pull the circuit down. Stellantis names this code in the same software bulletins as its low sibling: 18-071-26 for the 2025 RAM pickup with Hurricane power, plus 18-082-26 (SO engine) and 18-083-26 (HO engine) for the 2025 Wagoneer and Grand Wagoneer. All of them require a lit check engine light, and the fix is a reflash of the engine control module, sometimes alongside oxygen sensor and airflow codes. Before replacing hardware it is therefore worth checking for such an update. CARB expects outputs like this to be checked for circuit faults. The low case is P0E7C, an open circuit P0E7B, a networked actuator that stops talking U063C.
c: Valve B control wire shorted to a voltage source
Open circuit pulled high by the module input
s: Check engine light
Other stored codes after the same software issue

P0E7E.t: Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0E7E.d: P0E7E marks a control circuit of coolant bypass valve B that is electrically intact but does not respond as calibrated: actuator current, feedback or timing lie outside the window the software expects. Stellantis lists P0E7E most often of the valve B codes. Bulletin 18-106-25 from December 2025 covers model year 2026 RAM 1500 trucks with the high-output Hurricane built up to 7 October 2025 and calls for an engine control module update; the 2026 bulletins 18-071-26 and 18-082-26 repeat the code for the 2025 RAM and Wagoneer. Since a software fix is the documented remedy, a sluggish but working valve often turns out not to be the culprit. CARB requires functional monitoring of outputs, not only circuit checks. The pure wiring faults are P0E7B to P0E7D, mechanical sticking P0E7F and P0E80.
c: Engine control calibration fixed by bulletin 18-106-25 or 18-071-26 (Stellantis)
Valve B actuator moving slowly or not reaching its target
s: Check engine light
Usually no change in driving behaviour

P0E7F.t: Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Stuck/Open
P0E7F.d: P0E7F means coolant bypass valve B is judged to stay open while the module wants it closed. Stellantis documents it on the Chrysler Pacifica plug-in hybrid with the 3.6 litre engine: bulletin 07-008-23 (June 2023) covers cars built from 3 November 2022 to 10 February 2023, where machining debris from the cylinder head water jackets can collect inside the three-way valve. The MIL comes on and electric driving may be locked out while the petrol engine still works. To reproduce it, the bulletin has the car idle 10 minutes in engine mode, then run 5 minutes on battery with heat on and the blower below half; if P0E7F or P0E80 appears, the valve is replaced. The Hurricane software bulletins also list the code. P0E80 is the stuck closed case; P0E79 is the same fault on valve A.
c: Machining debris lodged in the three-way coolant valve (Pacifica Hybrid, bulletin 07-008-23)
Worn or broken internals in valve B
Calibration issue addressed by an engine control update (3.0 Hurricane)
s: MIL on
Electric drive mode unavailable, engine runs instead
Reduced or unstable cabin heat

P0E80.t: Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Stuck Closed
P0E80.d: P0E80 reports that bypass valve B has stayed shut although flow through it is requested. Stellantis gives the criterion for the Jeep Wrangler plug-in hybrid (2021 to 2023): the code sets once engine coolant and the inlet of the electric coolant heater differ by more than 40 °F, about 22 K. Its service case S2208000205 and bulletin 07-006-23 (cars built on 4 June 2022) trace this to hoses on the three-way valve that were fitted one port off; drivers notice a lit check engine light and at times no heat, and the fix is rerouting the hoses using the marks on the valve. On the 2022 to 2023 Pacifica plug-in hybrid, bulletin 07-008-23 blames a valve clogged by machining debris and replaces it. CARB covers such outputs under functional monitoring. P0E7F is the open counterpart.
c: Hoses at the three-way valve shifted by one port (Wrangler 4xe, bulletin 07-006-23)
Valve blocked by machining debris (Pacifica Hybrid, bulletin 07-008-23)
Valve B actuator seized in the closed position
s: Check engine light
Intermittent loss of cabin heat
Electric mode may be disabled

P0E81.t: Auxiliary Cooling System Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0E81.d: P0E81 is the general circuit code for temperature sensor A in an auxiliary cooling loop, a coolant circuit separate from the main engine loop, such as a heater loop of a plug-in hybrid or a loop that cools electric drive parts. The module sees a signal it cannot use at all, without classing it as too low, too high or implausible. No manufacturer documents P0E81 publicly. Ford's 2019 hybrid summary describes a comparable sensor, ECT2, placed between the electric PTC heater and the heater matrix, and checks its circuit through the analog input under P2184 and P2185. Volvo uses the term auxiliary cooling system for its T8 hybrids under P0EA7. CARB requires temperature sensors of this kind to be checked for circuit continuity. The more specific siblings are P0E82 to P0E84.
c: Loose, corroded or unplugged sensor connector
s: Check engine light
Heater or auxiliary pump runs on default values

P0E82.t: Auxiliary Cooling System Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0E82.d: P0E82 is set when temperature sensor A of the auxiliary cooling loop delivers a clean electrical signal whose value does not make sense against other temperatures. No manufacturer documents P0E82 publicly, but Ford's 2019 hybrid summary spells out such a plausibility test for its heater-loop sensor ECT2 under P2183. After at least 360 minutes of soak both coolant sensors must agree within 30 °F; with the loops joined and the electric pump above 2,500 rpm for 90 seconds, ECT2 plus a 7 °F hose loss must stay within 30 °F of the engine sensor; and the reading must stay between −30 and 275 °F. CARB includes hybrid component temperature sensors in its rationality requirements. A sensor that drifts, or a stuck bypass valve that keeps the loops apart, can trip it. Pure circuit faults are P0E81, P0E83 and P0E84.
c: Sensor A reading drifted out of tolerance
Stuck bypass valve keeping the loops from mixing
Low coolant or air around the sensor tip
s: Check engine light
Cabin heat regulation off target

P0E83.t: Auxiliary Cooling System Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0E83.d: P0E83 means the signal voltage of temperature sensor A in the auxiliary cooling loop has fallen below its valid floor. Coolant sensors are normally NTC thermistors whose resistance drops as they warm, so a low voltage reads as extremely hot coolant. When the value is beyond anything physically possible, the cause is usually a signal wire touching ground or a shorted sensor rather than real overheating. No manufacturer documents P0E83 publicly. On Ford's 2019 hybrids the equivalent fault of the heater-loop sensor ECT2 is P2184, recorded after 5 seconds of driver fault status. CARB requires out-of-range detection for such temperature inputs. The module may then run pumps or fans on safe defaults. P0E84 is the opposite, a reading stuck cold; P0E82 covers values inside the range that are implausible.
c: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Genuinely very hot coolant in the auxiliary loop
s: Check engine light
Coolant pump or fan running continuously
Implausibly high temperature shown on a scan tool

P0E84.t: Auxiliary Cooling System Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0E84.d: P0E84 is the high-voltage case for sensor A of the auxiliary loop: the signal sits near the reference voltage, which an NTC thermistor would only produce at extreme cold. Far more often the circuit is open, from an unplugged connector, a broken wire or a sensor with an internal break, or the signal line is shorted to a voltage source. The module then cannot judge the temperature of that loop and falls back to substitute values, which can make heater or pump control less precise. No manufacturer documents P0E84 publicly. Ford's 2019 hybrid summary uses P2185 for the equivalent fault of its heater-loop sensor ECT2, set after the driver signals a fault for 5 seconds. CARB wants temperature inputs tested for readings beyond their valid span. P0E83 is the low counterpart.
c: Unplugged connector or broken sensor wire
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
s: Check engine light
Scan tool shows the loop at minimum temperature
Less precise cabin heating

P0E85.t: Battery Charger B Temperature Too High
P0E85.d: P0E85 reports that the second charger stage or second on-board charger, labelled B, has become hotter than its own protection limit allows. Like the A counterpart P0D24, it is a heat verdict, not a sensor fault: the charger trusts its reading and cuts back power or stops to save its semiconductors. No manufacturer documents P0E85 with set conditions in public sources. Toyota shows that the letter B is real hardware: the 6.6 kW charger of the RAV4 Prime logs its input current fault as charger B (P0E89). CARB asks plug-in hybrids to flag charger failures that stop charging or reduce its rate. Typical triggers are poor coolant flow or air flow, a clogged heat exchanger or an internal defect. Expect slow or aborted AC charging, not loss of drive.
c: Too little coolant or air flow through charger B (low coolant, pump, blocked fins)
Internal defect in the power stage of charger B
Long full-power charging in very hot surroundings
s: AC charging slows down noticeably or stops before the battery is full
Charging fault message or flashing charge-port indicator

P0E86.t: Battery Charger B Input Voltage Too Low
P0E86.d: P0E86 means charger B sees less voltage at its input than it needs to work, although charging has been requested. It mirrors P0D27, which carries no letter and is used for the first charger. No manufacturer documents P0E86 publicly. Ford's plug-in hybrid summary (OBDSM1901) does list the opposite case on the same input, P0E87, which shows that the B input codes are in real use. A low input voltage is often caused outside the car: a weak or long house circuit, a faulty extension or charging cable, or a charging station that sags under load. Inside the car, worn inlet contacts or a bad high-voltage connection to the charger can do the same. CARB does not require faults originating in the supply to be detected, so an unconfirmed code may just reflect a poor socket.
c: Weak supply at the socket or charging station, long or undersized house wiring
Faulty charging cable, adapter or extension lead
Worn or burnt contacts in the charge inlet or its wiring to the charger
Voltage measurement inside charger B reads too low
s: AC charging does not start or stops shortly after starting
Charging works at another socket or station

P0E87.t: Battery Charger B Input Voltage Too High
P0E87.d: P0E87 flags an input voltage for charger B above what the charger accepts. Ford uses the code in its plug-in hybrid OBD summary (OBDSM1901) in an unusual way: it is part of a plausibility test run on the battery controller (BECM) and judges the charging voltage request that reaches the charger. Once the charger is in its ready state, a requested value above 450 V counts as a fault, and the check needs less than one second. In that reading the code points to a wrong command over the network rather than to the grid, so module software and data on the bus deserve attention first. On other designs a measured overvoltage at the input would set it. Ford lets charger faults request the amber wrench lamp instead of a specific charging message. The low case is P0E86.
c: Implausible charging voltage request from the battery control module (Ford logic)
Software fault in the charger or battery control module
Real overvoltage from the supply or charging station
s: Charging is refused or ends early
Amber wrench lamp in the instrument cluster (Ford)

P0E88.t: Battery Charger B Input Current Too Low
P0E88.d: P0E88 is set when charger B takes in less current than it should for the charging power it is asked to deliver, with voltage present. Its counterpart without a letter is P0D29. No manufacturer documents P0E88 in public sources. The neighbour P0E89 for too much current is documented by Ford, Toyota, Isuzu and Mercedes, so the input current of a B charger is clearly monitored. A low value with normal voltage suggests that the charger does not ramp up, that a resistive inlet or cable limits the flow, or that the charging station offers less current than expected. A measurement error is possible too, but those have their own sensor codes (P0E8A). CARB requires charger faults that limit the charging rate to be detected. Usually charging is just slow; driving is not affected.
c: Charger B power stage does not reach the requested power
High resistance at inlet contacts or in the charging cable
Charging station or cable signals a lower current limit than expected
s: AC charging takes much longer than usual
Charging stops or a charging fault is shown

P0E89.t: Battery Charger B Input Current Too High
P0E89.d: P0E89 reports more input current into charger B than permitted, and it is the best documented code of this series. Toyota lists P0E8919 on 2021 to 2023 RAV4 Prime XSE models with the 6.6 kW charger, together with P0D2A19 and PFC boost faults; the MIL is on, plug-in charging fails and the charger assembly is replaced (T-SB-0067-22). Ford's plug-in summary sets it when the charger, in ready state, receives a charging current request above 100 A. Isuzu logs it as excessive on-board charger input current in the VCU of the 2025-2026 NRR-EV with an amber EV warning and cures it with a VCU recalibration. Mercedes uses P0E8929 in the DC charging unit of several plug-in hybrids and the eSprinter, where the vehicle may refuse to start once a DC fast charge has ended. Too little current is P0E88.
c: Defective power factor correction or power stage in the charger (Toyota RAV4 Prime)
Calibration or software of the vehicle or charging control unit (Isuzu VCU, Mercedes DC charging unit, Ford request logic)
Current ripple or overcurrent from the charging station (Mercedes)
s: MIL or EV system warning lamp on
Plug-in charging stops or does not work at all
Vehicle does not start after DC fast charging (Mercedes)

P0E8A.t: Battery Charger B Input Current Sensor Circuit
P0E8A.d: P0E8A concerns the measurement, not the current itself: the sensor that tells charger B how much current enters at its input delivers no usable signal. It is the general circuit code; range, low and high faults of the same sensor sit at P2D85, P2D83 and P2D84, and the sensor of charger A uses P0D38. No manufacturer documents P0E8A publicly. That the B input current is evaluated is clear from P0E89, which Toyota sets on the RAV4 Prime as a circuit current above threshold and Ford tests against a 100 A limit. CARB requires inputs such as this to be checked for open circuits and out-of-range signals. In most chargers the sensor sits inside the unit, so a confirmed fault usually means repairing or replacing the charger. Without the reading, charging is refused or stopped.
c: Current sensor or its evaluation inside charger B defective
Open or shorted sensor wiring where the sensor is external
Charger software misjudges the sensor signal
s: AC charging does not start or is aborted
Charging fault indication; driving remains possible

P0E8B.t: Battery Charger B Input Voltage Sensor Circuit
P0E8B.d: P0E8B covers an electrical fault in the voltage measurement at the input of charger B: the controller gets no valid reading of the supply voltage. Range, low and high faults of this sensor have their own codes, P2E84, P2E85 and P2E86; charger A uses P0D3D for its first input voltage sensor. Some code lists call it input voltage sensor A of charger B. No manufacturer documents P0E8B publicly. Ford checks the voltage side of charger B through P0E87 with a 450 V limit, which is a judgment of the value, whereas P0E8B means the value cannot be read at all. CARB expects such inputs to be monitored for circuit continuity and range. The sensing is usually built into the charger, so after ruling out connectors the charger is the likely part. Charging is blocked until the fault clears.
c: Voltage sensing circuit inside charger B defective
Loose or corroded connector, damaged sensing lead
s: Plug-in charging is not possible
Charging fault message or charge-port indicator signals a fault

P0E8C.t: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit
P0E8C.d: The inverter of drive motor A may measure its high-voltage DC level at more than one point; sensor B is the second of those channels. P0E8C is the general circuit code for it, used when the signal is missing or electrically invalid without a clear low, high or plausibility verdict. Sensor A of the same inverter uses P0D2D, and a mismatch between both is P2E1A. No manufacturer documents P0E8C itself. Mitsubishi shows what sensor B can be: in the 2023 Outlander PHEV the power drive unit reads the boosted capacitor 2 voltage on a main channel, called V2M, and assigns its faults to P0E8D to P0E8F, while capacitor 1 belongs to sensor A. CARB requires such inputs to be checked for circuit faults. Without a trusted value the controller limits or blocks electric drive.
c: Sensing circuit for voltage channel B inside the power electronics defective
Low-voltage connector or harness of the inverter loose or damaged
Software fault in the motor control unit
s: Hybrid or EV system warning together with the MIL
Reduced electric drive power or vehicle not ready to drive

P0E8D.t: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0E8D.d: P0E8D says that voltage sensor B of the drive motor A inverter delivers a value that is electrically fine but disagrees with other readings of the same bus. Mitsubishi details the check for the 2023 Outlander PHEV, where sensor B is the main channel at capacitor 2 (V2M): with the boost converter switched off and the unit powered with 8 V or more for 0.5 s, a gap of at least 100 V to the rear motor unit, or of at least 50 V to capacitor 1, lasting 0.2 s sets the code, and the hint points to the power drive unit. Audi lists P0E8D00 with P0C0C00 in the electric drive of 2025-2026 Q6 and A6 e-tron models; if all entries appear together with a red high-voltage warning, the power electronics are replaced. Hard circuit faults are P0E8C, P0E8E and P0E8F.
c: Fault in the power electronics or its voltage measurement (Mitsubishi, Audi)
Drift of voltage channel B so that it no longer matches the other channels
Wrong reference value from another high-voltage unit (rear motor unit, battery management)
s: Red high-voltage system warning at start, stop safely (Audi)
MIL and hybrid warning, reduced or no electric drive

P0E8E.t: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit Low
P0E8E.d: P0E8E means the output of inverter voltage sensor B for drive motor A has fallen to the bottom end of its scale. On the 2023 Outlander PHEV Mitsubishi assigns it to the main measuring channel of capacitor 2 (V2M) in the power drive unit and sets it when that signal stays at no more than 0.45 V for 0.16 s, provided the unit has at least 8 V supply; monitoring runs continuously. Electrically this matches a short to ground, a broken signal path or a sensing circuit that has died, because the high-voltage bus itself would rarely read near zero while the system is active. The same channel reading high is P0E8F, while capacitor 1 on sensor A uses P0D2F for its low case. As the controller cannot trust the bus voltage, electric drive is limited or switched off and the MIL comes on.
c: Measuring circuit for capacitor 2 inside the power drive unit failed
Signal line shorted to ground or open
No high voltage on the bus because of a blown fuse or open contactor path
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Vehicle not ready to drive or only engine power available

P0E8F.t: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit High
P0E8F.d: P0E8F is the upper-limit fault of inverter voltage sensor B on drive motor A. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV sets it when the main channel at capacitor 2 (V2M) reports at least 4.75 V for 0.16 s, again with the unit supplied at 8 V or above, and lists it as a range check maximum. A reading pinned at the top usually comes from the signal touching the sensor supply, from a lost sensor ground or from a defect in the measuring circuit. A real overvoltage of the bus cannot be ruled out, but it has its own code, P0C79, and would normally show on several channels at once; if sensor A (P0D30) and the battery voltage are normal, the B channel itself is suspect. P0E8E is the low counterpart. The controller protects the inverter by limiting or stopping electric drive.
c: Measuring circuit for capacitor 2 inside the power drive unit defective
Signal shorted to sensor supply or lost sensor ground
Actual overvoltage on the high-voltage bus
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Electric drive switched off or strongly reduced

P0E90.t: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E90.d: P0E90 is meant for a voltage sensor B signal of the drive motor A inverter that flickers, jumps or drops out for moments without staying wrong long enough for the low or high code. No manufacturer documents P0E90 publicly. The documented siblings show how short the window is: Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV flags the same channel (V2M at capacitor 2) as too low or too high only after 0.16 s beyond 0.45 V or 4.75 V, and as implausible after 0.2 s of deviation, so shorter glitches need an extra stability test. CARB asks for input signals to be checked for circuit and rationality faults. In practice a loose low-voltage plug on the inverter, a chafed lead or a solder joint that opens with heat and vibration is the usual cause. Warnings may appear and vanish again.
c: Loose or corroded low-voltage connector on the inverter
Chafed or partly broken signal lead
Measuring circuit in the power electronics failing intermittently with heat or vibration
s: Hybrid warning that comes and goes
Short power interruptions or jerky electric drive

P0E91.t: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit
P0E91.d: P0E91 is the circuit code for the second DC voltage channel, sensor B, in the inverter of drive motor B, usually the second electric machine or the rear axle motor. It applies when this signal is absent or electrically unusable without a more precise verdict; its partner channel A is coded P0DA3, and the matching code for drive motor A is P0E8C. No manufacturer documents P0E91 or its B-sensor siblings for motor B publicly. Mitsubishi illustrates the frame with sensor A of the rear motor on the 2023 Outlander PHEV: the rear motor unit reports its inverter voltage, which the front power electronics compare with their own capacitor values. CARB requires inputs of hybrid drive components to be monitored for circuit faults. Motor B is then usually switched off, and the car may drive with reduced power.
c: Voltage channel B measuring circuit in the motor B inverter defective
Connector or harness of the motor B inverter loose or damaged
Software fault in the motor B control unit
s: Hybrid or EV warning with MIL
Loss of the second drive motor (for example no all-wheel drive), reduced power

P0E92.t: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0E92.d: P0E92 is stored when voltage sensor B of the drive motor B inverter gives a reading inside its electrical range that does not fit the other voltage values of the high-voltage system. No manufacturer documents P0E92 publicly. The closest published test is Mitsubishi's plausibility check P0DA4, written for the first voltage channel of the rear motor in the 2023 Outlander PHEV: with the boost converter off, the rear inverter voltage is compared with capacitor 1 and both capacitor 2 channels of the front unit, and a difference of 100 V or more to each of them for 0.2 s counts; the hints name the rear motor unit, battery management and the power drive unit. For drive motor A the same fault on sensor B is P0E8D. A drifting measurement or a wrong reference elsewhere are both possible, so all channels should be compared.
c: Voltage channel B of the motor B inverter drifts
Internal fault of the motor B inverter or motor unit
Wrong comparison value from battery management or the front power electronics
s: MIL and hybrid or EV system warning
Second drive motor switched off, reduced acceleration

P0E93.t: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit Low
P0E93.d: With P0E93 the controller sees the B voltage channel in the motor B inverter stuck near the bottom of its signal range, as happens with a short to ground, an open signal path or a failed measuring circuit. No manufacturer documents P0E93 publicly. Mitsubishi's rear motor sensor A on the 2023 Outlander PHEV gives a comparable limit: its low code P0DA5 sets once the signal sits at or below 0.55 V for 0.3 s with the rear motor unit powered at 8 V or more, and the checks start with the battery management and the high-voltage cables to the rear motor before the motor unit itself. Drive motor A has the equivalent sensor B fault as P0E8E. If several channels read low together, missing high voltage is more likely than a sensor fault. Motor B is normally disabled until the reading is valid.
c: Measuring circuit for channel B in the motor B inverter failed
Signal line shorted to ground or open
High-voltage cable or connection to motor B open, no voltage at the inverter
s: MIL and EV system warning
Rear or second motor without power, front-drive only

P0E94.t: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit High
P0E94.d: P0E94 records that voltage sensor B in the drive motor B inverter reports a value at the top of its signal range. A short from the signal to a supply, an interrupted sensor ground or a defective measuring stage are the usual explanations; a genuine overvoltage would normally show on the other channels too. No manufacturer documents P0E94 publicly. For sensor A of the rear motor Mitsubishi publishes the high limit on the 2023 Outlander PHEV: P0DA6 needs a signal of at least 4.76 V lasting 0.3 s, and only while the propulsion system is active, so the check is not run in standby. The low side of sensor B on motor B is P0E93, the high side of sensor B on motor A is P0E8F. CARB requires out-of-range checks for such inputs. Expect the second motor to be taken offline and a warning with MIL.
c: Measuring stage for channel B in the motor B inverter defective
Signal shorted to a supply or lost sensor ground
Real overvoltage on the high-voltage bus
s: MIL and EV system warning
Second drive motor deactivated, less traction and power

P0E95.t: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E95.d: P0E95 closes the sensor B series for drive motor B: the signal is unstable, with brief dropouts or spikes, rather than permanently low, high or implausible. No manufacturer documents P0E95 publicly. Published values for the neighbouring channels show why short events slip through the other tests: Mitsubishi rates sensor A of the rear motor (2023 Outlander PHEV) as low or high only after 0.3 s outside 0.55 V to 4.76 V, and its plausibility check needs 0.2 s of large deviation. CARB expects inputs to be monitored for circuit, range and rationality faults. Because a rear motor and its wiring are exposed to road spray and suspension movement, a corroded or loose connector is the first thing to check. The warning may appear only on rough roads and clear itself later.
c: Corroded or loose connector on the motor B inverter
Harness damaged where it moves with the axle or suspension
Measuring circuit in the motor B inverter failing intermittently
s: EV or hybrid warning that appears and clears again
Second motor drops out briefly, uneven traction

P0E96.t: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor C Circuit
P0E96.d: P0E96 opens the series for a third voltage measurement in a DC/DC converter, sensor C. It is the general circuit code, meant for a missing or electrically invalid signal; range, low, high and erratic faults of the same sensor follow from P0E97 to P0E9A. Where a converter has more than two voltage channels, for example input and output plus a redundant reading, C names the third. No manufacturer documents P0E96 or any sensor C code in public sources. For orientation, GM's 2025 engine tables (25OBDG03A) cover sensors A and B of a 12 V converter that supports engine auto-starts, with valid readings between 1 V and 28 V and Type B confirmation; FCA calls the first two channels voltage sensor 1 and 2. CARB asks for circuit faults of such inputs to be detected. Converter output may be cut back.
c: Measuring circuit for channel C inside the converter defective
Loose connector or damaged sensing lead
Software fault in the converter or its controller
s: 12 V or converter warning, possibly with MIL
Start-stop or 12 V support restricted

P0E97.t: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P0E97.d: P0E97 is the plausibility code for the third voltage channel of a DC/DC converter: sensor C delivers an electrically valid value that does not agree with what the controller expects. Two makers document it. Audi names P0E9700 for the 2020-2021 Q5 and 2021 A7 plug-in hybrids, stored now and then by the J841 electronics of the electric drive, with symptom code 45146; the revised bulletin explains that the software ignored the tolerance of two capacitors, so the ratio between capacity A and B fell outside its limit, and new software (version 0102) cures it. Mercedes-Benz lists P0E9700 for the converter of the EQB and the G-Class after a faulty wake-up of that unit. Hard faults of sensor C are P0E96, P0E98 and P0E99.
c: Converter or power electronics software with too tight plausibility limits
Converter stuck in an error state after an incorrect wake-up
Drifting voltage measurement inside the converter
s: MIL on, often without a noticeable driving fault
12 V battery or high-voltage warning messages in the cluster
Fault entry appears sporadically and returns after clearing

P0E98.t: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor C Circuit Low
P0E98.d: P0E98 is set when the C voltage channel of a DC/DC converter is stuck at the lowest end of its range, typically because the measuring line is grounded or the sensing stage has lost its supply. No manufacturer documents P0E98 publicly. GM's 2025 tables (25OBDG03A) show the matching test on channels A and B of the 12 V stabiliser used for auto-starts: below 1 V in 320 out of 400 readings at a 12.5 ms rate gives P0E33 or P0E38, rated Type B. A third channel would be judged the same way. CARB calls for range monitoring of inputs like this. If the converter output itself is normal on the other channels, the fault lies in the C path. The high counterpart is P0E99.
c: Sensor C signal line shorted to ground
Measuring stage without supply or with an open signal path
Internal defect in the converter's measuring circuit
s: MIL on, depending on the manufacturer's rating
Converter output reduced or switched to a fallback value
Start-stop or 12 V support may be disabled

P0E99.t: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor C Circuit High
P0E99.d: With P0E99 the controller finds the voltage sensor C reading of a DC/DC converter pinned near its upper limit. That points to the signal touching a battery feed or reference supply, or to a broken sensor ground that lets the input float up, rather than to a real converter overvoltage. No manufacturer documents P0E99 publicly. For channels A and B GM's 2025 engine tables (25OBDG03A) use more than 28 V as the limit for a 12 V converter, far beyond any genuine output, and confirm P0E34 or P0E39 after 320 of 400 failed samples as Type B. CARB demands such out-of-range checks. Comparing sensor C with the other channels and the battery voltage quickly separates a wiring fault from a converter problem; low readings are P0E98.
c: Sensor C signal shorted to battery voltage or reference supply
Open sensor ground letting the signal float high
Actual overvoltage from a faulty converter regulation
s: MIL and charging or 12 V warning possible
Converter limits or stops its output
Start-stop function unavailable

P0E9A.t: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E9A.d: P0E9A completes the sensor C voltage series of a DC/DC converter. It is meant for a signal that jumps, flickers or drops out for brief moments, which the low and high tests miss because they need a fault to persist. No manufacturer documents P0E9A publicly. The GM tables for channels A and B (25OBDG03A) illustrate the gap: their limit checks sample every 12.5 ms and require 320 failures in a window of 400, roughly four seconds, before a code is stored. Under CARB rules inputs need circuit and range tests and, if possible, a check for implausible values; an erratic code covers the cases in between. Corroded pins, a solder joint with a hairline crack or a wire that rubs through under engine movement are the usual causes, so the warning may come and go.
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the sensor C path
Harness chafing intermittently at a moving point
Cracked solder joint in the converter's measuring circuit
s: Warning lamp that appears and disappears
Short interruptions of start-stop or 12 V support
Code often stored as history only

P0E9B.t: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor B Circuit
P0E9B.d: P0E9B opens the series for the second current measurement of a DC/DC converter, sensor B. It covers a signal that is absent or unusable on the electrical level and that the controller cannot classify as low, high or implausible; those cases follow as P0E9C to P0E9F. No manufacturer documents P0E9B itself. Porsche confirms what sensor B is in practice: on the Taycan the high-voltage power electronics name the same channel current sensor 2 and store its short to ground as P0E9D00. Ford's hybrid summary shows what a current input check looks at, an offset below 15 A at power-up and a raw value kept inside 4.5-6.0 V. CARB makes circuit monitoring of such inputs mandatory. Without the reading the converter usually derates.
c: Fault in the converter's internal current sensing
Connector or wiring fault on the sensor B path
s: High-voltage or 12 V system warning
Converter output reduced, 12 V battery charged less
Possibly reduced drive power

P0E9C.t: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0E9C.d: P0E9C means current sensor B of a DC/DC converter gives a value within its electrical window that does not match the operating state, for example a current that stays put while the load changes, or that differs from the figure the controller derives from voltages and switching. No manufacturer documents P0E9C publicly. Ford describes such a rationality test for the boost converter of its hybrids under P0A94: a gap above 50 A between calculated and measured inductor current, lasting over 4 s in controlled operation, flags the converter. FCA treats the equivalent sensor A code P0E52 on the Ram 1500 eTorque as a one-trip fault after a software update. Circuit faults of sensor B are P0E9B, P0E9D and P0E9E.
c: Current sensor B drifting or with a shifted zero point
Fault in the converter power stage causing unexpected currents
Software with an unsuitable plausibility window
s: MIL, sometimes after a single trip
Reduced converter output and weak 12 V charging
Power reduction warning possible

P0E9D.t: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor B Circuit Low
P0E9D.d: P0E9D reports that the signal of DC/DC converter current sensor B has dropped below its valid range. Porsche documents it for the Taycan of model years 2020 to 2024 as P0E9D00, current sensor 2 of the converter with a short to ground, logged by the HV power electronics on the front axle (A49), the rear axle (A50) or both. A red warning tells the driver to stop safely because of an electrical fault, yet once the ignition has been cycled the entry is no longer active. Porsche blames a diagnostic threshold for current monitoring that was set too low and reprograms both control units, using PIWIS Tester version 43.500.000 or newer. Outside that case a real ground short or a dead sensor supply is the likely cause. The high counterpart is P0E9E.
c: Current monitoring threshold set too low in the software
Sensor B signal shorted to ground
Sensor supply missing inside the power electronics
s: Red warning to stop the vehicle safely
Fault no longer active after an ignition cycle
Drive power reduced or vehicle not ready to drive

P0E9E.t: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor B Circuit High
P0E9E.d: P0E9E flags the B current channel of a DC/DC converter reading above its ceiling: the raw signal lies above anything the sensor should output. With a Hall sensor whose zero lies mid-scale, this usually means the signal line touches the supply or the reference ground has opened. No manufacturer documents P0E9E publicly. Mercedes-Benz shows the same fault type on the first channel: on the EQB and G-Class, P0E5400 denotes a short to battery plus on the converter's current sensor A and shows up with red 12 V and HV warnings after a faulty wake-up; the workshop checks it with a buck-mode test of about 30 s in XENTRY and then resets the converter. Porsche calls the B channel current sensor 2 and has its low fault as P0E9D. A real overcurrent belongs to P0D33.
c: Sensor B signal shorted to supply voltage
Open reference ground of the current sensor
Converter in an error state after wake-up, cleared by reset
s: Red 12 V battery or HV warning
Converter stops supplying the 12 V network
Reduced drive power possible

P0E9F.t: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E9F.d: P0E9F is reserved for a current sensor B signal of a DC/DC converter that is unsteady: it spikes, drops out or shows noise yet never stays out of bounds for long. Publicly, no maker describes P0E9F. The Porsche case on the same channel shows how hard such events are to pin down: the Taycan's current sensor 2 low fault P0E9D00 is no longer active after an ignition cycle, and the remedy was a revised threshold rather than a part. Ford rates a current signal as valid only inside a raw band of 4.5-6.0 V; a value that leaves and re-enters that band briefly is exactly what an erratic code is for. CARB asks for inputs to be watched for open, shorted and implausible signals. Loose terminals, vibration or a marginal solder joint are typical; steady low or high faults are P0E9D and P0E9E.
c: Loose terminal or connector on the sensor B path
Solder joint that opens under heat or vibration
Electrical interference on the measuring line
s: Warnings that come and go
Brief converter derating
Code stored without a current fault

P0EA0.t: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor C Circuit
P0EA0.d: P0EA0 covers circuit faults of a third current channel inside a DC/DC converter, sensor C. Converters with several phases or with separate input and output sensing can carry more than two current channels; the letter C simply names the third. It is used when that reading is missing or cannot be decoded and no sharper diagnosis fits; plausibility, too-low, too-high and unstable signals have P0EA1 to P0EA4. No manufacturer documents P0EA0 or any other sensor C current code in public sources. Ford's hybrid summary describes the kind of current input check involved, where the raw value must stay between 4.5 V and 6.0 V and the offset at power-up under 15 A. Such checks are mandatory under CARB. The equivalent codes for channels A and B are P0E51 and P0E9B.
c: Defect in the converter's third current sensing channel
Damaged connector or wiring on the sensor C path
Software fault in the signal evaluation
s: Warning for the high-voltage or 12 V system
Converter limited to a reduced output
MIL depending on the manufacturer

P0EA1.t: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P0EA1.d: P0EA1 stands for a sensor C current reading that is electrically plausible yet disagrees with the converter's operating point or with its sister channels. If a converter measures several phase currents, those values should track each other, and one channel that deviates is a typical trigger. No manufacturer documents P0EA1 publicly. Ford's P0A94 test illustrates the approach for the boost converter of its hybrids: a deviation of over 50 A between measured and calculated inductor current, held for more than 4 s, counts as a fault. FCA shows how makers adjust such checks, turning the sensor A rationality code P0E52 into a one-trip fault for the Ram 1500 eTorque with flash 08-037-21. Hard circuit faults of sensor C use P0EA0, P0EA2 and P0EA3.
c: Sensor C channel drifting away from the other channels
Fault in the converter phase measured by sensor C
Plausibility software in need of an update
s: MIL, possibly after one trip
Reduced 12 V charging current
Converter or drive power derated

P0EA2.t: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor C Circuit Low
P0EA2.d: P0EA2 is stored when current sensor C of a DC/DC converter reports a raw value under its lower limit. Because current sensors in these units normally place their zero-current output at mid-supply, a value near zero volts rarely means low current; it points to a ground short, a lost sensor supply or a broken signal path. No manufacturer documents P0EA2 publicly. The closest published case is Porsche's P0E9D00 on the B channel of the Taycan converter, a short to ground that in fact came from a monitoring threshold set too low and was cured with new software. Ford rates current inputs as faulty below 4.5 V raw. CARB asks for out-of-range checks of such inputs. The high fault of sensor C is P0EA3.
c: Sensor C signal shorted to ground
Missing supply voltage of the current sensor
Monitoring threshold in the software set too tight
s: Warning lamp and possibly a stop request
Converter switched off or derated
12 V battery discharges while driving

P0EA3.t: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor C Circuit High
P0EA3.d: P0EA3 marks a current sensor C signal above the top of its accepted window. Electrically this means the signal line touching a voltage source, an open sensor ground or a failed output stage of the sensor; a genuine overcurrent of the converter is a different matter and has its own code, P0D33. No manufacturer documents P0EA3 publicly. Mercedes-Benz illustrates the fault type on the first current channel of the converter in the EQB and the G-Class, which logs P0E5400 for a short to plus; in that bulletin the entry comes from a wrong wake-up of the converter rather than from damaged wiring; a converter reset ends the error state. Ford treats raw current signals above 6.0 V as faulty. If only sensor C is affected, its path is the suspect. The low fault is P0EA2.
c: Sensor C signal shorted to supply
Open ground of the current sensor
s: 12 V or high-voltage warning in the cluster
Converter output stopped
Reduced performance possible

P0EA4.t: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0EA4.d: P0EA4 ends the current sensor C series and describes a signal that wavers or breaks off momentarily instead of failing steadily. No manufacturer documents P0EA4 publicly. A comparable published fault exists for the first channel: FCA bulletin 08-333-25 covers P0E55-00, the erratic code of current sensor A, on the 2025 Ram 1500 eTorque V6: there the 12 V battery loses charge, in bad cases until the pickup has to be towed, and FCA answers with a software update of the battery pack controller (BPCM). A software check is therefore worth doing before any part is replaced. CARB obliges makers to supervise such inputs. On the hardware side, a loose plug, a damaged pin or a joint that opens with temperature changes are the usual causes. Steady faults of sensor C are P0EA0, P0EA2 and P0EA3.
c: Loose plug or damaged pin on the sensor C path
Outdated control software evaluating the signal too strictly
Connection that opens with temperature changes
s: Sporadic warnings without a lasting fault
12 V battery not kept fully charged
Start-stop occasionally disabled

P0EA5.d: P0EA5 says that a second DC/DC converter, B, does not deliver what it is asked to, for example the commanded output voltage or current, although its sensors give no circuit fault. FCA documents it as DC/DC Converter 2 Performance for the 2019 Jeep Cherokee (KL) with the 3.2 litre V6 and engine start/stop: PCM flash bulletins 18-023-19 REV. B and 18-077-22 list it with P0EA6 and with communication codes for converter control modules A and B, alongside restart problems after a stop phase. The fix there is new PCM software, done with a charger keeping the battery between 13.2 and 13.5 V. Ford's equivalent test for converter A (P0A94) compares calculated and measured current, 50 A for 4 s. Overheating of converter B is P0EA6.
c: Engine or powertrain control software needing an update
Poor supply or ground connection of converter B
s: MIL on
Engine does not restart after an auto-stop, start-stop disabled
Voltage dips in the 12 V network, for example audio dropouts

P0EA6.d: P0EA6 means the second DC/DC converter, B, has reached a temperature beyond its permitted limit. Unlike a temperature sensor code, the reading itself is accepted as true; the unit is simply too hot and will normally reduce or stop its output to protect itself. FCA lists it as DC/DC Converter 2 Over Temperature for the 2019 Cherokee (KL) with the 3.2 V6 and stop-start (sales code EHK), in its PCM reflash bulletins (18-077-22, earlier 18-023-19 REV. B), which apply to MIL complaints with a list of start-stop related codes; no threshold is published. Under CARB the function of such parts has to be supervised. Blocked cooling air, high load on the 12 V network or a weak internal power stage are typical causes. Converter A uses P0D32 for the same fault.
c: Cooling air or heat sink of converter B obstructed
Sustained high load on the 12 V network
Control software misjudging the temperature condition
Weak internal power stage of converter B
s: MIL on
Start-stop unavailable while the converter is hot
Electrical consumers affected during engine restart

P0EA7.d: P0EA7 reports that an auxiliary cooling loop, a coolant circuit kept apart from the main engine circuit, does not achieve the cooling effect the controller expects. Volvo documents the code for its T8 plug-in hybrids of model years 2016 to 2019 (XC90, S90, XC60, S60 and others): the engine control module stores P0EA773, fault type actuator stuck closed, and turns on the check-engine light. Technical Journal 34123 traces it to the thermostat in the cooling coil of the electric rear axle drive and calls for a revised part with a small orifice, fitted in the correct orientation, followed by a coolant refill. Ford lists P0EA7:19 among codes that faulty dynamics-module software can leave in the PCM of the 2025-2026 Mustang GTD; reprogramming cures it there. Sensor faults of the same loop are P0E81 to P0E84.
c: Thermostat in the auxiliary loop sticking closed (Volvo T8, earlier part design)
Low coolant level or trapped air in the auxiliary loop
Weak or failed auxiliary coolant pump
Module software reporting the fault wrongly (Ford Mustang GTD)
s: Check-engine light on
Often no noticeable change in driving behaviour
Possible power limits on electric drive parts that run too warm

P0EA8.t: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor B Circuit
P0EA8.d: P0EA8 is the general circuit code for the second high-voltage measurement of an electric A/C compressor, labelled sensor B. Such compressors draw their power from the traction battery and convert it in a built-in inverter; the module reads the supply voltage to control the motor and protect its power stage. Here the B signal is missing or unusable as a whole, without being classed as low, high or implausible. No manufacturer documents P0EA8 publicly, and nobody states which point sensor B measures. For the A channel, GM's 2011 Volt tables show how such inputs are judged (P0D6A at 440 V or more, P0D6B at 190 V or less, each Type B). CARB demands circuit checks on inputs that hybrid battery cooling relies on. Expect the compressor to stop; specific faults are P0EA9 to P0EAC.
c: Interrupted voltage sense path inside or at the compressor
Fault on the compressor's inverter or control board
Poorly seated high-voltage or signal connector at the compressor
s: Air conditioning does not cool
Fault message for the climate system
Battery cooling via refrigerant may be unavailable during charging

P0EA9.t: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor B Circuit Performance
P0EA9.d: P0EA9 means the B voltage reading reported by the electric A/C compressor looks electrically valid but does not fit other information, usually the high voltage reported by the battery system that feeds the compressor directly. No manufacturer documents P0EA9 publicly. The matching check on sensor A (P0D69) shows typical limits: Mitsubishi's 2019 Outlander PHEV flags a gap of 20 V or more lasting 2 s once the compressor sees 205 to 415 V, the battery is above 15 °C and intake air above 0 °C; GM's 2011 Volt uses more than 15 V in 35 of 40 samples. Mitsubishi names the data bus, the compressor assembly and the hybrid ECU as causes, and a drifting measurement inside the compressor is just as likely for channel B. Hard circuit faults of sensor B are P0EA8, P0EAA and P0EAB.
c: Drifting voltage measurement inside the compressor module
Faulty data exchange between compressor and hybrid controller
Wrong battery voltage reference from the hybrid or battery controller
s: Air conditioning switches off or works only now and then
Fault often recorded without any other symptom

P0EAA.t: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor B Circuit High
P0EAA.d: P0EAA flags a B voltage reading at the top of, or beyond, the plausible range of the compressor supply. Since the battery cannot really deliver that much, the cause usually lies in the measurement itself: an open or shorted sense path, a failed voltage divider inside the compressor or a wrong reference. No manufacturer documents P0EAA publicly. GM's 2011 Volt judges the A channel this way (P0D6A): 440 V or more in 30 of 60 samples taken every 50 ms, Type B with MIL after two trips; a single sample at 480 V or more triggers a separate maker code. A genuinely high bus voltage would also show up in battery and inverter codes, which helps to tell the two apart. The compressor normally shuts down; the low counterpart is P0EAB.
c: Failed voltage divider or reference in the compressor module
Sense line shorted to a higher potential
Actual overvoltage on the high-voltage bus
s: Compressor stops, cabin is not cooled
Warning in the climate control display

P0EAB.t: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor B Circuit Low
P0EAB.d: P0EAB is set when the B voltage channel of the electric A/C compressor reports far less than the high-voltage battery actually supplies while the contactors are closed. Typical reasons are a sense line shorted to ground, a broken internal connection or a sensing stage without supply; a supply interrupted upstream, for instance by a high-voltage fuse, produces the same picture and should be ruled out first. No manufacturer documents P0EAB publicly. For the A channel (P0D6B), GM's 2011 Volt uses 190 V or less in 30 of 60 samples, contactors closed and no faults present, Type B. CARB calls for range checks of such inputs where hybrid cooling depends on them. The air conditioning, and possibly battery cooling, fails; the high counterpart is P0EAA.
c: Voltage sense line shorted to ground
High-voltage supply to the compressor interrupted (fuse, connector)
Measuring stage in the compressor module without supply
s: No cooling from the air conditioning
Charging power may be reduced if the battery cannot be cooled

P0EAC.t: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0EAC.d: P0EAC points to a B voltage signal that jumps or drops out for short moments instead of staying wrong. The module sees sudden changes no real battery voltage can make, or values that come and go. Loose high-voltage or signal connectors at the compressor, vibration damage to the harness, moisture in a plug and internal contact problems on the inverter board are the usual suspects. No manufacturer documents P0EAC publicly; GM and Mitsubishi only publish steady range and plausibility checks for the A channel (P0D6A, P0D6B, P0D69). The fault may vanish after a restart and return with vibration or temperature changes. Wiggle tests are only allowed after the high-voltage circuit is isolated and verified dead. Steady faults of the same sensor are P0EA8 to P0EAB.
c: Loose or corroded connector at the compressor
Harness chafed or cracked by engine and road vibration
Cracked solder joint on the compressor control board
s: Air conditioning cuts out briefly and then resumes
Fault entry returns after clearing

P0EAD.t: A/C Compressor Motor Current Sensor Circuit
P0EAD.d: P0EAD covers the current sensor of an electric A/C compressor, which measures how much current the motor drive takes from the high-voltage link. The controller needs this value to limit power and to shield the power stage and the high-voltage pack from overload. P0EAD is the general circuit code: the reading is absent or useless as a whole, with no low, high or plausibility verdict. Only Audi documents a sibling publicly (P0EAE on the 2016 A3 e-tron); P0EAD itself appears in no manufacturer source. GM's 2011 Volt shows how the measured value is used: above 27 A in 30 of 60 samples while the motor runs gives P0D6F, Type B. Because the sensor sits inside the compressor's power module, repair normally means the compressor assembly. Specific faults are P0EAE to P0EB0.
c: Failed current sensing element in the compressor power module
Open internal connection between sensor and control board
Compressor or climate module software error
s: Compressor does not start, no cooling
Fault stored in the climate or compressor module

P0EAE.t: A/C Compressor Motor Current Sensor Range/Performance
P0EAE.d: P0EAE says the compressor current reading is electrically valid but does not fit the operating state, for example a value that does not match motor speed or load. Audi documents the code for the 2016 A3 e-tron: P0EAE00 is stored as a passive or sporadic entry in the Climatronic module J255, the MIL is lit at the request of another module over the vehicle network while the engine module holds no code, and P26FD00 may appear alongside. Audi bulletin 2047037 blames a software calculation error in the compressor self-test and the refrigerant system check; technicians follow the guided test plan, replace the compressor only if it directs them to, and update J255 from software 0510 to 0520. CARB requires A/C components used by other diagnostics to be monitored. Circuit faults of this sensor are P0EAD, P0EAF and P0EB0.
c: Calculation error in the climate module software (Audi A3 e-tron, update available)
Drifting current measurement in the compressor
Internal compressor fault confirmed by the guided test
s: MIL on without an engine module fault code
Air conditioning may or may not be restricted
Entry stored as passive or sporadic

P0EAF.t: A/C Compressor Motor Current Sensor Circuit Low
P0EAF.d: P0EAF reports that the compressor current signal sits at the bottom of its measuring range. In a running compressor this cannot be true, so the module suspects the measuring chain: a grounded signal path, a sensing chip without supply or an offset error inside the power module. No manufacturer documents P0EAF publicly. GM's 2011 Volt supervises the measured current only against upper limits (27 A over 30 of 60 samples for P0D6F, 60 A on a single sample for a maker code), and Audi documents only the plausibility sibling P0EAE. Without a valid current value the controller cannot protect the inverter, so it shuts the compressor down. Air conditioning stops working while the car itself remains fully drivable. The high counterpart is P0EB0.
c: Current signal path shorted to ground
Offset error of the measurement in the power module
s: Compressor shut down, warm air from the vents
Climate system fault message

P0EB0.t: A/C Compressor Motor Current Sensor Circuit High
P0EB0.d: P0EB0 flags a current sensor signal at the top end of its range, beyond what the compressor drive could ever draw. It differs from a genuine overcurrent such as P0D6F, where the measurement is trusted and the motor is overloaded: here the signal itself is suspect, for example after a short to a supply voltage or a failed sensing element. No manufacturer documents P0EB0 publicly. GM's 2011 Volt gives a feel for normal limits: more than 27 A over 30 of 60 samples counts as excessive load there, Type B. CARB demands range checks for inputs that hybrid thermal management relies on. If the reading looks plausible after a restart, a stiff compressor or an overfilled refrigerant circuit should still be ruled out. The low counterpart is P0EAF.
c: Failed sensing element in the compressor inverter
Current signal shorted to a supply voltage
Real overload from a stiff compressor or excessive refrigerant charge
s: Compressor switches off right after starting
No cooling, fault message in the climate display

P0EB1.t: A/C Compressor Motor Phase U Current Sensor Circuit
P0EB1.d: Electric A/C compressors run a three-phase permanent-magnet motor whose inverter measures the phase currents in order to commutate it and limit torque. P0EB1 is the general circuit fault of the phase U current sensor: the controller gets no usable signal and gives no finer verdict on it. P0EB1 is not described in any public maker document. GM's 2011 Volt checked the same sensors under the older codes P0D7A to P0D7F, testing at standstill with zero speed request; any reading of 68 A or more in either direction (30 of 60 samples, 50 ms) counted as a sensor fault, Type B, and only a 12 V reset allowed a new pass. The sensor belongs to the inverter, so the usual repair is the compressor assembly. U-phase details: P0EB2 to P0EB4.
c: Failed phase U current sensor in the compressor inverter
Open signal path between sensor and inverter controller
Fault on the inverter control board
s: Compressor does not run, cabin stays warm
Climate system warning

P0EB2.t: A/C Compressor Motor Phase U Current Sensor Circuit High
P0EB2.d: P0EB2 is set when the phase U current sensor of the electric A/C compressor sends a signal above its valid window. Current sensors in such inverters often output a voltage centred on zero current, so a stuck-high output reads like a large current in one direction even with the motor at rest. No manufacturer documents P0EB2 publicly. GM's 2011 Volt ran a standstill test that catches exactly this: plus 68 A or more on phase U with no speed request set the older code P0D7A, Type B. A short to the sensor supply, a damaged Hall element or a fault on the inverter board are typical. The compressor controller stops the motor to protect the power stage. P0EB3 covers the low side; P0EB5 and P0EB8 report the same fault on phases V and W.
c: Damaged Hall element of the phase U sensor
Phase U signal shorted to the sensor supply
Defect on the inverter board affecting the U channel
s: Compressor will not start or stops at once
No cooling during hot weather

P0EB3.t: A/C Compressor Motor Phase U Current Sensor Circuit Low
P0EB3.d: P0EB3 means the phase U current signal has fallen below its permitted range. Depending on the sensor design this looks like a large negative current or like no signal at all; either way the controller can no longer trust the U-phase value it needs to drive the motor smoothly. No maker documents P0EB3 publicly. In GM's 2011 Volt, a phase U reading of minus 68 A or lower with the compressor at rest set the older code P0D7B, Type B with MIL after two trips, and a 12 V reset was needed before the test could pass again. Likely causes are a ground short in the sensing path, lost sensor supply or an internal inverter fault. Cooling stays off until the fault clears. Counterpart: P0EB2; the same fault on V and W: P0EB6, P0EB9.
c: Phase U sensing path shorted to ground
Supply to the phase U sensor missing
Internal fault in the compressor inverter
s: Air conditioning inoperative
Fault message after switching the A/C on

P0EB4.t: A/C Compressor Motor Phase U Current Sensor Range/Performance
P0EB4.d: P0EB4 concerns the plausibility of the phase U current reading of an electric A/C compressor. The value is in range but disagrees with what the controller can work out for itself: in a motor fed by three wires the phase currents must add up to roughly zero, and each phase should follow the commanded current pattern. A standing offset or a wrong gain while running are typical findings. No manufacturer documents P0EB4 publicly. GM's 2011 Volt looked for offsets on its compressor phases only with the motor stopped (plus or minus 68 A, older codes P0D7A and P0D7B). A weakening sensor element or inverter board is the usual cause, so the compressor assembly gets replaced. Electrical faults of phase U are P0EB1 to P0EB3.
c: Offset or gain drift of the phase U sensor
Ageing measurement circuit on the inverter board
Winding fault in the compressor motor distorting the currents
s: Compressor runs roughly or noisily before switching off
Reduced or intermittent cooling

P0EB5.t: A/C Compressor Motor Phase V Current Sensor Circuit High
P0EB5.d: P0EB5 is the high-range fault of the phase V current sensor in the compressor inverter. The reading lies above the window the sensor can produce in normal service, which points to a short towards supply voltage, a defective sensing element or an internal fault in the power module rather than to real overcurrent. Unusually, the V-phase codes start with high, low and plausibility, while the general V circuit code comes later as P0EBB. No manufacturer documents P0EB5 publicly. GM's 2011 Volt detected a stuck V-phase sensor at standstill at plus 68 A or more under the older code P0D7C, Type B. The compressor drive is switched off, and refrigerant-based battery cooling may be lost with it. Related codes: P0EB6, P0EB7 and P0EBB.
c: Phase V signal shorted towards supply voltage
Internal fault in the compressor power module
s: Compressor switched off, no cooling
Battery may warm up more during fast charging

P0EB6.t: A/C Compressor Motor Phase V Current Sensor Circuit Low
P0EB6.d: P0EB6 reports that the phase V current signal reads below its permissible minimum. The compressor's power module cannot regulate phase V without it and stops the motor. Candidates are a sensing path pulled to ground, a sensor that has lost its supply or a defect on the inverter board; a problem in the refrigerant circuit cannot produce this code. No manufacturer documents P0EB6 publicly. In the first-generation Chevrolet Volt, GM treated minus 68 A or lower on phase V with the motor at rest as a sensor fault (older code P0D7D, 30 of 60 samples, Type B). Because the sensor is built in, replacing the compressor unit is the normal fix. High range: P0EB5; general V circuit: P0EBB; the phase U and W equivalents are P0EB3 and P0EB9.
c: Phase V sensing path pulled to ground
Phase V sensor has lost its supply
Defect in the V channel of the inverter board
s: No air conditioning
Fault stored in the compressor control module

P0EB7.t: A/C Compressor Motor Phase V Current Sensor Range/Performance
P0EB7.d: With P0EB7 the compressor's phase V current value passes the electrical limits but is not credible. The controller compares it with the other two phases and with the current it is commanding; a persistent offset, a reading that lags or is scaled wrongly, or a three-phase sum far from zero all point at the V sensor. No manufacturer documents P0EB7 publicly. GM's 2011 Volt shows one form of such a check, performed at standstill (older codes P0D7C and P0D7D at plus or minus 68 A). Rough compressor running, noise or reduced cooling can appear before the controller gives up and switches off. Electrical faults of the same phase are P0EB5, P0EB6 and P0EBB; the matching checks on U and W are P0EB4 and P0EBA.
c: Persistent offset or scaling error of the phase V sensor
Slow or filtered V-phase measurement on the inverter board
Fault in the V winding or its internal lead
s: Uneven compressor running or humming noise
Cooling weakens, then fails

P0EB8.t: A/C Compressor Motor Phase W Current Sensor Circuit High
P0EB8.d: P0EB8 indicates that the phase W current sensor of the compressor inverter delivers a value above its usable range. Since the motor is not actually drawing such a current, a short to a positive supply in the sensing circuit or a failed sensor element is the most probable explanation. The W-phase series runs high, low and plausibility from P0EB8 to P0EBA, while the general W circuit code sits apart at P0EC0. No manufacturer documents P0EB8 publicly. GM's first-generation Volt flagged a W-phase reading of plus 68 A or more with the motor stopped under the older code P0D7E, Type B, and demanded a 12 V reset before the test could pass. Air conditioning stops. Counterpart: P0EB9; the same fault on U and V: P0EB2, P0EB5.
c: W-phase sensing circuit shorted to a positive supply
Fault in the W input of the inverter controller
s: A/C stops working, warning shown
Compressor will not restart until the fault is cleared

P0EB9.t: A/C Compressor Motor Phase W Current Sensor Circuit Low
P0EB9.d: P0EB9 is stored when the phase W current signal drops beneath its lower limit, for instance after the signal wire has made contact with ground or after the sensor has lost its feed. The value is then useless for motor control, and the compressor module shuts the drive down rather than run it on two phases of information. No manufacturer documents P0EB9 publicly. GM's 2011 Volt shows a comparable test: minus 68 A or lower on phase W at standstill set the older code P0D7F, rated Type B with MIL after two trips. Because the sensing sits inside the compressor, repair usually means replacing the compressor assembly once wiring and high-voltage plugs have been checked. High range: P0EB8; plausibility: P0EBA; general W circuit: P0EC0.
c: Phase W measuring line shorted to ground
Defect of the W measurement inside the compressor module
s: No cooling, compressor silent
Climate fault indicated

P0EBA.t: A/C Compressor Motor Phase W Current Sensor Range/Performance
P0EBA.d: P0EBA covers an implausible phase W current reading in an electric A/C compressor: the signal stays in range, yet it does not agree with the commanded current, the rotor position or the two other phases. No manufacturer documents P0EBA publicly. GM's 2011 Volt used a standstill check for sensor offsets on phase W, filed under the older codes P0D7E and P0D7F at plus or minus 68 A, 30 of 60 samples, Type B. In practice an ageing current sensor or a fault on the inverter board is behind it, and since both live inside the compressor, the assembly is replaced after the high-voltage system has been made safe and the connectors have been inspected. The compressor may run unevenly before the controller cuts it out. Electrical faults of phase W: P0EB8, P0EB9 and P0EC0.
c: Fault in the W measurement on the inverter board
Rotor position estimate disturbed, making the W current look wrong
s: Compressor runs unevenly, then stops
Cooling capacity drops

P0EBB.t: A/C Compressor Motor Phase V Current Sensor Circuit
P0EBB.d: P0EBB is the general circuit code for the compressor's phase V current sensor, numbered after the W-phase codes instead of at the start of the V series. The module receives no usable V-phase value at all and does not classify it further as high, low or implausible. Without that value the field-oriented control of the three-phase motor cannot work, so the drive stops. No manufacturer documents P0EBB publicly. GM's 2011 Volt monitored the phase sensors of its compressor at standstill under older codes (P0D7C and P0D7D for phase V, plus or minus 68 A, Type B). Causes are an open sensing path, a loose internal plug or a failed sensor or board. Detailed V-phase faults are P0EB5 to P0EB7; the general U and W circuit codes are P0EB1 and P0EC0.
c: Failed phase V sensor or inverter board
Loose internal plug between sensor and board
s: Compressor does not run
Air conditioning and possibly battery cooling unavailable

P0EBC.t: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0EBC.d: P0EBC is the general circuit fault of the first refrigerant temperature sensor in the air conditioning loop: the control module gets no usable reading from it and does not narrow the fault down to high or low. Volkswagen lists P0EBC00 for the 2021 ID.4 as an electrical fault of refrigerant temperature sensor 1 in the A/C module (address 0008). There the value comes from G395, a combined pressure and temperature sender on the low-pressure line, and bulletin 87-22-01 cures it by replacing that sender, which means draining and recharging the refrigerant. The A/C may stop cooling. Voltage faults of the same sensor are P0EBD and P0EBE, plausibility is P0EBF.
c: Internal electrical fault of the refrigerant pressure/temperature sender (VW G395)
Corroded connector or damaged wiring to the sensor
Faulty sensor input in the climate control module
s: Air conditioning inoperative or not cooling
Fault entry stored in the climate control module

P0EBD.t: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0EBD.d: P0EBD means the signal voltage of refrigerant temperature sensor A sits at the top of its range. With the usual NTC thermistor that equals an extremely cold reading, and in practice it points to an open signal path, a disconnected plug or a short to the reference voltage. No manufacturer documents P0EBD publicly. As a comparison for the same kind of sensor, GM's 2012 Volt flags its evaporator refrigerant sensor above 98 percent of the 5 V reference (about 4.9 V) in 40 of 50 samples, Type B, under P0538. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV treats a high input lasting 4 seconds as an open circuit. A wrong cold value can block compressor operation. The low-voltage counterpart is P0EBE.
c: Open signal or ground wire, or unplugged connector
Signal wire shorted to the reference or supply voltage
s: Compressor stays off or A/C output is reduced
Implausibly low refrigerant temperature in live data

P0EBE.t: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0EBE.d: P0EBE is logged when the voltage from refrigerant temperature sensor A falls close to zero. For an NTC element a low voltage stands for high temperature, so the controller sees refrigerant that seems far too hot. Real heat at that level is unlikely; a signal wire chafed through to ground or a thermistor shorted internally is the usual finding. No manufacturer publishes P0EBE. GM's 2012 Volt reacts to its evaporator refrigerant sensor below 2 percent of the reference (about 0.1 V) in 40 of 50 samples as P0537, Type B, which shows how such a check is built. Expect the compressor to be held off as protection. High-voltage fault of this sensor: P0EBD.
c: Signal wire chafed and shorted to ground
s: A/C compressor switched off as a precaution
Live data shows an unrealistically hot refrigerant

P0EBF.t: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor A Range/Performance
P0EBF.d: P0EBF reports that sensor A gives an electrically valid but implausible refrigerant temperature. Three makers name it. Audi stores P0EBF00 as passive or sporadic in the Climatronic module of the 2016 A3 e-tron; bulletin 2047037 blames a miscalculation in the refrigerant self-check and points to TSB 2046942. VW's 2021 ID.4 links it to the G395 sender, which is replaced. Volvo logs P0EBF24 in the engine module of its 2017 to 2019 S90, V60, XC60 and XC90, lighting the check engine lamp: when the car had been pre-heated or pre-cooled, or started remotely, while the traction battery was charged, the software misjudged the sensor, and Technical Journal 34446 ends with a software update. Circuit faults are P0EBC to P0EBE.
c: Software misjudgement after preconditioning or self-check (Volvo, Audi; update available)
Wrong refrigerant charge distorting the comparison values
s: Check engine lamp on (Volvo) or MIL requested by the climate module (Audi)
Fault stored as intermittent or sporadic
A/C may cool poorly or not at all

P0EC0.t: A/C Compressor Motor Phase W Current Sensor Circuit
P0EC0.d: P0EC0 is the umbrella circuit code for the phase W current sensor in the inverter of an electric A/C compressor. It applies when no valid W-phase value arrives at all, without a split into high, low or implausible; those cases have their own codes P0EB8 to P0EBA. Like the phase V circuit code P0EBB it is numbered out of sequence. No manufacturer documents P0EC0 publicly. For orientation, GM's 2011 Volt checked each compressor phase with the motor stopped and set a fault when the W reading stayed beyond plus or minus 68 A in 30 of 60 samples (older codes P0D7E and P0D7F, Type B, 12 V reset needed). Without the W value the motor control cannot run the compressor. U-phase circuit code: P0EB1.
c: Failed W-phase current sensor or inverter board
Interrupted W-phase sensing path inside the inverter
