Missing supply voltage for the current sensors
s: Electric A/C compressor does not start
No cabin cooling, battery cooling via refrigerant may be limited

P0EC1.t: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P0EC1.d: P0EC1 covers a circuit fault of a second refrigerant temperature sensor, found mainly on electrified cars whose heat pump or battery chiller measures the refrigerant at several points. The module receives no usable value from sensor B. No manufacturer publishes P0EC1 or says which of its sensors counts as B. Volkswagen's e-Golf shows how such networks look: up to five combined pressure/temperature senders (G395, G826 to G829) share two LIN lines, and because early parts could not be auto-addressed, bulletin 87-17-02 requires replacing every sender on the affected line. Without B the heat pump or A/C may shut down. Detailed faults of sensor B: P0EC2 to P0EC4; sensor A: P0EBC.
c: Failed sensor B or combined pressure/temperature sender
Wiring, connector or shared LIN line fault
Mixed part versions on one LIN line after a repair
s: Heat pump or A/C switched off or limited
Fault stored in the climate control module

P0EC2.t: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
P0EC2.d: With P0EC2 the signal of refrigerant temperature sensor B is stuck near the reference voltage. An NTC thermistor would only get there at extreme cold, so an open circuit somewhere in the loop is far more likely. No manufacturer documents P0EC2 publicly. Mitsubishi's procedure for the analogous evaporator outlet sensor of the Outlander PHEV shows the logic: the A/C amplifier sets its open-circuit code after 4 seconds of high input while READY is on or the battery is charging, and the technician measures about 5 V at the unplugged connector and checks both lines for continuity under 2 ohms. A false cold reading may lock out heating or cooling. Low counterpart: P0EC3.
c: Open signal or ground line between sensor B and module
Connector not fully seated after A/C work
s: Very low refrigerant temperature shown for sensor B
Heating via heat pump or cooling unavailable

P0EC3.t: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P0EC3.d: P0EC3 stands for a sensor B signal pulled down toward ground. Because a thermistor of the NTC type lowers its resistance as it warms, the module reads a refrigerant temperature far above anything the system could reach. Typical culprits are a harness pinched against the body, water inside the plug or a sensor that has failed shorted. P0EC3 appears in no public manufacturer document. GM's evaporator sensor check on the 2012 Volt (P0537, below roughly 0.1 V, two trips) is the nearest documented model. On cars that cool the traction battery through the refrigerant loop the controller may restrict that cooling as well as the cabin A/C. Open-circuit side: P0EC2; sensor A equivalent: P0EBE.
c: Harness pinched against the body, signal shorted to ground
Water ingress in the sensor plug
s: A/C compressor held off, cabin not cooled
Charging or driving power possibly limited if battery cooling depends on the loop

P0EC4.t: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor B Range/Performance
P0EC4.d: P0EC4 is a plausibility fault: sensor B delivers a voltage inside its normal window, yet the temperature it reports does not agree with other information. No manufacturer documents P0EC4 publicly. A well-described pattern comes from GM's 2012 Volt (P153B, Type B): once the compressor has been off for over an hour, the low-side refrigerant temperature must lie within 10 degrees Celsius of the raw ambient temperature and of the value derived from high-side pressure; the check runs only when no circuit codes are active. A drifting sensor, poor thermal contact or a wrong charge can fail such a comparison. The A/C usually still works but may be controlled poorly. Electrical faults of sensor B: P0EC1 to P0EC3.
c: Sensor B drifting out of tolerance
Sensor not seated properly on the pipe, poor thermal contact
Incorrect refrigerant charge shifting the comparison values
s: Uneven or weak cooling, compressor cycling oddly
Fault often appears only after a long standstill

P0EC5.t: A/C Compressor Motor Speed Sensor Range/Performance
P0EC5.d: P0EC5 means the speed information of the electrically driven compressor motor is implausible: the motor does not turn at the speed the controller expects, or the reported value contradicts other data. Mazda uses the code on the 2024 to 2026 CX-90 PHEV and 2025 to 2026 CX-70 PHEV, describing P0EC5:00 in the PCM as an error signal coming from the compressor. Bulletin 07-002/26b lists it beside P0D6D, U0605 and P0AA6 when an overcurrent shorts the compressor internally and the high-voltage A/C fuse blows; the A/C then stops cooling. GM's 2011 Volt ran a similar test as P1F0A, Type B: fault if the spinning motor stays below 1800 rpm for 20 seconds.
c: Internal short in the electric compressor after overcurrent (Mazda PHEV)
Blown high-voltage A/C fuse cutting compressor power
Mechanical drag or lack of oil keeping the motor below target speed
s: A/C does not cool
Accompanying compressor voltage, communication or insulation codes

P0EC6.t: A/C Power Supply Relay Control Circuit/Open
P0EC6.d: P0EC6 concerns the control side of the relay that switches power to air conditioning components, typically the compressor or climate electronics. The module driving the relay coil notices that its output does not behave as commanded, most often because the coil circuit is open. No manufacturer documents P0EC6 publicly, and the exact wiring differs by maker. CARB requires output components to be checked either functionally or for circuit continuity and shorts, and lets manufacturers report open and shorted states under one code, which is the role of this umbrella code. A relay that never pulls in leaves the A/C without power. Voltage-specific faults: P0EC7 and P0EC8; the clutch relay equivalent is P0645.
c: Relay coil burnt open or relay missing
Open control wire or loose relay socket terminal
Failed output driver in the controlling module
s: A/C or electric compressor completely without function
No relay click when A/C is requested

P0EC7.t: A/C Power Supply Relay Control Circuit Low
P0EC7.d: P0EC7 is set when the control line of the relay feeding the A/C reads too low a voltage, usually because it is shorted to ground. What the driver feels depends on how the coil is switched: with a low-side driver a grounded line can keep the relay energised even with the A/C off, while with a high-side driver the relay simply cannot be switched on. No manufacturer documents P0EC7 publicly. As a comparison, Mitsubishi monitors a relay-fed supply on its throttle actuator (P0657): with battery voltage above 8.3 V, the switched line must not sit at or below 6.0 V for 0.35 seconds. Open-circuit code: P0EC6; high counterpart: P0EC8; clutch relay analogue: P0646.
c: Relay control line chafed and shorted to ground
Shorted turns in the relay coil
Output stage of the module stuck low
s: A/C power stays on with A/C switched off, or never switches on
Possible battery drain while parked if the relay stays energised

P0EC8.t: A/C Power Supply Relay Control Circuit High
P0EC8.d: P0EC8 indicates that the relay control circuit for the A/C power supply carries too high a voltage, typically a short to a battery-fed wire. A low-side driver then pushes current straight into that short when it switches on; modern output stages detect the overcurrent, turn themselves off and log this code, so the relay stays open and the A/C components get no power. With a high-side driver the same fault can hold the relay on permanently. No manufacturer documents P0EC8 publicly. CARB explicitly lists shorts toward a higher voltage as a circuit fault that output component monitoring must catch. Look for wires rubbing on a powered conductor or a shorted coil. Low side: P0EC7; clutch relay analogue: P0647.
c: Control line shorted to a battery-fed wire
Relay coil with too low resistance overloading the driver
s: A/C has no power and stays off
Relay may stay energised permanently on high-side switched designs

P0EC9.t: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve A Stuck/Open
P0EC9.d: P0EC9 reports that refrigerant distribution valve A, a solenoid valve that splits refrigerant between branches of the A/C circuit, stays open or does not close on command. Such a fault is usually detected indirectly, because pressure or temperature behind the valve fails to react when it should be shut. Audi uses the code on the 2016 A3 Sportback e-tron: P0EC900 is logged passive/sporadic in the Climatronic module J255, and the MIL is switched on at the request of another module over the network, so the engine module J623 holds no code. Bulletins 2046942 and 2047037 trace it to a miscalculation in the refrigerant self-test and call for new J255 software; if the code returns after erasing, it has to be diagnosed as a real fault. Circuit faults of valve A are P2611 to P2613, valve B stuck open is P0EE2.
c: Faulty self-test calculation in the climate control software (Audi A3 e-tron, fixed by update)
Valve held open by dirt, debris or a sticking armature
Weak solenoid coil that no longer pulls the valve fully shut
s: MIL on without a code in the engine control module
Code stored passive/sporadic in the climate control module
Reduced or uneven cooling in one branch, or no noticeable change at all

P0ECA.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor System - Multiple Sensor Correlation
P0ECA.d: P0ECA treats the temperature sensors of the hybrid or traction battery as one system: the battery controller compares the readings with each other and flags the group when one of them strays from the rest or shows an impossible value. Ford documents it for its 2019 hybrid and plug-in models. The BECM runs the check all the time and sets P0ECA after three or more 5-second events in which a thermistor deviates from the average by more than 25 °C, reads above 95 °C or reads below −50 °C. Bentley stores P0ECA00 in address 0021, the 48 V super capacitor of the Bentayga's Dynamic Ride, alongside P0A9E and P0AC8; the cure is software version 114, after which the part number ends in F. GM files comparable checks under single-sensor codes such as P0A9C instead. Battery power is reduced.
c: One battery thermistor drifting away from the others
Battery controller software misjudging the comparison (Bentley super capacitor, update 114)
Loose or corroded connector on the temperature sense harness inside the pack
Genuine local hot spot, e.g. a blocked cooling channel at one module
s: Hybrid or battery warning, MIL depending on manufacturer
Reduced electric power or charging rate
On the Bentayga, Dynamic Ride fault message and no roll compensation

P0ECB.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sensor System - Multiple Sensor Correlation
P0ECB.d: P0ECB indicates that the voltage measurements of the hybrid/EV battery contradict each other. Battery controllers usually capture the same voltage along more than one path, for example the whole pack directly and as the sum of all cell readings, or each half of the pack against its own cells; once these paths drift apart, at least one sensor must be wrong. No manufacturer documents P0ECB publicly. GM runs exactly this comparison under P0ABB: a gap of more than 12 V between pack voltage and cell sum in 20 of 25 samples is a Type A fault. Ford checks each half pack against the total of its cells and fails above 42 V on plug-in and 38 V on full hybrids held for one second (P0B15, P0B1A). Since state of charge is no longer reliable, power is limited.
c: Drifting pack or half-pack voltage sensor in the battery controller
Loose or corroded cell sense lead falsifying the cell sum
Internal fault of the cell monitoring electronics
Measurement taken on the wrong side of a contactor that is not fully closed
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Limited electric power, unstable state of charge display
Contactors may stay open, vehicle may not reach ready mode

P0ECC.d: P0ECC is the general voltage code for hybrid/EV battery E. The letters A to F mark separately monitored sub-batteries, modules or energy stores of one system; E is the fifth, so the code can only occur where a manufacturer divides its storage into at least five such units. It signals a voltage of this unit that does not fit expectation, without saying whether it fluctuates (P0ECD), sits too low (P0ECE) or too high (P0ECF). No manufacturer documents P0ECC publicly. CARB asks for monitoring of the cells and voltage sensors of hybrid storage with codes that name the smallest replaceable unit, which explains such letter series. As a pack-level reference, GM's P0ABB compares pack voltage with the cell sum at a 12 V limit. The driver sees a battery warning.
c: Aged or damaged cells in unit E
Fault in the voltage sense leads or connectors of unit E
Battery controller measuring or software fault
s: Battery or hybrid warning, MIL
Reduced electric power and range

P0ECD.d: P0ECD flags an unstable voltage in hybrid/EV battery E: the value moves faster or further than the controller tolerates, whereas a lasting offset would set P0ECE or P0ECF. No manufacturer documents P0ECD publicly. How such a test can look is shown by Ford for battery A (P0B24) on its 2019 hybrids: the BECM watches continuously and fails the unit once any cell stays more than 0.5 V off the mean of all cells for 15 seconds. Applied to unit E, a weak cell sagging under load, a loose busbar screw or a corroded sense terminal create the same pattern. As these causes depend on load and vibration, the warning may show up while driving and disappear at rest. The general code of the unit is P0ECC; the same fault on unit F is P0ED1.
c: Cell with high internal resistance whose voltage collapses under load
Loose busbar screw or cell connector in unit E
Corroded or intermittent voltage sense terminal
Battery controller software, curable by update
s: Intermittent battery warning, often only under load
Power drops during acceleration
MIL on

P0ECE.d: P0ECE sets when the voltage of hybrid/EV battery E remains below the window the controller expects for the present load and charge. Its counterparts are P0ECF for too high and P0ECD for unstable readings. No manufacturer documents P0ECE publicly. Ford publishes a comparable low test for battery A (P0B25) on its 2019 hybrids, based on calculated state of charge: if any cell reaches 0 % for 10 seconds with the main contactors closed, or for 90 seconds with them open, the code is set. A unit that discharged itself during long standstill, a module with an internal short, or a balancing circuit that keeps draining one group can pull unit E down. The controller then reduces discharge power, so electric range and boost shrink and the engine runs more often on hybrids.
c: Unit E deeply discharged after long standstill or a high self-discharge cell
Internal short or capacity loss in a module of unit E
Balancing switch stuck on and draining one cell group
s: Reduced electric range and acceleration
Engine starts more often, EV mode unavailable
MIL and battery warning

P0ECF.d: P0ECF is stored when unit E of the hybrid/EV battery exceeds its upper voltage limit. It mirrors P0ECE, while unstable readings belong to P0ECD. No manufacturer documents P0ECF publicly. Ford's overcharge logic for its 2019 hybrids gives a sense of the limits involved: with the charge contactors open, a cell above 4.5 V on plug-in models or 4.35 V on full hybrids for 2 or 3 seconds counts as a fault under the state-of-charge code P0C30. Overvoltage in one unit typically follows broken cell balancing, a fault in charge or regeneration control, or a measuring channel that reads high. Because overcharged lithium cells are a safety risk, the controller blocks charging and regenerative braking and may open the contactors. Plug-in charging may be refused.
c: Cell balancing of unit E no longer works, group overcharged
Voltage sense channel reading too high
s: Charging or regenerative braking blocked
Battery warning, MIL
Vehicle may switch off the high-voltage system

P0ED0.d: P0ED0 is the general voltage code of hybrid/EV battery F, the sixth and last unit in this letter series. It reports an implausible voltage of the unit without separating unstable (P0ED1), low (P0ED2) and high (P0ED3) readings. Only storage systems divided into six or more separately monitored units can produce it, and no manufacturer documents P0ED0 publicly. Ford's 2019 hybrid BECM is an example of finely divided monitoring: it supervises the cells in groups of six per sense circuit and fails a circuit when any cell reads above 5 V or below 1 V for 11 seconds. CARB demands that the cells and voltage sensors of the energy storage are monitored with codes for the smallest replaceable unit. A battery warning and reduced power follow.
c: Aged or damaged cells in unit F
Open or high-resistance voltage sense lead of unit F
Cell monitoring electronics or software fault
s: MIL and battery warning
Reduced electric power

P0ED1.d: P0ED1 reports that the voltage of hybrid/EV battery F fluctuates beyond the permitted band instead of staying steadily off, which would be P0ED2 or P0ED3. No manufacturer documents P0ED1 publicly. CARB not only requires every cell and voltage sensor of the storage to be watched, it also asks for proof that cell balancing can hold each cell at its intended voltage, and an unsteady unit voltage is often the first hint that a cell group is running away from the others. Ford's comparable test for battery A uses a 0.5 V spread between one cell and the average, held for 15 seconds. Mechanical causes such as a loose busbar or a sense lead with poor contact make the reading jump with vibration. General code of unit F: P0ED0; the same fault on unit E: P0ECD.
c: Cell group of unit F drifting because balancing cannot keep up
Sense lead or connector with intermittent contact
s: Warning that comes and goes, often over bumps or under load
Short power reductions while driving
MIL on

P0ED2.d: P0ED2 means hybrid/EV battery F delivers less voltage than the controller predicts from current draw and state of charge. No manufacturer documents P0ED2 publicly. Published undervoltage limits exist for whole packs: GM's hybrid tables fail the pack below 24 V (P0ABC), and Ford sets P0A7D during cranking if its pack reads under 184.8 V on plug-in or 167.2 V on full hybrids, or if the weakest cell drops below 2.1 V for half a second. For one unit the limits scale with its number of cells. Typical causes are an aged module with lost capacity, a cell with internal leakage that drained during standstill, or a high-resistance joint that loses voltage under load. Discharge power is cut back. High voltage of unit F is P0ED3, low voltage of unit E is P0ECE.
c: Aged module in unit F with lost capacity
Cell with internal leakage drained during standstill
High-resistance connection inside unit F dropping voltage under load
s: Less power in electric mode
Shorter electric range
MIL and battery warning

P0ED3.d: P0ED3 is logged once battery F of the hybrid/EV system climbs above its permitted maximum voltage. It is the high member of the F series, next to P0ED2 (low) and P0ED1 (unstable). No manufacturer documents P0ED3 publicly. GM's hybrid tables show how strictly overvoltage is treated at pack level: above 479 V the P0ABD monitor fails within one trip. Ford sets P0AFB when its pack stays above 362.2 V on plug-in or 327.8 V on full hybrids for 10 seconds. Within a single unit an excess voltage usually means its cells were charged further than the rest, for instance because the balancing circuit of that unit quit, or that its measuring channel reads high. Charging and regeneration stay restricted until the cause is found; a warning appears and plug-in charging may be refused.
c: Balancing circuit of unit F failed, cells overcharged
Measuring channel of unit F reading too high
s: Charging refused or regenerative braking weak
MIL and battery warning

P0ED4.d: P0ED4 is the general current fault for phase X of the hybrid generator. J2012 names the generator phases U, V and W and adds a separate X, Y, Z series, which presumably serves machines with a second three-phase winding set fed by its own inverter bridge; which vehicles use it is not published, and no manufacturer documents P0ED4. Low and high cases are P0ED5 and P0ED6. Ford explains the role of its U-V-W codes on its 2019 power-split hybrids: the inverter is checked for overcurrent, current sensor and current regulation faults, and generator problems of this kind are stored as P0A6F, P0A72, P0A75 or their high variants. CARB requires electric drive components to be monitored. A faulty phase current limits generator output, engine start and charging.
c: Fault in the inverter bridge or current regulation for phase X
Phase X current sensor out of tolerance
Loose or damaged high-voltage connection of phase X
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Reduced charging, engine may start less smoothly

P0ED5.d: P0ED5 means that phase X of the hybrid generator carries, or appears to carry, too little current while the generator is supposed to deliver torque. No manufacturer documents P0ED5 publicly. Mitsubishi publishes a comparable check for the U, V and W phases of the 2023 Outlander PHEV: with at least 50 A requested and the generator between 500 and 4,500 rpm, a phase current that stays within roughly 17 A of zero for 0.4 s sets P0E0C, as does a failed comparison with the target current. In phase X the same result comes from a broken phase cable, a burnt winding joint, an inverter switch that never conducts, or a current sensor stuck at its zero point. P0ED6 is the high case; the low codes of phases Y and Z are P0ED8 and P0EDB. Generator torque and charging suffer.
c: Open or loose phase X cable or terminal
Inverter power switch for phase X not conducting
Burnt or broken winding connection in the generator
s: Weak or no battery charging by the generator
Rough engine start or vibration from the generator
MIL and hybrid warning

P0ED6.d: P0ED6 is stored when the current in phase X of the hybrid generator exceeds its permitted limit. No manufacturer documents P0ED6 publicly. Ford gives figures for the comparable U, V and W codes P0A71, P0A74 and P0A77 on its 2019 power-split hybrids: the motor/generator control unit declares overcurrent once the generator current magnitude passes 300 A for 400 microseconds, or 15 A for 200 ms just after power-up, when practically no current should flow. Genuine overcurrent points to a winding short, damaged insulation or a power switch that fails closed; a current sensor with too much gain triggers a false alarm. The inverter shuts down to protect itself, so the hybrid system may stop working. Low side: P0ED5; general code: P0ED4.
c: Turn-to-turn or ground short in the phase X winding
Current sensor reading too high (false overcurrent)
s: Sudden hybrid system shutdown or loss of ready mode
MIL and hybrid warning

P0ED7.d: P0ED7 is the general current code for phase Y, the middle phase of the generator's X-Y-Z set. Without being narrowed to low (P0ED8) or high (P0ED9), it says that the Y current no longer behaves as the inverter controller expects. No manufacturer documents P0ED7 publicly, and it is not known which production machines label their phases X, Y and Z. Ford describes what phase currents are used for in its 2019 hybrids: sensors on each phase feed the motor/generator control unit, which needs them to work out current magnitude and angle and also to confirm that the three AC cables are connected the right way. Monitoring of such electric drive parts is mandatory under CARB. Check the high-voltage connectors and look for other phase codes. Phase X: P0ED4, phase Z: P0EDA.
c: Inverter fault affecting the phase Y bridge
Phase cables mixed up or poorly seated after repair work
s: Hybrid warning and MIL
Limited generator operation

P0ED8.d: P0ED8 reports too little current in phase Y of the hybrid generator. No manufacturer documents P0ED8 publicly. Ford's 2019 hybrid summary describes a phase circuit test at power-up for the U-V-W phases: the motor/generator control unit declares a phase circuit fault if less than 5 A is seen over the 100 ms test window. Seen this way, a low Y current is first of all a question of continuity: an open cable or terminal, a failed winding joint or an inverter switch that does not turn on. A sensor that reads too low would make the controller drive more real current than intended, so a low code from the sensor side deserves the same attention. Generator torque and charging power drop. High counterpart: P0ED9; same fault on phases X and Z: P0ED5, P0EDB.
c: Open or corroded phase Y cable or terminal
Inverter switch for phase Y not turning on
Phase Y current sensor reading too low
s: Generator delivers less charging power
Uneven running or noise from the transaxle
MIL and hybrid warning

P0ED9.d: P0ED9 is set when phase Y of the hybrid generator draws more current than allowed. No manufacturer documents P0ED9 publicly. Overcurrent in a generator phase is a protection event: the inverter must switch off within fractions of a millisecond, before its power semiconductors are destroyed. The scale is illustrated by Ford's limits for the U-V-W phases, 300 A for 400 microseconds in operation. Causes include a short between turns or to ground in the Y winding, a chafed phase cable and an inverter switch stuck on; a sensor that reads high can imitate the fault. If several phases report high at the same moment, the inverter or its common supply is more likely than three separate defects. Low side: P0ED8; the same fault on phase X: P0ED6.
c: Short in the phase Y winding or to the housing
Chafed phase cable shorting to ground
s: Hybrid system shuts down, vehicle may lose ready mode
MIL and hybrid warning

P0EDA.d: P0EDA is the general current fault of phase Z, the last of the three X-Y-Z generator phases, without the detail of P0EDB (low) or P0EDC (high). No manufacturer documents P0EDA publicly. In a three-phase set the currents add up to almost zero at every instant, so a controller can calculate one phase from the other two or use the sum as a cross-check; Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV, for instance, fails its generator sum check P0DFA when, with the switches off, the sum stays at 140 A or above for 0.35 s. A faulty Z current therefore often shows up together with sum or correlation faults. Under CARB these drive components must be supervised as well. Expect a hybrid system warning and limited generator operation. Phases X and Y: P0ED4, P0ED7.
c: Phase Z current sensor offset or failure
Inverter fault on the phase Z bridge
Poor contact at the phase Z high-voltage terminal
s: Hybrid warning, often with further phase or sum codes
Reduced charging and generator assist

P0EDB.d: P0EDB means phase Z of the hybrid generator shows less current than the commanded operating point calls for. No manufacturer documents P0EDB publicly. Besides an absolute floor, published checks also look at the gap between actual and target current: Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV fails a U-V-W phase not only when it hovers near zero under demand but also when it misses its target current. If phase Z falls short, the machine runs unbalanced, which causes torque ripple, humming and extra heat in the remaining phases, so the inverter lowers generator power. Likely causes are a loose or corroded high-voltage terminal, a broken lead in the winding, a power switch that no longer conducts or a sensor offset. High counterpart: P0EDC; general code: P0EDA.
c: Loose or corroded phase Z high-voltage terminal
Power switch for phase Z no longer conducting
Broken conductor in the phase Z winding
s: Humming or vibration from the hybrid transaxle
Reduced generator power and charging
MIL and hybrid warning

P0EDC.d: P0EDC is the overcurrent code for phase Z of the hybrid generator and ends the X-Y-Z series. No manufacturer documents P0EDC publicly; the closest published logic is Ford's for its U-V-W generator phases (P0A71, P0A74, P0A77), which also flags any current above 15 A in the first 200 ms after power-up, a moment when the machine should be idle. A reading like that hints at a switch leaking or stuck on rather than at load. During operation a short between winding turns, an insulation fault to the housing, a damaged power module or a sensor with excessive gain can be behind the code; a sensor error usually also upsets the three-phase sum check. After the protective shutdown the generator no longer charges and electric engine starting may fail. Low side: P0EDB.
c: Damaged or leaking power module for phase Z
Insulation fault or turn short in the phase Z winding
s: Hybrid system shutdown, engine may not start
MIL and hybrid warning, possibly with sum check codes

P0EDD.d: P0EDD is the state-of-health verdict for the second section of a traction battery: section B has lost so much capacity or gained so much internal resistance that it falls below the maker's limit. P0A7F covers section A, P0EDE to P0EE1 sections C to F. Audi counts the Q5 PHEV (2020-2024) battery in groups and names P0EDD00 as group 2 deterioration in the battery management unit 008C; with the MIL on and guided fault finding silent, TSB 2079556/1 says to renew the module named by the entry. FCA uses the code on the Pacifica Hybrid: 08-299-25 extends warranty and replaces the 400 V pack, while a 2025 STAR case first checks fuses, wiring and BPCM software, then resets P0EDD in the BPCM. On the 2021 Wrangler, 08-168-23 calls it a false MIL fixed by BPCM software.
c: Battery module or cell group in section B aged beyond its limit
Battery controller software misjudging state of health (FCA reflash cases)
Pack defect covered by a warranty extension (Pacifica Hybrid)
s: MIL or hybrid system warning on
Noticeably shorter electric range
Engine runs more often, less electric assist

P0EDE.d: P0EDE flags the third battery section, C, as worn out. The controller estimates each section's usable capacity and resistance from voltage behaviour under load and at rest; if section C drifts too far from its new-state values, it is judged deteriorated. CARB asks for a state-of-health monitor and for codes that point to the smallest part a workshop can replace, which is why a multi-module pack gets one code per section. Only Audi documents P0EDE publicly: on the Q5 PHEV it stands for battery group 3 in control unit 008C. A February 2025 reporting obligation, 2076982/1, lists it with the yellow engine lamp and a displayed electric range that is too low, and asks dealers to call technical support before replacing parts. Sections B and D have P0EDD and P0EDF.
c: Cells in battery group 3 aged (capacity loss, higher resistance)
Strong voltage spread inside the section
Controller estimate wrong, module still healthy
s: Check engine lamp on
Displayed electric range too low
Electric driving mode cannot be selected or ends early

P0EDF.d: P0EDF belongs to the fourth section of the traction battery. It is not a sensor or wiring code but a capacity and power judgement: the battery controller has concluded that section D can no longer deliver what the maker expects of a healthy unit. Audi maps P0EDF00 on the Q5 PHEV to battery group 4 in the battery management unit 008C. Its bulletin 2079556/1 of September 2025 describes the workshop path: the MIL is on, guided fault finding offers no measure, so the high-voltage module behind the stored entry is removed and a new one fitted; if more than two modules are flagged, a technical assistance ticket comes first. Other makers have not published the code. Because only one module is replaced, the cost is far below a full pack. P0EDE and P0EE0 cover the adjacent sections.
c: High-voltage module of group 4 worn out
Single weak cell pulling the section down
Evaluation logic of the battery controller
s: MIL on
Reduced electric range and power

P0EE0.d: With P0EE0 the controller reports ageing of section E, the fifth part of the traction battery. A section is usually a module or a group of cell blocks with its own monitoring; once its share of the pack has lost too much capacity or become too resistive, the whole battery can no longer reach its rated energy, which shows up first as shorter electric range. Audi is the only maker with published references: on the Q5 PHEV, P0EE000 means battery group 5 in unit 008C, and both the 2025 reporting obligation 2076982 and the module replacement bulletin 2079556 list it, intermittent or static. The first also names P0BBD, a voltage spread beyond the limit, which often goes along with a weak section. Distinguishing feature: only section E is named; sections D and F use P0EDF and P0EE1.
c: Cell voltages in the section spread too far (often with P0BBD)
s: Electric range shown too low
Engine warning lamp on
Less power in electric mode

P0EE1.d: P0EE1 is the last code of the P0E range for section ageing and covers section F. The series runs A (P0A7F) and B to F (P0EDD to P0EE1); for further sections J2012 continues in the P2 block, with G and H as P2CCC and P2CCD. Audi uses exactly this chain on the Q5 PHEV: groups 1 to 8 of the battery are reported as P0A7F00, P0EDD00 to P0EE100, P2CCC00 and P2CCD00 in unit 008C, and P0EE100 is group 6. The 2025 bulletins treat it like its siblings: confirm the MIL complaint, find no other measure in guided fault finding, replace the affected module. No other maker has published P0EE1. CARB's rule that fault codes should isolate the smallest replaceable unit explains why such long letter series exist for large packs. Section E is P0EE0.
c: Section aged faster due to heat or poor cooling
Evaluation error of the battery controller
s: MIL on
Shorter electric range

P0EE2.t: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve B Stuck/Open
P0EE2.d: P0EE2 says the second refrigerant distribution valve, B, stays open or fails to close. In plug-in hybrids and EVs such shut-off valves route refrigerant either to the cabin evaporator or to a chiller that cools the battery; Egelhof sells solenoid versions with 12 V or 24 V coils for exactly this use. The fault is inferred, since the module sees pressures or temperatures that would not occur with the valve shut. Audi documents it on the A7 55 TFSI e (2021-2023): P0EE200 is stored in thermal management unit J1024, address 00C5, and the MIL comes on. TSB 2071040/1 blames the J1024 software and lists an SVM update from container 4K8909476J/K/L to 4K8909476V; the HV charging cable must be unplugged during flashing. Valve A stuck open is P0EC9.
c: Thermal management software misjudging the valve (Audi J1024)
Valve seat contaminated or armature stuck open
Weak coil that no longer moves the armature
s: MIL on
Weaker cabin or battery cooling
Often no noticeable effect beyond the warning

P0EE3.t: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve B Control Circuit/Open
P0EE3.d: P0EE3 concerns the wiring between the controlling module and refrigerant valve B, most often an interrupted path. With the output switched off, the driver normally sees a defined voltage through the coil; with it switched on, current flows. If neither picture appears, for instance because a pin has backed out of the connector or the coil winding is broken, the circuit is declared open. No manufacturer documents P0EE3 publicly. That valve B exists as a separately monitored part is shown by Audi's A7 PHEV, whose thermal management unit J1024 reports its mechanical fault as P0EE200. Typical hardware is a 12 V solenoid like Egelhof's shut-off valves. CARB requires every electronic output used for battery thermal management to be checked for open circuits. The matching valve A code is P2611.
c: Loose, corroded or pushed-back pin at the valve connector
Broken coil winding in valve B
Broken wire in the harness to the valve
s: Warning lamp on
Valve B no longer switches, affected refrigerant branch stays as it is

P0EE4.t: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve B Control Circuit Low
P0EE4.d: P0EE4 is stored when the control line of refrigerant valve B is pulled to a lower voltage than the driver commands, usually by a short to ground. With a high-side driver the valve would then stay energised or the output would be overloaded; with a low-side driver the coil may be switched on permanently. No manufacturer documents P0EE4 publicly. The closest published case is the valve A sibling P2612, which Ross-Tech describes for Volkswagen models as a short to ground at the N280 compressor regulator valve, a coil of about 10 ohms with a moulded connector that can turn brittle and let the pins corrode. A similar check on the valve B coil and its connector is a sensible start. Open and high faults of valve B are P0EE3 and P0EE5.
c: Control wire chafed through to ground
Coil winding shorted to the valve body
s: Warning lamp on
Valve B behaves as if permanently energised or not at all

P0EE5.t: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve B Control Circuit High
P0EE5.d: P0EE5 means the control line of refrigerant valve B carries more voltage than its commanded state allows. If the driver switches the coil to ground, a short to a 12 V feed is the classic reason; with some driver types an open coil can also float the line high. The practical effect depends on whether valve B is normally open or normally closed: either it cannot be energised any more, or it is energised when it should rest. No manufacturer documents P0EE5 publicly. Audi's A7 PHEV shows that valve B is watched by its own thermal management unit (J1024), and automotive shut-off valves of this kind run on 12 V or 24 V coils, according to Egelhof. CARB requires electrical checks of such battery thermal management outputs. P0EE4 is the low counterpart, P2613 the valve A code.
c: Control wire shorted to a 12 V feed
Open coil letting the line float high
Faulty output stage in the controlling module
s: Warning lamp on
Cabin or battery cooling not working as requested

P0EE6.t: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve B Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P0EE6.d: P0EE6 is reported by the output stage itself: the switch that powers refrigerant valve B has measured too much current or got too hot and has protected itself. Modern smart high-side switches do this on chip; TI's TPS1HB16-Q1, for example, has an adjustable current limit between 4.4 and 49 A, shuts down at about 150 C junction temperature with roughly 20 C hysteresis, and flags the event on its diagnostic output. A coil drawing more current than normal, through shorted turns or a partial short in the wire, is the usual cause; a hot mounting spot of the module can add to it. No manufacturer documents P0EE6 publicly. Unlike P0EE4, the circuit still conducts and is not simply grounded. The same driver fault on valve A is P266F; Audi's A7 PHEV logs a valve B fault in J1024.
c: Shorted turns in the valve B coil raising the current
Partial short in the valve wiring
s: Warning lamp on
Valve B switched off, cooling branch not served

P0EE7.t: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P0EE7.d: P0EE7 is the general circuit code for the second temperature sensor of the charging inlet. High-current inlets carry several sensors; the supplier Sailtran fits one PT1000 at the L1 pin and two independent PT1000 at DC+ and DC- of its CCS2 inlet, so A and B often stand for two different contacts. The code applies when the sensor B circuit is faulty in a way the module does not sort into low, high or implausible. No manufacturer documents P0EE7 on an official server. For sensor A, Mercedes lists P0D9900 as an electrical fault of the inlet contact sensor on the smart electric drive with 22 kW charger and traces it to loose low-voltage plugs at the charger (LI54.10-P-067823). CARB requires plug-in charger faults that stop or slow charging to be found. Sensor A is P0D99.
c: Loose low-voltage connector between inlet and charger
Damaged sensor wire in the inlet harness
Failed sensor element B (usually means a new inlet)
s: Charging refused or stopped
Charge indicator shows a fault

P0EE8.t: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0EE8.d: P0EE8 is set when sensor B in the charging inlet delivers an electrically valid value that does not fit the situation. A plausibility test may compare it with sensor A on the neighbouring pin, with the outside temperature after a long rest, or with the heating expected for the charge current. If B reads far colder than A during a high-current session, or shows a sudden rise without current, it fails. No manufacturer documents P0EE8 publicly. GM gives a hint for the A sensor equivalent P0D9A on the 2022 Hummer EV and BrightDrop EV600: worn or oversized terminals in public charge plugs are a suspect, and the test only runs again after about ten minutes of driving above 2 mph (PIT5904). Inlets with two DC pin sensors, as Sailtran builds them, make such a cross-check possible.
c: Worn station plug heating one contact unevenly
Sensor B lost thermal contact to its pin
s: Charging reduced or aborted
Fault only at certain stations

P0EE9.t: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P0EE9.d: P0EE9 reports that the voltage of coupler temperature sensor B lies under its valid window. What that means thermally depends on the element. An NTC thermistor loses resistance when heated, so a low signal reads as an extremely hot pin. The PT1000 platinum sensors that Sailtran places at the DC+ and DC- contacts of its CCS2 inlet behave the other way round, and in a pull-up circuit a low signal looks implausibly cold. A short to ground pulls the line down with either type, and water in the inlet can do the same. No manufacturer documents P0EE9 publicly. Bentley's TPI 2075291/1 for the 2024 Bentayga Hybrid shows for sensor A that Low is P0D9B, even though the charger unit 00C6 showed the texts of Low and High swapped. P0EEA is the high-signal sibling.
c: Sensor B signal wire shorted to ground
Moisture or water in the charging inlet
s: Charging not started or stopped
Reduced charging power

P0EEA.t: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
P0EEA.d: P0EEA is the opposite case: the sensor B signal of the charging inlet sits above the valid window. In a pull-up design that is what an unplugged connector, a broken sensor wire or a short to a supply voltage looks like. With a PT1000, whose resistance grows with heat, a high reading suggests an overheated contact, so the charger may stop at once; Sailtran fits PT1000 sensors at the DC+ and DC- pins of its CCS2 inlet. With an NTC it would read as far too cold, which hides real heating and is no safer. No manufacturer documents P0EEA publicly. For the A sensor, Bentley confirms on the 2024 Bentayga Hybrid that High is P0D9C and warns that the charger unit showed the wrong text, so diagnosis must follow the code number. P0EE9 is the low-signal sibling.
c: Unplugged connector or broken sensor B wire
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Open sensor element B inside the inlet
s: Charging aborted at once or refused
Fault in the charge indicator

P0EEB.t: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0EEB.d: P0EEB catches a sensor B signal from the charging inlet that jumps or drops out for moments. A metal contact and its plastic housing have real thermal mass, so a change of many degrees within milliseconds cannot be a true temperature and points to the circuit. No manufacturer documents P0EEB publicly. A Mercedes bulletin about the first inlet sensor of the third-generation smart with its optional 22 kW unit fits the pattern: inlet sensor codes there came from loose low-voltage contacts at the charger, the fix was to work the plugs gently and watch whether charging starts, and the bulletin warns the fault may only appear with warm or cold parts at the start or end of charging. Typical for P0EEB is a session that stops without visible reason and works next time. Steady faults are P0EE9 and P0EEA.
c: Loose contact in the sensor B circuit or at the charger plug
Moisture that comes and goes in the inlet connector
Cracked sensor element with temperature-dependent contact
s: Charging stops sporadically
Fault cannot be reproduced at once

P0EEC.t: Battery Energy Control Module B Performance
P0EEC.d: P0EEC says a second battery energy control module, B, has failed its own internal checks. Large or split packs can carry more than one such controller, each watching cell voltages, temperatures and current of its part. No manufacturer documents P0EEC publicly. GM shows how the module A version P0A1F works: in its 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables a single software watchdog reset of the controller is enough, checked at 9 V or more, and the code is Type A, so the MIL lights after one trip. That a B module exists in practice is visible at Audi: on the Q5 and A7 PHEV, U041300 reports invalid data from Battery Energy Control Module B, and TSB 2065722/2 links it to software 106 or 206 in the battery junction box SX6. Network loss of the module is a U code; P0A1F covers module A.
c: Software fault or watchdog reset in module B
Low or unstable 12 V supply to the module
Internal hardware fault of module B
s: MIL or hybrid warning on
Limited electric drive or charging

P0EED.t: Hybrid/EV Battery System Discharge Circuit Performance
P0EED.d: P0EED concerns the active discharge path on the high-voltage side, the circuit that drains the DC link capacitors once the contactors have opened so that no dangerous voltage lingers. The code says this path does not perform as intended, whereas P0C76 only judges how long the voltage takes to fall. FCA lists P0EED-00 for the 2017 Chrysler Pacifica Hybrid in bulletin 08-107-17, next to P0C76, P0C77 and P0AFA: a loose terminal bolt where the high-voltage lead joins the inverter module (PIM) could arc, the MIL came on and propulsion might be lost. Repair was a torque check to 25 N·m, or a new inverter module and cable if arcing marks were found. As a reference for the timing side, GM's P0C76 fails when the inverter still reads above 200 V 3.5 s after opening, Type A.
c: Loose or arcing high-voltage cable terminal at the inverter module (FCA 08-107-17)
Discharge resistor or its switching transistor open or degraded
Internal fault in the inverter or its voltage measurement
Main contactor sticking closed so the bus stays charged
s: MIL or hybrid system warning on
Loss of propulsion or vehicle will not enter ready mode
Further high-voltage codes such as P0C76 or P0C77 stored at the same time

P0EEE.t: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature B Too High
P0EEE.d: P0EEE is the overheating verdict for the second measuring point of the charging inlet: sensor B works electrically, but the contact it watches has become too hot, so charging is throttled or stopped. Electrical faults of sensor B have their own codes P0EE7 to P0EEB; overheating at point A is P0E5F, at points C and D P2E4E and P2E53. Ford documents P0EEE in special service message 55080 for certain Mustang Mach-E (2021 to 2023), E-Transit (2022 to 2025) and F-150 Lightning (2022 to 2023): DC fast charging at level 3 stations breaks off, and the vehicle stores P0EEE:27 together with P2E53:27 in the SOBDM. Ford traces this to module software, says a new charge port does not cure it and expects a software fix in Q3 2026; AC charging keeps working. Outside this case, worn or dirty pins are the usual cause.
c: Software of the charging diagnostic module misjudging the temperature (Ford SSM 55080)
Worn, dirty or corroded pins in the charging inlet
Loose crimp or screw connection behind the inlet pin raising contact resistance
Worn plug of the charging station heating the contact
s: DC fast charging stops or does not start
Charging power reduced while AC charging still works
Charging fault message in the cluster or app

P0EEF.t: Drive Motor A Control Module Overtemperature
P0EEF.d: P0EEF reports that the control module of drive motor A, the inverter electronics that switch the motor phases, has run too hot. The temperature reading itself is considered valid; faults of the inverter temperature sensors, such as P0AEF, are separate codes. No manufacturer documents P0EEF publicly. GM gives an idea of the limits on the 2016 Volt: its motor control processor A sets P0C11, P0C12 or P0C13 when power inverter phase U, V or W stays above 126 °C for 1.2 s within a 2 s window, rated Type A with the MIL after one trip. CARB demands that hybrid systems monitor electric motor performance. Low coolant in the electronics loop, a weak coolant pump, trapped air or long heavy load in hot weather heat the module, which then reduces motor torque to protect itself.
c: Low coolant level or air in the power electronics cooling loop
Electronics coolant pump weak or failed
Long full-load operation such as towing or climbing in high ambient heat
Degraded power semiconductors or thermal interface inside the module
s: Reduced drive power or hybrid system warning
MIL on (manufacturer-dependent)
Electric drive switched off until the module cools

P0EF0.t: Battery Charger Coupler Unlock Disabled - High Voltage Present
P0EF0.d: P0EF0 describes a safety lockout rather than a broken actuator: the vehicle keeps the charging connector locked because it still measures hazardous voltage at the inlet. CharIN's CCS design guide permits unlocking only below 60 V, and EVgo's interoperability guide for vehicle makers asks for release once current is close to zero, the inlet is under 60 V DC and the station has changed to state B1. If the voltage does not decay, for instance because a DC charging contactor has welded, the station leaves its output live or the vehicle's voltage measurement is wrong, the lock stays engaged and the code is logged. No manufacturer documents P0EF0 publicly. Electrical faults of the lock actuator are P0D91 to P0D98. The driver cannot remove the cable until the voltage is gone.
c: DC charging contactor stuck closed, inlet stays connected to the battery
Charging station does not switch off or discharge its output
Faulty inlet voltage measurement reporting voltage that is not there
Charging control software ending the session in the wrong order
s: Charging cable cannot be unplugged after charging
Charging fault message, sometimes only at certain stations
Emergency release of the connector needed

P0EF1.t: Drive Motor C Temperature Sensor Circuit
P0EF1.d: P0EF1 is the general circuit code for the temperature sensor of drive motor C, the third traction motor on vehicles with three or more electric machines. It must not be confused with P2DB1, which means sensor C inside drive motor A. Volvo Trucks lists P0EF1 with failure type 09, component failure, for its electric trucks in remote diagnostic bulletin RD21-022; it names connector, wiring harness, the motor temperature sensor itself and an unsupported configuration as possible causes and sends the technician to Tech Tool for the detailed steps. The general code is used when the fault is not classified as low or high, which have their own codes P0EF3 and P0EF4. Without a usable winding temperature the controller has to protect motor C and limits its output.
c: Loose, corroded or damaged connector of the motor C temperature sensor
Temperature sensor in the winding failed
Controller configuration not matching the installed motor (Volvo RD21-022)
s: Reduced drive power
Warning lamp for the electric drive
Motor temperature shown as invalid in the scan tool

P0EF2.t: Drive Motor C Temperature Sensor Range/Performance
P0EF2.d: P0EF2 flags a plausibility error of the drive motor C temperature sensor: its signal is electrically fine, yet the value does not fit what the controller expects. No manufacturer documents P0EF2 publicly. GM shows a typical check for drive motor B on the 2016 Cadillac ELR: after at least 21,600 s with the propulsion system inactive, the motor thermistor may differ by no more than 20 °C from the average of power electronics coolant and transmission fluid temperature, otherwise P0A31 sets as Type A. Ford compares motor coil, generator coil and transmission fluid temperatures on its 2019 hybrids after 200 minutes key-off, with limits of 10 °C and 30 °C. A drifting thermistor, a sensor that has lost contact with the winding or a high-resistance connection fails such a cold-start comparison.
c: Sensor no longer in thermal contact with the winding
Corroded pin adding resistance and shifting the reading
Comparison sensor such as coolant or oil temperature reading wrong
s: Warning lamp after a long standstill, often at the first start of the day
Usually no noticeable drivability change at first
Power limitation of motor C in some cases

P0EF3.t: Drive Motor C Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
P0EF3.d: P0EF3 is stored when the signal voltage of the drive motor C temperature sensor drops below its valid range. With the usual NTC thermistor on a pull-up resistor, a low voltage stands for an extremely hot winding, so electrically the suspects are a short to ground, a pinched harness or a sensor with an internal short. No manufacturer documents P0EF3 publicly. GM's motor B table for the 2016 Cadillac ELR shows the analogous limit: P0A32 trips once the reading corresponds to more than 184 °C, close to 0 V, after a 90 s warm-up, Type A. Ford's 2019 hybrids fail the motor coil sensor below 0.1 V held for 32 ms. Because the controller cannot tell such a short from real overheating, it derates motor C. P0EF4 covers the high-voltage side.
c: Signal wire shorted to ground or motor housing
Water or coolant in the connector bridging the pins
s: Drive power of motor C reduced immediately
Implausibly high motor temperature in the live data
Warning lamp on

P0EF4.t: Drive Motor C Temperature Sensor Circuit High
P0EF4.d: P0EF4 reports a drive motor C temperature signal above the plausible window. For an NTC sensor on a pull-up this equals an impossibly cold winding, the picture produced by an open sensor, a broken wire, an unplugged connector or a short to the reference voltage. No manufacturer documents P0EF4 publicly. GM's ELR motor controller treats the same situation for motor B as P0A33 once the value reads below −41 °C, near 5 V, while Ford flags the coil sensor of its 2019 hybrids once the voltage exceeds 4.8 V for 32 ms. A sensor that claims far too low a temperature would hide real overheating, so the controller switches to a substitute value and limits the output of motor C. Check the connector at the motor first; the low-side sibling is P0EF3.
c: Sensor connector unplugged, loose or with pushed-back pin
Broken signal or ground wire of the sensor
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference
s: Reduced power of motor C
Motor temperature stuck at the lowest value in the live data
Warning lamp on

P0EF5.t: Drive Motor C Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0EF5.d: P0EF5 covers a drive motor C temperature signal that jumps or drops out for short moments instead of staying wrong. Because of the thermal mass of a traction motor, the winding temperature can only change slowly; a step of many degrees within milliseconds therefore points to the wiring and not to the motor. Loose or corroded pins at the motor connector, leads chafing near moving parts or a cracked sensor lead are typical. No manufacturer documents P0EF5 publicly, and its drive motor A and B siblings P0A2E and P0A34 are not listed in the published Ford and GM tables either; Ford only runs open and short checks on its coil sensors with a 200 ms monitoring window. CARB requires hybrid systems to watch electric motor performance. Warnings that appear and vanish, sometimes with brief power cuts, are typical.
c: Loose or corroded pins in the motor connector
Harness chafing at brackets or moving parts
Cracked sensor lead inside the motor that opens with vibration or heat
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Short power interruptions of motor C, often on rough roads
Jumping motor temperature in the live data

P0EF6.t: Drive Motor C Temperature Sensor Over Temperature
P0EF6.d: P0EF6 is not an electrical fault: the drive motor C temperature sensor delivers a believable value, but that value has passed the motor's protection limit. No manufacturer documents P0EF6 publicly. For motor B on the 2016 Cadillac ELR, GM sets P0A35 when the temperature exceeds 149 °C and does not fall back below a reset threshold, Type A, and only while the range check P0A31 is passing. Ford's 2019 hybrids set P0A2F at a coil temperature above 140 °C or transmission oil above 115 °C. Causes are mostly on the cooling side, such as low coolant or oil, a failed pump or a clogged cooler, but long full-load phases or a winding with shorted turns also heat the motor. Torque of motor C is cut until it cools; sensor circuit faults belong to P0EF1 to P0EF5.
c: Low coolant or oil level, or air in the motor cooling circuit
Failed coolant or oil pump, or clogged cooler
Long full-load phases such as towing, track use or steep climbs
Shorted turns in the stator winding generating extra heat
s: Clearly reduced power until the motor has cooled down
Warning about drive system overheating
MIL on (manufacturer-dependent)

P0EF7.t: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor B Circuit
P0EF7.d: P0EF7 stands for an electrical fault in the second input voltage sensor of on-board charger A, the measuring channel that reads the AC supply voltage coming from a wallbox, station or household outlet. Chargers designed for several phases or split-phase supply may carry more than one such channel; the first one, sensor A, uses P0D3D to P0D41. This general code applies when the signal is unusable but not classified as range, low or high, which are P0EF8, P0EF9 and P0EFA. No manufacturer documents P0EF7 publicly. In its 2019 plug-in hybrid tables GM reads sensor A through a pulse duty ratio, so a broken line shows up as a stuck 0 % or 100 %. CARB requires plug-in vehicles to monitor charging system performance. As long as the supply voltage cannot be confirmed, AC charging is refused or limited.
c: Fault in the voltage sensing stage inside the charger
Open or high-resistance signal line between sensor and controller
Corroded low-voltage connector at the charger
s: AC charging does not start or stops shortly after start
Charging fault message in the cluster or app
DC fast charging usually unaffected

P0EF8.t: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0EF8.d: P0EF8 is set when input voltage sensor B of charger A delivers a value that is electrically valid but wrong for the situation. No manufacturer documents P0EF8 publicly. GM's rationality test for sensor A, P0D3E in its 2019 plug-in hybrid tables, illustrates the idea: while the car moves at 16 km/h or more, when no plug can be connected, the sensor duty ratio must stay between 8 and 12 %; if 60 of 80 samples taken every 25 ms fall outside, the code is stored as Type B. A charger with two input channels can additionally compare them with each other or with the supply voltage reported by the station. Offset drift or a partial fault in the sensing electronics is the likely cause, wiring less so. Charging may stop or continue at reduced power.
c: Offset drift of the voltage sensing electronics in the charger
Partial internal fault of the charger input stage
Charger software misjudging the plausibility window
s: AC charging interrupted or slower than expected
Code may set while driving without any charging attempt
Charging fault message

P0EF9.t: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor B Circuit Low
P0EF9.d: P0EF9 means the signal of input voltage sensor B in charger A has fallen below its valid range. No manufacturer documents P0EF9 publicly. GM's 2019 plug-in hybrid summary fails the matching sensor A code P0D3F when the duty cycle is 8 % or less but above zero, or stuck at 100 %, in at least 30 samples out of a window of 40 (Type B); a short to ground or a missing sensor supply produce that picture. Note that low refers to the measurement signal and not to a weak mains supply, which manufacturers report with input voltage too low codes such as P0D27. Because the charger cannot verify the incoming voltage, it does not begin AC charging. The high-side counterpart is P0EFA, the general circuit code P0EF7.
c: Internal fault of the charger measuring stage
Missing supply voltage of the sensing circuit
s: AC charging refused
Charging fault message right after plugging in
DC fast charging usually still possible

P0EFA.t: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor B Circuit High
P0EFA.d: With P0EFA, the signal from the second input voltage sensor of charger A, sensor B, lies above the plausible window. No manufacturer documents P0EFA publicly. GM's comparable check for sensor A, P0D40 in its 2019 plug-in hybrid tables, trips at a duty cycle of 92 % or more but below 100 %, or at exactly 0 %, in 30 of 40 samples, and is rated Type B. Electrically this points to a short to a supply voltage, an open signal line pulled up by the input stage, or a defective sensing stage inside the charger. Since the measuring channel normally sits on the charger board, the charger itself becomes the prime suspect once plugs and pins have been checked. AC charging is refused or ends soon after it started; the low-side sibling is P0EF9.
c: Defective measuring stage on the charger board
Open signal line pulled high by the input circuit
Signal shorted to a supply voltage
s: AC charging refused or ends after a few seconds
Charging fault message
Indicated charging power implausible

P0EFB.t: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor C Circuit
P0EFB.d: P0EFB flags an electrical fault on the third AC input voltage channel of on-board charger A, sensor C. Channel A reports through P0D3D to P0D41, channel B through P0EF7 to P0EFA; a third channel fits chargers that read each phase of a three-phase supply separately. This is the catch-all circuit code, used when the signal is unusable without being sorted into range, low or high (P0EFC, P0EFD, P0EFE). No manufacturer documents P0EFB publicly, and GM's hybrid tables for 2011, 2012 and 2014 to 2019 never list the matching circuit code P0D3D either, catching wiring faults on sensor A only through its low and high checks. In TI's 11 kW reference design every phase is scaled by a resistor chain and centred at 1.65 V in a 3.3 V converter, so a dead channel is easy to spot. AC charging is refused or limited.
c: Failed measuring channel C on the charger board (divider, amplifier or converter input)
Open or loose sense connection for this phase inside the charger or at the AC inlet harness
Charger software marking a valid channel as faulty
s: AC charging does not start or is limited
Possible reduced charging power on three-phase stations
Charging fault shown in the cluster or app

P0EFC.t: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P0EFC.d: With P0EFC, sensor C of charger A delivers an electrically sound signal whose value conflicts with the charger's other readings. No manufacturer documents P0EFC publicly. For sensor A, GM shows such a cross-check on the 2011 Volt: the charger module compares the AC peak voltage with two independent bulk voltage readings, and if both differ by more than 34 V for 512 ms within 640 ms, P0D3E is stored as Type A. GM preliminary information PIC5803 (Volt 2011 to 2013, Spark EV 2014) adds a warning: P0D3E together with P1E00 after an interrupted charge usually came from a brown-out, a power cut or a faulty cord set, not from the car. CARB likewise does not demand detection of faults that look the same as a weak supply. Check the outlet and station before blaming the charger.
c: Voltage dips, brown-out or power cut at the outlet or station during charging (GM PIC5803 for the sensor A code)
Faulty or poorly calibrated charging cord set or wallbox
Gain or offset drift of measuring channel C in the charger
s: Charging stops part-way or does not reach full charge
Fault appears only at certain outlets or stations
Charging fault message, sometimes with a warning lamp

P0EFD.t: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor C Circuit Low
P0EFD.d: P0EFD reports that the reading of input voltage sensor C in charger A sits below its plausible band. No manufacturer documents P0EFD publicly. GM's 2011 Volt charger module gives a reference for sensor A: once AC is detected at the inlet, a peak value under 90 V for 1500 ms within a 1875 ms window sets P0D3F, Type A with the warning lamp after one trip. Causes on the measuring side are a short to ground on the sense path, a shorted lower divider resistor or a missing reference for the converter. A phase that is genuinely dead at the supply, such as a tripped breaker on one leg of a three-phase station, can produce the same picture, so the incoming voltage is measured first. Mains undervoltage proper has its own codes such as P0D27; the high counterpart is P0EFE.
c: Defective divider or converter input for channel C in the charger
One phase missing at the supply (tripped breaker or fault in the station or cable)
Sense path of channel C shorted to ground
s: AC charging refused right after plugging in
Charging works on a different station or outlet
Charging fault message

P0EFE.t: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor C Circuit High
P0EFE.d: P0EFE is stored when channel C of charger A reports more input voltage than a household or station supply can deliver. No manufacturer documents P0EFE publicly. For sensor A, GM's 2011 Volt charger module trips P0D40 when the measured AC peak exceeds 422 V for 160 ms of a 200 ms window, rated Type A; this window is far shorter than the one for the low code, presumably because overvoltage endangers the input stage. In a divider front end like the one in TI's 11 kW design, an open lower resistor or a short to the converter reference pushes the signal toward the 3.3 V limit and causes exactly this reading. Real overvoltage from the grid is rare, so the measuring channel inside the charger is the main suspect once plugs have been checked. AC charging stops at once.
c: Open lower resistor in the voltage divider of channel C
Sense signal shorted to the converter reference or a supply rail
Actual overvoltage or surge from the supply
s: AC charging stops within seconds of starting
Displayed supply voltage unrealistically high
Charging fault message

P0FFF.d: P0FFF has no documented meaning. CARB requires the SAE J2012-defined codes such as P0xxx and P2xxx wherever possible and allows manufacturer-defined codes only in the ranges J2012 sets aside for them, such as P1xxx. None of the public J2012 title lists checked for obdex assigns a code in the P0Fxx block, and no vehicle maker, regulator filing or bulletin in the NHTSA archive uses P0FFF. If a scan tool reports P0FFF, the likely causes are a reading error, a tool with a faulty code table or a maker-specific code shown with the wrong prefix; check the raw data and the manufacturer's own code list.

P2000.d: A NOx adsorber (lean NOx trap) collects nitrogen oxides while a lean-running engine produces them and turns them into nitrogen during short rich purges. P2000 reports that the trap on bank 1 no longer stores or converts enough NOx; CARB wants this flagged before tailpipe NOx passes a fixed multiple of the standard. Chrysler documents the code on 2007 to 2011 Ram 2500/3500 pickups with the 6.7 L Cummins: bulletin 25-001-13 links it, often together with P2A00/P2A01, to sooted oxygen sensors has both sensors cleaned or replaced and a heat shield added, while 18-012-12 brings revised engine software for P2000 and other codes on the 2011 trucks. Sulphur poisoning, thermal ageing or purges that never complete are further reasons. The truck usually drives normally, but NOx output rises.
c: Sooted or drifting oxygen sensors that misjudge trap loading and purges
NOx trap poisoned by sulphur or aged by heat
Engine software that sets the code without a real fault (update available on some models)
Rich purges or desulphation not completed, e.g. because of short trips
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Often accompanied by oxygen sensor codes P2A00/P2A01
No noticeable change in driveability

P2001.d: P2001 belongs to the second cylinder bank: the NOx storage catalyst fed by bank 2 has lost so much capacity that it no longer holds and reduces the nitrogen oxides of lean running. The code is only possible on V or boxer engines that give each bank its own trap. No manufacturer documents P2001 publicly; the best documented trap application, the inline-six 6.7 L Cummins in Ram pickups, has a single bank and reports P2000. CARB sets the same emission-based limit for every NOx adsorber, so the bank 2 monitor works like its bank 1 sibling, comparing what the sensors behind the trap see during storage and purge with a model. Usual suspects are sulphur that desulphation can no longer burn off, a heat-damaged coating, misreading sensors on that side or purges cut short. The car keeps driving normally.
c: Bank 2 NOx trap poisoned by sulphur or thermally aged
Oxygen or NOx sensor on bank 2 reading wrongly
Rich purges on bank 2 repeatedly interrupted
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Driveability usually unchanged

P2002.t: Diesel Particulate Filter Efficiency Below Threshold (Bank 1)
P2002.d: P2002 means the particulate filter on bank 1 lets too much soot through, typically because the substrate is cracked, partly melted, emptied or bypassed. CARB requires diesel OBD to flag a filter whose filtering performance lets PM emissions exceed the limit. Older systems judge this from the pressure drop: GM's 2009 Duramax compares the flow resistance shortly after a regeneration (within 600 s or 18.6 miles, soot load at most 40 g) with a table and aims at a filter leaking eight times the standard. Newer systems use a resistive PM sensor behind the filter: on the 2014 Cruze 2.0 diesel, GM's 2018 diesel group and Ford's 2023 diesels the code sets when the sensor current exceeds 12 µA before the modelled amount of soot needed to trigger an intact sensor has passed. Ford names cracked substrates on Transit 3.2, F-150 3.0 and Super Duty 6.7 and replaces the filter; GM states that a filter with P2002 cannot be cleaned by service regeneration. Regenerating does not cure it.
c: Filter substrate cracked or melted, often after an uncontrolled regeneration
Faulty differential pressure sensor or leaking sensor hoses on pressure-based systems
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Usually no change in driveability
Visible soot at the tailpipe in severe cases

P2003.t: Diesel Particulate Filter Efficiency Below Threshold (Bank 2)
P2003.d: P2003 is set when the particulate filter of bank 2 lets too much soot slip through, which almost always points to a cracked, partly melted, hollowed-out or bypassed core. Separate filters per bank are uncommon, so the code is rare. No manufacturer documents P2003 publicly; GM and Ford explain the detection under the bank 1 code P2002: older systems judge the flow resistance of a freshly regenerated filter, newer ones use a resistive PM sensor behind it, which signals too early when soot gets past the filter. CARB requires the system to catch a filter whose leakage pushes PM beyond the limit and also one whose substrate is missing. A forced regeneration will not cure a broken filter; it has to be replaced. The warning lamp may be the only sign, with soot at the tailpipe if the leak is large.
c: Bank 2 filter core cracked or melted after an overheated regeneration
Filter on bank 2 removed, emptied or bypassed
PM sensor or differential pressure measurement on bank 2 giving false values
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Visible soot at the tailpipe with a large leak
Engine performance normally unaffected

P2004.t: Intake Manifold Runner Control Stuck Open (Bank 1)
P2004.d: Intake manifold runner control (IMRC) uses flaps in the intake manifold; petrol engines switch runner length or tumble, diesels close swirl flaps at low load. P2004 means the flaps on bank 1 stay open when the ECM has commanded them closed, judged from the position feedback. Ford checks commanded against actual plate position after coolant exceeds 40 °F (about 4 °C) and needs four events to set the stuck code; its 2012 summary covers both vacuum and electric actuators. Volkswagen's 2024 bulletin for Golf GTI, Golf R and Arteon lists P2004 as stuck open alongside P2006, P2014 and P2015, caused by contamination in the runner control valve N316. Volkswagen's 2017 bulletin for the 2.0T (BPY, CCTA, CBFA), by contrast, labels P2004 as flap stuck closed, so the manufacturer text in the scan tool may differ from the generic title. Typical causes are a sticking or broken flap shaft, a vacuum leak or a failed control valve.
c: Flap shaft sticking, worn or separated inside the manifold
Runner control valve contaminated or corroded
Vacuum hose or actuator diaphragm leaking
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Weaker low-speed torque

P2005.t: Intake Manifold Runner Control Stuck Open (Bank 2)
P2005.d: P2005 is the bank 2 version of the stuck-open check, so it only exists on V and boxer engines with a flap set per cylinder bank. The ECM has commanded the flaps on bank 2 closed, but the position feedback says they stayed open. Ford runs it on vacuum-operated V engines once coolant is above 40 °F and logs it after four failed events; on the 2017–2019 Super Duty 6.2L Ford found cracked vacuum hoses on the manifold and supplies the hoses alone instead of a new manifold. Audi links P2005 on the 4.0 TFSI (A8, S6, S7, RS 6, RS 7) to moisture in the flap potentiometer and fits a repair kit on both banks; the engine may be held to 4,000 rpm. Subaru names it on Forester Turbo and WRX, where EGR condensate corrodes the tumble valve shaft. Open flaps mostly cost low-speed torque and smooth idle.
c: Cracked or loose vacuum hose to the bank 2 flap actuator
Moisture in the flap potentiometer giving a false position (Audi 4.0 TFSI)
Flap shaft corroded or seized in the open position
Torn diaphragm in the vacuum actuator
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Less pulling power at low engine speed
Rpm limit on some Audi V8 engines

P2006.t: Intake Manifold Runner Control Stuck Closed (Bank 1)
P2006.d: P2006 means the intake manifold runner or swirl flaps on bank 1 stay closed when the ECM has commanded them open. Closed flaps choke the engine at higher load, so this is the case that costs power. On GM's 2018 diesels, with swirl flaps driven by a smart actuator that reports its position, the code sets at once (Type A, one trip) when the position after the P20F8 check exceeds the limit, with coolant at 60 °C or more and the actuator powered for at least 5 s. Ford checks commanded against actual plate position after coolant exceeds 40 °F and needs four events. Volkswagen's 2024 bulletin for Golf GTI, Golf R and Arteon traced P2006 to contamination inside the runner control valve N316 that made it stick closed, fixed in production by a better vacuum hose and valve assembly.
c: Flaps or shafts seized by deposits or wear
Runner control valve stuck from contamination
Electric actuator or its linkage failed
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Loss of power at higher rpm
Limp mode on some diesels

P2007.t: Intake Manifold Runner Control Stuck Closed (Bank 2)
P2007.d: P2007 reports that the runner or tumble flaps of bank 2 have not opened although the ECM asked for it. Because closed flaps narrow the intake path, the fault shows up mainly as missing power near the top of the rev range. On the 2013 Audi 3.0 TFSI (A6, A7, S4, S5, Q5, Q7) a torn diaphragm in one vacuum actuator caused P2006 or P2007; once the vacuum lines pass a leak test, Audi swaps the actuators on both banks to avoid a repeat visit. Audi's 4.0 TFSI bulletin also lists P2007, there with water in the potentiometer. Subaru counts it among tumble valve faults on Forester Turbo and WRX (corroded shaft, now stainless) and on Impreza and Crosstrek, where grease escaping from the actuator makes the valve erratic. Ford checks it like the bank 1 code: four failed events after coolant reaches 40 °F. Compare with P2005, the stuck-open case.
c: Torn diaphragm in the bank 2 vacuum actuator
Flap shaft seized by corrosion or deposits
Grease leaking from an integrated tumble valve actuator (Subaru Impreza/Crosstrek)
Vacuum supply or control valve not working
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Slight loss of power at high rpm

P2008.d: P2008 is the general circuit and open-circuit code for whatever drives the bank 1 flaps: a vacuum solenoid, a motor or a smart swirl actuator. GM's 2018 diesels with a feedback swirl actuator set it when the output stage sees more than 200 kΩ load in 12 of 15 samples (Type B, two trips), with the relay supply above 11 V; the 2014 Cruze diesel needs the open state for over 3 s, and the 2025 DC-motor design tests with the H-bridge off. On the Saab 9-5 2.0 TiD (2010) an open control line for 1 s is a Type A fault. Ford reports IMRC driver faults as P2008 after 5 s. FCA calls the same output the short runner valve: on the Ram 1500 a spread terminal in cavity 1 of the valve connector set P2008 with P2016/P2017. P2009 and P2010 separate short to ground and short to voltage; flaps usually rest in their default position.
c: Spread or corroded terminal in the actuator or valve connector
Broken control or supply wire to the bank 1 actuator
Open winding in the solenoid valve or actuator motor
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Flaps stay in their rest position, less low-end torque or top-end power

P2009.t: Intake Manifold Runner Control Circuit Low (Bank 1)
P2009.d: P2009 narrows the bank 1 flap control fault down to a low signal, which in practice means the control line has found a path to ground. GM's 2018 diesel tables flag a resistance to ground below 0.5 Ω in 12 of 15 checks every 100 ms (Type B), and the 2014 Cruze diesel waits until the short has lasted more than 3 s. In GM's 2025 DC-motor swirl drive the H-bridge is switched on and the code sets when its current exceeds 8 A in 240 of 300 samples. On the 2010 Saab 9-5 diesel the ECM uses P2009 for a grounded control circuit of the swirl solenoid. Subaru lists P2009, together with P2012 for bank 2, among codes on 2017–2020 Impreza and Crosstrek where grease from the tumble valve actuator leaks into the engine; the actuator is not sold alone, so the manifold is replaced. A chafed harness or water in the plug are the usual causes.
c: Control wire chafed through and touching ground
Internal short in the solenoid or actuator motor
Leaking integrated tumble valve actuator (Subaru Impreza/Crosstrek)
Water or corrosion in the actuator connector
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Flaps cannot be switched, uneven running at low speed

P200A.d: P200A is the functional check of the bank 1 flaps: the circuit is fine, but the flaps do not reach or report the expected positions. GM's 2018 diesels learn both end stops at key-off and fail if the closed stop lies outside 81–92 percent or the raw signal outside 25–40 percent of 5 V, or if a stroke takes over 5 s (coolant at least 60 °C, Type B). The 2014 Cruze diesel flags actual position lagging the command by more than 10 percent for 5 s. Saab's 2010 9-5 diesel uses P200A for an overheated driver stage (Type A). Kia ties it on the 2011–2013 Sorento 3.5 V6 to a dead variable charge motion actuator or a broken linkage inside the manifold; a weak battery can bring it back after repair, so test the battery and relearn the actuator. FCA reflashed it on the 3.0 EcoDiesel. P200B is the bank 2 twin.
c: Flap actuator worn, slow or failed
Broken or sticking linkage or flap inside the manifold
Weak battery disturbing the actuator relearn (Kia V6)
Control software that needs an update (FCA 3.0 diesel)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Weaker response at low or high engine speed

P200B.d: P200B judges whether the flaps of bank 2 move as commanded and settle where they should; it needs a V engine whose second bank has its own flap set or position feedback.
