The clearest public user is FCA's 3.0 V6 EcoDiesel: bulletins for the Jeep Grand Cherokee and Ram 1500 from 2014 onward, and 18-002-23 for the 2020 Ram 1500 with the third-generation engine, list P200A and P200B together and cure them by reprogramming the PCM, together with the cold-start variants P2D2D/P2D2E. That points to calibration as one cause rather than hardware alone. FCA publishes no thresholds; GM's inline-engine bank 1 check P200A shows the typical approach, comparing learned end stops with a window and timing each stroke. Before replacing a manifold, check for a software update, then the actuator and linkage on bank 2 only.
c: Engine software with an available update (FCA 3.0 EcoDiesel)
Flaps on bank 2 sticking from soot or carbon
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Often no noticeable change in driving

P200C.d: P200C reports that the exhaust at the bank 1 particulate filter has become hotter than the filter may tolerate, typically when a heavily loaded filter burns off during regeneration. GM's diesel tables set it as Type A, MIL on the first trip: the 2018 group uses more than 850 °C in regeneration and 800 °C otherwise ahead of the filter (30 of 40 samples), the 2020 table 900 °C behind it, the 2025 table 800 °C from 300 of 450 samples. Ford's 2023 diesels need over 830 °C upstream or 950 °C downstream, or a dead downstream sensor, for about 3 s. Hino's tech tip for 2011–2014 trucks has the DOC face checked for melting, the DPF replaced if soot passed it, and the SCR catalyst inspected. GM's PIP5468 for the L5P adds leaking charge-air ducts. Because heat can crack the filter, find the trigger before clearing.
c: Excess soot load burning off too fast during regeneration
Too much fuel reaching the exhaust (leaking injector, post injection, exhaust brake or injector problems)
Leaking charge-air ducting upsetting combustion and soot model
Faulty exhaust temperature sensor near the filter
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Regeneration aborted or blocked
Possible power reduction to protect the exhaust system

P200D.d: P200D is the overheating code for a particulate filter on bank 2 and therefore only appears where the exhaust of the second bank has its own filter and temperature sensors. No manufacturer documents P200D publicly; the published diesel layouts of GM, Ford and Hino run one filter and report its overheating as P200C. Those tables show how such a limit is built: a fixed ceiling between roughly 800 and 950 °C on the sensor ahead of or behind the filter, confirmed over many samples or a few seconds, and stored at once with the warning lamp. On a twin-filter engine the bank 2 check looks only at its own sensors, so a fault limited to one side, such as one leaking injector, an overloaded filter on that bank or a skewed sensor, separates the two codes. The control unit will usually stop regeneration and may limit power.
c: Bank 2 filter overloaded with soot before regeneration
Leaking injector or excess fuel on bank 2 cylinders
Exhaust temperature sensor on bank 2 reading too high
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Regeneration stopped
Power may be limited

P200E.d: P200E means the catalyst on bank 1 has run hotter than its design limit. On diesels this is the oxidation catalyst ahead of the particulate filter. GM reads the sensor behind the close-coupled DOC and stores a Type A code above 850 °C in its 2020 table and above 800 °C in 2025, each confirmed over hundreds of samples. Ford's 2023 diesels tie it to the filter check instead: P200E follows once the P200C condition has lasted 3 s while the vehicle stands still, in other words a parked regeneration that overheats. Heat comes from unburnt fuel reaching the catalyst, for instance leaking injectors, excessive post injection or misfire, from a soot-laden filter, or from charge-air leaks, which GM cites in PIP5468 for the 2017–2018 L5P. CARB does not accept overtemperature records as a catalyst health check, so conversion is judged separately.
c: Unburnt fuel reaching the catalyst (leaking injector, post injection, misfire)
Parked regeneration with high soot load running too hot
Exhaust temperature sensor behind the catalyst faulty
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Regeneration interrupted, possibly with reduced power
Hot smell or heat from the exhaust area

P200F.d: P200F flags excessive temperature in the catalyst of bank 2, so it needs an engine whose second bank feeds its own catalyst with its own temperature sensor. No manufacturer documents P200F publicly; GM and Ford describe only the bank 1 code P200E for their single-path diesels, with limits around 800 to 850 °C behind the oxidation catalyst or a link to a stationary regeneration that runs hot. A twin-path system would apply such a limit per side. Overheating confined to one bank usually has a cause on that bank: an injector dribbling fuel, misfire on those cylinders, or a sensor reading too high. Comparing both banks helps: if only bank 2 is hot, look at its cylinders and sensor first. CARB treats such temperature records as protection, not as proof that the catalyst still converts, so efficiency is monitored separately.
c: Fuel slipping into the bank 2 exhaust (dribbling injector, misfire)
Bank 2 exhaust temperature sensor reading too high
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Possible power reduction

P2010.t: Intake Manifold Runner Control Circuit High (Bank 1)
P2010.d: P2010 is the high-side counterpart of P2009 for the bank 1 flap drive: the control line carries voltage it should not, typically because it touches a supply wire or the actuator is shorted internally. GM's 2018 diesels judge a resistance to supply under 0.5 Ω, again 12 of 15 checks and Type B. The 2014 Cruze diesel looks at the line while the driver is switched on and needs the short for more than 3 s. GM's 2025 DC-motor swirl drive sets P2010 when more than 8 A flows through the H-bridge switches toward the supply in 240 of 300 samples. In the 2010 Saab 9-5 diesel it marks a swirl solenoid control line shorted to voltage; the shop check there uses a test lamp across the control and ignition pins while the valve is commanded between 95 and 5 percent. Output stages usually protect themselves, so the flaps simply stop moving.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Shorted winding in the solenoid or actuator motor
Output stage in the engine control module failed
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Flaps stuck in one position, change in low-speed torque

P2011.d: P2011 covers the electrical drive of the bank 2 flaps, so it appears only on engines with a separate actuator or solenoid per bank. Ford's petrol summaries list P2011 as the IMRC control circuit of bank 2 on vacuum-operated V engines; the PCM output driver itself reports the fault, the check runs continuously after coolant passes 40 °F and needs 5 s with at least 11 V battery voltage. Audi's 3.0 TFSI (A6, A7, A8, Q7, S4, S5, SQ5, 2012–2016) lists P2011 next to the stuck-flap codes in a bulletin where the vacuum-driven coolant pump drew too much vacuum and upset the flap control; the fix is an updated hose with a restrictor, so a P2011 there is not always a broken wire. GM's diesels are inline engines and use only P2008. Low and high faults of the same circuit are P2012 and P2013.
c: Open wire or loose connector at the bank 2 solenoid
Open coil in the bank 2 control solenoid
Vacuum-driven coolant pump drawing too much vacuum (Audi 3.0 TFSI)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Bank 2 flaps do not switch, slight loss of torque or power

P2012.t: Intake Manifold Runner Control Circuit Low (Bank 2)
P2012.d: P2012 means the ECM reads the control circuit of the bank 2 flap actuator too low, usually a short to ground in the wire or inside the actuator. Subaru is the one maker that names it publicly: on the 2017–2020 Impreza and 2018–2020 Crosstrek, including the plug-in hybrid, lubricant from the tumble generator valve actuator could leak and be drawn into the engine, after which the valve works erratically and P2009 or P2012 may set alongside the stuck codes. The TGV is part of the manifold, so the whole manifold is replaced with an updated one. No public table gives a threshold for bank 2; GM's bank 1 equivalent P2009 uses a ground resistance under 0.5 Ω or, on H-bridge drives, more than 8 A. CARB requires circuit faults of output components to be monitored continuously. Higher than expected readings are P2013, an open circuit is P2011.
c: Integrated tumble valve actuator leaking lubricant (Subaru Impreza/Crosstrek)
Bank 2 control wire shorted to ground
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Erratic idle or hesitation on light throttle

P2013.t: Intake Manifold Runner Control Circuit High (Bank 2)
P2013.d: P2013 points to a control line of the bank 2 flap actuator that sits too high, i.e. a short to battery voltage or an actuator whose winding has shorted so the driver sees supply where it expects a load. No manufacturer documents P2013 publicly. The logic can be taken from bank 1, where GM checks P2010 as a resistance to supply below 0.5 Ω and Saab's 2010 9-5 diesel uses it for the swirl solenoid control shorted to voltage. CARB requires circuit faults of such output components to be watched continuously, and runner systems are named among the outputs to monitor. Ford's V engines report bank 2 only as P2011, so a P2013 is more likely on other makes with one actuator per bank. Checking the wiring with the actuator unplugged usually separates harness from actuator. The flaps on that bank then stay in their rest position.
c: Bank 2 control wire shorted to a supply wire
Shorted winding in the bank 2 actuator
Engine control module output stage faulty
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Bank 2 flaps no longer switch

P2014.t: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit (Bank 1)
P2014.d: P2014 is the general electrical code for the flap position feedback on bank 1, used when the control unit sees a broken or shorted circuit without, or before, splitting it into low and high. Ford's 2012 summary calls it the IMRC input switch check: with coolant warmer than 40 °F it is checked all the time, and an open or shorted switch must persist for 5 s; from 2024 Ford treats P2014 as the base code whose failure bytes stand for low, high and over-travel. Volkswagen's quick reference for the 2014 Touareg sets it on the supercharged V6 hybrid (engine code CGFA) at a signal under 0.2 V. Volkswagen saw it on 2008–2011 2.0T engines (CCTA, CBFA) with failing manifolds and later told dealers on 1.8T/2.0T engines to replace only the sensor G336. The flaps then work unmonitored or are parked.
c: Runner position sensor (VW G336) failed internally
Manifold with integrated flap shaft and sensor damaged (VW 2.0T 2008–2011)
s: Check engine lamp on
Slightly weaker pull or rougher idle while the flaps are parked

P2015.t: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1)
P2015.d: P2015 means the position feedback of the intake manifold runner or swirl flaps on bank 1 is electrically present but implausible. How it is judged depends on the design. Diesels with a smart swirl actuator send position as a pulse-width signal: GM's 2018 diesels fail a pulse period below 0 or above 64 ms in 52 of 62 samples (Type B), and on the Opel/GM 2.0 CDTi in the Saab 9-5 (2010) the ECM flags a wrong frequency from the actuator, with sub-codes for period and high and low time (Type A). Ford's petrol engines call it position sensor over travel. Audi and Volkswagen use it widely on 2.0 TFSI: a corroded flap valve N316, a flap that separated inside the manifold, and on the 4.2 FSI a deformed seal behind the flap potentiometer that made the linkage stick. After a manifold or valve replacement the flap adaptation has to be run, or the code returns.
c: Flap linkage sticking or flap separated inside the manifold
Corroded or faulty flap control valve
Actuator electronics or position sensor faulty
Flap adaptation not performed after repair
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Rough idle or weaker low-speed torque

P2016.t: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Low (Bank 1)
P2016.d: P2016 says the bank 1 flap position signal sits at the bottom of its range, typically a shorted signal wire or a lost 5 V supply. Ford sets it below 0.24 V after 5 s; the 2014 Touareg 3.0 TDI (CNRB) below 0.15 V. GM's 2018 diesels read a smart swirl actuator whose feedback is a pulse train: a period frozen at 30 ms with 0 % duty in 50 of 62 samples, at least 5 s after the actuator woke and above 11 V, gives a Type B fault. On GM's 2025 SENT sensor a raw value under 1 % in 480 of 600 samples does the same. Chrysler's short runner valve feedback uses it too: a PCM reflash for 2013–2015 Ram 1500 V6/V8 trucks addresses P2016, and a 2023 Ram case traced P2008, P2016 and P2017 together to a spread supply terminal in the valve plug.
c: 5 V or actuator supply missing (spread terminal, blown fuse)
Position sensor or smart actuator electronics faulty
s: Check engine lamp on
Less torque at low revs or flat spot when the runner should switch

P2017.t: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit High (Bank 1)
P2017.d: P2017 is the mirror case of P2016: the bank 1 flap feedback is stuck near the supply rail. With a pulled-up input that happens when the signal or sensor ground opens, or when the signal wire touches a voltage source. Ford's limit is 4.7 V for 5 s, Volkswagen uses 4.85 V on the 3.0 TDI and 4.88 V on the 3.0 TSI hybrid of the 2014 Touareg. On GM's 2018 diesel swirl actuator the period is again pinned at 30 ms but the duty cycle reads 100 %, counted in 50 of 62 samples; the 2025 SENT version flags a raw value over 99 % in 480 of 600, both Type B with MIL after two trips. Chrysler's short runner valve bulletins cover P2017 together with P2016, which points to shared supply or connector faults rather than two failed parts.
c: Open sensor ground or signal circuit
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Spread or corroded terminal in the valve or sensor plug
Position sensor or actuator electronics faulty
s: Check engine lamp on
Flaps parked in default position, slightly changed running at part load

P2018.t: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Intermittent (Bank 1)
P2018.d: P2018 belongs to bank 1 and covers a flap position signal that drops out or jumps for short moments while it otherwise stays within limits, so neither the low nor the high code matures. Few makers publish it. Mitsubishi lists P2018 for the 2022 and 2023 Outlander with the 2.5 litre PR25DD engine as a bank 1 fault of the sensor that reports where the runner valve stands, logged after two trips with the warning lamp; a 2023 bulletin added its diagnostic page to the service manual. CARB requires such input components to be watched for circuit faults, which is why erratic feedback earns its own code. Loose pins, a cracked wire near the manifold or a worn sensor track are the usual suspects.
c: Loose or fretted pins in the sensor connector
Wire cracked by engine movement or heat near the manifold
Worn resistive track in the position sensor
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Often no noticeable change in driving

P2019.t: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit (Bank 2)
P2019.d: P2019 is the bank 2 counterpart of P2014 and only appears on V or boxer engines with separate flap feedback per cylinder row. It reports an electrical fault in the position circuit without stating its direction. Volkswagen's Touareg hybrid of 2014 (CGFA) stores it once the bank 2 signal drops under 0.2 V. Ford's 2024 summary uses P2019 as the parent code for bank 2: failure byte 11 corresponds to the low code P2021, 15 to the high code P2022 and 92 to over-travel (P2020), all checked once coolant is above 40 °F. Ford's 2014 code list marks P2019 as lighting the MIL. If P2014 is stored as well, look for a shared reference or ground before replacing both sensors.
c: Bank 2 sensor wiring open or shorted
Shared 5 V reference or ground faulty (both banks affected)
s: Check engine lamp on
Mild loss of low-speed torque if the control unit parks the flaps

P201A.t: Reductant Injection Valve Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2 Unit 1)
P201A.d: Engines with two SCR paths give each a DEF dosing valve. P201A concerns the first valve on bank 2: the circuit is not open or shorted, but what the control unit sees while dosing does not fit the command. No manufacturer documents P201A publicly; the pickup and truck SCR systems in the public record use one valve and report this fault as P202E. Those show the method: GM's 6.6 L LML counts commanded against actual valve states and fails after more than ten mismatches within 80 injection events, while Hino found that some faults came from software misjudging DEF pressure at the valve. CARB requires reductant delivery to be monitored. On bank 2 the same culprits apply: a valve stuck by crystals, a connector with added resistance, or wrong pressure. Too little DEF raises NOx and may start the inducement warnings.
c: Bank 2 dosing valve sticking from urea crystals or deposits
Corroded connector or harness adding resistance to the valve circuit
DEF pressure at the valve outside the expected range
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DEF system warning, possibly countdown to speed limitation

P201B.t: Intake Manifold Runner Control Actuator Supply Voltage Low (Bank 1)
P201B.d: P201B does not concern the control signal but the power feed of an electric flap actuator on bank 1. GM's 2025 diesel tables describe it for a swirl valve driven by a DC motor: if the supply seen by the driver falls below 6 V while the powertrain relay itself delivers more than 11 V, and this holds in 240 of 300 samples taken every 12.5 ms, a Type B fault is stored. So the voltage is lost between relay and actuator, for example at a fuse, connector or chafed wire. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 for the 2021 3.0L LM2 Duramax (Silverado, Sierra, Tahoe, Suburban, Yukon, Escalade) lists P201B among many codes caused by engine harness chafing that can blow fuses. GM's 2017–2018 diesels also include P201B in the fault group that switches swirl control off. The bank 2 version is P201C.
c: Chafed engine harness shorting or interrupting the actuator feed
Blown fuse in the actuator supply
High resistance at the supply pin of the actuator connector
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Swirl flaps no longer move, often with other electrical codes

P201C.t: Intake Manifold Runner Control Actuator Supply Voltage Low (Bank 2)
P201C.d: P201C reports that the electric flap actuator of bank 2 is not getting enough supply voltage. It only makes sense on V engines that give each bank its own powered actuator. No manufacturer documents P201C publicly. The bank 1 counterpart P201B is described by GM for its DC-motor swirl drive: the driver supply below 6 V while the relay feed is above 11 V, in 240 of 300 samples, Type B. That logic separates a weak battery, which would also pull the relay feed down, from a loss on the branch to the actuator. CARB treats such actuators as comprehensive output components and requires circuit faults to be found continuously. In practice the search starts at the fuse and supply pin of the bank 2 actuator. If both banks report a supply fault at once, look for a shared fuse or relay first.
c: Fuse or relay feeding the bank 2 actuator failed
Damaged supply wire or connector at the bank 2 actuator
Actuator electronics loading the supply down
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Bank 2 flaps stop working

P201D.t: Intake Manifold Runner Control Actuator Internal Performance (Bank 1)
P201D.d: P201D is for flap actuators with their own electronics: the bank 1 actuator, or the ECM's check of it, has found a fault inside the unit, such as a failed driver, sensor or self-test, while wiring and supply look normal. GM uses the code on its 2017 and 2018 diesels with a smart swirl actuator, but only as a member of the fault group that orders swirl control off, next to P2008–P2010, P201B, P2004 and P2006; the tables give no monitor row and no threshold for it. CARB requires flap systems that change charge motion to be checked for proper function, and lets makers check the shaft of one bank instead of every flap. Since internal faults cannot be repaired, the usual remedy is a new actuator or, where it is built in, a new manifold, after ruling out supply (P201B) and circuit codes. The bank 2 counterpart is P201E.
c: Internal electronics of the smart actuator failed
Actuator overloaded by sticking flaps, internal protection tripped
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Swirl control switched off, slightly rougher combustion at low load

P201E.t: Intake Manifold Runner Control Actuator Internal Performance (Bank 2)
P201E.d: P201E says the electronic flap actuator serving bank 2 has detected or caused an internal malfunction; the wires to it are not the issue. No manufacturer documents P201E publicly, and only engines with a separate smart actuator per bank can set it. On bank 1 GM lists the matching code P201D for its 2017–2018 diesels inside the group of faults that disable swirl control, but without its own thresholds, so even there the actuator decides what counts as internal. CARB asks for a functional check of every valve or flap system that alters charge motion. If P201E appears together with low supply (P201C) or circuit codes for bank 2, those come first; on its own it usually means the actuator, or a manifold with built-in actuator, must be replaced. Expect the bank 2 flaps to stay parked until the fault is gone.
c: Electronics inside the bank 2 actuator failed
Bank 2 flaps binding and overloading the actuator
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Little or no change in drivability

P201F.d: P201F says reductant pump A keeps running or keeps building pressure although the control unit has switched it off, for example when dosing pauses or after the line has been purged at shutdown. No manufacturer documents P201F publicly. The opposite fault is well described: Ford's 2023 diesels compare pump speed with its setpoint and set P208B when it deviates by more than 300 rpm or the control output sits at its limit for 30 s, while open, low and high faults of the drive circuit get P208A, P208C and P208D. A pump that will not stop usually has a driver or relay stuck closed, a control line shorted to supply voltage, or a pump controller that ignores the command. Effects are pressure where none is wanted, DEF left in lines that may freeze, and a drained battery. CARB requires output components to respond to commands.
c: Pump relay contacts welded or driver stage stuck on
Pump control wire shorted to supply voltage
Internal fault in the pump or dosing control unit
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Pump audible after switching off the engine
Battery discharged after standing

P2020.t: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2)
P2020.d: P2020 flags a bank 2 position signal that is electrically sound but does not fit what the flaps should be doing. On the CGFA hybrid V6 of the 2014 Touareg, Volkswagen triggers it when commanded and measured flap position are more than 40 % apart or the reported value leaves the 0–100 % window. Ford's summaries describe it as the bank 2 sensor travelling too far: the plates either miss the commanded position or the sensor reports travel beyond the normal stops, and four such events are needed. Because a sticking shaft, a broken lever or a vacuum fault looks the same to the sensor, P2020 often appears next to the stuck codes P2005 or P2007.
c: Bank 2 flap shaft sticking or carbon-fouled
Broken lever or linkage between actuator and shaft
Weak vacuum or leaking actuator diaphragm (vacuum systems)
Sensor shifted or adaptation missing after repair
s: Check engine lamp on
Reduced pull in the mid range or uneven idle

P2021.t: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Low (Bank 2)
P2021.d: P2021 is the low-signal code for the bank 2 runner position sensor. Ford documents it for vacuum-operated runner control on its V engines in the 2020–2023 summary: the position input below 0.24 V for 5 s, monitored continuously once coolant exceeds 40 °F. In the 2024 edition the same fault is shown as P2019 with failure byte 11. A low reading means the signal line is pulled to ground, the 5 V supply to the sensor is missing, or the sensor itself has failed short. On engines that share one reference for both banks, a simultaneous P2016 points to that common circuit. The ECM stops trusting the feedback and usually leaves the flaps in their default position.
c: 5 V reference to the bank 2 sensor open
s: Check engine lamp on
Slight loss of low-end torque

P2022.t: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit High (Bank 2)
P2022.d: P2022 sets when the bank 2 flap position input reads close to the supply voltage. Ford's limit is above 4.7 V for 5 s on its V engines with vacuum-operated runners (shown from 2024 as P2019 with failure byte 15); for the Touareg hybrid engine CGFA (2014) Volkswagen gives more than 4.88 V. Such a value is rarely real travel – it normally means the sensor ground or signal line is open so the input floats up, or the signal wire has contacted a 5 V or battery feed. Wiggling the harness while watching the live value helps to tell a broken wire from a failed sensor. With P2017 on bank 1 at the same time, check the common ground first. The flaps are usually left unpowered, so the engine runs on with slightly less low-speed torque.
c: Bank 2 sensor ground or signal open
Signal wire touching a 5 V or battery feed
s: Check engine lamp on
Little or no change in drivability

P2023.t: Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Intermittent (Bank 2)
P2023.d: P2023 is meant for a bank 2 flap position signal that briefly drops out or jumps without staying out of range long enough for P2021 or P2022. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; Ford's V-engine summaries stop at low, high and over-travel for bank 2, and Volkswagen's Touareg tables skip it. The closest published analogue is P2018 on bank 1, which Mitsubishi lists for the PR25DD-engined Outlander as a two-trip fault with warning lamp. CARB's rules for comprehensive components require circuit faults of emission-related inputs such as variable runner systems to be detected, so a calibration may use P2023 for unstable feedback. In practice it points to a loose connector, a chafed loom on the hot side of the engine or a worn sensor.
c: Bank 2 sensor plug with loose or corroded contacts
Harness rubbing through near exhaust or valve cover
Worn bank 2 position sensor giving dropouts
s: Warning lamp appears now and then
Usually no change in how the engine drives

P2024.t: EVAP Fuel Vapor Temperature Sensor Circuit
P2024.d: The fuel vapor temperature sensor tells the ECM how warm the vapor in the tank and canister is, which matters for leak tests that judge pressure or vacuum as the fuel cools after shutdown. P2024 is the unspecified electrical code for that circuit. On recent Audi models the sensor is built into the leak detection unit J909 at the charcoal canister. An Audi bulletin first issued in 2023 and revised in September 2026 covers 2022–2025 A3 to Q8 models: four-cylinder engines could store P2024, described as an electrical fault of the tank breather temperature sensor, although guided diagnosis expects P2026 for a low voltage at J909. The fix there is to follow the corrected test, not to replace parts. Without valid temperature the EVAP leak test cannot complete.
c: Open or shorted wiring to the temperature sensor or leak detection unit
Misassigned fault entry in the ECM software (Audi 2022–2025)
Leak detection unit with integrated sensor faulty
s: Check engine lamp on
EVAP readiness not set, possible inspection failure

P2025.t: EVAP Fuel Vapor Temperature Sensor Performance
P2025.d: P2025 means the vapor temperature reading is electrically valid but does not make sense against other inputs or over time. Audi documents a real-world cause on 2016–2018 A6 and A7 with the 3.0 litre engine: water gets into the tank ventilation path, runs past the leak detection pressure switch (NVLD) into the canister and turns to ice in cold weather. Owners notice the pump nozzle clicking off while refuelling, and P2025 can appear with P0441, P0451 and P0453. The bulletin has the canister weighed – above 2650 g it is replaced with switch and vent tube – and the filter relocated or the wheel liner updated. Volkswagen released ECM software for the 2022 Taos (24HV) and for Jetta and Taos (24iR) that also prevents P2025 entries. Ford's 2014 code list marks it as a MIL code.
c: Water or ice in canister and NVLD switch (Audi A6/A7 3.0)
ECM software setting the code falsely (VW Jetta/Taos 2022)
Temperature sensor drifted or slow to respond
s: Check engine lamp on
Fuel nozzle shuts off repeatedly when filling the tank
EVAP readiness incomplete

P2026.t: EVAP Fuel Vapor Temperature Sensor Circuit Low Voltage
P2026.d: P2026 reports a vapor temperature signal stuck near 0 V. With the usual NTC thermistor and pull-up resistor, a low voltage corresponds to an extremely hot reading, so the code nearly always points to a signal wire touching ground or a shorted sensor rather than real heat. Audi names this test explicitly: on 2022–2025 models with four-cylinder engines, guided diagnosis checks P2026 as a too-low voltage at the temperature sensor inside leak detection unit J909, the result an earlier software wrongly filed as P2024. Ford's 2014 code list includes P2026 as a MIL-on fault. No public source gives a numeric threshold. Because the EVAP leak checks use this temperature, they are suspended until the circuit is repaired and the monitor has run again.
c: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Temperature sensor or leak detection unit shorted internally
Moisture bridging pins at the canister-mounted connector
s: Check engine lamp on
Implausibly high vapor temperature in live data

P2027.t: EVAP Fuel Vapor Temperature Sensor Circuit High Voltage
P2027.d: P2027 is the high-voltage counterpart of P2026: the signal sits near the reference, which an NTC sensor would only produce at a temperature far below anything plausible. In practice the sensor circuit is open – a broken wire, an unplugged connector, a corroded pin – or the signal line is shorted to a voltage source. Ford's 2014 code list names P2027 among MIL-relevant faults, but no manufacturer publicly describes its threshold or timing. On Audi vehicles the sensor sits inside leak detection unit J909 at the canister, so an open there affects the whole unit. CARB treats sensors used by the EVAP monitor as input components that must be checked for out-of-range values. Until the circuit is fixed, the leak test cannot run and EVAP readiness stays open.
c: Open circuit – broken wire or unplugged connector
Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage
s: Check engine lamp on
Vapor temperature shown far below ambient

P2028.t: EVAP Fuel Vapor Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent
P2028.d: P2028 covers a vapor temperature signal that jumps or briefly drops out instead of changing smoothly, as vapor temperature normally does. Public manufacturer documentation for it is lacking: Ford's 2014 list ends with P2027, and the Audi bulletins concern P2024–P2026 only. The nearest documented case is Audi's sensor inside leak detection unit J909, mounted at the canister near the rear wheel arch where water and road salt reach the connector. CARB requires input components used by the EVAP monitor to be checked for circuit faults, which leaves room for a separate intermittent code. Suspects are a loose or corroded plug, a wire chafing on the body or tank straps, or moisture inside the leak detection unit. The lamp may come and go between trips.
c: Corroded or loose connector at the canister area
Wire chafing against body or tank straps
Moisture inside the leak detection unit with integrated sensor
s: Warning lamp that switches on and off
EVAP readiness slow to complete

P2029.d: A fuel fired heater burns a small amount of the vehicle's fuel to warm coolant or cabin air, a common add-on on diesels with little waste heat. P2029 is a state code: the controller has taken the heater out of service, usually after repeated failed starts, flame-outs, overheating or an electrical fault. CARB counts fuel-fired passenger heaters among other emission sources for which each maker must get its own monitoring plan approved. No manufacturer documents P2029 publicly. Webasto's Air Top Evo shows the pattern: no start, flame loss, overheating and glow plug faults have their own codes, and after too many failures the heater locks out until a workshop releases it. So the real fault, often logged alongside as P2030 or a circuit code, has to be fixed before the lock is cleared. The engine runs normally; the cabin stays cold.
c: Lock-out after repeated failed starts or flame-outs (fuel supply, glow plug, combustion air)
Heater shut down after overheating, e.g. low coolant flow
Supply voltage too low or wiring fault to the heater
s: Little or no auxiliary heat, slow warm-up
Heater does not start when requested
Warning lamp depends on the manufacturer

P202A.d: DEF freezes at about −11 °C, so the tank carries an electric, often PTC-type heater that thaws enough fluid for dosing after a cold start. P202A covers the control circuit of that heater with the emphasis on an open circuit: when commanded on, practically no current flows. Volkswagen documents it on the 2014 Touareg 3.0 TDI (CNRB) and judges the element by its conductance: during heating a value of 0.10 S or less, roughly 10 Ω or more, sets the code. Typical are a broken element, a burnt or loose connector at the tank, a blown fuse or an interrupted wire. With the heater dead, frozen DEF cannot be dissolved, so in winter the system soon reports it cannot dose and may begin the inducement countdown. P202B and P202C separate a weak or excessive heater current from this complete interruption.
c: Loose or burnt connector at the tank, or blown heater fuse
Interrupted wire between control unit and tank
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
In frost, DEF system warning and inducement countdown

P202B.t: Reductant Tank Heater Control Circuit Low
P202B.d: P202B belongs to the electric heater in the DEF tank and reports a low reading in its control circuit. Generically that means a signal sitting too low, for example a grounded wire or a drive output pulled down. Volkswagen gives a concrete test on the 2014 Touareg 3.0 TDI: right at the start of heating the element's conductance must reach a minimum, and a value under 0.30 S, i.e. more than about 3.3 Ω, sets P202B. The element still conducts, unlike the open-circuit case P202A, but draws too little current to thaw the tank in time. Corroded pins, a partly damaged element or a wire chafed against the body are typical. The heater is needed only in frost, so the code often surfaces in the first cold weeks; while temperatures are mild, DEF dosing usually continues.
c: Corroded heater connector pins adding resistance
Heater element partly damaged, resistance too high
Control wire chafed through to ground
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DEF stays frozen longer after cold starts

P202C.t: Reductant Tank Heater Control Circuit High
P202C.d: P202C is the high-side fault of the DEF tank heater circuit: the module sees a value above the allowed range, as when the wire touches battery positive or an element that conducts far too well. On the Touareg 3.0 TDI of model year 2014, Volkswagen flags it when the element's conductance at the start of heating exceeds 0.62 S, below roughly 1.6 Ω, which hints at an internal short. On 2025 Ram 2500 to 5500 with the 6.7 L Cummins, Chrysler's bulletin 08-076-26 lists P202C next to other DEF heater and pressure codes and cure them with new software for the DEF control unit; there the fault came from calibration, not from hardware. With a real short the fuse may blow or the driver protect itself, so the tank stays unheated. In winter the system may then warn and count down to a speed limit.
c: DEF control unit calibration (software update on some models)
Heater element with internal short, resistance too low
Heater control wire shorted to battery voltage
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Service DEF message, later speed limited
Heater fuse may blow

P202D.d: P202D reports that DEF is escaping somewhere between pump and dosing valve, which the controller typically notices as a pressure that cannot be held. Volvo and Mack use it on their 2014 and later trucks (OBD13 onwards). A 2015 tech tip handles it together with P208E and P20E8 and names poor electrical contact, which makes the pressure reading look low, and contamination that really lowers it. 2023 bulletins CBR-2298 and CBR-2303 add crystal crusts, a clogged tip or a weeping dosing valve, yet stress that returned valves were mostly fine: the valve is replaced only if a dosing test shows reduced flow. White urea crust on lines or the valve is a typical sign. CARB requires reductant delivery to be monitored. Neglected, the system cannot hold pressure, NOx rises and inducement follows.
c: Dosing valve weeping or crusted with crystals
Leaking DEF line, fitting or seal
Poor electrical contact faking a pressure loss
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
White crystalline deposits on DEF lines or dosing valve
Higher DEF consumption, later inducement warnings

P202E.t: Reductant Injection Valve Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1 Unit 1)
P202E.d: P202E concerns the first DEF dosing valve on bank 1, which in most SCR systems is the only one. The circuit itself is intact, but the valve does not behave as commanded. GM's 6.6 L LML (2014 table) checks what the valve driver was told to do against the actual state of its circuit and sets a Type A code after more than ten mismatches within 80 injections, checked only with the coil between about −7 and 100 °C. In GM's 2018 diesel tables an active stuck-tip fault of the valve also blocks the SCR efficiency test P20EE. Chrysler reflashed the dosing control unit of 2013–2014 Ram 2500 to 5500 with 6.7 L Cummins against needless P202E (bulletin 18-010-14), and Hino traced some cases on 2013 J08 trucks to software misjudging DEF pressure. Real faults are crystal-stuck valves or bad contacts; too little DEF raises NOx.
c: Dosing valve sticking from urea crystals or a clogged tip
Dosing or engine control unit software (updates available on some models)
DEF pressure at the valve outside the expected range
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DEF system warning, possibly countdown to speed limitation
Possibly additional SCR efficiency codes

P202F.d: P202F covers the commanded supply stage that feeds the reductant system or, in some layouts, the regeneration hardware, typically a supply pump or its power feed. The circuit is electrically present, but its behaviour does not match the command, for instance current or voltage that drifts outside the window expected for the requested state. J2012 leaves the exact component to the maker, and no manufacturer documents P202F publicly. Ford's 2023 diesels show how such a stage is watched under other codes: the reductant pump controller must keep its supply between 8.5 and 19 V (P21CB/P21CC) and its current below 15 A, and pump speed may not stray more than 300 rpm from target (P208B). CARB requires output components to respond properly. Likely causes are a weak relay or fuse contact, a pump that draws too much, or a faulty controller.
c: Weak relay or fuse contact in the supply feed
Supply pump drawing excessive current (wear, blockage)
Fault in the dosing or pump control unit
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DEF system warning, dosing reduced or stopped

P2030.d: P2030 is the functional check of a fuel fired heater: it is wired and commanded, but does not ignite, keep its flame or deliver the heat expected. Hino uses the code on 2011–2014 conventional trucks with the J08 engine, where a burner heats the exhaust for particulate filter regeneration. Its burner control unit confirms ignition through a flame temperature sensor and logs P2030 as burner misfire; campaign SCB-006-15 reprogrammed the unit because a flame not touching the sensor was read as a misfire, and SB-15-032 revised the troubleshooting. In cabin and coolant heaters the same idea appears as Webasto's start, flame-out and overheat faults. CARB lets each maker define the monitor for such devices. Typical causes are fuel starvation, a worn glow pin, blocked combustion air or a contaminated flame sensor.
c: Fuel starvation at the heater (dosing pump, filter, line)
Worn glow pin or contaminated flame sensor
Combustion air inlet or exhaust of the heater blocked, sooted chamber
Control unit software misjudging the flame (update on some models)
s: Heater fails to start or goes out
White smoke or fuel smell from the heater exhaust
Burner-assisted filter regeneration does not complete

P2031.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P2031.d: Exhaust gas temperature sensor 2 on bank 1 usually sits between the oxidation catalyst and the particulate filter, where the ECM uses it to control regeneration temperature. Under the generic circuit title, manufacturers set P2031 for different faults. On Ford's 2023 diesels it is a plausibility test: after at least 6 hours off, all sensors must agree within 50 °C at key-on, and while driving each must stay within ±80 °C of the modelled temperature for 200 to 400 s, with the fault confirmed after 20 s. Mack and Volvo trucks use P2031 with a failure mode identifier for open or shorted wiring, connector faults and failed sensors, and note that regeneration is then not possible. Stellantis found water and corrosion in the sensor and harness connectors and replaces both. P2032 and P2033 are the dedicated low and high signal codes.
c: Sensor failed or reading off from the model
Water or corrosion in the sensor or harness connector
Wiring open or shorted near the hot exhaust
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DPF regeneration inhibited

P2032.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P2032.d: P2032 means the signal of exhaust gas temperature sensor 2 on bank 1 is below its valid range. What that means electrically depends on the sensor type. On the Opel/GM 2.0 CDTi in the Saab 9-5 (2010) sensor 2 sits in the particulate filter and its voltage falls as it gets hotter, so a reading below 0.4 V for more than 1 s points to a short to ground; the code is Type A there. GM's 2009 Duramax uses the opposite characteristic and fails below 0.307 V, equivalent to -40 °C, for 300 s, which is typical of an open or grounded signal. GM's 2018 diesels compare against a resistance-equivalent limit below 142 Ω as a Type B code, Ford's 2023 diesels against 0.10 V within 2 s. So check the wiring diagram before deciding whether low means a short or an open. Without the sensor the ECM cannot control filter temperature and usually blocks regeneration.
c: Signal wire chafed to ground on the exhaust
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DPF regeneration inhibited, soot load rises

P2033.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P2033.d: P2033 means the signal of exhaust gas temperature sensor 2 on bank 1 is above its valid range. On the Opel/GM 2.0 CDTi in the Saab 9-5 (2010) the sensor in the particulate filter reads high voltage when cold, so more than 1.6 V for over 1 s means an open circuit, an unplugged connector or a short to voltage; it is Type A. GM's 2009 Duramax sets it above 3.37 V, equivalent to 1000 °C, for 300 s, which on that sensor is a short to voltage rather than an open. GM's 2018 diesels use a resistance-equivalent limit above 922 Ω (Type B), Ford's 2023 diesels 2.66 V within 2 s. Sensors near the filter see repeated heat cycles, and their leads and connectors are exposed to road water. The ECM loses the filter temperature and normally stops regeneration, so soot builds up until the fault is fixed.
c: Sensor element open after heat cycling
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DPF regeneration inhibited, soot load rises

P2034.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P2034.d: P2034 is the general electrical fault of the second exhaust temperature sensor on bank 2, so it only appears where the second bank has its own measuring point downstream. GM does not use it: the 2018 diesel tables number every exhaust temperature sensor on bank 1 (P0545/P0546, P2032/P2033, P242C/P242D, P2470/P2471), as one aftertreatment line serves the whole engine. Deutz assigns P2034 on its EMR L1 engine controller (industrial engines, list of November 2022) to the second temperature sensor upstream of the SCR catalyst, with failure-type bytes: -13 open, -11 shorted to ground, -12 shorted to battery, -F0 ground fault, -1C supply out of range. Others split low and high readings into P2035 and P2036. With the reading lost, temperature-dependent DEF dosing or filter regeneration is usually limited.
c: Sensor lead open or shorted where it runs along the hot exhaust
Sensing element failed after many heat cycles
Water or corrosion in the sensor connector
Sensor ground or supply from the control unit faulty
s: Engine warning lamp on
DEF dosing or particulate filter regeneration restricted
Engine power reduced on some applications

P2035.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P2035.d: P2035 reports that the signal of temperature sensor 2 on bank 2 has dropped below its plausible floor. Whether that is a short or an open depends on the sensor curve: with a thermistor pulled up by the control unit a grounded wire drags the voltage down, whereas some circuits read near zero when the loop is broken. No manufacturer documents P2035 publicly. Deutz, the one maker found using this sensor slot, keeps the short to ground under P2034-11 instead. The bank 1 counterpart P2032 shows typical limits: GM's 2018 diesels fail below a resistance equivalent of 142 ohms as a Type B code (MIL after two trips). CARB requires such out-of-range checks for every emission-relevant input. Expect the dosing or regeneration strategy that relies on this reading to be cut back.
c: Signal wire chafed through to ground on the exhaust or frame
Internal short in the sensing element
s: Engine warning lamp on
Temperature reading on bank 2 implausibly low or at the limit
Regeneration or DEF dosing limited

P2036.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P2036.d: P2036 is set when the bank 2, sensor 2 temperature signal climbs above the top of its valid window. On the usual pull-up input that is what an unplugged connector, a broken lead or an element gone open after heat cycling produces, while a short to supply voltage gives the same picture. No manufacturer documents P2036 publicly; Deutz files the short to battery of its second SCR inlet sensor as P2034-12, and GM's 2018 diesel tables carry all their sensors on bank 1. For the bank 1 code P2033 GM's 2018 diesel tables use a resistance equivalent above 922 ohms, confirmed by 10 failed samples, Type B. Because a dead sensor looks like an extremely hot exhaust here, the control unit may also trigger protective power reduction until the circuit is repaired.
c: Sensing element open after repeated heat cycles
Connector unplugged, loose or with pushed-back terminal
Sensor lead broken near the hot exhaust
Signal wire shorted to supply voltage
s: Engine warning lamp on
Bank 2 temperature shows an implausibly high value
Possible protective power reduction

P2037.t: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Sensor A Circuit
P2037.d: Some heavy-duty SCR systems do not spray DEF on their own pressure alone but blow it into the exhaust with compressed air, supplied by a compressor or an existing air system; Bosch's first Denoxtronic generation was built this way. A pressure sensor checks that this air is present before dosing. P2037 is the general circuit fault of that sensor. Deutz uses it on the EMR L1 controller (SPN 4335) for two failure types: a ground fault (-F0) and a sensor supply out of range (-1C), while a reading stuck low or open goes to P2039 and a short to battery to P2040. CARB names air assisted injection as part of the reductant delivery that must be monitored. With the air pressure unknown, dosing is normally stopped, and on trucks a power derate may follow.
c: 5 V supply or ground of the sensor interrupted or shorted
Damaged harness or corroded connector at the dosing module
s: Engine or emission warning lamp on
DEF dosing suspended
Engine power derate on trucks and machines

P2038.t: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P2038.d: P2038 does not mean a broken wire. The air pressure sensor A of an air-assisted DEF injector delivers a valid voltage, yet the value does not fit the operating state: it may show pressure while the air supply valve is closed, too little pressure while it is open, or fail to move when air is switched on and off. No manufacturer documents P2038 publicly. Deutz, which documents the electrical faults of the same sensor, reports such cases under its own codes instead: P1119 for an implausible air pressure signal, P1124 for air pressure too low and P13FF when air pressure and DEF pressure at the pump appear swapped. CARB requires plausibility checks on every input that the dosing strategy depends on. Leaks in the air line, a sticking valve or a drifting sensor are the usual reasons.
c: Leaking or kinked air line between valve and dosing unit
Sensor reading drifted or clogged pressure port
Air supply valve sticking open or closed
Insufficient pressure from the vehicle air system
s: Emission warning lamp on
DEF dosing reduced or stopped
Rising NOx emissions and possible derate

P2039.t: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Sensor A Circuit Low
P2039.d: P2039 is stored when the signal of injection air pressure sensor A sits below the lowest voltage a working sensor can deliver. Deutz documents it on its EMR L1 controller as P2039-00 under SPN 4335 and lumps two causes together: a grounded signal and an open circuit, since the input is pulled low when the signal wire is interrupted. A loss of the 5 V reference is another common reason for a reading near zero. Because the controller can no longer confirm that atomizing air is present, it stops DEF injection; Deutz engines then run without NOx reduction until the inducement logic of the machine steps in. The opposite fault is P2040, and electrical faults of the sensor supply fall under P2037.
c: Signal wire open or shorted to ground
5 V reference to the sensor lost
s: Emission warning lamp on
DEF injection stopped
Power derate after a while on machines with inducement

P203A.d: P203A is the general circuit code for reductant level sensor A, the first or only fill level element inside the DEF tank. Deutz lists it for the EMR L1 main and secondary ECU: the tank level input (J1939 SPN 1761) stores P203A with failure type 13 when the line is interrupted and with types 21 or 22 when the value drops under or climbs over its valid range. VW's 2014 Touareg (engine CNRB) files a gap of more than 80 s between watchdog pulses under P203A, even though VW's chart labels the code Circuit Low. FCA counts P203A among the faults that put the 6.7L Ram into the Service DEF – See Dealer inducement message. Low and high faults of the same sensor have their own codes P203C and P203D; sensors B and C use P21A8 and P21AD. Drivers get a DEF warning and, left alone, the usual speed or restart limits.
c: Loose, corroded or DEF-contaminated connector at the tank module
Broken or chafed level sensor wiring between tank and control unit
Failed level sensor or level electronics in the tank unit
Fault in the dosing or engine control unit, sometimes fixed by software
s: MIL and DEF system warning in the cluster
DEF level gauge missing, frozen or wrong
Countdown to speed limit or no-restart after some distance

P203B.t: Reductant Level Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P203B.d: P203B means the level reading of sensor A is electrically present but cannot be trusted. GM's 6.6L LML and 2014 Cruze diesel set it after 5 s (Type B) when the three discrete level contacts report a combination that is physically impossible, e.g. a higher contact wet while a lower one is dry. Ford's 2023 diesel summary sets P203B when the ultrasonic sensor reports no valid level, flags itself faulty or gives a height above the tank, checked only above 0 °C fluid and 3 kg contents. GM's 2025 DEF controller uses the sensor's readiness bit, which drops on a weak or missing echo (Type B). Jaguar (Ingenium 2.0D) and FCA point to overfilled tanks, Mercedes (Sprinter 906, SCR unit) to wrong filling and poor contact at tank module pins 3 to 5. Hard wiring faults are P203C/P203D.
c: Tank overfilled, so the ultrasonic sensor gets no usable echo
Ice or urea crystals on the sensor after cold soak
Wrong or diluted fluid in the DEF tank
Poor terminal contact at the tank module connector
Level sensor or tank unit defective
s: MIL, often with a DEF service message
DEF gauge stuck, jumping or showing empty with a full tank
Restart countdown on some models

P203C.t: Reductant Level Sensor A Circuit Low
P203C.d: P203C reports a level sensor A signal stuck at the bottom of its range. On GM's 6.6L LML and the 2014 Cruze diesel this is level contact 1: the tank electronics apply a test pulse, and a reading under 0.17 V for more than 3 s with over 8 V supply counts as a short to ground (LML Type A, Cruze Type B). GM's 2017/2018 diesel tables (1.6L Cruze, 2.8L Colorado) use a raw value below 2 in 40 of 50 samples, Type A, and the 2025 DEF controller sets the code on piezo excitation faults reported by the smart sensor. FCA lists P203C on 2014–2015 Ram 2500 to 5500 with the Cummins 6.7L and a radio frequency level sensor in the pump module; the fix was the pump/level module. GM's bulletin 12-06-04-002C ranks P203C among DEF codes that keep warnings active.
c: Signal wire shorted to ground or chafed at the tank
Level sensor or pump/level module internally faulty
DEF crept into the connector and bridges the terminals
s: MIL and DEF warning
DEF gauge reads empty or not at all
Speed or restart limit after a warning period

P203D.t: Reductant Level Sensor A Circuit High
P203D.d: P203D is the high-side fault of level sensor A. On the LML Duramax and the 2014 Cruze 2.0D, GM samples level contact 1 1.5 ms after a test pulse: 3.56 to 4.74 V means an open load, above 4.74 V a short to battery, either one for more than 3 s with Type A. GM's 2017 diesel table uses a raw value above 95 (Type B), while the 2025 DEF controller sets P203D when the ultrasonic sensor reports a level beyond its 400 mm measuring range for 6 s. Preliminary bulletin PIP4887B for 2010–2011 Duramax trucks names P203D with P21AB and P21B0 and asks for wiring and terminal checks even on history codes before a new DEF tank. FCA (Ram 6.7L, 2014–2015) and Jaguar (2.0D, overfilled tank reading zero) list P203D as well. Low-side faults are P203C.
c: Open circuit, unplugged or loose tank connector
Signal wire shorted to supply or battery voltage
Failed level sensor or tank assembly
s: MIL with Service Exhaust Fluid System or similar message
DEF gauge missing or showing full permanently
Speed or restart limit if not repaired

P203E.t: Reductant Level Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P203E.d: P203E stands for a level sensor A signal that keeps dropping out or jumping. FCA explains it best: Ram HD trucks with the 6.7L Cummins (2019–2021) carry an ultrasonic level sensor that needs an air gap above the fluid. Bulletin 18-034-21 and STAR case S2025000001 name an overfilled tank as the main trigger, because the echo no longer returns; residual ice or urea crystals in the focus tube after hard frost do the same. Returned parts were mostly found free of faults. The test only runs with ambient and tank above about 4 °C, so the fix is draining 2 to 3 gallons or thawing the tank, then about 15 min of steady highway driving. Jeep and Ram 3.0L EcoDiesel software updates (18-018-14, 18-018-15) also cover P203E. Steady circuit faults belong to P203C/P203D.
c: DEF tank overfilled, no air space for the ultrasonic echo
Residual ice or urea crystals covering the sensor
Intermittent contact at the tank connector
Control unit software needing an update
s: MIL and Service DEF message
DEF gauge jumps or reads 0 % with fluid in the tank
Warning returns after filling or after a cold night

P203F.d: P203F is not a sensor fault but the result of the level monitor: the DEF tank holds too little fluid to keep the SCR system working. CARB requires light and medium duty diesels to flag an empty reductant supply (13 CCR 1968.2 (f)(2.2.3)(B)); a maker can be exempted if a driver inducement prevents running without DEF and every input to it, such as the level sensor, is monitored. Deutz stores P203F-00 as DEF tank level low on the EMR L1 main ECU, and FCA lists it among the codes that trigger the Service DEF – See Dealer message and later the limits. FCA bulletin 18-034-21 shows a trap on 2019–2021 Ram HD: ice covering the ultrasonic sensor can set P203F although the tank is full enough. Refill first; if the code returns, check P203A to P203E.
c: DEF tank actually low or empty
Frozen fluid or ice covering the level sensor
Leak at tank, lines or pump unit
s: Low DEF warnings and range countdown
Speed limit or no restart once the countdown ends
MIL on some vehicles

P2040.t: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Sensor A Circuit High
P2040.d: With P2040 the injection air pressure sensor A reports a voltage above its upper limit, more than a real air pressure could produce. On Deutz's EMR L1 controller this is P2040-00 under SPN 4335, defined as a short circuit to battery. In practice that means the signal wire touches a powered conductor, the sensor ground is missing so the output floats up to the reference, or the sensor itself has failed high. A wrongly high reading is dangerous for the strategy because it could pretend that air is available when it is not, so the controller treats the signal as invalid and blocks DEF injection. Low readings are covered by P2039, implausible but in-range values by P2038. Check the ground pin first, then the harness for chafing against powered lines.
c: Signal wire shorted to battery or another powered line
Sensor ground open so the output floats high
Sensor failed with output stuck high
s: Emission warning lamp on
DEF injection blocked
Air pressure value shown at maximum

P2041.t: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
P2041.d: P2041 catches an air pressure sensor A whose signal keeps dropping out or jumping for brief moments, too short or too irregular to be confirmed as a steady low or high fault. On trucks and machines with air-assisted DEF dosing this typically comes from vibration: a terminal with lost contact tension, a cracked wire inside the loom or moisture entering the connector at the dosing module. No manufacturer documents P2041 publicly; Deutz, which uses the same sensor slot, lists only the permanent electrical faults (P2037, P2039, P2040). CARB counts erratic signals among the circuit faults an OBD system must detect. Since the fault comes and goes, wiggle-testing the harness while watching live data is more useful than measuring at rest; replacing the sensor without that test often does not help.
c: Terminal with lost contact tension at sensor or controller
Wire broken inside the insulation from vibration
s: Warning lamp coming and going
DEF dosing interrupted at times

P2042.d: P2042 concerns reductant temperature sensor A, which is a different part from the tank temperature sensor of P205A ff. The makers that document it place it outside the tank: Deutz assigns P2042 to the DEF temperature sensor of the SCR system (J1939 SPN 4337), while its tank sensor (SPN 3031) uses P205A; failure type 13 marks an open circuit, F0 a ground fault. Volvo and Mack describe P2042-01 (US17/OBD16 engines) as a test of the temperature sensor in the DEF pump and warn in KC-2015 that low battery voltage with ambient and tank below 0 °C logs it with nothing wrong; then the pump must not be replaced. Hino also separates tank and pump sensors. Short to ground and to battery are P2044 and P2045. Drivers see the MIL and a DEF warning.
c: Open circuit or loose connector at the pump/supply module
False setting at low battery voltage in frost (Volvo/Mack)
Temperature sensor in the pump unit defective
s: MIL and DEF system warning
DEF heating or dosing may be restricted

P2043.t: Reductant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P2043.d: P2043 flags a temperature reading from reductant sensor A that is electrically valid but does not fit the other temperatures the system knows. Deutz stores it as P2043-64, a plausibility error of the DEF temperature sensor in the SCR system (SPN 4337), separate from the tank sensor check P205B-64. Ford uses the code on 2011–2012 F-250/F-350 and 2011–2015 F-450/F-550 with the 6.7L diesel built up to 9 Dec 2014: per bulletin 18-2190, P2043 on its own only needs a PCM reprogram, while P2043 together with P205C or P205D calls for a new reductant heater and sender assembly as well. A plausibility code alone therefore often points to software or a cold soak case rather than to a broken part. Open and shorted circuits are P2042, P2044 and P2045.
c: Engine control software, fixed by reprogramming (Ford 6.7L)
Temperature sensor drifting or slow to respond
Frozen or partly thawed DEF around the sensor
Contact resistance in the connector shifting the reading
s: MIL, often without noticeable driving change
DEF heater may run at the wrong time

P2044.t: Reductant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P2044.d: P2044 is set when the signal of reductant temperature sensor A sits below its valid voltage window. As with other NTC thermistors, a low voltage corresponds to a hot reading, so a signal wire touching ground makes the fluid look extremely hot. Deutz lists P2044-00 as a grounded signal of the SCR-side DEF temperature input (SPN 4337) on the EMR L1 main and secondary ECU, kept apart from the tank sensor, whose low fault is P205C. No public table gives voltage or time limits for P2044; CARB only requires out of range and circuit checks for every input that feeds an emission control (13 CCR 1968.2 (f)(15.2.1)). A false hot value can switch off DEF heating in the cold, so frozen lines may follow. Measure the sensor and look for chafing before replacing parts.
c: Signal wire chafed through to ground
DEF residue in the connector bridging signal and ground
s: MIL and DEF warning
Scan tool shows an implausibly high DEF temperature
Lines may freeze because heating stays off

P2045.t: Reductant Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P2045.d: P2045 covers the opposite end: the voltage of reductant temperature sensor A is higher than any real temperature would produce. With an NTC element this reads as very cold, which is what an interrupted ground, a disconnected plug or a signal wire touching battery voltage cause. Deutz files P2045-00 as a short to battery for the DEF sensor outside the tank (SPN 4337); an open circuit gets its own entry, P2042-13. The tank temperature sensor counts separately, with its high fault under P205D. As no maker publishes thresholds for P2045, the CARB rule on input circuit monitoring (section (f)(15.2.1) of 13 CCR 1968.2) is the frame. A false cold value may keep the heater running and delay dosing after start. Check the plug, the ground and the sensor resistance at a known temperature.
c: Open sensor ground or unplugged connector
Signal wire shorted to battery or supply voltage
s: MIL and DEF warning
Scan tool shows DEF temperature near the lower limit
Dosing may start late after a cold start

P2046.t: Reductant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
P2046.d: P2046 records short dropouts or jumps in the signal of reductant temperature sensor A. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Deutz, the clearest user of the P2042 group, lists only an open line, a ground fault, both shorts and a plausibility error for this sensor, but no intermittent entry. How such a check can work is shown by GM's tank sensor test P205E in the 2025 DEF controller: it fails when the reading moves by more than 4 °C inside a ten-sample window, three times out of nine. CARB requires input circuits to be monitored for faults of this kind (1968.2, paragraph (f)(15.2.1)). In practice the cause is mostly a terminal losing contact under vibration or DEF residue in the connector. Wiggle tests with live data help; the tank sensor has its own code, P205E.
c: Corrosion from DEF residue in the connector
Harness rubbing through intermittently on the frame
s: MIL that comes and goes
Unsteady DEF temperature in live data

P2047.d: P2047 covers the electrical path of the first DEF dosing valve on Bank 1, which in nearly every SCR layout is the only one. The controller watches the valve's low-side driver and flags an open load: a broken wire, an unplugged connector or a burnt-out coil. GM's 6.6 L LML table expects roughly 200 kOhm between pin and load for 3 s (Type A); GM's 2018 diesel table counts 30 faulty samples out of 60. Ford's 2023 diesel summary reads 2.6 to 3.4 V on the idle output within 2 s. Ram found loose terminals at the injector plug, Volvo VNR trucks a harness chafed by a loose heat shield. On the LGH/LML GM ranks P2047 as a tamper-type fault, so the warning sequence toward a speed limit starts early; with no DEF sprayed, NOx rises.
c: Loose, corroded or pushed-out terminals at the DEF injector plug
Harness wire broken or chafed through near the exhaust
Open coil inside the DEF injector
Faulty output stage or software in the engine/dosing control module
s: MIL on, often together with a DEF system warning
Speed limitation countdown after continued driving
Increased NOx, failed emissions inspection

P2048.t: Reductant Injection Valve Circuit Low (Bank 1 Unit 1)
P2048.d: P2048 means the control line of the Bank 1, unit 1 DEF injector is pulled toward ground, typically a chafed wire touching the chassis or an internal short in the coil. GM's LML calibration treats less than about 0.5 ohm between signal and ground for 2 s as a failure (Type A). Ford's 2023 diesel logic reports the code once injector current exceeds 1.6 A; Deutz's EMR5 list files it under voltage below normal on the metering unit. Nissan reflashed the ECM of the 2016 to 2019 Titan XD with the Cummins 5.0 L V8 because P2048 appeared without a real defect, and Volvo traced it to a harness rubbed through on VNR trucks. While the code is active, dosing is normally blocked; the catalyst no longer reduces NOx and the inducement countdown may begin.
c: Control wire chafed against chassis or exhaust bracket
Shorted winding inside the DEF injector
ECM software setting the code without a fault (Nissan Titan XD reflash)
DEF residue or water bridging the connector pins
s: MIL on
DEF dosing suspended, warning in the instrument cluster
Inducement or reduced power after a countdown

P2049.t: Reductant Injection Valve Circuit High (Bank 1 Unit 1)
P2049.d: P2049 is the opposite electrical case for the Bank 1, unit 1 DEF injector: the low-side control line sees battery voltage, for instance through contact with a powered conductor or water inside the connector. On the 2014 Cruze diesel GM rates it Type B (two trips), whereas the LML and the 2018 diesel tables treat it as Type A; the 2018 test needs more than 11 V and counts 30 bad samples out of 60 at 100 ms. Deutz lists it for the EMR5 metering unit as an over-normal voltage or high-side short, and Ford's 2023 summary gives an injector current below 0.1 A as the trigger. GM's DEF bulletin sorts P2049 among non-tamper faults, so it brings up the emission service message rather than the tamper warning. The output stage shuts off to protect itself, which stops dosing.
c: Control wire shorted to a supply wire in the harness
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins at the injector connector
Internal fault of the DEF injector coil
Defective output stage in the control module
s: MIL on (on some GM diesels only after the second trip)
Service emission system message
Higher NOx because no DEF is injected

P204A.d: P204A is the general electrical fault of the sensor that measures DEF pressure between pump and injector; in most systems it is built into the pump module. The secondary ECU of Deutz's EMR L1 uses it for two states that are neither low nor high: a ground fault (failure type F0) and a sensor supply outside its window (1C), while shorts to ground or battery go to P204C and P204D. Mack trucks to US13 emissions report P204A-13 for an open signal or ground wire; repair instruction GDC18-058 has the harness checked and otherwise lists the complete DEF pump unit as the part to fit. Without a valid pressure value the controller cannot regulate dosing, so it stops the pump and the inducement timer starts. CARB requires such inputs to be monitored for circuit faults.
c: Open signal or ground wire to the pressure sensor
Sensor supply voltage out of range
Pressure sensor inside the DEF pump unit failed
s: MIL on, DEF system warning
No DEF dosing
Power or speed limitation after the countdown

P204B.d: P204B is a plausibility test: the DEF pressure sensor is electrically fine, but its value disagrees with the system state. GM uses moments when the true pressure is known. The 6.6 L LML sets it if more than 50 kPa appears while the line is empty and unpressurised (Type A, Type B on the 2014 Cruze diesel); GM's 2018 diesel table compares the reading with ambient after the end-of-trip purge, and GM's 2025 DEF controller fails it when the value strays more than 36.4 kPa from ambient before priming. Deutz marks the case on the EMR L1 with failure type 64. Hino released new DCU software in 2016 (SB-16-015) because the unit stored P204B falsely on conventional trucks. A genuine offset mostly means an ageing sensor in the pump module.
c: Pressure sensor offset drift inside the pump module
Dosing control unit software misjudging the reading (Hino SB-16-015)
Line not emptied at shutdown, e.g. afterrun interrupted or frozen DEF
s: MIL on, possibly only after a second trip
Emission service message
Often no noticeable driveability change

P204C.d: P204C means the DEF pressure sensor output has fallen below its valid range, which points to an open signal wire, a short to ground or a missing 5 V supply. On the 6.6 L LML, GM fails anything under 0.41 V lasting 0.4 s, GM's 2018 diesel table a raw value under 5 % of the supply, and the 2025 DEF controller less than 0.45 V in 6 of 100 samples, each Type A. Ford's 2023 diesels set it under 0.2 V. On 2017 to 2019 Super Duty trucks with the 6.7 L, Ford (TSB 19-2315) found water entering connectors C3613 and C4851 of the reductant harness and replaced harness, pump/heater assembly or tank. Deutz uses failure type 11 for it on the EMR5. Lacking a pressure value, the controller suspends dosing.
c: Water intrusion in the reductant harness connectors (Ford TSB 19-2315)
Signal wire open or shorted to ground
Missing 5 V reference to the sensor
Failed sensor in the pump/heater assembly
s: MIL on
DEF dosing stopped, DEF warning messages
Further reductant codes stored at the same time

P204D.d: P204D is the high-side counterpart: the pressure signal sits near or above the supply voltage, typically because the signal wire touches 5 V or battery voltage, the sensor ground is open, or the sensor has failed internally. Published limits are 4.80 V on GM's 6.6 L LML, 98 % of the supply in GM's 2018 diesel table, 4.90 V in GM's 2025 DEF controller and 4.85 V on Ford's 2023 diesels. GM's 2014 Cruze diesel logs it as Type B, the other GM tables as Type A. Deutz's EMR L1 calls the same state a short circuit to battery. To the controller such a reading could look like over-pressure, which is why it stops the pump; check the connector at the pump module and the sensor ground before replacing the module.
c: Open sensor ground or corroded ground terminal
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Internal failure of the pressure sensor in the pump module
s: MIL on (after two trips on some GM diesels)
DEF pump stopped, no dosing
DEF warning and later inducement

P204E.d: P204E covers a DEF pressure signal that jumps around although it stays inside the electrical limits, as with a loose terminal, a cracked wire or a sensor with an internal contact problem. GM's 2025 DEF controller is the public calibration: it adds up all absolute pressure changes over a moving window of 100 readings taken every 10 ms and counts a failure when that sum passes 1500 kPa while pumping forward, 1000 kPa when stopped or heating, or 200 kPa in reverse; ten failures within 100 runs store a Type A code. No other manufacturer documents the code in public. CARB expects input components to be checked for implausible as well as out-of-range signals. Besides the wiring, air in the line or a pump delivering unevenly can also make the pressure swing.
c: Loose or fretted terminal at the pressure sensor connector
Air in the DEF line or uneven pump delivery
Pressure sensor with internal intermittent fault
s: MIL on, fault may come and go
Dosing interrupted at times
Accompanying DEF pump or pressure codes

P204F.d: P204F (Bank 1) is the functional check of the whole DEF delivery path: the parts are electrically intact, yet the system cannot build or hold the pressure needed for dosing. GM's 6.6 L LML stores a Type A code if the pump module stays at or below 350 kPa after 30 build-up and venting attempts of at least 10 s each; the 2014 Cruze diesel uses 375 kPa and 20 attempts. GM treats P204F as a tamper fault. On Hino trucks P204F is the engine ECU's summary code for urea SCR faults seen by the dosing unit; per TT-14-025 it clears only after the DCU faults are repaired and the SCR memory has been reset. Ram's 3.0 L V6 EcoDiesel received PCM updates covering it (18-008-21). CARB demands this delivery check. Causes include frozen or clogged lines, a worn pump, air leaks or an empty tank.
c: DEF line clogged by crystals or frozen
Worn DEF pump that cannot reach target pressure
Air leak on the suction side or loose line couplings
Dosing unit faults repaired but SCR memory not reset (Hino)
Control module software needing an update (Ram 3.0 L)
s: MIL and DEF warning on
Countdown to speed or power limitation
Code returns after clearing until the cause is fixed

P2050.d: P2050 reports an open circuit at the first DEF injector of Bank 2, the cylinder bank opposite cylinder 1. The code only makes sense on engines whose two exhaust banks each feed their own SCR branch with a separate valve. No manufacturer publicly documents P2050; V-engines found in bulletins, such as the Cummins 5.0 L V8 in Nissan's Titan XD, combine both banks into one SCR line and report their only valve as Bank 1, unit 1. Detection would mirror P2047: GM's 2018 diesel logic reads the driver status every 100 ms with more than 11 V and needs 30 bad samples out of 60. CARB requires such actuators to be checked as comprehensive components. Suspects are plug and harness on the second exhaust branch and the coil itself; without dosing that branch emits more NOx.
c: Unplugged or corroded connector at the Bank 2 injector
Broken wire in the harness of the second exhaust branch
Open coil in the Bank 2 DEF injector
s: MIL on
Higher NOx from the Bank 2 branch
DEF warning, later inducement possible

P2051.t: Reductant Injection Valve Circuit Low (Bank 2 Unit 1)
P2051.d: P2051 reports a ground fault on the drive wire of the DEF injector assigned to Bank 2, unit 1. Like its siblings P2050 and P2052, it presupposes a twin-bank SCR system with a dedicated valve per exhaust branch, and no manufacturer publishes a calibration or bulletin for it. The comparable Bank 1 tests give an idea of the limits: GM's 6.6 L LML flags less than roughly 0.5 ohm to ground for 2 s, and Ford's 2023 diesel logic reacts to valve current above 1.6 A. Where the second branch's harness passes hot exhaust parts, damaged insulation is the first thing to inspect. CARB treats the valve as a monitored component; once the code sets, that branch stops dosing and its NOx conversion collapses.
c: Insulation melted or chafed near the Bank 2 exhaust
Shorted coil in the Bank 2 injector
DEF crystals in the connector creating a path to ground
s: MIL on
Dosing on Bank 2 switched off
Possible NOx efficiency code for Bank 2 later

P2052.t: Reductant Injection Valve Circuit High (Bank 2 Unit 1)
P2052.d: P2052 tells that battery potential is present on the switched line of the first Bank 2 injector, for example through a short to a powered wire or moisture bridging connector pins. It belongs to twin-bank SCR layouts in which each cylinder bank owns an injector; publicly, no manufacturer documents this code or its thresholds. For the matching Bank 1 code P2049, GM's 2014 Cruze diesel uses Type B (two trips) and the Deutz EMR5 list describes voltage above normal or a short to the high source, so P2052 would presumably follow the same logic. A driver that sees a short to positive normally switches off to protect itself, leaving the second branch without DEF. CARB's comprehensive-component rules apply; check plug, harness and coil resistance first.
c: Control line of the Bank 2 injector touching a supply wire
Moisture bridging pins in the Bank 2 injector plug
Faulty output stage for the Bank 2 valve
s: MIL on, possibly after two trips
No DEF on Bank 2
Higher tailpipe NOx

P2053.d: P2053 concerns a second DEF injector on the same exhaust line as Bank 1, unit 1, used where a manufacturer doses at two points, for instance ahead of two separate catalysts. GM's 2025 table (25OBDG04B, which also covers an inline-six diesel) monitors this DEF metering valve 2 with the same open-load logic as valve 1: more than 11 V, 30 faulty samples out of 60 at 100 ms, Type A; a separate P1C30 checks its coil temperature after a long soak. Deutz's EMR5 engines assign P2053 to metering unit 2, with failure bytes for current above normal (grounded) and below normal (open). If valve 2 drops out, valve 1 keeps working, so the downstream catalyst simply loses its DEF and NOx rises only partly, often noticed just through the MIL.
c: Disconnected or corroded plug at DEF injector 2
Broken wire between control module and injector 2
s: MIL on
Slightly higher NOx, little noticeable otherwise
DEF system message

P2054.t: Reductant Injection Valve Circuit Low (Bank 1 Unit 2)
P2054.d: P2054 flags a ground short in the switched circuit of the second DEF injector in the Bank 1 line. GM's 2025 diesel table (25OBDG04B) checks DEF metering valve 2 for this with the key on, the engine not cranking and more than 11 V, then sets a Type A code after 30 of 60 samples. Deutz uses P2054 on EMR5 engines for metering unit 2 with failure type 11, voltage below normal. Ford's 2023 diesel summary lists P2054 next to the circuit checks of its single injector but defines it as a resistance deviation below minus 2 ohm, so on a Ford the code points to a coil whose resistance has drifted low rather than to a second valve. Typical causes are a pinched wire, a shorted coil or a wet connector; the affected valve stops dosing.
c: Pinched or chafed wire to injector 2 touching ground
Coil resistance too low due to shorted turns (Ford definition)
Water or DEF in the injector connector
s: MIL on
Dosing at the affected valve stopped
DEF warning message

P2055.t: Reductant Injection Valve Circuit High (Bank 1 Unit 2)
P2055.d: P2055 is set when the control line of DEF injector 2 on Bank 1 is shorted to battery positive.
