In GM's 2025 diesel table (25OBDG04B) the power stage of metering valve 2 reports the short; with more than 11 V and 30 faulty readings out of 60 the ECM stores a Type A fault, just as P2049 does for valve 1. Deutz assigns failure type 12 (voltage above normal or short to the high source) to metering unit 2 on EMR5 engines. On Ford's 2023 diesels the code instead describes a coil resistance more than 2 ohm above expectation, which hints at corroded terminals or an ageing winding. Whatever the platform, a driver that detects overvoltage is disabled, so the second dosing point delivers nothing until the circuit is repaired.
c: Control line of injector 2 shorted to battery positive
Coil resistance too high, corroded terminals (Ford definition)
s: MIL on
Second dosing point inactive
Increased NOx emissions

P2056.d: P2056 refers to the fourth possible DEF injector position: the second valve in the Bank 2 exhaust line. It requires both a twin-bank layout and two dosing points per bank, a combination hardly any production engine uses; no manufacturer publicly documents the code. Detection would resemble GM's open-load check for metering valve 2 in its 2025 table (P2053): driver status read every 100 ms, more than 11 V on board, 30 bad samples out of 60, Type A. CARB lists reductant system valves among the electrical components whose circuits the OBD system has to verify. Before condemning a part, confirm which physical injector the scan tool assigns to Bank 2, unit 2, because confusing banks and units is an easy way to replace the wrong valve.
c: Connector of the Bank 2 second injector unplugged or corroded
Broken wire in the Bank 2 dosing harness
s: MIL on
Reduced NOx conversion on Bank 2

P2057.t: Reductant Injection Valve Circuit Low (Bank 2 Unit 2)
P2057.d: P2057 is the short-to-ground case for the second DEF injector of Bank 2. As with P2056 and P2058, it exists in the code list for engines with two exhaust banks and two dosing points each, yet no manufacturer publishes a calibration or service bulletin for it. Analogous logic is documented for Bank 1: GM's 2025 diesel table flags a low-side ground short at metering valve 2 (P2054) after 30 out of 60 samples, Type A, and the Deutz EMR5 list describes failure type 11 for that position. Likely culprits are a harness clamped against the frame or an exhaust bracket, shorted coil windings and DEF residue in the connector. Because the output stage switches the valve off, its catalyst segment converts noticeably less NOx.
c: Harness clamped against frame or exhaust bracket
Shorted windings in the injector coil
s: MIL on
Valve switched off, NOx conversion reduced

P2058.t: Reductant Injection Valve Circuit High (Bank 2 Unit 2)
P2058.d: P2058 indicates that the second DEF injector on Bank 2 sees battery voltage on its switched line. Like the other Bank 2, unit 2 codes it is reserved for twin-bank engines with two dosing points per bank, and no manufacturer documents it publicly. The Bank 1 counterpart P2055 appears in GM's 2025 diesel table as a power short of metering valve 2 (Type A after 30 of 60 samples), while Ford's 2023 summary uses that number for a coil resistance more than 2 ohm too high, a reminder that meanings can shift between makers. CARB's comprehensive-component rules require such circuit checks. Moisture in the plug, a short to a neighbouring supply wire or a failed output stage are the usual suspects; dosing at that point stops.
c: Short to a neighbouring supply wire
Failed output stage in the control module
s: MIL on
No dosing at the Bank 2 second valve

P2059.t: Reductant Injection Air Pump Control Circuit/Open
P2059.d: The air that atomizes DEF in an air-assisted system comes either from a small dedicated compressor or from an existing compressed-air system through a supply valve. P2059 concerns the driver circuit of that pump or valve, above all an open circuit: the output is switched on but no current flows. Deutz uses the code on its EMR L1 controller for the air pump or air supply valve (SPN 5796) with several failure types: -00 open circuit, -19 critically high output current, -31 load shorted and -2A unspecified electrical fault, while P2060 and P2061 cover high-side shorts to ground and battery. A blown fuse, a broken coil, an unplugged valve or corroded pins are typical. Without atomizing air the controller cannot dose DEF and NOx rises.
c: Open coil in the air valve or pump motor
Connector unplugged or corroded, wire broken
Fuse or relay in the supply path failed
Shorted valve coil causing overcurrent shutdown
s: Emission warning lamp on
No DEF dosing, NOx rises
Power derate on trucks and machines

P205A.t: Reductant Tank Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P205A.d: P205A is the general circuit code for the temperature sensor inside the DEF tank, usually built into the level or heater unit; the separate sensor in the supply path uses P2042 ff. Deutz assigns the tank temperature (J1939 SPN 3031) to P205A: failure type 13 for an open circuit, 21 and 22 for values under or over the valid range, while the SCR-side DEF sensor (SPN 4337) stays with P2042. VW's 2014 Touareg (CNRB) stores P205A when the signal exceeds 4.70 V, i.e. the high side that an open NTC circuit produces, and keeps the low side (below 0.30 V) for P205C. Other makers split these faults into P205C and P205D. The tank temperature decides when the tank heater runs, so a fault can mean frozen DEF and an SCR warning in winter.
c: Open circuit or loose tank connector
Tank temperature sensor in the sender unit defective
s: MIL and DEF warning
Tank heating not working in frost
Speed or restart limit on some models

P205B.t: Reductant Tank Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P205B.d: P205B is the rationality check of the DEF tank temperature: after a long cold soak every sensor should read about the same, so a tank value far off the rest is flagged. GM's 6.6L LML compares it with fuel temperature after 28,800 s engine off (beyond +35/−35 °C, Type B); GM's 2018 diesel table uses the exhaust gas temperature average (>35 °C, Type A), and the 2025 DEF controller needs at least four reference sensors and over 8 h off (>30 °C, Type A). Ford's 2023 diesels compare it with the quality sensor at start (>40 °C), VW's Touareg with outside air. Volvo/Mack (KC-2107) have it re-run before replacing the level sensor, and Ford (2019 6.7L), Land Rover (2016 TDV6) and GM (2021–22 3.0L) cured cases by software. Circuit faults are P205C/P205D.
c: Tank temperature sensor reading off (offset or gain)
Frozen tank or low fill level distorting the reading
Faulty reference sensor (fuel, exhaust or quality sensor)
s: MIL, sometimes with an emissions service message
Usually no change in driving

P205C.t: Reductant Tank Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P205C.d: P205C reports the DEF tank temperature signal at the bottom of its range. For voltage-read NTC sensors that means implausibly hot: Ford's 2023 diesels set it below 0.165 V, VW's Touareg below 0.30 V, GM's 2025 DEF controller below 0.3 V (about 75 °C) and GM's 2018 diesel table below 200 Ω, each as short to ground. Careful with older GM trucks: on the 6.6L LML and the 2014 Cruze the value arrives as a CAN raw value, and Low means a raw value under 1, i.e. −55 °C and over 1200 kΩ, the cold side (Type A, 3 s). Ford bulletin 18-2190 replaces the reductant heater and sender assembly on 2011–2015 6.7L Super Duty when P205C appears with P2043, and Hino has P205B to P205D checked before blaming the coolant valve. The high end is P205D.
c: Faulty sensor in the heater/sender assembly
DEF in the connector bridging the terminals
s: MIL and DEF warning
Tank temperature in live data stuck at an extreme
Tank heater not working in frost

P205D.t: Reductant Tank Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P205D.d: P205D is the top-of-range fault of the tank's temperature sensor. On voltage-read NTC sensors a high signal looks like extreme cold and typically comes from an open circuit, a lost ground or a short to supply: Ford's 2023 diesels set it above 4.3 V, GM's 2025 DEF controller above 4.75 V (about −40 °C, 0.5 s, Type A), and GM's 2018 diesel table above 60,000 Ω. On the 6.6L LML and 2014 Cruze GM reads a CAN raw value instead, where High means above 1022, i.e. 160 °C or more, the hot side (6 s, Type B). Ford's bulletin 18-2190 for 2011–2015 6.7L Super Duty treats P205D like P205C: new reductant heater and sender assembly plus PCM update. Hino names P205D next to P205B and P205C as a source of wrong DEF temperature input. The low end is P205C.
c: Open circuit, unplugged connector or broken ground
Sensor in the heater/sender assembly open internally
Signal wire shorted to supply voltage
s: MIL and DEF warning
Tank heater runs although the tank is warm
Dosing delayed after start

P205E.t: Reductant Tank Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P205E.d: P205E marks a DEF tank temperature that changes faster than any real tank could. GM describes two versions: the 2018 diesel table (1.6L Cruze, 2.8L Colorado) checks whether the signal's time evolution is plausible and fails after 8 out of 10 samples taken every 500 ms, provided no electrical fault of the sensor is present; the 2025 DEF controller flags readings that jump beyond 4 °C within ten values in three of nine checks, Type A. FCA used P205E on the 2013 Ram 2500/3500 with the 6.7L Cummins and released new PCM software (18-057-15 Rev. A) because the code set when the engine block heater was plugged in, and many later Ram updates list it too. A stored P205E without other codes therefore points to software or a loose contact. Steady faults are P205C and P205D.
c: Engine control software, fixed by reflash (FCA 6.7L)
Loose or corroded contact at the tank connector
Block heater use causing a fast temperature change
s: MIL, often after cold starts
Jumping tank temperature in live data

P205F.d: P205F is the Bank 2 version of the reductant system performance check, meant for engines in which the second cylinder bank has its own SCR branch with separate pressure supply or valve. It applies when that branch is electrically sound but fails to reach or regulate the pressure or quantity the controller asks for. No manufacturer publicly documents P205F; even a V-engine such as Ram's 3.0 L EcoDiesel V6 lists delivery problems as P204F in its bulletins. The Bank 1 logic gives orientation: GM's 6.6 L LML waits for 30 failed build-up attempts below 350 kPa before setting a Type A code. CARB requires every SCR system to detect delivery faults before emissions exceed the limits. Look for blocked lines, a sticking valve or crystallised DEF in the second branch.
c: Blocked or frozen DEF line to the Bank 2 branch
Bank 2 injector sticking due to DEF crystals
Insufficient pump or metering unit pressure for the second branch
s: MIL and DEF warning on
Higher NOx from Bank 2, possible inducement

P2060.t: Reductant Injection Air Pump Control Circuit Low
P2060.d: P2060 means the control line of the injection air pump or air valve is held at too low a level: when the output tries to switch it on, the voltage collapses because the wire or the load is connected to ground. Deutz defines exactly this on its EMR L1 controller as P2060-00, a high-side short to ground on output SPN 5796, which drives the air pump or valve. The driver protects itself, so the valve stays closed and atomizing air never reaches the dosing nozzle. Look for wires rubbed through on the frame or the engine block, a water-filled connector or a coil with a short to its housing. An open circuit of the same output is P2059, a short to battery P2061. DEF dosing is blocked until the short is removed.
c: Control wire chafed through to ground
Valve or pump coil shorted to its housing
Water in the connector bridging to ground
s: Emission warning lamp on
DEF dosing blocked
Possible blown fuse in the air valve supply

P2061.t: Reductant Injection Air Pump Control Circuit High
P2061.d: P2061 is the high-side counterpart: the pump or valve output that feeds atomizing air carries voltage when the controller expects it to be off, or the diagnostic sees a level that only a connection to battery positive can explain. Deutz documents it on the EMR L1 controller as P2061-00, short circuit to battery on the high side (SPN 5796). The consequence can be the reverse of P2060: the valve may stay energised and keep blowing air through the dosing unit even when no DEF is wanted, which wastes compressed air, while the controller still blocks dosing because it has lost control of the output. Typical are a wire pinched against a powered cable in the same loom or a damaged connector. Open circuits belong to P2059.
c: Control wire shorted to a powered cable in the loom
Output stage in the controller failed
s: Emission warning lamp on
Air valve may run continuously, air system loses pressure
DEF dosing blocked

P2062.d: J2012 keeps this title deliberately broad: the controlled supply that feeds the reductant system or, in some layouts, the regeneration hardware, mostly a supply pump or the relay powering it. P2062 reports an open control circuit, so the commanded stage draws no current. No manufacturer documents P2062 publicly. Published systems monitor this function under component codes: Ford's 2023 diesels set P208A when reductant pump voltage sits between 2.6 and 3.4 V or the pump controller supply drops below 6 V, and Deutz reports an open DEF pump drive as P05EE-00. Typical causes are a blown fuse, a relay that does not close, a broken wire or a failed pump. Without supply the reductant line cannot build pressure and dosing stops; CARB treats this as part of reductant delivery monitoring.
c: Blown fuse or relay not closing in the supply path
Broken wire or unplugged connector at the pump
s: Engine or emission warning lamp on
No reductant pressure, dosing stops
Restart countdown or speed limit on some vehicles

P2063.d: P2063 says the reductant or regeneration supply control circuit reads too low, the classic signature of a grounded control line or of a load drawing far more current than it should, which pulls the driver output down. No manufacturer documents P2063 publicly. The comparable component code in Ford's 2023 diesel summary is P208C, set when reductant pump current exceeds 5 A or the pump controller draws more than 15 A; Deutz files a grounded DEF pump high side as P05EF-00. Seized pump motors, especially after DEF has crystallised, and harness damage near the tank are the usual suspects. While P2062 means no current at all, here the stage is overloaded, and fuses or relays may be found burnt. Dosing is suspended until the circuit is repaired.
c: Supply control wire shorted to ground near the tank
Pump motor seized or blocked by DEF crystals
Internal short in the pump winding
s: Engine or emission warning lamp on
Fuse for the DEF supply blows repeatedly
Dosing suspended, possible speed or restart limitation

P2064.d: P2064 closes the supply control group that begins with P2062. The line that switches power to the reductant supply, in a few layouts to regeneration hardware, carries a level that only a connection to a positive feed can explain, or the stage stays live while the controller has it switched off. No manufacturer documents P2064 publicly. Related component codes show how such a fault is caught: Deutz files a DEF pump high side shorted to battery as P05F0-00 on its EMR L1 secondary controller, and Ford's 2023 diesels set P208D once pump voltage tops 16 V or the pump controller draws over 5 A with the driver on, confirmed within 2 s. Suspects are a chafed wire touching a powered circuit, a welded relay contact or a wet connector. Unlike P2063 the pump may keep running unbidden, yet dosing is still suspended.
c: Control line chafed through and touching a powered wire
Water or corrosion bridging pins in the supply connector
Faulty output stage in the controlling module
s: MIL and SCR or DEF warning in the cluster
DEF pump audible after it should have stopped
Countdown toward speed limit or no-restart after repeated faults

P2065.d: Sensor B is the second fuel level sender, used where one sender cannot cover the whole tank: the passive half of a saddle tank, a secondary tank on dual-tank trucks, or the secondary lever-type sender that Mercedes reads through its fuel pump module. Ford explains the saddle layout: a jet pump moves fuel to the active side, and both readings are averaged into one gauge value. P2065 is the general circuit code for this input, meaning an electrical fault not classified as low, high or intermittent. Ford's 2014 Boss 302S code list marks P2065 as a MIL code, and the 2024 Ford OBD summary uses P2065 as the base code for failure types such as -11, -12, -1C and -2A. CARB expects fuel level inputs to be monitored, because misfire and evaporative checks are suspended at low levels. Gauge and low fuel warning may mislead.
c: Loose or corroded connector at the second sender or pump module
Broken wire between sender and the module that reads it
Worn or failed sender card in the tank
Control module software that does not match the tank layout
s: Fuel gauge reads wrong, stuck or jumps
Low fuel warning comes on with a full tank or not at all
MIL on, evaporative monitor may not complete

P2066.d: P2066 flags a second fuel level sender whose reading is electrically valid but does not behave like real fuel. Makers test it differently. GM, on dual-tank trucks with an electric transfer pump, calls it Fuel Level Sensor 2 Performance and looks for a secondary reading that stays frozen while the engine burns 18 L or more, or that barely moves while the pump transfers fuel; Type B, two trips. Ford instead files a noisy signal here: more than 100 jumps of over 40 % between samples taken every 0.1 s, while a stuck sender B gets P25B1. Genesis compares calculated fuel use with the change the sender reports and revised that logic for the 2025 GV80 (25-01-026G). Jeep released PCM flashes for P2066 on 2021–2024 Grand Cherokee models, one symptom being a MIL after refuelling with the engine running. Mercedes uses P206600/P206609.
c: Float arm sticking or sender card worn in one spot
Transfer or jet pump not moving fuel between tank halves
Plausibility logic needing a software update (Jeep, Genesis)
Poor contact causing a noisy signal (Ford definition)
s: Fuel gauge stays put or lags behind real consumption
MIL after refuelling or long drives
Range display and low fuel warning unreliable

P2067.t: Fuel Level Sensor B Circuit Low
P2067.d: P2067 sets when the input from the second fuel level sender drops below its valid floor, usually a grounded signal wire or a sender resistance near zero. Ford's saddle-tank trucks flag it below 5 ohms (under one A/D count) and allow 30 s for the electrical check. GM's 2020 table, written for dual-tank vehicles, sets it when the secondary sender reads under 10 % of its 5 V range in 100 of 125 samples; Type B, two trips. Mercedes lists it as P206700, the secondary fill level sender grounded. Two bulletins point away from the tank: on 2021 Pacifica and Voyager the code appeared on front-drive vans running all-wheel-drive PCM software, and Genesis issued an ECM logic update for P2067 on the 2018 G80 5.0, where Hyundai calls sensor B the main sender. Driving is unaffected; the gauge is not.
c: Sender signal wire shorted to ground or chafed on the tank strap
PCM software for the wrong drivetrain or tank version
Diagnostic logic needing an ECM update (Genesis G80)
s: MIL on with no change in driving
Fuel gauge too low, empty or dropping suddenly
Low fuel warning without reason

P2068.t: Fuel Level Sensor B Circuit High
P2068.d: P2068 is the upper limit fault of the second fuel level sender: its signal sits above anything a working sender can produce, which normally means an open circuit, a lost sender ground or a short to a supply voltage. Ford reports it above 200 ohms, more than 253 A/D counts, using the same 30 s electrical check as for sender A. GM's 2020 dual-tank table needs 100 out of 125 samples with the secondary sender above 60 % of the 5 V span, Type B. Mercedes lists it as P206800, the secondary fill level sender shorted to plus. Ford SSM 52771 covers 2024 Bronco Sport, Escape and Corsair that displayed Fuel Level Low with the MIL and P2068 although the tank was not low; its pinpoint test was rewritten. Because the gauge combines both senders, one bad reading skews the whole display.
c: Open signal or ground wire, unplugged sender connector
Sender card worn through or wiper lifted off the track
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
s: Low fuel warning or empty gauge with fuel in the tank
MIL on
Range estimate jumps or is implausible

P2069.t: Fuel Level Sensor B Circuit Intermittent
P2069.d: P2069 covers brief dropouts on the second fuel level sender: the signal leaves its valid window for moments and comes back, too short for a hard low or high fault. Mercedes is the one maker found to document it, as P206900 in the FSCM_GEN4 fuel pump control unit, a sporadic malfunction of the secondary fill level sensor; a 2025 Mercedes bulletin on implausible gauge readings has connectors and harness routing checked. Ford handles a jumpy sender B under P2066 instead, so on Ford vehicles P2069 is unlikely. Behind such faults are worn spots on the sender card where the wiper loses contact, connectors at the tank flange that move with the body, or a harness rubbing on a bracket. CARB requires fuel level inputs to be monitored. The gauge may twitch and the low fuel light may flicker on and off.
c: Worn spot on the sender card at the usual fuel level
Loose or corroded terminal at the tank flange connector
Harness rubbing on a bracket or tank strap
s: Fuel gauge needle twitches or drops briefly
Low fuel light flickers on and off
Intermittent MIL

P206A.d: The quality sensor sits in the DEF (AdBlue) tank, usually inside a module that also holds level and temperature elements, and estimates urea concentration, in GM's case by timing ultrasonic echoes. P206A is the general circuit code: the module cannot deliver a usable quality value, without a finer split into range, low or high. Deutz uses it with failure-type bytes: on the EMR L1 controller P206A-21 and P206A-22 mean the quality value left its valid range at the bottom or top, on EMR5 P206A-01 stands for erratic or incorrect data. FCA lists P206A for its 3.0L diesel trucks from model year 2016 among the codes that start the Service DEF countdown: the engine can no longer be restarted once 150 miles pass without repair. Without a trustworthy reading the controller cannot detect wrong fluid, which CARB requires.
c: Corroded or loose connector at the tank sensor module
Failed quality sensor or tank sensor module
Damaged signal or supply wiring near the tank
Frozen, aerated or heavily contaminated fluid around the sensor
s: MIL and DEF system warning
Countdown to no-restart or speed limit
DEF quality value missing in scan data

P206B.d: P206B means the quality sensor answers, but its result cannot be used or does not fit what the SCR system does. GM sets it in its 2018 diesel table when the DEF controller keeps reporting the sensor as not ready, for instance because the ultrasonic echo is lost on a fouled sensor: 200 failed out of 250 samples, Type A, checked only with over 4 L of DEF and a sensor above 5 °C. GM bulletin 18-NA-124 for the 2018 Equinox and Terrain 1.6L diesel traces many cases to micro-bubbles from aerating filling equipment. Ford's 2023 diesels log an internal sensor error under P206B. Hino tests rationality: NOx conversion well below target while the sensor still claims usable fluid sets P206B with MIL. FCA lists it for its 3.0L diesels, and Ford SSM 51891 links it on 2023 Super Duty trucks with U02A2 and connector checks.
c: Air bubbles on the sensor after filling
Deposits or crystals on the ultrasonic sensor
Internal fault in the quality sensor or tank module
Drifting NOx sensor upsetting the rationality check (Hino logic)
s: MIL and Service Emission System or DEF message
Fault appears shortly or hours after refilling DEF
Possible countdown to speed limit

P206C.d: P206C is the low-side fault of the quality sensor, read in two ways. GM treats it as electrical: in its 2018 diesel table the piezo input of the ultrasonic sensor below 0.15 V in 40 of 50 samples sets the code, Type A. Ford uses it as a quality verdict: its 2023 diesels flag P206C when the filtered urea concentration stays at 28 % or less for over 900 s, and Ford SSMs 46890 to 50323 for 6.7L, 3.2L and 3.0L diesels say most cases come from diluted DEF, so the fluid is checked with a refractometer and replaced before parts are swapped, since low concentration also triggers a derate. GM PIP5602 for 2019 Colorado and Canyon 2.8L adds a false trigger: at roughly 30 % fill or less, a long right-hand curve can uncover the sensor; no parts are replaced, the tank is simply filled. Above-range readings belong to P206D.
c: Diluted or wrong fluid in the DEF tank (Ford definition)
Low tank level letting the sensor run dry in curves
Sensor signal shorted to ground or failed sensor element
s: MIL and DEF quality or emission system warning
Reduced power or speed limit on Ford diesels
Warning that appears after a long curve and then clears

P206D.d: P206D is the upper limit counterpart of P206C. In GM's 2018 diesel table it is electrical: the piezo input of the ultrasonic quality sensor above 4.5 V in 40 of 50 samples, Type A. Ford's 2023 diesels set it when filtered urea concentration reads 60 % or more for over 900 s, which real DEF never reaches, so either the sensor or a foreign fluid is to blame. GM PIP5635 for 2019 Colorado and Canyon 2.8L names a false cause: urea crystals that form around the sensor when the fluid freezes and thaws. Before repairs, sensor status should read OK, concentration 28 to 40 % and the tank above 5 °C; if not, warm the truck indoors and drive it in traffic for 10 minutes. FCA STAR case S2025000006 for 2020 Wrangler and Gladiator diesels calls the code mainly electrical but asks for a refractometer and hydrocarbon strip test too.
c: Urea crystals around the sensor after freeze and thaw
Sensor signal open or shorted to voltage, failed sensor
Foreign or over-concentrated fluid in the tank
s: MIL and DEF or emission system warning
Fault often after cold nights
Countdown toward speed limit or no-restart

P206E.t: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Stuck Open (Bank 2)
P206E.d: Reserved for engines whose second cylinder bank has its own intake manifold tuning valve, the flap that switches plenum volume or runner length for resonance charging. The code says the bank 2 flap was commanded shut but its position feedback still reports it open. No manufacturer documents P206E publicly; the GM and Ford tables checked cover only a single tuning valve, logged as P2070/P2071. By analogy with GM, a fault would be counted once the closed end stop is not reached for several seconds and confirmed on a second trip. CARB lists variable-length intake runner systems as monitored output components. The driver mostly notices a torque dip in one speed band; P206F is the reverse case, P2070 the bank 1 counterpart.
c: Flap or shaft of the bank 2 tuning valve gummed up by oil vapour and carbon from crankcase ventilation
Bank 2 actuator motor or gear worn, cannot drive the flap into the closed stop
Linkage between actuator and flap shaft detached or broken
End positions not relearned after actuator or manifold replacement
s: Check engine light after two drives (manufacturer-dependent)
Noticeably less pulling power in one rpm range
Changed intake sound under acceleration

P206F.t: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Stuck Closed (Bank 2)
P206F.d: Here the bank 2 tuning valve ignores an open request: the engine computer asks it to swing to the open end stop, yet the feedback still shows the closed position. The code only makes sense on a V-engine with a separately switched flap per bank, and no manufacturer publishes it; GM and Ford describe a single valve and use P2071 for the stuck-closed case. GM counts that fault when the open position is missing after at least 5 s and sets it as Type B. Electrical faults in the drive circuit belong to P0663 and onward, position sensor faults on bank 2 to P207A to P207E. A flap jammed shut usually costs top-end power more than low-speed torque, so the car may feel flat at higher revs; P206E is the opposite direction.
c: Bank 2 flap seized in its closed position by deposits or a dry shaft bearing
Bank 2 actuator internally defective, no longer produces the opening torque
On vacuum-operated designs a leaking hose or check valve leaves the actuator without vacuum
Broken flap seal or foreign object blocking the flap travel
s: Engine feels flat at high rpm
Check engine light (manufacturer-dependent)
Barely noticeable at moderate driving

P2070.t: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Stuck Open (Bank 1)
P2070.d: The tuning valve switches the manifold geometry for resonance charging; with a position sensor fitted, the engine computer can see whether the flap obeys. P2070 is logged when it was told to close and stays open. GM uses it in many tables: the 2006 and 2007 V6/four-cylinder sets flag a learn phase of 0.75 s or more, or five or more learn attempts, between 1000 and 3600 rpm; the 2015 and 2018 tables wait 5 s for the closed stop, count 320 of 400 samples at 12.5 ms and rate it Type B. The GM 2023/2024 tables print this code with a stuck-closed text, the reverse of J2012. Ford lists P2070 without MIL, although its own IMTV has no feedback. Without a sensor, P065E covers flap function; P2071 is the closed case.
c: Flap shaft sticking from oily carbon deposits fed by crankcase ventilation
Actuator motor or gear worn, flap stops short of the closed position
Actuator unclipped from the shaft or broken coupling
Learn routine of the end stops aborted, e.g. after repairs or low battery voltage
s: Check engine light after the second faulty drive (GM Type B)
Weaker pulling power in the speed range the closed flap is meant for
Louder or different intake noise

P2071.t: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Stuck Closed (Bank 1)
P2071.d: Counterpart to P2070: the bank 1 tuning valve receives an open command, but the position feedback keeps showing it shut. In GM's 2006 and 2007 tables the check simply compares commanded and actual flap position under load between 1000 and 3600 rpm, Type B. From 2015 on (also engine LWE in 18OBDG03A) GM requires that the open stop is reached within 5 s; 320 failed out of 400 samples set the code, and it stays blocked while P0660 to P0662 or the sensor codes P2077/P2078 are active. GM's 2023/2024 tables describe P2071 as stuck open, so on those vehicles the meaning of P2070/P2071 should be checked against the service data. Ford lists the code without MIL. Expect lost power at high rpm; bank 2 uses P206F.
c: Flap seized shut by deposits or corroded shaft bushings
Actuator defective, no longer turns the flap against its return spring
Weak supply to the actuator from a corroded connector or relay contact
s: Lack of power at high engine speed
Check engine light (GM Type B, Ford without MIL)
Engine otherwise runs normally

P2072.t: Throttle Actuator Control System - Ice Blockage (Bank 1)
P2072.d: Not related to the tuning valve: P2072 belongs to the electronic throttle system. If the throttle plate cannot move freely in frost, the controller assumes ice and runs repeated open and close strokes to break it loose; the code records that event. Ford's 2012 OBD summary lists it for second-generation throttle control as a non-MIL fault, and Ford's 2014 code list marks it for the wrench lamp only. FCA bulletin 09-023-23 covers the 2013 to 2023 RAM 1500 with the 3.6L V6: P2072 together with P2110 and P2118, sometimes a no-start below freezing, caused by moisture from the crankcase ventilation freezing on the throttle blade. The fix is drying throttle body and PCV parts, a kit with new air cleaner lid and make-up air hose, plus an oil change. Speed may be limited meanwhile.
c: Water from the crankcase ventilation condensing and freezing at the throttle plate
Frequent short trips in frost leave water in the engine oil and breather
Heater of the breather line or throttle body (where fitted) not working
Water entering the air intake through a loose duct or wet air filter
s: Wrench or engine light after a cold start in frost
Limited engine speed or reduced power
Engine may not start in deep frost

P2073.t: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Mass Air Flow - Throttle Position Correlation at Idle
P2073.d: The engine computer compares the measured air mass, or the manifold pressure, with what the throttle opening and engine speed predict. P2073 means the two disagree in the idle range. Ford's diesel OBD summary 2023 explains its approach: an airflow adaptation factor is learned in an idle cell and a load cell once per drive cycle; if the idle value ends up outside its band, P2073 is set. For the 6.7L Super Duty chassis that band is about +27 % and -13 %; the 3.0L diesel only checks the load cell. Ford bulletin 22-2115 reprograms the PCM of 2011 to 2012 F-Super Duty 6.7L trucks that set P2073 or P2074. Ford's 2014 code list also gives it MIL status. Air leaks, a dirty sensor or a clogged filter are typical; P2074 is the load case.
c: Unmetered air entering after the air flow sensor (loose clamp, cracked hose, leaking gasket)
Air flow sensor element contaminated or drifted, adaptation runs out of range
Deposits at the throttle plate distorting the idle air path
s: Check engine light
Unsteady or raised idle
Often no noticeable driving fault

P2074.t: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Mass Air Flow - Throttle Position Correlation at Higher Load
P2074.d: Same plausibility idea as P2073, but evaluated above idle, where the measured air mass or manifold pressure must match what throttle opening and rpm predict under load. Ford's diesels learn an airflow adaptation in a load cell; outside roughly +/-20 % (6.7L chassis and 3.0L), or if no stable value is learned within 20 learning events, P2074 is stored. Several Ford documents deal with it on the 6.7L Super Duty: a dirty air filter plus a MAF parameter reset instead of new parts (2013-2019 trucks), new calibration for 2017-2019 builds up to 9 January 2019, often with P0170. Hyundai bulletin 21-01-075H covers 2.5L Sonata, Santa Fe and Tucson (2020-22) with P2074 variants for low and for medium/high load, cured by ECM software; reduced power is possible.
c: Clogged air filter shifting the learned airflow value (Ford 6.7L)
Leak in charge air pipes or intercooler on turbo engines
Calibration issue fixed by software update (Ford 6.7L, Hyundai 2.5L)
Air flow sensor reading drifted at high flow rates
s: Check engine light
Reduced power or limited performance mode (Hyundai)
Hesitation under acceleration

P2075.t: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Position Sensor/Switch Circuit (Bank 1)
P2075.d: General circuit fault of the bank 1 tuning valve position feedback, which may be a potentiometer, a Hall sensor or a simple end-position switch. The code is meant for systems that do not split the fault into low, high or intermittent. No manufacturer publishes P2075: GM, which uses position sensing on its tuning valves, reports the same circuit through the specific P2077 and P2078, and Ford's IMTV has no feedback at all. CARB requires input components to be checked for open circuits and readings beyond their limits, but not with separate codes per fault type, which explains why such a catch-all code exists. In practice an open signal or ground wire or a bad plug is the usual cause; the flap may still work, but its function test is suspended.
c: Corroded or loose connector at the actuator with integrated position sensor
Signal, reference or ground wire chafed or broken near the hot manifold
Position sensor inside the actuator failed
s: Check engine light (manufacturer-dependent)
Flap position monitoring and stuck-valve tests no longer run
Usually no driveability complaint

P2076.t: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1)
P2076.d: The sensor signal is electrically within its limits, but it does not behave plausibly. GM defines this through the learn routine of the actuator in the 2015 and 2018 tables: if the reported position stays between 5 % and 35 % for 5 s or more while learning, or the learn routine starts ten or more times within a single key cycle, P2076 is stored as Type B after supply voltage of at least 11 V and one second of running. In GM's 2023 and 2024 tables the valve reports its position digitally over SENT, and P2076 flags a faulty or invalid data value from that interface. Hard-to-move flaps, a worn sensor track or a wrong actuator can cause it. It is less specific than P2077/P2078, which detect plain shorts and opens.
c: Flap binding so that the actuator cannot complete its learn sweep
Worn potentiometer track giving jumpy readings
Digital (SENT) position message corrupted by wiring or actuator electronics
s: Check engine light after two trips (GM Type B)
Actuator audibly cycling at key-on
Slight power loss in parts of the rev range

P2077.t: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Low (Bank 1)
P2077.d: The feedback signal of the bank 1 tuning valve has dropped below its plausible lower edge, typically because the signal is shorted to ground or the line is open with a pull-down. GM states it in percent of the sensor range: in 2006/2007 and again in the 2015/2018 tables a reading of 95 % or more counts as low, so GM's scaling is inverted; once 320 of every 400 checks (one each 12.5 ms) fail, it is stored as Type B. The Bosch-style logic in GM's 2023/2024 tables uses a raw voltage under about 0.7 V. FCA names P2077 for the manifold tuning valve of the 2007-2010 3.5L V6 (Sebring, Avenger, Journey, Pacifica) and advises checking the actuator duty cycle before replacing the manifold. Ford lists P2077 without MIL. P2078 is the high side.
c: Signal wire shorted to ground or chafed against the engine
5 V reference to the sensor interrupted
Actuator with integrated sensor defective (FCA 3.5L, check duty cycle first)
s: Check engine light (GM Type B; Ford without MIL)
Stuck-valve tests P2070/P2071 disabled
Driving often unchanged

P2078.t: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Position Sensor/Switch Circuit High (Bank 1)
P2078.d: Opposite of P2077: the bank 1 valve feedback sits above its upper plausible limit. Typical triggers are a short to battery or 5 V on the signal line, or an open sensor ground. Because GM's percentage scale is reversed, its tables treat a position of 5 % or less as high (2007, 2015, 2018; the 2006 table names 0.05 %), with 320 failures in 400 samples and Type B. GM's newer 2023/2024 logic instead watches for a raw voltage above roughly 4.8 V. On FCA's 3.5L V6 (2007-2010) P2078 is the second manifold tuning valve code next to P2077, and the Chrysler tip warns against replacing the whole manifold before testing the actuator output. Ford lists the code without MIL. Note that GM blocks its stuck-valve checks while this code is active.
c: Sensor ground open, e.g. pushed-back pin in the connector
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Electronics of the actuator unit defective
s: Check engine light (GM Type B; Ford without MIL)
Valve monitoring suspended
Possibly less power in one rpm band

P2079.t: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Intermittent (Bank 1)
P2079.d: Intended for brief dropouts or jumps in the bank 1 valve feedback that come and go rather than sticking at one limit. No manufacturer documents this meaning publicly. GM's tuning valve tables stop at P2076 to P2078, and Ford's 2014 code list even assigns P2079 to an intake air system leak, an older Ford-specific text that has nothing to do with the position sensor, so scan-tool texts on Ford vehicles can differ. Per CARB, intermittent faults of an input component are covered by the circuit and rationality checks. Loose crimp contacts, a cracked connector housing or a cable that moves with engine rock are the classic sources; wiggle testing while watching the live value is the most useful check.
c: Loose or fretted terminals in the sensor connector
Wire broken inside the insulation, contact lost with engine movement
Dead spot on the sensor track
s: Light comes and goes (manufacturer-dependent)
Fault often not present during workshop test

P207A.t: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Position Sensor/Switch Circuit (Bank 2)
P207A.d: Unspecified circuit failure of the position feedback on the bank 2 tuning valve. It presupposes a second, separately sensed valve, which in practice means a V-engine with one switchable flap per bank. Nobody publishes this code: the GM tables use a single sensed valve (P2076 to P2078), and in Ford's literature only the runner control flaps (IMRC, P2004 onward) are monitored bank by bank. Following CARB, the controller still has to detect an open or shorted input even if it does not tell those cases apart. Because the bank 2 sensor usually sits at the rear of the manifold, chafed wiring under the cowl is worth checking first; for a pure bank 1 fault see P2075, for refined bank 2 fault types P207C and P207D.
c: Poorly accessible bank 2 connector not latched or corroded
Harness chafed between manifold and bulkhead
Position sensor of the bank 2 actuator failed
s: Check engine light (manufacturer-dependent)
Mostly no change in driving behaviour

P207B.t: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2)
P207B.d: On bank 2, the valve feedback is electrically valid yet does not match what the flap should be doing, for instance it changes too slowly, sticks at an intermediate value or disagrees with the commanded state. No manufacturer documents P207B. The closest documented logic is GM's bank 1 code P2076, which fails the actuator learn sweep when the reported position lingers inside the 5-35 % band for five seconds, or when learning restarts ten times in one key cycle. A plausibility code like this often points at mechanics rather than electrics: a flap that binds or a slipping coupling falsifies the movement profile even with an intact sensor. Compare with P206E/P206F, which judge the end positions of the same flap.
c: Bank 2 flap binding, movement profile does not match the command
Coupling between sensor shaft and flap slipping
Sensor characteristic drifted with age and heat
s: Check engine light (manufacturer-dependent)
Possibly uneven power delivery

P207C.t: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Low (Bank 2)
P207C.d: Low signal on the position feedback of the bank 2 tuning valve: the controller sees a value below the window it accepts. Typical electrical causes are the signal shorted to ground or a missing 5 V supply. No manufacturer publishes P207C. Its bank 1 equivalent P2077 is well documented at GM, where the limit is given in percent and the scale runs backwards (95 % or more counts as low), and FCA cites P2077 for the 3.5L V6 manifold tuning valve; a bank 2 application would follow the same pattern. Ground faults can also kill other sensors on the shared 5 V circuit, so if several sensor codes appear together, look for the common reference first. P207D is the high-side fault.
c: Bank 2 signal wire shorted to ground
Shared 5 V reference pulled down or open
Internal short in the bank 2 sensor
s: Check engine light (manufacturer-dependent)
Other 5 V sensor codes at the same time

P207D.t: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Position Sensor/Switch Circuit High (Bank 2)
P207D.d: The bank 2 valve position signal reads above the highest value the controller accepts. Electrically that points at a broken sensor ground or a short from the signal to a supply voltage. There is no published manufacturer use of P207D; it mirrors GM's bank 1 code P2078, where 5 % or less counts as high due to the reversed scale, while GM's 2023/2024 logic compares the raw voltage with about 4.8 V. An open ground often comes from heat-damaged connectors on the rear bank, so inspect the plug before ordering a new actuator. Unlike P207B, a high code says nothing about the flap mechanics; the valve may move correctly while its feedback is simply not readable.
c: Sensor ground open at a heat-damaged connector
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
s: Check engine light (manufacturer-dependent)
No driveability change in most cases

P207E.t: Intake Manifold Tuning (IMT) Valve Position Sensor/Switch Circuit Intermittent (Bank 2)
P207E.d: Bank 2 version of the intermittent feedback fault: the valve position signal drops out or jumps for short moments, but returns to normal between events. No manufacturer documents P207E, and even its bank 1 twin P2079 has no published OEM use with this meaning. The diagnosis is therefore generic: since the fault may vanish before a scan tool is connected, freeze-frame data and the failure counter help to judge how often it happens. Heat cycling on the rear bank, vibration and water in the connector are the usual triggers. If the signal fails permanently, the code typically turns into the circuit or low/high variants P207A, P207C or P207D, which are easier to pinpoint.
c: Moisture or corrosion in the bank 2 sensor connector
Solder joint or wire breaking open intermittently under heat
Harness not clipped, contact lost under vibration
s: Intermittent warning light (manufacturer-dependent)
Fault not reproducible in the workshop

P207F.d: P207F is the verdict that the tank holds something other than proper DEF, which CARB explicitly requires the OBD system to detect. Without a quality sensor the fluid is judged by its effect: GM's 2011 diesel table names the code Incorrect Reductant Composition and compares measured SCR NOx conversion with a limit that depends on temperature and flow, Type B; Volkswagen's 2014 Touareg TDI flags average efficiency below 0.50. GM PIP5007D adds that its Exhaust Fluid Quality Poor message on 6.6L LGH/LML trucks only reports lost conversion, not necessarily bad fluid. With a sensor the verdict is direct: Deutz files poor AdBlue as P207F-00 and a wrong fluid type as P207F-29. Ford SSM 46706, Nissan NTB17-060 (Titan XD 5.0L Cummins) and Hino SB-14-028 updated tests or software. Pure catalyst ageing belongs to P20EE.
c: Water, coolant or other fluid in the DEF tank
Old DEF degraded by heat or long storage
NOx sensor reading wrong, faking poor conversion
Partly blocked dosing valve delivering too little fluid
s: Exhaust fluid quality warning in the cluster
MIL and countdown to speed limit or no-restart
Message persists until a quality test or relearn is passed

P2080.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2080.d: P2080 means the first exhaust temperature sensor on bank 1 passes its wiring checks, yet its reading does not fit the engine state. Each maker tests this differently. On the 6.6 L Duramax (GM 15OBDG09) the heat the exhaust flow should bring to the sensor is integrated and compared with what the sensor saw; the 3.0 L LZO (25OBDG04B) expects a minimum rise after more than 10,800 s of soak, which exposes a frozen value or a sensor no longer inside the pipe. Both are Type B. Ford's 6.7 L diesel cross-checks four sensors after 6 h off with a 50 °C key-on limit. VW's 2014 Touareg TDI allows 250 K above or 200 K below its model. Nissan cured false P2080 on the VK56VD and VR30DDTT petrol engines with new ECM software. Erratic jumps belong to P2081.
c: Sensor element drifted or slow after many heat cycles
Sensor loose, bent or not reaching into the exhaust stream
ECM calibration flags a good sensor (software update released, e.g. Nissan)
Exhaust leak upstream of the sensor cools the reading
s: Engine warning lamp on
Particulate filter regeneration blocked or aborted on diesels
Often no noticeable change in driving

P2081.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2081.d: P2081 is set when the signal of exhaust temperature sensor 1 on bank 1 jumps between consecutive readings faster than real exhaust gas can change. GM documents two versions. A diesel in table 18OBDG04 flags a change of more than 10 ohms between two samples taken 100 ms apart and needs 20 such failures out of 40. The 3.0 L LZO (25OBDG04B) looks at the raw temperature step instead, more than 100 °C, in 12 of 25 samples. Both are Type B, so the lamp lights after the second faulty trip. Infiniti lists P2081 with its siblings on the Q50 of 2016–2017 and the Q60 of 2017 (VR30DDTT) and fixes it by reprogramming the ECM. Ford's 2014 petrol code list carries it without a lamp marker. Loose contacts and heat-damaged leads are the classic causes; a steady but wrong value would be P2080.
c: Loose or corroded pin in the sensor connector
Sensor lead chafed or embrittled by exhaust heat, breaking contact on vibration
Cracked sensing element giving unstable resistance
s: Engine warning lamp on, sometimes only after the second trip
Exhaust temperature value jumping in live data
Regeneration or turbo protection strategy interrupted

P2082.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P2082.d: P2082 is the plausibility fault of the first exhaust temperature sensor on bank 2, the cylinder bank without cylinder 1. It only exists where both banks carry separate sensors ahead of the merge point, which in practice means V-type petrol engines with turbo or catalyst protection. The diesel tables from GM, Ford and VW number every sensor on bank 1 because one aftertreatment line serves the engine. Nissan is the documented user: bulletins NTB16-124 and ITB16-051 cover the 2017 Armada, Titan and QX80 with the VK56VD, where P2080 and/or P2082 came on although the sensors were fine; the cure is new ECM software, and the bulletin explicitly says not to replace the sensor. ITB17-050 does the same for the Q50 and Q60 with the VR30DDTT. Nissan does not publish the thresholds. Jumping values on this sensor are P2083.
c: ECM calibration error on affected Nissan/Infiniti models (reprogramming)
Exhaust leak on bank 2 ahead of the sensor
s: Engine warning lamp on
Usually no noticeable driving change

P2083.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P2083.d: P2083 reports an unsteady signal from exhaust temperature sensor 1 on bank 2: the value changes by more than the exhaust can physically manage between two readings, or briefly drops out. Only one maker documents it publicly. Infiniti bulletin ITB17-050 lists P2083 with P0544–P0549 and P2080–P2082 for Infiniti's Q50 (model years 2016–2017) and Q60 (2017) with the 3.0 L VR30DDTT twin-turbo V6, which has one sensor per bank, and prescribes an ECM reprogram. Ford's 2014 petrol code list includes P2083 with a lamp marker. No threshold is published for bank 2; GM's bank 1 counterpart P2081 shows the usual approach of counting fast steps in a window of samples. Before replacing parts, wiggle-test the connector and lead while watching live data. A plausible but wrong steady value would be P2082.
c: Intermittent contact in the bank 2 sensor connector
Lead damaged by turbocharger or exhaust heat
s: Engine warning lamp on
Bank 2 exhaust temperature flickering in live data

P2084.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P2084.d: P2084 applies the plausibility check to the second exhaust temperature sensor on bank 1, on diesels usually the one behind the oxidation catalyst or ahead of the particulate filter or SCR stage. GM runs the same tests here as for sensor 1: a heat balance on the 6.6 L Duramax (15OBDG09) and a cold-soak rise check on the 3.0 L LZO (25OBDG04B), both Type B. On the Ford 6.7 L diesel, P2084 sits next to P2080 in the sensor-to-sensor check that runs after 6 h off. VW's 2014 Touareg TDI is stricter in one direction only and fails sensor 2 once it reads more than 100 K below its model. Deutz stores the plausibility fault of the sensor ahead of the SCR catalyst as P2084-62 or -64 on its EMR L1 controller. A wrong value here can upset DEF dosing and regeneration control. Unsteady readings fall under P2085.
c: Sensor 2 reads low or responds slowly due to ageing or soot
Sensor connectors swapped with another exhaust temperature sensor after repair
Oxidation catalyst not producing the expected heat, so the reading looks implausible
s: Engine warning lamp on
Particulate filter regeneration or DEF dosing restricted
Reduced engine power on some diesels

P2085.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P2085.d: P2085 marks the signal of exhaust temperature sensor 2 on bank 1 as erratic. GM monitors it with the same logic as sensor 1 but on separate counters. In the diesel table 18OBDG04 a step of more than 10 ohms between two 100 ms samples counts as a failure, and 20 failures within 40 samples set the code; on the 3.0 L LZO (25OBDG04B) a raw jump above 100 °C in 12 of 25 samples is enough. Both carry Type B, so the lamp needs a second faulty trip. Ford's 2014 petrol list shows P2085 without the lamp marker. Because sensor 2 often sits under the vehicle, splashed water and road salt in the connector are frequent triggers. Implausible but stable readings set P2084.
c: Water or road salt in the underbody sensor connector
Lead rubbing on the exhaust or a bracket, intermittent break
Internal fault in the sensor causing unstable resistance
s: Engine warning lamp on after repeated occurrence
Erratic sensor 2 value in live data
Regeneration interrupted

P2086.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P2086.d: P2086 would report an implausible reading from the second exhaust temperature sensor on bank 2. Snap-on's code list confirms the wording. No manufacturer document available to us uses the code: GM, Ford and VW keep all diesel sensors on bank 1, Nissan's per-bank petrol layouts stop at sensor 1, and Ford's 2014 petrol list jumps from P2085 to P2088. Do not confuse it with the third sensor on bank 1: Ford's 6.7 L diesel checks sensors 1 to 4 against each other under P2080, P2084, P242B and P246F, with P24C2 for a multi-sensor mismatch. Bank 2 sensor 2 only makes sense with two separate exhaust trains that each carry a catalyst. CARB still requires a rationality check for every emission-relevant temperature input. The nearest documented analogue is P2084 on bank 1.
c: Bank 2 downstream sensor aged or sooted, reading off
Sensor loose or not reaching into the gas stream
Leak in the bank 2 exhaust ahead of the sensor
s: Engine warning lamp on
Catalyst or filter protection functions limited

P2087.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P2087.d: P2087 is reserved for a bank 2 sensor 2 exhaust temperature signal that is erratic or drops out. No manufacturer publishes it; we checked GM, Ford, VW, Deutz and the NHTSA bulletin index without a hit, and Ford's 2014 petrol list leaves it out. For a monitor in this style, GM's bank 1 counterpart P2085 is the reference: in table 18OBDG04 it counts resistance steps above 10 ohms between samples taken every 100 ms and sets a Type B code at 20 out of 40. CARB requires that intermittent faults of emission-relevant inputs be detected. If the code ever appears, the sensor connector and the lead along the second exhaust pipe are the first things to inspect. P2086 covers a steady but implausible value from the same sensor, P2034–P2036 its hard electrical faults.
c: Intermittent contact in the bank 2 sensor 2 connector
Lead chafing on the second exhaust pipe
s: Engine warning lamp on
Unstable exhaust temperature value for bank 2 sensor 2

P2088.t: "A" Camshaft Position Actuator Control Circuit Low (Bank 1)
P2088.d: P2088 concerns the control line of the oil control valve that moves the intake cam phaser (actuator A) on bank 1. On GM engines the ECM feeds the solenoid through a high-side driver; while the output is switched on, a voltage that falls below the controller window means the line has a path to ground (equivalent to less than 0.5 ohms). GM samples every 250 ms and sets the code after 20 failures in 25 samples, as a Type B fault on the 5.3 L L84 (19OBDG03B). GM bulletins PIP5553 (2018) and PIP5724 (2020) link P2088 and P2089 on V8 and V6 trucks and the Camaro to a jumper harness chafed or pinched at connector X154 on the lower left of the front cover. On many Fords open and shorted phaser circuits all land in P0010. The phaser then stays locked in its rest position.
c: Control wire chafed through to ground, e.g. GM jumper harness at connector X154
Oil control valve coil shorted internally
Engine oil wicked into the valve connector
Damaged output driver in the ECM
s: Engine warning lamp on
Less pull and higher consumption with cam timing fixed
Rough idle on some engines

P2089.t: "A" Camshaft Position Actuator Control Circuit High (Bank 1)
P2089.d: P2089 is the opposite fault on the intake phaser valve (actuator A) of bank 1: the control line carries voltage although the ECM has switched the output off. With GM's high-side driver that means a short to a supply, again judged against a 0.5 ohm equivalent. The sampling is the same as for P2088, 20 bad results within 25 at 250 ms each, but the 5.3 L L84 table 19OBDG03B rates P2089 more severely as Type A, so the lamp comes on in the first trip, while the 2018 hybrid table 18OBDG02 keeps it at Type B. GM's PIP5553 and PIP5724 name P2089 alongside P2088 for the damaged X154 jumper harness. Ford lists P2089 as a lamp code that its self-test can catch with key on and with the engine running. A wire touching a 12 V feed or a short inside the harness is more likely than a faulty valve.
c: Control wire shorted to a 12 V feed inside the harness
Pinched or chafed jumper harness at the front cover (GM X154)
s: Engine warning lamp on, on some GM engines in the first trip
Intake cam timing no longer adjusted, sluggish response

P208A.d: P208A reports an open or otherwise faulty drive circuit of the main DEF pump, the one that builds dosing pressure. Ford's 2023 diesels flag it when pump voltage sits between 2.6 and 3.4 V or the pump controller supply falls under 6 V, tested with the driver off and confirmed after 8 s. GM's 2018 diesel table takes a phase-open message from the DEF module, 32 of 40 samples, Type A; Volkswagen's 2014 Touareg TDI expects 4.70 to 5.40 V on an open line, and Deutz EMR5 files current below normal as P208A-13. Several bulletins blame software rather than parts: Volvo and Mack 2016–2017 chassis at cold start, Range Rover Velar 2.0 diesel together with P208C-11, and GM 23-NA-008 for 2022 trucks whose pump ran against frozen DEF. FCA counts it among inducement triggers.
c: Unplugged, corroded or broken pump connector or wire
Pump controller or ECU software (Volvo/Mack, JLR, GM 23-NA-008)
Low supply to the pump controller from fuse, relay or ground
Pump motor winding open, pump unit failed
s: MIL and DEF dosing malfunction message
No engine restart countdown
Fault often logged at cold start

P208B.t: Reductant Pump A Control Performance/Stuck Off
P208B.d: P208B is the functional check of DEF pump A: the circuit is intact, yet the pump ignores its command or stays off. Ford, titling it Reductant Pump Control Range/Performance, sets it on 2023 diesels when pump speed misses its setpoint by over 300 rpm or its speed control sits at a limit for 30 s, detected within 5 s and only after the circuit tests have passed. GM's 2014 diesel table reports Reductant Pump Performance when the pump motor's functional acknowledgement takes longer than 4 s, Type B. Deutz EMR5 adds an overheated output stage (P208B-4B) and an abnormal rate of change (P208B-92). In the field the hydraulics are usually to blame: FCA STAR S1925000008 (Grand Cherokee, Wrangler diesel) names trapped air in the tank filter and external leaks, and a Volkswagen 2.0 TDI tip rules out leaking lines first.
c: Air trapped in the tank filter or suction side after service
Leaking DEF line or connection between pump and dosing valve
s: MIL with DEF system message, often with P20E8
White urea crust on lines or fittings
Countdown to no-restart or reduced power

P208C.t: Reductant Pump A Control Circuit Low
P208C.d: P208C sets when the drive of DEF pump A is pulled low, either by a ground fault or by current far beyond normal. Ford's 2023 diesels look for pump current over 5 A or pump controller current over 15 A with the driver off, the same 8 s window as for the open fault P208A. In GM's 2018 diesel table the DEF control module itself reports the phase shorted to ground; 20 out of 25 samples, Type A. The 2014 VW Touareg TDI trips once the control line falls under 2.74 V, and Deutz EMR5 files it as P208C-11, too little voltage or a path to ground. Jaguar Land Rover found P208C-11 together with P208A-13 on 2018–2019 Range Rover Velar 2.0 diesels and fixed it with a PCM update. Real shorts are often chafed wires near the tank or a seized pump, which may also blow the fuse. Dosing stops.
c: Pump drive wire shorted to ground near the tank
Seized or crystallised pump drawing excessive current
Software error in the controlling module (JLR Velar)
s: MIL and DEF dosing malfunction warning
Pump fuse found blown
Countdown to no-restart

P208D.t: Reductant Pump A Control Circuit High
P208D.d: P208D means the drive of DEF pump A reads high, typically a wire touching battery positive, so the controller has lost authority over the pump. Unlike the open and low faults, Ford checks this one with the driver switched on: on 2023 diesels pump voltage over 16 V or pump controller current above 5 A sets it, confirmed in only 2 s. GM's 2018 diesel table relies on a phase-shorted-to-battery message from the DEF module, 20 of 25 samples, Type A, while the 2014 table watches for high voltage on the active driver. Volkswagen's 2014 Touareg TDI uses a control current above 4.00 A, and Deutz EMR5 files it as P208D-12. For 2013–2014 Ram 2500 and 3500 with the 6.7L Cummins, bulletin 18-010-14 reflashes the doser control unit when the MIL comes on with P208D or P202E. Check for wires pinched against powered cables and wet connectors.
c: Pump drive wire shorted to a battery feed
Moisture or corrosion in the pump connector
Internal fault in pump or pump controller
s: MIL and DEF system warning
No DEF dosing, rising NOx
Countdown to speed limit or no-restart

P208E.t: Reductant Injection Valve Stuck Closed (Bank 1 Unit 1)
P208E.d: P208E says the first DEF dosing valve does not open although it is energised correctly. Valve movement shows in the coil current: when the armature lifts, the trace kinks. Ford's 2023 diesels judge every stroke and need 50 failures; the test pauses while P2047 to P2049 report a circuit fault. Volkswagen's 2014 Touareg TDI counts more than 50 missing signal peaks, Deutz EMR5 files it as P208E-73, raised by its BIP check that looks for the valve opening. Usually urea crystals block the nozzle. Under Ford SSM 48539 the dosing test is repeated up to three times against a 40 to 50 mL target before the valve, never the pump, is replaced; Mack and Volvo describe intermittent clogging checked by timed flow tests; GM PIP5662 (low cab forward) replaces valve and pump filter. NOx rises and inducement follows.
c: Urea crystals blocking the dosing valve nozzle
Valve needle seized from deposits or heat
Contaminated fluid or debris from a dirty pump filter
s: MIL and DEF dosing warning
DEF consumption drops noticeably
Derate or countdown to no-restart

P208F.t: Reductant Injection Valve Stuck Closed (Bank 2 Unit 1)
P208F.d: P208F is the Bank 2 version of P208E: the first dosing valve on the second exhaust branch fails to open although its drive circuit is in order. It only applies to engines with two separate SCR branches, each with its own dosing valve, which is rare; most diesel cars and trucks run one valve on Bank 1. No manufacturer documents P208F publicly. The Bank 1 logic shows how the check works: Ford's 2023 diesels judge the valve stroke by stroke and need 50 failed strokes, the 2014 VW Touareg TDI needs over 50 absent current peaks. Ford pauses the test during circuit faults; for Bank 2 those would be P2050 to P2052. Crystallised urea in the nozzle is the most likely cause. CARB requires a reductant delivery fault to be detected. The second branch then receives no fluid, NOx rises and inducement may begin.
c: Urea crystals blocking the Bank 2 dosing valve
Valve needle stuck from deposits or overheating
Restricted supply line to the second valve
s: MIL and DEF or SCR warning
Higher NOx on one exhaust branch
Possible derate or countdown to no-restart

P2090.t: "B" Camshaft Position Actuator Control Circuit Low (Bank 1)
P2090.d: P2090 refers to actuator B, on engines with twin phasers the exhaust camshaft valve, on bank 1. What Low means depends on how the ECM drives the solenoid. GM's usual high-side output flags a ground short while the valve is energised; the 3.6 L LFX V6 (19OBDG03B) sets P2090 after 20 of 25 samples as Type A, the 2018 hybrid table 18OBDG02 as Type B. A GM controller with a low-side driver in table 23OBDG07 flips the test: it looks for a low voltage while the output is off and flags the code after only 0.2 s, two trips to the lamp. In both cases the threshold is below 0.5 ohms to ground. An open line on this valve is P0013, not P2090. With the exhaust phaser parked, the engine loses some internal exhaust recirculation and part-load efficiency.
c: Exhaust valve control wire shorted to ground or engine block
Shorted coil in the exhaust oil control valve
s: Engine warning lamp on, immediately on some GM V6 engines
Slightly higher consumption and emissions at part load

P2091.t: "B" Camshaft Position Actuator Control Circuit High (Bank 1)
P2091.d: P2091 says the control circuit of actuator B on bank 1, normally the exhaust phaser valve, sits too high. GM's high-side version on the 3.6 L LFX checks for a short to supply while the output is off and, like P2090, treats it as Type A after 20 of 25 samples; 18OBDG02 uses Type B. On the low-side controller of table 23OBDG07 the same code means the pin stays at supply voltage even though the driver should be pulling it to ground, and it takes about 1 s to confirm, two trips for the lamp. Ford shows P2091 in its 2014 petrol code list as a lamp code that both key-on and running self-tests can find. A short of this kind can overheat the driver, so the ECM usually switches the output off and leaves the exhaust cam at its default angle. Out-of-range timing of the same cam is P0014 or P0015.
c: Exhaust valve control wire touching a supply wire
Incorrect splice or pin swap after earlier wiring repair
Failed output stage in the ECM
s: Engine warning lamp on
Exhaust cam stays at default angle, slightly reduced performance

P2092.t: "A" Camshaft Position Actuator Control Circuit Low (Bank 2)
P2092.d: P2092 is the Low fault of the intake phaser valve (actuator A) on bank 2, which exists only on V and boxer engines with a separate valve per bank. Bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1. GM's 3.6 L LFX V6 in table 19OBDG03B checks this output with the high-side logic known from bank 1: a short to ground while energised, below 0.5 ohms, 20 bad samples out of 25, Type A, lamp in the first trip. The low-side controller in GM table 23OBDG07 tests the line while switched off and confirms after 0.2 s. Ford's 2014 petrol list includes P2092 but marks it only for the continuous monitor, not for the key-on or running self-test. If only bank 2 reports a fault, compare the valve resistance with the bank 1 valve and look for chafing where the harness crosses the cylinder head.
c: Bank 2 intake valve wire shorted to ground on the cylinder head
Shorted coil in the bank 2 intake oil control valve
s: Engine warning lamp on, immediately on GM LFX
Uneven running between banks, weaker torque

P2093.t: "A" Camshaft Position Actuator Control Circuit High (Bank 2)
P2093.d: P2093 reports too high a level on the control line of the bank 2 intake phaser valve (actuator A). Table 23OBDG07 shows why High and Low are not tied to one wiring fault: that GM controller switches the valve on the ground side, so it checks for voltage with the driver switched on and calls it a short to power after 1 s, with the lamp after two trips. The 3.6 L LFX (19OBDG03B) uses a high-side driver and looks for the same short with the output off; there P2093 is Type A after 20 of 25 samples. Ford's 2014 code list names P2093 as a lamp code covered only by the continuous monitor. Typical findings are a chafed wire touching an ignition or injector feed. If P2093 and P2089 appear together, suspect a shared supply or connector rather than two valves.
c: Bank 2 intake valve wire shorted to an ignition or injector feed
Fault in a shared engine harness connector
s: Engine warning lamp on
Bank 2 intake timing fixed, reduced low-speed torque

P2094.t: "B" Camshaft Position Actuator Control Circuit Low (Bank 2)
P2094.d: P2094 belongs to the fourth phaser valve of a twin-phaser V engine: actuator B, the exhaust camshaft, on bank 2. It is therefore absent on single-cam pushrod V8s and on inline engines. On GM's 3.6 L LFX the high-side output is checked for a ground short while on and treated as Type A after 20 out of 25 samples of 250 ms (19OBDG03B). The low-side GM controller of table 23OBDG07 detects the short to ground while off and reacts within 0.2 s; the lamp follows on the second trip. Ford's 2014 petrol list carries P2094 for the continuous monitor only. CARB requires output components of the valve timing system to be checked for circuit faults. An open circuit on this valve is P0023, wrong exhaust timing on bank 2 P0024 or P0025.
c: Bank 2 exhaust valve wire shorted to ground
Shorted coil in the bank 2 exhaust oil control valve
Insulation damaged by heat near the exhaust manifold
s: Engine warning lamp on
Slight loss of efficiency, higher part-load emissions

P2095.t: "B" Camshaft Position Actuator Control Circuit High (Bank 2)
P2095.d: P2095 closes the series: the bank 2 exhaust phaser valve (actuator B) shows a high level on its control line. For the 3.6 L LFX, GM table 19OBDG03B describes a high-side driver that finds a short to supply with the output off and sets a Type A code after 20 failures in 25 samples. In table 23OBDG07 a low-side controller watches the pin while the driver is on and confirms the short to power after 1 s, Type B style with two trips. Ford's 2014 petrol list contains P2095 with lamp marking, monitored continuously. In the workshop, measure the valve coil, then check the control wire for voltage with the connector unplugged and the ignition on; any voltage there points to the harness, not the valve. The engine runs on with a fixed exhaust cam. P2094 is the Low counterpart, P0023 the open circuit.
c: Bank 2 exhaust valve wire shorted to a supply wire
Bridged pins in the valve or engine harness connector
s: Engine warning lamp on
Exhaust cam on bank 2 fixed, minor drop in performance

P2096.t: Post Catalyst Fuel Trim System Too Lean (Bank 1)
P2096.d: Petrol engines run a slow outer control loop on the oxygen sensor behind the catalyst that shifts the mixture target of the front sensor. P2096 means this post-catalyst trim on bank 1 has hit its limit in the lean direction. The name describes the correction, not the engine: the rear sensor keeps reporting rich exhaust, so the loop keeps taking fuel away. GM's Bosch-based 2005 V6 calls it a rich shift with a correction below -0.03 lambda; GM's 2018 four-cylinders list it as the low limit, with the integral offset at -99 % and the total offset at -50 % or less (Type B); Ford's 2020 to 2023 engines set it 5 s after reaching a rear bias trim of -0.083. Causes are therefore a skewed rear sensor or an upstream sensor reading lean. Audi found a contaminated reference air duct in the rear sensor on 4.0 TFSI engines and warns against replacing the front sensor; GM saw P2096 on new Encore and Trax 1.4 catalysts before break-in and fixed a 2017 Malibu 1.5 by software.
c: Rear oxygen sensor skewed rich, for example a contaminated reference air duct
Front sensor reading lean, so the engine actually runs rich
Calibration issue fixed by an ECM update
New catalyst not yet broken in
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Usually no noticeable change in driveability

P2097.t: Post Catalyst Fuel Trim System Too Rich (Bank 1)
P2097.d: P2097 is the opposite limit of the post-catalyst trim on bank 1: the rear oxygen sensor keeps reporting lean exhaust, so the outer loop keeps adding fuel until it reaches its rich limit. GM's Bosch-based 2005 V6 sets it for a correction above +0.03 lambda; GM's 2018 four-cylinders list it as the high limit, with the integral offset at +99 % and total offset at +50 % or more (Type B); Ford's 2020 to 2023 engines set it 5 s after reaching a rear bias trim of +0.087. Air drawn in through an exhaust leak ahead of the rear sensor, a rear sensor skewed lean, or a front sensor reading rich all produce this pattern. Several manufacturers have issued software fixes: GM for the 2013 ATS and Malibu 2.5 (only when long-term trim stays within ±13 %) and for the 2017 Malibu 1.5, Mitsubishi for the 2014 Outlander V6 after a wrong threshold. Subaru's 2025 bulletin corrects the service manual steps for P2096 and P2097 across its range.
c: Exhaust leak ahead of the rear oxygen sensor drawing in air
Rear oxygen sensor skewed lean or aged
Calibration issue fixed by an ECM update
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Slightly higher fuel consumption

P2098.t: Post Catalyst Fuel Trim System Too Lean (Bank 2)
P2098.d: P2098 is the bank 2 version of P2096 on V and flat engines with a catalyst and rear oxygen sensor per bank. The post-catalyst trim of bank 2 has reached its lean-side limit because the rear sensor of that bank keeps reporting rich exhaust. Ford monitors both banks the same way and sets the code 5 s after the bank 2 rear bias trim reaches -0.083; GM's Bosch-based 2005 2.8 and 3.6 V6 and the 2008 3.6 LLT list it as a rich shift of the secondary trim beyond its calibrated limit. If only one bank reports it, compare the two banks' rear sensor signals and the front sensor readings: a fault on one side points to that bank's sensors or its exhaust, whereas both banks together hint at a common cause such as fuel or calibration. Audi saw P2098 with P2096 on 2013 to 2016 A8, S6, S7, S8, RS 6 and RS 7 4.0 TFSI, caused by contaminated reference air ducts in the rear sensors, not by the front sensors the guided test suggests.
c: Bank 2 rear oxygen sensor skewed rich
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Usually no noticeable change in driveability

P2099.t: Post Catalyst Fuel Trim System Too Rich (Bank 2)
P2099.d: P2099 is the bank 2 counterpart of P2097: the rear oxygen sensor of bank 2 keeps reporting lean exhaust, so the post-catalyst trim of that bank adds fuel until it reaches its rich-side limit. Ford sets it 5 s after the bank 2 rear bias trim reaches +0.087, with the closed loop running, coolant between 160 and 250 °F and at least 15 % fuel in the tank; GM's Bosch-based 2005 2.8 and 3.6 V6 and the 2008 3.6 LLT list it as a lean shift of the secondary trim beyond its calibrated limit, over two trips. A typical physical cause is air drawn into the exhaust ahead of the bank 2 rear sensor, at a cracked manifold, a leaking flange or a loose sensor, which makes that sensor read lean. A rear sensor that has aged lean or a front sensor reading rich gives the same result. Check fuel trims and front sensor data of both banks before replacing a sensor.
c: Exhaust leak ahead of the bank 2 rear sensor
Bank 2 rear oxygen sensor skewed lean or aged
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Slightly higher fuel consumption

P209A.t: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Sensor B Circuit
P209A.d: Air-assisted DEF dosing, as in Bosch's first Denoxtronic generation of 2004, mixes the fluid with compressed air before it reaches the exhaust, and a pressure sensor confirms that this air is there. A second sensor B can sit in another air branch or serve as a cross-check for sensor A. P209A is the general circuit fault of sensor B, set when its signal or supply cannot be evaluated at all; P209C and P209D split off the clearly low and high readings. No manufacturer documents P209A publicly, and Deutz, whose air-assisted EMR L1 system has only one such sensor, uses the P2037 family for it. CARB counts air-assisted injection among the delivery functions that must be monitored. Without a usable reading the controller usually suspends dosing, NOx rises and a derate may follow.
c: Corroded or loose connector at sensor B, often from DEF residue or road spray
Reference voltage or ground of the sensor interrupted or out of range
Internal electronic failure of pressure sensor B
Input stage in the dosing control unit defective
s: Malfunction indicator lamp or SCR warning on
DEF dosing suspended, higher NOx output
Engine power derate or inducement countdown on trucks

P209B.t: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P209B.d: Here the wiring of air pressure sensor B is intact and the voltage lies inside its valid band, yet the reported pressure makes no sense for the moment. Typical checks compare the value with the switching state of the air supply: pressure must rise when air is released to the mixing chamber and fall back when it is shut off, and with the system at rest it should sit near ambient. A sensor that sticks, drifts or reacts too slowly fails these tests. No manufacturer publishes P209B; Deutz reports such plausibility errors on its single air pressure sensor with its own code P1119. Besides the sensor, a leaking air line, a sticking supply valve or a clogged sensing port can produce the same picture. CARB requires rationality checks for every input the dosing strategy relies on.
c: Sensor B drifting or responding sluggishly
Leak in the atomizing air line between valve and dosing module
Sensing port blocked by urea crystals or dirt
Air supply valve sticking, so the expected pressure change does not occur
s: Check engine or SCR warning lamp
Dosing reduced or stopped, possible NOx efficiency codes later
No noticeable change in driving until an inducement starts

P209C.t: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Sensor B Circuit Low
P209C.d: P209C means the signal of the second air pressure sensor in an air-assisted DEF system has dropped below the lowest voltage a working sensor can deliver. With common three-wire pressure sensors this points to a signal wire shorted to ground, a lost 5 V reference or a sensor failed internally; with some input circuits an open signal line also reads low. The controller then cannot tell whether atomizing air is present. The opposite fault, a reading stuck above the valid band, is P209D, while P209B covers values that are electrically possible but implausible. No manufacturer documents P209C publicly; for sensor A, Deutz files the matching fault (short to ground or open) as P2039. Expect the dosing to be stopped and a warning on the dash; on heavy vehicles an inducement may follow.
c: Signal wire chafed through and touching ground
5 V sensor supply missing, for example pulled down by another sensor on the same rail
s: MIL or SCR warning on
Live data shows pressure at or below zero regardless of air supply
DEF dosing switched off

P209D.t: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Sensor B Circuit High
P209D.d: With P209D the second air pressure sensor reports a voltage above the top of its usable range, close to the supply or battery level. A real air pressure that high is not possible in the system, so the controller treats the value as an electrical fault.
