Usual explanations are a signal wire that touches a live conductor, a broken ground return so that the output floats up to the reference, or an open signal line on circuits that pull the input high. P209C is the mirror case with a reading too low, and P209A the umbrella code when the type of circuit fault cannot be narrowed down. P209D does not appear in any public manufacturer list; Deutz assigns the corresponding short to battery on sensor A to P2040. The SCR controller stops dosing because it can no longer confirm atomization, and the warning lamp comes on.
c: Sensor ground open at the connector or splice
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Sensor B output stage failed high
s: Warning lamp on, dosing stopped
Displayed air pressure stays at an impossibly high value
Inducement countdown on heavy vehicles if not repaired

P209E.t: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Sensor A/B Correlation
P209E.d: When an air-assisted DEF system carries two air pressure sensors, the controller can compare them under conditions where both should read alike, for instance with the air supply shut and the lines vented to ambient, or at a steady dosing point. P209E is set when the two values stay apart by more than the calibrated margin even though each lies within its own electrical range. The code says nothing about which sensor is wrong; a slow drift of one, a restriction in only one branch or a leak between them all show up this way. The individual sensor faults are P2037 to P2041 for A and P209A to P209D for B. No manufacturer documents P209E publicly. CARB asks for such cross-checks wherever redundant inputs exist. The SCR system typically limits or stops dosing until the cause is found.
c: One of the two sensors drifted; compare both against a reference gauge
Restriction or crystal build-up in only one air branch
Leak in the air path between the two measuring points
Replacement sensor with a different pressure range fitted
s: SCR or engine warning lamp on
Live data shows clearly different values for sensors A and B at rest
Reduced or suspended DEF dosing

P209F.t: Reductant Tank Heater Control Circuit Performance
P209F.d: DEF freezes at about minus 11 °C, so the tank is heated electrically or by engine coolant. P209F is not about a broken wire, which P202A to P202C report, but about the heating not behaving as expected: the tank does not warm up in the allowed time, or the heater or its valve runs too hot. Deutz uses the code on its MD1 controller as tank heater overtemperature with unknown cause (SPN 520312, FMI 11). On the Ram 2500 and 3500 with the 6.7 L Cummins, FCA lists P209F in bulletin 18-091-16 for 2013 trucks and again in 08-076-26 for model year 2025; both times new software for the PCM or the DEF control unit removes false detections. In winter a heating fault can leave the system unable to dose, which leads to warnings and eventually a speed limit.
c: Control unit software detecting a fault that is not there (FCA bulletins 18-091-16, 08-076-26)
Heater element partly degraded or poorly coupled to the fluid
Coolant heating valve sticking on coolant-heated tanks
Tank temperature sensor reading wrong, so heating looks ineffective
s: MIL and DEF system message, mostly in cold weather
Frozen DEF not thawed in time, dosing delayed after cold start
Speed limitation if the fault persists

P20A0.t: Reductant Purge Control Valve A Circuit/Open
P20A0.d: After the engine stops, many airless DEF systems suck the fluid out of the line and injector back into the tank so that nothing freezes there. In Bosch's Denoxtronic 2.2 this is done by a 4/2-way valve in the supply module that reverses the flow. P20A0 concerns the drive circuit of this valve, chiefly an interruption. GM checks it on the 6.6 L Duramax (LML/LGH) with the driver switched off: an impedance above 200 kΩ between ECM pin and load for 3 s sets the code, Type A. Volkswagen, on the 2014 Touareg 3.0 TDI (CNRB), uses a power-stage voltage between 2.97 and 4.70 V. Shorts to ground and to power are split off as P20A2 and P20A3. If the line cannot be emptied, DEF may stay in the injector and line and freeze there in winter.
c: Coil of the purge or reversing valve open
Connector at the supply module loose or corroded by DEF
Output stage in the engine or dosing control unit defective
s: MIL on (GM Type A, first trip)
DEF system or emission service message
Risk of frozen DEF line or injector in winter

P20A1.t: Reductant Purge Control Valve A Performance
P20A1.d: P20A1 judges the valve by its effect rather than its wiring. When the purge valve switches the pump into reverse, the pressure in the DEF line must drop. GM's 6.6 L Duramax (LML/LGH, tables 14OBDG10 and 16OBDG08) watches this pressure reduction phase: if the pump pressure at its end is less than 50 kPa below the value at its start, the code is stored, Type A, so the MIL comes on in the first trip. Hino describes the same code as a DEF pump reversing valve that stays shut; bulletin SB-16-015 for 2011 to 2017 conventional trucks reports false detections and supplies new DCU software. Real causes are a valve that does not shift, a blocked return path or a pressure sensor that misreads. Electrical faults of the same valve are P20A0, P20A2 and P20A3.
c: Reversing valve in the supply module not shifting, often from crystallized DEF
Dosing control unit software detecting falsely (Hino SB-16-015)
Return or suction path blocked so pressure cannot drop
DEF pressure sensor reading wrong during the test
s: MIL on after shutdown and restart
DEF warning message, possibly with other pump codes
Line not emptied, frost damage possible

P20A2.t: Reductant Purge Control Valve A Circuit Low
P20A2.d: The purge valve that reverses the DEF flow at shutdown is usually switched on the ground side. P20A2 reports that its control line is pulled too low, typically a short to ground somewhere between the driver and the coil, which would switch the valve on unintentionally or keep the driver from sensing it. GM tests the low-side driver of the 6.6 L Duramax with the output off and sets P20A2 when the impedance to controller ground is under 0.5 Ω for 2 s, Type A. Volkswagen flags the Touareg 3.0 TDI (CNRB, 2014) when the power-stage voltage falls below 2.97 V. Compared with P20A0, where the line is open, the fault here is an unwanted connection to ground. Chafed wiring near the tank and water in the connector are the usual findings; the controller may then block dosing.
c: Control wire chafed against the frame or tank bracket
Moisture or DEF in the valve connector creating a leakage path
Valve coil shorted to its housing
s: MIL on at once (GM Type A)
Service emission or DEF system message
Dosing possibly disabled

P20A3.t: Reductant Purge Control Valve A Circuit High
P20A3.d: P20A3 is the high-side fault of the purge valve circuit: the line carries voltage or current where it should not. GM detects it on the 6.6 L Duramax while the low-side driver is switched on; an impedance of less than 0.5 Ω to controller power lasting 3 s triggers it as a Type A fault. Volkswagen's test for the 2014 Touareg V6 TDI (engine CNRB) looks at current instead and reports P20A3 above 3.00 A, which indicates a short across the coil or to battery positive. A driver that sees such overcurrent switches off to protect itself, so the valve no longer reverses the pump, and the line is not emptied at shutdown. P20A2 covers the opposite short to ground and P20A0 the open circuit. Look for a shorted coil, a wire touching a supply cable or a damaged connector at the supply module.
c: Valve coil with shorted windings drawing excessive current
Control wire shorted to a battery-fed conductor
Damaged or DEF-contaminated connector bridging pins
s: MIL on in the first trip (GM Type A)
DEF warning and possibly further pump codes
In frost, risk of DEF freezing in the line

P20A4.t: Reductant Purge Control Valve A Stuck Open
P20A4.d: Stuck open means the purge valve stays in, or leaks into, its emptying position while the system is supposed to dose. Part of the pump output then flows back toward the tank, so working pressure builds slowly, collapses after the pump stops or needs a high pump duty to hold. No manufacturer documents P20A4 publicly; GM, Volkswagen and Hino describe only circuit faults and the opposite failure, the valve that does not move into purge (P20A1, P20A5). Bosch's workshop instructions for the Denoxtronic 2.1 or 2.2 show how such a fault looks: if pressure falls below 4.5 bar within about 120 s after a pressure test without any visible leak, a leak inside the supply module at the 4/2-way valve is suspected and the supply module is repaired. The consequence is poor dosing and rising NOx.
c: Worn or contaminated valve seat leaking internally in the supply module
Urea crystals holding the valve in the purge position
Valve energized permanently by a driver or wiring fault
s: Warning lamp on, often with low DEF pressure codes
Slow pressure build-up after start
Higher NOx, possibly SCR efficiency codes

P20A5.t: Reductant Purge Control Valve A Stuck Closed
P20A5.d: Stuck closed is the failure in which the purge valve does not switch to the reverse position when the system wants to empty the line. For the CNRB engine of the 2014 Touareg, Volkswagen bases P20A5 on the pressure difference between the start of the pressure reduction and the current value. Ford reports the code on 6.7 L diesel Super Duty trucks of model years 2023 to 2025, F-650/F-750 included: TSB 24-2055, 24-2379 and 25-2032 trace an illuminated MIL with P20A5 to a software issue of the glow dosing module, shown in the scan tool as secondary OBD control module, and cure it by reprogramming; driving is not affected. On other vehicles a jammed valve or a blocked return line is the real cause. P20A4 is the reverse case. A line left full can freeze and crack in winter.
c: Control module software (Ford 6.7 L, reprogram the glow dosing module)
Valve jammed in the delivery position by crystallized DEF
Return line to the tank kinked or blocked
DEF pressure sensor frozen at one value
s: MIL on, often found after a shutdown cycle
No change in driveability (Ford software case)
Frost damage to line or injector if a real valve fault persists

P20A6.t: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Control Valve Circuit/Open
P20A6.d: In an air-assisted DEF system the compressed air must reach the mixing point at a defined pressure, whether it comes from the vehicle's brake air supply or from a separate compressor. A solenoid valve sets or switches this air pressure. P20A6 marks an open circuit in its control: the controller commands the valve, but no current flows, so the atomizing air cannot be regulated. No manufacturer documents P20A6 publicly. Deutz, whose EMR L1 controller drives a similar air supply valve, files the open circuit under P2059 for the air pump or supply valve and under its own code P1062 for the air switching valve. Low and high faults of the same circuit are P20A8 and P20A9. Air-assisted dosing appeared with Bosch's Denoxtronic 1 in 2004 and was later replaced by airless systems.
c: Solenoid coil of the air pressure control valve open
Connector unplugged or wire broken near the valve
Fuse or supply feed for the valve missing
s: SCR warning lamp or MIL on
Dosing stops for lack of atomizing air
Power derate on heavy vehicles

P20A7.t: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Control Valve Performance
P20A7.d: With P20A7 the air pressure control valve is electrically fine, but the air pressure it should produce does not appear. The check relies on the air pressure sensor: after the valve is opened or its duty changed, the measured value must reach the target band within a set time. If pressure stays too low, overshoots or reacts sluggishly, the valve is judged ineffective. No manufacturer documents P20A7 publicly; Deutz reports comparable symptoms with its own codes, P1126 for a defective SCR air valve and P1124 for air pressure too low. Beyond a worn or dirty valve, an empty air reservoir, a leaking line or a blocked air filter upstream can explain the fault. Electrical problems belong to P20A6, P20A8 and P20A9; a valve clearly jammed in one position gives P20AA or P20AB.
c: Valve worn or contaminated with oil, water or urea deposits from the air supply
Insufficient supply pressure from the vehicle air system or compressor
Leaking air line or fitting downstream of the valve
s: SCR warning, often together with air pressure codes
Poor atomization, possible deposits in the exhaust pipe
Rising NOx and later efficiency faults

P20A8.t: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Control Valve Circuit Low
P20A8.d: P20A8 says the air pressure control valve's drive circuit sits at too low a level, which normally means a short to ground. Depending on whether the valve is switched on the high or the low side, this either stops the valve from opening at all or energizes it without command. In both cases the controller loses control of the atomizing air. The fault differs from P20A6, where the circuit is interrupted, and from P20A9, a short toward battery voltage. No manufacturer documents P20A8 publicly. For the comparable valves of its air-assisted system, Deutz lists the high-side short to ground as P2060 on the air pump or supply valve and as P1061 on the air switching valve. CARB requires such circuit checks on every electrical component of the SCR system. A chafed harness on the frame rail is the classic finding.
c: Harness chafed through to ground along the frame
Solenoid coil shorted to the valve body
Water in the connector creating a path to ground
s: MIL or SCR lamp on
Blown fuse possible on high-side switched valves
Dosing stopped, derate on trucks

P20A9.t: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Control Valve Circuit High
P20A9.d: If the control line of the air pressure control valve shows battery voltage or excessive current where it should not, P20A9 is stored. A wire touching a positive feed, a coil with shorted turns or a bridged connector can cause it. On a low-side driven valve the coil would then be live permanently; on a high-side driver the output often detects overcurrent and shuts down. Either way the atomizing air no longer follows the commands. P20A8 is the matching short to ground and P20A6 the open circuit. No manufacturer publishes P20A9. Deutz handles the comparable faults on its air pump or supply valve as P2061 for a short to battery and P2059-19 for critically high output current. Because the air supply is shared, check for further codes on the air pressure sensors before replacing parts.
c: Coil with shorted turns causing overcurrent
Control wire shorted to a positive feed in the harness
Output stage in the dosing control unit defective
s: Warning lamp on
Air pressure uncontrolled, often too high or permanently on
DEF dosing suspended

P20AA.t: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Control Valve Stuck Open
P20AA.d: P20AA describes a mechanical condition: the air pressure control valve lets air through even when it is commanded closed or to a lower setting. The air pressure sensor then shows pressure in phases where it should have fallen, for example after shutdown or during dosing pauses. Constant airflow can push DEF toward the nozzle unmetered, cool the mixing area and waste compressed air, which on trucks also strains the brake air supply. No manufacturer documents P20AA publicly; the closest documented case is Deutz's own code P1126 for a defective SCR air valve. Distinguish it from P20AB, where the valve blocks the air, and from P20A7, where the pressure is merely off target. Dirt, water or oil from the compressed-air system holding the valve off its seat is the usual reason.
c: Debris, water or oil from the air system on the valve seat
Valve held open electrically by a wiring or driver fault
s: SCR warning lamp
Air pressure remains present with the valve commanded closed
Audible air flow at the dosing module, compressor runs more often

P20AB.t: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Control Valve Stuck Closed
P20AB.d: The opposite of P20AA: the air pressure control valve does not open although the controller commands it, so no atomizing air reaches the DEF dosing point. The air pressure sensor stays near ambient during dosing requests. Without air, an air-assisted dosing module cannot spray the fluid into fine droplets, and the risk of liquid DEF and deposits in the exhaust grows; controllers therefore stop dosing, NOx rises and heavy vehicles move toward a derate. No manufacturer documents P20AB publicly; Deutz files low air pressure under its own code P1124 and a blocked air path at the injector under P1123. Before condemning the valve, check the supply pressure from the vehicle air system, a frozen or kinked line and the air filter. P20A6 to P20A9 indicate electrical causes instead.
c: Valve seized by corrosion or deposits
No supply pressure, for example low air reservoir or closed protection valve
Air line frozen with condensate or kinked
s: MIL or SCR warning on
Air pressure stays at zero when dosing is requested
Power derate or inducement on trucks

P20AC.t: Reductant Metering Unit Temperature Sensor Circuit
P20AC.d: P20AC is the general circuit code for the temperature sensor built into the reductant metering unit, meaning the DEF supply or dosing module that pressurises the fluid. The control unit typically relies on this value to judge whether the module has thawed and may start pumping. The code stands for an electrical fault the software cannot assign to a low or high signal; those cases carry their own numbers, P20AE and P20AF. No manufacturer documents P20AC publicly. Hino, for example, files faults of its DEF pump temperature sensor under the maker-specific P142A instead. CARB requires such inputs to be watched continuously for circuit continuity. Drivers see a DEF or engine warning and, if it is ignored, speed or restart limits.
c: Corroded or loose connector at the DEF supply/metering module
Damaged sensor wiring between module and control unit
Temperature sensor inside the metering unit failed (usually replaced with the module)
Input fault in the dosing or engine control unit
s: Malfunction indicator or DEF/SCR warning lamp on
Dosing delayed or stopped in cold weather
Inducement countdown with speed or restart limit

P20AD.t: Reductant Metering Unit Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P20AD.d: P20AD covers a metering unit temperature reading that is electrically valid but does not make sense. A typical check compares it after a long cold soak with other temperatures that ought to agree, or watches whether it climbs once the module heater or warm coolant has had time to act. Hino gives a practical yardstick in tech tip TT-16-014: with the engine at ambient temperature, DEF tank, DEF pump and coolant readings should lie within 8 °C (14 °F) of each other; Hino applies that to its coolant valve code P20B2, not to P20AD. No manufacturer publishes P20AD with its own limits. Because the verdict rests on behaviour over time, confirmation usually needs a complete drive cycle, and a skewed value can mislead the thaw and heating logic.
c: Temperature sensor in the metering unit drifted (reads plausible but wrong)
Comparison sensor (DEF tank or coolant temperature) itself faulty
Contact resistance in the connector shifting the signal
Module heating or coolant heating not working, so the expected rise never comes
s: Warning lamp after a cold start or longer drive
DEF dosing starts late or not at all in winter
Live data shows module temperature out of line with tank and coolant

P20AE.t: Reductant Metering Unit Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
P20AE.d: P20AE is stored when the signal of the metering unit temperature sensor falls below its valid band. If the sensor is an NTC thermistor, the common design, though no maker confirms it publicly for this part, a low voltage stands for a very high indicated temperature. Typical reasons are then a signal wire chafed through to ground, moisture or DEF crystals bridging the connector pins, or a shorted sensor element. No manufacturer reference names this exact code; CARB merely requires the input to be checked for out-of-range values. The control unit then usually discards the reading and may suspend dosing. The upper counterpart is P20AF, while unclear electrical faults go to P20AC.
c: Signal wire shorted to ground (chafing near tank or frame)
Water or DEF residue bridging the connector pins
Sensor element in the metering unit shorted
s: Warning lamp on immediately after key-on
Module temperature shown far too hot in live data
DEF dosing suspended, inducement countdown possible

P20AF.t: Reductant Metering Unit Temperature Sensor Circuit High
P20AF.d: P20AF means the metering unit temperature signal has risen above its permitted band. For an NTC thermistor, the likely design though not publicly confirmed for this part, that looks like an extremely cold module. Electrically it is usually an open signal or ground wire, a terminal backed out of the connector or a short to a voltage source. Corrosion deserves attention: Hino's bulletins SB-16-015 and SB-16-016 explain that frozen DEF can damage the pump and let fluid creep into the pump connector and SCR harness; Hino names its own P142A there, not P20AF. Believing the module frozen, the control unit holds back dosing and may keep heating. No maker publishes P20AF itself.
c: Open signal or ground wire to the temperature sensor
DEF intrusion and corrosion in the pump connector or harness
Sensor element in the metering unit open
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
s: Module temperature shown far below ambient in live data
DEF warning and delayed or missing dosing
Further SCR codes if the harness is corroded

P20B0.t: Reductant Metering Unit Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P20B0.d: P20B0 flags a metering unit temperature signal that jumps or drops out for brief moments instead of failing steadily. Housing, pump and fluid store a lot of heat, so the real temperature cannot change in leaps; the software treats such steps as a signal defect. Loose terminals, a harness rubbing against the frame near the tank and connectors exposed to road splash and thermal cycling are the main suspects. Since the fault comes and goes, it may well be inactive at the moment of inspection, and wiggling the harness while watching live data helps more than a single resistance reading. No manufacturer documents P20B0 publicly, so the actual jump limits remain unknown.
c: Loose or spread terminal in the module connector
Harness chafing intermittently against frame or tank bracket
Moisture entering the connector during wet or freezing conditions
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Temperature value jumping in live data
Fault often not reproducible in the workshop

P20B1.t: Reductant Heater Coolant Control Valve Circuit/Open
P20B1.d: Many heavy-duty SCR systems thaw the DEF tank and supply module with engine coolant, and an electrically switched valve decides when that warm coolant may circulate; Bosch offers its larger supply modules with either electric or cooling-water heating. P20B1 is set when the control unit finds the drive circuit of this valve open or otherwise defective. No manufacturer documents P20B1 publicly. Hino, which fits such a coolant cutoff valve, explains in TT-16-014 that once its dosing control unit detects an open load it stops powering the valve until a UREA SCR memory reset, so circuit tests only work while the valve stays connected. Without a working valve, DEF stays frozen longer in winter.
c: Valve connector unplugged, loose or corroded
Open solenoid coil in the coolant valve
Broken wire between control unit and valve
s: Malfunction indicator and SCR warning on
DEF thaws slowly or not at all in cold weather
Valve does not click during an actuator test

P20B2.t: Reductant Heater Coolant Control Valve Performance/Stuck Open
P20B2.d: P20B2 is a functional fault of the coolant valve that heats the reductant system: the circuit is intact, but temperatures do not follow the commanded valve position, most often because coolant keeps flowing while the valve should be shut. Hino uses the code in its dosing control unit and covers it in tech tip TT-16-014 for 2011–2017 conventional and 2013–2017 cab-over trucks. Most valves returned under warranty showed no defect, and a wrong DEF tank temperature input can set P20B2 falsely. Hino therefore asks to sort out any stored P205B to P205D or U02A2 first and, with the engine cold, to confirm that tank, pump and coolant temperatures agree within 8 °C (14 °F). Confirming the fault takes a drive with full warm-up.
c: Wrong DEF tank or pump temperature input misleading the valve check
Coolant valve mechanically stuck open (deposits, debris)
Valve test blocked by other stored SCR faults, valve wrongly condemned
s: Malfunction indicator with no other SCR fault stored
DEF tank temperature runs unusually high
Possible engine power restriction if left unrepaired

P20B3.t: Reductant Heater Coolant Control Valve Circuit Low
P20B3.d: P20B3 reports a low reading on the control line of the coolant valve that feeds the DEF heating, the classic picture of a control wire shorted to ground or a solenoid with shorted turns. Depending on how the output stage is wired, the valve then stays permanently energised or never responds, so the DEF can get too warm in summer or remain frozen in winter. No manufacturer is known to describe P20B3 publicly; the classification rests on the CARB rule that actuators in the SCR system be checked continuously for circuit faults. The valve exists mainly on coolant-heated systems, where it governs how quickly frozen DEF becomes available. Before replacing it, look for chafed wiring along the frame and for coolant or DEF inside the connector.
c: Valve control wire shorted to ground
Valve solenoid with shorted turns (low resistance)
Coolant or DEF inside the valve connector
s: Malfunction indicator and SCR warning on
DEF tank overheats or does not thaw, depending on valve position

P20B4.t: Reductant Heater Coolant Control Valve Circuit High
P20B4.d: P20B4 is the opposite electrical case to P20B3: the drive circuit of the reductant heater coolant valve reads too high, which points to a short to battery voltage on the control line or, with certain driver designs, an interrupted ground return. The control unit can then no longer switch the valve, and the heating loop stays in whatever position the valve spring holds. On coolant-heated installations, such as Bosch supply modules supplied with a cooling-water heating option, that decides whether the module thaws at all. No manufacturer documents P20B4 publicly; CARB's comprehensive component rules form the basis. Measure with the valve connected, because some controllers cut the output after a fault, as Hino describes for its valve.
c: Valve control wire shorted to battery voltage
Open ground return of the valve circuit
Output stage in the control unit defective
s: Malfunction indicator and SCR warning on
Valve cannot be actuated in an output test
Slow DEF thaw in winter

P20B5.t: Reductant Metering Unit Heater Control Circuit/Open
P20B5.d: P20B5 concerns the electric heater inside the reductant metering unit, the element that keeps the pump module from freezing. The control unit sets it when this heater circuit is open or otherwise broken. Volkswagen documents the code for the 2014 Touareg 3.0 TDI (engine CNRB): the engine control unit measures the conductance of the element while heating and stores P20B5 at 0.10 siemens or less, roughly 10 ohms or more. A burnt-out element, a broken wire or a corroded terminal are the usual reasons. With the heater dead, DEF in the module stays frozen longer after a cold start and dosing begins late. Too little and too much conductance have separate codes, P20B7 and P20B8, and the tank heater uses its own range.
c: Heater element in the metering unit burnt out (usually module replacement)
Broken heater supply or ground wire
Corroded heater terminals at the module connector
s: Warning lamp mainly in cold weather
DEF dosing starts late after a cold start
Inducement countdown possible

P20B6.t: Reductant Metering Unit Heater Control Circuit Performance
P20B6.d: P20B6 is the functional check of the metering unit heater circuit: wiring and driver pass the electrical tests, yet the heating falls short of what the control unit expects, for instance the module temperature barely rises during a commanded heating phase or the current drifts away from its target. Such a monitor needs the heater to be running, so it can only reach a verdict in cold conditions and across a drive cycle. Volkswagen's Touareg CNRB chart lists P20B5, P20B7 and P20B8 for this heater but no P20B6, and no other maker publishes the code with limits. Suspects include an aged element with changed resistance, poor thermal contact inside the module or a temperature sensor feeding a false value.
c: Aged heater element with reduced output
Metering unit temperature sensor reporting a wrong value
Low supply voltage to the heater (weak battery, poor ground)
s: Warning lamp after cold starts only
Long delay before DEF dosing begins in frost

P20B7.t: Reductant Metering Unit Heater Control Circuit Low
P20B7.d: P20B7 means the metering unit heater circuit reads low. Volkswagen gives this a concrete meaning for the 2014 Touareg CNRB: the control unit checks heater conductance at the start of heating and flags P20B7 below 0.33 siemens, so the element shows more than about 3 ohms; further stages at 0.18 and 0.04 siemens follow. In VW's logic, low therefore refers to conductance, not to voltage, and points to a degraded element, a high-resistance joint or a partly broken wire rather than a short to ground. Other makers may define the low case through the output-stage voltage instead, since their drivers differ. The module receives too little heat, and thawing after a frosty night takes longer.
c: Heater element resistance too high (aged or partly damaged)
Contact resistance at the heater terminals
Heater wire partly broken (few strands left)
s: Warning lamp at the start of a cold-weather heating phase
DEF dosing delayed in winter

P20B8.t: Reductant Metering Unit Heater Control Circuit High
P20B8.d: P20B8 marks the upper limit of the metering unit heater circuit. The 2014 Touareg CNRB table from Volkswagen sets it when the conductance measured at heating start exceeds 0.74 siemens, meaning the element is below about 1.35 ohms, with additional limits at 0.96 and 0.52 siemens. Such high conductance suggests shorted heater windings, wires touching each other or fluid bridging the terminals, and it implies excess current that strains the driver stage and wiring. The control unit will normally switch the heater off for protection, so in winter the outcome resembles an open heater (P20B5). Makers that judge their outputs by voltage may use the same code for a short to battery instead.
c: Heater element internally shorted (too low resistance)
Heater wires chafed and touching each other
DEF or water bridging the heater terminals
s: Warning lamp as soon as heating is requested
Heater switched off, DEF stays frozen longer
Possibly a blown heater fuse

P20B9.d: P20B9 flags an open or broken control circuit for reductant heater A, one of the electric elements that keep diesel exhaust fluid liquid in winter. Which element carries the letter A differs by maker: GM's 2025 DEF tables call it heater 1, the tank heater; Ford links the code to the pump/heater assembly in the tank, Deutz to the suction line heater. A Hino bulletin for 2015–2018 J05 cab-over trucks instead lists P20B9 as heater 2 of the heated DEF line, about 5.5 ohms per circuit at 20 °C. GM pinpoints the open with the output switched off and stores it after 2 s as Type A; VW sets it on the 2014 Touareg CNRB below 4.70 V signal voltage. Ford's TSB 21-2336 blames water inside reductant harness connectors on 3.0 L and 6.7 L trucks. Without heat, dosing waits until the fluid thaws.
c: Water or DEF residue inside the heater or tank harness connectors (Ford TSB 21-2336)
Heater A element burnt out, so resistance is far above specification
Broken supply or return wire between control module and heater
Heater output stage in the DEF or engine control module defective
s: Check engine light, often first noticed in cold weather
DEF dosing starts late or not at all after a cold start
DEF system warning followed by a countdown to a speed limit

P20BA.t: Reductant Heater A Control Circuit Performance
P20BA.d: P20BA is the plausibility test for heater A: the circuit is intact, yet the current, resistance or power the element takes does not match the command. GM's 2025 DEF tables compute the resistance of heater 1, the tank heater, and fail it below 1.00 or above 1.80 ohms, or when power strays more than 45 W from the request, after 8 s as Type A; the 2018 tables use a 1.05–1.93 ohm window. Ford checks circuit 1, also the tank heater, a single time each trip while it runs at full power: under 3 A and under 5 V at the output while switched on, or the reverse when off. FCA reflashed 2014 Ram 1500 EcoDiesel engines that logged P20BA without a real fault (18-028-14). Volvo and Mack advise diagnosing it like the pressure-build failure P20E8, including lines, filters and the coolant heating valve.
c: Aged heater element whose resistance has drifted out of the allowed window
Corroded or loose heater terminals adding resistance under load
Control software setting the code without a defect (FCA 18-028-14 reflash)
DEF pump unable to build pressure because of swapped or blocked lines (Volvo/Mack KC-4)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp with DEF system message
DEF tank stays cold or frozen in winter although the engine is warm
Possible speed limitation after the inducement countdown

P20BB.t: Reductant Heater A Control Circuit Low
P20BB.d: A low reading on the heater A control circuit usually means the output or its wire is grounded, or the element pulls far more current than it should. GM's 2025 DEF module checks heater 1 (tank heater 1) in both states: switched on, a low-side drain voltage above 0.45 V or a load current above 95 A counts; switched off, the high-side voltage sitting in a low band near 0.5–0.6 V. Two seconds of failures give a Type A fault. Ford logs P20BB on circuit 1 above 15 A and lets the glow plug module report it within 250 ms; VW uses a signal voltage under 2.97 V on the 2014 Touareg. On 2020–2022 Silverado and Sierra diesels GM found the test itself setting P20BB falsely and released new DEF module calibrations (22-NA-112). Expect a warning lamp and, later, a speed limit.
c: Heater A wire chafed through and touching ground
Internal short in the heater element, drawing excessive current
DEF control module calibration setting the code falsely (GM 22-NA-112)
Moisture bridging heater pins to ground in the connector
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, possibly with a blown heater fuse
Message that speed will be reduced if the system is not serviced
No DEF heating, so dosing is delayed in frost

P20BC.t: Reductant Heater A Control Circuit High
P20BC.d: P20BC means the heater A control circuit reads high: the wire or output has picked up battery voltage, so the element may run when it should be off or cannot be switched at all. GM's 2025 DEF tables spot this on heater 1 (tank heater 1) mostly in the off state, when the high-side voltage lies between roughly 2 and 4.3 V instead of near zero; Type A after a 2 s debounce. Ford's criterion is current below 3 A with more than 5 V at the output while the power stage is off. GM's 2014 tables for the 6.6 L LML, where the glow plug module drives the heaters, look for more than 3.5 V at the heater pin (Type B). On the Touareg CNRB, VW sets it above 2.20 A signal current. For 2025 Ram 2500–5500 with the 6.7 L Cummins, FCA names P20BC the suction line heater and fixes it with DCU software (08-076-26).
c: Heater A control wire shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
DEF control unit software fault (FCA 08-076-26 for 2025 Cummins Ram)
Heater output stage or relay stuck switched on
s: Check engine light and DEF system warning
Heater may stay energized, risking overheating or a drained battery
Reduced power or speed limit once the inducement starts

P20BD.d: Heater B's control circuit is open. In GM's tables heater 2 is the DEF line heater; the 2025 version detects the open state with the output off and sets a Type A code after two seconds, while the 2018 version relies on an open status reported by the DEF control module with battery voltage above 11 V. Deutz assigns B to the pressure line heater, the hose from pump to dosing valve. Hino numbers differently: its 2018 bulletin calls P20BD heater 1 of the heated DEF line on J05 cab-overs and asks for a resistance check at the 6-pin connector before the line assembly is replaced. On the Touareg CNRB, VW stores the code when the power stage's diagnostic signal drops below 4.70 V. A frozen pressure line delays or blocks dosing in cold weather. Short circuits of the same element are P20BF and P20C0.
c: Heating wire in the pressure line broken (line assembly replacement)
Corroded or unplugged line heater connector
Harness to the line heater damaged along the frame rail
s: Warning lamp, especially after cold nights
DEF pressure builds slowly or not at all in frost
Inducement countdown with eventual speed limit

P20BE.t: Reductant Heater B Control Circuit Performance
P20BE.d: P20BE judges whether heater B, in most designs the heated pressure line, behaves as expected once the wiring itself checks out. GM's 2025 DEF tables flag line heater resistance below 2.80 or above 7.50 ohms, or a power error above 16.5 W, after 8 s (Type A); the 2018 tables accept a voltage-to-current ratio only between 1.51 and 3.57 ohms. Ford tests circuit 2, the pressure line heater, continuously while it heats and fails it when conductance falls below 0.3 S within 2.2 s, in addition to an on/off current and voltage comparison. For the 3.0 L EcoDiesel FCA titles the code Reductant Pressure Line Heater Control Circuit Performance; its 2014 Ram 1500 bulletin cured spurious entries with PCM software. Deutz maps P20BE to over-temperature of its pressure line heater.
c: Pressure line heating wire degraded, resistance outside the window
High-resistance joint at the line heater connector
Engine control software setting the code erroneously (FCA 18-028-14)
Low heater supply voltage distorting the current measurement
s: Malfunction indicator lamp after a heating phase
Ice in the pressure line on cold starts, dosing late
Possible NOx efficiency codes as a consequence

P20BF.t: Reductant Heater B Control Circuit Low
P20BF.d: For heater B the code stands for a grounded control circuit or an overcurrent. Ford, where B is the pressure line heater, sets it when circuit 2 draws more than 15 A with the power stage on; the glow plug module can report such a short within 250 ms. GM's 2025 DEF module applies to heater 2 (line heater) the same low-band and overcurrent tests it uses on the tank heater, Type A, confirmed within 2 s, and in 2018 relied on a short-to-ground status from the DEF control module. VW's Touareg CNRB stores P20BF below 2.97 V signal voltage; Deutz lists FMI 4, a voltage too low, for its pressure line heater. Chafed line harnesses along the frame and water in connectors are typical. Because the driver shuts down or a fuse fails, the pressure line stays unheated in winter.
c: Line heater wire chafed on the frame and grounded
Water in the line heater connector creating a path to ground
Internal short in the heated pressure line
s: Check engine light, sometimes with a blown fuse
DEF pressure fault codes in cold weather
Speed limitation if the fault persists

P20C0.t: Reductant Heater B Control Circuit High
P20C0.d: P20C0 reports that heater B's control circuit is high, typically a wire touching a battery feed or a driver that will not switch off. On Ford diesels B is the pressure line heater: with the power stage off, a current below 3 A while the output still carries over 5 V triggers it, and the glow plug module flags the condition in 250 ms. GM's 2025 tables test heater 2 (line heater) with the output off and an elevated voltage window, Type A with a two-second filter; the 2018 tables use a short-to-battery status from the DEF control module. VW uses more than 2.20 A reported by the power stage on the Touareg CNRB, and Deutz FMI 3 for its pressure line heater. A line heater that is powered all the time can overheat the hose, while one the module has shut down leaves it frozen.
c: Line heater control wire shorted to a positive feed
Heater output stage in the DEF, engine or glow plug module stuck on
Bridged pins in a shared connector next to a supply terminal
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and DEF warning
Line heater may stay on with the engine off, draining the battery
Frozen pressure line once the module disables the heater

P20C1.d: Heater C's control circuit is interrupted. Where the third element sits again depends on the maker: GM's 2025 DEF tables make heater 3 a second tank heater and test it like the others (output off, 2 s, Type A); Deutz assigns C to the return line heater; FCA's EcoDiesel has a heater 3 of its own. Hino's 2018 bulletin for J05 cab-overs lists P20C1 as heater 3 of the heated DEF line, specified at 5.5 ohms ±1 at 20 °C and replaced as a complete line if out of range. On the 6.6 L LML in GM's 2014 tables the glow plug control module drives the DEF heaters and reports this fault after an active test that discharges its capacitor, about 3.4 s, Type B. The affected section stays frozen longer after a cold start, delaying dosing.
c: Heating circuit in the line or tank module open (resistance check at the connector)
Unplugged or corroded heater C connector
Glow plug control module fault where it drives the DEF heaters (GM LML)
s: Warning lamp mainly after cold soaks
DEF dosing delayed after a cold start
SCR warning and countdown if the fault persists

P20C2.t: Reductant Heater C Control Circuit Performance
P20C2.d: P20C2 says heater C is connected but does not take the power the control unit expects. In GM's 2025 tables heater 3, the second tank heater, must measure between 1.50 and 2.60 ohms and stay within 29 W of its command; otherwise Type A after 8 s. Ford reads the code differently on its diesels: there it means the heater supply voltage has dropped below 5 V, tested a single time per trip with the heaters at full load and again within the glow plug module diagnostics, so a weak feed or relay is the first suspect. FCA titles it Reductant Heater 3 Control Circuit Performance on the 3.0 L EcoDiesel and issued several PCM reflashes against false entries, among them 18-028-14 and 18-019-15. Deutz lists it for the return line heater as over-temperature. The usual result is late dosing in frost.
c: Heater supply below 5 V because of a weak relay, fuse or feed wire (Ford)
Engine control software setting the code falsely (FCA 18-028-14, 18-019-15)
Heater C element resistance outside its window
s: Check engine light after a heating cycle
DEF thaws slowly in cold weather
Further heater codes if the common supply is weak

P20C3.t: Reductant Heater C Control Circuit Low
P20C3.d: A low C circuit points to heater C being grounded somewhere or drawing excessive current. GM's 2025 DEF module treats heater 3, its second tank heater, exactly like heaters 1 and 2: a low-band voltage with the output off, or drain voltage and current limits with it on, Type A once 2 s have elapsed. On the 2014 LML Duramax (6.6 L) the glow plug control module reports heater currents above 25 A within about 1 s (Type B). The best-documented case is GM bulletin 22-NA-112: on 2020–2022 Silverado and Sierra with the 3.0 L LM2 or 6.6 L L5P, P20BB and P20C3 could set without any defect, and a recalibration of the DEF control module changed the test. Deutz maps the code to its return line heater (FMI 4). On those trucks software comes first; elsewhere look for a chafed harness.
c: Outdated DEF control module calibration on 2020–2022 GM diesel pickups (22-NA-112)
Heater C wire grounded through chafing
Shorted heater C element drawing overcurrent
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, possibly with no real fault present
Driver message that speed will be reduced without service
Unheated tank or line section in frost

P20C4.t: Reductant Heater C Control Circuit High
P20C4.d: P20C4 marks heater C's control circuit as high, meaning it sees battery voltage where none belongs. GM's 2025 tables test heater 3, a second tank heater, with the output switched off against a raised voltage window and set a Type A fault after 2 s of persistence. GM's LML documentation from 2014 (6.6 L) has the glow plug module react to over 3.5 V on the heater pin while the heater should be off (Type B). Deutz lists its return line heater with FMI 3, voltage above normal. No public service bulletin names P20C4, so the main suspects are harness damage near a supply wire and an output stage that stays on. An element that keeps heating with the engine off drains the battery; once the module locks it out, that section freezes. Open and low faults of heater C are P20C1 and P20C3.
c: Heater C control wire in contact with a battery feed
Heater driver in the DEF or glow plug module stuck on
DEF crystals or moisture bridging pins in the heater connector
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
Battery drained overnight if the heater stays powered
Inducement and speed limit if left unrepaired

P20C5.d: P20C5 covers an open control circuit in reductant heater D, the fourth heating element that only a few SCR layouts carry. Deutz is the one maker found that publishes the code: in its EMR5/MD1 fault list D is the downstream line heater, and P20C5 maps to SPN 520471 with FMI 5, an open or too little current. FCA's 3.0 L EcoDiesel also has a heater 4 (see P20C6), but no public document names P20C5 for it, and vehicle makers give no thresholds. Detection most likely follows the method GM documents for its heaters 1–3, which pinpoints an open with the output switched off, Type A once 2 s have passed. CARB requires output components to be checked for circuit faults. A broken wire, a loose connector or a burnt-out element in the heated downstream line are the likely causes.
c: Heating wire in the downstream DEF line burnt out or broken
Loose or corroded heater D connector
Wire break in the harness to heater D
s: Warning lamp in cold weather
Dosing delayed while the downstream line thaws

P20C6.t: Reductant Heater D Control Circuit Performance
P20C6.d: P20C6 is the functional check of heater D. FCA documents it for the 3.0 L EcoDiesel under the name Reductant Heater 4 Control Circuit Performance: bulletin 18-068-20 reflashed 2017 Ram 1500 engine computers that showed it, and a 2021 STAR case for 2020–2021 Ram 1500, Wrangler and Gladiator notes that it turns up mostly in severe cold, often without a defect. FCA asks technicians to confirm that ambient and tank temperatures read above 4 °C, inspect the supply line to the injector and run a dosing quantity test, which should capture 26–35 ml, before replacing anything; many returned pumps showed no fault. Deutz lists the code for its downstream line heater with an undetermined root cause (FMI 11). Only a failed dosing test or a leaking line justifies new parts.
c: False detection in extreme cold with a still-frozen tank (FCA STAR S2118000006)
Leaking or blocked DEF supply line to the injector
DEF pump unable to build pressure or injector delivering the wrong quantity
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, mostly after very cold nights
DEF system message, sometimes alongside pressure codes
Often no noticeable change in how the vehicle drives

P20C7.t: Reductant Heater D Control Circuit Low
P20C7.d: P20C7 reports that heater D's control circuit is grounded or overloaded with current. Only Deutz publishes the code: for its downstream line heater (SPN 520471) it maps to FMI 4, a voltage that is too low or a short to a low source. No vehicle maker documents thresholds for heater D. GM's tables for heaters 1–3 show the usual method, comparing the output voltage with the heater off against a low band and the current with it on, then setting Type A, set after a 2 s window; Ford uses 15 A on its two heater circuits. CARB requires such output circuits to be monitored for shorts that contradict what the module has commanded. Look for chafing on the line harness, water in a connector or an element with an internal short. Open and high counterparts are P20C5 and P20C8, the performance test is P20C6.
c: Heater D wire chafed through to ground
Water in the heater D connector
Internal short inside the heated downstream line
s: Warning lamp, possibly with a blown fuse
Unheated downstream line and delayed dosing in frost

P20C8.t: Reductant Heater D Control Circuit High
P20C8.d: Diesel exhaust fluid freezes at about -11 °C, so SCR systems carry several electric heating elements in the tank, pump and lines; which one a maker calls heater D varies. P20C8 reports that the control circuit of heater D reads high, meaning the output or its wiring has contact with battery voltage and the element can no longer be switched as commanded. GM names P20C8 for the 3.0 L LM2 Duramax in bulletin 21-NA-149, where a chafed engine harness blows fuses and sets a long list of codes. GM's 2025 DEF tables test the comparable heater C circuit (P20C4) through drain voltage and load current and rate it Type A after 2 s. Open, low and performance faults of heater D are P20C5 to P20C7. In frost the fluid may stay solid, dosing stops and the SCR warning follows.
c: Chafed harness letting the heater D control wire touch a battery-voltage feed
Moisture or DEF residue in the heater connector bridging pins
Internal short inside heater D or its integrated pump or line assembly
Faulty heater output stage in the engine or DEF control module
s: Check engine light and DEF or emission system warning
DEF dosing unavailable in cold weather, NOx warning or later speed limitation
Blown fuses and further unrelated codes when a chafed harness is the cause

P20C9.t: Reductant Control Module Requested MIL Illumination
P20C9.d: P20C9 is a forwarding code. Some diesel trucks use a separate DEF or SCR control module with its own fault memory; when that module detects an emission-relevant fault it asks the engine module to switch on the check engine lamp, and the engine module records P20C9. In GM bulletin 17-NA-366 for the 2018 Chevrolet Low Cab Forward 6500XD, every SCR code stays in the DEF module except this one, which the ECM stores and which turns the MIL on. Isuzu's 2011 N-Series with the 5.2 L diesel sets it automatically as soon as the DEF module logs a NOx sensor code such as P2201, P2206 or P2207 (special policy CB14-L-001). A generic reader therefore often shows only P20C9; the actual fault has to be read from the DEF module itself. Comparable request codes exist for other modules, for example P0700 for the transmission.
c: Emission-relevant SCR fault stored in the DEF control module (heater, pump, pressure, sensor)
Failed upstream NOx sensor reported by the DEF module
Outdated or mismatched software between engine and DEF control module
s: Check engine light with only P20C9 visible on a generic scan tool
DEF or SCR warning lamp, depending on the underlying fault
Possible power derate if the underlying SCR fault triggers inducement

P20CA.d: Air-assisted dosing, used mainly on older heavy and medium-duty diesels, mixes diesel exhaust fluid with compressed air from the vehicle's air system and blows the mixture through a nozzle into the exhaust. Airless pump systems in passenger cars and most current light trucks, such as Bosch Denoxtronic 2.2, have no air branch and cannot set this code. P20CA reports that compressed air is escaping from the dosing air circuit: the pressure expected downstream of the air shut-off or pressure control valve fails to hold. CARB names air-assisted injection among the reductant delivery functions that must be monitored. No maker documents P20CA publicly; a Cummins patent for an air-assisted urea doser lists leaks in the air supply, tank and lines as causes of its low-pressure fault. Too low and too high air pressure are P20E6 and P20E7.
c: Leaking air hose or fitting between air supply and dosing unit
Worn seal on the air shut-off or pressure control valve
Leak in the vehicle's compressed-air supply feeding the doser
Cracked or poorly sealed dosing unit housing on the air side
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
Audible hissing near the dosing unit or air lines
Poor DEF atomisation, higher NOx and later engine derate

P20CB.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector A Control Circuit/Open
P20CB.d: The engine computer checks the drive line of the hydrocarbon doser, a separate valve that sprays diesel into the exhaust ahead of the oxidation catalyst so the particulate filter can be heated for regeneration. This code means an open circuit: GM's diesel tables 18OBDG04 and 25OBDG04A watch the voltage on the switched-off driver output and flag a reading stuck in a mid band of roughly 2 to 3 V (Type B, MIL after two trips); the 6.6 L Duramax LML/LGH (15OBDG09) compares commanded and actual driver state. Short to ground and short to power have their own codes (P20CD, P20CE). Some makers use P2697 for the same injector instead. Without the doser the engine cannot finish active regenerations, so soot builds up.
c: Corroded or loose connector at the doser, which sits under the vehicle in the exhaust area
Heat- or chafe-damaged wire between engine computer and doser
Open solenoid winding inside the doser
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light on
Particulate filter regeneration does not start or is aborted
Soot load warning and, later, reduced engine power

P20CC.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector A Control Performance
P20CC.d: Unlike the circuit codes, this one judges what the hydrocarbon doser actually does. On the 6.6 L Duramax LML/LGH, GM table 15OBDG09 sets it when the outlet of the oxidation catalyst runs more than 300 °C hotter than its inlet for 180 s although no regeneration is under way and more than 900 s have passed since the last one; that heat can only come from fuel the doser should not be delivering. It is a Type A fault, so the MIL comes on after one trip. To keep the nozzle free, the same GM software pulses it briefly at 100 Hz at set soot levels. CARB requires makers to flag any injection fault that stops the filter from regenerating. Stuck positions have separate codes (P20CF, P20D0).
c: Doser leaking or dribbling fuel into the exhaust while closed
Coked nozzle tip with distorted spray
Exhaust temperature sensor before or after the catalyst reading wrong
s: Check engine light on
Unexpectedly high exhaust temperatures, possibly white smoke or fuel smell
Higher fuel consumption

P20CD.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector A Control Circuit Low
P20CD.d: Here the control line of the hydrocarbon doser has a short to ground. GM's diesel tables 18OBDG04 and 25OBDG04A test the output while the driver is off: if the voltage drops below about 2 V, the line is touching ground. GM rates it Type A, which lights the MIL after one trip, and the fault only clears after a calibrated count of good tests or a control-module reset. The LML/LGH Duramax lists it as Type B. A grounded line can make the doser open whenever its supply side is switched on, so fuel may enter the exhaust uncontrolled; that is why it is treated more strictly than the open circuit (P20CB) or the short to power (P20CE).
c: Control wire chafed through against the frame or exhaust
Water or salt in the doser connector bridging to ground
Internal short in the doser solenoid
s: Check engine light on after a single trip
Doser disabled, no active regeneration
Possible fuel smell or smoke from the exhaust

P20CE.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector A Control Circuit High
P20CE.d: The control line of the hydrocarbon doser is shorted to battery voltage. GM's diesel tables 18OBDG04 and 25OBDG04A detect it while the driver is switched on: current above roughly 8 to 11 A for a set time, or above about 16 to 22 A at once, counts as a short to power. GM rates it Type B, so the MIL follows after two trips; the LML/LGH Duramax (15OBDG09) uses a voltage check in the on state. The doser can then no longer be opened on command. Hino's J08E manual names P20CE among the codes to clear before diagnosing a regeneration complaint. Open circuit and short to ground are P20CB and P20CD.
c: Control wire touching a powered wire in a damaged harness
Doser solenoid with shorted turns drawing too much current
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light on
Active regeneration not possible
Rising soot load, later reduced power

P20CF.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector A Stuck Open
P20CF.d: The doser that adds diesel to the exhaust for filter regeneration is judged to stay open, so fuel keeps flowing after the command to close. On Volvo and Mack trucks the nozzle sits right at the turbo outlet and is fed by an AHI module; their troubleshooting guide KC-2157 points first to the fuel supply and then to that module. For 2016 US14 trucks Mack and Volvo released software because the code logged without a confirmed fault. Ram lists P20CF on the 2025–2026 2500/3500 with the 6.7 L Cummins HO among the codes cured by a PCM update. Unburned fuel can overheat the catalyst or leave as white smoke. The opposite failure is P20D0.
c: Dirt or deposits holding the doser valve off its seat
Upstream shutoff or dosing module letting fuel through
Calibration error, fixed by a software update
s: Check engine light on
White smoke or strong fuel smell from the exhaust
Very high temperatures at catalyst and filter
Higher fuel consumption

P20D0.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector A Stuck Closed
P20D0.d: The exhaust fuel doser is commanded to inject but no fuel gets through, typically because the nozzle tip is plugged. Detection usually relies on line pressure that fails to drop or on too little heat build-up across the oxidation catalyst. Volvo and Mack list P20D0 in their AHI troubleshooting guide KC-2157; the suggested steps are checking the AHI module and fitting a new nozzle after flushing both supply tubes, and the nozzle there is a maintenance part due at 150,000 miles. CARB demands a fault whenever the injection system can no longer reach regeneration. Without dosing the filter keeps filling with soot. Stuck open is P20CF.
c: Dosing module or supply valve not passing fuel
Kinked or blocked fuel line to the nozzle
s: Check engine light on
Regenerations fail or are requested constantly
Soot warning and reduced power

P20D1.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector B Control Circuit/Open
P20D1.d: Injector B is a second exhaust fuel doser, found only on layouts with two dosing points, for example twin exhaust paths. This code reports a broken control line or open coil on that second unit. No manufacturer documents P20D1 publicly; the logic would mirror injector A, where GM's diesel tables look for an off-state output voltage stuck in a mid band (P20CB, Type B). CARB wants every electrical part of an in-exhaust injection system covered by the comprehensive component checks. Most single-doser engines never set it, and many car diesels heat the filter by late in-cylinder injection instead of a doser at all.
c: Loose or corroded connector at doser B
Open solenoid winding in doser B
s: Check engine light on
Regeneration incomplete on the affected exhaust path

P20D2.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector B Control Performance
P20D2.d: With its wiring intact, the second exhaust fuel doser (B) is not delivering what was asked for: too little heat appears across the catalyst during dosing, or heat appears when it should be idle. No manufacturer documents P20D2 publicly. The comparable check for injector A on GM's 6.6 L Duramax (P20CC, 15OBDG09) watches for the catalyst outlet running far hotter than its inlet outside regeneration. CARB requires a malfunction whenever the injection system can no longer bring about regeneration, and a feedback-control fault if the system runs out of adjustment. Stuck positions of doser B are P20D5 and P20D6, the electrical faults P20D1, P20D3 and P20D4.
c: Partly coked nozzle on doser B
Low or unstable fuel pressure feeding doser B
s: Check engine light on
Longer or more frequent regenerations
Higher fuel consumption

P20D3.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector B Control Circuit Low
P20D3.d: The control line of the second exhaust fuel doser (B) is pulled toward ground. No manufacturer documents P20D3 publicly. For injector A, GM's diesel tables detect this by a switched-off output voltage below about 2 V and treat it as Type A with the MIL after one trip (P20CD), because a grounded line can open the valve without command. A similar strict rating is likely for B. CARB requires each electrical part of an in-exhaust injection system to be checked for circuit faults. The open circuit is P20D1, the short to power P20D4. Only engines with two dosing points can set this code.
c: Chafed control wire to doser B touching ground
Moisture in the doser B connector
s: Check engine light on
Doser B switched off, regeneration impaired

P20D4.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector B Control Circuit High
P20D4.d: On the second exhaust fuel doser (B), the control line sits at or near battery voltage, so the driver cannot pull it low to open the valve. No manufacturer documents P20D4 publicly. For injector A, GM's diesel tables flag excess current in the switched-on state as a short to power and rate it Type B (P20CE). With doser B out of action, the share of the exhaust it serves no longer gets enough heat for regeneration. CARB requires circuit monitoring for every electronic part of an in-exhaust injection system. For the same doser, P20D1 covers a broken line and P20D3 a grounded one.
c: Control wire to doser B shorted to a powered circuit
Shorted turns in the doser B solenoid
Faulty output stage in the control module
s: Check engine light on
Regeneration impaired, soot load rising

P20D5.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector B Stuck Open
P20D5.d: The second exhaust fuel doser (B) keeps passing fuel after it has been told to shut. No manufacturer documents P20D5 publicly; for the single doser A, Volvo and Mack trace the equivalent code P20CF to the fuel supply or the dosing module, and Ram fixed it on Cummins pickups with software. Detection usually relies on pressure in the doser feed line not rising again after closing, or on unexplained heat across the catalyst. Raw diesel in a hot catalyst can overheat it and causes smoke and fuel smell. CARB requires such injection faults to be caught. The stuck-closed counterpart is P20D6.
c: Deposits keeping doser B from sealing
Upstream shutoff valve leaking fuel through
Calibration error in the control software
s: Check engine light on
White smoke or fuel smell
Higher fuel consumption

P20D6.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector B Stuck Closed
P20D6.d: The second exhaust fuel doser (B) fails to deliver fuel even though the control unit commands it open. No manufacturer documents P20D6 publicly. For doser A, Volvo and Mack handle the matching code P20D0 by checking the dosing module and replacing the nozzle, whose tip tends to clog with carbon; the same weak spot applies to B. A blocked doser means the catalyst stays too cool for regeneration, so soot keeps accumulating in the filter until power is cut back. CARB requires a malfunction once the injection system cannot achieve regeneration. Stuck open on the same doser is P20D5.
c: Clogged nozzle tip on doser B
No fuel reaching doser B because of a blocked line or closed supply valve
Mechanically seized valve in doser B
s: Check engine light on
Failed or frequent regenerations
Reduced power once the filter is heavily loaded

P20D7.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Supply Control Circuit/Open
P20D7.d: Upstream of the exhaust doser sits a valve that releases fuel to it only when a regeneration is wanted, often called the shutoff or fuel cut valve. This code reports an open in its control circuit. Volvo and Mack store it as P20D713 (failure type 13 = open) and, in troubleshooting guide KC-2157, send the technician to the wiring and connector of the AHI module, where this valve is housed. Hino's J08E trucks use a fuel cut valve of the same kind. With the valve circuit open, no fuel reaches the doser and active regeneration stops. Shorts are P20D9 (low) and P20DA (high); mechanical sticking is P20DB and P20DC.
c: Loose or corroded connector at the dosing module
Broken wire in the dosing module harness
Open coil in the fuel shutoff valve
s: Check engine light on
Active regeneration not possible
Soot warning, later reduced power

P20D8.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Supply Control Performance
P20D8.d: The supply valve ahead of the exhaust doser is electrically sound, but the pressure it produces in the feed line does not follow its commands. A typical layout, described in a patent assigned to International Engine, measures that line pressure and uses it both to meter the dose and to diagnose the regulating valve. Hino's J08E manual lists P20D8 among the codes to resolve before chasing a regeneration fault; its trucks use a fuel cut valve ahead of the dosing injector. CARB treats a supply that runs out of control authority as a feedback fault. Circuit faults are P20D7, P20D9 and P20DA; a valve fixed open or shut is P20DB or P20DC.
c: Low feed pressure from a clogged fuel filter or weak low-pressure pump
s: Check engine light on
Regenerations take longer or fail

P20D9.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Supply Control Circuit Low
P20D9.d: For the fuel supply valve feeding the exhaust doser, the control line reads too low, which points to a short to ground. Volvo and Mack store P20D900 and, in AHI troubleshooting guide KC-2157, group it with the other electrical faults of the AHI module: check the module's connector and wiring harness. Depending on whether the valve is switched on its high or low side, a grounded line can either hold it shut or let it open unasked; most systems then disable dosing to be safe. The open circuit is P20D7 and the short to power P20DA. Valve sticking without an electrical cause is reported separately as P20DB or P20DC.
c: Chafed wire in the dosing module harness touching ground
Water in the dosing module connector
Internal short in the supply valve coil
s: Check engine light on
Dosing disabled, no active regeneration

P20DA.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Supply Control Circuit High
P20DA.d: For the supply valve ahead of the exhaust doser, the control line reads too high, typically because it touches battery voltage or, on some drivers, an open line pulled up internally. Volvo and Mack log it as P20DA00 and list it in guide KC-2157 among the AHI module electrical faults, with the instruction to check that module's wiring and connector. A circuit stuck high leaves the valve unable to follow commands, so the control unit stops dosing and active regeneration is lost until the fault is repaired. Its siblings are P20D7 (line broken) and P20D9 (line grounded); a mechanically stuck valve sets P20DB or P20DC.
c: Valve control wire shorted to a powered line
Damaged coil in the supply valve
Faulty output stage in the control module
s: Check engine light on
Active regeneration not possible

P20DB.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Supply Control Stuck Open
P20DB.d: The supply valve that should isolate the exhaust doser from the fuel system stays open after being switched off, so the feed line remains pressurized when no regeneration is running. If the doser itself then leaks, fuel can reach the hot exhaust unasked. Ram names P20DB together with P20CF (doser A stuck open) on 2025–2026 Ram 2500/3500 trucks with the 6.7 L Cummins HO, where a PCM software update is the fix. Hino found that its fuel cut valve could hang and leave too much pressure trapped in the doser feed pipe, and released an improved valve. The circuit is fine here; stuck closed is P20DC, electrical faults P20D7, P20D9 and P20DA.
c: Supply or fuel cut valve sticking open from wear or dirt
Detection or control calibration error, fixed by software
Contaminated fuel leaving deposits in the valve
s: Check engine light on
Fuel smell or smoke if the doser also leaks
Long cranking after fuel system work

P20DC.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Supply Control Stuck Closed
P20DC.d: The valve feeding the exhaust doser does not open when a regeneration starts, so the doser receives no fuel. A Hino patent shows how this is recognized: a pressure sensor between the shutoff valve and the dosing valve reads far below a threshold that depends on engine speed. Volvo and Mack list P20DC00 in AHI guide KC-2157 and tell technicians to look at the fuel supply first, then follow the guided diagnostics; a plugged fuel filter can mimic the fault. The electrical side is fine, which separates it from P20D7, P20D9 and P20DA. Stuck open is P20DB. Hino stores a stuck-closed fuel cut valve under P0005 instead.
c: Clogged fuel filter or water and dirt in the fuel
Internal fault in the dosing module
s: Check engine light on
Regenerations fail, soot load keeps rising
Reduced power in later stages

P20DD.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Pressure Sensor Circuit
P20DD.d: The pressure sensor in the feed line of the exhaust doser lets the control unit meter fuel and spot a stuck valve or plugged nozzle. This code is the general circuit fault of that sensor; signal too low, too high and unsteady have their own codes (P20DF, P20E0, P20E1). Volvo and Mack store it as P20DD13 (open circuit) and issued bulletins for Mack TD with MP10 and Volvo VNL/VNX with the D16 engine, where an internally failed AHI harness sets it together with P249F00 and P113413; the harness is replaced. Guide KC-2157 points to the sensor's wiring and connector. With no valid pressure reading, dosing and regeneration are blocked.
c: Internally damaged harness to the dosing module and its sensor
s: Check engine light on
Active regeneration blocked
Further codes for the reference voltage or the dosing system

P20DE.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P20DE.d: The doser feed pressure sensor gives a signal inside its electrical limits, yet the value does not fit what the system is doing, for example no pressure rise when the supply valve opens. Hino uses the code widely: SB-18-029 (2017–2019 J08 and J05 trucks, MIL on) has a specific sensor batch replaced, earlier notes blame a fuel cut valve that hangs or dirty fuel clogging a filter, and SB-22-007 swaps a 2020 bubbler filter. Volvo and Mack, in guide KC-2157, suspect the sensor, the air supply, the nozzle or the lines. So the fault often lies in the hydraulics, not the sensor. Electrical faults are P20DD, P20DF, P20E0 and P20E1.
c: Restricted fuel or separator filter from contaminated fuel
Sticking fuel cut or supply valve
Plugged nozzle or leaking fuel/air line
s: Check engine light on
Regeneration interrupted or blocked
Sometimes further fuel pressure codes such as P0087

P20DF.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Pressure Sensor Circuit Low
P20DF.d: The signal of the doser feed pressure sensor sits below its lower limit. Electrically that suggests a grounded signal line or a missing reference voltage. Hino describes its P20DF as the line pressure sensor reading too low and shows that real pressure loss can trigger it too: a fuel cut valve that hangs, or dirty fuel restricting the filter ahead of the dosing injector. Hino also changed the detection threshold by software on 2013–2016 cab-over trucks and corrected the measuring point in its workshop manual. So the check should cover both the sensor circuit and the fuel supply. High signal is P20E0, the generic circuit fault P20DD.
c: Real low pressure from a restricted filter or contaminated fuel
Signal wire shorted to ground or reference voltage lost
Outdated detection threshold, fixed by a software update
s: Check engine light on
Regeneration blocked

P20E0.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Pressure Sensor Circuit High
P20E0.d: The doser feed pressure sensor reports a signal above its upper electrical limit. On a typical three-wire sensor this happens when the signal line is open and pulled up, shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage, or when the ground is lost. Volvo and Mack store it as P20E000 and in guide KC-2157 direct technicians to the sensor's wiring and connector. In 2025 both brands also ran service campaigns on 2024–2025 trucks (at Mack with MP7/MP8 engines) built with an AHI fuel pressure sensor outside specification, which could set codes and upset aftertreatment control. Low signal is P20DF, plausibility P20DE and unsteady signal P20E1.
c: Signal wire open or shorted to reference or battery voltage
Sensor from a faulty production batch
s: Check engine light on
Active regeneration blocked

P20E1.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P20E1.d: The signal from the pressure sensor in the doser feed line jumps or drops out for short moments, faster than real line pressure could change. Usual reasons are a loose pin, a cracked wire flexing with engine movement, or moisture in the connector. No manufacturer documents P20E1 publicly. Comparable sensors exist on Volvo and Mack AHI modules, where a faulty sensor batch led to a 2025 service campaign, and on the Detroit hydrocarbon doser block, whose fuel compensation pressure sensor became a separate service part. CARB requires circuit checks for every sensor of an in-exhaust injection system. Steady faults belong to P20DD, P20DF and P20E0.
c: Loose or fretted pins at the sensor connector
Internal fault in the pressure sensor
s: Check engine light on, possibly coming and going
Regenerations interrupted

P20E2.d: P20E2 flags that bank 1 exhaust temperature sensors 1 and 2 disagree at a moment when both should show nearly the same value. Sensor 1 usually sits ahead of the oxidation catalyst and sensor 2 behind it. GM runs this check on the 6.6 L Duramax LML/LGH (table 15OBDG09) and on the diesel of table 15OBDG04: after at least 28,800 s (8 h) with the engine off, the two readings captured at start-up are compared, and a gap above a limit taken from a look-up table counts as a Type B fault, so the MIL lights after two failing trips. A sensor that is offset but still inside its valid voltage window passes the circuit checks P0544 and P2031–P2033 and is only caught here. Drivers rarely notice more than the lamp, although GM blocks some regeneration functions while this code is active.
c: Exhaust temperature sensor 1 or 2 drifted or aged (offset reading)
Corroded or loose connector adding resistance to one sensor signal
Sensors swapped or a non-matching replacement part installed
Engine control software needing an update
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on, often with no change in driving
Particulate filter regeneration delayed or blocked
Code returns after a long parking period

P20E3.d: P20E3 reports that exhaust temperature sensors 1 and 3 on bank 1 do not agree. In the usual diesel order, sensor 1 measures before the oxidation catalyst and sensor 3 after the particulate filter, so this pair brackets the whole aftertreatment line. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. Navistar's patent US7533519 explains the principle with sensors at the catalyst inlet, filter inlet and filter outlet: after a long stop all three must have cooled to almost the same value, and every pairwise difference is checked to expose a sensor stuck inside its range. Ford's 2023 diesels perform a comparable cold check (50 °C limit after 6 h off) but store P2080, P2084, P242B or P24C2 instead. CARB demands such plausibility checks for temperature sensors used by emission strategies. Expect the MIL; filter regeneration may be held back.
c: Sensor 1 or sensor 3 reading offset or responding sluggishly
Water or corrosion in the connector of the rear sensor
Exhaust leak near one sensor letting outside air cool its tip
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter regeneration postponed
Temperature values of sensors 1 and 3 differ noticeably on a cold engine

P20E4.d: P20E4 covers the pair around the particulate filter: sensor 2 at the filter inlet and sensor 3 at its outlet on bank 1 no longer agree. GM documents the code for the diesel in table 15OBDG04 (also 14OBDG04): after a soak of at least 28,800 s the start-up values of the filter upstream and downstream sensors are compared against a look-up limit, and a larger gap is a Type B fault. Because both sensors steer and protect filter regeneration, a biased one can lead to regenerations that run too cool or too hot. P20E2 covers the pair around the oxidation catalyst, while P2084 and P242B report range faults of a single sensor. The patent US7533519 uses the same inlet/outlet arrangement for its stuck-in-range test. Drivers usually see the MIL and may notice more frequent or aborted regenerations.
c: Filter inlet or outlet temperature sensor aged by heat cycling
Heat-damaged or corroded sensor connector or lead
Heavy soot or ash deposits on a sensor tip slowing its response
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Regenerations aborted or happening more often
Filter loading warning in some vehicles

P20E5.d: P20E5 is the bank 2 counterpart of P20E2: on engines with a separate exhaust and aftertreatment path per cylinder bank, sensors 1 and 2 of the second bank disagree after the system has cooled down. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; the GM tables that use P20E2 cover single-path diesels. The method is known from Cummins' patent US7771113: once the exhaust has cooled, the thermistors ahead of and behind the oxidation catalyst are checked against each other and an offset sensor is identified, even when its reading is still within range. CARB requires rationality monitoring of every temperature sensor used by an emission strategy. Bank 2 circuit or range faults use P0548, P2082 or P2034. The driver sees the MIL; regeneration of the bank 2 filter may be limited.
c: Contact resistance in a bank 2 sensor connector
Sensor connectors swapped between banks after a repair
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Bank 2 sensors show different values on a cold engine

P20E6.t: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Too Low
P20E6.d: This code belongs to air-assisted DEF dosing, where compressed air carries the fluid to the nozzle and breaks it into fine droplets; airless pump systems in cars and most current pickups do not use it. P20E6 means the air pressure in the dosing branch stays below the minimum the control unit needs while dosing is requested. A Cummins patent for such a system gives an example limit: if the combined air and DEF pressure remains under about 300 kPa for 10 s, a low-pressure fault is stored, pointing to a weak air supply or compressor, a shut-off valve that does not open, blocked or leaking lines, or crystallised DEF blocking the air path. Cummins bulletin TSB200096 describes crystal build-up on the air side of such dosing units that cuts air flow. No maker documents P20E6 itself publicly. Leakage is P20CA, excess pressure P20E7.
c: Insufficient air tank pressure from a leak or weak compressor
Air shut-off or pressure control valve not opening
DEF crystals restricting the air side of the dosing unit
Leaking, kinked or blocked air line to the doser
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
DEF dosing reduced or stopped, rising NOx emissions
Engine derate after the inducement period

P20E7.t: Reductant Injection Air Pressure Too High
P20E7.d: On air-assisted DEF dosing the control unit regulates the compressed air fed into the mixing chamber so that the nozzle sprays a stable mist.
