s: Check engine lamp on after two trips
Hesitation under load

P217A.t: Fuel Injector Group G Supply Voltage Circuit/Open
P217A.d: Group G only exists on engines with seven or more injector groups, in practice eight-cylinder engines with direct injection. GM's 2023 and 2024 summary tables (23OBDG07, 24OBDG07) name the cylinder 7 injector G and use P217A for a short on its high side: less than 0.5 ohm between the module pin and ground while the driver is off, or to the injector supply while it is on. Two such events with more than 9 V on the battery store the code within one trip. As with groups E and F, GM keeps open circuits on the separate per-cylinder injector codes, so the title's open wording is misleading on these engines. No bulletin naming this code was found. The injector is switched off, cylinder 7 misfires and the engine runs noticeably rough. P217B and P217C are the dedicated low and high codes.
c: Cylinder 7 injector feed shorted to ground or supply in the harness
s: Check engine lamp on, cylinder 7 misfire
Rough running under load

P217B.t: Fuel Injector Group G Supply Voltage Circuit Low
P217B.d: P217B reports the feed of injector group G as grounded, which on GM's direct-injection V8 engines is the injector of cylinder 7, at the rear of bank 1. GM's 2016 table 16OBDG07A and the 2018 LT4 table of the supercharged 6.2 V8 measure it with the driver switched on: if 25 A or more flows through the high side, the line is grounded somewhere. The check runs every 100 ms as soon as the battery has 11 V; 10 failures in 20 samples set the code as type A, so the MIL comes on in the same trip. Check the harness routing at the rear of the engine and the injector connector before suspecting the module. The module stops firing the injector, which shows up as a cylinder 7 misfire. P217C is the high fault, P217A the general one.
c: Cylinder 7 feed wire grounded at the rear of the engine
Engine control module output stage faulty
s: Check engine lamp on immediately
Cylinder 7 misfire, reduced power

P217C.t: Fuel Injector Group G Supply Voltage Circuit High
P217C.d: P217C means the group G injector supply, cylinder 7 on GM's direct-injection V8 engines, is pulled up to supply voltage. GM tests this while the high-side driver is off: if the line sits within 1 V of the controller supply, the module treats it as shorted to power. The tables 16OBDG07A (2016), 18OBDG03A for the 6.2 LT4 and 19OBDG03A apply the same counting of 10 failures out of 20 samples, 100 ms apart, at 11 V or more, and treat it as type A with immediate MIL. A wire rubbed against a powered circuit, a damaged injector connector and, more rarely, a faulty driver inside the module are the usual causes; a module fault often shows as several high codes at once. To protect the injector from staying open, cylinder 7 is shut off. P217B is the low counterpart, P217A the general code.
c: Cylinder 7 feed shorted to a powered wire
s: Check engine lamp on immediately
Cylinder 7 misfire

P217D.t: Fuel Injector Group H Supply Voltage Circuit/Open
P217D.d: Group H is the eighth injector group, on GM petrol direct injection the injector of cylinder 8, the last one on bank 2 of a V8. GM's 2023 and 2024 tables call it injector H and use P217D when its high side shows less than 0.5 ohm to ground with the driver off or to the injector supply with the driver on; two events above 9 V store the code in one trip. GM's service texts refer to it as the high control circuit of the cylinder 8 injector. Bulletin 24-NA-106 for the 2023 and 2024 Corvette with the 5.5 LT6 shows how a common cause hits a whole bank: water getting into a wrong twelve-pin intermediate connector to the bank 2 injector harness set P2149, P2155, P216D and P217D, the even cylinders, together with rail pressure codes. The fix is a connector with the correct part number.
c: Cylinder 8 injector feed shorted in the harness
Water in the bank 2 injector harness connector, Corvette LT6
s: Check engine lamp on, cylinder 8 misfire
Several bank 2 injector codes at once if the connector is wet

P217E.t: Fuel Injector Group H Supply Voltage Circuit Low
P217E.d: P217E flags the supply of injector group H as grounded, on GM's direct-injection V8 engines the injector of cylinder 8. GM lists it for the 6.2 LT4 in 2018 and in its 2016 table 16OBDG07A. With the high-side driver switched on, a current of 25 A or more means the line has found a path to ground; at 11 V or more, 10 bad samples out of 20 taken at 100 ms set the code as type A and light the MIL right away. Since the per-cylinder low-side codes P0282 and P0283 cover the return line, this code points specifically at the feed wire, the injector body or the driver. A practical check is to unplug the module and the injector and measure the feed wire to ground before suspecting the module. The engine loses cylinder 8. P217F is the high fault.
c: Cylinder 8 feed wire chafed to ground
Cylinder 8 injector shorted to its housing
Engine control module output stage faulty
s: Check engine lamp on immediately
Cylinder 8 misfire, engine shakes

P217F.t: Fuel Injector Group H Supply Voltage Circuit High
P217F.d: P217F is the last code of the injector group series: the feed of group H, cylinder 8 on GM's direct-injection V8 engines, shows supply voltage although the high-side driver is switched off. GM's tables 16OBDG07A, 18OBDG03A for the 6.2 LT4 and 19OBDG03A set it when the line stays within 1 V of the controller supply, counting 10 failures out of 20 samples at 100 ms with 11 V or more, type A, MIL on the first trip. A short to power can hold the injector partly open or stress the driver, so the module cuts cylinder 8. Wiring that touches a powered conductor, moisture in the plug or a failing module output are the candidates; high codes on several cylinders together suggest the module. P217E is the short to ground, P217D the general fault.
c: Cylinder 8 feed shorted to a powered wire
Moisture or corrosion in the injector connector
Engine control module output stage faulty
s: Check engine lamp on immediately
Cylinder 8 misfire, possibly rich running on bank 2

P2180.d: P2180 closes the series: bank 2's long-term trim must remove too much fuel above idle, so its multiplicative adaptation sits at the rich limit. GM's 2005 2.8 and 3.6 V6 and the 2008 3.6 LLT use a factor below 0.78, GM's 2024 tables below 0.77, both over two trips. VW's 2014 Touareg 3.0 TSI hybrid and 3.6 VR6 set it below -30 % on bank 2. Unlike P2190, which reacts to excess fuel at idle such as purge vapour, this code rises with load, so look at fuel delivered per injection: pressure regulator or high-pressure pump control, injectors leaking or over-delivering on bank 2, or a bank 2 front sensor reading rich. When P2178 is set as well, check the air mass reading and fuel pressure first. No bulletin naming this code was found.
c: Injector on bank 2 leaking or over-delivering
Fuel pressure too high or air mass sensor over-reading, usually with P2178
Bank 2 front oxygen sensor reading rich
s: Check engine lamp on after two trips
Higher fuel consumption

P2181.d: P2181 is the engine computer's verdict that the coolant warms up too slowly or settles below its target, almost always because the thermostat no longer closes. CARB requires the thermostat to be monitored and flags a failure when the warm-up stays more than 11.1 °C under the regulating point. GM (18OBDG03A) compares the block sensor with the radiator sensor during warm-up; if both rise together, the thermostat is open (Type B). VW's 2014 CC model expects 74–84 °C after a set amount of intake air; the Touareg with engine CNRB flags a gap of 7.5 K below the target. Audi, Bentley, Hyundai and Kia have bulletins tying P2181 to thermostats that stick or leak, Kia in part to software. Swapping the coolant sensor seldom helps. The heater stays lukewarm and fuel use climbs. P0128 is a similar thermostat code.
c: Thermostat not closing fully because of wear, corrosion or debris on the seat
Engine control software too sensitive, fixed by a reflash on some models (e.g. Kia SA463)
Radiator fan running constantly and overcooling the engine
Low coolant level or air in the system distorting the temperature reading
s: Check engine light, usually without any change in driving behaviour
Temperature gauge rises slowly or stays below normal
Weak cabin heating in cold weather
Higher fuel consumption on short trips

P2182.d: P2182 is the general circuit code for the second coolant temperature sensor: the module sees a fault in its wiring or signal but does not sort it into low, high or erratic. Where sensor 2 sits is up to the maker. Mazda fits it low on the radiator, VW calls it the radiator outlet sender, Ford's Escape plug-in hybrid uses it in the cabin heater loop, GM uses a second engine sensor. No maker documents P2182 itself publicly; GM, VW and others report the same sensor through the more specific P2184 to P2186. CARB demands that every coolant sensor be tested for broken circuits and readings beyond its valid span. Likely causes are an open signal wire, a loose connector or a dead sensor. Depending on the use of the sensor, fan control, thermostat diagnosis or cabin heating may run on substitute values.
c: Loose, corroded or water-damaged connector at sensor 2
Signal or reference wire to sensor 2 open or damaged
s: Check engine light
Radiator fan runs continuously as a precaution
Thermostat or cooling diagnostics unavailable

P2183.t: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 2 Circuit Range/Performance
P2183.d: P2183 means sensor 2 delivers a voltage inside the valid band, yet the temperature does not fit the other readings. Most makers test this after a long cold soak, when all temperatures should match. The VW Touareg with engine CNRB sets it when the radiator outlet sensor differs by more than 35 K from intake air, ambient or fuel temperature at start-up. RAM 1500 models with the rear axle heater compare that loop with engine coolant and oil after 8 hours and allow 30 °C; a block heater can trip it falsely. Ford reflashes Escape and Corsair plug-in hybrids where an active cabin heater soak timer set P2183 wrongly. Mazda3 sensors at the radiator bottom let water in and read too low. Real causes are corrosion and drift; others need a software update. Low, high and erratic signals are P2184 to P2186.
c: Water ingress or internal corrosion in sensor 2 shifting its reading
Control software misjudging soak time, block heater or cabin heater use
Coolant hoses at the sensor loop swapped or air trapped after service
Aged sensor element drifting out of tolerance
s: Check engine light, often right after a cold start
Remote start disabled on some trucks
Engine overheat message without real overheating on some hybrids

P2184.t: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 2 Circuit Low
P2184.d: Coolant sensors are NTC thermistors: the hotter they get, the lower their resistance and voltage. P2184 therefore reports a signal from sensor 2 so low that it would mean an impossibly hot engine, typically a signal wire touching ground or a shorted sensor. GM's 2019 tables (19OBDG03D) set it when resistance drops below about 47.5 ohms, matching 150 °C, for 5 s within 6 s (Type B, MIL after two trips). VW's 2014 CC flags the radiator outlet sensor above 141 °C, the Touareg CNRB a voltage under 0.22 V. GM lists P2184 among the codes caused by a chafed engine harness in bulletin 21-NA-149. Because a hot reading is accepted as real at first, fans may run flat out. P2185 is the opposite fault, P2186 the erratic case.
c: Signal wire of sensor 2 chafed through and touching ground
Coolant or water in the connector bridging signal and ground
s: Check engine light after two drives on GM vehicles
Radiator fans running at full speed
Further codes and warnings if a harness is chafed

P2185.t: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 2 Circuit High
P2185.d: P2185 is the high end of the sensor 2 circuit check. With an NTC thermistor a high signal stands for extreme cold, so the usual reason is an open circuit: a broken wire, an unplugged or corroded connector, or a sensor with an interrupted element; a short to voltage is rarer. GM (19OBDG03D) watches for a resistance in the order of 300 kOhm, the value at -60 °C, after 10 s of engine running or above -20 °C intake air, 5 s within 6 s, Type B. VW sets it at below -43 °C on the 2014 CC and above 4.92 V or 4.94 V on the Touareg. Audi issued a 2025 bulletin for the A4 and A5 family on P2185 at the radiator outlet sender G83. In bulletin 21-NA-149 GM traces it to a chafed harness. Low and erratic signals are P2184 and P2186.
c: Connector at sensor 2 unplugged, loose or corroded
Signal or ground wire of sensor 2 broken
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
s: Check engine light
Fans run permanently as a safety measure
Low coolant or temperature warning without a real cause on some models

P2186.t: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 2 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2186.d: P2186 covers a sensor 2 signal that jumps instead of changing smoothly. Coolant temperature moves slowly because of the mass of the liquid, so a step faster than physics allows points to a loose contact rather than a real change. GM's 2019 tables (19OBDG03D) work out an upper and lower limit for each new reading from the previous value and the sensor's time constant, about 7.4 s for sensor 2 within a -60 to 150 °C window; a reading outside this corridor for 5 s within 6 s sets the code as Type B, MIL after two trips. GM also lists P2186 among the effects of the chafed engine harness in bulletin 21-NA-149. Typical causes are worn connector pins, a wire broken inside the insulation or a sensor with an intermittent element. Steady low or high signals are P2184 and P2185.
c: Worn or loose pins in the sensor 2 connector
Wire broken inside its insulation or chafed harness making intermittent contact
Sensor 2 with an intermittent internal fault
s: Check engine light after two drives
Fans switching on and off irregularly
Temperature-related messages that appear and vanish

P2187.d: P2187 means the long-term fuel trim of bank 1 has to add more fuel than allowed in the idle and low-load range. Many systems, especially Bosch ones, split mixture adaptation into an additive part, which dominates at low airflow, and a multiplicative part for load. An air leak adds a fixed amount of unmeasured air, which matters most at idle, so it shows up in the additive part. GM's 3.6 V6 engines set the code above 7 % (2005) or 6.1 % (2008 LLT, at 520 to 1120 rpm, 1.7 to 7.8 g/s and coolant above 60 °C), and GM's 2024 tables above about 5.5 %, over two trips. On the Opel/GM 2.0 turbo in the Saab 9-5 (2010) the weighted long-term trim must exceed its limit for 4 s continuously or 50 s in total (Type B). Audi traced P2187 with P2279 on 2.0 TFSI engines to a crankcase ventilation valve that let boost into the crankcase; Mazda found A/F sensor wiring on the CX-7 2.3 turbo shorted after brake fluid was spilled on it.
c: Air leak after the air mass sensor, often at the crankcase ventilation
Damaged front oxygen or A/F sensor wiring
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Rough or hunting idle, hissing from the engine bay

P2188.d: P2188 means the long-term fuel trim of bank 1 has to remove more fuel than allowed in the idle and low-load range, the additive part of the mixture adaptation on Bosch-type systems. GM's 2008 3.6 LLT sets it below -6.0 % at 520 to 1120 rpm and 1.7 to 7.8 g/s, with closed loop and coolant above 60 °C. On the Opel/GM 2.0 turbo in the Saab 9-5 (2010) the weighted long-term trim must stay below its limit for 4 s or 50 s in total (Type B); Saab's test gives -22 to 0 % as normal trim and 19 to 42 kPa manifold pressure at idle. At idle the extra fuel typically comes from sources the ECM does not meter: Mercedes lists for the M132 engine a leaking PCV valve, leaking injectors or excessive fuel pressure, wrong intake pressure readings, a restricted or worn throttle and a contaminated oxygen sensor. A saturated charcoal canister purging at idle has the same effect. Stellantis found an airflow straightener in the air box clipped in wrong, which disturbed the air mass reading and set P2188 and P2190.
c: Leaking injector or fuel pressure too high
Fuel vapour from the purge valve or oil-diluted crankcase gases
Air mass or manifold pressure reading wrong
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Rough idle, fuel smell

P2189.d: P2189 is the bank 2 version of P2187: on engines with a front oxygen sensor per bank, the long-term trim of bank 2 has to add more fuel than allowed at idle and low load. GM's 2005 2.8 and 3.6 V6 set it when the additive correction exceeds 7 %, the 2008 3.6 LLT above 6.1 % at 520 to 1120 rpm, airflow of 1.7 to 7.8 g/s, engine load of 11 to 45 % and coolant above 60 °C, and GM's 2024 tables above about 5.5 % over two trips. Because both banks share the throttle, crankcase ventilation and brake booster vacuum, a leak there normally lifts the idle trim on both banks, setting P2187 and P2189 together. A code on bank 2 alone points to something only that bank sees: an intake manifold gasket or runner leak on that side, an injector on that bank, or the bank 2 front sensor or its wiring. Comparing both banks' trims at idle and at 2500 rpm narrows it down.
c: Intake gasket or runner leak on the bank 2 side
Shared vacuum leak, usually with P2187 present too
Bank 2 front sensor, its wiring or an injector on that bank
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Rough or hunting idle

P218A.t: Throttle Actuator B Control System - Idle Position Not Learned
P218A.d: P218A is the throttle B counterpart of P2176: on engines with a second electronic throttle, usually one per cylinder bank, that second unit failed to learn its closed rest position. GM's 2023 table 23OBDG07 runs the same three-step learn for bank 2 as for bank 1. First the plate must reach the closed target within 1.5 %, then the motor has to press it onto the stop with enough duty cycle, and finally the stored voltages must fall inside 0.33-0.58 V for sensor 1 and 4.42-4.67 V for sensor 2; any failed step stores the code within one trip. No other manufacturer documents P218A publicly. Ice, carbon, a weak motor or wiring faults at throttle B are typical causes, and engine power may be limited. Electrical motor faults of throttle B use P210A.
c: Carbon or ice keeping throttle B off its closed stop
Weak motor or gear wear in throttle unit B
Position sensors of throttle B outside the learn window
Supply or signal wiring fault at throttle B
s: Check engine lamp
Uneven idle between the banks
Reduced power

P218B.d: P218B is a general electrical fault in the second throttle/fuel inhibit line, B. An inhibit line carries a signal with which another unit can tell the engine computer to keep the throttle closed or stop fuelling. No manufacturer documents the B line publicly. The only published use of this function concerns the A line: GM's 2005 table for the 3.5-litre V6 (L66) places it in the throttle valve control section, where the injection and throttle processors check each other, and monitors it with P2553-P2555 once per drive cycle after ignition off, lighting the MIL on the next drive cycle. California's OBD rule requires inputs of this kind to be checked for circuit faults. Open wires, corroded pins and module connector faults come first; reduced power is possible.
c: Open or high-resistance inhibit B wire
Corroded or loose pins at the engine or throttle module connector
Fault in the unit that drives the inhibit signal
s: Check engine lamp on the following drive
Possible power limitation

P218C.d: P218C means the inhibit B line is electrically within limits, yet its state or response does not fit what the controller expects: it may signal a lock when none is requested, or fail to react during a function test. No manufacturer documents P218C publicly. GM's 2005 table for the 3.5-litre V6 (L66) shows the analogous test on line A as P2553: a function check of the relay path, judged by a normal signal on the serial data link with battery voltage above 7 V, run once per drive cycle after ignition off and lighting the MIL on the next drive. California's OBD rule asks for plausibility checks of such inputs. Likely causes are a sticking relay, a slow-switching driver or software mismatch between the modules. P218D/P218E cover hard low and high faults.
c: Relay in the inhibit path sticking or switching late
Software versions of the communicating modules do not match
Intermittent contact causing implausible line states
s: Check engine lamp on the next drive
Occasional power reduction without obvious reason

P218D.d: P218D reports that the voltage on inhibit line B sits below the lowest permitted value, which normally points to a short to ground, a missing supply from the sending unit or an open line pulled down by the input stage. No manufacturer documents P218D publicly. For the A line, GM's 2005 table for the 3.5-litre V6 (L66) gives a concrete limit: P2554 is set when the analogue throttle inhibit circuit reads under 0.498 V for 4 seconds, with the check running after ignition off and the MIL lit on the next drive cycle. California's OBD rule requires out-of-range checks on such inputs. Chafed insulation touching body ground, water in a connector or a failed driver in the sending module are the likely causes. P218E is the opposite fault, P218B the general circuit code.
c: Inhibit B wire shorted to ground
Water or corrosion in a connector of the inhibit line
Output stage of the sending module failed
s: Check engine lamp on the following drive
Possible power reduction

P218E.d: P218E says the inhibit B line carries more voltage than the controller allows, typically because it touches a battery-fed wire or the sending unit's output stage is stuck high. No manufacturer documents P218E publicly. On the A line, GM's 2005 table for the 3.5-litre V6 (L66) uses two limits for P2555: more than 10 V with the ignition on, or more than 4.5 V once the ignition is off, each judged over 4 seconds; the check runs after shutdown and the MIL lights on the next drive cycle. The lower limit with the ignition off shows that the line should be nearly dead when the system sleeps. California's OBD rule requires such range checks. Look for chafing against supply wires, a backfeed through a faulty module or a shorted relay. P218D is the low-side counterpart.
c: Inhibit B wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit
Voltage fed back through a faulty module after ignition off
Relay contacts welded, keeping the line energised
s: Check engine lamp on the following drive
Possible power reduction

P218F.d: P218F means the SCR system is dosing on paper, but nothing reaches the exhaust: the expected link between dosing commands, pump effort and line pressure is missing. Ford's 2023 diesel summary, which calls the test a reductant delivery check for clogging, runs it while dosing with the pressure error inside 0.5 bar for 5 s. It fails when the pressure barely reacts to changes in the injection rate and the mix of rate and pump duty misses its model by more than 0.15. Ford also lists it for the 6.7 L Power Stroke (18-2127, PCM update). Nissan reflashed Titan XD trucks with the Cummins 5.0 L V8 when P218F appeared at 0 °C or below. VW says P218F can stay after repairs on 2.0 TDI cars until a leak in the DEF line is fixed. Pressure codes are P20E8/P20E9.
c: Dosing valve or its nozzle crystallised and blocked
Leak in the DEF line between pump and dosing valve
Partly frozen line in frost or control software that needs an update
Worn DEF pump that cannot keep up delivery
s: Check engine light with a DEF or emission system warning
Restart countdown or speed limitation if the fault persists
DEF consumption lower than usual
White crystalline deposits at the dosing valve or line joints

P2190.d: P2190 is the bank 2 counterpart of P2188: the long-term trim of bank 2 has to remove more fuel than allowed at idle and low load. GM's 2008 3.6 LLT sets it below -6.0 % in the same window it uses for P2188 (520 to 1120 rpm, 1.7 to 7.8 g/s, closed loop, coolant above 60 °C, catalyst heating not active), and GM's 2005 2.8 and 3.6 V6 treat it in the same additive adaptation range. A rich fault on bank 2 only usually lies in that bank: a leaking injector, or a bank 2 front sensor reading lean so the ECM keeps leaning the mixture. Fuel pressure, purge vapour and air-mass errors act on both banks and tend to set P2188 and P2190 together. Stellantis is an example: an airflow straightener clipped in wrong in the air box upset the air mass reading and logged P2188 and P2190 together, sometimes with P0111 and an unstable idle; refitting it correctly cured it.
c: Shared cause such as air mass error or purge vapour, usually with P2188 too
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Rough idle, fuel smell

P2191.t: System Too Lean at Higher Load (Bank 1)
P2191.d: P2191 sets once bank 1's long-term trim has run into its enrichment limit in the upper load range, so the engine would be lean there without the correction. It is the third load zone next to P2187 (idle) and P2177 (off idle), and it is where a supply that copes at cruise first falls short: a tired fuel pump, a clogged filter, poor pressure regulation, injectors that flow too little, or an air mass sensor that reads low at high airflow. CARB demands a fault once adaptive control has used up the adjustment the maker allows (13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(6.2.2)). No manufacturer publishes its criteria for P2191; GM covers the load range with P2177 and a factor of 1.23 instead, and Kia lists only the rich sibling P2192 for the Rio and Soul 1.6 GDI. Drivers may feel hesitation when accelerating hard.
c: Fuel pump or pressure regulation unable to hold pressure at high demand
Air mass sensor under-reading at high airflow
Charge-air or intake leak behind the air mass sensor (turbo engines)
s: Check engine light on
Hesitation or flat spot under heavy throttle
Loss of power when climbing or towing
High positive long-term fuel trim at high load only

P2192.t: System Too Rich at Higher Load (Bank 1)
P2192.d: P2192 is the rich-side limit of the bank 1 trim in the upper load zone: the controller has pulled as much fuel as it may and the front sensor still reports excess fuel. Typical sources grow with demand, such as an air mass sensor reading high, fuel pressure above specification, or injectors that over-deliver or drip at high rail pressure; on direct-injection engines a leaking high-pressure injector is a prime suspect. Kia documents the code by name: bulletin ENG 146 (2015) lists P2192 with P2188 and other codes on 2012 to 2014 Rio and Soul with the 1.6 GDI engine and cures it with an ECM software upgrade rather than parts. GM handles the same load range as P2178 with a lower factor limit of 0.78. Expect higher consumption and possibly a fuel smell; P2188 is the idle counterpart, P2178 the off-idle one.
c: ECM calibration issue covered by a software update (e.g. Kia 1.6 GDI)
Air mass sensor reading too high
Injector leaking or over-delivering at high rail pressure
s: Check engine light on
Increased fuel consumption
Fuel smell or dark exhaust under load

P2193.t: System Too Lean at Higher Load (Bank 2)
P2193.d: P2193 reports for bank 2 what P2191 reports for bank 1: in the upper load zone the long-term trim of that bank sits at its enrichment limit. It only exists on engines with a separate front sensor per bank, such as V6, V8 and boxer engines. The useful question is whether bank 1 shows the same. Lean at high load on both banks (P2191 with P2193) points to something they share, chiefly fuel pump, filter, pressure regulation or the air mass sensor. Bank 2 alone narrows it to that side: injectors on bank 2, an intake gasket or runner leak there, or an exhaust leak ahead of the bank 2 sensor. No manufacturer documents P2193 publicly; GM monitors the comparable range as P2179, and CARB sets the general rule for exhausted fuel adaptation in 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(6.2.2).
c: Weak fuel supply (pump, filter, pressure regulation), usually with P2191
Intake gasket or runner leak on the bank 2 side
Exhaust leak ahead of the bank 2 front sensor
s: Check engine light on
Hesitation under heavy acceleration
Bank 2 long-term trim much higher than bank 1 at high load

P2194.t: System Too Rich at Higher Load (Bank 2)
P2194.d: P2194 means bank 2 has reached the lower limit of its trim in the upper load zone: the ECM is removing as much fuel as permitted, yet that bank still runs rich. Because air mass, fuel pressure and canister purge feed both banks, a rich error caused by them usually brings P2192 along. When P2194 stands alone, look at bank 2 itself: a leaking or over-delivering injector, an injector of the wrong flow class after a repair, or a bank 2 front sensor that reads lean so the controller keeps adding fuel. Comparing the trims of both banks while holding a high load on the road or a dynamometer separates the two cases. No manufacturer publishes P2194 criteria; GM uses P2180 with a factor limit of 0.78 for the corresponding range. The driver mainly sees higher consumption.
c: Leaking or over-delivering injector on bank 2
Air mass sensor reading high or fuel pressure too high (usually with P2192)
s: Check engine light on
Increased fuel consumption
Bank 2 long-term trim strongly negative at high load

P2195.t: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean (Bank 1, Sensor 1)
P2195.d: P2195 means the front oxygen or air-fuel sensor on bank 1 reports a lean mixture that the ECM does not believe, either because it stays lean or because it disagrees with other evidence. On GM's Bosch-based 2005 V6 the rear sensor has to read rich (above 0.85 V) while the front A/F sensor reads leaner than lambda 1.08 and the short-term trim sits at its maximum of 1.25, for about 100 s or 50 s in total. Ford checks narrow-band sensors for fewer than 5 switches in 30 s and wide-band sensors for 30 s at the short-term trim limit; from 2019 a sensor whose filtered lambda changes by less than 0.0001 for 30 s sets P2195 if the value is at or above 1. On the Opel/GM 2.0 turbo in the Saab 9-5 (2010) the code sets within 4 s continuously or 50 s in total. Ford replaced the heated oxygen sensors for P2195 and P2197 on 2015 to 2017 Explorer and F-150 3.5 GTDI. An exhaust leak ahead of the sensor can also make it read lean.
c: Front oxygen or A/F sensor aged or contaminated
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor
Sensor signal or reference wiring fault
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Possible rough running or higher consumption from wrong fuelling

P2196.t: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Rich (Bank 1, Sensor 1)
P2196.d: P2196 means the front oxygen or air-fuel sensor on bank 1 reports a rich mixture that the ECM does not accept. On GM's Bosch-based 2005 V6 this is a cross-check with the rear sensor: the rear sensor reads lean (below 0.15 V) while the front A/F sensor reads richer than lambda 0.92 and the short-term trim has pulled to its minimum of 0.75, for about 100 s or 50 s in total. Ford sets it for a narrow-band sensor that hardly switches and stays rich, a wide-band sensor that sits 30 s at the short-term trim limit, or, from 2019, a filtered lambda below 1 that changes by less than 0.0001 for 30 s; Ford blocks the stuck-rich test while fuel is boiling off the oil after a cold start. On the Opel/GM 2.0 turbo in the Saab 9-5 (2010) the code sets within 4 s continuously or 50 s in total. Because the ECM leans the engine to follow the false signal, a rear sensor reading lean and a lean real mixture often accompany it.
c: Front oxygen or A/F sensor contaminated or aged
Sensor signal shorted or reference circuit fault
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Possible hesitation or lean running

P2197.t: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean (Bank 2, Sensor 1)
P2197.d: P2197 is the bank 2 version of P2195 on engines with a front sensor per bank: the bank 2 front oxygen or A/F sensor keeps reporting lean in a way the ECM rejects. GM's Bosch-based 2005 2.8 and 3.6 V6 flag it when the bank 2 rear sensor reads rich (above 0.85 V) while the front sensor reads leaner than lambda 1.08 with short-term trim at its 1.25 maximum, a contradiction a real lean mixture would not produce. Ford applies its switching, trim-limit and, from 2019, stuck-lambda tests to bank 2 the same way, with a 30 s window. Ford's 2017 bulletin for 2015 to 2017 Explorer and 2015 to 2016 F-150 3.5 GTDI lists P2195 and P2197 with P2626 and P2629, the pumping-current trim circuits of the A/F sensors, and fixes them with new heated oxygen sensors. If only bank 2 is affected, an exhaust manifold leak on that side ahead of the sensor is worth ruling out before replacing the sensor.
c: Bank 2 front oxygen or A/F sensor aged or contaminated
Exhaust manifold leak on bank 2 ahead of the sensor
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Possible rough running or higher consumption

P2198.t: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Rich (Bank 2, Sensor 1)
P2198.d: P2198 is the bank 2 counterpart of P2196: the bank 2 front oxygen or A/F sensor reports rich in a way the ECM does not accept. On GM's Bosch-based 2005 2.8 and 3.6 V6 the bank 2 rear sensor must read lean (below 0.15 V) while the front sensor reads richer than lambda 0.92 and the short-term trim has dropped to its 0.75 minimum; the code then sets after about 100 s, or 50 s cumulatively, over two trips. Ford uses the same lack-of-switching, trim-limit and stuck-lambda logic as on bank 1, sets the stuck-rich code when the frozen lambda value is below 1, and suspends the stuck-rich test during cold starts while fuel boils off the oil through the crankcase ventilation. A sensor contaminated by oil or coolant, or one whose signal or reference wiring has a fault, gives this pattern; since the ECM leans bank 2 to follow the false reading, the rear sensor of that bank usually shows lean at the same time.
c: Bank 2 front oxygen or A/F sensor contaminated or aged
Sensor signal or reference wiring fault
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Possible hesitation or lean running

P2199.d: P2199 compares two intake air temperature readings that should be close, typically one in the air mass sensor and one further downstream in the intake manifold or a combined pressure and temperature sensor. Each circuit can be fine on its own; the fault is the disagreement. GM sets it when the two values differ by more than 55 °C in 40 of 50 samples taken every 100 ms, as a Type B code with MIL after two trips (2016 and 2018 tables). VW's 2014 Touareg uses a much tighter limit of 10 °C between the two manifold temperatures. CARB requires such rationality checks for input sensors under (e)(15). Stellantis lists it among the codes addressed by a PCM update for the 2020 RAM 1500 with the 3.0 EcoDiesel V6; there, check the software level first. Circuit faults are P0111 to P0114 (sensor 1) and P0096 to P0099 (sensor 2).
c: One temperature sensor drifted or contaminated
Corroded connector or added resistance in one sensor circuit
Calibration issue fixed by a PCM update (e.g. RAM 1500 3.0 EcoDiesel 2020)
Strong heat soak or hot-air leak near one sensor
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable driveability change
Scan data shows two clearly different intake temperatures with the engine cold-soaked

P219A.d: P219A means the ECM sees mixture differences between the cylinders of bank 1 that are large enough to raise emissions, even if the bank average is fine. CARB phased this monitor in from 25 % of 2011 to all 2014 model-year petrol vehicles (13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(6.2.1)(C)). GM measures how much the upstream sensor signal varies per firing event, normalises the result against a map of a healthy engine and flags a ratio above 1.05 (one 2016 engine, 1100 to 3500 rpm, Type A, one trip). Mitsubishi counts rich and lean peaks at 1750 to 3250 rpm and 40 to 70 % volumetric efficiency. On inline engines bank 1 is the whole engine. Toyota traced P219A on 2012 to 2014 Corolla 2ZR engines to compression escaping into the exhaust; from 2014 the Corolla adds the cylinder codes P219C to P219F.
c: One injector clogged, leaking or out of flow tolerance
Compression loss through an intake or exhaust valve
Air leak at one intake runner or gasket
ECM logic or sensor signal issue covered by software or wiring bulletins
s: Check engine light on
Often no noticeable symptom
Slight rough running or misfire codes when one cylinder is far off

P219B.d: P219B is the bank 2 counterpart for V and boxer engines. Ford's 2012 summary shows one way to find it: the ECM watches the fast ripple of the bank's wide-band sensor over windows of roughly 50 revolutions and sets the code when more than 75 % of them fail, after 300 to 700 s of driving at 1000 to 3000 rpm and 20 to 60 % load. On one GM 2016 engine the bank 2 limit is 1.15 against 1.05 for bank 1. Bulletins name leaking direct injectors (Ford F-150 2.7 EcoBoost 2018; Explorer and Aviator 3.0 EcoBoost 2023 to 2025, injectors of the affected bank replaced), faulty or contaminated injectors (Honda Pilot 2016), electrical noise in the A/F sensor lines (Mazda CX-9 2011 to 2013) and, at Infiniti on the QX80, a warning not to swap the A/F sensor first. A code on bank 2 only points to a part on that side.
c: Leaking or contaminated injector on bank 2
Interference or damage in the bank 2 A/F sensor wiring
Intake runner or gasket leak at one bank 2 cylinder
PCM calibration addressed by a software update
s: Check engine light on
Usually no driveability change
Possible misfire codes on bank 2 cylinders

P219C.d: P219C names cylinder 1 as the one whose mixture departs from the others. Not every system can do that: CARB lets the stored code point only as far as the monitoring method allows, so many engines just log P219A or P219B. Those that resolve single cylinders include Toyota (the 2014 Corolla 2ZR gained P219C to P219F) and VW, whose 2014 2.5 litre five-cylinder leans each cylinder in turn and judges the resulting roughness, flagging a ratio below 0.19 or above 1.50. Subaru reflashed 2019 to 2020 Crosstrek Hybrid ECMs because P219C to P219F set without a real fault. Where the fault is real, check the cylinder 1 injector, its intake port seal and valve tightness with a leak-down test, as Toyota prescribes for the 2015 Tacoma V6. Cylinder numbering differs between makers, so confirm which cylinder is number 1.
c: Cylinder 1 injector clogged, leaking or out of tolerance
Intake runner or injector seal leak at cylinder 1
False detection fixed by ECM reprogramming (e.g. Subaru Crosstrek Hybrid)
s: Check engine light on
Often no noticeable symptom
Possible P0301 or rough idle if cylinder 1 deviates strongly

P219D.d: P219D singles out cylinder 2. On engines with two banks, whether cylinder 2 sits on bank 1 or bank 2 depends on the maker's numbering, which decides whether P219A or P219B may appear alongside. Bulletins show three very different outcomes. Kia replaced the high-pressure injector and its clip plus the high-pressure and crossover fuel pipes on 2022 Carnival models with the 3.5 GDI V6 when any of P219C to P21A1 had set. Hyundai fixed P219C to P219F on the 2018 Sonata 2.0 turbo with ECM and TCM software and noted that drivers feel nothing. Stellantis found a charge-air cooler with a loose crimp on the 2025 RAM 1500 3.0 Hurricane, which set P219D among other cylinder codes along with a whistling noise and reduced boost. A real cylinder 2 fault is confirmed with an injector balance test and a leak-down test.
c: Faulty high-pressure injector at cylinder 2 (direct injection)
Charge-air leak upsetting cylinder filling (e.g. RAM 3.0 Hurricane)
Detection logic corrected by software update (e.g. Hyundai Sonata 2.0T)
s: Check engine light on
Often no driveability change
Reduced power or whistling noise if a charge-air leak is the cause

P219E.d: P219E points at cylinder 3. Two bulletins show that a mixture code does not always mean a fuel part. Audi stored P219C to P21A1, one code per affected cylinder, on 2010 to 2012 S4, S5 and A6 with the 3.0 TFSI because of an incorrect software setting; the fix was new engine software and, in a later revision, a new crankcase pressure regulating valve. Lexus traced P219A and P219C to P219F on the 2.0 turbo 8AR-FTS (NX, IS, RC, GS 2015 onward) to compression lost through exhaust valves with worn guides, sometimes with misfire codes and reduced engine power, and repaired the cylinder head. Toyota's 2015 Tacoma V6 bulletin also starts with a leak-down test. For a lone P219E, test the cylinder 3 injector and compression before replacing sensors; the bank sensor itself is shared by all cylinders.
c: Exhaust valve leakage at cylinder 3 (e.g. worn guides on Lexus 8AR-FTS)
Cylinder 3 injector delivering the wrong amount
Incorrect ECM software setting (e.g. Audi 3.0 TFSI)
s: Check engine light on
Possible P0303 or rough running
Reduced engine power in severe cases

P219F.d: P219F singles out cylinder 4, the last cylinder on four-cylinder engines. Infiniti issued a bulletin for 2017 to 2018 QX60 with the direct-injection VQ35DD that stored only P219F without any driveability complaint; the remedy was ECM reprogramming followed by the idle air volume learn. Honda found the opposite case on 2023 to 2025 CR-V Hybrid and Accord Hybrid: a leaking injector made the mixture rich, fouled spark plugs and caused rattling and rough running, with P219C to P219F, P0172 and A/F sensor heater codes; all injectors and the fouled plugs were replaced and Honda warned against changing the A/F sensor first. Hyundai's 2018 Sonata 2.0 turbo also set P219F through software. Reading the spark plug of the flagged cylinder is a quick first check for rich or lean burning.
c: Oversensitive detection fixed by ECM reprogramming (e.g. Infiniti QX60, Hyundai Sonata)
Fouled spark plug as a consequence of a rich cylinder
s: Check engine light on
Rough running or rattling noise when an injector leaks
No symptom when the cause is software

P21A0.d: P21A0 can only occur on engines with at least five cylinders. VW's 2014 specification books for the Golf, Jetta, Passat and Beetle with the 2.5 litre inline five list P219C to P21A0, one per cylinder, all judged the same way: the ECM briefly leans one cylinder, measures how much rougher the engine runs and derives an individual fuel correction; a result below 0.19 or above 1.50 is a fault. On a five-cylinder with a single front sensor, the bank code P219A belongs to the same engine. Six-cylinder users include Toyota's 2015 Tacoma 1GR-FE, Audi's 3.0 TFSI (software) and Kia's 2022 Carnival 3.5 GDI (injectors). Because the method uses roughness, a weak ignition coil or a compression problem in cylinder 5 can also influence the result.
c: Ignition or compression weakness at cylinder 5 affecting the roughness test
Software setting corrected by an update (e.g. Audi 3.0 TFSI)
s: Check engine light on
Possible P0305 or slight vibration at idle

P21A1.d: P21A1 marks cylinder 6, the last cylinder of an inline six or V6. The clearest example comes from the 2025 RAM 1500 with the 3.0 Hurricane twin-turbo inline six: the charge-air cooler housing had a loose crimp that let boost escape, the cylinders filled unevenly and P21A1 set together with other cylinder codes, accompanied by a whistle and lower boost; the cooler was inspected and replaced if needed. Toyota listed P219A, P219B and P219C to P21A1 for the 2015 Tacoma 1GR-FE and worked through a leak-down test to a valve job. Kia replaced high-pressure injectors and fuel lines on the 2022 Carnival 3.5 GDI, while Audi corrected a software setting on 2010 to 2012 3.0 TFSI models. A code for the last cylinder alone is no reason to suspect sensor or ECM before injector and compression are checked.
c: Charge-air cooler or boost leak (turbo engines, e.g. RAM 3.0 Hurricane)
s: Check engine light on
Whistling noise and reduced boost with a charge-air leak
Possible P0306 or rough running

P21A2.d: P21A2 places a mixture imbalance at cylinder 7, so it only exists on engines with eight or more cylinders. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the bulletin index of the US safety authority NHTSA contains no bulletin that names it. The requirement behind it is CARB's monitor for uneven mixture between cylinders (13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(6.2.1)(C)), which asks the code to identify the cause as far as the method allows. A V8 has four cylinders per front sensor, so the sensor signal alone separates them less clearly than on a four-cylinder; methods that work at the engine cycle frequency, as described in a Cummins patent, or VW's individual leaning test make cylinder-level codes possible. Check the cylinder 7 injector, its intake sealing and compression, and compare with misfire counts.
c: Intake runner or injector seal leak at cylinder 7
s: Check engine light on
Often no noticeable symptom
Possible P0307 if the deviation is large

P21A3.d: P21A3 blames cylinder 8, on a V8 the last cylinder in the numbering. No manufacturer documentation of this code is publicly available, and no bulletin in the NHTSA index refers to it; the basis is the general CARB requirement for detecting cylinder imbalance, phased in for 2011 to 2014 model years with an emission threshold of 3.0 times the FTP standard (4.0 for SULEV II) until 2014 and 1.5 times from 2015. Whether cylinder 8 lies on bank 1 or bank 2 depends on the maker's numbering, which tells you whether P219A or P219B should accompany it. As Toyota and Lexus bulletins on cylinder codes show, leaking or restricted injectors, an intake leak at one runner and leaking valves are the usual causes. An injector balance test and a leak-down test on cylinder 8 come before any sensor work.
c: Intake leak at the cylinder 8 runner
s: Check engine light on
Usually no driveability change
Possible P0308 with a strong deviation

P21A4.d: P21A4 is reserved for an imbalance at cylinder 9 and can therefore only appear on engines with ten or more cylinders, a small group of V10 and V12 petrol engines. No manufacturer documents the code publicly and no bulletin in the NHTSA index mentions it. CARB's rule (13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(6.2.1)(C)) still applies to these engines, and it allows a maker to store a bank code or even a misfire code instead when its hardware cannot single out a cylinder. With five or six cylinders feeding one front sensor, separating them needs extra effort, for example a frequency analysis tied to the engine cycle as in the Cummins patent, or an active test that changes the fuel of one cylinder at a time as VW does on its five-cylinder. Diagnosis follows the usual order: injector, intake sealing, compression of cylinder 9.
s: Check engine light on
Possible P0309 with a large deviation

P21A5.d: P21A5 flags cylinder 10, which on a V10 is the final cylinder and on a V12 sits near the end of its bank. Public manufacturer material for this code does not exist, and the NHTSA bulletin index has no entry for it. CARB requires detection of any cylinder imbalance that lifts emissions above one and a half times the FTP limit (from 2015) and that the fault code point as precisely as the method allows; since a phase-in from 2019 to 2021, petrol vehicles must also log how often the check actually runs in daily use. Before chasing cylinder 10 specifically, confirm that the flagged number matches the manufacturer's numbering and that no other cylinder of the same bank also shows a misfire count or a deviating injector, because a correction on one cylinder can shift its neighbours. Then test the cylinder 10 injector and compression.
c: Fault in another cylinder of the same bank shifting the result
s: Check engine light on
Possible P0310 or uneven idle

P21A6.d: P21A6 assigns the imbalance to cylinder 11, which exists only on twelve-cylinder engines. No manufacturer has published how it detects this code, and no NHTSA bulletin names it, so it is a placeholder that J2012 provides for large engines. The legal frame is CARB's cylinder imbalance monitor (13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(6.2.1)(C)). A V12 or W12 feeds six cylinders into each front sensor, and exhaust pulses overlap, which makes a clean per-cylinder reading hard; the Cummins patent describes estimating the signal content at the engine cycle frequency and then trimming the fuel of the cylinder that causes it, an approach suited to many cylinders. In practice the work is mechanical: confirm the numbering, compare injector delivery across the bank and run a compression or leak-down test on cylinder 11.
s: Check engine light on
Possible P0311 with a large deviation

P21A7.d: P21A7 is the last code of the cylinder series that starts with P219C and points to cylinder 12 of a twelve-cylinder engine. There is no public manufacturer description and no NHTSA bulletin for it. Under CARB's rule (13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(6.2.1)(C)) the monitor had to be in all 2014 and later petrol vehicles, with limits of 3.0 times the FTP standard until 2014 and 1.5 times from 2015 for non-LEV III cars, so twelve-cylinder engines are covered as well; many simply report the bank code P219A or P219B. The causes do not differ from smaller engines: a single injector, a leaking intake seal or a valve that does not close properly. Because a V12 has two separate banks, check whether the bank code and the misfire counter P0312 agree with cylinder 12 before parts are replaced.
s: Check engine light on
Possible P0312 or slight vibration

P21A8.d: P21A8 is the general circuit code for the second reductant level sensor, needed only where a DEF tank reports its fill level through more than one sensing element. GM's 6.6L Duramax (LML/LGH) and the 2014 Cruze diesel read three discrete level sensors, numbered 1 to 3 in GM's tables, which corresponds to A to C. GM does not use P21A8 itself but splits the fault into P21AA (below 0.17 V after a test pulse) and P21AB (open load or short to battery). A maker using the umbrella code stores it for any wiring fault it cannot assign to one side. CARB requires such input circuits to be monitored (13 CCR 1968.2 (f)(15.2.1)). Expect a DEF warning message and, if left unrepaired, the usual SCR warning sequence.
c: Damaged or corroded harness or connector at the DEF tank
Level sensor B in the tank assembly failed
s: Check engine light on
DEF system warning message in the cluster
DEF level or range display missing or wrong

P21A9.t: Reductant Level Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P21A9.d: P21A9 flags a level sensor B signal that stays inside its electrical limits but does not fit what else the system knows, such as the states of the other level sensors or the fluid consumed. GM's 2018 Cruze diesel (LH7) stores it in the module running the DEF system, under the name Level Sensor 2 Performance. Engineering bulletin PIE0453 asked dealers for freeze-frame data on ambient and fluid temperature, engine-off time and whether the car was parked outside, because the root cause was still unknown; cold soak is evidently under suspicion. On the 2014 Cruze GM still caught contradictory sensor states under P203B (5 s, Type B). Wiring faults of sensor B go to P21AA/P21AB. Drivers see the MIL and possibly a DEF message.
c: Frozen or very cold fluid giving an implausible reading
Level sensor B fouled by crystallised urea or degraded
Control module calibration flagging the sensor too early
s: Check engine light on
DEF level shown wrongly or jumping
Fault appears mainly after cold nights

P21AA.t: Reductant Level Sensor B Circuit Low
P21AA.d: P21AA means the second reductant level sensor reads too low a voltage, which GM takes as a short to ground. GM documents it for the 6.6L Duramax LML and the 2014 Cruze 2.0 diesel: the tank level electronics apply a test pulse, and if sensor 2 then shows less than 0.17 V for more than 3 s with over 8 V supply, the ECM receives an error status over CAN. The LML treats it as Type A (MIL on the first trip), the Cruze as Type B (two trips). GM bulletin 12-06-04-002C lists P21AA among the DEF codes that must run and pass before the warning tests can clear the driver messages. Look for chafed or wet harness sections first; as the sensors belong to the tank assembly, a failed element usually means a new tank unit.
c: Sensor 2 signal wire chafed through to ground
Fluid or water in the tank connector
Internal short in level sensor B (tank assembly)
s: Check engine light on
DEF warning message that stays on
DEF range or level display wrong

P21AB.t: Reductant Level Sensor B Circuit High
P21AB.d: P21AB is the high-side counterpart: GM sets it when level sensor 2 shows an open load (between 3.56 and 4.74 V, read 1.5 ms after the test pulse) or a short to battery voltage (above 4.74 V), each for more than 3 s, as Type A on the 6.6L LML and the 2014 Cruze diesel. GM's preliminary bulletin PIP4887B for 2010–2011 Silverado, Sierra, Express and Savana with the LML or LGH engine names P21AB together with P203D and P21B0 and the message Service Exhaust Fluid System: inspect wiring, connectors and terminal tension also when the faults are merely stored, and replace the DEF tank only when the wiring is sound. For the 2011 model year GM sorted P21AB into its tamper-related group.
c: Open signal wire or spread terminal at the tank connector
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
Level sensor B open inside the tank assembly
s: Check engine light on at once
Service Exhaust Fluid System message
Several level sensor codes stored together

P21AC.t: Reductant Level Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P21AC.d: P21AC reports that the level sensor B signal drops out or jumps for short moments instead of failing steadily. No manufacturer documents criteria for this code publicly. GM's Duramax and Cruze diesel tables cover sensor 2 only with the steady faults P21AA and P21AB, both requiring an error lasting over 3 s, so an intermittent code points to contact losses shorter than that: a terminal that has lost its grip in the tank connector, a harness section that moves with the tank, or corrosion where fluid has crept in. GM's bulletin PIP4887B on related level sensor codes stresses checking terminal tension even when codes are only stored in history. CARB requires input circuits to be watched for such faults (13 CCR 1968.2 (f)(15.2.1)).
c: Loose terminal in the tank connector
Harness flexing or rubbing near the tank mounting
Corrosion from fluid creeping into the connector
s: DEF warning that comes and goes
Jumping DEF level display
Check engine light, sometimes only stored code

P21AD.d: P21AD covers the electrical circuit of the third reductant level sensor, so it only exists on tanks with at least three level points. GM's 6.6L Duramax and 2014 Cruze diesel are such cases: the tank electronics test sensors 1 to 3 separately and pass each status to the ECM over CAN. GM uses the specific codes P21AF and P21B0 instead of this summary code. If P21AD shows up together with P21A8 and P203A, a shared supply, ground or the tank connector is far more likely than three failed sensors at once. Since the level information feeds the DEF range and refill warnings, drivers may see a missing or wrong range message besides the MIL. CARB asks for circuit monitoring of such inputs in 13 CCR 1968.2 (f)(15.2.1).
c: Fault in a supply, ground or connector shared by the level sensors
Level sensor C in the tank assembly failed
s: Check engine light on
DEF range message missing or implausible
Further level sensor codes stored

P21AE.t: Reductant Level Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P21AE.d: P21AE stands for an implausible level sensor C signal whose voltage is still electrically valid. No manufacturer describes a separate check for this code in public material. GM shows how such plausibility testing can work: on the 2014 Cruze diesel the ECM compares the readings of all three discrete level sensors after the test pulse and flags combinations that cannot physically occur together, but files the result under P203B rather than under a code for the sensor concerned. For the 2018 Cruze, GM did assign P21A9 to sensor 2. A maker using P21AE would point to sensor C itself, for instance after urea crystal deposits or partial freezing. Electrical faults of this sensor are covered by P21AF and P21B0.
c: Crystallised urea on level sensor C
Partly frozen fluid around the sensor
Level sensor C drifting or degraded
s: Check engine light on
DEF level display does not match the refill amount
Possible DEF warning sequence

P21AF.t: Reductant Level Sensor C Circuit Low
P21AF.d: P21AF is set when level sensor C, called level sensor 3 by GM, reads below 0.17 V right after the tank electronics apply their test pulse, which GM interprets as a short to ground. Supply must be above 8 V and the error must persist for more than 3 s. The 2014 Cruze diesel stores it as Type B, so the MIL lights after the second failing trip; on the 6.6L LML Duramax it appears in the same form, and GM bulletin 12-06-04-002C places it in the first group of DEF codes to be repaired before the warning tests can run again. When P203C or P21AA are present as well, several sensors reading low at once point to a common wiring or connector problem rather than to sensor 3 alone.
c: Sensor 3 signal wire shorted to ground
Water or fluid bridging contacts in the tank connector
Level sensor C shorted inside the tank assembly
s: Check engine light after two trips
DEF warning message
Implausible DEF level shown

P21B0.t: Reductant Level Sensor C Circuit High
P21B0.d: P21B0 means GM's level sensor 3 (sensor C) shows an open circuit or a short to battery: either 3.56 to 4.74 V or more than 4.74 V, measured 1.5 ms after a test pulse, for over 3 s. The 6.6L LML and the 2014 Cruze both rate it Type A, lighting the MIL on the first trip. PIP4887B names P21B0 next to P203D and P21AB on 2010–2011 Duramax trucks showing Service Exhaust Fluid System; when all three high codes appear together, GM directs technicians to wiring and terminal tension first and to the DEF tank assembly only afterwards. A tank connector left unplugged after other work would produce the same set of codes, so check that before ordering parts.
c: Tank connector loose, unplugged or with spread terminals
Sensor 3 signal wire open or shorted to voltage
Level sensor C open inside the tank assembly
s: Check engine light on at once
Service Exhaust Fluid System message
P203D and P21AB often stored as well

P21B1.t: Reductant Level Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P21B1.d: P21B1 marks level sensor C signals that come and go. Public manufacturer criteria do not exist; GM's diesel tables describe sensor 3 only through the steady faults P21AF and P21B0, each filtered over 3 s. A stored P21B1 therefore suggests interruptions too short for those monitors, typical of a connector that works loose under tank vibration, fluid seeping into the terminals, or a harness pinched under a tank strap. Moving the harness while watching the sensor data with a scan tool is the quickest way to reproduce it. If P21AC is present too, the cause probably lies in wiring both sensors share. Drivers mainly notice an unsteady DEF level display or a warning that appears and clears again.
c: Harness pinched under a tank strap
s: Unsteady DEF level display
DEF warning that appears and clears
Stored code without current fault

P21B2.t: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop NOx Adsorber Control
P21B2.d: P21B2 is set when the feedback control of a NOx adsorber (lean NOx trap) has not become active within the time the manufacturer allows once its enable conditions are met. CARB requires this check for vehicles with feedback control of the adsorber or its active injection (13 CCR 1968.2 (f)(8.2.3)(A)(i)). Cummins describes such a loop in patent US7594392: oxygen sensors before and after the adsorber, open-loop rich/lean cycling first, then a closed loop that holds the bed near 650 °C during regeneration. Ram 2500/3500 trucks with the 6.7L Cummins (2007–2011) carry a NOx absorber; Chrysler bulletin 25-001-13 links its P2000 to fouled oxygen sensors. No maker publishes criteria for P21B2; slow sensors or a cold exhaust are the usual suspects.
c: Fouled or slow oxygen sensor before or after the adsorber
Exhaust not reaching control temperature (short trips, low load)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensors
Exhaust temperature sensor reporting too low
s: Check engine light on
Regeneration of the NOx trap delayed or skipped
Higher NOx emissions, possible test failure

P21B3.t: Closed Loop NOx Adsorber Control At Limit - Too High
P21B3.d: P21B3 means the NOx adsorber feedback loop has reached its upper adjustment limit and still misses its target, the case CARB describes in 13 CCR 1968.2 (f)(8.2.3)(A)(iii). In practice the controller asks for more enrichment or longer rich phases than the calibration permits, because the downstream oxygen signal never shows the expected change or the bed stays below its target. Cummins patent US8065871 evaluates this upstream/downstream lambda difference to find the lean-to-rich transitions of the adsorber. Plausible reasons are a sulphur-loaded or aged adsorber, a lagging rear oxygen sensor, air leaks before the sensors, or fuel delivery that falls short. No manufacturer publishes thresholds for P21B3; read it together with P2000 and oxygen sensor codes.
c: NOx adsorber sulphur-loaded or thermally aged
Downstream oxygen sensor responding too slowly
Air leak in the exhaust ahead of the sensors
Too little fuel delivered for the rich phases
s: Check engine light on
Higher fuel consumption from long rich phases
Often stored together with P2000

P21B4.d: P21B4 reports that the NOx adsorber on bank 1 has run hotter than the manufacturer's protection limit. The risk is greatest during desulphation, when the adsorber is heated on purpose: Eaton patent US7251929 gives about 750 °C as the maximum desulphation temperature, beyond which the adsorber ages thermally, while Cummins aims for roughly 650 °C during regeneration (US7594392). Excess heat comes from too much fuel in rich phases, leaking injectors, unburnt fuel after misfires, or a temperature signal that reads wrong. No manufacturer documents its P21B4 limit publicly; the code can only occur on engines with such a catalyst, for instance the 2007–2011 Ram 6.7L Cummins. Act promptly: repeated overheating ruins the storage coating and leads to P2000.
c: Too much fuel during regeneration or desulphation
Leaking or dribbling injector on bank 1
Misfire sending unburnt fuel into the exhaust
Exhaust temperature sensor reading too high
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power while the engine protects the catalyst
Strong smell or heat from the exhaust

P21B5.d: P21B5 is the bank 2 version of the adsorber over-temperature fault and therefore only exists where each cylinder bank feeds its own NOx storage catalyst, which in practice means V engines with two exhaust paths. If only bank 2 overheats, the cause most likely sits on that side: an injector delivering too much, misfire limited to that bank, or a faulty temperature sensor there. If P21B4 is stored as well, look instead for something both banks share, such as the regeneration strategy, fuel quality or a skewed air mass reading. Eaton patent US7251929 puts the ageing limit near 750 °C during desulphation. No manufacturer publishes its P21B5 limit; the duty to monitor adsorber performance comes from CARB (13 CCR 1968.2 (f)(8)). Driving on risks permanent damage.
c: Injector on bank 2 delivering too much fuel
Bank 2 exhaust temperature sensor reading too high
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power to protect the catalyst
Uneven exhaust temperatures between the banks

P21B6.d: After a cold start, petrol direct-injection and diesel engines deliberately move the moment of injection – for example with an extra late pulse – so that more heat reaches the catalyst. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(11) wants every element of this strategy checked while it runs and reported apart from warm-engine faults. P21B6 pins such a deviation on cylinder 1. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM's 2025 diesel tables compare requested and scheduled start of injection on every cylinder but store only the system code P05EC. If cylinder 1 alone is flagged, a shared cause such as crank/cam synchronisation is unlikely; the injector, its wiring or its driver stage come first. Warm counterpart: P020A.
c: Injector of cylinder 1 responds late or inconsistently when cold
Corroded or loose connector or harness at injector 1
Injector driver stage in the engine control module faulty
Engine module software with an overly strict cold-start check
s: Check engine light after one or more cold starts
Slightly rough idle in the first minute after a cold start
No noticeable fault once the engine is warm

P21B7.d: P21B7 flags cylinder 2 during the cold-start phase only: the injection timing commanded for catalyst heating did not arrive as intended on that cylinder. The heating phase is brief and ends as coolant and catalyst warm up, so the monitor gets one chance per cold start and may need several cold starts before the code is confirmed. GM's 2025 diesel calibrations show the principle at system level: requested against scheduled start of injection, one sample per revolution, 88 failures out of 176 set P05EC with the lamp in the first trip. A cylinder-specific code like P21B7 appears in no public manufacturer document. If P020B (cylinder 2, warm) or P2B09 (cold-start pulse) are stored as well, the injector or its circuit is more likely than software.
c: Injector of cylinder 2 worn or coked, opening late at low temperature
Chafed or high-resistance wiring to injector 2
Weak battery lowering injector supply voltage during and after cranking
s: Check engine light that appears only after cold starts
Uneven running or slight smoke shortly after starting a cold engine
Code may take several cold starts to return after clearing

P21B8.d: Cylinder 3 is the last cylinder of three-cylinder engines such as Ford's 1.0-litre EcoBoost, a turbo direct-injection unit. There a single cylinder accounts for a third of all combustion events, so a cold-start fault on it tends to be felt more than on larger engines. P21B8 reports that while the cold-start heating strategy was active, the injection timing of cylinder 3 left its tolerance. The code belongs to a per-cylinder series made necessary by CARB's demand to keep cold-start faults apart from warm-running faults; no manufacturer documents its use publicly. On engines with four or more cylinders P21B8 simply marks cylinder 3. Neighbouring checks: P020C for the warm engine, P2B0A for the cold-start injection pulse, P0303 for misfire.
c: Injector of cylinder 3 with deposits or a weak coil
Moisture or corrosion in the plug of injector 3
Engine software update available for the cold-start calibration
s: Noticeable shaking at cold idle, especially on three-cylinder engines
Check engine light after cold starts
Normal running once warm

P21B9.d: Four-cylinder petrol direct injection is the most widespread engine type this code can apply to, and cylinder 4 is its last cylinder. Ford's 2011 OBD summary for its first turbo direct-injection engine explains the background: during catalyst heating the injection timing may be specific to that mode, possibly as two injections with one during the compression stroke, which in turn needs a rail pressure window (checked as P053F). P21B9 reports that this cold-start timing went wrong on cylinder 4 alone. No manufacturer lists the code publicly, so the description rests on CARB's cold-start rules and the documented system codes. Warm-engine counterpart: P020D; electrical injector fault: P0204; cold-start pulse: P2B0B.
c: Deposits on the tip of injector 4 changing its opening behaviour
Harness fault on the injector 4 circuit
Rail pressure barely inside its window during cold start, affecting the last cylinder first
s: Check engine light, usually without drivability complaints
Slightly longer catalyst warm-up and possibly higher cold-start emissions
Occasional hesitation right after a cold start

P21BA.d: P21BA can only occur on engines with at least five cylinders – inline fives, V6, V8 and larger. GM's 4.3-litre V6 and 5.3/6.2-litre V8 direct-injection engines use a dual-pulse injection in open loop after a cold start; a GM bulletin explains that the module watches crankshaft speed in this mode and sets P050D (cold start rough idle) if it varies too much. A per-cylinder timing code such as P21BA goes a step further and names the cylinder whose cold-start injection timing missed its target. No manufacturer has published use of P21BA. On which bank cylinder 5 sits depends on the manufacturer's numbering, so check the engine's cylinder layout before testing. Related: P020E (warm), P2B0C (cold-start pulse), P0305.
c: Injector of cylinder 5 sticking or delivering late when cold
Repair on the wrong injector because of a misread cylinder numbering
Open or high-resistance circuit to injector 5
s: Check engine light after cold starts
Rough idle during the first seconds after a cold start, possibly together with P050D

P21BB.d: Cylinder 6 exists on six-cylinder engines and anything larger – inline sixes and V6 units such as Ford's 3.5-litre EcoBoost petrol or the 3.0-litre EcoDiesel in the Ram 1500. For that diesel FCA listed the warm-engine timing codes P020A–P020F together with the over-advanced and over-retarded codes in a 2021 bulletin whose fix was reprogramming the engine module. P21BB is the cold-start version for cylinder 6: during the heating phase after start, its injection timing did not match the target. Diesels adapt injection timing to coolant temperature after a cold start to hold emissions down before NOx sensors are working, as a GM patent describes. No manufacturer documents P21BB publicly; a software update is worth checking before replacing parts.
c: Injector of cylinder 6 worn, coked or with drifting opening delay
Outdated engine module software (analogous timing codes were cured by reprogramming)
Damaged wiring or connector at injector 6
s: Check engine light after cold starts
On diesels, more white smoke or knocking in the first minutes
Hard start or rough idle when cold

P21BC.d: From cylinder 7 on, the code is limited to engines with at least seven cylinders – in practice V8, V10, V12 and W12. Common petrol V8 with direct injection are GM's 5.3- and 6.2-litre small blocks, which a GM bulletin describes with dual-pulse injection after a cold start, and Ford's 5.0-litre Coyote, which since 2018 combines port and direct injection. P21BC reports that during the cold-start heating phase the injection timing of cylinder 7 missed its target; on dual-system engines the direct injector is the part whose timing is shifted. No manufacturer publishes use of P21BC. If the code repeats on cylinder 7 only, test that injector cold and compare it with the others. Related: P021A (warm), P2B0E (cold-start pulse), P0207, P0307.
c: Direct injector of cylinder 7 slow to open or leaking at low temperature
Chafed or heat-damaged wiring to injector 7
Fault in the high-voltage injector driver of the engine module
s: Check engine light after cold starts
Rough cold idle, sometimes with P050D or a cylinder 7 misfire code

P21BD.d: P21BD covers cylinder 8, the last cylinder of a V8. GM's 2025 diesel tables show how close an existing monitor comes to this code: during cold start the module compares requested and scheduled start of injection, with every cylinder from A to H included in the enable checks, and a deviation beyond ±4 in 88 of 176 samples sets the lamp in the first trip. Yet GM stores only the system code P05EC, which does not say which injector misbehaved. A per-cylinder code like P21BD would point straight at cylinder 8; no manufacturer documents its use publicly. GM's petrol V8 with direct injection likewise use a special dual-pulse cold-start mode. Related: P021B (warm), P2B0F (cold-start pulse), P0208, P0308.
c: Injector of cylinder 8 with slow or varying response
Connector or wiring fault at injector 8
Cold-start calibration in the engine module needing an update
s: Check engine light after cold starts
Rough running or smoke in the first minute after a cold start
No symptoms at operating temperature

P21BE.d: A ninth cylinder exists only on V10, V12 and W12 engines, so P21BE is limited to a handful of models. Petrol engines in this class with direct injection include the 5.2-litre V10 of Lamborghini and Audi (Huracán, R8, S6 and S8) and the 6.3-litre W12 FSI of the Audi A8, which feeds its injectors from two high-pressure pumps and two rails. Whether their engine modules use P21BE is not documented publicly, and no other manufacturer source names the code. Its meaning follows from the series: during the cold-start heating phase the injection timing of cylinder 9 deviated from its target, a fault CARB wants reported apart from warm-engine faults. There is no cold-start injection pulse code beyond cylinder 8. Related: P021C (warm), P0209, P0309.
c: Direct injector of cylinder 9 with deposits or slow response
Wiring or connector fault at injector 9
Low pressure on the rail feeding cylinder 9 (engines with two rails)
s: Check engine light after cold starts
Slightly uneven idle while the engine is cold

P21BF.d: Cylinder 10 is the last cylinder of a V10 and exists otherwise only on twelve-cylinder engines. V10 engines are rare: Ford's 6.8-litre truck V10 (firing order 1-6-5-10-2-7-3-8-4-9, in the E-Series until 2019) and the 5.2-litre direct-injection V10 of Lamborghini and Audi. P21BF states that cylinder 10, during the cold-start heating phase, received its fuel at a different moment than targeted. No manufacturer documents the code publicly; the description rests on CARB's cold-start monitoring rules and on the system code P05EC, which GM checks across all cylinders of its diesels. If P021D (warm timing) or P0210 (injector circuit) are stored too, the cylinder 10 injector is the prime suspect; a cold-start pulse code does not exist for this cylinder.
c: Injector of cylinder 10 aged or contaminated
Wiring or connector problem at injector 10
Engine module software needing a cold-start calibration update
s: Check engine light after one or more cold starts
Uneven idle until the engine warms up

P21C0.d: P21C0 applies only to twelve-cylinder engines (V12 or W12), since passenger-car engines with exactly eleven cylinders do not exist. Examples with direct injection are BMW's N74 twin-turbo V12, found in the BMW 760i and in Rolls-Royce models such as Ghost, Wraith and Dawn, and the 6.3-litre W12 FSI. The code would report that cylinder 11 missed its cold-start injection timing, for instance when the extra injection for catalyst heating is shifted. Whether BMW, Rolls-Royce or Audi use P21C0 is not documented publicly. The legal basis is CARB's demand for separate cold-start diagnostics, allowing the module to tell such faults apart from warm-running timing faults (P021E). Related: P0211 (injector circuit), P0311 (misfire).
c: Direct injector of cylinder 11 with changed opening behaviour
Heat-damaged wiring or connector at injector 11
Injector driver for cylinder 11 in the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine light after cold starts
Barely noticeable on the road; a twelve-cylinder engine masks a single cylinder well

P21C1.d: Cylinder 12 is the last cylinder of V12 and W12 engines. Direct-injection V12 include Ferrari's F140 family (FF, F12berlinetta, 812 Superfast) and BMW's N74; among W engines there is the 6.3-litre W12 FSI. P21C1 reports that during the cold-start heating phase the injection timing of cylinder 12 deviated from its target. The code closes the series P21B6–P21C1, which exists because CARB requires cold-start faults to be kept apart from normal ones; the following code, P21C2, already belongs to the SCR reductant heater. No manufacturer publishes use of P21C1. Practical cross-checks: P021F (timing, warm engine), P0212 (injector circuit) and P0312 (misfire). Repairs on these engines are workshop jobs.
c: Injector of cylinder 12 with deposits or worn needle
Damaged wiring at the end of the cylinder bank (injector 12)
Cold-start calibration of the engine module out of date
s: Check engine light after cold starts
Hardly any drivability change, at most a slightly uneven cold idle

P21C2.d: P21C2 concerns the control line of the relay that supplies current to the DEF heaters. The control module drives the relay coil through an output stage and checks whether the circuit reacts; an open circuit means the coil, its wiring or a connector has lost continuity, so the heaters cannot be energised. Ford documents the code in its 2023 diesel summary: the check runs continuously while heating is requested, and with the relay stage on and every heater switched off, a heater current below 0.2 A sets P21C2 within at most 5 s. P21C3 and P21C4 are the low and high faults of the same line, P21C7 covers the power relay of the module itself. In frost the fluid may stay frozen, so dosing starts late and DEF warnings can follow.
c: Relay coil burnt open or relay not seated in its socket
Broken control wire between module and relay
Corroded or loose terminals at relay box or module connector
Faulty output stage in the controlling module
s: Check engine light on
DEF system warning, especially at low ambient temperature
Frozen DEF thaws slowly, dosing begins late after a cold start

P21C3.t: Reductant Heater Relay Control Circuit Low
P21C3.d: P21C3 is the low-side fault on the control line of the DEF heater relay: the signal is pulled toward ground, for example by a chafed wire touching the frame or a shorted relay coil, so the relay no longer follows the command. Ford's 2023 diesel summary uses the same continuous check as for P21C2, but here the relay stage is on, every heater has been told to stay off, and still more than 6 A of heater current is measured; the fault is confirmed within 5 s. Such a reading means power reaches the heater circuit by a path the module never requested. Whether the heaters then stay dead or run without control depends on how the relay is wired. P21C2 is the open-circuit counterpart, P21C4 the high-side fault, P21C7 the module power relay.
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Relay coil with internal short or welded contacts
Water or salt in the relay or heater connector
Output stage of the controlling module faulty
s: Check engine light on
DEF heating inactive or running when not commanded
Blown fuse in the heater supply

P21C4.t: Reductant Heater Relay Control Circuit High
P21C4.d: P21C4 means the control side of the DEF heater relay shows voltage when it should be dead. Ford's 2023 diesel summary sets it when the relay stage and all heaters are off and the heater circuit still carries more than 5 V, within at most 5 s; a short to the battery feed or contacts that no longer open are the classic reasons. FCA logs the code on Ram 2500 to 5500 trucks with the 6.7 L Cummins (2019 to 2024) with a title that names the line heater relay, often together with U11C1. Bulletin 25-008-24 traces this pairing to a replacement dosing control unit (68458603AB) and fixes it by reflashing; Stellantis case S1625000002 adds that new units ship without vehicle software and need programming. P21C2 and P21C3 cover the open and low faults.
c: Replacement dosing control unit not programmed or with outdated software (FCA)
Control or heater wire shorted to battery voltage
Internal fault in the controlling module
s: Check engine light on
Code appears shortly after a DEF control unit was replaced
Additional communication code such as U11C1 stored

P21C5.d: P21C5 is a plausibility code: the level sensor A reports valid readings, yet they hardly move when the fluid in the tank should be sloshing. GM spells this out for the ultrasonic sensor in its 2025 diesel tables, where it is sensor 1.
