As a guide, GM's LML logs P2200 when the smart sensor keeps signalling an interrupted wire for 0.5 or 10 s, and Ford adds probe-line shorts and checksum errors inside the sensor controller. CARB requires circuit faults on NOx sensors to be caught. P2214 to P2217 cover the other bank 2 signal faults.
c: Internal fault in the bank 2 NOx probe or its sensor control unit
Heat-damaged or chafed lead between probe and sensor control unit
Water or corrosion in the bank 2 sensor connector
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
No NOx value from the bank 2 sensor in live data
SCR warning, possibly with an inducement countdown

P2214.d: Under J2012, P2214 is the plausibility fault of the bank 2 NOx sensor: wiring intact, reading not credible. No maker uses it that way in public documents. Hino does use the number differently: on its J08E inline six (Hino 238, 258, 268 and 338 conventional models, 2011 to 2016) P2214 belongs to NOx sensor 2 behind the SCR catalyst. Hino bulletin SB-14-029 first checks DEF concentration (31.8 to 33.2 percent), exhaust leaks, temperature and airflow sensors and the dosing injector, then re-tests at a steady 45 to 50 mph after a regeneration. SB-15-038 and SB-16-002 link P2214 and P2201 to NOx heater elements cracked by condensation and add DCU software. For a real bank 2 sensor, P2201 logic applies (VW: 60 percent deviation).
c: Aged or poisoned NOx element reading with offset or slow response
Sensor heater cracked by condensation (Hino 2015-2016, SB-15-038/SB-16-002)
Diluted DEF or faulty dosing injector distorting the NOx reading
Exhaust leak upstream of the sensor
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Often stored with P2201 or SCR efficiency code P20EE
Higher DEF consumption or SCR warning

P2215.d: P2215 says the NOx value transmitted for bank 2 falls below the smallest figure a healthy sensor can deliver. Because smart NOx sensors talk over CAN, the limit is a concentration in ppm, not a wire voltage. No manufacturer publishes this bank 2 code; the diesels on record send both banks through one SCR system and use P2202 instead. Those bank 1 limits give the scale: GM's 6.6L and 3.0L Duramax flag readings below minus 90 ppm (on the LZ0 only after the dew point is reached, Type B over two trips), VW's 2014 Touareg TDI below minus 105 ppm. A strongly negative value usually comes from a drifted element or a fault inside the sensor electronics. P2216 is the high limit, P2213 the general circuit fault.
c: NOx element of the bank 2 sensor drifted low
Fault in the measuring electronics of the sensor module
Damaged lead between probe and sensor module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Negative NOx value for bank 2 in live data
DEF dosing switches to a substitute strategy

P2216.d: P2216 is set when the NOx concentration reported for bank 2 exceeds anything the engine could plausibly emit. It belongs to engines with an SCR line per cylinder bank; none of the documented diesels is built that way, and no manufacturer lists P2216 publicly. The bank 1 code P2203 shows what such a check looks like: GM trips at 1,500 or 2,500 ppm on the 6.6L LML and at 2,500 ppm on the 3.0L LZ0 (Type B, two trips), VW at 1,655 ppm on the 2014 Touareg TDI. An overreading probe can make the dosing controller inject too much DEF, risking ammonia slip, so the reading is discarded. Internal sensor failure is the most frequent reason. P2215 is the low limit, P2214 a believable but wrong value.
c: Bank 2 NOx sensor reading too high due to internal failure
Sensing element fouled by oil ash or DEF crystals
Calibration error in the engine or dosing control software
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Implausibly high NOx value for bank 2 in live data
SCR efficiency codes may follow

P2217.d: P2217 describes a bank 2 NOx sensor whose measuring path fails only now and then: the reading drops out or the sensor briefly reports an electrical error, then recovers. A smart NOx sensor evaluates its own probe lines and sends status flags for open or shorted circuits alongside the value over CAN; flags that toggle point to this code rather than to the steady fault P2213. No manufacturer documents P2217, nor its bank 1 twin P2204, with thresholds, so the debounce logic is calibration-specific; CARB generally requires continuous detection of NOx sensor continuity faults. Typical causes are a loose terminal, a lead that cracks when hot, or water entering the connector. The warning lamp may come and go.
c: Loose or corroded terminals at the bank 2 sensor connector
Lead near the exhaust cracked by heat or vibration
Sporadic fault in the sensor module electronics
s: Malfunction indicator lamp that comes and goes
Bank 2 NOx value briefly invalid in live data

P2218.d: A NOx sensor cannot measure until its built-in heater has taken the ceramic cell to several hundred degrees, and the sensor electronics switches that heater itself. P2218 reports a break in the heater control path of the bank 2 sensor, either inside the probe or in the lead to the sensor module. No manufacturer documents the bank 2 version. The bank 1 code P2205 is well described: GM's 6.6L LML sets it when an open heater is reported longer than 10 s with the battery at 11 V or more, the 3.0L LZ0 on an open load at the heater control pin, both Type A with the MIL after one trip. Without heating, the bank 2 sensor never becomes ready. P2219 and P2220 are the shorted cases, P2221 the heater sense side.
c: Heater element in the bank 2 NOx probe burnt through
Broken conductor between probe and sensor module
Pushed-back or corroded pin in the sensor connector
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after one trip
Bank 2 NOx sensor never reports ready

P2219.t: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit Low (Bank 2)
P2219.d: P2219 means the heater control line of the bank 2 NOx sensor is pulled toward ground when it should not be, typically a heater lead chafed against the exhaust or a shorted output stage in the sensor electronics. The control unit then switches the heater off to protect itself. Bank 2 use is not documented by any manufacturer, as known SCR diesels combine both banks. For the bank 1 counterpart P2206, GM's 3.0L Duramax (LZ0) counts 80 failures in 160 samples taken every 25 ms, with relay voltage above 11 V and the dew point passed, and stores a Type B fault lighting the MIL after two trips. Volvo and Mack treat P2206 on their inlet sensor as a sensor failure. P2218 is the open circuit, P2220 the short to power.
c: Heater lead of the bank 2 sensor chafed through to ground
Shorted heater or output stage inside the sensor
Salt water bridging pins in the connector
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Bank 2 NOx sensor stays cold and delivers no value

P221A.d: P221A compares the two NOx sensors of bank 1, upstream and downstream of the SCR catalyst. When conditions should make both read alike, the gap between them is too large, so the system cannot tell which value to trust. Volvo and Mack list P221A among codes that often lead to needless sensor swaps; before replacement a NOx conversion test must show the inlet and outlet readings disagreeing by more than about 40 ppm shortly before engine shutdown, or the cause lies elsewhere. Nissan bulletin NTB16-048 covers early 2016 Titan XD trucks with the Cummins 5.0L V8: P221A with P229E and P22A7 is fixed by a new outlet sensor and ECM reprogramming. P2201 and P229F judge each sensor alone, P221B is bank 2.
c: One of the two NOx sensors (often the outlet sensor) reading wrongly
Exhaust leak between the two sensors diluting the reading
Faulty DEF dosing distorting the comparison
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Often stored with P20EE or other SCR codes
Implausible NOx conversion values in live data

P221B.d: P221B compares the NOx sensors before and after the SCR catalyst of bank 2. When operating conditions should make them agree, their readings differ by more than the calibration allows, and the controller cannot decide which value is wrong. The code requires a separate SCR line on bank 2, which no publicly documented diesel has; no manufacturer lists P221B. The bank 1 twin P221A shows the practice: Volvo and Mack require a NOx conversion test before any part is changed and only accept a sensor fault if inlet and outlet readings differ by more than roughly 40 ppm shortly before shutdown, while Nissan bulletin NTB16-048 replaced the outlet sensor and reflashed the ECM on 2016 Titan XD trucks.
c: One of the two bank 2 NOx sensors reading wrongly
Exhaust leak between the two sensors
Dosing that does not stop or leaks, distorting the comparison
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Often stored with SCR efficiency codes
Inlet and outlet NOx values for bank 2 disagree in live data

P221C.t: Reductant Heater B Current Too Low
P221C.d: P221C reports that heater B of the DEF system draws too little current while switched on. GM and Ford both assign B to the heated pressure line that carries DEF to the dosing valve. GM's 2025 Duramax tables flag line heater current under 0.75 A with a PWM command above zero, 40 faulty readings spaced 0.1 s apart, Type A with the MIL after one trip. Ford's 2023 diesel summary watches heater B continuously while it runs and decides within 2.2 s: below 3 A with more than 5 V supplied, line power below 1 W or lower than expected. GM's 2014 tables for the 6.6L LML judged conductance instead (0.28 S or less), Type B. An open or burnt line heater is the usual find; P221D is the high-current partner.
c: Heating element in the DEF pressure line open or burnt
Corroded or loose connector at the heated line
Missing heater supply (fuse, relay or harness)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DEF line may freeze in winter, dosing starts late
DEF system warning, inducement possible if unresolved

P221D.t: Reductant Heater B Current Too High
P221D.d: P221D is stored when heater B, the electrically heated DEF pressure line at GM and Ford, takes more current or power than its design permits. That usually means a partly shorted element or a lead touching ground, and the controller cuts the heater to save its driver. GM's 2025 Duramax tables trip above 15 A, counted over 40 samples of 0.1 s while the vehicle is active, Type A with the MIL on the first trip and recovery only in the next drive cycle. Ford's 2023 diesel summary flags line heater power above the expected value within 2.2 s of continuous monitoring. On the 2014 6.6L LML, GM read the line heater conductance and set the code at 0.92 S or more, Type B. P221C is the low-current partner, P20BF a low control circuit.
c: Partly shorted heating element in the DEF pressure line
Water in the line heater connector
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after one trip (GM)
Line heater switched off, DEF may stay frozen in cold weather

P221E.t: Reductant Heater C Current Too Low
P221E.d: P221E says DEF heater C pulls too little current while commanded on. Which element is C depends on the system. In GM's 2025 Duramax tables heater 3 is a second tank heater; the code needs a PWM command above zero and trips under 0.75 A after 40 readings taken every 0.1 s, a Type A fault with the MIL after one trip. GM's 2014 tables for the 6.6L LML gave the letter to the heater in the supply (pump) module instead: conductance of 0.14 S or less, checked once per trip with the battery at 11 V or more, Type B. Ford's 2023 diesel summary has a heater C only with a supply voltage check (P20C2) and does not list P221E. In frost the thawing of DEF around that heater is slow. P221F is the high-current partner, P20C1 the open control circuit.
c: Heater C element open or burnt (tank or supply module, by system)
Corroded or wet connector at the tank or pump unit
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Slow DEF thawing in cold weather, dosing starts late

P221F.t: Reductant Heater C Current Too High
P221F.d: P221F flags excessive current through DEF heater C, pointing to a partial short in the element or its lead. GM's 2025 Duramax tables, where heater 3 is the second tank heater, set the code above 15 A over 40 samples of 0.1 s whenever the vehicle is active, Type A with the MIL after one trip, and zero all heater PWM commands while any heater fault is present. In GM's 2014 tables for the 6.6L LML, C denoted the supply module heater, and high conductance (0.46 S or more in one table, 0.35 S in the other) set a Type B fault once per trip. Ford's 2023 diesel summary does not use P221F. A shorted heater draws more than its driver tolerates, so the area it serves stays unheated. P221E is the low-current partner.
c: Heater lead chafed to ground at the tank or pump unit
Water or DEF crystals in the heater connector
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after one trip (GM)
DEF heating disabled, possible frozen-DEF warnings in winter

P2220.t: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit High (Bank 2)
P2220.d: P2220 is the high-side counterpart of P2219: on the bank 2 NOx sensor, the heater control line carries battery voltage when the heater should be off or regulated, so the element may overheat or the output stage cannot switch. A pinched lead touching a feed wire or a failed driver inside the sensor are the usual causes. The bank 2 code is not documented by any manufacturer. GM's 3.0L LZ0 describes the bank 1 version P2207 as a short to battery at the heater control pin, judged on 80 of 160 samples with over 11 V on the powertrain relay and confirmed as Type B after two trips. P2218 is the open circuit and P2224 a high signal on the heater sense side. Until repaired, SCR control for bank 2 runs without NOx feedback.
c: Heater control lead shorted to a supply wire
Failed heater driver inside the bank 2 sensor module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Bank 2 NOx reading missing or invalid

P2221.d: Alongside the heater drive, a NOx sensor has a sense path that tells the electronics how the heater is really behaving, usually by measuring its resistance, which tracks cell temperature. P2221 reports a general fault in that sense circuit on the bank 2 sensor. Public documentation exists only for the bank 1 code P2208: GM's 3.0L LZ0 checks the separate HTemp pin for an open load, 80 failures in 160 samples at over 11 V, Type A with the MIL after one trip, and notes that its Continental sensors debounce electrical faults internally for 1.5 s. No manufacturer lists the bank 2 version. Without valid feedback the sensor cannot regulate its temperature. P2222 to P2225 are the specific sense faults.
c: Fault in the heater measurement of the bank 2 sensor
Open sense conductor between probe and sensor module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Bank 2 NOx sensor not ready

P2222.t: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2)
P2222.d: With P2222 the heater feedback of the bank 2 NOx sensor is electrically present, yet what it reports does not match the heating command: the cell warms too slowly or settles at the wrong resistance. No manufacturer documents this bank 2 code. Two bank 1 descriptions show the approach. GM's 3.0L LZ0 (P2209) compares raw heater resistance with its target and fails a deviation over 3 percent in 50 of 100 samples, only after 45 s of good supply and 180 s past the dew point, Type B. Ford's diesel summary uses the matching rear sensor code P220F for heater current below 0.4 A or a duty cycle more than 20 percent off. An aged heater or weak supply is typical. P2221 is the general sense fault.
c: Aged heater in the bank 2 NOx probe with drifted resistance
Low supply voltage or poor ground at the sensor module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Bank 2 NOx sensor slow to become ready after a cold start
SCR monitor for bank 2 delayed

P2223.t: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Low (Bank 2)
P2223.d: P2223 indicates that the heater sense line of the bank 2 NOx sensor sits at or near ground potential, so the electronics reads an impossibly low value for heater resistance. A sense conductor rubbed through to the exhaust bracket or a shorted measuring input inside the sensor module are the usual explanations. No manufacturer publishes the bank 2 code. For bank 1, GM's 3.0L LZ0 tables carry the equivalent P2210 as a grounded HTemp pin, judged on 80 failed of 160 samples with the powertrain relay above 11 V, Type B, so the MIL waits for a second trip. With no usable feedback the sensor cannot hold its working temperature. P2224 is the opposite polarity, P2219 a low fault on the control side.
c: Sense lead of the bank 2 sensor shorted to ground
Shorted measuring input in the sensor module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
No valid NOx value from bank 2

P2224.t: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit High (Bank 2)
P2224.d: P2224 is logged when the heater sense signal of the bank 2 NOx sensor is too high, which the electronics sees as a short to supply voltage or as an interrupted heater reading near infinite resistance. The bank 2 code appears in no public manufacturer document. GM documents the bank 1 version P2211 for the 3.0L LZ0 as an HTemp pin shorted toward supply: 80 failed of 160 samples, powertrain relay above 11 V, sensor bus relay switched on, Type B over two trips. Since the sensor module cannot judge cell temperature, it holds back its NOx value and SCR control for that bank falls back on modelled emissions. P2223 is the low direction, P2220 a high fault on the control side, P2225 a sporadic sense fault.
c: Heater element in the bank 2 probe open, read as maximum resistance
Sense lead shorted to a voltage source
Fault in the sensor module input stage
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Bank 2 NOx sensor stays unready

P2225.t: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Intermittent (Bank 2)
P2225.d: P2225 covers a heater sense circuit on the bank 2 NOx sensor that fails only for moments: the feedback drops out or jumps, then returns to normal, which a steady open or short code would not describe. No manufacturer documents thresholds for P2225 or for its bank 1 twin P2212. GM's 3.0L LZ0 tables handle only the persistent faults on the HTemp pin (P2208, P2210, P2211) and mention that the Continental sensors debounce electrical errors for 1.5 s internally, so very short glitches may never reach the engine computer. Smart sensors flag heater faults over CAN. Look for a cracked conductor that opens when hot, a loose terminal or moisture. The warning lamp may switch on and off between drives.
c: Loose or corroded contact in the bank 2 sensor connector
Cracked sense conductor that opens with heat or vibration
Sporadic fault in the heater measurement of the sensor module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp that comes and goes
Bank 2 NOx value briefly invalid

P2226.d: P2226 is the general circuit code for barometric pressure sensor A, the sensor that tells the engine computer the outside air pressure for air-charge, fuel and boost calculations. Ford's OBD summary for 2024-2025 gasoline engines shows how the code appears in current software: every BARO fault is reported as P2226 plus a failure-type byte, -16 for a low voltage (formerly P2228), -17 for high (P2229), -92 for a plausibility error (P2227) and -1F for an erratic signal (P2230). The same list makes all four block auto start-stop. On Ford gasoline engines the sensor sits on the PCM circuit board. A plain P2226 without failure type is rare; sensor B has its own family from P222A. Expect the warning light and a default pressure value.
c: Fault of the barometric sensor built into the engine control module
Damaged wiring or loose connector on an external BARO sensor
5 V reference supply of the sensor pulled down by another faulty sensor
s: Check engine light
Auto start-stop no longer works
Failure-type suffix (-16, -17, -92, -1F) shown with the code on newer scan tools

P2227.t: Barometric Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P2227.d: P2227 means the barometric reading is electrically fine but does not fit the other pressure signals. Ford's 2012 summary compares BARO, throttle inlet and manifold pressure after at least 10 s engine-off; the sensor that disagrees with the other two is blamed. While driving at low airflow BARO must stay within 5.5 inHg of throttle inlet pressure. Ford's 2023 diesels set P2227 for a reading below 50 kPa held for 1 s. GM's 2018 diesel tables run the same three-way check at idle and before start, plus a 50-115 kPa window, as Type B. GM bulletins 22-NA-007 (Cruze 1.4 turbo) and 23-NA-002 (Silverado/Sierra 2.7 L) trace P2227 with P0299 to ice in the charge air cooler; the fix is new ECM software plus a baffle.
c: Ice or sludge in the charge air cooler on turbo engines in severe cold (GM 22-NA-007, 23-NA-002)
BARO sensor reading with an offset or drift
Faulty boost or manifold pressure sensor that skews the comparison
Engine control software that needs an update
s: Check engine light
Reduced power or hesitation in very cold weather on turbo engines
P0299 or misfire codes stored alongside

P2228.t: Barometric Pressure Sensor A Circuit Low
P2228.d: P2228 sets when the voltage from barometric pressure sensor A stays below the lowest value a real atmosphere could produce. Ford's gasoline summaries (2012 and 2020-2023) use under 2.0 V, which would mean an altitude above 15,000 ft, for 5 s; on these engines the sensor is mounted on the PCM circuit board. Ford's 2023 diesels flag under 0.25 V (about 6 kPa) after 0.5 s. GM's 2018 diesel tables attribute it to a grounded or broken signal line on a pull-down input: below 35.5 % of the 5 V supply (equal to 50 kPa) in 320 of 400 readings, Type B with the MIL after two trips. In Ford's 2024 software the same fault appears as P2226-16. P2229 is the high counterpart. The engine runs on a substitute pressure, so drivers mostly see only the lamp.
c: Signal wire of an external BARO sensor shorted to ground or open
Defective sensor inside the PCM (Ford, Mazda and others), PCM replacement
Low or missing 5 V reference to the sensor
s: Check engine light
Auto start-stop deactivated
Scan tool shows an implausibly low barometric pressure

P2229.t: Barometric Pressure Sensor A Circuit High
P2229.d: P2229 reports a barometric sensor A voltage above anything plausible for outside air. Ford's gasoline engines judge more than 4.4 V, an altitude below -1,000 ft, over 5 s; the 2023 diesels use 4.85 V (115 kPa) after 0.5 s. GM's 2018 diesel tables look for contact with a voltage source: over 94.1 % of the 5 V range (115.1 kPa) in 320 of 400 readings, Type B. Mazda bulletin 01-008/20 shows a less obvious cause on the 2018-2020 Mazda6 2.5 turbo: the BARO sensor lives inside the PCM and breathes through a filter hole on its underside. Wax sprayed into the engine bay can seal that hole, so the trapped air builds pressure as the PCM heats up. Mazda replaces the PCM with a reshaped bracket. Ford's 2024 software reports P2226-17 instead; P2228 is the low counterpart.
c: Breather filter of a PCM-internal BARO sensor clogged (e.g. engine-bay wax, Mazda 01-008/20)
Signal wire of an external sensor shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Internal fault of the sensor or the control module
s: Check engine light, often only after the engine bay has heated up
Auto start-stop deactivated
Scan tool shows barometric pressure far above the real value

P222A.d: P222A is the general circuit code for a second barometric pressure sensor, B. Only some engines carry one. GM's tables for the 3.0 L twin-turbo V6 (LGW, 2018) and for 2023-2024 twin-throttle engines monitor such a sensor B, but they report its circuit faults with the more specific codes P222C (low) and P222D (high) and do not use P222A. No maker documents P222A publicly. Read it as an unspecified electrical fault of sensor B, comparable to P2226 for sensor A, which Ford now stores with a failure-type byte that tells the type of fault. CARB requires circuit monitoring of every input sensor used by an emission-relevant function. Check wiring, connector and the 5 V supply; the engine usually keeps running on sensor A or a model value.
c: Damaged wiring or corroded connector at sensor B
Fault in the shared 5 V sensor supply
s: Check engine light
Usually no noticeable change in how the engine runs

P222B.t: Barometric Pressure Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P222B.d: P222B means sensor B delivers a clean signal whose value is wrong. GM documents two strategies. On the 3.0 L LGW (2018) and a 2016 engine family the ECM estimates outside pressure from boost pressure, airflow and rpm while driving; sensor B fails if it deviates by more than 20 kPa, or 25 kPa once more than 1.24 miles have passed since the last update. With the engine stopped for over 10 s, B must sit between 50 and 115 kPa, and if MAP, boost and BARO A agree within 10 kPa while B is further away, B is singled out. Both run as Type B over 320 of 400 readings. On GM's 2023-2024 twin-throttle engine, sensor B measures ahead of the bank 2 throttle and is checked against ambient pressure for 2 s.
c: Sensor B reading with offset or stuck at one value
Leak or restriction in the intake path that distorts the comparison
Boost or manifold pressure sensor fault affecting the estimate
s: Check engine light after two drives
Usually no driveability change

P222C.t: Barometric Pressure Sensor B Circuit Low
P222C.d: P222C flags a sensor B voltage that has dropped too low, as with a signal wire touching ground. GM's 2018 tables for the 3.0 L LGW set the code below 40 % of the 5 V range, equal to about 50.9 kPa, counted in 320 of 400 readings taken every 12.5 ms; it is a Type B fault with the MIL after two trips. GM's 2023-2024 tables for a twin-throttle engine use the pressure value itself: below 50 kPa for 2 s. In GM software the fault bundle for ambient pressure sensor 2 covers exactly P222C and P222D, which tells which sensor letter B refers to there. Compared with sensor A (P2228), the circuit is separate, so sensor A keeps working. P222D is the high-voltage counterpart, P222B the plausibility check.
c: Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground
5 V reference to sensor B open or shorted
s: Check engine light
Scan tool shows a very low reading for the second barometric sensor

P222D.t: Barometric Pressure Sensor B Circuit High
P222D.d: P222D is stored when sensor B reports an excessive voltage. GM's 2018 tables for the 3.0 L LGW name contact with a supply voltage or a broken line: on that input a broken wire drives the signal up, not down. The limit is 90 % of the 5 V range, about 115 kPa, met in 320 of 400 readings; Type B, MIL after two trips. GM's 2023-2024 twin-throttle engine evaluates the raw pressure of the sensor ahead of the bank 2 throttle and fails it above 115 kPa held for 2 s. Since an open line lands here, a disconnected connector after repair work is a typical find. P222C covers the low side, P2229 the same fault on sensor A. The engine keeps running on the remaining sensors.
c: Connector of sensor B unplugged or signal wire broken
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
s: Check engine light
Second barometric reading stuck near the top of its range

P222E.t: Barometric Pressure Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P222E.d: P222E catches a sensor B signal that jitters. Outside air pressure changes slowly, so GM measures noise directly: every 12.5 ms the difference to the previous reading is taken, and the absolute differences over 80 consecutive readings are added up into a so-called string length. If that total exceeds 100 kPa, the one-second sample counts as failed; four failures in five samples set the code as Type B, MIL after two trips. GM uses this in the 2018 tables for the 3.0 L LGW and in a 2016 engine family. The fault differs from P222C/P222D, where the voltage sits steadily outside its limits, and from P222B, where a smooth signal shows the wrong value. Loose pins, chafed wires and electrical interference are the usual suspects.
c: Loose or corroded terminal at sensor B or the ECM
Electrical interference, for example from a poorly grounded component nearby
s: Check engine light that may come and go
Second barometric value jumping on the scan tool

P222F.d: P222F is meant for engines with two barometric sensors whose readings should agree but drift apart, without the software being able to say which of the two is wrong. No maker documents this code publicly. GM, the one maker that publishes tables for a sensor B, resolves the comparison differently: it pulls in manifold and boost pressure as further references, singles out the deviating sensor and stores P222B for sensor B or P2227 for sensor A. Ford likewise uses a three-sensor vote for P2227. A pure A/B comparison has no tiebreaker, which explains why the code is rarely seen. CARB requires rationality checks of input sensors. Both sensors, their supply and any leaks in the lines feeding them should be checked.
c: One of the two barometric sensors has drifted
Supply or ground offset shifting one sensor's signal
Blocked port or breather of one sensor
s: Check engine light
The two barometric readings differ clearly on the scan tool

P2230.t: Barometric Pressure Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2230.d: P2230 flags a barometric pressure (BARO) signal that is electrically present but jumps or drops out for short moments instead of sitting permanently low or high. The engine computer uses BARO for air-charge, fuelling and boost calculations. Ford's 2020-2023 gasoline OBD summary lists P2230 with P2227-P2229 among the BARO faults that inhibit auto start-stop. GM bulletins for 2014-2017 trucks and SUVs with the 5.3/6.2 L V8 and for the 2012-2013 Equinox/Terrain 2.4 L trace P2230 to engine harness wires chafed through. Exact thresholds are not published. P2228/P2229 are steady low/high signals, P2227 a plausibility fault. Drivers usually notice only the warning light; start-stop may stay off.
c: Engine harness chafed against an engine component (e.g. vacuum pump pulley, cam cover)
Loose or corroded pin at the BARO sensor or ECM connector
Barometric pressure sensor with an internal contact problem
s: Check engine light, often coming and going
Auto start-stop inactive
Other sensor codes stored at the same time if a shared harness is damaged

P2231.t: O2 Sensor Signal Circuit Shorted to Heater Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2231.d: P2231 means the engine computer sees the heater supply of the upstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 leaking into the sensor's signal path - typically an internal short in the sensor or two neighbouring wires touching in the harness. VW's 2014 specification books for the Passat and Tiguan set it when the front sensor signal changes by more than 190 microamps, i.e. the measured sensor current is distorted. CARB requires circuit faults of every fuel-control oxygen sensor to be detected. P2232/P2233 cover sensors 2 and 3 of bank 1, P2234 the first sensor of bank 2. Because the mixture feedback can no longer be trusted, the engine may run on open-loop fuelling with higher consumption and emissions.
c: Internal short between heater and sensing element in the oxygen sensor
Heater and signal wires melted or chafed together (exhaust heat, routing)
Moisture or contamination bridging pins in the sensor connector
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption due to open-loop fuelling
Rough idle or hesitation in some cases

P2232.t: O2 Sensor Signal Circuit Shorted to Heater Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P2232.d: P2232 reports that the heater supply of the oxygen sensor behind the catalyst on bank 1 is bleeding into that sensor's signal line. A switching sensor only produces up to about 1 V, so the ECM watches its signal at the instant the heater is switched off. GM's tables for the 2005 2.8/3.6 V6, the 2008 3.6 LLT and the 2024 set 24OBDG07 flag a jump of more than 2 V within 0.04 s of heater turn-off in more than 4 out of 6 events, with the MIL after two trips. The Saab 9-5 (2010, 2.0 turbo) checks whether signal and heater voltage rise and fall together and treats the fault as Type B. P2231 is the front sensor, P2235 the rear position on bank 2. Mixture control continues, but catalyst monitoring loses its rear signal.
c: Internal leakage between heater and sensing element of the rear oxygen sensor
Signal and heater wires fused or chafed together near the exhaust
Water or corrosion bridging pins in the sensor connector
s: Check engine light after two drives
Catalyst monitor not completed or catalyst code stored alongside

P2233.t: O2 Sensor Signal Circuit Shorted to Heater Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P2233.d: P2233 is the heater-to-signal short for sensor 3 on bank 1, a third oxygen sensor that some engines fit after a second catalyst or between two catalyst bricks. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's checks for the rear-sensor codes P2232/P2235 show how such a fault is normally caught: the signal leaps by more than 2 V within 0.04 s whenever the heater is switched off. Jaguar Land Rover's 2015 bulletin for the 3.0 supercharged V6, which carries three sensors per bank, lists many sensor 3 faults but none of this type. CARB requires circuit faults of every monitored oxygen sensor to be detected. P2236 is the bank 2 counterpart. A third sensor serves only monitoring, so the car drives normally with the warning lamp on.
c: Internal leakage between heater and sensing element of sensor 3
Sensor 3 wiring melted or chafed along the exhaust or underbody
Corroded underbody connector of the third sensor
s: Check engine light without noticeable driving change
Emissions inspection failed because of the stored code

P2234.t: O2 Sensor Signal Circuit Shorted to Heater Circuit (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P2234.d: P2234 means the heater of the front air-fuel sensor on bank 2 couples into its measuring circuit. On a wide-band sensor the disturbance is small, so the check is finer than on rear sensors. GM's 2005 tables for the Bosch-equipped 2.8/3.6 V6 look for a signal step of 0.08-0.2 V appearing no later than 0.05 s after each heater switching edge; 18 such steps in a 10 s window count as a failure, the sensor must have been fully hot for 10 s, and the MIL follows after two trips. Jaguar Land Rover lists P2234 among the bank 2 front-sensor codes of the 2014-2016 LR4, Range Rover and Range Rover Sport 3.0 V6 and blames thermal shock from water hitting the hot element; the sensor is replaced. P2231 is the same fault on bank 1. Closed-loop fuelling on bank 2 may drop out.
c: Front sensor element cracked by thermal shock (water on the hot sensor)
Heater and signal wires of the bank 2 sensor touching in the harness
Moisture in the sensor connector bridging heater and signal pins
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption when bank 2 runs without lambda control
Other bank 2 front-sensor codes stored at the same time

P2235.t: O2 Sensor Signal Circuit Shorted to Heater Circuit (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P2235.d: P2235 concerns the post-catalyst oxygen sensor on bank 2, found on V engines with a catalyst per bank. The ECM sets it when switching off the heater makes the sensor voltage spike. GM runs the check only once the sensor is past its dew-point phase and the modelled exhaust has been above 250 °C for 90 s (and below 800 °C); the failure threshold, as for P2232, is a jump above 2 V within 0.04 s in more than 4 of 6 switch-offs. It appears in the 2005 2.8/3.6 V6 tables, the 2008 3.6 LLT tables and the 2024 set 24OBDG07, each with the MIL after two trips. Because the fault is tied to one sensor position, swapping banks is a quick plausibility check before parts are ordered. P2232 is bank 1, P2234 the front sensor of bank 2.
c: Internal leakage between heater and sensing element of the bank 2 rear sensor
Sensor wires damaged by heat or chafing near the bank 2 catalyst
Water ingress in the rear sensor connector
s: Check engine light after two drives
Bank 2 catalyst monitor not completed

P2236.t: O2 Sensor Signal Circuit Shorted to Heater Circuit (Bank 2 Sensor 3)
P2236.d: P2236 would be set if the heater of the third oxygen sensor on bank 2 leaked into its signal wire. Such a sensor sits furthest downstream and exists only on engines with two catalyst stages per bank. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and Jaguar Land Rover's 2015 list for its V6 with sensors 3 on both banks does not use it either. The mechanism matches P2232/P2235: the heater is pulsed with battery voltage while the sensor signal stays below about 1 V, so any coupling shows up as a voltage step when the heater switches; GM uses more than 2 V within 0.04 s. CARB requires every monitored oxygen sensor circuit to be checked. P2233 is bank 1. Driving is unaffected; the lamp and a failed inspection are the consequences.
c: Internal leakage between heater and sensing element of sensor 3 on bank 2
Long underbody wiring to the rear sensor chafed or heat-damaged
Road salt corrosion in the sensor connector
s: Check engine light with normal driving behaviour
Readiness for catalyst or oxygen sensor monitor not set

P2237.t: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2237.d: P2237 points to an open pump-current line (IP or APE) on the front wide-band sensor of bank 1. With that wire broken the output freezes near its stoichiometric value of roughly 1.5 V and lambda stops moving. Ford sets it on Bosch sensors when 20 s of fuel-control steps and reference-current pulses shift lambda by 0.05 or less; NTK interface chips report the open line directly. VW's 2014 books look for 1.49-1.51 V while the lambda controller deviates by more than 0.10 or fuel has been cut for over 3 s, and Saab's 9-5 2.0 turbo (2010) logs it as Type B. Software updates cure false or damaging cases on VW Jetta/Beetle 2.0 (2013-14, plus a new sensor) and Hyundai Kona 1.6 T-GDI (2024-25). P2238/P2239 are low/high, P2240 is bank 2.
c: Broken pump-current wire or pushed-back pin between sensor and ECM
Pump cell of the wide-band sensor damaged, for example by catalyst-heating strategy or thermal shock
Engine software that sets the code falsely (update available for some models)
s: Check engine light
Lambda reading stuck at 1.0 in live data
Higher fuel consumption in open-loop fuelling

P2238.t: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2238.d: P2238 is the low-side fault of the pump-current circuit of the front wide-band sensor on bank 1. Saab's 9-5 2.0 turbo (2010) shows a concrete test: on overrun with the injectors shut off, pure air should drive the signal well above its stoichiometric level, and if it stays below 1.7 V for 3 s the code sets as Type B. GM's 2005 V6 tables use the same fuel-cut check but book it under P2237. Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander lists P2238 as a two-trip code. Ford does not use it at all: a pump-current wire shorted to ground lands in P0131 there. P2237 is the open circuit, P2239 the high-side fault, P2241 the same on bank 2. Typical findings are a grounded IP wire or a sensor that can no longer pump oxygen.
c: Pump-current wire chafed through to ground
Aged or contaminated sensor that no longer reads lean in fuel cut-off
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM
s: Check engine light after two drives
Lambda value does not rise during coasting in live data

P2239.t: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2239.d: P2239 is the high-side counterpart for the pump-current circuit of the bank 1 front wide-band sensor. On the Saab 9-5 2.0 turbo (2010) it sets when, in closed loop with the mixture deliberately enriched, the signal still sits at 1.48-1.51 V for 1 s, meaning the sensor ignores a change it should report; it is a Type B code. GM's 2005 V6 tables check a similar window (1.48-1.52 V while target lambda lies outside 0.97-1.03) under P2237. Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander also lists P2239 as a two-trip code. Ford files this wire touching battery voltage under P0132 instead. A short to the heater supply can overload the sensor interface, so the wiring deserves a check before a new sensor goes in. P2238 is low, P2242 bank 2.
c: Pump-current wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Wide-band sensor with internal short or stuck output
Damaged sensor interface in the ECM
s: Check engine light after two drives
Lambda reading frozen near 1.0 regardless of load
New sensor fails again quickly if the wiring short is not found

P223A.d: P223A covers the control circuit of a fifth DEF heating element, heater E. Unlike heaters A to D, which each have four codes for open, performance, low and high, heater E gets only this one code, so any electrical fault of its driver or wiring ends up here. No maker documents P223A publicly. As a reference, GM's 2025 Duramax tables check comparable heater outputs by watching the low-side driver voltage and load current: a fault seen while heating forces the output off so the exact failure can be pinpointed, and heater circuits there are Type A. Which element carries the letter E depends on the system; most published SCR designs stop at three or four heaters. In frost an unheated section may stay frozen, so dosing and SCR monitoring suffer.
c: Open or shorted wiring or connector of heater E
Heating element E burnt out or shorted
Faulty output stage in the controlling module
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
DEF dosing delayed or blocked in freezing weather

P223B.d: P223B reports a fault in the control circuit of heater F, the sixth heating element of an SCR system. Like its neighbour P223A for heater E, it is a single catch-all code covering open lines and shorts alike. No maker documents P223B publicly, and the published systems show why: Ford's 2023 diesel summary names heaters A to C only (with A and B checked at peak heating power for under 3 A at more than 5 V), and GM bulletin 21-NA-149 lists the heater D codes P20C5 and P20C8 for the 3.0 L LM2 Duramax. Six zones would only appear on layouts with many separately heated lines or tanks. CARB requires every emission-relevant output to be checked for circuit faults. Expect an SCR warning and, in winter, the risk of a frozen line that ends in reduced power.
c: Damaged wiring or corroded connector of heater F
Heating element F open or shorted
Missing supply from the heater relay or fuse
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
Reduced power warning after a cold-weather DEF fault

P223C.d: P223C judges whether the pump current of the bank 1 wide-band sensor makes sense while the engine is coasting with fuel cut off. In that state the sensor sees almost pure air and, as Bosch's LSU 4.9 data show, must drive a clearly positive current. GM's tables (2016, 2018, 2019) start the test after 5 s of fuel cut-off and stop it at 12 s, with the reference cell above about 600 °C. Three windows count as faulty: current too large (above 5.0 mA, or 4.18 mA with the Delphi interface), close to zero (within ±0.3 or ±0.1 mA), or negative (below -0.10 mA). Each window has its own counter, e.g. 40 failures in 160 samples at 25 ms; the code is Type B. GM notes that it also catches open pump, reference-cell and reference-ground circuits. P223D is bank 2.
c: Aged or poisoned wide-band sensor with wrong pump current in air
Open pump-current, reference-cell or reference-ground wire
Exhaust leak or misfire that distorts the gas at the sensor
s: Check engine light after two drives
Usually no noticeable change in driving behaviour

P223D.d: P223D applies the pump-current plausibility test to the front wide-band sensor of bank 2 on V engines. GM's 2016 and 2018 tables describe it for engines with a Continental interface chip: during a fuel cut-off window between 5 s and 12 s, a reading above 5.0 mA, within ±0.3 mA of zero, or below -0.10 mA is counted, and 40 hits in 160 samples in any window set the code as Type B. The test is skipped while bank 2 heater faults (P0050-P0052) or P0155 are active, because a cold element pumps poorly. The Bosch LSU 4.9 data sheet shows why the check works: pump current is zero at lambda 1, negative when rich and positive when lean, so air must give a clear positive value. P223C is the bank 1 version; P2240, P2247 and P2254 isolate open wires.
c: Worn bank 2 wide-band sensor that no longer pumps correctly in air
Interrupted pump-current or reference circuit of the bank 2 sensor
Sensor heater too weak to keep the element at temperature
s: Check engine light after two drives
Often no driveability complaint

P223E.t: O2 Sensor Reference Resistance Out Of Range (Bank 1)
P223E.d: P223E checks the internal resistance of the reference (Nernst) cell in the bank 1 wide-band sensor. That resistance falls as the ceramic heats up, so the ECM uses it as a thermometer; Bosch specifies 300 ohms nominal for the LSU 4.9 at operating temperature. GM's tables (2016-2019) convert the value supplied by the interface chip into an element temperature and flag anything below 700 °C or above 1,000 °C in 80 % of samples (64 of 80 in 2018, 128 of 160 in 2016/2019), starting 20 s after heater warm-up; the code is Type B. GM bulletin 16-NA-266 covers 2016-2017 ATS, CTS, CT6, Camaro, Malibu and Envision with the 2.0 turbo LTG: a voltage spike inside the ECM sets P223E or P0132 and also blocks remote start, cured by reprogramming. P223F is bank 2, P0135 the heater itself.
c: Aged sensor whose reference cell resistance has drifted
Heater not holding the element at temperature (heater, wiring or control)
ECM calibration fault on GM 2.0 turbo LTG (bulletin 16-NA-266)
s: Check engine light after two consecutive drives
Remote start refuses to start the engine (GM LTG models)

P223F.t: O2 Sensor Reference Resistance Out Of Range (Bank 2)
P223F.d: P223F is the reference-cell resistance check for the front wide-band sensor of bank 2. GM's 2016 and 2018 tables translate the measured resistance into element temperature and count readings below 700 °C or above 1,000 °C; 64 of 80 samples (2018) or 128 of 160 (2016) at 25 ms set a Type B code. The monitor waits for heater warm-up plus 20 s and is blocked while the bank 2 heater codes P0050-P0052 or P0155 are present, so a pure heater fault shows up there first. A reading that is too cold despite a working heater points to a sensor whose ceramic has aged and become high-resistance; too hot suggests overheating, for example from misfire. Bosch's LSU 4.9 data sheet gives 300 ohms as the nominal cell resistance. P223E is bank 1, P223D the pump-current check of the same sensor.
c: Bank 2 sensor ceramic aged and high-resistance
Weak heater supply or high resistance in the heater wiring
Sensor overheated by misfire or very high exhaust temperature
s: Check engine light after two drives
Bank 2 lambda control slow to become active after a cold start

P2240.t: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit/Open (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P2240.d: P2240 is the open pump-current circuit of the front wide-band sensor on bank 2, so it only exists on V engines and boxers. Ford's summaries (2012 and 2020-2023) introduced it to replace P0154; detection works as on bank 1, by lambda failing to react to reference-current pulses or by the NTK interface chip. VW's 2014 Touareg and CC books flag 1.49-1.51 V combined with a lambda controller offset above 0.07 or a controller at its limit. GM's 2005 V6 adds a fuel cut-off test (signal below 1.7 V for 2 s). FCA reflashes the PCM for P2240 on the 2025 Ram 1500 and Wagoneer with the 3.0 Hurricane (bulletins 18-071-26, 18-082/083-26), and Jaguar Land Rover lists it among the 3.0 V6 sensor faults caused by water shock.
c: Open pump-current wire or loose pin at the bank 2 sensor connector
Bank 2 front sensor damaged by water or thermal shock
PCM calibration that sets the code without a hardware fault (FCA 2025 Hurricane)
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 lambda value stuck at 1.0 in live data
Higher fuel consumption

P2241.t: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P2241.d: P2241 reports the pump-current circuit of the bank 2 front wide-band sensor at too low a level, typically a grounded wire or a sensor that cannot pump enough oxygen. No manufacturer publicly documents P2241 with thresholds. The bank 1 twin P2238 is described by Saab for its 2.0 turbo, where the signal must climb past 1.7 V on overrun with the injectors off; a V engine would run the same logic per bank. Ford instead files a grounded pump-current wire under P0151 and keeps P2240 for the open line. CARB demands that fuel-control sensors be checked for broken or shorted circuits and for implausible readings, with separate codes where practical. P2240 is the open circuit, P2242 the high-side fault on bank 2. Bank 2 fuelling falls back to open-loop values.
c: Bank 2 pump-current wire shorted to ground
Aged bank 2 front sensor with weak pump cell
Fault in the ECM sensor interface for bank 2
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 2

P2242.t: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P2242.d: P2242 flags the pump-current circuit of the bank 2 front wide-band sensor as too high, usually a short to the heater feed or battery voltage, or a signal locked at its midpoint although the mixture is being changed. No manufacturer publicly documents P2242 with thresholds. Saab describes the bank 1 version P2239 for its 2.0 turbo: 1.48-1.51 V held for 1 s while closed loop enriches the mixture. Ford's 2020-2023 summary routes any short to battery on a wide-band sensor wire to P0152 instead. CARB requires fuel-control sensors to be checked for wiring faults and implausible readings. P2240 is the open circuit, P2241 the low fault, P2239 the same fault on bank 1. Since a voltage short can kill a replacement sensor, the bank 2 harness should be checked first.
c: Bank 2 pump-current wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Internal short in the bank 2 wide-band sensor
Damaged sensor interface in the ECM
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 lambda value stuck near 1.0
Replacement sensor fails again if the short remains

P2243.t: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2243.d: P2243 flags an open reference voltage line on the front wide-band sensor of bank 1, i.e. the Nernst-cell lead (RE/UN on Bosch sensors, VS on NTK). Ford's OBD summaries set it on Bosch parts when the sensor voltage sits above 4.7 V or below 0.2 V for 10 s; on NTK parts the interface chip reports the break itself. GM's 2005 V6 tables and the 2010 Saab 9-5 2.0 turbo use the same voltage window with cell resistance above 570 ohms, as a two-trip Type B code. On the 2004-05 Saturn Vue 3.5 V6 the pump-cell voltage must swing both above 4.8 V and below 3.4 V fifty times. Honda bulletin 14-002 ties it on 2010-11 V6 models to a broken sensor tip, often with P0420/P0430; Ford reflashes the 2020 Explorer 2.3 (20-2217). P2247 is bank 2, P2245/P2246 low/high.
c: Broken reference voltage (Nernst cell) wire or pushed-back pin between sensor and ECM
Sensing element cracked or tip broken off, for example by thermal shock
Engine software that sets the code falsely (update available for some models)
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 1
Catalyst efficiency code P0420 alongside it if a sensor fragment damaged the converter

P2244.t: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Performance (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2244.d: P2244 stands for a plausibility fault on the reference voltage side of the bank 1 upstream wide-band sensor: the Nernst-cell signal is electrically intact and within limits, but behaves in a way that does not fit the operating state, for instance offset or too slow. No manufacturer documents P2244 publicly. Ford treats this lead only as an open circuit (P2243) and books shorts on any sensor wire under P0131/P0132; GM, Saab and VW likewise publish only the open-circuit code. Bosch specifies the Nernst cell at a nominal 300 ohms and a load of at most 250 microamps, so ageing or contamination shows up as a shifted reading. CARB requires fuel-control sensors to be checked for implausible values as well as circuit faults. P2243 is the open line, P2245/P2246 low/high, P2248 bank 2.
c: Aged or contaminated wide-band sensor (oil ash, silicone, coolant)
High resistance in the reference voltage wire or connector
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor distorting the reading
s: Check engine light
Slightly higher fuel consumption
Possible failed emissions test

P2245.t: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2245.d: P2245 reports that the reference voltage side of the upstream air-fuel sensor on bank 1 reads too low, usually because the wire touches ground or the sensor has shorted internally. GM's tables for the Saturn Vue 3.5 V6 (L66, 2004-05) define it precisely: with the engine running for over 85 s, the heater active and the element signal between 3.2 and 4.6 V, a pump-cell circuit voltage below 1.5 V for 0.5 s stores the code in the first drive cycle. Jaguar Land Rover lists P2245 among the front-sensor codes in bulletin LTB00671 (2014-16 3.0 supercharged V6), where water caused thermal shock and the sensor is renewed. GM's 2018 Duramax table 18OBDG04 counts it among faults that invalidate the front sensor signal. P2243 is the open line, P2246 high, P2249 bank 2.
c: Reference voltage wire shorted to ground (chafed against exhaust or body)
Sensor element damaged internally, for example by water hitting the hot ceramic
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 1
Uneven idle or hesitation in some cases

P2246.t: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2246.d: P2246 means the reference voltage line of the bank 1 front wide-band sensor reads too high, typically from a short to battery or heater voltage or a short inside the sensor. No manufacturer publishes a threshold for P2246. GM's 2018 Duramax table 18OBDG04 names it, together with P2245, P2252 and P2253, as a fault that makes the front sensor signal unusable, but gives no setting criteria. Ford logs any wide-band lead that is shorted to supply voltage as P0132 and keeps P2243 for the open line, so Ford vehicles do not use this code. Bosch limits the Nernst cell to a 250 microamp load, which is why an external voltage on this wire can damage the sensor or the interface. CARB requires circuit faults of fuel-control sensors to be detected. P2245 is the low fault, P2250 bank 2.
c: Reference voltage wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Internal short between heater and Nernst cell in the sensor
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption
Repeat failure of a new sensor if the wiring short remains

P2247.t: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit/Open (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P2247.d: P2247 is the bank 2 version of P2243: the Nernst-cell reference line of the upstream wide-band sensor on the second cylinder bank is open. Ford's summaries trip it on Bosch sensors after 10 s outside 0.2-4.7 V and on NTK sensors via the interface chip, replacing the older P0150. VW's 2014 Touareg book names it an open Nernst-voltage circuit with limits of 0.25 and 4.80 V, while GM's 2005 V6 tables call it Type B. Field cases include Honda bulletin 14-002 (2010-11 V6 models, broken sensor tip, usually with P0430), Jaguar Land Rover LTB00671 (2014-16 3.0 supercharged V6, water shock) and a 2025 Ram 1500 3.0 engine software update (FCA 18-071-26). P2243 is bank 1, P2249/P2250 the low/high faults, P2254 the open ground line on bank 2.
c: Broken reference voltage (Nernst cell) wire or loose pin on the bank 2 sensor
Cracked element or broken sensor tip after thermal shock
Engine software that sets the code falsely (update for some models)
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 2
Catalyst efficiency code P0430 if a sensor fragment damaged the converter

P2248.t: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Performance (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P2248.d: P2248 is meant for a reference voltage signal on the bank 2 upstream wide-band sensor that is present but implausible, as opposed to an open or shorted line. No manufacturer documents P2248 publicly, and the published diagnostic tables of Ford, GM, Saab and VW cover the bank 2 Nernst-cell line only with the open-circuit code P2247, while Ford routes shorts to P0151/P0152. A drifting reading usually stems from an aged or poisoned sensor element or extra resistance in the circuit, which Bosch's 300-ohm nominal cell value makes measurable. CARB requires upstream sensors to be monitored for out-of-range and implausible output. P2244 is the bank 1 counterpart, P2247 the open line, P2249/P2250 low/high. Mixture control on bank 2 becomes less accurate.
c: Aged or contaminated wide-band sensor on bank 2
High resistance in the reference voltage wire or connector
Exhaust leak ahead of the bank 2 sensor
s: Check engine light
Slightly higher fuel consumption
Possible failed emissions test

P2249.t: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P2249.d: P2249 indicates that the reference voltage circuit of the front air-fuel sensor on bank 2 is pulled too low, most often by a grounded wire in the harness or a fault inside the sensor. The only public manufacturer criteria come from GM's tables for the Saturn Vue 3.5 V6 (L66, 2004-05), a Honda-built engine: after more than 85 s of running with the sensor heater active and the element signal at 3.2-4.6 V, a pump-cell circuit voltage under 1.5 V for half a second stores the code and lights the MIL in that drive cycle. The same table uses P2245 for bank 1. Ford, VW and GM's Bosch-equipped V6 tables do not list P2249. CARB requires circuit faults of fuel-control sensors to be detected. P2247 is the open line, P2250 high, P2255 the low fault of the ground line.
c: Reference voltage wire shorted to ground on the bank 2 sensor harness
Internal short in the bank 2 air-fuel sensor
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 2
Possible failed emissions test

P224A.d: P224A concerns the heater of the upstream NOx sensor on bank 1, the one before the SCR catalyst. Its electrical resistance rises with temperature, so the sensor electronics use it to hold the ceramic element at working heat. The code says that resistance is outside its allowed band, pointing to an aged or damaged element or a contact problem. No maker documents P224A publicly. GM performs the same test on the 3.0 L LZ0 Duramax (2025) but reports it as P2209: the measured resistance may differ from the target by no more than 3 %, judged on 50 of 100 readings once the supply has been above 10.8 V for 45 s and the dew point was passed 180 s earlier, Type B. A sensor with this fault reads NOx unreliably; P224B is the downstream sensor.
c: Heating element of the NOx sensor aged or cracked
Corroded or loose contacts in the sensor connector
Unstable supply voltage to the sensor module
s: Check engine light
SCR efficiency or NOx plausibility codes may follow

P224B.d: P224B is the heater resistance fault of the second NOx sensor on bank 1, mounted after the SCR catalyst. This sensor tells the control unit how much NOx is left after dosing, so its readings feed the catalyst efficiency monitor and the closed-loop dosing correction. If the heater's resistance leaves its expected band, the element may be running too cold or too hot. No maker documents P224B publicly. GM's 2025 tables for the 3.0 L LZ0 Duramax check the post-catalyst sensor heater against a 3 % resistance window as well, but file it under P22A7, the sensor 2 heater sense performance code, Type B. Hella describes the integrated heater as the part that keeps the sensor at operating temperature regardless of exhaust conditions. P224A is the upstream counterpart.
c: Heating element of the downstream NOx sensor aged or damaged
Corrosion in the sensor connector exposed to road spray
Element cracked by water droplets hitting the hot sensor
s: Check engine light
SCR efficiency monitor delayed or failing

P224C.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit/Open
P224C.d: P224C points to an open or otherwise faulty control circuit of shutoff valve A, the solenoid on a CNG or LPG tank that releases gas only when the engine runs on the alternative fuel. Such valves are normally closed. GM's 2015 bi-fuel Impala (bulletin PI1330) fits a high-pressure cut-off solenoid to the tank and energizes it in CNG mode while the engine cranks or runs; Ford's 2003 bi-fuel CNG documentation feeds its tank valve through the inertia switch and the ALT fuel relay. Neither publishes codes for the valve. No maker documents P224C publicly, and the CNG upfitter TransEco even files an open circuit under P224E. With the valve dead, bi-fuel cars carry on with gasoline; dedicated gas vehicles may not start.
c: Broken wire or unplugged connector at the tank valve
Solenoid coil of the valve open
Supply interrupted by relay or tripped inertia switch
s: Check engine light
Vehicle will not switch to gas operation or falls back to gasoline

P224D.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
P224D.d: P224D means tank shutoff valve A is electrically switched but the system behaves as if it stayed shut. Software can only infer that from a pressure response: once the valve is commanded open, line or rail pressure should climb toward the regulated value, which GM gives as 468-896 kPa for the bi-fuel Impala and Ford as about 724 kPa for its 2003 CNG trucks. Ford's control module also closes the tank valve itself if gas pressure sinks under 517 kPa. No maker documents P224D publicly; some code lists call it Range/Performance instead of Stuck Off. Possible reasons are a seized plunger, a closed manual tank valve or an empty tank. Bi-fuel vehicles return to gasoline, dedicated ones lose power or stall.
c: Manual tank valve closed or tank nearly empty
Valve plunger stuck closed, e.g. by contamination
Supply voltage too low to pull the solenoid open
Faulty gas pressure sensor misreporting the response
s: Check engine light
Engine switches back to gasoline or will not run on gas
Gas fuel gauge shows content although no gas is delivered

P224E.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit Low
P224E.d: P224E sets when the control line of tank shutoff valve A reads too low. The DTC list of CNG upfitter TransEco Energy for its alternative fuel control module (AFCM v1.4) blames the line touching ground or being interrupted, turns on the MIL in both dedicated and bi-fuel setups and lets the system keep operating normally rather than forcing a fallback. The same list uses P2A24 and related numbers for valves B to E. Ford's own Boss 302S code list also contains P224E. On a normally closed valve such as the one on GM's bi-fuel Impala, a grounded control wire may keep the solenoid from switching as intended. P224F is the high side, P224C the general open circuit. Gas lines must stay sealed during wiring repairs.
c: Control wire of the tank valve chafed through to ground
Open circuit, which some modules report under this code
Shorted solenoid coil in the valve
s: Check engine light
Gas operation unavailable or interrupted

P224F.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit High
P224F.d: P224F reports a control circuit of tank shutoff valve A that reads too high, typically a wire touching battery voltage. In TransEco Energy's AFCM fault list the cause is given as shorted to power, the MIL is lit and the gas system keeps working under the failure mode strategy. That matters because a valve held open by an external voltage can no longer be closed by the control unit: Ford's 2003 bi-fuel CNG system relies on closing the tank valve when gas pressure falls below 517 kPa, and GM's bi-fuel Impala keeps its cut-off solenoids energized only while the engine turns. Ford's Boss 302S list carries P224F too, though mislabelled as Low. P224E is the low side; CARB requires both directions to be monitored.
c: Control wire of the tank valve shorted to battery voltage
Output stage in the alternative fuel control module stuck on
Wiring mistake after a conversion or repair
s: Check engine light
Tank valve may stay open after switching off

P2250.t: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P2250.d: P2250 signals that the reference voltage line of the upstream wide-band sensor on bank 2 is too high, as happens with a short to the heater feed or battery voltage, or a breakdown inside the ceramic. No manufacturer documents P2250 publicly, and no bulletin in the NHTSA index names it. Ford sends any wide-band wire shorted to supply voltage to P0152 and uses P2247 only for the open line, so Ford engines never store it. Because Bosch allows the Nernst cell only a 250 microamp load, an outside voltage on this lead can ruin a replacement sensor unless the wiring is repaired first. CARB requires fuel-control sensors to be monitored for circuit faults, with distinct codes where practical. P2246 is the bank 1 counterpart, P2249 the low fault, P2247 the open circuit.
c: Reference voltage wire of the bank 2 sensor shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Internal short between heater and Nernst cell
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption
Repeat failure of a new sensor if the wiring short remains

P2251.t: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2251.d: P2251 points to an open negative current control line, i.e. the reference or virtual ground (VM on Bosch, COM on NTK) of the bank 1 upstream wide-band sensor. Ford detects it on Bosch parts by a sensor voltage stuck in a narrow band, or by a reference-current pulse that still moves lambda; NTK chips report the break directly. GM's 2005 V6 and Saab's 2010 9-5 look for 1.47-1.53 V with cell resistance above 570 ohms and exhaust below 900 °C (Type B); VW's 2014 Passat book uses a 950-ohm limit. GM calls it low reference circuit. Bulletins: ECM reflash for the 2020-22 Corvette (22-NA-019) and 2013-14 Dart 2.4 (18-011-14), new sensor for 2016-18 Range Rover TDV6 (LTB01191) and 2025 Wrangler (23-019-25). P2254 is bank 2, P2252/P2253 low/high.
c: Broken reference ground wire or pushed-back pin between sensor and ECM
Internal open circuit in the wide-band sensor
Engine software that sets the code falsely (reprogramming for some models)
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 1
Possible rough running or failed emissions test

P2252.t: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2252.d: P2252 means the negative current control side of the bank 1 front air-fuel sensor reads too low, typically because that line or the sensor cell is shorted to ground. GM's tables for the Honda-built 3.5 V6 in the Saturn Vue (L66, 2004-05) describe it as a sensor-cell short: once the engine has run for 85 s with the heater working and the element signal between 3.2 and 4.6 V, a sensor-cell voltage under 0.3 V for 0.5 s stores the code in the first drive cycle; P2255 is the bank 2 twin. Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander service manual update lists P2252 as a two-trip code, and GM's 2018 Duramax table 18OBDG04 counts it among faults that invalidate the front sensor signal. Ford instead books such shorts as P0131. P2251 is the open line, P2253 the high fault.
c: Reference ground or sensor-cell wire shorted to ground (chafed against exhaust or body)
Internal short in the air-fuel sensor
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 1
Possible hesitation or uneven running

P2253.t: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2253.d: P2253 reports that the negative current control side of the bank 1 upstream air-fuel sensor reads too high. On the Honda-built 3.5 V6 of the 2004-05 Saturn Vue (L66), GM's tables treat it as an open sensor-cell circuit: with the heater operating and the element signal above 4.6 V, a sensor-cell voltage over 6.0 V for 5 s sets it, and P2256 does the same on bank 2. A short to the heater or battery feed can drive the signal high in the same way. Mitsubishi lists P2253 as a two-trip code for the 2022 Outlander, and GM's 2018 Duramax table 18OBDG04 names it as a front sensor fault without giving limits. Ford logs high-side shorts on wide-band wires as P0132 instead. P2251 is the open ground line in Ford terms, P2252 the low fault.
c: Open sensor-cell wire or connector contact, letting the signal float high
Wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Internal defect in the air-fuel sensor
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 1
Repeat failure of a new sensor if a wiring short remains

P2254.t: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit/Open (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P2254.d: P2254 concerns the negative current control line - also called reference ground, virtual ground or COM - of the wide-band air-fuel sensor ahead of the catalyst on bank 2. Ford's OBD summaries (2012 and 2020-2023) set it for an open line: with Bosch sensors the PCM briefly injects a reference current and flags the line if lambda barely moves, within about 10 s; with NTK sensors the interface chip reports the open line directly. VW's 2014 Passat and CC books set it when the front signal sits at 1.47-1.52 V while the cell resistance exceeds 950 ohms. P2251 is the same fault on bank 1, P2255/P2256 are low/high faults. Closed-loop mixture control on bank 2 is lost.
c: Broken reference ground wire or pushed-out pin between sensor and ECM
Internal open circuit in the wide-band sensor
Corroded sensor connector with high contact resistance
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 2
Possible rough running or failed emissions test

P2255.t: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P2255.d: P2255 reports that the negative current control line (reference ground) of the bank 2 upstream wide-band sensor reads too low, typically a short to ground. No manufacturer publicly documents P2255 with thresholds. Ford's OBD summaries assign shorts to ground on any wide-band sensor line to P0151 and use P2254 only for an open line, and VW's 2014 specification books likewise list only P2254. The code therefore appears mainly where the sensor interface separates short-circuit faults by line. CARB requires circuit and out-of-range faults of fuel-control sensors to be detected and, where feasible, stored as separate codes. P2252 is the bank 1 counterpart, P2256 the high-side fault. Mixture control on bank 2 becomes unreliable.
c: Reference ground wire shorted to ground (chafed against exhaust or body)
Internal fault in the wide-band sensor
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption
Possible hesitation or uneven running

P2256.t: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P2256.d: P2256 means the negative current control line (reference ground) of the bank 2 upstream wide-band sensor reads too high, typically a short to battery or heater voltage. No manufacturer publicly documents P2256 with thresholds. Ford's OBD summaries send a short to battery on any wide-band sensor line to P0152 and reserve P2254 for the open line; VW's 2014 books also list only P2254 for this circuit. CARB requires fuel-control sensors to be checked for circuit continuity and out-of-range values, with separate codes where feasible. P2253 is the bank 1 counterpart, P2255 the low-side fault, P2254 the open circuit. A short to voltage can damage the sensor or the interface, so the wiring should be checked before a new sensor is fitted.
c: Reference ground wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Internal short in the wide-band sensor
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption
Repeat failure of a new sensor if the wiring short remains

P2257.t: AIR System Control A Circuit Low
P2257.d: P2257 concerns the control circuit of the secondary air (AIR) pump or its relay, which blows fresh air into the exhaust during cold starts so the catalyst lights off sooner. The code sets when that circuit reads low. GM's 2018 tables (LWE section) watch the low-side driver of the AIR pump control: a resistance of 0.5 ohm or less to controller ground, detected as low voltage with the driver switched off, in 20 of 25 samples of 250 ms with at least 11 V on the powertrain relay, Type B; some controllers also log P0418. VW's 2014 specification books for the CC and Touareg flag a relay control voltage between 0 and 3.26 V. P2258 is the short to power, P0418 the open circuit. Affected cars mainly emit more during warm-up.
c: Relay control wire shorted to ground
Secondary air relay with a shorted coil
Water ingress in the relay or pump connector
s: Check engine light
Secondary air pump silent during cold start
Secondary air flow codes such as P0411 may follow

P2258.t: AIR System Control A Circuit High
P2258.d: P2258 reports that the line controlling secondary air (AIR) pump A or its relay sits at too high a level, usually because it is shorted to battery voltage or the driver cannot pull it down. The pump only runs briefly after a cold start to heat the catalyst faster, so the fault mainly raises warm-up emissions. GM's 2018 tables (LWE section) check it while the low-side driver is switched on: 0.5 ohm or less between signal and supply, in 20 of 25 samples of 250 ms, Type B with the MIL after two trips. VW's 2014 book for the Touareg 3.0 TSI (CGFA) gives a signal current of 0.60 to 2.40 A as criterion. Ford names P2258 beside P0412 as a secondary air fault that disables its catalyst temperature model. P2257 is the low counterpart; P2259/P2260 belong to circuit B.
c: Control wire of the AIR pump relay chafed through and touching a battery-voltage feed
Secondary air relay with shorted coil or welded contacts
Moisture or corrosion in the relay or pump connector bridging terminals
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: MIL on, often without any noticeable change in driving
Secondary air pump silent after a cold start
Higher hydrocarbon emissions during warm-up, possibly a failed emissions test

P2259.t: AIR System Control B Circuit Low
P2259.d: P2259 is the low-level fault of the second secondary air control circuit, B. A second circuit exists where an engine uses two AIR pumps, two relays or a separately switched air valve; circuit A keeps its own codes P2257/P2258. A low reading usually means the control wire has contact with ground. If the relay is switched to ground by the ECM, such a short can energise it permanently, so the pump or valve keeps running after the warm-up phase and may overheat. No manufacturer publishes a threshold for circuit B; GM merely names P2259 in the keyword list of its connector-check bulletin PIP5094 for 2014 and older models. For circuit A, GM's 2018 tables judge the low-side driver over 20 of 25 samples as a Type B fault. CARB requires that secondary air systems be monitored. The engine itself runs normally.
c: Control wire of circuit B chafed against the body or engine and shorted to ground
Relay or air valve B with a shorted winding
Corroded connector at relay B or the air valve
s: MIL on
Secondary air pump audible for longer than usual or while warm
Blown fuse of the secondary air pump after a long run

P225A.d: P225A concerns the front NOx sensor of bank 1, the one ahead of the SCR catalyst. Modern NOx probes come with their own control unit that holds a sensor-specific calibration and reports finished values over CAN; this code means the stored calibration data of that unit cannot be read or fails its check. Ford's 2014 PCM code table carries P225A as a MIL code, but no manufacturer publishes the test or a threshold. Ford's 2023 diesels report memory errors inside the NOx sensor module under P2200 instead. CARB requires NOx sensor faults to be caught when the sensor can no longer serve as a feedback or monitoring input. P225B is the same fault on the downstream sensor. Usually the sensor assembly is replaced, as its memory cannot be repaired.
c: Internal memory or checksum fault in the NOx sensor control unit
Replacement sensor with a part number or calibration that does not suit the vehicle
Supply voltage dropout or poor connector contact while the module was storing data
Engine or aftertreatment control unit software that misreads the sensor data
s: MIL on, usually without any change in how the engine runs
SCR dosing runs without valid feedback, so NOx emissions may rise
Follow-up NOx catalyst efficiency codes possible

P225B.d: P225B is stored when the control unit of the downstream NOx sensor on bank 1 cannot provide valid calibration data from its memory. That sensor sits behind the SCR catalyst and is what the engine computer uses to judge how well urea dosing reduces NOx, so a sensor without trustworthy calibration leaves the catalyst monitor blind. Ford lists P225B as a MIL code in its 2014 PCM code table; a description of the check is not public from any manufacturer. Smart NOx sensors of the Continental type keep an OEM-specific calibration in their attached module, which is why a part for another vehicle can trip such a code. P225A is the upstream counterpart, while P229E to P22A1 cover the electrical faults of this downstream sensor.
c: Corrupted or unreadable calibration memory in the downstream NOx sensor module
Sensor installed with the wrong part number or an OEM calibration for another application
Moisture or corrosion at the sensor module connector disturbing its supply
s: MIL on with no driveability complaint
SCR efficiency monitor does not complete or reports P20EE
Possible emissions test failure because readiness stays incomplete

P225C.t: NOx Sensor Performance - Signal Biased/Stuck High (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P225C.d: P225C says the upstream NOx sensor of bank 1 reports more NOx than is plausible. Volvo describes its test on US17+OBD19 trucks: during engine motoring with zero fuel the engine makes no NOx, so the inlet sensor must fall below 50 ppm within about 10 s; each failure lights the MIL, which needs three clean drive cycles to go out. Volvo admitted false settings and told dealers not to replace the sensor. Mack and Volvo (KC-107) demand a NOx conversion test first; inlet and outlet should agree within 40 ppm before shutdown. Isuzu cured P225C on 2021 F-Series 5.2L trucks with a DCU update. FCA found most returned sensors from 3.0 EcoDiesel Ram and Jeep models fault-free and points to intake or EGR leaks, soot-clogged sensor ports and skewed MAF or coolant readings.
c: Engine or DEF control unit software that flags the sensor too eagerly
Leak in the charge air path or an EGR valve stuck partly open
Air mass or coolant temperature signal that skews the NOx model
Upstream NOx sensor with a genuine positive offset
s: MIL on, often without any noticeable driving fault
Code returns after the NOx sensor has been replaced
Higher DEF consumption or SCR efficiency codes in some cases

P225D.t: NOx Sensor Performance - Signal Biased/Stuck Low (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P225D.d: P225D is the opposite case to P225C: the upstream NOx sensor of bank 1 reads too little NOx or refuses to rise when the engine should be producing it. Volvo and Mack list P225D among NOx codes where the sensor is very unlikely to be at fault, because the probe is simply measuring fresh air; their guide says not to replace it. FCA uses P225D on the 3.0 EcoDiesel, from 2014 Ram 1500 and Grand Cherokee flash bulletins to 2020 Ram 1500 updates, and its 2021 case file for Wrangler, Gladiator and Ram 1500 reports mostly fault-free returned sensors; it names charge air or EGR leaks, fuel contamination that soots up the sensor ports and skewed MAF or coolant inputs. A low-reading sensor hides real NOx, so SCR control and the catalyst monitor lose accuracy.
c: Charge air, intake or exhaust leak that lets the sensor see diluted gas
Sensor ports clogged with soot, for example after fuel contamination
Low-pressure EGR valve partly stuck open
Outdated engine control software that a published flash corrects
s: MIL on
Code persists after a new NOx sensor
