Possible related intake, EGR or MAF codes

P225E.t: NOx Sensor Performance - Signal Biased/Stuck High (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P225E.d: P225E points at the downstream NOx sensor of bank 1, behind the SCR catalyst, reading persistently high. Because that sensor sees what is left after urea dosing, a high value can be a sensor offset or genuine NOx slipping through a weak catalyst, poor DEF or a faulty dosing valve. Volvo and Mack therefore put P225E in the group where either sensor or the aftertreatment itself may be the cause: their replacement guide and bulletin KC-107 require a NOx conversion test or the aftertreatment analysis in PTT before any part is changed, and for P225E they also send technicians to the DEF dosing valve diagnosis. No public bulletin from a passenger car maker covers P225E. P225C is the same fault upstream; P225F is the low-reading downstream case.
c: Real NOx slip from a weak SCR catalyst, poor DEF quality or a faulty dosing valve
Downstream NOx sensor with a positive offset
Control software that evaluates the sensor incorrectly
s: MIL on, often together with P20EE
Increased DEF consumption or DEF quality warnings
Power reduction possible if SCR efficiency codes follow

P225F.t: NOx Sensor Performance - Signal Biased/Stuck Low (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P225F.d: P225F is set when the downstream NOx sensor of bank 1 reports less NOx than expected or does not move away from a low value. A sensor behind the SCR catalyst that reads too low makes the catalyst look better than it is, so the efficiency monitor can no longer be trusted. The only public manufacturer source is the Volvo and Mack NOx sensor replacement guide for US10 and newer trucks: it lists P225F next to P225D among codes whose description mentions the NOx sensor although the sensor is rarely the cause, notes that the probe is reading fresh air, and tells technicians not to replace it. Leaks in the exhaust ahead of the sensor and harness faults are the more likely culprits. P225D is the upstream case; P225E the high-reading counterpart.
c: Exhaust leak upstream of the downstream sensor drawing in outside air
Chafed or corroded wiring between sensor module and probe
Downstream NOx sensor with reduced sensitivity
s: MIL on
SCR efficiency cannot be confirmed, readiness may stay open

P2260.t: AIR System Control B Circuit High
P2260.d: P2260 flags secondary air control circuit B sitting at too high a level, as with a short to the supply or a driver output that cannot switch. Circuit B drives the second pump, second relay or a separate air valve, depending on the engine. Where the ECM grounds the relay to switch it, a short to power means the relay can never pull in: pump or valve B stays idle, and the catalyst on that side heats up more slowly after a cold start. No manufacturer documents its threshold for circuit B; GM only lists P2260 among the codes in its connector bulletin PIP5094 (2014 and older). For circuit A, GM's 2018 tables treat 0.5 ohm or less between signal and supply, with the driver on, as a Type B fault, which shows the type of check involved. P2259 is the low-level counterpart, P2258 the same fault on circuit A.
c: Control wire of circuit B shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Relay or air valve B with an open coil, depending on how the driver is diagnosed
Output stage for circuit B in the engine control module defective
s: MIL on
Second secondary air pump or valve does not operate after a cold start
Increased cold-start emissions, possibly with a secondary air flow code on one bank

P2261.d: P2261 means bypass valve A of the turbocharger or supercharger, also called the recirculation valve, does not work mechanically. When the throttle snaps shut it should let charge air flow back to the compressor inlet so the compressor does not surge. GM's 2018 tables look for a valve stuck closed in coast-down: with the valve commanded open and at least 1,200 rpm, a high-pass filtered airflow signal above 30 g/s or a filtered boost slope above 500 kPa/s reveals surge; 8 failures in 10 tests give a Type B fault. GM bulletin 16-NA-020 (2016 Encore/Malibu 1.4/1.5 L) blames a sticking valve, 23-NA-033 (2023 Equinox/Terrain) an ECM whose short-circuit detection reacted to back voltage, and Kia campaign SC230 (2022 Seltos 1.6 T-GDI) a kinked recirculation hose. A flutter or rattle on lift-off is typical.
c: Bypass/recirculation valve sticking closed or with a torn diaphragm
Kinked, collapsed or wrongly routed recirculation or control hose
Electrical fault at the valve solenoid or its connector that prevents opening
Engine control module output reacting wrongly (software or hardware)
s: Fluttering, chuffing or rattling noise from the turbo when lifting off the throttle
MIL on
Slightly delayed boost after gear changes

P2262.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Pressure A Not Detected - Mechanical
P2262.d: P2262 says boost pressure A does not appear at all although the charging system should be producing it, and the cause appears to be mechanical rather than a sensor fault. The control unit sees the pressure after the compressor stay near ambient or close to manifold pressure. VW's 2014 book for the supercharged Touareg 3.0 TSI uses the ratio of boost to manifold pressure and flags it below a band of 1 to 1.25. Volvo technical journal 31319 (2016 four-cylinder B4204T23) traced P2262 together with P02CD to a fresh-air hose that had slipped off the air filter housing at the MAF; a spring clamp prevents a repeat. Unlike P0299, which measures a shortfall against the target, P2262 stands for boost missing altogether; P2263 rates overall control performance and P226B the opposite extreme. Acceleration feels flat, and many engines limit torque.
c: Intake or charge-air hose disconnected or split, so the compressor cannot build pressure
Wastegate or bypass stuck open, corroded or with a broken linkage
Damaged turbocharger or supercharger (bearing wear, broken drive, wheel damage)
Boost pressure sensor or its hose blocked or detached
s: Clear loss of power, no turbo or supercharger pull
MIL on, often with a reduced-power mode
Hissing or whistling from the intake if a hose has come off

P2263.d: P2263 means boost pressure measured in the intake manifold stays too far from the target set by the closed-loop boost control. CARB requires diesel OBD to detect underboost, overboost and slow response of the boost control. On the 2014 Cruze 2.0 diesel the allowed underboost deviation runs from 35 to 85 kPa with injection quantity and speed, and the code sets as Type A once the condition holds for 15 s; GM's 2018 diesels need 400 failures in 500 samples and name leaks after the compressor or in the manifolds, and exhaust obstructions, as targets. Ford's 2023 diesels count deviations above 35 kPa at 1500 rpm or more, typically over 100 s. The Opel/GM 2.0 CDTi in the Saab 9-5 (2010) waits for more than 200 s out of range and stores it as Type C. GM's Cruze bulletin found a charge-air cooler duct pulled off the throttle body, with P0299, P2002 and P2463 alongside. The engine usually limits torque.
c: Charge-air hose or cooler duct leaking or pulled off
Restricted exhaust, for example a heavily loaded particulate filter
s: Power loss or limp mode
Hissing or whistling from the charge-air system
Black smoke under load

P2264.t: Water in Fuel Sensor A Circuit
P2264.d: P2264 is the general circuit code for water-in-fuel sensor A, the probe in the diesel filter or separator that detects water by its conductivity. GM's 2018 diesel tables explain a neat self-test: after the ignition has been off for more than about 8 h, a healthy sensor briefly signals water during the first 0.3 to 1.8 s after power-up. If that pulse is missing in 10 of 14 samples of 100 ms, P2264 sets as a Type C code that turns on the Service Vehicle Soon lamp rather than the MIL; versions exist for sensors wired to the ECM and to the fuel tank zone module. Ford's 2014 PCM table also lists the code. With the circuit faulty, the warning for real water no longer works, so the separator should be drained by hand until it is fixed. P2265 to P2268 split the fault further.
c: Water-in-fuel sensor that no longer performs its power-up self-test
Corroded or loose connector at the filter housing, exposed to road spray
Open or damaged wire between sensor and ECM or tank zone module
Incompatible sensor fitted during a filter change
s: Service lamp or message on, engine runs normally
No warning if water actually collects in the separator

P2265.t: Water in Fuel Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P2265.d: P2265 means the signal from water-in-fuel sensor A is electrically present but does not behave plausibly, for example a self-test response that comes at the wrong time or a value that sits between the expected dry and wet states. No manufacturer documents P2265 publicly. A comparable check appears in GM's 2018 diesel tables under P2264: after a long ignition-off period the sensor has to signal water for a short moment right after power-up, and a missing response is judged as a fault. The probes measure conductivity between two electrodes in the water sump of the filter, so a film of dirt, biodiesel residue or a partly corroded probe can push the reading into an implausible zone. The code usually lights only a service or water warning; draining and cleaning come before replacing parts.
c: Sludge, emulsion or deposits coating the sensor electrodes
Sensor electronics drifting so the output lies between dry and wet
Corroded terminals adding resistance to the signal circuit
s: Water warning or service lamp that comes and goes
Water warning stays on even after the filter has been drained

P2266.t: Water in Fuel Sensor A Circuit Low
P2266.d: P2266 is set when the signal line of water-in-fuel sensor A stays below its valid range, typical of a grounded signal wire or of a conductive path that should not be there. Ford documents the code on 2017 and 2018 Super Duty trucks with the 6.7L diesel built up to 15 March 2018: bulletin 18-2133 links P2266, P2269 and P1140 with a lit water-in-fuel lamp to water entering connector C3080 at the sensor, which sits between tank and frame rail. The procedure checks the sensor across pins 1 and 2 for 795 to 815 kOhm, replaces it if out of range, then dries and wraps the connector. As water itself conducts, a wet plug can fake both a low circuit and a water alarm. P2267 is the high side, P2264 the general circuit code.
c: Water intrusion into the sensor connector bridging signal and ground
Sensor with internal resistance outside specification
Signal wire chafed against the frame and shorted to ground
s: Water-in-fuel lamp on although no water is in the separator
Often stored together with P2269

P2267.t: Water in Fuel Sensor A Circuit High
P2267.d: P2267 reports that the signal of water-in-fuel sensor A sits above its valid range, which usually indicates an open signal or ground path, a disconnected sensor or a short to a voltage source. Stellantis has a case file for 2025 and 2026 Ram 2500 to 5500 trucks with the Cummins 6.7L: after the fuel filter module has been drained, the warning lamp may stay on with P2267 and P2269. Instead of replacing parts, technicians drain both filter stages, remove the sensor, wipe residue off its probes, refit it at 3 Nm and prime the system with the lift pump. That points to the sensor reacting to leftover contamination as well as to wiring. P2266 is the low-side counterpart, P2268 the intermittent version.
c: Residual contamination on the probes after draining the filter
Unplugged sensor or open signal or ground wire
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
s: Water-in-fuel lamp stays on after draining
Often appears together with P2269

P2268.t: Water in Fuel Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
P2268.d: P2268 is reserved for a water-in-fuel sensor A circuit whose signal drops out or jumps for short moments instead of staying at a fault level. No manufacturer documents P2268 publicly. The neighbouring codes show where such faults arise on real trucks: Ford traced P2266 on 6.7L Super Duty models to water entering the sensor connector, and Stellantis linked P2267 on Cummins Ram trucks to residue on the probes after draining. Both effects can come and go with temperature, vibration or fuel sloshing in the filter, which is the typical picture of an intermittent circuit. The sensor itself is a simple pair of electrodes, so the search starts at connector, terminals and harness clips. P2266 and P2267 are the steady low and high faults.
c: Loose or corroded connector at the filter housing losing contact under vibration
Wire chafing intermittently near the frame or filter bracket
Moisture in the plug that changes with temperature and spray
s: Water warning flickers or appears briefly while driving
Code stored as history with no fault present at the workshop

P2269.t: Water in Fuel Condition - Sensor A
P2269.d: P2269 is not a wiring fault but a statement about the fuel: sensor A has detected water. On diesels it means the separator is full; Ram's 2025-26 Cummins 6.7L trucks set it with the MIL, and Stellantis traced a persistent case to incomplete draining, fixed by draining and swapping the sensor's signal and ground pins (TSB 14-004-26). Ford tied P2269 on 2017-18 Super Duty 6.7L trucks to water in connector C3080 and, in other bulletins, to PCM software. GM uses P2269 on flex-fuel petrol engines: if the flex fuel sensor's frequency exceeds 185 Hz in 50 of 63 samples, the fuel's conductivity points to water; Type B in 2018, Type A in 2025. Drain or replace contaminated fuel promptly; water damages injection pumps.
c: Water separator full and not drained at the service interval
Fuel from the tank or filling station containing water
Residual water after draining or a wet sensor connector faking the alarm
Engine control software needing an update
s: Water-in-fuel lamp or message, on some vehicles also the MIL
Rough running, power loss or hard starting if water reaches the injection system
Reduced power on some engines to protect the injection system

P226A.t: Water in Fuel Lamp Control Circuit
P226A.d: P226A concerns the output that switches the water-in-fuel warning lamp, not the sensor. The control unit drives the lamp circuit and checks it electrically; an open lamp, a broken wire or a shorted driver lets it set this code. No manufacturer documents P226A publicly, and on current vehicles the cluster usually receives the warning as a bus message, so a discrete lamp line that could fail is found mainly on older or commercial diesels. The practical risk is that the driver is no longer warned when the separator fills, while the sensor itself keeps working and P2269 can still be stored. CARB treats the warning lamp as part of the driver information, not as an emission input, so this code normally does not turn on the MIL. Check bulb, socket, wiring and driver output.
c: Burnt-out warning lamp or corroded lamp socket
Open or shorted wire between control unit and lamp
Faulty lamp driver in the control unit
s: Water-in-fuel lamp does not light during the bulb check at ignition on
Lamp stays on permanently regardless of the filter state

P226B.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger A Boost Pressure Too High - Mechanical
P226B.d: P226B reports boost from turbocharger or supercharger A rising too high for a mechanical reason, for instance a wastegate or bypass that will not open or a seized actuator linkage, rather than a sensor or wiring fault. VW's 2014 book for the supercharged Touareg 3.0 TSI sets it when boost passes 250 kPa. GM uses the code only for European calibrations: its 2018 diesel tables list P226B as an EOBD code in the boost-system fault groups, while the US software maps the same fault group to P2263. CARB requires boosted engines to detect overboost. Where P0234 judges a deviation above the target, P226B points to a mechanical cause; P2262 describes boost that does not appear at all. To protect the engine the ECM usually reduces torque, and some engines open a relief path.
c: Wastegate flap seized closed by corrosion or carbon
Seized or misadjusted wastegate or VGT actuator linkage
Vacuum or pressure line to a pneumatic actuator leaking or blocked
s: Sudden power cut or reduced-power mode under load
MIL on
Unusually strong surge of power just before the cut

P226C.t: Turbocharger Boost Control A Slow Response
P226C.d: P226C means the boost control actuator of turbocharger A does move, but too slowly, so boost lags behind changes in demand. Ford's 2023 diesel summary runs an intrusive check on the 3.0 L and 1.5 L at idle, once in each drive cycle: the variable vanes travel from closed to open, and within 7 s manifold pressure must change by at least 6.5 kPa at sea level (3.5 kPa at 8,000 ft). Mitsubishi's 2022 Eclipse Cross 1.5 turbo sets it when the wastegate angle stays more than 20 % off target for 5 s and then limits torque. FCA changed P226C on the 2014 Ram 6.7 L Cummins so that the MIL needs two trips instead of one; FCA case S2018000009 (Jeep) blames varnish in the VGT housing, Nissan NTB20-071 (Titan XD 5.0 diesel) a binding turbine control valve. P226F is the B side.
c: Variable vanes or turbine control valve sluggish from soot, varnish or corrosion
Worn electric or pneumatic boost actuator, or a weak control solenoid
Damaged wiring or connector between actuator and control module
Control module software that needs an update (cold-weather false sets)
s: Hesitant pull from low engine speed, turbo lag
MIL on, sometimes with a torque limit
More smoke on acceleration with diesel engines

P226D.d: P226D means the bank 1 particulate filter offers so little flow resistance that its core is likely broken, burnt out or removed. CARB requires detection of a destroyed or missing substrate, or a filter replaced by a pipe. GM's diesel tables test the filtered resistance of the DPF during soot loading above 500 rpm and 10 l/s exhaust flow: 5 failures in 10 samples (2018) or 20 in 30 below 0.01 kPa per l/s (2025), Type A. GM adds that a loose or blocked pressure-sensor pipe gives the same result; PIP5664 and an ECM update dealt with false P226D on 2020 6.6L L5P trucks, as did Mack and Volvo for 2015-16 MP engines. Ford also uses P226D for petrol particulate filters (2024-25: normalised back pressure below 1.0 for 5 s); 2025 Maverick and Bronco Sport 2.0L had the wrong pressure sensor fitted.
c: Filter core cracked, melted after an overheated regeneration, or removed
Differential pressure line disconnected, cracked, blocked or routed wrongly
Control software that sets the code without a hardware fault
Incorrect or faulty differential pressure sensor assembly
s: MIL on
Visible soot at the tailpipe if the filter core is damaged
Often no driveability change; regeneration behaviour may be affected

P226E.d: P226E reports a damaged or missing particulate filter core on bank 2, which only exists where each cylinder bank has its own filter. Ford documents it in its 2024-2025 OBD summary for petrol engines: the gasoline particulate filter check runs once the filter has been above 250 °C for 30 s and exhaust flow lies between 300 and 850 m³/h; if the lowest measured back pressure stays below the missing-brick threshold, a ratio under 1.0, for 5 s, P226E is stored for bank 2 and P226D for bank 1, with Mode 6 results under monitor ID $B3. No public bulletin covers P226E. CARB's missing-substrate rule for diesels follows the same idea. A pressure line problem can mimic a missing core, so check lines and sensor before condemning the filter.
c: Bank 2 filter core cracked, melted or removed
Pressure sensing line of bank 2 loose, cracked or blocked
Back pressure sensor reading too low
s: MIL on
Usually no noticeable change in driving behaviour

P226F.t: Turbocharger Boost Control B Slow Response
P226F.d: P226F is the slow-response fault of boost control B, meaning the actuator of a second turbocharger or of the second stage on twin-turbo, bi-turbo or sequential layouts. Which unit the letter B denotes is up to the manufacturer. The monitoring principle mirrors P226C: the control unit commands a change in vane or wastegate position and expects boost or manifold pressure to follow within a set time. No manufacturer documents P226F publicly. For the A side, Ford's 2023 diesel summary describes an idle test that sweeps the vanes and demands a pressure change within 7 s, and CARB requires diesel engines to detect slow boost response. Likely causes are a sluggish actuator, carbon or varnish in the B turbine housing, or a vacuum or wiring problem on that side. Boost builds hesitantly and the ECM may limit power.
c: Boost actuator of turbocharger B sluggish or worn
Carbon or varnish restricting vanes or flap on turbocharger B
Leaking vacuum line or damaged wiring to actuator B
s: Delayed boost in the speed range where the second charger takes over
MIL on, possibly with reduced power

P2270.t: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean (Bank 1, Sensor 2)
P2270.d: P2270 concerns the oxygen sensor behind the catalyst on bank 1. When the mixture turns rich, this sensor should rise to a high voltage; if it stays low, the ECM treats it as biased or stuck lean and can no longer rely on it for catalyst monitoring or the post-catalyst trim. GM's 2018 four-cylinders add fuel during a coast-down and set the code if the signal is still under 760 mV once 55 g of air have passed (Type B, two trips); Ford fails a sensor whose highest voltage stays under 0.42 V. P2096 reports the trim correction, P0136 a sensor without activity. Documented triggers include oil on the sensor (Honda Pilot 2023 to 2025), an oil-soaked connector (Mazda CX-9), a bent terminal (GM 2013 trucks) and ECM software (Subaru WRX 2015 to 2016, Forester turbo).
c: Rear oxygen sensor aged, contaminated or slow to reach rich voltage
Exhaust leak ahead of the rear sensor diluting the gas with air
Oil in the sensor connector or a bent terminal
Calibration issue fixed by an ECM update
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Catalyst and oxygen sensor readiness not completing
Usually no noticeable change in driveability

P2271.t: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Rich (Bank 1, Sensor 2)
P2271.d: P2271 is the opposite fault of the same bank 1 rear sensor: its voltage refuses to fall when the exhaust should be lean. It is usually checked during a deceleration fuel cut, when almost pure air passes the sensor. GM's 2018 four-cylinders set it if the signal is still above 100 mV after 25 g of air in fuel cut-off (Type B); GM's Bosch-based 2005 V6 looks for a reading above 0.2 V four seconds into the cut, VW's 2014 data books for CC and Tiguan use 0.15 V after 3000 mg of oxygen, and Ford added a fuel-cut stuck test from model year 2019. Causes are a sensor poisoned by coolant, oil or silicone, a signal wire touching voltage, or a front sensor misleading the ECM; Honda traced this on the 2007 to 2008 Acura TSX and replaced both sensors. P2097 and P0138 cover trim and circuit.
c: Rear oxygen sensor contaminated by coolant, oil or silicone
Faulty front A/F sensor making the rear sensor look stuck rich
Signal wire chafed against a voltage source
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Catalyst monitor not completing

P2272.t: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean (Bank 2, Sensor 2)
P2272.d: P2272 applies to V and flat engines with a separate catalyst and rear oxygen sensor on bank 2; that sensor fails to reach a rich reading when the ECM enriches bank 2. GM's 2016 tables (16OBDG05) set it if the voltage is still under 800 mV after 68 g of air during forced enrichment (Type B). GM's Bosch-based 2005 2.8 and 3.6 V6 first wait for 100 s below about 0.58 to 0.66 V, then ramp up the fuel and fail the sensor if it has not risen 10 s after the enrichment limit. Ford uses the same 0.42 V limit as on bank 1. Mazda found oil from a leaking oil pressure switch inside connector C-34 on the 2007 to 2015 CX-9, stored with P2A04, and fixed it with a new switch and a cleaned connector. If only bank 2 reports a fault, comparing its data with bank 1 narrows it down.
c: Bank 2 rear oxygen sensor aged or contaminated
Engine oil in the sensor connector, for example from a leaking oil pressure switch
Exhaust leak on bank 2 ahead of the rear sensor
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Catalyst monitor for bank 2 not completing

P2273.t: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Rich (Bank 2, Sensor 2)
P2273.d: P2273 means the rear oxygen sensor of bank 2 keeps a high voltage when the exhaust of that bank should be lean. GM's 2016 tables (16OBDG05) check this in fuel cut-off and set the code if the signal is above 100 mV after 9 g of air (Type B); GM's 2024 tables (24OBDG07) compare the lowest voltage during a commanded lean phase with 0.20 V over two trips. The Bosch-based 2005 GM V6 leans the bank after a long high-voltage phase and also fails the sensor above 0.202 V four seconds into a fuel cut. Ford treats bank 2 like bank 1 and uses fuel-cut events from model year 2019. Typical causes are a sensor fouled by oil or coolant on that side or a signal wire touching a supply line. P2099 is the post-catalyst trim of bank 2 at its rich limit; P0158 a voltage above the normal range.
c: Bank 2 rear oxygen sensor fouled by oil or coolant
Signal wire touching a supply or heater line
Bank 2 front sensor misreading so that the bank actually runs rich
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Catalyst monitor for bank 2 not completing

P2274.t: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean (Bank 1, Sensor 3)
P2274.d: Sensor 3 exists only where a bank has a third oxygen sensor, usually behind a second catalyst, so that sensor 2 sits between two bricks. P2274 says this last sensor on bank 1 stays lean when it should swing rich. VW's 2014 data books for the CC, Passat and Tiguan 2.0 TSI define it as a rear signal that does not oscillate and stays under about 0.62 to 0.65 V even after the ECM enriches the mixture by 27.9 %. Jaguar Land Rover lists P2274 with the bank 1 post-catalyst sensor codes of the 2014 to 2016 3.0 supercharged V6, blames thermal shock from water on the hot ceramic and fits a new sensor. CARB requires every secondary sensor to be checked for adequate output. P2270 is the same fault one position forward; P0142 and P0146 cover circuit faults and missing activity of sensor 3.
c: Third oxygen sensor aged or cracked by thermal shock from water
Exhaust leak ahead of sensor 3 drawing in air
Damaged wiring or connector of sensor 3
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
No noticeable change in driveability

P2275.t: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Rich (Bank 1, Sensor 3)
P2275.d: P2275 is the rich-side fault of the third oxygen sensor on bank 1, the last one on systems with two catalysts in series: it keeps a high voltage while the exhaust should be lean. VW's 2014 data books for the CC, Passat and Tiguan check it in fuel cut-off, comparing the voltage with 0.15 V once 4500 mg of oxygen have passed, more than the 3000 mg used for sensor 2 because the extra catalyst stores oxygen first. Jaguar Land Rover includes P2275 among the bank 1 post-catalyst sensor codes of its 2014 to 2016 3.0 supercharged V6 and replaces water-damaged sensors. Fouling by oil, coolant or sealant and a signal wire touching voltage are other plausible causes. P2271 is the same fault at sensor 2; P0144 reports a voltage above the valid range rather than a stuck reading.
c: Third oxygen sensor contaminated or damaged by water
Signal wire of sensor 3 touching a voltage source
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
No noticeable change in driveability

P2276.t: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean (Bank 2, Sensor 3)
P2276.d: P2276 needs three oxygen sensors on bank 2, so it only occurs on V or flat engines whose second bank carries a front, a mid-catalyst and a post-catalyst sensor. It reports that the post-catalyst sensor of bank 2 does not reach a rich reading. No manufacturer publishes a threshold for this exact code; Jaguar Land Rover lists it, with P2277 and the heater and circuit codes of that sensor, for the 2014 to 2016 3.0 supercharged V6 in the LR4, Range Rover and Range Rover Sport, where water on the hot element cracked the sensor. Ford's monitor runs the same switch-point test on sensors 2 and 3 and fails a rich peak below 0.42 V. CARB requires secondary sensors to be checked for sufficient output. If bank 1 is fault-free, compare both third sensors and look for an exhaust leak on bank 2.
c: Bank 2 third oxygen sensor aged or cracked by water
Exhaust leak on bank 2 ahead of sensor 3
Damaged wiring or connector of sensor 3
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
No noticeable change in driveability

P2277.t: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Rich (Bank 2, Sensor 3)
P2277.d: P2277 is the rich-side counterpart of P2276: the third, post-catalyst sensor on bank 2 does not drop to a lean reading. On such layouts the check normally runs during a fuel cut, when the second catalyst must fill with oxygen before the sensor can respond, so a slow or fouled element shows up here. No manufacturer publishes a threshold for P2277 itself; Jaguar Land Rover lists it among the bank 2 post-catalyst sensor codes of the 2014 to 2016 3.0 supercharged V6 and replaces water-damaged sensors. For reference, VW tests the bank 1 twin P2275 against 0.15 V after 4500 mg of oxygen, and Ford fails a sensor whose lean peak never drops below 0.48 V. A shorted signal wire or oil and coolant fouling are further causes. P2273 is the fault at sensor 2; P0164 a voltage above range.
c: Bank 2 third oxygen sensor contaminated or water-damaged
Signal wire of sensor 3 touching a voltage source
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
No noticeable change in driveability

P2278.t: O2 Sensor Signals Swapped Bank 1 Sensor 3/Bank 2 Sensor 3
P2278.d: P2278 reports that the third oxygen sensors of the two banks are connected the wrong way round, so the ECM reads the bank 1 sensor as if it sat on bank 2 and vice versa. The check changes the exhaust of one bank only, for example by cutting its injectors or feeding air into one exhaust line, and watches which sensor answers. A DaimlerChrysler patent describes this test and the risk for control sensors: crossed sensors push one bank leaner and the other richer until both controllers hit their limits. At the third position the effect is milder, since these sensors mainly watch the catalysts, but faults would be blamed on the wrong bank. No manufacturer documents a test for this code publicly; CARB requires usable secondary sensor output. The usual cause is crossed connectors after repairs.
c: Sensor 3 connectors of both banks plugged in crosswise after a repair
Harness routed to the wrong side or pins swapped in a connector
Wrong harness, ECM or calibration after a replacement
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Catalyst or sensor codes reported for the wrong bank

P2279.d: P2279 means the ECM has concluded that air enters the engine without being measured or expected, for example because the air mass sensor, manifold pressure and throttle position no longer agree with its air model. Volkswagen and Audi use it widely. On the 2013 to 2016 Audi A6, A7 and A8 4.0 TFSI, a leaking pressure-regulating valve in the crankcase breather module set P2279 with P0507 and a metallic whistle at warm idle; a fabric-reinforced membrane fixed it. On 2.0 TFSI engines (BPY, CCTA and others) a check valve that did not seal under boost let pressure into the crankcase, logging P2279, P2187 and P1297 with oil leaking at the filler cap. For the 2.5 litre five-cylinder Volkswagen advises checking cam timing first, since a timing offset changes the air the engine draws. Diesels set it too: the Mercedes OM651 2.2 in the international Jeep Compass and Patriot logged it with limp mode and got a new air filter and software.
c: Leaking crankcase breather or PCV pressure-regulating valve
Leak at intake manifold, hoses or seals after the air mass sensor
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Whistling at idle, unstable or high idle speed
Limp mode on some engines

P227A.d: P227A is the general circuit fault of barometric pressure sensor C, used when the control unit finds the signal missing or unusable without classifying it as too low or too high. Sensor C is not necessarily a separate ambient sensor: in GM's 2018 diesel tables the BARO C channel belongs to the turbocharger inlet pressure sensor, GM also uses it on the supercharged 6.2 L LT4, and on its 2023-2024 twin-throttle engine it reads pressure ahead of a throttle. No manufacturer documents P227A itself publicly; GM divides circuit monitoring of sensor C into P227C (low), P227D (high) and P227E (erratic). The matching general codes for sensors A and B are P2226 and P222A. With a substitute value the engine keeps running, but altitude and boost corrections lose accuracy.
c: Loose connector, corroded pins or damaged wiring at sensor C
5 V reference or sensor ground shared with other sensors disturbed
s: MIL on
Usually no noticeable change in driving; slight power loss at altitude possible

P227B.t: Barometric Pressure Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P227B.d: P227B means sensor C supplies an electrically sound signal that does not agree with the other pressure readings. In GM's 2018 diesel tables sensor C is the turbocharger inlet pressure sensor: the ECM compares it with BARO and MAP at idle and in the window between key-off and the next start, and if only sensor C is out of line it gets the blame, as a Type B fault after 320 failures in 400 samples. With the engine stopped a reading below 50 or above 115 kPa also fails. On GM's 2023-2024 twin-throttle engine the pressure ahead of a throttle is checked against ambient pressure while running and while stopped, with 2 kPa tolerance plus allowances for modelled air-filter loss; the code sets after 2 s within one trip. P227C to P227E cover electrical faults of the same sensor.
c: Sensor C drifting or with an offset
Sensor port blocked by dirt, oil or ice, or sensor not seated in its bore
Heavily clogged air filter shifting the pressure ahead of the compressor or throttle
s: MIL on
Mostly no driveability change; occasionally reduced boost

P227C.t: Barometric Pressure Sensor C Circuit Low
P227C.d: P227C flags a voltage from pressure sensor C that is too low. GM's 2018 tables show two variants. On the diesel, where sensor C measures turbocharger inlet pressure and the input has a pull-up, only a short to ground pulls it below 39.4 % of 5 V (about 50.2 kPa); 320 failures in 400 samples make it a Type B fault. On the supercharged 6.2 L LT4 the limit is 40 % (50.9 kPa), and both a grounded and an open line count, as Type A with the MIL on the first trip. GM's 2023-2024 twin-throttle engine looks at the pressure value: below 50 kPa for 2 s, two trips. GM bulletin 22-NA-188 (1.3 L L3T and 2.0 L LSY turbo) links P227C after an ECM replacement to a redesigned MAF sensor that requires the matching calibration. P227D is the high counterpart.
c: Signal wire of sensor C shorted to ground
Open signal or 5 V supply line on inputs that read an open circuit as low
Replacement control module without the calibration that matches the fitted sensor
s: MIL on, on some engines immediately
Engine runs on a substitute value, at most slightly less power

P227D.t: Barometric Pressure Sensor C Circuit High
P227D.d: P227D is the high-voltage counterpart of P227C. On GM's 2018 diesel the sensor C input has a pull-up, so both a short to the supply and a broken signal wire push it above 90.2 % of 5 V (about 115.4 kPa); after 320 failures in 400 samples it is a Type B fault. The supercharged LT4 uses 90 % (115 kPa) and attributes the code only to a short to power, here as Type A with the MIL on the first trip, because its input reads an open line as low. GM's 2023-2024 twin-throttle engine flags a reading above 115 kPa held for 2 s over two trips. Since the atmosphere cannot produce such a value at the sensor positions concerned, the ECM switches to a substitute, and corrections for altitude or boost become less exact.
c: Signal wire of sensor C shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Broken signal wire or sensor ground on inputs with pull-up
s: MIL on
Little change in driving; possibly reduced boost or poorer altitude compensation

P227E.t: Barometric Pressure Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P227E.d: P227E covers a sensor C signal that jumps although every single value is in range. GM measures this as a string length: the absolute difference between each reading and the one taken 12.5 ms earlier is summed over 80 consecutive readings, and a sum above 152 kPa (2018 diesel) or 150 kPa (supercharged LT4) counts as a failure. Four failures in five one-second samples set the code, as Type B with two trips on the diesel and as Type A on the LT4. Loose terminals, chafed insulation, a cracked sensor housing or interference from nearby actuators are typical triggers. P227C and P227D catch steady shorts, P227B values that are smooth but wrong. The engine normally keeps running on a substitute pressure.
c: Loose or corroded terminals in the sensor C connector
Interference from ignition or actuator wiring routed nearby
Sensor C with an unstable internal element
s: MIL on, possibly coming and going
Occasional brief hesitation or uneven boost

P227F.t: Air Flow Restriction/Air Leak Between Air Filter and MAF (Bank 2)
P227F.d: P227F means the passage between the air filter and the mass air flow sensor of bank 2 is restricted or lets air in that has bypassed the filter. By today's wording the code belongs to engines with a separate air path and MAF per bank; P2280 is the bank 1 version. FCA nevertheless sets P227F on Ram 2500 and 5500 heavy-duty trucks: STAR case S2218000013 (2022) reports it together with a prompt to service the air filter, sometimes alongside P0299 or P226C, on vehicles below 3,000 miles. The reason was factory filters whose paper media carried too much oil; a fresh filter is the first step. On the same trucks FCA treats the bank 1 sibling P2280 as a two-trip fault. A restricted filter starves the engine of air, so boost and power fall, and diesels may smoke more.
c: Air filter clogged with dust or soaked with too much oil
Intake opening blocked by snow, leaves or a collapsed duct
Loose clamp or cracked duct between filter box and MAF on bank 2
Faulty filter restriction or inlet pressure sensor
s: MIL on, on some trucks with an air filter service message
Reduced power and boost under load
More black smoke on diesel engines

P2280.t: Air Flow Restriction/Air Leak Between Air Filter and MAF (Bank 1)
P2280.d: P2280 is the bank 1 code for restricted airflow or an air leak between the air filter and the MAF sensor. A blocked filter lowers the pressure ahead of the sensor and limits the air the engine can take in. A leak in this section matters less for fuel metering, since the air still passes the MAF, but it lets unfiltered air and dust reach the engine. FCA's heavy-duty Ram trucks with the 6.7 L Cummins diesel are the documented users: with 2016 software, bulletin 18-027-16 made P2280 wait for two trips instead of one before the MIL, and FCA tech tip 9003821 (2017) notes MIL events where oil-soaked intake filters were being replaced. FCA's older wording names the code without a bank. P227F is the bank 2 counterpart, P2281 covers the stretch from the MAF to the throttle.
c: Air filter clogged or soaked with oil
Snow, ice or debris in the air inlet, or a collapsed intake duct
Cracked duct or loose clamp between filter box and MAF
Early software that flags the condition too readily
s: MIL on
Less power and slower boost build-up under load
More smoke from diesel engines when accelerating

P2281.t: Air Leak Between MAF and Throttle Body
P2281.d: P2281 points to air that escapes or enters between the MAF sensor and the throttle body, so the airflow the sensor reports no longer matches what reaches the cylinders. On turbocharged engines this section includes the compressor, the charge air cooler and their hoses: a loose clamp or split boot can blow off charge air under boost or draw in unmeasured air at idle. FCA is the documented user: across 2013 to 2026 Ram trucks with the 6.7 L Cummins diesel, flash bulletins such as 18-053-14 and 18-027-16 bring software meant to stop unwarranted MIL events for P2281. No manufacturer publishes the detection method or a threshold; an air-model comparison like Ford's speed-density check for P2282 is the likely principle. A real leak costs boost and power and leads to smoke on diesels. P2280 sits before the MAF, P2282 after the throttle.
c: Loose clamp, split hose or leaking charge air cooler between MAF and throttle
Contaminated or drifting MAF sensor that misreports airflow
Engine software that sets the code without a real leak (update available)
Disconnected crankcase vent or other hose joined to this section
s: MIL on
Hissing under boost and less power
Black smoke on diesels or rough idle on petrol engines

P2282.t: Air Leak Between Throttle Body and Intake Valves
P2282.d: P2282 means air enters the intake behind the throttle, so it reaches the cylinders without passing the throttle. Ford uses it as its PCV monitor on turbo engines with speed density: airflow worked out from manifold pressure is compared with airflow through the throttle, and a calculated leak of 1 lb/min or more for at least 5 s, with the throttle at 4 degrees or less, sets the code (2012, 2020-2023 and 2024 summaries). Ford designed the PCV inlet tube so that pulling it off leaves a large, detectable opening. Ford bulletins blame a stuck-open brake vacuum valve or tube on the 2.0 EcoBoost in the 2019-2020 Edge and Nautilus (TSB 20-2151), ice in the manifold of the 2020-2021 Escape hybrid (SSM 49654) and PCM software on the 2023 Maverick hybrid (TSB 23-2193). Land Rover found a detached brake vacuum pipe (LTB01186).
c: Brake booster vacuum pipe detached or its check valve stuck open
Crankcase ventilation hose disconnected or cracked
Leaking intake manifold gasket, throttle body seal or vacuum hose
Iced manifold pressure sensor or software miscalculating the leak
s: High or unstable idle speed
MIL on, sometimes with a hissing noise from the engine bay
Harder brake pedal if the brake vacuum line is affected

P2283.d: P2283 is the general circuit code for the injector control pressure (ICP) sensor. ICP describes the high-pressure engine oil that hydraulically actuated unit injectors (HEUI) use to pressurise fuel, as on Navistar-built Ford Power Stroke diesels; the sensor reports rail pressure so the injection pressure regulator can be closed-loop controlled. No manufacturer documents P2283 publicly. Ford's 6.0L summaries for 2003 and 2004 split the electrical check into P2285 (below 0.03 V) and P2286 (above 4.83 V), and Ford's 2014 PCM code table lists those two but not P2283. CARB requires diesel fuel-pressure control, explicitly including hydraulic fluid, to be monitored. Without a valid ICP signal the PCM substitutes a default value, so power and starting suffer.
c: Failed ICP sensor, often with oil inside the connector
Damaged signal, reference or ground wire of the sensor
5-volt reference circuit pulled down by another sensor
s: Low power and hesitation
Hard or long cranking, especially when hot
MIL on

P2284.t: Injector Control Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2284.d: P2284 means the measured injector control pressure does not follow what the PCM commands. Ford's 6.0L Power Stroke summaries (2003 and 2004) run the check continuously every 8 ms with the engine running: a fault is recorded once measured pressure stays more than 3.0 MPa above the target for longer than 7 s, the reverse case being P2290. Because the high-pressure oil pump is regulated through the IPR valve against the sensor reading, a biased sensor, a sticking regulator or an air-entrained oil supply can all open this gap. Ford also ran a 2003 owner programme replacing ICP sensors whose O-ring could shift and cause reduced power and rough idle. Unlike P2285/P2286 the circuit voltage is valid here; only its relation to the command is wrong.
c: ICP sensor reading offset, including a shifted internal O-ring
Injection pressure regulator valve sticking or contaminated
Wrong, aerated or low engine oil disturbing pressure control
Oil wicking into the sensor connector
s: Reduced power and rough idle
Engine runs on a substitute pressure value
MIL on

P2285.t: Injector Control Pressure Sensor Circuit Low
P2285.d: P2285 is set when the ICP sensor voltage falls almost to zero. Ford's 6.0L Power Stroke summaries for 2003 and 2004 define it precisely: below 0.03 V, checked every 8 ms without entry conditions, decided in under one second. Such a value cannot come from a working sensor on a 5-volt reference, so it points to an open signal wire, a short to ground, a lost reference voltage or an unplugged sensor. Ford lights the MIL for P2285 even on heavy federal trucks over 8,500 lb that otherwise run a reduced OBD calibration. On a HEUI engine the PCM then has to estimate rail pressure, so starting and response deteriorate. P2286 is the high-voltage counterpart; P2284 covers a valid signal that disagrees with the commanded pressure.
c: Signal wire open or shorted to ground
s: MIL on immediately
Hard starting and reduced power

P2286.t: Injector Control Pressure Sensor Circuit High
P2286.d: P2286 means the ICP sensor voltage has risen to the top of the range. In Ford's 2004 summary for the 6.0L Power Stroke the limit is above 4.83 V, checked every 8 ms and confirmed in less than one second; the 2003 edition already names the code alongside P2285. A reading that close to the 5-volt reference typically results from the signal wire touching the reference, a broken sensor ground or a sensor that has failed internally. Ford switches on the MIL for P2286 also on heavy federal trucks above 8,500 lb with their reduced OBD calibration, and its 2014 PCM code table marks the code as a MIL code. The engine runs on an estimated rail pressure until the fault is fixed. P2285 is the low counterpart, P2288 a real over-pressure condition.
c: Signal wire shorted to the 5-volt reference or another voltage
ICP sensor failed with output stuck high
s: MIL on
Reduced power and possibly harsh running

P2287.t: Injector Control Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent
P2287.d: P2287 covers an ICP sensor signal that drops out or jumps for brief moments, too short or too irregular to be judged as a steady low or high fault. No manufacturer documents P2287 publicly; Ford's 6.0L summaries and its 2014 PCM table contain the steady electrical codes P2285 and P2286 but not this one. On HEUI diesels the sensor is mounted on the engine in a hot, oily environment, so oil creeping into the connector, fretting terminals and harness rubbing are the usual reasons for an unstable signal. Since the PCM regulates high-pressure oil from this reading, short dropouts can make the engine stumble or surge before a substitute value takes over. CARB counts such inputs among the components whose circuit faults must be monitored.
c: Engine oil creeping into the sensor connector
Fretting or loose terminals at sensor or PCM
Harness rubbing on engine parts and shorting briefly
s: Occasional stumble, surge or hesitation
Code returns without a fault visible in the workshop

P2288.d: P2288 reports that the injector control pressure itself, not just its reading, has climbed above the allowed maximum while the engine runs. Ford's 6.0L Power Stroke summaries put the limit at 27.5 MPa in the 2003 edition and 29.5 MPa in 2004, sustained for more than 3 s. For comparison, Ford's high-pressure oil pump normally works between about 3 and 25 MPa on that engine. Excessive pressure means the injection pressure regulator fails to release enough oil to drain, because it sticks, its coil is driven wrongly or the control signal is stuck; a sensor reading high but still within circuit limits can also mislead. The PCM limits fuelling to protect the injectors and oil system. P2290 is the too-low case; P2289 the same check with the engine off.
c: Injection pressure regulator valve stuck or contaminated
Fault in the regulator drive circuit holding it at high duty
ICP sensor reading higher than the actual pressure
s: Reduced power with fuel limit active
Loud injection noise or knocking
MIL on

P2289.t: Injector Control Pressure Too High - Engine Off
P2289.d: P2289 is a plausibility test carried out with the engine stopped. On a HEUI diesel the high-pressure oil pump is driven by the engine, so once it stops, injector control pressure should drop to almost nothing. Ford's 6.0L Power Stroke summaries check this in engine-off mode: if the ICP reading stays above 10 MPa for more than 10 s (2003) or 12 s (2004), P2289 is stored. A real pressure that high without a running pump is unlikely, so the code mainly points to an ICP sensor with an offset or contamination, or to a signal circuit pulled up by a fault that stays within the electrical limits of P2286. Ford's 2014 PCM table marks it as a MIL code. P2288 is the counterpart with the engine running.
c: ICP sensor with a positive offset or oil contamination
Partial short between signal and reference voltage
Faulty input stage in the PCM
s: MIL on, possibly after the engine was switched off
Hard starting if the PCM trusts the false pressure value

P228A.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator A - Forced Engine Shutdown
P228A.d: P228A is a protective shutdown code: the engine computer has stopped the engine because rail pressure could not be held even with fuel pressure regulator A at full authority. In GM's 2018 diesel tables regulator 1 (A) is the fuel metering unit on the high-pressure pump; the fault is logged when actual pressure lags the setpoint by more than 40 MPa while the commanded pump flow is already at its maximum, in 640 of 800 samples taken every 12.5 ms (about 8 s), as a Type A code. GM bulletin 18-NA-103 lists P228A and P228B next to P0087 when gelled winter diesel starves the in-tank pump. P228B is the same reaction for regulator B, P228C the milder control-limit warning. Expect a stall or no restart until supply is restored.
c: Fuel supply starved (gelled or waxed diesel, clogged filter, failing in-tank pump)
Fuel metering unit on the high-pressure pump sticking or worn
High-pressure pump no longer reaching the required delivery
Leak in the high-pressure circuit or injector return
s: Engine stalls while driving or shuts off shortly after starting
Long cranking or no restart
Check engine light on, often with P0087
Whining in-tank fuel pump in cold weather

P228B.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator B - Forced Engine Shutdown
P228B.d: P228B mirrors P228A but concerns fuel pressure regulator B, which in GM's 2018 diesel calibration is the rail pressure regulator valve that spills surplus fuel from the rail. The ECM shuts the engine down when rail pressure stays more than 40 MPa below target although it already commands that valve fully closed, judged over 640 of 800 samples at 12.5 ms and stored as Type A. A fully closed spill valve should trap everything the pump delivers, so a remaining deficit points to a valve leaking internally, a weak pump, a starved supply (GM bulletin 18-NA-103: gelled diesel, together with P228A and P0087) or excessive injector leakage. P229A is the non-shutdown deviation check of the same regulator.
c: Rail pressure regulator valve not sealing when closed
Fuel starvation from gelled diesel or a blocked filter
s: Engine stops on its own and may not restart
Check engine light with low rail pressure codes
Loss of power just before the shutdown

P228C.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator A Exceeded Control Limits - Pressure Too Low
P228C.d: P228C means rail pressure has stayed below target long enough that regulator A, the path that sets pump delivery, is judged to have used up its correction. GM uses it widely on gasoline direct injection: in table 25OBDG03A the pump fails to keep up for 10 s within a 12.5 s window, logged as Type A; on its 2018 diesels the margin is 13 MPa with the metering unit in closed loop (Type B), and table 24OBDG07 uses a 3 MPa gap held for 5 s. GM bulletins tie it to pump plungers sticking after heavy E85 use on 2.4, 3.0 and 3.6 L engines (18-NA-072, PIP5385) and to a wrong connector letting water into the bank 2 injector harness of the Corvette LT6 (24-NA-106). Reduced power is common; P228D is the overpressure case.
c: High-pressure pump or its control valve sticking or worn (e.g. after heavy E85 use)
Low-pressure supply too weak or contaminated fuel
Water or corrosion in the injector or pump wiring
Rail pressure sensor reading too low
s: Reduced engine power message
Hesitation under load
Check engine light, sometimes clearing after a key cycle

P228D.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator A Exceeded Control Limits - Pressure Too High
P228D.d: P228D is the opposite of P228C: measured rail pressure stays above the setpoint for too long although regulator A should be cutting delivery. GM's gasoline table 25OBDG03A flags it when the high-pressure pump supplies more than requested for 10 of 12.5 s, as Type A; its 2018 diesel table uses minus 13 MPa with the metering unit in closed loop (Type B), and table 24OBDG07 minus 3 MPa for 7 s. Causes range from a pump control valve that will not shut off, via a pressure sensor reading wrong, to calibration: GM bulletin 17-NA-069 cures P228D on 5.3 L and 6.2 L V8s by reprogramming, and PACCAR bulletin E114 links it, with P0094, to defective unit pumps on MX-13 truck engines. Expect harsh running or derated power.
c: Pump control or metering valve not reducing delivery
Engine control software needing an update
Rail pressure sensor reading too high
Defective unit or high-pressure pump (truck engines)
s: Check engine light
Louder injection noise or rough idle
Reduced power in some cases

P228E.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator A Exceeded Learning Limits - Too Low
P228E.d: P228E reports that the self-learned correction of fuel pressure regulator A has reached its lower bound. Ford, which still calls the part regulator 1, explains the logic in its 2023 diesel summary for the 3.0 L and 6.7 L Power Stroke: whenever requested rail pressure is at least 600 bar, the PCM keeps adapting the pressure controller, and if the adaptation factor drifts beyond a limit equivalent to roughly a 20 % error in rail pressure sensor slope, it stores P228E or P228F after about 10 s. Ford's 2014 PCM code table marks both as MIL codes. A learned value at the floor suggests a pressure sensor whose characteristic has shifted or a pump and regulator no longer matching their model. P228F is the upper bound, P229C the same test for regulator B.
c: Pressure regulator or metering valve worn, characteristic changed
High-pressure pump delivery deviating from its model
s: Check engine light without noticeable drivability change
Occasional rough running or slower pressure response

P228F.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator A Exceeded Learning Limits - Too High
P228F.d: P228F is the upper counterpart of P228E: the learned correction for fuel pressure regulator A has run into its maximum. Ford's 2023 diesel summary applies one test to both codes on the 3.0 L and 6.7 L engines, with a limit near a 20 % rail pressure sensor slope error and about 10 s of monitoring at 600 bar or more. In heavy trucks, Volvo and Mack solutions K01029637 and K40914241 group P228F with P0087 and P016F for 11 L and 13 L common-rail engines; one cause they name is a damaged sealing lip on the second-stage filter that lets dirt reach the high-pressure side. Jaguar Land Rover message SSM 74588 lists P228F on the supercharged AJ126 petrol V6 together with high-pressure pump noise. Expect the MIL, possibly with rough running.
c: Dirt in the high-pressure system, e.g. via a leaking fuel filter seal
s: Check engine light
Noise from the high-pressure pump
Uneven running in some cases

P2290.d: P2290 belongs to the injector control pressure (ICP) family of hydraulically actuated unit injector (HEUI) diesels such as the Navistar-built Ford 6.0 L Power Stroke, where pressurised engine oil fires the injectors. Ford's 2003 and 2004 summaries run the check every 8 ms with the engine running and set it once actual ICP stays more than 3.0 MPa below the PCM's command for longer than 7 s; Ford's 2014 PCM code table marks it as a MIL code. Typical culprits are an injection pressure regulator that no longer seals, leaking high-pressure oil fittings or O-rings, a worn high-pressure oil pump, or low or aerated oil. Expect hard starting, low power and rough running. P2291 is the cranking variant, P2288 the overpressure case.
c: Injection pressure regulator (IPR) contaminated or not sealing
Leaking high-pressure oil rail fittings, stand pipes or O-rings
Low, wrong or aerated engine oil
s: Hard starting, especially when hot
Lack of power and rough running
Check engine light

P2291.t: Injector Control Pressure Too Low - Engine Cranking
P2291.d: P2291 judges pressure build-up while the starter is turning. On HEUI diesels the injectors only fire once injector control pressure has reached a minimum, so any leak in the pressurised oil circuit shows up as a long crank or a no-start; Wikipedia's Power Stroke article names a contaminated injection pressure regulator and failed high-pressure oil seals as typical no-start causes on the 6.0 L. Ford also reuses the code on its current common-rail diesels: the 2023 summary for the 3.0 L and 6.7 L sets P2291 when rail pressure stays under 14,000 kPa for 20 s of cranking. Ford's 2014 PCM code table lists the code as well. Unlike P2290, which watches the running engine, P2291 covers only the start phase.
c: Leak in the high-pressure oil (HEUI) or fuel (common rail) circuit
Injection pressure regulator or rail pressure valve not sealing
High-pressure pump delivering too little at cranking speed
Low cranking speed from a weak battery or starter
s: Engine cranks long or does not start
Starts only after repeated attempts
Check engine light after the start attempt

P2292.d: P2292 describes an injector control pressure that jumps around instead of sitting steadily below or above target. No manufacturer documents its detection logic publicly: Ford's 2014 PCM code table lists the code without a MIL marking, and the 6.0 L Power Stroke summaries only describe the steady checks P2284, P2288 and P2290. On a HEUI engine an unsettled pressure can come from air in the oil, an injection pressure regulator that sticks and releases, a failing high-pressure oil pump or a loose sensor connection. CARB requires diesel fuel pressure control, explicitly including hydraulic fluid, to be monitored. Drivers notice surging, stumbling or intermittent power loss. A pure dropout of the sensor signal fits P2287 better.
c: Air in the engine oil (foaming, wrong oil, overfill)
ICP sensor or its connector making intermittent contact
High-pressure oil pump starting to fail
s: Surging or bucking under steady throttle
Intermittent power loss
Rough idle

P2293.d: P2293 checks whether fuel pressure regulator B really controls rail pressure. In GM's 2018 diesel table regulator B is the rail pressure regulator valve; the code sets when, with that valve in charge, rail pressure rises above a calibrated ceiling of 67 to 217 MPa in 160 of 229 samples at 6.25 ms, Type A. VW's 2014 quick reference for the Passat, which still uses the older name regulator 2, flags a gap between commanded and measured pressure beyond plus or minus 1.5 MPa. GM preliminary information PIP5988 for the 2024 3.0 L Duramax (LZ0) advises replacing the high-pressure rail that carries the valve, not the pump, when P2293 appears alone or with P0089. P2294 to P2296 cover the electrical side of the same valve.
c: Rail pressure regulator valve sticking or worn (often replaced with the rail)
s: Check engine light
Reduced power or stalling in severe cases
Hard starting

P2294.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator B Control Circuit/Open
P2294.d: P2294 is the open-circuit check of the drive line to fuel pressure regulator B. GM's 2018 diesel ECM tests the low-side driver of the rail pressure regulator valve while the output is switched off: a voltage indicating more than 200 kΩ between signal and ground counts as open, and 44 failures in 88 samples at 6.25 ms set the code as Type B. VW's 2014 Passat quick reference uses a signal voltage between 1.40 and 3.20 V or an implausible signal pattern. Broken wires, a pushed-back connector pin or an interrupted valve coil are the usual findings. Without control of the valve the ECM cannot release rail pressure as intended and may limit power. P2295 and P2296 split shorts to ground and to supply.
c: Broken wire in the regulator harness
Loose, corroded or pushed-back connector pin
Open coil in the pressure regulator valve
Faulty output driver in the engine control module
s: Check engine light
Reduced power or emergency mode
Unstable idle or hard starting

P2295.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator B Control Circuit Low
P2295.d: P2295 stands for the control line of fuel pressure regulator B touching ground. GM's 2018 diesel ECM detects it with its low-side driver switched off: if the measured voltage corresponds to 0.5 Ω or less towards ground, the sample counts as failed, and 44 of 88 samples at 6.25 ms confirm the fault as Type B. VW's 2014 Passat quick reference describes the same fault as a ground short, with a signal voltage below 1.40 V. Chafed insulation near the rail or pump, water in the connector and a shorted valve coil are typical findings. Because a grounded low-side line can keep the valve energised regardless of command, rail pressure may drift from target and the ECM may reduce power. P2296 is the high counterpart.
c: Control wire chafed through to ground
Water or corrosion in the regulator connector
Shorted coil in the pressure regulator valve
s: Check engine light
Rail pressure too high or unstable, reduced power
Rough running

P2296.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator B Control Circuit High
P2296.d: P2296 is set when the control line of fuel pressure regulator B has contact with supply voltage. GM's 2018 diesel ECM checks this with its low-side driver switched on: if the line still shows a voltage equivalent to 0.5 Ω or less towards power, the sample fails, again with 44 of 88 samples and Type B. VW's 2014 Passat quick reference uses a signal voltage above 3.20 V and groups an open line with a battery-voltage short here. In that state the driver cannot pull the valve current through, so the valve stays unpowered and the ECM loses its means of holding the intended rail pressure; hard starting and reduced power follow. Look for the harness rubbing on a battery feed and for a damaged valve connector.
c: Control wire shorted to a voltage supply
Faulty output driver in the engine control module
s: Check engine light
Hard starting or stalling
Reduced power

P2297.t: O2 Sensor Out of Range During Deceleration (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2297.d: P2297 concerns the upstream oxygen sensor of bank 1 and the moment when fuel is cut on deceleration and the sensor should read almost pure air. Diesel calibrations compare the reading in overrun with a modelled value: GM's 6.6L LML faults a gap between measured and calculated value above 0.06 to 0.07, the 3.0L LZ0 a deviation beyond 5 percent (Type B). On the 2023 Jeep Gladiator 3.0L diesel, Stellantis TSB 25-002-24 checks the O2 adaptation after a coast-down and replaces the sensor above 0.0282. Bosch-based petrol engines read the code the other way: with all injectors firing, a signal looking like fuel cut-off sets it (Saab 9-5 2011 LDK: 4 s, Type B; GM 2005 V6 LP1/LY7: over 3.7 V for 10 s). GM bulletin 24-NA-094 lists it for the LZ0; P2298 is bank 2.
c: Upstream wide-band sensor aged or drifted (wrong reading in air)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor drawing in outside air
Air-mass or fuel model error (MAF, injector leakage, EGR) skewing the expected value
Engine software needing an update (GM 3.0L LZ0 2024, bulletin 24-NA-094)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Usually no noticeable change in driving behaviour
Possibly stored with P0133 or fuel-quantity codes

P2298.t: O2 Sensor Out of Range During Deceleration (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P2298.d: P2298 is the bank 2 version of P2297 and exists only on engines with two cylinder banks, each with its own upstream oxygen sensor. Three GM tables show the two readings of the code. The 2005 3.5L V6 (L66) tests during fuel cut-off with coolant above 69 °C and below 2,200 rpm, faulting a wide-band output above 4.5 V or below 2.9 V, over two drive cycles. The Bosch-managed 2005 V6 (LP1/LY7) works the other way round and flags a signal above 3.7 V for 10 s while every injector is firing and the target is richer than lambda 1.6. GM's 2024 tables (24OBDG07) set it for a lambda equivalent above 12 from the corrected pump current with the ceramic hotter than 655 °C, 10 s, two trips. No bulletin names P2298. Bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1.
c: Bank 2 upstream wide-band sensor aged or contaminated
Exhaust leak on bank 2 ahead of the sensor
Damaged sensor lead or connector on bank 2
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Usually no noticeable change in driving behaviour
Bank 2 fuel trim values may look unusual

P2299.t: Brake Pedal Position/Accelerator Pedal Position Incompatible
P2299.d: P2299 means the vehicle has seen the brake and the accelerator pressed together in a way it treats as implausible; engine torque is usually cut as a brake-override measure. GM documents the check in the brake control module of 2020 models with a pedal travel sensor: the code sets when the travel signal is not zero while the accelerator is applied above 4.47 mph (7.2 km/h) for 0.12 s, Type A. An FCA parts tip states it is mostly caused by drivers resting their left foot on the brake and warns against replacing the pedal; many FCA flash bulletins, e.g. 18-007-14 for the Fiat 500, and Nissan bulletin NTB17-063 (Titan XD, Cummins 5.0 L) clear it by reprogramming. A misadjusted brake light switch can also trigger it.
c: Driver resting a foot on the brake while accelerating
Control module software needing an update
Brake light switch or pedal travel sensor misadjusted or sticking
Floor mat or object keeping a pedal partly pressed
s: Engine power drops while braking and accelerating together
Check engine light
Car does not respond to the accelerator for a moment

P229A.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator B Exceeded Control Limits - Pressure Too Low
P229A.d: P229A is the low-pressure control-limit check for fuel pressure regulator B. In GM's 2018 diesel table regulator B is the rail pressure regulator valve; while it governs the rail in closed loop, the ECM compares setpoint and measured pressure and flags a deficit beyond about 13 MPa, using the same 640-of-800-sample window and Type B rating as the metering unit check P228C. The test pauses at low fuel level, ambient pressure under 60 kPa or ambient temperature below −7 °C. A valve that no longer seals, internal injector leakage or a pump short of delivery create the deficit. GM is the only maker found documenting P229A publicly. P229B is the overpressure case, P228B the stage that forces a shutdown.
c: Rail pressure regulator valve leaking internally
Restricted low-pressure supply or clogged filter
s: Check engine light
Lack of power under load
Longer cranking times

P229B.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator B Exceeded Control Limits - Pressure Too High
P229B.d: P229B flags rail pressure that stays above target while fuel pressure regulator B should be holding it. GM's 2018 diesel table, where regulator B is the rail pressure regulator valve, runs this check with the valve in closed-loop control and under the same enable conditions as P229A (fuel level, ambient pressure and temperature), mirroring the overpressure test P228D of the metering unit, and rates it Type B. A valve that sticks closed or cannot open far enough, a drive signal that keeps it energised, or a rail pressure sensor reading high are the classic causes. If pressure keeps climbing to the absolute ceiling, P2293 follows. P229A is the deficit case, P228D the same fault seen through regulator A.
c: Rail pressure regulator valve sticking closed
Rail pressure sensor reading too high
Valve drive signal stuck on (wiring or module)
s: Check engine light
Harder combustion noise
Reduced power in some cases

P229C.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator B Exceeded Learning Limits - Too Low
P229C.d: P229C means the learned correction for fuel pressure regulator B has reached its lower bound. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The matching check for regulator A is described by Ford for its 2023 diesels: the controller adapts at steady rail pressure of 600 bar or more and stores P228E or P228F when the adaptation would exceed roughly a 20 % sensor-slope error. On systems with two regulators, such as GM diesels with a pump metering unit (A) and a rail pressure valve (B), the B value describes the learned behaviour of that spill valve. CARB requires a monitor to report a pressure control that has used up its adjustment authority. Expect a lit MIL with little drivability effect; P229D is the upper bound.
c: Rail pressure regulator valve characteristic drifted
Adaptation values not reset after a component replacement
s: Check engine light
Usually no noticeable change in driving

P229D.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator B Exceeded Learning Limits - Too High
P229D.d: P229D reports that the learned correction for fuel pressure regulator B has climbed to its upper bound, the opposite of P229C. No manufacturer documents the code publicly, so its logic can only be inferred from the regulator A equivalent P228F: Ford's 2023 diesel summary sets that code after about 10 s when the controller adaptation passes a limit near a 20 % sensor-slope error, and Volvo and Mack link P228F on their truck engines to dirt that reached the high-pressure side. For regulator B, usually the rail pressure valve, a correction pinned at the top points to a valve that needs ever more drive to hold pressure, or a sensor out of calibration. CARB requires such exhausted control authority to be flagged.
c: Rail pressure regulator valve worn or contaminated
Contaminated fuel reaching the high-pressure side
s: Check engine light
Occasional unstable rail pressure or rough idle

P229E.d: P229E is the basic electrical fault of the second NOx sensor on bank 1, the one behind the SCR catalyst that shows how much NOx survives conversion. Its attached control unit checks the probe lines and passes the result to the engine computer over CAN. GM's 6.6L Duramax (LML) sets the code as Type A when an open or shorted status keeps arriving longer than 10 s, or 0.5 s in a later calibration. Ford's 3.0L and 6.7L diesels use it for shorts and opens on the Vs, COM, Ip1 and Ip2 lines and for a failed internal self-test of the sensor processor; VW's 2014 Touareg TDI for an error message or a validity ratio above 0.5. Volvo and Mack replace the outlet sensor, and Nissan bulletin NTB16-048 does the same on the 2016 Titan XD, adding an ECM update. P2200 is the front sensor.
c: Internal failure of the outlet NOx probe or its control unit
Damaged lead between probe and sensor control unit (heat, chafing)
Water or corrosion in the sensor connector
Engine control software needing an update (Nissan Titan XD 2016, NTB16-048)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
No valid downstream NOx value in live data
SCR warning; catalyst efficiency check cannot complete

P229F.d: P229F says the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 is electrically sound but its reading fails a plausibility test. Methods vary. GM's 6.6L LML waits for a burst of engine-out NOx and faults the sensor if its own value moves by less than 3 ppm (Type B); the 3.0L LZ0 watches the stability of the internal pump currents, failing above 0.5 percent unstable time. Ford checks offsets of roughly 30 ppm low or 50 ppm high and a missing rise on tip-in; VW's 2014 Touareg TDI checks offset, self-diagnosis results and oxygen plausibility. Volvo and Mack explain that P229F-64 can set when a fresh SCR leaves almost no NOx, so a single event is no proof of a bad sensor. Hino wants DEF quality and dosing checked first, and Ford warns that EGR cleaning fluids poison NOx sensors.
c: Outlet NOx element drifted, slow or poisoned (e.g. sodium from cleaning fluids)
Poor DEF quality or faulty dosing that distorts downstream NOx
Harness or connector fault at the outlet sensor (Volvo/Mack P229F-64)
Engine or dosing software needing an update (several FCA, Hino, Mazda notices)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Often stored together with SCR efficiency code P20EE
Downstream NOx value implausible compared with the upstream sensor

P22A0.d: P22A0 reports that the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 sends a raw value below the smallest figure a healthy sensor can produce. Because the sensor talks over CAN, the test looks at the transmitted number rather than a wire voltage. GM uses minus 90 ppm on the 6.6L LML, on its 2017 small diesels (table 17OBDG04) and on the 3.0L LZ0, in each case Type B after two trips with dew point reached and supply in range; the LZ0 needs 100 failed samples in 200. VW's 2014 Touareg TDI faults below minus 105 ppm or a lambda signal under minus 0.2. GM bulletin 24-NA-094 puts P22A0 on the list cured by an LZ0 software update on 2024 Silverado and Sierra 1500. A strongly negative value usually means element drift or an internal fault. P22A1 is the upper limit, P2202 the front sensor.
c: Outlet NOx element drifted low or internally faulty
Damaged lead between probe and sensor module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Live data shows a negative downstream NOx value
SCR efficiency monitor does not complete

P22A1.d: P22A1 flags a raw value from the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 that is higher than anything plausibly left behind the SCR catalyst. GM's 6.6L LML uses 1,500 ppm, or 2,500 ppm in table 14OBDG10; the 3.0L LZ0 and the 2017 small diesels also use 2,500 ppm, Type B after two trips. VW's 2014 Touareg TDI uses 1,655 ppm or a lambda signal above 1.54. Volvo and Mack count P22A1 among codes that point to a damaged outlet sensor and replace that sensor alone. For Ram ProMaster vans, a 2025 Stellantis case (S2525000001) reports P22A1 together with P20EE, asks for standard diagnosis including the DEF condition and states that engineering is still looking for the root cause. GM includes the code in LZ0 software bulletin 24-NA-094. P22A0 is the lower limit, P2203 the front sensor.
c: Outlet NOx sensor reading high due to internal damage
DEF quality or dosing problem raising real tailpipe NOx
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Implausibly high downstream NOx value in live data
SCR efficiency code P20EE stored alongside

P22A2.d: P22A2 describes a rear NOx sensor on bank 1 whose measuring circuit reports faults that come and go rather than staying present. Smart NOx sensors pass the state of that circuit (open wire, short or no error) to the engine computer over CAN, so brief, repeated fault reports fit this code. No manufacturer publicly documents a threshold for P22A2. The only trace is a Ford notice for 2015 to 2016 6.7L Super Duty trucks (SSM 45920, NHTSA index only) explaining that the code may stay stored after the actual fault has been repaired; CARB requires NOx sensors to be monitored continuously for circuit faults. Look for loose terminals, heat-damaged cable along the exhaust and water in the connector. P229E is the steady fault, P2204 the same pattern at the front sensor.
c: Loose or corroded terminals at the outlet NOx sensor connector
Harness along the exhaust damaged by heat or vibration
Sporadic internal fault in the sensor module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp that may go out and return
Downstream NOx value dropping out briefly
Code remains stored after the root fault is fixed

P22A3.t: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22A3.d: The ceramic element of a NOx sensor measures only after its built-in heater has brought it to several hundred degrees. P22A3 reports a break on the heater control side of the rear sensor on bank 1, behind the SCR catalyst. GM's 6.6L LML sets it when the sensor reports an open heater over CAN longer than 10 s, Type A. On the 3.0L LZ0 the heater control pin is tested for a missing load (80 failures in 160 samples), on the 2017 small diesels the H+ supply pin of the Gen 3.0 sensor; both Type A, so the MIL comes on after one trip. Volvo and Mack read P22A3-13 as a probable outlet sensor failure, and GM bulletin 24-NA-094 lists the code for an LZ0 software update. P22A4 and P22A5 are shorts, P22A6 the heater sense line, P2205 the front sensor.
c: Heater element in the outlet NOx probe burnt through
Broken conductor between probe and sensor module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after one trip
Outlet NOx sensor never reports ready
SCR warning on the display

P22A4.t: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22A4.d: P22A4 means the heater control line of the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 has a short to ground, so the sensor module can no longer drive the heater as commanded. GM documents it on the 3.0L LZ0 as a ground short on the heater control pin, judged once dew point is reached and sensor supply exceeds 9.9 V, 80 failures in 160 samples, Type B after two trips. Its 2017 small diesels watch the H+ supply pin of the Gen 3.0 sensor instead, 20 failures in 40 samples. Volvo and Mack count P22A4 among codes that indicate a damaged outlet sensor, and GM bulletin 24-NA-094 adds it to an LZ0 software update for 2024 Silverado and Sierra 1500. Expect the MIL after two trips and no downstream NOx data. P22A3 is the open circuit, P22A5 a short to voltage, P2206 the front sensor.
c: Heater element or probe lead shorted to ground inside the sensor
Probe lead insulation chafed against the exhaust or body
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Outlet NOx sensor stays not ready
SCR warning on the display

P22A5.t: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22A5.d: P22A5 is the opposite of P22A4: the heater control line of the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 has a short to supply voltage. The sensor module then cannot switch or regulate the heater, and the element risks running too hot or the module shuts the heater off to protect it. GM describes the check on the 3.0L LZ0 as a battery short at the heater control pin, 80 failures in 160 samples with dew point reached and supply above 9.9 V, Type B after two trips; the 2017 small diesels test the H+ supply pin of the Gen 3.0 sensor with 20 failures in 40 samples. GM bulletin 24-NA-094 lists P22A5 among codes an LZ0 software update clears on 2024 pickups. No public bulletin names a hardware fix. P22A3 is the open circuit, P22A4 the ground short, P2207 the front sensor.
c: Heater circuit inside the sensor shorted to supply voltage
Probe lead or connector touching a powered conductor
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Heater switched off, outlet NOx sensor not ready
SCR warning on the display

P22A6.t: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22A6.d: Besides the heater supply, a NOx sensor has a sense line through which its module measures the resistance of the heated element and so infers its temperature. P22A6 reports an electrical fault on that feedback line of the rear sensor on bank 1. GM's 3.0L LZ0 sets it for an open circuit at the HTemp pin, 80 failures in 160 samples, Type A after one trip; GM notes that the Continental Gen 3.5 sensor debounces electrical faults internally for 1.5 s. The 2017 small diesels use the same open-circuit check with 20 failures in 40 samples, also Type A. Volvo and Mack list P22A6 among codes that call for a new outlet sensor; GM bulletin 24-NA-094 names it Heater Feedback Circuit and covers it with an LZ0 software update. P22A8/P22A9 are shorts, P22A7 plausibility, P2208 the front sensor.
c: Open heater sense conductor inside the outlet NOx probe or its lead
Water or corrosion in the probe connector
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after one trip
