Outlet NOx sensor not ready, no downstream value
SCR warning on the display

P22A7.t: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22A7.d: P22A7 means the heater feedback of the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 shows a heater that does not reach or hold its target, although no open or short is found. GM's 3.0L LZ0 and 2017 small diesels compare the measured heater resistance with its target once supply has been in range for 45 s and dew point passed 180 s ago (Type B); the 6.6L LML fails the sensor if its heater never reports set-point temperature. VW's 2014 Touareg TDI allows 180 s after dew point; Ford uses the code as a signal readiness check. Ford traced it on 2017 to 2020 6.7L Super Duty trucks to water in the NOx connectors (TSB 20-2067, new harness 14406) and on 2023 models to that harness chafing on the EGR cooler, with fuse F18 blown (SSM 51750/51791). Nissan's NTB16-048 replaces the outlet sensor.
c: Aged heater or element in the outlet NOx probe
Water in the NOx sensor connectors (Ford 6.7L 2017-2020, TSB 20-2067)
Harness chafed on the EGR cooler with blown supply fuse (Ford 6.7L 2023)
Weak supply to the sensor module limiting heater power
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Outlet NOx sensor becomes ready late or not at all
Often stored with U029E or other NOx sensor codes

P22A8.t: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22A8.d: P22A8 means the heater sense line of the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 is shorted to ground; the sensor module uses that line to read the element temperature via its resistance. With that line pulled to ground, the module sees a temperature value it cannot trust and cannot regulate the heater properly. GM documents the test on the 3.0L LZ0: ground short at the HTemp pin, judged with dew point reached and sensor supply above 9.9 V, 80 failures in 160 samples, Type B after two trips; the Continental Gen 3.5 sensor debounces such faults internally for 1.5 s. GM's 2017 small diesels use the same check with 20 failures in 40 samples. No public bulletin names this code. P22A6 is the open circuit, P22A9 the short to voltage, P2210 the front sensor.
c: Heater sense conductor shorted to ground inside the probe
Probe lead insulation damaged against exhaust or body
Water bridging pins in the probe connector
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Outlet NOx sensor not ready
SCR efficiency check does not run

P22A9.t: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22A9.d: P22A9 is the high-side twin of P22A8: the heater sense line of the rear NOx sensor on bank 1 has a short to supply voltage. The module then reads an element resistance that is far off and loses its temperature feedback, so it cannot hold the probe at working temperature. GM's 3.0L LZ0 looks for a battery short at the HTemp pin once dew point is reached and supply exceeds 9.9 V, 80 failures in 160 samples, Type B after two trips; the 2017 small diesels need 20 failures in 40 samples. In both cases the Continental sensor itself confirms an electrical fault before reporting it. No manufacturer bulletin mentions P22A9. A short often sits where the probe lead runs close to other powered wiring or where a connector has taken in water. P22A6 is the open circuit, P22A8 the ground short, P2211 the front sensor.
c: Heater sense conductor shorted to supply inside the probe
Probe lead touching another powered conductor
Water bridging pins in the probe connector
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Outlet NOx sensor not ready
SCR warning on the display

P22AA.t: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Intermittent (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22AA.d: P22AA covers a heater sense line on the rear NOx sensor of bank 1 that fails only now and then. The module uses this line to read the element temperature and keep the heater on target; if the reading drops out or jumps for short moments, the temperature control briefly loses its reference and the sensor may fall out of its ready state. No manufacturer publicly documents a threshold or a bulletin for P22AA, and GM, Ford and VW do not list it in their published tables. CARB asks for continuous monitoring of NOx sensor heater circuits, and smart sensors report the heater circuit state (open, short, no error) over CAN. In practice, check terminal grip, cable routing near hot parts and water ingress. P22A6, P22A8 and P22A9 are the steady faults, P2212 the front sensor.
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the probe connector
Lead near the exhaust cracked by heat or vibration
Intermittent internal contact fault in the probe
s: Malfunction indicator lamp that may come and go
Outlet NOx sensor intermittently not ready

P22AB.t: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22AB.d: P22AB reports a break in the positive current control line of a wide-band probe mounted behind the catalyst or, on diesels, further down the aftertreatment on bank 1. On a Bosch-style five-wire probe this is the pump-current lead (IP/APE) through which the controller moves oxygen into or out of the pump cell. Chrysler lists the code for 2010-2012 Ram 2500/3500 pickups with the 6.7 Cummins in bulletins 25-004-12 and 25-002-14; the prescribed fix is new sensor connectors or an overlay harness before any sensor is replaced. GM names it in 21-NA-149 among faults from chafed harnesses on the 3.0 Duramax LM2. P22AC/P22AD cover low/high, P22B8 is bank 2, P2237 the upstream twin. The warning lamp comes on; the engine usually runs normally.
c: Corroded, loose or poorly crimped terminal in the sensor or sensor-module connector
Pump-current wire broken or chafed through along the exhaust
Internal open circuit in the downstream wide-band sensor
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen reading frozen or missing in live data
Related catalyst or aftertreatment monitors stay incomplete

P22AC.t: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22AC.d: P22AC means the pump-current (positive current) line of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe reads below its allowed window, usually because the wire touches ground or its insulation has worn through. GM includes the code in bulletin 21-NA-149 for 2019-2022 light-duty trucks and SUVs with the 3.0 Duramax LM2, where chafed engine wiring triggers a long list of faults; no public GM table gives a threshold. Not every maker uses this slot: Ford books a shorted lead on its upstream wide-band probes as P0131. Saab rates the upstream analog P2238 as a Type B fault. P22AB is the open-circuit case, P22AD the high one, P22B9 the bank 2 copy. Expect a lit warning lamp and stalled emission monitors rather than a change in driving.
c: Pump-current wire chafed against the body or exhaust and shorted to ground
Internal short in the downstream wide-band sensor
Water or contamination bridging the connector pins
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen value pinned at an extreme in live data
Possible failed emissions inspection because monitors are not ready

P22AD.t: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22AD.d: P22AD is the high-side fault on the positive current control line of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe: the pump-current wire is pulled above its expected level, for example by contact with the heater feed or another supply wire. On Saab's 2010 9-5 the pump-current pins measure roughly 2.8 V at the plug, which gives a feel for the normal bias. GM lists the code in bulletin 21-NA-149 for the 3.0 Duramax LM2, again tied to engine harness chafing, but publishes no limit. Ford sends shorts to power on its upstream wide-band probes to P0132 instead of a dedicated code. The upstream analog is P2239 (Type B at Saab); P22AB is the open circuit, P22AC the low reading, P22BA the bank 2 version. The lamp is lit; driving normally feels unchanged.
c: Pump-current wire shorted to the heater supply or another positive feed
Internal short between heater and pump cell in the sensor
Faulty sensor interface in the ECM or sensor module
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen reading implausibly high or fixed
Readiness monitors for catalyst or aftertreatment not completed

P22AE.t: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22AE.d: P22AE points to an open reference voltage line of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe, i.e. the lead of the Nernst (sensing) cell, called RE/UN by Bosch and VS by NTK. Through it the controller reads the cell voltage it regulates the pump current against, so a break leaves the oxygen value meaningless. Chrysler lists P22AE for 2010-2012 Ram 2500/3500 with the 6.7 Cummins; bulletin 25-003-13 found tin instead of gold terminals in five cavities of the 2011 sensor-module connector. For the upstream twin P2243, Ford, GM and Saab declare an open when the sensor voltage leaves 0.2-4.7 V and, at GM/Saab, the cell resistance exceeds 570 ohms. P22AF, P22B0 and P22B1 are performance/low/high, P22BB is bank 2. The lamp comes on.
c: Corroded or wrongly plated terminals in the sensor or sensor-module connector
Broken Nernst-cell wire in the harness
Cracked or aged sensing cell with very high internal resistance
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen or lambda value invalid in live data
Other downstream sensor codes may be stored at the same time

P22AF.t: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Performance (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22AF.d: P22AF is a plausibility fault on the Nernst-cell (reference voltage) side of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe: the wiring is intact, but the cell signal does not behave as the controller expects, for instance it cannot be held at its set point or drifts. Typical reasons are an aged cell whose resistance has risen above the roughly 300 ohms Bosch quotes for the LSU 4.9, soot or oil deposits, or a heater that keeps the element too cool. No maker documents this code publicly. CARB requires the OBD system to catch deterioration of voltage, impedance, current or offset of air-fuel sensors behind the aftertreatment before emissions rise too far. Siblings: P22AE open, P22B0/P22B1 low/high, P22BC bank 2, P2244 upstream.
c: Aged downstream wide-band sensor with raised cell resistance
Soot, oil or coolant deposits on the sensing element
Weak heater or heater control that leaves the element too cold
High-resistance contact in the Nernst-cell circuit
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen reading sluggish or offset compared with the upstream sensor
Catalyst or aftertreatment monitor may report errors as a follow-up

P22B0.t: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22B0.d: P22B0 says the reference voltage (Nernst-cell) line of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe sits below its permitted range. On a Bosch LSU the Nernst cell is a high-impedance source that tolerates at most about 250 microamps, so a chafed wire touching ground drags it down at once. No maker documents this exact code publicly. Ford's upstream logic treats a cell voltage under 0.2 V as part of its open-circuit check and books shorted leads under P0131, which shows that makers split these faults differently. JLR lists the upstream analog P2245 in a bulletin on cracked sensors. P22AE is the open case, P22B1 the high one, P22AF the performance check, P22BD the bank 2 equivalent. The driver mainly sees the warning lamp.
c: Nernst-cell wire shorted to ground through damaged insulation
Internal short in the downstream wide-band sensor
Moisture in the connector creating a leakage path
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen value implausible or unavailable

P22B1.t: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22B1.d: P22B1 is set when the reference voltage (Nernst-cell) line of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe reads above its valid range. Because the cell delivers only a few hundred millivolts across about 300 ohms, any contact with the heater feed or another live wire overrides it. A cracked ceramic letting the heater circuit leak into the cell can do the same. No maker publishes this code with a threshold; for the upstream sensor, Ford and Saab already treat a voltage above 4.7 V as an open reference line, while Ford sends shorts to power to P0132. CARB demands detection of out-of-range values on air-fuel sensors behind the aftertreatment. P22AE covers the open, P22B0 the low reading, P22BE bank 2 and P2246 the upstream twin.
c: Nernst-cell wire shorted to the heater supply or another live wire
Cracked sensor ceramic leaking heater voltage into the cell
Faulty sensor interface in the ECM or sensor module
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen reading stuck at a limit

P22B2.t: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22B2.d: P22B2 indicates an open negative current control line on the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe. This is the shared return of pump and sensing cell, the virtual ground (VM/IPN on Bosch, COM on NTK), which the controller holds at a mid-level bias of around 2.5 V. Chrysler lists the code for 2010-2012 Ram 2500/3500 with the 6.7 Cummins and repairs connectors and wiring first; GM names it in 21-NA-149 for the 3.0 Duramax LM2. For the upstream twin P2251, Ford sees an open return as a sensor voltage stuck near 1.5 V for 10 s, GM and Saab as 1.47-1.53 V with cell resistance above 570 ohms. P22B3/P22B4 cover low/high, P22BF bank 2. The warning lamp lights; drivability normally stays the same.
c: Loose, corroded or pushed-back terminal on the return wire
Return (virtual ground) wire broken in the harness
Internal open circuit in the downstream wide-band sensor
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen reading frozen near a fixed value
Aftertreatment readiness not set

P22B3.t: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22B3.d: P22B3 reports the negative current control line, i.e. the virtual ground of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe, as too low. Normally the controller lifts this common return to a bias near 2.5 V (Saab measures that at the plug of its 2010 9-5) so that pump current can flow in both directions; a short to chassis ground collapses the bias and with it the measuring range. No maker documents this exact code publicly. Mitsubishi lists the upstream analog P2252 as a two-trip code for the 2022 Outlander, and Ford handles upstream shorts under P0131 instead. P22B2 is the open-circuit code, P22B4 the high one, P22C0 the bank 2 version. Apart from the warning lamp, the driver rarely notices anything.
c: Return wire shorted to chassis ground through chafed insulation
Internal short inside the wide-band sensor
Faulty bias supply in the ECM or sensor module
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen value implausible or pinned

P22B4.t: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22B4.d: P22B4 is stored when the negative current control line (virtual ground) of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe climbs above its intended bias. Because this return sits at a mid-level voltage rather than at chassis ground, a short to the heater feed or battery voltage is the classic trigger, sometimes via moisture or a heat-damaged connector. No maker documents this exact code publicly; Mitsubishi lists the upstream analog P2253 as a two-trip code for the 2022 Outlander, while Ford treats upstream shorts to power as P0132. CARB asks for detection of out-of-range values on such sensors. P22B2 is the open, P22B3 the low variant, P22C1 the bank 2 code. The lamp is on and the related emission monitors will not complete.
c: Return wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Heat-damaged or wet connector bridging pins
Internal heater-to-cell leakage in the sensor
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen reading erratic or at a limit

P22B5.t: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22B5.d: P22B5 flags an open trim line on the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe. Bosch LSU probes carry a trimming resistor in the connector module, wired to pin 5 (RT/IA), that sets each sensor's individual characteristic; the controller reads it to scale the measured pump current. Lose that line and the oxygen value can still move, but with the wrong gain. Chrysler's wording speaks of the pump cell current trim of sensor 1/2 and lists the code for 2010-2012 Ram 2500/3500 with the 6.7 Cummins; after the wiring repair its road test compares both sensors during 10-second fuel cut-offs and allows no more than 4 % difference. Saab's upstream analog P2626 is checked in overrun below 750 °C and sets above 4.81 V. P22B6/P22B7 are low/high, P22C2 bank 2.
c: Corroded or loose trim-line terminal in the sensor connector
Trim wire broken between sensor connector and ECM or sensor module
Open trimming resistor in the sensor's connector module
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen reading disagrees with the upstream sensor during fuel cut-off
Follow-up aftertreatment or catalyst faults possible

P22B6.t: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22B6.d: By its name P22B6 is the low fault on the trim line of the bank 1 downstream wide-band probe, i.e. the lead to the calibration resistor in a Bosch-style sensor connector. GM's diesel tables use the slot differently: they set it when the oxygen value reported by the second NOx sensor falls below its physical minimum, less than -4 % in 200 of 250 samples in the 2016 table, with the engine in combustion mode and no NOx sensor fault pending. It is a Type B code with two trips. GM also lists P22B6 in PIP5468 for 2017-2018 Silverado/Sierra HD with the 6.6 L5P, where leaking charge-air ducting can set it, and in 21-NA-149 for the 3.0 LM2. P22B5 is the open, P22B7 the high counterpart, P22C3 bank 2. The lamp comes on.
c: Faulty downstream NOx/oxygen sensor delivering an impossible oxygen value
Trim or signal wire shorted to ground in the harness
s: Check engine light
Negative oxygen percentage shown for the downstream sensor in live data
Possible additional boost or air-flow codes when charge air leaks

P22B7.t: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P22B7.d: P22B7 is, going by its title, the high fault on the trim circuit belonging to bank 1's downstream wide-band probe. In GM's diesel tables (2016, 2018 and 2025 group 04) the code is a ceiling test on the oxygen value of the second NOx sensor: the 2016 table flags readings above 24 %, which is more oxygen than fresh air holds, in 100 of 200 samples. The test runs only while exhaust back-pressure stays below its limit, no exhaust brake is active and no NOx sensor pressure fault is pending; GM rates it Type B, two trips. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 lists it for the 3.0 Duramax LM2 alongside harness chafing. No public source gives a trim-resistor threshold. P22B5 is the open, P22B6 the low case, P22C4 bank 2. The lamp lights.
c: Faulty downstream NOx/oxygen sensor reporting excess oxygen
Chafed engine harness affecting the sensor lines (GM 3.0 LM2)
Trim or signal wire shorted to a voltage source
s: Check engine light
Downstream oxygen value above 21 % in live data

P22B8.t: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit/Open (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P22B8.d: P22B8 is the bank 2 version of an open positive current control line on a downstream wide-band probe: the pump-current wire (IP/APE on Bosch) of the sensor behind the catalyst or aftertreatment on the second cylinder bank has lost continuity. It only exists on engines with two exhaust banks and a wide-band probe after each catalyst, which is rare. No maker documents this code publicly. Its bank 1 twin P22AB appears in Chrysler bulletins for the 6.7 Cummins Ram; for the upstream P2240, Ford separates an open pump lead from an open return by pulsing a reference current and checking whether lambda moves by more than 0.05. P22B9/P22BA are low/high, P22BB the reference line. The warning lamp is the main sign.
c: Loose or corroded pump-current terminal in the sensor connector
Pump-current wire broken near the hot exhaust
Internal open circuit in the bank 2 downstream sensor
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream oxygen value missing or frozen

P22B9.t: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P22B9.d: P22B9 means the positive current control (pump-current) line of the bank 2 downstream wide-band probe reads below its allowed band, most often because the lead has worn through and touches ground. No maker documents this code publicly, so the logic can only be inferred from the bank 1 and upstream relatives: GM lists P22AC for the 3.0 Duramax LM2 without a threshold, Saab treats the upstream P2238 as a Type B fault, and Ford books upstream shorts as P0131. CARB requires out-of-range detection on air-fuel sensors behind the aftertreatment. The fault needs a V or boxer engine with a wide-band probe after each catalyst. P22B8 is the open, P22BA the high variant, P22AC the bank 1 code. A lit warning lamp is usually the only symptom.
c: Pump-current wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Internal short in the bank 2 downstream sensor
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream oxygen value at an extreme

P22BA.t: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P22BA.d: P22BA is set when the pump-current (positive current control) wire of the bank 2 downstream wide-band probe is held above its normal bias, typically through contact with the heater supply or a damaged connector letting battery voltage in. No maker documents this code publicly. Related evidence comes from bank 1 and the front sensors: GM names P22AD for the 3.0 Duramax LM2 in a harness-chafing bulletin, Saab measures about 2.8 V on the pump pins of a healthy upstream probe and rates P2239 as Type B, and Ford reports upstream shorts to power as P0132. The code only applies to dual-bank engines with a wide-band probe after each catalyst. P22B8 is the open, P22B9 the low code, P22AD bank 1. Expect the warning lamp.
c: Pump-current wire shorted to the heater feed or battery voltage
Faulty sensor interface in the ECM
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream oxygen value implausibly high

P22BB.t: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit/Open (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P22BB.d: P22BB reports an open reference voltage line on the bank 2 downstream wide-band probe, meaning the controller has lost the Nernst-cell signal (RE/UN on Bosch, VS on NTK) it needs to regulate pump current and compute oxygen content. No maker documents this code publicly. For the upstream bank 2 relative P2247, Ford flags an open reference lead once the sensor voltage leaves 0.2-4.7 V for 10 s, and VW's 2014 Touareg data book calls the same fault an open Nernst voltage below 0.25 V or above 4.80 V with cell resistance over 950 ohms. Its bank 1 twin P22AE is listed by Chrysler for the 6.7 Cummins Ram. Only engines with two exhaust banks and a wide-band probe after each catalyst can set it. P22BC-P22BE are the performance/low/high siblings. The lamp comes on.
c: Corroded or loose Nernst-cell terminal in the connector
Reference wire broken in the harness
Cracked sensing cell or internal open in the sensor
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream oxygen value invalid

P22BC.t: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Performance (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P22BC.d: P22BC concerns the plausibility of the Nernst-cell signal of the wide-band probe fitted after the bank 2 catalyst. The leads test fine, yet the cell voltage that the controller uses as its set point drifts, reacts slowly or cannot be held, so the computed oxygen value loses credibility. No maker documents this code publicly, and none publishes a limit for its upstream relative P2248 either. The usual reasons are physical: an aged cell whose resistance has climbed well above the nominal 300 ohms of a Bosch LSU 4.9, deposits from oil or coolant, or a weak heater. CARB requires a downstream sensor to remain good enough to judge the catalyst. Siblings: P22BB open, P22BD/P22BE low/high, P22AF bank 1. The lamp lights and catalyst results may be withheld.
c: Aged downstream wide-band sensor on bank 2 with raised Nernst-cell resistance
Oil, coolant or additive deposits on the sensing element
Heater output too low to keep the cell at working temperature
Contact resistance in the Nernst-cell terminal
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream oxygen reading lags behind or is offset from the other sensors
Catalyst monitor for bank 2 does not complete

P22BD.t: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P22BD.d: P22BD reports that the Nernst-cell (reference voltage) lead of the bank 2 post-catalyst wide-band probe sits below its valid window. Bosch allows the cell a load of only about 250 microamps, so a lead whose insulation touches ground, or moisture bridging the plug, pulls the signal down quickly. No maker documents this code publicly. Upstream practice shows how close low and open lie: VW's 2014 Touareg data book counts a Nernst voltage under 0.25 V with cell resistance above 950 ohms as an open circuit (P2247), and Ford sends shorts to ground on its front probes to P0151 for bank 2. JLR names the bank 1 front analog P2245 in a bulletin on probes cracked by water splash. P22BB is the open, P22BE the high case, P22B0 bank 1. Mostly only the lamp shows.
c: Nernst-cell lead chafed through and touching ground
Water or corrosion creating a leakage path in the connector
Sensing element cracked by water contact on the hot probe
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream oxygen value missing or at the lower end in live data

P22BE.t: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P22BE.d: P22BE is stored when the reference voltage lead of the bank 2 downstream wide-band probe carries more voltage than a working Nernst cell can produce. A healthy cell produces well under one volt from a source of roughly 300 ohms, so contact with the heater feed, a 5 V line or battery voltage swamps it, and a cracked ceramic can let heater potential leak into the cell. No maker documents this code publicly. On upstream probes the top of the scale is already an open-circuit criterion: Ford and Saab react above 4.7 V, VW's Touareg above 4.80 V, while Ford files shorts to battery under P0152 for bank 2. Under CARB rules a secondary sensor must also be checked for readings outside its range. P22BB is the open, P22BD the low reading, P22B1 bank 1. The lamp comes on.
c: Nernst-cell lead shorted to the heater supply or another live wire
Cracked ceramic letting heater voltage into the sensing cell
Faulty sensor interface in the engine control module
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream oxygen reading pinned at the upper limit
Heater codes for the same sensor may appear alongside

P22BF.t: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit/Open (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P22BF.d: P22BF means the negative current control lead of the bank 2 post-catalyst wide-band probe has lost continuity. That lead is the common return of pump and Nernst cell (VM/IPN on Bosch, COM on NTK); without it neither cell has a reference and the signal freezes near its bias. No maker documents this code publicly. How an open return is spotted shows in the bank 2 front code P2254: VW's 2014 Touareg data book looks for a signal of 1.47-1.52 V with cell resistance above 950 ohms, and Ford for Bosch-type probes waits for 1.45-1.55 V lasting 10 s. Chrysler lists the bank 1 twin P22B2 for the 6.7 Cummins Ram and replaces connectors first. P22C0/P22C1 are low/high, P22BB the reference lead. The lamp lights; driving feels normal.
c: Loose, corroded or pushed-out terminal on the return wire
Return wire broken by heat or vibration near the exhaust
Internal break in the sensor lead or element
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream oxygen value frozen at a constant reading
Further codes for the same sensor may be stored together

P22C0.t: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P22C0.d: P22C0 flags the negative current control line (virtual ground) of the bank 2 downstream wide-band probe as too low. The controller deliberately lifts this return above chassis ground, around 2.5 V on Saab's 2010 9-5, which lets the pump cell be driven both ways; once the wire touches ground, that bias and the lean side of the measuring range disappear. No maker documents this code publicly. Mitsubishi lists the bank 1 front analog P2252 as a two-trip code on the 2022 Outlander without giving a limit, and Ford reports shorts to ground on the VM pin of its front bank 2 probes as P0151 rather than a dedicated code. P22BF is the open, P22C1 the high reading, P22B3 bank 1. Apart from the lamp, little changes for the driver.
c: Return wire chafed against body or exhaust bracket, shorted to ground
Internal short from the sensor return to the housing
Faulty bias supply in the engine control module
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream reading cannot show lean values
Readiness for catalyst and oxygen sensor monitors stays open

P22C1.t: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P22C1.d: P22C1 covers a return line (virtual ground) reading too high on the bank 2 post-catalyst wide-band probe: the line is pushed above the mid-level bias the controller sets, which in practice means contact with the heater supply or battery voltage, often via a melted or wet connector. With the reference raised, the rich side of the scale is lost and the oxygen value becomes useless. No maker documents this code publicly. Mitsubishi names the bank 1 front analog P2253 as a two-trip code on the 2022 Outlander, and Ford's front-probe logic books shorts to battery on any Bosch pin as P0152 for bank 2. CARB expects out-of-range detection on secondary sensors. P22BF is the open, P22C0 the low case, P22B4 bank 1. The lamp lights; the engine runs on.
c: Return wire touching the heater feed or another positive supply
Heat-damaged or wet connector bridging the return to a live pin
Internal leakage from heater to sensing cells inside the probe
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream reading stuck high or implausible

P22C2.t: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit/Open (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P22C2.d: P22C2 reports an open trim line on the bank 2 downstream wide-band probe. Every probe ships with a calibration resistor in its plug (pin 5, RT/IA on a Bosch LSU) that corrects for spread in its diffusion gap; on Bosch probes it sits in parallel with the controller's sense resistor. Ford explains that if it opens, all pump current is forced through that measuring resistor, tilting the lambda curve, a small error near stoichiometry. No maker documents P22C2 publicly. Upstream on bank 2 it is P2629: VW's 2014 Touareg triggers above 4.81 V, Saab tests P2626 during overrun below 750 C, and Ford bulletin 17-2124 replaces the front probes of the 3.5 GTDI for P2626/P2629. P22C3/P22C4 are low/high, P22B5 bank 1. The lamp lights.
c: Corroded or loose trim-resistor terminal in the sensor plug
Trim resistor or its lead open inside the sensor connector
Trim wire broken between connector and control module
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream lambda reads slightly off, most visibly away from lambda 1

P22C3.t: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P22C3.d: P22C3 is the low fault on the trim (label resistor) circuit of the bank 2 post-catalyst wide-band probe. Ford's 2012 OBD summary shows how makers can read this for NTK probes: at each key-on the controller switches the heater off, samples a voltage divider and estimates the label resistor; a value too high is taken as a broken or grounded lead and sets the trim-low code (P2630 for the bank 2 front probe). The controller then falls back to the resistor rank stored in memory, so the reading stays usable but less exact. No maker documents P22C3 publicly, and GM reuses the bank 1 slot P22B6 for a NOx sensor oxygen check without a bank 2 equivalent. P22C2 is the open, P22C4 the high variant. The lamp lights.
c: Trim wire chafed and shorted to ground
High-resistance or corroded trim terminal raising the measured resistance
Defective label resistor in the sensor connector
s: Check engine light
Code typically appears right after engine start

P22C4.t: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P22C4.d: P22C4 is the high fault on the trim circuit of the bank 2 downstream wide-band probe. In Ford's key-on check of NTK label resistors, an estimated resistance that is too low means the line is shorted to power, which sets the trim-high code (P2631 for the bank 2 front probe); the stored resistor rank then stays in use. On Bosch-type probes a raised trim voltage looks much like an open: Saab and VW both trip their front trim code above 4.81 V, so makers may sort this fault into the open-circuit code. No maker documents P22C4 publicly, and GM's bank 1 slot P22B7 serves a NOx sensor oxygen ceiling with no bank 2 counterpart. Typical causes are a short to the heater feed or a damaged plug. P22C2 is the open, P22C3 the low case. The lamp lights.
c: Trim wire shorted to the heater supply or another positive feed
Heat- or water-damaged sensor plug bridging the trim pin
Internally shorted label resistor in the sensor connector
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 downstream lambda slightly off; heater codes may accompany it

P22C5.t: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Valve Control Circuit/Open
P22C5.d: P22C5 flags an open or broken drive circuit for the turbocharger compressor outlet valve. That valve sits in the charge-air path downstream of a compressor and decides whether this compressor feeds the engine, for example in register or two-stage charging or next to an electric auxiliary compressor. While the output is switched off, the engine control module compares the voltage on its driver with the level expected for an intact load; a reading typical of a cut wire or an unplugged connector sets the code. California OBD rules treat such boost actuators as monitored output components. No manufacturer publicly documents P22C5 itself; Mercedes-Benz uses the related stuck codes P22C8 and P22C9 on the M256 engine. With the valve unpowered, the module usually limits boost and power.
c: Valve connector loose, unplugged or corroded
Broken wire in the valve harness, often near hot turbo parts
Open actuator coil inside the compressor outlet valve
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power because boost is limited
Weak or delayed pull at the speed where the second boost path should join

P22C6.t: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Valve Control Circuit Low
P22C6.d: P22C6 is stored when the control line of the compressor outlet valve sits at a voltage that is too low for the current command, which normally points to a short to ground somewhere between the module and the valve. Whether the valve then stays permanently energized or never moves depends on whether the engine control module switches the ground side or the supply side of the coil. The module checks this electrically and needs no driving test, so the code can appear right after start. In a twin-path or two-stage boost layout the valve is meant to open or close one compressor branch on demand; a grounded line therefore leaves that branch in a fixed state. No manufacturer publicly documents P22C6; the description rests on the CARB output-component rules and published two-stage designs. Expect limited boost and a lit warning lamp.
c: Control wire chafed through and touching ground
Internal short in the valve actuator coil
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the connector
Damaged output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light on soon after starting
Boost limited, engine feels flat under load
Possible blown fuse if the short pulls heavy current

P22C7.t: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Valve Control Circuit High
P22C7.d: P22C7 means the drive line of the compressor outlet valve reads higher than the module expects, typically because the wire has a short to battery voltage or the coil draws excessive current while the driver is on. Modern output stages notice the overcurrent and switch off to protect themselves, so the valve then stops responding even though nothing is open. The valve itself belongs to the boost path of register, two-stage or e-compressor charging, where it controls whether a compressor delivers into the intake. Electrical checks like this run continuously under the CARB rules for monitored output components. No manufacturer publicly documents P22C7. Compared with the open-circuit code P22C5 and the low-voltage code P22C6, the search here focuses on rubbed wires touching a positive feed or a shorted actuator winding.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Shorted turns in the valve coil causing overcurrent
Replacement valve with unsuitable coil resistance
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light on
Valve no longer switches, boost reduced
Code returns immediately after clearing

P22C8.t: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Valve Stuck Open
P22C8.d: P22C8 is a functional fault: the compressor outlet valve stays open at a moment when the control strategy expects it shut, so pressure or airflow in the boost path does not follow the command. Mercedes-Benz uses it on the M256.8 inline six with its 48-volt electric auxiliary compressor. Bulletin LI09.41-P-078735 in its second version (March 2025) added P22C800 next to P22C900 for E, CLS, GLE and GLS 450, S 500/580 e and AMG 53 models and blames a jammed check valve in the charge-air pipe; the fix is a new charge-air line with integrated check valve. Listed symptoms are the warning lamp, weak output and faulty boost. Because the module must see the valve misbehave under suitable load, the code usually needs a test drive to confirm. P22C9 is the opposite case, a valve stuck shut.
c: Check valve in the charge-air pipe jammed (Mercedes M256)
Oil film or deposits holding the valve flap open
Actuator or linkage no longer able to close the valve
s: Check engine light on
Little or poor power output
Boost builds poorly or unevenly

P22C9.t: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Valve Stuck Closed
P22C9.d: P22C9 says the compressor outlet valve did not open when commanded, so air from the compressor it controls cannot reach the engine and the expected boost is missing. Mercedes-Benz documents the code for the M256.8 six-cylinder: the first version of bulletin LI09.41-P-078735 (December 2024) covers P22C900 in the MRG3 engine control unit on models from 2019 to 2025 and traces it to a check valve in the charge-air pipe that is jammed shut; the charge-air line with integrated check valve is replaced. Symptoms listed there are the engine lamp, reduced output and a boost malfunction. The check runs only under operating conditions that call for the valve to open, so confirmation usually takes a drive under load. Unlike P22C8, the risk here is a blocked path in which a compressor works against a closed outlet.
c: Check valve in the charge-air pipe jammed shut (Mercedes M256)
Valve actuator, vacuum or pressure supply unable to open the valve
Valve seized by deposits or corrosion
s: Check engine light on
Noticeable loss of power under load
Boost malfunction, possibly with underboost code

P22CA.t: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Switching Valve Control Circuit/Open
P22CA.d: P22CA reports an open drive circuit for the compressor outlet switching valve. In two-stage or register boost systems the outlet flap is often moved by vacuum or pressure, and this electrically driven switching valve decides when that actuating medium reaches it; Ford's two-stage patent notes such valves may be worked electrically or by vacuum. With the circuit open, the switching valve stays in its rest position and the outlet flap no longer changes over. Nissan names the part on the Cummins 5.0 V8 diesel of the 2016 Titan XD (TC outlet switching valve, see P22CE), but no manufacturer publicly documents P22CA. The module detects the fault electrically with the output off, so it is independent of driving style. Check plug, harness and coil resistance first.
c: Switching valve connector loose or corroded
Broken wire between module and switching valve
Open coil in the switching solenoid
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light on
Boost changeover no longer happens, power limited
Hesitation when accelerating through the switching speed

P22CB.t: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Switching Valve Control Circuit Low
P22CB.d: P22CB is set when the control line of the compressor outlet switching valve shows too little voltage for the present command, most often because the wire or the solenoid has a short to ground. On a low-side driven solenoid such a short can hold the valve energized all the time, so the outlet flap it supplies with vacuum or pressure stays in its switched position whatever the rpm and load. The module spots the fault through its driver diagnostics without any special driving. The solenoid is a small part in the actuating line of the outlet flap and is usually inexpensive; the wiring near the hot turbo area deserves a careful look. No manufacturer publicly documents P22CB. If P22C6 is present as well, look for a shared harness section or connector.
c: Control wire chafed and shorted to ground
Internal short in the switching solenoid
Water or corrosion in the solenoid connector
s: Check engine light on
Boost path stuck in one mode, uneven power across the rev range
Reduced power at low or high engine speed

P22CC.t: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Switching Valve Control Circuit High
P22CC.d: P22CC indicates that the drive line of the compressor outlet switching valve carries more voltage or current than allowed, usually a short to a battery feed or a solenoid with shorted windings. The output stage of the engine control module then tends to shut down for self-protection, which leaves the switching valve unpowered and the outlet flap in its rest position. On register or two-stage charging this typically means the second compressor branch is no longer brought in or taken out as planned. The test is electrical and continuous, as CARB requires for monitored output parts. No manufacturer publicly documents P22CC. Measure coil resistance against the specification and check whether the wire touches a positive feed; replacing the module is a last resort.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Shorted windings in the switching solenoid
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light on
Outlet flap no longer switches, power reduced
Fault returns as soon as the valve is commanded

P22CD.t: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Switching Valve Stuck Open
P22CD.d: P22CD is a plausibility fault: the engine control module commanded the compressor outlet switching valve shut, yet boost pressure, airflow or a position signal behave as if the switched path were still open. Because the switching valve feeds the actuator of the outlet flap, a mechanically stuck solenoid, a leaking control hose or a flap held open by the actuator all lead to the same result. In a sequential setup this can let charge air leak back through an idle compressor at low engine speed, so boost builds slowly. The check needs the operating point where the valve should be closed and is therefore confirmed during driving. No manufacturer publicly documents P22CD; Nissan uses the sister code P22CE on the Cummins 5.0 of the Titan XD. P22CE covers the reverse case.
c: Switching solenoid mechanically stuck in the open position
Leaking, cracked or swapped control hose to the flap actuator
Outlet flap or its actuator unable to close
s: Check engine light on
Sluggish boost build-up at low engine speed
Hissing or whistling noise from the intake side

P22CE.t: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Switching Valve Stuck Closed
P22CE.d: P22CE is set when the compressor outlet switching valve was told to open but the boost system shows no sign that the switched path changed over. Nissan documents the code as TC Outlet Switching Valve Stuck Closed for the 2016 Titan XD with the Cummins 5.0 litre V8 diesel and its two-stage turbocharger. Bulletin NTB16-051 (May 2016) links it to operation at or below 0 °C and to hesitation on acceleration after an overnight indoor soak followed by a cold drive below -18 °C; the remedy is reprogramming the ECM. The revised NTB16-051a (June 2017) keeps P22CE in the list. Besides software, frozen or collapsed control hoses and a sticking solenoid are plausible causes. The driver notices weak pull while the second stage should come in.
c: Engine control software reacting wrongly in cold weather (Nissan Titan XD bulletin)
Collapsed, kinked or frozen control hose to the outlet flap actuator
Switching solenoid stuck in the closed position
Insufficient vacuum or pressure supply for the actuator
s: Check engine light on, mostly in cold weather
Hesitation when accelerating until the engine is warm
Weak pull in the speed range where the second stage should help

P22CF.t: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Control Circuit/Open
P22CF.d: P22CF points to an open drive circuit of the turbocharger turbine inlet valve, the exhaust-side valve that either lets gas skip the small first-stage turbine of a series two-stage system or isolates a second turbine in a parallel-sequential layout. GM's diesel OBD tables (17OBDG04 and 18OBDG04) group P22CF, P22D0 and P22D1 as the faults of the high-pressure turbine bypass actuator (HTB); while one is active, boost control leaves closed-loop operation. A GM patent on a series-sequential turbo shows this bypass valve with both a current sensor and a position sensor. With the circuit open the valve sits in its spring position, often causing slow boost or a power cap. No public source gives GM's thresholds for P22CF; the electrical check runs whenever the actuator is in use.
c: Actuator connector loose, heat-damaged or corroded
Broken wire near the exhaust manifold or turbo
Open winding in the turbine valve actuator or its control solenoid
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power, boost control in fallback mode
Turbo lag or a missing second-stage push

P22D0.t: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Control Circuit Low
P22D0.d: P22D0 is logged when the drive circuit of the turbine inlet valve shows a voltage below the expected range, the classic sign of a short to ground in the wire or inside the actuator. GM lists P22D0 together with P22CF and P22D1 in the fault bundle of its high-pressure turbine bypass actuator in the 2017 and 2018 diesel OBD documents; any of them takes boost control out of closed loop. Because the exhaust valve sits right on the hot turbo housing, heat-brittle insulation that rubs through is a likely cause. Depending on how the driver is wired, the valve may then stay energized or never move, so exhaust skips the high-pressure stage at the wrong time or never. No public source gives GM's thresholds. P22D0 differs from P22CF by a short rather than a break.
c: Heat-damaged wire rubbing through to ground
Internal short in the valve actuator or control solenoid
Damaged output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light on
Power limited, boost too low or uneven
Code sets right after start without a test drive

P22D1.t: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Control Circuit High
P22D1.d: P22D1 tells you the drive circuit of the turbine inlet valve reads too high, which usually means a short to battery voltage or an actuator that draws overcurrent. GM assigns P22D1, along with P22CF and P22D0, to its high-pressure turbine bypass actuator in the 2017 and 2018 diesel OBD tables, and boost control drops out of closed loop when the fault is active. The GM patent on series-sequential turbocharging describes a current sensor on this valve, which is how an overcurrent can be seen directly. Once the driver protects itself and shuts down, the valve no longer follows commands. Compared with its siblings, the search concentrates on positive-feed contact and the actuator winding. No public source gives GM's threshold values for P22D1.
c: Actuator wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Actuator winding shorted or mechanically jammed, drawing overcurrent
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power, boost control in fallback mode
Fault comes back as soon as the valve is driven

P22D2.t: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Stuck Open
P22D2.d: P22D2 means the turbine inlet valve stays open after the module asked it to close. In a series two-stage system, an open valve lets exhaust skip the small high-pressure turbine, so low-speed boost and response suffer. In a parallel-sequential system such as Jaguar's 3.0 V6 diesel, where valves keep the secondary turbo out of the exhaust stream and intake until about 2,800 rpm, an open valve feeds that turbo too early and raises pumping losses. The module detects the fault by comparing commanded and measured valve position or the boost response, so it needs a drive at the relevant operating point. No manufacturer publicly documents P22D2 with thresholds. Soot and a seized pivot are typical; vacuum-driven designs add leaking control lines.
c: Soot or corrosion seizing the valve shaft in the open position
Leaking or detached control line on a vacuum-operated actuator
Actuator or linkage unable to close the valve
Position sensor reporting open although the valve moved
s: Check engine light on
Noticeable turbo lag at low engine speed
Higher fuel consumption
Reduced power mode

P22D3.t: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Stuck Closed
P22D3.d: P22D3 is stored when the turbine inlet valve does not open on command. In a series two-stage layout all exhaust must then pass the small high-pressure stage even at high load, raising back-pressure and risking overboost or turbo overspeed, so the module caps power. In a parallel-sequential layout the second turbo never comes in. Stellantis documents the code on the 2026 Jeep Cherokee with the 1.6 litre turbo hybrid: bulletin 18-052-26 Rev. A (June 2026) states that P22D3-00 sets falsely on vehicles built from mid-December 2025 to late April 2026 and adds PCM software that disables it. On other vehicles, check for a valve seized by soot, a failed actuator or a lacking vacuum supply. P22D2 is the opposite, a valve stuck open.
c: Valve seized closed by soot or corrosion
Engine software setting the code falsely (Jeep Cherokee 2026 bulletin)
Actuator, linkage or vacuum supply unable to open the valve
s: Check engine light on
Power capped at higher engine speed and load
Possible overboost code alongside

P22D4.t: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Position Sensor Circuit
P22D4.d: P22D4 is the general circuit fault of the sensor that reports how far the turbine inlet valve is open. Engineering literature explains why this valve, unlike most compressor bypass valves, has feedback: a Ford two-stage patent calls the high-pressure turbine bypass valve emissions-critical and therefore actively controlled with a position sensor, and a GM patent uses the measured opening to run the valve in position control. When the signal is missing or cannot be read at all, the module loses that feedback and typically switches to a fixed fallback position with reduced boost. No manufacturer publicly documents P22D4. The narrower sibling codes P22D6 and P22D7 name a too-low or too-high voltage; P22D4 is used when the fault cannot be assigned that precisely.
c: Loose, heat-damaged or corroded sensor connector
Damaged sensor wiring near the turbo
Failed position sensor, often integrated in the actuator
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power, turbo valve held in a fallback position

P22D5.t: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P22D5.d: P22D5 is a plausibility fault of the turbine inlet valve position signal. The voltage stays inside its electrical limits, yet it does not match what the module expects, for instance the reading lags the commanded position, fails to reach the learned end stops or does not change when the valve is moved. CARB requires input sensors of this kind to be checked for rationality as well as for circuit faults. Since a GM patent describes the valve being run in position control with sensor feedback, a wrong but believable reading directly corrupts the valve setting and thus boost. Causes include a sensor drifting with heat, a slipped magnet or linkage, and a valve that moves sluggishly so that position and command diverge. No manufacturer publicly documents P22D5.
c: Valve or linkage sluggish from soot, so position lags the command
Position sensor drifting or misaligned on the actuator
End positions not relearned after actuator replacement
s: Check engine light on
Jerky or delayed changeover between turbo stages
Boost fluctuates under steady throttle

P22D6.t: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Position Sensor Circuit Low
P22D6.d: P22D6 is set when the position sensor signal of the turbine inlet valve falls below its lowest valid voltage. Position sensors on such actuators normally work on a 5-volt reference with a signal that never reaches the rails in normal use, so a reading near zero means a lost reference, a signal wire shorted to ground or an internal sensor fault rather than a real valve position. The engine control module flags this electrically and quickly, without needing a test drive. It then ignores the reading and usually parks the valve in a safe position with reduced boost. Two-stage patents from Ford and GM describe exactly this kind of position feedback on the turbine bypass valve. No manufacturer publicly documents P22D6. Check the reference voltage at the plug first.
c: 5-volt reference open or pulled down by another shorted sensor
Internal failure of the position sensor
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power, valve in fallback position
Other sensor codes on the same reference circuit possible

P22D7.t: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Position Sensor Circuit High
P22D7.d: P22D7 is logged when the position signal of the turbine inlet valve rises above its highest valid voltage. A reading pinned near the reference level usually comes from an open sensor ground, a signal wire touching the 5-volt reference or battery voltage, or a failed sensor element, not from the valve itself. Like its low-voltage counterpart P22D6, this is a pure circuit check that runs continuously and does not depend on load. Without valid feedback, the module can no longer run the valve in position control as described in the GM two-stage patent, so it typically fixes the valve and limits boost. No manufacturer publicly documents P22D7. Inspecting the ground pin and wiring near the hot exhaust side usually finds the fault faster than swapping the actuator.
c: Signal wire shorted to the 5-volt reference or battery voltage
Internal failure of the position sensor
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power, valve held in fallback position

P22D8.t: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P22D8.d: P22D8 covers short dropouts or jumps in the position signal of the turbine inlet valve: the value leaps faster than the valve could physically move, or briefly disappears and returns. Such patterns typically come from a connector with fretting contacts, a wire breaking inside its insulation near the vibrating, hot turbo, or a sensor that fails under heat. Because the module uses this feedback to control the valve, as the Ford and GM two-stage patents describe, every glitch can make the valve hunt and boost wobble. The fault often appears only on rough roads or when the engine bay is hot, and may have vanished by the time the car is in the workshop. No manufacturer publicly documents P22D8. Wiggle testing with live data while watching the signal helps to find it.
c: Loose or fretting contacts in the sensor connector
Wire breaking intermittently from heat and vibration
Position sensor dropping out when hot
s: Check engine light on, sometimes only now and then
Boost surging or hunting
Brief loss of power on rough roads

P22D9.t: Cylinder 1 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit/Open
P22D9.d: P22D9 reports a broken control circuit at the gas injector of cylinder 1, the solenoid that meters CNG or LPG into the intake port whenever a bi-fuel or dedicated gas engine runs on the alternative fuel. The driver stage notices the break because no current flows when it switches on, or because the expected off-state voltage on its pin is missing. No maker publishes P22D9 itself: the TransEco AFCM list and Ford's 2014 code list only carry the Low/High pair P22DA/P22DB, and TransEco even files an open line under Low. GM's bi-fuel Silverado moves the injectors over to gas one by one starting with cylinder 1, so a break here tends to show up right at the changeover. Bi-fuel cars usually return to gasoline; a dedicated gas engine loses cylinder 1.
c: Open solenoid winding in the cylinder 1 gas injector
Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the gas injector
Broken wire or failed splice in the gas system harness
Defective driver stage in the gas or engine control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Engine changes back to gasoline or refuses to switch to gas
Misfire on cylinder 1 in gas mode (dedicated engines)

P22DA.t: Cylinder 1 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Low
P22DA.d: P22DA means the cylinder 1 gas injector control wire reads too low. TransEco Energy's DTC list for its CNG control module (AFCM v1.4) blames either a grounded wire or an open line, turns on the MIL in bi-fuel installations and reacts the same way it would to the matching gasoline injector fault. Ford's 2014 OBD code list carries P22DA as a MIL code as well. With a low-side driver, a control wire touching ground can keep the injector energized whenever its supply is live, so cylinder 1 may get gas without pause and run very rich; an interrupted wire leaves it without gas. P22DB covers the high side and P22D9 the plain open circuit. The gasoline injector of the same cylinder reports through P0261 instead.
c: Control wire of the cylinder 1 gas injector chafed through to ground
Interrupted control wire or connector (logged as Low by some modules)
Water or corrosion in the injector connector
Faulty output stage in the gas control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Very rough running on cylinder 1 in gas mode, possibly rich misfire
Gas system switches back to gasoline

P22DB.t: Cylinder 1 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit High
P22DB.d: P22DB flags a control circuit of the cylinder 1 gas injector that stays too high. TransEco Energy's AFCM fault list traces it to a short to battery voltage, lights the MIL for bi-fuel use and applies the same fallback as for the gasoline injector fault; Ford's 2014 code list also marks P22DB for the MIL. When the line is held at supply voltage, the driver cannot pull it down, so the injector never opens and cylinder 1 receives no gas: a lean misfire on that cylinder in gas mode is the typical result, often together with P0301. Many output stages also shut off to protect themselves from the excessive current. A coil with shorted turns can look the same. P22DA is the low side, P0262 the code for the gasoline injector.
c: Control wire shorted to battery or injector supply voltage
Shorted turns in the cylinder 1 gas injector coil
Output stage of the gas control module damaged
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Lean misfire on cylinder 1 in gas mode, often with P0301
Engine runs normally on gasoline

P22DC.t: Cylinder 1 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Range/Performance
P22DC.d: P22DC is meant for a cylinder 1 gas injector whose circuit is electrically intact but whose response looks wrong, such as a current trace that never reaches its peak or does not fall back to the hold level, or a coil whose resistance has drifted. A Ford patent on driving a second type of injector through an interface (US 8,161,946) describes this logic: the injector counts as degraded if it ignores on and off commands or stays at peak current. No vehicle maker publishes P22DC; TransEco and Ford's 2014 list stop at Low/High. A sticking injector is a plausible trigger, which is why GM's bi-fuel pickups filter the gas through a coalescing element that keeps oil and liquids away from the injectors. Expect a misfiring cylinder 1 or a return to gasoline.
c: Cylinder 1 gas injector sticking from oil residue or debris in the gas
Injector coil resistance outside its specification
Weak supply voltage to the injector bank
Injector of the wrong type or impedance installed
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Uneven running in gas mode, misfire counts on cylinder 1
Higher gas consumption or switch back to gasoline

P22DD.t: Cylinder 2 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit/Open
P22DD.d: P22DD signals an interruption in the circuit of the cylinder 2 gas injector. On many systems that circuit is not driven by the engine computer: Ford's 2003 bi-fuel CNG trucks used a separate alternative fuel control module holding drivers for both injector sets, with heavier stages for the gas injectors because they draw more current. GM's 2014 bi-fuel Silverado likewise stores gas faults in its own CNG control module (bulletin PIP5181), so a scan tool has to read that module as well. No maker documents P22DD publicly; TransEco and Ford list only the cylinder 2 Low/High codes P22DE and P22DF, and TransEco assigns an open line to Low. Look for a burnt coil or a separated connector before blaming the module.
c: Burnt-out or open coil in the cylinder 2 gas injector
Connector at the cylinder 2 injector loose or pulled off
Wire break between gas control module and injector
Failed injector driver in the separate gas control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Gas mode not available or ends shortly after switching
Misfire on cylinder 2 when running on gas

P22DE.t: Cylinder 2 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Low
P22DE.d: P22DE stands for a control line of the cylinder 2 gas injector whose voltage is too low. TransEco Energy's AFCM fault table blames a grounded or interrupted wire and turns on the MIL for bi-fuel vehicles; Ford's 2014 OBD code list includes P22DE as a MIL code too. California's OBD rule counts a bi-fuel car among alternate-fueled vehicles just for the periods it actually burns gas, so this monitor matters mainly in gas mode, and on gasoline the car normally behaves as usual. If the grounded wire keeps the injector energized, cylinder 2 is flooded with gas and the plug may foul; a separated wire starves it instead. P22DF is the high side, P22DD the open-circuit code, and P0264 belongs to the gasoline injector.
c: Cylinder 2 injector control wire grounded on engine or body
Open wire or pin, reported as Low by modules like the TransEco AFCM
Shorted output transistor in the gas control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Rich misfire or fouled spark plug on cylinder 2 in gas mode
Gas operation interrupted, engine runs on gasoline

P22DF.t: Cylinder 2 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit High
P22DF.d: P22DF indicates that the control circuit of the cylinder 2 gas injector reads high, which TransEco Energy's AFCM table attributes to a short to power; MIL on for bi-fuel use. Ford's 2014 code list likewise flags P22DF for the MIL. A line stuck at supply voltage keeps the injector closed, so cylinder 2 burns no gas and misfires lean, while running on gasoline is unaffected. On GM's 2015 bi-fuel Impala the ECM drives the CNG injectors itself and, if it sees a fuel delivery problem in one system, changes over to the other, so the driver may only notice a switch back to gasoline. A coil with internal shorts can produce the same overcurrent. P22DE is the low side; P0265 is the high-side code of the gasoline injector.
c: Cylinder 2 control wire touching a live supply wire
Internal short in the cylinder 2 gas injector coil
Driver protection in the control module tripping due to a fault
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Cylinder 2 misfires only on gas
Unexpected return to gasoline

P22E0.t: Cylinder 2 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Range/Performance
P22E0.d: P22E0 covers a cylinder 2 gas injector circuit that passes the plain open and short checks yet responds outside its expected window. California's OBD regulation asks for output components to be checked not only for circuit faults but also for a proper functional response; for alternate-fueled vehicles from 2004 to 2018 the gasoline rules applied unchanged, and from 2019 the maker submits its own monitoring plan. The Ford patent US 8,161,946 gives an example of such a functional check for an injector fed by an extra driver. No maker publishes P22E0 itself. Typical triggers are a sluggish or partly stuck injector, a coil past its specification or a driver that cannot deliver the needed current. Cylinder 2 then runs unevenly on gas.
c: Cylinder 2 gas injector opening or closing too slowly
Coil resistance of the injector out of tolerance
Driver stage or supply unable to provide the required current
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Uneven idle on gas, cylinder 2 misfire counts
Fuel trim drifts in gas mode

P22E1.t: Cylinder 3 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit/Open
P22E1.d: P22E1 marks an open control circuit at the cylinder 3 gas injector. Circuit continuity checks of this kind run all the time: California's OBD rule defines continuous monitoring as always enabled with at least two samples per second, so a break is caught within moments once the gas system is in use. No maker documents P22E1 openly. TransEco's AFCM list and Ford's 2014 code list give cylinder 3 only the Low/High codes P22E2 and P22E3, and TransEco counts an open line as Low. On GM's bi-fuel pickups the gas injectors sit on separate rails with hoses leading to nozzles at each intake runner, and their wiring runs along those rails; a pulled connector after work in that area is a common reason. Bi-fuel cars carry on with gasoline.
c: Cylinder 3 injector connector left off or not latched after service
Open coil in the cylinder 3 gas injector
Wire broken where the harness runs along the gas rail
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Gas mode switches off soon after changeover
Cylinder 3 misfire on dedicated gas engines

P22E2.t: Cylinder 3 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Low
P22E2.d: P22E2 is logged when the control circuit of the cylinder 3 gas injector reads low. In TransEco Energy's AFCM table the cause column says shorted to ground or open, the MIL comes on in bi-fuel systems and the reaction copies that for a gasoline injector fault. Ford's 2014 code list lists P22E2 as a MIL code. Because a grounded control wire can leave the injector energized, cylinder 3 may be flooded with gas; the catalyst then gets unburnt fuel, and prolonged driving in gas mode is a bad idea. With a broken wire the cylinder is simply starved. Typical spots are chafe points against brackets or the intake manifold. P22E3 is the high side and P22E1 the pure open-circuit code; the gasoline injector uses P0267.
c: Cylinder 3 control wire rubbed through against a bracket or the manifold
Broken wire or terminal in the cylinder 3 injector circuit
Shorted driver output in the gas control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Cylinder 3 runs rich or misfires in gas mode
Smell of unburnt gas at the exhaust

P22E3.t: Cylinder 3 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit High
P22E3.d: P22E3 tells that the cylinder 3 gas injector circuit is held high. TransEco Energy's AFCM list names a short to power, MIL on for bi-fuel use, and Ford's 2014 code list also ties P22E3 to the MIL. With the line stuck at supply voltage the injector cannot be switched on, so cylinder 3 gets no gas and misfires lean. In GM's bi-fuel Silverado layout the ECM calculates the pulse widths while a separate fuel injector control module passes them to the gas injectors, so the fault can sit in the wiring between that module and the injector, in the injector itself, or in the module output. Gasoline operation remains normal. P22E2 is the low side and P0268 the high-side code of the gasoline injector.
c: Cylinder 3 control wire shorted to a 12 V feed
Shorted turns in the cylinder 3 gas injector
Faulty output of the injector control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Lean misfire on cylinder 3 in gas mode, often with P0303
Noticeable loss of power on gas

P22E4.t: Cylinder 3 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Range/Performance
P22E4.d: P22E4 points to a cylinder 3 gas injector whose circuit works but whose electrical behaviour does not match the command. Peak-and-hold gas injectors first draw a high opening current and then a lower holding current; Ford's patent US 8,161,946 treats an injector that stays at peak or ignores commands as degraded and reports this back to the engine computer. No maker documents P22E4 publicly. The code is distinct from pressure problems: GM's bi-fuel pickups regulate gas to roughly 896 kPa ahead of the rail, and a wrong rail pressure has its own sensor codes. Here the injector or its driver is suspect, often after oil or debris from the gas has made the armature stick. Cylinder 3 then runs unevenly on gas.
c: Armature of the cylinder 3 gas injector gummed up by oil or debris
Injector coil aged or overheated, resistance out of range
Weak driver output or poor supply ground
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Intermittent cylinder 3 misfire on gas
Rising gas consumption

P22E5.t: Cylinder 4 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit/Open
P22E5.d: P22E5 is the open-circuit code for the cylinder 4 gas injector; on four-cylinder gas engines it is the last injector of the set. The driver sees no current when it switches the injector on. No maker documents P22E5 in public sources: TransEco and Ford's 2014 list stop at the cylinder 4 Low/High codes P22E6 and P22E7, and TransEco files an open line under Low. Ford's 2003 bi-fuel CNG trucks show a typical layout where gas enters through sleeves in the gasoline injector seats, with the gas injectors driven by a separate module, so connectors sit close to hot engine parts. Expect a switch back to gasoline on bi-fuel cars and a dead cylinder 4 on dedicated gas engines. P0204 is the gasoline counterpart.
c: Open coil in the cylinder 4 gas injector
Heat-damaged or brittle connector near the exhaust side
Broken wire in the cylinder 4 injector circuit
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Gas mode unavailable, car runs on gasoline only
Cylinder 4 dead on a dedicated gas engine

P22E6.t: Cylinder 4 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Low
P22E6.d: P22E6 reports a low signal on the cylinder 4 gas injector control wire. TransEco Energy's AFCM table gives short to ground or open as the cause and turns the MIL on in bi-fuel installations, keeping the same failure response as for gasoline; Ford's 2014 code list carries P22E6 with the MIL as well. On Ford's 2003 bi-fuel CNG system the control module would only start the engine on gas once rail pressure reached about 517 kPa, so a failed gas start alone does not prove an injector fault: check for this code first. A grounded line can hold cylinder 4 permanently open and flood it; an interrupted one leaves it dry. P22E7 is the high side, P22E5 the plain open circuit, and P0270 the gasoline injector code.
c: Cylinder 4 control wire grounded through damaged insulation
Separated terminal or broken wire in the cylinder 4 circuit
Damaged driver output in the gas control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Cylinder 4 runs rich or cuts out on gas
Engine stays on or returns to gasoline

P22E7.t: Cylinder 4 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit High
P22E7.d: P22E7 says the control circuit of the cylinder 4 gas injector reads high. TransEco Energy's fault table blames a short to power and lights the MIL for bi-fuel use; Ford's 2014 code list also marks P22E7 as a MIL code. The injector then cannot open and cylinder 4 misfires lean whenever gas is selected. Timing matters for diagnosis: GM's 2015 bi-fuel Impala starts on gasoline below about -20 °C and only moves to CNG once coolant reaches 50 °C, so on such cars the fault may appear only after warm-up. Check the wire for contact with a live feed and measure the injector coil for internal shorts. P22E6 is the low side; P0271 is the corresponding code for the gasoline injector of cylinder 4.
c: Cylinder 4 control wire in contact with a 12 V circuit
Cylinder 4 injector coil with internal short
Output stage of the controlling module defective
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Cylinder 4 misfire only after the switch to gas
Reduced power in gas mode

P22E8.t: Cylinder 4 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Range/Performance
P22E8.d: P22E8 applies when the cylinder 4 gas injector circuit is complete but the measured response lies outside the plausible range, for instance an opening current that rises too slowly or a hold phase that never settles. No vehicle maker documents P22E8 openly; the published lists from TransEco and Ford end at Low/High. Gas quality is a frequent background factor: GM fits a coalescing filter with a 6 micron element in its bi-fuel pickups because contaminants and liquids in the gas can damage the injectors, and the filter has to be drained and replaced at intervals. A neglected filter can therefore show up as this code. Cleaning rarely helps; the injector or the complete rail is usually replaced, then a drive on gas confirms the repair.
c: Cylinder 4 injector fouled by oil or liquids, often from a neglected gas filter
Aged injector coil with changed resistance
Low system voltage during cranking or at idle
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Rough idle on gas, smooth on gasoline
Gas mode ends after a while

P22E9.t: Cylinder 5 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit/Open
P22E9.d: P22E9 is the open-circuit code for the cylinder 5 gas injector and can only appear on engines with five or more cylinders, such as the V6 of GM's bi-fuel Impala or the 6.0-litre V8 of its bi-fuel Silverado and Sierra. The driver detects the break because current is missing when the injector is commanded on. No maker documents P22E9 publicly; TransEco's AFCM list and Ford's 2014 code list only use P22EA and P22EB for cylinder 5, and TransEco treats an open line as Low. On V engines the injector wiring of each bank often runs in its own harness branch, so check the cylinder 5 branch from the module to the injector. Bi-fuel vehicles fall back to gasoline; P0205 is the gasoline counterpart.
c: Open coil in the cylinder 5 gas injector
Loose connector in the harness branch for this bank
Open driver output in the gas or injector control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Engine returns to gasoline after switching to gas
Cylinder 5 misfire if gas operation continues

P22EA.t: Cylinder 5 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Low
P22EA.d: P22EA stands for a low voltage on the cylinder 5 gas injector control wire, a code limited to engines with at least five cylinders. TransEco Energy's AFCM table points to a grounded wire or an open line, lights the MIL in bi-fuel use and applies the gasoline injector fault response; Ford's 2014 code list, written for V8 engines among others, keeps P22EA as a MIL code. A control wire resting on ground can energize the injector without pause, so cylinder 5 may run far too rich and its spark plug may foul; with an open line it misses gas instead. Inspect the wire along the rail of the affected bank first. P22EB is the high side, P22E9 the plain open circuit, and the gasoline injector reports P0273.
c: Cylinder 5 control wire shorted to ground along the gas rail
Interrupted wire or terminal, flagged as Low by some modules
Shorted output stage in the gas control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Cylinder 5 runs rich or misfires in gas mode
Fouled spark plug on cylinder 5

P22EB.t: Cylinder 5 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit High
P22EB.d: P22EB reports that the cylinder 5 gas injector control circuit is too high, which TransEco Energy's AFCM list attributes to a short to power with the MIL on for bi-fuel use; Ford's 2014 code list likewise carries P22EB for the MIL. The injector stays closed, so cylinder 5 burns no gas and misfires lean, usually logged together with P0305. Gas injectors pull more current than gasoline injectors: Ford's 2003 bi-fuel CNG documentation notes that their drivers had to be stronger because of the extra heat, which also means a shorted coil quickly overloads the output. Measure the coil resistance and look for chafing against a live feed. P22EA is the low side; the gasoline injector of cylinder 5 reports P0274.
c: Cylinder 5 control wire chafed against a supply wire
Overheated cylinder 5 gas injector with shorted turns
Overloaded driver output in the gas control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Lean misfire on cylinder 5 in gas mode, often with P0305
Normal running on gasoline

P22EC.t: Cylinder 5 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Range/Performance
P22EC.d: P22EC is the plausibility code for the cylinder 5 gas injector circuit on engines with five or more cylinders: wiring and coil pass the basic checks, but the injector does not respond as commanded. California's OBD rule requires such output components to be checked for a proper functional response, and from model year 2019 the maker of an alternate-fueled vehicle submits its own plan for which monitors apply. Ford's patent US 8,161,946 describes one way to do it, judging an injector by whether its current follows the peak-and-hold pattern. No maker publishes P22EC itself. A sticking armature, a heat-aged coil or a weak driver are the usual suspects. Bi-fuel cars may keep running on gas with a rough cylinder 5 or drop back to gasoline.
c: Sticking armature in the cylinder 5 gas injector
Driver or supply not delivering the full opening current
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Rough cylinder 5 on gas or return to gasoline
Fuel trim on the affected bank drifts in gas mode

P22ED.t: Cylinder 6 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit/Open
P22ED.d: P22ED marks an open control circuit at the cylinder 6 gas injector, the last injector on six-cylinder engines like the 3.6-litre V6 of GM's 2015 bi-fuel Impala, where the ECM drives the CNG injectors directly. Current is missing when the injector should open, so the module records the break. No maker documents P22ED openly: the TransEco AFCM table and Ford's 2014 code list give cylinder 6 only P22EE and P22EF, and TransEco reports an interrupted line as Low, so the same fault may appear as P22EE on such systems. The Impala's ECM changes to the other fuel when one system cannot deliver, so the driver mostly sees gasoline operation and the MIL. Check coil resistance and connector first. P0206 is the gasoline counterpart.
c: Open coil in the cylinder 6 gas injector
Loose or corroded connector at cylinder 6
Broken wire between control module and cylinder 6 injector
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Vehicle runs on gasoline although gas is selected
Cylinder 6 misfire on dedicated gas engines

P22EE.t: Cylinder 6 Alternative Fuel Injector Control Circuit Low
P22EE.d: On engines that burn natural gas or propane through their own gas injectors, the control module watches the drive line of each gas valve. This code means the line to the cylinder 6 gas injector sits at a lower voltage than the switching state allows. The installer table of the Altech-Eco (formerly TransEco) CNG system for Ford F-150, Super Duty and Transit treats both a short to ground and a broken wire as this fault; it lights the MIL on bi-fuel trucks but not on dedicated CNG ones. Ford lists the code with MIL in its 2014 spark-ignition code list and checks it continuously. With a grounded line the valve may stay energised; an open line leaves it shut. Bi-fuel engines usually keep running on gasoline.
c: Control wire of the cylinder 6 gas injector chafed through to ground
Broken wire or loose plug at the gas injector (counted as Low by this system)
Faulty output stage in the PCM or gas control module
s: Check engine light on (bi-fuel versions)
Rough running or misfire on cylinder 6 in gas mode
