On a four-cylinder engine this is the last cylinder of the series, which is why Stellantis bulletin 09-009-26 lists exactly P2336 to P2339 for the 2.0L turbo PHEV (sales code ECX, Jeep Wrangler 4xe 2024–2025, Grand Cherokee 2023–2025): any of the four codes with the MIL on, often together with a knocking noise, qualifies for an engine replacement under an extended warranty because of machining debris and casting sand. In general the code means the knock control has seen vibration above the limit in the combustion window of cylinder 4 and retards that cylinder's spark. On six- and eight-cylinder engines the series continues with P2340; GM reports such cases as P0324, and Saab uses the sensor codes P0326/P0331 once more than one cylinder knocks.
c: Machining debris or casting sand damaging the engine (Stellantis bulletin 09-009-26)
Low-octane fuel or high intake temperature
s: MIL on
Knocking noise from the engine compartment
Reduced power

P233A.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator C Control Circuit/Open
P233A.d: Fuel pressure regulator C is a third pressure actuator that only a few high-pressure systems have; which valve carries the letter is up to the manufacturer. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B assigns C to a second fuel metering unit valve on the pump, driven by the ECM through a high-side and a low-side switch. P233A is logged when, with the valve commanded on, almost no current flows between the two drivers, i.e. the loop resistance looks higher than 200 kOhm; samples are taken every 100 ms above 11 V system voltage, and the fault is Type A, so the MIL comes on in the first trip. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 lists P233A for the 3.0L LM2 Duramax among codes caused by a chafed engine harness. P233B and P233C cover shorts; delivery can falter while the valve is dead.
c: Valve connector loose, corroded or a terminal pushed back
Engine harness wire broken where it rubs on brackets or clamps
Coil of the metering valve interrupted
Output driver in the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine light on in the first trip
Rail pressure deviates, hesitation or reduced power
Possibly hard starting or stalling

P233B.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator C Control Circuit Low
P233B.d: P233B points to the ground side of fuel pressure regulator C: the line between valve and low-side driver has contact with ground. In GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B, regulator C is the second fuel metering unit valve, and the ECM checks this line while the driver is switched off. If the voltage there is too low, meaning less than about 0.5 Ohm towards ground, the sample counts as failed; sampling runs at 100 ms with more than 11 V supply and the engine not cranking, and the code is Type A with the MIL in the first trip. A grounded low-side line can energise the valve permanently, so pump delivery no longer follows the command. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 names P233B for the 3.0L LM2 diesel after harness chafing. The open-circuit test is P233A, the opposite short P233C.
c: Insulation of the control wire worn through against engine or bracket
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the valve connector
Metering valve winding shorted to its housing
Low-side driver in the engine control module damaged
s: Check engine light on immediately
Rail pressure too high or unstable, rough running
Reduced engine power possible

P233C.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator C Control Circuit High
P233C.d: With P233C the ECM sees the control line of fuel pressure regulator C pulled towards battery voltage. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B runs this test while the low-side driver of the second metering unit valve is switched on: if the voltage across the driver stays high, the line evidently has a path to power of less than about 0.5 Ohm. The check samples every 100 ms with system voltage above 11 V and is Type A, lighting the MIL in the first trip. Because the driver can then no longer pull current through the coil, the valve stays without power and the ECM loses part of its control over high-pressure delivery; hard starting or reduced power can follow. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 lists the code for the 3.0L LM2 diesel with chafed harnesses. P233B is the ground-short counterpart.
c: Control wire chafed against a battery-fed wire in the harness
Damaged valve connector with pins touching
Shorted turns in the metering valve coil
Low-side driver in the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine light on immediately
Long cranking or no start
Reduced power, sometimes stalling

P233D.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator B Solenoid Supply Voltage Control Circuit/Open
P233D.d: Where the ECM switches the solenoid of fuel pressure regulator B on both sides, the ground-side line is checked under P2294 to P2296 and the feed from the high-side driver under P233D to P233F. P233D is the open-circuit code for that feed. No manufacturer documents it publicly: GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04A, where regulator B is the rail pressure regulator valve, contains only the low and high codes of this circuit and folds a broken feed into its regulator tests. The basis is therefore CARB's rule that output components be checked for circuit continuity. An open feed leaves the valve without current regardless of command, so the ECM loses its means of setting rail pressure; depending on the system the pressure rises or collapses, typically with reduced power.
c: Supply wire to the regulator solenoid broken or terminal loose
High-side driver in the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Rail pressure not controllable, reduced power
Possibly hard starting or stalling

P233E.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator B Solenoid Supply Voltage Control Circuit Low
P233E.d: P233E concerns the feed side of fuel pressure regulator B: the line from the ECM's high-side driver to the solenoid is shorted to ground. GM documents it for its 2025 diesels (table 25OBDG04A); there, regulator B means the rail pressure regulator valve. The ECM looks at the voltage across the high-side driver while it is switched on; if that voltage is high, the output is being pulled down, as through an impedance to ground under roughly half an ohm. 61 failures within 122 samples of 6.25 ms, enabled above 11 V and outside cranking, set the code as Type A, MIL in the first trip. The driver normally shuts off to protect itself, so the valve stops working and rail pressure can no longer be held. Ground-side faults use P2294 to P2296; P233F is the short to power.
c: Supply wire to the regulator rubbed through to ground
Regulator solenoid shorted internally or to its housing
Water or corrosion in the regulator connector
High-side driver in the engine control module damaged
s: Check engine light on in the first trip
Reduced power, rail pressure deviation
Hard starting or stalling possible

P233F.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator B Solenoid Supply Voltage Control Circuit High
P233F.d: P233F is set when the feed line of the fuel pressure regulator B solenoid carries voltage even though the ECM has its high-side driver switched off. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04A describes this test for the rail pressure regulator valve: in the off state the voltage across the driver should be large; if it is low, the line is fed from elsewhere, as if tied to power through less than half an ohm. As with the ground short, 61 failures in 122 samples of 6.25 ms decide, and the code is Type A. A permanently powered feed means the valve can only be controlled via the low side, or is energised continuously if that side is also faulty, so rail pressure may drift from target. Typical findings are a harness touching a battery feed or a damaged connector. P233E is the low counterpart.
c: Regulator supply wire touching a battery or ignition feed
Bent or bridged pins in the regulator connector
High-side driver in the engine control module stuck on
s: Check engine light on in the first trip
Rail pressure too high or unstable
Reduced engine power possible

P2340.t: Cylinder 5 Above Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Threshold
P2340.d: P2340 reports knock above threshold for cylinder 5, so it can only occur on engines with at least five cylinders – inline-five, six-cylinder, V8 or larger. The principle matches the rest of the series: the module evaluates the knock sensor signal in the crank-angle window of each combustion and retards spark individually when one cylinder knocks. No manufacturer was found that documents P2340 publicly; the Stellantis bulletin for P2336–P2339 concerns a four-cylinder engine and therefore stops at cylinder 4. GM and Saab detect the same condition but store P0324 (excessive knock on a single cylinder for more than 8 s). Causes are usually local to cylinder 5: deposits, a lean injector, a wrong plug or internal damage; poor fuel would affect several cylinders.
c: Carbon deposits or glowing particles in cylinder 5
Injector of cylinder 5 delivering too little
Wrong heat range or damaged spark plug
s: Check engine light on
Pinging or knocking under load
Less power, higher consumption

P2341.t: Cylinder 6 Above Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Threshold
P2341.d: Cylinder 6 is the last cylinder of inline-six and V6 engines, and P2341 reports that its share of the knock sensor signal has crossed the limit. Modern knock control adjusts ignition timing for every cylinder on its own, so a single cylinder can run retarded while the others keep optimum spark; the code tells which one keeps knocking. How a manufacturer reports this differs: GM and Saab use P0324 for excessive knock on one cylinder over more than 8 s, while knock on more than one cylinder or an improperly bolted sensor leads Saab to the sensor performance codes P0326/P0331. No public manufacturer document using P2341 was found. Check fuel quality, deposits, the plug and the injector of cylinder 6, and whether a loose part is making noise in that crank window.
c: Fuel octane too low for the engine
Deposits in the combustion chamber of cylinder 6
Loose component or valve train noise read as knock
Lean mixture in cylinder 6 from a restricted injector
s: MIL on
Knocking at full throttle or uphill
Reduced power

P2342.t: Cylinder 7 Above Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Threshold
P2342.d: P2342 applies only to engines with seven or more cylinders, in practice V8s and larger. It says the vibration picked up by the knock sensor during cylinder 7's combustion window has exceeded the threshold. On a V8 each bank usually has its own sensor, so the module has to combine sensor choice and crank angle to blame the right cylinder; noise from a loose bracket or the valve train in that window can mimic knock. Saab's GM-based tables therefore run a separate abnormal-noise check between 2,000 and 8,500 rpm to spot a sensor that is not properly bolted. No manufacturer was found that publishes P2342; GM and Saab report single-cylinder knock as P0324. If knock is real, cylinder 7 needs a look at deposits, plug, injector and compression before damage occurs.
c: Loose bracket, heat shield or valve train noise in cylinder 7's window
Deposits or hot spots in cylinder 7
Knock sensor of that bank loose or wrongly torqued
s: Check engine light on
Possibly audible knocking under load
Less power from retarded ignition

P2343.t: Cylinder 8 Above Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Threshold
P2343.d: P2343 belongs to cylinder 8, the last cylinder of a V8, and is stored when the knock intensity measured in that cylinder's crank-angle window stays above the calibrated limit. The knock control first answers with spark retard for cylinder 8 alone, and on turbocharged engines it may also lower boost; the code marks that this cylinder keeps knocking. Prolonged detonation can melt or hole a piston or crack the head, so the cause matters more than the light. Typical checks are fuel grade, carbon in cylinder 8, plug type and gap, injector delivery and, if the noise is mechanical, the parts near that bank's sensor. No manufacturer publishes P2343 in openly available documents; GM and Saab cover the same case with P0324 (one cylinder knocking for over 8 s).
c: Wrong plug type or gap in cylinder 8
Cylinder 8 running lean from low injector delivery
s: Check engine light on
Pinging or knocking, mostly under load
Reduced power, possibly less boost on turbo engines

P2344.t: Cylinder 9 Above Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Threshold
P2344.d: A ninth cylinder exists only on V10 and V12 engines, so P2344 is confined to a small group of vehicles: V10s such as Ford's 6.8L Triton in E-Series vans, Super Duty pickups and the Excursion, the Dodge Viper and Ram SRT-10, and performance cars from BMW, Audi and Lamborghini, plus the V12s. The code means the knock control has found the vibration level in cylinder 9's combustion window above the limit and is retarding that cylinder. No manufacturer was found that documents P2344 publicly; GM and Saab handle single-cylinder knock under P0324 instead. The usual suspects are deposits, fuel grade, plug, injector and noise sources near the sensor of that bank, examined for cylinder 9 specifically.
c: Deposits or hot spots in cylinder 9
Fuel of too low octane for a high-output engine
Wrong or fouled spark plug in cylinder 9
s: MIL on
Knocking or pinging under heavy load or towing
Reduced power

P2345.t: Cylinder 10 Above Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Threshold
P2345.d: P2345 is the knock code for cylinder 10, the last cylinder of a V10, so it appears mainly on engines such as Ford's 6.8L Triton truck V10, the Viper V10 used by Dodge, and the V10s of BMW M5/M6, Audi and Lamborghini. It sets when the knock signal belonging to cylinder 10's firing window stays over the calibrated limit; the module then keeps that cylinder's spark retarded. On a heavily loaded truck V10, towing, heat and low-octane fuel make real knock more likely, while on high-revving sports engines valve train noise can be mistaken for it. No manufacturer was found that documents P2345 publicly, and GM and Saab use P0324 for the same situation. Misfire on cylinder 10 is reported separately as P0310.
c: High load, towing or high intake temperature with marginal fuel
Valve train noise interpreted as knock
s: Check engine light on
Pinging when towing or climbing
Loss of power

P2346.t: Cylinder 11 Above Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Threshold
P2346.d: Cylinders 11 and 12 exist only on V12 engines, for example BMW's V12 in the 7 and 8 Series, Mercedes-Benz's M120 and its successors, and the V12s of Ferrari, Lamborghini and Aston Martin. P2346 reports that cylinder 11 has knocked above the threshold that the knock control allows in its crank-angle window. With twelve combustions per two crank turns the windows are short, so the module depends on clean crank and sensor signals to assign knock correctly; a fault on the bank sensor or noise from nearby parts can shift the blame. No manufacturer was found that publishes P2346; GM and Saab file a lone knocking cylinder under P0324. Retarded spark on one cylinder costs some power, but continuing knock can destroy the piston.
c: Deposits or hot spots in cylinder 11
Fuel below the required octane rating
Disturbed crank or knock sensor signal shifting the cylinder assignment
s: MIL on
Slight loss of power
Possibly audible pinging

P2347.t: Cylinder 12 Above Knock/Combustion Vibration Sensor Threshold
P2347.d: P2347 ends the per-cylinder knock series that starts with P2336 for cylinder 1; it is the code for cylinder 12 and thus appears only on V12 engines such as those from BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Ferrari or Lamborghini. The engine module has found that the vibration in cylinder 12's combustion window exceeds the threshold and is holding back that cylinder's spark. The J2012 title speaks of a knock or combustion vibration sensor, so the series is not tied to a particular sensor type. No manufacturer was found that documents P2347 publicly; the only bulletin seen for the series, from Stellantis, covers cylinders 1 to 4 of a four-cylinder engine, and GM and Saab use P0324. Work through fuel, deposits, plug and injector of cylinder 12 and check for mechanical noise.
c: Mechanical noise near the sensor of that bank
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power
Possibly knocking under load

P2348.d: A cylinder pressure sensor, usually built into the glow plug of a diesel, reports the combustion pressure of one cylinder so the ECM can trim injection for it. P2348 is the general circuit code for the sensor of cylinder 9, meant for modules that do not split faults into low and high. No manufacturer documents this code publicly: the systems found so far sit on four-cylinder diesels – the GM-built 2.0 CDTI of the Saab 9-5 relies on the split low/high codes, VW's US 2.0 TDI its own P13CE series – and an engine with a ninth cylinder and such sensors is not documented. The text therefore relies on CARB's circuit-monitoring duty for input sensors and on the cylinder-1 analogue P0395. Wiring, connector and sensor are the suspects; the ECM simply stops combustion control for that cylinder.
c: Sensor or glow plug connector of cylinder 9 loose or corroded
Reference, signal or ground wire damaged
s: Check engine light on
Often no noticeable change in driving
Possibly slightly harsher combustion noise

P2349.d: P2349 is the plausibility code for the combustion pressure sensor of cylinder 9: the signal is electrically valid but does not match what the ECM expects for the operating point. CARB requires input sensors to be checked for rationality where feasible, in both directions. A natural test point is overrun, when no fuel burns and the peak pressure should match the pure compression pressure; GM's European diesel in the Saab 9-5 already uses that peak to locate top dead centre. No manufacturer publishes this cylinder-9 code; its counterpart for cylinder 1 is P0396. Likely causes are carbon on the sensing element, a leaking glow plug seat or a plug fitted with the wrong torque, which detunes the sensor. The ECM ignores the signal, and the driver hardly notices anything.
c: Glow plug seat leaking or plug tightened to wrong torque
Genuinely low compression in cylinder 9 distorting the comparison
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable driveability change

P234A.d: P234A means the signal of the cylinder 9 combustion pressure sensor stays below its permitted minimum. No published manufacturer document covers cylinder 9; the closest pattern is the GM-built 2.0 CDTI diesel of the Saab 9-5, whose cylinder 1–4 low codes (P0397 for cylinder 1) set after more than 2 s below threshold with the engine running, checked once per operating cycle, as Type B – the MIL comes on after the second failing trip. A scan tool then shows a peak pressure of 0 kPa. Electrically this points to a lost 5 V reference, a reference shorted to ground or a signal wire touching ground. Saab expects 3 to 12 Ohm between reference and ground at the plug. Combustion control for the cylinder is suspended, which usually goes unnoticed. The high counterpart is P234B.
c: 5 V reference interrupted or shorted to ground
Sensor in the glow plug defective
s: Check engine light after two trips
Peak pressure reads 0 kPa on the scan tool
Driving behaviour mostly unchanged

P234B.d: P234B is stored when the cylinder 9 combustion pressure sensor signal sits above its upper limit. Nobody documents this cylinder-9 code openly, so the description borrows from the Saab 9-5 diesel (GM 2.0 CDTI): its high codes for cylinders 1–4 (P0398 for cylinder 1) need more than 2 s above threshold with the engine running, are tested once per operating cycle and are Type B. The live value then jumps to 10,000 kPa, beyond the normal span of up to 9,000 kPa. A signal pulled up usually means an open signal or ground wire – the input floats high – or a short to voltage on the reference or signal; Saab rates an unplugged connector as the most common finding. CARB demands such out-of-range checks for every input sensor. Like P234A, the code costs combustion control for the cylinder, rarely drivability.
c: Connector at the cylinder 9 glow plug not plugged in
Sensor ground or signal wire interrupted
Reference or signal wire shorted to voltage
s: Check engine light after two trips
Peak pressure shows an implausibly high fixed value
No obvious drivability complaint

P234C.d: P234C covers a cylinder 9 combustion pressure signal that jumps or briefly drops out instead of staying permanently low or permanently high. As an analogue only the Saab 9-5 diesel (a GM 2.0 CDTI) is published: its erratic codes for cylinders 1–4 (P0399 for cylinder 1) react much faster than the low/high codes, already once the signal has left its window for longer than 0.2 s while the engine runs, and they are Type B. Before a new glow plug is fitted, the test plan there verifies a 5 V reference within 4.8 to 5.2 V and less than 5 Ohm on the ground. Loose contacts at the plug connector, a harness rubbing on the cylinder head or electronics that fail when hot are typical. The code tends to come and go; for cylinder 9 no manufacturer documents it.
c: Intermittent contact at the glow plug connector
Harness rubbing on the cylinder head, breaking contact under vibration
Sensor electronics unstable at high temperature
s: Check engine light, often coming and going
Fault stored but hard to reproduce in the workshop

P234D.d: Unlike the sensor circuit codes, P234D judges the pressure itself: the value measured or modelled for cylinder 9 stays below what the ECM expects, while the sensor is electrically in order. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and the cylinder-1 analogue P039A is equally undocumented by code; the description therefore rests on CARB's duty to monitor combustion-sensor engines and on how pressure-sensing glow plugs work. Too little pressure can come from combustion that is weak or missing – an injector delivering short, low compression from a leaking valve or worn rings, a leaking glow plug seat – or from a sensor that has drifted downward. Running is rougher, smoke and consumption may increase, and a misfire code for cylinder 9 often appears as well.
c: Injector of cylinder 9 delivering too little or clogged
Compression loss from valve or piston ring wear
Combustion gas escaping at the glow plug seat
s: Check engine light on
Rough running, especially at idle
More smoke and higher fuel consumption

P234E.d: P234E reports that the pressure determined for cylinder 9 exceeds the expected maximum. No manufacturer documents the cylinder-9 code publicly. The sibling codes for cylinders 1–4 appear in two Audi bulletins for the 2015 S3, a petrol engine: they lit the EPC lamp together with misfire codes and turned out to be a software fault that misjudged combustion, cured by a software update. That shows the codes can be set from a calculated value, not only from a glow plug sensor. On diesels with pressure-sensing glow plugs, a real excess points to too much or too early fuel, for example a dripping injector, or to a sensor reading high. CARB asks combustion-sensor engines for sharper misfire detection. If the ECM shuts the cylinder off, power drops clearly; P234D is the low case.
c: Engine software misjudging combustion (update available at some makers)
Injector of cylinder 9 leaking or injecting too much
s: Warning lamp on, sometimes with misfire codes
Harsh, knocking combustion noise
Loss of power if the cylinder is shut off

P234F.d: P234F flags that the pressure signal of cylinder 9 changes too little: the rise and fall the ECM expects across each combustion cycle is missing or very small. For cylinder 9 there is no manufacturer documentation. In the Saab 9-5 with GM's 2.0 CDTI, the cylinder-1 analogue is P039C, labelled pressure variation too low, with three sub-faults; it reacts after more than 0.2 s out of range with the engine running and is grouped with the erratic code as a signal performance fault. Saab does not explain the exact measurement. A flat signal fits a sensing pin stuck in carbon that no longer passes on the pressure, a sensor that has lost sensitivity, or a cylinder that hardly builds up pressure. Usually only the warning lamp shows; the high counterpart is P2350.
c: Sensing element of the glow plug stuck by carbon
Cylinder 9 builds up little pressure (compression or injection fault)
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in engine behaviour

P2350.d: P2350 is the opposite of P234F: the cylinder 9 pressure signal swings more than plausible, with peaks or steps that do not fit the engine's operating state. No manufacturer publishes the code for cylinder 9. The analogue in Saab's 9-5 diesel workshop data is P039D, labelled as excessive pressure variation for cylinder 1, set as soon as the signal is outside its window for over 0.2 s and treated as a signal performance fault of Type B. A noisy signal comes mostly from the electrical side – interference on an unshielded or chafed signal wire, poor ground, failing sensor electronics. Less often the combustion itself is uneven, for instance through an injector that dribbles after closing. CARB requires such rationality checks of input sensors. Drivers rarely notice anything beyond the MIL.
c: Interference or chafing on the sensor signal wire
Sensor electronics in the glow plug failing
Injector of cylinder 9 dribbling after closing
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable symptoms

P2351.d: P2351 does not concern the sensor but the quality of combustion in cylinder 9, as judged from the pressure trace: the energy released per cycle, or its balance against the other cylinders, falls outside the permitted window. No manufacturer documents the code publicly, nor its cylinder-1 analogue P039E. CARB explains why such a check exists: engines fitted with combustion or combustion-quality sensors, such as homogeneous-charge compression-ignition designs, must catch misfire far more sensitively than others. Typical root causes are a coked or leaking injector, partial loss of compression, an air leak upstream or poor fuel. The engine runs unevenly, smoke rises, and the problem frequently shows up alongside a pressure too low/high code or a cylinder 9 misfire code.
c: Injector of cylinder 9 coked, leaking or sticking
Poor fuel quality or water in the fuel
s: Check engine light on
Uneven running and vibration
Increased smoke and fuel consumption

P2352.d: P2352 is the catch-all code for the electrical circuit of the cylinder 10 combustion pressure sensor, meant for engine computers that make no distinction between low and high. A tenth cylinder exists only on V10 and V12 engines. Under the bank-by-bank numbering of Ford and Audi it is the rearmost cylinder of the second bank; Chrysler counts along the crankshaft, which makes it the last one, at the back, on the even-numbered bank. Publicly, no maker lists this code: the known pressure-sensing glow plug systems sit on four-cylinder diesels, such as VW's US 2.0 TDI with its own codes P13CE to P13E3. CARB wants circuit faults of input sensors watched continuously, sampled at least twice per second. Suspects are the connector, the harness and the sensor itself; meanwhile the ECM lacks combustion feedback for this cylinder.
c: Glow plug/sensor connector of cylinder 10 not fully latched or corroded
Harness branch to the rear cylinder of the bank chafed or heat-damaged
Electronics in the pressure-sensing glow plug failed
s: Check engine light on
Engine usually runs as before
Combustion noise may become slightly harder

P2353.d: P2353 means the cylinder 10 pressure sensor delivers a signal that is electrically within limits but not believable for the current operating point – the reading is skewed, not cut off. CARB expects input sensors to be checked for such rationality faults, not just for open or shorted circuits. How an ECM can do this is visible in Saab's 9-5 diesel: it locates top dead centre from the pressure peak on overrun, corrects the offset of the crank trigger wheel and keeps the result in EEPROM. A drifted sensor, a heater rod that no longer passes pressure on to the measuring diaphragm, or a replacement plug whose calibration does not suit the engine would all fail such a test. No manufacturer documents P2353 for cylinder 10. The engine runs normally; only pressure-based control of this cylinder is lost.
c: Sensor offset drifted with age and heat
Carbon on the heater rod hampers pressure transfer to the diaphragm
Replacement glow plug with calibration for another engine
s: Check engine light on
No noticeable change in engine behaviour

P2354.d: P2354 reports that the signal of the cylinder 10 pressure sensor stays below its lower limit. The pattern known for this fault type comes from Saab's 9-5 diesel with its GM 2.0 engine: its low codes for the four cylinders (P0397 on cylinder 1) demand that a running engine sees the signal under the threshold for longer than 2 s, run once per trip and are Type B, so the MIL waits for a second failed trip. For cylinder 10 no manufacturer publishes the code. A quick check from that procedure: with the sensor connector unplugged, the scan tool should show more than 10,000 kPa; a lower reading points to a signal wire shorted to ground. A missing 5 V reference pulls the value down as well. On V10 engines cylinder 10 is the last one of its bank, so the plug is often awkward to reach.
c: Signal wire shorted to ground, e.g. chafed on the cylinder head
5 V reference interrupted or shorted to ground
Internal fault of the pressure-sensing glow plug
s: Check engine light after the second faulty trip
Scan tool shows peak pressure near zero for cylinder 10
Driving behaviour normally unchanged

P2355.d: P2355 means the cylinder 10 pressure signal is stuck above its upper limit. Taking the Saab 9-5 diesel with GM's 2.0 engine as the model, the Type B high codes for its four cylinders (P0398 on cylinder 1) wait until the signal has stayed above the threshold for over 2 s with the engine running. An interrupted signal or low reference circuit lets the input float upward, and the scan tool then displays a fixed 10,000 kPa instead of a value inside the normal 0 to 9,000 kPa. Saab's way to tell wiring from sensor: bridge signal and low reference at the harness plug with a fused jumper; the reading must then fall below 50 kPa, otherwise the fault lies in the harness or the ECM. No manufacturer documents P2355 for cylinder 10 itself; P2354 is the low counterpart.
c: Signal or low reference wire open, connector pulled off
Signal or reference shorted to a voltage source
Sensor electronics driving the output high
s: Check engine light after two trips
Peak pressure for cylinder 10 frozen at a very high value
No obvious driveability complaint

P2356.d: P2356 points to a cylinder 10 pressure signal that drops out or jumps for moments instead of failing permanently. No manufacturer covers cylinder 10 publicly. For four-cylinder TDI engines, a 2014 Volkswagen bulletin lays out a sensible order: first push and pull the glow plug connector – a felt click or a plug that comes off easily is already the fault – then swap the plug with a neighbouring cylinder to see whether the code moves with it, and finally move the harness while watching the maximum cylinder pressure value. On a V10 with bank-wise numbering the obvious swap partner is cylinder 9 in the same bank. According to VW, the MIL can need a second drive cycle. In Saab's GM-built diesel, the erratic codes react after only 0.2 s out of range.
c: Connector not fully seated, contact lost under vibration
Wire break inside the insulation or chafe point that opens intermittently
Glow plug sensor electronics failing intermittently
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Fault hard to reproduce in the workshop

P2357.d: P2357 is not about the wiring: the pressure measured or modelled for cylinder 10 itself is below expectation while the sensor circuit tests fine. No manufacturer publishes this code, and the cylinder-1 counterpart P039A is equally undocumented. On a V10 such an evaluation also has to know when low pressure is intended – Audi's R8 V10, for instance, cuts injection and ignition on a whole bank under light and moderate load. Outside such phases, too little pressure suggests weak combustion from an injector delivering short, compression lost through a valve or worn rings, gas escaping past the glow plug seal, or a sensor reading low. Expect rough idle, more smoke and higher consumption; the cylinder 10 misfire code P0310 frequently comes along.
c: Injector of cylinder 10 delivering too little fuel
Compression loss from valve leakage or worn rings
Combustion gas leaking past the glow plug seal
s: Check engine light on
Rough running, mainly at idle
More smoke and higher fuel consumption

P2358.d: P2358 indicates that the pressure determined for cylinder 10 exceeds its upper expectation. No manufacturer documents this cylinder-10 code. The closest published cases are Audi bulletins for the 2015 S3 with the 2.0 TFSI engine code CYFB: there the pressure-too-high codes of cylinders 1 to 4 (P039B00 to P03B900) showed up with misfire codes and P130A00, the entry for a cylinder the ECM has hidden, that is, switched off. The EPC lamp lit. Faulty software was to blame; an update to part number 8V0 906 259H, version 0002, cured it. So a petrol engine without glow plugs uses this family too. On a diesel with pressure sensors, a true excess points to surplus or early fuel, such as a leaking injector, or to a sensor whose output has crept upward. With the cylinder shut off, power drops noticeably.
c: Engine control software misjudging combustion (update available)
Injector of cylinder 10 leaking or over-delivering
s: Warning lamp on, sometimes together with misfire codes
Hard, knocking combustion noise
Reduced power if the cylinder is switched off

P2359.d: P2359 means the pressure trace of cylinder 10 changes too little: the build-up through compression and combustion is flatter than the ECM expects. No manufacturer documents this code for cylinder 10. Saab's 9-5 diesel lists the cylinder-1 analogue P039C with three sub-types, 00, 01 and 02, and counts it as a signal performance fault that reacts after 0.2 s out of range; what separates the sub-types is not explained there. BorgWarner's sensor glow plug passes the pressure through a flexible heater rod onto a measuring diaphragm, so a rod jammed by carbon or a stiff diaphragm flattens the curve. A cylinder with hardly any compression looks the same. In a V10 firing 1-6-5-10-2-7-3-8-4-9, as Ford's 6.8 L and Audi's 5.2 do, cylinder 10 is the fourth to fire.
c: Heater rod stuck in carbon, pressure no longer reaches the diaphragm
Cylinder 10 builds up hardly any pressure
s: Check engine light on
Engine behaviour usually unchanged

P235A.d: P235A is the counterpart to P2359: the cylinder 10 pressure signal swings more than the combustion can explain, with spikes or steps from one cycle to the next. A public manufacturer description of this tenth-cylinder code does not exist. In the Saab 9-5 diesel the cylinder-1 version P039D belongs to the signal performance group; it is Type B and responds within 0.2 s of leaving its window. Electrical noise is the usual reason: a signal wire with damaged shielding or chafed insulation, a poor engine ground, or unstable sensor electronics. Genuinely irregular combustion is rarer, for instance when an injector dribbles after closing. VW's TDI bulletin recommends watching the maximum pressure reading while flexing the harness – jumps then betray the wiring. The warning lamp is mostly the only sign.
c: Interference on a damaged or poorly shielded signal wire
Poor engine ground or corroded ground point
Sensor electronics delivering an unstable signal
Injector dribbling after closing, combustion varies
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable symptoms

P235B.d: P235B rates how well cylinder 10 burns, derived from its pressure curve – for instance from the energy each working cycle releases or from how it compares with the other nine cylinders of a V10. No manufacturer documents this code, nor the cylinder-1 equivalent P039E. CARB supplies the background: diesel passenger cars equipped with combustion or combustion quality sensors must, from model year 2010, flag misfire once it reaches 5 % of firings, counted over 1,000 revolutions – far tighter than the continuous-misfire rule other diesels long had to meet. Coked or worn injectors, partial compression loss, intake air leaks or poor fuel degrade combustion. The engine shakes, smoke and consumption rise, and the code tends to appear together with P2357 or P2358 or with the cylinder 10 misfire code P0310.
c: Coked or worn injector of cylinder 10
Air leak in the intake tract
s: Check engine light on
Uneven running and vibration
Increased smoke and fuel consumption

P235C.d: P235C stands for a fault in the circuit of the cylinder 11 combustion pressure sensor without saying whether the signal is too low or too high. A V10 ends at cylinder 10, so only twelve-cylinder engines have an eleventh one. With bank-wise numbering, cylinder 11 is the second-to-last of the second bank, between 10 and 12. Production engines combining twelve cylinders with combustion pressure sensors are not on public record, and no manufacturer documents P235C; the description rests on CARB's circuit monitoring rules and the cylinder-1 counterpart P0395. In Saab's 9-5 diesel the ECM wires each such sensor with a 5 V supply, a ground return and a signal line, and a fault in any of the three can trigger the code. Driving is normally unaffected.
c: Connector at the cylinder 11 glow plug loose or corroded
Reference, low reference or signal wire damaged
Sensor electronics in the glow plug failed
s: Check engine light on
No change in how the engine runs

P235D.d: P235D is set when the combustion pressure reported for cylinder 11 is electrically valid yet does not fit the engine's state – for example a compression peak that is clearly off while no fuel is being injected. Only engines with twelve cylinders have a cylinder 11, and none of them is publicly documented with pressure sensors, so no manufacturer describes this code. CARB demands rationality checks of input components in both directions, reading too high and too low. BorgWarner's piezo-resistive pressure glow plug is calibrated and programmed specifically for each customer: a plug taken from another engine application can therefore read wrong while being electrically sound. Carbon on the heater rod or a leaking seal at the plug seat are other likely causes. The cylinder-1 counterpart is P0396; drivers seldom notice more than the lamp.
c: Deposits on the heater rod distort the reading
Glow plug with calibration for another engine application fitted
Seal at the glow plug seat leaking
s: Check engine light on
Driving behaviour practically unchanged

P235E.d: With P235E the signal of the cylinder 11 combustion pressure sensor is too low, typically close to zero. No manufacturer documents this code, as twelve-cylinder engines with pressure sensors are not described publicly; the analogue is P0397 for cylinder 1 in Saab's 9-5 diesel, where a low signal must persist beyond 2 s with the engine running before the Type B code is logged. The first check there concerns the supply: 4.8 to 5.2 V on the reference terminal with ignition on; less voltage means the reference is interrupted or shorted to ground. Across reference and low reference of the plug itself, 3 to 12 Ohm are expected. A signal wire chafed through to the cylinder head also drags the input down. With bank-wise numbering the plug sits between cylinders 10 and 12, so their harness branches deserve a look too.
c: 5 V reference interrupted or shorted to ground
Signal wire chafed through to ground
Sensor glow plug outside its 3–12 Ohm specification
s: Warning lamp after the second faulty trip
Peak pressure of cylinder 11 shown as zero

P235F.d: P235F is logged when the cylinder 11 pressure sensor signal remains above its plausible maximum. Only twelve-cylinder engines have this cylinder, and no maker documents the code; the Saab 9-5 diesel serves as the model with P0398 for cylinder 1, a Type B code that needs more than 2 s over the threshold. In that wiring layout three faults produce a high reading: an open low reference, an open signal wire and a reference or signal shorted to battery voltage. Saab's test plan therefore measures less than 5 Ohm between the low reference and ground, and it requires infinite resistance between every sensor terminal and the plug body – broken insulation inside the glow plug would also distort the signal. The cylinder runs on without pressure feedback; P235E is the opposite case.
c: Low reference (ground) wire of the sensor open
Signal wire interrupted or connector off
Reference or signal shorted to battery voltage
Insulation failure between sensor terminals and plug body
s: Check engine light after two trips
Implausibly high fixed pressure value for cylinder 11

P2360.d: P2360 records a cylinder 11 combustion pressure signal that is unsteady – brief dropouts or spikes that do not last long enough for a low or high code. Since only twelve-cylinder engines have cylinder 11, and none is documented with pressure sensors, the code has no public manufacturer description. Saab's 9-5 diesel shows how quickly such a monitor acts: the erratic code for cylinder 1, P0399, is a Type B code that needs only a 0.2 s excursion beyond the permitted band with the engine turning. Contact problems dominate – a connector not fully latched, fretting corrosion on the terminals, a harness touching hot parts. Electronics in the plug head that only drop out once the engine is warm are another candidate. The fault often vanishes and returns days later.
c: Fretting corrosion or loose fit at the connector terminals
Sensor electronics in the plug head failing when warm
s: Check engine light that comes and goes
Fault stored without a lasting complaint

P2361.d: P2361 says the combustion pressure of cylinder 11 is too low although the sensor works electrically. No manufacturer documents this code, since no twelve-cylinder engine with combustion pressure sensing is publicly described. What the code judges is the cylinder itself: if its peak stays clearly below that of comparable cylinders or below the expected value, combustion or compression is lacking. Candidates are an injector with reduced flow or a clogged nozzle, worn rings or a burnt valve that lowers compression, a leak at the glow plug seat, or a sensor drifting low. A compression or leak-down test separates mechanical faults from injection faults. The engine runs unevenly, particularly at idle, and the cylinder 11 misfire code P0311 may be stored as well.
c: Injector of cylinder 11 with reduced flow or clogged nozzle
Worn piston rings or burnt valve lowering compression
Leak at the glow plug seat
s: Check engine light on
Uneven running, especially at idle
Possibly misfire code for cylinder 11 as well

P2362.d: P2362 is stored when cylinder 11 shows more combustion pressure than the ECM considers plausible. No manufacturer publishes it, because no twelve-cylinder engine with cylinder pressure monitoring is documented. On a diesel, excess pressure usually comes from the fuel side: an injector that leaks or hangs open adds fuel, injection timed too early raises the peak, and a sensor drifting upward fakes the effect. That this code family can also be triggered by software logic is shown by Audi's 2015 S3: a December 2018 bulletin, superseding one from 2015, cured the cylinder 1–4 versions with an ECM update. Sustained high peak pressure loads pistons and head gasket, so an ECM may shut the cylinder off. Harsh combustion noise and, after a shutdown, reduced power are the signs.
c: Injector of cylinder 11 leaking or hanging open
Engine control software misjudging the pressure
Injection timing too early for this cylinder
s: Warning lamp on
Harsh combustion noise
Loss of power if the cylinder is shut off

P2363.d: P2363 flags a cylinder 11 pressure signal with too little swing between its low point and the combustion peak. No manufacturer documents this code; cylinder 11 only exists on twelve-cylinder engines, none of which is publicly known with pressure-sensing glow plugs. Saab's 9-5 diesel files the related P039C for cylinder 1 as a Type B signal fault. A flat signal is mostly a sensor matter – the piezo-resistive element has lost sensitivity, or deposits hold the heater rod in place – while a genuine lack of compression in the cylinder is less likely. In Lamborghini's Aventador V12, firing 1-12-4-9-2-11-6-7-3-10-5-8, cylinder 11 is the sixth to fire; the older Lamborghini V12 fired it last. Apart from the warning lamp the driver rarely notices anything.
c: Piezo-resistive sensing element has lost sensitivity
Deposits holding the heater rod in place
s: Check engine light on
Engine runs normally in most cases

P2364.d: P2364 is stored when the pressure signal of cylinder 11 varies too strongly, from cycle to cycle or within one cycle. No maker publishes this code. Saab's 9-5 diesel has the analogous P039D for cylinder 1, a Type B signal fault reacting to 0.2 s outside its window. Excessive variation can stem from interference on the signal line, a ground connection whose resistance keeps changing, or moisture in the connector, but also from a cylinder whose combustion really scatters – an injector with an unstable spray pattern, or poor fuel. A variation limit is one way to meet CARB's demand for plausibility tests of input sensors. The MIL is usually the only symptom; P2363 covers the opposite, flat signal, and P2360 the short dropouts.
c: Interference coupling into the signal line
Ground connection with changing contact resistance
Moisture in the glow plug connector
s: Check engine light on
No noticeable effect on driving

P2365.d: P2365 means the ECM judges combustion in cylinder 11 to be poor, based on the pressure signal rather than on crankshaft speed alone. No manufacturer publishes this code; twelve-cylinder engines with pressure-sensing glow plugs are not documented. BorgWarner names the purpose of such sensors: letting the controller adjust injection quantity and timing per cylinder in closed loop. If the measured combustion of one cylinder stays outside its window despite that correction, a code of this kind results. CARB ties combustion sensors to stricter misfire detection on diesels. Causes include a fouled or leaking injector, compression loss, an intake air leak or contaminated fuel. Uneven running and more smoke are typical, often alongside P2361, P2362 or the misfire code P0311.
c: Fouled or leaking injector of cylinder 11
s: Check engine light on
Uneven running and vibration
More smoke from the exhaust

P2366.d: P2366 is the general circuit code for the combustion pressure sensor of cylinder 12; it does not tell whether the signal sits too low or too high. Twelve is the highest number on a V12 or W12. Whether a maker counts bank by bank or along the crankshaft, number 1 is normally the front cylinder, which places 12 at the opposite end of the engine. No twelve-cylinder engine with pressure-sensing glow plugs is publicly documented, so no manufacturer describes P2366; CARB's demand for circuit continuity checks and the cylinder-1 code P0395 frame it. A 2014 Volkswagen bulletin for its 2.0 TDI advises a push-and-pull test of the plug connector before any part is replaced, since a poorly seated connector is often the real culprit. The engine usually runs as before.
c: Glow plug connector not fully latched or loose
Damaged wire in the harness branch to the rearmost cylinder
s: Check engine light on
Pressure reading for cylinder 12 missing or fixed in live data

P2367.d: With P2367 the cylinder 12 pressure signal is electrically within its limits but makes no sense for the operating point. A natural yardstick is the motored cycle: on overrun nothing burns, so the curve has to peak at top dead centre. Saab's 9-5 diesel uses exactly this peak position to locate true TDC and keeps in EEPROM how far the crank trigger wheel sits off its nominal angle – which shows how closely the ECM follows each sensor. A sensor whose peak shifts, whose zero has drifted or whose seat lets gas escape would fail such a check. No manufacturer documents P2367, because no twelve-cylinder engine with this sensor is public; the cylinder-1 equivalent is P0396. In most cases only the warning lamp is noticed.
c: Sensor zero point or gain drifted
Combustion gas escaping at the glow plug seat
Glow plug of a different calibration fitted
s: Check engine light on
Implausible peak pressure value for cylinder 12 compared with the others

P2368.d: P2368 is stored when the voltage coming from the cylinder 12 pressure sensor stays below its lower limit. As the last cylinder of a V12 or W12, it has no publicly documented application, so Saab's 9-5 diesel code P0397 serves as the template. There, the scan tool shows peak combustion pressure in a normal band of 0 to 9,000 kPa; a signal wire touching ground or a missing 5 V reference pins the value at the bottom. In Saab's test an intact signal path jumps above 10,000 kPa once the plug is disconnected – a reading that stays low with the connector off therefore points to the harness rather than the sensor. Being a Type B code there, it needs two faulty trips before the lamp lights. The opposite case is P2369.
c: 5 V reference open or shorted to ground
Sensor electronics in the glow plug head failed low
s: Warning lamp after two trips with the fault
Peak pressure of cylinder 12 stuck near zero

P2369.d: P2369 means the cylinder 12 pressure input reads above its upper limit. Like the rest of the cylinder-12 family, it is not documented publicly by any maker. On Saab's 9-5 diesel the matching cylinder-1 code P0398 is set after more than 2 s above the threshold and is evaluated once per operating cycle. An unplugged sensor drives the value past 10,000 kPa, so to the ECM an open signal or open low-reference wire looks the same as a short to voltage. Saab tells the cases apart with a fused jumper between signal and low reference: the reading should then drop below 50 kPa; if it stays high, the fault lies in the wiring towards the ECM, otherwise in the plug. While the code is active, the ECM has no usable pressure feedback from this cylinder.
c: Signal shorted to a voltage source
Glow plug sensor electronics outputting a fixed high value
s: Check engine light after the second trip
Cylinder 12 shows an impossibly high pressure in live data

P236A.d: P236A covers brief, irregular disturbances of the cylinder 12 pressure signal – faults that come and go without settling into a lasting low or high state. Its model is the Saab 9-5 diesel code P0399, which responds as soon as the signal stays outside its band longer than 0.2 s. No manufacturer publishes P236A itself, since no twelve-cylinder engine with pressure glow plugs is documented. Volkswagen's 2014 bulletin for 2.0 TDI engines gives a practical routine for such cases: watch the maximum pressure value of every cylinder while flexing harness and connectors, and swap the suspect glow plug with one from a neighbouring cylinder. If the fault follows the plug, the plug is bad; if not, the harness is. Up to two drive cycles may pass before the lamp returns.
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the plug connector
Harness rubbing through under engine vibration
Glow plug sensor with intermittent internal fault
s: Warning lamp that switches on and off over several days
Pressure value of cylinder 12 jumps when the harness is moved

P236B.d: P236B reports that cylinder 12 builds too little combustion pressure while its sensor circuit itself is in order. No manufacturer documents the code, because no V12 or W12 with cylinder pressure measurement has been made public. A weak peak means this cylinder lacks air, fuel or sealing: a valve that does not close fully, a worn ring pack, a head gasket leaking towards a neighbour, or an injector delivering too little. Where cylinders are numbered bank by bank, 12 shares its bank with 7 to 11, so a compression test across that whole bank is worthwhile. A gas leak past the sealing element of the pressure glow plug also lowers the value. Rough idle and the misfire code P0312 often come with it; P236C is the deviation in the other direction.
c: Intake or exhaust valve of cylinder 12 not sealing
Worn piston rings or head gasket leak
Gas leaking past the glow plug seal
s: Check engine light on
Rough idle and vibration
Misfire code for cylinder 12 stored as well

P236C.d: P236C flags combustion pressure in cylinder 12 above its allowed value. A public twelve-cylinder application does not exist. That a code of this kind need not involve a pressure sensor at all is shown by its cylinder-1 to -4 relatives P039B, P03A5, P03AF and P03B9 on Audi's 2015 S3 with the CYFB petrol engine: faulty ECM software logged misfires in its primary detection window, switched on the EPC lamp and shut a cylinder off (P130A00); new ECM software solved it. On a diesel with real pressure sensing, a dripping injector, too much pilot fuel or a sensor drifting upward are the usual suspects. High peaks strain pistons, rings and gasket, so cutting the cylinder with reduced power is a plausible protective reaction.
c: Injector dripping or delivering too much pilot fuel
s: EPC or check engine lamp on
Loss of power when the cylinder is switched off
Harder combustion noise

P236D.d: P236D is stored when the cylinder 12 pressure trace swings too little – the curve stays flatter than compression and combustion ought to make it. No manufacturer documents this code for a twelve-cylinder engine. In Saab's 9-5 diesel the comparable cylinder-1 code P039C exists in three sub-variants, 00, 01 and 02, a sign that the ECM tells apart several ways in which a signal can be too weak. The likely culprits sit in the sensor: in BorgWarner's design a flexible heater rod passes the pressure on to a measuring diaphragm, so carbon that grips the rod dampens the signal, and ageing circuitry in the head of the plug lowers its amplification. If compression itself were missing, P236B would be the more likely entry. Driving is normally unaffected.
c: Carbon deposits restricting the heater rod
s: Check engine light on
Flat pressure curve for cylinder 12 in live data

P236E.d: P236E means the pressure signal of cylinder 12 scatters more than the ECM tolerates, either within one cycle or from one cycle to the next. No manufacturer publishes the code; the reference is Saab's P039D for cylinder 1, a Type B fault that needs only 0.2 s outside its window. Two groups of causes are possible. Electrical ones make the trace noisy: interference coupled into the signal wire, or a low-reference contact whose resistance changes with vibration. Combustion-related ones make the cylinder really unsteady: an injector whose delivery varies shot by shot, air in the fuel, or a sticking valve. Live data that are noisy even on overrun, when nothing burns, point to the electrical side. Drivers notice slight roughness at most.
c: Injector delivery varying from shot to shot
s: Check engine light on
Occasional slight roughness

P236F.d: P236F is the ECM's verdict that combustion in cylinder 12 falls short, judged from the evaluated pressure curve rather than from a single limit. No manufacturer documents it, as no twelve-cylinder engine with cylinder pressure sensing is public. BorgWarner states that its pressure glow plug lets the controller correct, cylinder by cylinder, how much fuel is injected and when, with the measured pressure as feedback. A performance code of this type follows when that trimming has used up its range for one cylinder and the result is still off target. For diesels, CARB links combustion sensors to more demanding misfire monitoring. Worn or coked injectors, poor compression, a restricted intake or contaminated fuel are typical findings. Rough running, extra smoke and P0312 may appear alongside.
c: Injector of cylinder 12 coked or worn
s: Check engine light on
Rough running
More visible exhaust smoke

P2370.t: Fuel Volume Regulator B Control Circuit/Open
P2370.d: A fuel volume regulator is the solenoid valve at the high-pressure pump that decides how much of the pump's stroke reaches the rail. Regulator B only exists where a second valve or second pump is fitted – the 5.2 litre V10 of Audi and Lamborghini, for instance, has two cam-driven high-pressure pumps for its two rails. No manufacturer documents P2370 publicly; GM's 2025 diesel table handles a second metering valve under P233A–P233C instead. The A counterparts show the logic: Ford wires its gasoline FVR with both high and low side to the PCM and monitors it continuously, and Ford's 2023 diesel sees an open valve as 2.8–4.8 V at the driver while the valve is off. Without current, delivery from pump B depends on the valve's resting state.
c: Connector at regulator B loose or corroded
s: Check engine light on
Rail pressure deviation and possible reduced power
Hard starting

P2371.t: Fuel Volume Regulator B Control Circuit Performance
P2371.d: P2371 is a functional fault of the second fuel volume regulator: the control circuit works electrically, but the valve does not achieve what the ECM asks of it. No manufacturer publishes a definition for regulator B, so the A side helps. Deutz's EMR controller, for example, compares the regulator current with its set point and records separate faults when it stays above or below it, plus a plausibility check of the current. Ford's 2023 diesel uses its P0002 for a different case – the driver stage in the ECM getting hotter than 170 °C. CARB also requires a fault when fuel pressure control reaches its limits and the commanded pressure can no longer be delivered. A sticking valve, dirt in the fuel or a worn pump are the usual causes.
c: Regulator B valve sticking from dirt or wear
s: Check engine light on
Rail pressure fluctuates or misses its target
Reduced power under load

P2372.t: Fuel Volume Regulator B Control Circuit Low
P2372.d: P2372 says the line driving fuel volume regulator B is pulled too low, as a rule by contact with ground. No manufacturer documents this B code publicly; it mirrors P0003 on regulator A. Ford's 2023 diesel detects that condition with the valve switched off: the voltage reported by the driver chip then falls below 2.8 V, where about 5 V would be normal. Deutz's EMR controller files a ground short on the feeding (high-side) wire of its volume control valve under P0003-00. Which side the short touches matters: on the feed side the valve loses its current, on the switched ground side it can be energised all the time, so delivery of pump B no longer follows the command. Chafed harness sections near hot engine parts are the classic finding.
c: Control wire chafed through to ground
Internal short in the regulator coil
s: Check engine light on
Rail pressure too high or too low depending on the affected side
Limp-home with reduced power

P2373.t: Fuel Volume Regulator B Control Circuit High
P2373.d: P2373 points to too much voltage or current in the control circuit of fuel volume regulator B, typically from a short to battery voltage or a shorted coil. No manufacturer publishes the B version; P0004 on regulator A is the model. Ford's 2023 diesel sets that code when the energised valve draws more than 3.7 A, while 2.2 A is the normal maximum. Deutz's EMR controller lists a short to battery on the high side as P0004-00 and treats critically high output current separately. Ford's gasoline summary explains why ECMs guard this circuit closely: the coil can overheat and fail when battery voltage sits on it permanently. A protecting driver switches off, so regulator B stops metering and rail pressure drifts, often with reduced power.
c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Regulator coil with shorted turns drawing excess current
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power or limp-home mode
Rail pressure deviation codes stored as well

P2374.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor B Circuit
P2374.d: P2374 covers any wiring or sensor-side failure of a second pressure sensor mounted upstream of a compressor. Where the letter B belongs is the manufacturer's choice; on parallel twin-turbo V engines, where each turbocharger serves one cylinder bank, a second inlet sensor for the other compressor is the obvious candidate. No manufacturer documents P2374 publicly – GM's supercharged V8 (P012B–P012D) and Ford's 2023 diesels (P012A) only use A codes. Ford's digital SENT sensor shows how such a general code can arise: it is set when the sensor itself signals an internal error or its data stay beyond a threshold for 5 s, while a lost data link counts separately as a U code. The ECM then substitutes a value, usually close to ambient pressure, and may limit boost on that side.
c: Connector or wire of sensor B open, corroded or shorted
Sensor B reports an internal error
s: Check engine light on
Reduced boost or power

P2375.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P2375.d: With P2375 the signal of compressor inlet pressure sensor B is electrically valid but implausible – stuck, offset or out of step with the other pressure values. No manufacturer publishes the B code; GM's 2018 table for the supercharged LT4 V8 describes the A counterpart P012B in detail. After a long enough engine-off period all induction pressures have equalised, so the reading must lie in the normal atmospheric range; with the engine turning between 400 and 6,200 rpm it is weighed against models of airflow, manifold pressure and throttle, where single model errors above 30 kPa count. GM rates the fault Type B, two trips. On a twin-turbo engine a clogged filter on one side or a leaking duct to compressor B can trigger it as readily as a drifting sensor.
c: Air filter on the side of compressor B clogged
Leaking or collapsed duct ahead of compressor B
s: Check engine light after two trips
Uneven boost between the two turbochargers
Reduced power

P2376.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor B Circuit Low
P2376.d: P2376 is set when the output voltage of compressor inlet pressure sensor B drops below its lower limit. No maker documents the B code publicly; GM's A version P012C on the supercharged LT4 gives an idea of the scale. There the threshold is 3 % of the 5 V reference, equal to roughly 6 kPa – a value no intake can reach in reality. The check runs continuously with one sample every 12.5 ms and fails once 320 of 400 samples are below the limit, so a steady fault is caught within a five-second window; the code is Type B. Typical reasons are a signal lead touching ground, a broken 5 V feed or a dead sensor. The ECM falls back on a substitute value and may cap boost on that compressor.
c: Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground
5 V reference to sensor B open
s: Check engine light on
Live data show an inlet pressure far below ambient
Possible boost limitation

P2377.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor B Circuit High
P2377.d: P2377 means sensor B ahead of the compressor delivers a voltage above its upper limit. Publicly no manufacturer defines this B code, so GM's P012D for the supercharged LT4 serves as a reference: it trips above 97 % of the 5 V reference, which equals about 124 kPa at that sensor, again with 320 failed samples out of 400 at 12.5 ms intervals and Type B. Upstream of a compressor the pressure cannot rise far above ambient, so such a reading is not physical. Typical faults are a signal wire touching the 5 V supply or battery voltage and an interrupted sensor ground, after which the output rises to the reference. Moisture that has crept into the connector can also create a path to the supply. P2376 is the opposite low-voltage case.
c: Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Sensor ground of sensor B open
Moisture bridging terminals in the connector
s: Check engine light on
Implausibly high inlet pressure in live data

P2378.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2378.d: P2378 records a signal from compressor inlet pressure sensor B that jumps or briefly drops out without staying beyond a limit. No manufacturer documents it publicly, and even for the A sensor a dedicated erratic code is rare: GM's LT4 table catches short spikes only through the counting window of its low and high checks (320 of 400 samples), and Ford's 2023 diesels fold faults of their digital sensor into P012A. An erratic monitor therefore has to look for brief limit violations or pressure changes faster than air in the intake can produce. Loose terminals, a harness touched by the hot turbocharger housing and moisture in the connector are typical. The fault tends to come and go; the ECM uses a substitute value while it is present.
c: Harness damaged by heat from the turbocharger
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Brief hesitation under boost

P2379.t: O2 Sensor Out of Range During Deceleration (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P2379.d: P2379 covers the oxygen sensor behind the catalyst on bank 2 at the moment the injectors are shut off on a closed throttle: the exhaust is then close to fresh air, and a sensor whose reading stays outside the expected lean window is suspect. No manufacturer documents P2379 publicly. The nearest published logic is GM's bank 1 code P232F on the 2023 6.6L L5P, which compares the O2 value of the rear NOx sensor with the front one during overrun (window +3.01 to −3.18 %, Type B); that engine has no second bank. Ford checks the same sensor during fuel cut but reports under P013C, P014A or P2272/P2273. CARB asks at least for a rich-to-lean check of rear sensors in fuel shut-off. Code lists also give P239F this title. The car drives normally; the light points to sensor ageing or an exhaust leak.
c: Bank 2 downstream sensor aged or contaminated, reacting too little to fuel cut
Exhaust leak near the bank 2 rear sensor diluting or distorting the sample
Chafed sensor lead or corroded connector on the bank 2 rear sensor
Leaking injector on bank 2 keeping fuel in the exhaust during overrun
s: Check engine light on
No noticeable change in how the car drives
Downstream O2 reading on bank 2 stays high during coasting in live data

P237A.t: O2 Sensor Exhaust Sample Error (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P237A.d: P237A says the rear oxygen sensor of bank 1 is not getting, or not reporting, a representative sample of exhaust: its reading does not fit the gas that should be flowing past it after the catalyst, typically because outside air enters through a leak or the sensing element is no longer exposed properly. No manufacturer documents P237A publicly. Volkswagen describes the front-sensor counterpart P2414 for the 2014 Golf with signal windows of 3.10 to 4.81 V and 2.5 to 3.2 V, which gives an idea of how such a plausibility check is built. CARB requires rear sensors to be monitored for faults that would spoil their use in catalyst and fuel control monitoring. P2414/P2415 cover sensor 1; code lists repeat this title under P23A0. Drivability is normally unaffected, but catalyst diagnosis becomes unreliable.
c: Leak at a flange, joint or cracked pipe ahead of the bank 1 rear sensor drawing in air
Rear sensor element damaged, coated or loose in its boss
Contaminated or blocked reference air path of the sensor (wiring or connector)
s: Check engine light on
Catalyst monitor not completing or reporting implausible results
Possible ticking exhaust noise from a leak

P237B.t: O2 Sensor Exhaust Sample Error (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P237B.d: P237B is the bank 2 version of the sample check on the post-catalyst oxygen sensor and therefore only appears on engines with two exhaust banks, mostly V6 and V8 units with a separate downstream sensor on each side. The ECM decides that what the sensor reports cannot be genuine exhaust from that bank, for example because a leak at the second-bank pipe lets air in or the probe is mounted badly. No manufacturer documents P237B publicly; a published example of the method exists only for the front sensor, Volkswagen's P2414 on the 2014 Golf. CARB demands monitoring of rear sensors because the catalyst check relies on them. Related codes are P237A for bank 1 and P2415 for the bank 2 front sensor; code lists use this title again for P23A1. Inspecting the bank 2 exhaust for leaks comes first.
c: Air leak in the bank 2 exhaust between catalyst and rear sensor
Bank 2 rear sensor damaged, poisoned or not seated correctly
Rear sensors of bank 1 and bank 2 swapped at the connectors after a repair
s: Check engine light on
Bank 2 catalyst monitor incomplete or failing
Engine runs as usual

P237C.t: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Control Circuit/Open
P237C.d: Some hybrids route the exhaust through a coolant heat exchanger after a cold start to warm the engine and cabin sooner, and flap A sends the gas around it once heat is no longer wanted. P237C is set when the drive circuit of that bypass actuator shows an open or a general circuit fault. Ford uses it on its full hybrids: on the Maverick 2.5L of 2022 and 2023, SSM 51921 traces P237C with P237D and P2C22 to water inside the heat exchanger, which is replaced; on 2021–2023 F-150 3.5L PowerBoost trucks built up to 1 March 2023, SSM 52050 blames the bypass control valve and replaces the muffler inlet pipe, while SSM 53003 offers an actuator kit. The bulletins report the MIL lit. P237D and P237E narrow the fault to low or high; P23A2 is valve B.
c: Water inside the heat exchanger assembly or actuator (Ford Maverick SSM 51921)
Bypass valve actuator with open winding or failed electronics
Broken wire or loose connector in the hot area under the vehicle
s: Check engine light on
Engine and cabin may warm up more slowly in cold weather
Further heat exchanger codes such as P2C22 stored alongside

P237D.t: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Control Circuit Low
P237D.d: P237D concerns the same drive line as P237C, the one that operates bypass flap A of an exhaust heat recovery unit, but here the module measures a voltage that sits too low – the usual picture of a control wire touching ground or an actuator shorted internally. Moisture in a connector under the car can produce exactly that. Ford names P237D in two full-hybrid bulletins: SSM 51921 for 2.5L Maverick hybrids built for model years 2022–23, where water inside the heat exchanger is the cause and the unit is renewed, and SSM 53003 for the PowerBoost F-150 hybrid of model years 2021 to 2023, which points to the heat exchanger actuator and supplies a replacement kit. Both bulletins describe a lit MIL. Unlike P237E, the short goes to ground; with the flap uncontrolled, warm-up can take longer.
c: Water in the heat exchanger or its actuator shorting the drive (Maverick)
Control wire chafed through against the body or exhaust bracket
s: Check engine light on
Slower heater response after a cold start
Car otherwise drives normally

P237E.t: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Control Circuit High
P237E.d: P237E is logged when the driver for exhaust bypass flap A on a heat recovery unit sees a control voltage above its expected range. The likely story is a short from the control wire to a supply feed or an actuator whose internal driver has failed in a way that pulls the line up. The flap then no longer follows the warm-up strategy. Ford is the one maker that names the code publicly, and only once: SSM 53003 lists P237E together with P237C, P237D, P237F, P2C22 and P2C23 for 2021–2023 F-150 hybrids with the 3.5L PowerBoost and blames the actuator mounted on the heat exchanger, which is replaced with a service kit after normal diagnosis. A lit MIL is reported. P237D is the low-side mirror image and P23A4 the same fault on valve B; a high signal rarely heals by itself.
c: Heat exchanger bypass actuator with failed internal driver (Ford F-150 SSM 53003)
Control wire shorted to a supply circuit in the harness
s: Check engine light on
Cabin heat may build up later on cold days

P237F.t: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Control Performance
P237F.d: P237F is not about wiring of the drive but about the result: the bypass flap A of the exhaust heat recovery unit was commanded, yet the effect the module expects does not appear. Ford judges this partly by temperatures, which is why SSM 52543 for the full hybrids F-150 3.5L (from 2021), Explorer 3.3L and Escape 2.5L (from 2020) and Maverick 2.5L (from 2022), all through 2024, first sends technicians to the connectors of exhaust coolant temperature sensors 3 and 4 – damaged seals, corrosion or water there can set P237F without a bad valve, so the heat exchanger need not be replaced. TSB 24-2173 fixes false P237F on 2024 Mavericks built up to 10 April 2024 with a PCM update. SSM 53003 covers a worn actuator on the F-150. The MIL comes on, driving is unaffected.
c: Water, corrosion or torn seal at the exhaust coolant temperature sensor 3/4 connectors (Ford SSM 52543)
PCM calibration setting the code falsely (2024 Maverick, TSB 24-2173)
Bypass actuator or flap sluggish, sticking or worn
s: Check engine light on
No effect on drivability
Often stored together with P2C23

P2380.d: P2380 is the general circuit code for EGR sensor D. Which sensor carries the letter D is up to the maker. Ford's 2024–2025 petrol OBD summary assigns it to the EGRP sensor, a smart EGR pressure sensor with a digital output covering 0.1 to 408.8 kPa: P2380 is stored when the sensor itself reports an internal malfunction, checked continuously while the EGR monitor runs, with 5 seconds to register the fault; a lost or corrupted data link sets U0669 instead. GM's 2025 diesel tables, by contrast, give its sensor D only the specific codes P2381 to P2384. CARB requires input components used by the EGR monitor to be checked for circuit faults. With the code stored the EGR flow check is not trustworthy and EGR may be cut back; the engine usually runs normally.
c: Internal fault reported by the smart EGR pressure sensor
Corroded or loose connector at the sensor
Unstable supply or ground to the sensor
s: Check engine light on
EGR monitor not completed
Possibly slight knock tendency or higher NOx with EGR reduced

P2381.d: P2381 means the signal of EGR sensor D is stuck at the top of its electrical range. GM's 2025 diesel ECM tables use it for the differential pressure sensor of the low-pressure EGR loop: if the raw voltage exceeds 99.83 % of the scale in 480 out of 600 samples, taken every 6.25 ms after cranking and with the powertrain relay above 11 V, GM records a Type A fault, lighting the MIL in the first trip. Typical reasons are an open sensor ground or a signal wire touching a 5 V or battery feed. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 for 3.0L LM2 trucks (Silverado, Sierra, Tahoe, Suburban, Yukon, Escalade) lists P2381 among codes that chafed engine harnesses can trigger. P2382 is the opposite limit and P2383 the plausibility check of the same sensor. The low-pressure EGR is usually shut off.
c: Open sensor ground or reference return
Chafed engine harness shorting the signal to a supply (GM 21-NA-149)
Differential pressure sensor failed with output at full scale
s: Check engine light on immediately
Low-pressure EGR disabled, NOx emissions rise
Other harness-related codes possible at the same time

P2382.d: P2382 reports that EGR sensor D delivers almost no signal voltage. In GM's 2025 diesel ECM tables this sensor measures the pressure difference across the low-pressure EGR path, and the code sets once the raw value drops below 0.02 % of range in 480 of 600 samples, sampled every 6.25 ms once the engine is out of cranking and the relay supply exceeds 11 V; it is a Type A fault with MIL on the first trip. Behind a reading that low there is usually a broken 5 V reference, a signal line shorted to ground or a sensor without output. For the 3.0L LM2 diesel, GM bulletin 21-NA-149 advises, for P2382 and P2383, pulling gently on each wire at the differential pressure sensor connector, since conductors may break there although they test good, and taping the harness afterwards. P2381 is the high-side code.
c: Conductor broken right at the sensor connector (GM 21-NA-149)
Open 5 V reference or signal shorted to ground
s: Check engine light on in the first trip
Low-pressure EGR switched off
Fault may come and go with engine vibration

P2383.d: P2383 flags an EGR sensor D whose signal is electrically fine but makes no sense. Two published strategies show how differently makers test it. GM's 2025 diesel ECM tables check the low-pressure EGR differential pressure sensor at key-off, when there should be no pressure difference: if the averaged reading exceeds 6 %, a Type A fault is set at once, provided no circuit or intermittent fault is present. Ford's 2024–2025 petrol summary uses P2383 for reversed hoses on its EGRP pressure sensor, judged by a signal off by more than 10 kPa or an internal temperature off by more than 27.7 °C for 5 seconds. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 adds harness checks at the sensor connector on 3.0L LM2 trucks. Mixed-up or cracked hoses, a drifting sensor and soot in the lines are the usual suspects.
c: Sensor hoses swapped, cracked or disconnected (Ford EGRP)
Sensor drifted so that it reads a pressure difference with the engine off (GM)
Sensing lines blocked by soot or condensate
Intermittent wire break at the sensor connector (GM 21-NA-149)
s: Check engine light on
EGR rate reduced or switched off
Often appears after work on the EGR or exhaust system

P2384.d: P2384 marks an EGR sensor D signal that jumps or drops out for brief moments without staying at a fixed fault level. GM's 2025 diesel ECM tables apply it to the differential pressure sensor of the low-pressure EGR loop: when two successive raw readings differ by more than 10 % in 300 out of 600 samples, taken every 6.25 ms with the relay supply above 11 V and no high or low circuit fault present, a Type A fault is logged and the MIL comes on in the first trip. GM bulletin 20-NA-039 lists P2384 among several codes on 2020 Silverado and Sierra 1500 trucks with the 3.0L LM2 diesel that a software anomaly could cause, cured by ECM reprogramming. Outside such cases loose terminals and chafed wiring are typical; P2381 to P2383 are the steady faults.
c: Loose or corroded terminals at the EGR sensor D connector
Harness chafing intermittently on engine or exhaust parts
Sensor with an internal contact fault
s: MIL on, often without noticeable driving change
Code stored, cleared and returning after some drives
EGR operation reduced as a precaution

P2385.d: P2385 is the general circuit code for a fifth EGR-related sensor, labelled E. The letter is assigned by each manufacturer, so the code only makes sense on engines with an extensive set of EGR sensors, such as diesels that pair high- and low-pressure loops with several pressure and temperature probes. No manufacturer documents P2385 publicly. The closest published logic is for sensor D: Ford's 2024–2025 petrol summary stores P2380 when its smart EGR pressure sensor reports an internal error, and GM's 2025 diesel tables use the D codes for the low-pressure EGR differential pressure sensor. CARB requires circuit checks on every input the EGR monitor depends on. P2386 and P2387 narrow the fault to high or low signal; with any of them stored, EGR diagnosis is suspended or EGR reduced.
c: Connector of EGR sensor E unplugged, damaged or corroded
Open or shorted wire between sensor and engine control unit
s: MIL on
EGR monitor not completing, readiness stays open
Possibly higher NOx and slightly changed engine response under load

P2386.d: P2386 says the signal of EGR sensor E sits at or above the upper end of its electrical range. With a typical three-wire 5 V pressure or position sensor that happens when the ground is open or the signal line touches a supply voltage; on a temperature sensor wired as a pull-up, an open circuit shows the same picture.
