No manufacturer documents P2386 publicly. The pattern GM publishes for sensor D on its 2025 diesels gives a sense of scale: P2381 sets once the raw value exceeds 99.83 % of range in 480 of 600 samples, as a Type A fault. CARB asks for out-of-range checks on EGR monitor inputs. P2387 is the low-side counterpart. Expect the MIL and reduced or disabled EGR; the engine itself normally runs on.
c: Open sensor ground wire or ground terminal
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
s: MIL on
EGR shut off or reduced
Scan data shows sensor E at full scale

P2387.d: P2387 is stored when the signal of EGR sensor E falls below its valid electrical range. On a pressure sensor with a 5 V reference that typically points to a lost reference feed, a signal wire shorted to ground or a sensor that no longer drives its output; a shorted thermistor would produce the same result on a temperature input. No manufacturer documents P2387 publicly. GM's published limit for the comparable sensor D code P2382 on 2025 diesels is a raw value below 0.02 % of range in 480 of 600 samples, sampled every 6.25 ms after cranking. Because a dead 5 V reference often feeds several sensors at once, other low codes sharing that rail are a useful clue. P2386 covers the high side; EGR usually runs in a fallback mode meanwhile.
c: 5 V reference open or pulled down by another sensor
s: MIL on
Further low-voltage codes on sensors sharing the same reference
EGR in fallback mode

P2388.d: P2388 covers an EGR sensor E whose signal is electrically valid but does not agree with what the engine controller expects from the operating state. Typical tests compare the reading with a known condition, such as zero pressure difference with the engine off, or with a modelled value from other sensors. No manufacturer documents P2388 publicly. Published sensor D logic shows the approach: GM's 2025 diesels flag P2383 if the low-pressure EGR differential pressure exceeds 6 % at key-off, while Ford's 2024–2025 petrol engines use P2383 for swapped hoses at the EGR pressure sensor. Plugged or cracked sensing hoses, soot build-up and sensor drift are the usual culprits rather than wiring. The car drives normally, but the EGR monitor cannot complete.
c: Sensing hoses blocked, cracked or swapped
Soot deposits at the sensor port
s: MIL on
EGR monitor readiness not set
Sensor E reading implausible at engine off

P2389.d: P2389 points to an EGR sensor E signal that is mostly plausible but now and then jumps, spikes or drops out. Engine controllers detect this by watching the rate of change between consecutive readings rather than absolute limits. No manufacturer documents P2389 publicly; the nearest published example is GM's sensor D code P2384 on 2025 diesels, which counts readings that change by more than 10 % from one sample to the next and sets a Type A fault after 300 such events in 600 samples. Such faults tend to follow engine vibration, heat cycles or moisture, so connector locks, pin tension and harness routing near hot exhaust parts deserve the first look. A fault that is absent during testing may still return; P2385 to P2387 describe steady faults.
c: Weak pin tension or unlatched connector
Harness damaged by heat or rubbing near the exhaust
Sensor with an intermittent internal fault
s: MIL on, sometimes going out again
Fault cannot be reproduced at the workshop
Jumps visible in the sensor E data stream

P238A.t: Water in Fuel Sensor B Circuit
P238A.d: P238A is the general circuit code for water-in-fuel sensor B, used where a diesel has two water-detecting points, for example a frame-mounted primary filter and a second separator. Stellantis case file S2214000004 for 2022 Ram 2500 to 5500 trucks shows that on these vehicles the B sensor is part of the fuel filter mounted on the frame; P238A itself is not named there. No manufacturer documents P238A publicly. The sensor works like sensor A: two electrodes in the water sump read the conductivity. GM's 2018 diesel tables describe a self-test for sensor A in which a healthy probe briefly reports water right after power-up; a missing pulse counts as a circuit fault. While the code is stored, real water in the filter may go unnoticed, so drain the separator regularly.
c: Water or corrosion in the sensor B connector at the chassis filter
Damaged harness along the frame rail
s: Water-in-fuel lamp or message on
No warning for real water in the chassis filter

P238B.t: Water in Fuel Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P238B.d: P238B means water-in-fuel sensor B delivers a signal that is electrically valid but implausible, for instance a value stuck between the clear dry and wet states, or a self-test answer that arrives at the wrong moment. No manufacturer documents P238B publicly. On 2022 Ram heavy-duty diesels sensor B is fitted to the frame-mounted filter, exposed to road spray (Stellantis case S2214000004). The probe judges conductivity, so a film of dirt, biodiesel deposits or a partly corroded electrode can shift its reading. For the sensor A codes on 2025–26 Ram trucks Stellantis advises draining both filter stages and wiping the probe before replacing anything, a sensible first step here as well. Unlike P238F it does not confirm water.
c: Dirt film or deposits on the sensor electrodes
Residual water or emulsion around the probe after incomplete draining
s: Water-in-fuel warning without water being found
Warning that persists after draining

P238C.t: Water in Fuel Sensor B Circuit Low
P238C.d: P238C is set when the signal line of water-in-fuel sensor B stays below its valid range. Because the sensor reads conductivity, anything that bridges its terminals or pulls the signal to ground can cause it: a chafed wire, a wet connector or a sensor body full of water. No manufacturer documents P238C publicly. For the matching sensor A code P2266 Ford bulletin 18-2133 on 2017–18 Super Duty 6.7L trucks traced the fault to water in connector C3080 and specified a sensor resistance of 795 to 815 kOhm across pins 1 and 2; on Ram trucks sensor B is the one in the chassis filter. Since a wet plug may imitate both a low circuit and real water, check for P238F as well. The opposite fault is P238D.
c: Water bridging the terminals in the sensor connector
Signal wire chafed through to ground on the frame
s: Water-in-fuel lamp on
Fault appears after washing or rain

P238D.t: Water in Fuel Sensor B Circuit High
P238D.d: P238D reports that the signal of water-in-fuel sensor B sits above its valid range, usually from an open circuit, a disconnected sensor or a short to voltage. Stellantis case file S2214000004 documents it for 2022 Ram 2500, 3500, 4500 and 5500 trucks: the water warning lamp or message comes on at low mileage, and the cause is water that a pressure washer or similar spray drove into the plug of the filter housing on the frame rail. Technicians inspect both connector halves; corrosion means replacing filter housing and harness connector, plain water means drying, dielectric grease and a retest, with a new housing if the code returns. Stellantis stresses that P238D is not P238F, which reports actual water. P238C is the low counterpart.
c: Spray water in the connector at the chassis-mounted fuel filter
Corroded terminals on harness or filter housing side
Sensor in the filter housing failed
s: Water-in-fuel lamp or message on at low mileage
No water found when draining

P238E.t: Water in Fuel Sensor B Circuit Intermittent
P238E.d: P238E is meant for a water-in-fuel sensor B circuit whose signal flickers or drops out for short periods instead of staying at one fault level. No manufacturer documents P238E publicly. The one published case for the same sensor explains well why such faults come and go: on 2022 Ram heavy-duty trucks Stellantis found water from road spray or pressure washing inside the plug of the frame-mounted filter, logged there as P238D. Moisture that evaporates, terminals that lose contact on rough roads and fuel sloshing over the probe can all produce brief changes. Since the sensor is a plain pair of electrodes, connector, pins and harness clips along the frame rail come first. P238C and P238D are the steady low and high faults.
c: Moisture entering and drying out in the connector
Loose terminals losing contact on rough roads
Broken harness clips letting the wire rub on the frame
s: Water-in-fuel lamp flickering or coming and going
Fault not present when tested at the workshop

P238F.t: Water in Fuel Condition - Sensor B
P238F.d: P238F is no wiring fault: it states that water-in-fuel sensor B has detected water, meaning the separator at that point has collected enough to bridge the probe. Ram's 2022 heavy-duty pickups (2500 to 5500) are covered by Stellantis case S2214000004, which keeps it apart from the circuit code P238D: with P238F stored, the filter on the frame has to be emptied completely and the fuel tested for water before any electrical diagnosis. For sensor A the equivalent is P2269, which Ram's 2025–26 Cummins trucks report with the MIL. Water in diesel fuel damages high-pressure pumps and injectors and promotes microbial growth, so drain promptly, find the source (tank, fuel station, condensation) and replace the filter if needed.
c: Water collected in the chassis filter separator
Fuel contaminated with water from tank or filling station
Separator drained incompletely after an earlier warning
s: Water-in-fuel lamp or message on
Rough running or power loss if water reaches the injection system
MIL on some vehicles

P2390.t: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Control Circuit/Open
P2390.d: P2390 concerns the drive circuit of the second electronically operated intake throttle that some diesel engines carry; which flap a maker labels A or B is its own choice. With the driver switched off, the engine module checks whether the motor circuit is closed; an open wire, a pulled connector or a burnt motor winding sets this code. No manufacturer publishes P2390 with thresholds. For the A valve (P02E0) GM's 2017 diesel tables look for a load resistance above 200 kΩ in 160 of 200 checks at 12.5 ms, provided the relay feeds more than 11 V, as a two-trip fault. A dead motor leaves the return spring to hold the flap open on most designs, so the vehicle drives normally while EGR control and regeneration heating lose authority.
c: Connector at the B throttle unplugged, loose or with pushed-back terminals
Broken motor lead in the harness between module and throttle
Open motor winding inside the throttle unit
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: MIL on, often without a noticeable change in driving
Particulate filter regeneration delayed or blocked
Engine may shake more when switched off because the flap no longer closes

P2391.t: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Control Performance
P2391.d: P2391 compares where the B intake throttle should be with where its position sensor says it is. If the gap stays too large under a steady command, the module concludes that the flap is sluggish or obstructed, typically by soot and oil deposits from EGR and crankcase gases, a worn gear stage or a weak motor. No published manufacturer table covers P2391. GM's 2025 diesels judge the A valve (P02E1) on a tracking error above 10 % in 960 of 1,200 samples at 6.25 ms, only once coolant has reached 40 °C and outside the cold-start strategy, and light the MIL in the first trip. Unlike the stuck codes P2394 and P2395, this one does not say in which direction the flap lags. Expect higher NOx, possibly blocked regeneration and sometimes reduced power.
c: Soot and oil deposits making the B flap stiff
Worn plastic gears or shaft bearing in the throttle unit
Weak motor or high resistance in the drive circuit
Position sensor reporting an offset angle
s: MIL on
Regeneration of the particulate filter does not complete
Occasionally reduced power or uneven response

P2392.t: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Control Circuit Low
P2392.d: P2392 is set when the module finds the motor output for the B intake throttle pulled towards ground, for example by a chafed wire touching the engine, water inside the connector or a shorted motor. The output stage protects itself and switches off. No manufacturer documents P2392 publicly. Ford's 2023 diesel summary checks the matching A-valve fault (P02E2) continuously while the power stage is active and needs only 0.2 s to register it. Because an H-bridge drives the motor, a ground short on either motor lead can be the trigger; whether the code points to one particular lead depends on the maker. With the motor dead the flap returns to its spring position, open on most designs: driveability changes little, but the EGR rate drops and the module may refuse to regenerate the particulate filter.
c: Motor lead chafed through and touching engine or body ground
Water or corrosion in the throttle connector
Internal short of the throttle motor to its housing
Damaged H-bridge in the engine control module
s: MIL on, code returns immediately after clearing
Regeneration blocked or aborted
Little or no change in driving

P2393.t: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Control Circuit High
P2393.d: P2393 is the counterpart of P2392: one of the B-throttle motor leads has contact with battery voltage, for example through a pinched harness or a bridged pin in the connector, so the output stage sees an overcurrent as soon as it switches. No manufacturer publishes P2393. For the A valve GM's 2017 diesels flag the analogous P02E3 when more than 9 A flows through the H-bridge in 160 of 200 checks and store it on the second trip. Ford's 2023 diesels need just 0.2 s to recognise the A-valve short. The ECM then disables the driver to protect itself. If P239B is stored as well, a shorted motor winding is a likelier culprit than the harness. Apart from the MIL the driver usually notices nothing; emissions and regeneration suffer.
c: Motor lead pinched against a live wire or terminal
Bridged pins in the connector (moisture, corrosion)
Shorted turns in the throttle motor
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: MIL on
Filter regeneration not carried out
Possibly blown fuse or further circuit codes on the same supply

P2394.t: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Control Stuck Open
P2394.d: P2394 means the B intake throttle remains wider open than requested even though the module drives its motor hard towards closing. A flap that cannot throttle fails to create the manifold depression that strong exhaust recirculation and regeneration heating depend on. No manufacturer documents P2394 openly. GM's 2017 diesel tables catch the A-valve version (P02E4) when the setpoint-minus-actual error is below -16 % while the duty cycle is beyond -34 %, in 1,280 of 1,600 samples at 6.25 ms, lighting the MIL at once; Ford's 2023 diesels use a deviation of more than 15 % held for 25 s. Coking, a broken gear tooth or a seized shaft are the usual reasons. Driving feels normal, but NOx and the soot load rise.
c: Deposits holding the flap in an open position
Broken gear tooth or stripped drive between motor and shaft
Motor too weak to overcome the return spring
Foreign object or broken part blocking the flap
s: MIL on
Frequent or failing particulate filter regenerations
Engine shakes when switched off

P2395.t: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Control Stuck Closed
P2395.d: P2395 reports a B intake throttle that remains nearer to its closed stop than the module asks for. Of the two stuck faults this is the more serious one, because a flap jammed near its seat starves the engine of air. No manufacturer publishes thresholds for P2395. The GM 2017 diesel check for valve A (P02E5) mirrors the stuck-open test: a positive error above 16 % while the motor is driven at more than 34 % duty towards opening, 1,280 of 1,600 samples, MIL in the first trip. Deposits that lock the flap close to its stop, an iced shaft after cold and damp nights, or a broken return spring are the usual reasons. The engine may smoke, lose power markedly, drop into limp mode or even stall; low-air-flow codes such as P239D often follow.
c: Deposits locking the flap near its closed stop
Broken return spring, flap no longer opens when unpowered
Jammed gear train or seized shaft bearing
Ice on the shaft or flap after cold, damp conditions
s: Marked loss of power, limp mode
Black smoke under load
Rough running or stalling in severe cases

P2396.t: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Position Sensor Circuit
P2396.d: P2396 is the general electrical fault of the sensor that reports the angle of the B intake throttle, a potentiometer or, on newer units, a contactless Hall sensor with analogue or SENT output. The code says only that the signal is electrically implausible, without telling whether the reading sits under or over its window; makers that separate the two would set P2398 or P2399 instead. No manufacturer was found that uses P2396. On the A side the LML 6.6 L Duramax tables from GM accept 0.40 to 4.72 V and Ford's 2023 diesels 0.08 to 4.92 V before they set their split codes. Without a valid position the module cannot run closed-loop control and usually de-energises the flap. Check the 5 V reference, ground and signal wire and the connector before replacing the throttle unit, which normally contains the sensor.
c: Damaged reference, ground or signal wire
Failed position sensor in the throttle unit
s: MIL on
Flap switched off, EGR runs with limited control
Regeneration postponed

P2397.t: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Position Sensor Range/Performance
P2397.d: P2397 covers a B-throttle position signal that stays inside its electrical window but does not make sense, for instance a reading that does not move when the motor is driven, or one that disagrees with the commanded angle. CARB asks for such rationality checks on inputs wherever feasible. No published manufacturer table covers P2397. The 6.6 L LML calibration from GM handles the A valve this way under P02E7 and flags a control deviation beyond ±10 % lasting 10 s. Because a sticking flap and a drifting sensor produce the same pattern, compare the scan-tool angle with the real flap position and check the sensor's contact resistance before blaming the actuator. The MIL and reduced EGR control are the main effects; some engines also cut power.
c: Sticking flap that lags behind the command
Worn potentiometer track or drifting sensor
Contact resistance in connector or signal wire
Play between gear and flap shaft
s: MIL on
Displayed flap angle does not follow the command
Occasionally reduced power

P2398.t: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Position Sensor Circuit Low
P2398.d: P2398 is logged when the position signal of the B intake throttle falls below its lower limit. Likely reasons are a signal lead shorted to ground, a lost 5 V supply, or a broken signal wire that the module input pulls low; on SENT sensors the transmitted raw value can also leave its range. No manufacturer documents P2398 itself. For the A valve, GM's LML reacts to less than 0.40 V persisting 5 s, its SENT-equipped 2017 diesels to under 1 % of 5 V in 200 of 250 checks (two trips), while Ford's 2023 diesels flag readings under 0.08 V lasting 3 s. If several 5 V sensors fail at once, suspect a shorted shared reference circuit. The flap is normally switched off, leaving the EGR loop with less control.
c: Open 5 V reference or open signal wire
Shared 5 V reference pulled down by another faulty sensor
s: MIL on
Further 5 V sensor codes at the same time
Regeneration suspended

P2399.t: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Position Sensor Circuit High
P2399.d: P2399 is the upper-limit counterpart of P2398: the B-throttle position signal reads higher than any real flap angle can produce. That usually points to a lost sensor ground, a signal wire touching the 5 V reference or battery voltage, or water bridging the terminals in the connector. No manufacturer is known to publish P2399. For the A valve the LML Duramax from GM uses P02E9 once the voltage exceeds 4.72 V during 5 s; Ford's 2023 diesels react when 4.92 V is passed for 3 s. Measure the ground lead back to the module first, since a weak ground lifts the signal without the sensor itself being damaged. The consequences resemble those of the other sensor codes: flap de-energised, MIL, EGR and regeneration compromised.
c: Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Moisture bridging terminals in the connector
s: MIL on
Flap stays at spring position
Regeneration suspended

P239A.t: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P239A.d: P239A describes a B-throttle position signal that keeps jumping or dropping out for short moments, too briefly to set the low or high code. Loose terminals, a harness that cracks as the engine rocks, corrosion or a worn potentiometer track are typical; on digital SENT sensors corrupted messages have the same effect. CARB requires circuit and range checks on inputs, and a separate code for erratic behaviour is left to the manufacturer. No maker documents P239A openly, and GM's 2017 diesel tables file SENT message errors of the A sensor under their own codes P16A0 to P16A2. Wiggling the harness while watching the angle in live data often reveals the fault. It tends to come and go, bringing the MIL and occasional EGR restrictions with it.
c: Loose or corroded terminals in the sensor connector
Wire breaking or rubbing intermittently with engine movement
Worn potentiometer track or faulty SENT sensor electronics
Electrical interference on the signal line
s: MIL that comes and goes
Short-lived jerks or EGR interruptions
Code stored without a permanent fault on testing

P239B.t: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Control Motor Current Range/Performance
P239B.d: P239B checks the current the B-throttle motor draws while its H-bridge is switched on. A blocked or very stiff flap, a partly shorted winding or the two motor leads touching each other push the current beyond what the module expects. No manufacturer publishes P239B with values. GM's 2017 diesels set the A-motor code P02EB once more than 5.5 A is seen in 160 out of 200 evaluations while the powertrain relay delivers over 11 V; the MIL follows on the second trip. What sets it apart from P2393 is the origin of the excess current: here it comes from the load itself rather than from a lead touching battery voltage. Checking whether the flap moves freely, with the unit removed if necessary, shows whether it binds. Once the driver shuts down, the spring opens the flap; the engine keeps running with restricted EGR control.
c: Flap blocked or very stiff, motor running at stall current
Short between the two motor leads in harness or connector
Faulty current measurement in the control module
s: MIL on
Flap switched off and resting at spring position
Often stored together with P2391 or the stuck codes

P239C.t: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Control System - High Air Flow Detected
P239C.d: P239C belongs to the air-mass control loop rather than to the throttle alone: with the B intake throttle taking part in that control, the module sees more fresh air than its target and cannot bring the reading down even at the limit of its authority. Too little recirculated exhaust gas is both the usual cause and the consequence, from an EGR valve stuck shut, a blocked EGR cooler, a flap that cannot close or an air-mass meter reading high. No manufacturer was found that uses P239C. Ford's 2023 diesels run this test for their single intake throttle under P02EC, comparing desired and measured air mass against a speed/torque map; the 6.7 L needs 10 s, the 3.0 L 5 s. NOx emissions rise; driveability normally stays unchanged.
c: EGR valve stuck closed or EGR cooler clogged
B throttle unable to close far enough
s: MIL on
No noticeable driving change in most cases
Often stored together with EGR flow codes

P239D.t: Diesel Intake Air Flow B Control System - Low Air Flow Detected
P239D.d: P239D is the mirror image of P239C: the measured fresh-air mass remains below target although the control loop involving the B intake throttle is already at its limit. Candidates are an EGR valve that will not close and floods the intake with exhaust gas, a B flap stuck partly shut (often together with P2395), a restricted air filter or charge-air path, a turbocharger delivering too little, or an air-mass meter reading low. No manufacturer is known to publish P239D. Ford's 2023 diesels check the same condition for their one intake throttle as P02ED, with a detection time of ten seconds on the 6.7 L engine and half that on the 3.0 L. As the engine is short of air, black smoke, rapid soot loading of the DPF and a loss of power are typical; limp mode is possible.
c: Clogged air filter or restricted charge-air path
Contaminated air-mass meter reading too low
s: Loss of power, possibly limp mode
Black smoke
Frequent particulate filter regenerations

P239E.t: O2 Sensor Out of Range During Deceleration (Bank 1 Sensor 2) - Duplicate Listing of P232F
P239E.d: P239E carries in common code lists exactly the same wording as P232F: a downstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 reading outside its expected window while fuel is cut on deceleration. No manufacturer, OBD summary or service bulletin on record uses P239E, and no source gives it a meaning of its own. The documented version is P232F, which GM applies to the 2023 6.6L L5P Duramax, comparing sensor 2 with sensor 1 in overrun (window +3.01 to −3.18 %, Type B). P239E is therefore best treated as a duplicate listing. Should a scan tool show it, read the maker's own code definition and freeze-frame data, then test the rear sensor as for P232F; CARB requires a rich-to-lean check of rear sensors during fuel shut-off.
c: Scan tool code table showing the duplicate number instead of the maker's code
Aged or drifting rear oxygen sensor on bank 1
Exhaust leak ahead of the rear sensor
s: MIL on without noticeable driving change
Code text in the scan tool contradicts the manufacturer's documentation

P239F.t: O2 Sensor Out of Range During Deceleration (Bank 2 Sensor 2) - Duplicate Listing of P2379
P239F.d: P239F appears in code lists with the identical title already given to P2379: the post-catalyst oxygen sensor of bank 2 is out of range while the injectors are switched off on a closed throttle. Neither code has a published manufacturer application; the only documented member of this deceleration check is GM's bank 1 code P232F on the single-bank 2023 L5P diesel, so a second bank never occurs there. No source assigns P239F a separate meaning, which makes it a duplicate listing of P2379. If it is ever read out, the manufacturer's code text decides; diagnosis would follow the bank 2 rear sensor: look for exhaust leaks ahead of it, check wiring and compare its overrun reading with the front sensor. CARB requires such fuel-cut checks for rear sensors.
c: Scan tool listing the duplicate number for a maker-specific fault
Aged rear oxygen sensor on bank 2
Air leak in the bank 2 exhaust ahead of the sensor
s: MIL on, engine runs normally
Catalyst monitor may not complete

P23A0.t: O2 Sensor Exhaust Sample Error (Bank 1 Sensor 2) - Duplicate Listing of P237A
P23A0.d: P23A0 repeats, word for word, the title of P237A in the usual code lists: the rear oxygen sensor of bank 1 does not see, or does not report, a representative sample of post-catalyst exhaust. No manufacturer uses P23A0 in any published OBD table or service bulletin, and no source defines it differently, so it is a duplicate listing of P237A. Even P237A has no public manufacturer application; the method is known only from the front sensor, where Volkswagen documents P2414 for the 2014 Golf with fixed signal windows. If a tool reports P23A0, check the maker's own code text first, then inspect the exhaust ahead of sensor 2 for air leaks and the probe's mounting. CARB requires monitoring of rear sensors used for catalyst checks.
c: Scan tool code table using the duplicate number
Air leak in the exhaust ahead of the rear sensor on bank 1
Sensor mounted poorly or element contaminated
s: MIL on, no drivability change
Catalyst diagnosis unreliable or incomplete

P23A1.t: O2 Sensor Exhaust Sample Error (Bank 2 Sensor 2) - Duplicate Listing of P237B
P23A1.d: P23A1 is listed with the same title as P237B: the bank 2 oxygen sensor behind the catalyst reports something that cannot be genuine exhaust from that bank. Only engines with two exhaust banks and a downstream sensor on each side could produce it. No published OBD summary or bulletin assigns P23A1, and no source gives it its own meaning; it is thus a duplicate listing of P237B, itself without public manufacturer use. A comparable plausibility check is documented only for a front sensor, Volkswagen's P2414 on the 2014 Golf. Should the code appear, the manufacturer's definition takes precedence; practical checks cover air leaks on the bank 2 pipe, sensor position and wiring. CARB demands that rear sensors are monitored because catalyst diagnosis depends on them.
c: Scan tool reporting the duplicate number
Leak in the bank 2 exhaust pipe ahead of the rear sensor
Damaged wiring or connector of the bank 2 rear sensor
s: MIL on, engine runs normally
Readiness for catalyst monitor stays open

P23A2.t: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve B Control Circuit/Open
P23A2.d: P23A2 reports an open or otherwise broken drive circuit for the second exhaust bypass flap, valve B, of an exhaust heat exchanger. Such units route the exhaust through a coolant heat exchanger after a cold start and send it past once engine and cabin are warm; a valve B only exists where the layout needs two flaps. No manufacturer documents P23A2 publicly. The closest published case is Ford's valve A on its full hybrids: SSM 51921 (Maverick 2.5L) and SSM 52050 (F-150 3.5L PowerBoost) treat the matching code P237C with a lit MIL and a new heat exchanger or muffler inlet pipe. CARB requires emission-related output components to be checked for circuit faults. P23A3 and P23A4 narrow the fault to low or high; P237C is valve A.
c: Connector at the valve B actuator loose, corroded or unplugged
Control wire broken near the hot exhaust or at a harness clip
Actuator coil or internal electronics of valve B open
s: Check engine light on
Slower engine and cabin warm-up in cold weather
No change in how the vehicle drives

P23A3.t: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve B Control Circuit Low
P23A3.d: With P23A3 the module sees the control line of exhaust bypass valve B sitting lower than its commanded state allows, which usually means that the wire or the driver stage of the actuator has found a path to ground. Water or road salt in a connector under the vehicle is a typical trigger. P23A3 itself appears in no public manufacturer document. For the valve A equivalent P237D, Ford's SSM 53003 on 2021–2023 F-150 PowerBoost hybrids blames the actuator mounted on the heat exchanger and supplies service kit PL3Z-5K245-B, while SSM 51921 links the code on Mavericks to water inside the heat exchanger. CARB expects such outputs to be monitored for out-of-range circuit states. If the flap cannot be driven, warm-up may take longer; P23A4 is the opposite short.
c: Control wire chafed through and touching body or exhaust ground
Moisture or salt bridging pins in the actuator connector
Internal short in the valve B actuator
s: Check engine light on
Heater output builds up slowly after a cold start
Fault may reappear after rain or washing

P23A4.t: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve B Control Circuit High
P23A4.d: P23A4 is stored when the control circuit of exhaust heat exchanger bypass valve B reads higher than expected – a short to a battery feed, a chafed wire touching another supply, or an actuator whose electronics pull the line up. Because the flap no longer obeys, the warm-up strategy has to run without it. There is no public manufacturer documentation for P23A4. Ford names the valve A counterpart P237E only once, in SSM 53003 for 2021–2023 F-150 hybrids with the 3.5L PowerBoost, together with the position sensor codes P2C22 and P2C23, and replaces the heat exchanger actuator. CARB requires circuit checks on emission-related output components. P23A3 is the low-side fault and P23A2 the open circuit; a high reading seldom clears by itself.
c: Control wire shorted to a 12 V feed in the harness
Failed electronics inside the valve B actuator
Output stage in the controlling module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Bypass flap does not respond to an actuator test
Driving behaviour unchanged

P23A5.t: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve B Control Performance
P23A5.d: Unlike the circuit codes, P23A5 judges the result: the module commanded valve B, the second exhaust bypass at the heat exchanger, but it does not see the response it expects, for example in position feedback or in how the exhaust-side coolant temperatures change. No manufacturer publishes P23A5. Ford's handling of valve A shows how such a check can mislead: for P237F on F-150, Explorer, Escape and Maverick full hybrids up to 2024, SSM 52543 first has the connectors of exhaust coolant temperature sensors 3 and 4 inspected for water or corrosion, and TSB 24-2173 cures false P237F on 2024 Mavericks with a PCM update. CARB requires a functional check of output components. Driving is usually unaffected; P23A6 and P23A7 name a flap stuck in one position.
c: Flap of valve B sluggish from soot or corrosion
Exhaust coolant temperature sensor connector wet or corroded, distorting the plausibility check
Overly strict calibration, fixed by a software update
s: Check engine light on
Cabin heat slow to arrive in winter
No effect on drivability

P23A6.t: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve B Stuck Open
P23A6.d: P23A6 says that bypass valve B of the exhaust heat exchanger stays open while the module wants it closed. In the usual layout the exhaust then keeps taking the bypass route, so the heat exchanger adds little or no heat after a cold start – noticeable as a slow engine warm-up and a weak cabin heater in cold weather, and on hybrids as the engine running longer just to make heat. The fault is judged mechanically, from position feedback or temperature response, not from the wiring. No manufacturer documents P23A6; the valve A twin is P00E3. Ford's valve A bulletins (SSM 52050, SSM 53003) show that faulty bypass valves and worn actuators on these units do occur. CARB requires functional monitoring of such outputs. P23A7 is the reverse case.
c: Flap seized in the open position by carbon or corrosion
Linkage between actuator and flap broken or detached
Actuator no longer able to move the flap
s: Check engine light on
Engine and heater take noticeably longer to warm up
Hybrid engine runs more often in cold weather

P23A7.t: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve B Stuck Closed
P23A7.d: P23A7 is the opposite of P23A6: the second bypass valve (B) on the exhaust heat exchanger does not open on command and stays closed. Depending on the layout, all exhaust is then forced through the heat exchanger even when the engine is fully warm, which adds heat to the coolant and some back pressure – most relevant under load and in hot weather. The module recognises the condition from position feedback or from temperatures that do not follow the command. No manufacturer publishes P23A7, and the valve A version is P00E4. Ford's valve A cases, water inside the heat exchanger (SSM 51921) and a replaceable actuator kit (SSM 53003), are the nearest public examples. CARB requires output components to be checked for proper function. Keep an eye on coolant temperature until it is repaired.
c: Flap stuck closed by deposits or corrosion
Damaged or water-filled heat exchanger obstructing the flap
s: Check engine light on
Coolant temperature higher than usual under load
Possibly reduced power or a changed exhaust note

P23A8.t: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve B Position Sensor Stop Performance
P23A8.d: P23A8 concerns the position feedback of exhaust bypass valve B at its mechanical end stops. Systems with a position sensor learn the readings at the fully open and the fully closed stop and compare later readings with them; if a stop value drifts out of its window, or the flap no longer reaches the stop at all, this code is set. Causes range from a carbon-fouled or bent flap to a slipping sensor or a worn actuator. No manufacturer documents P23A8; for valve A the equivalent is P25D6. Ford lists the valve A position sensor code P2C23 together with corroded exhaust coolant temperature sensor connectors (SSM 52543) and with a worn heat exchanger actuator (SSM 53003). CARB requires rationality checks on such inputs. Driveability normally stays unchanged.
c: Deposits or a bent flap keep valve B from reaching its end stop
Position sensor in the actuator drifted or loose
End stops not relearned after a repair
s: Check engine light on
Valve position in live data does not reach the expected end value

P23A9.d: P23A9 records that the engine was stopped, or kept from running, because the engine module lost contact with a control unit whose messages it needs to operate the engine safely. The title names only the consequence; which data link is meant is defined by each manufacturer, and none publishes P23A9. The underlying network fault normally shows up as a separate U code in the same or another module. CARB requires digital inputs to be monitored for missing communication. A comparable published check is GM's P06AF in its 2019 tables, where the ECM verifies a message pattern from the transmission module and may stop the engine on a mismatch. For the driver: the engine dies or refuses to restart; check CAN wiring and termination as well as supply and grounds of the modules involved.
c: Damaged CAN wiring, connector or termination
Partner module without power or ground, or low battery voltage
Failed or wrongly programmed partner module
Software versions of the modules not matching after repair
s: Engine stops while driving or does not start
Several U codes and warning messages from other modules
MIL or other warning lights on

P23AA.d: P23AA concerns bypass valve A of a turbocharger or supercharger, which opens a path around the compressor to relieve boost when the throttle closes or at part load. The code means the valve no longer follows its command and sits fixed. GM applies P23AA to the electronically positioned supercharger bypass valve of the 2019 Corvette LT5: if the measured position deviates from the target by more than 25 % for at least 1 s while the valve is barely moving (under ±10 % per second), 10 failures in 14 samples at 6.25 ms set a Type A fault with the MIL in the first trip. The circuit codes P0033 to P0035 and the mechanical test P2261 cover other faults of the valve. Stuck open it costs boost and power; stuck closed it can cause compressor surge and noise on lift-off.
c: Valve or actuator mechanically seized (deposits, wear)
Faulty electric actuator or position sensor of the valve
High resistance in wiring or connector
s: Reduced boost and power
Fluttering or surging noise when lifting off
MIL on, possibly limited power mode

P23AB.d: A NOx sensor is a smart part: the probe in the exhaust is wired to a small control unit with its own processor, which runs the heater, evaluates the cell currents and reports over CAN. P23AB means that this electronics in sensor 3 of bank 1 – usually the one behind a second SCR catalyst – reports an internal error or fails its self-checks. No manufacturer documents P23AB publicly. Ford's 2023 diesel OBD summary shows what such checks contain for its front sensor: RAM failure and ROM or EEPROM checksum errors, reported there under P2200. CARB requires NOx sensors to be monitored for faults that make them unusable for the SCR checks. P06EA and P06EB are the processor codes of sensors 1 and 2. Repair normally means a new sensor.
c: Internal electronics of the sensor 3 control unit defective
Supply voltage dips or poor ground resetting the sensor electronics
Sensor control unit damaged by heat or water ingress
s: Check engine light on
Sensor 3 values missing or frozen in live data
SCR or emissions warning on the display

P23AC.d: P23AC is the general electrical fault reported for NOx sensor 3 on bank 1. The sensor's own control unit watches the leads between its electronics and the ceramic probe and tells the engine computer over CAN whether a measuring circuit is open or shorted; the user manual of Drivven's NOx sensor module kit, published by NI, lists these status states for the NOx and O2 circuits. No manufacturer documents P23AC publicly. For its front sensor, Ford's 2023 diesel summary sets P2200 when the probe lines Vs, COM, Ip1 or Ip2 short to battery or ground. CARB requires NOx sensor monitoring to catch broken circuits and readings outside the possible range. More specific sensor 3 codes run from P23AD to P23B0; P2200 and P229E are sensors 1 and 2. Without a valid signal the final SCR check stops.
c: Lead between probe and sensor control unit damaged by heat or chafing
Corroded or loose terminals at the sensor 3 connectors
Probe or sensor electronics failed internally
s: Check engine light on
No NOx reading from sensor 3 in live data
SCR system warning

P23AD.d: P23AD flags the third NOx sensor on bank 1 as electrically intact but not trustworthy. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B describes the check for its post-second-catalyst NOx sensor: the internal stability flags of the NOx and lambda current control are watched, and a flag counts as off when, for instance, the V2 cell voltage leaves a 40 mV band around its set point or the pump currents Ip1 and Ip2 change faster than allowed. If the off share exceeds 0.50 %, with fuel request and its rate steady, dew point passed and the heater on target, the fault matures after 2 of 2 samples; Type B, MIL after two trips. CARB demands monitoring of NOx sensor performance. P23AE and P23AF are hard out-of-range values, P2201 the front sensor.
c: Aged or poisoned sensing cell giving unstable pump currents
High contact resistance in the sensor 3 wiring
Exhaust leak near the sensor upsetting the measurement
s: Check engine light after two trips
Sensor 3 NOx value jumps in live data
SCR efficiency monitor may not complete

P23AE.d: P23AE is set when the third NOx sensor on bank 1 reports a concentration below anything physically possible. GM's 25OBDG04B table for its 2025 diesels requires the raw NOx value of the sensor behind the second catalyst to fall under −90 ppm in 100 of 200 samples, taken every 25 ms once dew point is reached, supply exceeds 9.9 V and no CAN fault is present; it is rated Type B with the MIL after two trips. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 lists P23AE among the codes caused by chafed engine harnesses on 3.0L LM2 Duramax pickups and SUVs of 2021–2022 (Silverado and Sierra 1500, Tahoe, Suburban, Yukon, Escalade). CARB demands out-of-range checks on NOx sensors. P23AF is the high limit, P2202 and P22A0 are the low codes of sensors 1 and 2.
c: Engine harness chafed, disturbing the sensor 3 supply or signal
Sensor 3 with a negative offset from ageing or damage
s: Check engine light after two trips
Negative or zero NOx value for sensor 3 in live data
Other harness-related codes stored at the same time

P23AF.d: With P23AF the third NOx sensor on bank 1 delivers a value above its measuring range. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B sets the code when the raw reading of the post-second-catalyst sensor exceeds 2,990 ppm in 120 of 240 samples, provided the air system control is active or DEF dosing is ready; the rating is Type B, so the MIL follows on the second trip. For the 3.0L LM2 diesel in 2021–2022 light trucks, GM bulletin 21-NA-149 adds a practical hint: with P23AF the harness at the exhaust pressure differential sensor connector is checked by tugging on the single wires, because conductors may break there while still measuring fine, and extra tape is added afterwards. CARB requires detection of out-of-range NOx signals. P23AE is the low counterpart, P2203 the front sensor.
c: Wire broken inside the insulation near a connector in the exhaust sensor harness
Sensor 3 failed with a reading stuck high
Short between sensor lines in the harness
s: Check engine light after two trips
Sensor 3 shows implausibly high NOx even at idle
SCR efficiency code may follow

P23B0.d: P23B0 is meant for a third NOx sensor on bank 1 whose circuit faults come and go instead of staying present, so the status the sensor module reports over CAN keeps toggling between valid and faulty. No manufacturer documents P23B0 publicly, and none publishes a threshold for it; GM's 2025 diesel table, which details several other sensor 3 codes, does not list it. HELLA's workshop guidance on NOx sensors names plug connections and wiring harmed by moisture, grime and road salt and recommends checking supply and bus communication – a good fit for a fault that keeps returning. CARB requires circuit faults on NOx sensors to be detected. P23AC is the steady circuit fault; P2204 and P22A2 are the intermittent codes of sensors 1 and 2. The MIL may go out and come back.
c: Loose or fretting terminal in a sensor 3 connector
Harness rubbing or flexing near the exhaust, breaking contact under vibration
Moisture entering a connector in wet weather
s: Check engine light that goes out and returns
Sensor 3 value drops out briefly in live data

P23B1.t: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P23B1.d: A NOx sensor only measures once its built-in heater has brought the ceramic element up to temperature. P23B1 reports that the heater control side of the third sensor on bank 1 is open. GM's 2025 diesel calibration (table 25OBDG04B) looks for a missing load on the heater control pin of the post-second-catalyst sensor and fails after 80 of 160 samples at a 25 ms rate, with powertrain relay voltage above 11 V and the sensor bus relay switched on. GM rates it Type A, so the MIL comes on after a single trip. Bulletin 21-NA-149 includes P23B1 in its chafed-harness list for 2021–2022 3.0L LM2 trucks. CARB requires heater circuits to be checked for opens and shorts. P23B2 and P23B3 are shorts; P2205 and P22A3 cover sensors 1 and 2.
c: Heater element in the sensor 3 probe burnt through
Broken heater conductor between probe and sensor module
Probe connector not fully engaged after a repair
s: Check engine light after one trip
Sensor 3 never reports operating temperature
SCR warning on the display

P23B2.t: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P23B2.d: P23B2 points to the heater control line of bank 1's NOx sensor 3 being pulled to ground. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B checks that pin on the sensor downstream of the second catalyst for a short to ground and, unlike the open-circuit test, waits until the dew point has been reached, so that the heater is actually allowed to run; 80 failed out of 160 samples set the code. GM rates it Type B, two trips before the MIL lights. The bulletin for the 3.0L LM2 diesel, 21-NA-149 (model years 2021–2022), lists the code too and traces many faults to chafed engine harnesses. CARB demands detection of heater circuit shorts that contradict what the heater was told to do. The heater can then no longer be regulated; P23B3 is the short to power.
c: Heater control wire chafed against ground
Internal short in the heater of sensor 3
Water bridging the heater pins in the connector
s: Check engine light after two trips
Sensor 3 slow or unable to become ready

P23B3.t: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P23B3.d: If, on NOx sensor 3 of bank 1, the heater control pin sits at supply voltage when the electronics expect it to switch, P23B3 is stored. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B describes it, for the sensor behind the second catalyst, as a battery short at the heater drive pin, evaluated every 25 ms with sensor supply above 9.9 V and dew point reached, and failing at 80 of 160 samples; Type B with the MIL on the second trip. GM also lists P23B3 in bulletin 21-NA-149 for 3.0L LM2 Duramax light trucks of 2021–2022. CARB requires the OBD system to catch heater circuit states that contradict the command, naming a short to 12 V as the example. As electronics and heater form one unit, the complete sensor is usually replaced once the harness is ruled out. P23B2 is the ground short.
c: Heater control wire shorted to a supply line
Heater driver inside the sensor 3 electronics failed
s: Check engine light after two trips
Sensor 3 heater status shows an error in live data
SCR warning

P23B4.t: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P23B4.d: Besides its drive line, the heater of a NOx sensor has a sense connection through which its resistance, and with it the element temperature, is measured. P23B4 reports a fault in that sense path for the third sensor on bank 1. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B checks the HTemp pin of the post-second-catalyst sensor for an open circuit: 80 of 160 samples, Type A, MIL after one trip. A note in the table says that the Continental Gen 3.5 sensors debounce electrical faults internally for 1.5 s before reporting them, which lets the affected wire be pinpointed. Bulletin 21-NA-149 adds P23B4 to the harness-chafe list of LM2-powered 3.0L trucks from 2021–2022. Heater circuit monitoring is a CARB requirement. P23B5 is the plausibility check, P2208 and P22A6 the other sensors.
c: Heater sense lead broken between probe and module
Backed-out or corroded terminal at the probe connector
Internal break in the sensor 3 probe
s: Check engine light after one trip
Sensor 3 temperature status invalid

P23B5.t: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P23B5.d: P23B5 says the heater feedback from NOx sensor 3 (bank 1) is present but implausible: the element does not reach or hold the resistance that matches its target temperature. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B compares the raw heater resistance of the post-second-catalyst sensor with its target and fails it outside a relative band of 0.06, after waiting 200 s from supply in range and from dew point; 125 of 250 samples, Type A. Ford lists P23B5 for 2023 Super Duty trucks with the 6.7L diesel together with P2209, P22A7 and NOx sensor communication codes (SSM 51750, 51791): harness 14406 chafes on the right-hand EGR cooler near connector C146, so fuse F18 (20 A) is checked first. P23B4 is the open sense line.
c: NOx sensor harness chafing on a hot component such as the EGR cooler (Ford 2023 6.7L)
Aged heater element whose resistance no longer matches the target
Blown fuse in the NOx sensor supply after a short
High contact resistance in the heater connector
s: Check engine light after one trip
Several NOx sensor and communication codes at once
SCR warning, sensor 3 not ready

P23B6.t: NOx Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P23B6.d: P23B6 concerns the power feed of the third NOx sensor on bank 1, the smart probe behind the second SCR catalyst. Its built-in control unit needs a stable supply, and when the voltage it reports leaves the allowed range the engine module stores this code. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B fails it below 9.90 V while the engine runs, the powertrain relay delivers more than 11 V and the dew point has been passed; it needs 125 bad readings among 250 taken every 25 ms and is rated Type B (two-trip MIL). In bulletin 21-NA-149 GM counts P23B6 among the codes produced by a chafed engine harness with blown fuses on 2021-2022 trucks with the 3.0L LM2. P220A and P220B are the same check on sensors 1 and 2; without proper supply the sensor sends no NOx values.
c: Blown fuse in the NOx sensor supply after a short elsewhere in the harness
Supply or ground wire chafed through on the engine or frame (GM 3.0L LM2)
Corroded or loose pins in the sensor 3 connector under the vehicle
Weak battery or charging fault pulling the sensor supply down
s: Check engine light after two trips
Sensor 3 shows no NOx value in live data
Further NOx sensor or communication codes stored at the same time

P23B7.t: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P23B7.d: P23B7 is set when the heater drive of NOx sensor 3 on bank 1 looks electrically sound but does not behave as the control strategy expects, for instance a heater duty cycle far from what the element should need to reach operating temperature. No manufacturer documents P23B7 publicly; GM's 2025 table covers sensor 3 only with the plain heater circuit codes P23B1-P23B3 and the resistance check P23B5. Ford's 2023 diesel summary shows how the front-sensor counterpart P220E is judged: apart from open and shorted heaters a heater whose duty cycle misses the expected figure by over 20 percent is also treated as faulty. CARB requires sensor heater performance to stay within the supplier's limits. If the element never gets hot enough, sensor 3 stays inactive; P220F is the sensor 2 version.
c: Aged heater element that needs far more or less power than expected
High resistance in heater supply or ground contacts
Sensor supply voltage at the lower limit, so the heater cannot keep up
s: Check engine light on
Sensor 3 takes long to become ready or drops out of its active state
SCR efficiency monitor not completing

P23B8.t: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P23B8.d: Smart NOx sensors report heater temperature through a separate sense connection, which GM calls the HTemp pin. P23B8 means this line on sensor 3 of bank 1 is pulled to ground. GM's 2025 table 25OBDG04B looks for the ground short on the post-second-catalyst sensor once the powertrain relay is above 11 V, the relay feeding the sensor bus is switched on, the supply exceeds 9.90 V and the dew point is reached; 80 of 160 samples at 25 ms must fail, Type B with two trips. For Continental Gen 3.5 sensors GM adds that the sensor itself waits 1.5 s before passing on an electrical fault. Bulletin 21-NA-149 names P23B8 where the engine harness of 3.0L LM2 trucks has rubbed through. P23B9 is the short to power; P2210 and P22A8 cover sensors 1 and 2.
c: Sense wire chafed through and touching body, frame or exhaust ground
Water or salt bridging the sense pin to ground in the connector
Internal short in the sensor or its control unit
s: Check engine light after two trips
Sensor 3 does not report valid NOx values
Often stored together with other wiring-related codes

P23B9.t: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P23B9.d: P23B9 is the counterpart of P23B8: the temperature feedback wire of NOx sensor 3 on bank 1 carries a voltage that only a short to battery or to another live wire can explain. The sensor then cannot report a trustworthy heater temperature, so it withholds its NOx output. GM applies this check to the post-second-catalyst sensor in 25OBDG04B (2025) under the same frame as the ground short: powertrain relay above 11 V, sensor supply above 9.90 V, dew point reached, and half of 160 samples (80) must fail before this Type B code is stored. A harness overheated near the exhaust, where insulation melts between neighbouring wires, is a classic trigger; the same 21-NA-149 bulletin for the 3.0L LM2 includes P23B9. P2211 and P22A9 cover sensors 1 and 2.
c: Sense wire shorted to the heater supply or another battery-fed wire
Harness insulation melted by contact with hot exhaust parts
Internal fault in the sensor or its control unit
s: Check engine light after two trips
No NOx reading from sensor 3
Possibly a blown fuse in the sensor supply

P23BA.t: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Intermittent (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P23BA.d: With P23BA, the heater feedback signal from the third NOx sensor of bank 1 keeps vanishing or leaping for a moment and then recovers, rather than staying broken. P23BA itself is not described in any public manufacturer document. GM's 2025 table checks this sensor only for the lasting faults P23B4, P23B8 and P23B9, while remarking that a Continental Gen 3.5 probe only passes an electrical fault on after debouncing it for 1.5 s, so very brief dropouts may never reach the engine module at all. CARB asks for continuous monitoring of exhaust gas sensor heater circuits. Smart sensors send their heater circuit status over CAN, which is where an unstable state becomes visible. Loose terminals, a cracked lead near the rear of the exhaust and moisture drawn into the plug as it cools are the usual suspects; the MIL may come and go.
c: Terminal in the sensor 3 connector with weak contact pressure
Sense lead cracked by vibration or heat and opening only at times
Moisture entering the plug through a damaged seal
s: Check engine light that comes and goes
Sensor 3 briefly leaves its ready state
Fault often cannot be reproduced in the workshop

P23BB.d: P23BB says the heater element of NOx sensor 3 on bank 1 has a resistance outside its permitted band. Because the resistance of the ceramic heater climbs with temperature, it doubles as the thermometer of the probe, so an aged or cracked element heats poorly and reports a false temperature as well. No manufacturer publishes P23BB. GM runs the same kind of check on the post-second-catalyst sensor in 25OBDG04B but stores P23B5: the raw resistance may differ from its target by no more than 0.06 in relative terms, tested once supply and dew point have been valid for 200 s, 125 of 250 samples, Type A. Under CARB, the heater must be watched against the limits its supplier guarantees. P224A and P224B are the same fault on sensors 1 and 2; the usual remedy is a new sensor.
c: Heater element aged by long service at high exhaust temperature
Element cracked by water droplets hitting the hot ceramic
Added resistance from a corroded heater contact
s: Check engine light on
Sensor 3 slow to become ready after a cold start
Implausible NOx readings from the rear sensor

P23BC.d: Every smart NOx sensor carries its own control unit with a memory holding trim and reference data written for that individual probe at the factory. P23BC means this memory in sensor 3 on bank 1 cannot be read or fails its integrity check, so the engine module can no longer trust the readings. No manufacturer documents P23BC publicly. GM's 2025 table hints at what is stored there: for its sensing-element test P23C1, a reference value measured on the new sensor at the supplier plant sits in the sensor EEPROM. Ford's 2023 diesel summary files RAM, ROM and EEPROM checksum errors of the front sensor controller under P2200 instead. CARB treats NOx sensor faults as emission-relevant. P225A and P225B are sensors 1 and 2; a corrupt memory cannot be repaired.
c: Memory inside the sensor control unit corrupted or failed
Voltage dips or spikes on the sensor supply disturbing the memory
Replacement sensor with a calibration that does not match the vehicle
s: Check engine light on
Sensor 3 readings ignored by the engine module
SCR monitoring cannot complete

P23BD.t: NOx Sensor Performance - Signal Biased/Stuck High (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P23BD.d: P23BD means NOx sensor 3 on bank 1, the last probe downstream of the second SCR catalyst, reports more NOx than the operating state allows, or its value no longer comes down from a high level. A common test is engine overrun without fuel, when the exhaust contains no NOx at all: Volvo, for its inlet-sensor counterpart P225C, expects the reading to fall below 50 ppm within roughly 10 s. Ford's 2023 diesel summary allows the front sensor a positive offset of about 40 ppm under P2201. No manufacturer publishes P23BD itself. CARB names the offset-high failure mode for NOx sensors explicitly. A falsely high value behind the SCR system can make a healthy catalyst look worn out and lead to needless parts. P225C and P225E are sensors 1 and 2.
c: Measuring cell drifted upward with age or contamination
Sensor element damaged by thermal shock or poisoning
Monitor calibration too strict, fixed by an engine software update
s: Check engine light on
SCR efficiency code may follow although the catalyst is fine
Sensor 3 reading stays high in overrun

P23BE.t: NOx Sensor Performance - Signal Biased/Stuck Low (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P23BE.d: P23BE is the low-side mirror of P23BD: NOx sensor 3 on bank 1 shows less NOx than is plausible, or it stays near zero while the engine is clearly producing some. Behind a working SCR system the true value is small anyway, which makes a low-stuck sensor the more dangerous error for monitoring, because it can hide a failing catalyst. No manufacturer documents P23BE publicly. Ford's 2023 diesel summary sets a negative-offset limit of about 20 ppm for the front sensor under P2201. Volvo's troubleshooting guide treats the low-stuck counterparts P225D and P225F as a probe measuring outside air, so an exhaust leak or air entry is the likelier cause than the sensor. CARB lists gain-low failure modes for NOx sensors. P225D and P225F are sensors 1 and 2.
c: Exhaust leak or air drawn in ahead of sensor 3, diluting the gas
Measuring cell lost sensitivity and reads too low
Sensor not seated correctly so it samples too little exhaust
s: Check engine light on
Sensor 3 reads near zero under load
Possibly an audible exhaust leak at the rear section

P23BF.t: NOx Sensor Performance - Slow Response Low to High (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P23BF.d: P23BF concerns how quickly NOx sensor 3 on bank 1 follows a rise in NOx. The control module waits for an increasing transient and times the climb of the sensor signal against what a model predicts. No manufacturer publishes P23BF. GM's 2025 table demonstrates the method on the front sensor under P22F9: timing runs from 30 ppm up to 220 ppm, and the sensor fails when it trails by over 2 s or by more than a tenth of the model's time. For a probe behind two SCR catalysts this is harder, since little NOx is left to reach it. A Continental smart sensor is specified with a 33-66 % response time of 1300 ms when fresh and 1650 ms when aged. CARB counts response rate among NOx sensor performance faults. P22F9 and P22FC are sensors 1 and 2; P23C0 is the falling edge.
c: Soot, oil ash or urea residue blocking the gas inlet of the sensor
Measuring cells aged beyond their response specification
Element running too cold because the heater is weak
s: Check engine light on
Sensor 3 signal trails the front sensor during acceleration
No change in how the engine runs

P23C0.t: NOx Sensor Performance - Slow Response High to Low (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P23C0.d: With P23C0 the third NOx sensor on bank 1 is too sluggish when NOx falls, for instance when the driver lifts off and the engine goes into fuel cut-off. The module measures how long the reading takes to come down between two levels. No manufacturer documents P23C0 publicly. GM's 2016 diesel table judged the front-sensor counterpart P22FA during a load-to-overrun manoeuvre using a short and a long timer, failing it beyond 4 s on the first or 8 s on the second, Type B. Deposits from condensate, fuel or oil on the sensor element slow the gas exchange and age it faster, as HELLA notes. CARB expects such response-rate losses to be detected. A sensor that lags on the way down keeps reporting NOx that is already gone, which can make the SCR system look less effective than it is. P22FA and P22FD are sensors 1 and 2.
c: Deposits from condensate, fuel or oil on the sensor element
Holes in the protective tube partly blocked by soot or urea crystals
Sensor aged and no longer able to release its reading quickly
s: Check engine light on
Sensor 3 value stays raised for seconds after lifting off
Driveability unaffected

P23C1.t: NOx Sensor Performance - Sensing Element (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P23C1.d: P23C1 asks whether the measuring cells of NOx sensor 3 on bank 1 have lost sensitivity, for example because deposits clog the internal cavities. GM's 2025 table 25OBDG04B runs the test on the post-second-catalyst sensor during afterrun: the sensor shifts its internal pump currents so that oxygen in the second cavity rises to a target, and the outcome is set against a value the supplier recorded on the new part and wrote into the sensor EEPROM. A ratio above 125 % or below 75 % fails; results are smoothed with EWMA logic, the check runs once per trip at engine speeds under 1,500 rpm and exhaust temperatures below 400 °C, with Type A rating and a one-trip MIL. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 also lists P23C1 on 3.0L LM2 trucks. P22FB and P22FE are sensors 1 and 2.
c: Internal measuring cavities clogged by ash or other deposits
Sensing cells worn out after high mileage
Wiring fault upsetting the sensor supply during the test (GM 3.0L LM2)
s: Check engine light after one trip
SCR monitoring results become unreliable
No noticeable change in engine behaviour

P23C2.t: NOx Sensor Delayed Response - High to Low (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P23C2.d: P23C2 targets the dead time of NOx sensor 3 on bank 1 when NOx drops: the reading only starts to fall too long after the exhaust has changed, even if it then moves at a normal pace. CARB separates these two failure types in its oxygen sensor definitions, calling the time before a sensor first reacts delayed response and a sluggish transition slow response. No manufacturer documents P23C2 publicly. GM's 2025 table builds such a delay timer into the front-sensor test P22F9 for the rising edge: it runs from the moment the NOx model reaches 30 ppm until the sensor does, and more than 2 s counts as a fault. A partly blocked protective tube or aged cells are the usual reason. Sensors 1 and 2 use P24F4 and P24F5, while P23C0 stands for a slow falling transition.
c: Protective tube partly blocked, so new exhaust gas reaches the cell late
Aged sensing cells reacting late to a change
Condensate in the sensor housing after many short trips
s: Check engine light on
Sensor 3 value holds briefly before dropping in overrun
Engine runs normally

P23C3.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve C Position Sensor Circuit
P23C3.d: P23C3 is the general electrical fault on the feedback sensor that tells the engine module how far the third coolant bypass valve has turned. On modern thermal management modules this valve is a motor-driven rotary part, so without a valid angle the module loses its closed-loop positioning. No manufacturer documents P23C3 publicly. GM's 2025 engine tables read the same sensor digitally via SENT and only split it into low and high cases (P23C4, P23C5); a fault that fits neither window would fall under this umbrella code. CARB counts such cooling actuators and their sensors among the monitored comprehensive components. The driver may see slow warm-up, a higher or fluctuating temperature gauge and a warning lamp; motor driver faults are P26B7 to P26B9.
c: Loose, corroded or coolant-contaminated connector at the valve module
Damaged signal, 5 V reference or ground wire of the position sensor
Internal failure of the position sensor built into the valve actuator
Faulty sensor input or reference supply in the engine control module
s: Engine warning lamp
Engine takes longer to reach operating temperature
Coolant temperature gauge reads unusually high or unsteady

P23C4.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve C Position Sensor Circuit Low
P23C4.d: P23C4 says the angle reported by the bypass valve C position sensor has dropped below anything the sensor can produce in normal use, which GM traces to the signal line touching ground. GM's 2025 tables use the code on both its 3.0L Duramax diesel (25OBDG04B) and a gasoline family (25OBDG03B): the SENT sensor value must fall under 27 or under 50 counts respectively, for 4 seconds within a 5-second window, while SENT communication itself is healthy and the engine is not cranking. It is a Type B fault, so the lamp comes on after the second failing trip. With the feedback gone, the valve can no longer be positioned reliably and warm-up or cooling may suffer. The opposite case is P23C5; a wider position error is P26BB.
c: Position sensor signal wire chafed against ground
Coolant or water in the valve connector bridging the signal to ground
Defective position sensor inside the valve actuator
Missing sensor supply so the output stays at its lowest value
s: Engine warning lamp after two drives
Bypass valve C position shown as implausibly low in live data
Slow warm-up or unusual engine temperature

P23C5.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve C Position Sensor Circuit High
P23C5.d: With P23C5 the position feedback of coolant bypass valve C sits at the top end of its digital range, a reading GM explains as the signal line touching a voltage source. In GM's 2025 summaries for the 3.0L Duramax (25OBDG04B) and a gasoline engine family (25OBDG03B) the limit is identical: a SENT value above 4,050 counts present for 4 seconds within 5 seconds, checked only when the SENT link reports no error and the engine is not cranking. GM rates it Type B, two trips to the lamp. A high reading can also come from a broken ground at the sensor. Until it is fixed the module cannot trust the valve angle, so coolant routing may be wrong. Low readings are P23C4, general circuit faults P23C3.
c: Position signal wire shorted to a supply or reference wire
Open ground wire of the position sensor
Position sensor in the valve actuator reporting a stuck maximum value
Bent or spread terminals in the valve connector
s: Engine warning lamp on the second faulty trip
Live data shows bypass valve C near full scale regardless of command
Heater output or engine temperature behaves unusually

P23C6.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve C Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P23C6.d: P23C6 is set by the output stage itself: the H-bridge that drives the motor of coolant bypass valve C reports more current, or more heat, than it can tolerate. GM labels it a motor overcurrent in two 2025 summaries, the diesel table 25OBDG04B (3.0L Duramax) and the gasoline table 25OBDG03B; the driver flags it while energized, with a controller-specific trip point listed between 8.1 and 12.8 A, and the code matures after 2 seconds within 5 seconds as Type B. Typical triggers are a seized valve rotor, a motor with shorted windings or a partial short in the motor wires. To protect itself the driver switches off, so the valve stays where it is. Open and shorted motor circuits are P26B7 to P26B9.
c: Valve rotor stiff or seized by deposits or worn seals, so the motor stalls
Shorted windings in the valve motor drawing excess current
Motor wires partly shorted to each other or to ground
Overheated or faulty H-bridge driver in the engine control module
s: Engine warning lamp after two trips
Bypass valve C no longer moves and stays in its last position
Engine runs too cold or too warm depending on where the valve stopped

P23C7.t: Fuel Heater Control Module Power Control Circuit/Open
P23C7.d: Flex-fuel engines that must start on high-ethanol blends in the cold warm the fuel before injection, and a separate heating control unit switches the high heater currents on command of the engine module. P23C7 reports that the power control line to this unit is open or electrically faulty, so the heaters cannot be enabled. No manufacturer documents P23C7 publicly. Bosch describes its Flexstart heating control unit with a built-in relay for the heating current and full open/short diagnostics, and notes that ethanol ignites poorly below about 13 °C. CARB names heated fuel preparation systems as output components that need circuit monitoring. Expect long cranking or no start on ethanol in cold weather; P23C8 and P23C9 are the low and high cases.
c: Broken or disconnected power control wire between engine module and heater unit
Blown fuse or failed relay feeding the heater control circuit
Corroded or loose connector at the fuel heater control module
Internal fault in the fuel heater control module
s: Hard or failed cold starts on high ethanol blends
Rough running right after a cold start
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23C8.t: Fuel Heater Control Module Power Control Circuit Low
P23C8.d: P23C8 covers the case where the engine module finds the heater unit's power control line pulled to ground. The likely culprit is a chafed wire touching the body or engine, or a short inside the heater unit. Because the line is held low, the heating unit either never receives its enable or, depending on the circuit design, the fuse protecting it may blow. No manufacturer documents P23C8 publicly; the background is Bosch's Flexstart concept, in which the heating control unit drives the fuel heaters with roughly 260 W per circuit at 12 V and reports short-circuit diagnostics back. CARB requires circuit checks on heated fuel preparation. The car usually still runs on gasoline-rich fuel; cold starts with ethanol become difficult. Open is P23C7, high P23C9.
c: Power control wire chafed through to ground
Moisture in the heater unit connector creating a path to ground
Shorted control input inside the fuel heater control module
Faulty output driver in the engine control module
s: Long cranking in cold weather on ethanol
Blown fuse in the fuel heater circuit
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23C9.t: Fuel Heater Control Module Power Control Circuit High
P23C9.d: P23C9 is stored when the power control line to the fuel heater control unit shows battery voltage although the engine module has it switched off, pointing to a short to a live wire. The real risk here is the reverse of the low case: the heater stage may be enabled without being asked, warming the fuel after it is no longer needed and loading the electrical system. No manufacturer documents P23C9 publicly. Bosch lists reverse voltage and internal overtemperature protection for its Flexstart heating unit, which limits damage, and the engine module normally only heats depending on ethanol content and outside temperature. CARB requires output circuits of heated fuel systems to be checked. P23C7 covers the open and P23C8 the low fault.
c: Power control wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Welded relay contact keeping the circuit energized
Internal leakage in the fuel heater control module
Engine module output that does not switch off
s: Fuel heating active when not needed, possible battery drain
Heater unit or wiring gets unusually warm
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23CA.d: Some flex-fuel engines heat the fuel directly in the injector rail: a heating element in the rail brings ethanol up to temperature just before a cold start. P23CA flags the control circuit of that rail heater as open or otherwise faulty, so no heating current flows. No manufacturer documents P23CA publicly. Bosch's Flexstart rail uses such an element, rated at 260 W from a 12 V supply and able to warm E100 by up to 30 °C per second; the engine module commands it through the heating control unit based on ethanol share and ambient temperature. CARB lists heated fuel preparation among output components to be monitored. Cold starts on ethanol may fail; heaters mounted per cylinder have their own codes from P23D1 onwards.
c: Burnt-out heating element in the fuel rail
Broken wire or unplugged connector at the rail heater
Corroded high-current terminals at the heater
Failed output stage in the fuel heater control module
s: No start or long cranking on ethanol below about 13 °C
Misfiring or stumbling in the first seconds after a cold start
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23CB.t: Fuel Rail Heater Control Circuit Low
P23CB.d: P23CB means the control side of the fuel rail heater reads too low, normally a short to ground between the switching stage and the heating element. Since a rail heater draws a high current, a ground short on its feed can blow the fuse or trip the protection in the driving stage before the fuel gets warm. No manufacturer documents P23CB publicly. Bosch states that its Flexstart heating unit diagnoses shorts on each heating path and reports them to the engine module, which is how a code of this kind reaches the scan tool. CARB requires heated fuel preparation outputs to be monitored for circuit faults. In practice the engine still runs once warm, but cold starts on high ethanol content suffer. P23CA is the open and P23CC the high case.
c: Heater feed wire chafed to ground near the intake manifold
Heating element shorted to the rail body
Fuel or water in the heater connector
Shorted output stage in the fuel heater control module
s: Difficult cold start with ethanol
Fuel heater fuse blows repeatedly
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23CC.t: Fuel Rail Heater Control Circuit High
P23CC.d: With P23CC the fuel rail heater control circuit sits at supply voltage when it should not, most often because the line has shorted to a battery feed or the switching element is stuck conducting. The concern is uncontrolled heating: if the element keeps running, the fuel in the rail can get hotter than intended once the engine is warm. No manufacturer documents P23CC publicly. For reference, Bosch gives a target fuel temperature window of about 70 to 125 °C for its heated Flexstart rail, depending on system pressure, and says its heating unit diagnoses the switching FETs. CARB treats heated fuel preparation as a monitored output. Hot-start problems or vapour issues are possible alongside the warning lamp. Ground shorts are P23CB, an open circuit P23CA.
c: Heater control wire shorted to a battery feed
Switching transistor in the heater unit stuck conducting
Internal fault in the fuel heater control module
Damaged terminals letting adjacent pins touch
s: Rail heater stays on after start
Hard restart when the engine is hot
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23CD.t: Fuel Heater Control Module Feedback Signal/Open
P23CD.d: Besides being commanded, a fuel heater control unit reports back to the engine module, so the engine knows whether heating actually took place. P23CD indicates that this feedback line carries no usable signal or is open. Bosch describes exactly such a return path for its Flexstart unit: the delivered temperature and diagnostic status are measured and handed on to the engine module, which uses them to dose the heating energy. No manufacturer documents P23CD publicly. Without feedback the engine module cannot confirm heater operation, may stop using fuel heating and cannot evaluate the individual heater circuits. CARB requires monitoring of heated fuel preparation. Implausible feedback is P23CE; shorts of the line are P23CF and P23D0.
c: Broken feedback wire between heater unit and engine module
Loose or corroded pin for the feedback signal
Heater unit without supply or ground, so it sends nothing
Failed feedback output in the fuel heater control module
s: Cold-start fuel heating disabled or unconfirmed
Harder starts on ethanol in cold weather
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23CE.t: Fuel Heater Control Module Feedback Signal Performance
P23CE.d: Unlike the open and short codes, P23CE concerns a feedback signal that is electrically present but does not fit what the engine module expects. The heater unit may, for example, report no temperature rise during a commanded heating phase, a rise that is far too slow, or values that contradict the command state. Bosch's Flexstart heater unit measures the heat it delivers and passes it on, so a weak heating element, poor contact on a high-current path or a drifting measurement can all surface here. No manufacturer documents P23CE or its thresholds publicly. CARB asks for functional checks on heated fuel preparation, not only circuit checks. Cold starts on ethanol may be slow even though no wire is broken; a missing signal is P23CD.
c: Aged heating element delivering less heat than commanded
High resistance at heater power or ground terminals
Drifting temperature or current measurement inside the heater unit
Weak battery reducing heating power during cranking
s: Slow or rough cold starts on ethanol without a wiring fault
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23CF.t: Fuel Heater Control Module Feedback Signal Circuit Low
P23CF.d: P23CF is logged when the feedback line from the fuel heater control unit stays near ground, below its valid signal range.
