Mostly the wire is chafed against ground or the feedback output inside the unit is shorted. Depending on how the signal is coded, a permanently low level can also look like a heater that never reports a result, which is why the engine module treats it as a circuit fault rather than as real data. No manufacturer documents P23CF publicly; the background is the temperature and diagnostic feedback that Bosch describes for its Flexstart heater unit. CARB requires the inputs of monitored emission components to be checked for out-of-range values. Cold-start heating may be suppressed. The high-side counterpart is P23D0, a missing signal P23CD.
c: Moisture in a connector of the feedback circuit
Shorted feedback output in the fuel heater control module
Faulty input stage in the engine control module
s: Fuel heating not used for cold starts
Long cranking with ethanol in cold weather
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23D0.t: Fuel Heater Control Module Feedback Signal Circuit High
P23D0.d: P23D0 applies when the return signal from the fuel heater control unit is stuck above its plausible maximum. A short to a voltage source on the feedback wire is the usual explanation; with a pull-up input in the engine module an open ground at the heater unit can produce the same picture. Because a pinned-high signal could be misread as an overheated heater, the engine module discards it and records a circuit fault instead. No manufacturer documents P23D0 publicly. Bosch's Flexstart unit is described as sending heat and diagnostic data back to the engine module, which is the signal checked here. CARB requires out-of-range detection on such monitored inputs. Fuel heating is usually switched off as a precaution. The low case is P23CF, implausible values P23CE.
c: Feedback wire shorted to a voltage supply
Missing ground at the fuel heater control module
Feedback output of the heater unit stuck high
Faulty input stage in the engine control module
s: Fuel heating switched off as a precaution
Poor cold starts on high ethanol blends
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23D1.d: Instead of one heater for the whole rail, some flex-fuel systems give every cylinder its own heating path, either a heated injector or an element at each rail outlet. P23D1 is the open or general circuit fault on the path for cylinder 1, so that cylinder gets unheated ethanol during a cold start. Bosch's Flexstart heating control unit supervises four separate heat circuits of about 260 W each and recognises interruptions, which matches this per-cylinder layout. No manufacturer documents P23D1 publicly. CARB lists heated fuel preparation as an output component to be monitored. Typically cylinder 1 misfires or contributes nothing in the first seconds after a cold start. Cylinders 2 to 4 follow from P23D5 onwards; a rail-wide heater uses P23CA.
c: Burnt-out heater at cylinder 1 (heated injector or rail element)
Broken wire or unplugged heater connector at cylinder 1
Corroded terminals in the cylinder 1 heater connector
Failed channel 1 output in the fuel heater control module
s: Cylinder 1 misfire right after a cold start on ethanol
Rough idle until the engine warms up
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23D2.t: Cylinder 1 Fuel Heater Control Circuit High
P23D2.d: P23D2 is the high-voltage fault on the cylinder 1 heater circuit; note that in this series the high code comes before the low code (P23D3). The control side of the heater shows supply voltage while it should be switched off, so the switching stage has lost control: a short to a positive wire or a switching element that no longer turns off are the usual reasons. A heater left energized keeps warming fuel at cylinder 1 after start and draws current constantly. No manufacturer documents P23D2 publicly. Bosch credits its Flexstart heater unit with diagnosing the switching FETs of each of its four heat circuits, which is the kind of check behind this code. CARB requires circuit monitoring of heated fuel preparation. Opens are P23D1.
c: Cylinder 1 heater control wire shorted to a positive feed
Channel 1 switching element stuck on in the heater unit
Damaged connector letting the heater pin touch a supply pin
s: Cylinder 1 heater stays on, higher current draw
Possible hot-restart problems
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23D3.t: Cylinder 1 Fuel Heater Control Circuit Low
P23D3.d: P23D3 reports that the control circuit of the cylinder 1 fuel heater is pulled toward ground. It follows the high code P23D2 in the numbering, not the other way round. A ground short on a heater path rated at a few hundred watts lets far too much current flow, so the heater unit or a fuse cuts the channel and cylinder 1 starts with cold fuel while the other heaters still work. Bosch states that its Flexstart unit detects shorts on its four heat circuits individually and reports them to the engine module. No manufacturer documents P23D3 publicly. CARB demands circuit checks on heated fuel preparation outputs. Expect a one-cylinder stumble on cold ethanol starts and possibly a blown fuse. Open circuit is P23D1, the other cylinders follow from P23D7.
c: Cylinder 1 heater wire chafed to ground on the intake or engine
Heater at cylinder 1 shorted to its housing
Fuel or water in the cylinder 1 heater connector
Shorted channel 1 output in the heater unit
s: Single-cylinder misfire on cold ethanol starts
Blown fuse in the fuel heater circuit
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23D4.d: P23D4 is not about wiring at all: the cylinder 1 heater circuit is electrically intact, yet it fails to heat as it should. The heater unit measures what each heat circuit delivers, so a heater that draws too little current, warms too slowly or reaches a lower temperature than its neighbours stands out. Bosch notes that its Flexstart unit keeps track of the heat energy put out by each of four separate circuits and reports the measured temperature to the engine module. Aging elements, deposits on a heated injector or a high-resistance contact are plausible reasons. No manufacturer documents P23D4 or its limits publicly. CARB asks for functional monitoring of heated fuel preparation. Cold starts may be rough on one cylinder; P23D1 to P23D3 cover the electrical faults.
c: Aged cylinder 1 heater with reduced heating power
High-resistance connection in the cylinder 1 heater circuit
Deposits reducing heat transfer at a heated injector
Low battery voltage during the heating phase
s: Cylinder 1 runs rough for a while after a cold start on ethanol
Longer cranking in cold weather
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23D5.d: Cylinder 2 has its own fuel heating path on flex-fuel engines that warm the fuel per cylinder, and P23D5 says this path carries no current although the heater is commanded on, or the control line shows a general fault. To the heater unit the open simply looks like a missing load on channel 2. Bosch describes its Flexstart unit as checking each of four heat circuits for interruption and shorts and passing the result to the engine controller. No carmaker publishes P23D5 or its limits. CARB lists heated fuel preparation among the output systems to be monitored. Cylinder 2 then receives cold ethanol during the first seconds of a cold start. A quick check is to compare the resistance of heater 2 with that of its neighbours. Shorts on the same path are P23D6 and P23D7.
c: Heater at cylinder 2 burnt through (open element)
Cylinder 2 heater plug loose or not latched after intake work
Broken conductor in the cylinder 2 heater lead
Channel 2 output of the heater control unit failed
s: Cylinder 2 misfires briefly after a cold start on ethanol
Uneven idle in the first minute when cold
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23D6.t: Cylinder 2 Fuel Heater Control Circuit High
P23D6.d: P23D6 flags the control circuit of the cylinder 2 fuel heater as high. A heater driver typically checks the line both with the channel off and with it on; a level that stays near supply voltage in both states points to a control wire touching a positive feed or to a driver that no longer pulls the circuit down. Depending on the wiring, the heater then either stays energized or cannot be switched at all. Bosch documents that its Flexstart unit also diagnoses the FET switches of every heat circuit individually, and that is where a fault of this kind surfaces. P23D6 itself appears in no public manufacturer document, while CARB counts heated fuel preparation among the outputs to watch. Expect either a cold cylinder 2 at start or a heater that runs on. Low and open faults: P23D7, P23D5.
c: Cylinder 2 heater control wire touching a positive feed
Switching FET of channel 2 failed in the conducting state
Bent connector pin touching a supply terminal
s: Heater at cylinder 2 runs on or does not switch
Cylinder 2 starts cold on ethanol
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23D7.t: Cylinder 2 Fuel Heater Control Circuit Low
P23D7.d: For P23D7 the module reads the cylinder 2 heater control line as low, which on these power circuits nearly always means a path to ground: a chafed wire, a heater element shorted to its body, or fuel or water bridging the connector pins. The short draws more than the channel is meant to carry, so the heater unit protects itself; Bosch mentions reverse-voltage and internal overtemperature protection as well as short detection per circuit. In practice the heater on cylinder 2 is switched off and that cylinder starts cold while cylinders 1, 3 and 4 still get warm fuel; a blown heater fuse is possible. No manufacturer documents P23D7 publicly; CARB demands circuit checks on this output. High and open on cylinder 2: P23D6, P23D5; cylinder 1 equivalent: P23D3.
c: Cylinder 2 heater wire chafed through to ground
Heating element at cylinder 2 shorted to its housing
Fuel or water bridging pins in the cylinder 2 heater plug
s: Rough cold start on one cylinder
Fuel heater fuse blown
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23D8.d: P23D8 concerns how well the cylinder 2 heater works, not its wiring. According to Bosch, the Flexstart heated rail warms pure ethanol fuel at rates of as much as 30 °C a second, so a system of this kind knows roughly how quickly each heating point ought to warm up. If cylinder 2 rises clearly slower than expected, draws less current than its neighbours or never reaches its target temperature, the performance code follows. Typical reasons are an aged element, scale or varnish on the heated surface and a corroded contact that drops voltage under load. No manufacturer documents P23D8 or its thresholds publicly; CARB expects functional checks of heated fuel preparation. The driver mostly notices a rough first minute on cold ethanol. Electrical faults on this path are P23D5 to P23D7.
c: Cylinder 2 heater element with reduced output
Varnish or scale on the heated surface at cylinder 2
Corroded contact dropping voltage under heater load
s: Cylinder 2 runs rough for about a minute after a cold ethanol start
Longer cranking below freezing
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23D9.d: P23D9 is the open-circuit or general circuit fault of the heating path for cylinder 3. The fuel heater control unit drives each heater through a channel of its own; when channel 3 is switched on but no load current appears, the connection to the heater is considered broken. Bosch lists interruption among the faults its Flexstart unit diagnoses on all four heat circuits, and its heated rail can be configured for three- or four-cylinder engines, so on a triple cylinder 3 is the last heated outlet. No carmaker documents P23D9 publicly; CARB names heated fuel preparation as a monitored output. Below about 13 °C ethanol ignites poorly, so it is the unheated cylinder 3 that stumbles after a cold start. High and low faults on this path: P23DA and P23DB.
c: Terminal pushed out of the cylinder 3 heater connector
Wire broken where the harness flexes near the rail
Failed channel 3 output in the heater unit
s: Stumble on cylinder 3 after a cold ethanol start
Harder starting below about 13 °C
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23DA.t: Cylinder 3 Fuel Heater Control Circuit High
P23DA.d: P23DA tells that the control side of the cylinder 3 heater sits at a high level. The likely pictures are a control wire touching a positive feed, so voltage stays on the line when the channel is off, or an output stage that has failed conducting, so heater 3 runs without command. The second case is the costly one: Bosch rates one heat circuit at about 260 W at 12 V, which is more than 20 A, and a heater that keeps running after the engine is shut off will drain the battery within a few hours. A heater 3 that is still warm long after switch-off, or an unexplained flat battery, fits this code. No manufacturer publishes P23DA; CARB requires the circuit to be monitored. Low fault: P23DB, open: P23D9, cylinder 2 counterpart: P23D6.
c: Cylinder 3 control wire shorted to a positive feed
s: Flat battery after the car has stood for some hours
Heater at cylinder 3 warm long after switch-off
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23DB.t: Cylinder 3 Fuel Heater Control Circuit Low
P23DB.d: With P23DB the cylinder 3 heater control circuit is too low, meaning the line or the heater itself has found a path to ground. Because a single heat circuit is sized for several hundred watts, such a short trips the current limit at once; Bosch describes short detection per circuit and an integrated current relay in its Flexstart unit, which then cuts only the affected channel. Cylinder 3 starts on cold fuel while the remaining heaters keep working, so the engine shows roughness on one cylinder rather than a general cold-start problem. Water entering the connector, a damaged harness clip near the rail or an internally shorted heated injector are plausible causes. No manufacturer documents P23DB publicly; CARB requires circuit monitoring. Related: P23DA, P23D9, P23DC.
c: Water in the cylinder 3 heater connector
Harness chafed through at a damaged clip near the rail
Heated injector at cylinder 3 shorted internally
s: One-cylinder roughness when starting cold
Other cylinders start normally
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23DC.d: P23DC is set when the heating at cylinder 3 works electrically but delivers too little effect. Bosch writes that its heater unit follows the heat output of all four circuits and hands a temperature reading to the engine controller, so a channel that warms more weakly than the others can be singled out. Such systems exist because ethanol-rich fuel is hard to ignite in the cold: Brazilian flex cars long carried a small petrol tank for cold starts, and the 2009 VW Polo E-Flex was the first model to do without it. If cylinder 3 stays underheated, it misfires or runs lean during warm-up. Weak elements, deposits or a high-resistance joint are typical. No manufacturer documents P23DC or its limits; CARB asks for functional monitoring.
c: Cylinder 3 heating element below its rated output
High-resistance crimp or plug in the cylinder 3 heater circuit
s: Misfire on cylinder 3 during warm-up on ethanol
Lean running in the first minutes
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23DD.d: P23DD reports an open or general fault on the fourth and last heating channel. Bosch builds its heater unit with exactly four heat circuits and its heated rail for either three- or four-cylinder operation, so this code belongs to four-cylinder layouts. There the usual culprit is a heater at cylinder 4 that has burnt through or a plug that came loose during work on the intake manifold; a dead channel in the control unit itself is less likely. No manufacturer documents P23DD publicly, and CARB treats heated fuel preparation as an output that must be monitored. The engine then starts with one cold cylinder and runs unevenly on it for the first seconds, especially with high ethanol content. The shorts on this path are P23DE and P23DF.
c: Heater plug at cylinder 4 left loose after intake work
Dead channel 4 in the heater control unit
s: Uneven running on one cylinder for the first seconds after a cold start
Worse with high ethanol content
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23DE.t: Cylinder 4 Fuel Heater Control Circuit High
P23DE.d: P23DE means the cylinder 4 heater control circuit is at a high level where the module expects otherwise. Either the line has contact with a voltage source, or the driving stage no longer switches off, so heater 4 may keep running. The risk lies less in starting than in overheating: Bosch states that its heated rail works with fuel temperatures from 70 up to 125 °C depending on system pressure, and that the heating element can tell when it is running in air or vapour. If cylinder 4 keeps heating once the engine is warm, vapour bubbles form at that outlet and hot restarts can suffer. No manufacturer documents P23DE publicly; CARB requires circuit monitoring. Low fault: P23DF, open: P23DD, performance: P23E0.
c: Channel 4 driver no longer switching off
Cylinder 4 heater line touching a voltage source
Connectors swapped or mismated after repair
s: Hard restart when the engine is hot
Uneven idle after hot soak
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23DF.t: Cylinder 4 Fuel Heater Control Circuit Low
P23DF.d: P23DF marks the cylinder 4 heater control circuit as low, which in practice is a short to ground between the control unit and the heater. The channel then stays off until the next start. On four-cylinder engines cylinder 4 is the outermost rail outlet, where the harness often passes brackets and hot components; chafed insulation there, a heating element shorted to its housing and moisture in the plug are the usual suspects, an internally shorted output in the control unit less so. No manufacturer documents P23DF publicly; the CARB rule expects such outputs to be checked for circuit faults. In daily use the fault shows as a rough cold start on one cylinder, sometimes together with a tripped fuse. Its high counterpart is P23DE, the open circuit P23DD.
c: Chafed insulation on the cylinder 4 heater lead at the rail end
Heating element at cylinder 4 shorted to its housing
Moisture in the cylinder 4 heater plug
Shorted channel 4 output in the heater unit
s: Rough cold start on one cylinder
Tripped fuel heater fuse
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23E0.d: P23E0 judges the effect of the cylinder 4 heater rather than its wiring: the circuit is intact, but the heat delivered or the temperature reached falls short of what the conditions call for. One factor specific to resistive heaters is supply voltage. Bosch specifies 260 W per heating element at 12 V; since power falls with the square of voltage, a weak battery at 10 V during cranking leaves only about 180 W, and warm-up takes noticeably longer. A performance code on one cylinder alone, however, points to that heater: an aged element, deposits or a poor contact. The engine control sets the heating demand from ethanol content and outside temperature, so the fault shows mainly in cold weather on high-ethanol fuel. No manufacturer documents P23E0; CARB expects functional monitoring.
c: Aged heater at cylinder 4 with reduced output
Poor contact in the cylinder 4 heater circuit
Weak battery or low system voltage during heating
s: Rough start in cold weather on high-ethanol fuel
Longer cranking
Engine warning lamp, depending on manufacturer

P23E1.d: P23E1 covers the electrical drive of EGR valve C, a third exhaust gas recirculation actuator next to valves A and B. Which valve carries the letter C is up to the manufacturer; no carmaker documents P23E1 publicly. The code means the module has found the control circuit open or otherwise faulty. GM's 2018 diesel tables show how the A-side equivalent P0403 works: with the H-bridge driver off and the valve commanded away from closed, a load resistance above 200 kΩ in 96 of 120 samples sets the code as Type B, MIL after two trips. A similar check is plausible for valve C. CARB requires EGR components to be monitored for circuit faults. With this path disabled, NOx rises. Shorts are P23E3 and P23E4.
c: Unplugged or corroded connector at EGR valve C
Open motor winding or solenoid coil in valve C
Broken drive wire between engine module and valve C
s: Warning lamp with otherwise normal driving
Raised NOx at emissions testing

P23E2.d: P23E2 is raised when the drive circuit of EGR valve C is electrically intact but the valve does not respond to it as expected: commanded and measured position, or drive current and movement, drift apart. In GM's 2018 diesel calibration the A-side check P0404 compares setpoint and measured position of the high-pressure EGR valve and fails above a 10 % tracking error in 152 of 190 samples, with coolant at least 60 °C and outside air above −7 °C; it is a Type B code. Soot and lacquer, which over time stiffen EGR valves, are the usual reason, a worn gear train or a weak motor the next. No manufacturer documents P23E2 publicly; CARB asks that EGR control be checked for proper function. Circuit faults on valve C: P23E1, P23E3, P23E4.
c: Soot and lacquer making valve C sluggish
Worn gears or linkage in the valve C actuator
Actuator motor of valve C losing torque
s: Warning lamp after warm-up drives
Occasional hesitation when EGR is cut

P23E3.d: P23E3 says the control circuit of EGR valve C reads low. On motor or solenoid driven EGR valves this mostly means one of the drive lines has a short to ground, so the output stage would draw excessive current or sees a level it cannot produce by itself. The module then switches the driver off to protect it, and the valve falls back to its spring position, usually closed. For valves A and B the corresponding codes are P0489 and P045C; GM's 2018 diesel tables list both among the faults that request shut-off of the respective EGR position control. No manufacturer documents P23E3 publicly, and no thresholds for valve C are published. CARB requires EGR output circuits to be monitored. Expect higher NOx with little change in driving, plus the warning lamp. High fault: P23E4.
c: Drive wire of valve C shorted to ground
Internal short in the valve C motor or coil
Faulty output stage in the engine module
s: Warning lamp, little change in driving
EGR path C switched off

P23E4.d: P23E4 is the high counterpart: the control circuit of EGR valve C carries a level that is too high. Typical are a drive line touching a battery feed, a connector pin bent onto a supply terminal, or an output stage that no longer pulls its side low. Unlike a ground short, a short to voltage can leave the actuator partly energized, so depending on the design the valve may move unexpectedly or not at all. The equivalents for valves A and B are P0490 and P045D. Which component carries the letter C differs between manufacturers, and none publishes P23E4 with thresholds. Under the CARB rule such output faults have to be detected. The engine usually runs normally, EGR path C is switched off and the warning lamp comes on. Related: P23E1, P23E3.
c: Drive wire of valve C touching a battery feed
Bent pin in the valve C connector
Engine module output stage not pulling low
s: Warning lamp on
Valve C moves unexpectedly or not at all

P23E5.d: P23E5 means EGR valve C stays open although it is commanded closed. The 2018 GM diesel calibration decides the A-side code P042E like this: once the driver is switched off, the return spring should bring the valve to its closed default within 2 s; if the measured position is still above 5 % after that, the code sets at once as Type A, MIL on the first trip. Comparable logic would suit valve C. Too much exhaust gas at idle or under load causes rough running, misfire, stalling and, on diesels, smoke, which is why such faults are rated urgently. Carbon build-up holding the flap open is the usual cause; a broken spring or jammed linkage are others. No manufacturer documents P23E5 publicly. Stuck closed: P23E6, excessive flow: P23E8.
c: Carbon deposits holding valve C open
Broken return spring in valve C
s: Rough idle or stalling
Misfire and lack of power
Smoke on diesel engines
Warning lamp on the first trip

P23E6.d: With P23E6 the module concludes that EGR valve C does not open when commanded and stays at or near its closed stop. The consequence is the reverse of P23E5: the engine runs smoothly, but the exhaust share from this path is missing, combustion temperature and NOx go up, and a petrol engine may knock more readily. Typical reasons are a valve glued shut by soot, a seized shaft, a stripped drive gear or a motor that no longer delivers enough torque against the deposits. The counterparts for valves A and B are P042F and P045F; GM's 2018 diesel tables group P042F with P042E as position deviation faults. No manufacturer documents P23E6 publicly; CARB requires EGR systems to be monitored for insufficient flow and faulty control. Low flow from this path is P23E7.
c: Valve C glued shut by soot
Seized shaft or stripped drive gear
Actuator motor too weak to break the valve free
s: No change in driving, but higher NOx
Possible knocking on petrol engines
Warning lamp

P23E7.d: P23E7 means the module calculates less recirculated exhaust through path C than it expects for the current operating point. The valve may well move correctly; the gas simply does not get through, for example because the passage, cooler or valve seat is choked with soot. GM's 2018 diesel tables illustrate the A-side check P0401: measured air mass is compared with a value expected with EGR active, corrected for barometric pressure, and only at steady speed and fuelling, coolant above 60 °C, outside air above −7 °C and ambient pressure above 74.8 kPa; it is Type B after 350 failures. CARB requires low EGR flow to be detected before NOx exceeds its limits. No manufacturer documents P23E7 publicly. Excess flow is P23E8; valve C stuck closed is P23E6.
c: Soot-choked EGR passage or valve seat on path C
Clogged EGR cooler in path C
Air mass or pressure sensor reading off, skewing the calculation
s: Warning lamp after steady cruising
Raised NOx at emissions testing

P23E8.d: P23E8 reports that more exhaust gas passes through the third recirculation path, C, than the module allows for the current operating point – the reverse of P23E7. A valve C that does not seat fully, a leaking bypass or a flow sensor reading too high are the usual explanations. CARB requires the OBD system to recognise EGR flow so high that the system can no longer bring it down to the commanded rate. No manufacturer documents P23E8 publicly. GM's 2011 6.6 L LGH diesel shows the equivalent logic for path A (P0402): actual and desired air mass are compared, and a controller deviation between 0.4 and 1.2 g per revolution between 1150 and 1600 rpm, held for 8 s, sets a Type B fault. Expect rough idle, stalling, misfire or smoke.
c: EGR valve C held partly open by carbon deposits
Worn valve seat or leaking bypass in path C
Air-mass or EGR flow sensor reading off, so flow is overestimated
s: Rough or unstable idle
Engine stalls when coming to a stop
Hesitation or misfire under load
Visible smoke on diesel engines

P23E9.t: Camshaft A Position Signal Output Circuit/Open (Bank 2)
P23E9.d: P23E9 concerns a signal the engine control module sends out rather than one it receives: on some engines the ECM passes a conditioned copy of the bank 2 camshaft A position signal on to another module that needs engine phase information. The code flags a broken or otherwise faulty output line, typically an open circuit found when the driver stage is switched. No manufacturer documents P23E9 publicly. GM's tables for the bank 1 counterpart on the 2019 2.0 L LTG show the method: the driver voltage is compared with controller limits, and an open line above about 200 kOhm is caught during the low-circuit check, which is why P2614 may set alongside it. Ground faults belong to P23EA, shorts to voltage to P23EB. The engine itself usually keeps running normally.
c: Broken wire in the output line to the receiving module
Terminal pushed back or corroded in a connector
Receiving module unplugged or without its load resistor
Faulty output driver inside the engine control module
s: Stored code with no noticeable change in engine running
Fault entries in the module that receives the camshaft signal
Start-stop or shift functions may be restricted

P23EA.t: Camshaft A Position Signal Output Circuit Low (Bank 2)
P23EA.d: P23EA sets when the ECM's output line that relays the bank 2 camshaft A position signal to another control unit is pulled toward ground. The check is blocked during cranking: the module commands the output high and expects the line to rise; if it stays low, the wire is chafed against ground or the receiver has an internal short. GM's 2019 tables for the bank 1 equivalent P2615 give 0.5 ohm or less to ground, or 200 kOhm and more for an open, sampled every 100 ms, with 40 of 50 samples having to fail, rated Type C without MIL. No manufacturer lists P23EA publicly, so the GM values are an analogy. Depending on the receiver, shift quality or start-stop may suffer while the camshaft sensor itself is fine.
c: Output wire chafed through to ground on the engine or body
Receiving module with an input shorted to ground
Moisture or dirt bridging terminals in a connector
Output stage in the engine control module failed
s: Code stored, engine running normally
Harsher shifts or delayed engagement if the transmission module uses the signal
Start-stop function switched off

P23EB.t: Camshaft A Position Signal Output Circuit High (Bank 2)
P23EB.d: P23EB is the opposite fault to P23EA: the bank 2 camshaft A output line, which the ECM drives as a switched low-side signal for another module, stays high when it should be pulled low. Typical reasons are a wire touching a supply circuit, moisture in a connector or a defective driver in the ECM. GM checks the bank 1 version P2616 while the output is commanded low and declares a short to power at 0.5 ohm or less, with system voltage at least 11 V and 40 of 50 samples failing (Type C, no MIL). Nothing comparable is published for P23EB itself, so these figures only serve as a guide. Unlike sensor codes such as P0345, the engine's own timing is not affected; the risk lies with the module downstream, which loses its phase reference.
c: Output wire shorted to a battery or 5 V supply wire in the harness
ECM output transistor no longer switching to ground
s: Code present without drivability complaint
Related fault codes in the receiving control module
Comfort functions such as start-stop deactivated

P23EC.t: Camshaft B Position Signal Output Circuit/Open (Bank 1)
P23EC.d: P23EC belongs to the camshaft B group – on most layouts the exhaust camshaft – and refers to bank 1, the side with cylinder 1. The ECM rebroadcasts the phase signal of that camshaft on a dedicated output wire, and P23EC reports that this wire, or the driver stage feeding it, shows an open or undefined circuit condition. No manufacturer publishes P23EC; the closest documented logic is GM's for P2614 to P2616 on the camshaft A output, where an open of 200 kOhm or more is detected during the low-side test. CARB requires output circuits to be checked whenever another diagnostic relies on them. Low or ground faults are P23ED, high or battery faults P23EE. Drivability normally stays intact.
c: Open circuit in the camshaft B output wire
Connector at the ECM or receiver not fully latched
Input stage of the receiving module defective
s: Stored code, often found during a routine scan
Receiving module runs on substitute values

P23ED.t: Camshaft B Position Signal Output Circuit Low (Bank 1)
P23ED.d: With P23ED the ECM detects that its camshaft B output for bank 1 reads low although it has released the line to go high. Most often a harness section rubbing through to the engine block, a crushed connector pin or a shorted input in the receiving module is to blame. Measured analogies come from GM: the bank 1 camshaft A output code P2615 uses a ground resistance of at most 0.5 ohm, requires the engine to be out of crank and is rated Type C, so no warning lamp. Whether makers who use P23ED light the MIL is not published. Because the sensor feeding the ECM is not involved, replacing the camshaft sensor will not clear the code; a voltage-drop test of the output line between both modules is the sensible first step.
c: Harness rubbed through against the engine block
Crushed or bent connector pin touching ground
Shorted input in the receiving module
s: Code stored, engine performance unaffected
Downstream module reports missing camshaft signal
Possible fallback behaviour in transmission or hybrid functions

P23EE.t: Camshaft B Position Signal Output Circuit High (Bank 1)
P23EE.d: P23EE flags a camshaft B, bank 1 output line that the ECM cannot pull low: the voltage stays near supply level, pointing to a short to a battery-fed or 5 V wire, a faulty pull-up in the receiving unit or a failed ECM driver transistor. GM documents the test only for the bank 1 camshaft A counterpart P2616 on the 2019 LTG: monitored while the output is commanded low, a short once resistance to power drops to 0.5 ohm or below, a sample every 100 ms, 40 bad results in 50, Type C. No public manufacturer data exist for P23EE. A driver stage exposed to a hard short can overheat, so locating the short before replacing a module matters. Siblings: open circuit P23EC, low P23ED, the bank 2 high fault P23F1.
c: Output line shorted to a battery or sensor supply wire
Faulty pull-up circuit in the receiving module
s: Code logged while the engine runs normally
Faults or reduced functions in the module fed by the signal

P23EF.t: Camshaft B Position Signal Output Circuit/Open (Bank 2)
P23EF.d: P23EF covers the last combination of this series: camshaft B, usually the exhaust shaft, on bank 2, the cylinder bank without cylinder 1. On V-engines with four camshafts the ECM can provide a separate phase output per shaft, and P23EF says the bank 2 exhaust output has lost circuit continuity – a broken wire, a terminal backed out of its connector or a missing load at the receiving end. No manufacturer documents P23EF publicly. GM evaluates its comparable camshaft A outputs only with the engine not cranking and the powertrain relay at 11 V or more, and those faults do not turn on the MIL. Shorts are separated out as P23F0 (to ground) and P23F1 (to power); bank 1 has the same open-circuit check under P23EC.
c: Wire break in the bank 2 camshaft B output line
Terminal backed out of the connector housing
Receiving module disconnected or with failed input
s: Code stored without warning lamp on many vehicles
Module relying on the signal sets its own fault codes

P23F0.t: Camshaft B Position Signal Output Circuit Low (Bank 2)
P23F0.d: P23F0 is stored when the bank 2 camshaft B output stays at ground potential while the ECM expects it to float high. A low reading can come from insulation damage near the exhaust side, where heat makes harness sleeves brittle, or from a receiving module whose input has failed shorted. Following GM's published logic for P2615, the module samples every 100 ms and sets the fault after 40 bad samples out of 50; an open beyond about 200 kOhm is caught by the same test. These values are borrowed, since no maker publishes P23F0. A dead output leaves the downstream unit without engine phase information, so it may fall back to substitute values, which drivers notice as harsher shifts or disabled features.
c: Heat-damaged insulation on the exhaust side grounding the wire
Receiving module input failed short to ground
Defective output stage in the ECM
s: Code stored, engine itself unaffected
Harsher shifts or delayed gear changes
Features such as start-stop disabled

P23F1.t: Camshaft B Position Signal Output Circuit High (Bank 2)
P23F1.d: P23F1 means the camshaft B output for bank 2 sits at a high level that the ECM did not command. Its driver switches the line to ground to form the pulses; if the line stays high while switched, current is coming in from elsewhere – typically a short to a supply wire in a shared harness bundle, sometimes water bridging terminals. The GM bank 1 camshaft A analogue P2616 judges this at 0.5 ohm or less to power, with at least 11 V at the powertrain relay, and classes it as Type C. There is no published manufacturer description of P23F1. Measure the line with the receiver unplugged: if the voltage disappears, the receiving module is the source. Counterparts are P23EE for bank 1 and P23F0 for a line stuck low.
c: Short to a supply wire within a shared harness bundle
Receiving module feeding voltage back into the line
s: Code present, no change in engine behaviour
Communication or plausibility faults in the receiving module

P23F2.t: Cylinder 1 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance
P23F2.d: P23F2 says that the mixture in cylinder 1 has drifted away from the other cylinders and that the control unit holds the second injector of that cylinder, injector B, responsible. Only engines that feed each cylinder through two injectors can produce it. Toyota first paired a port and a direct injector in each cylinder with D-4S on the 2005 2GR-FSE V6. Ford's 2024 OBD summary shows what the letter means there: the port injectors are checked as Fuel System B (circuit codes P21CF to P21D6), the direct injectors as system A. CARB makes an imbalance check mandatory and asks that the code name the cause as exactly as the method permits. No maker documents P23F2 itself; Ford and GM still report imbalance per bank. Cylinder 1 is by definition on bank 1, so read P219C and P0301 alongside.
c: Injector B (usually the port injector) of cylinder 1 clogged or dripping
Leaking injector O-ring or intake runner gasket at cylinder 1
Loose connector on injector B of cylinder 1 (often with P21CF)
s: Check engine light on
Often no noticeable drivability change
Slightly rough idle or a misfire count on cylinder 1

P23F3.t: Cylinder 2 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance
P23F3.d: P23F3 points to cylinder 2 and to its injector B, the second of two injectors feeding that cylinder. The smallest engines able to raise it have three cylinders, for example Ford's 1.5 EcoBoost, which pairs port and direct injection and can switch one cylinder off at light load. On V engines the bank that holds cylinder 2 depends on how the maker numbers its cylinders, so read the service information before working on a side. Hyundai's Smartstream 1.0 and 1.2 MPi engines show that both injectors of a cylinder may also sit in the intake port; whether such a design calls one of them B is not published. No public document ties P23F3 to a vehicle. Compare with P219D for the same cylinder and with P21D0 for the injector B circuit.
c: Injector B of cylinder 2 delivering too much or too little fuel
Air leak at the intake port or injector seal of cylinder 2
Work done on the wrong cylinder because of the maker's numbering scheme
Chafed wire to injector B of cylinder 2 (check P21D0)
s: Check engine light on
Shaking at idle, most noticeable on small three- or four-cylinder engines
Slightly higher fuel consumption

P23F4.t: Cylinder 3 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance
P23F4.d: P23F4 refers to cylinder 3: the control unit has found that this cylinder burns leaner or richer than the others and traces the deviation to injector B. On a three-cylinder engine with port and direct injection, such as the Ford 1.5 EcoBoost, cylinder 3 is the last one; on four- and six-cylinder engines it lies in the middle of the block or bank. CARB lets a manufacturer store a misfire code instead of an imbalance code if exact identification would need extra hardware and misfire detection catches the fault reliably. A P0303 can therefore stand for the same cause. No maker documents P23F4 publicly. Port injectors that drip or clog and a leaking seal at the intake port of cylinder 3 should be checked first; P219E is the matching code without the injector letter.
c: Port injector (injector B) of cylinder 3 dripping or partly blocked
Leaking seal at the intake port of cylinder 3
Low compression or leaking valves on cylinder 3
s: Check engine light on
Possible misfire code P0303 at the same time
Uneven idle when the engine is warm

P23F5.t: Cylinder 4 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance
P23F5.d: P23F5 concerns cylinder 4, the end cylinder of a four-cylinder engine. Many four-cylinder units now carry two injectors per cylinder: Toyota's 8AR-FTS turbo (D-4ST) and its Dynamic Force engines such as the M20A (D-4S), Hyundai's Smartstream G2.5 GDi and T-GDi, and the updated Ford 2.3 EcoBoost of the 2024 Mustang. With a single bank, all cylinders share one wide-band sensor ahead of the catalyst; GM, for example, rates imbalance from how strongly that signal varies from one firing event to the next. No manufacturer links P23F5 to a vehicle in public papers. If P2BF0 or P2BF1 (Fuel Control System B lean or rich) appear as well, the whole port-fuel path is off rather than one injector. P219F and P21D2 cover the same cylinder.
c: Deposits or wear in injector B of cylinder 4
Air leak at the intake runner of cylinder 4
Low-pressure (port) fuel rail problem showing first at cylinder 4 (look for P2BF0/P2BF1)
s: Check engine light on
Slight vibration at idle
Fuel trim shifted on the single bank

P23F6.t: Cylinder 5 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance
P23F6.d: P23F6 flags cylinder 5 and is the first code in this row that a four-cylinder engine can never set. Engines with port plus direct injection and at least five cylinders are mostly V6 and V8 units: Ford's second-generation 3.5 EcoBoost V6, first shown in the 2017 Ford GT, Toyota's 2GR-FKS V6 with D-4S, and the V8s named at P23F8. On the Lamborghini Huracán V10, which combines direct and multi-point injection, cylinder 5 closes the first group of five. The code means the trim of that single cylinder points to its injector B, which in these designs is the port injector. Nobody publishes P23F6 with a threshold. Confirm the maker's numbering, then compare P21A0 and the misfire counter P0305 before replacing the injector.
c: Port injector of cylinder 5 out of tolerance
Intake manifold gasket leaking near cylinder 5
Intermittent contact in the injector B wiring of cylinder 5 (P21D3)
s: Check engine light on
Usually no change in performance
Fuel trim of the affected bank drifts

P23F7.t: Cylinder 6 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance
P23F7.d: P23F7 belongs to cylinder 6, the highest-numbered cylinder on a V6 or straight six. Toyota's GR V6 family is a typical carrier: the 2GR-FSE in the Lexus IS and GS and the later 2GR-FKS both use D-4S, in which the port injector supplies part of the fuel next to the direct injector, its share depending on load and engine speed. Ford's PFDI V6 engines follow the same idea. Because the split changes with the operating point, a faulty port injector may only show in the ranges where it delivers much of the fuel, which makes the fault hard to reproduce on a short test drive. CARB requires the imbalance check for these petrol engines, but no manufacturer documents P23F7 itself. Read P21A1, P0306 and the circuit code P21D4 for the same injector.
c: Port injector of cylinder 6 deviating in the ranges where it carries most of the fuel
Air leak at the intake runner or injector seat of cylinder 6
Injection split calibration needing a software update
s: Check engine light on
Fault comes and goes depending on driving style
Occasional roughness at low or medium load

P23F8.t: Cylinder 7 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance
P23F8.d: P23F8 identifies cylinder 7 and its injector B, so it needs at least seven cylinders, in practice a V8 or V10. Three V8 families using a pair of injectors in every cylinder are on record: Ford's 5.0 Coyote, which gained direct injection on top of port injection for the 2018 Mustang GT and F-150; Toyota's 2UR-GSE with D-4S in Lexus F models and the LC 500; and the supercharged GM LT5 in the 2019 Corvette ZR1, whose port injectors are driven by a separate fuel injection control module and listed as injector B (circuit codes from P21CF, Type A). None of them publishes P23F8; GM and Ford judge imbalance per bank. To narrow cylinder 7 down, use P21A2, the misfire code P0307 and the circuit code P21D5.
c: Port injector of cylinder 7 clogged or leaking
Fault in the separate injector B driver module, where fitted (e.g. GM LT5)
s: Check engine light on
Fuel trim of one bank off while the other bank is normal
Rarely a perceptible misfire

P23F9.t: Cylinder 8 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance
P23F9.d: P23F9 points to cylinder 8, the highest number on any V8. GM's 2019 tables for the LT5 Corvette show how far a V8 with port and direct injection resolves imbalance in practice: only bank by bank. For bank 2 the monitor samples the front oxygen sensor once per cylinder event, normalises the variance against a map and fails when the filtered ratio exceeds 0.75, a Type A fault that turns on the MIL after one trip. A cylinder code that also names the injector therefore needs more than the bank-level method can deliver, and no manufacturer has published that it uses P23F9. Ford's Coyote 5.0 since 2018 and Toyota's 2UR-GSE are further V8s with dual injectors. Which bank cylinder 8 sits on follows the maker's numbering; P21A3, P0308 and P21D6 help.
c: Injector B of cylinder 8 with wrong flow rate
Leak at the intake runner or PCV connection near cylinder 8
Front oxygen sensor of the bank giving a distorted signal
s: Check engine light on
Bank-level imbalance code (P219A/P219B) stored as well
Normal drivability in most cases

P23FA.t: Cylinder 9 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance
P23FA.d: P23FA concerns cylinder 9, which among passenger-car engines fitted with dual injection realistically means a V10. The best-known example is the 5.2 litre V10 of the Lamborghini Huracán, described as the first V10 to combine direct and multi-point injection. Its firing order 1-6-5-10-2-7-3-8-4-9 alternates between cylinders 1 to 5 and 6 to 10, so cylinder 9 belongs to the second group and fires last. Five cylinders feed each exhaust sensor here, so the share of one faulty cylinder in the measured signal is small; CARB therefore permits a bank-wide or misfire entry if the method cannot isolate the cylinder. No manufacturer publishes P23FA, and NHTSA's bulletin index holds no entry for it. Check P21A4, P0309 and the circuit code P21D7.
c: Leak in the intake path of cylinder 9
Valve seat or compression problem on cylinder 9
s: Check engine light on
Little or no effect on the high-revving engine's behaviour
Bank trim of the second cylinder group shifted

P23FB.t: Cylinder 10 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance
P23FB.d: P23FB marks cylinder 10, the highest cylinder number of a V10. Among dual-injection engines, the Huracán's 5.2 litre unit is the documented case; it adds multi-point injection to direct injection. In its firing order cylinder 10 follows directly after cylinder 5. On a ten-cylinder engine an injector B deviation in cylinder 10 shows up mainly in the bank that includes cylinders 6 to 10, which is why a bank code (P219B) or a misfire code (P0310) may be the only entry. CARB requires imbalance detection for such cars too, and since 2019 to 2021 also tracking of how frequently the check runs to completion in everyday use. No manufacturer documents P23FB publicly. P21A5 and the circuit code P21D8 are the companion codes.
c: Port injector of cylinder 10 dirty or worn
Injector seal leaking air at cylinder 10
Heat-damaged wiring to injector B of cylinder 10 (check P21D8)
s: Check engine light on
Bank 2 or misfire code stored alongside
Mostly no noticeable change

P23FC.t: Cylinder 11 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance
P23FC.d: P23FC is reserved for cylinder 11, so it can only belong to twelve-cylinder engines that add an extra injector in every cylinder. Such a pairing is hard to find in public engine data. Volkswagen's W12 illustrates the point: its early versions used twelve injectors in the intake manifold, one per cylinder, while the 6.3 FSI of the Audi A8 L W12 switched to direct injection with six-hole high-pressure injectors, again one per cylinder. Neither layout has an injector B. Any twelve-cylinder engine built with dual injection would still fall under CARB's imbalance rule, including the expectation that the code names the cylinder to the extent the detection strategy permits. No manufacturer documents P23FC. Should it appear, compare P21A6, P0311 and the circuit code P21D9 before replacing anything.
c: Second injector of cylinder 11 delivering a wrong quantity
Code read from an engine that has no injector B (scan tool or software issue)
s: Check engine light on
Hardly any change in smoothness on a twelve-cylinder engine

P23FD.t: Cylinder 12 Injector B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance
P23FD.d: P23FD closes the cylinder series at number 12. It states that the twelfth cylinder runs out of step with the rest and that the cause lies with its injector B. A matching engine needs twelve cylinders and two injectors in each, a combination that public engine references do not show: the VW W12, for instance, appeared with port injection and later as the 6.3 FSI with direct injection only. CARB nonetheless expects every petrol engine to detect imbalance that would lift emissions beyond the limits, and lets the stored code stay at bank or misfire level when the method cannot single out one cylinder. No manufacturer documents P23FD. On a V12 or W12 that stores it, compare the bank codes P23FE/P23FF and P219A/P219B with P21A7, P0312 and P21DA.
c: Second injector of cylinder 12 out of tolerance
Intake leak or valve sealing fault at cylinder 12
Code reported by a tool on an engine without a second injector
s: Check engine light on
Bank or misfire code stored at the same time

P23FE.t: Bank 1 System B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance
P23FE.d: P23FE reports a cylinder-to-cylinder imbalance on bank 1 that the control unit attributes to fuel system B, without naming a cylinder. Ford's 2024 OBD summary explains the letter for its dual-injection engines: the port path is Fuel Control System B with its own lean and rich codes (P2BF0/P2BF1 for bank 1), while direct injection forms system A. Ford's imbalance monitor itself still stores only P219A: it runs once per trip in closed loop after the fuel monitor has adapted, needs 300 to 700 s and fails above an imbalance ratio of 0.75. No manufacturer publishes P23FE. An inline engine has only bank 1, so the code then covers all its cylinders; on V engines it is the side with cylinder 1. A system-wide B code points to the port rail, its pressure or several port injectors at once.
c: Several port injectors on bank 1 fouled by deposits
Port fuel rail pressure or low-pressure supply wrong on bank 1
Intake manifold leak on the bank 1 side
Front oxygen sensor of bank 1 responding poorly
s: Check engine light on
Lean or rich fuel trim on bank 1, possibly P2BF0 or P2BF1
Slightly increased fuel consumption

P23FF.t: Bank 2 System B Air-Fuel Ratio Imbalance
P23FF.d: P23FF mirrors P23FE for bank 2 and can only occur on V, W or boxer engines, because inline engines have no second bank. It means the cylinders on the side without cylinder 1 deviate from each other and the fault is assigned to injection system B, which on Ford's PFDI engines is the port path (lean and rich codes P2BF2/P2BF3). Bank-level monitors on such engines are documented, but under the general codes: GM's 2019 LT5 Corvette V8 fails bank 2 when the normalised oxygen sensor ratio exceeds 0.75, rated Type A and lighting the MIL on the first failed trip, and Ford sets P219B. No manufacturer publishes P23FF. When the fault stays confined to bank 2, the culprit usually sits on that side, such as a port fuel rail, a manifold gasket or several injectors of that bank.
c: Several port injectors on bank 2 with deposits or wear
Intake manifold gasket leaking on bank 2
Supply problem in the port fuel rail feeding bank 2
Front oxygen sensor or its wiring on bank 2 distorting the signal
s: Check engine light on
Fuel trims of the two banks clearly apart
Possibly P2BF2 or P2BF3 as well

P2400.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Control Circuit/Open
P2400.d: P2400 is stored when the engine computer finds the drive line of the evaporative leak detection pump open, so the pump cannot be switched for the tank leak test. GM's tables for the sealed fuel system of the Volt (2011, 2016) compare the commanded and actual driver state and treat a low voltage in the off state, equal to more than 200 kOhm to ground, as an open; 20 failed samples out of 25 at 250 ms each set a Type B code. VW's 2014 Golf data book flags a signal voltage of roughly 4.4-5.6 V. Toyota names P2400 with failure types 7E/7F on A25A engines, and VW traced P2400 on the 2011-2014 Touareg 3.6 to coolant entering the pump's vacuum line. P2401 and P2402 are the short-circuit siblings. The leak test cannot run; the car drives normally.
c: Corroded or loose pump connector, broken wire in the drive line
Open winding or internal fault in the leak detection pump
Coolant in the pump's vacuum supply line from a failed coolant pump changeover valve (VW Touareg 3.6)
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light
EVAP readiness monitor stays incomplete
No noticeable change in driving behaviour

P2401.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Control Circuit Low
P2401.d: P2401 means the control line of the leak detection pump is pulled to ground level, usually by chafed insulation touching the body or by an internal pump fault. GM's 2016 Volt table checks the low-side driver while it is switched off; a near-zero impedance of about 0.5 Ohm to controller ground counts as a short, and 20 of 25 samples of 250 ms set a Type B code over two trips. VW's 2014 Golf and Touareg data books use a signal below about 2.15-3.26 V, depending on engine. Land Rover's SSM71298 (LR4, Range Rover Sport) and Subaru's ELCM bulletins also list P2401, Land Rover pointing to a defect inside the DMTL pump when the wiring checks out. Unlike P2400 the circuit is intact but shorted; the leak test is skipped while driving stays normal.
c: Control wire chafed through and touching ground near the tank or rear wheel arch
Internal short inside the leak detection pump
Water ingress in the pump connector causing a leakage path to ground
s: Check engine light
Leak test not completed, EVAP readiness missing

P2402.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Control Circuit High
P2402.d: P2402 points to the opposite fault of P2401: the pump control line sits at supply voltage or the pump draws too much current. GM's Volt tables call it a short to power detected while the driver is on; when it is active the ECM runs an intrusive check, running the pump for 15 s on command, with a Type B code after 20 failed samples out of 25. In VW's Golf data book of 2014 the limit is a pump current above 3.0 A or, on other engines, the voltage across the pump's current-measuring resistor (about 1.8-4.0 V). Acura recalled 2021-22 TLX Type S models (B22-007) because faulty PGM-FI software could keep the MIL on and P2402 stored after an ELCM circuit repair; Audi and Land Rover also publish P2402 cases. Driving is unaffected, but the evaporative leak check is skipped.
c: Leak detection pump motor seized or drawing excessive current
Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Control module software that does not clear the fault after repair (Acura TLX Type S recall)
s: Check engine light that may persist after repair until software is updated
EVAP readiness incomplete, inspection may fail

P2403.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Sense Circuit/Open
P2403.d: The sense circuit carries the feedback by which the engine computer knows what the leak detection pump is actually doing. P2403 is logged when that feedback is missing as if the line were open. The January 2014 Golf book from VW sets it once the sense signal stays at a low voltage for more than 0.5 s. Jaguar's bulletin JTB00436 for the XJ (X351, 2010 onwards) lists P2403 among the DMTL codes caused by road spray freezing or collecting in the pump filter, and Ford's code list for the 2014 Boss 302S carries the same title. Compared with P2400 the pump may run normally; only its feedback is lost. P2405/P2406 are the low/high siblings, P2404 the plausibility check. The tank leak test cannot be evaluated; drivability is not affected.
c: Broken feedback wire or backed-out terminal at the pump connector
Water or ice trapped in the pump or its filter (Jaguar XJ)
Failed feedback element inside the pump
s: Check engine light
EVAP monitor not completed
More often after winter driving or car washes

P2404.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Sense Circuit Range/Performance
P2404.d: P2404 is a plausibility code: the pump feedback is electrically present but does not behave as the leak test expects. VW's 2014 Golf data book sets it when the sense signal stays high for more than 30.4 s (12 s on another engine) over 30 checks, or when high signal time during pumping adds up to more than 10 s. Subaru has issued a series of bulletins since 2023 (09-102-23 to 09-131-25, many models) because condensation in the ELCM can trigger P2404 falsely; the fix is a leak test, a 35-minute ELCM pump active test and new ECM software. For the 2011-2014 Touareg 3.6, VW linked P2404 to coolant in the pump's vacuum line, and Land Rover lists P2404 with failure types 29 and 2F. P2403 covers a dead feedback, P2407 an unstable one.
c: Condensation inside the leak check module (Subaru ELCM, software update available)
Worn or sticking pump that no longer reaches its expected state in time
Coolant or debris in the pump's vacuum or vent line
s: Check engine light, often returning after clearing
EVAP readiness not set

P2405.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Sense Circuit Low
P2405.d: P2405 is set when the feedback signal of the leak detection pump stays below its permitted window, typically from a short to ground on the sense line or a fault inside the pump. No public source states a voltage threshold for this code. It appears in Maserati's sheet MAS002203 (2020) for DMTL-equipped M156/M157/M161 petrol models from MY17, which notes that most DMTL checks run with the key off; Land Rover's SSM69118 and SSM71298 treat a confirmed P2405 as a defect within the DMTL pump, and the 2021 bulletin JLRTB02068NAS1 blames dirt entering through the pump's dust filter and replaces pump and filter cover. P2406 is the high-side counterpart, P2403 a missing signal. The car drives normally, but the EVAP test result is lost.
c: Internal DMTL pump fault, often after dirt ingress through the dust filter
Corroded connector at the pump mounted near the rear wheel arch
s: Check engine light, possibly set while the car is parked
No effect on drivability

P2406.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Sense Circuit High
P2406.d: P2406 is the mirror image of P2405: the pump feedback reads above its allowed range, as with a short to a voltage source or a sense line that floats high. Thresholds are not published. Jaguar's JTB00436 for the XJ (X351) includes P2406 among DMTL faults caused by water or ice from tyre spray caught in the pump filter and has the canister and filler pipe renewed. Maserati's DMTL sheet MAS002203 and Land Rover's SSM69118/SSM71298 list it as well, and JLR's 2021 bulletin JLRTB02068NAS1 (Range Rover, Discovery, Range Rover Sport) replaces the pump with a new dust filter cover after contamination. It differs from P2404 in that the signal leaves its electrical range instead of merely being implausible. Driving is unaffected.
c: Water or ice from road spray in the pump filter (Jaguar XJ)
Sense wire shorted to a voltage feed or open ground at the pump
Pump damaged by contamination entering through the dust filter
s: Check engine light
Fault often appears after wet or freezing weather

P2407.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Sense Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2407.d: P2407 reports a pump feedback that jumps around instead of staying steady. On current-measuring DMTL pumps VW's 2014 Golf and Touareg books define it precisely: the pump current fluctuates by more than 1 mA during the reference measurement, or it drops by more than 6 mA for at least 3 s while pumping, checked with the engine off and on. Audi's TSB 2071770 (Q5, Q5 e, Q3, Q7 and others, 2022-23) calls the diagnosis too sensitive and cures it with new ECM software, and VW's 01-23-03 does the same for the 2022 Atlas and Atlas Cross Sport 2.0T before any parts are replaced. Maserati and Jaguar list P2407 too. P2404 is the steady implausibility, P2403 a lost signal. The car runs normally; the warning light is the main effect.
c: Over-sensitive diagnostic calibration, fixed by ECM software update (Audi, VW 2022-23)
Loose contact or corrosion at the pump connector
Worn pump motor with unstable current draw
s: Check engine light, sometimes only after the car has been parked
Code returns irregularly after clearing

P2408.d: P2408 is the general circuit code for a sensor or switch that tells the engine computer whether the fuel cap or filler is closed. It is set when that circuit shows a fault not narrowed down to low, high, plausibility or dropout, which are P2410, P2411, P2409 and P2412. No manufacturer publicly documents this code; most systems infer the cap state from pressure instead. Ford's OBD summary, for example, detects a missing or loose cap (P0457) when the tank does not pull down past -8 inH2O within 30 s after refuelling, lights a Check Fuel Cap lamp and shows a capless-filler message. CARB lets makers skip the MIL for a detected cap leak if a separate warning lamp exists. The vehicle drives normally; the cap and wiring should be checked.
c: Faulty fuel cap or filler switch
Damaged wiring or connector at the filler neck
Aftermarket cap that does not actuate the switch correctly
s: Check engine light or fuel cap warning
EVAP leak test may be skipped

P2409.d: P2409 is the plausibility code of the fuel cap sensor family: the circuit is electrically sound, but the reported cap state does not fit other information. A switch that never changes over a refuelling event, or one that reports closed while the leak test sees a gross leak, would be typical cases. No manufacturer publicly documents P2409. The closest documented logic is pressure-based: Ford's OBD summary flags a loose or missing cap (P0457) when the tank fails to reach -8 inH2O of vacuum within 30 s after refuelling, and clears it once purge vacuum is back above that level. CARB requires input components to be checked for rationality as well as circuit faults. P2408 is the generic circuit fault, P2410/P2411 the low/high signal codes, P2412 a dropout.
c: Cap switch mechanically stuck in one position
Wrong or damaged cap that does not operate the sensor
Misaligned filler door or neck after body repair
s: Check engine light or fuel cap message although the cap is tight
EVAP test results may be rejected

P240A.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Heater Control Circuit/Open
P240A.d: Some leak detection pump modules, such as the DMTL units on VW, Jaguar Land Rover and Maserati petrol engines, carry a small heating element that keeps moisture and ice from upsetting the pump and its pressure measurement. P240A is set when the heater's drive circuit appears open. The 2014 data books for the VW Golf and Touareg take a heater-line voltage of about 4.7-5.4 V as the criterion. Jaguar's JTB00436 for the XJ lists P240A next to other DMTL codes that water or ice in the pump filter can cause, and Land Rover's SSM69118 and SSM71298 cover it as well. P240B and P240C are the short-circuit siblings; P2400 concerns the pump drive itself. Without heating the leak test may become unreliable in cold, damp weather.
c: Burnt-out heating element inside the pump module
Broken heater wire or corroded terminal at the module connector
Missing supply voltage to the heater (fuse, relay)
s: Check engine light
Further EVAP pump codes in cold or wet conditions

P240B.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Heater Control Circuit Low
P240B.d: P240B covers a heater control line of the leak detection pump that is held at too low a voltage, which in practice means a short to ground on the wire or inside the module. Per VW's 2014 data books for the Golf and Touareg, the code appears when the heater signal falls below roughly 2.74-3.26 V. Land Rover lists P240B-00 in SSM71298 (LR4, Range Rover Sport L320) and SSM69118 (Range Rover L405, Range Rover Sport L494) and, once wiring is ruled out, has the DMTL pump replaced and returned. Maserati's sheet MAS002203 includes P240B for its DMTL models from MY17 and asks for the 12 V supply and connector to be checked first. Compared with P240A the circuit is closed but grounded; P240C is the over-current case. Drivability is not affected.
c: Heater wire shorted to ground near the pump
Internal fault in the DMTL pump module (Land Rover replaces the pump)
Moisture in the connector creating a path to ground
s: Check engine light
EVAP readiness not completed

P240C.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Heater Control Circuit High
P240C.d: P240C flags the heater circuit of the leak detection pump at the high end: VW's 2014 Golf and Touareg books set it when the heater current exceeds about 2.2-4 A, which points to a shorted element or a line touching battery voltage. Jaguar's JTB00436 for the XJ (X351) quotes both P240C-00 and P240C-85, the 85 suffix marking a signal above range, among faults from water or ice in the DMTL filter; Land Rover's SSM69118 lists P240C-85 and SSM71298 P240C-00, each leading to a DMTL pump swap when nothing else is found. Maserati names P240C on its DMTL engines too. P240A means no current flows at all, P240B a grounded line. Without heating, the leak test can suffer in cold and damp weather; the car itself drives normally.
c: Shorted heating element in the pump module, often after water ingress
Heater control wire shorted to battery voltage
Faulty heater output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light
Other DMTL codes after frost or heavy rain

P240D.t: Alternative Fuel Low Pressure System Leak
P240D.d: P240D applies only to vehicles running on a gaseous alternative fuel such as CNG or LPG, which CARB counts as alternate-fueled. It indicates a leak in the low-pressure part of the gas system, downstream of the pressure regulator. GM's bulletin PI1330 for the 2015 Impala bi-fuel shows this layout: the regulator reduces tank pressure to 68-130 psi, a low-pressure cut-off solenoid feeds a filter and oil separator and then the gas rail, and a relief valve caps that side at 290 psi if it is opened. How P240D is detected is not published by any manufacturer; a plausible approach is watching how pressure behaves with the shut-off valves closed. P240E is the matching code for the high-pressure side. A gas leak is a safety issue: stop using the gas system and have it inspected.
c: Leaking fitting or hose on the regulated low-pressure side
Leaking seal at the low-pressure filter or oil separator housing
Gas rail or gas injector seal leaking
s: Check engine light, gas mode may be disabled
Gas smell in the engine bay
Higher gas consumption

P240E.t: Alternative Fuel High Pressure System Leak
P240E.d: P240E concerns the high-pressure side of a gaseous alternative-fuel system, from the storage cylinder through the tank valve and high-pressure line and filter up to the regulator. Pressures there are far higher than in the rail: CNG is stored at about 200-250 bar, and GM's PI1330 rates the 2015 Impala bi-fuel tank at 3,600 psi, with a high-pressure cut-off solenoid at the tank and a coalescing filter that is drained every 15,000 miles. LPG systems run at up to about 300 psi according to GM. No manufacturer publicly documents how P240E is detected; a loss of tank pressure that is not explained by consumption is the likely trigger. CARB treats CNG and LPG engines as alternate-fueled. P240D covers the regulated low-pressure side. Treat any warning as urgent, since gas escapes quickly at these pressures.
c: Leaking high-pressure fitting or line between cylinder and regulator
Leaking tank valve or high-pressure cut-off solenoid
Leaking fill receptacle or its check valve
Leak at the high-pressure inlet of the regulator
s: Check engine light, vehicle switches to petrol or will not run on gas
Gas gauge falls while parked
Hissing noise or gas smell near the tank

P240F.d: P240F means the EGR system takes too long to follow a changed flow target. CARB has required diesel OBD to catch such slow response since model year 2010. VW's 2014 data call it EGR System Dynamic Check on the 2.0 TDI (CJAA) and rate rising and falling target air mass against a characteristic above 20; the Touareg 3.0 V6 TDI (CNRB) uses 35 for falling and 30 for rising demand. Volvo and Mack 2018–19 trucks may log P240F-00 with P0069, P0191 and P10EC; if two or more appear, solution K33593604 calls for a new engine harness. Hyundai traced it on 2024 Tucson and Sonata 2.5 GDI to an EGR valve sensor fouled by solder flux (24-01-080H). Too little or too much flow: P0401/P0402.
c: Faulty position sensor in the EGR valve (e.g. Hyundai solder-flux contamination)
Intermittent fault in the engine harness (Volvo/Mack D11/D13)
s: Check engine light
Hesitation or smoke during load changes
Engine power derate on heavy trucks

P2410.d: P2410 reports that the fuel cap sensor or switch circuit is held below its expected voltage window. Depending on how the switch is wired, this can mean a signal wire shorted to ground, a switch that is permanently closed to ground, or a sensor with a failed supply. No manufacturer publicly documents this code or its threshold; the evidence for the function itself comes from pressure-based cap checks such as Ford's P0457 logic, which watches tank vacuum after refuelling and triggers a separate Check Fuel Cap lamp. CARB requires electrical input circuits of emission-related components to be monitored for readings outside their range. P2411 is the high-voltage counterpart, P2408 the unspecified circuit fault. Expect a warning lamp and possibly an EVAP test that does not run; driving is unaffected.
c: Signal wire shorted to ground at the filler neck
Missing supply voltage to the sensor
s: Check engine light
Fuel cap warning stays on or never appears

P2411.d: P2411 is stored when the fuel cap sensor or switch circuit reads above its normal window. With a pulled-up signal line this is what an open circuit, an unplugged connector or a short to the battery feed looks like, so it is often the code that follows a bodywork job or a filler-neck replacement. No manufacturer publicly documents P2411 or a threshold for it. The function is known from pressure-based cap monitoring: Ford's OBD summary sets P0457 after refuelling if tank vacuum stays above -8 inH2O for 30 s and uses a dedicated Check Fuel Cap lamp. CARB allows a separate indicator instead of the MIL for a detected cap leak, but circuit faults of the sensor remain normal input-component faults. P2410 is the low counterpart, P2412 the intermittent case.
c: Open signal wire or unplugged connector, e.g. after body or filler-neck work
Signal wire shorted to battery voltage
s: Check engine light
Cap warning behaves as if the cap were permanently open

P2412.d: P2412 covers a fuel cap sensor or switch whose signal drops out or flickers rather than holding one state, for instance from a loose terminal, a cracked wire that flexes each time the filler door is opened, or a worn switch contact. Brief interruptions of this kind can make the cap look open for a moment and spoil an EVAP test. No manufacturer publicly documents P2412. Pressure-based cap detection, as in Ford's P0457 strategy with its -8 inH2O limit 30 s after refuelling, shows why a reliable cap signal matters for the leak monitor. CARB requires that input components be checked both for electrical faults and for plausibility. P2408 is the generic circuit fault, P2409 a steady implausibility, P2410/P2411 fixed low or high readings. Driving is not affected.
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the sensor connector
Wire cracked where it flexes at the filler door
s: Check engine light that comes and goes
Occasional fuel cap warning with the cap closed

P2413.d: P2413 is a broad EGR performance code, and makers fill it in different ways. GM's 2011 6.6 L LGH Duramax uses it for insufficient flow: the air-mass controller deviation must pass a map value of 1.8 to 2.4 g per revolution for 10 s under steady fuelling, rated Type B. GM's 2005 3.5 L L66 petrol engine compares valve lift instead: under 0.15 mm while more than 1 mm is commanded, below 4000 rpm, sets it after two drive cycles. VW's 2014 2.0 TDI (CJAA) links it to fuel mean-value adaptation, reporting four or more learning points at the ±6 mg per stroke limit. Typical results are higher NOx, a failed emissions test and, on diesels, reduced power. Narrower flow faults are P0401 and P0402, slow response P240F.
c: Soot or carbon restricting the EGR valve or passages
EGR valve not reaching commanded lift (actuator or position sensor)
Air-mass or pressure sensor error distorting the flow calculation
s: Check engine light
Reduced power or derate on diesels
Knocking or pinging under load on petrol engines
Failed emissions inspection

P2414.t: O2 Sensor Exhaust Sample Error (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2414.d: P2414 means the front air-fuel ratio sensor of bank 1 reports a reading that cannot come from real exhaust, usually a lean value caused by air leaking in ahead of the sensor or a sensor that is damaged. VW's January 2014 Golf/GTI data book uses two windows, a signal voltage of 3.10-4.81 V and a sensor signal of 2.5-3.2 V, with a second set near 2.5 V; another engine uses 3.1-4.77 V and 2.5-3.06 V. VW's bulletin 2038575 for the 2013-14 Jetta and Beetle 2.0 found that the catalyst-heating strategy could damage the front sensor, so the ECM is reprogrammed first and the sensor then replaced. GM's 2005 table for the 3.5 L L66 engine sets it when the A/F sensor stays above 2.3 V for 7 s. P2415 is bank 2. Expect a warning light and possibly higher consumption.
c: Air drawn in through a leak ahead of the sensor (manifold, gasket, cracked pipe)
Front sensor damaged by the catalyst-heating strategy (VW Jetta/Beetle 2.0, software update)
Loose, aged or contaminated air-fuel sensor
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption or uneven idle
Ticking noise from an exhaust leak

P2415.t: O2 Sensor Exhaust Sample Error (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P2415.d: P2415 indicates that the upstream air-fuel sensor on bank 2 is not reading a representative exhaust sample - typically because outside air is drawn in through a leak near the sensor or the sensor is not seated correctly, so the reading is implausibly lean. VW's 2014 specification books for the Passat, CC and Touareg evaluate the sensor signal voltage against two bands, 3.70-4.81 V and a lower band of 2.51-3.00 V or 3.0-3.70 V, the band being switched with the gain factor used for the sensor characteristic. P2414 is the identical check on bank 1. CARB requires fuel-control sensors to be monitored for every parameter that affects emissions. Expect a warning light and possibly rough running and higher consumption.
c: Exhaust leak ahead of or near the sensor (manifold, gasket, flex pipe)
s: Check engine light
Ticking exhaust noise when a leak is present
Higher fuel consumption or uneven running

P2416.t: O2 Sensor Signals Swapped (Bank 1 Sensor 2 / Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P2416.d: P2416 means the engine computer concludes that the two downstream oxygen sensors of bank 1 - sensor 2 after the first catalyst and sensor 3 after a second catalyst, as used mainly on SULEV/PZEV vehicles - are connected the wrong way round. No manufacturer publicly documents the detection logic for P2416. By analogy with P0040, which VW sets when the lambda controllers of the two front sensors move beyond their limits in opposite directions, the check compares the expected and actual response of each sensor. The usual cause is swapped connectors after a sensor replacement or harness repair. CARB requires secondary oxygen sensors to be monitored for proper function. P2417 is the bank 2 counterpart, P0041 a swap between banks.
c: Sensor 2 and sensor 3 connectors swapped after a repair
Wrong sensor type or harness length fitted in one position
Wires crossed in a harness repair
s: Check engine light shortly after an exhaust or sensor repair
Catalyst monitor not completing or giving implausible results
Usually no noticeable driveability change

P2417.t: O2 Sensor Signals Swapped (Bank 2 Sensor 2 / Bank 2 Sensor 3)
P2417.d: P2417 is set when the engine computer finds that the two downstream oxygen sensors on bank 2 - sensor 2 behind the first catalyst and sensor 3 behind a second one - respond as if their wiring were exchanged. Such three-sensor layouts are typical of V-engines built to SULEV/PZEV limits. No manufacturer publicly documents the detection logic for P2417; the closest documented analogue is P0040, which VW sets when two sensors drive their lambda controllers past opposite limits. In practice the fault follows a repair in which plugs or harness branches were mixed up. CARB requires secondary oxygen sensors to be checked for proper function. P2416 is the same check on bank 1, P0041 a swap between the banks.
c: Sensor 2 and sensor 3 connectors swapped after a repair
Wrong sensor type or harness length fitted in one position
Wires crossed in a harness repair
s: Check engine light shortly after an exhaust or sensor repair
Catalyst monitor for bank 2 not completing
Usually no noticeable driveability change

P2418.t: EVAP System Switching Valve Control Circuit/Open
P2418.d: P2418 is the electrical check of the control circuit of the EVAP switching valve - an extra valve in the evaporative system whose job depends on the design. Ford calls it EVAP switching valve or vapor blocking valve; its 2012 and 2020-2023 OBD summaries check the driver continuously and set P2418 when a short, open or intermittent fault persists for more than 5 s, so at Ford this one code covers all circuit faults. Karma's Revero and GS-6 bulletin uses P2418 for the open control circuit of the rear fuel tank isolation valve driven by the ECM. P2419/P2420 separate low and high circuit faults, P2450 is the mechanical stuck-open fault. While the valve cannot be controlled, leak tests are suspended and fuel vapour odour or refuelling trouble may follow.
c: Broken control wire or unplugged valve connector
Open solenoid coil in the switching valve
Corroded connector near the tank (road salt, splash water)
s: Check engine light
EVAP readiness not set
Possible fuel vapour odour or slow refuelling

P2419.t: EVAP System Switching Valve Control Circuit Low
P2419.d: P2419 reports that the control circuit of the EVAP switching valve reads low - usually the control line is shorted to ground, or the driver stage measures too little voltage. Karma's Revero/GS-6 bulletin lists P2419 for the rear fuel tank isolation valve controlled by the ECM. Subaru's bulletin 09-103-23 for 2015 Legacy and Outback with an evaporative leak check module (ELCM) tells technicians to look for P2419 and P2420 whenever the ELCM pump fault P2404 is stored, because the switching valve sits in the same module. Ford, by contrast, reports every circuit fault of this valve as P2418. CARB requires output components to be checked for circuit faults. P2420 is the high-side fault, P2418 the open circuit. The leak test is suspended and the warning light comes on.
c: Control wire shorted to ground (chafed near tank or frame)
Shorted coil in the switching valve or leak check module
Water ingress into the leak check module
s: Check engine light
EVAP readiness not set
Often stored together with leak detection pump codes
