P241A.t: O2 Sensor Signals Swapped (Bank 1 Sensor 1 / Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P241A.d: With P241A the engine controller has concluded that the oxygen readings of the sensor ahead of the bank 1 catalyst and of the sensor behind it fit the opposite mounting positions, so the two plugs or harness legs are most likely crossed. FCA uses the code on the 2011 Ram 2500/3500 with the 6.7L Cummins diesel and calls it an oxygen concentration mismatch between sensors 1/1 and 1/2; bulletin 18-012-12 Rev. A brings revised ECM software for it among other faults. CARB requires every sensor used for fuel control and catalyst checks to be monitored. P241B is the bank 2 pair, P2416 the pair behind the catalyst. In practice the code follows a sensor or exhaust repair; mixture control and catalyst diagnosis then work with wrong data.
c: Upstream and downstream sensor plugs connected the wrong way round after a repair
Sensor harness rerouted or wrong replacement harness fitted
Detection software needing an update (FCA 6.7L Cummins)
s: Check engine light after work on the exhaust or the oxygen sensors
Mixture adaptation drifts, fuel trims look implausible
Catalyst or sensor codes set as follow-up faults

P241B.t: O2 Sensor Signals Swapped (Bank 2 Sensor 1 / Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P241B.d: P241B concerns only engines with a second exhaust bank, typically V engines: the controller has decided that the front and rear oxygen sensors of bank 2 deliver signals that belong to each other's position. No manufacturer bulletin names P241B publicly; the only published use of this check found is FCA's bank 1 version P241A on the inline-six Cummins, where it is described as an oxygen concentration mismatch. A frequent variant on V engines is not a swap within bank 2 at all, but a sensor plugged into the bank 1 harness, which is why P241A and P0041 deserve a look as well. CARB sets the monitoring duty for oxygen sensors. Until the wiring is right, fuel control and catalyst testing of bank 2 cannot be trusted.
c: Bank 2 sensor plugs swapped during a sensor or exhaust repair
Bank 2 sensor plugged into the bank 1 harness side
Sensor with the wrong type or cable length fitted
s: Check engine light shortly after work on bank 2
Bank 2 fuel trims or catalyst monitor results implausible

P241C.t: Throttle Actuator Control System - Ice Blockage (Bank 2)
P241C.d: P241C is the bank 2 counterpart of P2072 and only makes sense on engines that use a separate electronic throttle per bank. The controller records that the throttle plate of that bank was frozen in place, recognised by a blade that will not follow its command in cold weather. No manufacturer publishes P241C. For bank 1, Ford's 2012 OBD summary lists ice blockage for its second-generation throttle control as a non-MIL fault, while FCA bulletin 09-023-23 (2013-2023 RAM 1500, 3.6L V6) reports P2072 with a MIL, forced limited rpm and no-start in frost, caused by moisture from crankcase ventilation freezing on the blade. Expect reduced power or a no-start until the throttle body thaws.
c: Condensate from crankcase ventilation freezing on the throttle blade
Water or snow drawn into the intake tract
Damaged or poorly routed ventilation or make-up air hose
s: Reduced power or capped engine speed in frost
Engine will not start after a cold night
Warning lamp depending on manufacturer

P241D.d: P241D marks the last step of the diesel SCR inducement: after repeated warnings about a reductant problem were ignored, the engine module blocks further engine starts. On FCA's 3.0L EcoDiesel (Ram 1500, Jeep Grand Cherokee from 2014) a DEF-related code first triggers a dash message, after 50 miles a restart countdown, and after 150 miles no restart; P241D is then stored and only sets alongside the causing code. A wiTECH routine allows up to 49 more miles. Jaguar Land Rover describes the same code on the Ingenium 2.0D when DEF was not topped up. CARB accepts such inducement strategies as a guard against running without proper reductant. The real fault is the companion code; repair it, then clear and re-run the monitors.
c: DEF tank run empty after warnings were ignored
Unrepaired SCR or DEF system fault (pump, pressure, quality, NOx sensor)
Causing code erased while the inducement remains active
s: Engine will not restart, message to service the DEF system
Earlier countdown warnings in the cluster
Check engine light with further SCR codes

P241E.t: Reductant Heater Coolant Control Valve Stuck Closed
P241E.d: Many SCR systems thaw frozen DEF with engine coolant routed through the tank or supply module; an electrically switched valve lets coolant in. P241E means that valve stays shut although the controller has opened it, so the expected warm-up does not appear. Deutz assigns P241E-00 in its EMR L1 list to the heating valve of the DEF pump and finds it through the defrost check; a closed tank heating valve gets its own code there (P1283). Unlike the circuit codes P20B1 to P20B4, wiring may be intact here; the valve or its coolant path is blocked. Hino bulletin TT-16-014 shows how a cutoff valve can be function-tested. In frost the SCR stays unavailable, NOx rises and an inducement can follow.
c: Valve seized or diaphragm stuck in the closed position
Kinked, blocked or air-locked coolant hoses to the DEF heater
Low coolant level or weak circulation
s: SCR or DEF warning in cold weather, DEF does not thaw
Higher NOx, possibly further SCR codes
Countdown to restart or power limitation if left unrepaired

P241F.t: EGR Cooler B Efficiency Below Threshold
P241F.d: Engines with two EGR loops can carry two coolers; P241F flags that the second one, cooler B, no longer removes enough heat from the recirculated gas. GM's 2020 diesel tables (20OBDG04) pin cooler B to the low-pressure EGR path: efficiency is derived from the gas temperatures before and after the cooler, corrected for flow, averaged and failed below 50 percent, a Type B fault (two trips) with coolant between 60 and 130 °C. The high-pressure cooler is checked there under P2457 against 72.61 percent. Ford monitors its single cooler only under P2457, via outlet temperature over coolant temperature. CARB demands detection of insufficient EGR cooling. Expect higher NOx and a fouled or bypassing cooler.
c: Soot or lacquer deposits on the cooler passages
Drifting EGR temperature sensor before or after the cooler
Weak coolant flow through the cooler (air pocket, thermostat, pump)
s: Check engine light after two trips
Higher NOx, possibly more frequent DPF regenerations

P2420.t: EVAP System Switching Valve Control Circuit High
P2420.d: P2420 means the control circuit of the EVAP switching valve reads high - typically a short to battery voltage on the control line or an overcurrent detected by the driver stage. Karma lists P2420 for the rear fuel tank isolation valve of the Revero and GS-6, which the ECM operates, and Subaru's bulletin 09-103-23 for 2015 Legacy/Outback with an evaporative leak check module (ELCM) includes P2420 among the codes to check alongside the pump fault P2404. Ford instead reports all circuit faults of its switching valve as P2418. CARB requires output components to be monitored for circuit faults. P2419 is the low-side fault and P2418 the open circuit. The evap leak monitor cannot run until the circuit is repaired.
c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Switching valve coil with too low resistance (overcurrent)
Faulty driver stage in the ECM
s: Check engine light
EVAP readiness not set
No noticeable driveability change

P2421.t: EVAP System Vent Valve Stuck Open
P2421.d: The vent valve closes off the evaporative system, letting a leak test hold pressure or vacuum. P2421 says the valve stays open when the controller has commanded it shut; the test then fails to seal, much like a gross leak. Which valve is meant depends on the design. GM's Volt with a sealed tank and leak check pump (16OBDG01) reports a stuck-open diurnal control valve as one result of its pump test sequence, Type B. Porsche applies P242100 on plug-in Cayenne and Panamera models to the tank isolation valve; carbon dust from the canister can spoil its sealing membrane, and the guided troubleshooting was revised. CARB requires the evaporative system and its valves to be monitored. Driving is unaffected, but the leak test stays incomplete.
c: Valve seat or membrane contaminated by charcoal dust or dirt
Vent or tank isolation valve mechanically stuck open
s: Check engine light, no driveability change
EVAP readiness not set, leak codes possible

P2422.t: EVAP System Vent Valve Stuck Closed
P2422.d: P2422 is the opposite case: the vent path stays shut even with the valve commanded open, so tank pressure or vacuum cannot equalise. GM's Volt table (16OBDG01) is specific: with more than 697 Pa of pressure or vacuum in the sealed tank, the diurnal control valve is opened, and a fuel tank pressure change of less than 249 Pa within 10 s fails the test, Type B. Honda (bulletin 15-010, 2013-2015 Accord; later Ridgeline and Pilot) blames dirt that plugs the vent tube of the canister and fits a new canister plus tube. Hyundai revised the detection logic for the 2020 Sonata 2.5 GDI by ECM update (campaign 962), and Porsche and Bentley plug-in hybrids use it for the tank isolation valve. Refuelling may become difficult.
c: Dust, dirt or insects blocking the canister vent tube or filter
Vent valve or tank isolation valve stuck closed
Detection logic needing an update (Hyundai 2020 Sonata)
s: Check engine light
Fuel nozzle shuts off early when refuelling
Hissing when the fuel cap or flap is opened

P2423.t: HC Adsorption Catalyst Efficiency Below Threshold (Bank 1)
P2423.d: Some very low emission petrol engines add a hydrocarbon trap: an adsorbing layer holds back unburned fuel during a cold start and releases it once the main catalyst has lit off. P2423 means the bank 1 trap no longer retains enough. Nissan uses the code, named HC adsorption catalyst function, on the 2010-2012 Altima with the QR25DE in California SULEV form. Its bulletin NTB20-020 stretches warranty on the front exhaust pipe that carries the catalyst to 16 years/170,000 miles for 2010-2011 cars and 10 years/120,000 miles for 2012, tied to an ECM reprogramming campaign. Nissan does not publish the threshold. CARB places such traps under other emission controls with an approved monitoring plan. The car drives normally.
c: Adsorber layer aged or saturated with deposits
ECM calibration affected by a manufacturer campaign (Nissan Altima SULEV)
Damage from misfires or oil consumption
s: Check engine light, no noticeable driving change
Higher cold-start hydrocarbon emissions

P2424.t: HC Adsorption Catalyst Efficiency Below Threshold (Bank 2)
P2424.d: P2424 applies the same check to the bank 2 hydrocarbon trap, so it can only appear on V or flat engines that have such a trap in each exhaust branch. No manufacturer documents P2424 publicly. The only published case of the family is Nissan's P2423 on the four-cylinder Altima SULEV, which has a single bank; there the trap sits with the front catalyst in the front exhaust tube, and the remedy is replacing that part under an extended emission warranty. CARB leaves the monitoring method for such traps to a plan the manufacturer must have approved, so thresholds are not public. With P2424 the engine runs normally; what suffers is the cold-start hydrocarbon output of the second bank.
c: Bank 2 adsorber layer aged or contaminated
Exhaust leak ahead of the bank 2 trap distorting the measurement
Thermal damage from misfires on bank 2
s: Check engine light
Possible failed emission inspection

P2425.d: The EGR cooling valve, often a bypass flap, decides whether recirculated gas passes through the cooler or around it, for example to warm up faster. P2425 reports that the driver stage sees no load on the control line, typically an open wire, a loose connector or a burnt-out actuator. Ford uses P2425 to P2427 for the EGR cooler bypass valve of its Power Stroke diesels: the open-load check runs continuously and needs 2 seconds to fail (2023 summary). VW's 2014 Touareg chart for the 3.0 TDI (CNRB) sets P2425 when the signal voltage falls below 4.70 V. P2426 and P2427 cover shorts. With the flap stuck, the engine may warm up slowly or EGR cooling may be lost.
c: Broken wire in the control circuit near the hot exhaust side
Loose or corroded connector at the valve
Open coil or motor inside the valve actuator
s: Check engine light
Slow warm-up or higher NOx depending on flap position

P2426.t: EGR Cooling Valve Control Circuit Low
P2426.d: P2426 is set when the command wire of the cooling valve reads too low, which on most driver stages means the wire is shorted to ground or the output cannot pull up. In Ford's Power Stroke summary the low and high faults are detected together by a short-circuit check of the cooler bypass actuator that runs all the time and fails after 2 seconds. Volkswagen instead applies a fixed limit to the CNRB 3.0 TDI of the 2014 Touareg: below 2.97 V on the signal the code is stored. Chafed insulation against the exhaust or the engine block is the usual cause. The bypass flap then stays in its default position, which can make the warm-up longer or the EGR gas hotter.
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Internal short in the valve actuator
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light
Bypass flap no longer moves

P2427.t: EGR Cooling Valve Control Circuit High
P2427.d: P2427 points to the high side: the control line of the EGR cooling valve is pulled towards battery voltage or the stage sees excessive current. VW's 2014 Touareg 3.0 TDI chart (CNRB) states the criterion as a current above 2.20 A, a sign of a short in the actuator winding or wiring to supply. Ford handles P2427 together with P2426 on its diesel engines within one permanently running short test of the cooler bypass actuator, 2 seconds to fail. To protect itself the driver stage usually switches off, so the flap remains wherever its spring holds it. Check the supply side of the harness and measure the coil resistance before replacing the valve; P2425 and P2426 are the open and low cases.
c: Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Shorted turns in the actuator, drawing excess current
Water ingress in the valve connector
s: Check engine light
Flap remains in spring position, possibly slower warm-up

P2428.d: P2428 is a protection code: the exhaust on bank 1 has become hot enough to endanger the aftertreatment, above all the diesel particulate filter. GM's 2014 diesel tables (14OBDG04) list five triggers, any of which fails the test after 6 seconds: about 800 °C ahead of the oxidation catalyst, 900 °C behind it, 800 °C behind the filter, or rises of more than 600 °C across the catalyst and 400 °C across the filter. The fault is Type A, so the lamp comes on at once. The usual origin is an uncontrolled soot burn in the filter, late fuel injected during regeneration or a leaking injector. CARB requires plausible EGT sensors, so a faulty sensor must be ruled out first. Engine power is usually limited.
c: Uncontrolled soot burn in an overloaded particulate filter
Leaking injector or excessive post-injection reaching the catalyst
Exhaust temperature sensor reading too high
s: Warning lamp on immediately, often with reduced power
Strong heat or burning smell from the exhaust
Particulate filter or catalyst damage in severe cases

P2429.d: P2429 reports excessive exhaust heat on bank 2 and therefore exists only on engines with two separately monitored exhaust branches, such as V diesels with an aftertreatment line per bank. No manufacturer publishes P2429. The bank 1 version P2428 is documented by GM for a 2014 diesel as an immediate Type A fault with several temperature and temperature-rise limits around the oxidation catalyst and the particulate filter; a bank 2 code would be expected to work the same way on its own sensors. CARB requires rationality monitoring for any exhaust temperature sensor that feeds a control strategy. Before replacing hardware, compare the bank 2 readings with bank 1 and look for a misfiring or leaking cylinder on that side.
c: Excessive soot burn in the bank 2 filter
Leaking injector or misfire on bank 2 sending fuel into the exhaust
Bank 2 exhaust temperature sensor reading high
s: Warning lamp with reduced engine power
Unusual heat or smell from one side of the exhaust

P242A.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P242A.d: P242A is the general circuit code for the third exhaust temperature probe on bank 1. Where that probe sits is up to each manufacturer: VW counts it behind the oxidation catalyst on the 2014 Touareg TDI, Deutz places it downstream of the SCR catalyst on its EMR L1 controller. VW sets P242A once the signal voltage climbs above 2.61 V, which fits an open circuit. Deutz splits the code by failure type, -13 for an open, -F0 for a ground fault and -1C for a supply out of range. Ford's 2023 diesels give the number a different job: a probe that strays more than 80 °C from its modelled value for 20 s within one trip. Dedicated low and high faults go to P242C and P242D. Without a trustworthy reading the ECM usually suspends regeneration or DEF dosing.
c: Open circuit or corroded terminal in the sensor connector or harness near the exhaust
Ground fault or sensor supply out of range (failure types -F0/-1C on Deutz)
On Ford diesels, sensor reading deviating from the exhaust temperature model
s: MIL on
Particulate filter regeneration or DEF dosing suspended
Implausible or missing value for sensor 3 in the scan tool

P242B.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P242B.d: P242B flags a reading from exhaust temperature sensor 3 on bank 1 that is electrically fine but makes no physical sense. Most checks start from a cold soak: GM's 3.0 L LZO (25OBDG04B) waits for more than 10,800 s engine-off and then expects the probe to warm up enough, which exposes a probe that has slipped from the gas stream or is frozen at one value (Type B). Ford's 2023 diesels want every probe within 50 °C of the others after 6 h off; VW's 2014 Touareg TDI compares sensor 3 with four other temperatures (60 K) and with its model (100 K). Not every case is a part fault: Volvo and Mack traced P242B on 2015–2016 trucks to a miscalculated soak time and issued software, and Jaguar found the DPF probe of the AJ20-D4 diesel loose or out of place. Jumpy signals go to P242E.
c: Sensor loose or no longer reaching into the exhaust stream
Sensor drifted or stuck at one value
ECM software miscalculating soak time (Volvo/Mack 2015–2016, software update)
Sensors swapped or wrong part fitted after repair
s: MIL on, often together with P2080 or P2084
No DEF dosing or parked regeneration refused
DPF warning lamp on

P242C.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P242C.d: P242C means the signal of exhaust temperature sensor 3 on bank 1 sits below its valid range. What that says about the wiring depends on the sensor type. GM's 2020 diesel tables (20OBDG04) read a resistance under 158 Ω as a grounded circuit and need 10 bad samples in a window of 20 (Type B); on the 3.0 L LZO a digital thermocouple module reporting below -72.8 °C counts the same way, with 19 of 25 samples. Ford's 2023 diesels use a voltage floor of 0.10 V, VW's 2014 Touareg TDI 0.68 V. Deutz describes P242C-00 as a grounded signal on the probe behind the SCR catalyst. A harness chafed through near the hot exhaust or a crushed connector is the usual find. The ECM then works with a substitute value and normally holds back regeneration.
c: Signal wire chafed and shorted to ground near the exhaust
Connector damaged, wet or with pushed-back terminals
s: MIL on after the second faulty trip on GM
Sensor 3 shows an implausibly low temperature in the scan tool
Regeneration blocked, filter load rising

P242D.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P242D.d: P242D is the mirror case of P242C: bank 1 probe 3 reports more than its plausible maximum, typically because the circuit is open or touches a supply. GM's 2020 diesel tables trigger above 900 Ω after 10 of 20 samples, the 3.0 L LZO above 100 MΩ for an analog probe or above 1,289.85 °C for a digital one; both tables rate it Type A, so the MIL comes on in the first faulty trip. Ford's 2023 diesels react to more than 2.66 V. Deutz describes P242D-00 as a short to battery. Stellantis lists P242D among the exhaust sensor codes of the 2025–2026 Ram 2500/3500 and asks technicians to check battery voltage first and to identify each sensor by name rather than number. Usually the fix is a connector, a harness repair or the sensor itself.
c: Open signal or return wire, broken by heat or vibration
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Low battery voltage during diagnosis (Ram 2025–2026 note)
s: MIL on in the first faulty trip (GM Type A)
Sensor 3 shows an implausibly high temperature or the maximum value
Regeneration and DEF dosing restricted

P242E.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P242E.d: P242E is set when exhaust temperature sensor 3 on bank 1 jumps between two samples faster than real exhaust gas can change, even though each single value is inside the valid range. GM documents this as a quick-change monitor that runs every 100 ms. The 2020 diesel tables look at the resistance step between consecutive samples and fail after 15 of 30 samples; the 3.0 L LZO evaluates the raw temperature step only while the reading is between 140 and 1,070 °C and needs 12 bad samples out of 25. Both are Type B, so the MIL waits for a second faulty trip. Loose terminals, corroded pins and a harness weakened by heat are the usual triggers, though the sensor can also fail internally. CARB asks for such checks on all emission-related inputs. A steady but wrong reading falls under P242B.
c: Loose or fretted terminal in the sensor connector
Harness insulation damaged by exhaust heat, intermittent contact
s: MIL after the second faulty trip
Sensor 3 value jumps in the scan tool live data
Code comes and goes, often after rough roads or washing

P242F.d: P242F reports that so much incombustible ash has collected in the bank 1 particulate filter that it restricts flow and no regeneration can clear it. Ash comes mainly from oil additives, builds up over the service life and leaves the filter only through cleaning or replacement. Deutz stores P242F-00 as a high ash load warning on its EMR L1 controller. GM's 2018 diesel tables watch for the same condition but file it under P24A4, which GM labels ash accumulation: a filtered flow resistance from differential pressure and exhaust flow, 5 failures in 10 samples, Type A. On 2015 Ram 2500/3500 with the 6.7 L Cummins, Stellantis issued PCM software (18-037-16) because P242F could set with no defect present, so check the calibration first. Soot overload belongs to P2463; the second filter has P243A.
c: Filter has reached its ash capacity after high mileage or operating hours
High oil consumption or unsuitable oil (high ash content) speeding up ash build-up
Calibration setting the code without a defect (Ram 6.7 L 2015, bulletin 18-037-16)
Differential pressure sensor or hoses reporting too much restriction
s: MIL or DPF service message
Regenerations becoming more frequent
Loss of power at high load due to back pressure

P2430.t: AIR System Air Flow/Pressure Sensor Circuit (Bank 1)
P2430.d: On engines with an electric secondary air (AIR) pump, a pressure sensor in the duct between pump and shut-off valve tells the engine computer whether air is really moving to bank 1. P2430 is the basic signal fault of that sensor. GM applies it in a special way: on the 2005–2006 3.8L V6 and the 2006 Corvette and CTS-V V8s it stands for a reading that stays frozen while the pump is commanded on (average error below 0.5 and variance below 1.0 for more than 5 s, once per trip, Type B with MIL after two trips); the 2018 tables keep this logic. Low and high voltage have their own codes, P2432 and P2433; P2435 is the bank 2 twin. The car drives normally, but the secondary air check cannot finish.
c: Pressure sensor no longer reacts, signal frozen at one value
Sensor port or duct blocked by water, ice or debris from the pump
Corroded connector or damaged harness at the sensor
s: Check engine lamp after two cold starts
Secondary air readiness not set, emissions test refused
No noticeable change in driving behaviour

P2431.t: AIR System Air Flow/Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1)
P2431.d: P2431 flags a bank 1 secondary air pressure signal that can be read but makes no sense. The usual check compares the sensor with barometric pressure: with the pump off both should agree, with the pump running the rise must stay within limits. GM sets the code on the 3.8L V6 (2005–2006) when the gap exceeds 10 kPa with the pump off or 50 kPa with it on for over 30 s, Type B; the 2018 table works with 15 kPa and 50 kPa. Volkswagen's 2014 Beetle 1.8 TSI allows a deviation of up to 60 hPa from ambient pressure, the Golf CBFA engine only 25 hPa. GM bulletin PIP4409E links P2431 on Colorado, Canyon and H3 to broken MAP sensor wires, because the comparison relies on a correct baro value. Pure circuit faults go under P2432/P2433.
c: Pressure sensor drifted or reacts too slowly
Wrong barometric reference, e.g. damaged MAP sensor wiring
Restricted or leaking air duct around the sensor port
s: Check engine lamp, often only after cold starts
Secondary air monitor not completed
Possibly further MAP or lean codes if the reference is wrong

P2432.t: AIR System Air Flow/Pressure Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 1)
P2432.d: P2432 means the bank 1 secondary air pressure signal has fallen below its valid band – typically a broken signal lead, a ground short or a missing 5 V reference. GM's tables give the limit as under 5 % of the reference (400 failed samples out of 1,000 on the 2005 3.8L V6) and, from 2018, under 6 % for 800 of 1,000 samples; the check runs all the time and is rated Type B. Volkswagen flags the code below 0.40 V on 2014 Beetle and Golf CBFA engines and below 0.5 V on the 2.5L five-cylinder. Because a dead signal makes every flow and valve test meaningless, those tests are suspended while the code is stored. The high-side twin is P2433, bank 2 uses P2437. Drivability is not affected.
c: Signal wire open or shorted to ground
5 V reference missing, often shared with other sensors
s: Check engine lamp, also while driving warm
Secondary air tests not run
Other sensor codes if the shared 5 V line is affected

P2433.t: AIR System Air Flow/Pressure Sensor Circuit High (Bank 1)
P2433.d: With P2433 the bank 1 secondary air pressure signal sits above its upper limit, pointing to a signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage, an open sensor ground or a failed sensor. GM uses more than 95 % of the reference on the 2005–2006 3.8L V6, more than 94 % on the 2006 Corvette and CTS-V V8s and in the 2018 tables (800 of 1,000 samples), always as a Type B fault watched without a break. Volkswagen's 2014 data put the threshold above 4.65 V (Beetle, Golf CBFA) or above 4.5 V (2.5L engine). A broken ground often shared with other sensors can make them report at the same moment, which helps narrow the search. P2432 is the low-side partner, P2438 the bank 2 version.
c: Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Open sensor ground or corroded ground terminal
s: Check engine lamp after two trips
Secondary air readiness stays incomplete

P2434.t: AIR System Air Flow/Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 1)
P2434.d: P2434 is meant for a bank 1 secondary air pressure sensor whose signal drops out or jumps for short moments instead of failing for good – typically a loose connector pin, a chafed wire or a sensor with an internal contact problem. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; GM, for example, covers the same sensor with P2430–P2433 only and folds signal noise into its stuck-in-range and performance checks. CARB wants each electrical component of the AIR system watched for circuit faults and implausible values. In practice this means moving the harness while watching live data and checking terminal grip. If the fault becomes steady, P2432 or P2433 appear instead; P2439 is the bank 2 code.
c: Loose or widened terminal in the sensor plug
Chafed or heat-damaged wire near engine or exhaust
s: Check engine lamp that comes and goes
Fault often not reproducible in the workshop

P2435.t: AIR System Air Flow/Pressure Sensor Circuit (Bank 2)
P2435.d: P2435 is the bank 2 version of the basic signal fault of the secondary air pressure sensor. It exists only where each cylinder bank has its own air path with a sensor, for instance Audi's R8 V10 with the bank 2 sensor G610. GM lists P2435 among its AIR pressure sensor codes in the 2018 tables, but the detailed rows there describe engines with one air path that use only the bank 1 codes, so no threshold is published for P2435 itself. By analogy with GM's P2430, the computer would look for a frozen or missing signal while the pump runs. One pump usually feeds both banks, so a bank 2-only code points to the sensor, its plug or its wiring on that side. P2430 is the bank 1 twin.
c: Bank 2 pressure sensor no longer reacts
Plug or harness on the bank 2 side damaged
Sensor port blocked by moisture or debris
s: Check engine lamp after cold starts
Secondary air readiness not reached

P2436.t: AIR System Air Flow/Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2)
P2436.d: P2436 says the bank 2 secondary air pressure reading is electrically valid but does not match what the system expects. Audi documents the code on the 2017 R8 and R8 Spyder V10: bulletin 2049142 (TSB group 01, 18-56) pairs P243600 with P243700 and has the bank 2 pressure sensor G610 replaced, following the guided fault finding. GM's 2018 tables note that the barometric-quality weighting used for P2431 also applies to P2436, but only on engines with two valves. As on bank 1, the reading is usually compared with ambient pressure with the pump off and on; a drifting sensor, a clogged sensing port or a wrong baro value can all trip it. P2431 is the bank 1 code; P2437/P2438 are the electrical faults.
c: Bank 2 pressure sensor drifted or failed (Audi R8 replaces G610)
Sensing port or hose on bank 2 clogged or leaking
s: Check engine lamp
Often stored together with P2437
Secondary air readiness incomplete

P2437.t: AIR System Air Flow/Pressure Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 2)
P2437.d: P2437 reports a bank 2 secondary air pressure signal stuck below its valid range. Audi lists it for the 2017 R8 and R8 Spyder, where it often shows up together with P2436; the bulletin's remedy is a new bank 2 pressure sensor G610. GM's 2018 tables name P2437 as a blocking condition for the bank 1 sensor tests, so a low reading on either side halts the whole secondary air diagnosis. Electrically, the usual suspects are an interrupted signal line, contact with ground or no 5 V supply; GM's bank 1 sensor treats a voltage under about 5–6 % of the reference as faulty, which gives an idea of the scale. Driving is not affected, but the secondary air readiness stays open. P2438 is the high-side code.
c: Bank 2 pressure sensor failed (Audi R8 bulletin replaces G610)
Signal wire open or shorted to ground
5 V supply to the sensor missing
s: Check engine lamp
Secondary air tests on both banks suspended

P2438.t: AIR System Air Flow/Pressure Sensor Circuit High (Bank 2)
P2438.d: P2438 is the bank 2 counterpart of P2433: the secondary air pressure signal of the second bank reads above its upper limit. GM mentions P2438 next to P2437 among the codes that block its AIR sensor and flow tests in the 2018 tables, but publishes no row of its own for it, because the engines described there have one air path. For comparison, GM's bank 1 sensor fails above 94–95 % of the 5 V reference. Typical triggers are a signal shorted to supply voltage, an open ground or an internal sensor defect; Audi's R8 V10, which carries a separate bank 2 sensor G610, shows where such a part sits. No public manufacturer document describes the conditions for P2438 itself. While it is stored, the pump and valve tests cannot be judged.
c: Signal wire shorted to reference or supply voltage
Open ground circuit of the bank 2 sensor
s: Check engine lamp
Secondary air readiness stays incomplete

P2439.t: AIR System Air Flow/Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 2)
P2439.d: P2439 covers brief dropouts or jumps in the bank 2 secondary air pressure signal. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the description rests on CARB's demand that every electrical AIR component be checked for circuit faults and rationality, together with the bank 2 sensor layout known from Audi's R8 V10 (sensor G610). Unlike with P2437 or P2438, the signal is valid most of the time, so the fault often vanishes at the workshop. Freeze-frame data, shaking the harness on the exhaust side and looking for heat-hardened insulation or green terminals are the practical steps. Bank 1 uses P2434; a lasting fault would show up as P2435–P2438 instead.
c: Loose or corroded terminal at the bank 2 sensor
Harness near the exhaust side brittle or chafed
s: Warning lamp appears now and then
Code returns after clearing without visible cause

P243A.d: P243A is the bank 2 counterpart of P242F: the ash load in the second particulate filter has grown so large that the filter chokes the exhaust and must be cleaned or replaced. A bank 2 filter only exists where each cylinder bank of a V engine feeds its own filter strand. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. Bank 1 monitoring shows how such a check works: GM's 2018 diesels judge ash by a filtered flow resistance derived from differential pressure and exhaust flow (Type A), and Deutz raises a warning once a modelled ash load limit is passed. Since ash does not burn, extra regenerations will not help and only waste fuel. If only one strand shows high back pressure or regenerates more often, the problem is confined to that side.
c: Bank 2 filter full of ash after long service
Oil burning on bank 2 (valve stem seals, turbo seal) adding ash
Bank 2 pressure sensor or hose reporting too much restriction
s: MIL or filter service message
Higher fuel consumption from frequent regenerations
Reduced power at high load

P243B.t: Particulate Filter Restriction - Forced Limited Power (Bank 2)
P243B.d: P243B means the second particulate filter is so restricted that the engine controller cuts power to protect engine and filter. Ford documents the code in its 2024–2025 OBD summary for gasoline engines, as part of the petrol particulate filter monitor next to P246C for bank 1. Once the filter has been above 250 °C for 30 s and exhaust flow lies between 400 and 850 m³/h, a normalised back pressure above 1.0 for 5 s sets the fault. That makes it one of the few bank 2 filter codes with public thresholds, and it shows the code is not limited to diesels. Likely causes are a filter overloaded with soot or ash, a dented pipe, or a pressure sensor or hose reading too high. Until the restriction is cleared the engine stays in reduced power. A high soot load on this bank without the power limit is P243F.
c: Bank 2 filter overloaded with soot or ash
Damaged or blocked exhaust pipe on bank 2
Pressure sensor or hose on bank 2 reporting too high a pressure
s: Noticeably reduced engine power
MIL on
Poor acceleration at higher speed

P243C.d: P243C is stored when the bank 2 particulate filter needs regeneration more often than its calibration allows. CARB requires diesel OBD to recognise regeneration so frequent that emissions would rise above the limit. No manufacturer documents this bank 2 code publicly, so the bank 1 code P2459 serves as the reference: Ford's 2023 diesels flag it once completed regenerations occur, on average, less than roughly 40 km apart. Excess soot from the engine side of that bank, for example a leaking injector, an EGR or boost fault, or a pressure reading that overstates the load, makes the filter look full too early. Every extra regeneration burns fuel and can thin the engine oil. If the other bank regenerates at normal intervals, compare what differs on this side.
c: Too much soot from bank 2 cylinders (injector, EGR or boost fault)
Pressure sensor or hose overstating the bank 2 soot load
Filter partly filled with ash, leaving little soot capacity
s: Regeneration running unusually often
Higher fuel consumption, rising oil level
MIL on

P243D.d: P243D says that a regeneration of the bank 2 particulate filter took longer than the calibrated limit. CARB expects the OBD system to notice when a filter fails to regenerate properly under conditions in which it was designed to. No manufacturer publishes this bank 2 code; the bank 1 version P2458 shows what such a limit looks like, for example on VW's 2014 Touareg TDI, where an accumulated regeneration timer above 93.35 min counts as a fault. Low exhaust temperature on that bank, a weak oxidation catalyst, an incorrect temperature or pressure signal and many short trips all drag the process out. A long regeneration costs fuel and puts extra heat into the filter. P243C covers regenerations that come too often, P243E those that end with soot left in the filter.
c: Exhaust on bank 2 not reaching regeneration temperature (short trips, low load)
Oxidation catalyst on bank 2 converting too little fuel into heat
Temperature or pressure sensor giving wrong values
s: Regeneration seems to run for a very long time (fan, idle speed)
Higher fuel consumption
MIL on

P243E.d: P243E is set when the second filter strand has finished regenerating but the soot was not burned off as planned. CARB requires a malfunction to be flagged whenever the filter does not regenerate properly under the manufacturer's intended conditions. Public manufacturer material covers only bank 1 here: for P24A2, Ford's 2023 diesels evaluate each regeneration, allow up to 40 minutes and store a fault if the soot estimate at the end is still above a threshold. Regenerations cut short by brief trips or switching off are the usual reason, followed by too little heat on that bank, a faulty temperature or pressure sensor or a fuel dosing problem. Ignored, the filter keeps loading until P243F or a power limit follows.
c: Regenerations interrupted by short trips or engine shut-off
Too little heat on bank 2 (catalyst, post-injection or dosing fault)
Faulty temperature or differential pressure signal
s: MIL on, filter warning
Regeneration restarts soon after the last one
Rising soot load in live data

P243F.t: Particulate Filter Restriction - Soot Accumulation Too High (Bank 2)
P243F.d: P243F means the soot load estimated for the bank 2 particulate filter has climbed past the level that a normal regeneration can still handle safely. Burning off too much soot at once can overheat and crack the substrate, so many engines then block automatic regeneration and call for a service regeneration or a new filter. No manufacturer documents P243F publicly. For the bank 1 analogue P2463, GM's 2018 diesels estimate soot from the differential pressure and confirm the fault after 120 failures in 150 samples; the same GM table, oddly, labels P24A4, the J2012 bank 1 twin of P243F, as ash accumulation. Typical causes are long stretches of short trips or idling, regenerations that keep aborting and engine faults that raise soot output on that bank. Power reduction (P243B) may follow.
c: Repeatedly aborted regenerations, short trips or long idling
Engine fault raising soot output on bank 2 (injector, EGR, boost)
Pressure sensor or hose overstating the soot load
s: MIL and filter warning on
Automatic regeneration blocked, service regeneration needed
Reduced power possible

P2440.t: AIR System Switching Valve Stuck Open (Bank 1)
P2440.d: P2440 means the bank 1 secondary air shut-off (switching) valve stays open when it should be closed. GM tests it in phase 2 of its air check: the pump runs while the valve is commanded shut, so pressure in the duct should build; if it stays more than 3 kPa below the model (2005–2006 3.8L V6) or under the 2018 table limit, the code sets as Type B. Volkswagen compares measured with modelled pressure while the valve is closed (2014 Beetle below 71.1 %, Golf 2.5L below 64.8 %). Toyota and Lexus see it on 2UZ-FE, 1UR-FE and 1GR-FE trucks, often after pump debris jams the valve (T-SB-0230-12, L-SB-0028-14, T-SB-0033-17); Subaru's 2011–2015 STI guidance says to check both banks. An open valve lets hot exhaust reach the pump.
c: Valve held open by debris from a damaged pump filter
Valve seat carboned up or corroded by condensate
Electric or vacuum actuator does not close the valve
s: Check engine lamp after a cold start
Pump noisy or failing later due to exhaust backflow
Often stored together with P2442 or P2445

P2441.t: AIR System Switching Valve Stuck Closed (Bank 1)
P2441.d: P2441 flags a bank 1 secondary air valve that does not open when commanded, so pump air never reaches the exhaust ports. Toyota documents it on 2005–2009 4.7L V8 (2UZ-FE) models such as 4Runner, Sequoia, Tundra and Land Cruiser: bulletin T-SB-0230-12 traces it to debris from the air pump contaminating the valves and lists it next to faults of the No. 2 valves. Subaru names P2441 for the 2011–2015 WRX STI and tells technicians to run the diagnosis for the opposite bank as well, since the root cause may sit there. On systems with a pressure sensor the duct pressure then rises unusually high while the oxygen sensor sees no extra air. Seized valves, a faulty actuator and carbon build-up are common causes. P2440 is the stuck-open partner, P2443 the bank 2 code.
c: Valve seized closed by debris or corrosion
Valve actuator, control solenoid or vacuum supply faulty
Kinked or collapsed air hose downstream of the valve
s: Check engine lamp after a cold start
Higher cold-start emissions, failed readiness check

P2442.t: AIR System Switching Valve Stuck Open (Bank 2)
P2442.d: P2442 is the stuck-open fault of the bank 2 secondary air valve: with the pump on and the valve commanded shut, air still passes, or exhaust flows back towards the pump. Lexus applies it to the 2010–2013 GX 460 with the 1UR-FE engine; bulletin L-SB-0028-14 replaces the bank 2 air switching valve and the pump, because a damaged pump filter sheds debris. Toyota's T-SB-0033-17 does the same for the 2012 Tacoma 4.0L V6 (1GR-FE) when P2440, P2442 or P2445 are stored. Subaru lists P2442 for the 2011–2015 WRX STI. Hot exhaust gas passing an open path can melt hoses and ruin the pump, so the fault should not be left for long. Bank 1 uses P2440, the stuck-closed counterpart is P2443.
c: Bank 2 valve held open by debris from the pump filter
Valve seat or diaphragm damaged by heat or condensate
Actuator does not close the valve
s: Check engine lamp after a cold start
Pump noise or later pump failure
Melted or brittle air hoses

P2443.t: AIR System Switching Valve Stuck Closed (Bank 2)
P2443.d: P2443 signals that the bank 2 secondary air valve stays shut although the engine computer commands it open, so the second bank gets no added air during warm-up. Subaru lists the code for the 2011–2015 WRX STI and recommends always following the diagnosis for the opposite bank too, since valve or hose faults on one side can show up on the other. Toyota's 2UZ-FE bulletin covers only the bank 1 equivalent. Under CARB rules, each bank's air supply must be judged on its own wherever a blocked bank would raise emissions measurably. Common causes are a seized valve, a leaking vacuum supply or control solenoid, and kinked hoses. Expect slightly higher cold-start emissions and a failed readiness check; driving is normal. P2441 is the bank 1 code.
c: Bank 2 valve seized in the closed position
Leaking vacuum line or faulty control solenoid
Kinked air hose on the bank 2 side
s: Check engine lamp after a cold start
Secondary air readiness not set

P2444.d: P2444 means the secondary air pump keeps blowing after the engine computer has switched it off. GM checks this in phase 3 of its sequence, with the pump commanded off and the valve closed: if duct pressure stays higher than predicted – by more than 1.5 kPa within 5 s on the 2005–2006 3.8L V6, by more than 4.2 kPa within 10 s for the 2006 V8s in Corvette and CTS-V – the code sets as Type A and lights the MIL on the first trip; the 2018 tables keep the Type A rating. The usual culprit is a welded or sticking pump relay or a driver circuit shorted to power, less often a pump with internal damage. A pump that never stops can overheat and drain the battery. P2445 is the stuck-off fault, P2446 the bank 2 code.
c: Pump relay contacts welded or sticking
Relay control circuit shorted to power
Output driver in the engine computer faulty
s: Check engine lamp on the first trip
Pump audibly running long after start or with engine off
Discharged battery

P2445.d: P2445 reports that the secondary air pump delivers no air although it is commanded on. Toyota and Lexus use it on several trucks: on 2UZ-FE 4.7L models (T-SB-0230-12, revised in 2013 to include P2445), on the 2010–2013 GX 460 (L-SB-0028-14) and on the 2012 Tacoma with the 1GR-FE (T-SB-0033-17). When the memory holds just P0418, P2445 or both, Lexus replaces the pump together with both switching valves, since debris from the pump may already have reached them. Typical root causes are moisture or debris that seizes the pump, a blown fuse, or a failed relay or driver. Unlike P2444, the pump stays silent at cold start. The engine runs normally, but cold-start emissions rise and the readiness check fails. P2447 is the bank 2 equivalent.
c: Pump seized by moisture or debris from a damaged filter
Blown pump fuse or failed pump relay
Open pump supply or ground, corroded plug
s: Check engine lamp after a cold start
No pump noise directly after a cold start
Often stored together with P0418

P2446.d: P2446 is the bank 2 entry for a secondary air pump that keeps running after being switched off. The code is meaningful only on engines with a separate pump per cylinder bank or where the system reports pump faults per bank; no manufacturer documents this code publicly. By analogy with GM's bank 1 code P2444, the check would run after the pump is commanded off and look for duct pressure that stays above the model, which points to a stuck relay, a shorted driver or a pump with an internal fault. Under CARB rules, AIR pumps, relays and valves count as comprehensive components and need their own monitoring. A pump that never stops can overheat, wear out quickly and load the battery. P2447 is the stuck-off code for bank 2; P2444 covers bank 1.
c: Relay of the bank 2 pump stuck closed
Faulty output driver in the engine computer
s: Check engine lamp
Pump keeps humming after the warm-up phase

P2447.d: P2447 indicates that the bank 2 secondary air pump does not deliver air when commanded. No manufacturer publicly documents this code; Toyota and Lexus, whose V6 and V8 trucks feed both banks from one pump through two valves, log a dead pump as P2445. On designs with a separate pump per bank, the cause usually lies with the second pump: a blown fuse, a failed relay, a corroded plug or a motor seized after water got in. CARB requires detection of a system that delivers too little or no air before cold-start emissions climb past the limit. Driving is unaffected; what suffers is the readiness status and the emissions after a cold start. P2446 is the stuck-on code for the same bank.
c: Bank 2 pump seized after water ingress
Blown fuse or failed relay of the bank 2 pump
Corroded pump connector or open ground
s: Check engine lamp after a cold start
Readiness for secondary air not set

P2448.d: P2448 means more secondary air reaches bank 1 than the system expects – for example when the shut-off valve leaks, the pump keeps blowing, or the control logic sees a stronger lean shift than modelled. Ford uses the code: its 2012 OBD summary names P0491, P0410 and P2448 as the bank 1 codes behind the secondary air readiness and in-use monitor counters, and Ford's 2014 code list (published for the Boss 302S) marks P2448 as a MIL code. Ford does not publish a threshold for it. CARB's secondary air rules focus on low flow but demand correct function of the whole system, valves included. Common causes are a valve stuck partly open, an air pump relay that sticks, or a leaking check valve. P0491 is the insufficient-flow counterpart, P2449 covers bank 2.
c: Shut-off valve does not seal fully
Pump relay sticks, pump runs longer than commanded
Leaking check valve in the air path
s: Check engine lamp
Lean-running codes or fuel trim deviation after cold start

P2449.d: P2449 is the bank 2 high-flow fault of the AIR system: during or after the air injection phase the second bank receives more air than predicted. Ford assigns it in its 2012 OBD summary to the bank 2 secondary air readiness, next to P0492 for too little flow, so the code belongs to Ford's AIR monitor even though no threshold is published. Likely causes mirror bank 1: a bank 2 shut-off or check valve that does not seal, a relay that keeps the pump running, or a lean signal that does not fit the model. Since excess air only leans out the mixture for a short time, drivers seldom notice anything beyond the warning lamp. The legal basis lies in CARB's AIR monitoring rules. P2448 is the bank 1 code, P0492 the low-flow partner.
c: Bank 2 shut-off valve does not seal
Pump keeps running due to a sticking relay
s: Check engine lamp
Usually no change in driving behaviour

P244A.t: Diesel Particulate Filter Differential Pressure Too Low (Bank 1)
P244A.d: P244A means the pressure difference across the bank 1 particulate filter is lower than exhaust flow and soot load predict. That points to a damaged or removed substrate or, far more often, to a pressure line that has slipped off, split or clogged. Ford's 2023 diesels use it as the missing substrate monitor: the measured filter inlet pressure stays below a flow-dependent limit, about 8 kPa at 300 m³/h, for 90 s. GM's 3.0 L LZO checks the upstream pipe and confirms a Type A fault after 240 of 400 samples. Ford replaced the pressure sensor on 2017–2018 Super Duty 6.7 L trucks when its key-on voltage was below 0.4 V, Land Rover the sensor on 2016 TDV6 models, and Volvo fits new sensor hoses on mild-hybrid petrol models from 2020. P2464 is the bank 2 version.
c: Upstream pressure hose disconnected, split or blocked
Differential pressure sensor reading too low (Ford 6.7 L, Land Rover TDV6 bulletins)
Filter substrate cracked, melted or removed
s: MIL on in the first faulty trip
Soot load shown near zero, regeneration not triggered
Visible smoke if the substrate is damaged

P244B.t: Diesel Particulate Filter Differential Pressure Too High (Bank 1)
P244B.d: P244B reports a pressure drop across the bank 1 particulate filter that is too large for the current exhaust flow. On GM's 3.0 L LZO the same monitor also catches a leaking or disconnected downstream pipe: depending on the sensor type it compares either the downstream pressure with a limit or the pressure-to-flow ratio, as a Type A code. A heavily loaded filter is the classic cause; on the 2020–2021 Cadillac XT4 with the 2.0 L diesel (LSQ), GM corrected an overstated soot reading that set P244B and reduced power with new ECM software. On 2025 L5P Silverado and Sierra HD, moisture that entered the sensor during washing can set it, so allow a night of drying before replacing parts. Hino calls P244B an incomplete regeneration and raised the torque cut to 70 % on 2013–2016 COE trucks. P2465 covers bank 2.
c: Filter heavily loaded with soot or ash
Downstream pressure hose leaking or disconnected (GM LZO)
Water in the differential pressure sensor after washing (GM L5P 2025)
ECM calibration overstating soot load (Cadillac XT4 diesel, update)
s: MIL on, often with reduced power
High soot level indication in the cluster
Regeneration requested repeatedly

P244C.t: Exhaust Temperature Too Low For Particulate Filter Regeneration (Bank 1)
P244C.d: During an active regeneration the engine raises exhaust temperature with late injections so the soot in the particulate filter can burn. P244C is stored when bank 1 does not get hot enough or does not stay hot long enough. GM's diesel tables of 2017 and 2018 count interrupted regenerations: the burn ran past its maximum time, the post injections were not released in time or the steady heating phase was never reached; a successful burn clears the counter, and the code is Type A after one trip. VW's 2014 TDI cars flag it when closed-loop temperature control upstream of the turbine is not active within 45 s, or ahead of the filter within 60 s. Deutz lists it as a failed regeneration. The bank 2 twin is P244E; P244D covers too much heat. Soot keeps building, so P2463 or P2459 may follow.
c: Oxidation catalyst aged or face-plugged, so the post-injected fuel does not light off
Regenerations repeatedly cut short by short trips, idling or engine shut-off
Exhaust temperature sensor ahead of catalyst or filter reading too low
Exhaust leak ahead of the catalyst cooling the gas
s: Malfunction indicator lamp and particulate filter warning on
Regenerations noticeably frequent or never finishing
Reduced power once the filter is heavily loaded

P244D.t: Exhaust Temperature Too High For Particulate Filter Regeneration (Bank 1)
P244D.d: This is the overheating side of the bank 1 regeneration check. While soot is being burned off, the controller keeps exhaust temperature inside a window; if it climbs past the upper limit, the substrate and the oxidation catalyst risk cracking or melting, so the burn is stopped and P244D is logged. GM names it Catalyst Temperature Too High During Regeneration in its 2011 Duramax tables, without publishing a threshold. Ram's 2025 to 2026 heavy-duty Cummins pickups group it with exhaust temperature sensor faults: the bulletin asks for correct battery voltage and for each sensor to be identified by name and position before parts are replaced. Deutz, in contrast, uses P244D for a burn stopped because it was too cold. Too little heat on bank 1 gives P244C, bank 2 has P244F, and general overtemperature is P2428.
c: Too much fuel reaching the exhaust (leaking injector or aftertreatment doser)
Heavily overloaded filter burning off too fast
Exhaust temperature sensor or its wiring giving implausibly high readings
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Regeneration aborted, filter warning stays on
Reduced power to protect the aftertreatment

P244E.t: Exhaust Temperature Too Low For Particulate Filter Regeneration (Bank 2)
P244E.d: P244E only exists on engines that have a separate particulate filter for the second cylinder bank, which is rare. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; it mirrors P244C, so the logic described for bank 1 applies here. GM, for example, counts regenerations on its 2017 diesels that end early because the heat-up never reached a stable phase, and gives that bank 1 fault a Type A rating. CARB requires diesel systems to detect a regeneration that fails to complete. On a two-filter layout the second bank lacks heat when its oxidation catalyst no longer converts the fuel, its exhaust temperature sensor reads low or the gas cools through a leak. Comparing both banks during a forced regeneration with a scan tool is the most direct check. Overheating of bank 2 is P244F.
c: Bank 2 oxidation catalyst no longer converting post-injected fuel
Bank 2 exhaust temperature sensor reading low
Driving pattern too short for a complete regeneration
Exhaust leak on bank 2 ahead of the catalyst
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Filter warning, regeneration does not complete

P244F.t: Exhaust Temperature Too High For Particulate Filter Regeneration (Bank 2)
P244F.d: The bank 2 counterpart of P244D: during a filter burn the second bank's exhaust gets hotter than the substrate tolerates. No manufacturer documents P244F publicly. The bank 1 version appears in GM's 2011 Duramax tables as a catalyst overtemperature during regeneration, and Ram links P244D on current Cummins trucks to exhaust temperature sensor faults, so a wrong sensor reading deserves suspicion before the hardware. On a real overheat the usual trigger is surplus fuel on that bank, from a dripping injector or a filter that was allowed to load up far too much before the burn started. The controller ends the regeneration, may reduce power and will retry later. Because overheating can crack the filter, a code that keeps returning should be diagnosed rather than repeatedly cleared. Too little heat on bank 2 is P244E.
c: Surplus fuel on bank 2 from a leaking injector
Bank 2 exhaust temperature sensor or wiring reading too high
Bank 2 filter heavily overloaded before the burn
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Regeneration stopped, possibly reduced power

P2450.t: EVAP System Switching Valve Performance/Stuck Open
P2450.d: The switching valve sits in the evaporative system and either seals off part of it during the leak test or redirects flow; P2450 means the valve does not do its job or remains open. Ford calls it the vapor blocking valve: in 2020 to 2024 gasoline models the check runs in the third phase of the 0.040 inch cruise leak test, lasts 2 to 3 s and fails when a calculated ratio stays below 2.75 (Mode 6 test $3D, component $82). VW's 2014 Golf builds the valve into the leak detection pump and fails it when pump current differs from the reference by less than 3 mA. Bentley's V8 models of 2019 to 2021 point to the pump wiring, a smoke test and then the pump itself; Ford fixed P2450 on 2018 F-150s with a PCM update. The electrical faults of the same valve are P2418 to P2420; stuck closed is P2451.
c: Switching valve sticking open or not sealing
Internal fault of a leak detection pump that houses the valve
Monitor software needing an update (known on some Ford trucks)
Cracked or loose vapor hose at the valve
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on, usually no noticeable driving change
Possible fuel odor near the tank area

P2451.t: EVAP System Switching Valve Stuck Closed
P2451.d: P2451 is the reverse fault of P2450: the evaporative system switching valve will not open when commanded, so vapor or test pressure cannot pass where the system expects it. It shows up mainly on vehicles with a sealed, pressurized fuel tank, such as plug-in hybrids. Mazda's CX-90 and CX-70 PHEV can set it together with P0451, P2422 and P0441; the bulletin suspects the tank pressure sensor or the tank shutter valve and replaces the shutter valve plus the vapor hose that carries the tank pressure sensor. Ford's C-MAX and Fusion hybrids and Energi models listed P2450 and P2451 in a bulletin warning that a software conflict could falsify a pinpoint test unless the fuel door was opened at a set step. A blocked valve can also keep the tank from depressurizing before refueling. Circuit faults of the valve are P2418 to P2420.
c: Tank shutter or switching valve stuck closed
Fuel tank pressure sensor giving wrong values to the monitor
Software or test-sequence issue (fuel door handling on some hybrids)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Fuel door or refueling release slow or not working on sealed-tank hybrids

P2452.t: Diesel Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor A Circuit
P2452.d: The pressure sensor A of the particulate filter, usually a differential sensor with hoses to the filter inlet and outlet, tells the ECM how loaded the filter is. Despite its generic circuit title, P2452 is in practice an offset check made when no exhaust flows. Ford's 2023 diesels run it in after-run and set the code when the sensor still reads more than 1 kPa. GM's 2018 diesels check the filter inlet pressure at the start of the drive cycle, after at least 10 s engine off, and set it as a Type B code when the offset is too big. A sensor that has drifted, moisture inside it or a hose holding pressure all give such an offset. Audi saw P2452 together with P2453, P2454, P2456 and P2002 on the 2009 to 2011 Q7 TDI and traced it to moisture entering the differential pressure sensor G505 through poor internal sealing; the fix was a sensor with better sealing. The soot model then works with wrong values, so regeneration timing suffers.
c: Sensor offset drifted or moisture inside the sensor
Sensor hose blocked by soot or condensate
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Regeneration too early, too late or inhibited

P2453.t: Diesel Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P2453.d: P2453 means the particulate filter pressure signal is electrically fine but does not behave like a real filter pressure. Manufacturers use two kinds of test. With the engine off there should be almost no pressure difference: GM's 2009 Duramax fails above 4.1 kPa, the 2014 Cruze 2.0 diesel above 3.2 kPa in after-run, and the Opel/GM 2.0 CDTi in the Saab 9-5 (2010) checks once at least 60 s after shutdown. With the engine running the signal has to follow changes in exhaust flow: the Duramax expects it to rise and fall when the flow changes by more than 200 m³/h per second, and Ford's 2023 diesels fail a reading under 1 kPa at 500 m³/h or more, which points to a disconnected or split hose. Saab adds that kinked braided hoses do not recover their shape. Audi (Q7 TDI) found moisture in sensor G505, Chrysler (2.8 diesel) checked sensor and connector, and Stellantis found open circuits and bad PCM grounds. Without a valid signal the soot load is estimated, often followed by P2463.
c: Sensor hose disconnected, split, kinked or blocked
Sensor skewed or stuck, for example from moisture ingress
High resistance in sensor wiring or ECM grounds
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DPF warning, regeneration inhibited or too frequent
Reduced power on some vehicles

P2454.t: Diesel Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor A Circuit Low
P2454.d: The particulate filter pressure sensor is a three-wire part: the ECM feeds it 5 V and ground and reads a signal that rises with the pressure difference across the filter. P2454 means that signal sits below the lowest plausible value. Ford's 2023 diesels fail below 0.10 V within 2 s, where 0.45 V corresponds to zero pressure difference; GM's 2018 diesels fail below 3 % of the supply with 80 of 160 samples. On the Opel/GM 2.0 CDTi in the Saab 9-5 (2010) an open circuit sets P2454 as well as a short to ground, after 2 s, so a disconnected plug reads low there. A shorted 5 V reference can also pull the signal down and usually sets P0641 alongside. Audi (Q7 TDI 2009 to 2011) saw P2454 from moisture inside sensor G505, and Chrysler lists it on the 2.8 diesel Town and Country with a sensor and connector check. Without the signal the filter load is estimated and regeneration may be limited.
c: Signal wire open or shorted to ground, connector unplugged
Internal sensor failure, for example from moisture
5 V reference shorted by another sensor on the same supply
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DPF warning or regeneration inhibited

P2455.t: Diesel Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor A Circuit High
P2455.d: P2455 means the particulate filter pressure sensor signal sits above the highest plausible value, at the top of the 5 V range. Ford's 2023 diesels and the Opel/GM 2.0 CDTi in the Saab 9-5 (2010) both use 4.9 V as the limit, Ford within 2 s and Saab after 1 s; on Ford's 6.7 L the signal follows roughly 0.082 V per kPa above 0.45 V, so 4.9 V would be about 54 kPa. Typical faults are a signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage, or an open low-reference (ground) circuit, which Saab lists among the circuit faults for this code. A real pressure that high from a blocked filter is unusual and would normally first raise soot codes such as P2463. Chrysler lists P2455 on the 2.8 diesel Town and Country with a sensor and connector check. The ECM falls back to a modelled soot load and may limit regeneration.
c: Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DPF warning or regeneration inhibited

P2456.t: Diesel Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2456.d: Here the pressure sensor A signal is within range but jumps in a way no real exhaust flow could cause. GM's 2017 and 2018 diesels compare each raw sample with the one before; a step larger than 20 % repeated over 80 or 160 samples sets the code after two trips, but only if no electrical fault is present. VW's 2014 TDI models check the rate of change and flag a pressure moving more than 10 hPa per second against the expected direction. Ford's 2024 gasoline particulate filter strategy files P2456 under its analog circuit checks with a 5 s detection time, and Deutz describes it as erratic differential pressure data. Loose terminals, a chafed harness, water in the sensor or a hose that flutters are the usual triggers. Hard opens or shorts go to P2452, P2454 and P2455; drift is P2453.
c: Loose or corroded sensor connector terminals
Harness chafing or heat damage near the exhaust
Condensate in the sensor or its pressure hoses
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Regeneration started at odd times or blocked

P2457.t: EGR Cooler A Efficiency Below Threshold
P2457.d: The EGR cooler is supposed to bring recirculated exhaust close to coolant temperature; P2457 says cooler A no longer removes enough heat, as CARB requires diesel systems to detect. GM rates efficiency as the drop across the cooler divided by the gap between inlet gas and coolant; in the 2017 tables the Duramax fails below 60 %, the MDE engine family below 50 %, each after two trips. Ford's 6.7 L diesel instead watches the outlet gas: above coolant plus 70 °C in 2013 and plus 88 °C in 2023 for 12 s, with the bypass in cooling position; gasoline engines with cooled EGR use a flow ratio. Ford traced P2457 on 2018 to 2019 F-150 3.0 L diesels to loose screws in the bypass module, and Hino fixed 2012 trucks by software. Soot fouling and a bypass flap stuck in bypass are common; cooler B is P241F.
c: Cooler passages fouled with soot and lacquer
Bypass flap stuck in bypass position or bypass module loose
EGR outlet temperature sensor reading too high
Low coolant level or poor coolant flow through the cooler
Monitor software misjudging efficiency (known on some trucks)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Higher NOx, sometimes reduced EGR or power
Coolant loss or white smoke if the cooler is also leaking

P2458.d: During a regeneration the engine raises exhaust temperature, mostly by late post-injection burned in the oxidation catalyst, until the soot in the particulate filter oxidises. P2458 means a regeneration took longer than the calibrated limit, so the filter was not cleaned in the expected time. CARB asks diesel OBD to detect regenerations that do not complete as intended. On the Opel/GM 2.0 CDTi in the Saab 9-5 (2010) the ECM runs the check with coolant at 73 to 96 °C and sets the code when regeneration times are too long; it is a Type C code there, stored without the MIL. Volkswagen saw P2458 with the MIL on 2011 Jetta and Golf 2.0 TDI (CJAA) and fixed it with an ECM software update, so the calibration is worth checking before parts are replaced. Otherwise the regeneration is slowed by low exhaust temperature, a weak oxidation catalyst, faulty temperature or pressure readings, or trips too short to finish. P2459 covers regenerations that happen too often.
c: ECM calibration that needs an update (documented by Volkswagen)
Short trips that keep regenerations from finishing
Oxidation catalyst too weak to reach regeneration temperature
s: DPF warning or MIL, depending on the manufacturer
Cooling fan and raised idle running on after shutdown
Higher fuel consumption

P2459.d: P2459 means the particulate filter is being regenerated more often than the calibration expects. CARB requires diesel OBD to flag regeneration so frequent that emissions would exceed the limit; frequent regeneration also dilutes oil and costs fuel. Ford's 2023 diesels set it when the average distance between completed regenerations falls below about 40 km. GM's 2014 Cruze 2.0 diesel compares the soot load that triggered a regeneration with a table built from the engine-out soot model, and GM's 2018 diesels flag a ratio of 10 or more between the pressure-based soot estimate and the engine-out model, citing dirty combustion, a leak in the intake or exhaust, or an inefficient filter. The Opel/GM 2.0 CDTi in the Saab 9-5 (2010) instead counts too many interrupted regenerations, as a Type C code. Stellantis replaced the filter on 2022 to 2023 Ram 2500/3500 6.7 Cummins over a manufacturing issue; left alone, the engine eventually derates.
c: High soot output from the engine (injectors, EGR, air leaks)
Differential pressure reading too high (sensor, blocked or swapped hoses)
Filter loaded with ash or defective from manufacture
s: MIL or DPF warning
Higher fuel consumption and rising oil level
Reduced engine power if the fault persists

P245A.d: The bypass lets cold-start EGR skip the cooler and is switched back to cooling once the engine is warm. P245A flags the bank 1 control circuit, usually as an open. GM's 2017 tables show both actuator types: on the Duramax with a DC-motor flap the controller sees a load resistance above 200 kOhm while the H-bridge is off and needs 160 failures in 200 samples, while the vacuum-switched version needs 24 of 30 samples with the flap commanded to cooling; both are Type B. Ford used P245A differently on its 2013 to 2015 6.7 L Power Stroke, as an intrusive check that fails when the gas temperature after the cooler moves by less than 3 °C per second after the flap switches; in 2023 that test carries P245B. Ford reflashed 2018 to 2019 Super Duty PCMs for P245A. Shorts are P245C and P245D, bank 2 is P248E.
c: Open wire or unplugged connector at the bypass actuator
Actuator motor or solenoid winding open
Control software needing an update (some Ford diesels)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EGR cooler bypass no longer switching; possible P2457 or P24A5 as follow-up

P245B.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1)
P245B.d: P245B is set when the bank 1 bypass is electrically intact but does not reach or hold the commanded position, or when switching it has no visible thermal effect. GM's 2017 Duramax with a position-controlled DC-motor flap compares setpoint and feedback; a tracking error above 16 % in 1280 of 1600 samples, with a steady setpoint, coolant over 70 °C and outside air above minus 23 °C, sets a Type B fault, and P24A5 follows if the flap is then found stuck. Ford's 2023 diesels, the 6.7 L and the 3.0 L, run an intrusive test once per trip: the flap is moved, and if the gas temperature after the cooler changes by less than 3 °C per second, P245B is logged. Carbon on the flap shaft, a worn linkage, a weak vacuum supply or a position sensor fault are typical causes. Pure circuit faults are P245A, P245C and P245D.
c: Bypass flap or shaft sticking from carbon deposits
Weak vacuum supply or leaking hose on vacuum-operated bypass
Slow EGR temperature sensor after the cooler
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Longer warm-up or higher NOx when the bypass stays in one position

P245C.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Circuit Low (Bank 1)
P245C.d: P245C reports that the control line of the bank 1 bypass actuator is pulled toward ground. GM documents this in its diesel tables: in 2014 the driver stage detects low voltage while it is switched off and treats it as a ground short, and in the 2017 tables the vacuum-switched bypass fails when the resistance to ground drops below 0.5 Ohm in 24 of 30 samples, rated Type B. With the line shorted the actuator may sit permanently in one position, so the cooler is either always bypassed or always used, which the efficiency check P2457 can then also notice. Typical findings are insulation rubbed through against the engine or exhaust, a pinched harness after repairs or a shorted solenoid winding. The open case is P245A, a short to supply P245D, and bank 2 has P2490.
c: Control wire chafed through and touching ground
Water or corrosion bridging connector pins
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Bypass stuck in one position, possibly with EGR cooler efficiency code

P245D.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Circuit High (Bank 1)
P245D.d: P245D is the short-to-supply case of the bank 1 bypass circuit. For the Duramax with a DC-motor bypass, GM's 2017 tables watch the current through the H-bridge while it drives the flap: more than 8 A in 160 of 200 samples sets a Type B fault. On the vacuum-switched version the check looks at resistance to the supply side, and the 2014 tables describe high voltage while the driver is on. Ram issued a PCM software update in 2025 for 2024 heavy-duty pickups with the 6.7 L Cummins that set P245D, together with other air handling codes, to remove false actuator faults, so the software level should be checked before the harness is opened. In a genuine case a wire touching a battery feed or an actuator with a low-resistance winding is found. Open circuit is P245A, short to ground P245C, bank 2 is P2491.
c: Control software reporting a false actuator fault (known on some Ram diesels)
Control wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Actuator motor drawing excessive current (low-resistance winding, binding)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Bypass actuator switched off by the controller and left in default position

P245E.t: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor B Circuit
P245E.d: Which sensor is B depends on the maker. Ford's 2013 6.7 L Power Stroke has an exhaust pressure sensor ahead of the filter as A and a two-port differential sensor across it as B. Despite its circuit title, P245E is there an offset test during after-run, with the key off and the controller still awake: since no gas flows, the differential reading should be zero, and more than 1 kPa for one second sets the code. On Ford's 2024 gasoline particulate filters with digital SENT sensors, P245E is the general circuit fault, detected within 5 s, while lost communication with the same sensor is U0602. So a sensor that drifted, a hose still holding pressure or water inside the sensor can set it as easily as a wiring fault. Low and high signals have their own codes, P2460 and P2461, and erratic signals P2462.
c: Sensor B offset drifted or moisture inside the sensor
Pressure hose kinked or blocked so pressure is trapped
Wiring or connector fault on the sensor B circuit
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Soot load estimate unreliable, regeneration timing affected

P245F.t: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P245F.d: With P245F the controller decides that the sensor B value is electrically fine but makes no physical sense. Ford's 2024 gasoline strategy runs three such tests on the B sensor of the gasoline particulate filter: an offset check with the engine stopped that fails once the average reaches 16 to 32 hPa; a rationality check that fails when the reading stays at or above the pressure expected for the current exhaust flow for a total of 20 s; and a derivative check that compares how fast pressure follows a change in flow over 2 s. Jeep released PCM software for 2018 Wranglers with a gasoline filter in Asia-Pacific and EMEA markets that set P245F together with P2453. Deutz assigns P245F to the pressure after the filter leaving its physical limits. Hoses, condensate and sensor drift are the usual suspects. Circuit codes are P245E, P2460 and P2461.
c: Sensor B hose cracked, disconnected or blocked
Condensate in the pressure line falsifying the reading
Sensor B drifted out of calibration
Control software needing an update (some Jeep models)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Filter regeneration triggered too early, too late or blocked

P2460.t: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor B Circuit Low
P2460.d: P2460 means the analog output of pressure sensor B has fallen below the lowest voltage a working sensor can deliver. On Ford's 2013 6.7 L diesel, sensor B is the differential pressure sensor across the filter; its output runs from about 0.45 V at zero to roughly 4.8 V near 38 kPa, and anything under 0.10 V for 2 s with the key on, battery between 9 and 16.25 V, sets the code. Ford's 2024 gasoline filter strategy uses a higher floor of 0.3 V held for 5 s. A missing 5 V reference, a grounded signal wire or an open in the signal line pulled down inside the controller all look the same here, so a check of reference, ground and signal at the connector comes first. The soot estimate loses one input and regeneration planning gets less accurate. The high case is P2461, erratic signals P2462.
c: 5 V reference to sensor B missing or shorted
Signal wire chafed and shorted to ground
Sensor B internally failed with output stuck low
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Regeneration based on a model only, possibly more frequent

P2461.t: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor B Circuit High
P2461.d: When pressure sensor B reports a voltage above its usable range, P2461 is stored. Ford sets the limit at 4.90 V for 2 s on the 2013 6.7 L diesel, where B is the differential sensor across the filter, and at 4.73 V for 5 s on the 2024 gasoline particulate filters. An open ground, a signal wire touching the 5 V reference or a battery feed, or a failed sensor are the classic electrical reasons. A Stellantis case from 2025 on the 2023 Jeep Renegade shows a different trigger: condensate inside the tubes between exhaust and differential pressure sensor gave false readings and set P2461 together with P2453 and P2455. The fix there was to dry the hoses with compressed air blown toward the filter, never into the sensor. Because the reading looks like a very full filter, the engine may limit power. The low counterpart is P2460.
c: Condensate in the sensor tubes producing false high readings
Sensor ground open or signal shorted to reference or battery voltage
Sensor B internally failed with output stuck high
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Reduced power because the filter appears heavily loaded

P2462.t: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2462.d: P2462 covers a sensor B signal that drops out or jumps for short moments without staying outside its range long enough for the low or high codes. Ford is the only maker found documenting it: the 2024 gasoline particulate filter summary lists P2462 next to P2460 and P2461 in the continuously running analog circuit check, with about 5 s needed to register a fault, and no separate threshold is published. On Ford's older 6.7 L diesel the B position belongs to the delta pressure unit mounted at the filter. The cause is nearly always mechanical or electrical intermittency: a terminal that loses contact as the engine shakes, a harness rubbing on a bracket, or moisture that comes and goes in the connector. Wiggling the harness while watching live data usually finds it. Sensor A has the matching code P2456.
c: Terminal losing contact under engine vibration
Harness rubbing on a bracket or exhaust part
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on, sometimes only after rough roads or rain
Pressure reading jumping in live data

P2463.t: Diesel Particulate Filter Restriction - Soot Accumulation (Bank 1)
P2463.d: P2463 means the soot load in the particulate filter has passed the level at which the engine still regenerates it on its own. GM's 2009 Duramax sets it at 70 g or more for 5 minutes, the 2014 Cruze 2.0 diesel at more than 32 g for 30 s, both as Type A codes; GM's 2018 diesels use the pressure-based soot model with 120 failures in 150 samples. On the Cruze the ECM then turns on the MIL, reduces engine power and blocks normal regeneration, so a dealer service regeneration is needed.
