GM's bulletin on the related driver messages notes that the filter cleans itself about once per tank and needs driving above 50 km/h; extended idling and stop-and-go traffic keep it from finishing. The underlying cause is not always the driving: Stellantis traced P2463 with P2453 to broken differential pressure sensor wiring and PCM grounds, Mack to a failed aftertreatment fuel doser. Check those before regenerating, or the code returns.
c: Regenerations not completed because of short trips or long idling
Differential pressure sensor, its hoses or wiring reading too high
Fault that prevents regeneration (fuel doser, temperature sensor)
s: DPF full or exhaust filter message in the cluster
MIL on and reduced engine power
Higher fuel consumption

P2464.t: Diesel Particulate Filter Differential Pressure Too Low (Bank 2)
P2464.d: P2464 is stored when the pressure drop across the second particulate filter stays smaller than the controller predicts for the current exhaust flow. Only engines that run a separate filter on each bank, typically larger V diesels, can log it. No manufacturer publishes a bank 2 calibration for this number, so the bank 1 partner P244A is the reference: Ford's 2023 diesels treat it as a missing substrate test and flag a filter inlet pressure below a flow-dependent limit, roughly 8 kPa at 300 m³/h, held for 90 s. CARB requires a check of this kind so that a cracked, melted or removed filter cannot go unnoticed. In the workshop a sensing hose that has come off, split or plugged is found far more often than a broken substrate. The MIL comes on; some engines also reduce power.
c: Pressure sensing hose of the bank 2 filter detached, cracked or leaking
Upstream sensing port or line blocked with soot or condensate
Filter substrate cracked, melted or removed
s: MIL on
Visible soot at the tailpipe if the filter is damaged
Regeneration suspended or reduced power on some engines

P2465.t: Diesel Particulate Filter Differential Pressure Too High (Bank 2)
P2465.d: P2465 means the second particulate filter builds up more back pressure than the controller accepts for the exhaust flow it calculates. The code is only possible where each cylinder bank has its own filter. No maker documents the bank 2 version in a public table; its bank 1 twin P244B gives the logic. On GM's 3.0 L LZO that check also reacts to a loose or leaking downstream pipe, comparing either the downstream pressure or the pressure-to-flow ratio, and it is a Type A fault there. CARB asks for monitoring that recognises a filter loaded so heavily that it endangers the engine. Typical findings are a filter packed with soot or ash, a plugged rear hose, a dented pipe or a sensor reading too high. A soot-model warning without a pressure test is P243F, and the stage with forced power reduction on this bank is P243B.
c: Bank 2 filter heavily loaded with soot or ash
Downstream sensing hose blocked, kinked or swapped
Dented or obstructed exhaust pipe behind the filter
s: MIL on
Frequent or prolonged regeneration attempts
Loss of power, possibly limp mode

P2466.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit (Bank 2 Sensor 3)
P2466.d: P2466 is the general circuit code for the third exhaust temperature probe in the bank 2 exhaust path, so it only appears on engines with two separate aftertreatment lines. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. The bank 1 counterpart P242A shows how makers fill such a general code: Ford's 2023 diesels use it for a probe that departs more than 80 °C from its modelled value for 20 s, while other makers attach open-circuit detection to it. CARB requires every emission-relevant sensor to be checked for circuit continuity and plausibility. Expect the controller to distrust the reading, to pause regeneration or DEF dosing that relies on it and to light the MIL. Clear low and high signal faults of this probe go to P2468 and P2469 instead.
c: Temperature probe failed internally or open
Connector or wiring near the exhaust damaged by heat
Probe loose or not reaching into the gas stream
s: MIL on
Implausible or missing value for this probe in live data
Filter regeneration or DEF dosing suspended

P2467.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2 Sensor 3)
P2467.d: P2467 means the third exhaust temperature probe on bank 2 delivers an electrically valid signal that does not match the operating state. A public threshold for this exact code is not available. On bank 1, Ford's 2023 diesels test the matching probe after at least 6 h off by demanding it stays within 50 °C of three other sensors, which reveals a probe that is stuck or out of position. Ford also names P2467 in special service message 48345 for Escape, Edge, Corsair and Nautilus of model years 2019–2020 with the 2.0 L EcoBoost, where coolant leaking from the EGR cooler into the exhaust can set it next to P0217 and P0401; the cooler is to be inspected and pressure-tested first. CARB requires such rationality checks on emission inputs. Wiring faults belong to P2466 and P2468 to P246A.
c: Probe aged, drifting or frozen at one value
Probe loose or pulled out of the gas stream
Coolant entering the exhaust through a leaking EGR cooler (Ford 2.0 L EcoBoost)
Controller software judging the probe too strictly
s: MIL on
Temperature value lags or deviates from neighbouring probes
White smoke and coolant loss if the EGR cooler leaks

P2468.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 3)
P2468.d: P2468 reports that probe 3 in the bank 2 exhaust line delivers a signal below the lowest value the input can produce with an intact circuit. With the usual resistive probes this nearly always means the signal line or the sensor itself has a ground short. No manufacturer lists this bank 2 code publicly; the neighbouring low codes show the scale. Ford's 2023 diesels treat anything below 0.10 V as a fault once ignition is on and supply lies between 9 and 16.25 V, judged within about 2 s, and GM's 2020 diesel tables flag a probe resistance below 158 Ω for sensor 4 as a Type B fault after 10 of 20 samples. CARB demands out-of-range checks for such inputs. Look for chafed insulation against the exhaust or a melted connector. The opposite fault, signal too high or open, is P2469.
c: Signal wire chafed through and touching ground
Connector melted or with water ingress
s: MIL on
Probe shows an implausible value at a standstill
Regeneration or DEF dosing inhibited

P2469.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 3)
P2469.d: P2469 is logged when bank 2 probe number 3 pushes its input above the permitted ceiling. An unplugged connector, a broken wire or a burnt-out sensing element produces exactly that, as does a signal line shorted to a voltage source. Public calibrations exist only for the sister inputs: Ford's 2023 diesels flag anything above 2.66 V, and GM's 2025 diesel tables treat an open-like resistance (beyond 100 MΩ) or a digital value hotter than roughly 1,290 °C as failed after 19 of 25 samples and rate it Type A, so the MIL comes on in the first trip. CARB requires that out-of-range highs on emission inputs are detected. Measure the probe resistance cold and check the plug before buying a sensor. A too-low signal is P2468, an erratic one P246A.
c: Connector unplugged or wire broken (open circuit)
Signal line shorted to a voltage source
s: MIL on, often already in the first trip
Probe shows a maximum or invalid value
Regeneration or DEF dosing inhibited

P246A.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 2 Sensor 3)
P246A.d: P246A flags a third bank 2 exhaust temperature probe whose reading jumps from sample to sample faster than real gas temperature could, even though every single value stays inside the legal range. The bank 2 code itself is not described by any manufacturer in public material. GM's diesel tables run the equivalent quick-change test for other probes every 100 ms: the 2025 tables count a step above 100 °C between samples, fail after 12 of 25 samples and confirm the fault in a second trip (Type B). CARB expects such erratic-signal checks on emission inputs. Loose terminals, corroded pins and harness strands weakened by heat and vibration are the usual reasons, sometimes a cracked sensor element. A steady but wrong value is P2467, a permanent short or open P2468 or P2469.
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the probe connector
Harness strands broken by heat and vibration
Cracked sensing element giving unstable contact
s: MIL on after a repeated fault
Temperature trace jumps in live data
Fault may come and go with bumps or engine heat

P246B.t: Vehicle Conditions Incorrect for Particulate Filter Regeneration
P246B.d: P246B says the controller wanted to clean the particulate filter but the vehicle did not offer the conditions its strategy needs, for example enough exhaust heat, a long enough run or a functioning air path. It describes a failed or blocked regeneration request rather than a defective part on its own, so the real cause is usually stored beside it. Land Rover documents exactly that on Range Rover and Range Rover Sport 2016–2018 and Discovery 2017–2018 with the 3.0 L TDV6: P246B-00 and P2463-00 can accompany P0234-77 when the intake air shutoff throttle has failed, and bulletins LTB01204NAS1 to NAS3 call for a new throttle followed by a dynamic regeneration. Short trips and long idling make it worse, and if soot keeps rising P2463 or a power limit follows. MIL behaviour differs by maker.
c: Another stored fault (e.g. intake throttle, sensors) blocking regeneration
Failed intake air shutoff throttle (Land Rover TDV6)
Short trips or long idling without enough exhaust heat
s: Regeneration does not start or is aborted repeatedly
Filter warning or rising soot load
MIL on together with the root-cause code on some vehicles

P246C.t: Particulate Filter Restriction - Forced Limited Power (Bank 1)
P246C.d: P246C is the final stage of the bank 1 filter loading monitor: the filter is judged so clogged that the controller reduces engine output to protect engine and filter. Ford uses it on diesels with an immediate MIL plus wrench light. In the 2015 summary a normalised restriction of twice the normal soot value above 625 rpm for 300 s sets it and EGR is switched off; the 2023 summary uses an estimated soot mass of 200 % of the normal regeneration trigger. Ford's 2024 petrol summary applies the code to the gasoline filter as well, with normalised back pressure above 1.0 for 5 s once the filter is above 250 °C at 400–850 m³/h. Ford bulletins for the 3.2 L Transit (18-2064) and 6.7 L Super Duty (21-2052) pair it with P2463 and fix it by forced regeneration or new PCM software. Bank 2 is P243B.
c: Soot overload after repeatedly missed or aborted regenerations
Mostly stationary or low-speed operation without full regenerations
Filter at the end of its life with high ash content
PCM calibration overestimating soot load (Ford bulletins)
s: MIL and service or wrench light on
Marked loss of power (limp mode)
Drive-to-clean or filter full message

P246D.t: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor A/B Correlation
P246D.d: P246D compares two pressure readings at the particulate filter that ought to agree under steady conditions. Which sensor is A and which is B is decided by each manufacturer. Ford's 2013 to 2015 diesel summaries use it as a rationality test between the filter pressure sensor DPFP and the delta pressure sensor DPS: with coolant above 70 °C, ambient pressure above 745 hPa, filter inlet temperature between 125 and 425 °C and exhaust flow of 200 to 600 kg/h, the code sets once the two differ by over 1.5 kPa, evaluated over about 2 s. Typical findings are swapped, kinked or leaking sensing hoses, water in a line or one sensor drifting while its circuit still passes. Pure electrical faults have their own codes (P2452 ff. and P245E ff.). With a doubtful pressure value the soot estimate and regeneration timing suffer.
c: Sensing hoses swapped, kinked or leaking
Water or soot in a sensing line
One pressure sensor drifting out of calibration
s: MIL on
Regeneration too early, too late or suspended
Pressure values of the two sensors disagree in live data

P246E.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 4)
P246E.d: P246E is the general code for the fourth exhaust temperature probe on bank 1, usually the last one in the aftertreatment line. Ford's diesels give it a model check rather than an electrical one: after a cold start the measured EGT14 value may differ from the modelled temperature by no more than 80 °C, the comparison lasting 200 to 400 s and the deviation having to persist for 20 s. Dedicated low and high signal faults of the same probe go to P2470 and P2471, and sensor-to-sensor plausibility to P246F. Volvo Trucks lists P246E-15 among the EGT faults on VNL tractors whose fix is replacing the affected exhaust temperature sensor (RD24-034). CARB requires continuity and rationality checks on emission-relevant inputs. A bad value often pauses regeneration or DEF dosing.
c: Probe aged or failed, reading far from the model
Probe loose or not reaching into the gas stream
Exhaust leak near the probe cooling the reading
s: MIL on
Value of the last exhaust probe deviates from expectation
Regeneration or DEF dosing suspended

P246F.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1 Sensor 4)
P246F.d: P246F stands for a fourth bank 1 exhaust temperature probe whose signal is electrically fine but physically implausible. Both main users test it after a long soak. Ford's diesels compare it with three other probes after at least 6 h off and allow no more than 50 °C between them, which unmasks a probe stuck at one value. GM's 2025 diesel tables wait for more than 10,800 s engine-off, then compare how far the probe warms within a calibrated time against a temperature map; too little rise points to a probe that has slipped from the pipe, or to a frozen signal, rated Type B with the MIL in the second trip. Electrical faults of the probe are P2470 to P2472, while P246E covers the model comparison on Ford. A plausibility fault often follows a loose probe after exhaust work.
c: Probe stuck at one value or drifting
Probe loose or backed out of the exhaust pipe
Probe connectors swapped with a neighbouring sensor
s: MIL on after the second faulty trip
Probe disagrees with neighbouring temperatures after a cold start
Usually no noticeable change in driveability

P2470.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 4)
P2470.d: P2470 means the signal of bank 1 probe number 4 has dropped below its valid floor, which on resistive probes indicates a short to ground. Ford's diesels flag a voltage under 0.10 V with the key on and 9 to 16.25 V supply, checked continuously over about 2 s. GM's diesel tables check whether the probe output stage is grounded: below 158 Ω in the 2017 and 2020 tables, below 500 Ω in 2018, and in the 2025 tables below 1 Ω or a digital reading under −72.8 °C after 19 of 25 samples, each time as a Type B fault. Ram lists P2470 for 2025–2026 Ram 2500/3500 in case S2625000003, which asks to check battery voltage before any exhaust sensor diagnosis. Chafed wiring at the exhaust and a shorted probe are the usual finds. Too high or open is P2471.
c: Signal wire chafed through and touching ground
Low battery voltage during diagnosis distorting readings (Ram)
s: MIL on
Implausible value for the last exhaust probe
Regeneration or DEF dosing inhibited

P2471.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 4)
P2471.d: P2471 is set when the fourth bank 1 exhaust temperature probe drives its input above the upper limit, the picture of an open circuit, an unplugged sensor or a short to voltage. Ford's diesels call more than 2.66 V a fault. GM checks both a short to power and an open driver circuit: above 900 Ω in the 2017 and 2020 tables, above 1,400 Ω in 2018, with 10 failed readings in 20; the 2020 and 2025 tables rate it Type A, so the MIL can come on in the first trip, and 2025 uses more than 100 MΩ or a digital reading above about 1,290 °C. Ram includes P2471 in case S2625000003 for 2025–2026 Ram 2500/3500 and points technicians to sensor names rather than numbers when locating the part. Start with the connector and a cold resistance check. Too low is P2470.
c: Connector unplugged or wire broken (open circuit)
Signal line shorted to a voltage source
s: MIL on, on GM possibly in the first trip
Last exhaust probe shows maximum or substitute value
Regeneration or DEF dosing inhibited

P2472.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 1 Sensor 4)
P2472.d: P2472 reports that the last bank 1 temperature probe (sensor 4) changes its signal too abruptly between two readings, although each reading on its own lies in range. GM documents it as a quick-change monitor with a 100 ms task: the 2017 and 2018 diesel tables look at the resistance step between consecutive samples (more than 10 Ω) and fail after 15 of 30 samples, the 2025 tables use a temperature step above 100 °C with 12 of 25 samples; all are Type B, so the MIL waits for a second trip. Stellantis case S2625000003 names it next to P2470 and P2471 for the 2025 and 2026 heavy-duty Ram pickups. Ford's diesel summaries do not use this number. Corroded pins, loose terminals and fatigued wires near the hot pipe cause most cases. A probe that is steady but wrong is P246F.
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the probe connector
Wire fatigue near the hot exhaust pipe
Cracked sensing element giving unstable contact
s: MIL on after the second faulty trip
Temperature value flickers in live data
Fault comes and goes, often after rough roads

P2473.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit (Bank 2 Sensor 4)
P2473.d: P2473 covers the wiring of probe number four in the bank 2 exhaust line as a whole, so it only occurs on engines with two separate exhaust paths and a long sensor chain on each. The controller sets it when the probe line delivers a value it cannot assign to a clean low or high fault, for instance an open circuit or a sensor reporting an internal error. No maker documents P2473 publicly. The bank 1 counterpart P246E shows how it can be used: Ford's 2023 diesel summary compares that probe against a temperature model after a cold start. CARB demands circuit continuity checks on every emission-relevant input. For the driver it means a lit MIL and often a paused particulate filter regeneration.
c: Broken wire or unplugged connector at the bank 2 probe
Fault in the control unit input stage
s: MIL on
No usable value for bank 2 probe 4 in live data
Filter regeneration suspended

P2474.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2 Sensor 4)
P2474.d: P2474 flags a plausibility problem: the electrical signal of bank 2 probe 4 is valid, yet the temperature it reports does not fit what the engine controller expects. Typical tests compare the probe with its neighbours after a long soak, when all should read about ambient, or with a modelled value during driving. Ford handles the bank 1 analogue P246F as a sensor-to-sensor check on its single-bank diesels; for the second bank no maker publishes P2474. CARB requires rationality monitoring for exhaust temperature inputs that feed emission strategies. A skewed probe can start or block regeneration at the wrong time, so the driver may notice higher fuel use or a regeneration that never completes.
c: Probe aged and reading off by a constant amount
Exhaust leak upstream of the probe falsifying the reading
s: MIL on after repeated detection
Probe 4 of bank 2 differs clearly from the other probes after a cold soak
Regenerations incomplete or more frequent

P2475.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 4)
P2475.d: P2475 is stored when the voltage from bank 2 probe 4 falls below the lowest value the probe can produce in normal use. With the resistive PTC probes common on diesels this points to a short between signal and ground, or to a sensor shorted internally. Published thresholds exist only for the bank 1 twin P2470: Ford's diesels treat less than 0.10 V as a fault after about 2 s with the key on, and GM's diesel tables test the probe input for a grounded condition as a Type B fault. No maker lists P2475 itself. The value of this probe is then replaced by a default, so the controller may restrict regeneration or reductant dosing until the repair.
c: Signal wire rubbed through against the exhaust or body
Water in the connector bridging the pins
s: MIL on
Bank 2 probe 4 shows an implausibly cold or fixed value
Regeneration or DEF dosing restricted

P2476.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 4)
P2476.d: P2476 covers the opposite end of the scale from P2475: the signal of bank 2 probe 4 sits above its usable ceiling. Because the probe forms a voltage divider with a pull-up resistor in the control unit, an interrupted wire, a disconnected plug or a short to a supply voltage all drive the input high. For the bank 1 equivalent P2471 Ford uses more than 4.90 V in its 2015 diesel summary and more than 2.66 V in the 2023 edition, both as continuous checks. P2476 is not listed by any maker in public documents; only engines with two banks and four probes per bank could set it. Expect a lit MIL and a substitute temperature, which can stop regeneration.
c: Open signal or ground wire, often heat-damaged
Connector loose or not locked after service work
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
s: MIL on
Probe reads maximum or an implausibly hot value
Regeneration blocked

P2477.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 2 Sensor 4)
P2477.d: P2477 targets a signal from bank 2 probe 4 that jumps around, while each individual sample may still be in range. Real exhaust temperature changes only gradually because the probe and pipe have thermal mass, so sudden steps between consecutive readings betray a wiring or contact issue. GM documents the method for the bank 1 sibling P2472: its 2017 diesel table counts samples with a resistance step above 10 ohms and fails at 15 of 30, as a Type B fault with the MIL on the second trip. P2477 itself appears in no public maker document. Faults tend to come and go with vibration or heat, so wiggling the harness while watching live data is the usual way to find them.
c: Loose or corroded pins in the probe connector
Wire strands breaking near the hot pipe
Cracked probe element with unstable contact
s: MIL on after the second faulty trip
Value of bank 2 probe 4 jumps in live data
Fault code returns after being cleared

P2478.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Out of Range (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2478.d: Unlike the circuit codes, P2478 judges the temperature itself at the first exhaust probe of bank 1, usually ahead of the oxidation catalyst. Ford's 2015 diesel summary for the 6.7L and 3.2L engines groups it with the EGT circuit check: the test is high-side only and trips at roughly 1150 °C, because the PTC probe curve leaves no separate low threshold. Volkswagen's 2014 Golf data for the 2.0L TDI CJAA sets it when the gap between target and measured temperature exceeds 40 K, and bulletin 01 12 28 updated the 2012 Passat TDI (CKRA) software because the check was too sensitive. Overheating from overfuelling or a failing turbo is the real-world trigger, so the cause deserves attention before the probe.
c: Real overheating from excess fuel or a leaking injector
Overly sensitive diagnosis needing a software update (VW Passat 2012)
Probe reading too high due to ageing
Lack of air from a boost leak or turbocharger fault
s: MIL on
Power reduced to protect the exhaust parts
Smoke or a hot smell from the exhaust in real overheating

P2479.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Out of Range (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P2479.d: P2479 applies the same temperature-limit idea to the second bank 1 probe. On the 2015 Ford 6.7L layout this is EGT12 at the oxidation catalyst outlet, where the exotherm of a regeneration shows up first, so a runaway burn or excessive post-injection can push the reading towards the limit. Ford's 2015 diesel summary lists P2479 alongside P2032 and P2033 and uses a high-side threshold of about 1150 °C; the 2023 edition no longer carries it. No other maker documents the code publicly. When the code appears together with circuit faults of the same probe, fix those first; on its own it calls for a check of injection and regeneration behaviour.
c: Excessive heat during regeneration, e.g. too much post-injection
Leaking injector adding unburnt fuel to the catalyst
s: MIL on
Regeneration aborted
Reduced power

P247A.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Out of Range (Bank 1 Sensor 3)
P247A.d: P247A is the out-of-range verdict for the third bank 1 probe, which sits further down the aftertreatment line. It is the best documented code of this series. Volkswagen's 2014 quick-reference books for the 2.0L TDI CJAA (Golf, Beetle) compare the control deviation with an engine-speed and torque map, while the 3.0L TDI in the 2014 Touareg flags a gap between target and measured temperature above 200 K or below -100 K. Ford's 2015 diesel summary includes it with the high-side limit of about 1150 °C. A reading too high here often follows an uncontrolled soot burn in the filter, one too low a regeneration that never got hot enough.
c: Overloaded particulate filter burning off too fast
Regeneration not reaching target temperature (VW low-side check)
s: MIL on
Filter regeneration aborted or repeated
Emergency mode with reduced power possible

P247B.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Out of Range (Bank 1 Sensor 4)
P247B.d: P247B concerns the last probe in the bank 1 chain. In Ford's 2015 6.7L overview that is EGT14, mounted downstream of the particulate filter, so it sees the heat that leaves the filter during regeneration. Ford's 2015 diesel summary is the only public maker document with this code; it pairs it with P2470 and P2471 and apply the same high-side limit of about 1150 °C, monitored continuously over some 2 s. The 2023 summary checks probe 4 against a model (P246E) instead. A real reading near the limit at the filter outlet hints at a thermal runaway in the filter, which can crack the substrate, so the vehicle should be inspected promptly.
c: Thermal runaway in the particulate filter
Unburnt fuel reaching the filter from injectors or a dosing valve
s: MIL on
Regeneration stopped, filter load warning possible
Power reduction

P247C.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Out of Range (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P247C.d: P247C is the bank 2 counterpart of P2478: the first exhaust probe on the second cylinder bank reports a temperature outside its permitted window, typically next to the turbine outlet or catalyst inlet of that bank. It needs a V engine with separate exhaust paths and its own probe per bank. No maker documents P247C in public material; Ford's 2015 diesels with their single exhaust stream use only the bank 1 numbers, with a high-side limit of about 1150 °C, and Volkswagen's 2014 2.0L TDI checks the target-to-actual gap. Comparing both banks helps: if only bank 2 runs hot, look at that bank's injectors, turbo and air supply before replacing the probe.
c: Bank 2 running hot from extra fuel or a faulty injector
Air shortage on bank 2 from a boost leak or turbo fault
s: MIL on
Reduced power to protect the exhaust
Bank 2 probe reads clearly above bank 1

P247D.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Out of Range (Bank 2 Sensor 2)
P247D.d: P247D applies to the second probe on bank 2, by analogy with P2479 normally downstream of that bank's oxidation catalyst, where the heat released by burning fuel during a regeneration is measured. It is set when the reported temperature leaves the plausible window, in practice mostly on the high side. There is no public maker document for P247D; the closest reference is Ford's 2015 diesel summary, which uses P2479 for the bank 1 position with a limit of about 1150 °C. CARB asks for out-of-range and rationality checks on such inputs. A one-sided hot reading on bank 2 often means that bank receives more fuel, while a probe that reads hot even when cold is simply faulty.
c: Too much heat in the bank 2 catalyst during regeneration
Probe reading high even on a cold engine
s: MIL on
Regeneration cancelled
Bank 2 probe 2 differs from its bank 1 twin

P247E.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Out of Range (Bank 2 Sensor 3)
P247E.d: P247E does not question the wiring but the value itself: the third exhaust probe on cylinder bank 2 reports a temperature the engine control unit will not accept, in practice mostly an implausibly hot one. The code only makes sense on a V engine whose two banks keep separate exhaust paths up to the third measuring point. No maker publishes P247E; the bank 1 twin P247A is used by Ford's 2015 diesels with a high-side limit of about 1150 °C and by Volkswagen's 2014 Touareg V6 TDI, which flags a target-to-actual gap above 200 K. CARB requires such inputs to be checked for range and plausibility. Look at the bank 2 regeneration and fuelling first; a probe that reads hot at a cold start is simply faulty.
c: Uncontrolled soot burn or too much post-injection fuel on bank 2
Probe drifted and reports values too high
Leaking injector or turbo oil leak on bank 2
s: Warning lamp on, regeneration may be aborted
Reduced power to protect the aftertreatment

P247F.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Out of Range (Bank 2 Sensor 4)
P247F.d: P247F flags an unacceptable reading from the fourth exhaust temperature probe of bank 2, the position that on most layouts sits behind the particulate filter. A genuine reading near the limit there means heat is leaving the filter, which points to a runaway regeneration. No manufacturer documents P247F publicly. The bank 1 counterpart P247B appears only in Ford's 2015 diesel summary, which trips it once the probe exceeds roughly 1150 °C; by 2023 Ford checked probe 4 against a temperature model (P246E) instead. CARB demands range and rationality monitoring for such inputs. Before the probe is replaced, compare it with the bank 1 probe 4 and inspect the filter, because a cracked substrate can follow repeated overheating.
c: Overloaded particulate filter burning off too fast
Probe ageing with readings drifting upwards
Probe swapped with another position after a repair
s: Engine warning lamp lit
Regeneration blocked or power limited

P2480.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 5)
P2480.d: P2480 is the general circuit or open-circuit fault of a fifth exhaust temperature probe on bank 1. Five probes in one line are rare; GM's small diesels with oxidation catalyst, SCR, second catalyst and filter are among the few layouts that use them. GM does not report P2480 there, however: its 2018 tables detect an interrupted probe 5 inside P2482, by a resistance above 1400 Ω with the output energised, and the 2025 tables treat values beyond 100 MΩ the same way. So no maker documents P2480 publicly; CARB only requires that the circuit be monitored. Typical findings would be a broken lead, a corroded plug near the hot exhaust, or a probe whose element has burned through. Low and High faults of the same probe are P2481 and P2482.
c: Broken or chafed lead to probe 5
Corroded or loose connector near the exhaust
Measuring element of the probe burned through
s: Warning lamp on
Missing or frozen value for probe 5 in live data
Filter regeneration may be suppressed

P2481.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 5)
P2481.d: P2481 means the signal of the fifth bank 1 exhaust probe has dropped below its lower electrical limit, which on a resistive probe usually indicates a short to ground. GM documents it codegenau for its diesel ECMs: the 2017 and 2020 tables fail a probe resistance under 158 Ω, the 2018 table under 500 Ω, each after 10 of 20 samples at 100 ms, as a Type B fault. The 2025 tables flag under 1 Ω, or for a digital thermocouple a reading colder than about −73 °C, after 19 of 25 samples. Ram lists P2481 for the 2025–2026 2500/3500 diesel and stresses using the sensor names in the scan tool, since the numbering is easy to mix up. P2482 is the opposite limit, P2484 an unsteady signal.
c: Signal lead chafed through and touching ground
Internal short in the probe after heat damage
Neighbouring probe replaced because positions were confused
s: Engine warning lamp after two trips
Probe 5 reads implausibly in live data

P2482.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 5)
P2482.d: With P2482 the fifth bank 1 exhaust probe delivers a signal above its upper electrical limit. On GM diesels this code also covers the open circuit: the 2018 table sets it above 1400 Ω, both as a short to power with the driver off and as an interruption with the driver on, after 10 of 20 samples, Type B. The 2020 table makes it Type A. In 2025 GM uses more than 100 MΩ, or a digital value hotter than about 1290 °C, after 19 of 25 samples, again Type A with the lamp on after one trip. Ram names P2482 together with P2481 for its 2025–2026 heavy-duty diesel pick-ups. A loose plug or broken lead is therefore as likely as a failed probe. Compare with P2481 for the short to ground.
c: Broken lead from heat or vibration
s: Warning lamp, on GM from 2020 after a single trip
Probe 5 shows a fixed extreme value
Regeneration suppressed

P2483.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1 Sensor 5)
P2483.d: P2483 is the plausibility test for the fifth bank 1 exhaust probe: the circuit is electrically fine, but the reading does not behave like a real exhaust temperature. GM's 2025 diesel tables describe the check in detail. After the engine has been off for more than 10,800 s (three hours), the value frozen at key-on serves as reference; if the probe then fails to rise by the amount a calibrated map expects while the engine runs, the ECM concludes it is stuck or no longer in the gas stream. It is a Type B fault and waits until the electrical codes P2481, P2482 and P2484 are clear. Hino also issued workshop-manual corrections for P2483 on its 2018–2019 J08E trucks. A probe pulled out of its boss after work on the exhaust is a classic cause.
c: Probe not fully seated in its boss after exhaust work
Probe output stuck or responding too slowly
Heavily sooted probe tip insulating the element
s: Warning lamp after two trips
Probe 5 barely changes while the other probes heat up

P2484.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 1 Sensor 5)
P2484.d: P2484 catches a fifth bank 1 exhaust probe whose signal jumps faster than any real exhaust temperature can change. GM's diesel ECMs compare consecutive samples taken every 100 ms. In the 2018 table the resistance difference between two samples is evaluated, and 15 failed samples out of 30 set a Type B code. The 2025 table uses a temperature step above 100 °C, needs 12 of 25 samples and runs only while the unfiltered value lies between 140 and 1070 °C and no electrical fault of the probe is present. GM lists internal probe faults, worn harnesses and connector problems as failure modes. Unlike P2481 and P2482, the signal stays within its limits, so wiggle tests on the harness while watching live data are the quickest way in.
c: Intermittent contact in the probe connector
Harness insulation worn by heat or rubbing
s: Warning lamp, sometimes going out again
Erratic jumps of probe 5 in live data

P2485.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit/Open (Bank 2 Sensor 5)
P2485.d: P2485 reports a circuit or open-circuit fault at a fifth exhaust temperature probe on bank 2. That requires a V engine with two separate aftertreatment lines carrying five probes each, a layout no public maker document shows. No manufacturer documents P2485. The closest reference is GM's single-bank diesel, which watches its probe 5 on bank 1 and folds the open circuit into the High code P2482 (above 1400 Ω in 2018, beyond 100 MΩ in 2025). CARB merely requires that every such input be monitored for circuit faults. If the code appears, check that the scan tool's probe numbering matches the vehicle, then the connector and lead. Bank 1 equivalent: P2480; Low/High of the same probe: P2486/P2487.
c: Interrupted lead between control unit and probe
Connector left unplugged after exhaust work
s: Warning lamp on
No valid value for this probe

P2486.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 5)
P2486.d: P2486 is set when the signal of the fifth bank 2 exhaust probe sits below its lower electrical limit, typically because the lead or the probe itself shorts to ground. No manufacturer documents P2486 publicly; it presupposes two exhaust banks with five probes each. As an analogy, GM's diesel tables handle bank 1 probe 5 under P2481 with a resistance limit of 158 to 500 Ω depending on the year (under 1 Ω in 2025) and a debounce of 10 of 20 samples, Type B. CARB calls for out-of-range low checks on every such input. In the workshop, measure the probe resistance cold and compare it with a probe of the same type, then look for chafed insulation along the exhaust. Opposite limit: P2487; bank 1: P2481.
c: Lead insulation damaged and touching ground
s: Engine warning lamp
Implausible reading of this probe

P2487.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 5)
P2487.d: With P2487 the control unit sees the fifth bank 2 exhaust probe above its upper electrical limit, the picture of a short to supply voltage or, on many designs, of an open circuit. There is no public maker document for P2487. For bank 1 GM treats probe 5 under P2482: above 1400 Ω in the 2018 tables, beyond 100 MΩ or about 1290 °C in 2025, rated Type A since 2020, so the lamp comes on after one trip. CARB requires out-of-range high detection for each input of this kind. Since a pulled connector produces the same reading as a dead probe, check the plug before buying parts; a probe that reads plausibly at ambient temperature after reconnection points to the harness. Low: P2486; bank 1: P2482.
c: Signal lead shorted to a supply line
s: Warning lamp after one trip
Probe shows maximum or no value

P2488.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2 Sensor 5)
P2488.d: P2488 is the rationality check for the fifth bank 2 exhaust probe: the signal is electrically valid but does not follow the operating state. No manufacturer documents P2488; a second bank with five probes is unknown in public maker material. GM's 2025 diesel tables show for bank 1 probe 5 (P2483) how such a check can work: after a soak of more than three hours the key-on value is frozen, and too small a rise during the following drive marks the probe as stuck or outside the gas stream, Type B. CARB requires rationality monitoring of inputs used by the OBD system. A comparison with the matching probe on bank 1 and with the neighbouring probes on bank 2 quickly shows whether one sensor lags behind.
c: Probe not reaching into the gas flow
Exhaust leak cooling the measuring point
s: Warning lamp after two trips
Regeneration may be inhibited

P2489.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 2 Sensor 5)
P2489.d: P2489 points to an unsteady signal from the fifth exhaust probe on bank 2: the value stays within its electrical limits but jumps or drops out briefly. This code is not documented by any manufacturer, as no public layout carries five probes per bank on a twin-bank engine. For the bank 1 position GM shows the method under P2484: samples every 100 ms are compared, and in 2025 a step above 100 °C in 12 of 25 samples, valid only between 140 and 1070 °C, sets a Type B fault. CARB requires monitoring of inputs for erratic behaviour where it affects emissions. Such faults usually come from loose terminals or a harness that touches hot parts, so a careful check of routing and clips pays off.
s: Warning lamp coming and going
Jumping value in live data

P248A.t: Reductant Heater A Sense Circuit Low
P248A.d: P248A concerns the sense line with which the control unit measures the supply voltage reaching DEF heater A, and reports that voltage as too low. GM uses it on its diesels with an SCR power module for the tank heater: the 2016 to 2018 tables subtract the heater supply voltage from system voltage and fail a gap of more than 3 V while heating is commanded, after 10 of 12 checks at 500 ms; cranking is excluded and a lost connection to the reductant module (U010E) blocks the test. The tables leave the lamp column blank. Ford's 2023 diesels also assign heater A to the tank. A voltage drop of this size usually comes from a corroded plug, a weak relay contact or a damaged supply lead.
c: Corroded heater supply connector at the tank
Worn heater relay contact causing voltage drop
Weak battery or charging fault during heating
s: Warning lamp or DEF system message
Frozen DEF not thawed in winter, dosing delayed

P248B.t: Reductant Heater A Sense Circuit High
P248B.d: P248B is the upper counterpart to P248A: the sense signal for the supply of DEF heater A reads higher than permitted, for example when the line shorts to battery voltage, when the supply stays live although the heater is switched off, or when the sense input itself fails. No manufacturer documents P248B in public material. GM's diesels only check the low side of this sense line (P248A, more than 3 V below system voltage); Ford's 2023 diesels flag a heater supply below 5 V and check the switched-off state of heater circuit 1, the tank heater, under P20BC. CARB requires reductant heaters and their circuits to be monitored. In practice, check whether the heater relay releases and whether the sense lead is intact.
c: Sense lead shorted to battery voltage
Faulty sense input in the control module
s: Warning lamp
Possible battery drain if the heater stays powered

P248C.t: Reductant Heater B Sense Circuit Low
P248C.d: P248C reports too little voltage on the sense circuit of DEF heater B. In GM's diesel tables from 2016 to 2018 heater B is the line heater, i.e. the heated hose from the pump to the dosing valve. The test mirrors P248A: if system voltage exceeds the measured line heater supply by more than 3 V while heating is requested, 10 failures in 12 checks at 500 ms set the code, with cranking excluded and U010E as a blocking condition; no lamp type is listed. Ford's 2023 diesels likewise give the pressure line heater the letter B. A frozen hose that does not thaw causes dosing faults in winter, so a voltage drop at the line heater plug or in its fuse and relay path should be found early.
c: Corroded plug at the heated DEF line
Voltage drop across fuse or relay of the line heater
Damaged supply lead along the frame
s: DEF warning or engine lamp
Dosing faults at low temperatures

P248D.t: Reductant Heater B Sense Circuit High
P248D.d: P248D means the heater B sense input reads too high, typically the heated line. Possible pictures are a sense wire shorted to battery positive, a supply that remains on after the heater has been switched off, or a faulty input stage. Public maker documentation for P248D does not exist. GM tests the line heater sense circuit only for undervoltage (P248C); Ford's 2023 diesels cover heater circuit 2, the pressure line heater, with P20C0 (switched off yet more than 5 V at the output) and the current codes P221C/P221D. CARB requires the reductant heating to be monitored. A line heater that never switches off wastes battery energy and can overheat the hose, so the relay is the first item to check.
c: Sense wire shorted to battery positive
Defective input stage in the module
s: Warning lamp
Battery discharging while parked

P248E.d: P248E is the bank 2 counterpart of P245A: the engine controller sees no proper load on the output that drives the EGR cooler bypass of the second cylinder bank, most often because the circuit is open. Only engines with a separate EGR path per bank can set it, which in practice means V engines with two coolers. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the published diesel tables we checked only list bank 1. For comparison, GM's 2017 Duramax tables flag the bank 1 DC-motor flap when the load resistance with the H-bridge switched off exceeds 200 kOhm, rated Type B. CARB requires such actuators to be checked as comprehensive components. With the flap unpowered, warm-up or cooling of the recirculated gas is no longer controlled on that bank.
c: Unplugged connector or broken wire at the bank 2 bypass actuator
Open motor or solenoid winding in the bank 2 actuator
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light on
Longer warm-up or higher NOx on one bank because the bypass stays put

P248F.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2)
P248F.d: With P248F the bank 2 bypass circuit is electrically sound, yet the flap does not do what the controller asks: it lags behind the setpoint, stops short of its end position or switching shows no effect on the gas temperature after the cooler. No manufacturer publishes a bank 2 version of this check. On bank 1 (P245B) GM's 2017 Duramax logic compares commanded and measured flap position and fails above a 16 % deviation, while Ford's 2023 diesels move the flap on purpose and expect a clear temperature response. A second bank would be judged the same way. Sticking from soot and oil carbon, a tired return spring, weak vacuum on pneumatic versions or wrong position feedback are the usual reasons. If the flap is later found fixed in place, the stuck code P24A6 may follow.
c: Bypass flap on bank 2 sluggish from soot and carbon
Leaking vacuum line or weak vacuum on pneumatic actuators
s: Check engine light on
Often no noticeable change in driving

P2490.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Circuit Low (Bank 2)
P2490.d: P2490 means the drive line of the bank 2 cooler bypass actuator sits too close to ground potential, typically a grounded wire between controller and actuator. It mirrors P245C on bank 1. No manufacturer documents P2490 publicly. GM's 2017 diesel tables give an idea of the bank 1 test: the vacuum-switched bypass is failed when the resistance to ground falls below 0.5 Ohm in 24 of 30 samples. Depending on the wiring, a grounded control line can keep the actuator permanently energised or permanently released, so bank 2 either always bypasses or always cools. Look for chafed insulation near the exhaust manifolds and turbocharger, harness clips lost after repairs and water in the connector. An open is P248E, a short toward the supply P2491.
c: Drive wire rubbed through and touching engine ground
Water or corrosion in the bank 2 actuator connector
s: Check engine light on
Bypass on bank 2 stuck in one mode, possibly followed by cooler efficiency codes

P2491.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Circuit High (Bank 2)
P2491.d: P2491 reports excess voltage or excess current in the drive circuit feeding the bypass actuator on bank 2, the classic sign of a short to supply or of a winding whose resistance has collapsed. It is the bank 2 sibling of P245D, and no maker publishes its own description of it. GM's 2017 tables show how a bank 1 DC-motor flap is protected: if H-bridge current climbs past 8 A in 160 of 200 samples, the output is flagged and the code is rated Type B. Many controllers switch off the affected driver to protect it, so the flap falls back to its spring-loaded rest position. A blown fuse feeding the actuator or a damaged controller output can accompany the code. Open circuit is P248E, ground short P2490.
c: Control wire touching a battery or ignition feed
Actuator winding with too low resistance or seized motor
Controller software reporting a false actuator fault
s: Check engine light on
Bypass flap on bank 2 rests in its default position

P2492.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Circuit (Bank 1)
P2492.d: The position sensor tells the controller where the bank 1 cooler bypass flap actually is; position-controlled flaps cannot be regulated without it. P2492 is the general circuit code for that sensor, used when the fault cannot be classed as a short to ground or to the supply. No manufacturer documents P2492 publicly. GM's Duramax tables from 2017 and 2018 monitor the same analog sensor, but split the electrical faults into P2494 (below 1 % of the 5 V reference) and P2495 (above 99 %), both Type B; a separate learning check at key-off is P24C4. Without a valid feedback signal the controller usually stops closed-loop flap control, which can then also set P245B. Damaged wiring, a loose connector or a lost 5 V reference are the main suspects.
c: Damaged sensor wiring near hot exhaust parts
Loose or corroded connector at the bypass valve
5 V sensor supply missing or shared circuit shorted
s: Check engine light on
Bypass flap no longer position-controlled

P2493.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Range/Performance (Bank 1)
P2493.d: P2493 is a plausibility fault: the bank 1 bypass position signal stays inside its electrical limits, but its value or behaviour does not fit the commanded flap position or the learned end stops. GM names the code in preliminary bulletin PI1449 for the 2015 Silverado and Sierra with the LML Duramax, where it showed up together with P2495, P24C4 and P06A3. The fix there was a complete new bypass valve, since the sensor sits in the valve and must not be taken apart. Range errors often come from a worn sensor track, a shaft that turns without the sensor following, or deposits that shift the end positions. The pure circuit faults are P2492, P2494 and P2495; bank 2 reports P2498.
c: Worn or defective bypass valve with integrated sensor
Deposits shifting the learned end positions
Unstable 5 V reference shared with other sensors
s: Check engine light on, often with further bypass codes
Bypass position in the live data does not match the command

P2494.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 1)
P2494.d: P2494 is set when the raw voltage of the bank 1 bypass position sensor drops toward zero. GM documents it for the Duramax diesel: in the 2017 tables the signal must be below 1 % of the 5 V reference in 200 of 250 samples, checked every 6.25 ms once cranking is over and the powertrain relay supplies more than 11 V. The 2018 tables keep the test and the Type B rating, so the lamp comes on after two trips. GM groups P2494 with P2495 and P24C4 in one sensor fault bundle, which makes the bypass control fall back to a default. A signal near zero points to a short to ground, a missing 5 V supply or a broken signal wire pulled down inside the controller. High voltage is P2495; on bank 2 the low case is P2499.
c: Open 5 V reference wire to the sensor
Internal sensor fault in the bypass valve
s: Check engine light after two trips
Bypass control falls back to a default position

P2495.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Circuit High (Bank 1)
P2495.d: P2495 covers a bank 1 bypass position signal that climbs close to the reference voltage. On GM Duramax diesels the 2017 calibration fails it above 99 % of 5 V in 200 out of 250 samples, with the same enable conditions as the low test, and rates it Type B. In the field GM saw it on 2015 LML-powered full-size pickups: preliminary bulletin PI1449 lists it with P2493, P24C4 and P06A3 and has the whole bypass valve replaced. That combination is a useful hint: a shared 5 V supply fault (P06A3) can drag several sensors along, so check the reference circuit before condemning parts. Otherwise an open ground wire or a signal wire touching supply is typical. Low voltage is P2494, bank 2 P249A.
c: Defective bypass valve with integrated sensor
Fault in the shared 5 V reference circuit
Signal wire touching a voltage source
s: Check engine light after two trips
Additional sensor supply codes stored at the same time

P2496.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 1)
P2496.d: P2496 targets a bank 1 bypass position signal that jumps, drops out briefly or changes faster than the flap can physically move, without staying outside the electrical limits long enough for P2494 or P2495. No manufacturer documents P2496 publicly; GM's Duramax tables, which do cover the same analog sensor, only list the low, high and learning checks. The fault pattern is typical of loose terminals, a wire that breaks inside its insulation when the engine rocks, moisture creeping into the connector or a worn contact track in the sensor. Because the signal looks fine most of the time, the code may come and go; wiggling the harness while watching live data is the most useful test. CARB treats such sensors as comprehensive components. Bank 2 uses P249B.
c: Loose or spread terminal in the sensor connector
Wire breaking inside the insulation from engine movement
Worn contact track inside the sensor
s: Check engine light that comes and goes
Bypass position value jumps in the live data

P2497.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Circuit (Bank 2)
P2497.d: P2497 is the generic circuit fault of the position sensor on the bank 2 cooler bypass, so it can only appear on engines whose second bank has its own EGR cooler with feedback-controlled flap. We found no manufacturer that documents a bank 2 bypass sensor; all published examples, such as GM's Duramax tables, are single-bank engines that use P2494 and P2495 on bank 1. The logic would be the same: the controller expects a voltage between fixed limits and flags the circuit when it is missing or implausible in a way not covered by the low and high codes. Bypass control on that bank is then usually suspended. A check of the connector, the 5 V supply and ground at the sensor comes first. The bank 1 equivalent is P2492.
c: Damaged wiring to the bank 2 position sensor
Failed position sensor or bypass valve
s: Check engine light on
Bypass on bank 2 no longer regulated

P2498.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Range/Performance (Bank 2)
P2498.d: With P2498 the bank 2 bypass position signal is electrically valid but not believable, for example because it does not change when the flap is commanded, settles at an unexpected value or no longer matches the end stops learned earlier. There is no public manufacturer description for this bank 2 code. The closest documented case is bank 1: GM's 2015 LML Duramax showed P2493 together with other bypass sensor codes, and GM's answer was a complete new bypass valve, because sensor and valve form one unit. On a twin-cooler engine the same reasoning applies to the second bank, so a sensor fault and a mechanically binding flap must be told apart with live data before parts are ordered. The bank 1 version is P2493; the actuator side of bank 2 is P248F.
c: Worn bank 2 bypass valve with built-in sensor
Flap binding so the sensor reads a position other than commanded
End-stop learn values invalid after a repair
s: Check engine light on
Measured and commanded bypass position differ on bank 2

P2499.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 2)
P2499.d: P2499 stands for a bank 2 bypass position voltage that has fallen to the bottom of its range. No manufacturer documents the bank 2 code publicly. For orientation, GM's 2017 Duramax tables fail the bank 1 sensor (P2494) once its output drops under one percent of the supply and need 200 bad results out of 250 before the Type B fault is stored. A comparable bank 2 check would react to the same electrical causes: the signal wire grounded somewhere along the harness, the sensor supply interrupted or shorted, or a sensor that no longer drives its output. If other 5 V sensors report low values simultaneously, the shared reference circuit is the better starting point. High voltage on bank 2 is P249A, the bank 1 low code P2494.
c: 5 V sensor supply interrupted or pulled down
s: Check engine light on
Bank 2 bypass position reads near zero

P249A.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Circuit High (Bank 2)
P249A.d: P249A is logged when the bank 2 bypass position signal sits near the top of the reference voltage. Like its siblings on this bank, it is not described by any manufacturer in public documents. The bank 1 analogue P2495 is set by GM's Duramax logic once the raw value exceeds 99 % of 5 V in most of a 250-sample window, rated Type B with the lamp after two trips. A reading stuck at the top usually means the sensor has lost its ground, so the signal floats up to the supply, or that the signal wire has contact with a voltage source. A water-damaged connector can produce the same picture. Because sensor and bypass valve are often one part, a new valve is only justified after wiring and ground check out. Low on bank 2 is P2499.
c: Lost ground at the bank 2 position sensor
Signal wire in contact with a supply line
Water ingress in the sensor connector
s: Check engine light after two trips
Bank 2 bypass position shows full scale

P249B.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 2)
P249B.d: P249B flags short dropouts or implausible jumps in the bank 2 bypass position signal that are too brief to count as a steady low or high fault. Public manufacturer documentation for it does not exist, and even the well documented bank 1 sensor on GM's Duramax only has low, high and learning checks, without an erratic test of its own. If a controller does use P249B, the cause is rarely the sensor itself: heat cycling near the turbocharger, vibration and road splash attack terminals and harness on the second bank. A freeze-frame or a recorded drive helps to see under which load and temperature the signal breaks up. Fixing a terminal is usually enough; a new valve only follows if the fault lies inside. The bank 1 code is P2496.
c: Fretting or loose terminal in the bank 2 sensor plug
Harness brittle from heat near the turbocharger
s: Check engine light appears now and then
Bank 2 position value flickers in the live data

P249C.t: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Reductant Injection Control
P249C.d: P249C covers the SCR dosing strategy rather than a part: after start-up the engine controller is expected to switch from fixed, map-based urea dosing to dosing corrected by the NOx sensor signal, and this code means that switch happened too seldom or too late. Ford's 2023 diesel summary checks how much of the operating time was really spent in closed loop compared with what was expected, with SCR temperature between 160 and 550 °C, coolant above 70 °C and a 300 s run. Usual reasons are a NOx sensor not yet ready, implausible exhaust temperatures or a cold SCR. P249D and P249E report the opposite case, a loop that runs but has run out of correction range. The driver usually only sees the warning lamp.
c: Downstream NOx sensor slow to become ready or faulty, so closed loop cannot start
Implausible exhaust gas temperature signal upstream or downstream of the SCR
Mostly short or cold trips keep the SCR below its working temperature
Engine control software calibration requiring an update
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Often no noticeable change in driving behaviour
NOx sensor or exhaust temperature codes may be stored as well

P249D.t: Closed Loop Reductant Injection Control At Limit - Flow Too Low
P249D.d: With P249D the NOx feedback loop of the SCR system has pushed its long-term correction as far as it may go because the delivered amount of DEF appears too small for the measured NOx. GM's tables judge this via the long-term adaptation value: above 1.69 in the 2014 diesel table and above 1.99 in the 2018 table; both rate it Type B, lamp after the second failing trip. Ford's 2023 diesel summary sets the code when the correction factor sits at its clip for 30 s while the SCR is warm and steady. Typical background is a partly blocked or worn dosing valve, weak pump pressure, crystallised urea or diluted fluid. The mirror code P249E means the loop had to take dosing back to its lower limit. Higher NOx output and possible later power reduction are the practical effects.
c: Dosing valve partly blocked by urea crystals or deposits
Weak DEF pump or restricted supply line and filter
Diluted or wrong fluid in the DEF tank
NOx sensor reading too high and misleading the controller
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Increased DEF warnings or later speed or power limitation
SCR efficiency code may follow

P249E.t: Closed Loop Reductant Injection Control At Limit - Flow Too High
P249E.d: P249E is the counterpart to P249D: here the SCR feedback has trimmed the dosing down to the lowest correction it is allowed, because more reductant seems to arrive than the NOx reading calls for. GM's 2014 diesel table flags a long-term adaptation factor below 0.41 (Type B); the 2018 table lists the low-side check as a two-trip Type B fault. Ford's 2023 summary uses the same 30 s clip rule as for P249D. A dosing valve that leaks or sticks partly open, overly concentrated fluid, ammonia slip being read by the NOx sensor as NOx, or a sensor that reads too low can all lead here. Ammonia smell at the tailpipe and white deposits around the injector are possible clues; drivability itself is rarely affected.
c: Dosing valve leaking or sticking partly open
Ammonia slip from an aged or overloaded SCR catalyst seen by the NOx sensor
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Ammonia smell from the exhaust
White crystalline deposits at the dosing point

P249F.t: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Particulate Filter Regeneration Control
P249F.d: During an active filter regeneration the controller is meant to steer the temperature ahead of the particulate filter with feedback from the exhaust temperature sensors, usually by adjusting late fuel injection or a hydrocarbon dosing valve in the exhaust. P249F is stored when the regeneration spent too little of its duration in that feedback mode. Ford's 2023 diesel summary judges the closed-loop share against a threshold that depends on total regeneration time, checked once per regeneration at 1000 to 3500 rpm. Volvo truck bulletin K86412082 (model years 2016 to 2018) pairs P249F with P24A0 on engines with a seventh, aftertreatment hydrocarbon injector and points first to engine and aftertreatment software. P24A0 and P24A1 cover a loop that runs but saturates. The driver normally notices only the lamp.
c: Engine or aftertreatment module software needing an update
Exhaust temperature sensor ahead of the oxidation catalyst or filter reading wrongly
Hydrocarbon dosing valve in the exhaust restricted or slow to respond
Regenerations repeatedly interrupted by short trips or changing load
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Regeneration may take longer or repeat more often
Often no change in driveability

P24A0.t: Closed Loop Particulate Filter Regeneration Control At Limit - Temperature Too Low
P24A0.d: P24A0 means the regeneration temperature loop is already giving all the extra heat it may, yet the gas ahead of the particulate filter stays below target. GM describes it as an HC injector control deviation: the gap between setpoint and measured temperature ahead of the DPF is watched while the filter warms up, and 10 failing out of 20 samples set a Type B fault; the 2014 table phrases it as insufficient hydrocarbon injector authority. Ford's 2023 summary uses P24A0 when the controller sits at a clip and the temperature error stays large long enough. Volvo truck bulletin K86412082 lists it with P249F. Likely culprits are a restricted HC doser or fuel supply, an aged oxidation catalyst that lights off poorly, or a faulty temperature sensor. Soot may build up because regenerations stay incomplete.
c: Hydrocarbon dosing valve or its fuel supply restricted
Oxidation catalyst aged or face-plugged, so the fuel does not burn ahead of the filter
Exhaust temperature sensor reading too low
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensors cooling the gas
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Regenerations take long or do not finish
Soot load codes may follow

P24A1.t: Closed Loop Particulate Filter Regeneration Control At Limit - Temperature Too High
P24A1.d: Here the regeneration loop has reduced its heat input as far as possible, but the temperature ahead of the filter still runs above target. GM lists P24A1 as the negative-deviation branch of the HC injector control check in steady regeneration, again a Type B fault counted over samples; the 2014 table calls it excessive hydrocarbon injector authority, and the 2018 table shows the check behind a calibration enable flag. Hino bulletin SB-22-007 names P24A1 and P24A2 on 2020 J08 conventional trucks fitted with a certain bubbler fuel filter, fixed by fitting a revised filter. Fuel leaking from a doser or injector, a sensor reading high or an uncontrolled soot burn can cause it. Unlike P24A0 the risk is thermal stress on the filter, so engines may cut the regeneration short.
c: Hydrocarbon doser or fuel injector leaking extra fuel into the exhaust
Fuel supply part causing unstable doser pressure (Hino 2020 bubbler filter)
Exhaust temperature sensor reading too high
Heavy soot load burning faster than the controller can follow
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Regeneration aborted early
Possible high exhaust temperature warning

P24A2.d: P24A2 judges the outcome of a regeneration on the bank 1 filter: the event ended, but the estimated soot left in the filter is still above the allowed level. Ford's 2023 diesel summary runs this once per regeneration for up to 40 minutes and compares the soot estimate at the end with a threshold. Deutz uses P24A2-00 for a regeneration stopped because the temperature got too high, and Hino bulletin SB-22-007 lists it together with P24A1 for a fuel filter issue on 2020 trucks. CARB demands detection of a filter that does not regenerate properly. Too low or too high exhaust temperatures, aborted regenerations and pressure sensor errors are common reasons. P243E is the bank 2 version; P24A4 follows if soot keeps rising.
c: Regenerations interrupted by short trips or engine shut-off
Exhaust temperature not reaching target (doser, oxidation catalyst, sensors)
Differential pressure sensor or its hoses giving a wrong soot estimate
s: Malfunction indicator lamp or filter warning on
More frequent regenerations, higher fuel consumption
Reduced power if soot keeps building

P24A3.d: P24A3 is the bank 2 entry for a particulate filter whose soot load, estimated from differential pressure, exhaust flow and a soot model, has climbed to the point where it noticeably restricts flow and needs a regeneration. It only appears on engines with two separate filter strands, such as some V engines. Public manufacturer documentation for this exact code is missing (the NHTSA bulletin index has no hit either), so this text leans on CARB's filter-clogging requirement and on the bank 1 equivalent P2463, which Deutz lists as a high soot load warning. The stronger level for bank 2, beyond which a normal regeneration may no longer be safe, is P243F, while ash build-up is reported separately. A long motorway drive or a workshop-initiated regeneration often clears it; repeated returns point to the cause behind the soot.
c: Mostly short trips so passive and active regeneration cannot finish
Excess soot from injectors, EGR or boost problems
Differential pressure sensor or hoses on bank 2 giving a false high reading
s: Particulate filter or engine warning lamp
Reduced power or slow response
Higher fuel consumption

P24A4.t: Particulate Filter Restriction - Soot Accumulation Too High (Bank 1)
P24A4.d: P24A4 marks the critical stage for the bank 1 filter: the soot load is so high that a normal regeneration risks overheating and cracking the substrate. Deutz names P24A4-00 a critical soot load. GM's 2016 and 2018 diesel tables use P24A4 for a clogged filter that has to be replaced, judged from the filtered flow resistance derived from differential pressure, 5 failures in 10 samples, Type A with one trip; the 2018 table labels the line ash accumulation, so GM appears to use the code for a load no regeneration can remove. P2463 is the earlier soot warning, P242F the separate ash code. Many engines then reduce power and block automatic regeneration, so only a controlled service regeneration, cleaning or a new filter will help.
c: Earlier soot warnings or failed regenerations not dealt with
Excess soot from injectors, EGR valve or turbocharger faults
Filter saturated with ash at end of service life
Differential pressure measurement reading falsely high
s: Marked loss of power, limp mode
Automatic regeneration no longer runs
Malfunction indicator and filter warning lamp on

P24A5.d: P24A5 means the bank 1 cooler bypass is mechanically stuck, and makers read that in both directions. GM's 2017 Duramax DC-motor flap is judged stuck in bypass if the position is still above 15 % after P245B; the 2018 vacuum version is moved between both modes and fails when the gas temperature after the cooler barely reacts, both Type B. Ford's 2013 and 2015 diesel summaries use it as an overcooling test on the 6.7 L and 3.2 L: with the flap commanded to cooling, gas after the cooler stays below a coolant-based limit for 12 seconds, a sign the flap sits in cooling. Ford traced early cases on 2016–17 Transit 3.2 L vans (TSB 17-0009) to a wrong EGR cooler; Ram reflashed 2014 6.7 L Cummins trucks to cut needless lamps (18-053-14). Bank 2 is P24A6.
c: Bypass flap seized by soot and carbon deposits
Actuator, linkage or vacuum supply no longer moving the flap
Incorrect EGR cooler fitted at the factory
Engine software that sets the fault too readily
s: Check engine light on
Slow warm-up or more soot when the flap is stuck in cooling
Higher NOx and EGR gas temperatures when stuck in bypass

P24A6.d: P24A6 is reserved for a mechanically stuck cooler bypass on bank 2. No manufacturer documents it publicly; the Ford and GM diesel summaries that describe the stuck test all apply it to a single bank and use P24A5. Their methods show how a second bank would be checked: either the measured flap position is compared with where it should rest, or the flap is switched and the gas temperature after the cooler must respond, as CARB's EGR cooler requirements expect. On a twin-cooler V engine a stuck bank 2 flap leaves that side either always bypassing, raising NOx, or always cooling, which slows warm-up and adds soot. Carbon build-up and a failing actuator are the likely reasons. Electrical faults on this bank are P248E, P2490 and P2491; the drift check is P248F.
c: Missing vacuum on a pneumatically switched bypass
s: Check engine light on
Uneven exhaust temperatures between the two banks

P24A7.t: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Control Circuit/Open
P24A7.d: Some diesel engines feed the EGR cooler with an electric auxiliary coolant pump so the cooler gets flow at low engine speed or after shut-off, independent of the main pump. P24A7 means the engine controller sees an open or otherwise faulty control line to this pump, typically when the driver stage detects no load while switching. No manufacturer documents this code publicly with thresholds, and no NHTSA bulletin index entry names it; the text relies on CARB's comprehensive component rules for outputs and on supplier information on EGR coolers in the coolant circuit. Check connector, wiring and pump fuse first. P24A9 and P24AA split the same circuit into shorts to ground and to supply. Without flow the cooler can overheat, so EGR may be reduced.
c: Loose, corroded or unplugged pump connector
Broken control wire in the harness
Open winding or electronics in the pump
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EGR may be reduced, NOx output rises

P24A8.t: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Performance/Stuck Off
P24A8.d: Unlike the circuit codes, P24A8 is about the pump's effect: it is commanded on, the wiring looks fine, yet the controller concludes that it does not deliver, for example because its speed feedback stays low or the expected temperature drop across the EGR cooler is missing. Air trapped after a coolant change, a blocked impeller, low coolant level or a seized motor are the usual reasons. How a maker detects the missing delivery is not published anywhere we could verify; CARB's requirement to test outputs for function and supplier material placing the cooler within the engine's coolant loop are the footing here. P24AB is the reverse, a pump that cannot be switched off. Continued operation risks boiling coolant in the cooler and cracking.
c: Air pocket in the auxiliary circuit after service or a leak
Pump motor seized or impeller blocked
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Coolant loss or bubbling at the expansion tank
EGR temperature or cooler efficiency codes may follow

P24A9.t: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Control Circuit Low
P24A9.d: P24A9 reports that the voltage on the control line of the electric EGR cooler coolant pump is lower than the driver stage expects in its current switching state, which usually points to a harness or pump-internal short to ground, or to a chafed wire touching the engine block. Whether low means switched on permanently or not at all depends on how the manufacturer drives the pump (low-side or high-side switching, or a PWM signal). Published limits are not available from any maker, so CARB's rules for monitoring actuator circuits and supplier notes on EGR coolers stand in. Inspect the harness near hot exhaust parts for melted insulation. P24AA is the short-to-supply counterpart, P24A7 the open line.
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Insulation melted near exhaust or EGR parts
Internal short in the pump electronics
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Pump may run continuously or not at all

P24AA.t: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Control Circuit High
P24AA.d: With P24AA the controller finds the control line of the EGR cooler coolant pump at a higher voltage than its switching state allows. The classic causes are a short circuit toward battery voltage, for example where the harness rubs against a powered wire, moisture in the connector, or a pump that no longer draws current so the line floats up. On some designs an open circuit can look like a high signal, so P24A7 and P24AA may appear together. Manufacturer limits are not public; the general CARB duty to watch actuator wiring plus supplier background on the cooler support this text. Measuring supply, ground and control voltage with the connector plugged in usually separates a wiring fault from a failed pump.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery voltage feed
Water or corrosion in the pump connector
Pump electronics failed so no current is drawn
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Pump may not run when commanded

P24AB.t: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Stuck On
P24AB.d: P24AB is set when the EGR cooler coolant pump keeps running although the controller has switched it off, seen for instance in continued speed feedback or current draw. Causes include a driver stage or relay that stays closed, a short that bypasses the switching side, or pump electronics that ignore the command. For the driver this is less urgent than a pump that will not run, but a constantly running pump drains the battery after shut-off and can slow engine warm-up. Public documentation of this check by a carmaker was not found; it follows from CARB's demand that switched outputs be verified in operation. P24A8 covers the opposite failure, P24A9 a short to ground that may keep the pump running.
c: Relay or controller output stage stuck closed
Short in the harness bypassing the switched side
Pump electronics no longer responding to the command
s: Pump audible after engine shut-off
Battery drained after standing
Malfunction indicator lamp on

P24AC.t: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Feedback Circuit Low
P24AC.d: Electronically commutated coolant pumps often report their state back to the controller on a separate feedback wire, typically as a speed or diagnostic signal. P24AC means that this return line sits below its valid range: shorted to ground, pulled down by a damaged pump, or permanently in an error level the pump uses to signal a dry run or blockage. The control side can be healthy at the same time, which separates it from P24A9. Signal limits are not disclosed by any maker; CARB's rules on rationality and range checks of inputs serve as the reference. Because the controller can no longer confirm pump operation, it may treat the EGR cooler as unprotected and limit EGR.
c: Pump signalling an internal fault, dry run or blockage
Corroded feedback pin in the connector
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EGR possibly reduced

P24AD.t: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Feedback Circuit High
P24AD.d: P24AD is the high-side counterpart of P24AC: the return signal from the EGR cooler coolant pump stays above its valid band. Since such feedback lines are usually pulled up inside the controller, a broken wire or a disconnected pump often shows as a constantly high level, as can a short to a voltage feed. The pump itself may still run normally, but the controller can no longer prove it. As with the low-side code, no maker discloses the band, so the general CARB input checks are the reference. A practical first step is to compare the feedback signal with the command while the pump is triggered from a scan tool, then check the line for continuity and for voltage from other circuits.
c: Feedback wire broken or pump unplugged, line pulled high
Feedback wire shorted to a voltage feed
Pump electronics no longer pulling the signal down
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Often no noticeable effect while driving

P24AE.d: The resistive particulate matter sensor behind the diesel particulate filter collects soot on interlocking electrodes; a rising current between them shows that particles are leaking through the filter. P24AE covers a fault in that electrode circuit. Ford's 2023 diesel summary checks it after each sensor regeneration at 200 to 425 °C over 120 s and sets the code if more than 5 µA still flows although the electrodes should be clean. VW's 2014 Touareg list ties P24AE to the electrode voltage leaving 0.30 to 4.70 V and to a functional check with too little or too unchanged measuring current. Special coverage 16018 from GM extended the warranty for Cruze 2.0 diesel sensors of model years 2014–2015 that set P24AE or P24AF after contamination or moisture damage. P24AF is the plausibility check during sensor regeneration.
c: Sensor element contaminated or damaged by moisture
Harness or connector to the sensor control unit damaged by heat or water
Fault in the separate sensor control unit
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Filter efficiency monitor cannot complete

P24AF.d: P24AF tests whether the particulate matter sensor behaves plausibly while it burns itself clean. During that heated phase the electrodes must show a small but definite current, and the heater must change the signal in an expected way. Ford's 2023 diesel summary sets P24AF when the current during sensor regeneration at 770 to 800 °C stays below 0.094 µA, judged over 120 s. VW's 2014 Touareg list uses the code when the accumulated change in heater voltage is no more than 0.25 V. A sensor that no longer reacts cannot detect a cracked or removed filter, which is why CARB requires this check. GM handled P24AF together with P24AE on 2014 and 2015 Cruze diesels under special coverage 16018. P24AE is the electrode circuit fault, P24B3 the heater circuit.
c: Sensor element aged or glazed, no longer responding
Sensor heater weak so the regeneration temperature is not reached
Element cracked by condensate after cold start
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Often no change in driveability

P24B0.d: P24B0 flags an electrode signal of the particulate matter sensor that sits too low, typically an open line or a cracked element that no longer conducts as expected. Ford's 2023 diesel summary watches the electrode supply continuously while the sensor measures and sets the code when it drops below 41.55 V for about 1.6 s. In GM's 18OBDG04 table the check runs during sensor regeneration at 600 to 820 °C, compares raw electrode current at two set temperatures and is Type B.
