VW's 2014 Touareg list ties the code to an electrode current above 5 µA. The code also shows up in FCA bulletin 18-008-23, a PCM update for the 2019 Compass diesel. P24B1 is the high side, P24AE the general electrode fault. Without a working sensor the filter monitor cannot run.
c: Sensor element cracked or electrode interrupted
Open electrode line between sensor and sensor control unit
Sensor control unit cannot supply the electrode voltage
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete

P24B1.d: P24B1 reports the electrode side of the particulate matter sensor reading high, which usually points to a short to a voltage source or to a soaked, conductive element. Ford's 2023 diesel summary sets it when electrode current exceeds 41 µA for about 3 s during measurement. GM's 18OBDG04 table looks for an electrode supply reading above 4.1 V in the sensor control unit (30 of 60 samples, Type B), and VW's 2014 Touareg list uses 0 V or more than 4.1 V. Mazda bulletin 01-005-22 for the 2018–2019 CX-5 SKYACTIV-D 2.2 blames condensate on the element and raised detection from one to two drive cycles. Ford 18-2225 replaces the sensor on 2017–2018 Super Duty 6.7L trucks. P24B0 is the low counterpart.
c: Condensate on the sensor element making it conductive
Electrode line shorted to a voltage source
Internal sensor fault, replacement sensor needed
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete

P24B2.d: P24B2 stands for a PM sensor electrode reading that cuts out or jumps for short moments rather than staying permanently low or high. Such dropouts usually come from a loose pin, a chafed harness near the hot exhaust or moisture in the connector. FCA documents the code for Jeep Compass diesels: bulletin 18-008-23 lists P24B2 for 2019 vehicles with the 2.0L engine (sales code EBS), and 18-026-23 for 2022 models, both fixed by reprogramming the PCM. Neither bulletin publishes a threshold. CARB requires the system to catch circuit continuity faults of the PM sensor. P24B0 and P24B1 are the steady low and high faults. Drivers mostly see only the warning lamp, but the filter monitor pauses while the signal is unreliable.
c: Loose or corroded pin in the sensor connector
Harness chafing on hot exhaust parts
Engine control software that needs reprogramming
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on, sometimes going out again
Particulate filter monitor does not complete

P24B3.t: Particulate Matter Sensor Heater Control Circuit/Open
P24B3.d: P24B3 means the heater inside the particulate matter sensor cannot draw the current it should while it is switched on, typically because the heater line is open. The heater is needed to burn soot off the electrodes. Ford's 2023 diesel summary checks continuously during sensor regeneration and sets the code when heater current stays below 0.2 A for about 2 s. GM's 18OBDG04 table watches for less than 0.5 A or more than 15 A while heating is requested (Type B); for the 2014 Touareg, VW judges the coil resistance. On 2019 L5P heavy-duty pickups, GM's PIP5607 warns that P24B3 or P24B5 could appear without any hardware fault. Ford's remedy in 18-2225 is a new sensor. P24B5 and P24B6 are the shorts.
c: Heater element burnt out inside the sensor
False detection in the control software
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete

P24B4.t: Particulate Matter Sensor Heater Control Circuit Range/Performance
P24B4.d: P24B4 is a plausibility check on the heater of the particulate matter sensor, and makers apply it differently. Ford's 2023 diesel summary looks during measurement, with the heater switched off, and sets the code if heater voltage still exceeds 7 V for 2 s. GM's 14OBDG04 table uses the heater to confirm that exhaust actually reaches the element inside its protection tube: if heater voltage varies by less than 100 % while exhaust velocity is above 30 m/s, the result is a Type B fault. GM's 16OBDG04 instead times how long the heater needs to reach the regeneration setpoint and lists P24B4 as Type X without MIL. A blocked protection tube, a weak heater or extra resistance in the harness can all set it. P24B3, P24B5 and P24B6 cover the pure circuit faults.
c: Protection tube of the sensor blocked by soot or deposits
Heater element aged and heating too slowly
Extra resistance in the heater harness
Heater output in the sensor control unit not switching off
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on (not with every manufacturer)
Particulate filter monitor does not complete

P24B5.t: Particulate Matter Sensor Heater Control Circuit Low
P24B5.d: P24B5 points to the heater line of the particulate matter sensor being pulled toward ground, so the heater control sees an implausible current while heating is requested. GM's 18OBDG04 table describes it as a ground fault on the heater line and flags it when current is under 0.5 A or above 15 A with the heater commanded on, 30 of 60 samples, Type B with two trips. VW's 2014 Touareg list uses a heater current below 1 A or above 15 A. GM issued PIP5607 for 2019 Silverado and Sierra 2500/3500 with the 6.6L L5P, telling technicians to clear P24B3 or P24B5 because engineering suspected false setting. While the heater cannot work, the sensor cannot clean itself and the filter monitor stops. P24B3 is the open circuit, P24B6 the short to power.
c: Internal heater fault in the sensor
False detection by the control software
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete

P24B6.t: Particulate Matter Sensor Heater Control Circuit High
P24B6.d: P24B6 reports the heater of the particulate matter sensor carrying current although it is commanded off, the classic sign of a battery-side short or a stuck driver stage in the sensor control unit. GM's 18OBDG04 table sets it when more than 0.2 A flows with the heater off or when the switch state disagrees with the command in one of the last five readings, Type B. GM's 14OBDG04 checks the heater voltage in the off state. VW's 2014 Touareg list names a current of 0.2 A or more. A heater that stays on can overheat and crack the ceramic element, so the sensor often has to be replaced together with the wiring repair. P24B5 covers a short to ground, P24B3 an open line, P24B4 implausible heater behaviour.
c: Heater line shorted to battery voltage
Heater output stage in the sensor control unit stuck on
Sensor element damaged by uncontrolled heating
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
Sensor may fail again quickly if the short is not fixed

P24B7.d: P24B7 concerns the resistance of the heater element in the particulate matter sensor, which drifts as the platinum track ages. Ford's 2023 diesel summary measures it once per drive right after key-on, with the sensor between -30 and 150 °C, and sets the code if resistance leaves 1.06 to 2.93 Ω at the cold end or 1.81 to 4.12 Ω at the warm end. GM's 14OBDG04 table runs a similar heater self-test after power-up and treats a calculated resistance above roughly 2.93 to 4.13 Ω as an aged heater, Type B. An out-of-range heater may still switch, but it cannot reliably reach the temperature for burning off soot. P24B3, P24B5 and P24B6 are circuit faults; P24D1 shows the effect when regeneration does not finish.
c: Wrong sensor temperature distorting the expected value
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Sensor regeneration may stay incomplete

P24B8.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Pressure Sensor Circuit
P24B8.d: P24B8 is the general circuit fault of the pressure sensor that sits inside an evaporative leak check module together with the pump and the switching valve. The sensor gets a 5 V reference from the engine computer and reports canister-side pressure during the engine-off leak test. No manufacturer documents P24B8 publicly; GM, Mitsubishi and Subaru use the more specific P24B9 to P24BB for this sensor. CARB requires such EVAP input components to be checked for circuit faults and implausible values. With this fault present, the leak test cannot be trusted and will not complete, so the EVAP readiness flag stays open. Typical findings are a broken reference or ground wire, a corroded module plug or a failed module.
c: Open or shorted 5 V reference, ground or signal wire to the leak check module
Corroded or loose connector at the leak check module near the canister
Pressure sensor inside the leak check module failed
Engine control module does not supply the sensor reference
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EVAP readiness monitor does not complete

P24B9.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P24B9.d: P24B9 means the leak check module's pressure sensor delivers a signal that is electrically valid but not believable. GM's 2018 Volt table (ELCP) compares the absolute sensor reading with barometric pressure from the MAP sensor while pump and valve rest; a gap above 3,000 Pa at the engine-off wake-ups (roughly 4 to 11 h after shutdown) or above 15,000 to 20,000 Pa while driving counts as a fail, 50 of 63 samples, Type B. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV instead counts signal noise during the key-off test and fails after more than 20 fluctuations. FCA fixed P24B9 with PCM software on the 2017 Pacifica and the 2025 Grand Cherokee 4xe (18-079-25). P24BA and P24BB are the hard voltage limits.
c: Pressure sensor in the leak check module drifted or noisy
Engine control software needing an update (FCA bulletins)
Moisture or dirt in the module's pressure port
Chafed wiring or loose pin causing signal disturbance
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EVAP leak test aborted, readiness not set
Usually no noticeable change in driving

P24BA.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Pressure Sensor Circuit Low
P24BA.d: P24BA reports that the voltage from the leak check module's pressure sensor has fallen below the lowest value a working sensor can produce. In GM's ELCP tables (2018 Volt) the limit is 0.70 V, about 14 % of the reference or roughly 47 kPa absolute, with 640 failures in 800 samples taken every 12.5 ms; the check runs whenever the controller is awake and is Type B. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV sets P24BA when the signal stays under 0.1 V for 2 s. Subaru asks technicians to clear P24BA before chasing P2404 in the ELCM. A low signal mostly means a lost 5 V reference, a signal wire shorted to ground or a dead sensor. P24BB is the high-side counterpart; the leak test is suspended until the fault is gone.
c: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
5 V reference open or pulled down by another sensor on the same supply
Pressure sensor inside the leak check module failed
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EVAP leak test not run

P24BB.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Pressure Sensor Circuit High
P24BB.d: P24BB is stored when the leak check module's pressure signal climbs above the top of its usable range. GM uses 4.85 V, about 97 % of the reference or roughly 120 kPa, again with 640 of 800 samples and Type B; the limit appears unchanged from the 2018 Volt up to GM's 2025 table 25OBDG03A for conventional ELCP systems. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV flags the code above 4.9 V lasting 2 s. Subaru lists P24BB with P24BA and P24B9 as faults to clear first when P2404 appears. A reading pinned high usually comes from an open ground, a signal wire touching a voltage source or an internal sensor fault, rarely from real pressure. P24BA covers the low side; P24B9 a signal that stays in range but disagrees with barometric pressure.
c: Open sensor ground or signal wire, letting the input float high
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Pressure sensor inside the leak check module failed
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EVAP leak test not run, readiness incomplete

P24BC.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent
P24BC.d: P24BC is meant for a pressure signal from the leak check module that drops out or jumps briefly, too short to latch the low or high limit. No manufacturer documents P24BC publicly. The closest published logic is Mitsubishi's noise check on the same sensor in the 2023 Outlander PHEV, which counts signal crossings during the engine-off test and fails above 20 events, but Mitsubishi reports that under P24B9. CARB expects EVAP sensors to be watched for circuit faults as well as erratic behaviour. Because the fault comes and goes, check the harness near the canister and fuel tank for chafing, water in the connector and loose terminals before replacing the module. Steady faults are P24BA (low) and P24BB (high).
c: Loose or spread terminal in the leak check module connector
Harness chafing near the canister or tank, intermittent short or break
Water or corrosion in the module connector
Sensor in the leak check module failing intermittently
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on, sometimes going out again
EVAP readiness monitor completes only occasionally

P24BD.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Switching Valve Control Circuit/Open
P24BD.d: P24BD points to the drive circuit of the switching valve inside the leak check module. This small solenoid moves the canister vent path between open air and the reference orifice, so the module can first measure a known leak and then test the real system. The code stands for an open or generally faulty control circuit. No manufacturer documents P24BD publicly; Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV splits the same valve into P24BE and P24BF, where the valve is fed from a relay and switched to ground by the engine computer. CARB requires output components like this to be checked for circuit faults. Without a working valve the leak test cannot run; in Mitsubishi's design purge is blocked and the fuel door stays locked.
c: Switching valve coil open inside the leak check module
Open control or supply wire, blown fuse or relay fault
Output driver in the engine control module faulty
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EVAP leak test does not run
On some designs fuel door locked or purge disabled

P24BE.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Switching Valve Control Circuit Low
P24BE.d: P24BE says the voltage on the switching valve control line is too low while the valve should be idle. Mitsubishi documents it for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: the valve sits in the ELCM leak check unit, is supplied by the MFI relay and grounded by a transistor in the engine computer, and the code sets when the line reads 3 V or less for 2 s with the valve not commanded. That pattern fits a missing relay supply, an open coil or a control wire shorted to ground. As a fail-safe the car stops purging, keeps the fuel filler door shut and shows a refuelling-system service message. P24BF is the over-current counterpart, P24BD the general circuit code; the related 0.020 inch leak test cannot finish meanwhile.
c: No supply from the relay to the valve (fuse, relay, wire)
Switching valve coil open inside the module
Control wire between module and ECM shorted to ground
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Fuel filler door does not open with the opener switch
Refuelling system service message on the display

P24BF.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Switching Valve Control Circuit High
P24BF.d: P24BF flags too much current in the switching valve circuit while the valve is energised. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV measures coil current through its low-side driver and sets the code when it reaches 2 A or more for 2 s with the valve commanded on. Such a value suggests a shorted coil or a control wire that touches battery voltage, so the driver is effectively feeding a dead short. The engine computer then blocks purge, keeps the fuel door locked and asks for a refuelling-system service. Check the wire between module and ECM for chafing before condemning the module, which carries pump, valve and sensor in one housing. The opposite electrical fault is P24BE; a valve that switches but does not seal is P24C0 or P24C1.
c: Switching valve coil shorted inside the module
Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Output driver in the engine control module faulty
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Fuel filler door stays locked
Canister purge switched off

P24C0.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Switching Valve Stuck On
P24C0.d: P24C0 is a mechanical fault found during the leak test itself: the switching valve stays in its energised position, or the pump around it does not do its job. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV checks this when the parked car wakes its controller 5 h, 6 h or 8.5 h after shutdown. While the reference pressure is being measured, the canister pressure must fall at a set rate; if it drops too slowly or the pump cannot pull it down, the code sets after 1 s below the limit. Mitsubishi groups a stuck valve with a pump stuck on or off and a frozen sensor, all inside the ELCM, and asks to clear P24BE or P24BF first. Mitsubishi then disables canister purging and locks the filler flap. A valve stuck in rest position is P24C1.
c: Switching valve mechanically stuck inside the leak check module
Leak detection pump stuck on or not running
Open or shorted pump circuit or connector damage
Module pressure sensor frozen at one value
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Fuel filler door does not open
Refuelling system service message

P24C1.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Switching Valve Performance/Stuck Off
P24C1.d: P24C1 means the switching valve does not respond when commanded, so the vent path stays where it was. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV recognises this after the reference measurement of the engine-off leak test: energising the valve should change the canister pressure, and if the difference to the first or second reference value stays below a limit for 10 s, the code is stored. Mitsubishi calls this valve stuck open and first rules out P24BE or P24BF, since a dead circuit looks the same from the pressure side. The fuel door locks and a refuelling-system message appears, but purge stays permitted. The fix is usually the complete leak check module. Stuck in the energised position is P24C0.
c: Switching valve stuck in rest position inside the module
Open or shorted valve circuit so the valve never moves
Dirt or water from the vent line jamming the valve seat
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Fuel filler door does not open
EVAP readiness not set

P24C2.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 1
P24C2.d: Diesel exhaust lines often carry three or four temperature probes in a row, ahead of the oxidation catalyst, the particulate filter and the SCR catalyst. P24C2 says that on bank 1 the readings of these probes no longer agree with each other, without pinning the error on one of them. Ford's 2023 diesel summary uses it in its EGT plausibility check: after a soak of at least six hours with the engine stopped, all probes should read alike at key-on (limit 50 °C), and during the following 200 to 400 s each probe is compared with a model (±80 °C), with a fault having to persist for 20 s. Ram lists the code in bulletin 18-028-14 for the 2014 Ram 1500 with the 3.0 L diesel, cured by new PCM software. Single-probe faults are P2080, P2084, P242B and P246F. Filter regeneration may be held back.
c: One exhaust temperature probe has drifted with age and reads too high or too low
Corroded or heat-damaged connector adding resistance to one probe signal
Engine control software with too tight correlation limits (update available on some models)
Probes swapped between mounting positions after a repair
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter regeneration suppressed or aborted
Often no noticeable change in driving behaviour

P24C3.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation Bank 2
P24C3.d: P24C3 is the bank 2 counterpart of P24C2 and only makes sense on engines whose two cylinder banks feed separate exhaust strings, each with its own set of temperature probes. The controller has found that the probes of the second string disagree among themselves beyond what the operating state allows. No manufacturer documents P24C3 publicly. Ford's 2023 diesel summary shows how such a group check works for bank 1: a key-on comparison after a long soak and a model comparison while driving, each probe weighed against the others. CARB requires that temperature sensors used for aftertreatment control be checked for rationality. The individual bank 2 probes have their own codes P2082, P2086, P2467 and P2474. A test with all probes cold after an overnight stop usually shows the outlier.
c: One bank 2 temperature probe has drifted and no longer matches the others
Contact resistance in a bank 2 probe connector or harness
Exhaust leak near one probe cooling its tip
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter regeneration may be inhibited

P24C4.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Exceeded Learning Limit Bank 1
P24C4.d: The bypass flap of the EGR cooler learns its end stops, and P24C4 means the learned values for bank 1 have left the window the software accepts. GM's diesel tables from 2017 on run the learning after key-off with coolant between 70 and 129 °C: the raw signal must lie between 16 and 24 % of 5 V in cooling position and between 72 and 85 % in bypass position; outside, the code is stored as Type B. GM's 2014 table 14OBDG10 instead judges the spread of the learned offsets (over 50 %) and a single offset beyond about ±16 %. Bulletin PI1449 for the 2015 Silverado and Sierra with the LML Duramax pairs it with P2493, P2495 and P06A3 and calls for a complete new bypass valve. Pure circuit faults are P2494/P2495; bank 2 reports P24C5.
c: Worn bypass valve whose integrated position sensor no longer reaches its learned values
Soot deposits shifting the end stops of the flap
Signal offset from connector corrosion or a weak 5 V reference
Learning repeatedly cut short because the controller is woken right after key-off
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after the second trip
Reduced EGR cooling, higher NOx output
Often no change in driveability

P24C5.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Exceeded Learning Limit Bank 2
P24C5.d: P24C5 belongs to engines with a second EGR cooler and bypass flap on bank 2. It reports that the end positions learned by that flap's position sensor fall outside the accepted window, so the controller can no longer trust where the flap really stands. No manufacturer documents P24C5 publicly; GM's diesel engines in the available tables use one bypass valve and only show the bank 1 code P24C4. There the learning runs after key-off with a warm engine and checks the raw voltage at both end stops against fixed bands, which gives a good picture of what the bank 2 test checks. CARB requires position feedback of emission-related actuators to be monitored for rationality. Electrical faults of the same sensor are P2497 to P249B; the bank 1 learning fault is P24C4.
c: Worn bank 2 bypass valve or sensor track
Deposits changing the end positions of the bank 2 flap
Signal shift caused by wiring or connector resistance
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Higher NOx emissions due to poorly controlled EGR cooling

P24C6.d: Inside the particulate matter sensor a meander-shaped platinum track measures element temperature, which the sensor needs to control its heater. P24C6 is the general circuit fault of that temperature signal. Ford's 2023 diesel summary flags a signal below 0.3 V or above 3 V for 2 s; VW's 2014 Touareg list and GM's 14OBDG04 table use the same band (GM Type B). On the 2018–2019 CX-5 SKYACTIV-D 2.2, Mazda (bulletin 01-005-22) links it to condensate cracking the element, sets it after one drive cycle and supplies a revised sensor. Ford fits a new sensor under 18-2225 (Super Duty 6.7L, 2017–2018), and GM special coverage 16018 covers 2014–2015 Cruze diesels. P24C8 and P24C9 split the fault into low and high.
c: Open or shorted temperature line in the harness
Fault in the sensor control unit
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete

P24C7.t: Particulate Matter Sensor Temperature Circuit Range/Performance
P24C7.d: P24C7 checks whether the temperature the particulate matter sensor reports fits the exhaust around it. Ford's 2023 diesel summary does an offset test after a cold soak of at least 6 hours, flagging more than 45 °C against the mean of the exhaust temperature sensors, and a dynamic test while driving that fails below -150 or above 60 °C against a model. VW's 2014 Touareg list uses 60 K and -100 K. GM's 18OBDG04 table sets it at more than 100 °C deviation in 200 of 250 samples (Type B) and names a damaged sensor or extra harness resistance as causes. Mazda treats it as a two-cycle code on the CX-5 SKYACTIV-D 2.2 (01-005-22); Ford 18-2225 and GM coverage 16018 replace the sensor. P24C6 is the electrical fault.
c: Sensor element damaged or temperature track drifted
Extra resistance between sensor and sensor control unit
Faulty exhaust temperature sensor used as reference
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete

P24C8.t: Particulate Matter Sensor Temperature Circuit Low
P24C8.d: P24C8 would be set when the temperature signal of the particulate matter sensor sits below its valid range, for example because the meander line is shorted to ground. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the available summaries fold low and high readings into other codes. Ford's 2023 diesel summary reports any reading under 0.3 V as P24C6, and GM's 25OBDG04A table includes values under 0.3 V in its P24C9 check. CARB requires PM sensor circuits to be checked for out-of-range values, so a low-side code is the logical place for such a fault. Expect a damaged sensor pigtail, a pinched harness or water in the connector. Without a temperature value the heater cannot be regulated and the filter monitor stays inactive. P24C9 is the high counterpart.
c: Internal fault of the sensor element
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete

P24C9.t: Particulate Matter Sensor Temperature Circuit High
P24C9.d: P24C9 reports the PM sensor temperature reading stuck at the high end, which GM explains as a short toward supply voltage or a broken meander line. In GM's 25OBDG04A diesel table the sensor control unit checks the meander signal and its reference: a signal under 0.3 V or over 3.5 V, or a reference under 4.5 V, counts as a failure, and 24 failures in a row or 24 of 96 samples set a Type B code with two trips. Other makers reviewed here, such as Ford in its 2023 diesel summary, report out-of-range temperature signals under P24C6 instead. A broken pigtail lead near the hot sensor body is a common cause. While the temperature is invalid the heater control and the filter monitor are suspended. P24C8 is the low side, P24C7 the plausibility test.
c: Broken temperature lead near the sensor body
Temperature line shorted to a voltage source
Reference voltage of the temperature circuit too low
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete

P24CA.t: Particulate Matter Sensor Temperature Circuit Intermittent
P24CA.d: P24CA is reserved for a PM sensor temperature reading that fails only now and then instead of staying out of range. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. For comparison, Ford's 2023 diesel summary treats any temperature signal outside 0.3 to 3 V for 2 s as P24C6, and GM's 25OBDG04A table uses a counter of 24 failures within 96 samples for P24C9, so short glitches can stay below those limits. CARB requires circuit faults of PM sensors to be detected. Intermittent faults of this kind usually come from a cracked solder joint, a connector that loosens with heat or a lead that chafes on the exhaust. The warning lamp may come and go, and while the reading is doubtful the soot filter check is put on hold. P24C6, P24C8 and P24C9 are the steady faults.
c: Cracked joint inside the sensor lead
s: Malfunction indicator lamp coming and going
Particulate filter monitor does not complete

P24CB.d: Some SCR diesels have a switch at the DEF filler neck that tells the engine controller when the cap is opened, so a refill can be recognised and the tank level and fluid quality reassessed. P24CB is the general circuit code for this switch: the controller sees a signal that fits neither the open nor the closed state. Audi documents it together with P24CC for the 2013 to 2015 Q7 TDI in bulletin 2051053: the microswitch at the AdBlue filler neck of the active tank tends to stick, above all in hot and humid weather, and then sets the codes after refilling while guided fault finding shows nothing. The fix is an improved switch, for which the tank has to come out. Short to ground or supply and intermittent faults have their own codes P24CD to P24CF.
c: Cap microswitch sticking, especially in hot and humid conditions
Corroded connector or chafed wire at the filler neck
Dried DEF crystals around the switch actuator
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on, often right after refilling DEF
Refill not recognised, DEF warnings may persist

P24CC.t: Reductant Tank Cap Switch Circuit Range/Performance
P24CC.d: P24CC is a plausibility fault: the cap switch at the DEF filler neck delivers an electrically valid signal, but its behaviour does not match what else the controller knows, for instance a switch that still reports an open cap long after refilling, or one that never changes state while the tank level clearly rose. Audi names the code in bulletin 2051053 (and its revision) for the 2013 to 2015 Q7 TDI, where the AdBlue cap switch on the active tank sticks in hot, humid climates; the bulletin lists it as P24CC00 next to P24CB00 and replaces the switch with an improved part after removing the tank. Because wiring checks pass, the stuck switch itself is the prime suspect. P24CB covers general circuit faults, P24CD and P24CE the electrical extremes.
c: Switch stuck in one position so it no longer follows the cap
DEF residue hindering the switch plunger
Damaged or non-original filler cap that does not actuate the switch
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after a DEF refill
Fill level or refill message not updated

P24CD.t: Reductant Tank Cap Switch Circuit Low
P24CD.d: P24CD means the signal line of the DEF cap switch sits below its valid voltage band. With the usual pull-up input that points to the line being pulled to ground: a short in the harness near the filler neck, a switch with an internal short, or moisture bridging the contacts. Whether the controller then reads the cap as permanently open or closed depends on how the switch is wired. No manufacturer documents P24CD publicly. The same switch appears in Audi's bulletin 2051053 for the Q7 TDI with the general and range codes P24CB and P24CC, which shows where it sits and that it can only be replaced with the tank out. CARB requires input circuits of emission-related components to be monitored for readings outside their valid band. The opposite case is P24CE; sporadic drops are P24CF.
c: Signal wire chafed through to ground near the filler neck
Moisture or DEF in the switch or connector bridging to ground
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Cap state shown permanently wrong, refills not detected

P24CE.t: Reductant Tank Cap Switch Circuit High
P24CE.d: With P24CE the controller sees the DEF cap switch signal above its permitted band. On a pull-up input this typically happens when the line is open, because the input then floats up to the reference, or when it touches a supply wire; a broken switch contact can look the same. Unlike P24CD, a simple unplugged connector after tank work is a frequent trigger here. No manufacturer documents P24CE publicly. The switch itself is known from Audi's bulletin 2051053 for the 2013 to 2015 Q7 TDI, which deals with the related codes P24CB and P24CC and places the switch on the filler neck of the active tank. CARB's comprehensive component rules call for detecting such out-of-range inputs. Checking the plug and measuring the line with the switch operated settles it.
c: Disconnected plug or broken wire letting the input float high
Signal wire touching a supply line
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Refill of DEF not registered

P24CF.t: Reductant Tank Cap Switch Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P24CF.d: P24CF is stored when the DEF cap switch signal jumps between states or drops out briefly although nobody touches the cap, typically while driving over rough roads. The controller counts unexpected changes and flags the circuit as unstable even if every single value lies within limits. Loose terminals, a cracked solder joint in the switch or a harness rubbing on the tank are the usual reasons. No manufacturer documents P24CF publicly. On the 2013–2015 Q7 TDI, Audi bulletin 2051053 found that the cap switch at the active tank sticks and sets P24CB/P24CC; a switch that sticks only partly can also produce erratic signals. CARB requires inputs to be checked for erratic behaviour. Wiggling the harness while watching live data usually reproduces the fault.
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the switch connector
Switch that sticks only partly and chatters
Harness rubbing on the tank or body
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, sometimes coming and going
Spurious refill or cap-open messages

P24D0.t: Particulate Matter Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit Low
P24D0.d: P24D0 concerns the power feed of the particulate matter sensor and its control unit, which sinks when the supply line has excess resistance or a short toward ground. Ford's 2023 diesel summary compares battery voltage with the voltage at the sensor while the heater runs at 35 % duty or more, and sets the code if the drop exceeds 1.1 V, 2.1 V or 3 V depending on battery level, within 2 s. VW's 2014 Touareg list uses comparable steps. GM's 18OBDG04 table flags supply under 9 V (Type B) and blocks its other PM sensor tests while P24D0 is active. It is also one of the codes in FCA's PCM bulletin 18-008-23 (Compass diesel, 2019). Check fuse, relay and ground first; P24D0 often comes with other PM sensor codes.
c: Corroded fuse, relay contact or ground adding resistance
Fault in the sensor control unit
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete
Further particulate sensor codes stored at the same time

P24D1.d: Before each measurement the particulate matter sensor heats its element to burn off collected soot. P24D1 means that this cleaning phase did not finish properly. Ford's 2023 diesel summary flags the code when the sensor cannot return to measuring after regeneration, judged over 120 s. GM's 18OBDG04 table fails it when the electrode stays at or below 775 °C for 43 s during steady regeneration (25OBDG04A: 715 °C), Type B, and calls it heater degradation. Ford special service message 49846 replaces the sensor on 2017–2019 Super Duty and F-650/750 6.7L trucks, and FCA lists P24D1 for 2019 Jeep Compass diesels in bulletin 18-008-23 (PCM update). P24B7 points to a heater resistance fault, P24AF to an implausible electrode during cleaning.
c: Sensor heater degraded, not reaching cleaning temperature
Heavy deposits on the sensor element
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete

P24D2.d: Besides the control output, many DEF heaters have a sense line on which the controller reads back the voltage actually reaching the element. P24D2 marks a general fault on this sense circuit for heater A, such as an open lead or a reading that makes no sense at all, as opposed to the voltage being merely too low (P248A) or too high (P248B). GM and Ford call heater A the tank heater. No manufacturer documents P24D2 publicly. GM's 2016 to 2018 diesel tables show the related sense test: system voltage minus heater supply must not exceed 3 V while heating is commanded, judged over 10 of 12 samples at 500 ms. CARB requires SCR heaters and their circuits to be monitored. If the sense signal is lost, the controller cannot confirm thawing, so dosing in frost may stay off.
c: Broken or disconnected sense wire to heater A
DEF creep or water corroding the heater connector
Faulty measuring input in the SCR or engine control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DEF warnings in cold weather, dosing delayed after a cold start

P24D3.d: P24D3 is the same kind of fault for heater B, which GM and Ford assign to the heated DEF line from pump to dosing valve. The read-back line of this heater is broken or delivers nonsense, so the controller cannot tell whether the hose is really powered; the narrower low and high cases are P248C and P248D. No manufacturer documents P24D3 in this sense. FCA uses the number differently: bulletin 18-008-23 for 2019 Jeep Compass diesels outside North America lists P24D3-00 as a particulate matter sensor supply voltage above threshold, fixed with new PCM software. GM's diesel tables from 2016 to 2018 describe a line heater sense check with a 3 V limit. A line that does not thaw blocks dosing in winter, so the fault deserves attention before frost.
c: Open sense wire or loose plug at the heated DEF line
Damaged heated line with internal conductor fault
Manufacturer-specific use of the code (FCA uses it for PM sensor supply), software update
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DEF dosing faults or warnings at low temperatures

P24D4.t: EGR Cooler Coolant Pump Feedback Circuit
P24D4.d: Where an electric auxiliary pump moves coolant through the EGR cooler, the pump usually reports back to the engine controller on a separate wire, for example with a speed or status signal. P24D4 is the general fault of that feedback circuit: the signal is missing or cannot be interpreted, while the narrower cases of a line stuck below or above its band are P24AC and P24AD. The drive side may be fine; faults in the control line are P24A7 to P24AA. No manufacturer documents P24D4 publicly. CARB requires the controller to check inputs from emission-related components for circuit faults and rationality. Pierburg describes EGR coolers as part of the coolant circuit. Without valid feedback the controller cannot prove the cooler is supplied and may cut back EGR to protect it.
c: Open feedback wire or loose connector at the pump
Failed pump electronics no longer sending a status signal
Blown fuse or failed relay leaving the pump without power
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EGR reduced, possibly higher NOx and changed engine noise
Coolant temperature warnings if the pump really stops

P24D5.t: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch B Circuit
P24D5.d: P24D5 is the general circuit code for a second EVAP pressure sensor, called B to tell it apart from the main sensor A (P0450 range). Which sensor is B depends on the maker: Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV uses it for an absolute fuel tank pressure sensor on its sealed tank, GM for a canister vapour pressure sensor, and Audi's bulletin 2069531 assigns sensor 2 to the G950 part in the purge path. No manufacturer documents P24D5 itself publicly; all three use the more specific P24D6 to P24D8. CARB requires circuit checks on every EVAP input. A stored P24D5 suggests a fault in the 5 V reference, ground or signal wire of that sensor; until it is fixed the leak or purge diagnostics depending on it are blocked.
c: Open or shorted reference, ground or signal wire of sensor B
Loose or corroded connector at sensor B
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EVAP readiness monitor incomplete

P24D6.t: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch B Circuit Range/Performance
P24D6.d: P24D6 is a plausibility fault of EVAP pressure sensor B. GM's 2023 table 23OBDG03A checks the canister vapour pressure sensor at the start of a cold drive: after more than 3,600 s soak the offset must sit within a window around barometric pressure; a filtered ratio above 0.73 sets the code, Type A. GM bulletins 24-NA-162 and 24-NA-258 trace P24D6 on 2024–2025 Silverado and Sierra HD 6.6L trucks to a narrow-range sensor fitted at the plant (about 1.5 V instead of 2.625 V at rest). Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV compares tank, differential and canister pressures for 180 s during the engine-off test. Audi lists it for V6/V8 sensor G950, FCA for 2017–2018 Giulia software. P24D7/P24D8 are hard voltage limits.
c: Wrong sensor version installed (GM HD trucks, narrow-range instead of wide-range)
Sensor offset drifted away from barometric pressure
Kinked hose or blocked port at the sensor
Engine control software needing an update (FCA, Audi)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Other EVAP codes such as a switching valve fault may appear alongside
No driveability change

P24D7.t: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch B Circuit Low
P24D7.d: P24D7 is set when EVAP pressure sensor B sends a voltage below its valid window. GM's 2023 table (23OBDG03A) watches its canister pressure sensor continuously and fails below 0.15 V, 3 % of the reference, with 640 of 800 samples, Type B; the sensor normally works between 0.5 and 4.5 V. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV uses a far higher floor for its absolute tank pressure sensor: under 1.0 V for 2 s. Audi's bulletin 2069531 shows P24D7 as pressure sensor 2 shorted to ground on 2022–2023 four-cylinder models and steers the test to sensor G950. Expect a signal wire grounded, a missing 5 V reference or a failed sensor. P24D8 is the high side, P24D6 a reading that is in range but wrong.
c: Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EVAP tests suspended

P24D8.t: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch B Circuit High
P24D8.d: P24D8 reports EVAP pressure sensor B reading above its valid voltage. In GM's 2023 table 23OBDG03A the canister pressure sensor fails above 4.85 V, 97 % of the reference, counted over 640 of 800 samples and treated as Type B. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV applies 4.1 V for 2 s to its absolute tank pressure sensor, which shows about 101 kPa at sea level when healthy. Audi's bulletin 2069531 lists P24D8 as pressure sensor 2 shorted to positive and also shows it among codes logged under a wrong label, to be tested as sensor G950. Common findings are an open sensor ground, a signal wire touching the 5 V or 12 V supply, or an internal failure. Compare P24D7 for the low side.
c: Open ground of sensor B, signal floats high
Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
EVAP readiness monitor incomplete

P24D9.t: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch B Circuit Intermittent
P24D9.d: P24D9 covers a sensor B signal that keeps flickering instead of failing outright. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV runs this check once per drive cycle inside the parked leak test, when the controller wakes at its scheduled times and coolant and intake air lie between 4 and 35 °C. It counts how often the tank pressure signal crosses the sensor's own filter value and stores the code after more than 20 crossings; the display then asks for a refuelling-system service. The service hints name the tank pressure sensor, the tank differential pressure sensor and their wiring. Shaking the harness while watching live data often reveals the spot. Steady low or high voltages fall under P24D7 or P24D8, implausible but stable readings under P24D6.
c: Loose terminal or poor contact at the tank pressure sensor
Harness chafed along the fuel tank
Tank pressure or tank differential pressure sensor unstable
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Refuelling system service message on the display

P24DA.t: Particulate Matter Sensor Exhaust Sample Error Bank 1
P24DA.d: P24DA checks that the particulate matter sensor actually samples exhaust gas, which is how the system detects a sensor that has been pulled out, sits in a blocked protection tube or is mounted wrongly. Ford's 2023 diesel summary runs it once per drive in protective heating mode and fails it if the summed sensor voltage change during exhaust flow changes stays under 0.5 V, over about 3 minutes. GM's 25OBDG04A table watches filtered heater power, sets the code below 1.66 and rates it Type A, so the lamp comes on after one trip. Bulletin 18-2225 lists P24DA among the codes cured by a new sensor on 2017–2018 Super Duty diesels. Because a sensor outside the exhaust would hide a failed filter, the code counts as emissions-relevant; P2002 reports the filter itself.
c: Sensor removed from the exhaust or installed wrongly
Sensor no longer responding to exhaust flow
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Particulate filter monitor does not complete

P24DB.t: Reductant Purge Control Valve B Circuit/Open
P24DB.d: After shut-down an SCR system empties its lines back into the tank so no fluid freezes in them; in Bosch's Denoxtronic 2.2 a 4/2-way valve in the supply module reverses the flow for this. Valve B is a second purge valve, for instance in layouts with two dosing branches. P24DB reports a drive circuit fault of valve B, mostly an interruption. No manufacturer documents P24DB publicly. GM documents the method only for valve A (P20A0) on its 6.6 L diesel: with the low-side driver off, an impedance above 200 kΩ between ECM pin and load for 3 s counts as open, Type A. CARB's heavy-duty rules require all electrical SCR components to be monitored. Shorts are split off as P24DD and P24DE. A line that is not emptied risks frost damage.
c: Broken wire or unplugged connector to purge valve B
Open solenoid winding in valve B
DEF-induced corrosion in the supply module connector
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DEF line not purged after shut-off, freezing risk in winter

P24DC.t: Reductant Purge Control Valve B Performance
P24DC.d: P24DC judges purge valve B by its effect, not by its wiring: once the controller switches the valve to purge, the pressure in the DEF line it serves should fall noticeably, and here it did not. No manufacturer documents P24DC publicly. On the 6.6 L Duramax, GM tests valve A under P20A1: if, when the pressure reduction phase ends, the pump pressure is less than 50 kPa below its starting value, the fault is set, Type A, sampled every 100 ms. Pico's description of the Denoxtronic 2.2 explains why: in purge mode the reversing valve makes the pump pull fluid out of the line, so a vacuum should build. A valve that does not shift, a blocked return or a misreading pressure sensor all end here. Electrical faults of valve B are P24DB, P24DD and P24DE.
c: Valve B mechanically stuck by crystallised DEF
Blocked return path or filter in the supply module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Frozen DEF line or dosing fault after cold nights

P24DD.t: Reductant Purge Control Valve B Circuit Low
P24DD.d: P24DD means the control line of purge valve B shows too little voltage at a moment when it should be high. With the low-side switching that GM uses for valve A, this is checked while the driver is off: the line should then carry battery voltage through the coil, and a low reading indicates a short to ground between valve and controller, so the valve may sit energised permanently. No manufacturer documents P24DD publicly; The valve A counterpart, P20A2, appears in GM's diesel tables for the 6.6 L engine. CARB's heavy-duty rules require detection of such circuit faults on SCR actuators. Typical spots are chafed wires near the tank and a coil that shorts to its housing. The opposite case is P24DE, an interruption P24DB.
c: Control wire chafed to ground near tank or frame
Valve coil shorted to its housing
Water or DEF in the connector
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Valve may remain in purge position, dosing pressure not reached

P24DE.t: Reductant Purge Control Valve B Circuit High
P24DE.d: With P24DE the control line of purge valve B stays at high voltage while the controller is actually pulling it to ground to switch the valve. That points to a short to the battery feed on the wire between valve and controller, or a valve coil with too little resistance, so that the driver protects itself and the valve never shifts. No manufacturer documents P24DE publicly. For valve A, GM runs the equivalent P20A3 check while the driver is switched on (6.6 L Duramax). CARB requires heavy-duty SCR actuators to be checked for this kind of circuit fault. The consequence is the reverse of P24DD: the valve stays in dosing position, so the line is not emptied at shut-down and can freeze. Interruptions are P24DB, the functional test P24DC.
c: Control wire touching a supply line
Valve coil with shorted turns and too low resistance
Damaged driver stage in the control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DEF line not purged, frozen line after frost

P24DF.t: Reductant Purge Control Valve B Stuck Open
P24DF.d: Stuck open means purge valve B remains in, or leaks toward, its emptying position while the system should be dosing. Part of the pump flow then goes back to the tank, so working pressure builds slowly, drops quickly when the pump stops, or needs a high pump duty to hold. No manufacturer documents P24DF publicly, and the public GM tables cover only the opposite failure of valve A (no pressure drop in purge, P20A1). The Denoxtronic 2.2 layout described by Pico explains the mechanism: one 4/2-way valve decides whether the pump feeds the injector or sucks the line empty, so a valve hanging halfway shortcuts the pressure side. CARB requires SCR delivery faults to be detected before emissions rise. P24E0 is the opposite fault; P24DC the general function test.
c: Internal leak or worn seat in purge valve B
DEF crystals preventing the valve from returning to dosing position
Control circuit fault keeping the valve energised
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
DEF pressure too low, reduced dosing and rising NOx
Warnings about reduced SCR function, possibly later engine power limits

P24E0.t: Reductant Purge Control Valve B Stuck Closed
P24E0.d: Stuck closed means purge valve B does not move into its emptying position when commanded after shut-down, so the line it serves stays filled with fluid under residual pressure. In normal dosing this goes unnoticed; the risk appears in frost, when the trapped DEF freezes in hose, pump or injector and can crack them. No manufacturer documents P24E0 publicly. How a blocked valve A is detected on GM's Duramax diesel: the pressure drop during the purge phase is measured, and less than 50 kPa sets P20A1, Type A. Pico's Denoxtronic 2.2 description shows that the purge relies on the reversing valve and the closed injector to create vacuum. CARB demands monitoring of SCR components. P24DF is the reverse failure.
c: Valve B seized by crystallised DEF or corrosion
Weak coil that no longer pulls the valve over
Intermittent open in the control circuit during shut-down
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Frozen or burst DEF line or injector after frost

P24E1.d: An NH3 sensor behind the SCR catalyst measures ammonia that slipped through unused, letting the controller trim dosing and detect overdosing or an aged catalyst. P24E1 is the general circuit code for this sensor: its signal is missing, implausible or erratic. Deutz lists P24E1 for its MD1 engine controller with SPN 4377 and FMI 2, i.e. unstable or wrong data. For the 2014 Ram 3500 to 5500 chassis cab with the 6.7 L Cummins, bulletin 18-042-20 offers two calibrations: one for trucks still equipped with the sensor, the other for trucks from which it has been taken off. CARB's heavy-duty rules require SCR sensors to be checked for circuit faults and rationality. Range, low, high and intermittent faults are P24E2 to P24E5; a lost CAN link to the sensor is U02A4.
c: NH3 sensor element or its electronics failed from heat and age
Heat-damaged wiring or connector near the exhaust
Software calibration issue, update available on some engines
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Less precise DEF dosing, possible ammonia smell or higher NOx

P24E2.d: P24E2 flags an NH3 sensor whose signal is electrically valid but makes no sense: the ammonia value sticks, drifts or contradicts what the dosing model expects from the SCR catalyst. On heavy trucks the sensor is a smart unit with its own electronics that test probe and circuitry and report over J1939. Navistar lets this self-test run on the 2013 N13 only after the middle of the SCR brick has stayed above 170 °C for five seconds, and lights the MIL after two failed trips. No manufacturer publishes P24E2 with thresholds. CARB's heavy-duty rule obliges makers to check such sensors for rationality. Wiring faults are P24E3/P24E4, dropouts P24E5. The driver sees a warning lamp; DEF dosing becomes less precise.
c: Sensing element aged or poisoned by deposits, giving a drifting ammonia value
Urea crystals around the sensor tip after overdosing
Exhaust leak near the sensor diluting the sample
s: Check engine light after two trips
DEF consumption noticeably higher or lower than usual
Possible ammonia smell at the tailpipe

P24E3.d: P24E3 means the NH3 sensor signal lies below the lowest value an intact sensor can deliver. Usual culprits are a short to ground between probe and its electronics module, a terminal pushed back in the connector or a defect inside the probe. On International trucks with the 2013 N13 engine, a matching condition is reported as SPN 5848 with failure mode 4, i.e. the signal voltage of the mid-bed ammonia sensor too low or grounded. No manufacturer publishes P24E3 itself. CARB requires out-of-range checks for emission sensors on heavy-duty engines. While the fault is present the controller cannot trust ammonia feedback and has to dose from its model. P24E4 is the high counterpart, P24E2 the plausibility fault.
c: Chafed harness between probe and sensor module shorting to ground
Internal fault in the ammonia probe
Corroded or pushed-back terminal at the probe connector
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Scan tool shows ammonia reading stuck at minimum

P24E4.d: P24E4 is set when the NH3 sensor signal climbs above anything a working sensor could report, so the value is rejected as electrically impossible rather than merely implausible. Typical reasons are a short to a supply voltage, a broken line pulled up internally, or failing electronics that output a saturated value. In Navistar's layout the ammonia measurement comes from a probe at mid-bed of the SCR catalyst plus a separate control module, so a reading at the upper stop usually points to the link between the two or to that module. No manufacturer publishes thresholds for P24E4. CARB's heavy-duty OBD rule calls for range checks on such sensors. P24E3 is the low fault; the general circuit code is P24E1.
c: Signal line shorted to a supply voltage in the harness
Open line between probe and module read as maximum value
Sensor electronics module outputting a saturated value
s: Check engine light on
Ammonia reading pinned at the upper limit
Possible reduced DEF dosing

P24E5.d: P24E5 covers an NH3 sensor signal that jumps or drops out for short moments while staying mostly in range. Vibration, heat cycling of the exhaust and road salt make loose connector pins and cracked insulation near the SCR can the main suspects. Ram fitted such a sensor to the 2014 3500 to 5500 cab chassis with the 6.7 L Cummins; bulletin 18-042-20 offers one engine calibration for trucks that keep it and another for trucks where it was removed, and warns that implausible-data or lost-communication codes appear when the wrong one is loaded. No manufacturer documents P24E5 publicly. CARB asks for erratic-signal detection on heavy-duty emission sensors. Steady faults are P24E3 and P24E4.
c: Loose or corroded pins at the sensor or module connector
Harness insulation cracked by exhaust heat and vibration
Sporadic internal fault in the sensor electronics
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Live data shows spikes in the ammonia value

P24E6.d: Like a NOx sensor, the ammonia sensor only measures once its ceramic element is hot, so it carries an electric heater. P24E6 reports that this heater circuit is open or otherwise electrically faulty: the driver commands heating but sees no current flowing. Common reasons are a burnt heater element, a broken wire in the pigtail or a terminal that lost contact. Without heat the probe stays cold and delivers no usable ammonia value, so dosing runs on the model alone. No manufacturer documents P24E6 publicly. CARB's heavy-duty rule requires a malfunction when heater current or voltage drop leaves the specified window. Low and high faults are P24E7 and P24E8; slow or unstable heating is P24E9.
c: Heater element inside the NH3 probe burnt through
Broken wire in the sensor pigtail near the hot exhaust
Heater terminal without contact in the connector
s: Check engine light on
No ammonia reading after warm-up

P24E7.d: P24E7 points to a heater circuit of the NH3 sensor that reads too low: the feedback voltage stays near ground, or the current is far below what the heater should draw. Most often the heater feed is shorted to ground, which can also blow the fuse or switch off the driver to protect it; a heater whose resistance has risen sharply gives a similar picture. The probe then heats slowly or not at all, and the ammonia value stays unavailable. No manufacturer publishes P24E7 with thresholds. CARB's heavy-duty OBD rule demands that heater current or voltage drop outside the maker's limits be flagged. The open-circuit fault is P24E6, the high fault P24E8 and heating performance P24E9.
c: Heater supply line shorted to ground
Heater element with strongly increased resistance
Blown fuse in the heater supply
s: Check engine light on
Ammonia value missing or delayed after start

P24E8.d: With P24E8 the heater circuit of the NH3 sensor reads too high. Either the line is shorted to a supply voltage so that the heater cannot be switched off, or the driver measures overcurrent because the element has failed with low resistance. A heater stuck on can overheat and crack the ceramic, so the controller normally shuts it down and stops evaluating ammonia until the fault clears. No manufacturer documents P24E8 publicly. CARB's heavy-duty regulation treats heater current or voltage drop outside the specified limits as a malfunction. Navistar's N13 shows that faults of this heater are reported by the smart sensor itself. P24E7 is the low counterpart, P24E6 the open circuit.
c: Heater control line shorted to battery voltage
Heater element failed with low resistance, causing overcurrent
Heater driver in the sensor module defective
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Ammonia sensor reading switched off

P24E9.d: P24E9 is not about a broken wire but about how the heater works: the circuit is intact, yet the NH3 probe does not reach or hold its operating temperature in the expected time, or its temperature control swings. Deutz lists P24E9 for its MD1 engine controller as SPN 4382 with FMI 2, meaning erratic or incorrect heater data. Navistar handles the similar case on the 2013 N13 as SPN 5848 FMI 10, an abnormal rate of change, where the probe or its module are the named suspects. Aged heater elements, cold exhaust from long idling and moisture on the ceramic play a role. CARB's heavy-duty rule requires heater performance checks. Electrical heater faults are P24E6 to P24E8.
c: Aged heater element no longer delivering full power
Condensate on the ceramic cooling it or causing thermal shock
Low supply voltage limiting heater power
s: Check engine light, often together with an NH3 sensor performance code
Ammonia reading available late or unstable

P24EA.d: The NH3 sensor is a smart unit: its electronics module needs its own power feed, usually switched battery voltage through a fuse or relay, to run the probe, the heater and the J1939 link. P24EA is the general fault of that supply, set when the measured feed voltage is missing, unstable or otherwise outside the valid window without being classed as clearly low or high. Navistar describes this type of module on the 2013 N13 as one that runs its own internal checks and reports them over the data link, which only works with clean power. No manufacturer publishes P24EA. CARB expects heavy-duty OBD to catch circuit faults on such components. P24EB and P24EC are the low and high cases.
c: Fuse or relay in the sensor feed faulty or loose
Damaged or corroded power or ground wire to the sensor module
Supply monitoring in the sensor module defective
s: Check engine light on
Further NH3 sensor or communication codes stored

P24EB.t: NH3 Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit Low
P24EB.d: P24EB reports that the power feed of the NH3 sensor module sags below its lower limit. Below that point the heater cannot bring the probe up to temperature and the electronics may reset, so ammonia readings and sensor messages become unreliable. Typical causes are a weak or discharged battery during cranking or long idle, a high-resistance ground strap, corroded fuse contacts or voltage drop along a long chassis harness. No manufacturer documents P24EB publicly; Navistar's N13 material shows the ammonia sensor as a separately powered probe-and-module unit. For heavy-duty engines, CARB wants such circuits checked for undervoltage. P24EA is the general supply fault, P24EC the high one.
c: Weak or discharged batteries pulling system voltage down
High resistance in the ground path of the sensor module
Corroded fuse or relay contacts causing voltage drop
s: Warning lamp, often after cold starts
NH3 sensor drops off the data link at times

P24EC.t: NH3 Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit High
P24EC.d: P24EC is stored when the feed voltage measured at the NH3 sensor module exceeds its upper limit. Overvoltage can damage the heater driver and the electronics, so the module may switch off heating and measurement to protect itself. Likely triggers are a charging system that regulates too high, jump-starting with a higher-voltage source, or a short from a higher feed onto the sensor supply line. No manufacturer publishes P24EC; for the component itself, Navistar's N13 bulletin describes the sensor as a probe paired with its own electronics module on the J1939 link. CARB's heavy-duty rule requires out-of-range detection on such circuits. Check the charging voltage first. P24EB is the low fault, P24EA the general one.
c: Overvoltage from jump-starting or a booster charger
Sensor supply line shorted to another higher feed
s: Check engine light on
Other modules may also report high system voltage

P24ED.d: Every NH3 sensor leaves the factory with individual correction values for offset and gain stored in its own electronics. P24ED means this memory fails its integrity check, for instance a checksum mismatch or unreadable data, so the module cannot convert the raw probe signal into a trustworthy ammonia value. The fix is normally a new sensor; wiring rarely plays a part. It differs from the engine software choice in Ram bulletin 18-042-20, where 2014 Ram 3500 to 5500 cab chassis trucks receive one controller calibration with the ammonia sensor and another without it. No manufacturer documents P24ED publicly. CARB demands that heavy-duty sensors be checked for faults. P24EE covers the sensor processor.
c: Calibration data in the sensor module corrupted
Power loss while the module was writing data
s: Check engine light on
No valid ammonia value although wiring tests pass

P24EE.d: P24EE says the microcontroller inside the NH3 sensor module has failed its own self-test, for example a watchdog reset, a RAM or ROM error or a timing fault. The engine controller only learns this through the status the sensor sends, because the processor is what runs the probe, the heater and the J1939 messages. Navistar explains for the 2013 N13 that its mid-bed ammonia sensor diagnoses itself and that probe and module are separate parts, ordered individually; a processor fault therefore normally means replacing the module. Repeated resets can also come from an unstable supply, so check that first. No manufacturer documents P24EE publicly. CARB requires fault detection on heavy-duty sensors. P24ED is the memory fault.
c: Electronics of the NH3 sensor module failed
Unstable supply voltage causing processor resets
Module damaged by heat or water ingress
s: Check engine light on
NH3 sensor data missing or frozen

P24EF.d: Some control modules drive a discrete wake-up output that switches other units on before or alongside the network. P24EF reports an open circuit on that line. GM uses it in the HPC2 battery-side processor of its 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables: with the output commanded off, a control voltage between 2.82 and 7.04 V counts as open, because an intact line would be pulled clearly low. The test samples every 12.5 ms and fails when 480 of 560 samples are bad, about seven seconds; it is Type A, so the MIL comes on after one trip. A broken wire, a backed-out pin or a module with a failed output are the typical reasons. The driver may face a module that does not wake up. P24F0 and P24F1 are the low and high faults.
c: Broken wake-up wire in the harness
Pin pushed back or corroded in a module connector
Wake-up output of the control module defective
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Connected module stays asleep, with related communication codes

P24F0.d: P24F0 means that a control module drives its wake-up output on, but the line voltage stays down, pointing to a ground short or a load drawing far too much current. In GM's 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables the HPC2 module runs this check whenever the output is commanded on and reports a fault if the control voltage is at or below 5.52 V. Sampling every 12.5 ms, it needs 480 failures in a window of 560, roughly seven seconds; as a Type A code it lights the MIL on the first trip. The unit at the far end then never sees its wake signal and may stay off or drop out. Search the harness for a chafed spot or a wet connector. P24EF is the open-circuit fault, P24F1 the high one.
c: Wake-up line shorted to ground at a chafe point
Moisture in a connector bridging the line to ground
Receiving module loading the wake-up input too heavily
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Hybrid or charging functions unavailable

P24F1.d: With P24F1 the wake-up line carries voltage while its driving module has the output switched off, so a short to a battery feed or a second source keeps it live. GM's HPC2 module in the 2016 and 2019 hybrid tables flags 13.21 V or more in the off state, using the same 480-of-560 sample count at 12.5 ms and Type A, MIL after one trip. Mercedes-Benz documents P24F100 in the 8-speed dual-clutch gearbox controller of CLA, GLA and GLB (XENTRY tip LI27.19-P-080869, 2026): the wake line appears shorted to positive, the car may briefly refuse to start, and the cause is signal timing with the ignition switch module, fixed by new SCN coding of that unit. P24EF is open, P24F0 low.
c: Wake-up line shorted to a battery feed
Signal timing between ignition module and receiving unit, solved by coding
Voltage fed back from another module that stays awake
s: Check engine light and several warning messages
Temporary no-start condition
Possible battery drain while parked

P24F2.t: EGR Temperature/Charge Air Cooler Temperature Correlation
P24F2.d: P24F2 compares two readings in the intake path of a diesel with cooled exhaust gas recirculation: the gas temperature after the EGR cooler and the air temperature behind the charge air cooler. When conditions say both should be close, for instance after the engine has cooled down, a wide gap shows that one of the two sensors cannot be trusted. Chrysler lists the code for the 3.0 L EcoDiesel (sales code EXF) in the 2014 Ram 1500 and Jeep Grand Cherokee; bulletins 18-028-14 and 18-018-14 cure false settings with new PCM software rather than parts. Chrysler publishes no thresholds. Circuit faults of the single sensors have their own codes such as P040C or P0097. The driver usually sees only the warning lamp; EGR use may be limited.
c: Outdated PCM calibration flagging the correlation without a real fault (Chrysler 3.0 L diesel)
EGR temperature sensor drifting or sooted up
Charge air cooler outlet temperature sensor reading wrong
Corroded connector adding resistance to one sensor signal
s: Check engine light, often without any noticeable driving fault
EGR operation reduced as a precaution on some calibrations
Implausible EGR or charge air temperatures in live data after a cold soak

P24F3.d: P24F3 sets the temperature reported from the DEF (reductant) tank against the fuel temperature. After a long soak both liquids rest close to ambient, so a clear mismatch exposes a sensor that reads wrong although each signal may be electrically valid. No manufacturer explains P24F3 in a public service document. Ford's 2023 diesel summary shows the same principle with other partners: P205B flags more than 40 °C between tank and DEF quality sensor temperature at start-up, and P0181 holds fuel temperature against the charge-air reading after six hours off. CARB requires such rationality checks for input sensors that feed emission controls. Where the DEF sensor is built into the tank module, the fix can mean a costly tank unit; driving is normally unaffected.
c: DEF tank temperature sensor (often integrated in the tank or sender module) reading wrong
Local heat source such as an exhaust leak warming one sensor
Contact resistance in a sensor connector
s: Warning lamp, often after a cold start
DEF tank and fuel temperature far apart in live data after an overnight stop

P24F4.t: NOx Sensor Delayed Response - High to Low (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P24F4.d: P24F4 concerns the dead time of the upstream NOx sensor on bank 1 when engine-out NOx falls, typically on lift-off into overrun: the reading stays put too long before it starts dropping, even if the later descent is normal. CARB defines this split for exhaust sensors, delayed response being the wait before the first reaction and slow response a sluggish transition. No manufacturer documents P24F4 publicly. GM's 2025 diesel table shows the method for the rising edge: inside the front-sensor test P22F9 a timer runs from the NOx model reaching 30 ppm until the sensor does, and over 2 s is a fault. Hella names deposits and ageing as reasons for late NOx readings. P22FA is the slow falling case, P24F5 sensor 2.
c: Soot or oil ash on the diffusion barrier of the front sensor
Aged measuring cells reacting late to falling NOx
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor distorting the transient
s: Check engine light on
Front NOx value lingers on lift-off
Engine runs normally

P24F5.t: NOx Sensor Delayed Response - High to Low (Bank 1 Sensor 2)
P24F5.d: P24F5 is the same delay check for NOx sensor 2 on bank 1, which sits behind the SCR catalyst and judges its conversion. If its value lags when NOx at the outlet falls, the efficiency estimate is distorted and the SCR monitor could pass or fail wrongly, so the sensor must react in time. A late reaction means the first visible change comes too long after the expected drop. No manufacturer publishes P24F5. CARB separates delayed from slow response in its sensor definitions; GM's 2025 diesel table shows a 2-second delay limit in its front-sensor test P22F9 as a model for such timing. Hella points to ammonia slip and crystal residue as threats to the element. P22FD is the slow falling case; P24F4 sensor 1.
c: DEF crystals or ammonia slip attacking the rear sensor element
Aged measuring cells of sensor 2 reacting late
Condensate in the cold tailpipe area affecting the sensor
s: Check engine light on
Possibly an SCR efficiency code alongside

P24F6.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Stuck Open
P24F6.d: Heavy Volvo and Mack trucks regenerate the particulate filter with an aftertreatment hydrocarbon injector (AHI, the 7th injector) that sprays diesel ahead of the oxidation catalyst; compressed air from the truck supply then blows the line to the nozzle clear. P24F6 means the fuel/air purge valve in the AHI module seems to stay open, so air keeps flowing when it should not. Solution K17696792 (US15 and later, 11, 13 and 16 L engines) lists checks when guided diagnostics finds nothing: 32 psi (221 kPa) at the doser air supply, a dry purge line, the right coalescing air-dryer cartridge and no aerated fuel. For the open case Volvo's AHI guide also replaces the nozzle and cleans the line. Regeneration can fail and soot builds up.
c: Oil or water in the purge air from an unsuitable or worn air-dryer cartridge
Debris holding the purge valve in the AHI module open
Damaged AHI nozzle or leaking fuel/air line toward the nozzle
Doser air supply pressure outside the 221 kPa specification
s: Particulate filter regeneration does not complete
Warning lamp and aftertreatment message on the dash
Rising soot load and more frequent regeneration requests

P24F7.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Stuck Closed
P24F7.d: P24F7 is the reverse case of P24F6: the purge valve of the aftertreatment fuel/air system will not open when commanded, so no compressed air reaches the dosing line and the 7th injector after a dosing phase. In Volvo and Mack trucks this valve sits in the AHI dosing block, mounted on the fuel filter housing from model year 2017 and on the engine block side before. Volvo's AHI troubleshooting guide points to the air supply, the module and the fuel/air lines up to the nozzle; contamination carried in with the air or fuel causes most module failures. The joint solution for both purge codes was reissued as KC-401 for trucks from model year 2016 and starts with the 221 kPa air pressure check. Without purging, fuel can coke in the line.
c: Purge valve jammed by oil, water or particles from the air system
Air supply to the AHI module restricted or below specification
Coked or kinked line between AHI module and nozzle
Internal fault of the AHI dosing module
s: Active regeneration aborted or not started
Warning lamp with aftertreatment message
Possible engine derate as soot load climbs

P24F8.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Control Circuit
P24F8.d: P24F8 is the electrical fault of the fuel/air purge valve: the control unit finds the solenoid drive circuit not working, typically an open wire or a coil that draws no current. Volvo and Mack report it as P24F813, the suffix 13 meaning open circuit. In their AHI diagnosis guide for US10+OBD13 engines onward it stands in the electrical fault table together with P24FA and P24FB, and the prescribed work is the AHI module connector and the harness, not the air or fuel supply. The dosing module carries the valve; on newer trucks it sits on the fuel filter housing. While the valve cannot be driven, the doser line is not blown clear after dosing, which puts filter regeneration at risk. CARB's heavy-duty rules require actuators like this to be checked for circuit continuity.
c: Broken wire or chafed harness between engine controller and AHI module
Corroded or loose plug at the AHI dosing module
Interrupted coil of the purge valve solenoid
s: Warning lamp right after the circuit test runs
Active regeneration blocked or incomplete

P24F9.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Control Circuit Range/Performance
P24F9.d: P24F9 covers a purge valve control circuit that is electrically present but behaves implausibly, for example when measured current or a feedback signal does not follow the commanded state within the expected time. Unlike P24F8, P24FA and P24FB, this variant appears in none of the Volvo/Mack AHI documents, and no manufacturer documents P24F9 publicly. The part involved is the same: a solenoid in the dosing module that admits compressed air to flush fuel out of the line to the exhaust injector after each dosing event. CARB's heavy-duty rule 1971.1 obliges systems that blow fuel into the exhaust with air assistance to detect any failure that leaves the filter unable to regenerate. Plausible triggers are a sluggish valve, drifting coil resistance or a high-resistance contact.
c: Purge valve moving slowly because of deposits
Solenoid coil resistance drifting with heat or age
High-resistance contact in the module plug
s: Warning lamp, sometimes only under heat
Irregular or aborted filter regenerations

P24FA.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Control Circuit Low
P24FA.d: P24FA reports that voltage on the purge valve control line is lower than the driver stage expects in the current switching state: a short to ground on the wire, a coil with too little resistance or a weak supply. Volvo and Mack name P24FA00 in the electrical section of their AHI troubleshooting guide for US10+OBD13 and newer engines; the work there is on the dosing module plug and the harness, not on the air or fuel side. Depending on how the driver is wired, a ground short can either keep the valve energised permanently or stop it from switching. In both cases the purge cycle after hydrocarbon dosing becomes unreliable, and the controller may suspend active regeneration until the fault is fixed. An open circuit is P24F8, the opposite polarity P24FB.
c: Control wire chafed through to chassis ground
Purge valve coil with shorted turns
Moisture in the AHI module connector
s: Warning lamp shortly after key-on or during dosing
Regeneration not possible

P24FB.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Control Circuit High
P24FB.d: With P24FB the purge valve control line sits higher than allowed, a pattern that points to a short to battery voltage or to a broken low-side path, so the controller cannot pull the line down. In the Volvo/Mack AHI guide P24FB00 is listed right beside P24FA00 among the electrical codes, and the first check is the harness and the plug at the dosing module. If the valve never energises, compressed air does not flush the feed to the 7th injector, and fuel left there can carbonise over time. A driver stage that shuts itself off against overcurrent may also log this code. The low counterpart is P24FA, a plain interruption P24F8. Expect a warning lamp and, on trucks, a dash message about filter regeneration.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed in the harness
Interrupted return path between valve and controller
Controller output stage protecting itself against overcurrent
s: Warning lamp and aftertreatment message
Filter regeneration unavailable

P24FC.t: Particulate Matter Sensor Heater Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P24FC.d: P24FC concerns the output stage that powers the heater of the particulate matter sensor: the driver reports excessive current or an internal temperature past its limit, which suggests a heater with shorted turns or too little resistance, or an overheating sensor electronics unit. On heavy trucks this sensor works as a self-diagnosing device after the SCR catalyst and reports over J1939. Volvo and Mack list P24FC00 in two editions of their PM sensor diagnosis guide for US14+OBD16 engines onward among the codes that justify replacing the sensor, whereas supply-voltage and communication codes point elsewhere. No public threshold exists. P24B5/P24B6 are plain heater circuit shorts, P24B7 the heater resistance. A sensor that cannot heat cannot burn off soot, so filter monitoring stops.
c: Internal failure of the smart PM sensor (heater or electronics)
Water ingress cracking the ceramic element or shorting the heater
Unusually high exhaust temperature at the sensor, e.g. during repeated regenerations
s: Warning lamp
No soot reading from the PM sensor, DPF monitoring not completed

P24FD.d: P24FD is intended to flag that the particulate filter in position A is not the expected part or is absent, for example after a filter delete or when an unsuitable replacement has been fitted. No manufacturer documents P24FD publicly. CARB's rules for light and heavy-duty diesels require the OBD system to notice a substrate that is destroyed, removed or swapped for a silencer or plain pipe. Makers usually report that through other codes: Ford's 2023 diesel summary catches a missing substrate as P244A when DPF inlet pressure stays under a flow-dependent limit (about 15 kPa at 600 m³/h) for 90 seconds, and P226D exists for a deteriorated or missing substrate. Expect a lit MIL and a failed emissions inspection until the correct filter is installed.
