c: Particulate filter removed or replaced by a straight pipe
Leaking or blocked pressure lines making a present filter look absent
s: Check engine light
Visible soot at the tailpipe if the filter is missing
Emissions inspection failed

P24FE.d: P24FE means the controller concludes that the SCR catalyst is missing or not the expected part. Ford runs this test on the 6.7 L diesel (2023 summary) for about 60 s with SCR inlet at 195–340 °C and feedgas NOx of 70–500 ppm, and sets the code when cumulative SCR efficiency falls below 0 %. Hino's J08E workshop text (SB-19-008, 2017–2020 conventional trucks) treats it as removal of the DEF SCR catalyst: average NOx conversion at or under 0.03 for 10 s, MIL off but service lamp on, low power. Hino alert SA-17-036 had first told dealers to clear and release trucks. Ford TSB 24-2136 links P24FE on 2020–2022 Super Duty to NOx sensor 11, fixed by a new sensor and software. Ordinary ageing is P20EE.
c: Upstream or downstream NOx sensor misreading (Ford sensor 11, Hino NOx sensors)
SCR catalyst removed or replaced by a non-matching part
Controller software detecting removal falsely, fixed by reprogramming
Diluted DEF or faulty DEF injector collapsing NOx conversion
s: Warning or service lamp (Hino sets the service lamp, MIL stays off)
Reduced engine power
NOx downstream of the SCR as high as upstream in live data

P24FF.d: P24FF signals that the diesel exhaust fluid itself has become too hot while the engine runs. The controller reads the DEF temperature sensor in the tank and flags a value above its limit during operation; hot urea solution ages faster and can form deposits. Deutz lists P24FF-00 in its EMR L1 secondary ECU code table (SPN 4337, FMI 11) as AdBlue overtemperature in operation, kept apart from its own warning and critical overtemperature codes. Volvo truck solution KC-10 names a typical hardware cause: when guided diagnostics finds the valve working yet the DEF is confirmed hot, the coolant solenoid valve that heats the tank may be fitted against its flow arrow; turning the valve body around fixes it. Sensor circuit faults are P205A to P205D.
c: DEF tank coolant solenoid valve installed against its flow direction (Volvo)
Tank heating valve stuck open so hot coolant keeps flowing
Missing heat shield or exhaust leak warming the tank or lines
DEF temperature sensor reading too high
s: Warning lamp with SCR or DEF message
DEF tank temperature far above ambient in live data

P2500.d: P2500 points to the L line, the turn-on wire between engine module and alternator regulator that on many older layouts also runs through the charge warning lamp. The module reads back the voltage on this wire; when it stays below the expected level, for instance because the line is chafed to ground or the regulator holds it down, this code is logged. A line pinned low can mean the regulator never receives its start command, so the field is not energised and the battery slowly drains. Ford lists P2500 in the code table of its 2014 BOSS 302S engine module, without a MIL marker; no maker publishes trigger values. P0621 covers the L circuit in general, P2501 is the high counterpart. The driver may see the battery lamp and later a weak or dead battery.
c: L wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Alternator regulator faulty and pulling the L terminal low
Corroded or loose plug at the alternator
Output stage for the L line in the engine module defective
s: Battery or charge warning lamp on
Battery voltage falls while driving
Hard or no start after some time

P2501.d: With P2501 the engine module sees too much voltage on the L line to the alternator regulator. The wire is then either touching a battery-fed conductor, or the module cannot pull it down because the regulator side or the lamp path is open, so the line floats up to supply level. Depending on the design, the regulator either stays switched on permanently or the module loses its ability to turn charging off and to signal a charging fault through the lamp. Ford names P2501 in the 2014 BOSS 302S code list, again without a MIL marker; trigger values are not published by any maker. Its low-side sibling is P2500, while P0621 describes the L circuit without saying which way it fails. Drivers may notice a lamp that never lights at key-on or one that stays on.
c: L wire shorted to a battery-fed wire in the harness
Break in the L circuit or plug off at the alternator
s: Charge lamp does not light during the bulb check or stays on
Charging voltage unusually high or not controlled
Battery drains if charging stops

P2502.d: P2502 is the general charging-system code: the engine module compares the voltage the generator actually delivers with what it has requested and finds a mismatch that it does not classify as simply too low or too high. Mazda uses it as a malfunction in the voltage produced by the generator. On 2022–2023 Mazda2 mild hybrids built in Mexico the charge lamp came on while driving; Mazda traced it to resistance at the ground terminal of the DC-DC converter under heavy current and replaced the converter with revised software. Ford lists P2502 for the 2014 BOSS 302S module. CARB lets makers pause other monitors at low or high system voltage, which is why charging faults matter for the OBD system. Directional faults are P2503 and P2504.
c: Alternator or regulator not reaching the requested voltage
High resistance at ground or B+ connections (Mazda mild hybrid DC-DC converter)
Slipping drive belt or worn tensioner
Battery with internal fault distorting the charging voltage
s: Charge warning lamp on while driving
Fluctuating battery voltage, flickering lights
Battery not fully charged

P2503.d: P2503 means the charging output is below target: with the engine running the module expects the generator to lift system voltage, but it stays too low. FCA calls the code Charging System Output Low. On the 2020 Dodge Durango its technical centre linked P2503 or P2504 with a lit battery lamp and no-start to a loose B+ stud on the feed from alternator to power distribution centre, or to a failed alternator pulley that turns freely both ways. A 2021 Ram 1500 case shows P2503 stored together with P2504 and a lit check engine lamp, traced by voltage-drop testing of the wiring. Unlike P0562, which reports a low supply at the module itself, P2503 judges the charging output. Expect a dim, weakening battery and possibly a stall or no-start.
c: Loose or burnt B+ connection between alternator and fuse box
Failed overrunning pulley or slipping belt
s: Battery lamp and check engine lamp on
Dim lights, electrical consumers dropping out
Engine stalls or will not start

P2504.d: P2504 is logged when the charging output overshoots: the measured voltage rises above what the module asked the generator to produce. FCA names it Charging System Output High and publishes several cases. A 2021 Ram 1500 lit the check engine lamp after a repair, with P2504 set and P2503 stored, and the advice was to voltage-drop every circuit involved. On a 2022 Ram 1500 that would not crank, the cause was the N1 connection at the high-current fuse array plus poor grounds from battery to body and from body to engine. The Durango bulletin treats P2504 alongside P2503 and the loose B+ post. Poor connections fool the measurement, so a sound alternator can be blamed. P0563 differs: it rates the module supply. Real overcharging can boil the battery and damage electronics.
c: High resistance at B+ fuse array or ground straps distorting the reading
Battery current or voltage sensor delivering wrong values
s: Check engine lamp, sometimes battery lamp
Very bright lights, bulbs failing early
No crank in connection-related cases

P2505.d: P2505 covers the supply inputs of the engine module in general. GM documents it in the 2014 diesel engine table 14OBDG04: the module checks its permanent battery feed, the line that keeps the engine-off timer alive while the ignition is off. If that constant supply was interrupted, the module flags P2505 as soon as the ignition is on; a single event is enough, the test is evaluated a single time per trip and the code is GM type B, so the MIL follows on the second failing trip. Without that feed the module cannot know how long the engine was off, which other diagnostics rely on. Ford lists P2505 without MIL marker for the 2014 BOSS 302S. P2506 to P2509 narrow the fault to plausibility, low, high and intermittent.
c: Battery disconnected or permanent-feed fuse removed or blown
Open or corroded permanent supply wire or connector
Supply monitoring inside the module defective
s: MIL after two trips (GM)
Often no drivability complaint
Learned values may be lost

P2506.d: P2506 is the plausibility variant: the supply reaching the engine module is electrically present but its value or behaviour does not fit the operating state. No passenger-car maker publishes how it detects this. The closest coded use is Deutz, whose EMR engine controller assigns P2506 with failure type 18 to a critical overcurrent in the ECU power supply, a reading that only makes sense as a performance check, not as a plain open or short. Ford lists P2506 with an M in the indicator column of its 2014 BOSS 302S code table. CARB requires makers to check input signals for rationality as comprehensive components. Clear low or high values belong to P2507 and P2508, dropouts to P2509. In practice the code points to supply wiring, relay or module.
c: Resistance in supply fuse, relay contact or connector
Excessive current drawn through the module supply (Deutz)
Internal supply monitoring of the module faulty
s: Check engine lamp (Ford lists it as MIL code)
Sporadic stalling or restarts of the module possible

P2507.d: P2507 reports that a supply input of the engine module sits too low. Makers read this differently. Mazda calls it a low PCM battery voltage input: on 2013–2020 models from CX-5 to MX-5 it appears together with P2610 when the engine was started three or more times after stops shorter than 15 s while the 15 A room fuse was pulled for transport; it concerns 2016 and later models and, as a stored past fault, usually goes unnoticed. On the 2024 CX-90 a loosely seated 25 A fuse F1 led to P2507, many warning lamps and a no-start. Ford's 2023 6.7 L diesel instead watches the module's internal 5 V rail and sets P2507 below 4.2 V, monitored continuously over about 5 s. P0562 is the system-voltage code; P2508 is the high case.
c: Supply fuse missing, pulled for transport or not fully seated
Weak battery or voltage dips during repeated starts
Corroded supply wire, ground or relay contact
Internal 5 V supply of the module failing (Ford diesel)
s: Often no symptom, code found during service (Mazda)
Several warning lamps, blank displays
No-start in severe cases

P2508.d: P2508 is set when a supply input of the engine module reads above its permitted range. Ford documents it for the 2023 6.7 L Power Stroke diesel: the module checks its internal 5 V supply rail and flags P2508 once that rail exceeds 5.5 V, with continuous monitoring, roughly 5 s to mature, and the module awake (key on, running or after-run). The same group also blocks the reductant quality sensor test while P2507 or P2508 is present. On the 2014 BOSS 302S module Ford gives P2508 an M in the indicator column. A raised internal rail suggests a regulator fault inside the module or an external short to a higher voltage. P0563 reports excessive system voltage instead, P06A6 a sensor reference out of range. P2507 is the low partner.
c: Internal 5 V regulator of the engine module defective
Supply or sensor wire shorted to battery voltage
Overvoltage from charging fault or jump start
s: Check engine lamp
Other diagnostics such as the DEF quality test suspended
Erratic sensor values possible

P2509.d: P2509 records a brief loss of the engine module's supply, a dropout rather than a lasting low or high value. Two Cummins-powered pickups show how easily it appears. Nissan warns for the 2016 Titan XD with the 5.0 L diesel: wait at least two minutes after switching off before disconnecting either 12 V battery, otherwise P2509 and P181B are stored; such codes may be erased but are not a warranty repair. FCA lists P2509 among faults addressed by a PCM reflash for 2018 Ram 2500/3500 with the 6.7 L Cummins, where customers saw the MIL. The module's after-run, interrupted by a cut supply, is what the check catches. Persistent values belong to P2507 and P2508, plausibility to P2506. Real loose battery clamps or relay contacts give the same code.
c: Battery disconnected before the module finished its after-run
Loose battery clamp, ground or supply connector
Module software too sensitive, fixed by reflash (Ram 6.7 L)
s: MIL on, often without drivability complaint
Code appears right after battery work

P250A.d: P250A is the general circuit code for the engine oil level sensor, a unit in the sump that today mostly measures by heated element or ultrasound and often reports oil temperature as well. Its use varies. GM's 2018 preliminary information for several trucks, SUVs and V8 cars lists P250A among codes caused by a jumper harness chafed near connector X154 on the front cover. Mazda tells technicians that on the 2016–2017 CX-9 an oil warning lamp with P250A can simply come from overfilled oil, so the level must be checked first. Deutz's EMR controller files a ground fault of the level sensor as P250A-F0. Specific low, high and erratic signals are P250C to P250E, a genuinely low level P250F.
c: Sensor harness chafed or pinched (GM X154 jumper harness)
Engine oil overfilled, sensor reading out of range (Mazda CX-9)
Oil level sensor defective or leaking at its seal
Corroded or oily connector at the sump
s: Oil level warning or message in the cluster
Oil level display missing or wrong
With harness damage, further engine codes and stalling (GM)

P250B.t: Engine Oil Level Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P250B.d: P250B fires when the oil level sensor answers electrically but its reading is implausible, for instance a level that jumps, stays frozen while the engine runs, or contradicts the value after a stop. Continuous sensors see a lower level in operation than at rest, so the plausibility logic has to account for running state, temperature and inclination. FCA treats P250B on the 2017 Alfa Romeo Giulia with the 2.0 L turbo (titled there Engine Oil Level Sensor Circuit Performance) as one of several codes corrected by a powertrain reflash, i.e. a logic issue rather than a broken part. Deutz's MD1 list ties P250B to the oil level parameter SPN 98 with a fault-present type. Circuit faults are P250C to P250E, real oil shortage P250F.
c: Plausibility logic in the engine module too strict, fixed by update (Alfa Romeo)
Sensor element aged or contaminated by sludge
Oil level far outside the calibrated range after a service
s: Oil level message without real oil loss
Level display jumps or stays fixed

P250C.t: Engine Oil Level Sensor Circuit Low
P250C.d: P250C means the oil level sensor's signal line is pulled too low, the classic picture of a short to ground or, depending on the input design, a break that lets the line drop. Deutz describes its P250C-00 the same way: level sensor line grounded or interrupted. Hyundai shows that software can trip it too: on 2023 Kona and Elantra with the 2.0 L Nu Atkinson engine, P250C turned on a warning lamp, and the cure was a PCM reflash that changes how the oil level warning is triggered. Ford also lists P250C for the 2014 BOSS 302S engine module. The opposite fault is P250D, dropouts are P250E. A low level of oil itself is P250F. For the driver the oil level information is lost.
c: Signal wire shorted to ground near the sump
Open circuit or unplugged sensor connector
Warning logic in the engine module, fixed by reflash (Hyundai 2.0 Nu)
s: Oil level warning lamp on
No oil level reading in the cluster

P250D.t: Engine Oil Level Sensor Circuit High
P250D.d: P250D is stored when the oil level sensor line rises above its valid range. The usual explanation is contact with a positive conductor; with pull-up inputs an interrupted line or missing sensor ground can also drive the signal high. Deutz gives the clearest definition: its EMR controller files P250D-00 as the level sensor shorted to battery. Ford lists P250D in the 2014 BOSS 302S engine code table. No passenger-car maker has published thresholds or a service bulletin for this code. A reading stuck high can mimic a full sump, so a real oil loss might go unreported until P250F logic or the oil pressure switch reacts. The low counterpart is P250C, the erratic one P250E, the generic circuit code P250A.
c: Signal wire shorted to supply voltage
Sensor ground open or signal line interrupted
s: Oil level warning or message
Level display permanently at maximum

P250E.t: Engine Oil Level Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P250E.d: P250E flags an oil level signal that drops out or jumps in an unrealistic way while the circuit otherwise looks intact. Typical sources are a loose terminal, a wire that breaks only under engine movement, or a sensor that loses its echo or heating cycle intermittently. Modern sensors deliver level and temperature as a timed or digital signal, so a single disturbed cycle can already be detected. Deutz's MD1 list assigns P250E to the oil level parameter SPN 98, and Ford lists P250E for the 2014 BOSS 302S module. Beyond that no maker publishes trigger criteria for this code. Unlike P250C and P250D, the value is not stuck at one end, and unlike P250B it is the signal itself that is unstable. The driver sees sporadic oil level messages.
c: Loose or oily terminal in the sensor connector
Wire breaking intermittently from engine movement
Sensor losing its measuring cycle sporadically
s: Oil level message appears and disappears
Jumping level display

P250F.d: P250F is not a wiring code: the oil level sensor works, and the measured level is below the minimum. Mazda used it on 2021 models with the 2.5 L turbo (Mazda3, Mazda6, CX-30, CX-5, CX-9) where a low-oil message and the check engine light appeared after roughly 5,000 to 7,500 km without visible leaks; Mazda suspected oil entering the combustion chambers past damaged valve stem seals and first topped up free of charge. Hyundai shows the reverse risk: on 2023–2024 Venue with the 1.6 L MPI engine the code could set with the level in range, and a PCM update changed the warning logic. Deutz files the same condition as P250F-00. Sensor circuit faults are P250A to P250E. Check the dipstick before driving on.
c: Oil burned past valve stem seals or piston rings
External oil leak or too little oil after a service
Warning logic triggering with correct level, fixed by update (Hyundai)
s: Low engine oil message and check engine light
Oil level near or below minimum on the dipstick

P2510.t: ECM/PCM Power Relay Sense Circuit Range/Performance
P2510.d: P2510 judges whether the main relay of the engine module behaves as commanded, based on what the module senses on the switched supply. GM's 2014 diesel tables describe two checks. A stuck relay is one that ignores the power-down command, recognised when timer values after the after-run are longer than possible; GM counts such events in EEPROM and sets the code once the count exceeds 2 (14OBDG04) or 1 (6.6 L LML, 14OBDG10). A relay that opens too early is seen when the EEPROM write that should close the previous after-run is missing. Both run once per trip in pre-drive, type B. Ford lists P2510 for the 2014 BOSS 302S. Pure sense-circuit faults are P0689/P0690, P2511 the intermittent case.
c: Main relay contacts welded or sticking
Relay dropping out early (weak coil, poor socket contact)
Battery disconnected or supply lost during after-run
Relay driver or EEPROM handling in the module faulty
s: MIL after two trips (GM type B)
Battery drain if the relay stays closed
Lost adaptations if the relay opens too early

P2511.t: ECM/PCM Power Relay Sense Circuit Intermittent
P2511.d: P2511 covers short dropouts on the line through which the engine module reads back the output of its main relay. The relay is commanded on, yet the sensed voltage briefly vanishes and returns, typical of a chattering contact, a cracked solder joint in the relay or a loose terminal in the fuse box. No manufacturer documents this code publicly with thresholds or a bulletin; even Ford's 2014 BOSS 302S list jumps from P2510 to P2512. CARB requires input circuits of the comprehensive components to be monitored, and GM's 2014 diesel tables show how the same sense signal is evaluated for P2510. Steady low or high readings are P0689 and P0690, a relay that does not follow commands is P2510. Possible effects: brief stalls or resets.
c: Worn or chattering main relay contact
Loose relay socket or fuse box terminal
s: Engine may stall briefly or hesitate
Several modules logging voltage-related codes

P2512.d: P2512 concerns the wired request line between the event data recorder and the engine module. The recorder, normally part of the airbag control unit, stores a short history of speed, throttle, brake and other pre-crash data when it senses a crash or near-crash, and needs powertrain values for that. Via the request circuit it can ask the engine module to deliver or freeze them. P2512 means the module sees this circuit as open or not in its expected state. Ford lists P2512 for the 2014 BOSS 302S engine module with a W rather than an M in its indicator column; no maker publishes wiring or thresholds. Low and high states are P2513 and P2514. The fault does not affect driving or emissions but may leave crash data incomplete.
c: Request wire broken or connector unplugged
Airbag/recorder module missing, replaced or not configured
Engine module configured for a recorder line that is not fitted
s: Code stored without noticeable symptoms
Possibly a service or wrench indicator

P2513.t: Event Data Recorder Request Circuit Low
P2513.d: P2513 is set when the event data recorder request line reads too low at the engine module. A wire rubbed through to body ground, a crushed harness after body work, or water in a floor connector are the obvious suspects; a low line may also be read as a permanent request. The recorder itself, usually housed in the airbag module, captures the seconds before and during a collision and depends on powertrain data for that picture. Ford is the only maker found listing P2513, in the 2014 BOSS 302S engine module table, marked W in the indicator column; thresholds are nowhere published. Unlike P2512 the circuit is not open but pulled down, and P2514 is the high side. Drivers notice nothing while driving; crash records may lack engine data.
c: Moisture or corrosion in an under-floor connector
Recorder or engine module input stage faulty
s: Code stored without drivability effect
Possibly a service or wrench indicator

P2514.t: Event Data Recorder Request Circuit High
P2514.d: P2514 tells you the request line between the event data recorder and the engine module sits at too high a level. The recorder, normally housed in the airbag control unit, keeps a short log of speed, pedal and brake data around a collision and fetches engine values through this line. A high reading points to a wire chafed against a powered conductor, a missing ground on the recorder side or an input stage pulled up internally. Ford is the only maker found listing P2514, in its 2014 BOSS 302S engine module code table, marked W rather than M in the lamp column, so no check engine light is expected; voltages are not published anywhere. An open line is P2512, a line pulled down is P2513. Driving is unaffected, though crash records may lack powertrain values.
c: Request wire chafed against a powered circuit
Missing ground or unplugged connector at the airbag/recorder module
Input stage in engine or recorder module faulty
s: Code stored with no effect on driving
Possibly a wrench or service indicator instead of the check engine light

P2515.t: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor B Circuit
P2515.d: P2515 is the general circuit fault of a second refrigerant pressure sensor, called B. Heat pump systems and vehicles with electric compressors often measure pressure at several points in the circuit; which position is B is up to the maker. Audi bulletin 87 22 35 (November 2022) ties P251500 to refrigerant pressure sensor 2 (G395/G827), read by thermal management module J1024 on 2020–2022 models from A6 to Q8 and e-tron: sensors produced prior to week 31 of 2021 had failing electronics, the cabin stopped cooling, sometimes with P053000 for sensor A as well, and a revised sensor is the cure. Ford's 2014 BOSS 302S engine table lists P2515 without a lamp mark. Low, high and plausibility faults of the same sensor are P2517, P2518 and P2516. Expect weak or absent cooling.
c: Pressure sensor electronics failed (Audi early build sensors)
Connector corroded or wiring to the sensor damaged
Evaluating module (thermal management or engine) faulty
s: A/C does not cool or cools only intermittently
Compressor stays off
Further A/C pressure codes such as P0530 stored

P2516.t: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P2516.d: P2516 flags a pressure sensor B whose reading is electrically valid but does not behave like real refrigerant pressure. In GM's hybrid OBD tables sensor B is the low-side sensor, evaluated by the hybrid processor that also runs the electric compressor. The 2019 edition looks for a stuck sensor: once the car has soaked and the compressor starts, the low-side value must shift by at least 4.0 kPa within 180 s of compressor running; if it barely moves, the test fails, type B with two trips. The 2011 edition used a sample counter of 32 fails in 40 checks at 250 ms intervals. GM also blocks its charge-loss check P0534 while P2516 is active. Out-of-range voltages are P2517 and P2518 instead. Typical result: compressor control falls back to defaults, cooling is weaker.
c: Pressure sensor stuck at one value
Compressor runs but hardly changes pressure (very low charge, blockage)
High resistance in signal or ground wire
s: A/C cools poorly
Check engine light after two drives (GM type B)
Refrigerant charge diagnosis not completed

P2517.t: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor B Circuit Low
P2517.d: P2517 means the signal of refrigerant pressure sensor B has dropped below its usable floor. GM's hybrid tables, where B is the low-side sensor, compute the ratio of signal to the 5 V reference and fail it below 2 % (0.10 V): in 2019 if that holds for 1.6 s of a 2 s window, in 2016 for 16 of 20 samples, in 2011 for 40 of 50 samples taken every 100 ms; each time type B, so the lamp comes on after two drives. A signal wire broken or shorted to ground, a lost 5 V reference or a sensor without output are the usual reasons; an empty system alone rarely pulls the voltage that far down. A merely implausible reading is P2516, the opposite extreme P2518. The compressor is normally locked out until the code clears.
c: Signal wire open or shorted to ground
5 V reference missing (wire or shared supply pulled down)
s: A/C compressor does not switch on
Check engine light after two drives on GM hybrids

P2518.t: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor B Circuit High
P2518.d: P2518 is stored when pressure sensor B reports a signal close to its supply voltage. GM, which uses B for the low-side sensor in its hybrid tables, sets the limit at 98 % of the reference, about 4.90 V. Interesting is how the rating changed: the 2011 edition counted 40 of 50 samples and treated it as type B with two trips, while the 2016 and 2019 editions make it type A, lighting the lamp after a single failed drive; 2019 needs 4 s out of a 5 s window. Typical causes are a signal conductor shorted to 5 V or battery voltage, an open sensor ground, or water in the connector. A real pressure peak normally stays inside the range and does not trigger it. Compare P2517 for the low extreme and P2516 for a frozen but valid value.
c: Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Moisture or corrosion in the sensor connector
s: Check engine light after one drive on newer GM hybrids
A/C compressor disabled, no cooling

P2519.d: P2519 covers the general circuit fault of a wired input through which the climate control asks the engine module for compressor operation. The engine module needs this request early, to raise idle speed, add torque reserve and then energise the compressor clutch relay. CARB therefore demands monitoring of electronic A/C components wherever switching the A/C changes fuel or ignition control, phased in from 2006 to 2008. Many current cars carry the request over CAN instead – Saab's 2011 9-5 is an example, with the HVAC module sending it as a message – and then network faults appear as U-codes rather than P2519. No maker documents P2519 publicly. P2520 and P2521 name a low or high level on the same input, P2522 the second input B. Expect A/C that does not start.
c: Request wire broken or connector loose
Climate control unit or A/C switch not sending a valid signal
s: A/C compressor never engages
Idle speed does not rise when A/C is selected

P251A.d: P251A concerns the switch the operator uses to arm the power take-off on a work truck. The control module reads this switch line and only allows PTO mode, often with a raised working idle, when the signal is plausible. This code means the module sees no valid state, typically an interrupted wire or a switch that no longer closes. GM documents it for 2019–2023 Silverado 4500HD to 6500HD medium-duty trucks in PIP6108: the PTO stops working, the fault may come and go, and before the switch is replaced the main PTO ground G120 on the left of the engine plus the frame, engine and body ground straps should be checked for paint, corrosion or a bolt without clamp load. P251B and P251C name a definite low or high level. The driver loses the PTO; the truck still drives.
c: Poor PTO or engine-to-frame ground (paint under the eyelet, corrosion, bolt bottoming out)
Broken or unplugged wire between PTO enable switch and module
Worn PTO enable switch that no longer makes contact
Faulty connection made during body or equipment installation
s: PTO cannot be engaged or drops out intermittently
Working idle speed is not raised when PTO is selected
Stored code with normal driving behaviour

P251B.d: With P251B the module reads the PTO enable switch input as stuck at a low level, below what either switch position should produce. A wire chafed through to chassis ground, water in a connector or a switch shorted internally are the usual explanations. No maker publishes P251B with thresholds; the closest documented case is P251A on GM medium-duty Silverado trucks, where bulletin PIP6108 traces PTO faults back to ground points, which shows how sensitive this switch circuit is to its reference. CARB lets OBD systems suspend selected monitors while a PTO unit is active, so a false PTO state also affects readiness. Depending on how the input is wired, a low reading may mean PTO is permanently refused or permanently requested. P251A is the open circuit, P251C the high side.
c: Switch signal wire chafed against frame or body
Moisture or corrosion in the switch connector
s: PTO will not engage, or engages without being selected
PTO indicator lamp behaves incorrectly
Readiness monitors may stay incomplete

P251C.d: P251C is logged when the PTO enable switch line sits above its valid window, close to supply voltage. That points to a signal wire touching a battery or ignition feed, a reference that has lost its ground, or a pull-up that the switch can no longer pull down. A lost ground matters here: GM's bulletin PIP6108 for P251A on 2019–2023 medium-duty Silverado trucks sends technicians to the PTO and frame grounds first. No manufacturer documents P251C itself or gives a voltage limit. Because CARB allows monitors to pause while PTO runs and Ford's summaries clear readiness during PTO mode, a falsely high input that reads as PTO active can keep monitors from completing. Sibling codes: P251A open circuit, P251B low.
c: Switch signal wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Missing ground on the switch or module reference
Switch stuck in the applied position
s: PTO engages or high idle starts without operator request
PTO cannot be switched off normally
Emissions readiness stays not ready

P251D.d: P251D covers the engine shutdown line of a power take-off installation. On trucks with body equipment such as cranes, pumps or aerial devices, a hard-wired signal lets the PTO controller or an equipment stop button tell the engine module to switch the engine off. P251D means the module cannot read a valid state on that line, usually because the wire or plug is open. No manufacturer documents P251D publicly or states how the engine reacts; the description rests on CARB's PTO definition and on GM's PTO bulletin PIP6108, which shows how ground and harness faults upset PTO circuits. Depending on calibration the PTO may be locked out, or a stop request from the equipment may no longer reach the engine. P251E and P251F name a fixed low or high level.
c: Open shutdown wire or loose connector at the body interface
Fault in the body equipment's stop switch or controller output
Shutdown input enabled in calibration but not wired by the upfitter
s: PTO locked out or equipment will not run
Equipment stop button no longer shuts down the engine

P251E.d: P251E reports that the PTO engine shutdown input reads too low. Whether low means stop now or all clear depends on the maker's wiring, so the practical effect varies: the module may treat the line as an active stop request and refuse to keep the engine running in PTO mode, or it may simply flag the line as shorted and ignore it. Typical causes are a chafed wire grounded on the frame, a corroded connector at the body interface or a stop switch shorted to ground. No manufacturer publishes P251E with a threshold or MIL rule; CARB defines the PTO unit, and GM's PTO bulletin PIP6108 for P251A shows that ground quality plays a big part in these body-builder circuits. Sibling codes: P251D for an open line, P251F for a high reading.
c: Shutdown wire chafed through to chassis ground
Corroded connector at the body builder interface
Equipment stop switch shorted to ground
s: Engine stops or will not stay running while PTO is used
PTO function disabled

P251F.d: P251F is the high-side fault of the PTO engine shutdown input: the voltage stays near supply level where the module expects a defined switching state. A shutdown wire touching a powered circuit in the body harness, a missing ground on the equipment controller, or an add-on module that drives the line permanently are typical. The main risk is that a real stop request from the body equipment is no longer recognised, or that the module locks out PTO operation as a precaution. Public maker documentation for P251F was not found; CARB covers PTO units in its OBD rules, and GM's PIP6108 on P251A illustrates how ground faults distort PTO-related inputs on medium-duty trucks. P251D is the open-circuit and P251E the low-level variant.
c: Shutdown wire shorted to a powered circuit in the body harness
Retrofitted control module holding the line high
s: Engine does not stop when equipment shutdown is triggered
PTO operation blocked

P2520.d: P2520 is set when the voltage on A/C request input A stays below the band the engine module accepts. Depending on whether the input is active-high or active-low, a grounded wire then reads as a permanent request or as none at all – either way the module distrusts it. Most often a harness rubbed through to body metal, a pinched wire behind the dashboard or a climate panel output stuck low is behind it. No maker publishes P2520 with thresholds; CARB only requires that A/C parts influencing fuel or spark control be checked, and on many cars with a networked request such as the 2011 Saab 9-5 the wired input does not exist. Unlike P2519 the circuit is not simply open, and P2521 is its high counterpart. The A/C may refuse to run or run unasked.
s: A/C does not switch on, or compressor runs although A/C is off
Idle speed behaves oddly when the A/C is toggled

P2521.d: With P2521 the engine module sees A/C request input A held above its valid range, typically because the wire touches a supply line, the input has lost its pull-down or the sending control unit drives it permanently high. Two makers list the code by number. Ford includes P2521 in the 2014 BOSS 302S engine module table without a lamp mark. FCA's emissions recall T21 for the 2004–2006 Dodge Sprinter names P2521 among the codes that the corrected engine software may newly report after reflashing. Neither publishes a voltage limit. CARB's A/C rules apply only where the request changes fuel or spark control. P2520 is the low counterpart, P2524 the same fault on input B. Drivers notice A/C that switches on by itself, will not switch off, or ignores the button.
c: Request wire shorted to a supply voltage
Climate control unit drives the line permanently high
Code newly reported after an engine software update (Sprinter T21)
s: A/C compressor runs although A/C is switched off
A/C button has no effect
Raised idle speed without A/C request

P2522.d: P2522 is the general circuit code for a second wired A/C request input, B. Why an engine module would need two such lines is left to each maker; plausible uses are a separate rear evaporator, a second request stage or a redundant line to cross-check input A. The common purpose stays the same: the module must learn of the coming compressor load in time to adjust idle and torque. CARB has required monitoring of electronic A/C components since the 2006–2008 phase-in, provided switching the A/C alters fuel or spark control. In networked systems, such as the 2011 Saab 9-5 that receives its A/C request as a CAN message, no such wire exists. No maker documents P2522 publicly. P2523 and P2524 denote low and high levels on B, P2519 the fault on input A.
c: Input B wire broken or connector loose
Sending climate module or switch faulty
s: A/C function served by input B unavailable
Idle dips when the compressor engages without notice

P2523.d: P2523 reports that A/C request input B is pulled below its valid range. On the wire level this usually means a conductor grounded against body metal, a sending module whose output transistor has failed shorted, or a wet connector draining the signal. Whether the engine module then assumes a constant request or none depends on the circuit design, and no maker states it publicly; P2523 has no codegenau manufacturer documentation. The regulatory basis is CARB's A/C component monitoring, required only where the A/C changes fuel or spark control. Cars that receive the request over CAN, like the 2011 Saab 9-5, cannot set it. P2522 is the generic circuit fault on B, P2524 the high side, and P2520 the same low fault on input A. Expect missing or unwanted compressor operation.
c: Input B wire shorted to ground
Output stage of the sending module shorted
Moisture in a connector of the request line
s: Compressor not engaging or engaging unasked
A/C-related idle compensation missing

P2524.d: P2524 indicates that A/C request input B reads above the level the engine module treats as valid. A line chafed against battery or ignition feed, an open pull-down inside the module or a control unit that latches its output high are the usual explanations. Ford is the one maker found to list it: its 2014 BOSS 302S code list shows P2524 without a lamp mark, just like its A-side counterpart P2521; no thresholds are given. A heavy-duty bulletin from Mack mentions a P252400 on MP10 engines, but in an oil pressure context, so that use is maker-specific and unrelated. CARB A/C monitoring applies only where the request alters fuel or spark control. P2523 is the low side, P2522 the general fault on B. Expect A/C behaving on its own.
c: Input B wire shorted to battery or ignition voltage
s: Compressor engages although not requested
A/C cannot be switched off or on as expected

P2525.d: P2525 is the general circuit fault of the pressure sensor on a vacuum reservoir. Diesels, and many hybrids and electric drives, lack usable intake vacuum and run a separate pump, often driven from the camshaft or by an electric motor, that fills a reservoir. That stored vacuum serves the brake booster and, on many diesels, pneumatic actuators for EGR, turbocharger control, swirl flaps or an exhaust brake. The sensor, normally a three-wire part with 5 V reference, lets the engine module verify the supply. CARB counts such inputs among comprehensive components that need circuit checks whenever they can affect emissions or other monitors. No maker documents P2525 itself. P2526 to P2529 split out plausibility, low, high and intermittent faults. Actuators may fall back to defaults.
c: Sensor wiring open or connector loose
Shared 5 V reference disturbed by another sensor
s: Check engine light depending on maker
Reduced boost or EGR function in default mode

P2526.t: Vacuum Reservoir Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2526.d: P2526 marks a vacuum reservoir pressure reading that stays inside the electrical range but does not fit the situation, for instance no rise in vacuum after the pump has run, or a value frozen while actuators draw on the reservoir. Because the sensor watches a real system, genuine vacuum faults such as a leaking hose, a worn pump or a cracked reservoir can set it as well as a drifting sensor. Two makers name it. FCA lists P2526 among the codes the revised engine software may newly log after emissions recall T21 on the 2004–2006 Dodge Sprinter. Hino's 2019 bulletin SB-19-013 for J05E cab-over trucks has technicians clear P2526 first before working through exhaust brake fault P0027, which uses vacuum-driven valves. Thresholds stay unpublished. Electrical faults are P2527–P2529.
c: Leaking vacuum hose, check valve or reservoir
Mechanical or electric vacuum pump delivering too little
s: Check engine light, often with boost or EGR codes
Weak exhaust brake or reduced power
Hissing noise from a leaking line

P2527.t: Vacuum Reservoir Pressure Sensor Circuit Low
P2527.d: P2527 means the signal from the vacuum reservoir pressure sensor has fallen below the lowest voltage a working sensor can produce. Whether low volts stand for deep vacuum or for atmospheric pressure depends on the sensor curve, but a reading at the floor is treated as an electrical fault, not as a vacuum value. Likely causes are a signal line shorted to ground, an open line on a sensor with pull-down, a missing 5 V reference, or a dead sensor. The 2004–2006 Dodge Sprinter is the documented case: FCA's emissions recall T21 names P2527 among the codes that may appear once the corrected engine software is installed; voltage thresholds were not published. P2528 is the high-side counterpart, P2526 a plausible voltage with an implausible value. Vacuum actuators may then run open-loop.
c: 5 V reference open or pulled down
s: Check engine light
Boost or EGR control in default mode, less power

P2528.t: Vacuum Reservoir Pressure Sensor Circuit High
P2528.d: P2528 is logged when the vacuum reservoir pressure sensor delivers a voltage near or at its supply, beyond anything the sensing element can output. A signal wire touching 5 V or battery voltage, a broken sensor ground, or corrosion bridging pins in the connector are the classic findings. A real loss of vacuum does not normally push the signal this far; it would appear as a range or performance fault instead. No vehicle maker documents P2528 publicly, so this rests on CARB's demand that comprehensive component inputs be checked for circuit faults, and on how such reservoirs work: a pump, often on the camshaft of diesels and hybrids, keeps them evacuated for the brake booster and actuators. P2527 is the low extreme, P2529 an intermittent signal. Expect default actuator control.
c: Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Corrosion bridging pins in the connector
s: Check engine light depending on maker
Reduced power with actuators in default position

P2529.t: Vacuum Reservoir Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent
P2529.d: P2529 covers a vacuum reservoir pressure signal that drops out or jumps for short moments rather than staying wrong. The engine module notices changes faster than a reservoir could physically empty or fill, or brief excursions to the electrical limits that recover again. Loose terminals, a cracked wire flexing with the engine, a harness rubbing on the pump bracket or moisture entering the connector are typical, and the fault often vanishes in the workshop. No maker documents P2529 publicly. CARB still expects circuit monitoring of such comprehensive component inputs, and the reservoir itself is the vacuum store a separate pump keeps up. Steady faults are P2527 and P2528.
c: Loose or spread terminal in the sensor connector
Harness chafing or wire breaking under engine movement
s: Check engine light comes and goes
Occasional brief loss of power or boost

P252A.d: P252A is the general circuit code for an engine oil quality sensor, a unit in the sump that judges the state of the oil from its physical properties. Hella's PULS+C variant, for example, adds measurements of viscosity, density and permittivity to ultrasonic level sensing, so oil changes can follow real wear instead of a fixed mileage. The engine computer stores P252A when it gets no usable signal at all, for instance because of a broken wire, an unplugged connector or a missing supply. No carmaker documents this code publicly with thresholds or bulletins. CARB demands monitoring only where a component can affect emissions or feeds another diagnostic. Low, high, erratic and implausible signals have their own codes P252C, P252D, P252E and P252B. For the driver the oil condition value and any adaptive service display are lost.
c: Sensor connector loose, unplugged or corroded by oil and moisture
Broken signal, supply or ground wire near the oil pan
Internal electronics of the oil quality sensor failed
s: Oil condition or service interval display missing or showing a fault
Warning message in the instrument cluster, usually without engine light

P252B.t: Engine Oil Quality Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P252B.d: P252B covers an oil quality sensor whose signal is electrically valid but makes no sense in context. Plausibility logic can weigh the reported oil properties against oil temperature, time since the last service or the engine's own oil ageing model; a value that stays frozen while conditions change, or leaps after a top-up without reason, is suspect. Sensors of the Hella PULS+C kind assess viscosity, density and permittivity, so deposits on the measuring element or an oil grade outside the calibration may also shift the result. No vehicle maker publishes criteria or bulletins for P252B. Open or shorted wiring belongs to P252A, P252C and P252D, short dropouts to P252E, while P253F reports oil that really is worn out. Usually only the oil condition display is affected.
c: Deposits or sludge on the sensing element distort the measurement
Oil grade or viscosity outside what the sensor calibration expects
Sensor aged or drifting, reading frozen or offset
Plausibility logic in the engine software too strict
s: Oil condition display shows implausible values or a fault message
Service interval calculated inconsistently after an oil change

P252C.t: Engine Oil Quality Sensor Circuit Low
P252C.d: P252C is stored when the oil quality sensor's signal sits below the range the engine computer accepts. Typical reasons are a signal wire chafed through to ground, a supply line that has lost its voltage or an internal short in the sensor; depending on the input circuit an open wire can also drag the reading down. As the sensor is mounted on the oil pan, its connector lives in a hot, oily and splash-prone spot, which makes corrosion and damaged insulation likely suspects. No manufacturer publishes a voltage threshold or a service bulletin for this code. CARB asks for circuit checks of such inputs only if the component can affect emissions or serves another monitor, so many applications leave the MIL off. P252D is the high-side counterpart, P252A the general circuit fault. The oil condition value disappears.
c: Signal wire chafed against the oil pan or engine block (short to ground)
Sensor supply voltage missing (fuse, supply wire)
Internal short in the oil quality sensor
s: Oil condition value missing in the cluster or service menu
Service reminder falls back to fixed intervals or shows a fault

P252D.t: Engine Oil Quality Sensor Circuit High
P252D.d: P252D means the oil quality sensor reports a voltage above its valid window. A short of the signal line to a positive conductor, a broken sensor ground or, with pull-up inputs, an interrupted signal wire can all push the value to the upper stop. Sensor electronics that latch high are a further possibility. Manufacturers do not document trigger values for this code. Depending on how the signal is scaled, a reading pinned at the top could pretend perfect oil or badly aged oil, so the computer ignores it and may rely on its calculated oil life instead. CARB only requires such checks where the sensor matters for emissions or other diagnostics, which is why a lamp is rarely involved. P252C is the low counterpart, P252E covers dropouts and P253F real oil deterioration. Expect a warning or a blank oil condition value.
c: Sensor ground or signal wire interrupted, connector pin pushed back
Signal wire shorted to a supply or battery-voltage wire
Sensor electronics stuck at a high output
s: Warning or blank oil condition value in the cluster
Oil change reminder appears too early, too late or not at all

P252E.t: Engine Oil Quality Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P252E.d: P252E points to an oil quality signal that briefly drops out or jumps while the circuit is otherwise intact. Typical sources are a terminal that loses contact when the engine shakes, a harness rubbing on the sump or a sensor whose internal measuring cycle is occasionally disturbed. Hella's oil sensors in the pan transmit their data as a repeating group of pulses roughly once per second, so on such designs even a single corrupted cycle can be detected. Hella's PULS+C extends the same sensor family to viscosity, density and permittivity. No vehicle maker documents P252E publicly. Unlike P252C and P252D the value is not stuck at one end, and unlike P252B the signal itself is unstable rather than merely implausible. Expect sporadic oil condition messages that come and go.
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the sensor connector
Harness rubbing on the oil pan with intermittent contact
Sensor electronics failing intermittently with heat or vibration
s: Oil condition message appears and disappears
Fluctuating oil condition or service interval values

P252F.d: P252F is not a wiring fault: the level sensor works and reports more oil in the sump than the permitted maximum. Deutz's EMR controller files the condition as P252F-00 under oil level parameter SPN 98 with FMI 15, and Ford's 2014 BOSS 302S code table lists P252F without a lamp entry. Besides overfilling at a service, fuel getting into the oil is a common reason. Mazda's Service Alert SA-026/18 for several 2013–2019 models explains that frequent short trips leave direct-injected fuel in the crankcase, raising the level; on a later long drive the fuel evaporates and can richen the mixture enough to set P0172. Coolant entering the oil also adds volume. Sensors that measure continuously while running, such as Hella's ultrasonic type, can catch this early. Low level is P250F. Check the dipstick and oil smell.
c: Too much oil added at the last oil change or top-up
Fuel dilution from frequent short trips or diesel particulate filter regeneration
Coolant entering the oil (head gasket, oil cooler)
s: Oil level warning in the instrument cluster
Dipstick reading above the maximum mark, oil may smell of fuel
Possible rich mixture codes after long drives

P2530.d: P2530 is the general fault of the hard-wired run signal that tells a powertrain module the ignition switch is in its run position. Modules use this line to wake up, power their outputs and decide when to start their internal shutdown routine; many also cross-check it against the ignition status sent over the network. The code says the signal is missing or unreadable without stating a direction. Ford lists P2530 in the 2014 BOSS 302S engine module code table without a MIL marker; no maker publishes trigger values. Typical causes are a blown fuse or relay in the run feed, a loose terminal or a worn ignition switch contact. P2531 and P2532 report a definite low or high level; P2533 to P2535 cover the run/start circuit.
c: Blown fuse or faulty relay in the run feed
Loose terminal at the module or ignition switch
s: Warning lamps or stored codes in several modules
Engine may stall or not start
Modules staying awake after key-off

P2531.t: Ignition Switch Run Position Circuit Low
P2531.d: The engine module logs P2531 if the run-position input stays low although the vehicle state says the ignition is on, for example while the engine runs or the network reports run. The supply side is the usual suspect: an open fuse, a relay that does not pull in, a wire grounded on the body or a switch contact that no longer carries current. The module then behaves as if the key were turned off and may start shutting down. Ford's 2014 BOSS 302S code table is the one public manufacturer listing; there P2531 carries the M marker, so Ford lights the MIL for it, unlike the neutral P2530 and the high-side P2532. No thresholds are published. Drivers may face a stall, a restart problem or several warning lamps at once.
c: Open fuse in the run circuit
Run signal wire shorted to ground
s: MIL on
Engine stalls or will not restart
Several warning lamps or communication codes at once

P2532.t: Ignition Switch Run Position Circuit High
P2532.d: P2532 means voltage is present on the run-position input when it should be absent, typically after key-off or while the network reports the ignition as off. A run feed backfed through another component, a relay with welded contacts or a wire touching a permanent battery feed can cause it. The module then cannot tell that the driver has switched off, stays awake and may drain the battery or delay its own shutdown tests. Ford includes P2532 in the 2014 BOSS 302S code table, without a MIL marker, whereas the low-side P2531 is flagged for the MIL there. No maker publishes voltages or timing. The open or general fault is P2530; the related run/start high fault is P2535.
c: Voltage backfeed into the run circuit through another component
Run wire touching a permanent battery feed
s: Battery drained after the vehicle is parked
Modules or fans keep running after key-off

P2533.d: P2533 is the general fault of the circuit that is live in both the on and the start position of the ignition switch, often called run/crank. Unlike the pure run line it must stay powered while the starter turns, so modules rely on it to remain awake during cranking. Ford lists P2533 in its 2014 BOSS 302S code table with the M marker for the MIL. Ford also published bulletin 21-2244 for 2021 Mustang Mach-E built before 7 July 2021: the MIL could come on with P061A, P1A1E and/or P2533 because of parameters in the powertrain control module, and the remedy is reprogramming the PCM and other modules. Wiring checks still come first on older vehicles. Low and high are P2534 and P2535.
c: Powertrain module software or parameters (Ford Mach-E 2021, reprogramming per TSB 21-2244)
Fuse or relay fault in the run/crank feed
Loose or corroded terminal at the module
s: MIL on
Possible no-start or stall during cranking

P2534.t: Ignition Switch On/Start Position Circuit Low
P2534.d: P2534 is the most widely documented of this group. GM's 2025 tables let the TCM fail it when its run/crank input is false while the ECM reports run/crank active, 99 failures out of 240 samples at 25 ms, Type A; the brake control module (EBCM) sets it when its primary wakeup line reads low for 3 s while the network says run or crank, Type B. On the 2016 Volt the line must drop below 2.0 V for 2.5 s. GM bulletins name an ECM harness rubbed through where it passes the left upper control arm bracket on 2020–2025 Silverado/Sierra 2500HD/3500HD (24-NA-124: MIL, stall, no start) and a TCM recalibration for 2008 CTS/STS with the 6L50 (PIP4276B). Ram's 08-037-21 lists it for the 2021 eTorque 1500. Ford's 2014 BOSS 302S table carries it without the M marker.
c: Engine harness chafed at a bracket (GM HD trucks, upper control arm bracket)
Module software needing an update (GM 6L50 TCM, Ram eTorque HCP)
Loose terminal on the wakeup line at TCM or BCM
s: MIL on
Stall or no start
Transmission or other modules set follow-up codes

P2535.t: Ignition Switch On/Start Position Circuit High
P2535.d: P2535 means the run/crank input stays active while it should be off. GM's 2025 tables fail it in the TCM after 320 of 400 samples with run/crank true while the ECM reports it inactive, Type A, and in the brake control module (EBCM) when the primary wakeup line stays high for 3 s against the network status, Type B; the 2016 Volt uses more than 6.0 V on the line with run/crank inactive. GM bulletin PIT6396 describes a concrete backfeed: once a new K111 fuel pump driver module goes into 2020–2023 Silverado/Sierra with the 3.0L or 6.6L diesel, about 2 V return on ignition circuit 439 via the wiring of the sensor that detects water in the fuel once the key is off. Ram also lists P2535 for the 2021 1500 eTorque. Ford's BOSS 302S table shows no MIL marker.
c: Voltage backfeed from another module (GM K111 fuel pump driver via water-in-fuel sensor circuit)
Run/crank wire touching a battery feed
s: MIL on, code returns at every key-on after clearing
Modules stay awake, battery drain

P2536.d: P2536 is the general fault of the accessory input, the signal that is live when the key or start button is in the accessory position and that on many vehicles also acts as a wake-up line between body and powertrain modules. The code does not say whether the line is open, low or high, only that its state cannot be used. No manufacturer documents P2536 publicly. The best analogue is P2537, which GM evaluates in engine and transmission modules; in bulletin PIT5308 GM explains that the ECM and TCM receive a 12 V accessory wake-up from the body module on circuit 5985. A faulty accessory line can disable functions that need modules awake with the engine off, such as remote start. Low and high levels are P2537 and P2538.
c: Fault in the accessory feed or wake-up output of the body module
Loose or corroded terminal on the accessory line
Worn accessory contact in the ignition switch
s: Remote start or key-off functions not working
Accessories behave inconsistently in the accessory position

P2537.t: Ignition Switch Accessory Position Circuit Low
P2537.d: P2537 reports that the accessory or accessory wake-up input sits low where a high level is expected. GM documents it in detail: on the 2016 Volt the ECM fails it when the accessory input is false while the propulsion system has been active for more than 0.5 s; it is a Type B fault over 2 trips, and the 6-speed TCM tables evaluate the same input with no MIL. GM bulletin PIT5308 for 2014–2015 Silverado, Sierra, Tahoe, Yukon, Suburban and Escalade links P2537 to remote start, and a power liftgate that only works with the ignition on, because ECM and TCM do not get the 12 V accessory wake-up from the BCM on circuit 5985; that wire is checked with a voltmeter, not a test lamp. A diesel follow-up (PIT5308A) adds a blower that keeps running after shutdown.
c: Open or high-resistance accessory wake-up circuit between BCM and ECM/TCM
Body control module not driving the wake-up output
Poor terminal contact at ECM or TCM connector
s: Remote start inoperative
Power liftgate works only with ignition on
Blower may keep running after engine shutdown (diesel)

P2538.t: Ignition Switch Accessory Position Circuit High
P2538.d: P2538 is set when the accessory input reads high in a state where it should be inactive, for instance once the vehicle is switched off and the body module should have released the line. Backfeed from an aftermarket device, a stuck accessory relay or a wire touching a battery feed are the obvious causes. A permanently high accessory line can keep modules awake and drain the battery. No manufacturer publishes P2538; the documented counterpart is GM's P2537, judged on the accessory wake-up signal against propulsion status, and GM's PIT5308 notes that some voltage after key-off is normal while the body module is still awake, so timing matters before calling the line faulty. P2536 is the general and P2537 the low fault.
c: Backfeed from aftermarket equipment connected to the accessory line
Accessory wire chafed against a battery feed
s: Battery drain while parked
Radio or accessories stay on after key-off

P2539.t: Low Pressure Fuel System Sensor Circuit
P2539.d: P2539 is the general circuit code of the sensor that reports the supply pressure ahead of the high-pressure pump. In VW's 2014 specification books for the Passat, CC and Touareg it is set once the signal exceeds 4.80 V, which the Passat book attributes to a broken line or contact with the positive supply; below 0.2 V VW stores P2541 instead. Deutz's EMR controller files P2539-F0 for a ground fault of the supply pressure sensor. Ford's 2015 Transit with the 3.2 L Duratorq TDCi has a pressure switch: per SSM 51033, units built from 6 March 2015 may log P2539 in a key-on engine-off self-test because no switch change is seen after shutdown, and the code can be ignored if the engine-running test and the MIL are clean. P2540 to P2543 narrow the fault down. Without the signal, supply pressure control runs on a substitute value.
c: Signal or ground wire open, connector not engaged
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Failed low-pressure fuel sensor or pressure switch
Code logged only in a static self-test without a real fault (Ford Transit 2015)
s: Check engine light
Hesitation or reduced power under load
Hard starting, especially after standing

P253A.d: The PTO sense circuit tells the powertrain modules whether the power take-off is really engaged, usually through a pressure or limit switch on the PTO unit. This feedback matters for OBD: CARB allows makers to suspend affected monitors only while PTO is active and requires readiness to be cleared after 750 minutes of cumulative PTO runtime, and Ford's 2012 summary notes that readiness flags are set to not ready during PTO mode with only circuit checks continuing. P253A means the feedback line is open or unreadable. No manufacturer publishes P253A with thresholds; the documented sibling is P253D on Ram heavy-duty trucks. With the signal missing, PTO-dependent functions and shift or idle strategies may be disabled.
c: Open sense wire or disconnected plug at the PTO unit
Failed PTO pressure or limit switch
PTO feedback configured in the module but no PTO fitted
s: PTO status not shown or PTO functions unavailable
Readiness monitors behave unexpectedly

P253B.d: P253B is not about a broken wire but about a PTO feedback signal that is electrically valid yet does not fit the situation. A module can compare the sense input with the operator request, engine speed or transmission state: PTO reported engaged although nobody selected it, or no engagement feedback although the PTO was commanded long enough ago. Sticking engagement mechanics, a slow pressure switch or a misadjusted limit switch typically cause this. No maker publishes P253B or its plausibility rules. The OBD relevance follows from CARB, which ties monitor suspension and readiness handling to the time a PTO unit is active, so a wrong PTO status distorts that accounting. Circuit faults are P253A, P253C, P253D; dropouts are P253E.
c: Limit or position switch on the PTO misadjusted
PTO engagement mechanism or clutch sticking
Low air or oil pressure at the PTO engagement and pressure switch
s: PTO engagement reported wrongly in the cluster or scan tool
Delayed or failed PTO engagement
Monitors not completing

P253C.d: P253C flags a PTO feedback input that reads too low for any valid switch state. Where the sense switch closes to ground on engagement, a grounded wire looks like a permanently engaged PTO; where it pulls up, the same fault hides every engagement. Common causes are a wire rubbed through near the transmission-mounted PTO, oil or water in the switch connector and a shorted pressure switch. No maker publishes P253C; Ram's bulletins on the high-side code P253D show that some makers evaluate this input in the transmission module, and Ford states that readiness is reset while PTO mode runs, so a false engaged signal can keep monitors from completing. Open circuit is P253A, high level P253D.
c: Sense wire rubbed through to ground near the PTO
Oil or water in the sense switch connector
s: PTO shown as engaged although it is off, or never shown as engaged
Readiness monitors stay incomplete
Possible MIL

P253D.d: P253D means the PTO feedback input reads above its valid range. Besides genuine shorts to voltage or an open ground on the sense switch, Ram documents a software cause: bulletin 21-013-15 (replacing 21-005-14) covers 2013–2014 Ram 3500 pickups and 3500, 4500 and 5500 chassis cabs with the 6.7L Cummins and Aisin AS69RC six-speed, where the MIL came on with P253D stored in the transmission module although no defect could be found. The fix was a TCM reflash followed by a quick learn. Its later successor 21-017-19, in revision A, repeats this for 2013–2017 models with that gearbox. So Ram evaluates the PTO sense line in the TCM and treats P253D as MIL-relevant. Open circuit is P253A, low P253C.
c: Outdated TCM calibration (Ram heavy-duty with Aisin AS69RC, reflash per bulletin)
Sense wire shorted to a voltage source
Open ground or reference at the PTO sense switch
s: MIL on without a noticeable PTO problem
PTO status wrong in scan data

P253E.d: P253E is stored when the PTO feedback signal flickers between states faster or more often than a real engagement could explain. Vibration on a frame-mounted or transmission-mounted PTO is the classic trigger: a loose terminal, a cracked wire near a bracket or a bouncing switch contact make the signal chatter. Because CARB lets makers pause monitors only while PTO is active and Ford clears readiness for the duration of PTO mode, a chattering sense line can repeatedly switch the OBD system into and out of its PTO state. No manufacturer publishes P253E with counts or time windows; Ram's P253D bulletins merely confirm that the sense input feeds the TCM on some trucks. Steady faults are P253A, P253C and P253D; implausible states P253B.
c: Loose or spread terminal in the sense switch connector
Wire cracked by vibration near the PTO
Worn sense switch with bouncing contact
s: PTO indicator flickers
PTO-related idle or shift strategy switches on and off
Readiness monitors keep resetting

P253F.d: P253F states that the engine computer considers the oil used up. Depending on the design this verdict comes from an oil quality sensor or, more often, from an oil life model that tallies operating conditions such as load, temperatures and estimated fuel dilution. Ford's 2014 BOSS 302S engine code table contains P253F without a lamp entry; exact criteria are published by no maker. Jeep shows how sensitive such a model is: for the 2022 Grand Cherokee 4xe with the 2.0 L turbo PHEV engine, bulletin 18-013-23 updates the PCM because the displayed oil life fell too fast once calculated dilution was high; the same update concerns electric mode being unavailable during the Fuel Oil Refresh Mode. Usual triggers are an overdue oil change, a counter not reset after service or heavy short-trip use. Quality sensor circuit faults are P252A to P252E.
c: Oil change overdue, oil actually aged
Oil life counter not reset after the last oil change
Strong fuel dilution from short trips, cold operation or frequent regenerations
Oil life calculation in the engine software too aggressive (update available)
s: Oil change or oil quality warning in the cluster
Remaining oil life shown as zero or dropping unusually fast

P2540.t: Low Pressure Fuel System Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2540.d: P2540 checks whether the low-pressure fuel sensor's reading is credible. The signal stays inside its electrical window, yet the pressure it reports does not fit what the supply side should be delivering. In VW's 2014 Touareg specification book the code appears only in the chapter for engine code CGFA, which also carries the hybrid high-voltage faults; the criterion is a deviation of actual pressure, with limits given as 800 and 80 kPa. The chapter for engine code CGRA lists only P2539 and P2541. Ram counts P2540-00 among the faults addressed by a PCM reflash in bulletin 18-021-25 for the 2025 Ram 3500 with the 6.7 L Cummins HO, so software can be involved. Genuine causes are a weak supply pump or a clogged filter. P2539, P2541 and P2542 are circuit faults, P2543 dropouts. Hesitation or hard starts are possible.
c: Weak in-tank or lift pump causing real pressure deviation
Restricted fuel filter or kinked supply line
s: Check engine light
Hesitation or power loss under load
Long cranking or hard starting

P2541.t: Low Pressure Fuel System Sensor Circuit Low
P2541.d: P2541 means the signal of the low-pressure fuel sensor is below its valid range - typically a short to ground on the signal line or a lost 5 V sensor supply. VW's 2014 specification books set it below 0.2 V on the Passat, CC and Touareg (VW labels it short to ground, low input or out of range low), whereas a signal above 4.8 V leads to P2539. Under CARB rules, inputs able to influence emissions must be watched for broken circuits and readings beyond their valid span. Without a valid reading the engine computer can only run the fuel supply pump on a substitute value, so pressure control becomes coarse. P2540 is the plausibility fault, P2542 the high-side fault, P2543 an intermittent signal. Symptoms range from none to hesitation under load or hard starting.
c: 5 V reference supply missing or pulled down by another sensor
s: Check engine light
Hesitation under load
Possible hard starting

P2542.t: Low Pressure Fuel System Sensor Circuit High
P2542.d: P2542 means the low-pressure fuel sensor reports a voltage above its permitted range. Deutz is explicit: its MD1 controller stores P2542 when the supply pressure sensor signal rises beyond its normal voltage or is shorted toward the high side (SPN 94, FMI 3), and the EMR system describes P2542-00 as a battery short. P2542 also appears in the list Ford published for the BOSS 302S engine module of 2014. VW, by contrast, does not use P2542 in its 2014 books for the Passat, CC and Touareg and files a signal above 4.80 V as P2539. Besides a short to the 5 V reference or battery voltage, a broken sensor ground can lift the signal. A falsely high reading can mask a real lack of supply pressure, so the engine may lose power without an obvious reason. P2541 is the low-side counterpart, P2540 the plausibility fault, P2543 short dropouts.
c: Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Sensor ground wire or pin interrupted
Failed low-pressure fuel sensor with high output
s: Check engine light
Reduced power or stalling if real pressure is low
Hard starting

P2543.t: Low Pressure Fuel System Sensor Circuit Intermittent
P2543.d: P2543 reports a low-pressure fuel sensor signal with brief interruptions or spikes, although it remains within its electrical range most of the time - a loose pin, a chafed wire or a sensor with an internal contact problem. Ram names P2543-00 for trucks with the 6.7 L Cummins HO in two PCM software bulletins, 18-013-26 (Ram 2500) and 18-021-25 (Ram 3500), each covering model year 2025 and each listing it next to P2540-00. Flawed calibration can therefore also produce entries. Other manufacturers do not publish thresholds for this code. CARB requires input components to be checked for circuit faults and, where feasible, rationality. P2541/P2542 describe a steady low or high signal, P2540 a plausibility fault. The code often comes and goes, sometimes with brief stumbling.
c: Loose or corroded pin at the sensor connector
Chafed signal or supply wire with intermittent contact
s: Check engine light, often intermittent
Brief stumbling or hesitation
No symptoms between events

P2544.t: Torque Management Request Input Signal A
P2544.d: P2544 concerns torque requests that another module, usually the transmission control module, sends to the engine module – for example to cut torque during a shift. GM's 2020 table 20OBDG04 checks each TCM message for a wrong protection value (16 of 20), a broken rolling counter (6 of 10), an increase request above 1,298 Nm (6 of 10) or the request type toggling too often (3 of 5), type B with two trips. GM's 2012 bulletin PIC4740C for 2006–2013 Cadillac ATS, CTS, SRX and STS with six-speed automatics traces P2544 with many U-codes, hard shifts and no-crank to loose pins in the transmission X1 connector. A GM engineering bulletin on the 2019–2022 Malibu 1.5 L turbo names it next to lost-communication codes; Ford's BOSS 302S list of 2014 has it without a lamp mark. P2545 is the plausibility fault.
c: Loose or unseated pins at the transmission connector
Data bus disturbance or failing gateway
Transmission module software or internal fault
s: Check engine light, often with several U-codes
Harsh shifts or reduced engine power
Multiple warning lamps, possibly no-crank

P2545.t: Torque Management Request Input Signal A Range/Performance
P2545.d: P2545 means torque request A arrives intact but carries values the receiving module cannot accept as plausible – a requested torque outside the expected window, a request that contradicts the operating state, or one that does not follow up as it should. Ford's 2014 BOSS 302S engine module table lists P2545 with M, i.e. with check engine light. Jaguar Land Rover shows that the code can live in the transmission module as well: bulletin SSM73291 (2018) covers Discovery Sport from 2015MY and Range Rover Evoque from 2014MY with the ZF 9HP48 nine-speed, where the TCM logs P2545-86 and/or P2546-86; dealers should first fix oil leaks and level, then load newer TCM software, and escalate only if it returns. P2544 is the general signal fault, P2546 and P2547 low and high.
c: Transmission oil leak or incorrect oil level (JLR 9HP48)
Requesting module sends implausible torque values
s: Check engine light (Ford) or transmission warning
Harsh or delayed shifts

P2546.t: Torque Management Request Input Signal A Low
P2546.d: P2546 says that torque request A, the channel over which one module asks another to raise or cut engine torque, reads below its permitted floor. On a hard-wired request this points to a line pulled toward ground; on a data-bus request it means a value pinned at or under the minimum the receiver accepts. Jaguar is the clearest user: SSM73594 (December 2017) covers the 2018MY E-Pace with the ZF 9HP48 nine-speed, whose transmission module stores P2546-86, sometimes together with P2545-86, while the root cause was still being investigated. The dealer sequence is leak check, oil level, newer TCM software, then clear and only call technical assistance if it returns; Land Rover issued a matching note, SSM73291, for its own 9HP48 models. P2547 is the high-side counterpart. Drivers may notice rough or delayed shifts.
c: Oil leak or low oil level in the transmission
Wired request line shorted to ground
s: Harsh or delayed gear changes
Transmission warning message or check engine light
Fault often stored together with P2545

P2547.t: Torque Management Request Input Signal A High
P2547.d: P2547 is logged when torque request A sits above the highest value the receiving module will accept. A wired input would read like a line touching a supply voltage or a lost ground at the sender; a bus message would carry an out-of-scale number. The receiver ignores such a request, since following it could mean an unwanted torque increase. No maker documents P2547 publicly. How input A is checked can be seen in GM's 2020 table 20OBDG04, where the engine module tests the transmission module's torque messages for protection value, rolling counter and an upper torque limit of 1,298 Nm, but under the general code P2544 rather than a separate high code. CARB requires such inputs to be monitored when they affect emissions or other diagnostics. P2546 is the low side, P2551 the high fault on input B.
c: Request line shorted to a supply voltage
Requesting module sends a value above the scale
Poor ground at the requesting module
s: Shift-related torque reduction no longer works, firmer shifts
Check engine light depending on make

P2548.t: Torque Management Request Input Signal B
P2548.d: P2548 is the general fault on a second torque request channel, B, used when a further module besides the transmission may ask the engine for less or more torque. GM spells out who sits on channel B: in the ECM part of its 2017 table 17OBDG04 and again in 19OBDG03A, P2548 checks the traction torque and speed request coming from the electronic brake and traction control module. A failure is counted when the message's two's-complement protection value does not match, at least 10 of 20 samples, or when the rolling counter fails to step up, at least 6 of 10. The test runs with run/crank active for over 0.5 s, ignition above 6.41 V and no lost-communication code U0121; GM rates it Type B, two trips. Traction or stability intervention via the engine may then be limited. P2549 to P2551 are its narrower faults.
c: Data bus disturbance between brake module and engine module
Brake/traction control module sends corrupted messages
Weak battery or poor module power supply
s: Check engine light after two trips (GM Type B)
Traction or stability control warning lamp
Reduced traction intervention on slippery roads

P2549.t: Torque Management Request Input Signal B Range/Performance
P2549.d: P2549 covers a torque request on channel B that arrives readable but makes no sense: a requested torque outside the expected band, a request that contradicts the current driving state, or one that changes in a way the sender could not plausibly mean. The wiring or bus link is assumed intact here, which separates it from the general fault P2548. No maker documents P2549 publicly. In GM's 2017 engine tables channel B carries the intervention wish of the brake/traction module, which GM validates under P2548 only. CARB obliges makers to check input components for rational values when they matter for emissions or for other monitors. The equivalent code on channel A is P2545; P2550 and P2551 are the low and high faults on B. Traction control may act less smoothly.
c: Requesting module (e.g. brake/traction module) computes implausible values
Software levels of sender and engine module do not match
Faulty input data at the requesting module, such as wheel speed
s: Check engine light depending on make
Traction control intervenes abruptly or not at all

P254A.d: P254A covers the first PTO speed selector: the switch or sensor an operator uses to choose one of the preset working speeds for a power take-off. The engine controller expects a defined signal on this line; with P254A it finds no valid state, typically a broken wire, an unplugged connector or a switch contact that never closes. No maker documents P254A publicly. GM's UI Bulletin 80c for 2008–2014 Silverado/Sierra 3500 chassis cabs shows why an open line is hard to catch: the remote set input reads 1.66–3.33 V as a legitimate standby request.
