Deutz files the same fault on its multi-stage speed selector under its own code P3045-13. P254B–P254E are the plausibility, low, high and intermittent faults. The truck drives normally; only the chosen PTO speed is not reached.
c: Broken selector signal or return wire
Selector or upfitter connector disconnected or pushed-out pin
Switch contact that no longer closes
s: PTO stays at standby speed instead of the selected step
Selected working speed cannot be called up
Stored code without effect on normal driving

P254B.d: P254B is the rationality fault of PTO speed selector 1. The wiring is intact and the voltage sits inside the electrical limits, yet the reading does not fit any configured position, or it contradicts other information the controller holds, for example two speed requests at once or a value that lingers between steps. CARB's OBD rule defines this kind of check as verifying an input against all other available data while it is within its normal range. No manufacturer publishes P254B; Deutz shows the idea with P3045-1C, value out of range, on its multi-stage speed selector. Typical culprits are a contaminated or worn rotary switch, a wrong resistor in an upfitter's coding ladder, or a selector configured for a different scheme. The PTO may refuse to leave standby speed.
c: Wrong resistor value in the upfitter's speed coding
Controller configured for a different selector type
s: PTO does not leave standby speed
Wrong working speed for the selected position

P254C.t: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 1 Circuit Low
P254C.d: P254C reports that the signal from PTO speed selector 1 sits below the lowest voltage the controller accepts, which in practice means the signal wire touches ground or the switch is shorted internally. Whether a maker can detect this at all depends on the design. In GM's UI Bulletin 80c a grounded remote set input is simply read as a request for Set Speed 1, factory 1250 rpm, so a chafed wire would quietly raise engine speed instead of setting a code; a resistor-coded selector leaves room for a separate fault band. Deutz records the same condition on its multi-stage selector as P3045-11, short to ground. No maker publishes P254C itself. The opposite fault, a reading above the top limit, is P254D. Expect PTO speed stuck at one step or PTO disabled.
c: Selector signal wire chafed through to ground
Internal short in the selector switch
Water in an exterior selector connector
s: PTO speed stuck at one step
PTO blocked by the controller

P254D.t: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 1 Circuit High
P254D.d: With P254D the controller sees the PTO speed selector 1 input above its upper limit. Causes are a signal wire rubbing against a battery-fed circuit, a broken ground or sensor return that lets the line float to the pull-up voltage, or a selector supply that is too high. Deutz separates these on its multi-stage speed selector: P3045-12 for a short to battery and P3045-A1 for a supply voltage outside its range. In GM's 2008–2014 chassis-cab PTO system a remote set input above 3.33 V is a valid choice, Set Speed 2 at 1700 rpm by default, which again shows that only a coded selector can flag this state. No manufacturer publishes P254D. P254C is the low-side counterpart. Operators notice the PTO jumping to the highest step or not engaging.
c: Signal wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit
Open ground or return line letting the input float high
s: PTO jumps to the highest preset speed
PTO does not engage

P254E.t: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 1 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P254E.d: P254E is set when the signal from PTO speed selector 1 changes faster or more often than a real switch operation can explain, or briefly drops out and returns. Each short glitch can be read as a new speed request, and engine speed then hunts between steps; on Ram chassis cabs with the VSIM interface the controller ramps between the remote presets at 200 rpm per second, so a chattering contact produces audible surging. No manufacturer documents P254E publicly. CARB requires circuit faults on monitored input components to be checked continuously rather than once per trip, which is how brief interruptions get caught. Vibration on a body-mounted switch panel, loose terminals and corroded upfitter splices are the usual sources. P254A covers a steady open circuit.
c: Loose terminal at the selector or upfitter connector
Corroded splice in the upfitter wiring
Vibration on a body-mounted switch panel
s: Engine speed surges while the PTO is running
PTO drops briefly to standby speed
Code comes and goes

P254F.d: P254F concerns the circuit of the hood switch, which tells the control units whether the engine hood is open. Engines that can start on their own, such as in hybrids or stop/start systems, need this to block an automatic start while someone works under the hood. GM documents the code in the ECM section of its 2012 table 12OBDG06 for the two-mode hybrid Tahoe, Yukon, Escalade, Sierra and Silverado: the engine module reads two hood switch states, checks every 25 ms with run/crank voltage between 11 and 32 V, and sets the fault after 0.5 s as Type B, two trips. GM's later 2017 table 17OBDG04 moved this kind of switch-versus-switch plausibility to P257D, which matches the J2012 range/performance wording. A broken switch or wiring can disable auto-start and raise a warning.
c: Hood switch dirty, corroded or misadjusted
Damaged wiring or connector at the hood latch
Bent hood latch after a front-end repair
s: Check engine light after two trips (GM Type B)
Auto-stop or hybrid engine start disabled
Hood-open warning while the hood is closed

P2550.t: Torque Management Request Input Signal B Low
P2550.d: P2550 marks the second torque request input, B, as stuck below its lower limit. A hard-wired line would be pulled to ground by chafed insulation or a fault in the sending stage; in a networked design the sender would be reporting a value that lies under the bottom of the defined range. The engine module then disregards input B and keeps running on its own torque calculation. No maker documents P2550 publicly. GM's 2019 table 19OBDG03A assigns the B channel to the traction request of the electronic brake and traction control module, sent in messages $1C8/$237, and checks it only with the general code P2548. CARB requires electronic inputs to be monitored for out-of-range values when they influence emissions. P2551 is the high-side fault, P2546 the low fault on input A.
c: Request line chafed through and shorted to ground
Output stage of the requesting module defective
s: Check engine light depending on make
Traction-related torque reduction no longer applied

P2551.t: Torque Management Request Input Signal B High
P2551.d: P2551 is the high-side fault of torque request B: the signal sits above the top of its valid window. Typical electrical causes would be a line touching a battery feed, an interrupted reference ground or a sender that drives its output to full scale. Because an unexpectedly high request could translate into unwanted torque, the engine module discards it and works without channel B. No maker documents P2551 publicly. GM's ECM table 17OBDG04 shows that a vehicle can fill channel B with the brake and traction module's request and validates it with protection value and message counter under P2548, with no separate high code. CARB requires monitoring of such electronic inputs whenever a failure could raise emissions or blind another monitor. P2550 is the low-side fault, P2547 the high fault on input A.
c: Request line shorted to battery voltage
Open ground or reference at the sender
Requesting module drives its output to full scale
s: Check engine light depending on make
Traction control warning, engine ignores intervention requests

P2552.d: P2552 is the general circuit fault of throttle/fuel inhibit A, a line over which the engine module can be told, or can itself command, that throttle opening or fuelling must be blocked. It acts as a safety path next to the normal pedal-to-throttle chain. Ford lists P2552 in the engine module code table of its 2014 BOSS 302S race car, worded as circuit/open; its lamp column stays empty, and Ford gives no thresholds. A 2005 GM diagnostic summary for the L66 3.5-litre V6 shows how such a line is monitored, though only with the narrower codes P2553 to P2555, which test the inhibit relay and the voltage on the inhibit circuit after ignition off. If the path is broken, the module may limit power to stay safe. P2553 is the plausibility fault, P2554 and P2555 low and high.
c: Inhibit line open, e.g. broken wire or pushed-out pin
Inhibit relay or its supply defective
Engine module input or output stage faulty
s: Usually no check engine light (Ford non-MIL)
Possible power limitation or no throttle response

P2553.d: P2553 means the throttle/fuel inhibit path A is electrically present but does not behave as commanded. GM's 2005 diagnostic table for the 3.5 L L66 engine files it under electronic throttle control and runs it as a function check of the inhibit relay over a serial data link: a healthy relay produces no serial data, so any data seen there counts as a failure. The test needs battery voltage above 7 V and the key off, and judges a fault within 0.2 s. Like the other inhibit checks in that table it runs once per driving cycle after the ignition is switched off, so the lamp comes on only during the following drive. In that table the throttle valve monitor also has two processors cross-checking each other. P2552 is the general circuit code, P2554 and P2555 voltage faults on the same line.
c: Inhibit relay sticking or contacts worn
Fault in the relay control or feedback wiring
Internal fault in the engine or throttle control unit
s: Check engine light on the drive after the fault was found
Possible reduced power or throttle limp mode

P2554.d: P2554 reports that the voltage on throttle/fuel inhibit circuit A is too low. In GM's 2005 L66 parameter sheet the limit is below 0.498 V on the analogue inhibit circuit, read by the powertrain module while it is still processing after the ignition has been switched off. The table lists a warm engine, coolant at 69.5 °C or more, among the enable conditions. Since the check takes place after shutdown, the lamp lights on the next drive rather than at once. A low reading usually comes from a short to ground somewhere in the inhibit wiring or a pull-down inside a connected unit. The relay itself is judged under P2553, an over-voltage on the same line under P2555, and P2552 is the general circuit fault. Drivers may meet a throttle that reacts sluggishly or a reduced-power mode.
c: Connected relay or control unit pulls the line down
s: Check engine light on the following drive
Sluggish throttle response or reduced power

P2555.d: P2555 indicates excess voltage on throttle/fuel inhibit circuit A. The same 2005 GM document for the L66 V6 uses two limits depending on key state: more than 10 V while the ignition is on, or more than 4.5 V once it is off, with the fault judged after 4 s. As with its sibling checks, monitoring happens after shutdown, a single time per drive cycle, and the lamp waits until the next trip. A line that should be at a low level reading close to system voltage hints at a short to a battery-fed wire, a relay stuck closed or a lost ground on the receiving side. P2554 is the low-voltage counterpart, P2553 the relay function check and P2552 the general circuit fault. CARB requires makers to monitor electronic inputs of this kind for out-of-range values. Effects can include limited throttle or reduced power.
c: Inhibit circuit shorted to a battery-fed wire
Missing ground on the receiving side
s: Check engine light on the next trip
Limited throttle opening or reduced power

P2556.d: P2556 is the general circuit code for the coolant level sensor or switch, normally fitted in the expansion tank. Deutz uses it on its EMR L1 engine control for industrial engines with the sub-code P2556-F0, a ground error, under SPN 111. Mercedes-Benz goes its own way and stores P2556-7B, meaning the sensor reports a fluid level that is too low. Bulletin LI20.30-P-078333 (August 2024) covers the EQB, where this code lands in the signal acquisition module SAM N10: air pushed into the circuit by the electric drive forms a cushion in the tank, so the level drops below the warning mark while driving; a red cap, filling 20 mm over max and if needed a revised tank fix it. LI09.41-N-079165 for OM654 Sprinter vans links the same code to coolant lost through an intercooler that leaks internally. P2560 is the plain low-level code.
c: Damaged wiring or ground at the level sensor
Air cushion in the expansion tank (Mercedes EQB)
Real coolant loss, e.g. internal charge air cooler leak
s: Low coolant warning in the cluster
Coolant level appears correct after opening the cap

P2557.t: Engine Coolant Level Sensor/Switch Circuit Range/Performance
P2557.d: P2557 means the coolant level signal is electrically present but not believable. The Deutz EMR L1 engine control is the one documented user and fills the code twice under SPN 111: P2557-00 for a sensor value outside the valid range, and P2557-1C when the supply voltage feeding the level sensor is itself out of range. The second case is worth checking first, because a weak or overloaded sensor supply skews the reading without any fault at the sensor. Mechanical effects can also confuse a level sensor; Mercedes describes for the EQB how an air cushion in the expansion tank pushed the measured level below the warning mark although enough coolant was present. Shorts to ground or open lines belong to P2558, a short to battery to P2559, and P2556 is the general circuit code. Expect a coolant warning that is unreliable.
c: Sensor supply voltage out of range (Deutz P2557-1C)
Level sensor element contaminated or failing
Air pocket or foam in the expansion tank distorting the reading
s: Coolant level warning appears and disappears
Engine protection warning on industrial engines

P2558.t: Engine Coolant Level Sensor/Switch Circuit Low
P2558.d: P2558 reports that the coolant level sensor or switch signal sits too low on the electrical scale. Deutz assigns it on the EMR L1 controller as P2558-14 under SPN 111 and groups two causes together: a grounded line or an interrupted one, which on that input both pull the reading to the bottom. The repair therefore starts by measuring the signal line to ground and checking it for continuity between control unit and tank, including the connector at the expansion tank, which sits in a hot and wet area. Note that a low signal is an electrical finding, not proof that coolant is missing; an actual low level is logged as P2560. On Mercedes passenger cars, by contrast, the level warning is coded P2556-7B. P2559 covers the opposite short to battery, P2557 an implausible value. The coolant level warning can no longer be trusted.
c: Broken wire or corroded connector at the expansion tank
s: Permanent low coolant warning despite a full tank
No warning possible if the level really drops

P2559.t: Engine Coolant Level Sensor/Switch Circuit High
P2559.d: P2559 is the high-voltage fault in the circuit of the coolant level sensor or switch. In the Deutz EMR L1 code list it appears as P2559-12 under SPN 111 meaning the line is shorted to battery plus; Deutz keeps open circuits under P2558 on that input, so a high reading there really points to contact with a positive feed. On other designs, especially simple float switches with a pull-up resistor, a broken wire could also produce a high level, so the maker's circuit logic decides what to measure. Wiring near the expansion tank often runs close to battery or fan feeds, which makes chafing a likely cause. P2558 covers the low side, P2557 an implausible but in-range value, P2556 the general circuit fault and P2560 a genuinely low coolant level. Until fixed, the low coolant warning may stay silent.
c: Signal line chafed against a positive feed
Open circuit on pull-up type switch designs
s: Low coolant warning does not work
Warning lamp or message for the level sensor

P255A.d: P255A belongs to the second PTO speed selector input, which lets the operator call up a further preset working speed in addition to selector 1. The controller finds no valid state on this line: a wire is broken, a connector is off, or the switch contact never closes. A real example of such a second input is the VSIM module of 2017 Ram chassis cabs, where grounding the PTO idle speed 2 wire (W542) selects Remote RPM Preset 2; it overrides preset 3 but gives way to preset 1. With that wire open, the second preset simply cannot be reached while preset 1 still works. No manufacturer publishes P255A. P254A is the same fault on selector 1; P255B to P255E describe the other failure types of selector 2.
c: Broken wire between selector 2 and the module
Upfitter connector for selector 2 not mated
s: Second preset speed unavailable
Selector 1 presets still work

P255B.d: P255B flags an implausible reading from PTO speed selector 2 although its circuit is electrically intact. Because a second selector normally works together with the first, the check can compare both: requests that cannot coexist, a level that sits between valid positions, or a selection that the configured number of presets does not allow. On Ram chassis cabs from 2012 the Cummins controller can be set to between one and five remote PTO speeds, so a selector reporting a step beyond the programmed count would be a candidate for such a fault. CARB calls this a rationality diagnostic. No manufacturer documents P255B publicly. Suspects are a sticky switch, an upfitter wiring mistake that ties both inputs together, or a configuration that does not match the hardware.
c: Upfitter wiring ties selector 1 and 2 together
Number of programmed presets does not match the switch
s: Second preset ignored or wrong speed reached
PTO speed control falls back to standby

P255C.t: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 2 Circuit Low
P255C.d: P255C means the input of PTO speed selector 2 reads lower than the controller's bottom limit, usually because the signal wire has a short to chassis ground or the switch is shorted inside. On designs where a grounded line is itself the command, as with the switch-to-ground inputs of Ram's 2017 VSIM, a short looks exactly like a permanently held preset 2 request; the controller can only tell the difference when the selector is resistor-coded or monitored with a diagnostic current. No manufacturer publishes P255C. P255D is the high-side fault on the same input, P254C the low fault on selector 1. Possible results are an engine that stays at the second working speed whenever PTO is active, or a PTO that the controller blocks.
c: Selector 2 wire shorted to chassis ground
Harness pinched under a body mounting
s: Engine always runs at the second preset in PTO mode
PTO blocked

P255D.t: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 2 Circuit High
P255D.d: P255D is stored when PTO speed selector 2 delivers a signal above the permitted maximum. A chafed wire touching a battery-fed circuit, a lost sensor ground, or an upfitter feeding 12 V into an input meant to be switched to ground are the realistic causes. Upfitter manuals show why the last point matters: Ram describes its VSIM preset inputs as switch-to-ground circuits, while GM's 2008–2014 remote set input interprets anything above 3.33 V as a speed request, so mixing up the conventions of different trucks produces readings outside the expected range. No manufacturer documents P255D publicly. P255C is the low-side code; P254D covers selector 1. The second preset may be unavailable or the PTO is shut off.
c: Selector 2 wire chafed against a battery-fed circuit
Upfitter applies 12 V to a ground-switched input
Lost ground or return line of selector 2
s: Second preset unavailable
PTO switched off by the controller

P255E.t: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 2 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P255E.d: P255E concerns short dropouts or rapid changes on the PTO speed selector 2 signal that do not match deliberate operation. Selector 2 is often the remote control on the body, close to pumps, booms or spreaders, so vibration, spray water and cable movement hit it harder than an in-cab switch. Ram's 2012 chassis cab guide shows the effect of spurious transitions: in remote mode a quick off-on toggle advances to the next of up to five preset speeds, so a flickering contact can step the engine through speeds nobody asked for. No manufacturer publishes P255E. CARB expects such circuit faults to be monitored continuously. P255A would be a permanent open circuit; P254E is the same symptom on selector 1.
c: Spray water or moisture in the body-mounted remote switch
Cable to the remote control flexing at a boom or hinge
Loose crimp or terminal in the selector 2 circuit
s: Engine steps through preset speeds unexpectedly
PTO speed unstable while working
Code appears only under vibration

P255F.d: P255F flags the A/C request A input as electrically sound but implausible: the request may switch on and off far more often than a real compressor demand would, stay set while the climate control is off, or disagree with what the engine module sees from the compressor side. The request lets the engine prepare for the compressor load by raising idle speed and torque reserve. CARB section (e)(12) requires monitoring of electronic A/C components when switching the A/C alters fuel or spark control, including failures that trigger the alternate strategy with the A/C off, phased in over 2006 to 2008. Saab's 2011 9-5 is an example of a design without such a wire, receiving the request as a bus message. No maker documents P255F publicly. P2519 is the general fault on input A, P256F the same check on input B.
c: Climate control module sends erratic requests
Loose contact on the request line causing chatter
s: Idle speed fluctuates when the A/C cycles
A/C cooling intermittent or switched off

P2560.d: P2560 is not an electrical fault but a level finding: the coolant level sensor works, yet it reports less coolant than the minimum. Deutz uses it on the EMR L1 control as P2560-00 under SPN 111 with failure mode 1, meaning the level has fallen under its warning threshold. Ford lists P2560 in the 2014 BOSS 302S engine module table, with no M in the lamp column, i.e. no MIL. Mercedes-Benz reports the same situation differently, under P2556-7B. The usual causes are leaks at hoses, radiator, water pump or heater core, internal leaks such as a charge air cooler or head gasket, or air trapped after a service. Because overheating can follow, top up only with the engine cool and look for the loss. P2556 to P2559 cover faults of the level sensor and its circuit.
c: External leak at hoses, radiator or water pump
Internal leak, e.g. charge air cooler or head gasket
Air trapped after a coolant service
s: Low coolant warning
Rising engine temperature or overheating
Visible coolant traces or sweet smell

P2561.t: A/C Control Module Requested MIL Illumination
P2561.d: P2561 is a messenger code. The climate control module has found an emission-relevant fault in its own area, such as a component that feeds the engine's A/C idle strategy, and asks the engine module to switch on the warning lamp, since only the master controller may drive it. The engine module stores P2561 as a pointer; the actual fault code sits in the A/C module and must be read there. GM's 2012 hybrid table 12OBDG06 illustrates this split: the ECM is the master that controls the lamp, while other controllers store their own codes. CARB's section (e)(12) explains why A/C faults can be emission-relevant at all: wherever the A/C changes fuel or spark control, its electronic parts must be monitored. No maker documents P2561 publicly. Clearing it without fixing the A/C fault brings it back.
c: Emission-relevant fault stored in the climate control module
Failed A/C sensor or actuator behind that fault
Climate control module internal or software fault
s: Check engine light on
A/C may not cool or may be switched off
Further codes stored in the climate control module

P2562.t: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor A Circuit
P2562.d: P2562 flags a general electrical problem in the circuit of the position sensor that reports where turbocharger boost actuator A stands - the variable vane linkage on many diesels, the electric wastegate actuator on turbo petrol engines. The engine computer receives a signal it cannot use at all, as opposed to a wrong position (P2563), a signal pinned low or high (P2564/P2565) or brief dropouts (P2566). Kia service actions SA078 and SA119A for the 2011 and 2012 Optima with the 2.0 T-GDI engine name P2562 together with P2565; the fix is to read the actuator position voltage with the scan tool and reset the rod length of the electronic wastegate actuator. With the code present, boost is usually cut back and the warning lamp is lit.
c: Open or corroded wiring or connector between position sensor and engine computer
Electronic wastegate actuator rod length out of adjustment
Position sensor inside the actuator failed
s: Reduced power because boost is limited
Check engine light on
P2565 stored at the same time on some engines

P2563.t: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P2563.d: P2563 means the position feedback of the turbocharger boost control actuator - variable vanes or wastegate - does not match the commanded position, without an open or short being reported. GM's 2009 Duramax diesel table sets it when vane position differs from target by 15 % or more for 5 s (Type B, warning light after two trips). VW's 2014 Passat book treats a position signal above 4.5 V or below 0.3 V as implausible on the 2.0 L TDI (CKRA), and VW bulletin 21-15-06 links P2563 on 2.0 L TDI engines to kinked vacuum hoses, a leaking vacuum diaphragm or a broken adjustment stud on the turbocharger. P2562/P2564/P2565 are circuit faults, P2566 an intermittent signal. Boost is often limited, so power drops noticeably.
c: Kinked, twisted or leaking vacuum hose to the boost actuator
Leaking actuator diaphragm or sticking vanes
Broken or missing adjustment stud, actuator travel out of tolerance
s: Noticeable loss of power, limp mode
Check engine light
Underboost code P0299 stored at the same time

P2564.t: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor A Circuit Low
P2564.d: P2564 is stored when the voltage from the boost actuator position sensor stays below the lowest value a working sensor can deliver, which usually points to a short to ground or a lost reference supply. GM's 2009 Duramax table uses 0.277 V (5.5 %, vanes fully open) held for 1 s once the engine has run 3 s, Type B. Ford's 2023 diesel OBD summary checks the signal continuously against 0.15 V over 2 s, and VW's 2014 Passat book applies the same 0.15 V limit on the 2.0 L TDI and calls it a short to ground. FCA bulletin 09-003-16 for the 2015-2016 Jeep Renegade 1.6 L sold in EMEA lists P2564 with P2565 and replaces the turbocharger. P2565 is the high-side counterpart, P2563 a position error with a usable signal. Expect reduced power.
c: Signal wire chafed through and touching ground near the turbocharger
5 V reference supply to the sensor missing or shorted
Failed position sensor or vane actuator
s: Noticeable loss of power or limp mode
Check engine light on
Other sensors on the same 5 V supply may report faults too

P2565.t: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor A Circuit High
P2565.d: P2565 means the boost actuator position signal sits above the highest plausible value, typically from an open signal wire, a short to the 5 V reference or battery voltage, or a failed sensor. GM's 2018 diesel ECM table flags it at an analog reading above 95 % in 200 of 250 samples (Type A, warning lamp on the first trip). Kia service action SA149 for the 2011-2012 Sportage 2.0 T-GDI pairs P2565 with P2562, updates the engine software and adjusts the wastegate rod until the position reading lands between roughly 3.8 and 4.1 V, depending on coolant temperature. Ford special service message 53328 offers a separate vane actuator for 2020-2022 F-Super Duty 6.7 L diesels showing P2564/P2565 among other codes. P2564 is the low-side fault. Power is usually limited.
c: Open signal wire or unplugged actuator connector
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Wastegate actuator rod set to the wrong length (electric wastegate engines)
Failed vane actuator with integrated sensor
s: Loss of power, sometimes limp mode
Check engine light on
Unusual turbocharger noise on some diesels

P2566.t: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
P2566.d: P2566 reports that the signal from the boost control position sensor flickers or drops out briefly instead of being steadily wrong. VW bulletins 21-15-04 (2015) and 21-15-06 (2020) for 2009-2014 Jetta, Golf and Jetta SportWagen with the 2.0 L TDI (CBEA, CJAA) list P2566 together with P2562-P2565 and P0299 for the complaint of lacking power; there the position sensor G581 sits in the vacuum diaphragm, and the repair path starts with vacuum hoses, diaphragm and the actuator travel. No thresholds are published. CARB requires turbocharger electronic components to be monitored as comprehensive components. P2563 is the plausibility fault, P2564/P2565 a steady low or high signal. Expect intermittent power loss and a warning light.
c: Loose or corroded pin at the position sensor connector
Heat-damaged or chafed sensor wiring near the turbocharger
Worn position sensor in the actuator
s: Intermittent loss of power or limp mode
Check engine light, sometimes going out again
Surging boost

P2567.t: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Temperature Sensor Circuit
P2567.d: P2567 is the general circuit fault of the sensor fitted to a direct ozone reduction (DOR) radiator - a radiator with a catalytic coating that converts ground-level ozone in the passing air and earns low-emission vehicles an NMOG credit. CARB section (e)(14) requires the OBD system to detect a missing or deteriorated DOR function. No manufacturer publicly documents P2567 itself. VW's 2014 books (CC, Tiguan) use the siblings P2568-P2570 for this sensor, with an identity check and LIN bus faults; MINI's 2015-2016 Cooper S with the B46M PZEV engine carries a LIN-linked catalyst sensor fixed to the radiator, logged under BMW's own fault codes. P2568 is the plausibility fault, P2569-P2571 low, high and intermittent. Often the radiator with its bonded sensor is replaced.
c: Damaged sensor wiring or connector at the radiator
Replacement radiator without coating or without sensor fitted
s: Check engine light
No change in driveability or engine cooling
Possible failed emissions inspection because of the stored code

P2568.t: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2568.d: P2568 is the plausibility check of the sensor on a direct ozone reduction (DOR) radiator, whose coating converts ozone in the cooling air. VW's 2014 specification books for the CC and Tiguan set it on a failed ID check or a failed functional check of the temperature sensor. VW Tech Tip 19-12-01 explains that on 2009-2015 Eos, Jetta, GTI, Passat and Tiguan with the 2.0 L TSI (CCTA, CBFA) this code refers to the radiator identification sensor G611; a new radiator comes with the sensor packed separately, to be bonded on. A non-coated aftermarket radiator or an unbonded sensor therefore triggers P2568. P2569/P2570 are LIN electrical faults, P2567 the general circuit fault. CARB section (e)(14) requires DOR monitoring.
c: Aftermarket radiator without ozone coating or without the identification sensor
Identification sensor not bonded after radiator replacement
s: Check engine light, often after a radiator replacement
No change in driveability or engine cooling
Possible failed emissions inspection

P2569.t: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
P2569.d: P2569 means the radiator-mounted sensor of a DOR system (direct ozone reduction: a radiator coating that breaks down ozone in the incoming air) shows an electrical fault toward ground. According to VW's 2014 data books for the CC with 2.0 L TSI (CBFA, CCTA) and the Tiguan (CCTA), the sensor talks to the engine computer over a LIN line, and P2569 is set when that link fails because the line is grounded. The same books assign an open line or a short to battery voltage to P2570, while P2568 covers the identity and function check. Typical triggers are a chafed LIN wire touching the body or a corroded radiator connector. The car drives normally, but the stored code can fail an emissions inspection.
c: LIN wire to the radiator sensor chafed and shorted to ground
Water or salt corrosion in the radiator sensor connector
Internal short in the radiator sensor
s: Check engine light on
No change in driveability or engine temperature
Emissions inspection may be refused

P256A.t: Engine Idle Speed Selector Sensor/Switch Circuit/Open
P256A.d: P256A refers to the switch or sensor with which the driver chooses a raised idle speed, for example to run a generator, an inverter or belt-driven equipment while parked, independent of any PTO. The controller sees no valid state on this input, which points to an open wire, a disconnected plug or a switch that no longer makes contact. No manufacturer documents P256A publicly. GM's bulletin PIT4529D for 2007–2018 Silverado/Sierra 2500/3500 shows that such selections exist side by side: an automatic cold-weather elevated idle on the 6.6L diesel, an optional High Idle (RPO UF3) operated through the cruise buttons, and a separate PTO mode. The engine keeps its normal idle; P0506 and P0507 instead concern an idle that misses its target.
c: Open wire in the idle selector circuit
Selector connector loose or not mated
s: Raised idle cannot be selected
Engine stays at normal idle

P256B.t: Engine Idle Speed Selector Sensor/Switch Range/Performance
P256B.d: P256B means the idle speed selector delivers a value that is electrically valid but makes no sense in context. The controller may, for instance, see a raised-idle request with the truck in motion, a position that does not exist, or a request that conflicts with an active PTO mode; Ram's 2012 chassis cab guide states that remote PTO outranks the Idle Up function, so the two inputs have a defined order the software can check. CARB defines a rationality diagnostic as comparing an input within its normal range with all other available information. No manufacturer publishes P256B. Likely causes are a sticking or misadjusted switch, aftermarket idle controls wired into the same circuit, or a configuration change. The idle request is usually ignored.
c: Aftermarket idle control wired into the same circuit
Idle or PTO configuration changed without matching hardware
s: Raised idle request ignored
Idle selection works only sometimes

P256C.t: Engine Idle Speed Selector Sensor/Switch Circuit Low
P256C.d: P256C says the idle speed selector input is pulled below its lowest valid level, typically by a signal wire shorted to ground or a switch with an internal short. Where the selector is a simple ground-switched input, the controller would read such a short as a permanent request, so a dedicated low code presupposes a coded or monitored circuit. No manufacturer documents P256C publicly. A raised idle that appears without driver input is not automatically this fault: Ram's 2025 6.7L Cummins bulletin S2509000007 lists automatic modes such as cab warm-up at 1000 rpm below 4.4 °C ambient or inverter support between 700 and 1500 rpm. P256D is the high-side code. Expect the raised idle to be unavailable or the code to return after every key cycle.
c: Idle selector wire shorted to ground
Internal short in the idle selector
s: Raised idle unavailable
Code returns after every key cycle

P256D.t: Engine Idle Speed Selector Sensor/Switch Circuit High
P256D.d: P256D is logged when the idle speed selector signal rises above the highest value the controller treats as valid. Causes include a wire chafed against a battery-fed circuit, an open sensor return that lets the input float high, or an accessory module that drives the line with system voltage. No manufacturer documents P256D publicly. On GM's 6.6L Duramax trucks covered by PIT4529D, the standard elevated idle lifts engine speed to 1050 rpm only below 0 °C outside and with coolant under 65 °C, and owners can switch it off; a selector fault should not be confused with that intended behaviour. P256C is the low-side counterpart and P256E the intermittent variant. Usually the raised idle cannot be selected, while normal driving is unaffected.
c: Selector wire chafed against a battery-fed circuit
Open return line letting the input float high
Accessory module feeding system voltage into the line
s: Raised idle cannot be selected
Normal driving unaffected

P256E.t: Engine Idle Speed Selector Sensor/Switch Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P256E.d: P256E records an idle speed selector signal that drops out or flickers for short moments, more often than real switch use would cause. Since the selector is usually operated with the engine idling for long periods, engine vibration, a worn rocker switch or a loose crimp can be enough; each interruption can cancel the raised idle and make the engine fall back and rise again. Ram's 2012 chassis cab guide describes an Idle Up set speed that is entered when the function is activated, so repeated on-off events are noticeable as speed changes. No manufacturer publishes P256E. CARB requires circuit faults on monitored inputs to be watched continuously. A steady break would set P256A instead. The driver mainly notices an unsteady raised idle.
c: Loose crimp or terminal in the selector circuit
Harness moving with engine vibration at idle
s: Raised idle drops out and comes back
Engine speed rises and falls at standstill
Code stored only intermittently

P256F.d: P256F is the plausibility fault of a second A/C request input, B. Its wiring checks out, yet the engine module finds the state or timing illogical, for instance a request present while the first input and the climate controller say no cooling is wanted, or one that flickers instead of holding steady. Why a vehicle has two request inputs is up to each maker; a rear evaporator, a second compressor stage or a redundant cross-check line are plausible reasons. No maker documents P256F publicly. The legal basis is CARB's A/C component monitoring, which also covers A/C parts used as inputs to other diagnostics. Networked designs like the 2011 Saab 9-5, which take the request over the data bus, report trouble as communication codes instead. P2522 is the general fault on B, P255F the matching test on A.
c: Climate control logic sends inconsistent B request
Intermittent connection on the B request line
Fault in a second evaporator or compressor stage control
s: Rear or second-stage cooling unreliable
Idle dips or surges with A/C operation

P2570.t: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Temperature Sensor Circuit High
P2570.d: P2570 is the high-side electrical fault of the sensor fitted to a DOR radiator, the ozone-converting coated radiator found on some low-emission petrol cars. VW's 2014 Tiguan book (2.0 L TSI, CCTA) logs it when LIN communication with the sensor breaks down because the line is interrupted or carries battery voltage; the 2014 CC book applies the same criterion to its CBFA and CCTA engines. A connector left unplugged after radiator work, a broken wire or a dead sensor are the usual reasons. VW Tech Tip 19-12-01 adds that a new radiator is delivered with this sensor loose, so it has to be glued on and connected. P2569 is the shorted-to-ground case. Cooling and driveability are unaffected; the MIL and inspection readiness are what matter.
c: Sensor not connected or not fitted after radiator replacement
Broken LIN wire or loose terminal
s: Check engine light, often right after radiator work
Engine runs and cools normally

P2571.t: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2571.d: P2571 stands for an unsteady or intermittently lost signal from the temperature sensor of a direct ozone reduction (DOR) catalyst. Unlike P2569 and P2570, which describe a lasting low or high fault, this code covers readings that jump around or vanish for moments. No manufacturer publicly documents P2571; the VW specification books that use this sensor family list only P2568 to P2570. On the VW 2.0 L TSI the part is the radiator identification sensor G611, which a VW Tech Tip says is bonded to the radiator, so a sensor that has come loose or a corroded plug is a plausible cause. CARB requires DOR systems to be monitored, and BASF's PremAir coating is the best-known DOR catalyst. Driving is unaffected.
c: Loose or corroded terminal at the radiator sensor plug
Sensor no longer firmly bonded to the radiator
Harness damaged by vibration at the radiator mounting
s: Check engine light that may come and go
No noticeable effect on driving or cooling

P2572.t: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Deterioration Sensor Circuit
P2572.d: P2572 points to a general fault in the circuit of a sensor meant to judge how much ozone-converting activity is left on a direct ozone reduction (DOR) catalyst, such as a coated radiator. CARB demands a real deterioration check only when the DOR credit is above 5 mg/mi NMOG on LEV III/IV vehicles (or half the NMOG standard on older ones); at or below that, the system merely has to notice a total loss of ozone reduction. BASF rates its PremAir NXT coating at a 5 mg/mi credit, which helps explain why no maker publicly documents P2572 or a dedicated deterioration sensor. Low, high and erratic signals have their own codes (P2574-P2576), the plausibility check is P2573. Driving is not affected.
c: Damaged wiring or connector at the DOR sensor
Replacement radiator without the sensor fitted
s: Check engine light on
No effect on engine power or cooling

P2573.t: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Deterioration Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2573.d: P2573 means the deterioration sensor watching a DOR (direct ozone reduction) catalyst delivers a signal that is electrically within limits but does not fit the expected behaviour, for example a value that never changes with conditions or contradicts other inputs. Such a sensor would estimate how much of the catalytic coating on the radiator still destroys ozone, which CARB requires on vehicles claiming a large DOR credit. No manufacturer publishes P2573 or its test criteria, so the exact check is unknown; on comparable VW systems the analogous plausibility code P2568 fires on a failed identity or function check of the radiator sensor. P2572 is the generic circuit fault, P2574/P2575 the low and high signals. Driveability is unchanged; the MIL may come on.
c: Deterioration sensor drifting or stuck at one value
Non-original radiator with a sensor that does not match
Radiator face heavily fouled, skewing the sensor reading
s: Check engine light after several drive cycles
No change in how the car drives

P2574.t: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Deterioration Sensor Circuit Low
P2574.d: P2574 is set when the deterioration sensor circuit of a direct ozone reduction (DOR) catalyst reads below its valid range, the usual signature of a short to ground or a failed sensor pulling the line down. No manufacturer documents P2574 publicly. The nearest documented analogue is P2569 on VW's 2.0 L TSI models, where the 2014 Tiguan book attributes a grounded LIN line of the radiator sensor to that code. A DOR catalyst only cleans the ambient air flowing through the radiator, so engine output, cooling and fuel use stay the same; the consequence is a warning lamp and possibly a failed OBD inspection. P2575 is the opposite fault, P2572 the general circuit code.
c: Sensor wire shorted to ground at the radiator
s: Check engine light on
Car drives and cools as before

P2575.t: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Deterioration Sensor Circuit High
P2575.d: P2575 reports a deterioration-sensor signal above the valid range on a direct ozone reduction (DOR) catalyst - typical for an open circuit, a missing ground or a short to a supply voltage. No vehicle maker has published how it uses P2575, and no service bulletin naming it turned up in the NHTSA index. As an analogy, VW's 2014 CC book sends an open LIN line or a short to battery from the DOR radiator sensor to P2570. Because the DOR coating sits on the radiator, a radiator swap is the most likely moment for a connector to be left off or a wire to be damaged. P2574 covers the low side, P2576 brief dropouts. The engine runs normally; only emissions monitoring is affected.
c: Connector left off or damaged during radiator work
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
s: Check engine light on
No change in power or engine temperature

P2576.t: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Deterioration Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2576.d: P2576 describes a deterioration-sensor signal on a direct ozone reduction (DOR) catalyst that comes and goes or jumps without a physical reason, rather than staying low (P2574) or high (P2575). Loose terminals, a cracked connector housing in the airstream ahead of the engine, or chafing where the harness meets the radiator are typical suspects, since that spot sees vibration, spray water and road salt. No manufacturer documents P2576 publicly. CARB's DOR rules describe what such a sensor would watch, and BASF positions its PremAir NXT radiator coating for the 150,000-mile durability that Tier 3 and LEV III demand. A stored code does not affect cooling or performance but counts as an emissions fault.
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the sensor connector
Harness chafing at the radiator support
Cracked connector housing letting water in
s: Check engine light, possibly only now and then
No noticeable driving symptoms

P2577.t: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Efficiency Below Threshold
P2577.d: P2577 means the OBD system has concluded that the direct ozone reduction (DOR) catalyst - usually a radiator coated with an ozone-destroying catalyst such as BASF's PremAir - no longer converts enough ozone. CARB ties the threshold to the credit claimed: for LEV III/IV vehicles with a DOR credit of 5 mg/mi NMOG or less, a malfunction is a system with no measurable ozone reduction left; above 5 mg/mi, it is a performance loss worth more than 5 mg/mi of credit. Earlier non-LEV III cars used 50 % of the NMOG standard instead. No manufacturer publicly documents P2577. Plausible causes are a non-coated aftermarket radiator or a coating worn or fouled by dirt; the usual fix is the correct coated radiator. Driving is unaffected.
c: Catalytic coating worn, damaged or covered with dirt
Faulty DOR sensor giving a false result
s: Check engine light on
No change in engine cooling or performance
Possible failed emissions inspection

P2578.d: P2578 is the catch-all electrical fault for speed sensor A, the pickup that counts revolutions of the turbocharger or supercharger shaft, normally by sensing a tone feature on the compressor wheel or its nut. The engine computer logs it when the sensor line is faulty in a way it cannot classify as too low, too high or sporadic; those cases have their own codes P2580, P2581 and P2582, and P2579 covers a readable but implausible speed. No manufacturer documents P2578 publicly with thresholds. CARB requires electronic parts used for boost control to be monitored as comprehensive components, and Bentley's W12 bulletin on its two shaft speed sensors calls for checks for an open line, shorts to ground or battery and shorts between wires. Boost may be limited and the warning lamp is usually on.
c: Loose, corroded or oil-soaked connector at the speed sensor
Harness chafed or heat-damaged near the hot turbocharger housing
Internal failure of speed sensor A
Fault in the engine control module input stage
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Reduced power because boost is limited as a precaution
Turbo speed missing or frozen in live data

P2579.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Speed Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P2579.d: P2579 means speed sensor A delivers a signal, but the shaft speed it reports does not fit the operating state the engine computer expects from boost, airflow and load. PACCAR bulletin E209 for 2017-2019 MX-11 and MX-13 truck engines treats P2579, alone or with P1581, as a fix-as-fail item: the sensor is replaced, because it tends to fail intermittently with a loss of power that disappears when the driver lifts off and presses the pedal again. Ram flash bulletins 18-019-20 to 18-007-24 for 2019 Ram 3500-5500 cab chassis with the 6.7 L Cummins list P2579 among codes cured by new engine software. Bentley sees it on the W12 in either engine control unit. Circuit faults are P2578 and P2580-P2582.
c: Speed sensor A dropping out intermittently
Engine software that misjudges the speed plausibility (update available on some models)
Intake or boost leak that makes the shaft speed differ from the model
Mechanical turbocharger problem such as bearing drag or wheel damage
s: Sudden loss of power that returns after lifting off the accelerator
Malfunction indicator lamp on
Turbo speed in live data jumping or inconsistent with boost

P257A.d: P257A is an output fault on the control line of the vacuum reservoir, usually a solenoid or switching valve the engine computer uses to connect, isolate or vent a vacuum storage tank. Such tanks occur mainly on diesels whose EGR valves, turbocharger vanes or flaps are worked by vacuum; GM bulletin PI1260 for the 2014 Cruze 2.0 L diesel, for example, shows the pump filling a tank built into the EGR cooler, which in turn feeds the turbo and EGR control solenoids. The driver stage logs it on an open circuit or on a fault it cannot assign to low or high. No manufacturer documents P257A publicly; CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 treats such outputs as comprehensive components to be checked for circuit faults. P257B and P257C cover shorts to ground and to voltage.
c: Loose or corroded connector at the reservoir control valve
Broken wire in the control or supply line
Open solenoid coil in the control valve
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Engine warning lamp on
Vacuum-driven actuators such as EGR or turbo vanes respond poorly

P257B.d: P257B points to a vacuum reservoir control circuit whose voltage is too low, which in practice usually means a ground short on the line between the control unit and the reservoir valve, or a driver stage that cannot hold the line at its proper level. The valve manages a vacuum store used by pneumatic actuators such as EGR valves or turbocharger vanes, mostly on diesel engines. No carmaker publishes P257B with thresholds, so the logic follows the CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 rules for output components. With the line shorted, the valve may stay permanently switched, and the actuators behind it lose or keep vacuum regardless of demand; GM bulletin PI1260 shows that vacuum problems in such systems then show up as turbo position codes. P257A is the open circuit, P257C the high-side fault.
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Shorted coil in the reservoir control valve
Damaged output stage in the engine control module
s: Engine warning lamp on
Follow-up codes for EGR or turbocharger position

P257C.d: P257C sets when the control line of the vacuum reservoir valve reads too high, typically from a short to battery positive or a fault in the driver stage, so the valve can no longer be switched as commanded. The reservoir serves pneumatic actuators on diesel engines; GM's bulletin PI1260 on the 2014 Cruze diesel names leaks anywhere in the vacuum system that feeds the turbo vane and EGR actuators as a cause of P003A, P2598 and P2599, which shows how a fault here spreads to boost control. No manufacturer documents P257C itself. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requires circuit checks on such output components. P257A covers an open line and P257B a short to ground, while sensor faults on the reservoir itself are reported as P2525-P2529. The driver will mostly notice the warning lamp and, at worst, weaker boost.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage line
Internal fault in the reservoir control valve
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Engine warning lamp on
Weaker boost or EGR response in some cases

P257D.d: P257D is the plausibility fault of the engine hood switch. The line is electrically readable, but the value falls into a band the module regards as impossible, or two redundant switches disagree. Hood status matters because stop-start, hybrid and remote-start logic must never crank the engine while someone is working in the bay. GM's 2018 engine table 18OBDG04 rejects a resistance-coded switch reading between 1,281 and 1,404 ohms, or two discrete switches showing the same state, after 80 bad readings out of 100 taken every 12.5 ms (Type B, two trips); the 2019 hybrid table 19OBDG01 uses percentage windows instead. GM bulletin PIC6460 traces P257D on 2014–2020 Impalas to coolant creeping from the temperature sensor into the ECM connector. Hood ajar messages and blocked auto-stop are typical.
c: Hood switch or plunger worn, misadjusted or contaminated
Fluid or corrosion in the switch or ECM connector shunting the signal
Second hood switch or latch switch reporting a different state
Replacement switch with wrong resistance coding
s: Check engine lamp after two drives
Hood ajar message although the hood is closed
Auto stop-start or remote start not available

P257E.d: P257E says the hood switch signal has dropped below its lowest valid level, which usually means the signal wire touches ground or the switch is shorted inside. GM's 2018 engine table 18OBDG04 sets it for a resistance-coded switch at 325 ohms or less, the 2019 hybrid table 19OBDG01 at 14.6 % of range or less, each with 80 failures in 100 samples and Type B. A Chrysler STAR case for the 2017–2018 Pacifica describes a lit hood ajar lamp, a dead stop-start system and P257E after a repair, caused by the hood ajar plug and the horn plug at the latch having been swapped – a dead horn gives it away. GM's engineering note PIE0834 lists the code on its 2022–2025 electric pickups and SUVs with front hood latch trouble. Depending on design a grounded line can look like an open hood.
c: Hood switch signal wire chafed to ground near the latch
Hood switch and horn connectors swapped after front-end repair
Switch shorted internally by water or impact damage
s: Hood ajar indicator on with the hood shut
Engine stop-start inoperative
Check engine lamp on

P257F.d: P257F is the high-side counterpart of P257E: the hood switch reading rises above the top limit, which points to an open signal line, a pin that has backed out of its connector, or a short to a voltage source. In GM's 2018 engine table 18OBDG04 the limit for a resistance-coded switch is 3,620 ohms or more, and the 2019 hybrid table 19OBDG01 uses 71.5 % of range; both need 80 failures within 100 samples and are Type B with two trips. A Stellantis STAR case for 2021–2023 Wrangler models sends technicians to connector XY103A at the left front of the engine compartment, where loose terminals can set P257F together with P152E or P0073. GM's PIE0834 also names it on its electric trucks with latch faults. The driver sees a check engine lamp, possibly a hood warning, and no automatic engine stop.
c: Open hood switch signal wire or unplugged switch
Loose or pushed-back pins in a front harness connector
Signal line shorted to a voltage source
s: Check engine lamp on
Engine stop-start stays inactive
Hood warning may be shown or may be missing when the hood is really open

P2580.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Speed Sensor A Circuit Low
P2580.d: P2580 says the signal from turbocharger or supercharger speed sensor A stays at the low end, so the engine computer sees too little or no usable pulse activity - typically from a short to ground, a weak sensor or a pickup that cannot read the target. A Stellantis STAR case from November 2023 for 2022-2024 Ram 2500 to 5500 trucks reports P2580 with the warning lamp, sometimes after few miles; besides the normal circuit tests it asks the technician to pull the sensor and inspect bore and tone wheel with a borescope, since debris or an extra O-ring left in the bore spoiled the signal. P2581 is the high-side counterpart, P2579 an implausible speed with a working circuit. Boost is often reduced.
c: Debris on the tone wheel or an extra O-ring in the sensor bore
Speed sensor A with weak or missing output
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Turbo speed reads zero or very low in live data
Possible boost limitation and reduced power

P2581.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Speed Sensor A Circuit High
P2581.d: P2581 is set when speed sensor A reports a level above what a healthy circuit can produce, so the engine computer cannot trust it. Typical triggers are a signal wire shorted to the supply or battery voltage, an open signal or ground path that lets the input float high, or a sensor with a shorted output stage. No manufacturer documents P2581 publicly; the closest evidence is Bentley's W12 bulletin, which lists the B-sensor high fault P2596 and demands checks for shorts to B+ before the sensor is replaced, and CARB's rule that electronic boost-control parts be monitored as comprehensive components. P2580 is the low-side fault, P2582 brief dropouts. The engine usually trims boost and lights the warning lamp.
c: Signal wire shorted to supply or battery voltage
Open ground or signal wire letting the input float high
Speed sensor A with a shorted output
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Implausibly high or fixed turbo speed in live data
Reduced boost and power

P2582.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Speed Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
P2582.d: P2582 points to a speed sensor A signal that cuts out or jumps for short moments while being fine in between, so the fault may be gone by the time the vehicle reaches the workshop. Loose terminals, a cracked wire that opens under vibration or heat, and a sensor failing internally when hot are the usual suspects. No manufacturer publishes P2582 under its own code; PACCAR's bulletin E209 on MX-11/MX-13 engines shows how hard such dropouts are to catch - its sensor fails intermittently, yet it is logged there under P2579, and the fix is a new sensor plus a 20-second high-idle check. CARB requires the boost-control electronics to be monitored for such faults. P2578, P2580 and P2581 describe faults that persist.
c: Loose or spread terminal in the sensor connector
Wire break that opens only under vibration or heat
Speed sensor A failing when hot
s: Brief power dips that come and go
Warning lamp that may switch off again
Turbo speed trace with dropouts or spikes

P2583.t: Cruise Control Front Distance Range Sensor Single Sensor or Center
P2583.d: P2583 points to the front distance sensor of adaptive cruise control – the only radar, or the centre unit where several are fitted. The engine module keeps the code because adaptive cruise acts directly on engine torque. Honda uses P2583 with failure type 76: bulletin 21-068 for 2017–2021 Accord, Civic, CR-V and Insight ties P2583-76, a temporary stop of the driver support system due to millimetre-wave radar misalignment, to snow and ice on the radar face in near-freezing weather and adds a radar software update; bulletin 26-036 covers unexpected ACC cancellation with the same code on 2023–2026 CR-V models, again fixed by software. Left and right sensors have P2591 and P2592. Until fixed, adaptive cruise and collision braking stay off.
c: Snow, ice, dirt or a non-approved grille trim in front of the radar
Radar software needing the manufacturer update
Radar misaligned after a knock or bumper repair
Radar unit or its wiring faulty
s: Adaptive cruise control switches off or cannot be engaged
Warning to clean the radar sensor
Collision mitigation braking unavailable, warning lamps on

P2584.t: Fuel Additive Control Module Requested MIL Illumination
P2584.d: P2584 belongs to diesel cars that add a fuel-borne catalyst to the tank so the particulate filter can burn off soot at lower exhaust temperatures. A separate additive module meters the fluid after each refuelling, in proportion to fuel added, and watches its pump, level sensor and its own circuits. If it finds an emission-relevant fault, it asks the engine module, which owns the lamp, to switch on the MIL; the engine module stores P2584 as a pointer. The approach goes back to PSA, whose 607 sedan, as presented in 1999, used Rhodia's cerium-based Eolys with on-board dosing. No manufacturer documents P2584 publicly. The real cause sits in the additive module: empty reservoir, failed dosing pump, lost refill count or wiring. Without dosing, regenerations fail and the filter clogs.
c: Additive reservoir empty or level sensor faulty
Additive dosing pump or injector failed
Additive module wiring, supply or CAN link faulty
Additive quantity counter not reset after refill or filter change
s: Check engine lamp on
Particulate filter warning, regenerations incomplete
Loss of power as soot load rises

P2585.t: Fuel Additive Control Module Warning Lamp Request
P2585.d: P2585 is the softer sibling of P2584. Here the fuel additive module asks for a warning lamp other than the MIL – typically a service or particulate filter indicator – because something needs attention before emissions suffer. The classic trigger is a reservoir running low, so the module warns that dosing will soon stop; a refill that was never registered with the scan tool can produce the same request. No manufacturer documents P2585 publicly. Rhodia's 1999 paper on Eolys explains why the warning matters: the catalyst alone cannot regenerate a filter in all driving conditions, it works only together with engine measures that raise exhaust temperature, and the dose is matched on board to the soot produced. Running dry therefore lets the filter load up and leads to harder faults later.
c: Refill or new additive bag not registered with the scan tool
Level sensor in the additive reservoir faulty
s: Service or particulate filter warning lamp on
Message about additive level in the instrument cluster

P2586.t: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor B Circuit
P2586.d: P2586 covers a general electrical fault at position sensor B, which reports where the second boost control actuator stands - the vane mechanism or electric wastegate of a second turbocharger on engines that regulate two of them separately. The engine computer cannot use the feedback, without the fault being pinned down as low (P2588), high (P2589) or sporadic (P2590); P2587 is a position mismatch with a working circuit. No manufacturer documents P2586 publicly. CARB requires the sensors of the boost control system to be monitored as comprehensive components. For sensor A, Kia service action SA078 on the 2011 Optima 2.0 T-GDI pairs the circuit code P2562 with an electric wastegate actuator whose rod length must be reset. Boost is usually limited.
c: Connector or terminal fault at the actuator B position sensor
Harness to actuator B damaged by exhaust heat
Position sensor inside actuator B failed (often replaced as a unit)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Reduced power because boost is capped
No valid position value for actuator B in live data

P2587.t: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P2587.d: P2587 is a plausibility fault: position sensor B gives an electrically valid reading, but the reported position of the second boost actuator does not follow the command, or the value lies outside what the mechanism can physically reach. No manufacturer documents P2587 publicly, so the logic is known only from sensor A. GM's 2009 Duramax table sets P2563 when vane position misses the target by 15 % or more for 5 s once the engine has run 30 s, and VW bulletin 21-15-06 traces P2563 on 2.0 L TDI engines to kinked vacuum hoses, a leaking diaphragm or a broken adjusting stud. Sticking vanes or wastegate linkage are therefore as likely as the sensor. Circuit faults of sensor B are P2586 and P2588-P2590.
c: Sticking variable vanes or wastegate linkage on turbo B
Kinked or leaking vacuum line or diaphragm on pneumatic actuators
Actuator rod or adjusting stud out of adjustment or broken
s: Noticeable loss of power or overboost cut
Malfunction indicator lamp on
Commanded and actual position of actuator B diverge in live data

P2588.t: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor B Circuit Low
P2588.d: P2588 is stored when the voltage from position sensor B of the second boost actuator drops below the lowest value a working sensor can deliver - most often a grounded signal line or a missing 5 V reference. No manufacturer documents P2588 publicly; the thresholds known for sensor A give the order of magnitude. Ford's 2023 diesel OBD summary flags P2564 below 0.15 V, and GM's 2009 Duramax table uses 0.277 V for 1 s once the engine has run 3 s. A shorted reference may also upset other sensors on the same supply. P2589 is the high-side fault, P2587 a position error with a usable signal, and P2564 the same low fault on sensor A. Power is normally reduced.
c: Signal wire of position sensor B shorted to ground
Lost or shorted 5 V reference supply
Failed position sensor B in actuator B
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Power reduced, boost held low
Further sensor codes if a shared reference is shorted

P2589.t: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor B Circuit High
P2589.d: P2589 means the signal that position sensor B returns for the second boost actuator sits above its plausible maximum, typically from an open signal or ground wire, a short to the reference or battery voltage, or a sensor with a defective output. No manufacturer documents P2589 publicly. For sensor A, GM's 2018 diesel engine table triggers P2565 at an analog value above 95 % in 200 of 250 samples, Type A with the lamp on the first trip, and Kia's service action SA149 for the 2011-2012 Sportage 2.0 T-GDI pairs P2565 with a software update and an adjustment of the wastegate rod until the position voltage reads about 3.8 to 4.1 V. P2588 is the low-side fault, P2565 the same fault on sensor A. Boost is usually reduced.
c: Open signal or ground wire of position sensor B
Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage
Wastegate rod set so the sensor reads at its upper end
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on, often on the first trip
Reduced power with boost capped
Position of actuator B stuck near the maximum in live data

P258A.d: P258A stands for an open or otherwise faulty control circuit A of an electric vacuum pump, which supplies the brake booster on engines that provide too little manifold vacuum, such as hybrids, downsized turbo petrol engines and diesels. Ford's 2018-2019 hybrid OBD summary assigns it to the brake system module: with the pump relay commanded off, a monitoring line voltage outside 1.3-5.0 V for 100 ms sets the code (legacy brake code C1035). Stellantis case S2209000006 explains that the PCM can log P258A after a crank longer than 2.5 s because the pump is unpowered while cranking; in that case the code may simply be cleared, but a P258B alongside points to the pump itself. P258B to P258D cover performance, low and high faults, P25EE the open fault of circuit B. Braking assist can be reduced.
c: Faulty pump relay, blown fuse or poor relay contact
False entry after a long engine crank while the pump is unpowered
Open wire or loose connector between module, relay and pump
s: Engine or brake warning lamp on
Harder brake pedal at low speed or after several stops
Start-stop function disabled

P258B.t: Vacuum Pump Control Circuit A Range/Performance
P258B.d: P258B is the range/performance code for control circuit A of the vacuum pump: the pump is commanded, but its monitoring feedback or the vacuum it produces does not fit. Ford's 2018-2019 hybrid OBD summary sets it from the brake module when the monitoring line sits outside 1.3-5.0 V with the relay off, or below 250 mV for 1 s with the relay on. FCA case S1805000006 for 2017-2020 Pacifica, Cherokee, Wrangler, Gladiator and Ram 1500 links P258B, often with ABS code C1252, to pumps that cannot keep enough vacuum and asks for checks of fuses, terminals, hoses and check valves plus a PCM update from 2019. Audi's Q3 bulletin 2072305 (2021-2024) traces P258B00 to a blown pump fuse after the ABS connector had been unplugged while the engine was running. The brake pedal may feel hard.
c: Worn or failed electric vacuum pump
Leaking hose or check valve that makes the pump run too long
Blown pump fuse, spread terminals or poor ground
Outdated engine software controlling pump duty cycle
s: Engine, brake or stability warning lamp on
Hard brake pedal, less brake assist
Start-stop fault message

P258C.t: Vacuum Pump Control Circuit A Low
P258C.d: P258C reports that control circuit A of the electrically driven vacuum pump reads too low, typically because the control or relay line is shorted to ground, the relay coil is faulty, or a blown supply fuse leaves the monitoring line without voltage. Depending on how the circuit is laid out, the pump may then run nonstop or not at all. No manufacturer publishes P258C itself. Ford's hybrid OBD summary shows the kind of window used on this circuit for P258A and P258B: the monitoring voltage should stay between 1.3 and 5.0 V with the relay off and must not drop below 250 mV with it on. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 treats such electrical outputs as comprehensive components. P258A is the open circuit, P258D the high side; if braking assist suffers, P050F for low brake vacuum can follow.
c: Control or relay wire shorted to ground
Faulty pump relay or relay coil
s: Engine or brake warning lamp on
Pump silent or running constantly
Firmer brake pedal

P258D.t: Vacuum Pump Control Circuit A High
P258D.d: P258D marks a control circuit A of the vacuum pump whose signal sits above the expected range, most often a short to battery positive on the relay or pump control line, so the control unit can no longer switch the pump as it wants. If the pump keeps running, it wears out early; FCA case S1805000006 notes that pumps forced into excessive run time tend to fail. No manufacturer documents P258D publicly, so CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 comprehensive component rules apply. Ford's hybrid OBD summary shows the reference for the same circuit, a monitoring voltage between 1.3 and 5.0 V while the relay is off. Stellantis case S2209000006 adds that pump codes logged during long cranking can be harmless. P258C is the low-side partner, P258B the plausibility code. The driver may hear the pump run constantly.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage line
Faulty output stage in the controlling module
s: Engine or brake warning lamp on
Vacuum pump runs continuously, even with the engine off in some cases

P258E.d: P258E is the plausibility check of the power take-off enable switch. The line is not open or shorted – those faults are P251A to P251C – but the state of the switch does not fit the other PTO inputs, for instance an enable request without a valid arming step or contact signals that contradict each other. GM lists P258E among the PTO module codes in UI Bulletin 80C for Silverado and Sierra chassis cabs: the in-cab rocker delivers three mode signals that the module decodes so that every press is cross-checked, and an upfitter's remote enable switch only works if the arming button was pressed within five seconds before. GM warns upfitters against load-engage switches because they defeat these diagnostics. The truck still drives; the PTO refuses to engage or drops out.
c: PTO switch contacts worn or contaminated, mode signals disagree
Upfitter wiring or load-engage switch interfering with the enable input
Remote enable used without arming sequence or with wrong switch type
PTO module configuration not matching the installed switches
s: PTO cannot be switched on or switches off unexpectedly
Driver information message about PTO conditions

P258F.d: P258F concerns the sending side of a torque management link. One controller – for example the engine module talking to a transmission or hybrid controller, or the reverse – transmits torque requests and finds that its own output is faulty, missing or not accepted by the receiver. The receiving side is better documented as P2544 and following: GM's 2020 table 20OBDG04 checks incoming torque requests from the TCM for a wrong protection value, a broken rolling counter and implausible magnitudes, Type B. No manufacturer documents P258F publicly. CARB's rule requires output components driven by a computer to be checked for correct functional response where feasible, which is the logic behind such a code. Typical causes are CAN wiring, mismatched software after programming or a faulty module. Harsh shifts or reduced power can follow.
c: CAN wiring or connector fault between the modules
Software levels of sending and receiving module do not match
Low voltage or poor ground at one of the modules
s: Check engine lamp on
Harsh or delayed shifts
Reduced engine power

P2590.t: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2590.d: P2590 is set when the position signal of the second boost actuator flickers, jumps or drops out for short moments instead of being steadily wrong. Unlike its sensor A counterpart P2566, this code is defined as intermittent/erratic, so an unsteady signal without full dropouts falls under it as well. No manufacturer documents P2590 publicly. For sensor A, VW bulletins 21-15-04 and 21-15-06 on 2009-2014 2.0 L TDI models group P2566 with the other position codes, locate sensor G581 in the vacuum diaphragm and start the repair at hoses, diaphragm and actuator travel. Typical are loose terminals or a sensor track worn by vibration. Steady faults on sensor B are P2586, P2588 and P2589.
c: Loose terminal or intermittent contact in the sensor B connector
Sensor track worn by vibration, giving a noisy signal
Chafed harness that shorts or opens briefly
s: Power surging or dropping intermittently
Warning lamp that may come and go
Jumping position value for actuator B in live data

P2591.t: Cruise Control Front Distance Range Sensor Left
P2591.d: P2591 is reserved for the left front distance sensor in cruise systems that combine several radars across the front; a single or centre unit uses P2583 and the right one P2592. No manufacturer documents P2591 publicly. Honda's bulletins on P2583 show what such a sensor typically reports: a view blocked by ice or dirt, or a misalignment the unit detects itself. A left corner sensor sits behind the bumper cover, so parking knocks, a repainted or replaced bumper, thick paint over the sensor area and bent brackets are prime suspects, before wiring or the sensor itself. CARB cites a cruise control that turns itself off on a detected fault as a diagnostic without emission impact, so a check engine lamp is not to be expected. Adaptive cruise and related assistance remain unavailable.
c: Bumper cover damaged, replaced or repainted over the left sensor
Left sensor bracket bent, sensor aimed wrongly
Ice, mud or stickers covering the sensor area
Sensor or wiring to the left corner faulty
s: Adaptive cruise control not available
Driver assistance warning message

P2592.t: Cruise Control Front Distance Range Sensor Right
P2592.d: P2592 marks a fault of the right-hand front distance sensor in multi-radar adaptive cruise layouts; the left unit reports P2591, a single or centre radar P2583. No maker publishes this code. Compared with a radar behind the grille emblem, a right corner sensor is more exposed to kerb and parking contact, stone chips and road salt reaching its connector, and it is often disturbed when a bumper is replaced on the passenger side. That is why aiming and mounting are checked before parts are swapped. Honda's P2583 bulletins illustrate the usual chain: dirt or ice on the radar face leads to a misalignment report and a temporary shutdown of the assistance. The engine module only keeps the record; the detailed cause is stored in the driver assistance or radar module. Driving itself is unaffected.
c: Right sensor knocked out of alignment by kerb or parking contact
Road salt or water corrosion at the right sensor connector
Sensor not recalibrated after bumper replacement
s: Adaptive cruise control switched off
Warning message for the radar or driver assistance system

P2593.d: P2593 concerns the second turbocharger speed sensor, found where an engine has two turbochargers, for example one per cylinder bank. It marks an electrical fault on that sensor's circuit that is not further classified; the specific forms are P2595 (low), P2596 (high) and P2597 (intermittent), while P2594 covers a plausibility error. Sensor A is reported separately under P2578-P2582. No manufacturer documents P2593 itself publicly. Bentley's W12 engine carries two such sensors (G688 for bank 1, G689 for bank 2), both engine control units store their faults, and the bulletin prescribes testing for opens, shorts to ground or B+ and wire-to-wire shorts before a sensor is changed. CARB requires these boost-control parts to be monitored.
c: Connector problem at speed sensor B
Harness to the second turbocharger damaged by heat or chafing
Internal failure of speed sensor B
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Power reduced, often only slightly with one turbo affected
No speed value for the second turbo in live data

P2594.t: Turbocharger Speed Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P2594.d: P2594 means the second turbocharger speed sensor produces a signal, but its reported speed does not agree with what the engine computer predicts for that turbo. Bentley documents it on the W12 in the Continental GT/GTC, Flying Spur and Bentayga (bulletin 2053348, versions 5 and 10): after a smoke test of intake and exhaust, a detached divider inside the air filter box on Continental and Flying Spur turned out to be one cause; with symptom code 23179 alone the code is cleared and retested without parts, while symptom code 32790 leads to a new speed sensor. P2593 and P2595-P2597 are circuit faults of the same sensor, P2579 the matching fault on sensor A. The warning lamp comes on.
c: Speed sensor B delivering an implausible signal
Detached divider in the air filter box disturbing the flow to one turbo
Intake or exhaust leak on the bank of the second turbo
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Fault often appears only under particular load or gradient conditions
Turbo speeds of both banks differ noticeably in live data

P2595.t: Turbocharger Speed Sensor B Circuit Low
P2595.d: P2595 is logged when the signal of turbocharger speed sensor B stays below the range the engine computer accepts, as with a short to ground or a sensor whose output has collapsed. Bentley names it for the W12 in Continental GT, GTC and Flying Spur from 2018 and later also in the Bentayga, stored in engine control unit 1 or 2. Unlike the plausibility code P2594, which may first be cleared and retested, the bulletin goes straight to the replacement of the affected sensor (G688 or G689) once wiring tests for opens and shorts pass; on the Bentayga the bank 1 sensor is much harder to reach. The opposite electrical fault is P2596, sensor A reports the same condition as P2580.
c: Speed sensor B with collapsed output
Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground
Corroded or contaminated connector at sensor B
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Speed of the second turbo shown as zero or very low
Possible reduction of boost

P2596.t: Turbocharger Speed Sensor B Circuit High
P2596.d: With P2596 the engine computer sees the line of turbocharger speed sensor B sitting above its valid window - the usual pattern for a signal shorted to supply voltage, an interrupted ground or a defective sensor output.
