The code was added to Bentley's W12 speed-sensor bulletin in its later revision (2053348/10, December 2022), which also brought in the Bentayga; it is handled like the low fault: work through the wiring checks including a short to B+, and if they pass, fit a new sensor for the affected bank and report back if the fault returns. P2595 is the low-voltage counterpart, P2594 a wrong but electrically valid speed, and P2581 the same fault on sensor A. Expect the warning lamp and possibly reduced boost.
c: Signal wire of sensor B shorted to supply or battery voltage
Defective output stage of speed sensor B
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Implausibly high speed for the second turbo in live data
Possible boost reduction

P2597.t: Turbocharger Speed Sensor B Circuit Intermittent
P2597.d: P2597 records short interruptions or jumps in the signal of the second turbocharger speed sensor, between which the circuit works normally. Such faults usually sit in a connector, a wire that breaks contact under engine movement or heat soak, or a sensor that drops out when hot. No manufacturer documents P2597 publicly. As an analogy, Bentley's W12 bulletin for the same sensor stresses reproducing the customer's driving situation - load, gradient, speed, light and hard acceleration - before deciding on a repair, which is exactly what a sporadic fault demands. CARB requires electronic boost-control components to be monitored. Continuous electrical faults on sensor B are P2593, P2595 and P2596; P2582 is the same pattern on sensor A.
c: Loose terminal or poor pin contact at sensor B
Wire breaking contact under engine movement or heat soak
Speed sensor B dropping out when hot
s: Occasional warning lamp, sometimes only after long drives
Short power dips under load
Dropouts in the speed trace of the second turbo

P2598.t: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor A Performance - Stuck Low
P2598.d: P2598 means the boost control position of turbocharger A, normally the vane or wastegate position reported by the actuator, appears stuck toward its low end: the measured value no longer follows the command although the signal is electrically valid. Ford's 2023 diesel OBD summary runs this check with closed-loop position control active above 500 rpm and flags a gap of more than 15 % in either direction lasting 25 s, with an extra variant during cold start. GM's 2018 table for its smaller diesels reads it as vanes jammed more open than requested (640 of 800 samples, Type A). GM bulletin PI1260 blames vacuum leaks for it on the 2014 Cruze with the 2.0 L diesel, and 17-NA-301 says a P2598 found at pre-delivery on 2017-2018 Cruze, Equinox and Terrain diesels may just be cleared. P2599 is the high-side partner. Expect reduced power.
c: Sooted or seized variable vanes that no longer follow the actuator
Vacuum leak or kinked hose on pneumatically driven actuators
Worn or failed electric vane actuator
One-off entry from unusual operation, e.g. after delivery transport
s: Engine warning lamp on
Lack of power under load, boost limited
Unusual turbo noise

P2599.t: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor A Performance - Stuck High
P2599.d: P2599 is the high-side stuck fault for position sensor A: the turbocharger actuator stays at, or reports, a position beyond where it should be, while the sensor circuit itself works. GM documents it twice. On the 2014 Cruze 2.0 L diesel the ECM compares commanded and actual vane position and logs P2599 when the deviation runs past 10 % in the direction opposite to P2598 for 10 s. The 2018 table for GM's smaller diesels checks instead whether the vanes spring back to their fully open rest position once the actuator is released after a P0046; if the reading stays above 15 % (vacuum actuator) or 5 % (smart actuator), the code sets at once as Type A. GM bulletin PI1260 names vacuum leaks as a cause. P2598 is the low-side partner; wiring faults use P2562-P2566.
c: Vanes or wastegate stuck toward the closed position by soot or corrosion
Weak return spring or binding linkage that keeps the actuator from its rest position
Vacuum control solenoid or hose fault on pneumatic actuators
Defective actuator electronics on smart actuators
s: Engine warning lamp on
Overboost cut-out or noticeable power reduction
Black smoke or rough response under load

P259A.t: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor B Performance - Stuck Low
P259A.d: P259A applies to engines with a second boost control actuator, for instance a twin-turbo layout or the second stage of a two-stage system, whose position is read by sensor B. The code is stored when that actuator's reported position stays at the low end and stops tracking the command even though the signal is electrically sound. No manufacturer documents P259A publicly. Its logic mirrors P2598 on the A side, where Ford compares requested with actual position and reacts to more than 15 % for 25 s, and GM counts samples with vanes more open than requested. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requires the boost control system to report faults that stop it from reaching its target. P259B is the high-side counterpart; circuit faults of sensor B fall under P2586-P2590. Reduced power is the usual result.
c: Sticking vanes, flap or wastegate on charger B
Weak vacuum or electrical supply to actuator B
Worn actuator B or misadjusted linkage
s: Engine warning lamp on
Weak acceleration, notably in the range where charger B works

P259B.t: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor B Performance - Stuck High
P259B.d: P259B is logged when the boost control actuator watched by position sensor B is found stuck at the high end of its travel, or fails to return to its rest position, while the sensor signal itself is plausible. A sensor B exists mainly on twin-turbo or two-stage engines. No manufacturer publishes P259B. On the A side, GM checks that the vanes spring back to fully open after the actuator is released and sets P2599 if they stay above 15 % (vacuum) or 5 % (electric); a comparable test for B is likely but not documented. GM bulletin PI1260 shows how vacuum leaks upset such pneumatic actuators. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 asks for boost control faults to be caught in both directions, including boost above the commanded level. P259A is the low-side partner. The engine may cut power to avoid overboost.
c: Mechanism of charger B seized toward the closed or high position
Return spring or linkage of actuator B binding
Vacuum solenoid or hose of actuator B faulty (pneumatic systems)
s: Engine warning lamp on
Power cut-out under full load to prevent overboost

P259C.t: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Turbocharger A Boost Control
P259C.d: P259C reports that closed-loop boost control of turbocharger A was not reached within the expected time after its enabling conditions were met. Instead of trimming the actuator from boost or position feedback, the controller stays in open-loop or default mode. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requires diesel OBD systems with feedback boost control to report it when control fails to start inside a time window set by the manufacturer, and P259C is the code for that case. No manufacturer publishes thresholds for P259C. Ford's 2023 diesel summary shows why it matters: its underboost check for turbocharger A runs only while boost feedback control is active. Typical root causes are inputs the loop needs, such as a faulty boost or position sensor, or a stored actuator fault. P259D is the turbocharger B equivalent.
c: Boost pressure or actuator position sensor fault that blocks closed-loop control
Actuator A fault, often with its own stored code
Charge air leak preventing boost from reaching the range where control starts
s: Engine warning lamp on
Sluggish or uneven boost build-up

P259D.t: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Turbocharger B Boost Control
P259D.d: P259D is the turbocharger B version of the closed-loop timing fault. On engines with two separately regulated chargers, the control unit expects the boost regulation of the second unit to switch to feedback operation within a set time, and here it did not. No manufacturer documents P259D publicly with thresholds; the basis is CARB 13 CCR 1968.2, which asks for a malfunction when feedback boost control does not start in time or falls back to default operation. GM's 2018 diesel table illustrates the dependency on the A side: its actuator plausibility checks only run while VGT position feedback is active and no fault is present on the position sensor or the actuator circuit. A stored sensor or actuator fault on charger B is therefore the first thing to repair. P259C covers turbocharger A.
c: Fault on position or pressure sensing for charger B
Actuator B or its control circuit faulty
Leak in the charge air path of charger B
s: Engine warning lamp on
Reduced power, especially at higher load

P259E.t: Turbocharger A Boost Control Position At Low Limit
P259E.d: P259E means the boost control of turbocharger A has run out of range at the low end: the actuator is at its limit, yet boost stays well under the target. Ford's 2023 diesel OBD summary places it in the underboost monitor. With closed-loop boost control active, at least 50 Nm (6.7 L) or 135 Nm (3.0 L) and 800 or 1300 rpm, it sets when desired boost exceeds actual boost by more than 120 kPa (6.7 L) or 80 kPa (3.0 L) for roughly 10-11 s. Ford's special service message 50564 for 2020-2022 Super Duty 6.7 L lists P259E among turbo-related codes and makes the variable vane actuator available on its own, so the whole turbocharger need not be replaced. P259F is the opposite limit, P2263 the slower general boost performance check, P0299 plain underboost.
c: Leak in charge air pipes, intercooler or clamps
Variable vane actuator or vane mechanism not reaching the commanded position
Exhaust leak upstream of the turbine
Boost pressure sensor reading too low
s: Engine warning lamp on
Clear loss of power under load
Whistling or hissing from the charge air side

P259F.t: Turbocharger A Boost Control Position At High Limit
P259F.d: P259F is the counterpart of P259E: the regulation of turbocharger A has hit its upper limit, and measured boost runs above the value the engine computer asked for. In Ford's 2023 diesel OBD summary it is the overboost monitor, checked continuously between 800 (6.7 L) or 1300 rpm (3.0 L) and 4000 rpm with at least 50 or 135 Nm of torque; it sets when actual boost exceeds the target by more than 120 kPa on the 6.7 L or 80 kPa on the 3.0 L for about 10-11 s. Ford bulletin 21-2074 for 2018-2019 Super Duty 6.7 L lists P259F among codes fixed by reprogramming the PCM, so software can be the trigger. More often a vane mechanism stuck toward closed or a wrong boost reading is to blame. P0234 is the separate absolute overboost code.
c: Vanes or wastegate stuck toward the closed position
Actuator or its vacuum/electrical control not opening as commanded
Engine control software needing an update
Boost pressure sensor reading too high
s: Engine warning lamp on
Sudden power cut at high load

P25A0.t: Turbocharger B Boost Control Position At Low Limit
P25A0.d: P25A0 says the regulator of turbocharger B has run to its low limit without reaching the boost target, so the second charger delivers too little pressure even with full control authority. It only exists on engines where two chargers are regulated separately. No manufacturer documents P25A0 publicly. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requires a fault once boost feedback control has used all of its adjustment and still misses the target, which describes this case. For the A side, Ford flags the same situation as P259E when requested boost exceeds measured boost by 120 kPa on its 6.7 L diesel for about 10 s. Leaks between charger B and the intake, a sticking wastegate or vanes and sensor errors are the usual suspects. P25A1 is the high-limit partner, P259E the turbocharger A version.
c: Leak in the charge air path served by charger B
Wastegate or vanes of charger B not closing as commanded
s: Engine warning lamp on
Lower power than usual, uneven pull

P25A1.t: Turbocharger B Boost Control Position At High Limit
P25A1.d: P25A1 is set when the boost control for turbocharger B is pinned at its upper limit and still cannot bring pressure down to the requested value, so the second charger overshoots. Like P25A0 it is limited to engines with two individually controlled chargers, and no manufacturer has published its own criteria for P25A1. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 asks the OBD system to detect boost control that has exhausted its authority as well as boost that climbs above the commanded level. Ford's overboost monitor for turbocharger A (P259F) gives a sense of scale: 120 kPa above target for about 10 s on the 6.7 L diesel. A wastegate or vane mechanism stuck toward closed, a blocked or misrouted control line, or false sensor readings are typical. Engines usually limit power to protect the turbo.
c: Wastegate or vanes of charger B stuck toward closed
Blocked, leaking or misrouted control line of actuator B
Boost pressure sensor giving wrong values
s: Engine warning lamp on
Power cut-out at high load

P25A2.t: Brake System Control Module A Requested MIL Illumination
P25A2.d: P25A2 is a messenger code: the brake system control module has stored an emission-relevant fault of its own and asks the engine module to light the check engine lamp. GM's 2017 engine table 17OBDG04 and 2019 hybrid table 19OBDG01 watch this request continuously from three seconds after power-up and class the engine module entry itself as Type A without a separate lamp request, because the lamp is already on the brake module's behalf. GM bulletins show the spread of causes: PIC6404 for 2020 Cadillac CT4 and CT5 links it to lost front camera communication, PIT6012 for 2023 Colorado and Canyon to a weak battery with C05D3 and a spongy pedal. Volvo's technical journal 36899 cures P25A268 on many 2017–2024 models by software. Read the brake module before replacing anything. Brake module B uses P25C9.
c: Emission-relevant fault stored in the brake control module
Weak battery or low system voltage upsetting the brake module
Brake or related module software needing an update
Lost communication with a partner module such as the front camera
s: Check engine lamp on
ABS, stability or driver assistance warnings at the same time
Brake pedal may feel soft in some cases

P25A3.d: P25A3 is a state code, not a wiring fault: the hood is reported open at a moment when the control strategy expects it closed, for example while an automatic restart, a remote start or a hybrid engine pull-up is pending. No manufacturer documents P25A3 publicly. A Stellantis STAR case on hood switch 2 explains the background: the PCM reads that switch directly, cross-checks it against the latch switch state sent by the body module over CAN, and if either reads open it disables stop-start until the trip ends and blocks remote start. CARB's OBD rule cites an override of start-stop disablement as an emissions-neutral diagnostic. Circuit faults of the switch itself are P254F and P257D–P257F. A hood not fully latched or a misadjusted switch striker is the usual reason.
c: Hood only on the safety catch, not fully latched
Hood switch or striker misadjusted after body work
Latch-integrated switch sticking in the open position
s: Hood open warning in the cluster
Auto stop-start and remote start locked out
Engine keeps running at standstill instead of stopping

P25A4.d: P25A4 is the general circuit fault for the fuel mode select switch – the button on bi-fuel vehicles with which the driver chooses between gasoline and an alternative fuel such as CNG or LPG. GM's 2015 bi-fuel Impala, described in PI1330, has it on the instrument panel left of the steering wheel; on the 2016 Silverado and Sierra 2500HD CNG trucks it sits in the centre stack and carries the fuel indicator. The engine module reads the switch line and logs P25A4 when it finds no valid signal at all, typically an open wire, a loose connector or a dead switch. No manufacturer documents P25A4 publicly. P25A5 covers plausibility, P25A6 and P25A7 low and high levels, P25A8 dropouts. The engine usually stays on gasoline or on the last mode, and switching by hand no longer works.
c: Open wire or unplugged connector at the fuel mode switch
Faulty connection in a bi-fuel conversion harness
s: Fuel cannot be changed with the switch
Engine runs on gasoline only
Fuel indicator light on the switch dark or flashing

P25A5.d: P25A5 flags a performance problem with the fuel mode select switch. The circuit is electrically sound, yet the switch behaves in a way that cannot be genuine, such as a momentary button that appears to be held down for minutes or a press that never returns to rest. On GM's bi-fuel trucks the chosen mode is kept across key cycles and each press toggles the fuel, so a stuck contact would keep requesting changes; GM's material on the bi-fuel Impala of 2015 notes that the switch light flashes while a fuel transition is under way. No manufacturer documents P25A5 publicly. Likely culprits are spilt drinks in the centre stack, a cap jammed after trim work or a switch from the wrong variant. The driver may lose manual fuel selection while the engine runs on.
c: Switch button sticking or contaminated by liquid
Panel trim pressing on the switch after installation work
Replacement switch of the wrong type or coding
s: Fuel mode changes by itself or not at all
Switch indicator keeps flashing

P25A6.t: Fuel Mode Select Switch Circuit Low
P25A6.d: P25A6 means the fuel mode select switch signal has fallen below the range the module accepts. On a switch that pulls a reference line towards ground when pressed, this is the signature of a signal wire rubbed through to the body or of moisture bridging the switch contacts; a grounded line could otherwise pass for a button held forever. CARB requires input components to be checked for out-of-range values, which is what this code reports. No manufacturer documents P25A6 publicly, though GM's bi-fuel Impala and 2500HD trucks show where the switch lives: dash panel or centre stack, close to cup holders and accessory wiring. Unlike P25A7, the cause is a path to ground, so isolating the switch from its harness is the first test. Fuel selection by hand is lost.
c: Switch signal wire chafed to ground behind the dash
Moisture or spilt liquid bridging the switch contacts
s: Fuel mode cannot be changed
Vehicle remains in one fuel mode

P25A7.t: Fuel Mode Select Switch Circuit High
P25A7.d: P25A7 reports a fuel mode select switch signal above the accepted window. With a pull-up input this mostly means the switch never closes its path – an open signal or return wire, a connector half off, a broken switch – or that the line has contact with a supply voltage, for example where an alternative-fuel conversion tapped into nearby wiring. No manufacturer documents P25A7 publicly; it follows CARB's demand that every computer input be checked for out-of-range readings. GM's 2016 Sierra and Silverado bi-fuel supplement shows the switch also carries the fuel indicator light, so a supply fault can affect both. Opposite to P25A6, measuring for voltage on the signal line with the switch unplugged separates a short to power from an open. Selection by switch stops working.
c: Open signal or return wire, connector not seated
Signal wire touching a supply voltage, e.g. after aftermarket wiring
s: Switch has no effect
Fuel indicator on the switch may stay dark

P25A8.t: Fuel Mode Select Switch Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P25A8.d: P25A8 records a fuel mode select switch signal that jumps or drops out briefly instead of staying in a stable state. The module sees transitions it cannot attribute to a real press, often while driving over rough roads, which points to a loose terminal, a cracked solder joint in the switch or a harness rubbing behind the trim. Because a press on GM's bi-fuel systems toggles the fuel even while driving, as GM states for its 2015 Impala, unwanted pulses could trigger needless fuel changes, which is why such glitches are flagged. No manufacturer documents P25A8 publicly. Wiggle tests with live data, checking terminal tension and inspecting any conversion harness are the right sequence. Short dropouts may come and go, and the code may return after clearing.
c: Loose terminal or poor contact at the switch connector
Cracked solder joint inside the switch
Harness rubbing behind the trim and shorting briefly
s: Occasional unexpected fuel mode changes
Switch light flickers
Code returns sporadically after clearing

P25A9.d: P25A9 covers the electrical circuit of the piston cooling oil control valve, the solenoid that switches the oil jets spraying the underside of the pistons. Under load the jets protect the pistons; when the engine is cold or lightly loaded they can be shut off to warm up faster and save oil pump work. GM's 2018 engine table 18OBDG04 checks the low-side driver of this valve on diesel engines while it is switched off and sets P25A9 when more than about 200 kilohm separate output and ground, meaning an open circuit, after 40 failures in 50 samples every 100 ms with at least 11 V supply (Type B, two trips); 17OBDG04 has the same check. Deutz EMR L1 engines log P25A9-13 for an open supply valve circuit and other subcodes for overcurrent or a shorted load. Stuck-off and stuck-on faults are P25AC and P25AD.
c: Valve connector unplugged, corroded or wire broken
Harness damaged by heat near the engine block
Output driver in the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine lamp on after two drives
Possible power reduction to protect the pistons

P25AA.t: Piston Cooling Oil Control Circuit Low
P25AA.d: P25AA flags a voltage at the piston cooling oil control valve output that sits too low for the commanded state, typically a short to ground between the module and the valve. This valve decides whether the oil jets under the pistons spray. GM's 2018 diesel engine table 18OBDG04 tests the low-side driver while it is switched off: if the output behaves like a connection of 0.5 ohm or less to ground in 40 of 50 checks taken every 100 ms, with at least 11 V from the powertrain relay, the code is stored as Type B and the lamp follows on the second trip. Deutz EMR L1 industrial engines report the same fault on their high-side switched supply valve as P25AA-11. An open circuit is P25A9, a short to power P25AB.
c: Valve control wire chafed through and touching ground
Internal short in the piston cooling valve
Water or oil in the valve connector bridging the pins
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp after two drives
Possible power limitation to protect the pistons

P25AB.t: Piston Cooling Oil Control Circuit High
P25AB.d: P25AB is the counterpart on the supply side: the control line of the piston cooling oil valve is pulled toward battery voltage. In GM's 18OBDG04 diesel table the check runs while the low-side driver is switched on; if the output then looks tied to power through 0.5 ohm or less, the module counts a short to power, again needing 40 failed samples out of 50 at 100 ms intervals with at least 11 V and logging a Type B fault with the lamp after the second trip. A shorted driver normally switches itself off for protection, so the valve then gets no command at all. Deutz lists P25AB-12 when the valve feeding the piston jets on EMR L1 engines is shorted to battery. Owners mostly notice only the warning lamp; some engines cut power to spare the pistons.
c: Control wire pinched against a live supply wire
Valve side of the circuit shorted to its own supply
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp after two drives
Piston cooling jets no longer switched
Possible reduced engine power

P25AC.t: Piston Cooling Oil Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
P25AC.d: P25AC is a functional fault rather than a wiring one: the valve is told to let oil reach the piston jets, but the feedback shows no flow. GM's 18OBDG04 diesel table reads a pressure switch in the jet circuit and fails the test when that switch stays without pressure while the engine turns, main oil pressure is at least 206 kPa and the command has been held for 8 s or more; 40 of 50 samples must fail, Type B. Porsche technical information 2306 from March 2023 for the Macan four-cylinder from model year 2022 explains that P25AC00, displayed there as an implausible oil pressure switch signal, mostly stems from machining swarf jamming the control valve; a new valve, cleaning and an oil change cure it. Without cooling oil the pistons run hotter under load.
c: Valve jammed by swarf or dirt in the oil
Piston cooling pressure switch faulty or unplugged
Low oil level or weak oil pressure feeding the jet circuit
Restricted oil passage to the jets
s: Check engine lamp after two drives
Engine power reduced under high load
Risk of piston damage if driven hard for long periods

P25AD.t: Piston Cooling Oil Control Circuit Stuck On
P25AD.d: P25AD describes the reverse mechanical failure: the piston cooling valve ought to be shut, yet oil keeps reaching the jets. GM's diesel table 18OBDG04 detects it when the pressure switch in the jet circuit reports pressure although the valve has been commanded to its off state for at least 8 s, with the engine turning and main oil pressure of at least 206 kPa; 40 bad samples out of 50 make it a Type B fault. Dirt or a broken return spring holding the valve open is the usual reason, a switch stuck closed the rarer one. The pistons are not at risk, but the jets bleed oil constantly, which can lower pressure at other consumers and lengthens warm-up after a cold start. Apart from GM, no manufacturer documents this code publicly.
c: Broken return spring in the valve
Piston cooling pressure switch stuck in the pressure position
s: Check engine lamp after two drives
Longer warm-up in cold weather
Slightly lower oil pressure reading at idle

P25AE.t: Piston Cooling Oil Pressure Too Low
P25AE.d: P25AE means the oil pressure reaching the piston cooling jets is below what the engine controller requires, even though the valve circuit itself shows no electrical fault. Volvo and Mack heavy trucks store it as P25AE00. Their bulletins KC-170 (2020, reissued 2021) and CBR 170-8 (May 2025, Mack and Volvo chassis from 2007 onward) cover an inactive P25AE00 set after a hard pull when engine oil pressure briefly drops, with SPN 4811 and SPN 100 named as related. Before parts are swapped, the oil temperature reading is compared with an infrared thermometer; a gap above 5 °F means a new sensor, otherwise technical support takes over. Real causes include low oil level, a tired pump or blocked jets. Lasting low cooling pressure endangers the pistons, so engines may derate.
c: Low oil level or oil starvation under hard load
Oil temperature sensor reading wrong (Volvo/Mack bulletin)
Worn oil pump or leaking pressure relief valve
Clogged oil filter or piston cooling jets
s: Inactive code after heavy pulling
Low oil pressure warning at the same time
Engine derate possible

P25AF.t: Coolant Temperature Control Module Requested MIL Illumination
P25AF.d: P25AF is a messenger code. A separate coolant temperature control module, used on some vehicles with electrically managed cooling for engine, battery or power electronics, has stored an emission-relevant fault of its own and asks the engine module to turn on the check engine lamp. CARB's OBD II rule expects lamp requests from other powertrain units to be passed on reliably. No manufacturer publicly documents P25AF with this meaning; the nearest documented relatives are GM's brake module requests P25A2 and P25C9, held in the engine module as Type A without a separate lamp command. Volkswagen's 2014 Touareg Hybrid data book still used P25AF for an engine hood switch message fault on CAN. The actual cause has to be read out of the thermal module.
c: Emission-relevant fault stored in the coolant temperature control module
Faulty coolant valve, pump or sensor handled by that module
Thermal module software needing an update
s: Check engine lamp on
Possible temperature warnings or reduced heating

P25B0.d: P25B0 means the main fuel level sender keeps reporting the same level although the engine has clearly been burning fuel. Ford runs this as a continuous check: the module totals the fuel injected, converts it into a share of tank capacity and compares that with how far the sender reading has moved. Depending on where the reading is frozen, the allowed mismatch is 60 % above a 90 % level, 30 % below 10 % and 25 % in between, and a full check can take 100 to 120 miles. Ford's 2012 summary still filed this fault under P0460; the 2014 Boss 302S list already marks P25B0 as a lamp code, and the 2024 summary reports it as P0460 with failure type 2A. GM covers a frozen sender with P0461 instead. CARB names the stuck fuel level sensor as a rationality check. The gauge stays put, so running dry is a real risk.
c: Float arm caught on the tank wall, baffle or pump module
Worn spot on the sender resistor track holding the wiper at one value
Float soaked with fuel and sunk to the bottom
Fuel consumption calculation in the PCM not matching the tank
s: Fuel gauge stays at the same mark over a long distance
Engine runs out of fuel while the gauge still shows fuel
Check engine lamp on

P25B1.d: P25B1 points at the second fuel level sender, the one found in the passive half of a saddle tank or in an additional tank. Its reading no longer changes in step with the fuel actually burned. Ford applies the same consumption comparison as for sender A, with mismatch limits between 25 % and 60 % depending on the frozen level, and the 2024 summary maps this fault to P2065 with failure type 2A. A frozen B reading is not always the sender's fault: if the jet pump that pulls fuel across from the passive side stops working, that half really does stay full while the other empties, which looks the same to the module. The averaged gauge value then drifts away from the true content and the range estimate becomes unreliable. Ford's 2014 Boss 302S list gives P25B1 the lamp; GM uses P2066 for a stuck second sender instead.
c: Float of sender B jammed or resistor track worn
Jet pump or its line no longer drawing fuel from the passive tank half
Blocked or kinked transfer line between the tank chambers
s: Gauge reading too high or barely falling as the tank empties
Engine stalls from fuel starvation with an apparently quarter-full tank
Check engine lamp on

P25B2.t: Fuel Level Sensor A or B Stuck
P25B2.d: P25B2 is the shared variant for tanks with two senders: the module has found that the level information is frozen but does not commit to which of the two senders is responsible. Ford lists it next to P25B0 and P25B1 under the same consumption-versus-reading check (100 to 120 miles, 25 to 60 % allowed mismatch) and, unlike the other two, keeps P25B2 as its own base code in the 2024 summary with failure type 00. When a calibration uses P25B2 instead of the single-sender codes is not explained publicly; a plausible case is a system that only evaluates the combined value of both senders. For the repair this means both senders, the jet pump and the wiring to each must be checked one after another, ideally by comparing each raw reading with the actual tank content. The 2014 Boss 302S list marks P25B2 as a lamp code.
c: One of the two senders mechanically stuck
Fuel no longer moved between tank halves by the jet pump
Corroded connector on the tank unit freezing one signal
s: Gauge stuck or moving far less than fuel used
Range display unreliable
Check engine lamp on

P25B3.d: P25B3 says the wastegate of turbocharger A stays further open than the module commands, so exhaust bypasses the turbine and boost falls short. On Ford EcoBoost engines with an electric wastegate actuator and position sensor, the PCM compares commanded and measured position; a gap above 20 mm held for 2.5 s sets the code, provided no circuit fault (P0243, P2ABD) is present. The 2024 summary reports it as P0243 with failure type 72. Ford bulletins SSM 49427 and 50171 cover 2.0/2.3 L EcoBoost models from 2019 (Edge, Escape, Ranger, Explorer, Bronco Sport and others) with a missing e-clip, a dead actuator or a damaged actuator rod; a service kit replaces actuator, rod and clips without a new turbocharger. Toyota lists P25B3-72 on the 2022 Tundra V35A and released new ECM software for it on the 2023 GR Corolla. Expect lack of power.
c: Missing retaining clip disconnecting actuator rod from the wastegate lever
Electric wastegate actuator failed or rod bent
Wastegate flap or bushing seized in the open position by heat or carbon
Diagnostic calibration needing an update (Toyota GR Corolla)
s: Clearly reduced power and slow boost build-up
Check engine lamp on, often with an underboost code
Wrench or reduced power warning on some models

P25B4.d: P25B4 is the reverse of P25B3: the module asked wastegate A to open, yet the valve stays shut or opens far too little. Ford uses the same position comparison for both directions (error over 20 mm for 2.5 s); in 2024 it appears as P0243 with failure type 73. Other makers infer the fault from pressure. Porsche explains that its DME judges the wastegate by the boost building up ahead of the throttle; on the 2021 Cayenne E3 PHEV during catalyst warm-up (bulletin 2230) and on Cayenne E-Hybrid models after a dynamic engine start from electric driving (250/22), a weak build-up was misread as a jammed valve, cured by DME software. Audi did the same for the 2018–2019 RS 5. Ford SSM 50670 for 2.3 L EcoBoost Ranger, Bronco and Explorer built from 14 Dec 2021 says: clear, road test under load, and replace the turbo if P25B4 returns.
c: Wastegate flap or spindle seized shut by carbon or corrosion
Actuator or linkage unable to move the valve
False detection by engine software (Porsche Cayenne, Audi RS 5)
Internal turbocharger fault requiring replacement (Ford SSM 50670)
s: Power reduced because the module limits boost
Possible overboost code alongside
Check engine lamp on

P25B5.d: P25B5 concerns wastegate B, which on twin-turbo V engines belongs to the second turbocharger, normally on the other cylinder bank. The valve remains open beyond what the PCM commands, so this turbo delivers too little boost while the A side may work normally. Ford monitors B separately from A with its own position sensor: more than 20 mm between target and actual for 2.5 s, checked only when the B circuit codes P0247 and P2ABE are absent; the 2024 summary lists it as P0247 with type 72. Ford TSB 23-2353 reprograms the PCM on 3.5 L EcoBoost F-150 (2022–2023) and Expedition/Navigator (2023–2024) for P25B3 to P25B6 and the related position sensor codes; the later SSM 54083 sends technicians back to the pinpoint tests because a real wastegate fault can be behind them. Toyota also names P25B5-72 for the 2022 Tundra V35A.
c: Wastegate B linkage loose or disconnected
Actuator B failed or its position sensor reading wrong
Flap of wastegate B seized open
s: Reduced power, especially when accelerating under load
Check engine lamp and/or wrench indicator on

P25B6.d: With P25B6 the second wastegate refuses to open when commanded, so turbo B cannot be regulated down and may push boost beyond the target; the module then usually caps torque. Ford detects it with the B-side position comparison (over 20 mm for 2.5 s, no P0247 or P2ABE present) and in 2024 files it as P0247 with type 73. A Ford case shows that loose hardware can trigger the closed-side codes too: TSB 24-2112 for the 2021–2023 Bronco with 2.7 L or 3.0 L engines lists P25B4, P25B6 and P0299 together and traces them to a loose nut on the turbo actuator arm, which leaves the valve out of its intended position and causes underboost. The same PCM update and later pinpoint advice as for P25B5 apply to 3.5 L EcoBoost trucks (TSB 23-2353, SSM 54083). Toyota lists P25B6-73 for the 2022 Tundra V35A.
c: Loose nut on the turbo actuator arm (Ford Bronco TSB 24-2112)
Wastegate B flap or spindle seized shut
Actuator B unable to drive the valve open
s: Power limited, sometimes after a short boost spike
Check engine lamp on, possibly with P0299 or an overboost code

P25B7.t: Auxiliary Ignition Switch On/Start Position Circuit
P25B7.d: P25B7 covers the hard-wired input from an auxiliary ignition switch that commands the On and Start positions from a second location, for example a rear panel behind the cab, a work platform or a remote station on a chassis-cab truck. The module flags a state on this line it cannot interpret, such as an open circuit, without saying whether the level is too low or too high. No manufacturer documents P25B7 publicly. The nearest published logic is the main run/crank input, for which the GM brake control module in table 25OBDG04A sets P2534 when its wake-up line stays low for 3 s while the ECM reports run or crank. Navistar describes remote start and shutdown panels for PTO bodies built on this principle. For the driver, the remote start point may stop responding while the key in the cab still works.
c: Open wire or loose connector in the harness to the body or remote panel
Worn or corroded contacts in the auxiliary switch
Input stage of the reading module damaged
s: Engine cannot be started or switched on from the auxiliary position
Normal key or push-button start still works
Stored code, often without other complaints

P25B8.t: Auxiliary Ignition Switch On/Start Position Circuit Low
P25B8.d: P25B8 means the auxiliary On/Start input sits at a low level when the module expects it to be active, or never rises when the remote switch is operated. Typical reasons are a switch contact that no longer closes, a blown fuse feeding the remote panel, a broken wire in the long harness run to the body or a short to ground at a frame connector. In practice it behaves like a dead remote switch: requests from the auxiliary position are ignored, so a crew working at the body or platform cannot start the engine or keep it on from there. As no maker publishes this code, the GM main-switch case serves as reference, where GM's brake control module needs its wake-up line low for 3 s against a run/crank message from the ECM before logging P2534 as a Type B fault. P25B9 covers the opposite direction.
c: Blown fuse or failed relay feeding the auxiliary switch
Signal wire shorted to ground on the frame or body
Auxiliary switch contact no longer closes
Corroded exterior connector with high resistance
s: Remote start or on request is ignored
Engine may shut down when the auxiliary position is used to keep it running
Remote panel indicator stays dark

P25B9.t: Auxiliary Ignition Switch On/Start Position Circuit High
P25B9.d: With P25B9 the module sees the auxiliary On/Start line at a high level when it ought to be inactive, for example after key-off or with no request from the remote panel. A switch stuck in the start position, a wire rubbing against a battery feed, backfeed through an upfitter relay or moisture bridging terminals in an exterior switch box can all hold the line up. The consequences differ from the low fault: a permanent start request can keep control modules awake and flatten the battery, and in the worst case could engage the starter unexpectedly. On its own wake-up input, GM's 2025 brake module (25OBDG04A) logs P2535 when the line stays high for 3 s although the ECM reports it should be low. P25B9 itself is not described publicly by any manufacturer, so diagnosis follows the upfitter wiring diagram.
c: Signal wire chafed against a battery or ignition feed
Auxiliary switch stuck in the On/Start position
Backfeed through an upfitter relay or accessory
Moisture in an exterior switch box or connector
s: Battery drains overnight because modules stay awake
Auxiliary start function disabled or behaving erratically
Starter may engage or click unexpectedly

P25BA.d: P25BA concerns the dash or panel switch with which the driver starts, or on some trucks blocks, a diesel particulate filter regeneration. The engine controller reads the switch as a discrete input and sets this code when the circuit is open or otherwise unusable, so a press no longer reaches it. Volvo describes a rocker of this kind: one half inhibits automatic regeneration below 40 km/h, the other starts a parked regeneration with the truck stationary, parking brake set, gearbox in neutral and engine warm. GM's L5P trucks with option FPF instead use the exhaust brake switch for the same job (bulletin 20-NA-203). No manufacturer documents P25BA publicly. Automatic regeneration while driving continues, but a requested parked regeneration cannot be started and soot can build up.
c: Switch connector loose or unplugged behind the dash
Broken signal or reference wire to the switch
Internal open circuit in the regeneration switch
s: Parked regeneration cannot be started when the cluster asks for it
Filter or regeneration warning lamp stays on longer than usual
Check engine lamp

P25BB.d: P25BB reports that the regeneration switch input reads a low level the switch itself cannot produce. Depending on the wiring, this points to a short to ground in the harness, a contact that is permanently closed to ground or a damaged switch module. On a ground-switching design such a fault would look like a button held down all the time, so the controller can no longer tell a genuine request from the defect and has reason to disregard the input. Regeneration switches are typical on vocational trucks, buses and chassis cabs that idle a lot and have to clean the filter while parked; the US Forest Service explains the procedure for its own diesel fleet. No manufacturer documents P25BB publicly. Its sibling P25BC covers the high side, P25BA an open circuit.
c: Switch signal wire shorted to ground
Switch panel damaged by liquid or impact
s: Regeneration switch has no effect
Parked regeneration may be unavailable when soot load is high
Check engine lamp

P25BC.d: P25BC is the high-voltage counterpart: the regeneration switch line carries a level near supply voltage that no switch position can produce. A wire chafed against a battery or ignition feed, water in a switch connector or a switch whose internal resistor network has failed are plausible causes. If the switch requests regeneration by pulling the line up, a stuck high could resemble a permanent start command. That matters because a parked regeneration raises idle speed and exhaust temperature sharply; GM bulletin 20-NA-203 tells drivers to stand on level ground outdoors, clear of anything that can burn. Without a reliable switch the engine controller has to rely on automatic regeneration while driving. No manufacturer documents P25BC publicly, so repair follows the vehicle's wiring diagram.
c: Switch signal wire shorted to battery or ignition voltage
Internal fault in the switch or its resistor network
s: Regeneration switch ignored by the engine controller
Unexpected regeneration messages in the cluster
Check engine lamp

P25BD.d: P25BD protects against engine runaway, where the engine keeps speeding up although the controller injects no fuel, for instance because oil from a failed turbocharger seal or combustible vapour drawn into the intake is being burned. GM documents the monitor in its diesel ECM tables. In 14OBDG04 the speed must pass 5,400 rpm for 0.01 s, after which the controller cuts the air supply with its intake air valve and disables the injectors; 18OBDG04 uses 5,500 rpm for 0.5 s and 20OBDG04 5,200 rpm for 0.1 s, both enabled above 1,500 rpm. Each table rates it Type A, so the MIL comes on in the first trip. Unlike P0219, which merely records an overspeed, P25BD means the engine was forcibly stopped. Before a restart, turbo, crankcase ventilation and intake tract should be checked for oil.
c: Turbocharger seal failure feeding oil into the intake
Oil carry-over from crankcase ventilation, e.g. overfilled or diluted oil
Combustible vapour drawn in from the surroundings
Erroneous engine speed signal or controller fault
s: Engine revs up uncontrollably and then shuts off
Heavy smoke from the exhaust before shutdown
Check engine lamp on immediately
Possible severe engine damage after the event

P25BE.d: P25BE concerns the output with which the engine controller tells an alternative fuel system, usually a CNG or LPG installation, to stop gas operation, for example after a fault, with an empty gas tank or while the engine warms up. The code reports an open circuit or a driver fault on this control line, so the command may no longer reach the gas controller or its shut-off valves. GM describes bi-fuel vehicles such as the Impala with the LFR engine, where one ECM runs both fuel systems and switches to the healthy one if a delivery problem appears; LPG retrofits often add a separate gas controller. No manufacturer documents P25BE publicly. CARB treats such a vehicle as alternate-fueled only while it burns the gas fuel. The vehicle normally keeps running on gasoline.
c: Open control wire between engine controller and gas system
Poor splice or connector in a retrofit gas installation
Open coil in a gas disable relay
Output driver in the engine controller defective
s: Vehicle stays on gasoline or will not switch to gas
Fuel mode indicator flashes or shows a system fault
Check engine lamp

P25BF.t: Alternative Fuel Disable Control Circuit High
P25BF.d: P25BF flags a voltage on the alternative fuel disable output that is too high for the state the engine controller is commanding. On a low-side driver this usually means a short to battery or ignition voltage, for instance where a gas kit harness has been routed along a hot feed or tapped into the wrong wire. Depending on design, a constantly high line may be read by the gas system as a permanent block, or the controller may switch the driver off to protect itself; either way the command it sends is no longer trustworthy. GM's 2016 Silverado and Sierra bi-fuel trucks show what the driver sees when gas operation is refused: the fuel indicator flashes and the truck stays on gasoline. No manufacturer documents P25BF publicly. Note that SAE lists High before Low in this group.
c: Control wire shorted to battery or ignition voltage
Retrofit gas kit tapped into the wrong circuit
Faulty input stage in the gas controller backfeeding voltage
s: Gas operation blocked, vehicle runs on gasoline only
Fuel mode indicator flashes
Check engine lamp

P25C0.t: Alternative Fuel Disable Control Circuit Low
P25C0.d: P25C0 is set when the alternative fuel disable output reads too low, typically a short to ground somewhere between the engine controller and the gas system. With a high-side driver that pin would then be unable to deliver its voltage; with a low-side driver the line would look permanently switched. The practical risk lies in which state the gas system reads as safe: if a missing block signal were taken as permission, gas could be released when the controller wants it off, so controllers generally stop gas operation as soon as such a fault is confirmed. CARB requires every 2019 and later alternate-fueled vehicle to run under an approved monitoring plan, which is where checks like this belong. No manufacturer documents P25C0 publicly; the open circuit is P25BE, the high fault P25BF.
c: Control wire shorted to ground, often where routed along the frame
Chafed insulation on a retrofit gas kit harness
Output stage in the engine controller damaged
s: Vehicle refuses to switch to gas
Fuel system fault message or flashing fuel indicator
Check engine lamp

P25C1.d: P25C1 relates to the incoming side of the alternative fuel disable function: a signal line on which the engine controller reads whether gas operation is blocked, either as feedback from the gas system or as a request from it, for example when a CNG or LPG controller detects low tank pressure or its own fault. The code says the signal is missing or unusable without naming a direction. In GM's bi-fuel Silverado and Sierra the system changes back to gasoline by itself when the gas tank runs empty and stops toggling after 20 transitions in one key cycle, which shows how much the engine controller depends on knowing the gas system's state. No manufacturer documents P25C1 publicly. P25C2 and P25C3 are the high and low variants; P25BE to P25C0 cover the control output.
c: Open signal wire from the gas system
Gas controller without power or ground, so no signal is sent
Corroded underbody connector of the gas system
s: Gas mode unavailable or drops out while driving
Fuel mode indicator flashes
Check engine lamp

P25C2.t: Alternative Fuel Disable Signal Circuit High
P25C2.d: P25C2 means the alternative fuel disable signal arriving at the engine controller sits above its valid range. Likely explanations are a short to a voltage feed, a missing ground at the gas controller that lets its output float up, or an open line combined with an internal pull-up in the reading module. Whether a high level reads as blocked or as released depends on the design, so the engine controller can no longer trust the gas system's status and will usually stay with or return to gasoline. GM's Impala bi-fuel information shows the logic behind this: with a delivery concern on one side, the ECM moves to the fuel system that is working. No manufacturer documents P25C2 publicly. In the SAE list the High code precedes the Low code here, unlike most groups.
c: Signal wire shorted to a voltage feed
Missing ground at the gas controller letting its output float high
Open signal wire pulled up inside the reading module
s: Vehicle stays on gasoline
Gas system fault indication
Check engine lamp

P25C3.t: Alternative Fuel Disable Signal Circuit Low
P25C3.d: P25C3 is logged when the alternative fuel disable signal reaching the engine controller is too low to be valid. A short to ground on the way from the gas system, a gas controller that has lost its supply, or a damaged output stage in that controller can each pull the line down. On a gas installation that announces a block by grounding the line, this would also be indistinguishable from a genuine stop request, so the engine controller has to treat gas operation as unavailable. GM's 2016 bi-fuel trucks illustrate the fallback: they start on gasoline and only change over once the conditions for gas operation have been met, and a failed changeover is shown with the fuel indicator. No manufacturer documents P25C3 publicly. The general signal fault is P25C1, the opposite case P25C2.
c: Damaged output stage in the gas controller
s: No change-over to gas operation
Fuel mode indicator flashes or shows a fault
Check engine lamp

P25C4.t: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P25C4.d: P25C4 covers the first temperature sensor of an electromechanical brake booster, in which an electric motor and gear set take the place of the vacuum diaphragm, as in Bosch's iBooster. The booster electronics use this value to protect motor and control unit from overheating during long or repeated braking. P25C4 reports an unusable sensor circuit without a direction. GM's 2023 Corvette Z06 table 23OBDG07 lists only the separate low and high codes P25C6 and P25C7 for this sensor in its EBCM section, plus C0579 and C057A for a second sensor; a generic circuit code does not appear there, and no manufacturer publishes P25C4. GM requires the booster temperature sensors to be fault free before it runs its rotor and ECU over-temperature checks, so a failed sensor removes that protection.
c: Temperature sensor inside the booster unit defective
Fault in the booster control electronics
s: Brake system warning in the cluster
Brake pedal may feel harder if assistance is reduced
Stored code, often together with chassis codes

P25C5.t: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P25C5.d: P25C5 is the plausibility fault for brake booster temperature sensor A: the circuit is electrically intact, but the reported temperature does not fit, for example a value that jumps implausibly, stays frozen while the motor works hard, or disagrees with the second sensor. No manufacturer documents P25C5 publicly. GM takes a different route on the 2023 Corvette Z06: rather than a separate rationality code, table 23OBDG07 adds up the signal voltages of temperature sensors 1 and 2 and logs the motor code C0582 as Type A once the sum exceeds 3.4 V for 0.6 s. That shows how two sensors can be checked against each other. A drifting sensor is the real hazard here, because the over-temperature protection of the electric motor relies on it.
c: Sensor drifted out of its characteristic curve
Contact resistance at the booster connector skewing the signal
Measurement error in the booster electronics
s: Brake warning message, sometimes only after long braking
Brake assistance reduced as a precaution

P25C6.t: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P25C6.d: P25C6 means the signal of brake booster temperature sensor A is too low, which GM describes as the sensor line being shorted to ground. GM uses the code on the 2023 Corvette Z06 (table 23OBDG07, EBCM section) and keeps the same logic in its 2024 and 2025 tables 24OBDG07 and 25OBDG03A: the check runs continuously with the ignition on, needs the condition five times in a row within 0.6 s and is rated Type B, so the MIL comes on after two trips. The voltage limit for the low side is left blank in the published tables. A low reading can also come from a pinched harness at the booster, from water in the connector or from a sensor that has failed internally. The sibling P25C7 covers a short to supply, C0579 the same fault on the second sensor.
c: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Internal short in the temperature sensor
s: Check engine lamp after two trips
Brake system warning message
Brake assistance may be limited

P25C7.t: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P25C7.d: P25C7 flags a sensor A signal that is too high; GM interprets it as the temperature line shorted to supply. In the EBCM part of table 23OBDG07 for the 2023 Corvette Z06 the voltage must exceed 3.27 V five consecutive times within 0.6 s with the ignition on, and the fault is Type B with two trips to the MIL. Tables 24OBDG07 and 25OBDG03A repeat these values. Beyond a real short, an open sensor or a broken ground can also pull the signal toward the top of the range on many sensor designs, so the wiring at the booster deserves a check before the unit is replaced. Its second sensor uses the slightly lower limit of 3.14 V and the chassis code C057A. P25C6 is the low-side counterpart.
c: Sensor signal shorted to the supply line
Open sensor circuit or missing sensor ground
s: Check engine lamp after two trips
Brake system warning message
Reduced brake assistance possible

P25C8.t: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P25C8.d: P25C8 is meant for a sensor A signal that drops out briefly or jumps faster than any real temperature in the booster could change, the typical footprint of a loose pin, a cracked solder joint or a wire that breaks under vibration. Each event may be too short for the low or high check to confirm, which is why this separate code exists. No manufacturer documents P25C8 publicly. GM's 2023 Corvette tables only confirm hard faults, requiring five consecutive out-of-range readings within 0.6 s for P25C6 or P25C7, so a fault that comes and goes might remain hidden there. Because an electromechanical booster such as Bosch's iBooster can also build brake pressure on its own for assistance systems, a jittery temperature input may make the unit limit its motor torque at unexpected moments.
c: Loose or spread terminal in the booster connector
Cracked solder joint inside the booster electronics
s: Brake warning that appears and disappears
Occasional change in pedal feel

P25C9.t: Brake System Control Module B Requested MIL Illumination
P25C9.d: P25C9 tells the engine module that a second brake system control module, labelled B, has found an emission-relevant malfunction and wants the check engine lamp switched on. GM uses the code in its hybrid OBD tables 16OBDG01, 18OBDG01 and 19OBDG01: the engine module listens to the lamp request message from module B continuously, starting three seconds after power-up, and logs P25C9 as Type A but without its own lamp request, since the brake module already asks for the lamp. Which fault lies behind it only module B can say, so its memory is read first; a low battery or network trouble can also upset it. Brake module A reports the same situation as P25A2. As braking functions may be involved, the car should be checked soon.
c: Fault stored in brake system control module B
Weak battery or low system voltage
Communication fault between module B and its partners
s: Check engine lamp on
Brake or stability warnings at the same time

P25CA.t: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit/Open (Bank 1)
P25CA.d: Some cam phasers carry a locking pin that holds the rotor in a fixed base or middle position for starting and while oil pressure is still building. Where that pin is released and engaged by its own solenoid, the controller supervises this extra circuit. P25CA reports that the lock control circuit for the intake phaser on bank 1 is open or otherwise not behaving electrically, so the lock can no longer be operated on command. GM's 2015 Volt and ELR table 15OBDG01 lists P25CA among the intake phaser fault groups that suspend the other cam phaser diagnostics; it gives no thresholds of its own. Passive designs such as BorgWarner's mid-position lock for Hyundai lack this circuit. Expect rough starts or idle and limited cam timing.
c: Open winding in the intake phaser lock solenoid
Connector off or terminal pushed back after engine work
Broken wire between module and lock solenoid
s: Check engine lamp on
Rough start or unsteady idle
Intake cam timing held at a default position, less power

P25CB.t: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit Low (Bank 1)
P25CB.d: P25CB points to a control line for the intake phaser lock on bank 1 that reads lower than it should, most often a short to ground on the wire or inside the lock solenoid. Depending on how the driver is wired, the solenoid may then stay energised or never receive current, so the lock pin is either released all the time or cannot be pulled back. Released permanently, the phaser can rattle at start before oil pressure arrives; stuck in, it keeps the intake cam at its base timing. GM's 2015 Volt and ELR OBD table 15OBDG01 places P25CB in the intake phaser fault bundles that pause the related phaser checks, without listing a threshold. CARB requires circuit checks on such output components. Low voltage events can set several lock codes together.
c: Lock control wire shorted to ground
Internal short in the lock solenoid
Weak battery or voltage dip during cranking
s: Check engine lamp on
Brief rattle from the timing drive at start
Reduced power with fixed intake timing

P25CC.t: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit High (Bank 1)
P25CC.d: With P25CC the controller sees the intake phaser lock control line on bank 1 sitting higher than expected, typically because it touches a live wire or the solenoid's ground path is shorted to supply. A protected output stage usually shuts down when it detects this, which leaves the lock solenoid without control: the pin falls back to whatever its spring dictates, and the intake phaser is then often parked at its locked base timing until the next restart. The GM 15OBDG01 table for the 2015 Volt and ELR counts P25CC among the intake phaser bundles that block further phaser diagnostics, but publishes no detection limits. Under CARB rules a circuit fault on such an output must be detected and stored. Inspect the harness near hot or moving parts first.
c: Lock control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Harness insulation melted near the exhaust or turbo
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp on
Sluggish response with intake timing fixed

P25CD.t: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit/Open (Bank 2)
P25CD.d: P25CD is the bank 2 version of the open-circuit lock fault and therefore only appears on V or boxer engines whose second cylinder bank has its own intake phaser with a separately switched lock pin. The controller finds the lock solenoid circuit on that bank interrupted or electrically implausible, so it can no longer release or set the pin deliberately. If bank 1 is free of faults, comparing both banks' lock circuits with a multimeter quickly isolates the broken side. GM's 15OBDG01 OBD table lists P25CD in its intake phaser fault bundles even though the Volt engine it covers has a single bank, which shows these entries are shared software rather than an engine-specific description. Symptoms are uneven idle and lower power from the affected bank.
c: Open circuit inside the bank 2 lock solenoid
Bank 2 lock solenoid connector unplugged or corroded
Wire break in the harness across the engine
s: Check engine lamp on
Uneven idle
Less power, bank 2 intake timing fixed

P25CE.t: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit Low (Bank 2)
P25CE.d: P25CE stands for a low signal on the lock control line of the bank 2 intake phaser: the wire or the solenoid winding has found a path to ground, or the module's output is stuck pulling low. Because the second bank's harness often runs along the back of the engine or under the intake manifold, chafing at brackets and heat damage are frequent findings. A grounded line may hold the lock solenoid energised permanently, leaving the pin withdrawn when the engine is shut down, which can cause a clatter on the next cold start. GM's 15OBDG01 table includes P25CE in the intake phaser fault groups that disable the other phaser monitors, without its own limits. Codes for both banks at once suggest a shared supply or low battery voltage rather than two bad solenoids.
c: Bank 2 harness chafed through at a bracket
Shorted winding in the bank 2 lock solenoid
Low system voltage setting lock codes on both banks
s: Check engine lamp on
Clatter at cold start

P25CF.t: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit High (Bank 2)
P25CF.d: P25CF is logged when the bank 2 intake phaser lock control line stays above its permitted voltage band. Common reasons are contact with a powered wire, moisture bridging connector pins to a supply terminal, or a failed output transistor in the controller. Once the driver protects itself and stops switching, the second bank's lock can no longer be released, so its intake cam may stay at the base timing while bank 1 still adjusts; the resulting imbalance shows up as a lumpy idle. In GM's 15OBDG01 table P25CF closes the list of intake phaser lock codes in the fault bundles that suspend the other phaser tests; no threshold is published. Before replacing the controller, measure the line with the solenoid unplugged.
c: Bank 2 lock control wire touching a powered circuit
Moisture in the connector bridging to a supply pin
Failed output transistor in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp on
Lumpy idle from uneven bank timing

P25D0.t: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit/Open (Bank 1)
P25D0.d: P25D0 moves the open-circuit lock fault to the exhaust side: the solenoid that releases the locking pin of the bank 1 exhaust cam phaser can no longer be driven because its circuit is interrupted or reads implausibly. The lock keeps the exhaust cam at a defined position while the engine starts, before the phaser has enough oil pressure to hold itself. No manufacturer documents P25D0 publicly; GM's 2015 Volt table names only the intake lock codes, and BorgWarner's mid-position lock for the Hyundai Gamma II four-cylinder is fitted on the intake cam while the exhaust phaser has none. The background therefore rests on CARB's rules for variable valve timing and output circuits. Without lock control the exhaust timing stays fixed, which costs economy and raises emissions.
c: Open winding in the exhaust phaser lock solenoid
Broken wire to the exhaust lock solenoid
s: Check engine lamp on
Slightly higher fuel consumption
Rough idle possible

P25D1.t: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit Low (Bank 1)
P25D1.d: P25D1 indicates that the control signal for the bank 1 exhaust phaser lock is too low, normally a grounded wire or a solenoid winding that leaks to ground. The exhaust side is the hotter one, so insulation that has hardened and cracked near the manifold or turbocharger is a typical finding. With the line grounded, the solenoid may stay powered and keep the pin retracted, or it never gets current, in which case the phaser stays locked. Either way the controller usually stops adjusting exhaust timing and falls back to a safe default. No public manufacturer document lists P25D1; the description follows the J2012 wording, CARB's requirement for circuit checks on output components and the general working of locking cam phasers.
c: Heat-cracked insulation grounding the lock wire
Engine oil wicked into the connector
s: Check engine lamp on
Exhaust timing fixed, slightly less power

P25D2.t: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit High (Bank 1)
P25D2.d: P25D2 is set when the bank 1 exhaust phaser lock control line carries more voltage than the controller allows in the current switching state, for example because it is shorted to an ignition-fed wire or the solenoid's return is tied to supply. Most output stages detect overcurrent here and switch off, so the lock solenoid loses its command and the pin goes to the position its spring defines. The engine then runs with a fixed exhaust cam until the fault clears. No manufacturer publishes material for P25D2; the explanation uses the J2012 title, CARB's demand for electrical monitoring of output components in variable valve timing systems, and the working principle of locking phasers. Unlike the Low code, a short to power can also damage the driver.
c: Lock control wire shorted to an ignition-fed circuit
Solenoid return path shorted to supply
Damaged output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp on
Weaker mid-range pull

P25D3.t: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit/Open (Bank 2)
P25D3.d: P25D3 concerns engines with two cylinder banks and a lockable exhaust phaser on each: the lock solenoid circuit of the bank 2 exhaust phaser is open or electrically implausible, so the module loses control over its pin. On many V engines the bank 2 exhaust solenoid sits at the rear or close to the firewall, where connectors are easily left loose after timing work. A loose plug sets only this code, whereas an open in a shared supply would usually trigger lock codes on several phasers at once. No manufacturer documents P25D3 in public material; the text is based on CARB's variable valve timing and output monitoring rules and on how locking phasers operate. The engine keeps running, but with fixed exhaust timing on bank 2.
c: Bank 2 exhaust lock connector left loose after timing work
Open winding in the bank 2 exhaust lock solenoid
Open in a supply shared with other phaser solenoids
s: Check engine lamp on
Uneven running between the banks

P25D4.t: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit Low (Bank 2)
P25D4.d: P25D4 reports a lock control line for the bank 2 exhaust phaser that is pulled down below its expected level. Grounding through damaged insulation, a solenoid with shorted turns or oil that has crept into the connector are the usual explanations. Because the exhaust manifold of the second bank radiates onto nearby harness sections, heat sleeving that has slipped out of place is worth checking. While the fault is active the controller cannot set the lock reliably and normally freezes exhaust timing on that bank. As with the other exhaust lock codes, there is no public manufacturer documentation; the account rests on CARB's circuit monitoring requirement and the operating principle of locking phasers. Repair is wiring work or a new solenoid.
c: Heat sleeve slipped, wire grounded at the manifold
Shorted turns in the bank 2 exhaust lock solenoid
s: Check engine lamp on
Bank 2 exhaust timing fixed

P25D5.t: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit High (Bank 2)
P25D5.d: P25D5 closes this series: the bank 2 exhaust phaser's lock control signal sits above its allowed voltage, pointing to a short to battery or ignition voltage, a return path tied to supply, or a defective output in the module. The protected driver then stops switching, and the lock solenoid stays without command until the next key cycle or until the fault vanishes. If P25D5 shows up together with high codes on other actuators, a shared harness fault or a module problem is more likely than a bad solenoid. There is no public manufacturer documentation for P25D5; the description draws on CARB's monitoring rules for variable valve timing and output components and on the design of locking phasers. Driveability suffers only mildly, but emissions and fuel use rise.
c: Bank 2 exhaust lock wire shorted to battery or ignition voltage
Harness fault affecting several actuator lines
Defective output in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp on
Slightly higher fuel consumption

P25D6.t: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Stop Performance
P25D6.d: An exhaust heat exchanger moves exhaust heat into the coolant after a cold start; a flap (bypass valve A) decides whether gas flows through it or around it, and a position sensor reports where the flap is. P25D6 targets the end-stop values of that sensor: at the fully open and fully closed stops the reading must sit inside a learned or calibrated window. If a stop is no longer reached, or the stop value has shifted, the code is set. No manufacturer documents P25D6 publicly; the B-side twin is P23A8. The closest documented case is Ford's general valve A position sensor performance code P2C23 on full hybrids (F-150, Explorer, Escape, Maverick), where SSM 52543 first checks the exhaust coolant temperature sensor connectors and SSM 53003 replaces a worn actuator. Driving usually feels normal; warm-up may slow.
c: Carbon build-up or a bent flap stopping short of its end stop
Worn valve actuator or linkage play
Position sensor shifted on its mount or drifting
End stops not relearned after parts replacement
s: Check engine lamp on without noticeable driving change
Slower engine warm-up or weaker cabin heat in winter

P25D7.d: Fuel level sensor C is a third level input, needed only where the fuel is spread over more chambers or tanks than two senders can cover, for instance on trucks with an extra tank. P25D7 is its general circuit code: the module sees an electrical fault on this input but does not classify it as low, high or intermittent. No manufacturer documents P25D7 publicly. The analogue at sender A shows how such a check works: Ford sets P0460 when the sender resistance stays below 5 ohms or above 200 ohms for 30 s. Regulators insist on supervising these inputs because misfire and evaporative tests may be suspended when the tank is at 15 % or less, and a wrong level can let them run or block them at the wrong time. For the driver the fuel gauge or range display may show nonsense or a substitute value.
c: Damaged wiring between tank C sender and module, often under the vehicle
Corroded or loose connector at the sender
s: Gauge or range wrong or replaced by a default value
Check engine lamp on

P25D8.d: P25D8 says that the third fuel level input delivers an electrically valid signal whose behaviour is not believable: it jumps, drifts or disagrees with the fuel actually used or transferred. A sender frozen at one value has its own code, P25DC, so P25D8 covers the remaining plausibility faults. No manufacturer documents P25D8 publicly. Comparable checks exist for the second sender: Ford treats more than 100 changes of over 40 % between samples taken every 0.1 s as a noisy signal (P2066), and GM's 2020 dual-tank logic checks whether the secondary sender reacts when its transfer pump moves fuel. A C-side check would likely follow similar ideas. CARB requires such rationality monitoring for fuel level inputs. The driver may see an erratic gauge or a range estimate that makes no sense.
c: Worn or dirty resistor track in sender C giving jumps
Transfer pump or line fault so the level in tank C does not change as expected
Damaged or loose float on sender C
s: Fuel gauge jumps or shows unrealistic values
Range estimate inconsistent
Check engine lamp on after repeated detection

P25D9.t: Fuel Level Sensor C Circuit Low
P25D9.d: P25D9 reports that the signal of the third fuel level sender has dropped below its lowest valid value. With the usual resistor-type sender this points to very low resistance, typically a signal wire shorted to ground or a sender shorted internally. Whether low means empty or full depends on how the sender is wired, so the gauge may stick at either end. No manufacturer documents P25D9 publicly. For sender A, Ford uses a fixed limit as reference: below 5 ohms, which equals less than one A/D count, the low code is set after 30 s (P0462). CARB requires out-of-range checks on all fuel level inputs. Distinct from P25DA, the high fault, and from P25D7, which only states a general circuit problem. Expect a gauge pinned at one end and a stored lamp code.
c: Signal wire of sender C chafed and shorted to ground
Water in the tank connector bridging signal and ground
s: Gauge pinned at full or empty
Check engine lamp on

P25DA.t: Fuel Level Sensor C Circuit High
P25DA.d: P25DA is set when the third sender's signal climbs above the top of its valid range. On a resistor sender fed through a pull-up, that almost always means an open path: a broken wire, a disconnected plug, a burnt-out spot on the resistor track or a missing ground return. A short to a voltage source has the same effect. No manufacturer documents P25DA publicly. The sender A counterpart gives an idea of the limits used: Ford flags the high fault when resistance exceeds 200 ohms, corresponding to more than 253 A/D counts, for 30 s (P0463). CARB requires out-of-range monitoring for fuel level inputs. Unlike P25D9, the cause here is usually an interruption rather than a short, so connectors and the harness at the tank deserve the first look. The gauge will usually rest at one end.
c: Broken signal or ground wire to sender C
Tank connector loose or unplugged after work on the tank
Interrupted resistor track inside sender C
Signal wire shorted to a voltage supply
s: Gauge stuck at one end of the scale
Check engine lamp on

P25DB.t: Fuel Level Sensor C Circuit Intermittent
P25DB.d: P25DB describes short, repeated dropouts in the third fuel level input: the signal leaves its valid range for moments and returns, rather than staying low or high. Typical culprits are a loose pin, a wire that breaks contact only when the vehicle flexes or the tank moves, and a sender whose wiper briefly lifts off the resistor track over rough roads. No manufacturer documents P25DB publicly. Ford does not use a separate intermittent code for senders A and B; it catches short-term jumps through its noisy-signal check (more than 100 jumps of over 40 % at 0.1 s sampling) under the performance codes, which is the closest documented logic. Under CARB this input falls under mandatory supervision as well. The gauge may flicker or briefly fall to empty, and the fault can be hard to reproduce in the workshop.
c: Loose or spread terminal in the sender C connector
Wire breaking contact when the frame or tank moves
Sender wiper lifting off a worn resistor track
s: Fuel gauge flickers or drops briefly to empty
Check engine lamp may come and go

P25DC.d: P25DC is set when a third fuel level sender, sender C, keeps returning the same reading although the engine has consumed a meaningful amount of fuel. Such a third input exists only on vehicles with extra or divided tanks, for example saddle tanks or auxiliary tanks on trucks. No manufacturer documents P25DC publicly. Ford's 2020–2023 gasoline OBD summary describes the equivalent check for senders A and B (P25B0 to P25B2): the PCM adds up injected fuel as a share of tank capacity and compares it with the sender movement, allowing a 25 to 60 % mismatch depending on where the reading is frozen. CARB requires a rationality check for a stuck fuel level sensor, since the level also enables the evaporative leak test. Electrical faults on sender C have their own codes, P25D7 and P25D9 to P25DB. The gauge or range display stops moving.
c: Float arm of sender C caught on a baffle, pump bracket or tank wall
Worn spot on the sender C resistor track holding the wiper at one value
Fuel transfer to or from tank C not working, so its level really does not change
s: Fuel gauge or range display frozen over a long distance
Risk of running out of fuel despite a displayed reserve
Check engine lamp on

P25DD.t: "A" Camshaft Position - Stuck In Locked Position (Bank 1)
P25DD.d: Many modern cam phasers hold their rotor with a spring-loaded pin at a defined angle, often in mid travel, so the engine starts with stable valve timing before oil pressure builds. P25DD means the intake phaser on bank 1 is still latched at that angle although the controller has asked it to unlock and move, so variable timing is lost on that camshaft. Ford's 2014 code list for the Boss 302S engine carries P25DD as a lamp code next to P25E0, P25E3 and P25E6. BorgWarner describes a passive mid-position lock on Hyundai's Gamma II engine that is released purely by oil flow, which is why thin, dirty or low oil and a sticking control valve are the usual suspects. CARB requires faults that keep the phaser from reaching its target to be detected. Expect weaker pull and higher fuel use.
c: Low oil level or pressure, or oil of the wrong viscosity, unable to push the pin out
Oil control valve for the bank 1 intake phaser sticking or its screen clogged
Lock pin seized in its bore by sludge or wear inside the phaser
s: Check engine lamp on
Less pulling power, especially in the mid-speed range
Higher fuel consumption

P25DE.t: "A" Camshaft Position - Unable to Achieve Locked Position (Bank 1)
P25DE.d: P25DE is the reverse of P25DD: the intake cam phaser on bank 1 should return to its lock angle and let the pin engage, typically as the engine is about to stop or idles before an automatic stop, but the controller never sees the expected locked position. If the pin is not in place at the next start, the rotor can rattle against its stops and timing wanders until oil pressure takes over. No manufacturer documents P25DE publicly. On mid-lock designs such as BorgWarner's unit for the Hyundai Gamma II, the pin only drops in when the rotor passes the slot under oil-driven cam torque, so a worn pin bore, debris in the phaser or a control valve that cannot reach its lock range are prime candidates. CARB names a pin failing to move to its position among the mechanical faults a VVT monitor has to catch. Symptoms: rough or noisy starts.
c: Debris or wear in the phaser keeping the pin from dropping into its slot
Oil control valve sticking so the lock range of the spool is never reached
Aged or contaminated oil slowing the phaser at hot idle
s: Check engine lamp on
Short rattle or knock from the timing drive right after starting
Rough start or unsteady idle in the first seconds

P25DF.d: P25DF belongs to the same block as the lock codes P25DD and P25DE, but it does not describe the latch itself. It flags that the intake phaser on bank 1 is not following its commanded angle as well as the calibration expects, judged as a check of control quality rather than as a plain deviation toward early or late timing (P0011, P0012) or a slow response (P000A). No manufacturer explains publicly where the line between P25DF and those older codes lies, so the exact trigger depends on the calibration.
