CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 asks every VVT system to detect both a missed target angle and sluggish movement. In hydraulic mid-lock phasers such as BorgWarner's for Hyundai, oil quality, the solenoid valve and the internal seals all decide how precisely the angle is held. Drivers notice uneven idle, hesitation or a drop in economy.
c: Worn or partly clogged oil control valve for the bank 1 intake phaser
Oil overdue, diluted or of the wrong grade
Internal leakage in the phaser letting the angle drift
s: Check engine lamp on
Uneven idle or slight hesitation when accelerating
Somewhat higher fuel consumption

P25E0.t: "A" Camshaft Position - Stuck In Locked Position (Bank 2)
P25E0.d: On engines with two cylinder banks, P25E0 is the bank 2 counterpart of P25DD: the intake camshaft actuator stays latched at its locking angle when the module wants it free to advance or retard. Because only one side is affected, the cam angles of the two banks no longer match, and the module may hold both sides in a fallback position. Ford's 2014 OBD-II code interpretation list for the Boss 302S V8 includes P25E0 among four lamp codes for a phaser stuck in its lock. A pin that fails to retract usually goes back to oil supply: too little pressure at that head, wrong viscosity, a clogged feed screen or a sticking control valve; less often the pin is jammed mechanically. CARB requires the OBD system to detect valve timing that cannot reach its target. Typical complaints are low power, rough idle and higher consumption.
c: Insufficient oil pressure at the bank 2 head, low level or clogged feed screen
Bank 2 intake oil control valve sticking
Lock pin mechanically jammed in the phaser
s: Check engine lamp on
Reduced power and rough idle
Higher fuel consumption

P25E1.t: "A" Camshaft Position - Unable to Achieve Locked Position (Bank 2)
P25E1.d: P25E1 is set when the intake phaser on bank 2 fails to re-engage its lock. The controller commands the phaser toward the locking angle, usually when shutting down or before an idle stop, and then checks whether the measured cam angle settles there; on bank 2 it does not. No manufacturer has published a description of P25E1. Mid-position locks like BorgWarner's, used on Hyundai's Gamma II, rely on oil-driven cam torque to swing the rotor into the slot, so low oil pressure at hot idle, varnish in the phaser or a control valve unable to reach the lock band are the likely culprits. Without the pin the following start is less stable and a brief rattle may be heard. CARB's VVT rules treat a pin that does not move into place as a mechanical fault to be detected. Bank 1 has its own code, P25DE.
c: Low oil pressure at hot idle from worn pump, bearings or thin oil
Varnish or debris in the bank 2 intake phaser
Control valve unable to move the spool into its lock range
s: Check engine lamp on
Brief rattle from the timing drive on start-up
Unsteady running right after a cold or warm start

P25E2.d: P25E2 points to poor position control of the bank 2 intake camshaft actuator: the measured angle tracks its target less accurately or with more oscillation than the calibration allows, while no clear lock fault is present. It is the bank 2 sibling of P25DF. No manufacturer publishes its trigger, so it remains unclear how it is separated from P0021 (bank 2 over-advanced or system performance) or the slow response code P000C; when one of those is stored too, it usually guides the diagnosis. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 wants every VVT system checked for missed setpoints and for being too slow. In hydraulic phasers of the mid-lock type, as BorgWarner supplies for the Hyundai Gamma II, contaminated oil, a weak solenoid valve or internal leakage reduce control precision. Symptoms tend to be mild: unsteady idle and lower efficiency.
c: Bank 2 intake solenoid valve worn or sluggish
Internal leakage across the phaser vanes
s: Check engine lamp on
Slightly unsteady idle
Lower fuel economy

P25E3.t: "B" Camshaft Position - Stuck In Locked Position (Bank 1)
P25E3.d: P25E3 concerns the exhaust side: the bank 1 exhaust phaser, camshaft B, remains held by its lock pin when the controller wants to move it. Exhaust timing then stays at its parking angle, which limits how the module can use valve overlap for internal exhaust gas recirculation and scavenging. The Boss 302S OBD-II list Ford published in 2014 marks P25E3 with the warning lamp, alongside the bank 2 exhaust code P25E6. BorgWarner's Gamma II system shows that exhaust phasers can use the same torsional-assist hardware as the intake side, although there only the intake phaser carries the mid-position lock. A pin that stays engaged mostly indicates low or contaminated oil at the phaser, a sticking control valve or a damaged rotor. CARB requires VVT target errors to be detected. The engine may idle roughly, emit more NOx and lose some power.
c: Low or contaminated oil at the exhaust phaser
Bank 1 exhaust oil control valve sticking
Damaged rotor or lock pin inside the exhaust phaser
s: Check engine lamp on
Rough idle
Slight loss of power, possibly failed emissions test

P25E4.t: "B" Camshaft Position - Unable to Achieve Locked Position (Bank 1)
P25E4.d: P25E4 means the bank 1 exhaust phaser does not reach and engage its locking position when the controller asks for it, for example before shutdown or an automatic engine stop. Stellantis lists P25E4 in several PCM reflash bulletins for Wagoneer and Grand Wagoneer models with the 3.0-litre Hurricane high-output twin-turbo inline six and stop-start, among them 18-022-25 Rev. A for 2025 and 18-040-26 for 2022; the remedy there is new software, and the listed complaints include no restart after a stop-start event. An inline six only has bank 1, so the bank 2 code P25E7 does not apply there. Outside such software cases, low oil pressure at hot idle, debris in the phaser or a sticking control valve keep the pin from dropping in. CARB lists a pin that fails to move into place as a fault the VVT monitor must find.
c: Engine control software needing an update (documented for Stellantis Hurricane engines)
Low oil pressure at hot idle so the phaser cannot swing into the lock
Debris in the exhaust phaser or a sticking control valve
s: Check engine lamp on
Engine fails to restart after an automatic stop, restarts after an ignition cycle
Rough start

P25E5.d: P25E5 reports that the exhaust camshaft actuator on bank 1 is controlled less precisely than intended: its angle lags, overshoots or oscillates around the target beyond calibrated limits, without a latch fault. It is the exhaust-side counterpart of P25DF and overlaps in meaning with P0014 and the slow-response code P000B; no manufacturer documents how P25E5 is told apart from them. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requires detection of missed targets and slow phasing for all VVT hardware. In a hydraulic phaser like those BorgWarner supplies for Hyundai's Gamma II, exhaust adjustment depends on cam torque pulses and on clean oil passages in the centre bolt valve, so oil condition and valve wear are the first checks. Drivers may notice unsteady idle, slightly reduced power or poorer economy.
c: Worn or dirty control valve for the bank 1 exhaust phaser
Degraded engine oil or a blocked oil filter
Noisy exhaust camshaft position signal making the angle look unstable
s: Check engine lamp on
Unsteady idle
Slightly reduced power or economy

P25E6.t: "B" Camshaft Position - Stuck In Locked Position (Bank 2)
P25E6.d: P25E6 tells that on bank 2 the exhaust cam phaser has not left its locked angle despite a command to adjust. The module then has one exhaust camshaft that can no longer be phased, which shifts valve overlap on that bank and can upset idle quality and the emissions balance between the two banks. Ford's 2014 list for the Boss 302S V8 includes P25E6 as a lamp code, together with the matching intake and bank 1 codes. The root causes resemble those of the other stuck-lock codes but should be checked on the bank 2 side specifically: oil feed and screen to that head, the bank 2 exhaust control valve and the phaser itself. CARB obliges OBD systems to flag VVT systems that do not reach their target angle. Expect the warning lamp, reduced power and possibly a rattle from the timing drive.
c: Restricted oil feed or clogged screen to the bank 2 cylinder head
Bank 2 exhaust oil control valve stuck
Lock pin seized in the bank 2 exhaust phaser
s: Check engine lamp on
Reduced power, uneven idle
Rattle from the timing drive

P25E7.t: "B" Camshaft Position - Unable to Achieve Locked Position (Bank 2)
P25E7.d: With P25E7 the module reports that the bank 2 exhaust phaser could not be brought into its locking position: when the lock is requested, the cam angle does not settle at the parking value or the pin does not hold it there. A start without the pin engaged tends to be rough, and on stop-start engines a smooth restart becomes less certain. No manufacturer documents P25E7 publicly; the closest documented case is P25E4 on bank 1 of Stellantis' Hurricane six, which was resolved by PCM software. Mechanically, mid-lock designs such as BorgWarner's need the rotor to swing past the slot on oil-driven cam torque, so degraded oil, a stuck spool valve or wear in the pin and its bore are usual causes. CARB treats a pin that does not move into position as a VVT fault the OBD system must detect.
c: Aged or sludged oil slowing the bank 2 exhaust phaser
Spool of the bank 2 exhaust control valve hanging
Worn lock pin or pin bore so the pin no longer holds
Calibration issue fixed by a control unit update
s: Check engine lamp on
Rough or rattling start
Hesitant restart after an automatic engine stop

P25E8.d: P25E8 is the last code of the locked-position block and covers the control quality of the bank 2 exhaust camshaft actuator: the module sees the angle wander from, overshoot or trail its setpoint more than allowed, while lock-related faults are absent. Older codes such as P0024 and P000D describe similar exhaust deviations on bank 2; which one a given calibration uses is not documented publicly by any manufacturer, so P25E8 should be read together with any accompanying cam codes and live phaser data. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 demands that any VVT system be watched for wrong angles and sluggish travel. In hydraulic phasers like BorgWarner's torsional-assist units, oil viscosity, filter condition and wear in the valve or rotor seals decide how well the angle holds. Symptoms are usually subtle, such as uneven idle or higher fuel use.
c: Wear in the bank 2 exhaust control valve
Wrong oil viscosity or a clogged oil filter
Worn rotor seals inside the exhaust phaser
s: Check engine lamp on
Uneven idle
Higher fuel use

P25E9.d: Some engines drive their mechanical supercharger through an electromagnetic clutch, so the blower only turns when extra low-speed torque is wanted. Eaton's TVS blower on the T6 Drive-E four-cylinder from Volvo is built this way, where the turbocharger takes over at higher revs. P25E9 means the engine computer has asked for the clutch to engage, but the supercharger is not being driven – the clutch stays open or slips, so no blower boost arrives. How the fault is recognised (blower speed, pressure rise) is not published. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; CARB treats supercharger electronics as monitored output components. The opposite failure is P25EA. Drivers notice a flat, hesitant pull-away until the turbo spools up.
c: Worn friction faces or too large an air gap, so the clutch slips or will not pull in
Clutch coil with an internal fault producing too little magnetic force
Low supply voltage or high resistance at the clutch connector
Accessory drive belt slipping or damaged at the supercharger pulley
s: Check engine lamp on
Weak acceleration from low engine speed
Normal pull once the turbocharger takes over

P25EA.d: Here the clutch between pulley and supercharger rotors stays engaged although the engine computer wants the blower uncoupled, for example at idle or steady cruising. The blower then keeps turning, costs drive power and fuel, and its air has to be routed past it. Audi documents P25EA00 on the 2017–2019 Q7 with the 3.0 TFSI (engine code CREC): bulletin 2048402 reports the lamp on with this code stored in the engine module J623 and prescribes an engine software update with improved diagnostics, explicitly without replacing parts for this fault. A genuinely seized or welded clutch is still possible on other cars. The reverse case, a clutch that will not engage, is P25E9. Drivers mainly see the warning lamp and slightly higher consumption.
c: Engine control software misjudging the clutch state (Audi Q7 3.0 TFSI, bulletin 2048402)
Clutch plates stuck together by wear debris, corrosion or overheating
Clutch coil kept energised by a wiring fault or a stuck driver stage
s: Check engine lamp on
Higher fuel consumption at part load
Supercharger whine also at idle or cruising

P25EB.d: P25EB covers the electrical drive of the supercharger clutch when it is neither cleanly shorted nor open, yet the values do not fit the command – for example a coil current that is too small or too large for the applied duty cycle, or a signal that drops out briefly. According to Eaton, the clutch needs only a 12 V signal but is engaged with a modulated signal so that it bites smoothly, which gives the controller something to compare. Typical reasons are a coil with altered resistance, a corroded plug or a chafed wire. Hard faults to ground or voltage are reported separately as P25EC and P25ED. No carmaker documents this code publicly; the regulation behind it is CARB's rule for output components. The clutch may be switched off as a precaution.
c: Clutch coil whose resistance has changed through heat or partial winding short
Corroded or loose connector at the clutch or engine module
Wire chafed near the hot supercharger housing causing intermittent contact
s: Check engine lamp on
Jerky or missing supercharger engagement at low revs

P25EC.d: The engine module measures a voltage on the supercharger clutch control line that is lower than expected for the commanded state. Most often the line has a short to ground. What that does depends on how the coil is switched: with a ground-side driver a grounded control wire can leave the coil permanently energised, so the blower keeps turning; with a supply-side driver the clutch simply stays off and the low-speed boost is gone. Neither the threshold nor a detection time has been published for this code, and no manufacturer documents it publicly; CARB requires output circuits to be checked for such faults. P25ED is the high-side counterpart, P25EB the plausibility fault. The control module usually disables clutch control.
c: Control wire shorted to ground, often chafed on brackets or the engine block
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp on
Supercharger permanently engaged or permanently off, depending on circuit design
Reduced power at low engine speed

P25ED.d: With P25ED the voltage on the clutch control line sits above the expected level. Common reasons are a wire shorted to battery voltage, or – on a ground-switched coil – an open coil or broken lead, because the line is then pulled up to supply voltage. A short to voltage can overload the driver stage, which protects itself by switching off. In practice the supercharger then stays uncoupled and only the turbocharger delivers boost, so the car feels sluggish from standstill. Volvo's twincharged T6 Drive-E and Audi's 3.0 TFSI are examples of engines with such a clutch, but neither has published this code. Thresholds are not public; CARB prescribes circuit checks for such outputs. Low-side faults are P25EC, implausible values P25EB.
c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Open clutch coil or broken wire on a ground-switched circuit
Output stage in the engine control module damaged
s: Check engine lamp on
Sluggish pull-away, supercharger does not cut in

P25EE.d: P25EE covers the second control circuit of an electric brake vacuum pump, the part of the wiring that should carry voltage while the pump is switched on. Ford's 2019 OBD summary for its hybrid and plug-in models assigns P25EE to the brake system module, mapped from that module's own code C1036: with the pump relay commanded closed, a monitoring line voltage below 250 mV for one second means the pump is not getting its supply, typically from an open circuit, a failed relay contact or a blown fuse. Circuit A (P258A) is judged with the relay open instead. On these vehicles the pump keeps the brake booster supplied when the combustion engine is shut down. P25EF to P25F1 are the performance, low and high codes of the same circuit. CARB treats such electrical outputs as comprehensive components. The pedal can turn hard.
c: Broken wire or loose connector between relay and pump
s: Hard brake pedal, especially with the engine off or in electric drive
Brake or traction warning lamp in addition to the check engine lamp
Vacuum pump never heard running

P25EF.t: Vacuum Pump Control Circuit B Range/Performance
P25EF.d: P25EF says that the B circuit driving the electric vacuum pump is electrically present but its behaviour does not match the command: the feedback on the switched side looks implausible, or the pump runs without the expected effect on brake vacuum. No manufacturer documents P25EF publicly. Ford's hybrid OBD summary shows the type of logic used on the neighbouring circuit A, where P258B combines an out-of-window monitoring voltage with the relay off and a reading under 250 mV with the relay on. FCA's bulletin S1805000006 ties the A-circuit performance code to pumps that cannot hold enough vacuum and has hoses, check valves, fuses and terminals inspected first. A similar approach suits circuit B. CARB requires plausibility monitoring of such outputs. The brake pedal may feel firmer than usual.
c: Worn vacuum pump that runs but builds too little vacuum
Leaking vacuum hose or faulty check valve
Corroded terminals causing an unstable feedback voltage
s: Brake pedal firmer than normal
Vacuum pump running longer or more often
Warning lamp on

P25F0.t: Vacuum Pump Control Circuit B Low
P25F0.d: P25F0 is stored when the pump's B control circuit reads lower than expected, usually because the switched supply or feedback line is shorted to ground or loaded down by a pump motor with an internal short. A short to ground on the supply side often blows the pump fuse, so the pump then stops altogether. No manufacturer documents P25F0 publicly. Ford's hybrid OBD summary uses a lower limit of 250 mV on the monitoring line for the open-type fault P25EE; a low fault on the same circuit would be judged against a comparable voltage window. The difference from P25EE: there the line is simply without voltage, here the module sees a load or a short pulling it down. CARB lists such outputs among the comprehensive components. Braking assist can fade, and P0556 or P050F may follow.
c: Chafed supply or feedback wire shorted to ground
Internal short in the vacuum pump motor
Water ingress in the pump connector
s: Hard brake pedal
Repeatedly blown vacuum pump fuse
Warning lamp on

P25F1.t: Vacuum Pump Control Circuit B High
P25F1.d: P25F1 marks a high reading on the vacuum pump's second (B) control circuit: the module sees voltage on the switched side when it should be low, for example because the line is shorted to battery voltage, the relay contacts have welded together or the pump has lost its ground. In the welded-relay case the pump keeps running after it has been switched off, which wears it out and drains the battery. No manufacturer documents P25F1 publicly. Ford's hybrid summary checks the comparable circuit A against a 1.3 to 5.0 V window with the relay open, a pattern that would also catch a supply that is stuck on. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requires electrical outputs to be checked for circuit faults. The opposite fault is P25F0, and P25EE is the open circuit. Drivers may hear the pump running constantly.
c: Feedback or supply line shorted to battery voltage
Lost ground connection at the pump
s: Vacuum pump running constantly, even with the vehicle switched off
Discharged 12 V battery
Warning lamp on

P25F2.d: A third boost pressure sensor, C, only makes sense on engines with several charging stages or chargers – for example a supercharger feeding a turbocharger, or a two-stage turbo system – where pressure is measured between the stages as well as ahead of the throttle. Which location carries the letter C is up to the manufacturer. P25F2 is the general circuit fault of this sensor, without separating low, high or implausible signals (those are P25F3 to P25F5); a networked sensor C would report lost communication as U060D instead. No manufacturer documents P25F2 publicly. For sensor A, GM-built Saab engines check the circuit all the time while the ignition is switched on and fall back to mechanical base boost with a clear loss of power, which is the likely reaction here as well.
c: Loose, corroded or oily connector at boost sensor C
Signal, 5 V reference or ground wire damaged
s: Check engine lamp on
Reduced power, boost limited to base level

P25F3.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P25F3.d: P25F3 means boost sensor C delivers a signal that is electrically valid but does not agree with what the other pressure readings and the engine model suggest. Saab's 2.0 litre turbo engine, developed with GM, shows how this is checked for sensor A: with the engine stopped the reading must lie between 50 and 115 kPa, roughly matching barometric pressure, and while running it is compared with a model built from barometric, manifold and throttle-inlet pressure and throttle position; a failure is a two-trip type B code. A comparable check would apply to C. Typical reasons are a leak or blocked port at the measuring point, oil fouling and sensor drift. No manufacturer publishes this code for sensor C. Expect reduced boost and a lamp.
c: Charge air leak near the measuring point of sensor C (hose, clamp, seal)
Sensor port fouled by oil from crankcase ventilation or a drifting sensor
Faulty barometric or manifold pressure sensor skewing the comparison
s: Check engine lamp on
Reduced power under load
Hissing noise if a charge air leak is present

P25F4.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor C Circuit Low
P25F4.d: Boost pressure sensors of this kind output a voltage that rises with pressure, so P25F4 – a signal below the lowest valid value – points to the wiring or the sensor rather than to the charge air. Usual reasons are a signal wire shorted to ground, a missing 5 V supply, or an open signal line on an input pulled down by the control unit. No public manufacturer data exist for sensor C; the GM-developed Saab engines give an idea for sensor A, setting the low code under 0.09 V for more than 5 s on the 2.0 litre and under 0.19 V for 4 s in one go or 50 s added up on the 1.6 litre. The control unit then typically disables boost control. The high-voltage counterpart is P25F5; a shared 5 V supply fault can bring up other sensor codes at the same time.
c: 5 V reference open or pulled down by another faulty sensor on the same supply
s: Check engine lamp on
Noticeable loss of power
Scan tool shows a pressure far below ambient for sensor C

P25F5.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Sensor C Circuit High
P25F5.d: P25F5 reports a signal from boost sensor C above the highest plausible value. Since the voltage climbs with pressure, a reading at the top end usually means an electrical fault: the signal shorted to 5 V or battery voltage, an open sensor ground, or an open signal wire where the input is pulled up. The limits differ widely by engine – for sensor A, Saab's GM-based 1.6 litre sets its code above 4.8 V (4 s at a stretch or 50 s cumulated, type C without lamp), whereas the 2.0 litre already flags a reading above 3.9 V lasting 5 s as a type B fault. No manufacturer documents these limits for sensor C. Because the engine would believe boost is excessive, it typically cuts boost control. P25F4 is the opposite fault.
c: Sensor ground open or high resistance
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
s: Check engine lamp on, depending on the manufacturer
Reduced power, boost cut back

P25F6.d: P25F6 is the overall monitor for a second secondary air injection system, lettered B, on engines with two separately controlled air delivery paths; system A reports through P0410 and P0411. During warm-up after a cold start a pump pushes fresh air into the exhaust, so leftover HC and CO burn off and the catalyst lights off sooner. CARB wants the complete delivery chain monitored, every switching valve included, and with separate paths the flow to each bank. No manufacturer documents P25F6 publicly; Toyota's 4.7 L 2UZ-FE V8 shows such a layout with one switching valve per bank but stores mostly its own codes for it. P25F6 is the general fault of system B, P25F7 the narrower flow complaint. The driver sees the MIL and fails an emissions test, while the car normally drives as usual.
c: Secondary air pump of system B worn, seized or water-damaged
Switching or check valve of system B stuck, often after debris from the pump
Cracked, loose or disconnected air hose or vacuum line
Faulty pump relay, fuse or wiring of system B
s: MIL on, usually after a cold start
Secondary air readiness monitor not complete, emissions test failed
Unusual whining or no pump noise during the first minute after a cold start

P25F7.t: AIR System B Incorrect Flow Detected
P25F7.d: With P25F7 the engine controller finds that the air delivered by secondary air system B does not match its expectation while the system is switched on after a cold start. Depending on the design, it judges the flow from how the oxygen sensors on that side react, from a pressure sensor in the air line or from pump behaviour. For 2006 and later vehicles outside LEV III, CARB demands detection before reduced flow pushes emissions beyond one and a half times the relevant FTP limit; LEV III vehicles use the threshold table instead, and with separate paths each bank counts on its own. No manufacturer documents P25F7 publicly. On Toyota's 2UZ-FE V8, a bulletin blames debris passing through the pump and fouling the valves for comparable faults. P0411 is the matching code for system A, P25F6 the general fault of system B.
c: Air pump of system B delivers too little air
Switching or check valve fouled or stuck partly closed
Air passages to the exhaust restricted by carbon deposits
Leaking air hose so that part of the flow escapes
s: MIL on after one or two cold starts
Emissions test failed or readiness incomplete
Driveability normally unchanged

P25F8.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve C Control Circuit
P25F8.d: Bypass valves in the intake let charge air flow around a compressor: on turbo engines they are the recirculation valves that open on a sudden throttle lift so the compressor does not surge, and on engines with a supercharger they can route air past the blower while it is idling or uncoupled. A third such valve, C, only appears on systems with several compressors; which valve gets the letter is manufacturer-specific. P25F8 is the general fault of its control circuit, typically an open circuit. No manufacturer documents P25F8. For valve A, Saab's GM-based 2.0 litre watches for open, short to ground or short to voltage for longer than 10 s at 11–32 V supply and sets a type B code. Expect surging noises on lift-off or less boost.
c: Broken wire or loose connector at bypass valve C
Open coil in the valve or its solenoid
s: Check engine lamp on
Fluttering noise when lifting off the throttle
Less boost or slower response

P25F9.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve C Control Circuit Low
P25F9.d: P25F9 tells that the control line of bypass valve C reads too low a voltage, normally because it touches ground somewhere or the coil is shorted. If the engine module switches the valve on the ground side, a grounded wire leaves the valve energised all the time; on an electric recirculation valve, which according to Pierburg works without a vacuum line, that means charge air keeps escaping back to the compressor inlet and boost stays short. If the valve is switched on the supply side, it simply stops opening and the compressor can surge when the throttle snaps shut. No manufacturer publishes P25F9; the Saab circuit check for valve A (10 s, type B) is the nearest documented analogue. The high-voltage counterpart is P25FA.
c: Output stage in the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine lamp on
Too little boost if the valve stays open
Surging or fluttering on lift-off if it stays shut

P25FA.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve C Control Circuit High
P25FA.d: With P25FA the control line of bypass valve C carries more voltage than the engine module expects for the commanded state. A wire shorted to battery voltage is the classic reason; on a ground-switched valve an open coil or broken lead also lets the line float up to supply level. A short to voltage can make the driver stage overheat and cut out, so the valve is no longer operated at all. On an electric recirculation valve, the effect is that it no longer opens on throttle lift-off and the compressor can surge, with the typical fluttering sound and some stress on the charger. No manufacturer documents P25FA for valve C; GM-based Saab engines monitor the same fault for valve A as part of a continuous type B circuit check. The low-side fault is P25F9.
c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Open valve coil on a ground-switched circuit
Damaged output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp on
Fluttering or surging noise when lifting off the throttle

P25FB.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve C Control Circuit Range/Performance
P25FB.d: P25FB is set when the control circuit of bypass valve C is not open or shorted, but its electrical behaviour does not match the command – for instance a current that rises too slowly or settles at the wrong level, or a signal that drops out now and then. That points to a coil whose resistance has changed with heat, contact resistance in the connector, or a valve whose armature moves sluggishly and so alters the current curve. Pure circuit faults are reported as P25F8 to P25FA, a valve that is mechanically stuck as P25FC. Which compressor valve C belongs to is decided by the manufacturer, and none documents this code publicly; CARB requires output components to be checked for proper function. Consequences range from surging on lift-off to reduced boost.
c: Valve coil resistance changed by heat ageing
Contact resistance or moisture in the valve connector
Sluggish valve armature due to deposits
s: Check engine lamp on
Occasional fluttering on lift-off
Uneven boost build-up

P25FC.d: P25FC concerns the valve itself, not its wiring: bypass valve C is electrically in order but does not move as commanded, sticking open, shut or somewhere in between. A valve stuck open lets charge air leak back to the compressor inlet, so boost falls short; one stuck shut cannot relieve pressure when the throttle closes, and the compressor surges audibly. Which of the two cases the engine module can tell apart, and from which signals, is not published; no manufacturer documents valve C publicly, so the comparable codes P2261 (valve A) and P00C4 (valve B) are the closest reference. Deposits from crankcase vapours, a torn diaphragm or a cracked housing are typical. Electrical faults belong to P25F8–P25FB; a stuck valve C may also be reported as P2CD5.
c: Oil and soot deposits from crankcase ventilation jamming the valve
Torn diaphragm or broken spring inside the valve
Cracked valve housing or leaking seal
s: Check engine lamp on
Loud fluttering when lifting off the throttle
Lack of boost and power

P25FD.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve C Temperature Too High
P25FD.d: This code says bypass valve C has become too hot. Recirculation valves are placed in the charge air path close to the compressor and thus near the hot turbine side, and an electric valve's coil adds its own heat when energised for long periods. How the engine module learns the temperature – a sensor in the valve or an estimate from current and duty cycle – is not stated in any public manufacturer document, and none documents P25FD itself. To protect the coil the module will usually limit or stop driving the valve, which can then lead to surging on lift-off or reduced boost. Separate codes cover the same overheating for valves A and B (P00D7, P00D8); a valve that is jammed rather than overheated is P25FC.
c: Heat soak from the turbocharger, e.g. after hard driving or with missing heat shields
Valve coil drawing too much current due to an internal fault
Sluggish valve held energised longer than intended
s: Check engine lamp on
Fluttering on lift-off or reduced boost after hard driving

P25FE.d: P25FE is the umbrella code for the supercharger disconnect clutch: it says the clutch function has failed without naming whether it is stuck, slipping or electrically faulty. Those cases have their own codes – P25E9 and P25EA for the mechanical states, P25EB to P25ED for the control circuit – so a control unit that sets P25FE either does not distinguish them or uses it as a summary. The clutch lets the engine computer switch the belt-driven blower on for low-speed torque and off at idle, cruise or high revs to save friction losses, as Eaton describes for its clutched TVS supercharger. No carmaker documents P25FE publicly; CARB requires such supercharger components to be monitored. Expect weaker low-speed response and higher consumption.
c: Worn or seized clutch on the supercharger pulley
Fault in the coil, wiring or connector of the clutch
Engine control software that misjudges the clutch state
s: Check engine lamp on
Weak response at low engine speed
Higher fuel consumption

P25FF.t: Electrical System Voltage Stabilizer Control Module Performance
P25FF.d: P25FF reports that the module which steadies the 12 V supply for sensitive electronics does not work as intended. Such stabilizers mainly appear on cars with automatic engine stop/start: every restart drags the battery voltage down hard, according to a semiconductor maker briefly below 4 V, which would otherwise reset radios, displays and similar loads. A DC/DC stage raises the voltage for those moments. No manufacturer publicly documents P25FF itself. GM's 2017 Chevrolet Malibu illustrates the circuit in practice: current fed back through the OnStar backup battery wiring into the DC-DC converter inhibited stop/start and lit the MIL, cured by removing a single fuse, without a code being named. Usually stop/start stays disabled and screens may reboot on restart; the engine keeps running normally.
c: Internal fault in the voltage stabilizer or DC/DC converter module
Aged or wrong-type 12 V battery so the module cannot hold the voltage
Current backfeed or poor supply/ground connection at the module
s: Automatic stop/start no longer active
Radio or display resets when the engine restarts
Warning light depending on the maker

P2600.d: P2600 means the controller sees an open circuit on the line that drives electric coolant pump A, directly or through its relay. GM's 2023 ECM table tests the auxiliary coolant pump relay output while it is off: more than 200 kOhm for 5 of 6 seconds sets the code as Type B, so the MIL follows after two trips. On Ford's 2020-2023 gasoline engines pump A serves the cabin heating loop. Hyundai traces P2600 on 2016-2019 Sonata Hybrid and Plug-in Hybrid to an internal open or short in the electric engine water pump or to low coolant; Kia found water seeping into the housing of the auxiliary pump on early 2019 Niro hybrids, and Audi chafed gearbox wiring on 2023 A6/S6. P2602 and P2603 are the low and high faults, P2601 the function check.
c: Internal open circuit in the electric pump or its electronics
Water or coolant ingress causing poor contact at the pump
Chafed or broken control wire, loose connector or failed relay
Coolant level too low (named by Hyundai as possible trigger)
s: MIL or hybrid warning lamp on
Little or no cabin heat
Rising coolant temperature in hybrid or after-run operation

P2601.t: Coolant Pump A Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
P2601.d: P2601 is set when electric coolant pump A is commanded on, yet its feedback or its effect shows that it is not really working, while the wiring itself tests sound. GM's 2008 table for the 3.6 L LLT judges its auxiliary pump indirectly: after a shutdown with coolant above 110 °C the pump runs on, and if the coolant does not cool down as the ambient-dependent calibration expects within about 80 s, the code is logged. Ford reprograms the PCM of 2021 F-150 trucks with the 3.5 L PowerBoost hybrid under bulletin 21-2053 for P2601 together with other codes. FCA lists P2601-00 for the electric coolant pump of the 2024 Dodge Hornet plug-in hybrid and cures it with control-module software. P2600, P2602 and P2603 report the electrical faults. Heating or post-shutdown cooling may suffer.
c: Electric pump seized, worn or running too slowly
Control module software misjudging the pump (update available)
Air pocket or low coolant so the pump runs dry
s: MIL on
Weak cabin heating
Coolant temperature stays high after shutdown

P2602.t: Coolant Pump A Control Circuit Low
P2602.d: P2602 reports that the control circuit of electric coolant pump A reads low - typically a ground short, or a matching fault report from the driver stage. Which pump is A varies: Ford's 2020-2023 gasoline OBD summary defines it as the auxiliary pump of the high-temperature loop for cabin heating, checked continuously over 5 s above 11 V; GM's 2008 3.6 L LLT table uses an after-run pump (P2602 = circuit to ground, stored only as pending code without warning light). VW's 2014 books set it below about 3.0 V on the Passat and CC and below 2.8-3.2 V on the Touareg. P2600 is the open circuit, P2601 the performance fault, P2603 the high-side fault. Without the pump, heater output or after-run cooling of a hot engine may suffer.
c: Internal fault in the electric coolant pump or its electronics
Coolant or water ingress into the pump connector
s: Fault code stored; MIL depends on the maker (GM 2008 LLT table none, GM 2023 ECM table Type B)
Weak cabin heating
No after-run of the pump after a hot shutdown

P2603.t: Coolant Pump A Control Circuit High
P2603.d: P2603 means the drive line of electric coolant pump A reads high - usually a short to the supply side, or an overcurrent seen by the driver stage. Ford's 2020-2023 gasoline OBD summary assigns pump A to the auxiliary high-temperature loop for cabin heating and sets P2602/P2603 when the smart driver reports a fault within 5 s. For the 3.6 L LLT, GM's 2008 table checks the after-run pump for a circuit fault to voltage (pending code only, no warning light). VW's 2014 books use a current threshold: about 0.60-1.20 A on the Passat and CC, 5.5-10 A on the Touareg. Under CARB, output components need monitoring for circuit faults. P2600 is the open circuit, P2601 performance, P2602 the low-side fault. Heater output or after-run cooling may be lost.
c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Seized or sluggish pump drawing excessive current
Faulty driver stage in the ECM
s: Fault code stored; MIL depends on the maker (GM 2008 LLT table none, GM 2023 ECM table Type B)
Weak cabin heating
Higher coolant temperature after hot shutdown

P2604.t: Intake Air Heater A Circuit Range/Performance
P2604.d: P2604 is the functional check of intake air heater A - the grid heater in the intake that warms the charge air of a diesel engine for cold starts. The circuit responds, but current, voltage drop or heating effect do not match the command. Under CARB, a glow plug or intake air heater has to be checked both for reacting correctly when commanded and for plausible current and voltage drop in its circuit. Volvo's heavy-truck engine bulletins (2020, 2022) list P2604-7F among the codes caused by a weak pre-heat relay and fix it with a software update, a check of terminal tension at heater and relay, and a new relay plus supply cable. P0540-P0543 cover the electrical faults of heater A, P2605-P2608 heater B, P2609 the system. Expect hard cold starts and white smoke.
c: Worn or sticking intake air heater relay
Loose or burnt terminals on the heater supply cable
Degraded or partly open heater grid
s: Hard starting in cold weather
White smoke and rough running after a cold start
Check engine light

P2605.d: P2605 points to an open circuit at intake air heater B, a second heating element in the intake of a diesel engine; the control unit finds no current path through the element, its relay or the cabling. Volvo's EMS code lists keep heaters A, B and C apart. An August 2020 Volvo software change log for heavy-truck engines names P2605-13 among the codes tied to a preheater relay robustness problem, and a 2022 Volvo/Mack instruction for 11 L and 13 L engines asks for terminal tension checks at element and relay and a software check before relay and supply cable are renewed together. CARB expects intake air heater circuits to be watched for current and voltage drop. P0543 is the open-circuit code of heater A, P2CE1 that of heater C. Harder cold starts and white smoke follow.
c: Loose, corroded or burnt terminal at heater element or relay
s: Hard starting in cold weather
White smoke after a cold start
MIL on

P2606.t: Intake Air Heater B Circuit Range/Performance
P2606.d: P2606 means heater B in the intake does respond, but the current it draws or the voltage drop across its circuit lies outside the window the engine controller expects. Mack documents P2604-7F and P2606-7F for 2014-2017 trucks with MP7, MP8 and MP10 engines and puts them down to extra circuit resistance from corrosion inside the master disconnect switch, so inspecting those contacts comes first. Volvo's 2020 software change log for heavy-truck engines lists P2606-7F next to the heater A code as a result of the preheater relay issue addressed by new EMS software. Unlike P2605, P2607 and P2608, the circuit is not open or shorted but merely implausible; P2604 is the same check for heater A. Cold starts may become sluggish and the engine may smoke white until warm.
c: Extra resistance from corroded contacts, e.g. in the master disconnect switch
Aged heater element with changed resistance
Outdated engine software (update published by the maker)
s: Sluggish cold starts
White smoke until the engine is warm
MIL on

P2607.t: Intake Air Heater B Circuit Low
P2607.d: P2607 says the signal from the circuit of intake air heater B stays too low, which normally means a grounded control or feedback line, or a relay output pulled down. No manufacturer documents P2607 publicly. The closest published equivalents are Deutz, whose MD1 code list files an under-voltage or ground short at the preheating relay of heater A as P0541, and Volvo, whose 2020 engine software list contains the low-side code P2CE3-11 for heater C but none for B. CARB asks for the heater circuit to be monitored for current and voltage drop, which is how such a low reading becomes visible. P2608 is the high-side counterpart, P2605 the open circuit, P2606 the plausibility check. With heater B unusable, cold starts take longer and the engine smokes white at first.
c: Control or feedback wire chafed through to ground
Internal short in the preheat relay
Moisture or corrosion in a connector of the heater circuit
s: Hard starting in cold weather
White smoke after a cold start
MIL on

P2608.t: Intake Air Heater B Circuit High
P2608.d: P2608 is logged when the circuit of intake air heater B reads too high, for instance a short to battery positive on the control line or a relay that stays energized when it should be off. Volvo is the one maker that names it in public bulletins: the August 2020 EMS change log for heavy-truck engines lists P2608-00 among the preheater codes reduced by a relay robustness update, and Volvo's 2022 instruction for the pre-heat relay on 11 L and 13 L engines includes P2608-7E in its scope before replacing relay and supply cable. Deutz uses P0542 with the same meaning for its preheating relay. A heater stuck on drains the batteries and can overheat cables; a dead heater makes cold starts hard. P2607 is the low-side code, P2605 the open circuit.
c: Preheat relay contacts welded or sticking closed
Control or feedback wire shorted to battery positive
Engine software needing the maker's update
s: MIL on
Batteries run down after short trips or standstill
Hard cold starts or white smoke

P2609.d: P2609 judges the intake air heating as a whole rather than one circuit: the controller compares what the grid heater should achieve with what it measures, for example via the current drawn or the rise in intake air temperature during preheat. Ram has published two service documents for its 6.7 L Cummins pickups. Bulletin 18-012-12 REV. A reflashes the engine module of 2011 Ram 2500/3500 trucks, with P2609 among the codes whose diagnosis was improved. A 2016 parts tip for 2012-2016 engines says that with heater faults or P2609 together with P0542 the heater grid and its relay are to be replaced as a set, and the cable between them checked for overheating. Volvo's 2022 pre-heat relay instruction also covers P2609-00. Hard cold starts and white smoke are the usual complaints.
c: Worn heater grid or relay (replace as a set)
Overheated or loose supply cable between relay and grid
Engine software with an outdated diagnostic (reflash available)
Intake air temperature sensor reading implausibly
s: Hard starting in cold weather
White smoke and rough idle after a cold start
MIL on

P260A.d: P260A reports an open circuit in the output a control module uses to engage the power take-off, typically the coil circuit of a PTO relay or engagement solenoid. GM's PTO module on 2008-2014 Silverado/Sierra 3500 HD chassis cabs, described in upfitter bulletin UI 80c, switches both the supply and the ground side of an upfitter-installed relay and refuses PTO operation unless both lines are connected; GM also notes that the relay output is disabled from the factory and must be programmed on. GM's PTO code table lists the low and high faults of this relay output, but not P260A, so no manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. CARB defines a PTO unit as engine-driven equipment for bodies such as dump beds or winches. The PTO stays disengaged, while normal driving is unaffected.
c: Relay coil wiring missing, broken or only one side connected by the upfitter
Open coil in the PTO relay or engagement solenoid
Corroded or loose connector in the chassis wiring
s: PTO does not engage
PTO indicator flashes or stays off

P260B.d: P260B is stored when the PTO control output reads too low, the classic case being a grounded wire leading to the PTO relay coil. GM documents the code as P260B.00, a low voltage on the PTO relay control line, among the faults the PTO module can set on 2008-2014 Silverado and Sierra 3500 HD chassis cabs. That module drives both ends of an upfitter-supplied relay, energizes it when the in-cab switch requests PTO and drops it again once engine speed is back at base idle; a ground fault on its control side therefore prevents engagement. Because the relay and its wiring are added by the body builder, their routing and protection deserve the first look. P260A is the open circuit, P260C the high-side fault. The truck still drives, only the PTO stays off.
c: Relay control wire chafed against the frame or body
Shorted coil in the PTO relay or solenoid
Relay wired incorrectly during body installation
s: PTO cannot be engaged
Message or flashing PTO indicator

P260C.d: P260C signals that the PTO control output reads too high, usually because the relay control line touches a powered wire or the relay coil draws too much current. GM lists it as P260C.00, a high voltage on the PTO relay control line, in the diagnostic table of the PTO module that GM fitted to Silverado and Sierra 3500 HD chassis cab trucks from 2008 to 2014. Since that module switches the relay on both its feed and its ground side, a short to voltage can leave the relay pulled in when it should have dropped out. Body builders splice into this circuit, so their added wiring is the likely suspect. CARB lets the OBD system pause selected monitors while a PTO runs, so a wrong PTO state matters beyond the work equipment. P260B is the low-side code, P260A the open circuit.
c: Relay control wire shorted to a powered circuit
Relay or solenoid coil with too low resistance
Faulty splice or add-on wiring from the body installation
s: PTO will not engage or will not release
PTO indicator behaves abnormally

P260D.d: P260D concerns the output that drives the lamp or LED telling the operator that the power take-off is engaged; the module has found a fault in that lamp circuit. For GM's heavy-duty pickup chassis cabs, upfitter bulletin UI 80c explains how such an indicator behaves: the LED in the PTO switch blinks quickly while the relay is energized, turns steady once load feedback confirms engagement or after 3 s without feedback, and blinks slowly when a memory speed is stored. A remote PTO indicator can be wired as well. GM's PTO code table does not list P260D, and no other maker documents it publicly. The PTO itself may work normally, but the operator loses the visual confirmation, which matters for safe work with tippers, cranes or pumps. P260A to P260C cover the control circuit itself.
c: Open or shorted wire to the indicator, often in add-on wiring
Fault in the PTO switch assembly with integrated LED
s: PTO indicator stays dark or lit regardless of PTO state
PTO itself works normally

P260E.t: Particulate Filter Regeneration Lamp Control Circuit
P260E.d: Diesel machines often have a separate dashboard lamp that tells the operator a particulate filter regeneration is needed or running. P260E covers the circuit that switches this lamp. Deutz documents it for its EMR5/MD1 engine controllers: fault type 11 (J1939 SPN 3697, FMI 4) means the lamp output reads below normal or is shorted to ground, type 12 (FMI 3) means it is too high or shorted to the supply. Deutz engines go into tractors, construction and other off-road equipment, so the code is mostly met there. For on-road heavy-duty engines CARB section 1971.1 requires electrical checks of such output components. A failed lamp output does not affect the filter itself, but the operator may miss a request for a parked regeneration, letting soot load build up until power is reduced.
c: Lamp wire shorted to ground or to supply
Lamp or bulb holder open, or lamp not fitted on this machine
Corroded connector at dashboard or engine controller
s: Regeneration lamp dark or permanently lit
Missed regeneration requests leading to high soot load
Later power reduction by the engine controller

P260F.d: Some evaporative leak tests run long after the engine is switched off, so Ford gives them a small dedicated processor that works during the soak. P260F is set when that monitoring processor does not behave as intended. In Ford's 2020–2023 gasoline OBD summary it belongs to the engine-off natural vacuum (EONV) test for 0.020 inch leaks, which may run at most twice a day after the vehicle has soaked for 3.5–6 hours; the processor check itself is continuous and takes about 5 seconds. Ford marks the code with a MIL in its 2014 list. Because the module also relies on CAN communication, tank pressure sensing and the vent solenoid, wiring or supply faults can trigger it as well as an internal fault. Without a working processor the small leak test (P0456) cannot complete, so readiness may stay incomplete.
c: Internal fault in the EVAP monitoring processor or module
Supply, ground or CAN wiring fault at the monitoring module
s: MIL on
EVAP readiness not set, small leak test not completed

P2610.t: ECM/PCM Internal Engine Off Timer Performance
P2610.d: Several emission monitors need to know how long the engine was off, for example to judge a cold start or an evaporative test after a soak. P2610 reports that the module's engine-off timer gives implausible values. Ford's 2020–2023 gasoline summary flags an engine-off time under 30 s after an inferred soak, an error above 15 s or a missing CAN timer message at start; its 2023 diesel compares 30 degrees of coolant cooling with at least 1200 s counted and checks an 8 s afterrun window (7.52–8.48 s). GM's 2013 tables test the initial value (below 0 or above 10 s) and tick spacing (0.8–1.2 s), Type B. Toyota and Lexus fixed false sets on 2014–2018 models by ECM reprogramming (T-SB-0146-16, T-SB-0336-17); Mazda keeps the timer in the cluster and logs P2610 with P2507 after short restarts in transport mode.
c: Engine module software prone to false timer faults (update available)
Battery disconnect, transport fuse removed or supply dropout during soak
Timer message from another module (e.g. cluster) missing on CAN
Internal timer fault in the control module
s: MIL on, usually without drivability change
Cold-start and EVAP monitors may not run

P2611.t: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve A Control Circuit/Open
P2611.d: A refrigerant distribution valve is an electrically switched valve in the A/C circuit that opens or blocks the refrigerant path to one branch, for example a rear evaporator or a battery chiller. P2611 tells you the engine or powertrain module can no longer drive valve A because its control line or coil is open. Ford's 2014 PCM code list for spark-ignition engines includes P2611, testable with key on, engine running and in continuous mode, but without a MIL mark. Audi uses the same valve naming in its thermal management module (valve B, P0EE2, A7 plug-in hybrid). P2612 and P2613 are the low and high faults of the same circuit. Typically the affected A/C branch stays shut or open, so cooling in one zone or of the battery suffers; engine operation is not affected.
c: Valve solenoid coil burnt out or internally open
Corroded or loose connector at the valve, often near condensation
Broken control wire between module and valve
Faulty output stage in the controlling module
s: One A/C zone (e.g. rear) blows warm or cannot be shut off
Reduced battery cooling on hybrids or EVs, possibly limited charging power
Stored code, often without warning lamp

P2612.t: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve A Control Circuit Low
P2612.d: P2612 is stored when the voltage on the drive line of refrigerant distribution valve A stays lower than the module expects, which normally points to a ground fault in the wire or inside the valve. Volkswagen is an unusual case: its engine control module reports P2612 as a ground short of the A/C compressor regulator valve N280, the electrically controlled valve of the variable-displacement compressor. Ross-Tech names a compressor that no longer works as the symptom and, on the New Beetle 2.5, a damaged four-pin plug near the starter; the valve coil has roughly 10 ohms. Where a real shut-off or distribution valve is used, a branch of the A/C system stays inactive. P2611 is the open circuit, P2613 the short to voltage.
c: Brittle or corroded connector at the valve (VW N280 plug near the starter)
Internal short in the valve coil
s: A/C does not cool or compressor does not engage (VW)
One cooling branch or zone remains inactive
Code stored, usually no other driveability symptom

P2613.t: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve A Control Circuit High
P2613.d: P2613 means the control circuit of refrigerant distribution valve A reads too high: the wire has a short to the supply side, or the driver stage senses excessive current when it switches the valve. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; Ford lists only the open-circuit code P2611, and the VW use of P2612 refers to the compressor regulator valve. Valves of this kind are simple solenoid shut-off valves, as suppliers such as Egelhof build them for systems that must close off one evaporator or the chiller completely. With the circuit shorted high the valve may stay energised, so refrigerant keeps flowing into a branch that should be idle, or the module switches the output off for protection. P2611 and P2612 cover the open and low faults.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Valve coil with shorted windings drawing too much current
Defective driver in the controlling module
s: An A/C branch keeps cooling although it should be off
Valve output switched off, so the branch does not work at all
Code stored without engine symptoms

P2614.t: Camshaft A Position Signal Output Circuit/Open (Bank 1)
P2614.d: Some engine computers pass a copy of the camshaft position signal on to another module, for example an injector driver unit or a valve timing controller. P2614 means that this outgoing line for camshaft A on bank 1 is broken or its pulses never reach the receiver. On the 2003 Ford 6.0 L Power Stroke diesel the PCM forwards the CMP pulse to the fuel injector control module (FICM); a counter in the FICM rises when that pulse is missing or out of step with the crank signal, checked above 90 rpm with 5 errors while cranking or 10 while running, and Ford lists the code with MIL. Mitsubishi names P2614 to P2616 for the 2022 Outlander, whose ECM feeds an electric intake valve timing module. P2615 and P2616 cover the shorted cases. Expect hard starting, stalling or a no-start.
c: Broken wire or loose terminal between sending module and receiving module
Camshaft sensor signal itself missing or out of sync with the crank signal
Receiving module (e.g. injector control module) not reading the signal
Defective output stage in the engine control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Long cranking or no-start
Engine stalls or misfires intermittently

P2615.t: Camshaft A Position Signal Output Circuit Low (Bank 1)
P2615.d: P2615 points to a camshaft A (bank 1) position output line that the engine module finds pulled to ground. GM documents it for the Cadillac CT6 in its 2018 tables: with the driver switched off and the line commanded high, the ECM measures the voltage and flags a short at an impedance to ground of 0.5 ohm or less; at 200 kilohm or more it treats the circuit as open, and some controllers then log P2614 instead. It takes 40 failing samples out of 50, read every 100 ms outside cranking and relay voltage is at least 11 V, and GM classes the code Type C without MIL. Mitsubishi lists it for the 2022 Outlander's valve timing module feed. The receiving module may lose cam phase information, so rough starts or a fallback timing strategy are possible.
c: Output wire chafed through and touching ground
Moisture or corrosion bridging the connector pins to ground
Internally shorted input in the receiving module
Faulty output driver in the engine control module
s: Stored code, often without warning lamp
Rough or delayed starting
Valve timing control in fallback mode

P2616.t: Camshaft A Position Signal Output Circuit High (Bank 1)
P2616.d: P2616 is the opposite fault to P2615: the outgoing camshaft A position line on bank 1 stays at supply potential although the module has switched its low-side driver on and wants the line low. In GM's 2018 CT6 tables the ECM declares a power short once the impedance toward the supply is 0.5 ohm or less, using the same window of 40 bad readings in 50 at 100 ms intervals, engine not cranking and at least 11 V; the code is Type C, so the warning lamp stays off. A chafed wire touching a battery feed or a failed output stage are the usual suspects. Mitsubishi also lists P2616 for the 2022 Outlander. The downstream controller sees a steady level instead of pulses, which can upset cam phasing or starting.
c: Output wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Low-side driver in the engine module no longer switching
Back-feed through a damaged or corroded connector
s: Stored code without warning lamp
Hard starting or hesitation after start
Cam phasing faults logged by the receiving module

P2617.d: When an engine module relays the crankshaft position signal to another controller, P2617 says that this forwarded line is open or the pulses go missing at the receiver. Ford's 2003 6.0 L diesel summary describes the clearest case: the fuel injector control module counts a fault whenever the crank pulse it gets from the PCM is absent or does not line up with the camshaft signal, monitored continuously above 90 rpm, and the code carries a MIL in Ford's lists. GM notes that some of its controllers may store P2617 alongside P2618 when the output is open, and Mitsubishi lists P2617 for the 2022 Outlander. Low and high shorts are P2618 and P2619; a fault in the crank sensor itself is P0335/P0336. Without the copied signal the injectors may not fire, so stalling or a no-start is typical.
c: Open wire or pushed-out pin on the crank output line
Crank sensor signal itself missing or out of sync with the cam signal
Receiving module (e.g. injector control module) faulty
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Engine cranks but does not start
Sudden stalling while driving

P2618.t: Crankshaft Position Signal Output Circuit Low
P2618.d: P2618 reports a crankshaft position output line that is shorted to ground. GM uses it widely, from the 2011–2012 hybrid tables to the 2019 ECM summaries, wherever the engine module provides a crank position output. The check runs while the output driver is off and the line is commanded high: 0.5 ohm or less toward ground counts as a short, 200 kilohm or more as an open (some controllers then add P2617). A failure needs 40 bad samples in 50 at 100 ms spacing, with the powertrain relay at 11 V or more and the engine not cranking; GM rates it Type B, so the MIL comes on after two trips. Mitsubishi lists P2618 for the 2022 Outlander. Typical findings are a pinched harness or water in a connector; the receiving module may switch to a substitute mode.
c: Harness pinched or chafed so the output touches ground
Water or corrosion in the output connector
Shorted input stage in the receiving module
Output driver failure in the engine control module
s: MIL on after two drive cycles
Related faults or substitute mode in the receiving module
Occasional hesitation or start problems

P2619.t: Crankshaft Position Signal Output Circuit High
P2619.d: P2619 is set when the crankshaft position output line is held at supply voltage while the module's low-side driver is switched on and expects it to be pulled down. GM's 2014 hybrid ECM table treats an impedance of 0.5 ohm or less toward power as the fault and evaluates it like the low case: 40 failures in 50 samples every 100 ms, engine not cranking, relay voltage of 11 V or more, Type B with MIL after two trips. GM also carries the code in its 2011, 2012, 2016 and 2023 tables, and Mitsubishi lists it for the 2022 Outlander. The usual cause is insulation damage that lets the line touch a positive feed, less often a defective output stage in the module. The listening controller then receives a constant level rather than teeth and may limit operation.
c: Damaged insulation lets the output touch a positive feed
Low-side driver in the engine module failed open
s: MIL on after two drive cycles
Receiving module reports implausible crank signal
Possible reduced power or start problems

P261A.d: P261A reports an open circuit in the drive of an auxiliary electric coolant pump labelled B. Ford's gasoline OBD summaries for 2020-2023 and 2024 define pump B as the high-temperature loop pump for component cooling and check it continuously over 5 s with at least 11 V on board. Ford's EcoSport 1.0 EcoBoost of 2018 (SSM 47359) set P261A because connector C1450 at that pump could not latch fully; a pigtail kit cures it. Audi bulletin 2043142 for 2012-2016 2.0 TFSI engines (CAE, CPM) links P261A to P261C to a failing after-run circulation pump and fits an updated pump. VW's 2014 Touareg book flags it at 4.8-5.3 V on the line. P261C/P261D are the shorts, P261B the performance fault.
c: Pump connector not fully seated or with spread terminals
Auxiliary pump with internal open (electronics or motor)
Broken supply or control wire, or failed relay where fitted
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on, sometimes only sporadically
No after-run circulation, heat soak after hot shutdown
Component temperatures (turbo, electronics) rise

P261B.t: Coolant Pump B Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
P261B.d: Unlike the wiring codes around it, P261B judges whether coolant pump B actually delivers when commanded. The verdict comes from pump feedback or from its effect on coolant temperatures, so the circuit can test fine while the pump does nothing. Ford's 2020-2023 and 2024 gasoline summaries list it for the component-cooling pump of the high-temperature loop, next to the circuit codes of that pump. Audi's 2.0 TFSI bulletin 2043142 (2012-2016) reports it as range/performance and traces it to a sporadically failing after-run pump that is replaced. GM's hybrid tables from 2014 group P261B with P261C in a no-flow fault bundle of the switchable water pump. Seized impellers, air in the loop or a weak pump are typical; P261E is the opposite stuck-on case.
c: Auxiliary pump motor or electronics failing intermittently
Air pocket after coolant service, pump runs dry
Impeller blocked by debris or deposits
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Engine or turbo runs hotter after shutdown, possible boiling noises
Heater or component cooling weak in certain conditions

P261C.t: Coolant Pump B Control Circuit Low
P261C.d: P261C points to a control line of coolant pump B pulled toward ground. VW's 2014 Touareg data book sets it when the signal voltage drops below 2.8-3.2 V. Ford (gasoline summaries 2020-2023 and 2024) relies on a smart driver that watches pump B, which cools components in the hot loop, and sets P261C or P261D as soon as it reports an output fault, within a 5 s window above 11 V. Audi's bulletin 2043142 (2.0 TFSI CAE/CPM, model years 2012 to 2016) names the low-side code alongside P261A and P261B and replaces the after-run pump with an updated part and bracket. GM's hybrid tables put P261C both in the control fault bundle and in the no-flow bundle of the switchable water pump. Look for chafed wires near hot parts, then for a pump with an internal short.
c: Chafed wire to ground near exhaust or engine parts
Internal short in the pump electronics, often after water ingress
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Auxiliary pump does not run, no after-run cooling
Rising temperatures at turbo or electronics in heavy use

P261D.t: Coolant Pump B Control Circuit High
P261D.d: With P261D the module finds the drive of coolant pump B too high, either a short to the supply side or a current above the permitted limit. VW's 2014 Touareg book uses a current test here, roughly 2.2 to 4 A as the threshold. Ford checks the component-cooling pump B of the high-temperature loop through a smart driver that reports output faults within 5 s at 11 V or more. GM's 2014-2018 hybrid tables include P261D in two fault bundles of the switchable water pump, one for control faults and one for a pump that keeps flowing. A sticking, overloaded pump can draw excess current as well, so check the pump before the module. P261A is the open circuit, P261C the low-side fault.
c: Stiff or partly seized pump drawing excess current
Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
Faulty driver stage in the engine module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Pump switched off for protection or running permanently
Possible battery drain if the pump keeps running after shutdown

P261E.t: Coolant Pump B Control Circuit Stuck On
P261E.d: P261E covers the case where coolant pump B keeps working although the module has commanded it off. That can be an output that stays energised, a relay with welded contacts, or, on switchable mechanical pumps, a shroud or valve that no longer closes, so coolant circulates during warm-up. GM's 2014-2018 hybrid tables name P261E only in the flow-stuck-on fault bundle of the switchable water pump, which also blocks the thermostat check P0128; GM does not publish its threshold there. No other manufacturer documents P261E publicly. Its counterpart for pump A, P261F, is set by GM when the feedback speed stays high while the pump is off. A stuck-on pump slows warm-up, raises fuel use and can drain the battery after shutdown.
c: Pump relay with welded contacts or output stage stuck on
Switchable pump shroud or vacuum/solenoid valve not closing
Control line shorted to battery voltage
s: Engine warms up slowly, heater stays cool longer
Pump audible after the engine is switched off
Warning lamp and possibly a thermostat code

P261F.t: Coolant Pump A Control Circuit Stuck On
P261F.d: P261F means electric coolant pump A reports activity while the module has it switched off. GM's 2025 ECM table 25OBDG04B describes the test: with the pump commanded off or below 299 rpm for 2 s and more than 11 V on board, a feedback speed of 3,100 rpm or more for 8 of 10 seconds sets the code as Type B; the warning lamp follows on the second faulty trip. Bulletin 22-NA-077 shows how that can fail without a defect: on 2021-2022 Blazer, Acadia, XT5 and XT6 with the 3.6 L LGX, high engine speed pushes so much coolant through the auxiliary pump that its impeller free-spins above the limit; GM reflashes the ECM and warns against replacing the pump. Mercedes lists P261F71 on the OM651 Sprinter with vacuum leaks or a damaged water pump. P261E is pump B.
c: Impeller driven by main pump flow at high rpm, fixed by ECM software (GM)
Vacuum leak or contaminated switching valve of a switchable pump (Mercedes OM651)
Pump electronics reporting wrong speed or not switching off
s: Check engine lamp after two faulty trips
Usually no noticeable driveability change
Slower warm-up when the pump really keeps running

P2620.d: P2620 concerns a line on which the engine module sends a throttle position value out to another unit, for instance a transmission or body controller, as an analogue or pulse-width signal. The code means the module detects that this output circuit is open, so the receiver gets nothing usable. No manufacturer documents P2620 publicly with thresholds; Ford includes it in its 2014 code interpretation list without a MIL marker, and the CARB rules require output circuits to be checked for continuity and shorts. GM's crank-output diagnostics (P2618) show how such a driver test typically works: the module compares the voltage on the line with what it commands. P2621 and P2622 are the shorted variants, while P0121–P0123 concern the throttle sensor itself. Shifting or idle control in the receiving module may be affected.
c: Open wire or loose pin on the throttle position output line
Corroded connector at the sending or receiving module
Output stage in the engine control module defective
s: Stored code, warning lamp behaviour depends on the maker
Irregular shift points or idle control in the receiving module

P2621.d: P2621 flags the throttle position output line as shorted to ground or reading below its permitted voltage band. A receiving module such as a transmission controller would then see a value that looks like a fully closed throttle all the time. No carmaker publishes a code-specific description with limits; the CARB requirement for output monitoring and GM's output-driver tests on the crank signal (0.5 ohm toward ground counted as a short, 40 failures in 50 samples) illustrate the usual method, but they are an analogy, not a documented P2621 strategy. Check the wire between the two modules for chafing against body ground and the connectors for corrosion before suspecting either controller. Compared with P2620 (open line) and P2622 (short to supply), the receiver here gets a steady low level.
c: Output wire chafed against body ground
Corrosion bridging the output pin to ground
Shorted input in the receiving module
s: Stored code in the engine module
Receiver behaves as if the throttle were always closed (late or odd shifts)

P2622.d: P2622 means the throttle position output line sits too high, typically because it is shorted to a supply wire or the driver in the sending module cannot pull it down. The receiver would read a value resembling wide-open throttle even at idle, which can confuse shift scheduling or torque calculations. There is no public manufacturer documentation for this exact code. CARB's comprehensive component rules oblige makers to detect shorts on output circuits, and GM's short-to-power check on its crank output (impedance toward power of 0.5 ohm or less, sampled every 100 ms) shows how such a test is commonly built. Inspect for a wire rubbing against a battery or ignition feed and for back-feed through a connector. P2620 is the open line and P2621 the short to ground.
c: Output wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Driver in the sending module unable to pull the line low
s: Stored code in the engine module
Receiver acts as if at full throttle (harsh or late shifts)

P2623.d: Engines with hydraulically actuated unit injectors (HEUI) fire their injectors with engine oil pressurised by a high-pressure pump; the injection pressure regulator (IPR) valve sets that oil rail pressure. P2623 says the PCM cannot drive the IPR because its circuit is open. Ford's OBD summaries for the 6.0 L Power Stroke from 2003 to 2009 call this the IPR actuator monitor: it runs continuously every 8 ms with engine off or running, needs less than a second and fails when the driver status shows an open or short. Ford's 2014 PCM code list marks P2623 as a MIL code. Without IPR control the oil rail cannot reach the pressure the injectors need, so expect a no-start or stalling. P2624/P2625 are the low and high faults; ICP sensor faults are P2284-P2288.
c: Loose or corroded IPR connector, broken wire on the high-pressure pump cover
Faulty IPR driver in the PCM
s: Engine cranks but does not start
Stalling or severe power loss
Malfunction indicator lamp on

P2624.t: Injector Control Pressure Regulator Circuit Low
P2624.d: P2624 is reserved for a control circuit of the injection pressure regulator that sits too low, typically a ground short on the line switched by the PCM. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. On the 6.0 L Power Stroke, the best-known HEUI application, Ford reports every open or short of the IPR driver under P2623 alone, according to its OBD summaries up to 2009; International's HEUI engines like the DT466 use their own heavy-duty fault codes. CARB requires engines whose injection pressure is built hydraulically to have that pressure control monitored like a fuel system. A grounded IPR output can leave the valve permanently energised, so oil rail pressure may run high or the module shuts the output down. P2623 is the open circuit, P2625 the high fault.
c: IPR control wire chafed to ground near the valley or pump cover
Damaged driver stage in the PCM
s: Hard start or no-start
Rough running, knocking or erratic power
Malfunction indicator lamp on

P2625.t: Injector Control Pressure Regulator Circuit High
P2625.d: With P2625 the module sees the injection pressure regulator circuit at too high a level: the switched line is shorted to battery voltage, or the IPR coil draws more current than the driver allows. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; Ford's 6.0 L Power Stroke summaries from 2003 to 2009 fold every IPR driver fault into P2623, and International's HEUI truck engines report through their own codes. The regulator matters because it alone decides how much oil pressure reaches the injectors; Navistar's HEUI design lets that pressure be set independently of engine speed. If the PCM cannot pull the IPR coil, rail pressure stays near minimum, so the engine may not start at all. CARB treats such hydraulic pressure control as part of fuel system monitoring.
c: IPR control line shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
IPR coil with reduced resistance causing overcurrent
Faulty IPR driver in the PCM
s: Long cranking or no-start
Low power, engine may stall
Malfunction indicator lamp on

P2626.t: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit/Open (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2626.d: Wide-band lambda probes such as the Bosch LSU 4.9 carry a calibration resistor in their plug; the engine module uses it to scale the pumping current. P2626 says this trim path at the front probe of bank 1 looks open. Makers detect it differently: GM's 2023 tables let the sensor chip measure the resistor after each start and fail an LSU 4.9 above 379.5 ohms (NGK ZFAS-U2: above 4,644 ohms), type B. VW's 2014 data books flag a probe signal above 4.81 V, and the 2010 Saab 9-5 applies that limit during fuel cut-off (type B). Ford's Bosch-equipped engines run an air test in overrun and fail a pump current above 3.09 mA held for 2 s. Ford's TSB 17-2124 for the 3.5 L EcoBoost in Explorer and F-150 (2015-17) cures it with a new probe. Low and high faults are P2627/P2628; bank 2 is P2629.
c: Front wide-band probe defective (trim resistor, pump cell or heater damage)
Trim line broken or pin pushed back in the six-pin probe connector
Moisture or corrosion in the probe connector raising the measured resistance
Engine software requiring an update after probe replacement (some makes)
s: Check engine light
Fuel control falls back to open loop on bank 1
Slightly higher fuel consumption or rough idle

P2627.t: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2627.d: P2627 marks a trim signal below its plausible range at the first wide-band probe of bank 1. On Ford petrol engines with NTK probes the interface chip sets it when the resistor line (RL) is open or touches ground; Bosch-equipped Fords do not use it. Honda-built 3.5 L V6 engines in GM's 2005 tables read a label resistor instead and log P2627 when its voltage stays above 4.7 V for 5 s, so the naming follows the resistor value rather than the voltage. On GM diesels the code covers the oxygen signal of the NOx sensor behind the turbine: the 2020 table fails readings below -4 percent in 200 of 250 samples, type B. GM's PIP5468D for 2017-18 Silverado and Sierra with the 6.6 L L5P links P2627 to loose charge-air ducts. Open trim is P2626, high is P2628, bank 2 low is P2630.
c: Trim/resistor line open or chafed to ground between probe and engine module
Wide-band probe or NOx sensor internally faulty
Loose or leaking charge-air ducts on diesel engines (GM L5P)
s: Check engine light
Further oxygen or NOx sensor codes stored at the same time
On diesels possibly boost or aftertreatment codes and reduced power

P2628.t: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
P2628.d: With P2628 the trim input of the front wide-band probe on bank 1 lies above its permitted range. Ford's 2020-23 petrol summary reserves it for NTK probes, where the interface chip reports the resistor line shorted to battery voltage. In GM's 2005 table for the Honda-sourced 3.5 L V6 it is the opposite end of P2627: the label resistor voltage drops under 0.29 V for 5 s. GM diesels apply it to the NOx sensor oxygen value downstream of the turbine; the 2020 table counts readings above 27 percent, i.e. more oxygen than air, in 100 of 200 samples and only while exhaust pressure is plausible (type B). A trim value out of range skews the lambda value the probe reports, so the module stops trusting the probe. Low is P2627, open P2626, bank 2 high P2631.
c: Trim line shorted to battery or another supply in the harness or plug
Wide-band probe or NOx sensor delivering an implausible value
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor drawing in outside air
s: Check engine light
Mixture control without probe feedback, higher consumption
On diesels NOx-related codes and possible SCR warnings

P2629.t: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit/Open (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
