P2629.d: P2629 is the bank 2 counterpart of P2626 and only exists on V or boxer engines with two front wide-band probes. The module finds the trim branch of that probe interrupted. GM's 2023 table 23OBDG07 calculates the parallel resistance between the probe's APE and MES pins and fails values above 240 ohms as an open compensation resistor, two trips. VW's Touareg V6 and VR6 data book of 2014 uses a probe signal above 4.81 V; Ford checks both banks during deceleration fuel cut for a pure-air reading. Mercedes-Benz bulletin LI49.00-P-054888 (2014) for M278 and M157 V8s blames a damaged probe heater and calls for both upstream probes plus new engine software; Ford's EcoBoost TSB 17-2124 also covers the left-side probe. Bank 2 low and high are P2630 and P2631.
c: Bank 2 front probe faulty, including heater damage (Mercedes M278/M157)
Open trim wire or loose terminal at the bank 2 probe connector
Outdated engine software (update called for together with new probes)
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 fuel control without wide-band feedback
Possibly further bank 2 fuel trim codes

P262A.t: Fuel Injector - Pilot Injection Not Learned
P262A.d: Common-rail diesels learn how long each injector must be energised to deliver its tiny pilot shot. Ford's 6.7 L Power Stroke does this with Zero Fuel Calibration: during overrun with rail pressure set to 300 bar, one injector fires small test pulses and the resulting rise in crankshaft speed tells the module the real quantity; the learned offset then corrects every pilot injection of that injector. P262A means the routine kept failing to learn. The 2013 Ford summary sets it after 100 s of valid conditions without a learned value (890-1,610 rpm, gears 4-6, converter locked, coolant at least 50 °C); the 2017 edition counts 30 attempts of 0.8 s or more. P02CC-P02DB cover offsets at their limits. CARB requires faults in pilot-quantity feedback control to be detected.
c: Driving pattern rarely offers long overrun phases in high gear (towing, city use)
Injector drift or wear so the test pulse does not give a usable response
Disturbed crankshaft speed or rail pressure signal
Non-original engine calibration interfering with the learning routine
s: Check engine light
Louder combustion knock, especially at idle and light load
Often no noticeable change in driveability

P262B.t: Control Module Power Off Timer Performance
P262B.d: P262B concerns the timer that keeps counting inside a control module while the vehicle is shut down, used to measure how long it has been off. GM runs two checks on it: a count-up test while run/crank is inactive, failing when two consecutive readings differ by over 1.5 s in 4 of 20 one-second samples, and a range test comparing the hardware timer with a mirror timer at shutdown or restart (deviation above 25 % in the 2014 tables). It is Type B, so the MIL follows on the second trip. GM saw false sets on 2019–2020 CT6 4.2 L engines when the engine cooled faster than expected, for example in wind or an air-conditioned garage (PIP5754: clear the code and keep the ECM), and links P262B to ECM supply or ground faults (PIP5609) and to a lost ignition relay feed (PIT5391).
c: Poor ECM power or ground connection, momentary supply loss
Ignition relay or its control circuit not supplying the module
Diagnostic calibration too sensitive to fast engine cool-down
Internal timer hardware fault in the control module
s: MIL on after two drive cycles
Possibly other control module codes stored at the same time

P262C.d: Engine modules supply groups of sensors from separately regulated 5 V outputs, lettered A, B, C and so on; G is the seventh such supply. P262C is the general fault of this output, typically an interruption so that the sensors behind it lose their feed and report signals near zero together. No manufacturer documents P262C publicly, and which sensors hang on circuit G depends entirely on the application. Comparable checks exist for earlier letters: GM monitors its fifth reference with a single collective code (P06D2) and a window of 4.875-5.125 V, type A; Ford checks reference A for shorts to earth or to the battery, with a 5 s debounce. CARB treats such outputs as monitored comprehensive components. Low, high and plausibility faults of circuit G are P262D, P262E and P262F.
c: Broken reference wire or splice feeding the sensors of circuit G
Loose or corroded pin at the engine module or a sensor plug
Internal regulator of the engine module for output G failed
s: Check engine light
Several sensor codes appearing at the same time
Reduced power or limp mode depending on the affected sensors

P262D.t: Sensor Reference Voltage G Circuit Low
P262D.d: P262D says the 5 V reference output G of the engine module is being dragged below its lower limit. Usually something on the line conducts to ground: a chafed wire, water in a plug, or one sensor with an internal short loading the whole group. A useful test is to unplug the sensors on circuit G one by one and watch whether the voltage recovers. No manufacturer documents P262D publicly; for its reference A, Ford's 2012 summary reads under 4.75 V lasting 5 s as a grounded line, and GM's 2019 tables apply a 4.875 V floor to its collective reference codes. The module may limit the output to protect itself, and all sensors on it then report low or invalid signals. P262C is the open or general fault, P262E the high fault of the same circuit.
c: Reference wire G chafed to ground or engine metal
One sensor on circuit G with internal short pulling the supply down
Water or corrosion in a connector of the group
Weak internal regulator of the engine module
s: Check engine light
Several sensors report low or invalid values together
Limp mode, reduced power or starting problems possible

P262E.t: Sensor Reference Voltage G Circuit High
P262E.d: With P262E the 5 V supply G that the engine module feeds to a sensor group sits above its upper limit. That points to an external voltage source getting onto the line, for example a reference wire rubbed through against a 12 V feed or a sensor signal wire, or to a regulator inside the module that no longer holds its setpoint. Sensors powered from G scale their outputs with this supply, so their readings rise and can become implausible; a hard short to battery voltage may also damage them. No manufacturer documents P262E publicly. Ford's 2012 summary treats more than 5.25 V on its reference A for 5 s as a short toward battery voltage, and GM's tables use 5.125 V as the ceiling for its collective reference codes. P262D is the low fault, P262F the plausibility fault on circuit G.
c: Reference wire G shorted to a 12 V feed or another powered circuit
Sensor on the group feeding voltage back into the reference
Internal regulator of the engine module out of tolerance
s: Check engine light
Readings of several sensors too high or implausible
Limp mode or reduced power possible

P262F.t: Sensor Reference Voltage G Circuit Range/Performance
P262F.d: P262F is the plausibility check of reference output G. The voltage is neither shorted nor missing, yet it wanders outside a tighter tolerance band or jumps around, which falsifies every ratiometric sensor on that circuit. Ford's 2012 summary shows the idea for its references A to C on Bosch Tricore modules: below 4.7 V or above 5.2 V for 0.5 s counts as a range fault. GM goes further on its numbered references and also compares the filtered with the unfiltered value, failing when they drift apart, so short dropouts are caught as well. No manufacturer documents P262F publicly. Typical sources are a poor ground at the module, a loose pin that opens briefly under vibration, or a sensor drawing too much current. P262C to P262E are the circuit faults on G.
c: Loose pin or splice on circuit G opening briefly under vibration
Poor ground connection of the engine module
Sensor on the group drawing excessive current
Drifting internal regulator of the engine module
s: Check engine light
Sporadic implausible values from several sensors
Occasional hesitation or limp mode

P2630.t: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P2630.d: P2630 reports a trim input that is too low at the upstream wide-band probe of bank 2, the cylinder bank without cylinder 1. Ford's petrol summaries of 2020-23 set it only with NTK probes, where the sensor interface chip sees the resistor line open or grounded; the same chip check runs for about 10 s before a fault is stored. GM documented the L66 3.5 L V6, a Honda design, in 2005: the bank 2 label resistor must not stay above 4.7 V for 5 s while the probe heater is active, and that table also files this under the low code. No service bulletin naming P2630 was found. Since only one bank is affected, the other bank keeps normal closed-loop control. The open fault on this probe is P2629, the high fault P2631, bank 1 low P2627.
c: Resistor line of the bank 2 probe open or rubbed through to ground
Damaged or heat-affected connector near the exhaust
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 running in open loop
Fuel economy slightly worse

P2631.t: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 1)
P2631.d: P2631 flags a trim value above the valid window for the first wide-band probe on bank 2. Ford assigns it to NTK probe installations: the interface chip notices the resistor line pulled up to battery voltage, as from a chafed wire touching a powered circuit. GM's 2005 table for the 3.5 L V6 of Honda origin uses the mirror logic, with the bank 2 label resistor voltage below 0.29 V for 5 s. CARB requires front air-fuel ratio sensors to be checked for wiring defects and for readings beyond their valid span that would disable closed-loop fuelling, which is what such a reading does. A harness short can also hit other circuits in the same loom, so check for neighbouring codes first. Bank 1 high is P2628; P2630 is the low fault and P2629 the open fault on this probe.
c: Bank 2 resistor line shorted to a powered wire in the harness
Bank 2 front probe with internal short
Non-matching replacement probe or repaired connector without the original resistor
s: Check engine light
Lambda control on bank 2 disabled
Possibly additional circuit codes from the same harness

P2632.d: Fuel pump B is a second pump beside the main one: a transfer pump between two tanks, an in-line booster or a second in-tank pump. P2632 reports an open in its control circuit. On the 6.6 L LML Duramax with dual tanks, GM's 2014 table 14OBDG10 drives the transfer pump relay through a low-side driver and sets the code as Type B after 3 s above 200 kOhm. In the 2020 diesel table 20OBDG04 it is a Type C code without MIL after 20 of 25 samples. Bulletin PIT5212B on 2013 Silverado/Sierra 3500 chassis cabs asks for a scan tool update before diagnosis. VW sets it below 0.8 mA for the in-line pump of 2014 Golf and Beetle; Ford's 2020-2023 summary uses P2632 for driver feedback faults of pump module B.
c: Failed transfer pump relay, fuse or relay socket
Open wire or corroded connector at the pump or tank
Pump motor or pump driver module open internally
Outdated scan tool cannot command the pump (GM PIT5212B)
s: Fuel from the second tank is not transferred, gauge drops faster
Possible stalling when the main tank runs dry
Warning lamp depending on manufacturer

P2633.t: Fuel Pump B Control Circuit Low
P2633.d: P2633 is the ground-short code of the second fuel pump circuit. GM's 2014 LML diesel table checks the ground-switched relay output of the fuel transfer pump while it is off and flags 0.5 ohm or less between signal and ground, held for 3 s, as Type B. The 2020 diesel table 20OBDG04 looks at the supply-side switch of the rear-tank transfer pump while it is on and stores a Type C code, without warning lamp, after 20 failures in 25 samples of 250 ms. VW's 2014 data books for Golf, GTI and Beetle set P2633 for the auxiliary in-line pump once the signal voltage stays under 2.0 V. GM bulletin PIT5212B groups it with P2632, P2634 and P2636 on 2013 dual-tank chassis cabs. A grounded wire usually blows a fuse or stops the pump.
c: Chafed pump wire grounded against frame or tank strap
Water in the connector under the vehicle
s: Blown fuse, second pump does not run
Fuel not transferred from the auxiliary tank
Warning lamp depending on manufacturer

P2634.t: Fuel Pump B Control Circuit High
P2634.d: P2634 indicates that the drive of the second fuel pump reads as shorted to battery voltage or carries too much current. For the 6.6 L LML with dual tanks, GM's 2014 table judges the transfer pump relay output while it is switched on and treats 0.5 ohm or less toward controller power, lasting 3 s, as a Type B fault. GM's 2020 diesel table checks the transfer pump driver while it is off instead and logs a Type C code after 20 of 25 samples; it notes that the open-circuit code P2632 may appear alongside. VW uses an overcurrent limit of 1.0 A for the in-line pump on 2014 Golf/GTI and Beetle. A pump with worn brushes or a shorted relay coil can cause it as well as damaged wiring. The open and low faults are P2632 and P2633.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage feed
Worn or binding pump drawing excess current
Relay with shorted coil or stuck contacts
s: Second pump runs constantly or is shut off by the module
Fuel level display between tanks inconsistent
Warning lamp depending on manufacturer

P2635.d: P2635 judges the main fuel pump by its result rather than its wiring: the module compares the measured fuel pressure with the commanded value and flags a pump that falls short or overshoots. GM's 2019 tables do this with filtered rail pressure error against calibrated low and high limits, with pump circuit and pressure sensor codes excluded first, and store it as Type B after two trips; the 2020 diesel table uses the same logic after 40 s of engine running. GM bulletin 16-NA-225 replaces the pump module on 2016-2017 Volt, Malibu, Colorado and Acadia because the pump leaks at the upper manifold. Bentley ties P263500 on the Bentayga W12 to fuel tank noise, and GM bulletin 18-NA-103 to gelled diesel in cold weather. P2636 is the same check for pump B.
c: Worn or leaking in-tank pump module
Clogged filter or blocked pickup, e.g. gelled diesel in cold weather
Low supply voltage or poor ground at the pump or pump control module
Fuel pressure sensor reading wrong without its own code
s: Hesitation, surging or loss of power under load
Hard starting or stalling
Whining noise from the fuel tank
Malfunction indicator lamp on

P2636.d: P2636 is the flow check for fuel pump B, in practice mostly the transfer pump of trucks with two tanks. GM's 2014 table for the 6.6 L LML compares how fast the levels in both tanks fall while the pump runs; if they do not move as expected for 140 s, a Type B fault is stored. The 2020 diesel table weighs a commanded transfer of 5 litres against the level change in the main tank (limit 2.5 litres, 1,000 s), or flags a rear tank still holding over 141 litres after 1,150 s of pumping; both give Type C. Emission recall 17067 for 2015-2016 Silverado/Sierra HD LML with tanks N2N notes that the MIL comes on, the fuel gauge drops to empty and transfer is blocked; dealers re-plumb the lines and reflash the ECM. PIT5208A attributes a false P2636 to refuelling with the engine or ignition on.
c: Weak transfer pump not moving enough fuel between tanks
Restricted transfer line or design-related flow limit (GM recall 17067)
Refuelling with engine or ignition on confuses the level-based check
Faulty fuel level sender in one of the tanks
s: Fuel gauge shows empty although the second tank holds fuel
Engine may stall when the main tank runs dry
Malfunction indicator lamp on

P2637.d: Many automatic transmissions ask the engine to cut torque briefly during an upshift and then check whether the engine actually did so. P2637 is stored by the transmission controller when that feedback for request A shows the engine did not follow. Allison names it Shift Energy Management (SEM) on its 3000/4000 series: behind Cummins L9 and X15 engines (EPA17 version) the engine failed to track the torque request closely enough, the CHECK TRANS lamp came on and Cummins fixed it with an ECM recalibration (TSB210020), with no change to Allison hardware or software. Cummins found the same on B6.7 engines in 2017 (J1939 SPN 513, FMI 7), and Navistar linked P2637 to Allison 1000/2000 calibrations causing quick, harsh upshifts. P2641 covers request B. Expect firm shifts or limited gears.
c: Engine control module calibration not following the torque reduction request
Transmission calibration not matched to the engine
J1939/CAN data link fault between engine and transmission
s: Check transmission lamp on
Harsh or too quick upshifts
Gear range limited

P2638.t: Torque Management Feedback Signal A Range/Performance
P2638.d: P2638 says the torque feedback for request A is present but its value does not fit the situation, for example an engine torque figure that drifts away from what the transmission expects during a shift. Honda documents it on its nine-speed automatic: on low-mileage 2016 Pilots the MIL lit and the gear indicator flashed because the idle learn had not been done properly before delivery, so the fix is a PCM reset with the HDS and a correct idle relearn. Service bulletins 16-008 (Pilot) and 16-012 (Acura TLX V6) later improved the torque accuracy monitoring behind P2638 by TCM software, again followed by an idle learn. Unlike P2637, where the engine ignores the request, here the reported torque is implausible. Drivers notice rough or delayed shifts.
c: Idle learn not completed after PCM reset or delivery
Outdated transmission software with oversensitive torque monitoring
Engine torque estimate skewed by air leaks or sensor errors
s: MIL on and gear position indicator flashing
Rough or delayed gear changes

P2639.t: Torque Management Feedback Signal A Low
P2639.d: P2639 means the torque management feedback signal A stays below its valid range, so the transmission controller cannot read a usable torque confirmation from the engine. No manufacturer explains this exact code publicly. The closest documented relatives are Allison's P2637, where the TCM checks over the SAE J1939 data link whether the engine honours shift torque reductions, and Honda's P2638 on its nine-speed gearbox. If the feedback travels as a network message rather than a wire, a low value usually stems from a calibration mismatch between engine and transmission software or a missing message; on a hard-wired signal, check for a ground short. CARB requires such inputs to be tested against range limits. Shift quality may suffer and torque reduction may be disabled.
c: Engine and transmission software versions not matched
Torque feedback message missing or corrupted on the data bus
Hard-wired feedback line shorted to ground
s: Transmission warning or stored code
Firm or flared shifts

P263A.d: P263A means the engine module has found the line that switches the malfunction indicator lamp shorted to ground. GM checks it while the low-side driver is off: if the voltage stays low with an impedance to ground of about 0.5 ohm, the lamp control is faulty; the 2014 tables need 50 of 63 samples at 50 ms intervals, the 2019 tables a single sample, with run/crank voltage of at least 11 V and remote start inactive. GM files it as Type B but marks it no MIL, which makes sense because the lamp itself is the affected part; some controllers also log P0650. GM preliminary information PIT5391 lists P263A and P263B among codes left behind when ignition 1 voltage drops out through a KR73 relay or terminal fault on 2014–2016 trucks. A permanently lit lamp is the main symptom.
c: MIL control wire chafed and touching ground
Loss of ignition 1 voltage via main relay or fuse block terminal
Faulty lamp input in the instrument cluster
s: Engine warning lamp lit permanently
Code stored even though the lamp cannot report it reliably

P263B.d: P263B is stored when the MIL control line is stuck at supply voltage while the module has switched its driver on to light the lamp. GM treats an impedance toward power of about 0.5 ohm as the fault and needs 4 failures within 5 samples, each 50 ms apart, provided run/crank voltage is at least 11 V and no remote start is running. As with P263A, GM labels the code Type B with no MIL, because a shorted control circuit cannot reliably show the warning. In practice the indicator stays dark even when other emissions faults are present, which is why reading stored codes matters, also before an emissions inspection. GM's PIT5391 bulletin ties P263B on 2014–2016 full-size trucks and SUVs to a missing ignition 1 supply. Check the cluster wiring and the driver output.
c: MIL control wire shorted to a positive feed
Ignition 1 supply interrupted at relay or fuse block
Lamp driver in the engine module failed
s: Engine warning lamp does not light, not even at key-on bulb check
Other emissions codes stored without warning

P263C.d: Modern diesel glow systems switch each plug through a semiconductor driver inside a glow plug control module (GPCM). P263C reports that such a driver does not behave as commanded. Ford's 6.7 L and 3.0 L Power Stroke GPCM talks to the engine module over a private CAN bus and flags any internal output, whether it serves the plugs, the DEF heaters or a relay, that fails to switch or overheats for more than 1 s; Ford's 2013 summary prints the code with a typo as P26C3. GM's 6.6 L L5P files comparable driver faults under P064C instead. Separate codes exist for the module as a whole (P064C, P06E5), its overheating (P263E) and open plugs (P0671 ff.). CARB counts all glow plugs as one monitored component. Expect slow cold starts and white smoke.
c: Output stage inside the glow plug control module failed
Glow plug or plug wire with short, overloading the driver
Poor GPCM power feed or ground causing erratic switching
s: Check engine light, glow indicator may flash
Hard or long cranking when cold
White smoke and rough running after a cold start

P263D.d: DEF turns solid at about -11 °C, so SCR systems heat the tank, pump and lines electrically. P263D concerns the power stage that switches these heaters rather than a heater element. On Ford's 6.7 L Power Stroke the heaters are switched by the glow plug module; the plausibility test runs once per trip at peak heater power and sets P263D when the driver circuits exceed 125 °C. Element faults are separate (P20BA, P20BE heater A/B performance, P20C2 heater C supply below 5 V). Deutz uses P263D-00 differently on its EMR engine controllers, namely when defrosting the AdBlue system fails. If the fluid cannot thaw, dosing starts late or not at all, NOx rises and the SCR warning sequence toward a speed or power limit can begin.
c: Heater power stage overheating from excessive load current
Partially shorted heater element or wiring drawing too much current
Internal fault of the module that drives the heaters
s: Check engine light and DEF/SCR warning
DEF not thawing in cold weather, dosing delayed
Countdown to speed or power limitation possible

P263E.t: Glow Plug Control Module 1 Over Temperature
P263E.d: The first glow plug control module measures its own internal temperature and reports P263E when it runs too hot, since its power semiconductors carry tens of amps during glowing. GM's 6.6 L L5P Duramax tables set it at a module temperature above 123 °C while the plugs are commanded on and coolant is below 60 °C, type B. Ford's 2023 diesel summary for the 6.7 L and 3.0 L names more than 125 °C inside the module. FCA bulletin 09-009-15 for 2014-15 Ram ProMaster vans with the 3.0 L diesel lists P263E among glow plug codes caused by plugs lacking an internal O-ring and replaces all four plugs. Heat can also come from repeated or very long glow cycles in deep cold. Driver faults are P263C, a second module would report P263F.
c: Defective glow plugs drawing excess current (e.g. Ram ProMaster plugs without O-ring)
Repeated start attempts or very long glow periods in severe cold
Internal fault or poor heat dissipation of the glow plug module
s: Check engine light, glow lamp flashing
Glowing cut short, hard cold starts
White smoke after cold start

P263F.t: Glow Plug Control Module 2 Over Temperature
P263F.d: P263F is reserved for engines with a second glow plug control module, for instance one per cylinder bank on large V engines; it reports that this second unit has exceeded its permitted internal temperature. No manufacturer documents P263F publicly, and the documented North American V8 diesels from Ford and GM manage all eight plugs with a single module, so they only use the module 1 code P263E. The logic would match that code: GM's L5P sets module 1 overheating above 123 °C during glowing, Ford's 6.7 L above 125 °C. CARB requires glow plugs to be monitored as one component. Likely triggers are high-current or shorted plugs on the bank served by module 2, extended glowing in severe cold, or an internal module fault. Cold starting suffers on one bank.
c: High-current or shorted glow plugs on the bank served by module 2
Long or repeated glow phases in severe cold
Internal fault or poor cooling of glow plug module 2
s: Check engine light, glow lamp flashing
Harder cold start, uneven running until warm

P2640.t: Torque Management Feedback Signal A High
P2640.d: P2640 is the high-range fault of torque management feedback signal A: the confirmation that the transmission controller receives after asking the engine for a torque change carries a value above the plausible upper limit. On Allison-equipped trucks this feedback is not a separate wire but part of the engine data broadcast on the J1939 link, so a high reading usually means the engine claims more torque than is physically possible or than was requested. No manufacturer documents P2640 publicly. For the related P2637 Cummins cured the fault with new ECM calibrations, a hint that software mismatches are a frequent root. P2637, P2638 and P2639 cover the general, plausibility and low faults of signal A. Expect harsher shifts and torque reductions that no longer work.
c: Engine ECM software reports torque values the transmission calibration does not accept
Outdated or wrong transmission controller calibration
Hard-wired feedback line shorted to voltage (where used)
s: Check transmission lamp or MIL on, depending on calibration
Firm or abrupt upshifts
Torque reduction during shifts no longer active

P2641.d: On Allison automatics, feedback B belongs to Low Range Torque Protection (LRTP): in the low ranges the TCM caps engine torque to spare gears and output shaft and checks that the engine respects the cap. P2641 sets when the engine reports more torque than permitted. Allison bulletin TT7401EN describes 2013 Cummins ISX12 engines with 4700/4800 transmissions: at idle in Low Reverse the ECM broadcast a wrong torque value, CHECK TRANS came on and Low Reverse was blocked until the ECM received calibration PH9.30.0.6 or later. Mack and Volvo tech tip TT-013-2015 sees the code under heavy load without drivability effects and also prescribes newer engine software. Navistar names it for Allison 1000/2000 calibrations. P2637 is the counterpart for request A.
c: Engine ECM software below the level required for the transmission (Cummins, Mack, Volvo)
Engine broadcasts torque above the low-range limit requested by the TCM
Transmission calibration not matched to the engine
s: CHECK TRANS lamp on
Low Reverse or other low ranges unavailable
Code appears under high load, often without noticeable drivability change

P2642.t: Torque Management Feedback Signal B Range/Performance
P2642.d: P2642 means feedback signal B arrives and lies inside its valid range, yet its value makes no sense for the current operating state, for example a torque figure that drifts away from what a limited request should produce or that changes implausibly fast. No manufacturer explains P2642 publicly. Allison ties request B to its low-range torque cap (LRTP) and logs the general code P2641 when the engine exceeds the cap; Honda documents the matching plausibility check for request A as P2638 on its nine-speed automatic and fixed false triggers with software and an idle relearn. By analogy, look first at engine and transmission software levels, then at the idle learn and at sensors feeding the torque model. Shifts may feel rough and low ranges can be restricted.
c: Engine and transmission software versions do not match
Idle or torque adaptation not learned after service
Faulty input to the engine torque model (air mass, intake air temperature)
s: Rough or delayed shifts
Transmission warning lamp on
Low ranges restricted

P2643.t: Torque Management Feedback Signal B Low
P2643.d: With P2643 the transmission controller sees feedback signal B below its lower limit, so it cannot confirm that the engine is holding the torque level it asked for. No manufacturer describes this exact code in public documents. Where the feedback is a data-link message, as with Allison transmissions behind Cummins, Mack, Volvo or Navistar engines, a low value tends to come from a missing or defaulted message, an incompatible calibration or a bus fault; on a wired signal a short to ground is the classic cause. CARB requires comprehensive components to be tested against their range limits. Because Allison ties request B to Low Range Torque Protection, the TCM may lock out low ranges when it cannot verify the limit. P2644 is the high counterpart.
c: Torque message missing or sent with a default value on the data link
Bus or signal wiring damaged, short to ground
s: Transmission warning lamp on
Low ranges or reverse low not selectable
Harsh shifts because torque reduction is missing

P2644.t: Torque Management Feedback Signal B High
P2644.d: P2644 reports that torque management feedback B exceeds its upper range limit. No manufacturer publishes a code-specific description. The closest documented case is Allison's P2641: a 2013 Cummins ISX12 calibration reported more torque than the low-range cap allowed, and Mack and Volvo trucks showed the same code under heavy load until the engine software was updated. A reading that is not just above the cap but beyond any valid value points to the same family of problems, namely engine software that scales or encodes the torque message differently from what the transmission expects, or a wired signal shorted to voltage. Low ranges may be locked out and the warning lamp lit. P2643 is the low fault, P2640 the high fault of signal A.
c: Engine software sends torque with a scaling the transmission does not expect
Engine calibration older than the level required by the transmission maker
Wired feedback line shorted to voltage
s: Transmission warning lamp on
Low ranges blocked
Shift quality reduced

P2645.d: Engines that switch valve lift or deactivate cylinders through their rocker arms use an actuator, usually an oil control solenoid, to send oil to the locking pins. P2645 means the engine controller sees the drive circuit of actuator A on bank 1 as open: the state it commands and the state it reads back on the line disagree. GM's 2015 four-cylinder table 15OBDG05 runs this check wherever VVL hardware is fitted, needs more than 11 V, counts 100 failures within 120 samples taken every 250 ms and sets a Type A fault with the MIL on the first trip. P2648 and P2649 cover shorts to ground and to power. The engine stays in its default lift, so power at high revs or economy suffers.
c: Open coil in the rocker arm oil control solenoid
Loose, corroded or oil-soaked solenoid connector
Broken wire in the control or supply line
Faulty output driver in the engine control module
s: MIL on, often on the first trip
No change to high lift, weak pull at high engine speed
Cylinder deactivation or economy mode no longer engages

P2646.t: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator System Performance/Stuck Off (Bank 1)
P2646.d: P2646 is a mechanical-hydraulic plausibility fault: actuator A on bank 1 was commanded to switch the rocker arms, yet the engine did not change lift, or responded too weakly. GM's 2015 table 15OBDG05 tests this intrusively by toggling between high and low lift at 1,200 to 1,800 rpm and 40 to 230 Nm with warm oil (30 to 130 °C) and judges the resulting phaser oil-pressure ripple with a filtered average; it normally completes once per drive and is classed Type A. Honda reuses the number on i-VTEC four-cylinders (bulletin 13-021) for a low-voltage reading of the rocker arm oil pressure switch and fits a new switch. Toyota fitted Valvematic Corollas (T-SB-0011-14, T-SB-0098-19) with new ECM software or a new lift controller. Low oil level, sludge or a sticking spool are typical; P2647 is the opposite case.
c: Low oil level, wrong viscosity or sludged oil
Sticking spool or clogged screen in the oil control solenoid
Seized locking pin in the switching rocker arm
Faulty lift controller or outdated ECM calibration (Toyota Valvematic)
s: MIL on after a completed test drive
Engine feels flat above mid-range speed
Higher fuel consumption

P2647.t: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator System Stuck On (Bank 1)
P2647.d: Here actuator A on bank 1 is believed to stay engaged: the rocker arms remain locked in the switched mode although the controller has asked for the default lift. GM's 2015 four-cylinder table 15OBDG05 detects this with the same intrusive lift toggle as P2646 but flags a filtered pressure-ripple value that falls below its limit; conditions are 1,200 to 1,800 rpm, 40 to 230 Nm, oil pressure 50 to 1,000 kPa, Type A after one trip. On the Honda-built 3.5 L V6 (L66) in GM's 2004 and 2005 tables, the VTEC pressure switch keeps signalling oil pressure for 5 s while the solenoid is off. On i-VTEC four-cylinders, Honda's bulletin 13-021 files a high-voltage switch reading under P2647 instead. Further causes: a solenoid leaking oil or a jammed locking pin. Expect rough idle, misfire or poor low-speed response.
c: Oil control solenoid leaks oil while switched off
Locking pin jammed in the engaged position
Faulty rocker arm oil pressure switch (Honda VTEC)
s: Rough or lumpy idle
Misfire at low load
Sluggish response when pulling away

P2648.t: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit Low (Bank 1)
P2648.d: P2648 points to a low-side electrical fault on the control line of rocker arm actuator A, bank 1: the line reads low, typically a short to ground or a solenoid with shorted turns. GM's 2015 table 15OBDG05 tests the driver for short-to-ground faults with ignition in crank or run and more than 11 V, trips after 100 bad samples out of 120 and lights the MIL at once (Type A). In GM's 2004 table for the Honda-made L66 V6 of 3.5 litres, the controller expects a return signal whenever it energises the VTEC solenoid; 0 V for 2 s sets the code. Check for chafed wiring against the head, a wet connector or a failed solenoid. Without switching the engine runs only in base lift.
c: Control wire chafed through to ground
Shorted turns in the solenoid winding
Moisture or oil bridging pins in the connector
s: MIL on immediately
No switching to the second lift stage
Reduced top-end power

P2649.t: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit High (Bank 1)
P2649.d: The counterpart to P2648: the control circuit of rocker arm actuator A on bank 1 reads high, which means a short to battery voltage or a driver that cannot pull the line down. In GM's 2015 table 15OBDG05 the check needs the output driver commanded on, ignition in crank or run and supply above 11 V; 100 failures in 120 samples set a Type A fault. The Honda V6 (L66) in GM's 2004 table looks at the opposite situation: with the VTEC solenoid commanded off, a return signal at 12 V lasting 2 s points to a high circuit. A harness shorted to a power feed or an internal controller fault are the usual suspects; the actuator can then stay energised or be shut down by the controller.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Output driver in the engine controller no longer switches
Open ground side of the solenoid circuit
s: MIL on immediately
Lift switching disabled or permanently active
Rough running at idle if the actuator stays energised

P264A.t: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit (Bank 1)
P264A.d: Some valve lift systems report back where the rocker arm actuator actually is, rather than relying on oil pressure; continuously variable designs driven by an electric motor, such as Toyota Valvematic, work this way. P264A is the general circuit fault for the position sensor of actuator A on bank 1: signal missing or implausible without a clear low or high pattern. No manufacturer documents this code publicly with thresholds; Toyota's Valvematic bulletin T-SB-0098-19 files its sensor fault under the B sensor code P265B. CARB demands monitoring of all electrical parts of such systems. Without valid feedback the controller usually freezes lift at a safe value, costing power and fuel economy.
c: Loose or corroded position sensor connector
Damaged signal, supply or ground wire
s: MIL on
Lift held at a fixed value, less power
Higher fuel consumption

P264B.t: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1)
P264B.d: Range/Performance means the bank 1 feedback sensor for actuator A delivers a signal inside its electrical limits that still does not fit what the engine expects, for example a position that lags or overshoots the commanded one, or that fails to move when the actuator is driven. CARB requires valve lift systems to catch target errors and slow response before emissions exceed set limits. No manufacturer documents P264B publicly; the closest documented case is Toyota's P265B on Valvematic engines (2014 Corolla, 2018–19 C-HR, 2020 Corolla), cured by ECM reprogramming or a new continuously variable lift controller. Worn linkage, a loose sensor, or a dragging actuator are plausible causes.
c: Sensor loose or misaligned on its mount
s: MIL on after a drive cycle
Hesitation or uneven power delivery
Idle speed fluctuating

P264C.t: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 1)
P264C.d: P264C is set when the signal from the position sensor of rocker arm actuator A, bank 1, sits below its valid window. Typical electrical explanations are a short of the signal wire to ground, a lost 5 V reference, or a sensor that has failed internally. CARB lists such out-of-range checks for every sensor in a lift or timing system under the comprehensive component rules. No carmaker publishes P264C with a threshold; it would only appear on engines whose actuator carries position feedback, such as motor-driven continuous lift designs. Expect the controller to stop adjusting lift, with weaker pull and higher consumption; P264D is the high-side counterpart.
s: MIL on
Weaker pull, lift no longer varied
Higher fuel consumption

P264D.t: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit High (Bank 1)
P264D.d: With P264D the position signal of actuator A on bank 1 reads above its plausible maximum. An open ground return, a signal line touching the 5 V or battery feed, or water in the connector can push it up. Because a reading at the upper stop looks like an impossible position, the controller rejects it and runs a fixed lift. No public manufacturer documentation gives a threshold; the regulatory basis is CARB's demand to check every input of a variable lift system for out-of-range values. Toyota's Valvematic engines show that such feedback exists, though Toyota files its sensor faults under the B codes. Compare with P264C (low) and P264E (intermittent).
c: Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Water ingress in the sensor connector
s: MIL on
Engine runs on a fixed lift setting
Noticeably less power

P264E.t: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 1)
P264E.d: P264E covers a feedback signal from the position sensor of actuator A, bank 1, that drops out or jumps for short moments rather than staying low or high. Loose terminals, a cracked wire flexing with engine movement, or interference on an unshielded line are the usual reasons, and the fault may vanish when the vehicle is parked. CARB requires lift system inputs to be monitored for such rationality and continuity problems. No manufacturer documents P264E publicly. Because the lift controller depends on a steady reading, jumps can make it hunt or fall back to a fixed lift, which drivers notice as surging or uneven idle. Wiggle tests on the harness help locate it.
c: Loose or spread terminal in the sensor connector
Wire cracked inside the insulation by engine movement
Electrical interference on the signal line
s: MIL on, sometimes clearing by itself
Surging or hesitation
Uneven idle

P264F.t: Engine Serial Number Not Programmed or Incompatible
P264F.d: Some engine controllers store the serial number of the engine they belong to, much like the VIN. P264F is logged when that entry is empty or does not fit. Ford Special Service Message 47823 covers 2013 to 2019 E-Series, Super Duty, F-53/F-59 and F-650/750 models: after a PCM replacement the MIL comes on with P264F until the engine serial number, taken from the build records in OASIS, is written into the new PCM with the Ford scan tool. Ford's 2023 diesel OBD summary groups the code with P0630 under vehicle configuration, and Ford's 2014 gasoline list marks it with MIL. GM's 2024 heavy-duty ECM tables set it when any stored serial digit still reads 0xFF, checked continuously, Type A after one trip. It is a configuration fault, not mechanical damage.
c: Engine serial number not written after PCM/ECM replacement
Serial number from another engine or used control module
Stored configuration lost through a memory fault in the module
s: MIL on after control module replacement
Usually no change in how the engine runs

P2650.d: Some engines split rocker arm switching into two stages or groups, each fed by its own oil control solenoid; the second one is called actuator B. P2650 is logged when the engine controller finds the drive line of that B solenoid on bank 1 open, so switching the output on or off brings no matching electrical response. No carmaker publishes this code with limits. GM's 2015 four-cylinder table 15OBDG05 shows how the equivalent test for actuator A is built: a driver check that only runs above 11 V and fails after 100 bad readings out of 120. CARB requires such circuit checks for every output of a valve lift system. Shorts on the same line are reported as P2653 (ground) and P2654 (power). Until repaired, the stage served by solenoid B remains in its rest position.
c: Open winding in the B rocker arm oil control solenoid
Terminal pushed out or corroded in the solenoid B connector
Wire chafed through near the valve cover or harness clips
Failed output stage for solenoid B in the engine control module
s: Check engine light on
Second switching stage never engages, less power or economy in that range
Possibly no other noticeable change in driving

P2651.t: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator System Performance/Stuck Off (Bank 1)
P2651.d: In the generic definition, P2651 says the B stage of rocker arm switching on bank 1 did not engage when requested, or engaged too weakly to be confirmed. Controllers usually verify the change through an oil pressure switch in the rocker gallery or through a measurable shift in engine behaviour. Honda gives the number a narrower meaning on many four-cylinder i-VTEC engines: Service Bulletin 13-021 (Accord L4 2003–12, CR-V 2002–09, Element 2003–11, Fit 2007–11, CR-Z 2011, Civic Si 2002–05 and Civic 2012–13) files P2646 or P2651 as a low-voltage fault in the rocker arm oil pressure switch circuit, may be intermittent, and the fix is a new switch. For the generic case, low or thin oil, a blocked solenoid screen and a seized locking pin are typical. P2652 is the opposite state.
c: Intermittently failing rocker arm oil pressure switch (Honda i-VTEC)
Oil level too low or oil of the wrong grade
Clogged filter screen or sticking spool in solenoid B
Locking pin in the switchable rocker arm seized by deposits
s: MIL on, sometimes only now and then
Engine lacks pull in the speed range served by stage B
Fault may not return right after clearing

P2652.t: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator System Stuck On (Bank 1)
P2652.d: P2652 means the controller thinks stage B of the bank 1 rocker switching stays engaged after release was commanded, usually because the confirming oil pressure switch still signals pressure. Honda documents it in two ways. For the 2017 Odyssey, Pilot and Ridgeline and the 2017 Acura MDX, RDX, RLX and TLX, Honda dealer messages from 2021–22 describe it as a stuck-on fault of rocker arm oil pressure switch B on bank 1, often stored together with P3400 for the cylinder-pausing Valve Pause System; owners may notice uneven running, and Honda asked dealers to hold such cars for inspection. Bulletin 13-021 for older four-cylinder i-VTEC models instead treats P2647/P2652 as a high-voltage fault in the switch circuit. A solenoid leaking oil while off also fits.
c: Rocker arm oil pressure switch B reporting pressure permanently
Solenoid B lets oil through in its closed position
Locking pin stuck in the engaged position
Switch signal line shorted to voltage (Honda four-cylinder meaning)
s: MIL on, possibly together with P3400 on Honda V6
Rough or uneven running, especially at low load
Cylinder deactivation no longer works

P2653.t: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit Low (Bank 1)
P2653.d: P2653 points to a voltage that is too low on the control line of rocker arm solenoid B, bank 1. On a solenoid switched from the supply side, a line rubbing against the engine block or a shorted coil pulls the signal down while the output is active; the controller's driver then reports an overcurrent or a low-voltage state. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. For actuator A, GM's 15OBDG05 runs the same kind of driver diagnosis on its 2015 four-cylinders above 11 V, with a fault after 100 of 120 samples and the MIL on at once. CARB treats such shorts as circuit faults that every lift system output must detect. Many drivers shut down to protect themselves, so the B stage drops out. P2650 covers an open, P2654 a short to power.
c: Control wire of solenoid B shorted to engine ground
Shorted turns inside the solenoid B coil
Engine oil inside the connector creating a leakage path
s: MIL on soon after the fault appears
B stage switched off, reduced power or economy

P2654.t: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit High (Bank 1)
P2654.d: P2654 reports a voltage that is too high on the wire that drives rocker solenoid B, bank 1, typically when the line touches a battery-fed wire or the driver's ground side is bridged. With a ground-switched solenoid, that kind of short can energise the valve permanently, so the B stage may stay engaged regardless of the command, which the engine feels as rough idle or misfire at low speed. No carmaker publishes this code with details. GM checks the matching A circuit (P2649) on its 2015 four-cylinders using an output test that needs at least 11 V and declares a Type A fault once 100 of 120 checks fail. CARB counts a short to power among the circuit faults a lift system must catch. Related: P2653 for the low side, P2650 for an open circuit, P2664 on bank 2.
c: Solenoid B control wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit
Internal short in solenoid B lowering its resistance
Shorted output transistor in the engine control module
s: MIL on
Rough idle or misfire if the B stage stays engaged
Possible blown fuse on the solenoid supply

P2655.d: P2655 is the bank 2 twin of P2645: on a V or boxer engine with a separate rocker arm actuator per cylinder bank, the drive circuit of actuator A on the side without cylinder 1 is open, so the state the controller sets and the state it sees on the wire differ. No manufacturer documents P2655 publicly. As an analogy, GM's 2015 table 15OBDG05 runs the bank 1 version with 100 failures out of 120 samples at 250 ms intervals and a Type A MIL. A broken wire in the harness running across the engine, a backed-out terminal or an open coil are plausible. Only bank 2 then loses lift switching, which can make the banks run unevenly and cause rough running.
c: Broken wire in the harness to the bank 2 solenoid
Terminal pushed out of the connector housing
Open coil in the bank 2 oil control solenoid
s: MIL on
Banks run unevenly, slight roughness
Reduced power or economy

P2656.t: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator System Performance/Stuck Off (Bank 2)
P2656.d: For bank 2, P2656 reports that actuator A was told to switch the rocker arms but the expected change in valve lift did not show up, or it was too small. Since such engines give every bank a separate oil feed and solenoid, a clogged screen or sticking spool on that side alone is enough. No manufacturer publishes P2656; GM's bank 1 test (P2646 in 15OBDG05) shows the usual method: an intrusive lift toggle at moderate load and warm oil, judged by oil-pressure ripple. CARB permits two-step systems to flag faults only once emissions exceed the threshold, but every such failure must then be caught. Low oil level, wrong viscosity and sludge deserve the first look.
c: Low, wrong or sludged engine oil
Clogged oil screen or sticking spool at the bank 2 solenoid
Seized locking pin in a bank 2 rocker arm
s: MIL on after a completed test
Weaker response at higher engine speed
Higher fuel consumption

P2657.t: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator System Stuck On (Bank 2)
P2657.d: P2657 is the stuck-on case for bank 2: actuator A keeps the rocker arms of the second bank in their switched mode after the controller has asked for the base setting. On a cylinder deactivation design that could mean valves stay closed on that side; on a two-step design the high-lift profile stays active at idle. No manufacturer documents P2657 publicly; GM's bank 1 test P2647 (2015, 15OBDG05) shows the principle, flagging a pressure ripple below its limit during a deliberate toggle. A solenoid that leaks oil when off, a jammed locking pin or debris in the oil passage of that bank are candidates. Misfires on one bank and a lumpy idle are typical.
c: Bank 2 solenoid passing oil while switched off
Locking pin stuck in the engaged position
Debris in the bank 2 oil passage
s: Misfire codes on bank 2 cylinders
Lumpy idle
Poor low-speed driveability

P2658.t: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit Low (Bank 2)
P2658.d: P2658 flags the bank 2 control line of rocker arm actuator A as too low, the classic sign of a short to ground or a coil with damaged windings. The test is purely electrical and runs whenever the controller drives the output, regardless of oil condition. No manufacturer documents P2658 publicly; GM's equivalent for bank 1 (P2648 in 15OBDG05) needs more than 11 V and 100 failures out of 120 samples, Type A. Inspect the bank 2 solenoid connector, harness clips near the exhaust manifold and the coil resistance. If only one bank can switch, the controller may disable the feature altogether, leaving reduced power or economy.
c: Bank 2 control wire shorted to ground
Damaged winding in the bank 2 solenoid
Harness insulation damaged by exhaust heat
s: MIL on immediately
Lift switching disabled
Less power or higher consumption

P2659.t: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit High (Bank 2)
P2659.d: P2659 covers the bank 2 control circuit of actuator A reading high: the wire is shorted to a voltage source or the controller's driver stage no longer switches it to ground. No manufacturer documents P2659 publicly. On bank 1, GM's 2015 table 15OBDG05 checks this as P2649 only while the driver is commanded on, again with 100 failures out of 120 samples and a Type A fault. A short of this kind may keep the solenoid powered, so the rocker arms of bank 2 could stay switched; alternatively the controller cuts the output. Compare with P2658 for the low side and P2655 for an open circuit; measuring the voltage at the unplugged connector separates harness from controller faults.
c: Bank 2 control wire shorted to a voltage source
Controller output stage no longer switching to ground
Neighbouring pins bridged in the connector
s: MIL on immediately
Bank 2 lift stays switched or switching is disabled
Rough idle in some cases

P265A.t: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit (Bank 1)
P265A.d: Lift systems that move the rocker geometry with an electric motor, such as Toyota Valvematic, need a sensor that tells the engine controller the actual adjustment angle. P265A flags a general electrical problem with the feedback sensor that reports where actuator B on bank 1 sits: the controller sees no usable signal but cannot classify it as simply too low or too high. Toyota's own bulletins place a Valvematic feedback complaint under the neighbouring B sensor code P265B, which shows Toyota uses this sensor letter; P265A itself is not documented publicly by any manufacturer. CARB requires circuit checks on all inputs of a valve lift system. A loose connector, a broken reference or ground wire, or a sensor failure are the likely reasons; P265B to P265E narrow the fault down.
c: Loose or corroded connector at the B position sensor
Open 5 V reference or sensor ground wire
Failed position sensor inside the lift controller
s: MIL on
Lift held at a fixed value, sluggish response
Higher fuel consumption

P265B.t: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1)
P265B.d: Toyota documents this code on Valvematic engines, where an electric lift controller turns a shaft that alters rocker geometry and reports its angle back. P265B is set when that feedback stays electrically valid but does not track the target. Bulletin T-SB-0011-14 (2014 Corolla, 2ZR-FAE) pairs it with P2646 and fixes it by reflashing the ECM. T-SB-0098-19 (2018–19 C-HR with 3ZR-FAE, 2020 Corolla with 2ZR-FAE) adds the Valvematic angle codes P10A0 and P1055 and replaces the lift controller if the code returns. Both start with a learn value reset and an engine-off active test in which the actual angle should drop to about 105–106° and climb above 108°. CARB demands that such systems recognise deviations from the target and sluggish reaction.
c: Continuously variable lift controller sticking or worn
Stored learn values no longer match the mechanism
Drifting angle sensor in the controller
s: MIL on, often together with P2646
Reduced power and slower throttle response
Fault may return after a short rev to 3,500 rpm

P265C.t: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 1)
P265C.d: The angle or position sensor of rocker arm actuator B, bank 1, normally works inside a voltage band that never touches the lower rail. If the reading falls below that band, the engine controller logs P265C, because a value near zero cannot correspond to any real actuator position. Possible reasons are a signal conductor grounded through damaged insulation, a supply feed that has dropped out, or an internal sensor defect. CARB treats out-of-range low signals of valve lift inputs as circuit faults to be detected. No carmaker documents P265C publicly; Toyota's published Valvematic cases concern the B sensor's range code P265B only. Without trustworthy feedback the controller generally parks the lift in a safe position. High side: P265D; range fault: P265B.
c: Sensor B signal wire grounded through damaged insulation
Internal fault in position sensor B
s: MIL on
Engine runs with fixed lift, less power

P265D.t: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit High (Bank 1)
P265D.d: P265D stands for a feedback signal from position sensor B, bank 1, that sits above its valid ceiling. A reading pinned near the supply voltage usually means the signal is no longer pulled toward a real value: the sensor ground has opened, the signal wire touches a reference or battery line, or moisture has bridged pins in the plug. Because such a value would describe a position the actuator cannot reach, the controller discards it and holds lift at a default. CARB requires out-of-range high detection for every input of a variable lift system. No manufacturer publishes P265D; Toyota's public Valvematic bulletins mention only P265B for this sensor. Check ground continuity first, then the connector. Low side: P265C; intermittent faults: P265E.
c: Open ground wire of position sensor B
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Moisture bridging pins in the sensor plug
s: MIL on
Lift frozen at default, weaker acceleration

P265E.t: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 1)
P265E.d: Here the bank 1 position signal for actuator B is neither stuck low nor high; instead it jumps, flickers or briefly vanishes faster than the mechanism could physically move. The engine controller compares successive readings and flags P265E when the rate of change or the number of dropouts exceeds what a motor-driven lift mechanism can produce. Typical culprits are fretting corrosion on the terminals, a conductor broken inside its insulation that only opens under vibration, or electrical noise from nearby ignition wiring. CARB asks for such signal quality checks on valve lift inputs. No manufacturer documents P265E publicly. The fault may come and go with temperature and road surface; the lift controller can hunt or fall back to a fixed setting.
c: Fretting corrosion on sensor B terminals
Conductor broken inside its insulation, opening under vibration
Interference from ignition or other high-current wiring
s: MIL on and off over several trips
Surging or uneven power delivery

P265F.t: Variable A/C Compressor Control Circuit Range/Performance
P265F.d: Variable-displacement A/C compressors change their output through an electric control valve on the back of the compressor housing. On Ford's externally controlled design the PCM drives that valve with a pulse-width signal and aims for an evaporator temperature of roughly 3 to 8 °C; Volkswagen calls the part regulator valve N280, a coil of around 10 ohms. P265F stands for a control circuit that is electrically intact but behaves implausibly, for example a measured valve current that does not follow the commanded duty cycle, or pressures that do not react. No manufacturer documents P265F publicly; Ford lists only the circuit codes P06A0 to P06A2, which this code complements. Expect weak or fluctuating cooling. Engine operation and emissions are usually unaffected.
c: Control valve sticking or internally worn
Refrigerant charge too low, so pressures do not follow the valve command
Corroded connector or high resistance in the valve circuit
s: A/C cools weakly or inconsistently
Compressor runs at fixed or minimum output

P2660.d: P2660 concerns V-type or boxer engines with switchable rocker arms on both cylinder banks: the controller sees the drive circuit of solenoid B on bank 2, the side without cylinder 1, as broken. An open coil, a disconnected plug after valve cover work, or a cut wire leaves the output without load, so the command and the electrical feedback disagree. No manufacturer documents P2660 publicly, and the Honda V6 cases on record involve bank 1 only. GM's 2015 table 15OBDG05 illustrates the method on actuator A with a driver check from 11 V upward and 100 failures in 120 samples. CARB requires circuit monitoring on every lift system output. The bank 1 equivalent is P2650; shorts on this line are P2663 and P2664.
c: Solenoid B plug on bank 2 left unplugged or not latched after repairs
Open coil in bank 2 solenoid B
Cut or broken wire on the bank 2 harness branch
s: MIL on
Bank 2 B stage inactive, uneven running between banks possible

P2661.t: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator System Performance/Stuck Off (Bank 2)
P2661.d: P2661 is the functional check of rocker arm stage B on bank 2: although the solenoid circuit is electrically sound, the commanded switch did not happen or the confirmation (an oil pressure switch reading or a change in cam phaser or engine response) stayed too small. Bank 2 means the engine has two cylinder heads, so the fault concerns only half of the cylinders, which may show as a difference between the banks. No manufacturer documents P2661 publicly with test conditions; CARB requires valve lift systems to detect hydraulic and mechanical faults that keep them from reaching the target. Oil starvation in that head, a partly blocked oil gallery, a sticking spool or seized pins are likely. Bank 1 counterpart: P2651; electrical fault: P2660.
c: Low oil level or poor oil supply to the bank 2 head
Partly blocked oil gallery or screen on bank 2
Sticking solenoid spool or seized locking pins on bank 2
s: MIL after a completed drive cycle
Less power in the range where stage B should engage
Higher fuel consumption

P2662.t: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator System Stuck On (Bank 2)
P2662.d: With P2662 the controller concludes that stage B on bank 2 stays switched after it has requested the default mode. Detection depends on the design: a pressure switch that keeps indicating oil pressure, or engine behaviour on that bank that still matches the engaged state. A solenoid that seeps oil when closed, a return path that cannot drain, or locking pins jammed by debris or wear keep the rockers coupled. Because only one bank is affected, the engine may idle unevenly or misfire on that side, especially when cold. No manufacturer documents P2662 publicly; Honda's published stuck-on case for stage B (P2652) refers to bank 1. CARB requires such stuck conditions in valve lift systems to be detected. Opposite fault on this bank: P2661.
c: Bank 2 solenoid B seeping oil when closed
Blocked drain path keeping oil pressure on the rockers
Locking pins jammed in the coupled position by debris or wear
s: MIL on
Uneven idle or misfire on bank 2, worse when cold

P2663.t: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit Low (Bank 2)
P2663.d: P2663 is stored when the control line to solenoid B on bank 2 reads too low, most often a short to ground somewhere between the module and the second cylinder head. On V engines that harness branch often runs along the back of the block or under the intake manifold, where heat and vibration wear through insulation. A coil whose resistance has collapsed gives the same picture. No carmaker documents P2663 publicly with thresholds. The principle can be seen in GM's 15OBDG05 table for 2015 four-cylinders on the matching actuator A circuit, with 100 failures in 120 samples above 11 V triggering a Type A fault. CARB counts circuit shorts among the faults to be caught. Many drivers switch off for protection, leaving stage B on that bank idle. Bank 1 equivalent: P2653.
c: Bank 2 control wire worn through and touching ground
Bank 2 solenoid B coil with collapsed resistance
Faulty output driver for bank 2 solenoid B
s: MIL on
Stage B on bank 2 out of action, power or economy reduced

P2664.t: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Control Circuit High (Bank 2)
P2664.d: P2664 signals excessive voltage on the control line of solenoid B, bank 2. Contact with a powered conductor, for example where several solenoid and injector feeds share a connector, or a driver that can no longer pull the line down, are the typical causes. Depending on how the output is wired, the valve may then be energised all the time, keeping stage B on that bank engaged, or not work at all. No manufacturer publishes P2664 or a threshold for it. GM monitors the corresponding A circuits on its 2015 four-cylinders with a Type A driver test above 11 V, which shows the usual approach. CARB lists shorts to power among circuit faults that lift system outputs must detect. Compare P2663 for a low reading, P2660 for an open and P2654 on bank 1.
c: Short to a powered feed inside a shared engine connector
Output driver in the control module stuck off
Internally shorted solenoid B on bank 2
s: MIL on
Misfire or rough idle on bank 2 if the stage stays engaged

P2665.t: Fuel Shutoff Valve B Control Circuit/Open
P2665.d: Engines that can burn a second fuel such as compressed natural gas use electric shut-off valves to keep that fuel locked in when it is not wanted. GM's 2015 Impala Bi-Fuel has two of them, both normally closed: a high-pressure cut-off at the tank and a low-pressure cut-off at the regulator, which the ECM energises only in CNG mode while the engine cranks or runs. P2665 means the control circuit of shut-off valve B is open, so the module cannot energise that valve. Ford's 2014 spark-ignition code list includes P2665 as a continuous test without MIL. Which physical valve carries the letter B is not published by either maker. With the valve unpowered, the gaseous fuel stays shut off and the engine typically falls back to gasoline. P0005 is the same fault on valve A.
c: Loose or corroded connector at the valve (often exposed under the vehicle)
Broken wire in the control circuit
s: Engine runs only on gasoline, gas mode not available
Fuel mode lamp flashes or shows an error

P2666.t: Fuel Shutoff Valve B Control Circuit Low
P2666.d: P2666 is stored when the control line of fuel shut-off valve B sits at too low a voltage, the typical sign of a short to ground between module and valve or inside the coil. Depending on how the driver is built, the valve may then open whenever the ignition is on, or the module switches the output off for protection. No manufacturer documents P2666 publicly. In bi-fuel vehicles such as GM's CNG Impala, the ECM controls normally closed cut-off valves on the gas side and changes over to gasoline as soon as it detects a problem in one fuel system; GM's Silverado and Sierra CNG models signal such errors with a rapidly flashing fuel indicator. P2665 is the open circuit and P2667 the short to voltage on the same valve, P0006 the low fault of valve A.
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Water ingress in the valve connector
s: Gas mode switched off, engine runs on gasoline
Fuel mode lamp flashes rapidly

P2667.t: Fuel Shutoff Valve B Control Circuit High
P2667.d: With P2667 the module measures excess voltage on the wire that drives shut-off valve B, usually because the wire touches a supply circuit. Safety matters here: on a low-side driven valve a short to voltage can keep the coil energised even when the module wants the valve closed, so the gaseous fuel may not be shut off reliably. No manufacturer explains P2667 publicly. GM's bi-fuel Impala relies on two normally closed cut-off valves that the ECM opens only while the engine runs on CNG, and falls back to gasoline whenever either fuel system reports a problem; Ford lists the open-circuit sibling P2665. P2665 and P2666 cover the open and grounded circuit, P0007 the high fault on valve A. Have it checked promptly and use the manual tank valve if gas can be smelled.
c: Control wire shorted to a voltage supply
Corrosion bridging pins in the valve connector
Faulty output stage in the control module
s: Gas mode disabled, operation on gasoline only
Fuel mode lamp indicates an error
Possible gas smell if the valve does not close

P2668.t: Fuel Mode Indicator Lamp Control Circuit
P2668.d: Bi-fuel vehicles tell the driver which fuel is in use through a small indicator, often built into the fuel selector button. On GM's 2016 Silverado and Sierra with CNG the light is off on gasoline, steady on natural gas, flashes once per second during a changeover and flashes about ten times per second when the CNG system has a fault; the 2015 Impala Bi-Fuel uses a similar light in its CNG switch. P2668 indicates that the module driving this lamp has found a fault in its control circuit, such as an open wire or a failed bulb or LED. No manufacturer documents the code publicly. Fuel switching itself is unaffected, but the driver loses the fuel mode display and the error warning. P26E2 and P26E3 are the low and high variants.
c: Indicator LED or bulb in the selector switch failed
Open wire or loose connector at the switch
Lamp driver in the control module defective
s: Fuel mode lamp stays dark in gas mode
No flashing during fuel changeover or on errors

P2669.d: Many transmission controllers feed their solenoids through internal high-side switches, called actuator supply A and B. Ford's 6R140 splits its Transmission Solenoid Power Control into two wires: TSPC-A powers shift solenoids A, C and E (fault P0657), TSPC-B powers SSB, SSD, TCC and line pressure control (P2669). Because both share one internal switch, any fault switches off all seven solenoids, leaving park, reverse, neutral and 5th gear with full line pressure; Ford lists P2669 with MIL. In GM's 16OBDG08 tables for Silverado/Sierra the TCM flags an open supply 2 when several solenoids on it read open at once while the supply line stays high; GM's 2023 TCM test checks at power-down and logs it as Type A. P2670 and P2671 cover low and high faults.
c: Open supply wire or connector between module and transmission bulkhead
Damaged internal transmission harness or lead frame
High-side switch inside the controller failed
s: Transmission stuck in a fixed gear (failsafe)
Harsh engagements due to maximum line pressure
MIL or transmission warning on

P266A.t: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit (Bank 2)
P266A.d: P266A is the basic circuit fault for the bank 2 position sensor of rocker arm actuator A. It only applies to engines that have a lift actuator with position feedback on each cylinder bank, which is rare; most switching rocker systems on V engines rely on oil pressure switches or none at all. No manufacturer documents P266A publicly, and even Toyota's Valvematic, which does use such feedback, is an inline design whose bulletins list a B code for its sensor. CARB still requires every electrical component of a lift system to be checked. If the controller loses this signal, it typically stops varying lift on bank 2, so power and refinement suffer.
c: Poor contact at the bank 2 sensor connector
Damaged wiring between sensor and engine controller
s: MIL on
Lift on bank 2 no longer adjusted
Reduced power and smoothness

P266B.t: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2)
P266B.d: For bank 2, P266B means the position reported for actuator A is electrically valid but does not match what was commanded or changes too slowly. CARB expects variable lift monitors to notice when the commanded position is missed or reached too late, and a sensor whose reading drifts from the real actuator position defeats both. No manufacturer publishes P266B; on the bank 1 side Toyota's comparable experience with P265B on Valvematic engines ended in recalibration or a replaced lift controller, which illustrates that software and mechanics can both be at fault. Check sensor mounting, linkage wear and actuator movement on that bank before replacing parts.
c: Sensor reading drifting from the true position
Control software calling for an update
s: MIL on after a drive cycle
Uneven running between the banks
Hesitation under load

P266C.t: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 2)
P266C.d: P266C reports a bank 2 position sensor signal for actuator A that has fallen under its lower plausibility limit. Grounded signal wires, a missing sensor supply or an internal sensor short pull it down; a connector left half unplugged after other work on the harder-to-reach side of the engine is another possible trigger. No manufacturer documents P266C publicly, so there are no published thresholds. Under CARB's comprehensive component rules, such a range check is mandatory for sensors in a lift system. The controller then holds bank 2 at a safe fixed lift. The high-side partner is P266D, the bank 1 equivalent P264C.
c: Bank 2 sensor signal shorted to ground
Connector not fully seated after other repairs
s: MIL on
Bank 2 held at fixed lift
Less pulling power

P266D.t: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit High (Bank 2)
P266D.d: P266D is logged when the bank 2 position feedback of rocker arm actuator A climbs above its upper limit. Typical reasons are an interrupted sensor ground, a signal wire chafed through onto a supply line, or corrosion that raises resistance. Since the value no longer represents a reachable actuator position, the engine controller discards it. No manufacturer documents P266D publicly; the requirement to detect it comes from CARB's monitoring rules for variable valve lift components. Only engines with position-sensed actuators on both banks could ever set it. Diagnosis starts with reference voltage and ground at the bank 2 sensor plug. Related: P266C, P264D.
c: Interrupted ground of the bank 2 sensor
Signal wire chafed onto a supply line
s: MIL on
Lift on bank 2 frozen
Reduced power

P266E.t: "A" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 2)
P266E.d: P266E describes a bank 2 position signal from actuator A that flickers: brief dropouts or spikes appear while the reading is otherwise fine. Heat cycling near the exhaust side, vibration on a loose pin or a harness rubbing on a bracket can produce it, and it often comes and goes. No manufacturer documents P266E publicly. CARB expects lift system inputs to be checked for continuity and rationality, which includes such short interruptions. A jumping signal makes the lift control on bank 2 unsteady or forces it to a default position, felt as hesitation or uneven running. Logging the sensor value while flexing the harness on that bank is the usual way to catch it.
c: Loose pin vibrating in the bank 2 sensor plug
Connector contact degraded by heat cycling near the exhaust
s: MIL comes and goes
Hesitation or uneven running
Fault often not present at the workshop

P266F.t: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve A Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P266F.d: Refrigerant distribution valve A is a solenoid that opens or closes one branch of the A/C circuit, for instance a rear evaporator or a battery chiller. Its driver stage in the control module protects itself: when the output current rises above its limit or the chip overheats, it switches off and reports P266F. That usually means the load draws too much, through a shorted coil, a short in the harness or a valve that is mechanically stuck. No manufacturer documents P266F publicly; Ford lists only the open-circuit code P2611 for the same valve, and suppliers such as Egelhof build these shut-off valves as simple on/off solenoids. Unlike P2611 to P2613, which flag open and shorted wiring, P266F concerns the protection of the driver itself. The affected branch then stays closed.
c: Valve coil with shorted turns drawing excessive current
Short in the valve harness or connector
Valve mechanically stuck so the coil stays loaded
Overheated or defective driver stage in the control module
s: One A/C zone or the battery cooling stays inactive
Fault may return after cooling down

P2670.t: Actuator Supply Voltage B Circuit Low
P2670.d: P2670 is set when the second high-side actuator supply delivers too little voltage while it is switched on, which nearly always means a short to ground somewhere on the supply line or in a load connected to it. GM documents it in several controllers. In the 16OBDG08 TCM tables for Silverado and Sierra a ground short is recognised at an impedance of 0.43 ohm or less, confirmed after three events, Type A. GM's 2023 TCM compares the supply voltage with battery voltage and also watches the average current, 60 ms to fail, Type A. In GM's hybrid tables (Volt THPC in 16OBDG01, HPC1 in 19OBDG01) high side driver 2 reports the short within about 0.13 s, again Type A after one trip. Solenoids on that supply drop out, so the transmission enters a failsafe mode.
c: Supply wire chafed and shorted to ground
Shorted solenoid on the supplied group pulling the line down
Faulty high-side driver in the controller
s: Failsafe gear, no normal shifting
MIL on immediately
Further solenoid circuit codes stored alongside

P2671.t: Actuator Supply Voltage B Circuit High
P2671.d: P2671 points to voltage on the second actuator supply when the controller has switched it off, so the line is fed from outside or the switch inside the module no longer opens. The solenoids on that supply can then no longer be de-energised as a group, which defeats the failsafe. GM tests this mostly at start-up or shut-down: in the 16OBDG08 TCM tables a short to power below 0.5 ohm is detected during initialisation with the driver off; the 2023 TCM checks at power-down whether the supply stays above 70 % of battery voltage, stores the result and sets the code at the next start as Type B. GM's hybrid HPC1 table of 2019 likewise rates it Type B. Ford's 2014 list contains P2671 without MIL. P2669 is the open circuit, P2670 the short to ground.
c: Supply line shorted to another powered circuit
High-side switch in the controller stuck closed
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the transmission connector
s: Warning lamp after the next start
Often no immediate shift complaint
Failsafe may not engage correctly if another fault occurs

P2672.d: On diesels with an electronically controlled rotary or distributor pump, the controller needs to know how far the pump's actual delivery start sits from its nominal position relative to the crankshaft. P2672 flags that this stored or measured offset is wrong or outside the window the software accepts. CARB requires 2010-on diesels to detect injection that is too early or too late. Dodge listed P2672 among the codes activated by the engine-controller update in emissions recall T21 for the 2004–2006 Sprinter; no public maker text gives a threshold. P2673 instead means the timing value was never learned. A driver may notice hard starting, knocking, smoke or reduced power.
c: Injection pump fitted or re-timed incorrectly after repair
Faulty pump timing or crank/cam reference signal
Worn pump drive (gear, belt, coupling) shifting the timing
Engine control software fault or wrong calibration
s: Check engine light on
Hard starting or rough idle
Diesel knock, smoke or reduced power

P2673.t: Injection Pump Timing Calibration Not Learned
P2673.d: This code says the engine controller holds no valid learned value for the start of delivery of its injection pump. Such a value is usually taught after the pump or the controller is replaced, or after a software reflash, and lets the controller correct the pump's individual timing tolerance. The same Dodge campaign (T21, new engine software for 2004–2006 Sprinter vans) also lists P2673 beside P2672; no public maker document explains its logic. CARB asks for tolerance compensation to be monitored on parts that are matched to the controller. Unlike P2672 the timing itself need not be wrong; the learning step is simply missing. A relearn with a scan tool is the usual cure.
c: Timing relearn skipped after pump or controller replacement
Software update interrupted or learned values lost
Relearn aborted because enable conditions (temperature, voltage) were not met
s: Check engine light on
Slightly rough running or more noise

P2674.t: Injection Pump Fuel Calibration Not Learned
P2674.d: Electronically governed diesel injection pumps meter the quantity per stroke themselves, and each unit differs slightly in how much it delivers for a given command. P2674 reports that the quantity correction for the installed pump has not been learned or stored in the controller. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; P2672 and P2673 cover the timing side of the same pump. CARB requires 2015-on vehicles whose fuel pumps or injectors carry production tolerance compensation, such as coded parts or trim resistors, to verify that the right compensation is in use. Without it, fuelling can drift, giving smoke, uneven idle or a shortfall of power until the learn routine is run.
c: Quantity learn not run after pump or controller replacement
Pump calibration data missing, wrong or not matching the installed pump
Fuel metering actuator fault preventing the learn from completing
s: Check engine light on
Smoke or uneven idle
Reduced power
