P2675.d: Some engines can change where the air cleaner draws its air, for example switching between a cold inlet at the front and a second opening in the engine bay, with a flap or valve moved by a solenoid or small motor. P2675 is the open or general circuit fault of this control: the module driving the flap detects that its output line carries no current or reports a fault it cannot classify further. No manufacturer documents P2675 publicly. Ford's 2014 gasoline code list contains only the low and high variants P2676 and P2677, both as continuous tests without MIL, which suggests the open case is treated inside those codes there. CARB demands circuit checks on outputs that can influence emissions. The flap then stays wherever it stopped.
c: Connector at the inlet flap actuator loose or unplugged, often after air filter service
Broken wire in the actuator circuit
Open coil or motor winding in the flap actuator
s: Warning light or stored code, often without MIL
Inlet flap no longer switches
Usually no noticeable change in driving

P2676.t: Air Cleaner Inlet Control Circuit Low
P2676.d: P2676 means the control line of the air cleaner inlet flap sits at too low a voltage for the state the controller has commanded. On a low-side driven solenoid this typically appears when the line is shorted to ground and the actuator is energised permanently; on other designs a shorted coil pulls the voltage down. Ford lists P2676 in its 2014 gasoline OBD code list as a continuous test with no MIL entry, so on those cars the code may sit in memory without a warning lamp. No public Ford text names the vehicles or the flap's job. CARB requires outputs that can change emissions to be checked for such faults. Expect the flap to stay in one position; drivability rarely changes. P2677 covers the opposite case.
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Shorted coil in the inlet flap actuator
s: Code stored, often without warning lamp
Inlet flap stuck in one position
Possibly changed intake noise

P2677.t: Air Cleaner Inlet Control Circuit High
P2677.d: The counterpart to P2676: the controller sees the drive line of the air cleaner inlet flap at too high a voltage, so it cannot pull the actuator in when asked. A short from the control wire to battery voltage, a failed output stage, or an open coil that leaves the line at supply level produce this pattern. In Ford's 2014 gasoline code list P2677 appears next to P2676, again as a continuous check without the MIL mark, meaning a stored code need not light the warning lamp. Beyond that list no manufacturer documents P2677 publicly. CARB's rules for monitored outputs explain why the driver stage is watched at all. The flap typically remains in its unpowered default position, and the car drives normally.
c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Open coil in the flap actuator
Failed output stage in the control module
s: Code stored, often without warning lamp
Inlet flap remains in its default position

P2678.d: In a sealed cooling system, air and vapour bubbles are carried through a thin vent line into the expansion tank, where they separate from the liquid; a bubble-free circuit avoids local hot spots, as cooling suppliers such as MAHLE point out. Some engines put an electrically switched valve in this degassing path so the controller can close it, for example to speed up warm-up. P2678 reports an open or unspecified fault in the drive circuit of that valve. No manufacturer documents P2678 or its valve publicly, so neither the purpose nor any threshold can be named. CARB requires electrical checks of controlled cooling system components. If the valve fails in the wrong state, warm-up can lengthen or venting may be impaired.
c: Unplugged connector or broken wire to the degassing valve
Open solenoid coil in the degassing valve
Faulty driver in the control module
s: Check engine light or stored code
Longer warm-up or slow heater output
Gurgling or air in the cooling system

P2679.t: Coolant Degassing Valve Control Circuit Low
P2679.d: P2679 indicates that the control line of the switched valve in the coolant vent path to the expansion tank reads too low. Usually the wire is grounded somewhere, or the solenoid has shorted turns; with a low-side driver the valve may then stay energised regardless of the command. The engine controller compares the line voltage with the state it set. Dodge lists P2679 among the fault codes that the reprogrammed engine controller of the 2004–2006 Sprinter can newly store under emissions recall T21, but the recall text gives no description of the circuit. Otherwise no maker explains P2679 publicly. CARB requires such circuit checks for controlled cooling components. A valve held in one state can slow warm-up or hinder venting.
c: Shorted turns in the degassing valve solenoid
Coolant or water leaking into the valve connector
s: Check engine light or stored code
Slow warm-up
Coolant level fluctuations in the expansion tank

P267A.t: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit (Bank 2)
P267A.d: Continuously variable lift systems turn a control or eccentric shaft with an electric motor and report the shaft angle back to the engine controller. On V engines each cylinder bank has its own mechanism; Nissan's VVEL on the VQ37VHR V6 and VK50VE V8 is an example of such a two-bank layout. P267A is the unspecific circuit fault of feedback sensor B on bank 2: the signal is unusable, but the controller does not classify it as too low or too high. No manufacturer documents P267A publicly; Toyota's bulletins use the B sensor letter only for its inline Valvematic engines and code P265B. CARB requires electrical checks on every input of a lift system. Expect connector, supply or ground problems first; P267B to P267E name more specific failure patterns.
c: Loose, corroded or damaged plug at the bank 2 position sensor
Broken or chafed signal, reference or ground wire
Internal fault of position sensor B, bank 2
Fault in the engine or lift control module input
s: Check engine light on
Variable lift on bank 2 held at a fixed default
Reduced power or rough idle

P267B.t: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 2)
P267B.d: P267B concerns the bank 2 feedback of lift actuator B when the signal is electrically sound but the angle it reports does not follow the commanded value, moves too slowly, or contradicts the mechanism's known travel. Faulty learning of the end stops, a slipping sensor mount, wear in the shaft drive or a sticking actuator can all produce this picture. No manufacturer documents P267B publicly. The closest published case is Toyota's bank 1 counterpart P265B on Valvematic engines: bulletin T-SB-0098-19 starts with a learn value reset and an active test of the shaft angle, then replaces the lift controller if the fault returns. CARB expects variable lift monitors to detect missed targets and slow response. Lift on bank 2 is usually frozen.
c: End-stop learn values lost or wrong after repair or battery disconnect
Worn or sticking shaft drive of actuator B on bank 2
Position sensor drifting or loose in its mount
Lift control software needing an update
s: Check engine light on
Hesitation or reduced power
Uneven idle when lift is frozen on one bank

P267C.t: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Low (Bank 2)
P267C.d: With P267C the engine controller reads the bank 2 position signal of lift actuator B below its lowest valid value. A sensor of this kind is designed so that even the end stop of the shaft keeps a margin to zero volts, so a reading near ground points to an electrical cause: the signal line shorted to chassis, a lost 5 V reference, or a sensor with an internal short. No manufacturer documents P267C publicly, and no thresholds are published. CARB treats out-of-range low inputs of variable lift systems as faults that must be detected. On a V engine the controller then usually stops adjusting lift on bank 2 only. Check the reference voltage at the sensor plug before replacing parts. P267D is the high-side counterpart.
c: Signal wire shorted to ground through damaged insulation
5 V reference supply to the sensor missing
Internal short in position sensor B, bank 2
s: Check engine light on
Lift on bank 2 fixed at a default position
Noticeably weaker acceleration

P267D.t: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit High (Bank 2)
P267D.d: P267D is stored when the angle feedback of lift actuator B on bank 2 rises above its upper valid limit. Typical causes are an open sensor ground, which lets the signal float toward the reference, a signal conductor touching a supply line, or water bridging contacts in the connector. Systems such as BMW's Valvetronic, where an electric motor swings an eccentric shaft through a fixed arc, never place the sensor at the supply rail in normal operation, so such a value is rejected. No manufacturer documents P267D publicly; detection follows from CARB's input checks for variable lift. The controller holds bank 2 at a safe setting. Measure ground continuity first. Low-side partner: P267C; dropouts: P267E.
c: Open or high-resistance ground of the position sensor
Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the sensor plug
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power with lift fixed on bank 2
Slightly higher fuel consumption

P267E.t: "B" Rocker Arm Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic (Bank 2)
P267E.d: Here the bank 2 angle signal of lift actuator B is mostly plausible, yet it drops out for moments or jumps by amounts the motor-driven shaft could not cover in the time between two readings. The engine controller counts such events and sets P267E once they exceed its tolerance. Loose terminals, a wire cracked inside its insulation near the cylinder head, and interference from ignition or actuator wiring are the usual suspects; the fault often depends on heat or vibration. No manufacturer documents P267E publicly. CARB asks lift system inputs to be checked for signal quality, not only for fixed limits. While the reading jumps, lift control on bank 2 can hunt or be parked. Recording the signal while moving the harness helps locate the fault.
c: Loose or fretted terminal in the sensor connector
Wire broken inside insulation, opening under heat or vibration
Interference from nearby ignition or actuator wiring
s: Check engine light that may come and go
Brief hesitation or surging
Uneven running when lift control on bank 2 hunts

P267F.t: Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P267F.d: Many control modules carry a temperature sensor on their own circuit board to protect output stages and, in transmission units, to back up fluid temperature. P267F adds an intermittent or erratic variant to the established family P0666 to P0669: the reading flickers, jumps or drops out briefly instead of being permanently too low, too high or implausible. Mercedes-Benz lists P267F00 as a temperature sensor fault of the control unit among the codes covered by its Intelligent Predictive Repair diagnosis for the 724.1 dual-clutch gearbox (bulletin LI27.00-P-077141, 2025), next to P0666 to P0669 and P0634. No thresholds are published. Since the sensor sits inside the module, repair usually means replacing or reprogramming that module.
c: Internal defect of the control module or its temperature sensor
Unstable module supply or ground causing erratic readings
Module software misinterpreting the sensor signal
s: Check engine or transmission warning light
Harsh or delayed shifts if the module uses substitute values
Often no noticeable symptom

P2680.t: Coolant Degassing Valve Control Circuit High
P2680.d: P2680 is the high-voltage fault of the degassing valve drive: the controller cannot pull the line down, so the valve stays in its unpowered state whatever is commanded. A wire touching a battery feed, an internally open solenoid, or a defective output transistor are the classic reasons. Because degassing only works when bubbles can reach the expansion tank, where the coolant calms and releases trapped gas, a valve stuck in the wrong state may leave air in the engine circuit or slow warm-up, depending on its default. No manufacturer documents P2680 publicly, and no threshold is published. The monitoring duty comes from CARB's comprehensive component rules. Check the coolant level and look for overheating signs.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery feed
Internally open solenoid of the degassing valve
Defective output stage in the control module
s: Check engine light or stored code
Air pockets, gurgling or weak cabin heat
Temperature gauge higher than usual

P2681.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Circuit/Open
P2681.d: Bypass valve A is an electrically driven coolant valve whose role differs by maker. P2681 flags an open or otherwise faulty drive circuit. GM's 2011 Volt table checks it in the HPC2/VICM: 40 failures in 50 samples at 100 ms, Type B. Ford's 2020–2023 gasoline summary defines valve A as the automatic transmission cooler flow (transmission warm-up) valve and sets the code when its smart driver reports a fault for 5 s. Toyota bulletin T-SB-0112-24 (A25A and M20A engines, 2018–2021) replaces the water valve for P2681 subtypes 11 (circuit grounded) and 15 (open circuit or battery short). Ram 1500 3.6 L trucks needed a new three-way coolant valve with a cracked gear (07-005-24); VW reflashed 2024 Atlas engine controllers.
c: Failed bypass valve (motor, gear or electronics)
Chafed harness or open fuse in the valve supply
Engine control software causing false detection
s: Check engine light on
Slow warm-up of engine or transmission
Maintenance or temperature warning message

P2682.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Circuit Low
P2682.d: P2682 narrows the drive fault of bypass valve A to the low side: the output is pulled toward ground when it should not be. In GM's 2016 table for the second-generation Volt, the VICM sets it when motor driver 1 reports a short to low while the valve is commanded to the low position, with 4 failures in 5 samples and Type B. Ford's 2019 hybrid summary flags P2682 after a driver fault longer than 5 s, and it must be present before the stuck-open test P26AB can finish. Volkswagen's 2014 Touareg Hybrid (CGFA) uses a signal voltage below about 2.8 to 3.2 V. Ford's 2014 gasoline list marks it as a MIL code. The valve stays where it was, so warm-up or heat distribution may suffer.
c: Drive wire to the valve motor shorted to ground
Internal short in the valve motor or electronics
Coolant or water corrosion in the valve plug
s: Check engine light on
Weak cabin heat or slow warm-up
Possible overheating warning under load

P2683.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Circuit High
P2683.d: For P2683 the drive of bypass valve A is shorted toward supply voltage or draws too much current. GM's 2016 Volt table has the VICM evaluate a short-to-high report from motor driver 1 while the valve is stopped or commanded to the high position; 16 failures out of 20 samples at 100 ms give a Type B fault. Volkswagen's 2014 Touareg Hybrid with the CGFA engine judges current instead and trips above roughly 2.2 to 4 A, which points to a jammed or shorted valve motor as well as wiring. Ford's 2019 hybrid summary uses a driver fault lasting over 5 s, and Ford's 2014 gasoline list shows P2683 with MIL. Coolant routing is then stuck, so heater output, warm-up or cooling of the affected circuit may change.
c: Jammed valve or shorted valve motor drawing excess current
Drive wire shorted to battery voltage
Faulty motor driver in the control module
s: Check engine light on
Changed heater output or warm-up time
Temperature warning in severe cases

P2684.d: Some transmission controllers power groups of solenoids through several internal high-side outputs; supply C is the third of these rails, after A (P0657) and B (P2669). P2684 reports an open load on it. GM's 2023 and 2024 TCM tables tie the code to high-side output 7 and test it while the module powers down: with the output off and a low-side driver on, the load should drag the line low, so a level above 40 % of battery voltage is remembered as an open load and reported after the next start, Type A. Ford's 2024 summary assigns P2684 to high side driver 7 of the TR9070 dual-clutch gearbox, and Ford's 2014 Boss 302S code list carries it as well. Whatever hangs on that rail stops working, so a default gear or limp mode is likely.
c: Broken wire or loose terminal between the module output and the supplied solenoids
Corroded or unseated transmission connector or internal lead frame
High-side output inside the controller defective
s: Transmission in default gear or limp mode
MIL on after restart
Several solenoid circuit codes stored together

P2685.t: Actuator Supply Voltage C Circuit Low
P2685.d: P2685 means the third actuator supply rail sags while it is switched on, almost always because the line or one of the loads it feeds has a path to ground. Unlike the open and switch faults of this rail, GM's 2023 and 2024 TCM tables check this one continuously during operation: if the voltage at high-side output 7 falls below a share of the supply, or the averaged output current runs too high, a timer counts up and the fault is confirmed after 60 ms. Battery voltage must lie between 8.75 and 18 V, the engine must not be cranking, and the test is suspended when P0882 or P0883 is present; GM rates it Type A. Ford's 2024 summary lists P2685 as the shorted-load fault of high side driver 7 in the TR9070 dual-clutch unit. The protected output switches off and the transmission falls back to a failsafe mode.
c: Supply wire chafed through and touching ground
Shorted solenoid coil on this rail drawing excess current
Weak battery or charging fault pulling the whole supply down
s: MIL on during the same trip
Failsafe gear, no normal shifting
Blown fuse possible on the transmission supply

P2686.t: Actuator Supply Voltage C Circuit High
P2686.d: The high case of supply C concerns voltage that should not be there: the rail stays live although the controller has turned it off. Causes are an internal high-side switch that no longer opens or an outside wire touching battery positive. GM's 2023 and 2024 TCM tables run this check during shutdown. With output 7 disabled, a reading above 70 % of battery voltage counts as a shorted switch; the module keeps that finding in permanent memory and reports it once restarted. Battery voltage must stay within 1.5 V during the test, and GM files it as Type B: two failing trips before the lamp lights. Ford lists P2686 as the shorted-switch fault of high side driver 7 in its 2024 TR9070 table and also in the Boss 302S code list. The solenoids can no longer be switched off safely, so a limp mode is likely.
c: Internal high-side switch of the controller stuck conducting
Supply wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit in the harness
Moisture in the transmission connector creating a leakage path
s: MIL after a second trip with the fault
Limp mode or fixed gear after restart
Code returns after clearing once the key has been off

P2687.d: Diesel engines warm the fuel at the filter so that wax crystals do not block it in frost. P2687 says the control line of that heater is open. In GM's diesel ECM tables the engine computer switches the heater relay with a low-side driver and judges the off-state voltage; more than 200 kOhm between pin and ground means open. The 2014 version (14OBDG04) needed 11 V for 3 s and 2 s of fault, Type B with MIL; the 2017 and 2020 versions use 10 bad readings out of 20 at 100 ms and rate it Type C without lamp. Ford used the same code differently: its 2015 and 2016 diesel summaries apply P2687 to the vaporizer glow plug of the 3.2 L Transit's downstream injection, open if the line sits at 2.9 to 3.2 V for 5 s; from 2017 that fault moved to P269B.
c: Heater relay coil open or relay not seated
Broken control wire or corroded terminal at the filter housing
Heater element open where it is switched directly without a relay
s: Hard starting or stalling in severe cold
Power loss from a waxed fuel filter
Often no warning lamp, depending on model year

P2688.t: Fuel Supply Heater Control Circuit Low
P2688.d: With P2688 the heater control line reads too low while the driver is off, which points to a grounded wire: the relay would then be energized all the time, and the filter heater runs even in summer and drains the battery after shutdown. GM's 2020 diesel table requires 0.5 ohm or less to ground and counts 10 failures in 20 samples taken every 100 ms; the code is Type C but, unlike its siblings, triggers a service-vehicle-soon message after one trip (the 2018 table matches). In 2014 GM still rated the same fault Type B with MIL. On the 2015 and 2016 Ford 3.2 L Transit diesel the code belonged to the vaporizer glow plug of the exhaust fuel system and was set after 5 s inside a 1.95–2.175 V window; later model years report that as P269D.
c: Control wire chafed against the engine or frame and grounded
Water or fuel in the filter-housing connector
s: Service message or MIL, depending on model year
Battery drained after the vehicle stands
Fuel heater running constantly

P2689.t: Fuel Supply Heater Control Circuit High
P2689.d: P2689 is logged when the fuel heater control line stays high even though the controller has commanded it on, so the relay coil is fed from battery positive and cannot be pulled in; the heater never works. GM's diesel ECM checks the low-side driver in its on state and treats 0.5 ohm or less to power as a short; the 2020 table uses 10 of 20 samples at 100 ms and Type C without lamp or message, while the 2014 table sets it as Type B. Ford's 2015 and 2016 diesel summaries give the code two jobs on the 3.2 L Transit: a vaporizer glow plug line held in the 10.9–12.32 V band for 5 s, and a relay status that contradicts the request for about 60 s, marked as provisional. In 2017 Ford split those into P269E and P26A0. Cold-weather starting is the main thing at risk.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-fed wire
Heater relay sticking so feedback no longer matches the command
Low-side driver in the engine controller defective
s: No fuel heating, gelling risk below freezing
Hard cold starts and rough idle until warm
Warning lamp only on some model years

P268A.d: P268A covers injector correction that relies on a learn routine rather than a printed code. GM's diesel tables 17OBDG04 to 19OBDG04A set it, Type A in one trip, when the small quantity learning (SQL) routine was not completed and stored before the vehicle left the assembly line. VW's 2014 Touareg 3.0 TDI (CNRB) lists it for a rail pressure deviation above 1,500–2,000 kPa lasting over 40 s. Audi's 2026 service note 2082225/1 reports it with the MIL on 2025–2026 A5 and Q5 2.0 TFSI petrol engines as a software issue. Deutz MD1 links it to a calibration fault of injector 1. Per-injector code faults use P268C–P2696. Symptoms range from none to rough idle and knock.
c: Injector quantity learn not completed after injector or controller replacement
Engine control software fault (e.g. Audi 2.0 TFSI 2025–2026)
Rail pressure deviation preventing correct learning
Injector worn beyond the correction range
s: Check engine light on
Rough idle or louder combustion noise
Often no noticeable change in driving

P268B.t: High Pressure Fuel Pump Calibration Not Learned/Programmed
P268B.d: Common rail and direct-injection petrol systems use a high pressure pump whose delivery is trimmed by a metering or volume control valve. Where the pump comes with individual correction data, or the controller has to learn its behaviour, P268B reports that this data is missing or was never taught. No manufacturer documents P268B publicly; GM's diesel tables, which carry P268A and the per-cylinder injector codes, do not list it. CARB names pumps corrected by in-line resistors as an example of parts whose compensation must be checked from 2015 on. Rail pressure control may then work with a generic pump model, so pressure faults such as P0087 or P0088 and weak starting can follow.
c: Pump correction data not entered after pump replacement
Controller replaced or reflashed without transferring pump data
Pump variant does not match the software
s: Check engine light on
Long cranking or hard start
Reduced power with rail pressure deviations

P268C.d: Every modern diesel injector carries a correction code from the factory flow test, and the controller must hold the code of the injector in cylinder 1. P268C sets when that code is missing, outside its range or fails the checksum. GM's 2014 four-cylinder diesel table (14OBDG04) checks the injector quantity adjustment (IQA) checksum once per drive cycle before driving, Type B. Later GM V8, six- and four-cylinder diesel tables rate it Type A, set if the code at DID $60 was never written. Ford's 2023 diesel summary (6.7 L and 3.0 L) runs the check continuously within about 0.5 s. Cylinder 1 exists on every engine, so this is the most widely used code of the series.
c: Correction code of a new cylinder 1 injector not entered
Code entered with a typing error, so the checksum fails
Controller replaced without transferring injector codes
s: Check engine light on
Uneven running or knock from cylinder 1

P268D.d: P268D concerns the stored flow correction for the injector in cylinder 2. In GM's 2016 four-cylinder diesel table (16OBDG04) the test runs with ignition on and passes once the end-of-line injector adjustment (EIA) value has been written via DID $61; a missing value only counts as a failure when the manufacturer enable counter is zero, i.e. on a finished production controller. The code is Type A there and in GM's 2020 V8 diesel table. Where cylinder 2 physically sits depends on the maker's numbering. Ford's 2023 diesel summary also uses P268D. CARB wants the stored code to point to the injector with the wrong compensation, hence one code per cylinder.
c: Adjustment value of the cylinder 2 injector not programmed after replacement
Injectors moved between cylinders without updating codes
Programming session aborted (voltage drop, communication loss)
s: Check engine light on
Slight misfire feel or noise from cylinder 2

P268E.d: For cylinder 3 the controller compares the injector's correction value with what its software accepts. Ford's 2023 diesel OBD summary explains the idea well: each injector's code, kept in EEPROM, describes how far that unit departs from an idealised mean part, and a DTC is logged if the value is absent, out of range or its checksum is wrong. The monitor runs continuously and needs about half a second. GM's 2019 V8 diesel table 19OBDG04A rates P268E Type A, so the lamp lights in the first trip. Because only the data is checked, the injector itself may be perfect; the usual fix is to read the code off the injector head and program it into the controller.
c: Cylinder 3 injector replaced, code not programmed
Code from an injector variant the software does not accept
Stored injector data corrupted in the controller
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable driveability change

P268F.d: P268F flags missing or unusable correction data for the injector in cylinder 4. On four-cylinder diesels it closes the series: GM's 2014 table 14OBDG04 and 2016 table 16OBDG04 list P268C to P268F and nothing beyond. The 2014 version checks the IQA checksum before each trip and rates the fault Type B, so the lamp waits for a second failed trip; the 2016 version uses the DID $63 write check and Type A. Six- and eight-cylinder engines from GM and Ford use the code as well. CARB requires that a wrong compensation be detected and, where feasible, traced to the specific injector. A single unmatched injector seldom causes clear symptoms, but emissions and noise can rise.
c: New cylinder 4 injector fitted without code programming
Code typed incorrectly into the scan tool
Used or replacement controller carrying another engine's codes
s: Check engine light on
Possible rough idle or higher combustion noise

P2690.d: P2690 is the first code of the series that a four-cylinder engine cannot set; it needs at least five cylinders. It reports that the flow correction for the cylinder 5 injector is absent or rejected by the controller. GM uses it in its 2025 six-cylinder diesel table 25OBDG04B as well as in its V8 diesel tables, Type A, with the value stored under DID $64. Ford's 2023 diesel summary, which spans the 3.0 L V6 and 6.7 L V8, includes it too. On V engines the location of cylinder 5 varies: Ford counts one bank first, GM alternates sides, so the service data must be checked before touching an injector. Expect a lit MIL rather than drivability trouble.
c: Cylinder 5 injector replaced without entering its code
Code entered for the wrong cylinder because of the bank numbering
s: Check engine light on
Rarely uneven running

P2691.d: P2691 refers to the injector in cylinder 6. For six-cylinder diesels it is the last of the per-cylinder codes: GM's 2025 table 25OBDG04B stops at P2691, while the V8 table 25OBDG04A goes on to P2693. In both 2025 tables the check is always active on production controllers and fails if the end-of-line adjustment value was never written; as a further guard, a separate plausibility test under P060C looks at the size of the computed adjustment values. GM rates P2691 Type A. Ford's 2023 diesel summary lists it for its 3.0 L and 6.7 L engines. Programming the code printed on the cylinder 6 injector normally clears it; a recurring fault after correct entry points to the controller.
c: Cylinder 6 injector code missing after replacement
Entered value rejected as implausible by the software
Controller memory fault losing stored injector data
s: Check engine light on
Possible knock or smoke from the affected cylinder

P2692.d: Only engines with seven or more cylinders can log P2692, which in practice means V8 diesels. It tells that the correction code for the cylinder 7 injector has not been stored or is unusable. GM carries it in every eight-cylinder diesel table from 17OBDG04 (2017) to 25OBDG04A (2025); the 2017 and 2020 versions evaluate it at ignition on, Type A in one trip, with the value expected under DID $66. Ford lists it in its 2023 diesel summary, where only the 6.7 L V8 has a seventh cylinder. Typical triggers are injector replacement on that cylinder or a swapped controller. Six-cylinder and smaller engines setting P2692 would point to a wrong software variant.
c: Injector in cylinder 7 replaced, code not programmed
Replacement controller without the vehicle's injector codes
Software variant for the wrong engine configuration
s: Check engine light on
Usually no drivability change

P2693.d: P2693 completes the series on V8 engines and covers the injector in cylinder 8. It is set when the controller finds no valid flow correction code for that position. In GM's 2018 table 18OBDG04 the code reads DID $67 and fails only once the manufacturer enable counter is zero; the 2025 table 25OBDG04A instead keeps the check permanently on in production units. Both rate it Type A. Ford's 2023 diesel summary covers it for the 6.7 L Power Stroke with a continuous check of about 0.5 s. When all eight codes appear together, a new or reset controller is far more likely than eight bad injectors; a lone P2693 points to work on that one injector.
c: Code of the new cylinder 8 injector not entered
New or reset controller lacking all injector codes
Typing error in the cylinder 8 code
s: Check engine light on
Possible rough idle or knock

P2694.d: P2694 would flag bad or missing correction data for the injector in cylinder 9 and therefore only fits engines with nine or more cylinders, in road vehicles essentially V10s. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's diesel tables end at P2693 for eight cylinders, and Ford's 2023 diesel summary covers the same eight codes; neither lists a cylinder 9 entry. The logic would follow theirs: a missing, out-of-range or checksum-failing code for that injector sets the fault, as CARB demands for coded injectors from 2015 on. If P2694 shows up on an engine with eight cylinders or fewer, suspect a scan tool decoding error or wrong software rather than an injector.
c: Cylinder 9 injector code not programmed (ten-cylinder engines)
Scan tool decoding error on engines without a ninth cylinder
Controller software for a different engine
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable symptoms

P2695.d: P2695 is reserved for the injector in cylinder 10, the highest cylinder number the J2012 series provides with its own data code. A ten-cylinder engine with individually coded injectors would be needed to set it, and none of the public OBD summaries reviewed here contains it: GM's 2025 V8 diesel table 25OBDG04A and Ford's 2023 diesel summary both stop at cylinder 8. CARB's rule that the stored code should, where feasible, identify the wrongly compensated injector explains why the series reaches this far. Engines with more than ten cylinders have to fall back on P2696. On ordinary cars and trucks P2695 is very unlikely to appear and should first be verified with a second tool.
c: Cylinder 10 injector code missing on a ten-cylinder engine
Misread code on engines with fewer cylinders
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable symptoms

P2696.d: P2696 is the collective version of P268C–P2695: the controller rejects stored injector correction data without naming a cylinder. That suits systems that check the data block as a whole, or engines with more than ten cylinders. No manufacturer documents P2696 publicly; GM and Ford use the per-cylinder codes instead. CARB allows a maker to flag only the minimum number of wrongly compensated injectors that raises emissions, which can make a shared code sensible. A real case of lost data is Mercedes-Benz campaign NCU-2023060006: on 2012 S-Class diesels the six injector codes could vanish during an emission software update, with a MIL and sometimes louder or rougher running.
c: Injector codes lost during a software update or controller replacement
Injector replaced without programming its code
Corrupted injector data block in the controller
s: Check engine light on
Louder engine noise or rough running

P2697.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector A Circuit/Open
P2697.d: Many heavy diesels do not raise exhaust temperature for filter regeneration by late in-cylinder injection, but spray diesel straight into the exhaust ahead of the oxidation catalyst through a separate doser, often called the seventh injector. P2697 means the solenoid that meters this fuel cannot be driven because its circuit is open. Volvo and Mack document it in their aftertreatment hydrocarbon injector (AHI) guide for US10 engines with 2013 OBD and later, as P2697 with failure type 13: the electric valve sits in the AHI dosing module, which moved onto the fuel filter housing from model year 2017, while the nozzle in the exhaust is purely hydraulic. The guide sends technicians to the module connector and harness. No dosing means no active regeneration, and soot builds up in the filter.
c: Loose, corroded or damaged connector at the dosing module
Harness to the dosing valve broken by heat or vibration
Dosing valve coil inside the module burnt open
s: Active particulate filter regeneration not possible
Rising soot load, later derate
MIL on

P2698.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector A Performance
P2698.d: P2698 is not about wiring but about whether the exhaust fuel doser does what it is told; most often the check looks for leakage when no dosing is requested. Ford's 3.2 L Transit (2017 and 2018 summaries) compares a measured temperature downstream of the injection point with a model after at least 6 h engine-off. The 2023 6.7 L Super Duty uses a model check after 21,600 s soak plus a second logic that balances oxygen mass before and after the catalyst. Volvo and Mack article KC-90 (model years 2016–17) warns the code can appear without symptoms and points to exhaust sensors, a low-flow nozzle, the AHI module and the catalyst; Mack bulletin GDC19-014 (US19) first updates engine software. Ram also lists P2698 in a 2026 PCM flash for 6.7 L Cummins chassis cabs.
c: Doser valve or nozzle leaking fuel into the exhaust
Coked nozzle or line causing low flow
Exhaust temperature sensor drifting and skewing the model comparison
Engine software needing the manufacturer update
s: MIL on, often without noticeable drivability change
Regenerations fail or take unusually long
Higher fuel use or white exhaust smoke

P2699.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector A Circuit Low
P2699.d: P2699 flags the drive circuit of the exhaust fuel doser as too low, usually a grounded control wire or a shorted valve coil. The difference to P2697 matters in practice: an open circuit simply stops dosing, while a grounded line can switch the valve on without command if the short sits behind the driver, so raw fuel may reach a cold catalyst. Volvo and Mack list P2699 with failure type 00 among the electrical faults of their aftertreatment hydrocarbon injector system and send the technician to the dosing module plug and harness, in the same guide that covers the open and high cases. No other maker documents the code publicly. Expect a lit MIL, cancelled regenerations and, if dosing stays blocked, a rising filter load with eventual power reduction.
c: Doser control wire grounded against the frame or exhaust bracket
Shorted coil of the dosing valve
Fuel or water inside the module connector
s: MIL on and regeneration inhibited
Possible white smoke if the valve opens uncommanded
Derate after prolonged soot build-up

P269A.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Injector A Circuit High
P269A.d: The high variant of the exhaust doser circuit means the control line shows supply voltage where the driver expects it to be pulled down, typically a short to battery positive or a driver that no longer conducts. In that state the valve cannot be opened, and a hard short can also overload the output, which the controller then switches off for protection. Volvo and Mack name P269A with failure type 00 first in the electrical fault table of the same AHI guide, with the same instruction as for its siblings: inspect the dosing module connection and wiring before replacing the module. Warranty only covers a new module when one of the listed module codes is active or confirmed. Without dosing the truck relies on passive regeneration and soot accumulates.
c: Doser control wire shorted to a positive supply
Output stage in the controller not switching
Pin damage in the dosing module connector
s: MIL on, regeneration requests fail
Filter soot level climbs over time
Derate in later stages

P269B.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Glow Plug Control Circuit/Open
P269B.d: Some diesels inject fuel into the exhaust through a small vaporizer whose glow plug turns the fuel into vapor before it reaches the oxidation catalyst. Ford calls this downstream injection (DSI) on the 3.2 L Transit, used so that filter regeneration needs fewer in-cylinder post injections and less oil is diluted. P269B covers an open in the circuit by which the engine computer controls that glow plug. Ford's diesel summaries from 2017 and 2018 watch the line continuously with key on at 9 to 16.3 V battery voltage and set the open fault when the voltage stays between 2.9 and 3.2 V for 5 s. The 2015 and 2016 summaries reported the same condition as P2687. With the plug dead the fuel cannot be vaporized, so regeneration is cut back and the lamp comes on.
c: Open wire or connector between engine computer and glow plug relay
Vaporizer glow plug relay coil open
Blown fuse in the glow plug control feed
s: MIL on
Particulate filter regenerations fail or become rare
More frequent in-cylinder regeneration, oil level may rise

P269C.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Glow Plug Control Performance
P269C.d: P269C is the plausibility counterpart to the electrical control codes: the wires test fine, yet the control stage of the exhaust glow plug does not behave as commanded, for example a relay or driver that does not report the expected state or reacts too slowly. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The closest documented case is Ford's 3.2 L Transit, where a vaporizer glow plug relay whose feedback disagrees with the command for about 60 s is a recorded fault, filed under P26A0 from 2017 and under P2689 before. CARB requires functional checks of such output components wherever feasible, beyond pure circuit continuity. An affected engine would lose or limit exhaust fuel vaporization, so regeneration suffers and the MIL can be expected.
c: Glow plug relay switching late or not at all
Faulty feedback signal from the relay or driver
Low system voltage during the control check
s: MIL on
Particulate filter regeneration incomplete

P269D.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Glow Plug Control Circuit Low
P269D.d: A low reading on the exhaust glow plug control line points to a path to ground before the load, so the control stage cannot set the right level and the vaporizer glow plug may be switched wrongly. Ford is the documented user: in its 2017 and 2018 diesel summaries the 3.2 L Transit judges the downstream injection glow plug circuit by voltage windows, and a reading held between 1.95 and 2.175 V for 5 s is classed as a short to ground (key on, battery 9–16.3 V). In 2015 and 2016 Ford used P2688 for the identical window. Typical findings are a pinched wire near the exhaust or a shorted relay coil. The DPF regeneration that relies on vaporized fuel is held back until the circuit is repaired.
c: Control wire chafed on the exhaust or body and grounded
Shorted coil in the glow plug relay
s: MIL on
Regeneration suspended, rising soot load
Possible blown fuse in the glow plug feed

P269E.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Glow Plug Control Circuit High
P269E.d: When the exhaust glow plug control circuit reads close to battery voltage at the wrong moment, the control side has contact with a positive feed or the switching stage hangs open, so the vaporizer glow plug may stay energized or ignore commands. On Ford's 3.2 L Transit diesel the 2017 and 2018 summaries set P269E once the circuit holds between 10.9 and 12.32 V for 5 s with the ignition on. The predecessor years filed this under P2689, together with the relay plausibility check that later became P26A0. A glow element that heats without stopping wears out quickly and can draw fuel-free current for long periods, so a later open element code may follow. Regeneration is curtailed and the MIL comes on.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit
Relay contacts welded, glow plug permanently powered
Output stage in the engine computer defective
s: MIL on
Glow plug failing early from constant heating
Regeneration curtailed

P269F.d: While P269B concerns the line that commands the exhaust glow plug, P269F targets the load circuit itself: the heating element or its power feed is open, so no current flows even when the control stage switches correctly. A burnt-out element is the usual reason, followed by a loose terminal at the plug in the hot exhaust area. There is no public manufacturer documentation for P269F. Ford's Transit with the 3.2 L engine, the documented user of this glow plug family, reports its vaporizer glow plug faults through the control codes P269B, P269D, P269E and P26A0 instead. CARB requires output components of an emission-related system to be checked for circuit faults. Without heat the injected fuel cannot vaporize, so the engine limits exhaust dosing and regeneration.
c: Loose or corroded terminal nut at the plug
Blown fuse in the glow plug power circuit
s: MIL on
Particulate filter regenerations fail

P26A0.d: P26A0 says the exhaust glow plug system does not perform as intended, even if no electrical fault is present. Ford gives the clearest picture for the 3.2 L Transit diesel: from the 2017 summary on, the code is set when the feedback of the vaporizer glow plug relay disagrees with its command for roughly 60 s while the key is on, a fault filed under P2689 in earlier years. Ford bulletin 18-2094, superseded by 19-2016, covers 2016–2018 Transits built up to 13 February 2018 that light the MIL with P26A0 and/or P24A0. When these are the only codes, the fix is a new fuel vaporizer glow plug plus a powertrain module update, and the newer bulletin adds checking a 3 A and a 20 A mini fuse. A failing plug starves the regeneration of heat, which is why P24A0 often appears alongside.
c: Blown fuse or relay feedback not matching the command
s: MIL on
Exhaust temperature control code P24A0 stored too
Regenerations take longer or fail

P26A1.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Glow Plug Circuit Low
P26A1.d: P26A1 describes a load circuit of the exhaust glow plug that reads too low: the feed or the element has found a path to ground, so the current bypasses the heater or exceeds what the circuit allows. Shorted elements, insulation damage at the hot plug body and wiring melted against the exhaust are the expected causes; a fuse in the glow plug feed may blow repeatedly. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Ford's 3.2 L Transit, which uses the neighboring codes for its vaporizer glow plug, files a grounded control line under P269D instead. CARB's output component rules call for detection of such circuit faults on emission-related heaters. The vaporizer cannot heat, so exhaust dosing and filter regeneration are restricted.
c: Glow element shorted to its housing
Feed wire melted or chafed against the exhaust
Fuse blown as a result of the short
s: MIL on
Fuse for the glow plug circuit blows again after replacement
Regeneration blocked

P26A2.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Glow Plug Circuit High
P26A2.d: The high case of the exhaust glow plug load circuit is set when the monitored point sits too close to supply voltage. Depending on how the module measures, this means the heater circuit is shorted to another positive feed or the element draws almost no current, so the voltage barely drops across it. The plug then stays cold or cannot be switched off. Public manufacturer data for P26A2 are lacking. The known user of the neighboring glow plug codes, the Ford Transit 3.2 L diesel, reports a high reading on its vaporizer glow plug control circuit as P269E. CARB treats such heaters as output components that must be monitored for circuit faults. Expect a lit MIL and limited particulate filter regeneration until the circuit is repaired.
c: Glow plug feed shorted to another battery-fed circuit
Element with greatly increased resistance near the end of its life
Glow plug relay contacts stuck closed
s: MIL on
Exhaust dosing and regeneration limited

P26A3.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Range/Performance
P26A3.d: P26A3 is a functional fault: the electrics of bypass valve A look fine, but the valve does not reach or report the position it should. GM's 2011 Volt table sets it, Type B, when the end-position learn fails with coolant above 50 °C, or when the valve has not arrived at its commanded position within 15 s. Honda calls the part an electric water valve: on the 2014 Accord Plug-In Hybrid, bulletin 20-033 blames climate control software that drove the three-way valve wrongly and replaces that unit; on the 2018 Clarity Plug-In Hybrid, 18-090 is an emissions recall with new engine software. Ram 1500 3.6 L trucks show it after a cracked valve gear or, per 07-007-24, contamination by stop-leak pellets requiring a flush.
c: Broken gear or jammed rotor inside the bypass valve
Contaminated coolant, e.g. stop-leak additives, blocking the valve
Engine or climate control software commanding the valve incorrectly
End-position learn not completed after replacement
s: Check engine light on
Weak or delayed cabin heat
Unusual coolant or transmission temperatures

P26A4.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Circuit
P26A4.d: Many electric coolant valves carry a potentiometer or Hall element that reports the actual valve angle back to the controller. P26A4 is the general circuit code for that feedback on valve A: the signal is missing or cannot be assigned to a more specific low, high or erratic fault. No manufacturer documents P26A4 itself in public. GM's Volt tables cover the same sensor only through P26A6/P26A7, and Subaru bulletin 09-80-21 (Forester, Outback, Legacy, Crosstrek 2019–2021) mentions P26A-series codes in general when water reaches the sensor portion of the thermo control valve. CARB requires input signals to be checked for continuity. Without valid feedback the controller loses track of the valve, so warm-up and cooling may run on a fallback setting.
c: Moisture or corrosion inside the valve's position sensor section
Loose, corroded or damaged connector or feedback wiring
Missing 5 V reference or ground for the position sensor
s: Check engine light
Slow warm-up or weak cabin heat
Possible additional valve or coolant temperature codes

P26A5.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P26A5.d: Here the feedback signal is electrically present but sits where a healthy valve should never be. In GM's 2016 Volt table the VICM treats readings between 5 and 30 % or between 70 and 95 % of the reference as invalid; 80 failures in 100 samples at 100 ms give a Type B fault, provided the drive codes P2682/P2683/P26AD/P26AE and P26A6/P26A7 are clear. The same GM document lists a faster 3-of-5 variant for the ELR. On the first-generation Volt (2011) this zone check was still part of P26A9. Subaru's bulletin 09-80-21 blames sensor corrosion for P26A-series codes and fits a redesigned valve. A worn sensor track, a damaged gear between motor and sensor or a mis-seated connector are the usual suspects.
c: Worn or corroded position sensor track inside the valve
Damaged gear or coupling between valve motor and sensor
High contact resistance at the valve connector
s: Check engine light after two drives
Engine runs too cool or warms up slowly
Fluctuating heater output

P26A6.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Circuit Low
P26A6.d: P26A6 means the valve A feedback voltage has dropped below its plausible floor, typically from a short to ground, a lost reference voltage or a failed sensor. GM sets it on the Volt (2011 HPC2/VICM and 2016 VICM) once the signal falls under 5 % of reference, about 0.25 V, in 40 of 50 samples at 100 ms; it is Type B, so the lamp comes on after two trips. Subaru issued a service manual correction for P26A6 (09-132-25: Forester from 2019, Outback/Legacy from 2020, Impreza/Crosstrek from 2021) telling technicians to skip the first diagnostic step. On 2022–2023 Ram 1500 trucks with the 3.6 L V6, bulletin 07-005-24 links P26A6 to a cracked gear and swaps the three-way coolant valve, a job of about 0.7 h.
c: Feedback wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Open 5 V reference supply to the sensor
Internal sensor failure, e.g. after coolant intrusion
s: Check engine light
Delayed warm-up or reduced heater output
Valve position shown at or near zero on the scan tool

P26A7.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Circuit High
P26A7.d: The counterpart to P26A6: the feedback from valve A reads too high. GM's 2016 Volt table counts both a signal above its window and a broken signal circuit here, because an interrupted wire lets the input float toward the reference. The limit is 95 % of the reference (4.75 V), checked as 40 failures in 50 samples at 100 ms, Type B. The 2011 Volt table uses the same 95 % rule but prints the voltage as 4.25 V. Subaru's correction bulletin 09-132-25 also covers P26A7 for its boxer engines and again drops the first step of the published test. Subaru's earlier bulletin 09-80-21 replaced the thermo control valve with a better sealed sensor section. Check for a broken signal or ground wire and for a short to the 5 V supply before condemning the valve.
c: Open feedback or sensor ground wire
Feedback wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Defective sensor in the valve housing
s: Check engine light
Scan tool shows valve position at maximum
Engine slow to reach operating temperature

P26A8.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P26A8.d: P26A8 targets a feedback signal that jumps or drops out briefly instead of staying wrong. No manufacturer publishes a definition for this exact code. The closest documented logic is in GM's 2011 Volt table, where under P26A9 the controller flags a reading that changes by more than 6 % between samples ten steps apart (8 of 10 or 80 of 100 samples) although no movement was commanded. Subaru's bulletin 09-80-21 lists P26A-series codes as consequences of moisture reaching the sensor of the thermo control valve on 2019–2021 models. CARB asks for rationality checks on inputs that affect emissions. In practice a loose terminal, a cracked solder joint or a worn sensor track causes it, often only with vibration or heat.
c: Loose or spread terminal in the valve connector
Worn or contaminated sensor track giving dropouts
Harness rubbing on engine parts and shorting intermittently
s: Check engine light that may come and go
Erratic heater output or engine temperature
Code returns after clearing, often on rough roads

P26A9.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Stop/Minimum Stop Performance
P26A9.d: The title refers to the learned end stop of valve A. GM's use of P26A9 shifted over time. On the 2011 Volt it covered feedback sitting in a forbidden zone (5–30 % or 70–95 %), sudden jumps above 6 % and slow drift above 3 %, all Type B. In the 2016 Volt table the VICM uses it when the valve misses its commanded position within 15 s, retries the end-position learn up to three times with 10 s each, and still fails; coolant must be above 58 °C, and GM notes that an open drive circuit also spoils the learn. The 2016 ELR section treats a failed end-position learn above 50 °C the same way. Subaru's 09-80-21 includes the P26A series. A sticking valve, deposits in the housing or a valve fitted without a relearn are typical causes.
c: Valve rotor sticking from deposits or contaminated coolant
End position not relearned after valve or module replacement
Open motor drive circuit preventing the learn routine
Drifting position sensor misreporting the stop
s: Check engine light after two drives
Engine overheats or stays too cool depending on stuck position
Weak or uneven cabin heat

P26AA.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Maximum Stop Performance
P26AA.d: P26AA is the upper-limit partner of P26A9: the controller cannot confirm or learn the maximum end stop of valve A, or the reported value at full travel lies outside the expected window. No manufacturer publishes criteria for this code. GM's Volt logic for P26A9 shows how such checks work: the valve is driven to an end, given a fixed time to arrive and relearned several times before a fault is stored. Subaru's bulletin 09-80-21 names the P26A family in general for sensor corrosion on its thermo control valve. CARB expects the OBD system to notice when such an output ignores its commands, wherever a test of its response is feasible. Likely causes are mechanical binding near full open, a damaged stop, or a sensor that saturates early.
c: Valve binding before reaching its maximum position
Worn or broken mechanical end stop or gear
Position sensor out of calibration near its upper end
s: Check engine light
Reduced cooling under high load
Heater or engine temperature not as expected

P26AB.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Stuck/Open
P26AB.d: P26AB is stored when valve A stays open although it was told to close. Ford's hybrid summaries (2014–2019) define the valve as the switch between a combined loop, with engine coolant through the heater core, and an isolated loop heated by a PTC heater; if the second coolant sensor reads more than 5 °F above the engine sensor within 60 s of a circuit fault, the valve is judged stuck in the combined loop, and P2682 must set first. On 2016–2017 smart fortwo cars a corroding vacuum change-over valve keeps the heater shut-off valve open, so Mercedes-Benz extended its warranty to 10 years. Ram 1500 trucks of 2013–2015 (3.6, 4.7 and 5.7 L) and 3.0 L diesels received PCM flashes that list P26AB.
c: Valve jammed open by deposits, wear or a broken drive part
Engine control software misjudging valve state (Ram flashes)
Drive circuit fault leaving the valve in its open default
s: Check engine light
Engine takes long to warm up, higher fuel use when cold
Heater works with engine off only poorly (hybrids)

P26AC.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Circuit/Open
P26AC.d: Which valve carries the letter B depends on the maker. Ford names it in its gasoline OBD summaries for 2020–2023 and 2024–2025: valve B is the active transmission cooling valve, which sends engine coolant to the automatic transmission oil cooler, while valve A heats the transmission. P26AC is set when the smart driver in the PCM reports a fault on that output for 5 s; in 2024 Ford also files it under the extended code P26AC_13 for an open circuit. CARB lets makers combine open, low and high faults of an output into one code, which is why P26AC is often the only electrical code used. With the valve unpowered, transmission oil may run hotter or colder than intended.
c: Broken wire or unplugged connector at valve B
Open solenoid or motor winding in the valve
Faulty output driver in the PCM
s: Check engine light
Transmission fluid temperature higher than normal when towing
Usually no change in normal driving

P26AD.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Circuit Low
P26AD.d: P26AD indicates a drive line of valve B pulled to ground. GM uses the code differently from the title: on the second-generation Volt (2016 table, VICM) the single coolant bypass valve has an H-bridge motor with two drive lines, and P26AD stands for driver 2 reporting a short to low while the valve is commanded toward the high position. Four failures in five samples at 100 ms set it as Type B; it is one of the codes that blocks P26A5, P26A9 and P15C5. Ford's 2014 gasoline list and its 2020–2025 summaries do not use P26AD. CARB requires output circuit faults to be detected but does not demand separate codes for each fault type. Expect a chafed wire to ground or a shorted motor winding.
c: Drive wire chafed and shorted to ground
Coolant or water in the connector creating a leak path
s: Check engine light after two drives (GM)
Valve no longer moves, heating or warm-up affected

P26AE.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Circuit High
P26AE.d: With P26AE the valve B drive output sees voltage where it expects none, typically a short to battery. GM's 2016 Volt table again applies it to the second drive line of the one bypass valve: the VICM sets it when driver 2 flags a short to high while the valve is stopped or commanded low, after 16 failures in 20 samples at 100 ms, Type B. Ford's 2024–2025 gasoline summary lists P26AE as the short-to-battery case of the active transmission cooling valve, also filed as P26AC_12, detected when the smart driver reports a fault for 5 s. A pinched harness touching a supply wire or an internally shorted valve motor are the main causes; drivers often protect themselves by switching off, so the valve stops moving.
c: Drive wire shorted to a battery-voltage wire
Internally shorted valve motor or solenoid drawing excess current
Damaged output stage in the control module
s: Check engine light
Valve stays in its last position
Transmission or cabin temperature control off target

P26AF.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B Stuck/Open
P26AF.d: P26AF is the functional fault for valve B remaining open against its command. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; Ford, for instance, monitors its valve B (transmission cooling) only electrically through P26AC/P26AE. How an open-stuck check can work is shown by Ford's hybrid logic for P26AB on valve A, which compares two coolant temperatures for 60 s after the valve should have changed state. CARB requires output components to be checked for proper functional response where feasible. A valve stuck open on an auxiliary coolant path wastes heat during warm-up, so the engine or transmission takes longer to reach temperature; causes include deposits, a broken return spring or gear, or a seized actuator.
c: Valve held open by deposits or debris
Seized actuator or broken drive gear
Coolant temperature sensor bias misleading the check
s: Check engine light
Longer warm-up, higher fuel use on short trips
Lower cabin heat in cold weather

P26B0.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B Range/Performance
P26B0.d: P26B0 covers a valve B that is electrically sound but does not perform: it moves too slowly, stops short of its target or reports a position that does not match the command. No manufacturer publishes criteria for P26B0. The closest public example is GM's logic for the valve A counterpart P26A3 on the 2011 Volt, Type B, which fails the valve when an end-position learn above 50 °C coolant fails or the commanded position is not reached within 15 s. Ford, which defines valve B as its transmission cooling valve, lists only circuit codes for it. Under CARB, an output that can affect emissions needs a functional check where feasible. Sluggish valves from contaminated coolant, worn gears or a weak motor are the expected causes.
c: Valve moving slowly due to contaminated or wrong coolant
Worn gear train or weak valve motor
Low supply voltage or high resistance in the drive circuit
s: Check engine light
Engine or transmission temperature outside its normal band

P26B1.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A Stuck Closed
P26B1.d: P26B1 reports that valve A does not open when it should. The best documented user is the Volkswagen group plug-in hybrids. Porsche stores P26B100 in the thermal management unit (TME) of the 2019–2022 Cayenne E-Hybrid and the 2019–2021 Panamera E-Hybrid for the valve that admits engine coolant to the heating circuit once the engine passes 40 °C. The TME infers its state from the gap between two coolant temperatures, with 7 °C as the limit, and certain conditions caused false entries; bulletins 116/22 and 193/22 reprogram the TME. Bentley found the same code on 2022 Flying Spur Hybrids (N91 valve) and also fixes it by software. A real fault leaves the heating circuit without engine heat and can affect warm-up strategy.
c: Thermal management software misjudging the valve (Porsche, Bentley)
Valve seized closed by deposits or a failed actuator
Swapped or kinked coolant lines after repair
Drifting coolant temperature sensor used for the check
s: Check engine light, sometimes only intermittent
Cabin heat relies on the electric heater longer than usual
Possible rise in engine temperature under load

P26B2.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B Stuck Closed
P26B2.d: P26B2 is the closed-stuck counterpart for valve B: the controller expects coolant to flow through the valve but sees no sign of it. No manufacturer documents P26B2 in public sources. Porsche's handling of the valve A code P26B1 on its E-Hybrids illustrates the method: the thermal management unit judges the valve from the temperature difference between two coolant sensors, so a borderline reading can trip the code even with a healthy valve. CARB requires a functional check of such outputs where feasible. If valve B serves an auxiliary circuit such as a transmission oil cooler, as at Ford, a closed valve can let that component run hot; possible causes are a seized valve, a failed actuator, a blocked line or calibration issues.
c: Valve seized in the closed position
Failed actuator motor or broken coupling
Blocked or kinked coolant line downstream of the valve
s: Check engine light
Rising temperature of the component served by the valve
Possible temperature warning under heavy load

P26B3.t: Fuel Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
P26B3.d: Fuel shut-off valves are electrically opened valves that isolate a gaseous or liquefied fuel, as on CNG or propane systems. P26B3 says valve A does not achieve its intended effect although it was commanded. Roush CleanTech documents it for its fourth-generation propane system on Ford E- and F-Series trucks (2016–2018), where it shares a check with P009E: at key-up the PCM reads rail pressure to see whether the rail was bled, and pressure still present at that point sets the code. Roush names a leaking check valve or a leaking supply solenoid in the rail pressure module, a clogged bleed restrictor or a kinked EVAP line. Its MIL status differs by vehicle. The result can be hard starting. P0005 is the electrical open on valve A; P26B4 is the stuck-on case.
c: Leaking check valve or supply solenoid in the rail pressure module
Clogged bleed restrictor or kinked EVAP line
Shut-off valve A not switching as commanded
Blown fuse in the valve supply
s: Hard starting after the vehicle has been parked
Check engine light on some vehicles
Possible fuel odour

P26B4.t: Fuel Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit Stuck On
P26B4.d: P26B4 is the opposite failure to P26B3: shut-off valve A stays open or energised when the module wants it closed. No manufacturer documents P26B4 in public sources. On the Roush propane system for Ford trucks, valve A is the tank solenoid (its open-circuit code is P0005), and GM's 2015 Impala Bi-Fuel uses two normally closed CNG cut-off valves that the ECM opens only in gas mode while the engine cranks or runs. A valve that cannot close defeats that safety function, so fuel may keep flowing into the lines after shut-off. Typical causes are a short to voltage on the control wire, a stuck driver or relay, or a mechanically jammed valve. CARB requires output monitoring. Have it fixed promptly; close the manual tank valve if fuel can be smelled.
c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Supply relay or driver stuck on
s: Check engine light
Fuel odour after shut-off
Fuel pressure remains in the lines with the engine off

P26B5.t: Fuel Shutoff Valve B Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
P26B5.d: With P26B5 shut-off valve B fails to open or pass fuel when commanded. Roush CleanTech documents the code for its Gen 4 propane system on 2016–2018 Ford trucks, where valve B is the supply solenoid in the module that regulates rail pressure (its circuit code there is P2665). Once a start is initiated, the system module checks how far rail pressure climbs; too small an increase stores P26B5. Listed causes include a tripped excess flow valve, a manual valve not fully open, a tank or supply solenoid that does not open, weak pumps, a blocked filter or kinked lines. The engine then cranks without starting or runs poorly, as the system cycles pumps and solenoids to build pressure. MIL status varies by model. P26B6 is the stuck-on case.
c: Supply or tank solenoid not opening
Manual valve partly closed or excess flow valve tripped
Weak fuel pumps, clogged filter or kinked lines
Blown fuse in the valve circuit
s: Engine cranks but does not start, or runs poorly
Long start sequence with pumps cycling repeatedly
Check engine light on some models

P26B6.t: Fuel Shutoff Valve B Control Circuit Stuck On
P26B6.d: P26B6 reports that shut-off valve B cannot be switched off: the control circuit or the valve remains in the on state after the module removes the command. No manufacturer documents P26B6 publicly. Where valve B is defined, it is a solenoid on the low-pressure side, for example the supply solenoid of the Roush propane rail pressure module (circuit code P2665) or, on GM's CNG Impala, one of two normally closed cut-off valves, the other sitting at the tank. Possible reasons are a control line shorted to power, a welded relay contact or a valve stuck open. Unlike P26B5, the engine usually still starts; the concern is that fuel is no longer sealed off when parked. CARB requires output components to be monitored. Repair soon and use the manual valve if gas is smelled.
c: Control line shorted to battery voltage
Welded relay contact keeping the valve powered
s: Check engine light
Fuel odour near the engine or regulator after shut-off

P26B7.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve C Control Circuit/Open
P26B7.d: P26B7 is the basic electrical test of the drive output for coolant bypass valve C, with an open load as its main case. The letter is not tied to one design. Ford defines valve C as the radiator bypass in the 2020–2023 and 2024–2025 editions of its gasoline OBD summary and logs P26B7 (in 2024 also as P26B7_13) once the PCM's smart driver reports an output fault, checked continuously over 5 s. Ford bulletin 16-0052 covers 2013 Escape 1.6L EcoBoost cars built up to 13 February 2013: replace the bypass valve, then reflash the PCM. GM powers its valve C through an H-bridge and stores the code after 4 s of open load within a 5 s window, Type B, in its 2019 L3B table and two 2025 tables. P26B8/P26B9 are the shorted cases. Warm-up and temperature control may suffer.
c: Failed actuator motor or coil inside bypass valve C
Unplugged, corroded or broken connector or drive wire
Engine harness chafed through near the valve
s: Check engine light
Engine warms up slowly or runs warmer than usual
Valve C stays in its default position

P26B8.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve C Control Circuit Low
P26B8.d: With P26B8 a drive line of valve C is pulled toward ground. The best public description comes from GM's 2025 ECM table 25OBDG04B for the six-cylinder diesel: valve C sits on an H-bridge, and the controller looks for a grounded line separately in the opening and the closing direction, each time only while the other direction is free of the same fault. The result is a Type B code, so the lamp normally lights on the second trip. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 lists P26B8 among many codes that a chafed engine harness can trigger on 2019–2021 trucks and SUVs with gasoline V6/V8, 2.7L turbo or 3.0L diesel engines. Ford has no separate low code here. A grounded line can stall the valve or blow the driver, leaving engine temperature less well controlled.
c: Drive wire chafed against the engine or body and shorted to ground
Internal short in the valve C motor
Water or coolant in the valve connector
s: Check engine light after two trips
Unstable or high coolant temperature
Further valve or harness codes stored at the same time

P26B9.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve C Control Circuit High
P26B9.d: P26B9 reports supply voltage where the valve C driver should see none, in practice a short to battery positive. Two makers document it. Ford's 2024–2025 gasoline summary pairs it with the open-circuit code as P26B9/P26B7_12: the smart driver for the radiator bypass valve flags the fault and the PCM stores it after 5 s of continuous monitoring. The 2020–2023 edition did not yet list a high code. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B watches both motor directions of the H-bridge for a line shorted to positive, Type B, and GM bulletin 21-NA-149 names P26B9 among the codes a chafed engine harness can cause. A shorted line may force the motor against an end stop or make the driver shut down, so cooling control is degraded until the wire is repaired.
c: Drive wire shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
Engine harness damaged by chafing or heat
Internal fault in the valve C actuator
s: Check engine light
Temperature gauge higher or more erratic than usual
Valve does not respond to scan tool commands

P26BA.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve C Stuck/Open
P26BA.d: P26BA is meant for a valve C that stays open although the controller wants it shut, while its circuit tests fine. No manufacturer documents this code in public sources. GM and Ford, which both use the letter C, cover their valve C functionally through other codes: GM's L3B and diesel tables treat a valve that misses its target angle as P26BB, and Ford watches its radiator bypass only electrically. How an open-stuck check can be built is shown by GM's block valve logic for P26C0, which needs a position error of at least 10° while the feedback still reports the open side. CARB requires a functional test of output components where feasible. If the valve hangs open, coolant flows when it should not, so warm-up is slow and the engine may stay below its target temperature.
c: Valve C jammed in the open position by wear or deposits
Dirty or mixed coolant hindering valve movement
Incorrectly learned end positions after a repair
s: Check engine light
Slow warm-up and lower temperature gauge reading
Weak cabin heating in cold weather

P26BB.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve C Range/Performance
P26BB.d: P26BB is GM's main functional code for its rotary coolant flow control valve. The ECM compares commanded and measured angle; a gap above 12° after the target has settled, or movement slower than calibrated, counts as a fault. In the 2019 L3B table this is Type A (4 of 5 s), in the 2025 diesel table Type B (8 of 10 s). Several GM bulletins concern it: 21-NA-256 (2019–2022 engines LSY, L3B, L3T) blames a break-in phase of the valve under about 2,000 miles and calls for a new valve only on repeat; 20-NA-100 (2.7L L3B pickups 2019–2020) and 22-NA-082 (3.0L diesel 2020–2022) prescribe new ECM software; PIE0697 gathered field data on the diesel with P2B60. A sluggish valve can let the engine run too warm or too cool.
c: New valve still in its break-in phase (GM, low mileage)
ECM calibration needing an update per GM bulletin
Valve or actuator sticking or worn
s: Check engine light
Coolant temperature higher or lower than normal
Code may disappear after further driving on a new valve

P26BC.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve C Stuck Closed
P26BC.d: P26BC covers a valve C that will not open on command even though its drive circuit is intact. Public criteria for this code are not available from any manufacturer. GM folds a valve C that fails to reach its target into the range/performance code P26BB, and Ford checks its radiator bypass valve C only for circuit faults. GM's stuck-closed logic for the block valve under P26C2 shows one way to detect it: a position error of at least 10° (5° in 2025) while the feedback stays below 50°. CARB asks for functional monitoring of outputs where feasible and for cooling system checks. This is the riskier direction: if valve C blocks flow to the radiator, heat cannot be shed, so watch the temperature gauge and stop before the engine overheats.
c: Valve C seized in the closed position
Actuator too weak to overcome friction or deposits
Low coolant level or trapped air distorting the temperature check
s: Check engine light
Rising engine temperature, possible overheat warning
Reduced engine power to protect the engine

P26BD.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve D Control Circuit/Open
P26BD.d: P26BD is the open-load or general circuit fault on the output that drives coolant bypass valve D. Ford is the documented user. Both editions of its gasoline OBD summary, 2020–2023 and 2024–2025, assign valve D to cabin heating, meaning the valve that routes engine coolant to the heater core, and set P26BD once the PCM's smart driver signals an output fault during continuous 5 s monitoring; the 2024 edition adds the extended form P26BD_13. Ford's 2014 code list for spark-ignition engines already names P26BD with the Circuit/Open wording. GM's public tables do not use P26BD. Because the valve mainly serves the heater, the usual effect is too little or uncontrolled cabin heat rather than an engine problem. P26BE and P26BF cover shorted lines.
c: Open coil or motor winding in valve D
Broken drive wire between PCM and valve
s: Check engine light
Weak or no cabin heat
Heater output that cannot be regulated

P26BE.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve D Control Circuit Low
P26BE.d: P26BE flags a drive circuit of valve D that reads too low, normally because the wiring or the valve itself is grounded. No manufacturer documents P26BE publicly. Ford, whose valve D is the cabin heating valve, reports only the general circuit code P26BD and, from 2024, the short-to-battery code P26BF. The closest documented logic belongs to valve C: GM's 2025 diesel table looks for grounded lines on that valve's H-bridge in each motor direction and grades it Type B. CARB requires output circuits to be monitored for circuit faults. A grounded line may keep a low-side driven valve energised or make the driver cut out. On a heater valve the result is mostly wrong cabin temperature, though a valve in the engine loop can also upset warm-up.
c: Moisture or corrosion in the connector
s: Check engine light
Cabin heat stuck at full or at minimum
Valve D does not react to commands

P26BF.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve D Control Circuit High
P26BF.d: P26BF stands for battery voltage on the valve D control line where the driver expects a switched or grounded level. Ford documents it in its 2024–2025 gasoline OBD summary: the cabin heating bypass valve is valve D, and a short to battery reported by the PCM's smart driver is stored as P26BF, internally also as P26BD_12, after continuous monitoring for 5 s. The 2020–2023 summary still listed only P26BD for this valve, so older Fords report the same fault under the general code. GM's public tables do not use P26BF. A short to positive can keep a low-side switched valve permanently on or trip the driver protection. Since this valve controls heater flow, expect heat that cannot be turned down or does not come at all.
c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Harness damaged near hot or moving engine parts
s: Check engine light
Heater stays hot or stays cold regardless of setting

P26C0.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve D Stuck/Open
P26C0.d: GM uses P26C0 for the block rotary valve, which controls coolant flow through the engine block between two mechanical end stops; its tables label it as the engine block coolant valve stuck open. The ECM counts a failure when requested and measured position differ by at least 10° while the raw feedback sits at 50° or more, i.e. on the open side. The 2019 L3B table grades it Type A, one trip; the 2025 table 25OBDG03B lowers the gap to 5° and grades it Type B. The check is suspended during the valve's calibration run and needs at least 11 V. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 lists P26C0 among codes caused by a chafed engine harness on 2019–2021 trucks. An open block valve lets the block stay cooler than intended, slowing warm-up.
c: Block valve jammed on the open side
Chafed engine harness disturbing drive or feedback (GM 21-NA-149)
Position feedback reporting a wrong angle
s: Check engine light
Longer warm-up, especially in cold weather
Higher fuel consumption on short trips

P26C1.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve D Range/Performance
P26C1.d: P26C1 means valve D works electrically but does not deliver the expected effect. Ford is the documented user, and on its plug-in hybrids valve D governs the cabin heating loop. Ford special service message 50325 and bulletin 22-2127 cover 2020–2022 Escape and 2021–2022 Corsair PHEVs that set P2183 for the second coolant temperature sensor, at times with an overheat warning; P26C1 can follow as a consequence. The root cause was a PCM soak timer that miscalculated how long the electric cabin heater had been off, so the fix is reprogramming several modules, starting with the PCM; checking coolant level and the ECT 2 connector came first. Ford's public summaries give no thresholds for P26C1. Diagnose P2183 before replacing the valve.
c: PCM software miscalculating heater soak time (Ford PHEV)
Contaminated connector of coolant temperature sensor 2
Valve D moving slowly or sticking
s: Check engine light
Engine overheat message in the cluster
P2183 stored at the same time

P26C2.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve D Stuck Closed
P26C2.d: P26C2 is the closed-side partner of P26C0, and GM again applies it to the block rotary valve of its engines. The test is the same comparison of commanded and actual angle, at least 10° apart in the 2019 L3B table (Type A, one trip) and 5° in the 2025 table 25OBDG03B (Type B), but here the raw feedback stays below 50°, so the valve is judged closed.
