The diagnostic is skipped while the end stops are being learned and when system voltage is under 11 V. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 includes P26C2 in its list of codes from a chafed engine harness. A block valve that stays shut stops coolant from circulating through the block, so local hot spots and engine overheating are the real risk; reduced power or a warning may follow.
c: Block valve seized on the closed side
Weak actuator motor unable to open the valve
s: Check engine light, immediately on GM 2019 L3B
Rising coolant temperature or overheat warning
Reduced engine power

P26C3.t: Internal Control Module Transmission Range Sensor Performance
P26C3.d: P26C3 comes from a second, independent checking layer inside the powertrain module: it recalculates the gear selector position (P-R-N-D) and logs a fault when it cannot confirm what the main signal path reports. Ford lists the code in its gasoline OBD summaries 2020–2024 as non-MIL; the 2024 edition splits it into sub-faults for range sensor A, range sensor B and the comparison of both. Ford special service message 47790 names P26C3 among the most frequent codes on 2013–2019 Fusion, MKZ and C-Max with the 2.0 L hybrid drive, caused by water or corrosion in several connectors. Faults in the sensor circuits themselves are covered by P0705, P2800 and P2805. Drivers usually notice a warning message or trouble selecting a gear.
c: Water ingress or corrosion in connectors of the range sensor or module wiring
Worn or misadjusted range sensor or selector giving inconsistent positions
Control module software fault, cured by a calibration update
s: Transmission or gear selector warning in the instrument cluster
Difficulty engaging a gear or leaving Park
Further codes such as P2800 or network faults stored at the same time

P26C4.t: Internal Control Module Clutch Pedal Performance
P26C4.d: On cars with a manual gearbox, the powertrain module reads the clutch pedal through its own sensors, and an independent monitoring path inside the module checks whether that reading is credible. P26C4 is set when this check rejects the pedal information. In Ford's gasoline OBD summaries for 2020–2024 it is a non-MIL code for manual transmissions; the 2024 issue breaks the check down into pedal sensor A, pedal sensor B and the cross-comparison of the two. The pedal state feeds the starter interlock, cruise control cut-off, stop/start and torque handling during gear changes, so these functions may be switched off. Pure circuit faults of the pedal sensors are reported as P08A7, P08B4 and P08B9; P26C4 points to readings that disagree or drop out intermittently.
c: Worn or misaligned clutch pedal sensor so that sensors A and B disagree
Loose or corroded pedal sensor connector or chafed wiring
Powertrain module software needing an update
s: Cruise control or stop/start not available
Engine cranks only reluctantly or not at all with the pedal pressed
Service warning without check engine lamp

P26C5.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve A Control Circuit/Open
P26C5.d: Exhaust flow control valve A is the electrically driven flap that switches the sound path or back pressure of the exhaust, mostly on sporty models with selectable exhaust modes. P26C5 means the output stage driving valve A finds the circuit open or otherwise unusable. In Ford's gasoline OBD summaries 2020–2024 a smart driver watches the output continuously and reports the fault after about five seconds; valve A belongs to bank 1 there, the second valve uses P2BF8 to P2BFA. Ford bulletins 21-2011 and 25-2146 (Mustang GT500, 2.3 L and 5.0 L) list it alongside a cluster notice that exhaust modes cannot be selected, traced to pinched wiring, a misaligned actuator bracket or a badly seated exhaust. Deutz names it for the exhaust flap of MD1 engines. The flap then stays where it last stopped.
c: Pinched, broken or unplugged actuator wiring near the exhaust
Misaligned actuator bracket or poorly seated exhaust straining the harness
Open winding or internal fault in the valve actuator
s: Exhaust mode selection not available message
Exhaust sound no longer changes between modes
Check engine lamp on some vehicles

P26C6.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve A Control Circuit Low
P26C6.d: P26C6 reports that the drive circuit of exhaust valve A sits at too low a voltage – typically because the wiring or the actuator has shorted to ground. Ford's 2024 OBD summary shows that the PCM handles it as failure type 11 of the valve A circuit check, which runs continuously and needs about five seconds; the gasoline summaries 2020–2024 carry a typo here and print P25C6 instead of P26C6 in the threshold table. Deutz lists the same code for its MD1 engines as a low voltage or short on the exhaust flap. Ford bulletin 22-2153 for the Mustang names P26C6 alongside other flap codes and a lit MIL, caused by an exhaust that was not seated correctly. With the circuit pulled low the flap can no longer be commanded; the sister codes P26C5 (open) and P26C7 (high) separate the other fault patterns.
c: Control wire chafed through against the body or exhaust and shorted to ground
Internal short in the flap actuator
Water or road salt in the actuator connector
s: Check engine lamp on
Exhaust mode cannot be changed
Flap stuck in one position, exhaust permanently quiet or loud

P26C7.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve A Control Circuit High
P26C7.d: P26C7 is the high-side counterpart: the control line of exhaust valve A carries more voltage than the driver expects, usually because the line touches battery positive or the actuator is damaged. In Ford's 2024 OBD summary it appears as failure type 12 of the valve A check, monitored all the time with a five-second window; the earlier summaries misprint it as P25C7 in their threshold list. Deutz's MD1 list uses it for an exhaust flap whose voltage is too high or shorted. Ford bulletin 25-2146 (Mustang 2018–2023 and Shelby GT500 2020–2022) groups P26C7 with the other flap codes, a lit warning lamp and a mode warning, and directs the technician to inspect the tailpipe actuator and its harness. Unlike P26C6, a high signal can also stem from a wire touching a powered circuit.
c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage or another powered circuit
Missing ground at the actuator pulling the line high
s: Check engine lamp on
Exhaust mode warning in the instrument cluster
No change in exhaust sound between modes

P26C8.t: Chassis Control Module 1 Requested MIL Illumination
P26C8.d: P26C8 is not a fault of the engine module itself. It is stored when a unit outside the powertrain, which the manufacturer designates chassis control module 1, has logged an emission-related code of its own and asks the engine module over the network to light the check engine lamp. GM lists it in the engine tables 18OBDG04 and in the hybrid tables 18OBDG01: the request message is watched continuously from three seconds after power-up, and the code is Type A but carries no lamp request of its own. GM preliminary information PIT6010 (Buick LaCrosse, Cadillac XT5 2017–2019) mentions P26C8 together with U135A after a transmission range control module was replaced and its software did not match. The real cause is found in the memory of chassis module 1, which has to be read first.
c: Emission-related fault stored in chassis control module 1
Replaced module with mismatched or missing software configuration
Low supply voltage or network disturbance during start-up
s: Check engine lamp on
Service transmission or chassis warning message
Additional codes stored in the chassis module

P26C9.t: Chassis Control Module 2 Requested MIL Illumination
P26C9.d: P26C9 is the message slot for a second chassis control module: if module 2 detects an emission-related fault, it can ask the engine module to switch on the check engine lamp, and the engine module records this request as P26C9. No manufacturer documents this code in public. The mechanism is known from its partner P26C8, which GM monitors in its 2018 engine and hybrid tables continuously from three seconds after power-up as Type A without its own lamp request. CARB's OBD rule requires that emission-relevant faults of other control units reach the driver through the MIL, which is why such forwarding codes exist. P26C9 says nothing about the actual defect – only reading the fault memory of chassis module 2 shows what lies behind it.
c: Emission-related fault stored in chassis control module 2
Incorrect configuration or software after module replacement
Low voltage or network fault corrupting the request message
s: Check engine lamp on
Codes stored in a chassis module in addition to the engine module

P26CA.d: Many engines replace the belt-driven water pump with an electric pump that has its own control electronics. P26CA flags a fault in the control connection to that pump. In the Ford 2.0 L hybrid system the pump is commanded over LIN and also has a backup run line wired to ignition; the PCM compares the state of this line reported by the pump with the real ignition state and sets P26CA after five seconds of mismatch. Toyota applies it to A25A engines (Camry, RAV4, Highlander, Sienna and Venza, 2020–2024) use the code with suffixes for a grounded or broken circuit and for a missing signal, in some cases with coolant leaking from the pump into its connector. Ford service messages 46857 and 47790 trace it to water in harness connectors. The pump may run on a fallback speed or stop.
c: Water or corrosion in the pump connector or harness connectors
Coolant leaking from the pump body into its electronics
Broken control or backup run wire between module and pump
s: Check engine lamp on
Rising coolant temperature or temperature warning
Coolant traces at the electric pump

P26CB.d: P26CB means the engine coolant pump does not deliver the expected work, typically because the impeller is blocked or turns too slowly. Ford's OBD summaries for hybrids let the pump's own electronics judge this from current and speed: too much current at too low a speed through four restart attempts is reported over LIN, and the PCM records P26CB after five seconds. Genesis campaign 916G (GV70 3.5 T, 2024–2025) replaces the electric pump of the water-cooled charge air cooler because a stuck impeller set P26CB. Jaguar Land Rover bulletin JLRTB02030NAS1 links it on Ingenium 2.0 L petrol engines to a switchable mechanical pump whose diverter shroud no longer moves, making the fans run at full speed. Toyota's A25A engines log it as speed stuck. Overheating protection may cut power.
c: Seized or obstructed impeller in the electric pump
Diverter shroud of a switchable mechanical pump not moving
Worn pump motor or bearing drawing excessive current
Engine module logic needing a software update
s: Check engine lamp on
Cooling fans running constantly at high speed
Rising engine temperature or reduced power

P26CC.t: Engine Coolant Pump Control Circuit Low
P26CC.d: P26CC reports that the circuit controlling the engine coolant pump stays at too low a voltage while the pump should be active. Honda uses the code on its two-motor hybrids and calls it a low voltage in the circuit of the electric pump: service bulletin 25-020 (Accord and CR-V Hybrid 2023–2024, Civic Hybrid 2025) explains that moisture in the pump relay can freeze at or below 0 °C, the relay then fails to switch, the MIL comes on and P26CC is stored as soon as the car is started cold. The fix is a revised relay, after checking the intake air temperature in the freeze frame. Under CARB's OBD rule, output components need a circuit check. Other causes are a short to ground or a missing supply. While the pump does not run, the engine warms up unevenly.
c: Moisture inside the pump relay freezing in cold weather
Pump control or supply wire shorted to ground
Blown fuse or poor supply to the relay
s: Check engine lamp on after a cold start
Poor cabin heating or rising engine temperature

P26CD.t: Engine Coolant Pump Control Circuit High
P26CD.d: P26CD is set when the control circuit of the engine coolant pump shows a higher voltage than the commanded state allows, for example while the driver is switched off. No manufacturer documents this code in public. CARB's OBD rule asks for output components to be monitored for circuit faults, and the same pump circuit is known from its low-side partner P26CC, which Honda documents on its hybrids in bulletin 25-020. Typical high faults are a control wire touching battery voltage, a relay whose contacts weld shut so the pump keeps running, or an open ground on the pump side. Depending on design the pump then runs permanently or cannot be regulated; the engine module usually stores the code at once and lights the MIL, while warm-up may take longer.
c: Pump control wire shorted to battery voltage
Open ground at the pump pulling the circuit high
s: Check engine lamp on
Pump running after the engine is switched off
Longer warm-up phase

P26CE.t: Engine Coolant Pump Overspeed/Air In System
P26CE.d: P26CE covers a pump that spins too fast for the current it draws – a sign that it is running dry or pumping air instead of coolant. Ford's hybrid OBD summaries spell out the check: the electronics in the pump report a dry-run state over LIN when speed exceeds 4,909 rpm while current stays too low, and the PCM sets the code after five seconds. Toyota lists P26CE with a 37 suffix among the A25A codes in Tech Tip T-TT-0714-22 for 2022–2023 hybrids and petrol models. Mercedes-Benz names it in information LI20.00-P-071399 for M256 engines built 07/2019 to 02/2020, together with a coolant temperature warning, and asks to check for leaks and trapped air. Unlike P26CB the pump is free to turn here, but coolant is missing around it, so the level should be checked first.
c: Low coolant level from a leak
Air pockets left after coolant service or pump replacement
Impeller loose or broken on the pump shaft
s: Coolant temperature warning in the cluster
Check engine lamp on
Gurgling noises or poor heater output

P26CF.t: Engine Coolant Pump Control Module System Voltage
P26CF.d: Smart coolant pumps carry their own electronics, which measure the supply voltage they receive. P26CF is the general code for that voltage when it is implausible but cannot be assigned to too low or too high. No manufacturer documents P26CF itself in public. Ford's hybrid OBD summaries show the principle with the sister codes P26D0 and P26D1: the pump module sends its electronics voltage over LIN, and the PCM compares it with its own battery reading. CARB requires electronic components that affect emissions to be checked for plausibility. A general system voltage fault usually points to a shared cause – loose grounds, a weak battery, charging problems or intermittent contact – rather than to the pump. The pump may reduce its output or stop.
c: Loose, corroded or intermittent pump supply or ground connection
Weak battery or charging system fault
Faulty voltage measurement in the pump electronics
s: Check engine lamp on
Other voltage-related codes stored at the same time

P26D0.t: Engine Coolant Pump Control Module System Voltage Low
P26D0.d: P26D0 means the electronics in the engine coolant pump see less voltage than they should. On Ford's 2.0 L hybrids (C-Max, Fusion, MKZ) the pump module reports its electronics voltage over LIN, the PCM compares it with the battery voltage it measures itself and sets the code when the gap reaches about four volts for five seconds. Ford special service message 46857 links P26D0 on 2017 C-Max built June to September 2017 to water in a jumper connector shared with the active grille shutter, together with P26CA and U019F; message 47790 extends the corrosion pattern to Fusion and MKZ up to 2019. A voltage drop usually sits in the feed or ground to the pump rather than in the battery as a whole. The pump may slow down, so coolant temperature should be watched.
c: Water or corrosion in a connector of the pump supply
High resistance in the pump ground or feed wire
Weak 12 V battery or low charging voltage
s: Check engine lamp on
Network codes such as U019F stored alongside
Rising engine temperature under load

P26D1.t: Engine Coolant Pump Control Module System Voltage High
P26D1.d: P26D1 is stored when the electronics of the engine coolant pump report a supply voltage clearly above the vehicle system voltage. Ford documents the check in its OBD summaries for hybrid and plug-in models: the pump module passes its measured electronics voltage on via the LIN link, and a reading more than about four volts above the battery voltage seen by the PCM for five seconds sets P26D1. The 2014 Boss 302S code list from Ford Performance also carries the code. A real overvoltage comes from a failing voltage regulator or a jump start with too high a voltage; more often the pump's own measurement drifts or the PCM reference is pulled low by a bad ground, so both sides need checking. The electronics may protect themselves by switching the pump off.
c: Faulty voltage regulator or overvoltage from jump starting
Poor PCM ground making the reference voltage look low
Voltage measurement drift inside the pump electronics
s: Check engine lamp on
Unusually bright lights or other overvoltage codes

P26D2.t: Engine Coolant Pump Control Module Over Temperature
P26D2.d: The electronics of a smart coolant pump also measure their own temperature. P26D2 is set when this value climbs too high: in Ford's hybrid OBD summaries the pump module reports the temperature over LIN and the PCM stores P26D2 once it passes 130 °C for five seconds. The electronics are cooled by the coolant flowing through the pump, so overheating usually means poor flow – a low coolant level, trapped air, a partly blocked impeller drawing excessive current, or very hot under-bonnet conditions. Ford also uses the over-temperature state as a reason to suspend its pump communication check. The code differs from P0217, which concerns the engine coolant itself. The pump may reduce power or shut down to protect itself, so engine temperature can rise quickly.
c: Low coolant level or air around the pump reducing cooling of its electronics
Stiff impeller or bearing making the motor draw high current
Internal fault in the pump electronics or temperature sensor
s: Check engine lamp on
Engine temperature rising or temperature warning
Reduced heater output

P26D3.t: Engine Coolant Pump Supply Voltage Circuit
P26D3.d: P26D3 concerns the power feed and ground of the engine coolant pump. On Ford's 2.0 L hybrids the pump module has no way of reporting a loss of these lines, since without power it goes quiet on the LIN bus. The PCM therefore draws a conclusion: if pump communication is lost (U019F) and the coolant has meanwhile warmed by more than 10 °C, it assumes the pump has stopped and sets P26D3 after five seconds; without the temperature rise only the communication code is stored. Ford's Boss 302S code list also contains P26D3. Typical causes are a blown fuse, a failed relay, a broken feed or a loose ground. As the pump does not run, the engine can overheat quickly, so the car should not be driven far.
c: Blown pump fuse or failed supply relay
Broken power feed or loose ground at the pump
Pump electronics dead so that the pump neither runs nor communicates
s: Check engine lamp on
Engine temperature climbing quickly
U019F stored at the same time

P26D4.t: Engine Coolant Pump Supply Voltage Circuit Low
P26D4.d: P26D4 narrows the supply fault of the engine coolant pump down to too low a voltage on its power feed. There is no public manufacturer documentation for this code. CARB's OBD rule requires circuit monitoring for electrical components, and Ford shows how the supply of a smart pump is judged with the general code P26D3: there the PCM infers a dead feed from lost pump communication plus a rising coolant temperature. A low reading, unlike a complete loss, typically comes from a corroded fuse holder or connector, a partially broken wire, a relay with burnt contacts or a short to ground that pulls the line down. The pump may then still run but slowly or with interruptions, so heating and engine temperature may become unsteady; the related P26D0 compares the pump's internal electronics voltage instead.
c: Corroded fuse holder or connector in the pump feed
Partial short to ground on the feed wire
s: Check engine lamp on
Fluctuating engine temperature or heater output

P26D5.t: Engine Coolant Pump Supply Voltage Circuit High
P26D5.d: P26D5 is set when the power feed of the engine coolant pump carries a higher voltage than the system allows. No manufacturer documents this code in public. It belongs to the same supply group as P26D3 and P26D4; Ford's hybrid OBD summaries explain the supply logic on the general code, and CARB requires electrical faults of monitored components to be detected. A high feed voltage can stem from an overcharging alternator or DC/DC converter, a jump start from a 24 V source, or a sensing line shorted to another powered circuit. In some designs a feed that stays live after shutdown, for example because of a stuck relay, is also judged as high. The pump electronics may switch off to protect themselves, and other modules often log overvoltage codes at the same time.
c: Supply relay stuck closed so the feed stays live
Feed or sensing wire shorted to another powered circuit
s: Check engine lamp on
Overvoltage codes in other control modules

P26D6.t: Engine Coolant Pump Clutch Control Circuit/Open
P26D6.d: Some engines drive their mechanical coolant pump through a switchable clutch: following a cold start the pump is left idle so the coolant stays still and the engine reaches temperature sooner, and once a target is met the clutch couples the pump to its drive again. P26D6 means the engine control module sees the control circuit of this clutch as open – typically a broken wire, a loose connector or a solenoid coil that has burnt through. No manufacturer documents this code in public. Ford's OBD summaries list clutched water pumps among the designs its thermostat monitor has to account for, and CARB demands an approved monitoring plan for any part other than the thermostat that regulates coolant temperature. Many clutches engage on loss of current, so the usual effect is slower warm-up rather than overheating.
c: Broken wire or corroded, loose connector in the clutch control circuit
Open solenoid coil in the coolant pump clutch
Blown fuse or missing supply to the clutch solenoid
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light on
Engine and cabin heater take longer to warm up
Coolant temperature behaves differently from normal after a cold start

P26D7.t: Engine Coolant Pump Clutch Performance/Stuck Off
P26D7.d: P26D7 is the serious case for a clutched coolant pump: the module has asked the clutch to couple the pump, but the cooling system shows no sign of circulation, so the pump is assumed to stay disconnected. The electrical side may be intact; worn friction faces, a seized armature or a pump that slips under load are typical mechanical reasons. No manufacturer documents P26D7 in public. A comparable failure is documented by Jaguar Land Rover bulletin JLRTB02030NAS1 for its switchable pump on Ingenium 2.0 L petrol engines, though under the general pump code P26CB: when the inner shroud did not move as commanded, the PCM ran the fans at full speed to protect the engine. Without coolant flow the cylinder head heats up locally, so the temperature gauge must be watched and the car should not be driven hard.
c: Worn or slipping clutch friction surfaces
Armature or switching mechanism seized in the disengaged position
Slipping or damaged pump drive belt
Implausible coolant temperature input or outdated engine software
s: Check engine light on
Coolant temperature rises quickly, possible overheating warning
Radiator fans run at high speed
Reduced engine power to protect the engine

P26D8.t: Engine Coolant Pump Clutch Stuck On
P26D8.d: With P26D8 the opposite of the warm-up strategy happens: the engine module wants the coolant pump decoupled after a cold start, but the pump keeps turning, so coolant circulates from the first second and the engine warms up as slowly as with a plain belt-driven pump. Behind this are usually a clutch that has welded or jammed shut, a return spring that no longer works or a control line that stays energised in designs where current disengages the pump. Public manufacturer documentation for P26D8 is lacking. CARB's OBD rule treats coolant-regulating parts other than the thermostat as subject to an approved monitoring plan, and a longer warm-up raises cold-start emissions and fuel use. Ford's thermostat monitor models warm-up time and must allow for clutched pumps, so P0128 may follow. Engine damage is not expected.
c: Clutch mechanically jammed or welded in the engaged position
Weak return spring or demagnetised holding magnet
No current at the solenoid in designs that need current to disengage
s: Check engine light on
Slow warm-up, heater gets warm late
Slightly higher fuel consumption on short trips

P26D9.t: Engine Coolant Pump Clutch Control Circuit Low
P26D9.d: P26D9 narrows the electrical fault of the coolant pump clutch down to a control line that sits too close to ground. The output stage in the engine module notices that the voltage on the line stays low when it should be high, which almost always points to a chafed wire touching the engine block or body, a coil with shorted turns, or water in a connector near the pump. There is no published manufacturer description of P26D9. CARB's rule asks for circuit checks on electronic components that influence coolant temperature control, and Ford names clutched water pumps as one such design. Because the solenoid can no longer be switched, the clutch remains in whatever state its springs or magnets give it without current; the driver mostly notices a lit MIL and a changed warm-up, while the short may also blow a shared fuse.
c: Chafed control wire shorted to ground
Moisture or coolant in the connector at the pump
s: Check engine light on
Changed warm-up behaviour of the engine
Possibly a blown fuse with further faults on the same circuit

P26DA.t: Engine Coolant Pump Clutch Control Circuit High
P26DA.d: P26DA is the high-side counterpart of P26D9: the control line of the coolant pump clutch shows more voltage than the commanded state permits, for instance while the driver should be pulling it low or while it is switched off. Typical causes are a wire rubbing against a live circuit, a missing ground at the clutch so the line floats up, or an open coil that the driver reads as high. None of the carmakers explains P26DA in public sources. CARB requires circuit monitoring for electronic parts that regulate engine coolant temperature, and Ford's OBD summaries confirm that clutched pumps are used on some applications. If the line is held at supply voltage the clutch may be stuck in one state; unlike P26D9 a fuse rarely blows. The MIL comes on and warm-up or cooling behaviour can change.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
Open ground or poor ground contact at the clutch solenoid
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light on
Pump clutch does not switch, warm-up or cooling behaves differently

P26DB.d: Some sporty cars shape the sound reaching the cabin or the tailpipe with an electrically driven part, such as a switchable flap in the silencer or a valve in an intake sound pipe. Circuit A is the first of up to two such actuators. P26DB flags an interrupted drive circuit: the module switches the output but sees no load, typically a cut wire, an unplugged connector or a burnt actuator coil. No manufacturer documents P26DB publicly with thresholds. Nissan links the sibling P26DE to the electric valve on the main muffler of the GT-R, and Ford checks comparable exhaust valve drivers for open circuits within 5 seconds. CARB requires checks of such outputs when they can influence emissions. The car still drives normally; the sound effect simply stays off.
c: Actuator connector unplugged or not fully seated, often after exhaust or intake work
Broken wire near the hot exhaust or at a moving section of the harness
Internal open circuit in the sound valve or actuator
Sound component removed or replaced by an aftermarket part without electrical equivalent
s: Check engine light, depending on the manufacturer
Sport sound or valve opening no longer noticeable
Driving behaviour otherwise unchanged

P26DC.t: Engine Sound Control A Circuit Low
P26DC.d: P26DC reports that the control line of sound actuator A sits at too low a voltage, which points to the wire or the actuator being grounded rather than interrupted. Depending on the design, the driver stage then cannot switch the flap or valve, or switches it permanently because the ground path bypasses it. Ford lists this code in its 2014 powertrain code interpretation with a check engine lamp marking but gives no thresholds; elsewhere no maker publishes details. Typical spots are insulation chafed through on the exhaust, a crushed harness under the car or water inside the actuator plug. Compared with P26DB (open) and P26DD (high), the repair here usually means tracing a bare conductor touching metal.
c: Control wire chafed through and touching body or exhaust metal
Moisture or corrosion in the actuator connector
Shorted winding inside the sound actuator
Faulty output stage in the controlling module
s: Check engine light
Exhaust or intake sound does not change between driving modes
Possibly a blown fuse for the actuator circuit

P26DD.t: Engine Sound Control A Circuit High
P26DD.d: With P26DD the module measures a voltage on the drive line of sound actuator A that is higher than the switching state allows. The usual reason is contact with a live conductor, for instance a neighbouring supply wire in a melted harness, or an internal fault in the actuator that feeds battery voltage back. The flap or valve may then stay energised regardless of the selected mode. Ford's 2014 code interpretation for its engine controllers carries P26DD with the lamp marking, without stating limits, and no other maker documents it. P26DB stands for an open circuit and P26DC for a grounded line, so here the search centres on harness sections where the drive wire runs alongside a supply line.
c: Drive wire shorted to a supply wire, often where heat has damaged the harness
Internal fault in the actuator feeding voltage back into the drive line
Incorrect or aftermarket actuator with different electrical layout
Output stage of the controlling module defective
s: Check engine light
Valve stays in one position, sound permanently loud or quiet

P26DE.t: Engine Sound Control A Circuit Performance
P26DE.d: Unlike the pure wiring codes, P26DE means the circuit of sound actuator A is electrically intact but the part does not behave as commanded, for example a flap that sticks, moves too slowly or reports an implausible position. The best documented case is Nissan's GT-R: bulletin NTB19-036, last amended in 2023 for model years 2017 to 2020, sets the check engine lamp with P26DE and names the electric control valve on the main muffler. The fix is either new engine software or replacing that valve on its own rather than the whole muffler. Ford's 2014 code list also carries P26DE with the lamp marking. Soot, corrosion and frozen moisture are typical reasons a flap binds. P26DB to P26DD cover open, low and high faults.
c: Exhaust sound valve sticking or worn
Engine software with too strict an evaluation, update available from the maker
Flap linkage blocked by deposits, ice or damage
Weak actuator motor or faulty position feedback
s: Check engine light
Exhaust note no longer changes, or changes late
Rattling or buzzing from the silencer area

P26DF.d: Sensor power supplies A to D are separate outputs of a control module that feed groups of sensors; they are a different family from the 5 V sensor reference voltages (P0641 and following). D is the fourth such output. P26DF is the general or open-circuit code for it. Deutz uses it in its EMR5/MD1 engine controllers for ECU sensor supply voltage 4 (SPN 3512), with fault types for special instructions and for an unknown root cause, but publishes no thresholds. Other makers do not document P26DF in public. If supply D drops out, every sensor fed by it reports implausible values at the same moment, so a cluster of unrelated sensor codes is the typical picture. Low and high faults of the same output are P26E0 and P26E1.
c: Broken supply wire or splice to the sensors on output D
Loose or corroded pin at the control module or a sensor
Supply output D inside the control module failed
s: Check engine light
Several sensor codes stored together
Reduced power or emergency mode depending on the sensors affected

P26E0.t: Sensor Power Supply D Circuit Low
P26E0.d: P26E0 means the fourth sensor supply output of the control module is pulled below its normal level. Deutz documents it for the fourth ECU sensor supply, SPN 3512, in two variants: excessive current or a grounded circuit (FMI 6), and a reading below the physical limit with top severity (FMI 1). In practice a single sensor with an internal short, or a chafed supply wire touching ground, loads the output so much that the module limits or switches it off. All other sensors on the same rail then lose their feed too. A good strategy is to unplug the sensors on supply D one by one and watch whether the voltage recovers. No other maker publishes the code; CARB requires such supplies to be monitored when emission-related sensors depend on them.
c: One sensor on supply D with an internal short pulling the output down
Supply wire chafed and touching engine ground
Moisture in a sensor plug bridging supply and ground
s: Check engine light
Group of sensor faults appearing at once
Engine derate or emergency mode

P26E1.t: Sensor Power Supply D Circuit High
P26E1.d: With P26E1 the fourth sensor supply of the control module reads higher than its regulated value. Deutz assigns it to SPN 3512 with FMI 0, meaning a reading beyond the upper physical limit, rated as most severe. Since the module regulates this output itself, an excessive reading normally comes from outside: a wire of supply D shorted to battery voltage or to another, higher supply, or a sensor feeding voltage back. Raised supply shifts every signal of the sensors connected to it and can damage them, so the module usually reacts strongly. Fewer real-world cases arise than for P26E0, but checking the harness for melted sections near hot or moving parts is the first step. Open circuits on the same output fall under P26DF.
c: Supply D wire shorted to battery voltage or a higher supply
Faulty sensor feeding voltage back into the supply rail
Regulator for supply D in the control module defective
s: Check engine light
Implausible readings from several sensors
Possible derate depending on the sensors involved

P26E2.t: Fuel Mode Indicator Lamp Control Circuit Low
P26E2.d: Bi-fuel vehicles show the active fuel with an indicator, often a lamp in the selector switch. GM's 2015 Impala bi-fuel lights it while running on CNG and flashes it during a fuel change; GM's 2016 CNG pickups also flash it fast to signal a gas system fault, and Ford's earlier bi-fuel trucks combined the ALT/GAS selector with its lamp in one assembly. P26E2 means the controlling module reads the lamp control circuit as too low. Where the module switches the lamp on the positive side, that typically points to a short to ground in the wire or the lamp; with a ground-side driver the same reading can mean an open path. No manufacturer documents P26E2 publicly. The fuel change itself still works, but the driver may see a lamp that is dark or always lit and loses the fault warning. P2668 is the general circuit fault.
c: Lamp control wire chafed to ground
Shorted LED or bulb in the fuel selector switch
Faulty lamp output in the controlling module
s: Fuel mode lamp dark or permanently lit
No visible warning when the gas system has a fault

P26E3.t: Fuel Mode Indicator Lamp Control Circuit High
P26E3.d: P26E3 is the opposite case of P26E2: the module that drives the fuel mode lamp sees a voltage on its control line that is higher than its commanded state allows. With a ground-side driver this is usually a short to a 12 V feed, or an open lamp that lets the line float to supply level; with a positive-side driver it points to outside voltage reaching the output. Many output stages switch off to protect themselves once they detect such a fault. The lamp matters on bi-fuel vehicles because it is the driver's only cue to the active fuel: on GM's 2016 Silverado and Sierra CNG it flashes once a second during a changeover and around ten times a second if the gas system has failed. No manufacturer documents P26E3 publicly, and a lamp circuit fault does not alter the exhaust emissions.
c: Lamp control wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Burnt-out bulb or open LED in the selector switch
Damaged or wet connector at the selector switch
s: Fuel mode lamp stays dark
Driver cannot tell which fuel is in use

P26E4.d: Stop-start systems often use a second starter relay, and P26E4 is the general circuit fault of this relay B. On GM's 12 V stop-start engines it switches the pinion of a tandem starter: the module's high-side driver flags an open circuit when, at standstill with at least 11 V, more than 200 kOhm appear toward ground in 40 of 50 samples (50 ms each); type B, so the lamp lights after two trips. FCA engines name it Starter Control 2. Jeep Compass bulletins 2019 to 2023 pair P26E4 with P0615 as a plausibility fault and failed restarts from stop-start, solved by new PCM or BCM software, and an Alfa Romeo Stelvio TCM update lists it as Starter Relay B Circuit. Low and high faults have separate codes, P26E5 and P26E6.
c: Open wire or loose terminal between module and relay B or pinion solenoid
Control module software misjudging the circuit, update available on some FCA models
Open coil in relay B or in the tandem starter pinion solenoid
Faulty high-side driver in the engine module
s: Check engine light
Engine does not restart from an automatic stop
Stop-start function disabled, occasional no-crank

P26E5.d: P26E5 indicates that the control circuit of starter relay B is shorted against ground. GM documents it for the tandem starter pinion relay of its 12 V stop-start engines: while the driver is switched on, an impedance of 0.5 Ohm or less toward ground in 8 of 10 samples of 50 ms sets the code, enabled at standstill once run/crank voltage is at least 6.41 V; the lamp follows as type B after two trips. The same entries appear in GM's 2019 tables for the 5.3 litre V8 and in 2023 tables. A GM preliminary information for 2019 to 2021 Silverado and Sierra 1500 with the 2.7 litre engine lists P26E5 among many codes caused by a shorting engine harness and blown fuses. Open and high-voltage faults are P26E4 and P26E6.
c: Engine harness chafed so the relay B control wire touches ground
Shorted coil in relay B or the pinion solenoid
Damaged high-side driver in the engine module
s: Check engine light
No crank or no restart after an automatic engine stop
Blown fuses and further unrelated codes if a harness short is the cause

P26E6.d: P26E6 reports a short to positive on the control line of starter relay B. GM tests for it while its driver for the tandem starter pinion relay is off: if the line still shows 0.5 Ohm or less toward a power source for 40 out of 50 checks taken every 50 ms, with the engine stopped and at least 11 V available, the code is stored as type B. The danger of this fault is a relay that is energised without a command, so the pinion could be pushed into the ring gear. The diagnostic appears in GM's 2018 and 2023 tables with the same thresholds. P26E4 and P26E5 cover open and grounded circuits.
c: Relay B control wire shorted to a battery-powered wire, e.g. under the battery tray
Relay B internally fed or contacts welded
Engine module driver output not switching off
s: Check engine light
Stop-start disabled
Starter noise or grinding without a start command

P26E7.d: Supply D is the fourth switched rail with which a control module powers a group of solenoids or other loads, after A (P0657), B (P2669) and C (P2684). P26E7 reports an open load on it. GM's 2023 and 2024 TCM tables assign the code to high-side output 8 and run the check only while the module shuts down: once the output is off and a low-side output on the same load is switched on, the load should pull the line down. If more than 40 % of battery voltage remains, the module keeps the finding in permanent memory and raises the code once it restarts, Type A. Ford's 2024 summary lists P26E7 as the open-load fault of high side driver 8 in the TR9070 dual-clutch gearbox. Everything fed from that rail is without power, so a substitute gear or limp mode is to be expected.
c: Broken wire or loose, corroded connector between the module output and the loads on supply D
Open coil in a solenoid powered from this rail
Internal fault in the high-side output of the transmission control module
s: Check engine or transmission warning light on
Transmission stays in a substitute gear or limp mode
Several solenoid or clutch codes stored at the same time

P26E8.t: Actuator Supply Voltage D Circuit Low
P26E8.d: P26E8 says the voltage on supply rail D drops too far while the rail is switched on. In GM's 2023 and 2024 TCM tables this is watched continuously at high-side output 8: a timer runs when the voltage falls below a share of the supply or the averaged current is too high, and after 60 ms the code is set, Type A; it is suspended while P0882 or P0883 is present. Ford's 2024 table lists P26E8 as the shorted-load fault of driver 8 in the TR9070 dual-clutch unit. On Volvo and Mack trucks of the US13 generation the aftertreatment module uses this rail to feed both NOx sensors upstream and downstream of the SCR, the particulate sensor plus the DEF quality sender; bulletins K31280406 and KC-415 describe brief dips when all four draw peak power, with communication codes for these sensors and a possible derate warning.
c: Supply line or a connected load shorted to ground
Loose or corroded battery, fuse or ground connections feeding the module, or weak batteries (Volvo/Mack aftertreatment module)
Faulty sensor or solenoid on the rail drawing too much current
Internal fault in the module output stage
s: Warning light on, often only briefly or intermittently
Transmission failsafe mode with loss of the solenoids on that rail
On trucks, lost communication with NOx, PM and DEF sensors and a derate warning

P26E9.t: Actuator Supply Voltage D Circuit High
P26E9.d: The high fault of rail D is about voltage where none should be: the controller has turned supply D off, yet the line stays live. Either the high-side switch inside the module no longer opens or an outside wire touches battery positive. GM's 2023 and 2024 TCM tables check this for output 8 during shutdown; if the line holds more than 70 % of battery voltage with the output disabled, a shorted switch is noted in permanent memory and reported once the module wakes up again. Battery voltage must stay between 8.75 and 18 V and change by less than 1.5 V during the test, and GM rates the code Type B, so two failing trips light the lamp. Ford's 2024 summary names P26E9 as the shorted-switch fault of driver 8 in the TR9070. Because the loads can no longer be cut as a group, the module will normally fall back to a safe mode.
c: High-side switch in the control module stuck closed
Supply D wire chafed against a battery or ignition feed
Water or corrosion in the module connector creating a leakage path
s: Warning light on after two drive cycles
Transmission in limp mode or with restricted gears
Code appears after restarting rather than while driving

P26EA.d: Vehicles with a second fuel pump give it its own driver module, and P26EA means that module B has reported an internal fault of its own. Ford documents the code in its gasoline OBD summary for 2020 to 2023 and again in 2024 as an internal error reported by the driver module of pump B. Module B reports its state to the PCM as a duty cycle on a fuel pump monitor wire: about 20 % flags invalid control data, 30 % plus or minus 4 % flags the internal error, while 0 or 100 % means no feedback at all (U016C). The check runs continuously at 11 to 16 V battery voltage and needs 2 to 5 seconds. Roush CleanTech's propane systems for Ford E- and F-Series route the same signal through a relay module to the PCM; there the code is non-MIL on the E-450 but MIL on F-650 and F-53. Fuel delivery from pump B may be reduced.
c: Internal failure of fuel pump driver module B
Open or corroded fuel pump monitor wire between module B and the PCM or relay module
Poor power or ground at module B
Worn or seized fuel pump B overloading the module
s: Warning light on, depending on the vehicle calibration
Hesitation or power loss at high load
Hard starting or stalling if the second pump is needed

P26EB.t: Alternative Fuel Control Module System Voltage
P26EB.d: On bi-fuel engines a separate alternative fuel control module often runs the gas side. In Ford's bi-fuel CNG documentation of 2002 it contains drivers for both injector sets, switches the fuel relays, picks the active fuel from the selector switch and shuts the tank valve when gas pressure falls below 517 kPa. In Roush CleanTech's propane systems for Ford trucks a smart relay module takes on that role and talks to the PCM over CAN. P26EB says the supply voltage measured by or at this module is outside its permitted window, from a weak feed, a bad ground or a charging fault. No manufacturer documents P26EB publicly. CARB requires an approved monitoring plan for alternate-fuel vehicles. The vehicle will usually refuse or drop gas mode and continue on gasoline.
c: Loose, corroded or undersized power or ground connection at the gas control module
Faulty fuse, relay or feed circuit of the gas system
Weak battery or alternator voltage outside the normal range
Internal fault in the alternative fuel control module
s: Gas mode not available or vehicle switches back to gasoline
Fuel mode indicator flashes or shows a fault
Warning light on

P26EC.d: Where a vehicle has two sound actuators, for instance one flap per tailpipe side or a valve in addition to an intake sound tube, B designates the second one. P26EC is stored when its drive circuit is broken, so switching the output produces no current. No manufacturer documents P26EC or the rest of the B row in public; information exists only for circuit A, such as Nissan's GT-R muffler valve, and for related exhaust valve drivers that Ford checks for open circuits over 5 seconds. Which physical part is B therefore has to come from the wiring diagram of the specific car. CARB treats outputs like this as monitored components where emissions can be affected. Expect the second valve to stay inactive while the engine runs normally.
c: Connector of the second actuator loose or disconnected
Wire to actuator B broken, for example by heat or vibration
s: Check engine light, depending on the manufacturer
Sound changes only on one side or not at all

P26ED.t: Engine Sound Control B Circuit Low
P26ED.d: P26ED concerns the second sound actuator and indicates a drive line pulled toward ground. A conductor rubbed bare on the exhaust bracket, a pinched loom or corrosion bridging the pins of a wet plug are the classic culprits, along with a shorted coil inside the actuator. No maker publishes this code or its limits; the A counterpart P26DC appears in Ford's 2014 code list, which is the closest reference. Where the second flap sits on the other exhaust branch, its wiring often takes a different route under the car than circuit A, so the A side being healthy says little about B. In everyday use the sound feature loses part of its effect, while engine power is not affected.
c: Insulation of the actuator B wire worn through against metal
Corroded or wet connector at actuator B
s: Check engine light
Second flap does not respond, sound only partly changes

P26EE.t: Engine Sound Control B Circuit High
P26EE.d: For the second sound actuator, P26EE signals a drive circuit carrying more voltage than expected, i.e. a short to battery positive or a feed coming back from a damaged actuator. Because the line is then powered from elsewhere, flap B may hold its position no matter what the driver selects. P26EE is not published by any maker; for orientation there are only the A codes in Ford's 2014 list and the exhaust valve driver checks in Ford's later summaries, which report output faults through a smart driver. When diagnosing, compare the B line with the unswitched supply wires running beside it and test the actuator off the car. Engine behaviour and emissions in normal driving are generally unchanged.
c: Actuator B wire in contact with a positive supply wire
Damaged actuator B feeding voltage back
Faulty output stage for circuit B in the module
s: Check engine light
Second flap stuck in one position

P26EF.t: Engine Sound Control B Circuit Performance
P26EF.d: P26EF is the functional fault of the second sound actuator: wiring checks pass, yet flap or valve B does not reach or report the commanded state in time. No maker documents P26EF publicly. The A-side equivalent P26DE is well described for the Nissan GT-R, where the electric valve on the main muffler was the cause and could be renewed separately after a software check, and Ford monitors its exhaust valves for a stuck flap via the PWM feedback of a smart driver. Those cases suggest the same suspects for B: binding from soot or rust, a seized shaft after long periods in one position, or a worn actuator gearbox. Unlike P26EC to P26EE, measuring voltages rarely finds the fault; a visual and movement check of the flap does.
c: Flap B binding due to soot, rust or a seized shaft
Worn gearbox or weak motor in actuator B
Evaluation in the module software too sensitive
s: Check engine light
Sound of the second branch changes late or not at all
Rattle from the flap housing

P26F0.d: P26F0 says that starter relay A remains closed even though the module has withdrawn its command, so current keeps flowing to the starter or its solenoid. Unlike the circuit codes P0615 to P0617, the wiring may be intact; the problem lies in the switching itself, typically welded contacts or a sticking armature. Detection works by feedback, for instance a crank sense signal that should vanish once the relay is released. No manufacturer documents P26F0 publicly. Jeep bulletins show that FCA drives some starters through two separately monitored relays, Starter Control 1 and 2, and GM runs extensive driver checks on its starter relay A, which are the closest references. Left unattended, a relay stuck on can overheat the starter and wear pinion and ring gear.
c: Welded or sticking contacts in starter relay A
Relay A control circuit fed from elsewhere so the coil stays energised
Faulty crank feedback signal suggesting a closed relay
s: Starter keeps running or grinding after the engine has started
Check engine light, stop-start disabled
Burning smell or flat battery after short trips

P26F1.d: P26F1 is the opposite case to P26F0: the module commands starter relay A on, but the expected reaction never arrives, so the starter receives no power. Possible reasons are burnt or contaminated contacts, a coil that no longer pulls in, or a missing feed on the load side, for example a blown fuse or a loose battery cable at the relay. No maker documents P26F1 publicly. As reference points remain FCA, whose Jeep bulletins treat its two starter relays as separately monitored outputs and describe intermittent no-crank conditions, and GM, whose 2018 tables monitor the starter relay A driver. Because a dead relay looks like a dead starter, check whether the starter terminal receives voltage during cranking before replacing the motor.
c: Burnt or dirty contacts in starter relay A
Blown fuse or loose power cable on the load side of the relay
Relay coil no longer pulling in
Feedback wire to the module interrupted
s: Engine does not crank, or only after several attempts
Check engine light
No restart after an automatic stop

P26F2.d: P26F2 concerns the second starter relay, which on stop-start vehicles may engage the pinion of a tandem starter (GM) or form the second switching path of a two-relay layout (FCA Starter Control 2). The code means relay B fails to drop out after its command ends. Depending on wiring, the pinion may then remain in mesh, or the starter could be energised as soon as relay A closes. No manufacturer documents P26F2 publicly; the GM tables only cover the electrical driver faults of relay B (P26E4 to P26E6), and FCA bulletins tie Starter Control 2 to plausibility faults. Welded contacts and a control line fed from elsewhere are the obvious suspects. Driving on with this fault risks damage to the pinion and the flywheel ring gear.
c: Contacts of relay B welded or stuck
Control line of relay B fed from another circuit
Pinion solenoid of the tandem starter sticking mechanically
s: Grinding or whining from the starter after the engine runs
Check engine light, stop-start unavailable

P26F3.d: P26F3 reports that starter relay B does not switch through when commanded, so the start sequence that depends on it cannot complete. It is the one code of this group with a public manufacturer case: an FCA STAR case for the Jeep Gladiator, released in March 2022, describes a check engine light and a no-start with P26F3, P00FD and P0562 stored, caused by loose power cables at the power control relay; tightening them to specification was the repair. That points to a missing supply on the load side rather than a failed relay. Otherwise burnt relay contacts or a coil that no longer pulls in are typical. P26F2 covers the opposite case, a relay B that will not release, and P26E4 to P26E6 its control circuit.
c: Loose power cable at the relay or power distribution unit
Burnt contacts in starter relay B
Weak battery or low system voltage so the relay does not pull in
s: Check engine light
Engine does not start or crank
Further codes for low system voltage or battery state

P26F4.d: Coolant pump C is a third electric pump next to pumps A and B; which circuit it serves is defined by each manufacturer. In Bentley's V8 models from the Volkswagen group it is the auxiliary pump for the heater circuit, while GM's diesel tables use the C codes for the pump of the low-temperature loop. P26F4 means the control line to this pump is open, so the module cannot command it or receives no feedback. No manufacturer documents P26F4 itself in public; the closest case is Bentley's bulletin 2058340/1 on the low-side code P26F5, where an internally corroded pump led to a lit MIL. CARB requires circuit checks on electric components that affect emissions or other monitors. Depending on the loop, heater output drops or charge air and electronics are cooled less.
c: Broken control wire or loose connector at pump C
Corroded pins from road splash or coolant ingress
Internal electronics of the pump failed
s: Check engine light on
Weak cabin heating at idle or with the engine stopped
Higher charge air or component temperatures, depending on the loop

P26F5.t: Coolant Pump C Control Circuit Low
P26F5.d: P26F5 reports that the control circuit of coolant pump C is pulled too low. Bentley documents the code in the engine electronics of the Continental GT/GTC and Flying Spur. Bulletin 2058340/1 (Continental 2018–2019, cars without parking heater) blames internal corrosion of the additional coolant pump that shorts it out; cars built before 15 July 2019 get a pump from another supplier together with a new bracket. Bulletins 2078799/1 to /3 (2024 V8 models) describe the code as intermittent and caused by over-sensitive self-diagnosis of the heater auxiliary pump; after checking the wiring for corrosion and coolant ingress the pump is replaced, and Bentley states that heating and engine are not affected. In both cases the MIL is lit, so the code is emission-related despite the harmless symptom.
c: Internal corrosion of the pump causing a short circuit
Over-sensitive internal diagnosis of the pump (known pump part number)
Control wire shorted to ground or coolant in the connector
s: Check engine light on
Often no noticeable change in heating or engine behaviour
Fault may come and go (stored as intermittent)

P26F6.t: Coolant Pump C Control Circuit High
P26F6.d: P26F6 is stored when the control line of coolant pump C carries a higher voltage than the commanded state allows. In practice that means the wire touches a live circuit, the pump has lost its ground so the line floats up, or the line is open between driver and pump in a way the output stage reads as high. No public service document covers P26F6 itself. The low-side sister P26F5 is documented by Bentley for the auxiliary heater pump of its VW-group V8 models, where internal corrosion and pump self-diagnosis were the causes; CARB requires electric parts serving emission control or other monitors to be checked for such circuit faults. A pump held permanently on may keep running after the engine is switched off and drain the battery; one that cannot start leaves its loop without flow.
c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Missing or corroded ground at pump C
Internal electronics of the pump failed
s: Check engine light on
Pump runs on after switch-off or does not run at all
Weak heater output with the engine idling

P26F7.t: Coolant Pump C Supply Voltage Circuit
P26F7.d: Unlike P26F4 to P26F6, which concern the control signal, P26F7 points to the power feed of coolant pump C: the voltage arriving at the pump is missing or implausible. A blown fuse, a relay with burnt contacts, a broken feed wire or a loose ground are the usual causes; a weak battery during cranking can also trigger it. No manufacturer documents P26F7 in public. Ford shows how such a supply fault is detected for its electric engine coolant pump: under P26D3 the PCM concludes that the feed has failed when pump communication is lost and coolant temperature still rises by more than 10 °C. CARB requires electrical faults of monitored components to be found. Without power the pump stops completely, so the loop it serves – heater, low-temperature or component cooling – loses flow until the feed is restored.
c: Blown fuse or faulty relay in the pump C feed
Broken feed wire or loose, corroded ground
Low system voltage from a weak battery or charging fault
s: Check engine light on
Pump C does not run at all
Further codes for the same fuse or for low voltage

P26F8.d: P26F8 is about mechanics rather than wiring: coolant pump C is powered and commanded but its rotor does not turn or stops under load. Smart pumps recognise this themselves from a high motor current at little or no speed, and report it to the controlling module. Debris or deposits in the pump housing, a seized bearing, a rotor stuck after a long standstill or ice in the loop are typical reasons. No manufacturer documents P26F8 in public. Ford describes the same principle for its electric engine coolant pump under P26CB: the pump electronics see excessive current at too low a speed, try to restart four times and only then report the fault, which the PCM logs after five seconds. CARB requires such functional faults of emission-relevant components to be detected. The loop served by pump C then has no circulation.
c: Seized bearing or rotor in pump C
Debris or deposits in the pump from contaminated coolant
Frozen coolant from an incorrect mixture
s: Check engine light on
Heating or component cooling of the affected loop fails
Pump may hum without turning

P26F9.t: Coolant Pump C Control Module Overtemperature
P26F9.d: Electric coolant pumps carry their own control electronics, which are cooled by the liquid passing through the pump. P26F9 means the electronics of pump C have reported a temperature above their limit. That rarely points to a defect in the module itself; far more often coolant is missing around it, air is trapped in the pump, the impeller is partly blocked and draws high current, or the pump sits in a very hot spot. No manufacturer documents P26F9 in public. Ford's OBD summaries show how such a check works on the engine coolant pump code P26D2: the pump reports its temperature over LIN and the PCM stores the code once 130 °C is exceeded for five seconds. CARB requires electronic components that serve emission control to be monitored. The electronics usually derate or stop the pump to protect themselves.
c: Low coolant level or air trapped in pump C
Partly blocked impeller causing high current
Faulty temperature sensing in the pump electronics
s: Check engine light on
Pump C runs at reduced speed or switches off temporarily
Heating or cooling of the affected loop varies

P26FA.t: Coolant Pump C Overspeed/Air in System
P26FA.d: P26FA flags a coolant pump C that turns far faster than it should – the classic sign of a pump moving air instead of liquid. GM uses the code in the engine module of its diesel calibrations for the pump of the low-temperature coolant loop: in table 20OBDG04 an actual speed of at least 4,500 rpm in 5 of 8 one-second samples sets it, in 25OBDG04A 4 of 5 samples suffice. Both list it as Type B, so the MIL comes on after two trips; the test needs at least 11 V at the powertrain relay and is skipped while the engine cranks. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 names P26FA among many codes caused by a chafed engine harness on Silverado and Escalade models. The first check is coolant level and bleeding; the sister codes P2BA0 (underspeed) and P26F8 (stuck) cover the opposite cases.
c: Low coolant level or air left in the low-temperature loop after service
Leak in the loop drawing in air
Chafed engine harness corrupting pump signals
Impeller slipping on its shaft or broken
s: Check engine light on after two trips
Gurgling from the pump area
Higher charge air temperature and possibly reduced power

P26FB.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Stuck Closed (Bank 1)
P26FB.d: A diesel engine routes recirculated exhaust around the EGR cooler while it is cold, so that the gas warms the engine and aftertreatment; later the bypass flap closes and the gas passes through the cooler. P26FB means the bypass on bank 1 does not open when commanded and stays in the closed, cooling position. FCA uses the code on the 3.0 L EcoDiesel (Ram 1500 2020, Jeep Wrangler). STAR case S2018000001 links it to a 0.6 mm brass restrictor that clogs inside the vacuum line running from the remote solenoid to the flap actuator; the tube must be replaced rather than cleaned, and the actuator is checked by hand for sticking. FCA's PCM software bulletins 18-008-21 and 18-002-23 list P26FB among the codes they address. CARB lists the bypass among parts that must respond during cold-start strategies, so warm-up emissions rise.
c: Blocked orifice or kinked vacuum line to the bypass actuator
Bypass flap sticking from soot and deposits
Faulty vacuum solenoid or weak vacuum supply
Outdated PCM calibration with too sensitive detection
s: Check engine light on
Longer warm-up of engine and exhaust aftertreatment
Usually no noticeable change in driveability

P26FC.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Stuck Closed (Bank 2)
P26FC.d: P26FC is the bank 2 version of P26FB and only exists on engines with a separate EGR cooler and bypass for each cylinder bank, typically V-configuration diesels. The engine module has commanded the bypass of the second bank open, but position feedback or the resulting gas temperature shows it is still closed, so the exhaust gas keeps flowing through the cooler during warm-up. No manufacturer documents P26FC in public. For bank 1, FCA's STAR case S2018000001 on the 3.0 L EcoDiesel shows how such a fault arises: a clogged orifice in the vacuum line to the actuator, or a flap that does not move freely. CARB requires the EGR cooler bypass to be checked for proper response while cold-start emission strategies are active. If P26FB and P26FC appear together, a shared vacuum supply or solenoid is the likely cause.
c: Blocked, leaking or kinked vacuum line to the bank 2 actuator
Bypass flap of bank 2 sticking from soot deposits
s: Check engine light on
Slower warm-up of the exhaust aftertreatment

P26FD.t: A/C Compressor Internal Control Module Performance
P26FD.d: Electric A/C compressors in hybrids and electric vehicles carry their own inverter and control electronics. P26FD says this built-in module does not work as expected, as judged by the module that supervises the compressor. Audi documents the code for the 2016 A3 e-tron: the Climatronic unit J255 logs it instead of the engine module, and the MIL comes on purely as a network request. Bulletin 2047037/1 attributes it to a software error in the self-check of the refrigerant system and the compressor diagnosis; the cure is new Climatronic software, with the compressor replaced only if guided fault finding demands it. CARB requires monitoring of electronic A/C components whose failure affects emission control or other monitors. Cooling may still work or be limited.
c: Software error in the climate or compressor control
Internal electronics or inverter of the compressor failing
Fault in the high-voltage supply or fuse of the compressor
s: Check engine light on without a code in the engine module
Air conditioning weak or not cooling
Further A/C codes stored as sporadic

P26FE.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve A Control Performance
P26FE.d: P26FE concerns the electrically driven exhaust flap A on models with selectable exhaust sound. The circuit is fine, but the flap does not reach the commanded position. Ford's OBD summaries 2020–2024 assign it to bank 1 and use two checks: the flap's smart driver reports a stuck valve over its PWM line, and a rationality test compares measured with commanded position, with a duration that depends on ambient conditions. Ford bulletins 17-2063 and 17-2217 (Focus RS 2016–2017) trace it to a valve freezing below 0 °C and fix it with new PCM software; 23-2132 (Mustang 2018–2023) blames a badly seated exhaust; 25-2144 (F-150 5.2 L, 2023–2025) requires PCM update and actuator alignment. Drivers see a lit MIL and a message that exhaust or drive mode is unavailable; bank 2 uses P2BFB.
c: Flap sticking from corrosion, soot or freezing moisture
Exhaust or actuator bracket not seated correctly
Actuator not aligned after replacement or outdated PCM software
s: Check engine light on
Message that exhaust or drive mode is not available
No audible change in exhaust sound between modes

P26FF.t: Auto Configuration Throttle Input Not Present (Bank 2)
P26FF.d: Some engine controllers set themselves up at power-on by checking which inputs are connected, so one module can serve several engine layouts. On V engines with a separate throttle body for each cylinder bank this includes a throttle position signal per bank. P26FF means the controller expects a throttle input for bank 2 but finds none during this self-configuration; P063E is the same finding for bank 1. Unlike circuit codes such as P0222/P0223, which judge a signal that is present but wrong, this one says the input was not detected at all. No manufacturer documents P26FF publicly. CARB requires throttle position inputs to be checked for wiring faults and for plausibility. Typical causes are an unplugged throttle body, an open signal wire or software meant for another engine; expect a reduced-power mode.
c: Bank 2 throttle body connector unplugged or not fully seated
Open signal, reference or ground wire to the bank 2 throttle position sensor
Engine controller programmed or replaced with software for a different engine variant
s: Check engine light on
Reduced engine power or limp mode
Poor throttle response or rough idle

P2700.t: Transmission Friction Element A Apply Time Range/Performance
P2700.d: Automatic transmissions shift by filling and releasing clutches or brakes, the friction elements, and the controller learns how long each one takes to apply. P2700 is set when element A engages too slowly, too quickly or not plausibly compared with the commanded shift. Which part A is depends on the gearbox. Ford's 2012 OBD summary notes that its newer units replaced these clutch-level codes with solenoid stuck on/off codes for service, yet Ford still uses P2700: bulletin 16-0057 links it with P0751 and P0730 on TorqShift units built up to 15 December 2015 in E-Series, Super Duty and F-53/F-59 chassis and renews the cylinder of the coast clutch together with its one-way clutch. On Roush's propane Ford chassis the code is MIL on the E-450 and non-MIL on others. Harsh or slipping shifts are typical.
c: Worn or damaged clutch A components, such as a cylinder, piston seal or one-way clutch
Sticking valve or solenoid in the main control valve body
Low, aged or incorrect transmission fluid
Adaptive shift values not relearned after repair or software update
s: Harsh, delayed or slipping shifts involving clutch A
Check engine or transmission warning light on
Incorrect gear ratio codes stored at the same time

P2701.t: Transmission Friction Element B Apply Time Range/Performance
P2701.d: P2701 concerns friction element B: the controller has measured an apply time for this clutch or brake that falls outside its learned window. The letter is assigned per gearbox, and bulletins show how varied the causes are. Ford's SSM 47361 pairs P2701 with P0757 on the 2018 Mustang 10R80 when it will not shift beyond second gear and traces it to one-way clutch damage in the front support. On 6F50/6F55 units built from November 2015 to February 2016, SSM 46069 and 50861 combine it with P0756 and loss of reverse, third and fifth gear, caused by a displaced direct clutch snap ring. A 2023 Stellantis case for Ram Heavy Duty trucks links P2701 and harsh shifts to a dislodged 2C clutch snap ring. Expect harsh shifts, flare or a missing gear.
c: Mechanical damage in clutch B, such as a displaced snap ring or damaged hub
Damaged one-way clutch working together with element B
Sticking valve or pressure control solenoid for clutch B
s: Harsh shifts or engine flare during shifts
One or more gears missing, e.g. no upshift beyond second
Warning light on

P2702.t: Transmission Friction Element C Apply Time Range/Performance
P2702.d: With P2702 the transmission controller reports that friction element C does not engage within the time it expects, measured from the shift command to the moment the speed ratio changes. Which clutch C stands for differs between gearbox designs. Ford names the code in several valve body bulletins. For 10R140 units in 2020 F-Super Duty trucks, TSB 20-2375 lists P2700 to P2705 among codes caused by sticking main control valves; below 8,000 km the dealer runs a break-in routine three times on the affected clutches, beyond that the valve body is replaced. SSM 54595 for 8F35 units in 2025 Maverick, Corsair, Escape and Bronco Sport built from September 2024 to September 2025 reports P2702 with P2706 and P2707 when the vehicle will not leave Park. Roush propane chassis store it without MIL.
c: Sticking valves in the main control valve body
Worn clutch C plates or leaking piston seals
Outdated transmission software or lost adaptive values
s: Harsh or delayed shifts on gears using clutch C
Vehicle may not shift out of Park on some Ford 8F35 units
Wrench or engine warning light on

P2703.t: Transmission Friction Element D Apply Time Range/Performance
P2703.d: P2703 points at friction element D: the time it needs to take up torque, as seen from turbine and output speed, no longer matches what the controller has learned. In Ford's eight-speed front-drive units the code turns up with reverse problems. TSB 21-2029 covers 2020 Escape models with the 1.5L EcoBoost and 8F24 built before 7 August 2020 that lose reverse while storing P0766 and P2703; fine particles keep the lever inside the electrically operated SOWC (selectable one-way clutch) from deploying, so that clutch and the filter are replaced. SSM 54825 reports P2703 with P0766 and P0767 plus harsh or missing reverse on 2023 to 2026 Escape 8F35 units and fixes it with a new selectable one-way clutch, rebuilt next to the A clutch, and an overhauled valve body. Ford's 10R140 bulletin lists it as well.
c: Faulty or contaminated selectable one-way clutch (Ford 8F24/8F35)
Sticking valve in the main control valve body
Worn clutch D plates or leaking seals
s: No reverse or harsh engagement into reverse
Harsh or delayed shifts on gears using clutch D
Check engine light on

P2704.t: Transmission Friction Element E Apply Time Range/Performance
P2704.d: P2704 is stored when friction element E takes too long or too short a time to apply, judged against the speed change the controller expects for the shift. Ford bulletins tie the code directly to the E clutch. TSB 23-2376 describes F-550/F-600 trucks of model year 2022 with the 6.7L diesel and 10R140: once they have covered over 8,000 km the input shaft wears against the E clutch hub, its O-rings fail and the E clutch circuit loses pressure, so P2704 appears with P0771 and the wrench lamp; hub and O-rings are renewed. On the 2020 Transit with the 10R80, TSB 20-2185 links P2704 and P0772 to harsh engagement into drive from sticking valves. Land Rover's SSM71847 lists P2704-07 among ZF 9HP48 faults on 2014-15 Evoque and Discovery Sport.
c: Pressure loss in the E clutch circuit from worn hub or damaged O-rings
Sticking valves in the main control valve body
Transmission control software needing an update
Low fluid level from a leak
s: Harsh engagement into drive or poor shift quality
Wrench, engine or gearbox warning on
Limp mode in a fixed gear on some gearboxes

P2705.t: Transmission Friction Element F Apply Time Range/Performance
P2705.d: P2705 covers the sixth friction element, F, so only transmissions with at least six shift elements use it, such as Ford's ten-speed and eight-speed families. The controller has found that F applies outside the time it has learned. Ford's SSM 50617 for Edge ST and Nautilus models from 2020 to 2022 with the 8F57 built up to 18 March 2022 reports cars returning to Park when drive or reverse is selected; the main code is P2707, and P2705 may accompany it. The cause is the F clutch piston, which serves second and eighth gear and whose rubber sealing surface can be damaged. On the 10R140, TSB 20-2375 includes P2705 among the codes from sticking main control valves and lets all six clutches be cycled. Roush's propane Ford chassis store P2705 without MIL.
c: Sticking valves in the main control valve body
Shift solenoid F not controlling pressure correctly
s: Harsh or slipping shifts in the gears using clutch F
Vehicle may fall back into Park when drive or reverse is selected (Ford 8F57)
Warning light on

P2706.d: P2706 is the general code for the sixth shift solenoid, F. Ford's 2024 OBD summary uses it as the base for all shift solenoid F faults in its 10R60/10R80, 8F35/8F40, 8F57 and 8F24 transmissions: with a fault-type byte added, P2706 marks an open, a short to ground, a short to supply, an intermittent connection, stuck off and stuck on, each also carrying its own two-byte code such as P097F, P2707 or P2708. Ford's electrical check flags a fault once the smart driver has reported a wiring problem for 1.5 s. Stellantis calls the same position the MS solenoid on the Ram 68RFE, where bulletin 18-061-20 lists P2706 among codes cleared by new engine controller software. Ford's SSM 54595 names it with P2707 on 8F35 units that will not leave Park. Shifts involving the related clutch become harsh or are blocked.
c: Open or shorted wiring or connector to shift solenoid F, often inside the transmission
Failed shift solenoid F or main control valve body
Control module software that needs reprogramming (Ram 68RFE)
Faulty solenoid driver in the PCM or TCM
s: Harsh shifts, missing gears or limp mode
Vehicle may not shift out of Park on some Ford 8F35 units
Warning light on

P2707.d: P2707 is not an electrical fault: the circuit to shift solenoid F is intact, but the clutch it controls does not apply when commanded, as if the solenoid stayed off. Ford stresses that a ratio-based check cannot tell a solenoid failure apart from other faults in the clutch hydraulics. In its 2024 summary P2707 equals P2706 with the functionally-failed-off byte for the 10R and 8F families. The test runs whenever the solenoid is switched from off to on; a bad event lasts about 2.5 s when not shifting or 1 s within a shift, adds 3 to a fault counter, a correct state takes 1 off, and the code sets at 9. Bulletins name a damaged F clutch piston on the 8F57 (SSM 50617) and a delaminated fluid pump gasket causing several stuck-off codes on 2021 Super Duty 10R140 units (SSM 50512). P2708 is the stuck-on case.
c: Leaking or damaged clutch F piston or seals
Shift solenoid F or its valve sticking in the off position
Insufficient supply pressure, e.g. damaged fluid pump gasket
s: Gears using clutch F missing or slipping
Return to Park or no engagement in drive or reverse
Check engine light on

P2708.d: P2708 means the clutch fed by shift solenoid F stays applied when the controller expects it released, although the wiring checks pass. Ford's 2024 OBD summary maps it to P2706 with the failed-on byte 7E for its 10R60/10R80, 8F35/8F40, 8F57 and 8F24 units. One bad event lasts roughly 2.5 s outside a shift or 1 s during one; each adds 3 to a counter, each correct reading removes 1, and 9 stores the code. Since a ratio test cannot separate valve and clutch, Ford's 10R80 bulletins (21-2315 up to 26-2395) treat it as a hydraulic fault, e.g. a shifting sleeve on the CDF clutch cylinder that leaks oil. Audi bulletin 2078831 lists P270800 with a gear actuator fault on 2025 A5/Q5 dual-clutch boxes. Expect harsh or late shifts and a lit MIL. P2707 is the opposite case.
c: Internal oil leak at a clutch cylinder or sleeve keeping the clutch applied (Ford 10R80 CDF cylinder)
Shift solenoid F mechanically sticking in the applied position (dirt, wear)
Outdated PCM/TCM calibration; Ford bulletins combine reprogramming with the repair
Debris or degraded fluid jamming valves in the valve body
s: Harsh or delayed engagement and shifts
MIL lit, often with other stuck-on or gear-ratio codes
Binding or shudder as two clutches work against each other
Transmission may hold a fixed gear for protection

P2709.d: P2709 flags an electrical fault on shift solenoid F, found by the output driver rather than by watching the gearbox shift. Hyundai and Kia list it as the circuit code for that valve: Kia bulletin TRA 051 and Hyundai 15-AT-010 call solenoid F SS-B on their six-speed transaxles and replace parts instead of the gearbox, Kia first the solenoid, then the harness to the PCM, and only then the PCM if the code returns; Hyundai 12-AT-015-1 does the same for the 2012-2013 Genesis eight-speed. Ford is inconsistent: its 2024 summary text sends shorts on solenoid F to P0998/P0999, yet its tables give P2709 for a short to ground on 10R and 8F35/8F40 units and as the general electrical fault on 8F57/8F24, flagged after 1.5 s of driver feedback. Shifts using that clutch are lost.
c: Defective coil in shift solenoid F (Hyundai/Kia replace the solenoid first)
Chafed or corroded wiring or connector between PCM/TCM and transmission
Damaged internal transmission harness or lead frame
Faulty output driver in the PCM/TCM
s: MIL lit and transmission in a fail-safe gear
Missing gears or sudden harsh shifts
Code returns immediately after clearing if the fault is permanent

P270A.t: Transmission Friction Element A Temperature Too High
P270A.d: P270A opens a row of six codes (A to F) for an overheated clutch or brake inside the gearbox.
