Less power because timing is pulled back as a precaution

P289B.t: Cylinder 3 Ion Current Sense Circuit High
P289B.d: P289B signals that the ion channel of cylinder 3 sits permanently above its upper limit. A conductor touching battery voltage, a coil that couples ignition energy into its measuring output, or a lost ground reference are the usual electrical reasons. Saab shows a comparable bank-level check on the Trionic T7 V6, where cylinder 3 belongs to bank 1 together with 1 and 5: its code P1313 is set when the combustion detection line stays above 5 V for 200 combustions and clears after 300 without fault. On the 2009 four-cylinder module, cylinder 3 has trigger input pin 2 and ion input pin 8, which makes targeted voltage checks easy. No manufacturer publishes P289B. The low-side counterpart is P289A.
c: Ion signal wire of cylinder 3 shorted to battery or supply voltage
Coil 3 coupling ignition energy into its measuring output
Missing ground reference at coil 3 or the processing module
s: MIL with high ion signal fault on cylinder 3
Knock on cylinder 3 may go undetected, so timing is retarded
Reduced pulling power

P289C.d: P289C stands for a general circuit fault in the ion measurement of cylinder 4, meaning no usable signal reaches the evaluation electronics from that plug. Cylinder 4 has a special role in Saab's Trionic four-cylinders: without a camshaft sensor, the engine fires cylinders 1 and 4 at the same time during start-up and decides from the ion response which of them is on the compression stroke. On the T8, coil 4 delivers its signal to processing module pin 15, and a combustion in cylinder 4 is passed on as a pulse to engine module pin 21(B). On a V6 with Saab's T7, cylinder 4 instead sits in bank 2 next to 2 and 6. Saab used in-house codes; no manufacturer publicly documents P289C.
c: Ion measuring stage in the coil of cylinder 4 failed
Open circuit between coil 4 and the processing module
Cylinder 4 input of the processing module defective
s: MIL with ion fault stored for cylinder 4
Extended cranking because cylinder 1 and 4 cannot be told apart reliably
Conservative ignition timing with reduced power

P289D.t: Cylinder 4 Ion Current Sense Circuit Range/Performance
P289D.d: P289D is a rationality fault: cylinder 4 supplies an ion trace that is electrically present but not credible, for instance a combustion peak far smaller than the others at equal load, or erratic changes between cycles. Low-pass filtering of this trace gives the combustion information, band-pass filtering the knock content, so a distorted signal degrades both functions for cylinder 4. On the 2009 Saab module, the cylinder 4 ion input is pin 15 and it is combined with cylinder 2 into the second combustion signal. Wear or fouling of the plug, an oil-wetted plug well, or a genuine mixture or compression problem in cylinder 4 are typical triggers. No manufacturer publicly documents P289D; P289C, P289E and P289F cover the electrical faults.
c: Worn or fouled spark plug in cylinder 4
Oil in the plug well of cylinder 4 from a leaking cover gasket
Mixture or compression problem in cylinder 4
s: MIL, sometimes accompanied by P0304
Noticeable vibration at idle
Fuel consumption rises slightly

P289E.t: Cylinder 4 Ion Current Sense Circuit Low
P289E.d: P289E means the ion signal of cylinder 4 remains below the range the module expects. A ground fault on the line from coil 4, a plug whose insulator conducts the bias voltage away, or a coil that has stopped generating that voltage are the main suspects. In Saab's T7 four-cylinder cassette, cylinders 3 and 4 share one detector that pulses engine module pin 6; Saab notes that a short to ground on such a combustion line produced only misfire codes, while an open line was flagged as P1334. A dedicated low code for cylinder 4 separates this case. Since cylinder 4 is also the start partner of cylinder 1, a dead signal can affect synchronisation. The opposite reading is P289F.
c: Ion signal line of cylinder 4 shorted to ground
Spark plug insulator of cylinder 4 leaking the bias voltage
Bias voltage generation inside coil 4 failed
s: MIL with low ion signal on cylinder 4
Possible start delay or misfire codes
Power reduced by safety timing on cylinder 4

P289F.t: Cylinder 4 Ion Current Sense Circuit High
P289F.d: P289F is set when the ion measurement of cylinder 4 is held above its plausible maximum. Electrically, look for a signal conductor in contact with a supply feed, an internally leaking coil 4, or a poor ground that lifts the reference level. On Saab's T7 V6, cylinder 4 is part of bank 2 with cylinders 2 and 6; there a combustion detection line above 5 V for 200 combustions sets Saab code P1324, which needs 300 fault-free combustions to report OK. On the 2009 four-cylinder module, the ignition trigger of cylinder 4 enters on pin 1, the ion signal on pin 15. A permanently high channel hides the knock oscillations, so timing is retarded. No manufacturer publishes P289F; P289E is the low case.
c: Ion signal conductor of cylinder 4 touching a supply feed
Internal leakage in coil 4 raising the measuring output
Poor ground lifting the reference of the cylinder 4 channel
s: MIL with high ion signal on cylinder 4
Reduced performance from retarded ignition
Knock protection on cylinder 4 weakened

P28A0.d: P28A0 reports that the ion current circuit of cylinder 5 delivers no evaluable signal. A cylinder 5 exists only on engines with five or more cylinders, which narrows the field considerably. The V6 of the Saab 9-5 with Trionic T7 is a documented ion-sensing example: cylinder 5 sits in bank 1 with 1 and 3, is triggered from engine module pin 31, and is fired together with cylinder 2 until synchronisation. That design, however, measures one combined voltage drop per bank, so a single-cylinder circuit fault cannot be isolated electrically; Saab instead counts missing combustion signals per cylinder for misfire code P0305. No manufacturer publicly documents P28A0.
c: Coil of cylinder 5 with failed ion measuring circuit
Connector or wire fault between coil 5 and the evaluation electronics
s: MIL with ion fault stored for cylinder 5
Misfire monitoring of cylinder 5 restricted
Retarded timing and slightly reduced power

P28A1.t: Cylinder 5 Ion Current Sense Circuit Range/Performance
P28A1.d: P28A1 flags a cylinder 5 ion signal that is electrically intact but implausible in size or shape compared with load, speed and the other cylinders. Ion current rises with chamber pressure and temperature, so a lean or poorly compressing cylinder 5 produces a weak trace exactly like a fouled plug does. Saab's T7 V6 shows how closely the signal is tied to misfire detection: its engine module accumulates missing combustion signals per cylinder over 1000 revolutions and compares them with a load- and speed-dependent limit before setting P0305. That discharge module also evaluates knock from the ion flow of its bank. No manufacturer documents P28A1 publicly; electrical faults on cylinder 5 are P28A0, P28A2 and P28A3.
c: Fouled or eroded spark plug in cylinder 5
Lean mixture in cylinder 5 from a clogged injector or intake leak
s: MIL, possibly with misfire code P0305
Uneven running under load
Higher fuel consumption

P28A2.t: Cylinder 5 Ion Current Sense Circuit Low
P28A2.d: P28A2 is stored when the cylinder 5 ion reading stays under its lower threshold. The measurement relies on a constant bias across the plug gap between sparks – about 80 V on Saab's T7 discharge modules – and anything that drains it to ground pulls the reading down: a chafed signal conductor, a cracked plug insulator, or a coil whose bias supply has failed. On Saab's four-cylinder T7, a combustion line shorted to ground produced no dedicated fault code and surfaced only as misfire codes, which illustrates the gap such a low-side code closes. On Saab's V6 the bank 1 module serves cylinders 1, 3 and 5 together. No manufacturer publicly documents P28A2. P28A3 is the high-side fault.
c: Signal conductor of cylinder 5 chafed against ground
Cracked insulator on the cylinder 5 spark plug
s: MIL with low ion signal on cylinder 5
Misfire codes for cylinder 5 may appear
Safety ignition map reduces power

P28A3.t: Cylinder 5 Ion Current Sense Circuit High
P28A3.d: P28A3 indicates a cylinder 5 ion signal locked above its permitted ceiling. Contact between the signal path and a voltage source, a coil 5 that injects ignition energy into its output, or a disturbed ground reference can cause it. The closest documented logic comes from Saab's T7 V6, where cylinder 5 is served by the bank 1 discharge module: Saab code P1313 detects an open or short to B+ on that bank's combustion line once it exceeds 5 V for 200 combustions, requires the engine to be running with ignition synchronised, and needs 300 clean combustions for the OK report. Naming cylinder 5 directly would require one measuring circuit per cylinder; no manufacturer documents P28A3 publicly. The low reading is P28A2.
c: Signal path of cylinder 5 in contact with a voltage source
Coil 5 feeding ignition energy into its measuring output
Disturbed ground reference of the evaluation circuit
s: MIL with high ion signal on cylinder 5
Ignition retarded on cylinder 5, less power
Knock events may not be recognised

P28A4.d: P28A4 is the general circuit code for the ion measurement of cylinder 6: the electronics get no usable signal from that plug. Only engines with six or more cylinders are affected, and among them ion sensing is rare. The V6 of Saab's 9-5 with Trionic T7 used it; there cylinder 6 is in bank 2 with 2 and 4, is triggered from engine module pin 32, and shares its start spark with cylinder 3. The V6 of the 2007 Saab 9-3 is a counterexample: its Motronic ME9 relies on two piezo knock sensors, one per bank, so no ion signal exists there at all. No manufacturer publicly documents P28A4; on an affected engine, coil 6, its wiring and the plug are checked first.
c: Ion measuring part of the cylinder 6 coil defective
Open ion signal circuit of cylinder 6 in the harness or connector
s: MIL with ion fault stored for cylinder 6
Reduced misfire and knock monitoring on cylinder 6
Moderate power loss from cautious timing

P28A5.t: Cylinder 6 Ion Current Sense Circuit Range/Performance
P28A5.d: P28A5 points to a cylinder 6 ion signal that exists but makes no sense for the operating point: too little combustion response, a trace that jumps between cycles, or one that departs from the remaining cylinders. Since ionisation follows the actual burn, a misfiring or lean cylinder 6 can trigger it as readily as a worn plug or a wet plug well. On Saab's T7 V6 the bank 2 module evaluates the ion flow of cylinders 2, 4 and 6 for knock, sending the result to engine module pin 62, and missing combustion signals on cylinder 6 feed misfire code P0306. If the signal is unreliable, knock control tends to retard timing more often. No manufacturer publicly documents P28A5; P28A4, P28A6 and P28A7 are the electrical siblings.
c: Spark plug of cylinder 6 worn or sooted
Water or oil in the plug well of cylinder 6
Poor combustion in cylinder 6 (injector, valve, compression)
s: MIL, often together with P0306
Rough running at idle or light throttle
Hesitation under acceleration

P28A6.t: Cylinder 6 Ion Current Sense Circuit Low
P28A6.d: P28A6 describes an ion reading from cylinder 6 that never leaves the bottom of its range. Between sparks the system keeps a small voltage across the plug, and the hot gas of a normal combustion lets a measurable current pass; if that voltage leaks to ground through a damaged conductor, a cracked ceramic or carbon deposits, or the coil stops supplying it, the reading collapses. With no usable value, the module treats cylinder 6 as unmonitored and usually falls back to safe timing. When tracing the fault, the harness along the cam cover deserves a close look for heat damage and chafed spots. No manufacturer documents P28A6 publicly; P28A7 is the high-side code.
c: Damaged ion conductor of cylinder 6 leaking to ground
Cracked ceramic or heavy deposits on the cylinder 6 plug
Coil 6 no longer supplies the measuring voltage
s: MIL with low ion signal on cylinder 6
Misfires on cylinder 6 possibly unrecorded
Engine noticeably weaker on safe timing

P28A7.t: Cylinder 6 Ion Current Sense Circuit High
P28A7.d: P28A7 is logged when the ion signal of cylinder 6 is held above the upper limit the module accepts. A conductor in contact with battery voltage, crosstalk from the primary side of coil 6, or an evaluation stage driven into saturation are the typical electrical explanations. Saab's T7 V6 handled the comparable fault per bank: cylinder 6 belongs to bank 2, whose combustion line triggers Saab code P1324 when it stays above 5 V for 200 combustions; the knock information of that bank travels separately to engine module pin 62. A saturated channel leaves no room for the knock oscillations, so the module retards timing on cylinder 6. No manufacturer documents P28A7 publicly. The low-side counterpart is P28A6.
c: Ion conductor of cylinder 6 touching battery voltage
Crosstalk from the primary side of coil 6
s: MIL with high ion signal on cylinder 6
Less power because of late ignition on cylinder 6
Knock on cylinder 6 may not be detected

P28A8.d: P28A8 covers a basic circuit fault in the ion current measurement of cylinder 7, so the module obtains no evaluable signal from that plug. A cylinder 7 only exists on engines with eight or more cylinders, and Saab, the best-known user of ion sensing, applied it to four-cylinder and V6 engines; no maker publicly describes an eight-cylinder version. No manufacturer publicly documents P28A8. Its physical position depends on the maker's numbering, which differs between brands on V8 engines. The principle stays the same: a bias voltage across the plug gap lets the burning gas conduct a small current, and a lost signal blinds misfire and knock assessment for that cylinder. Diagnosis starts at coil 7, its connector and the spark plug.
c: Coil of cylinder 7 with defective ion measuring function
Broken wire or loose connector in the cylinder 7 ion circuit
Cylinder 7 input of the evaluation electronics faulty
s: MIL with ion fault stored for cylinder 7
Misfire and knock monitoring of cylinder 7 unavailable
Some power loss from protective timing

P28A9.t: Cylinder 7 Ion Current Sense Circuit Range/Performance
P28A9.d: P28A9 means cylinder 7 returns an ion signal that is electrically sound but not believable for the current speed and load, or that stands out against the other cylinders of an eight-or-more-cylinder engine. Because the current through the plug gap grows with combustion pressure and temperature, a lean or misfiring cylinder 7 produces this picture as readily as a fouled plug or moisture in the well. The signal serves both misfire detection and knock control, as Saab's ion-sensing T7 V6 illustrates by analysing each bank's ion flow for knock. No manufacturer documents P28A9 publicly, and no production V8 with this measurement is publicly described. Electrical faults on cylinder 7 are reported as P28A8, P28AA and P28AB.
c: Fouled or worn spark plug in cylinder 7
Lean mixture or misfire in cylinder 7
Moisture in the plug well of cylinder 7
s: MIL, possibly together with P0307
Uneven idle
Knock control retards timing more often

P28AA.t: Cylinder 7 Ion Current Sense Circuit Low
P28AA.d: P28AA reports that the ion current reading from cylinder 7 has dropped below the floor the engine computer accepts. Ion sensing places a measuring voltage on the spark plug between firings; Saab's Trionic T8 coils generate about 120 V for this themselves. If that voltage leaks away through a carbon track inside the plug boot, a split insulator or a signal lead rubbing on the block, the evaluator sees almost no current even when the mixture burns normally. Because the reading then resembles a dead cylinder, a misfire code such as P0307 may be stored alongside. Cylinder 7 exists only on V8 and larger engines, and no maker publicly documents an ion-sensing engine of that size or this code. P28AB covers the opposite fault, P28A8 the open circuit.
c: Carbon track inside the cylinder 7 plug boot
Ion signal lead of cylinder 7 rubbed through to ground
Split ceramic insulator on the cylinder 7 plug
Measuring-voltage stage in coil 7 no longer working
s: MIL lit with a low ion reading stored for cylinder 7
Misfire code P0307 may appear although the engine runs smoothly
Reduced power from protective ignition timing

P28AB.t: Cylinder 7 Ion Current Sense Circuit High
P28AB.d: P28AB is set when the cylinder 7 ion signal sits above the highest value a healthy measuring circuit can deliver. Typical triggers are a signal lead touching a supply wire, moisture bridging the coil connector, or a coil whose ignition pulse bleeds into its measuring output. A constant high reading is treacherous for diagnosis because it can look like permanent combustion and so mask real misfire. Saab's T7 V6 shows comparable logic only per bank: its codes P1313 and P1324 flag a combustion line stuck above 5 V for 200 firings. No manufacturer publishes P28AB, and a V8 or larger engine using ion sensing is not publicly described. The low-side counterpart is P28AA; P28A9 handles readings that are in range but implausible.
c: Ion signal lead of cylinder 7 touching a supply wire
Moisture bridging contacts in the coil 7 connector
Coil 7 leaking its ignition pulse into the measuring output
s: MIL lit with a high ion reading stored for cylinder 7
Genuine misfire on cylinder 7 may go unreported
Timing pulled back on cylinder 7, slightly less power

P28AC.d: P28AC flags a general electrical fault in the ion current path of cylinder 8, typically an open connection, so no usable signal reaches the evaluation electronics. On a V8 this is the highest-numbered cylinder, on V10 and V12 engines a middle one; which bank it sits on depends on the maker's numbering. A cylinder-specific code presumes one input per coil, as in the CDM of Saab's later Trionic T8, which receives a separate ion line from each of the four coils. Older T7 modules merged cylinders into shared detectors and could not name a single one. No manufacturer documents P28AC, and no eight-cylinder ion-sensing engine is publicly known. Check coil 8, its plug, connector and wiring first; range and level faults are P28AD, P28AE and P28AF.
c: Loose or corroded connector in the cylinder 8 ion line
Broken conductor between coil 8 and the evaluation module
Cylinder 8 input of the evaluation module defective
s: MIL with a circuit fault stored for cylinder 8
No misfire or knock assessment for cylinder 8
Engine may run with conservative timing and lower power

P28AD.t: Cylinder 8 Ion Current Sense Circuit Range/Performance
P28AD.d: P28AD means the cylinder 8 ion signal is electrically intact but does not fit what the computer expects for the operating point, or it deviates clearly from the other cylinders. CARB treats such rationality checks as part of the monitoring of input components next to tests for wiring faults and for values outside the valid band. The current through the gap rises with pressure and temperature of the burning charge, so weak combustion from a worn plug, a partly blocked injector or poor compression in cylinder 8 lowers it, while oil deposits can distort it. On Saab's T8 the engine computer evaluates each cylinder only inside a crank-angle window after the spark. No manufacturer publicly documents P28AD. Circuit faults are P28AC, P28AE and P28AF; a confirmed misfire adds P0308.
c: Worn electrodes or wrong gap on the cylinder 8 plug
Oil deposits on the cylinder 8 plug
s: MIL, often together with P0308
Rough running under load
Knock control intervenes more often on cylinder 8

P28AE.t: Cylinder 8 Ion Current Sense Circuit Low
P28AE.d: P28AE stands for an ion reading from cylinder 8 that stays too low or near zero. Either the measuring voltage never reaches the plug, because the coil's bias stage or its supply has failed, or it drains away to ground through a damaged signal wire, a wet plug well or a tracked boot. With ion sensing the plug doubles as knock and combustion sensor, so a dead reading also takes knock protection for cylinder 8 away and the engine computer tends to fall back on retarded timing. A supply fault affecting the whole module would rather appear as P28C0 to P28C2 than as a single-cylinder code. No manufacturer documents P28AE in public; an eight-cylinder ion-sensing engine is not described. P28AF is the high-side fault.
c: Water or oil in the cylinder 8 plug well
Damaged cylinder 8 signal wire shorted to ground
Bias stage of coil 8 not producing measuring voltage
s: MIL lit with a low ion reading for cylinder 8
Knock protection of cylinder 8 lost, timing retarded
Possible misfire report for cylinder 8

P28AF.t: Cylinder 8 Ion Current Sense Circuit High
P28AF.d: P28AF is logged when cylinder 8 delivers an ion signal pinned at or above the upper limit. Possible reasons include the signal conductor shorted to battery voltage or to another live circuit in the harness, internal leakage inside coil 8 that lets the high-voltage side couple into the measuring line, or a lost reference ground at the evaluation input. CARB requires input components to be checked for values beyond their valid limits, and a reading stuck high would otherwise feed false combustion and knock data to the engine computer. How close high voltages sit to the signal is visible in Saab's T7 discharge modules, which fired from a 400 V capacitor while holding 80 V on the plug for measurement. No manufacturer documents P28AF publicly. The low reading is P28AE.
c: Cylinder 8 signal conductor shorted to battery voltage
Internal leakage in coil 8 coupling into the measuring line
Lost reference ground at the evaluation input
s: MIL lit with a high ion reading for cylinder 8
Misfire on cylinder 8 may stay undetected
Safety timing reduces power somewhat

P28B0.d: P28B0 marks an electrical circuit fault, usually an interruption, in the ion current measurement of cylinder 9. A ninth cylinder appears only on engines with ten or more cylinders, such as V10, V12 or W12 designs. Ion sensing as a production technique is publicly associated with Saab and Mecel, who brought it into series cars with the Trionic systems on four- and six-cylinder engines; for engines of ten or more cylinders no public application exists, and no manufacturer documents P28B0. The working principle would be unchanged: a small voltage across the idle plug gap, a current only when the hot gas ionises, and an evaluation channel per coil. Without that channel cylinder 9 loses misfire and knock evaluation; checks start at coil 9 and its connector.
c: Coil 9 connector not latched or with spread terminals
Ion output of coil 9 without function
Interrupted ion line of cylinder 9 in the harness
s: MIL with ion circuit fault for cylinder 9
Misfire and knock evaluation of cylinder 9 suspended
Slight loss of power from retarded timing

P28B1.t: Cylinder 9 Ion Current Sense Circuit Range/Performance
P28B1.d: P28B1 indicates that cylinder 9 produces an ion signal of believable electrical level whose shape or strength does not match engine speed, load or the neighbouring cylinders. Since the reading reflects combustion pressure and temperature, the root cause is often mechanical or mixture-related: a worn or oil-fouled plug, a leaking valve, a weak injector on cylinder 9, or condensation in the plug well. Saab used the same signal to count missing combustions per cylinder over 1000 crankshaft revolutions, the interval CARB also prescribes for emission-relevant misfire. No manufacturer documents P28B1, and engines with nine or more cylinders using ion sensing are not publicly described. P28B0, P28B2 and P28B3 are the electrical faults; P0309 may follow.
c: Worn or oil-fouled spark plug in cylinder 9
Weak spray from the cylinder 9 injector
Condensation in the cylinder 9 plug well
s: MIL, possibly with misfire code P0309
Noticeably uneven running at idle
Higher fuel consumption

P28B2.t: Cylinder 9 Ion Current Sense Circuit Low
P28B2.d: P28B2 is stored when the ion current measured at cylinder 9 remains under its lower plausibility limit. In an ion-sensing ignition each coil both fires the plug and supplies the measuring voltage, so a coil 9 with a weak bias stage, a cracked plug insulator or a signal wire grounded in the harness all reduce the current reaching the evaluator. Because the evaluation can hardly tell a dead circuit from a cylinder that does not burn, misfire code P0309 frequently accompanies it. On Saab's four-cylinder T7, a ground short on a combustion line triggered no special code at all, only misfire reports. No manufacturer publicly documents P28B2, and no ion-sensing V10 is known. P28B3 is the high fault, P28B1 the plausibility fault.
c: Cylinder 9 signal wire grounded in the harness
Cracked insulator on the cylinder 9 plug
s: MIL with low ion reading on cylinder 9
P0309 often stored at the same time
Reduced power under load

P28B3.t: Cylinder 9 Ion Current Sense Circuit High
P28B3.d: P28B3 shows that the cylinder 9 ion signal is held above the range a working circuit produces. Shorts from the sense line to a powered conductor, a coil 9 leaking high-voltage energy into its measuring output, or water in the connector can push it there. The fault matters for emissions monitoring, because a signal that always reports strong combustion would let real misfire on cylinder 9 go unnoticed. As an analogue, Saab's V6 bank codes needed 300 clean combustions before reporting the circuit OK again, after a sustained over-voltage had set them. No manufacturer documents P28B3, and no ion-sensing engine with nine or more cylinders is publicly known. P28B2 is the low fault, P28B0 the open circuit.
c: Cylinder 9 sense line shorted to a powered conductor
Coil 9 leaking high-voltage energy into its measuring output
s: MIL with high ion reading on cylinder 9
Real misfire on cylinder 9 can go unnoticed
Timing on cylinder 9 retarded as a precaution

P28B4.d: P28B4 is the basic circuit code for the ion current measurement of cylinder 10; typically the line from coil 10 to the evaluation module is interrupted or the coil's measuring stage is dead. Ten cylinders mean a V10 at minimum, where this is the last cylinder in the numbering, or a V12 or W12, where it is not. No production engine of that size with ion sensing is publicly described, and no manufacturer documents P28B4. Saab's systems illustrate the stakes: without the ion signal, misfire counting and cylinder-selective knock control lose their input, and the T7 V6 even cut fuel to every cylinder once a single discharge module lost its supply. Start at coil 10, plug and connector; P28B5, P28B6 and P28B7 are the range and level faults.
c: Open line between coil 10 and the evaluation module
Corroded terminals at the coil 10 connector
s: MIL with ion circuit fault for cylinder 10
Cylinder 10 excluded from misfire and knock evaluation
Possible power reduction through protective timing

P28B5.t: Cylinder 10 Ion Current Sense Circuit Range/Performance
P28B5.d: P28B5 reports an ion signal from cylinder 10 that is electrically valid yet implausible: its amplitude or timing after the spark does not fit the load point or departs from the remaining cylinders. Because ionisation depends on how hot and dense the burning charge is, causes include an eroded electrode gap, oil-wetted plugs, mixture errors on cylinder 10 or a compression loss. Saab's T7 V6 evaluated the ion flow of each bank for knock and retarded the affected cylinder step by step, so an untrustworthy signal tends to show up as erratic timing. No manufacturer publicly documents P28B5, and an ion-sensing V10 or V12 is not described. P28B4, P28B6 and P28B7 are the electrical faults; P0310 may accompany it.
c: Eroded electrode gap on the cylinder 10 plug
s: MIL, sometimes together with P0310
Erratic ignition timing on cylinder 10
Hesitation when accelerating

P28B6.t: Cylinder 10 Ion Current Sense Circuit Low
P28B6.d: P28B6 is set when the cylinder 10 ion reading is persistently too low. The measuring bias that should sit across the gap between sparks is missing or being drained: a coil 10 whose bias generator has failed, conductive deposits bridging the plug insulator, a wet boot, or a sense wire with insulation damage touching ground. Saab's T7 applied 80 V for this purpose, the later T8 about 120 V; either way, a short to ground collapses it. The engine computer then lacks combustion confirmation for cylinder 10, may log P0310 and usually falls back to cautious timing. No manufacturer documents P28B6 publicly, and no ion-sensing engine with ten or more cylinders is known. The high-side code is P28B7.
c: Conductive deposits bridging the cylinder 10 plug insulator
Cylinder 10 sense wire with damaged insulation touching ground
s: MIL with low ion reading on cylinder 10
P0310 may be stored as well
Cautious ignition timing, less pulling power

P28B7.t: Cylinder 10 Ion Current Sense Circuit High
P28B7.d: P28B7 means the ion signal of cylinder 10 is stuck above its valid window. The usual suspects are a sense lead shorted to a supply or to a neighbouring ignition circuit, breakdown inside coil 10 that lets spark energy into the measuring path, and a poor ground at the evaluation side that shifts the reference upward. A falsely high signal could pass as continuous combustion or as permanent knock, so the engine computer typically discards it and retards timing on that cylinder for safety. Saab's later T8 module, which processes the ion signal of each coil on its own input pin, shows the cylinder-selective layout such a code assumes. No manufacturer documents P28B7 publicly. The low-side fault is P28B6, module supply problems are P28C0 to P28C2.
c: Cylinder 10 sense lead shorted to a supply or adjacent ignition circuit
Poor ground at the evaluation side
s: MIL with high ion reading on cylinder 10
Timing on cylinder 10 retarded for safety
Misfire on cylinder 10 may be masked

P28B8.d: P28B8 is the general circuit code for ion sensing on cylinder 11: the evaluation electronics receive nothing usable from that cylinder, most often because the line from coil 11 is broken or its connector has lost contact. Eleven cylinders only occur on V12 and W12 engines, and none of them with ion sensing is publicly described; no manufacturer documents P28B8. The layout such a code presumes exists on Saab's Trionic T8, whose detection module has a dedicated ion input for every coil. Losing it leaves the engine computer blind to misfire and knock on that cylinder, and on T8, which has no camshaft sensor, ion pulses also serve to find the firing order. P0361 concerns the primary side of coil K, not the measuring path; P28B9 to P28BB cover the range and level faults.
c: Loose, corroded or pushed-back pin in the cylinder 11 coil connector
Broken ion signal wire between coil 11 and the evaluation module
Cylinder 11 input of the evaluation module damaged
s: MIL on with a circuit fault stored for cylinder 11
Misfire and knock detection for cylinder 11 no longer available
Cautious ignition timing with slightly reduced power

P28B9.t: Cylinder 11 Ion Current Sense Circuit Range/Performance
P28B9.d: P28B9 stands for an ion signal from cylinder 11 whose voltage stays inside the valid band but whose behaviour makes no sense: too weak or too strong for the current speed and load, or out of line with the other eleven cylinders. Such rationality tests belong to the input-component monitoring CARB demands. Since the reading follows the heat and pressure of the burning charge, the trigger is frequently in the cylinder itself, such as a worn or oil-fouled plug, a weak injector or a leaking valve. Saab's T7 V6 shows how strict this gets: it tallied missing combustions per cylinder and compared them with an allowance taken from a speed and load table, enabled only above 72 kPa ambient pressure and -7 °C. No manufacturer documents P28B9. P28B8, P28BA and P28BB are the electrical faults.
c: Worn or oil-fouled spark plug on cylinder 11
Cylinder 11 injector delivering too little or spraying poorly
Low compression on cylinder 11 (valve or ring leakage)
Water or oil standing in the plug well of cylinder 11
s: MIL on after the fault is confirmed on a second trip
Slightly rough running, sometimes with misfire code P0311
Unsteady ignition timing on cylinder 11

P28BA.t: Cylinder 11 Ion Current Sense Circuit Low
P28BA.d: P28BA means the cylinder 11 ion reading has fallen below its lower limit. Between sparks a bias voltage sits across the electrodes – 80 V on Saab's T7 – and burning gas lets a current flow that pulls this voltage down in proportion to pressure and temperature. If a fault drains the bias to ground, the evaluator registers the same collapse permanently: a sense wire chafed through, a plug insulator coated with conductive deposits, or water in the boot. Saab's manual notes that a combustion signal shorted to ground produced no dedicated code there, only misfire codes, so a separate low-signal code is a later refinement. No manufacturer documents P28BA, and no ion-sensing twelve-cylinder engine is publicly known. P28BB is the high-side fault, P28B8 the open circuit.
c: Ion signal wire of cylinder 11 chafed and touching ground
Conductive deposits on the cylinder 11 plug insulator
Moisture or a carbon track in the cylinder 11 plug boot
Bias voltage generation in coil 11 failed
s: MIL on with a low ion signal stored for cylinder 11
Misfire code P0311 possible although the engine runs smoothly
Power slightly reduced by conservative timing

P28BB.t: Cylinder 11 Ion Current Sense Circuit High
P28BB.d: P28BB is stored when the cylinder 11 ion signal remains above the highest value the measuring circuit can legitimately produce. Common reasons are a sense wire shorted to battery voltage or to another ignition circuit, an internal breakdown in coil 11 that couples spark energy into the measuring output, and a missing ground at the evaluator that lifts the whole reference. The nearest published logic is per bank on Saab's T7 V6: P1324 needs a combustion line above 5 V throughout 200 combustions and clears only after 300 clean ones; Saab handled it as a Type III fault without a warning lamp. A stuck-high reading looks like constant combustion and can hide genuine misfire. No manufacturer documents P28BB. Its low-side partner is P28BA; the module supply is checked by P28C0 to P28C2.
c: Ion signal wire of cylinder 11 shorted to battery voltage or another ignition circuit
Internal breakdown in coil 11 feeding spark energy into the signal
Poor ground of the evaluation module shifting the reference
s: Stored code for a high ion signal on cylinder 11, lamp behaviour depends on the maker
Real misfire on cylinder 11 may go undetected
Retarded timing on cylinder 11

P28BC.d: P28BC covers a wiring-level failure in the ion measuring path of cylinder 12 that keeps a valid signal from arriving, typically an open wire or a connector without contact. Cylinder 12 is the last one on a V12 or W12; no such engine with ion sensing is publicly known, and no manufacturer documents P28BC. On Saab's Trionic T8 each measuring channel needs two inputs at the detection module: the ion line from the coil and the ignition trigger of the same cylinder, which tells the module when to start listening. A break in either can leave the channel silent. With that, misfire counting and knock evaluation for cylinder 12 stop. The coil's primary circuit is a separate code, P0362. P28BD covers implausible signals, P28BE and P28BF the voltage levels.
c: Open ion signal wire or connector at coil 12
Ignition trigger for cylinder 12 not reaching the detection module
Cylinder 12 channel of the evaluation module faulty
s: MIL on with a circuit fault stored for cylinder 12
No combustion feedback from cylinder 12
Engine may run with reduced ignition advance

P28BD.t: Cylinder 12 Ion Current Sense Circuit Range/Performance
P28BD.d: P28BD reports that cylinder 12 delivers an ion signal of acceptable voltage whose content is not credible – its strength, timing or shape after the spark does not match the operating point or the rest of the engine. Saab's later detection module illustrates why content matters: it splits each raw ion trace with filters, a band-pass for the ringing that indicates knock and a low-pass for the slower part that describes combustion quality. A distorted trace corrupts both outputs. Likely sources are an eroded or oily plug, mixture errors on cylinder 12, carbon in the chamber or reduced compression. CARB counts such plausibility checks as part of input monitoring. No manufacturer documents P28BD. Electrical faults are P28BC, P28BE and P28BF; a real misfire adds P0312.
c: Eroded or oil-wetted spark plug on cylinder 12
Mixture error on cylinder 12 (injector, intake leak at that port)
Carbon build-up in the cylinder 12 combustion chamber
s: MIL on after the fault repeats on a later trip
Occasional roughness, sometimes with P0312
Knock control on cylinder 12 reacts erratically

P28BE.t: Cylinder 12 Ion Current Sense Circuit Low
P28BE.d: P28BE is set when the ion reading of cylinder 12 stays below its minimum. On Saab's Trionic T8 each coil generates its own measuring voltage of about 120 V and keeps it applied to the plug; the module then reads how much current the ionised gas lets through. When that voltage is never built up – coil 12 has lost its bias stage – or leaks away through a cracked insulator, a soaked plug well or a sense lead grounded on a bracket, the evaluator sees a near-zero signal on every cycle. The engine computer then cannot confirm combustion in cylinder 12 and may report P0312 although the cylinder fires. No manufacturer documents P28BE, and twelve-cylinder engines with ion sensing are not publicly described. P28BF is the high-side counterpart, P28BC the open circuit.
c: Water or oil in the cylinder 12 plug well draining the measuring voltage
Sense lead of cylinder 12 grounded against a bracket or the engine
Coil 12 no longer builds up its measuring voltage
s: MIL on with a low ion signal stored for cylinder 12
Misfire code P0312 without noticeable roughness
Fault often appears after washing the engine or in wet weather

P28BF.t: Cylinder 12 Ion Current Sense Circuit High
P28BF.d: P28BF signals that the cylinder 12 ion input sits above its permitted window. A sense wire touching a powered conductor, moisture bridging pins in the coil 12 connector or spark energy escaping inside the coil can all push it there. The consequence is easiest to see on Saab's T7 V6, where knock was read from the ion flow: a signal above the knock level made the engine computer retard that cylinder step by step, and if average retard across all cylinders grew too large it enriched the mixture and finally limited air mass. A false high reading can therefore cost power and fuel. Engine computers are expected to reject such a value and fall back to safe timing. No manufacturer documents P28BF publicly. P28BE is the low-side fault, P28C2 an overvoltage of the module supply.
c: Sense wire of cylinder 12 touching a powered conductor
Moisture bridging pins in the coil 12 connector
Internal flashover in coil 12 reaching the measuring path
s: Stored high ion signal code for cylinder 12, MIL depending on the maker
Noticeably less power from heavy timing retard
Higher fuel consumption from protective enrichment

P28C0.t: Ion Sense Module Supply Voltage Circuit
P28C0.d: P28C0 points to a fault in the power feed of the module that conditions ion signals – typically an open fuse, relay contact or wire, so the module is not powered at all. On Saab's Trionic T8 that module receives battery voltage via the main relay and its ground from a body point, and on the older T7 the ignition cassette took the same route. Saab's nearest code, P1310 (bank 2: P1320), required a turning crankshaft and more than 6 V at the main relay, then flagged the fault when every trigger output stayed under 2 V for one second. Saab cut fuel in response, on the V6 for every cylinder although just one cassette had failed, yet treated it as Type III without a warning lamp. No manufacturer documents P28C0 itself. P28C1 and P28C2 cover a supply that is present but too low or too high.
c: Blown fuse in the ion sense module feed
Main relay not switching through or burnt contact
Open supply wire or loose ground point of the module
Internal fault in the module's power stage
s: Engine cranks but does not start, or cuts out while driving
Ion-based misfire and knock detection lost on all cylinders
Warning lamp behaviour depends on the manufacturer

P28C1.t: Ion Sense Module Supply Voltage Low
P28C1.d: P28C1 means the ion sense module is powered, but its supply sits below the level it needs to work reliably. That matters because such modules turn 12 V into far higher voltages: Saab's T7 cassette converted battery voltage to 400 V DC stored in a capacitor and also kept 80 V across each plug for measuring. With a sagging feed the measuring voltage and thus the ion current shrink, and every cylinder can appear to burn weakly at the same time. Typical causes are a tired battery, voltage loss across a corroded main relay contact or connector, a high-resistance ground point, or deep dips during cranking. Saab enabled its supply check only above 6 V at the main relay. No manufacturer documents P28C1. P28C0 covers a missing supply, P28C2 one that is too high.
c: Voltage drop across a corroded main relay contact or connector
High-resistance ground point of the module
s: Hard starting, especially when cold or with a weak battery
Misfire codes on several cylinders at once
Stored supply-voltage code, often together with system voltage codes

P28C2.t: Ion Sense Module Supply Voltage High
P28C2.d: P28C2 is stored when the voltage feeding the ion sense module exceeds its upper limit. Since the module derives its measuring and, in cassette designs, its ignition voltages from this feed, an excessive input can raise the bias across the plugs, push signals toward the top of their range and stress the converter inside. The cause is rarely the module: a failing alternator regulator, a jump start from a 24 V source or a poor ground at the module that makes the measured difference look larger are more typical. Saab's published ignition diagnostics have no overvoltage check at all, only the loss-of-supply codes, so there is no maker analogue for this case; the code follows the CARB demand to check inputs for out-of-range values. No manufacturer documents P28C2. P28C0 and P28C1 are the open and low faults.
c: Alternator voltage regulator letting the system voltage rise too high
Jump start or charger with excessive voltage (e.g. 24 V)
Poor module ground distorting the voltage reading
Faulty voltage measurement inside the module
s: Stored overvoltage code, often together with P0563
Flickering or unusually bright lamps, battery gassing
Erratic misfire or knock reports on several cylinders

P28C3.t: EVAP System High Load Purge Line B Performance
P28C3.d: Under boost the intake manifold is above ambient pressure, so turbo engines add a high-load purge path: compressed air drives an ejector (venturi) that draws canister vapour into the compressor inlet, with check valves keeping boost out of the tank side. CARB requires every purge path to be checked for missing flow, from 2021 including disconnected lines, unless the high-load path carries under 1 percent of purge mass on the US06 cycle. P28C3 is the function check of a second such line, B. Line A is P04F0, used for example by Genesis on the 2.5T with a dual purge ejector that clogs with debris. No manufacturer publicly documents P28C3 or names line B. Volvo's 2019–2020 Dual Purge action shows the typical fault: a check valve upsetting ejector flow at high load, logging a code and the MIL.
c: Check valve in high-load line B sticking, leaking or fitted the wrong way round
Line B to the compressor inlet pulled off, cracked or kinked
Ejector nozzle blocked by debris or oil residue
Leak in the boost-side hose that drives the ejector
s: MIL on, usually without any change in driving behaviour
EVAP readiness not completed
Occasional fuel smell after long full-load driving

P28C4.t: Clutch A Motor Phase U-V-W Circuit Low
P28C4.d: P28C4 means the transmission controller finds the voltage too low on a phase lead (U, V or W) of the electric motor that operates clutch A. This layout belongs to wet dual-clutch gearboxes without a valve block, such as the Getrag/Magna 7DCT300 and its hybrid derivative 7HDT300: a brushless motor per clutch spins a gerotor pump that feeds oil directly to the clutch piston. A phase pulled towards ground, for example by chafed insulation or a shorted driver transistor, is the typical trigger. P28C5 covers the opposite direction, P28C6 an interrupted phase. No manufacturer publishes a code-specific threshold; the driver loses the gears carried by clutch A and gets a transmission warning.
c: Phase wire to the clutch A motor chafed through and touching ground
Winding inside the clutch A motor shorted to the housing
Defective output transistor for the motor phases in the transmission controller
s: Transmission warning lamp, often together with the MIL
Odd or even gears locked out, depending on which shaft clutch A serves
Jerky or delayed pull-away

P28C5.t: Clutch A Motor Phase U-V-W Circuit High
P28C5.d: With P28C5 the controller finds one or more phases of the clutch A motor sitting higher than the switching pattern allows, as if a lead were tied to battery voltage. The motor in question is the brushless drive of an on-demand pump actuator: Getrag introduced this concept with the 7DCT300, where one motor per clutch turns a gerotor pump and the pump pressure itself closes the clutch. Causes on the high side are a phase touching a supply wire in the harness, moisture bridging pins in the connector, or an output transistor that no longer switches off. Unlike P28C4 the fault points away from ground. Thresholds are not published by any manufacturer. The transmission typically drops clutch A and runs on the remaining shaft.
c: Motor phase lead shorted to a supply line in the harness
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins at the actuator connector
High-side switch in the controller that no longer turns off
s: Warning lamp for the transmission and stored DTC
Half of the gear set unavailable, vehicle continues with reduced choice
Clutch A may not open or close on command

P28C6.t: Clutch A Motor Phase U-V-W Circuit/Open
P28C6.d: P28C6 is the general circuit code for the three-phase supply of the clutch A motor and is set above all when a phase carries no current although the controller drives it, i.e. an open line. A brushless motor needs all three windings to produce torque; with one missing it stalls or runs roughly, and the gerotor pump behind it can no longer build the oil pressure that engages clutch A. Getrag fitted such ferrite motors as common parts for clutch actuation and shift drums in its pump-actuated DCT family. Typical faults are a backed-out terminal, a cracked solder joint in the actuator, or a broken wire near a moving bracket. P28C4/P28C5 instead describe a voltage pulled low or high. No manufacturer documents P28C6 publicly with values.
c: Terminal pushed back or loose in the clutch A motor connector
Cracked solder joint or winding connection inside the actuator
Phase wire broken at a bend or bracket
s: Clutch A does not engage, affected gears unavailable
Transmission warning and possibly MIL
Fault may come and go with vibration or temperature

P28C7.t: Clutch A Motor Phase U-V-W Performance
P28C7.d: P28C7 flags that the clutch A motor's phases are electrically intact but the motor does not respond as expected, e.g. currents and rotation do not match the commanded drive. Stellantis documents it in bulletin 21-040-26 (May 2026) for European 2022-2025 Jeep Renegade and Compass with the 1.5 MHEV engine and the 7HDT300 hybrid dual-clutch gearbox: together with P2787 it points to the actuator cylinder of the odd-gear clutch, which in this gearbox is clutch A. Cause given there is small debris in the transmission blocking a pump inside the actuator; the MIL comes on and odd gears may be lost. If the guided test fails, the actuator is replaced (1.5 labour hours). The even-gear counterpart is P28D5 with P27F3.
c: Debris from the transmission jamming the pump in the clutch A actuator (Stellantis 7HDT300)
Worn or sluggish clutch A actuator motor
Increased resistance in a phase connection causing unbalanced currents
s: MIL and transmission warning lamp on
Odd gears unavailable on the 7HDT300
Often stored together with clutch A temperature code P2787

P28C8.d: P28C8 concerns the motor-and-pump unit of clutch A as a whole: the controller sees that the delivered result, typically the clutch pressure reported by the sensor or the motor effort needed to reach it, does not fit the command. In on-demand designs the gerotor pump is connected straight to the clutch cylinder, so pressure follows pump speed directly; a Hyundai-backed EVS32 study modelled exactly this arrangement and its energy saving. A pump clogged by particles, a worn gerotor set, internal leakage at the piston seals or low oil level make the pump work harder or fall short. No manufacturer documents P28C8 itself in public; Stellantis blames debris jamming the actuator pump for the related P28C7 on the 7HDT300.
c: Clutch A pump obstructed by abrasion particles
Internal leakage at the clutch A piston or pressure line seals
Low transmission fluid level so the pump draws air
s: Slipping or delayed engagement of clutch A
Transmission warning, gears on clutch A may be locked out
Audible whine from the actuator under load

P28C9.d: P28C9 is stored when the clutch A motor turns faster than the controller considers plausible for the pressure it is asked to hold. Because the pump in such actuators delivers oil straight into the closed clutch circuit, the motor should slow down once pressure is reached; if it keeps racing, the oil is escaping or the pump is not loaded. Likely reasons are a leaking clutch piston seal, air drawn in at low fluid level, or a broken coupling between motor shaft and gerotor so that the motor spins free. A faulty rotor position signal can also fake a high speed, which is why P28CB/P28CC deserve a look first. P28CA is the opposite case. No carmaker publishes limits for P28C9.
c: Oil escaping from the clutch A pressure circuit, e.g. worn piston seal
Pump drawing air because of low fluid level or clogged suction filter
Broken drive between motor shaft and gerotor rotor
Faulty motor position signal reporting too high a speed
s: Clutch A slips or fails to transmit full torque
Transmission warning and restricted gear choice

P28CA.d: P28CA means the clutch A motor stays below the speed the controller commands, so the pump cannot deliver oil fast enough to build or modulate clutch pressure. Mechanical drag is the usual culprit: particles wedged in the gerotor, a seized bearing, or very thick oil in deep cold. Stellantis reports debris blocking an actuator pump on the 7HDT300 (bulletin 21-040-26), though it lists P28C7 rather than this code. Electrical limits can play a part as well, for instance low supply voltage or the controller derating its output stage because of heat, which would appear as P28D1. Overspeed of the same motor is P28C9. No manufacturer documents P28CA with a threshold; engagement of clutch A becomes slow or fails.
c: Particles jamming the gerotor pump of clutch A
Low supply voltage to the actuator or poor ground
s: Clutch A engages late or with a jolt
Transmission warning, especially after cold start
Affected gears may be withheld

P28CB.t: Clutch A Motor Position Sensor Circuit/Open
P28CB.d: A brushless motor can only be commutated correctly if the electronics know where the rotor stands; P28CB reports that the signal from the sensor tracking the clutch A motor's rotor position is missing or electrically unusable, mostly through an open line. Without it the controller cannot switch the U-V-W phases in the right order or count motor revolutions, so the pump of clutch A is shut down. In Getrag-type pump actuators these brushless ferrite motors are shared parts, and the position signal also serves to check motor speed against the pressure target. Typical causes: an open sensor feed or ground, a corroded pin, a failed sensor element. P28CC covers a signal that is present but implausible. No manufacturer publishes P28CB details.
c: Open signal, supply or ground wire of the clutch A motor position sensor
Corroded or loose pin at the actuator connector
Failed position sensor inside the actuator
s: Clutch A disabled, gears on that shaft unavailable
Transmission warning lamp
Possibly also motor speed codes stored

P28CC.t: Clutch A Motor Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P28CC.d: P28CC is the plausibility counterpart to P28CB: the position signal of the clutch A motor arrives, but its values or their sequence make no sense, for example jumps between rotor angles, a missing step in the pattern, or a speed that contradicts the phase currents. CARB expects rationality checks of this kind for input components where feasible. Electrical noise from a damaged shield, a partially broken wire, a loose sensor mount or magnet, and contamination of the sensor target are typical reasons. Since commutation depends on this signal, the motor may stutter, overshoot or stall, which can also produce P28C9 or P28CA. No manufacturer publicly documents P28CC; the result for the driver is lost or rough engagement of clutch A.
c: Partly broken wire or loose contact causing signal dropouts
Electrical interference on the position signal through a damaged shield
Loose sensor, shifted magnet or contaminated sensor target
s: Clutch A engages roughly or intermittently
Transmission warning, sometimes only while driving
Gear changes on one shaft delayed or withheld

P28CD.d: P28CD concerns the pressure sensor that tells the transmission controller how much oil pressure acts on clutch A. In pump-actuated wet DCTs there is no proportional valve to set pressure; instead Getrag places a pressure sensor downstream of the clutch pumps and closes the control loop over motor speed. P28CD is the general circuit fault, chiefly an interrupted signal, supply or ground line, so the controller receives no usable reading at all. Without feedback it cannot dose clutch torque and will normally take clutch A out of service. P28CE and P28CF describe a signal stuck at the low or high end, P28D0 a value that is in range but wrong. No manufacturer publicly documents P28CD.
c: Open signal, 5-volt supply or ground wire of the clutch A pressure sensor
Sensor connector not fully latched or pin pushed out
Internal open in the pressure sensor
s: Clutch A shut off, half of the gears unavailable
Transmission warning lamp and stored code

P28CE.t: Clutch A Pressure Sensor Circuit Low
P28CE.d: P28CE is logged when the clutch A pressure sensor output drops below the lowest voltage a working sensor can produce. Ratiometric pressure sensors are usually designed so that even zero pressure gives a small offset voltage; a reading underneath that band therefore means an electrical fault, not low pressure. Classic causes are a signal wire shorted to ground, a collapsed 5-volt reference shared with other sensors, or an internal short in the sensor. If the reference is the problem, several sensor codes often appear together. The pressure closed loop of the pump actuator then lacks feedback and clutch A is typically switched off. P28CF is the high-side twin; no manufacturer publicly documents P28CE values.
c: Pressure sensor signal wire shorted to ground
5-volt reference pulled down by another sensor on the same supply
Internally shorted clutch A pressure sensor
s: Clutch A disabled with transmission warning
Other sensor codes may be stored at the same time
Reduced choice of gears

P28CF.t: Clutch A Pressure Sensor Circuit High
P28CF.d: P28CF means the voltage from the clutch A pressure sensor climbs above the band a plausible measurement can reach, usually close to the reference or battery voltage. An open ground line is a frequent trigger, because many sensor circuits then float up to the supply level; a signal wire touching the 5-volt or 12-volt feed, or a sensor with a broken internal element, has the same effect. To the controller this would look like maximum clutch pressure, so it cannot trust the closed-loop pump control and normally deactivates clutch A to avoid unintended engagement. The low-side counterpart is P28CE and the general circuit code P28CD. No manufacturer publicly documents P28CF.
c: Open ground wire of the clutch A pressure sensor
Signal wire shorted to the 5-volt reference or battery voltage
Pressure sensor failed with output stuck high
s: Transmission warning, clutch A taken out of service
Pull-away or shifts only on the other clutch

P28D0.t: Clutch A Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P28D0.d: P28D0 is the rationality fault of the clutch A pressure sensor: its voltage lies inside the valid window, but the indicated pressure does not match what the system should be producing. In a pump actuator the controller can cross-check this well, because pressure in the clutch circuit rises with pump motor speed and current; an EVS32 paper describes how directly the gerotor flow translates into clutch pressure. A sensor that drifts, sticks at one value, or reacts slowly fails that comparison, as does a reading with no pressure at rest. CARB asks for such two-sided checks where feasible. Real pressure problems from leaks or a weak pump may show up together with P28C8. No manufacturer publicly documents P28D0.
c: Clutch A pressure sensor drifting or sticking
Real pressure deviation from leakage or weak pump, misread as a sensor fault
Contact resistance in the signal path shifting the reading
s: Harsh or slipping engagement of clutch A
Transmission warning, possibly after some time driving
Gears on clutch A may be withheld

P28D1.t: Clutch A Motor Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P28D1.d: P28D1 is set when the power stage that drives the clutch A motor exceeds its current limit or its internal temperature limit. This output stage, usually part of the transmission controller or the actuator electronics, protects itself by shutting down or derating, after which clutch A can no longer be operated normally. Overcurrent typically follows a motor that is hard to turn, such as a pump jammed by debris as Stellantis describes for the 7HDT300 actuator, or a shorted winding. Overheating also results from long periods of high pressure demand, for instance creeping in traffic or hill holds, and from a hot clutch already flagged by P2787. Phase circuit faults are P28C4-P28C6. No manufacturer publishes P28D1 thresholds.
c: Clutch A motor or pump hard to turn, e.g. jammed by particles
Long periods of high clutch pressure demand in stop-and-go or on gradients
Shorted motor winding drawing excess current
s: Transmission warning after heavy use, may clear after cooling down
Clutch A temporarily disabled
Possibly stored together with clutch temperature code P2787

P28D2.t: Clutch B Motor Phase U-V-W Circuit Low
P28D2.d: P28D2 reports that on the U, V or W lead feeding the electric drive of clutch B a voltage below its expected level is measured, pointing to a short towards ground. Such motor-driven clutches are found in wet dual-clutch units of the Getrag/Magna pump-actuator family; the 7DCT300 went into series in 2015 with the Renault Espace, and the hybrid 7HDT300 uses the same principle. In the Stellantis hybrid version clutch B carries the even gears. Frequent triggers are insulation rubbed through on a bracket, water in the actuator plug or a failed low-side transistor. Overvoltage on a phase is P28D3, an open lead P28D4; P28C4 is the clutch A twin. No carmaker publishes a limit; the even-shaft gears may be withheld.
c: Insulation of a clutch B motor phase rubbed through against ground
Water or corrosion in the clutch B actuator plug pulling a phase low
Failed low-side transistor of the clutch B motor driver
s: Transmission warning light, MIL possible
Gears on the clutch B shaft unavailable (even gears on the 7HDT300)
Harsh or hesitant gear changes

P28D3.t: Clutch B Motor Phase U-V-W Circuit High
P28D3.d: P28D3 is the high-voltage fault on the phase wiring of the clutch B motor: a lead reads above what the inverter pattern should produce, typically because it contacts a positive feed or the upper switch cannot turn off. In the Getrag 7DCT300 five brushless motors share the housing, two for the shift drums, two for the clutch pumps and one for the cooling pump, so motor harnesses run close together and a chafed spot can bridge to a neighbouring supply. Pin corrosion in the connector is a further candidate. P28D2 is the ground-side fault, P28D4 the interruption, and P28C5 the matching clutch A code. Values are not public. The transmission controller usually disables clutch B and drives on the other half.
c: Clutch B motor phase touching a neighbouring positive feed in the harness
Corroded pins bridging at the clutch B motor connector
Upper output switch for the clutch B motor stays conducting
s: Warning lamp and stored fault code
Vehicle drives on with only one clutch, gear choice reduced
Possible jerk when the controller drops clutch B

P28D4.t: Clutch B Motor Phase U-V-W Circuit/Open
P28D4.d: P28D4 covers the circuit of the three motor phases for clutch B in general and is mainly logged when the controller energises a phase and no current returns, meaning the path is broken. Getrag chose brushless ferrite motors without rare earths for this pump-actuator generation and reused them from the 6DCT250; if one winding path is lost, the remaining two cannot turn the rotor smoothly, and the gerotor pump of clutch B stops delivering oil to the clutch piston. Loose crimp terminals, a fractured wire near the actuator, or an internal connection cracked by heat cycles are the usual finds. P28D2/P28D3 describe phases forced low or high; P28C6 is the same fault on clutch A. No manufacturer has published P28D4 details.
c: Loose or spread crimp terminal on a clutch B motor phase
Phase wire fractured close to the clutch B actuator
Internal winding joint in the clutch B motor cracked by thermal cycling
s: Clutch B cannot be closed, its gears are blocked
Fault may appear only on rough roads or when hot
Transmission warning, MIL depending on make

P28D5.t: Clutch B Motor Phase U-V-W Performance
P28D5.d: P28D5 means the clutch B motor wiring passes the electrical checks, yet the motor's behaviour, its phase currents and resulting rotation, does not follow what the controller demands. It is one of the few codes in this group with a public manufacturer reference: Stellantis bulletin 21-040-26 (May 2026), valid for Jeep Renegade and Compass of model years 2022-2025 sold in Europe with the 1.5 MHEV and the 7HDT300 hybrid DCT, pairs P28D5 with the clutch temperature code P27F3. That pair points at the actuator cylinder for the even gears; particles inside the gearbox can jam one of its pumps. The MIL is lit, and if the activation routine fails, the even-gear actuator is renewed with 3.0 labour hours allowed. P28C7 is the odd-gear twin.
c: Particles from the gearbox jamming a pump in the even-gear actuator (Stellantis 7HDT300)
Clutch B actuator motor running stiff or weak
Raised contact resistance on one phase causing uneven currents
s: MIL on, transmission warning shown
Even gears not available on the 7HDT300
Often logged together with clutch B temperature code P27F3

P28D6.t: Clutch B Motor Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P28D6.d: P28D6 tells that the electronic switch stage powering the clutch B motor has hit its overcurrent or overtemperature protection. Normally these pump actuators draw very little; Getrag quotes roughly 31 W (NEDC) and 33 W (WLTC) for the complete 7DCT300 actuation, so a stage running into its limits indicates the motor is working against unusual resistance or a fault in the stage itself. Candidates include a pump seized by particles, which Stellantis reports for the 7HDT300 actuator under P28D5, a shorted motor winding, or long stretches of high clamping demand while the clutch is already hot, as P27F3 would show. Wiring faults on the phases fall under P28D2-P28D4; the clutch A counterpart is P28D1. Limits are not public.
c: Clutch B pump seized by particles, motor stalls and draws excess current
Turn-to-turn short in the clutch B motor winding
Prolonged high pressure demand with hot clutch, e.g. stop-and-go or towing
Defective output stage or poor heat transfer in the controller
s: Clutch B shut down temporarily, may recover after cooling
Transmission warning and restricted gears
May appear together with P27F3 or P28D5

P28D7.d: P28D7 judges motor and pump of clutch B as one unit: the oil pressure seen by the sensor, or the speed and current the motor needs for it, does not match the target. Getrag's hydraulic plan for the 7DCT300 has both clutch pumps drawing through a common suction filter, with a pressure sensor downstream of both pumps providing feedback. If P28D7 and the clutch A code P28C8 are stored together, the shared filter or the oil level is therefore a natural suspect; P28D7 on its own points more towards the clutch B pump, its gerotor set or leaking seals in the clutch B circuit. An EVS32 study with Hyundai found such on-demand pumps cut actuation energy by 96.5 % in the WLTP versus an engine-driven pump. No manufacturer documents P28D7 publicly.
c: Clogged common suction filter, especially if P28C8 is stored too
Leaking seals in the clutch B pressure circuit
Worn or contaminated gerotor set of the clutch B pump
s: Clutch B slips or engages late
Transmission warning, gears on clutch B possibly locked out
Unusual humming from the actuator area

P28D8.d: P28D8 sets when the clutch B motor spins faster than the controller expects for the commanded pressure. A gerotor works by positive displacement, the EVS32 model uses one with a seven-tooth outer rotor, so in a sealed clutch circuit its speed should fall once pressure is built; a motor that keeps accelerating means oil is escaping or the pump has lost its load. Plausible reasons are a worn piston or rotary seal in the clutch B circuit, aeration from low oil, or a sheared drive between motor shaft and inner rotor. A false speed reading from the rotor position sensor can mimic the same, so P28DA and P28DB should be cleared first. Slow running is P28D9; on clutch A the code is P28C9. No limits are published.
c: Worn piston or rotary feedthrough seal letting oil escape from the clutch B circuit
Aerated oil due to low level, pump runs without load
Sheared drive between clutch B motor shaft and inner rotor
Rotor position sensor reporting an excessive speed
s: Clutch B does not hold full torque, flaring on shifts
Transmission warning and limited gears

P28D9.d: P28D9 indicates that the clutch B motor cannot reach the speed it is commanded to, leaving the pump short of flow to raise or adjust clutch pressure. Getrag states that its pump actuators control pressure consistently down to low temperatures, so a motor that persistently lags points to extra drag rather than normal cold behaviour: particles caught in the gerotor, a tight bearing, or oil of the wrong grade. Stellantis names jammed actuator pumps on the 7HDT300 in bulletin 21-040-26, but lists P28D5 there, not P28D9. On the electrical side a weak supply or a driver stage that reduces output due to heat, logged as P28D6, can also hold the motor back. Excess speed is P28D8; P28CA is the clutch A version. No threshold is public.
c: Particles caught in the clutch B gerotor pump
Tight or damaged bearing in the clutch B motor or pump
Incorrect transmission fluid with too high viscosity
Low supply voltage or poor ground at the actuator
s: Delayed or jerky engagement of clutch B
Fault more likely after standing in the cold
Clutch B gears may be withheld

P28DA.t: Clutch B Motor Position Sensor Circuit/Open
P28DA.d: P28DA concerns the electrical circuit of the sensor that reports the rotor angle of the clutch B motor, and is chiefly stored when that signal disappears because a line is open. Electronic commutation of a brushless motor relies on this angle to energise U, V and W in the right order; it also lets the controller count revolutions and compare pump speed with the pressure sensor. Without a valid signal the clutch B pump is stopped and the gears on that shaft are no longer offered. Usual culprits are a broken sensor supply or ground, a pin pushed out of the connector, or a dead Hall or magnetic element inside the actuator. P28DB handles a signal that exists but is inconsistent; P28CB is the clutch A equivalent. Details are unpublished.
c: Open supply, ground or signal line of the clutch B motor position sensor
Pin pushed out or bent at the clutch B actuator connector
Failed sensing element inside the clutch B actuator
s: Clutch B out of service, half of the gears missing
Transmission warning lamp on
Motor speed codes for clutch B may be stored as follow-up faults

P28DB.t: Clutch B Motor Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P28DB.d: P28DB flags a rotor position signal for the clutch B motor that is electrically present but fails the plausibility tests: angle steps arrive in a wrong order, a transition is skipped, or the derived speed disagrees with the phase currents and the measured clutch pressure. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 calls for such rationality monitoring of input signals where it is technically feasible, beyond pure circuit checks. Interference through a damaged screen, a wire strand partly broken, a sensor or target magnet that has shifted, or metallic debris on the target are typical findings. Because commutation then goes wrong, the motor may judder or stall and P28D8 or P28D9 can follow. P28DA is the hard circuit fault, P28CC the clutch A twin. No carmaker documents P28DB.
c: Electrical interference through a damaged screen on the sensor lead
Partly broken strand in the clutch B position sensor wiring
Sensor or target magnet shifted, or metallic debris on the target
s: Clutch B engages roughly or drops out intermittently
Transmission warning, sometimes only after several trips
Motor speed codes for clutch B stored alongside

P28DC.d: P28DC concerns the sensor that reports the hydraulic pressure acting on clutch B of a dual-clutch or hybrid transmission. The code points to a broken connection: the module receives no usable signal at all, as happens when a signal, supply or ground wire is open or the connector has come off. No manufacturer documents P28DC publicly. A Getrag patent shows why the reading matters: each clutch has its own actuator pump with a dedicated electric drive, and the measured pressure closes the loop over motor speed; an Audi patent likewise gives every clutch its own pressure sensor. CARB requires circuit checks on such inputs. Which clutch carries the letter B is up to the maker. Without the signal the module runs clutch B on a fallback or takes it out of use.
c: Connector at the sensor or transmission plug loose, unplugged or with a pushed-back pin
Signal, supply or ground wire of the sensor broken
Sensor input in the transmission control module faulty
s: Transmission warning or check engine light on
Gears served by clutch B blocked, transmission in emergency mode
Jerky launch or harsh shifts

P28DD.t: Clutch B Pressure Sensor Circuit Low
P28DD.d: Set when the voltage from the clutch B pressure sensor falls below the lowest value the part can produce in normal service. Usually the signal line has a short to ground, the sensor supply is missing or the sensor has failed internally. Because the reading lies outside the valid band, the module treats it as an electrical fault rather than as low pressure. No manufacturer documents P28DD publicly. Patents from Getrag and Audi place one pressure sensor at every clutch of a twin-clutch gearbox so the controller can regulate clutch pressure directly; under CARB rules such inputs need an out-of-range check. P28DE is the high counterpart, P28DC the open circuit and P28CE the same fault on clutch A. Shifts that need clutch B may be blocked.
c: Sensor signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Sensor supply voltage missing or pulled down by another shorted sensor on the same supply
s: Transmission warning or check engine light on
Transmission in emergency mode, some gears unavailable
Harsh or delayed engagement

P28DE.t: Clutch B Pressure Sensor Circuit High
P28DE.d: P28DE means the clutch B pressure sensor delivers a voltage above anything a working sensor would show, even at full clutch pressure. Typical causes are a signal line touching a supply or battery feed, a broken sensor ground, or a signal line open at the sensor end where the input uses a pull-up resistor. No manufacturer documents P28DE publicly. In the actuator layout of a Getrag patent the pressure at each clutch is set by the speed of its own pump motor and checked by a pressure sensor, so a falsely high value would lead the controller to under-apply the clutch; an Audi patent shows the same one-sensor-per-clutch idea. Out-of-range checks on this kind of input are a CARB requirement. P28DD is the low fault and P28CF the clutch A version. The module usually disables clutch B.
c: Signal wire shorted to the sensor supply or to battery voltage
Sensor ground open or high resistance at the connector
Pressure sensor failed with output stuck high
s: Transmission warning or check engine light on
Emergency mode with limited gears
Slipping or weak pull when clutch B is in use

P28DF.t: Clutch B Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P28DF.d: Here the clutch B pressure signal is electrically valid, yet it does not fit the situation. Examples are a reading that stays well above zero while the clutch is released, a value that does not rise when the actuator builds pressure, or a mismatch between commanded and measured pressure that persists. No manufacturer documents P28DF publicly. A Getrag patent regulates each clutch by the speed of its own motor-driven pump and feeds the measured pressure back, which gives the controller an expected value to compare with; an Audi patent even uses a clutch pressure sensor to estimate accumulator pressure. CARB requires rationality checks on inputs. Besides sensor drift, a real pressure problem such as a leaking piston seal or a weak pump can trigger it.
c: Pressure sensor drifting or with offset at zero pressure
Actual clutch pressure wrong because of leaking seals, a weak actuator pump or low fluid
Corroded or loose contacts distorting the signal
Control software needs an update or new adaptation
s: Transmission warning or check engine light on
Shudder, slip or jerky engagement on clutch B
Emergency mode after a few drives

P28E0.t: Shift Motor Phase U-V-W Circuit Low
P28E0.d: The shift motor is the three-phase electric motor of an electronic range actuator: in shift-by-wire systems it turns the detent plate and selector shaft between P, R, N and D. A Denso patent describes such a motor whose driver energises the U, V and W phases in turn, with a motor relay in the supply; Hyundai Kefico sells its SBW actuator with a brushless motor. P28E0 reports a phase voltage below what the driver commands, typically a phase lead or winding shorted to ground. No manufacturer documents P28E0 publicly; Hyundai lists the open-circuit sibling P28E2. CARB requires circuit checks on outputs. The controller usually cuts the motor off, so the selected range can no longer be changed and the car may be stuck in P.
c: Phase lead to the actuator chafed and shorted to ground
Motor winding shorted to the actuator housing (moisture, insulation damage)
Output stage in the shift control unit faulty
s: Shift system warning in the cluster
Selected range cannot be changed, vehicle may stay in Park
Engine may not start because Park or Neutral is not confirmed

P28E1.t: Shift Motor Phase U-V-W Circuit High
P28E1.d: P28E1 is the opposite of P28E0: on any of the three shift motor phases the controller sees a voltage that is higher than the switching state allows, for example while the low-side switch should pull it down. Likely reasons are a phase lead touching a battery-powered wire, a winding with an internal short to a live part, or a high-side switch in the driver that no longer turns off. No manufacturer documents P28E1 publicly. The hardware is the same as described in a Denso shift range patent, where a motor driver feeds the U, V and W phases and a relay can disconnect the motor, and in Hyundai Kefico's brushless SBW actuator. CARB requires circuit checks on outputs. With a phase held high the motor cannot be commutated, so range changes stop.
c: Phase lead shorted to a battery-voltage wire in the harness
High-side switch in the shift control unit stuck on
Water or corrosion bridging pins in the actuator connector
s: Shift system warning in the cluster
No response to the gear selector
Vehicle may remain in Park

P28E2.d: P28E2 reports that no current can flow in at least one shift motor phase, usually a broken lead, a loose terminal or an open winding. Hyundai documents it in bulletin 22-AT-001H with failure type 14 (P28E214), an open UVW motor circuit, for the push-button shift-by-wire of the 2020-on Palisade and Sonata, the 2021-on Santa Fe and Santa Fe Hybrid and the 2022-on Tucson and Tucson Hybrid. Drivers see a shifter system malfunction message and may be unable to leave Park or start. For the Santa Fe the bulletin asks to remove air cleaner, battery and tray and check whether the actuator harness has rubbed through on the battery tray, then repair it. A Denso patent shows the U-V-W motor driver behind such actuators. CARB requires circuit checks on outputs.
c: Actuator harness chafed open, on the Santa Fe at the battery tray (Hyundai 22-AT-001H)
Loose or damaged pin in the SBW actuator connector
Open winding inside the SBW actuator
s: Shifter system malfunction message in the cluster
Cannot shift into or out of gear or out of Park
Wrong gear display or no start

P28E3.d: P28E3 covers the phase circuits of the shift motor when none of them is clearly open or shorted, yet they do not behave as expected: one phase draws noticeably more or less current than the others, or the current pattern does not match the commutation step. Such an imbalance comes from a phase with raised resistance, a partly shorted winding or a weak switch in the driver, and it shows up as uneven torque. No manufacturer documents P28E3 publicly. A Denso shift range patent describes the motor driver that energises U, V and W according to the rotor position and stops the motor at a target encoder count; Hyundai Kefico builds its SBW actuator around a brushless motor. CARB requires functional checks on outputs. Range changes may be slow, noisy or refused.
c: Corroded or loose contact raising the resistance of one phase
Partly shorted turns in a motor winding
Degraded switch in the motor driver
s: Shift system warning in the cluster
Slow or noisy range changes
Occasional refusal to change range

P28E4.t: Shift Motor Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P28E4.d: P28E4 says the output stage that powers the shift motor has reached its current or temperature limit and has protected itself. A blocked actuator is the classic trigger: if the detent plate, the park pawl linkage or the gear train inside the actuator binds, the motor stalls and current climbs. Shorts between phases, or many range changes in a row in hot conditions, can also heat the driver. No manufacturer documents P28E4 publicly.
