In a Denso shift range patent the motor driver energises the three phases and a motor relay sits between driver and battery, so the controller can cut power when a limit is hit; Hyundai Kefico integrates control unit and brushless motor in one SBW actuator. CARB requires circuit and functional checks on outputs. Until it cools down, the system may refuse shifts.
c: Detent mechanism, park pawl linkage or actuator gearing binding
Driver overheated after repeated range changes or high ambient heat
s: Shift system warning in the cluster
Range change stops halfway or is refused
Problem may disappear after the system cools down

P28E5.d: P28E5 judges the shift motor by its result: it is driven, but the actuator does not get to the commanded range as expected. Hyundai lists it in bulletin 22-AT-001H for the shift-by-wire Palisade, Santa Fe, Sonata and Tucson (including hybrids) with two failure types: P28E577, commanded position not reached, and P28E592, SBW motor performance. The bulletin tells technicians to watch the motor feedback current in the SCU data while pressing a shift button; a brief current means the SCU drives the actuator, no current points to the SCU or its wiring. It also compares target and actual lever positions to separate actuator from shifter faults. A Denso patent shows the motor being stopped at a target encoder count, which is the check this code relies on.
c: SBW actuator worn internally or mechanism stiff
Shift control unit or its harness not delivering motor current
Low 12 V supply during the shift
Shift control software needing an update
s: Shifter system malfunction message in the cluster
Range not engaged or engaged with delay
Wrong gear display

P28E6.d: P28E6 is set when the shift motor turns faster than its control allows. In a position-controlled actuator this is visible from the rotor feedback: the encoder count changes quicker than the commanded movement can explain. Plausible reasons are a load that suddenly disappears, for example a broken gear or coupling between motor and selector shaft, a control loop running away after a feedback error, or a faulty speed or rotor signal. No manufacturer documents P28E6 publicly. A Denso patent describes the logic: the motor is driven by feedback until the encoder reaches a target count, with output shaft sensors confirming the detent position; Hyundai Kefico uses a brushless motor in its SBW actuator. CARB requires functional checks on outputs. The actuator may overshoot the range or be shut down.
c: Broken gear or coupling inside the actuator, motor spins without load
Faulty rotor position or encoder signal
Control software error in the shift control unit
s: Shift system warning in the cluster
Wrong range engaged or range change aborted
Clicking or whirring from the actuator

P28E7.d: The shift motor position sensor tells the controller where the selector shaft of a shift-by-wire actuator stands. In a Denso patent it is a contactless magnetic sensor on the detent plate with two independent units, so two signals reach the ECU; Hyundai notes in bulletin 22-AT-001H that the readings of its two position sensors should add up to roughly 100 percent. P28E7 marks a broken circuit: no usable signal arrives, typically because the signal, supply or ground lead is interrupted or the plug has been pulled. No manufacturer documents P28E7 itself publicly; Kia uses the High variant P28E8. CARB requires circuit checks on inputs. Without a confirmed position the system cannot verify Park, so it may refuse to shift or to start.
c: Position sensor connector loose, corroded or unplugged
Signal, supply or ground wire of the sensor broken
s: Shift system warning in the cluster
Gear display missing or wrong
Vehicle refuses to shift or does not start

P28E8.t: Shift Motor Position Sensor Circuit High
P28E8.d: P28E8 means the shift motor position sensor reports a value above its permitted range. Kia documents it on the 2024-25 EV9: service action SA594 (bulletin ELE362, January 2025) covers cars built from 25 September 2023 to 4 September 2024 that may not leave Park while P28E812 is stored, which Kia attributes to an output shaft sensor reading above what it should be. The fix is new software for the shift control unit, event 787, an improvement of the fault judgment logic, also offered over the air. Outside that campaign the usual causes apply: a signal line shorted to a supply, an open sensor ground or a failed sensor. A Denso patent describes such output shaft sensors with two independent channels. CARB requires out-of-range checks on inputs. P28E9 is the low fault.
c: Shift control unit software on the 2024-25 Kia EV9 (service action SA594)
Sensor signal shorted to supply or battery voltage
Position sensor failed with output stuck high
s: Vehicle cannot be shifted out of Park
Shift system warning in the cluster

P28E9.t: Shift Motor Position Sensor Circuit Low
P28E9.d: P28E9 is stored when the signal of the shift motor position sensor sits below its valid band. Typical causes are a signal line shorted to ground, a sensor supply that has collapsed, for instance because another sensor on the same feed is shorted, or a failed sensor. No manufacturer documents P28E9 publicly; Kia documents the high counterpart P28E8 on the EV9. In a Denso patent the sensor sits on the detent plate and sends two independent signals, which lets the controller spot a single failed channel; Hyundai's bulletin 22-AT-001H gives the rule of thumb that both position sensor readings sum to about 100 percent, a quick check on the scan tool. Per CARB, inputs like this must be checked for out-of-range values. The actuator usually stays where it is and range changes are blocked.
c: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Sensor supply missing or pulled down
Position sensor failed with output stuck low
s: Shift system warning in the cluster
Range changes blocked or gear display wrong
Engine or drive system may not start

P28EA.t: Shift Motor Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P28EA.d: P28EA covers a position signal that is electrically valid but implausible: the two channels disagree, the value does not move although the motor runs, or the actuator ends up away from the expected detent. Hyundai uses the code in bulletin 22-AT-001H for its shift-by-wire models with two failure types, P28EA71, SBW actuator stuck, and P28EA77, commanded position not reached. The diagnosis compares target and actual lever positions in the SCU data and checks that both position sensor readings total about 100 percent; a related bulletin covers replacing the position sensor or actuator. A Denso patent explains why the check works: the controller relates the encoder count to changes of two output shaft signals. CARB requires rationality checks on inputs. Shifting is limited or refused.
c: SBW actuator stuck or not reaching the commanded position
Position sensor channels drifting apart (sum no longer near 100 percent)
Intermittent contact in the sensor or actuator harness
s: Shifter system malfunction message in the cluster
Cannot shift out of Park or into the requested range
Gear display does not match the selected range

P28EB.d: A shift-by-wire actuator has to learn which motor positions match P, R, N and D before it can work precisely. A Hyundai Autron patent does this from motor current: while the actuator travels between P and D, the load changes each time the detent spring passes one of the four notches of the detent plate, so R and N are found first and P and D derived by offset. A Denso patent learns a correction value at a limit of travel and the play between motor and output shaft. P28EB says these values are missing, typically after a new control unit or actuator, a software update or lost memory. It is a status code more than a hardware fault. No manufacturer documents P28EB publicly. The remedy is the learning routine with a scan tool; P28EC is a learned value out of limits.
c: Learning routine not run after replacing the control unit or actuator
Learned values cleared by a software update or memory loss
Learning aborted by low battery voltage or an active fault
s: Shift system warning in the cluster
Imprecise or refused range changes until learning is done

P28EC.t: Shift Motor Position Sensor Exceeded Learning Limit
P28EC.d: Unlike P28EB, learning did take place here, but the result lies outside the window the controller accepts. The learned sensor values for the end stop or for the P, R, N and D detents differ too far from the nominal ones, or the measured play is too large. Causes are mechanical wear or damage in the detent mechanism, an actuator mounted out of position on the selector shaft, a wrong or mismatched part, or a sensor with a large offset. No manufacturer documents P28EC publicly. In a Denso patent, encoder and output shaft signals yield a correction value at a travel limit plus the motor-to-output-shaft play; a Hyundai Autron patent derives the detent positions from changes in motor current. CARB requires rationality checks on inputs. Repeating the learning without a fix will fail again.
c: Actuator or sensor mounted out of position after a repair
Worn or damaged detent plate, detent spring or linkage
Wrong or mismatched actuator or sensor fitted
s: Shift system warning in the cluster
Learning routine fails repeatedly
Range changes imprecise or blocked

P28ED.t: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump B Overspeed
P28ED.d: Pump B is a second electrically driven transmission fluid pump that works independently of the engine, for example to hold pressure during start-stop or electric driving, or to feed clutch cooling. P28ED says its motor runs faster than commanded or faster than its permitted maximum. That typically happens when the pump loses its load because it draws air, at low fluid level or with a blocked suction filter, or when the speed estimate of a sensorless motor goes wrong. No manufacturer documents P28ED publicly. Analogous checks exist for single pumps: GM logs P179A on the 2016 Cadillac ELR when the pump motor exceeds its maximum speed of 6500 rpm, Type A, and Ford's 2019 plug-in hybrids flag a speed above 105 percent of command for 3 s under P0B0D. CARB requires functional checks.
c: Low fluid level or air drawn in, so the pump runs without load
Faulty speed feedback or control in the pump controller
s: Transmission warning or check engine light on
Start-stop or electric driving disabled
Whining from the pump area

P28EE.t: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump B Underspeed
P28EE.d: P28EE is the reverse of P28ED: electric transmission fluid pump B does not reach the speed its controller asks for. The motor is fed, but something holds it back, such as very cold and thick fluid, a binding or worn pump, debris in the gears or a low supply voltage. When the speed falls to zero the matching code is the stall P277C rather than this one. No manufacturer documents P28EE publicly. Comparable logic exists for single pumps: on the 2016 Cadillac ELR GM sets P1E3A, Type A, when commanded minus actual speed exceeds 200 rpm while more than 6.8 Nm is requested, while under P0B0D Ford's 2019 plug-in hybrids react to a speed under 95 percent of command for 3 s. CARB requires functional checks. The car then keeps the engine running or limits electric driving.
c: Pump binding, worn or contaminated with debris
Very cold, aged or wrong transmission fluid
Low supply voltage or high resistance in the pump feed
s: Transmission warning or check engine light on
Engine keeps running at stops, electric driving limited
Delayed engagement after an automatic engine restart

P28EF.t: Engine Disconnect Clutch Actuator Performance/Stuck Off
P28EF.d: In a P2 hybrid a clutch placed between combustion engine and e-machine lets the car drive electrically with the engine at rest and couples the engine back in when it is needed. P28EF says the device that applies this clutch is not doing its job: it is commanded to act, but the expected pressure or clutch response stays absent, so the actuator behaves as if switched off. No manufacturer documents P28EF publicly. On Audi's A3 e-tron the clutch is applied through a pressure regulating valve in the mechatronic unit, and a mechanically faulty valve there produced the neighbouring code P2884 (clutch stuck open); a Ford patent feeds the clutch valves from hydraulic pumps. CARB counts such hybrid parts as monitored output components. The engine may then fail to join in or to start.
c: Pressure regulating valve of the disconnect clutch sticking or mechanically faulty
Contaminated or low transmission fluid, so the actuator cannot build pressure
Electric or mechanical oil pump delivers too little pressure to the clutch circuit
Control software or learned clutch values out of date
s: Engine does not start or does not engage while driving in hybrid mode
Gearbox or hybrid system warning in the cluster
Reduced power or electric-only limp mode

P28F0.t: Engine Disconnect Clutch Actuator Stuck On
P28F0.d: P28F0 is the opposite of P28EF: the actuator of the engine disconnect clutch keeps applying the clutch although the controller wants it released. The engine then stays tied to e-machine and wheels, so electric-only driving and engine stop at standstill are no longer possible. No manufacturer documents P28F0 publicly. A Hyundai patent explains how such a fault is found: with the clutch commanded open, the speeds on both sides of it are compared, and if they still match, the clutch is judged stuck; the controller then blocks engine restarts that could push torque straight to the drive shaft. CARB treats the clutch actuator as a monitored hybrid output. P2886 names a clutch stuck closed itself, while P28F0 blames the actuator. Expect stalling or shudder at stops.
c: Clutch pressure valve stuck in the applied position, for example by debris
Valve or actuator driver permanently energised by a short in wiring or module
Clutch plates overheated and dragging so the actuator cannot release them
s: Engine stalls or shudders when the car comes to a stop
No electric-only driving, engine runs all the time
Hybrid system warning and restricted engine restarts

P28F1.t: Engine Disconnect Clutch Pressure Sensor Circuit
P28F1.d: A hydraulically applied disconnect clutch often has its own pressure sensor so the controller knows how firmly the clutch is held. Ford fits one to the 10R80 modular hybrid transmission of the 2021 Explorer, Aviator and F-150 hybrids; a Ford bulletin covers fluid seeping out at this sensor because its fasteners worked loose, fixed by retightening them. P28F1 is the general electrical fault of that sensor circuit, used when the module cannot tell low from high, typically an open signal, supply or ground wire or a connector that has lost contact. No manufacturer ties P28F1 to a threshold in public. CARB requires circuit checks on such inputs. Without a valid reading the clutch is run on a model or locked open, so the engine may stay off or engagement turns harsh.
c: Sensor connector loose, corroded or with a pushed-back terminal
Signal, reference or ground wire of the sensor broken
Pressure sensor electronics failed, possibly after fluid ingress at a leaking seal
Sensor input of the transmission or hybrid control module faulty
s: Hybrid or transmission warning light
Engine stays off or engages harshly when it should join in
Possible fluid wetness around the sensor

P28F2.t: Engine Disconnect Clutch Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P28F2.d: Here the wiring is intact and the voltage lies inside the valid band, yet the reading does not fit the situation. A Hyundai and Kia patent describes one such test: when the car is parked, the electric oil pump for the engine clutch is off, a soak time has passed and the vehicle stands still, no pressure can exist, so a sensor output above a set reference counts as a fault. The background is the zero-point learning of the sensor; a wrong offset makes the controller believe the clutch is open or closed when it is not, and slipping was observed. No manufacturer links P28F2 to this test in public. CARB requires such rationality checks on inputs. P28F3 and P28F4 are the out-of-range faults. Engagement quality suffers and the clutch may slip or bite hard.
c: Pressure sensor zero point drifted or wrongly learned
Real residual pressure from a sticking valve, so the sensor is not at fault
High resistance in sensor ground or signal line shifting the reading
s: Clutch slips or engages abruptly when the engine is coupled in
Hybrid or transmission warning light
Shudder during engine start while driving electrically

P28F3.t: Engine Disconnect Clutch Pressure Sensor Circuit Low
P28F3.d: P28F3 is stored when the voltage of the disconnect clutch pressure sensor drops below the smallest value a healthy part can output, a level that stands for an electrical fault, not for an open clutch. The usual suspects are a signal wire chafed against ground, a sensor reference supply that is missing or dragged down by another shorted sensor on the same feed, or a failed sensor. No manufacturer documents P28F3 with a threshold in public. Ford uses a separate pressure sensor at this clutch in its 10R80 hybrid gearbox, and a Hyundai patent shows the same single-sensor layout for the engine clutch. CARB requires out-of-range checks on such inputs. P28F4 is the high fault and P28F1 the unspecified circuit fault. The controller usually keeps the clutch open or runs it without feedback.
c: Signal wire shorted to ground through chafed insulation
Sensor reference supply missing or pulled low by another shorted sensor
Pressure sensor failed with output stuck low
s: Hybrid or transmission warning light
Engine coupling blocked, car runs electrically or in limp mode
Harsh engagement if the clutch is still used

P28F4.t: Engine Disconnect Clutch Pressure Sensor Circuit High
P28F4.d: With P28F4 the disconnect clutch pressure sensor sends a voltage above anything it could produce even at full clutch pressure. Typical reasons are a signal line touching the reference or battery supply, an open sensor ground, or on inputs with a pull-up resistor a signal wire that is broken at the sensor. No manufacturer publishes a threshold for P28F4. The sensor matters because the controller closes the clutch by pressure: Ford mounts one on the clutch of its 10R80 hybrid gearbox, while Hyundai notes in a patent that a reading wrongly offset from the real pressure makes the clutch slip. A falsely high value would suggest a firmly closed clutch. CARB obliges the maker to test such inputs against their valid range. P28F3 is the low fault. Most systems stop using the clutch until the fault clears.
c: Signal wire shorted to sensor reference or battery voltage
Sensor ground open or corroded at the connector
Pressure sensor failed with output stuck high
s: Hybrid or transmission warning light
Clutch slips when the engine is meant to drive
Electric-only operation or reduced power

P28F5.t: Engine Disconnect Clutch Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P28F5.d: P28F5 covers a pressure signal from the engine disconnect clutch that jumps, drops out briefly or changes faster than the hydraulics physically allow. Each sample may sit inside the valid band, but the pattern points to a loose contact, a wire that breaks under vibration or heat, or an unstable sensor. No manufacturer documents P28F5 publicly. Ford's bulletin for the 10R80 hybrid gearbox shows that this sensor sits on the outside of the clutch circuit with its own seal and fasteners; a loose fit there leaks fluid and can also disturb the connector. CARB requires checks for erratic input signals. In contrast to P28F2, which concerns a steady but implausible value, P28F5 is about an unsteady one. The driver may notice sporadic warnings and uneven engine engagement.
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the sensor or transmission connector
Harness wire breaking intermittently under vibration or heat
Sensor loose on its mounting or internally unstable
s: Hybrid warning that comes and goes
Occasional jerk when the engine is coupled in
Fluid seepage at the sensor in some cases

P28F6.t: Engine Disconnect Clutch Actuator Circuit Intermittent
P28F6.d: P28F6 points at the electrical side of the disconnect clutch actuator rather than at its mechanics: the drive circuit to the valve or motor that applies the clutch loses or regains its normal state for short moments, typically spotted as current or feedback that flickers between plausible and implausible. Loose pins, a harness rubbing through under engine movement and connectors with fluid inside are the usual culprits. No manufacturer documents P28F6 publicly. On the A3 e-tron, Audi's clutch actuator is a valve in the mechatronic unit that regulates pressure, while a Ford patent supplies the clutch valves from two hydraulic pumps, so a dropout cuts clutch pressure at once. CARB asks for circuit checks on output components. The permanent faults are P287E to P2881; P28F6 appears when the fault is sporadic.
c: Loose, spread or corroded terminal in the actuator circuit
Harness chafing intermittently against the transmission or body
Transmission fluid wicking into the connector
Actuator coil or motor winding with an intermittent break
s: Sporadic hybrid or transmission warning
Engine occasionally fails to couple in or drops out
Jerks or brief power loss in hybrid mode

P28F7.d: P28F7 reports that the pressure in the exhaust of bank 1 is higher than the engine model allows. GM documents it in its 2025 diesel ECM tables (25OBDG04B): the monitor looks at the low-pressure EGR differential pressure and fails above 80 kPa while torque demand exceeds a speed-dependent minimum (around 520 Nm at low engine speed, falling to 20 Nm at high speed), counting 480 failures in 600 samples; it is Type A, MIL on the first trip. GM names the cause as an exhaust throttle valve in the wrong position, for example with the link between its upper and lower shafts broken so the plate can stay shut although the actuated shaft has moved. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 lists P28F7 for the 3.0 L LM2 Duramax. Excess back pressure costs power and fuel and stresses the turbocharger.
c: Exhaust throttle valve stuck closed or its shaft linkage broken
Exhaust restricted downstream, for example by a heavily loaded particulate filter or damaged pipe
Chafed engine harness disturbing valve control (GM 21-NA-149)
Pressure sensor reading too high without a separate sensor code
s: Check engine light on
Reduced engine power
Higher fuel consumption and more frequent filter regenerations

P28F8.d: P28F8 is the bank 2 twin of P28F7 and only appears on engines whose two cylinder banks have separately measured exhaust paths, such as V engines with one turbocharger or flap per bank. It means the exhaust pressure on that side exceeds the modelled value. No manufacturer documents P28F8 publicly; GM's 2025 diesel tables cover only the bank 1 code on an inline engine, where a stuck exhaust throttle plate caused a reading above 80 kPa under load. By analogy, a bank 2 fault would come from a flap, turbine or pipe restricted on the second side. DieselNet explains that higher back pressure raises fuel use and emissions and hurts performance. CARB requires monitoring of boost and aftertreatment systems for such faults. Comparing both banks helps: if only bank 2 is high, look downstream on that side.
c: Exhaust flap or throttle on bank 2 stuck closed
Restriction downstream on bank 2, for example a blocked catalyst or filter section
Variable turbine of the bank 2 turbocharger stuck in a closed position
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power, possibly with uneven running between banks
Increased fuel consumption

P28F9.d: P28F9 flags exhaust pressure on bank 1 that stays below what the engine should produce at the current load. Too little pressure ahead of the turbine means the gas is escaping or not being held back: a leak at the manifold, gasket or turbine inlet, an exhaust flap jammed open, or a variable turbine stuck wide open. No manufacturer documents P28F9 publicly. Ford's 2023 diesel summary shows how such a deviation can be caught: it compares the measured turbine upstream pressure with a modelled value and flags differences beyond -100 or +500 kPa, but files them under P0474 as a sensor fault. A system-level code like P28F9 instead assumes the sensor is right. CARB requires underboost monitoring on boosted engines. Expect weak boost, sluggish response and possibly louder exhaust noise.
c: Exhaust leak at manifold, gasket or turbine inlet on bank 1
Variable turbine geometry stuck in the open position
Exhaust throttle or pressure flap jammed open
Leaking or cracked sensing tube to the exhaust pressure sensor
s: Check engine light on
Weak boost and sluggish acceleration
Ticking or hissing exhaust noise near the manifold

P28FA.d: P28FA is the bank 2 version of P28F9: the exhaust on the second cylinder bank carries less pressure than the load calls for. It presupposes an engine with a separate pressure reading per bank, such as a V engine with one turbocharger on each side. No manufacturer documents P28FA publicly. The likely chain mirrors bank 1: a cracked manifold or blown gasket on that side, a jammed-open flap, or the bank 2 turbine vanes stuck open. Ford's diesel summary of 2023 compares measured and modelled turbine upstream pressure but treats a mismatch as a sensor error (P0474), so a pure system code like P28FA is not what Ford uses. CARB requires underboost and exhaust system monitoring. A low value only on bank 2 while bank 1 reads normal narrows the search to that side.
c: Cracked manifold or leaking gasket on bank 2
Bank 2 turbocharger vanes or wastegate stuck open
Exhaust pressure flap of bank 2 jammed open
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power and slow boost build-up
Exhaust noise or soot traces on bank 2

P2A00.t: O2 Sensor Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1 Sensor 1
P2A00.d: Sensor 1 on bank 1 is the oxygen sensor ahead of the catalytic converter that the engine control module relies on for mixture feedback. P2A00 is a plausibility fault: a signal is present but does not behave the way fuel control expects. GM petrol engines (LCV, LEA, LHN) set it when the sensor never becomes ready for closed-loop fuelling or falls out of it again, counted as 200 failed samples out of 250 and logged as a two-trip Type B fault; on Saab's 9-4X with GM V6 engines 30 s with the fuel loop still open are enough. Ford's 2023 diesels compare the measured oxygen share with a value derived from injected quantity, boost pressure and exhaust gas recirculation and expect close to 20.95 % in overrun. On GM's 3.0 L diesel a leaking intake manifold triggered it (bulletin 22-NA-128).
c: Sensor aged or poisoned (oil ash, silicone, coolant), signal too weak or sluggish
Leak in intake manifold or exhaust ahead of the sensor distorts the oxygen reading
High resistance or corrosion in signal, reference or heater wiring
Fuel delivery or injector fault the sensor correctly reports but fuel control cannot correct
s: Check engine light on
Engine runs in open loop, fuel consumption rises
Uneven idle or hesitation
Failed emissions inspection

P2A01.t: O2 Sensor Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1 Sensor 2
P2A01.d: Sensor 2 on bank 1 sits behind the catalytic converter and mainly serves to judge how well the converter stores oxygen. Ford uses P2A01 for a signal that is out of range on the low side: on petrol engines with certain Continental control modules from 2011, and still in its 2020–2023 summary, a reading under −0.2 V lasting 10 s sets the code, usually because signal and return wires are swapped or the sensor is worn. On diesels this position is often taken by a NOx sensor with an oxygen output: Ford checks it against a calculated oxygen level, and GM's 2025 diesel tables let it differ from sensor 1 by at most 6 % at full load (120 of 240 samples, Type B). Mazda's CX-9 bulletin SA-004/19 links it to engine oil inside connector C-34 from a leaking oil pressure switch.
c: Engine oil or moisture in the sensor connector (Mazda CX-9 connector C-34)
Signal and return wires swapped, e.g. after a sensor replacement
On diesels, oxygen output of the second NOx sensor drifting
s: Check engine light on
Catalyst or aftertreatment monitor stays incomplete
Usually no noticeable change in driving behaviour

P2A02.t: O2 Sensor Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1 Sensor 3
P2A02.d: Sensor 3 on bank 1 follows a second converter or, on diesels, a further aftertreatment stage. GM is the only maker found that documents P2A02: in its 2025 diesel tables the oxygen value of the third NOx sensor is held against that of sensor 2 while the engine runs at full load, and a gap of more than 6 % in either direction in 120 of 240 samples sets a two-trip Type B fault. The test only starts once both sensors report themselves fully operational and the sensor-2 check has run, so a fault further upstream shows up as P2A01 first. For petrol engines with a third sensor no public description of this code exists; there CARB's rule applies that downstream sensors must stay good enough for converter monitoring. A drifting sensor 3 hardly changes how the car drives but stops the aftertreatment checks.
c: Oxygen output of the third NOx or oxygen sensor drifting with age
Exhaust leak between sensor 2 and sensor 3 lets outside air in
Sensor coated with soot, ash or urea deposits
s: Check engine light on
Aftertreatment monitor does not complete
No noticeable effect on driving in most cases

P2A03.t: O2 Sensor Circuit Range/Performance Bank 2 Sensor 1
P2A03.d: Bank 2 is the cylinder bank that does not contain cylinder 1, so P2A03 only occurs on V or flat engines; sensor 1 is the oxygen sensor ahead of that bank's converter used for fuel control. The fault is the bank-2 counterpart of P2A00: the sensor delivers a signal, yet fuel control cannot close the loop with it or keep it closed. In the Saab 9-4X (GM V6, LF1/LFW), P2A03 is logged when bank 2's fuel control loop is still reported open 30 s after the enabling conditions are met, as a two-trip Type B fault. GM's 2018 tables list P2A03 in the fault group for bank 2, sensor 1, which holds back the monitors that depend on that sensor. CARB demands detection when a sensor keeps the fuel system out of closed loop. Consumption and emissions of that bank rise while the loop is open.
c: Bank 2 front sensor aged or poisoned, too slow to reach closed loop
Sensor heater weak or wiring with high resistance, sensor stays too cold
Exhaust leak at the bank 2 manifold ahead of the sensor
Real mixture problem on bank 2 (injector, vacuum leak) the sensor reports correctly
s: Check engine light on
Higher fuel consumption
Rough idle or exhaust odour
Failed emissions inspection

P2A04.t: O2 Sensor Circuit Range/Performance Bank 2 Sensor 2
P2A04.d: Sensor 2 on bank 2 is the oxygen sensor behind that bank's catalytic converter, used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. Ford documents P2A04 together with P2A01 for certain Continental control modules on petrol engines from 2011, and again in its 2020–2023 summary: a rear-sensor voltage that stays below −0.2 V over 10 s sets the code – a value an intact switching sensor should not produce, normally pointing to swapped signal and return wires or a worn sensor. Mazda's CX-9 (2007–2015) logs P2A04 for the left-hand downstream sensor, often together with P2272; bulletins SA-004/18 and SA-004/19 send the technician to look for oil from a leaking oil pressure switch in connector C-34 before replacing the sensor. Driveability rarely suffers, but converter monitoring on bank 2 stops.
c: Oil in the sensor connector from a leaking oil pressure switch (Mazda CX-9)
Signal and return wires swapped or sensors of both banks plugged in crosswise
s: Check engine light on
Often stored together with a stuck-lean code for the same sensor
Catalyst monitor of bank 2 not ready

P2A05.t: O2 Sensor Circuit Range/Performance Bank 2 Sensor 3
P2A05.d: P2A05 refers to the third oxygen sensor on bank 2, mounted behind a further converter or aftertreatment stage of a V or flat engine. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The nearest documented case is its bank-1 counterpart: GM's 2025 diesel tables compare the oxygen value of sensor 3 with that of sensor 2 at full load and set P2A02 when the gap exceeds 6 % in 120 of 240 samples. Ford's downstream checks show the other route into a range fault, a reading that sinks below −0.2 V, which Ford, however, files only for sensor 2. CARB requires downstream sensors to stay good enough for the monitors that rely on them. An implausible sensor 3 goes largely unnoticed while driving, but the converter or aftertreatment check of bank 2 cannot finish.
c: Third sensor on bank 2 drifting or slow with age
Exhaust leak in the pipe between sensor 2 and sensor 3
Damaged or heat-affected wiring under the vehicle
s: Check engine light on
Readiness for the catalyst or aftertreatment monitor missing
Usually no change in driving behaviour

P2A06.t: O2 Sensor Negative Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 1
P2A06.d: P2A06 means the switching oxygen sensor ahead of the converter on bank 1 is delivering a voltage below zero. A zirconia sensor generates its voltage from the oxygen difference between exhaust gas and reference air, normally about 0.1–0.9 V; a negative value means the exhaust side looks richer in oxygen than the reference side, or the polarity at the module is reversed. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. A Denso patent uses exactly this symptom during fuel cut-off, with a time counter, to detect a cracked sensing element; Ford watches for rear-sensor readings under −0.2 V but stores them as P2A01/P2A04. The code only makes sense for switching sensors – many current engines use wide-range sensors in this position. Fuel control loses its feedback.
c: Cracked ceramic element, for instance after water shock or impact
Signal and signal-return wires swapped at connector or after a repair
Reference air path of the sensor contaminated by oil, sealant or water
s: Check engine light on
Mixture control falls back to open loop, consumption rises
Possible rough idle or poor emissions result

P2A07.t: O2 Sensor Negative Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 2
P2A07.d: Sensor 2 on bank 1 is the switching oxygen sensor behind the converter; P2A07 says its output has dropped below zero volts. Because the voltage comes from the oxygen difference across the zirconia element, a negative value points to reversed signal and return wires, a contaminated reference air path or a cracked element. No manufacturer documents P2A07 publicly. The closest documented test is Ford's: from 2011 a rear sensor held below −0.2 V for 10 s, put down to swapped wires or sensor degradation – Ford, however, files it as P2A01. A Denso patent watches for a negative output in overrun shut-off, a phase in which the exhaust behind the converter is almost pure air, to find element cracks. As long as the signal is negative, the converter cannot be assessed and the downstream trim switches off.
c: Signal and return wires swapped, e.g. after fitting a universal sensor
Sensor degraded or reference air contaminated
s: Check engine light on
Catalyst monitor of bank 1 not ready
Usually no noticeable change while driving

P2A08.t: O2 Sensor Negative Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 3
P2A08.d: P2A08 is the negative-voltage fault of the third oxygen sensor on bank 1, which sits behind a second converter or another aftertreatment stage. Such a sensor is normally a zirconia switching type whose output should stay above zero; an intact, correctly wired sensor does not deliver a negative reading in normal operation, so the code suggests swapped leads, a short between the signal return and another circuit, or a cracked element. No manufacturer documents P2A08 publicly; this description rests on CARB's duty to catch open circuits and readings outside the valid band, on Ford's −0.2 V limit for rear sensors (stored there under range codes) and on a Denso patent for crack detection. Sensor 3 hardly influences mixture control, so the main consequence is an incomplete converter monitor.
c: Signal return shorted to another circuit or leads swapped
Fault in the module's sensor input stage
s: Check engine light on
Converter monitor readiness missing
Normal driving behaviour in most cases

P2A09.t: O2 Sensor Negative Voltage Bank 2 Sensor 1
P2A09.d: P2A09 concerns the pre-converter oxygen sensor on bank 2, so it only arises on two-bank engines that use switching sensors ahead of the converters. The module reads a voltage below zero from it. Since a zirconia cell's output depends on the oxygen difference between exhaust and reference air, a negative value means swapped wires, a reference air path fouled by fluids or sealant, or a crack in the element; a Denso patent identifies such cracks by a lasting negative output in fuel cut-off. No manufacturer documents P2A09 publicly; Ford, for instance, records negative readings of its rear sensors under range/performance codes instead. P2A06 is the bank-1 counterpart. Bank 2 then loses its mixture feedback and may run in open loop, with higher consumption.
c: Cracked element in the bank 2 front sensor
Signal wires swapped or bank 1 and bank 2 connectors interchanged
Reference air path contaminated by oil, water or sealant
s: Check engine light on
Higher fuel consumption due to open-loop operation of bank 2
Possible rough idle

P2A0A.t: Manifold Absolute Pressure Sensor B Circuit
P2A0A.d: Engines with two intake manifold pressure sensors call the second one sensor B; in GM's tables for the Corvette's LT6 V8 it measures the manifold pressure of bank 2, next to the bank-1 sensor that uses the familiar P0105–P0109 codes. P2A0A is the general circuit fault of sensor B, meant for cases where the module sees a circuit problem without sorting it into low, high or intermittent. No manufacturer documents P2A0A publicly – the LT6 tables split electrical faults of this sensor into P2A0C and P2A0D. CARB requires checks for broken circuits and implausible extremes on every input that affects emissions. Without a usable MAP B signal the module estimates the air charge of the affected bank from a model, which can cost smoothness and power.
c: Loose connector, corroded terminal or damaged wire at sensor B
5 V reference shared with other sensors pulled down
s: Check engine light on
Uneven running or hesitation
Possible reduced power

P2A0B.t: Manifold Absolute Pressure Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P2A0B.d: P2A0B means the MAP B signal stays inside its electrical range but does not fit the operating state. GM documents it for the Corvette's LT6 V8, where sensor B reads the bank-2 manifold pressure, with several checks: before the engine turns, the raw reading has to agree with ambient pressure within a few kPa, otherwise one trip and 5 s are enough; with the engine running it is held against a modelled manifold pressure and may not overshoot the model's maximum or undershoot its minimum by more than about 2 kPa; and if the signal moves by less than 10 kPa although conditions should make it vary, the sensor is treated as frozen (two trips). Leaks downstream of the throttle, a blocked sensor port, ice or a drifting sensor are typical reasons.
c: Air leak in the bank 2 intake behind the throttle
Sensor port blocked by deposits or frozen condensate
Sensor B drifting so that its reading no longer matches ambient or model
s: Check engine light on
Hesitation or uneven idle
Mixture or load faults on bank 2

P2A0C.t: Manifold Absolute Pressure Sensor B Circuit Low
P2A0C.d: P2A0C reports that the MAP B signal voltage is too low. Manifold pressure sensors are usually three-wire parts fed from a 5 V reference; a signal close to zero means a broken reference or signal wire, a ground short or a dead sensor, because even deep vacuum would not pull a healthy sensor down that far. GM documents the code for the Corvette's LT6 V8, whose sensor B measures the manifold pressure of bank 2: a reading below 0.5 V for 1.5 s sets it after one trip. The bank-1 sensor reports the same condition as P0107. Once the signal is lost the module falls back on a modelled pressure for that bank, so the engine keeps running, but response and smoothness may suffer and power may be cut back.
c: 5 V reference or signal wire open
s: Check engine light on
Sluggish response or rough running
Possible reduced engine power

P2A0D.t: Manifold Absolute Pressure Sensor B Circuit High
P2A0D.d: P2A0D is the high-voltage counterpart: the MAP B signal sits close to the reference voltage. Typical reasons are an open ground wire, a signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage, or a sensor that has failed internally. For the Corvette's LT6 V8, GM sets P2A0D when the bank-2 manifold pressure sensor reads above 4.5 V for 1.5 s, after a single trip; the bank-1 sensor uses P0108 with practically the same limit. Such a voltage would stand for a pressure that the naturally aspirated intake cannot reach, so the module discards the value and works with a modelled pressure instead. Expect the warning light and, depending on the calibration, rough running or limited power.
c: Sensor ground wire open or connector not seated
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
s: Check engine light on
Rough running or hesitation
Possible limited power

P2A0E.t: Manifold Absolute Pressure Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2A0E.d: P2A0E flags a MAP B signal that jumps or drops out for short moments instead of failing for good. No manufacturer documents P2A0E publicly; GM's LT6 tables, the only public description of a sensor B, cover just its low, high and plausibility faults. The logic therefore follows the intermittent code of sensor A, P0109: Ford's 2012 summary sets it without MIL when the voltage briefly falls below 0.024 V or rises above 4.96 V, judged over 2 s, and another Ford strategy counts ten excursions beyond the limits in one drive cycle. Loose terminals, a chafed harness or moisture in the connector are the usual culprits, and the fault often comes and goes with vibration or temperature. The engine may stumble or hesitate during the dropouts.
c: Loose or widened terminal in the sensor B connector
Harness chafing on engine parts, intermittent short or open
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
s: Intermittent stumble or hesitation
Fault comes and goes, warning light depending on manufacturer

P2A0F.d: A fuel supply heater warms the fuel on its way to the engine. On diesels it sits at the filter so that paraffin wax cannot block it in frost; on flex-fuel engines running on high ethanol blends heated fuel eases cold starts, as a Kia patent with a heated ethanol path to a separate cold-start injector shows. P2A0F says the heater is being driven but does not achieve the expected effect, for example the fuel temperature fails to rise. No manufacturer documents P2A0F publicly. GM diesels supervise only the electrical side of their fuel supply heater, through the relay driver (e.g. P2688), and treat that as a Type C fault without MIL; CARB covers such parts as comprehensive components. Possible consequences are hard cold starts, rough running or loss of power in severe cold.
c: Heating element burnt out or with too high resistance
Heater relay, fuse or supply wiring not delivering full voltage
Fuel temperature sensor reports wrongly, so the heating effect seems absent
s: Hard starting in cold weather
Rough running or power loss in severe frost
Fault code stored, warning light depending on manufacturer

P2A10.t: O2 Sensor Negative Voltage Bank 2 Sensor 2
P2A10.d: The downstream oxygen sensor of bank 2, behind that bank's converter, is reporting a negative voltage. Bank 2 only exists on V and flat engines. A healthy switching sensor swings between roughly 0.1 and 0.9 V; readings below zero come from swapped signal and return wires, for instance after splicing in a universal sensor, from a fouled reference air path or from a cracked ceramic. No manufacturer documents P2A10 publicly. Ford monitors precisely this condition on rear sensors with a limit of −0.2 V held over 10 s but stores P2A04 for bank 2. A Denso patent treats negative readings during fuel cut-off as a sign of an element crack. The engine itself runs normally, but converter monitoring on bank 2 is blocked until the cause is fixed.
c: Signal and return wires swapped, e.g. on a spliced universal sensor
Cracked ceramic of the bank 2 downstream sensor
s: Check engine light on
Catalyst monitor of bank 2 not ready
No change in driving behaviour

P2A11.t: O2 Sensor Negative Voltage Bank 2 Sensor 3
P2A11.d: P2A11 is assigned to bank 2's third oxygen sensor, located after a second converter or additional aftertreatment of a two-bank engine, and says its signal has gone negative. For an intact, properly connected zirconia sensor that is not a normal state; likely explanations are reversed leads, a short within the harness or a cracked sensing element. No manufacturer documents P2A11 publicly, and for the whole series P2A06–P2A11 no public monitor description could be found; this text draws on CARB's rule on implausible sensor values, on Ford's rear-sensor test (below −0.2 V held over 10 s, filed as P2A01/P2A04) and on Denso's crack-detection patent. P2A08 is the bank-1 counterpart. Effects on driving are minimal, while the monitor that depends on this sensor stays incomplete.
c: Leads swapped or harness short near the exhaust
Fault in the module's sensor input
s: Check engine light on
Dependent catalyst or aftertreatment monitor incomplete

P2A12.t: Injection Pump Fuel Metering Control C (Cam/Rotor/Injector)
P2A12.d: The injection pump fuel metering codes cover electrically controlled actuators that decide how much fuel a diesel pump delivers – on distributor pumps the quantity solenoid, on common rail usually the inlet metering unit on the high-pressure pump, which a Bosch patent describes together with its flushing line. Actuators A and B have their own code groups (P0251 ff., P0256 ff.); C continues the series for pumps or engines with a third metering actuator, with its plausibility, low and high faults in P2A13–P2A15. P2A12 is the general fault of actuator C without a finer breakdown. No manufacturer documents P2A12 publicly; Saab's 2011 9-5 diesel, for example, reports an open circuit of its single pressure regulator as P0251. Depending on the system, rail pressure, power or speed are limited.
c: Open circuit or poor contact in the actuator C wiring or connector
Metering actuator C coil failed or valve sticking
Dirt or water in the fuel jamming the metering valve
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power or limp mode
Hard starting or stalling

P2A13.t: Injection Pump Fuel Metering Control C Range/Performance (Cam/Rotor/Injector)
P2A13.d: P2A13 flags metering element C of a diesel injection system as implausible: its circuit is electrically intact, yet the quantity or pressure it is supposed to produce does not follow the engine control module's command. The letter C stands for a third element – a further metering valve, a cam-driven pump plunger or a unit injector with its own solenoid. No manufacturer publishes P2A13. Volvo and Mack list this fault type for elements B, D and F on their 11 and 13 litre truck engines of the US17 emissions level, where it traced back to the rail pressure system or a slipping cam lobe. For C, the heavy-duty rule 13 CCR 1971.1 on injection quantity and pressure control is the basis. P2A14 and P2A15 cover low and high electrical readings. Output is usually derated.
c: Fault in the high-pressure system (leak, relief valve, low-pressure supply) that the element cannot compensate
Worn or sticking metering element C (valve, plunger or cam lobe)
Outdated engine control software or calibration
s: Check engine light on
Lack of power, especially under load
Engine power derated by the control module

P2A14.t: Injection Pump Fuel Metering Control C Low (Cam/Rotor/Injector)
P2A14.d: P2A14 reports that the signal in the drive circuit of fuel metering element C has fallen below its expected window. In practice the control module sees too little voltage or current on that output, as happens when the line touches ground or, depending on the driver design, an open wire. C denotes a third metering element besides A and B, found only on pumps or engines with several separately driven elements. No maker documents P2A14 publicly. Saab's 2011 9-5 diesel shows how such a check works for its single regulator: a control line shorted to ground for longer than one second sets P0253 as an immediate Type A fault. California's comprehensive component rules require this circuit check for every such actuator. Limited power and rough running are typical; P2A15 is the high-side counterpart.
c: Control wire of element C chafed through and shorted to ground
Broken wire or corroded, loose connector pin in the element C circuit
Coil of metering element C open or shorted to its housing
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power or limp mode
Rough running or misfire-like shaking

P2A15.t: Injection Pump Fuel Metering Control C High (Cam/Rotor/Injector)
P2A15.d: With P2A15 the engine control module finds the circuit of metering element C reading too high: voltage where the driver expects a pulled-down line, or a current beyond the limit. Causes are a chafed wire touching battery voltage, a short between windings inside the actuator, or a failing output stage. Element C is the third metering element on engines that control several pump plungers, valves or unit injectors individually. P2A15 has no public manufacturer documentation. Saab's V6 diesel of 2002, whose pump carries two pressure valves, logs an internal valve short after 2.1 s and then caps pedal travel at 30 %, fuel at 20 mm³ per stroke and rail pressure at 60 MPa – an example of how strongly such a fault restricts the engine. P2A14 is the low-side fault.
c: Shorted turns in the coil of metering element C drawing excess current
Control wire of element C shorted to battery voltage
Output stage in the engine control module no longer switching correctly
s: Check engine light on
Strongly limited power and accelerator response
Engine may stall or refuse to start

P2A16.t: Injection Pump Fuel Metering Control D (Cam/Rotor/Injector)
P2A16.d: P2A16 is the umbrella code for fuel metering element D, used when the control module registers a malfunction of that element without assigning it to the more specific plausibility, low or high codes (P2A17–P2A19). The D series only makes sense on systems with at least four individually controlled metering elements, such as engines whose camshaft drives several pumping units. On Volvo and Mack 11 and 13 litre truck engines from model year 2018, three of the six injectors are cam-actuated pumping injectors feeding the common rail; Volvo bulletins refer to D, though only with P2A17, not P2A16. A public description of P2A16 itself is missing, so the general CARB circuit and fuel system rules apply. Expect reduced power and a stored code with freeze frame.
c: Wiring or connector fault in the circuit of element D
Metering element D (valve, pumping unit or injector solenoid) defective
Engine control module fault or software error
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power
Hard starting or uneven running

P2A17.t: Injection Pump Fuel Metering Control D Range/Performance (Cam/Rotor/Injector)
P2A17.d: P2A17 means fuel metering element D is not delivering what the control module commands, although its circuit shows no electrical fault. Volvo and Mack document the code for their 11 and 13 litre engines (including Mack MP7/MP8) built to the US17 emissions level, together with P0257 and P2A1F. These engines pressurise the common rail with three cam-driven pumping injectors, each riding a double lobe that strokes it twice per camshaft turn. One bulletin points to an assembled camshaft whose injector lobe can twist on the shaft; it usually slips by 60°, and around 15° is already enough to trigger the code and lose power. Another groups P2A17 with low rail pressure, leak and regulator learning codes and asks for Tech Tool 2.7.85 or later plus guided diagnostics.
c: Injector lobe turned on the assembled camshaft (Volvo/Mack US17)
Rail pressure problem such as an internal leak or poor low-pressure supply
Worn pumping injector or rocker of element D
Outdated diagnostic software leading to wrong test results
s: Check engine light on
Lack of power
Further rail pressure codes stored at the same time

P2A18.t: Injection Pump Fuel Metering Control D Low (Cam/Rotor/Injector)
P2A18.d: P2A18 indicates a low reading in the control circuit of metering element D: the module detects that the output stays near ground or carries too little current. Typical triggers are a short to ground in the harness, a corroded connector pin or, with low-side drivers, an interrupted lead. Since the D range requires a fourth individually driven element, the code belongs to multi-element systems such as engines with several cam-actuated pumping units; Volvo bulletins mention element D only for its range/performance code. P2A18 itself is not described by any manufacturer. As a reference, Saab's V6 diesel of 2002 sets P0258 when the shared supply of its two pump valves has a ground fault or opens for over 1.05 s and then limits power. The high-side partner is P2A19.
c: Harness of element D shorted to ground
Corroded or spread connector pin at element D
Interrupted lead on the switched side of element D
Defective driver in the engine control module
s: Check engine light on
Limited power or limp mode
Fault may come and go with vibration or moisture

P2A19.t: Injection Pump Fuel Metering Control D High (Cam/Rotor/Injector)
P2A19.d: P2A19 is stored when the circuit of metering element D reads high – for instance a control line shorted to battery voltage, an actuator coil with shorted turns pulling excessive current, or a driver that no longer switches off. The fault is electrical; whether the element would still meter correctly cannot be judged until the circuit is repaired. Element D exists only on systems with four or more separately controlled metering elements. No manufacturer documents P2A19 publicly. Saab's 2011 9-5 diesel illustrates the pattern on its single regulator: a short to voltage lasting more than one second sets P0254 as a Type A fault, lighting the warning lamp at once. P2A18 covers the opposite direction, P2A17 the functional fault of the same element.
c: Control line of element D shorted to battery voltage
Actuator coil of element D with shorted turns
Output stage in the control module stuck switched on
s: Warning lamp on immediately
Severe power reduction
Possible stalling or no start

P2A1A.t: Injection Pump Fuel Metering Control E (Cam/Rotor/Injector)
P2A1A.d: P2A1A covers fuel metering element E in general: the engine control module has seen a malfunction of that element but files it under none of the more specific codes for plausibility (P2A1B) or low and high signal (P2A1C, P2A1D). A fifth separately driven element is rare; it presupposes engines that meter fuel per cylinder or per pumping unit. Delphi's F2E heavy-duty system, used by Volvo, Renault Trucks and Hyundai on six-cylinder engines, pairs a common rail with six injectors, half of them pumping and half plain, and the 16 litre version uses six pumping injectors – a layout where letters up to F could be assigned. Whether any maker actually reports P2A1A is not published; the CARB monitoring rules remain the basis. Reduced power is the likely reaction.
c: Wiring or connector fault at metering element E
Metering element E or its solenoid defective
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power
Uneven idle

P2A1B.t: Injection Pump Fuel Metering Control E Range/Performance (Cam/Rotor/Injector)
P2A1B.d: P2A1B reports that metering element E works electrically but its result is off: the pressure build-up or quantity attributed to it deviates from what was commanded, or its correction values sit at the limit. How a control module rates this is not published; rail pressure and fuel correction are the obvious inputs. No manufacturer documents P2A1B. Volvo and Mack use the matching range/performance code for B, D and F – three letters for the three pumping injectors of their 13 litre engines; E does not appear there. California's heavy-duty OBD rule requires detecting a fuel system that can no longer deliver the commanded quantity or pressure. Power is cut back, and a worn cam lobe, plunger or valve is a plausible cause.
c: Worn cam lobe, plunger or valve of metering element E
Insufficient low-pressure supply or clogged filter
s: Check engine light on
Lack of power under load
Longer cranking before start

P2A1C.t: Injection Pump Fuel Metering Control E Low (Cam/Rotor/Injector)
P2A1C.d: P2A1C is set when the drive circuit of the fifth metering element, E, reads below its permitted range. On solenoid-operated pump valves and unit injectors, a wire grounded against the engine block, water in a connector or a broken lead on the ground-switched side are typical. Because only a few injection layouts have five or more separately controlled elements, the code is rare, and no manufacturer documents it publicly. California's comprehensive component monitoring demands checking every such output for breaks and for values outside its range. Saab's two-valve V6 diesel pump of 2002 gives an analogy: a grounded or open common supply (P0258) restricts fuel quantity and rail pressure. Element E's high-side and functional faults are P2A1D and P2A1B.
c: Wire of element E rubbing on the engine block and grounded
Moisture or corrosion in the connector of element E
Broken lead on the ground-switched side
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power or limp mode
Rough running

P2A1D.t: Injection Pump Fuel Metering Control E High (Cam/Rotor/Injector)
P2A1D.d: P2A1D tells that metering element E's circuit sits above its plausible range. Faults that cause it include a lead rubbing through onto a powered wire, moisture bridging pins, an actuator winding shorted internally so that current climbs, or a defective output stage in the control unit. Element E only exists where five or more metering elements are driven individually. No manufacturer publishes P2A1D. Saab's 2002 V6 diesel offers a comparison: an internal short in one of its pump's two pressure valves persisting for more than 2.1 s sets P0259, and the workshop guidance recommends moving the harness while watching the meter to find intermittent shorts. The low reading of the same element is P2A1C.
c: Internal winding short in metering element E
Lead of element E chafed onto a powered wire or pins bridged by moisture
Defective output stage in the control unit
s: Check engine light on
Marked power limitation
Engine may cut out

P2A1E.t: Injection Pump Fuel Metering Control F (Cam/Rotor/Injector)
P2A1E.d: P2A1E is the general fault of the sixth fuel metering element, F – the last letter of this code family. The control module stores it for a failure of that element that it cannot pin down as a plausibility (P2A1F), low (P2A20) or high (P2A21) fault. Six individually metered elements would fit, for example, a six-cylinder engine with one pumping unit or unit injector per cylinder. Volvo and Mack, whose 13 litre truck engines use three cam-driven pumping injectors on a common rail, name element F in service bulletins, but only with the range/performance code P2A1F. No source describes P2A1E itself; the CARB rules for fuel system and electrical components set the frame. Typical consequences are a warning lamp and derated power.
c: Wiring or connector fault in the circuit of element F
Pumping unit, valve or injector solenoid of element F defective
s: Check engine light on
Derated power
Uneven running

P2A1F.t: Injection Pump Fuel Metering Control F Range/Performance (Cam/Rotor/Injector)
P2A1F.d: P2A1F says that metering element F does not reach its target although its wiring checks out. Volvo and Mack document it for their US17-generation 11 and 13 litre engines, alongside P0257 and P2A17. On these engines three pumping injectors, driven through rockers by double cam lobes, deliver fuel into the rail at up to roughly 35,000 psi. Two causes are named in their bulletins: an injector lobe on the assembled camshaft that has turned on the shaft – checked by barring the engine over and watching each lobe – and genuine rail pressure problems listed together with leak and low-pressure supply codes. For the latter, Volvo requires current Premium Tech Tool software and the guided test. Expect lack of power; repairs range from software to a new camshaft.
c: Injector lobe spun on the assembled camshaft (Volvo/Mack US17)
Low-pressure supply too weak or a leak in the rail system
Worn pumping injector of element F
Outdated workshop software misleading the guided test
s: Check engine light on
Lack of power
Rail pressure codes stored alongside

P2A20.t: Injection Pump Fuel Metering Control F Low (Cam/Rotor/Injector)
P2A20.d: P2A20 is the low-signal fault of metering element F: the module measures a voltage or current on that drive line that is lower than the switching state allows. Shorts to ground, broken conductors on low-side switched circuits and connectors pushed out of their housing are the usual suspects. Element F is the sixth individually controlled metering element, so the code only concerns engines with six such units. No manufacturer describes P2A20 publicly; even Volvo, which uses the letter F, lists it only for range/performance. As an analogy, Saab's 2011 9-5 diesel sets P0253 for its regulator line shorted to ground and P0251 for an open line, each after one second, both as Type A faults. The high-signal counterpart of P2A20 is P2A21.
c: Drive line of element F shorted to ground
Terminal pushed out of the connector housing or broken conductor
Open coil in metering element F
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power
Rough idle

P2A21.t: Injection Pump Fuel Metering Control F High (Cam/Rotor/Injector)
P2A21.d: P2A21 marks a high reading in the circuit of the sixth metering element, F. The control module sees battery potential on the line or a current exceeding the driver limit – for instance when the harness rubs through onto a supply wire or the actuator coil is partly short-circuited. A driver stage that protects itself may then switch the output off, so the element can no longer meter at all. No manufacturer publicly documents P2A21. Saab's 2002 V6 diesel shows the consequences of a comparable short in one of its two pump valves: P0259 after 2.1 s, with pedal response limited to 30 % and rail pressure to 60 MPa. The low-side fault of F is P2A20, the functional one P2A1F.
c: Partly short-circuited coil of metering element F
Harness of element F chafed onto a supply wire
Damaged output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light on
Severely limited power and throttle response
Possible stalling

P2A22.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve B Control Circuit/Open
P2A22.d: P2A22 covers the drive circuit of shutoff valve B, the electric lock on a further gas cylinder of a multi-tank CNG or LPG installation, when the module finds no current path at all. A broken lead, a loose plug or a burnt-out coil are the usual findings. No manufacturer documents P2A22 publicly; the upfitter TransEco lumps an open line into its Low code P2A24 instead. New Flyer's CNG bus bulletin SMB-169 suggests a quick test for a dead tank solenoid: swap its coil with the one from a neighbouring valve. CARB's comprehensive component rules require such outputs to be checked for wiring faults. With one cylinder isolated, the remaining tanks still feed the engine, so reduced range is often the first thing a driver notices.
c: Broken lead or disconnected plug at the valve on tank B
Burnt-out solenoid coil of valve B
Corroded terminals in the valve connector
s: Check engine light
Noticeably shorter range on gas
Gas left in one cylinder after the others are empty

P2A23.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve B Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
P2A23.d: P2A23 is stored when valve B is switched on electrically, but the gas system does not react as if that cylinder had opened. Software can only judge this from pressure: after the command, the reading downstream of the tank should rise, and a tank B pressure sensor, where fitted, should fall while gas is being used. No manufacturer publishes P2A23 or its thresholds. Bus maker New Flyer devotes bulletin SMB-169 to a tank solenoid stuck closed and explains how such a cylinder is vented through the purge line before the valve is replaced. Likely reasons are a jammed armature, a closed hand valve on that tank or debris. P2A22, P2A24 and P2A25 cover the electrical faults of the same valve, P2A42 the plausibility of its pressure sensor.
c: Armature of valve B jammed closed, e.g. by debris
Manual valve on tank B left closed
Tank or line pressure sensor reporting the response wrongly
s: Check engine light
Tank B stays full while the others empty
Reduced range on gas

P2A24.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve B Control Circuit Low
P2A24.d: P2A24 means the alternative fuel module sees the control line of shutoff valve B sitting too low. TransEco Energy, which converts trucks to CNG, assigns it in the fault table of its AFCM v1.4 to a lead shorted to ground or open, lights the MIL on dedicated and bi-fuel systems alike and does not force a fallback. The same table prints P2A14 in a second column beside it, a number that current code lists give to injection pump metering C. Ford's 2014 Boss 302S code list also includes P2A24, though without the MIL marker it shows for P224E. Chafed wires along the cylinder mounts are a classic cause. P2A25 is the high counterpart, P2A28 the matching fault on valve C.
c: Control wire of valve B chafed through to ground at a tank bracket
Open lead, which the TransEco module reports under this code
Shorted turns in the coil of valve B
s: Check engine light
Gas from tank B unavailable, range reduced

P2A25.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve B Control Circuit High
P2A25.d: P2A25 reports a voltage on the control circuit of tank valve B that is higher than the module expects, mostly because the wire touches a battery feed. TransEco Energy's fault table names a short to power as the cause, turns on the MIL and lets the gas system carry on. The real risk lies elsewhere: a solenoid held by foreign voltage stays open even when the module wants the cylinder isolated, for instance after the engine stops. Ford's 2003 bi-fuel CNG documentation shows why that matters, since its module shuts the tank valve once gas pressure falls under 517 kPa. Ford's Boss 302S list names P2A25 as well. P2A24 is the low-side partner; for valve A the equivalent code is P224F.
c: Control wire of valve B touching a battery feed
Output stage for valve B in the module stuck on
Wiring mistake during conversion or repair
s: Check engine light
Tank B may stay open with the engine off

P2A26.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve C Control Circuit/Open
P2A26.d: P2A26 is the open-circuit code for shutoff valve C, the solenoid on yet another gas cylinder. The module drives the coil and finds that no current flows, so the coil, its plug or the lead to it is interrupted. No manufacturer documents P2A26 publicly. What the repair costs depends on the design: in GM's single-tank bi-fuel Impala (bulletin PI1330) the high-pressure solenoid is threaded into the tank's manual valve and counts as non-serviceable, so a faulty one means a new tank, whereas New Flyer buses allow the coil alone to be exchanged. CARB requires output components to be watched for open and shorted circuits. Valves B, D and E have their own open-circuit codes, P2A22, P2A2A and P2A2E.
c: Interrupted lead or unplugged connector at valve C
Faulty driver for valve C in the control module
s: Check engine light
Gas in cylinder C cannot be used

P2A27.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve C Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
P2A27.d: P2A27 points to valve C: electrically commanded, yet apparently still shut. With several cylinders on one manifold, a single tank that stays isolated rarely stops the engine; the others keep supplying gas, and the fault appears as shorter range or a cylinder that never empties. Ford's 2003 bi-fuel CNG system regulates to about 724 kPa and closes its tank valve below 517 kPa, which shows how gas pressure serves as the yardstick for such checks. No manufacturer publishes P2A27 or how it is tested. Contamination, a sticking armature, too little coil voltage and a closed hand valve on that cylinder are the obvious suspects. Its electrical sister codes are P2A26, P2A28 and P2A29; P2A47 rates the tank C pressure sensor.
c: Sticking or contaminated armature in valve C
Hand valve on cylinder C closed
Coil voltage too low because of a poor feed or ground
s: Check engine light
Cylinder C never empties
Shorter range on gas

P2A28.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve C Control Circuit Low
P2A28.d: P2A28 tells that the control line of shutoff valve C reads too low. In TransEco Energy's AFCM table the cause is a lead to ground or an interruption; the MIL lights in both dedicated and bi-fuel conversions, and the vehicle continues without a forced change of fuel. Another number, P2A18, appears there alongside. Ford's Boss 302S list of 2014 carries P2A28 too. On cylinders mounted under a truck bed or on a bus roof the harness runs past brackets and clamps, where insulation can wear through. Whether a grounded line leaves the valve shut or pulls it open depends on whether the module switches the supply side or the ground side of the coil. P2A29 covers the high reading, P2A24 the same fault on valve B.
c: Insulation of the valve C wire worn through at a clamp
Interrupted lead, reported here by some modules
Coil of valve C shorted internally
s: Check engine light
Cylinder C not used or not shut off correctly

P2A29.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve C Control Circuit High
P2A29.d: P2A29 sets when the drive circuit of shutoff valve C sits at a high level, as with a wire touching battery voltage or a driver stage inside the module that will not switch off. TransEco's table for its AFCM v1.4 gives a short to power as the cause, with the MIL on and gas operation maintained. Ford names P2A29 in its Boss 302S code list. GM's bi-fuel Impala powers the cut-off solenoid on its tank only while the engine cranks or runs; a valve that remains live afterwards defeats the purpose of the lock, which is to hold gas in the cylinder when the vehicle stands or the fuel supply has been cut. Wiring mistakes after a conversion deserve a look. P2A28 is the low-side code for valve C.
c: Valve C control wire in contact with battery voltage
Driver stage for valve C will not switch off
Valve C wired to a permanent feed after a conversion
s: Check engine light
Cylinder C not sealed when the engine is off

P2A2A.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve D Control Circuit/Open
P2A2A.d: P2A2A marks an interrupted control circuit at shutoff valve D, which only exists on installations with four or more gas cylinders, mostly commercial trucks, vans and buses. When the module energizes the coil and measures no current, it stores this code. No manufacturer documents P2A2A publicly. If valves A to D all report open circuits at once, a shared feed is the suspect: in Ford's 2003 bi-fuel CNG design the tank solenoid draws its power through the inertia switch and the ALT fuel relay, and a multi-tank system wired that way would lose every valve together. A single code instead points to the coil, plug or lead of valve D. CARB's comprehensive component monitoring forms the legal basis.
c: Break in the branch of the harness leading to valve D
Common supply via relay or inertia switch interrupted (several valve codes at once)
s: Check engine light
Reduced usable gas quantity

P2A2B.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve D Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
P2A2B.d: P2A2B is the functional fault of valve D: the module has commanded it open, but the pressure picture suggests that cylinder D is not contributing gas. Bus builder New Flyer gives figures for the scale involved: its tanks hold between 1,375 and 24,800 kPa, while the regulated side should read 648 to 827 kPa once the engine runs. When a valve sticks shut, its cylinder stays full, and bulletin SMB-169 has the technician close the hand valves of that tank and its neighbours before venting it through the purge line. No car or truck maker publishes P2A2B. A failed coil whose circuit still tests intact can produce the same picture. The sister codes P2A2A, P2A2C and P2A2D deal with the wiring of this solenoid.
c: Weak coil that no longer pulls the armature
Hand valve on tank D closed after service
s: Check engine light
Tank D stays at full pressure
Reduced range on gas

P2A2C.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve D Control Circuit Low
P2A2C.d: P2A2C records too low a level on the control wire of shutoff valve D. TransEco Energy treats it in its AFCM v1.4 fault list as a short to ground or open circuit and switches on the MIL while letting gas operation continue; P2A1C is printed beside it as an alternative number. Ford's Boss 302S list from 2014 contains P2A2C too. On frame-mounted cylinder racks the plug of each tank valve is exposed to spray and road salt, so corrosion and chafing belong on the checklist. CARB asks for low and high circuit faults of output components to be told apart where practical, which explains the separate codes. The high side of this circuit is P2A2D; P2A2A stands for the plain open circuit.
c: Valve D wire grounded at a chafe point on the cylinder rack
Salt corrosion in the valve D connector
s: Check engine light
Gas from tank D not available

P2A2D.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve D Control Circuit High
P2A2D.d: P2A2D reports excessive voltage on the control circuit of shutoff valve D. The AFCM fault list from TransEco Energy names a short to power, lights the MIL and keeps the gas system in service; P2A1D stands next to it. Ford's 2014 Boss 302S list includes P2A2D without the MIL marker. A wire pinched against a supply cable, a module output that stays on or an error while wiring a conversion kit are the likely findings. The practical concern is that the solenoid may remain energized, so cylinder D is not sealed when the engine stops or a crash cuts the supply. Before any work on the harness, close the manual valves on the tanks. P2A2C covers the low readings of this valve, P2A29 the high fault on valve C.
c: Valve D lead pinched against a supply cable
Module output for valve D stays on
Error while wiring a conversion kit
s: Check engine light
Tank D possibly open with the engine off

P2A2E.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve E Control Circuit/Open
P2A2E.d: P2A2E is the open-circuit fault for shutoff valve E, the last letter of this series, so it only applies to systems with at least five gas cylinders, such as transit buses or heavy trucks. The module notices that the coil draws no current when commanded. No manufacturer documents P2A2E publicly, and TransEco's AFCM table lists valve E only with its Low and High codes. New Flyer offers a practical check: if the engine fails to start, confirm that the door of the fill box is shut and the solenoid wires are plugged in, because an open door also keeps all tank valves shut. Swapping the coil with a neighbour tells a coil fault from a wiring fault. CARB's monitoring rules for output components apply.
c: Valve E connector not plugged in after tank work
Broken wire in the harness branch to tank E
s: Check engine light
Gas in cylinder E remains unused

P2A2F.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve E Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
P2A2F.d: P2A2F signals that valve E was energized but the system did not see the expected gas flow from that cylinder. No manufacturer publishes this code or its test conditions; CARB only requires output components to be checked for a proper reaction to commands. New Flyer's bulletin explains that its tank solenoids switch on while the starter spins the engine to about 400 rpm. A weak battery or a voltage dip during cranking can therefore leave a coil unable to lift its armature, which looks exactly like a valve that hangs shut. GM's bi-fuel Impala regulates gas to 468 to 896 kPa, a useful reference when checking the low-pressure side. Contamination and a closed manual valve remain obvious mechanical causes.
c: Voltage drop during cranking, coil cannot lift the armature
Manual valve on cylinder E closed
s: Check engine light
Cylinder E does not empty
Fault appears mainly after cold or weak-battery starts

P2A30.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve E Control Circuit Low
P2A30.d: P2A30 sets when the control circuit of shutoff valve E reads low. TransEco Energy's AFCM v1.4 table names a short to ground or an open lead as the reason and keeps both dedicated and bi-fuel vehicles running, MIL on; P2A20 is listed beside it. Ford's Boss 302S code list contains P2A30 as well. A low reading on valve E alone points to the branch of the harness serving that cylinder. If B to E show low faults together, a shared ground or a connector close to the module is the more likely culprit. Tanks of this kind hold gas at up to about 24,800 kPa, so only trained staff should open any part of the system. P2A31 is the matching high fault, P2A2E the open circuit.
c: Control lead of valve E touching ground
Shared ground or connector near the module (several low codes together)
s: Check engine light
Gas from tank E not usable

P2A31.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve E Control Circuit High
P2A31.d: P2A31 closes the shutoff valve series with the high fault on valve E: the module measures voltage on the control wire where none should be. TransEco names a short to power and lights the MIL while the gas system continues; it prints P2A21 beside the code. Ford's Boss 302S list includes P2A31 without a MIL marker. In operation this can mean that cylinder E keeps supplying gas when the module wants it locked, for example after the inertia switch has tripped, the device through which Ford cut gas on its 2003 bi-fuel CNG vehicles. In the J2012 range the AFCM power relay codes follow from P2A32 onwards. P2A30 is the low-side code for the same valve, P2A2D the high fault on valve D.
c: Valve E wire shorted to a voltage source
Driver for valve E in the module stuck on
Valve E fed from a wrong circuit after an upfit
s: Check engine light
Cylinder E not locked when it should be

P2A32.d: Gas installations that carry a separate control unit for the gas side, the AFCM, may feed that unit through a relay whose coil is switched by a driver stage. P2A32 means this coil circuit shows no current path: the driver output sees an open line, a missing plug or a burnt coil. Ford's 2003 bi-fuel CNG pickups show how such a module manages relays itself; it energises the ALT fuel relay feeding the tank and rail solenoids. No manufacturer publishes P2A32 itself, so the logic is inferred from the engine-module counterpart P0685: on Saab's 2010 V6, GM Europe compares commanded and actual driver state and reports a mismatch lasting 4 s, or 30 s in total. If the relay never pulls in, the gas side stays dead and a bi-fuel vehicle keeps running on petrol.
c: Broken control wire or unplugged relay socket
Blown fuse in the coil feed of the relay
Output driver in the controlling module faulty
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Gas mode cannot be selected, vehicle stays on petrol
Dedicated gas engine: no start

P2A33.t: AFCM Power Relay Control Circuit Low
