P2A33.d: P2A33 concerns the control line that grounds the coil of the relay supplying the gas control module. Low means this line already sits near zero volts while the driver is switched off. A chafed wire touching the body is the classic finding; a coil with shorted windings can give the same picture. Since the coil is then permanently grounded, the relay may stay energised after the key is off, keeping the gas module awake and draining the battery overnight. Nobody publishes this code for a production gas system. Saab's GM Europe V6 manual, written for the engine relay twin P0686, lets the test run only between 10 and 18 V supply with the engine turning above 80 rpm and classes it as a Type C code, meaning no warning lamp there. CARB expects actuator outputs to be checked for such shorts.
c: Control wire chafed through and touching ground
Shorted turns in the relay coil
Moisture in the relay socket bridging to ground
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Battery flat after the vehicle has been parked
Gas module stays active after ignition off

P2A34.t: AFCM Power Relay Control Circuit High
P2A34.d: With P2A34 the coil control line of the gas module power relay stays at high voltage even when the driver tries to pull it to ground. Either the wire has contact with a battery-fed circuit, or the coil draws so much current that the driver shuts itself off for protection. In both cases the relay does not close. The consequence is the opposite of P2A33: the alternative fuel module receives no switched supply, so gas operation is impossible, and a bi-fuel car falls back to petrol from the start. Public documents for P2A34 are lacking; GM Europe treats the engine version P0687 on the 2010 Saab V6 with the same comparison of commanded against measured state. Ford's 2003 bi-fuel CNG design shows that the AFCM is a separate unit with its own power and relay outputs.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit
Relay coil with too low resistance overloading the driver
Wrong relay type fitted after a repair
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Gas operation unavailable, bi-fuel vehicle runs on petrol only
Dedicated gas engine: cranks but does not start

P2A35.d: Besides driving the relay coil, a control module can read back the voltage behind the relay contacts to confirm that power actually arrives. P2A35 is the general fault of this feedback line for the relay that supplies the gas control module, without a statement about too low or too high. Typical are an open sense wire, a corroded pin or a blown fuse between contact and sense point. Roush CleanTech's propane manual for Ford trucks lists a missing supply, a blown fuse or lost power and ground of its alternative fuel module as reasons for losing it on the bus (U0108), which shows how supply problems surface there. No published calibration uses P2A35; the engine-relay sibling P0688 is the analogue. Electrical symptoms may be absent while the relay itself still works.
c: Sense wire open or pin backed out
Blown fuse between relay contact and sense point
Corroded terminals in relay socket or module plug
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Often no drivability change
Occasional fallback to petrol if the supply really drops

P2A36.t: AFCM Power Relay Sense Circuit Low
P2A36.d: P2A36 is set when the relay feeding the gas control module has been commanded on, yet the voltage read back after its contacts stays too low. Burnt or pitted contacts, a high-resistance joint, a grounded sense wire or a blown fuse in the switched path all lead there, as does a weak battery during cranking. For the comparable engine relay code P0689, GM Europe on the 2010 Saab V6 uses a limit of 6 V held for more than 1 s and treats the result as Type C. No public calibration names P2A36 for a gas system. If the module really runs short of voltage, it may reset or drop off the network, which Roush's Ford propane trucks report as U0108; in a bi-fuel car the engine then returns to petrol.
c: Blown fuse in the switched supply
Weak battery or poor main ground
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Gas mode drops out, bi-fuel vehicle switches to petrol
Communication fault with the gas module stored as well

P2A37.t: AFCM Power Relay Sense Circuit High
P2A37.d: Here the read-back line of the gas module supply relay carries voltage at a moment when it should not: the relay is commanded off, yet power is still present behind its contacts. A welded contact pair is the main suspect, followed by a sense wire touching another live circuit. The practical effect is a gas control module that never shuts down, so stored values may not be saved correctly and the battery drains while parked. The 2010 Saab V6 manual from GM Europe covers the engine relay counterpart P0690 within the same feedback test as P0689. P2A37 itself appears in no public manufacturer document. Ford's 2003 bi-fuel CNG pickups illustrate that the alternative fuel module is a separate box with its own relay outputs, which explains why J2012 gives it a relay code set of its own.
c: Sense wire shorted to another live circuit
Miswired retrofit gas installation feeding voltage back
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Battery drained after standing
Relay clicks are missing at ignition off

P2A38.t: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit/Open Bank 1 Sensor 3
P2A38.d: P2A38 reports that the lead carrying positive current control for bank 1's third oxygen sensor has no continuity. That sensor sits behind a second converter or a later aftertreatment stage, and the code only makes sense where this position carries a wide-band probe: through this lead (pin APE/IP on a Bosch LSU 4.9) the controller drives between about −2 and +2.25 mA into the pump cell. No manufacturer documents P2A38 publicly. For the upstream twin P2237, Ford's 2012 summary spots a broken IP wire because lambda barely moves during deliberate reference-current pulses; its own third sensors are switching types with heater codes only. P2A39/P2A3A are the low/high faults, P2A3B the open return. The lamp lights, while driving feels unchanged.
c: Broken pump-current wire or pushed-back pin in the sensor plug
Sensor plug loose or not latched after exhaust work
Internal break in the pump cell of the probe
s: Check engine light
Sensor 3 value frozen near lambda 1 in live data
Downstream emission monitors not completed

P2A39.t: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit Low Bank 1 Sensor 3
P2A39.d: P2A39 is set when the pump-current lead feeding the rearmost wide-band probe on bank 1 (sensor 3) is pulled below its permitted window, typically because the wire rubs through to chassis ground near the hot rear exhaust section. At ignition-on Saab's 2010 9-5 shows roughly 2.8 V on the pump-current pins of its front probe, so a reading near zero points to a ground short. No manufacturer publishes P2A39 itself; Ford stores a short to ground on the IP wire of its front probes under P0131, and CARB only requires that such out-of-range signals be caught. P2A38 covers the open line, P2A3A the high side, P22AC the sensor 2 case. Apart from the warning lamp, the aftertreatment monitors using this probe stay incomplete.
c: Pump-current wire chafed through to body or exhaust bracket
Internal short in the probe after thermal shock or water ingress
Faulty sensor interface in the engine control module
s: Check engine light after repeated detection
Sensor 3 reading implausible or missing in live data

P2A3A.t: O2 Sensor Positive Current Control Circuit High Bank 1 Sensor 3
P2A3A.d: P2A3A means the voltage on the pump-current (positive control) lead of probe number three, bank 1, sits above its expected level. The usual culprit is contact with a supply: the heater feed runs in the same harness and connector, and moisture or heat damage at the plug can bridge the two. An offset pump current would falsify the lambda value, so the controller stops trusting it. P2A3A is not described by any manufacturer in public sources; Ford handles a short to battery on its front IP wires under P0132 instead. P2A38 is the open-circuit fault, P2A39 the low one, P2A3D the high fault on the return. The engine normally runs as before, but the lamp comes on and diagnosis starts with voltage checks at the connector.
c: Pump-current wire touching the heater feed in harness or plug
Water or corrosion in the sensor connector under the car
Internal short between heater and pump cell of the probe
s: Check engine light after repeated detection
Sensor 3 reports an implausibly lean value

P2A3B.t: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit/Open Bank 1 Sensor 3
P2A3B.d: P2A3B points to a break in the negative current control line of wide-band sensor 3 on bank 1, the common return of pump and Nernst cell. Bosch calls it virtual ground (IPN/VM, pin 2 on the LSU 4.9), NTK names it COM; the controller holds it at a bias of about 2.5 V, as Saab's 2010 9-5 shows at the plug, so current can flow both ways. No manufacturer documents P2A3B publicly. On the upstream analog P2251, Ford tells an open return from an open pump lead because lambda still shifts during reference-current pulses, and it flags a sensor voltage parked inside a band of 1.45–1.55 V, allowing 10 s before the fault is stored. P2A3C/P2A3D are low/high, P2A38 is the open pump lead. Expect the lamp, not a drivability change.
c: Broken virtual-ground wire or loose pin in the sensor plug
Corroded terminals in the connector near the rear exhaust
Internal break of the common electrode inside the probe
s: Check engine light
Sensor 3 signal stuck around its mid voltage in live data
Catalyst or aftertreatment monitor not completed

P2A3C.t: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit Low Bank 1 Sensor 3
P2A3C.d: P2A3C is stored when the virtual-ground return belonging to the third probe of bank 1 falls below its intended bias. Because this line normally floats around 2.5 V rather than at chassis potential, a chafed wire touching the body or an exhaust bracket drags it down and leaves the pump cell little room to reverse its current, so rich mixtures can hardly be measured. No manufacturer publishes P2A3C; this text relies on CARB's demand to detect out-of-range sensor circuits, on the Bosch LSU 4.9 pin layout and on the bias value Saab gives for its 2010 9-5 at the plug. P2A3B is the open return, P2A3D the high case, P2A39 the matching low fault on the pump lead. The lamp is lit and the downstream sensor checks will not complete.
c: Virtual-ground wire chafed through to chassis ground
Internal short from the common electrode to the sensor housing
Bias stage in the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine light after repeated detection
Downstream emission monitors stay incomplete

P2A3D.t: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit High Bank 1 Sensor 3
P2A3D.d: P2A3D flags the return line (virtual ground) of bank 1's sensor-3 wide-band probe as too high. Pulling this mid-level bias up to battery voltage usually takes a short to the heater supply, which shares the sensor plug, or water that has crept into a connector under the car. With its reference shifted, the controller can no longer centre the Nernst cell and rejects the lambda value. No public manufacturer material covers P2A3D; Ford's front-probe logic routes shorts to battery on VM to P0132, and the Bosch datasheet shows why the bias matters: zero pump current marks lambda close to 1. P2A3B is the open fault, P2A3C the low one, P2A3A the high fault on the pump lead. The driver usually notices only the lamp.
c: Virtual-ground wire shorted to the heater supply in harness or plug
Moisture bridging terminals in the sensor connector
Heater-to-electrode short inside a cracked probe
s: Check engine light after repeated detection
Sensor 3 lambda value rejected or shown as invalid

P2A3E.d: P2A3E is the alternative fuel version of P0148: the system cannot supply the gas or propane quantity the engine asks for. Ford had already defined its own code P1048 with this wording, listed with a lamp in the 2014 Boss 302S OBD table. Roush CleanTech's liquid propane system on Ford trucks shows how a delivery error is judged, there still under P0148: the pump voltage has climbed to its adaptive maximum while fuel trims run lean. Roush names a clogged filter, a tripped excess-flow valve, a closed tank or rail supply solenoid and a partly closed manual valve, and calls that code non-MIL. GM's 2015 bi-fuel Impala switches to the other fuel when one supply fails. No public source uses P2A3E itself; drivers mainly notice hesitation and a change to petrol.
c: Gas or propane filter heavily restricted
Tank solenoid, rail solenoid or manual valve not fully open
Excess-flow valve on the tank tripped
Weak propane pump or pressure regulator not holding pressure
Tank pressure too low because the tank is nearly empty
s: Hesitation or stalling on gas
Automatic switch to petrol
Lean fuel trim codes stored as well
Warning lamp depending on manufacturer

P2A3F.t: Excessive Time to Enter Alternative Fuel Control
P2A3F.d: On a bi-fuel or gas-start vehicle the control unit only changes over to gas once preconditions are met, for example warm coolant, enough pressure in the rail and a selected gas mode. P2A3F means this changeover did not happen within the calibrated time. GM's 2015 Impala bi-fuel bulletin PI1330 gives an idea of the conditions: below −20 °C ambient the engine starts on petrol and moves to CNG only when coolant reaches 50 °C. Ford's 2003 bi-fuel CNG pickups need at least 517 kPa rail pressure for a gas start and drop back to petrol below it. CARB treats the gas mode of such cars like a petrol engine up to model year 2018 and already demands a closed-loop entry time check (P0125 family). No maker documents P2A3F. Suspects are a slow thermostat, low tank pressure or a sticking valve.
c: Coolant warms up too slowly (thermostat stuck open, temperature sensor wrong)
Tank pressure too low for the switch-over
Regulator or vaporizer not heated enough by engine coolant
Tank or rail solenoid opening late or not at all
s: Vehicle keeps running on petrol much longer than usual
Gas indicator stays off or flashes
Check engine light, depending on calibration

P2A40.t: Alternative Fuel System - Injector Leakage to Rail Detected
P2A40.d: P2A40 reports that fuel is passing through an injector into a rail where it does not belong. The term fits dual-fuel direct injection, where one injector carries both diesel and gas: Caterpillar's patent US9422899B2 explains that the diesel is kept at a pressure equal to or a little above the gas to seal the gas needle, so liquid seeping into the nozzle space on the gas side is expected, and a check valve plus a purge routine keep it out of the gas common rail. A controller can spot such leakage from an unexplained pressure change in the affected rail. No manufacturer publishes the detection threshold for P2A40. Worn injector seals are the usual cause; the fix is normally new injectors, and the engine may be held in a reduced or single-fuel mode until then.
c: Worn internal seal or needle guide in a dual-fuel injector
Check valve between injector and gas rail leaking
Pressure difference between liquid and gas rail out of tolerance
Rail pressure sensor drifting and simulating a leak
s: Check engine light
Reduced power or operation on a single fuel
Rough running or smoke after a cold start

P2A41.t: Alternative Fuel Tank B Pressure Sensor Circuit
P2A41.d: Some multi-tank CNG installations give a second cylinder, tank B, its own pressure transducer, so the module knows the remaining gas per tank and can check that the tank valve responds. P2A41 is the general electrical fault of that sensor, set when the circuit is faulty without a clear verdict of low or high. Publications only describe the single sensor of tank A: on Ford's 2003 bi-fuel CNG trucks it is built into the regulator and drives the gauge, which the AFCM forces to empty when the sensor fails. The upfitter TransEco substitutes a fixed 3600 psi and keeps running. No manufacturer lists P2A41. Check the 5 V feed, signal and ground at the tank B sensor plug first; P2A43 and P2A44 separate the low and high cases, P2A45 brief dropouts.
c: Plug at the tank B sensor loose, corroded or harness damaged
5 V reference or sensor ground disturbed
s: Check engine light
Gas gauge wrong or showing empty
Tank B possibly no longer used

P2A42.t: Alternative Fuel Tank B Pressure Sensor Range/Performance
P2A42.d: Unlike its electrical siblings, P2A42 deals with a tank B pressure reading that is electrically valid but makes no sense. Examples: the value does not fall while gas is drawn from tank B, it stays frozen after refuelling, or it differs clearly from the pressure of the other cylinders after a long stop, when all tanks connected to one fill line should settle at about the same level. New Flyer's bulletin SMB-169 for CNG buses gives a sense of the scale: after filling, the high-pressure gauge is expected to show between 200 and 3,600 psi. A tank valve stuck closed (P2A23) or a closed hand valve also starves the reading of change. No manufacturer publishes P2A42 or its limits; CARB requires a rationality check for such inputs. Diagnosis compares the sensor with a mechanical gauge.
c: Tank B pressure sensor drifting or stuck
Tank B solenoid stuck closed or manual valve shut
Contact resistance in the sensor connector shifting the signal
s: Check engine light
Gas gauge implausible after refuelling or driving
Reduced range on gas

P2A43.t: Alternative Fuel Tank B Pressure Sensor Circuit Low
P2A43.d: P2A43 is stored when the signal of the tank B pressure sensor drops below its lower electrical limit, a level that no real tank pressure produces. The usual reasons are a signal wire grounded against the frame, a missing 5 V reference or an internal short in the sensor. For the tank A sensor, TransEco's AFCM list puts exactly these faults under its Low code, with a substitute value of 3600 psi and the lamp switched on in both dedicated and bi-fuel setups. Because a low signal looks like an empty cylinder, the gauge may drop to zero and tank B may be locked out although it still holds gas. No manufacturer documents P2A43 itself. Ford's 2014 Boss 302S table carries the tank A version P01A0 as a lamp code, a sign that the family is treated as emission-relevant.
c: 5 V reference open or pulled down by another sensor
Internal short in the tank B sensor
s: Check engine light
Gauge drops to empty for tank B
Less usable gas range

P2A44.t: Alternative Fuel Tank B Pressure Sensor Circuit High
P2A44.d: The counterpart to P2A43: the voltage on the tank B pressure sensor signal sits above its valid range. TransEco, for the tank A sensor of its gas conversions, names an open sensor or a short to power as the cause of the High code, which matches the usual pull-up layout of such inputs where a broken signal or ground wire drives the reading upward. A seemingly overfull cylinder is the risk here: the gauge may stay at full and the module may keep drawing on tank B as if gas were left, until the engine stumbles. No manufacturer lists P2A44 publicly, and the tank A variant P01A1 appears in Ford's 2014 Boss 302S code list. Start the check with the sensor ground and the plug, then measure signal voltage with the system depressurised.
c: Sensor ground or signal wire open
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
s: Check engine light
Gauge stuck at full for tank B
Stumbling when tank B actually runs empty

P2A45.t: Alternative Fuel Tank B Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2A45.d: P2A45 completes the tank B pressure group with the case that the other codes miss: the signal is mostly fine but jumps or drops out for moments, faster than any real gas pressure could change. Typical culprits are a plug that loses contact on rough roads, a wire rubbed through along the frame rail or a sensor with a cracked solder joint. Because the fault comes and goes, a single clean reading proves nothing. How such faults age out is described in Ford's material on its 2003 bi-fuel CNG trucks: once the condition stops, the lamp goes dark three trips later and the stored code disappears after forty. No manufacturer documents P2A45 itself; the logic follows the tank A counterpart P01A2 and the CARB rules for input components. Wiggle the harness while watching live data.
c: Tank B sensor plug with loose or corroded contacts
Harness chafed along frame or gas line
Intermittent internal fault in the sensor
s: Check engine light that comes and goes
Gas gauge flickering or jumping
Occasional unexpected switch to petrol on bi-fuel vehicles

P2A46.t: Alternative Fuel Tank C Pressure Sensor Circuit
P2A46.d: Larger CNG installations, for instance on trucks or buses, may carry three or more cylinders. Where a third one, tank C, has its own pressure transducer, P2A46 reports a general electrical fault in that sensor's circuit, stored when the module finds the signal unusable but cannot classify it as too low or too high. Publicly described is only the single tank sensor of simpler systems: Ford placed it inside the regulator of its 2003 bi-fuel CNG pickups and let the AFCM derive the gauge reading from it. No manufacturer lists P2A46. In practice the first checks are the three wires at the tank C sensor, the connector seal and the shared 5 V feed; the narrower codes P2A48 and P2A49 name a low or high signal, P2A4A short interruptions.
c: Wiring or plug at the tank C sensor damaged, loose or wet
Shared 5 V supply or sensor ground disturbed
s: Check engine light
Remaining gas shown wrongly
Tank C may be left unused

P2A47.t: Alternative Fuel Tank C Pressure Sensor Range/Performance
P2A47.d: P2A47 is not about broken wires: the tank C sensor delivers a voltage inside its window, yet the pressure it reports cannot be true. Plausible tests are a value that stays flat while the engine draws gas from tank C, one that does not rise during filling, or a clear gap to tanks A and B after a long rest, since cylinders on a common fill manifold settle to similar pressure. For scale, the bulletin SMB-169 that New Flyer issued for CNG buses expects the high-pressure gauge to read somewhere from 200 psi to 3,600 psi after refuelling. The cause can also be mechanical, such as a tank C valve that never opens (P2A27) or a closed manual valve. No manufacturer publishes P2A47 or its thresholds; CARB demands rationality monitoring of such inputs. Compare with a calibrated gauge before replacing parts.
c: Tank C sensor drifted or frozen at one value
Tank C solenoid not opening or manual valve closed
s: Check engine light
Gas level shown does not match refuelling or consumption
Shorter driving range on gas

P2A48.t: Alternative Fuel Tank C Pressure Sensor Circuit Low
P2A48.d: With P2A48 the voltage from the tank C pressure sensor has fallen beneath the lowest value a working sensor ever outputs, even with the cylinder empty. In such three-wire circuits a low reading points to the signal line touching ground, a dead 5 V supply or a short inside the transducer. The gas conversion specialist TransEco attributes its tank A Low code to a sensor shorted to ground and lets the AFCM continue with a fixed 3600 psi substitute while the lamp is on. For the driver, tank C looks drained: the gauge may sink and the module may skip that cylinder although it is still full. No manufacturer documents P2A48 itself. If the reference wire also feeds other sensors, a short elsewhere on it can trigger this code.
c: Signal wire of the tank C sensor touching ground
5 V reference open or shorted by another sensor on the same line
Internal short in the tank C transducer
s: Check engine light
Tank C reported empty despite being filled
Less gas range than expected

P2A49.t: Alternative Fuel Tank C Pressure Sensor Circuit High
P2A49.d: P2A49 is the mirror image of P2A48: the tank C pressure signal sits above the band a healthy sensor uses, so the module rejects it. In TransEco's AFCM table the tank A equivalent traces back to a sensor with an open circuit or a short to the supply. An open ground is a classic trigger too, because the input is then pulled toward its supply rail. The practical danger is a cylinder that seems full when it is not; the gauge stays high and the system may count on gas from tank C until the engine starts to falter on a near-empty supply. No manufacturer lists P2A49 publicly. With the system depressurised and the plug off, check whether the voltage at the module side still reads high; if so, the fault lies in the harness rather than the sensor.
c: Ground or signal wire of the tank C sensor interrupted
Signal shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
s: Check engine light
Gauge for tank C stays at full
Hesitation once tank C really runs low

P2A4A.t: Alternative Fuel Tank C Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2A4A.d: Unlike P2A48 or P2A49, which describe a signal stuck out of range, P2A4A covers a tank C pressure value that flickers: brief spikes, gaps or steps that no gas cylinder could produce, since pressure in a large tank changes only slowly. Vibration is the usual trigger, acting on a connector with weak pin tension, a cable clip that has let go, or water creeping past a seal near the back of the vehicle, where tank C often sits. A sensor failing internally is possible but rarer. Because the defect often vanishes in the workshop, freeze-frame data and a road test with live readings help. No manufacturer documents P2A4A; it mirrors P2A45 for tank B and P01A2 for tank A, and CARB covers such erratic inputs under its component rules.
c: Connector pins at the tank C sensor with weak contact
Water ingress at a connector seal
s: Check engine light appearing occasionally
Gas gauge jumps while driving
No noticeable effect between dropouts

P2A4B.d: Gaseous fuel changes density with temperature, so gas systems measure it to meter the right mass; Ford's 2003 bi-fuel CNG trucks, for example, use a thermistor at the rail for that density calculation and only switch to gas once both temperature and pressure allow it. The title of P2A4B names no location, which sets it apart from the tank temperature codes (P01AA ff.), the rail temperature codes (P01B4 ff.) and the vaporizer outlet sensors (P2A50 ff.). It is the general circuit fault of this gas temperature input, without a low or high verdict. No manufacturer documents P2A4B; Roush's propane systems report their fuel temperature under P0181–P0183 instead. Inspect plug, wiring and sensor resistance, since an NTC sensor can be checked against temperature with an ohmmeter.
c: Plug or wiring of the gas temperature sensor faulty
Input stage or data link of the gas module disturbed
s: Check engine light
Bi-fuel vehicle stays on petrol or switches back
Rougher running on gas

P2A4C.d: Here the gas temperature reading is electrically valid but implausible. A typical check compares it with other temperatures after a long cold soak, when gas, intake air and coolant should agree within a few degrees; another looks for the cooling that expansion in the regulator causes under heavy gas flow. A sensor that sticks at one value or lags far behind fails such tests. CARB requires rationality checks of this kind for inputs that affect fuel metering. Because the mass of gas injected depends on its density, a temperature that is wrong but in range quietly shifts the mixture, which the fuel trim then has to absorb. No manufacturer publishes P2A4C or its limits; Roush's propane equivalent is P0181. A sensor with a poor thermal contact can also cause it.
c: Sensor drifted, slow or stuck at one value
Sensor seated loosely or with poor thermal contact
s: Check engine light after a drive cycle
Fuel trim off while running on gas
Often no noticeable driving issue

P2A4D.t: Alternative Fuel Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
P2A4D.d: P2A4D means the voltage of the gas temperature sensor is below its valid limit. Gas temperature sensors are normally NTC thermistors whose resistance drops as they warm up, so a low voltage would correspond to extremely hot gas; in practice it nearly always means the signal wire is grounded or the sensor is shorted inside. TransEco shows how a gas module reacts to the comparable rail temperature Low code: dedicated installations replace the reading with the intake air temperature, bi-fuel ones are forced back to petrol, and the lamp comes on. No manufacturer lists P2A4D itself. Unplugging the sensor should make the reading jump to very cold; if it stays hot, look for the short in the harness rather than in the sensor.
c: Signal wire of the gas temperature sensor shorted to ground
s: Check engine light
Gas mode refused, bi-fuel vehicle runs on petrol
Live data shows an implausibly hot gas temperature

P2A4E.t: Alternative Fuel Temperature Sensor Circuit High
P2A4E.d: The counterpart to P2A4D: the gas temperature signal rises above its upper limit. With the usual NTC thermistor fed through a pull-up resistor, that equals an absurdly cold reading, and the most frequent reason is an open circuit, either a broken wire, a loose terminal or a sensor that has gone open inside. A short to a voltage source has the same effect. In TransEco's list the related rail temperature High code is attributed to exactly these causes and handled like the Low case, with a substitute value from the intake air sensor or a forced change to petrol. No manufacturer documents P2A4E publicly. Bridging the two pins at the plug should flip the reading to very hot; if not, the break lies between plug and module.
c: Broken wire or loose terminal in the sensor circuit
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
s: Check engine light
Live data shows gas temperature at its coldest limit
Bi-fuel vehicle falls back to petrol

P2A4F.t: Alternative Fuel Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2A4F.d: Temperature changes slowly, so a gas temperature reading that leaps by tens of degrees within moments is not physics but wiring. P2A4F is set for such spikes and dropouts of the gas temperature signal, while P2A4D and P2A4E cover signals that stay out of range. Engine vibration and heat cycles near the regulator loosen terminals and crack insulation, which is why the usual finds are a connector with fretting corrosion or a wire that breaks inside its insulation only when bent. Short glitches may cause a momentary change back to petrol on bi-fuel vehicles. No manufacturer documents P2A4F; it matches P01B8 for the rail sensor and P0184 on petrol engines. Check the circuit with a meter while flexing the harness at the sensor.
c: Fretting corrosion or loose terminal at the sensor plug
Wire broken inside its insulation near the regulator
s: Check engine light that comes and goes
Short switches to petrol on bi-fuel vehicles
Jumping gas temperature in live data

P2A50.t: Alternative Fuel Vaporizer A Outlet Temperature Sensor Circuit
P2A50.d: A vaporizer, often called reducer or converter on LPG systems, turns liquid gas into vapour with heat taken from the engine coolant. The sensor in P2A50 sits on the outlet side of vaporizer A and tells the control unit whether that unit is warm enough. Patent US7073489B2 explains why this matters: with too little heat the liquid does not fully evaporate and can block the regulator jet. P2A50 covers any fault in this sensor circuit that the module cannot classify as low or high. No vehicle manufacturer documents P2A50 publicly; aftermarket controllers such as AC STAG show the same problem as a missing or shorted reducer temperature sensor. Until the circuit works again, the system will usually stay on or return to petrol.
c: Plug or wiring of the vaporizer A outlet sensor faulty
Outlet temperature sensor of vaporizer A defective
Input stage of the gas control module disturbed
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Vehicle stays on petrol or switches back from gas
Gas mode indicator flashes or stays off

P2A51.t: Alternative Fuel Vaporizer A Outlet Temperature Sensor Range/Performance
P2A51.d: P2A51 does not point to a broken wire: the outlet temperature of vaporizer A is electrically valid but does not fit the operating state. Typical tests compare it with coolant and ambient after a long stop, expect it to climb as the engine warms up, and expect a dip when heavy gas flow draws heat out of the unit. A value that freezes, drifts or lags badly fails such checks. CARB demands rationality diagnostics of this kind and wants them stored apart from circuit faults. The mounting point matters: US7073489B2 notes that coolant may be at 50 °C while the converter body runs near 5 °C, so a sensor touching the wrong part reads very differently. No manufacturer publishes limits for P2A51. If the sensor checks out, consider P2A8B, a vaporizer A that lacks performance.
c: Sensor drifts or sticks at one value
Sensor badly seated or mounted at an unsuitable point
Vaporizer A really too cold (low coolant, air in the circuit, stuck thermostat)
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Late or no switch-over to gas after a cold start
Uneven running or hesitation on gas

P2A52.t: Alternative Fuel Vaporizer A Outlet Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
P2A52.d: Temperature sensors of this type are usually thermistors whose resistance falls as they get warmer, the same principle Ford describes for the fuel rail sensor of its 2003 bi-fuel CNG trucks. A signal under the lower limit would therefore mean an impossibly hot vaporizer A; in practice the signal line touches ground or the sensor is shorted inside. AC STAG lists this case as a reducer temperature sensor short. The danger is that a hot reading could let gas flow into a unit that is actually cold, so a control module will normally replace the value or fall back to petrol. No manufacturer documents P2A52. Pull the plug and watch the live data: a swing to very cold clears the harness, a hot value that remains points to a short in the wiring.
c: Moisture or coolant in the connector
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Gas mode blocked, vehicle runs on petrol
Live data shows an implausibly hot vaporizer

P2A53.t: Alternative Fuel Vaporizer A Outlet Temperature Sensor Circuit High
P2A53.d: P2A53 is the opposite case: the voltage of the vaporizer A outlet sensor sits near the supply reference, which a thermistor input reads as extreme cold. A broken wire, an unplugged or corroded connector, an open sensor element or a short to a voltage source all produce this. AC STAG names the open variant a missing reducer temperature sensor. Because its controllers only change over to gas once the reducer temperature allows it, such a reading keeps a bi-fuel vehicle on petrol; a dedicated gas engine may refuse to start or run with reduced output. TransEco handles the related rail sensor High code the same way, forcing petrol mode with the lamp on. No manufacturer publishes P2A53 itself. Bridging the plug pins should make the value jump to very hot.
c: Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
No switch-over to gas, bi-fuel vehicle stays on petrol
Live data shows a vaporizer far below freezing

P2A54.t: Alternative Fuel Vaporizer A Outlet Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2A54.d: A vaporizer full of coolant has a lot of thermal mass, so its outlet temperature can only change gradually. P2A54 is set when the vaporizer A signal jumps, drops out briefly or flickers in a way no real temperature could; the fault may be gone by the time a technician looks. Loose or corroded pins, a wire chafing on a hot hose and engine vibration are the usual reasons. CARB requires the module to catch such faults on inputs that affect emissions. AC STAG controllers keep a frozen frame of the conditions whenever an error occurs, which helps to tie the dropouts to bumps or engine load. No vehicle maker documents P2A54. The driver may notice repeated switching between gas and petrol.
c: Wire chafing on a hose or bracket
Sensor with an internal loose contact
s: Intermittent check engine light, depending on calibration
Occasional switching back to petrol
Jumping vaporizer temperature in live data

P2A55.t: Alternative Fuel Vaporizer B Outlet Temperature Sensor Circuit
P2A55.d: A second vaporizer appears where one heat exchanger cannot supply enough gas, for instance on large or heavy-duty engines. On LNG trucks the job is harder still: Westport's patent CA2862664C starts from liquid near −160 °C, heats it with engine coolant and places a gas temperature sensor downstream of the exchanger to choose how the coolant flows. P2A55 reports a circuit fault of the outlet sensor on vaporizer B that the module cannot sort into low or high. For heavy-duty alternative fuel engines from model year 2018, CARB section 1971.1 lets each maker submit its own monitoring plan, which helps explain why public code lists are scarce; none documents P2A55. The intact sensor on vaporizer A helps as a comparison while tracing plug and harness of B.
c: Plug or harness of the vaporizer B sensor damaged
Fault in the sensor input of the control module
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Reduced power or gas mode limited
Fall-back to the second fuel on dual-fuel engines

P2A56.t: Alternative Fuel Vaporizer B Outlet Temperature Sensor Range/Performance
P2A56.d: With two vaporizers fed by the same coolant, their outlet temperatures should behave alike, which gives the module a natural cross-check. P2A56 means the vaporizer B reading is electrically fine but out of line with that expectation, with the engine state or with its own history. The plausible window is wide: Westport's LNG patent gives vaporized fuel temperatures anywhere from about −20 °C to +80 °C depending on how the engine runs, so tests rely on comparisons rather than fixed values. Two causes look alike here: a drifting sensor, or vaporizer B really running colder because an air lock or kinked hose starves it of coolant. Feeling both coolant hoses settles it. The second case belongs to P2A8C. No manufacturer publishes P2A56 thresholds.
c: Vaporizer B sensor reads off or sluggishly
Vaporizer B gets too little coolant (air lock, kinked or blocked hose)
Sensor seated loosely in its port
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Power drop under high load on gas
Clear temperature gap between vaporizer A and B in live data

P2A57.t: Alternative Fuel Vaporizer B Outlet Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
P2A57.d: P2A57 sets when the outlet sensor on vaporizer B pulls its signal below the lowest valid voltage. On a thermistor that loses resistance with heat, as in the Ford CNG rail sensor, this would mean extreme heat, so the realistic causes are a signal lead grounded against the chassis and an internally shorted sensor. Long harness runs, common when the gas parts sit far from the controller, add chafing points. A falsely hot value is risky because the system could believe B is ready while it is cold. TransEco, for its comparable rail sensor fault, substitutes the intake air reading on dedicated systems and forces petrol on bi-fuel ones. No maker lists P2A57. Unplug the sensor: the reading must swing to cold, otherwise the harness is shorted.
c: Signal lead of the B sensor grounded
Insulation worn through on a long harness run
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Gas operation limited or switched off
Vaporizer B shown far hotter than vaporizer A

P2A58.t: Alternative Fuel Vaporizer B Outlet Temperature Sensor Circuit High
P2A58.d: Here the signal of the vaporizer B outlet sensor rests at or near the reference voltage, so the module would see a deep-frozen unit. Typical reasons are an open wire, a plug that has backed out, a sensor element that has failed open or a short to a supply line. Telling a wiring fault from a real problem matters on gas engines: CA2862664C warns that coolant inside and next to an LNG heat exchanger may turn to ice during a cold start, and such a frozen vaporizer would also read very cold, though not at the electrical limit. The control unit therefore stops trusting vaporizer B, which can mean reduced gas delivery or a fall-back fuel. AC STAG calls the open case a missing sensor. No manufacturer documents P2A58.
c: Open wire or plug of the B sensor backed out
Signal lead touching a supply line
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Gas delivery reduced or fall-back fuel used
Vaporizer B shown at an impossibly low temperature

P2A59.t: Alternative Fuel Vaporizer B Outlet Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2A59.d: On heavy vehicles the gas hardware sees constant shaking, and long harness runs to the vaporizers add connectors that can loosen. P2A59 records that the vaporizer B outlet signal changed faster or more erratically than real temperature can, or kept dropping out for short moments. Such faults tend to come and go with road surface, engine speed or coolant heat. The A sensor gives a good reference: if its value is smooth while B jumps, the problem is local to the B circuit. Look for green corrosion at the pins, cracked insulation and strain on the plug. No manufacturer documents P2A59; CARB still requires that sporadic faults on an input like this are detected. Expect occasional switching to petrol or a flickering gas indicator.
c: Connector of the B sensor loose or corroded
Harness damaged by vibration or strain
s: Check engine light comes and goes, depending on calibration
Sporadic switching to petrol
Flickering gas indicator

P2A5A.t: Alternative Fuel Vaporizer C Outlet Temperature Sensor Circuit
P2A5A.d: Vaporizer C is the third unit in a gas system that splits the conversion of liquid fuel over several heat exchangers, a layout that only makes sense for engines with very high gas demand. Each unit needs its own outlet sensor because a vaporizer that cannot keep up shows it first by a falling outlet temperature; patent US6755643B2 even uses an outlet sensor to shut a vaporizer down once the draw exceeds its capacity. P2A5A is the undirected circuit fault on the sensor of vaporizer C. No manufacturer documents this code, and public sources on three-vaporizer layouts are thin. CARB still requires circuit monitoring for such inputs. Depending on calibration, the module may limit gas operation or ignore unit C. Start with the connector and the sensor resistance.
c: Connector or wiring of the vaporizer C sensor faulty
Control module input for sensor C faulty
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Gas operation limited, less power at high load
Vehicle falls back to the other fuel

P2A5B.t: Alternative Fuel Vaporizer C Outlet Temperature Sensor Range/Performance
P2A5B.d: With three outlet sensors in one system, a plausibility check can use a majority: if A and B agree and C stands apart, vaporizer C or its sensor is the odd one out. P2A5B means the C value is electrically valid but fails such a comparison or does not follow warm-up and load as it should. The industrial vaporizer described in US6755643B2 shows the physical background: when more vapour is drawn than a unit can produce, its outlet cools. A C reading that sinks only under heavy load may therefore be true and point to a starved or fouled vaporizer (P2A8D) rather than to the sensor. A reading that stays flat whatever the engine does points to the sensor. No maker publishes the logic behind P2A5B.
c: Sensor C stuck, drifting or slow
Vaporizer C genuinely too cold from lack of coolant or fouling
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Power loss at full load on gas
Vaporizer C differs clearly from A and B in live data

P2A5C.t: Alternative Fuel Vaporizer C Outlet Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
P2A5C.d: P2A5C stands for a vaporizer C outlet signal below the valid range. Since such inputs are normally NTC thermistors, the module would read an implausibly hot unit; a signal lead touching ground or a sensor shorted internally is far more likely. Coolant that has seeped into the connector can also create a path to ground. AC STAG controllers show this as a short in the reducer temperature circuit and advise checking insulation and plug. A wrongly hot vaporizer C is a safety concern, since gas could pass through a unit that is in fact too cold to vaporize it fully. No manufacturer documents P2A5C. Disconnect the sensor and watch the value: a jump to cold means the sensor itself is shorted, no change means the fault sits in the wiring.
c: Signal lead of sensor C shorted to ground
Coolant or water in the connector
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Gas operation blocked or limited
Vaporizer C shown far too hot

P2A5D.t: Alternative Fuel Vaporizer C Outlet Temperature Sensor Circuit High
P2A5D.d: P2A5D says the vaporizer C sensor signal is stuck high, near the reference voltage, which reads as extreme cold. An interrupted wire, a disconnected or corroded plug, an open sensor or a short to battery voltage are the candidates. Gas controllers that use vaporizer temperature as a release condition, as AC STAG does before switching to gas, will hold off gas mode when they see such a value. With two other vaporizers still reporting, a control unit might be calibrated to carry on without C at reduced output, but no manufacturer documents P2A5D or its reaction. TransEco's analogous rail temperature High code names an open sensor or short to power. Measure resistance at the sensor and compare it with the coolant temperature.
c: Wire to sensor C interrupted or plug disconnected
Signal lead shorted to battery voltage
s: Check engine light, depending on calibration
Gas mode held back or output reduced
Vaporizer C shown at extreme cold

P2A5E.t: Alternative Fuel Vaporizer C Outlet Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2A5E.d: P2A5E marks an unsteady vaporizer C signal: brief dropouts, spikes or a jagged trace that a coolant-heated part cannot really produce. The fault often clears itself and returns, so it matters what conditions trigger it. Gas controllers such as AC STAG store a frozen frame of the moment an error occurs; logging the three outlet temperatures side by side during a test drive shows quickly whether only C misbehaves. Common culprits are a connector that has lost its grip, a pin pushed back in the housing and a cable rubbing against a bracket. CARB requires the detection of such sporadic faults on emission-relevant inputs. No manufacturer documents P2A5E. Until repaired, the gas system may drop out now and then.
c: Connector of sensor C without firm grip
Contact pin pushed back in the housing
s: Check engine light now and then, depending on calibration
Gas operation drops out occasionally
Spiky vaporizer C trace in recorded data

P2A5F.t: Alternative Fuel Tank B Level Sensor Circuit
P2A5F.d: How the content of a second gas tank is measured depends on the fuel. CNG has no liquid surface, so the level is worked out from pressure, often corrected by tank temperature; GM's 2015 Impala Bi-Fuel shows full near 3,600 psi and empty near 400 psi. LPG, being liquid, allows a float whose magnet passes its position through the tank wall to a Hall element, as in Rochester's R3D dials. P2A5F is the general circuit fault of such a sender on tank B, without a low or high finding. No manufacturer documents P2A5F. Roush's propane trucks with two tanks use the petrol codes P2067 and P2068 for the second sender instead, and the gauge then shows only the primary tank. Start with plug, wiring and supply of the tank B sender.
c: Plug or wiring of the tank B sender faulty
Tank B level sender or Hall module defective
Reading module or data link to the engine module disturbed
s: Check engine light
Gauge ignores the content of tank B
Range estimate on gas too low

P2A60.t: Alternative Fuel Tank B Level Sensor Range/Performance
P2A60.d: P2A60 flags a tank B level that is electrically valid but does not behave like a real fuel quantity: it fails to drop while gas is used from tank B, does not climb after filling, or swings wildly although the tank is at rest. Roush documents the stuck logic for its propane primary sender as P25B0, set when the value stays put over a considerable distance. On LPG the cause is often mechanical, a float arm bent or jammed inside the tank; with CNG, where the level is calculated, a drifting pressure sensor or a cold fill can mislead it, and GM notes that its gauge may read below full after refuelling in the cold. No manufacturer publishes P2A60 or its limits; CARB asks for rationality checks on such inputs. Compare the sender with the tank's own dial gauge.
c: Float arm in tank B bent or jammed (LPG)
Pressure or temperature input behind the calculated level drifting (CNG)
Contact resistance shifting the sender signal
s: Check engine light after several trips
Gas gauge does not move as fuel is used
Unexpected running out of gas

P2A61.t: Alternative Fuel Tank B Level Sensor Circuit Low
P2A61.d: P2A61 is stored when the tank B level signal falls below the smallest voltage the sender produces even with the tank empty. Roush's manual for its dual-tank propane trucks names a sender wire shorted to ground or a damaged sender as causes of the low case and adds that the second-tank code P2067 leaves only the primary tank on the gauge. A Hall-type float module with ratiometric output, such as Rochester's for LPG tanks, can also read low when its supply voltage is missing. The driver sees tank B as empty or ignored, and the usable range on gas appears shorter than it is. No manufacturer documents P2A61 itself. Check for chafed wiring near the tank mounting first, then measure supply and ground at the sender.
c: Sender signal wire of tank B shorted to ground
Supply voltage of a Hall-type sender missing
s: Check engine light
Tank B shown empty or left out of the gauge
Shorter displayed gas range

P2A62.t: Alternative Fuel Tank B Level Sensor Circuit High
P2A62.d: P2A62 is set when the tank B level signal climbs above the highest voltage a working sender delivers at full. For its dual-tank propane trucks Roush blames the high case on a disconnected sender or a wire shorted to more than 5 V, and with the second-tank code P2068 the gauge again falls back to the primary tank only. A broken ground at the sender gives the same picture on most pull-up inputs. The risk is the opposite of P2A61: if the reading were accepted, tank B would look full while it empties, so the module discards it. No manufacturer documents P2A62 itself. Check that the plug at the tank B sender is seated and locked, then test ground continuity before replacing the sender.
c: Tank B sender unplugged or wire open
Signal wire shorted to a voltage above 5 V
s: Check engine light
Gauge shows only the primary tank
Content of tank B unknown to the driver

P2A63.t: Alternative Fuel Tank B Level Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2A63.d: Fuel slosh makes any level reading wobble a little, and modules filter that out. P2A63 goes further: the tank B level signal drops out or jumps in steps no filter can explain, then returns to normal. Contacts at the sender are the main suspect, since the tank sits low on the chassis and is exposed to spray and road salt; a cable pinched by a tank strap or a Hall module losing contact in its housing are other options. Rochester presents its contact-free Hall design as more reliable than senders with a sliding wiper, and a worn wiper track is indeed a classic source of such jumps. No manufacturer documents P2A63; on petrol vehicles the counterpart is P2069 for the second sender. Watch the level reading while rocking the vehicle and flexing the harness.
c: Corroded contacts at the tank B sender from road spray
Cable pinched by a tank strap
Worn wiper track or loose Hall module in the sender
s: Gas gauge for tank B jumps or briefly drops
Check engine light from time to time
Range display unsteady

P2A64.t: Alternative Fuel Tank C Level Sensor Circuit
P2A64.d: A third gas tank, C, may have its own level input, either a real float sender in an LPG vessel or, on CNG, a value the module derives from that tank's pressure, the way Ford's 2003 bi-fuel trucks turned tank pressure into a gauge reading. P2A64 reports that the tank C level circuit is faulty without saying whether the signal is too low or too high; P2A66 and P2A67 make that distinction. Even the petrol-based code set ends at a second sender, so there is no conventional analogue for a third tank, and no manufacturer documents P2A64. The effect is mostly informational: the gauge or range shown may leave out tank C. Inspect the sender plug and its wiring run, which on rear-mounted tanks is often long and exposed.
c: Long harness run to tank C damaged or plug loose
Fault in the tank C pressure input the level is derived from (CNG)
s: Check engine light
Gauge or range leaves out tank C
Otherwise normal driving

P2A65.t: Alternative Fuel Tank C Level Sensor Range/Performance
P2A65.d: For tank C this code reports a level that stays within the valid voltage window yet contradicts what happens to the tank. Examples are a reading that remains unchanged over many kilometres although tank C supplies the engine, no rise after a fill, or a level that disagrees with the pressure in a CNG cylinder. With LPG a float that sticks or a sender fitted at the wrong angle are likely; with calculated CNG levels the error usually sits in the pressure or temperature input. GM's Impala bulletin explains one harmless case: after a cold fill, the gauge may stay below full even though the tank is correctly filled. No manufacturer publishes P2A65; CARB requires rationality monitoring. Cross-check against the mechanical gauge at tank C.
c: Float in tank C sticking or sender mounted at a wrong angle (LPG)
Pressure or temperature input of tank C drifting (CNG)
Contact resistance shifting the level signal
s: Check engine light after several trips
Level for tank C frozen or illogical
Range estimate unreliable

P2A66.t: Alternative Fuel Tank C Level Sensor Circuit Low
P2A66.d: P2A66 says the tank C level signal is below its lower electrical bound. With voltage-output senders that typically comes from a signal wire grounded somewhere along its route, a sender shorted inside, or a missing supply to a ratiometric Hall module such as those Rochester builds for LPG vessels, which needs a few volts to produce any output. The display consequence is an empty or missing tank C, so a driver may refuel early or think the gas supply is shorter than it is. No manufacturer documents P2A66, and since the petrol code family covers only two senders, the nearest documented relative is the tank B case P2A61. Disconnecting the sender should move the reading; if it stays low, trace the short in the harness.
c: Tank C sender signal wire grounded
No supply voltage at a Hall-type sender
s: Check engine light
Tank C displayed as empty
Refuelling earlier than needed

P2A67.t: Alternative Fuel Tank C Level Sensor Circuit High
P2A67.d: P2A67 is the high-side partner of P2A66: the tank C level voltage lies above anything a correctly working sender outputs at full. An unplugged connector, a broken signal or ground wire and a short to a supply voltage all push the input there. Roush names such faults for the high case of its propane senders and notes for the second-tank code P2068 that only the primary tank is then shown; for a third tank no such public text exists, and no manufacturer documents P2A67. Since a believed full tank C could leave the driver stranded, the module drops the value rather than display it. Look for a connector knocked loose during tank service and check ground continuity from sender to chassis.
c: Tank C sender plug loose or knocked off
Signal shorted to a supply voltage
s: Check engine light
Tank C missing from the gauge
Driver unsure about remaining gas

P2A68.t: Alternative Fuel Tank C Level Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2A68.d: The last code of this block covers a tank C level signal that flickers: it is valid most of the time but suffers short gaps or jumps unrelated to fuel movement. On vehicles with three tanks the wiring to tank C is often the longest and has the most joints, each a chance for a loose crimp or green corrosion; frame flex can open a fractured conductor for an instant. Where the level is computed from CNG pressure, a flickering pressure input (P2A4A) can be the real source. No manufacturer documents P2A68; it parallels P2A63 for tank B and P01B3 for tank A, and CARB treats erratic inputs as part of component monitoring. Stored freeze-frame values plus live level data on a test drive narrow it down.
c: Loose crimp or corroded joint in the long tank C harness
Conductor fractured, opening under frame flex
Unsteady tank C pressure input behind a calculated level (CNG)
s: Tank C level jumps on the display
Check engine light now and then
Range display unsteady

P2A69.t: Alternative Fuel Rail Pressure Regulator Inlet Pressure Sensor Circuit
P2A69.d: On a gaseous-fuel engine, the rail pressure regulator takes gas straight from the storage cylinders and steps it down for the injector rail. P2A69 covers the transducer on the high-pressure side of that regulator, set when its circuit is faulty without a clear low or high verdict. GM's 2015 Impala bi-fuel mounts a three-wire sensor on top of the regulator that reads cylinder pressure as high as 3,600 psi; Ford's 2003 bi-fuel CNG trucks build it into the regulator. ITT describes a CNG regulator with a transducer at its inlet port next to one at the outlet. None of them publishes P2A69 itself. Without the reading, remaining gas and regulator supply cannot be judged, so gas mode is usually blocked. P2A6B and P2A6C name the low and high cases.
c: Connector or harness at the regulator damaged by heat, vibration or corrosion
Inlet pressure transducer on the regulator faulty
5 V reference or sensor ground disturbed
Engine or alternative fuel control module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Gas mode not available, bi-fuel vehicle stays on petrol
Gas gauge implausible or showing empty

P2A6A.t: Alternative Fuel Rail Pressure Regulator Inlet Pressure Sensor Range/Performance
P2A6A.d: P2A6A flags a regulator inlet pressure reading that is electrically valid but implausible. Upstream of the regulator the value should fall slowly as gas is burned, jump after refuelling and, with the engine at rest, roughly equal cylinder pressure. A reading that stays frozen, climbs while driving, or sits below the regulated rail pressure although the engine runs normally points to a drifting transducer. For scale: GM regulates the Impala bi-fuel rail to 68–130 psi from a cylinder filled to 3,600 psi, and Blackstone's SAN209 regulator accepts up to 4,500 psig. No manufacturer documents P2A6A or its limits; CARB requires a rationality check for inputs like this one. Compare the sensor with a calibrated gauge before replacing parts.
c: Inlet pressure transducer drifted or contaminated by oil carried in the gas
Manual or solenoid tank valve closed, so the reading does not change
Contact resistance in connector shifts the signal
s: Check engine light on
Gas gauge does not match the actual fill level
Unexpected switch to petrol or gas mode refused

P2A6B.t: Alternative Fuel Rail Pressure Regulator Inlet Pressure Sensor Circuit Low
P2A6B.d: P2A6B is stored when the signal voltage of the regulator inlet pressure sensor drops below its valid band. With a typical three-wire transducer (5 V feed, signal, ground) that means a signal lead shorted to ground, a lost 5 V reference or a failed sensor element. A low voltage would read as an almost empty cylinder, so a bi-fuel vehicle may refuse gas mode or show an empty gauge with a full tank; Ford's 2003 bi-fuel CNG logic drove the gauge to empty whenever the sensor built into its regulator failed. GM uses the same reading on the Impala together with tank temperature to work out the fill level. No maker publishes P2A6B directly. Measure feed and signal at the plug with the key on before condemning the sensor.
c: Signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
5 V reference open or pulled down by another sensor on the same feed
s: Check engine light on
Gas gauge shows empty although the tank is full
Gas mode refused, bi-fuel vehicle runs on petrol

P2A6C.t: Alternative Fuel Rail Pressure Regulator Inlet Pressure Sensor Circuit High
P2A6C.d: P2A6C means the regulator inlet pressure signal sits above its plausible voltage ceiling. Typical causes are a signal wire touching a 5 V or battery-voltage circuit, an open sensor ground, an open signal line that the module pulls up internally (depending on its design), or an internal transducer fault. Unlike a genuinely excessive cylinder pressure, which P2A6F covers, the value here lies outside anything the sensor can physically deliver. On GM's Impala bi-fuel the regulator-mounted sensor covers a cylinder range of 3,600 psi; ITT's patented regulator places one transducer at the inlet port and a second at the outlet. No manufacturer documents P2A6C with thresholds. A broken ground often pins the reading at maximum, so check ground and connector first.
c: Sensor ground open or connector terminal pushed out
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
s: Check engine light on
Gas gauge stuck at full regardless of consumption
Gas mode blocked, bi-fuel vehicle switches to petrol

P2A6D.t: Alternative Fuel Rail Pressure Regulator Inlet Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2A6D.d: P2A6D is the dropout code of the regulator inlet pressure sensor: the signal jumps or briefly vanishes, but not long enough for a steady low or high verdict. The regulator normally lives in the engine bay, next to the right-hand strut mount on GM's 2015 Impala bi-fuel, and Blackstone requires warm engine coolant to circulate through its SAN209 unit so that it does not ice up. Its connector therefore sees heat, vibration and condensation. Loose terminals, a harness chafed against coolant hoses or moisture inside the plug are the usual suspects. No manufacturer publishes P2A6D; CARB expects circuit faults of such inputs to be detected. Wiggle-test the harness while watching live data, and look for corrosion in the connector.
c: Loose or widened terminal in the sensor connector
Condensation or corrosion in the plug near the coolant-heated regulator
Harness rubbing on hoses or brackets with intermittent contact
s: Check engine light on, sometimes clearing again
Gas gauge flickers or jumps
Sporadic switch from gas to petrol while driving

P2A6E.t: Alternative Fuel Rail Pressure Regulator Inlet Pressure Too Low
P2A6E.d: P2A6E is not a wiring fault: the inlet pressure sensor works, but the gas reaching the regulator is too weak for it to hold rail pressure. A regulator can only reduce pressure, so once the supply approaches its outlet setpoint, rail pressure sinks with it. ITT's CNG regulator patent addresses exactly this low-supply phase with a bypass that opens below a set inlet pressure. Common reasons are a nearly empty cylinder, a tank solenoid or manual valve that is not fully open, or a clogged high-pressure filter. Ford's 2003 bi-fuel CNG system closed the tank valve and fell back to petrol once system pressure dropped under 517 kPa (75 psia). No manufacturer publishes P2A6E; refuel first, then compare inlet pressure with a gauge.
c: Tank solenoid or manual shut-off valve not fully open
High-pressure filter clogged or line restricted
Inlet pressure sensor reading too low within its range
s: Check engine light on
Loss of power or stumbling in gas mode, especially at high load
Automatic switch to petrol or engine stalls on dedicated gas engines

P2A6F.t: Alternative Fuel Rail Pressure Regulator Inlet Pressure Too High
P2A6F.d: P2A6F reports a regulator inlet pressure above the calibrated maximum. Only cylinder pressure is present upstream of the regulator, so a genuinely high value usually comes from the tank side, such as overfilling at a dispenser without temperature compensation or a cold-filled cylinder that later warms up strongly; a transducer reading high but still in range is the other option. GM notes for the Impala bi-fuel, whose cylinder is rated at 3,600 psi, that stations limit fill pressure by temperature so that a car moved somewhere warmer is not overpressurised. Blackstone's SAN209 regulator allows up to 4,500 psig at the inlet and carries a relief device on the outlet. No manufacturer documents P2A6F. Verify the reading against a gauge before suspecting the tank.
c: Inlet pressure sensor reading too high within its range
Cylinder overfilled or strongly warmed after a cold fill
Sensor or calibration not matching the installed cylinder pressure rating
s: Check engine light on
Gas mode blocked as a precaution
Often appears right after refuelling

P2A70.t: Alternative Fuel Hydraulic Fuel Pump Select Valve Control Circuit
P2A70.d: Some heavy-duty LNG systems do not drive the cryogenic tank pump directly but through hydraulics: an engine- or motor-driven hydraulic pump supplies oil to a reciprocating hydraulic drive on each tank pump. Westport's patent US8726785B2 shows two LNG vessels whose pumps sit inside the tanks, plus a selector valve that the controller switches to decide which pump receives hydraulic flow. P2A70 covers the electrical control circuit of such a select valve and is set when the driver output detects a general fault. If the valve cannot be commanded, the system may be stuck on one tank or lose LNG supply. No manufacturer publishes P2A70; CARB's heavy-duty rule requires output components to be monitored. P2A72 and P2A73 separate the low and high cases.
c: Damaged harness or connector at the select valve on the frame
Output stage in the controlling module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Fuel drawn from one LNG tank only, range reduced
Loss of gas supply, dual-fuel engine falls back to diesel-only or derates

P2A71.t: Alternative Fuel Hydraulic Fuel Pump Select Valve Control Range/Performance
P2A71.d: P2A71 concerns the function of the hydraulic fuel pump select valve rather than its wiring: the circuit is intact, but the system does not respond as expected after a switch command. In Westport's design the controller links the hydraulic pressure it measures to whichever pump the selector valve should be feeding; if the pressure pattern does not match the commanded pump, or the empty-tank logic sees no change after switching, the valve is probably sticking or leaking internally. Contaminated hydraulic oil, a worn spool or a weak solenoid are typical. Caterpillar's patent describes a related directional valve whose actuator is shifted once pressure sensors detect the stroke end. No manufacturer publishes P2A71 or its limits.
c: Valve spool sticking due to contaminated hydraulic oil
Worn valve leaking internally, flow reaches both pumps
Solenoid force too low, for example from low supply voltage
s: Check engine light on
Tank changeover does not happen or happens late
Uneven LNG levels between tanks

P2A72.t: Alternative Fuel Hydraulic Fuel Pump Select Valve Control Circuit Low
P2A72.d: P2A72 is set when the control circuit of the hydraulic fuel pump select valve reads lower than expected for the commanded state. On a low-side driver this typically means the control wire is shorted to ground, so the valve coil may stay energised; on a high-side driver a short to ground or a shorted coil pulls the output down and may trip its protection. Either way the controller can no longer trust which LNG tank pump is being driven. Westport's patented system relies on knowing the valve position to assign hydraulic pressure readings to the right pump, so tank selection and empty-tank detection become unreliable. No manufacturer documents P2A72. Measure coil resistance and check the harness for chafing against the chassis.
c: Control wire chafed on the frame and shorted to ground
Select valve coil with shorted turns
Water in the connector bridging to ground
s: Check engine light on
Select valve stays switched, one tank pump runs permanently
Gas supply interrupted when the active tank runs empty

P2A73.t: Alternative Fuel Hydraulic Fuel Pump Select Valve Control Circuit High
P2A73.d: P2A73 signals that the select valve control circuit sits at a higher voltage than the commanded state allows. Typical faults are an open coil or broken wire on a low-side driven valve, which leaves the line at supply voltage, or a short to battery voltage that the output cannot pull down. The valve then stays in its spring-return position, so hydraulic flow keeps going to one tank pump whatever the command. On a multi-tank LNG truck the second tank may never be used, and the engine runs short of gas although LNG remains on board. Caterpillar's patent shows such a valve shifted by an actuator under controller command. No manufacturer publishes P2A73. Check coil resistance, the connector and the supply wire.
c: Valve coil or control wire open
Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Corroded connector pins with very high resistance
s: Check engine light on
Second LNG tank not used, range clearly shorter
Gas supply stops although fuel remains

P2A74.t: Alternative Fuel Hydraulic Fuel Pump Select Valve Control Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2A74.d: P2A74 covers brief, recurring faults in the select valve control circuit that clear before a firm low or high verdict. On LNG trucks the valve usually sits near the tank-mounted pump and hydraulic lines, where frame flex, road spray and very cold surfaces around the cryogenic tank stress connectors and insulation. A valve that drops out for a moment can cut hydraulic flow to the working pump mid-stroke; because Westport's control logic recognises the stroke end from pressure changes, such dropouts may also upset pump timing. Typical finds are loose terminals, corroded pins and wiring chafed along the frame rail. No manufacturer publishes P2A74. Wiggle the harness while watching the output status, and check the plug for moisture.
c: Loose terminal in the select valve connector
Moisture or ice in the connector near the cryogenic tank
Harness chafed along the frame rail with intermittent contact
s: Check engine light on, may go out again
Brief hesitation or pressure dips in gas mode
Irregular tank changeover

P2A75.t: Alternative Fuel Hydraulic Pump Pressure Sensor Circuit
P2A75.d: In a hydraulically driven LNG pump system the controller watches the oil pressure delivered by the hydraulic pump. Westport's patent US8726785B2 places this sensor in the supply line between the hydraulic pump outlet and the hydraulic drive, using it for three jobs: reversing the drive at each stroke end, spotting an empty tank when peak pressure stays low, and flagging leaks or other abnormal conditions. Caterpillar's design likewise feeds supply and return pressure to the controller to shift its directional valve. P2A75 is the general circuit fault of this hydraulic pump pressure sensor. Without the signal, the pump cannot be cycled correctly and LNG delivery may stop. No manufacturer publishes P2A75; P2A77 and P2A78 cover low and high.
c: Connector or harness at the hydraulic pressure sensor damaged
s: Check engine light on
LNG pump stops or strokes irregularly, gas pressure drops
Dual-fuel engine runs on diesel only or with reduced power

P2A76.t: Alternative Fuel Hydraulic Pump Pressure Sensor Range/Performance
P2A76.d: P2A76 is set when the hydraulic pump pressure reading looks electrically sound yet makes no sense for the operating state. Westport's patent explains why a fixed expectation is not enough: pressure rises with hydraulic pump speed, which follows engine speed when the pump is engine-driven, and with the LNG pressure the cryogenic pump works against. The controller therefore corrects its thresholds with a look-up table. A reading that stays flat while the pump strokes, shows no drop at stroke end, or disagrees with downstream fuel pressure points to a drifting sensor, but also to worn pump seals or low oil level. No manufacturer publishes P2A76 or its limits. Compare with a mechanical gauge on the test port and check the oil level.
c: Low hydraulic oil level or external leak
Worn hydraulic pump or drive seals
s: Check engine light on
Uneven LNG pressure or slow pressure build-up
Empty-tank warning although LNG remains

P2A77.t: Alternative Fuel Hydraulic Pump Pressure Sensor Circuit Low
P2A77.d: P2A77 is set when the signal from the hydraulic pump pressure sensor drops below the range a working sensor can deliver, typically because the signal wire or the 5 V reference is shorted to ground or the reference feed is open. On hydraulically driven LNG pumps this matters more than a mere missing value: Westport's patent US8726785B2 treats a peak hydraulic pressure that repeatedly stays low as the sign of an empty vessel, so a reading stuck near zero can mimic an exhausted tank and trigger needless tank switching or a fuel shutdown. No manufacturer publishes P2A77 or its voltage limits. Check the sensor connector, the reference voltage at the plug and the harness along the frame. P2A78 is the high counterpart.
c: Signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
5 V reference open or pulled to ground
s: Warning lamp with false empty-tank indication
Unexpected switching between LNG tanks
Gas supply stopped or reduced engine power

P2A78.t: Alternative Fuel Hydraulic Pump Pressure Sensor Circuit High
P2A78.d: P2A78 indicates that the hydraulic pump pressure sensor reports a voltage above its plausible maximum, as happens when the signal line touches the reference or battery voltage or the sensor ground is open. A false high reading is critical for the pump cycle, because rising oil pressure is the usual cue that a stroke has ended: Caterpillar's patent US9228574B2 names this as the conventional way to reverse the drive. With a pinned-high signal the controller may reverse too early or halt the pump, and LNG delivery collapses. Westport's design also uses this sensor to spot abnormal conditions, so an over-range value cannot be trusted. No manufacturer publishes P2A78. Inspect the sensor ground and look for chafed wires.
c: Sensor ground open or corroded at the connector
Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage
Pressure sensor failed with output at full scale
s: Warning lamp and very short or no pump strokes
Falling gas pressure and loss of power
Engine switches to reduced power or stops on gas

P2A79.t: Alternative Fuel Hydraulic Pump Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2A79.d: P2A79 records a hydraulic pump pressure signal that jumps or drops out for short moments without staying low or high long enough for P2A77 or P2A78. In a reciprocating LNG pump the controller reads this sensor continuously to find each stroke end, so a single spike can be mistaken for the end of travel and a brief dropout for a missing pressure peak. The pump may then run uneven strokes, and Westport's empty-tank logic, which counts low peaks over several strokes, can be misled. Vibration at the frame-mounted hydraulic unit, moisture in the plug and fractured crimps are typical causes. No manufacturer documents P2A79. Log the signal while flexing the harness; dropouts in an otherwise steady trace point to wiring.
c: Loose or fractured crimp terminal in the sensor circuit
Moisture or ice in the sensor plug
Harness damaged by vibration at the hydraulic unit
s: Uneven fuel pressure or surging power on gas
Sporadic warning lamp that clears again
Occasional false empty-tank message

P2A7A.t: Alternative Fuel Hydraulic Pressure Sensor Circuit
P2A7A.d: P2A7A is the general circuit fault of the alternative fuel hydraulic pressure sensor, a measuring point that the code list keeps apart from the hydraulic pump pressure sensor of P2A75. Where it sits is not defined publicly, and no manufacturer documents the split. Patents for hydraulically driven LNG pumps show the candidates: Caterpillar's US9228574B2 places one sensor in the supply line and another in the return line to the reservoir, while Westport's US8726785B2 suggests one sensor per side of the drive piston when pressure is taken at the drive unit. P2A7A is stored when the signal is faulty but fits neither a clear low nor a clear high case. Pump control then lacks one input and may restrict LNG delivery. P2A7C and P2A7D name low and high.
c: Damaged connector or harness at the hydraulic sensor
Fault in a sensor reference or ground shared with other sensors
s: Warning lamp on
Reduced LNG delivery or power limitation

P2A7B.t: Alternative Fuel Hydraulic Pressure Sensor Range/Performance
P2A7B.d: P2A7B covers a hydraulic pressure signal that is electrically valid but does not fit the operating state. Plausibility can be judged because pressures in the hydraulic drive of an LNG pump follow a known pattern: during a stroke the working side carries load pressure, while the return side stays close to reservoir level until the valve reverses. Westport's patent adds that pressure depends on hydraulic pump speed and on the LNG pressure the pump works against, so the expected values are corrected by table. A value frozen during strokes, a return pressure that climbs along with the supply, or a mismatch with the P2A75 sensor suggests drift, a blocked sensor port or a restricted return line. No manufacturer publishes limits for P2A7B.
c: Sensor port blocked by contaminated oil
Restricted return line or filter raising return pressure
s: Warning lamp after several drive cycles
Irregular pump strokes or reduced power on gas

P2A7C.t: Alternative Fuel Hydraulic Pressure Sensor Circuit Low
P2A7C.d: P2A7C is set when the hydraulic pressure sensor signal falls below its valid band, most often from a signal wire grounded against the chassis, an open 5 V reference or a sensor with an internal short. If this sensor watches the return side, as in one of Caterpillar's layouts, a dead-low reading would hardly stand out at first, since return pressure is low anyway; the range check against the minimum voltage still catches it. On the drive side a low value can mask the pressure rise that marks a completed stroke. The control may then rely on the remaining sensor or stop the LNG pump. Where both pressure sensors share a reference wire, check whether P2A77 is stored too. No manufacturer documents P2A7C or its thresholds.
c: Signal wire grounded against chassis or hydraulic lines
Open 5 V reference to the sensor
s: Warning lamp on
Pump stops or delivers less LNG
Additional sensor codes if the reference is shared

P2A7D.t: Alternative Fuel Hydraulic Pressure Sensor Circuit High
P2A7D.d: P2A7D means the hydraulic pressure sensor reads above its upper limit, typically because the signal line is touches the reference or battery supply, or its ground connection is broken. Unlike P2A7C, this fault is obvious at once: a full-scale reading while the pump is idle or retracting contradicts every other input. Caterpillar's patent notes that a sensor in the return line can also serve to shift the directional valve, though the supply-side sensor is preferred at high hydraulic pressure; on systems that use the return value, a falsely high reading could therefore upset stroke switching. No manufacturer publishes P2A7D. See whether the reading changes with the plug disconnected, and test the ground circuit.
c: Sensor ground open or high resistance
Signal line shorted to reference or battery voltage
s: Warning lamp on
Erratic or stopped pump strokes
Reduced power on gas

P2A7E.t: Alternative Fuel Hydraulic Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2A7E.d: P2A7E flags a hydraulic pressure sensor signal that breaks up or spikes briefly, then recovers before the low or high checks of P2A7C and P2A7D mature. Pressure in a pump drive pulses with every stroke anyway, so the controller has to tell genuine pressure swings from electrical noise; what it treats as erratic is a change faster than the hydraulics can produce, or a signal vanishing between strokes.
