Cold, damp surroundings close to the cryogenic tank, loose terminals and wiring rubbing on hydraulic hoses are typical causes. As long as the fault comes and goes, fuel delivery usually continues, but stroke timing may wander. No manufacturer documents P2A7E. Record the signal while moving the harness and compare it with the P2A75 sensor trace.
c: Loose terminal in the sensor connector
Condensation or ice near the cryogenic tank
s: Warning lamp that comes and goes
Uneven pump cycling or brief power dips

P2A7F.t: Alternative Fuel Pump A Compression Stroke Valve Control Circuit/Open
P2A7F.d: Hydraulically driven LNG pumps use solenoid valves to admit high-pressure oil to the drive side for the compression stroke and to vent it again for refilling. Caterpillar's patent US10060421B2 gives each of its six pumping elements, other counts being possible, a solenoid pilot that moves a spool between fill and drain positions; the controller sets timing and length of every stroke this way. P2A7F reports that pump A's compression stroke valve has an open or otherwise faulty control circuit. The valve then stays in its spring position and pump A no longer delivers. Which element or tank pump carries the letter A is not published, and neither is P2A7F itself. Check coil resistance and connector first.
c: Open wire or loose connector at valve A
Solenoid coil of valve A burnt open
Output stage in the control module faulty
s: Warning lamp on
Reduced LNG delivery and lower power
Gas pressure drops under load

P2A80.t: Alternative Fuel Pump A Compression Stroke Valve Control Circuit Range/Performance
P2A80.d: P2A80 concerns the compression stroke valve of pump A when its circuit is intact but the outcome of a command does not match. In the patented multi-element design, the time the solenoid holds the spool in the fill position sets the stroke, and a shorter command yields a partial stroke; the controller therefore expects a defined gain in gas pressure or hydraulic load per activation. If pump A contributes clearly less than its partners, or the spool reacts late, a sticking spool, varnished oil or a weak return spring are likely. Caterpillar also stresses that hydraulic pressure during the stroke must be held within tight limits to keep the LNG from vaporizing. No manufacturer publishes P2A80 or its test.
c: Spool of valve A sticking or slow
Weak return spring in the valve
s: Warning lamp after several drive cycles
Uneven gas pressure and slight power loss

P2A81.t: Alternative Fuel Pump A Compression Stroke Valve Control Circuit Low
P2A81.d: P2A81 is stored when the control circuit of pump A's compression stroke valve sits lower than the commanded state allows. With a low-side driver this mostly points to the control wire touching ground, which can energise the solenoid permanently; with a high-side driver a coil with shorted turns or a grounded feed pulls the output down until its protection trips. A valve held in the fill position keeps oil on the drive side, so the plunger cannot retract and refill, and pump A stays parked at full travel. In Caterpillar's six-element layout the remaining elements may cover part of the demand. No manufacturer publishes P2A81. Disconnect the valve and test the control wire for continuity to chassis ground.
c: Control wire of valve A shorted to ground
Shorted turns in the solenoid coil
s: Warning lamp on
Pump A stops delivering, power drops at high load

P2A82.t: Alternative Fuel Pump A Compression Stroke Valve Control Circuit High
P2A82.d: P2A82 shows the drive line to pump A's compression stroke valve at a higher level than the commanded state permits, most likely because the coil winding or its wire is broken where the valve is switched to ground, or because the line touches battery voltage and the output stage loses control of it. The solenoid then cannot move the spool into the fill position, so oil never reaches the drive side and pump A performs no compression stroke at all. Gas pressure downstream of the pump sinks faster than the controller expects, and on a single-element system the engine soon runs short of fuel. Caterpillar's patents show the spool going back to drain when the solenoid is de-energized, which is the state this fault produces. No manufacturer publishes P2A82. Measure coil resistance and feed voltage.
c: Open coil or broken wire at valve A
Control wire shorted to battery voltage
s: Warning lamp on
Falling gas pressure and power loss
Engine may stall on gas with a single pump element

P2A83.t: Alternative Fuel Pump B Compression Stroke Valve Control Circuit/Open
P2A83.d: P2A83 reports an open or otherwise faulty control circuit at the compression stroke valve of alternative fuel pump B. Whether a second pump exists depends on the layout: in Westport's patent US8726785B2, two LNG vessels each carry their own hydraulically driven pump, while Caterpillar's multi-element pump splits one unit into several separately switched elements. Either way, pump B's valve no longer admits drive oil, and its share of LNG delivery is lost. On a two-tank truck this can leave fuel stranded in the tank that pump B serves. The meaning of the letter B is not public, and no manufacturer documents P2A83. Where the valves are identical, swapping a connector with a neighbour shows whether the fault follows the coil.
c: Open wire or loose connector at valve B
Solenoid coil of valve B open
Output stage for valve B faulty
s: Warning lamp on
LNG in one tank cannot be used
Reduced power under high load

P2A84.t: Alternative Fuel Pump B Compression Stroke Valve Control Circuit Range/Performance
P2A84.d: P2A84 is set when pump B's compression stroke valve is electrically sound yet the pump does not respond as commanded. A controller that drives several pumps or elements in turn can compare them: in Caterpillar's multi-element patent, flow results from how often the elements are fired and how long each waits, so an element adding less pressure per command than its neighbours stands out. A slow spool, contaminated oil, internal leakage past the spool or worn plunger seals on the cryogenic side can all reduce pump B's output. With two tank pumps as in Westport's patent, the pressure behaviour before and after a switchover can also be compared. No manufacturer publishes P2A84. Check oil condition and compare delivery with pump A.
c: Spool of valve B slow or leaking internally
Worn plunger seals on the cryogenic side of pump B
s: Warning lamp after several drive cycles
Lower delivery from one tank or element

P2A85.t: Alternative Fuel Pump B Compression Stroke Valve Control Circuit Low
P2A85.d: P2A85 means the drive output for pump B's compression stroke valve reads too low for its commanded state. Typical are a control wire chafed through to the frame, which can keep the solenoid energised even when the controller wants it off, or a coil with shorted windings that draws excessive current. A valve stuck in the fill position leaves pump B's plunger parked at full extension; the pump stops delivering, and pressurised oil remains on its drive side. Caterpillar's six-element example can partly make up for this with the remaining elements, whereas a two-tank system loses the second tank's supply. No manufacturer publishes P2A85. Compare the measured coil resistance with that of an identical A or C valve.
c: Control wire of valve B chafed through to the frame
Coil of valve B with shorted windings
Output stage for valve B shorted
s: Warning lamp on
Pump B delivers nothing, reduced power or range

P2A86.t: Alternative Fuel Pump B Compression Stroke Valve Control Circuit High
P2A86.d: P2A86 is stored when pump B's compression stroke valve circuit shows a higher voltage than its state allows, pointing to an interrupted coil, a broken return wire where the valve is switched on the ground side, or a short to the supply. The valve then rests in its drain position: drive oil bypasses pump B and its plunger stays retracted. On a two-tank layout as in Westport's patent, the controller may keep drawing from the other tank, so the truck runs on while the second tank's LNG cannot be used and slowly warms up. Because the pump performs no strokes, its usual hydraulic pressure signature disappears, which helps to confirm the diagnosis. No manufacturer documents P2A86. Check the coil, the plug and the supply feed.
c: Open coil or broken wire at valve B
Control wire shorted to supply voltage
Corroded terminals in the valve B plug
s: Warning lamp on
One LNG tank is no longer emptied
Shorter range on gas

P2A87.t: Alternative Fuel Pump C Compression Stroke Valve Control Circuit/Open
P2A87.d: P2A87 covers the control circuit of the compression stroke valve on alternative fuel pump C, reporting an open or otherwise unusable circuit. A third pump valve only exists on systems with at least three separately switched pumping units. Caterpillar's patent US10060421B2 is such a case: it describes six elements arranged around one pump body, allows an odd number as well, and fires each through its own solenoid in a timed sequence. If valve C drops out, the sequence has a gap, delivery becomes uneven and the controller has to fire the others more often to hold gas pressure. No manufacturer publishes P2A87 or assigns the letter C. Check coil resistance and terminals, and whether codes for valves A or B are present as well.
c: Open wire or loose connector at valve C
Solenoid coil of valve C open
Output stage for valve C faulty
s: Warning lamp on
Uneven gas pressure, slight power loss at high load

P2A88.t: Alternative Fuel Pump C Compression Stroke Valve Control Circuit Range/Performance
P2A88.d: P2A88 reports that the compression stroke valve of pump C works electrically but its effect does not match the command. In a sequenced multi-element pump, each activation should add a similar amount of pressure to the gas accumulator or rail; an element that keeps falling short, or whose share fluctuates, stands out against its neighbours. Since Caterpillar's patent sets stroke length through the duration of the command, a spool that opens late shortens pump C's stroke without any wiring fault. Deposits on the spool, a partly blocked oil passage or worn cryogenic seals are plausible causes. Because the other elements keep running, the driver may notice little apart from the warning lamp. No manufacturer publishes P2A88 or its thresholds.
c: Deposits making the spool of valve C open late
Partly blocked oil passage to element C
Worn cryogenic seals on element C
s: Warning lamp after several drive cycles
Little noticeable change in driving

P2A89.t: Alternative Fuel Pump C Compression Stroke Valve Control Circuit Low
P2A89.d: P2A89 is set when the drive circuit of pump C's compression stroke valve reads low for the commanded state. Most often the control wire has found a path to ground, so the solenoid may stay on, or the coil has shorted turns and pushes the output stage into current limiting. A valve stuck in fill keeps pressurised oil behind element C; that element stops cycling, and the others have to carry its share. Expect reduced fuel delivery at high load rather than an immediate stall, at least on pumps with several elements like Caterpillar's design. No manufacturer publishes P2A89. Unplug valve C and check whether the short to ground remains in the harness; if it disappears, the coil is the likely culprit.
c: Control wire of valve C shorted to ground
Shorted turns in the coil of valve C
s: Warning lamp on
Reduced power at high load

P2A8A.t: Alternative Fuel Pump C Compression Stroke Valve Control Circuit High
P2A8A.d: P2A8A indicates that pump C's compression stroke valve circuit sits higher than the commanded state allows, from an open coil, a broken wire or a short to the supply rail. The solenoid cannot shift the spool, which stays in the drain position, and element C never starts a compression stroke. Unlike the low fault P2A89, nothing stays pressurised; the element is simply missing from the firing sequence, which the controller covers by firing the remaining ones more often. When P2A8A appears together with P2A82 or P2A86, a shared supply or ground for all valves is more likely than three failed coils. No manufacturer documents P2A8A. Check the common feed and ground before replacing valve C.
c: Open coil or broken wire at valve C
Fault in the supply or ground shared by the pump valves
Control wire shorted to the supply rail
s: Warning lamp on
Uneven gas pressure at high load

P2A8B.d: P2A8B means vaporizer A is not doing its job well enough, rather than reporting a wiring fault. On LPG engines this unit, also called reducer or converter, draws engine coolant heat to turn liquid gas into vapour at a steady pressure. Patent US7073489B2 explains the risk: evaporation chills the converter, the chill grows with gas flow, and an underheated unit can ice up until its regulator jet blocks. The AC STAG controller manual lets the system change to gas only after the reducer has warmed up and offers a pressure correction for a poorly performing reducer that floods the engine after overrun. Detection probably compares outlet temperature and gas pressure with expected values. No vehicle manufacturer documents P2A8B publicly.
c: Too little coolant reaching vaporizer A (air lock, kinked hose, thermostat stuck open)
Worn diaphragm or seat in the pressure stage of vaporizer A
Oily residues from the gas clogging the vaporizer chambers
Outlet temperature sensor reading wrong but still within range
s: Check engine or gas warning lamp on
System stays on petrol longer after a cold start or falls back to petrol under load
Hesitation, rough running or stalling after coasting on gas
Frost or condensation on the vaporizer body

P2A8C.d: P2A8C flags vaporizer B as underperforming: the gas leaving it is colder, or less completely vaporized, than the module expects for the current flow. With LNG the temperature gap is extreme, and Westport's patent CA2862664C describes the typical failure. At a cold start, at idle or under light load coolant crawls through the exchanger and can freeze inside it; flow then drops without stopping entirely, vaporizer capacity falls and the downstream gas temperature sinks, which can harm later components. Westport therefore runs fuel and coolant in parallel flow during start and idle and switches to counter flow afterwards. A stuck switching valve or ice can thus cause P2A8C. No manufacturer publishes the code or its limits.
c: Coolant partly frozen inside vaporizer B after cold start or long idling
Valve that switches between parallel and counter flow stuck
Low coolant level or too little antifreeze in the mixture
Deposits reducing heat transfer in vaporizer B
s: Malfunction lamp on
Reduced power or gas mode blocked, especially when cold
Ice on the vaporizer or gas lines behind it

P2A8D.d: P2A8D concerns a third vaporizer, found where large engines or several fuel branches need more heat exchange than one or two units provide. The code means unit C turns too little liquid into usable gas, or delivers it too cold, while its outlet sensor works. Where A and B run under the same conditions, the module can single out C by comparison, and that is the likely logic, though no maker publishes it. Timing matters for any such check: US7073489B2 points out that a thermostat sitting in the coolant reacts only slowly to changes in gas flow, and CA2862664C notes that no vaporizing is needed while the engine runs on another fuel. A fair test therefore waits for warm coolant and real gas demand. CARB lists such functional checks under its comprehensive component rules.
c: Coolant branch to vaporizer C restricted or unbalanced against A and B
Fouled heat exchange passages in vaporizer C
Pressure stage of vaporizer C sticking or leaking internally
Outlet sensor of C drifting so that the comparison fails
s: Warning lamp on, often with little noticeable change in driving
Loss of power at high load when all vaporizers are needed
One vaporizer housing noticeably colder than the others

P2A8E.d: P2A8E reports that alternative fuel pump A no longer delivers what it should, a mechanical or hydraulic fault rather than an electrical one. Such pumps move liquid fuel, typically LNG out of a cryogenic tank. A patent application now held by Cespira, US20080302111A1, shows how a controller can judge them from the delivery line pressure alone: each time the pump is commanded on, pressure has to climb from a lower to an upper set point within a known range of slopes. A clearly flatter rise means lost volumetric efficiency, and a falling pressure means the pump cannot even keep up with the engine. The document names worn piston seals, leaking static seals or check valves, dirt in the fuel and a weak hydraulic drive as causes. No manufacturer publishes P2A8E or its limits.
c: Worn dynamic piston seals in pump A
Leaking inlet or outlet check valve of pump A
Hydraulic drive of pump A delivering too little force or speed
Impurities in the fuel passing the filter and damaging the pump
s: Malfunction lamp on
Power loss at high load, gas pressure sagging
Pump runs noticeably longer to refill the accumulator
Engine switched to reduced output or diesel-only operation

P2A8F.d: P2A8F applies to a second alternative fuel pump whose output has fallen short of expectations. Layouts with two pumps usually give each LNG vessel its own pump, a redundancy Westport's documents mention explicitly. In US20080302111A1, a selector valve decides which pump delivers, and once the controller judges one pump degraded it can switch to the other. The difficulty lies in telling a weak pump from an empty tank: Westport's US8726785B2 notes that little drive work per stroke can mean either a nearly empty vessel or a broken component such as the drive shaft. A P2A8F shortly after refuelling therefore points to the pump itself. Pump B may also be the healthy one, so check which tank was active. No manufacturer documents P2A8F or how its letter is assigned.
c: Worn seals reducing the delivery of pump B
Tank served by pump B almost empty, mimicking a weak pump
Broken drive shaft or coupling between hydraulic drive and pump B
s: Malfunction lamp on
Usable range shorter, fuel left in one tank
System changes to the other tank earlier than usual

P2A90.d: P2A90 marks pump C of the alternative fuel system as delivering too little. A third pump may belong to a further tank or, in Caterpillar's design US10060421B2, be one of several pumping elements driven in sequence. Besides wear, cryogenic pumps have a typical weakness that Caterpillar's patent US9228574B2 describes: if the liquid at the inlet has warmed enough to form vapour, the pump cavitates and delivery stops, so centrifugal designs need a positive feed pressure. Short bursts of poor output after long parking, with warmer LNG in the tank, fit this picture; a permanent shortfall points to worn parts. The pump diagnosis in US20080302111A1 explains how a slow pressure rise reveals the loss. No manufacturer publishes P2A90; P2A87 to P2A8A cover pump C's stroke valve.
c: Vapour at the inlet of pump C after warm soak, causing cavitation
Worn seals or valves in pump C
Clogged inlet strainer or filter ahead of pump C
s: Warning lamp on
Weak pull or hesitation shortly after a long stop
Gas pressure recovers slowly after heavy acceleration

P2A91.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve A Control Circuit/Open
P2A91.d: A tank select valve decides which storage vessel feeds the fuel system. That sets it apart from a tank shutoff valve (P224C, P2A22 and onward), which simply opens or isolates one cylinder, and from the hydraulic fuel pump select valve (P2A70 and onward), which routes drive oil to a pump. Westport's patent US8726785B2 shows the idea with two LNG vessels and one external pump, where an insulated valve links the pump to either vessel. P2A91 means the control circuit of select valve A is open or otherwise faulty, so the valve stays in its rest position. Fuel is then drawn only from the vessel reached in that position and the rest may become unusable. No manufacturer documents P2A91 publicly; CARB requires output circuits to be checked for continuity.
c: Loose connector or broken wire to select valve A
Burnt-out solenoid coil of valve A
Faulty output stage in the alternative fuel module
s: Malfunction lamp on
Only one tank is used, range noticeably shorter
Fuel gauge shows content left although the engine runs short of gas

P2A92.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve A Control Performance
P2A92.d: P2A92 is the functional check for tank select valve A: the wiring tests pass, yet the fuel system does not behave as if the commanded vessel were connected. Software can judge this only through pressures. A patent by Cespira, the Westport and Volvo venture, outlines the logic for two compressed-gas supplies with their own pressure sensors: a supply-select valve assembly routes one supply to a compressor and the other to the regulator, and stages change whenever a supply falls under a set pressure. After such a command the newly chosen supply should start to lose pressure while the other holds steady. If nothing changes, or the wrong tank empties, valve A is probably sticking or leaking across its seat. No manufacturer publishes P2A92 or a threshold for it.
c: Select valve A sticking from dirt, ice or wear
Valve A leaking across its seat so both vessels are drawn
Tank pressure sensor giving a misleading reading
s: Malfunction lamp on
Tanks empty unevenly or in the wrong order
Short gas supply although one vessel still holds fuel

P2A93.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve A Control Circuit Low
P2A93.d: P2A93 is stored when the module measures a voltage on the control line of tank select valve A that falls short of the level expected for the commanded state. With a low-side driver this usually means the line touches ground, which can energise the solenoid permanently and keep valve A in its switched position regardless of the command. If the valve is fed from the positive side instead, the same fault overloads that output, which then usually switches itself off. In both cases the module can no longer choose the vessel, so the automatic change from an empty tank to a full one, as described in Westport's two-vessel patent, cannot be relied on. Valves near cryogenic lines collect condensation, so water in the connector is a plausible cause. No manufacturer documents P2A93; P2A94 is the high case.
c: Control wire of valve A chafed through to ground
Condensation or water in the connector of valve A
Shorted turns in the coil of valve A
s: Malfunction lamp on
Tank selection stuck, one vessel emptied completely
Fuse or output protection of the gas module trips

P2A94.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve A Control Circuit High
P2A94.d: P2A94 reports a control voltage at tank select valve A above what the module expects for the commanded state. On a valve switched to ground by the module, an open coil or broken lead leaves the line floating at supply voltage; alternatively a chafed wire contacts a battery feed that the output stage cannot pull down. Either way, valve A does not respond to commands and stays wherever its spring or the foreign voltage holds it. In the staged two-supply strategy patented by Cespira, the controller then cannot move to the second supply when the first falls below its threshold, or cannot leave it. Range shrinks or the engine falls back to its other fuel. No maker publishes P2A94. Check coil resistance, then the harness to the valve.
c: Open coil or broken lead on a ground-switched valve A
Control wire of valve A touching a battery feed
Corroded pins with high resistance at valve A
s: Malfunction lamp on
No change to the next tank, gas runs out early
Engine switches to its other fuel or reduced power

P2A95.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve B Control Circuit/Open
P2A95.d: P2A95 says the module finds no proper current path through tank select valve B. Where a second select valve exists, it typically serves the next vessel or supply in line. Cespira's patent for a gas engine fed from two compressed-gas supplies shows how much depends on such valves: the controller connects each supply either to a compressor or to the regulator, and only by switching can it keep using a supply whose pressure has dropped. With valve B dead, that step is missing and fuel held in the affected vessel is effectively stranded. Unlike P2A22, which concerns the shutoff solenoid on tank B, this code concerns the routing valve. No manufacturer documents P2A95. A broken lead, a loose plug or an open coil are the usual findings.
c: Loose plug or broken wire to select valve B
Open solenoid coil of valve B
Output stage for valve B in the module defective
s: Malfunction lamp on
Content of one vessel cannot be used
Range well below the usual figure

P2A96.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve B Control Circuit Performance
P2A96.d: P2A96 is about tank select valve B working electrically but not doing what it is told. In an LNG layout like the one in Westport's US8726785B2, where one pump draws from either of two vessels through an insulated select valve, the module can verify the switch from the pump's behaviour: right after selecting a full vessel, the drive work per stroke should be normal, whereas a reading that stays low suggests the pump still sits on the empty side. The same patent warns that low work can also come from a mechanical defect, so a plausible check compares readings before and after the command. Cold-stiffened seals, ice and debris can hold the valve back. No manufacturer publishes P2A96 or its test window.
c: Valve B held by ice or cold-hardened seals
Debris preventing valve B from shifting fully
Pump defect interpreted as a select valve problem
s: Malfunction lamp on
Gas supply drops right after a tank change
One vessel stays full while the other runs dry

P2A97.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve B Control Circuit Low
P2A97.d: P2A97 indicates that the drive line of tank select valve B reads too low. If the module feeds the valve from the positive side, a short to ground in the wire or a coil with shorted windings drags the output down, and the stage switches off to protect itself, so valve B falls back to its spring position. If the module switches the ground side instead, the same short can hold the valve energised all the time. The practical effect is that the choice of vessel no longer follows the strategy: in the staged scheme Cespira patented for two gas supplies, the controller cannot react when a supply reaches its lower pressure limit. No manufacturer documents P2A97. Look for chafing where the harness crosses tank straps and brackets. P2A98 is the high counterpart.
c: Wire to valve B chafed against a tank strap or bracket
Shorted windings in the coil of valve B
Moisture bridging the pins of the valve B plug
s: Malfunction lamp on
Tank change does not happen or happens at the wrong time
Gas mode ends early with fuel still on board

P2A98.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve B Control Circuit High
P2A98.d: P2A98 appears when the voltage on the control circuit of tank select valve B stays higher than the module allows for the commanded state. A ground-switched valve with an interrupted winding or lead shows this pattern, as does a wire that has picked up battery voltage. The valve will then not move on command, and the system keeps drawing from whichever vessel the resting valve connects. In Westport's two-vessel design with a single pump, that means one tank is used up and the second is never reached, so the engine runs short of gas while the gauge still shows reserve. CARB's heavy-duty rule expects such circuit faults to be detected and stored separately. No manufacturer publishes P2A98. A coil resistance check at the valve plug separates a dead coil from a wiring fault.
c: Interrupted winding or lead at valve B
Control line of valve B in contact with battery voltage
Corrosion at the valve B connector raising resistance
s: Malfunction lamp on
Second vessel never used, gas runs out early
Gauge shows reserve while power drops

P2A99.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve C Control Circuit/Open
P2A99.d: P2A99 belongs to installations with at least three selectable vessels or supplies and reports an open or otherwise broken control circuit at select valve C. Published designs mostly show two vessels, such as Westport's LNG arrangement with one pump and a valve choosing the tank, or Cespira's pair of compressed-gas supplies; a third valve extends the same principle. With valve C unpowered, its vessel can neither be brought on line nor, depending on the rest position, taken off line, so the selection sequence breaks at that point. Take care not to confuse it with P2A26, the shutoff solenoid on tank C, or with the hydraulic pump select valve. No manufacturer documents P2A99. Check the plug, the lead and the coil of valve C.
c: Disconnected plug or broken lead at select valve C
Coil of valve C burnt out
Module output for valve C failed
s: Malfunction lamp on
Third vessel stays full or is never isolated
Total range reduced

P2A9A.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve C Control Circuit Performance
P2A9A.d: With P2A9A, select valve C passes its electrical tests, but the effect of switching does not show up as expected. The likely evidence is pressure: once vessel C is selected, its own tank pressure sensor should begin to fall with consumption and the pressure ahead of the regulator should match that vessel's level. If tank C stays untouched, or the pressure jumps to a value that fits another vessel, the valve has not moved or leaks internally. Cespira's patent shows why the selection matters, since its controller decides which supply goes to compression and which to the regulator from measured supply pressures. A partial fault may only appear in the cold. No manufacturer publishes P2A9A or the comparison it uses; P2A46 and P2A47 cover the tank C pressure sensor.
c: Valve C not shifting fully because of wear or contamination
Internal leakage letting vessel C feed in the wrong position
Faulty tank C pressure reading misleading the check
s: Malfunction lamp on
Tank C level hardly changes over a tank cycle
Fault appears mainly in cold weather

P2A9B.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve C Control Circuit Low
P2A9B.d: P2A9B is logged when the control circuit of tank select valve C reads below the expected level. Common electrical findings are a lead grounded against the frame, a pinched wire under a tank strap or a coil with internal shorts. What follows depends on how the output is wired: a ground-side driver may now keep valve C switched permanently, while a supply-side driver shuts down and lets the valve drop back. Either way the selection of the third vessel no longer follows the commands. Westport's two-vessel patent ties tank changes to empty-tank detection; with the valve out of control, that change may be skipped or forced. No manufacturer documents P2A9B or its voltage limits. Check the circuit with the valve unplugged first, then with the coil reconnected.
c: Lead of valve C grounded against the frame or pinched under a tank strap
Internal short in the coil of valve C
Water in the plug of valve C
s: Malfunction lamp on
Third tank used constantly or not at all
Unexpected tank changes during the drive

P2A9C.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Select Valve C Control Circuit High
P2A9C.d: P2A9C reports a control voltage at select valve C above the level the commanded state permits. The usual reasons are an interrupted coil or wire on a valve the module switches to ground, which leaves supply voltage on the line, or a foreign voltage fed in from a damaged neighbouring wire. Valve C then ignores commands. In a staged strategy like the one Cespira patented, where the controller moves between supplies as their pressures drop below set limits, the step involving vessel C is lost, so its content is either never tapped or cannot be shut out of the sequence. Range falls and the engine may switch to its other fuel sooner. No manufacturer publishes P2A9C. Compare coil resistance with valves A and B where they are identical.
c: Open coil or wire on ground-switched valve C
Foreign voltage from a damaged neighbouring wire
s: Malfunction lamp on
Third vessel never drawn, range reduced
Earlier change to the other fuel

P2A9D.t: Alternative Fuel High Pressure System Small Leak
P2A9D.d: P2A9D points to a slow loss of gas from the high-pressure side, from the cylinders up to the regulator, too small to notice while driving. A Toyota and Denso patent, US6467466B1, explains the catch: with the valves open, a modest pressure drop cannot be told apart from consumption. The method therefore waits for a stopped engine with all shutoff valves shut, records the pressure, compares it after a set time and adds up the losses over several stops, so even traces show. Because tank pressure varies with content, it also offers a rate-based test. P240E is the general high-pressure leak, which a later Toyota and Aisan patent flags while running from a fast pressure drop. No manufacturer documents P2A9D publicly; CARB has gas vehicles under evaporative rules submit their own leak monitoring plan.
c: Seeping high-pressure fitting or loosened connection
Tank or shutoff valve not sealing fully when closed
Aged O-rings in the filter or regulator inlet
Drifting high-pressure sensor simulating a pressure loss
s: Malfunction or gas warning lamp on
Tank pressure noticeably lower after parking
Faint gas smell near the tanks or lines
Gas mode blocked at the next start on some systems

P2A9E.t: Alternative Fuel Return Line Valve Control Circuit/Open
P2A9E.d: Liquid-phase propane and LPG systems pump more fuel to the rail than the injectors use; the surplus flows back to the tank and carries heat and vapor away with it. A return line valve opens or blocks that path. With P2A9E the drive circuit of this valve is open or broken in some other way, so the module can no longer switch it and the valve rests in its unpowered state. The ROUSH CleanTech Gen 4 propane manual for Ford trucks shows what such a circuit looks like: a solenoid on the tank with a coil of 6 to 35 ohms, fed with battery voltage through a 10 A fuse and a relay, its ground side run to a relay module. Roush files its solenoid faults under other codes, and no manufacturer documents P2A9E publicly; CARB demands continuity checks on output circuits.
c: Corroded, wet or loose connector at the tank-mounted valve
Broken wire in the frame or tank harness
Open solenoid coil in the return valve
Blown fuse or faulty relay in the valve supply
Failed output stage in the fuel control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Hard or long cranking on a warm engine, as vapor is not flushed out of the rail
Switch to the base fuel or reduced power on bi-fuel or dedicated systems

P2A9F.t: Alternative Fuel Return Line Valve Control Circuit Range/Performance
P2A9F.d: P2A9F covers the grey zone between a clean open and a clean short: the control circuit of the return line valve is connected, but the current or voltage the output stage measures while driving it does not fit the command. Typical reasons are a coil whose resistance has drifted, a few shorted windings, or high contact resistance in a corroded connector that lets the coil pull in only weakly or late. For a comparable tank solenoid the ROUSH CleanTech propane manual gives 6 to 35 ohms as the acceptable window, which is a useful benchmark when measuring. No manufacturer documents P2A9F or a threshold for it publicly. A valve that switches unreliably can leave vapor in the rail after a hot soak; a hydraulic lack of return flow with a sound circuit is P2AA2.
c: Solenoid coil resistance out of range or partially shorted windings
High contact resistance from corrosion or water in the connector
Low supply voltage at the valve from a weak relay contact or ground
Output stage of the fuel control module measuring incorrectly
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Occasional hard starts after a hot soak
Fault comes and goes with temperature or moisture

P2AA0.t: Alternative Fuel Return Line Valve Control Circuit Low
P2AA0.d: P2AA0 means the module reads too low a voltage on the control line of the return line valve, which almost always points to a short to ground. What follows depends on which side the module switches. In the ROUSH CleanTech Gen 4 propane layout the valve has a fused battery feed and its ground wire runs to a relay module; if that ground wire chafes against the frame, the coil is energized whenever the supply is live and the valve can no longer be closed. With a high-side driver the same short would instead blow the fuse or make the driver shut down. No manufacturer documents P2AA0 publicly, and CARB only requires that such output faults be detected. Check the harness along the tank and frame first, then the coil.
c: Control wire chafed through and touching the frame or tank
Water in the valve connector bridging to ground
Internal short in the solenoid coil
Damaged output stage in the fuel control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Return valve stays open or the valve fuse blows, depending on the circuit layout
Irregular rail pressure or switch to the base fuel

P2AA1.t: Alternative Fuel Return Line Valve Control Circuit High
P2AA1.d: P2AA1 is the opposite electrical case to P2AA0: the valve drive wire sits at too high a voltage, usually because it touches a battery-fed wire. Where the module switches the ground side, as in the ROUSH CleanTech Gen 4 propane system with its relay-module ground, a line stuck at supply level leaves no voltage across the coil, so the valve cannot be energized at all and stays in its rest position. When the module then turns its transistor on, it may also see an overcurrent and shut the stage off. A wire nipped between harness bundles or a coil whose winding has shorted to its supply pin are the usual finds. Public manufacturer documentation for P2AA1 does not exist; CARB requires output circuit faults to be flagged.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-fed wire in the harness
Solenoid winding shorted to its supply terminal
Bent or bridged pins in the valve connector
Output stage in the fuel control module shorted internally
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Return valve cannot be switched and stays in its rest position
Poor hot starts or switch to the base fuel

P2AA2.t: Alternative Fuel Return Line Insufficient Flow
P2AA2.d: P2AA2 is a hydraulic fault, not an electrical one: too little liquid fuel comes back from the rail to the tank. The return keeps the fuel in the rail cool and liquid, so a weak return lets it warm up and boil. Patent US5623907A on a liquid propane delivery system shows the parts involved: a check valve in the return which only opens at roughly 15 psi differential to hold line pressure, and a solenoid-controlled bypass that flushes vapor out of the rail before start-up. A Hyundai patent on an LPI engine routes the return through a regulator unit with its own return valve. A sticking check valve, a kinked line, a valve that does not open or a weak pump all reduce the flow. No manufacturer documents P2AA2 publicly; circuit faults of the valve are P2A9E to P2AA1.
c: Return valve or return check valve sticking closed
Kinked, crushed or clogged return line or filter
In-tank pump delivering too little, leaving no surplus to return
Faulty pressure regulator in the return path
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Hard starting or stalling after a hot soak from vapor in the rail
Hesitation or lean running under load
Switch to the base fuel or reduced power

P2AA3.t: Cold Start EGR B Flow Insufficient Detected
P2AA3.d: P2AA3 belongs to the cold-start strategy (CSERS) newer diesels run in the first minutes after a long soak. CARB phases in from 2026 to 2028 that the OBD system must confirm, under defined monitoring conditions such as a soak of six hours or more, that the EGR valve and the EGR cooler bypass actually follow their cold-start setpoints by a clearly measurable amount, in the right direction and beyond normal start-up behaviour. P2AA3 is set when the second EGR path, B, delivers too little flow in that phase, so NOx rises while the catalysts are still cold. Which loop carries the letter B is up to the manufacturer. No manufacturer documents P2AA3 publicly; an FCA bulletin for a six-cylinder diesel with high- and low-pressure EGR lists only the A-side code P04DD, as a follow-on of low-pressure EGR sensor faults.
c: EGR valve B sticking or slow from soot at low temperature
Faulty position sensor on EGR valve B misleading the control
Clogged EGR cooler or passage in loop B
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Usually no noticeable change in driving
Higher NOx in the warm-up phase, possible inspection failure

P2AA4.t: Cold Start EGR B Flow Excessive Detected
P2AA4.d: P2AA4 is the mirror case of P2AA3: during the cold-start phase, EGR path B recirculates more exhaust than intended. Many calibrations deliberately keep EGR low in a cold engine, so a valve that leaks or hangs open is the classic cause. CARB's cold-start component checks require a response that is robustly detectable and in the commanded direction; where no feedback sensor exists, the monitor may judge the final command instead of the delivered flow. Too much exhaust in a cold combustion chamber shows up as rough idle, white or black smoke, more soot and in extreme cases stalling. No manufacturer documents P2AA4 publicly; FCA uses only the A-side code P04DD in its published bulletins. The A/B ratio check across both paths is P2D1C.
c: EGR valve B leaking or stuck partly open from carbon
Position sensor offset making the valve open further than commanded
Intake or exhaust throttle fault raising the pressure difference across loop B
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Rough idle and smoke after a cold start
Stalling or hesitation while the engine is cold

P2AA5.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High Bank 1
P2AA5.d: P2AA5 comes from the H-bridge that drives the DC motor of the bank 1 EGR cooler bypass flap: the driver chip itself reports that it is getting too hot. GM's diesel summary tables carry this monitor from 2017 (17OBDG04) to 2025 (25OBDG04A) as a motor overtemperature check. The fault flag comes from the hardware layer when the bridge exceeds 170 °C; the test runs outside cranking with powertrain relay voltage above 11 V, needs 160 failures in 200 samples at a 12.5 ms task and is Type B. GM bundles it with the open and shorted circuit codes P245A, P245C and P245D as an actuator fault. A flap that binds on soot, a motor with internal damage or a partial short make the bridge work too hard. A flap stuck in one position is P24A5; bank 2 is P2AA6.
c: Bypass flap binding on soot or corrosion, motor working against resistance
Internal fault in the bypass actuator motor
Partial short between the motor wires
Overheating or faulty H-bridge in the engine control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on after two trips
Bypass flap no longer driven, so warm-up EGR cooling stays at its last state
Possible further EGR or cooler efficiency codes

P2AA6.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High Bank 2
P2AA6.d: P2AA6 is the bank 2 version of the bypass driver protection code. It only exists on engines with a separate EGR cooler and bypass actuator for the second cylinder bank, typically V engines whose banks each have their own exhaust manifold feeding EGR. The output stage for that actuator reports excessive current or junction heat and shuts itself off, which leaves the flap where it was. No manufacturer documents P2AA6 publicly. GM's diesel tables, which define the bank 1 code P2AA5 with a 170 °C driver limit and a Type B rating, show no bank 2 counterpart, as those engines use a single bypass. Causes match bank 1: a binding flap, a damaged motor or a partial short. Circuit faults on bank 2 are P248E, P2490 and P2491; a stuck flap is P24A6.
c: Bank 2 bypass flap binding on soot or corrosion
Internal fault in the bank 2 actuator motor
Partial short in the bank 2 actuator wiring
Faulty driver stage in the engine control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Bank 2 bypass flap stays in its last position
Possible NOx or EGR temperature codes for bank 2

P2AA7.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B Position Sensor Circuit
P2AA7.d: Thermal management modules on modern engines use motor-driven rotary valves to split coolant between radiator, heater, oil or transmission cooler and engine block. A position sensor reports each valve's angle so the module can regulate it in closed loop. P2AA7 is the general circuit code for the sensor of valve B, used when the signal is unusable but cannot be classed as low (P2AA9) or high (P2AAA). No manufacturer documents P2AA7 publicly, and what valve B controls differs between makes. GM's 2025 diesel tables show how such a sensor is read on valve C: digitally over SENT, with readings outside a fixed count window filed as low or high faults after 4 seconds in 5, Type B. CARB counts these cooling actuators among the monitored components. Expect slow warm-up or temperature swings.
c: Loose, corroded or coolant-wetted connector, or damaged sensor wiring
Lost 5 V supply or ground to the position sensor
Failed position sensor inside the valve module
Faulty sensor input in the engine control module
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Slow warm-up or reduced cabin heating
Fluctuating or elevated coolant temperature reading

P2AA8.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2AA8.d: With P2AA8 the position sensor of coolant valve B delivers an electrically valid signal, but its content is implausible: it sticks while the motor turns the valve, jumps by more than a real valve could move, or lies outside the end stops the module learned. A worn sensor track, a magnet that has shifted on the valve shaft or a slipping gear between motor and sensor are typical findings. No manufacturer documents P2AA8 publicly. GM's 2025 diesel tables for the comparable valve C do not use a separate sensor plausibility code; they judge position against target and set the valve code P26BB once the deviation exceeds 12 degrees for 8 of 10 seconds, Type B. For valve B that valve-level check is P26B0, while P2AA8 is aimed at the sensor itself. Pure circuit faults are P2AA7, P2AA9 and P2AAA.
c: Worn or contaminated position sensor in the valve module
Slipping gear or shifted magnet between valve shaft and sensor
Intermittent contact in the connector causing signal jumps
Learned end stops lost after a module or valve replacement
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Engine warms up slowly or runs hotter than usual
Heater output varies

P2AA9.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B Position Sensor Circuit Low
P2AA9.d: P2AA9 is set once the position sensor on coolant valve B reports a value below its valid band, which nearly always means the signal wire or the sensor output is pulled toward ground. Rotary coolant valves in thermal management modules report their angle so the engine computer can steer coolant between radiator, heater and other loops. No manufacturer documents P2AA9 publicly. GM's 2025 diesel tables list the matching check for valve C as P23C4: the SENT reading has to drop under 27 counts for 4 of 5 seconds, rated Type B with two trips, and the test only runs while SENT communication itself is healthy. Ford, by contrast, gives the letter B to a transmission cooling valve without position feedback. The high-side fault is P2AAA.
c: Sensor signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Position sensor electronics in the valve module failed (often only as complete valve unit)
Coolant or moisture in the sensor connector creating a leakage path to ground
s: Check engine light on
Engine warms up slowly or runs cooler than usual
Cabin heating or transmission warm-up weaker, depending on what valve B serves

P2AAA.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B Position Sensor Circuit High
P2AAA.d: With P2AAA the position sensor of coolant valve B reports a value above anything a working sensor would deliver. Typical reasons are a signal line touching a supply wire, a damaged output stage inside the sensor or, depending on how the input is wired, an interrupted ground. Since the engine computer can no longer tell where the valve really stands, it loses closed-loop control and has to rely on a fixed default position. No manufacturer documents P2AAA publicly. GM's code for the comparable valve C, P23C5, flags a SENT value above 4,050 counts, again over 4 of 5 seconds and as Type B, and names a short to power as the cause. CARB requires input components to be checked for wiring faults and for readings beyond their limits. P2AA9 is the low counterpart, P2AAB the sporadic one.
c: Signal wire in contact with a supply or reference voltage wire
Sensor ground open at the connector or splice
Position sensor in the valve module defective
s: Check engine light on
Coolant temperature swings or stays off target
Possibly reduced engine power if the module protects against overheating

P2AAB.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2AAB.d: P2AAB covers a position signal from coolant valve B that is valid most of the time but drops out, jumps or flickers for short moments. Such patterns usually come from a contact that opens under vibration or heat, a lead that rubs against hot engine parts, or interference on the digital sensor line. No manufacturer documents P2AAB publicly, and GM's 2025 diesel tables contain no separate erratic code for the comparable valve C. There, brief disturbances would only surface indirectly, for example as the position deviation code P26BB (more than 12 degrees off target in 8 of 10 seconds) or as the end-stop learn fault P1098 checked after shutdown. CARB asks for circuit and plausibility checks on such inputs. Steady faults are P2AA9 and P2AAA; P2AA7 is the general circuit code.
c: Widened or loose terminal in the valve connector
Harness rubbing on hot or moving engine parts
Electrical interference or poor ground on the sensor line
s: Check engine light that comes and goes
Occasional temperature swings without a steady pattern
Often no noticeable change in driving behaviour

P2AAC.d: P2AAC is the general circuit fault of a sensor meant to recognise diesel where only gasoline belongs, so the system can react to misfuelling before damage occurs. No manufacturer documents this sensor or the code publicly, and its exact design is not described in sources available. Two Ford patents show why detection matters and how it can work without a dedicated sensor: diesel gives off far fewer vapours than gasoline, so tank pressure during refuelling (US10544031B2) or the warming of the carbon canister (US10611625B2) stays below the expected curve, while diesel in a gasoline engine can clog injectors and ignite uncontrolled. P2AAC applies when the sensor circuit fails in a way that is neither clearly low (P2AAE) nor clearly high (P2AAF). CARB requires circuit checks on such inputs.
c: Corroded or loose connector at the sensor near the tank or fuel line
s: Check engine light on
Misfuelling warning unavailable or shown without reason
Usually no change in how the engine runs

P2AAD.t: Diesel Fuel Presence Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2AAD.d: P2AAD means the diesel presence sensor delivers an electrically valid signal whose content does not make sense: it may report diesel although no refuelling has taken place, never change at all, or contradict other information the engine computer has about the fuel. No manufacturer documents this code or its test publicly. Ford patent US10544031B2 illustrates the kind of cross-check involved in misfuelling detection: its pressure limit is not fixed but follows the pressure expected in the tank during that particular refill, so the verdict rests on a comparison instead of a single raw value. CARB requires such plausibility faults to be stored under their own code, apart from the circuit faults P2AAC, P2AAE and P2AAF. A contaminated or aged sensing element is a likely cause.
c: Sensing element coated with deposits or residues
Calibration of the plausibility check not suited to the fuel quality in use
s: Check engine light on
Unjustified misfuelling message, or a real misfuelling going unnoticed

P2AAE.t: Diesel Fuel Presence Sensor Circuit Low
P2AAE.d: P2AAE is stored when the diesel presence sensor signal falls below the lowest value the input accepts, which points to a short to ground on the signal line or a sensor whose output has collapsed. Whether a low reading would otherwise stand for diesel or for gasoline is not published, so the code says nothing about the fuel in the tank, only that the reading cannot be used. No manufacturer documents P2AAE publicly. Ford's misfuelling patent US10611625B2 targets hybrids with sealed fuel tanks and watches the carbon canister temperature during refuelling, which shows that the task can be solved with sensors the vehicle already has. CARB requires out-of-range checks on inputs. Look first for chafed wiring near the tank, then at the sensor; P2AAF is the high counterpart.
c: Signal wire shorted to ground, often chafed on the underbody
Sensor supply or reference voltage missing
s: Check engine light on
Misfuelling protection inactive

P2AAF.t: Diesel Fuel Presence Sensor Circuit High
P2AAF.d: P2AAF reports the diesel presence sensor signal stuck above its upper limit. Common reasons are a signal wire touching a battery-fed line, an open ground or signal path that lets an internal pull-up drive the input high, or a sensor with a failed output stage. No manufacturer documents P2AAF publicly, and no public source states which signal level stands for diesel. The background is spelled out in Ford patent US10544031B2: diesel is heavier and oilier than gasoline, and once in a gasoline engine it can block injectors and burn uncontrolled, so the patent aims to stop the refill before the tank is full. With P2AAF set, such a warning can no longer be trusted. CARB demands range monitoring of such inputs; P2AAE is the low side, P2AAC the general circuit fault.
c: Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
Open sensor ground or signal wire
s: Check engine light on
Misfuelling warning unreliable

P2AB0.d: P2AB0 concerns the electronics of the particulate matter sensor rather than its sensing element: the sensor control unit, which feeds the electrodes, measures their current and reports over CAN, finds an internal error in its own measuring path. GM's 2025 diesel tables (25OBDG04A and B) describe it as an internal fault of the current switcher: the electrode current read in the small range must lie between a minimum and a maximum, tested while the sensor is regenerating, with its bus relay on and no CAN or electrical faults present; Type B, two trips. Bulletin KC-2080 for Mack and Volvo trucks adds that on PM sensors built before the end of 2017, P2AB0 logged together with U0080 points to a CAN fault rather than the sensor itself. Lost communication is U02A3.
c: Internal fault in the PM sensor control unit (sensor and control unit usually replaced as one part)
CAN wiring fault that older sensor versions also report as P2AB0
Unstable supply or ground at the sensor control unit
s: Check engine light on
Particulate filter monitoring cannot complete
Driving behaviour usually unchanged

P2AB1.d: P2AB1 reports that the control module of an electrically heated catalyst does not work as it should, for example because its self-test fails or the heating it delivers does not match the demand. Such heaters bring a catalyst to working temperature right after start or in low-load driving. According to DieselNet, Vitesco's Emicat heating disc went into two 48-volt mild-hybrid diesel van models from 2022 to warm up the SCR catalyst, after an earlier small-scale use on Audi's 3.0 TDI from model year 2014. No manufacturer documents P2AB1 publicly. CARB requires heated catalysts to reach their design temperature within a period the manufacturer sets after start. A failed switching stage or corrupt software are plausible causes; circuit faults of the heater itself are P0429 and P0439.
c: Internal fault in the heater control module (power stage or self-test)
Module software fault, update may be available
Module overheated due to poor cooling or high ambient heat at its mounting
s: Check engine light on
Higher emissions after cold start; inspection may fail
Driving behaviour largely unchanged

P2AB2.t: Catalyst Heater Control Module Supply Voltage
P2AB2.d: P2AB2 points to the power feed of the catalyst heater control module: the voltage it measures at its own supply input lies outside the window in which it may switch the heater. That window matters because these heaters draw several kilowatts; Vitesco's demonstration vehicle used a 4 kW disc, fed in 48-volt mild hybrids from energy recovered while braking, as DieselNet reports. Mitsubishi Electric's patent US5388404A shows the logic behind such a check: the controller first compares battery voltage with a reference and only then closes the heater current switch, guided by a catalyst temperature signal. No manufacturer documents P2AB2 publicly. A blown fuse, a corroded ground, a weak 48-volt battery or a faulty DC/DC converter are typical finds. P0562 and P0563 cover the general system voltage.
c: Blown fuse or faulty relay in the heater supply
Corroded or loose ground or high-current terminal
Weak 48-volt battery or faulty DC/DC converter in mild-hybrid systems
s: Check engine light on
Catalyst heating not available, higher emissions after cold start
Further voltage-related fault codes possible

P2AB3.t: Cold Start Intake Manifold Runner Control Stuck Open Bank 1
P2AB3.d: P2AB3 is part of the cold-start component checks that CARB phases in for 20, 50 and 100 percent of new vehicles in 2026, 2027 and 2028. Right after a start that follows a long standstill, charge motion, runner and swirl valves must follow the cold-start command clearly, toward the target and further than they would at a start without that strategy. The test only counts after at least six hours off, at -6.7 °C or warmer, with coolant no more than 15 °C above ambient. P2AB3 means the runner control on bank 1 stays in its open position when the cold-start strategy calls for a change. No manufacturer documents P2AB3 publicly. For comparison, Ford's ordinary IMRC check runs continuously above 40 °F coolant and judges stuck plates after 4 events (P2004). Weaker mixture motion raises cold emissions.
c: Actuator or vacuum unit too weak to move the flaps when cold
Flap shaft stiff from carbon or oil deposits
Linkage detached or broken between actuator and shaft
s: Check engine light on
Rougher idle in the first minutes after a cold start
Higher cold-start emissions, otherwise often unnoticed

P2AB4.t: Cold Start Intake Manifold Runner Control Stuck Open Bank 2
P2AB4.d: P2AB4 is the bank 2 version of the open-stuck check during cold start, so it only appears on engines with a separate runner control for each cylinder bank, typically V or flat engines. The runner flaps of the second bank fail to leave their open position as long as the cold-start routine runs, so that bank burns its mixture with less charge motion than intended. No manufacturer documents P2AB4 publicly; the requirement comes from CARB's cold-start component monitoring, which only applies once the engine has been off for six hours or longer. Ford's 2020 to 2023 gasoline summary shows the conventional split for vacuum-actuated V engines, with P2004 for bank 1 and P2005 for bank 2. Comparing bank 2 with bank 1 helps: if only one side lags, look at that actuator, its vacuum line and its linkage. Bank 1 is P2AB3.
c: Leaking vacuum line or diaphragm on the bank 2 actuator
Bank 2 flap shaft stiff from deposits
s: Check engine light on
Uneven running between the banks shortly after a cold start
Higher cold-start emissions

P2AB5.t: Cold Start Intake Manifold Runner Control Stuck Closed Bank 1
P2AB5.d: P2AB5 is the opposite of P2AB3: during cold start the runner control on bank 1 remains in its closed position and does not follow a command to open. CARB requires, for 2026 to 2028 phase-in vehicles, that such valves react measurably and in the commanded direction while the cold-start conditions hold, meaning a soak of six hours or more and coolant close to ambient. A flap that stays closed throttles the air path once the engine is asked for more load, so a lack of pull in the first minutes is possible, and the combustion pattern the calibration expects for the cold catalyst is lost. No manufacturer documents P2AB5 publicly. Ford's conventional counterpart outside the cold-start phase is P2006, judged against the commanded plate position. Bank 2 is P2AB6.
c: Flaps stuck closed by deposits or condensate freezing at low temperature
Actuator motor or vacuum valve does not move the shaft
Broken return spring or worn shaft bushing
s: Check engine light on
Less power in the first minutes after a cold start
Higher cold-start emissions

P2AB6.t: Cold Start Intake Manifold Runner Control Stuck Closed Bank 2
P2AB6.d: P2AB6 reports the runner flaps of bank 2 held in the closed position during the cold-start phase, against a command to open them. Like its siblings it exists only on engines that control each bank's runners separately and only becomes testable after a soak of six hours or more at ambient temperatures from -6.7 °C upward, as defined in CARB's cold-start rules. No manufacturer documents P2AB6 publicly. Ford's gasoline summary for 2020 to 2023 lists the everyday equivalent as P2007 and treats plates that miss the commanded position or overrun their travel as a functional fault. Because only one bank is restricted, the engine may run slightly unevenly between the banks until the flaps free up or the strategy ends. If P2AB5 is set as well, suspect a shared actuator supply. P2AB4 is the open-stuck case on this bank.
c: Bank 2 flaps seized by deposits or ice
Bank 2 actuator or its control valve defective
Shared actuator supply or vacuum source weak (often with P2AB5)
s: Check engine light on
Slightly uneven running and reduced pull after a cold start
Higher cold-start emissions

P2AB7.d: P2AB7 is the general circuit fault for the position sensor on wastegate A, found on engines whose wastegate is moved by an electric motor rather than a vacuum can. Turbo A is the first one in the exhaust flow on series layouts or the bank 1 unit on parallel layouts. Ford names P2AB7 in SSM 50485 for 2019-22 2.0L/2.3L EcoBoost models (Edge, Nautilus, Escape, Corsair, Bronco Sport), where a failed actuator, a lost e-clip or a bent rod led to a lack of power, and TSB 22-2357 cures false settings on 2021-22 F-150 2.7L trucks with new PCM software. Ford publishes no limit for this general code, only for the low and high variants P2AB8/P2AB9. GM reports a broken SENT link to the same sensor as U0644 instead. Bank 2 is P2ABA.
c: Electric wastegate actuator failed, e-clip missing or actuator rod damaged (sensor sits in the actuator)
Chafed harness or loose connector near the hot turbocharger
PCM calibration that sets the code falsely (reflash available for some models)
s: Check engine light on
Noticeable lack of power, boost limited
Often stored together with P0299 or the stuck wastegate codes P25B3/P25B4

P2AB8.t: Wastegate Position Sensor A Circuit Low
P2AB8.d: P2AB8 means the wastegate A position signal has fallen below its valid floor, which points to a short to ground, an open signal or reference wire, or a dead sensor. GM's 2019 tables for the 2.7L L3B read the sensor as a percentage of its reference and fail below 5 % in 30 of 38 samples taken every 100 ms; the 2025 tables use below 1 % in 10 of 12. Both run only outside cranking with powertrain relay voltage of at least 11 V and are Type A, so the lamp lights in the first trip. Ford's 2020-23 gasoline summary sets it under 0.50 V after 4 s. Stellantis case S2308000121 traces P2AB8 with P0245 on the Jeep Wrangler to a pinched harness between turbo and intake hose. P2AB9 is the high side, P2ABB bank 2.
c: Sensor harness pinched or chafed between turbocharger and intake hose (short to ground)
Open reference or signal wire, or pushed-out terminal in the actuator connector
Position sensor inside the electric actuator failed
s: Check engine light from the first trip
Reduced power because boost control is restricted
May appear together with P0245 when a shared harness section is damaged

P2AB9.t: Wastegate Position Sensor A Circuit High
P2AB9.d: P2AB9 is logged when the wastegate A position signal climbs above its valid ceiling. Typical reasons are a signal wire shorted to the sensor supply or to battery voltage, an open ground return that lets the input float upward, or an internal sensor fault. GM's ECM checks the raw position as a share of the reference: above 95 % in the 2019 L3B tables and above 99 % in the 2025 tables, each with 10 failures in 12 samples and Type A, lamp in the first trip. Ford flags it above 4.50 V for 4 s and has reflashed 2021-22 F-150 2.7L trucks (TSB 22-2357) as well as 2020-23 Explorer, 2022-23 F-150 3.5L and Expedition/Navigator (TSB 23-2353) against false settings. With the flap position unknown, boost is held back. P2AB8 is the low side, P2ABC bank 2.
c: Signal wire shorted to the sensor supply or battery voltage
Open sensor ground or corroded ground terminal
PCM calibration that sets the code falsely (Ford reflash for listed models)
Position sensor inside the electric actuator failed
s: Check engine light from the first trip
Lower power under load, boost held back
Powertrain fault (wrench) indicator on some Ford models

P2ABA.d: P2ABA covers a general circuit fault of the position sensor on the wastegate of turbocharger B, so it can only occur on engines with two turbos and electric wastegates: on a parallel layout the turbo of bank 2, on a series layout the second one downstream. Ford uses it on twin-turbo EcoBoost V6 engines. TSB 22-2357 reprograms 2021-22 F-150 2.7L trucks that log P2ABA, P2ABC, P2AB7 or P2AB9 because of software parameters; TSB 23-2353 and the later SSM 54083 cover 2020-23 Explorer, 2022-23 F-150 and 2023-24 Expedition/Navigator, first with a software update and then with the workshop manual pinpoint tests. No limit is published for this general code. CARB lists wastegate valve position among the data items an OBD system must report. Low/high are P2ABB/P2ABC.
c: PCM calibration that sets the code falsely (Ford reflash for listed models)
Damaged harness or connector at the bank 2 turbocharger
Electric wastegate actuator B with its built-in position sensor failed
s: Check engine light, on Ford also the powertrain (wrench) indicator
Reduced power, boost limited

P2ABB.t: Wastegate Position Sensor B Circuit Low
P2ABB.d: P2ABB reports that the position signal of the turbocharger B wastegate is too low, as a short to ground, a broken signal or supply wire or a failed sensor would cause. Ford's 2020-23 gasoline summary applies the same window as for turbo A and sets the code below 0.50 V after 4 s. In that document the threshold line for this sensor names sensor A, evidently an editing slip, since the heading and code title both refer to B. Ford lists P2ABB in TSB 23-2353 and SSM 54083 for twin-turbo applications such as the F-150 3.5L and Expedition/Navigator. The two GM tables reviewed here (2019 L3B, 2025) contain only the A codes. On a V6 the bank 2 flap can then no longer be positioned, so expect reduced boost and power. High is P2ABC, the bank 1 counterpart P2AB8.
c: Sensor wire chafed to ground near the bank 2 turbocharger
Open reference supply or signal wire, loose connector
Position sensor in wastegate actuator B failed
s: Check engine light
Less power, especially when accelerating hard

P2ABC.t: Wastegate Position Sensor B Circuit High
P2ABC.d: P2ABC is the high-voltage fault on the wastegate B position sensor: according to Ford's 2020-23 gasoline summary the input sits above 4.50 V for 4 s, a picture typical of a signal line shorted to the reference supply or an open sensor ground. On the 2.7L F-150 of model years 2021-22 Ford blames false P2ABC entries on calibration and fixes them by reprogramming the PCM (TSB 22-2357); TSB 23-2353 and SSM 54083 add it for the 3.5L V6 in F-150 and Expedition/Navigator. Since the driver cannot tell a sensor fault from a sticking flap, both show up as lower power or a fault light. Heat and vibration at the turbine housing loosen terminals, so the actuator connector deserves the first look. P2ABB is the low side, P2AB9 the same fault on turbo A.
c: PCM calibration that sets the code falsely (Ford reflash for listed models)
Open sensor ground or heat-damaged terminal at the actuator
Signal wire shorted to the reference supply or battery voltage
s: Check engine light, on Ford possibly the wrench indicator
Reduced power under load

P2ABD.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Wastegate Actuator A Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P2ABD.d: P2ABD is raised by the output stage that powers the electric wastegate actuator of turbocharger A when it detects excessive current or overheating. Ford's 2020-23 gasoline summary groups it with P0243 in the wastegate A circuit check: the PCM's smart driver chip recognises a short to battery or ground and an open load on its own and reports within 0.4 s, and the stuck open/closed tests P25B3/P25B4 are only allowed when neither code is present. No Ford bulletin naming P2ABD was found. GM runs a comparable self-protection check on the EGR cooler bypass motor (P2AA5, H-bridge above 170 °C). A linkage that binds and stalls the motor, an internally shorted motor or chafed supply wires make the driver protect itself. P2ABE is the same fault on turbo B.
c: Wastegate flap or rod binding from soot, corrosion or heat so the motor stalls
Actuator supply wires chafed to ground or to each other
Driver stage in the PCM faulty
s: Check engine light on
Clearly reduced power because the wastegate is no longer driven
Stuck wastegate checks P25B3/P25B4 not run while the code is stored

P2ABE.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Wastegate Actuator B Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P2ABE.d: P2ABE is the turbo B counterpart of P2ABD: the output stage driving the second electric wastegate actuator signals overcurrent or thermal overload. It therefore applies only to twin-turbo engines with two electric actuators, such as Ford's EcoBoost V6. Ford's summary treats it together with P0247 as the B circuit check, with the fault detected inside the smart driver chip and a monitoring time of 0.4 s; the functional checks P25B5/P25B6 are blocked while either code is stored. No public bulletin naming P2ABE turned up. A rod seized by corrosion, a shorted motor winding or a harness pinched against the turbo can make the driver shut down to protect itself. Because the bank 2 flap is then left unpositioned, the PCM is likely to limit boost on that side.
c: Wastegate B rod or flap seized by corrosion or heat
Shorted winding in electric actuator B
Actuator harness pinched against the turbocharger
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power, uneven boost between the two banks

P2ABF.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit/Open Bank 1
P2ABF.d: P2ABF points to an open circuit in the reference voltage line of the intake air oxygen sensor on bank 1. This sensor is a wide-band element placed in the intake tract, usually before the intercooler, that measures how much oxygen the incoming charge still contains and therefore how much exhaust has been recirculated. Ford's patent US8775011B2 describes it as a UEGO-type sensor that delivers either a pumping current or a voltage; a related Ford application reads the pumping current while a reference voltage is applied. With the reference lead broken, that loop cannot work and EGR control loses its feedback. No manufacturer documents P2ABF publicly; under CARB rules every engine input must be monitored for broken circuits. P2AC0 is the plausibility fault, P2AC1/P2AC2 low/high, P2AC3 bank 2.
c: Broken reference wire or pushed-back pin between sensor and ECM
Corroded or loose sensor connector in the damp intake area
Sensing cell of the intake oxygen sensor internally open
s: Check engine light on
EGR runs without sensor feedback or is reduced, higher NOx emissions

P2AC0.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1
P2AC0.d: P2AC0 is set when the reference voltage circuit of the bank 1 intake air oxygen sensor is electrically present but behaves implausibly, for example drifting or not matching what the ECM expects for the current EGR and pressure state. Stellantis documents it explicitly for the 2.0L turbo four (sales code EC2) of the Alfa Romeo Giulia and Stelvio: TSB 18-067-22 REV. B for 2022 Giulia and TSB 18-041-23 REV. A for 2022 Stelvio both cure a lit MIL with P2AC0 by flashing new engine software, so a false detection rather than a worn part. The 2017 Giulia bulletin 18-030-17 already listed it next to P2B89. Ford's intake oxygen patents show that intake pressure and humidity shift the sensor output, which any plausibility check has to allow for. P2ABF is the open circuit, P2AC4 bank 2.
c: Engine software that detects the fault falsely (Stellantis reflash for Giulia/Stelvio 2.0L)
Intake oxygen sensor aged or contaminated by oil mist from crankcase ventilation
High resistance in the reference wire or connector
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable change in driveability

P2AC1.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit Low Bank 1
P2AC1.d: P2AC1 flags a reference voltage below the range the ECM accepts on the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor. This usually means the reference lead is shorted to ground or the sensing cell inside the sensor has broken down. Without a stable reference the ECM cannot operate the cell, so the oxygen reading used to work out the EGR rate becomes useless and recirculation is typically cut back or run open loop. No manufacturer publishes a threshold or bulletin for P2AC1. Ford's patents describe the intake sensor as a wide-band element operated at a fixed reference voltage whose pumping current carries the oxygen signal, and CARB requires such inputs to be monitored for out-of-range values. Unplug the sensor and measure the lead against ground before replacing parts. P2AC2 is the high counterpart, P2AC5 bank 2.
c: Reference wire chafed through to ground
Sensing cell of the intake oxygen sensor broken down internally
Sensor interface in the ECM faulty
s: Check engine light on
EGR reduced or uncontrolled, possibly higher NOx and a failed emissions test

P2AC2.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit High Bank 1
P2AC2.d: P2AC2 means the reference voltage at the intake oxygen sensor of bank 1 reads above its permitted range. A reference lead shorted to a supply wire or battery voltage in the harness, a lost ground on the sensor side or water in the connector are the usual triggers; a sensor with an internally damaged cell can produce the same picture. The intake sensor sits in a damp, oil-misted environment near the crankcase ventilation and EGR inlet, so connector corrosion deserves a look. No manufacturer publishes P2AC2 with thresholds; CARB's rule for comprehensive input components and Ford's patents on the sensor itself are the basis here. As with the other faults in this family, the ECM loses its measurement of recirculated exhaust and falls back to model-based or reduced EGR, which can raise NOx. P2AC1 is the low counterpart, P2AC6 bank 2.
c: Reference wire shorted to a supply or battery voltage wire
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the sensor connector
Open ground on the sensor side
s: Check engine light on
EGR reduced, NOx emissions may rise

P2AC3.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit/Open Bank 2
P2AC3.d: P2AC3 is the open circuit fault in the reference voltage lead of the intake air oxygen sensor assigned to bank 2. A second intake sensor only exists where each cylinder bank has its own intake or EGR path, for example on V engines with two separate charge air routes; engines with a single sensor use the bank 1 code P2ABF. No manufacturer has published P2AC3 or a vehicle using it. Technically the check works as on bank 1: if the reference wire to the sensing cell is interrupted, the ECM can no longer operate the cell and receives no usable oxygen value, so EGR on that bank runs without feedback. Wiring routed close to the hot turbo or exhaust of the second bank is the first place to look. P2AC4 is the plausibility fault, P2AC5/P2AC6 low/high.
c: Broken reference wire or loose terminal at the bank 2 sensor
Harness damaged by heat near the bank 2 turbocharger or exhaust
Sensing cell of the bank 2 intake oxygen sensor internally open
s: Check engine light on
EGR on bank 2 reduced or uncontrolled

P2AC4.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit Range/Performance Bank 2
P2AC4.d: P2AC4 marks an implausible but electrically intact reference voltage on the second-bank intake oxygen sensor. It is the bank 2 twin of P2AC0, which Stellantis documents for the four-cylinder Alfa Romeo 2.0L; an inline four with one intake path has no bank 2, so P2AC4 would only appear on engines fitted with a second intake sensor. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. A plausibility test of this kind typically compares the sensor reading with what EGR valve position, intake pressure and air mass lead the ECM to expect; Ford's patents show that pressure changes and humidity shift the output and must be compensated. Ageing, contamination from crankcase vapours or an overly strict calibration are therefore likelier causes than a broken wire. P2AC3 is the open circuit.
c: Bank 2 intake oxygen sensor aged or contaminated by crankcase vapours
Calibration that judges the signal too strictly
High resistance in the reference wire or connector
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable change in driveability

P2AC5.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit Low Bank 2
P2AC5.d: P2AC5 reports that the bank 2 intake oxygen sensor sees a reference voltage below the permitted limit, typically a short to ground in the reference lead or a breakdown of the sensing cell. No manufacturer publishes this code, and engines with a separate intake oxygen sensor for bank 2 are rare. If a vehicle does set it, compare with P2AC1: a fault on only one bank points to that sensor or its own harness branch, while both banks together hint at a shared ground, the sensor supply or the ECM. While the reference is pulled low, the bank 2 EGR feedback is lost and the ECM is expected to reduce recirculation, which raises NOx output but rarely affects driveability. CARB and Ford's sensor patents frame the check. P2AC6 is the high side, P2AC3 the open circuit.
c: Reference wire of the bank 2 sensor shorted to ground
Shared sensor supply or ECM fault (if P2AC1 is present as well)
s: Check engine light on
Higher NOx, possibly a failed emissions test

P2AC6.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit High Bank 2
P2AC6.d: P2AC6 indicates an excessive reference voltage on the intake oxygen sensor serving bank 2, as happens when the reference wire touches a supply or battery feed, when the sensor ground is open or when moisture bridges the connector pins. Like the other bank 2 codes of this group, it is not documented by any manufacturer; the basis is CARB's general rule that input components must be checked for out-of-range values in both directions. Ford's patents on intake oxygen sensing describe the sensor element and the reference-voltage operation that this check protects.
