Before replacing the sensor, unplug it and measure the reference lead against ground and against battery voltage with the ignition on. P2AC5 is the low side, P2AC2 the bank 1 counterpart.
c: Reference wire of the bank 2 sensor shorted to a supply or battery feed
Moisture bridging pins in the connector
s: Check engine light on
EGR on bank 2 reduced, NOx may rise

P2AC7.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P2AC7.d: P2AC7 is the general circuit fault of the second coolant temperature sensor in the low-temperature loop that serves a water-cooled charge air cooler. Where two sensors exist, one usually sits at the cooler inlet and the other at its outlet, so the module can judge how much heat the cooler removes; in GM's 2025 diesel table, sensor A measures the water entering the cooler. No manufacturer publishes a description of P2AC7 itself. The code covers faults that cannot be classified as clearly low or clearly high, such as a signal the module rejects as invalid; those two extremes belong to P2AC9 and P2ACA. CARB requires circuit checks for every such input. The driver may notice the warning lamp and, on some engines, reduced boost as a precaution.
c: Loose, corroded or coolant-contaminated sensor B connector
Chafed or broken wire between sensor B and the module
Faulty sensor input or reference in the engine control module
s: Check engine light on
Implausible or missing value for sensor B in live data
Reduced boost or power on some engines

P2AC8.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P2AC8.d: P2AC8 sets when charge air cooler coolant temperature sensor B delivers an electrically valid value that makes no sense for the situation, for example after a long engine-off period when every temperature in the engine bay should have converged, or when it fails to change while the loop pump runs and the cooler heats up. No maker documents this exact check publicly; Ford and GM only publish thresholds for sensor A (P00DE to P00E2). Besides a drifting sensor, the low-temperature circuit itself can trigger it: low coolant, trapped air or a weak electric pump make the reading real but unexpected. Check level and bleeding first, then compare B in live data with sensor A and with the engine's own coolant reading. Hard limits of the signal are P2AC9 and P2ACA.
c: Low coolant level or air trapped in the low-temperature loop
Sensor B drifting out of its characteristic
Electric charge air cooler coolant pump weak or not running
Control module software needing an update
s: Check engine light on, often only after several drives
Sensor B reads clearly different from sensor A after a cold soak
Higher intake air temperature under load

P2AC9.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P2AC9.d: P2AC9 reports that the signal of charge air cooler coolant temperature sensor B has dropped below its permitted window. These sensors are NTC thermistors, so a low signal stands for an implausibly hot coolant and usually means the signal wire touches ground or the element is internally shorted. Public limits exist only for sensor A: Ford's 2023 diesels flag P00E0 below 0.162 V within 5 s, while GM's 2025 diesel table reads resistance and fails under 70 ohms in 30 of 38 samples as a Type B code. A B-sensor check from the same maker is likely built the same way, but no document states it. With a false hot value the control may run the loop pump constantly or cut boost. Measure resistance at a known temperature and inspect the harness for chafing.
c: Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground
Coolant in the connector bridging the terminals
s: Check engine light on
Live data shows an extremely high coolant temperature for sensor B
Coolant pump of the loop runs constantly or boost is reduced

P2ACA.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
P2ACA.d: P2ACA is the opposite end: the voltage from charge air cooler coolant temperature sensor B sits above anything a real temperature would produce. For a thermistor input this looks like extreme cold and is typical of an unplugged connector, a broken signal wire, a lost sensor ground or a short to a voltage source. For sensor A, Ford's 2023 diesel summary sets P00E1 above 4.928 V, and GM's 2025 diesel table above 166,297 ohms, again as Type B. Nothing comparable is published for B. A frozen-looking reading may keep the low-temperature pump idle or make the module distrust the cooler, which on some engines means less boost. Check plug fit and corrosion first; with the two terminals bridged, the live value should jump to the hot end.
c: Disconnected plug or broken signal wire of sensor B
Open ground or return line of the sensor
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
s: Check engine light on
Live data shows an extremely low coolant temperature for sensor B
Reduced boost on some engines

P2ACB.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Temperature Sensor B Intermittent/Erratic
P2ACB.d: P2ACB covers a sensor B signal that jumps or briefly drops out instead of following the slow temperature changes of a coolant loop. The title, without the word circuit, also includes erratic values while the wiring stays intact. No maker publishes the B-side check. GM's 2025 diesel table shows how the A-side version (P00E2) works: it builds moving limits around the last good reading using the sensor's filter time and counts 60 failed samples out of 75 against them, Type B. A test of this kind only runs while no steady circuit fault is present, so P2AC9 or P2ACA take priority. Typical causes are a terminal with poor contact tension, a connector loosened by vibration or coolant that has crept into the plug. Wiggle the harness while watching live data.
c: Terminal with weak contact tension in the sensor B plug
Harness rubbing through intermittently under vibration
Sensor B element with unstable output
s: Check engine light comes and goes
Sensor B value jumps in live data

P2ACC.d: P2ACC is the general circuit code for a second reductant (DEF) temperature sensor outside the tank; the tank sensors have their own series (P205A ff. and P2ADA ff.). Sensor A, coded P2042 ff., is placed by Deutz in the SCR supply path (SPN 4337) and by Volvo and Mack in the DEF pump. Where a B sensor sits is left to the maker, and no manufacturer publicly documents P2ACC. The code captures circuit faults that do not fall clearly under the low or high codes P2ACE and P2ACF. CARB requires circuit monitoring for every input that feeds an emission control. Because DEF heating and the release of dosing depend on this temperature, an SCR warning and, if the fault stays, the usual inducement steps may follow.
c: Connector of sensor B corroded by DEF residue
Damaged wiring between sensor B and the controller
s: Check engine light and DEF/SCR warning
Countdown or speed limitation if the fault persists

P2ACD.t: Reductant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P2ACD.d: P2ACD flags a reductant temperature sensor B reading that is electrically fine but disagrees with the other temperatures the SCR controller knows, typically checked after a cold soak, when DEF lines, tank and ambient should read about the same. No manufacturer publicly describes P2ACD. The sensor A counterpart shows the pattern: Deutz files P2043-64 as a plausibility error of the DEF temperature input, and Ford bulletin 18-2190 for the 2011–2015 6.7L Super Duty treats P2043 alone as a software case (PCM reprogram) and calls for a new heater and sender unit only when P205C or P205D appear as well. A B-side plausibility code without circuit codes therefore deserves a software check before parts are ordered. P2ACC, P2ACE and P2ACF cover the electrical faults.
c: Controller software with an overly tight plausibility check
Sensor B drifting from its characteristic
Line heater warming the sensor area during the check
s: Check engine light after a cold start
SCR warning with no noticeable driving change

P2ACE.t: Reductant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P2ACE.d: P2ACE means the signal of reductant temperature sensor B lies below its valid voltage band. With the NTC elements used for DEF temperature, a low voltage translates into an extremely hot reading, so a signal line rubbing through to ground, a crushed connector or DEF that has wicked into the plug and bridges the contacts are the usual suspects. No maker publishes a threshold for P2ACE. For sensor A, Deutz lists P2044-00 as a short to ground; GM's 2025 DEF controller sets the low limit of its tank sensor at 0.3 V, roughly 75 °C, which shows the order of magnitude. A false hot value can lead the controller to skip DEF heating in frost, so lines may freeze and dosing stop. Measure the sensor resistance against a temperature table and look for crystallised DEF at the connector.
c: Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground
DEF wicked into the connector bridging the terminals
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
Implausibly high DEF temperature in live data
Frozen DEF lines in winter

P2ACF.t: Reductant Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
P2ACF.d: P2ACF is set when reductant temperature sensor B reports a voltage above its valid band. For a thermistor that reads as deep cold, and it is what an open signal wire, a missing sensor ground, a disconnected plug or a short to supply voltage cause. No public document gives a limit for P2ACF; Deutz records the A-side equivalent as P2045-00, short to battery, and keeps the plain open circuit apart as P2042-13. For orientation, GM's 2025 DEF controller treats more than 4.75 V on its tank sensor, about −40 °C, as the high fault. A sensor that falsely reports frost can keep heaters running longer than needed and delay the start of dosing after a cold start, which raises NOx until it clears. Test the ground path and the sensor resistance at a known temperature.
c: Open signal wire or disconnected plug at sensor B
Signal wire shorted to supply voltage
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
Implausibly low DEF temperature in live data
Delayed start of dosing after a cold start

P2AD0.t: Reductant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent
P2AD0.d: P2AD0 stands for short interruptions or jumps in the signal of reductant temperature sensor B. The current title reads circuit intermittent only, without erratic. No manufacturer publishes this test. The closest documented logic is GM's tank sensor check P205E in its 2025 DEF controller, which counts a failure when the value moves more than 4 °C within a ten-sample window and needs three such failures out of nine; sensor A has the corresponding code P2046. Because DEF crystallises when it leaks, a slightly damp connector can produce exactly these spikes; vibration loosening a terminal is the other classic cause. Steady faults are reported as P2ACE or P2ACF instead. Clean and dry the connector, check terminal grip and repeat a wiggle test with live data running.
c: Moisture or DEF residue in the sensor B connector
Wire breaking intermittently inside the insulation
s: Check engine light that appears sporadically
Jumping DEF temperature in live data

P2AD1.t: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch C/G Voltage Correlation
P2AD1.d: P2AD1 compares the voltages of position signals C and G and sets when they stop describing the same position. What the letters mean depends on the layout; GM's 2023 table 23OBDG07 for an engine with two throttle bodies is the clearest public key: C is sensor 1 and G sensor 2 of the bank 2 throttle (P0227/P0228 and P212C/P212D), so C/G is the internal pair of that second throttle, the counterpart of the bank 1 pair A/B under P2135. GM's table itself checks each track against modelled air charge rather than listing P2AD1, and no maker documents the code publicly. Typical causes are a worn track in the bank 2 throttle, contact resistance in its connector or a shared ground or reference fault. The ECU then usually limits throttle opening.
c: Raised contact resistance in the throttle connector
Worn or drifting sensor track in the second throttle body
Fault on the shared 5 V reference or sensor ground
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power or limited throttle response

P2AD2.t: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch B/G Voltage Correlation
P2AD2.d: P2AD2 sets when signals B and G no longer agree in voltage. On engines with one throttle body per bank this is a cross-bank comparison: with GM's 2023 letter scheme, B is the second track of the bank 1 throttle and G the second track of the bank 2 throttle. Mercedes-Benz uses P2AD2 on its M177 twin-turbo V8 (AMG C63, E63, GLE63, GT63, also GLE/GLS 580 and Maybach GLS 600): the third version (August 2026) of bulletin LI07.10-P-080384 added P2AD200 to its list and traces it, together with P2135, P2136 and P2AD3, to high resistance in the pins of both throttle actuators, left and right; the fix is new silver- and gold-plated terminals and seals. Drivers notice the check engine light and possibly reduced power.
c: High resistance at the pins of the throttle actuator connectors
Drifting position track in one of the throttle bodies
Damaged wiring to one throttle actuator
s: Check engine light on
Possible loss of power
Further throttle codes such as P2135 or P2136 stored

P2AD3.t: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch A/G Voltage Correlation
P2AD3.d: P2AD3 compares tracks A and G. In GM's 2023 scheme A is the first sensor of the bank 1 throttle body and G the second sensor of the bank 2 unit, so the pair links both throttles of a V engine and can reveal that one plate is not where the other suggests. Mercedes-Benz is the documented user: on M177 V8s from the 2015 AMG C63 to the 2025 Maybach GLS 600, P2AD300 reads as an implausible relation between the A and G position values. Bulletin LI07.10-P-080384 already listed it in version 2 (May 2026) and blames raised contact resistance in the connectors M16/60 and M16/61 of the two throttle actuators. When P2135 or P2136 are stored alongside, a shared cause in the connectors is more likely than two failed throttles.
c: Raised contact resistance in the connectors of both throttle actuators
One throttle body with a faulty position sensor
Fault on a shared sensor supply or ground
s: Check engine light on
Possible loss of power or emergency throttle mode

P2AD4.d: P2AD4 reports that the voltage of an intermediate system, a supply level between the 12 V network and a high-voltage traction battery, has fallen below its lower limit. In practice this describes 48 V networks of mild hybrids, which carry a belt or integrated starter-generator and loads such as electric compressors; German makers agreed on such a level in 2011, and Audi and Mercedes-Benz use it since 2018. No manufacturer publicly documents P2AD4, so the exact meaning (which module measures, which threshold) remains maker specific. Plausible causes are a weak or deeply discharged 48 V battery, a DC/DC converter that drains the network, poor connections or a starter-generator that does not charge. CARB treats hybrid components in (f)(15.2.3) but grants mild-hybrid exemptions. Drivers lose start-stop and boost assistance.
c: Weak or deeply discharged 48 V battery
Starter-generator not charging the intermediate network
DC/DC converter drawing the network down
s: Warning lamp or message about the electrical system
Start-stop and electric boost unavailable
Engine may not restart via the starter-generator

P2AD5.d: P2AD5 is the high counterpart: the intermediate voltage level, in current vehicles mostly a 48 V mild-hybrid network, rises above its permitted maximum. Overvoltage typically arises when the starter-generator regenerates harder than the battery can accept, for example with a full or cold 48 V battery, a battery that has disconnected itself internally, or a faulty regulator in the generator or DC/DC converter. No manufacturer publishes P2AD5 or its threshold, so the details are maker specific; the assignment to 48 V follows from the term and the spread of such networks since 2018. Connected modules may switch off to protect themselves, so recuperation, electric boost and start-stop drop out and the 12 V side may show warnings. Diagnosis starts with the battery management data and the charge command of the generator.
c: Starter-generator regulating the voltage too high
48 V battery disconnected internally or unable to accept charge
Faulty DC/DC converter feeding back into the network
s: Warning message about the electrical system
Recuperation, electric boost and start-stop unavailable

P2AD6.t: Reductant Pump Motor Position Sensor Circuit
P2AD6.d: P2AD6 is the general circuit code of the position sensor in the motor of the reductant (DEF) pump. Modern supply pumps often use a brushless motor whose rotor position must be known for commutation and speed control; a Cummins Emission Solutions patent names a Hall-effect rotor position sensor as one option and back-EMF evaluation as the sensorless alternative. No manufacturer publishes a description of P2AD6. The code covers faults of the sensor circuit itself that are not clearly low or high (P2AD8, P2AD9), for example an implausible or missing pattern. In most designs sensor, motor and electronics form a sealed pump module, so the repair is a new pump unit after the harness and supply have been checked. If the pump cannot be controlled, dosing stops and the SCR warning sequence begins.
c: Position sensor or electronics inside the pump module defective
DEF residue or corrosion in the pump connector
Missing supply or ground for the pump electronics
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
DEF dosing stops; countdown to speed limitation

P2AD7.t: Reductant Pump Motor Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2AD7.d: P2AD7 sets when the motor position signal of the reductant pump is electrically valid but does not fit what the pump should be doing, for instance a rotor position or derived speed that is out of step with the commanded drive pattern. No maker documents P2AD7 publicly. Ford's 2023 diesel summary shows a related check from the speed side: P208B, the pump control performance code, fails when pump speed deviates from its setpoint by more than 300 rpm or the speed controller sits at its limit for 30 s. A stiff or partly frozen pump, crystallised DEF in the pump head or a shifted sensor magnet can all produce such mismatches. Because most pumps are sealed units, a confirmed P2AD7 together with pressure codes usually ends in a pump module replacement.
c: Pump stiff or partly frozen, crystallised DEF in the pump head
Position sensor inside the pump giving a shifted signal
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
Pressure build-up of the DEF system fails, often after cold nights

P2AD8.t: Reductant Pump Motor Position Sensor Circuit Low
P2AD8.d: P2AD8 reports a reductant pump motor position signal stuck below its valid range. For Hall-type sensors this mostly means the output is pulled to ground permanently: a signal wire shorted to ground, a sensor that has lost its supply, or an internal short in the pump electronics. Without a usable rotor position a brushless pump motor cannot be commutated reliably any more, so the controller may stop the pump to protect it. No manufacturer publishes P2AD8 or a threshold; the general frame is the CARB requirement for circuit checks on emission-relevant inputs. Where the sensor wiring runs inside a sealed pump module, check the external harness, fuses and supply voltage at the pump connector first; if those are sound, the pump unit is the likely replacement.
c: Internal short in the pump electronics
Sensor supply missing, e.g. blown fuse or open feed
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
DEF pump does not run, no dosing

P2AD9.t: Reductant Pump Motor Position Sensor Circuit High
P2AD9.d: P2AD9 is the high-side fault: the pump motor position signal stays above its permitted range. An open signal line pulled up by the controller's internal resistor, a broken sensor ground or a short to the supply rail produce this picture. Without changing position information, speed control fails and the pressure build-up may be aborted; faults of the pump drive itself carry their own codes, in Ford's diesel summary for example P208A to P208D. No public document describes P2AD9 itself or its limit. Look for white DEF residue in the pump connector, since the fluid creeps along wires and attacks terminals, and check the ground connection before condemning the pump. A failure that stops dosing triggers the driver warning and, if ignored, the speed or restart restrictions of the SCR system.
c: Open signal line or broken sensor ground
DEF residue corroding the pump connector
Signal shorted to the supply rail
s: Check engine light and SCR warning
No DEF pressure build-up, dosing stops

P2ADA.t: Reductant Tank Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P2ADA.d: P2ADA checks whether the second DEF tank temperature reading is plausible. GM documents it twice. In its 2017–2018 diesel tables (and again in 25OBDG06C) it is the DEF quality sensor temperature offset: after more than 28,800 s off, the quality sensor's thermistor may differ from the average of the exhaust temperature sensors by no more than 35 °C; 40 of 50 samples failing set a Type A code. The 2025 DEF controller compares, at key on after a soak of over 8 h, the tank sensor B value with the secondary device temperature and fails beyond 21 °C (3 s out of 6, Type A). GM bulletin 21-NA-149 lists P2ADA among the codes from engine harness chafing on 2021 3.0L LM2 trucks. Circuit faults are P2ADB to P2ADE.
c: DEF quality sensor with drifting temperature element
Chafed engine harness disturbing the signals
s: Check engine light after a cold start
DEF or SCR warning message

P2ADB.t: Reductant Tank Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P2ADB.d: P2ADB flags a value from the second DEF tank temperature sensor that lies below the lowest temperature the sensor can physically report, so the controller treats it as a circuit fault and not as cold fluid. GM is the documented user. In its 2017 and 2018 diesel tables sensor B is the thermistor inside the DEF quality sensor: a reading under −55 °C in 40 of 50 samples (100 ms task) sets a Type A code, MIL on the first trip. The 2025 DEF controller (25OBDG04A) leaves the range check to the smart tank unit, which sends an error flag over SENT; below −50 °C for 2 s P2ADB is stored. Without a valid value the SCR controller loses one input for managing the tank temperature. The upper limit is P2ADC, unsteady readings are P2ADD.
c: Defective thermistor in the DEF quality or tank sensor unit
Moisture or DEF crystals in the sensor connector
Damaged signal or supply wiring to the tank sensor
s: Check engine light right after the fault is detected
DEF or SCR system warning in the cluster
Countdown to reduced power or restart lock if left unrepaired

P2ADC.t: Reductant Tank Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
P2ADC.d: P2ADC is the upper limit check on the same sensor B: the reported DEF temperature is higher than the fluid in the tank could ever get. In GM's 2017 and 2018 diesel calibrations the quality sensor thermistor has to exceed 155 °C in 40 of 50 samples, with cranking finished and more than 11 V at the powertrain relay; the outcome is a Type A code. GM's 2025 DEF controller draws the line much lower at 90 °C, held for 2 s and again computed inside the smart tank unit. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 names P2ADC among the codes that a chafed engine harness produced on 2021 trucks and SUVs with the 3.0 L LM2 diesel. Such a high value usually means trouble in the sensor electronics or its wiring rather than real heat. Too low and unsteady signals are handled by P2ADB and P2ADD.
c: Internal fault in the quality sensor or smart tank sensor unit
Chafed engine harness disturbing the sensor circuit
Corroded or loose pins at the tank sensor connector
s: Check engine light on
DEF system message, often together with other harness-related codes
Possible inducement countdown toward reduced power

P2ADD.t: Reductant Tank Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2ADD.d: P2ADD judges how the sensor B signal moves over time instead of how high it is. Fluid in a tank warms and cools slowly, so sudden jumps suggest a loose contact or a failing element. GM's 2017 and 2018 diesel tables compare every raw thermistor sample with an envelope that starts at the last good value and widens toward the −55 °C and 155 °C limits as bad samples pile up; 40 failures in 50 samples give a Type A code. In the 2025 DEF controller the tank unit adds up the absolute temperature changes across a window of 14 samples taken every 1.3 s and fails above 6 °C, one fail in three windows being enough; while P2ADB or P2ADC is present this test is suspended. GM also lists P2ADD in bulletin 21-NA-149 on harness chafing with the 3.0 L LM2 diesel.
c: Loose or corroded contact at the tank sensor connector
Degrading thermistor in the quality or tank sensor unit
s: Check engine light that may return after clearing
Jumping DEF temperature in live data
DEF or SCR warning message

P2ADE.t: Reductant Tank Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P2ADE.d: P2ADE is the general circuit code for reductant tank temperature sensor B, intended for systems that report a fault on this input without splitting it into low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents P2ADE publicly. GM, where the sensor B family is on record, reports such faults through P2ADB, P2ADC and P2ADD plus the plausibility code P2ADA, and its 2025 DEF controller names exactly those four as the sensor B fault set. Deutz files an open circuit of its second tank temperature sensor at the suction point under its own code P1241 instead. CARB requires emission-related inputs to be checked for open circuits and for readings outside their possible range. Where P2ADE does show up, treat it as an open or unreadable sensor B circuit: inspect connector, wiring and the tank sensor unit.
c: Open signal line or unplugged tank sensor connector
Input fault in the SCR or engine control module
s: Check engine light on
DEF or SCR warning
Possible inducement countdown

P2ADF.d: P2ADF means the engine control module has concluded that air reaches the cylinders of bank 2 without passing the air measurement. Audi documents the code for the 4.0 litre TFSI V8 in the A8, S8, SQ7, SQ8, RS Q8, RS 6 Avant and RS 7 from model years 2019 to 2023. Drivers notice the check engine or exhaust warning lamp and a whistle from the engine bay; misfire codes for bank 1 and P2279 for bank 1 can be stored alongside. Audi's remedy is a new full-load crankcase breather line serving bank 2, while the oil separators and part-load lines stay in place. On other engines, split intake or boost hoses, leaking manifold gaskets and a stuck crankcase ventilation valve are the usual leak points. P2279 covers the same check for bank 1.
c: Leaking full-load crankcase breather line on bank 2 (Audi 4.0 TFSI)
Split intake or boost hose on bank 2
Leaking intake manifold gasket on bank 2
s: Check engine or exhaust warning light on
Whistling noise from the engine bay
Rough idle or misfire codes

P2AE0.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit Open Bank 1
P2AE0.d: P2AE0 says the calibration (trim) wire of bank 1's intake O2 sensor has lost continuity. On a Bosch-type wide-band element this is pin 5 (RT/IA), which connects a resistor in the plug that Bosch uses to set the characteristic of each individual sensor; without it the ECM scales the oxygen signal wrongly. No manufacturer documents P2AE0 publicly, and no bulletin lists it. On exhaust probes Ford spots an open IA line (P2626) on overrun with the injectors cut: if the pumping current in pure air stays above roughly 3.1 mA for 2 s, the code sets. Saab's 2010 9-5 uses a 4.81 V limit in the same situation. Ford's EGR patent also learns the intake sensor's zero point at idle or during fuel cut, so a wrong air reading skews the EGR estimate. P2AE1/P2AE2 are low/high, P2AE9 bank 2.
c: Trim lead (pin 5) broken in the harness
Trim contact pushed back or corroded in the sensor plug
Calibration resistor inside the sensor connector open
s: Check engine light on
EGR reduced or run without oxygen feedback
NOx emissions may rise

P2AE1.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit Low Bank 1
P2AE1.d: P2AE1 is stored when the voltage on the trim circuit of the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor falls below its window. With the ignition on, the 2010 Saab 9-5 expects roughly 2.8 V on terminal 5 of its wide-band probe, the trim connection; a value near zero suggests a lead rubbing on ground or a shorted resistor in the sensor plug. Ford's 2012 summary shows how makers sort such faults differently: on NTK probes an open and a grounded trim lead (RL) both set the low code P2627, while on Bosch probes a grounded IA lead lands in P0131. No manufacturer publishes P2AE1 for an intake sensor. With the trim value missing, the EGR rate derived from the oxygen reading becomes unreliable, so recirculation is cut back. P2AE0 is the open, P2AE2 the high fault, P2AEA bank 2.
c: Trim lead chafed through to ground
Calibration resistor in the sensor plug shorted
Open trim lead on sensors whose interface reports it as low
s: Check engine light on
EGR cut back, possibly higher NOx

P2AE2.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit High Bank 1
P2AE2.d: P2AE2 means the voltage on the trim lead of the intake air O2 sensor for bank 1 is too high. In the six-wire harness of a wide-band probe this line runs next to the heater feed, so a pinched wire or moisture bridging the pins in the connector can drag it towards battery voltage. Ford's 2012 OBD summary books a trim lead shorted to battery as P2628 on NTK probes and under the general high code P0132 on Bosch probes; neither covers an intake sensor, and no manufacturer documents P2AE2 publicly. CARB requires input circuits to be checked for values beyond their range in both directions. According to Bosch the trimming resistor fixes the sensor characteristic, so a falsified value shifts the oxygen reading that EGR control relies on. Check plug and lead against battery voltage before fitting a new sensor. P2AE1 is low, P2AEB bank 2.
c: Trim lead touching the heater supply
Moisture bridging contacts in the sensor plug
Internal short in the sensor or its connector module
s: Check engine light on
EGR reduced, NOx may rise

P2AE3.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Circuit Open Bank 1
P2AE3.d: P2AE3 reports a break in the pumping current lead of the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor, pin 1 of a Bosch LSU 4.9 (APE/IP). Through this wire the ECM drives current into the pump cell while the Nernst cell is kept on its set point; Ford's patent US9441564B2 explains that the size of that current reflects the oxygen share of the charge, from which the EGR dilution is calculated. With the lead open, no current flows and the reading freezes. For the exhaust twin P2237 Ford detects this when reference-current pulses shift lambda by 0.05 or less within 20 s. In the intake, where the gas always stays lean, such a test would have to rely on EGR changes instead; no manufacturer publishes P2AE3 to confirm how. P2AE4/P2AE5 are low/high, P2AE6 the open return, P2AEC bank 2.
c: Sensor plug loose or not latched
Pump cell inside the sensor open
s: Check engine light on
EGR runs without sensor feedback or is switched off

P2AE4.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Circuit Low Bank 1
P2AE4.d: P2AE4 flags too low a level in the pumping current circuit belonging to the bank 1 intake sensor, usually a pump lead chafed through to ground or an internal short in the pump cell. Saab's 2010 9-5 gives a useful reference for the same wire on its exhaust probe: about 2.8 V on terminal 1 at ignition-on with the sensor unplugged, and its low code P2238 sets when the signal stays under 1.7 V for 3 s on overrun. Ford instead stores a grounded IP lead as P0131. No maker documents P2AE4 for an intake sensor. Because the ECM can no longer pump oxygen through the cell, it loses the value it compares with the zero point learned without EGR, and recirculation is reduced or switched off. P2AE3 is the open lead, P2AE5 the high side, P2AED bank 2.
c: Pump current lead shorted to ground
Internal short in the pump cell
Sensor interface in the ECM faulty
s: Check engine light on
EGR reduced or switched off
Possibly higher NOx at an emissions test

P2AE5.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Circuit High Bank 1
P2AE5.d: P2AE5 is the high-side fault of the pumping current lead on the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor. A short to the heater supply or another battery feed in the harness is the classic cause; because the intake sensor works in damp air close to where blow-by gas and EGR enter, water in the plug comes next. Ford files a pump lead touching battery voltage on its exhaust probes as P0132, while Saab's 9-5 (2010) uses the high code P2239 when the signal stays between 1.48 and 1.51 V for 1 s despite enrichment, a Type B fault. Neither applies directly to the intake, and no manufacturer documents P2AE5 publicly; CARB supplies the obligation to catch out-of-range inputs. A shorted pump wire can damage the sensor interface in the ECM, so measure before swapping parts. P2AE4 is low, P2AEE bank 2.
c: Pump current lead shorted to the heater or another supply
Water or condensate in the sensor plug
Sensor interface in the ECM damaged by the short
s: Check engine light on
EGR reduced, NOx may rise

P2AE6.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit Open Bank 1
P2AE6.d: P2AE6 points to an open negative current control line on the bank 1 intake air oxygen sensor. This is the shared return of pump and Nernst cell, which Bosch names virtual ground (IPN/VM, pin 2); Saab's 2010 9-5 shows about 2.5 V on it at ignition-on, a bias that lets the pump current change direction. For the exhaust analog P2251, Ford separates an open VM from an open pump lead: lambda still reacts to reference-current pulses, and with the Bosch CJ125 chip the fault sets when for 10 s the sensor voltage remains between 1.45 and 1.55 V. No manufacturer publishes P2AE6 for the intake sensor. With the return missing, neither cell has a defined reference, the oxygen value is lost and EGR runs without feedback. P2AE7/P2AE8 are low/high, P2AE3 the open pump lead, P2AEF bank 2.
c: Corroded or loose return contact in the plug
Internal break of the common electrode in the sensor
s: Check engine light on
EGR runs without oxygen feedback

P2AE7.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit Low Bank 1
P2AE7.d: P2AE7 is set when the virtual-ground return of the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor is pulled below its bias. In operation this lead sits roughly 2.5 V above chassis, as Saab's 2010 9-5 documents for its wide-band probe; a wire touching the engine block, a bracket or the intake pipe drags it towards zero. The pump cell then has hardly any room to work, and both the measured oxygen share and the EGR rate derived from it become meaningless. Ford counts a grounded VM lead among the faults that set P0131 on its exhaust probes. No manufacturer documents P2AE7 itself, so this rests on CARB's range-check duty and the Bosch pin layout. P2AE6 is the open return, P2AE8 the high case, P2AE4 the low fault on the pump lead, P2AF0 bank 2.
c: Return lead chafed against engine or bracket
Internal short of the common electrode to ground
Bias source in the ECM faulty
s: Check engine light on
EGR cut back, possibly higher NOx

P2AE8.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit High Bank 1
P2AE8.d: P2AE8 reports that, on bank 1's intake air oxygen sensor, the negative current control line sits above its intended level. For the bias on this return to climb towards battery voltage, something must feed it: most often the heater supply sharing the six-pin plug, sometimes condensate in a connector that collects moisture from the intake air. With the reference raised, the ECM loses its anchor for regulating the Nernst cell and discards the oxygen value. Ford handles a VM lead shorted to battery on exhaust probes under P0132, and the Bosch LSU 4.9 sheet lists the trim, pump and return pins side by side, which shows how close these faults sit. No manufacturer documents P2AE8 publicly. P2AE6 is the open fault, P2AE7 the low one, P2AE5 the high fault on the pump lead, P2AF1 bank 2.
c: Return lead shorted to the heater supply
Internal short between heater and cell
s: Check engine light on
EGR reduced, NOx may rise

P2AE9.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit Open Bank 2
P2AE9.d: P2AE9 is the bank 2 version of the open trim circuit: the line from the ECM to the calibration resistor of the second intake air oxygen sensor has no continuity. A separate sensor for bank 2 only makes sense where each cylinder bank draws its charge or EGR through its own path; nobody has published a vehicle that uses P2AE9. The logic follows the exhaust analog P2629, which Ford sets for Bosch probes when the pumping current in air remains too high during a fuel cut-off event; Saab rates the bank 1 twin P2626 as Type B. As the Bosch datasheet explains, the resistor in the plug fixes the sensor's characteristic curve, so a broken trim lead leaves the reading of that bank uncalibrated. A pin pushed back in the connector is a frequent finding. P2AEA/P2AEB are low/high, P2AE0 bank 1.
c: Trim contact pushed back in the plug
Trim lead broken, often near the hot exhaust of bank 2
Calibration resistor in the sensor connector open
s: Check engine light on
EGR on bank 2 reduced or without feedback

P2AEA.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit Low Bank 2
P2AEA.d: P2AEA reports a trim circuit voltage below the permitted range at the bank 2 intake O2 sensor. Likely culprits are a trim wire grounded where the harness passes the second turbocharger, or a damaged resistor inside the sensor connector. Ford's 2012 summary assigns the exhaust analog P2630 to NTK probes for an open or grounded RL lead, a reminder that a low reading need not mean a short. Engines with a separate bank 2 intake sensor are rare and no manufacturer documents P2AEA. If P2AE1 is stored too, look at what both sensors share, such as a ground point or the ECM; alone, P2AEA points to the bank 2 sensor and its own wiring. Meanwhile the EGR on that bank loses its oxygen feedback; the lamp comes on and NOx can rise, but the car usually drives normally. P2AE9 is the open, P2AEB the high fault.
c: Trim lead grounded near the second turbocharger
Calibration resistor in the plug damaged
Fault in a ground or ECM path shared with bank 1
s: Check engine light on
Higher NOx, driveability usually unchanged

P2AEB.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit High Bank 2
P2AEB.d: P2AEB indicates excessive voltage on the trim wire serving the second bank's intake O2 sensor. A short to the heater or another supply wire, or moisture bridging contacts in the plug, can lift the line; Saab's 2010 9-5 test procedure for the comparable exhaust probe expects roughly 2.8 V on its trim terminal at ignition-on, so a reading near battery voltage is a clear sign. Ford's exhaust analog for bank 2 is P2631, used only on NTK probes for a trim lead shorted to battery. For an intake sensor on bank 2 no manufacturer documentation exists; CARB's comprehensive-component rule is the basis. Since the resistor sets the characteristic, a falsified trim value shifts the oxygen reading and with it the EGR calculation of that bank. P2AEA is low, P2AE9 open, P2AE2 bank 1.
c: Trim lead shorted to the heater or another supply
Moisture bridging contacts in the plug
Internal short in the sensor connector module
s: Check engine light on
EGR on bank 2 reduced, NOx may rise

P2AEC.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Circuit Open Bank 2
P2AEC.d: P2AEC means the pumping current wire of the second-bank intake oxygen sensor is interrupted. On a Bosch-style element the ECM uses this lead to push oxygen into or out of the measuring gap until the Nernst cell is balanced; the current needed is the oxygen signal. Ford's intake EGR patent US9441564B2 derives the recirculated share from the change in that current relative to operation without EGR, so an open lead removes the whole basis. For bank 2 exhaust probes Ford uses P2240, found by a lambda that hardly moves under test pulses. No manufacturer has published P2AEC or an engine fitted with a separate bank 2 intake sensor. Look first at wiring routed near hot exhaust parts of that bank. P2AED/P2AEE are low/high, P2AEF the open return, P2AE3 bank 1.
c: Pump current lead broken, often from heat near bank 2 exhaust
Sensor plug loose or not latched
Pump cell inside the sensor open
s: Check engine light on
EGR on bank 2 without feedback or switched off

P2AED.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Circuit Low Bank 2
P2AED.d: P2AED stands for a pumping current circuit on the bank 2 intake oxygen sensor that reads below its limit. A pump lead grounded on the engine or a breakdown inside the pump cell are the usual reasons. On exhaust probes Ford stores such a short for bank 2 under the general low code P0151 rather than a dedicated pump code, and Saab's 9-5 (2010) expects about 2.8 V on the pump terminal at ignition-on with the sensor disconnected. No manufacturer documents P2AED, and an engine using it would need one intake sensor per bank. If bank 1 reports P2AE4 at the same time, a common cause such as the ECM interface is more likely than two damaged leads. The EGR on bank 2 loses its oxygen feedback, so the ECM limits recirculation. P2AEC is the open, P2AEE the high fault, P2AE4 bank 1.
c: Pump current lead grounded on the engine
ECM sensor interface faulty (likely if bank 1 also reports)
s: Check engine light on
EGR on bank 2 limited, possibly higher NOx

P2AEE.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Pumping Current Circuit High Bank 2
P2AEE.d: P2AEE marks the pumping current lead of the bank 2 intake air oxygen sensor as too high. Contact with the heater feed in the shared plug, chafing against a live wire or water that has entered the connector can raise it. On exhaust probes of bank 2, Ford records a battery short of the IP wire as P0152, and CARB obliges the ECM to detect such out-of-range inputs; a code-specific description of P2AEE for the intake side has not been published by any manufacturer. Ford's patent US9441564B2 adds a quirk typical of this sensor: hydrocarbons from crankcase ventilation burn off oxygen at the hot element and distort the reading, but that is a plausibility issue, not an electrical one. Measure the lead against battery voltage before renewing the sensor. P2AED is low, P2AEC open, P2AE5 bank 1.
c: Pump current lead touching the heater feed
Harness chafed against a live wire
s: Check engine light on
EGR on bank 2 reduced, NOx may rise

P2AEF.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit Open Bank 2
P2AEF.d: P2AEF indicates that the return line, or virtual ground, of the bank 2 intake oxygen sensor is open. Both cells of a wide-band element reference this lead, pin 2 (IPN/VM) on the Bosch LSU 4.9, which the ECM biases so current can flow both ways. Ford's 2012 summary describes the bank 2 exhaust analog P2254: if the sensor voltage settles inside a narrow band (1.45-1.55 V with the Bosch CJ125, 1.95-2.05 V with the Conti ATIC42) for 10 s, the return is judged open. Nothing comparable is published for an intake sensor, and no maker documents P2AEF. A second intake sensor exists only where every bank has a separate intake or EGR route. While the return is open, bank 2 EGR loses its feedback; drivers usually see only the lamp. P2AF0/P2AF1 are low/high, P2AEC the open pump lead, P2AE6 bank 1.
c: Internal break of the common electrode
s: Check engine light on
Usually no noticeable change in driveability

P2AF0.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit Low Bank 2
P2AF0.d: P2AF0 is stored when the negative current control circuit of the bank 2 intake oxygen sensor falls below its window. Because the return is meant to sit at a bias of roughly 2.5 V, which Saab's 2010 9-5 lists as the test value on terminal 2 of its exhaust probe, any path to chassis ground pulls it down: insulation worn through at a clip, a crushed connector or an internal short in the sensor. Ford assigns a grounded VM lead on bank 2 exhaust probes to P0151. No manufacturer publishes P2AF0, so the description rests on CARB's range checks and the Bosch pinout. When bank 1 shows P2AE7 as well, suspect a shared harness section first. With the bias gone, the oxygen value of bank 2 is unusable and EGR is cut back. P2AEF is open, P2AF1 high, P2AED the low fault on the pump lead.
c: Return lead worn through at a clip or bracket
Internal short of the sensor to ground
s: Check engine light on
EGR on bank 2 cut back, possibly higher NOx

P2AF1.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit High Bank 2
P2AF1.d: P2AF1 is the high-side fault of the virtual-ground return on the bank 2 intake air oxygen sensor. Lifting this biased line towards supply voltage requires contact with a feed, most often the heater circuit in the same plug, or condensed water inside a connector. Once the return drifts up, the ECM can neither regulate the Nernst cell nor interpret the pump current, so the oxygen share of the bank 2 charge is lost. Ford's 2012 summary files a VM lead shorted to battery on its bank 2 exhaust probes as P0152; an intake sensor equivalent is not documented by any manufacturer, and CARB's comprehensive-component rule is the remaining basis. On a car that sets P2AF1, unplug the sensor and check the return pin against the Bosch pinout before replacing parts. P2AF0 is low, P2AEF open, P2AE8 bank 1.
c: Return lead shorted to the heater circuit
Bias source in the ECM faulty
s: Check engine light on
EGR on bank 2 reduced, NOx may rise

P2AF2.d: P2AF2 reports an open or otherwise faulty control line for a third starter relay. Such a relay appears where cranking is split across several switching stages, for instance on stop-start engines. No manufacturer documents P2AF2 publicly. The nearest documented user of relay C is Stellantis, which calls it Starter Relay 3: on Jeep and RAM stop-start models it is the power control relay that cuts the main battery off from the auxiliary one during an auto-start, yet published bulletins only cover its stuck codes P2AF5 and P2AF6. As an analogy for the circuit test, GM treats its tandem starter pinion relay output (P26E4) as open at 200 kΩ or more between signal and ground, after 40 failures in 50 samples of 50 ms, Type B. Shorts to ground and to voltage are P2AF3 and P2AF4.
c: Broken control wire or unplugged relay connector
Blown fuse or missing supply to the relay coil
Faulty output driver in the control module
s: Stop-start function disabled
Occasional or permanent no-crank
Warning lamp depending on manufacturer

P2AF3.t: Starter Relay C Control Circuit Low
P2AF3.d: P2AF3 sets when the control line of starter relay C is pulled toward ground at a moment the module expects a different level. What that does to the relay depends on the driver type: with ground-side switching the short acts like a permanent on command, with supply-side switching the coil never gets current. No manufacturer publishes a set condition for P2AF3. Stellantis uses relay C as Starter Relay 3, the battery isolation relay of its stop-start Jeep and RAM models, where an energised coil splits the two batteries; only the stuck codes of that relay appear in its bulletins. GM's comparable short-to-ground test on the tandem starter pinion relay (P26E5) looks for 0.5 Ω or less to ground with 8 failures in 10 samples, Type B. Open and short-to-voltage faults are P2AF2 and P2AF4.
c: Control wire chafed through to ground
Faulty output driver in the control module
s: Stop-start inoperative
Relay energised all the time or not at all, depending on circuit design
Possible no-crank

P2AF4.t: Starter Relay C Control Circuit High
P2AF4.d: P2AF4 points to a control wire of starter relay C that carries battery voltage when the module has switched its driver off, typically because it touches a 12 V feed or because the driver leaks. With supply-side switching that can keep the coil energised; with ground-side switching the module can no longer pull the relay in. No manufacturer publishes P2AF4. Relay C is known as Starter Relay 3 at Stellantis, the relay that isolates the auxiliary battery during stop-start restarts, but its published cases concern the stuck codes P2AF5 and P2AF6 only. As a reference, GM checks the tandem starter pinion relay (P26E6) with the driver off for a short toward supply, at 0.5 Ω or less to supply, 40 failures in 50 samples, Type B over two trips. Ground and open faults are P2AF3 and P2AF2.
c: Control wire shorted to a 12 V circuit
Water in the relay socket or power distribution box
s: Stop-start disabled
Relay may stay engaged with ignition off
Warning lamp depending on manufacturer

P2AF5.d: P2AF5 means starter relay C remains in its energised state when it should have dropped out. Stellantis uses it as Starter Relay 3 Stuck On for the power control relay of its dual-battery stop-start system: Jeep Grand Cherokee 2021 to 2025, Wagoneer and Grand Wagoneer 2022 to 2025, RAM 1500 2025, and earlier Pacifica, Durango, Compass, Wrangler and Gladiator. In normal driving the relay is released and closed, so the main battery also charges the auxiliary one; if the PCM still sees a voltage gap between the two above a calibrated limit, it stores P2AF5 and disables stop-start. Owners report no cranking, no start or a dead auto-stop function. Stellantis checks battery terminals, the 150 A fuses and distribution centre connections, and notes false fails with a flat auxiliary battery that a battery disconnect clears.
c: Loose or corroded B+ connection at main or auxiliary battery
Depleted auxiliary battery causing a false fail
Open or poorly seated 150 A fuse or fuse array
s: No crank or no start
Stop-start inoperative, service message for the system
Auxiliary battery not being charged

P2AF6.d: P2AF6 is the reverse fault on relay C: commanded to switch, the relay does not change state. Stellantis names it Starter Relay 3 Stuck Off, on some Wagoneers Dual Starter Relay Stuck. During an auto-start the PCM energises the relay to split the batteries; if it then finds hardly any gap between the auxiliary and the main battery voltages, the relay evidently stayed put, so P2AF6 is stored with MIL and stop-start shuts down. Bulletin 08-138-23 traced it on 2022–2023 Wagoneers to connector D3157A at the power distribution centre that had not clicked fully into place. The RAM 1500 2025 with the 3.0 L Hurricane and stop-start and later Wagoneers got PCM software that lets the permanent code clear. A drained auxiliary battery can also produce false fails.
c: Power distribution centre connector not fully seated
Depleted auxiliary battery causing a false fail
s: Check engine light on
Stop-start disabled
Occasional failure to restart after an auto-stop

P2AF7.d: P2AF7 is the open-circuit or general fault on the control line of a fourth starter relay, relay D. Four separately monitored starter relays only make sense where there is more than one cranking path, for example a pinion relay, a second starter or a battery isolation stage on a stop-start engine. No manufacturer documents P2AF7 publicly, and the Stellantis bulletins that use relay C do not name a relay D. CARB requires engine computers to monitor output components for lost continuity. As a comparison, GM considers its relay A and B outputs open once the circuit looks like 200 kΩ or more toward ground, after 40 failures in 50 samples. Typical causes are a broken wire, a corroded plug, an open coil or a blown supply fuse. P2AF8 and P2AF9 separate the grounded and the live control wire.
c: Broken control wire or corroded connector
Blown fuse feeding the relay coil
s: Auto-stop not available
Intermittent no-crank
Stored code, lamp depending on manufacturer

P2AF8.t: Starter Relay D Control Circuit Low
P2AF8.d: P2AF8 is logged when the control line of starter relay D shows a short to ground. Depending on whether the module switches the coil on its ground side or its supply side, the relay then either sits permanently energised or can no longer be operated. Stellantis lists P2AF8 in STAR case S2108000038 for the 2020–2021 Chrysler Pacifica, among codes such as U0100 and P0627 that arose from spread or bent terminals in the power distribution centre connectors, together with no-start and many electrical complaints; which relay the code covers there is not stated. Beyond that no maker publishes a set condition. For comparison, GM flags 0.5 Ω or less to ground on its starter relay outputs after 8 failures in 10 samples. P2AF7 covers the open line, P2AF9 the short to voltage.
c: Spread or bent terminals in the power distribution centre connector
s: No start or no crank
Several unrelated electrical faults at the same time
Stop-start unavailable

P2AF9.t: Starter Relay D Control Circuit High
P2AF9.d: P2AF9 indicates that the control line of starter relay D sits at supply voltage although the driver is switched off, mostly a short to a 12 V circuit or a leaking driver stage. With ground-side switching the module can then no longer energise the coil, because both coil ends see battery voltage; with supply-side switching the coil may stay energised and keep a cranking path live, which is the more critical case for starter and ring gear. No manufacturer documents P2AF9 publicly. CARB asks for output components to be tested for shorts as well as opens, and GM, as an analogue, treats a path of at most 0.5 Ω toward supply on its starter relay outputs as a short when the driver is off (Type B, 40 of 50). Check the wire for chafing against live circuits, then relay and module output.
c: Control wire chafed against a live circuit
Leaking output driver in the control module
s: Stop-start disabled
Starter may not engage, or in rare cases keep running
Stored code, lamp depending on manufacturer

P2AFA.d: P2AFA describes starter relay D staying engaged although the control module has commanded it to release; the module infers this from a feedback signal, a voltage or current that should have changed. No manufacturer documents P2AFA publicly. The closest published case is relay C at Stellantis, where Starter Relay 3 Stuck On (P2AF5) is detected from the voltage gap between main and auxiliary battery. A relay welded closed in a cranking path can keep the starter spinning after the engine fires, which risks damage to starter and ring gear, whereas a stuck battery isolation relay mainly blocks stop-start and the charging of the second battery. Causes are welded contacts, a live control wire (see P2AF9) or a faulty driver. The opposite stuck fault is P2AFB.
c: Control wire receiving voltage from another circuit
s: Starter keeps turning or grinding after the engine starts
Stop-start disabled
Battery drain while parked

P2AFB.d: P2AFB is set when starter relay D ignores an on command: the module energises it, but the expected change of voltage or current in the switched circuit never appears. No manufacturer documents P2AFB publicly. Stellantis shows on relay C how such a check works. Its Starter Relay 3 Stuck Off (P2AF6) is stored when both battery voltages stay equal during an auto-start although the relay should have separated them, and the published remedies range from a loose connector at the power distribution centre to new PCM software. For relay D, burnt or corroded contacts, a weak coil, low supply voltage and a poor ground are the usual suspects. Drivers may see a no-crank or an auto-stop that stays unavailable. The stuck-on counterpart is P2AFA; circuit faults are P2AF7 to P2AF9.
c: Low supply voltage or poor ground at the relay
Loose connector at the relay or distribution box
s: Engine does not crank on the affected path
Auto-stop permanently unavailable
Stored code, lamp depending on manufacturer

P2AFC.d: P2AFC is the general circuit code for a fourth engine coolant temperature sensor. Engines with split cooling, electric pumps or separate head, block, radiator and heater circuits carry several such sensors, and how they are numbered is up to each maker. No manufacturer documents a set condition for P2AFC publicly; for the 2019 L3B 2.7-litre engine GM instead assigns separate low and high codes to this sensor (P2AFE, P2AFF). Supplier NTN-SNR describes P2AFC in its coolant sensor catalogue as an electrical defect in the circuit of sensor 4. CARB requires coolant temperature inputs to be monitored for broken circuits and for values outside their range. Expect an open line, a loose plug or a failed NTC element; the engine computer then falls back on a substitute value.
c: Open wire or loose connector at sensor 4
Faulty input stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light on
Cooling fans running more than usual on substitute value
Thermal management in default mode

P2AFD.t: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 4 Circuit Range/Performance
P2AFD.d: P2AFD flags a sensor 4 coolant reading that stays inside the electrical limits but makes no sense, for instance a value that disagrees with the engine's other temperature readings once everything has cooled down for hours, or that hardly moves while the engine warms up. CARB requires such rationality checks for coolant temperature inputs used by emission controls. No manufacturer documents the set condition of P2AFD publicly; NTN-SNR names it a deviation or malfunction of the sensor 4 signal. The sister codes for sensors 2 and 3 (P2183, P01E4) work the same way: makers compare the readings after hours of standstill or follow the warm-up curve. Typical causes are a drifting element, corrosion in the plug, an air pocket around the sensor tip or software that needs updating. Hard circuit faults belong to P2AFC, P2AFE and P2AFF.
c: Corrosion adding resistance in the connector
Air pocket at the sensor after coolant service
s: Check engine light, often only after a cold start
Sensor 4 value clearly differing from the others in live data

P2AFE.t: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 4 Circuit Low
P2AFE.d: Coolant sensors are NTC thermistors, so a signal from sensor 4 that is too low stands for an impossibly hot reading, usually a signal wire grounded or a shorted element. GM documents P2AFE for the 2.7 L turbo four (L3B) in its 2019 tables: the configurable temperature input system sets it when the resistance of the sensor 4 channel drops below about 41 Ω, corresponding to 150 °C, for 5 s within a 6 s window; Type B, so the MIL follows on the second trip. In bulletin 21-NA-149 GM names P2AFE as one consequence of engine harness chafing on 2019 to 2021 Silverado and Sierra 1500 trucks, the 2.7 L included. Because a hot reading is first taken at face value, the fans may run at full speed. P2AFF is the opposite fault, P2AFD the plausibility check.
c: Signal wire shorted to ground, for example by harness chafing
Faulty input in the engine control module
s: Check engine light after two trips
Cooling fans running at full speed
Implausibly high coolant temperature in live data

P2AFF.t: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 4 Circuit High
P2AFF.d: P2AFF reports an excessive sensor 4 signal. For an NTC thermistor that means an implausibly cold reading, mostly from an open circuit, an unplugged connector or a line shorted to voltage. GM's 2019 tables for the 2.7 L L3B set P2AFF once the resistance rises above roughly 355 kΩ, equal to −60 °C, for 5 s in a 6 s window, with an engine run time above 10 s among the enabling conditions; Type B with MIL after two trips. Oddly, the same GM table names the radiator coolant sensor in the P2AFF row while assigning P2AFE to coolant sensor 4, but both channels share the same threshold. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 also lists P2AFF for chafed engine harnesses on its 1500 pickups. The engine computer then works with a substitute value. P2AFE is the short-to-ground case.
c: Open signal wire or unplugged connector
s: Check engine light after two trips
Implausibly cold coolant temperature in live data
Thermal management running on a default value

P2B00.d: P2B00 says the engine module could not confirm, with the engine past its cold-start phase, that injection pulses it commanded for cylinder 1 really happened. GM documents the check for its petrol direct-injection engines: the ECM digitises the voltage across both injector wires and looks for the small flux signature the armature leaves when it lifts. If that opening trace is missing too often – 100 failures in 200 samples in the 2018 four-cylinder table, Type B, lamp after two trips – the pulse counts as lost. GM only runs it with at least 5 MPa rail pressure, 5 s engine run time and 10 % fuel in the tank. GM bulletins name P2B00 on the 2.7 L L3B (chafed engine harness) and the 1.2 L LIH (ECM software). The cold-start twin for cylinder 1 is P2B08.
c: Engine harness chafed through to ground (GM L3B – above the camshaft carrier or near the left shock tower)
Armature or needle of the cylinder 1 injector sticking, so no opening signature appears
Outdated ECM calibration (GM service update for the 1.2 L LIH)
High contact resistance at the cylinder 1 injector connector
s: Check engine light after the second faulty trip
Rough running or misfire on cylinder 1 (P0301), sometimes no noticeable symptom
With a harness short, several unrelated codes at once and possibly a no-start

P2B01.d: P2B01 is stored when the ECM keeps missing the opening signature of the cylinder 2 injector in normal running, i.e. it has no proof that fuel was delivered on that cylinder's commanded pulses. GM uses the code on direct-injection petrol engines. The 2019 table for the 2.7 L L3B judges 100 failures out of 380 samples; the 2025 tables reach a verdict sooner, after 50 to 100 samples. Both are Type B with the warning lamp on the second trip. GM's preliminary information PIT5677 to PIT5677E for 2019–2021 Silverado and Sierra 1500 with the L3B lists P2B01 next to P2B00 and P2B03 among dozens of codes that a grounded, chafed engine harness can trigger. A misfire count on cylinder 2 (P0302) helps tell an injector problem from a wiring one; P2B09 is the cold-start version.
c: Engine harness shorted to ground at a chafe point (GM L3B bulletin series PIT5677)
Cylinder 2 injector opening sluggishly or not at all (deposits, worn armature)
Corroded or loose injector 2 connector distorting the feedback voltage
s: Warning lamp after two trips
Uneven idle, possibly misfire on cylinder 2
Together with many other codes and erratic behaviour when the harness is shorted

P2B02.d: P2B02 concerns cylinder 3: in warm operation the ECM did not see the voltage bump that marks the cylinder 3 injector actually opening, often enough to count pulses as not delivered. On GM's 1.2 L LIH three-cylinder, cylinder 3 is the last one, and the 2025 table for that family (cylinders 1–3 only) decides after 50 to 100 samples, Type B. GM service update A202310450 for this engine in the Encore GX (2020–2021) and Trailblazer (2021) (about 22,350 US vehicles) lists P2B02 with P2B00, P2B01 and the cold-start codes; the cure is reprogramming the ECM, not new parts. On four-cylinder engines GM also monitors cylinder 3 with this code. Cold-start faults on the same cylinder are P2B0A.
c: ECM calibration with false detections (GM 1.2 L LIH, service update A202310450)
s: Check engine light, often without any driveability complaint
On a real injector fault rough running on cylinder 3 (P0303)

P2B03.d: With P2B03 the engine module reports that cylinder 4 injection pulses went unconfirmed after warm-up: the coil voltage showed no proof of the armature moving. In GM's lists the code belongs to four-cylinder direct-injection engines – the three-cylinder tables end at P2B02 – and GM's 2025 four-cylinder table needs 50 to 100 samples for a Type B verdict with two trips. GM engineering information PIE0808 (Colorado/Canyon of model years 2023–2024 with 2.7 L) collects P2B03 with the offset-learning limit codes P10A9/P10AA of the same cylinder and the circuit code P02F1; steps are checking the harness near the turbo actuator, unplugging the fuel rail connector for 60 s and a 10-mile test drive. P2B03 also appears in the L3B harness bulletins. Cold start: P2B0B.
c: Harness chafed near the turbo actuator or elsewhere on the engine (GM 2.7 L)
Poor contact in the fuel rail injector connector
s: Lamp on after the second faulty trip
Possibly misfire on cylinder 4 (P0304) or under load
Further injector codes of the same cylinder stored at the same time

P2B04.d: P2B04 extends the warm-running missed-pulse check to cylinder 5, so it only matters on engines with five or more cylinders. No manufacturer documents P2B04 publicly as a monitor of its own. Among GM's 2025 V8 documents it turns up solely inside code lists attached to common calibration maps; the main entries there are the cold-start codes P2B08–P2B0F, while warm small-pulse faults of each cylinder go to GM's own offset-learning codes (P10AB/P10AC for cylinder 5). Where it is used, the idea follows the CARB rule that output parts need a functional check: the controller verifies the injector really opened on command. Which physical cylinder carries number 5 depends on the maker's numbering scheme, so check the engine's layout before pulling parts. Cold-start faults here are P2B0C.
c: Cylinder 5 injector sticking or opening too slowly
Chafed or high-resistance wiring to injector 5
Calibration error in the engine software
s: Engine warning lamp on
Rough running or misfire on cylinder 5 (P0305)

P2B05.d: P2B05 marks missed injection pulses on cylinder 6 outside the cold-start window; on a six-cylinder engine this is the last cylinder in the order of numbers. No manufacturer documents P2B05 publicly as a stand-alone check. GM's 2025 V8 calibration (25OBDG06A/06B) lists it only in the support tables shared by the pulse family. One of them shows why the check is tied to split injection: double or triple pulses are allowed only up to about 3,000–3,600 rpm, depending on mode and injector energy profile, and per GM's 2018 definitions single-pulse data are evaluated below 5,000 rpm. A fault therefore tends to show at low and medium speed. The injector of cylinder 6 is first suspect, wiring second; the cold-start counterpart is P2B0D.
c: Deposits or wear on the cylinder 6 injector hampering small pulses
Contact problem at the injector 6 plug
Injector driver or voltage sensing in the ECM faulty
s: Check engine light
Slight shaking at idle or low speed, misfire on cylinder 6 (P0306)

P2B06.d: P2B06 is the warm-engine pulse check for cylinder 7 and so practically limited to V8 and larger engines. No manufacturer documents P2B06 publicly in its own entry. In GM's 2025 V8 tables the code appears only in the lists of a shared calibration: a pulse counts as missing when the measured opening magnitude stays below a fixed value of 75 across rail pressures from 0.4 to 24 MPa. The warm per-cylinder faults GM actually reports on that V8 are its offset-learning limits P10AF/P10B0 for cylinder 7. CARB treats the injector as an output part whose response to a command must be verified. Typical follow-up is a misfire count on cylinder 7; the cold-start sibling is P2B0E.
c: Cylinder 7 injector with weak or missing armature lift
Wiring to injector 7 damaged by heat or chafing
Rail pressure outside the plausible range, distorting the opening signal
s: Engine light on after two trips
Misfire on cylinder 7 (P0307), rough idle

P2B07.d: P2B07 closes the warm-running row at cylinder 8, and the engine-wide check counting missed pulses over all cylinders is P2B96. No manufacturer documents P2B07 publicly as a separate monitor; GM's 2025 V8 tables mention it only in the code lists of shared calibration tables, while their cylinder 8 warm faults run as P10B1/P10B2. If a scan tool still shows P2B07, the logic matches the GM principle: injector coil voltage is sampled, and a missing opening trace means the pulse was not delivered. On many V8 designs cylinder 8 sits at the rear of a bank, close to the bulkhead and hot exhaust parts, so look at harness heat damage as well as the injector itself. Cold start: P2B0F.
c: Heat-damaged harness section at the rear of the engine
s: Check engine light
Misfire on cylinder 8 (P0308), especially at idle

P2B08.t: Cold Start Cylinder 1 Injection Pulse Performance
P2B08.d: P2B08 is the cold-start version of the cylinder 1 pulse check. While the catalyst is being heated, many direct-injection engines split each injection into two or three small pulses, and CARB requires for 20/50/100 % of model years 2026/2027/2028 that missing split or multiple pulses be detected during the cold-start strategy. CARB also wants faults found in that phase stored under their own codes, which is why P2B08 exists beside P2B00. GM used it earlier: its tables flag cylinder 1 when the opening signature is missing during catalyst warm-up, Type B. For the 1.2 L LIH in the 2020 Encore GX and 2021 Trailblazer, GM bulletin PIP5746 calls it a software anomaly appearing only on cold starts; verify after an overnight soak.
c: Cold-start software anomaly (GM 1.2 L LIH, fixed by ECM reprogramming)
Cylinder 1 injector sluggish when cold, missing the short split pulses
Contact fault in injector 1 wiring that shows mainly when cold
s: Warning lamp, often with the engine running normally once warm
Possibly slightly rough running in the first seconds after a cold start
Code returns only after a long standstill, not on warm restarts

P2B09.t: Cold Start Cylinder 2 Injection Pulse Performance
P2B09.d: P2B09 reports that while the catalyst is being warmed after a cold start the ECM missed the opening trace of injector 2 on too many commanded pulses. CARB defines the window: at least six hours engine-off, ambient at or above −6.7 °C and coolant no more than 15 °C warmer than ambient. GM already ran the test in 2019 on the 2.7 L L3B, setting it after 100 failures in 380 samples, Type B. For 2021 Malibu, Equinox and Terrain (LYX and LFV engines) GM bulletin 20-NA-230 lists P2B08–P2B0B with P2B95 as a software anomaly: vehicles built before 2 December 2020 get the current calibration, then codes are cleared and a cold start is repeated. If P2B09 comes back, normal diagnosis follows; the warm-engine code is P2B01.
c: Cylinder 2 injector not responding to the short cold-start pulses
Wiring or connector problem on injector 2
s: Check engine light after cold starts on two trips
Usually no driveability issue once the engine is warm

P2B0A.t: Cold Start Cylinder 3 Injection Pulse Performance
P2B0A.d: P2B0A stands for missed cold-start pulses on cylinder 3. For the GM 1.2 L LIH with its three cylinders it is the highest cold-start cylinder code, since that engine's 2025 table stops at P2B0A. The same table defines the cold-start window through the summary code P2B95: catalyst below 550 °C, coolant up to 66 °C, 250–3,000 rpm and less than 20 s after start, ending after 500 engine cycles at most – a very short test. Cylinder codes are Type B and decide after 50 to 100 samples. GM bulletin PIP5746 and service update A202310450 (2020–2021 Encore GX, 2021 Trailblazer) both list P2B0A; the cure is ECM reprogramming. Four-cylinder GM engines use the code for their cylinder 3 too. The warm-engine twin is P2B02.
c: ECM software anomaly on the GM 1.2 L LIH (service update A202310450)
Cylinder 3 injector reacting too slowly when cold
s: Lamp on, code stored only after a cold start
Engine runs normally once warm

P2B0B.t: Cold Start Cylinder 4 Injection Pulse Performance
P2B0B.d: P2B0B covers cylinder 4 during the cold-start strategy and in GM's tables belongs to four-cylinder and larger engines. GM's 2025 four-cylinder table sets the window via P2B95 differently from the three-cylinder: catalyst below 400 °C, 450–2,800 rpm, pedal up to 35 % and less than 100 s run time, so the test may continue while pulling away. The cylinder code itself is Type B after 50 to 100 samples. GM bulletin 20-NA-230 (2021 Malibu, Equinox, Terrain) treats P2B0B as a software issue solved by a new calibration; engineering information PIE0808 for the 2023–2024 Colorado and Canyon 2.7 L names it among codes still being investigated, with a harness check and fuel rail connector reseat. Warm-engine faults on this cylinder are P2B03.
c: ECM calibration needing an update (GM bulletin 20-NA-230)
Harness damage or poor contact at the fuel rail connector (GM 2.7 L)
Cylinder 4 injector sluggish at low temperature
s: Warning lamp after cold starts
Possibly slightly uneven running during the first minute

P2B0C.t: Cold Start Cylinder 5 Injection Pulse Performance
P2B0C.d: P2B0C flags cylinder 5 when its injector fails to show an opening signature on the split pulses used to heat the catalyst after a cold start. Publicly it is documented only by GM, in the 2025 V8 table 25OBDG06A, which lists the cold-start codes for all eight cylinders (P2B08–P2B0F): Type B, decision after 50 to 100 samples. For this engine GM's cold-start window is narrow – catalyst below 550 °C, coolant between 6 and 66 °C, 550–2,000 rpm, foot off the pedal (up to 1 %) and less than 100 s after start. No service bulletin naming P2B0C was found. The background is CARB's rule for model years 2026 to 2028 to check missing split pulses in the cold-start phase under separate codes. Warm-engine misses on cylinder 5 would be P2B04.
c: Cylinder 5 injector not lifting on the short cold-start pulses
Injector 5 wiring or connector with a contact fault
ECM calibration issue (check for software updates)
s: Check engine light after two cold-start trips
Usually unremarkable running once warm, maybe a short rough idle when cold

P2B0D.t: Cold Start Cylinder 6 Injection Pulse Performance
P2B0D.d: P2B0D belongs to the cold-start family and points at cylinder 6: while the engine was splitting injections to heat the catalyst, the ECM failed to register the armature-lift voltage signature on too many of that injector's pulses. GM publishes it in the 2025 V8 table 25OBDG06A as Type B with a verdict after 50 to 100 samples. What keeps the test short is its exit list: the cold-start strategy ends once the catalyst reaches 800 °C, barometric pressure drops below 72 kPa or an extended run-time limit expires, and multi-pulse mode stops above 2,350 rpm, beyond 3 % pedal or after 100 s. No bulletin naming P2B0D was found. Warm-engine misses on cylinder 6 are P2B05; misfire on that cylinder is P0306.
c: Cylinder 6 injector opening sluggishly on short pulses when cold (deposits, worn armature)
Corroded connector or chafed wire at injector 6 distorting the feedback voltage
ECM calibration detecting the opening signature unreliably in the cold-start phase
s: Check engine light after two cold starts with the fault
Uneven idle in the first minute after a cold start, later normal

P2B0E.t: Cold Start Cylinder 7 Injection Pulse Performance
P2B0E.d: P2B0E is the cylinder 7 entry of the cold-start pulse check. On engines that fire two or three short injections per cycle while heating the catalyst, the ECM expects each of them to show an opening signature on the injector feedback voltage; for cylinder 7 too many did not. GM's 2025 V8 supporting tables (25OBDG06B) show how the pulse count is chosen: double pulses are permitted up to 3,600 rpm and triple pulses up to 3,000 rpm, depending on the injector energy profile. The summary code P2B95 adds up the share of missed pulses over all cylinders once per trip, whereas P2B0E names the single cylinder (Type B, 50 to 100 samples, table 25OBDG06A). CARB phases this split-pulse check in over model years 2026 to 2028. The warm-running counterpart is P2B06.
c: Cylinder 7 injector not lifting on the very short split pulses (deposits, armature wear)
Enable or command wire of injector 7 damaged, falsifying the measured voltage
ECM software with an overly strict opening-signature evaluation
s: Warning lamp after the second faulty cold start
Slight shaking right after a cold start, often nothing noticeable

P2B0F.t: Cold Start Cylinder 8 Injection Pulse Performance
P2B0F.d: P2B0F closes the cold-start series with cylinder 8, so it only appears on eight-cylinder engines; publicly GM documents it, in table 25OBDG06A for its 2025 V8 family (Type B, two trips, 50 to 100 samples). The ECM reads the voltage across the injector enable and command wires and treats a pulse as undelivered when no opening magnitude shows up during catalyst heating. The same table watches cylinder 8 in other ways too: the warm-running pulse check P2B07 and GM's own codes P10B1 and P10B2, which set when the total small-pulse compensation of that injector falls below or rises above its limit. One enabling condition is that the enrichment for brand-new engines is no longer active. No service bulletin naming P2B0F was found.
c: Needle or armature of the cylinder 8 injector sticking on cold short pulses
Loose or corroded connector at injector 8
Chafed injector harness on the bank carrying cylinder 8
s: Check engine light, frequently without driveability complaints
With a real injector fault, rough cold idle and possibly misfire on cylinder 8 (P0308)

P2B10.t: Cylinder 1 Injection Pulse Offset Not Learned
P2B10.d: P2B10 means the engine control holds no valid learned offset for injector 1 – the correction of the opening time used for very small injection quantities has not been established. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Ford, the one maker with a published monitor for this group, lists only the exceeded-limit codes (P2B11 and siblings) for its Power Stroke diesels. The legal basis is CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (f)(4.2.4)(A)(i): a fuel system feedback that does not begin working within a time chosen by the manufacturer counts as a malfunction. A Bosch patent explains the learn itself: in overrun the activation time of a test injection is raised in small steps from a value too short to open the injector until the crankshaft speed reacts. P2B11 is the partner for a value that was learned but lies out of range.
c: Learn values cleared – after replacing injector 1 or the control unit, or after an adaption reset with a scan tool
Too few coasting phases with fuel cut-off for the learn to run
Injector 1 opening inconsistently, so no stable value is found
s: Warning lamp, otherwise often no noticeable effect
Possibly harder combustion noise at idle on cylinder 1

P2B11.t: Cylinder 1 Injection Pulse Offset Exceeded Learning Limit
P2B11.d: P2B11 says the learned small-quantity correction for injector 1 has drifted beyond what the engine control may apply. Ford documents the code for its 3.0 L and 6.7 L Power Stroke diesels under Zero Fuel Calibration: the PCM fires a tiny test injection, compares the energising time that produced a measurable effect with the target stored for that injector and sets the code when the result is at least 156 µs too short or 254 µs too long. Ford TSB 18-2015 for the 2017 F-Super Duty 6.7 L ties P2B11 and its siblings to a fuel knock at idle caused by wrongly learned injector timing; the fix was resetting the high-pressure side, the minimum fuel mass adaption and the crank sensor learn, then reprogramming the PCM. P2B10 is the not-learned state of the same injector.
c: Incorrectly learned injector values in the PCM (Ford TSB 18-2015, reset and reprogramming)
Injector 1 worn or coked so its opening behaviour has really shifted
Disturbed crankshaft speed signal falsifying the learn result
s: Check engine light
Diesel knock at idle, sometimes together with balance code P0263

P2B12.t: Cylinder 2 Injection Pulse Offset Not Learned
P2B12.d: P2B12 is stored when injector 2's pulse offset has not been learned, so the controller still relies on a default value for the smallest injections. The public record contains no manufacturer using this exact code; the explanation here follows from the title and from the neighbouring monitors.
