Learning of this kind needs repeated coasting phases with fuel cut-off, because only then can the effect of a single test injection be picked up through the crankshaft speed signal, as a Bosch patent on zero-fuel quantity calibration sets out. Engines that rarely coast – long motorway runs, towing – or a recent adaption reset after injector work can therefore leave the learn unfinished. CARB treats feedback that never starts in time as a fault. Once learned but too far off, cylinder 2 reports P2B13 instead.
c: Driving profile without enough fuel cut-off phases (constant load, towing)
Adaption values reset after work on injector 2 or the fuel system
Crankshaft speed signal too noisy to detect the test injection
s: Warning lamp without a clear driveability complaint
Possibly louder combustion on cylinder 2 at low load

P2B13.t: Cylinder 2 Injection Pulse Offset Exceeded Learning Limit
P2B13.d: P2B13 concerns injector 2 on Ford's Power Stroke diesels: its zero-fuel learn value has run past the permitted band. Ford's 2023 OBD summary shows when the learn runs: continuously, typically within about 30 s, with coolant of at least 50 °C, intake air between 0 and 75 °C, fuel of at least 10 °C, at least 10 V supply, almost no pedal (up to 2 %) and rail pressure within 50 bar of its target. A real deviation is not the only trigger, though. Special service message 48877 for 2017–2019 F-Super Duty 6.7 L trucks explains that abnormal steering wheel oscillation can put noise on the crank or cam sensor frequency and set these codes; if they stay away after clearing, no injector work is to be done. Balance code P0266 often appears alongside.
c: Steering wheel oscillation disturbing the crank or cam signal (Ford SSM 48877)
Injector 2 with genuinely shifted opening time due to wear or deposits
Implausible learned values in the PCM
s: Check engine light
Often no running fault; with a worn injector, knocking or rough idle

P2B14.t: Cylinder 3 Injection Pulse Offset Not Learned
P2B14.d: P2B14 tells that no offset has yet been learned for injector 3. No carmaker publishes this code for a specific engine, and the GM and Ford tables checked do not contain it. A GM patent on fast learning of diesel injector corrections shows why such a learn can take long: corrections are kept per injector and per rail pressure level, so a six-cylinder with four pressure levels needs 24 learned cells, each filled only during suitable fuel cut-off phases. The patent's answer is to extrapolate from one measured pressure to the others. Until the cells for cylinder 3 are complete, small pilot injections on that cylinder run without their individual correction. Under CARB (f)(4.2.4)(A)(i) such feedback must start within a set time; P2B15 is the out-of-limit partner.
c: Learn not yet completed for all rail pressure levels of injector 3
Injector 3 or control unit recently replaced without completing the learn
Rail pressure not holding steady enough during the test injection
s: Warning lamp, driving behaviour mostly unchanged
Slightly uneven idle in some cases

P2B15.t: Cylinder 3 Injection Pulse Offset Exceeded Learning Limit
P2B15.d: P2B15 reports that the zero-fuel correction learned for injector 3 has reached Ford's limit. For its 3.0 L six-cylinder diesel Ford adds conditions so the test injection takes place in a defined overrun: engine speed between 890 and 2,400 rpm, a gear from fourth to tenth held without shifting, the torque converter locked and the fuel balance wheel learn already finished. For the 6.7 L V8 engine, TSB 23-2076 from Ford (2020–2022 F-Super Duty) blames incorrect learned values after fuel system repairs and prescribes new PCM and TCM software plus the service function that resets the minimum fuel mass adaption for every cylinder, about 0.7 h of labour. A cylinder 3 balance fault (P0269) or injector performance fault (P02F0) should be ruled out first.
c: Learned values unsuitable after fuel system repairs (Ford TSB 23-2076, software and adaption reset)
Injector 3 drifted mechanically (wear, coking, internal leakage)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Possibly knocking or rough running at idle

P2B16.t: Cylinder 4 Injection Pulse Offset Not Learned
P2B16.d: P2B16 indicates a missing learned pulse offset for injector 4. Public manufacturer material does not tie it to any engine; Ford's published diesel monitor and its bulletins use only the exceeded-limit partner P2B17. Why the learn matters is set out in a Bosch patent: pilot injections are kept as small as possible, and if tolerances mean the injector does not open at all, combustion becomes noticeably louder. A typical trigger for a not-learned state is a fresh start of the learn – after replacing injector 4 or the engine control unit, or after a scan tool reset of the minimum fuel quantity adaption, a step Ford prescribes in TSB 23-2076. Clearing the code before the vehicle has seen suitable driving rarely helps; the conditions for the learn must occur first.
c: Injector 4 or PCM replaced, or adaptions reset, and the learn not yet completed
Learn conditions (warm engine, fuel cut-off) rarely reached
Injector 4 not opening on minimal pulses at all
s: Warning lamp
Louder combustion noise, especially at idle

P2B17.t: Cylinder 4 Injection Pulse Offset Exceeded Learning Limit
P2B17.d: P2B17 is set when injector 4's learned pulse offset goes past the allowed band. For the 6.7 L engine in 2020–2022 F-Super Duty trucks Ford saw this after fuel system work: stored learned values no longer matched the new parts. Special service messages 50646 and 50816 prescribe a relearn rather than a module swap – idle for at least six minutes with coolant at 75 °C or more and exhaust temperature EGT12 at 245 °C (pickups) or EGT13 at 230 °C (chassis cabs), then clear the code and retest; a new PCM is not needed. If P2B17 returns after that, a worn or leaking injector 4, a contribution fault (P0272) or a rail pressure problem remain the candidates. Ford's summary sets the code when the measured energising time misses the target by 156 µs downward or 254 µs upward.
c: Old learn values after fuel system work, cleared by a warm idle relearn (Ford SSM 50646/50816)
Rail pressure deviating from target during the test injection
s: Check engine light shortly after a fuel system repair
Usually unchanged driving behaviour

P2B18.t: Cylinder 5 Injection Pulse Offset Not Learned
P2B18.d: P2B18 means injector 5 has no learned offset. No manufacturer documents this exact code. On petrol direct injection GM covers a related idea with codes of its own: in the 2025 V8 table the ECM adds up the opening magnitude and closing time compensation of each injector, both derived from the feedback voltage, and P10AB or P10AC set for cylinder 5 when that sum is below the minimum or above the maximum limit (Type B, 50 to 100 samples). A not-learned status, by contrast, says that no usable value exists yet, for example after a new injector or control unit or after an adaption reset. For diesel engines CARB (f)(4.2.4)(A)(i) requires detection of feedback that does not start in time. The limit-exceeded twin is P2B19.
c: New injector 5 or control unit without a completed learn
Enabling conditions for the learn not met often enough
Faulty injector 5 wiring preventing a valid measurement
s: Warning lamp
Rarely noticeable; at most slightly uneven low-load running

P2B19.t: Cylinder 5 Injection Pulse Offset Exceeded Learning Limit
P2B19.d: P2B19 flags injector 5: its learned zero-fuel offset exceeds the calibrated limit. Ford's diesel OBD summary groups the code with the other odd numbers from P2B11 to P2B1F under the Zero Fuel Calibration monitor, which it files under fuel system feedback control. One distinct trigger is altitude: special service message 53340 covers 2020–2025 F-Super Duty 6.7 L trucks that store these codes when driven above 762 m (2,500 ft). The first step is the service function that clears the minimum fuel mass adaptions of all cylinders with Ford's FDRS tool; Ford told dealers a permanent fix was planned for the second quarter of 2025. CARB counts a fuel feedback loop that has used up its authority as a fault under (f)(4.2.4)(A)(iii).
c: Learned values skewed by driving above about 760 m (Ford SSM 53340)
PCM software without the later calibration fix
s: Check engine light after mountain or high-plateau driving
Possibly slightly rough idle

P2B1A.t: Cylinder 6 Injection Pulse Offset Not Learned
P2B1A.d: P2B1A reports that the pulse offset for injector 6 has not been learned. Public manufacturer sources do not name this code; on the 3.0 L V6 Power Stroke built by Ford, where cylinder 6 is the last one, Ford's summary lists only the exceeded-limit code P2B1B. CARB explains why such learning exists in diesel engines: since 2010, sections (f)(4.2.2) and (f)(4.2.3) demand checks that the right fuel quantity arrives at the right crank angle, and where no failure could push emissions over the threshold, reaching the control limits serves as the criterion instead. An unlearned offset means that pilot quantities on cylinder 6 rest on nominal data only. Few symptoms beyond the lamp are to be expected; the cure is completing the learn under suitable driving, then checking injector 6 if it never succeeds.
c: Learn for injector 6 still pending after a reset or parts replacement
Mostly short trips with a cold engine, so the learn rarely starts
Injector 6 delivering so erratically that no value can be fixed
s: Warning lamp
Perhaps slightly harder combustion noise at idle

P2B1B.t: Cylinder 6 Injection Pulse Offset Exceeded Learning Limit
P2B1B.d: P2B1B concerns injector 6. On Ford's 3.0 L V6 Power Stroke it is the last cylinder the zero-fuel monitor checks, on the 6.7 L V8 the sixth of eight. The code means the energising time at which injector 6 starts to deliver has moved too far from its stored target, beyond the learn limit. Ford TSB 25-2262 superseded TSB 23-2076 with newer PCM software: driving above 762 m could leave wrong learned values, the engine might idle slightly rough, and Ford states that driveability and durability are not affected. The procedure is reprogramming PCM and TCM and then resetting the minimum fuel mass adaptions. Mechanical causes remain possible, so a code that persists after reflash and reset calls for a contribution check (P0278) and a test of injector 6.
c: PCM software learning wrong values at altitude (Ford TSB 25-2262)
Injector 6 drifted by wear or deposits
Adaptions not reset after an earlier repair
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Slightly rough idle, driveability otherwise normal

P2B1C.t: Cylinder 7 Injection Pulse Offset Not Learned
P2B1C.d: P2B1C says no learned offset exists for injector 7, which only applies to engines with at least seven cylinders, in practice V8s. No manufacturer publishes a monitor for this code. A GM patent on small-quantity adaption shows that a learn can also fail to finish because results do not settle: several test injections during fuel cut-off are compared, and an injector whose consecutive values scatter too much gets a low confidence rating and is marked suspicious instead of passing. A noisy speed signal, an injector with erratic opening or a leak in the high-pressure system can therefore block a valid value. Bosch's zero-fuel calibration patent rests on the same speed-based detection. CARB (f)(4.2.4)(A)(i) asks for missing learning to be flagged; P2B1D is the out-of-range sibling.
c: Test results for injector 7 scattering too much to be accepted
Learn restarted after injector or control unit replacement
Leak in the high-pressure system disturbing the test injection
s: Warning lamp
With an erratic injector, uneven idle or knocking on one cylinder

P2B1D.t: Cylinder 7 Injection Pulse Offset Exceeded Learning Limit
P2B1D.d: P2B1D reports that the correction learned for injector 7 during Ford's zero-fuel calibration has gone beyond its limit; cylinder 7 exists only on the 6.7 L V8. Ford's TSB 25-2412 for 2023–2025 F-Super Duty trucks calls the warning lamp in many such cases incorrect: learned values skewed by operation above 762 m, sometimes with a slightly uneven idle. The repair is a calibration update for PCM and TCM, followed by resetting the minimum fuel mass adaptions. Ford's 2023 summary also shows the neighbouring fuel balancing control, which reports P0281 for cylinder 7 once more than 90 % of its permitted correction is used; both learns act on the same injector, so a balance code next to P2B1D points more towards real injector wear than towards a software issue.
c: Calibration learning wrong values at altitude (Ford TSB 25-2412)
Injector 7 worn, often with balance code P0281 as well
Interference on the crank or cam speed signal
s: Check engine light, sometimes without a real fault
Slightly uneven idle

P2B1E.t: Cylinder 8 Injection Pulse Offset Not Learned
P2B1E.d: P2B1E means injector 8 has not received a learned pulse offset. As the final cylinder in the group it belongs to V8 engines; Ford's 6.7 L V8 would be the obvious candidate, but Ford publishes only the exceeded-limit code P2B1F for it, so no manufacturer source for P2B1E exists. CARB leaves the time allowed for learning to the manufacturer: per (f)(4.2.4)(A)(i) a fault exists when feedback control has not begun within that interval. Because an eight-cylinder needs one learned set per injector and pressure level, GM patented an extrapolation of values to shorten the learning time. In service the code mostly points to a learn that was reset or never had suitable coasting phases; only if it comes back under good conditions do injector 8, its wiring or the crank signal come into question.
c: Learn values reset or injector 8 replaced, learn not finished
Few coasting phases with fuel cut-off in everyday use
Fault in the crank speed signal or the injector 8 wiring
s: Warning lamp
Mostly no noticeable change in running

P2B1F.t: Cylinder 8 Injection Pulse Offset Exceeded Learning Limit
P2B1F.d: P2B1F is the last code of the series: the offset learned for injector 8 has crossed the learning limit. Ford uses it on the 6.7 L V8 Power Stroke. For 2023–2025 F-Super Duty trucks, special service message 53896 links these codes to driving above 762 m; when symptoms are present the minimum fuel mass adaption of all cylinders is reset with FDRS, and if the fault persists, section 303-04 of the workshop manual takes over. The principle behind it is CARB's rule for diesel fuel feedback in (f)(4.2.4)(A)(iii): a fault once the control has used up its adjustment range. A GM patent on small-quantity learning describes the same idea with two codes per cylinder, one for negative and one for positive drift. P2B1E is the not-learned partner.
c: Adaption skewed by high-altitude driving (Ford SSM 53896, reset with FDRS)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Slightly rough idle in some cases, otherwise normal running

P2B20.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P2B20.d: Sensor B is a second temperature sensor in the coolant loop that serves the hybrid or EV power electronics, such as inverter, DC/DC converter or on-board charger; where it sits relative to sensor A is up to the vehicle maker. P2B20 is the undifferentiated circuit code: the controller finds the signal unusable without deciding between low and high. No manufacturer documents P2B20 publicly. Supplier NTN-SNR lists it in its coolant sensor catalogue as an electrical fault in the sensor B circuit, and CARB requires every input of inverter thermal management to be checked for circuit faults. GM's handling of sensor A (P0CF0/P0CF1 in its 2019 HPC2 table) shows the usual NTC logic behind such checks. Without the reading, the system tends to cut inverter and charging power.
c: Loose connector, corroded pins or broken wire in the sensor B circuit
Sensor B element open or shorted internally
Faulty input stage or reference supply in the controlling module
s: Hybrid or EV system warning and stored fault code
Reduced drive or charging power as a precaution
Electronics coolant pump running more often or at higher speed

P2B21.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P2B21.d: Here sensor B delivers a voltage inside its electrical window, yet the temperature it reports does not fit the rest of the vehicle: it may stay flat while the electronics warm up, or disagree with other temperatures after the car has stood for hours. No manufacturer publishes the set condition of P2B21. NTN-SNR names it a deviation or malfunction of the sensor B signal. For sensor A, GM's 2019 HPC2 table runs such a test once per key cycle after a long rest and checks the reading against outside air, transmission fluid and the refrigerant high side (limits 27–28 °C, 8 s in 10 s, Type B as P0CEF). Typical causes are a drifting element, trapped air at the sensor tip or corroded contacts. Hard electrical faults go to P2B22 and P2B23, the A/B comparison to P2D2A.
c: Sensor B element drifted out of its characteristic curve
Air pocket around the sensor after coolant service or a leak
Corroded or loose terminals adding resistance to the signal
Controller calibration that needs an update
s: Hybrid system warning, often only after a cold start
Cooling pump or fan behaviour that does not match conditions
Occasionally limited electric power

P2B22.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P2B22.d: P2B22 says the signal voltage of electronics coolant sensor B has fallen below its valid band. Since these sensors are NTC thermistors, a low voltage would mean an absurdly hot coolant, so the usual explanation is a signal wire touching ground, moisture bridging the connector or an internally shorted element. No manufacturer documents P2B22 publicly; NTN-SNR's catalogue calls it a too-small signal of sensor B. GM's 2019 HPC2 table shows typical numbers for the matching sensor A code P0CF0: below 4 % of the 5 V reference (0.2 V) for 4 s within 5 s, with more than 10.2 V supply, Type B. CARB requires such out-of-range checks on inverter cooling inputs. Because a hot value is taken seriously at first, the pump runs harder and power can be limited. P2B23 is the opposite case.
c: Sensor B signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Water or coolant in the sensor connector
s: Warning lamp or hybrid system message
Electronics coolant pump and fans running at high output
Reduced electric drive or charging power

P2B23.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
P2B23.d: With P2B23 the signal of electronics coolant sensor B climbs close to the reference voltage. For an NTC sensor that reads as extreme cold, which in practice nearly always points to an interruption: an unplugged or water-damaged connector, a broken signal or ground lead, an open element, or more rarely a short to a voltage source. No manufacturer documents P2B23 publicly; NTN-SNR records it as signal too high for sensor B. GM's tables for the sibling sensor A code P0CF1 set above 98 % of the reference (4.9 V) for 4 s in a 5 s window, Type B with MIL after two trips. A real-world hint comes from sensor A on the Chrysler Pacifica Hybrid, where water in an inline connector caused the same kind of high reading. The grounded counterpart is P2B22.
c: Open signal or ground wire, or connector not fully seated
Water intrusion and corroded pins in a connector of the sensor circuit
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
s: Hybrid or EV system warning with MIL
Coolant temperature for sensor B shown at about −40 °C in live data
Power reduced as a precaution

P2B24.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit
P2B24.d: Some electrified drivetrains measure the power electronics coolant at three points, for example ahead of the inverter, behind it and at the charger or DC/DC converter. P2B24 covers the third of these sensors, C, and reports a circuit fault the controller does not classify further. Which component sensor C watches is not standardised and varies by make. No manufacturer documents P2B24 publicly. NTN-SNR lists the code as an electrical fault in the sensor C circuit. CARB treats every input that serves the inverter's thermal management as a monitored component, so an open or shorted line has to be caught. More specific results for the same sensor are P2B26 (low) and P2B27 (high). With one of several readings missing, controllers usually carry on with the remaining sensors but may lower power limits.
c: Connector or wiring fault in the sensor C circuit
Input stage of the evaluating module faulty
s: Stored fault code, possibly with a hybrid system message
Lower charging or drive power in hot conditions

P2B25.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P2B25.d: P2B25 is the plausibility code for the third electronics coolant sensor. The signal is electrically sound, but its value cannot be right, for example because sensor C still reads cold while sensors A and B in the same loop have long warmed up, or because it jumps by an amount the coolant could not follow. No manufacturer publishes a set condition for P2B25. NTN-SNR describes it as a deviation or malfunction of the sensor C signal, and CARB asks for rationality checks on inverter thermal management inputs. GM's after-soak comparison for sensor A (P0CEF) illustrates the method. A sensor C that sits near a component with its own heat, such as the charger, can also mislead the test if the pump has stopped or the loop holds air. Electrical faults of sensor C go to P2B26 and P2B27.
c: Sensor C reading drifted away from the true temperature
Air in the loop or a weak pump leaving sensor C without flow
Corrosion in the sensor C connector
s: Fault code set after a cold start or a long drive
Cooling system reacting inconsistently
Possible limitation of charging power

P2B26.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit Low
P2B26.d: The voltage on the signal line of sensor C, the third coolant sensor in the power electronics loop, is lower than the controller accepts. Low means voltage here, not temperature: on an NTC sensor it corresponds to an implausibly hot value. A pinched or chafed lead touching the body, a short inside the sensor or coolant that has crept into the plug are the usual findings. No manufacturer documents P2B26 publicly; the NTN-SNR catalogue describes a signal of sensor C that is too small. CARB requires inverter cooling inputs to be checked for values outside their range; for sensor A, GM uses 4 % of the reference (0.2 V) as the lower limit. Since the reading suggests overheating, controllers tend to run pump and fans hard and may reduce power. The open or high case is P2B27, a plausible but wrong value P2B25.
c: Sensor C signal lead pinched or chafed against ground
Coolant wicking into the sensor plug
s: Warning lamp or system message
Pump and radiator fan running hard even when cool
Reduced power in some situations

P2B27.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit High
P2B27.d: P2B27 is logged when sensor C in the power electronics coolant loop sends a signal near the top of the reference, which the controller would have to read as deep frost. Far more often than real cold, the reason is a circuit that has opened: a connector that has backed out, a terminal pushed out of its cavity, a broken wire near a moving part or a failed element; shorting to the battery feed is rarer. No manufacturer documents P2B27 publicly; NTN-SNR names an excessive sensor C signal. As an order of magnitude, GM flags its sensor A above 98 % of the reference (P0CF1). CARB counts these sensors as monitored inverter cooling inputs. Unlike the low fault, a cold reading can hide real heat, so the controller usually switches to a substitute value and limits power. P2B26 is the grounded counterpart.
c: Connector backed out, terminal pushed out or wire broken
Signal line shorted to battery voltage
s: Warning lamp and hybrid system message
Sensor C shown far below outside temperature in live data
Limited electric power

P2B28.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump A Performance
P2B28.d: P2B28 means battery coolant pump A is electrically reachable but does not perform as the battery controller expects. VW and Audi store P2B2800 in battery management J840: VW bulletin 93-21-02 (2021 ID.4) traces it to air left when pump V590 did not run during the fill-and-bleed routine, and Audi's 2068363 series (Q4 e-tron 2022–2024, message Electric drive fault) names dry running from residual air, prescribes two bleed runs with the battery at 3–35 °C and replaces V590 only if the entry stays static. FCA lists P2B28 with MIL on the Jeep Wrangler eTorque mild hybrids (2.0 L, 3.6 L) and reflashes the battery pack module or hybrid control processor. Thresholds are not published. The dry-run code is P2B29, a stalled pump P0CFF.
c: Residual air in the battery coolant loop, often after service
Battery or hybrid controller software needing an update
Worn or failing battery coolant pump
Low coolant level from a leak
s: Electric drive fault message or MIL
Reduced drive or charging power
Short or missing engine auto-stops on mild hybrids

P2B29.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump A Overspeed - Dry Run
P2B29.d: A centrifugal pump that suddenly spins faster while drawing less current has lost its liquid: it is churning air. P2B29 reports exactly this for battery coolant pump A. Porsche describes the detection for the 2018 Panamera 4 E-Hybrid, where the pump watches its speed and current draw against the commanded speed and reports a dry run to the battery controller, but files it as P0C4A00 and notes it may take hundreds of miles to appear. Ford uses P2B29 itself: bulletins 20-2221 (2020 Escape HEV built up to 10 June 2020, stored in the BECM), 20-2293 and 20-2345 (hybrid Explorer, Aviator and Police Interceptor Utility) list it among MIL codes cured by reprogramming. Outside such software cases, look for leaks, low level or poor bleeding. P2B28 is the general performance code.
c: Air in the battery coolant loop after service or incomplete bleeding
Leak in a battery cooling line lowering the level
Battery controller software misjudging pump feedback (Ford 2020 hybrids)
s: MIL or hybrid system warning
Pump audibly gurgling or whining
Battery power or charging limited

P2B2A.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump A Overspeed - Dry Run
P2B2A.d: The pump in the low-temperature loop that cools power electronics and often the drive unit reports that it is turning too fast for its load, the sign of air instead of coolant. Mercedes documents P2B2A7A in the powertrain control unit of the 167 series (GLE/GLS) with M177 V8 and 48 V system before model year 2024: the 15 W pump beside the transmission switches to an emergency dry-run mode when the circuit holds air, the cluster shows a yellow coolant message; the fix is vacuum filling and staged venting with XENTRY, plus pumps of the correct part number. Audi logs P2B2A00 in thermal management 00C5 of the 2023–2024 e-tron and Q8 e-tron, with P0CE900 and low coolant, and replaces a damaged hose. Battery pump A has the equivalent P2B29.
c: Air in the low-temperature circuit after filling or a leak
Damaged or leaking coolant hose (Audi e-tron)
Pumps of the wrong part number or position (Mercedes 167)
s: Coolant or drive system warning in the instrument cluster
Churning noise from the affected pump
Reduced drive power until the loop is bled

P2B2B.d: Engines with split cooling, electric pumps or separate head, block, radiator and heater branches can carry five or more coolant sensors; the numbering is the maker's choice. P2B2B is the generic circuit code for number 5, meant for controllers that do not separate low from high. No manufacturer documents a set condition for P2B2B publicly. GM does use a fifth coolant sensor input, for instance in its 2019 tables for the 2.7 L L3B and in its 2025 engine tables, but reports its circuit faults only as P2B2D and P2B2E. NTN-SNR lists P2B2B as an electrical fault in the sensor 5 circuit, and CARB requires coolant temperature inputs to be monitored for opens and for readings outside their range. Typical reasons are a loose plug, a broken lead or a failed NTC element.
c: Loose connector or broken lead at sensor 5
Faulty sensor input in the engine control module
s: MIL with stored code
Cooling fans or thermal management running on default values

P2B2C.t: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 5 Circuit Range/Performance
P2B2C.d: P2B2C concerns a fifth coolant sensor whose signal is electrically valid but does not behave like coolant temperature: after a long cold soak it differs clearly from the other engine temperatures, it barely rises during warm-up although the engine heats normally, or it sits stuck at one value. CARB requires such rationality checks for coolant inputs that emission controls rely on. No manufacturer documents the set condition of P2B2C publicly; GM, which uses a sensor 5 input on the L3B and other engines, publishes only the electrical codes P2B2D and P2B2E for it. NTN-SNR names P2B2C a deviation or malfunction of the sensor 5 signal. Causes include a drifting element, a sensor in a branch with no flow because a valve or pump has failed, or poor contacts. Pure circuit faults are P2B2B, P2B2D and P2B2E.
c: No coolant flow in the sensor's branch (stuck valve, failed pump, air)
s: MIL, often after a cold start
Heater or fan behaviour that does not match engine temperature

P2B2D.t: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 5 Circuit Low
P2B2D.d: A low signal from coolant sensor 5 means its NTC resistance has collapsed, which the engine computer would read as an impossibly hot engine; a grounded signal wire or a shorted element is the usual reason. GM documents P2B2D in its configurable temperature input system: the sensor 5 channel fails when its resistance drops below 47.5 Ω in the 2019 L3B tables or 55 Ω in the 2025 ECM tables, a value tied to roughly 150 °C, for 5 s within a 6 s window; Type B, MIL on the second trip. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 lists P2B2D among the codes that chafed engine harnesses produce on 2019–2021 Silverado and Sierra 1500 trucks. NTN-SNR calls it signal too low for sensor 5. Fans may run at full speed until repair. P2B2E is the reverse fault.
c: Signal wire grounded, for example by a chafed harness
s: MIL after two trips
Radiator fans running constantly at high speed
Other harness-related codes stored at the same time

P2B2E.t: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 5 Circuit High
P2B2E.d: P2B2E is stored when the fifth coolant sensor shows a resistance so high that only an open circuit, an unplugged connector or a line shorted to voltage can explain it; the NTC curve would put the coolant below −60 °C. GM sets it once the channel exceeds about 298 kΩ in the 2019 L3B tables or about 174 kΩ in the 2025 ECM tables, for 5 s within 6 s, after an engine run time above 10 s or with intake air above −20 °C; Type B, MIL after two trips. As with sensor 4, GM's table names the radiator coolant sensor in this row although the low fault is assigned to sensor 5. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 includes P2B2E among the results of chafed engine harnesses on 2019–2021 light-duty pickups. Supplier NTN-SNR's catalogue has it as an excessive sensor 5 signal. The grounded case is P2B2D.
c: Open signal or ground wire, or unplugged connector
Chafed engine harness interrupting the circuit
s: MIL after two trips
Sensor 5 reads around −40 °C or lower in live data
Engine runs on a substitute temperature value

P2B2F.d: Unlike the circuit codes P0480, P0691 and P0692, P2B2F judges the result: radiator fan 1 is commanded on but does not deliver, up to not turning at all. Detection uses fan speed feedback from a PWM or LIN fan module, or the missing temperature drop when the fan should be cooling. FCA lists P2B2F-00 with the MIL for the 2017–2018 Alfa Romeo Giulia and 2018 Stelvio with the 2.0 L turbo four (EC2) in bulletins 18-097-19 and 18-026-20, among other codes fixed by a PCM software update; no thresholds are published. CARB requires output components such as fans to be checked for proper functional response. Beyond software, a seized motor, debris in the blades or a failed fan module are the usual finds. Overheating in traffic and weak A/C at idle follow. The stuck-on case is P2B30.
c: Fan 1 motor worn or seized, or blades blocked by debris
Fan control module or relay not switching the motor
Engine software judging the fan wrongly (FCA 2.0 L)
Poor power feed or ground at the fan
s: MIL
Rising coolant temperature in slow traffic
Weak air conditioning at standstill

P2B30.d: P2B30 states that radiator fan 1 does not follow the command to stop or to change speed, as judged from its speed feedback or module diagnosis. The classic electrical background is a welded relay contact or a fan module that keeps driving the motor. Audi uses the code on the 2022–2024 e-tron GT and RS e-tron GT, stored in thermal management J1024 (address 00C5) as symptom 59328: road dirt and stones entering through the wheel housing liner grille block the fan mechanically, so commanded and reported operation no longer match. Owners notice weak cabin heating or cooling, less drive power or a battery that will not charge fully. Audi fits revised fans, shrouds, liners and protective caps. CARB requires fan outputs to respond correctly to commands. Fan 2 has P2B32, the stuck-off case of fan 1 is P2B2F.
c: Road debris jamming the fan (Audi e-tron GT)
Fan control module ignoring the off command
s: Fan keeps running after switch-off, draining the 12 V battery
Weak cabin heating or cooling on electric vehicles
Grinding noise from the front wheel area

P2B31.d: P2B31 is the functional code for a second radiator fan: its circuits test fine (otherwise P0481, P0693 or P0694 would be set), yet the fan turns too slowly or not at all when commanded. Twin-fan cooling packs usually run fan 2 for high load or A/C demand, so a failure tends to show up only in heat or traffic. No manufacturer documents P2B31 publicly. FCA's 2.0 L Alfa Romeo models use the fan 1 sibling P2B2F with the MIL, and Audi's e-tron GT bulletins show how debris from the wheel housing can jam either of its two fans. CARB requires output components to be monitored for functional response where feasible. A worn motor, blocked blades or a fan module that stays off are the likely causes. Expect rising temperatures under load. Its stuck-on twin is P2B32.
c: Fan 2 motor worn, seized or jammed by debris
Fan module or relay for fan 2 not switching on
Weak supply or ground to fan 2
s: MIL or cooling warning
Temperature climbing at high load or with A/C on

P2B32.d: With P2B32 the controller finds that the second radiator fan keeps operating, or does not change state, against its command. On conventional cars this usually traces back to a relay stuck closed, a fan 2 control line shorted to its active level or a module that has lost control of the motor. Audi documents P2B32 for the RS e-tron GT and the plain e-tron GT of model years 2022 to 2024 as symptom 59342 in thermal management J1024: debris entering via the wheel housing liner blocks the fan, which leads to poor cabin climate, reduced drive power or incomplete charging; the cure is a revised fan, shroud and liner set for the affected side. CARB requires fan outputs to be checked for correct reaction to commands. A fan that never stops may also drain the 12 V battery. P2B31 covers fan 2 doing too little, P2B30 fan 1 stuck on.
c: Debris from the wheel housing jamming fan 2 (Audi e-tron GT)
Fan 2 control line shorted to its active level
s: Fan audible after the vehicle is switched off
Reduced heating, cooling or charging on electric vehicles
Flat 12 V battery after parking

P2B33.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit/Open Bank 1
P2B33.d: P2B33 concerns the second profile actuator on the intake camshaft (camshaft A) of bank 1. Such actuators are solenoids that extend a pin into a groove on a sliding cam sleeve and so move lobes of a different lift under the valves. GM uses the code on the 2.7-litre turbo four L3B (Silverado and Sierra 1500 from 2019), whose sliding cam system has four intake and two exhaust actuators; GM calls this one actuator 2. The ECM energises the output and flags an open circuit when it sees 200 kΩ or more between signal and ground in 4 of 5 samples, with supply above 11 V; MIL on the first trip (Type A). With the sleeve unable to move, lift switching and cylinder deactivation stay locked out. Low and High are P2B34 and P2B35.
c: Connector at the actuator on the camshaft carrier loose, corroded or not latched after valve cover work
Solenoid winding of actuator B open
Control wire broken in the engine harness
Output stage in the engine control module faulty
s: MIL on after the first drive with the fault
No change of intake lift profile, less pull or higher fuel use depending on the stuck profile
Cylinder deactivation no longer engages

P2B34.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit Low Bank 1
P2B34.d: On bank 1 the intake camshaft (A) carries a second shifting solenoid, actuator B, which GM's L3B 2.7-litre four labels actuator 2. P2B34 reports a short to ground on its control line: while the driver is switched on, the ECM measures 0.5 Ω or less from signal to ground and stores the fault after 4 failed out of 5 samples at more than 11 V, lighting the MIL at once (Type A). GM bulletin PIT5677, later 21-NA-149, names P2B34 among the codes a damaged engine harness can produce when it rubs through on the camshaft carrier or near the left shock tower; fuses may blow as well. The cam sleeve then cannot be shifted, so the engine runs without lift change or cylinder deactivation. The open circuit has its own code, P2B33.
c: Engine harness chafed through on the camshaft carrier or near the left shock tower (GM PIT5677)
Shorted turns or short to housing in actuator B
Oil or moisture in the actuator connector creating a path to ground
s: MIL on, often together with other codes from the same harness section
Lift switching and cylinder deactivation unavailable
With a chafed harness also rough running, reduced power or blown fuses

P2B35.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit High Bank 1
P2B35.d: P2B35 is the short-to-voltage counterpart for intake-side actuator B on bank 1, the second of the sleeve-shifting solenoids on camshaft A. In GM's L3B tables (2019 and again 2025) this test runs while the output is off: if the control line shows 0.5 Ω or less towards the controller supply, a short to power is assumed, and 4 hits in 5 samples set a Type A code with the warning lamp on in the same drive. A wire rubbing against a powered circuit in the harness or an internal short in the solenoid are typical reasons. Because the control line no longer behaves as commanded, the cam sleeve cannot be moved reliably and this actuator drops out of lift switching. Open and ground faults are covered by P2B33 and P2B34.
c: Control wire chafed against a powered circuit in the engine harness
Output stage in the engine control module faulty
s: MIL on during the drive in which the fault appears
Intake lift profile no longer changes as commanded
Higher fuel use because cylinder deactivation is blocked

P2B36.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit/Open Bank 2
P2B36.d: P2B36 describes an open control circuit at the second profile actuator of the intake camshaft (camshaft A) on bank 2. A second bank exists only on V or boxer engines. No manufacturer documents this code publicly: the one known user of the series, GM's L3B, is an inline four and only sets the bank 1 code P2B33, where it treats 200 kΩ or more with the driver on as open. V engines with cam-lobe switching do exist, for example Audi's V6 with the valvelift system acting on the intake valves, but their fault codes are not published. CARB requires that output components be checked for circuit continuity and shorts. An open actuator means its cam sleeve cannot change position, so this bank runs without lift switching.
c: Actuator connector on bank 2 unplugged, loose or corroded
Broken control wire between engine module and bank 2
s: Check engine light on
Bank 2 intake stays on one lift profile, possibly uneven running between the banks

P2B37.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit Low Bank 2
P2B37.d: Code P2B37 stands for a control line shorted to ground at intake-side actuator B of bank 2, the second lobe-switching solenoid on camshaft A of the other cylinder bank. Publicly, no maker assigns it to a vehicle. The bank 1 analogue P2B34 is defined by GM for the L3B four-cylinder, which flags a ground short at 0.5 Ω or less while the output is on; a V engine would need a mirror-image test for its second bank. The regulation (13 CCR 1968.2, comprehensive components) demands detection of such short circuits on output components. Typical causes are a harness rubbed through on the cylinder head or water and oil in the connector. With a grounded control line the actuator cannot work reliably, and lift switching on bank 2 is lost.
c: Harness to the bank 2 actuator chafed through on the cylinder head or a bracket
Oil or water in the actuator connector
s: Check engine light on
Lift switching inactive on bank 2, less power or more fuel use

P2B38.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit High Bank 2
P2B38.d: P2B38 marks a short to battery voltage in the control circuit of intake camshaft actuator B on bank 2. No published manufacturer documentation uses it; only the bank 1 version P2B35 is covered, by GM's L3B summary tables, which check with the output off and react to 0.5 Ω or less towards supply. Engines with two banks and stepped valve lift, such as V6 designs with sliding cam pieces on the inlet side, are the only possible carriers. Under the CARB rules for output components, a short to high voltage has to be recognised and reported. A pinched wire touching a live circuit or a solenoid with an internal short are the likely findings; the second bank then keeps its current cam profile instead of switching.
c: Pinched or chafed control wire touching a powered circuit
Faulty output stage in the engine module
s: Check engine light on
Bank 2 intake lift no longer changes, uneven power delivery

P2B39.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit/Open Bank 1
P2B39.d: Camshaft B is the exhaust camshaft, and actuator B is the second shifting solenoid on it. On GM's 2.7-litre L3B the exhaust side has only two such actuators, so this is the last of them; GM's tables call it exhaust camshaft profile actuator 2. P2B39 flags an open control circuit: with the output commanded on, the ECM reads an impedance of at least 200 kΩ to ground. It needs 4 failures in 5 samples, a supply above 11 V and key in crank or run, and it turns the MIL on in the first trip. A loose connector on the camshaft carrier, a broken wire or an open coil are the usual causes. The exhaust sleeve then stays put, so the engine cannot change profile on that side. The intake counterpart is P2B33.
c: Exhaust actuator connector loose or corroded on the camshaft carrier
Broken wire in the engine harness
Open solenoid coil in exhaust actuator B
s: MIL on in the first drive
Exhaust lift profile no longer switches, cylinder deactivation unavailable

P2B3A.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit Low Bank 1
P2B3A.d: P2B3A points to a short to ground in the control line of exhaust-side actuator B on bank 1, i.e. the second pin solenoid that slides the lobe sleeve along camshaft B. GM documents it for the L3B four-cylinder in its 2019 and 2025 OBD tables: driver on, a resistance to ground not above 0.5 Ω, 4 of 5 samples, supply over 11 V, Type A with immediate MIL. Unlike its neighbours, P2B3A is missing from the code list of bulletin PIT5677, which prints P2B39 twice instead, yet the harness chafing over the camshaft carrier described there produces exactly this kind of ground fault. With the exhaust sleeve stuck, the engine loses part of its lift switching. Open and short to power are P2B39 and P2B3B.
c: Engine harness rubbed through where it crosses the camshaft carrier
Shorted turns in exhaust actuator B
Oil wicking into the actuator connector
s: Check engine light on immediately
Exhaust profile and cylinder deactivation no longer switch
With harness damage often further codes and rough running

P2B3B.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit High Bank 1
P2B3B.d: For the second exhaust-camshaft profile actuator on bank 1 (camshaft B, actuator B), P2B3B means its control circuit is shorted to a voltage source. GM's L3B strategy checks this with the driver switched off: a resistance of no more than 0.5 Ω between the line and controller power counts as a fault, and four out of five such readings at a supply above 11 V store a Type A code, MIL on at once. Bulletin 21-NA-149, which covers chafed engine harnesses on 2019–2021 Silverado and Sierra 1500 pickups including the L3B, lists P2B3B among the possible codes. The affected exhaust sleeve can no longer be shifted on command, so the valve lift on that side stays as it is. P2B35 is the same fault on the intake side.
c: Control wire chafed against a live wire in the engine harness
Internal short in exhaust actuator B
s: Check engine light comes on during the drive
Exhaust lift stays in one profile, cylinder deactivation blocked

P2B3C.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit/Open Bank 2
P2B3C.d: This code reports an interrupted control circuit at actuator B on the exhaust camshaft (camshaft B) of bank 2. No vehicle manufacturer is known to use P2B3C in public documents. Its bank 1 twin P2B39 appears in GM's tables for the 2.7-litre L3B, an inline engine without a second bank, where an impedance of 200 kΩ or more with the output on counts as open. Audi's later 2.0 TFSI applies its valvelift system to the exhaust valves, which shows that exhaust lobe switching is in production, but that engine also has a single bank. CARB's requirement for circuit monitoring of output components is the basis. An unplugged connector, a broken lead or an open solenoid coil will stop the exhaust sleeve on bank 2 from moving.
c: Connector of the bank 2 exhaust actuator unplugged or loose
Open coil in exhaust actuator B
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust lift on bank 2 no longer switches

P2B3D.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit Low Bank 2
P2B3D.d: P2B3D: the control wire of the second exhaust-side profile actuator on bank 2 (camshaft B, actuator B) has contact with ground. Publicly documented use by a manufacturer is not known. For comparison, GM's L3B diagnostics define the bank 1 code P2B3A as a ground short of at most 0.5 Ω with the driver on and four failed tests out of five. Because 13 CCR 1968.2 requires engine control outputs to be monitored for such faults, a V engine with exhaust lobe switching on both banks would need this code. Look for chafing at brackets and valve cover edges or for a shorted coil. The exhaust valves on bank 2 then keep their current lift profile, and any function that relies on switching there is unavailable.
c: Wire chafed at a bracket or valve cover edge on bank 2
Shorted coil in exhaust actuator B
Oil or water in the connector
s: Check engine light on
Bank 2 exhaust stays on one lift profile

P2B3E.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Circuit High Bank 2
P2B3E.d: P2B3E is set when the control circuit of exhaust camshaft profile actuator B on bank 2 is shorted to supply voltage. No manufacturer documents the code publicly, so the details come from the analogue: GM's L3B tests the bank 1 counterpart P2B3B while the output is off and treats 0.5 Ω or less towards controller power as a short. CARB's comprehensive component section asks for detection of shorts to high voltage on actuators of this kind. Realistic causes would be insulation damage that brings the wire against a powered line or a solenoid shorted internally. The engine keeps running, but bank 2 loses exhaust lift switching, which costs efficiency. Open and ground faults on the same actuator are P2B3C and P2B3D.
c: Damaged insulation bringing the control wire against a powered line
Solenoid in exhaust actuator B shorted internally
Output stage in the engine module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust lift on bank 2 fixed, slightly higher consumption

P2B3F.t: A Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Bank 1
P2B3F.d: P2B3F is the general circuit code for position sensor B of the intake camshaft actuator (camshaft A) on bank 1, the side with cylinder 1; the NTN-SNR sensor guide also places it on the inlet side. Mercedes-Benz uses this code family on its M176/M177 V8 engines, where each CAMTRONIC lift actuator reports its own sensor signal and sensor B belongs to solenoid 2. No manufacturer documents P2B3F itself publicly. For comparison, GM's 2.7-litre L3B judges the feedback circuits of its sliding-cam actuators (P2C05 ff) as open once it sees 200 kΩ or more between signal and ground in 4 of 5 samples, Type A. Expect a broken wire, a loose plug or a failed sensor; the engine control then locks out the lift change. Low and High faults have their own codes, P2B41 and P2B42.
c: Connector at the actuator loose, corroded or wire broken
Position sensor in the actuator failed (actuator replacement)
Engine harness damaged by heat or chafing
s: Check engine light on
Lift switching or cylinder deactivation unavailable
Slightly higher consumption, sometimes less power

P2B40.t: A Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Range/Performance Bank 1
P2B40.d: With P2B40 the wiring of the intake-side sensor B (camshaft A, bank 1) is electrically fine, but its signal does not fit what the engine module commanded. Engines with switchable cam lift use such feedback to confirm that a pin really moved; GM's L3B, as a comparable case under P2C06, logs a fault when the Hall feedback shows movement although no shift was requested, or when the extending, extended and retracted states do not appear. Mercedes documents the same fault type for bank 2 as P2B44 (CAMTRONIC, M176/M177) and cures it with new software and revised actuators. For P2B40 itself there is no public manufacturer text. A sticking or worn actuator is more likely here than a wiring fault.
c: Actuator pin sluggish or sticking (wear, oil sludge)
Engine control software outdated (Mercedes CAMTRONIC update)
Sensor signal disturbed by loose contact
Cam sleeve or shift groove damaged
s: Check engine light on
Valve-lift change held in a safe position
Uneven running when the system tries to switch

P2B41.t: A Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Low Bank 1
P2B41.d: P2B41 reports a voltage below the permitted window from sensor B, which watches the intake actuator of bank 1. That usually points to a grounded signal line or a sensor that has failed internally. Mercedes describes the matching low fault on the exhaust side (P34BE, sensor of CAMTRONIC solenoid 1) literally as a short to ground, which shows how the family is meant; a public text on P2B41 itself is not known. GM's L3B, used here only as a comparison, sets its low codes on the sliding cam (P2C07) at 0.5 Ω or less between signal and ground while the driver is on, after 4 of 5 samples with more than 11 V supply. Chafed harness sections over the cylinder head deserve the first look. High is P2B42.
c: Signal wire shorted to ground (chafed harness)
s: Check engine light on
Cam lift switching disabled
Possibly further codes from sensors on the same supply

P2B42.t: A Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit High Bank 1
P2B42.d: Here sensor B of the bank 1 intake actuator reports a value stuck above its upper limit. Typical reasons are an open sensor ground, a signal line touching 5 V or battery voltage, or a defective sensor. No manufacturer explains P2B42 publicly; the supplier list from NTN-SNR only names it as the inlet-side sensor B with a signal that is too high. GM measures the related sliding-cam circuits of its L3B (P2C08) for contact with supply voltage while the output is switched off, again at 0.5 Ω and 4 of 5 samples, and lights the MIL on the first trip – a comparison, not a statement about this code. On Mercedes CAMTRONIC engines the sensor sits in the actuator, so a failed sensor means replacing the actuator. Low is P2B41.
c: Sensor ground open or connector corroded
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
s: Check engine light on
Intake lift change locked out
Usually no noticeable change in driving, sometimes reduced power

P2B43.t: A Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Bank 2
P2B43.d: P2B43 covers the wiring of sensor B at the bank 2 intake actuator, i.e. on the cylinder bank without cylinder 1, so it only appears on V or boxer engines. The engine module sees an open line or a signal it cannot accept at all. On Mercedes V8s with CAMTRONIC (M176/M177) the intake actuator of bank 2 is exactly where bulletin LI05.20-P-080192 places the sister fault P2B44; the same bulletin asks technicians to check the harness above the bulkhead for heat damage, which fits a circuit code as well. P2B43 itself is not described in any public manufacturer document. CARB demands that every sensor of a variable valve system is monitored for circuit faults. Bank 1 counterpart: P2B3F.
c: Harness near the bulkhead damaged by heat
s: Check engine light on
Cylinder deactivation or lift change switched off
Possibly limp-home message of the valve-lift system

P2B44.t: A Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Range/Performance Bank 2
P2B44.d: P2B44 is the one code of this group with a public manufacturer use. Mercedes-Benz bulletin LI05.20-P-080192 (January 2026) lists P2B4400 on M176/M177 V8 engines – AMG 63 models, S 580, G 550, GLS 580 – and reads it as an implausible sensor signal from CAMTRONIC solenoid 2 on the intake side of bank 2. The bulletin blames software and hardware: update the engine control unit, fit the newest actuator part numbers and inspect the harness near the windshield for heat damage. Related codes in the same bulletin show the system then going into limp-home mode (P164B). In short, the signal is electrically present but disagrees with the pin movement that was commanded. Bank 1 counterpart: P2B40.
c: Engine control software needs the CAMTRONIC update (Mercedes)
Actuator of an older part number (Mercedes replaces it)
s: Check engine light on
CAMTRONIC limp-home mode, cylinder deactivation off
Higher fuel consumption at part load

P2B45.t: A Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Low Bank 2
P2B45.d: P2B45 means the bank 2 intake actuator's position sensor B delivers an unusually low voltage – on bank 2, which a V engine places opposite cylinder 1. A grounded signal wire is the classic cause; an internally shorted sensor or a missing supply gives the same picture. Mercedes words the low faults of this family on CAMTRONIC V8s as a ground short (P34BE and P34C2, exhaust sensor A), though P2B45 itself appears in no public manufacturer text. Because the Mercedes bulletin on these engines found heat-damaged harnesses behind the engine, that area belongs on the check list. CARB requires out-of-range low signals of such sensors to be detected. Circuit High on the same bank is P2B46.
c: Signal wire grounded through chafing or heat damage
s: Check engine light on
Lift change on bank 2 stops working
Possibly limp-home message

P2B46.t: A Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit High Bank 2
P2B46.d: P2B46 flags a signal from position sensor B on the bank 2 intake camshaft actuator that is stuck too high. Most often the sensor has lost its ground, the signal line has contact with a supply line, or the sensor element itself has failed. There is no public manufacturer description of P2B46; NTN-SNR lists it simply as inlet sensor B, second bank, signal too high. On engines like the Mercedes M176/M177, whose CAMTRONIC actuators have the sensor built in, replacing the actuator is the usual repair once the wiring checks out. With the feedback lost, the engine control keeps the cam lift in its default position, so drivers mostly notice the warning lamp and a little more fuel use. Bank 1 counterpart: P2B42.
c: Signal line in contact with a supply line
Sensor element in the actuator failed
s: Check engine light on
Cam lift held in default position on bank 2
Slightly increased fuel consumption

P2B47.t: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Bank 1
P2B47.d: P2B47 moves the circuit fault to the exhaust side: it concerns position sensor B on the actuator of camshaft B, bank 1. NTN-SNR's supplier code list reads camshaft B as the outlet camshaft. Mercedes-Benz, in its CAMTRONIC bulletin for the M176/M177 V8, documents exhaust-side feedback faults only for sensor A of solenoid 1 (P34BD, P34BE); a second exhaust sensor and P2B47 itself are not documented publicly by any manufacturer. The comparable GM L3B judges an exhaust sliding-cam feedback circuit (P2C12) as open from 200 kΩ upward, 4 of 5 samples, MIL on the first trip. Look for an unplugged or corroded connector and broken wires first. The intake-side counterpart on bank 1 is P2B3F.
c: Connector unplugged or corroded, wire broken
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust cam lift change unavailable
Little change in driving behaviour

P2B48.t: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Range/Performance Bank 1
P2B48.d: P2B48 is the plausibility code for sensor B at the bank 1 exhaust actuator (camshaft B): the circuit works, yet the reported position contradicts the command. Mercedes handles this fault type on its CAMTRONIC V8s for the exhaust sensor of solenoid 1 as P34BD and fixes it through software and newer actuators; P2B48 itself is not found in any public manufacturer source. GM's L3B gives an idea of the logic under P2C13: the exhaust Hall feedback must pass through three states per shift, and a signal without a shift command also counts as an error. Carbon or sludge on the actuator pin, worn parts or a damaged shift groove can cause the mismatch. Bank 2 counterpart: P2B4C.
c: Actuator pin sticking from deposits or wear
Shift groove or cam sleeve damaged
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust lift switching held in one position
Possibly rough running during shift attempts

P2B49.t: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Low Bank 1
P2B49.d: With P2B49 the module reads too low a signal from position sensor B at the exhaust camshaft actuator of bank 1. A short between signal line and ground, a sensor with an internal short or a missing feed are the usual suspects. The nearest public manufacturer reference is P34BE on the Mercedes M176/M177: the sensor of exhaust solenoid 1 for CAMTRONIC, bank 1, described as shorted to ground. For P2B49 itself no manufacturer document is available. GM sets the comparable exhaust code of its L3B (P2C14) when the driver is on and the circuit shows at most 0.5 Ω to ground. Chafe points on the harness running along the cylinder head cover are worth checking first. Exhaust bank 1 high fault: P2B4A.
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust cam lift change switched off
Occasionally further sensor codes

P2B4A.t: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit High Bank 1
P2B4A.d: P2B4A says the position sensor B signal of the bank 1 exhaust camshaft actuator is above its limit. An interrupted sensor ground, a short to a voltage source or a failed sensor are typical. No manufacturer describes P2B4A publicly, and the Mercedes CAMTRONIC bulletin does not include any high fault of this family. As a comparison only, GM checks the exhaust sliding-cam circuits of the 2.7-litre L3B for an unwanted link to supply voltage with the output switched off (P2C15, 0.5 Ω, 4 of 5 samples, Type A). The engine module keeps the exhaust lift system in its safe position until the fault is gone. CARB counts such sensors among the comprehensive components that need circuit monitoring. Exhaust low fault on bank 1: P2B49.
c: Sensor ground interrupted or connector corroded
Signal line shorted to a voltage source
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust lift system kept in safe position
Usually unchanged driveability

P2B4B.t: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Bank 2
P2B4B.d: P2B4B is set when the circuit feeding the second position sensor (B) of the exhaust actuator on bank 2 is open or otherwise unusable. Bank 2 exists only on engines with two cylinder rows, such as the Mercedes M176/M177 V8, whose CAMTRONIC bulletin lists exhaust feedback faults on bank 2 for sensor A (P34C1, P34C2) but not for sensor B. No manufacturer has published a description of P2B4B, so the diagnosis follows the general pattern: check plug, wires and sensor supply, then the sensor in the actuator. Mercedes also found heat damage on the harness above the bulkhead on these engines. CARB expects electronic parts of valve-lift systems to be monitored for circuit faults. Bank 1 exhaust counterpart: P2B47.
c: Plug or wires at the actuator open
Heat damage to the harness above the bulkhead
Sensor in the exhaust actuator failed
s: Check engine light on
Cylinder deactivation or exhaust lift change unavailable
Somewhat higher consumption

P2B4C.t: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Range/Performance Bank 2
P2B4C.d: P2B4C stands for an implausible but electrically valid signal from the B sensor watching the exhaust actuator of bank 2. It is the exhaust-side mirror of P2B44, which Mercedes-Benz documents on CAMTRONIC V8s (M176/M177) for intake solenoid 2 of bank 2; for P2B4C itself there is no public manufacturer text. In the same bulletin Mercedes reports the exhaust sensor of solenoid 1 on bank 2 as P34C1 and points to engine software and revised actuator part numbers. CARB names a lift-mechanism pin that never arrives where it should as a failure the OBD system must find, which is what this feedback check exists for. Sticking pins and deposits are therefore the main suspects. Bank 1 counterpart: P2B48.
c: Intermittent contact in the sensor signal
s: Check engine light on
Lift system or cylinder deactivation in limp-home
Higher part-load consumption

P2B4D.t: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Low Bank 2
P2B4D.d: A too-low signal from position sensor B at the bank 2 exhaust camshaft actuator sets P2B4D. In practice this is a signal wire touching ground, a shorted sensor, or a sensor that gets no supply. The closest documented case is P34C2 on Mercedes M176/M177 V8s, where solenoid 1 on the bank 2 exhaust side reports a sensor short to ground; P2B4D is not described by any manufacturer in public. That bulletin also points at heat-damaged wiring near the windshield, so inspect the harness on the bank 2 side behind the engine. Repairs range from a wire splice to a new actuator with integrated sensor. CARB requires low-signal faults of such sensors to be recognised. Exhaust high fault on bank 2: P2B4E.
c: Signal wire touching ground (heat or chafe damage)
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust lift change on bank 2 out of action
Possibly limp-home message of the lift system

P2B4E.t: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit High Bank 2
P2B4E.d: P2B4E closes the group: the exhaust-side position sensor B of bank 2 sends a signal above its upper limit. Usually the sensor ground is open, the signal line is shorted to a supply, or the sensor is faulty. No manufacturer explains P2B4E publicly; the NTN-SNR code list only gives outlet sensor B, second bank, signal too high. In the CAMTRONIC family Mercedes uses on the M176/M177, the sensor is part of the actuator, so a confirmed sensor fault means a new actuator. Until then the engine runs on the fixed default cam profile on that bank, which mostly shows as a lit warning lamp and slightly more fuel use. CARB requires such circuit faults to be detected. Bank 1 counterpart: P2B4A.
c: Signal line shorted to a supply
s: Check engine light on
Bank 2 runs on the default cam profile
Slightly higher fuel use

P2B4F.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Performance/Stuck Off Bank 1
P2B4F.d: P2B4F covers the second profile actuator (B) on the intake camshaft of bank 1, a solenoid whose pin engages a groove on a sliding cam sleeve to change valve lift. Despite the title wording, GM's L3B 2.7-litre four (19OBDG03D, again in 25OBDG03B) uses it for the reverse case: a Hall element reports three pin states (extending 55, extended 45, retracted 68), and if the signal falls below 55 although no shift was commanded, the pin has fired on its own. Four wrong readings in five cylinder events with the engine running and more than 11 V set a Type A fault, MIL at once. The supplier NTN-SNR lists the code as actuator never active. A pin stuck out on the same actuator is P2B53; wiring faults sit under P2B33–P2B35.
c: Actuator B pin extends without a command (sticking solenoid, weak return spring)
Hall feedback of the actuator delivers wrong pin states
Shift groove on the cam sleeve worn so the pin is dragged out
s: MIL on in the first drive with the fault
Intake lift switching locked out, less pull or higher consumption
Cylinder deactivation no longer available

P2B50.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Performance/Stuck Off Bank 2
P2B50.d: Bank 2 of a V-engine has its own intake camshaft (A), and P2B50 reports that the second profile actuator on it does not do its job or stays in the off position. Mercedes-Benz documents the code for the M176 and M177 V8 with CAMTRONIC (for example AMG C63, GLC63 and S 580 models): in topic LI05.20-P-080192 of January 2026, solenoid 2 for the intake side of bank 2 is described as faulty or jammed off, with fault type 07 for a mechanical and 09 for a component fault. Mercedes recommends an engine ECU software update, newer actuator part numbers and an inspection of the harness near the bulkhead, where heat can damage it. The intake lift then cannot switch on that bank. Bank 1 counterpart: P2B4F; stuck on: P2B54.
c: CAMTRONIC actuator of an older part number, superseded by Mercedes
Engine control software that needs the available update
Harness heat-damaged above the bulkhead near the windscreen
Actuator pin mechanically jammed in the retracted position
s: Check engine light on
CAMTRONIC lift switching inactive on bank 2, possibly limp-home mode of the system
Slightly uneven running or higher fuel use at part load

P2B51.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Performance/Stuck Off Bank 1
P2B51.d: On the exhaust camshaft (B) of bank 1 the second sliding-cam solenoid is monitored by P2B51. GM applies it to the L3B 2.7-litre turbo four, whose exhaust side carries two such actuators. Its table entry mirrors the intake check: the ECM tracks the Hall feedback of the pin and treats a drop below the extending level of 55 without any shift request as an unintended firing. Four mismatches within five cylinder-event readings, engine running and supply above 11 V, store the code as Type A. In practice a pin that fires by itself can push the exhaust sleeve into the wrong profile, so exhaust lift and cylinder deactivation are blocked. NTN-SNR names it actuator never active. Intake equivalent: P2B4F; circuit faults: P2B39–P2B3B.
c: Exhaust actuator B pin releases without command, often heat-related sticking
Faulty Hall feedback in the actuator or its signal line
Sludge or debris at the actuator bore hindering the pin
s: MIL on immediately (Type A)
Exhaust lift profile no longer changes, turbo response may feel different
Cylinder deactivation disabled

P2B52.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Performance/Stuck Off Bank 2
P2B52.d: P2B52 is the bank 2 version for actuator B on the exhaust camshaft (B): the second shifting solenoid either does not move its cam sleeve or remains in the off position. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. NTN-SNR lists it in its camshaft sensor guide as actuator never active, and CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(13) requires valve control systems to be checked for failure to reach the commanded state. The closest documented analogue is Mercedes P005C on the M176/M177 V8, where exhaust solenoid 1 of bank 2 is reported faulty or jammed off (LI05.20-P-080192). Expect the exhaust lift profile to stay fixed on that bank. Bank 1 is P2B51, stuck on is P2B56, wiring faults are P2B3C–P2B3E.
c: Actuator B of the bank 2 exhaust camshaft does not extend its pin
Poor contact at the actuator connector or heat-damaged harness
Engine control calibration that judges the shift too strictly
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust lift switching inactive on bank 2
Possibly slightly lower power in the upper speed range

P2B53.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Stuck On Bank 1
P2B53.d: P2B53 means actuator B of the bank 1 intake camshaft is caught in the engaged position. GM documents it for the L3B 2.7-litre four as pin stuck: after a shift the Hall feedback must climb back above the retracted level of 68; if extending (55) or extended (45) was seen but the pin never reports home before the engine cycle ends, the ECM logs a stuck-out pin. One failure in five samples is enough, Type A, MIL on the first trip. GM bulletins PIT5677 and 21-NA-149 also list P2B53 among codes a chafed engine harness on 2019–2022 Silverado and Sierra can trigger. A pin left in the groove can hold the sleeve or wear it, so profile switching is disabled. Opposite fault: P2B4F.
c: Actuator pin does not retract (sticking plunger, varnish, weak spring)
Engine harness chafed on the camshaft carrier (GM PIT5677 / 21-NA-149)
Hall feedback does not report the home position although the pin is back
s: MIL on in the first drive
Lift switching and cylinder deactivation locked out
With a damaged harness also other codes, rough running or blown fuses
Possible ticking from the valve cover if the pin rubs in the groove

P2B54.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Stuck On Bank 2
P2B54.d: With P2B54 actuator B, the second shifter on the bank 2 intake camshaft, is reported as stuck on, meaning its pin or valve stays engaged after the command to release. A public manufacturer description of this exact code was not found. GM's L3B tables show how the bank 1 twin, P2B53, is judged: the Hall feedback must return to the retracted level within the engine cycle, otherwise a stuck pin is assumed. NTN-SNR describes P2B54 as component permanently active, and CARB requires valve control faults of this kind to be detected under (e)(13). On a V-engine only one bank would then run the wrong intake lift, which can cause uneven running between banks. Bank 1: P2B53; stuck off: P2B50.
c: Actuator B on the bank 2 intake camshaft stays engaged (sticking plunger)
Control line shorted so the solenoid remains energised
Position feedback of the actuator stuck at the engaged value
s: Check engine light on
Uneven running between the banks, especially at part load
Profile switching disabled by the engine control

P2B55.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Stuck On Bank 1
P2B55.d: P2B55 flags actuator B on the bank 1 exhaust camshaft as stuck on. Even GM, whose L3B four has a second exhaust actuator and uses P2B51 for it, lists no stuck-on code for that actuator in its 2019 and 2025 tables; no other maker documents P2B55 publicly either. The fault logic can be inferred from the intake twin P2B53: a pin that does not report back to its rest position after shifting. NTN-SNR lists the code as component permanently active, and CARB (e)(13) covers it as a valve control fault. A sleeve held in one exhaust profile changes scavenging and turbo response, and the engine control normally locks out further switching. Related: P2B51 (stuck off), P2B39–P2B3B (circuit).
c: Pin of exhaust actuator B does not retract, often from heat and deposits
Solenoid stays powered because of a wiring or driver fault
Damaged shift groove holds the pin
s: Check engine light on
Changed turbo response or reduced power
Possible metallic noise from the camshaft area

P2B56.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator B Control Stuck On Bank 2
P2B56.d: P2B56 completes the series: on bank 2 the second actuator of the exhaust camshaft remains engaged after it should have released. No manufacturer publishes a description of this exact code. NTN-SNR lists it as permanently active; CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(13) is the legal basis for monitoring such valve control functions. Mercedes uses the stuck-off counterparts on the exhaust side of its M176/M177 V8 (P005A/P005C), which shows that V8 sliding-cam systems monitor each bank separately. Typical reasons are a sticking solenoid, a worn shift groove or low oil quality that hinders the pin. One bank then keeps the wrong exhaust lift. Bank 1 equivalent: P2B55; stuck off: P2B52.
c: Solenoid of exhaust actuator B on bank 2 sticking in the engaged state
Aged or wrong engine oil slowing the pin
Worn shift groove on the exhaust cam sleeve
s: Check engine light on
Bank-to-bank imbalance felt as rough idle or part-load vibration
Lift switching locked by the engine control

P2B57.t: Low Engine Oil Pressure - Camshaft Control Disabled
P2B57.d: P2B57 is a status code rather than a circuit fault: the engine control has measured or calculated oil pressure too low for safe camshaft adjustment and has therefore switched the cam control off. Hydraulic cam phasers and oil-operated lift switching need a minimum pressure to hold position; below it the parts would rattle or drift. No manufacturer documents the code publicly; NTN-SNR lists it as camshaft timing deactivated because of low oil pressure, and CARB (e)(13) asks for monitoring of valve timing systems. Low oil level, wrong viscosity, a clogged pickup or a weak oil pump are the usual reasons, and a faulty pressure sensor can mimic them. Check pressure first: P0520–P0524 and P06DD/P06DE point to the sensor or pump control.
c: Oil level too low or oil of the wrong viscosity
Worn oil pump, faulty pump control or clogged pickup screen
Oil pressure sensor reading too low although pressure is fine
Worn bearings causing internal oil leakage at high temperature
s: Check engine light on, often together with an oil pressure warning
Camshaft adjustment inactive, weaker low-end torque and rough idle
Rattle from the cam phasers at start or when hot

P2B58.t: Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Motor Current High
P2B58.d: P2B58 reports that the electric motor driving the engine coolant flow control valve draws too much current. GM documents the check for its 3.0-litre inline-six Duramax diesel: in the 2025 table 25OBDG04B the driver stage flags a current above 5.5 A, and 80 failures in 100 samples taken every 12.5 ms set a Type B fault, so the MIL follows on the second trip. Enabling needs more than 11 V on the powertrain relay and an engine that is not cranking. A seized rotary valve, debris in the housing or a motor with shorted windings are typical reasons. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 lists P2B58 for LM2 trucks with a chafed engine harness. Heating and warm-up may suffer while the valve is stuck.
c: Rotary valve stiff or seized from deposits or debris in the housing
Chafed engine harness on GM LM2 (bulletin 21-NA-149)
s: MIL on after the second drive with the fault
Slow warm-up or weak cabin heat
Fans may run more often as a precaution

P2B59.t: Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Control Circuit/Open
P2B59.d: P2B59 is the open-circuit check for the drive of the coolant flow control valve. In GM's 25OBDG04B (3.0 L Duramax) the driver reports a load resistance above 200 kΩ, meaning one of the motor wires is disconnected; 80 of 100 samples set a Type B fault. Hyundai and Kia also use the code on the 2.5-litre Theta III engines with an integrated thermal management module (ITM): bulletins 26-EM-009H (Sonata, Tucson) and Kia TSB ENG 264 (K5, Sorento, Sportage, 2024–2025) describe P2B59F0 caused by an ECU logic error and fix it with new software, noting no driveability effect. Otherwise check the connector, the harness and the valve motor. Shorts to ground and to supply are reported separately as P2B5A and P2B5B.
c: ECU judgement logic on Hyundai/Kia 2.5 Theta III (software update 26-EM-009H / ENG 264)
Valve connector unplugged, loose or with a pushed-out terminal
Motor wire broken in the harness or valve motor winding open
s: MIL on, often without any noticeable driveability change
Valve stays in its default position, slower warm-up possible

P2B5A.t: Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Control Circuit Low
P2B5A.d: P2B5A stands for a short to ground in the control wiring of the coolant flow control valve motor. GM's 2025 table for the 3.0-litre Duramax describes the detection: the driver sees more than 9 A flowing, which it interprets as one motor wire touching ground, and 80 out of 100 samples at 12.5 ms set a two-trip Type B fault once relay voltage exceeds 11 V. Unlike P2B58, where the motor itself draws too much current, the cause here is normally insulation damage in the harness, a pinched wire near the valve or water in the connector. The valve stays in its last or default position, so coolant distribution becomes fixed. Short to power is P2B5B, open circuit P2B59.
c: Motor wire chafed or pinched against ground
Coolant or water in the valve connector
Internal short to housing in the valve motor
s: MIL on after two drives
Engine temperature control fixed, slower warm-up or higher running temperature

P2B5B.t: Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Control Circuit High
P2B5B.d: P2B5B covers a short to battery voltage on the motor leads of the coolant flow control valve. GM's diesel table 25OBDG04B evaluates it through the driver stage as well: a current above 9 A with a lead tied to supply counts as a failure, and the usual 80-of-100 rule with 12.5 ms sampling stores a Type B code. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 names P2B5B in its LM2 harness-chafing condition together with blown fuses and rough running, which points at wiring rubbing on powered circuits rather than at the valve. Because the driver shuts down to protect itself, the valve no longer reacts and warm-up control is lost. Ground short and open are P2B5A and P2B59.
c: Motor lead chafed against a powered circuit (GM LM2, 21-NA-149)
Corroded or wet connector bridging to supply
Driver stage in the engine control module faulty
s: MIL on after two drives, possibly further codes from the same harness
Blown fuses or rough running if the harness is chafed
Weak heater output during warm-up

P2B5C.t: Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Supply Circuit Low
P2B5C.d: With P2B5C the supply voltage reaching the driver of the coolant flow control valve motor is too low. GM monitors this on the 3.0-litre Duramax (25OBDG04B): if the motor driver sees less than 6 V while the powertrain relay delivers more than 11 V, the difference points at the feed path, and a Type B fault follows after 80 hits in 100 samples. Typical causes are a blown or loose fuse, a corroded relay contact or a damaged supply wire; 21-NA-149 includes P2B5C among the LM2 codes linked to a chafed harness. Without enough voltage the motor cannot position the valve, so engine temperature control falls back to a default. A weak battery alone rarely sets it, because the relay check would fail as well.
c: Blown or loose fuse, corroded relay contact in the valve feed
Supply wire damaged or chafed in the engine harness
High resistance at a ground or splice of the feed circuit
s: MIL on after two drives
Valve does not move, temperature control in fallback mode

P2B5D.t: Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Position Sensor Circuit
P2B5D.d: P2B5D is the general circuit code for the position sensor of the coolant flow control valve, the feedback that tells the engine computer how far the rotary valve has turned. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. GM's 3.0-litre Duramax, whose valve reports its position digitally over a SENT link, covers the sensor through the low and high codes P2B5E and P2B5F and a separate communication check instead.
