A system using P2B5D would flag an implausible or missing signal that fits neither low nor high. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15) requires such input circuits to be checked for continuity. With no valid position the engine computer cannot regulate coolant flow and usually parks the valve in a safe position.
c: Loose or corroded terminals at the valve connector
Signal, reference or ground wire of the sensor interrupted
Position sensor inside the valve faulty
s: Check engine light on
Coolant flow control in fallback, warm-up or heating behaviour changed

P2B5E.t: Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Position Sensor Circuit Low
P2B5E.d: P2B5E reports a position sensor reading below its valid window. On GM's 3.0-litre Duramax the valve sends its angle as a raw SENT value in percent of 5 V; anything under 2 % counts as too low, and 80 failures in 100 samples at 6.25 ms set a Type B fault, provided there is no SENT communication fault and the relay supplies more than 11 V. A broken 5 V reference, a sensor ground issue inside the valve or a damaged signal wire can produce such a value. GM includes P2B5E in the LM2 chafed-harness condition of bulletin 21-NA-149. The engine computer loses the actual position and stops closed-loop control of coolant flow. High reading: P2B5F; plausibility: P2B60.
c: 5 V reference or signal wire interrupted or shorted to ground
Chafed engine harness on GM LM2 (21-NA-149)
Position sensor in the valve faulty
s: MIL on after two drives
Coolant flow no longer regulated, warm-up slower

P2B5F.t: Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Position Sensor Circuit High
P2B5F.d: P2B5F is set when the valve position signal sits above the top of its window. The 2025 Duramax calibration (3.0 L, 25OBDG04B) treats a SENT raw value over 98 % of 5 V as implausibly high and stores a two-trip Type B code after 80 of 100 readings, sampled every 6.25 ms while the SENT link itself is healthy. A signal shorted to the 5 V reference or to supply, a moisture path in the connector or an internal sensor fault are the usual explanations; GM's 21-NA-149 lists P2B5F with the LM2 harness-chafing codes as well. Coolant flow control switches to a fallback, which can show as slow warm-up or weak cabin heat. Low counterpart: P2B5E.
c: Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage
Moisture or corrosion bridging contacts in the valve connector
Position sensor in the valve faulty
s: MIL on after two drives
Slow warm-up or weak cabin heat

P2B60.t: Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2B60.d: P2B60 checks whether the valve actually goes where it is told. On GM's 3.0 L Duramax the code sets when the gap between desired and measured position exceeds 12 % in 160 of 200 samples, only with a steady command, closed-loop control active and no coolant or outside temperature sensor fault (Type B). For LM2 trucks and SUVs GM issued 20-NA-039 and 22-NA-082 (ECM software), PIP5764 (corroded terminals at the centre actuator connector) and PIP5791, which has the valve swept from 25 to 95 % with GDS2 and then relearned. Hyundai and Kia link P2B60 to the cleaning routine of the ITM module on 1.6 T-GDI engines (23-EE-002H, 24-FL-003H, Kia ELE 285) and fix it with software.
c: Engine control software (GM 20-NA-039 / 22-NA-082, Hyundai/Kia ITM logic)
Corroded terminals at the valve actuator connector (GM PIP5764)
Valve sluggish or not learned, needs a relearn after test
Valve does not follow commands although wiring is fine
s: MIL on after two drives
Engine temperature fluctuates or warms up slowly
Often no driveability complaint beyond the warning lamp

P2B61.t: Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Stuck Closed
P2B61.d: P2B61 indicates that the coolant flow control valve stays closed although the engine computer asks it to open, so coolant cannot reach the radiator path as intended. Jaguar Land Rover uses it on the 2.0-litre Ingenium petrol four (2019–2020): in bulletin JLRTB02030NAS1, P2B61-73 appears with P26CB-72 when the movable shroud that diverts coolant in the electrically controlled pump stays put, and the PCM runs the fans at full speed to prevent overheating; a new pump and PCM software are the fix. FCA lists P2B61-00 for the Alfa Romeo Giulia and Stelvio 2.0 turbo (21-045-19, 21-035-20). Mazda uses the code on SKYACTIV-G engines but labels it a range/performance fault of its coolant control valve circuit.
c: Valve or diversion shroud mechanically stuck closed (JLR variable coolant pump)
Engine control software that needs an update
Valve drive or its wiring no longer moves the valve
s: Radiator fans running constantly at high speed, loud noise from the engine bay
Rising engine temperature under load
Check engine light on

P2B62.t: Coolant Pump B Supply Voltage Circuit
P2B62.d: P2B62 flags a supply voltage problem at coolant pump B, an electrically driven auxiliary pump with its own electronics. Ford's 2024 gasoline OBD summary files it as failure type 1C (supply voltage outside its permitted band) under base code P261A, in the check of pump B, which Ford defines as the high-temperature-loop auxiliary pump for component cooling #1. The check runs continuously, needs at least 11 V battery voltage and has a monitoring time of 5 seconds. Typical triggers are a blown fuse, a weak relay, corroded power or ground pins or a discharged battery. Faults on the control line are reported separately by P261A to P261D, the same supply fault on pump D by P2B69. With insufficient voltage the pump slows or stops, and the component it cools may overheat.
c: Pump fuse blown or supply relay not closing properly
Corroded or loose power or ground connection at the pump
Weak battery or charging system fault lowering supply voltage
Voltage detection inside the pump electronics faulty
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Auxiliary pump runs slowly or not at all
Rising temperature of the component cooled by pump B

P2B63.d: P2B63 means coolant pump B is powered and commanded but its rotor does not turn, or stays far below target speed. Brushless auxiliary pumps notice this themselves, for example from high current without rotation, and report it to the engine computer. Ford lists the code in its 2024 gasoline OBD summary as failure type 71 (actuator stuck) of pump B, base code P261A, checked continuously above 11 V battery voltage. Causes are a seized bearing, debris or deposits jamming the impeller, a pump frozen in a weak antifreeze mix, or an internally failed motor. GM's patent US20160047374A1 explains how comparing measured current and speed against expected values exposes such a pump fault. P2B65 signals the opposite case, too little load. Pump D has the twin code P2B6A.
c: Bearing seized or impeller jammed by debris or deposits
Electric motor or electronics inside the pump failed
Coolant frozen in the pump because antifreeze concentration is too low
s: Warning lamp with stored code
No audible pump run after the ignition is switched on
Overheating of the component served by pump B

P2B64.t: Coolant Pump B Control Module Overtemperature
P2B64.d: P2B64 reports that the electronics built into coolant pump B have become too hot and the pump has protected itself, usually by derating or shutting down. In Ford's 2024 gasoline OBD summary it is failure type 98 (system over temperature) of the pump B check under P261A, monitored continuously. Such overheating mostly follows a lack of cooling for the pump's own driver: coolant missing or full of air, a motor labouring against a sticking impeller, very hot surroundings near turbo or exhaust, or an ageing power stage. Because these pumps shed the heat of their electronics into the coolant they move, level and bleeding come first in diagnosis. P2B63 (stalled) and P2B65 (air) often share the root cause. Pump A has P2B9E, pump D P2B6B.
c: Coolant level low or air at the pump, so the electronics are not cooled
Sluggish impeller raises motor current and heat
Power stage inside the pump degraded
Damaged heat shield or high radiant heat at the mounting point
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Pump stops intermittently, often after long or hot drives
Reduced cooling of the served component

P2B65.t: Coolant Pump B Overspeed/Air in System
P2B65.d: When a coolant pump draws in air, its impeller loses load: speed climbs and current drops. P2B65 reports this for coolant pump B. Ford's 2024 gasoline OBD summary lists it as failure type B1 (overspeed/dry run) of pump B under P261A. Bentley stores P2B6500, labelled air in system and static, in both engine control units 0001 and 0011 of the W12 Continental GT, GTC and Flying Spur from model years 2018 to 2024, often together with P2B8600 for pump A and a coolant warning in the instrument panel. Bentley's bulletin 2066669 (revisions 1 to 4, latest November 2025) starts with a pressure test and then checks vent hose 975 122 447H, whose built-in check valve can restrict flow; after replacement the circuit is bled. Pump D has P2B6C.
c: Air left in the circuit after filling or repair
Coolant loss through a leak, level too low
Restricting check valve in the vent hose (Bentley W12, 975 122 447H)
Speed or current detection inside the pump faulty
s: Coolant or overheating warning in the instrument cluster
Falling coolant level in the expansion tank
Gurgling noise or fluctuating temperature display

P2B66.d: P2B66 is the open-circuit code for the control line of coolant pump D, the pump a manufacturer labels D in its thermal management. The driver stage in the engine computer detects a broken wire, an unplugged connector or a pump input that no longer draws current. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. Ford's 2024 summary shows the analogous logic for pumps A and B (P2600, P261A): a continuous check from 11 V battery voltage, in which the smart driver reports the output fault. Under CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15), output components must be watched for circuit faults. A short to ground is P2B67, a short to voltage P2B68; pumps C and E use P26F4 and P2DF4. Without control the pump stays off and its loop loses cooling.
c: Pump connector loose, corroded or unplugged
Control wire broken between engine computer and pump
Control input inside the pump open
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Pump D does not respond to commands
Higher temperature in the loop served by pump D

P2B67.t: Coolant Pump D Control Circuit Low
P2B67.d: P2B67 means the control line of coolant pump D sits too low, typically because it is shorted to ground or the driver stage sees excess current. No manufacturer publishes this code. Ford's comparable entries for pumps A and B (P2602, P261C) set when the smart driver in the engine computer reports an output fault, checked continuously above 11 V. Chafed insulation against body or engine, water in the connector and an internally shorted pump input are the usual suspects. Depending on how the output is wired, a ground short can leave the pump running nonstop or silence it completely. With the pump unplugged, measure the resistance of the signal wire to ground before replacing parts. Open circuit is P2B66, short to voltage P2B68; pump C has P26F5.
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion in the pump connector
Control input inside the pump shorted
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Pump D runs constantly or not at all

P2B68.t: Coolant Pump D Control Circuit High
P2B68.d: P2B68 flags a control line for coolant pump D that reads too high: it touches a voltage source or is pulled up while the driver should switch it. No manufacturer documents the code publicly. In Ford's 2024 summary the matching pump A and B codes (P2603, P261D) rest on the same principle, with the smart driver in the engine computer reporting an output circuit fault during a continuous check above 11 V. Likely causes are a wire rubbed through onto a battery-fed conductor, moisture bridging pins or a fault inside the pump electronics. With a line stuck high the pump may run at a fixed speed or ignore commands. Section (e)(15) of CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 wants this kept apart from the open and low faults. Open circuit is P2B66, ground short P2B67, pump E uses P2DF6.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Moisture bridging pins in the connector
Fault in the pump electronics pulls the line up
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Pump D runs at a fixed speed or ignores commands

P2B69.t: Coolant Pump D Supply Voltage Circuit
P2B69.d: P2B69 reports that coolant pump D does not receive a usable voltage on its power feed, as distinct from the control line covered by P2B66 to P2B68. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Ford shows the same failure type for pump B as P2B62 (type 1C, supply outside its permitted band) and for pump A as P2B9D, each checked continuously above 11 V battery voltage. A blown fuse, a relay that no longer closes cleanly, high resistance at a ground point or a weak battery can cause it, and a voltage drop test under load is the way to find them. Such output components fall within CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15). Without adequate power the pump slows or quits, so the circuit it serves overheats more easily.
c: Fuse blown or supply relay contacts worn
High resistance at the pump ground or ground point
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Pump D slow or inactive
Code returns mainly at low battery voltage or high electrical load

P2B6A.d: P2B6A reports that coolant pump D is blocked or stalled: supply and command are present, yet the rotor does not come up to speed. No manufacturer documents the code publicly. Ford uses the identical failure type 71 (actuator stuck) for pump B as P2B63 and for pump A as P2B9C, and GM's patent US20160047374A1 explains how deviations of measured current and speed from expected values expose a faulty electric coolant pump. Seized bearings, an impeller jammed by debris or sludge, frozen coolant and a failed motor winding are typical. Before condemning the pump, confirm its supply (P2B69) and its control signal. Air in the pump points to P2B6C instead, overheated pump electronics to P2B6B. Pump C has the counterpart P26F8.
c: Bearing seized or impeller jammed by debris or sludge
Motor winding or pump electronics failed
Coolant frozen because antifreeze concentration is too low
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Pump D silent although commanded
Overheating of the loop served by pump D

P2B6B.t: Coolant Pump D Control Module Overtemperature
P2B6B.d: With P2B6B the integrated electronics of coolant pump D report excessive temperature, and the pump derates or switches itself off to survive. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the equivalent for pump B is P2B64, which Ford lists as failure type 98 (system over temperature), and for pump A it is P2B9E. Heat in the driver usually builds when coolant around the pump is missing or aerated, when the motor fights a sticking impeller, or when the pump sits close to hot engine or exhaust parts. A failing power stage inside the pump can also trigger the report. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15) covers such output components. Check level, bleeding and free rotation before changing parts. While the pump rests, its circuit gets less flow and may run hot.
c: Too little coolant or air at the pump
Power stage inside the pump degraded
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Pump D cuts out after longer operation and restarts after cooling

P2B6C.t: Coolant Pump D Overspeed/Air in System
P2B6C.d: P2B6C means coolant pump D is spinning faster than its command would explain, the signature of an impeller moving air instead of liquid. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. For pump B, Bentley stores the counterpart P2B6500 on W12 models and traces it to a restricting vent hose, and Ford lists P2B65 as failure type B1 (overspeed/dry run). Patent EP2743509A1 describes how dry running and air bubbles in an electric coolant pump can be recognised from the way its speed rises and decays after a defined energy input. Typical causes are a low level after a leak, incomplete bleeding after service and air pockets that gather at high points of the loop. Bleed the circuit with the manufacturer's routine and look for leaks. A stalled pump D is P2B6A.
c: Circuit not fully bled after filling or repair
Vent line or bleed valve restricted, air cannot escape
s: Coolant warning or rising temperature display
Gurgling from the cooling circuit
Coolant level drops in the expansion tank

P2B6D.t: Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2B6D.d: P2B6D covers a position signal from the engine coolant flow control valve that drops out or jumps for short moments, even though single readings may still lie inside the valid window. This exact code appears in no public manufacturer document. In GM's 3.0 L Duramax diesel the valve sends its angle digitally via SENT; the engine computer tests that sensor for a low reading (P2B5E, under 2 %), a high reading (P2B5F, over 98 %) and plausibility (P2B60, more than 12 % deviation) and treats lost SENT communication as a separate fault, but names no intermittent code. A system using P2B6D would count unstable readings, for instance from a loose terminal, fretting corrosion or a harness that moves with the engine. Input faults of this kind must be caught according to CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15). Coolant flow control becomes unreliable.
c: Loose or widened terminal in the valve connector
Fretting corrosion on the signal or reference pins
Harness rubbing or flexing with engine movement
Position sensor inside the valve unstable
s: Warning lamp, code often stored as intermittent
Temperature display or warm-up behaviour fluctuates

P2B6E.d: P2B6E is the general circuit code for temperature sensor A on the turbocharger or supercharger. SAE J2012 names the sensor but leaves its measuring point open, so the manufacturer decides what it watches, and no manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. The engine computer reports P2B6E when the signal is missing or implausible without being clearly low or clearly high, typically an intermittent open circuit or a corroded connector. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15) calls for circuit checks on powertrain input sensors and names turbocharger electronics among monitored parts. GM's patent US11060525B2 shows, using compressor outlet temperature, how such a value protects the charger by trimming boost and how a sensor fault disables that function. Out-of-range codes are P2B6F and P2B70; sensor B has P2B8F.
c: Intermittent break in signal or ground wire
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Implausible or jumping turbo temperature value in live data

P2B6F.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger A Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
P2B6F.d: P2B6F reports that the signal of turbocharger/supercharger temperature sensor A has fallen below its valid range. If the sensor is an NTC thermistor, whose resistance drops as it warms, a low voltage stands for a very high temperature, so the usual electrical causes are a signal wire shorted to ground or a sensor failed internally short. With an element whose resistance rises with heat (PTC) the relationship is reversed, and low means very cold. Because no manufacturer documents this code publicly, the sensor type depends on the application. Per CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15), low and high out-of-range faults get separate codes. On a cold engine compare the displayed value with real conditions: a hot reading at rest points to a short. High reading: P2B70.
c: Signal wire shorted to ground, for example chafed near the exhaust
Input circuit in the engine computer faulty
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Live data shows an extreme value even with the engine cold

P2B70.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger A Temperature Sensor Circuit High
P2B70.d: P2B70 is set when sensor A on the turbocharger or supercharger delivers a signal above its valid range. For an NTC thermistor this corresponds to an implausibly cold reading, the classic result of an open signal or ground wire, an unplugged connector or a short to the 5 V reference; for a PTC-type element it would indicate extreme heat. No manufacturer publishes this code, so it remains open which point of the charging system the sensor watches. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15) has the fault stored apart from P2B6F and from the general circuit code P2B6E. The engine computer then usually works with a substitute value, and protective functions that rely on this temperature can only act in a limited way. Checking pin fit and continuity usually finds the cause.
c: Signal or ground wire open, connector unplugged
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or another voltage
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Live data shows a fixed extreme value

P2B71.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger A Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2B71.d: P2B71 covers a reading from temperature sensor A on the turbocharger or supercharger that is electrically valid yet does not fit the operating state. Typical plausibility tests compare the value after a long engine-off soak with other temperature sensors, or check it against a model; Cummins patent US8082736B2 shows how a turbine-side temperature can be derived from pressure signals, which gives the computer such a reference. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15.2.1) asks for two-sided rationality checks on input sensors where feasible. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, so limits and timing are unknown. Usual culprits are a drifting element, poor contact or a sensor that sits loose in its bore. Open or shorted wiring sets P2B6E to P2B70 instead; sensor B has P2B92.
c: Sensor element aged by heat and reading off
Contact resistance at the connector distorting the signal
Sensor loose or not fully seated in its bore
s: Warning lamp, often without noticeable driving change
Turbo temperature in live data differs clearly from other temperatures after a cold start
Boost may be trimmed back as a precaution

P2B72.d: P2B72 says the command line to coolant heater A is open or has lost continuity. Keep it apart from the engine coolant heater family P01E8–P01EF: the other J2012 codes for this heater – internal module, supply voltage and over-temperature under P2DA4–P2DA7, lost communication under U069E – point to a unit with its own electronics, such as the electric coolant heater of hybrids and EVs. GM's 2013–2014 Volt used a separate coolant heater control module for this job (bulletin PIC5943, no cabin heat in electric mode). No manufacturer documents P2B72 publicly, so limits and timing are unknown. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requires circuit monitoring of commanded outputs. In winter the cabin stays cold, or an engine runs more often to supply heat.
c: Command wire to the heater broken or connector not latched
Terminal pushed back or corroded in the heater connector
Input stage of the heater electronics open internally
Output stage in the commanding control module faulty
s: Little or no cabin heat, especially in electric driving
Engine starts more often in cold weather to provide heat (hybrids)
Warning or fault message, depending on the manufacturer

P2B73.t: Coolant Heater A Control Circuit Low
P2B73.d: P2B73 is the low case on the command circuit of coolant heater A: the commanding module reads the line at or near ground when it expects a higher level. Usual reasons are a chafed wire touching body ground, coolant or water in a connector, or an input in the heater that pulls the line down. Hyundai and Kia patent US11378000B2 shows why the line carries only a request: the heater has its own controller, which switches several sheath elements one by one and protects them. No manufacturer documents P2B73 publicly, and no thresholds are known. Under CARB rules, commanded outputs like this must be watched for circuit faults. The heater then normally stays off; an electrified car may start its engine more often for cabin heat. Open circuit is P2B72, high voltage P2B74.
c: Command wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Coolant or water in the heater connector
Input of the heater electronics shorted internally
Commanding module cannot drive the line high
s: Coolant heater does not switch on, weak cabin heat
Engine runs more often in the cold (hybrids)
Fuse for the request circuit may blow repeatedly

P2B74.t: Coolant Heater A Control Circuit High
P2B74.d: P2B74 is the opposite of P2B73: the command circuit of coolant heater A sits at or near supply voltage while the module expects it low, or the output stage measures excess current and shuts down. A wire rubbed through onto a 12 V feed, a crushed harness next to the heater's own supply cable or a shorted input in the heater electronics are typical. Depending on the wiring, the heater may run without a request or not at all. Designs with integrated control, such as Hanon's patent US11628706B2, add their own overheat sensing so that an unintended run does not destroy the element. No manufacturer documents P2B74 publicly. CARB wants such outputs monitored for electrical faults. Internal module and over-temperature faults have their own codes, P2DA4 and P2DA6.
c: Command wire shorted to a 12 V circuit
Harness crushed or melted near the heater supply cable
Heater electronics input shorted to its supply
Output stage of the commanding module faulty
s: Coolant heater off, or running without request
Higher 12 V or high-voltage battery drain when parked if the heater runs on
Weak cabin heat in cold weather

P2B75.t: Coolant Heater A Control Circuit Performance
P2B75.d: P2B75 is set when the command circuit of coolant heater A tests electrically sound but the heater's response does not match the request – the coolant leaving it fails to warm, for instance, or reported power or current stays off target. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15.2.2) asks for this kind of functional check on output components. GM's bulletin PIC5943 for the 2013–2014 Volt shows the practical test: with full heat requested in electric mode the heater core temperature should climb to about 54 °C and hold; if not, early coolant heater control modules were replaced (GM stores B101D there, not P2B75). No manufacturer documents P2B75 itself. Air in the loop, weak circulation, a failed element or faulty heater electronics are typical causes.
c: Air trapped in the heater loop or low coolant level
Heating element weak or partly failed
Internal fault in the heater control electronics
Coolant pump or valve in the heater loop not circulating enough
s: Cabin warms slowly or only with the engine running
Heater core temperature in live data stays low despite full heat request
Electric range reduced in winter because the engine starts for heat

P2B76.d: P2B76 reports an open command circuit for coolant heater B. Where a vehicle has two separately requested heaters or heating stages – Hyundai and Kia patent US11378000B2 describes one housing with several sheath elements that a controller switches individually – B stands for the second channel. Which physical heater carries the letter is up to the manufacturer, and none documents P2B76 publicly. Typical findings are a terminal pushed out of the connector, a wire broken where the harness flexes near the heater, or a blown feed for the request line. California's OBD rule covers outputs of this kind with a circuit test. Heater A often keeps working, so heating is only weaker; if both fail, look at P2B72 and the communication code U069E too.
c: Request wire for heater B broken at a flex point
Terminal pushed out of the heater connector
Fuse feeding the request circuit blown
Heater B input open inside the heater electronics
s: Reduced heating power, cabin warms more slowly
Defrosting takes longer in cold weather
Fault entry often without other noticeable effects

P2B77.t: Coolant Heater B Control Circuit Low
P2B77.d: P2B77 means the command circuit of coolant heater B reads low: the line is pulled toward ground although the module drives or expects a higher level. With a second heating stage this usually costs part of the heating power rather than all of it, because stage A can still run. A short to ground in a harness branch routed along the coolant hoses, corrosion from coolant seeping into the connector or a defective input in the heater electronics are the usual suspects. No manufacturer documents P2B77 publicly, so the setting limits are unknown. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 asks for circuit monitoring of outputs commanded by a powertrain computer. Open and high faults of heater B are P2B76 and P2B78; the engine coolant heater B family is P01EC–P01EF.
c: Harness branch along the coolant hoses shorted to ground
Coolant seepage corroding the heater connector
Heater B input shorted inside the heater electronics
s: Heating power noticeably lower than usual
Cabin and windows take longer to warm up
Possible traces of coolant at the heater connector

P2B78.t: Coolant Heater B Control Circuit High
P2B78.d: P2B78 flags the command line of coolant heater B as too high: voltage is present where the commanding module expects a low level, or its driver reports overcurrent. A short to a 12 V circuit is the classic cause; with a low-side driver, a heater input that has failed short can produce it as well. The risk is a stage that will not switch off on request, which is why heater designs such as US11628706B2 include independent overheat sensing in the housing. No manufacturer documents P2B78 publicly. The CARB regulation calls for an electrical check of such a line. If the fault lies in a shared harness, P2B74 for heater A may appear at the same time; measuring the request lines with the heater unplugged separates harness faults from heater faults.
c: Request wire for heater B shorted to a 12 V circuit
Heater B input failed short inside the heater
Damage in a harness section shared with heater A
s: Heater stage B off, or running although not requested
Unusual battery drain while parked
Lower heating power in winter

P2B79.t: Coolant Heater B Control Circuit Performance
P2B79.d: P2B79 says that coolant heater B is wired correctly but does not do what it is told: after a request the expected warming, current or status feedback fails to appear. In layouts with several stages, as in Hyundai and Kia patent US11378000B2, the controller switches the stages individually and shuts them down when outlet or housing surface temperature runs too high – a stage disabled by that protection can look like a performance fault from outside. No manufacturer documents P2B79 publicly. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15.2.2) demands functional checks on output components. Low coolant, trapped air, a weak heating element or an internal fault in the heater electronics are typical causes; the over-temperature code of heater A is P2DA6.
c: Low coolant or trapped air, so protection shuts the stage down
Heating element of stage B weak or open
Internal fault in the heater electronics for stage B
s: Heating power lower than expected
Heater outlet temperature rises slowly in live data
Fault may only appear at low outside temperatures

P2B7A.t: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch C Circuit
P2B7A.d: P2B7A is the general circuit fault of a third EVAP pressure sensor or switch, C, alongside A (P0450 range) and B (P24D5 range). Each maker assigns the letters itself. Audi V6 and V8 engines (bulletin 2069531, 2022–2025) call it tank ventilation pressure sensor 3, part GX49, and use P2B7A for its electrical fault; the bulletin adds that some control units logged this fault wrongly as P0450. VW uses the code for its fuel tank pressure sensor G400 with NVLD switch on the 2025–2026 Jetta and Taos FWD, where bulletin 01-26-01 blames a too-small orifice in the plug housing. CARB demands that every EVAP input be monitored for circuit faults. Until the fault is fixed, leak tests that rely on this sensor cannot run.
c: Sensor of an early design (VW G400 with narrow orifice)
Open or short in reference, ground or signal wire
Control unit logs a wrong fault entry (Audi bulletin 2069531)
s: Check engine light on
EVAP readiness monitor stays incomplete
Usually no change in driving behaviour

P2B7B.t: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch C Circuit Range/Performance
P2B7B.d: P2B7B means sensor C delivers a signal that is electrically valid but implausible. Mercedes-AMG documents it as P2B7B26 on the GT63 S E Performance (2024–2026): the ME control unit sees the signal change too slowly, caused by interference on the line, and bulletin LI07.70-P-078293 cures it by twisting the sensor leads that run between the engine computer and the EVAP sensors. Audi's V6/V8 bulletin 2069531 lists P2B7B as pressure sensor 3 implausible, but explains that this entry is mislabelled and the test really belongs to P24D6 on sensor G950. VW's 2025–2026 Jetta and Taos set it together with the narrowed G400 orifice. CARB asks for two-sided rationality checks on inputs where feasible. Leak tests may be suspended meanwhile.
c: Sensor port or orifice too narrow or blocked
Fault entry assigned to the wrong sensor (Audi bulletin 2069531)
Pressure sensor C drifting or sluggish
s: Check engine light on, no driveability complaint
EVAP readiness monitor not completing
Code returns after clearing, often after a few drives

P2B7C.t: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch C Circuit Low
P2B7C.d: P2B7C reports that the signal of EVAP pressure sensor C stays below its valid voltage window. The only public manufacturer reference is VW: on the 2025–2026 Jetta (engine DNKA) and Taos FWD (DYBA) the code points to fuel tank pressure sensor G400 with its NVLD switch, and bulletin 01-26-01 replaces the sensor assembly with the revised plug housing (part 5WA201700B) if the old version is fitted. No threshold is published for sensor C; Mitsubishi's comparable check on its own tank pressure sensor (P24D7) trips below 1.0 V for 2 s. A missing 5 V reference, a signal wire shorted to ground or a dead sensor are typical. Whether low means vacuum or pressure depends on the sensor's characteristic curve.
c: 5 V reference to the sensor missing or shorted
s: Check engine light on
EVAP leak tests not carried out, readiness incomplete
Other sensors on the same 5 V supply may report faults too

P2B7D.t: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch C Circuit High
P2B7D.d: P2B7D is the high counterpart to P2B7C: the signal of EVAP pressure sensor C sits above its valid range. VW lists it in bulletin 01-26-01 for the 2025–2026 Jetta and Taos FWD, whose fuel tank pressure sensor G400 came with a plug-housing orifice that proved too small; the first step is to check which housing version is installed. Public limits for sensor C do not exist; Mitsubishi's equivalent test on its own tank pressure sensor (P24D8) sets above 4.1 V for 2 s. An open sensor ground, a signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage and an internal sensor fault all push the signal up. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 requires out-of-range checks on all EVAP inputs; leak monitoring is held back until repair.
c: Sensor ground wire open or high resistance
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
s: Check engine light on
EVAP readiness not set after clearing codes
Car usually drives normally

P2B7E.t: EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch C Circuit Intermittent
P2B7E.d: P2B7E covers a signal from EVAP pressure sensor C that drops out or jumps for brief moments instead of failing for good. No manufacturer documents P2B7E publicly; Audi and VW use only P2B7A and P2B7B, VW also P2B7C and P2B7D, for this sensor. How such a check can work is shown by Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV for its tank pressure sensor (P24D9): during the parked leak test it counts how often the signal crosses its own filtered value and sets the code after more than 20 crossings. Loose terminals, a chafed harness near the tank, moisture in the connector or electrical interference – the cause Mercedes-AMG found behind P2B7B – are typical. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15) asks for circuit checks on EVAP inputs. Moving the harness gently while the reading is displayed helps locate the spot.
c: Loose or corroded terminal at the sensor connector
Harness chafing near the tank or along the underbody
Electrical interference on the signal line
Pressure sensor C with an intermittent internal fault
s: Check engine light comes and goes
Pressure reading jumps in live data
Fault often appears only on rough roads or in wet weather

P2B7F.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control Module A Calibration Not Learned/Programmed
P2B7F.d: P2B7F applies where boost control A is handled by its own electronic module, typically a smart actuator on the charger, and that module reports missing or invalid calibration data. Honeywell patent US7689376B2 describes such a controller holding a multi-point calibration measured for its individual turbocharger, and Melett notes for REA-type actuators that this data is unique to each unit, so swapped or new parts must be programmed or matched. The code therefore mostly appears after a module or charger replacement or an interrupted programming session. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 lists turbocharger electronics as monitored parts and requires a CAL ID from reprogrammable emission-critical modules. No manufacturer documents P2B7F publicly. Module B uses P2B80.
c: New or used module or charger fitted without programming or learn routine
Programming aborted, for example by low battery voltage
Module has lost its stored calibration (internal fault)
s: Warning lamp right after a repair on the turbo system
Reduced boost or emergency mode

P2B80.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control Module B Calibration Not Learned/Programmed
P2B80.d: P2B80 is the counterpart of P2B7F for the second boost control module, which only exists where two chargers or two separately driven actuators each carry their own electronics. It is set when module B has no valid calibration or its learn step was never completed. On twin-charger engines a frequent trap is fitting modules or chargers on the wrong side: Melett points out that REA-style actuator calibration belongs to one specific turbocharger and cannot be moved, and Honeywell patent US7689376B2 shows calibration recorded per unit. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 ties such reprogrammable modules to CAL ID reporting. No manufacturer documents P2B80 publicly. If both codes appear together, a programming or wiring issue in the engine computer is more likely.
c: Module B or its charger replaced without programming or learn routine
Modules or chargers fitted on the wrong side
s: Warning lamp after work on the second charger
Reduced power because boost on one side is limited

P2B81.t: Wastegate Position Sensor A Circuit Performance
P2B81.d: P2B81 reports that electric wastegate A does not behave as commanded although its sensor signal is electrically fine. GM documents it for the 2.7L L3B (table 19OBDG03D): with the actuator in normal operation the fault counts if the position error exceeds 20 % for over 1 s, actuator current exceeds 1.0 A for over 1 s or duty cycle exceeds 40 % for over 1 s, and 25 of 30 samples must fail; the 2025 table 25OBDG03B tightens the position limit to 10 % for 2 s with 29 of 30. It is Type A, so the MIL comes on in the first trip. GM bulletin PIP6007A names increased friction in the wastegate valve on the 2.0L LSY (Blazer, XT4 to XT6, CT4, CT5, Envision) and calls for turbocharger replacement. Wiring faults set P2AB7 to P2AB9.
c: Wastegate valve or linkage binding (GM PIP6007A, turbo replacement)
Electric wastegate actuator worn or drawing excessive current
Linkage clip missing or rod detached
s: MIL in the first trip
Boost too low or too high, flat or jerky acceleration
Reduced power mode possible

P2B82.t: Wastegate Position Sensor B Circuit Performance
P2B82.d: P2B82 is the performance fault for the second electric wastegate, found only on engines with two turbochargers and position-controlled wastegates. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. By analogy with GM's checks for wastegate A (P2B81 in 19OBDG03D), the computer would flag lasting gaps between commanded and measured position, or a motor that needs abnormal current or duty cycle to hold its target. GM letters a parallel layout so that charger A sits on bank 1, which would put B on bank 2. Ford's patent US9243553B2 adds that heat changes linkage length and shifts the sensor reading, so a worn or binding linkage can mimic a sensor fault. Circuit faults on side B are P2ABA to P2ABC; the stuck-type counterpart is P0248.
c: Wastegate valve B or linkage binding from heat and deposits
Actuator B worn, gear or motor weak
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Uneven or reduced boost, weaker pull

P2B83.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump A Overspeed/Air In System
P2B83.d: P2B83 concerns the electric pump that keeps coolant moving through a water-cooled charge air cooler. When the impeller runs in air instead of liquid, load vanishes and the motor spins up. GM documents this in its 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B: a reported pump speed of 8,500 rpm or more in 8 of 10 one-second samples sets the code, provided the pump is fitted and enabled, the engine is not cranking and relay voltage is at least 11 V; Type B, MIL after two trips. GM's 3.0-litre Duramax uses such a pump (M10, bulletin 23-NA-102). GM's bulletin 18-NA-291 for the supercharged LT4 notes that this pump switches off once it draws air, so the loop must be vacuum filled. Too little speed is P2B84, the B pump has P2CB1. Hot charge air can cut power.
c: Air pocket in the charge air cooler loop after service or a leak
Low coolant level in the separate low-temperature loop
Impeller loose or broken on the pump shaft
Pump electronics reporting an implausible speed
s: Check engine light after two drives with the fault
Reduced power under load because the intake air gets hot
Falling level in the charge air cooler coolant reservoir

P2B84.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump A Underspeed
P2B84.d: P2B84 reports that the electric charge air cooler pump is turning too slowly or not at all, judged by the speed its own electronics send back. GM lists the code next to P2B83 in the 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B as the low out-of-range case of the pump speed, with the limit printed as a reading below -115 rpm; 8 failed one-second samples out of 10 are needed, with the pump fitted and enabled, relay voltage at 11 V or more and the engine not cranking. Type B, so the MIL comes on after the second faulty trip. Typical reasons are a seized bearing, debris at the impeller, a weak supply or a corroded connector – GM's bulletin 23-NA-102 found water entering the M10 pump plug on the 3.0-litre Duramax. With little flow the intake air runs hot.
c: Worn or seized pump bearing, or debris blocking the impeller
Water or corrosion in the pump connector
Low supply voltage or poor ground at the pump
Pump motor or its electronics worn out
s: Check engine light after the second faulty drive
Less power under heavy load or when towing
High charge air temperature shown in live data

P2B85.d: P2B85 applies to engines whose main water pump is electric: the pump turns clearly slower than commanded. On GM's 2.7-litre L3B (table 19OBDG03D) the filtered gap between commanded and reported speed must exceed a map value – 200 rpm at low commands, up to 800 rpm at 8,000 rpm – during 8 of 10 seconds, with 300–6,250 rpm requested and more than 11 V; there it is Type A, MIL on the first trip, while the 2025 table 25OBDG03B rates it Type B. GM program N202320510 replaced pumps with faulty circuit boards on 2020–2021 CT4, CT5, Silverado and Sierra with L3B or LSY: overheating, MIL, P2B85 and reduced power, in the end engine shutdown. Mercedes links P2B8500 on the M254 to loose plugs at the high-temperature pump. Pump running when off: P2BA2.
c: Failed control board inside the electric water pump
Loose or poorly latched plug at the pump
Bearing wear or deposits slowing the impeller
Low supply voltage or high resistance in power or ground
s: Rising coolant temperature and overheating warnings
Reduced engine power to protect the engine
Check engine light, often on the first trip
Engine may be shut down if driving continues

P2B86.t: Coolant Pump A Overspeed/Air in System
P2B86.d: P2B86 says coolant pump A spins faster than it was told to – the typical sign of air at the impeller. In GM's 2025 tables (25OBDG03A, 25OBDG04B) the filtered gap between command and feedback must stay beyond a map limit, the pump running 200 to 348 rpm too fast depending on the 300–3,480 rpm request, over 8 s of a 10 s span at more than 11 V; Type B. On GM trucks pump A is the G17 auxiliary heater pump: bulletin PIT6505 (2024–2026 Escalade, Tahoe, Suburban, Yukon) found a stray O-ring lodged in it. Ford's 2024 gasoline summary has P2B86 as overspeed/dry-run type of the cabin-heating pump. Bentley sees P2B8600 with P2B6500 on W12 models (bulletin 2066669) and checks the bleed hose. Too slow: P2B87.
c: Air trapped in the loop after a repair or incomplete bleeding
Coolant loss through a leak, low level in the reservoir
Foreign object such as a loose O-ring at the pump ports
Restricted bleed or vent hose keeping air in the system
s: Check engine light after the second faulty trip
Weak or fluctuating cabin heat
Coolant warning or gurgling noise in the heater area

P2B87.d: With P2B87 the reported speed of coolant pump A stays below the commanded one. GM's 2025 tables (25OBDG03A, 25OBDG04B) compare filtered command and feedback against a calibrated limit while 300–3,480 rpm is requested and more than 11 V is present; 8 s in a 10 s window, Type B. Ford's 2024 gasoline summary lists it as the underspeed type of the cabin-heating auxiliary pump, checked continuously from 11 V. On GM vehicles the code often had no hardware cause: PIT5789 (2021 Tahoe, Suburban, Yukon, Escalade) cured it with new BCM software, bulletin 21-NA-024 (2021–2022 Acadia, Blazer, Enclave, Traverse, XT5, XT6) with an HVAC module update – the G17 pump was not to be replaced. PIT6505 later found a stray O-ring in it. Overspeed is P2B86, stall P2B9C.
c: Outdated software in the module that commands the pump
Impeller slowed by debris or a foreign O-ring
Worn bearing or motor in the auxiliary pump
Low voltage or poor contact at the pump connector
s: Check engine light, often without any other complaint
Reduced cabin heat at idle or with the engine stopped

P2B88.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 1
P2B88.d: P2B88 is the catch-all electrical code for the oxygen sensor that some turbocharged engines mount in the intake tract, behind compressor and charge air cooler, to judge how much exhaust the recirculation system is feeding back. Ford's patents describe this intake sensor as a heated wide-band element whose pumping current shrinks as recirculated gas dilutes the fresh charge. P2B88 is meant for a signal fault the module cannot sort into too low or too high, such as an open lead or a reading that keeps dropping out. No manufacturer documents P2B88 publicly; CARB requires every input used for emission control to be checked for circuit faults. Without the signal, EGR runs on a model or is switched off. P2B89 and P2B8A split the fault by voltage, heater faults are P2B8B to P2B8E.
c: Corroded or loose sensor plug, often wetted by charge air cooler condensate
Open or chafed signal wire between sensor and engine module
Intake oxygen sensor element internally failed
Fault in the sensor input stage of the engine module
s: Check engine light on
EGR reduced or switched off, with slightly higher fuel use or knock-limited power
Often no noticeable change in driving behaviour

P2B89.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Circuit Low Voltage Bank 1
P2B89.d: With P2B89 the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor signal sits below the lowest voltage the engine module accepts. Typical electrical reasons are a signal lead shorted to ground, a damaged element or a corroded plug near the charge air cooler, where condensate gathers. Stellantis is the one maker that names the code publicly: bulletin 18-030-17 (revisions B and D) and its successor 18-097-19 for the 2017–2018 Alfa Romeo Giulia with the 2.0-litre turbo four (sales code EC2) list P2B89, written without a bank, next to P2AC0 and P0402, and cure the lit MIL by flashing new engine software, so a false detection is possible there. Ford's patent on crankcase vapours shows that hydrocarbons burning at the hot element also pull the reading down. P2B8A is the high side, P2B88 the general fault.
c: Engine software detecting falsely (Alfa Romeo Giulia 2.0 EC2, fixed by reflash)
Signal wire shorted to ground or pinched in the harness
Moisture or corrosion in the sensor connector
s: Check engine light on
EGR flow limited or disabled by the engine module
Other stored codes such as P2AC0 or P0402 on the same vehicle

P2B8A.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Circuit High Voltage Bank 1
P2B8A.d: P2B8A is the mirror image of P2B89: the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor delivers a voltage above its valid window. On a wide-band element this usually comes from a signal wire touching a supply or the heater feed, from an open ground or reference return that lets the input float upward, or from water inside the connector. A value that high would mean more oxygen than fresh air can hold, so the module cannot derive EGR dilution from it and falls back to a model or stops recirculation. No manufacturer publishes P2B8A. Ford's patent DE102014220034A1 learns the sensor's zero point while no exhaust is recirculated, the reference against which an implausibly high reading stands out; US8775011B2 separates sensor faults from a leaking EGR valve. P2B89 is the low side, P2B88 the general circuit fault.
c: Signal wire shorted to a supply or to the heater feed
Open ground or reference return lead of the sensor
s: Check engine light on
EGR switched off, possibly slightly higher fuel consumption
Intake oxygen reading on the scan tool above the fresh-air value

P2B8B.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Heater Control Circuit/Open Bank 1
P2B8B.d: P2B8B is about the heater of bank 1's intake oxygen sensor: the module switches the heater on but sees no current, the classic sign of a broken heater coil, an open feed or control lead, or a blown fuse in the heater supply. A wide-band sensor only measures once its ceramic is hot. Ford's patent US9309838B2 gives about 800 °C as an example set point for the intake sensor, held by closed-loop heater control, and Bosch rates the LSU 4.9 heater at 7.5 W in steady state. With the heater dead the sensor never becomes ready, and EGR loses its oxygen feedback. No manufacturer documents P2B8B publicly; CARB treats sensor heaters as monitored components that must be checked for circuit faults. P2B8D and P2B8E are the shorts, P2B8C judges whether the heater does its job.
c: Heater coil inside the sensor burnt through or cracked
Blown fuse or failed relay in the heater supply
Open heater feed or control wire, loose connector pin
Heater driver in the engine module failed
s: Check engine light on
EGR stays inactive because the intake sensor never becomes ready
Possible companion code for the sensor signal

P2B8C.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Heater Control Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1
P2B8C.d: P2B8C is not about broken wires: the heater of the bank 1 intake oxygen sensor is electrically intact, yet the element does not reach or hold its temperature as expected, or the heater needs power that does not fit the conditions. Mounted right after the intercooler, this sensor gets hit by condensate. Ford's patents describe how water droplets make heater power jump, how long periods at full power can crack the element, and how the controller cuts heater power and pauses the intake sensor's heater diagnostics until consumption returns to its baseline, which shows what such a performance test watches. Ageing heaters with rising resistance, poor pin contact and low supply voltage are other triggers. No manufacturer documents P2B8C publicly. P2B8B is the open circuit, P2B8D and P2B8E the shorts.
c: Water from the charge air cooler reaching the hot sensor element
Heater aged with increased resistance, sensor slow to warm up
Corroded pins or high resistance in the heater supply
Low system voltage limiting heater power
s: Check engine light on
Fault often appears in humid or cold weather and with high boost
EGR temporarily reduced

P2B8D.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Heater Control Circuit Low Bank 1
P2B8D.d: P2B8D means the voltage the module sees on the heater control wire of bank 1's intake oxygen sensor is lower than the module expects for the commanded state, usually because the line is shorted to ground. Many engine modules switch such heaters on the ground side; there a control wire chafed against the body can keep the heater running even when it should be off, which overheats the ceramic and can crack it. A heater with shorted turns can likewise pull the line down. Bosch's LSU 4.9 data sheet shows the two heater pins separately from the measuring pins, so the heater can be checked on its own with a meter. No manufacturer documents P2B8D publicly; Ford's intake sensor patent US9719448B2 explains why uncontrolled heater power harms the element. P2B8E is the high side, P2B8B the open circuit.
c: Heater control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Heater coil with shorted turns inside the sensor
Water bridging the heater pins in the connector
Heater output stage in the engine module defective
s: Check engine light on
Heater switched off by the module, EGR feedback unavailable
Repeated sensor failure if the short is not repaired

P2B8E.t: Intake Air O2 Sensor Heater Control Circuit High Bank 1
P2B8E.d: With P2B8E, bank 1's intake O2 heater control wire shows more voltage than expected, as when it is shorted to battery voltage or when the driver cannot pull it down. If the module switches the heater on its ground side, such a short means the heater never receives current, the element stays cold and the sensor is never released for measuring. A driver that detects overcurrent may also switch off and report the line high. Ford's patent US9309838B2 shows how strongly the intake sensor relies on a closed-loop heater to hold its set point; without it, EGR control based on intake oxygen is suspended. Bosch's LSU 4.9 data sheet lists the heater pins for checking. No manufacturer documents P2B8E publicly. P2B8D is the low side, P2B8C the performance check.
c: Heater control wire shorted to battery voltage
Heater with too low resistance tripping the driver's overcurrent protection
Damaged connector with pins touching each other
Heater output stage in the engine module defective
s: Check engine light on
Intake oxygen sensor stays cold and not ready
EGR inactive

P2B8F.d: P2B8F is the general circuit fault for temperature sensor B, the second sensor of this kind on a charged engine, often belonging to a second turbocharger. Which spot it watches is left to the manufacturer, and none documents this code publicly. The engine computer sets it when the signal is lost or unusable without clearly sitting below or above its range, for example during short interruptions. Sensors near the exhaust side often use a platinum measuring resistor on a mineral-insulated lead, as Heraeus describes in patent US8328419B2, because ordinary NTC parts reach their limit at about 900 degrees Celsius. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15) requires circuit monitoring of such inputs. Out-of-range codes are P2B90 and P2B91; sensor A has P2B6E.
c: Loose or heat-damaged connector with intermittent contact
Wiring chafed or brittle near hot exhaust parts
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Sensor B value missing or jumping in live data

P2B90.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger B Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
P2B90.d: P2B90 means the signal of temperature sensor B has dropped below the lowest value the engine computer accepts. What that says about temperature depends on the element: an NTC thermistor loses resistance when hot, so a low signal reads as extreme heat, whereas a platinum resistor of the kind Heraeus patented for turbo protection (US8328419B2) gains resistance with heat, so a low signal reads as extreme cold. Electrically both point the same way: a signal wire touching ground or a shorted element. No manufacturer publishes this code, so the sensor type of a given engine must be taken from its service data. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15) keeps low and high faults apart. The high counterpart is P2B91, the matching code for sensor A is P2B6F.
c: Signal wire shorted to ground, for example melted insulation
Faulty input stage in the engine computer
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Sensor B shows a fixed extreme value even on a cold engine

P2B91.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger B Temperature Sensor Circuit High
P2B91.d: P2B91 is stored when temperature sensor B delivers a signal above its permitted window. By far the most frequent reason is a broken current path: an unplugged or corroded connector, a cracked wire or an element that has burned open, which pulls the input up to its reference voltage. A short to the 5 V supply or to battery voltage has the same effect. For an NTC part this looks like severe cold, for a platinum resistor like severe heat; the sensor patent US8328419B2 from Heraeus explains why lead strain and heat cycling make such breaks a known weak point. No manufacturer publishes this code. Per CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15) it is kept separate from the low fault P2B90 and the general circuit code P2B8F. Sensor A uses P2B70.
c: Signal or ground wire open, connector unplugged or corroded
Sensor element or its lead wires broken by heat cycling
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
s: Warning lamp with stored code
Sensor B stuck at an end value in live data

P2B92.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger B Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2B92.d: P2B92 says that temperature sensor B delivers a plausible voltage whose content is wrong: it may hang at one value, follow load changes too slowly or disagree with its partner sensor A on an engine with two chargers. A sensor that sits in a soot-coated or oil-wetted spot reacts sluggishly and is a classic trigger. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15.2.1) requires such rationality tests to look for readings that are wrongly high as well as wrongly low. GM's patent US11060525B2 illustrates why the value matters: boost is reduced when the charger runs too hot, and a sensor fault switches that protection off. No manufacturer documents P2B92 publicly. Clear electrical faults use P2B8F to P2B91; sensor A has P2B71.
c: Sensor tip coated with soot or oil, responds sluggishly
Sensor element aged and reading off
Contact resistance in connector or wiring
s: Warning lamp, usually without drivability change
Sensor B lags behind or contradicts sensor A in live data
Boost may be limited as a precaution

P2B93.t: Wastegate Position Sensor A Exceeded Learning Limit
P2B93.d: P2B93 concerns the learned closed position of electric wastegate A. The computer periodically drives the valve onto its seat and stores the sensor value found there; Ford's patent US9243553B2 explains why: linkage length drifts with temperature and the reference must be refreshed. GM documents the code for the 2.7L L3B (19OBDG03D) and in the 2025 table 25OBDG03B: it fails when the raw closed position learned is above 85 %, or when no valid closed position has ever been learned while the engine runs above 1000 rpm with a stable valve and coolant at least 80 degrees Celsius. It is Type A with one trip. The usual reasons are a worn seat, a bent or stretched linkage or a replaced charger not yet adapted; this differs from P2B81, which judges how the valve follows.
c: Wastegate linkage bent, stretched or wrongly adjusted
Wastegate flap or seat worn so the valve travels too far
Turbocharger or actuator replaced and relearn not completed
s: MIL in the first trip
Boost slightly low because the valve does not fully close

P2B94.t: Wastegate Position Sensor B Exceeded Learning Limit
P2B94.d: P2B94 is set when the learned end position of electric wastegate B falls outside the window the engine computer accepts. Stellantis documents it on the 2025 Ram 1500 with the 3.0L Hurricane twin-turbo: bulletin 09-008-25 (Rev. B) lists P2B94 together with P0248 and a MIL, with weak turbo response, caused by wastegate rod retention clips installed incorrectly at the factory. The fix is to measure the clips with a caliper and replace any that exceed 13.70 mm on the actuator side or 17.78 mm on the housing side. Ford's patent US9243553B2 explains the principle behind the learn step: the controller moves the valve against a mechanical stop and stores the sensor value there, so play in the linkage moves the learned point. Side A uses P2B93.
c: Wastegate rod retention clips incorrectly installed (Stellantis 09-008-25)
Play or bending in the wastegate B linkage
Charger or actuator B replaced without completed relearn
s: MIL on, often together with P0248
Lack of acceleration from the turbo

P2B95.d: P2B95 belongs to the cold-start strategy of petrol direct-injection engines: while the catalyst is heated, each injection is split into two or more small pulses, and the module checks via the injector coil voltage that every pulse really opened the injector. Unlike P2B08 to P2B0F, which name a cylinder, P2B95 is the engine-wide verdict. GM's 2025 table 25OBDG03A runs it once per trip during the strategy (catalyst under 550 °C, coolant −12 to 66 °C, 250–3,000 rpm, under 20 s run time) and relates missed pulses to all pulses; Type B. GM bulletins 18-NA-074 (2018 Malibu 1.5 l) and 20-NA-230 (2021 Equinox, Terrain, Malibu) cure false settings with ECM software. Stellantis uses the same name for the 2019 Jeep Cherokee 2.0 turbo (18-052-20). P2B96 is the warm counterpart.
c: Engine software setting the code falsely (GM and Stellantis reflash bulletins)
Injector opening sluggishly when cold due to deposits or wear
High resistance or chafing in injector wiring
Rail pressure outside the expected range during cold start
s: Check engine light after two cold starts with the fault
Usually no noticeable effect on driving
Possibly rough running in the first seconds after a cold start

P2B96.d: P2B96 is the engine-wide check, outside the cold-start phase, that injectors on a direct-injection petrol engine really open when commanded. The module digitises the voltage across each injector and looks for the small kink the moving armature leaves; if commanded pulses repeatedly show no opening, it assumes fuel was not delivered. GM's 25OBDG03A table runs this continuously in 100 ms steps as a global missing-pulse test beside the per-cylinder codes P2B00 to P2B07, Type B. GM's PIT5677 lists P2B96 among codes from chafed engine harnesses on 2019 Silverado/Sierra 1500 with the 2.7 l L3B, and the Encore GX/Trailblazer service update A202310450 cures it with ECM software. Mitsubishi files P2B96 under the injection system in its 2022 Outlander manual update. P2B95 covers the cold-start phase.
c: Engine harness chafed against underhood parts (GM 2.7 l L3B)
Engine software detecting falsely, fixed by reprogramming
Injector armature sticking or injector worn
High resistance in an injector circuit or connector
s: Check engine light after two drives with the fault
Misfire or rough running if fuel is really missing
Often other codes from the same harness or injector fault

P2B97.t: Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Position Exceeded Learning Limit
P2B97.d: P2B97 concerns the electrically driven exhaust back-pressure flap of GM's 3.0-litre Duramax diesel. After key-off the module moves the flap to its fully closed and fully open stops and stores what the SENT position sensor reports there. GM's 2025 table 25OBDG04B flags a learned value outside its window: closed below 4.8 % or above 14.7 % of 5 V, wide open below 80 % or above 96.5 %, enabled with coolant 30–150 °C and at least 9.5 V; Type A, MIL after one trip, no debounce. GM preliminary information PIP5874B for 2023 Silverado/Sierra with the 3.0 l LZ0 restricts the replacement part and asks for a borescope look at flap travel and welding slag before the valve is changed. P2B98 and P2B99 cover supply and driver faults, P0476 the general function check.
c: Flap travel blocked by welding slag, soot or corrosion
Position sensor in the actuator drifted
Actuator gear or motor worn so the stops are not reached
Weak battery during the key-off learn
s: Check engine light after one drive
Slower warm-up or reduced exhaust heating for aftertreatment
Possibly reduced engine power

P2B98.t: Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Supply Low
P2B98.d: P2B98 says the motor of exhaust pressure control valve A is not getting enough supply voltage. On GM's 3.0-litre Duramax, whose 2025 table 25OBDG04B documents the code, the H-bridge that drives the exhaust flap reports undervoltage below 6 V; 240 failed out of 300 samples taken every 12.5 ms set it, outside cranking and with the powertrain relay delivering more than 11 V. Type A, MIL after one trip. Because the main relay is fine in that case, the loss lies further on: a fuse, the feed wire, the connector or a weak ground of the driver. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 lists P2B98 among codes that chafed engine harnesses and blown fuses caused on 2019–2021 trucks, the 3.0 l LM2 included. Without power the flap stays put, so warm-up and back-pressure control suffer. P2B99 is the overheating driver.
c: Blown fuse or interrupted feed to the valve actuator
Corroded connector or poor ground at the actuator
Weak battery or charging fault causing voltage dips
s: Check engine light after one drive
Exhaust flap without function, slower warm-up
Further codes for the same fuse or harness

P2B99.t: Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P2B99.d: P2B99 reports that the output stage driving exhaust pressure control valve A is running too hot or carrying too much current. In GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B for the 3.0-litre Duramax, the H-bridge driver temperature has to exceed 170 °C in 240 of 300 samples at 12.5 ms intervals, outside cranking and with more than 11 V on the powertrain relay; Type A, one trip. GM names internal faults of the valve motor as a typical cause, for example shorted windings or a flap that binds so the motor stalls under load. A harness short can overload the driver as well; bulletin 21-NA-149 lists P2B99 on 2019–2021 trucks with the 3.0 l LM2 and chafed engine wiring. The driver then usually shuts down to protect itself and the flap is left uncontrolled. P2B98 is the supply fault, P2B97 the learn fault.
c: Valve motor with internal fault such as shorted windings
Flap binding from soot or corrosion so the motor stalls
Defective driver stage in the control module
s: Check engine light after one drive
Exhaust flap no longer controlled
Possibly reduced power or longer warm-up

P2B9A.d: P2B9A covers a DEF quality sensor whose signal drops out now and then or jumps between values, rather than sitting permanently too low or too high. The sensor in the tank module usually gauges urea concentration by timing an ultrasonic echo and passes the result on digitally. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B shows the weak spot: the sensor flags readings as not ready when the echo is weak, missing or inconsistent, but GM reports that under P206B, not P2B9A. No manufacturer documents P2B9A publicly. Likely triggers are a loose or corroded connector, bubbles or sloshing fluid, and a failing sensor. CARB requires detection of improper reductant, and an unstable quality value stalls that check; GM's patent US9050561B1 cross-checks the sensor against NOx conversion. P206A to P206D are the steady faults.
c: Loose, corroded or water-damaged connector at the DEF tank module
Air bubbles or sloshing DEF disturbing the ultrasonic echo
Urea crystals or deposits on the sensor face
s: Check engine light on
DEF warning message, possibly a countdown to reduced speed or no restart
Fault comes and goes, often after refilling or on rough roads

P2B9B.t: Vehicle Conditions Incorrect for Particulate Matter Sensor Regeneration
P2B9B.d: P2B9B is a status code of the particulate matter sensor behind the diesel particulate filter: the sensor needs to burn its electrodes clean before the next measurement, but operating conditions do not allow it. Heating the ceramic to around 780 °C is only safe once the exhaust is dry. GM's patent US9846110B2 holds the sensor just above the dew point until water vapour is gone, and Ford's 2023 diesel summary requires the dew point to be passed at the sensor before the filter check runs. Long idling, short cold trips or low exhaust temperature can keep postponing the sensor clean-up, and the filter monitor cannot finish. No manufacturer documents P2B9B publicly; it points to driving conditions rather than to a failed part. If the sensor does heat but fails to clean itself, P24D1 is set instead.
c: Short trips and long idling keeping exhaust below the dew point
Faulty exhaust temperature signal misjudging dew point conditions
Low supply voltage to the sensor control unit preventing heating
Engine software setting the enable conditions too narrowly
s: Usually no change in driving
Particulate filter monitor shown as not complete
Code disappears after a longer drive at steady speed

P2B9C.d: P2B9C signals that coolant pump A is powered and commanded but its rotor does not turn, or stops. Ford uses the code in its 2024 gasoline OBD summary as fault type 71 (actuator stuck) under P2600, where pump A is the auxiliary pump in the high-temperature loop for cabin heating; the check runs continuously above 11 V battery voltage over 5 seconds. Brushless pumps detect a locked rotor themselves, typically from high current without rotation, and report it to the engine computer; the GM patent US20160047374A1 explains how comparing measured current and speed with expected values exposes such faults. Usual reasons are a seized bearing, sludge or debris, frozen coolant or a burnt winding. Pump B has P2B63, pump D P2B6A. A pump that only runs slow sets P2B87.
c: Seized bearing or rotor in the auxiliary pump
Sludge, sealant residue or debris jamming the impeller
Coolant frozen in the pump due to weak antifreeze
Burnt motor winding or failed drive electronics
s: Little or no cabin heat
Check engine light
Pump silent when it should run

P2B9D.t: Coolant Pump A Supply Voltage Circuit
P2B9D.d: P2B9D means the power feed of coolant pump A is outside its usable range, as opposed to the command line covered by P2600 to P2603. Ford names it in the 2024 gasoline OBD summary as fault type 1C (feed voltage outside its window) of the cabin-heating auxiliary pump, monitored all the time from 11 V battery voltage with a 5-second window. Since these pumps carry their own electronics, they measure the voltage on their supply pin and report the deviation. Look for a blown fuse, a relay with burnt contacts, corrosion in the plug, a bad ground strap or a weak battery; a voltage-drop test with the pump running finds hidden resistance best. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15) demands monitoring of such outputs. The same fault on pump B is P2B62, on pump D P2B69.
c: Blown fuse or faulty relay in the pump supply
Corroded connector or poor ground at the pump
Weak battery or charging system voltage too low
s: Cabin heat weak or missing
Check engine light
Fault comes and goes with battery condition or electrical load

P2B9E.t: Coolant Pump A Control Module Overtemperature
P2B9E.d: P2B9E is raised by the electronics built into coolant pump A when their temperature gets too high; the pump then derates or shuts down to protect itself. Ford's 2024 OBD summary for gasoline engines lists it as fault type 98 (system over temperature) of the cabin-heating auxiliary pump, monitored continuously once the battery supplies 11 V or more. The drive stage is usually cooled by the coolant it moves, so heat builds up when the pump runs dry or partly in air, when a stiff impeller makes the motor work harder, or when the pump sits close to hot exhaust parts; an ageing power stage can add to it. Check level and bleeding first, then free rotation. Pump B has P2B64, pump D P2B6B. Air alone often shows as P2B86 first.
c: Low coolant or air at the pump, so the electronics lose cooling
Stiff bearing or impeller raising motor load
Heat from nearby exhaust parts or damaged heat shield
Ageing power stage in the pump electronics
s: Cabin heat drops off after some time of driving
Check engine light
Pump stops and restarts after cooling down

P2B9F.d: P2B9F means coolant pump B turns slower than requested. Ford's 2024 gasoline OBD summary places it as underspeed type B2 in the block of base code P261A, where pump B is the auxiliary pump of the high-temperature loop for component cooling no. 1; the check runs continuously from 11 V with a 5-second window. The text line there reads Coolant Pump A, but like P2B62 to P2B65 the entry sits in the pump B block and the J2012 title confirms B, so the A is a misprint. Slow rotation comes from bearing wear, debris or sludge at the impeller, a low supply voltage or tired pump electronics. Unlike P2B63 the pump still turns; with air it tends to run fast instead (P2B65). Pump A uses P2B87, pump C P2BA0, pump D P2BA1. The cooled part may overheat.
c: Worn bearing or dragging impeller in pump B
Debris or sludge slowing the impeller
Low supply voltage or poor ground at the pump
Weak motor or drive electronics in the pump
s: Check engine light
Temperature warning for the cooled component under load
Possible power reduction to protect hot parts

P2BA0.d: P2BA0 reports that coolant pump C does not reach its speed. GM names the code Low Temperature Coolant Loop Pump Underspeed in its diesel ECM tables and treats it as a low out-of-range speed reading: in 2020 (20OBDG04) the printed limit is below -100 rpm in 5 of 8 one-second samples, in 2025 (25OBDG04A) below -50 rpm in 4 of 5; enable conditions are an active pump, 11 V or more at the relay and no cranking. Type B, so the lamp waits for a second faulty trip. Bulletin 21-NA-149 lists P2BA0 among the many codes caused by a chafed engine harness on the 3.0-litre LM2 Duramax in 2021 trucks and SUVs, next to P2C48 for the same pump. Besides wiring, a stuck or worn pump and air in the loop are suspects. Pump B is P2B9F, pump D P2BA1.
c: Engine harness chafed against brackets, shorting pump circuits
Worn or partly seized low-temperature loop pump
Air or low coolant in the low-temperature loop
Low supply voltage at the pump relay
s: Check engine light after the second faulty trip
Parts on the low-temperature loop cooled less, reduced power possible
Further electrical codes when the harness is damaged

P2BA1.d: P2BA1 is set when coolant pump D, a further electric pump in the manufacturer's thermal management, turns slower than its command. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, so which circuit pump D serves and which limits apply is unknown. The same check exists for other letters: Ford's 2024 gasoline summary runs it for pumps A and B as fault type B2 (P2B87, P2B9F), continuously from 11 V, and GM's 2025 tables flag a filtered command-to-feedback gap that persists 8 of 10 seconds. Under CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15), outputs must be checked for a correct reaction to their commands. Likely causes are bearing wear, debris at the impeller, low supply voltage or poor contacts. A blocked pump is P2B6A, air P2B6C. Its loop then gets too little flow.
c: Worn bearing or dragging impeller in pump D
Debris or deposits slowing the impeller
Low supply voltage or high resistance in power or ground
Weak motor or drive electronics in the pump
s: Check engine light or cooling warning, depending on the vehicle
Rising temperature of the part cooled by pump D

P2BA2.d: P2BA2 belongs to the electric main water pump. GM uses it in a way the title does not suggest: on the 2.7-litre L3B (table 19OBDG03D) and in the 2025 table 25OBDG03B the test runs while the pump should be switched off – pump disabled or a request of 0–4 rpm for at least 3 s – and fails if the pump still reports 10 rpm or more for 8 of 10 seconds with over 11 V on board. So GM looks for a pump that keeps turning, Type B with MIL after two trips. A real blocked rotor shows up in GM's scheme as underspeed P2B85. Possible causes are faulty pump electronics, a speed signal that is not plausible, or coolant flow driving the impeller. When the pump will not stop, the engine warms up more slowly. Overspeed with air is P26CE, the command circuit P26CA.
c: Pump electronics ignoring the off command
Implausible speed feedback from the pump
Impeller turned by coolant flow from another pump
Command or enable line fault keeping the pump on
s: Check engine light after two trips
Engine takes longer to reach operating temperature
Pump audible after the engine is switched off

P2BA3.d: P2BA3 concerns the belt-driven starter-generator of mild-hybrid and stop-start engines: the controller has concluded that the machine does not turn the crankshaft or take torque from it as it should, although its electrics seem healthy. The exact detection rule is not published. FCA used the code on 2020 RAM 1500 and Jeep Wrangler 3.6 L eTorque models (bulletins 09-008-20 and 09-007-20), together with P0A92, after a batch of hydraulic belt tensioners let the belt slip; drivers saw the MIL and a flat battery. Audi lists P2BA300 for noisy or thrown belts on A4, A5, A6 and Q5 models and for squealing restarts on its 4.0 L V8 cars, where the generator itself was found intact and the tensioner damper is to be checked. Electrical faults of the machine have their own codes such as P2DC7.
c: Weak or defective belt tensioner or tensioner damper letting the belt slip
Worn, misaligned or thrown poly-V belt
Mechanical damage in the starter-generator (bearing, pulley)
s: Squealing, chirping or grinding from the belt drive, often at start
Engine fails to restart after an automatic stop
Battery runs flat because the machine no longer charges
Electrical system warning or MIL on the instrument panel

P2BA4.d: Many diesel SCR systems rely on the oxidation catalyst ahead of them to turn part of the NO into NO2, because a mix near half NO2 lets the SCR reaction run fast at low temperature. P2BA4 reports that this catalyst no longer delivers the needed gas mix. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (f)(1.2.3)(B) requires this check for 2015 and later diesels, but lets a maker cover it with the regular NMHC efficiency monitor; Ford's 2023 diesel summary does exactly that via P0420. GM and Cummins patents describe two methods: comparing SCR efficiency measured by the NOx sensors, or judging the catalyst's light-off heat after a hydrocarbon dose. No maker documents P2BA4 publicly. P2BA5 is the same check for a coated particulate filter; the driver mainly notices a lit MIL and possibly SCR codes.
c: Oxidation catalyst thermally aged or poisoned (sulphur, oil ash), little NO2 produced
Catalyst inlet face coated with soot or unburnt fuel after injector or EGR problems
Faulty NOx or exhaust temperature sensor distorting the evaluation
Exhaust leak upstream of the catalyst diluting the measured gas
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
SCR efficiency codes such as P20EE set as well
Usually no noticeable change in driving behaviour

P2BA5.d: Some diesel particulate filters carry a precious-metal coating that, besides helping burn soot, oxidises NO to NO2 for the SCR catalyst further down. P2BA5 says this coated filter fails to supply enough NO2. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (f)(9.2.4)(B) demands the check for medium-duty diesels from 2016 and for passenger cars and light trucks from 2019, and lets the maker evaluate the filter alone or together with the oxidation catalyst. Cummins describes judging both by the heat they release after a fuel dose; FEV tests feed gas quality with the NOx sensors around the SCR. No maker documents P2BA5 publicly. Unlike P2002, which flags filtration loss, this code is about the coating; the driver sees the MIL and may later notice weaker passive regeneration.
