c: Filter coating thermally aged, e.g. after very hot or uncontrolled regenerations
Ash or oil additives covering the catalytic layer
Weak upstream oxidation catalyst in a combined evaluation
Exhaust temperature or NOx sensor reading wrongly
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
More frequent active regenerations
SCR efficiency codes may follow

P2BA6.t: NOx Exceedance - SCR NOx Catalyst Performance
P2BA6.d: P2BA6 opens the group of NOx exceedance codes that grew out of the European rules on reagent-based NOx control. Each code names why tailpipe NOx has climbed above the diagnostic limit; here the blame lies with the SCR catalyst itself, while dosing, reagent and EGR still look plausible. Regulation (EU) 2017/1151 Annex XVI lets makers use exhaust NOx sensors to detect such excess, with the warning and inducement chain that follows. CARB separately asks for SCR conversion monitoring, usually reported as P20EE. FEV describes a test that tells a weak catalyst apart from poor feed gas. No maker documents P2BA6 publicly. Expect the MIL and an emissions warning; if not fixed, speed or restart limits may follow.
c: SCR catalyst aged, overheated or chemically poisoned
Urea crystal deposits on mixer or catalyst face
Too little NO2 from upstream oxidation catalyst
s: MIL and emission system warning in the cluster
Countdown to speed limit or no restart after some distance
Higher DEF consumption without better NOx reduction

P2BA7.d: P2BA7 records that NOx control has been lost because the DEF or AdBlue tank has run dry, so no reagent can be dosed. Regulation (EU) 2017/1151 Annex XVI requires a level warning no later than 2,400 km ahead of an empty tank and an inducement that keeps the vehicle from operating with an empty tank, typically by blocking the next engine start after a countdown. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (f)(2.2.3)(B) asks for an empty-reagent diagnosis but exempts makers whose inducement prevents running dry. Ford lists P2BA7 in its 2014 code interpretation table; no public document gives a threshold. The normal level code is P203F; P2BA7 is the consequence once the tank is empty. Refilling with enough fluid usually clears warning and limits.
c: DEF tank simply not refilled despite level warnings
Level sensor reading empty although fluid is present (fault, ice, deposits)
Leaking DEF tank or line emptying the system
Only a small amount refilled, below the quantity the system needs to recognise a refill
s: DEF empty message with restart countdown
Engine will not restart once countdown expires
MIL or emission warning on

P2BA8.t: NOx Exceedence - Interruption of Reagent Dosing Activity
P2BA8.d: With P2BA8 the controller states that NOx went up because reagent dosing stopped although the engine needed it. Regulation (EU) 2017/1151 Annex XVI, point 5.5, treats such an interruption as a case for the driver warning, unless the system paused dosing on purpose in conditions the maker declared to the authority; if dosing is not restored within 50 km, inducement starts. In California, section (f)(2.2.3)(A) of the OBD rule requires reagent delivery to be monitored. No maker documents P2BA8 publicly. The component fault behind the stop, such as pump P208B, pressure P20E8 or injector P2047, usually sets its own code; P2BA8 marks the emission consequence, while P2BA7 covers an empty tank and P2BAA too little consumption.
c: DEF injector clogged or stuck by crystals
Pump failure or pressure not built up
Frozen fluid because tank or line heater fails
Wiring or SCR control unit fault stopping dosing
s: DEF dosing malfunction message with distance countdown
MIL on, further SCR component codes stored
Reduced power or no restart if not repaired

P2BA9.d: P2BA9 blames high NOx on reagent that falls short of the specified quality, e.g. diluted or contaminated DEF. EU Annex XVI wants a wrong-fluid warning and inducement if not fixed within 50 km; CARB asks for improper reductant detection. Jaguar Land Rover bulletin SSM73330 links P2BA9-00/-92 on Range Rover diesels to an incorrect-DEF warning with a restart countdown, often with P2BAE and P2BAF, and points to intake or EGR leaks that fake poor fluid. FCA bulletin 25-003-15 replaced DEF parts on 2015 Grand Cherokee 3.0 diesels contaminated in the plant; for the Ram ProMaster FCA describes a refill monitor that must pass to clear the inducement. Unlike P207F or quality sensor codes, P2BA9 can stem from SCR efficiency alone; check the fluid before replacing parts.
c: DEF diluted with water, aged or replaced by the wrong fluid
Contaminated tank or lines (also from production, FCA 25-003-15)
Air leak after the MAF sensor or at EGR cooler joints misleading the NOx model (JLR)
Outdated engine software or faulty NOx sensor
s: Incorrect DEF quality message with restart countdown
MIL on, often with P2BAE and P2BAF
Speed or power limit if the countdown runs out

P2BAA.d: P2BAA means less reagent is actually reaching the exhaust than the dosing strategy asks for, so NOx stays too high. EU Annex XVI sets the frame: actual and demanded consumption are compared, and a gap above 50 % over 30 minutes triggers the warning. GM uses P2BAA on its diesel engines as Reductant Delivery Performance, Type A after one trip: 14OBDG04 checks a filtered DEF pressure drop against 365 kPa, while 16OBDG04 and 18OBDG04 compare the pressure drop after each injection with an expected value derived from pump duty. GM bulletin 25-NA-042 cures false P2BAA on 2023 Silverado 4500HD to 6500HD (L5D) with an ECM update. Neighbours: P2BA8 for stopped dosing, P2BA7 for an empty tank; drivers see a service emission system message.
c: Partially blocked DEF injector delivering too little
Weak DEF pump or clogged pump filter
Calibration error setting the code without a fault (GM 25-NA-042)
Leak in the pressure line returning fluid before the injector
s: Service emission or exhaust fluid system message
MIL on after one trip
DEF level falls more slowly than usual

P2BAB.d: P2BAB attributes excess NOx to exhaust gas recirculation that delivers the wrong amount of gas, so combustion temperature and raw NOx rise. It belongs to the European NOx control rules: Regulation (EU) No 582/2011, Annex XIII, handles tampering-related monitoring through UN Regulation 49 and keeps an EGR valve counter, so an impeded valve leads to warning and inducement. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (f)(6.2) separately demands low and high flow detection, normally reported as P0401 and P0402. No maker documents P2BAB publicly; it serves as the emissions link to those EGR flow codes, which point to the actual part. P2BAC is used when EGR is switched off entirely. The driver sees the MIL and, depending on the maker, a NOx warning and later reduced power.
c: EGR valve sooted up or sticking
EGR cooler or pipe partly blocked
Faulty EGR position sensor or air mass meter distorting flow estimate
Leak in the intake or EGR path
s: MIL on, EGR flow codes stored
Rough running or sooting with too much EGR
Power reduction possible if not repaired

P2BAC.d: P2BAC is reserved for the case where exhaust gas recirculation is not just off target but shut down altogether, whether by an unplugged valve, a blocked path, an unauthorised software change or a defect that leaves the valve closed. The European rules treat this as a typical tampering scenario: Regulation (EU) No 582/2011, Annex XIII, carries an EGR valve counter that ends first in a warning and then in inducement. California's rule, section (f)(6.2.1) of 13 CCR 1968.2, requires a malfunction when EGR flow is absent although expected. No maker documents P2BAC publicly. Compared with P2BAB, which covers wrong flow, this code needs a hard stop; component codes for valve circuit or position usually come along and point to the cause.
c: EGR valve unplugged, blanked off or disabled
EGR valve stuck closed or actuator failed
Modified engine software with EGR switched off
Open or short in the EGR valve circuit
s: MIL and NOx warning, later inducement
Harder, louder combustion
EGR circuit or position codes stored as well

P2BAD.d: P2BAD is the catch-all of the series: NOx after the SCR is measured too high, yet none of the specific causes from P2BA6 to P2BAC can be pinned down. GM uses it on the 2014 Duramax 6.6 L LML as Exhaust NOx Concentration High - Unknown Reason: the measured SCR efficiency, minus an offset-corrected model value, is filtered over time and fails once the difference drops below zero, with both NOx sensors active for over 60 s; Type A. GM PIP5007 notes that from 2012 this code takes over from P20EE/P207F as the diagnostic path when the DIC reports poor fluid quality. Nissan lists it as NOx Concentration Exceeded for the 2016 Titan XD with the Cummins 5.0 L and fixes it by reflashing the ECM. Diagnosis starts with DEF quality, dosing and sensors.
c: Poor DEF quality or partly blocked dosing without a specific code
Upstream or downstream NOx sensor drifting
Engine control software needing an update (Nissan Titan XD)
s: Exhaust fluid quality poor or emission warning
MIL on after the first failed run
Speed limit countdown if the condition persists

P2BAE.t: NOx Exceedence - NOx Control Monitoring System
P2BAE.d: P2BAE is tied to the system that watches NOx control itself, typically the NOx sensors and the logic that compares measured emissions with the permitted level. Regulation (EU) 2017/1151 Annex XVI allows exhaust NOx sensors to replace separate quality and consumption checks, with warning and inducement once the NOx OBD limit is passed; the heavy-duty rules keep counters for monitoring system faults. Deutz stores P2BAE-00 on its EMR L1 controllers under SPN 4090, FMI 15, as a high NOx warning from the SCR efficiency monitor. Jaguar Land Rover bulletins list P2BAE among the DEF inducement codes, mostly next to P2BAF and a root code such as P2BA9 or P249C; it clears once that cause is fixed. The driver sees the MIL and a DEF message.
c: Underlying SCR fault such as poor DEF quality or dosing pressure deviation
NOx sensor damaged, badly mounted or contaminated
Air trapped in the DEF system
s: MIL with DEF dosing malfunction message
No-restart countdown in the cluster
Stored together with P2BAF and a root cause code

P2BAF.d: P2BAF does not name a faulty part; it states that the driver inducement of the NOx control system has been activated. Regulation (EU) 2017/1151 Annex XVI requires such an inducement once reagent is lacking, of wrong quality, under-consumed or not dosed, typically counting down to a blocked engine restart; the reason and the distance driven with it go into non-erasable records kept for 30,000 km or 800 days. FCA bulletin 08-103-19 lists P2BAF-00 as Driver Inducement Active on the 2020 Jeep Compass 2.0 diesel, there caused by body control module software. Jaguar Land Rover lists P2BAF with P2BAE as DEF inducement codes next to root codes like P2BA9 or P208B. Repair the root code first; P2BAF then clears. P241D, by contrast, signals a forced shutdown.
c: Active SCR fault (DEF quality, dosing, level) that started the inducement
Control module software fault, e.g. BCM on Jeep Compass (FCA 08-103-19)
Root cause fixed but the clearing monitor has not yet run
s: Countdown message until no restart
MIL and DEF system warning on
Speed or power limited, engine may not restart

P2BB0.d: On engines that burn compressed natural gas, LPG or another fuel besides petrol or diesel, the controller can estimate how much gas it has injected and compare that with how fast the tank actually empties, judged by tank pressure or level. P2BB0 means the tank drains noticeably more slowly than the injection quantity implies. That points less to a leak than to wrong bookkeeping: a drifting tank pressure or temperature sensor, injectors or a regulator that deliver less gas than commanded (often with lean codes), or the engine having run on petrol longer than assumed. No manufacturer documents P2BB0 publicly. FCA patented exactly this consumption balance for CNG vehicles, and CARB counts such engines as alternate-fueled vehicles with their own monitoring plans. The opposite case is P2BB1.
c: Alternative fuel tank pressure or temperature sensor reading wrong
Gas injectors or filter restricted, less gas delivered than commanded
Pressure regulator supplying too little pressure
Fuel mode or control software not matching actual operation
s: MIL on, sometimes together with lean mixture codes
Gas range or gauge reading implausible
Engine switches to petrol more often than usual

P2BB1.d: P2BB1 is set when the alternative fuel store, typically a CNG cylinder, loses more gas than the injected quantity can account for. The main suspicion is a leak between tank and injectors, which is why this check doubles as a safety monitor. FCA's patent US9284895 describes it for natural gas vehicles: tank pressure is sampled at two moments, the gas mass delivered per cylinder charge is integrated over the same period, and a leak is flagged when actual use exceeds the expected figure by more than a tolerance, about 3 % or 2 mg per second and cycle in its example. No carmaker publishes P2BB1 itself. A sensor that exaggerates the pressure drop or an injector stuck open can produce the same result. Smell gas: park outdoors and have it checked. Too little use is P2BB0.
c: Gas leak at fittings, lines, regulator or tank valve
Gas injector leaking or sticking open
Tank pressure or temperature sensor exaggerating the pressure drop
s: Gas range much shorter than usual
Gas smell around the vehicle
MIL on, gas mode may be locked out

P2BB2.d: P2BB2 reports that the tank for the second fuel, mostly CNG or LPG, has been drawn down to its usable minimum. It is a status message rather than a component fault: a bi-fuel vehicle simply goes back to petrol. GM's bulletins for its bi-fuel models show the logic: the ECM derives the gas level from the tank pressure sensor, the 2013 Silverado and Sierra 2500HD gauge reads empty at roughly 500 psi and the 2015 Impala at about 400 psi, and when the gas is used up the engine changes to petrol on its own; GM's documents name no DTC for this step. No maker documents P2BB2 openly. If it appears with a full tank, suspect the tank pressure or level sensor (P019E, P01AF) or a closed tank shutoff valve (P224C). CARB treats such engines as alternate-fueled vehicles.
c: Gas tank actually used up to its reserve
Tank pressure or level sensor reading too low
Tank shutoff valve closed or not opening
s: Engine runs on petrol only, gas mode cannot be selected
Gas gauge shows empty or low-level warning

P2BB3.d: Where a separate driver module powers the fuel pump, the ECM sends a duty-cycle command and the module reports what it actually applies. P2BB3 means these two values disagree beyond a tolerance, so the pump is not running at the requested speed although no open or short has been found. GM documents this in its 2018 engine tables (18OBDG04) for vehicles with a fuel tank zone module: its fuel pump driver control module compares measured with received duty cycle every 12.5 ms once ignition voltage exceeds 6 V, sensor-bus data are valid and P0231, P0232, P023F and the driver overtemperature fault P1255 are absent; Type A, MIL on the first trip. Ford's petrol summary checks the pump secondary circuit only with P0231/P0232 and its own P1237. Expect weak fuel pressure.
c: Fuel pump driver or tank zone module not delivering the commanded output
High resistance in the pump supply or ground connection
Worn or binding fuel pump drawing abnormal current
Disturbed data link between ECM and pump module
s: MIL on
Hesitation or power loss under load
Long cranking or stalling

P2BB4.t: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 4 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2BB4.d: This code covers jumps in the signal of the fourth coolant temperature sensor that coolant cannot physically make. GM explains the method in the 2019 edition of its engine tables for the L3B and related engines (19OBDG03D): from each reading and the sensor's time constant the software predicts an upper and a lower bound for the next sample, and a step beyond either counts as erratic; 5 s of failures inside a 6 s window set the code as Type B, MIL on the second trip, and it stays blocked while a hard circuit low/high fault is present. P2BB4 itself is missing from the 2025 tables. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 names it among the effects of a chafed engine harness on 2019–2021 GM light-duty trucks. A loose terminal is the classic cause; steady open or short faults are P2AFE and P2AFF.
c: Loose or corroded terminal at the sensor 4 connector
Engine harness chafed, wire making intermittent contact
Internal intermittent break in the sensor element
s: MIL on after two drives
Jumping temperature value in live data
Cooling fans or thermal management reacting erratically

P2BB5.t: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 5 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2BB5.d: P2BB5 is the erratic-signal code for coolant sensor 5. Unlike the hard circuit faults P2B2D and P2B2E, the reading here stays within the valid range but changes faster than the sensor's thermal inertia allows, which betrays a contact that briefly opens or shorts. GM has carried the code in both its 2019 L3B/common tables (19OBDG03D) and its 2025 ECM tables (25OBDG03B) with the same rule: limits for the next sample are calculated from the previous one, and violations for 5 s within a 6 s window store P2BB5 as Type B, MIL after two trips. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 lists it among the codes a chafed engine harness causes on 2019–2021 Silverado and Sierra 1500 pickups. Wiggle-test the harness while watching live data before replacing the sensor.
c: Chafed engine harness with intermittent contact in the sensor 5 wires
Loose, spread or corroded connector terminal
s: MIL on after the second trip
Sensor 5 value spikes in live data
Often stored together with other harness-related codes

P2BB6.d: P2BB6 is the general circuit code for a sixth coolant temperature sensor, intended for control units that only know that the circuit is faulty and do not distinguish a grounded from an open or shorted-high line. Six or more coolant sensors appear on engines with split cooling, rotary coolant valves or separate branches for head, block, radiator and heater; which physical sensor gets number 6 is the manufacturer's decision. No manufacturer documents P2BB6 publicly. GM does read a sixth coolant channel in its 2019 and 2025 ECM tables, but reports its faults only through the specific codes P2BB8 and P2BB9. Under CARB rules each coolant temperature input must be tested for broken circuits and for readings beyond its plausible span. Unplugged connectors and broken leads are the likely reasons.
c: Sensor 6 connector unplugged, damaged or corroded
Open or shorted wire between sensor 6 and the ECM
s: MIL on
Sensor 6 shows a fixed substitute or implausible value
Fans may run continuously as a precaution

P2BB7.t: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 6 Circuit Range/Performance
P2BB7.d: With P2BB7 the sixth coolant sensor delivers an electrically valid value that nevertheless makes no sense. Plausibility tests of this kind compare the sensor with the other engine temperatures after a long cold soak, expect a clear rise once the engine warms up, and flag a value that never moves. CARB requires such rationality monitoring for coolant temperature inputs on which emission functions depend. No manufacturer publishes a set condition for P2BB7; GM, whose 2019 and 2025 engine tables do read a sixth coolant input, lists only the electrical codes P2BB8, P2BB9 and P2BBA for it. Possible reasons are a drifting element, a sensor sitting in a branch without flow because a pump or valve has failed, or contact resistance. Pure circuit faults are P2BB6, P2BB8 and P2BB9.
c: Sensor 6 element drifted out of its characteristic curve
No coolant flow at sensor 6 due to failed pump, valve or air pocket
Contact resistance at connector or terminals
s: MIL on, usually only after a cold start and warm-up
Sensor 6 value lags or stays flat compared with the other coolant sensors

P2BB8.t: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 6 Circuit Low
P2BB8.d: Coolant sensors are NTC thermistors, so a low signal from sensor 6 means a very small resistance that the ECM would have to read as extreme heat; in practice a signal wire touching ground or a shorted element. GM sets P2BB8 when the sixth coolant channel drops below 47.5 Ω in its 2019 L3B/common tables (19OBDG03D) or 55 Ω in the 2025 ECM tables (25OBDG03B), both roughly equal to 150 °C, if that persists for 5 of any 6 seconds; the fault is Type B, so the MIL comes on after the second trip. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 includes P2BB8 in the long list of codes caused by chafed engine harnesses on 2019–2021 light-duty pickups. Expect the cooling fans to run hard as a safeguard. If the same sensor's line is broken or touches battery voltage, P2BB9 is stored instead.
c: Sensor 6 signal wire shorted to ground, e.g. chafed harness
Moisture or coolant in the connector bridging the pins
s: MIL on after two trips
Sensor 6 shows an implausibly high temperature
Radiator fans running at high speed

P2BB9.t: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 6 Circuit High
P2BB9.d: A high signal from coolant sensor 6 corresponds to a resistance so large that only an interrupted circuit, a disconnected plug or a wire shorted to a voltage source explains it; read as temperature it would be colder than −60 °C. GM's tables check for this once the engine has run more than 10 s or intake air is warmer than −20 °C. For the sixth-sensor channel the limit is about 298 kΩ in the 2019 L3B/common edition (19OBDG03D) and about 174 kΩ in 2025 (25OBDG03B); 5 s of failures within 6 s give a Type B fault with the MIL on the second trip. As with P2B2E, GM's row names the radiator sensor while the low fault is tied to sensor 6. Bulletin 21-NA-149 lists P2BB9 for chafed harnesses on 2019–2021 pickups. The grounded counterpart is P2BB8.
c: Sensor 6 connector unplugged or not latched
Broken signal or ground wire, or signal shorted to voltage
s: MIL on after the second trip
Sensor 6 shows about −40 °C or lower
Fans may run continuously

P2BBA.t: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 6 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2BBA.d: P2BBA catches short dropouts or spikes in the sixth coolant sensor signal that never last long enough to count as a steady low or high fault. GM includes it in its 2019 L3B/common ECM tables (19OBDG03D) and in the 2025 edition (25OBDG03B): based on the last reading and the sensor time constant, the software allows only a limited change per sample, and if the signal leaps past that window for 5 s within 6 s the code is stored as Type B with the MIL on the second trip. The check pauses while P2BB8 or P2BB9 are active. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 lists P2BBA among the codes from chafed engine harnesses on 2019–2021 Silverado and Sierra 1500. Moving the harness during a live-data check usually reveals the spot; replacing the sensor alone rarely helps.
c: Chafed engine harness with intermittent contact
Loose or corroded terminal at sensor 6 or the ECM
Sensor element with intermittent internal break
s: MIL on after two trips, may go out again
Sensor 6 value jumps in live data
Other harness-related codes stored at the same time

P2BBB.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Circuit
P2BBB.d: P2BBB is the general fault of the position feedback from bypass valve A, the electrically driven valve that lets boosted air flow back from the compressor outlet to its inlet when the throttle closes or boost has to be trimmed. It is not the wastegate on the exhaust side. The engine module reads the sensor as a share of its 5 V reference; this code covers an open line or a signal it cannot sort into low or high. GM's 2019 tables for the supercharged 6.2-litre LT5 (Corvette ZR1) watch this sensor but publish only the low and high codes P2BBC and P2BBD; no manufacturer documents P2BBB itself publicly. An Achates Power patent explains why the feedback matters: without a valid position the commanded opening cannot be verified and boost control loses accuracy. Expect a warning light and reduced boost.
c: Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the bypass valve position sensor
Chafed or broken signal, reference or ground wire in the harness near the compressor
Internal fault of the position sensor in the valve actuator
Faulty sensor input or 5 V reference inside the engine control module
s: Check engine light
Reduced boost and noticeably less power
Whoosh or flutter noise when lifting off the throttle

P2BBC.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Circuit Low
P2BBC.d: P2BBC sets when the position signal of the bypass valve A sensor sits too low – usually an open signal wire, a short to ground or a lost 5 V supply to the sensor. GM uses the code on the 2019 Corvette ZR1 with the supercharged LT5, whose electronic compressor recirculation valve (eCRV) reports its position as a share of the reference voltage: a raw value under 10 % in 10 of 14 samples taken every 100 ms counts as a failure, checked while relay voltage is at least 11 V and the engine is not cranking. It is a Type A fault, so the MIL comes on in the first trip. The opposite case, a signal stuck near the reference, is P2BBD; a valve that does not follow its command is P23AA. Unable to trust the valve position, the module typically limits boost.
c: Signal wire shorted to ground or chafed against the engine
Open 5 V reference wire or reference shorted by another sensor on the same supply
Pushed-out or corroded terminal in the valve connector
Defective position sensor in the valve actuator
s: Check engine light on in the first trip
Limited boost and weaker acceleration
Possibly further 5 V reference codes if the supply is shorted

P2BBD.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Circuit High
P2BBD.d: P2BBD is the high-side counterpart: the position signal from bypass valve A rises toward the full reference voltage. That points to a short to the 5 V supply or to battery voltage, a broken sensor ground – the signal then floats upward – or a defective sensor. On GM's 2019 Corvette ZR1 with the LT5 V8 the module flags a raw position reading above 95 % of reference in 10 out of 14 samples at 100 ms intervals, with at least 11 V on the powertrain relay and outside of cranking; Type A, so the MIL lights at once. P2BBC covers the low side and P2BBB a general circuit fault of the same sensor. With the reading implausible, the module usually holds the valve in a safe position and reduces boost, so the car feels flat and may make noise when the throttle snaps shut.
c: Open sensor ground wire or corroded ground terminal
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage
Defective position sensor in the valve actuator
Moisture in the valve connector creating a leakage path
s: Check engine light on immediately
Reduced power because boost is limited
Unusual noise when lifting off the throttle

P2BBE.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Position Exceeded Learning Limit
P2BBE.d: P2BBE is not a wiring fault but a failed end-stop learn. GM's 2019 tables for the LT5 Corvette ZR1 describe how the electronic recirculation valve is taught after each engine shutdown: the module first drives it to the closed stop and stores the sensor value, then repeats this for the open stop. If the learned closed value falls outside 85–95 % of the sensor range, or the learned open value outside 10–20 %, the code sets at once (Type A, MIL in one trip). The learn only runs while no position-sensor or valve-circuit fault is active. Typical causes are carbon or oil deposits, a bent flap or shaft, a worn actuator gear or a sensor that has shifted. Since the learn needs a key-off, a repair is only confirmed after a full shutdown. Circuit faults of the same sensor are P2BBB to P2BBD.
c: Oil or carbon deposits keeping the valve from reaching its stops
Bent flap or shaft, or worn actuator gear
Position sensor shifted or drifted after a repair or with age
Non-matching replacement valve with a different travel range
s: Check engine light after the engine has been switched off and restarted
Boost limited or erratic on lift-off

P2BBF.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Supply Voltage Low
P2BBF.d: P2BBF concerns the power side of bypass valve A rather than its position feedback. Electric recirculation valves are moved by a small DC motor fed through an H-bridge in the engine module, and the bridge chip itself flags when its supply drops too far. GM documents exactly this for the eCRV of the 2019 Corvette ZR1: the motor driver reports low voltage in 80 of 100 samples at 12.5 ms, with relay voltage at least 11 V and the engine not cranking; Type A, MIL at once. Data sheets for throttle-type H-bridges such as NXP's MC33926 show how such an output stage switches off below its undervoltage lockout and reports this on a status line. Causes are a weak feed, a poor module ground or connector, or an internal driver fault. Without drive power the valve stays where it last stopped.
c: High resistance in the engine module feed, fuse or ground connection
Weak battery or charging fault causing voltage dips
Corroded pins at the engine module or valve connector
Internal fault of the H-bridge driver in the engine module
s: Check engine light on immediately
Valve no longer moves, boost limited or surging on lift-off
Often accompanied by other low-voltage codes

P2BC0.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P2BC0.d: P2BC0 sets when the output stage that drives bypass valve A reports too much current or overheating. GM applies it to the electric recirculation valve of the LT5-powered 2019 Corvette ZR1: when the H-bridge raises its flag in 80 out of 100 checks spaced 12.5 ms apart, with relay voltage of 11 V or more and no cranking, a Type A fault with immediate MIL results. Integrated H-bridges protect themselves by regulating current, folding it back as the chip warms and finally shutting off – NXP gives a thermal limit of about 175–200 °C junction temperature for its MC33926. Excess current usually comes from a sticking or jammed valve, a shorted motor winding or a short between the motor leads. P2BBF is the low-supply case of the same driver, P00D7 an overheated valve itself. The valve stops responding and boost is reduced.
c: Sticking or jammed valve making the motor draw high current
Shorted winding in the valve actuator motor
Motor leads shorted to each other or to ground in the harness
Overheated or damaged H-bridge driver in the engine module
s: Check engine light on immediately
Reduced boost and less power
Compressor surge noise when lifting off

P2BC1.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump A Stuck/Stalled
P2BC1.d: P2BC1 means the electric pump that circulates coolant through the charge air cooler loop is powered, but its rotor will not turn or stops under load; the pump electronics see high current at little or no speed and report this to the engine module. Audi documents the code as P2BC100 in bulletin 2080825 for 2025–2026 A5/S5 and Q5 models with engine codes DXBA and DXCA: after the car stood unused longer than two months, pump V188 may stick. The MIL and a reduced-power message appear. If the pump runs again on an actuator test and the entry was only intermittent, it is cleared, otherwise the pump is replaced. FCA lists P2BC1-00 on 2018–2019 Alfa Romeo Giulia and Stelvio 2.0 turbos among codes addressed by a software flash. Over- and underspeed of the same pump are P2B83 and P2B84.
c: Rotor stuck after a long standstill (Audi bulletin 2080825)
Debris, deposits or a worn bearing blocking the impeller
Engine module software needing an update (FCA bulletins for Giulia/Stelvio)
Ice in the loop due to insufficient antifreeze
s: Check engine light, often with a reduced-power message
Hot charge air and less power under load
No running noise from the pump during an actuator test

P2BC2.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump A Supply Voltage Circuit
P2BC2.d: P2BC2 points to the power feed of charge air cooler pump A: the pump or its controller sees a supply that is missing or outside its working window. Typical causes are a blown fuse, a relay with burnt contacts, a broken or corroded feed or ground wire, or a water-damaged plug; a weak battery can contribute. No manufacturer documents P2BC2 publicly. Ford's 2024 OBD summary shows the same fault type on its smart auxiliary coolant pumps: the pump driver flags a supply outside its permitted range (P2B9D for pump A), checked continuously from 11 V battery voltage and logged after five seconds. CARB requires charge air cooler systems and their electrical components to be monitored. Without a proper supply the pump stops, the charge air warms up and the engine may limit power. A pump that is powered but blocked is P2BC1.
c: Blown fuse or faulty relay in the pump feed
Broken or corroded supply or ground wire
Water ingress or corrosion in the pump connector
s: Check engine light or engine warning message
Pump does not run, charge air temperature rises
Reduced power in hot conditions or under load

P2BC3.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump A Control Module Overtemperature
P2BC3.d: The control electronics of an electric coolant pump sit inside the pump body and are cooled by the liquid flowing through it. P2BC3 means the electronics of charge air cooler pump A report a temperature above their limit. Far more often than a defective board, the reason is a low coolant level, air trapped in the pump after service, a partly blocked impeller drawing extra current, or a mounting spot exposed to engine heat. No manufacturer documents P2BC3 publicly. Ford's 2019 hybrid OBD summary shows how such a check works on its LIN-connected engine coolant pump (P26D2): the pump sends its module temperature and the PCM flags a value above 130 °C; the 2024 summary lists the same overtemperature type for the auxiliary pumps. The pump then derates or stops, and charge air temperature rises.
c: Low coolant level or air trapped in the low-temperature loop
Partly blocked impeller or worn bearing raising motor current
Fault in the pump's integrated electronics
Missing heat shield or pump placed close to hot engine parts
s: Check engine light or engine warning message
Pump runs slower or switches off, especially in hot weather
Hot charge air and reduced power

P2BC4.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor B Circuit
P2BC4.d: P2BC4 is the catch-all electrical code for positive contactor B of the charging system, the second charging switch on the plus side next to contactor A (P0D07). Which charging path B serves is up to the maker: Mercedes-Benz files its B codes under the DC charge connection unit of its plug-in hybrids, EQB and eSprinter, Mazda under the on-board charger branch of its two large plug-in SUVs, and Audi calls it charging contactor 2 on the Q8 e-tron. No manufacturer documents P2BC4 itself publicly. Under CARB the charging system of plug-in vehicles has to be supervised, and a GM patent judges such contactors by their coil current. Fused or non-closing contacts are P2BC5/P2BC6, driver faults P2BC7–P2BCA, the minus side P2BCB. Usually only the affected charging mode is lost.
c: Coil of positive contactor B open or shorted
Wiring or connector fault in the contactor B branch
Fault or software issue in the controlling module
s: DC fast charging or on-board charger charging (depending on design) refused
Charging fault message in the cluster or app
Driving usually still possible

P2BC5.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor B Stuck Closed
P2BC5.d: P2BC5 reports that positive charging contactor B still conducts after the open command, normally because its contacts have fused. Mercedes-Benz stores it, often with P2BCC, in the DC charge connection unit (N116/5, on the eSprinter N24/6) of GLE, E- and S-Class plug-in hybrids, the EQB and the eSprinter; after a DC session the vehicle refuses to start. Bulletin LI47.70-P-079912 blames current ripple, overcurrent or overvoltage from the station and contacts that part too late, and prescribes a software update plus a contactor-fault reset rather than a new unit. Mazda lists it as OBC contactor (+) stuck on in CX-90 (from 2024) and CX-70 (from 2025) plug-in hybrids and swaps Junction Box No. 2 (30-003-26). The reverse fault is P2BC6, the minus side P2BCC.
c: Contacts of positive contactor B welded, e.g. after current peaks at the end of charging
Software of the charging module judges the contactor state wrongly (Mercedes update)
Ripple, overcurrent or overvoltage from the charging station
Coil driver does not switch off
s: Vehicle will not start after DC charging (Mercedes)
High-voltage or hybrid system warning in the cluster
Further charging blocked

P2BC6.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor B Stuck Open
P2BC6.d: P2BC6 means positive charging contactor B does not close when commanded, so the plus side of that charging branch stays dead and the session aborts or never starts. The only maker documenting it publicly is Mazda: on the 2024–2026 CX-90 and 2025–2026 CX-70 plug-in hybrids it reads OBC contactor (+) stuck off, listed with the welded cases P2BC5 and P2BCC. Mazda traces all three to a contact-welding problem in these contactors and fits a new Junction Box No. 2 (bulletin 30-003-26). GM's analogous test for contactor A on the Chevrolet Volt (P0D09) shows the principle: during precharge the voltage on the charger side must build up, and a reading under 10 V ends the check as failed. Welding is P2BC5, the negative side P2BCD. Driving normally continues.
c: Contactor B damaged inside and no longer closing (Mazda junction box)
Coil supply or drive line interrupted
Charging control software misjudging the closing check
s: Charging session stops or does not start
Hybrid system malfunction message (Mazda)
Driving usually unaffected

P2BC7.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor B Control Circuit/Open
P2BC7.d: P2BC7 concerns the coil drive line of positive charging contactor B, not its main contacts: the module compares its command with the voltage and current it measures on that line and sets the code when the line is broken or the driver that does not follow. No manufacturer documents P2BC7 publicly. GM's test for the twin code of contactor A (P0D0A) on the Chevrolet Volt shows the method: with the driver off, more than 4 V on the output means an open, and with it on, a coil current under 57 mA counts as open too; the code needs 40 bad readings in a window of 50, taken every 12.5 ms. Monitoring of charging hardware on plug-in models is a CARB requirement. Usual causes: broken wire, loose plug, open coil. Range/performance, low and high are P2BC8–P2BCA, the minus side P2BCE. The charging mode behind contactor B is lost.
c: Control wire or connector to contactor B interrupted
Coil of positive contactor B open
Driver stage in the control module defective
s: Charging via the contactor B path not possible
Charging fault indication

P2BC8.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor B Control Circuit Range/Performance
P2BC8.d: P2BC8 flags a control circuit of positive charging contactor B that is connected but behaves implausibly: the coil draws a current that does not fit the command, the line voltage lies in an unexpected band, or pulling in takes too long. No manufacturer documents P2BC8 publicly. CARB demands rationality checks in addition to circuit checks for the charging components of plug-in vehicles. A GM patent explains one way to judge a coil: send a short pulse, record the current response and compare it with stored values, which reveals a winding or armature that no longer behaves as designed. Likely culprits are corrosion at the pins, a coil with drifting resistance and an ageing output stage. Opens are P2BC7, hard low or high readings P2BC9/P2BCA, the contactor A equivalent P0D0B. Charging may work only intermittently.
c: Contact resistance at connectors of the control line
Coil resistance of contactor B outside specification
Driver stage in the module degraded
s: Charging works only now and then
Charging aborts with a fault message

P2BC9.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor B Control Circuit Low
P2BC9.d: P2BC9 is the low-signal fault on the coil feed of plus-side charging contactor B: the module measures less voltage on that wire than its command calls for, most often because the wire touches ground or the output stage is being dragged down. With a high-side feed the coil is then starved and the contactor never pulls in, or the output stage trips its own protection. No manufacturer documents P2BC9 publicly. GM notes for its corresponding contactor A test on the Chevrolet Volt (P0D0A) that the open-circuit check cannot detect a short to ground, so this case needs a check of its own. CARB requires monitoring of the charging system on plug-in vehicles. Expect insulation rubbed through on the battery casing or moisture inside a plug. P2BCA is the high counterpart, P2BD0 the same fault on the minus side. That charging mode is then refused.
c: Control wire of contactor B shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion in a connector
Coil of contactor B internally shorted
s: Charging session does not start
Charging fault message

P2BCA.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor B Control Circuit High
P2BCA.d: P2BCA means the wire energising the coil of positive charging contactor B shows too much voltage, caused by contact with battery voltage or an output stage stuck in the on state; the contactor could then pull in uncommanded. Audi documents the code as charging contactor 2, short to positive, in the hybrid battery management module (address 008C) of the 2024 Q8 and SQ8 e-tron, including Sportback. Typical case: after AC charging the drive system refuses to come on, with U059B00, P0ADC00 and P0AE000 stored alongside. Audi attributes this to diagnostic software that reacts too sensitively and, in bulletin 2073482 (several revisions), suggests a 20-minute bus sleep before towing. P2BC9 is the low case, P2BD1 the minus side. Here the car may be immobilised.
c: Control wire of contactor B shorted to supply voltage
Driver stage does not switch off
s: Drive system cannot be activated after charging (Audi)
Drive system and electrical system fault warnings
Charging blocked

P2BCB.t: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor B Circuit
P2BCB.d: P2BCB is the general electrical code for negative contactor B of the charging system, which closes the return path of the second charging branch to the traction battery. No manufacturer documents P2BCB publicly. Where B serves DC fast charging, each pole usually has its own contactor so the inlet is isolated from the pack whenever no charger is connected; a Hyundai patent on quick-charge relays tests the plus and minus relay one after the other for exactly that reason. A Ford patent swaps the order in which the two charger contactors close from one session to the next and checks the last one closed for welding first. CARB requires monitoring of charging components on plug-in vehicles. Stuck closed and open are P2BCC/P2BCD, driver faults P2BCE–P2BD1, the plus side P2BC4, contactor A minus P0D0E.
c: Coil of negative contactor B open or shorted
Wiring or connector fault on the return-side contactor
Fault in the module that drives contactor B
s: Charging in the affected mode refused
Charging fault message
Driving usually still possible

P2BCC.t: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor B Stuck Closed
P2BCC.d: P2BCC says negative charging contactor B is still closed although the module ordered it open – in practice fused contacts on the return side. Mercedes-Benz lists it in the DC charge connection unit next to P2BC5 and P0E8929 (DC input current too high); the plug-in hybrid, EQB or eSprinter then cannot be started after DC charging. The bulletins name ripple and overvoltage from the station and contacts that open too late, and call for a software update and a contactor-fault reset instead of a new unit. Mazda names it OBC contactor (−) stuck on in the same bulletin and also prescribes a new Junction Box No. 2. Hyundai and Toyota patents find such welding by opening one pole while the other stays closed and checking the voltage behind it. P2BC5 is the plus side, P2BCD the reverse fault.
c: Contacts of negative contactor B welded at the end of charging
Current ripple or overvoltage from the DC station
s: Vehicle will not start after DC charging (Mercedes)
High-voltage system warning
Charging blocked

P2BCD.t: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor B Stuck Open
P2BCD.d: P2BCD is set when negative charging contactor B fails to close, so the charging branch lacks its return path and no current can flow even with the plus side connected. No manufacturer documents P2BCD publicly; Mazda lists the welded minus case P2BCC and the non-closing plus case P2BC6 for the CX-90 PHEV, but not this one. GM's Volt test for positive contactor A (P0D09) illustrates how a non-closing contactor shows up: with the charging and precharge contactors commanded on, the charger-side voltage stays below 10 V, and 8 failures in 9 samples end the check. Under CARB rules the charging hardware of plug-in vehicles must be supervised. Typical causes are burnt or contaminated contacts, a weak coil supply and module software. P2BCC is the welded variant, P2BC6 the plus side, P0D10 the contactor A twin. Charging aborts.
c: Negative contactor B burnt or mechanically not closing
Coil supply too weak or interrupted
Charging control software misjudging the check
s: Charging stops or never starts
Charging fault message

P2BCE.t: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor B Control Circuit/Open
P2BCE.d: P2BCE watches the coil drive of negative charging contactor B for an open line or a driver whose real state differs from its command. No manufacturer documents P2BCE publicly. The closest published test is GM's P0D11 for minus contactor A in the Volt and the ELR: an output above 4 V with the driver off, a voltage close to supply, or a coil current under 57 mA with the driver on all count as faults, and the status of the charging high-voltage interlock belongs to the enable conditions; GM rates it Type A. CARB makes such charging-circuit checks mandatory for plug-in models. Broken wires near the battery, pushed-back terminals and an open coil top the list. Range/performance, low and high are P2BCF–P2BD1, the plus side P2BC7. Without its return contactor that charging mode is lost.
c: Control wire or terminal of negative contactor B open
Coil of negative contactor B open
Driver stage in the module defective
s: Charging via the contactor B path not possible
Charging fault indication

P2BCF.t: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor B Control Circuit Range/Performance
P2BCF.d: P2BCF points to a control circuit on negative charging contactor B that is neither open nor shorted yet still implausible: coil current, line voltage or switching time fall outside the window that belongs to the commanded state. No manufacturer documents P2BCF publicly, and no published GM table has such a check for a charging contactor coil. CARB asks for rationality checks in addition to circuit checks on plug-in charging components. GM's patent on diagnosing the battery disconnect unit shows the kind of evidence available: how the coil current rises after a brief pulse, held against a stored profile, separates a healthy contactor from a sluggish one. A shifted coil resistance, corrosion in the connector and a poor module ground are typical. Opens are P2BCE, low and high P2BD0/P2BD1, the plus side P2BC8.
c: Corrosion or contact resistance in the control connector
Coil resistance of negative contactor B shifted
Poor ground of the controlling module
s: Charging drops out or will not begin
Charging fault message from time to time

P2BD0.t: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor B Control Circuit Low
P2BD0.d: With P2BD0 the coil drive line of minus-side charging contactor B is too low – usually insulation damage letting the wire touch the body, or an output stage stuck low. Starved of current, the coil leaves the return path of that charging branch open. No manufacturer documents P2BD0 publicly. GM states that its open-circuit test (P0D11) on the Volt and ELR minus contactor A cannot see a short to ground, so that case has to be caught elsewhere. CARB obliges makers of plug-in vehicles to check this hardware. Look for chafed wiring along the battery tray or underbody, moisture in connectors and an internally shorted coil. The high counterpart is P2BD1, the plus side P2BC9, the contactor A twin P0D13. The vehicle will normally not charge in that mode.
c: Control wire of negative contactor B shorted to ground
Moisture in a connector of the control line
Coil of negative contactor B internally shorted
s: Charging session will not start
Charging fault message

P2BD1.t: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor B Control Circuit High
P2BD1.d: P2BD1 flags excess voltage on the coil feed of minus-side charging contactor B, for instance from contact with a 12 V wire or an output stage that will not turn off. The risk is a coil that stays energised and keeps the return pole connected while the module believes it is open, so the module normally blocks charging. No manufacturer documents P2BD1 publicly. For negative contactor A on the Volt and ELR, GM catches this case under P0D11 when the off-state output remains within 0.4 V of supply. On the plus side Audi documents the counterpart P2BCA for the 2024 Q8 e-tron, where over-sensitive software caused the reports. CARB requires charging components to be monitored. Damaged insulation, a wiring mix-up after repair and a faulty output stage are the suspects. P2BD0 is the low case, P2BCC a welded contactor, P0D14 the contactor A twin.
c: Control wire of negative contactor B shorted to supply voltage
s: Charging blocked
High-voltage or charging fault warning

P2BD2.d: P2BD2 reports that the first aftertreatment line, or the only one, is not gas-tight, so exhaust escapes between engine and tailpipe or false air enters. A leak upstream of the catalysts lets untreated NOx and soot out and also confuses sensors: Foton Cummins patented a check that compares the measured aftertreatment pressure with a model value from exhaust back pressure and flags a leak beyond a limit, noting that leaks also cause urea crystals and false NOx efficiency faults. Ford describes telling a leak near the particulate filter apart from a slow catalyst sensor. CARB is studying how much such unfiltered leaks add to truck emissions. No maker documents P2BD2 publicly; P2BD3 covers system B. The driver may notice exhaust smell, ticking noises and the MIL.
c: Loose V-band clamp or failed gasket between aftertreatment modules
Cracked exhaust pipe, flex joint or catalyst housing
Leak at a sensor, DEF injector or pressure tap mounting
Pressure sensor hose cracked, making the system look leaky
s: MIL on
Exhaust smell, soot marks or ticking at a joint
Follow-up SCR or particulate filter codes

P2BD3.d: P2BD3 is the twin of P2BD2 for a second aftertreatment line, found on engines with two parallel exhaust paths, each with its own catalysts and filter. Which physical line is B is up to the maker; in practice it is usually the path of the second cylinder bank. Detection works the same way: an unexpected pressure across the line given the back pressure, or sensor patterns hinting at gas loss, as in the Foton Cummins and Ford patents. CARB research shows why it matters: gas escaping before the catalysts leaves the vehicle untreated. No maker documents P2BD3 publicly. If both codes are present, look for a common cause such as a shared joint or a pressure sensor used by both lines; a lone P2BD3 points to a leak on that side.
c: Loose clamp or leaking gasket in line B
Crack in pipe, flex joint or housing on side B
Leaking sensor or injector mounting on line B
Faulty pressure sensor or hose shared by both lines
s: MIL on
Exhaust noise or smell on one side
Uneven readings between the two lines

P2BD4.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump C Control Circuit/Open
P2BD4.d: Hybrid and electric drives cool the inverter, DC/DC converter and motor with one or more electric pumps; J2012 labels them A, B and C. P2BD4 means the controlling module has found an open circuit or an unclassified fault on the control line of pump C. No manufacturer documents P2BD4, or a third pump of this kind, publicly. Comparable checks exist for pump A: Ford's 2019 hybrid summary sets P0A05 when no reply arrives from the pump for more than 9.25 s with 6–19 V on the system, and GM's 2016 tables for the Cadillac ELR flag P0CE9 for an open or shorted pump control line in 16 of 20 samples at 250 ms, Type B. CARB requires the electronic parts of inverter cooling to be monitored. Low and high faults of pump C are P2BD5 and P2BD6. Overheating electronics lead to reduced drive power.
c: Unplugged, loose or corroded connector at pump C
Broken control or signal wire between module and pump
Faulty output or input stage in the controlling module
s: Hybrid or drive system warning, often with the check engine light
Reduced drive power when the electronics heat up
Pump C silent during an actuator test

P2BD5.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump C Control Circuit Low
P2BD5.d: P2BD5 flags the command line of the third electric coolant pump in the inverter and motor electronics loop as sitting at too low a level. With a low-side or PWM driver this usually means the wire or the pump input is shorted to ground, so the pump either runs unchecked or not at all. No manufacturer documents P2BD5 publicly. The nearest published logic is Ford's 2019 hybrid summary for pump A: P0A06 is stored once the pump output driver has reported a fault for more than 5 s, with 6 to 19 V on the 12 V system. CARB requires every electronic output of inverter thermal management to be checked for such circuit faults. P2BD4 covers an open line, P2BD6 a short to voltage. If the pump stops, drive power is cut back before the electronics overheat.
c: Pump C control wire chafed through and touching ground
Water or corrosion in the pump connector bridging the signal pin to ground
Shorted input stage inside pump C
Faulty output driver in the controlling module
s: Warning for the hybrid or drive system, often with the check engine light
Pump C runs constantly or stays silent regardless of command
Reduced drive power once the electronics warm up

P2BD6.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump C Control Circuit High
P2BD6.d: P2BD6 is stored when the control circuit of motor electronics coolant pump C reads higher than the commanded state allows. A short to battery voltage, or a driver stage that reports overcurrent, are the usual triggers; the pump may then keep running or ignore commands. No manufacturer documents P2BD6 publicly. Ford's 2019 hybrid summary shows how fast the pump A counterpart reacts: P0A07 sets after the output driver has signalled an overcurrent for just 0.25 s, which protects the stage early. GM's Volt and ELR tables fold a short to voltage on their equivalent pump line into P0CE9 (16 failures out of 20 checks spaced 250 ms apart, Type B). Ground faults on pump C are P2BD5, an open line P2BD4. A warning and reduced power follow if cooling suffers.
c: Control wire of pump C shorted to a supply wire in the harness
Pump C drawing excessive current because of an internal electrical fault
Bent or corroded pins in the pump C connector touching each other
Failed output stage in the controlling module
s: Hybrid system or check engine warning
Pump C keeps running after the vehicle is switched off, or does not respond at all
Power limitation during long climbs or fast driving

P2BD7.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump C Control Performance
P2BD7.d: P2BD7 means pump C in the motor electronics cooling loop is electrically reachable but does not deliver what the controller asks for: wrong speed, a fault report from the pump itself or too little cooling effect. No manufacturer documents P2BD7 publicly. Ford's 2019 hybrids judge pump A this way under P0C73, set once the pump has reported a confirmed internal fault for more than 1.25 s. GM's ELR infers weak flow under P0CEA by comparing loop and charger temperatures with the pump above 30 % speed, needing 32 failed readings out of 40 taken every 250 ms, Type B. For pump B, Stellantis cured P0C74 on 2024 Renegade 4xe models with new hybrid controller software (TSB 08-193-24). Air in the loop, low coolant and a worn pump are typical; drive power is limited.
c: Air trapped in the electronics loop after a repair or coolant loss
Low coolant level in the electronics loop reservoir
Worn, sticking or debris-blocked pump C
Outdated software in the hybrid controller that misjudges the pump
s: Check engine or hybrid warning light
Cooling fan running at high speed more often than usual
Reduced electric drive or charging power when the loop gets warm

P2BD8.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P2BD8.d: Some hybrid and electric drives measure the coolant in the inverter and motor electronics loop at more than one point; J2012 names these sensors A, B and C, and which spot each letter marks is left to the manufacturer. P2BD8 is the general circuit code for sensor B: the signal cannot be used, but none of the specific low, high or plausibility verdicts applies. No manufacturer documents P2BD8 publicly. For sensor A, GM's 2013 Two-Mode hybrid trucks only use the specific codes P0A01 to P0A03, and CARB obliges makers to monitor the electrical inputs used for inverter cooling. Low and high faults of sensor B are P2BDA and P2BDB, plausibility P2BD9. Without a reading the system usually runs the pump harder and may limit power.
c: Loose, unplugged or corroded connector at sensor B
Damaged signal or reference wire between sensor B and the module
Faulty input circuit in the controlling module
s: Hybrid or drive system warning, often with the check engine light
Electronics coolant pump and fan running more than usual
Possible reduction of electric drive power

P2BD9.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P2BD9.d: P2BD9 means coolant temperature sensor B in the motor electronics loop delivers a voltage inside its electrical window, yet the temperature it reports does not fit the rest of the vehicle. The circuit itself is intact; a drifting thermistor, a sensor sitting in an air pocket or a value that stays frozen are typical. No manufacturer documents P2BD9 publicly. GM's method for sensor A on the 2013 Two-Mode hybrid trucks, P0A01, shows the principle: after the vehicle has rested for over 28,800 s, the loop temperature at power-up may differ from engine coolant temperature by no more than 30 °C, provided engine coolant and intake air agree within 15.75 °C; a failure counts as Type B. Voltages outside the window for this sensor are reported as P2BDA and P2BDB; sensor C has its own check, P2BDD.
c: Sensor B thermistor drifted out of its characteristic
Air pocket or low coolant leaving sensor B partly dry
Added resistance from corroded terminals shifting the reading
Wrong value from a comparison sensor such as engine coolant or intake air temperature
s: Check engine light, usually without a noticeable driving issue at first
Cooling fan or electronics pump running at unexpected times
Occasional power limitation on hot days

P2BDA.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P2BDA.d: P2BDA is set when the sensor B signal in the electronics coolant loop falls below its valid window. These sensors are normally NTC thermistors, so a low voltage translates into an impossibly hot reading; a signal wire touching ground or a shorted sensor is the classic cause. No manufacturer documents P2BDA publicly. On sensor A of GM's 2013 Two-Mode hybrid trucks, the low fault P0A02 sets when the converted value reaches 162.1 °C in 30 of 50 samples taken every 100 ms, after propulsion has been active for more than 10 s; it is Type B. CARB requires such inputs to be tested against their valid limits. The opposite fault is P2BDB. The system may cut power because it believes the electronics are overheating.
c: Signal wire of sensor B shorted to ground
Moisture in the sensor connector creating a leakage path to ground
Faulty input stage in the evaluating module
s: Check engine light and hybrid system warning
Scan tool shows an implausibly high electronics coolant temperature
Power reduction even with a cold vehicle

P2BDB.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
P2BDB.d: P2BDB tells that the signal of coolant temperature sensor B sits above its valid voltage range. With a thermistor fed from a 5 V reference through a pull-up resistor, a broken wire, an unplugged connector or a sensor gone open lets the voltage rise to almost the reference, which the module would read as extreme cold. No manufacturer documents P2BDB publicly. GM's sensor A counterpart on the 2013 Two-Mode hybrid trucks, P0A03, uses a limit of -59.1 °C and the same 30-of-50 count at 100 ms, Type B. Since real overheating would go unseen, controllers usually fall back to a safe pump speed or reduced power. P2BDA covers the grounded case, P2BD8 an unspecified circuit fault of the same sensor.
c: Sensor B connector unplugged, not latched or with a backed-out pin
Broken signal or ground wire of sensor B
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
s: Check engine light or hybrid warning
Scan tool shows an implausibly low electronics coolant temperature
Electronics coolant pump running at a fixed high speed

P2BDC.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit
P2BDC.d: P2BDC reports a general fault in the circuit of coolant temperature sensor C, a third measuring point that some drives use in the loop cooling the inverter, converter and motor. The code stands for a signal the module cannot use without assigning it to the low, high or plausibility codes P2BDE, P2BDF and P2BDD. No manufacturer documents P2BDC, or a third sensor of this kind, publicly. As a guide to what such a module accepts as a valid signal, GM's 2011 Volt tables keep their single electronics coolant sensor between 2 % and 98 % of the 5 V reference and treat an exit from that window in 16 out of 20 readings, one every 250 ms, as a Type B fault. CARB requires circuit checks on these inputs. Without the value, cooling falls back to safe defaults.
c: Poor contact at the sensor C connector
Chafed or broken wiring between sensor C and the module
Fault on a 5 V reference or sensor ground shared with other sensors
s: Warning lamp for the hybrid or drive system
Fan and electronics pump running at high output as a precaution
Possibly reduced electric power

P2BDD.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P2BDD.d: P2BDD is the plausibility check of coolant temperature sensor C: electrically the signal looks fine, but the reported value cannot be right when set against other temperatures. No manufacturer documents P2BDD publicly. Two published approaches show how such a check can run while driving instead of after a cold soak. GM's 2011 Volt compares its electronics coolant sensor with the high-voltage charger temperature and flags a gap above 38 °C while the inverter module requests pump operation, or 40 °C otherwise, in 32 of 40 samples at 250 ms, Type B. A Nissan patent compares the inverter power element temperature with the coolant reading and applies a tighter limit when the element appears colder than the water, which physics rules out. Hard faults of sensor C are P2BDE and P2BDF.
c: Sensor C reading drifted away from the true coolant temperature
Air or weak flow at the sensor C location, so it sees a local hot or cold spot
Corroded terminals adding resistance in the sensor C circuit
Faulty comparison temperature from another sensor in the system
s: Check engine light without an obvious drivability problem
Cooling fan behaviour that does not match the conditions
Power or charging limitation under heavy load

P2BDE.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit Low
P2BDE.d: P2BDE reports that the voltage from coolant temperature sensor C has dropped below its lower limit. Low describes the voltage: for the usual NTC sensor it corresponds to a reading far hotter than the coolant can be, and the cause is mostly a grounded signal wire, a crushed pigtail or a sensor that has shorted internally. No manufacturer documents P2BDE publicly. GM's electronics coolant sensor in the Volt and ELR, monitored as P0CF0, shows typical limits: below 2 % of the 5 V reference (0.1 V) in the 2011 tables and below 4 % (0.2 V) in the 2016 Volt table, 16 of 20 samples at 250 ms, Type B. The open or high case is P2BDF, while the matching low fault of sensor B is P2BDA. Drive power may be limited as a precaution.
c: Sensor C signal wire shorted to ground or to the sensor ground
Crushed or melted sensor pigtail near hot components
Faulty analog input in the evaluating module
s: Hybrid warning or check engine light
Very high electronics coolant temperature shown in live data on a cold vehicle
Fan running at full speed shortly after start

P2BDF.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit High
P2BDF.d: P2BDF is stored when the signal of coolant temperature sensor C climbs to nearly the full reference voltage. For the module this looks like coolant colder than any climate allows; in practice a pin that has backed out of the connector, a corroded or broken signal wire, or a short to a voltage source is behind it. No manufacturer documents P2BDF publicly. GM sets the matching code for its single electronics coolant sensor, P0CF1, above 98 % of the 5 V reference (4.9 V): 16 of 20 samples at 250 ms in the 2011 Volt tables, 4 s within a 5 s window in the 2019 tables, Type B in both. CARB requires out-of-range checks on all inverter cooling inputs. The low counterpart is P2BDE, sensor B uses P2BDB. A warning lamp and reduced power are possible.
c: Backed-out or loose pin in the sensor C connector
Corroded or broken signal wire of sensor C
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or another supply
s: Check engine or hybrid system warning
Live data shows the lowest possible temperature for sensor C
Pump and fan running in a fixed protective mode

P2BE0.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Coolant Level Sensor Circuit/Open
P2BE0.d: P2BE0 concerns the wiring of the level sensor in the coolant reservoir of the high-voltage battery loop: its signal is missing or the line is broken. Stellantis documents the code as P2BE0-00 on the 2021-22 Chrysler Pacifica Hybrid, where the cluster asks for hybrid system service; Tech Tip 9004552 tells dealers to photograph the level in the battery coolant bottle before swapping sensor or bottle, so the real level is part of the diagnosis. GM watches the same part on the Chevrolet Volt under its own codes P1FFB to P1FFF; there an open line drives the signal above 4.0 V, 40 of 50 samples at 100 ms, Type A. Plausibility, low and high faults are P2BE1 to P2BE3. Expect a hybrid warning and possibly blocked charging.
c: Battery coolant level actually low (leak or after service), bulletin asks to check first
Level sensor defective, e.g. internal solder joints (GM Volt)
Open signal wire or loose connector at the reservoir
Internal break in the sensor jumper harness
s: Service hybrid system message on the cluster
MIL on
Plug-in charging disabled on some models

P2BE1.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Coolant Level Sensor Range/Performance
P2BE1.d: P2BE1 reports a battery coolant level signal that lies inside the electrical limits yet makes no sense, such as a value between the defined full and low states or one that flickers while the vehicle stands still. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM shows how such a check works on the Chevrolet Volt: its code P1FFB fails when the sensor voltage sits in a forbidden band of 2.85 to 3.11 V, 40 of 50 samples at 100 ms, Type A, while a genuine low level (1.38 to 2.84 V, judged only at standstill) has its own code. GM bulletin PI0961 adds cracked solder joints inside the sensor as a source of intermittent readings. CARB requires rationality checks for hybrid inputs. The pure circuit faults are P2BE0, P2BE2 and P2BE3.
c: Level sensor with internal fault, e.g. cracked solder joints
Intermittent contact in connector or jumper harness
Coolant level near the switching point or air in the loop
Evaluation software in the battery or hybrid controller
s: Hybrid system warning, often intermittent
MIL on
Coolant level looks correct at the reservoir

P2BE2.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Coolant Level Sensor Circuit Low
P2BE2.d: P2BE2 is stored when the voltage from the battery coolant level sensor falls below the lowest value the sensor can legitimately produce. That points to the signal touching ground or a sensor whose output collapses, not to a low coolant level, which normally reads inside the valid range. No manufacturer documents P2BE2 publicly. On the Chevrolet Volt GM uses its own code P1FFC for this case: below 1.37 V with the 12 V system above 10.2 V, 40 of 50 samples at 100 ms, Type A and MIL on the first trip. CARB requires out-of-range checks for such inputs. Because the controller no longer knows the level, it may restrict charging or hybrid operation. Open and high faults are P2BE0 and P2BE3.
c: Signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
s: Hybrid system warning
MIL on
Charging possibly disabled

P2BE3.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Coolant Level Sensor Circuit High
P2BE3.d: P2BE3 means the level sensor signal of the battery coolant loop is above its valid range, typically from a short to the sensor supply or to 12 V, or from a lost sensor ground. No manufacturer documents P2BE3 publicly. GM's code P1FFD on the Chevrolet Volt shows the same test with numbers: above 4.0 V, 40 of 50 samples at 100 ms, Type A. GM counts an open circuit as high there, so depending on the pull-up design a broken wire can end up under this code rather than P2BE0. GM bulletin PI0961 lists breaks inside the jumper harness of the sensor among the causes. CARB requires such range checks for hybrid inputs. The low side is P2BE2; the reservoir level should be checked before any part is replaced.
c: Open sensor ground or open signal with pull-up (read as high)
Signal wire shorted to sensor supply or 12 V
s: Hybrid system warning
MIL on
Charging possibly disabled

P2BE4.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor C Circuit
P2BE4.d: P2BE4 is the general circuit code for a third current measurement in the high-voltage battery, used where sensor A (P0ABF to P0AC3) and sensor B (P0B0E to P0B13) are already taken. What C measures depends on the design: a further Hall or shunt channel, or a sensor in a second current path; Continental patents a battery busbar with three independent current devices whose values are compared. No manufacturer documents P2BE4 publicly. GM's generic check for sensor A shows the method: before precharge the reading is stored as zero, and if it then moves by less than 1 A once loads draw current, the sensor is judged stuck. CARB requires circuit checks for hybrid inputs. Loss of a current value limits power; bus loss of sensor C is U064C.
c: Wiring or connector fault between sensor and battery controller
Input stage or software of the battery controller
s: Hybrid or EV system warning
Reduced electric power or range
MIL on

P2BE5.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P2BE5.d: P2BE5 flags current sensor C as implausible although its signal is electrically valid, for instance an offset with no current flowing or a value at odds with the other readings. Stellantis lists it, worded as current sensor C circuit performance, in bulletins 08-047-20 and 08-130-21 for the 2017-18 Chrysler Pacifica plug-in hybrid with the 3.6 litre engine: the MIL comes on, and the remedy is new software for the battery pack control module, not a new sensor. GM shows how two current readings are cross-checked: in its 2019 table P0B13 fails when sensors A and B differ by more than 10 A while both lie between -20 and 20 A, 400 of 500 samples at 25 ms, Type A. CARB demands rationality checks for hybrid inputs. Wrong current corrupts the charge estimate; circuit faults are P2BE4, P2BE6 and P2BE7.
c: Battery controller software (Stellantis Pacifica PHEV, reflash per bulletin)
High resistance at connector or sensor ground
s: MIL on
Hybrid system warning
Inaccurate state of charge or reduced electric range

P2BE6.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor C Low
P2BE6.d: P2BE6 is set when the output of current sensor C drops below the lowest value it can deliver in normal service. Unlike its A and B siblings, the official title omits the word circuit, but the meaning is the same out-of-range low check. No manufacturer documents P2BE6 publicly. GM's test for the coarse channel of sensor A (P0AC1) gives the scale: a converted current below -573 A (ADC count under 82) for 1.6 s within 2 s fails it, Type A, one trip. A signal shorted to ground, a missing sensor supply or a broken sensor are the usual reasons. CARB requires out-of-range checks for hybrid inputs. Without this value the controller reduces battery power; the high side is P2BE7, the plausibility code P2BE5.
s: MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
Reduced power, possibly no ready mode

P2BE7.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor C High
P2BE7.d: With P2BE7 the signal of current sensor C sits above its usable range, which after conversion would be an impossibly large current. As with P2BE6, the official wording drops the word circuit. No manufacturer documents P2BE7 publicly. GM's coarse-channel check for sensor A (P0AC2) shows typical numbers: above 303 A (ADC count over 4013) during 1.6 s out of every 2 s, Type A, MIL on the first trip. An open sensor ground, a signal touching the supply or an internal sensor fault are common causes. Where three current devices sit on one busbar, as in a Continental patent, the remaining two can still be compared, which helps the controller decide which one is wrong. CARB requires such range checks. Low is P2BE6.
c: Signal wire shorted to the 5 V supply or 12 V
s: MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
Battery power limited

P2BE8.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor Control Circuit B Open
P2BE8.d: P2BE8 reports an open in control circuit B of the battery precharge function, i.e. the coil drive of a second precharge contactor. Note the wording: the letter follows circuit, while the A codes P0AE4 to P0AE7 name contactor A. Such a second path exists, for example, in a Ford patent with one precharge resistor and switch on the positive side and another on the return side, so precharge still works if one main contactor is welded. No manufacturer documents P2BE8 publicly. GM's test for contactor A (P0AE4, 2019) shows the method: with the driver on, a coil current under 194 mA means open, 40 of 50 samples at 12.5 ms, Type B. CARB requires circuit checks of hybrid outputs. Without precharge the vehicle normally does not become ready.
c: Open control wire or loose connector at contactor B
Coil of precharge contactor B open internally
Driver stage in the battery controller defective
s: Vehicle does not become ready to drive
MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
Charging not possible

P2BE9.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor Control Circuit B Range/Performance
P2BE9.d: P2BE9 says control circuit B of the precharge function is connected but behaves implausibly: the coil current, the feedback voltage or the effect of switching does not match the command. No manufacturer documents P2BE9 publicly. A Ford patent shows why the result of precharge matters for a second path: if the main contactor stays welded, the controller switches precharge to the resistor bridging the return-side contactor, and it must then confirm that the bus voltage actually rises. GM judges the outcome of precharge separately (P0C78): in its 2019 tables the bus must reach 95 to 105 % of pack voltage within 0.7 s, Type A. CARB demands functional checks of hybrid outputs. Open, low and high are P2BE8, P2BEA and P2BEB.
c: Coil resistance out of tolerance or sluggish armature
High-voltage load or resistor fault keeping the bus from rising during precharge
Corrosion or high resistance in the control circuit
Battery controller software or driver stage
s: Vehicle sometimes does not become ready
MIL and hybrid or EV warning on

P2BEA.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor Control Circuit B Low
P2BEA.d: P2BEA is stored when control circuit B of the precharge function carries less voltage than its state requires, mostly because the coil feed touches ground or the output is pulled down. With a high-side driver the coil then gets no current and the second precharge path stays open. No manufacturer documents P2BEA publicly. GM's 2016 test of the contactor A equivalent (P0AE6) checks the driver output while it is commanded on and fails below 5.35 V, 13 of 16 samples at 12.5 ms, Type B, two trips, with the 12 V supply above 10.2 V. GM also notes that its open test cannot see a short to ground, which is why this case has its own code. CARB requires circuit checks on hybrid outputs. The high side is P2BEB.
c: Coil feed chafed and shorted to ground
Coil of precharge contactor B shorted internally
Driver stage of the battery controller pulled low
s: Vehicle does not become ready to drive
MIL and hybrid or EV warning on

P2BEB.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Precharge Contactor Control Circuit B High
P2BEB.d: P2BEB reports too much voltage on control circuit B of the precharge function while it should be off, usually a short to 12 V or a driver that does not switch off. The risk is a second precharge path closing on its own; the resistor can overheat if it stays in circuit. No manufacturer documents P2BEB publicly. For contactor A, GM's 2016 table (P0AE7) fails the off-state output between 5.27 and 19.7 V, 40 of 50 samples at 12.5 ms, Type B, two trips; in 2019 GM folds this case into P0AE4, set when the off-state output exceeds battery voltage minus 0.4 V. A coil stuck energised may later show up as a contactor that stays closed. CARB requires circuit monitoring of hybrid outputs. Low and open are P2BEA and P2BE8.
c: Driver stage stuck on in the battery controller
Damaged insulation between adjacent wires in the harness
s: MIL and hybrid or EV warning on
High-voltage system blocked as a precaution

P2BEC.t: Fuel Control System A Too Lean Bank 1
P2BEC.d: Engines that combine port and direct injection keep separate fuel trim adaptations for each injection mode. Ford, which uses this code on its PFDI engines such as the 2.7 L EcoBoost and 5.0 L V8 of the F-150, assigns system A to the direct-injection mode. In closed loop, with coolant at 70 to 110 C, at least 12 percent load, 10 percent fuel in the tank and purge switched off, the PCM sets P2BEC when bank 1 long-term trim adds more than 25 percent while short-term trim is still adding over 1 percent, for 2 seconds, and only while the engine runs on DI. A lean bank 1 in every mode would give P0171 instead. Suspects are therefore parts used only by DI: too little rail pressure because the high-pressure pump underdelivers, or restricted direct injectors. Ford also reflashes the PCM for it (20-2324, 22-2393).
c: PCM software fault on affected Ford models, fixed by reprogramming
High-pressure pump or its volume regulator delivering too little rail pressure
Direct injectors on bank 1 restricted or coked
Bank 1 upstream oxygen sensor reading skewed
s: Check engine light on
Hesitation under acceleration, when the engine relies on direct injection
Often no noticeable change in drivability

P2BED.t: Fuel Control System A Too Rich Bank 1
P2BED.d: P2BED is the rich counterpart of P2BEC: bank 1 has to remove fuel, but only while the engine is fed by direct injection, which Ford calls fuel system A on its port-plus-direct engines.
