The Ford monitor runs continuously in closed loop and reacts when long-term trim has pulled more than 25 percent and short-term trim keeps pulling beyond 1 percent for 2 seconds; purge must be off, so a saturated canister is not the reason. A rich bank in all modes is P0172 instead. For the 2018 F-150 2.7 L EcoBoost, Ford bulletin 20-2324 names leaking direct injectors: if, after a warm idle and shutdown, rail pressure decays under 10 psi in less than 30 seconds, all six DI injectors are replaced. Later 2.7 L trucks built up to July 2020 get new PCM software (20-2257, 21-2045).
c: Direct injector leaking or dribbling on bank 1
PCM software fault, Ford reprogramming bulletins
Rail pressure above target because of a faulty volume regulator or pressure sensor
s: Check engine light on
Long cranking or rough running right after a hot start
Fuel smell from the exhaust, higher consumption
Misfire codes on the same bank in some cases

P2BEE.t: Fuel Control System A Too Lean Bank 2
P2BEE.d: Here the lean correction concerns bank 2, the cylinder row without cylinder 1, and again only the direct-injection operating mode (fuel system A in Ford terms). Ford applies the same monitor as on bank 1: closed loop, warm engine, purge off, long-term trim above plus 25 percent combined with short-term trim above plus 1 percent for 2 seconds. Comparing banks narrows the search. If only P2BEE is stored, look at components that serve bank 2 alone, such as its direct injectors or its upstream oxygen sensor; if P2BEC appears as well, a shared item like the high-pressure pump or rail pressure sensor is more likely. Ford lists P2BEE in bulletins 20-2324 (2018 F-150 2.7 L) and 22-2393 (2019 to 2021 F-150 5.0 L, reflash and keep-alive memory reset).
c: PCM software requiring a Ford update
Bank 2 upstream oxygen sensor reading skewed
Low rail pressure, usually with P2BEC on bank 1 too
s: Check engine light on
Slight hesitation under load
Often no other complaint

P2BEF.t: Fuel Control System A Too Rich Bank 2
P2BEF.d: P2BEF says that the engine module has had to take away a lot of fuel on bank 2 while direct injection alone was supplying the cylinders. Ford sets it on port-plus-direct engines when long-term trim on that bank drops past minus 25 percent while short-term trim keeps subtracting more than 1 percent; two seconds in closed loop are enough. Because the common rich fault P0175 is reserved for enrichment seen in every mode, P2BEF points at the DI hardware of bank 2: a direct injector that sticks open or seeps after shutdown, or a rail pressure reading that is too low so the pump overshoots. On 2019 and 2020 F-150 2.7 L EcoBoost trucks built until 4 July 2020, Ford bulletins 20-2257 and 21-2045 cure this code, together with the other fuel-trim codes, by reprogramming the PCM.
c: Known PCM software issue on 2019-2020 F-150 2.7 L
Direct injector on bank 2 sticking open or seeping
Rail pressure sensor reading too low, pressure actually too high
s: Check engine light on
Rough running after a hot restart
Increased fuel use

P2BF0.t: Fuel Control System B Too Lean Bank 1
P2BF0.d: Fuel system B is, in Ford's monitor documents, the port fuel injection mode of engines that also have direct injectors. P2BF0 therefore means bank 1 runs lean only when the port injectors do the work. The decision rule matches the DI codes: long-term trim past plus 25 percent, short-term trim past plus 1 percent, held for 2 seconds during closed-loop operation with purge off. The suspects differ, though. Port injectors are fed by the low-pressure side, so a weak in-tank pump or low supply pressure, a clogged port injector or air entering past a port injector O-ring or intake gasket fit better than a high-pressure fault. Ford ships port injector O-rings with the 2.7 L injector repair in bulletin 20-2324 and lists P2BF0 in its reflash bulletins 20-2257, 21-2045 and 22-2393.
c: Low-pressure fuel pump or supply pressure too weak for the port injectors
Air leak at a port injector O-ring or intake manifold gasket
s: Check engine light on
Uneven idle or surging at light load
Hesitation when pulling away

P2BF1.t: Fuel Control System B Too Rich Bank 1
P2BF1.d: With P2BF1 the PCM has seen bank 1 too rich while fuel came through the port injectors, Ford's fuel system B. Ford flags it when the long-term value sits beyond minus 25 percent and the short-term value still takes away above 1 percent, for a 2 second window in closed loop. Since this monitor only runs with the canister purge valve closed, vapour from the evaporative system cannot explain the result; the excess fuel comes from the injection side or from a wrong air reading. Typical findings are a port injector that leaks into the intake runner, too much low-side fuel pressure or a mass air flow signal that reads low. If the rich condition is present in DI mode too, Ford stores P0172 instead. Ford names P2BF1 in its F-150 reflash bulletins for the 2.7 L and 5.0 L engines.
c: Port injector on bank 1 leaking or dribbling
s: Check engine light on
Fuel smell, black exhaust deposits
Rough idle when warm

P2BF2.t: Fuel Control System B Too Lean Bank 2
P2BF2.d: P2BF2 combines two restrictions: the lean correction is on bank 2, and it only occurs in the port injection mode that Ford designates fuel system B. The Ford threshold is identical to the other trim codes of this family, more than 25 percent added by long-term trim plus over 1 percent by short-term trim for 2 seconds. Using both letters and both banks together helps the diagnosis. A lean result on bank 2 alone in PFI mode suggests a port injector or an intake leak on that side; lean on both banks in PFI mode (P2BF0 and P2BF2) points to the shared low-pressure supply; lean in every mode is P0174. On the 2019 to 2021 F-150 with the 5.0 L V8, bulletin 22-2393 treats this code with a PCM reflash and a keep-alive memory reset.
c: Air leak at the bank 2 intake gasket or injector O-ring
Weak low-pressure supply, usually with P2BF0 as well
s: Check engine light on
Uneven idle
Mild hesitation at part throttle

P2BF3.t: Fuel Control System B Too Rich Bank 2
P2BF3.d: The last of the eight mode-specific trim codes: bank 2 is too rich while the port injectors (Ford fuel system B) are active. Ford triggers it when long-term trim has gone below minus 25 percent and short-term trim continues to subtract over 1 percent for 2 seconds, with the engine warm and purge disabled. Its value lies in what it excludes: a rich fault visible only in PFI mode and only on bank 2 rules out the canister, the high-pressure side and anything shared by both banks. That leaves a port injector on bank 2 that does not close cleanly, or a bank 2 upstream oxygen sensor that reads lean and drives the mixture rich. Ford includes P2BF3 in bulletins 20-2324, 20-2257, 21-2045 and 22-2393, covering F-150 trucks with either the 2.7 L EcoBoost or the 5.0 L engine.
c: Port injector on bank 2 not sealing
Bank 2 upstream oxygen sensor biased lean
s: Check engine light on
Fuel smell at idle
Higher consumption

P2BF4.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve A Position Circuit
P2BF4.d: Many electrically driven exhaust flaps report their actual angle back to the engine computer, either as an analog voltage or as a PWM duty cycle from a smart actuator. P2BF4 is the umbrella fault for that feedback path on valve A: the signal is missing, unusable or cannot be classed as clearly too low or too high. No manufacturer documents P2BF4 itself in public material. The closest relatives are Mazda, which reports a low position signal of its exhaust shutter valve as P2BF6, and Ford, whose bank 1 flap feeds its state back over a PWM line. CARB requires such inputs to be checked for circuit faults. Suspects are an unplugged or corroded connector, a broken signal or ground wire near the hot exhaust, or a failed position sensor inside the actuator itself.
c: Actuator connector loose, wet or corroded by road salt
Feedback or ground wire broken or heat-damaged near the exhaust
Position sensor inside the flap actuator failed
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust flap no longer switched, sound stays in one mode

P2BF5.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve A Position Circuit Range/Performance
P2BF5.d: Here the position signal of exhaust valve A is electrically fine, yet its value does not fit: the reported angle disagrees with the command, the end stops are not where the learned values say, or the signal jumps. Ford lists P2BF5 in its active exhaust bulletins for the 2018-2023 Mustang (21-2011 for the 2020 GT500, later 23-2132 and 25-2146), together with the matching valve B code P2BFD and the drive codes. The findings there were mechanical: pinched actuator wiring, a tailpipe bracket that was not welded flush, or a muffler and tailpipe not pushed far enough into their clamps. Mazda issued service alert SA-056-23 with revised diagnostic steps for P2BF5 to P2BF7 on the 2024 CX-5. Drivers typically get a lit MIL and a message that exhaust or drive mode is unavailable.
c: Muffler or tailpipe not fully seated in its clamps, straining the actuator
Actuator bracket bent or not welded flush to the tailpipe
Pinched actuator harness giving an unstable signal
Flap shaft binding from corrosion or soot
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust mode or drive mode not available message
Exhaust tone does not change between modes

P2BF6.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve A Position Circuit Low
P2BF6.d: P2BF6 means the position feedback of exhaust valve A sits below its valid range, as with a signal shorted to ground or a lost sensor supply. Mazda is the best documented user: its 2.5 litre Skyactiv-G with cylinder deactivation carries an exhaust shutter valve that Mazda patents describe as closing partly in two-cylinder mode to damp exhaust pulsation noise. Bulletin 01-004/20 calls P2BF6:00 a shutter valve position sensor low input detected within one drive cycle and reports the master warning light plus reduced power on 2019-2020 Mazda3 and 2020 CX-30; the cause was faulty PCM logic, cured by reprogramming. Mexican-market cars without deactivation are excluded. Deutz uses the same code on MD1 engines when the flap voltage drops under its normal band. Wiring and sensor must still be checked.
c: PCM software misjudging the sensor (Mazda bulletin 01-004/20)
Position signal wire shorted to ground
Sensor supply open or connector not latched
Position sensor in the shutter valve failed
s: Master warning or check engine light on
Reduced engine power

P2BF7.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve A Position Circuit High
P2BF7.d: P2BF7 is set when the position feedback of exhaust valve A rises above its plausible maximum. Electrically that points to the signal line touching the sensor reference or battery voltage, or to a lost sensor ground, which lets the input float up to its pull-up level. Deutz assigns P2BF7 with failure type 12 to a flap voltage that is too high or shorted to positive on its MD1 industrial engines, the counterpart to P2BF6. Mazda covers it for the 2024 CX-5 in service alert SA-056-23 together with P2BF5 and P2BF6, which concern the exhaust shutter valve used with cylinder deactivation; thresholds are not published there. CARB requires out-of-range checks on such inputs. Before condemning the valve, measure its ground and signal line with the actuator unplugged.
c: Open sensor ground letting the signal float high
Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage
Position sensor in the valve assembly failed
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust flap held in its default position
Exhaust sound no longer changes as expected

P2BF8.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve B Control Circuit/Open
P2BF8.d: Valve B is the second exhaust flap; Ford's gasoline OBD summaries 2020-2024 put it on bank 2, while valve A (P26C5) serves bank 1. P2BF8 reports that the drive circuit for flap B is open or unusable. On Ford a smart driver checks the output continuously and flags it within about 5 seconds; the 2024 summary files the open circuit as subtype 13. GM's 2023 and 2024 OBD tables (23OBDG07, 24OBDG07) watch the PWM control line of an exhaust valve the same way: open circuit, battery above 9 V, 4 seconds, two trips to the MIL. Ford names P2BF8 in its Mustang active exhaust bulletins, and 25-2144 for F-150 trucks with the 5.2 L engine, model years 2023 to 2025, lists P2BF8:78, an actuator that fails alignment, which a PCM update and relearn resolve. A broken wire or unplugged actuator is the usual find.
c: Broken or unplugged harness to the bank 2 flap actuator
Open circuit inside the flap actuator
Actuator not aligned after replacement or outdated PCM software (subtype 78)
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust mode not available message
One tailpipe flap no longer moves

P2BF9.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve B Control Circuit Low
P2BF9.d: With P2BF9 the control line of exhaust flap B is pulled toward ground. A bare spot rubbing on the body or exhaust, or a shorted actuator, is the classic cause, which is why the code tends to appear after exhaust work or with a sagging harness. Ford's 2024 OBD summary treats it as subtype 11 of the bank 2 flap check, run continuously over 5 seconds by the smart driver. GM's 24OBDG07 tables describe a ground short on the exhaust valve PWM control circuit with battery voltage above 9 V, 4 seconds and a two-trip MIL. Ford bulletin 21-2011 for the 2020 Mustang GT500 lists P2BF9 among the active exhaust codes and points to pinched wiring at the actuator mount. Compared with P2BF8, the circuit is intact but shorted, so check insulation along the whole run rather than continuity alone.
c: Control wire chafed through and touching ground
Harness pinched at the actuator bracket
Internal short in the flap B actuator
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust mode cannot be changed
Bank 2 flap stuck, uneven sound left and right

P2BFA.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve B Control Circuit High
P2BFA.d: P2BFA reports too high a level on the control line of exhaust flap B. Either the wire has contact with a powered circuit, or the actuator electronics feed voltage back, so the driver cannot pull the line down when it should. Ford's 2024 OBD summary lists it as subtype 12 of the bank 2 check, monitored continuously with a 5 second window. GM's 23OBDG07 tables describe a short to power on the exhaust valve PWM control circuit, enabled above 9 V battery voltage, failing after 4 seconds and lighting the MIL after two trips. Ford bulletin 25-2146 for the 2018-2023 Mustang and 2020-2022 Shelby GT500 groups P2BFA with the other flap codes and directs an inspection of the tailpipe actuator harness. A flap B that keeps moving although commanded otherwise fits this fault better than P2BF9.
c: Control wire shorted to a powered circuit
Flap B actuator electronics feeding voltage back
Damaged tailpipe actuator harness, Ford service part 14A411
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust mode warning in the cluster
Bank 2 flap in wrong position for the selected mode

P2BFB.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve B Control Performance
P2BFB.d: P2BFB is the functional fault of flap B: wiring checks pass, but the flap does not reach or hold the commanded angle. Ford runs two tests on its bank 2 flap. The smart driver reports a stuck valve over its PWM feedback line, and a rationality check compares measured with commanded position, its duration depending on ambient conditions. The 2024 summary maps subtypes 07 (mechanical), 4B (overtemperature) and 78 (alignment) of P2BF8 to P2BFB. Bulletin 23-2132 has the technician command the Mustang flap in 10 percent steps while watching its monitor status, then remove a sticking actuator or reseat the exhaust. For F-150 trucks with the supercharged 5.2 L (2023-2025), bulletin 25-2144 adds a PCM update and actuator alignment, needed when PID EFCV_B_MON_STAT reads 3.
c: Flap B binding from corrosion, soot or ice
Exhaust or actuator bracket not seated correctly
Actuator not aligned or outdated PCM calibration
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust mode not available message
No audible difference between exhaust modes

P2BFC.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve B Position Circuit
P2BFC.d: P2BFC covers a general fault in the feedback path that tells the engine computer where exhaust flap B is. It applies only to systems with a second position-monitored flap, such as one per tailpipe, so on single-flap vehicles it cannot occur. No manufacturer documents P2BFC in public material. Ford defines valve B as its bank 2 flap and reads its state through the smart driver's PWM line; GM's 23OBDG07 tables supervise the PWM feedback of two exhaust valves, but under GM-specific codes with duty cycle limits of 2 and 98 percent over 4 seconds. CARB requires circuit monitoring for such inputs. In practice, compare the B side with the A side: if only B fails, look at its connector and wiring first, since the actuators are usually identical.
c: Flap B connector loose, wet or corroded
Feedback wire to flap B broken or heat-damaged
Position sensing in actuator B failed
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust mode selection limited or unavailable

P2BFD.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve B Position Circuit Range/Performance
P2BFD.d: P2BFD flags a position signal from exhaust flap B that is electrically valid but implausible, for instance an angle that lags the command, end points that drifted from the learned values, or a reading that wanders while the flap should rest. Ford is the public user. Its active exhaust bulletins for the Mustang (21-2011 for the 2020 GT500, 23-2132 and 25-2146 for 2018-2023 models other than the GT350) list P2BFD next to P2BF5. If both appear together, a shared mechanical cause is likely, typically a muffler and tailpipe not fully engaged in the clamps, which loads both actuators. Alone, it points to side B: a pinched harness or a bracket not welded flush, which Ford checks with a 1 mm feeler gauge. Ford publishes no thresholds for this code.
c: Muffler and tailpipe not fully engaged in the clamps
Actuator bracket not welded flush to the tailpipe
s: Check engine light on
Drive mode or exhaust mode not available message
Exhaust tone stays the same in every mode

P2BFE.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve B Position Circuit Low
P2BFE.d: The position feedback of exhaust flap B reads below its lowest valid value. For an analog sensor that means a signal at or near 0 V, typically a short to ground or a missing 5 V supply; for a PWM feedback it means a duty cycle stuck near zero. No manufacturer publishes P2BFE. The nearest documented cases concern valve A: Mazda stores P2BF6 for a low shutter valve position signal and Deutz for a flap voltage below normal. GM watches the second valve of its 23OBDG07 application under its own code, failing below 2 percent duty cycle for 4 seconds. CARB requires such out-of-range checks. Because the two flap sensors often share a supply, a low reading on both sides at once suggests the common reference circuit rather than sensor B; a low on B alone points to its own wiring.
c: Flap B signal wire shorted to ground
Sensor reference supply open or shorted
Position sensor in actuator B failed
s: Check engine light on
Flap B no longer adjusted, exhaust sound unchanged

P2BFF.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve B Position Circuit High
P2BFF.d: P2BFF is the upper limit fault for the position feedback of exhaust flap B. An analog signal pinned near supply voltage, or a PWM feedback stuck near 100 percent, usually comes from a lost sensor ground, a signal wire touching voltage, or water bridging the connector pins. No manufacturer documents P2BFF publicly. Deutz uses the valve A counterpart P2BF7 when its flap voltage is too high, and GM's 23OBDG07 tables fail the second exhaust valve feedback above 98 percent duty cycle after 4 seconds, two trips to the MIL, under a GM-specific code. CARB asks for range checks on inputs of this kind. Unlike P2BFA, which concerns the drive line, this code points at the return signal, so the flap may still move while the computer no longer trusts the reported angle.
c: Open ground at the flap B position sensor
Water or salt bridging the actuator B connector pins
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust mode warning, flap B held in default position

P2C00.d: P2C00 reports that a third fuel pressure regulator, labelled C, cannot hold the pressure the engine module asks for, although its circuit tests fine. Letters beyond A and B are only needed on fuel systems with several pressure control elements, for example engines with two high-pressure pumps or separate control of low and high pressure. No manufacturer documents P2C00 publicly; regulator C's electrical faults have their own codes P233A to P233C. As a comparable performance check, GM's 2023 table 23OBDG07 watches the high-pressure controller output for its first and second quantity control valves (P0089, P2C01) and flags a fault when it stays beyond plus or minus 7.5 MPa for 10 seconds, on two trips. CARB requires fuel system and pressure control parts to be checked for proper function.
c: Regulator C or the pump it controls worn or sticking
Insufficient feed pressure to the controlled pump
Fuel pressure sensor drifting, so the regulator appears off target
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power at high load
Extended cranking

P2C01.d: GM uses P2C01 in its 2023 and 2024 summary tables 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 for an engine control module that drives two fuel quantity control valves on the high-pressure side: P0089 covers the first, P2C01 the second, labelled regulator D. The ECM compares the filtered output of the high-pressure controller with fixed bounds. If it stays above 7.5 MPa for 10 seconds, the pump cannot reach the target even at full demand; a shorter 6 second path applies when the tank is empty or on reserve. Below minus 7.5 MPa for 10 seconds means pressure stays too high despite maximum reduction. Both require two trips. Wiring faults of the same valve are separate codes, P2C02 to P2C04. Drivers usually notice a lack of power, hard starting or the MIL after the second trip.
c: Second high-pressure pump or its quantity control valve worn or sticking
Low tank level or weak low-pressure supply
s: Check engine light on after two trips
Reduced power or stumbling at full load
Hard or slow starting

P2C02.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator D Control Circuit/Open
P2C02.d: P2C02 is the open-circuit check on the control line of fuel pressure regulator D. In GM's tables 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 this is the second fuel quantity control valve of the high-pressure system, the twin of the valve watched by P0090. While the driver is switched off, the ECM expects a defined voltage on the line; if it reads low, it treats the load as disconnected, which corresponds to more than 200 kilohms between the ECU pin and the valve. Battery voltage must exceed 10.9 V and the engine must turn faster than 80 rpm, and the fault has to persist for 20 seconds. GM rates it as a one-trip fault. A broken wire, a corroded plug at the pump or an open valve coil are the usual causes; the affected pump can no longer be regulated.
c: Broken wire or loose terminal in the valve circuit
Corroded or unplugged connector at the high-pressure pump
Open coil in the quantity control valve
s: Check engine light on
Power reduction because one pump is no longer controlled
Possible rail pressure fault codes alongside

P2C03.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator D Control Circuit Low
P2C03.d: P2C03 is set when the switched low side of the regulator D control circuit has contact with ground. GM documents it in 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 for the second fuel quantity control valve, where it mirrors P0091 of the first valve. With the driver off, a healthy circuit shows a voltage on this line; if it is pulled low, the ECM concludes that less than about 0.5 ohm separates the pin from ground. The check needs more than 10.9 V supply and an engine speed above 80 rpm and counts 20 events before reporting, on the first trip. A short at the supply end of the same driver is a different GM code (P3138), so the code already tells which wire to inspect: typically the low-side lead chafed against the engine or a damaged valve connector.
c: Low-side wire chafed through to ground
Internal short in the quantity control valve
s: Check engine light on
Reduced engine power
Rough running at high load

P2C04.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator D Control Circuit High
P2C04.d: P2C04 covers the opposite electrical fault to P2C03: the switched ground end of the regulator D circuit is connected to battery voltage. In GM's 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 tables the circuit belongs to the second fuel quantity control valve, counterpart of P0092 on the first. The ECM detects it while the driver is switched on: the line should then be pulled down, and if the voltage stays high, the module assumes a short of less than 0.5 ohm to the injector supply. Enable conditions are supply above 10.9 V and engine speed above 80 rpm; 20 failed events set the code on the first trip. As long as the short exists the valve cannot be switched, so pump output for that circuit is lost. Look for insulation damage where the harness runs near hot or moving parts, and for moisture in the connector.
c: Low-side wire shorted to a supply voltage
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the valve connector
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power, possibly limp mode
Engine may hesitate under load

P2C05.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor A Circuit Bank 1
P2C05.d: Engines with switchable cam lobes use small solenoid actuators that push a pin into a groove of a sliding cam sleeve; a feedback signal confirms that the pin has moved. P2C05 is the general circuit fault for feedback A on the intake camshaft (camshaft A) of bank 1. GM uses it on the 2.7 L turbo four L3B in the Silverado and Sierra 1500 from 2019: in tables 19OBDG03D and 25OBDG03B the ECM tests the circuit while the output is energised and reports an open circuit at 200 kilohms or more between signal and ground in 4 of 5 samples, with supply above 11 V, as Type A with MIL on the first trip. Low and High are P2C07 and P2C08. GM bulletins PIT5677 and 21-NA-149 trace such codes on the L3B to engine harness chafing and blown fuses. Lift changes are locked out.
c: Engine harness chafed, sometimes with blown fuses (GM L3B bulletins)
Loose or corroded connector at the profile actuator
Open circuit inside the actuator or its feedback element
s: Check engine light on immediately
Cam lift switching and cylinder deactivation unavailable, slightly reduced power or economy
With harness damage, many other codes and possibly no start

P2C06.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor A Range/Performance Bank 1
P2C06.d: P2C06 deals with a feedback signal that is electrically intact but makes no sense. On GM's 2.7 L L3B, the ECM follows each shift of the intake profile actuator A on bank 1 through three Hall feedback states: extending once the reading falls below 55, extended below 45 and retracted, back at home, above 68. The code is logged when these states do not appear as expected after a command, or when the feedback reports pin movement although no shift was requested. It needs 4 faulty readings out of 5 with the engine running, supply above 11 V and no crank or camshaft sensor faults, and it is a Type A fault (19OBDG03D, 25OBDG03B). CARB names a single pin that fails to move as a failure the lift monitor must cover. A sticking actuator is more likely than wiring here.
c: Actuator pin sticking or slow because of wear or dirty oil
Worn groove or sliding sleeve on the intake camshaft
Hall feedback element in the actuator giving wrong values
s: Check engine light on immediately
Lift switching disabled, engine stays on one cam profile
Possible ticking noise from the cylinder head

P2C07.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor A Circuit Low Bank 1
P2C07.d: On GM's 2.7 L turbo four L3B (Silverado and Sierra 1500 from 2019) each of the four intake sliding-cam actuators reports its pin travel through a Hall element; GM calls the first one intake Hall sensor 1, which is position sensor A in J2012 terms. P2C07 means this circuit is pulled to ground. The ECM checks it with the output stage switched on and treats an impedance of 0.5 ohm or less between signal and ground as a short; 4 failures in 5 samples with more than 11 V supply set a Type A code, MIL in the first trip (19OBDG03D, 25OBDG03B). GM bulletin 21-NA-149 names P2C07 only in its keyword list for chafed L3B engine harnesses. Pin feedback is lost, so lift switching and cylinder deactivation are blocked. Open circuit is P2C05, short to power P2C08.
c: Engine harness chafed through to ground, e.g. over the camshaft carrier cover
Internal short to ground in the profile actuator or its Hall element
Oil or water in the actuator connector bridging to ground
s: Check engine light on from the first drive
Engine stays on one lift profile, no cylinder deactivation, slightly higher consumption
With harness damage, possibly blown fuses and many further codes

P2C08.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor A Circuit High Bank 1
P2C08.d: P2C08 flags a short to voltage on position sensor A, the Hall feedback of the first intake profile actuator on bank 1. GM's L3B 2.7 L four runs this check the other way round from the ground test: the output stage is switched off, and if the line still shows 0.5 ohm or less towards controller power, 4 of 5 such readings above 11 V store a Type A code with immediate MIL (19OBDG03D, again 25OBDG03B). Unlike the ground fault P2C07, P2C08 sits in the main code list of GM bulletins PIT5677 (2019) and 21-NA-149 (2019 to 2021 Silverado and Sierra 1500), which blame engine harness damage over the camshaft carrier and near the left shock tower and mention blown fuses. Lift switching stops until the fault is cleared. Open circuit: P2C05.
c: Chafed engine harness touching a live circuit (GM bulletins PIT5677, 21-NA-149)
Internal short to supply inside the actuator or its feedback element
Faulty output stage in the ECM
s: MIL lit immediately
No valve lift change and no cylinder deactivation
After harness damage also rough running, reduced power or no start

P2C09.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Bank 1
P2C09.d: Position sensor B belongs to the second of the four intake actuators that slide the cam sleeves on GM's L3B; GM's tables call it intake Hall sensor 2. The sensors are thus one per actuator, not one per lift step: sensors A to C get J2012 codes, while GM puts the fourth (sensor D) under its own codes P30B0 to P30B3. P2C09 is the open-circuit test for sensor B. With the output energised the ECM expects a low impedance; 200 kilohms or more between signal and ground in 4 of 5 samples, supply above 11 V, set a Type A fault (19OBDG03D, 25OBDG03B). GM bulletins PIT5677 and 21-NA-149 list P2C09 for L3B trucks with chafed harnesses. Without feedback the ECM cannot confirm shifts, so lift switching is disabled. Low and High are P2C0B and P2C0C.
c: Loose, unplugged or corroded connector on actuator 2
Wire broken by harness chafing on the camshaft carrier (GM L3B bulletins)
Open circuit inside the actuator or its Hall element
s: Check engine light on in the first trip
Lift switching and cylinder deactivation locked out
Usually no noticeable change in driving apart from fuel use

P2C0A.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor B Range/Performance Bank 1
P2C0A.d: Here the wiring of position sensor B is intact, but its report does not match what the second intake actuator on bank 1 was told to do. On the L3B, GM follows every shift through three Hall readings: below 55 while the pin is moving out, below 45 once fully out, and above 68 when it is back home. P2C0A is stored if this sequence is not seen after a command, or if the feedback shows pin activity although the ECM never asked for a shift. Four bad readings in five, engine running, more than 11 V and no crank or cam sensor codes are required; Type A, MIL at once (19OBDG03D, 25OBDG03B). A slow or sticking pin, a worn shift groove or poor oil are therefore likelier culprits than wiring. CARB requires the lift system to catch cylinders running on the wrong cam profile.
c: Pin of actuator 2 sticking or slow (wear, sludge, wrong oil)
Worn shift groove or detent on the intake cam sleeve
Hall element in the actuator reporting implausible levels
s: MIL on at once
Engine kept on a fixed cam profile, no cylinder deactivation
Possible ticking from the camshaft carrier or slightly uneven idle

P2C0B.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Low Bank 1
P2C0B.d: P2C0B reports that the circuit of position sensor B, the Hall feedback of the second intake actuator on bank 1, is shorted to ground. GM's L3B 2.7 L uses it with a resistance test while the output is on: at 0.5 ohm or less from signal to ground, 4 of 5 failed samples with supply over 11 V store a Type A code and the MIL comes on immediately (19OBDG03D, 25OBDG03B). Interestingly, GM's table wording for this test speaks of the sensor's solenoid driver, so the ECM judges the line from its output stage rather than from a sensor voltage. GM lists P2C0B only among the keywords of bulletins PIT5677 and 21-NA-149 on L3B harness chafing. Possible effects: stuck lift profile, no cylinder deactivation. Open: P2C09, short to power: P2C0C.
c: Insulation of the sensor B line worn through against engine metal
Shorted actuator 2 or its integrated Hall element
Moisture or oil in the connector
s: Check engine light on straight away
Valve lift no longer changes, fuel use may rise

P2C0C.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit High Bank 1
P2C0C.d: A short from the sensor B line to a voltage source triggers P2C0C. The sensor is the Hall feedback built into the second intake profile actuator on bank 1. For the L3B four in 2019 and later Silverado and Sierra 1500 trucks, GM tests with the output stage off; a reading of no more than 0.5 ohm against controller power, found four times in five checks while the supply exceeds 11 V and the key is in crank or run, gives a Type A code with MIL in the first trip (19OBDG03D, 25OBDG03B). Bulletins PIT5677 and 21-NA-149 include P2C0C in their main list for harness chafing at the camshaft carrier, the air cleaner housing and the left shock tower, where blown fuses can accompany the codes. An actuator whose position cannot be read is excluded from shifting. Ground short: P2C0B, open: P2C09.
c: Chafed harness bringing the line against a powered wire (GM PIT5677, 21-NA-149)
Internal short to supply in actuator 2
s: MIL on in the first trip
Cam profile switching and cylinder deactivation unavailable
With harness damage, further codes, rough running or no start

P2C0D.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor C Circuit Bank 1
P2C0D.d: Position sensor C is the third of the Hall feedback elements on the intake side of bank 1; on GM's L3B it sits in intake actuator 3 and is named intake Hall sensor 3. That engine has four intake and two exhaust profile actuators, so a fourth intake feedback exists beyond the J2012 letters and GM handles it with P30B0 to P30B3. P2C0D is the open-circuit check for sensor C: output on, at least 200 kilohms from signal to ground, four of five samples at over 11 V, key in crank or run, Type A with MIL on the first trip (19OBDG03D, 25OBDG03B). Both PIT5677 and its successor 21-NA-149 from GM list P2C0D for 2019 to 2021 L3B trucks with chafed engine harnesses. As long as sensor C reports nothing, the ECM blocks lift changes.
c: Harness rubbed through over the camshaft carrier, wire broken (GM L3B bulletins)
Connector on actuator 3 loose, damaged or corroded
Open circuit inside actuator 3 or its Hall element
s: Check engine light on in the first trip
No lift switching, no cylinder deactivation
Further codes, reduced power or no start if the harness is damaged

P2C0E.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor C Range/Performance Bank 1
P2C0E.d: P2C0E is the plausibility test for the feedback of the third intake actuator on bank 1. On the L3B, the ECM classifies each shift by the Hall signal of that actuator: extending when it drops below 55, fully extended under 45, retracted when it rises above 68 again. The code is set when a commanded shift does not produce this pattern, or when activity appears without any command. GM requires 4 faulty readings in 5 with the engine running, supply above 11 V and no active crank or camshaft sensor faults, and lights the MIL at once as Type A (19OBDG03D, 25OBDG03B). Unlike most of its siblings, P2C0E is not named in GM's harness bulletins; a mechanically sluggish actuator 3 or a damaged sleeve groove is the usual suspect. CARB demands detection of wrong-profile operation.
c: Pin of actuator 3 sticking or responding late
Damaged groove or detent on the cam sleeve served by actuator 3
Old or wrong-grade oil slowing the pin
s: MIL comes on immediately
Lift switching suspended, engine runs on one profile
Occasional ticking or uneven running if a sleeve sits halfway

P2C0F.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor C Circuit Low Bank 1
P2C0F.d: With P2C0F the ECM sees the position sensor C circuit of bank 1, the Hall feedback in the third intake actuator, connected to ground. In GM's L3B tables the test runs while the output is commanded on and looks for a signal-to-ground resistance not above 0.5 ohm; after 4 failures in 5 samples at more than 11 V the code is stored as Type A and the MIL lights at once (19OBDG03D; the 2025 table 25OBDG03B keeps the same limit). Of GM's harness bulletins, only the keyword section of PIT5677 and 21-NA-149 mentions P2C0F, while their main lists carry the open and high codes of this sensor. A pinched wire against the cylinder head or a shorted actuator is the probable cause; lift switching remains blocked. Open: P2C0D, high: P2C10.
c: Sensor C line pinched or chafed against ground
s: Check engine light comes on during the first drive
Engine no longer switches cam profile or deactivates cylinders

P2C10.t: A Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor C Circuit High Bank 1
P2C10.d: P2C10 completes the sensor C group for the bank 1 intake camshaft: the feedback line of the third profile actuator is shorted to voltage. GM's L3B logic switches the output off and checks the line against controller power; 0.5 ohm or less in 4 of 5 samples, with supply above 11 V, sets a Type A code and the MIL straight away (19OBDG03D, 25OBDG03B). The code appears in the main DTC list of GM bulletins PIT5677 and 21-NA-149, which trace no-start, rough running and reduced power on 2019 to 2021 L3B Silverado and Sierra 1500 to harness wear at the camshaft carrier cover and nearby brackets, sometimes with blown fuses. No other maker documents the code publicly. Until repaired, actuator 3 takes no part in lift changes. Open: P2C0D, ground short: P2C0F.
c: Harness wear at the camshaft carrier cover shorting to a live wire (GM bulletins)
s: MIL on immediately
No lift change and no cylinder deactivation
With harness damage, possibly stalling or no start

P2C11.t: Reductant Pump A Current Too Low
P2C11.d: P2C11 watches the electric motor of the DEF (AdBlue) pump from the other side than P214E: its driver output carries less current than a working motor should draw, which points to an open winding, a poor plug contact or a motor spinning freely or not at all. Only GM documents it publicly, in its 2025 diesel tables (25OBDG04A/B): the DEF control module flags under 0.75 A while the pump is used as a heater for frozen fluid, and under 0.5 A during priming and normal running. Failures over 4 s within 400 samples set it as Type A, so the MIL comes on after one trip, and the code only heals in the next drive cycle. While it is active the pump is stopped, no fluid is dosed and the SCR catalyst loses its NOx conversion; the exhaust fluid warning follows.
c: DEF pump motor with open winding or worn brushes/electronics (pump module in the tank)
Loose, corroded or spread terminals at the pump connector
Open or high-resistance control or low-reference wire between control module and pump
Faulty output stage in the DEF control module
s: MIL and exhaust fluid system warning in the instrument cluster
No DEF consumption, higher NOx emissions
Speed or restart limitation if the fault persists (inducement)

P2C12.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor A Circuit Bank 1
P2C12.d: Camshaft B is the exhaust camshaft in J2012 terms, and P2C12 reports an open circuit in the feedback of its first profile actuator on bank 1. GM's 2.7 L turbo L3B (Silverado and Sierra 1500 from model year 2019) is the documented user: its tables call this element exhaust Hall sensor 1. With the driver energised, the ECM flags a break once the signal-to-ground impedance reaches 200 kilohms or more; four failures out of five samples at system voltage above 11 V give a Type A code, MIL on trip one (19OBDG03D, 25OBDG03B). P2C12 is in the main DTC list of PIT5677 and its successor 21-NA-149, which point to engine harness damage at the camshaft carrier cover. Exhaust lift changes are then suspended. Low and high: P2C14, P2C15.
c: Engine harness worn through where it crosses the camshaft carrier cover (GM PIT5677, 21-NA-149)
Connector on exhaust actuator 1 not latched or corroded
Open Hall element inside the exhaust actuator
s: Check engine light from the first trip
Exhaust cam profile no longer switched, fuel economy mode unavailable
With harness damage, several other engine codes at the same time

P2C13.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor A Range/Performance Bank 1
P2C13.d: P2C13 is the rationality test for the first exhaust profile actuator's feedback on bank 1, so the wiring is not in question. GM's L3B tracks every exhaust shift through exhaust Hall sensor 1: the reading must drop below 55 as the pin starts to fire, below 45 when it is fully out and climb above 68 once the pin is home again. If a commanded shift does not produce these states, or the sensor reports a pin event that was never requested, four bad readings out of five with the engine running and supply over 11 V result in a Type A fault (19OBDG03D, 25OBDG03B). The test is suppressed while crank or cam position faults are active. GM names P2C13 only in the keyword index of its L3B harness bulletins. Prime suspects are a sluggish pin, sludge or a worn exhaust sleeve groove.
c: Pin of exhaust actuator 1 slow or sticking (sludge, overdue oil change, wrong oil grade)
Worn shift groove or weak detent on the exhaust cam sleeve
Hall element in actuator 1 delivering drifting levels
s: Warning lamp on at once
Exhaust lift locked on one profile, cylinder deactivation inactive
Occasional clicking from the top of the engine

P2C14.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor A Circuit Low Bank 1
P2C14.d: With P2C14 the ECM reports that the line of exhaust position sensor A on bank 1 is grounded. GM applies the check on the L3B 2.7 L while the driver is commanded on: a signal-to-ground impedance of 0.5 ohm or below, seen in four of five samples with the key in crank or run and more than 11 V, sets Type A with immediate MIL; the 2025 table 25OBDG03B adds a general enable flag but keeps the limit (19OBDG03D). Unlike P2C12 and P2C15, P2C14 does not appear in the main code list of PIT5677 or 21-NA-149, only among their search keywords. Typical causes are insulation worn through on the cylinder head or the generator bracket, or a shorted actuator. The exhaust sleeves of bank 1 stay where they are; the driver mostly notices the warning lamp.
c: Signal wire of exhaust sensor A rubbed bare against the head or a bracket
Internal short to ground in exhaust actuator 1
Engine oil wicked into the actuator plug
s: MIL on immediately
No exhaust lift change, slightly higher consumption under light load

P2C15.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor A Circuit High Bank 1
P2C15.d: P2C15 stands for a short to voltage on the exhaust position sensor A circuit, bank 1, i.e. the Hall feedback of GM's first exhaust actuator on the L3B four. This test runs with the output switched off: if a resistance of 0.5 ohm or less to controller power remains on the line, four failed reports in five at more than 11 V produce a Type A code, MIL at once (19OBDG03D, 25OBDG03B). P2C15 belongs to the main code list of PIT5677 and of 21-NA-149 for 2019 to 2021 L3B trucks. From the A revision on, these bulletins also mention blown underhood fuses alongside no-start, rough running and reduced power, so a short to power is often only one symptom of a larger harness fault. Exhaust lift changes stop. Open: P2C12, ground short: P2C14.
c: Chafed harness letting the sensor line touch a supply wire (GM PIT5677, 21-NA-149)
Short to supply inside exhaust actuator 1
Defective output stage in the ECM
s: MIL lit straight away
Exhaust cam profile stays fixed
Together with harness damage, blown fuses, no start or reduced power possible

P2C16.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Bank 1
P2C16.d: P2C16 is the open-circuit fault of position sensor B on the bank 1 exhaust camshaft. On GM's L3B this is exhaust Hall sensor 2, the second and last exhaust feedback: GM's tables list four exhaust pin drivers (control codes P002A, P2B39, P03F1, P3099) but only two exhaust Hall elements, which matches the two exhaust profile actuators described by GM TechLink. The ECM energises the driver and treats 200 kilohms or more from signal to ground in four out of five samples above 11 V as an open circuit, Type A, MIL immediately (19OBDG03D, 25OBDG03B). P2C16 is part of the main DTC list of PIT5677 and 21-NA-149. Possible causes are a pulled connector, a broken wire or an open Hall element; until fixed, exhaust lift switching is disabled.
c: Plug on exhaust actuator 2 pulled off or not locked after engine work
Wire broken where the harness rubs at the camshaft carrier (GM L3B bulletins)
Open circuit in the Hall element of actuator 2
s: Check engine light in the first trip
Exhaust lift switching and economy modes blocked

P2C17.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor B Range/Performance Bank 1
P2C17.d: P2C17 flags implausible feedback from exhaust Hall sensor 2, the position sensor of the second exhaust profile actuator on bank 1 of GM's L3B. The electrical circuit tests pass, yet the shift pattern is wrong: after a command GM expects the reading to pass below 55 (pin extending), below 45 (pin fully out) and back above 68 (pin retracted). A missing step, or a pin event reported without any command, counts as a failure; four such readings in five, with the motor turning, supply over 11 V and crank and cam sensors fault-free, lead to a Type A code, MIL straight away (19OBDG03D, 25OBDG03B). The harness bulletins only carry P2C17 in their keyword lists. Because CARB requires a single lift pin that fails to move to be caught, the engine falls back to a fixed exhaust profile. Look at oil condition and actuator 2 first.
c: Pin of exhaust actuator 2 binding because of deposits or degraded oil
Exhaust cam sleeve not snapping into its detent, worn groove
Low or aerated engine oil slowing the shift
s: Warning lamp on without delay
Engine runs on a fixed exhaust profile, no cylinder deactivation
Possibly a light tapping noise from the valve train

P2C18.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit Low Bank 1
P2C18.d: A ground short in the position sensor B line on the bank 1 exhaust side sets P2C18. On GM's L3B this is the feedback wire of exhaust actuator 2. GM's table phrases it as a fault of the sensor's solenoid driver: with the output commanded on, a signal-to-ground impedance not above 0.5 ohm in four samples out of five, supply over 11 V and ignition in crank or run, stores Type A and switches on the MIL (19OBDG03D, unchanged in 25OBDG03B). As with P2C14, GM's PIT5677 and 21-NA-149 list P2C18 only as a keyword, not under the codes found on affected trucks. Areas to inspect include the harness run over the camshaft carrier cover and below the air cleaner box, plus the actuator connector. The second exhaust actuator stays inactive until the short is repaired.
c: Harness insulation damaged at the camshaft carrier cover or under the air cleaner housing
Exhaust actuator 2 shorted internally to ground
Water or oil bridging contacts in the plug
s: MIL comes on in the first trip
Exhaust profile no longer changes, small rise in fuel use

P2C19.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor B Circuit High Bank 1
P2C19.d: P2C19 closes the sensor B group on the exhaust camshaft of bank 1: the feedback circuit of GM's exhaust Hall sensor 2 is shorted to a voltage source. For the L3B the ECM checks while the output is off; a path of at most 0.5 ohm to controller power, reported four times in five with supply over 11 V, gives a Type A code with the MIL on in the first trip (19OBDG03D, 25OBDG03B). P2C19 sits in the main code list of PIT5677 and 21-NA-149, which blame L3B harness damage at the camshaft carrier cover, at the base of the air cleaner box, or near the alternator bracket and the stud of the left front spring. Since no third exhaust Hall sensor exists on this engine, P2C19 is the last exhaust feedback code GM uses. Open: P2C16, ground: P2C18.
c: Harness chafed at generator bracket or coil spring stud, line touching a live wire (GM 21-NA-149)
Exhaust actuator 2 shorted internally to supply
s: MIL on in the first drive
Exhaust lift switching disabled
With extensive harness damage, stalling, no crank or blown fuses

P2C1A.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor C Circuit Bank 1
P2C1A.d: P2C1A would report an open circuit in a third position feedback on the bank 1 exhaust camshaft. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's L3B, the one engine with publicly documented exhaust feedback codes, has just two exhaust Hall sensors (P2C12 to P2C19), in line with the two exhaust profile actuators that GM TechLink describes; its 2019 and 2025 tables contain no P2C1A. A system with a third exhaust actuator would test it as with the analogous code P2C16: an energised driver and a very high signal-to-ground impedance pointing to a broken wire. CARB requires such sensors and actuators of a valve lift system to be monitored for circuit faults. Expect a warning lamp and a locked exhaust lift profile.
c: Disconnected or corroded plug at the third exhaust actuator
Broken feedback wire in the engine harness
Internal open in the position sensor
s: Engine warning lamp on
Exhaust cam profile switching locked out

P2C1B.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor C Range/Performance Bank 1
P2C1B.d: Range/Performance for exhaust position sensor C, bank 1: the signal is electrically fine but does not match the commanded pin movement of a third exhaust profile actuator. There is no public manufacturer documentation for P2C1B. The comparable test on GM's L3B (P2C13, P2C17) watches three Hall states per shift and also catches pin activity without a command; GM's engine has no third exhaust feedback, so the code stays unused there. CARB explicitly expects valve lift diagnostics to detect a single pin that does not reach its intended position, which is what such a code would cover. Mechanical causes such as a sticking pin, heavy oil sludge or a damaged sleeve groove would be more likely than wiring. Driving effect: lamp on, exhaust profile frozen.
c: Actuator pin sticking or reacting too slowly
Sludge or wrong oil viscosity in the valve train
s: Warning lamp on
Exhaust lift held on one profile, possibly ticking from the head

P2C1C.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor C Circuit Low Bank 1
P2C1C.d: P2C1C is reserved for a circuit-low fault, typically a short to ground, in the feedback of exhaust position sensor C on bank 1. It is not used in any public manufacturer documentation. GM's L3B tables show how its siblings work: P2C14 and P2C18 compare the line against ground with the driver on and declare a short at 0.5 ohm or less in four of five samples. Because that engine carries only two exhaust Hall sensors, the C position is not populated. CARB's comprehensive component rules would require a manufacturer that fits a third exhaust actuator to detect such out-of-range input. If it ever appears, check for chafed insulation and moisture at the actuator plug before replacing parts.
c: Sensor C wire chafed through to ground
s: MIL on
No change of exhaust cam profile

P2C1D.t: B Camshaft Profile Actuator Position Sensor C Circuit High Bank 1
P2C1D.d: P2C1D, the circuit-high code for exhaust position sensor C on bank 1, covers a feedback line pulled towards supply voltage, usually by a short to power. No carmaker publishes a use for it. On GM's L3B the matching codes P2C15 and P2C19 are evaluated with the output off, a short being declared at a resistance up to 0.5 ohm against the controller supply; there they also appear in the main list of harness chafing bulletins. With only two exhaust Hall sensors on that engine, sensor C does not exist. CARB obliges every electrical input of a lift system to be checked for out-of-range values, so a future user would likely flag this fault with a warning lamp and freeze exhaust lift switching. Inspect the wiring for contact with live circuits first.
c: Sensor C line rubbing against a powered wire
Internal short to supply in the actuator
Faulty driver stage in the ECM
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust lift switching suspended

P2C1E.t: Cold Start Fuel Pressure Regulator A Performance
P2C1E.d: Direct-injection petrol engines often run a catalyst-heating mode after a cold start, with split injections that need tightly held rail pressure. P2C1E says regulator A, which meters the high-pressure pump, ran out of authority in that phase. GM defines it in its engine tables from 2019 (19OBDG03D) to 2025 (25OBDG03B): fault when the commanded pump delivery angle sits at 92° or more, or at 0° or less, for 10 s within 12.5 s, with at least 11 V and over 0.275 MPa feed pressure; Type B, MIL after two trips. Unlike P2C1F/P2C20 it judges the actuator command, not the pressure gap. Because California wants cold-start faults kept apart from ordinary ones, the code exists next to P0089. Ford logs its cold-start pressure fault as P053F instead.
c: Worn high-pressure pump that needs full stroke to reach the target
Insufficient feed pressure from the in-tank pump or a clogged filter
Sticking quantity control valve on the high-pressure pump
Worn pump drive cam or follower reducing effective stroke
s: MIL after two cold starts with the fault
Rough idle or hesitation in the first minute after a cold start
Often no noticeable symptom once warm

P2C1F.t: Cold Start Fuel Pressure Regulator A Exceeded Control Limits - Pressure Too Low
P2C1F.d: P2C1F is the underpressure half of GM's cold-start fuel pressure check on direct-injection petrol engines: while the catalyst is being heated, measured rail pressure lags the target by more than a calibrated margin. Table 25OBDG03B uses a 3 MPa gap for desired pressures from 4 MPa up (2 MPa at 3 MPa), the same map as P228C; 10 s of failures within 12.5 s set the code as Type A, so the MIL lights after one trip. GM's 2019 table 19OBDG03D runs the same check but allows 5 MPa from 20 MPa desired, and table 23OBDG07 (2023) uses a filtered deviation above 3 MPa held for 5 s, also on one trip. Suspects are a weak high-pressure pump or quantity control valve, low feed pressure from the tank pump or a leaking injector. P228C is the same fault outside the warm-up phase, P2C20 the overpressure case.
c: High-pressure pump with worn plunger or sticking control valve delivering too little
Low feed pressure from in-tank pump, filter or pressure regulator
Leaking or sticking injector bleeding off rail pressure
Rail pressure sensor reading too low
s: MIL after a single faulty cold start
Long cranking, rough running or stalling when cold
Reduced power possible if pressure stays low

P2C20.t: Cold Start Fuel Pressure Regulator A Exceeded Control Limits - Pressure Too High
P2C20.d: P2C20 mirrors P2C1F: during catalyst heating after a cold start the rail pressure overshoots its setpoint because the high-pressure pump supplies more fuel than requested or cannot be throttled back. On GM direct-injection petrol engines the measured pressure must exceed the target by 3 MPa or more, on the map it shares with P228D, for 10 s within 12.5 s (25OBDG03B; in 19OBDG03D only 2 MPa from 20 MPa desired); Type A, MIL on the first trip. GM's 2023 table 23OBDG07 trips when the filtered deviation stays below minus 3 MPa for 7 s, again one trip. Most often a quantity control valve that sticks or a drive circuit fault keeps the pump at full delivery; a drifting rail pressure sensor or software can also be responsible. Too much pressure makes cold idle harsh and noisy; outside warm-up the same fault reads P228D.
c: Quantity control valve on the high-pressure pump stuck in the delivering position
Wiring or connector fault in the control valve drive circuit
Rail pressure sensor drifting so the controller overshoots
Engine control software that needs an update
s: MIL after one faulty cold start
Harsh, loud cold idle or ticking injectors
Possible reduced power or rich running smell

P2C21.t: Engine Oil Temperature Sensor A/B Correlation
P2C21.d: Engines with two oil temperature sensors can check them against each other; P2C21 means sensors A and B disagree although each signal is electrically valid. GM runs up to three tests in its 2019 and 2025 tables (19OBDG03D, 25OBDG03B): after a cold soak (engine off over 540 s or 2,100 s) oil, coolant and intake air must start within 16 °C of each other; the 2025 table also expects the oil to reach 70 °C once enough air has passed; and in operation A and B may differ by no more than 15.8 °C (8 of 10 samples). Type B, MIL after two trips. GM table 23OBDG07 sets it above 15 °C between the two sump sensors, likewise on two trips. A GM patent describes the coolant/intake comparison. Single-sensor faults are P0196 (A) and P01BA (B); typical causes are a drifting sensor or corroded contacts.
c: One oil temperature sensor drifting or stuck within its range
Corroded or loose contacts adding resistance on one sensor
Low oil level leaving one sensor partly uncovered
Block or oil heater use skewing the cold-start comparison
s: MIL after two trips
Oil life or oil temperature display may be wrong
Usually no change in driveability

P2C22.t: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Circuit
P2C22.d: Full hybrids with exhaust heat recovery pass hot exhaust through a coolant heat exchanger after a cold start and divert it around the exchanger with flap A once enough heat has been gathered. A sensor in the flap actuator reports the flap angle to the engine module. P2C22 is the general electrical fault of that feedback: the signal is missing or cannot be read. Ford uses it on its full hybrids. SSM 51921 ties P2C22 with P237C/P237D on the 2022–2023 Maverick 2.5L to water inside the heat exchanger, which is replaced; on 2021–2023 F-150 3.5L PowerBoost trucks SSM 52050 blames the bypass control valve and replaces the muffler inlet pipe, and SSM 53003 supplies an actuator kit. The MIL lights; P2C24/P2C25 name low and high signals, P2C23 an implausible one.
c: Water intrusion into the heat exchanger or its actuator (Ford Maverick hybrid)
Failed bypass valve actuator with integrated position sensor
Corroded or loose connector at the actuator under the vehicle
Harness near the exhaust chafed or heat-damaged
s: Check engine light
Slower engine warm-up and weaker cabin heating in cold weather
Engine of the hybrid runs longer before it may shut off

P2C23.t: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Performance
P2C23.d: P2C23 means the flap position reported for exhaust heat exchanger bypass valve A is electrically valid but does not make sense – for example it disagrees with the command or with how the coolant behind the exchanger warms up. A Ford patent shows that such plausibility can be judged from temperatures. Ford documents P2C23 on several full hybrids: SSM 49531 notes it on 2021 F-150 PowerBoost trucks at or below freezing, TSB 21-2053 reprograms the PCM on trucks built up to 15 February 2021, and SSM 52543 (F-150, Explorer 3.3L, Escape 2.5L, Maverick, up to 2024) first checks the connectors of exhaust coolant temperature sensors 3 and 4 for water and corrosion before the heat exchanger is condemned. Driving is unaffected; the MIL is on.
c: Water or corrosion in the connectors of exhaust coolant temperature sensors 3/4 (Ford)
Worn, sticking or frozen bypass actuator
Flap or linkage in the heat exchanger binding
s: Check engine light, often after frost
No noticeable change in driving
Heater warms up more slowly

P2C24.t: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Circuit Low
P2C24.d: P2C24 is stored when the position signal of exhaust heat exchanger bypass flap A drops below its permitted band. Typical reasons are a signal wire shorted to ground, an open sensor supply or an actuator whose sensor has failed low. CARB requires engine modules to check such inputs for readings outside their range and to keep separate codes for low, high and open where feasible. No manufacturer publishes P2C24 itself; Ford documents only the general circuit code P2C22 and the performance code P2C23 for the same sensor on its full hybrids, where SSM 53003 replaces the heat exchanger actuator on the F-150. An older Ford patent notes that such flaps often had no sensor at all, so the code only applies to actuators that report position. Warm-up may be slower; the MIL is expected.
c: Position signal wire shorted to ground near the exhaust
Open or missing 5 V supply to the position sensor
Position sensor inside the actuator failed low
s: Check engine light
Heat recovery switched off, slower warm-up

P2C25.t: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Circuit High
P2C25.d: P2C25 is the counterpart of P2C24: the feedback from the position sensor of exhaust heat exchanger bypass flap A sits above the highest value a working sensor can deliver. This usually points to a signal line touching a voltage source, an interrupted sensor ground or an internal sensor fault that pulls the output toward the reference. The check is a pure range test demanded by CARB for comprehensive components and does not judge whether the flap actually moves. No manufacturer documents P2C25 publicly; the nearest cases are Ford's full hybrids, where SSM 52050 fixes P2C22/P2C23 on F-150 PowerBoost trucks with a new muffler inlet pipe, naming the bypass valve as cause. Ford's patent describes estimating the flap state from coolant temperatures instead. Expect a lit MIL and reduced heat recovery.
c: Position signal wire shorted to a voltage source
Open ground circuit of the position sensor
Position sensor in the actuator failed high
s: Check engine light
Cabin heater slow to warm up in winter

P2C26.t: Fuel Injector Group B Supply Sense Circuit
P2C26.d: Many engines feed their injectors in groups from a switched supply, for example through an injector relay or a high-side driver. A separate sense line lets the engine module read back whether voltage really arrives at group B. P2C26 is the general fault of that read-back: the sensed value is missing, erratic or not consistent with the commanded supply state. It differs from P2149–P2151, which concern the supply path of group B itself. No publicly accessible manufacturer document explains P2C26; the code rests on CARB's comprehensive component rules. GM's injector logic on the Saab 9-5 2.0T shows the general pattern for supply faults: an incorrect voltage for over 1 s with the engine above 80 rpm sets a Type B code and the injector is shut off. Misfire is possible.
c: Open or high-resistance sense wire between injector supply and module
Injector relay or its socket making poor contact
Corroded connector in the injector supply harness
Faulty sense input inside the engine control module
s: Check engine light
Possible misfire or rough running on the cylinders of group B
Hard starting if the group is switched off

P2C27.t: Fuel Injector Group B Supply Sense Circuit Low
P2C27.d: P2C27 reports that the voltage read back on the supply sense line of injector group B is too low while the module expects the group to be powered. In practice the feed never reaches the injectors – a blown fuse, a relay that does not close, a broken supply wire or a grounded feed – or only the sense wire itself is grounded. In the first case the cylinders of group B receive no fuel and misfire or stay dead; in the second the engine may run normally. No publicly accessible manufacturer source documents P2C27; CARB requires out-of-range low checks of such circuits. GM's direct-injection logic, documented for the Saab 9-5 2.0T, disables an injector once its supply voltage is wrong for more than 1 s and stores a Type B fault. The high case is P2C28.
c: Blown fuse in the injector group B supply
Injector relay not closing or burnt contacts
Supply or sense wire shorted to ground
Internally shorted injector pulling the group supply down
s: Check engine light
Misfire on several cylinders, rough idle
Clearly reduced power or engine will not start

P2C28.t: Fuel Injector Group B Supply Sense Circuit High
P2C28.d: P2C28 is set when the sense line of the injector group B supply shows more voltage than allowed – either above the upper limit while the group is switched on, or voltage present while the module has switched the group off. Common reasons are a welded injector relay, a supply wire chafed against another powered circuit, or a sense wire shorted to battery voltage. A supply that cannot be switched off matters because the module can no longer isolate the group when it needs to protect an injector or the catalyst. No publicly accessible manufacturer document covers P2C28; it follows CARB's demand for separate high-range codes, and GM's handling of injector supply faults on the Saab 9-5 2.0T (wrong voltage for over 1 s, Type B, injector disabled) gives a comparable logic.
c: Sense or supply wire shorted to battery voltage
Excessive system voltage from the charging system
Internal fault of the supply switch in the engine control module
s: Check engine light
Often no noticeable change in running
Battery drain if the relay stays closed after switch-off

P2C29.d: Bypass valve B is the compressor recirculation valve of the second charger – the later one in series layouts, the bank 2 unit on parallel twin-turbo engines. It is not the wastegate. P2C29 means a position-controlled valve no longer follows its target and stays where it is. No manufacturer documents P2C29 publicly. The A-side twin P23AA shows the method on GM's 2019 Corvette LT5: a position error above 25 % lasting at least 1 s while the valve barely moves (under 10 %/s), 10 of 14 samples, Type A. GM's 2019 CT6 4.2L twin-turbo, by contrast, uses switched dump valves without a sensor for both banks and reports a sticking valve B as P00C4. Stuck closed causes surge noise on lift-off; stuck open costs boost.
c: Oil or carbon deposits binding the valve flap or piston
Worn gears or motor in the electric actuator
Bent shaft or damaged housing of the valve
s: Check engine light
Less boost and power
Fluttering compressor noise when lifting off

P2C2A.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Position Sensor Circuit/Open
P2C2A.d: P2C2A covers an open or otherwise unreadable position feedback from compressor bypass valve B, the electrically positioned recirculation valve of the second charger. Without a valid feedback the engine module cannot confirm how far the valve has opened, which an Achates Power patent names as the reason such sensors are monitored. No manufacturer documents P2C2A publicly. GM's 2019 tables describe the A-side sensor of the supercharged LT5 as a ratiometric signal relative to the 5 V reference, but publish only its low and high codes P2BBC/P2BBD. GM defines charger A as bank 1 in parallel layouts and first in exhaust flow in series layouts, so B is the other one. Wiring and connectors near the hot charger are the usual suspects; boost is often limited.
c: Unplugged, loose or corroded connector at valve B
Broken signal, reference or ground wire of the sensor
Internal open in the position sensor of the actuator
s: Check engine light
Boost limited, less power

P2C2B.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Position Sensor Circuit Low
P2C2B.d: With P2C2B the position signal of compressor bypass valve B lies below the lowest value a healthy sensor delivers. Likely reasons are a signal wire grounded against the engine, an open 5 V reference or a sensor that has failed low. For valve B no public manufacturer data exist. For valve A, GM's 2019 Corvette ZR1 (supercharged LT5) shows how such a test is built: a raw reading under 10 % of the reference in 10 of 14 samples taken 100 ms apart, only with relay voltage of at least 11 V and the engine not cranking, gives a Type A fault with immediate MIL (P2BBC). The open-circuit case is P2C2A, the high case P2C2C. Since valve position can no longer be confirmed, boost is typically reduced.
c: Signal wire of the position sensor shorted to ground
Missing 5 V reference at the sensor
Position sensor in the valve actuator failed low
s: Check engine light
Reduced boost pressure

P2C2C.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Position Sensor Circuit High
P2C2C.d: P2C2C flags a position signal from compressor bypass valve B that rises above the plausible top of its range, close to the sensor reference. A signal line touching 5 V or battery voltage, a broken ground wire or a defect inside the sensor are the typical findings. No manufacturer publishes P2C2C. GM's A-side counterpart P2BBD on the 2019 LT5 Corvette shows the pattern: a reading above 95 % in 10 out of 14 checks, one every 100 ms, relay voltage at least 11 V, no cranking, Type A. An Achates Power patent explains why a trustworthy reading matters: the controller compares commanded and measured opening to judge the valve. Unlike P2C29, the valve itself may still work; only its feedback is lost.
c: Signal wire shorted to reference or battery voltage
Open ground of the position sensor
s: Check engine light
Boost limited by the engine module

P2C2D.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Position Exceeded Learning Limit
P2C2D.d: Electrically positioned compressor bypass valves have their end stops relearned regularly so that the sensor reading can be converted into a true opening. P2C2D means that for valve B, belonging to the second charger, a learned stop came out beyond the allowed window. No manufacturer documents the B-side code. GM shows the routine for valve A on the 2019 Corvette ZR1: once the engine is switched off, the module first drives the valve closed and stores the reading, which must lie between 85 and 95 %, then the open stop, expected between 10 and 20 %; a value outside sets P2BBE immediately as Type A, provided no sensor or circuit fault is active. Deposits, a bent flap, gear wear or a shifted sensor are typical causes. A repair is only confirmed after the next key-off learn.
c: Carbon or oil deposits preventing the valve from reaching its stop
Worn actuator gear or loose sensor magnet
Valve replaced without relearn or with incorrect part
s: Check engine light after a key-off
Boost control less precise, possible surge noise

P2C2E.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Supply Voltage Low
P2C2E.d: P2C2E concerns the power stage of compressor bypass valve B, not its position signal. Such valves are moved by a small DC motor driven through an H-bridge, and the bridge reports when its own supply sags below a safe level. No manufacturer documents the B-side code publicly. GM's 2019 LT5 tables describe the equivalent for valve A (P2BBF): the motor driver flags low voltage in 80 of 100 checks spaced 12.5 ms apart, enabled at relay voltage of at least 11 V without cranking, Type A. NXP's MC33926 data sheet shows how a bridge of this kind disables its outputs under undervoltage and signals the fault. A weak battery feed, a poor module ground, a corroded relay or an internal driver fault are typical causes; the valve then remains in its last position.
c: Weak battery or voltage drop on the module feed
Poor ground or corroded relay contacts in the supply
Internal fault of the H-bridge driver
s: Check engine light
Valve no longer responds, boost reduced
Often accompanied by other low-voltage codes

P2C2F.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P2C2F.d: P2C2F is stored when the output stage driving compressor bypass valve B signals excessive current or overheating. The motor driver protects itself by limiting current and finally switching off, and reports this to the engine module. No manufacturer documents P2C2F; GM documents the A-side code P2BC0 for the supercharged 2019 LT5: a raised driver flag in 80 of 100 checks at 12.5 ms, with relay voltage of 11 V or more and no cranking, gives a Type A fault. NXP's MC33926 bridge, a typical part for such loads, regulates overcurrent and shuts down on overtemperature. Excess current mostly stems from a jammed valve working against its stop, a shorted motor winding or touching motor leads. Valve B overheating itself is P00D8; low supply to the same driver is P2C2E.
c: Jammed valve forcing the motor to stall against its stop
Shorted winding in the valve actuator motor
Motor leads shorted to each other or to ground
Overheated or faulty driver inside the engine module
s: Check engine light
Valve stops responding, boost reduced

P2C30.t: Ignition Coil Primary Circuit Fuse A
P2C30.d: On engines whose ignition coils are fed through more than one fuse, the module checks each fuse so that it notices when a whole group of coils loses power. P2C30 points to fuse A. A GM patent explains the reasoning: coils and injectors sit on separate circuits, so after a fuse blows fuel would still be injected into cylinders without spark; the module therefore watches the current through the fuse over a sampling window and cuts the matching injectors to spare the exhaust system. Stellantis uses P2C30 on the 3.0L Hurricane twin-turbo I6 with a separate ignition system control module (ISCM): bulletins 08-205-24 (2025 Ram 1500) and 08-221-24 (2023 Wagoneer) fix it by ISCM software. Expect MIL, misfire and hesitation. Which cylinders fuse A serves is not published.
c: Ignition system control module software (Stellantis 3.0L Hurricane)
Fuse A blown by a shorted ignition coil or supply wire
s: Check engine light
Misfire on several cylinders, hesitation
Reduced power while cylinders are shut off

P2C31.t: Ignition Coil Primary Circuit Fuse B
P2C31.d: P2C31 is the second of two fuse checks in the coil primary supply: the fuse B group of coils has lost voltage, or the module believes so. GM's patent on this monitor counts how often the current through the fuse falls below a threshold within a set number of samples before it declares the fuse open, then flags a service warning and stops fuel to the unfired cylinders. Stellantis lists P2C31 together with P2C30 for the 3.0L Hurricane I6 in the 2025 Ram 1500 and the 2023–2024 Wagoneer/Grand Wagoneer; later bulletins such as 08-136-26 and 08-194-26 add misfire codes P0300–P0306 and catalyst codes P0420/P0430, and the fix remains a reflash of the ignition system control module, partly with the PCM. A truly blown fuse usually means a shorted coil or chafed feed.
c: Ignition system control module calibration (Stellantis 3.0L Hurricane)
Shorted ignition coil in group B blowing the fuse
Chafed coil feed wire shorting to ground
s: Check engine light
Engine misfires or hesitates
Catalyst codes may follow

P2C32.d: A crankcase pressure sensor tells the engine module how the pressure in the crankcase ventilation compares with ambient, mainly so it can detect a disconnected or leaking breather line. P2C32 is the general circuit fault of sensor B: its signal is missing or cannot be decoded at all, without saying high or low. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. Ford shows the pattern for sensor A: on digital SENT sensors, invalid frames or signal patterns set P051A within 5 s, while analogue sensors report the range, low and high codes. Maserati lists the B codes P2C33–P2C35 for the blow-by sensor of its 2021 V6 and V8, but not P2C32. CARB requires the ventilation system to be monitored; with the sensor down that check cannot run, so the MIL is to be expected.
c: Unplugged, loose or corroded sensor connector
Open or chafed wire between sensor and engine module
Engine module input or software fault
s: MIL on
Crankcase ventilation leak check not available
Usually no change in driveability

P2C33.t: Crankcase Pressure Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P2C33.d: P2C33 means crankcase pressure sensor B delivers a signal inside its electrical limits that the engine module finds implausible, such as an offset from ambient pressure with the engine stopped or values a running engine cannot produce. Two bulletin families name it. Alfa Romeo reprograms both engine control modules of the 2.9 L V6 biturbo in the 2021–2022 Giulia and Stelvio (18-043-23, 18-007-25) because software set P2C33 among other codes; the later issue mentions limp-in. Maserati's MY21 bulletin MAS002969/A for its F160 six-cylinder and F154 eight-cylinder asks for a software update first when P2C33 is the only code, then checks the sensor, harness and blow-by valve; cold weather may play a part. For sensor A Ford sets P051B above a 0.15 inHg offset at rest or implausible pressure at low air flow.
c: Engine control software needing an update (Alfa Romeo and Maserati V6/V8)
Sensor offset or drift, partly due to moisture or ice in the port
Faulty blow-by (PCV) valve producing abnormal crankcase pressure
Harness or pin resistance shifting the signal
s: MIL on, often together with other PCM codes
Limp-in mode possible on affected Alfa Romeo models
Otherwise usually no driveability change

P2C34.t: Crankcase Pressure Sensor B Circuit Low
P2C34.d: Circuit Low means the voltage from crankcase pressure sensor B stays under the lowest value the sensor can deliver, typically because the 5 V reference is missing, the signal wire is shorted to ground or the sensor itself has failed. Maserati's bulletin MAS002969/A for MY21 Quattroporte, Ghibli and Levante with the F160 V6 or F154 V8 lists P2C34 next to the sensor-A codes P051B–P051D. Its checklist covers harness continuity and insulation, bent or corroded pins at sensor and ECM, the intermediate signal connection, and about 5 V between pins 1 and 2 at the sensor plug; the sensor sits on bank 1 of the V6 and bank 2 of the V8. As a yardstick, Ford sets the sensor-A low code P051C below 0.44 V after 5 s. While stored, the crankcase ventilation leak check is blocked.
c: 5 V reference open or shorted to ground
Signal wire shorted to ground or chafed insulation
Crankcase pressure sensor B internally failed
Bent or corroded pins at sensor or ECM
s: MIL on
Other sensors on the same 5 V supply may report faults too
Usually no driveability change

P2C35.t: Crankcase Pressure Sensor B Circuit High
P2C35.d: P2C35 is set when the signal of crankcase pressure sensor B sits above the highest voltage the sensor can legitimately produce. That usually means an interrupted signal wire pulled up inside the module, a broken sensor ground, or a short from the signal to the 5 V supply or to battery voltage. Maserati names P2C35 in bulletin MAS002969/A, on the MY21 blow-by sensor of the F160 six and F154 eight-cylinder engines, together with P2C33/P2C34 and the A-sensor codes; besides wiring and pins it lists a faulty sensor, outdated or corrupted ECM software. Ford's analogue sensor A uses P051D above 4.56 V for 5 s as its counterpart. Because the ventilation monitor depends on this signal, the MIL lights even though the engine runs normally.
