c: Open signal wire or unplugged connector
Signal shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Faulty sensor or outdated engine control software
s: MIL on
Crankcase ventilation monitor not completed
Usually no driveability change

P2C36.t: Crankcase Pressure Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2C36.d: P2C36 covers a crankcase pressure sensor B signal that drops out briefly or jumps faster than real crankcase pressure can change, while staying mostly inside its electrical range. That pattern points to a contact that opens for moments, a wire chafing on the engine, moisture in the plug or a sensor failing internally. No manufacturer documents P2C36 publicly: Maserati's bulletin on the blow-by sensor lists only P2C33–P2C35 for sensor B, and Ford's gasoline summary has no erratic code for its sensor A either, whose counterpart would be P051E. The description therefore rests on CARB, which requires inputs used by monitors to be checked for circuit faults and plausibility. A shake test of the harness while watching live data is the usual way to find the cause.
c: Loose or fretting contacts at the sensor or an intermediate connector
Wire rubbing on engine parts and shorting briefly
Moisture or oil in the connector
s: MIL that may come and go
Erratic crankcase pressure value in live data
Usually no driveability change

P2C37.t: Cold Start Engine Coolant Pump Performance
P2C37.d: Engines with a switchable or electric main coolant pump often keep the coolant still, or nearly so, right after a cold start so the cylinder head and catalyst warm up sooner. P2C37 reports that the pump did not behave as commanded during this cold-start phase, for example running when it should rest or failing to start when flow is requested. California rules require separate codes for faults detected during a cold-start strategy and ask makers of electric water pumps to submit a monitoring plan of their own. No manufacturer documents P2C37 publicly. An Audi patent shows one way to judge such a pump: once it is switched back on, the measured head temperature is checked against a model value derived from coolant temperature. Related are P2DE9/P2E82 (cold-start under- and overspeed) and P26CB.
c: Switchable pump stuck engaged or disengaged (clutch, shroud or valve actuator)
Electric coolant pump with failing motor or electronics
Air in the system or low coolant level
Coolant or head temperature sensor reading wrong and misleading the check
s: MIL on
Slow warm-up and weak cabin heat, or rising temperature when the pump stays off
Overheating warning possible in severe cases

P2C38.t: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P2C38.d: A cylinder head temperature sensor is an NTC thermistor seated in the head metal that tells the module how hot the engine really is, even without coolant. P2C38 is the general circuit fault of a second such sensor, B: the signal is open, shorted or otherwise unusable, without separating low from high (P2C3A/P2C3B do that, P2C39 judges plausibility). Ford uses it on the 2025 Explorer and Aviator with 2.3 L or 3.0 L EcoBoost: TSB 24-2393 (built until 15 Oct 2024) describes an over-temperature warning with P1299 plus P2C38 or P2C39 although fan and coolant are fine, and cures it by reprogramming the PCM. For sensor A Ford's 2024 summary flags below 0.244 V or above 4.96 V after 5 s. CARB treats head temperature sensors used for emission control like coolant sensors.
c: PCM software causing false faults (Ford 2025 Explorer/Aviator, TSB 24-2393)
Loose or corroded connector at the head sensor
Heat-damaged or chafed wiring near the cylinder head
s: MIL and engine over-temperature warning
Fail-safe cooling mode with reduced power possible
Temperature warning even though coolant level and fan are fine

P2C39.t: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor B Range/Performance
P2C39.d: P2C39 flags a second cylinder head temperature sensor, B, whose voltage is electrically valid but whose reading does not fit the engine's state, for instance a value that jumps, lags or disagrees with other temperature inputs. Ford is the documented user, all on EcoBoost engines: TSB 24-2441 and its successor 26-2217 (F-150 2.7 L, 2024–2025) pair it with P1299 or P1285 and an over-temperature warning while fan and coolant are fine; a 2024 truck with P2C39 gets new PCM software, the CHT sensor is renewed only if P1285/P1299 persist. TSB 24-2393 (2025 Explorer/Aviator 2.3/3.0 L built to 15 Oct 2024) and 25-2206 (Bronco/Ranger 2.7 L built to 17 Mar 2025) also cure it by reprogramming. Out-of-range voltages are P2C3A/P2C3B.
c: PCM calibration misjudging sensor B (Ford EcoBoost bulletins, cured by reprogramming)
Sensor B drifted or responding slowly
Sensor not seated properly in the head or corroded terminals
Genuine local overheating from low coolant or trapped air
s: Engine over-temperature warning although the gauge and coolant level look normal
Check engine light, often together with P1299 or P1285
Reduced power while the fail-safe cooling strategy is active

P2C3A.t: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P2C3A.d: P2C3A reports that the signal of cylinder head temperature sensor B sits below the lowest voltage the module accepts. Because these sensors are NTC thermistors, a very low voltage would stand for an impossibly hot head, so the usual reasons are a signal wire shorted to ground, water inside the plug or a sensor with an internal short. No manufacturer publicly documents this code. Ford's monitor for its first sensor shows the method: under 0.244 V for 5 seconds, checked continuously, sets the low-input code (P017C, older P1290). The ECM then has to substitute a value, and some calibrations play it safe with full fan operation or a warning. Expect a false overheat message or reduced power. High input is P2C3B, plausibility P2C39.
c: Signal wire of sensor B chafed through to ground
Moisture or coolant in the sensor connector
Internal short in the thermistor of sensor B
s: Overheat warning or very high head temperature in live data on a cold engine
Cooling fans running at full speed without reason
Check engine light, possibly reduced engine power

P2C3B.t: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
P2C3B.d: With P2C3B the voltage from cylinder head temperature sensor B stays above the valid ceiling, which the module would have to read as a head far colder than any real engine. An interrupted signal wire, a lost sensor ground, a terminal that has backed out of the plug or a thermistor cracked by heat cycling are the typical finds. No manufacturer publicly documents the code. For sensor A, Ford's 2024 OBD summary sets the high-input code above 4.96 V lasting 5 s. With the head temperature gone, the engine control falls back on coolant temperature or a default, may run the fans as a precaution and can keep warm-up settings longer than needed. Measure the voltage at the unplugged sensor first. The ground short case is P2C3A, the general circuit fault P2C38.
c: Open signal wire or terminal pushed out of the connector
Sensor return (ground) circuit open or high resistance
Thermistor of sensor B broken internally
s: Live data shows head temperature B at the lowest possible value
Check engine light
Fans run more often, idle and warm-up behaviour unusual

P2C3C.t: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2C3C.d: P2C3C is stored when the head temperature signal of sensor B drops out briefly or jumps in steps that no mass of hot metal could follow, while the samples on their own may still lie within the valid window. Loose terminals, a wire that touches ground only over bumps or with engine movement, corrosion in the plug and a cracked thermistor are the usual culprits. No manufacturer publicly documents P2C3C; Ford's bulletins for this sensor family deal with P2C38 and P2C39 and point to PCM software. California rules require engine component temperature sensors used for emission control to be monitored much like the coolant sensor. Wiggling harness and plug while watching live data is the most revealing check. A fault that stays low or high stores P2C3A or P2C3B instead.
c: Loose or spread terminal in the sensor B connector
Harness rubbing on engine parts and shorting only at times
s: Check engine light that comes and goes
Jumping head temperature B in live data
Occasional fan runs or brief warnings without real overheating

P2C3D.t: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor A/B Correlation
P2C3D.d: An engine with two head temperature sensors can check one against the other: after a long soak both should read close to each other and to coolant temperature, and while running their gap should stay inside an expected band. P2C3D means sensors A and B disagree beyond that limit although neither circuit shows a fault. No manufacturer publicly documents the code or its thresholds. From 2019, phased in until 2021, CARB asks makers that use extra component temperature sensors, also where those sensors sit in different coolant circuits, to have a monitoring plan approved. Ford's 2.7 L EcoBoost bulletins show that both PCM software and a revised CHT sensor can be to blame for implausible head readings. Compare both values on a cold engine; the one far from coolant temperature is suspect.
c: One of the two sensors has drifted out of tolerance
Contact resistance in one sensor circuit shifting its reading
Engine control software judging the pair too tightly
Real temperature difference from air pocket or poor flow in one head area
s: Check engine light without driveability complaints
Clearly different values for head temperature A and B after a cold start

P2C3E.d: P2C3E reports a fault on the control circuit of a fourth fan output: the driver in the engine or fan control module sees an open line, a missing load or an error it cannot sort into low or high. What counts as fan 4 is up to the maker. Saab's GM-based 9-5 of 2011 shows that such numbers follow control outputs rather than motors: three relays switch speed stages of two fans and report P0480 to P0482, or split into short to ground and short to voltage P0691 to P0696, all type B. No manufacturer publicly documents P2C3E. A blown fuse, an open relay coil, a broken wire or a loose plug at the fan are the likely finds. Depending on layout one fan stage stays off, and the engine may run hot in slow traffic. Low and high variants are P2C3F and P2C40.
c: Broken wire or loose connector in the fan 4 control line
Fan 4 relay coil open or relay missing
Blown fuse feeding the relay or fan module
Output driver in the control module defective
s: One fan or fan stage does not run when commanded
Rising temperature at idle or in traffic, weaker A/C at standstill
Check engine light

P2C3F.d: With P2C3F the module senses the control line of fan output 4 at too low a level, which in practice means a short to ground or, with a driver that switches to ground, a line held there by a fault downstream. Saab's 2011 9-5 workshop data define the matching codes for relays 1 to 3 (P0691, P0693, P0695) as a ground short in the relay control wiring, tested with ignition between 8 and 18 V and the engine above 400 rpm, and class them as type B with warning lamp. No manufacturer publicly documents P2C3F itself. Depending on the wiring, the short can switch fan 4 on for good or blow a fuse so it never starts. Check the insulation along the harness first, then the relay coil or module input. Circuit/open is P2C3E, high voltage P2C40.
c: Fan 4 control wire chafed through to body or engine ground
Shorted relay coil or fan module input
Water in the fan connector near the radiator
s: Fan 4 runs constantly or not at all
Blown fan fuse
Check engine light

P2C40.d: P2C40 states that fan control output 4 is held at too high a level: the line has contact with battery voltage, or the driver cannot pull it down when it should. In Saab's 2011 9-5 the counterpart relay codes P0692, P0694 and P0696 stand for a relay control wire shorted to a voltage source, and the manual adds that a stage stuck on can also occur without any stored code. No manufacturer publicly documents P2C40. Typical finds are insulation worn through against a live wire, moisture bridging two pins and a defective relay or fan module input. The fan may run without pause, even after the engine is off, or not respond at all, and a fan that keeps turning can flatten the 12 V battery. Low voltage is P2C3F, the general circuit fault P2C3E.
c: Fan 4 control wire in contact with a battery-voltage circuit
Relay or fan module input failed internally
Moisture bridging pins in the connector
s: Fan 4 runs constantly, sometimes after switch-off
Discharged 12 V battery after standing
Check engine light

P2C41.d: P2C41 judges the outcome rather than the wiring: fan 3 is commanded on and its circuit checks out (otherwise P0482, P0695 or P0696 would appear), yet the controller sees little or no response, usually through speed feedback from a fan module or a missing current draw. No manufacturer publicly documents this code. Audi's 2022–2023 e-tron GT shows what tends to be behind such faults: road debris entering through the wheel housing liner jammed the radiator fans, logged there under P2B30/P2B32. Porsche renewed corroded engine-compartment blowers in pairs on the 2017 911 after a fan failure warning. CARB asks for outputs to be checked for functional response where feasible. Rising temperatures under load follow. Speed deviations are P2CBB/P2CBC.
c: Fan blades blocked by dirt, stones or leaves
Worn or seized fan motor, corrosion from moisture
Fan control module does not drive the motor
Weak power or ground supply to the fan
s: Engine temperature climbs in traffic or under heavy load
Weak air conditioning at standstill
Warning lamp or fan failure message

P2C42.d: P2C42 reports that the fourth fan output does not deliver what is asked of it: the fan stays still or reaches far too little speed while its control line shows no electrical fault (those would be P2C3E to P2C40). No manufacturer publicly documents P2C42. Which part is fan 4 varies: a further radiator fan stage, an auxiliary fan for a charge air or oil cooler, or an engine compartment blower like the pair Porsche fits to the rear-engined 911, whose failure brings a warning to avoid full engine load. Mechanical blocking by dirt, as Audi found on the e-tron GT, worn bearings and a failed fan electronics module are the usual causes. Clean and spin the fan by hand before replacing parts. Fan 3 has P2C41, fan 2 P2B31.
c: Fan jammed by debris or a damaged shroud
Integrated fan electronics or fan module failed
s: Temperature warning or reduced power under high load
Fan 4 does not turn when activated with a scan tool
Grinding noise before the fan stops

P2C43.d: Some vehicles split their 12 V system with a switch so that a heavy starter load, typically an automatic restart, cannot pull the supply of control units and displays down. A Ford patent on start-stop cars puts that dip at roughly 5 to 7 V without such separation. The switch, a relay or semiconductor isolator, is commanded by a control module, and P2C43 is the general fault of this command line, usually an open circuit or a driver that sees no plausible load. No manufacturer documents P2C43 publicly; the only published case in this family is Ford's PowerBoost F-150 with an auxiliary battery isolator, which stores the performance code P2C44. Low, high and intermittent faults have their own codes P2C45 to P2C47. Expect auto stop-start or electric assist to be held back and a fault lamp; driving normally remains possible.
c: Open control wire or loose connector at the isolator
Isolator relay coil or electronic switch failed
Poor ground connection of the isolator circuit
Output driver in the control module defective
s: Warning lamp or powertrain fault indicator on
Automatic stop-start no longer stops the engine
Radio or displays may reboot during engine starts

P2C44.t: Battery Isolation/Voltage Stabilization Control Circuit Performance
P2C44.d: P2C44 means the isolation or voltage stabilization stage is wired and commanded, yet its behaviour does not match what the module expects. Ford is the one maker with published cases: 2021–2022 F-150 trucks with the 3.5 L PowerBoost hybrid and 10R80 MHT gearbox carry a second 12 V battery that an auxiliary battery isolator separates from the main battery. Two special service messages (SSM 50843, 50976) have the technician check ground circuit GD132 including G102, C146 and C1989C and test the auxiliary battery before swapping the isolator; bulletin 23-2031 then combined new PCM software with a new isolator (ML3Z-14526-B, up to 0.7 h). Ford shows the wrench indicator rather than the emissions lamp, sometimes together with U061E. Unlike P2C45/P2C46 the wiring voltage itself is not out of range.
c: Auxiliary battery isolator faulty (Ford replaces it per bulletin 23-2031)
Poor ground in the isolator circuit (Ford GD132, G102, C146, C1989C)
Weak or failing auxiliary 12 V battery
s: Wrench (powertrain malfunction) indicator on
U061E may be stored alongside
Electrical glitches during engine pull-up

P2C45.t: Battery Isolation/Voltage Stabilization Control Circuit Low
P2C45.d: P2C45 is stored when the line that commands the battery isolation or voltage stabilization switch reads lower than its commanded state allows, the classic picture of a short to ground or, with a high-side driver, an open coil pulling the sense voltage down. The switch exists so that the starter can draw its peak current from one battery while sensitive loads stay on a separate, stable supply; Ford's start-stop patent describes this split and notes that relays used for it wear and suffer from contact oxide. No manufacturer publishes P2C45 itself; Ford's PowerBoost F-150 cases are filed under P2C44. A chafed harness near the battery tray or a water-damaged connector is the usual find. Stop-start or engine pull-up support is typically blocked until the short is repaired.
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Corroded or water-damaged connector near the battery
s: Fault indicator on
Stop-start function unavailable
Possible blown fuse in the control circuit

P2C46.t: Battery Isolation/Voltage Stabilization Control Circuit High
P2C46.d: P2C46 is the opposite of P2C45: the control line of the battery isolation or voltage stabilization switch sits higher than expected, which points to a short to battery voltage, or, on a low-side driven relay, to an open circuit that leaves the sense input floating high. The consequence can be worse than with a low signal, because a switch that cannot be commanded may stay closed during restarts, so the supply dip the stage is meant to block reaches the electronics again; Ford's start-stop patent describes the main battery sagging to roughly 5–7 V while cranking. No manufacturer documents P2C46 openly, so the exact threshold is calibration-specific. Check for wires pinched against B+ cables, then for an open circuit, before replacing the isolator.
c: Control wire shorted to battery positive
Open circuit with low-side driver (input pulled high)
Control module input or driver fault
s: Fault indicator on
Stop-start disabled
Screens or radio may reset when the engine restarts

P2C47.t: Battery Isolation/Voltage Stabilization Control Circuit Intermittent
P2C47.d: With P2C47 the module saw the command line of the isolation or stabilization stage drop out and come back, rather than stay permanently open or shorted. Loose terminals, a cracked solder joint in the isolator or a ground strap that only loses contact when the engine rocks on a restart are typical, and the fault often sets only while driving or on bumpy roads. The battery area is a harsh place for connectors: heat, vibration and acid vapour. No manufacturer documents P2C47 itself; Ford's PowerBoost F-150 bulletins under P2C44 show how much a single ground path (GD132) matters in this circuit. CARB lets makers suspend other monitors at low system voltage, so a flickering supply can also leave readiness monitors incomplete. Wiggle tests with live data help to find the spot.
c: Loose or spread terminal in the isolator connector
Ground strap or ground point with intermittent contact
Cracked solder joint inside the isolator
s: Fault indicator comes and goes
Stop-start works only sometimes
Readiness monitors may stay incomplete

P2C48.t: Coolant Pump C Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
P2C48.d: P2C48 is a performance check on coolant pump C: the pump is driven, but what it draws or delivers does not match the request. GM uses it in its diesel tables, where pump C is the electric pump of the low-temperature loop: 20OBDG04 estimates the phase current expected at the actual pump speed and flags an error above 4 A for more than 5 s (5 failures in 8 samples), 25OBDG04A above 1 A with the pump over 2,800 rpm (10 of 12); both type B, two trips. In 19OBDG07 GM assigns P2C48 to the pump for the charge air cooler, using a speed-dependent current window. Bulletin 21-NA-265 (Silverado/Sierra 2500/3500 HD 2020–2022, L5P) links P2C48 and a coolant leak to the fuel cooler hose rubbing on the front drive shaft. Underspeed is P2BA0.
c: Low coolant or air in the low-temperature loop, e.g. from a chafed hose (GM 21-NA-265)
Worn, sluggish or partly blocked pump
Fault in the pump's integrated motor electronics
Weak supply from the powertrain relay or poor ground
s: Check engine light after two trips
Coolant leak under the vehicle
Higher intake air or fuel temperature, possibly reduced power

P2C49.t: Coolant Pump D Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
P2C49.d: P2C49 is the functional check of coolant pump D: the command arrives and the control line is intact, but the pump does not run or does not reach the effect the module expects. No manufacturer publicly documents P2C49. GM shows the method on pump C with P2C48: its diesel tables derive an expected phase current from the measured pump speed and set a type B fault once the difference persists for about 5 seconds. Ford's 2024 gasoline summary carries the same fault type for its auxiliary pumps A and B (P2601, P261B), monitored continuously above 11 V. Which loop pump D serves depends on the vehicle, often a second low-temperature or component circuit. Causes include a seized impeller, air, a weak motor or wiring resistance. The circuit it cools then runs hotter.
c: Air in the loop or low coolant after a leak or repair
High resistance in supply, ground or control wiring
Control module software judging the pump wrongly
s: Check engine light
Higher temperature in the circuit served by pump D
Possible power reduction to protect components

P2C4A.d: The clutch actuator position sensor reports how far the release mechanism of an automated or partly automated clutch has travelled, taken at the slave cylinder or inside the actuator rather than at the pedal. Typical designs are Hall sensors reading a magnet on the clutch piston. P2C4A is the general circuit fault of this sensor. Ford reports it in two ways: its 2024 OBD summary uses P2C4A as the base code behind the low and high faults P2C4C/P2C4D (failure types 11 and 12), and lists P2C4A_48 under P166F as an internal module check of the clutch actuation position, without MIL on manual gearboxes with stop in gear. Range, low, high and erratic faults have separate codes P2C4B–P2C4E. Without a valid signal the controller cannot judge clutch state, so start-stop or automated clutch functions are switched off.
c: Damaged or corroded sensor connector near the gearbox
Open supply, signal or ground wire
Position sensor on slave cylinder or actuator failed
Control module fault (Ford internal check P166F)
s: Stop-start or stop-in-gear disabled
Warning lamp or message
Automated clutch may refuse to engage or drive off

P2C4B.t: Clutch Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2C4B.d: P2C4B flags a clutch actuator position signal that is electrically valid but does not fit the situation, for example a reading that does not move when the actuator is commanded, or end stops that lie outside the learned window. Measuring position on the hydraulic side has its own pitfalls: Schaeffler (LuK) found on its electronic clutch management that brake fluid warming up after a drive shifted the apparent position by around 6 mm against a total travel of roughly 20 mm when the sensor sat at the master instead of the slave cylinder, and had to compensate in software. Air in the fluid acts similarly. No manufacturer publishes P2C4B; Ford only lists the low, high and correlation codes for this sensor. Expect start-stop or automated clutch functions to be limited and a relearn to be needed after repair.
c: Air or leakage in the clutch hydraulics
Sensor drift or loose sensor mounting
Clutch end positions not relearned after service
Clutch wear moving the engagement point out of range
s: Harsh or slipping clutch engagement
Stop-start disabled
Warning message about the gearbox or clutch

P2C4C.t: Clutch Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Low
P2C4C.d: P2C4C means the signal of the clutch actuator position sensor has fallen below its valid band. Ford documents it in its gasoline OBD summaries for 2020–2023 and 2024 under Clutch Actuation Position: the check runs continuously and needs less than one second to register the fault, and in the 2024 version it is reported as base code P2C4A with failure type 11. The section sits next to the clutch pedal sensor checks used for start-stop with manual gearboxes; Ford gives no MIL statement for it. A low reading usually comes from a signal wire shorted to ground, a missing 5 V supply or a sensor that has failed internally. Because the module then cannot tell whether the clutch is open, functions that depend on it, such as stopping the engine with a gear engaged, are disabled. P2C4D covers the high side.
c: 5 V reference supply missing or shorted
s: Stop-start or stop-in-gear unavailable
Warning lamp or message

P2C4D.t: Clutch Actuator Position Sensor Circuit High
P2C4D.d: P2C4D is set when the clutch actuator position signal rises above its upper limit. Ford lists it beside P2C4C in its 2020–2023 and 2024 gasoline OBD summaries: continuous monitoring, under one second to detect, and in 2024 reported as P2C4A with failure type 12. Ford does not state whether the MIL comes on. A high reading typically indicates an open sensor ground, a signal wire touching a supply voltage or a sensor whose output has gone to the rail; with three-wire Hall sensors an interrupted ground is a frequent cause because the signal then floats up to the reference. Unlike P2C4B the voltage itself is implausible, not just the position it represents. As with the low fault, start-stop features that rely on knowing the clutch state are switched off until the circuit is repaired.
c: Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
s: Stop-start or stop-in-gear unavailable
Warning lamp or message

P2C4E.t: Clutch Actuator Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2C4E.d: P2C4E covers a clutch actuator position signal that jumps, drops out briefly or changes faster than the mechanism could physically move. The sensor sits in a hot, vibrating spot on the gearbox or at the actuator, so connectors, fretting contacts and chafed wires are the main suspects; a Delphi patent for such sensors uses two Hall elements and a signal ratio precisely so that changes in the magnet gap matter less, which shows how mechanical play alone can disturb the reading. No manufacturer publishes P2C4E; Ford's documented checks for this sensor are limited to low, high and correlation. Because the controller cannot trust a jumping value, it typically blocks start-stop or automated engagement for the remaining drive. Watching the live signal while moving the harness usually narrows down the fault.
c: Fretting or loose contacts in the sensor connector
Wiring chafed against the gearbox housing
Sensor or magnet loose, changing the air gap
s: Intermittent warning message
Jerky or delayed clutch engagement
Stop-start works only sometimes

P2C4F.d: P2C4F concerns the actuator itself, the electric motor or electro-hydraulic unit that opens and closes an automated clutch, rather than its position sensor. The code means the actuator does not reach or hold the commanded position within the expected time or effort. Schaeffler describes such actuators for e-clutch and automated systems: a brushless motor driving a hydraulic master cylinder, with software continuously adapting the relation between position and transmitted torque. Mechanical sticking, a weak motor, air in the line or a worn clutch that needs more travel can all push the actuator outside its window. No manufacturer documents P2C4F publicly; CARB treats such gearbox actuators as monitored output components. See also P0810 (position control error) and P2785 (overheating). Limp mode or no drive-off is possible.
c: Actuator motor or gear worn or sticking
Air or leak in the clutch hydraulics
Worn clutch requiring travel beyond the learned range
Low supply voltage to the actuator
s: Difficult or impossible drive-off
Clutch slips or engages harshly
Gearbox warning and limp mode

P2C50.t: Clutch Pedal Position Sensor A/Clutch Actuator Position Sensor Correlation
P2C50.d: P2C50 compares two views of the same clutch: what the pedal sensor A says the driver is doing and what the sensor at the release side says the clutch is actually doing. In a hydraulic system both move together, so a lasting gap points to a fault in one sensor or in the hydraulics between them. Ford's OBD documents for gasoline engines (model years 2020–2023 and 2024) assign it to the in-range rationality check of the clutch actuation position sensor, reported as P2C50_00, monitored continuously with detection in under a second. Schaeffler's work on electronic clutch management shows why such a comparison needs tolerance: warming brake fluid alone shifted the measured position by about 6 mm. Circuit faults of each sensor have their own codes (P08A7 ff., P2C4A ff.). Start-stop is typically disabled.
c: Air or leak in the clutch hydraulics between pedal and slave cylinder
Release-side position sensor or slave cylinder faulty
Clutch pedal sensor A drifted or misadjusted
Positions not relearned after clutch or sensor work
s: Stop-start unavailable
Warning lamp or message
Clutch pedal feel may be soft or inconsistent

P2C51.d: Saddle tanks have two chambers and therefore two level senders, A and B; the engine module combines both resistances into one fuel level. GM's bulletin PI0926 for the 2011–2013 Equinox and Terrain shows this layout, with each sender reading about 40 Ω when full. P2C51 means the two senders disagree more than the tank design allows. A Hyundai patent describes such a check: it stores the voltage difference between both senders and starts its fault diagnosis when that difference stays the same although fuel has been used. No manufacturer publicly documents P2C51 itself; Ford and GM use P0461/P2066 and the stuck codes P25B0–P25B2 instead. CARB requires fuel level rationality because EVAP and misfire monitors rely on it.
c: Worn resistor track or sticking float on one sender
Jet pump not transferring fuel between the tank halves
Corroded connector adding resistance on one sender
Wrong or misassembled sender after tank work
s: Fuel gauge inaccurate or not reading full after filling
Check engine lamp
Range display jumps

P2C52.t: Cylinder 1 Fuel Injector B Offset Learning At Min Limit
P2C52.d: Engines with two injectors per cylinder call the second one injector B; with port plus direct injection that is usually one of the two sets, but which one is the maker's choice. For every B injector the engine control learns an offset, a correction for the dead time between the electrical command and the start of real fuel flow. P2C52 says this correction for cylinder 1 has been pushed to its lowest permitted value: the injector already passes more fuel than its model expects, and the pulse cannot be shortened any further. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(6.2.2) counts an adaptation that has used up its authority as a malfunction. No manufacturer publishes this exact code; Volvo's Technical Journal 36016 names only the Max partner P2C53.
c: Injector B of cylinder 1 leaking at the seat and adding fuel after closing
Replacement injector of a different flow rating or not matched to the engine software
Learned values or engine software not up to date (Volvo pairs an update with an adaptation reset for the related Max codes)
Supply pressure on this injector set higher than the model assumes (regulator)
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Long hot start or rough first seconds, possibly misfire on cylinder 1
Possibly fuel smell or higher consumption

P2C53.t: Cylinder 1 Fuel Injector B Offset Learning At Max Limit
P2C53.d: P2C53 is the opposite end of the injector B offset learn on cylinder 1: the engine control has lengthened the command as far as it may, and the cylinder still gets less fuel than requested. Ford patents describe the offset as the time the pintle and the driver circuit need before fuel moves, so a sticky or varnished valve or a weak supply raises it. Volvo documents the code: Technical Journal 36016 (2021) lists P2C53 together with P2C55, P2C57 and P2C59 as permanent ECM faults on 2022 model-year cars of types 224 to 246 with engine variants L1 and 06, usually without any drivability complaint. The remedy was new engine software followed by a reset of the injector adaptations in VIDA with the engine running, strictly in that order.
c: Engine software (Volvo TJ 36016: update, then reset injector adaptations in VIDA)
Varnish or deposits in injector B of cylinder 1, slow opening
Corroded or loose connector, chafed wire or voltage drop at this injector
Air leak at the intake runner of cylinder 1 (only where the learn uses exhaust oxygen)
s: Check engine light
Usually no change in how the car drives
Possibly uneven idle or lean misfire on cylinder 1

P2C54.t: Cylinder 2 Fuel Injector B Offset Learning At Min Limit
P2C54.d: P2C54 concerns injector B of cylinder 2 and the lower limit of its learned offset. Reaching the floor means the control had to keep cutting the opening time because the injector delivers too much, typically at the short pulses where dead time dominates. Plausible reasons are a seat that drips after closing, a replacement injector of a different flow class, or a rail pressure higher than the model assumes. Whether cylinder 2 sits on bank 1 or bank 2 depends on the numbering: in-line engines have one bank, GM V engines put even cylinders on bank 2, Ford V engines count cylinders 1 to 4 on bank 1. No maker documents P2C54 publicly, and Volvo's bulletin for this injector family lists only the Max code P2C55. The legal basis is CARB 1968.2 (e)(6.2.2).
c: Injector B of cylinder 2 leaking at the seat and adding fuel after closing
Replacement injector of a different flow rating or not matched to the engine software
Learned values or engine software not up to date (Volvo pairs an update with an adaptation reset for the related Max codes)
Supply pressure on this injector set higher than the model assumes (regulator)
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Long hot start or rough first seconds, possibly misfire on cylinder 2
Possibly fuel smell or higher consumption

P2C55.t: Cylinder 2 Fuel Injector B Offset Learning At Max Limit
P2C55.d: P2C55 reports that injector B of cylinder 2 needs the maximum offset the engine control allows: even with the longest permitted extension of its pulse it underdelivers. Volvo lists it in Technical Journal 36016 for 2022 model-year cars with engine variants L1 and 06. Version 4.0 of August 2021 still asked for model-specific special software, version 5.0 from September replaced that with a regular software release available from week 37 of 2021, again followed by an adaptation reset in VIDA. Cars treated before week 34 that showed the codes again had to be updated once more. Outside Volvo, a varnished or partly blocked injector, a high-resistance connector or, where the learn uses exhaust oxygen, a leak at the intake runner of cylinder 2 can drive the value up.
c: Engine software (Volvo TJ 36016: update, then reset injector adaptations in VIDA)
Varnish or deposits in injector B of cylinder 2, slow opening
Corroded or loose connector, chafed wire or voltage drop at this injector
Air leak at the intake runner of cylinder 2 (only where the learn uses exhaust oxygen)
s: Check engine light
Usually no change in how the car drives
Possibly uneven idle or lean misfire on cylinder 2

P2C56.t: Cylinder 3 Fuel Injector B Offset Learning At Min Limit
P2C56.d: P2C56 is set once injector B of cylinder 3 has its learned offset stuck at the minimum. How such a value is learned is shown in Ford patents for engines that combine both injection types: with the lift pump switched off, the port injectors fire one cylinder at a time while the others run on direct injection, and how far the low-pressure rail sags after every pulse shows how much fuel that injector really released. If cylinder 3 keeps releasing more than expected, the correction moves down until it reaches the floor. Typical sources are a leaking seat or an internal leak that adds fuel between pulses. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; it also exists on three-cylinder engines. CARB 1968.2 (e)(6.2.2) makes an exhausted adaptation a fault.
c: Injector B of cylinder 3 leaking at the seat and adding fuel after closing
Replacement injector of a different flow rating or not matched to the engine software
Learned values or engine software not up to date (Volvo pairs an update with an adaptation reset for the related Max codes)
Supply pressure on this injector set higher than the model assumes (regulator)
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Long hot start or rough first seconds, possibly misfire on cylinder 3
Possibly fuel smell or higher consumption

P2C57.t: Cylinder 3 Fuel Injector B Offset Learning At Max Limit
P2C57.d: P2C57 is the upper-limit counterpart for injector B on cylinder 3. A Ford patent on engines with two injector types explains why each injector needs its own learned offset: it is the time needed to overcome the inertia of the pintle and of the driver circuit, and it shifts with battery voltage and temperature. A valve that opens late, a corroded connector that drops voltage or deposits in the nozzle therefore push the correction toward its maximum. Volvo is the one maker with a public bulletin for this code (TJ 36016, model year 2022), where it usually appears without symptoms and is cured by a software update plus an adaptation reset in VIDA. CARB 1968.2 (e)(6.2.2) is the regulatory basis.
c: Engine software (Volvo TJ 36016: update, then reset injector adaptations in VIDA)
Varnish or deposits in injector B of cylinder 3, slow opening
Corroded or loose connector, chafed wire or voltage drop at this injector
Air leak at the intake runner of cylinder 3 (only where the learn uses exhaust oxygen)
s: Check engine light
Usually no change in how the car drives
Possibly uneven idle or lean misfire on cylinder 3

P2C58.t: Cylinder 4 Fuel Injector B Offset Learning At Min Limit
P2C58.d: P2C58 marks the minimum limit of the injector B offset on cylinder 4. Useful for diagnosis is a look at the A injector of the same cylinder: if P02D2 is stored as well, both valves seem to overdeliver, which points to something both learns share, such as the measurement or the cylinder itself, rather than to one injector. A lone P2C58 points to injector B, for example a seat that drips after shut-off and makes hot restarts long or the first seconds rough. On a four-cylinder engine this is the last cylinder of the row. No manufacturer publishes this code; Volvo's Technical Journal 36016 lists only the opposite code P2C59 for cylinder 4. Detection of an adaptation at its limit is demanded by CARB 1968.2 (e)(6.2.2).
c: Injector B of cylinder 4 leaking at the seat and adding fuel after closing
Replacement injector of a different flow rating or not matched to the engine software
Learned values or engine software not up to date (Volvo pairs an update with an adaptation reset for the related Max codes)
Supply pressure on this injector set higher than the model assumes (regulator)
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Long hot start or rough first seconds, possibly misfire on cylinder 4
Possibly fuel smell or higher consumption

P2C59.t: Cylinder 4 Fuel Injector B Offset Learning At Max Limit
P2C59.d: P2C59 tells that injector B of cylinder 4 has reached the maximum learned offset, so its delivery falls short even with the longest allowed correction. Volvo's Technical Journal 36016 includes it among four codes, one per cylinder from 1 to 4 and all at the Max limit, on 2022 model-year cars; the first step there is software, not parts. Outside such a bulletin, a swap test helps: move injector B of cylinder 4 to another cylinder, reset the adaptations and let the learn run again. If the Max code follows the injector, the valve is at fault; if it stays with cylinder 4, wiring, connector or the intake side of that cylinder are next. CARB 1968.2 (e)(6.2.2) treats an adaptation out of authority as a malfunction.
c: Engine software (Volvo TJ 36016: update, then reset injector adaptations in VIDA)
Varnish or deposits in injector B of cylinder 4, slow opening
Corroded or loose connector, chafed wire or voltage drop at this injector
Air leak at the intake runner of cylinder 4 (only where the learn uses exhaust oxygen)
s: Check engine light
Usually no change in how the car drives
Possibly uneven idle or lean misfire on cylinder 4

P2C5A.t: Cylinder 5 Fuel Injector B Offset Learning At Min Limit
P2C5A.d: P2C5A can only occur on engines with at least five cylinders and indicates that cylinder 5's injector B has had its learned offset pulled down to the lower bound. The control has removed as much opening time as it may, yet the cylinder still gets more fuel than intended from this valve. On V engines with Ford numbering cylinder 5 opens bank 2; GM numbering puts it on bank 1. Candidates are a dripping valve, a part with too high a flow rating after a repair, or fuel pressure that the model underestimates. No manufacturer documents P2C5A publicly, and Volvo's bulletin for this code family covers only cylinders 1 to 4. CARB's rule 1968.2 (e)(6.2.2) calls for detection once an adaptive correction has used up its range.
c: Injector B of cylinder 5 leaking at the seat and adding fuel after closing
Replacement injector of a different flow rating or not matched to the engine software
Old learned values not reset after injector or software work
Supply pressure on this injector set higher than the model assumes (regulator)
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Long hot start or rough first seconds, possibly misfire on cylinder 5
Possibly fuel smell or higher consumption

P2C5B.t: Cylinder 5 Fuel Injector B Offset Learning At Max Limit
P2C5B.d: P2C5B is the Max limit for injector B on cylinder 5, found on five-, six- and eight-cylinder engines. With two injection systems, one set may stay idle in parts of the map, and fuel left in a resting nozzle can varnish and slow the valve; the learned offset then climbs until it hits the ceiling. Ford builds such dual-injection V6 and V8 engines, yet its public OBD summaries for 2020 to 2025 list no offset-limit codes for injector B, and no other maker publishes P2C5B. The A-injector partner is P02D5. Before replacing parts, rule out a circuit fault on the same valve (P21D3) and reset the adaptations after any repair. CARB 1968.2 (e)(6.2.2) supplies the legal basis.
c: Varnish or deposits in injector B of cylinder 5, slow opening
Corroded or loose connector, chafed wire or voltage drop at this injector
Old adaptation values left at the limit after a repair or software change
Air leak at the intake runner of cylinder 5 (only where the learn uses exhaust oxygen)
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Possibly uneven idle or lean misfire on cylinder 5

P2C5C.t: Cylinder 6 Fuel Injector B Offset Learning At Min Limit
P2C5C.d: P2C5C reports that the injector B offset for cylinder 6 has been learned down to its minimum. In practice the most telling check is the learned value itself: a scan tool that shows the offsets of all B injectors makes one outlier obvious. For an overdelivering valve a pressure-hold test of the rail after shut-off helps, since a dripping injector lets pressure fall faster and may leave a fuel smell or a long hot start. On in-line sixes cylinder 6 is the last one on the rail; on V6 engines its bank depends on the maker's numbering. No manufacturer documents P2C5C publicly; Volvo's injector B bulletin stops at cylinder 4. Under section (e)(6.2.2) of CARB's 13 CCR 1968.2 the exhausted correction counts as a fault.
c: Injector B of cylinder 6 leaking at the seat and adding fuel after closing
Replacement injector of a different flow rating or not matched to the engine software
Old learned values not reset after injector or software work
Supply pressure on this injector set higher than the model assumes (regulator)
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Long hot start or rough first seconds, possibly misfire on cylinder 6
Possibly fuel smell or higher consumption

P2C5D.t: Cylinder 6 Fuel Injector B Offset Learning At Max Limit
P2C5D.d: P2C5D says injector B of cylinder 6 needs the largest learned offset allowed. Because the offset depends on how quickly the driver can energise the coil, electrical causes deserve the first look: a corroded or loose connector, chafed wiring or a supply voltage that sags on that injector lengthen the real opening delay. If a circuit code for the same valve (P21D4) is present, that comes first. Mechanical causes are deposits or a sticking pintle. On six- and eight-cylinder engines with port plus direct injection this valve is often under the intake manifold, which makes access costly. No maker documents P2C5D publicly; the only bulletin for the family, Volvo's TJ 36016, stops at cylinder 4. CARB 1968.2 (e)(6.2.2) applies.
c: Varnish or deposits in injector B of cylinder 6, slow opening
Corroded or loose connector, chafed wire or voltage drop at this injector
Old adaptation values left at the limit after a repair or software change
Air leak at the intake runner of cylinder 6 (only where the learn uses exhaust oxygen)
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Possibly uneven idle or lean misfire on cylinder 6

P2C5E.t: Cylinder 7 Fuel Injector B Offset Learning At Min Limit
P2C5E.d: P2C5E belongs to cylinder 7 and therefore to engines with at least seven cylinders, in practice V8s. It is stored when the learned offset of injector B has been driven to its floor: the valve gives more fuel than the model predicts even at the shortest permitted command. On Ford-numbered V8s cylinder 7 is on bank 2, on GM-numbered ones on bank 1, so a rich fuel trim for system B on the matching bank (P2BF1 or P2BF3) supports the finding. Leaking seats, a wrongly rated replacement valve or excess rail pressure are the usual suspects. No manufacturer documents P2C5E publicly; Ford's 2020 to 2025 OBD summaries for its dual-injection V8 do not list it either. It falls under CARB 1968.2 (e)(6.2.2).
c: Injector B of cylinder 7 leaking at the seat and adding fuel after closing
Replacement injector of a different flow rating or not matched to the engine software
Old learned values not reset after injector or software work
Supply pressure on this injector set higher than the model assumes (regulator)
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Long hot start or rough first seconds, possibly misfire on cylinder 7
Possibly fuel smell or higher consumption

P2C5F.t: Cylinder 7 Fuel Injector B Offset Learning At Max Limit
P2C5F.d: P2C5F, again a V8 code, flags injector B of cylinder 7 whose learned offset is pinned at its maximum. A point often missed is the learn history: when an injector is replaced or software changes, old adaptation values can sit at the limit until they are cleared. Volvo, for example, insists on resetting the injector adaptations with the engine running after its software update for the related four-cylinder codes. If the code returns after a reset and a full learn, the valve really underdelivers: varnish in the nozzle, a slow pintle or a poor connection. Comparing with the A-injector partner P02D9 shows whether only the B side is affected. No manufacturer publishes P2C5F; CARB 1968.2 (e)(6.2.2) defines the requirement.
c: Varnish or deposits in injector B of cylinder 7, slow opening
Corroded or loose connector, chafed wire or voltage drop at this injector
Old adaptation values left at the limit after a repair or software change
Air leak at the intake runner of cylinder 7 (only where the learn uses exhaust oxygen)
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Possibly uneven idle or lean misfire on cylinder 7

P2C60.t: Cylinder 8 Fuel Injector B Offset Learning At Min Limit
P2C60.d: P2C60 is the minimum-limit code for injector B on cylinder 8, the last cylinder of a V8 and the end of this code series. Its A-side twin P02DA is documented by GM for the L5P diesel and by Land Rover for a 5.0 V8, but the B version has no public manufacturer source at all. The physics are the same as on the other cylinders: the learned correction has shortened the pulse to the floor because this valve keeps overdelivering. On a V8 a dripping injector on cylinder 8 often shows up as a rough first few seconds after a hot start, sometimes with a misfire record for cylinder 8 (P0308). Under both Ford and GM numbering it sits on bank 2. CARB 1968.2 (e)(6.2.2) requires the check.
c: Injector B of cylinder 8 leaking at the seat and adding fuel after closing
Replacement injector of a different flow rating or not matched to the engine software
Old learned values not reset after injector or software work
Supply pressure on this injector set higher than the model assumes (regulator)
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Long hot start or rough first seconds, possibly misfire on cylinder 8
Possibly fuel smell or higher consumption

P2C61.t: Cylinder 8 Fuel Injector B Offset Learning At Max Limit
P2C61.d: P2C61 closes the series: injector B of cylinder 8 has driven its learned offset into the ceiling, so this valve stays short of fuel despite the longest correction allowed. Because a weak supply pump or low rail pressure would starve every injector of the same set, a Max code on a single cylinder narrows the search to that valve, its wiring or the air path of that cylinder. A lean system B trim on bank 2 (P2BF2) fits the picture on most V8 numbering schemes. Ford's published OBD summaries for the V8 with both injection types omit P2C61, and no other manufacturer documents it; Volvo's bulletin for the Max codes stops at cylinder 4. California's OBD rule (CARB 1968.2, section (e)(6.2.2)) makes an adaptation without remaining range a reportable fault.
c: Varnish or deposits in injector B of cylinder 8, slow opening
Corroded or loose connector, chafed wire or voltage drop at this injector
Old adaptation values left at the limit after a repair or software change
Air leak at the intake runner of cylinder 8 (only where the learn uses exhaust oxygen)
s: Check engine light
Often nothing else noticeable
Possibly uneven idle or lean misfire on cylinder 8

P2C62.t: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit/Open Bank 1 Sensor 3
P2C62.d: P2C62 points to an open trim circuit at the third oxygen probe of bank 1. Wide-band probes such as Bosch's LSU 4.9 carry a trimming resistor in the connector on a pin of its own (RT/IA) that sets each probe's characteristic; the engine module reads it to scale the pump current, so with the lead broken the signal still moves but with the wrong gain. A third probe sits behind a second catalyst, on diesels typically after the SCR stage. No carmaker documents P2C62 publicly: GM's 3.0L Duramax tables and bulletins use only P2C63, P2C64 and P2C65 for sensor 3. CARB requires circuit continuity checks on oxygen and air-fuel sensors. The front and middle analogues are P2626 and P22B5; low and high faults of this probe are P2C63/P2C64.
c: Trim line broken or terminal pushed back in the probe connector
Moisture or corrosion in the connector of the rear probe
Trimming resistor in the probe connector open (probe replacement)
s: MIL on, usually without noticeable driving change
Catalyst or aftertreatment monitors not completing

P2C63.t: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit Low Bank 1 Sensor 3
P2C63.d: P2C63 reports that the oxygen value from the third exhaust sensor of bank 1 has dropped below its physically possible minimum. Despite the trim wording, GM uses it on the 3.0L Duramax diesel for the O2 signal of NOx sensor 3, which sits behind the second catalyst: table 25OBDG04B (2025) fails a reading under -6 percent in 100 of 200 samples on a 25 ms task, with the engine running, supply above 11 V and the sensor ready; Type B, MIL after two trips. GM's PIT5751C and bulletin 21-NA-149 name P2C63 among many codes on 2020-21 Silverado, Sierra, Tahoe, Yukon and Escalade with the 3.0L LM2; the cause was an engine harness rubbed through above the generator or shorted against the clamp of the crankcase-pressure-regulator hose. P2C64 is the high side, P23AE the NOx circuit low code of this sensor.
c: Engine harness chafed or shorted (GM 3.0L LM2 - at the generator or the crankcase pressure regulator clamp)
Third exhaust sensor (on GM diesels NOx sensor 3) reporting an implausibly low O2 value
s: MIL on after two trips
On the GM LM2 often many other codes, rough running or blown fuses when the harness is damaged
Aftertreatment monitors not completing

P2C64.t: O2 Sensor Pumping Current Trim Circuit High Bank 1 Sensor 3
P2C64.d: P2C64 is the high-side partner of P2C63: the oxygen reading attributed to sensor 3 of bank 1 climbs above what the probe can physically deliver. On GM's 3.0L Duramax diesel the value comes from NOx sensor 3 behind the second catalyst, and table 25OBDG04B sets the code once that O2 reading exceeds 29 percent, clearly more than the roughly 21 percent of fresh air, in 100 of 200 samples under the same enable conditions as the low check; Type B, MIL after two trips. Such a figure hints at a signal fault in the sensor or its wiring rather than real exhaust oxygen. The harness bulletins PIT5751C and 21-NA-149 for 2020-21 GM models with the 3.0L LM2 list P2C64 as well. P2C62 is the open circuit, P23AF the NOx circuit high code of the same sensor.
c: Third exhaust sensor (on GM diesels NOx sensor 3) delivering an implausibly high O2 value
Engine harness chafed or shorted (GM 3.0L LM2, PIT5751C)
Moisture or corrosion in the sensor connector
s: MIL on after two trips
Further NOx sensor or aftertreatment codes stored

P2C65.t: O2 Sensor Out of Range During Deceleration Bank 1 Sensor 3
P2C65.d: P2C65 is the overrun plausibility check for the third oxygen sensor of bank 1: with fuel cut on deceleration the exhaust is close to fresh air, so the reading must land inside a known window. GM's 3.0L Duramax runs this test for sensor 1 under P2297, where table 25OBDG04B compares the measured O2 value with an estimate in overrun and flags a gap above 4 or below -3.25 percent (Type B). For sensor 3, NOx sensor 3 behind the second catalyst, GM publishes no threshold, but PIT5751C and bulletin 21-NA-149 list P2C65 together with P2C63/P2C64 on 2020-21 trucks and SUVs with the 3.0L LM2, where a chafed engine harness was the cause. CARB accepts a check during fuel shut-off where full rear-sensor monitoring is not feasible. The sensor 2 code is P232F, sensor 1 P2297.
c: Third exhaust sensor aged or drifting (wrong value in fresh air)
Exhaust leak ahead of sensor 3 distorting the overrun reading
Damaged sensor wiring or chafed engine harness (GM 3.0L LM2)
Leaking injector or model error disturbing the comparison in overrun
s: MIL on, usually without noticeable driving change
Possibly stored together with other sensor 3 or NOx sensor codes

P2C66.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump A Underspeed
P2C66.d: P2C66 reports that pump A of the electronics cooling loop, which carries heat away from inverter, DC/DC converter and often the on-board charger or drive motor, turns slower than requested. Pumps of this kind report their actual speed, and the controller compares it with the target. No manufacturer publicly documents P2C66. Ford's 2024 summary uses the same fault type, under-speed (B2), for engine coolant pump A, monitored continuously over 5 seconds above 11 V. GM's 2016 Volt judges pump A of its power electronics loop differently, as P0CEA, when coolant and charger temperatures drift apart. Worn bearings, sludge or debris, low supply voltage and partial air are typical. Expect reduced drive power or slower charging. Overspeed is P2C67, a stalled pump P2C68.
c: Worn bearings or a sluggish impeller
Debris or sludge in the pump or a restricted loop
Low supply voltage from fuse, relay or ground faults
Air pockets after a coolant service
s: Hybrid/EV system warning and check engine light
Reduced drive power or slower charging
Electronics temperature rises faster than usual

P2C67.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump A Overspeed
P2C67.d: With P2C67 the electronics coolant pump A runs faster than commanded. A centrifugal pump speeds up as soon as it loses load, so air in the loop is the leading suspect, followed by a loose impeller or a faulty speed signal. Mercedes logs the related dry-run code P2B2A7A on the GLE/GLS 167 with M177 V8 and 48 V system: air in the low-temperature loop sends the 15 W pump into an emergency dry-run mode, and the cluster shows a yellow coolant message. A Pierburg patent detects dry running by letting the motor coast after a defined energy pulse and counting rotor turns. No manufacturer documents P2C67 itself. Ford's 2024 summary treats overspeed/dry run (B1) as its own pump fault type. Underspeed is P2C66, dry run P2B2A.
c: Air in the electronics loop after service or from a leak
Low coolant level in the low-temperature reservoir
Impeller slipping on the shaft or broken
Implausible speed feedback from the pump electronics
s: Coolant or drive system warning in the cluster
Churning or gurgling noise from the pump
Reduced power when electronics temperatures climb

P2C68.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump A Stuck/Stalled
P2C68.d: P2C68 means the electronics coolant pump A has power and a command, yet its rotor does not turn or stops. Brushless pumps notice this themselves from a failed start attempt or high current with no rotation and report it to the controller. No manufacturer publicly documents P2C68. Ford's 2024 summary shows the matching fault type 71, actuator stuck, for engine coolant pump A (P2B9C), and a GM patent detects electric coolant pump faults by comparing measured with expected current. Seized bearings, sludge or debris, frozen coolant and burnt windings are the usual causes. Without flow, inverter and charger heat up quickly, so the vehicle limits power or stops charging. Audi's e-tron bulletin shows pump circuit faults (P0CE9) together with low coolant warnings.
c: Seized bearing or impeller in pump A
Foreign matter or sludge blocking the impeller
Burnt winding or failed pump electronics
Coolant frozen due to weak antifreeze
s: Drive system warning, check engine light
Strongly reduced power or charging interrupted
No pump noise when the pump is activated with a scan tool

P2C69.t: Drive Motor A Phase X Current
P2C69.d: P2C69 is the general fault for the current in phase X of drive motor A, as the inverter measures it. J2012 places the X, Y and Z series next to the U/V/W codes P0A5D-P0A65 without public explanation; in motor design those letters usually name the second three-phase winding set of a dual-winding machine. A Mitsubishi Electric patent for hybrid and electric drives shows such a layout, with its own inverter and a separate current sensor for each of X, Y and Z. No carmaker documents P2C69 publicly. By analogy with the U/V/W codes it covers a reading the controller cannot trust, a sensor circuit fault or a cable or winding defect that is not clearly a low or high value; those cases are P2C6A and P2C6B. The driver sees the hybrid or drive warning and limited or no electric power.
c: Phase X current sensor or its supply/signal circuit in the inverter faulty
High-voltage phase lead X loose, burnt or poorly joined at motor or inverter
Internal inverter fault (switching leg or measurement electronics of the X/Y/Z set)
Winding fault in phase X of drive motor A
s: Hybrid or electric drive warning and MIL on
Reduced electric drive power or vehicle not ready to drive
Further phase current or inverter codes stored at the same time

P2C6A.t: Drive Motor A Phase X Current Low
P2C6A.d: P2C6A means that too little current is seen in phase X of drive motor A while the inverter is driving it, which typically points to an open phase or a dead sensor. No carmaker documents the code publicly. GM's U/V/W counterpart shows how such a check works: in the 2016 Volt, the motor control processor samples each phase while the rotor sits within 30 degrees of that phase axis, with the inverter in normal PWM above 50 V and more than 900 A2 commanded; a peak below 9 A for 0.4 s within 0.6 s sets the code as Type A, MIL after one trip. In a dual-winding motor with a second X/Y/Z set, as in a Mitsubishi Electric patent, the same test would apply to phase X. P2C69 is the general X code, P2C6B the high side, P2C6D and P2C70 the low faults of Y and Z.
c: Phase X lead or terminal open or high-resistance between inverter and motor
Phase X current sensor reading near zero (sensor or its supply failed)
Switching leg for phase X in the inverter not conducting
Open winding of phase X inside drive motor A
s: Hybrid or drive system warning and MIL on
Noticeably weaker or jerky electric drive, or drive disabled

P2C6B.t: Drive Motor A Phase X Current High
P2C6B.d: P2C6B flags an overcurrent in phase X of drive motor A. X, Y and Z name the second three-phase winding set of a dual-winding machine, which a Mitsubishi Electric patent shows with its own inverter bridge and a current sensor per phase. No carmaker documents P2C6B publicly. Ford's 2019 hybrid summary gives the logic for the U/V/W counterparts (P0A5F, P0A62, P0A65): the motor control unit declares overcurrent above 600 A for 400 microseconds, or above 30 A for 200 ms right after power-up, when hardly any current should flow. Real causes are a short between windings or to the housing, or a power switch that stays conducting; a sensor reading too high fakes the fault. The inverter cuts drive to protect itself. P2C6A is the low side, P2C6E and P2C71 the high faults of Y and Z.
c: Turn-to-turn or ground short in the phase X winding of drive motor A
IGBT/MOSFET of the X leg in the inverter shorted or failing to turn off
Phase X current sensor reading too high (gain or offset drift)
Chafed or wet phase X lead touching another phase or the housing
s: Hybrid or drive system warning with MIL on
Sudden loss of electric drive, vehicle may not become ready
Isolation fault codes stored at the same time if the winding touches the housing

P2C6C.t: Drive Motor A Phase Y Current
P2C6C.d: P2C6C is the umbrella code for the current in phase Y of drive motor A, the middle phase of the second X/Y/Z winding set. No manufacturer documents it publicly. Ford's 2019 hybrid summary explains what such phase current codes collect: the inverter is watched for overcurrent, current sensor faults and current regulation faults, and the result is stored per phase. For Y that means the measured current does not follow the command, or the reading cannot be trusted, without being clearly low (P2C6D) or high (P2C6E). A failed sensor circuit has its own code, P2E1F. CARB leaves the drive motor monitoring plan to each manufacturer, so thresholds differ. In practice look at the Y phase lead, its terminals and the inverter, and expect a warning and reduced or no electric drive.
c: Inverter cannot regulate the phase Y current to its command (control or gate drive fault)
Loose, corroded or overheated phase Y terminal at inverter or motor
Phase Y current reading implausible against the other two phases
Partial winding fault in phase Y of the motor
s: Hybrid or drive warning, MIL on
Reduced electric torque or jerky drive
Vehicle not ready to drive in severe cases

P2C6D.t: Drive Motor A Phase Y Current Low
P2C6D.d: P2C6D is set when phase Y of drive motor A carries too little current while the inverter drives it, the typical signature of an open phase. No manufacturer documents P2C6D publicly. A test of this kind can run at start-up: on its 2019 power-split hybrids Ford checks the phase circuits right after power-up and declares a fault if less than 5 A flows during the 100 ms test. On a dual-winding motor of the kind shown in a Mitsubishi Electric patent, each winding set is driven separately, so an open Y lead in the second set does not affect U, V and W, but the machine loses torque and runs unevenly. Typical finds are a lifted or burnt terminal, a cracked busbar, a dead switching leg or an open winding. P2C6C is the general Y code, P2C6E the high side.
c: Phase Y lead, busbar or terminal open or high-resistance
Y switching leg of the inverter not conducting (switch or gate driver)
Phase Y current sensor or its supply failed, reading near zero
Open phase Y winding inside the motor
s: Hybrid or drive warning and MIL
Noticeably weaker electric drive, vibration or humming under load

P2C6E.t: Drive Motor A Phase Y Current High
P2C6E.d: P2C6E reports that too much current flows in the Y phase of drive motor A, which sits in the machine's second winding set. No manufacturer documents P2C6E publicly. A Hyundai bulletin shows what usually lies behind a phase overcurrent: on the 2017 Ioniq Hybrid, coolant leaking inside the traction motor set the high codes of phases U, V and W (P0A5F, P0A62, P0A65), often with the isolation fault P0AA6. Dealers ran an insulation breakdown test and replaced the motor if it failed, and drivers noticed weak acceleration and no air conditioning. The same applies to Y: moisture, coolant or damaged insulation lets current bypass the intended path. A shorted inverter switch or a sensor reading too high are the other suspects. P2C6D is the low side, P2C6B and P2C71 are X and Z.
c: Coolant or moisture inside the motor degrading winding insulation
Short between phase Y and another phase or the stator core
Shorted power switch in the Y leg of the inverter
Phase Y current sensor reading too high
s: Hybrid warning and MIL, often with an isolation fault code
Weak acceleration or electric drive switched off
Electric air conditioning compressor disabled

P2C6F.t: Drive Motor A Phase Z Current
P2C6F.d: P2C6F is the general current fault for phase Z, the third phase of the second winding set of drive motor A. No manufacturer documents it publicly. Whether Z is measured at all depends on the design: the Mitsubishi Electric patent fits a sensor to each of X, Y and Z, while a Hyundai patent describes inverters that measure two phase currents and calculate the third, since all three must add up to zero. In the second case a Z code can arise from an error in X or Y, so the other phases must be checked too. The code covers implausible readings and current that does not follow the command without a clear low or high case (P2C70, P2C71); a sensor circuit fault is P2E23. The driver sees a hybrid or drive warning with reduced or no electric power.
c: Error in the X or Y current measurement corrupting a calculated Z value
Phase Z terminal or busbar loose, corroded or overheated
Fault in the Z switching leg or its gate driver
s: Hybrid or drive system warning with MIL
Reduced electric power, possibly engine-only operation on hybrids
Other X/Y phase codes stored alongside

P2C70.t: Drive Motor A Phase Z Current Low
P2C70.d: P2C70 means phase Z of drive motor A delivers too little current although the inverter is commanding it. No manufacturer documents P2C70 publicly. GM's missing-phase check for the U/V/W set shows the principle: the 2016 Volt only judges a phase while the rotor angle sits near that phase axis and enough current is requested, and fails it when the peak stays under 9 A, Type A with MIL after one trip. The window matters, because a phase near its zero crossing carries little current even when healthy. For the Z phase of the second set the most likely finds are an open lead or terminal, a burnt connection at the inverter or a sensor stuck at zero. Torque drops and the motor may vibrate. P2C6F is the general Z code, P2C71 the high side, P2C6A and P2C6D the low cases of X and Y.
c: Phase Z lead or terminal open or burnt
Phase Z current sensor stuck near zero
Z leg of the inverter not switching
Open phase Z winding in the motor
s: MIL and hybrid or drive warning
Loss of torque and vibration from the motor under load

P2C71.t: Drive Motor A Phase Z Current High
P2C71.d: P2C71 reports overcurrent in phase Z of drive motor A, the last phase of the second winding set. No manufacturer documents P2C71 publicly. Once overcurrent is detected the inverter has to bring the machine into a safe state, and the Mitsubishi Electric patent on dual-winding drives deals with exactly that: when the battery link opens, each winding set is moved in steps from a phase short circuit to all switches off, at different times, so that the voltage induced by the spinning rotor cannot damage the inverter. For the driver this means a sudden loss of drive power and a warning. Ford's limits for the U/V/W case, 600 A for 400 microseconds, show how fast such checks are. Suspect a shorted switch, a winding or lead short, or a sensor error. P2C70 is the low side, P2C6B and P2C6E are X and Y.
c: Shorted power semiconductor in the Z leg
Short in the phase Z winding or lead, to another phase or ground
Phase Z current sensor reading too high or noisy
Inverter control software reacting wrongly to transients
s: Sudden loss of drive power with hybrid or drive warning
MIL on, vehicle may not restart into ready mode

P2C72.d: P2C72 says the coolant loop serving the hybrid or EV power electronics (inverter, DC/DC converter, often the charger) does not cool as expected. CARB requires a functional check of inverter cooling performance where feasible, on top of the circuit checks of pump and sensors. No manufacturer documents P2C72 publicly. The closest documented code is P0A93: Hyundai traced it on the 2011 Sonata Hybrid to the electric water pump, with a hybrid warning, no EV mode and weak acceleration (bulletin 14-HC-001). A Hyundai patent shows one way to judge the loop: with the car at rest a fixed pump output is applied, and an impeller turning faster than the reference reveals low coolant. Leaks, air, a weak pump, a clogged radiator or a failed fan are typical. Power is limited to protect the electronics.
c: Low coolant level or leak in the electronics loop
Air trapped in the loop after service
Electronics coolant pump delivering too little flow
Clogged low-temperature radiator or failed cooling fan
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Reduced power, no EV mode, especially in heat or under load
Inverter over-temperature codes stored as well

P2C73.t: Active Grille Air Shutter C Stuck On
P2C73.d: Some vehicles split the grille opening into several separately driven flaps; shutter C is a third one next to A (usually upper) and B (lower). P2C73 says flap C stays open although the engine module asks it to close – the counterpart of P05FE, which covers a flap that will not move to its target. Nobody publishes P2C73 itself. The nearest evidence is Hyundai: the 2026 Palisade and Palisade Hybrid run two lower flap actuators (left and right) and list other shutter C codes (P05FE, P2C74) in a 2026 campaign about corroded bumper connectors. Toyota records the same fault on shutter A as P05A0 subtype 72 when debris props the louvres open. Engine cooling is unaffected; the cost is drag, slower warm-up and a warning lamp.
c: Debris, snow or ice holding the louvres of shutter C open
Actuator motor or gear of shutter C failed in the open position
Linkage or flap frame bent or broken, e.g. after minor front damage
Water ingress and corrosion at the bumper connector of the actuator
s: Engine warning lamp, sometimes a grille shutter or air flap message
Slightly higher fuel consumption at motorway speed
Slower engine and heater warm-up in cold weather

P2C74.t: Active Grille Air Shutter C Control Circuit Range/Performance
P2C74.d: P2C74 judges the drive of grille shutter C: the command to the actuator or the feedback it returns does not fit the expected range, so the flap may move sluggishly, erratically or not at all. Hyundai is the documented user. In its 2026 Palisade and Palisade Hybrid (built May to December 2025) the lower air flap system has a left and a right actuator plus two flap sensors, and campaign 26-01-026H (revised as 26-01-026H-1 in August 2026) lists P2C74 with P05FE, P05AE and U0285. The cause there was water reaching the bumper connectors and corroding pins; the driver sees an air flap system message and the engine lamp, sometimes even a low oil warning. Repair means cleaning or replacing connectors, actuator, sensor or bumper harness. Unlike P2C73 (flap stuck open), this code points at the electrical drive path.
c: Water ingress and corroded pins at the bumper connectors of the flap actuator or sensor
Chafed or broken front bumper harness
Actuator of shutter C faulty or responding too slowly
Flap position sensor of the lower air flap faulty
s: Engine warning lamp and an active air flap warning message
Flap does not move or moves jerkily
Possibly an unrelated low engine oil message at the same time

P2C75.t: Active Grille Air Shutter Module C Over Temperature
P2C75.d: Smart grille shutter actuators carry their own driver chip and protect it by temperature. P2C75 is that self-protection for shutter C: the module reports its electronics as overheated and stops driving the motor. No manufacturer documents P2C75; the closest published logic is Ford's for shutters A and B (P05C0, P05C1): a chip junction temperature above 140 °C, confirmed after 10 s in the 2023 diesel summary and after 30 s in the 2024 petrol summary, with no further entry conditions. Heat builds when the motor keeps pulling against a frozen, jammed or bent flap, or when its winding is partly shorted; an internal fault is also possible. After cooling the flap often works again, which makes the fault look sporadic. Unlike P2C73 and P2C74, the verdict comes from the actuator's own electronics.
c: Flap frozen, jammed or bent so the motor works against a stop
Partly shorted motor winding drawing excess current
Internal fault of the actuator electronics
s: Engine warning lamp, often intermittent
Shutter C stops moving until the module has cooled down

P2C76.t: Active Grille Air Shutter D Stuck On
P2C76.d: Shutter D would be the fourth individually driven grille flap. P2C76 reports that this flap remains open when the engine module wants it shut. Not a single published document uses a shutter D: GM and Ford stop at A and B, and Hyundai's 2026 Palisade reaches C. The meaning therefore follows the stuck-open codes of the other flaps, P05A0 for A and P2C73 for C. Toyota's 2016–17 Prius illustrates the pattern on shutter A: debris lodged in the louvres kept them open, set P05A0 subtype 72 with the MIL and a dashboard message, and the cure was cleaning. An open flap leaves full cooling air, so overheating is unlikely; instead drag rises, the engine and catalyst warm up more slowly in winter, and fuel use creeps up.
c: Leaves, stones or other debris wedged in the louvres of shutter D
Actuator of shutter D failed while the flap was open
Flap frame or linkage damaged by a front impact
s: Engine warning lamp and possibly a grille shutter message
Longer warm-up and weaker heater output in winter
Marginally higher fuel use

P2C77.t: Active Grille Air Shutter D Control Circuit Range/Performance
P2C77.d: P2C77 flags the drive circuit of a fourth grille shutter D as implausible: the actuator does not respond to its command in the expected way, or the signal it returns lies outside the permitted window. No manufacturer publishes a shutter D, so the code is reserved for designs with four separately powered flaps. Comparable faults on other flaps show where to look. VW's 2015–16 Jetta (1.8 T and 2.0 TDI) set P05A3 for shutter A, often together with P05A0, because the software inside the grille motor was faulty; an updated motor cured it. Hyundai's 2026 Palisade sets P2C74 for shutter C when water corrodes the bumper connectors. So wiring, connectors and the actuator itself come before any module. Driving is normally unaffected beyond the warning lamp; the flap simply stays where it stopped.
c: Corroded connector or damaged wiring to the actuator of shutter D
Actuator of shutter D faulty, including faulty internal software
Stiff or partly blocked flap slowing the actuator response
s: Engine warning lamp
Shutter D no longer follows commands

P2C78.t: Active Grille Air Shutter Module D Over Temperature
P2C78.d: P2C78 is the over-temperature report of the actuator module for a fourth grille shutter D: its driver electronics have exceeded their thermal limit and the output stage has been switched off to protect it. No vehicle with a shutter D is documented, so the logic is borrowed from Ford's smart shutter actuators, which use P05C0/P05C1 for shutters A and B and set them when the controller chip reports more than 140 °C for 10 s (2023 diesel) or 30 s (2024 petrol). Typical triggers are a motor stalled against ice or a damaged linkage, a partly shorted coil, or heat soak near the radiator combined with constant repositioning. Because the protection releases once the chip cools, the code may come and go. Compared with P2C76 and P2C77 it says less about the flap than about the actuator's own health.
c: Motor stalled against ice or a damaged linkage
Heat soak near the radiator combined with constant repositioning
s: Intermittent engine warning lamp
Shutter D stops moving for a while

P2C79.d: P2C79 says the sulfur load held in the NOx adsorber (lean NOx trap) has reached the limit the engine computer allows. Sulfur from fuel and oil occupies the storage sites more firmly than NOx, so capacity shrinks until a desulfation is run: rich phases with the trap above roughly 550 °C, as a Volkswagen patent explains. A Ford patent models the stored sulfur and starts this cleaning once a calibrated amount is reached, naming typical values between 0.1 and 0.5 g per litre of trap. CARB requires the trap and its desulfation hardware to be monitored. No manufacturer documents P2C79 publicly; it suggests the load stayed high, for instance because the trap never got hot enough on short trips. P2000/P2001 judge NOx efficiency, P21B4 overheating. NOx output rises and fuel use may grow.
c: Desulfation never completes because the trap stays too cool (short trips, idling)
Fuel with high sulfur content (outside EU/US ultra-low-sulfur grades)
Increased oil consumption carrying sulfur-bearing additives into the exhaust
Faulty exhaust temperature or lambda signal that blocks or aborts the rich desulfation phases
Thermally aged trap whose sulfur can no longer be removed
s: Check engine light
Higher fuel consumption from repeated rich regeneration attempts
Occasional rotten-egg smell from the exhaust
Raised NOx emissions, possible failure at an emissions test

P2C7A.t: SCR NOx Catalyst Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 1 Catalyst 2
P2C7A.d: P2C7A concerns the second SCR catalyst on bank 1, typically an underfloor brick behind a first SCR stage.
