GM uses it on its 3.0-litre Duramax diesel: the 2020 table 20OBDG04 compares the efficiency of this catalyst, taken from the NOx sensors ahead of and behind it, with a reference built from the inlet NOx and a calibrated offset. A test is evaluated once 400 mg of NOx plus ammonia have entered the brick, results pass an EWMA filter, and the code is Type A with the MIL on after one trip; 25OBDG04B keeps this logic. GM bulletins PIP5682 (2020 LM2), PIP5888A (2022 LM2) and 23-NA-193 (2023 LZ0) cure false sets with new ECM software. P20EE covers the main SCR efficiency. Expect higher NOx and possibly a DEF warning.
c: ECM software that flags the second SCR falsely (GM 3.0 l diesel bulletins)
Second SCR catalyst aged, poisoned or with reduced ammonia storage
Drifting NOx sensor in front of or behind the second SCR
Poor DEF quality or under-dosing by the reductant injector
Exhaust leak between the sensors that distorts the NOx readings
s: MIL on after one trip
Exhaust fluid or emissions warning in the instrument cluster
Usually no noticeable change in driving behaviour

P2C7B.t: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Control Performance
P2C7B.d: The turbine inlet valve opens or blocks an exhaust path to a turbine: in a two-stage system it lets gas bypass the small high-pressure stage, in a sequential layout it brings the second turbo in. GM's patent US8276378B2 shows such a bypass valve run in closed loop with its own position control. P2C7B means the electrically driven valve does not follow its command closely or quickly enough, although no circuit fault is present. No manufacturer documents P2C7B publicly; CARB requires the boost control system to be checked for slow response as well as under- and overboost. Typical reasons are soot or corrosion making the valve stiff, a worn actuator gear train or a loose linkage. Boost becomes low or unsteady and the module may cut power. P22D2/P22D3 cover a valve stuck open or closed.
c: Valve or shaft stiff from soot and corrosion
Loose or bent linkage between actuator and valve
Position feedback that misreports the true valve opening
s: Reduced power or hesitation in the boost changeover range
Fluctuating boost pressure
Check engine light, possibly limp mode

P2C7C.t: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Supply Circuit Low
P2C7C.d: P2C7C reports that the voltage feeding the turbine inlet valve actuator is too low. Electric turbo actuators of this kind combine a DC motor, gearing and a position sensor and rely on a stable feed; BorgWarner's patent on such an actuator adds a spring that returns the valve to a default position when power is lost. No manufacturer documents P2C7C publicly. GM uses a comparable check on the exhaust pressure valve of its 3.0-litre diesel (P2B98, table 25OBDG04B): a fault when the motor supply drops below 6 V in 240 of 300 samples while the main relay delivers more than 11 V, Type A. Likely culprits are a blown fuse, a weak relay, corroded pins or a broken feed wire; a flat battery alone should not cause it. Boost control is curtailed. Faults in the control lines are P22CF to P22D1.
c: Blown fuse or faulty supply relay for the actuator
Corroded or loose pins at the actuator connector
Chafed or broken feed or ground wire near the hot turbo area
Defective supply output in the control module
s: Check engine light
Low boost and reduced power
Further turbo actuator codes stored at the same time

P2C7D.t: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Motor Driver High Current
P2C7D.d: P2C7D is set when the output stage driving the turbine inlet valve motor carries more current than permitted. H-bridge chips such as NXP's MC33926 limit motor current and flag overcurrent to the controller, and a Korean patent on electric turbo actuators explains how a DC motor that cannot reach its target draws excess current and is switched off before it burns out. No manufacturer documents P2C7D publicly. The usual trigger is a valve jammed by soot or corrosion so the motor stalls; shorted motor windings and chafed leads touching each other or ground are next. The driver then shuts down, the valve stays where it is and boost control is restricted. A valve that is merely slow without excess current leads to P2C7B, an overheated driver to P2C7E.
c: Valve jammed by soot or corrosion, motor stalls
Shorted windings in the actuator motor
Motor leads chafed and shorted to each other or to ground
Defective H-bridge driver in the control module
s: Sudden loss of boost and power
Check engine light, limp mode
Code returns immediately after clearing when the valve is commanded

P2C7E.t: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Motor Driver Overtemperature
P2C7E.d: P2C7E indicates that the driver circuit for the turbine inlet valve motor has grown too hot. Driver chips monitor their own junction temperature and switch off beyond a limit, as the data sheet of NXP's MC33926 H-bridge shows. No manufacturer documents P2C7E publicly; the closest published example is GM's 3.0-litre diesel, where P2B99 for the exhaust pressure valve sets once the H-bridge driver exceeds 170 °C in 240 of 300 samples (Type A, table 25OBDG04B). Heat builds up when the motor has to hold against a stiff or binding valve for long periods, when windings are partly shorted, or when an actuator with built-in electronics sits close to hot turbo parts, a risk the Korean actuator patent also names. After shutdown the valve is uncontrolled and boost is reduced. P2C7D is the overcurrent fault.
c: Binding valve that keeps the motor under constant load
Partially shorted motor windings raising current and heat
Actuator electronics overheated by missing heat shield or poor cooling
s: Loss of boost after a longer drive or under high load
Check engine light, possibly limp mode
Fault may disappear after the engine has cooled down

P2C7F.t: Turbocharger Turbine Inlet Valve Position Sensor Exceeded Learning Limit
P2C7F.d: P2C7F means the turbine inlet valve's position sensor has delivered an end-stop value outside the window the module accepts during its learning routine. Electric turbo valves are periodically driven against their stops and the reading there is stored as a reference; Ford's patent US9243553B2 explains for wastegates why this reference has to be refreshed, since hot linkages change length. No manufacturer documents P2C7F publicly. Comparable GM codes set when the learned closed position of wastegate A is above 85 % (P2B93, 2.7-litre L3B) or when the learned stops of the 3.0-litre diesel's exhaust flap leave their windows (P2B97). Typical causes are deposits keeping the valve off its seat, a bent linkage, a shifted sensor magnet or a new actuator not yet adapted. Without a valid reference boost control may be limited.
c: Carbon deposits preventing the valve from reaching its end stop
Replaced actuator or turbocharger without a completed learn procedure
Bent or worn linkage shifting the end positions
Position sensor or its magnet shifted on the shaft
s: Check engine light
Inconsistent boost during changeover between turbine paths
Reduced power in some engines

P2C80.d: P2C80 says the secondary air pump on bank 1 is turning faster than it should. Newer designs use a brushless motor whose speed is measured: an FCA patent describes a pump with a Hall sensor and target wheel so the controller can infer the air mass delivered from the revolutions and adjust pump speed. If the pump spins too fast for its command, it is working against little or no resistance, or its speed control has lost authority. No manufacturer documents P2C80 publicly; CARB requires secondary air systems and their electrical parts to be monitored. Possible causes are a detached or split outlet hose, a damaged impeller or shaft coupling, and a faulty speed signal or pump electronics. Cold-start emissions rise while the car drives normally. P2C81 is overheating, P2445 a pump that delivers nothing.
c: Outlet hose detached or split so the pump runs without back-pressure
Damaged impeller or loose coupling between motor and impeller
Faulty speed signal (Hall sensor) or its wiring
Defective control electronics inside the pump
s: Check engine light
Louder or higher-pitched pump noise after a cold start
Secondary air readiness not completed, emissions test may fail

P2C81.d: P2C81 reports that the secondary air pump on bank 1 has become too hot. The pump is only meant to run for a short time after a cold start, until the catalyst lights off, as Hella describes; a pump with integrated electronics can sense its own temperature and protect its motor. No manufacturer documents P2C81 publicly, so thresholds are unknown; CARB requires monitoring of secondary air delivery. Overheating points to a pump that ran far longer than planned, for example after many short cold starts in a row or with a relay stuck on (P2444), to a blocked intake filter or outlet, to worn bearings that add friction or to water inside the pump. The pump may shut itself off, so no air reaches the exhaust during warm-up and cold-start emissions climb. P2C80 is the overspeed fault, P2C82 the supply fault.
c: Pump running too long (many short cold starts, relay stuck on)
Clogged intake filter or blocked outlet path
Worn bearings or debris increasing friction
Moisture or condensate inside the pump
s: Check engine light
Pump stops early or does not run on the next cold start
Hot smell or grinding noise from the pump

P2C82.t: AIR System Pump Supply Voltage Circuit Bank 1
P2C82.d: P2C82 points to a fault in the supply voltage circuit of the bank 1 secondary air pump. Conventional pumps are switched on by a relay; pumps with their own electronics, like the brushless design in an FCA patent, receive a feed and can judge whether the voltage arriving there is plausible. No manufacturer documents P2C82 publicly; CARB demands that all electrical secondary air components be checked for circuit faults. Common causes are the high-current fuse, a corroded or loose connector, a damaged feed or ground wire and a relay with burnt contacts; heavy voltage dips during cranking may contribute. Without a proper feed the pump stays off, cold-start emissions rise and the secondary air readiness test fails. P0418 covers the relay control circuit, P2445 a pump that does not deliver.
c: Blown high-current fuse for the pump
Relay with burnt or sticking contacts
Damaged feed or ground wire to the pump
s: Check engine light
No pump noise for the first minute after a cold start
Secondary air readiness incomplete

P2C83.t: Cold Start Shift Time Too Short
P2C83.d: California requires every part of an emission-reducing cold-start routine to be checked while it is active and its faults to be stored apart from ordinary ones. Many automatics take part in that strategy: a warm-up gearshift mode lets the engine rev further before each upshift so engine and catalyst heat faster, as a ZF patent describes. P2C83 belongs to this family. It says a shift measured during the cold-start phase was too quick – the cold-start counterpart of P0895. Whether a maker times each ratio change or how long the warm-up mode lasts is not published, and no manufacturer documents P2C83. For comparison, Saab's 1994 automatic expected each shift to take 0.3–1.3 s. Too short a shift points to excessive clutch pressure or a fill adaptation off target with cold fluid; the result is a harsh first shift.
c: Clutch apply pressure too high while the fluid is cold
Fill or pressure adaptation for cold fluid outside its target, e.g. after a reset or software fault
Transmission fluid temperature signal implausible, so the wrong cold-start values are used
Pressure control solenoid sticking or overshooting
s: Harsh or jerky first upshifts after a cold start
Engine or transmission warning lamp
Shifting returns to normal once the gearbox is warm

P2C84.t: Cold Start Shift Time Too Long
P2C84.d: P2C84 is the opposite verdict to P2C83: a shift observed during the active cold-start phase took longer than its calibrated limit. Cold transmission fluid is thick, so clutches fill slowly and the engine can rev up between gears; a gearbox module normally compensates with temperature-dependent pressure and fill adaptation. When that is not enough, the shift stretches out. If a maker reads shift time as the length of the warm-up gearshift mode instead, a value that is too long would mean lower gears were held longer than intended, costing fuel without benefit. No manufacturer documents P2C84; the code sits next to the general P0896 because CARB wants cold-start faults kept separate. Likely causes are low or wrong fluid, a sticking valve or solenoid, worn clutch plates and a faulty fluid temperature signal.
c: Transmission fluid level low or wrong fluid specification
Shift valve or solenoid sticking when cold
Worn clutch plates needing more fill volume
Fluid temperature signal faulty, so cold-start shift values are misapplied
s: Slow, slipping upshifts with engine flare after a cold start
Engine or transmission warning lamp
Possible emergency program with a fixed gear

P2C85.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage External Isolation Fault
P2C85.d: P2C85 means the isolation monitor has found a fault-level loss of insulation on the vehicle side of the battery, in cables or components connected through the contactors. Mercedes-Benz uses the code in the battery management system with the text vehicle-side insulation fault. A 2024 warranty notice for C 350e, GLC 350e, GLE 550e and S 550e/560e plug-in hybrids lists it for a corroding high-voltage A/C compressor winding; the car could not be restarted once switched off. A 2025 bulletin for the 295, 296 and 297 model series traces it to moisture in a high-voltage PTC heater without a diaphragm. External versus internal follows from where the resistance is measured, as a Magna patent separates battery and component insulation. P2C87 is the earlier warning stage, P0AA6 the system fault.
c: Insulation breakdown in the high-voltage A/C compressor
Moisture in the high-voltage PTC heater or its connector
Chafed or crushed high-voltage cable touching the body
Coolant or water inside inverter, motor or charger
s: Red high-voltage or battery warning, do not restart message
Vehicle cannot be restarted after switching off
Electric heater or A/C not working

P2C86.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Internal Isolation Warning
P2C86.d: P2C86 is an early warning that the insulation inside the traction battery, between cells, busbars or module electronics and the pack housing, is dropping but has not yet reached the fault limit. The full internal fault is P0E74. No manufacturer documents P2C86 publicly. Mercedes-Benz shows the same content under its own code P142900 (warning, insulation inside the battery) on its 2015-2020 plug-in hybrids. How internal and external are told apart is explained in a Tesla tech note: the battery management system measures inside the contactors, so a low reading with contactors open points to the pack itself, and below 1,800 kOhm in that state the pack was replaced. Coolant or condensation in the pack and damaged module wiring are typical. CARB counts isolation detection as safety-only.
c: Coolant leaking inside the battery pack
Condensation or water ingress through a failed pack seal or vent
Damaged cell sensing or busbar insulation inside the pack
Isolation measurement in the battery controller drifting
s: Battery or high-voltage service message, often without immediate limits
Charging may be refused if the value keeps falling

P2C87.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage External Isolation Warning
P2C87.d: P2C87 is the warning stage for weakening insulation outside the battery, on the vehicle-side high-voltage network. Many systems use two limits; Volkswagen's ID.4, for example, shows a yellow lamp below 510 kOhm and a red one below 90 kOhm. Mercedes-Benz stores P2C8700 for an insulation warning on the vehicle side, listed in its 2024 extended warranty for plug-in hybrids with a corroding high-voltage A/C compressor and in a 2025 bulletin on a moist PTC heater. Volvo logs P2C871A in the BECM of the EX30: if it appears together with P128300 in VCU1 and the car will not engage a gear or reports reduced power, Technical Journal 37771 has the combined charger and DC/DC module replaced. If the fault grows, P2C85 follows.
c: Moisture or corrosion in an external HV component (compressor, heater, charger)
Insulation fault inside the on-board charger or DC/DC converter
s: Yellow high-voltage or battery warning
Reduced power or no gear engagement on some models
Intermittent, often after rain or washing

P2C88.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage System Isolation Warning
P2C88.d: P2C88 is the warning counterpart to P0AA6: the isolation resistance of the high-voltage system as a whole has fallen below a first limit without the monitor yet being able to say whether the battery or the vehicle side is to blame. Mercedes-Benz uses P2C8800 in the battery management system of the 295, 296 and 297 model series; its 2025 bulletin lists it with P2C8500 and P2C8700 when moisture builds up in a high-voltage PTC heater lacking a diaphragm, a fault that starts sporadically and worsens. Legally the complete system must stay above 500 ohms per volt, so the warning leaves time to find the leak before a lockout. Measure each branch separately, starting with components that are switched in only at times.
c: Moisture in a high-voltage component that is only switched in at times (heater, compressor)
Gradual insulation aging in cables or connectors
Beginning insulation loss inside the battery pack
s: High-voltage warning message, sometimes towing not allowed notice
Electric heater stays cold if it is the leaking part

P2C89.t: Hybrid/EV Battery System Precharge Current Too High
P2C89.d: Before the main contactors close, the DC link capacitors are charged through a current-limiting path. P2C89 is stored when the current in that phase exceeds its limit, which points to a short or an unexpected load on the high-voltage bus, a precharge resistor that is bypassed, or a measurement error. A Motiv Power Systems patent explains why this matters: the inrush into capacitance or a short can damage parts or weld contactor tips. Bentley names P2C8900 in the battery management unit (address 008C) of its 2025-26 Continental GT/GTC and Flying Spur plug-in hybrids, alongside P0C7800 and an insulation measurement fault; both precharge codes light the MIL, and the cure is a software update of the battery controller and DC/DC converter. P0C77 and P0C78 judge precharge time.
c: Battery management or DC/DC converter software misjudging the precharge
Short or active load on the high-voltage bus during precharge
Precharge resistor shorted or main contactor closing early
Pack current sensor reading too high
s: MIL and high-voltage system warning at start-up
Electric drive or charging unavailable, engine-only on plug-in hybrids

P2C8A.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Interface Control Module A Performance
P2C8A.d: Battery interface control modules are the satellite boards in the traction battery that measure cell voltages and temperatures and report them to the battery energy control module. P2C8A says module A is reachable but not working properly. GM uses the code on its Ultium EVs: preliminary information PIP6021 (Lyriq, Blazer EV, Equinox EV, later Optiq and Vistiq) blames a BECM calibration anomaly when P2C8A, P2C8B and U3577-U35AF are all set, with MIL or Service High Voltage and a draining 12 V battery; the fix is BECM programming and two manual resets. PIP6081 calls the same pattern a cell monitoring unit brownout on Hummer EV, Silverado EV and Escalade IQ. The earlier Volt checked comparable modules with its own code, a key value test, Type B.
c: Battery energy control module software or calibration error
Supply dip at the cell monitoring module (12 V battery weak, wake-up issue)
Damaged communication or supply harness inside the battery pack
s: MIL or Service High Voltage message
12 V battery discharging while parked
Many battery communication codes stored at the same time

P2C8B.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Interface Control Module B Performance
P2C8B.d: P2C8B is the performance fault for the second battery interface control module, B. In GM's Ultium bulletins it never appears alone: PIP6021 applies only if P2C8B is stored together with P2C8A and the module communication codes U3577 to U35AF, and the 2025-26 versions of PIP6081 extend it through U3584 and add U2BAA-U2BB1. That pattern, many modules failing at once, points to a common cause in the BECM software or the module supply rather than to board B itself, so GM tells dealers not to replace hardware but to reprogram, reset and recheck after 10 minutes in Ready. A lone, repeatable P2C8B is different and suggests module B or its harness. CARB asks for battery faults to be pinpointed to the smallest replaceable unit, which is why A and B are separate.
c: BECM software anomaly affecting several monitoring modules at once
Weak 12 V battery causing a brownout of the monitoring modules
Connector or harness fault at interface module B
s: MIL or high-voltage service message
Discharged 12 V battery

P2C8C.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor D Circuit
P2C8C.d: P2C8C reports a general fault in the circuit of the fourth temperature sensor of a DC/DC converter, after sensors A, B and C (P0C38, P0C3D, P0E58). Where sensor D sits inside the converter is up to each maker. That such a fourth sensor exists in practice is shown by FCA: the 2021 Ram 1500 with the 3.6 L eTorque mild hybrid watches converter sensors 1, 2, C and D, yet bulletin 08-037-21 lists only the plausibility code P2C8D for sensor D. No manufacturer documents P2C8C publicly. The code fits a signal the controller recognises as unusable but cannot sort into too low, too high or implausible. CARB requires circuit checks on hybrid input components. Without this reading the controller normally reduces converter output, which can weaken support for the 12 V system.
c: Sensor connector or wiring damaged or corroded
Temperature sensor D in the converter defective
Sensor reference or evaluation circuit inside the converter faulty
s: MIL or hybrid system warning
Converter output limited, 12 V charging voltage may drop

P2C8D.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor D Circuit Range/Performance
P2C8D.d: P2C8D is the plausibility test of DC/DC converter temperature sensor D: the voltage is electrically valid, but the temperature it implies does not match what the controller expects. Typical cross-checks compare the sensor with its neighbours after a long rest or look for a value that hardly changes while the converter works hard. FCA applies the code to its eTorque Ram 1500 pickup of model year 2021 (3.6 L V6), next to P0C39, P0C3E and P0E59 for the other converter sensors. Bulletin 08-037-21 flashes new Hybrid Control Processor software for trucks built up to 5 January 2021, and with it P2C8D becomes a one-trip fault, so the MIL lights after the first failed drive. FCA does not publish its limits. CARB demands rationality checks for hybrid component temperature sensors.
c: Hybrid control software level (FCA HCP update per 08-037-21)
Sensor D drifting and disagreeing with the other converter sensors
Uneven cooling of the converter, e.g. low coolant or air in the circuit
s: MIL on, with newer FCA software after one faulty drive
Reduced eTorque assist or start-stop availability

P2C8E.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor D Circuit Low
P2C8E.d: P2C8E is logged when the voltage from DC/DC converter temperature sensor D drops under the lower limit of its window. Power electronics mostly use NTC thermistors, where a falling voltage means rising temperature; an implausibly low value therefore reads as a converter far hotter than it can be. The usual culprits are a signal wire touching ground, a crushed harness or a thermistor that has shorted internally, much less often real overheating. No manufacturer documents P2C8E publicly; FCA proves sensor D exists on the 2021 Ram 1500 eTorque but names only P2C8D for it. CARB requires out-of-range checks on hybrid input components. Since the controller has to assume overtemperature, it tends to throttle the converter straight away. P2C8F covers the opposite direction.
c: Sensor D signal wire shorted to ground
Converter genuinely overheating because of a cooling fault
s: Hybrid or charging system warning
Converter derated right away, less electrical power available

P2C8F.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor D Circuit High
P2C8F.d: P2C8F stands for a sensor D signal stuck above the upper edge of its permitted range. With a thermistor fed through a pull-up resistor, the voltage climbs towards the reference as soon as the loop is broken, so an unplugged connector, a cracked wire or a corroded pin is the classic finding; a short to a supply voltage gives the same picture. The resulting reading would be a converter colder than any real ambient. No manufacturer documents P2C8F publicly; FCA shows sensor D on the 2021 Ram 1500 eTorque but lists only P2C8D for it. CARB requires range monitoring of hybrid input components. Because a false cold value could hide real overheating, the controller treats the temperature as unknown and usually limits power. P2C8E is the low-signal counterpart.
c: Connector unplugged or sensor wire broken
Corroded or pushed-back pin at the converter connector
Signal shorted to a supply voltage
s: Hybrid system warning, MIL possible
Electrical power limited as a precaution

P2C90.t: Crankcase Ventilation System - Hose A Disconnected
P2C90.d: Under California's phase-in (20 % of 2023, 50 % of 2024, all 2025 models) every PCV hose carrying crankcase vapour must be watched for a break as large as its smallest bore, so makers moved from the general P04DB to per-hose codes. P2C90 covers hose A. Ford's 2024 summary says P2C90 replaces P04DB: the dirty side is tested once per trip while cranking, the clean side once per trip above 5 lb/min airflow, backed by extrapolation and flow-model checks over up to 15 minutes. Bulletins come from Ford (2024 F-150 3.5 and 5.2, 2026 Transit 3.5: PCV check plus software), Toyota and Lexus (2023 Crown, RX 500h: false codes, ECM logic changed) and Stellantis (Jeep 2.0 turbo; Wagoneer 3.0 with a too short make-up-air valve spring).
c: PCV hose A pulled off, cracked or with a broken fitting
Detection software too sensitive (Ford, Toyota/Lexus and Stellantis updates)
PCV valve or make-up-air check valve not sealing
Crankcase pressure sensor or its signal faulty
s: Engine warning lamp, often without any other complaint
Oil mist or oily residue near the disconnected hose
Possibly unstable idle or lean mixture codes

P2C91.t: Crankcase Ventilation System - Hose B Disconnected
P2C91.d: P2C91 is the second hose-specific PCV disconnection code: crankcase vapour line B is detected as open or broken, separately from line A (P2C90). Which physical hose carries the letter is the maker's choice; the code slot exists so that systems with two monitored lines can name the faulty one. The documented user is Stellantis on the Alfa Romeo Giulia and Stelvio (2021–22) with the 2.9-litre twin-turbo V6. Their two engine computers were reflashed in bulletins of 2023 and 2025 because P2C91 appeared together with crankcase pressure sensor B faults (P2C33) without a real leak. A hose that is genuinely loose lets oil mist or unmetered air escape, can upset idle and fuel trims, and keeps the lamp lit. Since 2025 every hose of this kind must be monitored, which is why such second codes appear.
c: Engine control software reporting a disconnection that is not there (Alfa Romeo 2.9 V6)
PCV hose B loose, split or with a broken connector
Crankcase pressure sensor B or its wiring faulty
s: Engine warning lamp
Oil residue or hissing at a crankcase ventilation hose
Possibly rough idle

P2C92.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Contactor Control Supply Circuit/Open
P2C92.d: The main contactors of a traction battery are relays whose coils are energised by driver stages in the battery controller, and those drivers take their energy from a dedicated supply feed. P2C92 means this feed is missing or interrupted, for example because of a blown fuse, a broken wire or a feed relay that does not pull in. Why the feed is watched at all is explained in LG Energy Solution patent US12007445B2: a coil voltage that is too weak or not yet settled can leave a contactor only partly closed, so the controller checks the supply before closing each contactor and declares a fault after repeated failed checks. No manufacturer documents P2C92 publicly. With the feed gone, no contactor can close, so the car typically refuses ready mode and charging. CARB requires monitoring of hybrid components.
c: Fuse in the contactor supply feed blown
Supply wire or connector at the battery pack interrupted
Relay or switch feeding the contactor drivers not closing
Battery controller input or driver stage defective
s: Vehicle does not become ready to drive
Charging does not start
Hybrid or EV system warning

P2C93.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Contactor Control Supply Circuit Range/Performance
P2C93.d: With P2C93 the supply for the contactor drivers is present but does not behave as it should: it sags when a coil is switched on, ripples, or recovers too slowly before the next contactor in the closing sequence. A high-resistance contact or a weak feed therefore shows up here rather than as an open circuit. LG Energy Solution patent US12007445B2 describes the matching logic: before every contactor closes, the controller compares the supply with a minimum, waits and repeats the comparison if it is short, and only after a set number of failed tries records a supply fault. No manufacturer documents P2C93 publicly. For the driver the effect is often intermittent: the car may need several attempts to become ready or abort charging. CARB requires functional checks of hybrid components.
c: Corroded or loose contact in the supply feed causing voltage drop
Weak 12 V battery or ground connection sagging under coil load
Contactor coil drawing excessive current or driver stage faulty
s: Several attempts needed before the vehicle is ready
Charging stops unexpectedly
Intermittent hybrid or EV warning

P2C94.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Contactor Control Supply Circuit Low
P2C94.d: P2C94 says the supply feeding the contactor drivers lies below its lower limit. Ford is the maker that documents it: special service messages 51513 and 51783 (2023) describe 2021–2023 Escape, Corsair, Aviator, Mustang Mach-E, F-150 and Transit plug-in models whose AC charging at level 1 or 2 stops with the MIL on and P2C94 logged in the SOBDM, the on-board charger module. As a stopgap the charge handle is unplugged and reconnected; a new SOBDM does not help. TSB 23-2399, extended by 24-2027 to the 2023 E-Transit, blames SOBDM software and cures it by reprogramming. Ford does not say which supply it measures. On other vehicles a genuinely low feed, as described in patent US12007445B2, can stop contactors closing fully. Compare P2C95 for the high side.
c: Supply feed pulled down by a weak 12 V battery or poor ground
Partial short or high resistance in the supply wiring
s: AC charging stops while plugged in, MIL on
Charging resumes after unplugging and reconnecting
Vehicle may not become ready to drive

P2C95.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Contactor Control Supply Circuit High
P2C95.d: P2C95 is the upper-limit counterpart of P2C94: the voltage on the feed for the contactor coil drivers exceeds what the battery controller accepts. An excessive supply is less common than a weak one, but it heats the coils and stresses the driver transistors, and it can mean the measurement is wrong, for instance when the sense line touches a higher potential or the feed regulator inside the controller has failed. LG Energy Solution patent US12007445B2 shows that controllers measure this supply before each contactor closes; an upper limit is the logical extension, although the patent itself deals with undervoltage. No manufacturer documents P2C95 publicly. Depending on strategy the controller may refuse to close contactors or open them, so loss of ready mode is possible. CARB requires monitoring of hybrid components.
c: Supply or sense line shorted to a higher voltage
Supply regulator or measurement in the battery controller faulty
12 V system overvoltage from a faulty DC/DC converter or jump start
s: Hybrid or EV system warning
Vehicle may not become ready or may shut down HV

P2C96.d: Besides commands over the vehicle network, many high-voltage batteries have a separate wired input through which another controller can force the contactors open. The best-known use is the crash signal: in Volkswagen patent US9586481B2 the battery opens its contactor 10–100 ms after a hard-wired crash signal, versus roughly 20–200 ms when the message arrives over CAN, and blocks reclosing until the stored fault has been erased. Coda patent US20110304202A1 also ties battery disconnection to the airbag deployment decision. What exactly feeds the disable line is up to the maker. P2C96 means this line is open. No manufacturer documents the code publicly. Many designs read a lost signal as a shutdown request, so the car may not become ready. CARB requires monitoring of hybrid components.
c: Disable line or its connector at the battery pack interrupted
Sending controller (e.g. crash or airbag module) not driving the line
Connector left unplugged after body or battery repair
Input stage in the battery controller defective
s: Vehicle does not become ready to drive
High-voltage system warning

P2C97.d: P2C97 is set when the high-voltage battery's wired disable input sits below its valid range, typically because the line is chafed through to body ground or the sending module pulls it low permanently. Whether low means shut down depends on the design. Where the line is active-low, a short to ground looks like a constant request to open the contactors, and the battery stays switched off; where a defined level is expected, the controller simply loses a trustworthy signal. The safety value of a hard-wired path is shown in Volkswagen patent US9586481B2, where it opens the contactor faster than a CAN message. No manufacturer documents P2C97 publicly. A shorted line should be traced section by section between the sender and the battery connector. CARB requires monitoring of hybrid components.
c: Disable line chafed and shorted to ground
Sending module holding the line low permanently
Water in the connector creating a leakage path to ground
s: High-voltage battery stays switched off, no ready mode
High-voltage system warning

P2C98.d: P2C98 flags a battery disable line whose level is above the permitted range, usually through a short to 12 V or a sender that drives the line too high. Unlike the low case, the risk here can be hidden: if a high level means all clear, a stuck-high line would no longer pass on a real shutdown request. That is the point of such a wire in Volkswagen patent US9586481B2, which lets a crash signal open the contactor within 10–100 ms, and in Coda patent US20110304202A1, which disconnects the battery once airbag deployment is decided. The controller therefore flags the line even while driving seems normal; the CAN path normally remains as a backup. No manufacturer documents P2C98 publicly. CARB requires monitoring of hybrid components. Inspect the line for contact with feed wires.
c: Disable line shorted to 12 V supply
Sending module driving the line above the valid level
Input stage in the battery controller misreading the level
s: High-voltage system warning, often without noticeable driving fault
Ready mode may be blocked after the next restart, depending on maker

P2C99.t: Throttle Actuator A Control Exceeded Learning Limit
P2C99.d: An electronic throttle relies on learned values: the closed-stop position of its sensors and, in many systems, a correction that widens the commanded opening as carbon narrows the bore. P2C99 says a learned value for throttle A has run into its permitted limit, so the module can no longer compensate. No manufacturer publishes P2C99. GM shows both ideas elsewhere: its 2023 tables (23OBDG07) fail the lower-stop learn of throttle sensor bank 1 with in-house codes P30E3/P30E4 within one trip, and GM patents cap the learned throttle area correction and report how near it is to that cap as a coking value. Heavy deposits, a worn or replaced throttle body without relearn, or drifting sensors are typical. Idle may be unstable and power reduced. P2176 is the related idle-position code.
c: Heavy carbon deposits in the throttle bore needing more correction than allowed
Throttle body cleaned or replaced without resetting and relearning the adaptation
Worn throttle shaft, plate or end stop shifting the closed position
s: Engine warning lamp, possibly an electronic throttle warning
Idle speed too high, too low or hunting
Reduced power in a throttle emergency mode

P2C9A.t: Throttle Actuator B Control Exceeded Learning Limit
P2C9A.d: Throttle B exists only on engines with two electronically driven throttle bodies, usually one per cylinder bank on large V engines. P2C9A means a learned value of that second throttle – its closed-stop reference or the airflow correction stored for it – has reached the edge of the allowed range. Since both throttles must deliver matching air, a large learned offset on one side alone hints at deposits, a sticking plate or a replaced unit on that side. No manufacturer documents P2C9A. GM's 2023 tables handle the bank 2 throttle sensor with separate in-house codes (P30E5/P30E6) for the same stop-learn limit, judged within one trip. Expect rough or uneven idle, limited power if the module restricts the throttle, and possibly companion codes such as P218A (idle position of throttle B not learned).
c: Carbon deposits in throttle body B only
Throttle body B replaced or cleaned without relearn
Throttle plate B sticking or its return spring weak
Position sensor of throttle B drifting
s: Engine warning lamp
Uneven or hunting idle
Reduced power if the throttle is restricted

P2C9B.t: Cold Start Turbocharger/Supercharger Wastegate Actuator A Range/Performance
P2C9B.d: P2C9B checks wastegate A while the engine runs its catalyst warm-up strategy after a cold start, when the wastegate is commanded open so hot exhaust reaches the catalyst rather than the turbine. GM uses the code on the 2.7-litre L3B (table 19OBDG03D): it fails if the position error stays above 20 % for over 1 s, the actuator current above 1 A or the duty cycle above 40 %, judged on 25 of 30 samples at 100 ms; Type A, MIL after one trip. The 2025 table 25OBDG03B tightens the position limit to 10 % over 2 s (29 of 30). In the 19OBDG07 table for GM's twin-turbo 4.2-litre V8 the code flags a bank 1 bypass valve that sticks longer than 1 s during rapid heat-up. Causes are a stiff flap or linkage, a weak electric actuator or wiring. P2B81 covers the actuator outside cold start; P2C9C is turbo B.
c: Wastegate flap or linkage stiff from corrosion or deposits, worst when cold
Electric wastegate actuator with worn motor or gears
Poor contact at the actuator connector or wiring
s: Check engine light shortly after a cold start
Rattle or noise from the wastegate area when cold
Often no noticeable change in performance

P2C9C.t: Cold Start Turbocharger/Supercharger Wastegate Actuator B Range/Performance
P2C9C.d: P2C9C is the counterpart of P2C9B for wastegate B and only exists on engines with two turbochargers: GM's tables define turbo A as the first in a series layout or the bank 1 unit in a parallel one, so B is the second or the bank 2 charger. GM's 4.2-litre twin-turbo V8 (table 19OBDG07, test group KGMXV04.2088) watches the bank 2 turbine bypass valve during the cold-start rapid heat-up mode; if the valve is detected as jammed for more than 1 s, P2C9C sets, with separate paths for positions up to 50 % and above. The single-turbo 2.7-litre L3B has only actuator A, so 19OBDG03D lists no P2C9C. A valve that does not open while warming up delays catalyst light-off and raises cold-start emissions. Check the bank 2 actuator, linkage and plug; P2B94 is the learn limit of wastegate B.
c: Bank 2 wastegate flap or linkage stiff from corrosion or deposits
Worn or weak wastegate actuator B
Wiring or connector fault at actuator B
s: Check engine light shortly after a cold start
Uneven boost between banks later in the drive
Often no noticeable change during the cold start

P2C9D.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator C Exceeded Control Limits - Pressure Too High
P2C9D.d: P2C9D reports that the fuel pressure in the section governed by regulator C stays above its target although that regulator is already reducing delivery as far as it can. A third regulator letter is only needed where an engine has several pressure control elements, for instance two high-pressure pumps or separate rail circuits. No manufacturer documents P2C9D publicly. The closest published logic is GM's for regulators A and D (tables 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07): measured and desired rail pressure may differ by no more than 3 MPa for a few seconds before a one-trip fault is stored. CARB demands a fault once fuel pressure control runs out of authority. Expect a hard, noisy idle or reduced power; P2C9E covers the underpressure side of the same regulator.
c: Quantity control valve of circuit C sticking in the delivery position
Rail pressure sensor of that circuit reading too high
Wiring or connector fault keeping the valve from being switched
s: MIL on, often after a single trip
Harsh or noisy idle, especially when cold
Reduced engine power

P2C9E.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator C Exceeded Control Limits - Pressure Too Low
P2C9E.d: P2C9E is the underpressure counterpart of P2C9D: the circuit run by regulator C cannot reach its pressure target even with the regulator already asking for full delivery. No manufacturer publishes a definition of P2C9E, so the detail comes from analogous codes. GM's 2023/24 tables apply a 3 MPa deviation held for 5 s to its low-pressure codes and add a second path when the tank is empty or on reserve, because fuel starvation can mimic a weak pump. CARB requires such control-limit faults to be detected. Probable causes are a worn high-pressure pump, a valve stuck closed, insufficient feed pressure from the tank pump, a clogged filter or an injector leaking back. Drivers notice hesitation, long cranking or a power cut.
c: Worn high-pressure pump of circuit C
Low feed pressure from the tank pump or a clogged fuel filter
Quantity control valve stuck closed or open circuit to it
s: MIL on
Hesitation or stumbling under load
Extended cranking before the engine starts
Power limitation

P2C9F.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator D Exceeded Control Limits - Pressure Too High
P2C9F.d: P2C9F concerns regulator D, which GM uses for the second quantity control valve of a twin high-pressure system. GM's 2023 and 2024 tables 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 carry it in an ECM section that also lists the bank 2 rail sensor codes of bulletin 24-NA-106 for the 5.5 L LT6 Corvette. The table entry trips when the filtered rail-pressure control deviation exceeds 3 MPa for 5 s, with a second path while the tank is empty or on reserve, one trip. Note the oddity: this same criterion is the one GM gives bank 1 underpressure code P228C, while P2CA0 receives the mirror image, so the direction printed in the table appears reversed against the code title. In practice the code points to a valve or sensor of bank 2; P2C01 judges the valve's overall authority.
c: Second quantity control valve (bank 2) not regulating correctly
Water intrusion or fault in the bank 2 fuel harness connector (GM LT6)
Bank 2 rail pressure sensor reading implausibly
Very low tank level causing pressure dropouts
s: MIL on after one trip
Rough running or reduced power
Further fuel pressure or bank 2 injector codes stored

P2CA0.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator D Exceeded Control Limits - Pressure Too Low
P2CA0.d: P2CA0 is the low-pressure verdict for regulator D. GM bulletin 24-NA-106 names it as a bank 2 low-pressure fault on the 2023–24 Corvette with the 5.5 L LT6 and links it, together with P228C, P01BF, P312B and several injector high-side codes, to an incorrect twelve-pin inline plug with an unsealed cavity that admits water to the bank 2 injector wiring; the fix is inspecting the connector part number and, if wrong, renewing harnesses and the rail sensor. GM's tables 23OBDG07/24OBDG07 list P2CA0 with a filtered deviation beyond minus 3 MPa held for 7 s, one trip, a sign that in the same table belongs to overpressure code P228D. Expect stumbling, misfire-like running and the MIL.
c: Incorrect 12-way in-line connector admitting water to the bank 2 harness (GM 24-NA-106)
Weak bank 2 high-pressure pump or its quantity valve stuck
Insufficient feed pressure from the tank pump
s: MIL on after one trip
Stumbling or misfire-like running
Several bank 2 injector or rail sensor codes at the same time

P2CA1.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump Sense Circuit High
P2CA1.d: Some electric pumps in a water-cooled charge air cooler loop report back to the engine computer on a dedicated sense or feedback wire, kept apart from the line commanding them. P2CA1 means the level on that return wire stays above its plausible band. Usual reasons are a chafed wire touching a battery feed, a break in the line where the controller input is pulled up internally, or pump electronics that no longer switch the line at all. The title carries no pump letter. No manufacturer documents P2CA1 publicly. Pierburg's patent US8392060B2 explains that such pumps announce faults by tying a line to ground for coded periods, so a line that never drops hides every message. CARB requires circuit checks on emission-related inputs. Unable to confirm the pump, the controller may cut boost.
c: Feedback wire chafed through and touching a battery or ignition feed
Broken feedback wire or backed-out pin, input floats to its high level
Pump electronics no longer pulling the feedback line down
Damaged input stage in the engine control module
s: MIL on
Reduced power or boost under load, especially in hot weather
Pump fault messages from the pump no longer reach the controller

P2CA2.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump Sense Circuit Low
P2CA2.d: P2CA2 is set when the return wire from the intercooler pump sits below its valid range for longer than allowed. Insulation worn through against the body, water in the plug, or pump electronics that keep pulling the line down are the usual suspects. The last case is tricky: pumps working on the principle in Pierburg's patent US8392060B2 report a fault by grounding the line for a coded duration, so a line that never comes back up looks the same as a pump stuck in its error state, and a real pump defect may stand behind the code. MACS stresses that electric water pumps work with a PWM input plus a feedback signal, so both should be scoped side by side. No manufacturer documents P2CA2 publicly; CARB requires the circuit check. P2CA1 is the high case.
c: Feedback wire chafed against body or engine ground
Pump electronics holding the line low because of an internal fault
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the pump connector
s: MIL on
Engine power limited when charge air temperature rises
Code may appear together with pump speed or performance codes

P2CA3.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump Sense Circuit Performance
P2CA3.d: With P2CA3 the feedback signal from the intercooler pump is electrically inside its limits but does not fit what the controller expects: a reported speed or status that contradicts the command, a pulse pattern it cannot decode, or a reply that changes although the request stayed constant. Rheinmetall offers auxiliary pumps for exactly these loops that talk to the engine computer by PWM or LIN and carry extensive self-diagnosis, so the controller relies on this answer to know the loop is circulating. Contact resistance in the plug, interference on the wire, a failing pump circuit board or mismatched software in pump or engine module are possible causes. No manufacturer documents P2CA3 publicly; CARB asks for rationality checks of such inputs. Fixed high or low levels are P2CA1 and P2CA2.
c: Loose or corroded terminal distorting the feedback signal
Pump circuit board sending erratic or implausible feedback
Interference from ignition or alternator on a poorly routed wire
Pump or engine module software not matching each other
s: MIL on, sometimes only intermittently
Power reduction on long climbs or in hot weather

P2CA4.t: Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor Signals Swapped A/B
P2CA4.d: P2CA4 means the engine module believes the readings of particulate filter pressure sensors A and B arrive on each other's inputs, typically because connectors, sensors or sensing hoses were interchanged during service. Such a mix-up yields values that look electrically sound but invert the pressure picture across the filter. No manufacturer documents P2CA4 publicly. Comparable checks exist: Ford's 2015 diesel summary cross-checks its absolute and delta filter pressure sensors under P246D and sets it above 1.5 kPa disagreement, and Ford's 2020–23 petrol summary flags reversed EGR delta-pressure hoses (P139A) once its signal sits under −0.5 kPa for half a minute. CARB requires plausibility checks on PM filter sensors. Wrong soot loading and mistimed regeneration follow.
c: Sensing hoses of sensors A and B fitted to the wrong ports
Electrical connectors of the two sensors interchanged after service
Replacement sensor with different pin assignment or range
Crossed wires after a harness repair
s: MIL on, usually right after work on the exhaust or sensors
Regeneration too frequent or not taking place
Implausible filter pressure values in live data

P2CA5.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor E Circuit
P2CA5.d: P2CA5 is the general circuit fault of the fifth temperature sensor in a DC/DC converter, the one carrying letter E. Converters measure several hot spots because each part heats differently: a Hyundai patent for a hybrid high-side converter places separate sensors on the inductor and on both IGBT switches, high side and low side, and changes the switching frequency when their readings drift apart. No manufacturer documents P2CA5 publicly; the highest letter found in a bulletin is sensor D on the 2021 Ram 1500 eTorque (FCA 08-037-21). The code fits a signal that is unusable but cannot be classed as low, high or implausible. CARB requires circuit checks for such hybrid inputs. Expect the converter to be derated, which can strain the 12 V battery.
c: Loose, corroded or pushed-out terminal at the converter connector
Temperature sensor E inside the converter failed
Evaluation circuit of the converter control board faulty
s: Hybrid or electrical system warning and MIL on
DC/DC converter output limited, 12 V battery discharges

P2CA6.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor E Circuit Low
P2CA6.d: P2CA6 is logged when the voltage of DC/DC converter temperature sensor E sits below the lower edge of its window. Converter sensors are usually thermistors whose resistance falls as they warm, so a signal that collapses towards zero would mean a converter hotter than physically plausible. A chafed signal wire touching ground or an internally shorted thermistor is the normal explanation; genuine overheating would first produce smooth, believable readings. No manufacturer documents P2CA6 publicly, and published bulletins only go up to sensor D. CARB requires out-of-range detection on hybrid input components. Because the controller has to assume excess heat, it typically cuts converter power at once. The opposite signal fault is P2CA7.
c: Signal wire of sensor E chafed through and shorted to ground
Thermistor of sensor E shorted internally
Actual severe overheating of the converter, e.g. coolant loss
s: MIL and hybrid or charging warning on
Converter switched off or strongly limited immediately after start
Low 12 V voltage message on longer drives

P2CA7.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor E Circuit High
P2CA7.d: P2CA7 means the signal of DC/DC converter temperature sensor E is stuck above its upper limit. In a thermistor input fed through a pull-up resistor, an interrupted loop lets the voltage rise to the reference, so a pin pushed out of the connector, a broken conductor or a short to a supply line gives this result. The implied reading would be colder than any real surroundings. No manufacturer documents P2CA7 publicly; the converter sensors named in bulletins stop at letter D. CARB asks for range checks on such hybrid inputs. As a false cold value could hide real heat, the controller treats the temperature as unknown and limits the converter, leaving more of the 12 V load to the battery. P2CA6 is the low-side counterpart.
c: Open circuit in the sensor E signal or return line, e.g. pushed-out pin
Signal line shorted to a supply voltage
s: MIL and hybrid or charging warning on
Implausibly cold converter temperature in live data
Reduced converter output, 12 V battery charge drops

P2CA8.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor E Circuit Range/Performance
P2CA8.d: P2CA8 covers sensor E of the DC/DC converter when its voltage is electrically fine but the temperature it reports does not make sense. Typical plausibility tests compare all converter sensors after a long soak, when they should agree, or check whether a reading moves at all while the converter is under heavy load. FCA shows the pattern for lower letters: on the 2021 Ram 1500 eTorque, bulletin 08-037-21 lists performance codes for sensors 1, 2, C and D, turning them into one-trip faults with new hybrid control software, but sensor E is not named. No manufacturer documents P2CA8 publicly. CARB explicitly demands rationality monitoring for hybrid component temperature sensors. Drift, poor thermal contact of the sensor or software are the usual suspects.
c: Sensor E drifting away from the other converter sensors
Sensor E has lost thermal contact with the part it measures
Outdated converter or hybrid control software with too tight limits
Contact resistance in the connector shifting the signal
s: MIL on, possibly after a single drive
Converter temperature in live data not following load or ambient

P2CA9.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor F Circuit
P2CA9.d: P2CA9 is the general fault code for the circuit of the sixth DC/DC converter temperature sensor, letter F. Which component this sensor watches is left to the manufacturer. No manufacturer documents P2CA9 publicly; the converter sensors visible in bulletins end at D (Ram 1500 eTorque, FCA 08-037-21). Why a converter has several measuring points is shown by a Hyundai patent: inductor and both IGBTs are measured separately so that the controller can balance how hot they get. The code serves for input faults that cannot be sorted into low, high or implausible. CARB demands circuit monitoring of hybrid inputs. A derated converter can gradually drain the 12 V battery; sensor E's general circuit code is P2CA5.
c: Damaged harness or poor contact in the sensor F circuit
Temperature sensor F inside the converter failed
Input stage on the converter control board faulty
s: MIL and hybrid system warning on
Converter output limited, 12 V voltage may sag

P2CAA.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor F Circuit Low
P2CAA.d: P2CAA reports that the input for DC/DC converter temperature sensor F reads too low. With the usual thermistor circuit this corresponds to an impossibly hot reading, so the controller suspects the signal path before the hardware: a ground short in the harness, moisture in the connector or a thermistor that failed short. A useful check is whether the value stays low with the vehicle cold and the converter idle, since a real temperature would have dropped long ago. No manufacturer documents P2CAA publicly, and the lettered converter sensors named in bulletins end at D. CARB requires hybrid input components to be monitored for out-of-range signals. The converter is normally throttled or shut off. Siblings: P2CAB (high), and P2CA6 for sensor E.
c: Sensor F signal shorted to ground in the harness
Moisture or contamination in the converter connector
Thermistor of sensor F failed short
s: MIL and hybrid or charging warning on
Very high converter temperature shown even with a cold vehicle
Converter limited or switched off

P2CAB.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor F Circuit High
P2CAB.d: P2CAB is set when DC/DC converter temperature sensor F delivers a voltage above the top of its valid band. For a thermistor input this is the typical signature of an open circuit, since the pull-up drags the line to reference voltage, or of a short to a higher voltage. The resulting value would be colder than the surroundings, which a working converter can never be. No manufacturer documents P2CAB publicly; bulletins name converter sensors only up to letter D. CARB requires range monitoring of hybrid input components. Checking the connector at the converter, its locking and the terminals for spread or corrosion comes first, as the sensor is frequently built into the converter assembly. P2CAA is the low counterpart, P2CA7 the same fault for sensor E.
c: Converter connector not latched or terminals spread
Broken signal or return wire of sensor F
Signal line shorted to a higher voltage
s: MIL and hybrid system warning on
Converter temperature shown far below ambient
Reduced 12 V supply from the converter

P2CAC.t: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor F Circuit Range/Performance
P2CAC.d: P2CAC flags DC/DC converter temperature sensor F as implausible although its signal is electrically valid. With six sensors in one converter the controller has plenty of reference values: after a cold soak all should read close to ambient, and during operation sensor F should rise and fall in step with the load on the part it watches. The Hyundai patent shows that converter software already evaluates temperature differences between sensors, there to tune the switching frequency. No manufacturer documents P2CAC publicly; FCA's Ram 1500 eTorque bulletin 08-037-21 only covers performance codes up to sensor D. CARB requires rationality checks for hybrid component temperature sensors. A sensor detached from its heat sink, drift or outdated software are typical. Sensor E uses P2CA8.
c: Sensor F detached from its heat sink or measuring point
Sensor F drifting against the other converter sensors
Outdated converter or hybrid control software
Uneven cooling of the converter, e.g. air in the coolant circuit
s: MIL on, sometimes after a single drive
Sensor F reading out of line with the other converter temperatures

P2CAD.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump B Control Circuit/Open
P2CAD.d: Where a charge air cooling loop has a second electric pump, it carries the letter B. P2CAD reports that the control line to that pump is open, so the driver stage in the engine computer sees no load. No manufacturer documents a pump B or this code publicly. GM publishes the matching test for pump A (P023A) on the supercharged LT5 in table 19OBDG03A: with the low-side driver switched off, more than 200 kΩ between output and ground counts as open; 50 failed samples out of 63 at 100 ms, main relay at least 11 V, Type A with MIL on the first trip. Unplugged or corroded connectors, a broken wire or an open motor winding are the common finds. A pump driven only over LIN has no such line and would report through U01BC instead.
c: Pump B connector loose, unplugged or corroded
Broken control wire between engine module and pump B
Open motor winding or internal board fault in pump B
s: MIL on, often after the first trip
Pump B silent; charge air temperature rises under load
Reduced engine power

P2CAE.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump B Control Circuit Low
P2CAE.d: P2CAE concerns the second electric pump of a charge air cooling loop: its control line is held at ground potential where the driver expects a higher level. No manufacturer documents pump B publicly. GM's published test for pump A (P023B, LT5, table 19OBDG03A) runs with the low-side driver off and flags a short to ground when output and controller ground are connected by less than 0.5 Ω, again 50 of 63 samples, Type A. What the pump then does depends on its design: a plainly switched motor may run all the time, while a smart pump that reads a missing PWM signal may fall back to an emergency mode. Look for a harness chafed on a bracket, water between pins, or an internal short in pump B. The opposite fault, a short to power, is P2CAF.
c: Control wire of pump B rubbed through to ground
Water or corrosion in the pump B connector
Internal short in the electronics of pump B
s: MIL on
Pump B runs continuously or stays in a fallback mode
Possible power reduction when the charge air gets hot

P2CAF.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump B Control Circuit High
P2CAF.d: P2CAF says the control line of charge air cooler pump B is tied to supply voltage, so the engine computer cannot pull it down when it switches the pump on. As with the rest of the pump B series, no manufacturer documents the code publicly. For pump A, GM's LT5 table 19OBDG03A (P023C) carries out this check while the driver is on: below 0.5 Ω between output and controller power counts as a short to power, 50 of 63 samples, Type A with MIL in the first trip. Because the driver may shut itself down to avoid overheating, pump B then usually stops and the second half of the cooling loop loses flow. Typical causes are a wire pinched against a 12 V feed, moisture bridging two pins, or a shorted pump. A short to ground is P2CAE, an open line P2CAD.
c: Control wire of pump B pinched against a 12 V feed
Moisture bridging supply and control pins at the pump
s: MIL on after the first faulty trip
Pump B does not start when commanded
Reduced power at high load

P2CB0.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump B Performance
P2CB0.d: P2CB0 flags that charge air cooler pump B is electrically in order but does not work the way its operating data say it should. No manufacturer documents the code publicly. GM shows how the same check runs on pump A (P026E) in its 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B: the motor phase current expected for the measured pump speed is compared with the actual current, and an error above 5 A for more than 5 s, with the pump above 1,000 rpm and coolant between 10 and 126 °C, sets the code after 16 failures in 20 samples – Type A, MIL on the first trip. Bosch describes such pumps as brushless units whose own circuit board handles motor control and diagnosis. Worn bearings, a damaged impeller, a restricted loop or low coolant are typical. Pure over- or underspeed has its own codes, P2CB1 and P2CB2.
c: Low coolant level or air pockets in the charge air cooler loop
Worn bearing or damaged impeller in pump B
Kinked hose, clogged cooler or debris restricting flow
s: MIL on
Charge air temperature higher than normal, power reduced
Unusual whining or rattling from the pump

P2CB1.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump B Overspeed/Air In System
P2CB1.d: P2CB1 means pump B in the charge air cooling loop turns faster than it should. An electric pump loses its hydraulic load when the impeller churns air instead of coolant, so overspeed is mostly a symptom of a low level or poor bleeding. No manufacturer documents P2CB1 publicly. For pump A (P2B83), GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B treats 8,500 rpm or more in 8 of 10 one-second samples as a fault, at 11 V or higher, Type B with MIL after two trips. GM's LT4 bulletin 18-NA-291 adds that this kind of pump shuts itself off once it draws air, which is why the loop there has to be vacuum filled. Check level, leaks that suck in air, and the bleed procedure before replacing pump B. If the pump then overheats, P2CB5 may follow.
c: Air trapped in the loop after service or incomplete bleeding
Low coolant from a leak in the charge air cooler circuit
Impeller loose or broken on the shaft of pump B
s: MIL on after two trips
Gurgling or a high-pitched pump noise
Low coolant warning or falling expansion tank level

P2CB2.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump B Underspeed
P2CB2.d: With P2CB2 the speed reported by charge air cooler pump B stays below what it should reach. The motor is braked mechanically or gets too little power: a dragging bearing, debris or sludge at the impeller, a weak supply or a high-resistance connector. No manufacturer documents P2CB2 publicly. GM's pump A version, P2B84 in table 25OBDG04B, trips on a reported speed below −115 rpm, effectively a stopped or backward-turning rotor, in 8 of 10 samples with at least 11 V, Type B. GM bulletin 23-NA-102 traced such pump faults on the 3.0-litre Duramax to water getting into the plug of pump M10, a reminder to inspect the connector first. Less flow means warmer charge air and possible power loss. A rotor that cannot move at all is P2CB3.
c: Dragging bearing or sludge slowing the rotor of pump B
Water or corrosion in the pump connector raising resistance
Low supply voltage from a poor ground or weak battery
s: MIL on after two trips
Charge air runs hot, engine power reduced under load

P2CB3.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump B Stuck/Stalled
P2CB3.d: P2CB3 is reported when charge air cooler pump B receives power and a command but its rotor does not turn. The pump's own electronics usually detect this from current flowing without rotation and pass the result to the engine module. No manufacturer documents P2CB3 publicly. Ford's 2024 gasoline OBD summary uses the same fault type, 71 (actuator stuck), for its auxiliary coolant pump B (P2B63), checked continuously from 11 V over 5 s. Audi bulletin 2080825 shows a typical trigger on pump A (P2BC1): the V188 pump of 2025–2026 A5, S5 and Q5 can stick after the car stood unused for over two months. Seized bearings, debris, frozen coolant or a burnt winding are other causes. A pump that turns, only too slowly, sets P2CB2.
c: Rotor stuck after a long period without use
Debris or deposits jamming the impeller of pump B
Burnt winding or failed drive electronics in the pump
Coolant frozen because of insufficient antifreeze
s: MIL on, often with a reduced-power message
No flow in the second branch of the charge air cooling loop

P2CB4.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump B Supply Voltage Circuit
P2CB4.d: P2CB4 concerns the power feed of charge air cooler pump B rather than its command line: the pump finds its supply missing or outside the window in which it can run. No manufacturer documents P2CB4 publicly. Ford's 2024 gasoline OBD summary contains the same fault type, 1C (supply out of range), for auxiliary coolant pump B (P2B62); it is monitored all the time from 11 V battery voltage and logged after 5 s. Because the pump electronics sit inside the housing, as Bosch describes for its PCE pump, the pump measures its own supply pin and reports the result. A blown fuse, a relay with burnt contacts, a corroded ground, a damp plug or a weak battery are the usual causes; a voltage-drop test with the pump running finds hidden resistance. Without power the pump stops.
c: Blown fuse or faulty relay in the pump B feed
Corroded or loose ground connection of the pump
Moisture or corrosion at the supply pins of the connector
Weak battery or charging fault pulling the voltage down
s: MIL on
Pump B silent, charge air temperature climbs
Other supply-related codes may be stored at the same time

P2CB5.t: Charge Air Cooler Coolant Pump B Control Module Overtemperature
P2CB5.d: P2CB5 is raised by the electronics inside charge air cooler pump B when their temperature exceeds the limit; the pump then throttles back or stops to protect itself. No manufacturer documents P2CB5 publicly. Ford's 2024 gasoline OBD summary lists the same fault type, 98 (system over temperature), for its auxiliary coolant pump B (P2B64), monitored continuously from 11 V. Ford's 2019 hybrid summary shows the principle on the LIN-linked engine coolant pump (P26D2): the pump sends its module temperature and the PCM flags readings above 130 °C. The board is cooled by the liquid passing through, so overheating mostly follows a dry run, air in the pump, a stiff impeller or a hot mounting spot. Check level and bleeding first; air alone often appears as P2CB1.
c: Pump running dry or partly in air because of low coolant
Stiff impeller making the motor draw more current
Pump mounted close to hot exhaust or turbo parts
Ageing power stage in the pump electronics
s: MIL on
Pump B slows down or switches off, charge air gets warmer
Reduced power in hot weather or on long climbs

P2CB6.d: P2CB6 rates the boost control loop of charger B as a whole: the pressure produced by the second turbocharger or supercharger strays too far, upward or downward, from what the engine module requests in steady closed-loop operation. It is the B counterpart of P2263 and only applies to engines with two separately controlled chargers. No manufacturer documents P2CB6 publicly. GM's A version on its 2018 diesels counts 400 failures in 500 samples between 2,250 and 4,500 rpm at a desired boost of 130–300 kPa and names leaks after the compressor or exhaust restrictions as targets, Type A. CARB requires underboost, overboost and slow-response detection. Unlike P02CA/P02CB, which name the direction, this code judges overall control quality.
c: Leak in the charge air path of charger B
Sticking wastegate or variable vanes of charger B
Restriction in the exhaust upstream or downstream of turbine B
Boost pressure sensor B reading inaccurately
s: MIL on
Uneven or reduced power under load
Hissing or whistling from the charge air system

P2CB7.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Pressure B Not Detected - Mechanical
P2CB7.d: P2CB7 states that charger B delivers practically no boost although the operating point calls for it, and that the reason is likely mechanical rather than electrical: the pressure measured after the second compressor hardly rises above ambient. It mirrors P2262 for charger A and is relevant only to engines with two separately monitored boost paths. No manufacturer documents P2CB7 publicly. For the A version, Volvo technical journal 31319 traced P2262 on a 2016 four-cylinder engine to a fresh-air hose that had slipped off the air filter housing. CARB requires boosted engines to detect underboost. While P02CB measures a shortfall against target, P2CB7 stands for boost missing altogether; acceleration is flat and torque is often limited.
c: Intake or charge air hose of charger B detached or split
Wastegate or bypass of charger B stuck open
Actuator linkage or vacuum supply to charger B failed
s: Clearly flat acceleration
MIL on, power limited
Unusual hissing or no turbo sound

P2CB8.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Pressure B Too High - Mechanical
P2CB8.d: P2CB8 reports that the second charger, B, produces more boost than the engine module allows, and attributes this to a mechanical cause such as a wastegate or bypass of charger B that no longer opens, a seized actuator rod or sooted variable vanes stuck in the closed position. It is the B twin of P226B. No manufacturer documents P2CB8 publicly. GM's A-side performance check on 2018 diesels watches the same overboost direction with a barometric correction and lists exhaust restrictions as a trigger. CARB requires overboost detection on boosted engines. Unlike P02CA, which only notes boost above target, P2CB8 points at hardware. To protect the turbine and engine, the module usually cuts torque or opens a relief path.
c: Wastegate of charger B stuck closed
Variable turbine vanes of charger B sooted and sticking
Seized actuator rod or linkage on charger B
Boost pressure sensor B reading too high
s: Sudden power cut under full load
MIL on
Surging or jerky boost build-up

P2CB9.d: P2CB9 means the second electric cooling fan reports a lower speed than its command calls for, while communication and wiring are judged sound. GM uses it in two ways. In tables 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 the fan must stay below a speed-dependent floor of up to 3550 rpm for 20 s once it has been commanded above 7.65 % for more than 5 s. The 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B models the expected speed of a LIN fan and flags 16 bad samples out of 20 at one per second, for example under 2300 rpm when 2500 rpm is asked for; both are two-trip codes with the lamp. GM's PIE0601 of 2020 lists P2CB9 with P0494, U0632 and U0633 on 2020–2021 full-size trucks and SUVs and asks for a look at fuses and debris in the blades. Fan 1 has P0494, overspeed of fan 2 is P2CBA.
c: Fan blades slowed by debris, leaves, snow or ice
Fan 2 motor or its integrated electronics worn or faulty
Blown fuse, weak supply or poor ground at the fan
Sporadic entry without fault found (GM investigated without a fix)
s: Check engine light after two trips
Coolant temperature rises at idle or when towing
Weaker air conditioning at standstill

P2CBA.d: With P2CBA the controller finds fan 2 spinning clearly faster than its own estimate of what the current command should produce. GM documents the check in tables 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07: the reported speed minus the estimated speed must exceed a margin of 1400 to 4050 rpm, depending on the operating point, for 20 s with more than 9.5 V on board, and the lamp follows on the second trip. A separate GM code covers readings beyond 4999 rpm that cannot be real, so P2CBA points to a fan that really turns too fast or a motor controller that ignores its command. Typical reasons are a broken or missing blade section, a damaged shroud letting the rotor run free, or a fan module that drives at full power. GM's 2025 diesel table does not use P2CBA. Underspeed of the same fan is P2CB9, fan 1 overspeed P0495.
c: Fan blade broken or partly missing, less load on the motor
Fan electronics drive the motor harder than commanded
Implausible speed feedback from the fan module
Shroud damaged or detached so the rotor runs free
s: Check engine light after two trips
Unusually loud or vibrating fan noise
Fan runs at high speed even with a cool engine

P2CBB.d: P2CBB concerns vehicles with three electric radiator fans: the third one turns slower than modelled for its command. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B describes the check for a LIN-controlled fan 3. The controller converts the request into an expected speed, allows for start-up and ramp delays and for supply voltage, and compares the reported speed with a lower limit; at a 925 rpm request the floor is 725 rpm, at 2800 rpm it is 2600 rpm. Sixteen failures in twenty one-second samples set a Type B code, two trips to the lamp. The test only runs above 875 rpm and is blocked while U067C or the out-of-range fan 3 codes are active. Not every GM triple-fan setup uses P2CBB: table 23OBDG07 logs fan 3 underspeed under its own code P14D7. Overspeed is P2CBC, fan 2 underspeed P2CB9.
c: Fan 3 slowed by debris, ice or a distorted shroud
Fan 3 motor bearings or integrated controller worn
Voltage drop on the fan 3 power feed or ground
s: Check engine light after two trips
Engine runs warmer under high load or in heat
Reduced A/C cooling at low speed

P2CBC.d: P2CBC is the counterpart to P2CBB: the third cooling fan turns noticeably faster than the controller expects for the present request. No manufacturer publicly documents this code. The closest published logic is GM's: table 23OBDG07 flags fan 2 overspeed as P2CBA when the reported speed exceeds the estimate by 1400 to 4050 rpm for 20 s, and treats fan 3 the same way under its own code P14D8 with a margin of 1300 to 4800 rpm. GM's 2025 diesel table watches the LIN fan 3 for underspeed and for readings of 4000 rpm or more, but assigns no P2CBC. CARB requires output devices such as fans to be checked for correct response to their commands. A damaged rotor, a fan module running at full power or false speed feedback would explain the fault. Overspeed is rarely a cooling risk but hints at a component that will fail.
c: Fan 3 blade broken or rotor unbalanced
Fan 3 electronics ignore the speed command
Wrong speed value reported by the fan module
s: Check engine light, depending on the maker
Loud or rough fan noise

P2CBD.d: Some engines heat the crankcase ventilation path so that moisture and oil carried by blow-by gas cannot freeze and block it; engines with two such paths, for example a PCV line and a separate make-up air line feeding the turbo intake, may carry a second heater, B. P2CBD reports that the control circuit of heater B is open, so the element never receives current. No manufacturer documents P2CBD publicly. For heater A (P053A), GM's 2016 diesels check the driver pin with 20 failures in 40 samples below 90 °C coolant as Type C, without lamp, while the Saab 9-5 2.0 diesel treats the same fault as Type A. A broken wire, corroded connector or burnt-out element are usual; only frost reveals the effect.
c: Corroded or loose connector at heater B
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: MIL on (depending on manufacturer) or code stored only
No noticeable effect in mild weather
In hard frost, iced ventilation path with oil leaks or rough idle

P2CBE.t: PCV Heater B Control Circuit High
P2CBE.d: P2CBE says the switched control line of PCV heater B carries too high a voltage, usually because it touches battery positive. Since the module normally completes the heater circuit by pulling this line to ground, a short to supply means the output can no longer switch the element on, or the driver shuts down to protect itself, so heater B stays cold. No manufacturer documents P2CBE publicly. GM checks the A-side equivalent P053C on 2016 diesels with the same 20-of-40 sample counter below 90 °C as its open and ground tests, Type C; the Saab 9-5 2.0 diesel looks for 3–4 V on the low reference with the connector unplugged. Look for chafed insulation near hot parts. Note that in the B group the High code comes before Low.
c: Control wire chafed through and touching battery voltage
Moisture bridging pins in the heater B connector
Internal short in heating element B
Damaged output stage in the engine control module
s: Code stored, MIL depending on manufacturer
Heater B inactive, risk of an iced ventilation path in frost

P2CBF.t: PCV Heater B Control Circuit Low
P2CBF.d: P2CBF is set when the control line of PCV heater B sits at ground potential at a moment the module expects a voltage on it. On the usual low-side layout, with supply fed directly to the heater and the module providing the ground, a short to ground on that line turns heater B on permanently regardless of command. The ventilation stays protected against frost, but the element draws current continuously and may age faster. No manufacturer documents P2CBF publicly; the A-side code P053B is checked by GM's 2016 diesels at coolant below 90 °C with 20 of 40 failing samples, Type C without lamp. A pinched harness against the engine block or a damaged connector is the typical find.
c: Control wire pinched or chafed to engine ground
Output stage in the engine module shorted internally
s: Code stored, MIL depending on manufacturer
Heater B constantly on, slightly higher electrical load
Usually no driveability complaint

P2CC0.d: P2CC0 covers PCV heater B when its wiring passes the electrical tests but the heater does not behave as expected: current outside the plausible window, an overheated output stage, or no sign of the commanded warming. It complements the circuit codes P2CBD to P2CBF, which only detect opens and shorts. No manufacturer documents P2CC0 publicly, and the A-side code P053D is not published either; GM Europe files the closest function, an over-temperature of the heater output stage while switched on, under P052E as a Type A fault on the Saab 9-5 2.0 diesel. An FCA patent explains why the heaters matter: frozen blow-by in the make-up air line can block flow and harm the compressor wheel. Aging elements or high-resistance contacts are typical.
c: Heating element B with drifted resistance
High-resistance contact in connector or supply
Output stage overheating in the engine control module
