P2D07.d: P2D07 is the underspeed report for the second motor electronics pump: B is moving, so it is not stalled as in P2D05, yet its actual speed stays well short of the request for too long. Friction in a worn bearing, a partly obstructed impeller, a pump motor that has lost strength or a supply that drops when the pump draws current are the usual chain of suspects. No manufacturer publicly documents P2D07. The closest published logic is Ford's: its 2024 summary keeps under-speed (B2) as a distinct fault type for auxiliary pumps, checked continuously above 11 V for 5 s, and its 2020 hybrids store the pump A version, P2D02. CARB wants the electronic outputs that cool the inverter checked for function. Measure supply and ground under load before replacing the pump. Temperatures climb and power may be capped.
c: Worn bearing or friction inside pump B
Impeller partly obstructed by deposits or debris
High resistance in feed or ground causing the voltage to sag under load
Pump motor or its electronics losing performance with age
s: Warning lamp on
Pump B speed in live data clearly below the target value
Power limitation during long climbs or towing

P2D08.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump B Supply Voltage Circuit
P2D08.d: P2D08 watches the line that actually powers motor electronics coolant pump B, typically a fused 12 V feed plus ground: the voltage there is too low, too high or absent. The control-line faults of the same pump have their own codes, P0B38 to P0B3A, so P2D08 sends the search to fuses, relays, splices and the ground point rather than to the signal wire. Because many modules share the 12 V net, look for other low-voltage codes and check the auxiliary battery and DC/DC converter first. No manufacturer publicly documents P2D08. Ford's 2024 summary shows the same fault type (1C, supply voltage out of range) for its auxiliary pumps, with a 5 s check enabled from 11 V; the 2020 Ford hybrids carry the pump A version, P2D03. Pump B then fails to cool its electronics and power may be reduced.
c: Corroded connector, loose terminal or poor ground at pump B
Blown fuse or faulty relay in the pump B feed
Weak 12 V battery or DC/DC converter delivering too little voltage
Chafed supply wire with intermittent contact
s: Warning lamp on
Pump B works only intermittently
Additional voltage codes in neighbouring modules

P2D09.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump B Control Module Overtemperature
P2D09.d: P2D09 is raised when the controller inside motor electronics coolant pump B reports that it has become too hot. The pump's own electronics are cooled by the fluid it moves, so the code often follows dry running, a blocked line that makes the motor draw high current, or a mounting spot exposed to heat; an internal defect in the pump board is the other possibility. No manufacturer publicly documents P2D09. Ford's 2024 summary contains the same fault category (98, system over temperature) for its auxiliary pumps, while on pump A the 2020 Ford hybrids log P2D04, which the bulletins cured with new software. Unlike the supply code P2D08 the wiring is usually fine here. When the pump throttles itself, the inverter it serves can overheat and the drive limits power.
c: Low coolant or air, so pump B electronics lose their cooling
Restricted line or clogged component raising pump load and current
Internal defect of the pump B control board
s: Code appears mainly in hot weather or under sustained load
Pump B switches off temporarily
Warning lamp and reduced power

P2D0A.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump C Stuck/Stalled
P2D0A.d: P2D0A starts the five codes for pump C, a third electric pump that some layouts add to the motor electronics loop, for example for a further drive unit or a separate charger and DC/DC branch. The code means pump C is driven and powered but its rotor stays still. Seized bearings, foreign bodies in the impeller and burnt windings are the usual mechanical and electrical reasons. No manufacturer publicly documents P2D0A, and none of the other pump C codes in this block appear in public service material either. CARB requires monitoring of every electronic output used for inverter cooling; Ford's 2024 summary records the matching fault type (71, actuator stuck), and the pump A equivalent P2D00 is known from 2020 Ford hybrids. For a pump C wiring fault use P2BD4 to P2BD7 instead. Without flow the cooled branch heats up and power is reduced.
c: Seized bearing or blocked rotor in pump C
Foreign bodies or deposits jamming the impeller
Burnt motor winding or failed start electronics in the pump
s: Warning lamp on
Pump C silent while commanded on
Rising temperature in the branch cooled by pump C and reduced power

P2D0B.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump C Overspeed/Air in System
P2D0B.d: P2D0B is stored when pump C of the motor electronics loop reaches a speed above the commanded value. Since a pump with air around its impeller loses load and accelerates, the code is first of all a hint at a low level, a leak or incomplete bleeding; a third pump in a branch that sits high in the vehicle is especially prone to trapping air. No manufacturer publicly documents P2D0B. A published example of the same fault on another pump exists: on certain 2022–2023 F-150 Lightning trucks Ford found P2D06, the pump B version, after leaking battery coolant tubes (programme 23B09). In Ford's 2024 summary, overspeed together with dry running forms fault type B1. Fill and bleed per the service procedure and pressure-test the loop. A stalled pump C is P2D0A, a slow one P2D0C. Left alone, the electronics heat up and power drops.
c: Air trapped in the pump C branch after incomplete bleeding
Coolant loss through a leak in the loop
Loose impeller or false speed signal from the pump
s: Warning lamp on, sometimes without other effects
Coolant level below minimum or visible leak traces
Gurgling noise from the pump area

P2D0C.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump C Underspeed
P2D0C.d: P2D0C tells you that pump C, the third pump of the motor electronics loop, is turning too slowly for longer than its controller accepts. Compared with P2D0A the rotor is free, and compared with P2D0B the problem is lack of speed, not lack of load: think of a dragging bearing, a partly clogged impeller or filter screen, or a feed that cannot hold its voltage while the motor draws current. No manufacturer publicly documents P2D0C. Ford's 2024 summary separates under-speed (B2) from the other auxiliary pump faults and runs the check for 5 s once the battery has at least 11 V; on pump A, Ford's 2020 hybrids record the same failure as P2D02. CARB requires a functional check of inverter cooling outputs where feasible. Rising component temperatures and reduced power follow.
c: Dragging bearing or internal friction in pump C
Partly clogged impeller or screen in the pump C branch
Voltage drop on feed or ground of pump C under load
s: Warning lamp on
Pump C speed below target in live data
Higher component temperatures and power limits under load

P2D0D.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump C Supply Voltage Circuit
P2D0D.d: P2D0D flags the supply side of motor electronics coolant pump C: the voltage on its power feed is outside the permitted window or missing. Its counterparts on the command line are P2BD4 (open), P2BD5 (low) and P2BD6 (high), so a technician who sees P2D0D alone should check the fuse, relay, power splice and ground of pump C before touching the signal wire. No manufacturer publicly documents P2D0D. For comparison, Ford's 2019 hybrid summary runs the pump A circuit checks only while system voltage stays between 6 and 19 V, and its 2024 summary lists supply voltage out of range (1C) as an auxiliary pump fault type with an 11 V threshold. CARB requires the electrical monitoring of all inverter cooling outputs. A pump C without a stable feed may stop, so the cooled branch warms and power is limited.
c: Poor ground or corroded supply terminal at pump C
Blown fuse or faulty relay in the pump C feed
Weak 12 V battery or low DC/DC converter output
s: Warning lamp on
Pump C runs intermittently or not at all
Other voltage-related codes stored at the same time

P2D0E.t: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump C Control Module Overtemperature
P2D0E.d: P2D0E closes the motor electronics pump series: the control electronics integrated in pump C have reported an internal temperature above their limit. Smart pumps protect themselves by derating or switching off, and the module storing the code learns of it through the pump's status feedback. Heat usually comes from running without coolant, from a high load against a blocked branch, or from a defect on the pump board itself. No manufacturer publicly documents P2D0E. Ford's 2019 hybrid summary still covered such pump self-reports as one performance code (P0C73), while its 2024 summary names system overtemperature (98) as a separate auxiliary pump fault type; the 2020 Ford hybrids store P2D04 for pump A. A short to voltage on the pump C command line would be P2BD6, not this code. If pump C shuts down, power is limited.
c: Pump C running with too little coolant or air
Blocked branch raising pump load and electronics temperature
Defective control board inside pump C
s: Code sets mainly in heat or after long high-load operation
Pump C switches off and restarts after cooling
Warning lamp and reduced power

P2D0F.d: Pre-ignition means the charge ignites by itself ahead of the spark, mostly at low engine speed and high load in small turbocharged direct-injection engines. Ford patents describe how such events are found: the knock sensor signal is judged in an early crank angle window against a higher limit than ordinary knock, and a counter per cylinder keeps the history. P2D0F reports that this count has passed its calibrated limit while full power is still allowed. No manufacturer documents P2D0F publicly; Lexus uses its own P1378 on the 8AR-FTS 2.0 turbo, and VW lists the power-limiting sibling P2D10. Typical triggers are low-octane fuel, oil droplets or diluted oil, and glowing deposits. Repeated events can crack pistons, so the cause should be found quickly.
c: Fuel with too low an octane rating or poor quality
Oil droplets in the chamber, unsuitable oil or oil diluted by fuel
Glowing carbon deposits on pistons or valves
Spark plugs with too hot a heat range or worn electrodes
Engine control calibration that needs a manufacturer update
s: Check engine light, often after hard acceleration from low speed
Sharp knocking or a single loud bang under load
Rough running or misfire if a piston has already been damaged
Rising oil consumption after repeated events

P2D10.t: Engine Pre-Ignition Above Threshold - Forced Limited Power
P2D10.d: P2D10 is the escalated form of P2D0F: pre-ignition events have exceeded the threshold, and the engine computer now restricts power to protect pistons and rings. A Ford patent gives an idea of the scale, cutting engine load by about 10 percent after three detected events while also capping boost and enriching the mixture. Volkswagen uses P2D10 on the 2022 Jetta and Taos with the 1.5 L turbo: its 24iR update (November 2022, revised March 2023) and Taos bulletin 01-22-05 name P2D10 when P0196 for the oil temperature sensor is stored as well, and tell technicians not to replace parts before reflashing the ECM. Lexus shows the same pattern under P1378 with a reduced power message. Expect a warning lamp and weak acceleration until the fault is cleared.
c: Repeated pre-ignition from low-octane or contaminated fuel
Engine software fault, known on VW 1.5 L turbo together with P0196
Oil droplets, wrong oil grade or fuel-diluted oil in the cylinder
Piston or ring damage that already keeps causing hot spots
s: Noticeably reduced power, often with a warning message
Check engine or EPC light on
Knocking noises under load before the limit kicks in

P2D11.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve A Position Not Learned
P2D11.d: Electrically driven exhaust flaps need their end stops taught to the control unit, so that commanded and actual angles line up. P2D11 says this adaptation is missing or invalid for valve A, as after a new actuator, a new muffler, a reflashed ECM or a flat battery. Maserati lists P2D11 together with its own P1217 on the Grecale 2.0 L4 mild hybrid, where owners see the MIL and hear abnormal exhaust noise. Bulletin MTB 24-22 asks about fuel or oil additives and wants fuel and oil samples; DS 26-06 adds an endoscope check of the bypass valve in the rear silencer for corrosion, which leads to a new rear silencer. GM runs a comparable end stop check under its own codes and offers a learn routine in the scan tool. Unlike P2BF5, the signal is valid; only the reference is missing.
c: Learn procedure not run after actuator, silencer or ECM work
Learned values lost after a flat or disconnected battery
Corroded or binding flap that cannot reach its end stops
Control software that rejects the learn result
s: Check engine light
Unusual exhaust noise, rattling or a flap hunting for position
Exhaust sound modes no longer change

P2D12.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve B Position Not Learned
P2D12.d: P2D12 is the counterpart of P2D11 for the second flap or bank 2: the stored end positions of exhaust valve B are missing or were rejected. No manufacturer documents P2D12 publicly. The closest public logic sits in GM's 23OBDG07 table, which decides from the PWM feedback of exhaust valve 2 whether its end stops have been learned, over 4 seconds with more than 9 V on board, as a two-trip fault under its own code P3181. Ford needs the same alignment on the 2023-2025 F-150 with supercharged 5.2 L V8 (bulletin 25-2144) if the B monitor status PID shows 3, yet stores P2BF8 subtype 78 or P2BFB for it. GM bulletin PIC6289C warns that a disconnected battery can force a relearn. A scan tool learn run usually cures it; if it fails again, the flap or its mounting binds.
c: Alignment or learn run for valve B skipped after repair
Adaptation erased by a discharged or disconnected battery
Actuator mounted out of position or flap shaft binding
Outdated engine software that makes the learn fail
s: MIL on, sometimes with an exhaust mode not available message
Flap B noisy or searching for position
No audible change between sound modes on one side

P2D13.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve C Control Circuit/Open
P2D13.d: P2D13 tells that the drive circuit of a third exhaust flap, valve C, is open or cannot be evaluated. Such a valve only exists on layouts with more than two controlled flaps, for instance a separate bypass in the rear silencer next to one flap per bank. No manufacturer publishes P2D13 or any other valve C code. Ford's 2020-2024 OBD summaries know only valve A on bank 1 and valve B on bank 2; there a smart driver watches the output all the time and flags an open within about 5 seconds under subtype 13. GM's 23OBDG07 tables run the same open-circuit test on an exhaust valve PWM line, but report it as the valve B code P2BF8 after 4 seconds. Under CARB rules, output components like this need circuit monitoring. A connector left off after exhaust work, a broken wire or an internal open in the actuator are the usual finds.
c: Actuator connector unplugged or loose after exhaust work
Broken control wire near the hot exhaust or at a bracket
Internal open in the valve C actuator
Failed output stage in the control module
s: Check engine light
Flap C stays in its rest position, exhaust sound does not change
Message that an exhaust or drive mode is unavailable

P2D14.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve C Control Circuit Low
P2D14.d: With P2D14 the drive wire of flap C is dragged toward ground when the driver expects a higher level. Chafed insulation touching the body or the exhaust, a crushed harness after the car was jacked up, or a shorted actuator winding are the classic reasons. No manufacturer documents P2D14. For the A and B flaps, the Ford 2024 OBD summary handles a ground short as subtype 11 of its smart driver check, run over a 5 second window, and GM's 24OBDG07 tables store P2BF9 for a grounded exhaust valve PWM line after 4 seconds once the supply exceeds 9 V, lighting the MIL on the second trip. CARB wants actuator circuits checked for values outside their range. As the wire is intact but shorted, a continuity test can pass; check the insulation to ground along the whole run instead.
c: Control wire chafed through and touching ground
Shorted winding or electronics in the valve C actuator
Water or salt bridging pins in the connector
s: MIL on
Flap C does not move or stays at its default angle
Exhaust louder or quieter than the selected mode

P2D15.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve C Control Circuit High
P2D15.d: P2D15 is set when the drive wire of flap C carries too high a level, so the output stage cannot pull it down as commanded. Either the wire touches something live, or the electronics inside the actuator push voltage back onto it. No manufacturer publishes P2D15. Analogies exist for flaps A and B: in its 2024 OBD summary Ford books a short to power as subtype 12 of its continuous driver check, which runs for 5 seconds, while the GM 23OBDG07 tables flag the same fault on an exhaust valve PWM line as P2BFA, with more than 9 V supply once 4 seconds have passed, MIL after the second trip. CARB requires such circuit checks on output devices. A flap that keeps moving or sits fully open although nothing was requested fits this code better than P2D14.
c: Control wire shorted to a voltage-carrying circuit
Defective electronics in the valve C actuator feeding voltage back
Output stage in the control module stuck high
s: Check engine light
Flap C open or moving without being commanded
Exhaust sound modes unavailable

P2D16.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve C Control Performance
P2D16.d: P2D16 covers the case where flap C passes every wiring test but still fails to follow its command: it moves too slowly, stops short of the target or drifts away from it. No manufacturer documents valve C codes publicly. Ford's handling of its A and B flaps shows the idea. The actuator electronics flag a jammed flap through the PWM return line, and a plausibility test sets the measured against the requested angle. The 2020-2023 summary lumps both under control performance; the 2024 edition breaks them down into subtypes 07 for a mechanical fault, 4B for an overheated actuator and 78 for failed alignment. In bulletin 23-2132 the Mustang flap is driven open and shut in 10 percent steps to locate the problem. Soot or rust on the shaft, a seized bearing, a bent silencer or a tired motor are typical; CARB asks for such functional checks.
c: Flap shaft seized by soot or corrosion
Worn or overheated actuator motor or gearbox
Silencer or actuator bracket misaligned after exhaust work
s: MIL on, possibly with an exhaust mode warning
Rattle or buzzing from the flap area
Exhaust sound no longer matches the selected mode

P2D17.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve C Position Circuit
P2D17.d: P2D17 is the catch-all fault for the return signal by which actuator C reports its angle to the engine computer. The signal is missing or unusable, yet it does not fit the clear low or high pattern of P2D19 and P2D1A. The code can only appear where a third flap with its own position output exists. No manufacturer documents P2D17. GM's 23OBDG07 tables illustrate how such returns are supervised: for each of two exhaust valves the period and duty cycle of the PWM signal are read and judged over 4 seconds, under GM codes. Ford reads the state of its two flaps over the PWM line of the smart driver. CARB rules call for circuit checks on such inputs. Begin at connector, pins and ground of actuator C, and compare with the other flaps, which are usually of identical design.
c: Corroded or loose connector on actuator C
Damaged feedback or ground wire near the exhaust
Failed position sensor inside the actuator
s: Check engine light
Flap C held in a default position by the control unit
Sound modes partly unavailable

P2D18.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve C Position Circuit Range/Performance
P2D18.d: With P2D18 the position signal of flap C is electrically sound, but its value makes no sense: the reported angle lags or contradicts the command, the end points have wandered off the stored values, or the reading creeps while the flap is idle. No manufacturer publishes P2D18. GM's 23OBDG07 tables separate the two levels clearly: the raw PWM feedback is checked first, and only if it is valid is the computed valve position judged, failing below 3.5 or above 96.5 percent for 4 seconds under GM codes. Ford's 2020 Mustang GT500 bulletin 21-2011, covering the valve A and B codes P2BF5 and P2BFD, found mechanical reasons such as pinched wiring or a tailpipe bracket not welded flush. CARB also requires plausibility checks on such inputs. Unlike P2D16, the fault lies in what the sensor reports.
c: Actuator or silencer shifted so the end points no longer match
Worn or drifting position sensor in the actuator
Pinched or chafed wiring causing an unsteady signal
Learned values no longer valid after parts were replaced
s: MIL on after a drive cycle
Exhaust note changes at the wrong moment or flap C hunts
Drive or exhaust mode reported unavailable

P2D19.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve C Position Circuit Low
P2D19.d: P2D19 is stored when the angle feedback from actuator C drops beneath the bottom of its permitted band. With an analog sensor the line then reads close to zero volts, mostly through a ground short or a lost 5 V supply; with a PWM return the duty cycle hangs close to zero. No manufacturer documents P2D19. The nearest public examples belong to valve A: in bulletin 01-004/20 Mazda links P2BF6 to a low reading from the shutter valve sensor on its cylinder deactivation engine, curing it with new PCM software, and Deutz MD1 engines store P2BF6 when flap voltage falls too low. In GM's 23OBDG07 tables an exhaust valve feedback under 2 percent duty cycle fails after 4 seconds. If flaps share a sensor supply, a low on several of them points to that reference rather than to sensor C.
c: Missing sensor supply voltage or open supply wire
Position sensor in actuator C failed low
Faulty evaluation logic in the engine software
s: Check engine light
Flap C no longer adjusted, default position held
Possible power reduction on engines that tie the flap to cylinder deactivation

P2D1A.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve C Position Circuit High
P2D1A.d: P2D1A flags an angle feedback from actuator C that sits above the top of its permitted band: an analog line close to the supply level, or a PWM return hanging near full duty. Typical reasons are a broken sensor ground, a feedback wire chafed against a live conductor, or water creeping between the connector contacts. Because an input without ground drifts up to the pull-up voltage, an open ground shows up as a high reading. No manufacturer documents P2D1A publicly. On MD1 engines Deutz logs P2BF7, the valve A twin, for excessive flap voltage or a short to positive, while GM in its 23OBDG07 tables rejects an exhaust valve return above 98 percent duty once it lasts 4 seconds, with a two-trip MIL under a GM code. In contrast to P2D15, which concerns the drive wire, the flap itself can keep moving here.
c: Feedback wire touching a voltage-carrying wire
Moisture or road salt in the actuator connector
Position sensor in actuator C failed high
s: MIL on
Control unit ignores flap C feedback and stops adjusting it
Exhaust sound stuck in one mode

P2D1B.t: Exhaust Flow Control Valve C Position Not Learned
P2D1B.d: P2D1B closes the valve C series: the control unit holds no valid end stop values for the third exhaust flap, so it cannot translate its position feedback into a reliable angle. No manufacturer documents P2D1B publicly, and so far even the A and B versions P2D11 and P2D12 are rare in published material. GM's 23OBDG07 tables show the principle for two exhaust valves: during an end stop learn phase the feedback is watched for a valve stuck at a stop, and a separate test flags end stops that were never learned after 4 seconds, with the MIL on the second trip. GM bulletin PIC6289C ties such faults to new cars and recent exhaust work and prescribes a scan tool relearn instead of new parts. Ford's 25-2144 likewise needs an alignment after fitting a new actuator.
c: Learn run for flap C not completed after installation or repair
Learned end stops lost after battery disconnection
Flap blocked or binding so the learn run aborts
Engine software that needs an update before the learn succeeds
s: Check engine light shortly after exhaust or battery work
Flap C hunting, buzzing or rattling
Sound modes do not switch as expected

P2D1C.t: Cold Start EGR A/B Ratio Performance
P2D1C.d: P2D1C belongs to engines with two exhaust gas recirculation paths, A and B, whose share of the total recirculated flow is scheduled differently right after a cold start. The code says that during the cold start strategy the split between both paths did not follow its target. CARB obliges diesels to verify EGR valve position and EGR cooler bypass while the cold start monitoring window applies (at least 6 h soak, ambient from -6.7 °C). GM's 2025 table for the 3.0 l LZ0 diesel shows the layout: EGR A is the high pressure loop (P0401), EGR B the low pressure loop (P049B), steered by a desired LP split; there the cold start HP valve is checked under P034F (tracking error over 10 %, Type B). No manufacturer documents P2D1C publicly. P04DD and P04DE judge EGR A flow alone; expect higher NOx after cold starts.
c: EGR valve A or B sooted or sluggish, so it cannot reach its cold start position
Restricted EGR cooler or leaking pipe in one of the two loops
Faulty pressure, temperature or position signal used to estimate the flows
Engine control software that misjudges the split in cold weather
s: Check engine light after cold starts, often without noticeable driveability change
Rough or smoky running in the first minutes after starting
Further EGR flow codes such as P0401 or P049B stored alongside

P2D1D.t: Reductant System Leak Detected - Small Leak
P2D1D.d: P2D1D reports that the pressurised DEF (AdBlue) circuit between pump, line and dosing valve loses fluid slowly, too little to collapse pressure but enough to be measurable. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. A supplier patent from Plastic Omnium shows how such leaks are found: with dosing at zero the pump should idle near 1,500 rpm at 5 bar, and a speed above 1,750 rpm raises suspicion; the line is then drawn into vacuum and a rise above -200 mbar within about 20 s confirms the leak. California requires reductant delivery to be monitored. P2D1E is the large leak, P202D the older general leakage code. Expect white crystal crusts at fittings, higher DEF use and, if ignored, an SCR warning.
c: Seeping quick connector or damaged O-ring on the DEF pressure line
Worn seal or gasket at the DEF dosing valve on the exhaust pipe
Hairline crack in the DEF line, often after freezing or chafing
Pump module leaking internally or at its housing seal
s: Check engine light, usually with an exhaust service message
White crystalline deposits at line fittings or the dosing valve
DEF consumption noticeably higher than usual

P2D1E.t: Reductant System Leak Detected - Large Leak
P2D1E.d: P2D1E is the severe form of the DEF leak verdict: the pump cannot build or hold working pressure because fluid escapes freely, for example from a split or disconnected line. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's 2025 diesel tables catch the same physical result under P20E8, which fails when measured DEF pressure stays more than 63 kPa below its setpoint for 30 s with over 3 litres in the tank (Type A, MIL on the first trip). California requires the reductant delivery system to be monitored, and a leak of this size stops dosing, so NOx conversion collapses. Unlike P2D1D, fluid is often visible as a puddle or wet trail. Most trucks soon start the service countdown toward a speed limit.
c: DEF line pulled off or connector not latched after service
DEF line split by ice expansion or road debris
Cracked dosing valve body or blown seal at the exhaust
Cracked pump module housing in the tank unit
s: Check engine light and DEF system warning soon after start
Puddle or wet trail of DEF under the vehicle
Countdown to restricted speed or no restart

P2D1F.d: P2D1F means DEF still moves, but less than the dosing command implies, typically because a filter, line or dosing valve tip is partly clogged. Stellantis lists it on 2025–2026 Ram 2500 to 5500 heavy-duty trucks together with P208B, P218F and P20E8 and advises a bucket test before replacing the doser: with doser fitted, pressure should hold 80–94 psi for over 6 minutes; with doser removed, 55–75 psi for over 30 s. Many returned dosers showed no fault. Ford's 2023 diesels detect clogging under P218F by correlating injection rate with pump duty. Plastic Omnium's patent reads a lower than expected pump speed as a clog sign. P2D20 is complete blockage.
c: Urea crystals partly blocking the dosing valve nozzle
Clogged DEF pump filter or suction strainer
Kinked or pinched DEF line after body or exhaust work
Contaminated or aged DEF leaving deposits
s: Check engine light with exhaust fluid service message
Code returns intermittently, often without a lasting fault
Possible NOx efficiency code if dosing stays low

P2D20.d: P2D20 is the hard verdict after P2D1F: no measurable DEF passes, so the pump keeps pressure but nothing reaches the exhaust. A public manufacturer description of P2D20 does not exist; GM's 2025 diesel tables flag the matching symptom under P20E9 when DEF pressure stays more than 63 kPa above its setpoint for 4 s during closed loop control (Type A). Ford's 2023 diesels check flow plausibility under P218F and the dosing valve itself under P208E, stuck closed. California requires the delivery system to be monitored because without reductant the SCR catalyst stops reducing NOx. Frozen fluid, a fully crystallised nozzle or a closed valve are typical. Expect a fast countdown to reduced speed.
c: Dosing valve stuck closed or nozzle fully crystallised
Frozen DEF in line or valve due to a failed line heater
Crushed or fully kinked DEF line
Pump filter completely blocked by deposits
s: Check engine light and DEF warning, often in frost
Countdown to speed limitation or start inhibit
Follow-up NOx efficiency codes

P2D21.t: Turbocharger Interstage Pressure Sensor A Circuit
P2D21.d: Engines with two turbochargers in series can measure the pressure between the low-pressure and the high-pressure compressor. GM's patent on two-stage boost control uses this mid-stage value to split the pressure ratio between both stages and to steer the low-pressure wastegate; Cummins describes the same sensor between the stages and the intercooler. P2D21 is the general circuit code: the module rejects the signal but does not assign it to the low, high or erratic codes. No manufacturer documents P2D21 publicly. California requires input sensors to be checked for circuit faults and boost systems for under- and overboost. Single-turbo engines never set it. Expect reduced boost and power.
c: Loose, corroded or oil-soaked sensor connector
Chafed or heat-damaged harness near the turbochargers
s: Check engine light
Reduced power, boost held to a safe value
Sluggish response while accelerating

P2D22.t: Turbocharger Interstage Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P2D22.d: P2D22 flags an interstage pressure reading that is electrically valid but implausible, for instance offset, stuck or out of step with the other pressures. No manufacturer documents a detection rule. A Cummins patent on a two-stage engine shows what plausible means: with the compressor bypass valve open, interstage and charge pressure should be almost the same, about 102 kPa at 600 rpm and 119 kPa at 2,000 rpm; a service test compares both speeds, and if charge pressure and turbo speed check out while a code is stored, the interstage sensor is the suspect. California requires rationality checks for such inputs. A sensor that reads wrong can mislead the boost split between the stages.
c: Sensor port clogged with oil or soot deposits
Leak in the duct or intercooler between the stages
Stage bypass valve stuck, giving pressures the model does not expect
s: Check engine light
Uneven boost build-up or reduced power
Possible boost deviation codes alongside

P2D23.t: Turbocharger Interstage Pressure Sensor A Circuit Low
P2D23.d: P2D23 says the interstage pressure signal sits below the lowest voltage a working sensor can produce. Typical causes are a signal wire shorted to ground, a lost 5 V supply or an internal sensor short. No public table gives a threshold for this sensor; for comparison, Ford's 2023 diesels treat a DEF pressure sensor below 0.2 V as circuit low. The sensor itself sits between the two compressors of a series turbo system, as GM's two-stage control patent describes, where its value guides the low-pressure stage. California requires out-of-range checks on every such input. With the value missing, the controller usually falls back to a model and caps boost. A high reading is P2D24.
c: 5 V reference open or pulled down by another sensor
s: Check engine light
Boost limited, noticeably less power
Further codes if the shared sensor supply is affected

P2D24.t: Turbocharger Interstage Pressure Sensor A Circuit High
P2D24.d: P2D24 is the opposite case to P2D23: the interstage pressure signal is pinned near or above the top of its range. On a three-wire sensor this usually points to an open ground, a signal wire touching the 5 V reference or battery voltage, or an open signal line pulled up inside the controller. Ford's 2023 diesels, as a comparable pressure sensor example, set circuit high above 4.85 V. No manufacturer documents P2D24 or its threshold. Cummins places the sensor between the low- and high-pressure stages ahead of the charge air cooler. California requires out-of-range monitoring. A falsely high value can make the controller think the low-pressure stage overboosts and cut its output.
c: Open sensor ground or corroded ground pin
Open signal wire pulled up by the controller
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
s: Check engine light
Power reduced, boost held back
Interstage pressure reads high even with the engine off

P2D25.t: Turbocharger Interstage Pressure Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2D25.d: P2D25 is set when the interstage pressure signal jumps or drops out faster than any real pressure between two turbo stages could change, typically through brief interruptions in the circuit. No manufacturer documents the code or its rate limit publicly. The sensor matters because GM's two-stage control patent feeds the measured mid-stage pressure back to the low-pressure wastegate loop, so spikes can make that loop hunt. California requires input sensors to be monitored for faults, and the boost system for slow response. Vibration and heat near the turbochargers make loose terminals and cracked insulation the leading suspects; a wiggle test while watching live data usually finds them.
c: Loose or spread terminal in the sensor plug
Moisture or oil in the connector
s: Check engine light that comes and goes
Surging or hunting boost
Brief power loss over bumps

P2D26.t: Coolant Pump E Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
P2D26.d: P2D26 belongs to the general auxiliary coolant pumps, not to the motor electronics family above: pump E is the fifth electric pump of a vehicle, and its assignment (low-temperature loop, charge air cooler, turbo or component cooling) depends entirely on the manufacturer. The code says the control circuit is intact but the pump does not run or does not deliver the expected effect. No manufacturer publicly documents P2D26. GM's diesel tables show the method on pump C (P2C48): they compute the phase current expected at the measured speed and set a type B fault after about 5 s outside the window. Ford's 2024 summary handles performance/stuck off (fault type 92) for its pumps continuously above 11 V. A seized rotor, air, a weak motor or wiring resistance are typical. Electrical faults on pump E have their own codes from P2DF4.
c: Pump E seized or mechanically worn so it does not reach its target
Air or low coolant in the loop served by pump E
High resistance in connector, feed or ground of pump E
Control module software requiring an update
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Higher temperature in the circuit cooled by pump E
Possible reduced power, depending on what pump E cools

P2D27.t: Coolant Pump F Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off
P2D27.d: P2D27 is the functional check for coolant pump F, the sixth auxiliary pump in the lettering scheme and thus only relevant on vehicles with very many electric pumps, typically plug-in hybrids, electric vehicles or heavy diesels with several separate loops. The control line answers, yet the pump stays off or falls short of what the module expects from speed, current or temperature response. No manufacturer publicly documents P2D27, and unlike pump E no further pump F fault codes appear in common code lists. Published logic exists only for siblings: GM's 2025 diesel table judges pump C (P2C48) by comparing phase current with speed above 2,800 rpm, 10 failures out of 12, type B. Ford's 2024 gasoline summary watches its pumps A and B (P2601, P261B) for 5 s from 11 V. Check the loop, then pump and wiring.
c: Pump F blocked or worn so it runs too weakly
Air pocket or low coolant in the circuit of pump F
Corroded connector or high resistance in the pump F supply
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Overtemperature in the component or loop served by pump F
Power limitation if the cooled component protects itself

P2D28.d: P2D28 concerns the torque side of a cold start strategy. To heat the catalyst, the engine control asks for a torque reserve: spark is retarded and airflow raised so the wheels still get the requested torque while extra heat goes into the exhaust. A GM patent describes this, with a heat estimate turned into a reserve request that enters the propulsion torque calculation. The code means the torque delivered or commanded in this phase strayed from what the strategy planned. CARB allows cold start heating to be judged by the last commanded reserve of torque over the first 30 s at idle. Stellantis lists P2D28 for the 2026 Dodge Charger with the 3.0 l Sixpack engine; bulletin 18-022-26 says it was set falsely through a non-robust monitor and is cured by PCM software. P032F is the general low torque code.
c: Engine control software with a monitor that sets the code without a real fault
Throttle, intake leak or airflow error, so retarded spark cannot be balanced by more air
Misfires or weak ignition while spark is heavily retarded
Implausible temperature or speed input to the torque model
s: Check engine light shortly after a cold start
Hesitant or uneven pull while the engine is still cold
Often no noticeable symptom when the cause is software

P2D29.d: Hybrids and electric vehicles drive the A/C compressor with its own high-voltage motor and inverter. P2D29 reports that this motor is commanded to turn but does not rotate. No manufacturer documents P2D29 publicly. GM's 2019 hybrid tables cover a related check under its own code P1F0A: the filtered gap between commanded and fed-back compressor speed must stay inside limits while 960 to 8,600 rpm is requested, high-side pressure is below 2,800 kPa and pack voltage above 270 V; failure is Type B. A Tecumseh patent explains why current alone misses a stall and why high head pressure right after shutdown can hold the rotor. Without the compressor, cabin and often battery cooling are lost.
c: Mechanically seized compressor, often after oil loss or refrigerant leak
Fault in the compressor's integrated inverter or phase output
Restart against high head pressure or overcharged system
High-voltage supply to the compressor interrupted or weak
s: Air conditioning blows warm air
Warning about reduced battery cooling or charging power
Compressor phase current or overload codes stored alongside

P2D2A.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A/B Correlation
P2D2A.d: Some drives measure the coolant of the inverter and power electronics loop at two points. After a long rest both should read nearly the same, so P2D2A records that sensors A and B disagree by more than the allowed margin; the code does not say which one is wrong. No manufacturer documents P2D2A publicly. GM's 2019 hybrid tables run the idea with one sensor and other references under P0CEF: after at least 3,600 s with compressor, pump and propulsion off, the electronics coolant reading must stay within 27 °C of outside air or transmission fluid, or 28 °C of a refrigerant-based value (Type B). CARB requires inputs of inverter thermal management to be monitored.
c: One of the two sensors has drifted
Added resistance in a connector or wire shifting one reading
Air pocket at one sensor after coolant service
Replacement sensor with a different characteristic
s: Hybrid or EV system warning
Electronics coolant pump runs more often or at full speed
Possible power reduction to protect the inverter

P2D2B.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor A/B Correlation
P2D2B.d: Liquid-cooled traction batteries often have coolant sensors at pack inlet and outlet. When the pack has rested long enough, sensors A and B should agree; P2D2B records a gap beyond the limit without naming the faulty one. No manufacturer documents P2D2B publicly. GM's 2019 hybrid tables test the pack inlet sensor alone under P0C43: after all high-voltage contactors have been open for at least 14,400 s, it fails only when it is off from both references, by 23 °C or more from the average cell temperature and by 22 °C or more from outside air, Type B. California asks for monitoring of every input used for battery thermal management. A wrong reading can make heating or chilling of the pack misjudge, limiting charging or power.
c: One pack coolant sensor has drifted
Corroded or loose connector at a sensor
Air trapped in the battery coolant loop after service
Faulty measuring input in the battery control module
s: Hybrid or EV battery warning
Reduced charging power or range
Battery heater or chiller running unexpectedly

P2D2C.t: Engine Coolant Temperature Measurement System - Multiple Sensor Correlation
P2D2C.d: Engines with split or map-controlled cooling carry several coolant sensors, for example at head, block, inlet, outlet, radiator and heater core. After a cold soak all should read alike; P2D2C reports that the set as a whole disagrees and the module cannot single out one sensor. No manufacturer documents P2D2C publicly. GM's 2025 tables do the comparison under P0116 instead: once per valid cold start the coolant sensor is checked against two others from a configurable list that also includes oil, intake and outside air, Type B over two trips. CARB demands rationality checks of the ECT sensor and an approved plan for engines that read two sensors placed in different coolant loops. Warm-up enrichment and thermostat diagnosis may suffer.
c: One coolant sensor in the set has drifted
Uneven soak, e.g. block heater or short stop, misread as a fault
Low coolant or air leaving one sensor dry
s: Check engine light
Temperature gauge or fan behaviour unusual
Rough cold running or higher fuel use when warming up

P2D2D.t: Cold Start Intake Manifold Runner Performance Bank 1
P2D2D.d: P2D2D reports that the intake manifold runner or swirl flaps of bank 1 did not reach the position the cold start strategy asked for. Many engines hold these flaps in a special setting after a cold start to stir the charge and stabilise combustion while the catalyst warms up. CARB names intake runner, charge motion and swirl valves among the features that must respond to their cold start command, robustly and beyond what they would do without the strategy. The outside-cold-start counterpart is P200A. Stellantis uses P2D2D on the 2020 Ram 1500 with the 3.0 l EcoDiesel Gen 3 and eight-speed automatic: bulletins 18-008-21 and 18-002-23 list it with P2D2E and remedy it with new PCM software. Beyond software, a stiff flap shaft, a carbon-coated runner or a weak actuator are typical reasons.
c: Engine control software that judges the cold start flap check too strictly
Flap shaft or runner coated with soot and oil deposits, stiff when cold
Worn actuator or loose linkage on bank 1
Position sensor signal or wiring fault
s: Check engine light, usually without a noticeable driving change
Slightly rougher idle in the first minutes after a cold start
P2D2E or P200A may be stored too

P2D2E.t: Cold Start Intake Manifold Runner Performance Bank 2
P2D2E.d: P2D2E is the bank 2 version of the cold start runner check, so it only appears on V or boxer engines whose second cylinder row has its own flaps or actuator. The module compares the position commanded for the cold start phase with the feedback from that bank and flags a flap that stays short of target. Both FCA bulletins for the 2020 Ram 1500 3.0 l EcoDiesel V6 (18-008-21, 18-002-23) list it together with P2D2D, and the cure is a PCM reflash; when both banks report at once, software or a shared supply is more likely than two failing flaps. If only bank 2 is stored, inspect that side's shaft, linkage and connector. CARB demands the check for charge motion and swirl valves during cold starts; outside that window the same fault is P200B.
c: Engine control software, especially when P2D2D is stored at the same time
Deposits making the bank 2 flap shaft stiff in the cold
Bank 2 actuator, linkage or connector worn or corroded
s: Check engine light, often with no other complaint
Uneven idle shortly after a cold start
P2D2D or P200B may appear alongside

P2D2F.d: P2D2F means boost from turbocharger or supercharger A stayed below its target during the cold start strategy; P0299 is the same complaint in normal operation. CARB counts electronic wastegate position on petrol engines and variable turbine geometry on diesels among the features that must follow their cold start command. Stellantis uses the code on the 3.0 l EcoDiesel. Recalls 19V-757 (Ram 1500 2014-2016) and 20V-699 (Grand Cherokee 2014-2019) deal with EGR coolers that crack inside; the coolant vapour can ignite in the intake, and if P0299 or P2D2F is stored the intake manifold must be pressure tested and replaced when perforated. For the 2022 Ram 1500 EcoDiesel, bulletin 18-133-22 lists P2D2F among codes fixed by PCM software. Leaks in charge piping or a sticking turbine vane are other causes.
c: Leak in charge air pipes, intercooler or intake manifold
Intake manifold damaged by combustion after an internal EGR cooler crack (FCA EcoDiesel recalls)
Variable turbine vanes or wastegate sticking in the cold
Engine control software that needs an update
s: Weak pulling power shortly after a cold start
Check engine light, sometimes together with P0299
Hissing noise under load if the charge air path leaks

P2D30.d: P2D30 is the opposite of P2D2F: during the cold start strategy, boost from turbocharger or supercharger A rose above the permitted value. Outside that phase P0234 covers it. CARB lists electronic wastegate position as a cold start feature that has to follow its command, so a gate that stays shut when the strategy wants it open is the classic trigger. No manufacturer documents P2D30 publicly. For the related wastegate check GM's 2019 table for the 2.7 l L3B fails P2C9B when position error exceeds 20 % for more than 1 s under cold start conditions, Type A. GM bulletin 22-NA-002 (Equinox and Terrain 1.5 l) shows how cold causes boost faults: frozen oil and water in the wastegate regulator solenoid and ice inside the intercooler set P0234 or P0299. The module usually cuts power to protect the engine.
c: Wastegate flap or linkage stuck closed or stiff in the cold
Wastegate regulator solenoid blocked by frozen moisture or oil deposits
Electric wastegate actuator or its position feedback faulty
Boost pressure sensor reading too high
s: Sudden power reduction shortly after starting in the cold
Check engine light, sometimes with P0234 or a wastegate code
Unusually strong surge of power while the engine is cold

P2D31.t: Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Exceeded Learning Limit Bank 1
P2D31.d: An intake manifold tuning valve switches the effective volume or length of the intake to use pressure waves for more cylinder filling. Electrically positioned versions learn the feedback value at their end stop, and P2D31 says that learned value lies outside its tolerance band. GM uses the code on the 2023 and 2024 Corvette Z06 with the 5.5 l LT6, whose two plenums are linked by three servo-driven communicator valves. Tables 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 average the feedback voltage of tuning valve 1 at the closed stop and fail it above 4.5 V or below 4.25 V for 1 s, battery 9 to 17.5 V, with P2076 to P2078 and P0660 absent; MIL after two trips. Tuning valve 2 has its own GM codes. Typical reasons are a worn stop, a bent valve or a drifting sensor; power can suffer in certain rev bands.
c: Worn end stop or deposits changing the closed position of the valve
Bent valve plate or shaft after mechanical stress
Position sensor inside the actuator drifting
Actuator replaced without completing the relearn
s: Check engine light
Less torque in some engine speed ranges
Changed intake sound under load

P2D32.t: Intake Manifold Tuning Valve Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High Bank 1
P2D32.d: P2D32 is an electrical self-protection code: the power stage that drives the motor of intake manifold tuning valve 1 has reported excessive current or overheating. Smart drivers watch both values internally and switch off before damage. Unlike P0661 and P0662, which describe a line shorted low or high, this code comes from the driver itself, often because the motor is overloaded. GM applies it to the LT6 V8 of the Corvette Z06 (model years 2023 and 2024), where servo-operated valves connect the two intake plenums. Tables 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 store it when the stage flags overcurrent or overtemperature for 1 s with battery voltage between 9 and 17.5 V; MIL after two trips. Valve 2 has a separate GM code. Look for a jammed or stiff valve, a shorted motor winding or chafed wiring.
c: Valve jammed or stiff, so the motor draws excessive current
Internal short in the actuator motor
Chafed control wiring touching ground or another circuit
Faulty driver stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light
Tuning valve stays in one position, with less torque in some rev ranges
Code may return soon after clearing if the valve stays jammed

P2D33.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Inductive Charger Control Module Processor Performance
P2D33.d: P2D33 concerns the electronics on the vehicle side of a contactless charging system and states that the processor of the inductive charger module has failed one of its own self-tests, for example a memory checksum, a RAM test or a watchdog. Inductive charging moves energy across a gap between a ground coil and a vehicle coil; GM's EV1 used the Magne Charge paddle to SAE J1773, while SAE J2954 now defines wireless power classes up to 11 kW. No manufacturer documents P2D33 publicly. Its wired counterpart P0E5E shows what such a test covers: Mitsubishi sets it on the 2023 Outlander PHEV for a ROM CRC or RAM read/write error in the charger control. CARB asks for charger faults that stop or slow charging to be detected. Wireless charging is then refused; driving and cable charging normally still work.
c: Internal fault of the inductive charger control module (memory, processor, watchdog)
Corrupted or outdated module software, for example after an interrupted update
Unstable 12 V supply or poor ground at the charger module causing resets
s: Wireless charging does not start or stops shortly after starting
Charging fault message in the instrument cluster or app
Code returns after clearing even though the vehicle is correctly positioned

P2D34.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Inductive Charger Control Circuit Range/Performance
P2D34.d: P2D34 points at the control line of the inductive charger, the wired path over which a vehicle controller wakes, enables or commands the charger module. The circuit is not open or shorted, but its level or duty cycle lies outside the expected window or does not follow the command. No manufacturer documents P2D34 publicly, and which signal the line carries depends on the design. Wireless systems need such coordination because the vehicle side sets how much power it takes: the Magne Charge paddle used an infrared link to report the demand of the on-board charge controller, and a Hyundai patent (US10245962B2) has the vehicle assembly controller read coil current and battery data before it drives its active rectifier. CARB requires charger faults that block or slow charging to be found. Check connectors, ground and software first.
c: Corroded or loose connector raising the resistance of the control line
Software levels of charger module and commanding controller that do not match
Faulty output or input stage in one of the two modules
s: Inductive charging is not offered or ends without a clear reason
Charging works intermittently depending on vibration or temperature

P2D35.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Inductive Charging System High Voltage Interlock Circuit Performance
P2D35.d: The inductive charger feeds its rectified DC power into the high-voltage system, so its connectors are usually part of a high voltage interlock loop (HVIL), a low-voltage circuit that breaks as soon as a plug or cover is opened. P2D35 means this loop delivers a signal, but not the one expected, for instance a level that does not track the test source being switched. A clear open is P2EB4. No manufacturer documents P2D35 publicly. GM's Volt tables show how a charging interlock is judged: the module sources 5 V into the loop and treats a reading below 30 % of that reference as a fault, Type A (P0D17 in 14OBDG01). Partly seated plugs, worn or corroded terminals and chafed wires are typical. CARB expects charging faults to be detected. Wireless charging stays blocked until the loop is sound.
c: Interlock or high-voltage connector at the inductive charger not fully latched
Oxidised or spread interlock terminals with high contact resistance
Chafed interlock wire near the underbody pad, which is exposed to water and stone impact
Faulty interlock source or sense stage in the monitoring module
s: Inductive charging is refused
Fault appears after work on the underbody or after driving through deep water

P2D36.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Inductive Charger Output Voltage Performance
P2D36.d: P2D36 judges the DC side of the inductive charger: the voltage it hands to the traction battery is outside what the controller expects for the current state, too low to push charge current or above what the battery may accept. No manufacturer documents P2D36 publicly. How the vehicle side regulates this output is shown in Hyundai patent US10245962B2: the vehicle assembly rectifies the coil power with a bridge whose two switching legs change timing to raise or lower output, can shift its pad to alter coupling, and fine-tunes until the measured secondary current matches the target; the example runs at about 400 V. SAE J2954 sets the wireless power classes this must cover. Causes include a failing rectifier or filter, a drifting voltage sensor or a badly aligned car. P2D37 covers the input side. Charging is usually stopped.
c: Faulty rectifier, switching stage or output filter in the vehicle assembly
Output voltage sensor drifting against the battery voltage measurement
Vehicle parked off-centre over the ground pad, so the output cannot be held
Regulation software of the charger module
s: Inductive charging stops shortly after it begins
Charging power far below the expected value

P2D37.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Inductive Charger Input Circuit Range/Performance
P2D37.d: P2D37 looks at the input of the inductive charger, the high-frequency AC that arrives from the vehicle pickup coil before rectification. The measured input is present but implausible: it fits neither the power being transferred nor the other readings, or it does not react when the transfer ramps up. Clear low and high readings have their own codes, P2EB5 and P2EB6. No manufacturer documents P2D37 publicly. The input depends on coupling across the air gap: the Magne Charge paddle worked at 130 to 360 kHz, current J2954 systems at 85 kHz, and coil offset or a foreign object changes what reaches the vehicle. Hyundai patent US10245962B2 has the vehicle controller read the secondary-coil voltage or current for exactly this regulation. Check pad alignment and coil connectors before replacing modules.
c: Damaged or loose connection between pickup coil and charger module
Large coil offset, excessive ground clearance or metal object on the pad
Faulty input voltage or current sensing inside the charger module
s: Inductive charging starts with low power or not at all
Positioning aid reports the car as aligned, but charging still fails

P2D38.d: P2D38 is the functional check of the traction battery heater: it was switched on, yet the pack or its coolant did not warm as expected, or the heater ran too hot. CARB asks for such a heating check wherever feasible. Toyota uses the code on the 2023 bZ4X as P2D384B, the failure type standing for over temperature; tech tip T-TT-0727-23 lists it with an illuminated MIL and asked dealers to call technical support first because the cause was still under investigation. GM's Volt shows the usual logic under its own code P1EC6: in 2011, heater on for more than 40 s with less than 9 °C rise of the pack inlet coolant; in 2014, a rise slower than 0.15 °C/s within up to 161 s while charging; both Type B over two trips. Wiring faults of heater circuits use other codes. In cold weather, charging and power may be restricted.
c: Heater element or its power switch delivering no or too little heat
Air, low coolant or a weak pump so that heat does not reach the pack sensors
Pack inlet or cell temperature sensor reading wrong, faking a missing rise or overheating
Control software that judges the heating too strictly (Toyota bZ4X case under investigation)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp or hybrid/EV system warning on
Slow charging or reduced power in cold weather
Battery stays cold although preconditioning was requested

P2D39.d: P2D39 is an event record: the traction battery opened its contactors because another system demanded it, not because the battery found a fault of its own. The classic trigger is a crash. In Volkswagen patent US9586481B2 the airbag unit grades crash severity; at the highest level the battery opens its contactor within about 10 to 100 ms of a hard-wired signal, or 20 to 200 ms via CAN, then blocks reclosing until the fault memory is erased while the power electronics discharge the bus below about 60 V. No manufacturer documents P2D39 publicly. It differs from P2D3A, a shutdown of the whole hybrid system, and from P2C96 to P2C98, which judge the wired disable line itself. After a collision the car will not become ready again, and the high-voltage system needs inspection before the code is cleared.
c: Collision or crash signal from the airbag control module
Shutdown request from another controller after a safety fault (isolation, interlock)
Spurious signal on the hard-wired disable line or network message error
s: Vehicle cannot be switched to ready or drive mode
High-voltage system warning in the instrument cluster
Code persists until it is erased with a scan tool

P2D3A.d: P2D3A records that the high-voltage system as a whole was shut down by force rather than in the normal power-down sequence. Stellantis uses it in the battery pack control module (BPCM) of its 400 V STLA Large electric cars, the 2025 Dodge Charger Daytona (bulletin 08-025-25) and the 2024–2025 Jeep Wagoneer S (08-011-25, 08-128-25). In these bulletins the code is not the complaint itself: after the BPCM has been reprogrammed, the technician checks whether P1614 (ECU reset), P2D3A or U029A (lost sensor module) are present, and for P2D3A runs the BPCM Soft Reset routine in wiTECH. The code can therefore follow a module reset, a software fault or a safety reaction elsewhere. A disconnect of the battery alone is P2D39. While it is active the car may refuse to become ready.
c: Battery control module reset or reprogramming leaving the shutdown latched (Stellantis BPCM)
Software fault in the battery or vehicle control module
Safety reaction to another high-voltage fault, which is stored alongside
s: Vehicle does not enter drive-ready mode
Wrench or service warning in the instrument cluster

P2D3B.d: After the contactors open, the capacitors of inverter and DC link still hold high voltage, so a discharge system, either a resistor or an active circuit in the power electronics, drains them within seconds. P2D3B is the general fault code for this system; the narrower ones are P0C75 and P0C76 for discharge time and P0EED for the discharge circuit. No manufacturer documents P2D3B publicly. GM's 2019 hybrid table shows how the drain is checked under P0C76: if the inverter still reads above 200 V 3.5 s after the main contactors opened, a Type A fault is set after two runs. Volkswagen patent US9586481B2 requests active discharge after a severe crash and treats it as complete below about 60 V. The car may refuse to restart, and nobody should work on the system without measuring that it is voltage-free.
c: Faulty active discharge switch or driver in the inverter
Open or degraded passive discharge resistor
Wrong high-voltage reading in the inverter or battery module
Contactor that does not open, so the bus stays fed from the battery
s: Hybrid/EV system warning lamp on
Vehicle does not become ready on the next start

P2D3C.t: Cold Start Hybrid/EV Drive Motor Performance
P2D3C.d: In a hybrid the electric drive motor can be part of the strategy that cuts emissions after a cold start, and P2D3C says it did not perform as that strategy required. CARB demands separate diagnostics for elements of the cold start strategy that are also monitored in normal operation, so a motor fault found during warm-up is kept apart from the general P0A90. No manufacturer documents P2D3C publicly. GM patent US8838316B2 explains the role: the motor drives the car and spins the unfuelled engine to roughly 1,000 to 1,800 rpm, ideally 1,200 to 1,400 rpm, so it can light off the catalyst with retarded spark; if the motor cannot cover the driver's request within its limits, the strategy is abandoned. A motor that falls short therefore costs catalyst heating and raises cold start emissions. Look for further motor, inverter or battery codes.
c: Motor output derated by temperature or another motor fault
Cold or weak traction battery limiting the power available to the motor
Calibration of the cold start strategy in the hybrid controller (software update)
Resolver or motor position sensor fault affecting torque delivery
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Engine starts earlier or runs rougher after a cold start than usual
Often no noticeable change in driving

P2D3D.t: Cold Start Hybrid/EV Drive Motor Inverter Torque Performance
P2D3D.d: P2D3D narrows the cold start check to the inverter: during the cold start strategy, the torque it produced through the drive motor did not match the torque the hybrid controller commanded. Precise torque matters in this phase because motor and engine share the work. In Toyota application WO2015092509A1 the engine idles with retarded ignition at roughly zero to 3 kW while the second motor supplies most of the drive torque; in GM patent US8838316B2 the motor must cut its torque at the moment the engine fires so the driver feels no jolt at the wheels. No manufacturer documents P2D3D publicly. CARB asks for cold start faults to be stored apart from ordinary ones, which is why P0A78 exists beside this code. Typical reasons are inverter current sensing, temperature derating or calibration; expect a MIL rather than a loss of drive.
c: Phase current sensing error in the inverter distorting the delivered torque
Torque derating because of very low or high power electronics temperature
Torque coordination of the cold start strategy in software
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Slight jerk when the engine fires after a cold start

P2D3E.d: P2D3E states that the traction battery could not support the cold start emission strategy as planned, typically because it could not deliver the power the strategy relied on. While the engine heats the catalyst at low output, the battery has to carry most of the driving load. Toyota patent US12679331B2 starts from the weakness that warm-up fails when the demand exceeds the battery output limit; its answer is a lower minimum voltage and a higher steady limit during warm-up, sized to reach that minimum in 5 s instead of 10 s, while the short-term extra is reduced. CARB requires battery health monitoring to catch faults that prevent emission strategies from running and wants cold start faults kept separate, hence the distance to P0A7F. No manufacturer documents P2D3E publicly. Cold, aged or low-charged packs are the usual reasons.
c: Aged traction battery with raised internal resistance and voltage sag
Very cold pack after a long rest, limiting discharge power
State of charge too low to carry the load during warm-up
Weak module or cell imbalance pulling a single cell to its limit early
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Engine has to work harder right after a cold start, electric assist feels weak
Other battery capacity or temperature codes stored

P2D3F.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cooling System B Performance
P2D3F.d: P2D3F is the functional check of a second cooling path of the traction battery, alongside A (P0C32) and C (P2D40). Which path carries which letter is the manufacturer's choice; packs may be cooled by air, by a coolant radiator or by a refrigerant chiller, and some switch between them. No manufacturer documents P2D3F publicly. CARB requires a cooling performance check where feasible, and published tests show the principle: GM's 2012 Volt fails its battery cooling check under P0C32 when the average pack temperature stays above 40 °C during active cooling, Type A. Ford, which uses letter C for the chiller path of its Explorer and Aviator hybrids, tests that path by commanding maximum chiller flow and expecting the inlet coolant to fall by 3 °C. Expect reduced power or charging when the pack runs hot.
c: Low coolant or trapped air in the battery loop
Blocked radiator, cooler or air duct of this cooling path
Diverter valve or pump that does not route enough flow through path B
Coolant or cell temperature sensor reading wrong
s: Malfunction indicator lamp or hybrid system warning on
Reduced electric power or slower fast charging in hot weather

P2D40.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Cooling System C Performance
P2D40.d: P2D40 is the functional check of the third cooling path of the traction battery. Ford uses it for the refrigerant chiller on the 2020–2023 Explorer, Aviator and Police Interceptor Utility hybrids (FHEV and PHEV); the code is stored in the secondary OBD module SOBDMC and lights the MIL. Bulletin 22-2342 tests the path: after the pack has warmed to at least 18 °C, maximum chiller flow is commanded for 2 minutes and the inlet coolant must drop by 3 °C; otherwise cooler fins, coolant pump and diverter valve are checked. On the road the chiller should engage above about 51 °C battery temperature on FHEV and 42 °C on PHEV. Ford lists squeezed hoses, trapped air, a refrigerant charge under 80 % of specification or a partly blocked cooler; SSM 51297 points to an updated workshop procedure. Other paths are P0C32 and P2D3F.
c: Low refrigerant charge in the A/C circuit feeding the battery chiller
Air in the coolant or pinched, kinked battery coolant hoses
Partly blocked battery chiller (high voltage battery cooler)
Coolant diverter valve or battery coolant pump not delivering flow through the chiller
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Battery temperature rises during hard driving or towing, power may be reduced
Weak cabin air conditioning if the refrigerant charge is low

P2D41.t: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage B Performance
P2D41.d: P2D41 is a plausibility check on the second voltage value that an electric A/C compressor reports for its motor drive: the reading is electrically valid but disagrees with a reference, for example the traction battery voltage or the first compressor voltage value. Which voltage the letter B stands for is up to the manufacturer; no manufacturer documents P2D41 on an official public source. GM shows the principle for voltage A in the Volt: P0D69 compares compressor input voltage with the pack voltage and fails above a 15 V gap (2011) or 30 V (2016), Type B. California only demands such monitoring where the compressor serves battery cooling or engine control. Low and high signal: P2D42, P2D43.
c: Faulty voltage measurement inside the compressor control module
Contact resistance at the high-voltage connector of the compressor
Implausible reference value from the battery or hybrid control module
s: Hybrid or EV warning message, warning lamp depending on the manufacturer
A/C cooling reduced or switched off

P2D42.t: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage B Low
P2D42.d: P2D42 is stored when voltage B at the electric A/C compressor motor stays below the lower limit of its working range, so the inverter cannot drive the motor properly and usually switches it off. Unlike a sensor circuit code, it refers to the voltage that is actually present. No manufacturer documents P2D42 on an official public source. Mazda's bulletin 07-002/26 for the CX-90 and CX-70 plug-in hybrids shows the classic cause on the voltage A side (P0D6D): an internal short blows the A/C high-voltage fuse. GM's 2011 Volt flagged a compressor input of 190 V or less as P0D6B. A loose high-voltage connector or open contactors also fit. The A/C stops cooling; plug-in hybrids may lose battery cooling too.
c: Blown A/C high-voltage fuse, often after an internal compressor short
Loose or corroded high-voltage connector at the compressor
Internal fault in the compressor inverter or measurement
s: A/C blows warm air
Hybrid system warning, possibly reduced battery cooling or charging power

P2D43.t: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage B High
P2D43.d: With P2D43 the controller reports that compressor motor voltage B has climbed above the level its power stage can withstand; the compressor controller normally stops the motor to protect its transistors. No manufacturer documents P2D43 on an official public source. GM's hybrid tables show how the voltage A side is treated: the 2011 Volt logs a single sample of 480 V or more as P1ECA, while the 2016 tables classify a reading above 527.25 V as out of range under P0D6A, each Type B. Real overvoltage is rare because the battery holds the bus steady; spikes during charging or regeneration, a faulty converter or charger, or a wrong measurement inside the compressor are more likely. The A/C cuts out; repeated cases call for a check of the high-voltage system.
c: Faulty voltage measurement in the compressor control module
Voltage spikes on the high-voltage bus during charging or regeneration
Faulty DC/DC converter or on-board charger
s: A/C switches off, sometimes only for a while
Hybrid or EV system warning

P2D44.d: P2D44 is the overall function check of the electric A/C compressor motor: it is commanded to run but does not deliver what is expected, typically a speed feedback that does not follow the request, while no single voltage or current fault is flagged. No manufacturer documents P2D44 on an official public source. GM runs the comparable test under its own code P1F0A, Type B: the 2011 Volt fails it when the spinning motor stays below 1800 rpm for 20 s; the 2019 tables filter the gap between requested and reported speed across a request range of 960 to 8,600 rpm. A rotor that does not turn at all has its own code, P2D29. Causes include internal wear, too little refrigerant or oil, excessive head pressure and controller faults. Cooling becomes weak or stops.
c: Internal mechanical wear or lack of oil in the compressor
Wrong refrigerant charge or excessive high-side pressure
Fault in the compressor inverter or its speed evaluation
s: A/C cools poorly or not at all
Unusual noise from the compressor
Battery cooling restricted on plug-in hybrids and EVs

P2D45.d: P2D45 means the diesel exhaust fluid in the tank does not warm up as it should while the tank heater is working, so frozen or very cold fluid cannot be dosed. GM uses the code in its diesel OBD tables from 2021 to 2025 in two variants. In the separate reductant control module, after over 28,800 s engine-off, with fluid between -40 and -14 °C, more than 5 L in the tank and a heater command of at least 10 W, the module compares the measured mean temperature with what a just-acceptable heater would reach; staying below it fails the test, judged once per trip on a 600 s basis. A 2023 engine module variant checks that the tank warms from a start below 0 °C. Both are Type B. Heater circuit faults: P20B9 ff.; too hot: P24FF.
c: Tank heater element degraded or partly failed
Low supply voltage to the heater, e.g. weak battery or poor ground
Tank temperature sensor reading too low
s: MIL after two trips in cold weather
DEF or SCR warning message, dosing delayed
Possible countdown to speed limitation if the fault persists

P2D46.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack B Over Temperature
P2D46.d: P2D46 extends the pack over-temperature check to a battery that is split into several separately watched sections: section B has run hotter than its protection limit, while section A, on undivided batteries the whole pack, uses P0A7E. No manufacturer documents P2D46 publicly. GM shows how the parent code works: its 2019 table 19OBDG02 takes the hottest module reading and fails above 65 °C in 80 of 100 samples at 100 ms, Type A, so the MIL comes on after one trip. A divided pack would run that comparison per section. CARB asks for monitored battery temperature inputs and a functional check of battery cooling. The car usually cuts charge and drive power until section B cools down.
c: Restricted coolant or air flow through section B (blocked channel, kinked hose, clogged intake)
Sustained high load or repeated fast charging in hot weather
Temperature sensor in section B reading too high without a circuit fault
Aged modules in section B with raised internal resistance
s: Hybrid or EV system warning and check engine light
Reduced electric drive power and regeneration
Charging slowed or interrupted

P2D47.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack C Over Temperature
P2D47.d: With P2D47 the battery controller reports that the third section of a divided traction battery, C, has exceeded its temperature limit. Because neighbouring sections share the same coolant or air supply, a fault confined to one letter usually points to a local cause: a blocked cooling channel, a cold plate that lost contact with its modules, or an air duct obstructed in that area. No manufacturer documents P2D47 publicly. For whole-pack overheating GM's 2011 Chevrolet Volt used P0A7E with a module limit of 73.5 °C, 50 failures in 60 samples, Type A, and skipped the test while a temperature sensor rationality fault was active. California's rule also expects the cooling performance of the battery to be verified. Expect reduced power until the section cools.
c: Blocked cooling channel or air duct serving section C
Poor thermal contact between section C modules and the cooling plate (missing or displaced thermal paste/pad)
Temperature sensor in section C reading high
s: Check engine or hybrid system warning light
Less electric power, especially after longer drives
Battery cooling fan or pump running at high speed

P2D48.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack D Over Temperature
P2D48.d: P2D48 is the over-temperature code for the fourth section, D, of a sectioned high-voltage battery. Before treating it as real heat, a technician should ask whether the temperature value itself can be trusted. Porsche's 2025 911 GTS T-Hybrid shows why: P0A7E00 was stored together with a thermal run-through code and a red fire warning that blocked starting, yet no hot surface or smell was found; a software condition interrupted communication inside the battery, so its sensors sent implausible values. No manufacturer documents P2D48 itself. CARB requires battery temperature sensors to be monitored as inputs, and genuine sensor faults normally carry their own codes. Real overheating of section D limits power and charging.
c: Implausible temperature data from the battery electronics (internal communication or software fault)
Insufficient cooling of section D (coolant flow, pump, chiller, air path)
Genuine cell overheating in section D due to an internal cell defect
s: Hybrid system or battery warning, possibly a fire hazard message
Vehicle may refuse to start or enter drive-ready mode
Reduced electric power and charging

P2D49.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack E Over Temperature
P2D49.d: P2D49 says that section E, the fifth separately monitored part of a traction battery, is hotter than permitted. One trap with every pack over-temperature code is heat produced after the car has been switched off. Subaru's 2014–16 Crosstrek Hybrid illustrates it: bulletin 11-185-18 explains that the battery warms itself slightly by self-discharge after shutdown, the original controller logic allowed too little for this, and motor assist, regeneration and auto start-stop then stopped working under P0A7E; reprogramming solved it without a new battery. No manufacturer documents P2D49 publicly. CARB calls for monitored battery temperature inputs and cooling. A code that only appears after parking with no other finding hints at software.
c: Battery controller logic or threshold too strict for normal post-shutdown warming (software update)
Reduced cooling of section E (coolant flow, fan, duct)
Parking in strong sun or heat after hard use
s: Hybrid warning light, sometimes only after the car has stood
Motor assist and regeneration unavailable
Auto start-stop no longer works

P2D4A.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack F Over Temperature
P2D4A.d: P2D4A covers section F, the sixth part of a battery whose controller watches temperature section by section. It pairs naturally with P0EE1, the deterioration code of the same section: aged cells with higher internal resistance turn more current into heat, and repeated overheating speeds up ageing, so both entries on one letter point at the modules themselves rather than at cooling. No manufacturer documents P2D4A publicly. How strictly a lamp follows varies even for the whole-pack code: GM's eAssist table 13OBDG05C sets P0A7E above 72.3 °C, taken from the maximum of the healthy sensors, as a Type B code with the MIL after two trips, while its plug-in tables rate it Type A. CARB requires cooling performance checks. Power is limited.
c: Aged modules in section F producing extra heat (often with P0EE1)
Insufficient cooling flow to section F
Sensor in section F reading too high
s: Warning light; timing depends on manufacturer (first or second trip)
Shorter electric range and weaker electric drive
Battery fan or coolant pump louder than usual

P2D4B.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack G Over Temperature
P2D4B.d: P2D4B reports overheating in section G, the seventh separately supervised part of the traction battery. Such a letter only makes sense for big packs with many groups. The Audi Q5 PHEV is a documented example of such a split: its hybrid battery unit 008C reports eight battery groups through the deterioration codes P0A7F00 to P2CCD00, group 7 being P2CCC00, and Audi bulletins 2076982/1 and 2079556/1 of 2025 deal with replacing single modules.
