Those bulletins cover ageing only; no manufacturer documents P2D4B. For battery components such as cells and temperature sensors, CARB requires codes that isolate the smallest unit replaceable in service. Before a module is changed, the cooling circuit for section G should be checked, since overheating alone is not proof of a worn module.
c: Insufficient cooling of section G (coolant distribution, trapped air, pump)
Worn module in section G (compare with P2CCC)
Temperature sensor of section G reading too high
s: Engine or hybrid warning lamp
Displayed electric range shorter than usual
Reduced charging power

P2D4C.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack H Over Temperature
P2D4C.d: P2D4C stands for overheating of section H, the eighth monitored portion of a traction battery. Eight sections is also the largest split found in public service information, the Audi Q5 PHEV with groups 1 to 8, so H marks the edge of documented practice; Audi publishes only the ageing code P2CCD00 for its group 8, and no manufacturer documents P2D4C. Before suspecting the modules, look at the cooling system as a whole: CARB requires a functional check of battery cooling, which surfaces as separate cooling-performance codes such as P0C32, P2D3F and P2D40. If these are set too, the cause is the loop, not section H. GM's plug-in table 16OBDG02 shows a typical pack limit of 72 °C, 80 of 100 samples, Type A. Power drops until it cools.
c: Battery cooling loop fault (low coolant, pump, chiller, valve) affecting section H
Local flow restriction or poor cold-plate contact at section H
Worn module in section H (see P2CCD)
s: Warning lamp and possibly further battery cooling codes
Limited acceleration in electric mode
Charging stops or slows down

P2D4D.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack I Over Temperature
P2D4D.d: P2D4D is meant for section I, the ninth subdivision of a battery that is supervised section by section; no published battery has that many monitored groups, and no manufacturer documents the code. Where it is used, the reaction depends on how much margin the controller keeps. GM's 2019 table 19OBDG01 is an example of a tight setting for the whole pack: P0A7E fails once the hottest reading exceeds 54 °C for 5 s within a 6.3 s window, Type A. Fast charging, towing or long climbs in summer are the usual moments when such a limit is reached. CARB requires battery temperature inputs and cooling to be monitored. The battery management first lowers charge and discharge current; only if that does not help is a fault stored.
c: Heavy charging or discharging current (fast charging, towing, climbs) beyond cooling capacity
Temperature sensor of section I reading high
s: Charging power drops sharply during fast charging
Reduced drive power with warning message
Check engine or EV system light

P2D4E.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack J Over Temperature
P2D4E.d: P2D4E marks overheating of section J, the tenth separately judged part of a sectioned pack; its ageing counterpart is P2CCF. No manufacturer documents P2D4E publicly. The useful first step is to compare the temperatures of section J with those of its neighbours in live data. If only one sensor stands out while the others agree, a drifting sensor is more likely than real heat; GM's eAssist controller in table 13OBDG05C runs that kind of check under P0A9C, flagging a sensor that differs from the battery average by more than 8.55 °C, Type B. If the whole section is warm, look at its cooling and its modules. CARB asks for both: monitored temperature inputs and a working cooling system. Power is reduced until the reading drops.
c: One temperature sensor in section J drifting high while neighbours read normal
Worn modules in section J (check P2CCF)
s: Warning light with reduced electric power
Section J temperature clearly above its neighbours in live data
Charging limited

P2D4F.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack K Over Temperature
P2D4F.d: P2D4F reports that section K, the eleventh supervised section of a high-voltage battery, has gone over its temperature limit; overheating and ageing of the same section are kept apart, the latter being P2CD0. No manufacturer documents P2D4F publicly. In a liquid-cooled pack, sections far from the coolant inlet see the warmest coolant, so a weak pump, a low level or air left in the loop after service tends to show up there first. GM's 2016 table 16OBDG01 still checks the whole pack against 73.5 °C with 50 failures in 67 samples at 100 ms, Type A, and suspends the test while voltage, current or temperature sensor faults are active. Under CARB, the cooling performance of the pack has to be checked in operation. The car protects the cells by cutting power.
c: Low coolant level or air trapped in the battery loop, often after service
Weak or intermittently failing battery coolant pump
Worn modules in section K (compare with P2CD0)
s: Warning light, often under load or in summer
Reduced electric drive and charging power
Coolant pump or fan audible for a long time after driving

P2D50.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack L Over Temperature
P2D50.d: P2D50 is the last code in the lettered over-temperature series: after P0A7E for section A, or the whole pack if it is undivided, and sections B to K (P2D46 to P2D4F), L is the twelfth section. The deterioration series runs further to N (P2CD3), but sections M and N have no matching heat code in the current lists. No manufacturer documents P2D50 publicly. The logic would follow the parent code, which GM's 2019 table 19OBDG02 runs on the hottest module against 65 °C as a Type A code. Its ageing partner is P2CD1. In service, cell voltages and temperatures of section L are compared with the rest of the pack, and cooling faults are ruled out before any module is changed. CARB requires monitored battery temperature sensors. Power is reduced.
c: Worn or imbalanced modules in section L (see P2CD1, P0BBD)
Temperature sensor of section L reading high
s: Hybrid or EV warning lamp
Reduced electric power and regeneration
Slower charging

P2D51.d: P2D51 is the general electrical code for the control circuit of an air-assist injection system, the circuit counterpart to P0065 to P0067. Assist air flowing around the injector tip breaks the fuel spray into finer droplets. In Ford's patented layout the air bypasses the throttle and is metered by a solenoid valve that the engine computer drives with a pulse-width signal, so a circuit fault concerns this valve, its wiring or the driver stage. Another Ford patent shows a passive variant in which only a shroud on the injector meters the air and nothing electrical can fail. No manufacturer documents P2D51 publicly. Without the valve, atomisation suffers mainly at idle and in cold starts. Low and high: P0066, P0067. Air-assisted DEF dosing uses separate reductant codes such as P2059.
c: Open or shorted coil in the air-assist solenoid valve
Damaged wiring or corroded connector at the valve
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: MIL on
Unsteady idle or harder cold starts
Slightly higher hydrocarbon emissions

P2D52.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit
P2D52.d: P2D52 is the general circuit code for a third coolant temperature sensor, C, in the liquid loop of a hybrid or EV battery. Sensors A and B are commonly the pack inlet and outlet; where C sits is not published and depends on the design. The code says only that the signal is unusable, without saying whether it lies under or over its limits. No manufacturer documents P2D52 publicly. The closest published case is sensor A: Volvo stores the general code P0C4200 in the battery control module of the XC90 T8 from 2016, and technical journal TJ 33546 has the workshop confirm the latest software and then simply clear it. CARB requires battery thermal management inputs to be monitored. Without this value the controller may limit charging or power.
c: Loose connector, damaged wire or corroded pin in the sensor C circuit
Battery controller software flagging the circuit wrongly (update)
s: Check engine or hybrid system light
Battery heating or cooling not working as expected
Charging or electric power may be limited

P2D53.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P2D53.d: P2D53 means coolant temperature sensor C of the battery loop delivers an electrically valid value that does not fit its surroundings. Unlike P2D2B, which only sees that sensors A and B disagree, this code blames sensor C itself. No manufacturer documents P2D53 publicly. GM's 2019 table 19OBDG01 shows the analogous test for sensor A (P0C43): after the HV contactors and battery heater have stayed off for 14,400 s or longer, the inlet value is compared with average cell temperature and outside air and fails at 23 °C or 22 °C difference, 8 s within 10 s, Type B. Audi's 2020 Q5 TFSI e set P0C4300 without a defect because the thermal management limits were too tight; software campaign NVLW fixed it. CARB demands such rationality checks.
c: Sensor C drifting or reacting slowly
Plausibility limits in the controller software too tight (update)
Contact resistance in the connector or air pocket at the sensor
s: Warning light, often after the car has stood for hours
No obvious driveability change at first
Battery conditioning less effective

P2D54.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit Low
P2D54.d: P2D54 flags the signal voltage of battery coolant temperature sensor C as too low. These sensors are NTC thermistors pulled up to a reference, so a falling voltage reads as rising temperature; a short to ground or an internally shorted sensor therefore looks like boiling coolant, while the loop itself may be cold. No manufacturer documents P2D54 publicly. GM uses the same logic for sensor A as P0C44: its battery controller fails the inlet value at 87.9 °C, an ADC count of 133 or less in the 2019 tables and 130 or less in the 2011 Volt, for 1.75 s within 2.5 s, Type B. CARB requires out-of-range checks on battery thermal inputs. Expect warnings and possibly limited power; the high counterpart is P2D55.
c: Signal wire of sensor C shorted to ground (chafed harness)
Moisture or coolant in the connector bridging the pins
s: Live data shows an implausibly hot coolant reading for sensor C
Battery cooling runs constantly
Warning light and possibly reduced power

P2D55.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit High
P2D55.d: P2D55 is the counterpart to P2D54: the signal of battery coolant temperature sensor C sits at or near the reference voltage. On an NTC circuit with pull-up that is what an open circuit produces, so the controller sees an impossibly cold coolant value. Typical findings are a connector not plugged back after battery work, a broken wire, a spread terminal, or a short to a supply line; an open sensor element is less common. No manufacturer documents P2D55 publicly. GM's sensor A equivalent P0C45 fails below -40 °C, at an ADC count above 3890 (2019) or 3823 (2011 Volt); either must persist for 1.75 of 2.5 s, Type B. CARB demands such out-of-range checks. Battery heating may not work properly in winter.
c: Open circuit: connector unplugged, broken wire or spread terminal
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
s: Live data shows about -40 °C for sensor C
Battery heating or cooling uses substitute values
Warning light; reduced power in cold weather possible

P2D56.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2D56.d: P2D56 points to a coolant temperature signal from sensor C that jumps around faster than liquid in the battery loop can really change temperature, while mostly staying inside the electrical limits. No manufacturer documents P2D56 publicly. GM runs such a test for sensor A as P0C46 in table 19OBDG01: every 100 ms the step to the previous inlet reading is taken, ten absolute steps are summed, and a sum above 64 °C counts as a failure; 4 s within 5 s set a Type B code, and the test pauses while the hard faults P0C44 or P0C45 are active. For sensor B, Volvo's TJ 36929 notes that P0CD900 after charging in air above 20 °C can be a false detection cured by software 3.2.4. CARB requires circuit continuity checks. Loose pins and moving harnesses are the usual suspects.
c: Loose or corroded terminal in the sensor C connector
Harness rubbing or moving with the battery, causing brief interruptions
Detection logic reacting to normal conditions (software update)
s: Warning light that comes and goes
Sensor C value jumps in live data, especially when wiggling the harness
Usually no noticeable driveability change

P2D57.d: P2D57 belongs to a second alternator, called generator B, as fitted to some heavy trucks; GM, for instance, offered a secondary generator (option KHB) on 2019 Silverado medium-duty trucks with the 6.6 L diesel. The code concerns the control channel of that machine: the engine computer's command and the regulator's response do not fit together, or the signal leaves its plausible band. No manufacturer documents P2D57 publicly. Infineon's LIN regulator chip TLE8881-3 shows what such a regulator reports: an electrical error flag for a field terminal shorted to ground or battery, an open field winding or excessive battery voltage, debounced over 250 or 1,000 ms; if communication stops, it falls back to a default set point. Generator A uses P065B. The charge lamp may light.
c: Damaged control line (LIN or command wire) or corroded connector
Faulty voltage regulator of the second alternator
Replacement alternator with an incompatible regulator
s: Charge warning lamp or message
Second alternator charges at a fixed default voltage or not at all

P2D58.d: P2D58 reports that generator B, the second alternator of a dual charging system, does not deliver as commanded for mechanical reasons, most often because its drive slips. Such machines often sit on their own belt and idler. GM's customer satisfaction program N192255140 for 2019 Silverado medium-duty trucks with secondary generator option KHB shows how sensitive that mounting is: a bolt that missed its clamp load could work loose, so dealers fitted a new bracket for the A/C compressor together with the idler and inspected the belt. No manufacturer documents P2D58 publicly. Infineon's LIN regulator TLE8881-3 recognises a broken belt or stalled alternator when the phase signal stops swinging above a cut-in speed. Check belt, tensioner, pulley and bearings first. Generator A: P065C.
c: Worn, glazed or oil-soaked drive belt slipping
Weak tensioner or loose idler pulley mounting
Stiff alternator bearing or faulty overrunning pulley
s: Charge warning lamp, low charging voltage
Belt squeal or noise from the second alternator

P2D59.d: P2D59 indicates that generator B has become too hot. Which machine B means is up to the manufacturer: a second alternator in a dual charging system or a second motor-generator in a hybrid. No manufacturer documents P2D59 publicly. For generator A, Mitsubishi describes the hybrid case under P0A3B on the 2023 Outlander PHEV: a W-phase coil temperature of 199 °C or more for one second sets the code. On the alternator side, Infineon's LIN regulator TLE8881-3 raises a high-temperature flag as soon as the chip passes a programmable compensation threshold, where it also starts lowering the voltage set point. Typical causes are blocked cooling air or oil flow, sustained overload, a failed fan or a misreading sensor. Output is cut back, so charging or hybrid power may be limited.
c: Obstructed cooling air path or reduced oil/coolant flow to the generator
Sustained high electrical load at low engine speed
Temperature sensor or regulator measuring wrongly
s: Reduced charging output or charge warning
On hybrids, limited electric or series-mode power

P2D5A.d: P2D5A compares two level sensors of the diesel exhaust fluid system: each delivers a valid signal, yet together they describe a fill level that cannot be true. Tanks with several level contacts, or vehicles with a main and an auxiliary tank, can cross-check their sensors this way. No manufacturer documents P2D5A on an official public source. GM's 2014 diesel tables show the idea under P203B: the module pulses three discrete level contacts and reports a fault after 5 s, Type B, when the readings form an impossible combination, for instance sensor 2 in its 0 to 1.7 V band while sensor 1 sits at 1.71 to 3.56 V. California requires the level sensor to be monitored as input to driver inducement. A wrong reading can bring early warnings or the inducement countdown.
c: One level sensor failed or contaminated
Urea crystals or deposits on the sensing elements
Corrosion or poor contact at the tank sensor connector
s: Implausible or jumping DEF level display
MIL and DEF warning message
Possible inducement countdown despite sufficient fluid

P2D5B.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor C Circuit
P2D5B.d: P2D5B is the umbrella electrical fault for charging-system contactor C on the plus pole, a third plus-side switch next to contactors A (P0D07) and B (P2BC4). Which charging path C serves is left to each maker, and none states it in public: the bulletins that cite contactor B codes (Mercedes, Mazda, Audi) never mention a C contactor, nor do the published GM tables, and no document lists P2D5B itself. CARB obliges plug-in hybrids to catch charger faults that stop or curb charging. One GM patent assesses this kind of contactor from its coil current after a brief test pulse. Welding and failure to close have their own codes (P2D5C/P2D5D), coil-drive faults P2D5E–P2D61. Expect the charging mode behind C to be unavailable.
c: Coil of contactor C open or shorted internally
Damaged wiring or loose plug at the contactor or its module
Output stage or software of the controlling module
s: One charging mode refused or aborted
Charging or high-voltage warning in the cluster
Driving otherwise normal

P2D5C.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor C Stuck Closed
P2D5C.d: P2D5C is set when positive charging contactor C still conducts after the module commanded it to open; fused contacts are the usual reason. No manufacturer documents P2D5C publicly. Patents describe how a weld shows up: Ford opens its charge contactors one at a time after a session and treats one as welded if the voltage measured at the charger stays within a set margin of the battery voltage; one welded pole blocks further charging, both welded also block driving. GM spots a stuck contactor before start-up from the coil current of a short pulse that is too brief to close a healthy one. Because the plus pole of that charging path can stay live, the module usually locks the path. P2D5D is the reverse fault, P2D63 a welded minus contactor C, P2BC5 the contactor B twin.
c: Main contacts of contactor C welded, e.g. after switching under load
Coil output stage does not switch off
Faulty voltage measurement on the charger side simulating a weld
s: Charging blocked after the previous session
High-voltage warning, possibly no ready mode
Code appears at the end of a charging session or at start-up

P2D5D.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor C Stuck Open
P2D5D.d: P2D5D means positive charging contactor C stays open although it was commanded closed, so the plus pole of that charging path never connects and the session fails right at the start. No manufacturer documents P2D5D publicly; Mazda, which lists the non-closing case for contactor B (P2BC6), says nothing about a C contactor. GM's comparable check for the Volt's plus contactor A (P0D09) illustrates detection: while the charger precharges, its terminal voltage ought to climb; if 8 of 9 readings, spaced 12.5 ms apart, remain under 10 V, the contactor counts as stuck open (Type A). CARB requires plug-in hybrids to detect charger faults that prevent charging. Suspects are burnt contacts, a weak coil feed and a jammed armature. Welding is P2D5C, the minus side P2D64.
c: Contactor C does not pull in (burnt contacts, jammed armature)
Insufficient coil supply due to wiring or connector resistance
Control software misjudges the precharge voltage
s: Charging in the affected mode does not start
Charging station reports an aborted session
Driving not affected

P2D5E.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor C Control Circuit/Open
P2D5E.d: P2D5E concerns the wire that energises the coil of plus-side contactor C, not its power contacts: the module finds that the state of its output driver and that of the line disagree, typically because a wire or the coil winding is broken. No manufacturer documents P2D5E publicly. GM's check of the contactor A counterpart (P0D0A) gives typical criteria: an output reading above 4 V while switched off, or under 57 mA of coil current while on, counts as an open; 40 bad results out of 50, sampled every 12.5 ms, are needed, and the 2016 Volt rates it Type B (two trips), the ELR Type A. Look for a broken wire, a terminal backed out of its plug or an open coil. Range, low and high are P2D5F–P2D61. Contactor C cannot pull in, so its charging mode is lost.
c: Broken coil feed wire or pushed-back terminal
Coil winding of contactor C open
Output stage in the module defective
s: Charging in the affected mode not possible
Fault present continuously, not only while charging
Charging warning in the cluster

P2D5F.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor C Control Circuit Range/Performance
P2D5F.d: P2D5F reports that the coil circuit of plus-side charging contactor C is intact yet behaves in a way that does not match the command: the coil current, the voltage on the line or the pull-in delay drift out of their expected band without amounting to a clear open, low or high condition. No manufacturer documents P2D5F publicly, and the published GM tables contain no range test for the coil of any charge contactor. Under CARB, hybrid parts the maker chooses to monitor must show a proper response to commands. A GM patent lists usable measures: rise rate, derivative and integral of the coil current after a short pulse, compared with a reference recorded in advance. Raised resistance in a plug, a coil whose resistance has shifted and a worn driver fit this code. Opens are P2D5E, low and high P2D60/P2D61. Charging may cut out now and then.
c: Corroded or loose pins raising resistance in the coil circuit
Coil resistance of contactor C out of tolerance
Ageing output stage in the module
s: Charging interrupts sporadically
Contactor clicks late or audibly chatters
Code returns after clearing

P2D60.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor C Control Circuit Low
P2D60.d: P2D60 is logged when the coil feed of positive charging contactor C reads lower than commanded – usually the wire has found ground or the driver output is dragged low. Where the driver switches the supply side, the coil then gets too little current and the contactor stays open, or the driver shuts itself off for protection. No manufacturer documents P2D60 publicly. GM's table for the contactor A twin (P0D0A) on the Volt states that its open-load test is blind to a ground short, so a low fault needs a separate check. CARB lets makers report open, shorted-low and shorted-high output faults under one code, so some systems may never set this one. Typical finds: insulation rubbed through at the battery housing, water in a plug. P2D61 is the high case, P2D67 the minus side.
c: Coil feed wire shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion in the contactor plug
Shorted turns in the coil of contactor C
s: Affected charging mode refused
Fault may appear only in wet weather
Charging warning shown

P2D61.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor C Control Circuit High
P2D61.d: P2D61 points to excess voltage on the wire feeding the coil of plus-side contactor C, caused by touching a 12 V feed or by an output stage that no longer switches off. The real danger is a coil energised without command, closing the plus pole of the charging path while the module assumes it is open; charging is therefore normally inhibited. No manufacturer documents P2D61 publicly. GM's contactor A test (P0D0A) detects this as a short to battery when the switched-off output is less than 0.4 V below supply (2016 tables; the 2011 Volt minus contactor test uses 1.2 V). Audi documents the comparable high fault for contactor B (P2BCA) on Q8 e-tron models of model year 2024, but not for C. Chafed or swapped wires after repair work and a faulty driver are the usual causes. P2D60 is the low case, P2D68 the minus side.
c: Coil feed wire shorted to a 12 V supply
Output stage does not switch off
Wires swapped at a connector after repair work
s: Charging blocked as a precaution
Contactor may click without a charging request
High-voltage or charging warning

P2D62.t: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor C Circuit
P2D62.d: P2D62 is the collective electrical code covering minus contactor C, which connects the return conductor of the third charging path to the traction battery. Neither the code nor the meaning of C is documented by any manufacturer. Separate switches in both poles are common on charging paths because only then can the inlet be fully isolated, and diagnosing the pair needs one pole held closed while the other is tested: a Hyundai quick-charge patent checks the plus relay first and then the minus relay against the voltage at the charging inlet, so a minus-side fault is pinned down separately. Under CARB, a plug-in hybrid must flag charging faults that disable or limit charging. Welded and non-closing cases are P2D63/P2D64, driver faults P2D65–P2D68, the plus side P2D5B. The charging mode via C is typically disabled.
c: Coil of minus contactor C open or shorted
Wiring or plug fault on the minus contactor
s: One charging mode unavailable
Charging warning in the cluster
Driving unaffected

P2D63.t: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor C Stuck Closed
P2D63.d: P2D63 says negative charging contactor C has not opened on command; the return-side contacts are almost certainly fused. No manufacturer documents P2D63 publicly, and the Mercedes and Mazda bulletins that report a welded minus contactor B (P2BCC) do not mention C. Detection relies on isolating one pole at a time: Toyota opens the minus charge relay while the plus relay stays closed and treats it as stuck if the charging inlet voltage stays above a threshold; it repeats the test with the main relays open to exclude a charger that keeps supplying power. Hyundai uses the same pairing at the end of quick charging. With a welded minus pole the inlet is no longer isolated on that side, so the module blocks the path. P2D64 is the opposite fault, P2D5C the plus side.
c: Fused main contacts of minus contactor C
Charger still supplying voltage during the check (false detection)
s: Charging blocked after a session
High-voltage warning at start-up
Vehicle may not become ready if the plus side is welded too

P2D64.t: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor C Stuck Open
P2D64.d: P2D64 appears when minus charging contactor C does not close; the third charging path then lacks its return conductor and no current flows even with the plus contactor in. No manufacturer documents P2D64 publicly. The principle mirrors GM's Volt check of plus contactor A (P0D09): once charge and precharge contactors are commanded closed, charger-side voltage should rise, and under 10 V in 8 of 9 readings fails the test. Seen from outside, a missing minus connection looks just like a missing plus one, so telling P2D64 from P2D5D needs both coil drives to be checked. CARB requires charger faults that prevent charging to be detected on plug-in hybrids. Burnt contacts, a weak coil feed and software are typical. P2D63 is the welded variant.
c: Minus contactor C does not pull in or contacts burnt
Weak coil supply from wiring or connector faults
s: Charging in the affected mode never starts
Charging station aborts immediately
Driving unaffected

P2D65.t: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor C Control Circuit/Open
P2D65.d: P2D65 concerns the line that drives the coil of minus-side charging contactor C: the module notices that what it commands and what the line actually shows do not match, which usually means a broken wire, a loose terminal or an open coil. No manufacturer documents P2D65 publicly. The closest published test is GM's P0D11 for the minus charge contactor of the 2011 Volt: with the output off, more than 2 V on it counts as an open load, and the code needs 40 bad samples out of 50 taken every 12.5 ms (one trip, Type A); a short to ground stays invisible to that check. P2D5E is the plus-side twin, P2D73 the same fault on contactor D. The return pole of path C cannot be closed, so that charging mode drops out.
c: Broken coil-drive wire or terminal pushed out of the connector
Open winding in the coil of minus contactor C
Faulty output stage in the controlling module
s: The charging mode routed through contactor C does not start
Code is stored even without a charging request
Charging fault message in the cluster

P2D66.t: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor C Control Circuit Range/Performance
P2D66.d: P2D66 flags a coil circuit of minus charging contactor C that is connected but responds outside its expected band while showing neither a break nor a short. P2D66 is not described by any manufacturer, and GM's public tables list no range test for charge contactor coils. A GM patent shows why such a check needs care: the coil current of the same contactor differs markedly between -40, 25 and 85 °C, so the patent compares readings with a reference stored offline for each contactor. CARB requires output parts that a maker monitors on a hybrid to respond properly to commands. Corroded terminals and an aged coil fit this pattern. P2D65 is the open, P2D67/P2D68 low and high, P2D5F the plus side.
c: Corroded or loose terminals raising circuit resistance
Coil resistance drifted through ageing or overheating
Module software with an unsuitable reference or calibration
s: Charging via contactor C drops out now and then
Fault occurs mainly in very cold or very hot conditions
Code returns after clearing

P2D67.t: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor C Control Circuit Low
P2D67.d: P2D67 is stored when the drive line of minus charging contactor C sits lower than the module expects, typically because the wire touches ground or the connector has taken in water. No manufacturer documents P2D67 publicly. A separate low check is needed because the usual open-load test misses this fault: GM states in its 2011 Volt table for the minus charge contactor (P0D11) that the test cannot detect a short to ground. CARB, on the other hand, allows opens and shorts on outputs to share one code, so certain systems log this case under P2D65. The effect of the short depends on which coil end is switched: contactor C may remain open, or the output stage protects itself by cutting out. P2D68 is the high case, P2D60 the plus side.
c: Drive wire chafed against the battery housing or body
Moisture or corrosion in the contactor connector
Shorted turns in the coil of minus contactor C
s: Charging mode via contactor C refused
Fault more frequent after rain or washing
Charging warning in the cluster

P2D68.t: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor C Control Circuit High
P2D68.d: P2D68 means the wire energising minus charging contactor C carries more voltage than commanded, for instance where it rubs on a 12 V line or the output stage keeps conducting. No manufacturer documents P2D68 publicly. GM's published tests show how such a short is judged and how the margin has tightened: for the 2011 Volt minus charge contactor (P0D11) GM calls it a short to supply once the idle output comes within 1.2 V of the supply voltage; the 2016 tables cut that margin to 0.4 V. If the coil is fed from the high side, a short can pull contactor C in without command and close the return pole while the module thinks it is open, so charging is normally locked. P2D67 is the low case, P2D61 the plus side, P2D76 contactor D.
c: Drive wire chafed against a 12 V supply line
Output stage in the module no longer switches off
Wires swapped or pinched after repair work
s: Charging blocked as a precaution
Contactor may click without a charging request
High-voltage or charging warning

P2D69.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor D Circuit
P2D69.d: P2D69 collects electrical faults of positive charging contactor D, a fourth plus-side switch after A (P0D07), B (P2BC4) and C (P2D5B). What D connects is not public: none of the makers documents P2D69, and the NHTSA bulletin index since 2015 names neither P2D69 nor any contactor D. Under CARB a plug-in hybrid must notice charger faults that prevent or slow down charging, but does not make them switch on an idle output only for a functional check, so a rarely used path may only be checked while it is in use. A GM patent offers a check at key-on: a coil pulse too short to close a healthy contactor still shows by its current whether the contacts are already shut. Specific faults: P2D6A–P2D6F; minus side: P2D70.
c: Defective coil or contacts of plus contactor D
Wiring or connector fault between module and contactor D
Fault in the module that switches contactor D
s: One charging mode unavailable
Fault may only show when that charging mode is used
Driving unaffected

P2D6A.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor D Stuck Closed
P2D6A.d: P2D6A reports that positive charging contactor D still conducts after being told to open, nearly always because its contacts have welded. No manufacturer documents P2D6A publicly. A Ford patent explains where welds come from and how they are found: of the two charge contactors, the one closing last completes the circuit and takes the arcing, so Ford alternates the closing order between sessions. After charging, that last one is opened first and, once the charger-side voltage has had time to decay, is judged welded if that voltage still roughly equals the battery voltage. A single weld ends charging until repair; with both poles welded the car will not drive either. P2D6B is the opposite fault, P2D71 the minus side, P2D5C the C twin.
c: Contacts of plus contactor D welded by arcing
Coil kept energised by a faulty output stage
Faulty charger-side voltage measurement simulating a weld
s: Charging locked after the previous session
Vehicle may not become ready if the other pole is welded too
Fault appears at the end of a charging session

P2D6B.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor D Stuck Open
P2D6B.d: P2D6B is logged when positive charging contactor D fails to close on command, leaving the plus pole of its charging path disconnected. No manufacturer documents P2D6B publicly. GM's Volt test for plus contactor A (P0D09) shows the usual principle: once charging and precharge are commanded on, the charger-side voltage has to climb, and the test fails when 8 of 9 samples, taken every 12.5 ms, stay below 10 V (Type A). The tricky part is attribution. CARB exempts failures that look identical whether the vehicle or the charging station is at fault, so the code is meant for faults that clearly lie inside the vehicle. Typical finds are pitted contacts, low coil voltage or a stuck armature. P2D6A is the welded case, P2D72 the minus side.
c: Burnt contacts or jammed armature in plus contactor D
Insufficient coil supply voltage or poor ground
Module software misjudging the voltage rise
s: Charging in the affected mode never starts
Charging station reports an immediate abort
Driving unaffected

P2D6C.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor D Control Circuit/Open
P2D6C.d: P2D6C covers the coil supply of positive charging contactor D rather than its main contacts. The module finds the line in a state that contradicts the command to its driver, mostly due to an interrupted wire or coil. No manufacturer documents P2D6C publicly. GM's 2016 check of plus contactor A (P0D0A) looks at both driver states: with the driver off, more than 4 V on the line means open; with it on, a coil current below 57 mA does too; the code needs 40 of 50 samples failing, Type B on the 2016 Volt and Type A on the ELR. CARB requires output circuits to be checked for lost continuity. Contactor D then stays out and the charging mode it serves is unavailable. P2D6D–P2D6F are the other drive faults, P2D73 the minus side.
c: Interrupted coil supply wire or backed-out terminal
Open coil in plus contactor D
Output stage of the module defective
s: Affected charging mode not possible
Fault present permanently, not only while charging
Charging warning displayed

P2D6D.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor D Control Circuit Range/Performance
P2D6D.d: P2D6D points to a coil circuit of positive charging contactor D that works but behaves implausibly: current or voltage on the line drifts out of its normal window although no open or short is present. No manufacturer documents P2D6D publicly, and GM's published tables contain no such range test for charge contactors. A GM patent explains what the coil current can reveal: the position of the armature shapes the current response, so a contactor that is fully or partly closed draws a recognisably different curve, judged by its derivative and integral against a stored reference. CARB expects monitored hybrid outputs to answer commands properly. Contact resistance and a sluggish armature fit this code. P2D6C, P2D6E and P2D6F cover open, low and high.
c: Raised contact resistance in the coil circuit
Sluggish or partly jammed armature in contactor D
Ageing output stage delivering too little current
s: Charging via contactor D interrupted sporadically
Contactor pulls in late or chatters
Code returns after clearing

P2D6E.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor D Control Circuit Low
P2D6E.d: P2D6E is set when the voltage on the coil supply of plus contactor D reads too low, usually a wire touching ground. No manufacturer documents P2D6E publicly. In a layout where the module switches the supply side of the coil, which a GM patent names as one option besides switching the ground side, a ground short means the driver works into a short circuit: the coil gets no usable current, contactor D stays open and the stage may cut out to protect itself. GM's 2016 contactor drive tests (P0D0A/P0D11) note that their open-load logic cannot see a ground fault, so detecting this case takes a dedicated test. Look for rubbed-through insulation and water in plugs. P2D6F is the high case, P2D75 the minus side.
c: Coil feed wire shorted to ground
Water or corrosion in the connector of contactor D
Shorted coil in plus contactor D
s: Charging mode via contactor D refused
Fault set as soon as the contactor is commanded
Charging warning shown

P2D6F.t: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor D Control Circuit High
P2D6F.d: P2D6F says the supply wire to the coil of plus contactor D sits above its commanded level. No manufacturer documents P2D6F publicly. GM's 2016 drive test for plus contactor A (P0D0A) treats an idle output within 0.4 V of the supply voltage as shorted to power. Where the coil is switched on its supply side, one of the two layouts a GM patent describes, such a short energises the coil with no command, so plus contactor D may close and put the plus pole of its path, up to the inlet, on battery potential. Modules therefore lock charging when they see this code. Causes are a wire chafed against a 12 V line, swapped wires or a driver that stays on. P2D6E is the low case, P2D76 the minus side.
c: Coil feed shorted to a 12 V supply
s: Charging locked
Contactor clicks unexpectedly with ignition on
High-voltage warning possible

P2D70.t: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor D Circuit
P2D70.d: P2D70 groups electrical faults of negative charging contactor D, the return-side partner of plus contactor D (P2D69). What D switches and when P2D70 is set remain undocumented. Separate contactors in both poles of a charging path exist so that the inlet can be fully cut off; for diagnosis that means each pole must be tested alone. A Hyundai quick-charge patent does this once a session ends, with charge current already below about 5 A: it keeps one charge relay on, switches the other off and reads the inlet voltage, which must fall below the 60 V level that permits unlocking the connector. Under CARB, charging faults that stop the battery from charging must be detected. Specific faults: P2D71–P2D76.
c: Defective coil or contacts of minus contactor D
Wiring or connector fault on the contactor D circuit
s: One charging mode unavailable
Charging connector may stay locked after a session
Driving unaffected

P2D71.t: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor D Stuck Closed
P2D71.d: P2D71 indicates that negative charging contactor D has stayed closed after an open command, as happens when the contacts fuse. No manufacturer documents P2D71 publicly. A Toyota patent addresses a pitfall of this check: after DC charging the car asks the station to stop, but some stations keep feeding, and the leftover inlet voltage would wrongly suggest welded relays. Toyota therefore repeats a suspicious result after opening the main relays and draining the capacitor, then opens one charge relay at a time against a threshold of a few to a few tens of volts. A Ford patent adds the consequence: one weld locks charging, a weld on both poles also stops the car from driving. P2D72 is the opposite fault, P2D6A the plus side.
c: Fused contacts in minus contactor D
Station kept supplying voltage during the check
Coil held on by a faulty output stage
s: Charging locked after a DC session
Vehicle may refuse to become ready if the plus side is welded as well
High-voltage warning at start-up

P2D72.t: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor D Stuck Open
P2D72.d: P2D72 appears when negative charging contactor D will not close, leaving its path without a return lead; even with plus contactor D pulled in, nothing can be charged. No manufacturer documents P2D72 publicly. Detection can work like GM's Volt test P0D09 for plus contactor A, which expects the charger-side voltage to rise once the contactors are commanded on and fails below 10 V. A missing minus pole and a missing plus pole look the same from that voltage, so the module must use the coil drive states to tell P2D72 from P2D6B. CARB does not require faults to be flagged that cannot be told apart from a failing station. Burnt contacts and a weak coil supply are typical. P2D71 is the welded case.
c: Minus contactor D does not close mechanically
Weak coil supply or poor ground at contactor D
Module software misattributing a station fault
s: Charging in the affected mode never begins
Station aborts right after plugging in
Driving unaffected

P2D73.t: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor D Control Circuit/Open
P2D73.d: P2D73 concerns the coil drive of negative charging contactor D: commanded and measured state of the line differ, pointing to an open wire, terminal or winding. No manufacturer documents P2D73 publicly. GM's test for the minus charge contactor (P0D11) is the direct analogue. In the 2016 tables it shares one entry with the plus contactor test and adds a current check: under 57 mA with the driver on means open, as does more than 4 V with it off. The 2011 Volt version only looked at the off state, with a 2 V limit. Both need 40 bad samples of 50 and cannot detect a ground short. The return pole of path D stays open. P2D74–P2D76 are the other drive faults, P2D6C the plus side, P2D65 contactor C.
c: Open coil drive wire or loose terminal
Broken winding in minus contactor D
Defective driver or current sensing in the module
s: Charging mode via contactor D not available
Code present at every key-on
Charging fault message

P2D74.t: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor D Control Circuit Range/Performance
P2D74.d: P2D74 says the coil circuit of minus charging contactor D answers commands in an unexpected way, although it is neither open nor shorted. No manufacturer documents P2D74 publicly, and no published GM table has a range test for charge contactor coils. One measure a GM patent proposes is timing: how quickly the coil current climbs to a set level after the driver switches on. A slow rise suggests extra resistance in the circuit or a changed coil. That patent runs its test at key-on or remotely by telematics. CARB asks for a functional check of monitored outputs where feasible. Typical are aged plugs, a degraded coil and a weak driver. P2D73 is the open, P2D75/P2D76 low and high, P2D6D the plus side.
c: Aged connector adding resistance to the coil circuit
Coil of minus contactor D with changed resistance or inductance
Output stage no longer delivering full current
s: Charging via contactor D stops intermittently
Delayed contactor click when charging starts
Code reappears after clearing

P2D75.t: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor D Control Circuit Low
P2D75.d: P2D75 is stored when the drive line of negative charging contactor D reads low. No manufacturer documents P2D75 publicly. How serious this is depends on wiring: a GM patent shows the coil switch either on the supply side or on the ground side. If the module switches the ground side, a short to ground at that end bypasses the switch, so the coil can energise and minus contactor D can close although nothing was commanded; charging is then locked for safety. With supply-side switching the same short simply leaves the contactor open. CARB permits makers to combine open and short faults of an output under one code, so not every system sets a separate low code. Chafed wires and wet plugs are typical. P2D76 is the high case, P2D6E the plus side.
c: Drive wire of contactor D shorted to ground
Moisture in the contactor D connector
Output stage shorted inside the module
s: Charging locked
Contactor may click without a command
Fault worse in damp weather

P2D76.t: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor D Control Circuit High
P2D76.d: P2D76 means the control wire of minus contactor D shows more voltage than the module asked for. No manufacturer documents P2D76 publicly. GM's 2016 test for the minus charge contactor (P0D11) flags a power short when the idle output gets within 0.4 V of the supply. The effect hinges on which coil end is switched, which a GM patent leaves open: on a ground-side switched coil, a short to supply at the switched end means both coil ends sit at the same potential, so contactor D never pulls in and the driver may see overcurrent when it turns on; on a supply-side switched coil the contactor may close by itself. Either way charging via path D stops. P2D75 is the low case, P2D6F the plus side, P2D68 contactor C.
c: Drive wire of contactor D touching a 12 V feed
Output stage that no longer switches off
Crossed wires after work on the battery
s: Charging mode via contactor D blocked
Fault appears as soon as ignition is on
Charging or high-voltage warning

P2D77.t: Battery Charger Control Module B Performance
P2D77.d: P2D77 says the control electronics of charger B, a second on-board charger or charger stage, do not work as intended; faults of its processor are filed separately under P2D78. No manufacturer documents P2D77 publicly. The A-side twin P0D67 shows what such a check covers: Ford's 2014 hybrid OBD summary flags it during an active charge for internal faults that prevent charging, such as overvoltage in the low- or high-voltage section, a failed PFC stage or a broken high-voltage current sensor. On the 2022 Outlander PHEV, Mitsubishi watches the charger's internal 3.3, 6 and 12 V rails for 1 s and then stops charging. That a charger B exists is shown by Toyota's 6.6 kW RAV4 Prime charger, whose B stage has its own codes. Plug-in charging fails; driving continues.
c: Internal power or control stage of charger B failed (unit replacement)
Internal low-voltage supply rail of charger B out of tolerance
Weak 12 V supply or poor ground at the charger
Charger software fault, cured by an update where one exists
s: AC charging does not start or stops after a short time
Charging fault message or warning in the instrument cluster
Charging possible only at reduced power, if the other charger path still works

P2D78.t: Battery Charger Control Module B Processor Performance
P2D78.d: P2D78 points at the processor inside the control module of charger B: its self-tests of program or working memory have failed, so the module no longer trusts its own computations. All other functional faults of that module belong to P2D77. No manufacturer documents P2D78 publicly. The kind of test meant is visible in the A-side twin P0E5E, for which Mitsubishi's 2023 PHEV code table names two triggers in the charger controller: a failed CRC check of the ROM and a failed RAM write/read test. CARB requires plug-in hybrids to detect charger malfunctions that disable charging or reduce charging performance. A charger that cannot vouch for its processor will not switch grid power into the battery, so charging is refused. Reprogramming may clear a corrupted memory image; a hardware fault means a new charger.
c: Memory or processor hardware in the charger B control unit defective
Corrupted charger software, e.g. after an interrupted update
12 V supply dip while the charger boots
s: Plug-in charging is refused right after connecting
Charging system warning in the cluster

P2D79.d: P2D79 covers the circuit of a charging stop switch as a whole, a button the driver presses to end external charging before the battery is full. The code is set when the switch line carries no valid signal at all; high, low, performance and intermittent faults of the same line have their own codes P2D7A to P2D7D. No manufacturer documents P2D79 publicly. The part itself is described in patents: in Toyota's design the charging ECU receives a stop signal for as long as the button is held, and Honda's older EV charger ran until the battery was full or its stop switch was turned on. Under CARB, hybrid parts a maker chooses to monitor are judged like any other input, circuit faults included. With an unreadable stop button, the car may refuse to charge or may simply ignore the button.
c: Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the stop switch
Broken wire between stop switch and charging control unit
s: Charging cannot be ended with the stop button
Charging may be refused as a precaution

P2D7A.d: P2D7A means the voltage on the charging stop switch line stays above the band the control unit accepts. This refers to the signal, not to the button position: typical causes are a broken wire or switch contact on a line held up by a pull-up resistor, or a short to a supply voltage. No manufacturer documents P2D7A publicly. What the driver notices depends on the circuit layout. If high is the idle level, an open line looks like a button never pressed, so charging can only be ended by unplugging. If the switch pulls the line up when pressed, the fault mimics a held button, the case Toyota's patent calls a closed failure, and charging will not start at all. The low counterpart is P2D7B, the start switch equivalent P2D7F.
c: Open circuit in the stop switch line or connector (pull-up design)
Stop switch signal wire chafed through and touching a supply voltage
Burnt or broken contact inside the stop switch
s: Charging does not start although the plug is connected
Pressing the stop button has no effect during charging

P2D7B.d: P2D7B is stored when the charging stop switch line is pulled below its permitted voltage, most often by a short to ground in the wiring, water in the switch or a contact that no longer opens on a switch that grounds the line when pressed. No manufacturer documents P2D7B publicly. Here the effect is mostly the reverse of P2D7A: on the common ground-switching layout a grounded line reads as a stop button held down. Toyota describes exactly this situation for its charging stop switch, where a permanent stop request blocks the start of charging, and adds a user procedure to override the stuck button. If instead low is the idle level, the stop request is lost. The high counterpart is P2D7A; the start switch has its own low code, P2D80.
c: Stop switch signal wire shorted to body ground
Moisture or corrosion bridging the stop switch contacts
Stop switch contact stuck closed (ground-switching design)
s: Charging does not begin or ends immediately after plugging in
Charging indicator shows no active session

P2D7C.d: P2D7C covers a stop switch signal that is electrically valid but does not make sense. A typical rationality test asks whether the reported state fits the situation, for instance a stop request that never ends although no one can hold a button that long, or a switch that reports pressed before any charging session has begun. No manufacturer documents P2D7C publicly. CARB requires such rationality checks for inputs where feasible and wants them stored under a code separate from circuit faults, which is the role of this code next to P2D7A and P2D7B. Toyota's patent illustrates the stuck-button problem behind it. A sticking key, a mechanically jammed trim panel or a switch with internal leakage are the usual suspects; charging may be blocked or the button ignored.
c: Stop button mechanically sticking in the pressed position
Internal leakage in the switch giving an in-between signal
Trim panel or object pressing on the button
s: Charging blocked although the plug is seated correctly
Stop button feels stiff or does not spring back

P2D7D.d: P2D7D flags a stop switch signal that jumps between states without a matching button press, or drops out briefly and returns. Since the charging control treats a stop signal as an order to end charging, as both the Toyota and the Honda patents describe, a flickering line can end a session without anyone touching the button. No manufacturer documents P2D7D publicly. Faults that come and go point to a loose terminal, a cracked solder joint in the switch, a chafed wire that touches metal only when the body flexes, or moisture that dries out again. Unlike P2D7A and P2D7B, the measured level is mostly in range, so stored freeze-frame data and a wiggle test are the main tools. Owners typically find that charging stopped overnight for no visible reason.
c: Loose or fretting terminal at the stop switch connector
Cracked solder joint or worn contact inside the switch
Wire chafing that shorts only intermittently
s: Charging stops unexpectedly, e.g. overnight
Battery not full in the morning despite being plugged in

P2D7E.d: P2D7E is the umbrella circuit code for a charging start switch, the control with which a person begins a charging session by hand, for example to override a charging timer. It is set when the start switch line delivers no usable signal; the split into high, low, performance and intermittent follows in P2D7F to P2D82. No manufacturer documents P2D7E publicly. Patents show the part: Honda's early electric vehicle charger began charging only after its charge start switch was turned on, and Toyota's wireless charging system lets a passenger in the car or a person on the ground start charging with such a switch. CARB treats monitored hybrid parts as inputs that must be tested for circuit faults. Charging by button fails, while plug-in or timer charging may still work.
c: Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the start switch
Broken wire between start switch and charging control unit
s: Pressing the start button does not begin charging
Charging only begins at the programmed timer time

P2D7F.d: P2D7F reports a start switch line sitting above its allowed voltage, caused by an open wire or contact on a pulled-up input or by contact with a supply voltage. No manufacturer documents P2D7F publicly. With a start button the consequences run the other way than with the stop switch P2D7A. If the input idles high and the button grounds it, an open circuit hides every press, so a timer-delayed session cannot be brought forward. If the button drives the line high, the fault resembles a permanent start command, and a well-designed control unit will not act on a signal it has flagged as faulty, so charging may wait for the timer or the next plug-in. Honda's early charger shows why the input matters: there the start switch alone released charging. Low counterpart: P2D80.
c: Open circuit in the start switch line or connector (pull-up design)
Start switch signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Start switch contact no longer closes
s: Start button has no effect
Charging begins only by timer or after re-plugging

P2D80.d: P2D80 is set when the start switch line is dragged below its valid voltage, typically through a short to ground or a contact that stays closed on a button that grounds the input when pressed. No manufacturer documents P2D80 publicly. In that common layout a grounded line reads as a start button held down forever. The risk differs from the stop switch: a stuck start request could begin charging against a timer setting or keep re-requesting a session, so the control unit is expected to set the code and stop acting on the input. Where low is instead the idle state, presses are simply lost. CARB demands that distinct out-of-range faults of such inputs get separate codes, hence this code beside P2D7F. The stop switch has its own low code, P2D7B.
c: Start switch signal wire shorted to ground
Start switch contact stuck closed or bridged by moisture
Corrosion in the connector creating a path to ground
s: Charging ignores the timer or starts unexpectedly before the code is set
Start button no longer works after the fault is detected

P2D81.d: P2D81 is the plausibility code of the charging start switch: the wiring reads as healthy, yet the reported switch behaviour cannot be right. Examples of what a control unit can check are a start request lasting far longer than any real press, a request that appears while no charging connector is plugged in, or a press that never produces the expected change of state. No manufacturer documents P2D81 publicly. CARB asks for rationality checks on inputs where feasible and for them to be stored separately from circuit and range faults, which is why this code stands apart from P2D7F and P2D80. The start switch in Honda's patent only mattered with the connector in place, which shows why plug state is a natural cross-check. Charging by button becomes unreliable or is disabled.
c: Start button sticking or not returning
Worn switch contacts giving an unclear signal
Connector detection signal wrong, so a valid press seems implausible
s: Start button works only sometimes or not at all
Charging message about a switch fault

P2D82.d: P2D82 describes a start switch signal that toggles on its own or vanishes for moments. Because a start command is a trigger rather than a stop order, the visible effect is different from P2D7D: a flickering contact may start a charging session nobody asked for, for example ahead of a cheaper overnight tariff set in the timer, or swallow a deliberate press. No manufacturer documents P2D82 publicly; the switch type is known from Honda's and Toyota's patents, where turning the start switch on begins charging. Loose terminals, cracked solder joints, switch bounce on worn contacts and moisture that comes and goes are the usual reasons. The stored level is often in range, so watching the live switch status while moving the harness and pressing the key is the practical test.
c: Loose or fretting terminal at the start switch connector
Worn contacts bouncing inside the start switch
Wire damage that makes contact only at times
s: Charging starts at unexpected times despite a timer
Start button needs several presses

P2D83.t: Battery Charger B Input Current Sensor Circuit Low
P2D83.d: P2D83 says the current sensor at the input of charger B outputs a signal under its valid range. No manufacturer documents P2D83 publicly. For charger A the same fault is P0D3A, which Mitsubishi interprets on the 2022 Outlander PHEV as a ground short. Below 0.344 V of sensor output (roughly -54 A) for half a second, with 10-16 V on the charger, ends the charge, and the repair is a replacement charger/DC-DC assembly. In GM's 2011 Volt, the charger module treats an AC reading below 0.8 A in 160 out of 200 ms as Type A. Toyota's RAV4 Prime proves that a B stage has its own input current monitoring. The sensor usually sits inside the charger. Too high is P2D84, implausible values P2D85, the general circuit code P0E8A.
c: Current sensor of charger B or its signal path shorted to ground inside the unit
Sensor supply inside the charger missing
Damaged internal connection or external harness where the sensor is separate
s: AC charging aborts shortly after starting
Reduced charging power if only charger A is still used

P2D84.t: Battery Charger B Input Current Sensor Circuit High
P2D84.d: P2D84 is the high-side fault of charger B's input current sensor: its signal climbs above what the measuring range allows. No manufacturer documents P2D84 publicly, so the A-side code P0D3B serves as reference. For the 2022 Outlander PHEV, Mitsubishi counts half a second of sensor output above 4.658 V (around +54 A) as a supply-side short and halts charging. GM's Volt module of 2011 sets its Type A fault once more than 24.78 A of AC is reported in 160 out of 200 ms. Real currents of that size would exceed what the charger draws by design, so the fault almost always lies in the measuring chain. P2D84 differs from P0E89, where the current is judged too high, not the sensor. Low counterpart: P2D83.
c: Charger B current sensor output shorted toward its supply inside the unit
Current sensor of charger B failed (charger repair or replacement)
Reference or ground of the sensor lost, pushing the signal up
s: AC charging does not start or stops within seconds
Charging fault warning in the cluster

P2D85.t: Battery Charger B Input Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2D85.d: P2D85 is for an input current reading of charger B that lies within the electrical limits yet cannot be true. No manufacturer documents P2D85 publicly. Its A-side model P0D39 shows the usual test, a check of the zero point while no current should flow: Mitsubishi sets it on the 2022 Outlander PHEV if at least 1.5 A shows up for 2 s while charging is not yet permitted by the PHEV control unit; GM's 2011 Volt module reacts once the offset hits 5.4 A in 512 out of 640 ms. CARB wants such rationality faults filed separately from circuit faults, and allows sensors mounted on a control unit's circuit board to share one code for circuit and range faults. A drifting sensor makes the charger misjudge its power. Hard low or high faults are P2D83 and P2D84.
c: Zero-point drift of the charger B current sensor
Real residual current through a defective input stage while charging is not released
Calibration or software fault of the charger
s: Charging refused or stopped soon after plugging in
Charging power lower than expected

P2D86.d: P2D86 checks two fuel temperature sensors against each other. Where both ought to show nearly the same value, because they measure the same fuel or after a long engine-off soak, a gap larger than a calibrated margin makes the pair implausible, without telling which sensor lies. No manufacturer documents P2D86 publicly. GM runs exactly this test on direct-injection gasoline engines under its own number P111F: two SENT temperature sensors on the high-pressure rail may differ by no more than 10 °C, and 100 bad readings out of 125, one every 100 ms, set a Type B fault after two trips. Ford's 2023 diesels instead compare sensor A with the charge air cooler outlet after six hours off (P0181, 20 °C). Circuit faults of the single sensors are P0182/P0183 and P0187/P0188.
c: One of the two fuel temperature sensors has drifted and reads too warm or too cold
Corroded or loose connector adding resistance to one sensor signal
Replacement sensor of the wrong type or fitted in the wrong position
Engine control software with too tight a comparison limit
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, usually after two drives
Often no noticeable change in how the engine runs
Occasionally rougher hot restarts if fuel quantity correction is off

P2D87.d: Current electric radiator fans carry their own electronics, which turn the PWM or LIN request of the engine controller into motor current. P2D87 means this control module of fan 1 reports that it has become too hot. The supplier Brose, for example, rates its brushless fan modules with built-in LIN or PWM electronics for stable output up to 120 °C, so overheating points to a stiff or blocked motor drawing too much current, poor airflow at the radiator or an ageing power stage. No vehicle maker publicly documents P2D87 in this sense; Deutz uses the same number in its MD1 engine list for an unrelated fan drive output fault. CARB requires such output devices to be checked for correct response. A hot module usually cuts fan speed, so coolant temperature and air conditioning suffer. Fan 2 has P2D8A.
c: Worn bearings or debris make the fan motor stiff, so the module overheats from excess current
Clogged radiator or condenser fins, missing air guides, heat build-up at standstill
Ageing power stage or thermal contact inside the fan control module
s: Fan runs slower or switches off temporarily
Rising coolant temperature in slow traffic
Weaker air conditioning at standstill

P2D88.d: P2D88 means the electronics of fan 1 do not behave as expected although supply and communication are present: the module reports an internal fault, or the speed it sends back does not fit the request. Audi documents the code for 2025 Q5, Q5 Sportback, SQ5 and SQ5 Sportback in TSB 2081184/1. The thermal management control unit stores P2D88, P2D8B or the LIN error U366500, the engine warning lamp comes on and the air conditioning may stop. The reason was an incorrectly fitted ground of the electric fan at earth point 642 on cars built before 28 May 2025; the workshop inspects and reworks it. A Hyundai patent shows the principle behind such checks: the fan controller returns its measured speed to the engine unit and falls back to fixed duty values when the link fails. Fan 2 has P2D8B.
c: Poor or wrongly fitted ground connection of the fan
Internal fault of the fan control electronics
Fan blocked or slowed by debris or bearing wear
Moisture or corrosion in the fan connector or LIN line
s: Engine warning lamp on
Air conditioning stops cooling
Fan does not run or runs irregularly

P2D89.t: Fan 1 Control Module Supply Voltage Circuit
P2D89.d: P2D89 concerns the power feed of the fan 1 control module: the voltage at its supply terminal, or the value the module reports back, is missing or outside the permitted window. Porsche uses the code in the DME of the 2021–2023 718 Cayman GTS 4.0, Boxster GTS 4.0, Cayman GT4 and Spyder and names it radiator fan 1 (left), power supply. Technical Information 198/22 explains that a software fault could set P2D89 together with P2D8C under certain start-up conditions; drivers noticed weak air conditioning and sometimes an engine control warning, and reprogramming the DME cures it. Where no such software issue applies, check the fan fuse, the heavy supply cable, its ground and the plug for corrosion or heat damage, ideally measuring voltage drop under load. Fan 2 has P2D8C.
c: Blown fuse, loose terminal or high-resistance supply cable to the fan module
Engine control software that misjudges the fan supply during start-up (Porsche 198/22)
Corroded or loose ground of the fan module
Weak battery or charging system dropping the supply during high fan load
s: Radiator fan intermittently without function
Reduced air-conditioning performance
Engine control warning in the instrument cluster

P2D8A.d: P2D8A is the second-fan twin of P2D87: the electronics that power fan 2 signal that they have reached their temperature limit. On cars with two radiator fans the second one usually sits on the other side of the shroud; Porsche, for instance, calls its right-hand fan number 2. No manufacturer publicly documents P2D8A. Since supplier modules such as those from Brose are specified for stable output only up to about 120 °C, heat soak in the engine bay after a hard run, a jammed motor pulling high current or clogged fins that starve the fan of air are the first suspects. CARB requires output devices to be checked for proper response, and a module that throttles itself no longer delivers the requested airflow. Expect higher coolant temperature in traffic and weaker air conditioning.
c: Stiff or partly blocked fan 2 motor overloading its electronics
Heat build-up around the module, e.g. clogged fins or damaged air guides
Defective temperature sensing or power stage in the fan 2 module
s: Second fan slows down or cuts out after long idling
Coolant temperature climbs at standstill
Air conditioning blows warmer

P2D8B.d: With P2D8B the module that drives fan 2 fails a plausibility or self-test: it has supply and receives a request, yet the status or speed it reports does not fit. Audi's TSB 2081184/1 for the 2025 Q5 family lists P2D8B next to P2D88 and the local LIN bus error U366500, all stored in the thermal management control unit (address 00C5). In those cars earth point 642 of the electrically controlled fan at the front right had been fitted incorrectly; production changed on 28 May 2025, and in service the ground is checked and repaired, with photos for the warranty claim. On other vehicles a worn motor, foreign objects in the blades or water in the connector are more likely. Typical complaints are a lit engine warning lamp and an air conditioning that no longer cools. Fan 1 has P2D88.
c: Damaged or incorrectly fitted ground point of fan 2
Foreign objects or worn bearings slowing fan 2
Internal electronics fault of the fan 2 module
Water ingress or corrosion at connector or LIN line
s: Engine warning lamp on
Air conditioning without cooling
Fault stored intermittently or permanently

P2D8C.t: Fan 2 Control Module Supply Voltage Circuit
P2D8C.d: P2D8C concerns the supply circuit of the fan 2 control module. The engine controller registers that the module does not get proper operating voltage, whether through an open or high-resistance feed, a blown fuse, a poor ground or a reported voltage outside its window. Porsche lists P2D8C in the DME of the 718 GTS 4.0, GT4 and Spyder from model years 2021 to 2023 as radiator fan 2 (right), power supply. Bulletin 198/22 traces the joint appearance with P2D89 to a software error during control unit start-up and fixes it with a DME update; the fan then failed now and then, the air conditioning lost performance and an engine control warning could appear. Before condemning a fan, measure the voltage drop at the module under load. Fan 1 has P2D89, internal faults of the module are P2D8B.
c: Blown fuse or high-resistance supply line to the fan 2 module
Engine control software error at start-up (Porsche 198/22)
s: Second radiator fan fails now and then
Air conditioning loses cooling power
Engine control warning displayed

P2D8D.d: In a P2 hybrid a disconnect clutch between combustion engine and electric machine lets the car drive on electric power alone and couples the engine in when needed. P2D8D aims at the clutch hardware itself, not at its actuator, pressure sensor or wiring, which have their own codes: the clutch does not take up or release torque the way the control expects. No manufacturer documents P2D8D publicly. Related cases show where such faults arise: Audi's A3 e-tron logged P2884 (clutch stuck open) when the pressure regulating valve for this clutch in the mechatronic unit failed mechanically, and a Ford patent opens the clutch again if a fault is signalled while it is held at its touch point. CARB treats such hybrid parts as monitored components. The engine may fail to join in, and starts may jerk.
c: Worn or glazed clutch plates that slip or no longer hold torque
Mechanically binding piston or plates so the clutch does not release fully
Pressure regulating valve of the clutch mechanically faulty
Wrong, aged or contaminated transmission fluid changing friction behaviour
s: Engine does not couple in or starts with a jerk
Transmission or hybrid warning in the cluster
Limp mode with reduced power or electric-only driving

P2D8E.t: Engine Oil Pressure Sensor/Switch C Circuit
P2D8E.d: Some engines have more than one oil pressure sensor or switch; which one is labelled A, B or C is up to the manufacturer. P2D8E is the general circuit code for sensor or switch C: the controller sees an electrical fault, or with a digital SENT sensor a message or internal error, that it cannot classify as too low or too high. No manufacturer documents P2D8E publicly; Audi's EA888 evo5 does use a sensor C, but only its low fault P2D8F appears in a bulletin. The matching checks for sensor A are published: Ford's 2024 engines report an internal or communication fault of a SENT pressure sensor as P0520 within 5 s, and GM tests a plain switch while the engine has been stopped for a long time, setting P0520 as a Type C code without lamp if it still shows pressure for 5 s. Low and high are P2D8F/P2D90.
c: Oil-soaked, corroded or loose connector at sensor C
Internal electronics fault of the sensor or switch
Chafed or broken wire between sensor and engine control unit
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, depending on make
Oil pressure warning may come on without real pressure loss
Switchable oil pump may stay in its safe high-pressure stage

P2D8F.t: Engine Oil Pressure Sensor/Switch C Circuit Low
P2D8F.d: P2D8F means the signal of oil pressure sensor C lies below its valid electrical range, which usually points to a short to ground, a lost supply or a defective sensor. Audi uses the code on 2025–2026 A5, S5, Q5 and SQ5 models with the 2.0 TFSI EA888 evo5 (TSB 2079097): engine control unit J623 stores it with symptom 17004, and the cluster may show the oil pressure and emission warnings. The first release blamed the control unit calibration. The revision adds that a voltage spike from a powerful charger switched on together with the ignition can set it, so the charger is connected first, the memory cleared and no parts replaced unless the code comes back. For sensor A, Ford flags an analog signal under 0.25 V for 5 s and a GM 2024 engine table under 0.25 V for 1 s. High is P2D90.
c: Signal or supply wire of sensor C shorted to ground
Voltage spike from a workshop charger switched on with the ignition (Audi EA888 evo5)
Sensor C defective with output stuck near zero
Engine control calibration that sets the fault too readily
s: Oil pressure warning without real pressure loss
Emission control warning lamp
Warning message in the instrument cluster

P2D90.t: Engine Oil Pressure Sensor/Switch C Circuit High
P2D90.d: P2D90 is set when sensor C delivers a voltage above its valid range. Typical reasons are a broken ground or signal wire that lets the input float up, a short to battery voltage or a sensor with a failed output stage. No manufacturer publicly describes P2D90; for the EA888 evo5 Audi documents only the low counterpart P2D8F. Sensor A gives the yardstick: Ford's 2024 engines flag an analog sensor above 4.75 V for 5 s (P0523), and a GM 2024 engine table sets P0523 above 4.5 V after 1 s as a two-trip fault. Because the controller can no longer read real oil pressure from that sensor, it may light the oil warning or hold functions that rely on it, such as a variable oil pump, in a safe setting. Measure reference, signal and ground at the plug first. Low is P2D8F.
c: Open ground or signal wire of sensor C
Signal wire shorted to battery or reference voltage
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, depending on make
Oil pressure gauge or warning shows implausible values
Variable oil pump may stay in its safe stage

P2D91.t: Engine Oil Pressure Sensor/Switch C Circuit Range/Performance
P2D91.d: P2D91 says sensor C is electrically in range, but its reading does not fit the engine's state: pressure while the engine stands still, too little at speed, or a value that stays frozen while conditions change. Ford's 2024 summary handles sensor A this way under P0521, catching a signal stuck high, low or mid-range and readings that depart from a modelled pressure in either direction for 5 to 10 s. A GM 2024 engine table sets P0521 after 3 s, two-trip, when relative pressure exceeds 500 kPa under defined conditions or stays below 50 kPa above 1520 rpm. No manufacturer documents P2D91 publicly. A tired sensor, sludge in its bore, wrong oil grade, a worn pump or a sticking pressure control valve can be behind it; confirm real pressure with a mechanical gauge. Electrical faults are P2D8F/P2D90.
c: Sensor C drifted or stuck at one value
Real oil pressure deviation from worn pump, wrong oil or low oil level
Sticking oil pressure control valve of a variable pump
Sludge or debris in the sensor bore
s: Malfunction indicator lamp after two drives on some makes
Oil pressure warning flickers or appears without reason
Possible engine noise if pressure is really low

P2D92.t: Starter/Generator Phase X Current Sensor Circuit High
P2D92.d: P2D92 is set when the signal from the phase X current sensor of a belt or crankshaft starter/generator rises above the range the control electronics treat as valid. Such sensors, commonly Hall devices placed around the phase conductor, put out a voltage that tracks the current, so a value stuck near the top of the scale points to the circuit rather than to real current: a signal lead touching a supply voltage, a damaged connector or a sensor whose output has failed high. No manufacturer documents P2D92 publicly. The closest published logic is GM's eAssist belt machine, coded as drive motor A: a reading above 440 A within about 42 ms, Type B over two trips, after which current control carries on without the sensors. Low side: P2D95; Y and Z: P2D93, P2D94.
c: Phase X sensor signal wire shorted to a supply or reference voltage
Current sensor output failed at the upper end of its range
Damaged, corroded or water-contaminated connector at the starter/generator
Fault in the evaluation circuit of the starter/generator control module
s: Warning lamp or MIL, often only after the fault has been seen on two trips
Reduced electric assist and weaker restarts after automatic engine stop
Automatic stop-start no longer active

P2D93.t: Starter/Generator Phase Y Current Sensor Circuit High
P2D93.d: P2D93 reports that the current reading for phase Y of the starter/generator has climbed past its upper validity limit. Y is the middle letter of the X/Y/Z set this code series uses; the same list also has U/V/W variants (P2D9B to P2D9D), and no maker explains publicly how it assigns them. Not every design measures every phase. GM's eAssist belt system lists sensor circuit checks only for phases U and W, since with three phases one current can be calculated from the other two. A system that stores P2D93 therefore has a dedicated sensor on Y. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Real phase currents do not get that high, so suspect a shorted signal lead, the sensor itself or the control module. P2D96 is the low fault, P2DC3 the general Y circuit code, P2DC4 the range check.
c: Phase Y sensor signal lead chafed and touching a voltage-carrying wire
Internal fault of the phase Y current sensor in the machine electronics
Defective input stage in the starter/generator control module
s: Hybrid or charging system warning on the instrument cluster
Boost function during acceleration missing or reduced
Engine restarts by the conventional starter or not at all after auto stop

P2D94.t: Starter/Generator Phase Z Current Sensor Circuit High
P2D94.d: P2D94 completes the high-side series: the phase Z current sensor of the starter/generator outputs a value above its valid window. Inverters for 48 V starter/generators are built for three- or six-phase machines, and the controller relies on measured phase currents to set torque for engine restarts, boost and energy recovery.
