CARB's OBD rule requires input components, including the hybrid parts a manufacturer has to monitor, to detect wiring faults and readings outside the plausible range; a high-side code like this one is such an out-of-range finding. No manufacturer documents P2D94 publicly. Typical finds are a pinched lead or a loose plug at the machine, moisture in the electronics or a sensor defect, which often means replacing the starter/generator assembly. P2D97 is the low counterpart, P2D9A the intermittent fault.
c: Pinched sensor lead or loose plug at the starter/generator
Water ingress into the machine-mounted electronics
Phase Z current sensor defective, output reads too high
s: MIL or system warning lamp
Stop-start and recuperation switched off
Battery warning because the machine charges less or not at all

P2D95.t: Starter/Generator Phase X Current Sensor Circuit Low
P2D95.d: P2D95 means the phase X current sensor of the starter/generator delivers a signal below the lowest value the controller accepts. The machine works as motor and as generator, so its phase currents change direction and the sensor reports signed values; GM's eAssist table, for example, uses limits of minus and plus 440 A. Low therefore does not mean little current, but an implausibly large reading in the negative direction or an output that has collapsed. Likely reasons are a signal wire shorted to ground, a lost sensor supply or a broken sensor. No manufacturer documents P2D95 publicly; in the GM analogue the U-phase low code sets below -440 A as a two-trip Type B fault. P2D92 is the high side, P2DC1 the general phase X circuit fault and P2DC2 its range check.
c: Phase X sensor signal wire shorted to ground or housing
Sensor supply voltage missing because of an open wire or terminal
Current sensor output failed at the lower end of its range
s: Warning lamp after repeated detection
Starter/generator runs in a restricted mode with less torque
Stop-start unavailable

P2D96.t: Starter/Generator Phase Y Current Sensor Circuit Low
P2D96.d: P2D96 covers the phase Y current sensor of the starter/generator when its signal drops below the valid range, for instance through a short to ground or a missing sensor supply. For the driver the more important part is how the controller reacts: without a trustworthy phase current it will usually limit or stop electric assist, stop-start can be suspended and charging through the machine may fall back, with a warning lamp. In GM's eAssist analogue the switch to sensorless current control happens within about 0.19 s, and the code is stored as Type B over two trips. No manufacturer documents P2D96 publicly. Check sensor supply and ground at the machine first. P2D93 is the high fault of Y; the series goes on with P2D97 for phase Z low, and P2D99 is the intermittent Y fault.
c: Phase Y sensor signal pulled to ground by damaged insulation
Open circuit in the sensor supply or a backed-out terminal
s: Electric assist reduced or switched off
Stop-start suspended
Battery or system warning, charging may be reduced

P2D97.t: Starter/Generator Phase Z Current Sensor Circuit Low
P2D97.d: P2D97 is the last of the three low codes: the Z-phase current sensor of the starter/generator reports a value under the bottom of its valid window. Because the machine both drives the engine and charges, its phase current is signed, so a low fault stands for an impossible negative reading or a collapsed output, not for a weak current. Z is no mere placeholder: Mazda's bulletin 01-004-25 for its integrated starter generator lists the stator driver circuits in a U-V-W group and a separate X-Y-Z group. No manufacturer documents P2D97 publicly. In GM's eAssist analogue the low codes trip below -440 A after roughly 42 ms, Type B. Suspect a grounded signal lead or a lost sensor supply. High side: P2D94; X and Y low: P2D95, P2D96.
c: Phase Z sensor signal lead shorted to ground or to the machine housing
Sensor supply interrupted by an open wire or a pushed-back terminal
Phase Z current sensor output stuck at the bottom of its range
s: Warning lamp or MIL, typically after the fault has repeated on a second trip
Electric boost and recuperation reduced or switched off
No automatic engine stop, or restarts via the conventional starter

P2D98.t: Starter/Generator Phase X Current Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2D98.d: P2D98 points to a phase X current signal of the starter/generator that briefly drops out, jumps or flickers, even though most individual samples may still sit inside the accepted range. That pattern usually comes from a contact that opens under vibration or heat, a chafed lead or an ageing sensor; in many designs the signal is produced by a Hall element sitting in a ferrite ring around the phase conductor. X, Y and Z name a second phase group in some machines, as a 2025 Mazda bulletin on its integrated starter generator (01-004-25) shows. No manufacturer documents P2D98 publicly, and no threshold for the erratic check has been published. Unlike the steady faults P2D92, P2D95 and P2DC1, this one tends to come and go, so freeze-frame data and a wiggle test at the machine matter most.
c: Connector contact at the starter/generator opening under engine vibration
Phase X sensor lead chafed against the belt drive or a bracket
Ageing current sensor with unstable output at high temperature
s: Warning that appears and disappears between trips
Stop-start occasionally unavailable
Electric assist briefly cut during acceleration

P2D99.t: Starter/Generator Phase Y Current Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2D99.d: P2D99 is stored when the phase Y current value of the starter/generator behaves in a way a real winding current cannot: sudden steps, dropouts to zero or noise between consecutive samples. The winding inductance smooths the true current, so such jumps implicate the measuring path. Only systems that actually sense phase Y can raise this code; GM's eAssist table, for example, lists current sensor checks for phases U and W alone. Mazda's ISG bulletin 01-004-25 confirms that a starter/generator may carry an X-Y-Z phase group. No manufacturer documents P2D99 publicly. Check the connector for corrosion and pin drag first, then the harness route near hot or moving parts. Steady counterparts: P2D93 (high), P2D96 (low), P2DC3 (circuit); X and Z intermittent: P2D98, P2D9A.
c: Corrosion or weak pin tension in the phase Y sensor connector
Harness damaged by heat from the exhaust side or by contact with moving parts
Phase Y current sensor producing a noisy or unstable signal
s: Sporadic hybrid or charging system warning
Recuperation occasionally interrupted

P2D9A.t: Starter/Generator Phase Z Current Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2D9A.d: P2D9A marks an unsteady current signal on phase Z of the starter/generator. Before replacing hardware it is worth asking whether the detection itself is too sharp. Mazda met exactly that on 2022 and 2023 CX-30 and Mazda3 models built in Mexico: its integrated starter generator flagged faults in the U-V-W and X-Y-Z stator driver groups because its overcurrent detection logic misjudged the current, and bulletin 01-004-25 cured it with ISG software carrying a revised threshold. Mazda used its own codes there, not P2D9A, and no manufacturer documents P2D9A publicly. Such a second X-Y-Z driver group is where a Z phase comes from; CARB wants hybrid input parts like these sensors checked for erratic signals. Other causes: loose terminals or water in the plug. Steady faults: P2D94, P2D97, P2DC5.
c: Starter/generator software with overly sensitive detection, update available
Loose or spread terminal in the phase Z sensor plug
Water in the connector after washing or driving through deep water
s: Battery and engine warning lamps that come on now and then
Mild-hybrid functions occasionally unavailable

P2D9B.t: Starter/Generator Phase U Current Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2D9B.d: P2D9B concerns phase U, the first phase of the starter/generator's main U-V-W group, when its current signal is unsteady rather than permanently out of range. GM's eAssist system, whose belt-driven machine appears in its tables as drive motor A, shows how a manufacturer separates hard limits from short events: the U sensor fails high or low beyond 440 A in either direction within 41.6 ms, while a fast, repeated overcurrent is handled by switching the inverter off for one 2.08 ms loop, counting the event and re-enabling, with the code following the third count. No manufacturer documents P2D9B itself publicly. Typical causes are a marginal plug contact, a damaged lead or a failing sensor. V and W intermittent: P2D9C, P2D9D; X to Z: P2D98 to P2D9A.
c: Marginal contact in the phase U sensor connector
Phase U sensor lead with damaged insulation or a partly broken strand
Phase U current sensor beginning to fail
s: Intermittent warning lamp, sometimes only after several trips
Sudden loss of electric assist, returning after a restart

P2D9C.t: Starter/Generator Phase V Current Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2D9C.d: P2D9C reports an erratic current signal on phase V of the starter/generator. V is the phase that some designs never measure: in a star-connected three-phase winding the three currents add up to zero, so GM's eAssist table runs sensor checks only on U and W. Other inverters fit a sensor to every phase conductor, often a Hall chip in a ring core whose output voltage follows the current. A system that stores P2D9C therefore evaluates phase V on its own, and an unsteady value there leads to the V sensor, its plug or its leads rather than to the other two phases. No manufacturer documents P2D9C publicly. Drivers notice a sporadic warning and short gaps in stop-start or boost. Neighbours: P2D9B (U) and P2D9D (W).
c: Phase V sensor plug not fully latched or with fretting corrosion
Intermittent break in the phase V sensor wiring
Phase V current sensor with unstable output
s: Sporadic system warning on the instrument cluster
Short interruptions of stop-start or boost

P2D9D.t: Starter/Generator Phase W Current Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2D9D.d: P2D9D covers phase W of the starter/generator when its current signal flickers or drops out for moments. The W sensor is one of the two that GM's eAssist belt machine monitors. GM's checks there look at solid failures: below -440 A or above 440 A for 41.6 ms, Type B, and a learned zero offset beyond 30 A while the inverter is off. A brief glitch that never crosses such limits is what an intermittent code is meant to catch. No manufacturer documents P2D9D publicly. Hall sensors around the phase conductors deliver a voltage that follows the current, so a drifting reference, moisture or a cracked solder joint in the electronics can make the reading jump. Steady W faults belong to other codes; U and V intermittent: P2D9B, P2D9C.
c: Cracked solder joint in the sensor path after many heat cycles
Poor contact in the phase W sensor connector
s: Warning lamp that shows up mostly when the engine is hot or the weather is wet
Charging through the starter/generator briefly interrupted

P2D9E.d: P2D9E reports that the voltage of the high-voltage system – the DC network joining traction battery, inverters, DC/DC converter and other HV consumers – has dropped below its lower limit while the system is switched on. P0AFA judges the battery pack itself; P2D9E looks at the network side. No manufacturer documents P2D9E publicly or names its threshold. GM's 2013 eAssist mild-hybrid table shows both viewpoints: the battery module sets P0AFA once pack voltage stays under its limit for 320 of 1595 samples (Type A), while the motor control processor separately watches its own HV sensor. A deeply discharged pack, a contactor that drops out, a failing precharge or a loose HV connector are typical causes. Expect reduced power, no ready mode or a refused start.
c: Traction battery deeply discharged or cell groups weak
Main contactor dropping out or precharge circuit faulty
Loose or corroded HV connector or busbar under load
Voltage sensing in the inverter or controller reads too low
s: Hybrid or EV system warning and check engine light
Noticeably reduced drive power or limp mode
Vehicle does not reach ready mode or engine does not start

P2D9F.d: P2D9F is the over-voltage case: the DC voltage on the high-voltage network rises above the permitted maximum. Too much voltage stresses capacitors, power semiconductors and cells, so controllers react within milliseconds by cutting regeneration or charging. No manufacturer documents P2D9F publicly. GM's eAssist table of 2013 gives a comparable check under its own code P1AEE: the motor control processor flags system voltage high when its HV sensor reads more than 150 V or a hardware over-voltage flag is set, two trips, Type B. Typical triggers are strong regenerative braking with a full battery, a contactor opening while the motor still generates, or a drifting voltage measurement. Expect reduced regeneration, limited power and a warning light.
c: Regenerative braking or charging while the battery is already full or cold
Contactor or HV connection opening while the motor generates
Voltage measurement in the inverter or controller reads too high
Voltage limits in control software too tight, update available
s: Hybrid or EV system warning and check engine light
Little or no regenerative braking, more wear on the friction brakes
Power limited or HV system shut down

P2DA0.d: P2DA0 is the plausibility code of this group: the high-voltage system is neither clearly too low nor too high, but its readings or behaviour do not fit together. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 asks for such rationality checks on inputs, stored separately from circuit and range faults. No manufacturer documents P2DA0 publicly. A typical cross-check appears in GM's 2013 eAssist table under P1AEC: with contactors closed, the motor control processor compares its own bus voltage with the pack voltage and the sum of the mid-pack readings and flags a difference of 15 V or 10 V, two trips, Type B. Differing sensors, a high-resistance HV joint, contactor contacts that have burnt or a slow precharge lead there. Power is usually limited.
c: Voltage sensors in battery and inverter disagree
High resistance in an HV connector, busbar or fuse
Main contactor contacts burnt or welded
Calibration or software of a controller, update available
s: Hybrid or EV system warning, check engine light
Reduced drive power or no electric drive
Fault appears under heavy load or after a long stop

P2DA1.t: Gear Shift Control Module B Supply Voltage Low
P2DA1.d: With shift-by-wire, the selector the driver touches is an electronic module; module B is a second one, such as a further selector station or a redundant unit. Allison's 6th-generation controls show such a pair: for module 2 they list performance, lost communication, incompatibility and invalid data (P085E, U0291, U0333, U0592), but no supply codes. P2DA1 means the 12 V feed of module B, as measured by the module or the transmission controller, is below its lower limit. No manufacturer documents P2DA1 publicly. Audi's selector lever J587 on 2019–21 A6/A7 shows how much depends on this voltage check: its evaluation logged faults and blocked range selection until new software was loaded. Battery, fuse, feed wire and ground come first.
c: Weak 12 V battery or voltage dip during cranking
Corroded ground, loose connector or high-resistance feed to module B
Fuse for module B blown or with poor contact
Voltage evaluation in module software too strict
s: Shifter warning in the instrument cluster
Range selection at the second selector ignored, vehicle stays in P
Fault appears together with other low-voltage codes

P2DA2.t: Gear Shift Control Module B Supply Voltage High
P2DA2.d: P2DA2 is the over-voltage counterpart of P2DA1: gear shift control module B, the second selector unit of a shift-by-wire system, sees a supply above its permitted maximum. No manufacturer documents P2DA2 publicly or names the limit. Excess voltage usually comes from the charging side – a failed alternator regulator or DC/DC converter, a 24 V jump start, a battery charger left connected during diagnosis – and only rarely from a short between the module feed and a higher-voltage circuit. To protect itself the module may stop accepting inputs. Allison's 6th-generation controls show that a second selector is handled as a unit of its own with separate codes, so a fault there need not disable the first one. Measure charging voltage before replacing anything.
c: Alternator regulator or DC/DC converter delivering too much voltage
Jump start with 24 V or charger connected during operation
Module feed shorted to a circuit with higher voltage
Voltage measurement inside module B faulty
s: Shifter warning in the instrument cluster
Second selector does not respond, main selector may still work
Further overvoltage codes in other modules, flickering lights

P2DA3.t: Gear Shift Control Module B Overtemperature
P2DA3.d: P2DA3 is a condition code: gear shift control module B reports that its internal temperature exceeds the safe limit. The circuit is fine, the module simply runs too hot. No manufacturer documents P2DA3 or a threshold publicly; Allison's 6th-generation controls, which give module 2 its own performance and communication codes, do not list it. Heat can enter from outside – a selector in a sun-heated console, a mounting close to heater ducts or other warm components – or arise inside, when output stages for display, lock solenoid or illumination draw too much current. A hot unit may reduce its functions until it cools. A code that also appears at normal temperatures points to an internal defect.
c: Strong sun load or nearby heat source at the mounting location
Output stage for lock solenoid, display or lighting drawing excess current
Internal defect or faulty temperature sensing in module B
s: Shifter warning, mainly in hot weather or after long operation
Second selector temporarily ignores range requests
Fault disappears after the module has cooled down

P2DA4.t: Coolant Heater A Internal Control Module Performance
P2DA4.d: Coolant heater A here is an electric heater with built-in electronics, usually a high-voltage PTC or wire-element unit that warms coolant for cabin and battery in hybrids and EVs; it is separate from the engine block heater codes P01E8 ff. P2DA4 says that heater's own controller has found a fault in itself – a power switch that shorted, a temperature or current measurement that fails, or a processor error. Texas Instruments describes the usual layout: one controller on the 12 V side for LIN or CAN, one on the HV side that drives the elements and cross-checks current, voltage and temperature. No manufacturer documents P2DA4 publicly; Ford stores the sister code P2DA6 in the module SOBDMC on the F-150 Lightning. The heater is switched off, so expect little heat in electric mode.
c: Power switch inside the heater shorted or failed
Internal temperature or current measurement faulty
Coolant or moisture inside the electronics housing
Software fault in heater or commanding module, update available
s: Little or no cabin heat in electric mode
Engine of a hybrid runs more often just to supply heat
Climate system message, usually without check engine light

P2DA5.t: Coolant Heater A Supply Voltage Circuit
P2DA5.d: P2DA5 concerns the feed that powers coolant heater A, the electric coolant heater with its own electronics found in hybrids and EVs. The heater's controller finds its supply input missing or outside the expected window and reports it as a circuit fault, unlike P2DA7, which rates the voltage level of the module. Which feed is meant is up to the maker. Texas Instruments shows that such heater modules run their logic from the 12 V rail and can watch that rail for leaving its operating range, while the heating elements draw from the HV battery. No manufacturer documents P2DA5 publicly. Typical findings are a blown fuse, a corroded pin in the low-voltage connector, a poor ground or an open HV fuse in the distribution box. The heater stays off until the feed is restored.
c: 12 V or HV fuse for the heater open
Corroded or loose pin in the heater supply connector
Poor ground connection of the heater electronics
Supply input inside the heater electronics faulty
s: No heat from the electric coolant heater
Cabin heat only when the engine of a hybrid runs
Possibly lost communication with the heater stored at the same time

P2DA6.d: P2DA6 says coolant heater A, the electric coolant heater of a hybrid or EV, has become too hot. Such heaters measure outlet coolant or housing temperature and switch off above a limit; a Hyundai/Kia patent (US11378000B2) does exactly that, mainly to protect the elements when coolant is missing. Ford is the one maker documented: on 2023 F-150 Lightning trucks built from 31 July 2023 the module SOBDMC can store P2DA6 because of its software. In SSM 52211 the pinpoint test points to software when the ECT2 reading exceeds 70 °C; TSB 23-2375 cures it by reprogramming the SOBDMC and running maximum heat for five minutes. Without symptoms Ford needs no further work; with too little cabin heat, low coolant, air or a pump that does not run are the usual causes.
c: Software of the controlling module (Ford Lightning SOBDMC), reprogramming
Low coolant level or air trapped in the heater loop
Heater loop coolant pump not running or valve blocking flow
Temperature sensor in heater or loop reading too high
s: Often no noticeable symptom, code found during service
Heater switches off, cabin warms only weakly
Climate system message, no check engine light

P2DA7.t: Coolant Heater A Control Module System Voltage
P2DA7.d: P2DA7 is logged when the electronics built into coolant heater A – the HV heater of a hybrid or EV – see a system voltage outside the window in which it may work. While P2DA5 points to the feed circuit, this code judges the level. High-voltage heaters have a defined range; DBK's 400 V unit, for example, runs from 195 to 450 V DC, and Texas Instruments notes that heater controllers must cope with a varying DC bus and may monitor their supply rails. No manufacturer documents P2DA7 publicly or states whether it rates the HV or the 12 V side. Typical reasons are a strongly discharged or very full traction battery, a weak 12 V battery or a measuring fault in the heater. The heater stays off while the voltage is out of range and usually resumes afterwards.
c: Traction battery voltage at the edge of the heater's range (very low or very high charge)
Weak 12 V battery or poor ground of the heater electronics
Voltage measurement inside the heater faulty
s: Electric heater temporarily without function
Fault occurs with very low or very high battery charge
Cabin heat only from the engine of a hybrid

P2DA8.t: DC/AC Converter Control Module A Switch A Circuit
P2DA8.d: DC/AC converter control module A is the inverter that turns direct current from the vehicle battery into household AC for sockets in the vehicle; Ford calls it DCACA and uses it for Pro Power Onboard on the F-150, where TSB 21-2127 handles a related fault, P0364 in the PCM. P2DA8 reports an electrical fault – open, short or no valid signal – in the circuit of switch A of this module. J2012 does not say what switch A is. In Ford's patent US11043801B2 the DCACA controller switches each socket group on and off through relays and can also read a manual button in the bed or cab; comparing voltages ahead of and behind the switch tells it whether the switch works. No manufacturer documents P2DA8 publicly. The affected outlets stay dead; driving is not affected.
c: Open or shorted wire or corroded connector between switch A and the module
Switch A or its relay failed
Water ingress at an outlet panel in the bed or cargo area
Internal fault of the DC/AC converter module
s: AC outlets of group A without power
Message that onboard power is unavailable
Outlet button without reaction

P2DA9.t: DC/AC Converter Control Module A Switch A Circuit Range/Performance
P2DA9.d: P2DA9 belongs to switch A of the DC/AC converter control module A, the inverter that supplies AC sockets in the vehicle. Unlike P2DA8 the circuit is intact, but the switch does not behave as expected: its signal sits between valid states, or the commanded state does not show up at the output. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 describes this type of check as a rationality or functional test kept apart from circuit faults. Ford's patent US11043801B2 gives a practical example: the controller compares voltage ahead of and behind each socket switch and reports a switch error when voltage arrives upstream but not downstream. No manufacturer documents P2DA9 publicly. Worn or sticking contacts, a relay that does not pull in, contact resistance or a jammed button are typical; outlets then work only intermittently.
c: Worn, sticking or burnt contacts of switch A or its relay
High contact resistance in connector or outlet wiring
Outlet button jammed by dirt or damage
Voltage sensing in the converter module implausible
s: Outlets of group A work only intermittently
Outlet power switches off unexpectedly under load
Switch position in the display does not match the outlet state

P2DAA.t: DC/AC Converter Control Module A Switch B Circuit
P2DAA.d: P2DAA flags an electrical fault in the line of switch B belonging to DC/AC converter control module A, the vehicle's inverter for 120/230 V sockets. The module finds the switch B line open, shorted to ground or to supply, or without a usable signal. Having a second switch makes sense where outlets are split into groups – in Ford's patent US11043801B2 every socket, or a set of sockets, gets its own ON/OFF switch, driven by the DCACA through relays, and the controller sheds low-priority sockets when total load gets too high. No manufacturer documents P2DAA publicly, and which outlet group B serves is set by the maker. Only the sockets behind switch B should be dead; if group A fails at the same time, a common feed, ground or the module itself is the more likely culprit than two separate switches.
c: Open or shorted wire or corroded connector in the switch B circuit
Switch B or its relay failed
Shared feed, ground or converter module faulty (when group A also fails)
s: AC outlets of group B without power, other outlets work
Message that onboard power is limited or unavailable

P2DAB.t: DC/AC Converter Control Module A Switch B Circuit Range/Performance
P2DAB.d: With P2DAB, switch B of converter module A – the unit feeding the vehicle's AC sockets – fails a plausibility test. Wiring tests pass, yet switch B does not deliver what was asked of it: it stays closed after an off command, opens under load, or reports a position that disagrees with the measured output. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 calls for such functional checks on output components. In Ford's patent US11043801B2 the controller opens socket switches on its own – after a timer, above a user current limit or when total power is too high – so a state the module did not expect can also come from this logic. No manufacturer documents P2DAB publicly. A switch that welds shut is the more serious case, because the socket can no longer be switched off; contact wear and moisture are the usual reasons.
c: Contacts of switch B or its relay welded, sticking or worn
Moisture or dirt at the outlet panel of group B
Load management or software in the converter module, update available
s: Outlets of group B switch off unexpectedly or cannot be switched off
Warning about onboard power in the display
Fault appears mainly with high loads connected

P2DAC.t: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P2DAC.d: P2DAC is the general circuit fault of a second temperature sensor (B) in drive motor A; sensor A has its own series from P0A2A. A motor carries a second probe either as a backup element beside the first – Sensata's hairpin sensor patent allows two NTCs, or an NTC plus a PTC, in one housing – or as a probe on another phase winding. No manufacturer documents P2DAC publicly. Mitsubishi shows the multi-probe layout on the 2023 Outlander PHEV, with coil sensors on the U, V and W phases, but files sensors 2 and 3 under its own codes from P3052 and only accepts voltages between 0.1 and 4.93 V. Which side the voltage left is recorded by P2DAE (low) and P2DAF (high), not by P2DAC. Losing the reading usually means derated electric drive.
c: Broken or shorted sensor B lead between motor and inverter
Loose, corroded or pushed-out terminal at the motor connector
Sensor B thermistor failed inside the stator
Faulty sensor input in the inverter or motor control unit
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Electric drive power limited
Sensor B shows a fixed or missing value in live data while sensor A looks normal

P2DAD.t: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P2DAD.d: P2DAD covers a sensor B signal that stays inside the electrical window yet does not fit the situation. CARB asks for rationality checks on hybrid input components where feasible, logged under a code of their own apart from circuit and range faults. The obvious reference is a neighbouring probe: on the 2023 Outlander PHEV Mitsubishi compares its V-phase coil sensor (sensor 2, own code P3054) with the U-phase value after more than 90 minutes off and with the inverter switched off, and rejects it when the gap exceeds 26 °C for longer than 0.8 s. A UAES patent adds a running check: when winding current should heat the stator but the reading does not rise, the sensor is flagged as reading low. No manufacturer publishes P2DAD. Thermistor drift and extra contact resistance are the usual causes.
c: Sensor B thermistor drifted from its resistance curve
Added resistance at a worn or corroded terminal
Probe no longer seated firmly against the winding
Fault in the reference value, e.g. sensor A or coolant temperature
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Sensor B differs clearly from sensor A after the car has stood overnight
Electric drive power limited in some situations

P2DAE.t: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P2DAE.d: P2DAE means the sensor B voltage has fallen below the lowest value a healthy sensor can deliver. Winding probes are mostly NTC thermistors whose resistance collapses as they heat – Thinking Electronic quotes roughly 0.46 kOhm at 180 °C for its stator probes – so with the usual pull-up circuit a near-zero voltage would read as an impossibly hot winding. In practice it points to a short: signal lead to ground or to the motor housing, a shorted thermistor, or a lead pinched during assembly. On the 2023 Outlander PHEV, Mitsubishi's own code P3053 catches its V-phase probe when the signal stays at or under 0.1 V for half a second, provided the power drive unit has at least 8 V. No manufacturer documents P2DAE publicly. P2DAF is the opposite fault; real overheating would be P0A2F.
c: Sensor B signal lead shorted to ground or motor housing
Thermistor shorted internally (often replaceable only with the motor)
Lead pinched or chafed after work on the drive unit
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Sensor B shows an extremely high fixed temperature in live data
Electric drive power reduced

P2DAF.t: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
P2DAF.d: P2DAF is the high-side counterpart: the sensor B voltage rises close to the reference. For an NTC probe that would be an impossibly cold winding, so the controller treats it as an interrupted circuit – broken lead, unplugged or corroded connector, cracked thermistor – or, less often, a short to a supply voltage. A UAES patent on stator sensor diagnosis describes the principle: upper and lower voltage limits sit just inside the supply rails, and a reading outside them counts as a circuit fault before any plausibility logic runs. Mitsubishi's equivalent for the V-phase probe of its Outlander PHEV (2023) is P3052, set once the signal reaches 4.93 V and stays there half a second. No manufacturer publishes P2DAF. The low side is P2DAE. Without sensor B the inverter may hold back torque to protect the winding.
c: Open signal or ground lead of sensor B
Connector unplugged or terminal backed out, often after drive unit work
Thermistor open or cracked inside the stator
Signal lead shorted to a supply voltage
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Sensor B shows an implausibly low temperature in live data
Electric drive power limited

P2DB0.t: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent
P2DB0.d: P2DB0 logs short dropouts or jumps in the sensor B signal that come and go too fast for the steady low and high checks. Because CARB requires circuit monitoring of input components to run continuously, such glitches are caught while driving. No manufacturer documents P2DB0, but Bentley's 2025 bulletin for the 2020–23 Bentayga and Flying Spur hybrids describes the same pattern on sensor A under P0A2E00: at high temperature the crimped joint of the motor temperature sensor shifts its resistance abruptly and the reading spikes. Only the sensor is renewed, yet engine and gearbox must come out to reach it. Heat cycling, vibration and loose terminals along the run from stator to inverter are the usual suspects. Expect a fault that is often heat-related and hard to reproduce on a cold car.
c: Resistance jumps in the sensor crimp at high temperature
Worn or loose terminals in a connector of the sensor B line
Chafed lead with intermittent contact under vibration
s: Warning light that comes and goes, often after hard driving
Sensor B value spikes briefly in live data
Electric drive power briefly limited on some models

P2DB1.t: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor C Circuit
P2DB1.d: P2DB1 reports a circuit fault on a third temperature sensor (C) in drive motor A. Three probes in one motor make most sense when each phase winding of the three-phase machine gets its own: Mitsubishi equips the front motor of the 2023 Outlander PHEV with U-, V- and W-phase coil sensors, and a fault on any of them lights both the hybrid warning and the MIL. The W-phase probe, its sensor 3, uses the maker's own codes P3055 to P3057 rather than P2DB1, and no manufacturer documents P2DB1 publicly. The direction of the fault is left to P2DB3 (signal low) and P2DB4 (signal high). With two other probes still working the car usually drives on, but the control unit may cap power.
c: Broken or shorted sensor C lead between motor and inverter
Loose or corroded terminal at the motor connector
Sensor C thermistor failed in its phase winding
Faulty sensor input in the inverter or motor control unit
s: Hybrid system warning and check engine light
Sensor C missing or frozen in live data while the other motor sensors read normally
Electric drive power capped

P2DB2.t: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P2DB2.d: P2DB2 flags a sensor C reading that is electrically valid but disagrees with what the motor should show. With three probes a cold-soak comparison is the natural test: Mitsubishi checks its W-phase sensor (sensor 3, own code P3057) on the 2023 Outlander PHEV once per driving cycle after more than 90 minutes off, inverter switched off, and rejects it when it lies over 26 °C away from the U-phase reading for 0.8 s or longer; the V-phase check runs continuously instead. CARB asks for two-sided rationality checks where feasible. A UAES patent also compares a stator probe with coolant and power-switch temperatures after a long stop. No manufacturer documents P2DB2. Thermistor drift, a poor contact or a probe that has lost touch with its winding are typical causes.
c: Sensor C thermistor drifted from its resistance curve
Extra resistance at a corroded or worn terminal
Probe loose on its phase winding
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Sensor C stands well apart from the other motor sensors after a cold start
No noticeable driving change in many cases

P2DB3.t: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor C Circuit Low
P2DB3.d: P2DB3 sets when the sensor C voltage drops below its valid floor. For an NTC probe this would stand for a temperature far beyond any real winding heat, so a short is much more likely than a genuine hot spot: signal lead to ground or motor housing, insulation damaged inside the stator, or a thermistor shorted internally. Mitsubishi, which reads its W-phase coil probe as sensor 3 on the 2023 Outlander PHEV, uses its own code P3056 and the same floor as on the other phases: no more than 0.1 V over half a second. Thinking Electronic rates its stator probes for −40 to 200 °C and tests them at up to 2000 V AC, a reminder that the probe sits in the high-voltage winding. No manufacturer documents P2DB3. P2DB4 is the high side, P2DAE the same fault on sensor B.
c: Sensor C signal lead shorted to ground or motor housing
Probe insulation damaged inside the stator
s: Hybrid system warning and check engine light
Sensor C reads extremely hot while the other sensors look normal
Electric drive power reduced

P2DB4.t: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor C Circuit High
P2DB4.d: P2DB4 is the open-circuit side of sensor C: the voltage climbs toward the reference because hardly any current still flows through the thermistor. A broken wire, a terminal backed out of the motor connector, corrosion or a cracked thermistor are the likely finds; a short to a supply voltage is rarer. With an NTC the value shown would be an impossibly cold winding. For the W-phase probe of the same Mitsubishi (sensor 3, own code P3055) the limit is likewise 4.93 V held half a second with at least 8 V at the power drive unit, and the repair path ends with a new power drive unit or front motor. The UAES patent places the upper limit just below supply voltage. No manufacturer documents P2DB4 itself. P2DB3 is the low side, P2DAF the same fault on sensor B.
c: Open signal or ground lead of sensor C
Terminal backed out or corroded in the motor connector
Signal lead shorted to a supply voltage
s: Hybrid system warning and check engine light
Sensor C reads far below ambient temperature in live data
Electric drive power limited

P2DB5.t: Drive Motor A Temperature Sensor C Circuit Intermittent
P2DB5.d: P2DB5 is set when the sensor C signal drops out or jumps briefly and then recovers – a flickering contact rather than a lasting open or short. No manufacturer documents P2DB5. The closest published case concerns sensor A: Bentley's P0A2E00 bulletin for 2020–23 Bentayga and Flying Spur hybrids traces temperature jumps to a sensor crimp whose resistance changes suddenly when hot, cured by a new sensor rather than a new motor. CARB expects circuit checks on input components to run without pause, which is why even short glitches end up in memory. The warning may disappear for days; testing the harness while the drive unit is warm helps to catch it.
c: Crimp of sensor C changing resistance when hot
Loose or fretted terminals in the sensor C connector
Lead rubbing through and touching intermittently
s: Warning light that disappears and returns
Brief spikes or gaps in the sensor C value in live data
Fault mainly after long or hard drives

P2DB6.t: Battery Charger B Cooling System Performance
P2DB6.d: P2DB6 is set when the cooling of a second on-board charger, charger B, cannot hold the unit inside its permitted temperature window, so the charger has to cut its power or stop. No manufacturer documents P2DB6 publicly. Mercedes shows the A-side case P0D8F on the AMG GLE 53 Hybrid (LI47.70-P-079963): AC charging ended after about 15 minutes because the low-temperature coolant lines of charger and power electronics had been connected the wrong way round, and the charger's two coolant temperature sensors also disagreed. CARB requires plug-in hybrids to flag charger faults that stop charging or slow it down. A charger B temperature beyond its limit is reported separately as P0E85. For the driver, plug-in charging becomes slow or aborts.
c: Low coolant level or trapped air in the charger cooling circuit
Electric coolant pump of the low-temperature circuit weak or failed
Coolant hoses connected to the wrong circuit after assembly or repair
Low-temperature radiator clogged or its airflow obstructed
s: Charging power reduced at the charge station
Plug-in charging stops after some minutes
Charging fault message in the instrument cluster

P2DB7.t: Battery Charging System B High Voltage Interlock Circuit/Open
P2DB7.d: P2DB7 reports that the high voltage interlock loop of charging system B is broken. Such a loop is a low-current wire run in series through the HV plugs and covers of a charging path; once it opens, the control unit treats the path as unsafe and keeps it switched off. B denotes a second charging path, for example a further on-board charger. No manufacturer documents P2DB7 publicly. The A-side code P0D15 shows a typical cause: on 2021–2023 XC40 Recharge cars Volvo found that the plant had not closed the latches on the AC high-voltage plug linking inlet and charger (TJ 36522, P0D1513), and AC charging was lost; seating and latching the plug fixed it. CARB wants plug-in hybrids to detect faults that disable charging. Signal-level faults of this loop are P2DB8 to P2DBB.
c: HV connector in the charging path not fully seated or its catch not closed
Broken interlock wire or pushed-out terminal
Service cover or HV cover of the charger not closed properly
Fault in the interlock evaluation of the control module
s: No charging through charging path B
Charging system warning in the instrument cluster

P2DB8.t: Battery Charging System B High Voltage Interlock Circuit Performance
P2DB8.d: P2DB8 means the interlock loop of charging system B carries a signal, but one that does not behave as the control unit expects. A common test switches the module's test source on and off and checks that the sensed level follows; a reading that stays put or hovers between the valid bands points to contact resistance, a half-seated plug or corrosion rather than a clean break. No manufacturer documents P2DB8 publicly. GM's Volt summary tables (2011, 2014) judge the A-side charging loop in exactly these two states, sourced and unsourced, against separate limits (P0D17, P0D18). The hard open is P2DB7, fixed low or high levels P2DB9 and P2DBA. While the fault is present, path B is normally not used for charging.
c: Raised contact resistance in an interlock terminal
Plug in the charging path inserted only partway
Corrosion or moisture in an interlock connector
Test source or measuring stage of the module not working correctly
s: Charging via path B refused or interrupted
Charging system warning message

P2DB9.t: Battery Charging System B High Voltage Interlock Circuit Low
P2DB9.d: P2DB9 is stored when the sensed voltage of the charging system B interlock loop stays too low. Since the module feeds a test voltage into the loop, a low reading usually means current is escaping to ground: a chafed wire touching the body, moisture in a connector, or a failing measuring stage inside the module. No manufacturer documents P2DB9 publicly. For the A-side loop of the Chevrolet Volt, GM's 2011 and 2014 tables call the reading faulty when it drops under 30 % of the sourced 5 V in two of two 12.5 ms samples, rated Type A (P0D17); that logic is a fair model for loop B. The high counterpart is P2DBA, a clean open P2DB7. Path B will not be used for charging until the fault is cleared.
c: Interlock wire chafed through and touching ground
Water or dirt in an interlock connector causing leakage to ground
Defective interlock source or measuring stage in the control module
s: Charging through path B not possible
Charging system warning message

P2DBA.t: Battery Charging System B High Voltage Interlock Circuit High
P2DBA.d: P2DBA flags an interlock signal of charging system B that reads too high. A loop fed from a test source and measured at its far end shows a raised level when it is shorted to a supply voltage, or, depending on the circuit, when added resistance or a break lets the measuring input float upward. No manufacturer documents P2DBA publicly. GM checks the A-side loop of the Volt in two states (P0D18): with the 5 V source off, a reading above 24 % of reference counts as a fault, with it on, one above 44 %; both are Type A in the 2011 and 2014 tables. Telling a short to voltage from an open therefore needs both states. The low counterpart is P2DB9. Charging through path B stays blocked.
c: Interlock wire shorted to a supply voltage
Added resistance or partial break in the interlock loop
Faulty measuring input in the control module
s: No charging via path B
Charging system warning message

P2DBB.t: Battery Charging System B High Voltage Interlock Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2DBB.d: P2DBB covers an interlock loop of charging system B that keeps dropping out and recovering, so its state flips between valid and invalid. The trigger is usually mechanical: a terminal with low contact pressure, a plug that is not fully latched, or a wire that only loses contact when the body flexes or the parts heat up. No manufacturer documents P2DBB publicly. A useful parallel is Mercedes bulletin LI54.10-P-067823 for the smart electric drive with the 22 kW charger option: loose low-voltage contacts at the charger produced sporadic interlock faults, filed there under the general codes P0A0A and P0A0E, and the car would not charge. CARB expects plug-in hybrids to catch faults that block charging. Steady faults are P2DB7 to P2DBA. Charging may stop for no visible reason.
c: Loose or widened terminal in an interlock connector
Connector in the charging path not fully latched
Chafed interlock wire that loses contact only with movement or heat
s: Charging via path B stops without warning
Fault comes and goes, often depending on temperature

P2DBC.t: Battery Charger B Coupler Lock Position Sensor Circuit
P2DBC.d: P2DBC is the general circuit fault of the lock position sensor at charger B's coupler, the feedback telling the vehicle whether the pin that holds the charging plug in the inlet has moved out or back in. B marks a second inlet or charging path. No manufacturer documents P2DBC publicly. GM's patent US8936482B2 shows how such feedback can work: an angle sensor on the actuator motor shaft yields the pin travel, and fast charging is withheld if the lock cannot be confirmed. On the A side Ford stores P0D9E:00 in the SOBDM of 2021–2023 Mach-E, F-150 Lightning and e-Transit after the DC plug was pulled without pressing the release button, which damages the pin (TSB 23-2014); only the lock actuator is replaced. Specific fault types follow in P2DBD to P2DC0.
c: Open or shorted wire between lock actuator and control module
Lock pin broken after the plug was pulled while still latched
Corroded or loose connector at the lock actuator
Faulty sensor input in the control module
s: DC fast charging not possible at inlet B
Charger service warning in the instrument cluster

P2DBD.t: Battery Charger B Coupler Lock Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2DBD.d: P2DBD is the plausibility fault of the coupler lock feedback on charger B: the signal is electrically valid yet does not fit what the lock is doing, for example a travel that is too short after a lock command, or longer than the pin could ever move with a plug inserted. No manufacturer documents P2DBD publicly. GM's patent US8936482B2 uses that second case to spot a broken or missing pin, since the computed travel then passes the locked end stop. Mercedes lists the A-side code P0D9F00, a malfunctioning position sensor of the charging cable lock, for the 22 kW charger of the smart electric drive (LI54.10-P-067823); loose low-voltage contacts at the charger were behind it. While the lock state is doubtful, charging is usually refused. Hard low or high faults are P2DBE and P2DBF.
c: Lock pin broken off or missing, so the measured travel is implausible
Lock mechanism sticking or jammed by dirt or ice
Loose low-voltage contacts at the charger or actuator
s: Charging at inlet B refused
Plug cannot be locked or released normally

P2DBE.t: Battery Charger B Coupler Lock Position Sensor Circuit Low
P2DBE.d: P2DBE means the coupler lock sensor of charger B delivers a voltage below its valid band. No manufacturer documents P2DBE publicly. The A-side code P0DA0 is documented by Mitsubishi for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: with the ignition-controlled supply on, the PHEV-ECU sets it on a low input from the inlet's lock sensor. The repair flow first checks the signal line for a ground short between ECU and lock actuator connector, then checks the sensor itself, which should measure about 16.8 kΩ between its two pins. Damaged harness, the inlet cable assembly with its actuator, or the ECU are the named suspects. Ford also lists P0DA0 among the codes after a broken lock pin (TSB 23-2014). Too high is P2DBF. Charging via inlet B may be refused.
c: Sensor signal line shorted to ground
Lock position sensor with internal short or wrong resistance
Damaged lock actuator after the plug was pulled while latched
Faulty sensor input in the control module
s: Charging at inlet B refused
Charging system warning lamp or message

P2DBF.t: Battery Charger B Coupler Lock Position Sensor Circuit High
P2DBF.d: P2DBF is set when the lock position signal of charger B's coupler stays above its permitted range. No manufacturer documents P2DBF publicly. Mitsubishi's procedure for the A-side code P0DA1 on the 2023 Outlander PHEV points to the usual culprits of a high reading: the sensor's ground pin at the lock actuator connector must show continuity to body ground (2 Ω or less), its supply pin must carry battery voltage, and the signal line to the PHEV-ECU is checked for an open; only then are the inlet assembly and the ECU suspected. GM's patent US8936482B2 explains why this matters: without a confirmed lock, fast charging is not allowed. The low counterpart is P2DBE. With an unbelievable lock state, inlet B is not released for charging.
c: Open ground connection of the lock position sensor
Open signal line between sensor and control module
Signal line shorted to a supply voltage
Faulty inlet assembly with integrated lock actuator
s: Fast charging at inlet B not possible
Charging system warning message

P2DC0.t: Battery Charger B Coupler Lock Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2DC0.d: P2DC0 describes lock feedback at the charger B inlet that jumps or drops out for short moments instead of failing steadily. Because the lock state is a release condition for charging, a flickering signal can end a session or stop it from starting even though the plug is held properly. No manufacturer documents P2DC0 publicly. GM's patent US8936482B2 names the consequence of an unconfirmed lock: fast charging is prohibited. As a model on the A side, Mercedes traced a lock position sensor fault (P0D9F00) on the smart electric drive's 22 kW charger to loose low-voltage plugs at that charger (LI54.10-P-067823), with complaints tied to cold or warm components. Worn terminals, a chafed wire at the inlet and water ingress are typical. Steady faults are P2DBC to P2DBF.
c: Loose low-voltage plug at the lock actuator or charger
Sensor wire chafed near the charging inlet
Water ingress into the inlet or actuator connector
s: Charging at inlet B stops or fails to start sporadically
Fault appears only at certain temperatures

P2DC1.t: Starter/Generator Phase X Current Sensor Circuit
P2DC1.d: P2DC1 is the general circuit code for the phase X current sensor of the starter/generator: the controller sees an electrical fault in the sensor path without, or in place of, a separate high or low verdict. CARB's OBD rule normally wants wiring faults and out-of-limit readings stored apart, yet it allows them to share one code when the sensor sits on a circuit board inside the control unit. Starter/generators with inverter and sensors built into the machine can fall under this, so P2DC1 may stand where P2D92 and P2D95 would otherwise appear. Mazda's starter generator, for one, splits its stator drivers into a U-V-W and an X-Y-Z group (bulletin 01-004-25). No manufacturer documents P2DC1 publicly. Range check: P2DC2; intermittent: P2D98.
c: Phase X current sensor on the integrated electronics board defective
Open or shorted lead between an external phase X sensor and the controller
Unstable 12 V supply or ground of the starter/generator electronics
s: MIL or system warning lamp
Starter/generator in a reduced mode or switched off
Stop-start and boost unavailable

P2DC2.t: Starter/Generator Phase X Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2DC2.d: P2DC2 means the starter/generator's phase X current sensor delivers values that are electrically valid but do not make sense. CARB requires such rationality faults to be detected where feasible and kept in a code of their own, separate from wiring and out-of-limit faults. One published method is the zero check: when the inverter is not switching, no phase current flows, so the reading should be near zero. GM's eAssist machine filters this offset over eight loops and treats more than 30 A as a fault on its U and W sensors, which GM files under the Range/Performance codes of drive motor A. No manufacturer documents P2DC2 publicly. A drifting sensor zero, a corrupted reference voltage or a sensor slowly failing are likely. Circuit fault: P2DC1; high and low: P2D92, P2D95.
c: Zero point of the phase X sensor drifted, for example through ageing or heat
Sensor reference voltage out of tolerance
Phase X current sensor with gain error or slowly failing
s: Warning lamp after the plausibility check has failed on two trips
Less electric torque because current control runs in a substitute mode

P2DC3.t: Starter/Generator Phase Y Current Sensor Circuit
P2DC3.d: P2DC3 flags an electrical fault in the circuit of the phase Y current sensor of the starter/generator. Such a sensor needs a supply, a ground and a signal line, and a break or short in any of the three can end up here when the controller cannot or does not tell high from low. Under CARB's rule the hybrid parts a manufacturer chooses to monitor are checked like any other input component, and the manufacturer has to get its hybrid monitoring plan approved. Not every machine has a Y sensor: GM's eAssist table covers only phases U and W, so a vehicle storing P2DC3 uses a different layout. No manufacturer documents P2DC3 publicly. Measure supply and ground at the sensor plug before condemning the machine. Range check: P2DC4; high and low: P2D93, P2D96.
c: Missing supply or ground at the phase Y sensor
Open phase Y signal line between sensor and controller
Phase Y current sensor without output
s: MIL or hybrid warning
Automatic stop-start disabled
Battery charged less by the starter/generator

P2DC4.t: Starter/Generator Phase Y Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2DC4.d: P2DC4 says the phase Y current reading of the starter/generator is inside its electrical limits but fails a plausibility test. One way to test it is an energy balance: the power drawn or delivered on the phase side must match the current on the DC side. GM's eAssist machine compares the sum derived from its phase sensors with the DC-DC converter input and battery pack current; a gap above 40 A in 90 of 96 checks, run every 2.08 ms, sets a two-trip Type B code, and current control then continues without the sensors. GM measures U and W only, so this is an analogue, not P2DC4 itself, which no manufacturer documents publicly. A sensor with a gain error or a drifting zero is the usual suspect. Circuit: P2DC3; X and Z range: P2DC2, P2DC6.
c: Phase Y current sensor reading consistently too high or too low
Zero offset of the phase Y sensor drifted
Comparison value wrong because the DC-side current measurement is faulty
s: Warning lamp after two trips with the fault
Noticeably weaker boost and smoother but slower restarts

P2DC5.t: Starter/Generator Phase Z Current Sensor Circuit
P2DC5.d: P2DC5 records a circuit fault of the phase Z current sensor in the starter/generator. A Z phase only exists on machines with more than one phase group. Mazda, for one, gives an integrated machine a second set of stator drivers labelled X, Y and Z, and CARB asks for circuit checks on such hybrid inputs. Since such sensors usually sit inside the machine electronics, a confirmed internal fault often means replacing the complete starter/generator, while a harness or plug problem can be fixed on its own. Rule out the external side first: supply, ground, connector and the low-voltage leads. No manufacturer documents P2DC5 publicly. Range check: P2DC6; high and low: P2D94, P2D97; intermittent: P2D9A.
c: Phase Z sensor inside the starter/generator electronics failed
Low-voltage connector of the starter/generator damaged or not latched
Supply or ground fault of the machine electronics
s: MIL and battery warning
No recuperation and no electric boost

P2DC6.t: Starter/Generator Phase Z Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2DC6.d: P2DC6 is the plausibility code for the starter/generator's phase Z current sensor. The reading stays within its electrical window but does not match what the controller expects from commanded current and machine state. Care is needed to separate this from a real winding problem: GM's eAssist logic, for example, watches the peak current of each phase as the rotor turns and stores a separate open-phase code when it stays under 9 A although at least 25 A are commanded. A low Z value can thus mean a weak sensor or a phase that truly carries little current. CARB demands rationality faults in their own code, apart from circuit faults. No manufacturer documents P2DC6 publicly. Circuit: P2DC5; Z high and low: P2D94, P2D97; phase correlation: P2DCB.
c: Phase Z sensor has lost sensitivity or drifted
Real current deviation from a poor phase Z connection or winding fault
Controller software or calibration judging the signal wrongly
s: Warning lamp, usually after two trips
Reduced starter/generator output or rough automatic restarts

P2DC7.d: P2DC7 is the general fault for the excitation current of a starter/generator, meaning the DC current in the rotor field winding does not behave as commanded. Only wound-field machines have one. Valeo's 48 V belt starter generator, for instance, is a synchronous claw-pole machine; in such designs the stator gets three-phase current from an inverter, while a separate H-bridge drives direct current through brushes and slip rings into the rotor coil. Permanent-magnet starter/generators need no excitation, so the code does not apply to them. Regulator chips for wound-field alternators measure this current and can limit it, which is the basis for such checks. Switching the field off is also a safety tool against DC-link overvoltage. No manufacturer documents P2DC7 publicly. Low: P2DC8; high: P2DC9.
c: Worn brushes or contaminated slip rings on the rotor
Fault in the excitation H-bridge of the starter/generator electronics
Rotor field winding with interrupted turns or a short
s: Battery or charging warning lamp
Starter/generator stops charging and assisting
Stop-start disabled

P2DC8.d: P2DC8 reports that too little excitation current reaches the rotor field winding of a wound-field starter/generator. With a weak field the claw-pole machine produces little torque and little voltage, so both charging and electric assist fade. Infineon's LIN alternator regulator TLE8881-3 shows how such a check works: if the field driver runs at full duty cycle and four current measurements stay below a programmable minimum, it reports a broken excitation coil; it measures the field current with about 250 mA accuracy up to 5 A. A 48 V starter/generator controller can apply the same idea. No manufacturer documents P2DC8 publicly. Worn brushes, dirty slip rings or an open coil are typical finds. General code: P2DC7; high: P2DC9; intermittent: P2DCA.
c: Brushes worn down so they no longer contact the slip rings reliably
Open circuit in the rotor field coil or its connections
Excitation driver stage in the electronics unable to deliver current
s: Charging warning and falling battery voltage
No electric boost and weak or no belt-driven restarts

P2DC9.d: P2DC9 means a starter/generator with an electrically excited rotor draws more field current than its controller expects or allows. In such machines, for example Valeo's 48 V claw-pole belt starter generator, the stator windings get their three-phase supply from an inverter, and an extra full bridge sets the rotor's DC field via brushes on slip rings. Too much field current points to shorted turns in the rotor coil, a field driver that no longer regulates, or a faulty current measurement. It matters because a strongly excited machine turning fast can drive the 48 V bus to unsafe voltages; TI describes switching off the excitation bridge as the way to de-energise such a rotor. No manufacturer documents P2DC9 publicly. General code: P2DC7; low: P2DC8; intermittent: P2DCA.
c: Excitation driver stage in the controller shorted or no longer regulating
Shorted turns in the rotor field coil lowering its resistance
Faulty field current measurement inside the controller
Field lead chafed and shorted to a supply voltage
s: Check engine light and 48 V or charging system warning
Start-stop and electric boost switched off
Overvoltage protection cuts in, electrical consumers may flicker

P2DCA.d: P2DCA is set when the field current of a starter/generator with electrically excited rotor does not stay steady but drops out or jumps for short moments, without staying beyond the low or high limit long enough for P2DC8 or P2DC9. The rotor coil of a claw-pole machine such as Valeo's 48 V iBSG receives its current through brushes running on slip rings, so worn or sticking brushes and dirty or worn rings are typical sources of such dropouts; a loose plug on the field leads or a cracked solder joint in the excitation bridge can do the same. Each dropout briefly collapses the rotor field, making torque and charging current fluctuate. No manufacturer documents P2DCA publicly. Drivers may notice uneven engine restarts or a flickering charge warning. General fault: P2DC7.
c: Worn or sticking brushes, dirty or worn slip rings
Loose connector or terminal on the field leads
Cracked solder joint in the excitation bridge of the controller
s: Charge warning that comes and goes
Jerky or delayed restarts after start-stop
Electric boost and recuperation work only at times

P2DCB.t: Starter/Generator Phase X-Y-Z Current Sensor Correlation
P2DCB.d: P2DCB compares the three current sensors of the starter/generator's X-Y-Z phase group with one another or with the DC side. In a star-connected winding the instantaneous phase currents must add up to roughly zero; if they do not, at least one sensor is wrong, even though each may sit inside its own limits. Mazda's bulletin 01-004-25 shows that an integrated starter generator can carry a second stator driver group called X, Y and Z beside U, V and W. GM's eAssist instead balances currents: if the value derived from the phase sensors differs from DC-DC converter plus battery pack current by more than 40 A in at least 90 out of 96 checks, one every 2.08 ms, P0BFD sets as Type B and current control runs without sensors within 187.2 ms. No manufacturer documents P2DCB publicly. Single-sensor faults: P2DC1 to P2DC6.
c: Gain or zero drift of one phase current sensor
Disturbed supply or reference voltage shared by the sensors
Calibration or software fault in the starter/generator controller
s: Check engine light with hybrid or 48 V system warning
Reduced electric boost and recuperation in substitute mode
Start-stop may be disabled

P2DCC.d: P2DCC reports that the rotor position or speed the starter/generator derives from its own sensor disagrees with an independent reference. For a belt-driven machine the natural reference is the crankshaft: engine speed times the pulley ratio has to match machine speed. GM's eAssist runs this comparison under the drive motor performance code P0A90: more than 1,000 rpm between machine and ECM speed for 1.5 s within 2 s sets it as a one-trip Type A, while gaps above 500 rpm are counted over two key cycles. GM also watches the resolver for a tracking error above 5 degrees. A slipping belt can therefore look like a sensor fault. No manufacturer documents P2DCC publicly. Lacking a reliable angle, the controller usually stops assist and auto-start; CARB asks that such generator faults be detected.
c: Slipping drive belt or weak belt tensioner
Rotor position sensor degraded or shifted
Faulty engine speed reference from the crankshaft sensor or its CAN signal
s: Start-stop and electric assist disabled
Belt squeal or engine restart via 12 V starter instead
Check engine light

P2DCD.d: P2DCD is meant for a second particulate filter, labelled B, that the engine control unit finds to be absent or not the specified part, for instance after the filter has been cut out, replaced by an empty housing or swapped for an unsuitable aftermarket unit. No manufacturer documents P2DCD publicly, and makers catch such tampering with other codes. CARB's rules for diesel vehicles and heavy-duty engines require a fault when the filter body is wrecked or taken out, or the whole unit gives way to a silencer or plain tube. Ford's 2024 gasoline summary performs this check on its second filter as P226E (bank 2): with exhaust flow of 300 to 850 m³/h and the filter above 250 °C for 30 s, normalised backpressure under 1.0 for 5 s means a missing brick. Filter A: P24FD. Expect a MIL and a failed inspection.
c: Filter B removed or replaced by an empty housing or pipe
Filter substrate cracked, melted or blown out
Leaking or blocked pressure lines misleading the detection
s: Check engine light on
Failed emissions inspection
Louder exhaust or visible soot at the tailpipe

P2DCE.t: Control Pilot Charging Switch B Circuit/Open
P2DCE.d: P2DCE reports an open or otherwise faulty control circuit of charging switch B, a vehicle-side switch on the control pilot line. Under SAE J1772 the car first loads the pilot with about 2.74 kΩ, pulling the 12 V supplied by the station down to roughly 9 V; closing a charging switch puts another 1.3 kΩ in parallel, the level falls to about 6 V and the station energises the cable. With the circuit of switch B interrupted, the module cannot place this request through it. Which hardware the letter B stands for, such as a second charge inlet or a redundant path, is not published, and no manufacturer documents P2DCE. CARB asks plug-in hybrids to detect charger faults that stop or limit charging. Switch A counterpart: P0CF8. Expect a car that the station recognises but that does not charge.
c: Broken wire or pushed-back pin in the switch B circuit
Switch or its driver inside the charging module open
Corroded contacts at the charge inlet or module connector
s: Station detects the car but charging never starts
Charging fault message in the instrument cluster

P2DCF.t: Control Pilot Charging Switch B Range/Performance
P2DCF.d: P2DCF means charging switch B responds electrically, but the pilot level it creates is not plausible. The only public description of such a test concerns switch A: in a GM check for the Chevrolet Volt, run only while no cable is inserted, the module shuts its internal test switch and the charging switch simultaneously, and the pilot-to-battery voltage ratio then has to lie from 0.14 to 0.28; 30 failures in 50 samples taken every 100 ms set P0CF9 as Type A. An equivalent check of switch B would catch a drifted resistor, a switch with high contact resistance or a fault where the module measures the pilot. No manufacturer documents P2DCF publicly; the MIL depends on how the maker classifies it. Circuit faults: P2DCE, P2DD0, P2DD1. Charging may be refused or stop.
c: Resistor in the switch B branch drifted out of tolerance
High contact resistance in switch, inlet or connector
Fault in the pilot voltage measuring path of the charging module
s: Charging refused or stopping after a short time
Charging error message

P2DD0.t: Control Pilot Charging Switch B Circuit Low
P2DD0.d: P2DD0 says the drive or sense wire of switch B reads below its valid range. The usual reasons are a wire chafed through to body ground or a shorted transistor stage in the charging electronics. Depending on how the switch is driven, a grounded line can hold it permanently closed, so the pilot stays at the charge-request level of about 6 V, or keep it from ever closing. CARB requires plug-in hybrids to recognise charger faults that block or limit charging, but exempts failures that cannot be told apart from problems at the station; a short inside the vehicle is clearly on the car side. No manufacturer documents P2DD0 publicly. Owners may see charging begin as soon as the cable is connected, or not at all. High: P2DD1; open: P2DCE; switch A low: P0CFA.
c: Switch B wire chafed and shorted to ground
Output stage in the charging module failed shorted
Moisture in the charge inlet creating a leakage path
s: Charging starts immediately on plug-in or not at all
Timed charging not followed
Charging fault message

P2DD1.t: Control Pilot Charging Switch B Circuit High
P2DD1.d: P2DD1 reports a voltage on the drive or feedback wire of switch B that is higher than it should be. Likely culprits are a wire touching battery voltage or another feed somewhere between inlet and module, or a transistor stage that has lost the ability to pull its output low. Whether the switch then stays open or closed depends on the design. If it stays open, the pilot remains at about 9 V, the J1772 state of a connected vehicle that does not ask for energy, and the station keeps the cable dead. No manufacturer documents P2DD1 publicly; CARB's plug-in rules ask for detection of on-board charger faults that prevent charging. Low side: P2DD0; plausibility: P2DCF; switch A high: P0CFB. Check connectors for moisture and pushed-back pins before replacing the module.
c: Switch B line shorted to a supply voltage
Driver stage in the charging module no longer pulling low
Moisture or pushed-back pins at inlet or module connector
s: Car stays in plugged-in state, station supplies no power
Charging session cannot be ended cleanly

P2DD2.t: Control Pilot Charging Switch B Intermittent/Erratic
P2DD2.d: P2DD2 is stored when the signal of charging switch B changes state erratically: it drops out or toggles for brief moments, while lasting faults would end up as P2DCE, P2DD0 or P2DD1. Loose terminals, green corrosion at inlet pins or the module plug, and conductors that break contact only when the car moves or temperatures change are the usual suspects. On the pilot line each lost request counts: a J1772 station supplies power only while it sees roughly 6 V, the level that asks for current, so every dropout makes it switch off and possibly on again. No manufacturer documents P2DD2 publicly; under CARB rules a plug-in hybrid must notice a charger fault that breaks off charging. Switch A counterpart: P0CFC. Charging sessions stop and restart for no visible reason, and the battery may not be full in the morning.
c: Loose terminal in the charge inlet or module connector
Corrosion from water ingress at the charge inlet
Chafed wire losing contact with movement or temperature
s: Charging stops and restarts repeatedly
Battery not fully charged after a charging session

P2DD3.t: Control Pilot Charging Switch B Stuck Off
P2DD3.d: Stuck Off: although the module orders charging switch B to close, nothing changes on the pilot; the voltage sits near 9 V, the plugged-in level, rather than dropping to about 6 V. Through this switch the station thus never sees a request for energy. A contact or relay that will not close, a broken 1.3 kΩ resistor or an error in the pilot measurement can each cause this. CARB generally treats a missing functional response to a command as an output component fault, and its plug-in section adds charger faults that stop charging. No manufacturer documents P2DD3 publicly. The opposite case is P2DD4; circuit faults are P2DCE to P2DD1; the switch A equivalent is P0CFD. At the station the car is recognised and may show as plugged in, yet no energy flows.
c: Switch or relay B no longer closing
Open resistor in the charge-request branch
Pilot voltage measurement in the module faulty
s: Car recognised at the station but no charging
Charging error message

P2DD4.t: Control Pilot Charging Switch B Stuck On
P2DD4.d: P2DD4 describes the reverse case: switch B remains closed against the module's command to open, and the pilot goes on asking for energy at about 6 V although charging should have ended or paused. Welded or sticking contacts, a driver stage shorted on, or software that does not release the switch are all possible. For switch A, Mercedes-Benz traced the corresponding code P0CFE to the AC charger software and cured it by SCN coding, advising against swapping parts, so an update check comes first. No manufacturer documents P2DD4 publicly. CARB requires plug-in hybrids to monitor the on-board charger. Counterpart: P2DD3; circuit faults: P2DCE to P2DD1. Scheduled charging pauses may be ignored, or the session may end with an error message instead of finishing normally.
c: Charger software not releasing the switch
s: Charging does not end or pause as planned
Charging error message after the session

P2DD5.t: Fuel Injection Quantity B Lower Than Expected
P2DD5.d: P2DD5 reports that the injection path the manufacturer calls B delivers less fuel than the engine control commanded. SAE leaves open what B is: a second injector set, an injector group or a separate operating mode. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The underlying check is the one CARB has demanded from diesels since 2010: the module compares requested fuel with what airflow and lambda say was burned. GM does this for system A as an adaptation (FSA) with a lower threshold map, 200 of 400 samples, Type B; Ford diesels report a fueling error below -0.15 as P0171. P2DD6 is the opposite direction, P2DD7 the cold-start version. Expect weak pull and possibly rough running.
c: Injectors of group B coked or partly blocked
Supply or rail pressure for this path too low (filter, pump)
Airflow or lambda measurement off, so the computed fuel looks too small
Engine control software or injector calibration data
s: Check engine light on
Less power, sluggish response under load
Uneven idle

P2DD6.t: Fuel Injection Quantity B Higher Than Expected
P2DD6.d: With P2DD6 the engine control has found that path B injects more fuel than requested, so the mixture ends up richer than planned. Typical reasons are an injector that drips after closing, a worn nozzle passing extra fuel, or rail pressure above target; a sensor that under-reads airflow can fake the same result. On diesels this shows up as soot: more black smoke and shorter intervals between filter regenerations. No manufacturer publishes P2DD6 itself. Ford's 2023 diesels flag the matching global fault as P0172 once the filtered fueling error exceeds +0.15; GM scales its upper limit for A with ambient pressure. P2DD5 is the shortfall in path B, P2DD8 the same excess during cold start.
c: Injector in group B dripping or nozzle worn
Rail pressure above target (regulator, pressure sensor)
Airflow sensor reading low or intake leak after the sensor
s: Check engine light on
Black smoke, more frequent particulate filter regeneration
Higher fuel consumption

P2DD7.t: Cold Start Fuel Injection Quantity B Lower Than Expected
P2DD7.d: P2DD7 limits the shortfall of P2DD5 to the cold-start phase. Many engines inject differently just after a cold start, with extra or shifted injections that heat the catalyst or SCR system. CARB section 1968.2 (f)(12.1.2) requires diesels to keep faults found while this strategy runs apart from the same faults in normal operation, and (f)(12.2.3) adds a check that the commanded injection quantity actually responds, phased in over 2026 to 2028. GM's 2025 diesels show the pattern with separate cold-start codes for rail pressure (P2C1F) and injection timing (P05EC), but not for quantity. No maker documents P2DD7. Fuel thickened by cold, a clogged filter or slow pressure build-up fit here; the engine may run roughly until warm.
c: Fuel filter restricted, fuel waxing in cold weather
Rail pressure builds too slowly after start
Injectors of group B sluggish or partly blocked
Coolant or fuel temperature signal implausible
s: Check engine light on after a cold start
Hard cold start, rough running while cold
Longer warm-up

P2DD8.t: Cold Start Fuel Injection Quantity B Higher Than Expected
P2DD8.d: P2DD8 means path B delivered more fuel than requested while the cold-start routine ran. A cold engine burns surplus fuel poorly, so it leaves as white or blue smoke and raw hydrocarbons before the catalyst is warm, and some of it can reach the oil. No manufacturer uses P2DD8 in public documents. Ford shows how such an excess is caught on its 6.7 litre diesel: a cold-start version of the fuel balancing check runs only in cold start mode and sets a fault when an injector correction exceeds 90 percent of its allowed authority, but it reports through the cylinder codes P0263 and up. A leaking injector, a pressure regulator overshooting in the cold or a wrong temperature signal are the usual suspects. P2DD7 is the shortfall.
c: Injector of group B leaking or sticking slightly open
Coolant temperature signal reads colder than real, too much start fuel
Cold-start calibration in engine control software
s: Check engine light on after a cold start
White or blue smoke and fuel smell after a cold start
Rising oil level from fuel dilution

P2DD9.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Control Circuit Performance
P2DD9.d: P2DD9 means the drive circuit of the evaporative leak detection pump is electrically intact, yet the pump does not react the way the command implies: the feedback the engine computer reads back, usually motor current or driver state, does not match the on or off request. Bosch-style DM-TL pumps on European cars are judged by their motor current, first while blowing through a 0.5 mm (0.020 in) reference orifice and then against the closed tank, so a sluggish motor or a resistive plug skews the entire leak test. CARB wants EVAP parts checked for proper functional response as well as for opens and shorts. GM's 2025 tables suspend their pump tests while a pump circuit fault is active. No maker documents P2DD9 publicly; plain circuit faults are P2400 to P2402. Driving is unaffected, only the leak check is lost.
c: Pump motor worn or sluggish, current draw off target
Corroded connector or chafed wire adding resistance in the pump feed
Water or ice in the pump module (mounted near the wheel arch)
Faulty output stage or current sensing in the engine control module
s: Check engine light on
EVAP readiness monitor stays incomplete
No noticeable change in driving

P2DDA.t: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Performance/Stuck Off
P2DDA.d: P2DDA is stored when the leak detection pump fails to create the pressure change the leak test expects, as if it never started or moves too little air. GM performs this check on its electric leak check pumps (ELCP) under its own code P145C: at engine-off wake-ups between roughly 4.3 and 11 hours after shutdown the pump runs against a 0.020 in reference orifice, and if vacuum stays under 100 Pa after 60 s on the first measurement or 30 s on the second, the pump is judged stuck off; Type B, two trips. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV reports a pump stuck on or off under P24C0, after canister pressure falls too slowly. No manufacturer documents P2DDA publicly. The leak test cannot finish; the car drives normally. A pump running when told to stop is P2DDB.
c: Pump motor or vane inside the leak check module seized or worn out
Fresh-air filter or vent line of the module blocked by dirt or water
Switching valve in the module not moving, so the pump works against the wrong path
