Electric drive limited or switched off
Fault may come and go with vibration or temperature

P2E24.t: Drive Motor A Phase Z Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2E24.d: P2E24 concerns a phase Z current reading of drive motor A that passes the electrical checks yet fails a plausibility test. No manufacturer documents P2E24 publicly. Z completes the second winding group of a two-group motor; in the Mitsubishi Electric patent X, Y and Z are star-connected and controlled separately from U, V and W, so a biased Z sensor upsets only its own group. GM's 2019 hybrid table shows the typical test on the U/V/W side: the offset learned while no motor current flows must stay within 35 A, otherwise the code sets after 0.4 s, Type A. Ford also uses the motor phase sensors to confirm that the three AC leads are connected correctly, so a skewed reading can look like a wiring problem. Circuit: P2E23; low and high: P2E25, P2E26; group sum: P2E27.
c: Zero offset of the phase Z sensor drifted
Gain error of the phase Z sensor
Faulty measuring stage on the inverter control board
s: Hybrid warning lamp and MIL
Electric drive limited
Uneven torque or motor noise

P2E25.t: Drive Motor A Phase Z Current Sensor Circuit Low
P2E25.d: P2E25 means the phase Z current sensor of drive motor A reports below its valid minimum. No manufacturer documents P2E25 publicly. A zero reading is not the same thing: if phase Z carries no current because a lead is open, the sensor correctly reads about zero and the open phase is judged by P2C70. Low here means beyond the negative end of the scale; GM places that limit for its U/V/W sensors between -440 A on eAssist and -800 A on the 2016 Cadillac ELR. When X and Y log low codes as well, a common cause such as the shared sensor reference or a ground in the inverter's low-voltage wiring is more likely than three failed sensors; Ford, for one, watches that reference separately. High side: P2E26.
c: Phase Z sensor signal shorted to ground
Shared sensor reference or ground faulty
s: Hybrid warning lamp and MIL
Reduced electric drive
Low codes of other phases possibly stored too

P2E26.t: Drive Motor A Phase Z Current Sensor Circuit High
P2E26.d: P2E26 reports a phase Z current sensor signal of drive motor A that sits above its permitted range. No manufacturer documents P2E26 publicly. The consequence goes beyond one lost reading: in GM's eAssist table the overcurrent check P0C01 and the missing-phase check P0C05 only run while no current sensor code is active, and current control falls back to a mode that ignores the sensors. The inverter therefore loses part of its own protection and has to hold back torque. GM's U-phase high limit there is 440 A, two-trip Type B. Causes on the measuring side include the signal touching the supply line or an interrupted ground return; true overcurrent in phase Z is P2C71. A Mitsubishi Electric patent names Z as the third phase of a separately controlled second set. Low side: P2E25.
c: Phase Z signal shorted to the sensor supply
Open ground of the phase Z sensor
Phase Z current sensor failed high
s: Hybrid warning lamp and MIL
Electric drive torque clearly reduced
Vehicle continues only in a reduced-power mode

P2E27.t: Drive Motor A Phase X-Y-Z Current Sensor Correlation
P2E27.d: P2E27 compares the three current sensors of phases X, Y and Z of drive motor A with each other. Mitsubishi Electric's patent joins the X, Y and Z windings in a star, so their currents must add up to almost zero at every instant; a clear residual means at least one sensor is wrong, even if every reading passes its own checks. No manufacturer documents P2E27 publicly. GM's U-V-W counterpart P0BFD shows the limits: an absolute sum of 110 A for 0.02 s on the 2016 Volt or for 0.0032 s within 0.0038 s in a 2019 table, and above 156 A on the 2016 Cadillac ELR, all Type A. GM's eAssist skips its balance check while a single sensor code is set, because that code already names the culprit; the correlation alone cannot. Single faults: P2E1B to P2E26.
c: One of the three X/Y/Z sensors drifted in offset or gain
Disturbed common reference of the current sensors
Leakage current from the X/Y/Z winding group to the housing
s: Hybrid warning lamp and MIL
Electric drive limited or temporarily switched off
No single sensor code stored alongside

P2E28.t: Drive Motor A Excitation Current Sensor Performance
P2E28.d: P2E28 concerns a drive motor with an electrically excited rotor, the type Nissan uses in the Ariya and BMW in its fifth-generation eDrive. Such a rotor carries a field coil that receives direct current through brushes and slip rings; a sensor measures that current for the closed field-control loop. P2E28 means the sensor signal is electrically valid but does not make sense, for instance it disagrees with a second sensor or with what the commanded duty cycle should produce. CARB wants rationality faults stored apart from circuit faults. No manufacturer documents P2E28 publicly, nor its thresholds. Wiring faults are P2E7B, P2E29 and P2E2A; a real overcurrent is P2E2B. Without a trusted reading the field cannot be regulated, so expect reduced or no drive power.
c: Excitation current sensor drifted (offset or gain no longer correct)
Faulty excitation power stage, so actual and expected current differ
Worn brushes or dirty slip rings changing the field circuit resistance
Inverter or motor control software fault
s: Electric drive warning or service message
Noticeably reduced drive power
Vehicle may refuse to drive or stop driving

P2E29.t: Drive Motor A Excitation Current Sensor Circuit Low Voltage
P2E29.d: P2E29 reports that the signal voltage of the excitation current sensor of drive motor A has dropped below the band the controller accepts. The sensor sits in the excitation stage that feeds direct current to the rotor field coil of an electrically excited motor; TI names shunts with isolated amplifiers or isolated Hall-effect sensors for this job. A reading pinned low is an electrical fault: a short to ground, a lost sensor supply or reference, or a dead sensor. No manufacturer documents P2E29 publicly. Implausible but valid readings are P2E28, a high signal P2E2A, the general circuit fault P2E7B. Because the field current can no longer be measured, the controller will likely switch the field off, as TI recommends for faults, and drive torque from this motor is lost.
c: Sensor signal line shorted to ground
Sensor supply or reference voltage missing
Excitation current sensor or its isolated amplifier failed
s: Electric drive warning lamp on
Loss of drive power from motor A
Vehicle may not become ready to drive

P2E2A.t: Drive Motor A Excitation Current Sensor Circuit High Voltage
P2E2A.d: P2E2A is the counterpart to P2E29: the signal from the sensor that measures the rotor field current of drive motor A sits above the highest voltage a working sensor can deliver. Typical reasons are a signal line touching a supply rail, an open ground or reference connection that lets the input float up, or a failed sensor output stage. Electrically excited traction motors, such as BMW's fifth-generation eDrive units, rely on this measurement to set rotor flux, because the field current sets how strong the rotor's magnetic field is. No manufacturer documents P2E2A publicly. It must not be confused with P2E2B, where the current itself is too high; a merely implausible value is P2E28. Expect a drive system warning and loss of power from this motor until the fault is repaired.
c: Sensor signal line shorted to a supply voltage
Open sensor ground or reference connection
s: Electric drive warning lamp on
Reduced or no drive power
Fault returns immediately after clearing

P2E2B.t: Drive Motor A Excitation Current Too High
P2E2B.d: P2E2B does not blame the sensor: the measured field current of drive motor A itself exceeds what the controller allows. In TI's example of an excitation stage, two switches and two diodes sit between the high-voltage rails; with both switches on, the rotor coil sees the entire DC-link voltage, and switches of this kind are rarely sized above about 50 A. A switch that sticks closed or a control loop that stops regulating therefore lets the current climb. Excess field current overheats the rotor coil, brushes and switches. The safe reaction TI describes is to command zero field current, which also removes rotor flux and back-EMF. No manufacturer documents P2E2B publicly. Sensor faults are P2E28 to P2E2A. The motor is usually shut down, so drive power from it is lost.
c: Excitation power switch shorted or stuck on
Field current control or gate driver fault in the inverter
Shorted turns in the rotor field winding
s: Electric drive warning lamp on
Sudden loss of drive power from motor A
Vehicle may not restart the drive system

P2E2C.t: Battery Charger A Module Supply Voltage Performance
P2E2C.d: P2E2C covers the low-voltage supply that powers the control electronics of on-board charger A, not the AC input. The code means this supply voltage is present but behaves implausibly, for example it fluctuates or disagrees with what other modules see on the same 12 V network. Mitsubishi shows why the value matters: the Outlander PHEV only judges the charger's internal 3.3, 6 and 12 V rails while the charger supply is between 10 and 16 V. Mitsubishi files those faults under P0D67, and no maker documents P2E2C itself. CARB requires plug-in hybrids to detect charger faults that stop or slow charging. Out-of-range values are P2E2D and P2E2E, AC input voltage P0D27/P0D28, charger B P2E2F. Driving is normally unaffected, but charging can be refused or break off.
c: Loose or corroded supply or ground connection at the charger
Ground offset between charger and other modules
Unstable 12 V supply from weak battery or DC/DC converter
Faulty voltage measurement inside the charger module
s: Plug-in charging does not start or stops early
Charging system warning message
Fault comes and goes with electrical load or vibration

P2E2D.t: Battery Charger A Module Supply Voltage Low
P2E2D.d: P2E2D is set when the 12 V feed of the control board in on-board charger A stays below its lower limit. The usual suspects sit outside the charger: a discharged or failing 12 V battery, a DC/DC converter that is not keeping the network up, a blown fuse in the feed, or resistance in supply or ground wiring that eats voltage under load. For orientation, Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV accepts its charger's supply only between 10 and 16 V before checking the internal rails (P0D67); the limit behind P2E2D is not published, and no manufacturer documents the code. CARB requires plug-in hybrids to catch charger faults that block charging. Too high is P2E2E, implausible P2E2C, low AC input P0D27. The car often still drives, but charging may fail.
c: Blown fuse or failed relay in the charger supply
High resistance in supply or ground wiring
DC/DC converter not maintaining the 12 V network
s: Plug-in charging refused or interrupted
Further low-voltage faults in other modules
Charging status display behaves erratically

P2E2E.t: Battery Charger A Module Supply Voltage High
P2E2E.d: P2E2E reports the opposite of P2E2D: the low-voltage feed of on-board charger A rises above its upper limit. On a plug-in vehicle the 12 V network is held by the DC/DC converter, so a converter regulating too high is the first suspect; an external charger or jump-start device at excessive voltage can do the same, and a faulty measurement inside the charger can fake the reading. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV, for comparison, treats charger supply voltages above 16 V as outside its test window for P0D67; P2E2E itself appears in no public manufacturer documentation, threshold included. Under CARB rules, a plug-in hybrid must flag charger faults that prevent or limit charging. Low is P2E2D, implausible P2E2C, system overvoltage P0563. Charging may stop to protect the electronics.
c: DC/DC converter regulating the 12 V network too high
External battery charger or jump starter with excessive voltage
Faulty voltage measurement inside the charger module
s: Plug-in charging stops or will not start
Overvoltage faults stored in other modules as well
Lamps unusually bright or 12 V battery overcharged

P2E2F.t: Battery Charger B Module Supply Voltage Performance
P2E2F.d: P2E2F concerns the 12 V feed of the control electronics in a second on-board charger, charger B, not its grid input. The voltage is within limits but behaves implausibly, for example it jumps around or disagrees with the system voltage that other modules report. No manufacturer documents P2E2F publicly. The A-side pages from Mitsubishi show why the feed matters: the Outlander PHEV runs its charger checks, such as P0D67 on the internal 3.3/6/12 V rails or the ROM test P0E5E, only while the charger supply sits between 10 and 16 V. A supplier unit like Holley's 30-8405 specifies the same 9–16 V working range. CARB wants plug-in hybrids to catch charger faults that stop or slow charging. Out-of-range values are P2E30/P2E31; the A twin is P2E2C. Charging may become unreliable.
c: Loose or corroded supply or ground terminal at charger B
Ground offset between charger B and the reference module
Fluctuating 12 V network from weak battery or DC/DC converter
Faulty supply voltage measurement inside charger B
s: Plug-in charging starts late, pauses or stops
Fault appears with electrical load changes or vibration
Charging system warning in the instrument cluster

P2E30.t: Battery Charger B Module Supply Voltage Low
P2E30.d: P2E30 is stored when the 12 V feed reaching the control board of charger B stays under its lower limit. Most causes lie upstream: a flat or aged 12 V battery, a blown fuse or failed relay in the charger feed, or corroded supply and ground contacts that lose voltage under load. No manufacturer documents P2E30 publicly, and no threshold is published. For a sense of scale, Holley's 30-8405 charger unit names 9–16 V as its normal range and keeps CAN alive only down to 6 V; Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV lists a faulty charger supply circuit among the causes of lost communication with the charger (U019B). Under CARB rules a charger fault that blocks charging must be flagged. Too high is P2E31, charger A low is P2E2D. Charging via path B is likely refused; driving normally continues.
c: Blown fuse or failed relay in the charger B feed
Voltage drop across corroded supply or ground contacts
DC/DC converter not holding up the 12 V network
s: Charging through charger B does not start
Low-voltage or communication faults in other modules too
Reduced charging power if only one charger works

P2E31.t: Battery Charger B Module Supply Voltage High
P2E31.d: P2E31 is the high-side counterpart of P2E30: the low-voltage feed of charger B climbs above what its control electronics accept. On plug-in cars the DC/DC converter holds the 12 V network, so a converter regulating too high is the main suspect; a workshop charger or jump pack set too high, or a faulty measurement inside charger B, can give the same reading. No manufacturer documents P2E31 or a threshold publicly. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV pages put the upper edge of the charger test window at 16 V, for P0D67 as well as for the ROM check P0E5E, and Holley's 30-8405 charger unit is rated up to 16 V. Charger faults that get in the way of charging are covered by CARB. System overvoltage is P0563, the A-side twin P2E2E. Charger B likely stops to protect itself.
c: DC/DC converter regulating the 12 V network too high
Workshop charger or jump starter with excessive voltage
Faulty supply voltage measurement inside charger B
s: Charging via charger B stops or will not start
Overvoltage codes stored in several modules
12 V battery gassing or lamps unusually bright

P2E32.t: Battery Charger A Module Forced Shutdown Voltage Performance
P2E32.d: P2E32 belongs to the forced shutdown input of on-board charger A, a hardwired signal with which another module can switch the charger off regardless of bus messages. The code means this signal does not behave as expected although its level is in range, for instance the charger keeps converting power after a shutdown request, or the line reports shutdown while none was commanded. No manufacturer documents P2E32 or the circuit behind it publicly. Watt & Well's EVCC charging controller offers a comparable supplier example: its hardwired emergency stop halts charging when the loop current drops to zero. CARB obliges plug-in hybrids to detect charger faults that disable or degrade charging. Low and high levels are P2E33/P2E34, charger B's twin is P2E3E. Charging is usually blocked.
c: Contact resistance or partly corroded terminal in the shutdown line
Shutdown input stage inside charger A not responding correctly
Fault or software issue in the module driving the shutdown signal
s: Plug-in charging refused or ended unexpectedly
Charging system warning message

P2E33.t: Battery Charger A Module Forced Shutdown Voltage Low
P2E33.d: P2E33 reports that the voltage on the forced shutdown line of charger A sits below its valid band. What that means in practice depends on the logic, which no manufacturer publishes for this code. Shutdown lines are often built fail-safe, as in Watt & Well's EVCC charging controller, where a missing loop current counts as an emergency stop. With such logic a wire broken or shorted to ground looks like a permanent shutdown order, so charger A stays off even though nobody asked for it; the code then separates a wiring fault from a genuine request. Typical findings are a chafed wire touching the body, water in a connector or a pulled-out pin. Charger faults that stop charging fall under CARB's plug-in hybrid rule. High is P2E34, implausible behaviour P2E32, charger B low P2E3F.
c: Shutdown line chafed through and shorted to ground
Broken wire or backed-out pin in the shutdown circuit
Moisture or corrosion in the charger signal connector
Output stage of the commanding module stuck low
s: Charger A never starts charging
Charging aborts when the car or harness is moved
Charging system warning message

P2E34.t: Battery Charger A Module Forced Shutdown Voltage High
P2E34.d: P2E34 is set when the forced shutdown line of charger A reads above its permitted voltage. The usual cause is contact with a battery-fed or switched 12 V wire in the same harness, or an internal leak inside the charger or the commanding module. No manufacturer documents P2E34 publicly. The danger is the reverse of P2E33: on a fail-safe line such as the EmShut input of the EVCC by Watt & Well, where current flowing means normal operation, a line stuck high can no longer carry a stop request. A well-designed control unit therefore distrusts the charger and keeps it disabled instead of risking charging it cannot switch off. The CARB charger rule for plug-in hybrids applies. Low is P2E33, implausible P2E32, charger B high P2E40. Expect no charging through charger A.
c: Shutdown line shorted to a 12 V feed in the harness
Internal leakage in charger A or the commanding module
Incorrect wiring after a previous harness repair
s: Charger A disabled, plug-in charging not possible or slower
Charging system warning message

P2E35.d: P2E35 covers the enable line of charger B, the hardwired 12 V signal that wakes the charger or allows it to work, and reports a general circuit fault, usually an open. No manufacturer documents P2E35 publicly. The A-side code P0E61 is documented by GM: the 2016 Volt (VICM) and the 2019 hybrid tables (HPC2) evaluate a fault flag from the line driver at 10.2 V system voltage or more, 30 bad samples out of 40 at 25 ms, Type B. Holley's 30-8405 charger unit shows why the line counts: the charger only runs with 12 V on its wake-up pin, and without it even its CAN stays silent. Specific level faults are P2E36 and P2E37, plausibility P2E38. With an open line charger B stays asleep; a car with a second charger may still charge slowly through the first.
c: Broken enable wire or backed-out terminal
Signal connector at charger B not fully latched
Failed enable driver in the commanding module
s: Charger B does not wake when the cable is plugged in
Charging slower than usual or not at all
Charging system warning message

P2E36.t: Battery Charger B Enable Circuit Low
P2E36.d: P2E36 means the enable signal to charger B is pulled under the level its commanded state allows, most often by a short to ground or by a driver stage that cannot pull the line up. No manufacturer documents P2E36 publicly. On the common active-high layout, which Holley's 30-8405 charger unit uses with a 12 V wake-up input drawing about 20 mA, a grounded line simply means the charger never receives its wake request. Lear's patent on waking an on-board charger from the pilot signal explains the background: the charger sleeps to spare the 12 V battery and needs a valid wake signal to start. A hard short may also overload the output stage in the commanding module. GM documents only the general A-side code P0E61. High is P2E37, open P2E35, charger A low P0E62. Charging via charger B fails.
c: Enable wire chafed and shorted to ground
Water or corrosion in the charger B signal connector
Damaged high-side driver in the commanding module
s: Charger B stays off whenever charging is requested
Lower charging power or no charging

P2E37.t: Battery Charger B Enable Circuit High
P2E37.d: P2E37 is stored when the enable line of charger B carries more voltage than its commanded state allows, typically because it touches a powered wire or the driver in the commanding module is stuck on. No manufacturer documents P2E37 publicly. The effect differs from P2E36: on an active-high wake line the charger is told to stay awake although no charging is planned. Lear's patent on a wake-by-pilot circuit points out why that hurts, since the charger is meant to sleep together with the whole car to keep the 12 V battery healthy, so a stuck enable can drain it overnight. The control unit may also lose the ability to switch charger B off by hardware. GM's 2016 Volt tables list only the general A-side enable fault P0E61. Low is P2E36, charger A high P0E63.
c: Enable wire shorted to a 12 V feed
Enable driver in the commanding module stuck on
Internal leakage in the charger B input circuit
s: 12 V battery discharged after standing
Charger B fan or pump runs with nothing plugged in
Charging via charger B disabled

P2E38.t: Battery Charger B Enable Circuit Range/Performance
P2E38.d: P2E38 flags an enable circuit of charger B that is electrically sound, while the charger or its partner modules do not react to it as expected. No manufacturer documents P2E38 publicly. Ford shows the A-side logic for P0E64 in its 2019 plug-in hybrid OBD summary: once the charger is ready and the wake-up line Chrg_Wkup is high, the battery energy control module must report ready; if it still says not ready after 30 s, the test fails. Slow start-up, a module that does not wake or mismatched software can therefore trigger the code without any wiring fault. GM's 2019 hybrid tables check the hardware side of the line separately (P0E61). CARB asks for rationality checks where feasible. Circuit faults are P2E35 to P2E37, output power deviations P2E3A. Charging may start late or not at all.
c: Software mismatch between charger B and battery control module
Battery control module not waking or starting too slowly
Enable level marginal due to contact resistance
s: Charging begins only after a long delay or not at all
Fault appears only on some charging sessions

P2E39.d: P2E39 concerns the high-voltage fuse in the branch between the traction battery and charger B. Battery management units usually judge such fuses by comparing the voltage behind the fuse with the pack voltage; Volvo's technical journal TJ 37376 on BECM codes P0A9500 and P0E2F00 has technicians read exactly those values at the fuse outputs. No manufacturer documents P2E39 publicly. For the A-side code P0E2E00 Audi describes a 2022 Q5 plug-in hybrid case: the J840 battery regulation module logs it intermittently after very dynamic cornering through a diagnostic irregularity, replacing the switching unit does not help, a software update does. A really blown charger B fuse stops charging through that path. Other HV fuses are P0A95 and P0E2F, the A twin P0E2E.
c: Fuse opened by an internal short in charger B
Spurious entry from battery management software
Faulty voltage sensing behind the fuse
s: Charging through charger B no longer possible
Electrical system or high-voltage warning

P2E3A.t: Battery Charger B Output Voltage Performance
P2E3A.d: P2E3A says the high-voltage output of charger B does not follow its target, typically in the constant-voltage phase near the end of a charge, without being clearly too low. No manufacturer documents P2E3A publicly. The A-side code P0D20 shows two readings of the same check. GM's 2011 Volt sets it in constant-voltage mode once the output deviates by 15 % or more, 30 times in 50 samples at 100 ms, One Trip Type A. Ford's 2019 plug-in hybrid summary files P0D20 when the charger, connected and fed with AC, delivers less output power than expected. Holley's 30-8405 unit specifies an output voltage accuracy of 1 %. CARB covers faults that keep the battery from filling completely. Clearly low output is P2E3B, current deviation P2E3C. Charging may end early or below full.
c: Degraded power stage or regulation inside charger B
Charger or battery module software needing an update
s: Battery does not reach full charge
Charging stops early or takes longer
Charging system warning message

P2E3B.t: Battery Charger B Output Voltage Too Low
P2E3B.d: P2E3B is set when the high-voltage output of charger B stays below what the control unit expects while charging. No manufacturer documents P2E3B publicly. For the A-side code P0D21, GM's 2016 tables for the Cadillac ELR use a fixed floor: in constant-current as well as constant-voltage mode the charger bus must not drop under 150 V, and 8 failures in 10 samples set the code as Type B. Stellantis stores P0D21-00 in the integrated dual charging module (IDCM) with the MIL on and the car refusing to charge, on the 2021 Wrangler 4xe (TSB 08-260-26, some cars also tripping the house circuit breaker) and the 2022 Pacifica plug-in hybrid (TSB 08-334-26); the fix in both is IDCM software. CARB requires such charger faults to be caught. Imprecise output is P2E3A, a short P2E3D.
c: Charger module software fault fixed by reprogramming
Failed power stage inside charger B
High resistance in the HV output connection
s: MIL on and vehicle will not charge
Level 2 charging fails, wall box breaker may trip

P2E3C.t: Battery Charger B Output Current Performance
P2E3C.d: P2E3C means charger B does not deliver the high-voltage current it has been asked for. No manufacturer documents P2E3C publicly. Its A-side model P0D22 is well covered: the 2011 Volt compares actual and desired current in constant-current mode against a table and sets the code after 150 bad samples in 300, One Trip Type A. Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander PHEV stops charging if target and actual current differ by 3 A or more for 3 s while the PHEV-ECU permits charging. GM bulletins PIP4884B (2011 Volt, mostly in cold weather) and PIP5077D (2013 Volt) trace a MIL with P0D22 after charging to calibration and order a reflash of the hybrid powertrain control module 2, not a new charger. Voltage faults are P2E3A/P2E3B, a shorted output P2E3D. Charging slows or stops.
c: Control software or calibration of charger or hybrid module
Weak power stage inside charger B
s: MIL after or during charging
Charging takes noticeably longer or aborts
Problem more frequent in cold weather

P2E3D.d: P2E3D points to a short on the high-voltage output side of charger B. No manufacturer documents P2E3D publicly. GM's test for the A-side code P0D23 shows how such a short is found: while the charger contactor is only precharging and the multi-purpose contactor is open, hardly any current should flow, so more than 0.35 A on the charger bus in 4 of 5 samples at 100 ms sets the code as One Trip Type A, both in the 2011 Volt and in the 2016 Cadillac ELR tables. The test is suspended while output current sensor faults are active. Supplier chargers such as Holley's 30-8405 build in output short-circuit protection that shuts the stage down. Causes are an internal short in charger B, a damaged HV cable or a contactor path that leaks. Charging is blocked; current deviations alone are P2E3C.
c: Internal short in the charger B output stage
Damaged high-voltage cable between charger B and battery
Leaking or stuck contactor path in the charging circuit
s: Charging blocked as soon as the cable is plugged in
High-voltage or charging system warning

P2E3E.t: Battery Charger B Module Forced Shutdown Voltage Performance
P2E3E.d: P2E3E is the charger B version of P2E32: the forced shutdown signal of the second charger is electrically in range but its behaviour is implausible. Examples are a shutdown request that the charger ignores, or a level that changes state without a matching command, so the control unit can no longer trust its hardwired off-switch for path B. No manufacturer documents P2E3E or the underlying circuit publicly. What such a line is for can be seen at Watt & Well, whose EVCC controller ends a charging session in hardware as soon as current in its EmShut loop vanishes. CARB demands that plug-in hybrids detect charger faults that prevent or degrade charging. Its low and high faults are P2E3F/P2E40. Expect charger B to be locked out; a first charger may keep charging at reduced power.
c: Shutdown input stage inside charger B not responding correctly
Intermittent contact in the charger B shutdown line
Software issue in the module issuing the shutdown
s: Charging slower than usual because charger B is locked out
Charging system warning message

P2E3F.t: Battery Charger B Module Forced Shutdown Voltage Low
P2E3F.d: P2E3F reports a forced shutdown signal at charger B that stays below its permitted voltage. No manufacturer documents P2E3F or the shutdown logic behind it publicly. If the line is fail-safe, as at the EVCC controller from Watt & Well, where zero loop current or an unconnected input triggers the stop, then a ground short or a break looks like a standing shutdown command and charger B stays switched off for good. The code lets the system tell that wiring fault from a deliberate request. Likely findings are a damaged wire near the charger mount, a corroded or loose pin in the signal plug, or a commanding output stage stuck low. A charger that cannot run is exactly what CARB wants a plug-in hybrid to report. High is P2E40, implausible P2E3E, charger A low P2E33.
c: Shutdown line of charger B shorted to ground
Broken wire or loose pin in the signal plug
Output stage of the commanding module stuck low
s: Charger B never takes part in charging
Reduced charging power or no charging

P2E40.t: Battery Charger B Module Forced Shutdown Voltage High
P2E40.d: P2E40 means the forced shutdown signal of charger B reads above its valid band, typically from a short to a 12 V wire or a leak inside the charger or the module that drives it. No manufacturer documents P2E40 publicly. With fail-safe logic, as Watt & Well specifies for the EVCC, where flowing current stands for normal operation, a line held high can no longer pass on a stop order, so the hardware path that should end charging in an emergency is lost. For that reason a control unit would rather keep charger B disabled than run it without a working off-switch. CARB's onboard charger requirement covers this too. Low is P2E3F, implausible P2E3E, charger A high P2E34. The driver mainly notices slower or no charging.
c: Shutdown line of charger B shorted to a 12 V wire
Internal leakage in charger B or the commanding module
Miswiring after a harness or charger repair
s: Charging slower or impossible with charger B locked out
Charging system warning message

P2E41.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump B Control Circuit/Open
P2E41.d: P2E41 flags an electrical fault on the line over which the controller commands electronics coolant pump B, the second pump serving inverter, DC/DC converter and frequently the charger; the maker decides which pump is B. No manufacturer publicly documents P2E41. GM's 2018 hybrid tables show the logic for the pump A counterpart P0CE9: the controller watches the current on the PWM command line and fails it below 200 mA or above 3 A while active, after 16 failures in 20 samples taken every 250 ms, Type B. Ford's 2024 summary checks the command line of its auxiliary pump B for an open circuit (fault type 13) within 5 s at 11 V or more. Broken wires, corroded pins and pumps with dead input electronics are typical. Audi logged pump A's circuit code on the e-tron alongside low coolant. Low and High are P2E43 and P2E44.
c: Broken or disconnected control wire between module and pump B
Corroded or pushed-back pins at the pump connector
Pump B electronics no longer load the command line
Faulty output stage in the controlling module
s: Hybrid or electric drive warning and MIL
Pump B does not run, electronics loop warms up faster
Reduced drive power or interrupted charging under high load

P2E42.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump B Performance
P2E42.d: P2E42 is the functional verdict on electronics coolant pump B: the circuits test fine, yet the controller concludes the pump is not doing its job. Two ways of reaching that verdict are documented for pump A. For the 2016 Cadillac ELR, GM checks the result, setting P0CEA when power electronics coolant and charger temperatures drift too far apart after the pump has been enabled for more than 300 s. GM's 2018 tables check the pump itself by filtering the gap between commanded and reported speed (P19FC, Type B). No maker documents P2E42. Stellantis cleared a related performance code of a motor electronics pump B, P0C74, on 2023 Renegade and Compass 1.3 PHEV models by reprogramming. Air, debris, a weak pump or software are candidates; CARB asks for a cooling check where feasible.
c: Air pocket after service or slow coolant loss
Worn pump B delivering too little flow
Debris, kinked hose or clogged cold plate in the loop
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Higher inverter or charger temperatures than usual
Power reduction or slower charging in hot conditions

P2E43.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump B Control Circuit Low
P2E43.d: P2E43 means the command signal of electronics coolant pump B sits too low, typically because the line has contact with ground or the output stage cannot drive it up. On PWM-controlled pumps this usually stops the pump outright. Pierburg's CWA pumps, a widespread design, read a duty cycle of 0 to 1 % as stop and pull their PWM input to ground through 10 kΩ, so a grounded line leaves the rotor standing. Ford's 2024 summary treats circuit low (fault type 11) on its auxiliary pumps as a report from the smart driver, checked over 5 s at a battery voltage of at least 11 V. GM's 2016 hybrid tables fold grounded, voltage-shorted and open lines into a single pump A code, P0CE9. No manufacturer publicly documents P2E43. Chafed insulation and wet connectors are usual finds. The high-side code is P2E44, pump A's version P0CEB.
c: Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the pump connector
Shorted input stage inside pump B
Output stage of the module stuck low
s: Pump B stops, electronics coolant heats up
MIL with hybrid or drive system message
Limited power or charging rate under load

P2E44.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump B Control Circuit High
P2E44.d: P2E44 is the opposite fault: the command line of electronics coolant pump B reads higher than its commanded state allows, mostly because it touches a battery-fed wire or the driver can no longer pull it down. Many PWM pumps react to a permanently high input with an emergency mode; Pierburg's interface runs the pump at about 95 % speed for a duty cycle of 98 to 100 %. The loop may therefore stay cooled while the controller has lost all influence on the speed, which also wastes energy and adds noise. Ford's 2024 summary lists circuit high (fault type 12) as a separate failure type of its auxiliary pumps. No manufacturer publicly documents P2E44. Look for harness sections rubbing against live wires, moisture and a defective output stage in the module. P2E43 covers the low side, P0CEC is pump A's equivalent.
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-voltage circuit
Module output stage unable to pull the line low
Moisture linking supply and signal pins in the connector
s: MIL with hybrid system message
Pump B runs continuously at high speed, audible hum
Pump does not respond to commanded speed changes

P2E45.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump B Enable Circuit
P2E45.d: Some designs switch electronics coolant pump B on through a separate enable line or a relay, independent of the speed command; P2E45 reports a fault in that path. GM's 2018 hybrid tables show the scheme for pump A: with the enable output active, more than 0.6 A on the line counts as a short to ground (P1F44); with it inactive, more than 35 µA or a line voltage under 4.5 V counts as a short to voltage (P1F45), each after 16 of 20 samples at 250 ms, Type B. The 2016 tables list the same pair. Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander PHEV powers its electric water pump through a relay energised by the PHEV-ECU and names that relay among the causes of its pump speed code P10D9. No manufacturer documents P2E45 itself. Without enable the pump stays dead although the command signal is fine. Pump A's code is P0CED.
c: Enable wire open or shorted between module and pump
Pump relay or its fuse failed, where the design uses one
Faulty enable output in the controlling module
s: Pump B never starts although commanded
MIL and hybrid or charging warning
Power or charging limited as electronics heat up

P2E46.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump B Overspeed - Dry Run
P2E46.d: P2E46 is the dry-run report of electronics coolant pump B: faster than commanded at lower current, the signature of air at the impeller. Porsche describes such self-monitoring on the traction-battery pump of the 2018 Panamera plug-in hybrid (code P0C4A00 there). On Mercedes 167-series SUVs with the M177 V8 and 48 V, trapped air forces the 15 W low-temperature pump into a protective dry-run state and sets pump A's P2B2A7A with a yellow coolant warning; Mercedes prescribes vacuum filling and repeated venting. For BAE hybrid buses the pump maker EMP warned that filling with the pump at only 20 % speed leaves air at the inlet and ruins the shaft seals. No manufacturer publicly documents P2E46. Bleed the loop and find the leak first. Plain overspeed is P2E48, pump A's dry-run code P2B2A.
c: Low coolant level from a leaking hose, joint or component
Air left in the loop after service without vacuum fill
Pump B damaged by earlier dry running
s: Coolant warning message and MIL
Pump starts briefly, then stops again
Gurgling noise or falling level in the electronics reservoir

P2E47.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump B Underspeed
P2E47.d: P2E47 is set when electronics coolant pump B keeps turning but clearly slower than requested. GM's 2018 hybrid tables describe the check for pump A (P19FC): the filtered difference between commanded and reported speed must stay within a calibrated band once the pump has run for 5 s at 11 to 90 % duty, otherwise a Type B fault results. Ford's 2024 summary keeps underspeed (B2) as a fault type of its own, and a Toyota patent for cooling a vehicle drive unit (US20130030643) uses pump speed together with flow and coolant temperature to locate the faulty part. No manufacturer publicly documents P2E47. Unlike a stall (P2E49) the rotor still moves, so bearing friction, impeller deposits, a partial blockage, thick cold coolant or a weak supply are more plausible than a failed motor. Pump A: P2C66.
c: Stiff bearing or worn pump B
Deposits or debris slowing the impeller
Voltage drop on pump supply or ground under load
Incorrect or aged coolant, too viscous when cold
s: MIL and hybrid system warning
Electronics temperatures rise during long drives or fast charging
Occasional power limitation

P2E48.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump B Overspeed
P2E48.d: With P2E48 the controller sees electronics coolant pump B turning faster than commanded, without the separate dry-run test (P2E46) having fired. The usual reason is lost load, since a centrifugal pump accelerates when its impeller gets less liquid, whether from a low level, a collapsed suction hose, partial air or an impeller slipping on its shaft. A Continental patent for electric fuel pumps (US20120245819) compares pump current with voltage or speed to spot leakage or dry running without a pressure sensor. Mercedes' bulletin on pump A's P2B2A7A in the 167 series links excessive speed to leakage or a failed seal. Ford's 2024 summary combines overspeed and dry run in one fault type (B1). No manufacturer publicly documents P2E48. A false speed signal is rarer.
c: Low level or residual air in the electronics loop
Collapsed or kinked hose on the pump inlet side
Impeller slipping on the pump shaft
Implausible speed feedback from the pump electronics
s: MIL, sometimes with a coolant level warning
Louder pump noise than usual
Rising electronics temperatures and power limits

P2E49.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump B Stuck/Stalled
P2E49.d: P2E49 reports that electronics coolant pump B is powered and commanded, but its rotor does not turn or comes to a standstill. Mitsubishi's 2022 Outlander PHEV shows such a test for its electric water pump: with more than 9 V supply the PHEV-ECU sets P10D9 once the reported speed stays under 100 rpm for 0.5 s, against about 500 rpm when healthy. A GM patent (US9599011) checks electric coolant pumps by comparing the measured current with the current expected for the operating point; a blocked rotor shows up as a mismatch. Ford's 2024 summary names the matching failure type actuator stuck (71). No manufacturer publicly documents P2E49. Seized bearings, debris after repairs, frozen coolant and burnt windings are usual causes. Underspeed is P2E47, pump A's stall code P2C68.
c: Seized bearing or failed pump B motor
Debris or sealant residue jamming the impeller
Frozen coolant due to insufficient antifreeze
Supply or ground lost under load
s: MIL and hybrid or drive system warning
Rapid temperature rise in inverter or charger
Strong power reduction or charging stops

P2E4A.t: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor C Circuit
P2E4A.d: P2E4A is the general electrical fault of a third temperature measuring point in the charging inlet, logged when the module sees a defective circuit but does not sort it into low, high or implausible. Unlike sensors A and B, the C row has no intermittent code of its own. Why a third sensor exists: a TE Connectivity patent (US11329436) recalls that above 200 A each DC contact needs its own permanent temperature watch, and inlets such as Sailtran's CCS2 add one at the L1 pin. Which contact C watches is up to the maker, and none documents P2E4A publicly. A Phoenix Contact patent (US10256579) shows that one sensor input may even be a series chain of PTC elements on several pins, so one broken lead silences the whole chain. CARB expects charger faults that block or slow plug-in hybrid charging to be detected.
c: Sensor lead or crimp between inlet and evaluating module broken
Low-voltage connector of the inlet harness loose or corroded
Temperature element C (or one element of a PTC chain) failed inside the inlet
Measuring input in the charger or charge control module defective
s: Charging refused or only possible at reduced power
Charging system warning in the cluster or the app
Charge indicator at the inlet signals a fault

P2E4B.t: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P2E4B.d: P2E4B concerns a sensor C value that is electrically valid yet does not fit the situation, for instance a reading that ignores a heavy charge current, departs from the other inlet sensors or jumps without cause. CARB wants such rationality faults kept under their own code, apart from codes for wiring faults and values beyond the limits. TE Connectivity (US11117478) explains why inlet readings can be off: to keep the sensing circuit isolated, sensors often sit away from the power contact, so they lag behind it and read cooler. No manufacturer documents P2E4B. For the A sensor, GM's PIT5904 on the 2022 Hummer EV and BrightDrop EV600 suspects software or oversized, damaged terminals in heavily used station plugs, and says the test reruns only after about 10 minutes of driving above 2 mph. Hard circuit faults belong to P2E4A, P2E4C and P2E4D.
c: Worn or widened terminals in the charging station plug heating the contact unevenly
Sensor no longer in good thermal contact with its pin
Plausibility logic in the charging software too strict, update available
Temperature element drifted from its characteristic curve
s: Charging stops or starts at reduced power, often at busy public stations
Fault does not reappear until the car has been driven for a while
Charging warning message

P2E4C.t: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor C Circuit Low
P2E4C.d: P2E4C says the voltage on the sensor C input has fallen under its lower limit. Low is about the signal; the temperature it implies depends on the element. Volex fits its NACS inlet with NTC thermistors of 100 kΩ at 25 °C and a B value of 4150 K, whose resistance shrinks as they warm, so with a pull-up a very low voltage stands for an absurdly hot contact. Amphenol's NACS inlet watches DC+ and DC- with PT1000 elements instead; there the same low signal reads as implausibly cold. A short to ground pulls the line down whatever the element, and so can water or corrosion bridging the sensor pins. No manufacturer documents P2E4C publicly, and no thresholds are published. Unlike a true overheat verdict (P2E4E), the circuit is suspect here. P2E4D is the high-signal counterpart.
c: Sensor C signal wire shorted to ground
Water or corrosion bridging the sensor terminals in the inlet or its connector
Measuring input of the evaluating module defective
s: Charging blocked at once or ended shortly after start
Charging system warning
Fault may follow rain or a car wash

P2E4D.t: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor C Circuit High
P2E4D.d: P2E4D is stored when the sensor C input rises above its upper limit. In a pull-up circuit that is the signature of an open loop, an unplugged connector or a short to a supply voltage. Read as temperature, it means very cold for an NTC, but very hot for a PT1000 or a PTC element. The Phoenix Contact patent US10256579 describes PTC elements wired in series on several contacts whose resistance climbs steeply once a set temperature is passed; seen from the module, a broken chain looks the same as a tripped one. Charge controllers such as Watt&Well's EVCC accept either PT1000 inputs, measured in a Wheatstone bridge, or NTC inputs on bias resistors, so what high means depends on how the input is configured. No manufacturer documents P2E4D publicly or gives limits. P2E4C is the low-signal sibling; P2E4E is real overheating.
c: Sensor C loop open, for example a broken wire or unplugged connector
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Temperature element C or one link of a PTC chain open inside the inlet
Measuring input of the evaluating module defective
s: Charging does not start or stops immediately
Charging system warning
Displayed inlet temperature stuck at an extreme value

P2E4E.t: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature C Too High
P2E4E.d: P2E4E is no sensor fault: measuring point C works, but the contact it watches has become too hot, so charging is cut back or ended. For orientation, a DOE laboratory report from August 2025 compares the IEC 62196-1 ceiling, 90 °C when the air is at 40 °C, with the fixed 100 °C of SAE J3400. No manufacturer documents P2E4E publicly. Others show the same logic under their own codes: Porsche stops Taycan charging when the NTC of the left or right charging inlet stays at 90 °C or above for more than 14 s (P31D200), and Hyundai addresses P1BAD on the 2022-2023 Ioniq 5 with a charge-management software update. Honda's Fit EV bulletin names a poor contact to the station plug as the heat source and lets the car finish at lower current. Heat from worn pins, dirt or a weak cable is typical. Sensor C circuit faults are P2E4A to P2E4D.
c: Worn, widened or dirty pins in the station plug or the vehicle inlet
Charging cable with thin conductors heating up at high current (Porsche)
Long high-current session in strong heat or direct sun
Temperature logic in the charging software, update available
s: Charging slows down or stops partway through
Charge indicator at the inlet flashes a fault or reduced-power state
Discoloured or heat-marked pins at the plug or inlet

P2E4F.t: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor D Circuit
P2E4F.d: P2E4F is the general circuit fault of the fourth inlet temperature sensor, used when the wiring is clearly wrong but not classed as low, high or implausible; the D row has no intermittent code either. Ford is the one maker whose public papers show a sensor D in use: SSM 55080 names P2E53, the overheating verdict for point D, stored in the secondary OBD module (SOBDM) of the Mustang Mach-E, E-Transit and F-150 Lightning, so that module reads sensor D. Ford does not publish P2E4F or say which pin D watches. A fourth point makes sense because, as TE patent US11329436 puts it, each DC contact above 200 A needs its own monitoring and a 90 °C contact must be reported within 30 s. On the smart with 22 kW charger, Mercedes traced inlet sensor codes to loose low-voltage plugs at the charger (LI54.10-P-067823).
c: Low-voltage connector between inlet harness and evaluating module loose (smart for sensor A)
Sensor D wiring chafed or broken
Temperature element D failed (normally replaced with the inlet)
Measuring input in the SOBDM or charger defective
s: DC fast charging refused or limited
Charging warning in the cluster
Fault may only show with a warm or cold inlet

P2E50.t: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor D Circuit Range/Performance
P2E50.d: P2E50 flags sensor D for delivering a believable voltage that the logic still rejects. A module can test this in several ways: compare D with a sensor on a contact that carries the same current, check whether it warms as expected under load, or look for steps no metal pin could make. Inlets that monitor both DC+ and DC-, as Amphenol's NACS inlet does with PT1000 elements, offer such a partner. Ford's special service message 55080 proves that its electric pickup, van and crossover read a sensor D, since it cites the overheating code P2E53, yet Ford publishes nothing on P2E50. No other maker documents it. CARB asks for rationality checks to be two-sided where feasible and stored apart from circuit codes. When D is distrusted, the car usually limits or refuses fast charging. P2E4F, P2E51 and P2E52 cover electrical faults.
c: Sensor D has lost good thermal contact with its pin
One contact heating far more than its partner due to wear or dirt
Plausibility thresholds in the module software, update available
s: DC fast charging limited or ended early
AC charging may still work
Charging warning message

P2E51.t: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor D Circuit Low
P2E51.d: P2E51 reports a sensor D voltage below the valid band. TE Connectivity lists thermistors, thermocouples and resistance temperature detectors as candidate elements for inlet sensing (US10960781), and the patent also explains the stakes: contact resistance heats the inlet at high current and could melt parts or start a fire if nobody watches. With an NTC thermistor a low signal suggests a contact far too hot to be real; with a resistance detector such as a PT1000 it suggests a pin colder than the climate allows. Either way the most common physical cause is a short to ground or moisture across the sensor leads. The only public trace of a sensor D is Ford's SSM 55080 on P2E53 for three of its electric models; P2E51 itself appears in no maker's published documents. High signal is P2E52, real overheating P2E53.
c: Sensor D signal wire shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion in the inlet harness connector
Measuring input of the evaluating module defective
s: DC fast charging refused
Charging warning message
Inlet temperature reading implausible in live data

P2E52.t: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor D Circuit High
P2E52.d: P2E52 is the mirror case of P2E51: the sensor D input sits above its valid band, usually because of an interrupted sensor lead, a connector that has backed out, or a short to a supply line. Volex quotes for its NACS inlet NTC thermistors with an operating range of -40 to +125 °C; an open NTC loop looks like a contact colder than that range, which hides any real heating. With a PT1000 an open loop looks like a hot pin and stops charging at once. Only Ford is known to read a sensor D, as its bulletin on overheating code P2E53 shows, but it gives no thresholds or details for P2E52. CARB asks for circuit checks on input components and, on plug-in hybrids, for detection of charger faults that stop or slow charging. Real overheating at point D is P2E53.
c: Sensor D lead broken or connector backed out
Signal wire shorted to a supply line
Temperature element D open inside the inlet
Measuring input of the evaluating module defective
s: DC fast charging does not start or stops at once
Charging warning message
Inlet temperature reading fixed at an extreme value

P2E53.t: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature D Too High
P2E53.d: P2E53 means measuring point D in the charging inlet reports a contact that is too hot, and charging is throttled or halted. Ford documents this exact code in SSM 55080: on Mustang Mach-E built up to 25 June 2023, E-Transit 2022-2025 and F-150 Lightning 2022-2023, DC fast charging can stop with P2E53:27 and/or P0EEE:27 in the SOBDM. The 27 is the J2012 subtype for a signal changing faster than allowed. Ford blames SOBDM software, says a new charge port will not help, keeps AC charging available and expected a fix in Q3 2026. That differs from SSM 51866, where P0E5F at 48 A AC led to a new charge port. A Ford patent (US10377264) describes the port sensor feeding the charger, which derates or shuts down above a threshold. A DOE report cites 90 to 100 °C contact limits. Circuit faults of sensor D are P2E4F to P2E52.
c: SOBDM software misjudging DC fast-charge heating (Ford SSM 55080)
Worn or contaminated DC pins in the station plug or the inlet
Very high charging current in hot weather
Heat-damaged inlet contacts needing a new charge port
s: DC fast charging stops at level 3 stations
AC charging at home or level 2 still works
Charging power reduced during fast charging

P2E54.d: P2E54 is the general circuit fault of a third exhaust pressure sensor, C. Its position is set by the manufacturer; engines can carry several such sensors, as in a GE patent with one pressure sensor in each of two exhaust manifolds. No manufacturer publicly documents P2E54; Ford's 2023 diesels and its EcoBoost petrol engines use sensor A only. For that sensor Ford's diesel summary uses the general circuit code when the digital SENT sensor reports an error status or delivers raw data above a limit, while lost communication goes to U0691; for sensor C that is U069F. CARB's heavy-duty rule lists exhaust pressure sensors among monitored input components. Expect the MIL and, depending on use, limited boost or EGR. Low and High are P2E56 and P2E57.
c: Exhaust pressure sensor C failed internally
Wiring near the exhaust damaged by heat or chafing
Corroded or loose connector at sensor C
s: MIL on
Reduced power if boost or EGR control falls back to substitute values
Other exhaust or EGR monitors may not run

P2E55.t: Exhaust Pressure Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
P2E55.d: P2E55 is the plausibility test of exhaust pressure sensor C: the voltage is in range, but the pressure does not suit the operating state. CARB wants such rationality faults stored apart from circuit faults. No maker documents P2E55; Ford's 2023 diesel summary shows the pattern for sensor A. With the engine stopped for at least 10 s the reading may differ from ambient pressure by no more than 15 kPa; while driving it is set against a model and may not exceed it by 500 kPa or fall 100 kPa below it. A Ford patent (US7779633) computes the pressure ahead of the turbine; a Bosch patent checks two sensors on either side of a flow restriction against a modelled pressure drop. FCA warns that real back pressure from a clogged particulate filter sets the code on Cummins diesels, so check the exhaust first.
c: Real back pressure from a clogged particulate filter or catalyst
Sooted or cracked sensing tube to sensor C
Sensor C offset drifted or stuck mid-range
Exhaust leak near the measuring point
s: MIL, often without noticeable driveability change
Particulate filter or EGR codes alongside
Reduced power if the pressure is really too high

P2E56.t: Exhaust Pressure Sensor C Circuit Low
P2E56.d: P2E56 means the signal of exhaust pressure sensor C stays under the lowest voltage a working sensor can produce. Analogue exhaust pressure sensors return a share of their 5 V reference; Ford's petrol transfer function for sensor A puts 49 kPa at 0.3 V and flags anything under 0.21 V for 5 s, while its 2023 diesels use 0.1 V for 2 s. No manufacturer publicly documents P2E56. A signal wire shorted to ground, a lost 5 V reference or a sensor with a failed output stage are the usual reasons; if several sensors on the same reference set low codes at once, the reference or the module is the better suspect. Functions that use the value, such as EGR or turbocharger control, then rely on substitute values, so power may be limited. The high-side code is P2E57, sensor A's low code P0472.
c: Signal wire of sensor C shorted to ground
5 V reference open or pulled down by another sensor
s: MIL on
Possible loss of power from substitute values
Further low codes of sensors sharing the reference

P2E57.t: Exhaust Pressure Sensor C Circuit High
P2E57.d: P2E57 reports a signal from exhaust pressure sensor C above the plausible ceiling. For sensor A Ford sets that ceiling at 4.80 V, on petrol engines checked while the EGR monitor runs and with 5 s to fail, on 2023 diesels with 2 s; in Ford's petrol transfer function 4.7 V already equals about 378 kPa. On a three-wire sensor a high reading usually comes from an open ground, a signal line in contact with the 5 V supply or a battery-fed circuit, or, depending on the input circuit, an open signal line pulled up inside the module. Soot or moisture in the sensing path rarely produce this electrical fault. No manufacturer publicly documents P2E57. After repair, clear the code and confirm that sensor C reads ambient pressure with the engine off. Low is P2E56, sensor A's high code P0473.
c: Open ground circuit of sensor C
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Open signal wire pulled high by the module input
s: MIL on
Boost or EGR control in substitute mode, possibly less power

P2E58.t: Alternative Fuel Random/Multiple Cylinder Misfire Detected
P2E58.d: P2E58 is the collective misfire code for running on the second fuel, mostly CNG or LPG: misfires are counted while gas is burned, but no single cylinder can be blamed, or several each carry a large share. CARB treats a bi-fuel car as alternate-fueled only while it runs on gas and asks for the same misfire monitor as on petrol; EPA likewise requires converters to keep OBD working on the conversion fuel. No carmaker documents P2E58 openly; Honda's Civic CNG and Roush propane trucks log gas-mode misfire with the ordinary P03xx codes. A GM patent checks both fuels: misfire on gas only points to the gas side, on both fuels to ignition. Likely culprits are an iced or poorly heated regulator or vaporiser, a clogged filter, low gas pressure or a lean mixture. One-cylinder faults are P2E59 to P2E60.
c: Gas pressure regulator or LPG vaporiser iced up or not heated enough (low coolant flow, moisture in the gas)
Too little gas pressure at the rail – clogged gas filter, nearly empty tank or weak regulator
Worn plugs or weak coils on several cylinders that cope with petrol but not with the harder-to-ignite gas mixture
Lean gas mixture from an intake air leak or wrong gas-system calibration
s: Rough running or jerking only while the engine runs on gas
Bi-fuel vehicle switches back to petrol on its own
Check engine light on or flashing, gas-mode indicator may flash

P2E59.d: P2E59 means that, while the engine is burning its gaseous fuel, the misfire monitor puts the dropouts on cylinder 1; CARB allows a single-cylinder code once more than 90 % of counted misfires fall on one cylinder. In most numbering schemes cylinder 1 is the frontmost. No manufacturer publishes P2E59. Honda logged misfire on its 2008 Civic CNG as P0301 to P0304 and had dealers swap coils to see whether the fault moved with the coil. On GM's 2013 Silverado/Sierra bi-fuel the injector module hands over from petrol to CNG injectors one cylinder after another, starting at cylinder 1, so a misfire seen only at changeover should be told apart from one in steady gas mode. Check the CNG injector, its hose and nozzle on cylinder 1, then coil and plug. Misfire on petrol too: P0301.
c: Sticking or leaking gas injector on cylinder 1
Cracked injector hose or loose nozzle in the intake port of cylinder 1
Weak coil or worn plug on cylinder 1 that fails only under gas
Fault in the fuel changeover module or its programming (misfire only at the switch from petrol to gas)
s: Rough idle on gas that disappears in petrol mode
Stumble at the moment the system changes over to gas
Check engine light, possibly flashing under load

P2E5A.d: P2E5A says cylinder 2 is the one losing combustion while the engine is supplied with alternative fuel; P0302 is its petrol twin. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. On inline engines cylinder 2 follows cylinder 1; on V engines it is either the foremost cylinder on the other bank (GM, Chrysler) or the second one of the first bank (Ford, Audi). The gas injector is the typical gas-specific suspect: compressor oil carried in CNG condenses after the pressure regulator, reaches the injectors unevenly and can gum single valves or make them close erratically, as GM and Siemens patents describe. Landi Renzo's service manual for its 6.0-litre CNG conversion asks for misfire codes to check the injector plug, the nozzle seated in its port, the drive signal and injector wiring not crossed between cylinders.
c: Gas injector on cylinder 2 gummed or sluggish from compressor oil in the gas
Injector harness of the conversion routed crosswise, so cylinder 2 receives another cylinder's pulse
Injection nozzle of cylinder 2 not properly seated in the manifold port
Coil or plug on cylinder 2 too weak for gas operation
s: Uneven running on gas, normal on petrol
Higher gas consumption and loss of power
Check engine light

P2E5B.d: P2E5B flags misfire on cylinder 3 during operation on CNG or LPG; on petrol the matching code is P0303. No manufacturer publishes P2E5B. One cause that belongs to gas engines in particular is valve seat wear: dry gaseous fuels leave few combustion products, so valve and seat insert rub metal on metal and the seat recedes, as a Honda patent on seat materials explains. Once a valve stops sealing, compression in that cylinder falls and combustion becomes unreliable. For this reason natural-gas engines usually carry hardened exhaust valves and seats, and Ford's 2014 F-150 gaseous-fuel prep package added hardened valves, seats, pistons and rings. A compression or leak-down test on cylinder 3 separates this from injector or ignition faults; engines converted without hardened parts deserve extra suspicion.
c: Valve seat recession on cylinder 3 from dry gas operation, valve no longer seals
Worn plug or failing coil on cylinder 3
Retrofit gas conversion on an engine without hardened valves and seats
s: Misfire on gas that slowly gets worse, later also on petrol
Low compression on cylinder 3, sometimes a ticking valve noise
Check engine light

P2E5C.d: P2E5C is stored when the misfire counter blames cylinder 4 while gas is being burned; in petrol mode the code would be P0304. No manufacturer documents P2E5C publicly, and Deutz's fault list for its eControls LPG, CNG and bi-fuel engines reports such events with the ordinary P0301 to P0304. On four-cylinder engines cylinder 4 is the last one in the block. Ignition is the main gas-related suspect: NGK points out that a gas/air charge needs a clearly higher firing voltage than petrol, which loads the coils and wears the plugs faster, and the US Department of Energy notes that natural gas reacts more sensitively to spark quality. A coil or plug that still works on petrol can therefore drop out on gas alone. Check plug type and gap for gas, coil and boot, then move the coil to another cylinder.
c: Spark plug on cylinder 4 worn or unsuited for gas (gap too wide, wrong heat range)
Coil or plug boot on cylinder 4 breaking down under the higher firing voltage
Gas injector on cylinder 4 sticking or delivering too little
s: Misfire mainly under load or acceleration on gas
Engine runs cleanly after switching to petrol
Check engine light, flashing during heavy misfire

P2E5D.d: P2E5D assigns gas-mode misfire to cylinder 5, which exists only on engines with five or more cylinders, such as the 3.6-litre V6 in GM's 2015 Impala bi-fuel, V8 trucks or inline-six gas engines in buses. P0305 is the petrol equivalent. No manufacturer publishes P2E5D. With bank-wise numbering (Ford, Audi) cylinder 5 opens the second bank; with crank-order numbering (GM, Chrysler) it lies on the odd-numbered bank. In the Impala, GM placed an oil separator with filter in the low-pressure line before the CNG rail and set a 36,000-mile change interval; an overdue element lets oil reach the injectors. For its heavy natural-gas engines, Cummins names worn, damaged or mishandled spark plugs as a leading cause of unplanned misfire downtime. CARB §1971.1 covers such heavy-duty gas engines.
c: Spark plug on cylinder 5 past its change interval or damaged when handled
Low-pressure oil separator/filter not serviced, oil reaches the gas injector of cylinder 5
Cracked coil extension or boot on cylinder 5 (heavy-duty gas engines)
s: Vibration and power loss on gas
Bi-fuel vehicle drops back to petrol
Check engine light

P2E5E.d: P2E5E names cylinder 6 as the misfiring one while the engine runs on alternative fuel; P0306 is its petrol twin. No manufacturer documents the code openly. On inline sixes cylinder 6 is the rearmost. With liquid propane injection, fuel turning to vapour in the rail is a known gas-specific cause: Roush CleanTech's diagnostic manual names running in the vapour region as a reason for P03xx misfire, a Ford patent notes that propane left in a hot rail boils off after shutdown and expands about 250-fold, and an Agility patent describes vapour forming when pressure sags along a rail feeding its injectors in series, so too little fuel is metered. Note whether misfire follows hot restarts or a low tank. A Texas training manual on propane conversions recommends the scan tool's cylinder balance test to confirm the cylinder.
c: Gas or liquid-propane injector on cylinder 6 sticking or leaking
Propane vapour in the liquid-injection rail (hot restart, low rail or tank pressure)
Plug or coil on cylinder 6 failing under gas
Low tank pressure in cold weather or nearly empty tank
s: Misfire or rough running shortly after a hot restart
Long cranking time when the engine is warm
Check engine light

P2E5F.d: P2E5F puts alternative-fuel misfire on cylinder 7, so it concerns eight-cylinder engines, for instance GM's Vortec 6.0 V8 in the bi-fuel Silverado/Sierra or the dedicated CNG and LPG Express/Savana vans that GM lists in its gaseous-fuel overview bulletin. P0307 is the petrol counterpart. No maker documents P2E5F publicly. On GM V8s cylinder 7 is the rear cylinder of the odd-numbered bank; on Ford V8s it is the third cylinder of the second bank. Conversion hardware adds failure points per cylinder: Ford's 2003 bi-fuel CNG system fed gas through sleeves set into each petrol injector seat, with a separate module driving the gas injectors, and Landi Renzo's 6.0-litre manual tells technicians to verify each nozzle in its port and the routing of the injector harness. Check these before the coil.
c: Gas injector on cylinder 7 faulty or sticking
Leaking injector sleeve or loose nozzle at cylinder 7's intake runner
Conversion injector harness damaged or misrouted near the rear of the engine
Coil or plug on cylinder 7 too weak for gas
s: Rough running on gas, smooth on petrol
Gas-mode indicator flashing or automatic return to petrol
Check engine light

P2E60.d: P2E60 is the last cylinder-specific code of the alternative-fuel misfire group and points to cylinder 8; the next code, P2E61, covers misfire with low fuel. Petrol twin: P0308. No manufacturer documents P2E60 openly. On GM V8s cylinder 8 is the rear cylinder of the even-numbered bank, on Ford V8s the rear of the second bank. In Ford's 1999 bi-fuel LPG/CNG system for the 5.4-litre V8 a metering unit called Compuvalve supplied gas, and an adjustable tuning tee split the flow between the two rails, so a poor split can starve one side. A patent on cleaning Compuvalve injectors names compressor oil as the main deposit. A GM patent shows the protective idea behind such codes: switch a misfiring cylinder to liquid fuel instead of cutting it, which would cost about a quarter to a third of torque.
c: Deposits from compressor oil in the gas injector serving cylinder 8
Coil or plug on cylinder 8, often hard to reach at the rear of the engine
Uneven gas split between the two rails starving the bank with cylinder 8 (older bi-fuel systems)
Valve seat wear on cylinder 8 after long gas operation
s: Misfire on gas, possibly with lean codes on one bank
Engine shakes at idle on gas
Check engine light

P2E61.t: Alternative Fuel Misfire Detected With Low Fuel
P2E61.d: P2E61 records misfire that occurs while the engine burns its gaseous fuel and that fuel is almost used up. No manufacturer documents the code publicly. CARB treats a bi-fuel car as alternate-fueled only while it runs on gas and lets makers seek approval to suspend misfire monitoring at 15 % fuel or less, since a nearly empty tank can cause misfire by itself. Ford patents explain it for CNG: the regulator keeps the rail at a few bar, but near 500 psi tank pressure the flow chokes and rail pressure wavers, so metering suffers; one known answer is switching to petrol at low tank pressure. Another Ford patent reads low rail pressure despite gas in the tank, e.g. from ice, as a supply restriction. Refill and recheck; misfire with ample gas is P2E58 to P2E60.
c: Gas tank close to empty, so the regulator can no longer hold rail pressure
Tank pressure or level signal reads too high, so the system stays on gas too long
Restriction in the gas line (clogged filter, ice) that only shows when tank pressure is low
Worn plugs or coils that cannot ignite the leaner gas mixture near empty
s: Stumbling or power loss on gas when the gas gauge is near empty
Vehicle changes over to petrol on its own
Check engine light on

P2E62.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve E Control Circuit/Open
P2E62.d: Coolant bypass valve E is the fifth electrically driven coolant valve in the SAE lettering; which coolant path it controls (heater, radiator, transmission, block) is up to the carmaker. P2E62 says the engine computer sees an open or otherwise faulty drive circuit. No manufacturer documents valve E publicly. Ford's 2020–2023 gasoline summary shows the usual logic for its valves A to D: a smart driver reports an output fault during continuous monitoring and the code sets after 5 s. Driver chips find a broken line by feeding small test currents and checking where the pin voltage settles, as an AMI Semiconductor patent describes. VW fixed P2681 entries on 2024 Atlas models with new engine software instead of parts, so check for updates. Shorts to ground or supply are P2E63 and P2E64.
c: Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the valve
Broken wire in the drive or supply line
Open winding in the valve actuator motor or solenoid
ECM software fault or defective output stage
s: Check engine light or service message
Heating, warm-up or cooling behaves differently, depending on what valve E controls
Valve stays in its de-energised default position

P2E63.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve E Control Circuit Low
P2E63.d: P2E63 flags a drive line for coolant bypass valve E whose voltage is lower than the commanded state allows, typically a grounded wire or a heavy leakage path to ground in the harness or the actuator. No carmaker documents valve E publicly. CARB does not even force separate codes for open and shorted outputs, so many systems use only one code. Toyota shows the subtype idea on valve A: P268111 marks a grounded circuit, P268115 a battery short or a broken line; bulletin T-SB-0112-24 fits a new water valve or water bypass hose assembly, depending on model, on A25A and M20A engines (2018–2021). A 1995 US patent on solenoid drivers suspends its checks for a broken line or a battery short for as long as a ground fault persists. Check the harness for chafing at hot or moving parts before replacing the valve.
c: Chafed drive wire touching engine ground
Internal short in the valve actuator, often after coolant got into it
Corrosion bridging pins in the connector
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light, sometimes a maintenance message
Valve does not move or stays in its default position
Slower warm-up or changed heater output

P2E64.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve E Control Circuit High
P2E64.d: P2E64 is the high-side counterpart: the control line of coolant bypass valve E carries more voltage than expected, usually because it touches a supply wire, or the load has gone open in a way the output stage reads as high. Valve E itself appears in no public manufacturer document. Ford's 2024 summary shows how this is commonly grouped: for its valves A to D the smart driver's short-to-battery result (fault byte 12) is filed under the High code, for example P26BF for valve D, alongside the general circuit code. Toyota pairs short to battery and open circuit in one subtype, P268115. A supplier patent (AMI Semiconductor) separates the cases by driving test currents into the pin and comparing the resulting voltage with thresholds. Check for chafing against live wires and water in the connector.
c: Drive wire chafed through and touching a battery-voltage wire
Moisture or coolant in the connector creating a path to supply voltage
Open actuator winding that the output stage reads as high voltage
Defective output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine light
Valve is not driven and stays in its de-energised position
Possible change in heater output or warm-up time

P2E65.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve E Stuck/Open
P2E65.d: P2E65 is a functional fault: the electrics of valve E are fine, but the valve remains open although it was told to close. The official title is written Stuck/Open, though it means stuck open, the partner of P2E67. No carmaker documents valve E publicly. GM shows the method on its block rotary valve D (P26C0): commanded and measured angle differ by 10° or more while the raw feedback sits at 50° or above, 4 of 5 seconds, Type A in the 2019 L3B tables. Without a position sensor, a Ford patent infers a stuck warm-up valve from coolant and transmission fluid temperatures before and after the command. GM bulletin 21-NA-149 adds that a chafed engine harness can trigger such valve codes. Open valves waste heat during warm-up.
c: Valve body jammed open by deposits or worn seals
Broken gear or weak actuator that cannot drive the valve closed
Position sensor or its wiring reporting an open valve that is actually closed
Chafed engine harness disturbing drive or feedback signals
s: Engine and cabin heat take longer to come up
Check engine light
Slightly higher fuel use on short trips

P2E66.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve E Range/Performance
P2E66.d: P2E66 is the broad plausibility code for valve E: the valve moves, but not to the right place, not fast enough, or its feedback does not match the command, without a clear stuck-open or stuck-closed verdict. No manufacturer documents valve E publicly. A Hyundai patent outlines such a test for a rotary coolant valve: drive it to its end positions, compare what the housing-mounted position sensor reports, try a release routine if it seems stuck, and otherwise park it in a limp-home position that keeps coolant flowing to the radiator and warn the driver. Ram bulletin 07-005-24 (2022–2023 Ram 1500, 3.6 L) traces the comparable valve A code P26A3 to a cracked gear inside the three-way coolant valve and replaces it.
c: Cracked or worn gear inside the valve actuator
Valve sluggish from deposits, degraded coolant or worn seals
Position sensor drifting or lost end-stop learn values
Low supply voltage slowing the actuator
s: Check engine light, sometimes a coolant or maintenance message
Uneven heater output or warm-up
Possible fallback to a fixed valve position

P2E67.t: Engine Coolant Bypass Valve E Stuck Closed
P2E67.d: P2E67 means valve E stays shut although the control asked it to open. No manufacturer documents valve E publicly. GM's closed-side test on block valve D (P26C2) shows the pattern: a gap of more than 5° between commanded and measured angle while the raw feedback stays below 50°, 4 of 5 seconds, Type B in the 2025 table 25OBDG03B; the test pauses during end-stop learning. Ford patents describe temperature-based checks instead: valves are closed one at a time and the coolant temperature reaction is compared with the expected one, and a transmission warm-up valve counts as stuck closed when the fluid fails to warm as expected after the open command. A closed valve can be harmless (heater path) or serious (block or radiator path, risk of hot spots).
c: Valve jammed closed by deposits, debris or swollen seals
Actuator motor or gearing unable to open the valve
Position feedback stuck at the closed value
Wrong coolant or trapped air after service upsetting the temperature-based check
s: Check engine light
Little or no heat from the heater, or rising engine temperature, depending on the circuit
Possible reduced engine power to protect the engine

P2E68.t: System Too Lean During Cylinder Deactivation Bank 1
P2E68.d: P2E68 is a fuel trim fault that is judged only while cylinders are shut off: in that mode bank 1 needs more fuel correction than allowed. GM uses it on its 4.2-litre twin-turbo V8 (LTA, table 19OBDG07): the engine learns a separate multiplicative long-term trim for deactivation mode, and the code sets when that factor for bank 1 rises above 1.23 and has been steady for at least 10 s; Type B, MIL after two trips. Enables include coolant at 54.8 °C or more, intake air under 90 °C and no wide-open throttle. Full-engine lean faults use other codes, such as P2177. On that engine half the cylinders run in this mode, two per bank. A Ford patent explains why a faulty valve deactivator shows up as a bank-specific trim shift.
c: Restricted injector on one of the cylinders that keep firing on bank 1
Unmetered air entering bank 1 (intake leak, seal, PCV)
Deactivating rocker or lifter on bank 1 not holding the valves shut, pumping air into the exhaust
Bank 1 oxygen sensor reading biased rich
s: Check engine light after two trips
Slight shake or surge at light cruise when cylinders are shut off
