Cylinder deactivation may be used less often

P2E69.t: System Too Rich During Cylinder Deactivation Bank 1
P2E69.d: P2E69 is the rich mirror of P2E68: with cylinders deactivated, bank 1 has to pull fuel out beyond the permitted range. In GM's 19OBDG07 tables for the 4.2-litre twin-turbo V8 the separate long-term trim factor learned for deactivation mode must drop below 0.77 and stay steady; it shares the enable logic of P2E68 and is Type B, MIL on the second trip. A Ford patent on variable displacement V8s shows how such a rich shift arises: if one cylinder fails to deactivate, air blows through it, the airflow meter reports more air, fuel rises accordingly, and the bank that is working normally runs rich. A leaking injector on a firing cylinder or a fuel-diluted crankcase can do the same. The running-mode rich codes are separate.
c: A cylinder that should be off still breathing, so measured airflow and fuel delivery are too high
Leaking or dribbling direct injector on bank 1
Fuel vapour from diluted oil or a stuck-open purge valve
Bank 1 oxygen sensor reading biased lean
s: Check engine light after two trips
Higher fuel use, possible fuel smell
Rough running in deactivation mode

P2E6A.t: System Too Lean During Cylinder Deactivation Bank 2
P2E6A.d: P2E6A applies the lean test to bank 2, the cylinder row without cylinder 1. GM sets it on the 4.2-litre twin-turbo V8 of the 2019 table 19OBDG07 when the trim factor learned for deactivation mode on bank 2 exceeds 1.23 while stable; Type B. The engine closes the valves of four cylinders and fires in the order 1-4-6-7, so on GM's odd/even bank split only cylinders 4 and 6 keep working on bank 2, and a single weak injector there weighs heavily. A separate camshaft-driven high-pressure pump feeds each bank, so a pump problem can also stay on one side. CARB requires the fuel system to be watched for any fault that pushes emissions over the limits. A lean trim on both banks during deactivation points to a shared cause such as an intake leak.
c: Weak injector on cylinder 4 or 6, which carry bank 2 in deactivation mode
Bank 2 high-pressure fuel pump delivering too little
Deactivating rocker on bank 2 letting air pass into the exhaust
Exhaust leak ahead of the bank 2 oxygen sensor
s: Check engine light after two trips
Hesitation at light load in deactivation mode
Often no noticeable change in normal driving

P2E6B.t: System Too Rich During Cylinder Deactivation Bank 2
P2E6B.d: P2E6B closes the set: bank 2 runs rich while cylinders are switched off. GM's 19OBDG07 tables (4.2-litre twin-turbo V8, LTA) fail the test when bank 2's deactivation-mode trim factor falls below 0.77 and has settled; Type B, two trips, same enable conditions as the other three codes. Typical systems keep the valves of the idle cylinders shut and stop fuelling them, so the shut cylinders act as air springs; if a valve or injector of a cylinder that should be off keeps working, measured air and real air per firing cylinder no longer match. Compared with P2E69 the fault sits on the other bank; a rich result on both banks suggests a common source such as purge vapour or fuel-diluted oil. GM calls the system Active Fuel Management.
c: Leaking injector on bank 2, including one on a cylinder that should be shut off
Deactivation rocker or its oil-control solenoid not switching on one cylinder
Excess purge vapour or fuel-diluted engine oil
Bank 2 oxygen sensor reading biased lean
s: Check engine light after two trips
Higher fuel consumption on the highway
Possible sooty tailpipe on bank 2 side

P2E6C.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack A Cell Thickness
P2E6C.d: P2E6C means the cells of high-voltage pack A have become thicker than the battery controller tolerates: the cells are swelling. A healthy cell only breathes a little while charging; GE and University of Michigan measured about 0.1 mm, 1 % of its thickness, on the Sanyo cell of Ford's Fusion HEV pack. Lasting growth comes from aging or from gas after overcharge or overheating. No manufacturer documents P2E6C publicly. Kia shows a comparable guard: on the 2017 Niro hybrid a switch on the pack closes when cells bulge after overcharge, and the BMS then opens the main relays (P1BA7). A Ford patent likewise lets the BECM reduce current or open contactors when cell pressure is too high. Expect power limits or no READY; P2E6D to P2E6F are faults of the sensor itself.
c: Aged cells in pack A that have grown permanently thicker
Gas build-up in cells after overcharging or overheating
Module clamping or end plates loosened, so cells can expand further
s: Hybrid or EV system warning, often with reduced power
Vehicle may not switch to READY because the main contactors stay open
Charging blocked or limited

P2E6D.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack A Cell Thickness Sensor Circuit High
P2E6D.d: P2E6D says the signal from the cell thickness sensor of pack A sits above the range the controller accepts as a real reading. The code describes the voltage, not swollen cells. No manufacturer documents P2E6D publicly, and how such a sensor is built varies: a Ford patent uses a resistive gauge on a thinned cell wall whose resistance climbs as the wall bulges, LG uses a fibre grid read by a photoresistor, and classic strain gauges are read through a Wheatstone bridge. With a pull-up input, an open wire or lost ground drives the value high; a short to a supply can do the same. Ford's BECM keeps the contactors open if a self-check finds cells no longer monitored. CARB wants separate codes for low and high out-of-range faults; low is P2E6E.
c: Open signal or ground wire, unplugged or corroded connector inside pack A
Signal wire chafed against a supply or reference line
Thickness or pressure sensing element itself failed open
s: Hybrid or EV warning light
Power or charging limited as a precaution
In some designs the vehicle will not go to READY

P2E6E.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack A Cell Thickness Sensor Circuit Low
P2E6E.d: P2E6E is the low-side counterpart to P2E6D: the thickness or swelling sensor of pack A delivers less signal than any intact circuit should, typically from a short to ground, a missing supply or a dead sensor amplifier. No manufacturer documents P2E6E publicly. Two patents show why a low reading can hide a real problem. LG places piezo elements in the cooling gap between cells; they produce a voltage only when expanding cells press on them, which the BMS evaluates. Bosch and Samsung SDI describe a pressure film around the electrode winding whose charge is turned into a voltage by an amplifier fed from the battery. If that output collapses, the controller can no longer see swelling, so it flags the circuit. CARB requires each out-of-range fault of an input to be stored separately.
c: Signal wire shorted to ground or to the module housing
Sensor supply or amplifier supply missing
Sensing element or its amplifier failed
Moisture or coolant in a connector inside the pack creating a leakage path
s: Hybrid or EV warning light
Reduced power or limited charging

P2E6F.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack A Cell Thickness Sensor Circuit Performance
P2E6F.d: P2E6F covers a thickness sensor in pack A whose reading is electrically valid but does not behave as the controller expects. Cell thickness is not static: it rises and falls with state of charge, which is why Bosch and Samsung SDI propose using the swelling force of the winding to estimate charge and health, and a graphene film sensor studied at Warwick tracked charge level from expansion alone. A sensor that stays frozen while the pack is charged and discharged, or drifts against that pattern, is therefore suspect. Nebraska and Oak Ridge researchers found that expansion also depends on current, charge voltage and clamping force, so limits must be wide. No manufacturer documents P2E6F publicly. CARB asks for such rationality checks where feasible.
c: Sensor loosened, shifted or no longer bonded to the cell or end plate
Sensor drifting with age or temperature
Contact resistance in connectors distorting the reading
Missing calibration or relearn after module replacement
s: Warning light without noticeable driving change at first
Charging or power may be restricted later

P2E70.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack B Cell Thickness
P2E70.d: P2E70 is the swelling code for a second high-voltage pack, B, in vehicles that carry two; which pack is A and which B is set by the maker. The controller judges that cells in pack B have grown too thick. No manufacturer documents P2E70 publicly. Research explains why thickness is watched at all. A University of Michigan patent reads the force on the module end plates and uses it to estimate capacity loss, and Southwest Research Institute derives aging from the strain at equal charge level, new versus aged. In real failures far more happens: in tests by the UK HSE a heated 5 Ah pouch cell released about 4 litres of gas on average, and the force of that swelling matters most where cells sit tightly packed. Pack A swelling is P2E6C.
c: Cells in pack B aged and permanently thicker
Gas generation after overcharge, deep discharge or heat
Poor cooling of pack B accelerating cell degradation
s: Hybrid or EV warning with power reduction
Reduced range or charging blocked
Vehicle may refuse READY

P2E71.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack B Cell Thickness Sensor Circuit High
P2E71.d: P2E71 flags the thickness sensor circuit of pack B as reading too high. Not every swelling detector is analog: LG's module patent uses a panel that slides along a ramp until it touches a contact sensor, and a Lithium Energy and Power patent fits cells with insulated contact elements that close under pressure. Ford also describes a thin wire across a weakened cell wall that tears once the wall bulges, cutting the current through it. In such switch-type layouts an open circuit and a triggered sensor can look alike, so the controller needs a defined resting level to tell them apart. No manufacturer documents P2E71 publicly. Check connectors after pack B service first; low signal is P2E72.
c: Sensor connector in pack B not fully seated after battery work
Broken signal or ground wire to the sensor
Signal line shorted to a supply voltage
s: Hybrid or EV warning light
Possibly limited power or charging

P2E72.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack B Cell Thickness Sensor Circuit Low
P2E72.d: P2E72 means the pack B thickness sensor reports a signal below its valid floor. On a bridge-type strain gauge, the output is a small fraction of the excitation voltage that grows with strain, so losing that excitation or shorting a bridge leg to ground pulls the reading towards zero. Capacitive designs, such as a patented pressure-sensitive QTC sensor coated with indium tin oxide, depend on a measuring module that can fail the same way. LG's piezo elements in the cell gaps only output voltage under pressure, so a short across them hides real expansion. No manufacturer documents P2E72 publicly. CARB demands separate codes for low and high faults; the high side of this circuit is P2E71, pack A's low code P2E6E.
c: Signal line or sensor shorted to ground inside pack B
Sensor excitation or reference supply lost
Fault in the measuring circuit of the battery monitoring module
s: Hybrid or EV warning light
Power or charging may be reduced as a precaution

P2E73.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack B Cell Thickness Sensor Circuit Performance
P2E73.d: P2E73 indicates that the thickness sensor of pack B delivers values within range that the controller cannot reconcile with what it otherwise knows about the pack. Free expansion of a healthy cell is small, about 1 % of its thickness on the Ford Fusion HEV cell measured by GE, so a sensor must resolve fractions of a millimetre; GE's thin eddy-current coils between cells covered 0 to 2 mm. Plausibility can also come from other signals: LG patents detecting swelling from the temperature sensors already in a module, and the Michigan force method links end-plate load to capacity fade, giving references to compare against. No manufacturer documents P2E73 publicly. CARB asks for rationality checks where feasible; pack A's version is P2E6F.
c: Sensor mounting or gap changed, for example after module work
Sensor drift or degraded sensing element
Plausibility limits in the battery controller software too tight
s: Warning light, often with no other complaint
Battery controller may limit power or charging rate

P2E74.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor D Circuit
P2E74.d: P2E74 covers any circuit fault of coolant temperature sensor D, the fourth such sensor a maker can fit to the battery's liquid cooling. Battery controllers typically watch coolant at the pack inlet and outlet; GM's Volt and ELR tables use sensor A for the inlet and B for the outlet. Where a sensor D sits is not public. No manufacturer documents P2E74 publicly. Such sensors are sealed NTC thermistors; one supplier part for battery coolant reads 2828 ohms at 25 °C. GM's 2011 Volt runs its coolant sensor range checks only while no fault is active on the battery controller's 5 V reference circuit. CARB requires the inputs of battery heating and cooling to be monitored. Without the value, cooling may run on substitute data and power can be limited.
c: Damaged wire, loose connector or corroded terminal at sensor D
Fault on the shared 5 V reference circuit of the battery controller
s: Hybrid system or check engine light
Battery cooling or heating not working as intended
Reduced electric power or charging rate

P2E75.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor D Circuit Range/Performance
P2E75.d: P2E75 means battery coolant sensor D gives a reading that is electrically fine yet does not match the other temperatures in the loop. No manufacturer documents P2E75 publicly. GM's sensor B (outlet) shows how such a check works: with the pump above 20 % the outlet value is compared with inlet and average cell temperature. The 2011 Volt fails it at more than 10 °C, 80 of 100 samples at 100 ms; the 2016 ELR allows 20 °C, 32 of 40 samples at 250 ms; both two-trip Type B. Software can be the culprit: Volvo had P0CD6 set wrongly on 2016–17 XC90 T8 (TJ 32193), Audi had P0C4300 with emissions lamp on the 2020 Q5 TFSI e, fixed by thermal module software. CARB requires rationality checks where feasible.
c: Sensor D drifting or responding slowly
Plausibility logic in controller software too strict (update available)
Air pocket or poor coolant flow around the sensor
s: Warning light, frequently with no other symptom
Less effective battery cooling or heating

P2E76.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor D Circuit Low
P2E76.d: P2E76 reports that the voltage on battery coolant sensor D has dropped below its lower limit. Because these sensors are NTC thermistors whose resistance falls as they warm, a low voltage stands for very hot coolant, and a grounded signal wire or a sensor with an internal short produces exactly that picture. No manufacturer documents P2E76 publicly. GM's comparable sensor B code, P0CD7, sets at a reading of 87.9 °C or more, equal to an ADC count of 130 or less, for 1.75 s within a 2.5 s window; the 2016 ELR table marks it two-trip. Coolant genuinely that hot in a battery loop is rare, so suspect wiring first. CARB requires out-of-range detection for battery thermal inputs. The high-voltage counterpart is P2E77.
c: Signal wire of sensor D shorted to ground
Sensor D shorted internally, for example after coolant entered it
Actual overheating of the battery coolant loop
s: Hybrid or check engine warning
Cooling may run at full effort or power may be cut back

P2E77.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor D Circuit High
P2E77.d: P2E77 is set when the signal of battery coolant sensor D rises to or near the reference voltage. In a pull-up NTC circuit that is the signature of an open: a disconnected plug, a broken wire, a spread pin or a sensor element that has gone open, and the controller then sees a coolant temperature colder than physically plausible. No manufacturer documents P2E77 publicly. GM's sensor B analogue P0CD8 fails below -40 °C, an ADC count above 3823, persisting for 1.75 s of a 2.5 s window; the 2011 Volt runs it only while the 5 V reference of the battery controller is fault-free. CARB requires such out-of-range checks. In cold weather battery heating may misjudge the loop; the low counterpart is P2E76.
c: Sensor D connector unplugged or not latched after cooling system work
Broken wire or spread terminal in the sensor D circuit
s: Hybrid or check engine warning
Battery heating may switch on needlessly or behave oddly in winter

P2E78.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor D Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2E78.d: P2E78 stands for a coolant temperature from sensor D that jumps around, mostly without leaving the electrical limits. A liquid loop changes temperature slowly, so fast swings point to a loose contact rather than to the coolant. No manufacturer documents P2E78 publicly. GM's 2019 hybrid table shows a matching test for inlet sensor A (P0C46): it adds up the absolute changes between ten successive readings and counts a sum above 64 °C as a fail; 4 s out of 5 s set a two-trip Type B code, and it is skipped while the hard faults P0C44/P0C45 are present. Volvo found that P0CD900 for sensor B on 2021–22 PHEVs after charging in warm weather might be a spurious entry; software release 3.2.4 resolves it (TJ 36929). CARB requires circuit continuity monitoring.
c: Loose or fretting terminal in the sensor D connector
Harness rubbing through near moving or vibrating parts
s: Warning light that comes and goes
Coolant temperature in live data jumping

P2E79.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump C Performance
P2E79.d: P2E79 is the functional verdict on a third pump in the coolant loop of the traction electronics: command and wiring look healthy, yet the pump does not move coolant the way the controller expects. No manufacturer documents P2E79 or says which pump it calls C. GM has published two strategies for its electronics pump: the 2016 ELR sets P0CEA when the spread between power-electronics coolant temperature and charger temperature grows too large once the pump has been on for over 300 s (32 failures in 40, Type B), and the 2019 tables smooth the difference of commanded versus fed-back pump speed (P19FC). A GM patent adds a comparison of measured with expected pump current. Trapped air, blocked passages, a worn impeller or software can be behind it; Stellantis cured a comparable pump B code (P0C74) by a reflash.
c: Air trapped in the electronics coolant loop after service or a leak
Pump C worn or impeller fouled, delivering too little flow
Kinked hose or clogged cooler passages in the loop
Control software misjudging pump function (update available)
s: Hybrid or EV system warning lamp, possibly MIL
Drive power or charging rate limited because electronics run warm
Gurgling or whirring noise from the electronics coolant loop

P2E7A.t: Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump C Overspeed
P2E7A.d: P2E7A means the third electronics coolant pump spins faster than the speed it was given. A centrifugal pump that draws air instead of liquid loses its load and races, so a low coolant level, a leak or a poorly bled loop come first, a slipping impeller or false speed feedback later. No manufacturer documents P2E7A. GM's 2019 hybrid tables show how such a fault is caught on its electronics pump: P19FC fails once filtered feedback speed exceeds the command by a calibrated margin, and with the pump switched off a reported speed above 250 rpm in 8 of 10 s also counts. HELLA's MP150e pump detects dry running from speed and start current, stops and stores a fault. Mercedes ties P2B2A7A in the 167 series to air and leaks; Ford keeps overspeed/dry run as fault type B1. Performance of pump C is P2E79.
c: Coolant level low or air pocket at the pump inlet
Leak or defective seal in the electronics coolant loop
Impeller loose on its shaft or broken
Faulty speed feedback from the pump electronics
s: Coolant or hybrid system warning, possibly MIL
Coolant reservoir level dropping, traces of leakage
Pump runs loud or churns; power or charging may be reduced

P2E7B.t: Drive Motor A Excitation Current Sensor Circuit
P2E7B.d: P2E7B is the general circuit fault of the measuring element for the DC field current in the rotor of drive motor A. It exists only in electrically excited synchronous motors, whose rotor field comes from a winding, as in Renault's Megane E-Tech, Nissan's Ariya and BMW's fifth-generation eDrive. The controller stores P2E7B when the signal is missing or unusable without a clear low or high reading, e.g. after a lost supply, a broken connection or a dead sensor. In TI's excitation stage a single or a pair of sensors, shunt amplifiers or isolated Hall parts, closes the field loop. No manufacturer documents P2E7B publicly. Low and high signal are P2E29 and P2E2A, implausible values P2E28. Without a trusted value the field is cut, as Audi describes for fault signals, and the motor stops pulling.
c: Supply or reference of the excitation current sensor lost
Open or corroded connection between sensor and motor controller
Excitation current sensor or its isolated amplifier failed
Measuring input inside the inverter or motor controller defective
s: Electric drive warning lamp and MIL
Noticeably reduced power or no drive from motor A
Vehicle may refuse to enter ready mode

P2E7C.t: A/C Compressor Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P2E7C.d: P2E7C covers the second internal temperature sensor in the control electronics of an electric A/C compressor. Their inverter sits on the housing: a Mitsubishi Heavy Industries patent places a sensor next to the power switches, Denso measures at the switches and at the motor stator, and TI's compressor inverter reference feeds IGBT temperature back for overheat protection. The maker decides what B denotes; GM already uses separate code blocks for its CPU sensor (P0D70) and IGBT sensor (P0D75). No manufacturer documents P2E7C publicly. As the generic circuit code it only says that no usable reading arrives, with neither a low nor a high signal identified. The compressor may limit speed or shut down; since the sensor is soldered to the board, repair normally means a complete compressor.
c: Sensor B or its circuit on the compressor control board defective
Compressor controller fails to evaluate or transmit the value
Unstable 12 V supply, ground or data link to the compressor
s: A/C cools weakly or switches off
On plug-in hybrids and EVs, battery cooling and fast charging may be limited
Warning message on the climate display; MIL depends on the manufacturer

P2E7D.t: A/C Compressor Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor B Performance
P2E7D.d: P2E7D is the plausibility check for internal temperature sensor B of the electric A/C compressor controller: the reading is electrically in range yet conflicts with other temperatures. The test runs after a long rest, when all sensors should read alike. No manufacturer documents P2E7D. GM applies the method to its IGBT sensor (P0D76): the 2011 Volt tolerates 11 °C difference from ambient air and 7 °C from the CPU sensor after 21,600 s off, the 2019 tables 22 °C after 7,200 s in 8 of 10 s, Type B. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV compares two temperatures inside its front drive unit after a 3,600 s soak and fails at 18 °C; a Nissan patent judges an inverter switch sensor against coolant temperature. Drift, a still-warm compressor or a faulty reference can trigger it.
c: Sensor B drifted or poorly coupled to its measuring point
Comparison value wrong, e.g. outside air or second internal sensor faulty
Compressor still warm from recent use or preconditioning when the test ran
s: Usually no noticeable effect at first; fault stored after a cold start
Compressor may derate early or shut off on a wrong temperature
MIL on some vehicles after two drive cycles

P2E7E.t: A/C Compressor Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor B Circuit High
P2E7E.d: P2E7E reports that internal temperature sensor B of the A/C compressor controller delivers a signal above its valid range. Most sensors of this kind produce a voltage that falls as temperature rises; TI's compressor inverter reference uses such an analog part, so a high signal stands for an impossibly cold reading. GM applies exactly this to the IGBT sensor of its compressor: P0D77 sets when the reported value falls under −40 °C, in the 2011 Volt after 30 failures within 60 samples taken every 50 ms, provided ambient exceeds −7 °C, in 2018 at a 100 ms rate and in 2019 after 4 of 5 s, always Type B. No manufacturer documents P2E7E. An open sensor path, a cracked solder joint or a lost reference on the board are usual causes. In J2012 this High code precedes the Low code P2E7F.
c: Sensor B path open, e.g. cracked solder joint on the board
Reference or ground of the measuring circuit lost inside the module
Analog input of the compressor controller defective
s: Compressor runs restricted or not at all
Cabin and, where present, battery cooling weaker
MIL possible after two drive cycles depending on manufacturer

P2E7F.t: A/C Compressor Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P2E7F.d: P2E7F is the low-signal counterpart: sensor B inside the compressor control module reports a value below its valid band, which for a sensor with falling output means an impossibly hot reading. GM's comparable code on the compressor IGBT sensor is P0D78: the 2011 Volt fails above 274 °C, the 2018 and 2019 tables above 150 °C, with the compressor detecting the condition itself and passing it on over GMLAN, Type B. No manufacturer documents P2E7F. A short on the sensor path is the usual explanation. Genuine overheating of the power stage, for instance from too little refrigerant flow, should still be ruled out, because controllers like the one in a Mitsubishi Heavy Industries patent slow or stop the compressor when it runs too hot. The cold side is P2E7E.
c: Short circuit in the sensor B path on the control board
Measuring circuit of the compressor controller defective
Power stage genuinely overheating, e.g. low refrigerant charge
s: Compressor derates or shuts down for overheat protection
Air conditioning blows warm, battery cooling may be limited
MIL possible after two drive cycles depending on manufacturer

P2E80.t: A/C Compressor Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2E80.d: With P2E80 the controller sees the reading of sensor B, a second internal thermometer in the compressor electronics, flicker: values leap or vanish for an instant and then look normal again. Set criteria for P2E80 are not published by any manufacturer. For the 2019 Volt, GM lists the IGBT counterpart P0D79 merely as a code that must be inactive before its rationality check P0D76 starts. A Hyundai patent dealing with sensors on inverter power switches separates the patterns: dropouts spread irregularly over time point to bad contact, whereas a value stuck at one number suggests a short. Loosened board connectors, cold solder joints and interference are prime suspects. Rule out the low-voltage feed, ground and network line first; when the fault stays, the compressor assembly is normally replaced as one unit.
c: Loose contact or cold solder joint in the sensor B circuit
Electrical interference from the inverter switching on the measuring line
Fluctuating 12 V supply or ground of the compressor controller
s: A/C cuts out and recovers sporadically
Fault may be stored without any noticeable effect

P2E81.t: Cold Start Engine Coolant Bypass Valve D Stuck Closed
P2E81.d: P2E81 is the cold-start version of P26C2 for valve D, which GM uses as the block rotary valve between two mechanical end stops. Its 2025 ECM tables (25OBDG03B) count a failure when commanded and measured position differ by more than 5° while raw feedback stays below 50°, i.e. on the closed side, in 4 of 5 seconds; Type B, MIL after two trips. It only runs in low-flow coolant mode (also with auto-stop) and with catalyst warm-up active, at 11 V or more, with block coolant above −34 °C and no calibration run for 37 s. CARB asks that faults found during the cold-start strategy carry their own codes. Keeping coolant still in the block is intended at first, as a Ford patent explains, but a valve that will not open later risks hot spots. The open side is P2DE8.
c: Block rotary valve stuck on the closed side (deposits, wear)
Valve actuator too weak to turn the valve when coolant is cold and thick
Chafed or corroded harness to the valve actuator
Invalid end-stop learn values after repair or battery disconnect
s: Check engine light after two trips
Engine temperature rising faster or unevenly after a cold start
Usually no driveability change

P2E82.t: Cold Start Engine Coolant Pump Overspeed
P2E82.d: P2E82 flags an electric main coolant pump that spins faster than requested while the cold-start warm-up strategy runs. GM's 2025 ECM tables (25OBDG03B) subtract reported from requested speed, filter the result and fail the test when it falls below −200 rpm in 8 of 10 seconds; Type B, MIL after two trips. Required: low-flow coolant mode, catalyst warm-up active, a request that changes by less than 50 rpm per sample for 3 s, and inlet coolant at −40 °C or warmer. Outside cold start GM uses P26CE with a speed-dependent limit of −200 to −800 rpm. A pump that turns too freely often moves air instead of coolant, so low coolant or trapped air are the first suspects. A GM patent compares pump speed and current with targets to find such faults.
c: Low coolant level or air trapped after service, so the impeller runs dry
Impeller loose or damaged, so the motor turns without load
Faulty pump electronics or speed feedback signal
Flow path blocked by a stuck valve, changing the pump load
s: Check engine light after two trips
Gurgling noises or weak heater output
Rising engine temperature if coolant is missing

P2E83.t: Fuel Rail Pressure Performance - Engine Off
P2E83.d: P2E83 covers a fuel rail pressure check that runs once the engine is shut down: the residual pressure in the rail falls too fast, stays too high or behaves implausibly. No manufacturer documents the code publicly. For monitors active at standstill, CARB extends the driving cycle through the shutdown period until the next start. Patents show what such a check looks at: GM measures rail pressure a set time after shutdown, fires an injector to bleed it if it is still above a limit (about 5 MPa in the diesel example) and flags a fault if it stays high; Ford lists rail pressure decay with the engine off as a way to find leaking direct injectors. Ford's 2024 summary covers rail pressure only while running, cranking and in cold start (P0087, P0088, P00C6, P053F).
c: Injector leaking into the cylinder, so rail pressure decays too quickly
Leaking pump check valve or pressure relief valve
Rail pressure sensor with offset or drift, implausible at rest
Pressure rising after shutdown from heat soak with no way to relieve it
s: Check engine light
Long cranking or rough start after the car has stood
Possible fuel smell or smoke right after starting

P2E84.t: Battery Charger B Input Voltage Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2E84.d: P2E84 questions the plausibility of the grid voltage that charger B reads at its input: the sensor answers within its electrical limits, yet the figure does not suit the moment, such as a voltage with no supply connected or a value that contradicts other readings. No manufacturer documents P2E84 publicly. How such a check works is shown on charger A: GM's 2011 Volt compares the AC peak voltage with two internal bulk voltages and fails when both differ by more than 34 V (Type A), while Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV reacts to 25 V or more held for 2 s. On the Polestar 3, whose AC charger reports as charger B, input sensor faults appear as P0E8B16 and lead to replacement of the unit if DC charging still works. Hard low or high readings are P2E85/P2E86. AC charging is usually refused.
c: Voltage sensing inside charger B drifting or faulty
Corroded or loose AC contacts between charge inlet and charger B
Unstable or unusual supply from the charging station or house circuit
s: AC charging does not start or stops after a short time
DC fast charging still works normally
Charging fault message in the instrument cluster or app

P2E85.t: Battery Charger B Input Voltage Sensor Circuit Low
P2E85.d: P2E85 means the input voltage signal of charger B sits too low, so the car sees little or no grid voltage while it expects AC. GM uses the code on its battery-electric models, from the 2017 Bolt EV to the Lyriq, Hummer EV, Blazer, Equinox and Silverado EV and BrightDrop vans, under the wording input voltage sensor circuit low voltage. Bulletin PIT6353 and TechLink March 2025 name a typical trigger: a DC-only NACS adapter used at a household outlet or AC wallbox, which routes the shared pins to the DC contacts, so no AC reaches the charger; P0D3F, P0F71 and on the Bolt P1EE6 may set with it. A 2026 TechLink lists P0E8B-11 beside it. With the right adapter the fault is gone; otherwise check inlet, wiring and the charger. Too high is P2E86.
c: DC-only NACS adapter used on an AC charger
Charging station or house circuit not delivering AC voltage
Open or high-resistance AC path between inlet and charger B
Sensing circuit inside charger B shorted to ground
s: Vehicle does not charge on a Level 1 or Level 2 AC charger
DC fast charging works without the adapter problem
Further charger codes such as P0D3F or P0F71 stored

P2E86.t: Battery Charger B Input Voltage Sensor Circuit High
P2E86.d: P2E86 flags an input voltage signal of charger B above the highest value the measurement can plausibly produce. Home sockets and AC stations stay far below that, so the fault normally lies in the sensing path or its signal line, rarely in the grid. No manufacturer documents P2E86 publicly. The charger A versions give the scale: GM's 2011 Volt treats an AC peak above 422 V for 160 of 200 ms as sensor high (Type A, MIL), and Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV sets P0D40 when the sensor output passes 3.161 V, equal to more than 492 V, for 0.5 s, then halts charging and names the charger/DC-DC unit as the part to replace. CARB wants hybrid monitoring plans to cover charging system performance. Too low is P2E85, plausibility P2E84. AC charging usually stays blocked.
c: Voltage sensing circuit inside charger B faulty
Sensor signal line shorted to a supply voltage
Lost reference ground of the measurement
s: AC charging refused or ended immediately
Charging system warning in the cluster
Fault returns at once after clearing, even on a known good charger

P2E87.d: P2E87 is the general fault of a second plug-detection circuit, B, whose job is to tell the vehicle that a connector is seated in an inlet. Under SAE J1772 this proximity pin is tied to earth through resistors and a switch in the latch button, so the car can lock out driving and wind down current before the plug comes out; CHAdeMO inlets have their own proximity contact for the same interlock. A second circuit is needed where a car carries two inlets, as the Outlander PHEV does with its normal and quick-charge sockets: Mitsubishi reports the normal one as proximity A (P0D58/P0D59) and reads a separate quick-charger connecting voltage, without publishing a B code. No manufacturer documents P2E87. Lear patented a circuit that also wakes the charger through this line. Expect no charging on that inlet.
c: Damaged or corroded proximity contact in inlet B
Open or poorly seated connector between inlet B and the controller
Faulty charging cable or plug resistor
Evaluation circuit in the charger or control unit faulty
s: No charging through the affected inlet
Plug not recognised or vehicle reports a cable while none is fitted
Vehicle may refuse to enter drive readiness

P2E88.d: P2E88 flags plug sensing on circuit B whose value is electrically valid but makes no sense, typically a voltage that falls between the defined steps for no plug, plug latched and release button pressed. Those steps come from fixed resistors: J1772 uses 150 Ω plus 330 Ω once the latch is opened, and IEC 62196 cables code their current rating with values from about 100 Ω to 1.5 kΩ, each read within a tolerance band. Supplier controllers such as Watt & Well's EVCC bias the pin with 5 V and treat less than 3.5 kΩ as a plug, more than 4 kΩ as none. No manufacturer documents P2E88; for circuit A FCA cured P0D57 on the 2017 Pacifica plug-in hybrid by reflashing its hybrid control processors. Worn contacts or an off-standard cable are common. Hard faults are P2E89 and P2E8A.
c: Worn or dirty proximity contact raising the resistance
Charging cable or adapter with off-standard coding resistor
Moisture in inlet B creating leakage paths
Control software judging the signal wrongly
s: Charging aborts or the current is limited unexpectedly
Plug status changes without anyone touching the connector
Fault appears only with certain cables

P2E89.d: P2E89 stands for a voltage on proximity circuit B below the band the controller accepts in a state where no plug can be present. The rule for circuit A shows how this is judged: GM's Volt checks the line with the charge door closed or while driving out of Park and sets P0D58 below 4.2 V, in 2011 after 30 failures out of 50, in the 2019 tables after 240 out of 400 samples above 20 km/h, as a Type A code with MIL. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV sets P0D58-00 on a low input of the charger connection signal and checks the line to the PHEV-ECU for a ground short, the charging cable and even outside supply equipment. No manufacturer documents P2E89 itself. A Lear patent protects the 5 V feed of such circuits against shorts. Expect a car that believes a plug is in.
c: Proximity line of circuit B chafed and shorted to ground
Water or dirt in inlet B bridging the contact to earth
Defective charging cable left in the inlet
Input stage in the evaluating control unit damaged
s: Message that a charging cable is connected although none is
Vehicle cannot be put into drive mode
Warning lamp, depending on manufacturer the MIL

P2E8A.d: P2E8A is the opposite of P2E89: the proximity line of circuit B sits above the accepted band. Because the evaluating controller usually pulls the pin up to a reference such as 5 V, as described for Watt & Well's EVCC, an open wire or a missing earth path reads high just like a short to a supply. For circuit A GM's Volt sets P0D59 above 4.8 V under the same conditions as the low test, charge door closed or moving out of Park, again Type A with MIL. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV logs P0D59-00 on a high charger connection signal and points to the harness between charger and PHEV-ECU or the PHEV-ECU itself. No manufacturer documents P2E8A. The usual result is a plug on inlet B that is never recognised, so charging there does not start.
c: Broken proximity wire or unplugged connector at inlet B
Missing protective-earth path in inlet or cable
Proximity line shorted to a supply voltage
s: Charging cable on inlet B is not detected
Charging does not start on that inlet
Warning lamp, depending on manufacturer the MIL

P2E8B.d: P2E8B describes a plug-detection signal on circuit B that drops out or jumps for moments, so the car sees a connector appear and vanish although nobody touched it. The consequences follow from the purpose of the line: under SAE J1772 the proximity state is what lets the vehicle stop drawing current before the plug is released and block driving off while connected, so a flickering signal can end charging for no visible reason or let a drive lock come and go. In Lear's patented design the same line also wakes the charger, so glitches can rouse it needlessly. No manufacturer documents P2E8B. Mercedes describes the classic cause for circuit A on the smart with 22 kW charger: loose low-voltage plugs that act up only with warm or cold parts, alongside P0D5800/P0D5900. Hard faults are P2E89/P2E8A.
c: Loose low-voltage connector on the proximity line
Worn proximity contact in inlet B or on the cable plug
Chafed wire with intermittent contact to ground
Moisture in the inlet after rain or washing
s: Charging stops and restarts at random
Cable-connected message appears and disappears
Fault more frequent at the start or end of charging

P2E8C.t: Battery Charger B Charge Sequence Signal 1 Circuit High
P2E8C.d: Charge sequence signals 1 and 2 belong to DC fast charging to CHAdeMO, used for example on the Nissan Leaf, the Mitsubishi i-MiEV and the Outlander PHEV. Signal 1 runs over connector pin 2: the station closes its switch d1 and applies 12 V to the line, which tells the car it is ready and starts the CAN dialogue. P2E8C means the vehicle sees this line high when it should not, for instance with no station connected or after the station has opened d1 once a session is over, or the level exceeds the allowed range. Likely reasons are a short to a 12 V source in the harness or inlet, or a faulty input stage. No manufacturer documents P2E8C publicly. The car can then no longer trust the start and stop handshake and usually refuses DC charging. The low counterpart is P2E8D.
c: Sequence signal 1 line shorted to a 12 V source
Moisture or debris in the DC inlet bridging pins
Faulty input stage in the evaluating control unit
Station switch d1 not opening at the end of a session
s: DC fast charging refused or ending with an error
AC charging continues to work
Charging fault message in the cluster

P2E8D.t: Battery Charger B Charge Sequence Signal 1 Circuit Low
P2E8D.d: P2E8D means the vehicle finds the first CHAdeMO sequence line low while the fast charger should be driving it. Signal 1 is the opening move of a session: once the plug is detected the station closes d1 and applies 12 V, and only after that does the CAN exchange of battery limits begin. If the vehicle side sees no voltage, the session stalls before any current flows. The line can also supply contactor coils in the car, which is why the standard allows up to 2 A on it; a short to ground therefore loads the station switch hard. No manufacturer documents P2E8D publicly. Reasons include a short to ground, a broken wire or pin 2 contact, a corroded inlet, and, on the station side, a switch d1 that never closes, so trying another charger helps narrow it down. The high counterpart is P2E8C.
c: Sequence signal 1 line shorted to ground
Open wire or damaged pin 2 in the DC inlet
Fast charger not closing its switch d1
Faulty input stage in the evaluating control unit
s: DC fast charging does not start
Station reports a communication or vehicle error
AC charging unaffected

P2E8E.t: Battery Charger B Charge Sequence Signal 2 Circuit High
P2E8E.d: P2E8E concerns the second CHAdeMO sequence line, which works differently from the first: the station closes switch d2 to tie the line to ground, completing the circuit that sequence signal 1 feeds, and only then may the vehicle close its high-voltage contactors. Before that the connector has been latched and the vehicle has given charge permission. If the vehicle measures this line and finds it high at the moment d2 should be closed, the go-ahead for the contactors never arrives and the session ends just before power transfer; a high level outside a session points to a short to a supply. An open wire on pin 10 or a station whose d2 fails can look the same. No manufacturer documents P2E8E publicly. The low counterpart is P2E8F; faults on signal 1 are P2E8C/P2E8D.
c: Open wire or damaged pin 10 in the DC inlet
Fast charger switch d2 not closing
Sequence signal 2 line shorted to a supply voltage
Faulty input stage in the evaluating control unit
s: DC session stops after insulation test without current flowing
Station shows a vehicle-side error
AC charging still possible

P2E8F.t: Battery Charger B Charge Sequence Signal 2 Circuit Low
P2E8F.d: P2E8F reports the second CHAdeMO sequence line pulled low at a time it should be released. Because the station uses d2 to connect this line to ground as the very last step before the vehicle closes its contactors, and opens d2 first when the session ends, a line already at ground early, or still at ground once d2 is open, contradicts the sequence. A ground short in the inlet or harness, a station switch d2 that sticks closed, or a faulty input stage can be the cause. The vehicle then cannot be sure its contactor release is controlled by the station and normally refuses or aborts DC charging. No manufacturer documents P2E8F publicly; Siemens' CHAdeMO library for charging stations shows the station side, with relays d1 and d2 rated for 2 A. The high counterpart is P2E8E.
c: Sequence signal 2 line shorted to ground
Fast charger switch d2 stuck closed
Water or dirt in the DC inlet
Faulty input stage in the evaluating control unit
s: DC fast charging refused right after plugging in
Session ends with an error instead of a normal stop
AC charging unaffected

P2E90.t: Battery Charger A Internal Power Supply Performance
P2E90.d: P2E90 says the internal power supply of charger A, the rails that feed its control and gate-driver electronics, does not behave as intended. Kia uses the code: technical bulletin ELE409 (service action SA639, December 2025) covers 2025 EV6 and 2026 EV9 built between 21 February and 18 September 2025 that store P2E9092, performance or incorrect operation, and can no longer charge on Level 1 or 2; the fix is a new integrated charging control unit (ICCU). Mitsubishi watches the same rails under P0D67 on the Outlander PHEV: 3.3, 6 and 12 V supplies must stay in their windows for 1 s, otherwise charging stops. TI explains that such bias supplies draw on the 12 V or high-voltage battery. Charger B is P2E91; the 12 V feed of the module itself is P2E2C.
c: Internal supply stage of charger A or the ICCU failed
Weak 12 V feed or loose low-voltage connector at the charger
s: No AC charging at home or on Level 2 stations
DC fast charging may still work
Charging system warning in the cluster

P2E91.t: Battery Charger B Internal Power Supply Performance
P2E91.d: P2E91 is the same verdict for charger B: one of its internally generated supply voltages is wrong, so the charger cannot run its power stages safely. Polestar uses the code on the Polestar 3, whose grid-to-high-voltage converter GHCA reports as charger B. Technical journal TJ 37630 (version 3.0, December 2025) lists P2E9117 and P2E9119, by failure-type byte voltage and current above threshold, among the GHCA codes and says to replace the GHCA when DC charging works but AC charging does not. Mercedes shows that the trigger may sit outside the unit: its bulletin for the 22 kW smart charger blames loose low-voltage plugs for P1D0BFD, an internal supply fault. Mitsubishi checks such rails under P0D67. The A-side twin is P2E90, the 12 V feed of charger B P2E2F.
c: Internal supply stage of charger B failed
Loose low-voltage connector or weak 12 V feed at charger B
s: AC charging fails while DC fast charging still works
Charging time much longer or charging stops early
Charging socket light signals a fault

P2E92.t: Charge Port Door B Open Request Switch Wake-Up Circuit
P2E92.d: P2E92 concerns cars with a second electrically opened charge door. Its open-request switch or sensor must be able to rouse sleeping control units, so besides its normal signal it drives a wake-up line, and P2E92 records that the two disagree. Porsche's Taycan campaign WLK2 shows the naming, door A at the driver and door B at the passenger side, both opened by a hand gesture over a sensor; Audi's newer models put an extra AC inlet with its own flap on the opposite side, also opened at the flap. No manufacturer documents P2E92. GM's 2011 Volt tests the A version, P0CC6: wake-up active with the switch released, or pressed without wake-up, filtered in 50 ms steps, Type B over two trips. The usual result is a door B that sometimes ignores a press.
c: Open or shorted wake-up wire between switch and control unit
Worn switch or sensor at door B giving mismatched signals
Water ingress or corrosion at the door B connector
Wake-up input of the control unit faulty
s: Charge door B does not open on request every time
Door opens only from the screen or the other side works normally
Increased standby drain if the line keeps waking modules

P2E93.t: Charge Port Door B Open Request Switch Circuit
P2E93.d: P2E93 is the basic circuit fault of the input with which the driver asks the second charge flap to open. On cars with a flap on each side this input is usually a touch or wipe sensor on the flap itself: Porsche's Taycan and Cayenne Electric open each flap when a hand passes over a sensor area at its rear, and Porsche's WLK2 parts list calls the passenger-side flap door B. No manufacturer documents P2E93 publicly. GM shows how the A version P0CC7 works on the 2011 Volt: a reading in the forbidden band from 65.9 to 81.6 percent of reference, seen in six of eight 50 ms samples, sets a Type B code. Low and high faults belong to P2E95 and P2E96, implausible behaviour to P2E94. Typically flap B ignores the hand but still opens from the screen.
c: Touch or wipe sensor of flap B with a wrong internal resistance
Partly broken or corroded signal wire to the flap B sensor
Moisture in the connector at the flap module
Faulty input stage in the control unit reading the sensor
s: Charge flap B does not react to touch or hand gesture
Flap B still opens via the central display or app
Charging flap warning in the instrument cluster

P2E94.t: Charge Port Door B Open Request Switch Circuit Performance
P2E94.d: With P2E94 the open request input of charge flap B is electrically sound, yet its behaviour cannot be right, for example a request that stays active for far too long. Audi describes exactly this pattern for the Q6 e-tron in bulletin 2076776/1: tension in the left or right flap module can deform the flap so that it sinks into the body and the button inside the module stays pressed; the flap can then no longer be opened from outside, while the display still opens it. No manufacturer ties this to P2E94 publicly. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15.2.1) asks for rationality checks on inputs where feasible and for separate codes from circuit faults, which is the role of this code next to P2E93, P2E95 and P2E96. A GM patent shows the basic chain: release button, controller, latch actuator.
c: Deformed or recessed flap B keeping the request button pressed
Sensor of flap B shifted or not seated correctly
Ice or dirt acting on the sensor area
s: Flap B cannot be opened from outside
Opening via the display or charging menu still works
Flap B sits deeper than the surrounding body panel

P2E95.t: Charge Port Door B Open Request Switch Circuit Low
P2E95.d: P2E95 says the request signal from charge flap B has dropped under the bottom of its permitted range. Usual reasons are a signal wire touching ground, water bridging the connector pins or an internally shorted sensor. Depending on the wiring, the control unit may take this as a button held down all the time. No manufacturer documents P2E95 publicly. For the A flap, GM's 2011 Volt table sets P0CC9 once 6 out of 8 readings stay under 22.9 percent, and treats it as Type B. Water at flap connectors is a known weak point on two-sided designs: Audi's campaign 93H6 for the e-tron sealed or replaced the connectors in the charge door units on both sides because moisture could leave the flap openable only with the manual release. High readings are P2E96, invalid middle values P2E93.
c: Signal wire of the flap B sensor shorted to ground
Water in the flap B connector bridging the contacts
Request sensor of flap B failed short internally
s: Flap B does not open on touch, or only with the manual release
Control unit may stay awake longer, raising standby drain
Charging flap warning displayed

P2E96.t: Charge Port Door B Open Request Switch Circuit High
P2E96.d: P2E96 is stored when the request signal of charge flap B climbs past the top of its permitted range. Contact with a 12 V supply raises it, and so does a broken sensor ground or switch path that lets a pulled-up input float. The control unit then usually sees a request that never arrives. No manufacturer documents P2E96 publicly. GM's Volt table for flap A sets the matching P0CCA when readings pass 94.5 percent in 6 out of 8 cases, Type B. On Porsche's Taycan each flap can be moved both from the centre console and by the touch-free sensor; bulletin 186/24 has technicians test both ways on both sides and check lines and plug connections before replacing parts. Low readings are P2E95, the invalid middle band P2E93.
c: Sensor signal wire shorted to a 12 V supply
Interrupted ground or switch path at the flap B sensor
Pushed-back or loose pin in the flap module connector
s: Flap B never reacts to the hand or touch
Opening from the centre console or display still works
Warning that the charging flap is impaired

P2E97.t: Charge Port Door B Open Request Switch Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2E97.d: P2E97 points to a request signal from charge flap B that briefly vanishes or jumps, while no permanent fault can be found. A real case with the same sensor type comes from Porsche: on the Macan Electric of model years 2023 to 2025 the optional electric flaps open when a flat hand rests on the rear third, and bulletin WRP7 explains that production tolerances could make the gesture go undetected now and then; the fix replaces the adhesive strips that hold the sensors on both flaps. No manufacturer links that case or any other to P2E97 publicly. Electrically, loose terminals, a harness bent by the flap and a poorly fixed sensor are the usual reasons. Permanent faults are coded as P2E93, P2E95 and P2E96. Drivers notice a flap B that responds only sometimes.
c: Sensor on flap B not held firmly, adhesive strip loosened
Loose terminal in the flap B connector
Harness to flap B damaged by repeated movement
s: Flap B opens only on some attempts
Code stored without a lasting fault in the workshop

P2E98.t: Charge Port Door B Position Sensor Circuit
P2E98.d: P2E98 is the general circuit code for the sensor that reports whether charge flap B is open or shut. Mercedes-Benz documents it: in its plug-in hybrids the separate DC charging socket has its own flap, and information LI47.70-P-078563 lists P2E9873 for a supposed electrical fault of that flap's position sensor, stored in the DC charge-connection unit N116/5 and the powertrain controller, with the MIL lit and the note that the actuator does not open. Starting and charging stay normal; the cause is software, the fix a DCCU update plus SCN coding, after which the code no longer lights the MIL, and parts must not be replaced. Porsche's Taycan detects flap end positions with a reed sensor. Low, high and erratic faults are P2E9A, P2E9B and P2E9C, plausibility P2E99.
c: Software fault in the DC charging unit reporting a false sensor fault (Mercedes)
Position sensor of flap B with a wrong internal resistance
Damaged wire or connector between sensor and control unit
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on, charging and starting normal (Mercedes)
Flap B may stay shut or show a wrong status

P2E99.t: Charge Port Door B Position Sensor Circuit Performance
P2E99.d: P2E99 means the position signal of charge flap B is within its electrical limits yet contradicts what the flap is doing, for instance closed although the flap was just opened. On cars with two flaps such an error has side effects, because the flaps lock each other: Porsche found on the 2020 Taycan that a bad sensor signal led to a wrong end-position decision, which then blocked the flap on the other side, and replaced both flap harnesses (campaign WLK2); a GM patent describes the same interlock with a magnet sensor per door. Audi reports two e-tron GT cases where a closed flap was read as open: a faulty actuator with oxidation or particles (2064953/4) and, later, cockpit software (2079475/1). No manufacturer ties these to P2E99 publicly. Pure circuit faults belong to P2E98, P2E9A and P2E9B.
c: Position sensor or its harness giving a wrong end-position signal
Oxidation or particles in the flap actuator that houses the detection
Software misreading the flap state at start-up
s: Message asking to close a charging flap although both are closed
Opposite flap A locked and not operable
Charging refused

P2E9A.t: Charge Port Door B Position Sensor Circuit Low
P2E9A.d: P2E9A reports that the flap B position signal has fallen under its lowest valid value. A signal wire chafed against ground, water in the connector or an internally shorted sensor are the usual reasons. Tesla's latch patent shows a common build in which a reed or Hall element inside the latch senses a magnet disc on the door, so the signal follows the gap between them. No manufacturer documents P2E9A publicly. For the A flap of the 2011 Volt, GM sets P0CCE as Type B when 6 out of 8 readings fall under 22.9 percent, and while a position code is active it holds back the control pilot test P0CF4 and the opening check P0CD2. P2E9B is the high counterpart, P2E98 the general circuit code. Expect a flap state that never changes and possibly blocked charging.
c: Position signal wire of flap B shorted to ground
Water in the sensor connector at flap B
s: Flap B status in the display does not change
Charging blocked or charging flap warning

P2E9B.t: Charge Port Door B Position Sensor Circuit High
P2E9B.d: P2E9B is the high-side position fault of charge flap B: the reading lies above anything a working sensor can deliver. A signal wire touching 12 V, or a missing sensor ground, letting the input drift upwards, are typical explanations. No manufacturer documents P2E9B publicly. GM's Volt tables show the A version P0CCF flagging readings over 94.5 percent of the reference once six of eight samples agree, spaced 50 ms in 2011 and 500 ms in the 2013 table, as a Type B code. In GM's magnet sensor patent the door signal mainly drives an open-door warning and the interlock between two doors, so a stuck reading tends to produce a permanent flap-open message. Low readings are P2E9A, implausible but valid ones P2E99. The driver typically cannot charge on either side until the fault is gone.
c: Position signal wire shorted to a 12 V feed
Broken ground wire of the flap B position sensor
Corroded or loose connector at the flap module
s: Permanent message that a charging flap is open
Charging not possible on either side

P2E9C.t: Charge Port Door B Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P2E9C.d: P2E9C covers a flap B position signal that flickers or drops out briefly instead of failing for good. Common sources are loose terminals, a harness bent at every flap movement, or a sensor sitting loose in its holder. No manufacturer documents P2E9C publicly. Two official cases show how fragile this signal path can be on two-flap cars. Porsche replaced the harnesses of flap A on the driver side and flap B on the passenger side of 2020 Taycans because an incorrect sensor signal made the car misread the end position. Audi traced wrongly shown flap states on the e-tron GT to the actuator, naming oxidation and foreign particles inside it. Lasting faults are P2E98, P2E9A and P2E9B, plausibility errors P2E99. Drivers see a flap status that changes on its own or charging warnings that come and go.
c: Loose terminal in the position sensor connector
Harness to flap B strained or chafed by flap movement
Oxidation or particles in the flap actuator with integrated detection
s: Flap status in the display switches without reason
Sporadic charging flap warnings or interrupted charging

P2E9D.t: Charge Port Door B Unlock Control Circuit
P2E9D.d: P2E9D concerns the output that releases or drives charge flap B, not its sensors. Depending on the design this is a latch actuator or a small motor: Audi's e-tron family uses lock actuators F496 and F497 for its high-voltage charging flaps on the two sides, and Porsche's Taycan a servo motor per charge port door. No manufacturer documents P2E9D publicly. GM's 2011 Volt shows how the A version P0CD1 is judged from the fault flag of the driver stage: a short to ground while the release is commanded (3 of 4 samples), a short to 12 V or an open circuit while it is not (64 of 80 samples, 50 ms each), Type B. Split low and high codes are P2E9F and P2EA0, the movement check P2E9E. The driver finds flap B shut and has to use the other side or the emergency release.
c: Flap B actuator or motor winding open or shorted
Damaged control wire or connector to the flap B actuator
Faulty output stage in the control unit
s: Flap B does not unlock or move at all
Charging only possible on the other side
Charging flap warning in the cluster

P2E9E.t: Charge Port Door B Unlock Control Circuit Performance
P2E9E.d: P2E9E is a function check: the control unit commands flap B to unlock and then expects the position sensor to confirm an open flap. GM's tables for the A flap of the Volt set P0CD2 when that report is missing after 5 seconds (2011) or 13 seconds (2013, only above minus 12 °C), skip the test while position or output codes are active, and use Type B. No manufacturer documents P2E9E publicly, but Audi bulletins show the mechanical side on two-flap cars: on the e-tron the flap lock actuator can break if the flap is forced (2080912/1), on the Q6 e-tron broken gears in the flap motor leave it rocking at one spot (2077931/1), and on the A6 e-tron software could release the second flap's lock before the first was fully shut (2079918/1). P2E9D covers the electrical circuit.
c: Flap B lock actuator or motor gears broken, often after force on the flap
Flap B frozen, dirty or binding in its housing
Software sequencing error between the two flaps
Position sensor not reporting the opened flap
s: Flap B pops slightly or rocks but does not open fully
Flap B moves freely by hand because the actuator is broken
Charging flap warning, charging only on the other side

P2E9F.t: Charge Port Door B Unlock Control Circuit Low
P2E9F.d: P2E9F is the low-voltage form of the flap B release output fault: the driver stage measures its control line close to 0 V where a higher level is expected. A control wire chafed to body ground or an actuator winding that has shorted are the usual culprits, and a protective fuse or driver shutdown can follow. No manufacturer documents P2E9F publicly. GM's Volt folds this case into the combined A code P0CD1, judging a short to ground only while the release is commanded. A GM patent shows what the line feeds: a briefly energised actuator retracts a post so a spring can push the flap open, after which power is removed. Porsche's Taycan bulletin 186/24 has technicians check the lines and plugs of the flap servo motors before replacing modules. High-level faults are P2EA0, the function test P2E9E. Flap B then stays shut.
c: Control wire of the flap B actuator shorted to ground
Shorted winding in the flap B actuator or motor
s: Flap B does not release on any request
Blown fuse for the flap circuit possible

P2EA0.t: Charge Port Door B Unlock Control Circuit High
P2EA0.d: P2EA0 marks the opposite case at the flap B release output: the line sits at a high voltage while the driver stage should be pulling it down or keeping it off. Contact with a 12 V circuit does this, and on low-side switched outputs an interrupted actuator or wire gives the same reading. No manufacturer documents P2EA0 publicly. GM's Volt checks the A output for a short to battery or an open line only while no release is commanded, needing 64 of 80 samples at 50 ms, and reports it within P0CD1. Tesla's latch patent explains why a permanently powered release is unwanted: the electromagnet is fed only briefly through a normally open switch to cancel the holding magnet. Audi's e-tron campaign 93H6 shows the fallback when a flap stays shut, the manual release. Low-level faults are P2E9F, the movement check P2E9E.
c: Control wire of the flap B actuator shorted to 12 V
Open actuator winding or broken wire on a low-side driven output
Output stage in the control unit stuck on
s: Flap B never releases, only the manual release helps
Actuator may run warm if powered permanently

P2EA1.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 6
P2EA1.d: P2EA1 is the general electrical fault of a sixth exhaust temperature probe on bank 1, counting from the engine towards the tailpipe. No manufacturer documents this code publicly: the diesel tables that are published stop at probe 5, which GM's 2025 table 25OBDG04A places behind the particulate filter. GM's logic for that probe hints at the use of a general circuit code: a broken lead appears as more than 100 MΩ and is booked as High, while digital thermocouple modules also watch their communication. P2EA1 thus fits interruptions or contact faults the module cannot assign to one limit. Stellantis warns for the 2025–2026 Ram heavy-duty diesel to go by sensor names, not numbers, when locating a probe. Low and High are P2EA3 and P2EA2.
c: Corroded or heat-damaged plug of the sixth probe near the exhaust
Probe lead or internal wire broken by exhaust vibration
Harness chafed or melted along the aftertreatment
Faulty input stage or temperature evaluation module
s: Check engine lamp on
Particulate filter regeneration delayed or blocked
Live data for probe 6 missing or jumping

P2EA2.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit High Bank 1 Sensor 6
P2EA2.d: P2EA2 says the signal of the sixth bank 1 exhaust probe sits above its upper electrical limit. Which temperature that implies depends on the element. Most probes form a voltage divider with a pull-up resistor in the module; an open lead then drives the input to the reference, which an NTC part reads as extreme cold and a platinum (PTC) part as extreme heat. Heraeus notes that both platinum resistors and thermocouples are used beyond 900 °C. No maker documents P2EA2; the closest public analogue is GM's probe 5 code P2482 in 25OBDG04A: more than 100 MΩ, or above about 1290 °C on a digital thermocouple, in 19 of 25 samples, Type A with the lamp after one trip. An unplugged connector or broken lead is therefore the prime suspect.
c: Open signal or ground lead, or connector not latched
Probe element burnt open after overheating or vibration
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
s: Check engine lamp, often after a single trip
Probe 6 shows an impossible extreme value in live data
Filter regeneration or SCR dosing restricted

P2EA3.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Low Bank 1 Sensor 6
P2EA3.d: With P2EA3 the input of the sixth bank 1 exhaust probe drops below the lowest value a healthy circuit can deliver. Electrically this is nearly always a short: the signal wire touching ground or the exhaust, or an element whose insulation has broken down. What the module displays differs by type, as Hella explains for divider circuits: a shorted NTC probe looks red hot, a shorted platinum (PTC) probe looks frozen. No manufacturer documents P2EA3; GM's code P2481 for probe 5 serves as a guide, set below 1 Ω or, with a digital thermocouple, colder than about −73 °C in 19 of 25 samples as Type B, i.e. MIL after two trips. A wrong low value can mislead the module about exhaust heat, so regeneration or SCR dosing may be held back.
c: Signal wire chafed through to ground or to the exhaust pipe
Probe with internal short after thermal or mechanical damage
Water or road salt bridging the connector pins
s: Check engine lamp after the second faulty trip
Probe 6 reads far too hot or far too cold depending on type
Regeneration or SCR dosing held back

P2EA5.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1 Sensor 6
P2EA5.d: P2EA5 is the plausibility fault of the sixth bank 1 exhaust probe: the voltage is electrically valid, yet the temperature does not match what the exhaust is doing. California's rule 13 CCR 1968.2, section (e)(15.2.1), like §1971.1 for heavy-duty engines, asks for two-sided rationality checks and names exhaust temperature sensors that steer a catalyst temperature strategy. No manufacturer publishes P2EA5. GM's 2025 diesel check for probe 5 (P2483) shows the method: after more than 10,800 s engine off, the value frozen at key-on is the reference, and if the probe then rises less than a calibrated map expects, it is judged stuck or out of the gas stream. Typical causes are a probe pulled from its boss, soot-coated or drifting elements, or two probes swapped at their plugs.
c: Probe loose or pulled from its boss after exhaust work
Drifting element or soot-coated tip reacting too slowly
Neighbouring probes swapped at their connectors
Contact resistance in the connector shifting the reading
s: Check engine lamp after two trips
Probe 6 stays flat or lags while other probes heat up
Regeneration interrupted or not started

P2EA6.t: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Temperature Sensor Circuit
P2EA6.d: P2EA6 is the general circuit fault of the temperature sensor in the charge pipe between the turbo compressor and the charge air cooler. Squeezing the air heats it a lot; Cummins notes in patent US6401457 that excessive outlet temperature can melt the compressor housing or harm the wheel, and still estimated the value in 2001 because no series sensor lasted there. GM's later patent US11060525 fits a sensor in exactly this duct and trims the boost target in closed loop once a limit is reached; with a sensor fault that function is disabled. No manufacturer documents P2EA6 publicly. It covers missing or intermittent signals that are neither clearly low (P2EC0) nor high (P2EC1); implausible values belong to P2EC2.
c: Loose or corroded connector on the charge pipe sensor
Wire breaking intermittently near the hot turbocharger
Faulty input in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp on
Compressor outlet temperature missing or jumping in live data
Boost limitation at high load possibly less refined

P2EA7.t: DC/AC Converter A Input Voltage Too Low
P2EA7.d: A DC/AC converter turns direct current into household AC for sockets in the vehicle. P2EA7 means the DC voltage reaching converter A is below the range in which it is allowed to run. Which supply that is depends on the design: Toyota Industries' patent US10050558 describes a 12 V-fed unit that only works between about 11 and 16 V, pauses its output when a weak or aged battery pulls the input down and restarts on its own once the voltage is back. Ford's patent US11043801 instead feeds the Pro Power sockets of a hybrid from the high-voltage bus. No manufacturer documents P2EA7 publicly. The driver notices dead sockets; the cause usually lies in the supply rather than in the converter.
c: Weak, discharged or aged 12 V battery
Voltage drop at the supply fuse, cable or ground point of the converter
Hybrid high-voltage supply restricted, for example at very low state of charge
Faulty input voltage measurement inside the converter
s: AC sockets in the vehicle deliver no power or cut out
Message about the power outlet or inverter in the cluster
Problem appears mainly with engine off or at low battery charge

P2EA8.t: DC/AC Converter A Input Voltage Too High
P2EA8.d: P2EA8 is the reverse of P2EA7: the DC input of converter A lies above its permitted window. In the 12 V design of Toyota Industries' patent US10050558 the inverter stops once the battery side exceeds about 16 V, for example after a jump start from a 24 V source or with a failed alternator regulator. Unlike the low-voltage case it does not simply resume, but waits for a reset such as switching the vehicle off and on or unplugging the loads. Where the converter hangs on the high-voltage bus, as in Ford's Pro Power layout (US11043801), an overvoltage points to the traction system rather than to the converter. No manufacturer documents P2EA8 publicly. The sockets switch off to protect the unit and the connected devices.
c: Charging system overvoltage from a faulty alternator regulator or DC/DC converter
Jump start or charging with too high a voltage
Faulty input voltage measurement inside the converter
s: AC sockets switch off and stay off until a restart
Other overvoltage messages or flickering lights

P2EA9.d: P2EA9 reports that converter A has become too hot. The converter watches the power devices that switch and invert the current – MOSFETs, diodes and transistors – and in Toyota Industries' patent US10050558 it stops once their temperature passes a set limit, then waits for a manual reset, the same handling as an input overvoltage. Heat builds up with long use near full load, a blocked air path behind trim or under a seat, high cabin temperatures or a cooling fan that no longer runs. Ford's high-voltage Pro Power layout (US11043801) also lowers the power ceiling while driving compared with standing. No manufacturer documents P2EA9 publicly. The sockets stay dead until the unit has cooled; if it repeats without heavy load, the sensor or converter itself is suspect.
c: Long operation near the rated power
Cooling air path blocked or cooling fan failed
High temperature at the mounting location
Faulty temperature sensing or power stage in the converter
s: AC sockets switch off under load
Output only returns after cooling and a restart

P2EAA.t: Active Radiator Air Flow Control Module A Control Circuit Performance
P2EAA.d: The active radiator air flow system meters cooling air with motor-driven flaps between bumper opening and radiator; J2012 keeps its control module apart from the grille shutter modules (P05C0, U0284). Hyundai and Kia's patent US11225900 shows such a system with two flap zones, each moved by its own actuator according to vehicle speed, outside and coolant temperature and refrigerant pressure. P2EAA means the control circuit of module A responds but does not behave as expected, for instance a drive signal outside its plausible range. No manufacturer documents P2EAA publicly. GM's smart shutter actuators show the comparable setup: they talk to the engine module over LIN, which only judges them with a supply between 11 and 32 V. A fault mostly costs fuel and warm-up speed.
c: Corroded or loose connector in the exposed front-end area
Supply or ground of the module outside its range
Internal fault in control module A
s: Check engine lamp on, where the maker assigns a MIL
Flaps stay in one position
Slower warm-up or slightly higher fuel consumption

P2EAB.t: Active Radiator Air Flow Control Module A Over Temperature
P2EAB.d: P2EAB means module A of the active radiator air flow system reports that its own electronics have overheated. Such smart actuators carry their motor driver on board and protect it: J2012 records the matching case for the grille shutter as P05C0, where the actuator switches its output stage off when the chip runs too hot. Typical triggers are a motor straining against ice, dirt or a jammed linkage, a mounting place close to the radiator in hot weather, or an internal fault. Hyundai and Kia's patent US11225900 shows where such modules sit, directly between bumper opening and radiator. No manufacturer documents P2EAB publicly. While the module is off, the flaps remain where they stopped; if they stay closed under load the engine can run hotter, otherwise fuel use and warm-up suffer.
c: Flaps blocked by ice, dirt or a damaged linkage, motor overloaded
High heat at the mounting place near the radiator
Internal fault in the module or its temperature sensing
s: Check engine lamp on, where the maker assigns a MIL
Flaps stop moving for a while
Higher coolant temperature under load if the flaps are stuck closed

P2EAC.t: Active Radiator Air Flow Control Module A Performance
P2EAC.d: P2EAC is the general performance fault of module A: the module can be reached, but the flap system does not do what it is told. GM's check of the comparable smart shutter actuator on the 3.0 L diesel LZ0 shows the approach: a gap of more than 5 % between commanded and reported position starts repeated attempts to free the flaps, and only after a calibrated number of failed retries is the fault confirmed, type B with the MIL after two trips. A Chrysler patent application, US20130338870, names ice as a frequent reason and has the system try again once the temperature is above 0 °C. No manufacturer documents P2EAC publicly; Hyundai and Kia's US11225900 shows the flap hardware involved. Usual causes are frozen or blocked flaps, a broken linkage and a worn actuator.
c: Flaps frozen or blocked by debris
Worn gearbox or motor in the actuator
s: Check engine lamp on, where the maker assigns a MIL
Flaps do not open or close, sometimes only in frost
Warmer engine under load or slower warm-up

P2EAD.d: Some diesels dose DEF at two points, each with its own metering unit or injector. P2EAD means the second one no longer delivers what it should. GM documents it for the 3.0 L Duramax LZ0, where its table calls it injector 2 performance with low consumption: the control unit compares the pressure drop expected while the second injector doses with what it measures and builds a correction factor; once the averaged factor passes the calibrated limit, proper delivery is no longer assured and the code sets as type A, MIL after one trip. Unit 1 has P20FE. GM bulletin 23-NA-193 lists P2EAD among codes on 2023 Silverado and Sierra 1500 caused by software and cured by an engine module update. Otherwise a crusted or partly blocked injector or a kinked line is usual.
c: Second DEF injector crusted or partly blocked by urea crystals
Kinked, frozen or blocked line to the second injector
Engine control software needing an update (GM LZ0 2023)
Weak DEF pump or pressure sensor deviation
s: Check engine lamp on
DEF warning and, if not repaired, speed limitation
Higher NOx emissions

P2EAE.t: Reductant Injection Valve Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1 Unit 2
P2EAE.d: P2EAE concerns the second DEF injector on bank 1. Open, low and high circuit faults have their own codes, P2053 to P2055; here the circuit works, yet its signal does not fit a properly moving valve. GM uses it on the 2023 3.0 L Duramax LZ0 to detect a stuck second injector: from the current trace of each injection it takes the second derivative, in which the armature movement shows up as a kink, and fails the test when too few samples cross a threshold that depends on injector temperature and battery voltage, judged over 5 of 10 samples, type A with MIL after one trip. Delphi's patent US11280245 explains this kink method and its limits with chopped drive voltage. The 2025 GM table no longer lists P2EAE. Causes are urea crystals, a seized armature and contact faults.
c: Armature of the second injector sticking from urea crystals
Corroded contacts distorting the current trace
s: Check engine lamp on
DEF system warning
Higher NOx emissions

P2EAF.t: Reductant Injection Valve Stuck Closed Bank 1 Unit 2
P2EAF.d: P2EAF means the second DEF injector on bank 1 stays shut although it is commanded open, so the SCR stage it serves gets no reductant. It is the unit 2 counterpart of P208E. Control units spot the case in two ways. One looks at the coil current: when the armature lifts, the trace shows a small kink, and Delphi's patent US11280245 describes finding it even with chopped drive voltage. The other compares pump effort with the commanded flow; in Cummins' patent US9664092 a shortfall of 90 % or more stands for a stuck-closed injector or a blocked line. No manufacturer documents P2EAF publicly; GM's LZ0 files a stuck second injector under P2EAE instead. Usually crystallised fluid or corrosion holds the needle. NOx emissions rise and the vehicle may later limit speed.
c: Corrosion inside the injector after poor fluid or long standstill
Blocked or frozen supply line to the second injector
s: Check engine lamp on
DEF warning with countdown to speed limitation
Higher NOx emissions

P2EB0.t: Throttle Valve Intake Air Pressure Sensor Circuit
