P2EB0.d: P2EB0 concerns the sensor that measures air pressure at the inlet of the throttle valve, i.e. between charger or air filter and throttle. On turbo engines this is the reading Ford calls TIP and GM TIAP; both makers, however, report faults of that sensor under the boost sensor codes P0236–P0238, and no manufacturer documents P2EB0 publicly. Ford's gasoline summary shows how widely the value is used: its PCV monitor P2282 needs a healthy TIP sensor before it runs. Bosch's comparable sensor sends pressure and temperature either on two analogue lines or digitally over a single SENT line, where garbled or missing messages would fit a general circuit code like this one. Low and high faults are P2EB1 and P2EB2.
c: Loose, corroded or oil-wetted connector at the sensor
Intermittent break in signal, reference or ground wire
Failed sensor electronics, e.g. SENT output
s: Check engine lamp on
Reduced boost or hesitant acceleration if a substitute value is used
Other air system checks such as the PCV monitor may not run

P2EB1.t: Throttle Valve Intake Air Pressure Sensor Circuit Low
P2EB1.d: P2EB1 says the pressure signal at the throttle inlet is below the lowest valid voltage. These sensors are linear: Ford's transfer curve gives about 0.4 V at 20 kPa and 4.5 V at 300 kPa, so a low voltage reads as an absurdly low pressure. A missing 5 V reference, a signal shorted to ground or a failed sensor are the usual causes. No manufacturer documents P2EB1; for the same sensor under the boost code P0237 GM's 2025 gasoline table 25OBDG03B sets a fault below 14.4 % of 5 V (about 50 kPa) in 320 of 400 samples taken every 12.5 ms, Type A, and Ford below 0.19 V for 5 s. Since boost control relies on this pressure, the engine may limit boost. P2EB2 is the opposite limit.
c: 5 V reference open or shorted, often shared with other sensors
s: Check engine lamp, often after the first trip
Noticeable loss of power under load
Pressure reading far below ambient in live data

P2EB2.t: Throttle Valve Intake Air Pressure Sensor Circuit High
P2EB2.d: P2EB2 is stored when the throttle inlet pressure signal exceeds its upper limit. Since voltage climbs with pressure, the module would read a boost no charger can deliver. Electrically this points to a signal wire touching the 5 V reference or battery voltage, or to an open sensor ground that lets the output float up. No manufacturer documents P2EB2 publicly. GM files the high fault of its TIAP sensor under P0238 and sets it above 85.8 % of 5 V, about 371 kPa, again 320 of 400 samples and Type A; Ford's throttle inlet sensor fails above 4.88 V for 5 s. GM's patent US8090522 shows that the throttle controller works directly with this pressure, sampled every 12.5 ms, so a wrong value disturbs throttle control. P2EB1 is the low limit.
c: Open sensor ground or corroded ground pin
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
s: Check engine lamp, often after the first trip
Boost limited, sluggish response
Pressure reading far above ambient with the engine off

P2EB3.t: Throttle Valve Intake Air Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2EB3.d: P2EB3 covers a throttle inlet pressure that is electrically fine but wrong. With the engine stopped, the pressure ahead of the throttle must equal manifold and barometric pressure; Ford checks this at key-up after at least 10 s off, allowing about 2.7 inHg between boost and manifold sensor. While running, GM compares its TIAP reading with an airflow model and fails it if the gap exceeds 30 kPa, reported as P0236. Nira Automotive's patent US5083434 shows why the value matters: the pressure drop across the throttle can replace the throttle angle when setting the boost target. No manufacturer documents P2EB3 publicly. Typical causes are a sensor drifting with age, a blocked or iced port, or a charge air leak that drags the model apart.
c: Sensor offset or drift with age
Pressure port blocked by oil residue or ice
Leak in the charge air path upsetting the model comparison
s: Check engine lamp on
Pressure reading differs from manifold and barometric pressure with engine off
Uneven boost or reduced power

P2EB4.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Inductive Charger High Voltage Interlock Circuit/Open
P2EB4.d: With inductive charging, the vehicle coil picks up high-frequency power from a ground pad and an on-board rectifier turns it into DC for the traction battery; SAE J2954 defines classes up to 11 kW around 85 kHz. Because this path carries high voltage, its plugs and covers sit in a high voltage interlock loop, a low-voltage signal wire that breaks as soon as a connector is pulled or a lid removed. P2EB4 says this loop of the inductive charger is open, and the charging path stays switched off. GM shows how a charging loop is checked on the Volt: the module feeds 5 V and compares the returned share, with a low reading set as type A. P2D35 covers implausible loop signals. No manufacturer documents P2EB4 publicly. Typical causes are an unseated connector after repair, a bent pin or a broken loop wire.
c: HV connector or cover of the charger not fully latched
Fault in the interlock evaluation of the module
s: Inductive charging does not start or stops
Charging fault message

P2EB5.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Inductive Charger Input Voltage Low
P2EB5.d: P2EB5 reports that the input of the inductive charger receives too little voltage during power transfer. That input is the AC the vehicle coil collects from the ground pad across the air gap, so the level depends on alignment, gap and the power sent by the ground side. For its reference coil SAE J2954 allows vertical gaps of up to about 250 mm and a sideways offset of up to 100 mm. In the patent US10826565 of Momentum Dynamics, now InductEV, the vehicle side keeps reporting its voltage and current to the ground unit, which drops the charging signal when a fault is flagged. No manufacturer documents P2EB5 publicly. Low readings come from a poor parking position, an object between the pads, a weak ground unit or a faulty sense circuit. Charging slows or stops; cable charging is unaffected.
c: Vehicle not parked accurately over the ground pad
Object or ice between ground pad and vehicle coil
Ground unit delivering too little power
Faulty input voltage measurement in the charger
s: Inductive charging slow or interrupted
Charging fault message

P2EB6.t: Hybrid/EV Battery Inductive Charger Input Voltage High
P2EB6.d: P2EB6 is the counterpart to P2EB5: the voltage at the input of the inductive charger is higher than its electronics accept. Too much induced voltage can stem from a ground unit sending more power than requested, a ride height that shifts the coupling, for example when the vehicle is loaded or unloaded during charging, or a control loop between both sides that has lost step. Momentum Dynamics' patent US10826565 explains why the vehicle side reports voltage, current and the gap in near real time, and how the ground unit halts transfer at once when the vehicle signals a fault. SAE J2954 sets the 85 kHz band and the power classes within which these limits work. No manufacturer documents P2EB6 publicly. The charger shuts down to protect itself and the battery; cable charging stays possible.
c: Ground unit sending more power than requested
Coupling changed by ride height or position during charging
Disturbed communication between vehicle and ground unit
Faulty input voltage measurement in the charger
s: Inductive charging stops shortly after starting
Charging fault message

P2EB7.d: P2EB7 is a request rather than a classic fault: the vehicle considers its 12 V battery due for replacement. Energy management judges battery condition through a sensor or a battery with its own electronics on the LIN bus; HELLA's intelligent battery sensor, for example, measures voltage, current and temperature and works out state of charge, health and function. Bentley stores P2EB700 in the engine electronics of the 2025 Continental GT, GTC and Flying Spur. Its bulletin 2079155/2 states that the code lights no MIL and can stem from a brief communication fault between LIN bus and battery module; the remedy is to disconnect battery and LIN plug for 15 minutes, not a new battery. On other vehicles the code may truly point to an aged battery, so a proper battery test comes first.
c: 12 V battery worn, low remaining capacity
Brief LIN communication fault with the battery module (Bentley 2025)
New battery fitted but not registered or of the wrong type
s: Code stored without warning lamp
Possibly weak starting or reduced start-stop operation

P2EB9.t: Reductant Injection Valve Circuit Range/Performance Bank 2 Unit 2
P2EB9.d: P2EB9 is the bank 2 twin of P2EAE: the circuit of the second DEF injector on the second exhaust bank works electrically, but its signal does not match a valve that opens and closes as it should. Bank 2 implies a separate exhaust line for the second cylinder bank, and unit 2 a further dosing point on that line. No manufacturer documents P2EB9 publicly. GM's 3.0 L Duramax LZ0 shows how such a test runs for bank 1 unit 2: it takes the second derivative of the injector current and fails when too few injections show the armature moving. Delphi's patent US11280245 describes the same kink detection. Open circuit, low and high on this injector are P2056 to P2058. Usual causes are crystal deposits, a sticking armature and corroded contacts; NOx emissions can then exceed the limits.
c: Corroded contacts distorting the current trace
s: Check engine lamp on
DEF system warning
Higher NOx emissions

P2EBB.d: P2EBB is the general circuit fault of a sensor that reports the temperature inside the crankcase, i.e. of the blow-by gas or the space above the oil. Patents show what engines do with it: Ford (US9228557) feeds exhaust-heated air into the crankcase, checks the arrival with such a sensor and stores a code, possibly with MIL, if the reading stays below the expected value; GM (US5897597) diagnoses the ventilation by the temperature rise of the gas between fresh-air inlet and PCV valve. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(9) requires the crankcase ventilation to be monitored, so a dead sensor can block that check. No manufacturer documents P2EBB publicly. The code fits signal loss or intermittent contact; out-of-range faults are P2EBE and P2EBD.
c: Connector loose or contaminated with engine oil
Harness wire breaking intermittently on the engine block
s: Check engine lamp on
Crankcase temperature missing or jumping in live data
No noticeable change in how the engine runs

P2EBC.d: P2EBC means the crankcase temperature sensor delivers an electrically valid value that does not suit the engine state: it may stick, react too slowly or sit far from the coolant and oil temperatures after a long stop. The CARB rule 13 CCR 1968.2 calls in (e)(15.2.1) for rationality checks that catch readings that are wrongly high as well as wrongly low. Why the value must be right is shown by patents: Ford (US9394843) uses an oil temperature sensor on the crankcase as a gate for purging fuel from diluted oil, and a hydrogen-engine application (US20230313750) compares crankcase gas temperature with the blow-by dew point to decide how much air prevents water condensing. No manufacturer documents P2EBC. Electrical faults use P2EBB, P2EBD and P2EBE.
c: Sensor drifted or slow because of sludge or oil coking on the tip
Contact resistance in the connector shifting the value
Replacement sensor with a different characteristic fitted
s: Check engine lamp after the fault is confirmed
Crankcase reading disagrees with oil and coolant temperature on a cold start
Crankcase ventilation checks may not complete

P2EBD.d: P2EBD is set when the crankcase temperature signal rises above its highest valid voltage. With the usual pull-up arrangement this happens when the current path through the sensor is interrupted, for example by an unplugged or oil-soaked connector, a broken wire or an open element, or when the signal touches the 5 V reference or battery voltage. For an NTC thermistor, whose resistance grows as it cools, the module then sees an impossibly cold crankcase; a PTC element would read as overheated instead. No manufacturer documents P2EBD, so limits and debounce times are not public. Under (e)(15.2.1) of 13 CCR 1968.2 the high fault has to be stored separately from the low fault P2EBE and from the rationality fault P2EBC.
c: Connector unplugged, oil-soaked or with spread terminals
Signal shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
s: Check engine lamp on
Crankcase temperature fixed at an extreme value
Engine runs normally

P2EBE.d: P2EBE reports a crankcase temperature signal below the lowest voltage the circuit can produce when intact. In practice a short is behind it: either the signal lead has rubbed through to ground on the engine block, or the insulation inside the sensor has given way, for instance after oil has crept into the housing. If the sensor is an NTC thermistor, a low voltage stands for great heat, so the module would believe the crankcase is overheating; a PTC element would appear frozen. No manufacturer publishes this code. The reading matters because systems such as Ford's crankcase heating in US9228557 use it to judge whether warm air arrives. CARB's 13 CCR 1968.2 keeps the low fault apart from P2EBD (section (e)(15.2.1)). The engine itself usually runs on unchanged.
c: Signal wire chafed through to ground on the engine
Sensor shorted internally after oil ingress
Faulty input stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp on
Live data shows an implausible crankcase temperature
Crankcase heating or ventilation checks suspended

P2EBF.d: P2EBF reports that the control used to select a battery charging mode stays in one state, most likely a button that reads as permanently pressed. On plug-in hybrids such a control makes the engine recharge the traction battery while driving: Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV had a separate Battery Charge (CHRG) switch that runs the engine until about 80 percent state of charge, and the 2026 model reaches the same mode through its EV button. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 defines such a driver-chosen mode that raises the state of charge, citing a charge now button as example, and requires distance and fuel used in it to be tracked. No manufacturer documents P2EBF publicly; Mitsubishi's 2023 PHEV code chart lists no such code. A stuck switch can leave the mode on or make it unselectable.
c: Button mechanically jammed or contact welded in the pressed state
Spilled liquid or dirt in the console switch panel
Short in the switch signal wire imitating a held button
s: Engine keeps running to charge the traction battery
Charging mode cannot be switched on or off
Higher fuel use and less electric driving

P2EC0.t: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
P2EC0.d: P2EC0 reports that the compressor outlet temperature signal has fallen under the lowest valid voltage. Air temperature sensors on the intake side are usually NTC thermistors, as Bosch states for its combined boost pressure and temperature sensor; their resistance shrinks as they warm, so a signal pulled towards ground is read as extreme heat. A signal wire touching ground or a sensor shorted internally is the usual cause. With a PTC element the meaning would be reversed. No manufacturer documents P2EC0, so thresholds and timing are unknown. Section (e)(15.2.1) of California's 13 CCR 1968.2 has the low fault stored apart from the high one (P2EC1). In GM's patent US11060525 a faulty sensor switches the closed-loop boost reduction off.
c: Signal wire shorted to ground, e.g. chafed on the charge pipe
Oil or moisture bridging the connector pins
s: Check engine lamp on
Live data shows an implausibly hot charge air temperature
Possible loss of power if a substitute value limits boost

P2EC1.t: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Temperature Sensor Circuit High
P2EC1.d: P2EC1 is set when the compressor outlet temperature sensor delivers a voltage above its permitted window. Because the module feeds the sensor through a pull-up resistor, any break in the current path lifts the input to the reference: an unplugged or corroded connector, a cracked wire or a burnt-out element. A short to 5 V or battery voltage has the same effect. For an NTC thermistor this shows up as severe cold, for a PTC part as severe heat. No manufacturer documents the code publicly. The outlet sensor works in a harsh spot, where charge air can reach about 200 °C, a value Ford's diesel charge air cooler check still covers, so heat and vibration at the plug are a known strain. Low reading: P2EC0; general fault: P2EA6.
c: Connector unplugged, corroded or with spread terminals
Signal shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
s: Check engine lamp on
Live data shows a fixed extreme value
Usually no noticeable change in driving

P2EC2.t: Turbocharger Compressor Outlet Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P2EC2.d: P2EC2 flags a compressor outlet temperature that is electrically valid but does not fit the operating point. A reference is easy to build: Cummins (US6401457) derives the outlet temperature from inlet temperature and pressure, turbo speed, air mass and pressure ratio, and after a long soak the sensor should also agree with intake and ambient readings. Under 13 CCR 1968.2 CARB wants such two-sided checks (section (e)(15.2.1)) and, in (f)(7), a watch on charge air cooler performance, which relies on the temperature entering the cooler; Ford's diesel test P026A scales its limits with compressor outlet temperature. No manufacturer documents P2EC2. Typical causes are a slow, drifted or oil-coated sensor, or one that has worked loose in its port.
c: Sensor drifted or reacting too slowly
Tip coated with oil from crankcase or turbo seals
Sensor loose or not reaching into the air stream
s: Check engine lamp after the fault is confirmed
Reading disagrees with intake and ambient temperature after a cold soak
Charge air cooler diagnosis may be suspended

P3400.d: P3400 is the bank-level verdict: the engine computer has concluded that cylinder deactivation on bank 1 as a whole does not behave as commanded, without blaming a single circuit. Makers fill it differently. On the 2019 LT4 Corvette, GM compares a manifold pressure model with all cylinders firing against the same model while cylinders are off; 100 failed samples out of 200 give a Type B code. Mazda's 2.5 l four-cylinders store it when a deactivation oil control valve is clogged, for example by plastic from the filter wrapper (SA-061/20). In Honda's VCM V6 it stems from a rocker arm oil pressure switch, and the Hemi Ram 1500 got a PCM update for it. Bank 2 is P3497. The lamp comes on; misfires or rough running may follow.
c: Deactivation oil control valve or its screen clogged by debris
Low oil level, wrong grade or overdue oil change
Switchable rocker arm or lifter broken, dislodged or not latching
Oil pressure too high on cold start, e.g. weak relief valve spring
Engine control software needing an update
s: Check engine lamp on
Rough idle or misfire codes on the deactivating cylinders
Ticking or clattering from the valve train
Reduced-cylinder mode no longer used, higher fuel use

P3401.d: P3401 points to a broken control path to the solenoid that switches off cylinder 1, a cylinder that GM and Chrysler V8s and Ford's 1.5 l three-cylinder EcoBoost all deactivate. On the 2019 L84 and L86 V8s, GM looks at the low-side output while it is off: over 200 kilohm to ground counts as open, and 20 failures among 25 readings at 250 ms intervals make it a Type B fault. GM adds that some controllers store P3403 alongside. Ford's VDE monitor relies on the fault status of its smart driver and decides within 5 seconds. For the 5.7 l Hemi, a Chrysler STAR case describes a deformed manifold heat shield that rubs the MDS solenoid harness open. P3403 and P3404 cover shorts, P3402 the mechanical function. Deactivation is then locked out.
c: Control wire broken or worn through, e.g. by a hot exhaust heat shield
Loose, corroded or oil-soaked solenoid connector
Open coil in the cylinder 1 deactivation solenoid
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp on, on GM after the second trip
Engine stays in all-cylinder mode
Slightly higher fuel consumption

P3402.d: This code reports that cylinder 1 does not respond as expected when the engine computer switches it off or back on, although the control circuit itself tests fine. Ford lists P3402 in its Variable Displacement Engine monitor for 2020-2023 gasoline engines: it runs continuously during deactivation, entry and exit, between 400 and 4500 rpm and once oil pressure has had about two seconds to build. GM handles the mechanical check for cylinder 1 under its own code P3498 instead. Wiring faults on the same channel set P3401, P3403 or P3404. A driver typically notices a warning lamp, a shake when the engine changes modes, or a misfire on cylinder 1.
c: Low oil level, wrong viscosity or aged oil slows the hydraulic switching
Switchable lifter or rocker of cylinder 1 sticking or not latching
Deactivation solenoid valve sticking or its oil screen blocked
Leaking solenoid seal lets control pressure bleed off
s: Check engine lamp on
Shudder or jerk when the engine enters or leaves reduced-cylinder mode
Misfire on cylinder 1 (P0301)
Cylinder deactivation no longer used, higher fuel use

P3403.t: Cylinder 1 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit Low
P3403.d: The engine computer drives the deactivation valve for cylinder 1 through an output stage that checks its own wiring. P3403 means that check found the control line pulled to ground. GM documents it for the L84 and L86 V8s (2019): with the driver off, an impedance below 0.5 ohm to ground counts as a fault, and 20 failures in 25 samples taken every 250 ms set a Type B code, so the lamp comes on after the second trip. Ford's VDE monitor flags the same short via its smart driver within 5 seconds. An open line is P3401, a short to battery voltage P3404, a mechanical failure P3402. The engine then stays in all-cylinder mode, mainly costing fuel.
c: Control wire chafed against the engine and shorted to ground
Internal short in the cylinder 1 deactivation solenoid
Oil or water in the solenoid connector
Faulty output driver in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp on after two trips
Engine no longer switches to reduced-cylinder mode
Somewhat higher fuel consumption

P3404.t: Cylinder 1 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit High
P3404.d: P3404 is the short-to-power counterpart within the cylinder 1 group. GM tests it while the low-side driver is switched on: if the output still shows less than 0.5 ohm to supply voltage, the current has no proper path through the solenoid, and 20 of 25 samples at 250 ms set a Type B fault. The test only runs with at least 11 V at the powertrain relay and about 425 rpm (L84; 400 rpm on the L86). Ford names P3404 for the single deactivating cylinder of its VDE engines. Typical culprits are a control wire touching a supply line or a solenoid with shorted windings. Compare P3403 (short to ground) and P3401 (open).
c: Control wire shorted to a supply voltage in the harness
Shorted winding in the cylinder 1 deactivation solenoid
Damaged output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp on
Cylinder deactivation disabled
Possible further circuit codes on other solenoids if a shared supply is affected

P3405.d: J2012 reserves P3405 for an open control circuit of a separate exhaust valve actuator on cylinder 1. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The common systems do not need it: in GM's Dynamic Fuel Management one solenoid per cylinder feeds oil to both intake and exhaust lifters, and Ford's VDE only lists intake codes for cylinder 1. A GM patent application uses one shared hydraulic valve and only sets the order, with the exhaust valves switched off and back on before the intake valves; a Ford patent watches the exhaust valve via exhaust pressure. A separate exhaust actuator would fall under CARB's output component rule, which asks for continuity checks. If used, an open coil or wire would set P3405, while P3401 covers the intake side and P3406-P3408 the other exhaust faults.
c: Broken wire or loose terminal to the exhaust valve actuator
Open coil in the cylinder 1 exhaust valve actuator
Output driver fault in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp on
Cylinder deactivation or valve switching disabled

P3406.d: Where an engine controls the exhaust valves of cylinder 1 separately, P3406 would mean the exhaust side does not follow the command although the circuit checks pass. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Ford holds a patent that detects an exhaust valve still opening after deactivation through pressure changes in the exhaust, and a GM patent, using one shared control valve, has the exhaust valves deactivate and also reactivate before the intake valves, so a lagging exhaust side is a real failure mode. Production systems from GM and Ford instead check the whole cylinder (GM P3498, Ford P3402). Electrical faults on this channel are P3405, P3407 and P3408; if the cylinder keeps pumping exhaust, the driver may feel roughness.
c: Insufficient or degraded oil delays exhaust-side switching
Exhaust lifter or rocker of cylinder 1 not latching or unlatching
s: Check engine lamp on
Rough running or vibration in reduced-cylinder mode
Cylinder deactivation suspended

P3407.t: Cylinder 1 Exhaust Valve Control Circuit Low
P3407.d: P3407 stands for a short to ground in the control circuit of a dedicated exhaust valve actuator on cylinder 1. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, so there are no published thresholds. As an analogy, GM's intake-side code P3403 counts an impedance under 0.5 ohm to ground, seen with the driver off, as a fault. CARB requires such output circuits to be checked for shorts. Engines with one shared solenoid per cylinder, like GM's AFM and DFM V8s, report this fault under the intake-side codes instead. An open exhaust circuit would be P3405, a short to power P3408. The car usually keeps running normally on all cylinders, with a warning lamp.
c: Actuator control wire shorted to ground
Internal short in the exhaust valve actuator
Engine control module output stage fault
s: Check engine lamp on
No change to reduced-cylinder mode

P3408.t: Cylinder 1 Exhaust Valve Control Circuit High
P3408.d: If an engine has its own actuator for the exhaust valves of cylinder 1, P3408 marks a control circuit that reads high, usually a short to battery voltage. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. For comparison, GM checks the intake-side P3404 with the driver switched on and flags under 0.5 ohm to supply. A GM patent application switches intake and exhaust valves together through one shared hydraulic valve, exhaust side first, and describes no separate exhaust channel either. With one solenoid per cylinder, as on GM's DFM, the code is not needed. Siblings: P3405 open, P3406 function, P3407 short to ground; P3404 is the intake-side equivalent.
c: Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Shorted coil in the exhaust valve actuator
Output stage fault in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp on
Cylinder deactivation disabled

P3409.d: P3409 is the open-circuit code for the deactivation control of cylinder 2. GM uses it on two very different engines. On the 3.6 L V6 (LGX, LGZ) cylinder 2 is one of the two active fuel management cylinders, and an engineering bulletin links P3409 to oil leaking from the rocker arm oil control valve in the camshaft cover. On the L84 V8 with Dynamic Fuel Management every cylinder has a solenoid; GM flags an open circuit when it sees more than 200 kohm with the driver off, 20 of 25 samples at 250 ms, Type B. Shorts are P3411 and P3412, a mechanical failure P3410. The driver sees a warning lamp and loses the fuel-saving mode.
c: Oil leaking at the control valve and soaking its connector (GM 3.6 L V6)
Broken wire or loose pin in the cylinder 2 solenoid circuit
Open coil in the cylinder 2 deactivation solenoid
Engine control module output driver fault
s: Check engine lamp on
Oil residue around the valve cover control valve (V6)
No reduced-cylinder operation, higher fuel use

P340A.d: P340A is meant for engines that switch the intake valves of a whole bank through a shared control circuit, rather than one solenoid per cylinder. It reports an electrical fault in that bank 1 circuit, without saying whether it is open or shorted. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, which leaves it without known limits; CARB merely demands that outputs of this kind be monitored for breaks and shorts. The common systems are built per cylinder: GM's DFM V8 has one solenoid per cylinder in the valley, so faults go to codes such as P3401. Honda's VCM V6 reports bank-level trouble as P3400. Bank 2 is P340B, the exhaust side P340C, the bank 1 function check P341A. Expect a warning lamp and no reduced-cylinder mode.
c: Damaged, open or shorted wire in the bank 1 control circuit
Corroded or loose connector at the bank 1 actuator
Bank 1 intake deactivation actuator with open or shorted coil
Output stage fault in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp on
Cylinder deactivation disabled on bank 1
Higher fuel consumption at light load

P340B.d: P340B mirrors P340A for bank 2, the bank that does not contain cylinder 1, so it only applies to V or boxer engines. It marks an electrical fault in a control circuit that switches the intake valves of that whole bank at once. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The widespread V8 systems put the deactivating cylinders of bank 2, cylinders 4 and 6 on GM and Chrysler engines, on their own solenoids and report them as P3425 or P3441. Honda's VCM V6 watches bank 2 via a rocker arm oil pressure switch and stores P3497. CARB asks for circuit checks of such outputs. The bank 1 counterpart is P340A, the bank 2 exhaust circuit P340D, the function code P341B. Usually the only effects are the lamp and lost economy.
c: Chafed, open or shorted wire to the bank 2 actuator
Oil or moisture in the bank 2 actuator connector
Defective bank 2 intake deactivation actuator coil
Engine control module output stage fault
s: Check engine lamp on
Engine runs on all cylinders permanently
Slightly higher fuel consumption

P340C.d: P340C concerns a separate electrical circuit that disables the exhaust valves of bank 1 as a group. A fault in its wiring, connector or actuator coil sets the code. No manufacturer documents it publicly, and none of the known production systems needs it: GM's DFM engines feed the intake and exhaust lifters of each cylinder from one shared solenoid, and a GM patent application describes one hydraulic valve per pair of cylinders that drops the exhaust valves before the intake valves purely by cam timing. Under CARB rules every output of this type needs an electrical integrity test. The intake-side circuit is P340A, bank 2 exhaust P340D, the bank 1 exhaust function P341C. Drivers mainly see the lamp; deactivation is suspended.
c: Open or shorted wire in the bank 1 exhaust actuator circuit
Exhaust deactivation actuator coil open or shorted
Connector or wiring damaged by heat near the exhaust side
Engine control module output stage fault
s: Check engine lamp on
Reduced-cylinder mode not available

P340D.d: P340D is the bank 2 version of the exhaust-side group circuit: the engine computer sees an electrical fault on the line that is supposed to disable the exhaust valves of the bank without cylinder 1. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Separate exhaust control matters because a cylinder can only act as a gas spring if its exhaust valves stay shut too; a Ford patent shows how an exhaust valve that keeps opening can be detected from exhaust pressure. On known engines, though, intake and exhaust are switched together per cylinder, as with GM's DFM. CARB rules call for monitoring of outputs like this one. Related: P340C for bank 1, P340B for the bank 2 intake side, P341D for the function check. Deactivation stays off.
c: Damaged wiring to the bank 2 exhaust deactivation actuator
Faulty coil in the bank 2 exhaust actuator
Output stage fault in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp on
Engine no longer drops cylinders at light load

P3410.d: P3410 covers a cylinder 2 deactivation system that is electrically intact but does not do what is commanded, such as valves that keep opening or fail to return. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM checks this behavior on the L84 under its own code P3499, by watching manifold pressure while cylinder 2 should be off; Ford uses the matching cylinder 1 code P3402. GM bulletin 21-NA-036 for 3.6 L V6 engines shows how such faults appear in practice: oil leaking past the control valve or rockers that do not latch cause misfires on cylinder 2 (P0302). Circuit faults belong to P3409, P3411 and P3412. Expect roughness and lost economy.
c: Oil bleeding past the control valve seal, pressure lost
Rocker or lifter of cylinder 2 not latching
Broken solenoid tip left in the bore keeps a new valve from seating
s: Misfire on cylinder 2, often after a reduced-cylinder phase
Check engine lamp on
Vibration at light load

P3411.t: Cylinder 2 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit Low
P3411.d: P3411 means the control output for the cylinder 2 deactivation valve sees a short to ground. GM lists it for the L84 V8 (2019), whose Dynamic Fuel Management can switch off any cylinder: below 0.5 ohm to ground with the low-side driver off, 20 failures in 25 samples every 250 ms, at least 11 V on the powertrain relay and 425 rpm. It is a Type B fault, so the lamp lights after two trips in a row. GM notes that some controllers set P3409 together with it. On engines where cylinder 2 cannot be deactivated the code has no use. The fix is usually in the wiring or the solenoid in the engine valley; P3412 is the short to power.
c: Damaged insulation lets the control wire touch ground
s: Check engine lamp after two trips
Dynamic Fuel Management inactive, engine stays on all cylinders

P3412.t: Cylinder 2 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit High
P3412.d: On GM's L84 V8 each cylinder, including cylinder 2, has a valve lifter oil solenoid bolted into the block valley. NHTSA's description of the system notes these solenoids are driven with peak-and-hold current for fast response. P3412 is set when the control line for cylinder 2 is shorted to supply voltage: GM checks it with the driver on and treats under 0.5 ohm to power as failed, 20 of 25 samples at 250 ms, Type B. In that state the computer cannot pull the solenoid properly and drops cylinder 2 from deactivation. Related codes are P3409 for an open circuit, P3411 for a short to ground and P3410 when the circuit is fine but the cylinder does not respond.
c: Control wire shorted to a voltage feed in the harness
Low-resistance coil in the cylinder 2 solenoid
Engine control module output stage fault
s: Check engine lamp on
Cylinder deactivation no longer active

P3413.d: P3413 belongs to the exhaust half of the cylinder 2 block and reports an open control circuit for a separately driven exhaust valve actuator. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The engines known to deactivate cylinder 2, GM's L84 V8 and the 3.6 L V6, switch intake and exhaust valves through one control valve per cylinder and therefore report circuit faults as P3409. The code would only apply to designs with their own control valve for the exhaust side; a GM patent application instead switches both sides with one shared valve and merely staggers them, exhaust first. CARB requires a continuity check for such output components. P3414 to P3416 complete the exhaust group. The driver would see a lamp and lose deactivation.
c: Open wire or connector to the cylinder 2 exhaust actuator
s: Check engine lamp on
Cylinder deactivation unavailable

P3414.d: P3414 would be set when the exhaust valves of cylinder 2 do not follow a deactivation or reactivation command on an engine with separate exhaust valve control. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The underlying problem is described in a Ford patent: an exhaust valve that still opens after deactivation shows up as pressure changes in the exhaust, and the controller can reactivate the cylinder or block further deactivation. GM's DFM engines report a cylinder whose intake and exhaust valves stay active under their own code P3499 instead. Electrical faults on this channel are P3413, P3415 and P3416, the intake-side function code is P3410.
c: Exhaust-side lifter or rocker of cylinder 2 not switching
Low oil pressure or aerated oil
s: Check engine lamp on
Rough running when cylinders are switched off
Deactivation suspended by the engine computer

P3415.t: Cylinder 2 Exhaust Valve Control Circuit Low
P3415.d: P3415 describes a control circuit for a dedicated cylinder 2 exhaust valve actuator that is pulled toward ground. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Cylinder 2 itself is a common deactivation candidate: GM switches it off on its 3.6 l and 3.0 l V6 engines (bulletin 21-NA-036) and on DFM V8s, but there one oil control valve serves the whole cylinder, so wiring faults land on the intake-side codes P3409, P3411 and P3412. On the L84, GM treats a resistance to ground below 0.5 ohm, read while the output stage is inactive, as a short. CARB wants these outputs tested for shorts. Siblings: P3413 open, P3414 function, P3416 short to power; cylinder 1 uses P3407. The engine keeps running on all cylinders.
c: Control wire of the cylinder 2 exhaust actuator touching ground
Internal short in the cylinder 2 exhaust actuator
Damaged output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp on
Cylinder deactivation inhibited

P3416.t: Cylinder 2 Exhaust Valve Control Circuit High
P3416.d: P3416 means the control line of a separate cylinder 2 exhaust valve actuator sits too high, typically because it touches a supply voltage or the coil has shorted turns. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The closest published test is GM's for the intake-side P3412 on the L84: once the output stage is active, any resistance to supply below 0.5 ohm is a failure, and 20 hits out of 25 lead to a Type B entry. NHTSA's review of GM's DFM V8 describes one valve lifter oil solenoid per cylinder that serves intake and exhaust alike, which is why such engines need no exhaust-only code. CARB requires shorts in outputs to be detected. Related: P3413 open, P3415 short to ground, P3408 for cylinder 1.
c: Actuator control wire shorted to a supply line
Shorted turns in the cylinder 2 exhaust actuator coil
Engine control module output stage fault
s: Check engine lamp on
Engine stays in full-cylinder mode

P3417.d: P3417 flags a broken path in the drive circuit of the cylinder 3 deactivation solenoid. GM documents it twice: its 2007 Displacement on Demand table covers solenoid circuits on cylinder 1, 3 and 5 and needs 30 bad readings in 100 with the engine turning faster than 800 rpm; for the 2019 DFM engine L84, the ECM expects over 200 kohm whenever its low-side output rests, 20 of 25 checks, Type B. That controller also watches a high-side driver for the same solenoid under separate codes, and GM warns that P3419 may appear alongside. The LTA and LT2 V8s also put cylinder 3 to rest, together with 2, 5 and 8 (bulletin 20-NA-038). As long as the circuit is open, every cylinder keeps firing.
c: Broken or chafed wire between control module and cylinder 3 solenoid
Open winding in the cylinder 3 deactivation solenoid
Loose, oily or corroded solenoid connector
Failed output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp on
Reduced-cylinder mode no longer engages
Slightly higher fuel consumption

P3418.d: P3418 is meant for a cylinder 3 deactivation that is wired correctly yet does not respond as requested: the cylinder keeps breathing when it should rest, or fails to come back. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM tests the hardware of cylinder 3 under its own code P349A; bulletin 20-NA-204 for the 2021 L84 and L87 notes that a voltage dip during cranking can briefly disable the outputs and set that code without a real fault. Honda shows the same failure pattern in another form: in bulletin 13-055 excess cold-start oil pressure pushed cylinders 1 to 4 into cut mode uncommanded, logged as P3400/P3497 with misfires. Circuit faults belong to P3417, P3419 and P3420. Expect rough running and a misfire code.
c: Low oil level, wrong viscosity or aged oil
Lifter or rocker of cylinder 3 not locking or unlocking
Cylinder 3 control valve sticking or its screen blocked
Oil pressure too high or too low for the switching window
s: Misfire code for cylinder 3 (P0303)
Shudder when the engine changes between modes
Check engine lamp on

P3419.t: Cylinder 3 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit Low
P3419.d: P3419 says the line feeding the cylinder 3 deactivation solenoid is dragged toward ground. The L84 V8 in GM's 2019 OBD documents shows the test: while the low-side output rests, a resistance to chassis ground under half an ohm is wrong, and once 20 out of 25 readings, one every 250 ms, agree, with the powertrain relay above 11 V and the engine at 425 rpm or faster, a Type B fault is logged. The lamp therefore follows on the second trip, and some controllers add P3417 at the same moment. The older 2007 Displacement on Demand table still merged short and open for cylinder 3 into one solenoid test. P3420 is the opposite fault, P3427 the cylinder 4 equivalent. Driving stays normal apart from the lost fuel saving.
c: Insulation of the cylinder 3 control wire worn through to ground
Internal short of the cylinder 3 solenoid to its housing
Oil or water bridging pins in the connector
Defective driver in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp after two drives
Engine no longer drops cylinders under light load

P341A.t: Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit Performance Bank 1
P341A.d: P341A is the function check behind P340A: the bank 1 intake deactivation circuit is electrically sound, yet the valves do not end up where they were commanded. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Comparable checks exist under other numbers. GM's LT4 compares a modeled and a measured manifold pressure with and without deactivation and reports the bank result as P3400; per-cylinder failures on DFM engines go to P3498 onward. A Delphi patent notes why averaged manifold pressure alone separates working and failed intake deactivation poorly and cannot name the cylinder. Typical causes are hydraulic: low or dirty oil, a sticking control valve, lifters that do not latch. Misfires and rough running are possible.
c: Low oil level or aged, contaminated oil
Bank 1 deactivation control valve sticking or screen blocked
Switchable lifters or rockers on bank 1 not latching or releasing
Insufficient oil pressure from a worn pump or leaking seal
s: Check engine lamp on
Jerk or vibration when cylinders switch off or on
Misfire codes on bank 1

P341B.t: Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit Performance Bank 2
P341B.d: With P341B the controller judges that intake deactivation on bank 2 is not doing its job even though no circuit fault is present: cylinders keep breathing when they should be sealed, or stay sealed after reactivation. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. One way to catch it is described in a Delphi patent: pressure pulses in the intake are timed against crank angle, and a missing or extra pulse shows which cylinder misbehaves. In practice, makers use their own codes instead, such as GM's P3498 series per cylinder or Honda's bank code P3497. CARB requires a functional check of such outputs. Electrical faults on the same bank are P340B; bank 1 is P341A. Oil level and quality are the first things to check.
c: Oil level too low or oil past its service life
Lifter or rocker on bank 2 stuck in one switching state
Control valve on bank 2 sticking or leaking past its seal
s: Check engine lamp on
Rough running, mostly at light load
Misfire codes on bank 2

P341C.t: Deactivation/Exhaust Valve Control Circuit Performance Bank 1
P341C.d: P341C covers exhaust valves on bank 1 that ignore a deactivation command while their wiring and actuator coil check out. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. A Ford patent explains why it matters and how to spot it: a sealed cylinder whose exhaust valve keeps lifting leaves a trace in exhaust pressure, and the controller can respond by reactivating the cylinder, blocking further deactivation and storing a fault. Production engines control both valve sets per cylinder jointly, so GM, for instance, files such faults under its own per-cylinder codes from P3498. Electrically this circuit reports P340C; intake function on bank 1 is P341A, bank 2 exhaust P341D.
c: Exhaust-side lifter or rocker on bank 1 not switching
Low oil pressure or foaming oil
s: Check engine lamp on
Popping or uneven exhaust note in reduced-cylinder mode
Deactivation suspended

P341D.t: Deactivation/Exhaust Valve Control Circuit Performance Bank 2
P341D.d: P341D appears once the bank 2 exhaust valves respond wrongly to a deactivation or reactivation request while the electrical side is intact. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Timing is the critical part: a GM patent application has the exhaust valves stop before the intake valves when a cylinder is switched off and resume before them when it comes back, so that burnt gas is expelled and no fresh charge is trapped. GM's DFM V8, as NHTSA describes it, reverses this and stops the intake side first. If the exhaust side lags, the planned order breaks. CARB expects outputs like this to be checked for proper function. The circuit code for this bank is P340D, the bank 1 equivalent P341C, the intake function on bank 2 P341B. Expect a lamp, harsh mode changes and higher fuel use.
c: Exhaust lifter or rocker on bank 2 switching late or not at all
Oil too thin, too old or too low for fast switching
s: Check engine lamp on
Bump or shudder during mode changes
Higher fuel consumption

P3420.t: Cylinder 3 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit High
P3420.d: P3420 reports that the cylinder 3 deactivation control line carries supply voltage where the module expects to pull it low. On GM's L84 the test runs only while the low-side output is switched on: a connection to battery voltage below 0.5 ohm, confirmed in 20 out of 25 samples, sets a Type B code. According to NHTSA's 2025 investigation into GM's DFM V8s, every cylinder has exactly one lifter oil solenoid, run by a peak-and-hold driver, so a single short disables the whole cylinder's switching. The Gen IV controller also has a separate high-side stage for this solenoid with its own codes, which helps tell which half of the circuit failed. P3419 covers the short to ground. The engine just keeps all eight cylinders working.
c: Control wire of cylinder 3 touching a powered conductor
Shorted turns in the cylinder 3 solenoid winding
Output transistor in the engine control module damaged
s: Check engine lamp on
Fuel economy mode unavailable

P3421.d: P3421 opens the exhaust group of cylinder 3 and stands for an interrupted circuit to an actuator that would switch only the exhaust valves. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Engines that are known to idle cylinder 3, such as GM's LTA and LT2 V8s (bulletin 20-NA-038) and the L84, let one lifter control both valves of the cylinder, so an open circuit there shows up as P3417. A GM patent application on deactivation hardware keeps a single oil-switching valve and only shapes the cam timing so that the exhaust side drops out first and returns first. Should a design ever give the exhaust side its own actuator, CARB's continuity check for outputs would apply to it. The owner would see a warning lamp and lose the economy mode.
c: Broken lead or loose terminal at the cylinder 3 exhaust actuator
Fault in the control module output
s: Check engine lamp on
Cylinder deactivation locked out

P3422.d: P3422 would apply if cylinder 3's exhaust valves disregard an order to stop or restart even though the wiring checks out. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. How such a fault can be spotted is shown in patents: Ford patented a way to catch an exhaust valve still lifting after shutdown by its mark in the exhaust pressure trace; the engine then brings the cylinder back, blocks further deactivation and may store a code. A Delphi patent does the same for the intake side by timing pressure pulses against crank angle. GM folds both valves of cylinder 3 into one mechanical check, P349A. A leaking exhaust valve pumps air through the cold cylinder, which upsets fuel trim and can cause a misfire count on cylinder 3.
c: Exhaust-side switching lifter or rocker of cylinder 3 stuck
Oil level or quality outside specification
Restricted oil passage to the exhaust switching element
s: Uneven running in reduced-cylinder mode
Fuel trim or misfire codes alongside
Check engine lamp on

P3423.t: Cylinder 3 Exhaust Valve Control Circuit Low
P3423.d: P3423 points to a grounded control wire at a dedicated cylinder 3 exhaust actuator. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and NHTSA's 2025 look at GM's DFM engines shows why: each cylinder has just one lifter oil solenoid, and it feeds both lifters, intake and exhaust, so there is no separate exhaust output that could fail. For that same solenoid on cylinder 3, GM's L84 table flags a resistance to ground under half an ohm at rest and files it as P3419. The 2007 Displacement on Demand application likewise lists only one solenoid circuit for cylinder 3. Any design with its own exhaust output would fall under the CARB duty to detect shorts. Effect: warning lamp, cylinder 3 stays active.
c: Exhaust actuator wire of cylinder 3 shorted to engine ground
Actuator winding shorted to its housing
Faulty output stage in the control module
s: Check engine lamp on
No switch to reduced-cylinder operation

P3424.t: Cylinder 3 Exhaust Valve Control Circuit High
P3424.d: P3424 closes the cylinder 3 block and stands for an exhaust actuator control line that is held at supply voltage. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The L84 from GM shows how far one shared solenoid can be monitored without it: for cylinder 3 the ECM checks a low-side driver under P3417, P3419 and P3420 and a high-side driver under extra codes of its own, yet none of them is exhaust-only. A GM patent application explains why: one hydraulic switching valve per cylinder pair serves intake and exhaust, the order being set by the cam lobes. The nearest documented test is the one behind P3420, in which a supply connection of less than half an ohm, seen with the output active, is judged a short. A driver would notice only the lamp.
c: Exhaust actuator wire chafed against a supply line
Shorted turns in the exhaust actuator of cylinder 3
s: Check engine lamp on
Engine runs on all cylinders permanently

P3425.d: Cylinder 4 is one of the four cylinders that classic V8 cylinder deactivation shuts off, together with 1, 6 and 7, both at GM (Active Fuel Management) and on the Chrysler 5.7 L Hemi with MDS. That makes P3425 one of the best documented codes in this range. GM's 2019 tables for the L84 and L86 flag an open when the off-state output shows more than 200 kohm, 20 of 25 samples, Type B. Chrysler lists it as Cylinder 4 Deactivation Control Circuit; a STAR case describes the driver-side exhaust manifold heat shield wearing through the solenoid harness and asks for at least 15 mm clearance. P3427 and P3428 cover shorts on the same circuit.
c: Solenoid harness chafed through by the exhaust manifold heat shield (5.7 L Hemi)
Open coil in the cylinder 4 deactivation solenoid
Control module software needing an update (Chrysler TSB 18-002-25)
s: Check engine lamp on
Engine stays in eight-cylinder mode
Further circuit codes for cylinders 1, 6 and 7 if the shared harness is damaged

P3426.d: P3426 is one of the few performance codes in this range that makers really use. FCA calls it Cylinder 4 Deactivation Control Performance on the 6.4 l Heavy Duty Hemi with MDS; bulletins 18-082-16 and 18-036-20 list it with P3402, P3442 and P3450 and fix it with new PCM software. Ford stores it on the 2025 F-150 5.0 l: bulletin 25-2487, replaced by 26-2093, traces P3402 and P3426 to a restricted oil feed tube for the right-bank deactivation solenoids, which is replaced under the valve cover. GM checks cylinder 4 mechanically under P349B instead. Circuit faults are P3425, P3427 and P3428. The lamp comes on, and the engine may run rough or stay in full-cylinder mode.
c: Restricted oil feed tube to the deactivation solenoids (Ford 5.0 l, TSB 26-2093)
Control software needing an update (FCA 6.4 l Hemi)
s: Check engine lamp on
Misfire on cylinder 4 or rough running
Drone or shudder at light throttle

P3427.t: Cylinder 4 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit Low
P3427.d: P3427 is set when the cylinder 4 deactivation solenoid circuit has a path to ground. GM uses it on several 2019 V8s: the DFM engine L84, the AFM engine L86 and the LT4 of the Corvette. Once the low-side output is switched off, less than half an ohm toward ground fails the check; 20 of 25 samples, relay voltage at least 11 V, 425 rpm (L84) or 400 rpm (L86, LT4), Type B. In all three tables the criteria column names cylinder 1, an apparent copy slip. For the MDS-equipped Hemi from Chrysler, one STAR case documents an exhaust manifold shield that rubs the solenoid harness open; a bared wire touching metal there can end up as this kind of short. P3428 covers the opposite short, to battery voltage.
c: Control wire to the cylinder 4 solenoid rubbed through to ground, e.g. by a heat shield
Moisture or oil in the solenoid connector
Damaged driver in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp after two drives
V4 or reduced mode never engages
Further circuit codes on other deactivating cylinders if the harness is damaged

P3428.t: Cylinder 4 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit High
P3428.d: P3428 means the wire that switches cylinder 4's deactivation solenoid is tied to voltage. GM's bulletin 20-NA-038 lists cylinders 1, 4, 6 and 7 as the ones its AFM V8s switch to V4 mode, which makes cylinder 4 a standard candidate. In the 2019 documents for L84, L86 and the Corvette LT4, GM judges the circuit with the low-side stage switched on: a supply path of less than half an ohm counts as a short, and 20 bad results within 25 produce a Type B entry and the lamp after two trips. Because the low-side stage sinks the current, a line stuck at battery voltage can push the output into overcurrent, so after repair the module should be checked too. P3427 is the short to ground, P3425 the open. The truck or car keeps all cylinders running.
c: Cylinder 4 control wire shorted to a 12 V feed
Low-resistance winding in the cylinder 4 solenoid
Overloaded output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp on
No V4 or reduced-cylinder operation

P3429.d: P3429 stands for an open circuit to an actuator that would switch nothing but cylinder 4's exhaust valves. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, although few cylinders are deactivated as often: GM's AFM V8s (bulletin 20-NA-038), the Hemi with MDS and Mazda CX-5 and Mazda6 four-cylinders with deactivation all idle cylinder 4; Mazda's alert SA-041/18 names cylinders 1 and 4 as the deactivation area where rocker arms can fall out. In the GM design reviewed by NHTSA in 2025, one solenoid per cylinder works the intake and exhaust lifter together, so interrupted wiring is reported as P3425. A layout with a separate exhaust output would still owe CARB a continuity test. P3430 to P3432 complete this exhaust group.
c: Open conductor or pushed-out pin to the cylinder 4 exhaust actuator
s: Check engine lamp on
Fuel-saving mode inactive

P3430.d: P3430 would cover exhaust valves on cylinder 4 that keep opening, or stay shut, against the command while the circuit itself is sound. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Ford shows both sides of the problem: a Ford patent recognises an exhaust valve opening after shutdown from changes in exhaust pressure and responds by reactivating the cylinder and storing a code, while in practice the 2025 F-150 5.0 l reports a cylinder 4 switching fault as P3426 and traces it to a restricted solenoid oil feed tube (bulletin 26-2093). An exhaust valve that does not stay closed lets fresh air reach the catalyst and the oxygen sensors, which can show up as fuel trim errors, misfire counts and vibration.
c: Restricted oil supply to the cylinder 4 switching elements
Exhaust lifter or rocker of cylinder 4 not changing state
Oil too thin, too old or too low
s: Vibration in reduced-cylinder mode
Lean or rich fuel trim codes
Check engine lamp on

P3431.t: Cylinder 4 Exhaust Valve Control Circuit Low
P3431.d: P3431 reports a cylinder 4 exhaust actuator line shorted to ground. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Cylinder 4 is switched off by Chrysler's MDS Hemi as well as by GM's V8s with AFM or DFM, but each of them runs a single solenoid per cylinder, so their bulletins and tables only list intake-side circuit codes: Ram's 2025 software bulletin 18-002-25 names P3425 next to P3401, P3441 and P3449, and for GM's 2019 L84, P3427 handles a grounded line of under half an ohm, checked while the output rests and confirmed 20 times in 25 (Type B). That is the closest documented test; CARB would demand the same kind of short detection for a separate exhaust output. Drivers would see the lamp, and cylinder shutdown would cease.
c: Cylinder 4 exhaust actuator lead grounded on the block or a bracket
Internal short to ground in the exhaust actuator
s: Check engine lamp on
Engine stays on all cylinders

P3432.t: Cylinder 4 Exhaust Valve Control Circuit High
P3432.d: P3432 is the last code of the cylinder 4 block and denotes an exhaust actuator control line sitting at supply voltage. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The intake-side counterpart P3428 is well covered: For GM's L84, L86 and Corvette LT4 of model year 2019, a supply path below half an ohm, measured while the low-side stage conducts, is logged as a Type B short. Exhaust valves are not forgotten in those engines, they simply switch with the same lifter oil. A GM patent application lets a single hydraulic valve serve both sides, and the cam timing makes the exhaust side drop out earlier than the intake side and also come back sooner. Without a separate exhaust output, this code has nothing to watch. Expect only the lamp.
c: Exhaust actuator wire of cylinder 4 in contact with battery voltage
Exhaust actuator coil with shorted windings
Output stage of the engine control module defective
s: Check engine lamp on
Deactivation unavailable

P3433.d: P3433 reports an open control circuit to the deactivation valve of cylinder 5, and GM has used it across three generations. The 2007 V6 with Displacement on Demand, which shut off cylinders 1, 3 and 5, already flagged a short or open after 30 failures in 100 samples at 250 ms above 800 rpm. On the 3.6 L V6 (LGX, LGZ) cylinder 5 is an active fuel management cylinder, and GM tied P3433 to oil leaking from the rocker arm control valve in the camshaft cover. The 2019 L84 V8 tests every cylinder with a 200 kohm limit. Each time it is a Type B code. P3434 to P3436 are the function and short codes for the same cylinder.
c: Oil leaking at the cylinder 5 control valve into its connector (GM 3.6 L V6)
Broken wire or spread terminal in the solenoid circuit
Open coil in the cylinder 5 solenoid
s: Check engine lamp on
Oil seepage at the valve cover control valve (V6)
Reduced-cylinder mode no longer used

P3434.d: With P3434 the computer has found that cylinder 5 does not switch off or back on correctly, while the control circuit tests fine. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's L84 runs the equivalent test under P349C: manifold pressure stays too high while cylinder 5 is commanded off, meaning its valves keep working. For 3.6 L V6 engines, GM bulletin 21-NA-036 describes the field picture: misfires on cylinder 5 (P0305), sometimes only after a reduced-cylinder phase, from oil leaking past the control valve or rockers that do not latch, and asks to check for a solenoid tip broken off in the bore. Wiring faults for this cylinder are P3433, P3435 and P3436.
c: Oil leaking past the cylinder 5 control valve seal
Switching rocker or lifter of cylinder 5 not latching
Solenoid tip broken off in the bore
s: Misfire on cylinder 5 (P0305)
Check engine lamp on
Shaking after reduced-cylinder operation

P3435.t: Cylinder 5 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit Low
P3435.d: P3435 flags a short to ground on the control line of the cylinder 5 deactivation valve. GM documents it codewise twice: in the 2019 tables for the L84 V8, with under 0.5 ohm to ground in the driver-off state, 20 of 25 samples at 250 ms and Type B, and in an engineering bulletin for 3.6 L V6 engines (LGX, LGZ) where P3435 appears along with P3433 and P3409 when oil leaks from the rocker arm control valve. Oil that wicks into the connector can create exactly such a leakage path. P3433 is the open circuit, P3436 the short to power, P3434 a mechanical failure. In daily driving the engine simply stays on all cylinders.
c: Oil in the cylinder 5 valve connector creating a leakage path (GM 3.6 L V6)
s: Check engine lamp on
Oil wetness at the valve cover around the control valve (V6)
No fuel-saving cylinder deactivation

P3436.t: Cylinder 5 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit High
P3436.d: P3436 is the short-to-power code for the cylinder 5 deactivation valve. Publicly it is documented by GM for the L84 V8 (2019), where Dynamic Fuel Management uses a dedicated valve lifter oil solenoid for each of the eight cylinders. The engine computer checks the line while its low-side driver is on; an impedance below 0.5 ohm toward supply voltage counts as a fault, confirmed by 20 of 25 samples at 250 ms, with at least 11 V and 425 rpm. As a Type B code it lights the lamp after two consecutive trips. Because the solenoid then cannot be switched in a controlled way, cylinder 5 is excluded from deactivation. Siblings: P3433 open, P3435 short to ground, P3434 function.
c: Control wire touching a voltage supply
Shorted coil in the cylinder 5 solenoid
Engine control module output stage defect
s: Check engine lamp after two trips
Dynamic Fuel Management disabled

P3437.d: P3437 is reserved for an open circuit in a separate exhaust valve actuator on cylinder 5. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM, the main user of cylinder 5 deactivation codes (2007 V6, 3.6 L V6, L84 V8), only publishes the intake-side group P3433 to P3436, because its systems switch both valves of a cylinder together; NHTSA's description of Dynamic Fuel Management states that each solenoid feeds intake and exhaust lifters. CARB still expects any emission-relevant actuator to be checked for continuity, which is what this code would report. P3438 to P3440 are the other exhaust codes for cylinder 5, P3433 the intake-side open.
c: Broken wire or connector to the cylinder 5 exhaust actuator
s: Check engine lamp on
Cylinder deactivation locked out

P3438.d: P3438 describes an exhaust side of cylinder 5 that is commanded to deactivate or reactivate but does not follow, with an intact circuit. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Two patents show why the exhaust side matters: in a GM patent application one shared valve switches the exhaust valves off, and back on, before the intake valves, so an exhaust lifter that lags breaks that order, and Ford detects an exhaust valve still opening after deactivation from exhaust pressure. If the exhaust valve keeps opening while the cylinder is off, the engine can run rough. GM's DFM engines report a cylinder whose valves stay active as P349C. The electrical codes for this channel are P3437, P3439 and P3440.
c: Exhaust lifter or rocker of cylinder 5 slow to switch
s: Check engine lamp on
Roughness or noise while cylinders are switched off

P3439.t: Cylinder 5 Exhaust Valve Control Circuit Low
P3439.d: P3439 would report a short to ground in the control circuit of a dedicated exhaust valve actuator on cylinder 5. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and no threshold is published for it. The closest documented reference is the intake-side P3435, which GM's L84 sets at under 0.5 ohm to ground with the driver off, after 20 of 25 samples. CARB's output component rules call for exactly this kind of short-circuit check on any actuator that can affect emissions. Engines that switch both valves of cylinder 5 with one solenoid report a short only through P3435. Exhaust-side siblings are P3437 (open), P3438 (function) and P3440 (short to power).
c: Control wire of the exhaust actuator grounded
s: Check engine lamp on
Engine runs on all cylinders only

P3440.t: Cylinder 5 Exhaust Valve Control Circuit High
P3440.d: P3440 closes the cylinder 5 block and stands for a high signal, usually a short to supply voltage, in the circuit of a separate exhaust valve actuator. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The code only makes sense on an engine with a separate exhaust actuator; a Ford patent, for example, checks via exhaust pressure whether an exhaust valve still opens after deactivation. Current production systems that deactivate cylinder 5 drive both valves from one solenoid, and GM reports a short to power there as P3436, checked with the driver on and a 0.5 ohm limit. If a dedicated exhaust channel did short high, the computer would stop using deactivation and light the lamp. Compare P3437, P3438 and P3439.
c: Exhaust actuator control wire shorted to voltage
Engine control module output stage fault
s: Check engine lamp on
Cylinder deactivation unavailable

P3441.d: Cylinder 6 belongs to both classic V8 deactivation groups, so P3441 is a code that real engines set. On GM V8s with Active Fuel Management, which park cylinders 1, 7, 6 and 4, the 2019 tables list it for the L86 truck engine and the LT4 Corvette: with the low-side driver off, more than 200 kohm between output and ground counts as an open, and 20 failures in 25 samples (every 250 ms, from 400 rpm) store a Type B code. The L84 with Dynamic Fuel Management runs the same check from 425 rpm. Chrysler names P3441 for the 5.7 L Hemi with MDS; a STAR case blames a heat shield rubbing through the solenoid harness. Shorts on this circuit are P3443 and P3444.
c: Solenoid harness broken or chafed through (on the 5.7 L Hemi by the manifold heat shield)
Open coil in the cylinder 6 deactivation solenoid
Loose or corroded connector at the cylinder 6 solenoid
Control module software that needs an update (Chrysler TSB 18-002-25)
s: Check engine lamp on
Engine no longer drops to four-cylinder mode
Possibly circuit codes for cylinders 1, 4 and 7 as well if the shared harness is damaged

P3442.d: P3442 reports that cylinder 6 does not switch off or back on as commanded although its control circuit tests fine. FCA uses it as Cylinder 6 Deactivation Control Performance on the 6.4 l Heavy Duty Hemi with MDS in RAM 2500 to 5500 trucks: bulletins 18-082-16 and 18-036-20 list it with P3402, P3426 and P3450 under a lit MIL and fix it with new PCM software. Ford stores it on 2025 F-150 5.0 l trucks built January to April 2025: bulletin 25-2487, replaced by 26-2093, traces P3442 and P3450 to a restricted oil feed tube for the left-bank deactivation solenoids, which is renewed under the valve cover. GM's L84 judges cylinder 6 under its own code P349D. Electrical faults on the same channel are P3441, P3443 and P3444.
c: Outdated PCM calibration (FCA 6.4 l, bulletins 18-082-16 and 18-036-20)
Restricted oil feed tube to the left-bank solenoids (Ford 5.0 l, TSB 26-2093)
Oil level too low, wrong grade or worn oil, so pressure builds too slowly
Deactivating lifter of cylinder 6 not locking or unlocking
s: Check engine lamp on
Jerk or vibration when the engine changes between eight and four cylinders
Misfire on cylinder 6 (P0306)
Fuel consumption rises because deactivation is locked out

P3443.t: Cylinder 6 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit Low
P3443.d: Here the engine computer has found the cylinder 6 solenoid's switched lead pulled to ground. GM spells out the test for its 2019 V8s (L84, L86 and the LT4 Corvette): while the low-side driver is off, an impedance under 0.5 ohm toward ground is a fault, and 20 hits among 25 checks while the powertrain relay supplies at least 11 V store a Type B code. GM adds that some controllers record the open-circuit code P3441 at the same moment, so the pair does not prove two separate faults. On the L84 each solenoid also has a high-side feed, and a short to ground there carries GM's own code P3114. P3444 is the short to voltage on this channel. Cylinder deactivation stays off until the fault is repaired.
c: Insulation of the cylinder 6 control wire worn through to ground
Cylinder 6 solenoid shorted internally to its housing
Moisture or oil bridging the pins of the solenoid connector
Output stage in the engine control module damaged
s: Check engine lamp on from the second faulty trip
Four-cylinder mode no longer available
P3441 stored at the same time on some GM controllers

P3444.t: Cylinder 6 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit High
P3444.d: P3444 is set when the output that switches the cylinder 6 deactivation solenoid to ground still sees supply voltage while it is turned on, meaning the line has a short to power instead of a path through the coil. GM tests this on the 2019 L84, L86 and LT4 V8s with a limit of 0.5 ohm to controller power, 20 errors out of 25 samples at 250 ms intervals and Type B lamp logic. On the L84, whose solenoids also have a switched high-side feed, a short to voltage on that feed has the separate GM code P3115. Because the ECM can no longer energize the valve, cylinder 6 simply keeps firing and the engine gives up four-cylinder operation. Compare P3441 (open) and P3443 (short to ground).
c: Cylinder 6 control wire in contact with a supply wire in the harness
Shorted turns in the cylinder 6 solenoid coil
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp on
Engine runs on all eight cylinders permanently
Slightly higher fuel consumption at light load

P3445.d: P3445 is defined for a break in the wiring of a stand-alone actuator that would control the exhaust valves of cylinder 6. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The engines that deactivate cylinder 6 today, GM's AFM and DFM V8s and Chrysler's Hemi with MDS, publish only intake-side codes for this cylinder (P3441, and at GM also P3443 and P3444). NHTSA's description of GM's DFM hardware explains why: a single solenoid per cylinder sends oil to the intake and the exhaust lifters alike, which then unlock one after the other. An engine with its own exhaust-side actuators would have to check their wiring for continuity under CARB's rules for output components, and that is the fault this code names. P3446 to P3448 complete the exhaust group.
c: Broken wire or loose connector at the cylinder 6 exhaust actuator
Output stage in the control module faulty
s: Check engine lamp on
Cylinder deactivation disabled

P3446.d: P3446 stands for an exhaust valve on cylinder 6 that does not follow a deactivation or reactivation command although its circuit is intact. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM watches a closely related failure under a code of its own: on the 2019 L84, P318E (Cylinder 6 Trapped High Pressure Exhaust Charge) looks for an exhaust valve that fails to open and let the burned gas out, recognised by crankshaft jerk in 66 of 100 samples, Type B, with immediate protective action. A Ford patent covers the opposite case, an exhaust valve that keeps opening after shut-off, detected from exhaust pressure. The electrical codes for this exhaust channel are P3445, P3447 and P3448.
c: Exhaust lifter of cylinder 6 switching late or not at all
Oil pressure too low for reliable switching
s: Check engine lamp on
Knock-like noise or vibration when the cylinder is switched back on
Possible misfire on cylinder 6 (P0306)

P3447.t: Cylinder 6 Exhaust Valve Control Circuit Low
P3447.d: P3447 is about a ground fault on the lead of a stand-alone exhaust actuator for cylinder 6. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM, the one maker publishing the full set of cylinder 6 circuit codes, switches both valves of the cylinder with one solenoid and reports a ground short as the intake-side P3443: impedance below 0.5 ohm toward ground while the driver is off, 20 of 25 samples, Type B. A comparable test would apply here, because CARB requires circuit monitoring for every emission-relevant output. NHTSA notes that GM inhibits deactivation as soon as a solenoid driver circuit fault is present, so the practical result is an engine running on all cylinders. P3445 (open) and P3448 (short to power) are the neighbouring exhaust codes.
c: Exhaust actuator wire of cylinder 6 chafed against the engine
Internal short to ground in the exhaust actuator
Damaged driver in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp on
Engine stays in full-cylinder mode

P3448.t: Cylinder 6 Exhaust Valve Control Circuit High
P3448.d: If cylinder 6 had its own exhaust valve actuator, P3448 would report its control line shorted to battery voltage. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. A GM patent application on cylinder deactivation switches both sides through one shared hydraulic valve and only lets the exhaust valves go first, off and back on, so it shows no separate exhaust control either; GM's production V8s likewise put both lifters on one solenoid and publish only P3444 for a short to power on cylinder 6. That test, below 0.5 ohm to power with the driver switched on and 20 of 25 samples, is the reference for how such a fault would be judged. With the actuator unusable, deactivation is blocked. P3445 to P3447 are the sibling exhaust codes.
c: Exhaust actuator wire touching a supply line
Shorted turns in the exhaust actuator coil of cylinder 6
Engine control module output stage faulty
s: Check engine lamp on
No switch to reduced-cylinder operation

P3449.d: P3449 tells you the engine computer lost continuity in the circuit to the cylinder 7 deactivation solenoid. Chrysler documents it twice for the 5.7 L Hemi with MDS: a 2025 bulletin for the 2023 RAM 1500 eTorque lists it next to a cylinder 7 misfire (P0307) and fixes it with new PCM software, and a STAR case names P3449 first when the driver-side manifold heat shield has worn through the MDS harness at the rear of the cylinder head. GM uses the code on AFM V8s (L86, LT4 Corvette) and on the DFM L84, flagging more than 200 kohm in the off state, 20 of 25 samples, Type B. P3451 and P3452 report shorts, P3450 a mechanical fault on cylinder 7.
c: MDS harness at the rear of the driver-side head worn through by the manifold heat shield (5.7 L Hemi)
PCM calibration needing an update (Chrysler TSB 18-002-25)
s: Check engine lamp on
Engine stays in eight-cylinder mode
Rough idle or misfire on cylinder 7 (P0307) on the 5.7 L Hemi

P3450.d: P3450 reports that cylinder 7 does not deactivate or reactivate as commanded while its solenoid circuit checks out. FCA lists it as Cylinder 7 Deactivation Control Performance for the 6.4 l Heavy Duty Hemi with MDS (RAM 2500 to 5500, bulletins 18-082-16 and 18-036-20): the MIL lights and a PCM reflash cures it, with an optional calibration that also eases drone and shudder in MDS mode. On the 2025 F-150 5.0 l, Ford bulletin 26-2093, which replaces 25-2487, pairs it with P3442 and has the left-bank solenoid oil feed tube replaced under the valve cover. In GM's system, as NHTSA describes it, oil pressure moves locking pins so the lifter body travels without opening the valve. GM's L84 uses P349E. Electrical faults: P3449, P3451, P3452.
c: Restricted oil feed tube to the left-bank solenoids (Ford 5.0 l, TSB 26-2093)
Outdated PCM calibration (FCA 6.4 l, bulletins 18-082-16 and 18-036-20)
Locking pins in a cylinder 7 lifter sticking from wear or dirt
Insufficient or aged oil delaying the switch
s: Check engine lamp on
Ticking noise from the valve train
Misfire on cylinder 7 (P0307)
Reduced-cylinder mode switched off

P3451.t: Cylinder 7 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit Low
P3451.d: P3451 means the switched ground line of the cylinder 7 deactivation solenoid has contact with ground somewhere along its way. GM documents the check for the L84 and L86 trucks and the LT4 Corvette (2019): with the driver off, less than 0.5 ohm to ground, 20 hits in 25 samples taken every 250 ms, Type B, meaning the warning lamp waits for a second faulty trip. According to GM, certain controllers log the open-circuit code P3449 along with it, so both codes together need not mean two faults. On the L84 the high-side feed of the same solenoid reports a ground short under its own code P3117. P3452 is the short to power on this channel, P3450 the mechanical fault.
c: Cylinder 7 control wire pinched or chafed to ground
Oil or water inside the solenoid connector
Defective driver in the engine control module
s: Check engine lamp on after two trips
P3449 may be stored as well
No four-cylinder mode, higher fuel use

P3452.t: Cylinder 7 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit High
P3452.d: Unlike the open and ground-short checks, GM can only detect P3452 while the cylinder 7 solenoid driver is switched on, because a short to supply voltage shows up as an output that will not pull low when it should. The 2019 tables for the L84, L86 and LT4 set the limit at 0.5 ohm to controller power and need 20 errors out of 25 samples, Type B. The check therefore depends on the ECM actually commanding deactivation; on GM's DFM engines that only happens with coolant above 40 °C, more than 20 s after start and above 13 km/h, according to NHTSA. Typical causes are a harness pressed against a feed wire or a solenoid with shorted windings. P3449 and P3451 are the other circuit codes for cylinder 7.
c: Cylinder 7 control wire shorted to a voltage feed
Low-resistance coil in the cylinder 7 solenoid
s: Check engine lamp on, often only after longer warm drives
Cylinder deactivation unavailable

P3453.d: P3453 is the code SAE assigns to an open circuit in a dedicated exhaust valve actuator for cylinder 7. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's description of Dynamic Fuel Management, published by NHTSA, shows how exhaust control works without such an actuator: the same oil signal unlocks the intake lifter at once, while the exhaust lifter waits until the valve spring load drops on the base circle of the cam. Separate wiring exists only in designs with an extra exhaust actuator, and CARB would require its continuity to be monitored. Actual cylinder 7 circuit faults on GM and Chrysler V8s show up as P3449 instead. P3454 to P3456 are the other exhaust codes; P3455 is the short to ground.
c: Interrupted wire to the cylinder 7 exhaust actuator
s: Check engine lamp on
Cylinder deactivation locked out

P3454.d: P3454 covers an exhaust valve on cylinder 7 that does not switch as commanded, with no electrical fault on its control circuit. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's own cylinder 7 check P318F on the 2019 L84 shows why the exhaust side matters: if the exhaust valve fails to open and release the burned gas, the trapped charge is compressed again, cylinder pressure climbs and the intake mechanism can be damaged on reactivation, so the ECM reacts at once (crankshaft jerk test, 66 of 100 samples, Type B). A Ford patent tackles the reverse problem, an exhaust valve still opening after deactivation, spotted through exhaust pressure. P3453, P3455 and P3456 are the electrical codes.
