P34BB.d: P34BB is stored when the bank 2 exhaust actuator's temperature signal stays above its window – typically a broken signal line, a loosened ground connection or contact with a supply wire. Because the module can no longer see how warm the actuator driver is, it lacks what it needs to protect it; Aisin's design, for comparison, ends its current reduction only after the reading has stayed below a return threshold for some time. With the value missing, the exhaust phaser on this bank will usually be kept in a safe position, so the warning lamp is often the only sign. No manufacturer publication covers P34BB, and NTN-SNR simply calls it too high a signal on the outlet side, second bank. High fault on bank 1: P34B7; low on bank 2: P34BA.
c: Signal line broken or sensor ground loose
Signal line touching a supply wire
Sensor open inside the bank 2 actuator
s: Malfunction indicator lamp lit
Bank 2 exhaust cam held in a safe position

P34BC.t: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor A Circuit Bank 1
P34BC.d: P34BC means the module cannot make sense of the wiring of sensor A, which reports where actuator B on bank 1 stands. Read against the NTN-SNR list, actuator B is the exhaust-side one. Where such actuators are electric, sensor A reports the motor or phaser angle; Mitsubishi shows the intake equivalent P34AC, set after a voltage outside the window for one second or more. Mercedes-Benz files the feedback of its CAMTRONIC exhaust solenoid on its M176/M177 eight-cylinder units in this very group, yet its bulletin lists only the range and low codes P34BD and P34BE, not the general circuit code. No public source covers P34BC itself, so diagnosis stays generic: unplugged connector, broken wires, missing sensor supply, then the actuator. Bank 2 counterpart: P34C0.
c: Connector at the exhaust actuator unplugged or corroded, wire broken
Sensor integrated in the actuator failed (actuator replacement)
s: Malfunction indicator lamp lit
Exhaust-side adjustment on bank 1 switched off
Possibly slightly higher fuel consumption

P34BD.t: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor A Range/Performance Bank 1
P34BD.d: P34BD has a documented user. Mercedes-Benz lists P34BD09 in bulletin LI05.20-P-080192, dated 14 January 2026, for M176/M177 V8 engines with CAMTRONIC, used for example in the AMG C 63 and E 63, the G 550 and the Maybach GLS 600. Its fault text reports the feedback from exhaust-side CAMTRONIC solenoid 1 of bank 1 as faulty and classes it as a component fault. Mercedes names software and hardware as the cause: update the ME engine control unit, check the part numbers of all CAMTRONIC actuators and replace older ones (A177 982 03 03 or 17 00 by 19 00, 02 03 or 16 00 by 18 00), and look for heat-damaged wiring at the bulkhead. P005A (exhaust solenoid 1 jammed off) and the limp-home code P164B often come along. Bank 2: P34C1.
c: Engine control software outdated (Mercedes M176/M177: update)
CAMTRONIC actuator of a superseded part number
s: Check engine light on
CAMTRONIC in limp-home mode, often with further CAMTRONIC codes

P34BE.t: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor A Circuit Low Bank 1
P34BE.d: For P34BE, too, a Mercedes-Benz text exists: the CAMTRONIC bulletin covering the M176 and M177 eight-cylinders reads P34BE00 as the signal of exhaust solenoid 1, bank 1, being grounded. That fits the generic meaning, a signal under its lower limit. Mercedes points to the engine cover and the wiring routed over the bulkhead, close to the windshield, where heat damage was found; harness damage is to be reported with photos and a lambda graph test. Beyond the wiring, the remedy includes fitting the latest CAMTRONIC actuators and updating the engine software. Once the feedback is lost the system can enter limp-home (P164B), and the exhaust cam profile of that bank stays fixed. High on bank 1: P34BF; low on bank 2: P34C2.
c: Heat-damaged harness above the bulkhead, signal shorted to ground
Sensor inside the CAMTRONIC actuator shorted (older part number)
Engine control software not up to date
s: Check engine light on
CAMTRONIC limp-home, exhaust valve lift on bank 1 no longer switched

P34BF.t: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor A Circuit High Bank 1
P34BF.d: P34BF: on bank 1, sensor A of the camshaft B actuator, i.e. the exhaust side, sends more voltage than allowed. An open ground, a signal wire in contact with a feed or an internally open sensor are the usual explanations. Mercedes-Benz documents low and implausible signals for this sensor on its CAMTRONIC V8 (P34BE, P34BD), but no high fault; other manufacturers do not mention the code either. On Mitsubishi's electric intake phaser the matching high code P34AF parks the motor in its reference position, and an electric exhaust actuator would presumably react in a similar way. CARB counts the sensors of a VVT system among the comprehensive components, whose out-of-range values must be detected. Low on bank 1: P34BE; high on bank 2: P34C3.
c: Sensor ground interrupted or plug corroded
Signal line shorted to a supply wire
Sensor in the exhaust actuator open internally
s: Malfunction indicator lamp lit
Exhaust adjustment on bank 1 kept in its reference position

P34C0.t: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor A Circuit Bank 2
P34C0.d: P34C0 is the generic circuit fault of position sensor A belonging to camshaft actuator B of bank 2 and therefore appears only on V-type or other two-bank engines. Mercedes-Benz files the bank 2 exhaust feedback of its CAMTRONIC V8 (M176/M177) under neighbouring codes – P34C1 for an implausible signal, P34C2 for a grounded one – but P34C0 itself is absent from its bulletin, and no other carmaker has published it. Diagnosis therefore stays general: supply, ground and signal line between module and actuator, then the actuator with its built-in sensor. If P34BC is set as well, shared feeds and grounds deserve a look before any part is swapped. NTN-SNR describes P34C0 as an electrical fault at the outlet side. The remaining fault types for this sensor are P34C1 to P34C3.
c: Wiring or plug at the bank 2 exhaust actuator open
Shared sensor feed or ground faulty (if P34BC is also stored)
Sensor in the bank 2 actuator failed
s: Malfunction indicator lamp lit
Exhaust adjustment on bank 2 disabled

P34C1.t: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor A Range/Performance Bank 2
P34C1.d: Mercedes-Benz names P34C109 for the exhaust side of bank 2 on its CAMTRONIC V8s: the signal from the sensor at solenoid 1 is wrong although the circuit is intact, entered as a component fault. CARB explains why such a check exists, since even a single cylinder pin on a lift mechanism not moving into place is a failure mode that VVT monitoring has to cover. The same bulletin, LI05.20-P-080192, also carries P005C (solenoid 1, exhaust, bank 2: faulty or jammed off) and P164B (CAMTRONIC limp-home). The Mercedes remedy: engine software, current actuator part numbers, and a look at the harness for heat damage. Because the solenoid sensor is integrated, a confirmed fault calls for replacing the actuator. Bank 1 counterpart: P34BD.
c: CAMTRONIC actuator of an older part number (Mercedes: replace)
Engine control software needs an update
Actuator pin sticking or moving too slowly
s: Check engine light on
CAMTRONIC limp-home, often together with P005C

P34C2.t: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor A Circuit Low Bank 2
P34C2.d: Mercedes-Benz documents this code as P34C200: on cylinder bank 2, the feedback line of CAMTRONIC exhaust solenoid 1 is grounded. The code is one of sixteen that bulletin LI05.20-P-080192 groups together for engine types M176 and M177, found in AMG 63 models as well as S-Class, G-Class and GLS cars. Since heat damage turned up on wiring that runs over the firewall beside the windscreen, a harness inspection comes first, before parts are replaced; Mercedes also wants actuators with the older numbers ending 02 03, 16 00, 03 03 and 17 00 exchanged for the current versions and the engine software updated. A low signal can also come from an actuator with internal damage. Bank 1 low: P34BE; bank 2 high: P34C3.
c: Harness near the windshield heat-damaged, signal to ground
Sensor in the bank 2 CAMTRONIC actuator shorted
s: Check engine light on
CAMTRONIC limp-home, exhaust lift on bank 2 fixed

P34C3.t: B Camshaft Position Actuator Position Sensor A Circuit High Bank 2
P34C3.d: P34C3 completes the sensor group of actuator B: on bank 2, sensor A watching the exhaust-side actuator puts out a voltage beyond its permitted range. A broken sensor ground, an open signal path or contact with a feed line are the usual causes. No manufacturer publishes P34C3. Mercedes-Benz, whose CAMTRONIC V8 uses neighbouring codes on this bank (P34C1, P34C2), lists no high fault, and the 2022 Mitsubishi Outlander has no electric exhaust actuator at all – its exhaust camshaft is shifted through an oil control solenoid that the fail-safe fixes in its reference position together with the electric intake motor. Until the cause is found the bank 2 exhaust adjustment stays in its default state, so drivers mainly see the warning lamp. Bank 1: P34BF.
c: Signal line in contact with a supply wire
Sensor in the bank 2 exhaust actuator faulty
s: Malfunction indicator lamp lit
Bank 2 exhaust adjustment held in base position

P34C4.t: A Camshaft Position Actuator Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High Bank 1
P34C4.d: P34C4 is logged when the output stage feeding the bank 1 intake actuator A reports that its current or its own temperature has passed the permitted limit. The code belongs to electric phasers, where a small motor instead of an oil valve turns the camshaft. An Aisin patent shows the protective logic: a current sensor and a board temperature sensor sit on the motor driver, and if the board stays hot the controller first eases the motor off its end stop and later cuts the current. NTN-SNR files P34C4 under inlet adjustment, bank 1. Nissan drives both intake cams of the 2018 Pathfinder electrically from a separate module (NTB18-016), yet no public manufacturer text covers P34C4 itself. A binding phaser, sludged oil or a shorted motor winding are typical triggers. Bank 2 is P34C5.
c: Phaser stiff or held against its stop, motor draws high current for long
Low or sludged engine oil making the phaser hard to turn
Winding or motor lead of the bank 1 actuator shorted
Output stage or its sensors in the phaser control module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Intake timing on bank 1 no longer adjusted, held at a fixed angle
Weaker pull at low revs, rougher idle on a cold engine

P34C5.t: A Camshaft Position Actuator Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High Bank 2
P34C5.d: P34C5 mirrors P34C4 on bank 2 for intake actuator A: the driver powering the electric phaser motor on the second cylinder bank has measured too much current or run too hot and protects itself. Only V or boxer engines with one electric intake phaser per bank can log it. Two banks give a handy cross-check: if the fault stays on bank 2 after the motors trade places, wiring or the module are to blame; if it moves with the motor, the motor is. The Aisin patent explains why heat and current are judged together, as pressing the phaser hard against its stop lifts both at once. NTN-SNR places it on the bank 2 inlet side. No carmaker publishes P34C5; Nissan's module bulletin NTB18-016 for the 2018 Pathfinder only shows the hardware type. Bank 1: P34C4.
c: Bank 2 phaser stiff or stuck at an end stop
Motor lead to the bank 2 actuator chafed or shorted
Electric motor of the bank 2 actuator worn or internally shorted
Bank 2 output stage in the phaser control module faulty
s: Check engine light on
Bank 2 intake timing frozen, banks run unevenly
Slightly rough idle and less torque at low engine speed

P34C6.t: B Camshaft Position Actuator Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High Bank 1
P34C6.d: P34C6 concerns actuator B, which NTN-SNR assigns to the exhaust camshaft, on bank 1: the stage driving it signals overcurrent or overheating. That presumes an electrically powered exhaust phaser, and none is documented in public sources. The 2022 Mitsubishi Outlander shifts its exhaust camshaft hydraulically via a solenoid valve, which fail-safe holds at a reference angle, and Mercedes-Benz uses B-side codes on its M176/M177 V8 only for CAMTRONIC position feedback, not for driver load. So no manufacturer is known for this code. Should it appear, the logic of the Aisin patent applies: a hot driver board or a motor fighting a stiff phaser pushes current up, and the controller backs off or switches the motor off. Exhaust timing then rests at its default, which mainly costs smoothness and some economy. Bank 2: P34C7.
c: Exhaust phaser on bank 1 stiff, motor overloaded
Short in the motor wiring of actuator B, bank 1
Output stage for actuator B damaged or overheated
s: Check engine light on
Exhaust cam timing on bank 1 fixed in its default position
Slightly higher fuel use, minor loss of smoothness

P34C7.t: B Camshaft Position Actuator Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High Bank 2
P34C7.d: P34C7 closes the group of four driver-load codes: on bank 2 the power stage of the exhaust-side actuator B reports current or temperature above its limit. NTN-SNR ties it to outlet adjustment on the second bank. It is the rarest of the set, because electric phasers have so far appeared on the intake side; no public manufacturer document names P34C7. The fault type means the module is guarding itself, not that a sensor reads wrong, since position and temperature sensor faults of this actuator have their own codes (P34C0 to P34C3, P34B8). Plausible triggers are a motor working against a seized or poorly oiled phaser, a short in its wiring, or a driver that runs hot because it sits close to the exhaust side. CARB treats such phasers as monitored outputs. Driving continues, just with exhaust timing locked. Bank 1: P34C6.
c: Bank 2 exhaust phaser seized or poorly lubricated
Motor wiring of actuator B, bank 2, shorted or heat-damaged
Driver overheating from poor cooling or a module fault
s: Check engine light on
Bank 2 exhaust timing no longer varied
Usually only small changes in how the engine runs

P34C8.d: P34C8 does not point at one actuator or bank; it says the separate controller for cam adjustment is not working properly in itself. Mitsubishi defines it for the 2022 Outlander: with the ignition on, the controller of the electric intake phaser detects an internal CPU error, and the module is the only listed cause. Fail-safe then parks the electric intake motor and the exhaust oil control solenoid at their reference angle, lets the runner flap open, stops EGR, drops stratified cold starts and runs idle at a set speed. Mercedes-Benz lists P34C800 for M176/M177 V8s as a general CAMTRONIC fault (LI05.20-P-080192), with a software update, newer actuators and a check for heat-damaged harness as remedy. Unlike P34C4 to P34C7, which judge one output stage, this code concerns the module as a whole.
c: Internal processor fault in the cam adjustment control module
Module supply or harness heat-damaged or with poor contact
s: Check engine light on
Cam phasing held at its reference position
Rougher cold start and fixed idle speed
Noticeably less torque, higher fuel use

U0001.d: U0001 is the umbrella code for trouble on the high-speed CAN, the fast two-wire network joining engine, transmission, brake and steering modules. GM/Saab logs it once a module's transmit error counter climbs past 255: that module disconnects itself, stops sending and works with substitute values. Older GM calibration tables treat it as a bus-off, Type B after 5 s (2006 V8 ECM), and a 2006 five-speed TCM flags it after 64 bus-off events with the MIL on at once. FCA names U0001 CAN C Bus (Ram 1500 steering gear harness, Jeep Compass wiring crushed by a console bolt); Volvo and Mack trucks store it together with U0010 in the aftertreatment module, with MIL and possible derate. Usually several modules report it at once; individual wire faults have their own codes U0003 to U0009.
c: Bus pair chafed, pinched or crushed in the harness
Corroded, loose or bent pins at a module or splice connector
One module or its transceiver disturbing the whole bus
History entry after a voltage dip or tester connected with ignition on
s: Several warning lamps and messages at the same time
Scan tool reaches some modules only or none at all
Shifting, steering assist or brake functions in fallback mode
Many lost-communication codes stored alongside

U0002.t: High Speed CAN Communication Bus Performance
U0002.d: U0002 stands for impaired rather than lost traffic on the high-speed CAN, and makers fill the slot in different ways. GM/Saab sets it when a supervised periodic message, which also tells the receiver that its sender is alive, has not shown up within the 250 ms supervision time; the receiver then carries on with a default value. FCA calls U0002 CAN C Bus Off Performance: a reflash for the 2013 Ram 2500/3500 6.7 L diesel PCM changed it from a one-trip to a two-trip MIL fault, whereas the 2024-26 Dodge Charger steering column module stores it without MIL because dips in supply voltage lasting about 40 ms trip a software bug. In contrast to U0001 the bus mostly keeps working, so complaints come and go: sporadic warnings or single functions dropping out briefly.
c: Intermittent contact at connectors or splices of the bus pair
Module software reacting to short voltage dips (reflash available)
Weak battery or poor ground causing brief module resets
Electrical interference from retrofitted devices on the bus
s: Warning lamps that appear and disappear again
Single functions briefly unavailable
Code stored as history without a current fault

U0003.t: High Speed CAN Communication Bus (+) Open
U0003.d: U0003 reports a break in the (+) wire of the high-speed CAN, which GM and FCA also call CAN-High. At rest this line idles near 2.5 V and is lifted about one volt for each dominant bit. Once it is cut, modules on the far side of the break lose the differential pair and drop out, while nodes on the intact section may keep talking. Standard high-speed transceivers cannot report a wire interruption on their own, as NXP points out, so whether a module stores U0003 depends on its own monitoring. Harley-Davidson lists U0003 together with U0001 as history codes in the ABS unit of 2017 Touring models when the TechLink interface was plugged in with the ignition already on; there no repair is due. Genuine breaks come from chafing, pushed-back terminals or corrosion.
c: CAN-High conductor broken at a flex point or after a repair
CAN-High terminal pushed back or corroded in a connector
Diagnostic interface connected with ignition on (history code only)
s: Modules beyond the break no longer reachable
Several warnings and fallback modes at once
Fault appears or disappears when the harness is moved

U0004.t: High Speed CAN Communication Bus (+) Low
U0004.d: U0004 means the (+) wire of the high-speed CAN, CAN-High, is dragged below its valid range, usually by a short to ground. This is one of the faults the physical layer cannot absorb: a sending node is unable to produce a dominant bit, every frame attempt fails, the error counters rise and the controllers end up bus-off, as onsemi's bench measurements show. Transceivers with bus diagnosis, NXP's TJA1043 for example, recognise this short up to roughly 50 ohms. Typically all powertrain and chassis modules on the network fall silent at the same moment, accompanied by U0001 and a string of lost-communication codes. No manufacturer documents U0004 publicly; an FCA bulletin describes the same picture under U0001, caused by a harness pinched beneath a console bolt.
c: CAN-High insulation damaged and touching body ground
Harness clamped by a screw, bracket or seat rail
Defective transceiver in one module pulling CAN-High down
s: Network-wide communication loss, scan tool cannot connect
Engine, gearbox, ABS and steering warnings together
Vehicle may not start or run in limp mode

U0005.t: High Speed CAN Communication Bus (+) High
U0005.d: U0005 flags CAN-High, the (+) wire of the high-speed bus, sitting above its permitted range, generally because it touches battery voltage or a 5 V feed. Unlike a ground short this does not have to halt traffic: onsemi and NXP both found that frames still pass, but the voltage picture is distorted, noise immunity worsens and, on networks with a large capacitive load, bit timing can be violated. NXP therefore classes it as a hidden bus failure that only transceivers with diagnosis can see. The usual result is occasional message loss, intermittent warnings, or a single module that reports the fault while the car drives normally. No manufacturer documents U0005 publicly. Measuring CAN-High against ground with ignition on shows a value near supply voltage instead of about 2.5 to 3.5 V.
c: CAN-High chafed through against a battery or ignition feed
Moisture bridging CAN-High to a supply pin in a connector
Incorrectly connected accessory or retrofit module
s: Sporadic warnings, often with no lasting malfunction
Individual messages or modules dropping out under load or in damp weather

U0006.t: High Speed CAN Communication Bus (-) Open
U0006.d: U0006 points to an interrupted CAN-Low conductor, i.e. the (-) line on the high-speed network. That line rests near 2.5 V and sinks by about a volt whenever a dominant bit is sent. Nodes isolated by the break no longer receive a usable differential signal from the rest of the network, while the modules still joined on both wires can go on exchanging data. A line interruption is outside what common high-speed transceivers can diagnose themselves (NXP), so the code relies on module-specific checks such as missing acknowledgements. No manufacturer documents U0006 publicly. Frequent findings are a conductor fractured at a door or tailgate hinge, a backed-out terminal or a corroded splice. With the battery disconnected, a check across the two lines often shows about twice the normal 60 ohms when the break separates one of the terminators.
c: CAN-Low conductor fractured at a hinge or flex point
Corroded splice or connector in the CAN-Low path
CAN-Low terminal backed out after work on the harness
s: Part of the modules unreachable, others still respond
Warnings from the affected systems, sometimes only when moving doors or harness

U0007.t: High Speed CAN Communication Bus (-) Low
U0007.d: U0007 reports that the (-) line CAN-Low on the fast bus is held below its valid band, normally by a short to ground. The physical layer copes with this particular case: onsemi recorded ongoing transmission with a distorted level pattern and raised transceiver current, and NXP counts it among the hidden failures. Traffic therefore continues, yet the reserve against interference shrinks, which may surface as an occasional lost frame or a brief warning. Only modules whose transceiver offers bus diagnosis can spot the condition directly. No manufacturer documents U0007 publicly; FCA field cases describe ground shorts on the CAN C (+) and (-) lines under U0001. Inspect sections near sheet-metal edges, brackets and seat rails, then measure CAN-Low to ground with the battery disconnected.
c: CAN-Low insulation worn through against body metal
Water in a connector bridging CAN-Low to a ground pin
Module transceiver internally shorted on its CAN-Low pin
s: Usually no noticeable malfunction, code found during a scan
Occasional short-lived warnings, worse with moisture

U0008.t: High Speed CAN Communication Bus (-) High
U0008.d: U0008 means CAN-Low, the (-) wire of the high-speed CAN, is forced too high, typically through contact with the 12 V system or another supply rail. This fault blocks the bus: CAN-Low can no longer be driven down, no dominant state develops, and both onsemi and NXP found that transmission becomes impossible. Senders accumulate errors until they reach bus-off, so U0001 and lost-communication codes nearly always appear alongside, and engine, transmission or brake electronics may switch to stored default values. No manufacturer documents U0008 publicly. With ignition on, CAN-Low reading close to battery voltage instead of about 1.5 to 2.5 V confirms it; the contact point is usually where the bus pair runs beside a supply feed, for example after an accessory installation.
c: CAN-Low chafed against a battery or ignition supply wire
Retrofit wiring tapped into the bus pair by mistake
Bent pin or moisture linking CAN-Low to a supply contact
s: Total communication loss on the high-speed network
Many warning lamps, possible no-start
Scan tool cannot reach powertrain modules

U0009.t: High Speed CAN Communication Bus (-) Shorted to Bus (+)
U0009.d: U0009 describes CAN-Low and CAN-High of the high-speed bus being shorted to each other. The voltage difference between them then stays at zero, which every receiver interprets as recessive, so a dominant bit can never form; onsemi's tests show transmission stopping entirely and controllers running into bus-off. According to NXP, transceiver bus diagnosis cannot detect this short, so a module infers it from protocol errors instead. No manufacturer documents U0009 publicly. With the battery disconnected, the resistance between both lines reads close to zero ohms instead of the usual 60. Likely sources are a crushed harness section, water inside a splice or connector, or a damaged transceiver in one module bridging its two bus pins. Unplugging modules one by one narrows the location down.
c: Bus pair crushed so that both conductors touch
Water or corrosion bridging CAN-High and CAN-Low in a splice or connector
Failed transceiver shorting both bus pins inside a module
s: No communication on the high-speed network at all
Numerous warnings, fallback modes, possibly no start
Scan tool reaches only modules on other networks

U0010.d: U0010 is the general fault code for the medium-speed CAN, a slower two-wire network that several makers run next to the fast powertrain bus. Saab/GM documents it as mid-speed GMLAN with (+) and (-) wires and a terminating resistor across them, Ford as MS-CAN; on the F-Super Duty an unplugged connector C408 interrupts it and takes climate control, front control panel and headlamp logic down with it. Code-specific users are Volvo and Mack: their aftertreatment module logs U0010-88 together with U0001-88 when chafed wiring cuts communication, with MIL and possible derate. Ford, by contrast, tells Transit technicians to ignore a U0010 in the rear camera module after BCM programming if the camera works. On passenger cars a fault here mainly costs comfort functions, not driveability.
c: Connector in the medium-speed network unplugged or not seated
Harness chafed or wet at doors, tailgate or body mounts
Residual code after module replacement or programming
s: Climate control, lighting or infotainment functions inoperative
Several body modules unreachable with the scan tool
On heavy trucks MIL and engine derate possible

U0011.t: Medium Speed CAN Communication Bus Performance
U0011.d: U0011 says the medium-speed CAN is running but not dependably: expected periodic messages come late or not at all, error frames accumulate, or a node briefly goes bus-off and rejoins. No manufacturer publicly documents U0011 in its J2012 sense with thresholds. The nearest model is GM's high-speed counterpart U0002, where a supervised message missing for more than 250 ms sets the code. Alfa Romeo even assigns the number to something else: in the Giulia and Stelvio drive style control module, U0011-14 and U0011-15 mark a faulty down circuit of the DNA rotary selector. Typical causes are loose or corroded connectors, water ingress, voltage dips during cranking and module software. Body and comfort functions then work only intermittently while the car itself drives normally.
c: Loose or corroded connector on the medium-speed pair
Low battery voltage or poor ground causing module resets
Module software miscounting or missing messages (update needed)
s: Comfort functions such as windows, locks or climate controls work intermittently
Code stored as history in body modules

U0012.t: Medium Speed CAN Communication Bus (+) Open
U0012.d: U0012 reports an interruption of CAN-High, the (+) wire of the medium-speed CAN. Saab's mid-speed GMLAN uses the same two-wire layout as the fast bus, with a terminating resistor between (+) and (-), so a break isolates the modules downstream and alters the resistance seen between the lines. Ford's F-Super Duty illustrates the effect at vehicle level: if connector C408 stays unplugged after the pickup box is removed, MS-CAN traffic is cut and climate control, front controls and headlamp logic stop working. No manufacturer documents U0012 with its J2012 meaning; Alfa Romeo uses U0012-14 and -15 for the up circuit of its DNA selector instead. Check terminals and splices of the medium-speed pair, especially at doors, tailgates and upfitter bodies.
c: Body or upfitter connector in the medium-speed (+) path left open
CAN-High conductor broken in a door or tailgate harness
s: Comfort and body modules behind the break inoperative
Climate, lighting or switch panel functions missing

U0013.t: Medium Speed CAN Communication Bus (+) Low
U0013.d: U0013 indicates that CAN-High on the medium-speed bus, the (+) wire, is pulled toward ground. Where this network uses the same differential layout as high-speed CAN, as Saab's terminated mid-speed GMLAN suggests, a grounded CAN-High rules out any dominant bit; onsemi and NXP list this short among those that end all communication. Every node on the segment, usually body, climate and infotainment units, therefore goes quiet together, and the gateway or body controller stores missing-message codes for them. No manufacturer documents U0013 publicly. Powertrain functions on the separate fast bus normally carry on. With the battery off, a resistance of only a few ohms from CAN-High to ground locates the short; typical spots are door boots, seat rails and trim fasteners.
c: Medium-speed CAN-High insulation damaged against body ground
Wires broken open in a door boot or tailgate grommet
Comfort module transceiver pulling CAN-High down
s: All comfort and infotainment modules fail together
Engine and transmission keep working normally

U0014.t: Medium Speed CAN Communication Bus (+) High
U0014.d: U0014 means CAN-High of the medium-speed bus lies above its normal range, most often because the (+) wire touches battery voltage. On a differential CAN of the high-speed type this is a fault the network rides through: onsemi and NXP found frames still being delivered, but with shifted levels, reduced noise margin and higher current draw in the transceivers. NXP calls such a short hidden because only transceivers with built-in diagnosis notice it. On the comfort bus the result tends to be subtle: an occasional unresponsive switch, a flickering display or a stored code without complaint. No manufacturer documents U0014 publicly, and Saab's description shows only the two-wire terminated layout that makes this analogy plausible. A CAN-High reading close to battery voltage with ignition on confirms the short.
c: Medium-speed CAN-High rubbing against a supply wire
Moisture in a door or roof connector linking CAN-High to plus
Aftermarket device wired to the comfort bus incorrectly
s: Occasional unresponsive switches or flickering displays
Stored code without obvious malfunction

U0015.t: Medium Speed CAN Communication Bus (-) Open
U0015.d: U0015 stands for a break in CAN-Low, the (-) conductor of the medium-speed CAN. Modules separated by the break stop exchanging data with the rest of the network, whereas units still connected on both wires keep working; which functions disappear therefore depends on where the line is cut. Ford's F-Super Duty bulletin shows how a single open connector in the MS-CAN switches off the HVAC controls, the front switch panel and the headlamp function together. Common high-speed transceivers cannot diagnose a line interruption themselves (NXP), so the code results from the module's own reasoning about missing replies. No manufacturer documents U0015 publicly. Wiring that moves, such as door, tailgate and seat harnesses, and connectors opened during body or upfit work are the first places to check.
c: CAN-Low conductor fractured in a moving harness section
Connector not reconnected after body or upfit work
s: Only some comfort functions lost, depending on break location
Fault varies when doors or seats are moved

U0016.t: Medium Speed CAN Communication Bus (-) Low
U0016.d: U0016 reports CAN-Low of the medium-speed bus, the (-) wire, sitting below its valid range, typically through a short to ground. Transferred from the high-speed physical layer, which Saab's two-wire terminated mid-speed GMLAN resembles, this is a fault the bus tolerates: onsemi measured continuing transmission with deformed levels, and NXP files it as a hidden failure visible only to transceivers with diagnosis. The comfort network therefore usually keeps working, but becomes more sensitive to interference; drivers rarely notice anything beyond sporadic glitches. No manufacturer documents U0016 publicly. Because the fault hides so well, the code itself is often the only clue; measure CAN-Low against ground with the battery disconnected and follow the harness near sharp edges.
c: Medium-speed CAN-Low chafed against a ground point or sheet edge
Water ingress in a footwell or door connector
Comfort module transceiver internally shorted on CAN-Low
s: Usually no lasting malfunction, code found during a scan
Sporadic glitches in comfort functions

U0017.t: Medium Speed CAN Communication Bus (-) High
U0017.d: U0017 means CAN-Low on the medium-speed CAN, the (-) wire, is held too high, as a rule by contact with battery or another supply voltage. On a differential bus of the high-speed type this short is fatal for traffic: the line cannot be pulled down, no dominant bit appears, and onsemi and NXP both class it among the shorts that make transmission impossible. All body and comfort modules on the segment drop out at once, the gateway records missing messages, and functions such as climate control, locking or the radio may stop responding until the short is removed. No manufacturer documents U0017 publicly; the analogy rests on Saab's terminated two-wire mid-speed GMLAN. With ignition on, CAN-Low near battery voltage confirms the fault.
c: Medium-speed CAN-Low chafed against a supply wire
Moisture or bent pin linking CAN-Low to a supply contact
Accessory wiring connected to the comfort bus by mistake
s: All comfort and infotainment modules out at once
Climate, locking or radio not responding

U0018.t: Medium Speed CAN Communication Bus (-) Shorted to Bus (+)
U0018.d: U0018 describes the two medium-speed CAN lines, CAN-Low and CAN-High, shorted together. With no voltage difference left, receivers see only recessive bits, nobody can win arbitration, and the controllers on the segment eventually go bus-off; onsemi's measurements on the comparable high-speed layer show transmission stopping completely. NXP notes that transceiver diagnosis does not catch this short, so it is inferred from protocol errors. No manufacturer documents U0018 publicly. Expect the complete comfort network to fail together while the powertrain bus stays unaffected. With the battery disconnected, a near-zero resistance between (+) and (-) in place of the normal termination value confirms it; separating connectors section by section narrows the location, often a crushed or wet harness.
c: Medium-speed bus pair crushed so both wires touch
Water in a connector bridging (+) and (-)
Failed transceiver shorting both bus pins in a comfort module
s: Entire comfort network fails, powertrain unaffected
Body modules unreachable with the scan tool

U0019.d: U0019 is the general fault slot for the low-speed CAN, the slow body network serving doors, lighting, locks and comfort electronics. Two physical forms exist: the two-wire fault-tolerant CAN of ISO 11898-3, which NXP's TJA1055 runs at up to 125 kBd and keeps alive on one wire after a single break or short, and the one-conductor low-speed GMLAN that GM runs at 33.33 kbit/s. FCA names U0019 CAN B Bus; on the 2015 Ram ProMaster the BCM logged U0019-01 (general electrical failure) with a lit MIL, cured by a BCM reflash under bulletin 08-230-22. Mercedes-Benz lists U001988 among the codes behind false anti-theft alarms in 2019-25 models and has supply, ground and CAN lines to the overhead panel checked. Comfort functions suffer rather than driveability.
c: Damaged low-speed bus wiring or corroded, loose connector pins
Poor supply or ground at a module on the body bus
Module software logging the code without a real fault (FCA ProMaster BCM)
Faulty module or transceiver disturbing the low-speed bus
s: Comfort functions such as locks, lighting or windows fail or act erratically
Anti-theft alarm triggers without obvious reason
Lost-communication codes for several body modules
MIL on in some vehicles (FCA ProMaster 2015)

U0020.t: Low Speed CAN Communication Bus Performance
U0020.d: U0020 reports a low-speed CAN that still runs but delivers its traffic unreliably. GM documents it for the 2011 Saab 9-5, whose low-speed GMLAN is a single wire: a module sets U0020 when a monitored cyclic message, which doubles as proof that the sender is available, fails to arrive, and then substitutes a default value. Saab adds that some modules store it when the bus wakes up or the supply returns before they have learned which partners are present; diagnosis follows the symptoms or the U0100-U02FF codes. GM told technicians to ignore a current U0020 in the video processing module of 2019 Silverado/Sierra trucks as a software artefact, and lists it for 2017 trucks whose gateway module hangs until its fuse is pulled. Unlike U0019 the bus itself is usually intact.
c: Code stored while modules wake up or after the supply was interrupted
Software anomaly in one module (GM video processing module 2019)
Gateway module stops communicating or has loose terminals
Intermittent contact in the low-speed bus wiring
s: Often no noticeable symptom, code found during a scan
Sporadic dropouts of comfort or display functions
Several modules store communication codes at the same time

U0021.t: Low Speed CAN Communication Bus (+) Open
U0021.d: U0021 marks a break in the (+) wire of a two-wire low-speed CAN, called CAN-High in the fault-tolerant layout of ISO 11898-3. There the wire rests close to 0 V and is pulled toward 5 V for a dominant bit, the reverse of the high-speed pattern. NXP's TJA1055 treats an interrupted CAN-High as failure 1: drivers, termination and differential reception stay unchanged, and its error pin only reacts when the gap lies between sender and receiver, so it toggles rather than staying low. Communication therefore usually continues and the code mainly records lost redundancy. GM's low-speed GMLAN uses one wire only, so a (+)/(-) split does not apply there. No manufacturer documents U0021 publicly; CARB merely demands that missing communication of digital inputs be detected and coded separately.
c: CAN-High wire broken at a flex point such as a door transition
Pushed-back or spread terminal in a connector
Corrosion in a connector or splice
s: Usually no noticeable effect, the bus keeps running
Occasional comfort function glitches, especially with interference
Code stored only in modules on one side of the break

U0022.t: Low Speed CAN Communication Bus (+) Low
U0022.d: U0022 indicates a ground short on CAN-High, the positive conductor of a dual-wire low-speed CAN. In the fault-tolerant design of ISO 11898-3, where CAN-High idles at about 0 V and only rises for dominant bits, a ground short simply takes that rise away. NXP's TJA1055 lists CAN-High to ground as failure 5 and keeps transmitting and receiving differentially, since its receiver threshold is chosen so that reception stays correct in this case as well. The network therefore keeps working, and the driver often notices nothing apart from the stored code. On GM's single-wire low-speed GMLAN the (+)/(-) naming does not fit. No manufacturer documents U0022 publicly. With the battery disconnected, a reading near zero ohms from CAN-High to ground confirms the short; trim screws and seat rails are typical culprits.
c: CAN-High insulation chafed through against body ground
Wire pierced by a trim screw or trapped under a seat rail
Internal transceiver fault pulling CAN-High low
s: Frequently no symptom besides the stored code
Rare sporadic comfort function faults

U0023.t: Low Speed CAN Communication Bus (+) High
U0023.d: U0023 means CAN-High, the (+) conductor of a dual-line low-speed CAN, sits too high, typically shorted to battery voltage or a 5 V supply. Under ISO 11898-3 this pins the line at a level the receivers read as permanently dominant. NXP's TJA1055 handles it as failure 3 or 3a in two steps: once an initial delay expires it falls back to single-wire operation, and if the line is still too high it moves over to CAN-Low, switches its CAN-High driver off and weakens that line's termination; detection takes about 1.6 to 8 ms. Traffic continues on one wire, though electromagnetic robustness is worse in that mode. No manufacturer documents U0023 publicly; GM's low-speed GMLAN, being a single conductor, offers no (+)/(-) pair. CAN-High measuring near battery voltage against ground instead of its resting level close to 0 V points to the short.
c: CAN-High chafed against a battery feed or ignition wire
Water in a connector bridging CAN-High to a supply pin
Retrofitted accessory tapped into the wrong wire
s: Comfort functions mostly still work, occasional glitches
Increased sensitivity to interference, e.g. with radio transmitters nearby
Code stored in several body modules

U0024.t: Low Speed CAN Communication Bus (-) Open
U0024.d: U0024 reports an interruption of the (-) line, CAN-Low, of a two-wire low-speed CAN. Under the ISO 11898-3 fault-tolerant scheme this wire idles near 5 V and is pulled toward ground for dominant bits. NXP's TJA1055 counts a broken CAN-Low as failure 2, keeps drivers and termination as they are and goes on receiving differentially; it can flag the break only when the gap separates transmitter and receiver, which makes its error output flicker. Because the network keeps running, the fault often surfaces only as a stored code in modules beyond the break. Places where wires flex, such as door or tailgate transitions, are obvious suspects. The single-wire GM low-speed GMLAN has no (-) line, so the code has no meaning there. No manufacturer documents U0024 publicly.
c: CAN-Low wire broken in a door or tailgate harness
CAN-Low terminal backed out of its connector
Corroded CAN-Low contact after water entry
s: Typically no symptom, code found during a scan
Comfort functions behind the break react sluggishly or sporadically

U0025.t: Low Speed CAN Communication Bus (-) Low
U0025.d: U0025 flags CAN-Low pulled toward ground on a low-speed CAN with two conductors. In the fault-tolerant physical layer of ISO 11898-3 CAN-Low idles near 5 V, so a ground short forces it into its dominant state for good. NXP's TJA1055 (failure 4) first sees a permanently dominant receive signal; after about 0.3 to 1.6 ms it switches the CAN-Low driver off, changes that line's termination to a weak pull-up and continues in single-wire mode on CAN-High. Messages keep flowing, but with weaker immunity to interference, so sporadic dropouts of comfort functions are possible. The transceiver goes back to differential mode by itself once the short is gone. No manufacturer documents U0025 publicly; GM's one-conductor bus has no (-) side at all. Resistance from CAN-Low to ground near 0 Ω with the battery off confirms the fault.
c: CAN-Low insulation damaged and touching body ground
Harness trapped by a panel, bracket or seat mechanism
Module transceiver internally shorting CAN-Low to ground
s: Comfort functions work but drop out now and then
Body modules store the code repeatedly

U0026.t: Low Speed CAN Communication Bus (-) High
U0026.d: U0026 means CAN-Low, the (-) line of a two-wire low-speed CAN, is held too high. Since this wire already sits near 5 V at rest in an ISO 11898-3 network, the outcome depends on where the short goes. Against the 5 V supply (failure 6a in NXP's TJA1055) the transceiver stays in differential mode with normal drivers and termination. Against battery voltage (failure 6) its comparator trips after roughly 0.3 to 1.6 ms, the CAN-Low driver is switched off, the termination becomes a weak pull-up and reception continues over CAN-High alone. Either way the bus normally survives, which is why the code is often found without a clear complaint. No manufacturer documents U0026 publicly, and the GM low-speed GMLAN gets by with one conductor. Look for chafing against a feed wire or water in a connector.
c: CAN-Low chafed against a battery or ignition feed
Moisture in a connector linking CAN-Low to a supply pin
Faulty transceiver driving CAN-Low to its supply
s: Often no noticeable effect
Occasional comfort function dropouts when the bus runs on one wire

U0027.t: Low Speed CAN Communication Bus (-) Shorted to Bus (+)
U0027.d: U0027 describes the two wires of a low-speed CAN, (+) and (-), touching each other. On a high-speed bus such a short ends all traffic, but the fault-tolerant layer of ISO 11898-3 is built to ride it out. NXP's TJA1055 counts it as failure 7: the receive signal first sticks at dominant, then within about 0.3 to 1.6 ms the transceiver turns off its CAN-Low driver, leaves that wire with only a weak pull-up and carries on in single-wire mode. Comfort functions usually still work, though with less margin against interference, and differential operation resumes by itself once the short is cleared. No manufacturer documents U0027 publicly; a single-wire bus like GM's low-speed GMLAN cannot have this fault at all. Squeezed harness sections and wet splices are the likely spots; compare the high-speed sibling U0009.
c: Harness crushed so that both bus wires make contact
Water in a splice or connector bridging the two wires
Damaged transceiver bridging its two bus pins
s: Comfort network keeps running, sometimes with dropouts
Higher sensitivity to electrical interference
Code stored in several body modules at once

U0028.d: U0028 is the general code for Vehicle Communication Bus A, a neutral label each maker assigns to a network of its choosing. GM uses it in the radio of many 2013-19 models as the health indicator of the MOST infotainment ring, which the radio masters: a current U0028 symptom 00 points to a MOST module with a power, ground or wake-up fault, found by bypassing modules with kit EL-51578 until the code turns to history. In the 2026 Tahoe/Escalade family the brake control module stores U0028-88, whose diagnostic path is swapped with U0037-88 by a software slip. Audi assigns Bus A to the sensor/hybrid CAN of its 48 V mild hybrids and lists U002800 on the Q5 PHEV after a chafed power-electronics harness. Isuzu N-Series trucks show it with a misconfigured FMS-CAN interface.
c: Power, ground or wake-up fault at a module on the bus (GM MOST ring)
Bus or supply wiring chafed or pinched (Audi Q5 PHEV, GM dash harness)
Connectors not fully seated or locked, spread pins
Wrong module configuration or software fault (Isuzu FMS, GM brake module 2026)
s: Infotainment functions dead: blank radio display, no audio, steering wheel controls inoperative (GM)
Battery or electrical system warning in the cluster (Audi mild hybrid)
Several warning lamps, vehicle may not be drivable (Audi Q5 PHEV)
Further communication codes stored alongside

U0029.d: U0029 reports that Vehicle Communication Bus A works, but not reliably; which network that is depends on the maker. In Audi's 48 V mild hybrids (A6 up to Q8, 2019-23) the engine control unit logs U002900 for its sensor/hybrid CAN, labelled there as no communication, together with U002800; the belt starter-generator is then set to freewheel, the battery is no longer charged and a yellow or red battery warning appears. Audi blames connectors not plugged in or locked properly, spread pins or shorted wires, and states that a new starter-generator does not help. The Q5 PHEV stores it after the 12 V wiring feeding its power electronics rubs on the underbody trim. GM names U0029 for 2014-20 full-size trucks and SUVs with a dash harness pinched at the left instrument panel bracket, and for 2017 trucks with a hung gateway module.
c: Connector not fully seated or locked, spread or bent pins
Harness chafed on underbody trim or pinched at a dash bracket
Faulty sensor on the bus disturbing communication (Audi brake servo pressure sensor)
Gateway module stops communicating until reset
s: Yellow or red battery warning, battery not charging (Audi mild hybrid)
Intermittent warning messages from several systems
Comfort or infotainment functions drop out briefly

U0030.d: U0030 stands for an open circuit in the (+) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus A. What that wire is depends on the network a maker assigns to Bus A; where it is a two-wire CAN, like the sensor/hybrid CAN Audi files under this name in its 48 V mild hybrids, the (+) line is CAN-High. A break splits the bus: nodes on opposite sides lose each other, while modules sharing an intact section may still exchange frames. NXP points out that ordinary high-speed transceivers cannot recognise an interrupted wire themselves, so the module has to deduce it from missing partners or error counters. No manufacturer documents U0030 publicly; CARB only requires missing communication from digital inputs to be detected and coded separately. Check terminals, splices and the resistance between (+) and (-).
c: (+) wire of Bus A broken in the harness
Terminal backed out or spread in a connector
Connector left unplugged after a repair
s: Functions served by modules beyond the break stop working
Lost-communication codes for some modules on Bus A

U0031.d: U0031 indicates a ground short on the (+) conductor of Vehicle Communication Bus A. Where Bus A is a high-speed-style two-wire CAN, such as the sensor/hybrid CAN Audi assigns to this slot in its 48 V mild hybrids, the (+) wire is CAN-High, which has to rise by about a volt to form a dominant bit. Grounded, it cannot: onsemi's measurements list CAN-High to ground among the shorts under which transmission becomes impossible, so the controllers keep retrying in vain. Every node on Bus A then falls silent together, and modules on other networks record lost-communication codes for them. No manufacturer documents U0031 publicly. With the battery disconnected, a few ohms or less between CAN-High and ground locate the short; chafed harness sections are the usual cause.
c: (+) wire chafed through against body ground
Harness trapped under a panel or bracket
Transceiver of one module shorting the (+) line internally
s: All functions served by Bus A fail at once
Many lost-communication codes in other modules
Warning lamps or fallback modes depending on the modules involved

U0032.d: U0032 reports excess voltage on the (+) line of Vehicle Communication Bus A, usually from contact with battery voltage. If Bus A is a two-wire CAN of the high-speed type, as Audi's sensor/hybrid CAN, the (+) wire is CAN-High. onsemi's bench tests show frames still getting through with CAN-High at 12 V, only with distorted levels; NXP counts such shorts among hidden bus failures that a plain transceiver does not report. Faults therefore show up as sporadic message errors or a single module complaining while the vehicle behaves normally, quite unlike the hard stop of U0031. No manufacturer documents U0032 publicly. A reading close to battery voltage on CAN-High against ground, instead of somewhere between 2.5 V and 3.5 V, confirms it; a harness rubbed through next to a supply cable or a wet connector is the usual cause.
c: (+) wire chafed against a battery or ignition feed
Water in a connector bridging the (+) wire to a supply pin
Aftermarket device connected to the bus wire
s: Sporadic warnings or brief function dropouts
Only one module reports the fault, vehicle otherwise normal

U0033.d: U0033 reports an interruption of the (-) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus A; on a dual-line CAN like the sensor/hybrid CAN Audi lists as Bus A, that is CAN-Low. As with U0030, the network falls apart into pieces that can no longer hear each other, and NXP stresses that a standard high-speed transceiver has no means of detecting an open wire on its own. The control module infers the fault indirectly, for example from expected messages that stop arriving or from rising error counters, so the code often appears next to lost-communication entries for modules beyond the break. No manufacturer documents U0033 publicly. With the battery disconnected, a resistance between (+) and (-) that differs from the normal termination value hints at the break; check recently separated connectors first.
c: (-) wire of Bus A broken in the harness
Pushed-back or corroded terminal in a connector
Connector not reconnected after a repair
s: Modules beyond the break stop responding
Lost-communication codes stored alongside

U0034.d: U0034 flags the (-) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus A pulled toward ground. On a high-speed-type CAN, the layout Audi uses for the sensor/hybrid CAN behind this slot, that wire is CAN-Low, which normally drops by about a volt for dominant bits. onsemi found that with CAN-Low grounded, frames still pass, but the bus levels are distorted and the sending node draws more current, because its high-side driver now feeds the termination against ground. NXP lists this case among the hidden failures that go unnoticed without transceiver diagnosis. Expect intermittent errors or one module reporting the code rather than a dead network. No manufacturer documents U0034 publicly. A resistance near zero between CAN-Low and ground with the battery off confirms it.
c: (-) wire insulation damaged and touching ground
Harness pinched by a bracket or panel
Faulty transceiver pulling the (-) line to ground
s: Intermittent communication errors, vehicle mostly normal
Code reported by a single module

U0035.d: U0035 means the (-) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus A is held too high, typically shorted to battery voltage. On a two-wire high-speed-type CAN, such as Audi's sensor/hybrid CAN filed under Bus A, this is CAN-Low. onsemi's tests place CAN-Low at 12 V among the shorts that make transmission impossible: frames can no longer be sent and the controllers repeat them without success. All modules on Bus A drop out together, and units on other networks register their absence. This is the opposite of U0034, where traffic survives. No manufacturer documents U0035 publicly. Measuring CAN-Low against ground with ignition on shows battery voltage instead of roughly 1.5 to 2.5 V; chafing against a supply wire or a water-filled connector are the usual reasons.
c: (-) wire chafed against a battery or ignition feed
Water in a connector linking the (-) wire to a supply pin
Damaged transceiver driving the (-) line high
s: All functions on Bus A fail together
Lost-communication codes in modules on other networks
Warning lamps or fallback modes depending on the modules involved

U0036.t: Vehicle Communication Bus A (-) Shorted to Bus A (+)
U0036.d: U0036 describes a short between the (+) and (-) wires of Vehicle Communication Bus A. On a CAN-type bus the differential voltage then stays at zero, receivers see only recessive bits and, as onsemi's measurements on high-speed CAN show, no frame can be sent any more; NXP adds that transceiver diagnosis cannot detect this short. Audi documents U003600 under exactly its J2012 name for the 2018-21 Q5 plug-in hybrid: together with U002800, U002900 and drive-motor and power-electronics codes it appears when the 12 V harness of the power electronics chafes against the underbody trim, with warning lamps and in some cases a car that cannot be driven. The fix is repairing the wires and rerouting the harness. With the battery off, near zero ohms between the bus wires confirms the short.
c: Harness chafed so that both bus wires touch (Audi Q5 PHEV: underbody trim)
Water in a splice or connector bridging the two wires
Damaged transceiver shorting its bus pins
s: Several warning lamps on at once
Vehicle may refuse to drive (Audi Q5 PHEV)
Drive-motor and power-electronics codes stored alongside

U0037.d: U0037 is the umbrella code for Vehicle Communication Bus B, the second neutral network slot after Bus A; each maker decides which network sits behind it, and published uses differ widely. Volkswagen's 2014 Touareg data book sets it when a CAN frame sent on Bus B goes unacknowledged. FCA calls U0037-00 the LIN bus on the 2018-22 Jeep Wrangler, where it came with U0121 and an intermittent ABS lamp caused by a loose ground point G907A. Volvo's brake control module 2 stores U003700 alongside ECM code P25A268 and a lit check-engine lamp on 2017-24 models; software 3.0.3 cures it. On GM's 2026 full-size SUVs and Silverado/Sierra EV the brake module's U0037-88 procedure is swapped with U0028-88, and Ford reflashes the Mustang GTD dynamics module over false U0037 entries.
c: Loose or corroded ground or supply of a module on Bus B (FCA: ground G907A)
Module software misreporting or mishandling the bus (Volvo BCM2, Ford VDM, GM brake module 2026)
Damaged bus wiring or a poorly seated connector
A module on Bus B that has stopped answering
s: Warning lamps of the systems on Bus B, e.g. ABS lamp (Jeep) or check-engine lamp (Volvo)
Stop/start or chassis functions unavailable
Lost-communication codes stored alongside

U0038.d: U0038 flags Vehicle Communication Bus B as present but unreliable: frames arrive late, incompletely or for a while not at all, rather than the bus being dead outright. Volkswagen's 2014 Touareg data book describes the trigger as a global time-out in which no messages come in any longer. Honda uses U0038 for the TM-CAN link between transmission and engine control: on 2016-17 Civic CVT models it appeared together with U0101 when an internal TCM fault cut the link, leaving the car stuck in Park without cranking and with several warning lamps lit. Honda replaces the TCM and on 2016 cars also updates the PCM software. Compared with U0037 the code describes a bus that still exists but whose traffic breaks off, so intermittent contacts, a failing node or software are the usual suspects.
c: Internal fault in a module on Bus B (Honda Civic: transmission control module)
Loose or corroded terminals interrupting traffic now and then
Software mismatch between modules on the bus
s: Selector stuck in Park, engine does not crank (Honda Civic CVT)
Several warning lamps on at once
Functions drop out intermittently

U0039.d: U0039 reports a break in the (+) conductor of Vehicle Communication Bus B, which on a CAN-type network is CAN-High. Deutz assigns this code to the third CAN channel of its EMR L1 engine controller and lists it for main and secondary ECU simply as an open circuit on CAN 3, without naming the wire. On a classic high-speed CAN the interruption stays invisible to the transceiver; NXP notes that even diagnosing transceivers cannot flag a wire break, so the module infers it from partners falling silent. A fault-tolerant low-speed CAN behaves differently: NXP's TJA1055 keeps sending and receiving after a CAN-High break without spoiling frames already on the line. In practice, functions beyond the break drop out while others carry on. Look for unplugged connectors, backed-out pins and breaks near moving parts.
c: (+) wire of Bus B broken, often at a flex point
Terminal backed out or spread in a connector
Connector left open after repair work
s: Functions of modules beyond the break unavailable
Lost-communication codes for individual modules

U0040.d: U0040 indicates the (+) line of Vehicle Communication Bus B pulled down to ground potential. On a high-speed-type CAN that is CAN-High, and onsemi's bench tests list it among the shorts that stop all transmission: each failed start of frame raises the transmit error counter by eight, the controller turns error passive after a handful of attempts and goes bus-off once the count passes 255. Meanwhile the CANH driver runs into its current limit. The same short is one of the failures that NXP's fault-tolerant TJA1055 rides out without corrupting frames. So the effect ranges from a completely silent Bus B to a degraded but working one, depending on the bus type. No manufacturer documents U0040 publicly. Measure CAN-High against ground with the battery off; chafed insulation is the usual culprit.
c: (+) wire chafed through against body ground
Harness crushed by a seat rail, bracket or panel
Transceiver of one module pulling the (+) line to ground
s: All functions on Bus B fail at once (high-speed type)
Many lost-communication codes in modules on other networks
Fallback modes or warning lamps depending on the modules involved

U0041.d: U0041 means the (+) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus B sits at too high a voltage, typically because it touches a battery or 5 V supply. For a high-speed-type CAN this is CAN-High, and NXP classes a short of CAN-High to battery or to VCC as a hidden failure: frames keep flowing, so only a transceiver with bus diagnosis, such as the TJA1043, reports it. On a fault-tolerant low-speed CAN NXP's TJA1055 reacts in two steps after time-outs and finally switches off its CANH driver, running on CAN-Low alone. Either way the vehicle often behaves normally, and the code may sit in memory long before anything fails. No manufacturer documents U0041 publicly. A reading near supply voltage on CAN-High against ground confirms it; check for chafing against feed wires and moisture in connectors.
c: (+) wire chafed against a battery or 5 V feed
Moisture in a connector bridging the (+) wire to a supply pin
Faulty transceiver driving the (+) line high
s: Often no noticeable symptom, code found during a scan
Sporadic warnings from one module

U0042.d: U0042 points to an interrupted (-) wire on Vehicle Communication Bus B; on a CAN-type bus that is CAN-Low. The network then splits along the break, and on a standard high-speed CAN neither side's transceiver can tell what happened, since NXP states that line interruptions escape even transceiver diagnosis. Detection rests on time-outs for messages from nodes on the far side. On a fault-tolerant low-speed CAN, the TJA1055 data sheet from NXP treats a CAN-Low interruption as a failure that frames in progress survive. A resistance check across the two bus wires at a central connector helps: with both terminations reachable it reads about 60 ohms, a break in one wire leaves only the near terminator at about 120 ohms. No manufacturer documents U0042 publicly; start with connectors that were opened recently.
c: (-) wire of Bus B broken in the harness
Corroded or pushed-back terminal in a connector
Connector not reconnected after a repair
s: Modules beyond the break no longer respond
Lost-communication codes stored alongside

U0043.d: U0043 reports the (-) line of Vehicle Communication Bus B shorted toward ground. Where Bus B is built like a high-speed CAN, that line is CAN-Low, and the fault is sneaky: onsemi measured frames still getting through, with distorted levels and the node drawing about 72 mA instead of 65 mA, because the CANH driver now pushes current through the termination into ground. NXP lists the case among hidden failures. NXP's fault-tolerant TJA1055 transceiver instead detects the short, switches off its CAN-Low driver and carries on single-wire over CAN-High. In both cases the vehicle tends to run normally, with the code logged by one module or showing up only now and then, which sets it apart from U0040, where the bus goes quiet. No manufacturer documents U0043 publicly; near-zero ohms from CAN-Low to ground confirms it.
c: (-) wire insulation damaged and touching ground
Harness trapped under a panel or bracket
Faulty transceiver pulling the (-) line to ground
s: Vehicle mostly normal, code stored by a single module
Occasional communication errors

U0044.d: U0044 means the (-) conductor of Vehicle Communication Bus B is held at an excessive voltage, mostly through contact with battery plus. Where Bus B is a high-speed-type CAN, the conductor is CAN-Low, and onsemi found that with CAN-Low at 12 V no frame gets out any more; the node's current even drops, to about 48 mA, because its transmit pin is driven low only some 2 % of the time while the controller retries and backs off. All Bus B members fall silent together. A fault-tolerant low-speed CAN handles the same fault differently: NXP's TJA1055 detects it after a filter delay, turns off the CAN-Low driver and listens on CAN-High only. No manufacturer documents U0044 publicly. Ignition on, CAN-Low against ground near battery voltage confirms it; look for chafing at supply wires and water in connectors.
c: (-) wire chafed against a battery or ignition feed
Water in a connector linking the (-) wire to a supply pin
Damaged transceiver driving the (-) line high
s: All functions on Bus B fail together (high-speed type)
Lost-communication codes in modules on other networks
Fallback modes or warning lamps depending on the modules involved

U0045.t: Vehicle Communication Bus B (-) Shorted to Bus B (+)
U0045.d: U0045 describes the two wires of Vehicle Communication Bus B touching each other. Deutz uses this code in the EMR L1 engine controller for a short circuit on its third CAN channel, without further detail. On a high-speed-type CAN, bridged wires leave no differential voltage, every bit reads recessive and, per onsemi, nothing can be transmitted while the CANH driver works into its current limit; NXP adds that transceiver diagnosis cannot see this short. On a fault-tolerant low-speed network, NXP's TJA1055 first sees a permanent dominant level, then after a time-out switches off CAN-Low and keeps going on CAN-High. Typical causes are crushed harness sections, water in splices and a damaged module input. No car maker documents U0045 publicly; near-zero ohms between the wires with the battery off confirms the fault.
c: Harness crushed so that both bus wires touch
Water in a splice or connector bridging the two wires
Damaged module input shorting its bus pins
s: Every function on Bus B unavailable (high-speed type)
Several warning lamps on at once
Lost-communication codes in modules on other networks

U0046.d: U0046 covers Vehicle Communication Bus C in general, the third manufacturer-assigned network slot after Bus A and Bus B. Public uses are rare. Stellantis lists U0046-00 among the faults addressed by powertrain control module flash 18-071-26 for the 2025 Ram 1500 with the 3.0-litre Hurricane twin-turbo six; the bulletin pairs its long code list with a possible MIL but does not single out the bus fault as the reason for the lamp. Ford's 2014 Boss 302S code table names U0046 as well, without marking it as a MIL code. Behind the code there may be a wiring fault, a module that stops talking or plain software, so check for accompanying lost-communication codes first, then supply, ground and bus wiring of the modules on that network before replacing parts.
c: Control module software that misjudges the bus (Ram 1500: PCM flash)
Damaged bus wiring or poorly seated connector on Bus C
Supply or ground fault at a module on Bus C
s: Check-engine lamp possible together with other stored codes (Ram 1500)
Functions of modules on Bus C unavailable
Lost-communication codes stored alongside

U0047.d: U0047 says that Vehicle Communication Bus C is up but its traffic is not dependable, for instance through sporadic error frames, messages arriving too late or brief dropouts. CAN controllers keep score with error counters: as onsemi explains with reference to ISO 11898-1, every failed transmission adds eight to the transmit counter, beyond about 128 the node turns error passive and past 255 it takes itself off the bus, rejoining only after 128 runs of eleven recessive bits. A performance code is typically set somewhere along that path, before or between short bus-off episodes. No manufacturer documents U0047 publicly; CARB only requires faults in digital communication to be detected and stored separately. Loose terminals, corroded connectors, interference and a node that resets now and then are the usual causes.
c: Loose or corroded terminals on Bus C
A module on Bus C resetting because of weak supply or ground
Interference coupled into the bus wiring
s: Functions drop out briefly and return
Sporadic warning messages from several systems

U0048.d: U0048 stands for an open (+) wire on Vehicle Communication Bus C, CAN-High where Bus C is a CAN. Deutz places the code on CAN 4 of its EMR L1 engine controller, listed for main and secondary ECU as an open circuit on that channel, just as U0039 covers CAN 3. Electrically, an interrupted CAN-High wire splits a high-speed CAN into islands that keep working internally; NXP points out that transceiver diagnosis cannot report such a break, so the controller relies on missing messages. A fault-tolerant low-speed transceiver such as NXP's TJA1055 rides through the same break with its drivers left active. Expect lost-communication entries for nodes located past the interruption. No car maker documents U0048 publicly. Check connector seating, crimp terminals and harness flex points first.
c: (+) wire of Bus C broken at a flex point or splice
s: Modules on the far side of the break unreachable
Lost-communication codes in several modules

U0049.d: U0049 reports the (+) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus C shorted to ground. If Bus C is a high-speed-type CAN, the affected conductor is CAN-High; for a dominant bit it should climb to roughly 3.6 V, which a grounded line cannot do, and onsemi's tests show the node unable to send anything while its CANH output works into a current limit of up to about 120 mA. Every module on Bus C drops out at the same moment, and members of other networks begin logging missing messages. The fault-tolerant low-speed variant reacts more gracefully, since NXP's TJA1055 counts a grounded CAN-High among the failures that leave ongoing traffic intact. No manufacturer documents U0049 publicly. With the battery disconnected, CAN-High at a few ohms or less to ground confirms the short.
c: (+) wire of Bus C chafed through to ground
Harness pinched during assembly or repair
Shorted transceiver in a module on Bus C
s: All functions on Bus C fail together (high-speed type)
Missing-message codes in modules on other networks

U0050.d: U0050 flags excess voltage on the (+) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus C. On a high-speed-style CAN bus, the conductor is CAN-High sitting at battery or 5 V level, a condition onsemi found survivable: frames still pass, the dominant bits merely look different and the transceiver draws about as little as when idle, since its high-side driver delivers no current. NXP therefore lists it with the hidden failures that need transceiver diagnosis to surface at all. Fault-tolerant low-speed transceivers such as NXP's TJA1055 confirm the fault in two timed steps and then fall back to single-wire operation on CAN-Low. Because driving rarely changes, the code is often found by chance during a scan. No manufacturer documents U0050 publicly. CAN-High near supply voltage against ground confirms it.
c: (+) wire of Bus C touching a battery or 5 V feed
Moisture in a connector linking the bus wire to supply
Aftermarket device tapped into the bus wire
s: Usually no symptom, code found during a scan
Occasional single warning from a module on Bus C

U0051.d: U0051 stands for a severed (-) conductor on Vehicle Communication Bus C, CAN-Low where Bus C is a CAN. Deutz, which places Bus C on the fourth CAN channel of the EMR L1 engine control unit, does not use this code and books CAN 4 faults only as open circuit (U0048) or short circuit (U0054). A high-speed transceiver cannot see the interruption itself, as NXP points out, so the module only notices that partners on the far side stop acknowledging or sending. NXP's fault-tolerant low-speed TJA1055 instead compares the edge counts on both wires and flags a difference of four pulses; since that works only when the break lies between sender and receiver, its error output tends to toggle. No car maker documents U0051 publicly. Check CAN-Low continuity connector by connector.
c: (-) wire of Bus C broken at a flex point or splice
Terminal pushed back or spread in a Bus C connector
s: Modules beyond the break no longer respond
Code comes and goes while other modules keep working

U0052.d: U0052 signals a ground short on the (-) line of Vehicle Communication Bus C; where Bus C follows the high-speed CAN layout, the affected line is CAN-Low, and NXP's application note for the TJA1041 lists this short among the hidden bus failures: nodes keep communicating, so a controller only learns of it from a transceiver with bus diagnosis. Such a transceiver needs at least four dominant phases of 4 µs or more on the wire before its failure flag is valid, and it reliably catches shorts between 0 and 50 ohms. The price of the fault is a smaller noise margin; with high bus capacitance dominant periods can stretch until bit timing is violated. The vehicle therefore usually drives normally and the code appears in a single module. No manufacturer documents U0052 publicly. Battery off, CAN-Low shows practically zero ohms to chassis.
c: (-) wire of Bus C chafed against body metal
Harness trapped under a trim panel or seat rail
Transceiver in one module pulling CAN-Low to ground
s: Often no noticeable symptom, code found during a scan
Occasional brief warning from a module on Bus C

U0053.d: U0053 reports too much voltage on the (-) conductor of Vehicle Communication Bus C, meaning CAN-Low if Bus C is built as a high-speed CAN, and NXP's TJA1041 application note states that a short of CAN-Low either to battery or to the 5 V transceiver supply makes communication impossible, while onsemi's measurements show the transmitting node stuck in endless failed attempts. All Bus C members go quiet together. A fault-tolerant low-speed bus separates the two cases: the TJA1055 data sheet treats CAN-Low at 5 V as a failure it simply tolerates, but at battery voltage it switches off its CAN-Low driver after a delay and receives over CAN-High alone. No manufacturer documents U0053 publicly. With the ignition on, CAN-Low near 5 V or battery voltage against ground confirms the fault.
c: (-) wire of Bus C touching a battery or 5 V feed
Moisture in a connector bridging the (-) wire to a supply pin
s: All functions on Bus C drop out at once (high-speed type)
Lost-communication codes in modules on other networks
Warning lamps or fallback modes depending on the affected modules

U0054.t: Vehicle Communication Bus C (-) Shorted to Bus C (+)
U0054.d: U0054 describes a short between the two wires of Vehicle Communication Bus C. Deutz uses it in main and secondary EMR L1 engine controllers as a short circuit on CAN 4, the same channel whose open circuit is U0048. On a high-speed CAN the bridged pair carries no differential voltage, so no dominant bit can form; onsemi measured the node's draw falling to about 47 mA, the lowest of all short types, because almost no transmission takes place. NXP's TJA1041 note adds that bus diagnosis in the transceiver cannot recognise this case. On fault-tolerant low-speed hardware like NXP's TJA1055, the bridged pair first looks like an endless dominant state; after 0.3 to 1.6 ms the chip disables CAN-Low and continues on one wire. Resistance across the pair close to zero, measured without battery, confirms it.
c: Harness crushed so that both Bus C wires touch
Water in a splice or connector bridging the pair
Damaged module input shorting its two bus pins
s: All modules on Bus C unreachable (high-speed type)
Engine controller reports CAN fault, connected machine functions fail (Deutz)

U0055.d: U0055 covers Vehicle Communication Bus D as a whole, the fourth network slot a manufacturer can assign freely. Volvo documents it for the 2016-17 XC90 T8 plug-in hybrid: the engine control module stores U005500 with fault type intermittent, the driver information display shows the turtle symbol and the car lacks power. Volvo classifies it as a software fault, tells technicians not to replace parts, and announced new software for week 16 of 2017, until then the code was simply cleared. Bentley assigns Bus D to a private chassis CAN and documents its performance code U0056. Without such a bulletin, look first for lost-communication codes that show which module on Bus D is missing, then check its supply, ground and connectors.
c: Control module software misjudging Bus D (Volvo XC90 T8: ECM update)
Supply or ground fault at a module on Bus D
Damaged wiring or loose connector on Bus D
s: Turtle symbol and reduced engine power (Volvo XC90 T8)
Functions of modules on Bus D unavailable
Lost-communication codes stored alongside

U0056.d: U0056 says Vehicle Communication Bus D works, but its traffic is disturbed. Bentley documents it for the Continental GT (2018-20), GTC (2019-20) and Flying Spur (2020): U005600 with symptom numbers 12689537, 12689541 or 12689542 lands in the chassis control unit (address 0074) or in roll control systems 1 and 2 (00D4, 00D5). Bus D is a private CAN there, and its errors pull in a series of suspension codes; the driver sees a red or yellow suspension lamp and a dynamic ride fault message. Bentley has technicians check the connectors and harness of the three units, then update the chassis control software, or replace the unit if it is on another software level. A production change came with a software update. Elsewhere, loose contacts or a resetting node are the usual causes.
c: Chassis control software level prone to Bus D errors (Bentley)
Loose or dirty connector at a module on Bus D
Damaged harness between the modules on Bus D
A module on Bus D restarting because of weak supply
s: Red or yellow suspension warning lamp (Bentley)
Dynamic ride fault message, several suspension codes stored
Functions drop out briefly and return

U0057.d: U0057 indicates an interrupted (+) wire on Vehicle Communication Bus D. Where Bus D is a two-wire CAN, such as the private chassis CAN Bentley files under that name, it is CAN-High. Apart from splitting the bus, a break changes the line itself: Texas Instruments describes high-speed CAN as a 120-ohm twisted pair terminated at both far ends, and warns against placing a terminator inside a node because the line loses it when that node is unplugged. A break that cuts one terminator off leaves part of the wire unterminated, so reflections can distort edges for the remaining nodes. The transceiver cannot detect the interruption itself (NXP). No manufacturer documents U0057 publicly. Look for connectors left open after repairs and conductors fractured where the harness flexes.
c: (+) wire of Bus D broken where the harness flexes
Connector left unplugged or not latched after a repair
s: Modules beyond the break unreachable
Sporadic errors among the remaining modules

U0058.d: U0058 reports the (+) conductor of Vehicle Communication Bus D shorted to ground. If Bus D is a high-speed-style CAN, that conductor is CAN-High, and NXP's TJA1041 application note puts this short on the list of failures that stop communication completely. A diagnosing transceiver can still flag it, but the note explains why the controller rarely gets that far: when communication is fully corrupted, the routine that would read the flag after a sent frame is never reached.
