In practice the modules on Bus D drift into bus-off one after another and partners on other networks record them as missing. onsemi measured the node's supply current dropping from about 65 to 50 mA. No manufacturer documents U0058 publicly. With the battery disconnected, CAN-High shows a few ohms or less to ground.
c: (+) wire of Bus D chafed through to ground
Harness pinched by a bracket or fastener
Shorted transceiver in a module on Bus D
s: All functions on Bus D fail together
Lost-communication codes in modules on other networks
Warning lamps or fallback modes depending on the modules involved

U0059.d: U0059 means the (+) line of Vehicle Communication Bus D sits at too high a voltage, typically from contact with a battery or 5 V feed. On a high-speed CAN layout the line concerned is CAN-High, and the fault belongs to the shorts NXP calls hidden: communication goes on, and only a transceiver with bus diagnosis can report it. NXP's TJA1041 note mentions a further side effect, namely that the bus wake-up logic of that device was designed so that a CAN-High short to battery does not wake the network while it goes to sleep; a hint that such a short can otherwise interfere with the network going to sleep. Fault-tolerant low-speed hardware like the TJA1055 handles it in two timed steps and ends on CAN-Low alone. No manufacturer documents U0059 publicly. Measured against ground, CAN-High sitting near supply voltage settles the diagnosis.
c: (+) wire of Bus D touching a battery or 5 V feed
Moisture in a connector bridging the bus wire to supply
Aftermarket device tapped into the bus wire
s: Usually no symptom, code found during a scan
Occasional single warning from a module on Bus D

U0060.d: U0060 stands for a break in the (-) line of Vehicle Communication Bus D, CAN-Low on a two-wire CAN such as Bentley's private chassis network. Nodes cut off by the break still see CAN-High move, but a high-speed receiver judges only the voltage difference between both wires, so frames from the other side become unreadable to them. NXP notes that a high-speed transceiver has no way to detect a line interruption itself, which leaves time-outs and missing acknowledgements as the evidence. NXP also designed the wake-up detection of its TJA1041 so that a CAN-Low interruption causes no unwanted wake-up while the bus goes to sleep. No manufacturer documents U0060 publicly. Test CAN-Low continuity between the modules, starting with connectors recently opened.
c: (-) wire of Bus D broken in the harness
Connector not fully latched after work on the vehicle
s: Functions of modules beyond the break fail
Lost-communication codes for individual modules on Bus D

U0061.d: U0061 reports the (-) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus D held at ground potential; a Bus D designed as high-speed CAN has CAN-Low in that role, which normally swings only between about 2.5 V and 1.5 V. Texas Instruments gives the tolerated common-mode range of ISO 11898 receivers as anything between -2 V and +7 V, so a grounded CAN-Low still lies inside the window and the receivers keep decoding; onsemi confirms that frames continue with distorted levels. What changes is current: the upper output stage of the sending node now feeds the 60-ohm load directly into ground, raising its draw to roughly 72 mA in onsemi's test. The code typically sits in one module with diagnostic transceiver while Bus D keeps working. No manufacturer documents U0061 publicly. With the battery off, CAN-Low reads near zero ohms to ground.
c: (-) wire of Bus D chafed against a ground point or body edge
Water in a connector linking CAN-Low to a ground pin
Faulty transceiver pulling the (-) line down
s: Often no symptom, code stored in a single module
Occasional interference-related message errors

U0062.d: U0062 means the (-) conductor of Vehicle Communication Bus D is forced high, usually by contact with battery plus. Built as high-speed CAN, Bus D carries this fault on CAN-Low, which can then no longer be pulled down any more; onsemi and NXP both list this short among those under which no frame gets through, so every Bus D member eventually ends up bus-off and other networks log its absence. Diagnosing transceivers such as NXP's TJA1041 recognise the short when its resistance is between 0 and 50 ohms. Texas Instruments adds a hardware angle: termination resistors should be rated for such a short, since a bus wire shorted to a 24 V line loads them with the transceiver's short-circuit current times that voltage, enough to destroy a quarter-watt part. No manufacturer documents U0062 publicly. CAN-Low near battery voltage confirms it.
c: (-) wire of Bus D chafed against a battery or ignition feed
Water in a connector linking the (-) wire to a supply pin
Termination or transceiver damaged by a lasting short to supply
s: All functions on Bus D fail together
Lost-communication codes in modules on other networks
Warning lamps or fallback modes depending on the modules involved

U0063.t: Vehicle Communication Bus D (-) Shorted to Bus D (+)
U0063.d: U0063 covers a short circuit between both conductors of Vehicle Communication Bus D. On a CAN-type Bus D the receivers then measure no voltage difference, read every bit as recessive and cannot see any frame start; onsemi lists this short with those that block transmission completely. It is also one of the two fault classes, along with wire breaks, that NXP's TJA1041 bus diagnosis explicitly does not detect, so modules infer it from error counters and silent partners. A useful check uses the termination: with the battery disconnected, a healthy high-speed pair reads about 60 ohms between the wires, while this fault gives close to zero. If the short sits inside a module, unplugging modules one at a time brings the reading back. No manufacturer documents U0063 publicly.
c: Harness crushed so that both Bus D wires touch
Water in a splice or connector bridging the pair
Damaged transceiver shorting its two bus pins
s: All modules on Bus D unreachable at once
Several warning lamps or fallback modes

U0064.d: U0064 is the umbrella fault for Vehicle Communication Bus E, the fifth freely assignable network slot. Jaguar Land Rover documents it for the 2022-25 Range Rover (L460) and 2023-25 Range Rover Sport (L461): modules store U0064-88 (bus off) and U0064-87 (missing message), often together with U0080 codes for Bus F, when connector CM32B3/4 between the main body and instrument panel harnesses is not fully latched. Owners report electrical faults around power mode zero and FlexRay module functions, sometimes only intermittent and depending on movement in the cabin or on temperature. JLR has the connector unplugged, its pins inspected and relatched even when it looks secure. Volkswagen Group uses the neighbouring code U0065 for the infotainment CAN in the gateway.
c: Harness connector between body and instrument panel not fully latched (JLR CM32B3/4)
Bent or spread pins in that connector
Supply or ground fault at a module on Bus E
s: Electrical faults that come and go with cabin movement or temperature (JLR)
Modules on Bus E not responding, bus-off or missing-message entries
Codes for further networks stored alongside

U0065.d: U0065 reports that Vehicle Communication Bus E is present but its communication is unreliable. In Audi and Volkswagen gateways this slot stands for the infotainment CAN. Audi lists U006500, labelled there as no communication on the infotainment CAN, in gateway J533 of the 2015-18 A3, paired with U111000 in the instrument cluster: the infotainment unit will not switch on, cannot be operated or goes blank now and then. The cause is a grey 12-pin contact carrier not slotted correctly into the quad-lock connector of control unit J794; both parts are replaced. Volkswagen's 2017 Golf family campaign 91Q1 warns that the gateway may store U0065 during the infotainment software update because J794 drops off briefly; such entries are intermittent and clear.
c: Contact carrier not seated in the infotainment unit's quad-lock connector (Audi A3)
Brief dropout of the infotainment unit during a software update (VW Golf)
Loose or corroded terminals on Bus E
s: Infotainment cannot be switched on or operated, screen sporadically blank (Audi A3)
Instrument cluster reports restricted functions
Stored only as a passive entry after a software update

U0066.d: U0066 indicates a break in the (+) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus E. Where Bus E is a two-wire CAN, like the infotainment CAN Audi and Volkswagen monitor under that slot, the (+) wire is CAN-High. The physical layer decides how visible the fault is. With fault-tolerant low-speed hardware, NXP's TJA1055 rides through a CAN-High interruption with drivers, termination and differential receiver left as they were, and only counts edges: once CAN-High and CAN-Low differ by four pulses, its error output goes low. A high-speed transceiver offers no such check, so modules notice only that partners beyond the break fall silent. No manufacturer documents U0066 publicly; Audi's A3 case of a badly seated contact carrier in a multi-pin connector shows how such interruptions arise.
c: (+) wire of Bus E broken in the harness
Contact carrier or terminal not seated in a multi-pin connector
Connector left unplugged after a repair
s: Modules beyond the break, often infotainment units, unreachable
Lost-communication codes for individual modules

U0067.d: U0067 tells of the (+) conductor of Vehicle Communication Bus E being grounded. For a Bus E built as a high-speed CAN that is CAN-High, which a dominant bit needs to raise by about a volt; grounded, it cannot. onsemi describes the resulting cycle: the controller attempts a start-of-frame, fails, flags errors, becomes error passive and finally bus-off, then must wait for 128 groups of eleven recessive bits before it may try again, so its transmit line is active only about 2 % of the time. Every Bus E node goes silent, and modules on other networks log them as missing. NXP's fault-tolerant TJA1055 low-speed chip, by contrast, carries on despite the same short. No manufacturer documents U0067 publicly. CAN-High at a few ohms to ground with the battery off confirms it.
c: (+) wire of Bus E chafed through to body ground
Harness trapped behind the dashboard or a trim panel
Shorted transceiver in a module on Bus E
s: All functions on Bus E fail together (high-speed type)
Missing-message codes in modules on other networks

U0068.d: U0068 flags the (+) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus E at an excessive voltage, from battery or a 5 V rail. If Bus E is a high-speed CAN, the line in question is CAN-High, and traffic continues: onsemi saw frames pass with altered dominant levels, NXP files the case under hidden failures. Detecting it therefore depends on the module. NXP's TJA1041 note explains that a diagnosing transceiver must itself send at least four sufficiently long dominant phases before its failure flag is valid, and recommends reading the flag once a frame has finished, because arbitration with other senders can distort the measurement. That is why only some modules on Bus E, or none, may store the code. No manufacturer documents U0068 publicly. A meter on CAN-High showing roughly supply voltage to ground proves it.
c: (+) wire of Bus E chafed against a battery or 5 V feed
Moisture in a connector bridging the bus wire to supply
Aftermarket device connected to the bus wire
s: Usually no symptom, code found by chance
Code stored in only one module on Bus E

U0069.d: U0069 concerns a severed (-) line on Vehicle Communication Bus E, CAN-Low where Bus E is a CAN such as the infotainment CAN Volkswagen Group gateways supervise. Beyond splitting the network, the break matters for signal quality: Texas Instruments points out that stubs on a high-speed CAN are unterminated and should stay short, around 0.3 m, because reflections in them must die out ahead of the sampling point. A break that isolates a terminating node turns the remaining wire into exactly such an open end. Transceivers do not detect line interruptions themselves (NXP), so a module infers the fault from missing acknowledgements or time-outs. No manufacturer documents U0069 publicly. Check CAN-Low continuity and connector latching, especially behind the dashboard.
c: (-) wire of Bus E broken in the harness
Connector not fully latched, contacts lifting
Terminal backed out of its housing
s: Modules beyond the break unreachable
Sporadic message errors among the remaining modules

U0070.d: U0070 points to a (-) line of Vehicle Communication Bus E with a path to ground, CAN-Low wherever Bus E is a high-speed CAN. Traffic survives the short, which onsemi and NXP both confirm, so drivers rarely notice anything; onsemi traced a higher node current, because the upper driver stage now pushes current through the 60-ohm termination into ground. On a fault-tolerant low-speed bus the effect is a mode change instead: NXP's TJA1055 reads a never-ending dominant state, needs 0.3-1.6 ms to confirm it, then disables the CAN-Low output stage and keeps going single-wire via CAN-High, with weaker immunity to interference in that mode. Either way the code often lingers in memory unnoticed. No manufacturer documents U0070 publicly. An ohmmeter between CAN-Low and chassis that reads close to zero confirms it.
c: (-) wire of Bus E chafed against body ground
Harness pinched during installation of trim or accessories
Faulty transceiver pulling CAN-Low to ground
s: Usually no symptom, code found during a scan
Occasional interference with audio or display functions on Bus E

U0071.d: With U0071 the (-) conductor of Vehicle Communication Bus E sits too high, mostly by a short to battery voltage. Where Bus E is a high-speed CAN this is CAN-Low, and the bus dies: the line can no longer be pulled down, onsemi's node failed every start of frame, and NXP's TJA1041 note lists CAN-Low at battery or at 5 V as faults that prevent any communication. All Bus E modules drop out, and the gateway or other networks log them as lost. A fault-tolerant low-speed transceiver reacts differently; NXP's TJA1055 detects CAN-Low at battery voltage after a filter delay, turns its CAN-Low output off and receives via CAN-High alone. No manufacturer documents U0071 publicly. With ignition on, a CAN-Low reading at battery level rather than in the 1.5-2.5 V band confirms it.
c: (-) wire of Bus E chafed against a battery or ignition feed
Water in a connector linking the (-) wire to a supply pin
Damaged transceiver driving the (-) line high
s: All functions on Bus E fail together (high-speed type)
Gateway or other modules report lost communication

U0072.t: Vehicle Communication Bus E (-) Shorted to Bus E (+)
U0072.d: U0072 describes the (-) and (+) wires of Vehicle Communication Bus E touching each other. On a high-speed CAN this ends communication: with the pair bridged there is no differential voltage, onsemi found transmission impossible, and NXP's TJA1041 note lists the short with the faults its bus diagnosis cannot detect. A fault-tolerant low-speed CAN degrades more gently. NXP's TJA1055 treats the short as a dominant level that never ends, confirms it in 0.3-1.6 ms, shuts down its CAN-Low driver and falls back to working over one wire, and returns to differential mode once the short is gone and the recessive state holds for a while. No manufacturer documents U0072 publicly. Separating connectors along the bus while measuring the resistance between the wires narrows the location down.
c: Harness crushed so that both Bus E wires touch
Water in a splice or connector bridging the pair
Damaged module input shorting its bus pins
s: All modules on Bus E unreachable (high-speed type)
Several warning messages, gateway reports lost communication

U0073.t: Control Module Communication Bus A Off
U0073.d: U0073 is logged by a module whose own CAN controller has withdrawn from Bus A. Each failed transmission adds eight to its transmit error counter; above 255 the chip goes bus off and may rejoin only after 128 runs of 11 recessive bits (onsemi). GM's 2019 tables flag more than five bus-off events, about 0.06 s, inside a 0.81 s window as Type A with MIL on the first trip, and the ECM suspends lost-communication tests such as U0101 while it is active. Around 2006 GM still reported this state as U0001. A Ford TCM turns the MIL on at once because engine speed is missing. Bulletins trace U0073 to a loose ground (Trax, G103), backed-out terminals in the 6L80 transmission connector and harness rubbing on a cylinder head (Silverado LV3). Expect several warnings, possibly a gearbox held in one gear.
c: Bus A wires chafed through or shorted to ground in the harness
Loose or corroded ground point of a module on Bus A
Backed-out or loose terminals, e.g. in the transmission connector
s: MIL and several cluster warnings at the same time
Transmission stuck in one gear or shifting harshly
Gauges fluctuate or drop out briefly
Lost-communication codes such as U0100 or U0101 in other modules

U0074.t: Control Module Communication Bus B Off
U0074.d: U0074 tells that a module dropped into bus off on Bus B, which the makers that use it assign to an extra powertrain network. GM's 2019 ECM tables call it the Powertrain Expansion CAN, and the LT5 injection module rates its Bus B check Type B, two trips. On 2014-18 trucks and SUVs, PIP5427 ties U0074 to a lost link between ECM and fuel pump module that drives fuel pressure far above target and sets P2635; the communication fault is to be fixed first. FCA's label for the code refers to its Dedicated Powertrain CAN (D-PT): a PCM reflash cures it on the 2019 Ram 1500 eTorque, and on 2022-24 Wranglers it comes with a binding shifter. Ford lists it on 2017-18 F-150s with a badly secured transmission harness, and its diesel PCMs set it when a line stays shorted or open longer than 10 ms.
c: Damaged or poorly routed powertrain harness on Bus B
Engine module software fault, fixed by reprogramming
Loose connector, bent pin or badly seated fuse on a Bus B module
s: Service Engine Soon lamp or MIL on
Fuel pressure well above the requested value (GM trucks)
Shifter binds or shift concerns
No crank or start-stop inoperative

U0075.t: Control Module Communication Bus C Off
U0075.d: Which traffic runs on Bus C differs from brand to brand, so U0075 means little until the storing module is known. On the 2015 Cadillac Escalade with Driver Assist, the active safety module records it alongside radar and camera codes; GM found that a worn diagnostic interface or cable on DLC pins 3 and 11, where the object detection network ends, can create these entries falsely. On the 2020-24 CT5, U0075 together with lost-communication codes led to CAN 1 wires 4986/4987 chafed on the passenger seat frame, with steering, stability and airbag messages. The 2026 Dodge Charger 3.0 turbo uses the code under the J2012 name, set falsely with MIL and cured by new PCM software. First identify the module and its network, then measure.
c: Bus C wires chafed on a seat frame or body edge
Engine module software setting the code falsely
Defective diagnostic interface or cable creating false entries
s: Service messages for steering, stability control or airbag
Driver assistance, radar or front camera unavailable
MIL on with no driveability complaint (FCA)

U0076.t: Control Module Communication Bus D Off
U0076.d: GM is the main public user of U0076. In the 2019 tables for the Corvette LT5 engine, Bus D is the Powertrain Sensor CAN, a private link between the ECM and engine-side devices. The ECM sets the code when that bus has been off for one second after the controller has run for three seconds, Type B with MIL after two trips, and holds back its lost-message check toward the fuel level module meanwhile. On the 2020-22 Malibu 1.5 L, bulletin 21-NA-186 traces U0076 together with U18A2 and message counter faults to an ECM harness rubbing on its bracket; owners notice a Service Engine Soon lamp or an erratic fuel gauge. Unlike U0055, which describes the bus D wiring as a whole, this code reports that the ECM's own controller has fallen silent.
c: ECM harness rubbing through on its bracket
Poor contact at a connector of the engine-side sensor bus
Faulty CAN transceiver inside the ECM
s: Service Engine Soon lamp or MIL on
Fuel gauge erratic or wrong
Message counter codes stored alongside

U0077.t: Control Module Communication Bus E Off
U0077.d: At GM, Bus E is usually a chassis-side network. In the 2018 tables for the LYX engine variant, the ECM watches it the same way as Bus A, more than five bus-off events within 0.81 s, but rates the result Type X without MIL; the transmission's default-to-park checks stay disabled while U0077 is set. On the 2015 Escalade, high resistance under the sill plates in circuit 5986, which wakes the modules for communication, left the brake, steering and suspension modules without a proper wake-up signal; on 2010-15 Equinox and Terrain models corrosion in connector X411 behind the fuel tank caused it. Volvo mild hybrids may store U007700 in the medium-voltage battery module together with P0A7B at pre-delivery; Volvo advises clearing it and reloading software only if it returns with MIL.
c: Corroded underbody connector in the Bus E harness
High resistance in the communication enable (wake-up) circuit
One-off software event in a module, cleared without repair
s: Service ABS, StabiliTrak or power steering messages
Suspension or all-wheel-drive warnings
Heavy steering when the steering module drops off

U0078.t: Control Module Communication Bus F Off
U0078.d: At GM the bus behind U0078 is often the single-wire low-speed GMLAN that ties body modules together. Equinox and Terrain models from 2010 to 2015 set it with lost-communication codes for body module, cluster and liftgate when water corrodes connector X901 above the liftgate glass. On the 2013-16 Acadia the low-speed wire to the remote door lock receiver got pinched between the rear HVAC duct and the roof, giving intermittent no-crank, a dead radio and erratic gauges. A poor body control module ground at G218 on the 2015 Escalade produced U0078 together with U0073. Because these modules handle comfort and access, owners mostly notice dark interior lights, a dead liftgate or blank displays. GM's published OBD tables do not list U0078, so no MIL type is documented.
c: Water intrusion and corrosion in a body harness connector
Low-speed bus wire pinched behind trim or headliner
Poor ground of the body control module
s: Interior lamps or liftgate inoperative
Radio, climate panel or cluster go blank
Intermittent no-crank

U0079.t: Control Module Communication Bus G Off
U0079.d: No manufacturer documents U0079 publicly, so what Bus G is depends entirely on the vehicle. The code belongs to the bus-off family: the controller of the reporting module has collected enough transmit errors to stop sending in order to protect the other nodes. That sets it apart from U0089, the general Bus G fault, and from lost-communication codes such as U0100, which other modules store once they no longer hear the silent one. CARB requires that missing communication of digital inputs and outputs be detected and stored under its own code, which is why a module records its own disconnection. Read all modules first: if only one holds U0079, its transceiver, supply or connector is suspect; if several do, look at the Bus G wiring and termination.
c: Short between the Bus G wires or to ground
Faulty transceiver in the reporting module
Supply or ground dropouts at the reporting module
s: Functions of the reporting module unavailable
Lost-communication codes in other modules

U007A.t: Control Module Communication Bus H Off
U007A.d: Bus H appears in no public manufacturer document for U007A; the code merely says that one module's CAN controller has switched to bus off on the network its maker labels H. A sensible check order follows from the physics. A high-speed CAN carries a 120 ohm resistor at each end, so with the battery disconnected the two wires should show roughly 60 ohms between them; about 120 ohms points to a missing terminator, near zero to the wires touching. With ignition on, a dominant bit pulls CAN-High toward 3.5 V and CAN-Low toward 1.5 V. As onsemi shows, a bus that is held recessive pushes a sender into bus off within a few dozen bit times, so shorts and transceiver damage come before software in the search.
c: Terminating resistor open or a terminating module disconnected
s: Functions on Bus H fail or work only intermittently
Warning messages from several systems

U007B.t: Control Module Communication Bus I Off
U007B.d: U007B is tied to no published manufacturer use; a Bus I only exists on vehicles split into many separate networks. The cause need not sit in the wiring at all. Onsemi describes a node whose transmit pin cannot produce a dominant level: every start-of-frame attempt fails and raises the error counter by eight, after 17 attempts it is error passive and shortly afterwards bus off, although the remaining bus may keep running normally. A damaged transceiver, a supply dip at the module or a cracked solder joint can therefore produce U007B in a single module only. If the code returns after clearing, check that module's power and ground under load and swap it against a known good unit before opening the harness.
c: Transceiver in the reporting module unable to drive the bus
Weak supply or ground at the reporting module
Short or open in the Bus I wiring
s: Only the reporting module's functions drop out
Code returns soon after clearing

U007C.t: Control Module Communication Bus J Off
U007C.d: For U007C no manufacturer publishes a use; a Bus J only exists where the electrical architecture splits the vehicle into ten or more CAN segments. Bus off is self-healing by design: once the controller has seen 128 sequences of 11 recessive bits it may rejoin, as onsemi explains, and the error counters start again from zero. A short-lived short circuit, a loose pin or a voltage dip during cranking can therefore leave U007C as a history code while everything works again by the time the car reaches the workshop. Such intermittent cases need the fault reproduced, for instance by flexing harness sections and connectors of Bus J while watching the module's communication status. Replacing modules on a history code alone rarely helps.
c: Loose pin or connector on Bus J opening briefly
Harness chafe causing brief shorts on Bus J
s: Stored history code without a current complaint
Brief, self-clearing dropouts of single functions

U007D.t: Control Module Communication Bus K Off
U007D.d: U007D is one of the few late-alphabet bus-off codes with a public trace, all from GM's 2017 full-size trucks and SUVs (Silverado, Sierra, Tahoe, Suburban, Yukon, Escalade). There a serial data gateway module connects many CAN segments, and PIT5586 lists U007D next to U0073, U0078 and a long row of lost-communication codes. GM names two causes: bent, backed-out or loose terminals at gateway connectors X1 and X2, and a microcontroller fault that keeps the gateway powered but silent on every channel. For the latter GM's interim remedy is to pull the gateway's power fuse for a minute (F26DL on trucks, F28DL on SUVs) until a software update is installed, without replacing parts. Complaints range from dead gauges to no crank or start-then-stall.
c: Bent, backed-out or loose terminals at the gateway connectors
Gateway microcontroller locks up and stops communicating
s: Instrument cluster gauges dead or fluctuating
No crank, no start or stall after starting
Radio, climate controls or steering wheel buttons inoperative
Numerous lost-communication codes in many modules

U007E.t: Control Module Communication Bus L Off
U007E.d: There is no public manufacturer documentation for U007E; the letter L is reserved for vehicles with a dozen or more networks. The code marks the last step of the CAN error ladder. A node stays error active while its counters are below 128 and signals faults with dominant flags; between 128 and 255 it becomes error passive and may flag errors only recessively; once transmit errors exceed 255 it goes bus off and stops sending, as Wikipedia's CAN bus article describes. U007E therefore means that a module has failed repeatedly, not once. What the driver notices depends on what the silent module controls, from a missing comfort function to warning lamps, and partner modules then store their own lost-communication codes.
c: Persistent short or bad contact on Bus L
Fault inside the reporting module's CAN interface
s: Single comfort or assistance function missing
Partner modules report lost communication

U007F.t: Control Module Communication Bus M Off
U007F.d: U007F closes the range of bus-off codes that SAE runs from U0073 for Bus A to Bus M; the next code, U0080, already belongs to the general Bus F faults. No manufacturer publishes a use, and which physical network carries the letter M has to be read from the maker's service data. CARB only demands that missing digital communication be detected and stored separately, not how buses are named. One detail helps narrow the cause: according to Wikipedia, a sender whose frames simply go unacknowledged, for example because it is alone on the bus, keeps repeating them and reaches error passive, not bus off. U007F thus points to active disturbance, such as a shorted line or a node that cannot drive the bus. Begin at the storing module's supply, ground and connector.
c: A node unable to drive the bus, e.g. defective transceiver
Poor supply, ground or connector contact at the storing module
s: Functions of the storing module unavailable
Several warning messages or none, depending on the module

U0080.d: U0080 is the general fault of Vehicle Communication Bus F, and makers give that letter very different networks. In the 2019 Audi A6 and A7 3.0 TFSI the transmission module stores U008000 (Bus F) when its harness chafes on the crossmember or the FlexRay feed rubs on a module bracket, together with parking lock codes P17F4-P17F6 and U010100 in the engine module. Range Rover L460/L461 log U0080-88 (bus off) and U0080-81 (invalid data) if connector CM32B3/4 is not latched. Stellantis security gateways call it Ethernet Bus 1; when the telematics box answers more than 5 s late after start-up, a stored U0080-00 is simply cleared. Volvo and Mack trucks use U008088 for CAN faults on datalink 7 at engine or aftertreatment module. Effects range from none to a transmission warning.
c: Bus F wiring chafed on a crossmember or bracket
Inline connector of Bus F not fully latched
Module on Bus F starts communicating too late after wake-up (stored code only)
Supply or ground fault of a Bus F module
s: Transmission or other warning messages in the cluster
Stored code without any noticeable fault
Telematics or app services report errors

U0081.d: U0081 marks Vehicle Communication Bus F as working but unreliable: frames arrive damaged, late or not at all from time to time, while the network as a whole stays up. No manufacturer documents U0081 publicly. Jaguar Land Rover shows how close the boundary is by recording invalid serial data on Bus F as failure type 81 of U0080 instead. Where Bus F is FlexRay, as on Audi's A6/A7 link to the transmission, each transceiver can check its own output: NXP's TJA1081B raises a bus error flag whenever the level it reads back on the BP/BM pair disagrees with the data it is sending, which happens with collisions, interference or a damaged pair. CARB asks for communication errors on digital signals to be detected, not only total loss. Intermittent contacts and moisture are the usual culprits.
c: Loose or corroded contact in a Bus F connector
Twisted pair of Bus F damaged or untwisted near a repair
Electrical interference from an aftermarket device
Module software that handles bus timing incorrectly
s: Functions on Bus F drop out briefly and return
Several modules store communication codes at the same time

U0082.d: U0082 reports an interrupted (+) wire on Vehicle Communication Bus F. Where Bus F is FlexRay, as Audi's A6/A7 bulletin suggests, this is bus plus (BP); in a CAN it would be CAN-High. FlexRay signals by the voltage difference between BP and BM, and NXP's TJA1081B only accepts activity once that difference exceeds a threshold of about 150 to 300 mV. Nodes beyond a broken BP therefore receive a reduced or missing signal, while the sender keeps seeing its own output intact on its side of the break, so its bus error flag stays quiet. The fault shows as partners that stop answering. No manufacturer documents U0082 publicly; Volvo and Mack trucks fold line breaks on their datalink 7 CAN into U008088. Check BP continuity connector by connector.
c: (+) wire of Bus F broken at a flex point or after chafing
Terminal of the (+) wire pushed back in a connector
Inline connector of Bus F not fully latched
s: Modules on the far side of the break no longer respond
Warnings that come and go with vehicle movement

U0083.d: U0083 means the (+) line of Vehicle Communication Bus F is held too low, normally by a short to ground. On FlexRay, which Audi links to Bus F, the line is bus plus (BP). NXP builds its TJA1081B to survive such a short and lists short-circuit detection on the bus lines among its diagnostic features; with BP at ground instead of its idle level of roughly half the 5 V supply, the difference to BM no longer swings the way the receivers expect. If Bus F is a CAN, a grounded CAN-High stops dominant bits, which onsemi found blocks the bus. Among Volvo's typical triggers for the truck code U008088 is CAN-High grounded. No manufacturer documents U0083 itself. With the battery disconnected, measure the (+) wire to chassis.
c: (+) wire of Bus F chafed through to body metal
Harness pinched by a trim panel or bracket
Faulty transceiver pulling the (+) line to ground
s: Several functions on Bus F fail at once
Many lost-communication codes in other modules

U0084.d: U0084 is set when the (+) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus F carries too much voltage, typically after contact with battery power. For a FlexRay Bus F, as in Audi's A6/A7, the wire is bus plus (BP); NXP rates the bus pins of its TJA1081B to withstand shorts to 14, 24 and 48 V and caps the output current at about 72 mA, so the hardware usually survives while signal levels are wrong. If Bus F is a CAN, CAN-High at supply voltage is one of the faults that may leave traffic running: onsemi still saw frames pass, and NXP counts it among hidden failures that only a diagnosing transceiver reports. Volvo lists shorts of CAN-High to power behind its truck code U008088. No manufacturer documents U0084 itself. Look for wiring touching a feed or a wet connector.
c: (+) wire of Bus F touching a battery or ignition feed
Water in a connector bridging the bus to a supply pin
Faulty aftermarket wiring tapped into the bus
s: Often no symptom, code found during a scan
Sporadic dropouts of functions on Bus F

U0085.d: U0085 points to a severed (-) conductor on Vehicle Communication Bus F, that is bus minus (BM) where Bus F is FlexRay, as in the Audi A6/A7, or CAN-Low in a CAN. How hard the break hits depends on the topology. FlexRay may run two independent channels, and Wikipedia notes that traffic can carry on with reduced bandwidth when one of them fails, so a break on one channel may cost little more than redundancy. In a single-channel layout every node beyond the break goes silent. Transceivers cannot see an open wire directly, as NXP explains for CAN; the module infers it from missing frames. Volvo's truck bulletin KC-2079 also lists open CAN-Low as a trigger of U008088. No manufacturer documents U0085 itself. Check continuity of the (-) wire through every connector.
c: (-) wire of Bus F broken after chafing or repeated flexing
Spread or corroded terminal of the (-) wire
Poor earlier repair splice in the bus pair
s: Individual modules on Bus F stop responding
Code present with little or no effect when a second channel takes over

U0086.d: U0086 says the (-) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus F sits too low, usually shorted to ground. On a FlexRay Bus F, as in the Audi A6/A7, that wire is bus minus (BM). At rest both FlexRay lines float near half the transceiver supply, and NXP specifies a near-zero difference between them in idle. A grounded BM leaves BP well above it, a permanent positive difference that receivers read as DATA_1 instead of idle, which disturbs wake-up and frame recognition across the cluster. On a CAN the comparable fault, CAN-Low to ground, is usually harmless for traffic and stays hidden unless a transceiver with bus diagnosis reports it, as NXP describes. No manufacturer documents U0086 publicly. Measure the (-) wire to chassis with the battery disconnected.
c: (-) wire of Bus F chafed against body metal
Harness trapped under a seat rail or trim
Transceiver of one module pulling the (-) line to ground
s: Modules on Bus F fail to wake or drop out
On CAN layouts often no noticeable symptom

U0087.d: U0087 stands for a (-) wire on Vehicle Communication Bus F pulled too high, most often through contact with battery voltage. If Bus F is the FlexRay of an Audi A6/A7, the wire is bus minus (BM); held above BP, it creates a constant negative difference that receivers treat as DATA_0, so the channel looks permanently busy and no node can place a frame. NXP's TJA1081B tolerates such a short on its bus pins without damage. On a CAN, CAN-Low at supply voltage cannot be pulled down for a dominant bit; onsemi and NXP both describe the bus as blocked. Volvo includes a short of CAN-Low to power among the causes of its truck code U008088. No manufacturer documents U0087 itself. With ignition on, a (-) wire near battery voltage confirms the fault.
c: (-) wire of Bus F shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Moisture in a connector linking the (-) pin to a supply
Internally shorted transceiver in one module
s: All functions on Bus F fail together
Warning lamps and messages from several systems

U0088.t: Vehicle Communication Bus F (-) Shorted to Bus F (+)
U0088.d: With U0088 the two conductors of Vehicle Communication Bus F are bridged to each other. Signalling on both FlexRay and CAN rests on the difference between the wires, so with them joined there is none: a FlexRay receiver such as NXP's TJA1081B sees a difference below its activity threshold and treats the line as idle, while every sending node reads back something other than what it transmits and sets its bus error flag. On a single channel this ends all exchange on Bus F, which is why modules elsewhere then log the silent partners as lost. Volvo names a short between CAN-High and CAN-Low as one cause of U008088 on its truck datalink 7. For CAN, onsemi's bench tests likewise show a bridged pair stopping all traffic. Isolate sections by unplugging connectors while measuring between the wires.
c: Bus F pair crushed so both wires touch
Water or corrosion bridging both wires in a splice or connector
Transceiver with an internal short between its bus pins
s: Complete loss of the functions served by Bus F
Lost-communication codes for several modules

U0089.d: U0089 covers Vehicle Communication Bus G as a whole, the seventh of the network letters that SAE leaves for manufacturers to assign. No manufacturer documents U0089 publicly, and neither a service bulletin nor an OBD table names a network for the letter G, so the bus behind it can only be identified from the service information for the specific car. Such umbrella codes rest on CARB's demand that a digital input which stops communicating be recognised and given its own fault code. The code says only that the module has a problem with Bus G as a whole; the neighbouring codes narrow it down: U008A for unreliable traffic, U008B to U0091 for single-wire faults, U0079 for a module that switched itself off the bus. What the driver notices depends on which systems share Bus G.
c: Damaged wiring or connector on Bus G
Supply or ground fault of a module on Bus G
Internal fault of a module disturbing the bus
s: Functions handled by Bus G modules fail or act erratically
Several modules hold communication codes

U008A.d: U008A means Vehicle Communication Bus G still carries traffic, but not cleanly. No manufacturer documents U008A publicly. If Bus G is a CAN, every node counts its own transmit and receive errors; Wikipedia describes that a node turns error passive once a counter exceeds 127 and leaves the bus only after the transmit count passes 255, which is the bus-off case coded as U0079. U008A covers the range below that, with repeated frames, delays and occasional corrupted data. Signal quality is a frequent reason: Texas Instruments recommends unterminated stubs of no more than about 0.3 m on high-speed CAN, because reflections in longer branches, such as from tapped-in accessories, can distort bits at the sampling point. CARB requires communication errors to be detected alongside total loss.
c: Loose or corroded contact in a Bus G connector
Aftermarket device tapped into Bus G with a long branch
Termination of Bus G missing or out of tolerance
s: Short dropouts of functions on Bus G
Messages that appear briefly and vanish

U008B.d: On Vehicle Communication Bus G, U008B flags an open (+) conductor, which on a CAN means CAN-High. No manufacturer documents U008B publicly. A useful clue comes from the termination: Texas Instruments describes a high-speed CAN line ending in a 120-ohm resistor at each end, which a meter across CAN-High and CAN-Low sees as about 60 ohms. With CAN-High broken, only the resistor on the measuring side remains in the loop and the reading rises to roughly 120 ohms; on the other side of the break it is the same, which helps locate the gap. Meanwhile the far nodes miss part of the signal and fall silent or drop frames, and as NXP notes, transceivers do not report open lines themselves. Check the (+) wire through every connector of Bus G.
c: (+) wire of Bus G broken at a hinge, seat or door passage
Terminal of the (+) wire pushed out of its connector cavity
s: Some modules on Bus G not reachable with a scan tool
Intermittent faults that change with temperature or movement

U008C.d: U008C indicates a (+) wire on Vehicle Communication Bus G pulled too low, usually grounded. No manufacturer documents U008C publicly. On a high-speed CAN the (+) wire is CAN-High, which Texas Instruments describes as rising from about 2.5 V to 3.5 V for every dominant bit while CAN-Low drops to 1.5 V, giving the 2 V difference receivers decode. A grounded CAN-High cannot rise, so no node can assert a dominant bit; onsemi saw transmission fail outright in this state. Each failed frame raises the sender's error counter, so the same module may also log U0079 once it goes bus off. The whole network falls silent and other networks log the missing modules. With the battery disconnected, CAN-High showing only a few ohms to chassis confirms the short.
c: (+) wire of Bus G chafed against body metal
Harness pinched by a screw, panel or seat
Defective transceiver holding CAN-High to ground
s: All modules on Bus G drop out together
Many warnings and lost-communication codes at once

U008D.d: U008D is stored when the (+) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus G carries excessive voltage, from a short to battery or another supply. No manufacturer documents U008D publicly. On a high-speed CAN this concerns CAN-High, and traffic often continues: NXP lists the fault among those that stay hidden unless a transceiver with bus diagnosis catches it, and onsemi saw frames still pass. The repair needs a second look, though. Texas Instruments warns that a bus wire in contact with a 24 V line drives the transceiver's short-circuit current through the terminating resistor and can burn out a 1/4 W part. After removing the short, measure the resistance between CAN-High and CAN-Low again; about 120 instead of 60 ohms means one terminator, often inside a module, has been damaged.
c: (+) wire of Bus G touching a battery or 24 V feed
Water in a connector linking the bus to a supply pin
Terminating resistor damaged by an earlier short
s: Often no symptom, code found during a scan
Sporadic dropouts on Bus G after a wiring fault

U008E.d: With U008E the (-) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus G is open, CAN-Low where Bus G is a CAN. U008E is not documented publicly by any maker. Seen with an oscilloscope, CAN-Low beyond the break no longer drops from about 2.5 V to the 1.5 V that Texas Instruments gives for a dominant bit, so receivers there get only the CAN-High half of the signal and less margin against noise. Termination suffers as well: TI recommends that the 120-ohm resistors sit at the line ends and not in a node, because a disconnected node takes its terminator with it, and a broken CAN-Low can cut one of them off in the same way. Transceivers do not flag the open line themselves, as NXP points out. Checking resistance between the wires from both sides of the vehicle helps locate the gap.
c: (-) wire of Bus G broken at a flex point
Bus G connector not fully latched or a terminal backed out
s: Modules beyond the break respond only sometimes
Code comes and goes with temperature or road shocks

U008F.d: U008F is the low-voltage fault on the (-) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus G, which on a CAN means CAN-Low touching ground. No public manufacturer document uses U008F. On a high-speed CAN this is one of the faults that let messages through: onsemi measured working transmission with distorted levels, and the node drew about 72 instead of 65 mA because a terminating resistor now drains to ground. NXP lists CAN-Low to ground among the shorts its TJA1043 reports although traffic continues, and warns that such tolerated faults raise current draw and spoil electromagnetic compatibility. A car can therefore run normally with U008F stored. With the battery disconnected, a (-) wire showing near zero ohms to chassis confirms it.
c: (-) wire chafed through to the body or a bracket
Moisture in a connector bridging the (-) pin to a ground pin
Damaged transceiver in one module pulling the line down
s: Often no noticeable effect, code found during a scan
Sporadic dropouts on Bus G

U0090.d: U0090 is logged when Bus G's (-) wire is pulled up, typically by a short to a supply feed; in CAN terms this is the CAN-Low line. U0090 is not described in any public manufacturer source. Unlike a grounded CAN-Low, this fault normally stops the bus: onsemi found transmission impossible with CAN-Low at 12 V, and NXP rates it as a short under which communication fails. The search is easier once you know which feed is involved. Nissan's CAN diagnostic chart measures each bus wire to ground both with the key off and with it on, and keeps separate entries for shorts to battery and to an ignition feed. A fault that is present only with the ignition on points to a switched circuit, one that persists with the key off to a permanent battery feed.
c: (-) wire shorted to a permanent battery feed
(-) wire touching a switched ignition feed in the harness
Retrofitted equipment spliced into the bus wires
s: All modules on Bus G stop responding at once
Warning lamps and lost-communication codes in several systems
Fault may come and go with the ignition switch position

U0091.t: Vehicle Communication Bus G (-) Shorted to Bus G (+)
U0091.d: U0091 closes the Bus G block: the (-) and (+) wires of Vehicle Communication Bus G are joined, on a CAN CAN-Low to CAN-High. No manufacturer has published a use of U0091. With both wires bridged no voltage difference can form, so a high-speed CAN carries no frames at all. Transceiver self-diagnosis is of little help here; NXP notes that its TJA1043 reports shorts to ground and supply but not a short between the two bus wires, so the module concludes the fault from the silence. Measuring is quick: Nissan gives about 60 ohms between the wires as normal and lists zero ohms for a short between them. To find the spot, unplug modules and harness sections one at a time until the reading returns to normal.
c: Bus wires crushed together, e.g. under a seat rail or panel
Corroded or wet splice bridging both wires
Internal short in one module's transceiver
s: Complete loss of the functions served by Bus G
Scan tool cannot reach any module on Bus G

U0092.d: U0092 stands for Vehicle Communication Bus H as a whole, the eighth network letter in SAE's list. Which network a carmaker files under H is not stated in any public bulletin or OBD table, and no manufacturer documents U0092 itself; the service data of the specific model has to tell. The code reflects CARB's rule that a digital input which stops communicating must be detected and get its own fault code. U0092 does not narrow the fault down; U0093 stands for degraded traffic, U0094 to U009A for single-wire faults and U007A for a module that went bus off. Supply problems can look the same: Nissan observes that below about 10 V modules drop off the bus one by one at different voltages, and that a few main fuses feed many modules at once. Check battery and feeds first.
c: Wiring or connector fault on Bus H
Weak battery or voltage drop so modules fall off the bus
Blown main fuse or bad feed supplying several Bus H modules
s: Several functions handled by Bus H modules fail together
Problems worse at cranking or with a low battery

U0093.d: U0093 says Vehicle Communication Bus H works, but with too many errors or too much delay. U0093 appears in no public manufacturer document. Unlike the wire codes U0094 to U009A, nothing is open or shorted; the signals are merely unreliable. A frequent background is a ground offset between modules. Texas Instruments describes the potential difference between the grounds of sender and receiver as common-mode voltage, with ISO 11898 requiring tolerance from -2 to +7 V, and lists erratic resets, lock-ups and corrupted data as results when it is exceeded. In a car this happens with loose or corroded ground points. On a CAN, each corrupted frame triggers an error frame and a repeat, which costs bandwidth long before any node is shut off.
c: Loose or corroded ground point of a Bus H module
Interference coupled in from nearby loads or retrofitted devices
s: Functions on Bus H drop out briefly and recover
Modules restart or freeze sporadically

U0094.d: U0094 reports that the (+) wire of Bus H is interrupted, CAN-High where Bus H is a CAN. No manufacturer documents U0094 publicly. How much the break matters depends on the kind of CAN. A fault-tolerant low-speed CAN up to 125 kBd, built with transceivers such as NXP's TJA1055, keeps receiving differentially with a broken CANH wire, and the chip's error output toggles only if the gap separates the sending node from the listening one, so the module may see the fault only now and then. A high-speed CAN loses the far nodes. For locating it, Nissan's chart separates a break in the main line from one in a branch to a single module, judged by the resistance and voltages measured at the diagnostic socket.
c: Broken (+) wire, e.g. at a hinge or flexing harness section
Terminal pushed out of a connector
s: Single modules on Bus H not reachable
Fault appears intermittently or with movement

U0095.d: U0095 indicates that the (+) wire of Vehicle Communication Bus H is held too low, usually through a ground short (CAN-High on a CAN). No public manufacturer document uses U0095. The effect depends heavily on the bus type. On a high-speed CAN, onsemi found that no frame can be sent with CAN-High grounded; the stuck node kept retrying in short bursts, its transmit line active only about 2 % of the time, and the supply current fell to about 50 mA. Repeated failures end in bus off, which would add U007A. NXP's fault-tolerant TJA1055, by contrast, copes with a grounded CANH without even leaving differential reception. The same code can therefore mean a dead network on one car and an unnoticed defect on another.
c: Harness pinched during a repair or installation
Faulty transceiver holding the (+) line low
s: On high-speed CAN: all Bus H modules fail together
On fault-tolerant CAN: little or no noticeable effect

U0096.d: U0096 is set once excessive voltage appears on the Bus H (+) wire, as from a short to battery or to the module supply; on a CAN this is CAN-High. U0096 is not documented by any manufacturer in public. On a high-speed CAN such a short often leaves traffic running; NXP lists CAN-High to battery and to the 5 V supply among hidden failures. A fault-tolerant low-speed CAN reacts in steps. NXP's TJA1055 first switches to single-wire reception over CANH after a time-out and, if the line stays high, moves on to CANL and shuts off its CANH driver; the delays keep radio interference from triggering it. When the short is gone, the chip returns to normal by itself. Look for chafing against a supply wire or water in a connector.
c: Water in a connector bridging the (+) pin to a supply pin
Faulty transceiver driving the (+) line high
s: Often no symptom, code found during a scan
Sporadic dropouts on Bus H

U0097.d: U0097 points to an open (-) wire on Vehicle Communication Bus H, CAN-Low if Bus H is a CAN. The code is absent from public manufacturer documents. Effects vary: NXP's fault-tolerant TJA1055 keeps receiving differentially with a broken CANL, while on a high-speed CAN the nodes beyond the break lose part of their signal. Sleep behaviour matters too; NXP designed the wake detection of its TJA1043 so that a broken CAN-Low does not wake the network while it is going to sleep. A car with U0097 should still be checked for battery drain. To locate the break, Nissan advises splitting a harness with inline connectors into sections, testing one at a time and fitting a 120-ohm resistor in place of the terminating module.
c: Spread or bent terminal losing contact
Poor earlier repair or splice in the (-) wire
s: Modules beyond the break respond only sometimes
Code with little effect on fault-tolerant layouts

U0098.d: U0098 is stored once the Bus H (-) wire, CAN-Low on a CAN, sits too low, normally from a short to ground. No manufacturer has made a use of U0098 public. With fault-tolerant low-speed CAN the short unfolds in stages: the receive pin of NXP's TJA1055 initially stays dominant without pause; once a time-out has passed, the chip disables its CANL driver and goes on receiving single-wire over CANH. Once the short is removed, normal levels return and the chip goes back to differential mode. Communication thus survives, but with less noise margin. A high-speed CAN also keeps running in this state, as onsemi measured, though with distorted levels. A resistance check of that wire against chassis, battery disconnected, confirms it.
c: Harness pinched by a fastener or panel
Faulty transceiver pulling the (-) line to ground
s: Usually no noticeable symptom
Occasional errors on Bus H in electrically noisy conditions

U0099.d: U0099 describes a (-) wire on Vehicle Communication Bus H held at too high a voltage, most often through contact with battery power; on a CAN that wire is CAN-Low. Nothing public from a manufacturer covers U0099. NXP's data sheet for the fault-tolerant low-speed TJA1055 separates two cases: CAN-Low at battery voltage is recognised once the line stays above a comparator threshold for a set time, after which the chip turns off its CANL driver and listens over CANH alone; CAN-Low at the 5 V supply is tolerated without leaving differential mode. Recovery happens automatically after a run of recessive bits. On a high-speed CAN, by contrast, onsemi found that CAN-Low at 12 V blocks all transmission, so U007A for bus off may follow.
c: (-) wire shorted to a battery feed
Corrosion or water in a connector between (-) and a supply pin
Faulty transceiver driving the (-) line high
s: On high-speed CAN: Bus H goes silent
On fault-tolerant CAN: degraded but working communication

U009A.t: Vehicle Communication Bus H (-) Shorted to Bus H (+)
U009A.d: U009A means the two wires of Vehicle Communication Bus H touch each other, on a CAN CAN-Low against CAN-High. No manufacturer documentation of U009A is public. On a high-speed CAN this ends all traffic; onsemi's bench node could not send and drew about 47 mA against roughly 65 mA on a healthy bus. A fault-tolerant low-speed CAN can live with it: the TJA1055 from NXP initially reads the bus as constantly dominant, and only once a time-out has run does it disable its CANL driver and carry on single-wire, returning to differential operation once the wires are separated. So on some cars U009A comes with a dead network, on others only with a stored code. Separating harness sections while measuring resistance between the wires narrows down the spot.
c: Wet or corroded splice joining both wires
Internal short in a module's transceiver
s: On high-speed CAN: complete loss of Bus H functions
Lost-communication codes for several modules

U009B.d: U009B addresses Vehicle Communication Bus I overall, the ninth network letter. Which network sits behind I is left to the manufacturer and not named in any public bulletin; U009B itself is not documented publicly by any maker. CARB requires that a lost digital input be detected with a separate code, which is the role of this group. Bus I has no wire-level codes of its own in the list, so U009B must also cover line faults. One cause is easy to overlook: a single module with a fault in its controller can hold the bus dominant. NXP's TJA1042 and TJA1051 transceivers counter this with a time-out that switches off the transmitter, so that the remaining nodes keep talking. Unplugging modules one by one finds such a node.
c: Open or shorted wire on Bus I
One module holding the bus dominant
Missing supply or ground at a Bus I module
s: Functions of Bus I modules fail or act erratically
Lost-communication codes in several modules

U009C.d: U009C reports that Vehicle Communication Bus I carries traffic, but not at the quality the module expects. U009C has not been documented in public by any manufacturer. The causes lie in signal integrity rather than a hard fault. Texas Instruments ties the possible bus length to the data rate, roughly 40 m when running at 1 Mbit/s and 100 m at half that rate, and names cable bandwidth and intersymbol interference as the limits; repairs with long added wire or untwisted cable eat into that margin. TI cites the standard's twisted pair with 120 ohms impedance. CAN detects such distortion as protocol errors: Wikipedia explains that after five identical bits the sender adds one of the inverse value, and six identical bits in a row count as an error, prompting a repeat.
c: Repair with untwisted or overly long wire
s: Brief dropouts of functions on Bus I
Delayed reactions of displays or controls

U009D.d: U009D covers Vehicle Communication Bus J in general, the tenth letter, and like I it has only this code and a performance code in the list, so open or shorted lines also end up here. No public bulletin names the network behind J, and no manufacturer documents U009D publicly. CARB's requirement for a separate code when a digital input stops communicating is the regulatory basis. Faults that appear after parking deserve attention. Nissan points out that with the key off and the network asleep both CAN wires read 0 V, so voltages must be measured with the bus awake. NXP notes that a single frame at a 500 kbit/s rate may not be enough to wake its TJA1043 reliably, and asks for two in a row. A module that wakes late can therefore look like a bus fault.
c: Open or shorted wire on Bus J
Module not waking or waking late
Supply or ground fault at a Bus J module
s: Functions of Bus J modules missing after start
Lost-communication codes, sometimes only after parking

U009E.d: U009E flags unreliable traffic on Vehicle Communication Bus J without a total loss. No manufacturer publishes a use of U009E. Interference is a likely source. Texas Instruments names fluorescent lamps, switching power supplies and motor drives as typical emitters of common-mode noise that couples onto bus lines, and explains that a receiver without good rejection may take it for data. A twisted pair and differential signalling keep this in check, so opened twists or retrofitted electronics near the harness are suspects. NXP adds that tolerated wiring faults also worsen electromagnetic behaviour. Where messages go unacknowledged, Wikipedia notes that nodes often resend them repeatedly, which can drive them into the error-passive state.
c: Interference from nearby loads or retrofitted electronics
Bus wires untwisted at a repair
Loose contact in a Bus J connector
s: Short dropouts on Bus J, often with certain loads switched on
Warnings that appear briefly and clear

U0100.d: U0100 is stored by a module that has stopped hearing the engine or powertrain controller, ECM/PCM A; a second engine controller has its own code, U0115. Usually the transmission controller logs it, often alongside other listeners. GM's 2019 ten-speed TCM rates it Type A (MIL on the first trip) and holds it back while its own bus-off code U0073 is active; GM's 2016 tables set it once frame $0C9 is absent in 12 of 12 one-second samples at 11–32 V (Type B). Ford's 2012 summary has the TCM switch on the MIL at once, because engine speed and torque are gone. The gearbox then falls back to a limp-home program; GM bulletin 08-07-30-021H traces such cases to harness terminals, bus wiring and corroded connectors.
c: ECM/PCM without power or ground (fuse, main relay, ground point)
Damaged CAN lines or loose, corroded terminals between ECM and TCM
Weak battery or voltage dip during cranking (history code)
ECM internally faulty or software not running
s: MIL on, often several U codes in other modules
Transmission stuck in a substitute gear or harsh shifts
Gauges for engine speed or temperature drop out
Engine may stall or not crank

U0101.d: U0101 means the transmission controller has dropped off the bus as seen by another node, mostly the engine controller. GM's 2019 truck ECMs watch eight TCM frames, most of them at 500 ms intervals, and set the code as Type A after battery and run voltage have exceeded 11 V for 3 s, provided U0073 is not active; GM's electronic range selector logs it as Type B after 1 s, the hybrid processor in the same table after 5 s. Ford's 2023 diesel summary flags the code when the TCM's master frame has been absent beyond 1 s, while the 2012 summary checks it only where the TCM is a separate unit. U0402 covers implausible TCM data, U0302 a software mismatch. Typical effects: dead gear display, fixed gear, MIL.
c: TCM without power or ground (fuse, relay, connector)
Spread or corroded terminals at the transmission harness connector
Chafed or open CAN lines to the TCM
TCM internally faulty, overheated or not programmed
s: MIL on, transmission warning in the cluster
Gear indicator blank or flashing
Transmission locked in one gear
Scan tool cannot reach the TCM

U0102.t: Lost Communication With Transfer Case Control Module
U0102.d: U0102 is logged when the transfer case control module, which shifts between two- and four-wheel drive and between high and low range, stops sending. GM's 2025 engine controllers expect frame $035 and fail it when gaps exceed 425 ms within a 5 s window; the code is Type C, emissions-neutral and without MIL. The earlier two-mode hybrid trucks (2012 table) used Type B with 500 ms detection between 10 and 18 V. Ford's 2023 diesel controllers allow 5 s before flagging the TCCM. Bulletin 08-07-30-021H lists U0102 among GMLAN codes caused by shared bus faults. The driver mostly sees a 4WD warning and a transfer case left in its last range; engine and gearbox keep running. U0403 covers implausible data from the same module.
c: Transfer case module without power or ground
Water or corrosion in the module connector (often mounted low on the frame)
Damaged CAN lines to the transfer case module
s: 4WD or AWD warning, range selection ignored
Transfer case stays in its last mode
Usually no MIL

U0103.t: Lost Communication With Gear Shift Control Module A
U0103.d: U0103 points to gear shift control module A, the electronic selector (lever, rotary knob or buttons) in shift-by-wire cars. GM's 2025 engine controllers talk to it over a LIN line and set the code as Type B once its response is absent for at least 500 ms. Stellantis calls it Electric Gear Shift Module: on the Ram 1500 (case S2208000168) U0103-00 appears with U11E3 and U1267 when the rotary selector will not leave Park, and new ESM software is the cure. Ford's Mach-E TSB 21-2405 stores U0103:87 in a secondary OBD module with a wrench lamp and Shift System Fault, fixed by reprogramming; for Explorer/Aviator, SSM 49329 blames loose grounds G210/G214. U0404 is the invalid-data sibling.
c: Selector module software fault (update available from the maker)
Loose ground or blown fuse feeding the selector
Open or shorted LIN/CAN line to the selector
s: Service Shifter or Shift System Fault message
Selector stuck in Park or gear changes refused
MIL or wrench lamp on
Intermittent no-crank

U0104.t: Lost Communication With Cruise Control Module
U0104.d: U0104 names the cruise control module, today usually the radar unit of adaptive cruise control that sends speed and distance requests to the engine. GM's 2019 truck ECMs check its frames $2CB and $2CD, treat gaps beyond 500 ms that persist for 3 s as a failure and classify the result as Type C, emissions-neutral and without MIL; detection pauses while the bus-off code of the carrying bus (U0073, U0074) is active. Saab's 2011 9-4x code list carries U0104 with sub-codes for short to ground, invalid data, wrong message counter and checksum error. While the code is active, cruise or distance control switches off or cannot be armed; driving and emissions are unaffected. U0405 covers implausible data from this module.
c: Radar/cruise module without power or with a wet, loose connector (front bumper area)
Front-end damage or bumper repair affecting module or wiring
Damaged CAN lines to the module
s: Cruise or adaptive cruise unavailable, warning message
Forward collision alert may switch off as well
No MIL

U0105.t: Lost Communication With Fuel Injector Control Module
U0105.d: U0105 concerns a separate fuel injector control module that drives the injectors on command of the engine controller. GM's 2005 Duramax 6.6 L (LLY) received a status message from this injector driver via CAN (J1939) whose toggle bit must flip every 20 ms; if it stalls for three updates, 30 failures in 50 checks give a Type B code. On the 2019 Corvette LT5 the ECM watches frame $1EA from a dedicated injector module and, after 10 s without it, logs U0105 as Type A on the first trip. Losing this link usually means misfire, power reduction or a stall, since the ECM can no longer confirm injection. U0406 covers invalid data and U0306 a software mismatch with the same module.
c: Injector module supply low or missing (fuse, relay, battery voltage)
Loose or corroded connector or damaged CAN lines to the module
Injector module internally faulty (heat, power stage)
s: MIL on
Misfire, rough running or reduced power
Engine stalls or will not start

U0106.t: Lost Communication With Glow Plug Control Module 1
U0106.d: U0106 reports that glow plug control module 1 of a diesel engine no longer communicates. In Ford's 2023 diesel summary (6.7 L and 3.0 L) the GPCM is declared lost after 5 s of silence. GM's 2015 Cruze diesel table fails it when no GPCM message arrives for 0.25 s over a 10 s test (Type B); GM's 2018 diesel table also lets the GPCM report that it misses ECM frames $C9, $4C1 or $4F1 and sets U0106 after 11 s as Type B over two trips. Isuzu's N-Series bulletin SB18-N-001A (4HK1, 2011–2018) links the MIL with U0106 to water running down the glow plug harness into the GPCM plug; sealed terminals fix it. Expect hard cold starts, white smoke and an unreliable wait-to-start lamp.
c: Water or corrosion in the glow plug module connector or harness
Module supply fuse, relay or ground faulty
Damaged CAN lines to the glow plug module
Glow plug module internally faulty (overtemperature, driver)
s: MIL on
Long cranking or no start when cold
White smoke after cold start
Wait-to-start lamp behaves oddly

U0107.t: Lost Communication With Throttle Actuator A Control Module
U0107.d: U0107 targets a stand-alone throttle actuator control (TAC) module, as used before throttle control moved into the engine controller. In GM's 2004 and 2005 truck tables (4.3–6.0 L and 8.1 L) the PCM and TAC module traded data over a dedicated serial link; the PCM declared a gap after 18.75 ms and the TAC module after 25 ms. Each missing or corrupt message added 10 to a counter, each valid one took 1 away, and 500 ms without valid data produced a Type A code with MIL on the first trip. Without this link the electronic throttle is no longer cross-checked, so the engine usually runs with restricted power. U0408 covers invalid TAC data and U0308 a software mismatch.
c: Open, shorted or chafed serial data lines between PCM and TAC module
TAC module supply or ground faulty
Corroded connector at the TAC module
s: MIL on
Reduced engine power, throttle barely opens
Idle unstable or engine stalls

U0108.t: Lost Communication With Alternative Fuel Control Module
U0108.d: U0108 covers a separate controller for an alternative fuel such as LPG or CNG, added to an engine that otherwise runs a gasoline control strategy. Roush CleanTech's fourth-generation propane systems for Ford E- and F-Series trucks (2016–2018) are a documented user: the PCM expects CAN traffic from the system's Smart Relay Module and stores U0108 when those messages keep missing. Roush lists broken wiring between SRM and PCM, a blown fuse and lost power or ground at the SRM as causes, rough idle as a symptom. Under CARB rules, every electronic powertrain part that can raise emissions falls under comprehensive component monitoring, which makes the link emission-relevant. U0409 covers implausible data, U0309 a software mismatch.
c: Alternative fuel module without power or ground (fuse, relay)
Damaged CAN wiring between conversion module and PCM
Water or corrosion in the module connectors
s: MIL on
Rough idle or poor running on the alternative fuel
System may stay on or revert to gasoline

U0109.t: Lost Communication With Fuel Pump Control Module A
U0109.d: U0109 means the engine controller no longer hears fuel pump control module A, the electronics that drive the in-tank pump at variable speed. GM's 2019 Corvette LT5 table watches frames $1EB and $4D9 and sets the code after 10 s as Type B over two trips. Ford instead returns the module status on a duty-cycle line: its 2020–2023 gasoline summary flags feedback stuck at 0 % or 100 %, the 2023 diesel summary a pump duty below 5 % or above 95 % for 0.5 s. Ford TSB 16-0060 (Super Duty 6.2/6.8 L, MIL) replaces the module; GM PIC5655A (Volt 2011–2013) points to a loose feed on circuit 1540 or its fuse in the rear fuse block. Pump B has U016C. Expect hard starts, stalling or no start.
c: Loose fuse, relay or feed terminal supplying the pump module
Fuel pump module internally faulty (common on some trucks, replaced by bulletin)
Corroded connector or damaged wiring near the tank or frame
Engine controller software setting the code falsely
s: MIL on
Long cranking, stalling or no start
Hesitation under load from low fuel pressure

U010A.t: Lost Communication With Exhaust Gas Recirculation Control Module A
U010A.d: U010A is set when a stand-alone control module for exhaust gas recirculation A stops communicating. J2012 reserves this slot for engines whose EGR valve or EGR system is run by its own electronics on the bus rather than as a plain output of the engine controller; module B (U010B) would be a second such unit. No manufacturer documents U010A publicly, and the NHTSA bulletin index holds no entry for it. Because EGR lowers combustion temperature and NOx, CARB requires it to be monitored, so a lost EGR controller counts as emission-relevant. The nearest documented case is GM's boost control module (U010C), a smart actuator on a sensor bus. Expect EGR shut off and possibly reduced power. U040B covers invalid data.
c: EGR module A without power or ground
Heat-damaged wiring or connector near the exhaust side
Open or shorted bus lines to module A
s: MIL on
EGR deactivated, higher NOx
Possible reduced power mode

U010B.t: Lost Communication With Exhaust Gas Recirculation Control Module B
U010B.d: U010B names the second exhaust gas recirculation control module, B. Its existence implies an engine with two separately controlled EGR units, for example a high- and a low-pressure loop on a diesel or one unit per cylinder bank; which one is B is the maker's choice. The code itself only says that a node expecting periodic messages from module B no longer receives them. Neither a manufacturer document nor any entry in the NHTSA bulletin index names U010B. Diagnosis therefore follows the generic path: supply, ground and bus lines of module B first, then the module. If only B is silent while A (U010A) still talks, the fault sits in B's branch. Invalid data from B is U040C; CARB's EGR monitoring makes the code emission-relevant.
c: EGR module B without power or ground
Open or chafed bus branch to module B
Loose or heat-damaged connector at module B
s: MIL on
Second EGR path inactive, possible NOx increase
Module B not reachable with a scan tool

U010C.t: Lost Communication With Turbocharger/Supercharger Control Module A
U010C.d: U010C reports that turbocharger/supercharger control module A, in practice the electronic actuator that positions variable-geometry vanes or a wastegate, has gone silent. GM's 2017 small-diesel table (2.8 L Duramax and Cruze diesel) watches its frames $099 and $499 on a dedicated sensor bus and logs U010C once 10 s pass without them, rated Type B with two trips, provided that bus is not off (U0076). On FCA's 2015 Ram 2500/3500 with the 6.7 L Cummins, bulletin 09-005-22 reports MIL with U010C next to P003A, P00AF, P0046 or P0234 and replaces the turbo actuator under a warranty extension. Without the actuator boost cannot be steered, so the engine limits torque. U040D is the invalid-data sibling, U010D the second module.
c: Electronic turbo actuator faulty (heat, internal electronics)
Actuator supply, fuse or ground faulty
Heat-damaged connector or bus lines at the turbo
s: MIL on
Low power, reduced boost
Other boost codes such as P003A or P0234 stored

U010D.t: Lost Communication With Turbocharger/Supercharger Control Module B
U010D.d: U010D is the counterpart of U010C for a second charger control module, B. It applies to engines with two independently actuated chargers, such as sequential or twin turbo layouts, or a turbo plus an electronically controlled supercharger. Every node that expects cyclic data from module B logs the code once that traffic stops. No manufacturer documents U010D publicly and the NHTSA bulletin index lists it nowhere, so thresholds are unknown; GM's handling of module A (10 s, Type B, two trips) shows the usual pattern. With one charger uncontrolled, the engine controller typically caps boost and torque and may light the MIL, because boost control is emission-relevant under CARB. U040E covers invalid data from module B.
c: Charger module B without power or ground
Heat-damaged wiring or connector at the second charger
s: MIL on
Reduced power, second charger not used
Module B not reachable with a scan tool

U010E.t: Lost Communication With Reductant Control Module
U010E.d: U010E concerns the reductant control module that runs dosing, pump and heaters of a diesel SCR system with urea solution (DEF/AdBlue). GM's 2017 small-diesel table expects frame $092 and several $4Cx/$4Ex frames on bus B and, after 10 s of silence, records a Type A fault with MIL on the first trip, unless bus B is off (U0074). GM's 2025 central gateway judges its DEF controller differently: messages overdue by 2.5 periods for 6.5 s with battery above 7 V give Type B. For Ram 3500–5500 cab chassis with the 6.7 L Cummins (2012), bulletin 18-012-13 brought ECM software against needless MIL with U010E. Without the module no reductant is dosed, NOx rises and the inducement logic may cap speed. U040F covers invalid data.
c: Reductant module without power or ground (fuse, relay)
Corroded or wet connector at the tank-mounted module
Damaged bus lines along the frame to the module
Engine controller software setting the code falsely
s: MIL and DEF/AdBlue warning
Countdown to speed limit or restart block
Further SCR codes such as P20EE

U010F.t: Lost Communication With Air Conditioning Control Module
U010F.d: U010F is logged when the air conditioning control module stops reporting. J2012 keeps it apart from the HVAC control module (U0164): the A/C unit governs the refrigerant side, such as compressor clutch or electric compressor drive and pressures, while the HVAC module handles blower, flaps and temperature choice. Saab's 2011 code lists for the 9-5 and 9-4x carry U010F 00 next to U0164 00, which documents GM/Saab use. Neither list gives a threshold; Saab's general U0100–U02FF procedure applies, a missing state-of-health message at 9–16 V. The compressor then usually stays off, so cooling and demisting are lost; the engine is not affected and no MIL is expected. U040A covers invalid data from the same module.
c: A/C module without power or ground (fuse, connector)
Damaged bus lines to the A/C module
Condensate or water at module or connector
s: Air conditioning does not cool
Windows fog up, demisting weak
No MIL

U0110.t: Lost Communication With Drive Motor Control Module A
U0110.d: U0110 means drive motor control module A, the power electronics running the electric traction motor of a hybrid or EV, has stopped talking. Audi's TSB 2065538/1 (Q5 and A7 PHEV, 2019–2021) finds U011000 in the transmission controller after a brief 12 V dip trips the low-voltage monitor; a full bus sleep of about 20 minutes plus clearing codes cures it. Mazda bulletin 09-027-26 (CX-70/CX-90 PHEV) sees U0110 with U0100, U0115 and P0AB9 when water corrodes connector 3002-411 and READY fails in the cold. GM's 2025 gateway table sets it as Type B over two trips once a monitored frame lags 2.5 times its cycle across 6.5 s. Toyota flagged it on the 2017–2019 Highlander Hybrid. Expect no READY, red warnings or limp mode.
c: 12 V battery weak or voltage dip, inverter electronics drop off the bus
Water or corrosion in high- or low-voltage connectors of the drive system
Damaged CAN lines to the inverter
Drive motor control module internally faulty
s: Vehicle does not enter READY or will not start
Red drive-system or electrical warning
Electric drive unavailable, limp mode

U0111.t: Lost Communication With Battery Energy Control Module A
U0111.d: U0111 indicates that battery energy control module A, which measures cell voltages, temperatures and current of the high-voltage or 48 V battery, has dropped off the network. GM's 2018 Volt hybrid controller expects it on bus A and sets the code as Type B over two trips once messages have been absent for 5 s above 10.2 V; while it is pending, GM suspends pack voltage and current plausibility checks. GM PIC5829 (Volt 2011–2013) advises updating the BECM calibration instead of replacing it. In the Jeep Wrangler 4xe the battery module may fail to wake in severe cold, so the hybrid controller logs U0111-00 (case S2108000056). Land Rover reports 48 V MHEV BECMs going offline with MIL and lost start-stop. U0112 is module B.
c: Battery module software or calibration fault (update released)
Module fails to wake up in extreme cold or after a 12 V dip
Damaged CAN lines or connector at the battery pack
Battery energy control module internally faulty
s: MIL or service-hybrid/charging warning
No READY, electric drive or charging unavailable
Start-stop inoperative (mild hybrid)
12 V battery drained
