It is set when that unit's data reach the head unit or gateway but fail the plausibility, counter or checksum test; U0196 means contact is lost. In the Saab code lists GM published for 2011, that partner is the rear audio control module. Large GM SUVs with the U42 entertainment package show how faults look in practice: PIC6003A (2015 Tahoe, Suburban, Yukon) traced a rolling picture after switching to rear video to the centre stack, and 17-NA-378 (2017) swapped the media player for sound out of step with the film. No manufacturer documents U0497 itself. Rear screens, headphones or controls misbehave; no MIL.
c: Software of the rear unit or the head unit mishandling shared video or audio data
Internal fault of the rear entertainment unit or its media player
Supply, ground or bus connection fault at the rear unit
s: Rear screens show a rolling or missing picture
Rear headphones or controls without function
Front audio system usually keeps working

U0498.t: Invalid Data Received From Telephone Control Module
U0498.d: U0498 is logged when the telephone control module, the hands-free or Bluetooth unit, still sends frames but the head unit or body controller rejects their content. For Chrysler the lost-contact partner U0197 is the hands-free phone module (HFM); its bulletins 08-112-14 (2013-2015 Town & Country, Grand Caravan, Wrangler, Challenger and others) and 08-055-17 Rev. A (2012-2017 Journey, Charger, 300) restore dead Bluetooth or an HFM stuck at its loading screen with new module software. GM's Saab lists call the same partner the telephone control module. Where the phone unit also places emergency calls, the telematics code U0499 is the closer neighbour. No manufacturer documents U0498 publicly. Expect failed pairing or calls; no MIL.
c: Hands-free module software fault, cured by reprogramming
Module not booting fully or resetting, so its status values are invalid
Internal hardware fault of the telephone module
s: Bluetooth pairing or hands-free calls fail
Phone menu unavailable or stuck on a loading message

U0499.t: Invalid Data Received From Telematic Control Module
U0499.d: U0499 means the telematic control module, which carries the cellular modem for remote services and, in the EU, the 112 eCall required by Regulation 2015/758, sends data a receiver rejects. GM's 2025 tables (25OBDG04B) let the object calculation module EOCM3 check ARC, checksum or MAC on the telematics unit's precise positioning frames (heading, latitude, longitude): 6 of 10 faulty, judged over 8 s of a 10 s window, 9-16 V, partial network on, over 5 s after reset; Type D, no MIL, Super Cruise and adaptive cruise switch off. Stellantis (08-216-26, 2026 Charger; S268A000004, 2026 Cherokee) finds U0499-00 in the BCM, to be solved by TBM software, not by new parts. U0198 is lost contact.
c: Telematics module software sending faulty or unprotected frames, fixed by an update
Corrupted positioning data from the telematics unit (GPS antenna or receiver issues)
Internal fault of the telematics module
s: Super Cruise or adaptive cruise unavailable on GM vehicles
Connected services or an infotainment service message
Often no noticeable effect, code cannot be cleared

U049A.t: Invalid Data Received From Door Control Module A
U049A.d: U049A reports implausible data from door control module A, usually the driver's door: the unit that runs window lift, lock and mirror and reads the door switches. The body controller or gateway still hears it but rejects the content because a value is undefined, a counter jumps or a checksum fails. Chrysler's bulletin 08-061-12 for the 2005-2010 300 and Charger names the lost-contact partner U0199 the driver door module (DDM), with front windows and locks dead; a Yazaki patent shows how such a door unit relays CAN commands to its motors over a LIN sub-bus. No maker documents U049A publicly; U0501 to U0503 cover doors B to D. Expect a driver's door that ignores its switches or central locking; no MIL.
c: Chafed wires or loose pins in the door harness between body and door
Driver door module internally faulty, for example after water ingress
Wrong configuration or software after module replacement or retrofit
s: Driver window or mirror switches without function
Central locking ignores the driver's door

U049B.t: Invalid Data Received From Tachograph Module
U049B.d: U049B is set when the tachograph still transmits but its data are rejected. In trucks and buses EU Regulation 165/2014 has the device record speed, distance and driving times from a motion sensor, and units such as Continental VDO's DTCO 4.1a pass these values on through two CAN interfaces. Engine, transmission or body controllers then rely on the tachograph speed, so implausible frames matter beyond the logbook. Allison's tech tip TT7546EN (2000 and 3000 series, 2014) shows the effect: the calibration tool of a tachograph broadcast a road speed on the data link, the TCM saw speed without output-shaft rotation, stored N/V = 0 and fell back to the performance shift schedule until calibration C142 was flashed. No maker documents U049B publicly; U019A is lost contact.
c: Tachograph calibration or parameters not matching the vehicle, e.g. after a tyre or axle change
Faulty motion sensor or sensor wiring producing implausible speed values
Internal fault of the tachograph unit
s: Speedometer or tachograph speed missing or erratic
Cruise control, speed limiter or shift behaviour affected
Tachograph fault message

U049C.t: Invalid Data Received From Battery Charger Control Module A
U049C.d: U049C means the on-board charger, battery charger control module A, is heard on the bus but reports values the battery controller considers invalid. Ford's 2019 OBD summary for hybrid and plug-in vehicles has the BECM set it when the charger's CAN signal shows invalid states for 5 s; U019B is the same charger missing for 5 s. Ford calls this unit SOBDM or BCCM: it turns mains AC into high-voltage DC and also feeds the 12 V battery. Ford TSB 24-2445 (2023-2024 Mustang Mach-E) finds U049C in the BECM when DC fast charging fails with an error on the charger, and cures it by reprogramming the SOBDM. Charging is refused or stops while driving stays normal; Ford flags charger faults with the amber wrench lamp.
c: Charger module software reporting invalid states, cured by reprogramming
Software levels of charger and battery controller not matching
Internal fault of the on-board charger
s: High-voltage battery does not charge, error shown at the charging station
Charge fault message or wrench lamp in the cluster
Driving itself unaffected

U049D.t: Invalid Data Received From Glow Plug Control Module 2
U049D.d: U049D is logged when a controller, normally the engine control module, still hears from the second glow plug control module but cannot trust what it reports, for instance because a counter, checksum or plug status value is out of line. A second unit is found on diesels that split their glow plugs between two drivers. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; it mirrors U0407, which covers module 1. CARB 1968.2 obliges diesel OBD to verify that glow plugs respond to commands and draw proper current, a check the engine controller can only make with valid module data. A GM patent shows both controllers exchanging timed messages and flagging late ones as faults. U019C means the module is silent, U030B a software mismatch. Hard cold starts and a lit MIL are likely.
c: Corroded or loose connector or data wire at glow plug module 2
Supply voltage sagging while the glow plugs draw high current
Glow plug control module 2 internally faulty
Module or engine controller software not matched after replacement
s: Check engine or glow plug warning light on
Long cranking or misfire on cold starts
White smoke until the engine warms up

U049E.t: Invalid Data Received From Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Temperature Sensor
U049E.d: Direct ozone reduction (DOR) means a catalytic coating on the radiator, sold by BASF as PremAir, that turns ground-level ozone into oxygen while air flows through the core. CARB grants an emissions credit for it and, under section (e)(14) of 1968.2, wants OBD to watch the coating on cars that claim the credit; a temperature sensor on the radiator serves this purpose. U049E applies where that sensor reports over a data link and its messages arrive but fail plausibility. A hard-wired sensor instead uses P2567 to P2570. No manufacturer documents U049E publicly. U019D marks a sensor that has gone silent. The car drives normally; the result is a MIL, a suspended ozone catalyst check and possibly a failed inspection. Check wiring and the sensor before suspecting the radiator.
c: Damaged connector or wiring near the radiator (impact, corrosion)
Replacement radiator or sensor not matching the original DOR version
Sensor or engine controller software version not matching
s: Check engine light on without noticeable drivability change
Emissions inspection failed or readiness not set

U049F.t: Invalid Data Received From Transmission Range Control Module
U049F.d: The transmission range control module (TRCM) is the shift-by-wire actuator that physically moves the transmission between P, R, N and D after the driver selects a range electronically. U049F is stored by a module that receives TRCM messages whose content it rejects. Ford lists U049F in its 2014 OBD code chart without the MIL marker it gives to other codes such as U04A4. GM fitted a TRCM to the 2017 LaCrosse and XT5: under program 17075 a broken actuator gear left cars stuck in Park, and bulletin 16-NA-373 cured a calibration fault that lit the MIL with a transmission warning by reprogramming. U019E stands for lost contact, U031A for software mismatch, U04BD for the park lock module. Drivers may see a shift warning, a wrong gear display or a car that will not leave Park.
c: TRCM electronics or actuator position sensing faulty
Outdated TRCM calibration (GM 16-NA-373 calls for reprogramming)
Bus wiring or connector fault at the transmission-mounted module
Low or unstable battery voltage while shifting
s: Shift system or transmission service message
Vehicle stays in Park or does not engage the selected range
Gear indicator disagrees with the selected range

U04A0.t: Invalid Data Received From Engine Coolant Pump Control Module
U04A0.d: Engines with an electric main coolant pump carry a pump whose built-in electronics set the speed on request and send back status and fault information. Rheinmetall, for example, builds such pumps for main engine cooling with a LIN interface and extensive self-diagnosis, and Hella notes that electric pumps can stay off after a cold start so the engine warms faster. U04A0 means the engine controller still receives pump messages but finds speed, status or check values implausible. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. It matters for emissions because CARB 1968.2 expects coolant temperature to reach its closed-loop threshold in time, which depends on a correctly controlled pump. U019F and U0672 stand for lost contact. Watch the temperature gauge: the engine may run hot, limit power or keep the fan on.
c: Pump electronics faulty, often after overheating or coolant ingress
LIN or CAN wire or connector at the pump corroded or loose
Pump running dry or blocked (air in system, debris), reported as error state
Pump or engine controller software not matched after replacement
s: Check engine or coolant temperature warning
Engine runs hot or the cooling fan runs continuously
Reduced engine power to protect the engine

U04A1.t: Invalid Data Received From Hybrid/EV Battery Interface Control Module A
U04A1.d: U04A1 means the battery management controller keeps receiving messages from interface control module A, one of the slave boards that measure cell voltages and temperatures inside the high-voltage pack, but rejects their content as invalid. Volkswagen names the code: its on-car analysis list of 31 July 2024 for the ID.4 (2021–2024) files U04A1 together with U04A5 and U04A9 under the topic CMCe faults, stored in diagnostic address 8C, with an electrical system warning and no other relevant code there; dealers have to call the VW helpline before repairing. Silence from module A would be U01A0, a software mismatch U033A. Data errors of the battery energy control module itself are a separate code, U0412. Reduced power or no charging is possible until it is fixed.
c: Software issue in battery management or cell module controllers (VW ID.4 CMCe case, helpline first)
Interface control module A internally faulty
Loose or corroded connector on the pack-internal data link to module A
Weak 12 V battery disturbing the start-up of the battery electronics
s: Electrical system or high-voltage battery warning in the cluster
Reduced drive power
Charging interrupted or refused

U04A2.t: Invalid Data Received From Hybrid/EV Battery Interface Control Module B
U04A2.d: U04A2 covers the second interface board of the high-voltage pack, module B: its frames reach the battery controller but carry implausible content. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. The closest published logic is GM's 2016 hybrid table 16OBDG02, where the battery systems module talks to eight interface boards, A to H, over a serial UART daisy chain. If no data at all arrive from B for 5 s at more than 10.2 V, GM logs the lost-link sibling U01A1 as Type A, after first trying a loop-back test that bypasses the chain. U04A2 is the opposite case: the link exists, the content fails. CARB lists battery voltage sensors among the hybrid storage inputs that OBD has to check. Software issues fall under U033B.
c: Poor contact in the chain connection between interface boards A, B and C
Interface control module B internally faulty
Outdated calibration in the battery controller
s: Hybrid or EV system warning, MIL on plug-in hybrids
Electric range or power reduced

U04A3.t: Invalid Data Received From Hybrid/EV Battery Interface Control Module C
U04A3.d: U04A3 concerns interface module C. Such boards do more than measure: they also switch the balancing resistors that bleed charge from individual cells. CARB 1968.2 section (e)(15.2.3) requires hybrid OBD to confirm that cell balancing still holds the cell voltages where intended, and GM checks this per board in 16OBDG02 by closing the odd and even balancing gates in turn and comparing readings, for module C under P1E9E. When the battery controller cannot trust what module C sends, it can neither balance nor judge those cells, so it usually limits power. No manufacturer publishes U04A3 itself. U01A2 marks a silent module C, U033C incompatible software; module D's data fault is filed as U02A0, because U04A4 belongs to the particulate sensor.
c: Interface control module C faulty (measurement or balancing stage)
Damaged cell sense lead or connector at module C
Interference or contact fault on the pack-internal data link
s: Hybrid or EV warning, MIL on plug-in hybrids
Power limited, state of charge shown inaccurately

U04A4.t: Invalid Data Received From Particulate Matter Sensor A
U04A4.d: Diesel particulate matter (PM) sensors have their own control unit that measures soot on the element and sends the result to the engine controller. GM's 2025 ECM tables (25OBDG04A) check the alive rolling count, protection value and checksum of about twenty soot sensor signals and set U04A4 after 3 bad frames in 10, with battery voltage of at least 11 V for 5 s; it is a Type B code, so the MIL comes on after two trips. VW's 2014 Touareg TDI chart sets it when the sensitivity factor leaves 0.75 to 1.25, when an invalid sensitivity signal lasts 2 s or when sensor messages fail for 0.6 s. Ford's 2014 chart also lists it as a MIL code. U02A3 is total loss, U04B2 the second sensor, U05A4 the reverse direction. The filter monitor pauses until data are valid.
c: PM sensor control unit or sensing element faulty (heat, soot, moisture)
Replacement sensor of the wrong variant or not yet matched
Damaged wiring or connector between sensor unit and engine controller
Low supply voltage disturbing the sensor unit
s: Check engine light on
Particulate filter monitor not completing, readiness missing
Usually no change in how the engine runs

U04A5.t: Invalid Data Received From Hybrid/EV Battery Interface Control Module E
U04A5.d: Module E is the fifth interface board in a high-voltage pack, and U04A5 says its data reach the battery controller in a form that fails the checks. This is one of three letters Volkswagen spells out: for the ID.4 of model years 2021 to 2024 the on-car analysis list of July 2024 groups U04A5 with U04A1 and U04A9, all stored in address 8C, and asks dealers to phone the VW helpline before any repair. The list gives no thresholds and does not explain why only A, E and I appear; the gap of four letters between them is visible but not documented. Wikipedia describes the ID.4 pack as nine or twelve modules. Silence from E is U01A4, a software mismatch U033E. The car shows an electrical system message.
c: Software issue in the battery electronics (VW ID.4, clarify with helpline)
Interface control module E internally faulty
Contact fault on the internal link to module E
s: Electrical system warning message
Drive power or charging limited

U04A6.t: Invalid Data Received From Hybrid/EV Battery Interface Control Module F
U04A6.d: U04A6 is set when interface control module F delivers messages the battery controller cannot accept. A board like this checks itself as well: in GM's 16OBDG02 table every interface module, F included, runs four processor performance tests once at each ignition change, for example confirming that its analogue-to-digital converter shows no stuck bits when the input is forced to its limits, Type A after 8 failures in 10 samples. Such internal faults get their own GM P1 codes; U04A6 is meant for the case where the receiver itself judges the incoming data unusable. No manufacturer documents U04A6 publicly. U01A5 means F has stopped talking, U033F that its software does not fit. Expect a hybrid or EV warning and restricted output.
c: Processor or converter fault on interface board F
Contact fault on the internal data link to module F
Supply dropouts of the battery electronics during switch-on
s: Hybrid or EV warning, MIL on plug-in hybrids
Reduced power output

U04A7.t: Invalid Data Received From Hybrid/EV Battery Interface Control Module G
U04A7.d: U04A7 points to interface module G. In a modular battery management system each board sits at a different potential: the ground of the top module can be hundreds of volts above that of the bottom one, so the boards talk through isolated links such as optocouplers or radio. Interference, moisture in a connector or an ageing isolator can corrupt the frames of a single board without breaking the link altogether, and the battery controller then logs an invalid-data code for that letter. No manufacturer publishes U04A7 or thresholds for it. In GM's table 16OBDG02, G is the seventh of eight boards. U01A6 stands for lost contact with G, U0340 for a software mismatch. Charging or drive power may be limited.
c: Moisture or corrosion at internal connectors (leaking pack seal)
Failing isolated communication stage on board G
Interface control module G otherwise defective
s: Battery or hybrid system warning
Charging or drive power limited
Fault may come and go with humidity or temperature

U04A8.t: Invalid Data Received From Hybrid/EV Battery Interface Control Module H
U04A8.d: U04A8 is the invalid-data code for interface module H. In GM's 2016 hybrid table 16OBDG02, H is the last of eight boards that the battery systems module reaches through a daisy chain; a pack of that design needs no higher letter. GM explains that a break anywhere in such a chain cuts off every board behind it, so lost contact is reported for the first board that cannot be recovered. An invalid-data code is different: if only H's frames fail the checks while A to G pass, the cause is more likely local to H, its connector or its cell inputs. No manufacturer documents U04A8 publicly. U01A7 means H is silent, U0341 a software mismatch. The driver sees a hybrid warning and may lose power.
c: Interface control module H internally faulty
Connector or lead fault at the last board of the chain
Faulty cell input on board H producing impossible values
s: Hybrid system warning, MIL on plug-in hybrids
Reduced propulsion power

U04A9.t: Invalid Data Received From Hybrid/EV Battery Interface Control Module I
U04A9.d: U04A9 refers to interface module I, the ninth position in the series. It is the third of the codes Volkswagen lists for the ID.4: in the dealer analysis list of July 2024, U04A9 appears beside U04A1 and U04A5 as a CMCe fault in address 8C, valid for model years 2021 to 2024, with an electrical system message as the complaint. According to Wikipedia the smaller ID.4 battery has nine modules and the larger one twelve, so a ninth position exists in both, though VW does not say how letters map to modules. As with the other two, the helpline must be called before parts are changed. U01A8 marks loss of contact with I, U0342 a software conflict. From J (U04AA) on, the series presupposes larger packs.
c: Software issue in the battery electronics (VW ID.4 case)
Interface control module I internally faulty
Contact fault on the pack-internal link to module I
s: Electrical system warning message
Charging or power restricted

U04AA.t: Invalid Data Received From Hybrid/EV Battery Interface Control Module J
U04AA.d: U04AA flags invalid data from interface module J, the tenth slot. From here on the series only matters for packs with ten or more monitored sections; a nine-module ID.4 battery or an eight-board GM pack like the one in table 16OBDG02 has no J at all. GM's Ultium family, by contrast, assembles packs from anywhere between six and 24 modules of one design, per Wikipedia, and the larger ones clearly exceed ten. No manufacturer publishes U04AA or a threshold for it, and none of the indexed service bulletins mentions it. Likely triggers are the same as for the lower letters: a disturbed isolated link, a damaged connector or a faulty board. U01A9 means J is silent, U0343 incompatible software.
c: Disturbed isolated data link inside the pack
s: Battery or EV system warning
Power or charging rate reduced

U04AB.t: Invalid Data Received From Hybrid/EV Battery Interface Control Module K
U04AB.d: U04AB means interface module K, the eleventh, delivers data the battery controller judges invalid. What those boards report, cell voltages and temperatures, are exactly the inputs that CARB rule 1968.2, paragraph (e)(15.2.3)(A)(iv), names for monitoring in a hybrid energy storage system; this is why plug-in hybrids light the MIL for such faults, while battery-electric cars, which fall outside these rules, show a battery or system warning instead. With part of the pack unreadable, the controller has to assume the worst for those cells: tighter charge and discharge limits or a blocked charge. No manufacturer documents U04AB publicly, and an eleventh board only exists in larger packs. U01AA covers loss of contact, U0344 a software mismatch.
c: Faulty temperature or voltage input on board K
Contact fault on the internal data link to module K
Interface control module K internally faulty
s: MIL (plug-in hybrid) or battery warning (EV)
Charging blocked or slowed
Reduced acceleration

U04AC.t: Invalid Data Received From Hybrid/EV Battery Interface Control Module L
U04AC.d: U04AC covers interface module L, the twelfth letter. Twelve is a common pack size: Wikipedia gives twelve modules for the larger ID.4 battery and for the Ultium pack of the Cadillac Lyriq. Where one board serves each module, L would be the last board present there. Whether a maker actually wires it that way is not public; the 2024 Volkswagen list names only A, E and I for that car, and no source names U04AC. The code means messages from L arrive but fail the controller's checks, not that L has gone quiet (U01AB) or carries the wrong software (U0345). Tracing it requires the manufacturer's scan tool and, beyond the external low-voltage connections, work on an opened high-voltage battery.
c: Loose plug on the internal link to module L
Fault at the pack's external low-voltage connector
s: High-voltage battery warning
Power reduced, possibly no charging

U04AD.t: Invalid Data Received From Hybrid/EV Battery Interface Control Module M
U04AD.d: With U04AD the series reaches module M, the thirteenth interface board, which only exists in packs larger than the common twelve-module layout. One example of such a size is GM's Hummer EV: Wikipedia describes its Ultium battery as 24 modules in two layers that can be switched from parallel to series for 800 V fast charging. How GM names the monitoring electronics in that pack is not published, and no maker documents U04AD. The code says the battery controller receives M's frames but rejects their content; corrupted counters, checksums or impossible cell values are typical reasons in this code family. Loss of contact would be U01AC, a software mismatch U0346. Reduced power or charging is the likely consequence.
c: Corrupted frames on the internal link (counter or checksum errors)
Measurement input on board M reporting impossible values
s: Battery system warning
Fast charging slower or refused

U04AE.t: Invalid Data Received From Hybrid/EV Battery Interface Control Module N
U04AE.d: U04AE stands for invalid data from interface module N, the fourteenth. Like the other high letters it can only appear on a large pack, and no manufacturer documents it publicly. What changes for the workshop is mostly practical: the board sits inside the sealed high-voltage battery, so after reading the freeze-frame data and ruling out the 12 V supply and the low-voltage connectors outside the pack, every further step means de-energising the system, measuring isolation and opening the housing, a job for trained staff with the maker's tester. Polestar, for example, bills a high-voltage battery disconnect with insulation measurement as a labour step of its own when a high-voltage part is replaced. U01AD means module N is silent, U0347 a software conflict.
c: 12 V supply or low-voltage plug of the pack at fault (check first)
Contact fault on the internal link to module N
s: Battery or EV system warning
Output and charging power limited

U04AF.t: Invalid Data Received From Hybrid/EV Battery Interface Control Module O
U04AF.d: U04AF concerns interface module O, the fifteenth board. In practice a data fault of this kind often follows work on the pack: if a replaced board and the battery controller interpret messages differently, frames arrive formally intact but fail range or counter checks. The software sibling U0348 and a search for available updates therefore belong next to this code, as does U01AE for a module that stopped sending. GM's 2015 note PIC6080 for the 2011–2014 Volt, ELR and Ampera says to reprogram the battery and hybrid controllers first when cell codes are spread over several pack sections, and to call technical assistance only when all of them sit on one interface board. No maker documents U04AF; the letter O only exists on very large packs.
c: Software levels of replaced board and battery controller do not match
Plug not fully seated after pack repair
s: Battery warning shortly after a battery repair
Reduced power or charging

U04B0.t: Invalid Data Received From Hybrid/EV Battery Interface Control Module P
U04B0.d: U04B0 closes the series: interface module P is the sixteenth and last letter the code lists provide for these boards, with U01AF for lost contact and U0349 for a software mismatch. Packs with more than sixteen monitored sections do exist, such as Ultium batteries with up to 24 modules, so either several modules share one board or the maker uses its own codes beyond P; which applies is not published. The next code, U04B1, already belongs to a different device, the battery monitor module. As with the other letters, U04B0 means the battery controller receives P's messages but finds their content unusable, which leads to power limits and a warning. No manufacturer documents U04B0 publicly.
c: Contact fault on the internal link to module P
Battery controller software misreading module P
s: High-voltage system warning
Power and charging limited

U04B1.t: Invalid Data Received From Battery Monitor Module
U04B1.d: Despite its place after the high-voltage interface series, U04B1 usually concerns the 12 V side: in GM's 2024 OBD table 24OBDG07 the battery monitor module is the intelligent battery sensor on the 12 V battery, read by the body control module over LIN. GM sets U04B1 when the alive rolling counts of the sensor's signals, among them charged and discharged amp-hours, state of charge, temperature and crank data, are wrong in 8 of 10 samples, polled every 250 ms, with the car in run, above 11 V and at least 5 s after power-up; Type B, two trips. Alfa Romeo reported U04B1-00 in the PCM of 2017–2019 Giulia and Stelvio after a module flash and cleared it with a BCM configuration restore. U01B0 means the sensor is silent.
c: Body control module configuration lost or mismatched after reprogramming (Alfa Romeo)
Intelligent battery sensor on the negative terminal faulty
LIN lead or plug at the battery sensor damaged or corroded
s: Check engine light (GM Type B, after two trips)
Start-stop disabled or charging strategy of the generator changed

U04B2.t: Invalid Data Received From Particulate Matter Sensor B
U04B2.d: U04B2 is the B counterpart of U04A4, intended for vehicles that carry a second smart PM sensor, for instance one per exhaust line or one ahead of and one behind a filter. Messages from sensor B still reach the engine controller, but their content is rejected. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the public examples all use the single sensor A. By analogy with GM's handling of sensor A in 25OBDG04A, a receiver would count frames with a wrong rolling counter, protection value or checksum and set the code once too many fail within a short window. CARB 1968.2 demands that OBD detect PM sensor faults before the sensor can no longer serve filter monitoring. U01B1 means sensor B has gone silent. Expect a MIL and an incomplete filter check, with no change in drivability.
c: Control unit or element of PM sensor B damaged by heat, soot or moisture
Wiring or connector of sensor B chafed or corroded
Sensors A and B swapped or wrong variant fitted
s: Check engine light on
Particulate filter readiness not set

U04B3.t: Invalid Data Received From Planetary Gear Set Control Module
U04B3.d: Several hybrid transmissions use planetary gear sets whose shift elements are switched to change the operating mode; two-mode hybrids, for example, combine two extra planetary sets with four clutches to move between electric, power-split and fixed-gear driving. Where a separate module controls such a set and reports its state, U04B3 marks messages from that module that arrive but carry implausible data. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and SAE gives little more than the name. CARB 1968.2 counts transmission controllers among the emission-critical powertrain units and requires hybrid components to be monitored. U01B2 covers a module that no longer talks. Depending on design, the hybrid system may fall back to a limited mode with a warning light.
c: Planetary gear set control module or its position sensing faulty
Bus wiring or connector at the transmission damaged or oil-soaked
Software of module and hybrid controller not matching
s: Hybrid system or transmission warning
Reduced power or electric-only driving unavailable

U04B4.t: Invalid Data Received From Brake Blending Actuator
U04B4.d: In hybrid and electric cars, brake blending decides how much of the requested deceleration the drive motor recovers as energy and how much the friction brakes supply; at low speed the hydraulic brakes take over completely. An electromechanical booster such as Bosch's iBooster, paired with a matching ESP, is rated for blending up to about 0.3 g of regenerative deceleration. U04B4 is stored when messages from the blending actuator arrive but their values are not credible. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. CARB 1968.2 requires hybrids to flag faults that disable or degrade regenerative braking, so a MIL is possible. U01B3 marks a silent actuator. Expect less regeneration, a changed pedal feel and a brake warning.
c: Blending actuator or its pedal/position sensing faulty
Chassis bus wiring or connector fault
Brake and drive controller software not matching after update or replacement
Low 12 V supply affecting the actuator electronics
s: Brake system or hybrid warning light on
Little or no regenerative braking, shorter range
Brake pedal feels different or harder

U04B5.t: Invalid Data Received From Brake System Control Module B
U04B5.d: Brake system control module B is a second brake controller. Bosch, for instance, adds a second, redundant brake unit to its Integrated Power Brake on automated vehicles so the car can still be stopped if the main unit fails, and the iBooster plus ESP pairing serves the same purpose. U04B5 is stored when a receiver gets messages from module B that fail plausibility, for example a wrong counter, checksum or pressure value. U0418 is the matching code for the primary brake module, U01B4 marks lost contact with module B and U031C a software mismatch. No manufacturer documents U04B5 publicly. As a safety system it rarely lights the MIL; expect brake or stability warnings, and driver assistance or automated functions may be switched off.
c: Brake control module B internally faulty
Chassis or private brake bus wiring or connector fault
Software of the two brake modules not matching after update or replacement
Weak supply on the redundant power path
s: Brake, ABS or stability control warning
Driver assistance or automated driving functions unavailable

U04B6.t: Invalid Data Received From Catalyst Heater Control Module
U04B6.d: An electrically heated catalyst brings the converter to working temperature right after a cold start. Vitesco's EMICAT heater runs at 12, 24 or 48 V and can draw up to 300 A, has been ordered for 48-volt mild hybrid diesel vans with production planned from 2022, and in high-voltage hybrids is fed by a dedicated DC/DC converter. The electronics that switch this power report heater state and energy to the engine controller. U04B6 is stored when those messages arrive but fail plausibility; no carmaker has published its use of the code. Section (e)(2) of CARB 1968.2 requires OBD to confirm that a heated catalyst reaches its target temperature in time, so the check cannot run without valid data. U01B5 marks lost contact. Expect a MIL and higher cold-start emissions.
c: Heater control electronics or DC/DC stage faulty
High-current connection to the heater loose or overheated, giving implausible feedback
Bus wiring or connector near the hot exhaust damaged
Module and engine controller software not matching
s: Check engine light on
Catalyst monitor readiness not set
Engine may idle longer at raised speed after cold start

U04BA.t: Invalid Data Received From Switch Input Module A
U04BA.d: A switch input module collects the positions of several buttons and reports them to other control units as network frames. U04BA means that frames from module A keep arriving, but the receiver, usually the body controller, rejects their content: a switch state outside the defined values, a wrong message counter, a failed checksum or an unexpected length. An Eaton patent describes such a module in which a controller polls each switch address and acts only on replies carrying a valid address and state. Which buttons belong to module A is up to the carmaker; no maker documents this code publicly. If module A falls silent, U01B7 is set instead. For the driver, the buttons handled by this module may do nothing or trigger the wrong function.
c: Switch module or receiving controller with incompatible software or coding after repair
Switch input module A internally faulty (moisture, damaged switch contacts)
Corroded connector or chafed data lead corrupting the frames
s: Buttons served by the module inoperative or acting intermittently
Code stored in the body controller without a warning lamp

U04BB.t: Invalid Data Received From Switch Input Module B
U04BB.d: U04BB concerns the second switch input module. A receiving controller still hears module B on the bus, but the switch information inside its frames fails the plausibility, counter or checksum test. Where buttons are split across several housings, a modular layout like the one in a BCS Automotive Interface Solutions patent is typical: a main module identifies each attached satellite by a coded type and translates its signals for the CAN or LIN bus. A satellite reported with the wrong type or a coding mismatch after a part swap can produce exactly this kind of unusable data. No carmaker publishes a text for U04BB. U01B8 stands for total silence of module B. Expect individual buttons, often a group in one console or panel, to stop responding.
c: Replacement switch module of the wrong variant or not coded to the vehicle
Switch input module B internally faulty
Loose or corroded plug between satellite and main module
s: A group of buttons in one panel not responding
Functions switching on by themselves or not switching off

U04BC.t: Invalid Data Received From Switch Input Module C
U04BC.d: With a third switch input module, addressing becomes a weak point. Several near-identical switch units often hang on one LIN line as slaves, and each needs its own node address, assigned either by part variant or by an auto-addressing routine at start-up. If two units end up with the same address, or a reply arrives with a bad LIN checksum, the master receives data it cannot assign and the controller records U04BC for module C. Nothing public ties this code to a specific make or to a fixed location in the car. U01B9 covers the case where module C does not answer at all, and U04BD, which follows in the list, belongs to the park lock module rather than to this series. Effects stay limited to the buttons wired to module C.
c: Two switch units with the same LIN node address after replacement or failed auto-addressing
Switch input module C internally faulty
Interference on the shared LIN line, e.g. damaged insulation
s: Buttons of module C ignored while other switch groups work
Button presses assigned to the wrong function

U04BD.t: Invalid Data Received From Park Lock/Pawl Control Module
U04BD.d: With park-by-wire, an electronic unit drives an actuator that pushes the parking pawl into the toothed park wheel on the gearbox output and pulls it out again; there is no mechanical link to the selector. Software holds back engagement until the vehicle has stopped, since the pawl would otherwise ratchet over the teeth. U04BD is stored when the park lock module keeps sending messages but their content, such as the reported pawl position, is implausible. It differs from U049F, which covers the module that moves the whole transmission range. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. How a maker checks such data is shown by Ford's 2024 OBD description: on park-by-wire vehicles the engine module rejects implausible monitoring data from the gear shift module and the transmission range control module as non-MIL faults, and the two park position sensor inputs are compared with each other (P07B5). Per Ford's 2012 description, it is a value that arrives but lies outside its valid range that makes a network fault an invalid-data code rather than a lost-communication one (U0422 instead of U0140). U01BA marks a module that has gone quiet. Expect a warning to secure the vehicle, a car that refuses to leave Park, or a Park state that the display does not confirm.
c: Pawl position sensing or actuator inside the module faulty
Bus wiring or connector at the transmission corroded or loose
Weak 12 V battery during park lock actuation
Software or learned values missing after module replacement
s: Warning to secure the vehicle or apply the parking brake
Vehicle will not shift out of Park
Park not confirmed on the display

U04BE.t: Invalid Data Received From Battery Charger Control Module B
U04BE.d: U04BE is logged when a module receives data from battery charger control module B that it cannot accept. Charging hardware can come in more than one stage: the Audi e-tron, for example, was sold in Europe with 11 kW AC charging as standard and 22 kW as an option. Which unit counts as A or B is up to the maker. Polestar shows one assignment: on the Polestar 3 the control unit GCCC stores U01BB00, the lost-contact sibling for charger B, when the on-board AC charger GHCA has failed; AC charging then stops while DC charging still works, and the fix is a new GHCA. No maker documents U04BE itself. It is not emission-related; expect slow or no AC charging.
c: On-board charger B internally faulty (Polestar 3 analogy, grid disturbances)
Charger or charging-control software out of date
Bus wiring or plug at the charger damaged
s: AC charging slow, interrupted or impossible
DC fast charging usually still works
Charging fault message

U04BF.t: Invalid Data Received From Drive Motor A Clutch Actuator
U04BF.d: Some electric and hybrid drivetrains can separate a drive motor from its wheels with a clutch so that an unused axle does not drag the motor along. A Rivian patent describes such a disconnect without a position sensor: the motor speed is brought within a small window of the output speed before engaging, and the control system judges success from how the motor responds to the load. U04BF is set when the actuator for drive motor A sends messages that the receiving controller finds implausible, for example a clutch state that contradicts the speeds. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. On hybrids CARB 1968.2 calls for monitoring of drive motor performance. U01BE marks a silent actuator. Expect reduced power, all-wheel drive or the second motor locked out, and a drive system warning.
c: Clutch actuator motor or its electronics faulty
Worn or sticking disconnect clutch giving a state that does not match the command
Bus wiring or connector at the drive unit damaged
Software of actuator and drive controller not matching
s: Drive system or all-wheel-drive warning
Reduced power or one motor not used
Clunk or jerk when the motor is coupled

U04C0.t: Invalid Data Received From Battery Management Control Module
U04C0.d: The battery management control module behind U04C0 is not always the main controller of the high-voltage battery. Mazda uses the code on the CX-90 (2024–2026) and CX-70 (2025–2026) plug-in hybrids for their backup power unit: the PCM stores U04C0:00, which Mazda describes as an internal malfunction there, often together with P143B, U3008 or U3003 and a lit hybrid system warning. Bulletin SA-030-26 traces this to the small AGM sub battery under the passenger floor and has it replaced. GM's 2024 table 24OBDG07 has only the lost-contact sibling U01BF, set by the gateway after 6.5 s without messages from a module called LIBI, Type B, and no U04C0 entry. Not the same as U0412, the invalid-data code of the battery energy control module.
c: Weak backup sub battery (Mazda CX-90/CX-70 PHEV, AGM YTZ7S)
Battery management or backup power unit internally faulty
Bus wiring or connector fault to the module
s: Hybrid system warning light on
Further codes for the backup power supply stored

U0500.t: Invalid Data Received From Communication Module
U0500.d: The public code lists checked do not carry U0500 at all, so neither its status as a generic code nor its wording can be confirmed. In the generic numbering, an invalid-data code usually mirrors the lost-communication code of the same module 0x301 lower (U0200 to U0501, U0199 to U049A); for U0500 that partner would be U01FF, which is not assigned in those lists either, so a reserved slot is likely. No manufacturer bulletin found uses U0500. If a tool shows it, read the make-specific meaning first. By analogy only: a telematics unit links the car to mobile networks for remote and emergency services, and invalid frames from it would disable those services without affecting the engine; the defined code for that unit is U0499.
c: Code read with a manufacturer-specific definition that differs from the generic list
Scan tool decoding the stored fault number incorrectly
Telematics or communication unit sending corrupted frames (analogy to U0499)
s: Code present without any noticeable fault
Remote app, emergency call or online services unavailable (if it concerns the telematics unit)

U0501.t: Invalid Data Received From Door Control Module B
U0501.d: Many cars give each door its own electronics: a door unit receives commands over CAN and drives window lift, lock and mirror, as a Yazaki patent describes with a LIN sub-bus inside the door. Module A has its invalid-data code in U049A; U0501 is the same check for the second door unit. The body controller or another listener gets B's frames, for instance lock status, window position or switch inputs, but finds them implausible, out of sequence or with a bad checksum. Which door B serves is not standardised, and no carmaker documents U0501 publicly. GM's Saab 9-5 list, for one, has no partner entry U0200 for it. Silence from B gives U0200. The driver may notice one door that no longer locks centrally or whose window switch is ignored.
c: Water ingress into the door module through a failed door membrane
Broken wires in the harness grommet between body and door
Door module not programmed or configured after replacement
s: One door not following central locking
Window, mirror or door-ajar display of that door erratic

U0502.t: Invalid Data Received From Door Control Module C
U0502.d: For door control module C the letter is a weak guide. In the generic list its lost-communication partner is U0201, yet GM's 2011 Saab 9-5 code list uses U0201 for the transfer case control module. So on some makes the slot is not a door at all, and the vehicle's own fault text decides. Where it does mean a third door unit, the check is the usual one: frames from C arrive, but their content is rejected because a signal is undefined, the alive counter does not step correctly or the checksum fails. Saab sorts such findings into subtypes 71, 72 and 74 after the code. No public bulletin names U0502. Door-related effects, if any, are confined to the door C controls; total loss of contact is U0201.
c: Door control module C internally faulty
Damaged wiring in the door hinge area
Manufacturer uses this code slot for another module
s: Lock, window or mirror of one door working only sometimes
Stored code without noticeable fault

U0503.t: Invalid Data Received From Door Control Module D
U0503.d: U0503 is the invalid-data code for door control module D. It is rarely seen in published service material: Ford, the most visible user of lettered door modules, labels the latch controllers of its four-door electronic-latch cars E to H (DCME–DCMH, e.g. Mustang Mach-E), leaving D unused there. In a four-door car with one unit per door, D would typically be the last of the four, but that is not fixed. When a receiver gets D's lock, window or switch data and the content fails its checks, the code is stored; if the frames stop, U0202 follows. No manufacturer documents U0503 publicly. Expect a single door with an unreliable lock, window or interior switch rather than a car-wide fault.
c: Door control module D internally faulty or water-damaged
Broken data lead in the door harness grommet
Weak 12 V battery causing faulty frames during wake-up
s: One door not unlocking or locking with the others
Window switch on that door ignored

U0504.t: Invalid Data Received From Door Control Module E
U0504.d: U0504 is the one door code of this series with a public manufacturer case. Ford names the electronic door latch controllers DCME to DCMH, and its programming applications list DCME as door control module E. In 2024–2026 Lincoln Nautilus and 2025–2027 Aviator, latch software stored B1262:92 in several of these modules, and U0504 could appear in the gearshift module, which evidently uses door status. The cluster then warned of a door fault, of the transmission not being in Park or of hill start assist being unavailable; the fix was a software update of DCME–DCMH (SSM 54938, 54978, 55241). No check engine light is mentioned. In GM's Saab 9-5 list the lost-communication partner U0203 is the left rear door switch panel.
c: Door latch module software (Lincoln Aviator/Nautilus, update DCME–DCMH)
Door control module E internally faulty
Damaged wiring between body and door
s: Door fault warning in the cluster
Transmission Not In Park or Hill Start Assist Not Available messages (Lincoln)
Door latch or electronic door release erratic

U0505.t: Invalid Data Received From Door Control Module F
U0505.d: At Ford, F is the second of the electronic latch modules (DCMF). Its typical troubles are documented, though not with U0505 itself: 2020–2023 Aviators logged latch circuit codes in DCME–DCMH when low battery voltage met fault thresholds set too low (SSM 50556), and Mach-E cars raised false alarms through latch module software (SSM 51292). Both show that supply voltage and software are where such modules fail. U0505 is set when a listener receives DCMF's frames but discards them as implausible. GM's Saab 9-5 list maps the partner slot U0204 to the right rear door switch panel. Losing the frames completely gives U0204. Symptoms are door ajar warnings, an alarm going off or a door that will not open electrically.
c: Low 12 V battery voltage disturbing the latch module (Ford/Lincoln)
Door control module F internally faulty
s: Door ajar or door fault warning
False alarm after locking

U0506.t: Invalid Data Received From Door Control Module G
U0506.d: G is the seventh door slot and in practice belongs to cars that number their door electronics from E upwards. Ford does so with DCMG, the third of four latch modules in Mach-E, Aviator and Nautilus; Ford service messages name DCMG together with its siblings whenever latch software is updated. GM's Saab 9-5 code list contains no partner entry U0205, so the slot appears unused there. The code means a receiving controller judged DCMG's lock and door-state messages invalid, while U0205 stands for missing messages. Because e-latch doors have no mechanical outside release in normal use, a module sending bad data can leave one door that does not open from the handle or triggers door warnings.
c: Latch module software needing update (Ford DCMG)
Weak 12 V supply during locking or wake-up
Door control module G internally faulty
s: Door not opening with the electronic handle
Door fault message in the cluster

U0507.t: Invalid Data Received From Folding Top Control Module
U0507.d: The folding top control module runs the power soft top or retractable hardtop of a convertible: it moves the top through hydraulics or motors, watches latch and position sensors and blocks the sequence when something is in the way. Other units need its status, for example to drop the windows, warn while driving or release the trunk lid. U0507 is logged when that status arrives in an unusable form. BMW shows how much hinges on clean data: in 16,286 convertibles of the 4 Series built 2013–2015, the CVM misread luggage compartment sensors due to software, which could defeat obstruction detection and damage the hydraulics (SI B54 02 17, reprogramming). No maker publishes U0507 itself. U0206 means no contact.
c: Top control module software error (BMW F33/F83 example)
Damaged wiring to top position or latch sensors in the folding area
Water reaching the module from a leaking top drain
s: Top refuses to open or close or stops midway
Top not secure warning while driving

U0508.t: Invalid Data Received From Moveable Roof Control Module A
U0508.d: The moveable roof control module drives an electric sunroof or panoramic glass panel, typically through a cable-driven motor with stored end positions and pinch protection. GM uses the same module name: its Saab 9-5 code list files the loss of contact with this module as U0207, the partner of this code. U0508 is stored when the roof module's position and status frames arrive but fail validation. BMW's SI B54 02 13 illustrates the kind of internal fault behind it: F30-series sunroofs stuck or moved in small steps, the FZD module logged checksum and calibration errors, and reprogramming fixed it. Separate generic codes exist for a sunroof control module (U046A); which name a car uses depends on the maker.
c: Roof module software or lost initialisation of end positions
Water damage from blocked roof drains
Damaged wiring or connector in the headliner
s: Sunroof stuck, moving jerkily or one-touch function lost
Roof not closing with the remote key

U0509.t: Invalid Data Received From Seat Control Module A
U0509.d: Seat control module A is usually the electronics of the first powered seat, often the driver's memory seat. The Saab 9-5 code list published by GM spells this out: there, the lost-communication partner U0208 is the memory seat control module. Its frames carry seat positions for memory recall, heating or ventilation states and switch inputs; when another controller receives them but finds them corrupted or implausible, U0509 is the result. Ford names its driver seat electronics DSM rather than by letter, so the A slot is not universal. No public bulletin covers U0509 itself. If the data is bad, memory positions may not recall, easy-entry movement may stop and climate seat functions may be shut off; driving is unaffected.
c: Seat module configuration or software not matching the vehicle
Under-seat harness or connector damaged by seat travel or objects
Seat control module A internally faulty
s: Seat memory positions not recalled
Seat heating or ventilation unavailable

U050A.t: Invalid Data Received From Seat Control Module B
U050A.d: For seat control module B there is a fairly clear manufacturer assignment. Ford calls the front passenger seat unit SCMB, for example in the 2024–2026 Lincoln Nautilus, where it held B120A:2A with an inoperative heated seat (SSM 54647), while the driver side is the DSM. Ford's letters follow the generic slots: after a seat module G/H update, F-Super Duty APIMs stored U024B and U024C, the generic codes for seat modules G and H (SSM 53226). GM's Saab 9-5 uses the B partner slot U0209 for the front seat heating module. U050A therefore points to the front passenger seat electronics on many cars; it is stored when that module's data is received but rejected. Missing data is U0209.
c: Seat module configuration lost or wrong after programming (Ford SCMB)
Harness under the passenger seat pinched or connector loose
Seat control module B internally faulty
s: Passenger seat heating or adjustment not working
Seat settings missing in the center display

U050B.t: Invalid Data Received From Moveable Roof Control Module B
U050B.d: A second moveable roof module only makes sense where the roof has more than one powered element, for instance a sliding front glass panel plus a separately driven rear panel or sunshade, or a large panoramic roof split into sections. U050B records that data from this second unit reached the network but was unusable. GM's Saab 9-5 code list knows only one moveable roof module (U0207), and no manufacturer publishes a case for the B module, so the code is uncommon. Its lost-communication partner is U020A. Because each panel keeps its own end positions and pinch protection, faulty data from B usually affects only that panel: it may stay closed, stop part-way or need re-initialising.
c: Second roof drive lost its end-position learning
Moveable roof control module B faulty, often after water entry
Connector or lead to the rear roof drive damaged
s: Rear roof panel or shade not moving while the front one works
Panel stopping part-way

U050C.t: Invalid Data Received From Door Control Module H
U050C.d: Door control module H, the last door slot, is used by Ford in two different ways. In the Mach-E, Aviator and Nautilus it is the fourth electronic latch module, DCMH, updated together with DCME–DCMG. In the 2020–2022 Transit it controls the power sliding door: TSB 22-2305 describes a sliding door that partly moves or fails to open or close, with U201A possibly stored in DCMH, fixed by a new latch, conical washers and door adjustment. So on a van, U050C most likely concerns the sliding door, on a passenger car a latch. The code is set when a receiver rejects DCMH's frames as invalid; U020B stands for lost contact. No bulletin shows U050C itself.
c: Power sliding door latch or adjustment fault feeding wrong states (Ford Transit)
Worn wiring in the sliding door track or hinge
s: Power sliding door moving only partly or not at all
Door ajar or door fault message

U050D.t: Invalid Data Received From Wireless Accessory Charging Module A
U050D.d: The wireless accessory charging module is the inductive pad for phones, almost always following the Qi standard, which Toyota was first to offer from the factory, on the 2013 Avalon. The module reports charging state, phone detection and faults to the infotainment or body controller, which shows the charging icon. Ford calls it WACM; for 2018–2022 models it documented slow or no charging and phone mispositioning messages with MagSafe iPhones, advising a check with another Qi phone before replacing parts (SSM 50982). That is a compatibility issue, not U050D. The code itself means the WACM's status frames arrive but are invalid. No maker publishes it. U020C means the module is not heard at all.
c: Charging module software outdated or mismatched
Module overheating, e.g. blocked fan or foreign object on the pad
Wireless charging module A internally faulty
s: Phone not charging on the pad or charging icon missing
Repeated phone position warnings

U050E.t: Invalid Data Received From Wireless Accessory Charging Module B
U050E.d: U050E belongs to a second inductive charging pad, found in cars that offer one pad up front and another for the rear seats or a second front position. Each pad runs its own transmitter coil, object detection and temperature monitoring, so a fault in B leaves pad A working. The fault is logged once the controller that displays charging status gets frames from module B whose values or protection fields do not check out. No manufacturer bulletin mentions a B module; Ford's documented WACM cases concern single pads. Before replacing anything, test with a known Qi-compatible phone and clear coins or cards from the pad. U020D is the matching code for no communication with module B.
c: Metal object or card on the second pad triggering protection
Software of charging module B not matching the vehicle
Wireless charging module B internally faulty
s: Second charging pad inactive while the first works
No charging indication for the rear or second pad

U0511.t: Invalid Data Received From Seat Control Module C
U0511.d: Seat control module C usually serves a seat beyond the two front ones. GM's Saab 9-5 code list assigns the partner slot U0210 to the rear seat heating control module, and Ford labels its rear seat electronics with later letters altogether (SCMK and SCML for the second-row power seats of the 2025 Navigator, SCMJ for the third-row fold module), so module C is anything but uniform. U0511 is stored when frames from module C reach the network but their content is rejected. No public document names U0511. Rear seat modules often sit under carpets or folding mechanisms where harnesses get pinched, a cause more typical here than at the front. Effects: rear seat heating, folding or adjustment unavailable.
c: Harness pinched by rear seat folding or rail mechanism
Configuration of the rear seat module missing after replacement
Seat control module C internally faulty
s: Rear seat heating not switching on
Power folding or adjustment of a rear seat inoperative

U0512.t: Invalid Data Received From Seat Control Module D
U0512.d: U0512 has a documented GM case that goes beyond comfort functions. On the 2020 Cadillac CT5 with option UGN, the image processing module, which handles camera data for driver assistance, could set U0512 and display Service Driver Assist. GM named software as the cause, told technicians to clear the code and recheck, and to follow normal diagnosis only if it returned at once (PIC6408, revised as PIC6408A in October 2020). The bulletin does not say which seat information the camera module uses. In other cars, module D is simply a fourth seat unit; Ford's matching of letters to generic slots is shown by U024B/U024C for its seat modules G and H. Lost contact with module D gives U0211.
c: Software in the receiving module (Cadillac CT5 image processing module)
Seat module D configuration or software mismatch
Damaged harness or connector under the seat
s: Service Driver Assist message (Cadillac CT5)
Driver assistance features temporarily unavailable
Seat functions served by module D not responding

U0513.t: Invalid Data Received From Yaw Rate Sensor Module
U0513.d: A yaw rate sensor reports how quickly the body rotates about its vertical axis, and stability control weighs that rotation against steering angle, wheel speeds and sideways acceleration. U0513 means frames from a separate yaw rate sensor module do arrive, but the receiver rejects them: value out of range, invalid-status bit, wrong counter or checksum. No manufacturer publishes setting criteria for this code. GM's 2011 Saab 9-5 shows a different layout: yaw and lateral sensing share one multi-axis unit, and corrupt frames are stored as U0125 with failure types 71, 72 or 74. Toyota's Sequoia case (NHTSA PE16-006) shows the physical risk, as a drifting offset produced unwanted brake pulses until VSC switched itself off. Expect ESC and traction lamps and no stability intervention; U0123 means the module is silent.
c: Sensor element drifting or giving an offset the receiver flags as implausible
Loose mounting or corroded connector at the sensor module
Sensor module or brake controller software/configuration not matching after replacement
Disturbed CAN signals (wiring, terminating resistor, interference)
s: ESC/stability control and traction control warning lamps on
Stability control interventions unavailable
Driver assistance relying on vehicle motion data switched off

U0514.t: Invalid Data Received From Mirror Control Module A
U0514.d: J2012 provides two mirror control units, and U0514 concerns unit A: its frames keep arriving, but the receiver finds the content unusable, for instance a signal flagged invalid, a wrong counter or checksum, or a value outside the defined range. FCA ties the letter to the cabin mirror. In its Grand Cherokee case S2108000013 the partner code U0213 is called interior mirror control module A and was logged in the BCM after a configuration restore had wrongly declared a combined rear view mirror module fitted. Jaguar Land Rover shows the invalid-data side with its own code B1974-86 on the 2020 Evoque, caused by mirror software and without any effect on function. Depending on the unit, auto-dimming, a camera mirror view or memory settings may be unavailable. U0213 means silence; module B uses U044F.
c: Software error in the mirror module sending invalid signal values
Vehicle configuration in the BCM not matching the fitted mirror variant
Mirror control module A internally faulty
Loose or corroded connector at the mirror (headliner or door)
s: Often no noticeable effect; code found only during a scan
Auto-dimming or camera mirror view unavailable
Mirror memory or folding function not working

U0515.t: Invalid Data Received From Remote Function Actuation Module
U0515.d: The remote function actuation module picks up the radio signals of key fobs and, on newer vehicles, of a phone used as a key, and hands lock, unlock, liftgate or remote start requests to the body controller. U0515 means its messages reach the network but fail the receiver's checks. Ford calls the unit RFA: on the Mustang Mach-E of model years 2021–2023 (SSM 51571, following an OTA software push) and the Lincoln Nautilus (SSM 54773) an RFA stuck in programming mode switched off the phone key function and left partner code U0214 in several modules; pulling the RFA fuse for a minute and reflashing with FDRS restored it. GM's bulletin 15-NA-004 lists U0214 on 2013–2016 Acadia where the keyless receiver's data line on the low-speed LAN got trapped by the rear HVAC duct. Fob, passive entry or phone key may then work erratically.
c: Module software hanging or outdated, e.g. after an over-the-air update
Chafed or pinched data wire to the receiver module in the roof area
Supply interruption or internal fault of the receiver module
s: Key fob or phone-as-a-key not working or only intermittently
Passive entry or remote start unavailable
Network codes stored in several body modules at the same time

U0516.t: Invalid Data Received From Door Switch A
U0516.d: Here a door switch is a networked switch pack in a door trim panel that reports window, lock or mirror requests as data instead of through separate wires. U0516 is stored when frames from switch unit A arrive but fail the receiver's validity checks. No manufacturer publishes which door letter A stands for or documents this code; FCA lists the driver's switch as unit B, so A cannot simply be taken as the driver's side. NXP's car door keypad note AN2205 illustrates the scheme: the body controller polls the keypad over LIN about every 100 ms and receives a short status reply in which the slave also flags its own bus errors. Requests from a rejected switch are ignored or treated as released, so its buttons seem dead. U0215 is the lost-communication counterpart.
c: Electronics of switch unit A faulty (moisture, cracked solder joints)
Damaged data or ground wire in the door harness
Replacement switch of the wrong variant or software level
s: Buttons on one door switch pack without function
Window or lock on that door only operable from other switches

U0517.t: Invalid Data Received From Door Switch B
U0517.d: Door switch B is the only letter of this series with a published manufacturer assignment. FCA bulletin 08-013-15 for the 2014 Jeep Cherokee (KL) gives the partner code U0216 as lost communication with the driver door switch; it showed up after the battery had been disconnected, together with a Start/Stop Not Available message, and was cured with new BCM software and a restored proxi configuration. U0517 itself is not documented by any manufacturer: here the driver's switch pack keeps sending, but the content is rejected. Since this pack usually holds the master buttons for every window, the rear window lockout and often lock and mirror controls, corrupt data can disable several functions at once. Battery voltage, BCM software and the driver door harness are the first checks.
c: BCM software or vehicle configuration out of step after battery disconnection (FCA KL)
Driver door switch pack faulty, e.g. after liquid ingress
Chafed data or ground wire between body and driver door
s: Driver's master window switches or window lockout not working
Lock or mirror adjustment from the driver's door unavailable
Start/Stop Not Available message (FCA, with partner code)

U0518.t: Invalid Data Received From Door Switch C
U0518.d: U0518 is set when a receiving controller gets data from door switch unit C that it cannot trust. Which door that is remains unpublished, and no manufacturer documents the code. Door switch packs are usually LIN slaves, and LIN protects every frame with a parity-checked identifier and a checksum; NXP's keypad design even reports bit, checksum, parity and no-response errors back in its status bytes. A cracked wire in the flexing harness between body and door, a weak ground or voltage dips while window motors start can therefore corrupt frames without silencing the unit, which would instead give U0217. The effect stays limited to whatever switch C commands: windows, locks or mirrors may ignore it. Inspect the hinge-area harness before replacing the switch.
c: Partly broken data or ground wire in the door hinge area
Supply dips while motors start (weak battery, poor ground)
s: Controls on one door respond only sometimes
Fault appears when the door is opened or closed

U0519.t: Invalid Data Received From Door Switch D
U0519.d: Door switch unit D reports the positions of its buttons as coded data. Inside such packs several contacts often share one input through resistor networks or comparators, as Microchip explains for the switch interface of its LIN chips ATA6641/ATA6642, and the stages of a window rocker are distinguished by voltage level. Worn or wet contacts can then yield combinations the receiver regards as impossible, such as up and down at the same time, and the frame is thrown away. No manufacturer assigns D to a particular door or documents U0519; GM's Saab 9-5 code list, for example, handles the rear door switch panels under separate codes, U0203 and U0204. A sticky or water-damaged switch pack is the most likely cause; U0218 covers complete loss of the unit.
c: Worn, sticky or wet contacts producing impossible switch combinations
Electronics of switch unit D faulty
Poor ground or damaged data wire to the switch
s: Window moves the wrong way or not at all from this switch
Express function triggered or missing unexpectedly

U051A.t: Invalid Data Received From Door Switch E
U051A.d: U051A concerns door switch unit E. On a car with four side doors, A to D would already be enough for one unit per door, so E suggests an additional switch location; no manufacturer documents this code or says what E means. Rear or sliding doors with their own electronics are plausible candidates: Yazaki's patent US8304928 describes doors with dedicated controllers, each serving a window switch module, joined to the body network through a LIN sub-bus. One interaction matters for any rear switch: the driver's window lockout blocks rear requests deliberately, so a rear switch that does nothing is not by itself a fault. The code becomes meaningful when frames from unit E contain implausible values; U0219 indicates the unit has gone silent.
c: Switch unit E internally faulty or water-damaged
Fault on the LIN sub-bus wiring between door controller and switch
Switch variant not matching the vehicle configuration
s: Switch at an additional door position without function
Window at that position operable only from the driver's door

U0521.t: Invalid Data Received From Door Switch F
U0521.d: Door switch unit F lies beyond the usual four side doors. Vans and large SUVs may carry further switch panels, for example at sliding doors or for a third seat row, but no manufacturer states which position F denotes or documents this code. Whether the switch acts as a LIN slave polled by a door or body controller, or, as in NXP's LIN application overview, as the master of a small door network that drives the window lifter slaves, the receiving side sets U0521 when the unit keeps answering yet its content fails the checks: contradictory button states, a wrong frame length or a corrupted checksum. Windows or locks served by this switch then stop reacting to it. U0220 is the matching lost-communication code.
c: Worn wiring or contacts at a sliding or rear door transition
Switch or controller software not matching after replacement
s: Switch panel at a sliding door or rear row not working
Windows or locks served by that panel do not respond to it

U0522.t: Invalid Data Received From Door Switch G
U0522.d: J2012 provides seven door switch units, and G is the last of them. Few vehicles need that many networked switch packs, and no manufacturer publishes what G stands for or documents U0522. Where such a unit exists it works like its siblings: it supplies its button states when asked, and the receiver ignores them once a frame is malformed, out of range or carries an invalid counter. After a switch pack has been replaced or the body controller reconfigured, a variant or software level that does not suit the vehicle can produce exactly this pattern; FCA's Cherokee bulletin 08-013-15 shows door-switch codes being cleared by BCM software and a restored configuration. All other doors and switches carry on working. U0221 is the partner for complete silence.
c: Switch variant or body controller configuration not matching
Data or supply wire to switch unit G damaged
s: One additional switch panel ignored by the vehicle
Code appears after a switch or module replacement

U0523.t: Invalid Data Received From Door Window Motor A
U0523.d: A door window motor in the J2012 sense is a lift motor with its own electronics that talks to the network, usually as a LIN slave of a door or body controller. Such a unit reports where the glass is, based on its Hall pulses, whether it stopped for an obstacle or a stall and whether its sensor or supply has failed, as NXP's MM908E624 reference design (AN3147) shows. U0523 is stored when these reports from motor A reach the master but cannot be used. No manufacturer documents the code or the door behind letter A. Typical consequences are a window that only moves while the switch is held, a missing express function or no automatic closing on locking. Lost communication with the same motor is U0222.
c: Electronics or Hall sensor in window motor A faulty
Window position not learned after battery disconnection or repair
Damaged LIN, supply or ground wire to the motor
s: Window moves only while the switch is held
Express up/down or comfort closing unavailable
Window stops part way

U0524.t: Invalid Data Received From Door Window Motor B
U0524.d: U0524 means the master accepts frames from window motor B but not what they say. A common reason is a position value the controller cannot reconcile. Smart lift motors count Hall pulses between a learned lower and upper end, and Atmel's anti-pinch application note AVR480 describes acquiring such parameters during initialisation and spotting a defective Hall sensor from a run of apparent direction changes. After a battery disconnection, a motor replacement or a regulator that has slipped, the stored travel no longer matches reality, and many systems fall back to manual operation until the window has been re-initialised. No manufacturer publishes setting criteria for U0524 or the door assigned to B. U0223 covers a motor that has stopped answering.
c: End positions lost after battery disconnection, motor or regulator work
Hall sensor in motor B faulty, giving erratic position counts
Regulator cable or glass clamp slipped, so travel no longer matches
s: One-touch operation lost on that window
Window stops short of the top or reverses near the seal

U0525.t: Invalid Data Received From Door Window Motor C
U0525.d: Data from window motor C include what the door controller needs for automatic closing, which in the United States falls under FMVSS 118. A window able to close without the switch being held must stop and reverse before it presses on a test rod of 4 to 200 mm with 100 N or more, and then open again by at least 125 mm or far enough for a 200 mm rod. If the reports from motor C are corrupt, the controller can no longer rely on that reversal, so a cautious design blocks one-touch and remote closing for this window. No manufacturer documents U0525 or names the door behind C. Raising and lowering with the switch held usually still works; U0224 is the lost-communication partner.
c: Motor C electronics sending corrupted status
Voltage drop at the motor during start-up (weak battery, poor ground)
Chafed LIN wire in the door harness
s: Automatic closing on locking does not close this window
Window only operable with the switch held

U0526.t: Invalid Data Received From Door Window Motor D
U0526.d: Not every lift motor carries Hall sensors. Patent US11611297 describes a cheaper approach in which the controller derives speed, current and how quickly current changes from the ripple that commutation leaves in the motor current, and recognises a pinch from those values. Positions obtained this way are sensitive to supply noise and brush wear, so the data reported by window motor D may drift out of the plausible range and lead to U0526. No manufacturer publishes this code or says which door uses letter D. Practical effects resemble the sister codes: express and comfort closing disabled, a lost end position, sometimes a window that halts part way. U0225 is stored instead when motor D does not answer at all.
c: Position counting from current ripple disturbed (brush wear, supply noise)
Window motor D or its electronics faulty
Poor ground or connector at the door
s: Window halts part way or misjudges its end position
Express and comfort closing unavailable

U0527.t: Invalid Data Received From Door Window Motor E
U0527.d: U0527 is logged when a receiver rejects the content sent by window motor E. Mechanics can play a part. Subaru's bulletin 07-189-21 for the 2020 Legacy and Outback deals with front regulators whose glass tilted in the sash frame and bound, so the anti-entrapment function reacted erratically and the glass closed slowly or not at all; revised regulator and motor assemblies fixed it. Binding of that kind produces current and speed profiles a motor controller may treat as implausible, even though the bulletin itself names no network code. No manufacturer links U0527 or the letter E to a particular door. Check glass run channels and the regulator before suspecting electronics; U0226 means communication with motor E is lost entirely.
c: Glass binding in the run channel or sash, distorting motor load
s: Window reverses without an obstacle while closing
Glass closes slowly or stops before the seal

U0528.t: Invalid Data Received From Door Window Motor F
U0528.d: Window motor F is one of the slots beyond the four usual side doors; it could serve, for instance, powered rear quarter glass or a sliding door window, but no manufacturer documents which window F stands for or publishes U0528. Such motors report through status signals: in NXP's LIN 2.0 window lift example (AN2960) the slave returns an error flag for its last action plus a LIN response-error bit, which lets the master keep watch over every node. When these signals arrive in an inconsistent form, for example after a motor with a different variant or node configuration has been fitted, the master discards them and stores U0528. The window concerned then moves only in a limited way or not at all, while the others remain usable. U0227 is the lost-communication partner.
c: Replacement motor with a different variant or node configuration
Damaged wiring at a sliding door or rear body transition
s: An additional power window moves only partly or not at all
Code appears after a motor has been replaced

U0529.t: Invalid Data Received From Door Window Motor G
U0529.d: With G, J2012 reaches the seventh and last window motor slot, more than most vehicles will ever use. No manufacturer publishes U0529 or names a window for G. Should the code appear, it follows the logic of its siblings: motor G is heard on the network, yet its frames are rejected because of a checksum or counter error, a signal marked invalid or a value outside the agreed range. Supply problems are a frequent trigger, since lift motors draw high starting currents; NXP's MM908E624 design reports overvoltage and overtemperature in its status for that reason. For diagnosis, watch the reported position while operating the window and check supply and ground before replacing the motor. U0228 means the motor is silent.
c: Weak supply or ground causing faults under starting current
Window motor G or its electronics faulty
Motor electronics overheated after repeated operation
s: Window stops responding after several operations
