U060F.t: Lost Communication With Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A
U060F.d: Modern hot-film air flow meters often transmit digitally; Bosch lists SENT, frequency and LIN outputs, and many units also carry pressure, temperature or humidity. U060F means sensor A's messages are missing. GM's 2025 tables run it on LIN: no answer to the pressure request for at least 62.5 ms or to the temperature/humidity request for 250 ms, Type A or B by calibration. GM bulletin 24-NA-158 traces P0102 with U060F on 2023/2024 full-size SUVs with L84/L87 V8 engines to water that got into the sensor connector during assembly and replaces sensor and connector. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV sets U060F-00 after a 2 s SENT timeout or data error and then estimates air mass from throttle opening. Ford uses it for SENT units too.
c: Water, corrosion or loose terminals in the air flow sensor connector
LIN or SENT line, battery feed or ground to the sensor interrupted
Sporadic communication error without hardware fault (cleared and rechecked)
s: Check engine light, often together with an air flow circuit code
Engine runs on a modelled air mass, with reduced response
Rough idle or hesitation

U0610.t: Lost Communication With Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor B
U0610.d: Air flow sensor B is the second meter on engines that measure each intake path separately, typically one per bank on V engines with two air boxes. In GM's documents 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07, written for an engine with two throttle bodies, U060F stands for bank 1 and U0610 for bank 2: the code sets when the digital sensor itself reports a time overflow or a maximum-period violation for 1.5 s with battery voltage above 9 V, and the MIL follows on the second trip. Ford's 2024 gasoline summary is an exception, filing its digital air flow sensor B under U0612. P010A to P010E concern an analog sensor B, and P010F compares the two meters. Without sensor B the controller relies on sensor A and models for that bank.
c: Signal, supply or ground wire to air flow sensor B damaged
Air flow sensor B electronics failed or contaminated
Moisture or loose terminal at sensor B connector
s: Check engine light after the second trip on GM
Uneven running or slightly reduced power

U0611.t: Lost Communication With Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Bank 1
U0611.d: Intake air temperature is often no longer a separate NTC wire to the controller but a value inside a digital frame: combined air flow meters send it over LIN or SENT, and pressure chips such as Infineon's KP276 digitize an attached NTC and pass it on in the same SENT message. U0611 concerns sensor 1 of bank 1, typically the upstream sensor in the air filter or air flow path. GM documents it for a two-throttle calibration of 2023/2024, paired with U0613: it sets when the temperature message from the sensor upstream of throttle 1 stops arriving or its line reads as stuck high or stuck low; the MIL comes on after two trips. P0110 to P0114 are the analog circuit codes. Fuel and spark corrections then use a fixed substitute temperature.
c: Wiring fault to the combined sensor that carries the temperature value
Electronics of the combined air flow or pressure sensor failed
Corroded or loose connector in the intake path
s: Check engine light, on GM after two trips
Usually no noticeable change in driving

U0612.t: Lost Communication With Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Bank 2
U0612.d: Bank 2 needs its own intake temperature sensor only where the engine has two separate air paths, as on V engines with one air box and throttle per bank. U0612 is the lost-communication code for that sensor 1 of bank 2. GM's 23OBDG07/24OBDG07 treat it as the bank 2 twin of U0611: the second bank's temperature message is missing, or its line is reported stuck high or low, and the MIL follows after two trips. Ford's 2024 gasoline summary, however, assigns U0612 to communication with its digital air flow sensor B (lost for more than 5 s), so on Ford vehicles the code points to that meter instead. P00AA to P00AE cover the analog circuit. Without the value the controller substitutes a fixed temperature.
c: Wiring fault on the bank 2 intake sensor branch
Bank 2 temperature sensor or its host sensor failed (on Ford the air flow sensor B)
Corroded connector on the bank 2 intake
s: Check engine light
Little effect on driving; with Ford's air flow sensor B reduced response possible

U0613.t: Lost Communication With Intake Air Temperature Sensor 2 Bank 1
U0613.d: Intake air temperature sensor 2 sits further downstream than sensor 1, for example after the charge air cooler or in the manifold, where it is frequently combined with a pressure sensor (a TMAP unit). Digital versions send the temperature together with pressure; Melexis' MLX90818 can carry a medium temperature in its SENT frame and replaces the value with a reserved error code when measurement fails. U0613 means this digitally delivered temperature for bank 1 is no longer received. The only public manufacturer use is GM (23OBDG07/24OBDG07), whose dual-throttle calibration stores U0613 jointly with U0611 when the bank 1 temperature message is lost or stuck high or low, MIL after two trips. P0095 to P0099 are the analog codes. Charge temperature then runs on a substitute value.
c: Damaged wiring to the combined temperature/pressure sensor
Temperature element or electronics of the combined sensor failed
Oil from the charge air path in the connector
s: Check engine light, on GM after two trips
Possible spark retard or boost reduction as a precaution

U0614.t: Lost Communication With Intake Air Temperature Sensor 2 Bank 2
U0614.d: This is the bank 2 counterpart of U0613: the downstream intake temperature sensor of the second bank, usually after that bank's charge air cooler or in its manifold half, delivers its value digitally and the controller has stopped receiving it. Typical carriers are TMAP-style sensors whose SENT frames hold pressure and temperature, protected by a CRC and status bits, as described for Infineon's KP276. No manufacturer documents U0614 publicly; even GM's twin-throttle tables, which use U0611 to U0613, leave it out. The code therefore rests on CARB 1968.2, which demands a separate fault code when a digital input stops communicating. P00A5 to P00A9 describe the analog circuit of the same sensor. The engine controller falls back to a modelled charge temperature for that bank.
c: Wiring fault to the bank 2 combined temperature/pressure sensor
Corroded or oily connector at the bank 2 sensor
s: Check engine light
Little effect on driving, occasionally less boost

U0615.t: Lost Communication With Engine Coolant Bypass Valve A
U0615.d: Engines with split cooling circuits often route coolant through an electrically driven valve that reports its position and status digitally. U0615 is stored when the engine controller gets no answer from bypass valve A. In GM's 2019 hybrid tables (19OBDG01) the valve sits on a LIN bus: once Run mode and at least 11 V have held for 400 ms, three missed responses fail the test as Type B, and the valve's own position check (P15C5) is suspended meanwhile. Ram's bulletin 08-171-26 for 2025-26 Ram 2500 to 5500 trucks links U0615 on the coolant three-way valve to a contaminated connector under the coolant bottle; the fix is dielectric grease, or a new valve plus pigtail. Drivers notice the lamp and weak cabin heat. Circuit faults of the valve are P2681 to P2683.
c: Moisture or corrosion in the valve connector (Ram bulletin 08-171-26)
LIN, supply or ground wire to the valve open, shorted or chafed
Valve actuator electronics failed (valve no longer answers)
LIN master in the engine controller faulty
s: Check engine light
Little or no cabin heat
Engine warms up slower or coolant temperature behaves unusually

U0616.t: Lost Communication With Engine Coolant Bypass Valve B
U0616.d: Valve B is a second electronically controlled coolant valve, for example one that splits flow between the block and the head or toward a heater or oil cooler; which valve carries the letter B depends on the manufacturer. No manufacturer documents U0616 publicly. The code means the controller has stopped receiving valid replies from that valve over its digital link, while valve A may still answer, so the fault is likely in the branch of wiring, the connector or the electronics of valve B itself. Suppliers such as Hella and Rheinmetall build these valves with LIN, PWM or SENT interfaces and internal position feedback. CARB requires a monitoring plan for engines that regulate temperature with more than one flow control device. P0E7B to P0E7E cover the electrical circuit of valve B.
c: Damaged signal, supply or ground wire in the branch to valve B
Loose, corroded or wet connector at valve B
Controller software or configuration does not match the fitted valve
s: Warning lamp, often without a noticeable change in driving
Unusual warm-up behaviour or coolant temperature swings

U0617.t: Lost Communication With Engine Coolant Bypass Valve C
U0617.d: Unlike its LIN-based neighbours, GM uses U0617 for a coolant bypass valve whose position sensor transmits SENT frames (SAE J2716) to the engine controller. The tables 25OBDG03B and 25OBDG04B count a failure when the input hardware flags a message fault, when pulses arrive but the newest frame is older than 6.25 ms, or when the SENT pin voltage stays above or below a controller limit while frames go stale. Four failures within a five-second window set the code as Type B over two trips; the 2019 table 19OBDG03D still ran it as Type A after one trip. Suppliers such as Rheinmetall offer coolant valves with SENT position feedback. Typical causes are wiring and connector faults on the three-wire sensor line. The valve may stop being regulated, so warm-up and heater output can suffer.
c: SENT signal, 5 V supply or ground wire of the valve position sensor open or shorted
Corroded or loose connector at the valve
Position sensor inside the valve failed (usually replaced with the valve)
SENT input of the engine controller faulty
s: Check engine light (on GM after two trips, on 2019 calibrations after one)
Slow warm-up or reduced heater output
Possibly further coolant valve codes stored at the same time

U0618.t: Lost Communication With Engine Coolant Bypass Valve D
U0618.d: Bypass valve D is a fourth smart coolant valve and appears only on engines with several separately controlled coolant paths. GM's 2025 table 25OBDG03B is the one public document found that uses U0618: the engine controller polls the valve over LIN and expects its response frame (BRV_Rsp). If that reply is missing for 250 ms or longer while the LIN channel is initialised, the valve is configured as present and the battery has held above 11 V for five seconds, the code fails as Type B and needs two trips to light the MIL. A single silent valve with working neighbours narrows the search to its own branch, connector or electronics; several LIN codes at once point to the shared bus or the master. Coolant flow in that branch may stay at its default position.
c: LIN wire, supply or ground to valve D interrupted or chafed
Poor contact at the valve connector
Fault on the shared LIN bus or in the LIN master (several LIN codes)
s: Check engine light after two trips
Unusual coolant temperature or warm-up behaviour

U0619.t: Lost Communication With Reductant Level Sensor A
U0619.d: Reductant level sensor A reports how much diesel exhaust fluid (DEF, AdBlue) is left in the SCR tank. Newer tank units are smart sensors: a sensing element plus electronics that transmit level, temperature and often concentration as digital frames over CAN, SENT or LIN. U0619 means the engine or aftertreatment controller gets no valid frames from that level sensor, whether the line is silent, frames time out, checksums fail or the sensor flags an internal fault. CARB requires a digital input that stops talking to store its own code, apart from the circuit and plausibility codes P203A to P203E. No manufacturer publicly documents a detection rule for U0619. Without a level value the low-DEF warning is lost and the controller can no longer rule out an empty tank, which California treats as an SCR fault.
c: Corroded, water-soaked or loose connector at the DEF tank sensor
Data line, supply or ground of the tank sensor chafed or broken along the frame
Electronics of the tank level sensor failed (often replaced as a tank sender unit)
Controller software or configuration not matching the installed sensor
s: Check engine light or SCR warning
DEF gauge blank or frozen at a fixed value
No warning before the DEF tank runs empty

U061A.t: Lost Communication With Reductant Level Sensor B
U061A.d: Some SCR tanks carry more than one level measurement, for example a second sensing element, a second tank chamber or a separate sender; which point counts as B is the manufacturer's choice, and no public document assigns it. U061A is stored when the controller stops receiving usable digital frames from level sensor B while sensor A may still report normally. That pattern points to the wiring branch, connector or electronics of the second sensor rather than to the network as a whole. Supplier sensors such as SSI's ultrasonic DEF unit put level and temperature on a J1939 CAN link, so a dead sensor looks to the controller like any missing node. Circuit-type faults of the same sensor are P21A8 to P21AC. Expect a warning lamp and a DEF reading that no longer matches the tank.
c: Open or chafed wire in the branch that feeds only level sensor B
Water or corrosion in the connector of sensor B
s: Check engine light or DEF system warning
DEF level shown wrongly or not at all

U061B.t: Lost Communication With Reductant Level Sensor C
U061B.d: Level sensor C is a third level input of a reductant system and exists only on layouts with more than one tank or measuring point. No manufacturer publicly documents U061B or explains which part carries the letter C. The code says that this third sensor's digital messages have stopped or keep arriving corrupted, so its reading is treated as unknown. Because CARB counts the reductant supply among the SCR functions an OBD system must watch, and asks for a separate code whenever a digital input stops communicating, the fault is emission-related even if levels A and B still report. Volvo's guide for its CAN-connected truck tank sensor starts with the harness and the pins, looking for damage, corrosion and water, which is also the sensible first step here. P21AD to P21B1 cover the circuit faults of sensor C.
c: Damaged pins, corrosion or water in the connector of sensor C
Harness to the additional tank or measuring point damaged
Internal failure of level sensor C
s: Malfunction indicator lamp
Implausible DEF quantity on the display

U061C.t: Lost Communication With Reductant Temperature Sensor A
U061C.d: Reductant temperature sensor A tells the controller how warm the diesel exhaust fluid is. That value decides when tank and line heaters must run, when dosing may begin after a cold start, and the concentration reading relies on it, since it is calculated from how fast sound travels through the fluid. On digital units the temperature element shares a housing with the level or quality measurement; SSI's ultrasonic tank sensor, for example, sends temperature, level and concentration together over J1939. U061C is logged when frames that carry temperature A no longer arrive or fail their checks. No manufacturer publicly documents a threshold or delay for this code. The analog circuit faults of the sensor are P2042 to P2046. In winter, a missing temperature can hold off SCR dosing for longer, so NOx emissions rise.
c: Connector of the combined DEF tank sensor corroded or loose
Damaged data, supply or ground wire to the sensor
Sensor electronics failed, sometimes after freeze damage
s: Check engine light
DEF heater or SCR dosing starts late or not at all in cold weather
DEF quality reading unavailable

U061D.t: Lost Communication With Reductant Temperature Sensor B
U061D.d: Temperature sensor B is a second temperature input of the reductant system. Where it sits depends on the maker: at another spot in the tank unit, in the pump or supply module, or along the dosing line. Volvo's truck tank sensor, for instance, measures temperature at two points on its circuit board, yet sends everything over one CAN connection and reports a lost connection as U02A2 rather than with this code. U061D therefore belongs to designs in which temperature B arrives as its own digital message. If only B drops out, the controller can usually keep working with A but loses the cross-check between the two values and the heater control for that zone. No manufacturer publicly documents U061D. Circuit faults of an analog sensor B are P2ACC to P2AD0.
c: Wiring to the second temperature point (pump module or dosing line) damaged
Connector of temperature sensor B corroded or not latched
Temperature sensor B or the module housing it failed
s: Malfunction indicator lamp
Line or pump heating may not work properly in frost

U061E.t: Lost Communication With Battery Isolation/Voltage Stabilization Control Module
U061E.d: A battery isolation or voltage stabilization module separates a second 12 V battery or protected loads from the starter circuit, so that cranking during an automatic restart does not drag the voltage of the rest of the vehicle down. A GM patent (US 9,803,608) describes such an isolator built from MOSFET switches. U061E means the powertrain controller has lost contact with this module. Ford documents it on 2021 and 2022 F-150 trucks with the 3.5 L PowerBoost hybrid (special service message SSM 50843): U061E, often with P2C44, turns on the powertrain malfunction (wrench) lamp rather than the check-engine light. Ford blames a poor ground circuit GD132 or a failed auxiliary battery isolator and wants the ground and the auxiliary battery tested before the isolator is replaced. U041A covers invalid data from the same module.
c: Poor ground connection of the isolator circuit (Ford ground GD132)
Weak or deeply discharged auxiliary battery
Communication wire or connector to the module damaged
s: Powertrain malfunction (wrench) lamp on Ford trucks
Additional battery or isolator code such as P2C44

U061F.t: Lost Communication With Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Bank 1 Sensor 1
U061F.d: Many current exhaust temperature sensors are active: a thermocouple probe, often type N, feeds a small electronics module that turns the reading into SENT or CAN messages, as in the Sensience 22J sensor. U061F means valid messages from the bank 1, position 1 sensor (normally the most upstream one) have stopped. GM's 2025 diesel tables (25OBDG04A and 25OBDG04B) define it for a SENT sensor: any message fault, or messages that are too old, counted in 19 of 25 samples taken every 100 ms once the sensor start-up delay has passed and the engine is not cranking; Type A, so the MIL lights in the first trip. GM also stores a second code tied to the controller input the sensor is wired to. Bentley saw it with U0621 on 2020-on V8 Continental and Flying Spur cars whose harness chafed on a wheel-arch bracket.
c: Sensor harness rubbing through on a bracket or subframe edge (Bentley V8)
Connector or module of the sensor damaged by exhaust heat
Internal fault of the active sensor that shuts its SENT output off
Missing 5 V supply or ground from the controller
s: Check engine or emission warning lamp
Further codes for the controller input or the second bank
Particulate filter regeneration may be postponed

U0620.t: Lost Communication With Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Bank 1 Sensor 2
U0620.d: Sensor 2 on bank 1 is the next exhaust temperature measuring point downstream of sensor 1; on diesels it usually sits ahead of the particulate filter or the SCR catalyst, depending on how the maker numbers its sensors. U0620 is the lost-communication code for this point when it is a digital sensor: its frames have stopped, are too old, or its own diagnosis has switched the SENT output off. GM uses it in the same 2025 diesel tables as U061F with an identical rule (19 bad out of 25 samples at 100 ms, Type A), and again a second code identifies the controller input the sensor is connected to. Monitors and regeneration decisions that need this temperature cannot use it while the link is down. An analog sensor at the same position reports circuit faults as P2031 to P2033.
c: Signal, supply or ground wire of the sensor damaged near the exhaust
Moisture or corrosion in the underbody connector
s: Malfunction indicator lamp in the first trip on GM diesels
Diesel particulate filter or SCR warnings may follow

U0621.t: Lost Communication With Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Bank 2 Sensor 1
U0621.d: U0621 mirrors U061F on bank 2: messages from the first exhaust temperature sensor of the second cylinder bank no longer reach the controller, so the code only appears on V engines or other layouts with two exhaust paths. Bentley documents it for the V8 in the Continental GT, GTC and Flying Spur, model years 2020 to 2023 (bulletins 2065698/1 and 2065698/2): the emission warning lamp is lit and the fault memory shows U0621, often alongside U061F, as intermittent or static. The cause was the sensor harness routed close to the subframe and worn through on a bracket inside the wheel-arch liner; the repair is mending the wires and re-securing them so they cannot touch nearby parts again. GM's SENT diesel tables contain no bank 2 code. Analog circuit faults at this position are P0547 to P0549.
c: Harness rubbed through on the subframe or a wheel-arch bracket
Electronics of the bank 2 sensor failed
s: Emission warning lamp on
Code logged as intermittent first, later static

U0622.t: Lost Communication With Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Bank 2 Sensor 2
U0622.d: U0622 covers the second exhaust temperature measuring point on bank 2 when it is a digital sensor that transmits its value as SENT or CAN messages. The controller sets it once those messages stop or keep failing their checks, for instance after a broken signal wire, a lost 5 V supply or a fault inside the sensor module, an electronics box that on active sensors must tolerate up to 140 °C beneath the car. No manufacturer publicly documents U0622: GM's diesels with SENT temperature sensors have only one bank, and the Bentley V8 bulletins name only the sensors at position 1. CARB requires a dedicated code for a digital input that stops communicating, which is the role of this code. Judging by the documented neighbours, the harness routing near the exhaust is the first thing to inspect. Analog faults here are P2034 to P2036.
c: Sensor wiring chafed or melted along the bank 2 exhaust
5 V supply or ground to the sensor interrupted
Heat-damaged electronics module of the sensor
s: Malfunction indicator lamp
Exhaust temperature for bank 2 sensor 2 missing in live data

U0623.t: Lost Communication With Coolant Pump A
U0623.d: Coolant pump A is an electric pump whose speed is set over a digital link, typically LIN, and which reports its status back. GM's 2025 tables (25OBDG03A, 25OBDG04B) call it the auxiliary electric water pump and fail U0623 as Type B when its response frame is absent for 2.5 s although the LIN channel is ready and either the actuator relay or the powertrain relay is energised. On the Duramax 3.0 diesel GM bulletin 23-NA-102 names it the heater coolant pump; it shares ECM LIN bus 1 with grille shutters and fans, so chafed wiring sets several codes together. Stellantis bulletin 08-399-25 for the 2024 Dodge Hornet PHEV (also Alfa Romeo Tonale) lists U0623 alongside P2601 and fixes it by reflashing the hybrid control processors. Effects range from weak heating to blocked cabin preconditioning.
c: Chafed or pinched LIN harness shared with other actuators (GM 23-NA-102)
Outdated hybrid or inverter controller software (Stellantis 08-399-25)
Blown fuse, relay or open supply/ground to the pump
s: Check engine light
Reduced cabin heat or failed scheduled preconditioning on plug-in hybrids
Other LIN device codes (grille shutters, fans) stored at the same time

U0624.t: Lost Communication With Coolant Pump B
U0624.d: Some engines carry a second electric coolant pump, for instance one that keeps coolant moving through the turbocharger after shutdown or feeds a separate heater or low-temperature loop. Which pump is B is decided by the manufacturer. No manufacturer documents U0624 publicly; GM uses U0623 and U062F for its LIN pumps instead. The code means that pump B no longer answers on its data link. Bosch's PAD2 and PCE 2.0 pumps illustrate the design: speed set by PWM or LIN and a built-in diagnostic function that reports faults to the controlling unit. CARB asks for an approved monitoring plan when an electric pump rather than a thermostat governs engine coolant temperature. Wiring and connectors come first; P261A to P261D cover the pump's control circuit.
c: Signal, supply or ground wire to pump B damaged
Fuse or relay feeding pump B open
Pump electronics failed, sometimes after overheating or a seized rotor
s: Warning lamp
Reduced heater output or higher component temperatures after shutdown

U0625.t: Lost Communication With Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor Bank 1
U0625.d: Direct-injection engines increasingly use rail pressure sensors that send pressure, and sometimes fuel temperature, digitally via SENT. U0625 says the engine controller has lost this link for the bank 1 sensor. GM's 2025 tables (25OBDG03A) set it when the SENT line stays low with at most four pulses received, in 400 of 500 samples taken every 6.25 ms, Type A; a line stuck high is GM's own code U101B, and corrupted or stale frames are logged as P128F. In 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 GM stores U0625 together with U101B when the line sits high or low for 0.5 s, again in one trip, while protocol errors go to U1374. As long as the code is active, GM suspends the fuel temperature checks of the same sensor. The bank 2 sensor has U0665; analog circuit faults are P0190 to P0194. Expect reduced power or hard running.
c: SENT signal wire shorted to ground or to voltage, or open
Fuel or oil contamination, corrosion or loose pins in the sensor connector
Rail pressure sensor electronics failed (on some engines only with the rail)
SENT input of the engine controller faulty
s: Check engine light in the first trip
Reduced power, rough running or hard starting
Further SENT codes such as U101B stored at the same time

U0626.t: Lost Communication With A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor A
U0626.d: Without a refrigerant pressure reading the climate controller cannot protect the compressor or schedule the condenser fan. When pressure sensor A digitizes its value itself and transmits it as a LIN or SENT frame, U0626 marks that the frame has stopped arriving; which point of the circuit gets the letter A is up to the manufacturer. No manufacturer documents U0626 publicly. Audi illustrates the pattern with its combined sensor G395, which the body module polls as a LIN slave: if the air quality sensor drops out together with it, the shared LIN wire is usually pinched (Audi stores its own codes). The A/C normally shuts down until contact returns. Hardwired sensors report P0530 to P0533 instead, and P2CD4 compares sensor A with B.
c: LIN wire to the sensor pinched, chafed or cut (Audi documents this for G395)
Corroded, loose or pushed-back terminals at the sensor connector
Sensor supply voltage missing or ground intermittently open
Sensor electronics failed, often after moisture or refrigerant leaking at the sensor
s: A/C compressor stays off, no cooling
A/C fault message or flashing A/C indicator
Other LIN devices on the same line may also report no communication

U0627.t: Lost Communication With A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor A
U0627.d: Refrigerant temperature matters most where a controller adjusts superheat itself, as with electronic expansion valves and heat pumps; it also guards against overheated discharge gas. U0627 is set once the digital temperature value from sensor A is no longer received. Many suppliers build temperature and pressure into one housing; Sensata, for example, offered such R744 sensors with LIN, PWM or analog output. If U0626 appears at the same moment, the shared plug, LIN line or supply of that combined part is the first suspect; if only U0627 is present, the temperature channel or a separate sensor is more likely. No manufacturer documents U0627 publicly. Depending on the strategy, cooling or heat-pump output drops or stops. Analog equivalents are P0EBC to P0EBF.
c: Connector, LIN line or supply of a combined pressure/temperature sensor faulty
Temperature channel or sensor electronics failed
Climate or thermal controller no longer polls the sensor (software or LIN master fault)
s: Reduced cooling or heat-pump output
Heat-pump mode unavailable, auxiliary heater takes over
A/C fault message

U0628.t: Lost Communication With A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor B
U0628.d: A second pressure transducer appears mainly in heat pumps and CO2 (R744) systems, where both the low and the high side are measured to control efficiency and detect leaks; the Sensata R744 presentation lists heat-pump control and leak diagnosis among those uses. U0628 means that the digital pressure value from sensor B no longer reaches its controller. If sensor A still reports while B is silent, the fault is likely in B's own branch, plug or electronics rather than in the controller. No manufacturer documents U0628 publicly. Losing the second pressure value usually ends heat-pump operation or forces a conservative compressor mode. Hardwired faults of the same sensor show as P2515 to P2518 or P05E2; disagreement between A and B is P2CD4.
c: Damaged LIN, supply or ground wire in the branch to sensor B
Wet, corroded or loose connector at sensor B
s: Heat pump does not heat, cabin heating relies on the auxiliary heater
Weak or no A/C cooling
A/C or thermal system warning message

U0629.t: Lost Communication With A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor B
U0629.d: A second refrigerant temperature point is typical where an electronic expansion valve meters flow, for instance at the evaporator or chiller outlet, so that superheat can be calculated from temperature and pressure. U0629 is logged when the controller stops getting answers from temperature sensor B over its serial link. A digital sensor can diagnose its own measuring element, so U0629 points to the transmission path or to a sensor that has gone completely silent, not to a merely implausible reading. When U0628 is stored as well, a combined pressure/temperature unit B or its line is the likely common cause. No manufacturer documents U0629 publicly. Often only one operating mode, such as battery chilling or heat pump, is lost. Analog circuit faults are P0EC1 to P0EC4.
c: LIN line or connector at temperature sensor B open, shorted or corroded
Combined pressure/temperature unit B failed (often together with U0628)
Fuse or supply feed for sensor B open
s: Battery cooling or heat-pump mode unavailable
Uneven or reduced A/C performance

U062A.t: Lost Communication With A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve Actuator A
U062A.d: Heat pumps and battery-cooling circuits need valves that redirect refrigerant, for example hot gas from the outer heat exchanger to an inner one when the system switches from cooling to heating. Suppliers such as Egelhof build these as motor-driven switching valves that replace two or more solenoid valves and are commanded digitally, partly via LIN. U062A is set when actuator A no longer answers its controller. No manufacturer documents U062A publicly. How serious it is depends on what the valve feeds: BMW, for one, lit the MIL on the i3 for a jammed refrigerant shutoff valve in the battery cooling branch (its own code 21F0D0). Hardwired versions of valve A report P2611 to P2613, P266F or the mechanical fault P0EC9.
c: LIN, supply or ground wire to valve actuator A damaged
Moisture or corrosion in the actuator connector
Software fault in the controlling module (reprogramming may be needed)
s: Switching between cooling and heat-pump mode fails
No cabin heat from the heat pump or no cooling in one branch
Thermal system warning, possibly reduced charging or drive power

U062B.t: Lost Communication With A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve Actuator B
U062B.d: Valve B is a further refrigerant switching point, for instance one that opens or closes a rear evaporator or a battery chiller path; the assignment of letters differs from maker to maker. U062B records that actuator B has stopped responding to its digital commands. While A still answers, the shared LIN master and the main feed are probably sound and the search narrows to B's branch. Egelhof's multi-way valve shows another design: one LIN-controlled motor unit with up to seven positions takes the place of up to four solenoid valves, so a single silent actuator can block several flow paths at once. No manufacturer documents U062B publicly. P0EE3 to P0EE6 cover the electrical circuit of valve B and P0EE2 a stuck valve.
c: Wiring fault in the branch to valve actuator B
Loose or corroded connector at actuator B
Actuator B electronics or motor unit failed
s: One cooling branch (rear A/C or battery chiller) does not work
Several heat-pump modes unavailable at once with a multi-way valve
Thermal system warning message

U062C.t: Lost Communication With A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve Actuator C
U062C.d: A third distribution valve only exists in elaborate thermal systems that combine cabin cooling, heat pump, dehumidification and battery conditioning in one refrigerant loop. U062C is stored when valve actuator C fails to reply on its serial line. In such layouts several actuators often hang on one LIN segment; if C and D are lost together while A and B still answer, check the common wiring section, splice or supply of that segment before replacing any valve. No manufacturer documents U062C publicly. CARB asks for a dedicated fault for missing communication with digital components only where they are monitored for emissions or other diagnostics, which is rarely the case for cabin climate valves.
c: Shared LIN segment, splice or supply feeding valve C damaged (often with U062D)
Connector at actuator C loose, wet or corroded
s: A single heat-pump or dehumidifying mode no longer works
Windows fog more easily in heating mode
Climate system warning or reduced comfort without warning

U062D.t: Lost Communication With A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve Actuator D
U062D.d: Actuator D is the fourth refrigerant switching valve and appears only in loops with many separately controlled paths; because a single multi-way unit can replace up to four solenoid valves, many vehicles never use the letter D. U062D means the controller sent requests to valve D and got no valid answer within its expected schedule. No manufacturer documents U062D publicly. A useful check is whether the actuator wakes up and draws current when commanded: no current hints at supply or ground, current without reply at the LIN line or the actuator itself. Replacing a valve body means opening the refrigerant circuit, so recovery, evacuation and recharge are part of the job. Related actuators are U062A to U062C.
c: Supply or ground of actuator D missing (no current draw when commanded)
LIN line to actuator D open or shorted
s: One refrigerant path cannot be opened or closed
Reduced heating or cooling in certain modes

U062E.t: Lost Communication With A/C Refrigerant Expansion Valve Actuator
U062E.d: An electronic expansion valve uses a geared or stepper motor to set the refrigerant flow into an evaporator or battery chiller, guided by pressure and temperature readings instead of a thermostatic bulb. Units such as Egelhof's EXV and KXV accept their target position over LIN and carry a position sensor, so they can also shut a branch completely. U062E is logged when that actuator stops answering. No manufacturer documents U062E publicly. The consequences can reach the drivetrain: on Mercedes EQE and EQS models (series 294 to 297) a faulty chiller expansion valve Y140/1 triggered a cooling-system warning announcing reduced energy input, though there the valve hung open (code B3A0077) rather than going silent. Distribution valves are covered by U062A to U062D.
c: LIN, supply or ground wire to the expansion valve damaged
Connector at the valve wet or corroded (often near the evaporator or chiller)
Software fault in the thermal or powertrain controller
s: No cooling at the affected evaporator or chiller
Cooling-system warning, possibly reduced drive or charging power on electrified vehicles
Heat pump unavailable

U062F.t: Lost Communication With Coolant Pump C
U062F.d: GM assigns coolant pump C to the pump of its low-temperature coolant loop, a separate circuit that runs well below engine temperature. The 2020 table 20OBDG04 fails U062F once LIN communication errors reach three counts, provided the bus itself is not already faulted (U1345), the pump is configured as present and run/crank voltage is at least 11 V. In 2025 (25OBDG04A) the test watches the pump's response frame CWP_Rsp and fails after 2.5 s without it. Both versions are Type B, so the MIL comes on after two trips. If the pump stays silent, the loop loses its circulation and the parts it cools can run hotter. Electric pumps like Bosch's PDE receive their speed command over LIN or PWM and report their own diagnosis.
c: LIN wire, supply or ground to the low-temperature loop pump damaged
LIN master in the engine controller faulty
s: Check engine light after two trips
Parts on the low-temperature loop may run hotter than normal

U0630.t: Lost Communication With Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 4
U0630.d: Engines with split or multi-zone cooling may measure coolant temperature at more than three points, and a sensor that sends its value as a digital message instead of a resistance can be checked for silence. U0630 means the engine controller no longer receives such messages from coolant temperature sensor 4. No manufacturer documents U0630 publicly, and where sensor 4 sits is not standardised. Since 2021 CARB requires an approved monitoring plan when an engine judges its operating temperature from sensors placed in several distinct coolant loops, so a lost sensor counts as an emission fault. Such a bus sensor has just three wires (supply, ground, data), and those plus the connector are the first suspects. The controller then works with a substitute value, and the cooling strategy may become more conservative.
c: Data, supply or ground wire to sensor 4 open or shorted
s: Check engine light
Cooling fan may run more than usual

U0631.t: Lost Communication With Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 5
U0631.d: Sensor 5 is the highest-numbered engine coolant temperature input in the J2012 list and is found only on engines that monitor many coolant zones, for example block, head, radiator outlet and separate loops. U0631 records that the controller has stopped receiving digital messages from that sensor. No manufacturer documents it publicly. Because sensor 4 and sensor 5 usually sit on different branches, U0631 on its own points to its own connector, wire or sensor electronics, while both together suggest a shared data line or supply. CARB folds sensors that watch distinct coolant loops into the cooling system monitor, so the MIL is plausible. LIN messages carry a checksum, and a sensor that answers with bad frames counts as missing too. Expect a substitute value and cautious fan control.
c: Wiring to sensor 5 damaged (open, short, chafing)
Connector at sensor 5 corroded or not latched
Sensor 5 electronics failed or sending corrupt frames
Shared supply or data line fault (often with U0630)
s: Check engine light
Fan running more often or longer

U0632.d: Many radiator fans now contain their own speed controller and take commands over LIN instead of relays. U0632 is set when fan 1 stops responding. GM (25OBDG03A, 25OBDG04B) fails it as Type B after 2.5 s without the fan's response frame and then suspends the fan speed checks P0494 and P30EE; the 2023/24 tables 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 allow three missed frames. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV assigns fan 1 to the right-hand radiator fan on LIN2 and sets the code after 2 s of failed communication. Mercedes bulletin LI20.00-P-076708 (GLC 254, GLE 167) reports the fan at full speed with a coolant warning and blames drivetrain controller software or LIN wiring; Audi bulletins for the Q7 cite chafed fan harnesses. Fans usually default to full speed.
c: Fan harness chafed or pinched near the radiator or plenum (Audi bulletins)
Fan power feed (fusible link) or ground open
Outdated software in the controller that runs the LIN bus (Mercedes PTCU)
Electronics in fan 1 failed (replaced as fan assembly)
s: Fan running continuously at full speed, loud
Check engine light and coolant warning message
On some Audi models limited engine speed or drive system fault message

U0633.d: U0633 is the counterpart for a second LIN-controlled radiator fan. GM's 2025 table 25OBDG04B checks the frame CFM2_RSP and fails after 2.5 s of silence as Type B; 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 count three missing frames, and on those engines fans 3 and 4 have their own codes on another LIN line. In the Outlander PHEV 2023 Mitsubishi's fan 2 is the left-hand unit. Audi bulletin 2072000/1 for the 2020-24 Q7, Q8 and RS Q8 family lists U0633 with fan circuit codes and the warning of limited performance with engine speed capped at 2000 rpm; the harness rubs on the right front frame rail. GM bulletin 23-NA-102 finds it on the Duramax 3.0 together with other LIN devices. Fan 2 alone failing while fan 1 still answers points to its own branch or motor.
c: Fan 2 harness rubbing on the frame rail or radiator support
Power feed or ground of fan 2 interrupted
s: Remaining fan runs at full speed or noise from the fan area
Warning lamp; on Audi models limited performance and engine speed
Rising coolant temperature in slow traffic

U0634.t: Lost Communication With Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor A
U0634.d: Liquid-cooled traction batteries check how warm the coolant is where it enters or leaves the pack to decide whether to cool or heat. Where that sensor is a digital node rather than a plain thermistor, the battery or thermal controller can detect when its messages stop, and U0634 records exactly that for sensor A. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; GM, for instance, reads its battery coolant sensors as analog thermistors, with P0C42 to P0C46 for their circuit faults. For hybrids CARB requires every electronic input used for battery thermal management to be monitored like any comprehensive component, so a MIL is to be expected there. Without the reading the controller must estimate pack temperature and may reduce charge or drive power.
c: Data, supply or ground wire to sensor A damaged
Connector at the battery coolant line corroded or loose
Battery or thermal management controller fault
s: Hybrid or battery warning lamp, on hybrids also the MIL
Reduced charging power or limited electric performance

U0635.t: Lost Communication With Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor B
U0635.d: Sensor B is the second battery coolant temperature point, commonly placed on the opposite side of the pack from sensor A so the controller can see how much heat the coolant picks up. U0635 means sensor B no longer delivers digital messages. No public manufacturer document uses the code. With sensor A still working the controller keeps one reference but loses the temperature difference across the pack, which it uses to size pump speed and chiller or heater demand. CARB's hybrid rules count such inputs among the battery thermal management parts that must be monitored, and also ask for a functional check of cooling where feasible. The analog circuit faults of the same sensor are P0CD5 to P0CD9. Check the wiring branch to B before replacing parts.
c: Wiring branch to sensor B open, shorted or chafed
Moisture or corrosion at the sensor B connector
s: Battery or hybrid system warning
Battery cooling runs more often or charging power is reduced

U0636.t: Lost Communication With Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve A
U0636.d: Battery thermal loops use motor-driven valves to send coolant through the chiller, the heater or a bypass, or to link the battery loop with the drive unit circuit. Many of these valves have a small controller of their own: Hutchinson's rotary three-way valve for electric vehicles talks LIN, and Thomas offers its coolant valves with PWM, LIN or CAN control and an optional self-diagnosis. U0636 is stored when valve A stops replying to the battery or thermal controller. No manufacturer documents the code publicly. Valve A then holds its last or default position, so the pack may be cooled or heated too little; CARB treats such valves on hybrids as monitored thermal management outputs. P0CDF to P0CE3 cover the electrical control circuit of the same valve.
c: LIN, supply or ground wire to valve A damaged
Thermal or battery controller software fault
s: Battery or hybrid system warning
Reduced fast-charging power or limited drive power when the battery is hot or cold
Cabin heating or cooling behaving differently

U0637.t: Lost Communication With Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve B
U0637.d: Valve B is a second smart valve in the battery coolant loop, for example a mixing valve that blends chilled and warm coolant or a switch-over valve to the drive unit circuit. U0637 is set when valve B goes silent on its data link while the controller may still talk to valve A. No manufacturer documents U0637 publicly, so which function the letter B stands for varies. Thermal management actuators of this kind, such as Hella's 360-degree rotary actuators, take LIN or PWM commands; on a LIN link the controller notices quickly when a node stops answering. A single silent valve points to its own connector, wiring branch or actuator. Expect a warning and limited charge or drive power in hot or cold conditions. P0D1A to P0D1E cover the valve's control circuit.
c: Wiring branch to valve B open, shorted or chafed
Valve B connector loose or corroded
Valve B actuator failed, sometimes after a jammed valve body
s: Battery or hybrid system warning
Limited charging or drive power in hot or cold weather

U0638.t: Lost Communication With Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor A
U0638.d: The coolant loop that serves the inverter and other high-voltage electronics needs its own temperature reading so the controller can size pump speed and decide when to derate. When sensor A on that loop is a bus node that sends its value digitally, for instance over LIN, the receiving controller notices when frames stop coming, and U0638 records that silence. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15.2.3)(B)(ii) requires every electronic input that serves inverter cooling to be checked like other input components, so a MIL is expected on hybrids. An analog sensor of the same position reports wiring faults through P0CEE to P0CF2 instead. Without a reading the system usually assumes a warm loop and limits electric power.
c: Data, supply or ground line to sensor A open, shorted or chafed
Corroded or loose connector at the electronics coolant line
Internal electronics of sensor A failed
Fault or outdated software in the controller that polls the sensor
s: Hybrid system warning, on hybrids usually the MIL as well
Reduced electric drive power, especially under load or in hot weather
Electronics coolant pump running continuously at high speed

U0639.t: Lost Communication With Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor B
U0639.d: A second temperature point in the electronics cooling loop, labelled B, lets the controller compare inlet and outlet or watch a separate branch, and the pair is checked against each other by P2D2A. U0639 means that sensor B, read as a digital bus participant, has gone quiet while the bus itself is still working. No manufacturer documents U0639 publicly, so its exact mounting point stays vehicle-specific. CARB treats such inputs of inverter thermal management as monitored components under (e)(15.2.3)(B)(ii). While sensor B is missing, any plausibility check between A and B cannot run, and the cooling strategy falls back to sensor A alone or to a model. Wiring faults of an analog sensor B would appear as P2B20 to P2B23.
c: Harness to sensor B damaged, for example near hoses or brackets
Moisture or bent pins in the sensor B connector
Sensor B itself no longer transmits
s: Hybrid or EV system warning lamp
Correlation checks between the electronics coolant sensors disabled
Occasional power limitation on long climbs or fast charging

U063A.t: Lost Communication With Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Temperature Sensor C
U063A.d: Sensor C is the third digitally connected temperature sensor in the cooling loop for the hybrid or EV power electronics. It is found where a system splits the loop further, for example to give a DC/DC converter or onboard charger its own reading. U063A is stored when its frames stop arriving. No public manufacturer documentation names this code or the location of sensor C. California's OBD II rule lists inverter cooling inputs among the monitored parts, so a hybrid has to flag the loss. If only U063A is present while A and B still answer, a local fault at sensor C or its branch of the harness is far more likely than a bus-wide problem. The analog counterparts are P2B24 to P2B27.
c: Open or chafed wire in the branch that feeds sensor C only
Sensor C connector unplugged after service work or corroded
s: Hybrid or EV warning lamp
Possible reduction of charging or drive power

U063B.t: Lost Communication With Coolant Bypass Valve Actuator A
U063B.d: Rotary coolant valves are often moved by a smart actuator that takes its target angle over LIN and reports back. U063B covers the case where actuator A no longer replies. Mercedes-Benz uses it in the drivetrain controller N127 (PTCU, CPC3) for the control valve of the high-temperature circuit; bulletin LI20.00-P-076708 for the GLC 254 and the facelifted GLE 167 (model year 2024) lists U063B00 and U063B87 (message missing) together with codes for fan 1, coolant pumps and an exhaust flap on the same LIN line. The check engine lamp comes on, a coolant service message appears and the radiator fan runs flat out. For the GLC with PTCU version 22A the cure is new software; otherwise connectors and LIN wiring are inspected. Electrical faults of the valve drive itself are P0E75 to P0E7A.
c: Outdated drivetrain controller software (Mercedes PTCU version 22A)
Damaged, chafed or corroded LIN wiring or intermediate connectors
Electronics in valve actuator A failed
Missing supply voltage or ground at the actuator
s: Check engine light with coolant service message
Radiator fan permanently running at full speed and noisy
Further LIN codes (fan, coolant pumps, exhaust flap) stored together

U063C.t: Lost Communication With Coolant Bypass Valve Actuator B
U063C.d: U063C is the counterpart for the second networked coolant bypass actuator, B. Stellantis lists it for the 3.0-litre Hurricane straight six: bulletin 18-071-26 (2025 Ram 1500) and bulletins 18-082-26 and 18-083-26 (2025 Jeep Wagoneer and Grand Wagoneer) name U063C next to the circuit and performance codes P0E7C to P0E7F of the same valve. In these cases the root cause is powertrain control module software, and the repair is a PCM check and reflash of about 0.2 hours; no hardware has to be replaced. The MIL is lit. Where no such update applies, a lost bus link to actuator B still points to wiring, connector or the actuator. A failed valve can disturb warm-up, cabin heat or coolant temperature control.
c: Bus, supply or ground wire to actuator B damaged
Loose or corroded actuator B connector
s: Malfunction indicator lamp on
Codes P0E7C to P0E7F for bypass valve B stored at the same time
Irregular warm-up or weak cabin heat

U063D.t: Lost Communication With Hybrid/EV Electronics Coolant Pump A
U063D.d: The first electric pump of the power electronics loop, A, circulates coolant through the inverter, DC/DC converter and similar parts. Pumps of this class, such as Bosch's PAD2, take their speed command via PWM or LIN and run their own diagnosis; with LIN the controller also expects regular status replies. U063D is set when pump A stops answering. No manufacturer documents U063D publicly. California's OBD II regulation covers the outputs of inverter cooling too, which makes a lit MIL likely on hybrids. If the pump is dead rather than just mute, P2C68 (stalled) or P0CEA (performance) tend to follow. Pumps B and C report the same fault as U02BA and U02C1. The electronics heat up and the system cuts power.
c: Blown fuse or open supply/ground to electronics coolant pump A
LIN wire to the pump open, shorted or chafed
Pump electronics failed, often after running dry or overheating
Fault in the hybrid or thermal controller acting as bus master
s: Hybrid system warning and MIL
Reduced electric drive power or engine kept running on hybrids
Inverter or electronics overtemperature messages

U063E.t: Lost Communication With Exhaust Heat Exchanger Bypass Valve Actuator A
U063E.d: Exhaust heat recovery passes hot exhaust through a coolant heat exchanger after a cold start, so the engine and cabin warm up sooner; a flap later diverts the gas around it. When that flap's actuator is a LIN slave, losing it gives U063E. GM documents the check in its hybrid tables 16OBDG02 through 19OBDG02, run by the second hybrid powertrain control processor: with the controller on, Run/Crank active, LIN enabled for at least 2 s and battery voltage at least 10.2 V, 80 missed replies at 40 ms intervals (3.2 s) fail it as Type B, MIL after two trips. A stuck flap can slow warm-up or keep heating the coolant when it should not. Circuit and position faults of the flap are P237C to P237F and P2C22 to P2C25; actuator B is U066C.
c: Actuator electronics damaged by heat near the exhaust
LIN or supply wiring under the vehicle damaged or corroded
Water ingress or corrosion in the actuator connector
Weak 12 V supply interrupting LIN communication
s: MIL after two drive cycles
Slower engine and cabin warm-up in cold weather
Engine runs longer on hybrids to reach operating temperature

U063F.t: Lost Communication With Engine Coolant Flow Control Valve Position Sensor
U063F.d: The coolant flow control valve meters how much coolant passes through the engine, and its position sensor often transmits over SENT, a one-way digital protocol with a frame every few milliseconds. U063F flags the loss of that stream. GM's 2025 diesel tables (25OBDG04B) treat it as a Type B fault, with the MIL on the second trip, when 80 of 100 samples taken every 6.25 ms are bad: the last valid SENT frame is older than 6.25 ms while the line sits steady low or high, SENT frame errors are counted, or the pulse counter stops updating. The powertrain relay must supply more than 11 V and the engine must not be cranking. GM's harness chafing bulletin 21-NA-149 for 2019 to 2022 trucks and SUVs lists U063F among many codes. Analog-type sensor faults are P2B5D to P2B60 and P2B6D.
c: Engine harness chafed through to the SENT, supply or ground wire (GM 21-NA-149)
Corroded or loose connector at the flow control valve
Position sensor electronics in the valve failed (usually replaced with the valve)
SENT input of the engine control module faulty
s: Check engine light after two trips
Coolant temperature control less precise, slower warm-up or higher temperatures

U0640.t: Lost Communication With EVAP Fuel Vapor Temperature Sensor Circuit
U0640.d: Many fuel tank pressure senders also measure the temperature of the vapor in the tank, and when such a sender reports digitally, typically over SENT, both values share one data stream. U0640 is stored when the engine controller no longer receives valid temperature data from this sensor. Despite the word circuit in the title, the fault concerns the digital link; an analog vapor temperature sensor reports wiring faults as P2024 to P2028. Audi documents U0640 together with U0641 for 2021–2023 A4 and A5 models with the 2.0 TFSI EA888: electrical interference on the vent system signal sets both codes sporadically, the cure is swapping two wires of a twisted bundle in the harness, and a new sender does not help. The MIL comes on, while the car drives normally.
c: Interference or chafing on the shared signal line of the tank pressure/temperature sender
Loose or corroded connector at the tank sender
Electronics of the sender failed (only if the code is stored permanently)
Engine controller software or input fault
s: Check engine light on
Often stored together with U0641
Evaporative system monitor does not complete

U0641.t: Lost Communication With EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch Circuit A
U0641.d: Pressure sensor A is the main input for the evaporative leak test that CARB 1968.2 (e)(4) requires: with the system sealed, the controller follows how pressure in tank and canister rises or falls. Newer designs often use a relative pressure sensor with SENT output; Melexis' MLX90821, for example, spans about −0.06 to 0.26 bar in its SENT version and can add a media temperature. U0641 means these digital messages are missing or unusable, which (e)(15.2.1)(B)(i) treats as its own fault; an analog sensor would log P0450 to P0454. Audi's 2.0 TFSI bulletin for 2021–2023 A4/A5 separates sporadic entries, caused by interference and fixed in the harness, from permanent ones that need normal diagnosis. The leak test stays blocked and the MIL is on.
c: Electrical interference or damage on the sensor signal line
Connector at the tank or canister sensor loose, wet or corroded
Pressure sensor A itself no longer sends
s: MIL on
EVAP leak monitor not ready, possible inspection failure
No noticeable change in driving

U0642.t: Lost Communication With EVAP System Pressure Sensor/Switch Circuit B
U0642.d: A second EVAP pressure sensor, B, appears where one reading is not enough, for instance when tank and canister are separated by an isolation valve and each side needs its own value, as in sealed tanks of plug-in hybrids that see higher pressures. Which location is called B is up to the manufacturer. U0642 is the lost-communication code for this sensor when it reports digitally; its analog counterpart logs P24D5 to P24D9. No manufacturer documents U0642 publicly. Because CARB 1968.2 (e)(15.2.1)(B)(i) demands a separate code for a digital input that stops talking, the code exists independently of U0641. While B is silent, the controller cannot compare both sides or check the isolation valve, so the leak test is suspended and a MIL is to be expected.
c: Signal, supply or ground line to sensor B open or chafed
Corroded or unplugged connector at sensor B
Receiving controller input or software fault
s: MIL on
EVAP monitor incomplete
On sealed tanks possibly a delayed fuel door release

U0643.t: Lost Communication With Turbocharger/Supercharger A Temperature Sensor
U0643.d: This sensor reports a temperature at charger A, whose exact measuring point the J2012 title leaves open; depending on the design it can watch the compressor outlet or the hot side. GM's tables define charger A as the first one in the exhaust path on series layouts and the bank 1 charger on parallel ones. When the sensor is a digital part, for instance with SENT output, the controller sets U0643 as soon as valid frames stop arriving; analog wiring and range faults go to P2B6E to P2B71 instead, and charger B uses U0689. No manufacturer documents U0643 publicly. Without the temperature the engine management loses a protection input for the charger and usually caps boost, so the engine can feel weak under load.
c: Wiring near the charger damaged by heat or chafing
s: MIL on
Reduced boost and power
Further boost-related codes stored

U0644.t: Lost Communication With Wastegate Position Sensor A
U0644.d: Pneumatic wastegates have largely given way to electric actuators, and these carry a position sensor so the controller knows how far the bypass flap around the turbine is open. GM reads that sensor on charger A over SENT and, in the 2025 table 25OBDG03B, stores U0644 when message faults appear or a frame is older than 3.13 ms in 10 out of 12 samples taken every 100 ms, with relay voltage of at least 11 V and the engine not cranking; it is Type A, so the MIL comes on in the first trip. GM's harness bulletin PIT5677 for the 2.7L L3B in 2019–2021 Silverado and Sierra 1500 lists U0644 among codes caused by a chafed engine harness. Analog faults would be P2AB7 to P2AB9. Expect reduced power.
c: Engine harness chafed at brackets or covers
Connector at the wastegate actuator loose or corroded
Position sensor in the actuator failed
Low supply voltage or poor ground
s: MIL on from the first trip
Reduced engine power, boost limited
Several other engine codes when the harness is damaged

U0645.t: Lost Communication With Active Air Dam Module
U0645.d: An active air dam is a motor-driven panel below the front bumper that drops at highway speed to cut drag and retracts for low speed or rough ground. Its small control module talks to the powertrain controller over a serial line; on the 2.7L F-150 Ford runs it on a LIN bus shared with the generator and the grille shutters. U0645 is logged once that module no longer replies. Ram uses it on the 1500 DT: TSB 23-029-22 covers 2019 trucks built up to 21 January 2019 (sales code MXB) with the MIL lit, and a new air dam under an eight-year warranty extension. A 2025 Ram case asks for impact damage, connector corrosion and resistance checks first. Ford's SSM 50737 blames a LIN wire grounded at the left engine mount. Actuator faults are C0601 to C0630.
c: Air dam unit with built-in module failed (early Ram 1500 DT)
Air dam damaged by curb, snow or debris impact
Water or corrosion in the air dam connector
Shared LIN wire chafed to ground near the engine mount (Ford F-150 2.7L)
s: Air dam stays in one position
Check engine light on some trucks (Ram)
Charging system warning if the shared LIN line is shorted (Ford)

U0646.t: Lost Communication With Motor Electronics Coolant Pump A
U0646.d: In these titles, motor electronics stands for the power electronics that feed an electric drive motor in a hybrid or EV, and coolant pump A is the main electric pump of that loop. When it is commanded by LIN rather than a plain PWM wire, the controlling module can tell when the pump stops talking, which is what U0646 stores. No manufacturer documents U0646 publicly; the same pump with conventional wiring would instead set P0A05 to P0A07 for its control circuit or P0C73 for poor performance. Pumps that cool an inverter count as monitored thermal management outputs in CARB's rules, which argues for a MIL. Without confirmed flow the controller limits motor torque to protect the electronics, so the car may feel down on power.
c: Fuse, relay or power feed of motor electronics pump A interrupted
LIN line between controller and pump damaged
s: Hybrid or EV system warning and MIL
Limited drive motor torque or power
Motor electronics over-temperature message, see P0A7C

U0647.t: Lost Communication With Motor Electronics Coolant Pump B
U0647.d: Cars fitted with two or more drive units, or with separate loops for the motor and its inverter, may fit a second networked pump in the motor electronics circuit, called B. U0647 is logged when this pump no longer returns its status frames. Public manufacturer documentation for U0647 does not exist. Since it is a separate node, the typical clue is that pump A and the rest of the bus still communicate, which narrows the search to pump B's own branch of wiring, its connector and its fuse. The conventional circuit codes for this pump are P0B38 to P0B3A, with P0C74 for performance and P2D05 to P2D09 for internal pump faults. Electric pumps such as Bosch's PCE generation take LIN commands and diagnose themselves. Expect reduced power from the axle that pump B cools.
c: Wiring branch or fuse that serves only pump B open
Pump B connector corroded or not fully seated
s: Hybrid or EV warning lamp, MIL on hybrids
Power limited on one drive unit

U0648.t: Lost Communication With Motor Electronics Coolant Pump C
U0648.d: U0648 belongs to a third digitally controlled pump in the motor electronics cooling, labelled C, which only more elaborate layouts carry, for example a generator inverter with its own loop. The fault means the pump has dropped off the bus. No carmaker publishes a description of U0648, so which component pump C cools has to be taken from the vehicle's own service information. CARB's rule for inverter thermal management, (e)(15.2.3)(B)(ii), still applies to hybrids. A pump with plain wiring would report P2BD4 to P2BD7 or the internal faults P2D0A to P2D0E. If A, B and C drop out together, look for a shared cause such as a common fuse, ground point or bus master rather than three failed pumps.
c: Data or supply line to pump C damaged
Shared fuse or ground point of the pumps faulty (several pump codes at once)
s: Hybrid or EV warning lamp
Reduced power from the electric machine cooled by pump C

U0649.t: Lost Communication With Coolant Pump D
U0649.d: Coolant pump D is the fourth auxiliary electric pump in the generic lettering that runs from A (U0623) through B and C (U0624, U062F) to E (U0698). What D circulates is up to the manufacturer; GM, for example, assigns C to its low-temperature loop, while Mercedes uses the E code for a pump of its low-temperature circuit. U0649 is set when pump D, controlled over LIN or a similar link, no longer sends a response. No manufacturer documents U0649 publicly. Pumps of this kind receive speed commands over LIN or PWM and report their own diagnosis, as Bosch describes for the PDE. Its circuit and internal faults are P2B66 to P2B6C, with P2C49 and P2BA1 for performance and underspeed. Loss of the pump leaves its loop without circulation.
c: LIN, supply or ground wire to pump D damaged
Controller acting as LIN master faulty or needing a software update
s: Warning lamp, depending on manufacturer the MIL
Components on the affected loop run warmer than normal

U064A.t: Lost Communication With Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor A
U064A.d: Battery management needs the pack current to count charge in and out and to judge state of charge and state of health. Many packs measure it with a self-contained sensor that sends its value over CAN; LEM's CAB series, for example, transmits on high-speed CAN at 500 kbit/s and is built for ASIL C. U064A records that current sensor A has stopped sending, while an analog sensor would report wiring faults via P0ABF to P0AC3. No manufacturer documents U064A publicly. CARB 1968.2 (e)(15.2.3)(A)(iv) requires the electronic inputs of the energy storage system to be monitored, which on hybrids points to a lit MIL. Without a current value the battery controller cannot track charge and normally restricts charging and discharging sharply.
c: CAN, supply or ground wiring of sensor A inside or at the pack damaged
Moisture or corrosion at the pack's low-voltage connector
Battery energy control module fault or software
s: Hybrid or EV battery warning, on hybrids also the MIL
Strongly reduced drive power or charging refused
Implausible state-of-charge display

U064B.t: Lost Communication With Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor B
U064B.d: Some packs carry a second current sensor, B, often a different measuring principle than A, so that the battery controller can cross-check the two through P0B13 and still have a value if one fails. U064B is stored when that second digital sensor goes silent. No manufacturer publishes U064B. With only one remaining sensor the controller loses its redundancy; depending on the safety concept it may keep driving with sensor A but flag the fault, or reduce power until the plausibility check can run again. Sensors like LEM's CAB family send their readings as periodic CAN frames, so a missing frame stands out quickly. Section (e)(15.2.3)(A)(iv) of the CARB rule covers this input as well. An analog sensor B would instead log circuit faults P0B0E to P0B12.
c: Bus or supply wiring of sensor B damaged
Missing or faulty CAN termination in the pack sub-network
s: Battery system warning lamp
Correlation check between the current sensors no longer possible
Possibly reduced charging or drive power

U064C.t: Lost Communication With Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Current Sensor C
U064C.d: A third pack current sensor, C, appears where a battery has parallel strings or a separate measuring point, for instance in a battery junction box, that each need their own current value. U064C means that this sensor no longer delivers its data frames to the battery controller. No manufacturer documents U064C or the place of sensor C publicly. Because the remaining sensors cannot see the current in the branch that C watches, the controller usually lowers the permitted current for the whole pack instead of guessing. CARB's energy storage provisions treat it as a monitored input. For an analog sensor C, P2BE4 to P2BE7 would cover the circuit. LEM offers its CAB sensors up to 1,500 A, which shows the current class involved.
c: Data or supply wiring of sensor C damaged
Loose connector at the battery junction box
s: Battery warning lamp
Reduced power and slower charging

U064D.t: Lost Communication With Trailer Brake Control Switch
U064D.d: Trucks with a factory trailer brake controller carry a dash switch with gain buttons and a manual slider that lets the driver apply only the trailer brakes. On current designs this switch is a small electronic unit that reports to the brake controller, which is why GM's 2024 campaign N242442100 for the 2022 Silverado and Sierra pairs a new switch with reprogramming of the cluster and the brake module. U064D marks a broken data link to that switch. No maker documents this code in public; GM logs switch faults as C159C, and in PIT5948B and campaign N222384930 a defective switch brought up the Service Trailer Brake warning and disabled trailer braking for that key cycle. The whole controller module silent is U0137, bad data from it U0438. Brake the trailer only with caution until fixed.
c: Trailer brake control switch electronics failed
Switch connector behind the dash trim loose or not seated
Damaged data or supply wire to the switch
Brake or cluster software not matched to a replaced switch
s: Service trailer brake message in the cluster
Gain buttons and manual slider have no effect
Electric trailer brakes not applied when braking

U064E.t: Lost Communication With EGR Cooler Bypass Position Sensor Bank 1
U064E.d: Many diesels steer recirculated exhaust around the EGR cooler while the engine is cold and through it once warm, using a bypass flap with its own position sensor. CARB 1968.2 (f)(6.2.5) requires the cooler system to be checked for poor cooling, and that check only makes sense if the controller knows the flap position. U064E is set when this sensor on bank 1 is a digital part and its data no longer arrives. No manufacturer documents U064E publicly, and the published code lists show no separate bank 2 counterpart. An analog sensor would report P2492 to P2496 instead, and a learned end stop outside its limit is P24C4. While the position is unknown, the cooler performance monitor cannot run; warm-up emissions may rise slightly.
c: Wiring to the cooler bypass actuator damaged by heat or vibration
Corroded or loose connector at the bypass actuator
Position sensor in the bypass actuator failed
s: MIL on
EGR cooler monitor not completed
Usually no change in driving behaviour

U064F.t: Lost Communication With Intake Manifold Runner Position Sensor Bank 1
U064F.d: Diesel swirl flaps partly close one intake port per cylinder at low load so the charge spins and mixes better; a motor moves them and a sensor reports the angle. In GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B that sensor transmits by SENT, and U064F covers a missing or corrupt stream: an internal fault flag or message error, or position data not refreshed for over 6.25 ms with the line held steadily high or low. It must show in 480 of 600 checks taken every 6.25 ms, after cranking and with more than 11 V at the relay. As Type B it turns on the MIL only after a second failed trip. While U064F is active, GM does not judge the raw value (P2016 below 1 %, P2017 above 99 %); motor circuit faults are P2008 to P2010, failed end-stop learning P200A.
c: Oil or soot in the actuator connector, corroded pins
Position sensor in the swirl flap actuator failed
SENT signal wire chafed, open or shorted on the engine
s: MIL after two trips with the fault
Swirl flaps left in default position, slightly rougher or smokier low-load running
Often no noticeable change in driving

U0650.t: Lost Communication With Exhaust Pressure Control Valve A Sensor/Switch
U0650.d: The exhaust pressure control valve is a throttle flap in the exhaust that diesels use to raise back pressure and exhaust temperature, for example during warm-up or filter regeneration. In GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B this flap is called ETV and reports its position by SENT. U0650 is stored when 480 of 600 checks at 6.25 ms intervals find the position protocol steady low or high with outdated data, a message error, or stalled counters, with relay voltage above 11 V and the engine past cranking. Being Type A, it lights the MIL during the first faulty trip. The same table keeps the drive circuit (P0475) and tracking errors above 10 % (P0476) apart; analog sensor faults are P048B to P048F, valve B has U067E.
c: Wiring at the exhaust flap damaged by heat
Connector at the flap actuator corroded or loose
Position sensor in the flap actuator failed
s: MIL on from the first trip
Particulate filter regeneration delayed or blocked
Slower warm-up in cold weather

U0651.t: Lost Communication With EGR Sensor A
U0651.d: EGR sensors A to D are generic slots: a maker may assign them to valve position, pressure or another EGR measurement. In GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B, which has both a high-pressure and a low-pressure EGR loop, sensor A is the SENT position sensor of the high-pressure valve. U0651 is set there if at least 480 out of 600 tests, one every 6.25 ms, find stale data with the line stuck low or high, a message error, or counters that stop, provided the relay supplies more than 11 V and no start is in progress; Type A, MIL in the first trip. A raw signal below 1 % of 5 V on the same sensor is P0405 instead. Other analog faults run through P0405 to P0409 and P046C. EGR flow monitoring stops while the position is missing.
c: SENT line to the EGR valve damaged by heat or chafing
EGR valve connector corroded or loose
Position sensor in the EGR valve failed
s: MIL on from the first trip
EGR switched off, possibly louder combustion
EGR monitor not ready

U0652.t: Lost Communication With EGR Sensor B
U0652.d: U0652 covers a digital EGR sensor labelled B that has stopped delivering data. What B measures depends on the maker; it may be the position of a second valve or a pressure or temperature signal of the EGR path. No manufacturer documents U0652 publicly. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B shows how loose the lettering is: it uses U0651 for the high-pressure valve and U0653 for the low-pressure valve, whose text even calls it the B position sensor, yet U0652 does not appear at all. Sections (e)(15.2.1)(B)(i) and (f)(15.2.1)(B)(i) of the CARB rule require a separate code when a digital input stops communicating. An analog sensor B reports P0486, P0407, P0408 and P046E. Whatever B serves, its EGR function and monitor are suspended until data returns.
c: Wiring to EGR sensor B open, shorted or heat-damaged
Connector at sensor B corroded or loose
s: MIL on
EGR monitor incomplete
Possibly reduced EGR operation

U0653.t: Lost Communication With EGR Sensor C
U0653.d: On GM's 2025 diesel with high- and low-pressure EGR (table 25OBDG04B), EGR sensor C is the SENT position sensor of the low-pressure valve, which as usual for such loops takes exhaust after the particulate filter and feeds it ahead of the compressor. Oddly, the table's text calls this valve the B position sensor while filing its codes under C. U0653 is stored when 480 of 600 checks every 6.25 ms see outdated data while the protocol sits permanently low or high, a corrupt message, or counters that froze; GM rates this Type A, lighting the MIL on the first trip. A raw level below 1 % on the same sensor is P044C, and P044A to P044E cover the analog faults of sensor C. While the low-pressure valve position is unknown, its loop is shut and the high-pressure loop has to cover alone.
c: Wiring to the low-pressure EGR valve damaged near the exhaust
Position sensor in the low-pressure EGR valve failed
s: MIL on from the first trip
Low-pressure EGR disabled, higher NOx
EGR monitor not ready

U0654.t: Lost Communication With Diesel Intake Air Flow A Position Sensor
U0654.d: Diesel intake air flow valve A is the throttle ahead of the intake manifold: it creates the vacuum for high EGR rates, trims airflow for filter regeneration and shuts at switch-off. GM's 2025 diesel tables 25OBDG04A and 25OBDG04B read its angle by SENT and set U0654 when the data stop refreshing for more than 6.25 ms while the line is stuck low or high, a frame is faulty, or the counters freeze. 04A needs 200 of 250 checks, 04B 480 of 600, both every 6.25 ms after cranking with over 11 V at the relay. Type A means MIL in the first trip. GM evaluates the out-of-range codes P02E8 and P02E9 only while no such link fault exists. Ford's 2023 diesels monitor the same throttle with P02E8/P02E9 and do not list U0654. Sensor B has U0655.
c: Oil, soot or corrosion in the throttle body connector
SENT signal, supply or ground wire damaged
Position sensor in the throttle unit failed (usually replaced with the unit)
s: MIL in the first trip
EGR control restricted, particulate filter regeneration delayed
Engine may shake more at switch-off

U0655.t: Lost Communication With Diesel Intake Air Flow B Position Sensor
U0655.d: Some diesels carry a second intake air flow valve, labelled B; which flap gets that letter depends on the engine layout and the maker. When its angle sensor is a digital SENT unit, U0655 reports that the engine controller no longer receives usable position frames from it. No manufacturer documents this code in public. GM's 2025 diesel tables give SENT link codes only to valve A (U0654, Type A, 6.25 ms checks), and CARB requires a separate code whenever a digital input stops communicating. Analog sensor faults on the B side are P2396 to P239A, drive faults P2390 to P2395. Expect the flap to be switched off and left to its spring, with EGR control and regeneration limited and a likely MIL on emission-certified engines.
c: Contaminated or loose connector at throttle unit B
Signal, supply or ground wire to sensor B damaged
Digital position sensor of valve B failed
s: Check engine light
Particulate filter regeneration postponed or blocked
Little change in drivability in many cases

U0656.t: Lost Communication With Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control A Position Sensor
U0656.d: On a variable geometry turbocharger the boost control position sensor reports where the guide vanes stand, and the controller needs that feedback to regulate boost and to check, as CARB 1968.2 (f)(7.2.3) asks, that the vanes reach their target in time. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B reads this VGT position by SENT and sets U0656 when 480 of 600 checks, run every 6.25 ms, find the protocol stuck low or high with stale data, a message error, or counters that no longer update; it is Type A with the MIL in the first trip.
