Low raw signal level on the same sensor is a different code there, P2564. Analog circuit faults are P2562 to P2566, charger B uses U02B0. The vanes usually go to a safe position and power drops.
c: SENT, supply or ground line to the VGT actuator damaged
Connector at the actuator exposed to heat, oil or water
Position sensor or electronics in the VGT actuator failed
Engine controller input or software fault
s: MIL on
Limp mode with clearly reduced power
Boost control codes stored at the same time

U0657.t: Lost Communication With Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Position Sensor
U0657.d: The bypass valve meant here sits on the intake side: on turbocharged petrol engines it lets compressed air recirculate when the throttle shuts, and on supercharged engines it routes air around the blower at light load. When the valve is electrically driven and reports its position digitally, U0657 marks that the position data from valve A has stopped arriving. No manufacturer publishes a description of U0657, so the exact valve and its protocol come from the vehicle's own service information. Analog circuit faults of the same sensor are P2BBB to P2BBD and an adaptation problem is P2BBE; valve B has U066B. Without position feedback the controller cannot tell whether surplus air is being released, so it may restrict boost to protect the compressor.
c: Wiring to the bypass valve open, shorted or chafed
Position sensor in the valve failed
s: MIL on
Less boost or hesitant throttle response
Unusual whoosh or flutter when lifting off

U0658.t: Lost Communication With Windshield Temperature Sensor
U0658.d: To keep the glass clear before it mists, an automatic climate system can compare the temperature of the inner windshield surface with the cabin air's dew point right in front of it. Suppliers such as Sensirion (SAAF) and ScioSense (WSS2) build this into one small module at the mirror base that computes the dew point itself and reports over LIN at 19.2 kBd. U0658 is stored when the climate master stops getting answers from that glass sensor. No maker documents this exact code in public; FCA logs the same kind of loss as its own U1190 in the BCM, and a Pacifica case shows it appearing during remote start with nothing to replace. Without the reading the controller can only react once fog is visible, so the windshield may mist up in damp or cold weather.
c: Sensor not clipped back, unplugged or without glass contact after windshield replacement
Loose or damaged plug or LIN wire at the mirror base or headliner
Electronics of the humidity and glass temperature module failed
Code logged in a wake-up phase such as remote start without a real fault
s: Windshield fogs before the climate system responds
Automatic defog or anti-fog function inactive or less effective
Other sensors on the same mirror-base LIN line may also be missing

U0659.t: Lost Communication With Left Front Temperature Actuator
U0659.d: In a two-zone system the left front temperature actuator turns the blend door that sets how much of the air for the left side passes the heater core. As a smart LIN node it takes position requests from the climate master and replies with its state. GM documents U0659 in the body control module of its 2025 OBD tables (25OBDG03B, 25OBDG04B): the actuator reply frame missing for at least 11.5 s, evaluated every 600 ms with the battery above 11 V and no sooner than 5 s after power-up, Type B, so the MIL comes on after two trips. While it is active GM holds back the door checks B2B05, B2B28 and B2B29; corrupt counters from the same motor are GM's own U140F. The left zone, on US cars the driver, then stays at one temperature. U065A is the right-hand twin.
c: Electronics of the left temperature actuator failed
LIN, supply or ground wire to the actuator open or chafed under the dash
Actuator plug not latched after dash or footwell work
Configuration or software fault in the module that polls the actuator
s: Left zone stuck hot or cold regardless of the setting
Check engine light on GM vehicles that list the code as Type B
Climate display may show a fault or ignore left temperature changes

U065A.t: Lost Communication With Right Front Temperature Actuator
U065A.d: The right front temperature actuator only exists where the right-hand front seat gets its own blend door, as in dual-zone systems; single-zone cars move one door for both sides and never run this check. GM lists U065A next to U0659 in its 2025 BCM tables, watching the frame AHDA05_Rsp with the same 11.5 s limit and Type B rating; in 25OBDG04B that slave is calibrated as not present, so the monitor stays idle on that build. Its GM partners are U1410 for corrupt counters and B2B06, B2B2B and B2B2C for travel faults. FCA shows how a failing right door feels: 2014-15 Town and Country and Grand Caravan blew hot air from the right vents until the actuator passed a wiTECH calibration or was renewed. Here the link itself is gone, so the right side holds its last mix.
c: Right temperature actuator electronics or motor failed
Wire to the actuator damaged behind the glovebox or console side panel
Climate module configured for the wrong number of zones after replacement
s: Passenger side blows hot or cold no matter what is selected
Right temperature setting has no effect while the left side works
MIL possible on GM models with the code rated Type B

U065B.t: Lost Communication With Left Front Mode Actuator
U065B.d: The mode actuator decides where the air leaves the dash: face vents, footwell or windshield. A separate left front unit points to a layout where each front zone has its own distribution door; when the climate master gets no reply from it over LIN, U065B is stored. No maker documents this code publicly. GM's PIT5660 for the 2019 Silverado and Sierra shows the opposite case on a single mode door: the actuator lost its count of position when modes changed with vents shut and the blower on high, set no code, and relearned after about 20 key cycles. With the link down, the left outlets stay in their last mode, which matters when defrost is selected and that side cannot follow. Door range or position faults belong to codes such as B0150 or B0170.
c: Break or short on the LIN branch to the left mode actuator
Shared actuator supply or ground missing
s: Left outlets keep blowing at face, floor or glass regardless of mode
Defrost selection does not move air to the left part of the windshield
Climate fault message or flashing mode indicator

U065C.t: Lost Communication With Right Front Mode Actuator
U065C.d: A right front mode actuator lets the passenger side choose its own outlets, or in some designs close its share of the air altogether; Denso's US 2020/0189351 describes a passenger-side door driven by its own actuator so that only the driver is served. U065C means the climate master can no longer reach that right-hand unit over LIN. No maker publishes the code, so detection time and fallback depend on the vehicle. In practice the right outlets keep their last position while the left side still follows commands, so the two halves of the cabin drift apart: the passenger may get floor air when the driver asks for vents, or no air at all if the door stopped closed. Windshield defog is mostly handled by the left or a common door and stays usable.
c: Connector on the passenger side of the HVAC case loose or wet
Damaged LIN branch toward the passenger side
s: Passenger outlets ignore mode changes
Little or no airflow on the passenger side
Uneven comfort between driver and passenger

U065D.t: Lost Communication With Air Intake Actuator
U065D.d: The air intake actuator swings the inlet door between outside air and cabin air. Modern controllers move it on their own: Ford's SSM 51726 notes that the 2021-23 Bronco opens the inlet door to about half every 30 to 60 minutes in recirculation to refresh the cabin, and onsemi's TND416 describes stepper-driven recirculation flaps that find their end stop by stall detection and save compressor energy by reusing cooled air. U065D is set when the climate master hears nothing more from this actuator. No maker documents the code in public. Which way it hurts depends on where the door stopped: stuck in recirculation, humidity builds and the glass fogs; stuck on fresh air, exhaust odour enters in traffic and maximum cooling weakens.
c: Water ingress at the blower housing reaching the actuator plug
LIN or supply wire to the inlet actuator damaged
s: Recirculation button has no effect
Windows fog quickly when the door is stuck on recirculation
Outside smells enter the cabin when it is stuck on fresh air

U065E.t: Lost Communication With Ram Air Actuator
U065E.d: At speed, the wind pushes extra outside air through the cowl inlet into the climate housing. Some vehicles therefore fit the fresh-air path with a motorised ram air flap that narrows the opening as dynamic pressure rises, so airflow and noise stay steady; Behr's US 5,645,479 nests it with the recirculation flap, and Daimler's DE 10 2010 025 623 drives it through a non-linear linkage for fine throttling near closed. Others, like Honda in WO 2012/115719, use the inlet door for the same job and have no separate flap. U065E means the master has lost its LIN link to that flap's actuator. No maker documents the code publicly. A flap stuck open lets the cabin airflow surge and rush at motorway speed; one stuck nearly shut starves the vents at low speed.
c: Ram air flap actuator electronics failed
Moisture or debris from the cowl reaching the actuator connector
LIN wire to the ram air actuator chafed or disconnected
s: Airflow rises noticeably with road speed
Air rush noise from the vents at high speed
Weak airflow at low speed if the flap stopped nearly closed

U065F.t: Lost Communication With Left Rear Temperature Actuator A
U065F.d: Vehicles with a separately controlled rear climate zone need their own temperature doors for the rear outlets, and in a split rear system the left side may use two of them, labelled A and B. Hanon's US 11,305,608 shows why two can be needed: one door ahead of the heater core and a second behind it mixing warm air into the rear cold-air duct. Which door counts as A is up to the maker. GM uses this code: bulletin 23-NA-206 lists U065F-00 in the body control module of the CT4, CT5, Corvette, Escalade, Tahoe, Suburban and Yukon from model year 2020 or 2021 on as a history code from software anomalies that turns on no lamp and may be ignored; if it is current, normal diagnosis applies. A real loss leaves the rear left air at one temperature.
c: Software timing between modules logs a false history code (GM)
Left rear temperature actuator A failed
Rear HVAC harness or connector damaged in the floor or rear quarter
s: Often none when the code is only stored as history
Rear left air stays hot or cold
Rear temperature control has no effect on the left

U0660.t: Lost Communication With Left Rear Temperature Actuator B
U0660.d: Temperature actuator B is the second door for the same rear left zone that A serves. Where a rear zone uses two doors, one typically sets the split between cold and heated air and the other trims the mix further downstream, like the downstream rear door in Hanon's US 11,305,608; makers do not publish which letter goes to which. U0660 means the climate master gets no answer from actuator B over its LIN line. There is no public maker document for U0660; GM's 23-NA-206 lists only the A actuator on the left rear. Because A still answers, the rear left zone usually keeps some control: temperatures can be reached but overshoot, lag or sit a few degrees off. B alone missing is a narrow fault that points to that actuator or its own branch of wiring.
c: Actuator B electronics or motor failed
Fault in the wiring branch or plug that only actuator B uses
Replacement actuator not assigned or calibrated by the scan tool
s: Rear left temperature drifts or overshoots the set value
Rear left zone reacts slowly to temperature changes

U0661.t: Lost Communication With Right Rear Temperature Actuator A
U0661.d: A right rear temperature actuator is only fitted where the rear seats are split into left and right climate zones, as in four-zone systems of large sedans, SUVs and vans. Actuator A on the right is the counterpart of U065F on the left, so when this code is stored the passenger behind the front passenger seat loses temperature control while the left rear zone still works. No maker documents U0661 publicly; GM's bulletin 23-NA-206 names only the left-hand rear actuators. Hanon's US 11,305,608 shows the door arrangement that such zones rely on. Because both rear sides often share one harness and LIN segment, a single right-side code points toward the actuator itself; right and left together point toward the common wiring or the master.
c: Right rear temperature actuator A failed
Actuator plug in the right rear duct area loose or corroded
Shared rear LIN segment faulty (then usually several rear codes)
s: Right rear zone stays at one temperature
Rear right temperature buttons have no effect
Left rear zone continues to work normally

U0662.t: Lost Communication With Right Rear Temperature Actuator B
U0662.d: With four rear temperature actuators, A and B on each side, plus front units, a climate system may run many look-alike motors on LIN, where one master serves up to 15 slaves. Identical parts must be told apart, either by part variant or by position detection along a daisy chain, as the LIN article explains. That makes right rear actuator B prone to a specific trap: a new or swapped unit that was never assigned its address answers on the wrong identifier, and the master logs U0662 although the part works. No maker documents this code publicly. A genuine loss only affects the fine mixing on the right rear side; actuator A keeps basic control there. Chips such as NXP's MM908E626 show the usual three-wire hookup of supply, ground and LIN.
c: Replacement or swapped actuator B without the correct LIN address
Open supply, ground or LIN pin at actuator B
s: Right rear temperature imprecise or slow to settle
Code appears right after an actuator was replaced

U0663.t: Lost Communication With Rear Mode Actuator
U0663.d: The rear mode actuator steers rear-seat air between upper outlets, such as console or roof vents, and the rear footwell. Hanon's US 11,305,608 shows a dome-shaped rear mode door doing exactly this between console vent and rear floor vent. GM uses the code: bulletin 23-NA-206 lists U0663-00, under GM's own name with the suffix Left, in the body control module of Cadillac, Corvette, Tahoe, Suburban and Yukon models from 2020 or 2021 on, as a history entry caused by software that sets no lamp and can be ignored unless it is current. The added word Left suggests GM may split rear distribution by side. When the link is truly lost, rear passengers get air only from the outlets that were open last, for instance warm air at the face or cold air at the feet.
c: Software timing in the body or climate module storing a false history code (GM)
Harness to the rear HVAC unit or console damaged
s: No symptom if the code is only stored as history
Rear air stuck at the console or roof vents or at the floor
Rear mode button has no effect

U0664.t: Lost Communication With Rear HVAC Air Cutoff Actuator
U0664.d: Some climate units carry a door that opens or shuts the whole air supply to the rear seats, so the system can send everything forward when nobody sits in the back or when the front needs full airflow. Hanon's US 11,305,608 places such an on-off door on the rear cold-air passage, and Denso's US 2020/0189351 moves its rear airflow door to feed or close the rear vent and heat outlets. U0664 means the climate master has lost contact with the actuator of this door. No maker documents the code in public. The impact depends on where the door stopped: closed, the rear gets no conditioned air at all; open, the rear keeps blowing even when switched off and the front loses some airflow, most noticeable during maximum cooling or defrost.
c: Actuator plug at the rear outlet of the HVAC case not seated
LIN or supply wire to the cutoff actuator damaged
s: No air at the rear outlets
Rear outlets keep blowing although rear climate is off
Reduced airflow at the front during maximum cooling or defrost

U0665.t: Lost Communication With Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor Bank 2
U0665.d: Engines with one fuel rail per cylinder bank may give each rail its own pressure sensor, and newer ones send the reading digitally via SENT. U0665 says the controller has lost the bank 2 sensor's data. GM's 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 tables pair it with GM's own code U101C: path 1 trips when the signal line stays at high level, path 2 when it stays low, each after 0.5 s and within one trip. An out-of-range raw value from the same sensor is logged separately (GM P312B), and the plausibility tests of P01BF run on top. The bank 1 sensor follows the same logic with U0625 and U101B. Analog bank 2 circuit faults are P01BE to P01C2. Without a rail pressure value the controller falls back to a substitute model; reduced power and rough running are possible.
c: Bank 2 sensor signal wire open or shorted to ground or voltage
Fuel-soaked, corroded or loose sensor connector
Rail pressure sensor electronics on bank 2 failed
s: Check engine light after one trip
Reduced power, hesitation or rough running
GM-specific code U101C stored alongside

U0666.t: Lost Communication With Reductant Pressure Sensor
U0666.d: The reductant pressure sensor watches the DEF line between the supply pump and the dosing valve. Bosch, for instance, offers its supply module with or without such a sensor; with it, the pump only runs when dosing is requested, the line stays pressurised through stop-start phases and is purged at key-off against freezing. If the sensor speaks a digital protocol, U0666 means its messages have stopped reaching the controller. No manufacturer documents this code in public. CARB places each SCR sensor under its comprehensive component rules and demands both a dedicated code for a silent digital input and detection of faulty reductant delivery. Analog faults are P204A to P204E, pressure too low or high P20E8 or P20E9. Dosing usually stops, followed by DEF warnings and possibly a MIL.
c: DEF crystals or corrosion in the supply module connector
Harness to the tank or pump module damaged
Pressure sensor failed (often only with the pump module)
Fault in the dosing or engine control unit input
s: DEF system warning in the cluster
Dosing stopped, higher NOx output
Check engine light possible

U0667.t: Lost Communication With Engine Oil Temperature Sensor A
U0667.d: Engine oil temperature feeds warm-up strategies, injection and protection functions, and on recent engines the sensor sends it digitally over SENT. U0667 says that link has failed. Ford's 2023 diesel OBD summary lists the code in its group of SENT sensor monitors, together with the oil pressure sensor (U0600), the mass air flow sensor and others: it sets when the SENT sensor reports a communication error, checked continuously, with 5 s needed to mature. In that table P0195 is also triggered by a SENT communication error, so both may appear together, while the range check P0196 is a separate test. Analog sensors use P0195 to P0199. With no valid reading the controller substitutes a modelled temperature, which can cost some smoothness or power; Ford treats the fault as part of its OBD monitoring.
c: Oil wicking into the sensor connector
Sensor signal, 5 V supply or ground wire damaged
s: Check engine light
P0195 stored at the same time
Oil temperature reading missing in the cluster or scan tool

U0668.t: Lost Communication With Engine Oil Level Sensor Circuit
U0668.d: Despite the word circuit in its name, U0668 concerns the data link to the oil level sensor, not a voltage fault. Sensors in the sump measure the oil height either thermally or by ultrasound; Hella's PULS type packs an ultrasonic transducer, a temperature sensor and an ASIC into one module that sends its result to the engine controller over a single signal line, and loss of supply or ground is one listed failure cause. When that signal no longer arrives or is unreadable, a separate lost-communication code can be stored. No manufacturer documents U0668 in public. Because oil level is normally not emission-relevant, CARB's rule on separate codes for silent digital inputs hardly applies. Electrical sensor faults are P250A to P250E, low or high oil P250F and P252F. Check the dipstick until fixed.
c: Missing supply voltage or ground at the sensor
Sensor electronics failed or oil inside the housing
Corroded or damaged connector or harness at the oil pan
s: Oil level warning or service message in the display
Oil level reading unavailable

U0669.t: Lost Communication With EGR Sensor D
U0669.d: Two makers document sensor D as an EGR pressure sensor with SENT output. Ford's 2024–2025 gasoline OBD summary lists U0669 as EGR sensor D communication for the SENT EGR pressure sensor it calls DPFE (range 0.1 to 408.8 kPa): it is checked continuously while the EGR monitor runs and flags a fault when the sensor stops talking or sends corrupt data, after about 5 seconds. Ford's EGR flow test (P0401, P0402) waits until U0669 and the circuit codes P2380 and P2383 have passed. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B uses U0669 for the low-pressure EGR delta pressure sensor, Type A, 480 of 600 samples at 6.25 ms. Analog faults are P2380 to P2384, sensor E is U066A. Without the pressure, EGR flow cannot be judged.
c: SENT, supply or ground line to the EGR pressure sensor damaged
Connector at the pressure sensor corroded or loose
Engine controller input or software fault
s: MIL on
EGR flow monitor does not run
Sometimes rough idle or pinging when EGR is shut off

U066A.t: Lost Communication With EGR Sensor E
U066A.d: EGR sensors A to E are open slots in the code set: each maker decides whether a slot carries a valve position, a pressure or a differential pressure in the recirculation path. U066A means the engine controller no longer gets usable digital frames from the device it calls sensor E, typically a SENT part. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. In the published tables GM gives slot A to the high-pressure valve position and C to the low-pressure one, while Ford and GM use D for a SENT EGR pressure sensor (U0669); an E appears nowhere. CARB demands its own code when a digitally coded input goes silent. Analog faults of this slot are P2385 to P2389. Most systems then cut or limit EGR, and the EGR monitor stays incomplete.
c: Signal, supply or ground wire to EGR sensor E damaged by heat or chafing
Connector at the sensor loose, corroded or contaminated with soot
Engine controller input or software fault
s: Check engine light
EGR switched off or limited, sometimes harsher combustion noise
EGR readiness monitor not complete

U066B.t: Lost Communication With Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve B Position Sensor
U066B.d: When the throttle snaps shut, a compressor bypass valve lets boosted air recirculate to the inlet side instead of surging against the closed plate. Engines with two chargers or two compressor stages can carry a second such valve, and if its electric actuator reports the opening angle as a digital message, U066B means the engine controller no longer gets valid position frames from valve B. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Ford's 2024 gasoline summary checks bypass valve B only for circuit faults (P00C1/P00C2 after 5 s) and lists no position feedback for it. Analog position faults on valve B would be P2C2A to P2C2C; valve A has U0657. CARB demands a separate code for lost communication of digital inputs. Boost is usually limited.
c: Signal, supply or ground wire to the bypass valve B actuator damaged
Connector at the valve loose, corroded or heat-damaged near the turbo
Position sensor electronics in the valve actuator failed
Engine controller input or software fault
s: Check engine light
Boost limited, reduced power
Compressor surge noise when lifting off the throttle

U066C.t: Lost Communication With Exhaust Heat Exchanger Bypass Valve Actuator B
U066C.d: Exhaust heat recovery sends hot gas through a coolant heat exchanger after a cold start and later steers it past; the steering is done by bypass flaps. Actuator B is the second such flap, present only where the layout has two paths or stages. U066C is logged once that actuator, linked over a serial bus such as LIN, stops answering the controller. No maker has published a definition for this code. The nearest published check covers actuator A: GM's hybrid tables from 16OBDG02 on set U063E after 80 unanswered LIN requests at 40 ms (about 3.2 s), Type B with the MIL after two trips; no table lists a B actuator. CARB requires lost communication of digital parts to be detected separately. Hardware faults of flap B are P23A2 to P23A8. Expect slower warm-up in cold weather.
c: Actuator B electronics damaged by exhaust heat
LIN, supply or ground wire under the vehicle damaged
Water or salt corrosion in the actuator connector
Low supply voltage during the check
s: Check engine light, on some systems only after two drive cycles
Engine and cabin heater warm up more slowly
Hybrid engine runs longer to reach temperature

U066D.t: Lost Communication With Charge Air Cooler Temperature Sensor Bank 1
U066D.d: The temperature of the charge air behind the intercooler tells the engine controller how dense the intake charge is and whether the cooler still removes enough heat; CARB lists charge air cooler temperature in the data diesel vehicles must report and requires an undercooling monitor in (f)(7.2.4). U066D is reserved for a bank 1 sensor that delivers its reading as a digital frame, for example as the NTC channel of a SENT pressure sensor such as Infineon's KP276. No manufacturer documents U066D publicly: Ford (2024 gasoline, 2023 diesel) and GM (25OBDG04A, Type B) read their bank 1 sensors analog and set P007C/P007D when voltage or resistance leaves its range. Without the value the controller works from a model, and boost may be trimmed.
c: Signal or supply wire to the charge air sensor open or chafed
Oily or corroded connector at the charge air pipe
Digital sensor (often combined with boost pressure) failed
Engine controller input or software fault
s: Check engine light
Slightly reduced power at high load
Often no noticeable change in normal driving

U066E.t: Lost Communication With Charge Air Cooler Temperature Sensor Bank 2
U066E.d: A bank 2 charge air temperature only exists on V or boxer engines that run one turbocharger and one intercooler per cylinder bank. There the controller can compare both sides, and a mismatch belongs to P007F, the bank 1/bank 2 correlation code. U066E is the digital-link failure for the bank 2 sensor: its frames are missing or unusable, so that comparison and any per-bank boost correction lose their input. None of the Ford or GM OBD summaries examined shows a bank 2 charge air sensor at all, let alone a digital one, so no manufacturer can be named; analog faults would be P00A0 to P00A4. CARB's (f)(7.2.4) undercooling monitor applies per cooler. The controller substitutes the bank 1 value or a model; the driver rarely notices more than the warning lamp.
c: Wiring to the bank 2 charge air sensor damaged, often routed near the hot side
Connector at the bank 2 charge air pipe loose or oily
s: Check engine light
Possible additional bank correlation code (P007F)
Mostly unchanged driving behaviour

U066F.t: Lost Communication With Low Pressure Fuel System Sensor
U066F.d: The low-pressure side of a direct-injection fuel system runs from the tank pump to the high-pressure pump, and a sensor there lets the controller regulate the lift pump. If that sensor transmits a digital value, for example over SENT, U066F records that its messages have stopped. None of the public manufacturer documents uses the code. GM's 2025 table 25OBDG03A reads its low-side sensor, labelled fuel pressure sensor B, as a 5 V analog input at the engine controller or the pump module and fails P018C below 4 % of reference (64 failed samples in 80, Type B). Ford's 2024 summary flags its low-pressure rail sensor below 0.049 V or above 4.88 V within 8 s. Analog faults of this sensor are P2539 to P2543. Expect a MIL and possibly hard starting or hesitation under load.
c: Signal, supply or ground wire to the low-pressure sensor damaged
Connector at the sensor or fuel line corroded or not latched
Sensor electronics failed and no longer transmit
Receiving input or software of the engine or pump control module faulty
s: Check engine light
Longer cranking or hard starting
Hesitation or power loss under heavy load

U0670.t: Lost Communication With Fuel Temperature Sensor A
U0670.d: GM's 2025 direct-injection engines measure fuel temperature in the high-pressure rail with digital SENT sensors, and sensor 1 is the one GM files under U0670. The test counts pulses on the signal wire: if the line sits permanently high and four or fewer pulses arrive (25OBDG03A; 40 or fewer in 25OBDG03B), a sample fails, and 400 bad samples in a window of 500, one every 6.25 ms, set the code; being Type A, it lights the MIL during the first trip. While it is active, GM holds back the range checks P0182/P0183 and the sensor comparison P111F. CARB requires a separate code when a digital input stops talking. The controller then substitutes a fuel temperature, so drivability rarely changes; the fault lies in wiring, connector or sensor.
c: SENT signal wire to sensor A shorted or open
Connector at the fuel rail loose or contaminated
Fuel temperature sensor A internally failed
SENT receiver in the engine controller faulty
s: Check engine light from the first trip
Usually no noticeable change in driving
Occasionally rougher hot restarts

U0671.t: Lost Communication With Fuel Temperature Sensor B
U0671.d: Sensor B is the second SENT temperature sensor in GM's high-pressure fuel rail (sensor 2 in 25OBDG03A and 25OBDG03B). Its link test mirrors that of sensor A, line stuck high with too few pulses, 400 of 500 samples at 6.25 ms, Type A. What sets B apart is its job: GM compares it with sensor 1 and stores P111F when the two differ by more than 10 °C in 100 of 125 samples, and it checks the raw digital value of sensor 2 against limits below 145 and above 1,865 counts (P0187/P0188, Type B). Without B both checks go blind, so a drifting sensor A could go unnoticed. If U0670 and U0671 appear together, look first at a shared connector, supply or ground; if only B is missing, its own branch or sensor is more likely.
c: Signal wire of sensor B chafed, shorted or open
Shared 5 V supply or ground of both rail sensors faulty
Engine controller input or software fault
s: Check engine light
Sensor comparison and range checks of sensor B not completed
Often no drivability complaint

U0672.t: Lost Communication With Engine Coolant Pump
U0672.d: GM's 2.0 L LSY and 2.7 L L3B four-cylinders circulate coolant with an electric main pump that the engine controller commands over LIN. U0672 sets when the pump's response frame MWP_Rsp is missing for at least 250 ms (25OBDG03B; same logic in 19OBDG03D for the L3B) once the LIN channel is up, the relay is powered and battery voltage exceeds 11 V; as a Type A fault it turns the MIL on at once. GM bulletin PIP5863C covers 2019-2024 Silverado/Sierra 1500, Colorado/Canyon, Blazer, Acadia, Envision and Cadillac CT4 to XT6: check terminals and crimps, unplug and reconnect the pump, clear the code; if it stays away, release the car. U019F names a separate pump control module, U04A0 its invalid data. Watch engine temperature.
c: Poor terminal tension, crimp or lock at the electric pump connector
LIN, supply or ground wire to the pump chafed or contaminated
Pump relay or fuse supplying the pump faulty
s: Check engine light immediately
Rising coolant temperature or overheating warning
Weak cabin heating
Reduced engine power to protect the engine

U0673.t: Lost Communication With Ion Sense Module
U0673.d: After each spark, a small bias voltage across the plug gap lets the ignition system measure the current carried by ions in the burning mixture; Ford's patent US20170030322A1 shows such an ion sensing module passing this signal to the controller for combustion and knock assessment. U0673 means the engine controller no longer hears from that module. Stellantis lists U0673-00 among the MIL codes in a series of powertrain controller reflash bulletins for the 3.0 L Hurricane twin-turbo six (sales codes EFC and EFH): 18-022-25 Rev. A for the 2025 Wagoneer and Grand Wagoneer, 18-106-25 for the 2026 Ram 1500 and 18-071-26 for the 2025 Ram 1500. The stated cause is controller software, so updating it comes before replacing hardware.
c: Bus, supply or ground wiring of the ion sense module faulty
s: Check engine light
Other stored codes from the same software issue
Usually no change in how the engine runs

U0674.t: Lost Communication With Wastegate Position Sensor B
U0674.d: Electric wastegate actuators need position feedback so the controller can hold the turbine bypass at the commanded opening. On twin-turbo engines the second charger gets its own sensor, and U0674 says the digital frames from that sensor B have stopped or are corrupt. GM uses the sibling U0644 for wastegate A over SENT (25OBDG03B, Type A), yet none of the GM tables lists U0674. Ford's 2024 gasoline summary goes the analog way for charger B: P2ABB below 0.50 V or P2ABC above 4.50 V within 4 s, and a position error beyond 20 mm sets P25B5/P25B6. So no published source uses U0674 itself. CARB counts wastegate valve position among the diesel data items. Expect boost on that charger to be reduced or the wastegate held open.
c: Wiring to the wastegate B actuator heat-damaged or chafed
Position sensor inside the actuator failed
Weak supply voltage or poor ground
s: Check engine light
Reduced power, boost limited on one charger
Sluggish response under load

U0675.t: Lost Communication With Turbocharger/Supercharger Speed Sensor A
U0675.d: A speed sensor in the bearing or compressor housing lets the controller watch how fast the turbocharger rotor spins, mainly to keep it below its overspeed limit; a BorgWarner patent (US9353760B2) describes such a sensor and gives that reason, and CARB names turbocharger/turbine speed among the data diesel vehicles must output. Classic sensors send a pulse train whose faults are P2578 to P2582. U0675 applies when sensor A delivers the speed as a digital message and those messages are missing or invalid. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Without a speed value the controller cannot tell how close the rotor is to its limit, so it will usually cap boost and engine power until the fault is gone.
c: Sensor wiring near the turbocharger heat-damaged or broken
Engine controller input or software fault
s: Check engine light
Boost and power limited
Noticeably weaker acceleration at higher loads

U0676.t: Lost Communication With Fuel Level Sensor A
U0676.d: Fuel level sensor A is the main tank sender. Usually it is a float-driven resistor read as a voltage, and U0676 only applies where the sender itself reports digitally and its messages stop. Public documentation of this code from any manufacturer is lacking. In its 2024 summary Ford treats sender A as a resistance: below 5 ohms or above 200 ohms within 30 s are circuit faults, more than 100 jumps of over 40 % are noise, and stuck checks need 100 to 120 miles. GM's 25OBDG03A lets the float feed the engine controller directly or a fuel tank zone module, which forwards the value, and pauses its range checks while a communication fault is active. CARB needs the level for EVAP testing and misfire disablement at low fuel, so the gauge may be wrong and those monitors stay incomplete.
c: Wiring at the tank or fuel pump flange damaged or corroded
Electronics of the level sender failed
Module that reads or forwards the level faulty
Connector under the vehicle not latched or water-damaged
s: Fuel gauge reads empty, full or freezes
Range display missing or wrong
Check engine light, EVAP readiness not set

U0677.t: Lost Communication With Fuel Level Sensor B
U0677.d: A second level sender is needed when a tank has two chambers, as in saddle tanks that straddle the driveshaft, or when a vehicle carries a second tank. GM's 25OBDG03B calls it sensor 2 of the secondary tank, used on vehicles with two senders and a mechanical transfer pump; its circuit checks fail below 10 % or above 60 % of the 5 V range in 40 of 50 samples (P2067/P2068, Type B). Ford's 2024 summary runs sender B through the same resistance, noise and stuck checks as A and adds P25B2 for a stuck reading on either. U0677 is the digital variant: sender B's messages stop arriving. No manufacturer documents it publicly. The gauge then misjudges the part of the tank sender B covers, and range and EVAP readiness suffer.
c: Wiring to the secondary-chamber sender damaged
Connector at the secondary flange corroded
s: Gauge drops suddenly or never shows full
Range estimate inaccurate
Check engine light

U0678.t: Lost Communication With Fuel Level Sensor C
U0678.d: A third level sender only makes sense where the fuel volume is split further, for example a tank with three chambers or a main tank plus an auxiliary one. U0678 would be stored when such a sender C reports its value as a message and that message is lost. No manufacturer documents U0678 publicly, and the public OBD summaries checked here stop at two senders: GM's 2025 tables and Ford's 2024 summary, which covers A and B and a combined stuck code P25B2. The analog counterparts for C exist as P25D7 to P25DC. CARB lists stuck fuel level sensors among inputs that need extended monitoring, and the level enables EVAP tests, so a missing third reading keeps those monitors from running and leaves the gauge inaccurate.
c: Wiring to sender C damaged or corroded
Module receiving the level data faulty
s: Gauge or range wrong when the third chamber is involved
Check engine light
EVAP readiness not completed

U0679.t: Lost Communication With Transmission Fluid Pressure Sensor/Switch A
U0679.d: Automatic transmissions measure hydraulic pressure to confirm that a clutch or pulley really received the pressure the controller asked for. Which sensor is A varies: Ford's 2024 summary calls the sensors of its 10R60/10R80 and 8F units TFP A and B, analog with 0.5 to 4.5 V for 0 to 2,500 kPa, and sets P0841 when the reading sticks although the clutch still applies and releases. GM's 24OBDG07 assigns A to clutch 1 (P0842 below 220 mV, P0843 above 4,530 mV after 150 ms), while its CVT table 25OBDG03A uses A for the primary pulley. U0679 covers a digital sensor A that has gone silent. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The transmission controller then loses its pressure feedback and may hold a gear or shift harshly.
c: Transmission internal harness or lead frame to sensor A damaged
Transmission case connector leaking oil or corroded
Transmission control module input or software fault
s: Harsh or delayed shifts
Transmission stays in a fixed gear
Check engine or transmission warning light

U067A.t: Lost Communication With Transmission Fluid Pressure Sensor/Switch B
U067A.d: Sensor B is the second pressure measuring point. In GM's CVT table 25OBDG03A it reads the secondary pulley, whose pressure sets the clamping force on the belt; its plausibility check runs only above 1,200 rpm with line pressure over 1,000 kPa and a secondary command above 500 kPa. In GM's 24OBDG07 B belongs to clutch 2, fed from its own reference VREF2, and Ford's 2024 summary checks TFP B with P0846 to P0848. U067A stands for a digital sensor B whose messages have stopped. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. With the clamping or clutch pressure unknown, the controller has to work with assumed values, which can mean firmer shifts, limited torque or a fixed gear. If A is still readable, the fault sits in B's own branch.
c: Internal wiring to sensor B damaged
Separate sensor supply for B faulty
s: Firm shifts or engagement
Reduced engine torque, limp mode
Warning light on

U067B.t: Lost Communication With Engine Disconnect Clutch Pressure Sensor
U067B.d: Parallel hybrids put a clutch between engine and electric motor so the car can drive electrically with the engine stopped. Many close it hydraulically, and a pressure sensor confirms the clamping: in Ford's 10R80 MHT hybrid transmission, as Gears Magazine explains, the auxiliary pump closes the clutch and a pressure sensor watches that supply. Schaeffler's application WO2018233759A1 places a pressure sensor in the clutch actuator's master cylinder next to a travel sensor. If such a sensor reports digitally and its messages stop, U067B is stored. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Analog faults of the same sensor are P28F1 to P28F5; U02AA concerns the clutch actuator. Engine starts and electric driving may then be restricted.
c: Wiring or connector of the clutch pressure sensor damaged
Transmission or hybrid controller input or software fault
s: Hybrid system warning, electric driving unavailable
Engine runs continuously or starts roughly
Check engine light

U067C.d: Some engines need a third electric cooling fan, for instance for a charge-air or auxiliary radiator, and LIN lets each fan carry its own speed electronics. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B uses U067C for cooling fan 3: the response frame CFM3_Rsp must be missing for at least 2,437.5 ms, the LIN channel enabled and battery voltage above 11 V; the code is Type B, so the MIL lights after two trips. While it is active GM suspends the fan 3 speed checks, P2CBB for running slower than modelled and P30F2/P30F3 for feedback out of range, the high limit being 4,000 rpm. On the engines of GM's 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 the same fan instead sets the GM-specific U112A on a third LIN line. Watch engine temperature under load.
c: LIN wire to fan 3 chafed or open
High-current supply, fuse or ground of fan 3 faulty
Fan connector corroded by road spray
s: Check engine light after two trips
High coolant or charge-air temperature at low speed or when towing
Fan 3 silent or running constantly

U067D.d: U067D is meant for a fourth cooling fan with its own network interface that has stopped answering. Four electrically commanded fans are rare. No manufacturer documents U067D publicly: GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B ends at fan 3, and the engines in GM's 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07, which do have a fourth LIN fan, report it with the GM-specific code U112B once its response frame ECM_LIN3_CFM4_RSP has been missed three times, maturing over two trips. LIN suits such small motor nodes, and cooling fan motors are a classic application. If fan 4 is wired conventionally, its faults appear as P2C3E to P2C40 for the control circuit and P2C42 for performance. Losing one of four fans mostly shows when cooling demand is high.
c: Fan 4 power feed or ground interrupted
s: Temperature climbs in traffic or under heavy load
Warning light depending on manufacturer
Fan 4 does not run

U067E.t: Lost Communication With Exhaust Pressure Control Valve B Sensor/Switch
U067E.d: An exhaust pressure control valve is a flap in the exhaust that diesels close partly to raise back pressure, which speeds warm-up and helps reach filter regeneration temperatures. Valve B is a second flap of this kind, and U067E concerns its position sensor or switch when that reports digitally: the controller has lost its messages. Public manufacturer documentation for U067E is lacking. GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B shows the pattern for valve A, a SENT position sensor whose silence gives U0650 after 480 failed checks out of 600 at 6.25 ms, Type A. For valve B, drive faults run from P049F to P04A5 and analog position faults from P04A6 to P04AA. CARB wants a separate code for a mute digital input. Warm-up and regeneration may be impaired.
c: Sensor wiring at valve B damaged by exhaust heat
Connector at valve B corroded or loose
Position sensor in the valve B unit failed
Engine controller input or software fault
s: Check engine light
Particulate filter regeneration delayed or not started
Longer warm-up in cold weather

U067F.t: Lost Communication With Barometric Pressure Sensor A
U067F.d: Barometric pressure sensor A is normally the ambient sensor that corrects fueling, boost targets and many diagnostics for altitude; CARB requires barometric pressure, measured or estimated, in the OBD data stream. U067F covers a digital version of that sensor whose messages stop arriving. GM's dual-throttle program 23OBDG07 does read a digital ambient sensor, but files its faults under P-codes: a CRC error or a short reported in message A sets P2228 or P2229, and defect or queue-full flags set P2227, each after 2 s with MIL in one trip. Ford's 2024 gasoline and 2023 diesel summaries keep sensor A analog (P2228). No published table therefore assigns U067F. Because ambient pressure may also be estimated, as CARB allows, drivability rarely suffers.
c: Data, supply or ground wire to the barometric sensor interrupted
s: Check engine light
Slightly off fueling or boost at altitude
Other diagnostics may be suspended

U0680.t: Lost Communication With Barometric Pressure Sensor B
U0680.d: The letter B need not mean a second ambient sensor; it can be any further pressure input that sees near-atmospheric air. GM's 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 tables, written for a program with two throttle bodies, use barometric sensor B for the pressure ahead of the bank 2 throttle and send it over SENT. U0680 is stored when the frames carrying the high and low line pressure of bank 2 come in with a wrong data length code for 1.5 s; the MIL follows after two trips. The checks of the value itself are P222C and P222D (raw reading under 50 or over 115 kPa) and P222B (plausibility against ambient pressure). U068A covers the bank 1 counterpart. Air mass on bank 2 then has to be estimated without its reference.
c: SENT signal, supply or ground wire to the bank 2 pressure sensor faulty
Connector at the sensor ahead of the throttle loose or wet
Engine controller software or SENT input fault
s: Check engine light after two trips
Uneven running between banks possible
Additional pressure plausibility codes

U0681.t: Lost Communication With Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch D
U0681.d: In the generic code scheme the letters D, E and F normally mark the accelerator pedal tracks, while A to C and G belong to throttle bodies. U0681 is meant for a pedal module whose first track D reports digitally, for example over SENT or SPC as offered by Melexis' MLX90377 position IC, which lists pedal sensors as an application and comes as a fully redundant dual die. No manufacturer documents U0681 publicly. Ford (2024 gasoline) and GM read pedal D analog: Ford sets P2122/P2123 below 0.25 or above 4.75 V within a second, with wrench lamp and MIL. Ford also explains the fallback when one pedal input is lost: driver demand follows the remaining track at a limited rate. CARB requires pedal and redundant pedal position in the diesel data stream.
c: Wiring to the pedal module chafed in the footwell or at the bulkhead
Pedal module connector loose or corroded
Sensor electronics in the pedal module failed (replaced as a unit)
Engine controller input or software fault
s: Check engine light and possibly a powertrain warning
Sluggish, rate-limited throttle response
Reduced power

U0682.t: Lost Communication With Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch E
U0682.d: Track E is usually the redundant second signal of the accelerator pedal, which the controller compares with track D before trusting any torque request. U0682 marks the loss of digital frames from that track. No manufacturer documents it publicly; GM and Ford wire pedal E analog, with Ford setting P2127/P2128 on voltage limits and P2138 when D and E disagree by more than 0.9 degrees. What matters to the driver is described in Ford's 2024 failure-mode table: with one track lost, demand is rate limited; with both gone, the engine ramps to a fixed high idle and ignores the pedal until the brake brings it back to idle. A digital pedal that sends both tracks in one SENT stream can therefore lose D and E together. CARB requires redundant pedal position data.
c: Signal or reference wire of track E damaged
Water or corrosion in the pedal connector
s: Check engine light and powertrain warning
Delayed throttle response
Fixed elevated idle with no pedal response if both tracks fail

U0683.t: Lost Communication With Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch F
U0683.d: A third pedal track F is rare. It appears where a pedal module carries three signals, or where the F letter is used for an extra switch or a throttle input; the correlation codes P2139 (D/F), P2140 (E/F) and P212F (F/G) show that the scheme pairs F both with the pedal tracks and with throttle sensor G. U0683 means that digital frames for input F have stopped or fail their checks. No manufacturer documents the code publicly, and neither the Ford nor the GM tables examined contain any F input at all: both work with two pedal tracks, D and E. Analog faults of F would be P2130 to P2134. The effect depends on the role of F; with one redundant track gone, the controller usually limits power and the warning lamp comes on.
c: Wiring for input F open, shorted or chafed
Connector at the pedal or sensor module loose or corroded
Sensor electronics for input F failed
s: Check engine light
Reduced power or limited throttle response
Additional correlation codes possible

U0684.t: Lost Communication With Catalyst Temperature Bank 1 Sensor 1
U0684.d: A catalyst temperature sensor tells the controller when the converter is hot enough to work and to be tested. Sensor 1 on bank 1 is the first such probe on the bank that holds cylinder 1. U0684 applies when the probe sends its reading as a digital message and that message has stopped. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and many makers fit no sensor here: Ford's 2024 gasoline summary works with an inferred mid-bed temperature and only runs its catalyst test between 510 and 815 °C of that model value. CARB accordingly lets the catalyst temperature in the data stream be measured or estimated, but wants a separate code for every silent digital input. Analog circuit faults at this point are P0425 to P0428; U0685 covers sensor 2.
c: Sensor lead near the converter burnt or chafed
Evaluation electronics of the temperature sensor failed
Engine controller input or software fault
s: Check engine light
Catalyst readiness monitor does not complete

U0685.t: Lost Communication With Catalyst Temperature Bank 1 Sensor 2
U0685.d: Where a converter carries two temperature probes, one usually sits ahead of the brick and one behind it, so that the heat released by the reaction shows up as a rise between them. Sensor 2 on bank 1 is the second, downstream position. U0685 means this probe reports over a digital link and its messages no longer arrive. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, so thresholds and debounce times are unknown. Without the second reading, the comparison with sensor 1 is lost: the correlation code P046A cannot be judged, and any strategy that uses the temperature rise as a sign of catalyst activity loses its input. Analog faults of the same probe are P042A to P042D; sensor 1 has U0684. CARB requires a separate code for digital inputs that fall silent.
c: Lead of the downstream probe damaged by heat, stones or road salt
Connector corroded or not fully latched
s: Check engine light
Catalyst monitor or sensor comparison stays incomplete

U0686.t: Lost Communication With Catalyst Temperature Bank 2 Sensor 1
U0686.d: Bank 2 exists only on engines whose cylinder rows feed separate exhaust paths, so U0686 belongs to V or flat engines with one converter per side. It means the first catalyst temperature probe of that second bank has stopped delivering digital messages. Such probes are often a thermocouple paired with a small electronics unit; Sensience, for example, sells N-type probes rated to 1000 °C whose module converts the reading to SENT or CAN. The module and its lead sit close to hot exhaust parts, which makes heat damage a typical cause. None of the carmakers describes this code in public material. The analog equivalents are P0435 to P0438; the same position on bank 1 is U0684. CARB requires a dedicated code once a digital input goes mute.
c: Sensor electronics on bank 2 damaged by heat
Harness on the bank 2 side chafed or melted
s: Check engine light
Catalyst monitor for bank 2 not completed

U0687.t: Lost Communication With Catalyst Temperature Bank 2 Sensor 2
U0687.d: U0687 refers to the rear catalyst temperature probe of bank 2, the one behind the converter brick on the second cylinder row. Once its digital messages stop, the controller can no longer compare bank 2 inlet and outlet temperatures (P046B) and loses an over-temperature guard: such probes have long been used to warn when a converter runs hotter than it can tolerate, which on older two-way designs was around 750 °C. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, so MIL timing and debounce are not known; CARB only requires that silence of a digital input sets its own code. Analog faults at this point are P043A to P043D, and sensor 1 of the same bank is U0686. The car usually drives normally, but the fault should not be left, since misfires could go on overheating the converter.
c: Lead of the rear bank 2 probe damaged
s: Check engine light
Bank 2 temperature comparison not possible
No noticeable change in driving

U0688.t: Lost Communication With Throttle Position Sensor/Switch G
U0688.d: Throttle sensor G is the second track of a second throttle body. GM's 23OBDG07 and 24OBDG07 tables, for a program with one throttle per bank, use it for throttle position sensor 2 on bank 2. Both tracks of that throttle travel in one SENT stream, so GM sets U0688 together with U0608 (sensor 1, bank 2) when the line carries no signal, pulse widths fall outside their window or the calibration pulse is off, within 0.13 s and MIL in one trip. NXP's KMA215 shows why: its dual throttle format packs the angle and its inverted copy into a single frame. Raw value checks of track G are P212C under 0.195 V and P212D over 4.805 V, P212B checks synchronisation. Bank 2's throttle can then no longer be positioned reliably, so power is reduced.
c: SENT, supply or ground wire to the bank 2 throttle body faulty
Throttle body connector loose, wet or corroded
Sensor electronics in the throttle body failed (replaced as a unit)
s: Check engine light on the first trip
Reduced power, uneven running between banks
U0608 stored at the same time

U0689.t: Lost Communication With Turbocharger/Supercharger B Temperature Sensor
U0689.d: Twin-charger engines may monitor a temperature at the second charger, for instance to protect the compressor or turbine of charger B from overheating; CARB's diesel data list includes compressor inlet as well as turbine inlet and outlet temperatures. U0689 means the reading of the temperature sensor for charger B arrives over a digital link and that link has failed. Such a channel can be built into a combined pressure sensor, as Infineon's KP276 shows with its SENT-transmitted NTC input. No manufacturer documents U0689 publicly, and none of the Ford or GM summaries examined contains it. Circuit faults of an analog sensor are P2B8F to P2B92, charger A's link loss is U0643. With the value gone, the controller may protect the charger by limiting boost.
c: Wiring near charger B damaged by heat
Temperature sensor or its interface electronics failed
s: Check engine light
Boost reduced as a precaution
Otherwise often unchanged driving

U068A.t: Lost Communication With Barometric Pressure Sensor C
U068A.d: Barometric sensor C appears in two very different layouts. In GM's dual-throttle tables 23OBDG07/24OBDG07 it measures the air ahead of the bank 1 throttle; P227C and P227D judge its raw value (under 50 or over 115 kPa, 2 s), and U068A is set once the bank 1 SENT frames carry an incorrect length for 1.5 s, two trips to MIL. Oddly, GM's description calls the part pressure sensor 2 although the frames are labelled bank 1. GM's diesel tables 25OBDG04A/04B place sensor C inside a LIN air-mass meter instead: a low reading there sets P227C (Type B), but a missing reply is logged as U060F for the meter, not as U068A. U0680 is the bank 2 partner. The controller falls back on modelled pressure.
c: Signal, supply or ground wire to sensor C damaged
Connector at the intake pressure sensor loose or corroded
s: Check engine light after two trips
Bank 1 fueling less precise
Accompanying pressure codes P227B to P227D possible

U068B.t: Lost Communication With Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor A
U068B.d: The inlet pressure sensor sits between air filter and compressor. Its reading shows filter restriction and, together with boost pressure, the pressure ratio the compressor works against. Ford's 2023 diesel summary connects sensor A via SENT and lists U068B in its SENT sensor group: U068B follows when the low-level SENT driver sees the signal line pinned to one voltage level, either up or down, monitored without pause and judged over 5 s. A sensor that still talks but raises its own error flag or reports data above a threshold sets P012A instead. Combined pressure and temperature chips such as Infineon's KP276 deliver this kind of SENT signal. U068C is the code for a second inlet sensor. Without the value the controller estimates inlet pressure, and boost or filter monitoring become less precise.
c: SENT signal wire shorted to ground or voltage, or open
Connector on the intake duct loose, oily or corroded
s: Check engine light
Air filter restriction no longer monitored
Possibly somewhat reduced boost

U068C.t: Lost Communication With Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor B
U068C.d: A second inlet pressure sensor makes sense where each bank breathes through its own filter and charger, or where a two-stage system needs the pressure ahead of the second compressor. U068C means the digital frames from that sensor B no longer arrive in usable form. No manufacturer documents U068C publicly; Ford's 2023 diesel summary, the only examined table with an inlet pressure U code, runs just sensor A over SENT (U068B), and no GM table lists either code. Faults of an analog sensor B are P2374 to P2378. CARB lists compressor inlet pressure among the required diesel data. The controller then models the pressure on that side, so filter restriction there goes unseen and boost targets get more cautious.
c: Signal, supply or ground wire to inlet sensor B damaged
Connector loose or contaminated with oil
s: Check engine light
Filter restriction on that side no longer detected
Slightly lower boost possible

U068D.t: Lost Communication With EGR Temperature Sensor A
U068D.d: EGR temperature sensors show how hot the recirculated gas is, mostly behind the EGR cooler, so the controller can judge cooler efficiency and correct the gas density. U068D is the digital-link failure for sensor A. No public manufacturer source covers U068D. In the published tables sensor A is analog: GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04A calls it the downstream EGR temperature sensor 2 and flags a resistance below 159 ohms as P040C, and Ford's 2023 diesel summary sets P040C under 0.69 V and P040B if the reading rises less than 10 °C after start. Neither has a SENT variant for A. CARB requires the EGR cooler to be checked and a separate code for any digital input that goes quiet. Analog faults are P040A to P040E; the A/B comparison is P040F.
c: Wiring to EGR temperature sensor A damaged near the cooler
s: Check engine light
EGR cooler monitoring not possible

U068E.t: Lost Communication With EGR Temperature Sensor B
U068E.d: GM documents this code in its 2025 diesel tables 25OBDG04A and 25OBDG04B, where sensor B is named EGR temperature sensor 1. Its circuit tests (P041C, P041D) are written for either a resistive probe or a digital thermocouple unit; the digital one counts as low below -72.8 °C. U068E covers the digital case: the check looks for SENT output switched off by an internal sensor fault, protocol errors or messages that are too old, and fails once 19 of 25 samples taken every 100 ms are bad while Run/Crank is active. It is Type A, so the MIL comes on in the first trip, and GM also logs a code for the input the sensor is wired to. Ford's 2023 diesels place sensor B behind the EGR cooler but read it as an analog signal. U068D, U068F and U0690 cover the other slots.
c: SENT signal, supply or ground wire to sensor B damaged
Internal fault in the sensor that shuts off its output
Connector corroded or contaminated by soot and oil
Fault at the controller input the sensor uses
s: Check engine light, on GM diesels in the first trip
Second code for the controller input stored alongside
EGR cooler efficiency not monitored

U068F.t: Lost Communication With EGR Temperature Sensor C
U068F.d: Engines with both a high- and a low-pressure EGR loop need more temperature points, which is where slots C and D come in. U068F means the controller lost the digital messages of EGR temperature sensor C. There is no public manufacturer documentation for it. In GM's 2025 diesel table 25OBDG04B, sensor C is an air temperature point upstream in the low-pressure EGR path, read as a resistance: below 7 ohms it gives P04D0 after 30 of 38 counts, Type A, and after more than 8 hours off it may not stray over 20 °C from the mean of intake air and fuel temperature at key-on (P04CF). A SENT version with its own lost-communication check is not listed there. CARB requires separate detection when a digital input is silent. Analog faults are P04CE to P04D2. Low-pressure EGR is then usually reduced or switched off.
c: Wiring to sensor C near the exhaust aftertreatment damaged
s: Check engine light
Low-pressure EGR reduced or disabled

U0690.t: Lost Communication With EGR Temperature Sensor D
U0690.d: Sensor D is the last of the four EGR temperature slots, used only on systems with many measuring points, for example on both sides of a cooler in each of two EGR loops. U0690 says its digital messages have stopped reaching the controller. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and none of the reviewed GM and Ford tables uses a D position at all. From 2013 on, CARB lists EGR temperature among the values the OBD system must report where fitted, and it requires EGR coolers to be checked for too little cooling; a missing reading can leave that check without data. CARB also asks for a separate code when a digital input falls silent. Analog faults are P04E5 to P04E9, and U068D to U068F cover the other three slots.
s: Check engine light
EGR cooler check incomplete

U0691.t: Lost Communication With Exhaust Pressure Sensor A
U0691.d: On Ford's 6.7 L and 3.0 L diesels of 2023, exhaust pressure sensor A measures pressure ahead of the turbine and is a SENT device. Ford's diesel OBD summary sets U0691 when the low-level SENT driver sees a communication error or no data within the expected window, when the line is held at one voltage level, or when the sensor reports an internal fault; the check runs continuously and needs 5 s. P0470 is kept for a SENT status error or a raw value above a limit. The same sensor has two plausibility tests: with the engine off it may differ from barometric pressure by no more than 15 kPa (P0471), and while driving it is compared against a model (P0474). Without this pressure, turbo and EGR control lose an input. U0692 covers sensor B.
c: SENT line shorted to ground or supply, or open, near the hot turbo
Sensor reports an internal error or stops sending
Sensor damaged by soot or condensate in the pressure line
s: Check engine light
Reduced boost or power on some engines
EGR and turbo running on substitute values

U0692.t: Lost Communication With Exhaust Pressure Sensor B
U0692.d: Exhaust pressure sensor B is a second pressure point in the exhaust, whose location the maker defines, for instance on the other bank or behind the turbine. U0692 means its digital output, usually SENT, has stopped delivering valid frames. Code-specific documentation from a manufacturer is not public. Ford's 2023 diesel summary has only one exhaust pressure sensor, the SENT unit ahead of the turbine with U0691, and GM's 2025 diesel tables list no B sensor. CARB names exhaust pressure sensor output among the values diesel OBD systems must report and requires a separate code when a digitally coded input stops communicating. Analog circuit faults of sensor B are P047A to P047E; sensor C has U069F. What the driver notices depends on what the reading is used for, ranging from nothing beyond the lamp to reduced power.
c: Wiring to pressure sensor B damaged by exhaust heat
s: Check engine light
Possibly reduced power

U0693.d: Intake air humidity influences combustion temperature and NOx, so some engines measure it, usually with a capacitive element built into the air-mass meter; Bosch offers such meters with optional humidity sensing over SENT, FAS or LIN. GM's dual-throttle tables 23OBDG07/24OBDG07 use U0693 for a SENT humidity sensor on bank 1, stored when the sensor itself reports a maximum or minimum error for 1 s, MIL after two trips; the same program has P00F4 to P00F6 for the reading and GM codes for invalid data. Other layouts avoid U0693: GM's 25OBDG04A treats a silent LIN air-mass meter as U060F, and Ford's 2023 diesel sets P00F2 for bad SENT humidity message timing. Fuel and EGR then run on default humidity.
c: Humidity element in the air-mass meter contaminated or failed
Signal or supply wire to the sensor faulty
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
s: Check engine light after two trips
Usually no noticeable drivability change
Accompanying humidity or air-mass codes possible

U0694.t: Lost Communication With Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump A
U0694.d: Liquid-cooled traction batteries rely on an electric pump to move coolant through the pack, and pumps like Bosch's PCE accept their speed command by PWM or LIN and report faults themselves. U0694 records that battery pump A no longer communicates. Published manufacturer data do not mention it. GM's hybrid table 19OBDG01 drives its battery pump by a discrete or PWM line and judges the line current (under 200 mA or over 3 A, 4 s within 5 s, Type B), so faults surface as P0C47. Hyundai uses its own U1118 for the battery pump on the 2019 Kona Electric; campaign T4G traced it to coolant entering the pump's electronics housing and replaces the housing or the pump. Expect reduced power, slower charging and a hybrid or EV warning.
c: Coolant entered the pump electronics housing
Bus, supply or ground wire to the pump damaged
Battery or hybrid controller software fault
s: Hybrid/EV system warning
Reduced drive power
Slower DC fast charging

U0695.t: Lost Communication With Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump B
U0695.d: Pump B is a second pump in the battery thermal circuit; what it serves, for instance a parallel branch or a heater or chiller loop, is up to the manufacturer. U0695 is set when that pump stops answering on its data link. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The public GM tables show a single battery pump only: the 2016 Volt table 16OBDG01 checks its PWM control line at commands between 5 and 95 %, 40 bad readings within 50, sampled every 100 ms, Type B. Hyundai's campaign T4G shows how such pumps fail on the network, using maker-specific codes for the battery and the motor electronics pumps. Pumps like Bosch's PAD2 take PWM or LIN commands and offer diagnostics. Wired faults of pump B are P0E1A to P0E1E.
c: Wiring or connector of pump B damaged or wet
Pump B electronics or motor failed
s: Battery temperature warning or power limit
Charging power reduced
Hybrid/EV system warning

U0696.t: Lost Communication With Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor C
U0696.d: In GM's 2025 diesel tables 25OBDG04A and 25OBDG04B, sensor C is the downstream relative pressure sensor, which reads the gauge pressure behind the particulate filter and carries its own temperature element (lost communication there is U06B6). U0696 is set when the sensor reports message faults above a fixed count or when its newest message is too old, judged as 158 failures in 200 samples at 12.5 ms intervals. Being Type A, it turns on the lamp in the first trip. GM keeps offset errors at standstill (P2CE5) and a frozen signal (P2CE6) apart. Ford's 2024 gasoline summary lists U0696 with P2CE5 for SENT filter pressure sensors, checked continuously with 5 s to register. Without this value, back pressure and filter load are estimated. Sensor D is U0697.
c: Wiring to the downstream pressure sensor damaged by heat or chafing
Internal sensor fault that switches off the SENT output
s: Check engine light, on GM diesels in the first trip
Particulate filter regeneration based on estimates or delayed

U0697.t: Lost Communication With Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor D
U0697.d: Sensor D is the fourth filter pressure slot and appears only in Ford's 2024 gasoline OBD summary, which watches particulate filters on both banks (P226D and P226E for a missing substrate). There U0697 sits with P2CEA in the circuit and lost-communication check for SENT-type pressure sensors A to D: it runs all the time and needs 5 s to log a fault. Ford keeps a separate functional check (P2CEB) and, for analog parts, low and high limits of 0.3 and 4.73 V. GM's 2025 diesel tables go no further than C. A missing D reading leaves the filter it serves without a measured pressure drop, so soot load and the missing-substrate test fall back on models or wait. U0696 refers to sensor C, U0601 and U0602 to A and B.
c: Wiring to filter pressure sensor D damaged
s: Check engine light
Particulate filter monitor for one bank incomplete

U0698.t: Lost Communication With Coolant Pump E
U0698.d: Coolant pump E continues the generic letter series of auxiliary electric pumps after A to D. Mercedes-Benz uses it for the second coolant pump in its low-temperature circuit: bulletin LI20.00-P-076708 lists U0698E4 and U0698E5 in the powertrain control unit N127 together with other LIN devices such as fan, charge-air cooler pump and high-temperature control valve. Affected are the GLC (254) and the 2024 facelift GLE (167); drivers see the check engine lamp, a coolant warning and the radiator fan at maximum speed. On the GLC with control unit software 22A the fix is a software update; otherwise connectors, wiring and intermediate connections on the LIN bus are checked. Pumps like Bosch's PDE take speed commands via PWM or LIN and diagnose themselves.
c: Powertrain control unit software (Mercedes N127 version 22A)
LIN wiring or intermediate connector chafed or corroded
s: Check engine light
Coolant warning message
Radiator fan running at full speed

U0699.t: Lost Communication With Coolant Pump F
U0699.d: Pump F is the sixth auxiliary electric coolant pump in the generic lettering, and the code flags that this pump has stopped responding on its data line. No manufacturer documents U0699 publicly; even the Mercedes bulletin that uses the E code for a low-temperature pump lists no F. Six separately addressed pumps point to elaborate thermal systems, for example vehicles with several cooling loops for engine, charge air, electronics and cabin. Such pumps typically take a PWM or LIN speed command and report their own condition, as Bosch describes for the PDE, and LIN is widely used for small motor nodes of this kind. CARB asks for an approved monitoring plan when an electric pump rather than a thermostat regulates engine temperature. P2D27 covers pump F's control performance.
c: Data, supply or ground wire to pump F damaged
Pump F electronics or motor failed
s: Warning light depending on manufacturer
Loop served by pump F runs too warm
Radiator fan running more often or at full speed

U069A.t: Lost Communication With Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Bank 1 Sensor 3
U069A.d: The third exhaust temperature sensor on bank 1 usually sits in the aftertreatment, ahead of the filter or SCR stage. GM covers U069A in both 2025 diesel tables, 25OBDG04A and 25OBDG04B: a SENT sensor whose output was switched off by an internal fault, or that sends faulty or outdated messages, fails the check once 19 readings out of 25, taken every 100 ms, are bad. The test waits for the sensor start-up delay and skips cranking; Type A, so the lamp lights in the first faulty trip. GM's regeneration control reads EGT 3 as the temperature ahead of the particulate filter, and the circuit-low test P242C treats a digital reading under -72.8 °C as faulty. Ford's 2023 diesels have sensor 3 as an analog probe (P242C/P242D, below 0.10 V or above 2.66 V). Sensor 4 is U069B.
c: Sensor harness along the aftertreatment burnt or chafed
Electronics module of the thermocouple sensor failed
s: Check engine light, on GM diesels in the first trip
Particulate filter regeneration blocked or postponed
Further code for the controller input

U069B.t: Lost Communication With Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Bank 1 Sensor 4
U069B.d: Sensor 4 is the fourth temperature point along the bank 1 exhaust. Of GM's 2025 diesel tables only 25OBDG04A contains U069A's partner U069B; 25OBDG04B ends at sensor 3. The logic is the same SENT check as for sensor 3, 19 bad samples of 25 at 100 ms after the sensor's start-up delay, Type A. What differs is the role: in the second stage of GM's hydrocarbon dosing control (P144E) EGT 4 supplies the temperature ahead of the filter, so losing it disturbs regeneration. GM rates an open or high circuit on this probe (P2471) as Type A. Ford's 2023 diesels read sensor 4 as an analog probe (P2470/P2471) and check it against the other sensors after a cold start (P246F). Sensience offers such probes with SENT or CAN output.
c: Harness to sensor 4 damaged by heat during regeneration
s: Check engine light
Regeneration interrupted or not started

U069C.t: Lost Communication With Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Bank 2 Sensor 3
U069C.d: U069C refers to the third temperature probe in the bank 2 exhaust path, so it can only occur where each cylinder bank feeds its own aftertreatment line, as on some V engines. Such a probe is a digital unit that reports its reading as SENT or CAN frames; the code is stored when those frames stop or keep failing their checks. No manufacturer documents U069C publicly. GM's 2025 diesels have one bank and test only the bank 1 positions, declaring a probe lost after 19 bad samples within 25 and rating it Type A. Bentley's V8 bulletin 2065698/1 proves that digital bank 2 probes are in use, yet names only the first position (U0621). An analog probe at this spot reports through P2466 to P246A, and the fourth probe on bank 2 has U069D. The MIL and a postponed filter regeneration are the likely consequences.
c: Sensor harness on the bank 2 exhaust side chafed or heat-damaged
Electronics box of the probe failed
Probe has lost its supply or ground
s: Check engine light
Filter regeneration on bank 2 postponed or blocked
Probe shows no value in live data

U069D.t: Lost Communication With Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Bank 2 Sensor 4
U069D.d: Sensor 4 is normally the final measuring position in the bank 2 exhaust, often placed further down the aftertreatment where the controller judges how hot the gas leaves the filter or catalyst stages. U069D reports that this digital probe has gone silent on its data link. Code-level documentation from a maker is not public; CARB only demands that a coded digital input which stops talking gets a code of its own. Sensience builds such probes from a type N thermocouple and a control module that handles up to four probes on J1939 CAN or one or two on SENT, so one failed module can silence several positions at once. On bank 1 only GM's 25OBDG04A contains the matching code U069B, rated Type A. Wiring faults of an analog probe at this point use P2473 to P2477, while U069C is the third probe. Expect a lit MIL and regeneration being delayed.
c: Probe lead melted or torn near the rear aftertreatment
Electronics unit of the probe dead
Supply fuse or feed wire of the probe faulty
s: Check engine light
Regeneration delayed or cancelled

U069E.t: Lost Communication With Coolant Heater A
U069E.d: Coolant heater A is an electric heater with its own control electronics that warms coolant for the cabin and, in some designs, for the traction battery – usually a high-voltage PTC unit in hybrids and EVs. The vehicle commands it over a data link, mostly LIN: DBK's 400 V heater is driven via LIN 2.0 plus a PWM input, and Webasto's 800 V range adds CAN on its larger models. U069E is stored when the commanding module stops getting answers from the heater. No manufacturer documents U069E publicly. The 2013–2014 Chevrolet Volt shows the layout with a separate coolant heater control module; GM diagnosed it with its own code B101D (PIC5943), and heat returned once the engine ran. Circuit and internal faults of this heater are P2B72–P2B75 and P2DA4–P2DA7. The driver mainly notices little or no heat in electric mode.
c: LIN or CAN line to the heater broken, shorted or connector loose
12 V supply or ground of the heater electronics missing
Control electronics inside the heater failed
Heater or master module software fault
s: Little or no cabin heat in electric mode
Engine starts more often in cold weather to supply heat (hybrids)
Slow battery warm-up or reduced charging power in frost, where the heater serves the battery

U069F.t: Lost Communication With Exhaust Pressure Sensor C
U069F.d: Exhaust pressure sensor C is a third pressure measuring point in the exhaust; where it sits is up to the manufacturer, for example behind the turbine or on a second exhaust branch. U069F: this digital sensor, typically a SENT device, no longer supplies usable frames. No manufacturer documents U069F publicly. The nearest documented case is sensor A on Ford's 2023 diesels (6.7 L, 3.0 L): Ford stores U0691 for a transmission error or data gap, a signal wire pinned at one level, or a self-reported sensor fault, watched continuously over 5 s. Letters differ between makers, so these limits are not transferable. CARB requires a coded digital input that falls silent to have a code of its own. Wired analog versions of sensor C report P2E54 to P2E57. Expect the MIL and substitute values for boost or EGR control.
c: Signal, supply or ground wire of sensor C damaged by exhaust heat
Sensor C reports an internal fault or stops sending
Moisture or corrosion in the sensor connector
s: Check engine light
Possibly less boost or power
Pressure value missing or frozen in live data

U0901.t: Invalid Data from Ion Sense Module
U0901.d: An ion sense module evaluates the tiny current that the burning mixture conducts between the plug electrodes after ignition for the engine controller, which uses it to spot misfire, knock and poor combustion; Ford's patent US20170030322A1 places such a module in the ignition system. U0901 means the module's messages still arrive but their content is rejected – a value out of range, an implausible signal or a wrong checksum or counter. No manufacturer documents U0901 publicly. Stellantis' 3.0 L Hurricane six runs a networked ion sense system: its bulletins name U0673 (module silent) and P2F64 (ion sense feedback circuit A), both cured by PCM software. Saab's Trionic T8 module still fed knock and combustion pulses to the controller over separate wires. With bad ion data, misfire and knock detection lose their basis.
c: Software of the engine controller or ion sense module (update available)
Disturbed data line, for example from ignition interference or a poor ground
s: Check engine light
Possibly reduced power from knock protection
Misfire or ion sense codes stored alongside
