U3000.d: U3000 is the catch-all for a fault inside the module that stores it; the attached failure-type byte says what kind. GM's front camera module uses :41 checksum, :42/:44 memory, :49 internal electronics and :51 not programmed, all without MIL, and then drops adaptive cruise. In a GM brake module the same code covers hardware self-tests and is Type A, while Ford's 2014 Boss 302S list marks U3000 in the PCM as MIL-relevant. Ford SSM 47982 notes that the cruise module of 2017–2019 Super Duty trucks can log U3000:49 after a weak battery: if it stays away after clearing, the module is kept. Mazda (15-002/19) replaced forward cameras that stored a permanent U3000:04. The module named in the scan matters more than the code.
c: Weak or discharged battery leaving a stored internal-fault entry
Module software or calibration that needs an update or reprogramming
Real internal defect such as memory or processor failure in the module
Module running too hot, e.g. a windshield camera in strong sun
s: Warning or service message for the system run by the affected module
Assistance or comfort function switched off, e.g. adaptive cruise or lane keeping
Often no noticeable fault if the entry came from a one-off voltage dip

U3001.d: U3001 tells you that a module did not finish its orderly power-down: supply vanished or dipped before it had closed its tasks and saved its data, so it notes the abrupt end at the next start. Low voltage is the usual trigger. Audi found U300100 static in the engine computer of 2019 A6, A7, A8 and Q8 3.0 TFSI models after a low-voltage event, with the check engine light on and sometimes a no-start, and released new ECM software. Volkswagen saw the same entry in the engine module of 2018–2020 Tiguan, Passat and Beetle after battery work and clears it by switching transport mode on and off. Ford pairs U3001:68 or :89 with U3000:96 in the F-150 steering module (SSM 51226) when voltage is too low at start-up, which costs steering assist until voltage recovers.
c: Discharged battery, battery swap or jump start cutting power mid-shutdown
Module software that logs the event too readily and needs an update
Loose feed, ground or fuse contact dropping out after key-off
Main or power-hold relay opening before the module is done
s: Stored code found during service, often with no complaint
Check engine light on and occasionally a no-start when the engine computer stores it
Missing steering assist right after start-up when the steering module stores it

U3002.d: With U3002 a module reports that its own stored VIN is either blank or differs from the VIN that the rest of the car sends on the bus. GM's front camera module splits this into :51, memory still erased, and :56, any digit not matching the broadcast VIN; both run at start-up in Run with 9–16 V and do not light the MIL. Ford's SSM 51903 covers Ford- and Lincoln-badged 2021–2023 vehicles whose cruise, blind-spot and other modules store U2100 or U3002 after replacement, fixed by writing VIN and configuration in FDRS; SSM 53569 adds that a tail lamp moved from another car can trigger it. CARB requires the VIN to be readable through the diagnostic connector, which is why modules check it. The typical case is a used or unprogrammed part.
c: Used module or lamp from another vehicle still holding its old VIN
New module fitted without writing VIN and configuration
Programming session broken off, leaving the VIN memory blank
s: Stored code right after a module or lamp replacement
Driver assistance or the affected function disabled until the VIN is written

U3003.d: U3003 is logged when the supply a module measures at its own pins leaves the band it needs; the byte gives the direction: :16 too low, :17 too high, :1C out of range, :68 a logged event. GM's front camera module sets it below 9.0 V or above 16.0 V after 3 s in Run and then switches off adaptive cruise, without MIL. Mazda's MT-006/18 links U3003:16 in the CX-5 and CX-9 power liftgate module to a flat battery: recharge, reset, done. Volvo's TJ 34142 ties PSCM U30031C at cranking in start/stop cars to a battery support module switch and asks for both batteries above 12.4 V; Ford's SSM 49662 reports U3003:68 in the 2018 F-150 steering module after auto start-stop on a low battery. Each module stores its own entry, so several at once point to the battery or charging.
c: Low state of charge or aged 12 V battery
Alternator or DC/DC converter charging too little or too much
Voltage dip while cranking or restarting in start/stop mode
Corroded fuse, connector or ground in the feed to that module
s: Comfort or assistance function inoperative, e.g. power liftgate or adaptive cruise
Reduced steering assist message during cranking or after start-stop
The same code stored in several modules at once

U3004.d: U3004 concerns the relay, or electronic switch, that feeds the accessory (ACC) circuits once the car is in accessory or run mode. On GM trucks the body module reads the ignition inputs, decides the power mode and energises the matching relays itself. Mazda documents the code in the start stop unit as U3004:17, an ACC relay line above its threshold. Its bulletin SA-023-23 for the 2017–2022 CX-5 traces it to drink spilled near the front cupholder, which corrodes connector C-16: the ignition then cannot be switched off, infotainment stays on and the battery runs flat. Mazda's MT-001/21 lists the same entry among faults caused by aftermarket dongles plugged into the diagnostic connector. The stuck accessory feed matters more to the driver than the code; no MIL.
c: Spilled liquid corroding a connector in the relay control or feed circuit
Aftermarket device on the diagnostic socket or accessory circuit feeding back voltage
Accessory relay sticking or its coil damaged
Fault in the module that drives the relay
s: Ignition or accessory mode cannot be switched off, radio stays on
Flat battery and no-start after the car has stood
Accessory functions dead in accessory mode

U3005.d: U3005 relates to retained accessory power (RAP), which keeps radio, windows or sunroof alive for a while after the key is switched off. GM's truck manual explains the logic: the body module holds its internal RAP relay for about ten minutes after key-off, and ends RAP early when a door opens or battery voltage sinks below a calibrated limit; some modules get the RAP state as a bus message instead. No manufacturer documents U3005 itself publicly, so the code most likely flags a RAP output or message that does not follow these rules. GM's PIE0724 for 2022 Silverado, Sierra and Envision shows the typical consequence of a RAP fault: radio still on afterwards and a dead battery, checked with a parasitic draw test against 50 mA. Not emission-related, no MIL.
c: RAP relay or output stage staying on or not switching on
Faulty door switch signal, so RAP is not ended on door opening
Body module or radio software handling the RAP state wrongly
Wiring fault or add-on device back-feeding the accessory circuit
s: Radio, windows or sunroof working long after key-off or not at all after key-off
High parasitic drain and flat battery

U3006.t: Control Module Input Power A Circuit/Open
U3006.d: Modules with heavy loads often take more than one battery feed, and U3006 says feed A is missing or open. Which pin is A depends on the maker. In one GM brake module (25OBDG04B) feed A means KL30_1, which supplies the pump motor: if it falls below 53.85 % of the second feed KL30_2 for 75 ms, a blown fuse or short to ground is assumed, Type B with MIL. A second GM brake supplier (25OBDG03B) sets U3006 when the motor supply is under 5 V before the start-up motor test, also Type B. Both feeds there are permanent battery positive, not an ignition line. Jeep's 08-106-21 lists U3006-00 next to U3007-00 on 2021 Wrangler 4xe with a weak 12 V battery and MIL, and Mazda's SA-023-23 shows U3006:01 in the CX-5 parking brake module after battery drain.
c: Blown or loose fuse in the feed A path
Discharged 12 V battery pulling the feed below the check limit
Corroded terminal, loose pin or chafed wire on supply A
Internal power switch or board fault in the module
s: ABS, stability or parking brake warning lamps on
Function of the module limited or switched off
Check engine light on in some vehicles

U3007.t: Control Module Input Power B Circuit/Open
U3007.d: U3007 is the partner code for the second battery feed, B. In GM's 25OBDG04B brake module B is KL30_2, the supply for the valve coils: the module compares it with KL30_1 and sets U3007 when it stays below 53.85 % of that value for 75 ms, and also when the switch for valve power reports less than half the supply voltage for 50 ms; Type B with MIL. The other GM brake supplier (25OBDG03B) uses U3007 differently, for charge-pump tests that could not run three times because both internal supply paths were in undervoltage. So B is a separate fused feed, not a backup of A, and a fault on B alone points to its own fuse or pin. Jeep's 08-106-21 for the 2021 Wrangler 4xe lists U3007-00 first among codes cured by charging or replacing the 12 V battery.
c: Blown or poorly seated fuse feeding input B
Low battery voltage making feed B fail the comparison
Damaged wire or spread terminal on supply B
Valve power switch or internal supply path in the module faulty
s: ABS and stability control warnings, functions shut off
Check engine light on in some vehicles
Often stored together with U3006 when the battery is weak

U3008.d: Modules that switch large currents are often grounded through two separate wires, and U3008 marks the loss of ground A. GM's 19OBDG03B brake module measures the voltage on both grounds and forms (G1 − G2)/(G1 + G2); each wire should carry half the current, so a result above 0.9 for 200 ms means ground 1 is gone, Type A with MIL. Ford's TSB 26-2150 for 2025–2026 Explorer, Police Interceptor and Aviator ties U3008:1B in the steering module, the byte meaning resistance too high, to ground G104 or G116 on the passenger frame rail; the repair enlarges the hole and fits a self-tapping M8 bolt. On the road this shows as a steering assist warning and heavier steering. Mazda uses U3008:01 on CX-90 and CX-70 plug-in hybrids for an over-current or voltage fault in the backup power unit instead.
c: Loose or poorly clamped ground eyelet at the body or frame
Corrosion or paint under the ground connection raising resistance
Broken or chafed ground wire A in the harness
s: Steering assist or brake system warning in the cluster
Reduced power steering assist or limited ABS function
Check engine light where the maker classes it as MIL-relevant

U3009.d: U3009 is the counterpart for the second ground path, B. In the GM brake module of 19OBDG03B the same ratio test runs the other way round: if (G1 − G2)/(G1 + G2) drops below −0.9 for 200 ms, ground 2 is judged disconnected, Type A with MIL. Ford's steering module on the 2025–2026 Explorer, Police Interceptor and Aviator shows that B is a different physical point: TSB 26-2150 sends U3009:1B to the right-hand shock tower ground, G103 on the Explorer and G119 on the Aviator, while ground A sits on the frame rail, and the repair there renews the fastening. Because one good ground can carry the module for a while, the fault may come and go with load, heat or moisture. If both U3008 and U3009 appear, check the shared ground circuit and the battery negative first.
c: Loose nut or stud at the ground B mounting point
Corroded contact face at the strut tower or body ground
Damaged ground wire B or crimp in the harness
s: Intermittent steering assist or brake warning messages
Heavier steering or reduced brake control while the fault is active

U300A.d: U300A is a module's complaint about the ignition switch as a whole: the position or key information it receives does not add up, so it cannot be sure whether the driver wants off, accessory, run or start. The failure-type byte narrows it down. Ford's SSM 52606 covers 2023–2024 Super Duty trucks with a keyed ignition that display Vehicle May Not Start/Restart Service Now with U300A:01 stored by the body control module; a grommet around the lock cylinder had shifted and hindered the key, and reseating it is the repair. On Ram's 2025 heavy-duty pickups the LED headlamps, i.e. smart lamp modules left and right, log U300A-29, signal invalid, as the key moves from run to start. Ram says to leave it alone if it only comes back as stored, but to check the hardwired ignition line if it is active 10 s after start.
c: Key travel hindered at the lock cylinder, e.g. by a displaced grommet or trim
Module software that flags the run-to-start transition as invalid
Worn or dirty contacts inside the ignition switch
Open, chafed or corroded hardwired ignition line or connector
s: Start or restart warning in the cluster, possibly a no-start
Stored code in a lamp or body module with no noticeable effect
Key turns stiffly or does not reach every position cleanly

U300B.d: Judging by its name, U300B concerns the ignition line that should carry voltage in Accessory, On and Start, i.e. in every key position except Off. A module sets it when the level on that wire contradicts the power mode it has been told or sees on its other inputs, for example live with the vehicle off, or dead while the bus reports run. No manufacturer documents U300B publicly. GM's 2012 pickup wiring manual shows the principle: the body control module reads several discrete switch circuits, decides on the power mode and broadcasts it, and modules with their own switched inputs may fall back to a default mode when that message disagrees with their own pins. GM also shows that such lines are cut differently, e.g. its accessory feed drops out while cranking, which this input type should not do.
c: Blown fuse or faulty relay in the switched feed to this input
Input wire open, shorted or backfed from another circuit
Worn ignition switch contact for this position group
Body control module sending a wrong power mode on the bus
s: Functions on the accessory and run feed missing or behaving oddly
Affected module running in a fallback mode with a warning

U300C.d: U300C covers an ignition input that, going by the title, is meant to distinguish Off, On and Start rather than simply switching between live and dead. GM's 2012 light-duty truck wiring manual has exactly such a circuit, labelled Off/Run/Crank: unlike the plain accessory and run/crank feeds it takes separate states for key out or accessory, key in and off, run, and crank. A module reading a coded line of this kind sets U300C when the state it decodes is invalid or disagrees with the power mode on the network. No manufacturer documents U300C publicly. Because one wire carries several states, a slight resistance in the switch or a poor connector can shift the level into the wrong state without breaking the circuit, so measuring the line in every key position beats a simple continuity test.
c: Contact resistance in the ignition switch shifting the coded level
Corroded or loose pin at the switch or module connector
Input wire open or shorted to ground or voltage
Faulty input stage in the reading module
s: Vehicle does not switch power modes as expected, e.g. no start or no shutdown
Intermittent warnings that depend on key position or switch movement

U300D.d: U300D concerns the line that should be live in On and Start only, which GM calls Run/Crank Ignition 1; in GM's 2012 truck wiring manual it is active in run and crank and inactive in off and accessory. A module sets the code when this line and the power mode on the bus disagree. GM's PIT5817A for 2020–2021 Envision, CT4, CT5, Escalade, Corvette, Tahoe, Suburban and Yukon shows the typical case: the instrument cluster stores U300D while the ECM, TCM and brake module log P2535, often after remote start, and the customer finds a dead battery and a service engine lamp. The BCM's driver for the ignition main relay stays on after key-off and keeps circuit 5199 powered, so the line remains live with the car off; the fix is a new BCM. The cluster's code itself is the witness, not the cause.
c: Body control module keeping the run/crank relay energized after key-off
Run/crank relay sticking closed or failing to close
Blown fuse or open wire in the run/crank feed to the module
Backfeed from an aftermarket device tapped into the run/crank circuit
s: Battery repeatedly discharged after the car was parked
Service engine lamp at start-up with P2535 in other modules
Cluster or other modules staying awake with the ignition off

U300E.d: U300E deals with an ignition input that should be live only in On, without Start. Such run-only feeds exist because many loads are shed while the starter turns; GM's 2012 truck wiring manual, for instance, keeps its retained accessory power relay energized in all modes but two, crank and off-awake. If a module sees this run-only line high in Off or Accessory, or low while the network reports run, it stores U300E. A brief drop during cranking is intended and must not be judged as a fault, so a module that flags the code right after every start points more to a timing or software issue than to wiring. No manufacturer documents U300E publicly. A real wiring fault usually leaves functions on that feed dead with the engine running, which helps to separate the two cases.
c: Blown fuse or faulty run relay on the run-only feed
Input wire open, shorted or backfed
Module software misjudging the intended drop during cranking
Worn run contact in the ignition switch
s: Functions on the run-only feed dead with the engine running
Code logged right after each start with no other complaint

U300F.d: U300F refers to the accessory input, the line that powers comfort loads such as audio or power windows when the key is in accessory. In GM's 2012 pickup wiring manual this accessory voltage circuit is active in accessory and run but switched off in crank and in both off positions. A module stores U300F when that pattern breaks: voltage on the accessory input with the key out, or none while the body controller broadcasts accessory or run. No manufacturer documents U300F publicly. Since the accessory feed is often routed through a relay and shared by many consumers, a stuck relay can leave radio and windows working with the key removed and slowly flatten the battery, whereas an open feed simply kills those functions; checking which of the two applies is the first step.
c: Accessory relay sticking closed or not pulling in
Blown accessory fuse or open feed wire
Worn accessory contact in the ignition switch
Aftermarket equipment backfeeding the accessory line
s: Radio, windows or sockets dead in accessory, or still on with the key out
Battery drained after parking when the feed stays live

U3010.d: U3010 concerns the start or crank request input, which should be active only while the key or button is held in Start. A module sets it when it sees a start signal outside a valid crank event, or misses one although the network reports crank. In GM's 2012 truck wiring manual the start position is the only one in which the run/crank line is active while the accessory line is off, so the start state is recognised from a combination of lines that must change together. No manufacturer documents U3010 publicly. The moment of transition is delicate: Ram found that the 2025 heavy-duty LED headlamp modules flag the run-to-start change as invalid (U300A-29) and treat it as harmless if stored only, which shows that a code logged exactly at cranking can be a software artefact rather than a wiring fault.
c: Worn start contact or push-button in the ignition switch
Start request wire open or shorted to voltage
Module software misreading the run-to-start transition
Supply dip during cranking upsetting the input reading
s: Engine does not crank or cranks with a delay
Code stored at each start with no further complaint

U3011.d: U3011 relates to the input that tells a module the ignition is off, for instance a key-in or off-state line. The code is set when that input reports off while the network says the car is running, or fails to report off when every other source does. This matters because modules plan their shutdown around it: Ford's patent US5945745A describes control modules that run fully while an ignition detector sees the ignition and drop into a low-current sleep once the signal disappears. A false off can therefore cut functions while driving, and a missing off can keep modules awake and draw the battery down. GM's 2012 truck wiring manual likewise lets the body controller sleep only with the switch off and the key out. No manufacturer documents U3011 publicly.
c: Faulty key-in or off-position contact in the switch
Off-state input wire open or shorted
Body control module reporting a wrong power mode
Faulty input stage in the reading module
s: Modules not going to sleep, battery drained after parking
Functions switching off briefly while driving

U3012.d: Some modules must wake themselves while the car is parked, for example to run engine-off tests or battery checks, and U3012 reports that this went wrong. Ford's 2023 diesel OBD summary describes the PCM monitor: the code sets if more than two wake-ups happen in the ten minutes before a scheduled alarm wake, or if a requested alarm wake is still missing ten minutes later. GM's 2016 Volt hybrid module checks at power-up whether a self wake-up requested at the last shutdown actually happened, Type A, one trip. In practice the cause is often software: Ford TSB 23-2077 reprograms PCM and TCM on 2022 Super Duty 6.7L trucks with MIL and U3012, and TSB 25-2245 reflashes the ABS module of 2025 F-150s storing U3012:68 with a soft pedal after start-up.
c: Module software handling timed wake-ups incorrectly
Another module or add-on keeping the network awake or waking it repeatedly
Battery disconnected or supply lost while a wake-up was pending
Fault in a hard-wired wake-up line or its connector
s: Check engine light on with no drivability concern
ABS or brake warning and soft pedal right after start-up when the brake module stores it

U3013.t: Control Module Input Power C Circuit/Open
U3013.d: U3013 extends the input power family to a third feed, C, and reports it as missing or open. It only exists on modules with at least three separately fused supplies, such as large body or brake units. No manufacturer documents U3013 publicly, and nothing defines which pin is C; that is up to each maker's wiring. The detection principle can be taken from GM's brake module, which compares two battery feeds and flags one as open when it drops to about half of the other for 75 ms (U3006/U3007). CARB requires electronic inputs that the OBD system relies on to be checked for circuit faults, which is the basis for such checks. In practice a single blown fuse, a pushed-out pin or a weak battery is behind it; if C and D appear together, look for a shared fuse or a supply common to both.
c: Blown fuse in the feed C path
Pushed-out pin, corroded terminal or broken wire on supply C
Weak battery or voltage dip during cranking
s: Part of the functions of the affected module dead
Lost communication codes in other modules if the unit shuts down

U3014.t: Control Module Input Power D Circuit/Open
U3014.d: U3014 is the fourth member of the input power series and means feed D of a module is absent or open. Four separate feeds are rare, so the code appears mainly on central body controllers or power distribution units with several power stages. As with U3013, no maker publishes a definition for it, and the letter only follows that module's pin plan. Where maker data exists for the A and B codes, the supplies are compared with one another, as in GM's brake module, or a single feed must reach a minimum voltage before a load test. Mazda's SA-023-23 shows how a drained battery leaves supply codes in several modules at once, which is why a single D entry is better explained by its own fuse or pin. Not emission-relevant; whether a lamp lights depends on the module.
c: Loose terminal or damaged wire on supply D
Flat battery, then usually with further supply codes in other modules
s: Individual consumers or functions of the module not working
Often stored together with other input power codes after a battery problem

U3015.d: U3015 reports that the third ground path of a module, labelled C, is missing or no longer plausible. Three or four separate grounds are found mainly on units that drive heavy loads, such as brake, steering or power distribution modules, where control electronics and power stages return current through their own wires. No manufacturer documents U3015 publicly. The published logic for grounds A and B gives the pattern: GM's 19OBDG03B brake module compares the voltages on two grounds and flags one as lost once the ratio leaves ±0.9, and Ford's 26-2150 ties each ground letter to a specific body point. Which pin is C is defined only by that module's wiring diagram. A failing ground C can bring warning lamps, a disabled function or erratic readings from the same module.
c: Corroded or loose ground eyelet at the body or frame point
Chafed or broken ground wire between module and ground point
Spread or corroded ground pin in the module connector
Internal fault in the module's ground measurement
s: Warning lamp or message for the system run by the affected module
Function cut back or switched off, often depending on load or moisture
Stored together with other supply or ground codes of the same module

U3016.d: U3016 closes the ground series and stands for a fourth return path, D, that the module considers open or out of line with its other grounds. Four grounds on one unit are rare, so before chasing the D pin it pays to check whether grounds A to C are logged as well; several ground codes at once point to a shared splice, the battery negative cable or a body-to-engine strap rather than to one wire. No manufacturer publishes a definition for U3016. GM's ratio check for two brake module grounds (19OBDG03B) and Ford's bulletin 26-2150, which assigns grounds A and B of a steering module to different bolts, show that each letter means a real, separate fastening point. CARB expects electrical faults of such components to be caught by continuous circuit checks.
c: Poor shared ground, battery negative or engine-to-body strap
Corroded or loose eyelet at ground point D
Damaged ground pin or water in the module connector
Fault in the module's own ground monitoring
s: Warning or service message for the affected system
Several ground or supply codes logged at the same time
Intermittent loss of the module's function

U3017.d: U3017 means a module distrusts its own time base: the clock or timer it counts with disagrees with what it expects, often time received from another unit over the network. In practice it is mostly a software matter. Ram's 6.7 L Cummins trucks list U3017 in a long series of ECM reflash bulletins from 2014 on (e.g. 18-002-14, 18-019-20) to stop the MIL when nothing is defective, and Ram's 2019 eTorque battery module got new software for it (08-030-24). Nissan's NTB17-066 reprograms the Titan XD 5.0 L diesel ECM for a lit MIL with U3017. Volvo and Mack trucks of 2016–2017 set it intermittently, about 18 min after start; the advice is not to swap the ECU or cluster but to update software or wait 5 s with key on before cranking. Audi traces U301700 in the A3's 48 V battery module to a flat 12 V battery after long standstill.
c: Module software that flags timing differences too readily; fixed by reprogramming
Time or key-off information from another module arriving late or implausible at start-up
Discharged 12 V battery after a long standstill
Real defect of the module's clock circuit
s: MIL on without any drivability complaint
Code appears some minutes after start and later goes inactive
Reappears after clearing until the module software is updated

U3018.t: Control Module Input Power Circuit A/B Correlation
U3018.d: Where a module has two separate battery feeds, U3018 says that feed A and feed B no longer agree. In GM's 2025 body control module tables (25OBDG04B, 25OBDG03B) the two measured voltages are compared while a battery is detected and the starter is not engaged; a gap above 4 V in 4 s of a 5 s window fails the test, Type B. GM's electric brake booster in the 2016 and 2018 hybrid tables checks battery supply against the module's own supply instead and fails at a difference above 7 V within 0.01 s, Type A, because the booster's master switch needs a firm supply. In practice one feed is usually dead: GM's PIT5869/PIT5869A for 2021–2024 Tahoe, Suburban, Yukon and Escalade pair U3018 with U3505 and warm A/C when a shorted console lamp wire blows fuse F4DR of the second BCM feed.
c: Blown fuse on one of the two feeds, often from a short on a load circuit sharing it
High resistance or loose terminal in one feed wire
Weak battery causing uneven voltage drops between feeds
Faulty voltage measurement inside the module
s: Service engine soon lamp or system warning, depending on the module
Functions on the dead feed stop working, e.g. A/C blowing warm
Logged together with a low-voltage code for feed A or B

U3019.t: Control Module Input Power Circuit B/C Correlation
U3019.d: U3019 pairs the second and third supply of a module and reports that they drift apart. The one published use comes from GM's electric brake booster module in the 2016 and 2018 hybrid tables (16OBDG02, 18OBDG01). There, one voltage sensor watches the booster circuit supply and a second one the supply of the motor driver; the module divides the two readings and sets U3019 when the ratio rises above 1.321 or falls below 0.766 for 2 s while running or shutting down. GM describes this as a check for drift of the voltage divider, so besides a weak feed a measuring fault inside the module is a real candidate. The code is Type A, meaning MIL on the first trip, and it passes after about 5 s with ignition on. Because the booster supports braking, expect a brake warning and possibly reduced assist.
c: Voltage loss on one feed from a corroded fuse, terminal or splice
Drift of the voltage divider or sensor inside the module
Motor driver supply sagging under load from a faulty booster motor stage
s: MIL and brake system warning on the first trip
Reduced or harder brake pedal assist
Often stored with input power low or high codes of the same module

U301A.d: A wake-up circuit is a separate wire that rouses a sleeping module without bus traffic, for example when a charge cable is plugged in or another controller needs it. U301A reports that line A has lost continuity, so no valid signal reaches the input. Ford's 2019 hybrid OBD summary shows such a line in use: the battery energy control module relies on a hardwired charge wake-up signal before it runs its charging and contactor checks. No manufacturer documents U301A publicly. GM's PIT6198 for 2019–2022 Silverado and Sierra shows the consequence of a lost wake input at the ECM (circuit 5985, about 12 V with the BCM awake): other modules report U0100 and the service engine lamp comes on, with possible shift complaints. An open wake line usually means the module stays asleep or joins late.
c: Broken wake-up wire or pushed-out connector pin
Corroded or loose contact at the sending or receiving module
Sending module or charger not driving the wake-up output
Blown fuse in a supply-fed wake circuit
s: Module does not respond, other modules report lost communication
Charging or a function that needs the wake-up does not start

U301B.t: Control Module Wake-up Circuit A Low
U301B.d: U301B means wake-up line A sits below its expected level, typically because it touches ground or is pulled down by a faulty sender. What happens next depends on how the receiving chip works. NXP's CAN transceiver TJA1043, for example, wakes on a change of the WAKE pin in either direction once the new level has stayed stable for a short filter time, and its switching threshold lies a few volts below battery voltage (typically battery minus 2.5 V). A line clamped to ground therefore produces no further edge and acts like an unused pin, so the module stays asleep when it should start. A wire that only sags, for example through corrosion, can drop under the threshold too. No manufacturer documents U301B publicly; compared with U301A, look first for chafing against body metal.
c: Wake-up wire chafed through and touching ground
Corrosion or moisture pulling the level down at a connector
s: Module stays asleep, function or charging unavailable
Lost-communication codes in other modules

U301C.t: Control Module Wake-up Circuit A High
U301C.d: U301C is the opposite of U301B: wake-up line A is stuck high, usually shorted to a battery-fed wire or held up by a sender that never releases it. The receiving module then gets a permanent wake request. In Ford's 2019 hybrid OBD summary, a high charge wake-up signal is one of the conditions under which the battery energy control module runs its charge contactor and pack contactor checks, so a line stuck high makes the module behave as if charging were requested. The likely result is a module that never falls asleep and a 12 V battery that is flat after a few days of parking. A transceiver like NXP's TJA1043 also needs a change of level to register a wake, so a permanently high line cannot deliver a fresh wake event either. No manufacturer documents U301C publicly.
c: Wake-up wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Sending module or charger holding the wake output on
Moisture bridging the wake pin to a neighbouring supply pin
s: 12 V battery drained after the vehicle has been parked
Module or fan audible or active with the vehicle switched off

U301D.t: Control Module Wake-up Circuit A Performance
U301D.d: U301D says wake-up line A is electrically intact but its level does not fit what the module expects at that moment. Ford uses it in the battery energy control module of the 2019 Fusion Energi plug-in hybrid. Its OBD summary files the code under the charging performance checks: while the charger is precharging and its output voltage is already within the window for closing the charge contactors, the BECM still sees the charge wake-up line low before it has asked for the contactors to close. Ford's TSB 18-2386 and SSM 47630 report U301D with a lit MIL after charging on cars built up to 2 Oct 2018; if it is the only BECM code, the PCM and BECM are reprogrammed together (0.5 h) under the emissions warranty. Charging is normally unaffected, but the MIL stays on until cleared.
c: BECM and PCM software judging the wake-up timing too strictly
On-board charger raising its wake-up signal late or unsteadily
High resistance in the charge wake-up wire or connector
s: MIL on after a charging session
Code is the only entry in the battery control module

U301E.d: U301E is the open-circuit code for a second wake-up line, B, on modules that can be roused by more than one source, for example by a door or key event and separately by a charge or timer signal. Ford's patent US5945745A explains why such paths exist at all: a module may sit in a low-current state with the ignition off and still has to answer certain demands, such as panel lighting when the headlamps are switched on. No manufacturer documents U301E publicly; Ford's 2019 hybrid OBD summary shows only the A-side logic of a charge wake-up line. When only line B is open, the module still wakes through A and the bus but ignores the source wired to B, so the fault often shows as one specific function failing to start. If A and B are logged together, check the common sending module or a shared splice first.
c: Broken wake-up wire B or loose pin
Fault at a splice or sender shared with line A
Source wired to line B not driving its output
s: One wake-dependent function, e.g. timed or remote action, does not start
Module otherwise works normally once awake

U301F.t: Control Module Wake-up Circuit B Low
U301F.d: U301F reports wake-up line B held below its valid level, most often by a short to ground. Since B is a second, independent wake path, the module can still be roused through line A or the network; what it loses is the wake source wired to B. With an edge-triggered input such as the WAKE pin of NXP's TJA1043, which only reacts to a level change that remains stable for a short filter time, a grounded line simply never delivers that change. Its threshold sits only a few volts under battery voltage, so a partly shorted or corroded wire can count as low as well. No manufacturer documents U301F publicly. Unlike U301E, the circuit is not open, so a resistance check to ground with both connectors unplugged is the quickest way to find the fault.
c: Wake-up wire B chafed and touching ground
Moisture or corrosion pulling line B down
Source on line B with its output stuck low
s: Function tied to wake source B unavailable
No other complaint while the module is awake

U3020.t: Control Module Wake-up Circuit B High
U3020.d: U3020 sets when wake-up line B stays above its valid level, typically through contact with a battery or ignition feed, or because its source holds it on. The practical effect differs from U301F: a permanently active B line keeps asking the module to stay awake even when line A and the bus have gone quiet, so the module cannot enter sleep and the 12 V battery runs down while parked. Ford's 2019 hybrid OBD summary shows how much a high wake level can trigger, since its battery module starts contactor checks whenever the charge wake-up is high. At the same time a transceiver such as NXP's TJA1043 only wakes on a level change, so the fixed high line cannot pass on a real request from source B. No manufacturer documents U3020 publicly. A parasitic draw test with the line unplugged confirms the cause.
c: Wake-up wire B shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Source on line B holding its output on
Moisture bridging line B to a supply pin
s: 12 V battery flat after parking
Module stays awake with the vehicle locked

U3021.t: Control Module Wake-up Circuit B Performance
U3021.d: U3021 is the plausibility code for wake-up line B: the wire is neither open nor shorted, but the wake signal arrives at the wrong time or does not match what other inputs say. No manufacturer documents U3021 publicly. The closest published logic is Ford's U301D for line A in the 2019 Fusion Energi battery module, which fails when the charge wake-up is still low although the charger output voltage is already in the window for closing the contactors. Chrysler's powertrain counterpart P06E4, wake-up circuit performance, appears in 2024 Jeep Wrangler 4xe bulletins (e.g. 21-017-24) that cure it with new module software. Both cases point the same way: a performance fault on a wake line is often a timing question between two modules and is more often solved by a software update than by new wiring.
c: Software in sender or receiver judging the wake timing wrongly
Source on line B raising or dropping its signal late
Contact resistance on line B slowing the level change
s: Warning lamp or message after a wake event, e.g. after charging
Function works, but the code returns sporadically

U3022.d: U3022 is the last of the ignition input codes and, by its name, covers a line or line state that belongs to Accessory and Off together, i.e. to all positions in which the engine is not meant to run. GM's 2012 pickup wiring manual has a comparable case: its coded Off/Run/Crank circuit shows one common state for key out and for accessory, separate from key in, run and crank. A module that sees this accessory/off state while the network reports run or crank, or the opposite with the vehicle parked, logs U3022. No manufacturer documents U3022 publicly. In practice the code is less about a single dead wire than about two signals disagreeing, so stored codes for U300C, U300F or U3011 in the same module are useful hints as to which circuit is wrong.
c: Contact resistance in the ignition switch giving an in-between level
Input wire open, shorted or backfed
Body control module broadcasting a wrong power mode
s: Accessory functions behaving wrongly for the key position
Stored together with other ignition input codes in the same module

U3023.t: Control Module Input Power Circuit A - Ignition Input On/Start Circuit Correlation
U3023.d: U3023 means a module sees clearly different voltages on its permanent battery feed A and its switched run/crank input while both should be live. GM's 2025 engine and transmission control modules (25OBDG04B, 25OBDG03B and others) run this check once a battery is detected, run/crank is active and the starter is not engaged: a difference above 3 V in 40 of 50 samples fails it, in some ECM variants 50 of 63. The TCM entries are Type A and most ECM entries Type B, both with MIL; one 2025 ECM list (25OBDG04A) keeps it as Type C without MIL. GM bulletin 24-NA-124 shows a typical cause on 2020–2025 Silverado and Sierra 2500/3500: the ECM harness rubs through at the driver-side upper control arm bracket, giving U3023 with P2534, P0700 and others, a lit MIL, a stall or a no-start; the harness is repaired and tied away from the bracket.
c: Module harness chafed against a bracket, interrupting feed or ignition wire
Faulty run/crank relay or fuse feeding the ignition input
Voltage drop on the battery feed from a loose terminal or corroded fuse
Faulty voltage sensing inside the module
s: MIL on, often with several other codes from the same module
Engine stalls or does not start
Transmission faults when the TCM stores it

U3024.t: Control Module Input Power Circuit B - Ignition Input On/Start Circuit Correlation
U3024.d: U3024 is the same plausibility test as U3023, but against the module's second battery feed, B: with the key in run or start, feed B and the switched ignition input should show about the same voltage, and a lasting gap points to a fault on one of the two paths. The code only makes sense on modules with two permanent feeds plus an ignition line. No manufacturer documents U3024 publicly. For guidance, GM's 2025 tables describe the A variant in engine and transmission modules: battery present, run/crank active, starter not engaged, and a difference above 3 V in most of 50 samples. If only U3024 is stored and not U3023, feed B itself is the more likely culprit, since a missing ignition signal would upset both comparisons. Effects depend on what feed B powers inside the module.
c: Blown fuse or damaged wire on battery feed B
Run/crank relay or ignition wire delivering too little voltage
Loose or corroded pin for feed B in the module connector
Faulty voltage sensing inside the module
s: Warning lamp or message, depending on the module
Loss of functions supplied through feed B

U3025.d: Safety-relevant systems often give a supervising controller a hard-wired line through which it can switch off another module or its power stage, independent of the bus. Bosch patent US6804564B2 describes a first control unit that de-energizes a faulty second unit over such an output line, and FCA patent US10676100B2 shows a hybrid where control processor, motor processor and a monitor each have their own shutoff line to the inverter gate driver. U3025 says this disable line to module A is open or electrically missing. No manufacturer documents U3025 publicly. A broken line is serious either way: depending on the logic, module A may treat it as a permanent shutdown request and refuse to run, or stopping it in an emergency becomes impossible, which is why the system usually keeps the function off.
c: Broken disable wire or unplugged connector between the two modules
Corroded or pushed-out pin on the disable line
Output driver of the supervising module no longer driving the line
Input stage of module A misreading the line
s: Function of module A unavailable, e.g. drive system not ready
System warning message in the cluster

U3026.t: Control Module A Disable Circuit Low
U3026.d: U3026 is logged when the disable line to module A sits below its valid voltage range, typically because it is shorted to ground. What that means depends on the polarity the maker chose. In the Siemens control unit of patent US7596436B2 the enable signal is high for run and low for shutdown, and a monitoring circuit cuts the output stages by pulling the shutdown paths to vehicle ground. With such active-low logic a short to ground looks exactly like a permanent shutdown command, so module A stays off and the driver loses that function, although nothing else is wrong. Where low is the run state, the danger is the opposite, since the shutdown can no longer be signalled. No manufacturer documents U3026 publicly. Look for a chafed wire touching the body between the two modules.
c: Disable wire chafed through and touching body ground
Moisture in a connector creating a leak path to ground
Supervising module holding the line low permanently
s: Module A stays switched off, function unavailable
Warning message for the affected system

U3027.t: Control Module A Disable Circuit High
U3027.d: U3027 is the high-side counterpart: the disable line to module A reads above its valid range, as with a short to battery voltage or a neighbouring wire. In an active-low design such as the one in Siemens patent US7596436B2, where pulling the shutdown path to ground blocks the output stages, a line stuck high means module A keeps its enable and can no longer be switched off over the hard-wired path. That removes the independent safety layer FCA's patent US10676100B2 is built around, where losing a shutoff line could let a hybrid keep producing torque. Systems therefore treat this case strictly and usually disable the function by other means. No manufacturer documents U3027 publicly; check for a short to a powered wire in the harness and for water in connectors.
c: Disable wire shorted to a battery or supply wire
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in a connector
Output driver of the supervising module stuck high
s: Function locked out by the safety concept, system warning shown
Vehicle may not become ready to drive

U3028.t: Control Module A Disable Feedback Circuit
U3028.d: A disable line is only useful if someone can prove it works, so many designs read back what actually arrives at the switched module. U3028 reports a fault in that feedback path for module A: the returned signal is missing or does not match the state that was commanded. GM's patent US9122662B2 shows the principle: while the ignition is off, several processors set their outputs in a fixed series of test states and compare the resulting output of the inhibit path with the expected value, flagging a fault on any mismatch. FCA's patent US10676100B2 likewise steps through six combinations of shutoff signals. No manufacturer documents U3028 publicly. Unlike U3025, the shutdown line itself may be fine; the system just cannot confirm it, so it often withholds the function until a test passes.
c: Open feedback wire or loose pin between module A and the monitoring module
Self-test disturbed by low voltage or an early shutdown
Faulty readback stage in module A or the monitoring module
s: Function of module A blocked after the self-test, system warning
Fault may appear only at start-up or shutdown

U3029.t: Control Module A Disable Feedback Circuit Low
U3029.d: U3029 narrows the feedback fault to a signal that stays below its valid range, typically a readback wire shorted to ground. The consequence follows from the readback idea in GM's patent US9122662B2, where the inhibit path is driven through known test states and its actual output compared with the expected one: if the feedback is pinned low, every state that should read high fails, and the monitor cannot tell a working shutdown from a broken one. Depending on the design, a permanently low readback may also be taken as module A already being disabled. No manufacturer documents U3029 publicly. The usual suspects are a chafed readback wire touching the body, water in a connector or a defective input stage; the disable line itself should be checked separately.
c: Feedback wire shorted to body ground
Moisture or corrosion pulling the readback pin low
Defective readback input stage in the monitoring module
s: Function of module A locked out, system warning displayed
Code returns at every start until the short is found

U302A.t: Control Module A Disable Feedback Circuit High
U302A.d: U302A means the readback from module A's disable path is stuck above its valid range, for example through a short to a supply wire. The risk is a false all-clear or a false alarm, depending on which level stands for disabled. In a test sequence like the six-step shutoff check of FCA patent US10676100B2, a feedback that never drops will fail the steps where a shutdown is commanded, and the controller must assume the shutdown path does not work. FCA notes that such a result would eventually need a fault flag, and that blocking the vehicle outright could strand the driver, so it proposes rerouting the signal through another processor to keep availability. No manufacturer documents U302A publicly. Check the readback wire for contact with powered circuits and the connectors for moisture.
c: Feedback wire shorted to a battery or supply wire
Corrosion bridging the readback pin to a neighbouring supply pin
Module A driving its feedback output permanently high
s: System warning and function of module A unavailable
In hybrids, possibly no ready mode or reduced drive power

U302B.d: U302B belongs to the ignition outputs, i.e. a feed that a module switches itself instead of merely reading it. The Accessory/On/Start variant should carry voltage in every power mode except Off and, unlike most accessory feeds, should stay on while the engine cranks. The driving unit, typically a body controller or the power supply unit of a keyless start system, compares its command with what it reads back on its own pin and stores U302B when the two differ: voltage in Off, or none in accessory, run or crank. No manufacturer documents U302B publicly. Tokai Rika's patent US6900552B2 shows such a unit switching separate relay coils for accessory, two ignition stages and the starter through FET drivers. A driver stuck on or a welded relay contact on this feed can flatten the battery overnight.
c: Welded relay contact keeping the feed live in Off
Faulty driver stage in the switching module, stuck on or not switching
Output wire or a connected load shorted to ground, tripping the driver protection
Blown fuse between the relay and the loads on this feed
s: Battery flat after the car has been parked
Several loads on the feed dead although the vehicle is switched on
Warning about the power supply or ignition system in the cluster

U302C.d: U302C covers an ignition output that encodes several states on one wire: Off, On and Start each get their own level, so a single conductor passes the power mode on to other units. It is the sending counterpart of coded inputs like the Off/Run/Crank circuit that GM's wiring manual for its 2012 light-duty trucks shows between ignition switch and body controller, which uses separate levels for key removed, key in at off, running and cranking. A module producing such a coded line stores U302C once the level read back at its own pin differs from the state it means to transmit. No manufacturer documents U302C publicly. Since receivers evaluate voltage bands rather than on or off, a partial short, an extra load or a corroded pin can turn run into start or off without the line going dead, so measure it in each mode with receivers connected.
c: Corroded or loose pin shifting the coded level
Faulty input in a receiving module pulling the line out of its band
Chafed wire with a partial short to ground or voltage
Faulty output stage in the sending module
s: Other modules acting on a wrong power mode, e.g. shutting down or not waking
Sporadic warnings that change with key position or button presses

U302D.d: U302D concerns the output that powers the On/Start circuits, i.e. everything that has to work with the engine running and through cranking but not in Off or Accessory. On GM's 2012 pickups the body control module handles this by switching the coil of the run/crank relay over circuit 5199. GM bulletin PIT5817A, covering 2020–2021 models such as Escalade, Tahoe, Corvette and CT5, shows what goes wrong on that side: the BCM keeps driving ignition main relay KR73 after shut-off, circuit 5199 stays live and the battery runs down, while engine, transmission and brake controllers store P2535 and the cluster stores U300D; the repair is a new BCM. GM records that case through input codes in the receivers, not as U302D. A module that checks its own on/start output would catch the same fault at the source. No manufacturer documents U302D publicly.
c: Relay driver in the body control module staying on after shut-off
Ignition main relay contact welded or relay not pulling in
Relay coil control wire open or shorted to voltage
Retrofitted device feeding voltage back into the run/crank circuit
s: Battery repeatedly flat, often after a remote start
Engine lamp at start-up with P2535 stored in engine and transmission modules
No start or modules without power if the output fails open

U302E.d: U302E applies to an output intended to carry voltage in On alone, which means it has to switch off while the starter turns. The driving module must blank out that intended gap during cranking and judge the output only in steady power modes, otherwise every start would log the code. How such a check can be built is shown in Yazaki's patent CN106797120A: a controller measures the voltage behind a second ignition relay, treats a reading below a threshold set between nominal voltage and 0 V as a relay that failed open, warns the driver on a display and moves the affected loads over to the first ignition feed. Transferred to U302E, a dead output in On points to a relay stuck open, a blown fuse or a broken wire, while voltage in Off points to a welded contact or a driver stuck on. No manufacturer documents U302E publicly.
c: Run relay not closing, e.g. burnt contacts or open coil
Blown fuse or broken wire behind the relay
Welded contact or driver stuck on, leaving the output live in Off
Module software judging the intended cut during cranking as a fault
s: Loads on the run-only feed dead with the engine running
Power supply warning in the cluster
Battery discharged when the output stays on after shut-off

U302F.d: U302F is logged by the module that switches the accessory feed for audio, sockets or windows when that feed is out of step with its own command. Two normal behaviours have to be ruled out first. Keyless systems cut accessory power during cranking: in Tokai Rika's patent US7254466B2 the power supply unit releases the accessory relay when start is requested and re-energizes it only once the engine controller reports that combustion has begun. GM's 2012 pickups, on the other hand, keep accessory voltage on after key-off through a relay inside the BCM for roughly 10 minutes, unless a door is opened. Outside those windows, a live feed in a locked car suggests a welded relay or a driver stuck on, and a dead feed in accessory an open relay, fuse or wire. No manufacturer documents U302F publicly.
c: Accessory relay welded or its driver stuck on
Blown accessory fuse or open feed wire
Retrofitted equipment overloading or backfeeding the accessory feed
s: Radio, sockets or windows dead in accessory mode
Accessories still on long after locking, battery drained

U3030.d: U3030 points to the start output, the line through which a module energizes the starter relay or passes on a crank request; it should be active for seconds at most. In Tokai Rika's push-button start patents the power supply unit switches the starter relay on together with the ignition relays once brake pedal and button are confirmed, and off as soon as the engine controller reports that the engine has fired. Which unit owns this output varies: on GM's 2012 pickups the engine control module, not the body controller, drives the starter enable relay. A module logs U3030 when the line stays dead although cranking is commanded, leaving the engine unable to crank, or stays live after the command ends, which can keep the starter engaged. No manufacturer documents U3030 publicly; starter relay circuit faults have their own codes, P0615 to P0617.
c: Faulty start driver in the module, not switching or stuck on
Start control wire open or shorted to ground or voltage
Open or shorted coil in the starter relay loading the output
Weak battery pulling the output level down during cranking
s: Engine does not crank when start is requested
Starter keeps running or grinding after the engine has fired
Start only on a second or third attempt

U3031.d: U3031 relates to an output whose task is to announce the off state, for example a discrete line that tells other units they may shut down, or the off branch of a power-mode output. Shutdown in many vehicles hinges on such a signal: in Ford's patent US5945745A, modules work normally while an ignition signal is present and fall back to a sleep mode with minimal current draw once it disappears, and GM's 2012 pickups allow the BCM to sleep only when none of its outputs is commanded. If the generating module finds this off output in the wrong state, it records U3031. Stuck in the not-off state, receivers stay awake and drain the battery; signalling off while driving could shut functions down on the move. No manufacturer documents U3031 publicly, so where this output sits has to be taken from the wiring diagram of the vehicle.
c: Faulty output stage in the module that generates the off signal
Off-signal wire open or shorted to ground or voltage
Corroded or loose pin at the sending or receiving module
Module software setting the off output at the wrong moment
s: Battery drained because modules do not go to sleep
Functions switching off unexpectedly with the vehicle on

U3032.d: U3032 is the output counterpart of U3022: a line that a module drives to express the grouped state Accessory or Off, i.e. every power mode where the engine should stay off. Such grouping exists in real wiring. GM's 2012 pickup electrical manual shows a coded ignition circuit whose level is identical for a pulled key and for accessory, and changes once the key is inserted, the engine runs or cranks. A module generating a comparable output monitors the level at its pin and logs U3032 when the level differs from what it means to send, for instance accessory/off appearing while the vehicle runs. Receivers may then switch functions off on the move or stay awake when parked. No manufacturer documents U3032 publicly; codes such as U3022 or U302C stored in the receiving units show which side is wrong.
c: Output stage in the driving module stuck or failed
Output wire shorted to ground or voltage, or broken
Corroded or loose pin shifting the coded level
Retrofitted accessory tapped into the line
s: Accessories such as radio or sockets not matching the key or button position
Modules staying awake after shut-off, battery drained overnight
Related ignition input codes stored in other modules

U3033.d: U3033 reports that a module's own security certificate is absent or fails validation, so the unit cannot prove its identity in signed or encrypted exchanges. Stellantis uses the code in the security gateway (SGW) and in connected radios. For 2020 Durango and Pacifica radios, case S2008000164 explains that the certificate is fetched once the car is online and that a stored entry may need as many as 40 key cycles before it disappears; no part is to be replaced. Later bulletins for Ram, Jeep Wagoneer, Grand Cherokee and Dodge Charger (08-322-25, 08-173-26, 9100701) name U3033-00/-01 in the SGW, state that it leaves the MIL off and fix it by reflashing the SGW when the over-the-air update failed. Bulletin 9100386 adds checks of connectivity and the Ethernet network and reloading the certificate store.
c: Certificate not yet downloaded because the vehicle had no connectivity
Gateway software setting the code erroneously, fixed by reflash
Certificate store empty or holding a wrong certificate
s: Code active or stored and cannot be cleared, usually without MIL
Security gateway not answering the diagnostic tester
Message asking for an over-the-air update or a service visit

U3034.d: U3034 concerns the secret keys or certificates that modules use to authenticate messages to each other: the module finds that key material missing or not matching its partners. Ford's TRON (Trusted Real-Time Operation Network) on 2023–2025 models from F-150 to Mustang Mach-E shows the usual trigger. If a TRON module is replaced and fresh keys are not distributed, the gateway and the other TRON modules can log U3034 together with U3035, U3036 and U211A–U211C; SSM 53638 and 53759 call for the TRON Module Authentication routine, started from the gateway in Ford's diagnostic software. Volkswagen's bulletin 01-24-02 lists U303400 as a sporadic, irrelevant entry in the brake electronics of 2024 ID.4 with one gateway software level. No MIL is documented; the cause is setup or software far more often than hardware.
c: Module replaced without running the key distribution routine
Gateway software logging the code without real fault
Partner module offline during key exchange
Key storage in the module damaged
s: Code appears in several modules at once after a repair
Functions relying on secured messages unavailable or degraded
Often no noticeable symptom, sporadic entry only

U3035.d: U3035 means a secured message arrived but its authentication part did not check out, so the receiver treats the content as invalid. In AUTOSAR Secure Onboard Communication the receiver recomputes the message authentication code over data ID, payload and freshness value; a mismatch or an unusable key counts as failed verification and the message is dropped. Ford's SSM 51497 for 2023 Super Duty says the PCM sets U3035 when authentication fails after key initialization, harmless without other codes, MIL or drivability issues; TSB 23-2421 reflashes the 6.8L/7.3L PCM when the MIL is on with P061B, U0140 and U3035/U3036. Audi's TSB 2077740 ties U303500 with U029400 and U012900 to Q6 e-tron that cannot select a gear in cold weather. Ford TRON module replacement without new keys also causes it.
c: Module software rejecting valid messages, fixed by update
Keys not aligned after a module replacement
Messages checked before key initialization or wake-up finished
Corrupted frames from wiring or bus faults
s: Code found during a self-test without complaints
MIL with further network or processor codes on some engines
Function refused, e.g. gear selection not possible in the cold

U3036.d: U3036 judges authentication over time rather than a single bad frame: checks keep failing, cannot be completed, or sender and receiver lose step, for example in their freshness counters. AUTOSAR SecOC shows why this differs from U3035: a receiver retries when no freshness value is available or the crypto service is busy and only gives up after a configured number of build or verify attempts. Ford stores U3036 in the 2023 Super Duty PCM; SSM 51497 explains that it is logged while the PCM keeps monitoring as the CAN bus goes to sleep, and needs no action without other codes, MIL or drivability faults. TSB 23-2421 covers 6.8L and 7.3L trucks with MIL, P061B and U0140, cured by new PCM software. After a TRON module swap Ford also lists U3036 among codes from keys that were not redistributed.
c: Monitoring software flags authentication during bus sleep or wake-up
Freshness counters of sender and receiver out of step
Keys not redistributed after module replacement
Sending module intermittently missing on the bus
s: Code stored after a self-test or key-off without complaints
MIL together with P061B or U0140 on some engines
Secured functions working only intermittently

U3500.t: Control Module Input Power A Circuit Range/Performance
U3500.d: U3500 says that supply input A of a module is present but its voltage is implausible, for example outside the window expected for the current power mode or contradicting other measurements, without clearly passing a lower or upper limit. It thus sits between U3006, which reports a missing or open feed, and the hard limit codes U3501 and U3502. Which pin is A is up to the manufacturer; in GM's electric brake booster tables (2016–2019 hybrid) A is the module's own logic and CAN supply, watched for under 7.5 V and over 16 V, but GM uses only the Low and High codes there. No manufacturer documents U3500 publicly. Typical causes are a high-resistance contact that sags under load, a poor ground or a drifting internal measurement.
c: High-resistance terminal or fuse contact on feed A
Poor module ground shifting the measured supply
Drifting voltage measurement inside the module
s: Functions of the module dropping out or behaving inconsistently
Code returns mainly under electrical load

U3501.t: Control Module Input Power A Circuit Low
U3501.d: U3501 reports that supply A of a module is below its permitted range. GM's electric brake booster (BSC2) in the 2016–2019 hybrid OBD tables runs two checks: the CAN/logic supply under 7.5 V for 0.09 s, and the internal sensor for the module supply under 4.9 V for 0.2 s, a level below the point where the hardware should already have shut down. Both are Special Type C, so no MIL. The weight of the code lies elsewhere: GM lists U3501 among the conditions that suspend many other booster tests, because motor and sensor checks are meaningless without proper supply. It passes after 30 s with ignition on. Usual causes are a weak or discharged battery, a deep dip while cranking, a corroded fuse or terminal on the feed, or a bad ground.
c: Deep voltage dip during engine start
Corroded fuse, terminal or ground in the A feed
Internal supply stage of the module faulty
s: Module resets or drops off the network at low voltage
Other self-tests of the module suspended
Warning lamp for the affected system, usually without MIL

U3502.t: Control Module Input Power A Circuit High
U3502.d: U3502 means supply A rises above its allowed limit. In GM's 2016–2019 hybrid OBD tables the electric brake booster checks its CAN supply voltage and sets U3502 above 16 V lasting 0.09 s while its software runs; this is Type B, so the MIL comes on after two failing trips, and the test passes after 30 s with ignition on. Unlike low voltage, which a module can often ride out, overvoltage endangers electronics and power stages, which explains the short reaction time. Common causes are a regulator fault in the generator or DC/DC converter, jump-starting from a 24 V source or a wrongly set charger, and a load dump when a battery cable comes loose while charging. If several modules report high voltage at the same moment, the charging system is at fault, not the module.
c: Generator regulator or DC/DC converter overcharging
Jump start or external charger with excessive voltage
Loose battery terminal causing voltage spikes
Faulty voltage measurement inside the module
s: MIL after repeated trips
Several modules logging overvoltage at once
Flickering lights or battery warning

U3503.t: Control Module Input Power A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
U3503.d: U3503 stands for a supply A that keeps jumping: mostly correct, but with brief dropouts or spikes, so the module sees erratic readings or restarts. What sets it apart from U3501 and U3502 is the pattern rather than the level: short interruptions, fast swings between samples or repeated resets. No manufacturer documents U3503 publicly. GM's brake booster tables show how short supply check windows can be (0.09 s), and that is the time scale on which a loose crimp or a cracked solder joint becomes visible. Look for loose terminals, fuses with weak clamping, chafed wires near moving parts and grounds shared with large loads; wiggle tests while the engine idles, with a scope or min/max recording help, because a plain multimeter averages such events away.
c: Loose crimp, pin or fuse contact in feed A
Ground shared with heavy loads causing dips
Cracked solder joint inside the module
s: Sporadic resets or brief function dropouts
Code returns over bumps or when loads switch

U3504.t: Control Module Input Power B Circuit Range/Performance
U3504.d: U3504 checks the plausibility of the second supply input, B. Modules with high-power stages often split their supply: in GM's electric brake booster tables B is the battery feed of the booster circuit (voltage sensor 1), checked separately against low and high limits and compared with feed C. U3504 applies when B is present but implausible, for example disagreeing with the logic supply or failing to follow battery voltage under load, without crossing a hard limit. No manufacturer documents U3504 publicly. Because B often feeds valves or motors, a high resistance tends to show only while current flows, as a drop that is invisible at rest. Measure the voltage drop across fuse, connector and ground under load and check whether U3018 or U3505 are stored as well.
c: Resistance in fuse, connector or ground of feed B under load
Feed B supplied from a different source than expected
Drifting measurement of feed B inside the module
s: Power stage functions weak or switched off under load
Code mainly when motors or valves are active

U3505.t: Control Module Input Power B Circuit Low
U3505.d: U3505 reports that supply input B is too low. In GM's 2016–2019 hybrid tables the electric brake booster treats B as the battery feed of the booster circuit and checks it at several levels: sensor reading under 6 V for 30 s, battery voltage under 9.3 V for 90 s, and quick 0.2 s checks with reduced assist once it falls below 9.3 V (level 1) or 7.5 V (level 2); all Special Type C, no MIL. Body controllers use the code too: GM bulletin PIT5869 (revised as PIT5869A) on 2021–2024 full-size SUVs such as Escalade and Tahoe pairs U3505 with U3018 and B1AA3, warm A/C and the SES light; a shorted circuit to the front console compartment lamp opens fuse F4DR on the BCM's second feed. Check fuse and battery first.
c: Fuse of feed B blown by a short elsewhere on the circuit
Corroded terminal or ground in feed B
Internal measurement or supply path faulty
s: Functions on the second feed missing, e.g. warm A/C
Reduced brake assist with warning on booster modules
Stored together with U3018

U3506.t: Control Module Input Power B Circuit High
U3506.d: U3506 reports overvoltage on supply input B. In GM's electric brake booster (2016–2019 hybrid OBD tables) three checks feed this code: battery voltage of the booster circuit above 17 V for 90 s, the supply of the internal motor driver above 18 V for 1.1 s, and battery voltage above 16.5 V for 1.1 s, at which booster performance is cut back. All are Type B, MIL after two trips; passing takes 90 s with ignition on. The graded limits reveal the idea: brief excursions are tolerated, lasting ones or those that put the power stage at risk are not. Check the charging voltage at idle with loads switched on first, then external chargers, jump starters and loose battery terminals that produce voltage spikes.
c: Charging voltage too high from regulator or DC/DC converter
Jump starter or charger delivering excessive voltage
Faulty measurement of feed B in the module
s: MIL after two trips
Reduced assist of the supplied power stage
Overvoltage codes in further modules

U3507.t: Control Module Input Power B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
U3507.d: U3507 covers an unsteady supply B: the voltage is mostly in range but drops out or jumps for short moments. Since B often powers stages such as motors or valves, the dropouts typically appear when these draw current, for instance while braking or steering. GM's brake booster tables show that the module judges B over short and long windows (0.2 s up to 90 s); a fault that merely flickers fits neither the low nor the high code and counts as erratic. No manufacturer documents U3507 publicly. Suspect loose crimp contacts, worn fuse holders, corroded grounds and chafed wires, and test under load with a recording meter or scope. If U3505 or U3018 are stored as well, the feed has probably dropped out completely at times.
c: Loose crimp or worn fuse holder in feed B
Corroded ground point of the module
s: Brief function dropouts when power stages switch on
Code returns sporadically and is hard to reproduce

U3508.t: Control Module Input Power C Circuit Range/Performance
U3508.d: U3508 checks the plausibility of a third supply input, C. Only modules with large or separately protected loads have three feeds; in GM's electric brake booster (2016–2019 hybrid tables) C is the motor driver feed, measured by voltage sensor 2 and compared with feed B through U3019 (ratio outside 0.766 to 1.321). U3508 would apply if C is present but its value does not suit the operating state, for instance staying high while the motor draws current or departing from battery voltage, without crossing a hard limit. No manufacturer documents U3508 publicly; GM uses only the Low and High codes for C. Check the motor feed and its ground under load and look for related U3019 or U3013.
c: Resistance in the motor supply path of feed C
Poor ground of the power stage
Drift of the internal voltage divider
s: Reduced function of the motor-driven system
Correlation codes between feeds stored as well

U3509.t: Control Module Input Power C Circuit Low
U3509.d: U3509 says supply C is too low. In GM's 2016–2019 hybrid OBD tables the electric brake booster sets it when voltage sensor 2, which watches the motor driver supply, reads below 6 V for 90 s while the car travels faster than 4 mph. Unlike the A and B low codes, which are Special Type C without MIL, this one is Type A, lighting the MIL after one failing trip, because the booster motor cannot build assist without this feed. Passing requires a straight drive of at least 3.1 miles. Less than 6 V for that long almost always means an open fuse or wire, a failed connector or a deeply discharged battery rather than a brief dip. Drivers may see a brake warning and feel a harder pedal; check the motor fuse and its ground first.
c: Fuse of the motor supply open
Broken wire or failed connector in feed C
Internal measurement of feed C faulty
s: MIL and brake warning on the first trip
Harder brake pedal through missing assist

U350A.t: Control Module Input Power C Circuit High
U350A.d: U350A is the overvoltage code for supply C. GM's electric brake booster (2016–2019 hybrid tables) logs it when voltage sensor 2 on the motor driver supply exceeds 19.8 V for 90 s at speeds above 4 mph, Type A, so a single failing trip lights the MIL. The limit is higher than the 16 to 18 V thresholds used for feeds A and B because the motor stage tolerates more, yet a lasting excess is treated as serious since it threatens the power transistors. The pass condition is a straight drive over 3.1 miles or more. Such values rarely arise in a healthy 12 V system: think of a failed generator regulator or DC/DC converter, jump-starting from a 24 V source, or, with normal battery voltage, an internal sensing error.
c: Generator regulator or DC/DC converter overcharging
Jump start from a 24 V source
Faulty measurement of feed C inside the module
s: MIL and brake warning on the first trip
Brake assist reduced or switched off

U350B.t: Control Module Input Power C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
U350B.d: U350B reports that supply C fluctuates: it drops or spikes briefly without staying out of range. Where C feeds a motor stage, as in GM's electric brake booster (motor driver supply, voltage sensor 2), such faults surface at moments of peak current, because a loose contact then loses voltage or opens for an instant. GM itself uses only the Low, High and correlation codes for this feed, and no manufacturer documents U350B publicly. The difference from U3509 lies in the timing: short events rather than a steady low level. Typical findings are a fuse with weak clamping, a loose ring terminal on the ground, chafing near the module or corroded pins; check with a recording meter while the load is operating and look for U3019 as a companion code.
c: Loose fuse contact or ring terminal in feed C or its ground
s: Brief loss of assist from the motor-driven function
Sporadic warning lamp that clears again

U350C.d: U350C reports that the fan built into or attached to a control module draws no current, or its circuit is open, at the moment the module switches it on. Some electronics carry their own blower: on the 2021 Toyota RAV4 Prime the plug-in charger has a fan with a speed sensor (bulletin T-SB-0021-21, code P1CE931), and the central infotainment unit of the Karma Revero has one under a shroud (TB-24-94-01). For electrical parts that cool inverters and traction batteries, CARB requires circuit and function monitoring. No maker documents U350C itself. With the fan dead, the module heats up and may cut its own output, charge more slowly or shut down. Shorts are split off into U350D/U350E; U350F covers a fan that is wired correctly but runs wrong.
c: Fan motor winding or brushes open
Fan plug loose or not latched after the module was removed
Broken fan supply or control wire
Fan output stage inside the module failed open
s: Module fan silent when it should run
Module overheats, reduces output, charges slower or restarts
Temperature warning or function message for the affected module

U350D.t: Control Module Cooling Fan Circuit Low
U350D.d: U350D is set when the voltage or current feedback in a control module's fan circuit sits below the window the module expects. Usually the fan supply or control wire touches ground, or the motor itself has shorted turns, so the output stage limits current or switches off and the fan stands still; a blown fan fuse produces the same picture. Electronics with a dedicated fan exist, for example the charger of the 2021 Toyota RAV4 Prime with its fan speed sensor (T-SB-0021-21), and CARB demands that electrical outputs cooling inverters and batteries be checked for circuit faults. No manufacturer publishes U350D. Once warm, the module will most likely protect itself by lowering its output. An open circuit is U350C, a short to voltage U350E.
c: Fan supply or control wire chafed through to ground
Fan motor with shorted windings drawing excess current
Fan fuse blown as a result of the short
Output stage in the module pulling the line low
s: Module fan does not run
Reduced function or shutdown of the module when hot
Blown fan fuse

U350E.t: Control Module Cooling Fan Circuit High
U350E.d: U350E points to a fan circuit whose level is higher than the module expects, typically because the control or feedback line is shorted to battery voltage or the output stage is stuck on. Unlike the low and open faults, the fan may then run all the time, even with the module cold or the car parked, which is audible and can drain the 12 V battery. Fan-cooled electronics are found in infotainment units such as the central unit of the Karma Revero (TB-24-94-01) and in on-board chargers; CARB treats electrical cooling outputs for inverters and batteries as monitored components. U350E is not documented by any manufacturer in public. Check the harness for chafing against supply wires before suspecting the module.
c: Fan control or feedback wire shorted to a 12 V supply
Fan output stage in the module stuck on
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the fan connector
s: Module fan running continuously, also after switch-off
12 V battery discharged after standing
Fan does not react to temperature changes

U350F.t: Control Module Cooling Fan Circuit Range/Performance
U350F.d: U350F means the fan circuit is electrically sound but the fan does not do what it is told: its speed feedback disagrees with the command, or the module keeps heating up although the fan is switched on.
