Dust, a blocked or rubbing blade, worn bearings or a lost speed signal are typical. A related case is Toyota's bulletin T-SB-0021-21 for the 2021 RAV4 Prime: the charger fan's speed sensor reported no signal (P1CE931), charging took longer, and the cure was new charger software rather than a new fan. Karma fixed noise from the infotainment unit fan with a redesigned shroud (TB-24-94-01). CARB asks for a functional check of cooling performance where feasible. No maker lists U350F itself; U350C to U350E cover wiring faults.
c: Fan blade blocked by dust, debris or a deformed shroud
Worn fan bearing slowing the fan down
Fan speed sensor signal missing or misread
Module software misjudging the fan feedback (Toyota RAV4 Prime charger)
s: Fan noise, rattling or whining from the module
Module runs hot, charging or function slowed
Code returns after clearing once the fan is commanded again

U3510.d: U3510 says a control module lacks a calibration it needs: either the data set that adapts its software to the vehicle was never written or got lost, or a learned calibration such as a sensor alignment has not been done. CARB makes every emission-critical unit report a calibration ID and a verification number, so empty or invalid data cannot pass unnoticed. No maker publishes U3510 itself, but related codes show both meanings: Hyundai's chassis code C2702, worded the same way, appears on 2019 Elantra blind-spot radars (bulletin 19-BE-016H, new radar plus mounting-angle check), and Stellantis' C0529-00 for the steering angle sensor of the 2023 Dodge Hornet lit the MIL until the wheel was turned lock to lock (08-148-23, EPS update).
c: New or used module installed without programming or setup
Software update aborted, e.g. by low 12 V voltage or lost connection
Required learn or alignment routine not performed after repair
Internal memory of the module losing its stored data
s: Function of the affected module unavailable or limited
Warning lamp of the related system, MIL if the module is OBD-relevant
Fault appears right after a module replacement or software update

U3511.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit B
U3511.d: U3511 is the general fault of a second high-voltage interlock loop, circuit B. Many vehicles need more than one loop: a Volvo truck patent gives each separate HV bus its own interlock circuit, and a Samsung SDI patent describes extra loops for battery-internal parts such as the service disconnect or the junction box, each with its own source, detector and diagnosis. Which plugs belong to loop B is not published by any maker; GM's OBD tables and Mercedes' model line 243 report all interlock faults with the loop A codes P0A0A–P0A0D. The module sets U3511 when loop B is disturbed but no more precise low, high or performance result applies. The contactors stay open and the vehicle cannot reach ready mode. CARB lists interlock loops as safety-only systems.
c: HV connector, cover or disconnect in loop B open or not latched after service
Bent, pushed-back or corroded interlock pins
Interlock wiring of loop B chafed or cut
Source or sense stage for loop B in the monitoring module faulty
s: Vehicle does not enter ready mode
High-voltage or hybrid system warning in the cluster
Charging refused

U3512.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit B Performance
U3512.d: U3512 is stored when interlock loop B still conducts but behaves implausibly: its resistance drifts outside the permitted window, the returned signal does not follow the test pattern in time, or two readings of the same loop disagree. CATL's interlock patent explains why loops misreport: contact impedance between HV parts, supply fluctuations and static discharge can cause false alarms. Samsung SDI points out that different loops may have different detection and reaction times, so loop B can be judged by other rules than loop A. Oxidised pins, a connector not fully latched or a harness rubbing on the body are likely causes, as Mercedes lists for its interlock codes P0A0A00 to P0A0D00. No maker documents U3512 itself. The HV system may drop out repeatedly rather than stay off.
c: Oxidised interlock pins raising the loop resistance
Connector in loop B seated but not fully latched
Harness rubbing on the body with intermittent contact
Interference or supply ripple distorting the loop signal
s: HV system switches off and on again unexpectedly
Ready mode lost while driving or at start
Interlock codes in several modules at once

U3513.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit B Low
U3513.d: U3513 reports a signal on interlock loop B that stays below its lower limit while the loop is energised by the module. What that means depends on the circuit: where the module feeds a test voltage in and reads it back at the far end, an opened plug reads low just like a wire touching ground. GM's documented loop A gives a sense of scale: its low code sets when less than 30 % of its 5 V check voltage comes back in two 12.5 ms samples, Type A. Texas Instruments' reference design shows how a current-fed loop can tell both apart: a grounded wire makes the loop current vanish while the supply current rises, with an open loop both drop. No maker publishes U3513. The contactors stay open; check loop B for chafed wires and unplugged connectors.
c: Interlock wire of loop B chafed through to ground
Plug or cover in loop B open, read as low by the sensing circuit
Interlock source in the monitoring module not delivering its signal
s: No ready mode, HV contactors stay open
Hybrid or EV warning lamp, MIL depending on maker
Charging not possible

U3514.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit B High
U3514.d: U3514 means loop B reads higher than allowed: a wire of the loop touches 12 V or another supply, or the loop does not fall back to its low state once the module turns its source off. GM's loop A code checks both states, allowing 24 % of 5 V while the source is off and 44 % while it is on. Ford's interlock patent tests the source line for a short to 12 V before releasing the loop, then stores a trouble code and turns on the Service Soon lamp rather than a general warning. In the reference design from Texas Instruments a short to battery shows up as loop current that no longer follows the commanded on/off pattern. No manufacturer lists U3514 itself. Disconnecting segments one at a time shows where the foreign voltage enters loop B.
c: Interlock wire of loop B shorted to 12 V or another supply
Interlock source in the module not switching off
Water in a connector bridging an interlock pin to a supply pin
Incorrect splice or add-on wiring after a repair
s: Vehicle will not start or enter ready mode
Service or HV warning lamp on
Fault stays present with all HV connectors properly mated

U3515.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit C
U3515.d: U3515 is the general fault of a third interlock loop, circuit C. Such a loop exists where one or two are not enough: Caterpillar's patent for battery machines forms a separate interlock circuit from each battery group with its disconnect and contactor pair, and Samsung SDI mentions designs with more than two independent loops for parts inside the pack. Volvo couples two loops through an isolated relay so that a fault in one opens the other, which is why codes for several loops can be logged together. Which component a manufacturer wires into loop C is not documented publicly for any vehicle. U3515 applies when loop C fails without a more specific low, high or performance result; HV power remains off until the loop is closed again.
c: Connector or cover belonging to loop C opened during work and not refitted correctly
Interlock harness of loop C damaged
Fault in a coupled loop opening loop C as well
Monitoring module unable to drive or read loop C
s: No ready mode, HV system switched off
Interlock codes for more than one loop stored together
Charging blocked

U3516.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit C Performance
U3516.d: U3516 flags loop C as electrically present but untrustworthy: resistance, timing or pattern of the returned signal fall outside what the module accepts, often only for moments. As the U35xx series has no intermittent code for loops B and C, unlike P0A0E for loop A, short dropouts will probably be stored here. The interlock patent from CATL names contact impedance, supply ripple and static discharge as sources of false trips, and Mercedes' bulletin for model line 243 links its interlock codes to oxidised low-voltage pins, bent pins at HV components and twisted harness runs; it adds that the HV component itself is rarely to blame. No maker documents U3516. Drivers notice HV shutdowns that come and go, often after rough roads or rain.
c: Loose or spread contact in a connector of loop C
Twisted or strained harness section moving with the body
Static discharge or interference on the interlock line
s: Sporadic loss of ready mode
HV warning that appears and clears by itself
Fault hard to reproduce in the workshop

U3517.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit C Low
U3517.d: U3517 says the level read back on interlock loop C stays too low. Depending on the design, an opened plug in loop C, a wire chafed to ground or a failed source in the monitoring module all lead to it. In current-fed designs such as the Texas Instruments reference circuit, a short to ground draws extra supply current while an opened loop does not, which helps to separate the two. For loop A, GM uses a 5 V test voltage and a 30 % lower limit, which indicates the margins involved. Mercedes has technicians measure interlock loop resistance segment by segment on model line 243, a method that suits loop C just as well. No manufacturer publishes U3517 itself. Until the fault is cleared, the contactors remain open.
c: Interlock wire of loop C chafed to ground at a module or the body
Connector in loop C unplugged, sensed as a low signal
Broken interlock connector housing or terminal
Source stage for loop C failed in the monitoring module
s: Vehicle cannot be started
HV system warning in the instrument cluster
Charging unavailable

U3518.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit C High
U3518.d: U3518 is stored when loop C reads above its upper limit, usually a loop wire shorted to 12 V, to the wire of another loop in a shared connector, or a source stage that no longer switches off. Volvo's two-loop patent couples loops only through a galvanically isolated relay, so foreign voltage from one loop is not meant to reach another; where wires of different loops share a connector, damage can still bridge them. Ford's patent stores a code and switches on its Service Soon lamp once an interlock circuit is shorted high, and Texas Instruments shows that the loop current then stops following the commanded pattern. No maker documents U3518. The HV system stays off; inspect connectors that carry interlock pins of several loops first.
c: Interlock wire of loop C shorted to 12 V
Loop C bridged to another loop's wire in a shared connector
Interlock source for loop C stuck on in the module
s: No ready mode despite all HV connectors being in place
Service or HV warning lamp lit
High codes for more than one interlock loop

U3519.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit D
U3519.d: U3519 marks a fault on the fourth interlock loop of the high-voltage system, circuit D, that the module does not classify further. A fourth independent loop mainly makes sense where one vehicle carries several battery packs. Caterpillar explains why for battery-powered mining, building and farm machines: with only one loop, charging or servicing a single pack would cut off all of them, so each battery group is watched on its own and the charging port gets yet another loop. No manufacturer publishes which parts belong to loop D. The contactors guarded by it open, and the branch behind them stays unavailable.
c: Disconnect of the battery group on loop D left open or not locked after charging or service
Connector in loop D not fully latched
Loop D wiring damaged between packs or distribution units
Controller that drives and reads loop D faulty
s: One battery pack or high-voltage branch not available
Reduced range or power, or no ready mode at all, depending on design
High-voltage system warning in the instrument cluster

U351A.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit D Performance
U351A.d: U351A says that loop D returns a signal, but not the one the module sent out. Many designs feed the loop with pulses rather than a steady level. In a Corun battery patent a microcontroller sends a 0 to 5 V square wave at 100 Hz with half on, half off through the interlock switches of pack, motor controller and vehicle controller, and treats the loop as sound only if frequency, on-time and amplitude return unchanged. A rounded, shifted or weakened pattern hints at contact resistance, moisture or coupled interference rather than a clean break. No maker documents U351A. High voltage may drop out without warning.
c: Corroded or worn interlock contacts adding resistance to loop D
Moisture in a low-voltage connector of the loop
Loop wiring routed too close to switching high-voltage cables
Signal input of the evaluating controller faulty
s: Sudden loss of high-voltage power while driving or charging
Fault appears after rain, washing or on rough roads
Restart sometimes possible after switching off and on

U351B.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit D Low
U351B.d: U351B reports that too little level comes back from interlock loop D while the module drives it. GM's hybrid tables for the loop A code P0A0C give a frame of reference: the test only runs when on-board voltage exceeds 10.2 V, judges what fraction of a 5 V test signal returns against a 30 % limit and logs a Type A fault after two failed 12.5 ms readings. A weak 12 V battery thus pauses the check instead of tripping it. No maker publishes a calibration for U351B. Typical causes are a wire crushed against the body, a loop plug left off, or a dead source; the contactors behind loop D may not close.
c: Loop D wire pinched against the body and shorted to ground
Plug within loop D not seated after a repair
Test voltage source in the controller failed
s: No ready mode or high-voltage branch D unavailable
Warning to have the high-voltage system checked
Fault stays present after clearing until the wiring is repaired

U351C.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit D High
U351C.d: U351C is stored when loop D carries more voltage than its present state allows. GM's high check for loop A, P0A0D, shows why both states are tested: with the source commanded to 0 V, more than 24 % of 5 V counts as a failure, five times in eight samples; with the source at 5 V the limit is 44 %, four times in six. A loop that fails to fall when its source switches off reveals foreign voltage even if it looks normal while fed. No maker lists U351C. Likely are a loop wire touching a 12 V feed, a source that no longer turns off, or a bad repair splice. Readiness is withheld until the loop is clean.
c: Loop D wire in contact with a 12 V supply line
Source driver in the controller no longer switches off
Earlier repair splice joined the loop to a wrong wire
s: Vehicle does not reach ready mode
Fault returns immediately after clearing
Other 12 V consumers may show faults if a supply wire is involved

U351D.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit E
U351D.d: U351D covers a disturbed fifth interlock loop, circuit E, where the module cannot narrow the fault down. Five loops arise naturally if every protected housing gets its own circuit. A GM patent describes this: each high-voltage enclosure has a functional interlock tied to its access point, and the low-voltage signal inside only gets through while that opening is closed. Removing a cover is thus noticed by the circuit of that very housing. Which enclosure belongs to loop E is not published. Check covers, lids and their screws first, then the plugs of the housings involved; high voltage stays off until loop E is closed.
c: Cover of a high-voltage housing on loop E not fitted or not fully tightened
Interlock contact or bridge in the cover bent or broken
Loop E wiring damaged between housings
s: No ready mode after work on a high-voltage component
High-voltage warning in the instrument cluster

U351E.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit E Performance
U351E.d: U351E points to loop E giving results the module cannot trust, and the doubt may concern the monitoring hardware as much as the wiring. Designers do test their own test circuits: CATL first checks its current-generating stage so that a failing source is not blamed on high-voltage parts, and Sanden's interlock at the plug of an electric A/C compressor also recognises defects of the monitoring device and its loop, not only an unplugged connector. A performance code on loop E can therefore come from a drifting source or detector. No maker publishes U351E. Once wiring and plugs test fine, suspect the controller running the loop.
c: Current or voltage source for loop E drifting in the controller
Loose contact in a loop E connector
Detection circuit or its reference faulty
Controller software with outdated plausibility limits
s: High-voltage shutdowns without a recognisable pattern
Fault returns although wiring and connectors test good
Possibly further self-test codes in the same controller

U351F.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit E Low
U351F.d: U351F reports a low reading on interlock loop E, the usual result when a plug in that loop is separated or one of its wires is grounded. The US standard FMVSS 305a explains the hurry: a high-voltage connector that can be pulled without tools may, as one permitted option, bring its live parts to 60 V DC or less within one second of separation. The interlock gives the early signal for that; Texas Instruments describes the follow-up of stopping traction, opening the power relays and discharging the DC-link capacitors. No maker documents U351F. Expect abrupt loss of drive power and no restart until loop E reads normal.
c: High-voltage plug with interlock in loop E pulled or backed out
Loop E wire chafed through to ground
Interlock pin pushed back in its housing
s: Abrupt loss of drive power, often with a stop-safely message
Vehicle cannot be restarted in ready mode
Charging aborted or impossible

U3520.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit E High
U3520.d: U3520 means the fifth interlock loop sits above its permitted range, usually because a loop wire has picked up battery voltage or another low-voltage feed. Lear's patent for a pulsed interlock tester shows how to pin this down further: it measures current at generator and detector pins and, by comparing them, works out at which end the unwanted link to the 12 V side lies. Simpler controllers only see the raised level. No manufacturer has published U3520. In the workshop, test each loop E wire against 12 V with the plugs at both ends disconnected; wet or corroded connectors next to fused feeds are typical spots.
c: Loop E wire shorted to a 12 V supply
Water or corrosion bridging a loop pin to a supply pin
Loop source in the controller stuck on
s: No ready mode, high-voltage warning shown
Fault reappears directly after clearing

U3521.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit F
U3521.d: U3521 flags an unspecified fault in loop F, the sixth interlock loop. Extra loops often guard service openings rather than cables. FMVSS 305a defines the service disconnect as the device that switches the circuit off for checks and service and demands finger protection wherever it opens without tools; its interlock tells the controller when it is pulled. Covers can be watched without contacts too: GM patented an interlock switch built from a magnet and a reed relay that stays closed only while the magnet is near. No maker publishes which opening belongs to loop F. Check that the service plug is fully locked and that magnet covers sit correctly.
c: Service disconnect not fully inserted or its lever not locked
Cover with interlock magnet missing, swapped or mounted out of position
Reed relay or switch contact of the cover interlock failed
s: No ready mode after battery or service work
High-voltage system message in the cluster

U3522.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit F Performance
U3522.d: U3522 is set when loop F behaves inconsistently, for instance when redundant evaluation channels reach different verdicts or the signal timing is off. Such checks exist because the interlock belongs to a safety function: Samsung SDI notes that it then needs an ASIL rating and failure-rate figures for its parts, so hidden faults in the monitoring path have to be caught, not just an open loop. CARB counts the interlock among safety-only systems, which is why this code concerns electrical safety rather than emissions and why lamp behaviour differs between makers. No manufacturer publishes U3522. Expect sporadic refusals to become ready.
c: Redundant measuring channels for loop F disagree because of a sensing fault
Intermittent contact in a loop F connector
Internal fault of the evaluating controller
s: Ready mode occasionally refused, then available again
High-voltage warning that comes and goes

U3523.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit F Low
U3523.d: U3523 is logged when loop F reads too low, typically from an open plug or a wire shorted to ground. Tracing it means working close to high-voltage parts. The German statutory accident insurance DGUV lets only trained high-voltage staff de-energise the system and insists on the order: isolate, secure against switching back on, then prove absence of voltage with a suitable tester, not a multimeter. Only then open loop F plugs, measure sections or bridge the loop for a test; a bridge must never stay in place, as it defeats the protection. No maker documents U3523. The vehicle stays without high voltage until the cause is fixed.
c: Plug in loop F open or not engaged after service
Loop F wire shorted to ground
Broken interlock connector housing or locking tab
s: Vehicle not ready to drive, high-voltage warning shown
Charging not possible

U3524.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit F High
U3524.d: U3524 indicates a level on loop F above its upper threshold. Pulsed test schemes recognise this easily: if the loop is driven with a fixed square wave, as in Corun's 100 Hz battery design, a wire stuck at 12 V returns a flat level without any edges, which no intact connection could produce. Texas Instruments rates its interlock reference design to survive a direct connection to the 12 V battery, and it offers a third, high-impedance output state for diagnosis. No manufacturer publishes U3524. Look for chafing against fused 12 V wires and for low-voltage plugs in which a loop pin sits right beside a supply pin.
c: Loop F wire chafed against a fused 12 V wire
Loop pin bridged to a neighbouring supply pin by corrosion or a bent terminal
Source driver for loop F no longer switches off
s: High-voltage system remains off, vehicle not ready
Code returns at once after clearing

U3525.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit G
U3525.d: U3525 stands for a fault on the seventh interlock loop, circuit G, that the module does not classify further. Auxiliary high-voltage consumers are candidates for loops of their own: Sanden runs an interlock loop beside the HV plug between an electric A/C compressor and the traction battery, and a Chinese design cited by Caterpillar links an air-conditioning interlock circuit to the main one over CAN. On Mercedes model line 243 the PTC heater's control unit logs its own interlock code, P154700. Which consumer sits on loop G is not public. A dead loop G may only disable heating or cooling, or may block the whole system.
c: HV plug of an auxiliary consumer such as compressor or heater not latched
Loop G wiring to the auxiliary consumer damaged
Interlock contacts inside the consumer's connector damaged
s: Air conditioning or electric heater unavailable
In some designs no ready mode at all
High-voltage or climate warning in the cluster

U3526.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit G Performance
U3526.d: U3526 reports an implausible result for loop G. Not every interlock is a wire loop: Rivian patented a virtual interlock in which a controller first brings the DC bus up to a low, safe voltage only, gathers the voltages that the high-voltage components report over CAN, and raises the bus to operating voltage only if those reports are acceptable. With such a scheme a performance fault means values that contradict each other rather than a broken wire, for example one component seeing a bus voltage far from the battery's. No maker documents U3526. Missing or stale CAN data, a faulty voltage sensor or a loose HV plug are the main suspects.
c: Voltage sensing inside one high-voltage component faulty
Voltage message missing or late on the CAN bus
HV plug not fully seated, so one component sees no bus voltage
s: Start-up of the high-voltage system aborted
Communication codes in other control units at the same time

U3527.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit G Low
U3527.d: U3527 sets when the level on loop G drops below what the module expects. When several controllers watch interlock lines, the reporting unit already narrows the search. A Mercedes service bulletin on the 243 model series shows this with loop A codes: the DC charging unit and the AC charger each store a ground-short code, the battery management a short to positive, and the PTC heater has a separate code. For loop G, start measuring at the controller storing U3527, follow its section outward and compare the codes in the other units. No maker publishes U3527. While the low reading persists, the contactors behind loop G stay locked.
c: Loop G wire cut or chafed to ground near a control unit
Plug in the section of the reporting unit not connected
Loop source of the reporting controller failed
s: Vehicle does not become ready, or charging is refused
Interlock codes in more than one control unit

U3528.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit G High
U3528.d: U3528 means something lifts loop G to a level the controller never expects from it. Texas Instruments notes that automotive interlocks, unlike industrial ones, must survive a short to the 12 V battery and to ground; its reference design feeds the loop through an intelligent switch on the supply side with current limiting and thermal shutdown. Such electronics may come through a short undamaged, whereas a simpler output stage can fail, and then the code returns even after the wiring is repaired because the driver now stays on. No manufacturer documents U3528. Remove the foreign voltage, clear the code and test again before replacing a controller.
c: Loop G wire shorted to the 12 V supply
Loop output stage damaged by an earlier short and stuck on
Moisture bridging pins in a loop G connector
s: No ready mode, high-voltage warning
Code persists after the harness repair

U3529.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit H
U3529.d: U3529 marks a fault on circuit H, the eighth interlock loop, without a more specific result. Texas Instruments distinguishes one central loop running through all high-voltage parts from individual loops inside each subsystem that confirm its own assembly. Eight separate loops are realistic mainly for trucks, buses and machines with several packs and distribution boxes, such as Volvo's electric-road trucks with at least two HV buses or Caterpillar's multi-pack machines; in passenger cars a fourth to eighth loop is hardly to be expected. No manufacturer documents U3529. On a car, compare codes in other units before assuming a wiring fault.
c: Connector or disconnect on loop H open
Loop H wiring damaged on chassis or between packs
Code logged by a controller with faulty software rather than a real loop H fault
s: One HV branch or pack unavailable, or no ready mode
Warning about the high-voltage system

U352A.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit H Performance
U352A.d: U352A says the eighth loop is closed but its electrical values leave the calibrated band. In CATL's interlock patent the decision thresholds follow from the loop current, a sensing resistor and the impedance of every HV part in the chain. A long loop through many parts therefore has narrow margins: each extra contact, a replacement part with different internal resistance or a lengthened harness shifts the result. That makes a performance fault on a late loop plausible after repairs or conversions. No maker publishes U352A. Compare part numbers of recently fitted HV parts with the originals and look for added plugs in loop H.
c: Replacement HV component with different interlock resistance fitted
Extra connector or harness extension added to loop H
Rising contact resistance at several loop H terminals
s: Fault appears after a repair or conversion
High-voltage system switches off occasionally

U352B.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit H Low
U352B.d: U352B reports too low a level on interlock loop H. Apart from a pulled plug or a grounded wire, a deliberate opening can cause it: Texas Instruments mentions feeding a crash signal into the loop so that high voltage shuts off after an accident. The DGUV warns that such a crash shutdown does not establish absence of voltage and that disconnection following the maker's rescue sheet is still advisable; FMVSS 305a takes its post-crash voltage readings in a window from 10 s to one minute after the impact. No maker documents U352B. After a collision, replace damaged loop sections rather than patching them, and have trained staff isolate the system.
c: Loop H opened on purpose by a crash signal after an accident
Loop H wiring or plug damaged in a collision
Loop H wire shorted to ground
s: High voltage off after an accident or airbag deployment
Vehicle cannot be made ready

U352C.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit H High
U352C.d: U352C reports an excessive reading on loop H. Whether that points to foreign voltage or to a break depends on the quantity the controller evaluates. If it reads voltage, a wire touching 12 V is the usual reason. If it works out the loop's resistance, as Lear's tester patent does, a value beyond the maximum is treated as open and one under the minimum as shorted, so high may mean corrosion or a loose terminal. The service data of the specific vehicle settles which reading applies; for U352C no maker publishes it. Measure loop H resistance with every plug latched and compare it with a sound loop of the same vehicle.
c: Loop H wire in contact with a 12 V supply
Corroded or loose terminal raising loop H resistance
Loop source stuck on in the controller
s: No ready mode, high-voltage warning
Fault sometimes disappears after moving connectors

U352D.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit J
U352D.d: U352D is the summary code for interlock circuit J, the ninth loop in J2012 lettering, which leaves out the letter I. What the loop contains is up to the maker, and none has published it. A loop need not pass through plugs only: a Ford patent for a centralised interlock leads the circuit across mating body parts such as the hood or trunk latch and its receptacle, so that opening the lid by itself switches high voltage off; floor access panels are named as a further option. Where a design like this is used, a lid that has not fully latched can explain a fault on loop J. Check latches before wiring; the vehicle cannot become ready until the loop is complete.
c: Connector in loop J not fully latched
Hood, trunk or access panel latch wired into loop J not fully engaged
Controller that drives and reads loop J faulty
s: No ready mode, often right after a hood, trunk or underbody panel was opened
High-voltage system warning in the instrument cluster
Charging blocked

U352E.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit J Performance
U352E.d: U352E reports an implausible result from loop J. Interlocks also guard auxiliary drives outside the traction system. Copeland patented a contactless version for the inverter of a trailer refrigeration unit, which may be fed from a 460 V generator through a rectifier at about 650 V DC: a magnet on each terminal cover faces a Hall sensor in the housing, and the drive releases voltage only while that field is sensed. The patent wants the detection range small, so a cover sitting slightly askew, a deformed gasket or a loosened magnet screw can leave the sensor near its switching point and let the reading flicker. No maker documents U352E. The drive on loop J may cut out at random.
c: Cover with interlock sensing seated unevenly or gasket deformed
Loose contact in a loop J connector
Sensing element or its actuating magnet loose or damaged
Signal input of the evaluating controller faulty
s: High-voltage consumer on loop J switching off intermittently
Fault more frequent on rough roads or after work on covers
High-voltage system warning that comes and goes

U352F.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit J Low
U352F.d: U352F means loop J reads below its lower threshold, the picture an interrupted loop gives. In high-voltage plugs the interlock pins are shorter than the power pins, so they part first when the plug is withdrawn. A TE Connectivity product manager puts the resulting lead at just one to three milliseconds for a plug pulled quickly, while switching the whole system off can take close to a second, and adds that a closed loop does not prove full mating. A Hyundai and Kia connector patent names the same weakness of fast separation. A plug in loop J that has been pulled back slightly, or a dropped interlock pin, is thus the first suspect. No maker lists U352F; the contactors stay open.
c: High-voltage plug in loop J partly withdrawn, interlock pins already apart
Interlock pin in loop J pushed back in its cavity
Loop J wire chafed through to ground
s: High-voltage system switches off and stays off
No ready mode after work near high-voltage plugs
Charging not possible

U3530.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit J High
U3530.d: U3530 flags loop J above its upper threshold. Foreign voltage is one explanation, but in a design that pushes a constant current through the loop and reads the drop across it, any added resistance lifts the measured value too. Tesla's HVIL tech note for early Model S cars, filed with NHTSA, names a poor solder joint at a charger board connector that exceeded 90 ohms only when hot. To reproduce it, technicians drove about 20 minutes at highway speed, charged for at least half an hour and measured the loop pins on the still warm charger. A loop J fault that turns up only after long trips or charging sessions points to such heat-sensitive joints. No maker documents U3530 itself.
c: Cracked solder joint or crimp in loop J whose resistance rises when warm
Loop J wire in contact with a 12 V supply
Loose or spread terminal in a loop J connector
s: Fault appears after long drives or charging, not on a cold start
Charging session or drive interrupted by a high-voltage warning
Loop measures normal once the components have cooled down

U3531.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit K
U3531.d: U3531 stands for an unspecified fault on interlock circuit K, the tenth loop. An interlock need not be a dedicated wire pair. For hybrid trucks, International patented running the hybrid CAN bus through the same connector as the power cable: once the plug is parted, data traffic on that bus stops and one terminating impedance drops out, and a traffic detector then opens an interrupter in the high-voltage feed. A loop K built along these lines would react to a dead or disturbed bus section as well as to an open plug, so network faults stored in the same controllers deserve attention. No maker discloses the members of loop K. High voltage stays blocked while the fault is active.
c: Connector in loop K not fully latched
Communication line routed with loop K interrupted or disturbed
s: No ready mode or one high-voltage branch unavailable
Network or communication codes stored alongside
High-voltage system warning in the instrument cluster

U3532.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit K Performance
U3532.d: U3532 indicates that loop K does not respond the way the controller expects. Some checks run only while the system powers up. A Ford patent describes one: during precharge a switch holds the high-voltage bus between an upper and a lower level far below operating voltage, and the interlock test takes place inside that window. Too little current then suggests a connector that is not seated, too much a short, and only a passed test lets precharge carry on. A start-only test of this kind can let a marginal contact pass on one key cycle and fail on the next, so the code may come and go between trips. No maker publishes U3532. Expect occasional refusals to become ready.
c: Marginal contact in a loop K connector that passes some start checks and fails others
Fault in the precharge path disturbing the start-up check
Controller software with outdated check limits
s: Vehicle sometimes does not become ready at switch-on, then works on the next attempt
Fault stored at start-up rather than while driving

U3533.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit K Low
U3533.d: U3533 says loop K reads too low. Apart from an open plug, part of the loop current may be escaping somewhere. Tesla's HVIL tech note for the Model S describes two such cases: a drive inverter whose control board leaked some of the nominal 20 mA loop current to ground, and a loop wire squeezed against ground close to a seat belt pretensioner. The fault therefore need not sit in a connector at all; a component on the loop or a wire trapped by seat or trim parts can cause it. When every plug of loop K is latched and the value stays low, measure the loop current at each component and inspect wiring near seat mounts. No maker documents U3533; the contactors remain open.
c: Loop K wire squeezed against ground by seat, trim or mounting parts
Plug within loop K not connected
High-voltage component on loop K leaking loop current to ground internally
s: Vehicle does not reach ready mode
Fault may follow work on seats or interior trim
Warning to have the high-voltage system checked

U3534.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit K High
U3534.d: U3534 reports loop K above its upper threshold. Besides a loop wire chafed onto a 12 V feed, the timing of the electronics can be behind it. In the Texas Instruments reference design TIDA-020069 a 10 mA constant current feeds the loop, and that source can be disabled to save power or to hold the loop in a deliberate fault state until the other systems are ready. Its current then shrinks to one hundredth, and send and return voltages look like a short to battery. If software reads loop K before enabling the source, or the enable line hangs, a high result appears although the wiring is sound. No maker documents U3534. Rule out foreign voltage first, then ask about controller software updates.
c: Loop K wire in contact with a 12 V supply
Loop source still disabled when the controller evaluates loop K
Controller software with faulty start-up sequence
s: Vehicle does not become ready
Fault may appear right at switch-on although no wiring damage is found

U3535.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit L
U3535.d: U3535 is the umbrella code for interlock circuit L, the eleventh loop. Large vehicles carry many guarded compartments. On New Flyer battery buses the energy storage units sit on the roof at front, centre and rear, and each access door is watched by an interlock limit switch. A service instruction from the bus maker, filed with NHTSA, swaps the switch bracket for one with a stop and bonds a striker plate to the door so the switch is pressed reliably; the same procedure turns a separate HV interlock switch off for lockout. A misadjusted door switch, or a lockout switch not turned back on, can open a loop such as L. Which compartments belong to it is not published.
c: Door or lid limit switch on loop L misadjusted or not actuated
Manual high-voltage interlock or lockout switch left off after service
Connector in loop L not fully latched
s: Vehicle or one energy storage unit unavailable after maintenance
High-voltage system warning on the dashboard
Fault linked to opening or closing a compartment

U3536.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit L Performance
U3536.d: U3536 means loop L delivers values the controller considers implausible without a clear limit being crossed. Shaky contacts are a typical reason. Tesla's Model S HVIL note has technicians wiggle each plug while a second person watches the live loop voltage, and stresses that a weak spot may make the value drift long before it is bad enough to set a fault; pin drag tests then reveal loose terminal tension. Multi-Contact markets a dedicated short-contact module tested for shock and vibration to DIN 50467, because ordinary shortened contacts can end up wrongly placed. No maker documents U3536. Expect brief shutdowns, often on bad roads.
c: Terminal in a loop L connector with too little contact force
Loop L connector without proper strain relief, moving with vibration
Signal input of the evaluating controller faulty
s: Short high-voltage dropouts while driving, especially over bumps
Warning disappears after a restart

U3537.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit L Low
U3537.d: U3537 is logged for an insufficient reading on loop L. The cause may lie outside the loop itself. In a Volvo patent with paired loops for trucks with separate high-voltage buses, neither loop is closed before the current sources start; one loop only closes once the source of the other energises the coil of an isolated relay. If that partner source stays off, or the relay coil or its contacts fail, the dependent loop reads as open though its own plugs are fine. With such a design, a low result on loop L calls for checking the codes and source of the coupled loop and the relay before any wiring is opened. No maker documents U3537; the contactors behind loop L stay open.
c: Plug within loop L disconnected or wire shorted to ground
Source of a coupled loop not running, so the coupling relay stays open
Coupling relay between loops with failed coil or contact
s: Vehicle or one high-voltage bus does not become ready
Interlock codes for more than one loop stored at once

U3538.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit L High
U3538.d: U3538 is stored when loop L overshoots its permitted maximum. In a constant-current loop that can be a contact problem rather than foreign voltage. Tesla's Model S tech note records its most frequent HVIL field failure as high-voltage plugs serving the cabin PTC heater, the heater for battery coolant and the A/C compressor harness whose interlock pins were too short: the supplier had changed the housing without lengthening the pins, and in the worst case male and female never met. Higher resistance raised the loop voltage until the fault set. Replacement plugs with longer pins carry a yellow dot. Comparable part revisions can matter on any loop L. No maker documents U3538; high voltage stays off.
c: Connector revision in loop L with interlock pins too short for reliable contact
Loop L wire in contact with a 12 V supply
Spread female terminal in a loop L connector
s: Vehicle does not become ready or switches off high voltage
Heating or air conditioning affected if their plugs are part of the loop

U3539.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit M
U3539.d: U3539 covers a non-specific fault on circuit M, the twelfth interlock loop. Loops J to M only make sense in very extensive high-voltage systems such as trucks, buses, construction or mining machines with interfaces for battery, charging, drive and auxiliaries such as hydraulic pumps or heaters. In a 2026 article a TE Connectivity product manager argues against fitting HVIL everywhere: if analysis shows that only 20 of 50 interfaces on a truck need it, leaving out 30 removes 30 potential failure points, since each loop can trip and halt a working vehicle. No maker documents what loop M covers. A fault there can idle the vehicle while its high-voltage parts are undamaged.
c: Connector of an auxiliary or charging interface in loop M not fully latched
Loop M wiring damaged on a long run through the vehicle
s: Vehicle or a high-voltage auxiliary unavailable
High-voltage warning without visible damage

U353A.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit M Performance
U353A.d: U353A flags loop M as questionable rather than plainly open or shorted. Redundant monitoring can produce exactly that state. NIO patented an interlock fed by two signal generators whose pulse trains overlap on one line; with duty ratios A and B the detector expects a combined average of A plus B minus their product. If only one part arrives, the system can keep the contactors closed and name the generator whose share is missing as a fault candidate, though the real cause may sit outside it. The aim is to avoid needless shutdowns caused by a failing monitoring part. Under such logic a performance code may be logged while the vehicle still drives. No maker documents U353A.
c: One of the loop M signal sources weak or failed
Loose contact in a loop M connector distorting the signal
Detection circuit for loop M faulty
s: Warning lamp while the vehicle keeps driving
Occasional loss of high voltage if the second channel also degrades

U353B.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit M Low
U353B.d: U353B is set when loop M reads too low. A lever-type plug can leave it in exactly that state on purpose. A connector patent by Hyundai and Kia adds an intermediate lock to the lever: on the way out it stops at a point where the interlock contacts are already apart while the power terminals still touch, so the system has time to switch off before the second lever movement separates the plug. If such a plug is left at the intermediate stage after service, or not pushed fully home, loop M stays open although the plug seems attached. Check every lever on the loop for its final locked position. No maker documents U353B; the contactors remain open.
c: Lever-type connector in loop M left at its intermediate position
Loop M wire shorted to ground
Loop M source in the controller failed
s: No ready mode after service on high-voltage plugs
Fault persists after clearing

U353C.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit M High
U353C.d: U353C indicates that loop M exceeds its upper threshold. A loop built from known resistances can be checked point by point. In Tesla's Model S tech note the battery management sends a constant 20 mA through four resistance stages of 60 ohms, 240 ohms in total, so about 4.8 V appears at the start and the value falls to 3.6, 2.4 and 1.2 V at the following connectors. Back-probing each point and comparing it with these steps shows in which section extra resistance or foreign voltage sits; resistance to ground with the loop off runs in matching 60-ohm steps. A wiring diagram with such reference values makes loop M quick to trace. No maker documents U353C itself.
c: Corroded or loose contact adding resistance in one section of loop M
Loop M wire in contact with a 12 V supply
High-voltage component with internal loop resistance out of specification
s: Vehicle does not become ready
High-voltage warning returns after clearing

U353D.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit N
U353D.d: U353D is the general code for interlock circuit N, the thirteenth loop in J2012 lettering; designs with that many loops are only conceivable on very large high-voltage systems. No maker documents U353D publicly. Moisture is a frequent root cause on interlocks of any letter: FCA bulletin 08-131-21 for the 2021 Jeep Wrangler plug-in hybrid traces a no-start with P0A0A to water getting past a pinched orange seal into the P1 and P2 HV connectors under the car, often logged together with an isolation fault (P0AA6). Where corrosion has set in, the harness or the power inverter module has to be replaced. Inspect seals before cleaning pins.
c: Water in a loop N connector because a seal is pinched or damaged
Connector in loop N not fully seated
Interlock pins corroded after earlier moisture
Controller that drives and reads loop N faulty
s: No ready mode or no start, often after rain, washing or wading
Isolation fault stored alongside the interlock code
Hybrid or high-voltage system warning in the cluster

U353E.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit N Performance
U353E.d: U353E marks loop N as implausible. Such a verdict can stem from electrical interference rather than from the loop wiring. Tesla bulletin SB-25-17-005 for 2023 and 2024 Model Y cars describes the centre high mounted stop lamp disturbing the supply line of the high-voltage controller, which set HVIL alerts on an intact loop; the fix is a ferrite clipped around the thickest tan wire of that harness branch. A fault that coincides with braking or with other loads switching on suggests similar coupling on loop N. No maker documents U353E. Wiring checks then find nothing, and the warning may clear by itself.
c: Interference from another load coupling into the supply of the monitoring controller
Loose contact in a loop N connector
Ferrite or shielding missing after harness repair
Evaluation software of the controller too sensitive
s: High-voltage warning that appears briefly, sometimes when braking
No fault found on loop resistance checks
Occasional refusal to become ready

U353F.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit N Low
U353F.d: U353F covers a loop N value under the permitted minimum. The defect can sit inside a consumer rather than in the harness. For the Cummins battery electric systems BES CM2450 EV110B and EV111B, bulletin TSB250044 ties fault codes 8174 (interlock level too low or grounded) and 8175 to the electric air compressor: once the interlock contacts of the HV cable to the compressor pass, the measurement moves to the interlock pins of its low-voltage connector, and above 2 ohms (1 ohm in the first issue of February 2025) the compressor gets replaced. No maker documents U353F. While it is set, the vehicle is likely to lose high-voltage readiness.
c: Interlock path inside an HV consumer such as an electric air compressor open or high-resistance
HV cable plug on loop N not reconnected properly
Loop N wire shorted to ground
s: High voltage switches off and stays off
Interlock fault returns although all cable plugs test fine
Auxiliary drive such as the air compressor not running

U3540.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit N High
U3540.d: U3540 reports loop N on the high side of its permitted window. In converted or repowered vehicles the installer often assembles the loop. The hardware manual of BorgWarner's Cascadia Motion CM inverters offers a pin pair, HVIL_IN and HVIL_OUT, that is bridged inside once every HV plug of the inverter is fitted, and leaves the safety of the whole installation to the installer. Each unit chained in this way adds pins, crimps and splices. Where the controller injects a fixed current, as in Tesla's Model S loop, every added ohm lifts the measured voltage. No maker documents U3540. Check adapter harnesses and added joints first.
c: Extra contacts, splices or adapter harnesses from a conversion raise loop N resistance
Loop N wire shorted to a 12 V or 24 V feed
Poorly crimped or loose interlock terminal
s: No ready mode right after a conversion or component swap
High-voltage system warning
Charging blocked

U3541.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit O
U3541.d: U3541 denotes trouble on interlock circuit O, the fourteenth loop. What happens next may depend on the operating state. Tesla's 2013 HVIL diagnostic guide for the Model S, published through NHTSA, splits the reaction: in the modes Standby, Support and Charge the battery management stores a fault and opens the contactors, or leaves them open if they already are, whereas in Drive it only raises a warning so that the car does not lose propulsion. A loop O fault that occurs on the move may thus first be noticed as a car that will not restart after parking. No maker documents U3541 or the parts of loop O.
c: Connector in loop O not fully latched
Internal fault in an HV component on loop O
s: Warning while driving without loss of drive
No ready mode after the vehicle was switched off
Charging refused

U3542.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit O Performance
U3542.d: U3542 marks loop O as implausible. Interlock trouble often clusters around charging. Mercedes bulletin LI54.10-P-067823 for the third-generation smart electric drive with the optional 22 kW on-board charger, built before 25 March 2013, links sporadic or permanent interlock codes (P0A0A00, P0A0E00), a no-start with a charging-cable message and a battery that will not charge to loose low-voltage contacts at that charger. Technicians push or pull those plugs gently and wait up to 5 seconds each time to see whether charging begins; the fault may appear solely with cold or warm components. No maker documents U3542.
c: Loose low-voltage contact at the on-board charger carrying loop O
Contact that opens only when components are hot or cold
Internal fault in the on-board charger
s: Vehicle will not start and reports a plugged-in charging cable
Charging does not start or stops
Fault at the beginning or end of a charging session

U3543.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit O Low
U3543.d: With U3543, loop O has dropped under its minimum. Some plug designs let the fitter see the reason. An LG Electronics patent describes a high-voltage connector closed by turning a cover housing: the rotation moves an inner cap up or down so that the power terminals mate first and the shorter interlock tab last, while a scale on the plug housing shows how far the cover has turned. A cover left short of its end stop keeps the power pins engaged with the interlock still apart, exactly the picture of a low reading. No maker documents U3543. Turn each rotary plug on loop O fully home and check the scale.
c: Rotary HV plug on loop O not turned to its end position
Interlock tab or socket in a loop O plug bent or pushed back
Loop O wire shorted to ground
s: High voltage stays off after work on HV plugs
No ready mode
Charging not possible

U3544.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit O High
U3544.d: U3544 sets when loop O delivers too high a value. A plug can hold its specified torque and still sit crooked. FCA's STAR case S2108000121 (Rev. B, 2026) for Wrangler and Grand Cherokee 4xe models describes P0A0A after HV repairs although the connector bolts reached 9 Nm: the plug had gone on at an angle, the C3 connector of the power inverter module in particular. Three windows around its shield must show bare aluminium housing with no gap; spread interlock terminals mean replacing the HV component. In a current-fed loop such poor contact appears as a higher value. No maker documents U3544. Seat each plug squarely before tightening.
c: HV plug on loop O torqued down while tilted
Interlock terminals spread by a crooked fitting
Loop O wire shorted to a 12 V feed
Connector bolt thread stripped so the plug cannot be clamped
s: Check engine light and hybrid system message right after an HV repair
No ready mode

U3545.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit P
U3545.d: U3545 is the general fault code for interlock circuit P, the fifteenth loop. Interlock electronics can be harmed by events elsewhere in the drive. Allison service letter SIL 3-EP-14 (Rev. C, 2017) for the H 40/50 EP hybrid system used in buses offers a separate HVIL circuit card for the DPIM2 inverter: if the check list shows 3 to 4 µF between DC+ or DC− and chassis, for example after an internal stator short, that card is damaged and can be swapped instead of the whole inverter, which first has to come out of the vehicle; an ESD wrist strap is mandatory. No maker documents U3545.
c: Interlock circuit board inside the inverter damaged, e.g. after a motor winding short
Connector in loop P not fully latched
Electrostatic damage to monitoring electronics during service
s: Vehicle cannot be made ready
Other drive faults stored at the same time, such as motor or isolation faults

U3546.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit P Performance
U3546.d: U3546 marks loop P as implausible. On large vehicles the mechanical routing of HV cables affects the interlock too. Gillig's field service campaign FSC 22-13-2479 for its Gen 2.0 and 2.5 battery electric buses found that HV battery cables in one equipment compartment lacked adequate support brackets; the outcome was an intermittent HVIL fault 8175, sometimes with the HV exposure lamp lit, and the fix was added bracketry. A heavy cable that swings with every bump can tug at its plug just enough to upset the loop for an instant. No maker documents U3546. Look for unsupported cable runs close to the plugs of loop P.
c: HV cable without adequate brackets pulling on a loop P plug
Loose contact in a loop P connector
Cable clamp or bracket not refitted after repair
s: Interlock fault that comes and goes, more often on rough roads
High-voltage warning lamp lighting briefly
Brief loss of high-voltage power

U3547.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit P Low
U3547.d: U3547 reports a low value on loop P, and the contactors drop out with it. A design flaw can be the cause too. Kenworth (campaign 25KWC) and Peterbilt (25PBC) recalled battery electric T680E, 520EV and 579EV trucks under NHTSA number 25V181: with certain HVIL circuit layouts in their Accelera power control accessory subsystem, high voltage could be lost and the contactors open without warning, cutting propulsion. The remedy pairs a software check with two overlay harnesses. If a commercial vehicle keeps losing power on loop P, ask for open campaigns before hunting for wiring faults. No maker documents U3547.
c: Interlock circuit layout covered by a recall, overlay harness not yet fitted
Plug in loop P open or interlock pin pushed back
Loop P wire shorted to ground
s: Sudden loss of propulsion while driving
Contactors open without prior warning
No restart until the loop reads normal

U3548.t: High Voltage System Interlock Circuit P High
U3548.d: U3548 is the high-side code of loop P. When each unit adds a known share of loop resistance, a single suspect can be isolated by substitution. Tesla's Model S HVIL guide has technicians, after consulting a field engineer, place a 60-ohm resistor across the drive inverter's interlock pins at connector X250 and also bridge its CAN lines; if the contactors then close, the inverter's internal section is to blame. Such a stand-in serves only as a short test by trained staff and must be removed afterwards. No maker documents U3548. A raised reading calls for measuring the share of each component on loop P.
c: Internal interlock section of an HV component too resistive
Loop P wire shorted to a 12 V feed
Loose or poorly crimped interlock terminal in loop P
s: Contactors stay open, no ready mode
High-voltage system warning
Charging blocked

U3549.t: Hydrogen Tank High Pressure Sensor 1 Circuit
U3549.d: U3549 covers the electrical circuit of the high-pressure sensor that reads hydrogen pressure on the storage side, upstream of the regulator, where a full system holds up to 70 MPa, the ceiling set by FMVSS 308. Its value feeds the fuel gauge, fill logic and leak checks: a Hyundai patent watches it while the parked car briefly wakes, a GM patent trims it against the more precise low-pressure sensor whenever the regulator stands wide open, and Toyota compares the filling-side and supply-side sensors after refuelling. U3549 itself appears in no public manufacturer document. An open, a short or a signal outside its range leaves the gauge and leak monitoring blind; expect a warning and possibly limited power. The supply-line sensors have their own codes, U3564 and U3565.
c: Corroded or damaged connector or wiring between sensor and storage controller
Sensor supply voltage or ground missing
s: Hydrogen system warning in the instrument cluster
Fuel gauge or range display missing or implausible
Fuel cell power limited

U354A.t: Hydrogen Tank A Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit
U354A.d: U354A reports an electrical fault on the first temperature sensor of hydrogen tank A. Tank sensors matter most while refuelling: compression heats the gas, and FMVSS 308 slows the pressure ramp once the gas inside passes 85 °C; on the Mirai the tank temperature is passed to the dispenser by infrared. No maker publishes U354A, but Honda shows how such faults appear on the 2017 Clarity Fuel Cell under its own codes P1F76 (main tank) and P1F77 (sub tank): they set during fuelling, and because the sensor sits inside the tank, the first remedy in Tech Line article ATS 170903 was a new tank. Bulletin 19-001 later blamed many cases on outdated software in the fuel cell communication unit. Sensor 2 of the same tank is U354B.
c: Outdated software in the unit that evaluates the tank sensors
Temperature sensor inside the tank failed (often only as tank assembly)
Open or short in the sensor wiring or connector at the tank
s: Code sets while refuelling
Hydrogen system warning
Refuelling slower or ends before the tank is full

U354B.t: Hydrogen Tank A Temperature Sensor 2 Circuit
U354B.d: U354B is the circuit code for the second temperature sensor in tank A. One probe cannot capture a long tank during a fast fill: in tests published in the HySafe journal, sensors in on-tank valves at both ends of a Type IV tank finished a fill around 30 °C apart, and the authors concluded that even two positions miss the hottest zone. A second sensor thus gives the controller a cross-check and a second view of the gas. Honda's 2019 dealer notice for the Clarity Fuel Cell describes the flip side: a false reading between two tank sensors kept the tank from being filled completely. No maker documents U354B publicly. With sensor 2 lost, expect a warning and cautious, perhaps incomplete fills; sensor 1 of the same tank is U354A.
c: Wiring or connector fault at the far tank end
Second temperature sensor of tank A failed
Evaluation software misjudging the sensor pair
s: Tank cannot be filled completely
Hydrogen system warning

U354C.t: Hydrogen Tank B Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit
U354C.d: U354C flags the circuit of the first temperature sensor in tank B. The maker decides which tank is B, and every series fuel cell car has at least two: the first Mirai carried tanks of 60.0 and 62.4 litres, the Clarity a main and a sub tank. With several tanks the readings can be checked against each other. A Hyundai patent monitors the sensors of three tanks, judges one defective once it sits 20 °C away from the others and replaces its value with a healthy one, so fill control still respects 85 °C and the fuel quantity stays right. Such comparison targets drifting values; an open or shorted sensor as in U354C is recognised directly. No maker documents the code. Sensor 2 of tank B is U354D.
c: Open or short in the wiring to tank B
Temperature sensor 1 of tank B failed
Input stage of the storage control unit faulty
s: Hydrogen system warning
Refuelling limited or interrupted

U354D.t: Hydrogen Tank B Temperature Sensor 2 Circuit
U354D.d: U354D marks an electrical fault on the second temperature sensor of tank B. Apart from fill control, tank temperature is needed to convert pressure into fuel quantity, because cold gas at a given pressure holds more hydrogen than warm gas. Sensors and wiring sit at the tank under the floor, often inside the on-tank valve. Hyundai's venting bulletin 20-FL-008H-1 for the Nexo has the underbody covers removed to reach the tank valves, requires tank pressure below 500 psi before work on hydrogen parts and full venting before welding or open flame within 18 inches. A sensor fault on the tank can therefore become a job involving defuelling. No maker publishes U354D. Its partner on the same tank is U354C.
c: Moisture or damage at the underbody connector of tank B
Temperature sensor 2 of tank B failed
Harness chafed after underbody or tank work
s: Hydrogen system warning
Fuel gauge less accurate
Refuelling ends early

U354E.t: Hydrogen Tank C Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit
U354E.d: U354E points to an electrical fault on sensor 1 of tank C, a tank that exists only on three-tank vehicles: the second-generation Mirai, whose long central tank is joined by two smaller ones crosswise under the rear seat and the boot, or the Nexo with three tanks holding 156 litres. On a two-tank car such as the first Mirai or the Clarity the code would suggest a configuration or software mismatch. The sensor is not the overheat protection: a thermally activated relief device opens on its own, on Toyota's FCHV at 110 °C, without electronics. A lost sensor costs information, not the fire safeguard. No manufacturer documents U354E publicly; sensor 2 of tank C is U354F.
c: Wiring or connector fault at tank C
Temperature sensor 1 of tank C failed
Controller coded for a different number of tanks
s: Hydrogen system warning
Refuelling slower or stopped early

U354F.t: Hydrogen Tank C Temperature Sensor 2 Circuit
U354F.d: U354F is set when the circuit of the second temperature sensor in tank C fails. During refuelling the car hands tank data to the station; Toyota describes infrared links between the tank temperature sensors, nozzle and dispenser that set the flow so the gas does not overheat. In a published test series the fill was stopped as soon as either of two tank sensors showed 85 °C, which explains why a missing channel matters: the controller has to fill more cautiously or quit early. FMVSS 308 likewise ties a slower pressure ramp to gas above 85 °C. No maker documents U354F. Expect a hydrogen system warning and refuelling that takes longer or ends short of full, which in turn trims range. The paired sensor is U354E.
c: Open or short in the wiring of sensor 2 at tank C
Temperature sensor 2 of tank C failed
Evaluation software needing a manufacturer update
s: Refuelling takes longer or stops before full
Hydrogen system warning
Reduced range after refuelling

U3550.t: Hydrogen Tank A Valve Control Circuit
U3550.d: U3550 indicates an electrical fault in the control circuit of the solenoid valve on hydrogen tank A. This on-tank valve is the primary closure between tank and fuel system, and FMVSS 308 requires it to default to closed when unpowered. Toyota's FCHV guide lists when the controller shuts the valves of all tanks: vehicle off, abnormal pressure loss or rise, airbag or fuel cell crash sensors, a hydrogen sensor alarm, hood or fuel door opened, or a malfunction of a shut valve. An open coil, a short or a failed driver stage thus leaves tank A closed. No manufacturer documents U3550 publicly. With several tanks the others may keep the car moving with less range; the enable path is U3551, the mechanical function U3552.
c: Wiring or connector fault between controller and valve
Solenoid coil of the tank A valve open or shorted
Valve driver stage in the storage control unit faulty
s: Hydrogen system warning
Reduced range, or no READY if the car depends on this tank

U3551.t: Hydrogen Tank A Valve Enable Circuit
U3551.d: U3551 concerns the enable circuit of the valve on tank A: not the switched control line, but the path that permits the valve to be powered at all, typically a relay, fuse or supply-side switch. Designs keep it apart so a crash can cut hydrogen reliably. In a Honda patent the fuel cell controller opens a collision cutoff relay as soon as the airbag unit reports an impact, and FMVSS 307 demands valve closure no later than 5 seconds after a crash. Toyota's FCHV guide follows the same idea: pulling two fuses disables the vehicle and closes every tank valve. If this path is open or shorted, tank A cannot open. No manufacturer documents U3551. Enable codes on several tanks at once point to a shared supply.
c: Enable or crash cutoff relay faulty
Blown fuse or missing supply in the valve enable path
Open or short in the enable wiring to valve A
s: No READY or fuel cell does not start
Hydrogen system warning

U3552.d: U3552 is the performance code for the valve on tank A: the circuit tests good, but the valve does not act as commanded, either staying shut or failing to seal. With several tanks this is hard to see, because one pressure sensor where the tank lines merge cannot tell that a single tank no longer delivers. Hyundai's answer in a 2018 patent is to estimate how much hydrogen is supplied and compare it with what the stack consumes and purges; another Hyundai patent, with a sensor on each tank, flags the tank whose pressure drifts about 50 bar from the rest. No maker documents U3552 publicly. The driver mainly notices less range and a warning, and the tank with the faulty valve is kept closed. U3555 is tank B.
c: Tank A valve stuck closed or opening sluggishly
Implausible tank pressure reading misleading the check
s: Noticeably lower range than the gauge suggests
Hydrogen system warning

U3553.t: Hydrogen Tank B Valve Control Circuit
U3553.d: U3553 means the controller sees a fault in the drive circuit of the solenoid valve on tank B, such as an open coil, a short to ground or supply, or an output that does not follow its command. Hyundai shows in a patent how such valves can be checked: one current sensor reads the operating current of several tank solenoids; if it falls below a reference, the controller switches the PWM duty from 100 to 90 % and looks whether the fed-back duty appears inverted. If not, the valve is judged faulty. In the workshop that means measuring coil resistance and following the harness from tank to controller. No maker documents U3553. Until repaired, tank B stays closed; U3550 and U3556 are the same fault on tanks A and C.
c: Damaged wiring or corroded connector to the tank B valve
Output stage of the control unit faulty
s: Hydrogen system warning
Range reduced because tank B is not used

U3554.t: Hydrogen Tank B Valve Enable Circuit
U3554.d: U3554 refers to the enable path that powers the tank B solenoid. Its purpose is a second, independent way to withdraw the permission for the valve to open. Toyota patented a layout in which the valve controller and the controller for high voltage sit at opposite ends of the car and back each other up: after a crash at one end, the controller at the undamaged end shuts the hydrogen valve. Toyota's FCHV guide also lists an opened hood or fuel door among the triggers that close the valves. A fault in such a release path keeps tank B shut even with an intact coil. No maker documents U3554 publicly. Check fuses, relays and the release wiring before the valve itself; U3553 covers the control side of the same valve.
c: Enable relay or switch in the supply path faulty
Open or short in the enable line to valve B
Faulty input that withdraws the release, such as a crash or flap signal
s: Hydrogen system warning
Range reduced or no READY

U3555.d: U3555 reports that the valve on tank B does not behave as expected although its circuit tests good. Leakage through the closed valve is one form. Hyundai patented a check for it while the car is parked: at wake-ups, hydrogen left in the supply line is fed into the stack with the tank valves shut, so the high-pressure reading should fall slightly; if it stays the same at each wake-up, the tank is feeding gas past the seal. The opposite is a valve that will not open. On the Nexo, venting for service closes the manual valve on each tank with a hex key, and a manual valve left shut afterwards would look like a stuck valve. No maker documents U3555. U3552 and U3558 are the siblings for A and C.
c: Tank B valve seat leaking when closed
Manual tank valve not reopened after service
s: Hydrogen system warning, sometimes after parking
Range lower than expected

U3556.t: Hydrogen Tank C Valve Control Circuit
U3556.d: U3556 is the control circuit code for the valve on tank C, the third tank found only on three-tank layouts such as the Nexo or the current Mirai. On the Mirai the two crosswise tanks behind the long central one are the smaller ones, so losing one costs only part of the range. That makes the fault easy to overlook while driving. The controller recognises an electrical fault in the valve drive directly and stores U3556, whereas a valve that sticks mechanically only shows up as missing hydrogen, which Hyundai's patent finds by comparing supply with consumption. Check coil, connector and driver first. No manufacturer documents U3556 publicly. Tank C stays shut; expect a warning and less range. The enable path of the same valve is U3557.
c: Wiring or connector fault at the tank C valve
Driver stage for valve C faulty
s: Hydrogen system warning
Range noticeably shorter after a full fill

U3557.t: Hydrogen Tank C Valve Enable Circuit
U3557.d: U3557 is stored for a fault in the enable circuit of the tank C valve, the third tank of three-tank vehicles. Permission to open is not tied to driving alone: a Honda patent describes the cutoff valve being open with the ignition off, for example when the stack keeps operating after shutdown, so collision detection stays powered in that state and a cutoff relay can still close the valve. The enable path therefore has to work when the car is parked, and faults may surface after switch-off. FMVSS 307 asks for valve closure within 5 seconds of any crash. No manufacturer documents U3557. Expect tank C to stay shut, a warning and less range. If U3551 and U3554 are also stored, look for a supply common to all valves.
c: Cutoff or enable relay for valve C faulty
Fuse or common valve supply interrupted
Enable line to tank C damaged
s: Hydrogen system warning, possibly right after switch-off or at start
Reduced range

U3558.d: U3558 is listed only as Hydrogen Tank C Valve, without a fault type, so it serves as the general valve code for tank C on three-tank vehicles. FMVSS 308 shows what such a valve must withstand: tens of thousands of pressure cycles, partly at extreme temperatures, chatter flow, and afterwards no more than 10 NmL of leakage per hour. Toyota treats tank and valve as one service part on the Mirai and has it replaced every 15 years. A valve fault on the third tank costs range rather than mobility as long as tanks A and B work. No manufacturer documents U3558 publicly; the diagnosis starts with the freeze frame data and with U3556 and U3557 for the electrical side of the same valve.
c: Tank C valve sticking or not sealing
Electrical fault at the valve without its own circuit code
Tank and valve beyond their service life
s: Hydrogen system warning
Shorter range

U3559.d: U3559 flags a wiring or signal fault on the first pressure sensor of the air supply that feeds the stack, located behind the air filter and ahead of the electric compressor. Its reading is the suction pressure of the compressor: in a Toyota patent the delivery pressure is divided by it to place the operating point on the compressor map and keep clear of the surge line, and Nissan derives the compressor inlet pressure the same way from a barometric sensor. Altitude and a clogged filter also show up here. No maker documents U3559 publicly. Without the value the controller has to work with a substitute, the margin to surge shrinks, and output is likely held back. Honda's Clarity shows that air supply faults in such cars light the MIL. Sensors further downstream report as U355A and U355B.
c: Connector or wiring at the air filter housing wet, corroded or damaged
5 V supply or ground of the sensor missing
Fuel cell control unit faulty or needing a software update
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Reduced power, especially under high load or at altitude
Unusual compressor noise

U355A.t: Charge Air Cooler Outlet Pressure Sensor 1 Circuit
U355A.d: U355A concerns the first of two pressure sensors behind the charge air cooler, where compressed and cooled air heads for the humidifier and the stack. This is the pressure the system really regulates: in a Nissan patent a sensor between intercooler and water recovery unit is the feedback for compressor torque and the outlet pressure valve, and the controller caps this pressure so that compressor and humidifier stay below their heat limits. Toyota takes its counterpart behind compressor and intercooler as the delivery pressure for the surge check. No public manufacturer document names U355A. An open or shorted circuit takes away the main pressure feedback; expect a fuel cell warning and reduced output. Where sensor 2 (U355B) is fitted it can serve as a fallback.
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of sensor 1
Shared 5 V supply or ground faulty (often with other sensor codes)
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Noticeably reduced power
Compressor speed fluctuates or stays high

U355B.t: Charge Air Cooler Outlet Pressure Sensor 2 Circuit
U355B.d: U355B points to a circuit problem with pressure sensor 2 at the charge air cooler outlet. J2012 lists two at this spot, which points to a pair used for cross-checking; how a maker splits the roles is unpublished, and no public document uses U355B. A GM patent shows the principle: before start-up, while the compressor stands still and the cathode holds only atmospheric pressure, readings are compared, and a doubtful sensor is replaced by a value calculated from the remaining ones. Ford names a winter risk on the wet air side: water on a sensor diaphragm can freeze and give no or false output at a cold start, which may lead to a shutdown. Sensor 1 at the same spot is U355A. With only one valid sensor left, output may be limited.
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of sensor 2
Condensed water frozen on the sensor (occurs at cold start, may clear when warm)
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Start refused or system shuts down shortly after a cold start
Reduced power while only one pressure sensor is valid

U355C.t: Charge Air Cooler Outlet Temperature Sensor Circuit
U355C.d: U355C reports a circuit fault on the temperature sensor behind the charge air cooler. Compression heats the air strongly: Honda gives about 120 °C at the compressor outlet, while the stack works at 80 to 90 °C, so the air is first brought down to roughly 60 to 75 °C. The sensor confirms this cooling before the air reaches the humidifier. In a Toyota patent it sits between intercooler and humidifier, and if the intercooler coolant pump fails, the controller slows the compressor to keep air temperature below a set limit; Nissan derives an upper pressure limit from the same reading. No maker documents U355C publicly. Without a valid temperature, humidifier and membrane lose their protection, so a warning and a careful cut in power should follow. Pressure here is U355A/U355B.
c: Open or short in wiring or connector of the temperature sensor
Sensor ground or reference circuit faulty
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Power limited, especially under sustained high load
Compressor runs at reduced speed

U355D.d: U355D covers the first pressure sensor in front of the expander, a turbine in the cathode exhaust that turns leftover pressure from the stack outlet into shaft power for the compressor. Garrett states that its optional turbine expander, developed among others for the compressor of the BMW iX5 Hydrogen, lowers the electricity needed for compression by up to 20 %. In a Toyota patent a waste gate valve divides exhaust between turbine and bypass, because the flow resistance of the turbine raises the pressure the compressor must supply and can push it toward surge. A sensor at the turbine inlet shows this back pressure directly. No maker documents U355D. Losing it takes an input from energy recovery and cathode pressure control. Toyota's Mirai bulletin T-SB-0043-23 shows that faults on the cathode air side light the MIL.
c: Wiring or connector of sensor 1 at the wet exhaust side corroded, open or shorted
Expander inlet pressure sensor 1 faulty internally
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Higher hydrogen consumption because less energy is recovered
Reduced peak power
