U355E.d: U355E names a circuit fault on pressure sensor 2 at the expander inlet. Conditions there are harsh: cathode exhaust carries the product water of the stack, and Volkswagen notes in a turbine patent that the pressure drop inside the turbine makes water condense even behind a droplet separator, eroding the blades. A Hannover study on fuel cell turbines likewise asks for robustness against droplets and lets the turbine set the cathode operating pressure. Ford describes how wet pressure sensors in a fuel cell can freeze and give no or false signals at a cold start. A second sensor lets the controller spot such a reading. No maker documents U355E publicly. A failure of sensor 2 alone mainly removes this cross-check; together with U355D the expander control is blind and power is likely limited.
c: Wiring or connector of sensor 2 corroded by exhaust moisture, open or shorted
Water frozen in the sensor port at cold start
Expander inlet pressure sensor 2 faulty internally
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Fault appears mainly after cold starts
Reduced power if sensor 1 is affected as well

U355F.d: U355F reports a wiring or output stage fault on the actuator of the valve at the cathode outlet, which throttles the air leaving the stack and thereby sets the pressure the air side runs at. GM moves such a valve in closed loop on a pressure reading, in steps or continuously. U355F itself is absent from public maker documents. For the 2021–22 Mirai, Toyota bulletin T-SB-0043-23 ties a lit MIL to a stuck air pressure regulating valve (P1F6E71), fixed by new EV control software or, since the 2025 revision, a new valve. In a Toyota patent air pressure that repeatedly exceeds about 270 kPa counts as a fault: compressor stopped, air routed into the bypass, valve opened. An open or shorted drive leaves cathode pressure uncontrolled; expect a warning and cut power. Position feedback has its own code, U3560.
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of the valve actuator (wet exhaust area)
Valve motor or actuator winding faulty
Driver stage of the fuel cell control unit faulty or software outdated
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Noticeably reduced power
Fuel cell system shuts down or vehicle does not reach READY

U3560.t: Cathode Backpressure Valve Position Sensor Circuit
U3560.d: U3560 is set when the signal of the position sensor on the cathode backpressure valve is missing, shorted or outside its electrical range. Outlet valves of this kind are often throttle flaps whose angle is reported back, as a Hydrogenics patent shows for the cathode and purge valves of a stack. The reading matters beyond the valve: in a GM patent the controller turns the valve position into an expected air-side pressure and compares it with the measured one to reveal leaks or blockages in the air path, so without a believable angle that check loses its footing. No manufacturer publishes U3560. The controller may carry on regulating from pressure alone or park the flap in a safe position; a warning and limited output are likely. Faults in powering the same valve are logged as U355F.
c: Open, short or moisture in the position sensor wiring or connector
Position sensor faulty (often only available with the valve unit)
Sensor 5 V supply or ground missing
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Reduced power
Further air path codes stored at the same time

U3561.d: U3561 points to a break, a short or an output stage fault in the actuator circuit of the cathode bypass valve. This valve lets part of the compressor delivery skip the stack and flow straight into the exhaust. Nissan gives two reasons: keeping the compressor clear of surge when the stack needs little air, and putting enough air into the exhaust to dilute the hydrogen released when the anode is purged. Because opening the bypass lowers stack pressure, Nissan closes the pressure control valve a little further at the same moment. Toyota uses a three-way valve that can send the entire flow into the bypass when air pressure has to be dumped. No public maker document lists U3561. If the valve cannot be driven, a fuel cell warning is likely, along with limited power and possibly no start. Its mechanical behaviour is judged under U3562.
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of the bypass valve
Bypass valve motor or actuator faulty
Driver stage of the fuel cell control unit faulty
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Reduced power, compressor speed fluctuating at low load
Fuel cell system does not start

U3562.d: Unlike U3561, this code concerns how the cathode bypass valve itself behaves: it does not reach or hold the opening the controller asks for, for instance because it sticks. A Toyota patent shows why a valve stuck shut is serious. While a cold stack is warmed by deliberately inefficient generation, bypass air is supposed to thin out hydrogen in the exhaust; if ice holds the valve closed, all of that air enters the stack, which then produces more power than intended. Toyota spots this from compressor outlet pressure above a limit or from stack current straying from its command, then opens the backpressure valve and slows the compressor. A valve stuck open costs stack pressure instead, as Nissan notes. No maker publishes U3562; that stuck air valves switch on the MIL is documented by Toyota for the Mirai (T-SB-0043-23).
c: Valve frozen in place after a cold soak
Valve sticking from deposits or wear
Actuator too weak or gear damaged
Position feedback reading wrong, valve itself fine
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Reduced power or failed start in frost
Unusual compressor or air noise

U3563.t: Cathode Bypass Valve Position Sensor Circuit
U3563.d: U3563 means the position sensor on the cathode bypass valve delivers no usable signal because of a broken wire, a short or a voltage outside its window. Toyota's patent mounts such a valve body position sensor right at the bypass valve, with pressure sensors before and after it; the angle tells the controller how the compressor air is really being split between stack and bypass. A Hydrogenics patent likewise fits angle sensors to the throttle-type valves of its stack. No public manufacturer source names U3563. Without the feedback, the controller has to infer the valve state indirectly, for example from compressor outlet pressure or stack current as Toyota describes, and will usually restrict operation. Drive faults of the valve are U3561, a mechanically misbehaving valve U3562.
c: Open, short or moisture in the position sensor wiring or connector
Position sensor in the valve unit faulty
Shared 5 V supply or ground faulty (often with other sensor codes)
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Reduced power, especially at low load

U3564.t: Hydrogen Supply Line A Pressure Sensor 1 Circuit
U3564.d: U3564 deals with the wiring of pressure sensor 1 on hydrogen supply line A, most likely the medium-pressure section behind the tank regulator; J2012 does not fix the spot. Toyota's patent shows such a layout: a mechanical reducing valve brings tank hydrogen down to roughly 1.1–1.6 MPa, an intermediate pressure sensor watches that section, and the injector then lowers the pressure to about 200–300 kPa for the stack. To find an offset, Toyota closes the tank valve, lets the injector draw the line down until the reducer stands wide open, and compares readings up- and downstream of it. Hyundai's Nexo has two hydrogen pressure sensors, numbered 1 and 2, with their own codes (P315200/P315300) and renewed both in campaign T4E; U3564 itself is in no public document. Without the value, regulator monitoring suffers and power may be limited.
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of pressure sensor 1
Pressure sensor 1 faulty internally (maker may supply a revised part)
5 V supply or ground of the sensor missing
Fuel cell control unit faulty or needing a software update
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Reduced power
Fuel cell system may refuse to start

U3565.t: Hydrogen Supply Line A Pressure Sensor 2 Circuit
U3565.d: U3565 signals that the second pressure sensor of hydrogen supply line A has a wiring problem. Two sensors on one line let the controller cross-check them, and Hyundai's Nexo shows how such a pair is handled in service: when hydrogen pressure sensor 1 or 2 (P315200, P315300) set codes, campaign T4E from 2019 had both swapped for a revised part at an outdoor venting spot, followed by an offset reset and a leak test; the thin metal membrane of the sensors must touch nothing. A later Hyundai update (20-01-029H) reworked the MIL logic in the Nexo's fuel cell controller and names the sensor 1 code P315292 in that context. No maker documents U3565. A warning is likely; relying on sensor 1 alone, the system may keep running, perhaps with less power. Sensor 1 on this line is U3564.
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of pressure sensor 2
Sensor membrane damaged during a previous repair
Fuel cell control unit faulty or needing a software update
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Often no noticeable change while sensor 1 still works
Reduced power

U3566.d: U3566 is set for an electrical fault at anode inlet pressure sensor 1, sitting between hydrogen injector and stack. A GM patent explains why this value is central: it closes the loop for the injector and also feeds anode valve control and the handling of hydrogen in the exhaust. A wrong value derails that loop; in GM's example the injector is held at full duty because a 200 kPa target never shows on a sensor stuck at 100 kPa. GM flags such a sensor when its readings vary by less than 6 kPa over a time window and then runs the anode open loop, about 50 kPa above cathode pressure. Hyundai checks its stack supply pressure sensor against recirculation blower speed and warns in the cluster. As a circuit code U3566 covers opens and shorts; no public source uses it. Expect a warning and reduced power.
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of sensor 1 at the stack
Anode inlet pressure sensor 1 faulty internally
Shared 5 V supply or ground faulty (often with other sensor codes)
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Noticeably reduced power
Rough or interrupted fuel cell start

U3567.d: U3567 belongs to the second pressure sensor at the anode inlet. Its signal carries safety weight: GM uses anode pressure to catch an injector stuck open, then shuts the tank valves, opens the anode bleed valve, lifts cathode pressure with compressor and backpressure valve and opens the cathode bypass so hydrogen in the exhaust stays diluted. Another GM patent treats a gap of more than a calibrated margin, typically 3 kPa, between actual and desired pressure as an injector fault. Sensors in this wet zone can ice up, so GM checks the anode sensor before start against ambient pressure plus the anode-to-cathode differential. A second sensor allows a similar comparison while driving. No maker publishes U3567. Expect a warning; with sensor 1 as the only source, power may be reduced. Sensor 1 is U3566.
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of sensor 2 at the stack
Anode inlet pressure sensor 2 faulty internally
Water in the connector, fault mainly after frost
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Often no noticeable change while sensor 1 still works
Reduced power

U3568.d: U3568 flags trouble in the electrical drive of the anode multifunction valve: an open wire, a short against ground or battery voltage, or a failed output stage. The code title does not say which duties the valve combines; known designs merge draining water and purging nitrogen in one solenoid below the anode water separator. GM routes such a combined valve into the cathode inlet so that escaping hydrogen reacts on the catalyst, and Hyundai calls its version an integrated discharge valve. If the controller cannot switch it, the anode loses both its water outlet and its nitrogen outlet; in Hyundai's patent the system stops when no gas leaves the valve. No manufacturer documents U3568 publicly. A fuel cell warning with lost drive power is the likely result. Mechanical misbehaviour of the valve is U3569.
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of the valve (wet area below the stack)
Solenoid coil of the valve open or shorted
Driver stage of the fuel cell control unit faulty
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Power dropping off the longer the drive lasts
Fuel cell system shuts down or does not start

U3569.d: With U3569 the multifunction valve can be driven but does not do what it is told: it stays shut, leaks or reacts too slowly. A solenoid of this kind usually lacks position feedback, so its state is inferred. For an integrated drain and purge valve Hyundai lifts anode pressure a fixed amount over ambient while no current is drawn and the air path is closed, opens the valve and checks after the expected drain time plus a settling period whether pressure has dropped to ambient; if not, the valve counts as stuck closed. GM reads the injector duty instead, which climbs once gas rather than water passes. Stuck shut, the valve lets water flood the anode and nitrogen dilute the hydrogen; stuck open, hydrogen escapes. No public source names U3569. Typical results are a warning, less power or a shutdown.
c: Valve frozen shut after parking in frost
Valve sticking or leaking from deposits or worn seat
Water level sensor of the separator reads wrong, valve itself fine
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Reduced power, uneven fuel cell output
Start refused or shutdown, mainly after frost
Higher hydrogen consumption

U356A.d: U356A concerns the electrical drive of the solenoid sitting under the anode water trap, which lets condensate leave the hydrogen loop. Hyundai opens it when a level sensor reports a full trap and closes it at a low mark so no hydrogen follows; if that sensor fails, the valve is closed as soon as anode pressure falls faster than a set rate. GM also gives the drain valve an emergency role: after an injector sticks open, hydrogen may be let out through it until the concentration in the exhaust reaches a limit. A broken or shorted drive circuit takes away both jobs. No maker documents U356A publicly. Since water keeps collecting in the anode, a warning and reduced or interrupted operation are plausible. The valve's mechanical state is U356B, the header drain circuit U356C.
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of the drain valve
Drain valve solenoid coil open or shorted
Driver stage of the fuel cell control unit faulty
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Reduced power after some driving time
Fuel cell system shuts down

U356B.d: U356B is about how the drain valve behaves, not its wiring. Hyundai shows how such faults are separated: if the level in the trap fails to drop within a set time after an open command while the position sensor still reports closed, the valve is judged stuck shut; the system then limits current, drains on a schedule derived from accumulated charge and runs the stack warmer so water leaves as vapour. If the level stays low after a close command and the sensor reports open, hydrogen could escape, so the system is shut down. A dead level sensor can mimic a jammed valve; another Hyundai patent forces the valve open and watches whether a sagging cell voltage recovers to tell the two apart. In winter frozen condensate is a likely cause. No public source cites U356B; expect a warning plus reduced power or a shutdown.
c: Drain valve frozen after parking in frost
Valve sticking or not sealing due to deposits or a worn seat
Water level sensor of the trap faulty, valve itself fine
Drain line downstream of the valve blocked or iced
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Power limited, fuel cell running hotter than usual
System shutdown if the valve stays open

U356C.t: Anode Header Drain Valve Control Circuit
U356C.d: U356C covers the drive circuit of a second drain valve mounted directly on the anode exhaust header, the channel inside the stack that gathers the gas leaving every cell. GM lists three valves behind the stack: a bleed valve at the top of the anode sump, a drain valve at its bottom and this header valve, which empties into the cathode exhaust. Condensate pooling in the outlet header harms cell durability, above all when the car stands on a steep slope, and GM has also patented heating of these manifolds against ice. Older logic opened the header valve only at shutdown or on a tilt sensor signal; GM's newer scheme lets it serve a share of bleed requests, by default the fifth. If the drive is open or shorted, the water stays put. No maker documents U356C publicly; a warning and limited operation are likely. The sump drain circuit is U356A.
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of the header drain valve
Valve solenoid coil open or shorted
Driver stage of the fuel cell control unit faulty
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Power limited, especially after parking on a slope
Often no noticeable effect at first

U356D.d: U356D is set when the header drain valve responds electrically yet does not empty the header as intended. GM splits each opening into two phases: first water runs out of the header, then nitrogen-rich gas is bled off. The end of the water phase is recognised from stack voltage or from an estimated gas flow across the valve, and the bleed phase is sized by the hydrogen content of the anode. If the water phase takes unusually long, GM concludes the stack is tilted or the header overfilled and calls on the valve more often. A valve stuck closed lets water build up and starve the cells farthest along the header; one stuck open keeps venting hydrogen into the cathode exhaust. Ice is a further risk at outlet manifolds. No maker publishes U356D. A warning and less power follow; circuit faults are U356C.
c: Header drain valve or its line frozen
Valve sticking or leaking from deposits or a worn seat
Header drain line to the cathode exhaust blocked
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Reduced power, uneven cell voltages
Higher hydrogen consumption if the valve stays open

U356E.t: Anode Drain Valve Heater Relay Control Circuit
U356E.d: U356E refers to the relay that powers the heater on the anode drain valve, more precisely to its coil drive from the fuel cell controller. Drain valves sit in the wettest corner of the hydrogen loop and can freeze shut after a cold night. Hyundai fits PTC heaters to its purge valves, fed by the battery and switched on when a start below freezing is detected; Parker Hannifin places a PTC element right at the seat of a fuel cell drain valve, and Hilite sells drain valves with built-in heating that still open at minus 40 °C. If the relay cannot be driven, the heater stays off, or stays on and drains the battery. In mild weather nothing may be noticeable; in frost an iced drain valve can delay or prevent the start. No maker documents U356E publicly, and its MIL handling is unknown.
c: Open, short or corrosion in the relay coil wiring or connector
Fuse or supply of the relay circuit missing
Relay driver in the fuel cell control unit faulty
s: Fuel cell warning message
Delayed or failed start in frost
Often no noticeable effect in warm weather

U356F.t: Anode Header Drain Valve Heater Relay Control Circuit
U356F.d: U356F reports that the relay feeding the heater on the anode header drain valve cannot be driven properly because its coil circuit is open or shorted. That valve hangs on the stack's anode outlet header, where condensate gathers and can freeze during a cold soak. GM targets exactly this zone with heated outlet manifolds so ice does not block them during subzero starts. Whether the header valve carries its own heater and when it is switched is not described in public maker documents; the code only implies a relay separate from the one for the sump drain valve (U356E). Such a fault can leave the heater dead, risking an iced valve and a delayed or failed cold start, or keep it powered, which costs battery energy. In warm weather the effect is rarely noticeable. U356F has no public manufacturer source.
c: Open, short or corrosion in the relay coil wiring or connector
Relay driver in the fuel cell control unit faulty
s: Fuel cell warning message
Start problems after a frosty night
Battery discharged if the heater stays on

U3570.t: Stack Inlet Coolant Temperature Sensor Circuit
U3570.d: U3570 signals that the sensor for coolant entering the stack sends a broken, shorted or out-of-range reading. Thermal control is steered by this value: Hyundai describes a three-port valve which gets the stack inlet temperature from the fuel cell control unit over CAN and sets its opening from it, and in a Nissan patent the current drawn from the stack is capped once inlet coolant passes a set point, so that the outlet cannot overheat. GM shows that the inlet figure can also be estimated from pump inlet temperature, flow rate and a heat exchanger model. No maker documents U3570 publicly. Without a valid reading the system has to run on a substitute; a warning lamp and held-back power are to be expected. Outlet sensors report as U3571 and U3572.
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of the inlet sensor
Inlet coolant temperature sensor faulty internally (drift, internal open)
Coolant seeping past the sensor seal into the connector
Input stage of the fuel cell control unit faulty
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Reduced power, especially under high load
Implausible stack inlet temperature in live data

U3571.t: Stack Outlet Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit
U3571.d: U3571 concerns the wiring and signal of sensor 1 in the coolant stream leaving the stack. Coolant is hottest here, so the reading serves as the main overheat guard: GM holds stack outlet temperature mainly with a three-port valve sending coolant past or through the radiator and shuts the stack off when coolant at this point gets too hot. A wrong outlet value can therefore force a needless shutdown or hide genuine overheating. GM cross-checks the sensor against end cell temperatures and treats it as suspect when it reads more than 3 °C above their average. Hyundai can fall back on the exhaust temperature of the air side as a stand-in. No public maker document names U3571. Warning and lower output follow; U3572 covers sensor 2 at this location, U3570 the inlet.
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of outlet sensor 1
Outlet temperature sensor 1 faulty internally or drifting
Connector or wiring near the hot outlet line damaged by heat
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Power reduced or fuel cell system switched off as a precaution
Outlet temperatures of sensor 1 and sensor 2 disagree in live data

U3572.t: Stack Outlet Coolant Temperature Sensor 2 Circuit
U3572.d: U3572 is logged when the second coolant temperature sensor at the stack outlet has a wiring or signal problem. No maker explains in public why two sensors share this spot; mutual checking is the obvious reason. A Toyota patent for systems with several stacks shows one way: outlet temperature is estimated from inlet temperature and stack output, and an outlet sensor whose reading departs from that estimate is reported as faulty. GM compares the outlet value with an expected figure to spot a failed coolant pump and may then lower stack output. Hyundai campaign 21-01-045H-1 for the Nexo shows that a stack coolant fault (pump code P1D3D94) lights the check engine lamp. No maker documents U3572 publicly. With sensor 1 still valid a warning may be all; with both lost, power will be cut. Sensor 1 is U3571.
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of outlet sensor 2
Shared sensor ground faulty (often with U3571 at the same time)
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Little or no change in driving as long as sensor 1 is valid
Reduced power if both outlet sensors are affected

U3573.d: U3573 concerns how the coolant mixing valve is powered: its actuator line may be interrupted or shorted, or the output stage may have failed. This three-way valve splits stack coolant between radiator and bypass and so decides how warm it is when it returns to the stack. Designs vary: in a Hyundai application a solenoid pushes a spool and its current sets the split, while Toyota describes a rotary valve turned by a stepper motor through a gear train. In the conventional Hyundai layout the valve takes the stack inlet temperature over CAN from the fuel cell control unit. If the actuator cannot be powered, coolant temperature is no longer regulated. U3573 appears in no public maker document. Likely consequences are a warning and capped output; how the valve itself responds is judged under U3574.
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of the valve actuator
Actuator motor or solenoid coil of the mixing valve faulty
Driver stage or CAN link of the controlling unit faulty
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Stack temperature too high or too low, reduced power
Slow warm-up of the fuel cell system

U3574.d: U3574 serves as the catch-all for the coolant mixing valve when the trouble lies in its behaviour rather than its wiring: it sticks, moves too slowly or misses the commanded split between radiator and bypass. Temperatures reveal it, because GM sets stack outlet temperature with this valve and the inlet-to-outlet difference with pump speed, so a jammed valve upsets both. Toyota plans for the case: before each start the valve runs to a fully open end position to reset its zero point, and in one variant it is left open toward the radiator at shutdown, so a valve that seizes later still cools the stack. Hyundai patented a lower-friction plunger seal for its stack coolant valve against leaks and wear. No maker documents U3574 publicly. Expect a warning, swinging temperatures and less power.
c: Valve element sticking from deposits, worn seal or unsuitable coolant
Actuator gear or motor worn, valve moves sluggishly
Internal leak, coolant passes the closed port
Air in the stack coolant loop after service distorting the temperature response
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Stack temperature swings or stays too high under load
Reduced power, slow warm-up in cold weather

U3575.t: Coolant Mixing Valve Position Sensor Circuit
U3575.d: U3575 deals with wiring and signal of the sensor reporting how far the coolant mixing valve is open. GM lists feedback of the valve position, next to two temperature sensors, among the parts its stack outlet temperature control relies on. In Toyota's design the sensor is built into the valve and returns the angle of the valving element; since it can drift, the controller re-zeroes it against an end position before the coolant pump starts. If the signal is missing or shorted, the controller no longer knows where the valve stands and may regulate from temperatures alone or move the valve to a safe setting. No maker documents U3575 publicly. Probable results: a warning lamp and capped output. Faults in driving this valve fall under U3573.
c: Open, short or moisture in the position sensor wiring or connector
Position sensor faulty (usually replaced together with the valve)
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Stack temperature regulated less precisely, reduced power
Valve opening shown as invalid in live data

U3576.d: U3576 is set when the stack differential pressure sensor delivers no signal, a shorted one or one outside its valid range. The title leaves open which two pressures it compares. In a GM patent such a sensor is plumbed between anode and cathode side, as the anode is normally kept slightly above the cathode. GM also uses it ahead of start-up, with the cathode still at ambient pressure, to verify the anode pressure sensor: ambient plus differential reading should match the anode value. Ford keeps the difference across the membrane within a tolerance of around 600 mbar, may shut the system down when it is breached and heats such sensors so that ice cannot blind them. No maker documents U3576 publicly. Expect a warning, reduced power or no start; anode inlet pressure is U3566/U3567.
c: Open, short or corrosion in wiring or connector of the differential pressure sensor
Water or ice in the sensor ports or a failed sensor heater
s: Fuel cell system warning, MIL on
Reduced power or fuel cell system shuts down
No start, especially after a cold night
